## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest care; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers have commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they have done so. An extremely accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following features are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the entire work, the modest price, and especially this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

# Preliminary dissertation by Peter Francis Chifflet on the author of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*

## Chapter I. On the age of Saint Bede the priest, and therefore on the true day and the true year of his death

[Col. 0009A]

This treatment of the question will, I think, not be unwelcome to the learned reader, once he learns that nearly eight hundred years have been spent in investigating it, and that the dispute is still unresolved. Cardinal Bellarmine aptly called Bede the Sun of the West, so that it may truly be said that nothing is clearer than the light of this sun, and nothing darker than its setting.

Bede himself writes about himself at the end of his English History, which he concludes in the year 731 of the Lord’s Incarnation, that he had then completed the fifty-ninth year of his age. From this it follows that he was born in the year of Christ 672.

But there is such diversity of opinion concerning his age and concerning the year and day of his death that it is astonishing that, on so illustrious a subject, English, Italian, German, French, and writers of every nation have so far been unable to agree. Hermannus Contractus, the Chronicle of Reichenau, the Annals of Saint Nazarius, the Anonymous of Fleury, Hepidanus, Sigebert, and Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, among others, assign his death to the very year 731 in which he brought his History to an end.

Yet Bede himself refutes all of them—his death is commonly assigned to the month of May—when, at the end of his History, he mentions that in the same year 731 Tacuin was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury on the tenth day of June.

William of Malmesbury and Matthew of Westminster write that Bede died in the year 734, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. So too does the continuator of the English History after Bede, book I, chapters 6 and 8. Commelinus, who printed this anonymous author in the Heidelberg edition of the *Writers of Britain* of 1587, seems to have distinguished him from William of Malmesbury, although the work consists entirely of Malmesbury’s text except for the last three chapters of book III, and does not contain the whole of that book. Hence Balaeus rightly omitted him from his *Catalogue of the Writers of England*.

But this day does not agree with that year, as is evident from the rules of computation. Michael Alford, in his *Anglo-Saxon Annals*, assigns Bede’s death to the same year of Christ, 734, but refers it to another day, which he does not adequately explain.

Simeon of Durham gives the year 735, on Ascension Day, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. The author of the chronological recapitulation appended to the end of Bede’s History adopted this view in the Heidelberg edition. Their stumbling block seems to have been that in that year Ascension Day actually fell on May 26, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. But they did not foresee the other difficulties inherent in their position, which will become clear from what follows.

Lambert of Hersfeld placed the event in the year 736. Finally—not to gather them all here—Baronius vacillated in this chronology. In the *Martyrology*, under May 27, he fixed Bede’s life at ninety-four years; but in the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 721, number 19, he judged that Bede had reached the one hundred and fifth year of his life, namely, the year 776 of Christ. I shall examine his arguments below.

[Col. 0009B]

For me, everything is settled by the letter of Cuthbert to Cuthwin concerning Bede’s passing. Surius and Baronius published it, but Simeon of Durham gave a much more accurate version in book I, chapter 15, of his *History of Durham*. From this letter, written by an eyewitness, I conclude that Bede the priest departed this life in the year of Christ 762, in the ninetieth year of his age, on May 26, a Wednesday, toward evening, on the eve of the Lord’s Ascension—and therefore on the ecclesiastical day of the Ascension, which began with first vespers—not on the natural day of Ascension, reckoned from midnight.

This is clear from the very words of Cuthbert’s letter, where he expressly says that Bede breathed out his blessed soul on Wednesday evening, the seventh day before the Kalends of June, that is, on May 26. Quite accurately. For in the year of Christ 762, Easter fell on April 18 and the Ascension on May 27.

What Cuthbert had said earlier, that Bede lived until the day of the Lord’s Ascension, must therefore be understood exclusively, or as referring to the ecclesiastical day of the Ascension, which began with first vespers and thus at the end of Wednesday.

To this assertion drawn from Cuthbert’s letter must be added the ancient testimonies to Bede’s age of ninety. For in the years of Christ 751 and 773, Easter likewise fell on April 18, and the sequence of the movable feasts, including the Ascension, was the same. But in 751 Bede was seventy-nine years old; whereas in 773, if Bede had still been alive, he would have reached the one hundred and first year of his life.

We must therefore prove that Bede died at the age of ninety, so that his departure from this life may be placed in the year 762 rather than in either of the other two years.

[Col. 0009C]

This is expressly asserted in Bede’s epitaph, which Wion reports in *The Tree of Life*, book V, chapter 101. He aptly warns that it was inscribed upon the sacred remains of Saint Bede after they had been transferred from Girvo, where they had first been buried, to the city of Durham, and enclosed in the same chest with the body of Saint Cuthbert, which was still incorrupt at that time. From Simeon of Durham, book I, chapter 14, and book III, chapter 7 of the *History of Durham*, and from Richard the prior, book II, chapter 1, *On the Bishops of Hexham*, it may be inferred that this occurred around the year 1000.

The epitaph was of the following kind. It could still be read in his sarcophagus in our own time, as Possevinus testifies in his *Apparatus*, and it is reported in the Antwerp edition of the *History of the English People* of 1550 and in the Cologne edition of 1601:

> Bede, servant of God, noble star of monks,  
> Benefited the Church at the ends of the earth.  
> This diligent man, searching everywhere into the thought of the Fathers,  
> Flourished in eloquence and composed very many works.  
> In this life he lived three times thirty years,  
> A priest in office, useful in talent.  
> On the seventh day before the Kalends of June, deprived of his flesh,  
> He earned the angelic homeland of the English.

He also reports another epitaph of only four hexameter verses, inscribed upon Bede’s first tomb, and the anonymous continuator of the English History rightly observes that it was utterly shameful and unworthy of so great a man’s mausoleum, book I, chapter 8.

[Col. 0010A]

The Carthusians of Cologne likewise confirm this same age of ninety in their additions to the *Martyrology of Usuard*, published in 1521, under the seventh day before the Kalends of June. They note that his feast was celebrated on that day, or, according to others, on the following day.

The diversity of the sacred calendars seems to have arisen from the hour of Saint Bede’s death, which occurred on Wednesday evening, and therefore on May 26, as we have reported from Cuthbert. His burial, however, commonly called his deposition, fell on Thursday, which was Ascension Day itself, May 27. Hence in the necrologies Bede’s final day was recorded sometimes as May 26 and sometimes as May 27, the first reckoning referring to the departure of his soul and the second to the burial service.

Thus the Carthusians of Cologne write under the seventh day before the Kalends of June:

> On this same day—or, according to others, on the following day—in England occurred the deposition of the Venerable Bede, priest and confessor, outstanding doctor. As he himself reports about himself, when he had been entrusted to the monastery at the age of seven, amid the observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in the church, he always found it a delight either to learn, teach, or write. At length, full of days and holiness, he died at the age of ninety on the day he had requested, namely, the day of the Lord’s Ascension. For on that day, with his understanding unimpaired and his face cheerful, after he had sung the antiphon “O King of glory,” etc., he gave up his spirit.

[Col. 0010B]

The author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, once Bede’s disciple, adds his testimony. There we read:

> Bede the priest, beloved of God, migrated to the Lord on the day he desired and requested—namely, on the day when Christ, the King of glory and conqueror, ascended above all the heavens—on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the year 731 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the 127th year from the death of Saint Gregory, having completed ninety years of age, as some affirm. For he became a deacon in the nineteenth year of his age, and a priest in the thirtieth. From that time, after he had spent thirty years learning what would benefit the Church, until his fifty-ninth year he diligently endeavored, with no idle labor, to commit worthy books to memory through his own pen. For another thirty years, they say, he corrected what he had written and instructed his disciples to no small degree in the studies of all the liberal arts.

This author wrote nearly eight hundred years ago, “from what he had learned through Sigulf, his teacher, who in turn reported it as the most faithful disciple of Alcuin.” Exactly as in the printed editions, I read this in the manuscript codex of Saint Mary of Reims, so that no one may suspect a typographical error here.

Nevertheless, this passage cannot escape suspicion of an error introduced by an ancient copyist. For how can Bede be said to have died in the year of Christ 731 at the age of ninety, when he himself testifies that in that same year he was no more than fifty-nine? Or how could he have corrected for thirty years the books he had written and first published in 731, if he did not reach the age of ninety? Finally, how can it be said that Bede died in 731 on the day of the Lord’s Ascension and on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, when the rules of the ancient computation make it absolutely certain that in the year 731 the Lord’s Ascension occurred not on the seventh day before the Kalends of June but on the sixth day before the Ides of May?

This passage is therefore corrupt—not through the author’s error, but through the copyist’s fault—and the author undoubtedly wrote 762 instead of 731. In that year Bede was ninety, thirty years having elapsed since the first publication of his books. Accordingly, the year “127 from the death of Saint Gregory the pope” must be changed to 159, since the great Gregory had departed to heaven in 604, in the seventh indiction, on March 12.

[Col. 0010C]

This chronology of Bede’s age is splendidly confirmed by four letters among the letters of Saint Boniface, once separately edited by Nicholas Serarius and later transferred into more recent editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, numbers 89, 95, 111, and 150.

The first of these in chronological order is number 111, the letter of Lull, archbishop of Mainz, to Cuthbert the abbot. In it he sends him a silken pallium and asks him for all the books of “Bede of blessed memory: *On the Building of the Temple*, or *On the Song of Songs*, or the epigrams composed in heroic or elegiac meter, if possible; but if not, the three books *On the Building of the Temple*. Perhaps this is a difficult request; but I believe that nothing is difficult for true charity.”

The second in chronological order, number 89, records that Cuthbert the abbot had received from Lull the silken pallium intended for the relics of Bede of blessed memory. He sends Lull two little books from Bede’s writings about the man of God Cuthbert—who had been bishop of Lindisfarne—composed in verse and prose. He excuses himself for not being able to send more because of the severity of winter, which had caused the hands of the scribes to grow weak and numb, and promises to send him whatever of Bede’s minor works he lacked as soon as it became possible to prepare them.

His words are these:

> I gratefully received the little gifts of your affection, and all the more gratefully because I learned that you had sent them with the deepest devotion: namely, the silken pallium which you destined for the relics of Bede, our teacher, of blessed memory, in remembrance and veneration of him. It seems right to me that the entire English people in all the provinces, wherever they are found, should give thanks to God because God bestowed upon them in their own nation so remarkable a man, endowed with various gifts, so devoted to exercising those gifts, and likewise living in good morals. For through experience, having been raised at his feet, I learned what I am telling you, and so forth.
>
> But now, since you have asked for something from the minor works of the blessed Father, with my boys I have prepared for your affection, according to our ability, what I could: I have sent to your desire the little books about the man of God Cuthbert, composed in verse and prose. If I could have sent more, I would gladly have wished to do so, because the recent winter kept the island of our people under a terrible burden of cold and frost, and of storms of wind and rain, for a long time and over a wide area. Consequently the scribe’s hand was delayed, lest the work reach the number of many books, and so forth.
>
> As for the minor works of Bede of blessed memory that you do not yet possess in copies, I promise that, if we live, I shall assist your desire by sending them.

[Col. 0011A]

In the third letter, number 95, Cuthbert the abbot, mindful of his promise, sends Lull Bede’s book *On the Building of the Temple*.

In the fourth letter, whoever its author may be, he asks for the remaining minor works of Bede and indicates that Bede had recently departed from the living. For he says:

> Meanwhile, we ask that you kindly send us the remaining writings of that most diligent investigator of the Scriptures, the monk Bede, whom we have recently heard shone in the house of God, like a candle of the Church, through his knowledge of the Scriptures.

This is letter number 150, transferred from volume IX of Baronius’s *Annals* into Serarius’s collection and wrongly attributed to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, although it truly belongs to Lull, his successor. I demonstrate this by two arguments.

First, it is requested on the basis of the three letters mentioned above. In the first letter, Lull had asked Cuthbert for all Bede’s minor works. Since he received only a few—the ones mentioned in Cuthbert’s letters 89 and 95—he then requested the works that were still lacking. This is what letter 150 does.

The second argument is that Bede is known to have survived Boniface. For according to Serarius’s accurate calculations, Boniface won the glorious martyr’s crown in the year of Christ 755. After Boniface, Lull, already a bishop, sent a silken pallium to honor Bede’s recently extinguished relics. Therefore that letter to Cuthbert the abbot, which is number 150 in the collection and mentions Bede as one who had recently shone in the Church—and therefore as already dead—belongs to Lull.

[Col. 0011B]

Since it is therefore plainly evident from these facts that Bede was alive beyond the year of Christ 755, the exact age of ninety that we established from his epitaph and other arguments fixes his death in the year 762, which was Lull’s seventh year in office after Boniface. Lull reached the age of eighty-seven and held the episcopate for thirty-two years after Boniface.

It is certainly astonishing that Alford, in his *Annals*, referred these letters concerning Bede’s death to the year 734 and failed to attend to the chronology of Boniface and Lull, which he could have understood from Nicholas Serarius’s *Mainz*.

It is no less astonishing that William of Malmesbury and the other English historians who followed him wandered so far from the correct year of Bede’s death. Malmesbury himself touches upon the reason for this when he says, in book I of the *Kings*, chapter 3:

> Almost all knowledge of events was buried with Bede, until his own times.

Alford adds in his *Annals of the Anglo-Saxon Church*, under the year 734:

> We know and mourn that this is true; for Malmesbury is rightly regarded as the first writer after Bede in the narration of historical events.

Balaeus places the death of William of Malmesbury in the year of Christ 1142. He must have begun writing thirty years earlier. On this hypothesis, nearly three hundred and fifty years elapsed between Bede’s death and the publication of Malmesbury’s books.

After so long an interval, during which knowledge of chronology lay dormant among the English, is it surprising that it awoke to certain phantoms of dreams and deviated by nearly thirty years from the actual date of Bede’s death? We have demonstrated that this did happen by conclusive arguments.

[Col. 0011C]

It remains for me to answer the objection Baronius raised at the beginning. Under the year of Christ 731, number 19, he asserts either that Bede reached the one hundred and fifth year of his life or that the letter to Wicrheda the priest, concerning the equinox according to Anatolius, is not Bede’s. Yet he seems to count this letter among Bede’s writings at the end of the English History, because in it he gives an example concerning the Easter of the year in which he was writing, 776, and of the following year, 777. He accurately sets out the epacts, regular numbers, concurrents, the fourteenth moons of the first month and their weekdays, and finally the Sundays of Easter, as they are contained in the thirteenth nineteen-year cycle of Bede.

He then prudently adds:

> If these statements concerning Bede’s long life are not acceptable because they are novel and hitherto unheard of, then the burden falls upon those who deny that the letter recently cited is Bede’s and who must demonstrate that it is falsely listed among his writings. We shall willingly accept what they produce as more truthful, always ready to follow the person who presents the stronger evidence.

To this I reply that I recognize as a true and genuine work of Bede the letter concerning the equinox according to Anatolius, which begins, “I gladly received the letter of your kindness,” and ends with the words, “confirm that it was before the equinox.” But I reject as spurious the appendix that begins, “In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle,” and mentions the years 776 and 777.

[Col. 0011D]

I saw Bede’s letter concerning the equinox in an old codex of the Library of Geneva, considerably more accurately printed than the common version. It was immediately followed by chapter 29 of the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, concerning the agreement of the sea and the moon.

The cited appendix was absent, as having no relevance to the subject. It can be seen in what appears to be its proper place, in the book *On the Phases of the Moon*, volume I, among Bede’s works. Hence it is clear that the appendix is not Bede’s, but belongs to an unknown author who was writing in the year 776, fourteen years after Bede’s death.

As for the fact that Ulpericus is praised in the same treatise *On the Phases of the Moon*, do not hesitate to regard this as a gloss by a later hand. Ulpericus, or Helpericus, lived long after the year of Christ 776. We have seen two editions of his *Computus* in manuscripts, the earlier from the year 903 and the later from 930. For in the chapter entitled “How the Years from the Incarnation of the Lord Are Found,” he says that he is writing in those years.

You may therefore also refute Josias Simler, who says in his abridgment of Gesner’s *Bibliotheca* that Ulpericus flourished in the year of the Lord 1069. As for his further statement that Ulpericus was a monk of Saint Gall, this can scarcely be proved by us, since the preface to his *Computus* seems to indicate that he was instead from Auxerre.

Nevertheless, since in that preface he accuses himself of instability and indicates that he wandered through several monasteries, I would not dare deny that he may at some time also have lived among the monks of Saint Gall.

As proofs, so to speak, of this preface, I append here Cuthbert’s letter concerning the death of Saint Bede; Bede’s letter concerning the equinox according to Anatolius, rendered better in many places from the Geneva codex; and the preface of Helpericus’s *Computus* addressed to Asprius, whom he calls “most holy Father,” perhaps the abbot or co-abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, together with another preface and an epilogue.

[Col. 0012A]

As a conclusion, I shall add, in place of the story circulated about the title “Venerable” being written by an angelic hand in the verse of his epitaph—

> Here in the grave lie the bones of Venerable Bede—

the actual origin of this designation, from Gabriel Bucelinus’s *Benedictine Menology*, under the sixth day before the Kalends of June:

> His writings, he says, possessed such authority that, by order of the bishops of Britain, they were read publicly in the churches. When, according to custom, the name of their author, “the Venerable Bede the priest,” was prefixed to the readings from his homilies, since no one dared to call him anything else while he was alive, the custom has continued to the present day: the man who from the beginning, during his lifetime, was called not “Saint” but “Venerable” has, because of the very reason for this illustrious designation, thereafter been called “Venerable” forever.

[Col. 0012B]

It remains for me to bring together here what I have observed in various places concerning the burial, tombs, and relics of Saint Bede.

I stated above that his body was first buried at Girvo, from which his blessed soul flew forth and entered into the joy of its Lord, in the Christian year 762. From there, about 238 years later, it was transferred to the sacred church at Durham together with the body of Saint Cuthbert, which was still incorrupt at that time.

I next read in Helinandus, the monk of Frigidus Mons, book XLVIII of the *Chronicles*, that the clerics of Laon, after their church had been consumed by fire, resolved to undertake a supplication through France and England in order to collect some assistance for its repair. They carried with them certain relics of Saint Mary of Laon, renowned for miracles.

> These men from Salisbury, he says, came to the abbey of nuns called Wilton—scarcely three miles away, as Alberic adds when reporting this in his *Chronicle* under the year 1115—where the burial place of the Venerable Bede the priest was shown to them. Beside him was buried that famous woman poet. A certain man who had long been suffering from fever lay there at the tomb of the Venerable Bede the priest, because many people were accustomed to be healed there.

Alberic adds on his own account:

> Here a question arises: should one investigate what the truth is concerning the burial of the Venerable Bede? Or can both accounts stand—the statement made here and what is written in the legend of the translation of Saint Cuthbert concerning the body of the Venerable Bede? Some say that there were two Bedes: the first was the author of the homilies, and he is the one from Wilton, beside whom the famous woman poet was buried.

In the *Monastic Register of England*, volume I, part I, page 4, I read that in the church of Glastonbury “lie the bones of the Venerable Bede, the most discerning doctor.”

But Volaterranus says in book XIV of his *Anthropology*:

> Bede’s burial is seen at Genoa.

[Col. 0012C]

Bede the Venerable himself indicates a third Bede, earlier than the other two, in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert* preserved by Surius and Henschenius, March 20, chapter 57:

> I did not dare to ask Saint Cuthbert what the temptations were of which he had spoken. I only asked him to accept ministers. He agreed and kept some of us with him. Among them was the elder Bede the priest, who had always been accustomed to attend him familiarly in his ministry and was unquestionably aware of his gifts and receptions. For this reason especially he wished him to remain with him, so that if he had not repaid anyone’s gift with a worthy recompense, Bede might recall this to his mind by admonition and, before he died, restore to each person what belonged to him.

I would gladly accept what Helinandus reports about the tomb of this elder or earlier Bede, and what Hermannus and most others say: that he died in the year 431.

Thus the younger Bede survived that elder Bede by exactly forty-one years, since, as we have shown, he died in the year of Christ 762, on May 26.

Those who failed to distinguish these two Bedes of Girvo, the elder and the younger, necessarily fell into various chronological errors.

# Chapter II. On Bede’s passing and his way of life

[Col. 0015C]

## Letter of Cuthbert, his disciple and an eyewitness, to Cuthwin, his fellow disciple

[Note: [Col. 0015D] From the *History of the Church of Durham*, by Simeon, monk of Durham, book I, chapter 15. We have nevertheless supplied or corrected a few items from an edition of this letter published long ago with Bede’s works, and also in Surius and Baronius’s *Annals*. [Col. 0016D]]

To Cuthwin, most beloved in Christ, the Collector, Cuthbert, his fellow disciple, eternal salvation in God.

I received the little gift you sent with great pleasure, and I read with profound gratitude the letter expressing your devoted learning. In it I found—what I desired above all—that Masses and sacred prayers for our beloved father in God and our teacher Bede are being diligently celebrated by you. Therefore, out of affection for him, I am all the more delighted to say in a few words, insofar as I enjoy the exercise of my intellect, in what manner he departed this world, since I understand that you too desired and requested this account.

He was afflicted by a very severe illness, with frequent difficulty in breathing, though without pain, beginning before the Lord’s Resurrection, that is, almost two weeks beforehand. Thereafter, cheerful and joyful, giving thanks to almighty God every day and night—in fact, at every hour—until the day of the Lord’s Ascension, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June [May 26], he continued to live and gave us, his disciples, daily lessons. Whatever time remained in the day he devoted to chanting psalms; and he spent the whole night awake in joy and thanksgiving, except when a little sleep interrupted him. When he awoke, he immediately resumed his customary practices and did not forget to give thanks to God with outstretched hands.

I truly confess that I had never seen with my eyes, nor heard with my ears, anyone else giving such diligent thanks to the living God. O truly blessed man! He sang the saying of blessed Paul the Apostle: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10), as well as many other passages from Holy Scripture, by which he urged us to rise from the sleep of the soul, anticipating the final hour. He also said several things in our own language, that is, English, for he was learned in our poetry. Indeed, at that time, composing this English poem, he said with deep contrition [approximately four lines in English, written in English characters, follow in Simeon], which sounds as follows in Latin:

> Before the necessary departure, no one becomes wiser than is needful: namely, in order to consider, before the soul departs from here, what good or evil it has done, and how it will be judged after its departure.

He also sang antiphons according to our custom and his own. One of them was:

> O King of glory, Lord of hosts, who today ascended triumphantly above all the heavens, do not leave us orphans, but send upon us the Spirit of truth promised by the Father. Alleluia.

When he came to the words, “Do not leave us orphans,” he broke into tears and wept bitterly. After an hour he began again to repeat what he had started, and he continued doing so throughout the day. Hearing this, we mourned with him: at one moment we read, at another we wept; indeed, we always read with tears.

In such joy we passed the fifty days up to the day mentioned above. He rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God because he had been judged worthy to be afflicted in this way. He often repeated: “The Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12), together with many other passages from Holy Scripture. He also repeated the saying of Saint Ambrose:

> “I have not lived in such a way that I should be ashamed to live among you; but neither am I afraid to die, because we have a good Lord” (Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*).

During those days he worked diligently on two little works of great memorial value, apart from the lessons we received from him and the chanting of psalms. He translated the Gospel of Saint John into our language, for the benefit of the Church, up to the passage where it says, “But what are these among so many?” He also made some excerpts from the books of Bishop Isidore’s *Rotarum*, saying: “I do not want my disciples to read falsehood and, after my death, labor over it without profit.”

When Tuesday came, the day before the Lord’s Ascension, he began to grow more seriously ill in his breathing, and a slight swelling appeared in his feet. Yet throughout that entire day he taught and dictated cheerfully, and occasionally said among other things: “Learn with haste; I do not know how long I shall remain, and whether my Maker may take me away after a short while.” It seemed to us that he knew his own death very well.

Thus he spent the night awake in thanksgiving. At dawn, on Wednesday, he carefully ordered that what we had begun should be written down. When this had been done, until the third hour, we then walked with the relics of the saints, as the custom of that day requires. One of us remained with him and said: “There is still one chapter lacking, most beloved teacher. Does it seem difficult to you to be questioned further?” He replied: “It is easy. Take your pen, trim it, and write quickly.” The man did so.

At the ninth hour he said to me: “I have some valuable things in my little chest: pepper, altar-cloths (*oraria*), and incense. But run quickly and bring the priests of our monastery to me, so that I too may distribute among them the little gifts God has granted. The rich of this world take pains to give gold, silver, and other precious things; but I shall give my brothers, with great affection and joy, what God has given.”

He addressed each one, urging and entreating them to celebrate Masses and offer prayers for him diligently; and they gladly promised that they would do so. All mourned and wept, especially because he had said that they would never again see his face in this world. Yet they rejoiced because he said:

> “It is time for me to return to him who made me, who created me, who formed me from nothing. I have lived for a long time, and the merciful Judge wisely foresaw my life. The time of my dissolution is at hand, for I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

After speaking many other things of this kind for our instruction, he passed the day joyfully until evening. Then the boy named Wilberch said: “There is still one sentence, beloved teacher, that has not been written down.” He replied: “Write it quickly.”

After a short while the boy said: “The sentence has now been written down.” He answered: “You have spoken the truth. It is finished. Take my head in your hands, for it greatly delights me to sit opposite my holy place, where I used to pray, so that, while sitting, I may call upon my Father.”

And so, seated on the floor of his little cell and chanting, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” when he had named the Holy Spirit, he breathed his last breath from his body and thus departed to the heavenly kingdoms.

All who witnessed the death of the blessed father said that they had never seen anyone else end his life with such great devotion and tranquility. For, as you have heard, as long as his soul remained in his body, he sang “Glory be to the Father” and other words to the glory of God, and he never ceased giving thanks with outstretched hands to the living and true God.

Know, dearest brother, that I could recount many things about him; but the poverty of my language imposes brevity upon my account. Nevertheless, with God’s help, I intend in due course to write a fuller account of what I saw with my eyes and heard with my ears.

## Chifflet’s Notice on Bede’s Ecclesiastical History

First of all, dear reader, you should be advised concerning the various editions of this work on the deeds of the English, which lies before you. No one, I think, who has seen John Gravius’s preface to his Antwerp edition of 1550 will regret not having known the oldest—and therefore the first—edition known to us:

> “Here, dear reader, we give you the Ecclesiastical History of the English by the venerable Bede, printed only once, so far as I know, fifty years ago; but so corruptly that you might find it difficult to judge whether it would have been preferable for it never to have been committed to type at all rather than to have come into people’s hands in this form. I am lying if I did not discover more than 1,050 errors in a single ternion of this work; and perhaps we have had more trouble restoring it than the author had in composing it.”

We believe that the Strasbourg edition of 1514 is meant here; a copy of it survives in the library of the Republic of Augsburg. Since we ourselves have not seen that edition, Gravius’s account is presently sufficient for our knowledge of it. Yet Gravius could have been assisted in correcting Bede’s work by the Paris edition of 1544, prepared by François Jamet, who was the first to publish Bede’s collected works in three volumes.

Thus far Bede’s English History has appeared in three forms. First, by itself: at Strasbourg in 1514, Antwerp in 1550, in small folio; Cologne in 1601, in sextodecimo; and Cambridge in Anglo-Saxon, in folio, in 1644, with the English translation of King Alfred. Second, it appeared together with several older writers on British affairs, at Heidelberg, printed by Commelin, in folio, in 1587. Of that very edition the Lyon printer René Potelier falsely claimed that he had printed numerous copies in the same year, 1587, at Lyon, after altering the title page; he placed them on sale under his own name. Consequently, anyone who lists a Lyon edition of that year as different from the Heidelberg edition is listing it without justification.

Third and finally, Bede’s English History appeared together with his other works: in Paris, through Jamet, in three volumes, in 1544; there again, in eight volumes, in 1554; likewise at Basel, in eight volumes, through Johann Hervagius, in 1563; and finally at Cologne, in the same number of volumes, through Antonius Hierat, in 1612.

Of all these, the Heidelberg edition of 1587 and the Cambridge edition of 1644 are more accurate than the others; yet they are not entirely free from blemishes, as will appear from the notes below. We declare our own edition to be the most complete and corrected of all, on the basis of several manuscript codices, among which the principal place is held by the Codex of Saint Maximin at Trier, of excellent quality and great antiquity. From it especially I dare hope that I have restored this distinguished work to the author’s original purity, with no small benefit and adornment alike to French and English history.

Concerning orthography, I note that I have everywhere retained from the Trier Codex, a manuscript of good quality and great antiquity, the ancient form of writing, because I had no doubt that it proceeded from Bede’s own mind and character—namely, in such forms as *Gaius*, *reverentissimus*, *inluminare*, *Brittania*, *adsertio*, *adtestatio*, *adicere*, *Nordanhymbrorum*, *adlati*, *conlisae*, *inlisae*, *adsistere*, *inlusus*, *inruptio*, *adlaturus*, *conlocarunt*, *adceleranti*, *Scotti*, *conroderet*, *conlapsus*, *inlatus*, *adsumpto*, *adsertiones*, *applicavit*, *adsentatio*, *adpropinquare*, *intellegunt*, *intellegentia*, *adplicuit*, *adfligunt*, *adgregatis*, *inlicita*, *adsensum*, *adsedit*, *adflictiones*, *adsurgere*, *inlustravit*, *exspectatis*, *suppositis*, *idolatria*, *supplantatio*, *inlecebris*, *exsolvamus*, *adquirere*, *Doruvernensis*, *neglegentia*, *utillimus*, *exsecretur*, *proicere*, *contemtus*, *redemtus*, *aquilonalis*, *Hrofensis*, *Agilberctus*, *Cuthberctus*, and many similar forms.

We have not reproduced these forms from the Trier manuscript in order to introduce them into common usage, but so that we might not depart from the mind of the most learned Bede, whose orthographic practice we cannot doubt this to have been.

## Smith’s Notice on the Same History

Here, reader, we give you the Ecclesiastical History, long ago printed many times in various places. The oldest and first printing of all was made in the distinguished city of Strasbourg in the year 1500. At that time the work did not appear alone, but together with Peter of Troyes’ scholastic History, otherwise known as Comestor, and Eusebius’ Ecclesiastical History through Rufinus, with Rufinus’ continuation.

My father was supplied with this edition by the distinguished John Battelev, Archdeacon of Canterbury. It teems with typographical errors—gross ones, indeed, though not especially dangerous. Otherwise, it appears to have been made from a sufficiently ancient codex, for it agrees with the best manuscripts in proper names, chapter divisions, and many variant readings.

Second, it appeared together with the histories mentioned above at the imperial town of Hagenau in 1506, under the supervision of Heinrich Gran, a resident there. He does not appear to have corrected or revised the earlier edition on the authority of any manuscript codex, but merely to have printed it anew word for word.

The opportunity to consult this printing was given to me by the celebrated and exceptionally learned antiquarian Thomas Baker, Bachelor of Sacred Theology, from the library of Christ’s College, Cambridge. I name him here because of his outstanding kindness toward me and as a mark of honor.

Afterward this same history of Bede was printed at Antwerp in 1550, Louvain in 1566, Heidelberg and Lyon in 1587, and Cologne in 1601. Among the other works of the same author it also appeared in Paris through Jamet in 1544, again there in 1554, likewise at Basel through Johann Hervagius in 1563, and finally at Cologne through Antonius Hierat in 1612.

More carefully corrected than all these was the edition published at Cambridge in 1644, in Latin and Saxon, through the work and study of Abraham Wheelock. The distinguished scholar edited the Latin text on the authority of three manuscript codices and illustrated it with extensive historical and ecclesiastical commentaries. The work is certainly worthy of every praise, but it is not complete in every respect; indeed, it suffers from numerous and serious defects.

Finally, in 1681, our author’s work appeared in Latin at Paris, more accurately edited through the efforts of Peter Francis Chifflet, a priest of the Society of Jesus—or, if one believes the most learned editor himself, edited with the greatest possible accuracy—on the basis of several manuscript codices, among which the principal place is held by the Codex of Saint Maximin at Trier, of excellent quality and great antiquity. Chiffletius proves this most clearly from the very ancient orthography retained by that codex. Yet this printing too is not entirely free from blemishes, as will become abundantly clear to anyone who turns his eyes to the bottom of our edition’s pages, where Chifflet’s blunders are chiefly noted.

Accordingly, men distinguished for learning judged that a new edition of Bede would be not merely useful but almost necessary. The first to undertake this burden was the distinguished Thomas Gale, Doctor of Sacred Theology, not long ago Dean of York. By making many other British and English historians available to the public, he had already rendered great service to his homeland.

After collating many manuscript codices and collecting various notes and observations, he declined the burden, I believe because he was occupied with other affairs, and persuaded my father to undertake it. The same celebrated man, with singular courtesy, shared with my father various readings and most learned observations.

My father therefore finally assumed the labor. In order to purge his edition of the errors and defects of earlier ones, he devoted great effort to seeking out and comparing manuscript codices, and, by his own efforts and those of his friends, carefully collated all those he could find in the libraries of Britain.

Overwhelmed by the infinite mass of variant readings, he judged it necessary to devise some method by which he could lighten so great a burden. Observing that many codices were inferior both in age and quality, and that the more recent they were, the fuller they were of variant readings and errors, and recognizing also that they had been copied from older manuscripts, he immediately treated the readings of the more recent codices as entirely worthless and concentrated chiefly on collating several of the oldest.

The oldest manuscript codex of all had recently been in the possession of that distinguished patron of letters, John Moore, formerly Bishop of Ely; today it is preserved in the royal library at Cambridge. It was written in ancient Anglo-Saxon letters around the year 737, two years after the death of our author, as is clear from certain chronological notes placed at the end of the book, which converge upon that year. They are written in these words:

> “In the year 547 Ida began to reign; from him the royal line of the Northumbrians takes its origin, and he remained in the kingdom for twelve years. After him Glappa, one year; Adda, eight; Aethelric, four; Theodric, seven; Friduuald, six; Hussa, seven; Aethelfrid, twenty-four; Edwin, seventeen; Oswald, nine; Oswiu, twenty-eight; Ecgfrid, fifteen; Aldfrid, twenty; Osred, eleven; Coenred, one; Osric, eleven; Ceolwulf, eight.

> “Paulinus baptized 111 years ago.

> “An eclipse 73 years ago.

> “Penda died 79 years ago.

> “Ecgfrid’s battle 63 years ago.

> “Aelfwine 58 years ago.

> “The monastery and Uiuraemonda 64 years ago.

> “Comets were seen 8 years ago.

> “In the same year Father Ecgberct departed to Christ.

> “The English came to Britain 292 years ago.”

Since almost all these dates converge upon the year 737, the distinguished Wanley, who was extremely familiar with Anglo-Saxon manuscripts, considers it probable that this very codex was written in that year, while Ceolwulf was still reigning, or at least before Eadberht’s inauguration—also two years after Bede’s death—in the monastery at Wearmouth.

Moreover, the hand of this codex agrees closely with the copy of Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Care* written by the deacon Willibald, that is, between the year 731, when he received the diaconate, and the year 740, when he was ordained priest. It also agrees with other books and charters of indisputable antiquity, especially with the letter of Walharius, Bishop of London, to Berctwald, Archbishop, which we print in the appendix, no. 24.

It is probable that the codex was carried into Gaul a few years after it was written. For it contains many distinctions, corrections, and so forth written by a Gaul who read the Anglo-Saxon hand with difficulty; and these annotations, occurring here and there in a French hand, appear to have been written roughly nine hundred years ago, near the beginning of the book.

Finally, at the end the following is also written:

> “Also from the Decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger, who now governs the Roman Catholic Mother Church.”

Here Gregory seems to mean Gregory III, who succeeded Gregory II in the papacy in 731 and died in 741.

This codex was preserved in Gaul with sufficient care until the conclusion of the treaty made at Ryswick between William, King of Great Britain, and Louis, the Most Christian King. At that time a certain very learned man purchased it at public auction, together with many other exceedingly rare Greek and Latin codices, and sold them all to a most reverend gentleman who was their owner.

This *keimḗlion* [treasure], venerable for its antiquity, possessing the greatest authority and the most excellent and certain reliability, apparently copied from Bede’s own autograph in the very monastery where Bede composed his History, was lent to my father for use by that bibliophile bishop.

After it had twice been collated with the greatest care against Chifflet’s edition, we print it here word for word. My father considered it a religious duty not to depart from the testimony of a codex of such astonishing antiquity, except where it was plainly discovered that the scribe had written incorrectly, or where a slight withdrawal from its reading was necessary.

Nor was this without good reason. When it is compared with two codices written in Saxon letters and preserved in the Cotton Library—Tiberius C. 2 and A. 14—and also with a third in the royal library, apparently written before the Norman Conquest, they agree with it in proper names, in the ancient method of writing compound words, and in almost every other respect. They differ only in readings that are plainly trivial, and even those differences are few. Therefore there was no reason at all why the text, excellently established from the Morian Codex, should be altered even slightly.

# Bede’s Ecclesiastical History

## Bede’s Preface

*(Smith, English Ecclesiastical History)*

### To the Most Glorious King Ceolwulf

*[Note: Ceolwulf: namely, king of the Northumbrians; see History V.24. There was another king of this name among the West Saxons in A.D. 527, and another among the Mercians in A.D. 819.]*

Bede, servant of Christ and priest, sends greetings to the most glorious King Ceolwulf.

The Ecclesiastical History of the English people, which I recently published, I first gladly sent to you, my king, at your request, for reading and approval; and now I send it back to you for copying and more thorough reflection upon its contents. I greatly appreciate your sincere devotion, by which you not only diligently lend your ear to hearing the words of Holy Scripture, but also zealously devote attention to learning the deeds or sayings of those who came before us, especially the distinguished men of our own nation.

For whether history reports good things about good people, the attentive hearer is earnestly encouraged to imitate what is good; or whether it recalls evil deeds of wicked people, the religious and devout hearer or reader is nonetheless more diligently stirred, by avoiding what is harmful and perverse, to carry out those things which he recognizes as good and worthy of God.

Recognizing this most carefully, you desire that the History mentioned above be more widely disseminated for the sake of general salvation, so that it may become known both to you and to those whom divine authority has appointed you to govern. To remove from you or from the other hearers or readers of this History any occasion for doubt concerning the sources from which I learned what I have written, I shall briefly explain them.

The principal author and helper in this little work was the most reverend Abbot Albinus, a man learned in every respect. He had been carefully instructed in the Church of Canterbury by the blessed Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian, venerable and most learned men. He had learned everything that had taken place in the province of Canterbury itself, or in the neighboring regions, through the disciples of blessed Pope Gregory, whether from written records or from the tradition of elders.

He transmitted these materials to me through the religious priest of the Church of London, Nothelm, either in written form or through Nothelm’s own oral reports.

*[Note: Nothelm was only a priest of the Church of London; see the textual apparatus above.]*

Nothelm later came to Rome and, after searching the archive of the same holy Roman Church with the permission of the reigning Pope Gregory, found there several letters of blessed Pope Gregory and other pontiffs. On his return, he brought them to be inserted into our History, with the approval of the aforementioned most reverend Father Albinus.

*[Note: Albinus. Writers of the highest reputation—Baronius, Contius, and even Leland himself—confuse this Albinus with Flaccus Albinus, otherwise known as Alcuin. Yet the latter, who lived almost a full century later, was a disciple of Archbishop Ecgberht of York and died as Abbot of Tours in 804; this Albinus, however, was a disciple of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian of Canterbury and himself died as Abbot of Canterbury in 732. Bede wrote a letter to this Albinus concerning the benefit of the assistance he had received; see it in its proper place.]*

*[Textual apparatus: At the address, some witnesses add “magnanimous king.” At “Holy Scripture,” the common codices read “sacred,” having been misled by manuscript abbreviations. At “disseminated,” the common codices read “propagated,” thereby correcting the author. Some witnesses read “the most reverend abbot” for “the most reverend Abbot Albinus.” Chifflet places a comma after “carefully” in “carefully instructed,” which he thought improved the sense, but contrary to the author’s style. Some witnesses read “the same regions” for “regions adjoining it,” and omit the “and” introducing “he transmitted these things to me.” Nothelm was only a priest of the Church of London, though he became bishop of Canterbury in 735, beyond the chronological limit of Bede’s History; the author of the *History of the Antiquity of the British Church* calls him bishop of London by a slight error. The Pope Gregory then governing the Roman Church was Gregory III, not Gregory II: Gregory II died on 17 January 731, Gregory III succeeded on 22 February, and Bede mentions 10 June of the following year in connection with Tatwine’s consecration (History V.24). Thus, when sending, indeed resending after revision, this preface to Ceolwulf, Bede wrote the clause during Gregory III’s pontificate. Some witnesses read *promemus* for *promeremus*. On the boundaries of the Saxon provinces, see Appendix no. 2. Common editions place “Saxons” after “Eastern.” Some witnesses read “Daniel also” for “Daniel too.” Some read “Ceadda’s”; for the present reading see History IV.2–3.]*

From the beginning of this volume up to the time when the English people received the faith of Christ, I learned what I have set forth by collecting material here and there, chiefly from the writings of earlier authors. From that point down to the present time, I learned, through the diligence of the aforementioned Abbot Albinus and the reports of Nothelm, as I have said, what had taken place in the Church of Canterbury through the disciples of blessed Pope Gregory or their successors, and under which kings these events occurred.

They also reported to me, at least in part, what happened in the provinces of the East Saxons, the West Saxons, the East Angles, and the Northumbrians, and through which bishops or under which kings they received the grace of the Gospel.

I was especially encouraged by Albinus himself to dare undertake this work. Daniel, too, the most reverend bishop of the West Saxons, who survives to the present day, communicated to me in writing certain matters concerning the ecclesiastical history of his own province and of the neighboring province of the South Saxons, as well as the Isle of Wight.

*[Note: Province. On the boundaries of the Saxon provinces, see the appendix, no. 2.]*

We learned carefully from the brothers of the monastery founded by Cedd and Ceadda, and called Lastingham after them, how, through the ministry of these religious priests of Christ, the province of the Mercians came to the faith of Christ, which it had not previously known, and how the province of the East Saxons recovered the faith which it had once rejected; we also learned what kind of life and death those fathers had.

In the province of the East Angles, we learned what ecclesiastical events had taken place partly from the writings and traditions of earlier generations, and partly from the account of the most reverend Abbot Esi.

In the province of Lindsey, I learned what had taken place concerning the faith of Christ and what succession of priests had existed, either from the writings of the most reverend Bishop Cyniberct or from the spoken testimony of other faithful men.

What had taken place in the province of the Northumbrians from the time when they received the faith of Christ down to the present, throughout its various regions and in the Church, I learned not from any one author, but from the reliable testimony of countless witnesses who were able to know or remember these things, except for those matters which I myself could know.

Among these things, it should be noted that what I have written in this volume or in the booklet of the Deeds of the most holy Father and Bishop Cuthbert, I partly took simply from what I found previously written about him by the brothers of the Church of Lindisfarne, lending the History I was reading my faith; but partly I carefully added what I myself was able to learn from the most certain testimony of faithful men, accepting the authority of the History I read.

*[Note: “By myself.” Some manuscripts read *me ipsum*. On our correction, see Bede, concluding section of History V.25.]*

I earnestly beseech the reader that, if he finds anything in what we have written set down otherwise than the truth requires, he not attribute this to us. For, following the true law of history, we have sought simply to commit to writing, for the instruction of posterity, what we gathered from commonly circulating reports.

*[Note: “Moreover, all.” I long wondered why so many codices placed this clause at the end of the History contrary to the best copies. At last, when I came to Cottonian Manuscript I, I found a gap left at this point, and the clause inserted obscurely at the end of the book. The scribe had before his eyes an original exemplar which he did not dare contradict, but there may have been other matters to which he was still conforming according to the custom of his time. Suspending judgment, therefore, he restored the clause here, where, subsequently neglected and lying forgotten, it gave all who copied this manuscript in later centuries an opportunity to err.]*

Moreover, I earnestly ask all readers or hearers of our nation to whom this same History may come to remember to intercede frequently for my weaknesses of mind and body before the heavenly mercy.

*[Note: “Mercy.” Chifflet’s copy alone reads *patriam* (“fatherland”).]*

Let them repay me for this return of their reward in their respective provinces: I have carefully taken pains to record, concerning each province or the more distinguished places within it, whatever I believed worthy of remembrance and pleasing to its inhabitants; may I therefore find among all of them the fruit of pious intercession.

# The Ecclesiastical History of the Venerable Priest Bede, an Anglo-Saxon

*(Smith, English Ecclesiastical History)*

## Book One

### Chapter One: On the Situation of Britain and Ireland, and Their Ancient Inhabitants

*[Note: Britain. Bede excerpted this description from various authors, especially Pliny, Solinus, Orosius, and Gildas.]*

Britain, an island of the Ocean formerly called Albion, lies between the north and the west, opposite Germany, Gaul, Spain, and the greatest parts of Europe, at a considerable distance. It extends for eight hundred miles toward the north and is two hundred miles broad, except for the longer stretches of its various promontories, by which its circumference is made to total 3,600 miles.

*[Note: “Forty-eight times.” Three thousand six hundred miles.]*

To the south it has Belgic Gaul, whose nearest shore is approached by travelers through a city called the harbor of Rutupiae, now corruptly called Reptacaestir by the English. Across the intervening sea, the nearest shore is that of Gessoriacum, belonging to the Morini, a distance of fifty miles—or, as some have written, 450 stadia.

*[Note: Harbor of Rutupiae. In the *Antonine Itinerary*, Ritupae; in the inscription of Amerbach and the scholia of Battely on Juvenal, Riputia; in Bede’s time among the English, Reptacaestir; in the manuscript of Nennius at Durham and others, Ruoichyn; today, Richborough.]*

*[Note: Gessoriacum. Now Boulogne, according to the Peutinger Tables.]*

*[Note: The Morini. A people of Gaul extending from Neufchâtel to Étaples, perhaps including the district of Ponthieu.]*

*[Note: “As some have written.” Namely, Dio Cassius and the *Antonine Itinerary*.]*

*[Note: 450 stadia. Fifty-six miles.]*

Behind it, where it opens toward the boundless Ocean, it has the Orkney Islands.

The island is rich in crops and trees and suitable for raising cattle and livestock. In some places it even produces vines; and both on land and in the sea it is fertile in birds of various kinds. It is also distinguished by rivers teeming with fish and by numerous abundant springs, especially rich in salmon and eels.

Seals and dolphins are very frequently caught, as are whales, apart from various kinds of shellfish. Among these are mussels, within which they often find pearls of every color and of excellent quality—red, purple, hyacinth-colored, and green, but especially white.

There are also snails in sufficient and more than sufficient abundance, from which a dye of scarlet color is made. Its red is exceedingly beautiful and cannot be made pale by the heat of the sun or by any damage caused by rain; rather, the older it is, the more attractive it is customarily considered.

The island has springs of salt water, as well as hot springs, and from them streams of hot baths, conveniently adapted in different places to every age and sex according to each person’s needs. For water, as Saint Basil says,

*[Note: Saint Basil, *Hexameron*, Homily IV: “Having already acquired, in its passage, a hotter quality from the nature of the minerals, it becomes boiling from the same cause that sets it in motion, and for the most part fiery.”]*

receives a burning quality when it flows through certain particular minerals, and becomes not merely hot but fiery.

The island is also fertile in veins of metals—copper, iron, lead, and silver—and produces a great deal of excellent jet. This stone is black and gem-like; when brought near fire it burns, and when ignited it drives away snakes. Heated by friction, it adheres to objects just as amber does.

It was once also distinguished by twenty-eight most noble cities, apart from countless fortresses, which likewise were equipped with very strong walls, towers, gates, and bolts.

*[Note: Twenty-eight cities. See the appendix, no. 3.]*

Because it lies close beneath the northern summit of the world, it has bright summer nights, so that in the middle of the night observers often question whether the evening twilight still remains or whether morning has already arrived—since the nocturnal sun, passing not far beneath the earth toward the east, returns through the northern regions.

For this reason it has extremely long days in summer, just as it has, by contrast, extremely long nights in winter, when the sun withdraws toward the Libyan regions—that is, eighteen hours. Likewise, it has extremely short nights in summer and days in winter, namely only six equinoctial hours. In Armenia, Macedonia, Italy, and the other regions lying on the same latitude, the longest day or night lasts fifteen hours, while the shortest lasts nine.

At present, in accordance with the number of books in which the divine law was written, it searches out and professes one and the same knowledge of supreme truth and true sublimity in the languages of five peoples—namely, English, British, Scottish, Pictish, and Latin—which, through the study of the Scriptures, has been made common to all the rest. In the beginning, however, this island had only Britons as inhabitants, from whom it received its name. They are said to have been brought over from the Armorican region and to have claimed for themselves the southern parts of the island.

[Note: From the Armorican region. Lesser Britain, called Armorica—meaning “by the sea”—which lies opposite the island of Britain.]

After they had possessed the greater part of the island, beginning from the south, it happened that the people of the Picts, as they relate, entering the Ocean in a few longships from Scythia, reached Ireland beyond all the borders of Britain, driven there by the changing winds. They entered its northern shores, and, finding there a people of Scots, asked that they too might be granted settlements in that region, but they could not obtain this. Ireland is the largest of all the islands after Britain. It lies to the west of Britain; but just as it is narrower toward the north, so it extends much farther southward beyond Britain’s borders, reaching as far as the northern regions of Spain, though a great expanse of sea lies between them.

[Note: Scythia. It is generally assumed that Bede here means Nearer Scythia, now called Scandinavia, comprising Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. In this sense the sea lying between the homeland of Hengist and Britain is also called the Scythian gulf by Nennius.]

Thus the Picts, reaching Ireland by sea, as we have said, asked that they too be given settlements and dwelling places there. The Scots replied that the island could not contain them both, but said: “We can, however, give you sound advice about what you can do. We know that there is another island not far from ours, toward the rising of the sun, which we often see from a distance on clearer days. If you wish to go there, you can make it habitable for yourselves; or, if anyone resists you, make use of us as your auxiliaries.”

Accordingly, the Picts went to Britain and began to inhabit the northern parts of the island, for the Britons had occupied the southern parts. Since the Picts had no wives, they asked the Scots for them. The Scots agreed to provide them only on the condition that, whenever the succession became doubtful, they should choose their king from the female line of the royal family rather than the male. This custom is known to have been maintained among the Picts to the present day.

[Note: As time went on. It is uncertain when the Scots first came to Britain; Bede nevertheless seems to place their arrival before the Roman period.]

As time went on, Britain received, after the Britons and Picts, a third nation—the Scots—within the territory of the Picts. They came from Ireland under their leader Reuda and, whether by friendship or by force, claimed for themselves among the Picts the settlements which they still possess. From this leader they are called Dalreudini to the present day, for in their language *daal* means “a part.”

[Note: Dalreudini. The name was brought from Ireland itself, where Dalriada, now called Rout, lies close to modern Scotland. The territory of King Eda, whom Bede calls Reuda in abbreviated form, was called Reuther by later historians. This people’s settlements in Scotland extended through the regions of Kintyre, Knapdale, Lorna, Argyll, and Breadalbane, together with the adjacent islands.]

Ireland surpasses Britain greatly both in the breadth of its territory and in the healthfulness and clarity of its climate, so that snow rarely remains there for more than three days. No one, because of winter, cuts hay in summer or builds stables for beasts of burden. No reptile is usually seen there, and no snake can live there. For snakes often brought from Britain die as soon as the ship approaches land and they are affected by the smell of that air. Indeed, nearly everything that comes from that island is effective against poison.

Finally, we ourselves saw that, when certain people had been bitten by a snake, leaves were scraped from books that had come from Ireland; the scrapings were placed in water and given to them to drink, and immediately they consumed and quieted the entire force of the spreading poison and the whole swelling of the distended body.

The island is rich in milk and honey, not without vineyards, and abundant in fish and birds; it is also renowned for hunting deer and roe deer. This, properly speaking, is the homeland of the Scots. Departing from it, as we have said, they added a third nation in Britain to the Britons and Picts.

There is a very large inlet of the sea which in ancient times separated the nation of the Britons from the Picts. It breaks far into the land from the west, and on it stands, to this day, the most strongly fortified city of the Britons, called Alcluith. When the Scots whom we have mentioned arrived at the northern part of this inlet, they made that place their homeland.

[Note: Alcluith. *Brittanodunum*, now corruptly called Dumbarton, a fortress on the River Clyde. Shortly after Bede’s time—that is, in 756—it was surrendered to King Eadberht of Northumbria and King Óengus of the Picts; in 869 it was completely destroyed by the Danes.]

## CHAPTER II  

[Col. 0027D]
### How Gaius Julius, the first of the Romans, came to Britain

[Note: Chapter II. This entire chapter is taken from Orosius, Book VI, chapter 9.]

Britain remained inaccessible and unknown to the Romans until Gaius Julius Caesar. In the six hundred and ninety-third year from the founding of the City, but in the sixtieth year before the Lord’s Incarnation, while serving as consul with Lucius Bibulus and waging war against the peoples of the Germans and Gauls, who were separated only by the Rhine River, he came to the Morini, from whom the nearest and shortest crossing to Britain lies.

[Note: Three. This year should be understood not as referring to Julius Caesar’s arrival in Britain, but to his consulship with Bibulus.]

[Note: Sixtieth. This is the one detail Bede added to Orosius: namely, the year of the Incarnation in relation to the year from the founding of the City.]

[Note: Lucius. Bibulus had both a father and a son named Lucius, whereas he himself was Marcus.]

After preparing about eighty cargo and transport ships, Caesar crossed over to Britain. There he was first exhausted by a fierce battle and then overtaken by a storm, losing most of his fleet and almost all his cavalry, together with a considerable number of soldiers. Returning to Gaul, he sent the legions into winter quarters and ordered six hundred ships of both kinds to be built.

[Note: Legions. Other copies read “three legions,” or “twelve”; others, “six,” or “twelve.”]

Crossing again to Britain at the beginning of spring, while he himself marched against the enemy with a large army, he saw the ships lying at anchor overtaken by a storm: some were dashed against one another, others struck the sands and were shattered. Forty of them were lost, while the remainder were repaired only with great difficulty.

Caesar’s cavalry was defeated by the Britons in the first engagement, and Labienus, a tribune, was killed there.

[Note: Labienus. Quintus Laberius Durus, Caesar, *Gallic War*, Book V. Labienus, however, was left by Caesar in Gaul; after accomplishing many deeds there, he later defected to Pompey and did not perish until the battle of Munda. The people of Kent claim Labienus—that is, Laberius—as their own, and even point out his burial place by the River Stour near Chilham. Ledandus, drawing on an Old Chronicle, says that Labienus, that is, Laberius, was killed near Chestonwood by Rochester.]

In the second battle, after great loss on his own side, he put the defeated Britons to flight. From there he proceeded to the River Thames.

[Note: Proceeded. Other copies read: “he proceeded,” and report that the river could be crossed at only one place by a ford.]

[Note: Thames. Other copies read *Tamensium*.]

On the farther bank, under the leadership of Cassivellaunus, an immense multitude of the enemy had taken its position and had obstructed the bank of the river and almost the entire ford beneath the water with extremely sharp stakes. Traces of those stakes can still be seen there today, and observers think that each was as thick as a man’s thigh and, encased in lead, had been fixed immovably in the depths of the river.

[Note: Stakes. From these, the ford is called “Coway stakes” near Lalham by Camden. Orosius’s statement that the river could be crossed at only one place is evidently mistaken, since native authorities have supplied so many supposed fords for Caesar: Brentford, Kingston, Chertsey, and Wallingford. For this reason the clause is not found in Bede’s manuscripts. See also King Alfred’s Saxon paraphrase of this passage of Orosius.]

When the Romans discovered and avoided this obstacle, the barbarians, unable to withstand the attack of the legions, hid themselves in the forests. From there they repeatedly burst forth and inflicted heavy losses on the Romans.

Meanwhile, the very strongly fortified city of the Trinovantes, under the leadership of Androgeus, surrendered to Caesar after giving forty hostages.

[Note: Androgeus. Mandubracius in Caesar, *Gallic War*, Book V. *Mandu* occurs in many names: Veromandui, Cartismandua, Manduessedum, and Maudubii. Androgeus may perhaps be a corruption of Mandubrogus, which comes close to both names.]

Following this example, many other cities entered into alliance with the Romans. With their guidance, Caesar at last captured in a severe battle the town of Cassivellaunus, situated between two marshes, fortified also by the cover of forests, and abundantly supplied with everything.

[Note: The town of Cassivellaunus. It is thought to have been Verulamium, now St Albans. In that region the Cassii, whom Caesar mentions and from whom Cassivellaunus perhaps received his name, had their settlements. If you wish to see the stories which our native historians have attached to this Cassivellaunus and Androgeus, consult Geoffrey of Monmouth and Matthew of Westminster.]

After this, Caesar returned from Britain to Gaul, having sent the legions into winter quarters, and was surrounded and harassed on every side by sudden disturbances of war.

[Note: Britain. Other copies read “from the Britons” instead of “from Britain,” owing to the abbreviation used in the earliest manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER III  

[Col. 0029B]
### How Claudius, the second Roman to visit Britain, added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire; and how Vespasian, sent by him, also brought the Isle of Wight under Roman rule

[Note: Chapter III. This chapter too is owed to Orosius.]

In the seven hundred and ninety-eighth year from the founding of the City, the emperor Claudius, fourth after Augustus, wishing to display himself as a ruler useful to the state, sought war and victory everywhere and from every direction. Accordingly, he undertook an expedition to Britain, which appeared to have been thrown into rebellion because defectors had not been returned.

[Note: Seven hundred and ninety-eighth. Paris reads “the ninth”; the Antwerp and Cologne editions read “the seventh.” Chiffletius, defending his Trier manuscript, vigorously argues for the ninth year and criticizes those who give the eighth or seventh, although it is certain that either of the latter two is closer to the chronology than the ninth. Bede places Claudius’s expedition in the fourth year of his reign and in the year of Christ 46. When these years are adapted to the year from the founding of the City, we must arrive at 797 or 798. Gaius was killed on 24 January in the year 794 from the founding of the City, corresponding to A.D. 42. Therefore the fourth year of Claudius, his successor, includes part of the year 797 from the founding of the City, but most of the year 798, which corresponds to A.D. 46, and which all of Bede’s ancient manuscripts clearly give.]

He crossed into the island, which no one had dared to visit either before Julius Caesar or after him, and there, without any battle or bloodshed, within a very few days he brought the greater part of the island into submission.

[Note: No one after him. Augustus came to Gaul in the year 727 from the founding of the City against the Britons, but returned after their ambassadors had declared them pacified. In the following year, the Cantabrian disturbances prevented him from preparing arms against them. Tiberius scarcely ever set foot outside Rome. Gaius merely visited the Ocean and, bringing back ridiculous spoils, sought a triumph in vain.]

He also added to the Roman Empire the Orkney Islands, situated in the Ocean beyond Britain. Six months after his departure he returned to Rome and gave his son the name Britannicus. He completed this war in the fourth year of his reign, which is the forty-sixth year from the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: The year in which there was famine. The authors of the annals assign this famine to the second year of Claudius. Orosius and Bede, however, follow Eusebius.]

In that same year a very severe famine occurred throughout Syria, which is remembered as having been foretold in the Acts of the Apostles by the prophet Agabus.

Vespasian, who later ruled after Nero, was sent by Claudius to Britain and also brought under Roman authority the Isle of Wight, situated near Britain to the south. The island is about thirty Roman miles from east to west and twelve from south to north; in its eastern parts it is six miles by sea, and in its western parts three miles, from the southern coast of Britain.

[Note: Thirty miles. Camden counts only twenty.]

Nero succeeded Claudius in the empire but attempted nothing at all in military affairs. Thus, among the countless losses of the Roman realm, he almost lost Britain, for under him two very famous towns there were captured and destroyed.

[Note: Two towns. Camulodunum and Verulamium, captured by the forces of Queen Boudica. Suetonius Paulinus nevertheless restored the province. Tacitus.]

## CHAPTER IV  

[Col. 0030B]
### How Lucius, king of the Britons, sent a letter to Pope Eleutherus asking to become a Christian

In the one hundred and fifty-sixth year from the Lord’s Incarnation, Marcus Antoninus Verus, fourteenth after Augustus, assumed the kingdom together with his brother Aurelius Commodus.

[Note: During whose reigns. Up to these words Bede takes the beginning of this chapter from Orosius. I would not, however, attribute to Orosius the difficulty which seems to exist in the dates of the emperors Marcus and Commodus and of Pope Eleutherus. The year 911 from the founding of the City, which Orosius assigns to the joint rule of the brothers, corresponds to A.D. 161. There is no difficulty concerning Lucius’s letter to Eleutherus in that year; indeed, it is the very year in which Eusebius and Bede agree in their Chronicles concerning the beginning of the brothers’ reign, as I noted at that passage. But here, in the *History*, Bede, converting Orosius’s era from the founding of the City into the era of the Incarnation, assigns A.D. 156 to the year 911 and nevertheless requires that Lucius’s letter be admitted to the same period. It is uncertain why he did this, and there is no need to linger over the explanation. It is enough to observe that just as Bede here anticipates the common chronology—and even his own chronology—in the years of Marcus and Commodus, so he must be understood to anticipate it also in the years of Eleutherus. Just as he places the beginning of Marcus and Commodus in A.D. 156 and their end in A.D. 167, so he wished the pontificate of Eleutherus to be placed in the corresponding years, so that the final year of the brothers would always coincide with the first year of the pope. That this was Bede’s intention is clear from the summary at the end of this *History*, where he says that Eleutherus became bishop in A.D. 167. Whatever explanation we accept, Bede’s intention in both books will be the same: namely, to align the end of the emperors’ reign with the beginning of the pontificate. There is no need, as many have done, to introduce Commodus the son here, since the brothers’ joint reign provides sufficient time in which this correspondence between the king and Eleutherus could have taken place, as indeed it should have.

As for the reign, deeds, and death of Lucius, which Bede does not mention, I leave them to those who have collected the traditions concerning Lucius.]

During their reign, while Eleutherus, a holy man, presided over the pontificate of the Roman Church, Lucius, king of the Britons, sent him a letter, begging that through his command he might be made a Christian. He soon obtained the fulfillment of his pious request, and the Britons preserved the faith they had received inviolate and intact in peaceful security until the reign of the emperor Diocletian.

## CHAPTER V  

[Col. 0030D]
### How Severus distinguished the part of Britain recovered by the Romans from the rest by a rampart
