In the one hundred and eighty-ninth year from the Lord’s Incarnation, Severus, an African by birth, from Tripolitan Leptis, seventeenth after Augustus, obtained the empire and held it for seventeen years.

[Note: One hundred and eighty-ninth. Eusebius reads “one hundred and ninety-third,” but Bede continues the same calculation that he followed in the preceding chapter. I therefore conclude that the variation was not due to scribes but to the author.]

[Note: Seventeen years. Eusebius and most chronologists give eight; but it must be admitted that Bede’s manuscripts, both in the *Chronicle* and in the *History*, have seven. I acknowledged their authority there and follow it here. According to an exact calculation, Severus ruled for seventeen years, seven months, and three days.]

Severus was naturally savage and constantly harassed by many wars. He ruled the state with great courage, but at great cost. Having therefore conquered the civil wars which had confronted him with the greatest difficulty, he was drawn to Britain when almost all his allies had defected. After repeatedly fighting great and serious battles there, he decided to separate the part of the island that had been recovered from the remaining unconquered peoples, not by a wall, as some suppose, but by a rampart.

[Note: A wall is made of stone; a rampart of turf. Apart from this distinction, nothing has been added to Orosius in this chapter. Critics have strongly questioned whether Bede correctly distinguishes a wall from a rampart. In the authors who have handed down an account of this work of Severus, the terms are used indiscriminately, but there is no certainty about the matter that overturns Bede’s supposition. Bede explains himself more fully on this point in Chapter 12 of this book.]

A wall is made of stones, whereas a rampart, by which camps are fortified against the force of the enemy, is made of turf. The turf is cut from the earth and built up like a wall above ground, so that in front there is a ditch from which the turf has been removed; above it, stakes of very strong wood are set in place.

Thus Severus constructed a great ditch and a very strong rampart, further strengthened by frequent towers, extending from sea to sea. There, at the town of Eboracum, he died of illness. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Geta, declared a public enemy, perished; Bassianus, having assumed the surname Antoninus, succeeded to the kingdom.

## CHAPTER VI  

[Col. 0031D]
### On the reign of Diocletian and his persecution of the Christians

[Note: Chapter VI. This entire chapter too is from Orosius.]

In the two hundred and eighty-sixth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, Diocletian, thirty-third after Augustus, was chosen emperor by the army. He held power for twenty years and made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, his colleague in the empire.

During their reign, a certain Carausius, low in birth but quick in judgment and action, had been stationed to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then ravaging. But he acted more to the ruin than to the advancement of the state: when he recovered plunder from the pirates, he returned none of it to its owners but claimed it all for himself. This aroused suspicion that, through calculated negligence, he was allowing the enemies themselves to attack the borders. Therefore, when Maximian ordered him to be killed, he assumed the purple and seized Britain. After vigorously claiming and holding it for seven years, he was finally killed through the treachery of his colleague Allectus.

Allectus afterward held the island, which he had wrested from Carausius, for three years. The prefect of the praetorian guard, Asclepiodotus, overthrew him and recovered Britain after ten years.

Meanwhile, Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the churches to be destroyed and Christians to be oppressed and killed, in the tenth persecution after Nero [304]. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those that had preceded it, for it continued uninterruptedly for ten years through the burning of churches, the proscription of the innocent, and the slaughter of martyrs.

[Note: For ten years. That is, from Diocletian’s nineteenth year, which for Eusebius is A.D. 304, to the sixth year of Constantine the Great, which for him is A.D. 313; when that year ended, the persecution ceased. The history of this and the following chapter falls within those years. See Appendix, no. 4. Also consult Bede’s *Chronicle* under Diocletian.]

Finally, Britain too was greatly exalted by the glory of her many confessors devoted to God.

## CHAPTER VII  

[Col. 0032B]
### The passion of Saint Alban and his companions, who shed their blood for the Lord at that time

[Note: In that place. Apparently in the first or second year of the persecution just mentioned, before Diocletian and Maximian laid down the purple.]

For in Britain Saint Alban suffered [305]. The presbyter Fortunatus, when mentioning the blessed martyrs who came to the Lord from every part of the world, says in his *Praise of Virgins*:

[Note: The illustrious Alban. Fortunatus, VIII.4.]

> Fruitful Britain produces the illustrious Alban.

[Note: This Alban. Gildas disposes of the martyrdom of this saint in a few words; Bede gives a fuller account from the Acts of the Martyrs, whose first author is unknown. Capgrave—or rather John of Tynemouth—provided more details, but the English Church that followed adopted only Bede’s account, distributing it into nine lessons and transferring it into the public offices. See also Cotton Library, Julius D. VII.29; Tiberius D. III; Faustina B. IV.1.]

This Alban, still a pagan, received into his home a certain cleric fleeing from the persecutors, while the commands of the wicked rulers were raging against Christians. When Alban saw him devoting himself continually to prayer and keeping watch day and night, he was suddenly visited by divine grace and began to imitate that man’s example of faith and devotion. Gradually instructed by his saving exhortations, he abandoned the darkness of idolatry and became a Christian with his whole heart.

After the aforementioned cleric had lodged with him for several days, word reached the ears of the wicked ruler that a confessor of Christ, for whom no place of martyrdom had yet been appointed, was hiding with Alban. He immediately ordered soldiers to search for him diligently. When they reached the martyr’s hut, Saint Alban at once presented himself to the soldiers in place of his guest and teacher, wearing that man’s clothing—that is, the *caracalla* in which he was dressed—and was led bound before the judge.

[Note: Caracalla. A priestly garment. See the Saxon paraphrase of this passage. Regarding this garment, which was discovered many centuries later in the monastery at Ely, see Thomas Walsingham, p. 103, under A.D. 1313.]

It happened that, at the hour when Alban was brought before him, the judge was standing at the altars and offering sacrifices to demons. When he saw Alban, he was immediately consumed by overwhelming anger because Alban had dared voluntarily to offer himself to the soldiers in place of the guest he had received. He ordered Alban to be dragged before the images of the demons at whose altar he was standing.

“You preferred,” he said, “to conceal a rebel and sacrilegious man rather than hand him over to the soldiers, so that, as a despiser of the gods, he might suffer the punishment deserved for his blasphemy. If you attempt to abandon the worship of our religion, you will have to pay whatever penalties were owed by him.”

But Saint Alban, who had voluntarily declared himself a Christian to the persecutors of the faith, was not at all afraid of the ruler’s threats. Girded with the weapons of spiritual warfare, he openly declared that he would not obey the ruler’s commands.

Then the judge said: “Of what family or race are you?”

Alban replied: “What does it matter to you from what stock I was born? But if you desire to hear the truth of religion, know that I am already a Christian and devote myself to Christian observances.”

The judge said: “I ask your name. Tell it to me without delay.”

He replied: “My parents call me Alban, and I always worship and revere the true and living God, who created all things.”

Then the judge, filled with anger, said: “If you wish to enjoy the happiness of everlasting life, do not delay sacrificing to the great gods.”

Alban replied: “These sacrifices which you offer to demons can neither help those subject to them nor fulfill the desires or prayers of those who supplicate them. Rather, whoever offers sacrifices to these images will receive eternal punishments in hell as his reward.”

When he heard this, the judge, moved by overwhelming fury, ordered the holy confessor of God to be beaten by the torturers, thinking that he could soften—or rather break—the firmness of his heart by blows when he could not do so by words. While he was subjected to the most severe tortures, he bore them patiently, indeed joyfully, for the Lord.

When the judge perceived that Alban could neither be overcome by tortures nor recalled from the worship of the Christian religion, he ordered him to be beheaded.

As he was being led to his death, he came to a river whose swift current divided the wall and the sandy ground where he was to be executed. There he saw a considerable crowd of people of both sexes, of various conditions and ages, who had unquestionably been summoned by divine inspiration to serve the blessed confessor and martyr. They occupied the bridge over the river so completely that it could scarcely be crossed before evening.

At last, when almost everyone had crossed, the judge remained behind in the city without his attendants. Saint Alban, whose mind burned with devotion to reach martyrdom quickly, approached the stream and, raising his eyes to heaven, immediately saw that the riverbed had dried up: the water had withdrawn before him and made a way for his feet.

When the executioner himself, who was to strike him, saw this among the others, he hurried to meet him when he had reached the appointed place of death.

[Note: The appointed place. Formerly, as it is commonly read, Holmhurst; but in the best copy of John of Tynemouth, in the Lambeth Library, Holynhirst.]

Moved by divine inspiration, the executioner threw down the sword he had held ready and fell at Alban’s feet, earnestly desiring that, with the martyr or in place of the martyr whom he had been ordered to strike, he himself might rather deserve to be struck.

Thus, when the man had changed from a persecutor into a companion of truth and faith, and the sword lay on the ground while there was a proper delay among the executioners, the most revered confessor of God climbed the hill with the crowds. It stands conveniently about five hundred paces from the sandy ground, joyfully adorned—and indeed everywhere clothed—with flowers of various herbs. Nothing on it is suddenly steep, nothing precipitous, nothing abrupt; nature has spread it broadly on every side and leveled it like a plain, making it worthy, because of the beauty inherent in its appearance, to be consecrated one day by the blood of the blessed martyr.

[Note: Most fitting. Chiffletius alone reads “most fitting.”]

At its summit Saint Alban asked God to give him water. Immediately, a perennial spring burst forth from an enclosed channel before his feet, so that everyone might recognize that the stream too had paid its service to the martyr. For it could not have happened that, on the steep summit of the hill, the martyr would ask for water which he had not left in the river, unless he had perceived that this would be appropriate.

The river, having completed its service and fulfilled its devotion, left behind its testimony of duty and returned to its natural course.

Thus beheaded, the most steadfast martyr received the crown of life which God promised to those who love him. But the man who had brought impious hands against the pious neck was not permitted to rejoice over the dead, for his eyes fell to the ground together with the head of the blessed martyr.

That soldier too was beheaded—the one who earlier, seized by a heavenly impulse, had refused to strike the holy confessor of God. It is evident of him that, although he was not washed in the water of baptism, he was nevertheless cleansed in the washing of his own blood and made worthy to enter the heavenly kingdom.

Then the judge, struck by such an extraordinary display of heavenly miracles, immediately ordered the persecution to cease, beginning to show honor to the slaughter of the saints through which he had previously thought they could be forced to abandon their devotion to the Christian faith.

Blessed Alban suffered on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, near the city of Verulamium, which is now called by the English people Verlamacaestir or Waetlingacaestir.

[Note: Verlamacaestir or Waetlingacaestir. The former name comes from the River Ver, which lay east of the old city; the latter from the Roman road called Watling Street, which lay to the west.]

There, when the peace of Christian times later returned, a church of marvelous workmanship was built, worthy of his martyrdom.

[Note: Where afterward there was a church. This British church, destroyed in the Saxon wars, was restored by King Offa around A.D. 793. After it had again been devastated by the Danes, the faithful renewed it under Abbot Geoffrey in A.D. 1229.]

At that place, to this day, the healing of the sick and the frequent working of miracles do not cease to be celebrated.

At that time Aaron and Julius, citizens of the city of the Legions, suffered, as did many others of both sexes in various places. They were tortured with different torments and mangled by the unheard-of dismemberment of their limbs, and after a perfect struggle sent their souls to the joys of the heavenly city.

[Note: At that time. From this point to the end of the chapter, the material comes from Gildas, section 8.]

[Note: Aaron and Julius. Each of them had in the City of the Legions a distinguished church adorned with his name. In ancient times there were three notable churches: one of the martyr Julius, adorned with a choir of virgins dedicated to God; another founded in the name of blessed Aaron, his companion, and distinguished by its notable order of canons; and a third marked by the metropolitan see of all Wales. Gerald of Wales, *Journey through Wales*, I.5.]

[Note: The city of the Legions. Stapleton called this place Leicester in his translation of Bede. Camden’s interpreters call it Exeter.]

[Note: Very many. Ancient martyrologies, including Bede’s, commemorate the holy martyrs Socrates and Stephen in Britain, and writers assign them to this persecution, on 17 September. Notker, under 22 June, counts 889. Nauclerus says that they were innumerable.]

## CHAPTER VIII  

[Col. 0035D]
### How, after the persecution had ceased, the Church in Britain enjoyed some measure of peace until the time of the Arian madness

[Note: Chapter VIII. The first part of this chapter, up to “poured it into the island, which held nothing certain firmly,” is from Gildas; the remainder is from Orosius, although Bede cites only Eutropius.]

When the storm of persecution had subsided [313], the faithful of Christ who during the time of danger had hidden themselves in forests, deserts, and concealed caves came out into public. They restored the churches that had been destroyed to the ground, founded, built, and completed basilicas of the holy martyrs, openly displayed everywhere, as though victorious standards, the signs of their sufferings, celebrated feast days, and performed sacred rites with pure heart and mouth.

Thus the peace that existed in the Churches of Christ in Britain continued until the time of the Arian madness. That madness, after corrupting the whole world, infected this island too, remote as it was from the rest of the world, with the poison of its error. Once this path of pestilence had been opened across the Ocean, every plague of heresy poured into the island, which was always eager to hear something new and held nothing certain firmly.

[Note: This island also, and below, the churches of the islands. The general condition of the Church in that age is here applied to our Britain. From the testimonies of Constantine, Athanasius, Hilary, and others, however, it is abundantly clear that the bishops of Britain always adhered to the orthodox faith.]

At this time Constantine, who, while Diocletian was alive, ruled Gaul and Spain [407], a man of the greatest gentleness, died in Britain.

He left Constantine, his son by his concubine Helena, appointed emperor of the Gauls.

[Note: Appointed. Chiffletius alone reads “begotten.”]

Eutropius writes that Constantine was made emperor in Britain and succeeded his father in the kingdom.

[Note: Made emperor in Britain. Eutropius, Book X. The royal paraphrast deserves praise here, for in his Saxon interpretation he claims for this island the birth of its former ruler Constantine. And rightly so, but Eutropius does not attest this: he says that the son was made emperor, not that he was born there.]

During his reign the Arian heresy arose, was exposed and condemned at the Council of Nicaea, and nevertheless spread the destructive poison of its faithlessness—not only throughout the whole world, as we have said, but also among the churches of the islands.

## CHAPTER IX  

[Col. 0036A]

## Textual apparatus to Chapters I–IX

The following readings occur in the supplied text and are associated here with their clauses in source order. Purely inflectional or orthographic alternatives retain their Latin forms because English cannot reproduce the distinction.

1. In the account of the first British and Pictish settlements, *Austrina* (“southern things/parts”) is alternatively *Austrinas*, the accusative form agreeing with “parts”: the Britons had occupied the southern parts.
2. In “as time went on Britain, after the Britons and Picts, received a third nation,” *post Brittones* (“after the Britons”) is alternatively *praeter Brittones* (“besides the Britons”).
3. Caesar left the legions *in Hiberna*; the alternative name-form is *in Hibernia* (“in winter quarters,” as the narrative understands it, though the printed forms coincide with the name Ireland).
4. When Caesar advanced against the enemy, another text adds *ingenti*: he went with “a huge army.”
5. The river name *Tamesim* (“the Thames,” accusative) is alternatively printed *Tamensium*, an inflectionally different or corrupt form. [Col. 0028B]
6. After the stakes are described as fixed immovably in the river bed, another text adds *haereant*, “that they might remain fixed there.”
7. The Britons “hid themselves” in the woods: *obdidere* is alternatively *abdidere*, with the same substantive meaning.
8. The strongly fortified city of the Trinovantes “gave itself” to Caesar, *dedit*; the alternative *dedidit* makes the military sense explicit, “surrendered itself.” [Col. 0028C]
9. Caesar took Cassivellaunus’s stronghold after a severe *pugna*, “battle”; another text has *bello*, “war.”
10. Claudius wished to display a ruler useful to the commonwealth; another text adds *se*, “to display himself as such a ruler.”
11. Britain had been stirred to revolt because fugitives were not *redhibitos*, “returned as demanded”; another text has *redditos*, “given back.” [Col. 0029C]
12. Pope *Eleutherus* is alternatively named *Eleutherius*.
13. Lucius is called king *Brittaniarum*, “of the Britains”; another text has *Britannorum*, “of the Britons.” [Col. 0030B]
14. Severus held the empire for seventeen years; another text reads eight years. The accompanying editorial note further records that Bede’s manuscripts read seven, while the exact calculation given there is seventeen years, seven months, and three days.
15. Severus “left” (*reliquit*) two sons; another text has the participle *relinquens*, “leaving” two sons. Of Bassianus another text adds *vero*, “but/indeed”: “Bassianus, however, assumed the surname Antoninus and obtained the kingdom.”
16. Carausius “kindled” (*accendens*) suspicion by not returning the pirates’ booty; another text reads *accedens*, “adding to/approaching” suspicion.
17. He appeared to permit incursions through *artifici negligentia*, “crafty negligence”; another text reads *artificii negligentia*, “neglect of the scheme/artifice.”
18. After Carausius, Alectus held the stolen island; another text adds *vero*, “Alectus, however.” [Col. 0032A]
19. Asclepiodotus is called prefect *praetorio*; another text has the genitive form *praetorii*, “prefect of the praetorium.”
20. Britain was exalted by *plurima* glory, “very great glory,” devoted to God in confession; another text has *complurima*, “very abundant/manifold glory.”
21. The companions of Saint Alban shed their blood in the “same” time, *eodem*; another text has *eo*, “that” time. [Col. 0032B]
22. Fortunatus mentioned the martyrs who “were coming” from the whole world to the Lord, *venirent*; another text has *venerunt*, “came.”
23. Alban saw that the cleric devoted himself to continual prayers and vigils *die noctuque*, “by day and by night”; another text has *diu noctuque*, “for a long time and by night.”
24. Alban asks, “What does it concern you?” (*pertinet*); another text has *refert*, “what does it matter to you?” [Col. 0033B]
25. The judge thought he could “soften” (*emollire*) Alban’s constancy by blows; another text has *emoliri*, “overcome or work upon” his constancy. [Col. 0033C]
26. After the persecution Britain had “a little” peace: *aliquantulam* agrees with *pacem*; another text has the adverbial/neuter *aliquantulum*.
27. The faithful had hidden themselves in woods, deserts, or concealed caves: *occulerant* is alternatively *occultaverant*, with the same meaning.
28. Constantius died in Britain: *morte obiit*, literally “met death”; another text has the regular accusative *mortem obiit*. [Col. 0035D]
29. Maximus returned to Gaul; another text adds *in*, explicitly “returned into Gaul.” [Col. 0036A]

One editorial note absent from the earlier draft belongs to the Orkneys at Col. 0029D: “Orkneys. Tacitus by no means concedes this, wishing this laurel to belong peculiarly to his Agricola; under Agricola’s command, only when Domitian was emperor, he says that the Roman fleet discovered and subdued the Orkney Islands, which until then had been unknown. But since the British war in Claudius’s time was waged under the command of Aulus Plautius, who was victorious for seven continuous years, it is not impossible that the assertion here, taken from Eusebius and Eutropius, that the Orkneys were received by Claudius is correct.”
### How, during the reign of Gratian, Maximus was made emperor in Britain and returned to Gaul with a great army

[Col. 0036A]

In the year 377 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Gratian, forty-second from Augustus, held the imperial power for six years after the death of Valens, although he had already long before been ruling together with his uncle Valens and with his brother Valentinian. When he saw the condition of the state afflicted and almost ruined, he invested Theodosius, a Spaniard, with the purple at Sirmium, out of necessity for restoring the state, and appointed him simultaneously to rule the East and Thrace.

At that time Maximus, a vigorous and honorable man, and worthy of the title of Augustus had he not risen through tyranny against his sworn allegiance, was created emperor in Britain by the army, almost against his will, and crossed over into Gaul. There he terrified Gratian Augustus by a sudden attack while Gratian was planning to cross into Italy; having ensnared him by deceit, Maximus killed him and drove his brother Valentinian Augustus out of Italy. Valentinian fled to the East, where Theodosius received him with paternal affection and soon restored him to the imperial power—Maximus the usurper having meanwhile been shut up within the walls of Aquileia, captured, and killed by them.

[Note: [Col. 0036C] “A Spaniard.” Chiffl. alone has “a Spanish man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0036C] “A man of honor.” Gildas, in his customary satirical manner, gives us a very different conception of Maximus; but here Bede follows other authorities, Orosius and Prosper.]

[Note: [Col. 0036C] “Almost against his will.” Maximus himself professed this to Saint Martin, as Sulpicius Severus records in the closing part of the Life of Martin.]

[Note: [Col. 0036C] “There Gratian.” Gratian, defeated at Paris by the treachery of Merobaudes, master of the soldiers, fled and was captured and killed at Lyons. PROSPER, under the year 385. But see Gregory of Tours, I, 38, 43, and Socrates, Ecclesiastical History V, 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0036D] “Within the walls of Aquileia.” OROS., VII, 35. “At the third milestone from Aquileia.” PROSPER, under the year 389.]

## CHAPTER X  
### How, while Arcadius was reigning, Pelagius the Briton undertook proud wars against the grace of God

[Col. 0036C]

In the year 394 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Arcadius, son of Theodosius, assumed the kingdom with his brother Honorius, forty-third from Augustus, and held it for thirteen years. In his time Pelagius the Briton spread the poisons of his unbelief far and wide against the aid of heavenly grace, using as his associate Julian of Campania, whom an ungoverned desire for the bishopric he had lost was agitating. Saint Augustine, as did the other orthodox Fathers, answered them with many thousands of Catholic doctrinal pronouncements, yet could not correct their madness. But, more seriously, after their madness had been rebuked, it chose rather to increase by contradicting than to be cleansed by assenting to the truth. Prosper the rhetorician aptly suggests this in heroic verse when he says:

> Against Augustine, it is said, there creeps a certain  
> Writer, whom devouring envy has long consumed.  
> Who drove the wretched little serpent, its head  
> Somewhat covered in dark caverns, to raise itself from the ground?  
> Either the sea-dwelling Britons fed this one on their own grain,  
> Or the Campanian grass makes his heart swell.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] “In his time.” The Pelagian heresy arose in the time of Arcadius, but spread chiefly during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger. See Prosper, under the year 414. Garnerius has expressly arranged the sequence of years in his notes to Marius Mercator, p. 127 onward.]

[Note: [Col. 0036D] “The Briton.” To distinguish him from the Pelagius who is called Pelagius of Tarentum. AUGUSTINE, Letter to Paulinus 106. Also to distinguish him from any fictitious Pelagius who might be called Gaul or Scot.]

[Note: [Col. 0036D] “Julian of Campania.” In the preface to Bede’s Commentary on the Song of Songs, the common editions call this man “Julian of Celano in Campania.” In Peter the Deacon’s book On the Incarnation he is called “of Aedianum,” but in Prosper’s Chronicle he is correctly called “of Eclanum.” Eclanum was a city of the Hirpini on the borders of Campania and Apulia, assigned to either province according to the various divisions of the empire. After Eclanum was destroyed, its see was transferred to Frequentum, commonly called Fregento. HOLSTENIUS, in Cluverius’s Italy.]

[Note: [Col. 0037C] “The bishoprics they had lost.” These are Prosper’s words under the year 440. Celestine, pope of Rome, deprived Julian, Florus, Orontius, Fabius, and others of the same sect of their bishoprics.]

[Note: [Col. 0037C] “Cleansed.” The Vulgate has “corrected” throughout, except in the Mori manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0037B] “In heroic verse.” That is, in a poem Against the Detractor of Augustine, apparently Caelestius, whom the poetic allusion describes as filled with envy by “the sea-dwelling Briton”—that is, Pelagius—and “the Campanian grass”—that is, Julian.]

[Note: [Col. 0037D] “Rhetorician.” Vossius, History of Latin Literature II, conjectures that “of Rhegium” should be read here, assuming that Prosper was bishop of Rhegium, although he was never a bishop.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### How, while Honorius was reigning, Gratian and Constantine were created usurpers in Britain, and soon the former in Britain and the latter in Gaul were killed

[Col. 0037B]

In the year 407 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Honorius Augustus, the younger son of Theodosius, held the empire, forty-fourth from Augustus, two years before the Roman invasion carried out by Alaric, king of the Goths, when the peoples of the Alans, Suebi, Vandals, and many other nations with them, after crushing the Franks and crossing the Rhine, were raging throughout the whole of Gaul, Gratian, a townsman, was created and killed as a usurper in Britain.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] “The younger.” All the manuscripts read *minoris* (“of the younger”), not excepting the Mori manuscript; some printed editions have *majoris* (“of the elder”), others *junioris* (“of the younger”). It is remarkable how all the manuscripts agree in the unhappy reading *minoris*. Chifflet rightly professes to restore, according to the truth and Bede’s own intention, *minore* (“the younger”): “The elder,” he says, “was Theodosius’s son Arcadius.” The matter itself speaks, as does Bede himself in the Chronicle under the year 4377: “Honorius,” he says, “with Theodosius the Younger, the son of his brother, for fifteen years.”]

[Note: [Col. 0037D] “Two years before.” From these words through “killed at Vienna,” the passage is copied from Orosius, VII, 40, 42.]

In his place Constantine, taken from the lowest ranks of the army, was chosen solely because of the hope inspired by his name and without any merit of character. As soon as he seized the imperial power, he crossed into Gaul. There he was repeatedly deceived by the barbarians through unreliable treaties and became more a burden than a benefit to the state. Therefore, soon afterward, at the command of Honorius, the general Constantius set out for Gaul with an army, shut him up in the city of Arles, captured him, and killed him. His son Constans, whom he had made Caesar after taking him from a monastery, was killed at Vienna by his own general, Gerontius.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] “Gratian.” Concerning him, those emperors, and the generals of this chapter, see Zosimus VI; Sozomen, IX, chapters 11–17; and Olympiodorus, in Photius, Codex 80.]

[Col. 0037C]

Rome was captured by the Goths in the 1064th year from its foundation [409], from which time the Romans ceased to rule in Britain, nearly 470 years after Gaius Julius Caesar had first reached the island. They lived within the rampart which, as we have stated, Severus built across the island, on its southern side. The cities, lighthouses, bridges, and roads constructed there still testify to this. The more distant parts of Britain, however, and even the islands beyond Britain, they possessed by right of dominion.

[Note: [Col. 0038C] “Ceased to rule.” This is true with respect to their former authority; but otherwise the Roman Empire again exerted its strength in Britain under Honorius and for some time also under Valentinian III.]

[Note: [Col. 0038C] “By right of dominion.” Alas, how many wounds on both sides were required to establish the succession of Roman rule, until in our own times the whole rivalry for empire yielded to universal obedience through the happy union of the inhabitants under the most august monarchy.]

## CHAPTER XII  
### How the Britons, ravaged by the Scots and Picts, sought aid from the Romans, who came a second time and built a wall across the island; but when this was immediately breached by the aforementioned enemies, the Britons were overwhelmed by a greater calamity

[Col. 0038B]

After this, Britain was stripped of all its armed forces, its entire military strength, and all the vigor of its flourishing youth. These forces had been taken away through the recklessness of the usurpers and never returned home. The island therefore lay open to plunder, being completely ignorant of every form of warfare. At last, when two fiercely savage peoples from across the sea suddenly attacked it—the Scots from the northwest and the Picts from the north—it was stunned and lamented for many years.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] “From across the sea.” Whatever may be said about the evidence of classical authors, I cannot doubt from this description that, according to Bede, the Scots at that time, together with the Picts and for many years previously, had established settlements north of the Straits, within the island properly called Britain.]

We call these peoples “from across the sea,” not because they were situated outside Britain, but because they were separated from the Britons by two sea-inlets lying between them—one breaking into the British lands from the eastern sea, the other from the western sea—far and wide, although they cannot meet one another. In the middle of the eastern inlet is the city of Giudi [or Guidi]. The western inlet has above it—that is, on its right—the city of Alcluith, which in their language means “the rock of the Clyde,” for it stands beside the river of that name.

[Note: [Col. 0038C] “In its middle.” I do not know why writers, including Buchanan himself, have sought the city of Giudi in the middle of the isthmus at the River Carron, or even toward the west, as others have done at Cairpentaloch, when in fact it was situated in the middle of the sea or eastern inlet, on the island of Inchkeith or Inchcolm. The western inlet, opposite it, has above it, on the right, Alcluith, or Dumbarton.]

Because of the attacks of these peoples, the Britons sent envoys to Rome with letters [414] and begged for assistance in tearful prayers. They promised continual submission, provided only that the threatening enemy might be kept at a greater distance. A legion was soon sent to them under arms. When it had been transported to the island and engaged the enemy, it slaughtered a great number of them and drove the remainder from the territory of the allies. Having meanwhile freed the Britons from their cruel oppression, the legion urged them to build a wall across the island between the two seas, so that it might serve as a defense against the enemy. It then returned home in great triumph.

The islanders built the wall they had been ordered to build, not so much with stones as with turf, since they had no craftsman capable of such a great work, and erected it without any usefulness. They constructed it for many miles between the two straits or inlets of the sea mentioned above, so that where the protection of water was lacking, the defense of the rampart might guard their borders against enemy invasion. The remains of this work, that is, of the very broad and lofty rampart, may still be seen there with complete certainty.

It begins about two miles from the monastery of Abercorn, toward the west, at a place called Peanfahel in the language of the Picts and Penneltun in the language of the English, and, extending westward, ends near the city of Alcluith.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] “Abercorn.” The name of this place still remains at the mouth of the River Carron, but no monastery remains. It was the see of Trumwine, bishop of the Picts, concerning whom see Bede IV, 12, 26.]

[Note: [Col. 0039D] “Peanfahel.” In English, Penneltun; from its sound one might suppose Vindovalam. Nennius calls it Cenail in Scottish, chapter 19, and even today it is called Kenneil with slight variation.]

But when the former enemies saw that the Roman soldiers had departed, they immediately arrived in ships, invaded the territory, slaughtered everything, and, like a ripe field of grain, reaped, trampled, and passed over everything that lay before them. Therefore envoys were again sent to Rome [416], imploring aid in a voice of lamentation, lest their wretched homeland be utterly destroyed and the name of the Roman province, which had long been glorious among them, be buried beneath the wickedness of foreign peoples and become contemptible.

A legion was sent again. Arriving unexpectedly in the autumn, it inflicted great slaughter on the enemy and drove across the seas all who were able to escape—those who had previously been accustomed to gather their annual plunder from across the sea without any soldier opposing them. Then the Romans declared to the Britons that they could no longer exhaust themselves in such laborious expeditions for their defense. Rather, they urged the Britons themselves to take up arms and undertake the struggle against the enemy, who could be stronger than them for no other reason than that the Britons themselves were weakened by indolence.

Moreover, because they thought that this too would bring some advantage to the allies whom they were compelled to abandon, they built a wall of solid stone from sea to sea in a straight line, between the cities which had been established there out of fear of the enemy, where Severus had once built a rampart. This wall, famous and conspicuous to the present day, they constructed at public and private expense, with a body of Britons [or Romans] working alongside them. It was eight feet wide and twelve feet high, running in a straight line from east to west, as is clear to those who look upon it even today.

When it had been completed, they gave the sluggish people strong warnings and provided models for the preparation of weapons. They also placed towers at intervals along the southern shore of the Ocean, where their ships were kept, because an invasion of barbarians was feared from that direction as well, so that the sea might be watched. Then they bade farewell to their allies as though they would never return.

When the Romans had gone back to their own country, the Scots and Picts, learning that their return had been refused, immediately came back themselves. Growing more confident than usual, they seized the whole northern and farthest part of the island as though it belonged to its native inhabitants, right up to the wall.

At this, a feeble army was stationed on high ground, where it languished day and night in terror and stupefaction. Meanwhile the enemies’ hooked weapons did not cease; the cowardly defenders were dragged most miserably from the walls and dashed to the ground. What more need be said? They abandoned the cities and the wall and fled [or were scattered]. The enemy pursued them, and the slaughter became more cruel than before. Just as lambs are torn apart by wild beasts, so the wretched citizens were torn apart by their enemies. Driven from their dwellings and little possessions, they moderated the famine threatening them by mutual robbery and plunder, increasing foreign calamities through domestic violence, until the whole region was deprived of every means of food except the solace of hunting.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### How, while the younger Theodosius was reigning, Palladius was sent to the Scots who believed in Christ, and the Britons, seeking assistance from the consul Aetius, failed to obtain it

[Col. 0040D]

In the year 423 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Theodosius the Younger, forty-fifth from Augustus, assumed the kingdom after Honorius and held it for twenty-six years. In the eighth year of his reign, Palladius was sent by Celestine, pontiff of the Roman Church, as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ [430].

[Note: [Col. 0039D] “He held it for twenty-six years.” Thus in the Treves manuscript and the Cambridge manuscript, correctly. The printed editions falsely read “twenty-seven years.” Honorius died in the year of Christ 423, on 15 August, as Theophanes observes; Theodosius died in 450, on 28 July. Therefore it cannot be said that Theodosius the Younger ruled for twenty-seven years after Honorius, since according to the dates just given he did not complete even the twenty-sixth full year of his reign.]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] “In the eighth.” Baronius, under the year 429, VII, says that Bede should be corrected from Prosper, since Bede says that Palladius was sent by Celestine, bishop of Rome, in the eighth year of the reign of Theodosius the Younger, whereas Celestine’s pontificate occurred eight years later, namely in the sixteenth year of the same Theodosius. The error of Baronius, which I noted above in the Chronicle concerning the years of Honorius, recurs here concerning the years of Theodosius. Bede rightly counts the years during which Theodosius reigned before Honorius’s death as belonging to Honorius. Accordingly, it is not Bede who should be corrected from Prosper, but Baronius from Bede.]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] “Believing … first.” These words are found in the most ancient manuscripts of Bede and admit no suspicion of alteration, just as there can be no doubt that the Scots, wherever they were, had received the Christian faith, at least in part, when Palladius was sent to them. See also the Chronicle under number 4403.]

In the twenty-third year of his reign, Aetius, an illustrious man who had also been a patrician, held the consulship for the third time with Symmachus. The impoverished remnant of the Britons sent him a letter [445], whose opening is: “To Aetius, consul for the third time: the groans of the Britons.” In the course of the letter they explained their calamities as follows:

> The barbarians drive us toward the sea; the sea drives us back toward the barbarians. Between them arise two kinds of death: either we are slaughtered, or we are drowned.

Nevertheless, even by these actions they could obtain no aid from him, since at that time he was occupied in the most serious wars against Blaedla [Bleda] and Attila, kings of the Huns. Although, in the preceding year, Bleda had been killed by the treachery of his brother Attila, Attila himself remained such an intolerable enemy of the state that he ravaged almost the whole of Europe, destroying and invading its cities and forts.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] “In the course of the letter.” Polydore Vergil, I do not know from what source, gives the letter in full, but without the authority of any manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] “Famine.” These are the words of Marcellinus Comes under the consulates of Aetius III and Symmachus, indiction 14, and under the consulates of Ardabur and Callep(i)us, indiction 15. Bede applies them to the Britons from Gildas’s satire in the following chapter.]

Indeed, at the same time famine invaded Constantinople. Pestilence followed without delay. Moreover, many of the walls of that city collapsed, together with fifty-seven towers. When many cities also had fallen, famine and the pestilential stench of the air destroyed many thousands of human beings and animals.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### How the Britons, compelled by a notorious famine, drove the barbarians from their territory; and how abundance of grain, luxury, pestilence, and the destruction of the people followed without delay

[Col. 0041C]

Meanwhile, the aforementioned famine afflicted the Britons more and more [446], leaving their descendants an enduring report of their wickedness. It compelled many of them to surrender to the hostile raiders, while others never did so; rather, trusting in divine aid when human help failed, they continually rebelled from the mountains, caves, and wooded places. Then for the first time they began to inflict slaughter on the enemies who had been plundering the land for many years.

Thus the shameless Irish raiders returned home [or returned to their homes], although they were to come back again after a short time. The Picts, in the farthest part of the island, then for the first time and thereafter remained quiet; nevertheless, from that time onward they did not cease occasionally to carry off plunder and inflict devastation upon the Britons.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] “The Irish.” The precision of the name is certainly worth noting here. He calls the Scots who repeatedly returned from Ireland to the Britons, in alliance with the Albanians, “Irish”; but he includes under the Picts those who remained with the Picts in the farthest part of the island, although they too did not cease to carry out raids.]

When the hostile devastation ceased, the island began to abound in such an abundance of grain as no former age remembered. Along with it, luxury grew, and this was immediately and rapidly accompanied by every plague of vices, especially cruelty, hatred of truth, and love of falsehood. Thus, if any one of them appeared gentler and somewhat closer to the truth, all their hatred and weapons were hurled without restraint against him as though he were the destroyer of Britain.

These things were done not only by secular men but also by the very flock of the Lord and its shepherds, who subjected their necks to drunkenness, anger, quarrels, contention, envy, and other crimes of this kind, casting aside Christ’s easy yoke.

Meanwhile, a bitter pestilence suddenly seized people of corrupt minds. In a short time it struck down such a multitude of them that the living were not even sufficient to bury the dead. Yet neither the death of their own people nor the fear of death could recall those who survived from the death of the soul into which they were being struck down by sin. Therefore, not long afterward, a sharper vengeance for dreadful wickedness followed the sinful people.

A council was therefore held to decide what should be done and where protection should be sought to avoid or repel the savage and very frequent invasions of the northern peoples. It pleased everyone, together with their king Vortigern, to summon the Saxon people from across the sea for assistance. It is clear that this was arranged by the will of the Lord, so that evil might come against the wicked, as the outcome of events more clearly proved.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] “Abundance, luxury, pestilence.” Chiffl. alone reads “abundance, pestilence.”]

## CHAPTER XV  
### How the people of the Angles, invited into Britain, first drove their adversaries far away, but soon afterward, having made a treaty with them, turned their weapons against their allies

[Col. 0042C]

In the year 449 from the Incarnation of the Lord [or 409], Marcian, having obtained the kingdom with Valentinian, forty-sixth from Augustus, held it for seven years.

At that time the people of the Angles, or Saxons, summoned by the aforementioned king, came to Britain in three longships. The same king granted them a place to settle in the eastern part of the island, as though they were going to fight for their homeland, but in reality to conquer the island.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] “In the eastern part.” Ethelwerd and the Saxon Annals, under the year 449, say that Hengist and Horsa were brought to a place commonly called Hypwinesfleot, now believed to be Ebbsfleet on the Isle of Thanet. Nennius, chapter 28, says that the king granted them that island as a place in which to remain; William of Malmesbury follows him.]

They engaged in battle with the enemies who had come from the north to meet them and the Saxons won the victory.

When this was reported at home, together with the fertility of the island and the sluggishness of the Britons, a longer fleet carrying a stronger force was immediately sent there. It joined the contingent previously sent and made the army invincible.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “A stronger force.” Five thousand men, transported in eighteen keels.]

Those who had arrived received a place of settlement among the Britons, who granted it on the condition that the newcomers would fight for the peace and safety of the homeland against its enemies, while the Britons would provide the soldiers’ proper pay.

They had come from the three stronger peoples of Germany, namely the Saxons, Angles, and Jutes [or Vites].

The Cantware and the Victuarii [or Vectuarii] originate from the Jutes: that is, the people who occupy the Isle of Wight, and the people who are still called the nation of the Jutes in the province of the West Saxons, situated opposite the island itself.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “Of the Jutes.” In these names the ancient names of the Getae and Goths remain, despite all the efforts of copyists who prefer “Vites.” Their homeland also remains well known as Jutland, a province of the Danish kingdom.]

From the Saxons—that is, from the region now called that of the Old Saxons—came the East Saxons, South Saxons, and West Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “Of the Old Saxons.” In Bede’s time, Ealdsexe included Holstein properly so called, Dithmarschen, Stormarn, and Wagria on the Cimbric Peninsula.]

From the Angles—that is, from the homeland called Angulus, which from that time until today is said to have remained deserted between the provinces of the Jutes and the Saxons—came the East Angles, Middle Angles, Mercians, the entire race of the Northumbrians, that is, the peoples living north of the River Humber, and the other peoples of the Angles.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “The Angles.” Old Anglia, still called Angeln, lies between the Saxons and the Jutes. Its chief town is called Schleswig in the Saxon language, but Haithabu among the Danes. ETHELWERD, book I.]

Their first leaders are said to have been two brothers, Hengist and Horsa [or Hengistus and Horsus]. Horsa was later killed in battle by the Britons, and to this day he has a monument bearing his name in the eastern parts of Kent.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “A monument.” The battlefield was at Aeglesthrep, and the monument was in the village of Horsted.]

They were sons of Wictgils, whose father was Witta, whose father was Wecta, whose father was Woden, from whose stock the royal lineage of many provinces derived its origin.

[Note: [Col. 0043C] An alternative reads: “They were the sons of Wictgils, whose father was Wecta.”]

Thereafter, as the bands of the peoples mentioned above flocked competitively into the island, the population of the newcomers began to grow, until they became a terror even to the natives who had summoned them.

Then, after briefly making a treaty with the Picts whom they had already driven farther away by warfare, they began to turn their weapons against their allies. First, they compelled the Britons to supply them more generously with provisions. Seeking an opportunity for separation, they declared that unless a more abundant supply of food were given them, they would break the treaty and lay waste to every part of the island.

Nor did they ever fail to follow up their threats with actions. To speak briefly, the fire kindled by pagan hands exacted God’s just vengeance for the crimes of the people, like that fire which was once kindled by the Chaldeans and consumed the walls of Jerusalem—indeed, all its buildings.

So here too, while the wicked conqueror acted—or rather while the just Judge ordained it—the fire continued its course without anyone opposing it, ravaging the nearest cities and fields from the eastern sea to the western sea, and covering almost the whole surface of the dying island.

Public and private buildings alike collapsed. Priests were slaughtered everywhere before the altars; bishops and peoples were consumed together by sword and flames, without regard for rank; and there was no one to bury those cruelly killed.

Thus some of the wretched survivors, captured in the mountains, were slaughtered in heaps. Others, exhausted by hunger, came forward and surrendered to the enemy, about to undergo perpetual servitude in exchange for food—if indeed they were not immediately slaughtered. Others sorrowfully sought regions across the sea. Others remained in their homeland and, trembling, led an impoverished life in mountains, forests, or steep crags, always living in fear.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### How the Britons won their first victory over the people of the Angles under the leadership of Ambrosius, a Roman

[Col. 0044C]

But when the hostile army, having exterminated and scattered the native inhabitants of the island, returned home, the Britons gradually began to regain their strength and courage. Emerging from the hiding places in which they had concealed themselves, they prayed with unanimous agreement for heavenly aid, lest they be utterly destroyed everywhere to the point of annihilation.

At that time they were led by Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man [466], who alone perhaps of the Roman people had survived that calamity; his parents, who bore the royal name and insignia, had been killed in it.

Under this leader the Britons recovered their strength. Challenging the victors to battle, they themselves, with God’s favor, gained the victory. From that time onward they prevailed, sometimes over their fellow citizens and sometimes over their enemies, until the year of the siege of Mount Badon [492], when they inflicted no small slaughter on those same enemies, approximately forty-four years after their arrival in Britain. But this will be discussed later.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “Ambrosius.” Bede places this Ambrosius in the Chronicle under Zeno. Consequently, some observers, noting that the Roman Empire was then suffering from problems of succession, have reported that Ambrosius was raised to the imperial purple. But the things we read about him, his parents, and his deeds, with which the History is filled for thirty-two years, I judge to be either wholly fabulous or at least uncertain. The book On the Victory of Aurelius Ambrosius, mentioned by Geoffrey of Monmouth, II, 1, has either completely perished or was never seen.]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] “Now citizens, now enemies.” Concerning the various battles of those times, see the Saxon Chronicle from the year 455 to 597 on the one side, and Nennius from chapter 35 on the other. There one may briefly see whatever other writers have left in differing forms on both sides.]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] “Mount Badon.” Polydore Vergil places this site at Blacamore in the region of York, contrary to the evidence of all who agree on the city of Bath or Bannesdown.]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] “Approximately the forty-fourth.” Gildas’s words are: “And the forty-fourth year, as I know, is beginning”; another reading is “is arising,” and another, “the first month, or first, having elapsed”; he also says that this was the year of his birth. When these points are considered, the number of years given by Gildas seems to concern the time of his writing rather than the arrival of the Saxons—namely, that Gildas wrote in the forty-fourth year after the battle of Badon, a year especially notable to him and also the year of his birth. If this interpretation is correct, it will give us a different chronology for this period. See Usserius, under the year 520.]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### How Bishop Germanus, sailing to Britain with Lupus, calmed first the storm of the sea and afterward that of the Pelagians by divine power

[Col. 0045C]

[Note: [Col. 0043D] Chapter XVII. The five chapters following, through chapter 22, are taken from Constantius, a presbyter of Lyons, who wrote the Life of Saint Germanus. See Surius, under 31 July, and the manuscript in the Cotton Library.]

[Additional textual apparatus: At the account of Maximus, one alternative reads “where” for “there,” and another adds “and” before “captured.” The date in Chapter X has the alternative 397; *Britto* has the forms *Brito*, *Breito*, and *Bruto*; and the final poetic line alternatively reads *huic tument* (“for this one the hearts swell”). In Chapter XI, *farus* (“lighthouses”) has the alternatives *fana* (“shrines”) and *fores* (“doors”). The Chapter XII heading alternatively has “they, being interrupted” for “when this was interrupted”; its opening alternatively reads “Britain as a whole”; *sinibus maris* (“sea-inlets”) alternatively reads *finibus mari*; and “Peanfahet” is the Pictish form. The old manuscripts read “when it had been brought to the island” for “when it had been brought into the island.” One reading adds “with no soldier opposing them”; another has “we have seen to this day” for “famous and conspicuous to the present day”; and *instituendorum armorum* (“of weapons to be provided/trained for”) alternatively reads *instruendorum armorum* (“of weapons to be equipped”). *Aquilonalem* (“northern”) alternatively reads *Aquilonarem*, and *die* (“by day”) alternatively *diu* (“for a long time”).

In Chapter XIII, Aetius is alternatively named Boetius; Blaedla has the forms *Bledda* and *Bleda*; and *plura* (“many [thousands]”) alternatively reads *plurima* (“very many [thousands]”). The Chapter XIV heading alternatively omits *famosa* (“notorious”); *fames sua* (“the famine aforesaid”) has the alternatives *fames illa* (“that famine”) and *fames*; *impudentes* (“shameless”) alternatively reads *imprudentes* (“unwary”); *domus* (“home”) alternatively *domum* (“to home”); *quantas* alternatively *quantis*; and *Aquilonalium* (“northern [peoples]”) alternatively *Aquilonariarum*.

The Chapter XV heading alternatively adds “into” before Britain and reads “compelled [them] to go away” for “drove [them] far away.” The date has the alternative 409. *Jutis* (“Jutes”) alternatively reads *Vitis*, and *Jutarum* (“of the Jutes”) *Vitarum*; *Victuarii* alternatively reads *vectuarii*. Chifflet alone reads “East Angles, Mercians” in place of “East Angles, Middle Angles, Mercians.” *Immo* (“indeed”) alternatively reads *imo et* (“indeed, and”); and *acervatim* (“in heaps”) alternatively *catervatim* (“in bands”). In Chapter XVI, *unanimo consensu* (“with unanimous accord”) alternatively reads *unanimi consensu* (“with united accord”).]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] “A few years earlier.” Bede does not say how many years before the arrival of the Saxons Saint Germanus came to Britain. Prosper dates his arrival to 429 and adds another connected entry under 432, namely, Palladius’s arrival in Scotland. Bede records both events in the History: Palladius under 430 or 431, in Prosper’s very words; Germanus in this passage, using Prosper’s words concerning the reason for his arrival, but otherwise following Constantius, a contemporary author of the highest reputation who wrote the saint’s Life as his specific subject. Yet the discrepancy between this calculation based on Prosper and the dates assigned by Constantius—and followed by Bede—is so great that it is difficult to decide which authority to follow. “A few years earlier” is indefinite and could be extended to include Prosper’s dates among the years of Saint Germanus, were it not for Caelestine, whose dates are too far removed from this calculation.]

Certainly, a few years before their arrival, the Pelagian heresy, introduced through Agricola, [Note: [Col. 0045D] “Agricola, son of Severianus.” Little is known with certainty about Agricola and Severianus. Nearly everyone, against Bale, has concluded that Agricola was not Leporius and that Severianus was not Sulpitius Severus.] the son of Bishop Severianus, had polluted the faith of the Britons with its foul plague. But since the Britons were unwilling either to accept the perverse doctrine by blaspheming the grace of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0046C] “Nor were they sufficient …” Although the Pelagian heresy derived from a Briton, it spread in distant regions and left its homeland enveloped in the fortunate ignorance of error.] or to refute the cunning of its wicked persuasion by contending in argument, they found a salutary plan: to seek from the Gallican bishops assistance in the spiritual conflict. For this reason, a great synod was assembled [Note: [Col. 0046C] “A great synod.” Prosper says that, at the urging of the deacon Palladius, Pope Caelestine sent Germanus in his place so that, after expelling the heretics, he might guide the Britons back to the Catholic faith. Prosper himself confirms this again in his work Against the Collator, chapter 41, a work less exposed to the ravages of time than his Chronicle. Nevertheless, it is certain that neither Bede nor Constantius mentions Caelestine in connection with Saint Germanus’s mission. Jacobus Sirmondus, therefore, inserting this council—which he calls of uncertain location—into his chronological series, does not place it with Prosper under 429, but with Sigebert under 446. Among other things he adds: “Since, in the common version of Prosper’s Chronicle, the embassy of Germanus is attached to the year 429, the suspicion of an interpolated error is not without foundation, apparently introduced by those who, having read that Palladius was sent by Pope Caelestine to those regions, believed that Germanus likewise had been dispatched by him to Britain—something reported neither by Bede, nor by Constantius, nor by Erricus, nor by any ancient writer.” Sirmondus’s Posthumous Notes, volume III of Labbe, p. 1508.] to deliberate jointly whom they ought to send there to succor the faith. By the unanimous judgment of all, the apostolic priests Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Of Auxerre.” Besides Constantius’s prose account, Erricus, a monk of Auxerre, wrote a Life of Saint Germanus in verse in six books, and also two books about his miracles.], and Lupus, Bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Of Troyes.” Troyes in the Gallic province of Champagne. See Lupus’s Life in Surius, under 29 July.], were chosen to come to the Britons to strengthen the faith of grace.

When they had received the prayers and commands of Holy Church with ready devotion, they entered the Ocean. As far as the middle of the journey from the Gallic gulf to Britain, the ship sped safely with favorable winds. Then suddenly a hostile force of demons confronted the travelers [Al.: the hostile force confronted them]. They envied such great and eminent men as they hastened [Al.: pressed on] to restore the salvation of the peoples [Al.: to the peoples]. They raised storms; they obscured the sky and daylight with the night of clouds; the sails could not withstand the fury of the winds; the sailors’ efforts, overcome, gave way; the vessel was carried forward by prayer, not by human strength. By chance the leader himself—or rather the bishop—was overcome in body and relaxed by weariness and sleep.

Then, as though the opponent had ceased resisting, the storm that had arisen grew stronger, and the vessel was already being submerged beneath the waves pouring over it. Blessed Lupus and all the others, terrified, roused the elder to confront the raging elements. More steadfast because of the enormity of the danger, he invoked Christ and, taking water in the name of the Holy [or Most Holy] Trinity, subdued the raging waves with a light sprinkling [or aspersion]. He admonished his companion and encouraged everyone. Prayer poured forth from a single mouth and cry. The Godhead was present; the enemies were put to flight; clear calm followed; and the winds, turning contrary, returned to serve the journey. After traversing the sea a short distance, they reached the desired shore in peace.

[Col. 0046B] There a multitude gathered from different regions to receive the priests, whose coming had also been foretold by an adverse prophecy. For evil spirits announced what they feared: when driven from possessed bodies by the priests’ command, they confessed both the sequence of the storm and the dangers they had caused, and did not deny that they had been defeated by the priests’ merits and authority.

Meanwhile, the apostolic priests rapidly filled the island of Britain with their reputation, preaching, and miracles. Through them the divine word was preached every day not only in churches but also at crossroads and throughout the countryside. Thus the Catholic faithful everywhere were strengthened, while the depraved recognized the path of correction. In them there were, as it were, the glory and authority of the apostles in their integrity of conscience, doctrine in their writings, and miraculous powers in their merits. Accordingly, the whole region readily adopted their judgment.

The authors of the sinister persuasion remained hidden away. Like wicked spirits, they groaned that the peoples were escaping them and perishing to their cause. At last, after long deliberation, they presumed to enter the conflict. They came forth conspicuous for their wealth, resplendent in clothing, and surrounded by the flattery of many. They preferred to undergo the danger of battle rather than incur, among the people whom they had subverted, the shame of silence, lest they appear to have condemned themselves by keeping quiet.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “There.” H. Boethius says that this assembly took place at London, book VIII. The Florilegus calls it a synod and says that it was held at Verulamium in 446. Some writers confuse this British assembly with the Gallican synod.]

There, indeed, an immense multitude had gathered, including wives and children. The people were present as spectators and future judges. The two sides stood opposed under unequal and dissimilar conditions: on the one side divine faith, on the other human presumption; on the one side piety, on the other pride; on the one side Pelagius the author, on the other Christ.

At first the most blessed priests gave their opponents an opportunity to argue. Their argument, consisting only of the nakedness of words, occupied ears and time for a long while to no purpose. Then the venerable bishops poured forth torrents of their eloquence together with apostolic and evangelical rains. [Note: [Col. 0047D] “They poured forth.” The place where Saint Germanus preached to the people is still shown, marked by a chapel consecrated in his name.] Their own discourse was mingled with the divine word, and the most vexatious assertions were followed by the testimony of the readings. [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Most vexatious.” Chifflet alone has “most moderate”; Constantius has “most violent,” which agrees in sense with “most vexatious.”] Their vanity was convicted and their perfidy refuted, so that at each objection raised against their words they confessed that they were in error, since they could not answer. The people, acting as judge, could scarcely restrain their hands, yet testified to their judgment by shouting.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How he restored sight to the blind daughter of a tribune and, afterward, reaching Saint Alban’s, received relics of Alban himself there and deposited relics of the blessed apostles and other martyrs

[Col. 0047C]

Then suddenly a man holding the authority of a tribune came forward with his wife, offering his ten-year-old blind daughter to the priests for healing. They instructed that she be offered to their opponents. But those men, deterred by the reproach of conscience, joined the parents in prayer and begged the priests to cure the little girl. Seeing their opponents humbled in spirit, the priests briefly offered prayer. Then Germanus, filled with the Holy Spirit, invoked the Trinity. Without delay, he seized with his hands the small reliquary hanging at his side, containing relics of the saints, and applied it before everyone to the girl’s eyes. Immediately, when the darkness had been driven away, the light of truth filled them.

The parents rejoiced, and the people trembled at the miracle. [Col. 0047D] After that day the wicked persuasion was so completely erased from everyone’s hearts that they followed the priests’ teaching with eager longing.

Thus, after the destructive perversity had been suppressed, its authors refuted, and everyone’s minds established in the purity of faith, the priests asked to visit the blessed martyr Alban, in order through him to give thanks to God. There Germanus, carrying with him relics of all the apostles and of various martyrs, offered a prayer and ordered the tomb to be opened, intending to deposit precious gifts there. [Note: [Col. 0048D] “The tomb … intending to deposit gifts.” See the Florilegus under 794 concerning their discovery and the devotion of the age toward what was found over them.] He judged it fitting that the members of saints gathered from different regions—those whom heaven had received as equals in merit [Note: [Col. 0048D] “Equals.” Chifflet alone has “equal.”]—should also share the hospitality of a single tomb.

After these relics had been honorably deposited and joined together, he removed from the very place where the blessed martyr’s blood had been shed a mass of dust, intending to carry it with him. [Note: [Col. 0048D] “To carry with him.” He built a basilica within the walls of Auxerre to house these relics and dedicated it in the name of Saint Alban. Erricus, book I, On the Miracles of Saint Alban. Concerning other relics of the saint claimed by monks at Mainz, Otto, and Cologne, let those who care for such disputes read elsewhere.] In it, the slaughter of the martyrs appeared to have reddened the dust, the blood having been preserved, while the persecutor grew pale. [Note: [Col. 0048D] “Of the martyrs.” The good manuscripts, though not the best, read “of the martyr.”] When these things had been accomplished, an innumerable multitude of people was converted to the Lord on that same day.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the same men, detained there because of illness, extinguished fires in houses by prayer, and how he himself was cured of his illness through a vision

As they were returning, the enemy who lays ambushes prepared traps of chance and, taking advantage of Germanus’s slipping, crushed his foot. He did not know that bodily affliction was advancing his merits, as in the case of the most blessed Job. Since Germanus was consequently detained for some time in one place by the necessity of his illness, a fire broke out in the nearby little house where he was staying. After consuming the houses there, which were covered with marsh reeds, the fire was driven by the bellows of the wind toward the dwelling in which he lay.

Everyone rushed together to the bishop, so that, with his hands raised, he might avert the danger that threatened. But he rebuked them and refused, through confidence in his faith, to allow himself to be moved. The whole multitude, terrified by despair, ran to meet the fire. Yet so that God’s power might appear more clearly, whatever the crowd tried to protect was consumed. But what the sick man had defended while lying there—the lodging of the holy man—was spared: the terrified flame leapt over it, raging on either side, and amid the masses of blazing fire the unharmed dwelling, guarded by the inhabitant enclosed within, emerged intact.

The crowd rejoiced at the miracle and congratulated itself that it had been defeated by divine powers. Day and night an innumerable common people kept watch before the poor man’s hut: some wishing to care for souls, others for bodies. The things Christ performed through his servant cannot be recounted—through one who worked miracles while ill.

Since he allowed no remedy to be applied to his weakness, one night he saw a figure in shining white garments standing beside him. The figure seemed to raise him from where he lay with an outstretched hand and ordered him to stand firm on his feet. After that moment, when the pains had been driven away, he recovered his former health so completely that, when day returned, he undertook the hardships of the journey without fear.

## CHAPTER XX. How the same bishops brought heavenly assistance to the Britons in battle and then returned home

Meanwhile, [Note: [Col. 0049C–D] “Saxons.” The presence of Saxons in Britain during Saint Germanus’s first visit has caused scholars no little difficulty. Some maintain that “Saxons” here stands for “Scots,” through an error in the manuscripts of Constantius and Bede; others seek the error in Prosper’s Chronicle, which they think should be corrected from Bede and Constantius; still others say that the Saxons came at that time not for permanent settlement but only on a military expedition, under an alliance made with the Picts. The first of these solutions is refuted by all the manuscripts; Prosper’s own explanation in Against the Collator overturns the second. The last has its difficulties, but also arguments which for the most part outweigh them.] the Saxons and Picts joined forces and undertook war against the Britons, whom the same necessity had drawn together into camp. When the Britons, trembling, judged their own forces almost unequal to the enemy’s, they sought the assistance of the holy bishops. The bishops hastened their promised arrival and inspired such confidence in those who were afraid that their coming was believed to signify the arrival of a vast army. Thus Christ fought in the camp under apostolic commanders.

The revered days of Lent were also at hand, made more devout by the presence of the priests. The people, instructed by daily preaching, rushed eagerly to the grace of baptism. A very large part of the army sought the waters of saving baptism, and a church was constructed of branches for the day of the Lord’s Resurrection and set up in the open field near the city. The army proceeded wet with baptism; faith burned among the people; and, with confidence in the protection of arms crushed [or broken off; another reading: “with the armed defense despised”], they awaited divine assistance.

The enemy was informed of the discipline—or the camp-arrangement—of chastity. They presumed that victory over an unarmed army would be easy and hastened forward with renewed eagerness. Their approach, however, was discovered by scouts.

When the Easter solemnity had passed, and the greater part of the army, newly risen from the bath, began to take up arms and attempt to prepare for battle, Germanus declared himself commander of the battle. [Note: [Col. 0049D] “Commander.” No one should think it inappropriate that Germanus led an army. Before becoming a bishop, he had administered the temporal command and government of the territory of Auxerre. The author of his Life says of this: “The warfare of the world is abandoned; heavenly warfare is assumed.”] He chose the swiftest men, traversed the surrounding area, and from the direction where the enemy was expected to come, observed a valley enclosed by mountains. There he formed a new army, himself the commander of the host.

The fierce multitude of the enemy was already at hand, and those lying in ambush watched it approach. Then suddenly Germanus, acting as standard-bearer, warned them all and proclaimed that they should answer his voice with one cry. While the enemy were secure in the belief that they had arrived unexpectedly, the priests shouted “Alleluia” three times. [Note: [Col. 0049D] “Alleluia.” Saint Gregory, in Job XXVII.6, has these words: “Behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to growl barbarously, has long since begun to resound with the Hebrew [Ebraeum] ‘Alleluia’ in divine praises.” Bede applied this to the conversion of the English, II.1, and after him John the Deacon did the same in the Life of Gregory, without observing that that book was written before the conversion of the English. Consequently, Gregory’s words refer to the battle in this chapter and to its Alleluia, especially since he says that it had already happened long ago.]

A single voice followed from everyone, and the raised cry, rebounding from the air and multiplied by the surrounding mountains, terrified the hostile army. The enemy seemed to feel not only the encircling cliffs collapsing upon them but even the structure of heaven itself trembling. They were so overcome with panic that the speed of their feet could scarcely save them. They fled everywhere, threw down their weapons, and rejoiced if they could rescue their bare bodies from danger. Many, falling headlong in terror, were swallowed by the river they had crossed. The innocent army watched the vengeance inflicted upon the enemy and became an idle spectator of the victory granted to it. The exposed spoils were gathered, and the devout soldier embraced the joys of the heavenly palm.

The bishops triumphed over the enemy’s defeat without bloodshed; they triumphed in a victory obtained through faith, not strength.

Thus, after the island had been secured by manifold safety, and after enemies both invisible and visible in the flesh had been overcome, the bishops prepared to return. Their own merits and the intercession of the blessed martyr Alban secured them a peaceful voyage, and a fortunate keel restored them safely to their homeland, to the longing of their people. [Note: [Col. 0050D] “Restored.” “Remained” is found in the common manuscripts: “Both kinds of people, enemies and citizens, English and Britons, remained on the island; the English fought for dominion, the Britons for life.” This clause, which follows in various readings, has no authority in any ancient manuscript. It nevertheless shows what was meant at the time when these words were added: namely, that during Saint Germanus’s first arrival the Saxons remained in Britain, fighting for mastery.]

## CHAPTER XXI. How, when the Pelagian plague was springing up again, Germanus returned to Britain with Severus; how he first restored walking to a lame young man and then restored the people of God to the path of faith, after condemning or correcting the heretics

[Note: [Col. 0050D] “Not long afterward.” These words also disturb Prosper’s chronology. If Germanus’s first arrival was in 429, either a considerable interval must be inserted before the second arrival, or more years must have elapsed during the second mission than can be reconciled with the events and history of Germanus, as becomes clear below.]

Not long afterward, news came from the same island that Pelagian perversity was again being spread by a few authors. Once more, the prayers of all the priests were brought to the most blessed man, asking him to defend the cause of God which he had previously upheld. He promptly complied with their request. Taking with him Severus, a man of complete holiness, who had been a disciple of the most blessed Father Lupus, Bishop of Troyes, and who had then been ordained bishop at Trier and was preaching the word [of God] to the peoples of First Germany, he boarded ship and, with the elements cooperating, sailed to Britain in a calm vessel.

Meanwhile, evil spirits flew throughout the whole island and announced by unwilling prophecies that Germanus was coming. So great was the effect that a certain Elafius, a leading man of that region, hastened to meet the saints without any report from a visible messenger. He brought with him his son, whom a grievous infirmity had condemned in the very flower of youth.

The boy’s sinews had withered, and his knee was contracted; because of the dryness of his leg, he could not use his foot to walk. The whole province followed Elafius. The priests arrived, and an uninformed multitude came to meet them. At once the blessing was given and the teaching of the divine word poured forth. They recognized that the people remained in the faith in which they had left them. They understood that the guilt belonged to a few, sought out the authors, and condemned them when they were found.

Suddenly Elafius fell at the priests’ feet, offering his son, whose need was proclaimed even without prayers by the infirmity itself. A common grief arose among all, especially among the priests, who entrusted the mercy they had conceived to divine compassion. At once blessed Germanus made the young man sit down. He touched the knee bent by infirmity, and his healing right hand passed over the whole extent of the disease. Health quickly followed the salutary touch: dryness received moisture, the sinews recovered their functions, and in the sight of all the son was restored to health and the father was restored his son.

The people were filled with amazement at the miracle, and Catholic faith was firmly implanted in every heart. The preaching then turned toward correction of the transgression.
