By the unanimous judgment of all, the authors of the depravity, who had been expelled from the island, were brought to the priests to be taken to the Continent, so that both the region might enjoy absolution and the heretics correction. As a result, undefiled faith continued in those places for a long time thereafter.

When everything had thus been set in order, the blessed priests returned with the same success with which they had come. Germanus, however, [Note: [Col. 0051C] “After this.” Constantius states that, after returning from Britain, Germanus soon undertook another journey to Arles, at the time when Auxiliaris was prefect of the Gauls. According to Sirmondus, Auxiliaris held the prefecture in 449 and the following years. Germanus then went immediately to Ravenna to appease Aetius, who was hostile to the Armoricans because they had rebelled; because of this crime, the unfortunate Alemanni were to be punished and avenged. While Germanus was at Ravenna, he died, and his possessions were distributed. It is worth noting in passing that the reliquary of relics fell by lot to Placidia, the emperor’s mother—and in it perhaps some blood-colored dust carried from Verulamium. It is entirely clear that Germanus returned from Britain a second time only during the final years of his life and, if Bede’s and Constantius’s chronology is rejected, after he had spent the greater part of his long episcopate in Britain. Readers of Nennius and our native historians would nevertheless be persuaded of this, unless they had transmitted so many absurdities about Saint Germanus and his conduct in Britain. In short, there are two chronologies for this great man’s British missions: Prosper’s, from 429 to 435, and Constantius’s and Bede’s, from approximately 446 to 453. Each has its own knots, and so far I have found no one equally capable of untying them.]

after this, came to Ravenna to plead for peace for the Armorican people. There he was received with the greatest reverence by Valentinian and his mother Placidia, and he departed to Christ. His body, accompanied in an honorable procession by the works of his virtue, was carried back to his own city. Not long afterward Valentinian was killed by the retainers of the patrician Aetius, whom he had himself killed, in the sixth year of Marcian’s reign; with Valentinian the Western Empire also fell.

## CHAPTER XXII. How, when foreigners had for a time ceased their attacks, the Britons wore themselves out in civil wars and likewise plunged themselves into greater crimes

[Note: [Col. 0052C] “Chapter XXII.” See Gildas, section 26. There he compressed much into a few words and brought the historical portion of his work to an end. From that point he proceeds to rebuke the kings, priests, and people of his own time. It was not necessary, therefore, for Bede to attribute further crimes to them, namely, their withholding of the Gospel. Yet I would not believe that Bede did so because he was a Saxon historian, as some maintain, for Gildas, a historian of the Britons, did not spare his own people in this matter. I would readily excuse the Britons for not preaching the Gospel to the hostile Saxons, but Bede alone did not note this neglect; Pope Gregory inquired about it not only with regard to the Britons but also the Gauls. Gildas’s work, On the Ruin of Britain, is sufficiently well known today. The author Gildas is generally overlooked, being obscured by an excessive proliferation of distinctions. Hence so many surnames—Albanius, the Wise, Badonicus, the Historian—although in truth there is one and the same Gildas, whose age is given above, chapter 16, in the history covering a large part of Bede’s work up to this point.]

Meanwhile, Britain had indeed been free for a short time from external enemies, but not from civil wars. The ruins of cities destroyed and deserted by the enemy remained; citizens who had escaped the enemy fought one another. Nevertheless, while the memory of the disaster and calamity inflicted was still fresh, the kings, priests, common people, and nobles still preserved, in some fashion, each their proper order.

But when they died and a generation succeeded that knew nothing of that time of calamity, having experienced only the condition of the present serenity, all restraints of truth and justice were so shaken and overturned that not merely a trace but not even a memory of them appeared anywhere except among a very few—indeed, among exceedingly few.

Among the other indescribable crimes which their historian Gildas describes in mournful language, they added this: they never entrusted the word of faith by preaching it to the Saxon or English people who inhabited Britain alongside them. Yet divine mercy did not abandon the people whom it had foreknown. Rather, it sent to that nation preachers of the truth far more worthy, through whom it might believe.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How Saint Pope Gregory, sending Augustine with monks to preach to the English, also strengthened them with an exhortatory letter so that they would not cease from their labor

[Col. 0052C]

In the year 582 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Maurice, the fifty-fourth emperor from Augustus, assumed the imperial power and held it for twenty-one years. In the tenth year of his reign [592], Gregory, a man distinguished in learning and action, having obtained the pontificate of the Roman and apostolic see, governed it for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. Moved by divine prompting, in the fourteenth year of that emperor, approximately the one hundred and fiftieth year after the arrival of the English in Britain, he sent the servant of God Augustine, together with several other monks who feared the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0053C] “Several.” See chapter 25 below.] to preach the word of God to the English people.

When they had begun to undertake the work they had been commanded by the bishop, and had already completed part of the journey, [Note: [Col. 0053C] “A little.” From Gregory’s letters to Stephen, abbot of Lérins; Prothasius, Bishop of Aix; and the patrician Arigius, it can be inferred that Augustine’s companions settled in Provence, not far from the island of Lérins.] they were struck by an inactive fear and considered returning home preferable to approaching a barbarous, savage, and unbelieving people whose language they did not even know. By common agreement they decided that this would be safer.

Without delay they sent Augustine, whom Gregory had arranged to have ordained bishop if the English received them, back home to obtain from blessed Gregory, by humble entreaty, permission for them not to undertake such a dangerous, laborious, and uncertain pilgrimage. He sent them an exhortatory letter, urging them to proceed with the work of the word while trusting in divine assistance. [Note: [Col. 0053C] “Letters.” For a collection of the letters Gregory wrote concerning this mission, together with the course of this British journey, see the appendix, no. 6.] Its wording was as follows:

> Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord.
>
> “Since it would have been better not to begin a good work than to turn back in thought from what has been begun, you must, dearest sons, apply the greatest zeal to completing the good work which, with the Lord’s help, you have begun. Therefore let neither the labor of the journey nor the tongues of evil-speaking men deter you. With all persistence and fervor, carry through what you have begun, with God as your guide, knowing that a great labor is followed by a greater glory of eternal reward.
>
> “As for Augustine, your superior, whom we have also appointed your abbot, when he returns, obey him humbly in all things, knowing that whatever you complete at his instruction will be wholly profitable to your souls. May Almighty God protect you by his grace and grant me to see the fruit of your labor in my eternal homeland, so that, although I cannot labor with you, I may nevertheless be found together with you in the joy of reward, since I desire to labor. May God keep you safe, dearest sons. [Note: [Col. 0053D] “Given.” Baronius attacks Bede here without justification concerning the years of Maurice: he both used a corrupt manuscript and was deceived in calculating the beginning of Maurice’s reign. In place of the year after Maurice’s thirteenth consulship, which Bede’s genuine manuscripts provide, he read the fourteenth year from a corrupt manuscript. He then made Maurice’s fourteenth year his eleventh, assigning or rather omitting Maurice’s first years too late.] Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, was emperor, in the fourteenth year, after the consulship of the same lord of ours in the thirteenth year, in the fourteenth indiction.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. How he sent a letter to the Bishop of Arles on their reception

At that time the same venerable bishop also sent to Etherius, Bishop of Arles [616], [Note: [Col. 0053D] “To Etherius of Arles.” It is generally assumed that there is an error here, Etherius being written in place of Virgilius, since Etherius was Bishop of Lyon at that time. But whether the error lies there is very doubtful. First, the letter found in Bede addressed to Etherius of Arles is not found under that title in Gregory’s Register. The Register contains another letter to Virgilius of Arles, of the same substance but in a different form. I therefore conclude that the error is more likely in the letter than in the name. When Augustine departed, Gregory wrote several letters on the same day. Their originals lay together in the apostolic archive, and Nothelmus copied them. Why could he not have taken one for another and brought to Bede the letter written to Etherius of Lyon in place of the one written to Virgilius of Arles, the names and titles having been transposed through a copying error? SMITH.—“To Etherius of Arles.” Rather, to Aetherius of Lyon, as Sirmondus aptly asserts in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, in the note to p. 420. Aetherius presided over Lyon from 589 to 602, as can be gathered from the acts of the councils and from the letters of the Roman pontiffs. This letter of Gregory the Great was given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth indiction, and therefore in 596. A duplicate of it is found in book VI of the Register, letter 52, addressed “To Palladius, bishop of Saintes; Pelagius, of Tours; and Serenus, of Marseille, bishops of Gaul, from their peers” (see Migne, Patrologia, volume LXXXVII, column 836). It therefore appears to have been a circular letter of recommendation. Bede seems to have been led into this error about Aetherius’s see by the presbyter Nothelmus, from whom Bede himself states in the preface to his History, addressed to King Ceolwulf, that he received and obtained this and other letters concerning England from the archive of the Roman Church. CHIFFLET.] that he might receive Augustine, who was traveling to Britain, kindly. He sent a letter whose text was as follows:

> “To the most reverend and most holy brother Etherius, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “Although religious men who possess a love pleasing to God need no recommendation from anyone, nevertheless, since a suitable occasion for writing has arisen, we have taken care to send our letter to your Fraternity. We inform you that we have sent there [or thither], with the help of the Lord and for the benefit of souls, the bearers of this letter: Augustine, the servant of God, whose zeal we know to be reliable, together with other servants of God. Your holiness must hasten to assist him with priestly zeal and provide him with your support.
>
> “So that you may be more ready to offer him assistance, we have thought it necessary to explain the matter to you carefully, knowing that, once you have learned it, you will devote yourself entirely, for God’s sake, to supporting him as the matter requires. We also commend to your charity in all things Candidus, a presbyter and our common son, whom we have sent to administer a small patrimony of our Church. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, was emperor, in the fourteenth year, after the consulship of the same lord of ours in the thirteenth year, in the fourteenth indiction.”

## CHAPTER XXV. How Augustine, coming to Britain, first preached to the king of the people of Kent on the island of Thanet and, having received permission from him, entered Kent to preach

[Col. 0055A]

Textual apparatus not otherwise reflected above:

- In the council passage: *illic* (“there”) has the alternative *illuc* (“thither”); *electi sunt* (“were chosen”) has *eligebantur* (“were being chosen”); *Trecasenae* has the spelling *Trecassinae*; and “to the Britons” (*Brittanias*) has the singular *Brittaniam* (“to Britain”).
- In the sea voyage: “Holy Trinity” has *sanctissimae* (“Most Holy”); “sprinkling” (*spargine*) has *aspergine* (“aspersion”); and “the divine word” has the addition *et* (“and”).
- In the assembly: “gathered” (*excita*) has *excitata*; “spectator and future judge” has the alternative reading “and one who will be a spectator and … is awaited” (*et spectator futurus et … expectatur*); “the most blessed priests” has the addition “Germanus and Lupus”; and *molestissimas* (“most troublesome/vexatious”) is replaced in Chifflet alone by *modestissimas* (“most moderate”), while Constantius reads *violentissimas* (“most violent”).
- In Chapter XVIII: *acturi* (“about to give thanks”) has *auctori* (“to the author”), with another reading adding *acturi*; *pares* (“equal [in merit]”) has *paribus* (“as equals”); and the text’s “slaughter of the martyrs” has the singular reading “of the martyr” in good, though not the best, manuscripts.
- In Chapter XIX: “the lodging … was opened” (*reserato hospitio*) has *reservato hospitio* (“the lodging … was preserved”).
- In Chapter XX: “the protection of arms crushed” has *contrito* (“broken”) or *contempto armatorum praesidio* (“the defence of armed men despised”); “attempted” has the addition *et*; “declared himself” has the subjunctive *profiteretur*; “Alleluia” has the lower-case form *alleluia* and *repetitum* in place of *repetitam*; “raised cry” has *elevatum*; the enemy “seemed to feel” has an addition *ruisse* (“to have fallen”); and “the river which they had crossed” has the reading *mensi erant* (“they had measured/crossed”).
- In Chapter XXI: “Not long afterward” has the addition *post* (“after”); “defend” (*tutaretur*) has *tueretur*; “the word” has the addition *Dei* (“of God”); “flew about” (*pervolantes*) has *provolantes* (“rushed forth”); “to meet” (*occursu*) has *occursum*; and “in which he had left them” has the plural *reliquerant*.
- In Chapter XXII: *Brittania* has *Brittaniae*; *praeter* (“except”) has *praeterquam*; “Gildus” has *Gildas*; and “they added” has the singular *addebat* (“he added”).
- In Chapter XXIII: “twenty-one years” has the alternate order *uno et viginti*; and *aliquantulum* (“a little”) has *aliquantum*.
- In Chapter XXIV: “bishop” has *archbishop*; “there” (*illic*) has *illuc* (“thither”); and *patrimonioli* (“a small patrimony”) has *patrimoniali* (“patrimonial”).

Strengthened, therefore, by the confirmation of the blessed Father Gregory, Augustine returned with the servants of Christ who were with him to the work of preaching, and reached Britain [597]. At that time Aedilberct was the most powerful king in Kent; he had extended the boundaries of his dominion as far as the great River Humber, by which the southern and northern peoples of the English are divided.

On the eastern side of Kent there is the fairly large island of Thanet—that is, according to the customary English reckoning of its size, [Note: “families,” that is, hides or carucates. A portion of land consisting of approximately one hundred acres, whose cultivation is sufficient to support a household.] six hundred households. It is separated from the mainland by the River Wantsum, which is about three stadia wide and fordable in only two places, for each of its extremities stretches out into the sea. It was there, then, that the servant of the Lord Augustine and his companions—nearly forty men, as they say—landed.

By the command of the blessed Pope Gregory they had taken interpreters from the Frankish people. Sending a message to Aedilberct, they announced that they had come from Rome and were bringing a most excellent message: to those who obeyed it, they promised, without any doubt, eternal joys in heaven and a kingdom without end with the living and true God.

When the king heard this, he ordered them to remain on the island to which they had come and to be supplied with whatever they needed until he could determine what to do with them. For news of the Christian religion had already reached him, since he had a Christian wife from the Frankish royal family, named Bercta [Note: Bercta. She was the daughter of Charibert, king of the Franks, and granddaughter of Clotarius I.] [variant: named Berctam]. He had received her from her parents on the condition that he should be permitted to preserve inviolate the practice of her faith and religion, together with the bishop whom they had given her as an assistant in the faith, named Liudhard [Note: Liudhard. A bishop of Silvanectum in Gaul, according to Thomas Sprott, author of the *History of the Monastery of Saint Augustine of Canterbury*, and, following him, William Thorn in his *Chronicle*, chapter 2, although no mention of him occurs among the bishops of Silvanectum in the works of the Sanmarthani. Concerning him, see Henschenius, under 24 February.]

After some days [variant: after several days] the king came to the island and, sitting in the open air, ordered Augustine and his companions to come there to meet with him. He had taken care that they should not enter any house to meet him, following an old superstition lest, if they possessed some kind of magical art, their arrival should enable them to deceive and overcome him.

But they came endowed not with demonic power, but with divine power, carrying a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord and Savior painted on a panel [Col. 0055D]. Singing litanies, they entreated the Lord for their own eternal salvation and for that of those on whose account and to whom they had come.

When, at the king’s command, they had taken their seats and were preaching to him the word of life, together with all his companions who were present, he replied:

> “The words and promises that you bring are certainly beautiful; but because they are new and uncertain, I cannot assent to them, abandoning what I have preserved for so long a time together with the whole English people. Yet because you have come here as foreigners from a distant land and, as far as I can see, have desired to share with us what you believed to be true and excellent, we do not wish to be troublesome to you. Rather, we intend to receive you hospitably and to provide whatever is necessary for your sustenance. Nor do we forbid you to join to your faith, by preaching, all whom you are able to persuade.”

[Note: He gave them a residence. According to W. Thorn, it was in that part of the city called Stablegate.]

Accordingly, he gave them a residence in the city of Doruvernum, which was the capital of his entire kingdom, and, as he had promised, together with the provision of temporal sustenance he also granted them permission to preach.

It is reported that, as they approached the city, they sang this litany in unison, according to their custom, carrying the holy cross and the image of the great King, our Lord Jesus Christ:

> “We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned. Alleluia.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. How he likewise imitated the teaching and life of the primitive Church in Kent, and received the episcopal see in the king’s city

When they had entered the residence granted to them, they began to imitate the apostolic life of the primitive Church [597]: serving through continual prayers, vigils, and fasts; preaching the word of life to those whom they could; rejecting all the things of this world as though they were foreign to them; accepting from those whom they taught only what appeared necessary for sustenance; living in every respect according to what they themselves taught; and keeping their minds ready to endure every adversity, even to die for the truth they preached.

What need is there to delay? Some believed and were baptized, marveling at the simplicity of their innocent life and the sweetness of their heavenly teaching.

Near the city itself, toward the east, there was an ancient church built in honor of Saint Martin, while the Romans still inhabited Britain [Note: Saint Martin. A bishop was later established in this church to assist the archbishop, who was occupied with the public affairs of the king and the Church, in confirmations, ordinations, and other duties assigned to him. This continued until, in the time of Lanfranc, when the bishop died, it was decided that no one should be appointed in his place; thus the name and office of bishop there came to an end.] It was there that the queen, whom we have already said was a Christian, was accustomed to pray.

In this church they too began at first to assemble, sing psalms, pray, celebrate Mass, preach, and baptize, until, after the king had been converted to the faith, they received full permission to preach and to build or restore churches.

When the king himself, delighted by the exceedingly pure life of the saints and by their most gracious promises—which they had also confirmed by the display of many miracles—believed and was baptized [Note: Baptized. Tradition relates that this occurred on Pentecost. Indeed, it took place in 597, before Augustine crossed into Gaul to be ordained; both the narrative and the circumstances require this.], more people began to flock together to hear the word. Abandoning the rites of paganism, they joined themselves through faith to the unity of Christ’s holy Church.

The king is said to have rejoiced so greatly in their faith and conversion that, nevertheless, he compelled no one to become a Christian. Rather, he embraced believers with deeper affection, as fellow citizens with him of the heavenly kingdom. For he had learned from the teachers and authors of his salvation that service to Christ ought to be voluntary, not compelled.

Nor did he delay in giving his teachers themselves a place of residence appropriate to their rank in his metropolitan city of Doruvernum [variant: Dorovernia] [Note: Doruvernum. Aedilberct himself moved to Regulbium and built a new palace there.], while also granting them the necessary properties of various kinds [Note: “Of various kinds.” See the properties donated by Aedilberct in *Monumenta Anglicana*, I, under “The Monastery of Canterbury.” It may also be noted in passing that certain of the charters recording these donations contain several typographical errors, which can be corrected from the manuscript of the Trinity College Library at Cambridge.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. How, after becoming bishop, he reported to Pope Gregory what had taken place in Britain and at the same time received his answers to the necessary questions

[Note: Meanwhile. Some deny that Augustine crossed the sea again and maintain that he was ordained during his first journey through Gaul. This is contrary not only to Bede but also to the circumstances themselves. Who could suppose that Augustine was made a bishop before he knew that he would have a people over whom he would preside? Furthermore, if he was to be ordained before entering Britain, why was he not ordained at Rome by Gregory himself rather than at Arles by Aetherius? Bede therefore rightly says that Augustine was selected from among the others to be ordained if the Angles received them, chapter 23. Once this had been ascertained, he then—and not before—considered his ordination. The argument sometimes pressed from the short interval between Augustine’s ordination and the celebrated baptism mentioned by Gregory in his letter to Eulogius of Alexandria has no force. Even the briefest calculation allows sufficient time for both tasks to have been completed. Who would doubt that a bishop would return to his own people as quickly as possible, or that the people would flock as quickly as possible to the bishop who had returned? From this I conclude that Gregory received news of this baptism of the English and of Augustine’s episcopate, which he transmitted to Eulogius, at precisely this time, through Laurence and Peter, whom Augustine expressly sent to Rome immediately after his return.]

Meanwhile the man of God Augustine came to Arles [Note: Arles. The reason for his ordination by the bishop of Arles rather than by another is partly given in the answer to the seventh question in this very chapter. The Church of Arles had possessed singular prerogatives from ancient times and, when others encroached upon them, had not lacked either prayers or arguments in its defense. On this matter see Quesnellus, under Leo I.] and was ordained archbishop for the English people by Aetherius, archbishop of that city, in accordance with the instructions that they had received from the holy Father Gregory [597]. After returning to Britain, he immediately sent Laurence the priest and Peter the monk to Rome, so that they might report to the blessed pontiff Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he had been made a bishop [598]. At the same time he asked for his advice concerning matters that appeared necessary.

Without delay he received answers appropriate to his questions, which we have also thought it useful to insert into this history.

### I. Question of the blessed Augustine, bishop of the Church of the Cantwaru

How are bishops to conduct themselves with their clergy, and what is to be done with the offerings of the faithful that are brought to the altar? How many portions should be made, and how should a bishop act in the Church?

Pope Gregory of the city of Rome replied:

Holy Scripture bears witness—a Scripture that there is no doubt you know well—and especially the Letters of the blessed Paul to Timothy, in which he took care to instruct him how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God.

[Note: “It is the custom . . .” Gratian, *Causa* XII, question 2, canon 30.]

It is the custom of the apostolic see to give instructions to bishops who have been ordained, so that of every income that comes in, four portions should be made: one, namely, for the bishop and his household, on account of hospitality and the reception of guests; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for the repair of churches.

[Note: “Because your fraternity.” Gratian, *Causa* XII, question 8, canon 8.]

But because your fraternity, trained in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live separately from your clergy, in the Church of the English—which, by God’s will, has only recently been brought to the faith—you should establish the form of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church. Among them no one claimed as his own anything of what he possessed; everything was held in common.

[Note: “But if there are any.” The Paris edition of 1518, printed in Spelman, inserts here another question: “I wish to be instructed whether clerics unable to remain continent may marry; and if they marry, whether they ought to return to the secular life.” The first part of the answer in Bede, beginning with the words “But if there are any,” is applied to it. Gratian, Part I, distinction 32; also XII, question 1.]

If there are any clerics who are not in sacred orders and who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally. For concerning those same fathers—or, according to another reading, “those same communities”—of whom we have spoken above, we know that it is written: “It was distributed to each according to his need” (Acts 4:35). Provision must also be made for their support, and they must be kept under ecclesiastical discipline, so that they live uprightly, devote themselves to singing psalms, and, by God’s authority, preserve their heart, tongue, and body from every unlawful act.

But what need is there to speak of making portions, offering hospitality, and fulfilling mercy to those who live a common life? Everything that remains must be distributed for pious and religious purposes, as the Lord, the teacher of all, says: “Give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

### II. Augustine’s question

Since there is one faith, there are diverse customs among the Churches [variant: why are there diverse customs?], and one custom of celebrating Mass is observed in the holy Roman Church, while another is observed in the Churches of Gaul?

Pope Gregory replied:

Your fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember having been nourished [Distinction 3]. But if you have found something in the Roman Church, or in the Churches of Gaul, or in any Church whatsoever, that may please almighty God more, I wish you to select it carefully and introduce it into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, as a special institution. Gather into it what you have been able to collect from many Churches.

For places are not to be loved on account of things, but places are to be loved on account of good things. From each Church, therefore, choose whatever is pious, religious, and right; gather these things, as though into a single bundle, and establish them as a custom among the minds of the English.

### III. Augustine’s question

I ask what punishment should be imposed if someone steals something from the Church?

Gregory replied:

Your fraternity can judge from the person of the thief how he may be corrected [Gratian, *Causa* XII, question 2, canon 11]. Some commit theft despite having resources; others offend in this matter because of poverty. Therefore some must be corrected by damages, others by beatings; some more strictly, others more leniently.

When the correction is somewhat stricter, it must be administered out of charity, not fury, because the correction is being given for the benefit of the one corrected, so that he may not be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. We ought to impose discipline upon the faithful just as good fathers customarily discipline their bodily children: they strike them with blows for their faults, yet they seek to have as heirs the very children whom they afflict with pain, and they preserve their possessions for those whom, in anger, they appear to be pursuing.

This charity must therefore be kept in mind, and it must itself determine the measure of correction, so that the mind does nothing wholly outside the rule of reason.

You should also add how those who have stolen things from the churches are to restore them. But far be it from the Church to receive with increase what it appears to have lost from earthly goods, and to seek profits from vanities [Note: “To seek.” Chifflus alone reads: “To seek; but, having received the goods themselves, the Church should not demand more.”]

### IV. Augustine’s question

May two full brothers marry two sisters who are descended from them by a distant line of generation?

Gregory replied:

This is entirely permissible, for nowhere in the sacred writings is anything found that appears to contradict this matter.

### V. Augustine’s question

Up to which generation may the faithful marry their relatives? And is it permitted to marry stepmothers and relations?

Gregory replied:

A certain secular law [Gratian, XXXV, question 2, canon 20] permits in the Roman state that a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, may have intercourse. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot grow from such a union. The sacred law also forbids the exposure of the shame of kinship.

Therefore the faithful ought to be permitted to join in marriage in the third or fourth generation; for the second generation, as we have said, must in every way abstain from one another.

To have intercourse with a stepmother is a grave crime, because it is also written in the law: “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness” (Leviticus 18:7). A son cannot, of course, uncover his father’s nakedness. But because it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), whoever dares to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother, who was one flesh with his father, has plainly uncovered his father’s nakedness.

It is likewise forbidden to have intercourse with a relation, because through the earlier union she had become the flesh of a brother. For this reason John the Baptist was also beheaded and brought to completion through holy martyrdom. He was not told to deny Christ and then killed for confessing Christ; rather, because our Lord Jesus Christ himself had said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), John was killed for the truth and thus shed his blood for Christ.

[Note: “But since there are many.” The Paris edition of 1518 inserts here a seventh question: “I ask that it be explained whether, if those who have entered into a shameful union are to be separated, the offering of holy Communion must also be denied to them.” The corresponding part of the fifth answer in Bede, beginning with the words “But there are many,” is applied to it.]

Since there are many among the English who, while still unbelievers, are said to have entered into this abominable union, they must be admonished, upon coming to the faith, to abstain and to recognize that this is a grave sin. They must fear the dreadful judgment of God, lest, for the sake of carnal affection [variant: pleasure], they incur the torments of eternal punishment.

Nevertheless, on this account they must not be deprived of communion in the holy body and blood of the Lord, lest they appear to be punished for acts into which they entered through ignorance before the washing of baptism. At the present time the holy Church corrects some things through fervor, tolerates others through gentleness, and overlooks others through prudence. In this way it bears and overlooks matters so that often, by bearing and overlooking the evil that opposes it, it may restrain it.

All who come to the faith must be admonished not to dare to commit anything of this kind. But those who do commit it must be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord. For just as guilt is to some extent tolerated in those who acted through ignorance, so it must be pursued with force in those who are not afraid to sin knowingly.

### VI. Augustine’s question

If a great distance intervenes between places, so that bishops cannot easily assemble, may a bishop be ordained without the presence of other bishops?

Gregory replied:

In the Church of the English, where at present you alone are found as a bishop [see Book III, 28; IV, 2], you can ordain a bishop only without other bishops. For when bishops come from Gaul, who will be present as witnesses at the ordination of a bishop?

Nevertheless, we wish your fraternity to ordain bishops in such a way that the bishops themselves are not separated from one another by a great distance [Gratian, distinction 80, canon 6], so that there is no necessity in which, at the ordination of a bishop, other pastors—whose presence is extremely useful—cannot easily assemble.

Therefore, when, by God’s authority, bishops have been ordained in places near one another, an episcopal ordination should in every respect not be carried out without three or four bishops assembled.

For even in spiritual matters, so that they may be arranged wisely and maturely, we can draw an example from bodily affairs. Certainly, when marriages are celebrated in the world, married people are summoned, so that those who have already gone before on the path of marriage may share in the joy of the subsequent union.

Why, then, should not those also assemble for this spiritual ordination, through which a person is joined to God by sacred ministry—those who may either rejoice in the progress of the bishop who has been ordained or pour out prayers together to almighty God for his protection?

### VII. Augustine’s question

How ought we to deal with the bishops of Gaul and Britain?

Gregory replied:

We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul [Gratian, XXV, question 2, canon 3], because from the ancient times of my predecessors the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we ought not to deprive him of the authority he has received.

If, therefore, your fraternity should happen to travel to the province of Gaul, you should act together with that same bishop of Arles so that, if there are any faults among the bishops, they may be corrected. If he should perhaps prove lukewarm in the vigor of discipline, he must be inflamed by the zeal of your fraternity.

We have also written to him [Book XI, indiction 4, letter 68], so that, in the presence of your holiness in Gaul, he too may assist with his whole mind and restrain from the conduct of the bishops whatever is contrary to the command of our Creator.

You yourself, however, may not judge the bishops of Gaul apart from the proper authority [variant: by your own authority]. Instead, by persuasion, gentleness, and by showing them good works worthy of imitation, reform the minds of the wicked toward the pursuit of holiness. For it is written in the law: “Passing through another man’s harvest, one must not put in a sickle, but one may rub the ears with the hand and eat” (Deuteronomy 23:25; Gratian, VI, question 3).

You cannot put the sickle of judgment into the harvest that appears to have been entrusted to another. But through the affection of good works, strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of their vices and, by admonishing and persuading, convert it—as though by chewing it—into the body of the Church.

Whatever, however, must be done by authority should be undertaken together with the aforementioned bishop of Arles, so that what the ancient institution of the Fathers established may not be neglected [variant: may not fail to achieve its effect].

As for all the bishops of Britain, we entrust them to your fraternity, so that the unlearned may be taught, the weak strengthened by persuasion, and the perverse corrected by authority.

[Note: “May be corrected.” The Paris edition which Spelman calls the new edition—that is, apparently, the edition of 1545—introduces here a petition of Augustine:

> “I ask that the relics of Saint Sixtus the martyr be sent to us.”

Gregory’s concession:

> “We have done what you requested, so that the people who formerly said that the body of Saint Sixtus the martyr was venerated in that place—although it does not appear to your fraternity to be truly or genuinely holy—may receive the certain benefits of the most holy and approved martyr and not venerate what is uncertain. It seems to me, however, that if the body which the people believe to belong to a certain martyr does not shine with any miracles, and if none of the elders exists who claims to have heard from his parents the account of the martyr’s passion, the relics you requested should be deposited separately, so that the place where the aforementioned body lies may be blocked off in every way, and the people may not be permitted to abandon what is certain and venerate what is uncertain.”

The occasion for this petition is said to have been that Augustine found in Kent a tradition concerning a certain Sixtus whose relics had formerly been venerated by the Britons. Suspecting, rightly, that this was false, he requested what he believed to be the true relics. But Bede says nothing about this petition or response. Spelman supplied these additions without the authority of any manuscript. The Benedictine editors printed them in Gregory’s letters, Letter 64 of Book XI, indiction 4, on the authority of certain Gregorian manuscripts; therefore, so that the reader might lack nothing, I have placed them after Bede’s genuine text.]

### VIII. Augustine’s question

Should a pregnant woman be baptized? After she has given birth, how long should she wait before entering the church? Or, lest the child she has borne be overtaken by death, after how many days may it receive the sacrament of holy baptism? After how long may her husband join with her in sexual intercourse? If she is subject to her menstrual period, may she enter the church or receive the sacrament of holy Communion? If a man has had intercourse with his wife, may he enter the church before washing with water, or even approach the mystery of holy Communion? All these matters ought to be made known to the inexperienced English people.

Gregory replied:

I do not doubt that your fraternity has asked this question, and I think that I have already given you an answer. But I believe that you have wished what you yourself were able to say and think to be confirmed by my response.

Why should a pregnant woman not be baptized, since there is no guilt in the fruitfulness of the flesh before the eyes of almighty God? When our first parents sinned in paradise, they lost, by the just judgment of God, the immortality they had received. Since almighty God did not wish to destroy the human race utterly on account of its sin, he took immortality away from human beings because of their offense, yet in the kindness of his compassion he preserved for them the fruitfulness of offspring.

What was therefore preserved for human nature by the gift of almighty God—by what reasoning could it be prevented from receiving the grace of holy baptism? In that mystery in which every sin is utterly extinguished, it would be exceedingly foolish to imagine that the gift of grace could be opposed.

When a woman has given birth [Gratian, distinction 5, canon 1], you have learned from the commandment of the Old Testament how many days she should remain apart: thirty-three days for a male child, but sixty-six days for a female [Note: “By the commandment.” The common manuscripts read: “It is clear from the commandment,” which runs as follows: “If a woman has conceived and borne a male child, she shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification; she shall touch no holy thing and shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification have been fulfilled. But if she has borne a female child, she shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of her purification.”]

This, however, must be understood mystically. If she enters the church at the very hour when she has given birth in order to give thanks, she is not burdened by any weight of sin. For in sexual intercourse there is pleasure, whereas in the bringing forth of offspring there is groaning. Hence it was said even to the first mother of all [Note: “It is said.” The Vulgate says that, because she transgressed God’s commandment, it was said to her: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions,” and so forth.]: “In pains you shall bring forth” (Genesis 3:6).

If, therefore, we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we turn her own punishment into guilt. A woman who has given birth may be baptized without any prohibition; and if she or the child she has borne is in danger of death, either she herself at the very hour when she gives birth [variant: gave birth] or the child at the very hour when it is born may likewise be baptized without any prohibition.

For just as the grace of the holy mystery must be provided with great discretion to those who are living and capable of understanding, so it must be offered without any delay to those threatened by death, lest, while time is still being sought to provide the mystery of redemption, a brief delay intervene and no one remain who can be redeemed.

Her husband, however, ought not to approach her for intercourse until the child who is born has been weaned.

A wicked custom has arisen in the conduct of married people: women refuse to nurse the children whom they bear and hand them over to other women to be nourished. This appears to have been invented solely because of incontinence: since they do not wish to remain continent, they disdain to nurse the children they have borne.

Therefore women who, because of this wicked custom, hand their children over to others to be nursed ought not to have intercourse with their husbands until the period of purification has passed. Indeed, even apart from the reason of childbirth, when they are held by their customary menstrual period, they are forbidden to have intercourse with their husbands, so that the sacred law strikes with death anyone who approaches a menstruating woman (Leviticus 10).

Yet a woman who is undergoing her menstrual period ought not to be forbidden to enter the church, because the bodily discharge of nature cannot be counted as guilt against her. Since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not right that she be deprived of entry into the church.

For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her illness departed from her (Luke 8). If, then, while placed in a flow of blood, she was rightly able to touch the Lord’s garment, why should a woman who suffers the monthly flow of blood not be permitted to enter the church of the Lord?

But you say: “Illness compelled that woman; the women of whom we are speaking are constrained by custom.” Consider, dearest brother, that everything we suffer in this mortal flesh was ordered by the just judgment of God after sin, as a consequence of the weakness of nature.

To hunger, thirst, suffer heat or cold, and grow weary belongs to the weakness of nature. And what else is it to seek food against hunger, drink against thirst, breezes against heat, clothing against cold, and rest against weariness, except to seek a remedy against illnesses?

The menstrual flow of women, therefore, is an illness. If, then, the woman who was placed in sickness rightly presumed to touch the Lord’s garment, why should what is granted to one sick person not be granted to all women who are sick through a defect of their nature?

They should not be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy Communion during those same days. If, out of profound reverence, a woman does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she does receive it, she is not to be judged.

It belongs to good minds to recognize their faults in some way even where there is no fault. For often something is done without fault that arises from fault. Thus, when we are hungry, we eat without fault, although it was because of the fault of the first human being that we came to be hungry.

The menstrual period is not a fault for women, since it comes naturally [variant: occurs naturally]. Yet the fact that nature itself has been so corrupted that it appears to be polluted even without the intention of the will arises from sin. In this defect human nature may recognize what it has become through judgment. The person who willingly committed sin bears the guilt of sin unwillingly.

Therefore women should consider themselves carefully. If, during their menstrual period, they do not presume to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, they are to be praised for their upright reflection. But when, through the habit of a religious life, they are carried by love of the same mystery toward receiving it, they ought not, as we have said, to be restrained.

For just as external works are observed in the Old Testament, so in the New Testament attention is directed carefully not so much to what is done outwardly as to what is conceived inwardly, so that it may be judged with subtle discernment.

Although the law forbids the eating of many things as unclean, in the Gospel the Lord says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—this is what defiles a person” (Matthew 15:11). A little later, explaining this, he added: “From the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:19).

It is abundantly shown there that what is demonstrated to be polluted in action is generated from the root of polluted thought. The apostle Paul likewise says: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1:15). Immediately, announcing the cause of their defilement, he adds: “For their mind and their conscience are defiled.”

If food is not unclean to one whose mind is not unclean, why should what a woman with a pure mind suffers by nature be counted as uncleanness?

Source/review notes: The supplied witnesses preserve several grammatical and textual alternatives; the apparatus retains their actual forms and distinct meanings.

A man who sleeps with his own wife (Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction VII, question 4, chapter 7), unless he has washed with water, ought not to enter the church; but even after washing he ought not to enter immediately. The old law, however, prescribed for the people that a man who had joined himself to a woman should wash with water and not enter the church before sunset—something that can nevertheless be understood spiritually. For a man is joined to a woman when the mind, through pleasure in thought, is joined to unlawful desire; and unless the fire of desire has first cooled in the mind, he ought not to consider himself worthy of the assembly of the brethren if he sees that he is weighed down by the wickedness of a perverse will.

Although different peoples have different opinions about this matter and seem to observe different practices, it has nevertheless always been the custom of the Romans, from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s wife, to seek purification by washing and reverently to abstain for a short time from entering the church. In saying this, we do not consider marriage itself to be a fault; but because even lawful intercourse with one’s wife cannot take place without the pleasure of the flesh, one ought to abstain from entering the holy place, since that pleasure itself can in no way be without fault.

For the man who said, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50:7), was not born of adultery or fornication, but of a lawful marriage. He who knew himself to have been conceived in iniquities lamented that he had been born in sin, because he carries in the branch the sap of vice that he drew from the root. In these words, however, he does not call the intercourse of married people itself iniquity, but rather the pleasure of the intercourse.

There are many things that are recognized as lawful and legitimate, yet in performing them we are nevertheless stained to some degree. Thus, often in our anger we pursue faults and disturb the tranquillity of our spirit; and although what is done is right, it is nevertheless not commendable that the mind is disturbed in doing it. He was angry against the vices of sinners who said, “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8). Since a tranquil mind alone can raise itself to the light of contemplation, he mourned that his eye had been troubled by anger; for while pursuing evil deeds below, he was compelled to be confused and disturbed in contemplating higher things. Anger against vice is therefore praiseworthy, yet he considered himself to have incurred guilt through the distress by which he was disturbed.

Accordingly, lawful union of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and intercourse of the flesh ought to be for the purpose of begetting children, not the satisfaction of vice. But if someone uses his wife not carried away by the desire for pleasure, but solely for the purpose of begetting children, then, whether he may enter the church or receive the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, he should be left to his own judgment. For we ought not to forbid him to receive who, being placed in the fire, is unaware that he burns.

But when, in the act of intercourse, not love for begetting offspring but desire holds sway, married people have something in their intercourse for which they should mourn. Holy preaching grants them this, yet by that very concession it shakes the mind with fear. For when the apostle Paul said, “If he cannot contain himself, let him have his wife,” he immediately took care to add, “But this I say by way of indulgence, not by way of command” (1 Corinthians 7:9). What is lawful is not therefore indulged because it is just. What he called an indulgence, then, he showed to be a fault.

It must also be carefully considered that, when the Lord was about to speak to the people on Mount Sinai, he first commanded that same people to abstain from women. If, in the place where the Lord spoke through a creature subject to human beings, such bodily purity was required that those who were to receive the words of God should not be joined to women, how much more ought women who receive the body of the almighty Lord to preserve bodily purity in themselves, lest they be weighed down by the immense greatness of the mystery itself?

For this reason it is also said to David by the priest concerning his young men that, if they were clean from women, they should receive the loaves of the Presence; they would certainly not have received them unless David had first acknowledged that they were clean from women. A man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may then receive the mystery of holy communion when, according to the sentence already established, he is also permitted to enter the church.

### IX. Augustine’s Question

After the pollution that commonly occurs through a dream, may anyone receive the Lord’s body? Or, if he is a priest, may he celebrate the sacred mysteries?

### Gregory’s Response

The Testament of the old law (Gratian, distinction VI, chapter 1), as we have already said in the preceding chapter, calls such a man polluted and does not permit him to enter the church until evening unless he has washed with water. The spiritual people, however, understanding this in another way, will accept it in the same sense that we have described above: the person who is tempted by impurity is, as it were, deceived in a dream and polluted in thought by true images; but he must be washed with water so that he may cleanse the sins of his thought with tears. Unless the fire of temptation has first withdrawn, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

Yet in this pollution there is a very necessary distinction, which must be carefully weighed: from what cause does it happen to the sleeping mind? Sometimes it arises from drunkenness, sometimes from an excess or weakness of nature, and sometimes from thought. When it has occurred through an excess or weakness of nature, this pollution is not to be feared at all; for it is more a matter for regret that the mind, unaware, has endured it than that it has caused it.

But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in eating, and the receptacles of the bodily fluids are consequently burdened, the mind incurs some guilt as a result—not, however, to the point of forbidding the reception of the holy mystery or the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass, if perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity compels the mystery to be offered because another priest is absent. If others are present who can perform the ministry, pollution caused by overeating ought not to prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, as I think, one should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that the sleeping mind has not been shaken by a shameful image [variant: suggestion].

For there are some in whom this pollution usually arises in such a way that their minds, even while their bodies are sunk in sleep, are not defiled by shameful images. In such a case, one thing is shown: the mind itself is guilty, though it is not free even by its own judgment, since, although it remembers nothing seen while the body slept, it nevertheless remembers, in the body's waking state, that it had fallen into gluttony.

But if the pollution of the sleeping person arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. It sees from what root that impurity proceeded, because what it knowingly thought, it unknowingly endured. Yet one must consider whether that thought arose through suggestion, through pleasure, or—what is more serious—through consent to sin.

Every sin is completed in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, pleasure through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. For the serpent suggested the first fault, Eve, like the flesh, took pleasure in it, and Adam, like the spirit, consented. Great discernment is therefore necessary, so that the mind may act as its own judge between suggestion and pleasure, and between pleasure and consent.

When an evil spirit suggests sin in the mind, if no pleasure in sin follows, sin has not in any way been committed. But when the flesh begins to take pleasure, sin begins to be born; and if the mind also consents deliberately, then sin is recognized as completed. Thus in suggestion there is the beginning of sin, in pleasure its nourishment, and in consent its completion.

It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought, the flesh draws into pleasure; yet the soul does not consent to that pleasure. Although the flesh cannot take pleasure without the mind, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is nevertheless unwillingly bound in carnal pleasure to some degree, so that it contradicts it through reason and does not consent, yet remains bound by pleasure and groans bitterly that it is bound.

Hence that distinguished soldier of the heavenly army also groaned, saying: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:23). If he was captive, he was not fighting; but he was fighting as well. Therefore he was both captive and fighting: he was fighting, then, against the law of his mind, against which the law existing in his members was fighting.

If he was fighting, he was not captive. Thus a human being is, so to speak, both captive and free: free because of the righteousness that he loves, captive because of the pleasure that he bears unwillingly.

[Note: “Therefore he was also captive.” The sense here is easy to see, but it is difficult to reduce it to the wording of the manuscripts. Each editor has indulged his own conjectures. Some have, “He was not captive . . . in the law of the mind.” Chifflet, placing a full stop after *pugnabat* (“he was fighting”), prints, “He was fighting, therefore.” I have inserted into the text the wording of the ancient manuscripts, those of More and two of the Cotton manuscripts, because here they agree exactly. Let others choose the reading they prefer.]

[Note: “Unwillingly.” Editors of Gregory’s works ordinarily place these questions and answers in the register of that pope’s letters, book XI, indiction 4, letter 64. This writing indeed has the character of a decretal letter. Bede, however, does not call it a letter, but a little book (see II.1), since it exceeds the ordinary length of a letter and treats several subjects of considerable importance at once. Whatever name it is given, we owe its preservation to Bede. For in the very century in which it appeared, around the year 740, Boniface of Mainz wrote to Nothelm, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning it as though it were uncertain or lost, as follows: “I beg you to arrange to send me a copy of that letter which, as they say, contains the questions of Bishop Augustine, the first preacher of the English, and the answers of the holy Pope Gregory—[including the statement] that the faithful may contract marriages within the third degree of relationship—and to investigate carefully whether the aforesaid writing can be proved to be by our father Gregory or not. For, as the keepers of the archives affirm, it was sought in the archive of the Roman Church among the other copies of the aforesaid pontiff, but could not be found.” What Nothelm replied is unknown. But that from the beginning this was a letter in Bede is shown, apart from the fact that More’s manuscript is older than Boniface’s writing, by the fact that it was sent to Nothelm, as well as by the continuous testimony of subsequent centuries—not only in Bede’s books, but also in the works of other authors who wrote about the matters treated there and praised this letter as possessing the highest authority. As a further accumulation of evidence, there are the confirmations of Gregory’s successors and of the whole Church in the body of canon law, by which these replies of Gregory passed into the form of ecclesiastical laws. Citations of them have been placed in the notes below the text at their appropriate locations.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII  

[Col. 0068D]
### How Pope Gregory sent a letter to the bishop of Arles to assist Augustine in the work of God

Thus far extend the responses of the blessed Pope Gregory to the inquiries of the most reverend Bishop Augustine. The letter that he mentions having written, he had given to the bishop of Arles, Virgilius [Note: “The successor of Etherius.” Unless Gregory of Tours had supplied another predecessor of Virgilius accepted by others, I would readily have suspended judgment concerning Bede’s Etherius of Arles. For Bede does not speak of Etherius only incidentally or only once, but throughout the course of his history and in connection with the succession of the see of Arles. Virgilius was not unknown to him; and why should there not have been something in the chronology of these bishops that was lost during those obscure times?]—the successor of Etherius [601]. This was its form:

> To the most reverend and holy brother Virgilius, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.
>
> How great is the affection that should be shown to brothers who come of their own accord is understood from the fact that they are often invited for the sake of charity. Therefore, if it should happen that our common brother Augustine the bishop comes to you, may your affection receive him, as is fitting, with such warmth and kindness that it may both refresh him with the benefit of its consolation [variant: honor] and teach others how brotherly love ought to be cultivated.
>
> Since it often happens that those who live far away first learn from others what needs correction, if he should perhaps bring before your fraternity any faults of priests or others, investigate everything carefully while residing with him. Show yourselves so strict and attentive toward those things that offend God and provoke him to anger that punishment may strike the guilty for the correction of others, while false opinion does not afflict the innocent.
>
> May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in the nineteenth year [of his reign], and, after his consulship, in the eighteenth year of our same lord, in the fourth indiction.

[Note: “After the consulship.” More’s manuscript has *PC.*, an abbreviation that some manuscripts expanded as “of the pontificate.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX  

[Col. 0069D]
### How he sent Augustine the pallium, a letter, and several ministers of the word

Moreover, because Bishop Augustine had reported to Pope Gregory that there was indeed a great harvest there but few laborers, the same Pope Gregory sent with his aforementioned messengers several fellow workers and ministers of the word [601]. The first and chief among them were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus. Through them he also sent, in general, everything necessary for the worship and ministry of the Church: sacred vessels, altar vestments, church ornaments, priestly and clerical garments, relics of the holy apostles and martyrs, and very many books.

He also sent letters in which he stated that he had forwarded the pallium to Augustine and explained how he ought to establish bishops in Britain. The text of these letters is as follows:

> To the most reverend and holy brother Augustine, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.
>
> Since it is certain that ineffable rewards in the eternal kingdom are reserved for all who labor for the almighty God, it is nevertheless necessary for us to bestow honors upon them, so that through the reward they may be able to labor with still greater zeal in spiritual work. And because the new Church of the English has, by the gift of the same Lord and through your labor, been brought to the grace of almighty God, we grant you the use of the pallium for the celebration of Masses alone. In each place, you are to ordain twelve bishops who shall be subject to your authority, so that the bishop of the city of London may thereafter always be consecrated by his own synod and receive the pallium of honor from this holy and apostolic see, which, by God’s authority, I serve.
>
> As for the city of York, we wish you to send a bishop whom you yourself judge fit to ordain, provided only that, if that city and the neighboring places receive the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan honor. For, if his life is spared, we also intend, with the Lord’s favor, to grant him the pallium. He shall nevertheless be subject to the direction of your fraternity. After your death, he is to preside over the bishops whom he has ordained in such a way that he may in no respect be subject to the authority of the bishop of London.
>
> Between the bishops of the cities of London and York, let this distinction of honor henceforth be maintained: the one who was ordained first is to be regarded as senior. By common counsel and harmonious action, however, let them unanimously arrange whatever must be done for Christ’s sake, think rightly, and carry out what they have judged necessary without disagreement between them.
>
> Your fraternity is to have subject to you, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, not only the bishops whom you ordain, nor only those who are ordained by the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain. Thus, from the speech and life of your holiness, they may receive a pattern of right belief and good living; and, faithfully carrying out their office in faith and conduct, may they reach the heavenly kingdom when the Lord wills.
>
> May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in the nineteenth year [of his reign], and, after the consulship of our same lord, in the eighteenth year, in the fourth indiction.

[Note: “Of London and York.” The disputes that these letters later produced among the sees of Canterbury, York, London, and Saint Andrew’s in Scotland have been sufficiently narrated in the histories. See William of Malmesbury, Hoveden, Eadmer, T. Stubbs, and others. Concerning the neighboring places of York, I have added some material in the appendix, no. 8.]

## CHAPTER XXX  

[Col. 0070B]
### A copy of the letter that he sent to Mellitus the abbot as he was going to Britain

When the aforementioned messengers had departed, the blessed Father Gregory sent after them letters worthy of remembrance [601], in which he clearly showed how diligently he watched over the salvation of our people. He wrote as follows:

> To his most beloved son Mellitus, abbot, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.
>
> Since the departure of our community that is with you, we have been left in great suspense, because we have had no opportunity to hear anything about the success of your journey. When, therefore, almighty God has brought you to our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop, tell him what I have long considered and discussed with myself concerning the matter of the English: namely, that the temples of idols in that people should by no means be destroyed, but that the idols themselves within them should be destroyed; that blessed water should be made and sprinkled in those same temples; that altars should be built and relics placed there.
>
> For if those temples are well constructed, they must be converted from the worship of demons to the service of the true God, so that when the people see that their temples are not destroyed, they may remove error from their hearts and, recognizing and worshiping the true God, may more familiarly gather in the places to which they are accustomed.
>
> And because they are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should also be changed for them in this matter: on the day of the dedication, or on the feast days of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, they should make for themselves booths from branches of trees around those same churches that have been converted from temples, and celebrate the feast with religious banquets. They should no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for food to the praise of God and give thanks to the giver of all things for their nourishment. Thus, while some outward joys are preserved for them, they may more readily consent to inward joys.
>
> For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut off everything at once from hard hearts, since even one who strives to climb to the highest place is raised by steps or paces, not by leaps. Thus, when the Lord made himself known to the Israelite people in Egypt, he nevertheless retained for their own worship the sacrificial practices that they had been accustomed to offer to the devil, commanding them to sacrifice animals in his own worship. In this way, as they changed their hearts, they would lose one part of their sacrifice and retain another: although the animals they were accustomed to offer remained the same, when they sacrificed them to the true God and not to idols, the sacrifices themselves were no longer the same.
>
> You must therefore tell the aforesaid brother this, so that, being present there, he may judge how he ought to arrange everything. May God preserve you unharmed, my most beloved son. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in the nineteenth year [of his reign], and, after the consulship of our same lord, in the eighteenth year, in the fourth indiction.

[Note: “After considering it with myself.” Gregory had written to King Æthelberht that the worship of idols should be abolished and the buildings of the temples destroyed. But, fearing that he had been carried away there by excessive zeal, he sent Mellitus with additional instructions and caught up with him during the journey. The letter to Æthelberht appears below, in chapter 32. This letter to Mellitus has plainly been placed outside its proper order, as have others.]

## CHAPTER XXXI  

[Col. 0071B]
### How he exhorted Augustine by letter not to glory in his miracles

At this time he also sent Augustine a letter concerning the miracles that he had learned were performed through him. In it he exhorted him, in the following words, not to incur the danger of pride through their abundance:

> I know, dearest brother, that almighty God has shown great miracles through your love among the people whom he willed to choose [variant: *gente*, “among the people”]. Therefore it is necessary for you both to rejoice in and fear this heavenly gift, and to fear it even while rejoicing.
>
> You should rejoice because the souls of the English are being drawn through outward miracles to inward grace; but you should fear lest, amid the signs that are performed, a weak mind raise itself through presumption, and lest, by the very means through which it is lifted outwardly to honor, it fall inwardly through empty glory.
>
> We must remember that when the disciples returned from preaching with joy and said to their heavenly Teacher, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name,” they immediately heard: “Do not rejoice over this, but rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” They had placed their minds in private and temporal joy by rejoicing in miracles; but they were recalled from private to common joy and from temporal to eternal joy when they were told: “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven.”
>
> Not all the elect perform miracles, but the names of all of them are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples of the Truth ought not to find joy except in that good which they possess in common with everyone and in which they have no private ground for rejoicing.
>
> It remains, then, dearest brother, that amid the things you perform outwardly through the Lord’s working, you should always judge yourself inwardly with close attention and understand with close attention both who you are and how great is the grace present among the people for whose conversion you have received the gifts of performing signs.
>
> Whenever you remember that you have sinned against our Creator, whether through speech or through deeds, always recall these things to mind, so that the memory of your guilt may press down the rising glory of your heart. Whatever you have received or do receive for performing signs, attribute it not to yourself but to those for whose salvation it has been granted to you.

[Note: “Concerning miracles.” This is only part of the letter; its beginning and conclusion have been omitted. See the appendix among the British letters. After reading the complete letter, I have no doubt that it was a response to Augustine’s report in chapter 27, by which Gregory was informed of Augustine’s consecration and of the miracles about which he had written to Eulogius of Alexandria.]

## CHAPTER XXXII  

[Col. 0072B]
### How he sent a letter and gifts to King Æthelberht

At the same time the blessed Pope Gregory also sent a letter to King Æthelberht [601], together with very many gifts of various kinds [variant: very splendid gifts]. He sought to honor with temporal honors the king whose knowledge of heavenly glory he rejoiced had come through his labor and zeal. A copy of the aforementioned letter follows:

> To the most glorious and excellent son, Æthelberht, king of the English, Gregory, bishop.
>
> For this reason almighty God brings good men to rule over peoples: so that through them he may bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all those over whom they have been placed. We know that this has been done among the English, over whom your glory has therefore been set, so that through the good things granted to you, heavenly benefits might also be bestowed upon the people subject to you.
>
> Therefore, glorious son, carefully preserve the grace that you have received from God. Hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you; multiply the zeal of your righteousness in their conversion; pursue the worship of idols; overthrow the buildings of their temples; and build up the conduct of your subjects through great purity of life, exhorting, frightening, encouraging, correcting, and showing examples of good works. Thus you may find in heaven as your rewarder the one whose name and knowledge you have spread on earth. He himself will make your name more glorious even among posterity, since you seek and preserve his honor among the nations.
>
> Thus, in former times, the most devout emperor Constantine, recalling the Roman state from the perverse worship of idols, subjected himself with it to our almighty Lord God Jesus Christ and turned himself and the subject peoples wholly toward him. As a result, that man surpassed the name of the ancient rulers by his praises, and he exceeded his predecessors in reputation by as much as he surpassed them in good works.
>
> Therefore let your glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—into the kings and peoples subject to you. Let it surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit; and by as much as it has wiped away the sins of others among your subjects, let it become more secure concerning its own sins before the terrible judgment of almighty God.
>
> Our most reverend brother Augustine the bishop, trained in the rule of a monastery [variant: learned in a monastery], filled with knowledge of sacred Scripture, and endowed, by God’s authorship, with good works: listen to whatever he admonishes you, carry it out devotedly, and preserve it carefully in your memory. For if you listen to him in what he speaks on behalf of the almighty Lord, that same almighty God will more quickly hear him interceding for you [variant: will hear him].
>
> If, God forbid, you disregard his words, how will almighty God be able to hear him on your behalf, when you refuse to hear him on behalf of God? Therefore bind yourself to him with your whole mind in the fervor of faith, and assist his effort with the strength that the Godhead grants you, so that he himself may make you participants in his kingdom, whose faith you cause to be received and preserved in your own kingdom.
>
> Moreover, we wish your glory to know that, as we learn from the words of the almighty Lord in sacred Scripture, the end of the present world is already near [Note: “The end is near.” Do not be surprised that Gregory introduces this abruptly concerning the end of the world. Influenced by various calamities that had then invaded the world, he had absorbed the belief that the end of the world was imminent in that age. For this reason, not only in this letter to the king but also in other writings, he repeatedly offers exhortations based on this principle.] and the kingdom of the saints is to come, which can never be ended.
>
> As that end of the world approaches, many things are imminent that did not occur before: changes in the air, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places. Yet not all these things will come in our own days; they will all follow after our days.
>
> If, therefore, you recognize any of these things occurring in your land, do not allow your mind to be disturbed in any way. These signs of the end of the age are sent beforehand so that we may be concerned for our souls, remain mindful of the hour of death, and be found prepared in good works for the judgment that is to come.
>
> I have now spoken these few words, glorious son, so that when the Christian faith has grown in your kingdom, our own speech among you may also grow broader, and we may desire to speak all the more as the joy in our mind over the complete conversion of your people increases.
>
> I have sent a few small gifts, which will not be small to you when you have received them as a blessing from the blessed apostle Peter. May almighty God perfect in you the grace that he has begun, prolong your life here through the course of many years, and after a long time receive you into the assembly of the heavenly homeland. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed, lord son. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in the nineteenth year [of his reign], and, after the consulship of our same lord, in the eighteenth year, in the fourth indiction.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  

[Col. 0073C]
