### How Augustine restored the Church of the Savior and established the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter; and concerning its first abbot, Peter

When Augustine had received an episcopal seat in the royal city, as we have said above, supported by royal assistance he recovered there the church that he had learned had been built in ancient times through the work of Roman Christians. He consecrated it in the name of Saint Savior, God and our Lord Jesus Christ [598] [Note: “In the name.” After the name was changed several times, it is now called Christ Church and bears the name of the holy Savior.] and established there a residence for himself and for all his successors.

He also built a monastery not far east of the city itself. At his urging, Æthelberht built there from the foundations a church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and enriched it with various gifts [Note: “He endowed it.” We have three charters of donations in the *Monumenta Anglica*, where I noted them above, and a fourth in manuscript A.T.C., which I have placed in the appendix, no. 9. There has long been a dispute concerning the antiquity and authority of these charters. The monks, especially those of Canterbury, had such license in forging charters that they even cast suspicion upon the authenticity of genuine documents. See what Papebrochius in the *Propyleum*, volume II of the April volume, and Mabillon in *De re diplomatica* have collected on both sides concerning these matters. Besides the king’s charters, the monks also possessed a bull of Augustine, although its authenticity has always been questioned; and manuscript A.T.C., in its own defense of it, has proved the matter abundantly.]

In that monastery the bodies of Augustine himself, all the bishops of Canterbury, and the kings of Kent could be buried [Note: “That the bodies might be placed there.” According to the laws of that age, burial within cities is said to have been unlawful. The bodies of the kings and bishops of Canterbury were placed in this monastery of Peter and Paul until Cuthbert, archbishop, obtained permission for burial in Christ Church, where he too was buried in the year 758.]

The church, however, was consecrated not by Augustine himself but by his successor Laurence [Note: “His successor.” Certainly Augustine’s death was not long afterward.] The first abbot of the same monastery was the priest Peter [Note: “The first abbot. His successors were John, Rufinianus, Gratiosus, Petronius, and Nathanael, who came to England with Augustine or later with Mellitus and Justus.]. Sent as a messenger to Gaul, he was drowned [Note: “Drowned.” The *English Martyrology* and Ferrarius place Peter’s feast on the eighth day before the Ides of January; the Benedictine calendar and Molanus on the third day before the Kalends of January. Perhaps one date was the day of the translation and the other the day of his death.] in a gulf of the sea called Amfleat [Note: “Amfleat.” Commonly Ambleteau], and the obscure inhabitants of the place handed him over for burial.

But almighty God, to show what kind of man he had been in merit, caused a heavenly light to appear every night above his grave. When the neighbors [Note: “The neighbors.” Malebranc, in *Morini*, book III, chapter 4, attributes this piety to Count Fumertius. Peter rests in great honor at Boulogne in the church of the Canons. See Gotselinus, *On the Translation of Saint Augustine*, II.28.] noticed that the man buried there had been a saint and investigated where he came from and who he was, they took away his body and placed it in the city of Boulogne, in a church, with the honor appropriate to so great a man.

## Textual apparatus to Chapters XXVII–XXXIII

The readings below occur in the supplied text and follow its order. Latin forms are retained where English cannot display an inflectional, orthographic, or word-order distinction.

1. In the discussion of abstinence after marital intercourse, “this lawful union” has *ipsa* (“that very union”) or *ista* (“this union”).
2. The union cannot take place without *voluntate carnis*, “the will of the flesh”; another text reads *voluptate carnis*, “the pleasure of the flesh,” which fits the following explanation. [Col. 0065A]
3. Another text adds *arbor*, “tree,” to the branch-and-root image: “the tree carries in its branch the moisture of the fault drawn from the root.”
4. The qualification that the words do not call marital union itself iniquity reads *non*, “not,” or *tamen non*, “nevertheless not.”
5. Many acts are *licita … ac legitima*, “lawful and legitimate”; another text has the compressed wording *licita ac*.
6. The Psalm says the eye was troubled *prae ira*, “because of anger”; another reading is *a furore*, “by fury.” [Col. 0065C]
7. Praiseworthy anger is nevertheless burdensome, *qua*, “by which”; another text reads *quia*, “because.”
8. The angry person “thought” that being troubled incurred guilt, *aestimabat*; another text has *aestimat*, “thinks.”
9. Lawful union is *legitimam carnis copulam*, “a lawful union of flesh”; another text has *legitima copula*, “lawful union.”
10. One uses *suam conjugem*, “his wife”; another text prints the ablative *sua conjuge*, “with his wife.”
11. The paired conjunction is *sive … seu*, “whether … or”; another text repeats *sive*.
12. The desire for offspring has the corrupt alternatives *ortandi*, *ortandae*, *optandae*, *oriendae*, and *procreandae sobolis*, suggesting offspring “to be raised,” “arising,” “to be desired,” “to arise,” or, most plainly, “to be begotten.” [Col. 0065D]
13. With Paul’s quotation another text adds *Corinthiis scribens*, “writing to the Corinthians.”
14. “Hence also” is *Hinc etiam*; another text reads *etenim*, “for indeed.”
15. In an involuntary nocturnal emission the phrase is *animum nescientem*, “the unknowing mind”; another text has *animus nesciens*, “the mind, unaware.”
16. The event is *dolendum*, “to be grieved over”; another text has *dolendus*, “the sufferer is to be pitied.” [Col. 0066D]
17. Other priests may fulfill the *ministerium*, “ministry”; another text reads *mysterium*, “mystery or sacramental rite.”
18. A shameful *imaginatione*, “image or imagining,” may shake the sleeping mind; another text reads *suggestione*, “suggestion or prompting.” [Col. 0067A]
19. Although the flesh cannot *delectare*, “give pleasure,” without the mind, another text has *delectari*, “be delighted.” [Col. 0067C]
20. The mind resists “lest it consent,” *ne consentiat*; another text reads “and does not consent,” *nec consentiat*.
21. It groans that it is bound *vehementer*, “violently”; another text omits “violently.”
22. The difficult sentence reads *et pugnabat igitur*, “and he was fighting, therefore”; another text punctuates and expands it as *et pugnabat. Repugnabat igitur*, “and he was fighting. Therefore he was resisting the law of the mind.”
23. Augustine is to “refresh him with the good of his consolation,” *bono refoveat*; another text has “cherish him with the honor of his consolation,” *honore foveat*. [Col. 0068C]
24. Gregory plans, *Domino favente*, “with the Lord favoring,” to grant the pallium; another text has *faciente*, “with the Lord bringing it about.” [Col. 0069D]
25. The bishops “of the cities of London and York,” *Lundoniae et Eburacae civitatis*, are alternatively styled *Londoniensis et Eboracensis*, “the bishop of London and the bishop of York.”
26. Those subject to the bishop are to receive a *formam*, “pattern,” of right faith and life; another text has *normam*, “rule.” [Col. 0070B]
27. The heading says Gregory “sent” (*misit*) a letter to Mellitus; another text has *miserit*, “that he sent.”
28. In the greeting to Augustine another witness preserves only *…tissimum fratrem*, a defective ending corresponding to “most reverend brother.”
29. Pagan temples are to be converted *in obsequio veri Dei*, “to the service of the true God”; another text has *in obsequia*, “into acts of service.” [Col. 0070D]
30. The solemnity may occur on the dedication or *natalitii*, “feast,” of the martyrs; another text has plural *natalitiis*, “feast days.” [Col. 0071A]
31. The people are no longer to sacrifice animals to the devil “and” (*nec*) are to kill them for food in praise of God; another text has *sed*, “but,” making the contrast explicit.
32. It is impossible to cut everything away at once: *abscidere* is alternatively the synonymous *abscindere*.
33. A weak mind may be raised *foras*, “outwardly,” in honor; another text has *foris*, “outside.” [Col. 0071D]
34. The gift of miracles was given not to Augustine but to those whose salvation it served; another text adds *eis*, explicitly “given to them.” [Col. 0072B]
35. Gregory sent a letter and gifts to King Æthelberht; another text adds *et*, “also,” before the king.
36. The gifts were *perplura*, “very many”; another text reads *perpulcra*, “very beautiful.”
37. The king is to discipline his subjects’ morals *et magna vitae munditia*, “and by great purity of life”; another text has *ex magna vitae munditia*, “from great purity of life.”
38. Constantine subjected the nations with himself to Christ and turned wholly to *eum*, “him”; another text reads *Deum*, “God.” [Col. 0073A]
39. Augustine was *edoctus*, “thoroughly instructed,” in the monastic rule; another text has *doctus*, “instructed.”
40. Almighty God *exaudit*, “hears,” him praying for you; another text has future *exaudiet*, “will hear.”
41. “When” (*quando*) can God hear him for you if you neglect him? Another text reads *quomodo*, “how can” God hear him?
42. Support his *adnisum*, “effort”; another text divides the form *ad nisum*, “toward the effort.”
43. The imperative is *adjuvate*, “support his effort”; another text has *adjuvante*, “with the power/divinity helping,” changing the construction.
44. You are to cause Christ’s faith to be received, *faciatis*; another text has indicative *facitis*, “you cause it to be received.”
45. Portents will occur contrary to the *ordinationem temporum*, “appointed arrangement of the seasons”; another text has *ordinem temporum*, “order of the seasons.”
46. Augustine recovered the church made by the work of *antiquo Romanorum fidelium*, “an ancient faithful Roman”; another text reads *antiquorum Romanorum fidelium*, “the faithful Romans of old.” [Col. 0073D]
47. He *ditavit* the church, “enriched it”; another text has *dotavit*, “endowed it.”

Six editorial notes absent from the earlier draft are restored in source order:

- [Col. 0068D] “The letter which he mentions.” Namely, in the preceding chapter, in the seventh response: how Augustine should deal with the bishops of Gaul and Britain.
- [Col. 0069D] “Things pertaining to worship.” A book of Trinity Hall, Cambridge, treats these matters specifically; Wanley supplied a transcript from its books in his *Catalogue of Manuscripts*, page 172. See it newly edited in the Appendix, no. 7.
- [Col. 0071D] “The people.” Most common and old editions read *gente*, “among or by the people,” but More’s manuscript and Chiffletius read *gentem*, “the people” as direct object.
- [Col. 0072D] “Hasten … zeal.” For how greatly Gregory regretted this, see above in the letter to Mellitus.
- [Col. 0073D] “Monastery.” Manuscript A.T.C. and others mention an ancient shrine and the church of Saint Pancras, also giving the reason drawn from the name why Augustine dedicated a church to that saint. But Bede says nothing of them, nor indeed do Æthelberht’s charters.
- [Col. 0073D] “Peter and Paul.” From Dunstan’s time the name Augustine was added to this name of the apostles, and in common usage it absorbed the older designation.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### How King Aethelfrid of the Northumbrians, crushing the peoples of the Scots in battle, drove them from the territories of the English

At this time the very powerful and glory-loving king Aethelfrid ruled the kingdom of the Northumbrians. More than all the leading men of the English, he devastated the nation of the Britons, so that he seemed comparable to Saul, once king of the Israelite nation—except only that he was ignorant of divine religion. For no tribune and no king had ever made more of their lands, after exterminating or subjugating the natives, either tributary to the English nation or habitable.

To him, deservedly, could be applied what the patriarch said when blessing his son, speaking in the person of Saul: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will devour the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoil.”

Moved by his successes, Aedan [Chiffl.: Edam], king of the Scots who inhabit Britain, came against him with a vast and powerful army; but, defeated, he fled with only a few survivors. Indeed, at the celebrated place called Degsastan—that is, “Degsa’s Stone”—almost his entire army was slaughtered.

In that battle also Theodbald [Al.: Theobaldus], Aethelfrid’s brother, was killed together with the whole army that he commanded. Aethelfrid completed this war in the year 603 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eleventh year of his reign, which lasted twenty-four years; and in the first year of Phocas, who then held the summit of Roman power.

[Note: Degsastan. This place, so famous in Bede’s age, is unknown today. There are several towns in that region whose names make them plausible locations for this battle. The editor of the *Anglo-Saxon Annals* places it at Dalston, near Carlisle; the bishop of Carlisle at Dawston, near Jedburgh.]

[Note: Neither thereafter did any king. Fordun, III.31, says that Eugene, Aedan’s son, succeeded in the year 106 and “harassed the regions of the Saxons, and sometimes those of the Picts, with severe incursions.” But this contradicts Bede, who attests to the Scots’ peace up to the year 731, in which he himself lived. See V.24.]

From that time onward, no king of the Scots dared to come into battle in Britain against the English nation, down to the present day.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0075]

## CHAPTER I  
### On the death of the blessed Pope Gregory

[Col. 0075C]

At this time—that is, in the year 605 of the Lord’s Incarnation—the blessed Pope Gregory died,

[Note: Fifth. In the eighth indiction; see the *Chronicle* under Phocas. Paul the Deacon, following Bede, likewise gives this in Book IV of his *History of the Lombards*. John the Deacon and most others put it in 604, indiction 7. He died at the beginning of March, which, by Julian reckoning, falls in 605. Florence of Worcester, Matthew of Westminster, and the manuscripts A, T, C agree on 605, placing Saint Gregory’s death on the fourth day before the Ides of March, Friday.] after having governed the Roman and apostolic Church with the greatest glory for thirteen years, six months, and ten days,

[Note: Ten. That is, counting the days of his consecration and death.]

and was transferred to the eternal seat of the heavenly kingdom.

Because through his efforts he converted our nation—that is, the nation of the English—from the power of Satan to the faith of Christ, it is fitting for us to speak of him at greater length in our *Ecclesiastical History*. We may rightly and ought to call him our apostle. For although he held the pontificate throughout the whole world and had long presided over Churches already converted to the faith of truth, he made our nation, until then enslaved to idols, into the Church of Christ. Thus we may appropriately apply to him the apostolic saying: “Though he is not an apostle to others, yet he is to us; for we are the seal of his apostleship in the Lord.”

He was Roman by birth, descended from his father Gordianus from ancestors who were not only noble but also religious. Finally, Felix, once bishop of the same apostolic see, a man of great renown in Christ and in the Church, was his great-great-grandfather.

[Note: Felix. John the Deacon writes “the Fourth,” as does the Roman Martyrology before Baronius’s correction, which prefers “the Third,” though on weak arguments.]

[Note: Great-great-grandfather. This need not be understood strictly as the father of a great-grandfather, and grandfather of a great-grandfather; the word may signify one of the ancestors without regard to degree or blood relationship.]

[Note: “That nobility.” From this point Paul the Deacon copied almost all Bede’s words in his *Life of Gregory*; John likewise did so with a few changes, although he says that, with the pope’s permission, he followed the authority of the papal archives in nearly everything.]

Gregory himself also practiced the nobility of religion with no less strength of devotion than did his parents and relatives. He turned wholly, by the generosity of divine grace, toward attaining the glory of heavenly dignity—that nobility which he seemed to possess in worldly terms. For, suddenly changing his secular clothing, he entered a monastery, where he began to live with such perfection of grace that, as he later used to testify with tears, all passing things lay beneath his mind; he rose above all things that turn and change; he was accustomed to think of nothing except heavenly things; and, although still confined in the body, he already passed beyond the prison of the flesh through contemplation. He even came to love death—which is nearly everyone’s punishment—as the entrance into life and the reward of his labor.

[Note: “As he himself later used to testify, with his Peter.” In the preface to the *Dialogues*. He writes similarly in the preface to the *Moralia* addressed to Leander, and in Book I, letters 4, 5, 6, and elsewhere.]

He was accustomed to speak of this not by boasting of his progress in virtue, but rather by lamenting the decline which he seemed to have incurred through pastoral care. Once, in private conversation with his deacon Peter, after enumerating his former spiritual virtues, he immediately added sorrowfully:

> “But now, because of the opportunity afforded by pastoral care, my mind suffers the affairs of secular people, and, after so beautiful an appearance of quiet, is stained by the dust of earthly activity. When it has scattered itself outward because of the descent of many, even when it desires inward things it undoubtedly returns to them diminished. Thus I consider what I endure; I consider what I have lost. And while I look upon what I have lost, what I carry becomes heavier.”

This the holy man said out of profound humility. We ought nevertheless to believe that he lost nothing of monastic perfection through the demands of pastoral care; rather, he then gained a greater advancement from the labor of converting many than he had formerly gained from the quiet of his own way of life.

This is especially so because, even while exercising the pontifical office, he took care to make his own house a monastery; and when, first withdrawn from the monastery, he had been ordained to the ministry of the altar and sent from the apostolic see to Constantinople as *apocrisiarius*,

[Note: His house. Under the patronage of Saint Andrew the Apostle, beside the basilica of Saints John and Paul at the Clivus Scauri on the Caelian Hill.]

[Note: *Apocrisiarius*. A representative and administrator of affairs. He was sent by Pope Pelagius II to Tiberius Constantine Augustus. At that time two matters especially troubled the Roman Church and all Italy: the schism over the Three Chapters and the Lombard war.]

he nevertheless did not interrupt his purpose of heavenly life while living in an earthly palace. He began to keep with him, as a protection for regular observance, certain brothers from his monastery who had followed him to the imperial city out of the grace of brotherly love. Their example, as he himself writes, continually bound him, as though with an anchor-rope, to the calm shore of prayer whenever he was tossed by the unceasing surge of secular affairs; and among them he daily strengthened his mind, shaken by worldly activities, through the disciplined discourse of reading.

Through their companionship he was not only protected from earthly attacks but also increasingly inflamed for the practices of heavenly life.

For they urged him to expound mystically the book of blessed Job, which was wrapped in great obscurities. He could not refuse a work which brotherly affection imposed upon him as something that would be useful to many. He therefore explained, in thirty-five books and with admirable method, how that book should be understood according to the literal sense, how it should be referred to the mysteries of Christ and the Church, and in what sense it should be applied to each of the faithful.

He began this work while serving as *apocrisiarius* in the imperial city and completed it after becoming pope at Rome.

While he was stationed in the imperial city, he crushed, with the help of the grace of Catholic truth, a new heresy that had arisen there concerning the condition of our resurrection, attacking it from the very beginning of its origin. For Eutychius, bishop of that city, taught that our body in the glory of the resurrection would be intangible, more subtle than winds and air. When Gregory heard this, he proved, both by reasoning from the truth and by the example of the Lord’s resurrection, that this doctrine was entirely contrary to orthodox faith.

Catholic faith teaches that our body, exalted in that glory of immortality, is indeed subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the reality of its nature, in accordance with the example of the Lord’s body. Of that body, raised from the dead, he himself says to the disciples: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

In defending this faith, the venerable Father Gregory labored so earnestly against the rising heresy, and with the assistance also of the most devout emperor Tiberius Constantine so shattered it,

[Note: With the help. See the *Chronicon*, no. 4536.]

that thereafter no one was found to revive it.

He also composed another excellent book called *The Pastoral Rule*, in which he clearly revealed what sort of men should be admitted to the government of the Church, how those rulers ought to live, with what discernment they should instruct each of their hearers individually, and with how much consideration they ought daily to weigh their own weakness.

He also composed forty homilies on the Gospel, which he divided equally between two books. He wrote four books of *Dialogues*, in which, at the request of his deacon Peter, he collected for the example of posterity the deeds of the saints whom he could learn about or hear of as the most renowned in Italy. Thus, just as in his books of exposition he taught what virtues should be earnestly pursued, so by recording the miracles of the saints he showed the splendor possessed by those same virtues.

He also demonstrated, in twenty-two homilies, how much inner light was contained in the first and last parts of the prophet Ezekiel, which seemed to be more obscure.

Besides the little book of *Responses*, which he wrote in answer to the questions of Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English nation—as we have already explained, inserting the whole booklet into this history—

[Note: The synodical booklet. Written, according to the custom of the Church, to the other patriarchs. See this booklet in John the Deacon’s *Life of Gregory*, Book II, section 3. Several such examples from other pontiffs may be found in the *Book of the Roman Pontiff’s Daily Register*, p. 26 and elsewhere.]

[Note: “Which with bishops.” Manuscript Mori reads “which [he composed] with bishops”; other witnesses read “with fellow bishops.”]

he also composed a synodical booklet with the bishops of Italy concerning the Church’s necessary affairs, and letters to various friends.

It is all the more remarkable that he was able to produce so many and such substantial volumes because for nearly the whole period of his youth, to use his own words, he was tormented by frequent pains in his vital organs; at every hour and moment he grew weary from the weakened strength of his stomach; and he suffered from slow but continuous fevers. Yet amid these afflictions, while he attentively considered that, according to the testimony of Scripture, “Every son who is received is scourged,” the more harshly he was pressed down by present evils, the more confidently he breathed in expectation of eternal things.

These things may be said of his immortal intellect, which so great bodily pain could neither extinguish nor restrain.

[Al.: restrict.]

Other pontiffs devoted themselves to building and adorning churches with gold or silver; but he gave himself entirely to the gain of souls.

Whatever money he possessed, he diligently took care to distribute and give to the poor, so that “his righteousness might remain for ever and ever, and his horn be exalted in glory.” Thus he could truthfully say the words of blessed Job:

> “The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I clothed myself with righteousness, and I covered myself with it as with a garment and a diadem, according to my judgment. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case which I did not know I investigated with the greatest diligence. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job 29:11, 17).

And shortly afterward:

> “If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it—for from my infancy compassion grew with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb” (Job 31:17–18).

To the work of this piety and righteousness also belongs the fact that, by means of the preachers whom he sent here, he snatched our nation from the teeth of the ancient enemy and made it a participant in eternal freedom. Rejoicing in its faith and salvation, and commending it with worthy praise, he himself said in his *Exposition of Job*:

[Note: He said this in the *Exposition of Job*, Book XXVII, chapter 8.]

> “Behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to roar barbarously, has already begun to sound Hebrew ‘Alleluia’ in divine praises. Behold, the once-swollen Ocean, now subdued, serves beneath the feet of the saints; and its barbarous waves, which earthly rulers could not tame with the sword, priests restrain through the fear of God by simple words. The man who, while unbelieving, had no fear whatsoever of the armies of combatants now, as a believer, fears the tongues of the humble.
>
> “For when heavenly words have been received and miracles have also shone forth, the power of divine knowledge is poured into him; he is restrained by terror of that same divinity, so that he fears to act perversely and longs with all his desires to come to the grace of eternity.”

By these words blessed Gregory also makes clear that Saint Augustine and his companions led the English nation to knowledge of the truth not by preaching words alone, but also by displaying heavenly signs.

Among other things, blessed Pope Gregory arranged for Masses to be celebrated over the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in their churches.

[Note: Over their bodies. After acquiring very numerous olive groves, and so forth. See John the Deacon, I, section 20.]

At the celebration of the Masses themselves he also added three words full of the greatest perfection:

[Note: “He added.” John the Deacon, Book II, §17. Pope Gelasius revised the ancient Missal, and Gregory the Gelasian Missal; from it arose the *Book of Sacraments*, in which he appended these words to the canon.]

> “And order our days in your peace; rescue us from eternal damnation; and command us to be numbered among your elect.”

[Note: Another version adds, “Through Christ our Lord.”]

He governed the Church during the reigns of the emperors Maurice and Phocas. In the second year of Phocas, passing from this life, he migrated to the true life that is in heaven.

His body was buried in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, before the sacristy, on the fourth day before the Ides of March. At the end of time he will rise in glory there with the other pastors of the holy Church. The following epitaph was written on his tomb:

> Receive, O earth, this body taken from a body,  
> which you may be able to restore through God, the giver of life.  
> The spirit seeks the stars; the laws of death will harm nothing  
> that regards death itself as the way to another life.  
>   
> Here in this tomb are enclosed the limbs of the supreme pontiff,  
> who always lives everywhere through innumerable good works.  
> He overcame hunger with food and cold with clothing,  
> and by sacred admonitions shielded souls from the enemy.  
>   
> He fulfilled by his actions whatever he taught in speech,  
> so that, speaking mystical words, he might be an example.  
> With pious guidance he converted the English to Christ,  
> gaining to the faith a multitude from a new nation.  
>   
> This was your labor, this your devotion, this your care, O shepherd:  
> to offer to the Lord the abundant gains of the flock.  
> And now, made God’s consul, rejoice in these triumphs,  
> for you already possess the reward of your works without end.

[Note: “Nor should it be passed over in silence.” Manuscript Barlow begins Chapter 2 here.]

Nor should the tradition concerning blessed Gregory, handed down from our ancestors to our own day, be passed over in silence. It explains the reason why he showed such diligent concern for the salvation of our nation.

They say that one day, when many goods for sale had recently been brought into the marketplace by arriving merchants and many people had gathered to buy them, Gregory himself came among the others and saw, among the merchandise, boys being offered for sale. They had fair bodies, handsome faces, and remarkably beautiful hair.

[Note: Boys. In many places in the Low Countries there still survives the custom of having boys enter school on Saint Gregory’s feast to learn the alphabet; Saint Gregory is regarded there as the patron of those learning letters.]

When he saw them, they say, he asked from what region or land they had been brought. He was told that they came from the island of Britain, whose inhabitants had such an appearance.

Again he asked whether those islanders were Christians or were still entangled in pagan errors. He was told that they were pagans.

Then, drawing a long sigh from the depths of his heart, he said: “Alas, what grief, that people of such a bright appearance should be possessed by the author of darkness, and that such grace of countenance should bear a mind empty of inward grace!”

Again he asked what the name of that nation was. He was told that they were called Angles.

Then he said: “Good—for they have an angelic appearance, and such people ought to be fellow-heirs of the angels in heaven.”

[Note: Angelic. Some confirmation is lent to this tradition by the fact that, when Gregory himself had set out to convert the English, he was recalled by the arrival of a *locusta* (“locust”), whose name suggested *loco standum esse* (“that he ought to remain in place”). John the Deacon records this seriously. See Book I, section 24.]

“What is the name of the province from which these have been brought?” he asked.

He was told that the people of that province were called Deiri.

“Good,” he said, “Deiri—from *de ira*, ‘rescued from wrath’ and called to the mercy of Christ. What is the king of that province called?”

He was told that he was called Aella [Al.: Elle, Aelle, Alle, Ealle].

Playing upon the name, he said: “Alleluia! The praise of God the Creator ought to be sung in those regions.”

[Note: Pontiff. Paul the Deacon identifies him as Pelagius; John the Deacon as Benedict, Pelagius’s predecessor.]

He approached the pontiff of the Roman and apostolic see—for he had not yet himself become pontiff—and asked him to send some ministers of the word to the English nation in Britain, through whom it might be converted to Christ. He declared himself ready, with the Lord’s help, to complete this work, if the apostolic pope approved it.

He was unable to carry this out at that time. Although the pontiff wished to grant what he had requested, the Roman citizens could not allow him to withdraw so far from the City. As soon as Gregory himself had assumed the pontifical office, he completed the work he had long desired: he sent other preachers, while assisting their preaching so that it might bear fruit through his own exhortations and prayers.

[Note: Prayers. Indeed, also with money. From his small patrimony—whose collection he entrusted to Candidus, as stated in Book I, chapter 24—and from letters to Aetherius and other letters, it is clear that a considerable part was spent on purchasing the children of pagans so that they might be raised for Christ.]

We have thought it appropriate to insert these matters into our ecclesiastical history according to the tradition we received from the ancients.

## CHAPTER II  
### How Augustine, bishop of the Britons, urged them to Catholic peace—even by a heavenly miracle performed before them—and what punishment followed their rejection of his counsel

[DCIII.]

[Note: Meanwhile. Bede does not give the year of this synod. Ranulf of Chester places it in 599, Spelman in 601, Sigebert in 602, and Florence of Worcester in 603. Since Bede assigns it a place after the battle of Degsastan, which occurred in 603, I cannot place this synod earlier than that year.]

Meanwhile Augustine, with the assistance of King Aethelberht, summoned to a conference with him the bishops or teachers of the neighboring province of the Britons,

[Note: Bishops or teachers. See II.14, where he gave his teacher and bishop his episcopal see.]

at a place which to this day in the English language is called Augustine’s Oak—that is, “Augustine’s Oak”—on the boundary between the Hwiccas [Al.: Huicti, Uuicti, Vect] and the West Saxons. He began to persuade them by brotherly admonition to maintain Catholic peace with him and undertake together, for the Lord, the labor of evangelizing the nations.

[Note: Augustine’s Oak. Most people seek a village here: Ausrick, according to Spelman; Ossentree, according to Hammond; Ake or Rock, according to Tomkins. Two letters by Tomkins on this matter may be seen in Corpus Christi College, Oxford, among Fulman’s collections, vol. II. It seems, however, that this conference was held not in any village but in the open air, beneath some notable oak. Our ancestors were accustomed to assemble in this way, not from superstition but to allow the people freer access.]

For they did not celebrate the Lord’s day of Easter at its proper time, but from the fourteenth to the twentieth day of the moon; this calculation is contained within an eighty-four-year cycle. They also practiced many other things contrary to ecclesiastical unity.

[Note: Easter. On this controversy, see Appendix IX.]

After a lengthy discussion, they refused to yield either to the prayers, exhortations, or rebukes of Augustine and his companions. Instead, they preferred their own traditions to all the Churches throughout the world that were united with them in Christ.

The holy Father Augustine therefore brought this laborious and prolonged dispute to an end by saying:

> “Let us entreat God, who makes those who are of one mind dwell in the house of his Father, that he himself may deign to show us by heavenly signs which tradition ought to be followed and by what paths we should hasten to enter his kingdom. Let someone who is ill be brought forward, and let the faith and work devoted to God of the person by whose prayers he is healed be regarded as true and to be followed by all.”

Although unwillingly, the adversaries consented to this. A man of English birth who had been deprived of the sight of his eyes was brought forward. When he was presented to the British priests, he received no cure or healing through their ministry. At last Augustine, compelled by righteous necessity, bent his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He prayed that he would restore the sight which the blind man had lost, and that, through the bodily illumination of one man, he would kindle the grace of spiritual light in the hearts of many believers.

Without delay the blind man was given sight, and Augustine was proclaimed by everyone a true herald of the highest light.

Then the Britons admitted that they understood Augustine’s teaching to be the true way of righteousness, but said that they could not abandon their ancient customs without the agreement and permission of their own people. They therefore requested that a second synod be held, with more people attending.

When this had been arranged, seven British bishops and many highly learned men came, as is reported,

[Note: Seven. There are authors who identify episcopal sees suitable to this number: Llandaff, or Taff, also called Morgannwg from the county; Saint Asaph, or Llan-Elwy; Saint Padarn in Cardiganshire, later included within the see of Menevia; Bangor; Chester; Hen, or Hereford; and the Hwiccan see, or Worcester. Saint Kebius and Guentonia could also be added if we do not wish to wander beyond the Severn. Indeed, among so many catalogues, why do we not see Caerleon, the mother of them all, which later withdrew to Menevia? Its bishop is said not to have attended Augustine’s synod, evidently guarding his metropolitan right. That would be a reasonable explanation for his absence, but also a reasonable argument for his presence. Bede says nothing about this matter, and I think nothing should be inferred from it except that historians of later times chose to establish seven bishops besides the metropolitan.]

especially from their most renowned monastery, called in the English language Bancornaburg.

[Note: Bancornaburg. Near the River Dee, not far from Chester, commonly Bangor-is-y-Coed, “Bangor beneath the Wood,” to distinguish it from Bangor on the Menai or Strait of Menevia, where the episcopal see is located. William of Malmesbury records extensive remains of the Bancornian monastery in his own day, although they have almost entirely disappeared. I suspect, however, that a considerable part of them belonged to the ancient fort of Bonium, because Roman coins have been unearthed there.]

At that time Dinoot [Al.: Dinooth] is said to have presided over the monastery. As they were on their way to the council mentioned above, they first went to a certain holy and prudent man who habitually lived an anchorite’s life among them, and asked him whether they ought to abandon their traditions at Augustine’s preaching.

He replied: “If he is a man of God, follow him.”

They said: “How can we prove that?”

He answered: “The Lord says, ‘Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). Therefore, if that Augustine is gentle and humble in heart, it is believable that he himself also bears Christ’s yoke and offers it to you to bear. But if he is harsh and proud, it is clear that he is not from God, and that we should pay no attention to his teaching.”

They asked again: “And how can we recognize this?”

“Arrange,” he replied, “for him to arrive first with his companions at the place of the synod. If he rises when you approach, know that he is Christ’s servant and listen obediently to him. But if he despises you and refuses to rise before you, although you are more numerous, let him be despised by you.”

They did as he had said. When they arrived, Augustine was sitting in a chair. Seeing this, they immediately turned to anger, accused him of pride, and strove to contradict everything he said.

He said to them:

> “In many matters you act contrary to our custom, indeed to that of the universal Church. Yet, if you are willing to obey me in these three things—celebrating Easter at its proper time; completing the ministry of baptism, through which we are reborn to God, according to the custom of the holy Roman and apostolic Church; and preaching the word of the Lord to the English nation together with us—we shall patiently tolerate all the other things you do, although they are contrary to our customs.”

[Note: But they. On this reply, see Appendix X.]

They replied that they would do none of these things and would not recognize him as archbishop. They said among themselves: “If he would not rise for us now, how much more will he despise us as worthless once we begin to submit to him?”

The man of God Augustine is said to have foretold to them with a threat that, if they refused to accept peace with their brothers, they would receive war from their enemies; and if they refused to preach the way of life to the English nation, they would suffer the vengeance of death at their hands.

This was accomplished in every respect as he had foretold, by the judgment of God.

For afterward the very powerful English king whom we mentioned, Aethelfrid, gathered a large army and inflicted a great slaughter upon that faithless nation at the city of the Legions, which the English call Legacaestir but which the Britons more correctly call Carlegion.

[Note: Carlegion. On the Dee, commonly Westchester. The city of the same name on the Usk lay far to the south and was held by the Britons as a metropolitan city.]

[DCXIII.]

When he saw, as he was preparing for battle, their priests standing apart in a safer place—priests who had gathered to pray to God for the army engaged in battle—he asked who they were and what they had assembled there to do.

Many of them were from the monastery of Bancor. It is said that the number of monks there was so great that, although the monastery was divided into seven portions with superiors governing them, none of those portions contained fewer than three hundred men, all of whom customarily lived from the labor of their hands.

[Note: Such a number. It should also be noted that there was another monastery called Bangor in Ulster, Ireland, near the Bay of Fergus, commonly Cnocfergus. Saint Bernard describes it in the *Life of Saint Malachy* as having both a number of monks and other circumstances so similar that it is plainly evident that one was the model of the other.]

Many of these men had come to the battle line mentioned above, after completing a three-day fast, together with the others for the sake of prayer. They had as their protector a man named Brocmail, who guarded them from the swords of the barbarians while they remained intent upon prayer.

When King Aethelfrid understood the reason for their arrival, he said:

> “Therefore, if they cry out to their God against us, then surely, although they carry no weapons, they are fighting against us, since they pursue us with hostile prayers.”

He therefore ordered the weapons to be turned first against them, and then destroyed the remaining forces of the accursed army, though not without great loss to his own army.

It is said that about twelve hundred of those who had come to pray were killed in that battle, and that only fifty escaped by flight. At the first arrival of the enemy, Brocmail turned his back with his men and abandoned to the striking swords those whom he ought to have defended, unarmed and exposed.

Thus the prophecy of the holy pontiff Augustine was fulfilled, although he had long before been taken up to the heavenly kingdom: the faithless men who had rejected the counsels of perpetual salvation offered to them were made to experience even temporal destruction as punishment.

[Note: Although he had already been taken up to the heavenly kingdom long before. This clause is not found in the Saxon paraphrase. Many therefore conclude that it was interpolated after the time of King Alfred in order to remove the stain of the massacre of the Banchor monks, which might have been attributed to Augustine had he still been alive. See those who have argued on both sides of the matter for other considerations. As for the reading, I can and ought to state that in all the Latin manuscripts I have examined I have never found one lacking this clause, and that without any suspicion of error or fraud. I also see Wheloc testify to the same concerning the three manuscripts he possessed, in a letter to Mr. Simmons Dewes dated 26 January 1639, preserved in the *Most Ample Treasury* of the Honorable Robert, Earl of Oxford. Since Augustine’s threats are there noted as carrying some blame, he answers the question concerning the monks’ massacre: “I do not know; but nothing should be inferred from the Saxon omission, since it is the Paraphrast’s custom in almost every line to remove something and occasionally to add something.” Thus he.]

## CHAPTER III  
### How he made Mellitus and Justus bishops, and concerning his death

[Col. 0085A]

### Editorial variants and readings omitted above

- At the comparison with Saul, *in personam* has the alternative *persona* (“in the person [of Saul]”); Aedan is alternatively *Edam*, and Theodbald alternatively *Theobaldus*.
- In the Gregory chapter, *denique* is alternatively *deinde* (“then”); *Haec* (“these things”) replaces *Hoc* (“this”); and the quotation beginning “But now” has the longer alternative opening, “But now my unhappy mind …” The source also reads *magnae* with the alternative *magna*, and *propriae* with *propria*.
- *Apocrisiarius* is alternatively spelled *apocrisarius*; the work on Job is said alternatively to have been *implevit* (“completed”) rather than *explevit*; and some witnesses add *in* before “that glory of immortality.” The form *omelias* has the alternative *homilias*.
- In the quotation from Gregory’s *Exposition of Job*, *infidelis* (“an unbeliever,” singular) has the alternative *infideles* (“unbelievers”); *perceptis caelestibus verbis* (“after heavenly words have been received”) has *praeceptis* (“after heavenly commands have been received”); and *gratiam aeternitatis* (“the grace of eternity”) has *gloriam* (“the glory of eternity”). “Churches of the holy apostles” has the alternative “Churches of the blessed apostles.”
- The Mass prayer has the additional ending in some witnesses: “Through Christ our Lord.” In “He governed the Church during the reigns of the emperors Maurice and Phocas,” some witnesses omit “of the emperors.”
- In the epitaph, “converted the English to Christ” has the alternative word order, “turned the English to Christ”; *fidei* (“to the faith”) is printed in John the Deacon’s edition as *fideique* (“and to the faith”).
- At Augustine’s Oak, the readings are *Huicciorum*, alternatively *Huictiorum*, *Uuicti*, or *Vect.* The Easter sentence has *ecclesiasticae unitati* (“ecclesiastical unity”) with the alternative *Ecclesiae unitati* (“unity of the Church”). In Augustine’s appeal, *habitare facit* (“makes dwell”) has *fecit* (“made dwell”); “in the heart” has the alternative “in the hearts”; and “the grace of spiritual light” has “the light of spiritual grace.” The request for a second synod has the grammatical alternative *secunda* for *secundo*.
- Dinoot is alternatively *Dinooth*. In the anchorite’s words, “offers it to you to bear” has the alternative “offers it to us to bear”; and “we should pay no attention to his teaching” has the added *est* in some witnesses. The Britons’ first response is introduced by *At illi* (“but they”), and the note on that response refers to Appendix 10.
- Augustine’s three requests include the variant spellings and forms preserved in the source: “Easter at its proper time,” “the ministry of baptism,” and “the holy Roman and apostolic Church.” In the final sentence, *ultione* has the alternative accusative *ultionem* (“vengeance”).
- The source’s note on the Bangor monastery identifies the Ulster site more exactly as being near the Bay of Fergus’s Rock (*sinus Petrae Fergusianae*), commonly Cnocfergus. The final textual note’s “Banchor monks” represents the printed form *Banchorenstum*.

## CHAPTER III  
### How he made Mellitus and Justus bishops, and concerning his death

[Col. 0085A]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 604, Augustine, archbishop of the Britons, ordained two bishops, namely Mellitus and Justus. Mellitus was appointed to preach to the province of the East Saxons, who are separated from Kent by the River Thames and border the eastern sea. Their capital is the city of London, situated on the bank of that river and itself a marketplace for many peoples arriving by land and sea. At that time Sabert, nephew on his sister’s side of Æthelberht, was ruling among this people, although he was subject to the authority of Æthelberht, who, as stated above, ruled over all the nations of the Angles as far as the River Humber. When this province too had received the word of truth through Mellitus’s preaching, King Æthelberht built in the city of London a church of Saint Paul the Apostle, in which he and his successors might have the seat of an episcopal see.

Justus, however, Augustine ordained bishop in Kent itself, in the city of Durobrivae, which the English people called Hrofaescaestrae, after the first ruler of that place, who was called Hrof.

[Note: Hrof. Harpsfeld says of this name: “That family, or at least one of the same name, still remains among the people of Kent,” p. 67. In the ancient Itinerary the name of the place is Durobrovis. Ancient charters written in the Hroffensis text six hundred years ago have Hrofbrevi, city of Roibi. In the Peutinger Tables of military stations: Roibis.]

[Note: *Saint Andrew.* With reference to the monastery from which Augustine and his companions were sent to preach.]

It lies approximately twenty-four miles west of Durovernum. There King Æthelberht built a church of the blessed apostle Andrew. He also offered many gifts to the bishops of both churches, just as he did to the church at Durovernum, and he added territories and possessions for the use of those who were with the bishops.

[Note: *He died.* Bede does not specify the year of Augustine’s death. Hence arose a variety of opinions, which there is no need to enumerate, since Bede has reduced the matter to a narrow interval. For in 604 Augustine ordained Mellitus and Justus bishops (II.3). In the eighth year of Phocas, the thirteenth indiction—that is, the year 610—Mellitus brought letters from Rome from Pope Boniface to Archbishop Laurence. Augustine’s life and death, therefore, must have fallen within this interval. Mabillon, from a table in *Cantuariensis Monasterii Anglicani*, I, p. 24, calculates the year as 607, adding the legend of Ely, according to which that church was founded by Augustine in 607. But this appears so fabulous that it does injury even to the Canterbury tradition.

The chronology of the monastery of Saint Augustine, which is appended without an author’s name to the chronicle of G. Thorn among the Ten Writers, but which comparison shows to have had T. Helmham as its author, if indeed it belonged to his manuscript A.T.C., gives the deaths of Gregory and Augustine in the same year: Gregory’s on the fourth day before the Ides of March, a Friday; Augustine’s on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, a Wednesday. The year, however, is 605. Wharton produces two arguments for 604, but one of them—namely, that concerning Gregory, which Wharton regards as certain—is directly opposed to Bede, who places Gregory’s death in 605. The other derives from a computational error in W. Thorn’s chronicle, *Ten Writers*, p. 1765, where Augustine’s death is placed on a Tuesday, although the chronology mentioned above, from which Thorn derived his calculation, clearly gives Wednesday, both in the edition of the Ten Writers, p. 2229, and in manuscript A.T.C. I therefore conclude that Augustine died in 605, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, a Wednesday.]

The beloved Father Augustine died [605], and his body was placed outside, beside the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul mentioned above, because that church had not yet been completed or dedicated.

[Note: *Dedicated.* The year was 613.]

As soon as it had been dedicated, however, his body was brought inside and decently buried in its northern portico.

[Note: *Buried.* In the same year.]

In that portico the bodies of all the succeeding archbishops were also buried, except for only two, Theodore and Berctuald, whose bodies were placed in the church itself, because the aforementioned portico could not contain more.

[Note: *Portico.* This portico was in the old church, where the chapel of the Blessed Virgin now stands. Thorn.]

Almost in its center stands an altar dedicated in honor of the blessed Pope Gregory. Every Saturday the solemn offices for him are celebrated there by the priest of that place.

[Note: *Offices.* So also in the Council of Clofesho in 747: “It was established by the seventeenth decree that the birthday of the blessed Pope Gregory, and also the day of his deposition, which is the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and likewise that of Saint Augustine, archbishop and confessor, who, sent to the English nation by the aforesaid pope and our father Gregory, first brought it knowledge of the faith, the sacrament of baptism, and knowledge of the heavenly homeland, should all be honored solemnly, as is fitting. Thus each day should be kept as a holiday by clergy and monks, and the name of that blessed Father and teacher of ours, Augustine, should always be spoken in the chanting of the Litany after the invocation of Saint Gregory.” Spelman, *Councils*, vol. I, p. 250.]

The following epitaph was inscribed on Augustine’s tomb:

> HERE RESTS THE LORD AUGUSTINE, FIRST ARCHBISHOP OF DUROVERNUM,
>
> Formerly sent here by the blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, and supported by God through the working of miracles, he led King Æthelberht and his people from the worship of idols to faith in Christ. Having completed in peace the days of his ministry, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, while that same king was reigning.

## CHAPTER IV  
### How Laurence, together with his fellow bishops, urged the Scots to follow the unity of the holy Church, especially in observing Easter; and how Mellitus came to Rome

[Column 0086C] Augustine was succeeded in the episcopate by Laurence [605], whom he had ordained while still alive precisely so that, after his death, the condition of the Church—still so new—orphaned even for an hour of its shepherd, might not begin to falter. In this he also followed the example of the first shepherd of the Church, namely the most blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, who is said, after founding the Church at Rome, to have consecrated Clement as his assistant in preaching the Gospel and at the same time as his successor.

After attaining the rank of archbishop, Laurence worked with the utmost energy to enlarge the foundations of the Church, which he had seen nobly laid, and to advance them toward the fullness of their proper height, both by frequent exhortation and by continual examples of godly conduct. Indeed, he cared not only for the newly gathered Church of the English, but also for the pastoral welfare of the ancient inhabitants of Britain and of the Scots who inhabit Ireland, an island close to Britain.

When he learned that the life and profession of the Scots in their homeland, and likewise those of the Britons in Britain itself, were in many respects less ecclesiastical than they should be—especially because they did not celebrate the solemnity of Easter at its proper time, but, as we have explained above, thought that it ought to be observed from the fourteenth moon to the twentieth, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection—he wrote, together with his fellow bishops, an exhortatory letter to them. He earnestly appealed to them and solemnly urged them to maintain the unity of peace and catholic observance with the Church of Christ spread throughout the whole world. The beginning of this letter is as follows:

[609]

> “To our most beloved lords and brothers, the bishops or abbots throughout all Scotland: Laurence, Mellitus, and Justus, bishops, servants of the servants of God.
>
> “When the Apostolic See sent us, according to its custom, as throughout all the lands of the world, to preach to pagan peoples in these western regions, and it happened that we entered this island which is now called Britain before we knew its circumstances, we believed that its inhabitants followed the custom of the universal Church. Accordingly, we held both the Britons and the Scots in great reverence for their holiness. But after learning more about the Britons, we judged the Scots to be better.
>
> “Yet through Bishop Daganus, when he came to this island which we mentioned above, and through Abbot Columbanus, who came among the Gauls, we learned that the Scots differ in no respect from the Britons in their manner of life. For Bishop Daganus, when he came to us, would neither eat with us nor even take food in the same lodging in which we were dining.”

[Note: *Daganus.* He was from the Irish monastery of Bangor and, as is reported, was sent as a bishop and representative of the Scots to confer with Laurence concerning matters disputed between the Churches. I believe that, while he was still only an abbot, he presented the rule of Saint Molua or Lugid to Pope Gregory, for the objections brought against this are insignificant. Bale also states that he wrote one book to the Churches of the Britons; had anyone seen it, we would possess fuller and more reliable information about Daganus.]

[Note: *Columbanus.* Columbanus retained these prejudices not only throughout Britain but also in Gaul. Indeed, his disciples clung stubbornly to the Irish tonsure and other Irish rites. Eustasius, his successor in the monastery of Luxeuil, defended the practice, but, conscious of the scandal, later labored to remove it and attempted to bring the rules of Saints Benedict and Columbanus into unity. Note that a Life of Columbanus was published at Basel and Cologne among the works of Bede, volume III, although Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, claims in his preface to be its author.]

Laurence also sent letters, worthy of his office, to the priests of the Britons, seeking to confirm them in catholic unity.

[Note: *But how much.* I do not know why some interpret this in a favorable sense.]

But how much he accomplished by these efforts is still shown by the present circumstances.

At this time Mellitus, bishop of London, came to Rome to discuss with Pope Boniface matters necessary for the Church of the English.

[Note: *Necessary matters.* Bede does not say what those matters were. Baronius supplies the omission from the legend of Saint Edward; see William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, II, near the beginning. He supposes that Mellitus went to consult about the validity of the consecration of Westminster church by the hands of the apostle Peter, but in my opinion this explains very little.]

When that same most reverend pope convened a synod of the bishops of Italy to establish regulations concerning the life and quiet of monks, Mellitus himself also sat among them, in the eighth year of the reign of the emperor Phocas, the thirteenth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of March [610], so that he might confirm by his own authority whatever had been decreed according to the rule, and, returning to Britain, carry with him instructions to be delivered to and observed by the Churches of the English. He also brought letters which the same pontiff addressed to Laurence, the beloved archbishop of God, and to all the clergy, and likewise to King Æthelberht and the English people.

[Note: *And when the same.* Mellitus’s arrival in connection with this synod appears entirely accidental. The life and quiet of the monks, concerning which the synod was compelled to legislate, affected the English Church no more than any other Church. But since Mellitus was present, he gave his vote and brought the decrees home, together with letters to Laurence and Æthelberht. See the synod’s decree and the letter to Æthelberht in the appendix, no. 11.]

This Boniface was the fourth bishop of Rome after the blessed Gregory. He obtained from the emperor Phocas that the temple in Rome which the ancients called the Pantheon, as though it were an image of all the gods, should be given to the Church of Christ. Having expelled all its impurity, he made it a church of the holy Mother of God and of all the martyrs of Christ, so that, once the multitude of demons had been excluded, a multitude of saints might possess there a memorial.

## CHAPTER V  
### How, after the deaths of Kings Æthelberht and Sabert, their successors revived idolatry, and how Mellitus and Justus consequently departed from Britain

[Note: *In the year of our Lord 616.* This is how it appears in manuscript Tr.; the printed edition erroneously gives 613, changing, as often happens, the symbol for six into that for three. The year 616 appears in the summary at the end of the *History*. King Alfred’s Saxon version cautiously gives approximately 616. Chifflet.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 616, which was the twenty-first year from the time when Augustine [the bishop] was sent with his companions to preach to the English people, King Æthelberht of Kent, after a temporal reign which he had held with great glory for fifty-six years,

[Note: *Fifty-six.* Other manuscripts have “fifty-three,” owing to the same confusion of numerals noted above.]

entered the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom. He was the third among the kings of the English nation to rule all their southern provinces—those separated from the northern provinces by the River Humber and the territories adjoining it—but he was the first of them all to ascend to the heavenly kingdom.

The first to hold such authority was Aelle, king of the South Saxons; the second was Cealin, king of the West Saxons, called Ceaulin in their language; the third, as I have said, was Æthelberht, king of Kent; the fourth was Reduald, king of the East Angles, who, even while Æthelberht was alive, exercised leadership over his own people; the fifth was Edwin, king of the Northumbrian people—that is, of those inhabiting the northern side of the River Humber—who ruled with greater power than all who inhabit Britain, both English and Britons, except only the people of Kent. He also subjected to English rule the islands called the Mevanias, belonging to the Britons and lying between Ireland and Britain; the sixth was Oswald, likewise king of the Northumbrians and a most Christian ruler, who held the kingdom within these same boundaries; the seventh was his brother Oswiu, who, ruling for some time over almost the same territory, also subdued for the most part and made tributary the peoples of the Picts and Scots who occupy the northern regions of Britain. But these matters will be treated later.

King Æthelberht died on the twenty-fourth day of February,

[Note: *Twenty-fourth.* Other manuscripts have “twenty-seventh,” owing to the same error mentioned above.]

after twenty-one years since he had received the faith. He was buried in the portico of Saint Martin, within the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, where Bertha was also buried.

Among the other benefits which he conferred on his people for their welfare, he also established legal decrees according to Roman models, with the counsel of wise men.

[Note: *Decrees.* These decrees still survive in the famous Rochester text left by Bishop Ernulf. Spelman published their beginning in *Councils*, I, p. 127. Hickes printed the remainder in his *Thesaurus*, *Dissertation on the Epistles*, p. 89. Elstob undertook a new edition but, overtaken by death, was forced to leave the distinguished work unfinished.]

They were written in the language of the English and are still preserved and observed. In them he first established how the person who stole anything belonging either to the Church, to a bishop, or to any other order should make restitution. He clearly wished to provide protection for those whose faith and teaching he had received.

Æthelberht was the son of Irminricus,

[Note: Other manuscripts have Hirminricus.]

whose father was Octa, whose father was Oeric,

[Note: Other manuscripts have Orric.]

surnamed Oisc, from whom the kings of Kent are customarily called Oiscingas.

[Note: *Oiscingas.* A Saxon patronymic, like Geuissing, Wodening, Aetheling, and so forth.]

His father was Hengist, who, together with his son Oisc, entered Britain first when invited by Vortigern,

[Note: Other manuscripts have Vurtigerius.]

as we related above.

But after Æthelberht’s death, when his son Eadbald assumed the government of the kingdom, this proved a great injury to the Church, whose tender growth was still very recent. For he not only refused to receive the faith of Christ but was also defiled by an act of fornication such as, as the Apostle testifies, had not even been heard of among the Gentiles, so that he took his father’s wife.

[Note: *His father’s wife.* After Bertha’s death Æthelberht had taken another wife, whom historians, because of the incest, do not honor by naming.]

By both crimes he gave an opportunity to return to their former vomit to those who, under his father’s rule, had accepted the laws of faith and chastity either through royal favor or through fear of the king. Nor were the scourges of heavenly discipline lacking to chastise and correct the treacherous king, for he was afflicted by frequent madness of mind and by the invasion of an unclean spirit.

[Column 0090B] The storm of this disturbance was increased also by the death of Sabert, king of the East Saxons. When he sought the everlasting kingdoms and left his three sons, who had remained pagans, as heirs to the temporal kingdom, they immediately began openly to serve the idolatry which, while he was alive, they had seemed to interrupt for a time, and they gave the peoples subject to them free permission to worship idols.

When they saw the bishop celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass in the church and giving the Eucharist to the people, they said to him, as popular report has it, puffed up with barbarous stupidity:

> “Why do you not also give us the shining bread which you used to give to our father Saba, and which you do not cease to give to the people in the church?”

[Note: *Saba.* It was not unusual among the ancient Saxons to abbreviate and contract names: thus Cuthulf and Cuthwin became Cutha, Ceolric became Ceola, Sabert became Saba, and so forth.]

They were accustomed to call him Saba.

The bishop answered them:

> “If you wish to be washed in that saving fountain in which your father was washed, you may also share in the holy bread of which he partook. But if you despise the bath of life, you cannot in any way receive the bread of life.”

They replied:

> “We do not wish to enter that fountain, for we know that we have no need of it; but we do wish to be refreshed by that bread.”

After he had carefully and repeatedly warned them that no one could share in the holy offering without purification, they were finally moved to fury and said:

> “If you will not agree to our request in this small matter, you can no longer remain in our province.”

They expelled him and ordered him to leave their kingdom with his companions.

[Column 0090D] [617] Having been expelled, he came to Kent to consult with his fellow bishops Laurence and Justus about what should be done in these circumstances. By common counsel it was decided that it would be better for them all to return to their homeland and serve the Lord there with a free conscience than to remain fruitlessly among barbarians who rebelled against the faith.

Mellitus and Justus therefore departed first and went to the regions of Gaul, intending to await the outcome there. But those who had expelled the herald of truth did not long remain unpunished in their service of demonic worship. For they went into battle against the nation of the Genissae, and all fell together with their army. Although the authors of the crime had perished, the people whom they had stirred to wickedness could not be recalled to their senses or restored to the simplicity of the faith and love that is in Christ.

## CHAPTER VI  
### How Laurence, chastised by the apostle Peter, converted King Eadbald to Christ, and how the king soon recalled Mellitus and Justus to preach

When Laurence too was preparing to follow Mellitus and Justus and leave Britain [617], he ordered a bed to be prepared for him that very night in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of which we have often spoken. After he had poured out many prayers and tears before the Lord for the condition of the Church, laid down his limbs to rest, and fallen asleep, the most blessed chief of the apostles appeared to him. For a long time in the secrecy of the night he scourged him with severe blows and demanded, with apostolic sternness, why he was abandoning the flock entrusted to him by the Lord, or to which shepherd he was fleeing while leaving Christ’s sheep among wolves.

> “Have you forgotten my example?” he said. “For the little ones of Christ, whom he had entrusted to me as a sign of his love, I endured from the unbelieving and the enemies of Christ bonds, beatings, prisons, afflictions, and finally death itself—death on the cross—so that I might be crowned with Christ?”

[Note: *Severe.* So the old manuscripts read; other manuscripts have “harsher.”]

Strengthened both by these blows from blessed Peter and by his exhortations, the servant of Christ Laurence came at once, when morning arrived, to the king. He opened his clothing and showed him how terribly he had been lacerated by the blows. The king was greatly astonished and asked who had dared inflict such wounds on so great a man. When he learned that, for the sake of the king’s salvation, the bishop had suffered such tortures and wounds from Christ’s apostle, he was very afraid. He anathematized all worship of idols, renounced the unlawful marriage, received the faith of Christ, and, after being baptized, took every possible care to support and favor the affairs of the Church.

He also sent to Gaul and recalled Mellitus and Justus, ordering them to return and freely establish—or restore—their Churches.

After a year from their departure they returned [618]. Justus returned to the city of Hrof, over which he had presided, but the people of London refused to receive Mellitus as bishop, preferring to serve idolatrous priests. Eadbald did not possess as much royal power as his father had, so that he could restore the bishop of his Church even against the will and opposition of the pagans.

Nevertheless, from the time when he was converted to the Lord, he and his people devoted themselves to the divine commandments. Finally, in the monastery of the most blessed chief of the apostles, he built a church of the holy Mother of God, which Archbishop Mellitus consecrated.

## CHAPTER VII  
### How Mellitus the bishop extinguished by prayer the flames of his burning city

During the reign of this king [619], the blessed archbishop Laurence ascended to the heavenly kingdom

[Note: *Ascended to the heavenly kingdom.* The same Goscelin who wrote the Life and Translation of Augustine also wrote the Life of Laurence, Mellitus, and others. Goscelin was, incidentally, a monk of Bertin, summoned to England by Saint Anselm of Canterbury. He first settled at Ramsey and then at Canterbury. William of Malmesbury mentions this author and work in *On the Bishops*. What he wrote about Laurence no longer survives, although Molanus saw it and Capgrave abridged it. Laurence is said not only to have written letters but also to have undertaken a journey to Scotland, held a synod on the Isle of Man to establish peace among the Churches, and performed many miracles everywhere. None of these things is mentioned by Bede. His memory is celebrated in the martyrologies on 2 February.]

and was buried in the church and monastery of the holy apostle Peter beside his predecessor Augustine, on the fourth day before the Nones of February. After him Mellitus, who had been bishop of London, assumed the see of the Church of Durovernum as its third bishop after Augustine. Justus, who was still alive, continued to govern the Church of Hrof. While they governed the Church of the English with great care and labor, they received an exhortatory letter from Boniface, bishop of the Roman and apostolic see, who had presided over the Church after Deusdedit, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 619 [or 618].

Mellitus was burdened in body by an illness, namely gout, but in the movements of his mind he was sound and, with vigor, passed beyond all earthly things, flying always toward heavenly things, which he loved, sought, and desired. He was noble by birth, but nobler still in the height of his mind.

To give one testimony to his virtue, from which the rest may be understood: once, through negligence, the city of Durovernum caught fire, and as the flames grew stronger it began to be consumed. No quantity of water thrown upon them could resist them. A considerable part of the city had already been devastated, and the fire was raging toward the bishop’s residence. Trusting in divine assistance where human help was lacking, the bishop ordered himself to be carried toward the flames that were raging and the fiery masses flying in every direction.

At the place where the force of the flames pressed most fiercely stood the martyr shrine of the blessed Four Crowned Martyrs. Carried there on the hands of those serving him, the bishop began by prayer, though weak, to drive away the danger which the strong hands of able men had been unable to overcome despite great labor.

Immediately the wind, which had been blowing from the south and spreading the fires throughout the city, turned back toward the south. First it withdrew the force of its fury from the buildings lying opposite; then, soon becoming entirely still, it restrained the flames as they simultaneously subsided and went out.

Because the man of God burned mightily with the fire of divine love, and because he was accustomed, by frequent prayers and exhortations, to repel from himself and his people the storms of the powers of the air, he deservedly had power over the world’s winds and flames and was able to prevent them from harming himself or his people.

After governing the Church for five years, he too departed to heaven during the reign of Eadbald. He was buried with his fathers in the aforementioned monastery and church of the most blessed chief of the apostles, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 624, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

[Other manuscripts: March.]

## CHAPTER VIII  
### How Pope Boniface sent the pallium and a letter to Justus, his successor

[624] Justus, who had been bishop of the Church of Hrof, immediately succeeded him in the pontificate. For that Church he consecrated a Roman bishop, having received from Pope Boniface authority to ordain bishops. We have already mentioned that Boniface was the successor of Deusdedit. The form of the authority was as follows:

> “To his beloved brother Justus, Boniface.
>
> “How devoutly and vigilantly your fraternity has labored for the Gospel of Christ has been shown not only by the substance of the letter sent by you but also by the perfection granted from above to your work. For almighty God has not abandoned either the sacrament of his name or the fruit of your labor, since he himself faithfully promised the preachers of the Gospel: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matthew 28:20).
>
> “His mercy has shown this especially in the ministry entrusted to you, opening the hearts of the nations to receive the unique mystery of your preaching. He has illumined the course of your labors with the support of his goodness, granting abundant fruit through the faithful exercise of the talents entrusted to you and preparing it for him whom you might mark out through multiplied generations.
>
> “This too has been granted to you as a recompense: by persevering continually in the ministry entrusted to you, you have awaited with praiseworthy patience the redemption of that people, and, as they progressed through your merits, their salvation has been brought near. For the Lord says: ‘Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved’ (Matthew 24:13).
>
> “You have therefore been saved through the hope of patience and by the virtue of endurance, so that the hearts of unbelievers, cleansed of their natural and superstitious disease, might obtain the mercy of their Savior. When we received the letters of our son, King Adulwald, we learned with what instruction in sacred eloquence your fraternity had led his mind to the belief of true conversion and unquestioning faith.

[Note: *Adulwald* (also *Adelwald, Edilwald, Aethelwald,* and *Eadbald*). He is the Eadbald of the preceding chapter, son and successor of Æthelberht, whom the pope repeatedly calls Auduvald.]
>
> “From this we take certain confidence in the long-suffering mercy of heaven, and we believe that, through the ministry of your preaching, not only the fullest salvation of the peoples subject to him but also that of their neighbors will follow. Thus, as it is written, may the reward of your completed work be granted you by the Lord, the giver of all good things. Truly, may the universal confession of the nations testify that their sound has gone out through the whole earth and their words to the ends of the world, through the sacrament of the Christian faith which has been received.”

[Note: *Of your labors.* So manuscript Tr. Bede used *fatigia* for the labors undertaken for the salvation of souls. Although this is an unusual word, we have retained it in place of the reading found in the Vulgate, *of your eminence*. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés I read *of your fatigues*. Chifflet.]

> “Moreover, at the invitation of your zeal for goodness, we have sent the pallium to your fraternity by the bearer of this letter. We have ordered that you may use it only in celebrating the most sacred mysteries. We also grant you authority, when necessity requires and the Lord’s mercy goes before you, to celebrate the ordination of bishops, so that the Gospel of Christ may be spread through the preaching of many among all the nations that have not yet been converted.
>
> “Let your fraternity therefore strive to preserve with undefiled sincerity of mind what it has received through the kindness of the Apostolic See. Consider the likeness of that for which you have undertaken to carry so distinguished a garment upon your shoulders. With the mercy of the Lord invoked, strive to show yourself such that you may present the rewards of the gift granted to you, not with guilt but with the benefit of souls, before the tribunal of the supreme and coming Judge. May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.”

## CHAPTER IX  
### Concerning the reign of King Edwin, and how Paulinus, coming to evangelize him, first instructed his daughter in the sacraments of the Christian faith

At this time the nation of the Northumbrians—that is, the nation of the English which lived on the northern side of the River Humber—received the word of faith through the preaching of Paulinus, whom we mentioned above, together with its king Edwin [625].
