As a sign that this king would receive the faith and the heavenly kingdom, his power in the earthly kingdom had also increased, so that—something no Englishman before him had done—he brought under his authority all the territories of Britain wherever the provinces of the English or Britons were situated.

Indeed, as we explained above, he also subjected the islands called the Mevanias to the rule of the English.

[Note: *Mevanias.* Camden says that one should read *Menavias*, and perhaps he is not wrong; nevertheless, it is true, as he himself admits, that *Mevanias* is the reading found in the manuscripts, for the oldest manuscripts have it so. There is no need to say that the first island is today called Anglesey and the second Man.]

The first island, which lies to the south, is larger in area and more fertile in the production and abundance of crops; according to the reckoning of the English, it contains the equivalent of 960 households. The second contains more than 300.

The occasion for this people’s reception of the faith was that its aforementioned king was related to the kings of Kent. He had taken as his wife Æthelberga, daughter of King Æthelberht, also called Tate.

When Edwin first sought her marriage by sending envoys to her brother Eadbald, who then ruled the kingdom of Kent, the answer was that it was not lawful to give a Christian virgin in marriage to a pagan, lest the faith and sacraments of the heavenly King be profaned by union with a king who was wholly ignorant of the worship of the true God.

When the messengers reported these words to Edwin, he promised that he would in every respect do nothing contrary to the Christian faith practiced by the virgin. Rather, he would permit her to observe the faith and worship of her religion, according to Christian custom, together with all who came with her, whether men or women, priests or ministers. Nor did he deny that he too would accept the same religion, if, after examination by prudent people, it could be found holier and more worthy of God.

The virgin was therefore promised to Edwin and sent to him. As had been arranged, Paulinus, a man beloved of God, was ordained bishop. He came with her and strengthened her and her companions by daily exhortation and by the celebration of the heavenly sacraments, so that they might not be polluted by association with the pagans.

[Textual apparatus not otherwise represented above, in source order: *Cantia* [Al. *Cantio*]; *emporium* [Al. *emptorium*]; *Dorubrevi* [Al. *Doroverni*]; *Doruvernensis* [Al. *Doroverniensis*]; *inlatum* [Al. *inlatum in*]; *corpora* omitted in Al.; *Successit* [Al. adds *autem*]; *augmentare* [Al. *augmentari*]; *profectum* [Al. *perfectum*]; *satagit* [Al. *sategit*]; “matters necessary for the Church of the English” [Al. adds *causis*, “causes”]; “synod of the bishops of Italy” [Al. “in Italy”]; “third day before the Kalends of March” [Al. fourth]; *quaeque* [Al. *quaecunque*]; “instructions to be delivered” [Al. “commands”]; *episcopo* [Al. *episcopus*].

In Chapter V: “sixteenth” [Al. third or seventh, through confusion of the old numeral forms VI, III, VII]; Augustine [Al. adds “bishop”]; “fifty-six” [Al. fifty-three]; *Cantuariis* [Al. *Cantuarios*]; Oswiu [Al. Oswi or Oswin]; “and correct” [Al. “or correct”]; “this disturbance” [Al. “this kind of disturbance”]; “could share” [Al. “may share”]; “agree” [Al. infinitive *adsentiri*]; Mellitus and Justus departed “first” [Al. “as the first”]; “not long [after]” [Al. adds *post*, “after”]; “expelled” [Al. *depulerant*, “drove out”]; “could not be recalled to their senses” [Al. “corrected”].

In Chapter VI: “When Laurence too” [Al. omits *too*]; “before the Lord” [Al. “before God”]; “with severe blows” [Al. *acrioribus*, “harsher”]; “opened his clothing” [Al. *rejecto*, “having cast off [his clothing]”]; “establish—or restore—their Churches” [Al. *restituendas*, “restore,” or *instruendas*, “instruct”].

In Chapter VII: “fire” [Al. *igne*]; “the wind … spreading the fires throughout the city” [Al. *ubi*, “where,” for *urbi*, “throughout the city”]; “because” [Al. *who*]; the date is eighth day before the Kalends of May [Al. March].

In Chapter VIII: “his work” [Al. *mundi*, “world,” for *saeculi*, “age”]; *fatigia* is retained in the underlying text as “fatigations/exertions,” rather than the Vulgate reading *fastigiorum*, “eminence”; “as a recompense” [Al. “who”]; “awaited” [Al. present *await*].

In Chapter IX: “wherever the provinces of the English or Britons were situated” [Al. past “were inhabited”]; Æthelberga’s alternative name *Tatae* [Al. *Tate*]; “when he sought” [Al. past “had sought”].]

Paulinus was ordained bishop by Archbishop Justus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 625; and thus he came with the aforesaid virgin to King Edwin as the companion of a carnal union. But he himself applied his whole mind rather to presenting to Christ, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, a chaste virgin to one husband [Al., omits “husband”], by calling to the knowledge of the truth the people to whom he was going. When he had come into the province, he labored greatly, with the Lord’s help, both to keep those who had come with him from falling away from the faith [Al., departing from it] and, if he could, to convert some of the pagans to the grace of faith by preaching. But, as the Apostle says, although he labored there for a long time in the word, the god of this age blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine upon them.

In the following year there came into the province an assassin named Eumer [Al., Eumerus], sent by King Cuichelm of the West Saxons, hoping to deprive King Edwin of both his kingdom and his life. He carried a two-edged dagger smeared with poison, so that, if the wound from the iron should not be sufficient to kill the king, the venom might complete the work.

He came to the king on the first day of Easter, beside the river Derwent [Al., Boruventionem], where there was then a royal estate [Note: *Deruventionem*. Derwent.]. He entered as though delivering a message from his lord; and while he rolled out his feigned embassy with deceitful speech, he suddenly rose, drew the dagger from beneath his clothing, and attacked the king. When Lilla, the king’s most devoted minister [Al., the king’s minister], saw this, and had no shield at hand with which to defend the king from death, he immediately placed his own body before the assailant’s blow. But the enemy drove the blade in with such force that, passing through the slain soldier’s body, it wounded the king as well. When the attacker was then assaulted from every side with swords, in the midst of the tumult he also killed with his infamous dagger another soldier named Frodheri [Al., Fordheri].

That same night, on the holy feast of the Lord’s Easter, the queen had borne a daughter to the king, named Eanfled. While the same king, in the presence of Bishop Paulinus, was giving thanks to his gods for the daughter born to him, the bishop, by contrast, began to give thanks to the Lord Christ and to assure the king that he himself had obtained from him by his prayers that the queen should give birth safely and without severe pain. Delighted by these words, the king promised that, renouncing his idols, he would serve Christ if he granted him life and victory while he fought against the king who had sent the murderer who wounded him. As a pledge that he would fulfill his promise, he assigned this same daughter of his [Al., omits “his”] to Bishop Paulinus to be consecrated to Christ. She was baptized on the holy day of Pentecost, the first of the Northumbrian people, together with eleven [Al., twelve] others from the queen’s household.

[Note: “Eleven.” Matthew of Westminster says thirty. The printed manuscripts of Bede, except A. 1, have twelve; but see how wrongly the Saxon manuscript paraphrase of C. C. C. expresses the passage: “with eleven other women from the queen’s household, and the infant was the twelfth.”]

At that time, having recovered from the wound previously inflicted upon him, the king gathered an army and went against the people [Al., king] of the West Saxons. When battle had been joined, he either killed or received into submission all whom he had learned had conspired for his death. Thus, returning victorious to his homeland, he did not immediately and rashly wish to receive the sacraments of the Christian faith, although from the time when he had promised that he would serve Christ he no longer served idols. Rather, from that time onward [Al., adds “from that time”] he took care to learn more diligently the account of the faith from the venerable man Paulinus himself, and to consult with his leading men, whom he knew to be wiser, about what they thought should be done concerning these matters. He himself, being naturally very shrewd, often sat alone for a long time, outwardly silent but inwardly conversing much with himself in his heart, considering what he ought to do and what religion ought to be observed.

## CHAPTER X. How Pope Boniface exhorted the same king to the faith by letters

[DCXXV.] [Note: “At that time.” Although Bede places these letters of Boniface after the events of the preceding chapter, to which he assigns the year 626, they must nevertheless have been written in the year 625. For Boniface died in that year, on 22 October. Thus, “at that time” here has the same meaning as Bede’s *interea* (“in the meantime”) elsewhere.]

At that time he received letters exhorting him to the faith from Boniface, pontiff of the Apostolic See, of which the following is the form:

[Note: “Copy of the letter,” etc., is omitted by the Cambridge and Lyons editions and by certain manuscripts.]

### Copy of the letter of the most blessed and apostolic Boniface, pope of the Church of the city of Rome [Al., of Rome], addressed to the glorious man Edwin, king of the English

> To the glorious man Edwin, king of the English: Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.
>
> Although the power of the supreme Divinity cannot be explained by the offices of human speech—for by its greatness it exists in such invisible and inscrutable eternity that no intelligence, however acute, is sufficient to comprehend and express how great it is—nevertheless, because his kindness, when the doors of the heart have been opened for his self-disclosure, mercifully pours into human minds by inward inspiration the mysteries that are revealed concerning him, we have extended our priestly solicitude to announce to you the fullness of the Christian faith, so that, implanting in your understanding the gospel of Christ our Savior, which he commanded to be preached to all nations, we may offer you the remedies of salvation [Al., the remedy of salvation].
>
> The mercy, therefore, of the majesty on high, which by the mere word of its command established and created all things—namely, heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them—ordering the ranks by which they should subsist, governing all things through the counsel of its coeternal Word and the unity of the Holy Spirit, fashioned humanity from the clay of the earth in its own image and likeness. It granted humanity so great a privilege of reward that it placed human beings above all other creatures and, once the limit of its command had been observed [Al., the time of its command], fortified them with the permanence of eternity.
>
> This God, therefore—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who is the undivided Trinity—the human race, from the rising of the sun to its setting, venerates and worships in saving confession of faith as its Creator and Maker. To him the highest authorities and powers of the world are subject, because by his ordering the precedence of all kingdoms is granted. By the mercy of his goodness, he has also deigned wonderfully to kindle, with the fervor of the Holy Spirit for the knowledge of himself, the cold hearts of nations situated even at the ends of the earth, for the extension and subjection of his whole creation.
>
> [Note: The wording *dilatandi subdi* is uncertain. The variants read: *dilatandi gratia, subdi*, “for the purpose of extending and subduing”; *dilatandi gratia, subdendique*, “for the purpose of extending and bringing under subjection”; *dilatandae subsidio*, “by the aid of extending”; *dilatandae subsidii*, “of the aid of extending”; and *dilatandae subsidiis*, “by aids for extending.”]
>
> For what the mercy of the Redeemer accomplished in the illumination of our glorious son King Andubald and of the peoples subject to him, we confidently infer that your Glory has learned more fully from the proximity of the places. We trust that his wonderful gift will likewise be conferred upon you, with the certain hope of heavenly perseverance [Al., the hope of heavenly perseverance]. For we have learned that your glorious wife, who is known to be a part of your body, has been illuminated by the reward of eternity through the regeneration of holy baptism.
>
> Therefore, by this letter, with all the affection of inward charity, we have taken care to exhort you, glorious sir [Al., more gloriously], so that, rejecting idols and their worship, despising the follies of shrines and the deceitful allurements of augury, you may believe in God the almighty Father, and in his Son Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit [Al., and believe in the Holy Spirit]. Thus, believing, and with the power of the holy and undivided Trinity cooperating, you may be freed from the bonds of the devil’s captivity and become participants in eternal life.
>
> How great a guilt of wickedness binds those who embrace and cultivate the most destructive superstition of idolatry [Al., the most destructive supposition of idolatry] is shown by the ruinous examples of those whom they worship. Hence the Psalmist says of them: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm 95:5). And again:
>
> “They have eyes, but they do not see;  
> they have ears, but they do not hear;  
> they have noses, but they do not smell;  
> they have hands, but they do not touch;  
> they have feet, but they do not walk.
>
> “Therefore they become like those who place the hope of their confidence in them” (Psalm 113:5–8).
>
> For how can those beings possess any power to help anyone who are constructed from corruptible material by the hands of those beneath and subject to you, and to whom human craftsmanship has given the lifeless likeness of limbs? Unless moved by you, they cannot walk; but, constructed [Al., bound together] like a stone placed in one spot, possessing no understanding and overwhelmed by their very insensibility, they have acquired no ability either to harm or to help. By what deception of mind, then, you worship and follow as gods those to whom you yourselves have given the image of a body, we cannot discover by sound judgment.
>
> Therefore you ought, having received the sign of the holy cross by which the human race was redeemed, to cast from your hearts the accursed overthrow wrought by the devil’s cunning—he who stands as the envious and hostile rival of the works of divine goodness—and, laying hands upon these objects whom until now you have fashioned for yourselves as gods from a structure of material, take the greatest care to break and destroy them [Al., “take care to break and destroy them”].
>
> For their very dissolution and corruption—since they never possessed a living spirit and could in no way receive sensibility from their makers—should plainly show you how worthless was that which you worshiped until now. You, who have received a living spirit from the Lord, are nevertheless better than their fabrication [Al., *constructione* rather than *constructioni*]; for almighty God ordained that you, descended through kinship from the human being whom he formed, should multiply through the ages by countless generations [Al., *deductus*; *deductos*, for *deductis*].
>
> Come, therefore, to the knowledge of him who created you, who breathed into you the spirit of life, who sent his only-begotten Son for your redemption, so that he might rescue you from original sin and, having rescued you from the power of wicked demonic depravity [Al., omits “depravity”], reward you with heavenly gifts.
>
> Receive the words of the preachers and the gospel of God that they announce to you. Believe, as has often been said, in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit and the inseparable Trinity. Put demonic suggestions to flight and expel from yourselves the prompting of the poisonous and deceptive enemy. Being reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, may you be worthy, by the help of his munificence, to dwell with him whom you have believed in the splendor of everlasting glory [Note: “By the help of his munificence,” etc. Al., “by his help and munificence”; “by his helping munificence”; “by the help of munificence.”]
>
> Moreover, we have sent you a blessing from your protector, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: namely, one shirt with gold ornamentation [Note: “One in gold.” Al., “one in gold and one Ancyrian cloak.”] and one Ancyrian cloak [Note: An *Ancyrian cloak*. For a priest it would be a *capa*, while for a soldier it is a *pallium*; it was brought from Ancyra.]. We ask that your Glory receive it in the spirit of kindness in which it is known to have been sent by us.

## CHAPTER XI. How he warned the king’s wife by letter to take diligent care for his salvation

[DCXXV.]

The same pontiff sent the following kind of letter to his wife Aethelberga as well.

### Copy of the letter of the most blessed and apostolic Boniface, pope of the city of Rome, addressed to Aethelberga, queen of King Edwin

> To the glorious lady, daughter Aethelberga, queen: Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.
>
> The goodness of our Redeemer, who rescued the human race from the bonds of the devil’s captivity by the outpouring of his precious blood, has offered it many remedies of providence by which it might be saved. Thus, making the knowledge of his name known to the nations in various ways, he enabled them to recognize their Creator by receiving the sacrament of the Christian faith.
>
> That this gift has indeed been bestowed upon the understanding of your Glory is plainly indicated by the mystical cleansing of your regeneration [Al., “the regeneration of your cleansing”]. Our mind therefore exulted with great joy at the great benefit of the Lord’s generosity, because he deigned to kindle in your confession a spark of orthodox religion [Note: “Confession”: only the manuscript of Mori; the others have “conversion”]. From this, not only the understanding of your glorious husband but also that of the whole people subject to you might easily be inflamed with love of him.
>
> For we have learned from those who came to us announcing the praiseworthy conversion of our glorious son King Audubald that your Glory too, having received the wondrous sacrament of the Christian faith, shines continually through pious works pleasing to God; that you carefully abstain from the worship of idols and from the allurements of shrines and auguries; and that, remaining steadfast in unaltered devotion [Al., “unchanged devotion”] to the love of your Redeemer, you watch so that you may never cease to contribute your efforts toward extending the Christian faith.
>
> When fatherly charity had diligently inquired about your glorious husband, we learned [Al., omits “we learned”] that, until then, he had served abominable idols and delayed offering his obedience to the voice of the preachers. From this, no small bitterness has accumulated for us, because a part of your body has remained a stranger to the knowledge of the supreme and undivided Trinity.
>
> Therefore, in the duties of a father, we have not delayed bringing our admonition to your glorious Christianity [Al., “bringing it without delay”], exhorting you not to postpone acting urgently and at a suitable time, having been imbued with the support of divine inspiration, so that, through the cooperating power of our Savior the Lord Jesus Christ, he too may be joined to the number of Christians, and so that you may maintain the rights of marital union through an undefiled bond of fellowship. For it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). How, then, can it be said that the unity of your union exists if he remains alienated from the brightness of your faith, separated by the darkness of detestable error?
>
> Therefore, devoting yourself to continual prayer [Al., “to continuous prayer”], do not cease to obtain from the long-suffering mercy of heaven the benefits of his illumination, so that those whom carnal union is shown to have made, in a certain sense, one body may also be preserved by unity of faith in perpetual fellowship after the passing of this life.
>
> Persist, therefore, glorious daughter, and hasten with all your strength to soften the hardness of his heart by the devout presentation of the divine commandments. Pour into his understanding how glorious is the mystery that you have received by believing, and how marvelous is the reward that, having been reborn, you have deserved to attain. Kindle the coldness of his heart by the proclamation of the Holy Spirit, so that, when the sluggishness of his most destructive worship has been removed, the warmth of divine faith may kindle his understanding through the frequent repetition of your exhortations [Al., “your earnest exhortations”]. Thus it will unquestionably become clear that the testimony of holy Scripture has been fulfilled through you: “The unbelieving husband will be saved through the believing wife” (1 Corinthians 7:14).
>
> For this purpose you have obtained the mercy of the Lord’s compassion: so that you might return to your Redeemer a multiplied fruit of the faith and benefits entrusted to you. We do not cease to ask in constant prayers that, with the support of his own goodness, you may be able to fulfill this.
>
> Having said these things, and showing you the duties of fatherly affection, we exhort you, whenever an opportunity is found through a courier, to relieve us as quickly as possible with favorable news concerning the things that the power from above has deigned wonderfully to accomplish through you in the conduct [Al., “conversion”] of your husband and of the people subject to you. In this way our concern—which eagerly awaits desirable news about the salvation of your soul and of all yours—may be relieved by your report; and, recognizing more abundantly the illumination of divine favor spread among you, we may rightly render abundant thanks, with joyful confession, to God, the giver of all good things, and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.
>
> Moreover, we have sent you a blessing from your protector, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: namely, a silver mirror and a gilded ivory comb [Al., “an ivory comb”]. We ask that your Glory receive them in the spirit of kindness in which they are known to have been sent by us.

## CHAPTER XII. How Edwin was summoned to believe by a vision once shown to him while he was in exile

[DCXXVI.]

The aforesaid Pope Boniface dealt with the salvation of King Edwin and of his people in these letters. But the heavenly oracle that divine compassion had once deigned to reveal to him while he was an exile at the court of King Redwald of the English also contributed not a little to preparing his mind to receive and understand the admonitions of saving doctrine.

When Paulinus saw that it was difficult to incline the king’s lofty spirit toward the humility of the way of salvation and toward receiving the mystery of the life-giving cross, and when he was laboring for his salvation, as well as for that of the people over whom he ruled, both by words of exhortation addressed to human beings and by words of supplication addressed to divine compassion, he finally, as seems credible, learned in the spirit what kind and nature of oracle had once been shown to the king from heaven. From then on he did not delay to urge the king immediately to fulfill the vow that, in the oracle shown to him, he had promised to fulfill if he were rescued from the miseries of that time and reached the height of royal power.

The oracle was as follows:

[Note: “With Aethelfrid pursuing him.” Edwin was the son and heir of Aella, king of Deira. When his father died, Edwin was left a minor and was excluded both from kingdom and homeland by Aethelfrid, king of Bernicia, who had married Aella’s daughter Acca. He fled to Redwald, the most powerful king of the East Saxons. It should be noted here that this Aella, Edwin’s father, was the king to whose name Gregory alludes in the first chapter. For the tradition is absurdly twisted in Codex A. T. C., p. 14, into Aella, king of the West Saxons, the father of Cissa.]

While he was wandering in exile for many years, concealed in various places or kingdoms, pursued by Aethelfrid, who had reigned before him, he finally came to Redwald, begging him to preserve his life by protecting it from the plots of so great a persecutor. Redwald received him willingly and promised to do what was requested [Al., what he requested].

But when Aethelfrid learned that Edwin had appeared in that province and was living familiarly with his companions at the king’s court, he sent messengers who offered Redwald a large sum of money for Edwin’s death. This achieved nothing. He sent a second time, and a third, offering more abundant gifts of gold [Al., adds “of gold and”] and silver, and in addition threatening Redwald with war if his request were despised.

Redwald, broken either by threats or corrupted by gifts, yielded to the petitioner and promised either to kill Edwin or to hand him over to the messengers. When a very faithful friend of Edwin noticed this, he entered the chamber where Edwin intended to sleep—for it was the first hour of the night—and, calling him outside, told him what the king had promised to do against him. He added:

> “If you wish, at this very hour I will lead you out of this province and bring you to places where neither Redwald nor Aethelfrid will ever be able to find you.”

Edwin replied:

> “I give thanks indeed for your goodwill; nevertheless, I cannot do what you suggest, namely, be the first to violate the pact I made with so great a king, since he has done me no harm and has not yet inflicted any hostility upon me. Rather, if I am to die, let him deliver me to death rather than some more ignoble person. For where shall I flee now, when for so many years and through so many stretches of time I have wandered through all the provinces of Britain avoiding the snares of my enemies?”

When his friend departed, Edwin remained alone outside. Sitting sadly before the palace, he began to be afflicted by many surges of thought, not knowing what to do or where to turn his steps.

When he had long been tormented by silent anguish of mind and consumed by an unseen fire, he suddenly saw, in the stillness of the deep night, a man approaching him whose face and clothing were unfamiliar. When he saw him, he was greatly frightened, as one would be by a stranger and an unexpected visitor.

The man approached, greeted him, and asked why, at that hour, while all the others were resting and held in deep sleep, Edwin alone was sitting sorrowfully awake upon a stone. Edwin in turn asked what concern that was of his, whether he himself would spend the night indoors or outside.

The man replied:

> “Do not suppose that I am unaware of the cause of your sadness, sleeplessness, and outdoor solitude. I know with complete certainty who you are, why you grieve, and what evils you fear are about to come upon you. But tell me what reward you would be willing to give, if there were someone who could release you from these sorrows and persuade Redwald neither to do you any harm himself nor to hand you over to your enemies to be killed.”

When Edwin answered that he would give this person everything within his power as a reward for such a benefit, the man continued:

> “What if he also truly promised that you would become king, once your enemies had been destroyed, so that you would surpass in power not only all your ancestors but also all who had previously been kings among the English?”

Edwin, made more resolute by the questioning, did not hesitate to promise that he would respond with fitting acts of thanksgiving to anyone who granted him such great benefits.

Then the man spoke for a third time:

> “But if the one who truly foretold that such great and such wonderful gifts were to come to you could also show you counsel concerning your salvation and life, better and more useful than any of your parents or relatives had ever heard, would you agree to obey him and receive his saving admonitions?”

Edwin did not delay but immediately promised that in everything he would follow the teaching of the one who would rescue him from so many and such great calamities and raise him to the height of royal power.

When he had received this answer, the speaker immediately placed his right hand upon Edwin’s head and said:

> “When this sign comes to you [Al., omits ‘this sign’], remember this time and our conversation, and do not delay to fulfill what you now promise.”

After he had said these things, as they report, he suddenly disappeared, so that Edwin understood that the one who had appeared to him was not a human being but a spirit.

While the royal youth was still sitting alone there, rejoicing indeed at the consolation granted to him [Al., pious and kindly consolation] but also greatly troubled and carefully considering who the one who had spoken these things to him might be and where he had come from [Al., where he had come], the aforementioned friend came to him and greeted him with a joyful face:

> “Rise,” he said, “go inside, and, putting aside the anxieties of your cares, compose both your body and your mind for rest, because the king’s heart has been changed [Al., unchanged]. He has decided not to do you any harm but rather to keep the faith he promised. For after revealing privately to the queen the intention of which I told you earlier, she recalled him from it, warning him that there was no justification for so great a king to sell his best friend, placed in need, for gold, or rather to lose his faith—which is more precious than all ornaments—for love of money.”

What more is there to say? The king did as he had been told. He not only did not hand the exile over to hostile messengers [Al., to enemies], but also helped him reach the kingdom. For, as soon as the messengers had returned home, Redwald gathered a large army to defeat Aethelfrid. Redwald killed Aethelfrid, who met him with a much smaller army—for Redwald had not given him time to assemble and unite his entire force—at the eastern side of the river called the Idle, in the territory of the Mercians [Note: “On the eastern side.” Near Idleton.]. In that battle Redwald’s son, named Raegenheri, was also killed. Thus Edwin, in accordance with the oracle he had received, not only escaped the plots of the king hostile to him but also succeeded the slain man in the glory of the kingdom.

When, therefore, King Edwin delayed believing while Paulinus preached the word of God, and for some time, as we have said, used to sit alone at suitable hours, diligently examining within himself what he ought to do [Al., adds “and”] and what religion he ought to follow, the man of God entered to him one day, placed his right hand upon his head, and asked whether he recognized this sign.

When Edwin, trembling, tried to fall at his feet, Paulinus raised him and addressed him in a familiar voice:

> “Behold, by the Lord’s gift, you have escaped the hands of the enemies whom you feared. Behold, through his generosity, you have received the kingdom that you desired. Remember not to delay doing the third thing that you promised: receive the faith of him who, rescuing you from temporal adversities, raised you to the honor of a temporal kingdom, and observe his commandments. If thereafter you are willing to obey his will, which he preaches to you through me, he will also free you from the everlasting torments of evil and make you a participant with him in the eternal kingdom in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XIII. What counsel the same king held with his leading men concerning receiving the faith of Christ, and how his high priest profaned his altars

When he had heard these things, the king replied that he both wished and ought to receive the faith that Paulinus taught. Yet he said that he would still confer about it with his friends, princes, and counselors [Al., principalities; Al., leading men], so that, if they too wished to share his opinion, they might all together be consecrated to Christ in the font of life. With Paulinus’s approval, he did as he had said.

After consulting with the wise men, he asked each of them individually what they thought of this doctrine, hitherto unheard of among them, and of the new worship of the divinity that was being preached.

The first of his high priests, Coifi [Al., Coefi; Al., Cyfi], immediately answered:

> “See, O king, what sort of thing this is that is now preached to us. But I declare to you most truthfully what I have certainly learned: the religion that we have hitherto held has no power at all and no usefulness [Al., “the religion has no usefulness”]. For none of your people devoted himself more diligently than I to the worship of our gods, and nevertheless there are many who receive from you greater benefits and higher honors than I do, and who prosper more in everything they undertake to do or acquire. But if the gods had any power, they would rather wish to help me, who have taken pains to serve them more zealously. Therefore, if, after examination, you perceive that the things now preached to us as new are better and stronger, let us hasten to accept them without any hesitation.”

Another of the king’s nobles agreed with this persuasion and these prudent words, and immediately added:

> “The present life of human beings on earth seems to me, O king, comparable to the time concerning which we are uncertain. Suppose that, while you are seated at dinner with your commanders and ministers in winter, with a fire burning in the midst and the dining hall made warm, while outside storms of winter rain or snow rage everywhere, one of the sparrows should suddenly fly very swiftly through the house. It enters through one door and immediately goes out through another.
>
> “During the brief time it is inside, it is untouched by the storm of winter; but after passing through a tiny stretch of clear weather for a moment, it immediately returns from winter to winter and slips from your sight. So this life of human beings appears for a little while; but what follows or what preceded it, we are entirely ignorant. Therefore, if this new doctrine has brought something more certain [Al., shall have brought something more certain], it rightly appears that we ought to follow it.”

The other elders and counselors of the king, divinely admonished, continued with similar observations.

Coifi added that he wished to hear Paulinus himself speak more carefully about the God whom he preached. When Paulinus did so at the king’s command, Coifi exclaimed after hearing his words:

> “I understood long ago that there was nothing in what we worshiped. For the more diligently I sought truth in that worship, the less I found. But now I openly confess that in this preaching the truth shines forth—the truth that is able to grant us the gifts of life, salvation, and eternal blessedness. Therefore, O king, I suggest that we quickly consign to curse and fire the temples and altars that we have consecrated without any useful result” [Al., “consign them to fire”].

What more is there to say? The king openly gave his assent to blessed Paulinus, who was preaching the gospel [Al., to the preaching of the gospel], and, renouncing idolatry, confessed that he received the faith of Christ.

When the king asked the aforesaid high priest of his rites who should first profane the altars and shrines of the idols, together with the enclosures surrounding them, he replied:

> “I. For who is more fit than I, through the wisdom given me by the true God, to destroy for the example of all what I worshiped in folly?”

Immediately casting aside the superstition of vanity, he asked the king to give him weapons and a stallion, so that, mounting it, he might go to destroy the idols [Al., “he went”]. For it had not been permitted the high priest either to carry weapons or to ride any horse except a mare.

Thus, girded with a sword, he took a spear in his hand and, mounting the king’s stallion, proceeded toward the idols. The people watching him thought that he had gone mad. But as soon as he approached the shrine, he did not delay to profane it by throwing into it the spear he held. Rejoicing greatly at the knowledge of the worship of the true God, he ordered his companions to destroy and burn the shrine, together with all its enclosures.

The place where the idols once stood is shown not far east of York, beyond the river Derwent, and is now called Godmunddingaham [Note: *Godmunddingaham*. It still retains the name Godmundham, that is, “the enclosure of the gods.” The place was famous not only for Saxon but also for Roman, indeed British, idol worship. Nearby lies Delgovitium, which Camden derives from the British *Delgwe*, which in his view denotes statues of the gods; today it is Wigton, that is, “the town of idols.”]. There the high priest himself, under the inspiration of the true God, polluted and destroyed the altars that he himself had consecrated.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Edwin himself was made a believer with his people, and where Paulinus baptized

King Edwin, together with all the nobles of his people and a very large number of the common people, received the faith and the washing of holy regeneration in the eleventh year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 627, and approximately the 180th year from the arrival of the English in Britain.

He was baptized at York on the holy day of Easter, on the day before the Ides of April [12 April], in the church of the holy apostle Peter. While he was being catechized and instructed there for the reception of baptism, he had rapidly built this church of wood. In the same city he also granted his teacher and bishop, Paulinus, an episcopal seat.

As soon as he had received baptism, he took care, under the instruction of Paulinus, to build on the same site a larger and more magnificent basilica of stone, enclosing within its center the oratory that he had first constructed. After the foundations had been prepared in a square around the earlier oratory, he began to build the basilica. But before the height of the walls had been completed, the king himself was killed by an impious death and left the same work to his successor Oswald to complete.

[Note: “To be completed.” It was completed by King Oswald and burned in the year 1069. Restored by Archbishop Thomas I, it burned down in 1137. Finally, in the time of King Edward I, under Treasurer John and the archbishops Romanus, Melton, and Thoresby, it was raised to its present size. — Simeon of Durham; Stubbs.]

From that time Paulinus preached the word of God in that province continuously for six years, that is, until the end of that king’s reign, with the king himself approving and supporting him. All who were predestined to eternal life believed and were baptized. Among them were Osfrid and Eadfrid, sons of King Edwin, both born to him in exile by Quoenburga, daughter of Cearl, king of the Mercians.

They were baptized at a later time, along with other children of his born to Queen Aedilberga: Aedilhun, Aedilthryd the daughter [Al., daughters], and another son, Vuscfrea. The first two, while still wearing the white garment of baptism, were taken from this life and buried at Eboracum in the church. Yffi, the son of Osfrid, was also baptized, as were not a few other noble and royal [Al., distinguished] men.

So great, it is said, was the fervor of faith and the desire for the saving bath among the people of the Northumbrians at that time that, on one occasion, Paulinus came with the king and queen to a royal estate called Adgefrin [Al., Adgebrin] [Note: Adgefrin. Today, Yeverin in Glendale.] and stayed there with them for thirty-six days, devoted to the work of instructing and baptizing. Throughout all those days, from morning until evening, he did nothing else than instruct in the word of salvation the people who flocked there from every village and place, and then wash those whom he had instructed in the river Gleni [Note: Gleni. Bowent.], which was nearby, with the bath of remission.

In the time of the kings who followed, this estate was deserted, and another was established in its place at a site called Maelmin [Note: Maelmin. Millfield.] [Al., Melmun; al., Malmin; al., Melmin]. This was in the province of Bernicia. But also in the province of Deira, where he was accustomed to stay more often with the king, he baptized in the river Sualua [Al., Sualica; al., Suala], which flows past the settlement of Cataracta [Note: Sualua. The writers of Augustine’s miracles have transmitted an account of Augustine’s baptism comparable to this baptism of Paulinus. We certainly have Pope Gregory’s authority, in the letter mentioned above to Eulogius of Alexandria, that Augustine baptized a great number of the faithful, as many as ten thousand. But that he did so in the river Sualua near Cataracta appears to be an error arising from the confusion of Augustine with Paulinus. For if Augustine baptized in the river Sualua, it is not likely that this was the Sualua at Cataracta, but rather the Sualua at the mouths of the Medway. Yet Augustine’s writers assign to him a northern journey for a very different reason: on the one hand, to enhance his labors, authority, and miracles; on the other, to attach to him the massacre of the monks of Bangor—on both sides, as it seems, with an equal appearance of truth.] [Note: The settlement of Cataracta. The editions, except A.1 and C.1, read “the settlement near Cataracta.” Manuscript C.1 has Cataractum.]

For at the very beginning of the Church’s birth, oratories and baptisteries could not yet be built there. Nevertheless, at Campodono [Note: Campodono. The similarity of the name seems to fix the site of this place at Cambodunum, which the authors interpret as Almondbury, corrupted from Albanbury, because this basilica consecrated by Paulinus was dedicated in memory of Saint Alban. It is not unworthy of notice, however, that the Saxon Paraphrase translates Campodono as Donafelda, from which Gale infers that it may perhaps have been Tanfield. This lies near Ripon, closer to the river Sualua, where Paulinus baptized.]—where at that time there was also a royal estate—he built a basilica. Later the pagans, by whom King Edwin was killed, burned it together with the entire estate. In its place later kings made themselves an estate in the region called Loidis [Note: In the region of Loidis. Not in the town itself, but in the estate of Oswinthorpe, which lies nearby and displays the name of its royal founder. See III.24.].

The altar, however, escaped the fire because it was made of stone, and it is still preserved in the monastery of the most reverend abbot and priest Thryduulf [Al., Tridulf], which is in the forest of Elmete [Note: Elmete. The size of this forest was recorded in an ancient Saxon schedule, found in many manuscripts and published by Gale in *Hist. Script.*, vol. I. According to it, Elmedsaetna contains six hundred hides. The estate of Berwick takes its name from it; the ruins of its walls gave occasion for the conjecture that Bede’s royal estate stood there. Bede, however, says nothing of a royal estate in the forest of Elmete, but only of Thryduulf’s monastery, which in the recent edition of Camden is assigned also to this town; no one has yet discovered any definite information about it. The territory of Elmete includes not only Berwick but also the other surrounding districts. Robert of Graystanes, *Anglia Sacra*, I, p. 739, says that Robert of Stichill, bishop of Durham, was confirmed by Geoffrey of York at Sherburn in Elmete. For the antiquities of this region, see the recently published book of Thoresby.]

## CHAPTER XV

How the province of the East Angles received the faith of Christ.

[DCXXVII.] Edwin had such devotion to the worship of truth [Note: “So great, however, etc.” Al., “such devotion, as is reported.”] that he even persuaded Earpwald [Al., Carpwald; al., Erpwald; al., Eorpwald], son of Redwald, king of the East Angles [Note: That he persuaded Earpwald. Florence of Worcester, Matthew of Westminster, and the Saxon Chronicle place Earpwald’s conversion in the year 632 and the beginning of Sigeberht’s reign in 636. But the sequence of events in Bede’s *History* seems to contradict this calculation. For Earpwald was killed immediately after his conversion, and after Ricberht’s three years of usurpation Sigeberht succeeded to the kingdom; Felix was then sent to him by Honorius of Canterbury. After seventeen years, Thomas was given to him as Felix’s successor by the same Honorius; and after five years, Berctgils, or Boniface, was appointed Thomas’s successor by the same Honorius. Thus we arrive at the year 653, when Honorius died. When these twenty-two years—seventeen of Felix and five of Thomas—are reckoned back, Sigeberht’s accession falls in the year 631, and Eorpwald’s conversion and death, together with Ricberht’s tyranny, in the year 627.] to abandon the superstitions of idols and receive, with his province, the faith and sacraments of Christ.

Indeed, his father Redwald had long before been instructed in the sacraments of the Christian faith in Kent, but without lasting effect. For when he returned home, he was led astray by his wife and by certain perverse teachers, and corrupted in the sincerity of his faith. His latter state was worse than his former, so that, in the manner of the ancient Samaritans, he appeared both to serve Christ and the gods whom he had previously served; and in the same temple he had an altar for the sacrifice of Christ and a small altar for sacrifices to demons. Aldwulf, king of that province in our own time, testified that this temple had survived until his day and that he had seen it in his youth.

The aforementioned King Redwald was noble by birth, though ignoble in conduct. He was the son of Tytil, whose father was Wuffa, from whom the kings of the East Angles are called Wuffings.

But Eorpwald, not long after he had received the faith, was killed by a pagan man named Ricberht [Al., Richberht]. For three years thereafter the province remained in error, until his brother Sigeberht [DCXXXI] received the kingdom. He was in every respect a most Christian and learned man. While he was still in exile in Gaul during his brother’s lifetime, he had been instructed in the sacraments of the faith; as soon as he began to reign, he took care to make his entire province share in them.

His efforts were most gloriously supported by Bishop Felix [Note: Domnoc. Today Dunwich, now submerged by the sea. The see was first divided with Elmham, then transferred there; afterward it was established at Thetford, and finally at Norwich.], who came from the region of the Burgundians [Al., Burgundiones]. He had been born and ordained there, and when he came to Archbishop Honorius and declared his desire to him, Honorius sent him to preach the word of life to the aforementioned nation of the English.

Nor did Felix’s hopes fall in vain. Rather, this pious cultivator of the spiritual field found abundant fruit among the believing peoples. For, in accordance with the meaning of his name, he freed the whole province from long-standing wickedness and misery and led it to faith, works of righteousness, and the gifts of everlasting happiness. He received the episcopal see in the city of Domnoc [Al., Dumnoc; al., Dummoc], and after presiding over that province for seventeen years [Al., having presided], he ended his life there in peace.

## CHAPTER XVI

How Paulinus preached in the province of Lindsey, and concerning the character of King Edwin.

[Col. 0108B]

[DCXXVIII.] Paulinus also preached the word in the province of Lindsey, which lies on the southern bank of the river Humber, extending to the sea. He first converted to the Lord the prefect of the city of Lincoln, whose name was Blaecca [Note: Blaecca. Bede is content to report his name; others have also traced his lineage from Woden to Eanferth and have related that the prefecture of Thong Castle was entrusted to him by Hengist, together with all the forces of the Lincolnshire district. As far as I know, this rests on no other foundation than Florence of Worcester’s general conclusion concerning the ancestry of the Lindisfari.] together with his household.

In that city he also built a church of outstanding workmanship in stone. Its roof has since fallen, whether through prolonged neglect or an enemy’s hand, but its walls appear to stand to this day; and every year some miracles of healing are customarily displayed there for the benefit of those who seek faithfully. In this church [Note: The church. It is conjectured that this church stood where Saint Paul’s now stands and that it was formerly Saint Paulinus’s. The similarity of the names easily won acceptance for this identification.] Paulinus, when Justus had passed to Christ, consecrated Honorius as his successor, as we shall say in its proper place below.

A certain priest and abbot, a most truthful man from the monastery of Peartaneu [Al., Partanei; al., Peartanig; al., Peortaneu] [Note: Peartaneu. Nothing remains in the authors concerning the foundation of this monastery. The site lay not far from Bardney, in whose endowment the neighboring remains of piety seem to have been absorbed. Walter of Gaunt, in a charter concerning the restoration of the monastery of Bardney, grants a tithe from all his domain at Parteney: “In the aforesaid Parteney, a church with its appurtenances, the hospital of Saint Mary Magdalene … together with the view of frankpledge at Parteney.” *Monumenta Anglicana*, I, p. 143. See Bede, III.11.] named Deda, told me that an elder had related to him that he himself had been baptized at midday by Bishop Paulinus, in the presence of King Edwin and a great crowd of people, in the river Trent near the city which in the language of the English is called Tiouulfingacaestir [Note: Tiouulfingacaestir. There is little certainty concerning the site of this place. Nevertheless, Southwell claims the memory of the baptism for itself; the piety of the kings, the possessions of the bishops of York, the successors of Paulinus, and the collegiate church of priests established there have consecrated the claim to this private local history.] [Al., Tuilf-Tuisf-Tulf-Uulfingcaestir].

He was also accustomed to describe Paulinus’s appearance: he was a man of tall stature, slightly stooped, with black hair, a lean face, a hooked and very slender nose, and an appearance at once venerable and terrifying. He had with him in the ministry James the deacon, a man industrious and noble in Christ and in the Church, who survived down to our own times.

So great, it is said, was the peace in Britain at that time, wherever King Edwin’s authority extended, that, as is still said in a proverb, even if a woman with her newborn infant wished to walk across the whole island from sea to sea, she could do so without anyone harming her.

The same king took such care for the welfare of his people that in many places, where he had constructed clear springs beside the public crossings of roads, he ordered bronze drinking cups [Note: Cups. Matthew of Westminster reads, “he conveyed [water] through bronze pipes,” incorrectly; for Bede expressly says that he ordered cups to be hung up. These were vessels set out for drinking. Concerning them Trebellius Pollio writes: “Also, into cups and goblets, eleven pounds.” King Aethelberht of Kent, in a letter to Saint Boniface of Mainz, mentions “a silver cup, gilded within, weighing three pounds.”] to be hung there for the refreshment of travelers. No one dared touch them, whether out of the greatness of his authority and fear of him, or refrained from doing so out of love, except for necessary use.

He possessed such majesty in his kingdom that not only were banners carried before him in battle, but also in peacetime, whenever he rode among his cities, estates, or provinces with his ministers, a standard-bearer always preceded him. Moreover, whenever he walked anywhere through the streets, that kind of banner which the Romans call a *tufa* [Note: *Tufa*. These are mute standards: eagles, dragons, banners, pennons, *tufae*, and feathers. Vegetius, book III, chapter 5. Among the Romans, a kind of standard made from closely packed balls of feathers. Among our own people it survived even to the time of Richard II. A charter of Gervase of Clifton, knight, grants and confirms to Robert of Bevercotes “one plume-tufa.” Some describe the *tufa* as consisting of a cross and a globe, and suppose that the cross brought back to Kent in chapter 20 was Edwin’s *tufa*.], while the English call it a *tuuf*, was accustomed to be carried before him.

## CHAPTER XVII

How Edwin received exhortatory letters from Pope Honorius, who also sent the pallium to Paulinus.

At that time Honorius, the successor of Boniface, held the episcopate of the apostolic see [Note: “When he learned.” This letter to Edwin has no date attached to it, but from the accompanying letter in the following chapter to Honorius of Canterbury it is clear that both were written in the year 634, although Edwin was then dead; his death had not yet reached the pope’s ears. The fact that so many years elapsed from Edwin’s conversion in 627 until news of it was conveyed to the pope, or at least until the pope replied with the pallia, may be attributed either to the slow progress of the faith in much of the Northumbrian kingdom, concerning which see II.12–13 and III.2, or to difficulties that arose concerning the mutual consecration of metropolitans and could have delayed the matter. Nor was it necessary for the pallia to be sent immediately after consecration; indeed, we do not read in Bede that any pallia were sent to Laurence, Mellitus, or Justus, the predecessors of these men.]. When he learned that the nation of the Northumbrians, together with its king, had been converted to the faith and confession of Christ through the preaching of Paulinus, he sent Paulinus a pallium. He also sent King Edwin exhortatory letters, kindling him with paternal affection so that they might always persevere and advance in the faith of truth which they had received [Al., which he had received]. The order of those letters was as follows:

[DCXXXIV.]

“To the most excellent and pre-eminent son Edwin, king of the English, Honorius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greeting.

“So brightly does the integrity of your Christianity burn with zeal for the worship of its Creator that it shines far and wide; and, proclaimed throughout the whole world, it bears abundant witness to the fruit of your work. For you recognize that you are kings when, taught by orthodox preaching about your King and Creator, you believe by venerating God and render to him, as human nature permits, the sincere devotion of your mind.

“For what else shall we be able to offer to our God except that, persisting in good works and confessing him as the author of the human race, we hasten to worship him and return our vows to him? Therefore, most excellent son, we exhort you with the paternal affection that is fitting to hasten by every means, with watchful purpose and constant prayers, to preserve what divine mercy has deigned to call you to by its grace, so that he who has deigned to release you from every error in the present age and bring you to knowledge of his name may prepare for you a dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

“Therefore, occupy yourselves frequently with reading the apostolic memory of your preacher, my lord Gregory, and keep before your eyes the affection of his teaching, which he willingly exercised for the sake of your souls, so that his prayer may increase your kingdom and people and present you blameless before almighty God.

“As for those things which you hoped would be arranged by us for your priests, in accordance with the sincerity of your faith, which has been commendably made known to us through many reports by the bearers of this letter, we foresee that we should freely grant them without any delay. We have sent two pallia for the two metropolitans, namely Honorius and Paulinus, so that, when either of them has been summoned from this world to his Creator, the other may, by this authority of ours, appoint a bishop in his place.

“We have been moved to grant this both by our affection for your charity and by the great distances of the provinces known to lie between us and you, so that in all things we might provide our assistance to your devotion and comply with your desires. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency in safety.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

How Honorius, who succeeded Justus in the episcopate of the Church of Canterbury, received the pallium and letters from the same Pope Honorius.

[Note: “Meanwhile.” Bede did not give the year of Justus’s death, and hence this part of the history is shrouded in darkness. Many hold that Justus occupied the see for only three years and died in 627, and that Honorius then either succeeded him or the see remained vacant. Others assign several more years to Justus, down to 632, 633, and so on. Bede says nothing of a vacant see, nor of Justus’s death before the period covered by the letters below. Yet Honorius had to be consecrated at Lincoln before 633, before Paulinus withdrew from the province of York; and not after 631, so that there would remain twenty-two years—those of Felix and Thomas—before Honorius’s death, which certainly occurred in 653. See the note above on chapter 15. I have therefore placed Justus’s death in 630, Honorius’s consecration in 631, and the pallium in 634.]

Meanwhile, Archbishop Justus, having been raised [Al., taken] to the heavenly kingdoms, died on the fourth day before the Ides of November [DCXXX], and Honorius was made [Al., elected] bishop in his place. When he came to Paulinus to be ordained, Paulinus met him at Lincoln, and Honorius was consecrated as the fifth bishop of the Church of Canterbury after Augustine [DCXXXI].

The aforementioned Pope Honorius also sent him a pallium and letters in which he decreed [Al., had decreed] the same thing that he had decreed in the letter sent to King Edwin: namely, that when the bishop of Canterbury or York had departed this life, the one who remained, as his associate in the same rank, should have authority to ordain another bishop in the place of the one who had died. Thus there would be no need always to undertake the exhausting journey to the city of Rome, across such vast stretches of land and sea, for the ordination of an archbishop.

We have also thought it useful to insert the text of these letters in our *History*.

[DCXXXIV.]

“To our dearest brother Honorius, Honorius.

“Among the many gifts of good things which the mercy of our Redeemer deigns to bestow upon his servants, his clemency also grants this through the munificence of his goodness: whenever, through brotherly communications, it presents unanimous love to one another’s sight in a kind of contemplation. For these things we continually render thanks to his majesty and beseech him with suppliant prayers that he may confirm your charity, laboring and bearing fruit in the preaching of the Gospel, following the rule of your holy master and head, Gregory, with perpetual stability, and through you raise greater growth for the enlargement of his Church.

“Thus may your acquisition and that of your predecessors, which has sprung from the beginnings established by the lord Gregory, grow stronger and spread more widely in faith and works, in the fear of God and charity; so that the promises of the Lord’s word may look upon you in the future, and that voice may summon you to eternal festivity: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11:28). And again: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things: enter into the joy of your lord’ (Matthew 25:21).

“And indeed, dearest brothers, while prefacing these words of exhortation to you in the interest of eternal charity, we do not cease to grant what we perceive may be appropriate to the privileges of your churches. Both at your request and at the request of our sons, the kings, by this present decree of ours, in the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we grant you authority that, whenever divine grace commands one of you to be called to itself [Al., summoned away], the one who survives must ordain the other as bishop in the place of the deceased.

“For this reason also we have sent individual pallia to your charity, for the celebration of that ordination, so that by the authority of our decree you may carry out an ordination pleasing to God. The long intervals of land and sea that lie between us and you compelled us to condescend to this concession, so that no loss might in any way arise for your churches under the pretext of any circumstance, but rather that you might more fully extend the devotion of the people entrusted to you.

“May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

“Given on the third day before the Ides of June, while our lords the Augusti were reigning: Heraclius in his twenty-fourth year, in the twenty-third year after his consulship; and his son Constantine in his twenty-third year and his third consulship; and Heraclius the most fortunate Caesar, likewise his son, in his third year, in the seventh indiction; that is, in the six hundred and thirty-fourth year of the Lord’s incarnation.”

[Note: Heraclius in his twenty-fourth year, etc. This passage was corrupt and mutilated in all editions. There the initials P.C. were incorrectly rendered as *proconsulatus*, although they mean nothing other than *post consulatum* (“after the consulship”); and the words “and his son Constantine in his twenty-third year” were omitted, thereby confusing the meaning of the whole subscription. Heraclius began to reign on 5 October, indiction 14, in the Dionysian year 610, but in the year 602 from the divine incarnation according to Theophanes, who generally reduces the years of the incarnation by eight, as do George Syncellus and most other Greeks. The same Heraclius began his consulship in the year 611. Heraclius the younger, called the new Constantine, was born to Heraclius by the empress Eudocia on 3 May, indiction 15, in the year 612. In the seventh year of Heraclius his father, in the year 617, on 1 January, indiction 5, he was proclaimed consul. Heraclius, the son of the new Constantine and grandson of the elder Heraclius, was born and baptized on 3 November, indiction 5, in the twentieth year of the great Heraclius, the Dionysian year 631. Therefore, in 634, on the third day before the Ides of June, the third year of the boy Caesar Heraclius was in progress. Hence there remains a difficulty in the words “and his third consulship,” which refer to Constantine. For if Constantine’s consulship began in 617, as we have reported from Theophanes, then in 634 Constantine’s seventeenth year of consulship was in progress. It therefore seems that we should read “and his seventeenth year of consulship,” unless perhaps a new consulship began for him when his son Heraclius was born—something which I find noted by no Greek author. Chifflet.]

[Note: Seventh indiction. Baronius places “sixth” in the margin here, to make the calculation fit the year 633, which he either found in his manuscript or thought ought to be found there. Chifflet and others struggled to determine the date of this letter, each correcting his own manuscripts, but all unsuccessfully. For the ancient codices themselves agree on one and the true reading.]

## CHAPTER XIX

How first Honorius, and afterward John, sent letters to the nation of the Scots concerning Easter and at the same time concerning the Pelagian heresy.

[Col. 0113A]

[DCXXXIV.] The same Pope Honorius [Al., the pontiff of the Roman see] also sent letters to the nation of the Scots. He had discovered that they were mistaken in their observance of holy Easter, as we explained above. He earnestly exhorted them not to consider themselves, though few in number and situated at the ends of the earth, wiser than the ancient or contemporary Churches of Christ throughout the world, and not to celebrate Easter contrary to the Paschal calculations and the decrees of the synodal bishops of the whole world.

[DCXL.] John also, who succeeded Severinus, the successor of the same Honorius, while he was still elected to the pontificate, sent them a letter full of great authority and learning for the correction of this same error. He clearly affirmed that the day of the Lord’s Easter ought to be sought from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first, as had been established at the Council of Nicaea.

He also took care to warn them in the same letter to guard against and repel the Pelagian heresy, which he had learned was reviving among them. The beginning of his letter is as follows:

“To the dearest and holiest Tomianus [Al., Thomianus], Columbanus, Cromanus [Al., Chromanus], Dinnaus [Al., Dinnanus], and Baithanus, bishops; to Cromanus [Al., Chromannus], Ernianus [Al., Hermianus], Laistranus, Scellanus, and Segenus [Al., Segianus], priests; to Saranus and the other Scottish teachers or abbots: Hilarius, archpriest and serving in place of the holy apostolic see; John the deacon and, in God’s name, the designated successor; likewise John, chief secretary and serving in place of the holy apostolic see; and John, servant of God and counselor of the same apostolic see.

[Note: Tomianus, etc. Tomianus was archbishop of Armagh; Dinnaus, bishop of Connor; Baithanus, of Clonmacnoise; Cromanus, abbot of Roscrea; Segenus, of Iona. I do not find the sees or titles of the others.]

“The writings which the bearers brought to Pope Severinus of holy memory, and, after he departed from this light, the replies to what had been requested, remained unanswered. When these matters were disclosed, so that the darkness of so great a question should not remain unexamined for long, we discovered that certain people in your province were attempting, against the orthodox faith, to renew a new heresy from an old one [Note: A new heresy from an old one. The old heresy was always to celebrate Easter with the Hebrews; the new one was to do so only occasionally, namely, in those years in which the day of Easter fell on the fourteenth moon. See Appendix, no. 9.], rejecting in a clouded darkness our Easter, on which Christ was sacrificed, and striving to celebrate it with the Hebrews on the fourteenth moon.”

The beginning of this letter plainly declares both that this heresy had only recently arisen among them and that not the whole nation, but only certain individuals among them, had become entangled in it.

After explaining the method of observing Easter, they add the following concerning the Pelagians in the same letter:

“We have also learned this: that the poison of the Pelagian heresy is reviving among you once again. We urge you by every means to remove from your minds this poisonous crime of superstition. For it ought not to be hidden from you how that execrable heresy has been condemned; for it has not merely been abolished for these two hundred years, but is also daily condemned and buried by us under a perpetual anathema. We urge you not to revive among you the ashes of those whose weapons have been burned.

“For who would not execrate their proud and impious attempt, when they say that a human being can exist without sin by his own will and not by the grace of God? The first foolish blasphemy is to say that a human being can be without sin; this is wholly impossible except in the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who was conceived and born without sin.

“For all other human beings are born with original sin. Even when they exist without actual sin, they are known to bear the testimony of Adam’s transgression, according to the Prophet’s saying: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me’ (Psalm 50 [51]:7).”

## CHAPTER XX

How, after Edwin was killed, Paulinus returned to Kent and assumed the episcopate of the Church of Rochester.

When Edwin had ruled the nation of the English and Britons most gloriously for seventeen years—six of which, as we have said, he himself spent in service to Christ—Caedualla, king of the Britons, rebelled against him [Note: Caedualla. See especially how Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates all these wars throughout book XII of his *History of the Kings of Britain*]. Penda, a most vigorous man of royal Mercian stock, gave him assistance; at that time Penda himself ruled that nation for twenty-two years with varying fortune.

They joined battle in a fierce engagement on the plain called Haethfelth [Note: Haethfelth. A wooded district in the county of York between the river Don and the isle of Axholme.], and Edwin was killed on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the year 633 of the Lord’s incarnation, when he was forty-eight years old [Note: Forty-eight. The editions read “forty-seven,” as does the Saxon translator, but this is contrary to the manuscripts.]. His entire army was either slain or scattered.

In that battle his son Osfrid, a young and warlike man, fell before him [Note: Osfrid. Together with Godbold, king of the Orkneys, who had come to his aid. Radulph of Diceto, p. 784.]. His other son Eadfrid, compelled by necessity, fled to King Penda; later, during the reign of Oswald, he was killed by Penda in violation of his oath.

At that time a great slaughter took place in the Church—or among the people—of the Northumbrians [Col. 0115A], especially because one of the leaders responsible for it was a pagan, while the other was a barbarian more savage than a pagan. Penda was devoted to idols together with the whole Mercian nation and was ignorant of the Christian name. Caedualla, on the other hand, although he bore the name and profession of a Christian, was so barbarous in mind and conduct that he spared neither the female sex nor the harmless age of little children, but handed them all over to death amid tortures with the ferocity of a wild beast. For a long time he ravaged their entire provinces and determined to wipe out the whole race of the English from the borders of Britain.

Nor did he show any respect for the Christian religion that had arisen among them. Indeed, it remains the custom of the Britons even to this day to regard the faith and religion of the English as worthless and to associate with them in nothing more than with pagans [Note: Than with pagans. See above, chapter IV of this book.].

Edwin’s head was brought to York [Note: The head. His body, however, was buried in the church at Hatfield.] and afterward carried into the church of the blessed apostle Peter, which he had begun and his successor Oswald completed, as we explained above. It was placed in the portico of Saint Pope Gregory, from whom Edwin himself, as his disciple, had received the word of life.

When the affairs of the Northumbrians had been thrown into confusion by this disaster, and there seemed to be no protection anywhere except in flight, Paulinus took with him Queen Aedilberga, whom he had brought there some time before, and returned by ship to Kent. He was received with great honor by Archbishop Honorius and King Eadbald.

He arrived there under the leadership of Bassus, a very brave soldier of King Edwin. With him were Edwin’s daughter Eanfled [Al., Eanfreda], his son Vuscfrea, and Yffi [Al., Iffi], the son of his son Osfrid. Later, out of fear of Kings Eadbald and Oswald, their mother sent them to Gaul to be raised by King Dagobert [Al., Dagbert] [Note: Dagobert. Son of Chlothar and grandson of Chilperic; his brother Charibert was the father of Bertha, the mother of Aedilberga. Aedilberga herself founded a monastery at Liming, an estate given to her by her brother the king, where she took the veil as the first of the English and ended her life. Her memory is celebrated in the English Martyrology on 10 September.], who was his friend. Both died there in childhood and were buried in the church with the honor appropriate either to royal children or to Christ’s innocent ones.

He also brought with him very many precious vessels belonging to King Edwin, including a large golden cross and a consecrated golden chalice for the service of the altar. These are still displayed as preserved in the church of Kent.

At that time the Church of Rochester had no shepherd, because its bishop Romanus, who had been sent by Archbishop Justus as a legate to Pope Honorius, had been swallowed by the waves of the Italian sea. Therefore, at the invitation of Bishop Honorius and King Eadbald, the aforementioned Paulinus assumed and held its care [Col. 0116B] until he too, in due time, ascended to the heavenly kingdoms with the glorious fruit of his labor.

When he died in that Church, he also left behind the pallium that he had received from the Roman pope.

He had left in his Church at York the deacon James, a truly ecclesiastical and holy man, who, remaining in the Church for a long time thereafter, rescued great spoils from the ancient enemy by teaching and baptizing. The village in which he especially used to live, near Cataract, is to this day called by his name.[^c0012-1] Since he was exceedingly skilled in singing in the church, after peace had later been restored in the province and the number of the faithful had increased, he also began to serve as a teacher of ecclesiastical song according to the custom of the Romans or of Canterbury.[^c0012-2] And he himself, an old man and full of days, followed, according to the Scriptures, the way of the Fathers.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER ONE. How the first successors of King Edwin betrayed [Al., “lost”] the faith of their people, and how Oswald, a most Christian king, restored both kingdoms

[Col. 0115]

After Edwin had been killed in battle, Osric, the son of his paternal uncle Aelfric, succeeded him in the kingdom of Deira, from which province Edwin had derived his family lineage and the beginnings of his kingdom. Osric had been instructed in the sacraments of the faith through the preaching of Paulinus [633]. The kingdom of Bernicia, however—for the people of the Northumbrians had from ancient times been divided into these two provinces—was received by Eanfrid, the son of Aethelfrid, who had derived the origin of his family and kingdom from that province.[^c0012-3]

Throughout the whole period in which Edwin reigned, the sons of the aforesaid King Aethelfrid, who had ruled before him, were living in exile among the Scots or Picts with a great company of nobles. There they were instructed in the teaching of the Scots and refreshed by the grace of baptism. When, after the death of their hostile king, they were permitted to return to their homeland, the first of them, Eanfrid, whom we have mentioned, received the kingdom of Bernicia.[^c0012-4] But as soon as each of these two kings had obtained the earthly kingdom allotted to him, he betrayed by condemning them the sacraments of the heavenly kingdom into which he had been initiated, and restored himself to be polluted and destroyed by the ancient filth of idolatry.

Without delay, the king of the Britons, Cadwallon, killed both of them with impious hand but by a just vengeance [634]. First, in the following summer, while Osric had rashly besieged him in a municipal town,[^c0012-5] Cadwallon suddenly burst out with all his forces and destroyed Osric, unprepared with his army. Then, after possessing the provinces of the Northumbrians for a full year—not as a victorious king, but as a raging tyrant laying them waste and tearing them apart with tragic slaughter—he finally condemned Eanfrid to a similar fate when Eanfrid foolishly came to him with twelve chosen [Al., “select”] soldiers to request peace.

That ill-fated year, hated by all good men, remains so to this day, both because of the apostasy of the kings of the English, by which they had stripped themselves of the sacraments of the faith, and because of the mad tyranny of the British king. Hence all who reckoned the years of the kings agreed that, once the memory of the treacherous kings had been removed, the same year should be assigned to the reign of the succeeding king, Oswald, a man beloved by God. When Oswald arrived after the killing of his brother Eanfrid with a small army but one armed with the faith of Christ, the impious leader of the Britons was killed, together with those immense forces with which he boasted that nothing could resist him. This took place at a site called in the language of the English Denisesburna, that is, Denis’s Stream [Al., “rising stream”].

## CHAPTER TWO. How, among countless miracles of healing, a certain man was cured of the weakness of a painful arm by the wood of the Cross that the same king had raised when he was about to fight against the barbarians

The place where Oswald came to this battle and raised the sign of the holy cross [635], praying on bended knees to the Lord that in such great need he would come to the aid of his worshipers with heavenly help, is still shown and held in great veneration.[^c0012-6] It is said that, after the cross had been made with great speed and a pit prepared in which it was to be set, Oswald himself, burning with faith, seized it, placed it in the pit, and held it upright with both hands until, earth having been heaped around it by the soldiers, it was fixed firmly in the ground. When this had been done, he raised his voice and proclaimed to the whole army:

“Let us all bend our knees and together pray to the living and true almighty Lord, asking him in his mercy to defend us from the proud and savage enemy; for he himself knows that we have taken up arms for the salvation of our people.”

They all did as he had commanded. Thus, advancing against the enemy at the beginning of dawn, they gained the victory in accordance with the merit of their faith.

At the place of this prayer countless miracles of healing are known to have been performed, as a sign and memorial, clearly, of the king’s faith. Even to this day many people are accustomed to cut off splinters from the wood of the most holy cross. When these are placed in water and sick people or animals are given the water to drink or are sprinkled with it, they are immediately restored to health.

That place is called in the language of the English Hefenfelth [Al., Heofenfeld], which may be rendered in Latin as “Heavenly Field.” It received this name in ancient times as a sure omen of future events: signifying, of course, that there a heavenly trophy was to be raised, a heavenly victory begun, and heavenly miracles celebrated to the present day.
