The place lies beside that wall, to the north, which the Romans once built across Britain from sea to sea in order to repel the attacks of the barbarians, as we have related above. At this place the brothers of the church of Hagustald, which is not far away, had for a long time been accustomed to come every year on the day before the anniversary of King Oswald’s death, keep a vigil for the salvation of his soul, celebrate it with abundant praise of the psalms, and offer a sacrifice of sacred oblation for him in the morning. As this good custom grew, they recently built a church there [Al. adds: “and dedicated it”], making the place holier and more honored by all.[^c0012-7] And rightly so, because, as we have learned, no sign of the Christian faith, no church, and no altar had been erected in the whole nation of Bernicia before this standard of the holy cross was set up by the new leader of the army, who, prompted by the devotion of faith, was about to fight against the most monstrous enemy.

It is not beside the point to recount one of the many miracles of power performed at this cross. A certain brother of the church of Hagustald, named Bothelm, who survives to the present day, a few years ago was walking carelessly at night on the ice when he suddenly fell and crushed his arm. He began to suffer the most severe pain from the fracture, so that the pain prevented him from bringing the arm even to his mouth.

One morning, when he heard that one of the brothers intended to go up to the site of the same holy cross, he asked him to bring back some portion of that venerable wood, saying that he believed that, through it and by the Lord’s gift, he might obtain healing. The brother did as he was asked. Returning in the evening, when the brothers were already seated at table, he offered Bothelm some of the old moss with which the surface of the wood was covered. Since, while sitting at table, Bothelm had nowhere at hand to put the gift that had been offered him, he placed it in his bosom. When he went to bed, he forgot to put it elsewhere and allowed it to remain in his bosom.

In the middle of the night, when he awoke, he felt something cold touching his side. He put out his hand to discover what it was and found his arm and hand so completely healed that they were as if he had never suffered any such illness [Al., “they had never suffered”].

## CHAPTER THREE. How the same king requested a bishop from the nation of the Scots, received Aidan, and gave him an episcopal see on the island of Lindisfarne

The same Oswald, therefore, as soon as he had received the kingdom, desired that the whole people whom he had begun to govern should be imbued with the grace of the Christian faith, whose great power he had already experienced in defeating the barbarians. He sent to the elders of the Scots, among whom, while living in exile, he had obtained the sacraments of baptism together with the soldiers who were with him, asking that a bishop be sent to him. Through the bishop’s teaching and ministry, the English people whom he ruled might learn and receive both the gifts of the Lord’s faith and its sacraments [635].

He obtained what he had asked for without much delay. He received Bishop Aidan [Al., Aidanum], a man of exceptional gentleness, piety, and moderation, possessing zeal for God, although not fully according to knowledge. He was accustomed to observe the Lord’s day of Easter, according to the custom of his people, of which we have often spoken, from the fourteenth moon through the twentieth.[^c0012-8] At that time the northern province of the Scots and the whole nation of the Picts likewise celebrated the Lord’s Easter according to this reckoning, believing that in this observance they followed the writings of the holy and praiseworthy Father Anatolius. Whether this is true, anyone learned in the matter can easily discover.[^c0012-9] The peoples of the Scots who lived in the southern parts of the island of Ireland had long before learned, at the admonition of a bishop of the apostolic see, to observe Easter according to the canonical rite.[^c0012-10]

When the bishop had come to him, the king granted him the site of an episcopal see on the island of Lindisfarne, where he had requested it.[^c0012-11] This place is surrounded twice each day by the waves as the tide comes in and goes out, like an island; when the shore is laid bare again, it is restored to the mainland. The king humbly and gladly obeyed Aidan’s instructions in everything and took great care to build up and extend the Church of Christ throughout his kingdom.

There was often a most beautiful spectacle there: when the bishop preached, although he did not perfectly know the language of the English, the king himself became an interpreter of the heavenly word for his commanders and ministers, since during the long period of his exile he had thoroughly learned the language of the Scots.

From that time many men began to come day after day from the region of the Scots into Britain. With great devotion they preached the word of faith in those English provinces over which King Oswald ruled, and, whoever among them had been ordained to the priestly rank, administered the grace of baptism to those who believed. Churches were therefore built in various places; peoples came together gladly to hear the word; royal gifts of estates and territories were granted for establishing monasteries; and English children, together with adults, were instructed by Scottish teachers in the study of the Scriptures and the observance of regular discipline.

For they were monks, especially those who had come to preach. Bishop Aidan himself was a monk, having been sent from the island called Hii,[^c0012-12] whose monastery for a very long time held authority over nearly all the monasteries of the northern Scots and over all those of the Picts, and presided over the governance of their peoples. This island indeed belongs by right to Britain, from which it is separated by a narrow strait; but it had long before been handed over by the Picts who inhabit those regions of Britain to the monks of the Scots, because through their preaching they had received the faith of Christ.

## CHAPTER FOUR. When the nation of the Picts received the faith of Christ [Al., “accepted”]

In the year 565 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Justin the Younger [Codex Mori: Justinian] received the government of the Roman Empire after Justinian, a priest and abbot named Columba [Al., Columbanus, Columban], distinguished by the habit and life of a monk, came from Ireland to Britain to preach the word of God to the provinces of the northern Picts—that is, to those separated from their southern regions by lofty and rugged mountain ranges.[^c0012-13]

The southern Picts, who had their settlements within those same mountains, had, as is reported, received the faith of truth long before, abandoning the error of idolatry. The word was preached to them by Bishop Nynia, a most reverend and holy man of the nation of the Britons [394], who had been regularly instructed at Rome in the faith and mysteries of the truth.[^c0012-14] His episcopal see, distinguished by the name and church of Saint Martin the Bishop, where he himself also rests bodily together with many saints, is now held by the nation of the English. This place, belonging to the province of Bernicia, is commonly called “At the White House,” because there he built a church of stone in a manner unusual among the Britons.[^c0012-15]

Columba came to Britain when Bridius, son of Meilochon, a most powerful king, was ruling the Picts. In the ninth year of Bridius’s reign, Columba converted that people to the faith of Christ by word and example. They therefore granted him the aforesaid island for the establishment of a monastery.

The island is not large, measuring about five households, by English reckoning.[^c0012-16] His successors still possess it to this day, and he himself is buried there [597]. He was seventy-seven years old, about thirty-two years having passed since he first came to Britain to preach.

Before coming to Britain, he had founded a renowned monastery in Ireland, called in the language of the Scots Dearmach, that is, “Field of Oaks,” because of the abundance of oak trees.[^c0012-17] From these two monasteries many other monasteries were subsequently spread by his disciples both in Britain and in Ireland. Among them all, the insular monastery in which he rests bodily held the primacy [Al., “holds it”].

The island itself is accustomed always to have as its ruler an abbot who is a priest. To his jurisdiction the whole province, and even the bishops themselves, in an unusual order, are subject, following the example of that first teacher, who was not a bishop but a priest and monk.[^c0012-18] Some writings about his life and words are said to have been preserved by his disciples.

Whatever sort of man he himself may have been, we know this with certainty about him: he left successors distinguished by great continence, divine love, and regular discipline. At the time of the greatest festival, they followed uncertain cycles, since, being situated far beyond the world, they had received from no one the synodal decrees concerning the observance of Easter. Nevertheless, they diligently observed all the works of piety and chastity that they were able to learn from the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings.

This form of Easter observance remained among them for a considerable time, namely until the year 715 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Al., “716”], for one hundred and fifty years.

At that time the most reverend and holy Father and priest Ecgberht, an Englishman who had lived for a long time in exile in Ireland for Christ’s sake, came to them. He was highly learned in the Scriptures and outstanding in the perfection of a long life. Through him they were corrected and transferred to the true and canonical day of Easter.

Even previously, however, they had not always celebrated it on the fourteenth day of the moon with the Jews, as some supposed. They did celebrate it on a Sunday, but on a Sunday belonging to a different week from the one that was appropriate. For, as Christians, they knew that the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week, must always be celebrated on the first day of the week. But, like barbarians and rustics, they had not learned precisely when that first day of the week—which is now called the Lord’s Day [Al., “named”]—was to occur.

Nevertheless, because they did not cease to burn with the grace of charity [Al., “had not ceased”], they also deserved to receive the knowledge of this matter perfectly, according to the Apostle’s promise: “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you” [Al., “has revealed it”]. More must be said about this in its proper place below.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the life of Bishop Aidan

[Col. 0123B]

From this island, from this community of monks, Aidan was sent to establish the province of the English in Christ, having received the rank of the episcopate [635]. At that time Segenius, an abbot and priest, presided over the same monastery.[^c0012-19] Among his other lessons of conduct, Aidan left the clergy a most salutary example of abstinence and continence. His teaching was especially commended to everyone by the fact that he himself taught nothing other than what he practiced with his companions.

He took care to seek nothing and love nothing of this world. Whatever was given to him by kings or wealthy men of the world, he immediately rejoiced to distribute to the poor who happened to appear. He was accustomed to travel through every kind of place, both urban and rural, not carried on horseback but walking on foot, unless some greater necessity compelled him otherwise. Thus, wherever he saw rich or poor people while traveling, he immediately turned aside to them, inviting unbelievers to receive the sacraments of the faith, or, if they were believers, strengthening them in that faith and encouraging them both by words and deeds to give alms and perform good works.

His life differed so greatly from the sluggishness of our own time that everyone who traveled with him, whether tonsured clerics or laymen, was required to meditate—that is, either to devote themselves to reading the Scriptures[^c0012-20] or to learning [Al., “reciting”] psalms. This was his daily work and that of all who were with him, wherever they might arrive.

If it happened—which was rare—that he was invited to a king’s banquet, he entered with one or two clerics. After refreshing himself briefly, he hurried immediately either to read with his companions or to go out to pray.

Inspired by his example, all religious men and women of that time adopted the custom throughout the year, except during the relaxation of the fifty days of Easter, of extending their fast on Wednesdays and Fridays until the ninth hour.

He never concealed the faults of the wealthy out of regard for their rank or fear of them, but corrected them with severe criticism. He never gave money to the powerful of this world, except only food when he had received anyone as a guest. Rather, the gifts of money that he received from the wealthy he either distributed, as we have said, for the needs of the poor or employed for the redemption of those who had been unjustly sold. Indeed, he redeemed many people by paying their price, and afterward made them his disciples, advancing them through instruction and training even to the priestly rank.

It is reported that when King Oswald had requested from the province of the Scots a bishop who would minister the word of faith to him and his people, another man of a sterner disposition was sent first.[^c0012-21] After preaching for some time to the English people without making any progress, and after the people had been unwilling to listen to him, he returned to his homeland and reported at a meeting of the elders that he had been unable to accomplish anything by teaching the people to whom he had been sent, because they were untamable men of a harsh and barbarous mind.

They then, as is reported, began to hold a lengthy discussion in council about what should be done. They desired the salvation of the people who had requested them, but they were distressed that the preacher they had sent had not been received.

Then Aidan, who was also present at the council, said to the priest under discussion:

“It seems to me, brother, that you were too harsh toward unlearned hearers, and that, in accordance with apostolic discipline [Al., “teaching”], you did not first give them the milk of gentler doctrine, until, gradually nourished by the word of God, they became capable of receiving more perfect things and accomplishing the higher commandments of God.”

When he had said this, all those seated there turned their faces and eyes toward Aidan and carefully considered his words. They decided that he was worthy of the episcopate and that he ought to be sent to instruct the unbelieving and unlearned, since he had first been shown to be imbued with the grace of discernment, which is the mother of the virtues. They therefore ordained him and sent him to preach. Once he had received the opportunity, he appeared adorned not only with the discernment he had previously displayed but afterward with the other virtues as well.

## CHAPTER SIX. On the remarkable religion and piety of King Oswald

[Col. 0125A]

Instructed by the teaching of this bishop, King Oswald, together with the English people whom he ruled [635–642], learned not only to hope for the kingdoms of heaven, unknown to his ancestors, but also obtained more earthly kingdoms than any of his predecessors from that one Lord who made heaven and earth.[^c0012-22] In the end he received under his authority all the nations and provinces of Britain, which are divided among four languages: those of the Britons, Picts, Scots, and English.

Raised to such a height of kingship, he nevertheless—and this is remarkable to say—was always humble, kind, and generous toward the poor and strangers. It is reported that once, on the holy day of Easter, while he was seated at dinner with the aforementioned bishop, a silver dish filled with royal food had been placed before him, and they were just about to extend their hands to bless the bread. Suddenly his servant entered—the man entrusted with caring for the reception of the needy—and informed the king that a very great multitude of poor people had come from every direction and were sitting in the streets, asking the king for alms.

The king immediately ordered the dishes set before him to be carried to the poor, and also commanded that the dish be broken into pieces and distributed among them. When the bishop who was seated beside him saw this act of piety, he delighted in it, seized Oswald’s right hand, and said, “May this hand never grow old.”

The bishop’s blessing was fulfilled according to his prayer. After Oswald was killed in battle and his hand and arm had been cut off from the rest of his body, they remained incorrupt to the present day. They are preserved in a silver casket in the church of Saint Peter in the royal city called after a former queen, Bebba—today Bamburgh.[^c0012-23] They are venerated by everyone with fitting honor.[^c0012-24]

Through the activity of this king, the provinces of Deira and Bernicia, which until then had been at odds with one another, were joined into one peace and, as it were, fitted together into a single people. Oswald was the nephew of King Edwin through his sister Acha.[^c0012-25] It was fitting that so great a predecessor should have from his own family such an heir both of religion and of the kingdom.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. How the province of the West Saxons received the word of God through the preaching of Birinus, and concerning his successors Agilberht and Leuthere

[Note: “At that time.” Since Bede does not state the year of Birinus’s arrival, the authorities vary here, as they often do. I have chiefly followed the Saxon Chronicle, not only because it surpasses the other historians after Bede in authority everywhere, but especially because it deserves particular trust in matters concerning the West Saxons, having been written by an inhabitant of that kingdom, as Warton observes.]

At that time [634] the people of the West Saxons, who in ancient times were called Gewissae,[^c0012-26] received the faith of Christ while Cynegils [Al., Cynigils] was reigning. The bishop Birinus preached the word to them. He had come to Britain with the counsel of Pope Honorius, promising that, in his presence, he would scatter the seeds of the holy faith in the innermost regions beyond the English, where no teacher had preceded him.

By order of the same pontiff, he was consecrated to the episcopal rank by Asterius, Bishop of Genoa. But when he reached Britain and first entered the country of the Gewissae, finding all the people there to be completely pagan, he judged it more useful to preach the word there rather than go farther and search for those to whom he ought to preach.

[^c0012-1]: **On the village called by his name.** Today, Akeburg.

[^c0012-2]: **Ecclesiastical song.** See Appendix, no. 12.

[^c0012-3]: **Into these two provinces.** Deira began at the Humber and ended at the River Tees; Bernicia extended from the Tees to the Tweed. Hence some kings of the Northumbrians ruled only over the Deirans, such as Aelle; some only over the Bernicians, such as Adda, Aelle’s son; and some over both, such as Edwin, Aelle’s son, and Saint Oswald, followed by his brother Oswiu. From Oswiu’s time onward the two regions remained under one kingdom. So Richard of Hexham, *Ten Writers*, p. 286. Some, however, assigned the boundaries of these provinces very differently, extending Deira to the Tweed and Bernicia to the Firth of Edinburgh. We find Bernicia extending to the Firth, but Deira no farther than the River Tees.

[^c0012-4]: **“Whom we have mentioned.”** The manuscripts commonly read: “We have mentioned Osric as king of Deira, and Eanfrid as king of Bernicia. Both …”

[^c0012-5]: **“In a municipal town.”** Not “of the town,” as writers have absurdly corrupted Bede’s text, but “in a municipal town”: a town regarded as a *municipium*, or called a *municipium*. The Saxon Paraphrase also translates this correctly. We know only one such place in this province, and why should it not have been York, which Aurelius Victor explicitly calls a *municipium* in his *History of the Caesars*? The word *municipium* could indeed have been used in later centuries in a broader sense, but Bede’s expression here involves a particular designation: the chief city of the kingdom of Deira, which in fact had long been a *municipium*.

[^c0012-6]: **The sign of the holy cross.** Many charters still remain in the archives of Durham with the ancient seal of Saint Cuthbert attached. On it the head of Saint Oswald is displayed on one side and his cross on the other. See the reproduction in Appendix, no. 13.

[^c0012-7]: **A church there.** A church of Saint Oswald still remains to the northwest of Axelodunum. More about these matters may be found in Appendix, no. 13.

[^c0012-8]: **The fourteenth through the twentieth moon.** The reference is to the disputed Paschal reckoning, according to which Easter could be celebrated on a Sunday falling between the fourteenth and twentieth days of the lunar month.

[^c0012-9]: The editor refers the reader to chapter 25 below and to Bede’s *Chronicle*, no. 4230.

[^c0012-10]: See Book II, chapter 19.

[^c0012-11]: **The island of Lindisfarne.** “It takes its name from the River Lindis, which runs out into the sea. The river is two feet wide and cannot be seen except when the sea has receded. The island is eight miles in circumference. It is now called Holy Island because Saints Aidan, Finan, Tuda, and Cuthbert, together with other bishops of the same Church, rested there in body; afterward many monks and various laypeople were martyred and buried there by the Danes.” Simeon of Durham, pp. 68–69. See the same work for the territory of this island.

[^c0012-12]: **The island of Hii.** “It is two thousand paces long and more than a thousand wide. Two monasteries have been founded there, one of Black Monks and the other of holy nuns of the order of Saint Augustine wearing the rochet; there is also a refuge. The monks’ monastery remained until the time of King Malcolm and Saint Margaret as a burial place and royal seat, as it were, of nearly all the kings of Scotland and Pictland.” Fordun, *Scotichronicon* II, 1. “In the old monastery of Saint Columba, the bishop’s seat of the islands was established, in place of the former residence in Eubonia—that is, Man—which had been seized by the English. Among the ancient ruins there still remains a burial ground or common cemetery of all the noble families who lived in the Western Isles. Three burial mounds stand out, separated by modest intervals, with little houses erected over them facing east. On the western side of each is an inscribed stone indicating whose tomb it is. In the middle is the TOMB OF THE KINGS OF SCOTLAND; on the right, OF THE KINGS OF IRELAND; on the left, OF THE KINGS OF NORWAY. In the rest of the cemetery, the distinguished families of the islanders have their own separate tombs. Six nearby islands, small but not unproductive, were granted by ancient kings and the rulers of the islands to Columba’s monastery.” Buchan.

[^c0012-13]: **Mountain ranges.** The Grampian Mountains. Their highest ridge is today called Drumalban, “the Ridge of Albion.”

[^c0012-14]: **At Rome.** Nynia is said to have gone to Rome in the time of Pope Damasus, to have been ordained for the Britons by Siricius in 394, and, on his return, to have visited Saint Martin, a man renowned for regular discipline, though not his uncle, as Hector Boethius reports. On this occasion Nynia dedicated his church to Saint Martin, as was customary in those times.

[^c0012-15]: **At the White House.** Whithorn in Galloway. Nynia died there in 432. In the same year Saint Patrick entered Ireland, while Palladius had entered Scotland the preceding year. The Thoresby manuscript codex at this passage has the following note, written in large letters in the body of Bede’s text: “Where the Premonstratensian Order has its episcopal see and election.”

[^c0012-16]: **“Five households, by English reckoning.”** One manuscript reads *milliarium* (“a mile”), incorrectly.

[^c0012-17]: **Dearmach.** Adamnan, *Life of Saint Columba* I.3, says that Columba founded in central Ireland a monastery called in Scots *Dairmach*. This is the Augustinian monastery now called Durrow or Durmach in County King’s, and it is incorrectly confused by some with the monastery of Armagh.

[^c0012-18]: **The bishops themselves.** But not with respect to spiritual authority. See Adamnan, *Life of Saint Columba* I.26: “At another time a proselyte from the province of the Numinenses came to the saint. He conducted himself humbly as far as he could, so that no one knew that he was a bishop; nevertheless, this could not be hidden from the saint. On another Sunday, when the saint ordered him to prepare the body of Christ according to custom, he summoned the saint so that the two of them might break the Lord’s bread together, as though they were two priests. The saint therefore approached the altar, and, suddenly looking at his face, addressed him: ‘Christ bless you, brother. Let the bishop alone break the bread in the episcopal manner. Now we know that you are a bishop. Why have you tried to conceal this until now, so that the veneration owed to you might not be shown by us?’ On hearing these words, the humble pilgrim was deeply astonished, honored Christ in the saint, and all who were present greatly marveled and glorified God.” In Canisius, vol. V, part II, p. 579.

[^c0012-19]: **Segenius.** He was the fourth abbot after Saint Columba. The second was Baithan; the third, Virgnous or Fergnaus. This is the Segenius to whom Pope John, among others, sent a letter (II.19), and to whom Cummian also wrote in the collection of Irish letters, both concerning Easter.

[^c0012-20]: **The Scriptures.** If Hector Boethius is to be believed, they had other books as well to occupy themselves in reading. Fergus, the king, carried away from Rome a chest filled with books when Rome was captured, and transported it with him to the Hebrides, placing it on the island of Iona, together with books containing the distinguished deeds of his people. Hence the long-standing expectation concerning the lost Decades of Livy. Hector supported this not merely by a general assertion but by the personal testimony of his own eyes: he claimed to have seen part of the documents and prepared a description of them, explaining their circumstances with such minute detail that, unless the author’s integrity is impugned, it would be sacrilegious to doubt the truth of his account. See Boethius, Book VII.

[^c0012-21]: **Another man first.** His name was Cormannus, according to Hector Boethius, Book IX.

[^c0012-22]: **The reign of Oswald.** The dates given here are 635–642.

[^c0012-23]: **In the royal city.** Bebbanburgh, now Bamburgh. It is said to have been founded by Ida, king of the Northumbrians, according to the Saxon Chronicle.

[^c0012-24]: **They are preserved.** Simeon of Durham, p. 2, says: “They display their incorruptibility even to our own age, through the grace of the king’s and bishop’s merits. Suardebrand, a monk of our Durham Church who recently died while William was administering the bishopric, repeatedly testified that he had seen them.” Walter of Whittlesey writes that the arm was brought to Peterborough Monastery by Winegot of Bebberch. Ingulf, under the year 1018, mentions a prior who, during the Danish devastations, fled from Peterborough with several brothers, taking with him the arm of King Saint Oswald to the island of Ely. Nevertheless, after many years it was displayed at Peterborough to King Stephen, Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln, and others.

[^c0012-25]: **Acha.** Besides Anfrid and Oswald, she bore Aethelfrid five other sons—Oswiu, Ostaf, Osa, called Florilegus, Oswiod, Oslac, and Offa—and one daughter, Aebba, abbess of Coldingham. Fl. of Worcester.

[^c0012-26]: **Gewissae.** This is the Saxon term for “West Saxons.” The same formation appears in “Visigoths,” with only the expletive Saxon prefix *Ge-* added.

Therefore, while he was preaching the Gospel in the aforesaid province [DCXXXV], when the king himself had been instructed in the faith and was being washed in the baptismal font together with his people, it happened at that time that the most holy and victorious king of the Northumbrians, Oswald, was present. He received him as he came out of the font and, in a most beautiful and truly God-worthy union—for he was to take the king’s daughter as his wife—first received him, dedicated to God in a second birth, as his own son.

Both kings gave the same bishop the city called

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Both Kings. For Oswald held superior authority over both kingdoms, as Bede says in the preceding chapter. Thus kings Æthelberht and Sæberht agreed in the church of Paul; II, 3.]

Dorcic [Al. Dorcinca, Dorkecaester],

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Dorcic. Dorchester in Oxfordshire, at the confluence of the Thames; for there is another village of the same name in Dorset. Note also that, although this region later passed to the Mercians, it then obeyed the kings of the West Saxons. At first the West Saxons had one bishop, namely the one at Dorcic; later they had two, one at Winchester and the other at Sherborne. In the time of King Edward three were added to these two: those of Wells, Crediton, and Cornwall; and not long afterward a sixth at Ramsbury. W. Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus* III. This remained the episcopal see until the time of William I, when Bishop Remigius transferred it to Lincoln.]

to establish there an episcopal see. After churches had been built and dedicated there, and after he had called many peoples to the Lord through his devout labor, he departed to the Lord and was buried in the same city. Many years later, through the agency of Bishop Haedde,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Transferred. Hedde was a monk and abbot of Streaneshalch; concerning his succession in the episcopate, see IV, 12. He transferred the see from Dorchester, together with the body of Saint Birinus, to Winchester in the year 683, the tenth year of his episcopate—unless the brief Winchester Annals, Ang. Sacr. I, 193, have reckoned incorrectly. From this translation arose endless disputes between the monks of Winchester and the canons of Dorcic around the year 1224. The memory of Saint Birinus is celebrated on 3 December.]

he was transferred from there to the city of Venta and placed in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

When the king also had died, his son Coinualch [DCXLIII] succeeded him in the kingdom. He refused to accept both the faith and the sacraments of the heavenly kingdom, and not long afterward lost the power of the earthly kingdom as well. For after repudiating the sister of Penda, king of the Mercians, whom he had married, he took another wife. Consequently, Penda attacked him in war, deprived him of his kingdom, and drove him into exile with the king of the East Angles, whose name was Anna. While he lived there in exile for three years, he came to know and embraced the faith of the truth [Al., the truth]. For the king with whom he was staying was himself a good man, blessed with good and holy offspring, as we shall explain below.

[Col. 0127B] When Coinualch had been restored to the kingdom, a certain bishop named Agilberctus [DCL] came into the province from Ireland. He was by nationality a Gaul, but had then spent a considerable time in Ireland for the sake of studying the Scriptures. He joined the king, voluntarily undertaking the ministry of preaching. Seeing his learning and diligence, the king asked him to remain as bishop of his people, once he had received an episcopal see there. Agilberctus agreed to his request and governed that people for many years by priestly authority.

At length the king, who knew only the language of the Saxons, grew weary of the foreign speech and introduced into the province another bishop of his own language, named Uini [DCLXIV], who had been ordained in Gaul. Dividing the province into two dioceses, he granted Uini an episcopal see in the city of Venta, which is called Uintancaestir by the Saxon people. Therefore Agilberctus was deeply offended that the king had done this without consulting him.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] He returned. I do not place Agilberctus’s return to Gaul before the year 664, because he took part in the Synod of Paris in that year; III, 25.]

He returned to Gaul and, having received the episcopate of the city of Paris, died there in old age and full of days.

Not many years after his departure from Britain, Uini was expelled from the episcopate by the same king [DCLXVI].

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Uini … purchased. Hence, after his death, he did not deserve to be included in the succession of the bishops of London. M. Westmonasteriensis, year 666.]

He withdrew to the king of the Mercians, named Wulfhere, and purchased from him, for a price, the see of the city of London; he remained its bishop until the end of his life. Thus the province of the West Saxons remained without a bishop for a considerable time.

At that same time, the aforementioned king of that people, repeatedly afflicted by his enemies with the gravest losses to his kingdom,

[Col. 0127D] finally recalled that it was treachery which had once driven him from the kingdom, while the faith of Christ, once recognized, had restored him to it. He understood that, just as the province was then deprived of a bishop, so it had rightly been deprived of divine protection as well. He therefore sent envoys to Agilberctus in Gaul, humbly entreating him to return to the episcopate of his people.

But Agilberctus excused himself and declared that he could not come, since he was bound by the episcopate of his own city and diocese. Nevertheless, so as not to offer no help to one who pleaded so earnestly, he sent in his place the presbyter Leutherius, his nephew, so that, if the king wished, he might be ordained bishop for him. Agilberctus said that he himself judged Leutherius worthy of the episcopate.

The people and the king received him honorably and asked Theodore,

[Col. 0128B] then archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, to consecrate him as their bishop. He was consecrated in that city [DCLXX] and, in accordance with synodal decree, alone governed the episcopate of the Gewissae with careful administration for many years (see IV, 12).

## CHAPTER VIII. How Earconberht, king of the Kentish people, ordered idols to be destroyed; and concerning his daughter Ercongota and Æthelberga, his kinswoman, virgins consecrated to God

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 640, Eadbald, king of the Kentish people, passed from this life and left the governance of the kingdom to his son Earconberht. Having received it, Earconberht held it with great distinction for twenty-four years and several months.

He was the first of the kings of the English to order, by royal authority throughout his entire kingdom, that idols be abandoned and destroyed, and likewise that the fast of forty days be observed. To ensure that this command could not easily be disregarded by anyone, he prescribed suitable and appropriate punishments for transgressors.

His daughter Earcongota, a daughter worthy of such a parent, was a virgin of great virtues. She served the Lord in a monastery built in the territory of the Franks by a most noble abbess named Fara.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Fara. She is called Burgundofara, that is, “noble Fara,” or “noble family,” born among the Burgundians. The monk Jonas of Bobbio wrote a book on her virtues, included in editions of Bede’s works, vol. III, and later edited again by Surius and Mabillon.]

The place is called

[Note: [Col. 0128D] In Brige. The district of Brie and the Forest of Brie derive their names from this forest; the province is now called Brie. In this region Fara founded the convent of virgins at Eboriacum, which is still called Faremoustier after its founder.]

In Brige. For at that time, when not yet many monasteries had been built in the territory of the English, many people from Britain used to visit the monasteries of the Franks or of Gaul for the sake of the monastic way of life. They also sent their daughters there to be educated and joined to the heavenly Bridegroom, especially to Brige and

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Cale. Chelles in the Parisian district, about one hundred stadia from Paris. It was once a royal estate on the River Marne; there Bathildis built a convent of consecrated virgins.]

to Cale, and to

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Andilegum. Chiffletius supplied an extensive note on the location of this place and—strangely enough—abandoning the true location that he had before his eyes, sought a false one far away. Hadrianus Valesius, in his *Notitia Galliarum*, under the word *Andeliacum*, commonly called Andelys-sur-Seine, pointed out to us almost with his finger the monastery of Andilegum of which Bede speaks. For from the royal codex he reports the following words concerning Saint Clotilde, queen of the Franks: “She also built another monastery above the River Seine, in a place called Andeleius, not far from the walls of the city of Rouen, in the name of the Mother of God.” “It is situated,” says Valesius, “about seven leagues from Rouen,” though Mabillon says only four miles; and a few years ago it passed from being an old cell or priory into a Benedictine abbey. The year of death of both the holy Fara and Earcongota is unknown. Smith.

—In the monastery of Andilegum. [Col. 0129B] It is exceedingly strange that neither in *Gallia Christiana* nor among the abbeys of the Frankish kingdom is any mention made of this most illustrious nunnery, although it is clear, on Bede’s own testimony, that more than a thousand years ago consecrated virgins were sent there—as also to Brige, Cale, and the island of Britain—to be dedicated to God.

The learned Hadrianus Valesius seemed to point this place out to us almost with his finger in his *Notitia Galliarum*, under the word *Andeliacum*. There he reports, from the royal codex, the following concerning Saint Chlotilde, queen of the Franks: “She also built another monastery above the River Seine, in a place called Andeleius, not far from the walls of the city of Rouen, in the name of the Mother of God.” It is about seven leagues from Rouen, and this is the monastery of Andelagum mentioned in the *Chronicle of Fontanelles*, volume III of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 243. But how can this monastery be said to be not far from the walls of Rouen if it is about seven leagues distant from them?

A different place occurs to one for Bede’s Andilegum: namely, that it was situated in Alsace, that Saint Salaberga began its construction, and that it was later completed and enlarged by the empress Richarda. Hermannus Contractus, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 887, writes: “The empress Richarda, accused by the emperor and others of adultery with Luitward, bishop of Vercelli, who enjoyed intimate favor with her and the emperor at court, proved by divine judgment that she was untouched by any intercourse with men and had remained a virgin, although she had already appeared for twelve years in the emperor’s marriage. Soon separated from him, she withdrew to the convent of virgins at Andelach, which she had built, and there the virgin queen remained devoted to divine service.”

Among the papers of Father Stephen Voyrin, beside this passage of Hermannus, I found the following note: The divine judgment he mentions was her not being harmed by fire. For, dressed in a white garment, she entered a blazing pyre and could not be injured. That remarkable garment, untouched by the fire, is preserved in the Premonstratensian convent at Stivagium in Lorraine. She had received it from the emperor Charles, long before it came into the possession of the Premonstratensians; [Col. 0129D] and she joined Stivagium to Andelacum, as is clear from letters both of Richarda herself and of Pope Lucius III. These clearly state that Charles outlived his wife, which nevertheless does not agree sufficiently with the historian Hermannus.

The letters of Lucius, issued in 1181, read as follows: “The place of Stivagium, in which the abbey has been founded, is known to be subject in perpetuity to the monastery of Andelacum, which the same empress built from its foundations and, in the presence of the said emperor, assigned to the Roman Church, after the death of Richarda, his wife, who had held that place as her own possession, by virtue of the institution of the late Charles, emperor of the Romans.”

The letters of Richarda herself, dated on the Kalends of May in the year 880, concerning the property of the abbey of Stivagium, are extant at Stivagium.

So wrote Voyrinus, a man of angelic innocence and piety in character, indefatigable zeal, and outstanding intellect, who would have deserved much from the public through the composition of books had he not died in the flower of his age.

Gaspar Bruschius, in his *Chronology of the Monasteries of Germany*, writes: “Andlow, anciently Andelaha, named either from the river of that name or from the convent of Helio, in the district of Alsace, sacred to Saints Fabian and Felicitas, is a wealthy and celebrated college of canonesses born of distinguished families, situated near the Vosges Mountains. It was founded and most liberally endowed for twelve canonesses and an equal number of canons in the year of Christ 880—or, as others hold, 888—by Saint Richarda, daughter of the king of the Scots and wife of Charles the Fat, emperor of the Romans. Separated from her husband by divorce, she lived there, died there, and was buried in an honorable tomb raised behind the high altar.”

Stephanus Vitus, on the authority of Bruschius, maintains that Richarda was Irish, that is, born in Greater Scotland. Molanus mentions her in his *Additions to Usuard*, under 18 September. Wion does so on the same day in Book III of *The Wood of Life*, and in Book IV, chapter 3, among the holy empresses of the West. Raderus wrote her life in *Holy Bavaria*. Joannes Ruyr also wrote about her and her monastery in *Antiquities of the Vosges*, part III, book I, chapter 10.

Yet when all these writers say that the monastery was founded by Richarda, you should not understand this to mean that she first erected this sacred house. Rather, having been founded long before and later neglected and partly ruined, it was restored, enriched, and enlarged by her with buildings and revenues, so as to provide a suitable residence for pious and noble virgins.

In my opinion, it had originally been founded by Saint Salaberga. The following passage comes from the life of Salaberga, whose author was nearly contemporary with her: “Why say more? With God as author, committing all her hope, after God, to the blessed man Walbert, abbot of Luxeuil, her husband having converted and her children having been consecrated to God, after receiving the religious habit and taking counsel with the blessed Walbert, and with her husband’s consent, she endeavored to build a convent of girls in the suburb of the city of Langres, on her paternal inheritance or succession. By making Christ heir to her paternal inheritance, she nobly endowed it from the revenues of her own estates.”

And shortly afterward: “Although that place lay near the borders of Austrasia, it was nevertheless close to Burgundy, being somewhat less than forty miles from the monastery of Luxeuil. There she dedicated to the Lord Christ a hundred or more girls, both daughters of nobles and girls from her own household. But when most of the monastery’s structure had been built, the servant of Christ, filled—as she was—with the prophetic Spirit of God, began to weigh the matter with the man of God and to judge that the convent of girls was not secure in that place and possessed no stability or fortification. For although the barbarians were far away, the fact that the frontiers of kingdoms were intermingled on every side gave warning of danger in the future—and we later witnessed that danger.

“Not long afterward, civil war was waged between the Frankish kings Theuderic and Dagobert in those very regions. Every neighboring place was devastated; fields, villages, houses, and—most grievously—the bodies of the saints themselves were burned by fire.”

Understand *suburbium* as a diocese or territory, as it is commonly read in ancient authors. Andilegum is in Upper Alsace, where the borders of the ancient kingdoms of Burgundy and Austrasia lay; hence it was sometimes reckoned within one and sometimes within the other. It was about forty miles from Luxeuil, that is, approximately thirteen ordinary leagues by road.

No monastery could be identified more accurately than the one that Salaberga had prepared for a hundred girls on the advice of Walbert, abbot of Luxeuil, and whom she later transferred to Laon. But, as I believe, two hundred years later the heroine Richarda restored the ruins of Andilegum—or rather rebuilt them even better. Chiffletius.]

the monastery of Andilegum. Among them was Saethryd, the daughter of the wife of Anna, king of the East Angles, whose name we mentioned above, and Æthelberg, that same king’s natural daughter. Since both were foreigners, they were appointed abbesses of the same monastery at Brige on account of the excellence of their virtues.

The elder daughter of that king, Sexburh, wife of Earconberht, king of Kent, had a daughter named Earcongota, of whom we are about to speak.

Many deeds of virtue and signs of miracles performed by this virgin dedicated to God [Al., consecrated to God] are still commonly related by the inhabitants of that place. But it will suffice for us to say briefly something about her passing, by which she sought the heavenly kingdoms.

As the day of her calling approached, she began to go around the small dwellings of the sick servants of Christ in the monastery, especially those who were advanced in age or distinguished by the excellence of their character. Humbly commending herself to the prayers of them all, she did not conceal that her imminent death, which she had learned through a revelation, was at hand.

She said that the revelation had been of the following kind: she had seen a crowd of men dressed in white entering the same monastery. When she asked them what they were seeking or what they wanted there, they replied that they had been sent there for this purpose: to take with them the golden coin that had come there from Kent.

That very night, in the latter part of it—that is, at the beginning of dawn—she passed from the darkness of the present world into the light above. Many of the brothers of the same monastery, who were in other buildings, reported that they had clearly heard the singing of angels already chanting, as well as a sound like that of a great multitude entering the monastery. They immediately went out to discover what it was and saw that an immense light had been sent down from heaven. It was leading that holy soul, freed from the bonds of the flesh, to the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland [Al., leading her onward].

They also relate other miracles divinely displayed in the same monastery that night; but since we are moving on to other matters, we leave them to tell those stories themselves.

The venerable body of the virgin and bride of Christ was buried in the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. On the third day it was decided that the stone covering the tomb should be removed and placed higher in the same spot. When this was done, such a fragrant sweetness [Al., such a fiery fragrance] welled up from below that all the brothers and sisters standing there seemed to see the storerooms of balsam opened.

Her maternal aunt, whom we have mentioned, Æthelberg, also preserved the glory of perpetual virginity beloved by God through great bodily continence. The extent of her virtue became clearer after her death.

While she was abbess, she began to build in her monastery a church in honor of all the apostles, in which she wished her body to be buried. But when the work had been brought almost halfway to completion, death took her before she could finish it, and she was buried in the very place in the church where she had desired.

After her death, while the brothers were occupied with other matters, the building was abandoned for seven years. When that period had elapsed, they decided, because of the excessive labor involved, to abandon the construction of the church completely and to transfer the abbess’s bones from that place to another church that had been completed and dedicated.

When they opened her tomb, they found her body so undefiled that it was free from the corruption of carnal desire. They washed it again, clothed it in other garments, and transferred it to the church of the blessed martyr Stephen, whose feast is customarily celebrated there with great honor on the Nones of July.

## CHAPTER IX. How frequent miracles of healing occurred at the place where King Oswald was killed; and how first the beast of a traveler and then a paralytic girl were healed there

The most Christian king Oswald of the Northumbrians reigned for nine years, counting also that year which the savage impiety of the British king and the insane apostasy of the English kings had made detestable. For, as we explained above (Chapter I), it was established by the unanimous agreement of all that the name and memory of the apostates should be entirely erased from the list of Christian kings and that no year of their reign should be recorded.

When this period of years had been completed, he was killed in a great battle by the same pagan people and pagan king of the Mercians by whom his predecessor Edwin had also been slain, at a place called in the language of the English

[Note: [Col. 0131D] Maserfelth. Two counties secretly claim this place for themselves. Lancashire, near Winwick, has produced the place-name Maserfelth and preserves an inscription in the church of Winwick from ancient times, without neglecting the argument that it lies within the kingdom of the Northumbrians, where Penda attacked Oswald. Shropshire also has its own Maserfeld, today Oswestry or Oswaldstre, which is called in British “Oswald’s Cross,” and lies in that county because Oswald had recently taken it after defeating Penda. The author of Saint Oswald’s Life in Capgrave stands by this view, and Camden confirms his authority. Oswestry lies about seven miles from the city of Shrewsbury toward Wales, and less than half a mile from Offa’s Dyke. In that field a church called White Church was founded in honor of Saint Oswald. *Monumenta Anglicana* I, p. 38.]

Maserfelth, in the thirty-eighth year of his life,

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The fifth of August. His memory is celebrated in the Martyrology on that same day. See IV, 14.]

on the fifth day of August [DCXLII].

The greatness of his faith in God and the devotion of his mind became evident even after his death through miracles of virtue. For at the place where he was killed by pagans while fighting for his homeland, healings of both human beings and animals have continued to be celebrated down to the present day.

It happened, therefore, that many people took away dust from the very place where his body fell to the ground, put it into water, and thereby brought great relief to their sick dependents [Al., through this]. This practice became so widespread that the earth gradually removed from the place produced a pit as deep as a man is tall.

Nor is it surprising that the sick are healed at the place of his death, since throughout his life he never ceased to care for the sick and poor, to give alms, and to offer assistance. Many miracles of virtue are reported as having occurred at that place or through dust taken from it, but we have thought it sufficient to relate only two that we heard from our elders.

Not long after his killing, when some time had passed, it happened that a certain man, riding on horseback, was traveling near that place. His horse suddenly grew weary, stopped, lowered its head to the ground, let foam fall from its mouth, and, as the pain increased greatly, began to collapse onto the ground.

The rider dismounted, spread straw beneath the animal, and began to await the moment when he would either recover his beast improved or abandon it as dead. While the animal was long tormented by severe pain and twisted itself in various directions, it suddenly rolled into the place where the famous king had fallen.

Immediately the pain subsided, it ceased its violent movements, and, following the customary manner of horses, rolled from one side to the other as if after weariness. Then it rose at once, apparently sound in every respect [Al., sound], and began eagerly cropping the green grass.

When he saw this, the man, being of keen intelligence, understood that this place where the horse had been healed possessed some remarkable holiness. He set up a marker there, mounted his horse shortly afterward, and proceeded to the lodging he had intended to reach.

When he arrived, he found there a girl, the niece of the head of the household, who had long been afflicted with paralysis. As the members of the household complained in his presence about the girl’s grievous illness, he began to tell them about the place where his horse had been healed.

Why say more? They placed her on a cart and took her to that place [Al., added: that place], where they set her down. Once she had been placed there, she fell asleep briefly. When she awoke, feeling herself healed of that bodily paralysis, she asked for water, washed her face herself, arranged her hair, covered her head with a linen cloth, and returned on foot, sound in health, with those who had brought her.

## CHAPTER X. How the dust of that place proved effective against fire

At the same time [DCXLIII], another man, as they say, of the British nation, traveling near the very place where the battle mentioned above had been fought, saw one portion of the ground greener and more beautiful than the rest of the field. With an intelligent mind he began to reason that there could be no other cause for the unusual greenness of that place than that some man holier than the rest of the army had been killed there.

He therefore took some of the dust of that earth with him, tying it in a linen cloth, thinking that the dust would eventually be useful for healing the sick. Continuing on his journey, he reached a village in the evening and entered a house in which the villagers [Al., neighbors] were dining and feasting.

Received by the masters of the house, he too sat down with them at the meal, hanging the small linen cloth containing the dust he had brought on one of the wall-posts [Al., on one wall-post].

While they continued for a long time to devote themselves to food and drunkenness, a great fire was lit in the middle of the house. Sparks flew high, and the roof of the house—which was woven from branches and covered with hay—suddenly caught fire.

When the guests saw this, terrified and confused, they fled outside, unable to help the burning house, which was already on the point of destruction. When the house had been consumed by the flames, only the doorpost on which the dust was enclosed and hanging remained safe from the fire and untouched.

When they saw this miracle, they were greatly astonished. Investigating more carefully, they discovered that the dust had been taken from the place where the blood of King Oswald had been shed [Al., was shed].

When these miracles had been disclosed and widely reported, many people began for days afterward to frequent that place and to receive there the grace of healing for themselves and their own.

## CHAPTER XI. How a heavenly light remained above his relics throughout the entire night; and how demoniacs were healed through them

Among these events, I think that what virtue and heavenly miracle were displayed when his bones were discovered and transferred to the church where they are now kept [DCXLIII] must by no means be passed over in silence.

This was accomplished through the diligence of Osthryth, queen of the Mercians, who was the daughter of his brother Osuiu,

[Col. 0134B] [Al., his brother Osuiu], who held the summit of the kingdom after him, as we shall relate below.

There is a famous monastery in the province of Lindsey called

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Beardaneu. Bardney. The first foundation of this monastery is uncertain, since its fortifications were so thoroughly destroyed by the Danes. Nevertheless, from ancient times it rose to such greatness that it once had three hundred monks, and its abbot is said to have been lord of Lindsey. Its restoration is owed to Walter de Gaunt in the year 1115. *Monumenta Anglicana* I, p. 142.]

Beardaneu, which the same queen greatly loved, revered, and honored with devotion together with her husband Æthelred. She desired to bury there the honored bones of her uncle.

When the cart carrying these same bones arrived at the aforesaid monastery toward evening, those who were in the monastery refused to receive them willingly. Although they knew him to be holy, they nevertheless pursued him even after death with their old hatred, because he had come from another province and had received rule over them.

It therefore happened that the relics remained outside that night, with only a large tent stretched over the cart in which they lay [Al., nevertheless].

But a manifestation of heavenly power revealed how reverently they ought to be received by all the faithful. For throughout that entire night a column of light, extending from that cart all the way to heaven, stood visible from almost every place in the same province of Lindsey.

When morning came, the brothers of that monastery, who the previous day had refused them, began earnestly to ask the queen that the same holy relics, beloved by God, be buried among them.

They therefore washed the bones, placed them in a coffin that they had prepared for this purpose, and set it in the church with appropriate honor. To give the memory of the holy man’s royal person eternal remembrance, they placed above the tomb his standard, fashioned of gold and purple. They also poured into a corner of the sacristy the water in which they had washed the bones [Al., had washed them].

From that time onward, the earth that had received the venerable bath came to have a healing power for driving demons from possessed bodies.

Later, while the aforementioned queen was staying in the same monastery, a venerable abbess came to visit her. She is still alive today and was named Æthilhild, sister of the holy men Æthelwin and Aldwin. The former was bishop in the province of Lindsey; the latter was abbot

[Col. 0135A] in the monastery called Peartaneu (see Book II, 16), not far from which she also had a monastery.

When she arrived there and was speaking with the queen, and, among other matters, the conversation turned to Oswald, she said that she herself had seen that night a light above his relics, rising high to heaven. The queen added that many sick people had already been healed by dust from the pavement on which the water from that washing had been poured.

The abbess asked that a portion of the healing dust be given to her. She received it, tied it in a cloth, placed it in a small box, and returned.

Some time afterward, while she was in her own monastery, a certain guest arrived who was often suddenly and severely afflicted by an unclean spirit during the night. He was kindly received, and after supper he had laid his limbs down in bed when the devil suddenly seized him. He began to shout [Al., cry out], gnash his teeth, foam at the mouth, and twist his limbs in various movements.

Since no one could either hold or bind him, a servant ran and, knocking at the door, notified the abbess.

She opened the monastery gate and went out with one of the consecrated women to the men’s quarters. Calling for a presbyter, she asked him to come with her to the afflicted man.

When they arrived, they saw that many people were already present and were trying to hold the man and restrain his insane movements, but they were entirely unable to do so. The presbyter recited exorcisms [Al., an exorcism] and did everything he could to calm the wretched man’s fury. Yet even he, though laboring greatly, could accomplish nothing.

When no hope of healing seemed to remain for the raging man, the aforesaid dust suddenly came to the abbess’s mind. She immediately ordered a servant to go and bring the small box in which it was kept.

When the woman entered the courtyard of the house, bringing what she had been ordered to fetch, the demoniac suddenly became silent. As though released into sleep, he lowered his head and settled all his limbs into repose.

All fell silent, holding their faces attentively, anxiously waiting to see what the outcome would be.

After a short interval, the afflicted man sat up and, breathing heavily, said: “Now I am of sound mind, for I have regained the sense of my mind.”

They diligently questioned him about how this had happened. He replied: “As soon as this virgin approached the courtyard of this house with the small box she was carrying,

[Col. 0135D] all the evil spirits that were oppressing me departed. Having left me, they appeared nowhere.”

Then the abbess gave him a small portion of that dust [Al., all of it]. After the presbyter had offered a prayer, he passed a very peaceful night and from that time onward suffered no nocturnal fear or torment from the ancient enemy.

## CHAPTER XII. How a little boy was cured of fever at his tomb

[Col. 0136A]

Some time later [DCLXIII], a little boy in the same monastery was severely afflicted by a long illness of fever. One day, as he anxiously awaited the hour of the attack, one of the brothers entered to see him and said:

“My son, shall I teach you how to be cured of this troublesome illness [Al., this kind of illness]? Rise,” he said, “enter the church, approach Oswald’s tomb, sit there, and remain quietly close to the tomb. Be careful not to leave it or move from that place until the hour when the fever subsides has passed. Then I myself will enter and lead you away.”

The boy did as he had advised. As he sat beside the saint’s tomb, the illness did not dare touch him at all; indeed, it fled in such fear that it did not venture to touch him on the second day, the third day, or ever afterward.

The brother who related this to me, having come from that place, added that at the time when he was speaking with me the boy—now a young man—was still alive in the same monastery, where this miracle of healing had once occurred.

Nor is it surprising that the prayers of that king, now reigning with the Lord, had great power with the One whose earthly kingdom he had once governed, while he had always labored and prayed more earnestly for the eternal kingdom.

Finally, they say that he often remained in prayer from the time of the morning praises until daylight. Because of his frequent practice of praying or giving thanks to the Lord, he was accustomed always to sit with his hands turned upward upon his knees wherever he was.

It is also commonly reported, and has become proverbial, that he ended his life even while speaking the words of a prayer. For when he was surrounded by weapons and enemies and saw that he was on the point of being killed, he prayed [Al., to the Lord] for the souls of his army.

Hence they say in the proverb: “God, have mercy on the souls,” said Oswald as he fell to the ground.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Bones. During the Danish invasions, in the year 910, the bones of Saint Oswald are said to have been transferred from Bardney to Gloucester, through the agency of Æthelred, king of the Mercians. SIM. DUN. BROMPT. There are indeed countless places, not only in England but also in Belgium and Ireland, that claim the relics of Saint Oswald, so that several legends would scarcely suffice for investigating them.]

His bones, therefore, were transferred and buried in the monastery we have mentioned. As for his head,

[Note: [Col. 0136D] Head. As I think everyone concedes, Saint Oswald’s head was later placed in the coffin with the body of Saint Cuthbert, and was eventually carried with it to Durham and found between his arms. See William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, Book III, under the bishops Edmund and Ranulf of Durham.]

and his hands with the arms severed from the body, the king who had killed him ordered them to be hung upon stakes. When Osuiu [Al., Osuin], his successor in the kingdom, came there with an army a year later, he took them away: the head he placed in the cemetery of the church of Lindisfarne, but the hands with the arms he buried in the royal city. (See above, chapter 6.)

## CHAPTER XIII. How in Ireland someone was recalled from the point of death through his relics

The fame of this illustrious man not only traversed all the regions of Britain, but, scattering far across the Ocean the rays of its life-giving light, reached the regions of both Germany and Ireland [DCLXXIX]. The most reverend Bishop Acca is accustomed to relate that, when he was on his way to Rome and was staying with the most holy Archbishop Vilbrord of the Frisian people, together with his own bishop Vilfrid, he frequently heard Vilbrord recount the wonderful things that had taken place in that province in connection with the relics of that most reverend king.

He also reported that, while he was still a priest and was leading a life of pilgrimage in Ireland for the sake of his eternal homeland, the report of Oswald’s holiness had already spread far and wide throughout that island. Among the miracles he related, we have thought it appropriate to insert the following into our present History.

“During the time,” he said, “of the pestilence that devastated Britain and Ireland with widespread destruction, among those struck by that plague was a certain scholar from the Scottish people, a learned man devoted to literary study, but one who had shown absolutely no zeal or diligence in caring for his everlasting salvation. When he saw that death was near, he began to fear and tremble, lest, once dead, he should be carried to the gates of hell because of the merits of his sins. He called for me, while I was nearby, and, trembling amid the labored sighs of his illness, he addressed me in a mournful voice as follows:

“‘You see that, as the affliction of my body continually increases, I am now being forced to face the point of death. I have no doubt that, immediately after the death of my body, I shall be carried away to the everlasting death of my soul and subjected to infernal torments, since for a considerable time, amid my studies of divine reading, I have habitually served the entanglements of vice rather than the divine commandments. Yet I have resolved in my mind that, if heavenly mercy grants me some additional time to live, I shall correct my vicious habits and transfer my whole mind and life entirely and completely to obedience to the divine will.

“‘But I know that I have no merit by which I may either receive, or hope to receive, a reprieve for living, unless perhaps he should deign to show mercy to me, wretched and unworthy as I am, through the help of those who faithfully served him. We have heard—and the report is most widespread—that among your people there was a king of wondrous holiness named Oswald, whose excellence in faith and virtue became renowned even after his death through the frequent working of miracles. I therefore ask you, if you have any of his relics in your possession, to bring them to me, in case the Lord should wish to have mercy on me through his merit.’

“I replied: ‘I do possess a fragment of the wood upon which his head, after he had been killed by the pagans, was fixed. If you believe with a steadfast heart, divine mercy may, through the merit of so great a man, grant you a longer span of this life and make you worthy to enter eternal life.’

“He immediately replied that he had complete faith in this.

“Then I blessed water and, putting into it a splinter of the aforesaid oak, gave it to the sick man to drink. At once he began to improve, and, recovering from his illness, lived for a great many years thereafter. Turning to God with all his heart and in all his actions, wherever he went he proclaimed the mercy of the gracious Creator and the glory of his faithful servant.”

## CHAPTER XIV. How, after Paulinus’s death, Ithamar assumed the episcopate of the Church of Rochester in his place; and concerning the remarkable humility of King Oswin, who was killed by Osuiu in a cruel slaughter

[Col. 0138B] After Oswald had been transferred to the heavenly kingdom, his brother Osuiu [DCXLII] took his place upon the throne of the earthly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] His brother. I do not know why certain writers have stated that Osuiu was the illegitimate son of Æthelfrith, contrary to the authority of all trustworthy historians.]

He was about thirty years old and held the kingdom, with great difficulty, for twenty-eight years. He was attacked, on the one hand, by the pagan people of the Mercians, who had killed his brother, and also by his own son Alchfrid, as well as by his nephew, that is, the son of his brother who had reigned before him, Oidilvald [Al., Adilvald].

In the second year of Osuiu’s reign—that is, in the six hundred and forty-fourth year from the Lord’s Incarnation—the most reverend Father Paulinus, once bishop of York but then bishop of the city of Rochester, passed to the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Nineteen years. Wharton, *Anglia Sacra* I, p. 329, rashly thinks that Bede should be corrected here by substituting eleven years for nineteen. He failed to notice that, besides the eleven years during which Paulinus presided over the Church of Rochester, from 633 to 644, eight years had elapsed during which he sat at York, from 625 until the death of King Edwin in 633. Bede does not say nineteen years during which he presided, as Wharton incorrectly reads, but nineteen years during which he held the episcopate.]

He had held the episcopate for nineteen years, two months, and twenty-one days.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Buried. During the episcopate of Gundulf, Archbishop Lanfranc utterly demolished the old church of Saint Andrew and built a new basilica, raising the bones of Saint Paulinus from the earth and placing them honorably in a shrine. This was done on the fourth day before the Ides of January, on which day his annual memorial is solemnly celebrated in the Church of Rochester.]

He was buried in the sacristy [Al., sanctuary] of the blessed apostle Andrew, which King Æthelberht had built from the foundations in that same city of Rochester. In his place Archbishop Honorius ordained Ithamar, who was indeed descended from the people of Kent, but was equal to his predecessors in life and learning.

During the early years of his reign, Osuiu had as a partner in royal dignity a man named Oswin, of the stock of King Edwin—that is, the son of Osric—of whom we have spoken above, a man of extraordinary piety and religious devotion. He ruled the province of the Deirans [Al., Dierans] amid the greatest abundance of all things, and was himself beloved by everyone [DCLI]. Yet he could not maintain peace with the man who governed the remaining part of the Trans-Humbrian people to the north, namely, the province of the Bernicians. Rather, as the causes of their disagreement grew more serious, Osuiu put him to death in a most wretched slaughter.

For when an army had been gathered against him, Oswin saw that he could not engage in battle with Osuiu, who had the greater number of auxiliaries. He therefore thought it more useful at that time to lay aside his intention of fighting and preserve himself for better times. He dismissed the army he had assembled and ordered each man to return home, from a place called

[Note: [Col. 0139C] Vilfaraesdun. Although Bede describes this place fairly carefully, I have not been able to find it. The learned Ellerton conjectured that it was Ellerton; there are indeed several places of that name in the region, but all are too near waterfalls to fit the location given by Bede. The manuscript Durham Chronicle calls it Wolfrethdon, but nothing can be inferred from this, since no place of that name exists there; and even if it did, the authority of later manuscripts would not justify departing from the ancient reading.]

Vilfaraesdun, that is, Vilfari’s Hill, situated about ten miles from the village of Cataracton toward the setting of the summer sun. He himself withdrew with only one soldier, his most faithful companion, named Tondheri [Al., Condheri], intending to conceal himself in the house of the earl Hunwald, whom he believed to be especially friendly toward him. But, alas, it was far otherwise. Osuiu [Al., Osuin] had him betrayed by that same earl and killed, together with the soldier just mentioned, by his prefect Ætheluin, in a death detestable to all.

This took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the ninth year of Osuiu’s reign, at a place called

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The thirteenth. Hence, on this day, the margin of the Durham Martyrology reads: “In Britain, the feast of Saint Oswin, king and martyr.” Matthew Paris incorrectly gives the fourteenth.]

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Ingetlingum. Today Gilling, near Richmond. No remains of the monastery survive there. It was founded by Eanfled, the wife of Osuiu and a relative of Oswin, and its abbot was Trumhere, a kinsman of Oswin. See below, III.21 and 24. The body of Saint Oswin was carried to Tynemouth and lay there until the passage of time consigned it to oblivion. At last, in the year 1065, during the time of Earl Tostig and Bishop Ægelwin of Durham, a stone sarcophagus was found, not without a revelation, by the king himself in the chapel of the blessed Virgin Mary, 415 years after his burial; his bones were placed in a shrine with great honor. See the history in the manuscript *Life of Saint Oswin*, Cotton Library, Julius A. 10, and in Matthew of Westminster under the year 1110. Richard, abbot of Saint Albans, transferred Oswin’s relics from the ancient chapel into a new bier. The same source, *Florilegium*. In the meantime, however, the monks of Jarrow transferred Saint Oswin’s bones to Jarrow and, after Earl Waltheof of Northumbria had given them the church of Saint Mary and Oswin, kept them with themselves for a considerable time before later returning them to the former place. *Book of Benefactors of Durham*, Cotton Library, Domitian A. 7. The monuments of the Church of Durham likewise attest this.]

Ingetlingum. A monastery was later built there to atone for this crime, so that prayers might daily be offered to the Lord for the redemption of the souls of both kings, namely, the one who had been killed and the one who had ordered his killing.

King Oswin was handsome in appearance, tall in stature, pleasant in speech, courteous in manner, and generous with his hand to all, both noble and humble. Thus it happened that everyone loved him on account of the royal dignity of his spirit, his countenance, and his merits, and that men of the highest rank came from nearly every province to serve him. Among the other glories of his virtue and modesty, or, so to speak, of his particular blessing, his humility is also said to have been especially great; one example will be sufficient to prove this.

He had given Bishop Aidan an excellent horse, on which Aidan could ride, cross the waters of rivers, or, if any other necessity arose, complete a journey. When a poor man encountered him after a short interval and asked for alms, Aidan dismounted and ordered the horse, still adorned with its royal trappings, to be given to the poor man. He was indeed very merciful, a lover of the poor, and, as it were, the father of the needy.

[Col. 0140A] When this was reported to the king, he said to the bishop, as they were about to enter to dinner: “Why, my lord bishop, did you give the royal horse, which you ought to have kept as your own, to a poor man? Did we not have many cheaper horses, or other possessions sufficient for gifts to the poor, even if you had not given them that horse which I specifically chose for you to possess?”

The bishop immediately replied: “What are you saying, O king? Is that son of a mare dearer to you than that Son of God?”

After these words they entered to dine. The bishop took his place in his usual seat. The king, who had come from hunting, began to warm himself standing by the fire with his attendants. Suddenly, while warming himself, he remembered the words the bishop had spoken. He unbelted his sword, gave it to an attendant, and hurried to the bishop’s feet, falling before him and asking him to be reconciled with him.

“Never again,” he said, “will I speak about this or judge what or how much of our property you give to the sons of God.”

When the bishop saw this, he was very frightened. He immediately rose, lifted the king up, and promised that he was fully reconciled to him, provided only that, sitting down to the meal, he would lay aside his sadness. As the king, at the bishop’s command and request, recovered his cheerfulness, the bishop, on the contrary, began to grow sad, even to the point of shedding tears. When his priest asked him in his native language—for the king and his household did not understand it—why he was weeping, he replied:

“I know that the king will not live for long. Never before have I seen so humble a king. From this I perceive that he will soon be taken from this life; for this people is not worthy to have such a ruler.”

Not long afterward, the bishop’s dreadful prediction was fulfilled by the king’s mournful death, which we have described above.

Bishop Aidan himself, only twelve days after the killing of the king whom he loved—that is,

[Note: [Col. 0140D] The day before the Kalends. On this day the margin of the Durham Martyrology reads: “In Britain, Saint Aidan, first bishop of Lindisfarne. On the same day, the commemoration of the holy relics of that Church.” See the list of these relics in the appendix, no. 14. It is worthy of note that this day marked the beginning of Saint Cuthbert’s monastic vocation, following a vision concerning Saint Aidan’s death. See Bede’s *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 4.]

on the day before the Kalends of September, was taken from the world and received from the Lord the everlasting rewards for his labors [DCLI].

## CHAPTER XV. How Bishop Aidan foretold to sailors a coming storm and gave them holy oil with which to calm it

What his merit was, the inward judge also revealed through signs of miracles [DCXLIII–DCLI]. Of these, it is enough to set down three for the sake of remembrance. A certain priest named

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Utta. An illustrious priest and abbot of the monastery called Capra’s Head. See below, III.21.]

Utta [Al., Witta], a man of great seriousness and truthfulness, and therefore honorable to everyone, even to the princes of this world, was sent to Kent to bring from there a wife for King Osuiu, namely Eanfled, the daughter of King Edwin.
