(See Book II, chapters 9 and 20.) She had been taken there after her father was killed. He intended to travel there by land but return with the maiden by ship. He approached Bishop Aidan and begged him to pray to the Lord on behalf of himself and those who were about to undertake so long a journey.

The bishop blessed them and commended them to the Lord, and also gave them sanctified oil.

“I know,” he said, “that when you board the ship, a storm and contrary wind will come upon you. But remember to cast into the sea this oil that I give you; immediately the winds will cease, the sea will become calm, and fair weather will happily accompany you and bring you home by the desired route.”

Everything happened in order as the bishop had foretold. At first, when the waves of the sea were raging, the sailors tried to hold the ship by casting anchors into the water, but their efforts achieved nothing. As waves swept around them, began to fill the ship, and they all saw that death was threatening and already at hand, at last the priest remembered the bishop’s words. Taking up the flask, he poured some of the oil into the sea, and immediately, just as had been foretold, the sea ceased its raging.

Thus it came about that the man of God, through the spirit of prophecy, foretold the coming storm and, through the power of that same spirit, though bodily absent, calmed the storm after it had arisen. The sequence of this miracle was not related to me by some doubtful informant, but by the most faithful priest of our Church, named Cynimund, who declared that he had heard it from Utta [Al., Witta] himself, the priest in whom and through whom it had been accomplished.

## CHAPTER XVI. How he removed by prayer the fire brought against the royal city by its enemies

[Col. 0141D]

Many who were able to know it relate another memorable miracle of the same Father [DCXLII–DCLV]. During his episcopate, the hostile army of the Mercians, under the leadership of Penda, devastated the regions of the Northumbrians far and wide with impious destruction and reached the royal city, which is called Bamburgh from the name of Queen Bebba. Since they could capture it neither by arms nor by siege, they tried to consume it with flames.

They tore down the huts [Al., bonds] that they found near the city, brought there a great mass of beams, timbers, walls, wattlework, hay thatch, and other materials, and surrounded the city with these at a great height on the side adjoining the land. When they saw a favorable wind, they set fire to the pile and attempted to burn the city.

At that time the most reverend Bishop Aidan was staying on the island of Farne, which lies about two miles from the city. He often withdrew there for the sake of solitary prayer and silence. Even today they customarily point out on that island the place of his solitary dwelling.

When he saw the balls of fire and smoke being carried by the winds and rising above the walls of the city, he is said to have raised his eyes and hands toward heaven and said with tears:

“See, Lord, how many evils Penda is doing.”

At these words the winds immediately changed direction away from the city and turned the flames back upon those who had kindled them. Several of them were injured, all were terrified, and they ceased attacking the city, recognizing that it was being divinely aided [Al., preserved].

## CHAPTER XVII. How the beam placed against the church in which the same bishop died could not be consumed by the flames while the rest of the house burned; and concerning his inner life

[Note: [Col. 0141D] *Apposta* … *Destina* … Bede calls *apposta* or *destina* a wooden beam by which, as a support, a sacred building constructed of wood was strengthened on its western side. Yet Vitruvius, who was considerably earlier than Bede, uses *destinae* in Book V, chapter 12 of *On Architecture*, where he discusses harbors and structures made in water. The manuscripts cited by Philander read *vincula* or chains, by which wooden chests made of masonry and destined to be rolled into the water were bound; hence *destinae* are called bonds in the ancient glossaries. I combine these two senses of the word as follows: a *destina* is something by which anything else is restrained or held back, either so that it does not disperse or so that it does not collapse. CHIFFLET.]

When the day of death forced him to leave the body [DCLII], after completing sixteen years of his episcopate [Al., seventeen], he was in a royal estate not far from the city we have mentioned. Since he had a church and chamber there, he often turned aside and stayed there, and from there he used to go out to preach throughout the surrounding region. He did the same in other royal estates, possessing no property of his own except his church and the small fields adjoining it.

They therefore pitched a tent for him in his illness on the western side of the church, so that the tent touched the church wall. Thus it happened that, leaning against the *destina* that had been placed outside the church as a protection, he breathed out his final breath of life. He died in the seventeenth year of his episcopate, on the day before the Kalends of September.

His body was immediately transferred from there to the island of Lindisfarne and buried in the cemetery of the brothers. After some time, when a larger basilica had been built there and dedicated in honor of the most blessed prince of the apostles, his bones were transferred there and buried at the right side of the altar, with the veneration due to so great a bishop.

Finan succeeded him in the episcopate [DCLII]. He too had been sent there from the Scottish island of Iona and its monastery and remained in the episcopate for a considerable time.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Sent from the monastery. The position of these words is sufficient to refute the absurd error of those who have called the island of Hii by the name “Hiidestinatus.”]

After several years it happened that Penda, king of the Mercians, came into these regions with a hostile army. While destroying everything he could with sword and flame, he also burned the village in which the bishop had died, together with the church mentioned above. But, in a remarkable manner, the single *destina* against which he had leaned when he died could not be consumed by the flames that devoured everything around it.

When this miracle became known, the church was soon restored there, and this same *destina* was again placed externally as a support for the wall, as it had been before. After some further time, however, through negligent carelessness, the same village and the church itself were again consumed by fire. Yet even then the flames could not touch the *destina*. Although the fire entered with great force into the holes by which it had been fastened to the building and consumed them [Al., destroyed them], it was nevertheless in no way allowed to damage the *destina* itself.

Therefore, when the church was built there for the third time, they did not place that *destina* outside as a support for the house, as before; instead, they placed it inside the church in memory of the miracle, where those entering were to bend the knee and implore heavenly mercy. It is established that from that time many obtained the grace of healing in that place. Indeed, several people obtained remedies for illnesses affecting themselves and their families by cutting splinters from the *destina* itself and placing them in water.

I have written these things about the person and deeds of the man mentioned above, not praising or approving in him his imperfect understanding concerning the observance of Easter. Rather, I strongly condemn that matter, as I have demonstrated most clearly in the book I composed *On Times*. But, as a truthful historian, I have simply described the things that were done by or through him, praising in his actions what deserves praise and commending it to the memory of readers for their benefit: his devotion to peace and charity, continence and humility; his mind victorious over anger and greed, and contemptuous alike of pride and empty glory; his diligence both in carrying out and teaching the heavenly commandments; his skill in reading and keeping vigils; an authority worthy of a priest; his correction of the proud and powerful; and his gentleness in consoling the weak and refreshing or defending the poor.

In short, to gather much into few words, as far as we have learned from those who knew him, he took care to omit none of the things he understood from the evangelical, apostolic, or prophetic writings to be required, but to fulfill them all in action according to his strength.

These qualities I greatly embrace and love in the bishop mentioned above, since I do not doubt that they were pleasing to God. But that he did not observe Easter at its proper time, whether because he did not know its canonical date or because he was overcome by the authority of his own people and refused to follow what he had recognized, I neither approve nor praise.

Nevertheless, I approve this in him: that in celebrating his Easter he held in his heart, venerated, and preached nothing other than what we do—namely, the redemption of the human race through the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ. Accordingly, he celebrated it not, as some falsely suppose, with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon on whatever weekday it might fall, but always on Sunday, from the fourteenth day of the moon through the twentieth. He did so because of his faith in the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week, and because of his hope in our resurrection, which he believed would truly take place on that same first day of the week, now called the Lord’s Day, together with the holy Church.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the life and death of the religious King Sigeberht

In those times [DCXXX], after Earpwald, the successor of Rædwald, had ruled the East Angles, his brother Sigeberht became king.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Of the East Angles. Having completed the history of the conversion of the Northumbrians under the kings Edwin, Oswald, Osuiu, and Oswin, from II.15 through this chapter, Bede now resumes what remained concerning the conversion of the East Angles.]

He was a good and religious man.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Good. In II.15 he is called “very learned,” since in Gaul he had been closely associated with educated men and had exchanged letters with Desiderius, bishop of Cahors. According to Pits, these letters are said to survive among the Swiss, in the monastery of Saint Gall.]

While he had formerly been living in exile in Gaul, fleeing the hostility of Rædwald,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Hostility. Sigeberht was only Earpwald’s half-brother and was driven into exile by King Vitrico out of envy.]

he received the baptismal washing. After returning to his homeland and obtaining the kingdom, he immediately wished to imitate the good arrangements he had seen in Gaul and established a school in which boys might be instructed in letters.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] School. Several historians—William of Malmesbury, Florence, and Huntingdon—place multiple schools here, in various suitable places. But Bede speaks of only one, in which the establishment of schools began and in which it appeared in a more distinguished form. See concerning these matters the brief discussion in the appendix, no. 15.]

Bishop Felix, whom he had obtained from Kent, assisted him and provided them with teachers and instructors according to the custom of the people of Kent.

The king became such a lover of the heavenly kingdom that at last, abandoning the affairs of the kingdom [DCXXXIV] and entrusting them to his kinsman Ecgric [Al., Ecgrico], who had previously held part of that same kingdom, he entered the monastery that he had built for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Monastery. At Bedrichsuurde, today Bury St Edmunds. THOMAS OF ELY, *Life of Saint Æthelthryth*.]

Having received the tonsure, he devoted himself to serving the eternal kingdom instead.

[Col. 0144D] After he had done this for a long time, it happened that the people of the Mercians, led by King Penda, went to war against the East Angles. When they saw themselves inferior to their enemies in battle, they asked Sigeberht to come with them to strengthen the army. Although he refused and protested, they dragged him unwillingly from the monastery and took him into battle, hoping that the soldiers would be less afraid and that, in the presence of a former commander of great courage and distinction, they would be less likely to think of flight.

But he, mindful of his profession, although surrounded by an excellent army, would carry nothing in his hand except a staff. He was killed together with King Ecgric, and their entire army, as the pagans pressed upon it, was either slaughtered or scattered.

Anna became their successor in the kingdom [DCXXXV], the son of Eni,

[Note: [Col. 0145C] Of royal descent. Eni was the brother of Rædwald. EL. UIG. *Chronology*.]

a man of the highest virtue and the father of excellent offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Excellent offspring. See chapter 7 of this book. Note also that Uithberga, a nun of the monastery of Ely, must be added to the offspring listed there. According to Thomas of Ely, after her father’s death she lived as a solitary at Dereham. Anna’s daughters must also be joined by two sons, Aldwulf and Jurmin. SAME AUTHOR.]

The details concerning them will be given in their proper place.

[Col. 0145B] He too was later killed by the same pagan leader of the Mercians who had killed his predecessor.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] He was killed. According to the historians, Anna’s death took place in the year 654. Thomas of Ely, in the passage cited, no. 7, adds that it occurred in the nineteenth year of his reign. From this we may infer the dates of these kings according to Bede’s method. Sigeberht came to power in 630; Egric around 633. Both were killed in 635. King Anna was buried at Blythburgh, where his son Jurmin was also buried before being transferred to Bury St Edmunds.]

He was killed [DCLIV].

## CHAPTER XIX. How Fursa founded a monastery among the East Angles; concerning his visions and holiness, to which his incorrupt flesh after death also bore witness

While Sigeberht still held the insignia of the kingdom [Al., islands],

[Note: [Col. 0146C] While he still held them. Those who begin Sigeberht’s reign in 636 place Fursa’s arrival in 637, certainly earlier than is appropriate. For Fursa did not come at the very beginning of Sigeberht’s reign, but only while the king still held the royal insignia; nor did the king lay aside insignia that he had only recently received, but did so only at the end, after abandoning the affairs of the kingdom. I have therefore chosen the middle year for Fursa’s arrival.]

a holy man named Fursa came from Ireland [DCXXXIII], distinguished in word and deed and marked by exceptional virtues. For the sake of the Lord, he wished to lead a life of pilgrimage wherever he found a suitable opportunity. When he reached the province of the East Angles, he was honorably received by the king mentioned above. Carrying out his customary work of evangelizing, he converted many unbelievers to Christ by both the example of his virtue and the encouragement of his preaching, and strengthened those who already believed in faith and love of Christ.

When he was seized by a bodily illness, he was granted the enjoyment of an angelic vision. In it he was admonished to persist diligently in the ministry of the word that he had begun and to devote himself indefatigably to his customary vigils and prayers, because his departure was certain, but the hour of that departure was unknown, as the Lord says: “Watch therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

Strengthened by this vision, he took care to build as quickly as possible the site of the monastery he had received from King Sigeberht and to establish it according to the rules of monastic discipline. The monastery was wooded and attractive because of its proximity to the sea. It was built in a certain fort which, in the language of the Angles,

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Cnobheresberg. Today Burgh Castle in Suffolk, at the mouth of the River Yare.]

is called Cnobheresburg, that is, Cnobhere’s city. Later, Anna, king of that province, and other nobles adorned it with larger buildings and gifts.

This man was of the most noble lineage of the Scots, but far nobler in spirit than in flesh. From the time of his childhood he devoted no small care both to sacred reading and to monastic discipline. And, as is especially fitting for the saints, he diligently endeavored to do everything he had learned ought to be done.

Why say more? As time passed, he also built a monastery for himself in which he might devote himself more freely to heavenly pursuits. There, after being seized by illness, he was taken from the body, as the little book written about his life sufficiently relates. From evening until cockcrow, separated from his body, he was granted the sight of angelic hosts and the privilege of hearing their blessed praises.

He was accustomed to report that, among other things, he clearly heard them chanting:

“The saints will go from strength to strength.”

And again:

“The God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

He was restored to his body, and on the third day was again taken out of it. He saw not only the greater joys of the blessed but also the greatest struggles with evil spirits, who, shamelessly accusing him repeatedly, attempted to block his heavenly journey. Yet, protected by angels, they accomplished nothing.

If anyone wishes to know more fully about these matters—namely, with what cunning the demons repeated, as though written in a book, his deeds, his idle words, and even his very thoughts, and what joyful or sorrowful things he learned from the holy angels and from the righteous men who appeared among the angels—let him read the little book of his Life mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0146D] The little book of his Life. Three ancient authors, each in two books—the first concerning his life, the second concerning his miracles—described the deeds of Saint Fursa. The first anonymous writer lived not long after Fursa, since Bede praises him so often and occasionally follows his wording. The date of the second anonymous author cannot easily be determined. The third was Arnulf, abbot of Lagny, who, around the turn of the eleventh century, condensed the two works of the anonymous authors into two books, namely, the *Life* and the *Miracles*, and interpolated several passages. MABILLON, *Acta Benedictina*, vol. II, p. 299.]

From that book, I believe, he will gain much spiritual benefit.”

Among these things there is one account which we too have thought it worthwhile to include in this history. When he had therefore been carried high into the air, he was ordered by the angels who were leading him to look down upon the world. Then, lowering his eyes toward the regions below, he saw beneath him, at the lowest depth, what seemed to be a dark valley. He also saw four fires in the air, not far apart from one another. When he asked the angels what these fires were, he heard that they were fires which would set the world ablaze and consume it.

One was the fire of falsehood, because we do not at all fulfill what we promised in baptism, namely, to renounce Satan and all his works. The second was the fire of greed, because we prefer the riches of the world to love of heavenly things. The third was the fire of discord, because we are not afraid to offend the minds of our neighbors, even in matters of no importance. The fourth was the fire of impiety, because we consider it nothing to strip the weaker and to defraud them.

The fires gradually grew, extending themselves until they reached one another, and, joined together, became an immense flame. When they drew near, he, terrified, said to the angel: “Lord, behold, fire is coming near me.” But he replied: “What you did not kindle will not burn in you. For although this pyre appears terrible and immense, it examines each person according to the merits of his deeds; each person’s desire will burn in this fire. Just as a person burns in the body through unlawful pleasure, so, once freed from the body, he will burn through the punishment he has deserved.”

Then he saw one of the three angels who had served as his guides throughout both visions go before him and divide the flames of the fire, while two others flew around on either side, protecting him from the danger of the fires. He also saw demons flying through the fire and devising the conflagrations of wars against the just.

There follow accusations against him by evil spirits, the defenses of good spirits, and a more abundant vision of the heavenly hosts. He also saw holy men from his own people [Al.: Scots], whom, as he had formerly heard from widespread report, he had known to have held the rank of priest honorably. From them he heard many things that were highly beneficial either to himself or to all who might wish to listen.

When they had finished speaking, and when they too were returning to heaven with the angelic spirits, the three angels of whom we have spoken remained with blessed Fursey in order to return him to his body. When they drew near the great fire mentioned above, the angel divided the flames of the fire as before. But when the man of God had reached the opening made between the flames, unclean spirits seized one of the men whom they were tormenting in the fires, threw him at Fursey, and, striking his shoulder and jaw, set them on fire. He recognized the man and recalled that he had received his garment as the man was dying.

The holy angel immediately seized him and threw him back into the fire. The evil enemy said: “Do not cast away the one whom you formerly received; for just as you received his goods as a sinner, so you ought also to share in his punishments.” The angel replied: “He received him not because of greed, but in order to save his soul.” And the fire ceased.

Then the angel turned to Fursey and said: “What you kindled burned in you. For if you had not accepted the money of this man who died in his sins, his punishment would not be burning in you.” After saying many other things, he taught him in salutary speech what ought to be done for the salvation of those who repent as death approaches.

Afterward, when he had been restored to his body, he carried visibly upon his shoulder and jaw, throughout the whole of his life, the mark of the burning which he had endured in his soul. In a wondrous manner, his flesh publicly displayed what his soul had suffered in secret. He always took care, as he had previously been accustomed to do, to show and proclaim to everyone the work of virtue, both by his example and in his preaching. He wished to explain the sequence of his visions only to those who asked about them out of a desire for repentance.

There still survives an elderly brother of our monastery who is accustomed to relate that a very truthful and devout man told him that he had seen Fursey in the province of the East Angles and had heard those visions from his own mouth. He added that it was the depth of winter and that everything was bound by ice, while Fursey, sitting in a thin garment, sweated as he spoke, as though in the heat of midsummer, because of the intensity of the fear or sweetness he remembered.

When, then, to return to what was said above, he had proclaimed the word of God to everyone for many years in Scotland and could not easily endure the commotion of the invading crowds, he left behind everything he seemed to possess and departed even from that native island. With a few brothers he came through the Britons into the province of the English, and there, preaching the word as we have said, he built a noble monastery.

When these matters had been properly accomplished, wishing to withdraw from all the affairs of this world and even from the business of the monastery itself, he relinquished the care of the monastery and of souls to his brother Fullan and to the priests Gobban [Al.: Gabban, Galban, Golban] and Dicullus.

**Note:** Fullan. After Fursey’s death he went with his brother Ultan to Brabant, founded the monastery of Fosses, and, leaving its care to Ultan, lived for some time in the Nivelles convent as a companion of Saint Gertrude the virgin. Later, while traveling to the monastery of Fosses, near the town of Rhodo in the diocese of Cambrai, to visit his brother, he was killed with three companions by a wicked man in the forest or village of Sonesia, on the day before the Kalends of November, around the year 656. He was buried in the monastery of Fosses.

Freed himself from all worldly things, he resolved to end his life in an anchoritic way of life [Al.: having become a hermit]. He had another brother, named Ultan.

**Note:** Ultan. Several years later he was appointed abbot of the monastery of Péronne, where his brother lay buried. He died around the year 680. He is commemorated in the Benedictine Martyrology and elsewhere on the Kalends of May. He is to be distinguished from Ultan, a monk of Lindisfarne, who is commemorated on the sixth day before the Ides of August.

Ultan had reached the hermit life after a long testing in the monastery. Fursey therefore sought him out alone and lived with him for a whole year in continence and prayer, engaged in daily manual labor.

Afterward, seeing that the province had been disturbed by the incursions of the pagans and foreseeing that the monasteries too were in danger, he dismissed everything in an orderly fashion, sailed to Gaul, and there was honorably received by the Frankish king Hloduio [Al.: Chlodoveus] or by the patrician Ercunualdus [Al.: Erchenaldus]. He built a monastery at a place called Latiniacum.

**Note:** Latiniacum. Commonly Lagny, situated in the Brie region on the bank of the River Marne, six French miles above Paris. The monastery began to be built when Erchinoald, prefect of the palace, supplied the estate and assistance, under Chlodoveus, King Dagobert’s son, around the year 644. Fursey was its head until the final year of his life, when, having appointed Emilianus or Eminianus as his successor, he returned to Britain and died in the village of Ponthieu called Macerias.

Not long afterward he was struck by illness and brought his final day to a close, around the year 650. The patrician Erchinoald took his body and kept it in a portico of a church which he was building at his own estate called Péronne.

**Note:** Péronne. Today Péronne, a fortress or palace of the ancients, which must be distinguished from the village of Perona on the River Savus, where the fortress of Cambrai and the abbey of Saint Andrew of the Order of Saint Benedict now stand.

When this had been done after twenty-seven days, and the body itself had been removed from the portico in order to be placed near the altar, it was found so completely uncorrupted that it seemed to have departed from this life at that very hour. Four years later, when a more honorable little building had been constructed as a resting place for his body, it was again found there, east of the altar, still without any mark of decay. It was transferred to that place with due honor, where it is often attested that his merits shone forth through many miracles worked by God.

**Note:** Twenty-seven. Various dates are given for Fursey’s solemn commemorations, one of which concerns his burial. Bede is accused of making the burial date uncertain: he says that Fursey was buried twenty-seven days after his body had been placed in the portico, whereas the anonymous author of his Life says thirty. But it is not particularly important to debate which of the two should be believed.

**Note:** His body. The relics of Saint Fursey are kept at Péronne in the collegiate church dedicated in his name, apart from the skull-bone, which is said to be at Latiniacum.

We have briefly touched upon the incorruption of his body so that the greatness of the man might become more evident to readers. Whoever reads his little book will find all these matters treated more fully, as well as accounts of his other fellow soldiers.

**CHAPTER XX**

**How, after the death of Honorius, Deusdedit served as archbishop, and who at that time were the bishops of the East Angles and of the Church of Rochester**

**Note:** After his death. When Felix died, he was buried at Domnoc, his own see, and was later translated to Seham—now Soham—a village by the mere which was once dangerous for boats bound for Ely, but is now crossed on foot by a way made through the marshy reed-bed. There are still traces there of the church which the Danes destroyed and burned, burying its inhabitants, burned as well, beneath its ruins. Much later the saint's body was sought, found, and buried in Ramsey Abbey. William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, II. His commemoration is observed on 8 March.

Meanwhile, after Felix, bishop of the East Angles, had died in the seventeenth year after receiving the episcopate [647], Honorius ordained Thomas, his deacon from the province of the Gyrvii, in his place. When Thomas too was taken from this life five years after his episcopate, Honorius substituted for him Berctgils, surnamed Boniface, from the province of Kent [652].

Honorius himself, after completing the course appointed for him, departed from this life in the year 653 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the day before the Kalends of October. After the episcopal see had remained vacant for one year and six months, Deusdedit, a man of the West Saxon people, was elected sixth archbishop of the see of Canterbury. Ithamar, bishop of the Church of Rochester, came there to ordain him [655].

He was ordained on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, and governed the Church for nine years, seven months [Al.: four months], and two days. After Ithamar’s death, he consecrated Damianus in his place; Damianus was of the people of the South Saxons [664].

**CHAPTER XXI**

**How the province of the Middle Angles became Christian under King Peada**

At this time the Middle Angles, that is, the Angles of the central region, received the faith and sacraments of the truth under Peada [Al.: Penda], son of Penda, king [653]. He was an excellent young man, worthy of the name and dignity of king, and his father placed him over that people’s kingdom. He came to Osuiu, king of the Northumbrians, asking that his daughter Alchfled be given to him in marriage.

He could obtain what he requested only if he accepted the faith of Christ and baptism, together with the people over whom he ruled. But after hearing the preaching of the truth, the promise of the heavenly kingdom, and the hope of resurrection and future immortality, he willingly confessed that he wished to become a Christian, even if he did not receive the maiden. He was especially persuaded to receive the faith by Osuiu’s son, named Alchfrid, who was his kinsman and friend and whose sister, Cyniburg, daughter of King Penda, he had as his wife.

He was therefore baptized by Bishop Finan, together with all the companions and soldiers who had come with him and all their servants, in the royal village called Ad Murum.

**Note:** Ad Murum. Commonly Walton. But the site of that place cannot agree with the distance from the sea which Bede assigns. Not far from Newcastle, however, is Waubottle, whose name itself indicates a building beside a wall. I therefore think that the royal village where Peada was baptized should be placed there, about twelve thousand paces from the sea.

Having received four priests who seemed suitable both in learning and in life for teaching and baptizing his people, he returned with great joy. The priests were Cedd [Al.: Cedda], Adda, Betti, and Diuma; the last was a Scot by nationality, while the others were English. Adda was the brother of Uttan, an illustrious priest and abbot of the monastery called Ad Caprae Caput.

**Note:** Ad Caprae Caput. Today Gateshead. No remains of Uttan’s ancient monastery survive there. We see a very beautiful chapel of later construction, scarcely yet overcome by ruins. Tradition says that it was a nunnery, although one can scarcely find its history in the authorities.

We have mentioned this monastery above. The priests came into the province with the prince, preached the word, and were gladly heard. Many people every day, both noble and infirm [Al.: lowly], having renounced the filth of idolatry, were washed in the fountain of faith.

King Penda did not prevent the word from being preached even in his own people, that is, among the Mercians, if anyone wished to hear it. Rather, he hated and despised those whom he found, though imbued with the faith of Christ, not to possess the works of faith. He said that those people were contemptible and wretched who refused to obey the God in whom they believed.

These things began two years before the death of King Penda. After Penda was killed [656], and the Christian King Osuiu received his kingdom, as we shall relate below, Diuma, one of the four priests mentioned above, became bishop of the Middle Angles and Mercians alike, having been ordained by Bishop Finan. The scarcity of priests compelled one bishop to be placed over two peoples.

After he had acquired not a few people for the Lord in a short time, he died among the Middle Angles [658], in a region called Infeppingum.

**Note:** Infeppingum. It is unknown what region this was. On the border of Mercia lies Reppington, a name not entirely consistent with the rules of etymology in sound, but not very far removed from it. The whole hundred takes its name from that place; several Mercian kings lived there and were buried there—why not a bishop as well? There were not only dwellings for nobles there, but also a monastery formerly founded for divine services. Heppingham comes closer to the name; it is specially mentioned in the third cartulary of Durham.

Ceollach succeeded him in the episcopate. He too was of the Scottish people, and not long afterward, having abandoned the episcopate, he returned to the island of Iona, where the Scots had the chief seat and stronghold of many monasteries. He was succeeded in the episcopate by Trumheri, a religious man trained in monastic life [659], an Englishman by nationality but ordained bishop by the Scots. This took place during the reign of King Wulfhere, of whom we shall speak below.

**CHAPTER XXII**

**How the East Saxons, having long ago abandoned the faith, received it again under King Sigberct through the preaching of Cedd**

At that time [653] the East Saxons also received, at the urging of King Osuiu, the faith which they had formerly abandoned after expelling Mellitus, their bishop. Their king was Sigberct, who reigned after Sigberct surnamed the Little.

**Note:** The Little. The succession of the kings of the East Saxons was as follows: Erchenuini; Sledda; Seberct; Sexred; Seward; the brothers Sigeberct; Sigberct the Little; and Sigberct the Good, who was the convert of this chapter.

Sigberct was a friend of King Osuiu. Whenever he frequently came to him in the province of the Northumbrians, Osuiu used to urge him to understand that those could not be gods who had been made by human hands; that wood or stone could not be the material from which gods were created, since their chips would either be consumed by fire, shaped into vessels for human use, or, being held in contempt, thrown outside and trampled underfoot until they became earth.

Rather, he urged him to understand as God one whose majesty was incomprehensible, invisible to human eyes, omnipotent, eternal, who had created heaven and earth and the human race, governed them, and would judge the world with equity. His eternal dwelling, he said, ought to be believed to be in heaven, not in base and perishable metal. It was rightly to be understood that all who learned and practiced the will of the one by whom they had been created would receive eternal rewards from him.

When King Osuiu had often impressed these and many similar ideas upon King Sigberct in friendly and almost brotherly counsel, Sigberct finally believed, with the help of the agreement of his friends. After taking counsel with his people, and with the exhortation and unanimous approval of all, he was baptized with them by Bishop Finan in the royal estate mentioned above, called Ad Murum.

**Note:** Ad Murum. It lies beside the wall with which the Romans once encircled the island of Britain, twelve thousand paces inland from the eastern sea.

Thus King Sigberct, now a citizen of the eternal kingdom, returned to the seat of his temporal kingdom and asked King Osuiu to give him some teachers who might convert his people to the faith of Christ and wash them in the saving font. Osuiu sent to the province of the Middle Angles and summoned to him the man of God Cedd. Giving him another priest as companion, he sent him to preach the word to the people of the East Saxons.

After Cedd and his companion had traveled throughout the whole region and gathered a great Church for the Lord, it happened that Cedd returned home for a time and came to the church of Lindisfarne to confer with Bishop Finan. When Finan learned that Cedd’s evangelical work had prospered, he made him bishop for the people of the East Saxons, summoning two other bishops to assist in his ordination.

After receiving the episcopal rank, Cedd returned to the province and, completing the work he had begun with greater authority, established churches in various places and ordained priests and deacons to assist him in the word of faith and in the ministry of baptism. He did so especially in the city called in the Saxon language Ythancaestir.

**Note:** Ythancaestir. Called Othona by the Romans, it is now Saint Peter’s Chapel on the Wall, situated on the promontory at the end of the Dengie hundred. In English, Saint Peter’s on the Wall.

He also did so in the place called Tilaburg.

**Note:** Tilaburg. Tilbury, where Camden is criticized for placing Cedd’s see. I do not think, however, that Camden intended a strictly episcopal see, for that would have been London, but rather a larger residence established for the convenient access of the people, just as he had another at Ythancestria in the other part of the diocese.

The first of these places is on the bank of the River Penta, the second on the bank of the Thames.

**Note:** Penta. Freshwell, from whose springs one still retains the genuine name Pante, although both the river and the city have now disappeared.

Gathering there a community of Christ’s servants, he taught them to observe the discipline of regular life insofar as people still inexperienced in it could manage.

After the institution of the heavenly life had for a considerable time been daily increasing in the province mentioned above, with the king rejoicing and the whole people sharing his joy, it happened that the king himself was killed by the hands of his kinsmen, at the instigation of the enemy of all good things [660].

The perpetrators were two brothers. When they were asked why they had done this, they could give no other answer than that they had been angry with the king and hostile to him because he was accustomed to spare his enemies excessively and, whenever they pleaded with him, to forgive the injuries they had inflicted with a tranquil mind.

Such was the king’s fault for which he was killed: that he faithfully observed the evangelical commandments. Yet, in accordance with what the man of God had foretold, his guilt was truly punished by this innocent death. One of the companions of those who killed him had contracted an unlawful marriage. When the bishop could neither prevent nor correct it, he excommunicated the man and ordered all who wished to obey him not to enter his house or receive food from him.

The king disregarded this command and, being asked by the companion, entered his house to feast. When he had left, the bishop met him. Seeing the bishop, the king immediately trembled, dismounted from his horse, fell at his feet, and asked pardon for his offense. The bishop also dismounted, for he too had been riding.

But in anger he touched the prostrate king with the staff he held in his hand and declared with episcopal authority: “I tell you: because you refused to keep away from the house of that lost and condemned man, you must die in that very house.”

It must nevertheless be believed that such a death for a religious man not only cleansed away such a fault but also increased his merit, since it occurred for the sake of piety, because of his observance of Christ’s commandments.

Suidhelm, son of Sexbald, succeeded Sigberct in the kingdom [660]. He was baptized by Cedd himself in the province of the East Angles, in the royal village called Rendlaesham, that is, Rendil’s Residence.

**Note:** Rendlaesham. A small village in Suffolk on the River Deben.

Aedilvald, king of that people and brother of their king Anna, received Suidhelm as he came up from the holy font.

**CHAPTER XXIII**

**How the same Bishop Cedd, having received from King Oidilvald a place for building a monastery, consecrated it to the Lord with prayers and fasts; and concerning his death**

When the same man of the Lord was carrying out the office of bishop among the East Saxons, he also frequently visited his own province, that is, the province of the Northumbrians, to exhort it.

**Note:** His own. The dual sphere of Cedd’s office has also made his homeland uncertain. Some have wanted him to have been born in the territory of York, others in London. But since Bede deliberately identifies Cedd’s province here by saying “his own,” that is, the province of the Northumbrians, there seems to be little doubt about which region was his native land.

When Oidilvald, son of King Osuald [653–664], who ruled in the regions of Deira,

**Note:** He held the kingdom. M. West does not mention this Oidilvald in his catalogue of the Northumbrian kings. The power of the lesser king had been almost entirely extinguished by the growing authority of King Osuiu. Nevertheless, both his close kinship and the foundation of the monastery under a royal title sufficiently prove that he was a king; hence Bede rightly attributes to him the name and authority of king.

saw that Cedd was a holy and wise man, upright in character, he asked him to accept from him some possession of land on which to build a monastery. There the king himself might come more frequently to pray to the Lord and hear the word, and, when he died, might be buried. For he faithfully believed that he would be greatly aided by the daily prayers of those who served the Lord in that place.

The king had with him the bishop’s own brother, named Caelin, a man equally devoted to God. Since he was a priest, he was accustomed to minister the word and the sacraments of the faith to the king and his household. Through Caelin’s acquaintance with Cedd, the king had come especially to love and know the bishop.

The bishop therefore favored the king’s wishes and chose a place for building a monastery in steep and remote mountains, where there seemed to be more hiding places and lairs of robbers and wild beasts than dwellings of human beings. Thus, in accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy, greenery of reed and rush—that is, the fruit of good works—might spring up in dens where dragons had formerly lived, where previously either beasts had dwelt or human beings had been accustomed to live like beasts.

The man of the Lord was eager first to cleanse the place he had received for the monastery from the former pollution of wickedness by prayers and fasts, and only then to lay the monastery’s foundations there. He therefore asked the king to grant him the opportunity and permission to remain there for the approaching entire period of Lent for the sake of prayer.

Throughout all those days, except Sunday, he prolonged his fast until evening according to custom. Even then he took nothing more than a very small piece of bread, one hen’s egg, and a little milk mixed with water. He said that this was the custom of those from whom he had learned the rule of regular discipline: newly acquired places intended for a monastery or church were first consecrated to the Lord by prayers and fasts.

When ten days of Lent remained, someone came to summon him to the king. But, so that the holy work would not be interrupted because of royal business, Cedd asked his priest Cynibill, who was also his own brother, to complete the pious undertaking. When the latter willingly agreed, Cynibill, after completing the observance of fasting and prayer, built there the monastery now called Laestingaeu.

**Note:** Laestingaeu. This monastery’s location was sought for a long time, no less than the founder’s homeland. Alford first found it in the territory of York, then in that of the East Saxons, and finally in the province of the Northumbrians—but in reality nowhere. It is now no longer doubted that it was at Lestingham, not far from Streaneshalch. Dugdale inserted the place into his Monasticon, but added nothing to this chapter of Bede.

He established it according to the religious customs of Lindisfarne, where he had been educated.

After he had administered the episcopate in the aforementioned province for many years and had also directed this monastery, having appointed its superiors,

**Note:** Having appointed. So the old manuscripts read—not as though he had proposed statutes, but because he appointed superiors, whence the Saxon paraphrase translates that he “appointed a provost and aldermen.”

it happened by chance that, when he came to the monastery itself during a time of pestilence, he fell ill there and died [664]. At first he was buried outside. As time passed, however, a stone church was built in the same monastery in honor of the blessed Mother of God, and his body was placed in it to the right of the altar.

**Note:** Placed. His memory is celebrated on the seventh day of January.

The bishop left his monastery to be governed afterward by his brother Ceadda, who later became a bishop, as we shall relate below. For these four brothers whom we have mentioned—Cedd, Cynibill [Al.: Cenibill], Caelin, and Ceadda—all, something rarely found, were distinguished priests of the Lord, and two of them also held the rank of high priest.

When the brothers in his monastery in the province of the East Saxons heard that the bishop had died and been buried in the province of the Northumbrians, about thirty men came from their monastery, wishing either to live beside the body of their father, if that pleased God, or to die and be buried there.

They were gladly received by their brothers and fellow soldiers, but all of them died there when the aforementioned plague arrived, except for one little boy, who is known to have been preserved from death through the prayers of his father.

He lived for a long time afterward and devoted himself to reading the Scriptures. Eventually he learned that he had not been regenerated by the water of baptism. He was immediately washed in the font of saving baptism and was later promoted to the order of the priesthood; he became useful to many in the Church.

I would not doubt that, through the intercessions, as I have said, of his father—in whose love he had come to the bishop’s body—he was held back from the point of death, so that he himself might escape eternal death and might also provide other brothers with the ministry of life and salvation by teaching them.

**CHAPTER XXIV**

**How the province of the Mercians received the faith of Christ after the killing of King Penda, and how Osuiu, in return for the victory he had gained, gave possessions and territories for the building of monasteries**

At this time [655], King Osuiu was often suffering bitter and intolerable attacks from the frequently mentioned king of the Mercians, who had killed his brother. At last, compelled by necessity, he promised that he would give him countless royal ornaments or gifts, greater than could be believed, as the price of peace, provided that Penda returned home and ceased laying waste to his kingdom’s provinces to the point of annihilation.

But when the treacherous king would in no way heed his pleas, having resolved to destroy and exterminate his entire people, from the least to the greatest, Osuiu turned to the aid of divine mercy, by which he might be rescued from barbaric impiety. Binding himself by a vow, he said: “If the pagan does not know how to accept our gifts, let us offer them to the one who does know how to accept them, the Lord our God.”

He therefore vowed that if he emerged victorious, he would offer his daughter to the Lord, consecrated to perpetual virginity, and would also donate twelve estates for the construction of monasteries. Thus, with a very small army, he entered the contest.

It is said that the pagan army was thirty times larger. They had thirty legions, led by the most noble commanders and equipped for war. Against them King Osuiu came with his son Alchfrid, possessing, as I have said, a very small army, but trusting in Christ as his leader.

For his other son Ecgfrid was at that time being held hostage in the province of the Mercians by Queen Cynuise.

**Note:** Cynuise. By this wife Penda had five sons: Peada, Wulfhere, Aethelred, Merowald, and Mercelm, besides an illegitimate son named Osward; and two daughters, Cyneburh and Cyneswith. They also report that another daughter of his, named Wilburh, was married to Friduuald, sub-king and founder of the monastery of Chertsey; this is recorded by Ralph of Diceto and by the author of the Life of Saint Osyth.

Oidilvald, son of King Osuald, who ought to have come to their aid, was on the side of the adversaries and had become their leader as they prepared to fight against his own country and his uncle. At the very time of battle, however, he withdrew from the fighting and awaited the outcome of the danger in a secure place.

When the battle was joined, the pagans were put to flight and slaughtered. Almost all of the thirty royal commanders who had come to give aid were killed. Among them was Aethelheri, brother of Anna, king of the East Angles, who had himself initiated the war. He was killed along with his soldiers or auxiliaries.

The battle had been fought near the River Winwaed.

**Note:** The River Winwaed. Today the Broad Are, which flows past the town of Leeds.

At that time the river had overflowed its broad channel and all its banks because of the abundance of rain. Consequently, the sword killed far more of the fugitives in the water than of those engaged in battle.

Then King Osuiu, giving thanks to God for the victory granted him in accordance with his vow to the Lord, gave his daughter Aelfled, who had scarcely completed her first year, to be consecrated to him in perpetual virginity. In addition, he donated twelve small estates of land, so that, once earthly military service had been set aside, there might be places and means for the monks’ devoted service in the heavenly warfare and for their continual prayers for the eternal peace of his people.

Of these estates he gave six in the province of Deira and six in Bernicia. Each estate consisted of ten households, making one hundred and twenty altogether.

The aforementioned daughter of King Osuiu, who was to be dedicated to God, entered the monastery called Heruteu, that is, “Deer Island.”

**Note:** Heruteu. Today Hartlepool in the county of Durham.

At that time Hild was its abbess. After acquiring, two years later, a possession of ten households at a place called Streanaeshalch, she built a monastery there.

**Note:** Streanaeshalch. Whitby, the harbor of the territory of York.

In that monastery the king’s daughter mentioned above was first a student of the regular life and afterward also its teacher, until, when the number of fifty-nine years had been completed, the blessed virgin entered the embrace and wedding feast of the heavenly Bridegroom.

In that monastery she herself, her father Osuiu, her mother Eanfled, her mother’s father Edwin, and many other nobles were buried in the church of the holy apostle Peter.

King Osuiu brought this war to an end in the region of Leeds, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, with great benefit to both peoples. He freed his own people from the hostile devastation of the pagans and, with the treacherous head cut off, converted the Mercians and the neighboring provinces to the grace of the Christian faith.

**Textual apparatus additionally represented**

The following readings in the supplied text are not otherwise displayed above. They are given with their anchors and English sense; where the variation is purely grammatical, orthographic, or a word-order distinction, the paired Latin forms are retained.

- At Fursey's ascent: *elatus* (“carried up”) is alternatively *elevatus* (“raised”); the alternative omits *in* in “will not burn **in** you”; *etsi* (“although”) is alternatively *et* (“and”); and “divide the flames of the fire” is alternatively *ignis flammam* (“the fire's flame”).
- At the return through the fire: plural *adpropiarent* (“they drew near”) is alternatively singular *adpropiaret*; *ad memoriam reduxit* (“recalled”) is alternatively *in memoriam reduxit*; the angel's “No” alternatively adds *hoc* (“this”); the alternative omits *ad mortem* (“at death”) in “those who repent as death approaches”; and “publicly” alternatively adds *omnibus* (“to all”).
- In the elderly brother's report: *tenui veste* (“in a thin garment”) is alternatively *iste* [materially uncertain in this OCR]; the alternative adds *Dei* (“of God”) after “man”; and *multitudinem* (“multitude”) is alternatively *magnitudinem* (“greatness”).
- In the withdrawal to the hermitage: the printed *reliquit monasterii* (“he relinquished [the care] of the monastery”) is alternatively *reliquit monasterium* (“he left the monastery”); *alterum* (“another”) is omitted in the alternative; and *pervenerat* (“had reached”) is alternatively *perveniret* (“might reach”).
- In the French episode: the alternative has *cum* (“when”) for *dum*; *cui nomen est* (“whose name is”) is alternatively *erat* (“was”); *prope* (“near”) is alternatively *propter* (“because of”); and the alternative reads six, rather than twenty-seven, days. “We have briefly touched upon the incorruption of his body” is alternatively “these matters, and the visions, and the incorruption of his body”; the alternative omits *sed* (“but”) before “also”; and *quisque* (“whoever”) is alternatively *quisquis* (“whosoever”).
- In Chapter XX: the alternative adds *et* (“and”) to the heading; omits *hoc* (“this”) in “and this [occurred]”; and has *antistes Hrofensis* for *antistes Ecclesiae Horfensis* (“bishop of the Church of Rochester”).
- In Chapter XXI: *Ad Caprae caput* (“Goat's Head”) is alternatively *Ad Capreae caput*; *Infeppingum* is alternatively *Infebbingum*; and, as corrected above, *infirmorum* means “the infirm,” while the alternative *infimorum* means “the lowly.”
- In Chapter XXII: the alternative has a lacuna from *aeterna* (“eternal”) to *meritoque* (“and rightly”), rather than the complete sentence about eternal rewards; *repetiit* (“returned”) is alternatively *petiit* (“sought”); and *in gentem Orientalium Saxonum* (“for the people of the East Saxons”) is alternatively *in gente* (“among the people”). In the account of Sigberct's death, *audirent* (“heard”) is alternatively *audissent* (“had heard”); *cur hoc fecerint* (“why they had done this”) replaces *quare hoc facerent*; *nimium* (“excessively”) is alternatively *nimirum* (“certainly”); the alternative adds *hoc* (“this”) to the king's disregard; adds *de* to *desiluit equo* (“dismounted from his horse”); and has *protestans* (“declaring”) for *protestatus* (“having declared”). Finally, *quai* is alternatively *quae* (“which”), and *frater Anna* is alternatively *frater Annae* (“brother of Anna”).
- In Chapter XXIII: *ritus* (“customs”) is alternatively *ritum* (“custom”); the alternative omits *usque* (“until”) in the duration of the fast; *ne* (“lest”) is alternatively *nec* (“nor”); and *statutis propositis* means “after setting regulations in place,” whereas the variant *praepositis* means “after appointing superiors,” as the accompanying note explains. The alternative also omits *eodem* (“same”) in “the same monastery.”
- In Chapter XXIV: *sacra virginitate dicandam* (“to be dedicated in holy virginity”) is alternatively *sacrandam* (“to be consecrated”); *pugnaturis* (“as they were about to fight”) is alternatively *pugnaturus* (“as he was about to fight”); and *praefata regis Osuiu filia* (“the aforesaid daughter of King Osuiu”) is alternatively *praefata Osuii filia* (“the aforesaid daughter of Osuiu”).

The first bishop appointed over the province of the Mercians, and likewise over the Lindisfarners and the Middle Angles, was Diuma, as we said above (see Book III, chapter 21). He died and was buried among the Middle Angles [Al. adds: “he was”] [656]. The second was Cellach, who, while still alive, abandoned the office of bishop and returned to Scotland; both were of Scottish origin. The third was Trumhere, an Englishman by nation, but taught and ordained by the Scots. He was abbot of the monastery called Ingetlingum. This is the place where King Oswini was killed, as we mentioned above (see Book III, chapter 14).

For Queen Aeanfled, who was related to him, in order to atone for his unjust death, asked King Osuiu [Al., Osuiu] to grant the aforesaid servant of God, Trumhere, a place there for building a monastery, since he too was a kinsman of the murdered king. In that monastery, continual prayers were to be offered for the eternal salvation of both kings—that is, both the one who was killed and the one who ordered the killing.

King Osuiu ruled the people of the Mercians, and also the other peoples of the southern provinces, for three years after the killing of King Penda. He also subjected most of the people of the Picts to the kingdom of the English.

At that time he granted the kingdom of the Southern Mercians to Peada [Al., Penda], son of King Penda, because he was his relative. These Southern Mercians, they say, numbered five thousand households and were separated by the River Trent from the Northern Mercians [Al., Northern Mercians], whose territory contained seven thousand households. But Peada was treacherously and most wickedly killed the following spring, as they say, by the betrayal of his wife, at the very time of the Easter festival [658].

[Note: His wife, Alchfled, the natural daughter of King Osuiu. Although some maintain that Peada was not killed by his wife, who was a Christian, but was removed through the evil arts of a pagan mother.]

When three years had been completed after the killing of King Penda, the leaders of the Mercian people—Immin, Eafha [Al., Eafba, Eabba, Eaba], and Eadberct—rebelled against King Osuiu. They raised to the kingship Wulfhere, the adolescent son of Penda, whom they had kept hidden, and, choosing leaders who were not the king’s own appointees, boldly recovered both their territory [Col. 0158A] and their freedom. Thus, free under their own king, they rejoiced to serve Christ, the true King, for his eternal kingdom in heaven.

That same king ruled the Mercian people for seventeen years. His first bishop was Trumhere, whom we mentioned above (chapter 21); the second was Jaruman; the third, Ceadda; and the fourth, Winfrid. All these, succeeding one another in order under King Wulfhere, held the episcopate of the Mercian people.

## CHAPTER XXV

### How a controversy arose concerning the date of Easter against those who had come from Scotland

Meanwhile, after Bishop Aidan had been taken from this life, Finan, ordained and sent by the Scots, received the episcopal office in his place [652]. On the island of Lindisfarne he built a church suitable for an episcopal see. Yet, following the custom of the Scots, he constructed it entirely not of stone but of cut timber, and covered it with reeds. In a later period the most reverend Archbishop Theodore dedicated it in honor of the blessed apostle Peter. But Eadberct, bishop of that place [Al., “of that man”], after removing the reeds, saw to it that the whole building—that is, both the roof and the walls themselves—was covered with sheets of lead.

At this time a frequent and serious controversy arose concerning the observance of Easter (see Appendix, no. 9), because those who had come from Kent or from Gaul maintained that the Scots celebrated the Lord’s day of Easter contrary to the custom of the universal Church. Among them the most vigorous defender of the true Easter was a Scot named Ronan [Al., Sonan]. Although Scottish by nation, he had been instructed in the rule of ecclesiastical truth in the regions of Gaul or Italy. In disputing with Finan, he corrected many people or stirred them to a more diligent investigation of the truth. Yet he could not correct Finan; rather, because Finan was a man of fierce temper, Ronan’s correction made him harsher and turned him into an open opponent of the truth.

James, formerly deacon of the venerable Archbishop Paulinus, as we have shown above, observed the true and Catholic Easter, together with all whom he could instruct in the more correct way [Al., “the more reformed way”]. Queen Eanfled also observed it with her household, according to what she had seen practiced in Kent. She had with her from Kent a presbyter named Romanus, who followed the Catholic observance. Hence it is said to have happened in those days that Easter was sometimes celebrated twice in the same year. When the king kept the Lord’s Easter after breaking his fast, the queen and her household, still continuing their fast, were celebrating Palm Sunday.

This disagreement in the observance of Easter was patiently tolerated by everyone while Aidan was alive. They clearly understood that, although he could not celebrate Easter contrary to the custom of those who had sent him, he nevertheless carefully carried out the works of faith, piety, and love customary among all the saints. For this reason he was rightly loved by everyone, even by those who held a different opinion about Easter. He was honored not only by ordinary people but also by the bishops themselves, Honorius of the Kentish people and Felix of the East Angles.

After Finan, who succeeded Aidan, had died, Colman succeeded him in the episcopate [662]. He too had been sent from Scotland. A more serious controversy then arose concerning the observance of Easter and also other disciplines of ecclesiastical life.

[Note: All the Vulgate manuscripts, except Mori’s; hence the reading “moved” is rightly adopted.]

This controversy consequently stirred the minds and hearts of many people, who feared that, having received the name of Christians, they might be running—or might have run—in vain. It reached the ears of the rulers themselves, namely King Osuiu and his son Alchfrid. Osuiu had been taught and baptized by the Scots and was thoroughly familiar with their language; he therefore believed that nothing was better than what they had taught him.

Alchfrid, however, had as his teacher of Christian learning the highly learned Wilfrid. Wilfrid had previously gone to Rome for ecclesiastical instruction and had spent a considerable time at Lyons with Dalfinus, archbishop of the Gauls, from whom he had also received the crown of the ecclesiastical tonsure. Alchfrid knew that Wilfrid’s teaching was rightly preferable to all the traditions of the Scots. He had therefore given him a monastery of forty households at a place called Inhrypum. He had shortly before given this place as a monastic possession to those who followed the Scots. But when they were later given the choice, and preferred to leave the place rather than change their custom, he gave it to the man who had a doctrine and a life worthy of the place.

At that time Agilberct, bishop of the West Saxons, whom we mentioned above, came to the province of the Northumbrians. He was a friend of King Alchfrid and of Abbot Wilfrid, and stayed with them for some time. At Alchfrid’s request, he made Wilfrid a presbyter in the monastery mentioned above. Agilberct himself had with him a presbyter named Agatho.

A controversy therefore arose there concerning Easter, the tonsure (see Appendix, no. 9), and other ecclesiastical matters. It was decided that a synod should be held in the monastery called Strenaeshalch, which means “Bay of the Lighthouse,” where Hild, a woman devoted to God, was then abbess, and that the controversy should be settled.

Both kings came there, father and son; the bishops Colman, with his clerics from Scotland, and Agilberct, with Agatho and the presbyters Wilfrid. James [Col. 0159D] and Romanus were on their side. Abbess Hild and her people were on the side of the Scots; among them was also the venerable Bishop Cedd, who had long before been ordained by the Scots, as we have shown above. He served as interpreter at the council and most diligently represented both sides.

King Osuiu first prefaced his remarks by saying that those who served one God together ought to follow one rule of life and not differ in their celebration of the heavenly sacraments, since all alike expected one kingdom in heaven. Rather, they should investigate which tradition was more correct and then all follow it together. He ordered his own bishop, Colman, to speak first: what rite did he follow, and from where did it derive its origin?

Then Colman said:

“The Easter which I am accustomed to observe I received from my elders, who sent me here as bishop. All our fathers, men beloved by God, are known to have celebrated it in the same way. Lest anyone think that this practice should be despised or rejected, it is the very practice which the blessed evangelist John, the disciple especially beloved by the Lord, is said to have observed with all the Churches over which he presided.”

When he had said this and similar things, the king ordered Agilberct also to state the custom of his observance, its origin, and the authority by which he followed it.

Agilberct replied:

“I ask that my disciple, the presbyter Wilfrid, speak in my place, because we both hold the same view as the other guardians of ecclesiastical tradition who are present here. He can explain our position better and more clearly in the language of the English than I can through an interpreter.”

Then Wilfrid, ordered by the king to speak, began as follows:

“The Easter which we celebrate we have seen observed by everyone in Rome, where the blessed apostles Peter and Paul lived, taught, suffered, and were buried. We saw it celebrated by everyone in Italy and in Gaul, which we crossed for the sake of learning and prayer. We discovered that this same Easter was observed by Africa, Asia, Egypt, Greece, and the entire world wherever the Church of Christ is spread, among diverse peoples and languages, according to one and not differing reckoning of time—except only by these people and their obstinate accomplices, namely the Picts and Britons, with whom, from the two remotest islands of the Ocean—and not even from the whole of those—they struggle against the entire world in foolish labor.”

When he had said this, Colman replied:

“Why do you wish to call our labor foolish, when we follow the example of so great an apostle who was worthy to recline upon the Lord’s breast, while the whole world knows that he lived with the greatest wisdom?”

Wilfrid answered:

“Far be it from us to accuse John of foolishness. He observed the ordinances of the Mosaic Law according to the letter, while the Church was still Judaizing in many respects, and the apostles could not suddenly renounce every observance of the Law instituted by God. In the same way, all who come to the faith must reject the idols invented by demons, so that they may not cause scandal to the Jews living among the nations. This is why Paul circumcised Timothy, sacrificed offerings in the temple, and had his head shaved at Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla—all, plainly, for the purpose of avoiding scandal to the Jews. This is why James said to that same Paul: ‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law.’

“Yet now that the Gospel is shining throughout the world, it is neither necessary nor lawful for the faithful to be circumcised or to offer bodily sacrifices to God. Thus John, following the custom of the Law, began the celebration of the Paschal festival on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, without caring whether that day fell on a Sabbath or on any other weekday.

“But Peter, when he was preaching at Rome, remembering that the Lord rose from the dead on the first day after the Sabbath and brought the hope of resurrection to the world, understood that Easter should be celebrated in this way: according to the custom and commands of the Law, he too always awaited the evening of the fourteenth moon of the first month, just as John did in the East. When it appeared, if the Lord’s Day—which was then called the first day after the Sabbath—was to come on the following morning, he began to celebrate the Lord’s Easter that very evening, as we all do today.

“But if the Lord’s Day was not to come on the morning immediately after the fourteenth moon, but on the sixteenth, seventeenth, or any other moon up to the twenty-first, he awaited it and began the sacred solemnities of Easter on the evening of the preceding Sabbath. Thus it came about that the Lord’s Day of Easter was observed only from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first.

“This evangelical and apostolic tradition does not abolish the Law but rather fulfills it. For the Law commands that Easter be observed from the evening of the fourteenth moon of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first moon of that same month. All the successors of the blessed John in Asia after his death, and the entire Church throughout the world, turned to imitate this observance. The Council of Nicaea did not establish this as something newly devised, but confirmed it as the true Easter and the only Easter to be celebrated by the faithful, as ecclesiastical history teaches.

“Therefore, Colman, it is clear that in your observance of Easter you agree neither with John, as you claim, nor with Peter, whose tradition you knowingly oppose, nor with the Law, nor with the Gospel. John, observing the Paschal season according to the decrees of the Mosaic Law, paid no attention to the first day after the Sabbath; but you do not act as he did, because you celebrate Easter only on the first day after the Sabbath.

“Peter celebrated the Lord’s Easter from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first day; but you do not act as he did, because you observe the Lord’s Easter from the fourteenth through the twentieth moon, so that you often begin Easter on the evening of the thirteenth moon. Of this moon neither the Law made any mention, nor did the Lord, the author and giver of the Gospel, do anything upon it. Rather, on the fourteenth moon he either ate the ancient Passover in the evening or entrusted the sacraments of the New Testament, in remembrance of his Passion, to be celebrated by the Church.

“Moreover, you entirely exclude from your Easter celebration the twenty-first moon, which the Law especially commends for observance. Thus, as I have said, in the celebration of the highest feast you agree neither with John, nor with Peter, nor with the Law, nor with the Gospel.”

In reply Colman said:

“Did the holy man Anatolius, who is greatly praised in the ecclesiastical history mentioned above, hold opinions contrary to the Law or the Gospel when he wrote that Easter should be celebrated from the fourteenth through the twentieth? Should we believe that our most reverend father Columba [Al., Columban] and his successors, men beloved by God, who celebrated Easter in the same way, thought or acted contrary to the divine Scriptures? Many among them were such that heavenly signs and the miracles of the miraculous powers they exercised bore witness to their holiness. Since I do not doubt that they were saints, I never cease to follow their life, conduct, and discipline.”

Wilfrid replied:

“It is certain that Anatolius was a most holy and learned man, worthy of the highest praise. But what have you to do with him, since you do not observe his decrees? In his Easter calculation he certainly followed the rule of truth and established a cycle of nineteen years, which you either do not know or, having learned it and knowing that it is observed by the whole Church of Christ, despise as worthless.

“He calculated the fourteenth moon for the Lord’s Easter in such a way that, on that very day, he acknowledged it to be the fifteenth moon according to the Egyptian reckoning at evening. Likewise, he designated the twentieth moon as the Lord’s Day of Easter in such a way that, as that same day declined, he held it to be the twenty-first moon. That you have failed to understand his rule of distinction is proved by the fact that you sometimes celebrate Easter unmistakably before the full moon—that is, on the thirteenth moon.

“As for your father Columba and his followers, whose holiness you claim to imitate and whose rule and commands, confirmed by heavenly signs, you claim to follow, I could answer that when many say to the Lord at the judgment that they prophesied in his name, cast out demons, and performed many miracles, the Lord will reply that he never knew them. But far be it from me to say this about your fathers. It is much more just to believe good of those unknown to us than evil.

“Therefore I do not deny that they were servants of God and beloved by God, who loved God with rustic simplicity but pious intention. Nor do I think that such an observance of Easter greatly harmed them, so long as no one had come to show them the decrees of a more perfect discipline to follow. I believe that, if a Catholic calculator had come to them at that time, they would have followed his instructions just as they are proved to have followed the commandments of God as they knew and had learned them.

“But you and your companions sin beyond doubt if, after hearing the decrees of the apostolic see—or rather, of the universal Church—and knowing that they are confirmed by the sacred writings, you refuse to follow them. Even if your fathers were holy, is their small number from one corner of a remote island to be preferred to the universal Church of Christ spread throughout the world? And if your Columba was holy and powerful in miracles—indeed, ours too, if he belonged to Christ—could he be preferred to the most blessed chief of the apostles, to whom the Lord said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven’?”

When Wilfrid had finished, the king said:

“Is it true, Colman, that these words were spoken by the Lord to Peter?”

He replied:

“True, O king.”

The king then said:

“Can you produce anything of such power that was given by the Lord to your Columba?”

He replied:

“Nothing.”

The king again said:

“If both of you agree without any dispute that these words were spoken principally to Peter and that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to him by the Lord—”

They replied:

“Yes, certainly.”

Then he concluded:

“And I say to you that he is the doorkeeper whom I do not wish to contradict. Rather, insofar as I know and am able, I desire to obey his decrees in everything, lest, when I come to the gates of the kingdom of heaven, there be no one to unlock them because the one who is proved to hold the keys is turned against me.”

When the king had said this [Al. adds: “with his hands raised to heaven”], all those seated or standing there, the great together with the ordinary people, approved. Rejecting the less perfect institution, they hastened to transfer themselves to what they had recognized as better.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### How Colman, defeated, returned home; how Tuda performed the episcopal office in his place; and how those teachers were regarded in the Church

When the dispute had ended and the assembly had been dismissed, Agilberct returned home. Colman, seeing that his teaching had been rejected and his sect despised, took with him those who wished to follow him—namely, those who refused to accept the Catholic Easter and the tonsure in the form of a crown, for there was also a considerable dispute about this—and returned to Scotland to discuss with his people what he ought to do about these matters.

Cedd, abandoning the practices of the Scots, returned to his own see, since he had recognized the observance of the Catholic Easter.

This controversy took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 664, which was the twenty-second year of King Osuiu. The episcopate of the Scots, which they exercised in the province of the English, had then lasted thirty years. Aidan held the episcopate for seventeen years, Finan for ten, and Colman for three.

When Colman returned to his homeland, the servant of Christ Tuda assumed the episcopate [Al., “bishopric”] of the Northumbrians in his place. He had been educated and ordained bishop among the Southern Scots. In accordance with the custom of that province, he wore the crown-shaped ecclesiastical tonsure and observed the Catholic rule concerning the date of Easter. He was a good and religious man, but governed the Church for only a very short time.

He had come from Scotland while Colman was still holding the episcopal office, and diligently taught everyone, both by word and by example, the things belonging to faith and truth.

For the brothers who preferred to remain in the Church of Lindisfarne when the Scots departed, the most reverend and gentle Eata was appointed as superior with the authority of an abbot. He was abbot of the monastery called Mailros.

[Note: Mailros. This inland monastery, situated on the border of Scotland, is wrongly confused with Lindisfarne by William Lambarde. Vespasian Collection, A. 5.]

[Note: He was placed in charge with the authority of an abbot. The form of government instituted by Colman from the beginning in the Church of Lindisfarne has also been retained to the present day in the Church of Durham, which succeeded it: the superior of that church, although only a prior by name, is in reality and dignity an abbot.]

It is said that Colman, when he was about to depart, asked King Osuiu for Eata and obtained him, because Eata was one of the twelve boys whom Aidan, at the beginning of his episcopate, had accepted from the English people to educate in Christ. The king greatly loved Bishop Colman because of the prudence naturally belonging to him.

This Eata was the man who not long afterward became bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne.

[Note: “Not long afterward.” After Eata had presided over the Church of Lindisfarne in the place of an abbot for fourteen years, he governed it for seven years with episcopal authority, from the year 678, when he was worthy to be consecrated, until the beginning of 685, when he received Cuthbert as his successor. Eata is commemorated on 26 October.]

When Colman departed for home, he took with him part of the bones of the most reverend Father Aidan. He left the other part in the church over which he had presided and ordered it to be buried in its sacristy.
