[Note: “Part of the bones.” This distribution of Aidan’s relics makes it sufficiently clear on what grounds the people of Glastonbury claim that he was buried among them. Their claim is not, however, entirely without foundation. A manuscript belonging to John Wessington, prior of Durham, says that King Edmund brought certain bones of Bishop Aidan to Glastonbury while he was on a northern expedition (p. 38).]

The great frugality and self-control of these men and their predecessors was also demonstrated by the very place which they governed. When they departed, only a very few houses were found there besides the church—only those without which civil life could in no way exist.

They possessed no money apart from livestock. If they received any money from the wealthy, they immediately gave it to the poor. There was no need either to collect money or to prepare houses for the reception of the powerful of this world, since such people never came to the church except for prayer and to hear the word of God.

The king himself, whenever necessity required it, came with only five or six attendants [Al. omits “attendants”]. After completing his prayer in the church, he departed. If it happened that they took refreshment there, they were content with the simple daily food of the brothers and asked for nothing more.

All the concern of those teachers at that time was to serve God, not the world; their whole care was to cultivate the heart, not the belly. Hence the religious habit was held in great honor at that time. Wherever a cleric or monk arrived, everyone gladly welcomed him as a servant of God. Even if he was found traveling along the road, people ran to him and rejoiced either to receive the sign of the cross from his hand or to be blessed by his mouth. They also listened attentively to the exhortations of such men.

On Sundays they flocked eagerly to the church or monasteries, not for the refreshment of the body but to hear the word of God. If a priest happened to come to a village, the villagers immediately gathered together and made it their concern to hear the word of life from him.

The priests and clerics had no other reason for visiting the villages than to preach, baptize, visit the sick, and, in short, care for souls. They had been so thoroughly disciplined against every plague of greed that no one accepted territories or possessions for building monasteries unless compelled by the powerful of this world [Al., “by the authorities of this world”] [Al., “unless those compelled accepted them”] (see above, chapter 23).

This custom continued for some time afterward in all the Churches of the Northumbrians. But enough has been said about these matters.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### How Ecgberct, a holy man of the English people, lived the monastic life in Ireland

In the same year of the Lord’s Incarnation, 664, there was an eclipse of the sun.

[Note: On the third day of May. Bede mentions this eclipse several times: once in his book *On Times*, and again in the *Chronicle* properly so called, no. 4622. In both places he dates it to the fifth day before the Nones of May, which corresponds to the third day of the month. This nevertheless causes no small difficulty for astronomers, since it is entirely inconsistent with the rules of the science.

“Gerhard Mercator, convinced that this eclipse, seen by Bede, was observed by him on that third day of May, relied so heavily on Bede’s authority that he did not hesitate to use it as the foundation for constructing a new hypothesis. But for those examining Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 25, it will be clear that this eclipse preceded his birth by nine years.

“Since he had learned from others that the eclipse occurred at the beginning of May, and from his own science knew that it could have occurred only at the time of the new moon, he thought that the day of the new moon had to be determined from the table of the nineteen-year cycle of Dionysius. When he discovered from it that the golden number of that year, XIX, indicated the first moon on May 3, he concluded that the eclipse of the sun had occurred on no other day than that.

“For it had not yet been sufficiently understood how deceptive that cyclical method of determining the new moons was. Marianus Scotus declared that its error was later exposed to the whole world by the phenomena themselves. Concerning the year 1082, when that same nineteenth year of the cycle was running, he wrote: ‘The first Paschal moon appeared to the whole world on the fourth day before the Nones of April, although it ought to have been on the second day before the Nones of April, where the golden number XIX was displayed in the commonly used calendars.’ Usserius, *British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 491.]

It occurred on the third day of May, at approximately the tenth hour of the day. In that same year a sudden epidemic of plague, after first devastating the southern regions of Britain, also attacked the province of the Northumbrians and raged for a long time with bitter destruction over a wide area, striking down a great multitude of people.

By this plague the aforementioned priest of the Lord, Tuda, was taken from the world and honorably buried in the monastery called Paegnalaech.

[Note: Paegnalaech. Waghele, *Saxon Chronicle*, p. 40, under the year 664; Wemalet, *History of Huntingdon*, Book III, p. 191. The various readings of this place-name arise from an erroneous interpretation of Saxon letters. The monastery itself, however, is not clearly identified. The name most closely resembles Pincanheale, today Finchale, two miles from Durham on the River Wear.

“Its certain antiquities do not extend beyond Saint Godric, who lived in the time of King Henry I and Hugh de Puiset, its founding bishop. Nevertheless, the councils convened there in the eighth century themselves clearly show that the place was already famous in Saxon times; nor is any other location known where they were held.

“Until some other burial place claims Tuda’s remains with stronger right, let us be permitted to enjoy the relics of so great a man.”]

This plague also afflicted the island of Ireland with a similar disaster. At that time many nobles and commoners from the English people were living there. During the episcopates of Finan and Colman, they had left their homeland and withdrawn there either for the sake of divine learning or for a more disciplined life.

Some of them immediately devoted themselves faithfully to the monastic life; others preferred to travel from one teacher’s cell to another and gladly devote themselves to study. The Scots welcomed all of them most willingly and took care to provide them with daily food without payment, books for reading, and free instruction.

Among them were two young men of outstanding ability, from the English nobility, Aedilhun and Ecgberct. The former was the brother of Aediluini, a man equally beloved by God. Aediluini himself, in a later age, went to Ireland for the sake of study, returned to his homeland well instructed, and became bishop in the province of Lindsey. He governed that Church for a long time with great distinction.

[Note: “For a long time.” From the year 679 to the year 701. Aediluini was the second bishop of Sidnacester. The first was Eadhed, whom we shall discuss in the following chapter.]

[Note: Rathmelsigi. In the language of the Scots, *rath* denotes a village or fortress. Mellis and Mellifont belonged to the same monastery, although the place that still bears the name Mellis is three miles from Mellifont. Both places seem to have been named after Saint Mel, bishop, disciple of Saint Patrick, and son of Patrick’s sister Darerca; see Jocelin, *Life of Patrick*, chapters 50, 102, and 186.]

When these two were in the monastery which in the language of the Scots is called Rathmelsigi, and all their companions had either been carried away from the world by death or scattered through narrow places, both were seized by the same mortal illness and gravely afflicted.

Concerning Ecgberct, a most truthful presbyter of venerable gray hair, who declared that he had heard these things from Ecgberct himself, related the following to me. When Ecgberct thought that he was about to die, he went out in the morning from the room where the sick were resting. Sitting alone in a suitable place, he began carefully to reflect on his actions. Struck by the memory of his sins, he washed his face with tears and prayed to God from the depths of his heart that he might not yet die before he had either more fully corrected, in the time remaining to him, the negligence he had committed in childhood or infancy, or exercised himself more abundantly in good works.

He also made a vow: he would live as an exile so completely that he would never return to the island in which he had been born, namely Britain; that, apart from the customary psalmody of the canonical hours, if bodily health did not prevent him, he would sing the entire Psalter every day in praise of God; and that every week he would pass one day and night fasting.

When his tears, prayers, and vows were finished, he returned to the house and found his companion asleep. He too climbed onto his bed and began to relax his limbs into rest. After he had rested for a short while, his companion awoke, looked at him, and said:

“O brother Ecgberct, what have you done? I had hoped that we would enter eternal life together. Nevertheless, know that you will receive what you have asked.”

For he had learned through a vision both what Ecgberct had requested and that his request had been granted.

What more need be said? Aedilhun died the following night. Ecgberct, however, was relieved of the burden of his illness and recovered. He lived for a much longer time and, having received the priestly rank, adorned it with worthy conduct. After many good works of virtue [Al., “gifts”], as he himself had desired, he recently—that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 729—when he was ninety years old, departed to the heavenly kingdoms.

He lived with great perfection of humility, gentleness, self-control, simplicity, and justice. Thus he was of great benefit both to his own people and to the Scottish and Pictish nations among whom he lived in exile: by the example of his life, the persistence of his teaching, the authority of his correction, and the mercy with which he distributed what he received from the wealthy.

He added to the vows already mentioned that throughout Lent he would take food no more than once a day, tasting nothing but bread and the thinnest milk, and that only in measured quantity. He used to place this milk, fresh from the previous day, in a flask; after removing the thicker surface that formed overnight, he drank the remainder with a little bread, as we have said.

He also always took care to observe this measure of self-restraint for forty days before the Nativity of the Lord and for an equal number of days after the completed solemnity of Pentecost, that is, the Quinquagesima.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### How, after Tuda’s death, Wilfrid was ordained bishop in Gaul and Ceadda among the West Saxons, for the province of the Northumbrians
Meanwhile King Alchfrid [Note: [Col. 0167D] His father Oswiu had entrusted him with the province of Deira to govern under himself.] sent the priest Wilfrid to the king of the Franks, so that he might have him consecrated bishop for himself and his people [DCCLXIV]. But that king sent him to Agilbert for ordination—the man mentioned above, who, having left Britain, had become bishop of the city of Paris [Col. 0167C]. He was consecrated with great honor by Agilbert himself, in the royal village called Compiègne, with many bishops assembled there [Note: [Col. 0167D] In Compendio, Compiègne, a royal estate in the territory of Soissons, at the confluence of the Aisne and Oise. While Pippin was ruling among the Franks, a synod was held there, and [Col. 0168D] Charles the Bald built a monastery in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, which is now called Saint-Corneille.]

While he was still staying overseas on account of [Al., “after”] his ordination, King Oswiu, imitating the zeal of his son, sent to Kent a holy man, modest in character, adequately instructed in the reading of Scripture, and skillfully carrying out in his works what he had learned from Scripture ought to be done, to be ordained bishop of the Church of York. He was a priest named Ceadda, brother of the most reverend bishop Cedd, whom we have often mentioned (above, chapters 21, 22, 23, and 26), and abbot of the monastery called Lastingham.

The king sent with him his own priest, named Eadhaed [Col. 0167D] (see Book IV, chapter 12), who later, during Ecgfrith’s reign, became bishop of the Church of Ripon. But when they reached Kent, they found that Archbishop Deusdedit had already departed from this world and that no other pontiff had yet been appointed in his place. Therefore they turned aside to the province of the West Saxons, where Bishop Wine was. By him the man mentioned above was consecrated bishop, two bishops of the British people being admitted to participate in the ordination; as has often been said, they celebrate the Lord’s day of Easter contrary to canonical custom, from the fourteenth to the twentieth day of the moon [Col. 0168A]. For at that time there was no canonically ordained bishop anywhere in Britain except Wine [Note: [Col. 0168D] Except for Wine. He had, namely, been ordained in Gaul. See Book III, chapter 7.]

After Ceadda had been consecrated bishop, he immediately began to devote himself to ecclesiastical truth and chastity; to apply himself to humility, continence, and reading; and to travel through towns, countryside, cottages, villages, and strongholds for the purpose of evangelizing—not by riding, but by going on foot after the manner of the apostles. For he had been one of Aidan’s disciples [Al., “a disciple”], and he took care to instruct his hearers by the same actions and practices, following the example of Aidan and of his brother Cedd.

When Wilfrid came to Britain, already made a bishop, he too contributed many regulations of Catholic observance to the churches of the English through his teaching. Thus it came about that, as Catholic instruction increased day by day, all the Scots who lived among the English either yielded to them or returned to their own country.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### How the priest Wighard was sent from Britain to Rome to be ordained archbishop, but died there, as was reported when the letter of the apostolic pope [Al., omits “apostolic”] was soon sent back

At this time [DCLXVII], the most noble kings of the English, Oswiu of the province of Northumbria and Ecgberht of Kent, having taken counsel together about what ought to be done concerning the condition of the English Church—for Oswiu had come to understand truly, although he had been educated by the Scots, that the Roman Church was Catholic and apostolic—selected, with the election and consent of the holy Church of the English people, a good man and a priest suited for the episcopate, named Wighard, from the clergy of Deusdedit the bishop [Al., “archbishop”]. They sent him to Rome to be ordained bishop, so that, having received the rank of archbishop, he might ordain Catholic bishops for the churches of the English throughout Britain.

But when Wighard reached Rome, he was seized by death before he could be consecrated bishop [Al., “as bishop”], and the following letter was sent back to King Oswiu in Britain:

> “To the excellent [Al., “most excellent”] son, Oswiu, king of the Saxons, Vitalian, bishop and servant of the servants of God.
>
> “We have received the desirable letter of Your Excellency [Col. 0168D]. On rereading it, we recognized the profoundly pious devotion and most fervent love which you possess for the blessed life, and that, protected by the right hand of the Lord, you have turned to the true and apostolic faith, hoping that, just as you reign among your own people, so also you may reign with Christ [Al., “in Christ”] in the future. Blessed, therefore, is the people that has deserved to have so wise and God-fearing a king; for not only has he himself proved to be a worshiper of God [Al., “is a worshiper of God”], but he also meditates day and night on turning all his subjects to the Catholic and apostolic faith for the redemption of their souls.
>
> “For who, hearing these pleasing things, would not rejoice? Who would not exult and be glad at these pious works? Your people too have believed in Christ, almighty God, in accordance with the words of the divine prophets, as it is written in Isaiah: ‘On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, the nations will entreat.’ And again: ‘Listen, islands, and pay attention, peoples from afar.’ And shortly afterward: ‘It is too little,’ he says, ‘for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to restore the remnants of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.’
>
> “And again: ‘Kings shall see, and princes shall rise and worship.’ And shortly afterward: ‘I have given you as a covenant of the people, to raise up the earth, to possess the desolated inheritances, and to say to those who are bound: “Come out”; and to those who are in darkness: “Be revealed.”’
>
> “And again: ‘I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness, and I have taken your hand and preserved you; and I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light to the nations, so that you may open the eyes of the blind and bring out the bound man from confinement, from the prison house those sitting [Al., “the one sitting”] in darkness.’
>
> “Behold, most excellent son, how clear as daylight it is that it was prophesied [Al., “of the prophets”] not only concerning you but also concerning all the nations that they would believe in Christ, the creator of all. Therefore it is fitting that Your Highness, since you are a member of Christ, should perpetually follow in all things the pious rule of the chief of the apostles, whether in celebrating Easter or in all the things handed down by the holy apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0169C]. Like two lights of heaven, they illuminate the world; so their teaching daily enlightens the hearts of believers.”

[Note: [Col. 0169D] And afterward, having said some things concerning its celebration. The question of Easter recurs so often that Bede refrained from repeating in the papal letters and elsewhere what had been written about it—both in the letter of Pope Honorius to the Irish clergy, in the year 639 (II, 19), and in the letter of Laurence of Canterbury to the same people (II, 4). He does the same in this letter of Pope Vitalian. Concerning this, Usserius, in his notes on *Epistolae Hibernicae*, collection 9, p. 126, observes that this deficiency can in some measure be supplied from the oldest documents of the monastery of Whitby. In them, under a heading prefixed with the name Vitalian—undoubtedly Vitalian, pope of the city of Rome—he found the following:

> “For we ought never to celebrate the holy Easter except according to the apostolic and Catholic faith, as it is celebrated throughout the whole world by the Christian people, that is, according to the apostolic rule of the 318 holy Fathers and the computation of the holy Cyril and Dionysius. For throughout the whole earth the one dove of Christ, that is, the immaculate Church, thus celebrates the holy day of the Resurrection of Easter. For the apostolic see did not approve Victor’s rule for Easter; therefore it does not follow his arrangement concerning Easter.”

And afterward he says some things about celebrating one true Easter throughout the whole world [Al., omits “whole”].

> “Finally,” he says, “we have not now been able to find, in accordance with the tenor of your writings, a teachable man and a bishop adorned in every respect, because of the length of the journey. Indeed, as soon as such a suitable and proven person has been found, we shall send him instructed to your country, so that, both by the living voice and through the divine oracles, he may, with divine permission, root out all the tares of the enemy from your entire island.
>
> “We have received the gifts sent by Your Highness to the blessed chief of the apostles for his eternal remembrance, and we thank you for them; together with the clergy of Christ, we continually pray to God for your safety [Col. 0170A]. The one who offered these gifts, however, has been removed from this light and laid at the threshold of the apostles, at which we were greatly saddened, since [Al., “why”] he had died here. Nevertheless, through the bearers of this letter whom we have sent to you, we have caused the benefits of the saints [Al., adding ‘martyrs’]—that is, relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy martyrs Laurence, John and Paul, and of Gregory and Pancratius—to be given to them, so that they may certainly all be handed over to Your Excellency.
>
> “We have also sent through the aforesaid bearers to your wife, our spiritual daughter, a cross containing a golden key, made from the most sacred chains of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Learning of her pious devotion, the entire apostolic see rejoices with us as greatly as her pious works before God are fragrant [Al., “burning”] and flourishing.
>
> “Let Your Highness therefore hasten, as we desire, to dedicate your entire island to God Christ. Indeed, you have as protector the Lord Jesus Christ, redeemer of the human race, who will grant you all prosperity, so that you may gather together a new people of Christ and establish there the Catholic and apostolic faith. For it is written: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.’ Surely he seeks it and has obtained it, and, as we desire, all the people of his island will be subjected to him.
>
> “Greeting Your Excellency with paternal affection, we continually pray for the divine mercy, that it may deign to assist you and all your people in every good work, so that you may reign with Christ in the future age [Col. 0170C]. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellency unharmed.”

Who was found and appointed as bishop in place of Wighard will be more suitably related in the following book.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### How, during a time of plague, the East Saxons returned to idolatry, but were soon corrected from their error through the zeal of Bishop Jaruman

At the same time [DCLXV], the province of the East Saxons was ruled, after Suidhelm, whom we mentioned above [above, chapter 22], by Kings Sigheri and Sebbi [Note: [Col. 0170D] The former was the son of Sigberht, surnamed the Little; the latter was the son of Seaward, who, having shamefully betrayed the Christian faith, was killed by the king of the West Saxons. Harpsfeld incorrectly calls this man the son of Æthelred.], although they themselves were subject to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians.

When this province was afflicted by the calamity of the aforementioned plague, Sigheri, together with the portion of the people under him, abandoned the sacraments of the Christian faith and turned to apostasy. For both the king himself and many of the common people and nobles, loving this present life and not seeking the future one—or even believing that it did not exist—began to restore the abandoned temples and worship idols, as though by these means they could be protected from the plague.

But his companion and fellow heir to the same kingdom, Sebbi, preserved with great devotion the faith he had received together with all his people, and, as we shall relate below, completed his faithful life in great blessedness. When King Wulfhere learned that the faith of the province had been profaned in part, he sent Bishop Jaruman, who had succeeded Trumhere, to correct the error and call the province back to the faith of truth.

Jaruman acted with great skill. According to the report given to me by a priest who had been his traveling companion and fellow worker in the word—and who was a religious and good man—he traveled far and wide, and brought both the people and the king mentioned above back to the way of righteousness. Thus, after abandoning or destroying the temples and altars they had made, they opened the churches and rejoiced to confess the name of Christ, which they had opposed. They preferred to die in him with faith in the resurrection rather than live amid idols in the filth of unbelief. When these things had been accomplished, their priests and teachers themselves returned home rejoicing.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER I  
### How, after Deusdedit’s death, Wighard was sent to Rome to receive the episcopate [Al., “bishop”; al., “to receive the bishopric”]; but, after Wighard died there, Theodore was ordained archbishop and sent to Britain with Abbot Hadrian

In the year of the aforementioned eclipse and of the plague that immediately followed it, when Bishop Colman, defeated by the unanimous resolve of the Catholics, returned to his own people, Deusdedit, the sixth bishop of the Church of Canterbury, died on the day before the Ides of July [DCLXIV] [Note: [Col. 0171D] Deusdedit. Codex A.T.D., p. 25b, says that his original name was Fritonas.]. King Erconberht of Kent also died in the same month and on the same day, leaving the seat of the kingdom to his son Ecgberht, who, having received it, held it for nine years.

Then, after the episcopate had remained vacant for a considerable time [Note: [Col. 0171D] “For no short time.” From the day before the Ides of July in the year 664 to the seventh day before the Kalends of April in the year 668. Wharton, however, counts from 28 July.], Wighard, a priest and a man most learned in ecclesiastical disciplines, of English origin, was sent to Rome by Ecgberht himself and by Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, as we briefly stated in the preceding book, so that, at their request, he might be ordained archbishop of the English Church. At the same time, gifts were sent to the apostolic pope, including many gold and silver vessels.

When he reached Rome, where [Al., “to which”] Vitalian presided over the apostolic see at that time, and had explained the purpose of his journey to the aforesaid apostolic pope, not long afterward both he himself and nearly all the companions who had come with him were carried off by the plague.

Then the apostolic pope, having deliberated about these matters, carefully sought whom he might send as archbishop to the churches of the English. In the monastery of Hiridano [Al., “Niridano”] [Note: [Col. 0172D] Thus Codex Mori, but the manuscripts of earliest authority differ in this word. Some have *Niridano*, and rightly so. It is a place near Mount Cassino.], which is not far from Naples in Campania, there was an abbot named Hadrian, a man African by nationality, diligently instructed in sacred letters, trained in both monastic and ecclesiastical disciplines, and highly skilled in both the Greek and Latin languages.

The pope summoned him and ordered him, after accepting the episcopate, to come to Britain. But he, declaring himself unworthy of so great a rank, said that he could point out another whose learning and age were more suitable for receiving the episcopate [Col. 0172B]. When he offered to the pontiff a certain monk from a nearby monastery of virgins, named Andrew, the man was judged worthy of the episcopate by all who knew him [Al., “knew him”]. But the burden of bodily infirmity prevented him from becoming a bishop. Once again Hadrian was urged to accept the episcopate; he requested [Al., “requested”] a delay, in case someone else suitable for episcopal ordination might meanwhile be found.

At that time there was in Rome a monk known to Hadrian, named Theodore, born [Al., adds “from”] in Tarsus of Cilicia. He was learned in both secular and divine literature, instructed in Greek and Latin, upright in character, and venerable in age—that is, he was sixty-six years old [Al., “forty-six”].

When Hadrian offered him to the pontiff for ordination as bishop [Col. 0172C], he obtained it, but on these conditions: that he himself would lead Theodore to Britain, since he had already visited the regions of Gaul twice for various reasons [Note: [Col. 0172D] He had already visited them twice for different reasons. Hence the greater suspicion fell upon Hadrian rather than Theodore; see below.], and therefore had greater knowledge for undertaking this journey and was sufficiently provided with attendants of his own; and that, as his associate in teaching, he would carefully ensure that Theodore introduced nothing contrary to the truth of the faith, in the Greek manner, into the Church over which he would preside.

After being ordained subdeacon, Theodore waited four months, until his hair grew long enough for it to be cut into a crown. For he had worn the tonsure in the manner of the Easterners, that of the holy apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0172D] Of Paul. See the appendix on the tonsure, no. 9.]. He was ordained by Pope Vitalian in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 668, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, a Sunday. Thus he was sent to Britain together [Al., omits “together”] with Hadrian on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

When they had traveled by sea together to Marseille and then by land to Arles [Al., “Arelatem”], and had presented themselves to John, archbishop of that city, together with Vitalian’s commendatory letters, they were detained by him until Ebroin, mayor of the royal palace, granted them permission to proceed wherever they wished.

After receiving this permission, Theodore went to Agilbert, bishop of Paris, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0173D] Above, III, 25, 26, and 28]. Agilbert received him kindly and kept him for a long time. Hadrian, however, first went to Emme, bishop of Sens, and afterward to Faro, bishop of Meaux, and remained with them [Al., “under them”] for a considerable time in good circumstances; for the approaching winter had compelled them to stay wherever they could find rest.

When reliable messengers reported these things to King Ecgberht—namely, that the bishop whom they had requested from the Roman pontiff was [Al., “had arrived”] in the kingdom of the Franks—he immediately sent his prefect Raedfrid [Al., “Regetfrid”] to bring him. When Raedfrid arrived, he took Theodore, with Ebroin’s permission, and led him to the port called Quentavic [Note: [Col. 0173D] Quentavic. A village of Gaul in the territory of Ponthieu on the river Canche. The monastery of Saint-Josse was situated there, and it retains the name Saint-Josse-sur-Mer. Baluze. It is commonly called Étaples.]. There Theodore, exhausted by illness, stayed for a short time. When he began to recover, he sailed to Britain.

Ebroin, however, detained Hadrian, because he suspected that he had some embassy from the emperor [Note: [Col. 0173D] The emperor Constantine Pogonatus, who had recently come to power and, in the troubled affairs of the Franks, might have been able to inflict new losses upon them. Especially since in that very year, after the death of Chlothar III, Ebroin had raised his brother Theuderic to the throne against Childeric. What later happened to him sufficiently demonstrates that the suspicions he conceived on every side were not groundless.] to the kings of Britain against the kingdom over which Ebroin then exercised the greatest authority.

But when he had ascertained with certainty that Hadrian had neither such an embassy nor any such commission, he released him and allowed him to follow Theodore. As soon as Hadrian reached him, Theodore gave him the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, where, as I have said, the archbishops of Canterbury customarily are buried [Note: [Col. 0173D] As stated above, I, 33, and II, 3.]. For the apostolic lord had instructed Theodore, when he departed, to make provision for Hadrian within his diocese and to give him a place where he could live suitably with his companions.

## CHAPTER II  
### How, after Theodore had traveled throughout the country, the churches of the English began to be imbued not only with Catholic truth but also with the study of sacred letters; and how Putta became bishop of the Church of Rochester in place of Damian

Theodore reached his own Church in the second year after his consecration, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, a Sunday [DCLXIX], and governed it for twenty-one years, three months, and twenty-six days.

Having soon traveled throughout the entire island [Note: [Col. 0173D] “The entire island.” He had received from Pope Vitalian a papal privilege by which the bishop of Canterbury possessed authority over the whole English Church. It should nevertheless be noted that this privilege was not first granted to him as something peculiar to himself, as some suppose, but had either truly been granted in common with his predecessors or at least claimed as such. See Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus*, I.]—wherever the peoples of the English lived, for he was received and heard most willingly by all—he spread everywhere the right order of living and the canonical rite of celebrating Easter, with Hadrian accompanying and assisting him in all things.

He was the first among the archbishops [Al., “archbishop”; [Col. 0173D] omits *in*] to whom the whole English Church consented to submit. Since, as we have said, both men were abundantly instructed in sacred and secular letters, a crowd of disciples gathered around them, and the rivers of saving knowledge flowed out daily to water their hearts. Thus they also taught their hearers the disciplines of metrical art, astronomy [Al., “the astronomical discipline”], and ecclesiastical arithmetic [Note: [Col. 0174D] Ecclesiastical arithmetic—not merely ordinary arithmetic, but the branch that deals with calculations directed toward the use of the Church, an art that Bede transmits in his books *On the Reckoning of Time*.]

The evidence is that, even to this day, some of their disciples survive who know the Latin and Greek languages equally as well as their own native language [Note: [Col. 0174D] Greek as well. See the appendix, no. 15.]. Never, since the English came to Britain, had more prosperous times existed: they possessed kings who were both powerful and Christian, and so were a terror to all barbarian nations; everyone’s hopes were directed toward the joys of the heavenly kingdom recently heard of; and whoever desired to be instructed in sacred readings had teachers readily available to teach them.

From that time the musical tones sung in the church, which until then were known only in Kent, also began to be learned throughout all the churches of the English. Except for James, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0174D] Above, II, 16 and 20; III, 25.], the first singing master of the churches of Northumbria was Aeddi, surnamed Stephen. He had been invited from Kent by the most reverend Wilfrid, who was the first of the bishops of English origin to learn and transmit the Catholic manner of life to the churches of the English.

Thus Theodore, surveying everything, appointed bishops in suitable places and, with their help, corrected whatever he found to be less than perfect. Among these matters, when he reproved Bishop Ceadda for not having been duly consecrated [Note: [Col. 0174D] For not having been properly consecrated. Theodore charged Ceadda’s ordination with two errors. First, he had been ordained to a see that had already been filled by Wilfrid’s election. Second, in his ordination the bishops who had been admitted to participate with Wine in the ministry were among those who followed the British custom concerning Easter; see III, 28.], Ceadda answered in the deepest humility:

> “If you know that I have not rightly received the episcopate,” he said, “I willingly withdraw from the office, since I never judged myself worthy of it. But because I was ordered to undertake it for the sake of obedience, I consented to do so, although unworthy.”

When Theodore heard the humility of his reply, he said that Ceadda ought not to resign the episcopate; instead, he himself completed Ceadda’s ordination anew according to Catholic practice.

At the time when, after Deusdedit’s death, a bishop of the Church of Canterbury was being sought, ordained, and sent, Wilfrid too was sent from Britain to Gaul to be ordained. Since he returned before Theodore, he himself ordained priests and deacons in Kent until the archbishop reached his see.

When Theodore arrived, he immediately ordained in the city of Rochester, where the episcopate had long been vacant after Bishop Damian’s death, a man more trained in ecclesiastical disciplines and content with the simplicity of life than energetic in worldly affairs. His name was Putta. He was especially skilled in singing in the church according to the Roman manner, which he had learned from the disciples of the blessed Pope Gregory.

## CHAPTER III  
### How Ceadda, mentioned above, was appointed bishop of the province of the Mercians; and concerning his life, death, and burial

At that time [DCLXIX] Wulfhere was king of the province of the Mercians. When, after Jaruman’s death [Note: [Col. 0175D] Jaruman’s death provided a timely opportunity for Ceadda’s withdrawal, so as to preserve the unity of the Church.], he asked Theodore to provide a bishop for himself [Al., “who also”] and his people, he did not wish to appoint a new bishop for them. Instead, he requested from King Oswiu that Bishop Ceadda be given to them.

Ceadda was then living a quiet life in his monastery at Lastingham, while Wilfrid administered the episcopate of the Church of York and of all the Northumbrians, as well as of the Picts, insofar as King Oswiu could extend his authority.

Since it was the custom of that most reverend bishop to carry out the work of the Gospel by traveling on foot through the regions rather than by riding [Note: [Col. 0175D] “By walking.” See above, III, 28.], Theodore ordered him to ride whenever a longer journey lay ahead. When Ceadda resisted for a long time, out of zeal and love for pious labor, Theodore himself lifted him onto the horse with his own hands. For he had discovered that Ceadda was truly a holy man, and he compelled him to ride when necessity required it.

Having therefore received the episcopate of the Mercian people and of the Lindisfarans [Al., “Lindisfarnans”] [Col. 0175C], Ceadda took care to administer it according to the examples of the ancient Fathers, with great perfection of life. King Wulfhere also gave him land sufficient for fifty households, to build a monastery in a place called Ad Barwa, that is, “At Barwa” [Note: [Col. 0175D] *Ad Barude*. Knowledge of this place has disappeared; I do not know whether it could be identified with Barton upon Humber.], that is, “At the Grove,” in the province of Lindsey. There, even to this day, traces of the regular life established by him remain.

He had his episcopal see in a place called Lichfield, where he also died and was buried [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Having died.” His memory is celebrated on 2 March.]. There, even to this day, the see of the succeeding bishops of that province remains [Note: [Col. 0175D] “He had his see.” Before Ceadda, Lichfield had the following bishops: Diuma in 656, Ceollach in 658, Trumhere in 659, and Jaruman in 662. See Book III, 21. Ceadda succeeded Jaruman in 669. When, at the synod of 1075, the episcopal sees were transferred to more prominent places, Bishop Peter moved his see to Chester, and Robert, his successor, to Coventry. Shortly afterward Roger restored it to Lichfield, where in 1148 he founded a magnificent church in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Ceadda. After being destroyed in the civil wars, it was restored by Bishop Hacket with greater splendor than before. This see was raised to an archbishopric under Offa, king of the Mercians. After Mercia and the East Angles had been made into a province by Pope Hadrian, its former authority immediately returned to Canterbury under his successor Leo.].

He had made himself a dwelling [Note: [Col. 0176D] “A residence.” See the appendix, no. 16.] somewhat farther away from the church. Whenever he was free from labor and the ministry of the word, he used to pray and read there in greater seclusion with a few brothers—seven or eight.

After he had ruled the Church in that province with great glory for two and a half years, the time arrived, by the dispensation of heavenly judgment, of which Ecclesiastes speaks: “There is a time for throwing stones and a time for gathering them.” For a divinely sent calamity came upon them, transferring, through the death of the flesh, the living stones of the Church from earthly dwellings to the heavenly building.

When many members of the Church of that most reverend bishop had been taken from the flesh, and his own hour came to depart from this world to the Lord, it happened one day that he was staying in the aforementioned residence with only one brother, named Owin [Note: [Col. 0176D] In the Benedictine Martyrology, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, there is a commemoration of Blessed Owin, a monk who had been chief steward of Saint Æthelthryth when she went as a bride to King Ecgfrith. He followed the same example when he entered religious life.]. The rest of his companions had returned to the church for a necessary purpose.

This Owin was a monk of great merit. He had renounced the world with a pure intention of receiving the heavenly reward and was altogether worthy that the Lord should reveal his mysteries especially to him, and worthy that those who heard him tell of them should believe him.

He had come with Queen Æthelthryth from the province of the East Angles and had been the first of her servants and the chief officer of her household. When, as the fervor of his faith increased, he decided to renounce the world, he did not do so half-heartedly. He stripped himself so completely of worldly possessions that, leaving behind everything he had, dressed only in a simple garment and carrying an axe and a hatchet in his hand, he came to the monastery of the same reverend father, called Lastingham.

He did not signify, like some others, that he was entering the monastery for leisure, but for labor. He also demonstrated this by his actions: the less he was able to devote himself to meditation on Scripture, the more eagerly he applied himself to manual work.

Indeed, while he was honored among the brothers in the aforementioned residence because of his devout reverence for the bishop, whenever the bishop and the others were occupied inside with reading, Owin worked outside at whatever seemed necessary.

One day, while he was doing some such task outside, and his companions had gone to the church—as I began to say—the bishop was alone in the oratory of the place, devoting himself to reading or prayer. Suddenly he heard, as he later reported, a most beautiful voice of singers rejoicing, descending from heaven all the way to earth.

He said that he first heard this voice from the southeast, that is, from the height of the winter sunrise [Al., “arising from the southeast”]. Then he heard it gradually drawing nearer, until it reached the roof of the oratory in which the bishop was. After entering it, the voice filled the entire place and surrounded it on every side.

While he anxiously focused his mind on what he was hearing, after the passage of approximately half an hour he heard the same song of joy rise from the roof of that oratory and, by the route through which it had come, return to heaven with indescribable sweetness [Col. 0176D].

He remained for a short while almost stunned, carefully pondering what this might be [Al., “what this was”]. Then the bishop opened the window of the oratory and, making a sound with his hand, as he often used to do [Al., “as he was accustomed to do”], ordered anyone who might be outside to come in.

Owin entered hurriedly. The bishop said to him:

> “Go quickly to the church and bring the seven brothers here. You too must be present.”

When they came, he first admonished them to preserve among themselves and toward all the faithful the virtue of love and peace. He also urged them to follow with tireless perseverance the rules of the regular discipline, whether they had learned them from him and observed them in him, or had found them in the deeds or sayings of the Fathers who had gone before.

Then he added that the day of his death was already close [Col. 0177B]:

> “For that beloved guest,” he said, “who used to visit our brothers has deigned to come to me also today and to call me from this world. Therefore, when you return to the church, tell the brothers both to commend my departure to the Lord in their prayers and to remember to anticipate their own departure, whose hour is uncertain, by vigils, prayers, and good works.”

After he had spoken these and many similar words, and the brothers had received his blessing and gone out in great sadness, the one who had heard the heavenly song returned alone and fell prostrate on the ground.

> “I beg you, Father,” he said, “may I [Al., “may I indeed?”] ask you something?”
>
> “Ask whatever you wish,” he replied.
>
> “I beg you,” said Owin, “tell me what that song of rejoicing was which I heard, coming from heaven over this oratory and, after a time, returning to heaven.”
>
> The bishop replied: “If you heard the sound of the song and recognized that heavenly hosts had come, I command you in the name of the Lord not to tell anyone about it before my death. They were truly the spirits of angels who came to call me to the heavenly rewards that I have always loved and desired. They promised that they would return after seven days and take me with them.”

This was indeed fulfilled in action just as it had been told [Al., “foretold”] to him. Immediately he was struck by bodily illness, which grew worse day by day. On the seventh day, as had been promised to him, after strengthening his approaching death by receiving the body and blood of the Lord, his holy soul was released from the prison of the body and went to seek eternal joys, carried, as it is right to believe, by angelic companions.

It is not surprising that he looked joyfully toward the day of his death—or rather, the day of the Lord—for he had always carefully and anxiously awaited its coming.

For among the many merits of self-restraint, humility, learning, prayer [Al., of prayer], voluntary poverty, and the other virtues, he was so subject to the fear of the Lord, so mindful in all his works of his last things, that, as a certain brother named Trumbert used to relate to me—one of those who instructed me in the Scriptures [Al., om. “of him”], and who had been brought up in his monastery and under his direction—if, while he was reading or doing something else, a stronger gust of wind suddenly arose, he would immediately invoke the Lord’s mercy and beseech that it might be propitious to the human race. But if a more violent wind persisted, he would close the book, fall on his face, and devote himself more earnestly to prayer. If, however, a stronger storm or driving rain came, or even lightning and thunder terrified the earth and air, then, hastening to the church, he would apply himself attentively to prayers and psalms until the serenity of the air returned. When his people asked why he did this, he replied:

“Have you not read: ‘The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice [Al., sound]. He sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied his lightning and confused them’? For the Lord moves the air, stirs up the winds, hurls lightning, thunders from heaven, in order to rouse earthly beings to fear him, to recall their hearts to the remembrance of the future judgment, to scatter their pride, and to confound their boldness by bringing to mind that dreadful time when he himself, with heaven and earth burning, will come in the clouds with great power and majesty to judge the living and the dead. Therefore,” he said, “we ought to answer his heavenly admonition with the fear and love that are its due: whenever, with the air stirred, he stretches out his hand as if threatening to strike, yet does not strike, let us immediately implore his mercy, search the innermost chambers of our hearts, clear away the rubble of our vices, and act anxiously lest we ever deserve to be struck.”

The revelation and report of the aforementioned brother concerning the death of this bishop are also confirmed by the account of the most reverend Father Ecgberct, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0177D] Above, III, 27]. Long ago, when he was still a young man, he too was diligently leading in Ireland, together with the young Ceadda, a monastic life of prayer, self-restraint, and meditation on the divine Scriptures. But after Ceadda later returned to his homeland, Ecgberct remained abroad for the Lord until the end of his life.

When, therefore, after a long time, the most holy and self-restrained man Hygbald came from Britain to visit him—he was abbot in the province of Lindsey—and when, as was fitting for saints, they were speaking about the life of the earlier Fathers and rejoicing in imitating it, mention was made of the most reverend bishop Ceadda. Ecgberct said:

“I know of a man who is still living in the flesh on this island, who, when that man departed from the world, saw the soul of Ceadda, his brother, descend from heaven with a company of angels, and, taking his soul with him, return to the heavenly kingdoms.”

Whether he was speaking of himself or of someone else remains uncertain to us [Note: [Col. 0177] From “Dum tamen” through “incertam” is absent from A. I. and Chiffl.]; nevertheless, it cannot be uncertain that what so great a man said was true.

Ceadda died on the sixth day before the Nones of March and was first buried beside the church of Saint Mary. Later, when the church of the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, had been built there, his bones were transferred into it. In both places, as a sign of his virtue, frequent miracles of healing are customarily performed.

Recently, a certain madman, wandering about everywhere, arrived there in the evening. The custodians of the place either did not know of him or did not care for him. After resting there throughout the night, he went out in the morning with his senses restored, and, to the amazement and joy of all, showed what healing the Lord had granted him there. The tomb itself is covered by a wooden structure made in the form of a little house, with an opening in the wall through which those who come there out of devotion customarily insert their hand and take out some of the dust. When they put it into water and give this to sick animals or people to drink, the affliction of the illness is immediately removed, and the joys of the desired health return [Al., return].

In his place Theodore appointed Uynfrid, a good and moderate man, who, like his predecessors, presided in the episcopal office over the provinces of the Mercians, the Middle Angles, and the Lindisfaras. Uulfheri, who was still alive, held the royal scepter over all these territories. Uynfrid belonged to the clergy of the bishop whom he succeeded, and for a considerable time had exercised the office of deacon under him.

## CHAPTER IV. How Bishop Colman, having left Britain, established two monasteries in Ireland: one for the Irish and the other for the English whom he had brought with him

[Col. 0179C]

Meanwhile Colman, who was an Irish bishop, left Britain [667] and took with him all the Irish whom he had gathered on the island of Lindisfarne, as well as about thirty men from the English people who were trained in the practices of monastic life. Leaving several brothers in his church, he first came to the island of Iona, from which he had been sent to preach the word [Al., add. of God] to the English people. Then he withdrew to a certain small island, situated far to the west of Ireland and isolated from it. In the Irish language it is called [Note: [Col. 0179D] Inisboufinde. Colman withdrew to this island, which still retains its name, in the year 667, as Ussher cites the Ulster Annals under the year 667: “The voyage of Bishop Columbanus with the relics of the saints to the island of the White Cow, on which he founded a church.” And under the year 675: “The repose, or end of the life, of that same Bishop Columbanus on the island of the White Cow.” “By the name Columbanus,” says Ussher, “there can be no doubt that Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne, is meant; Bede also records that, when returning home, he took with him a portion of the bones of the most reverend Father Aedan.” On this island Saint Rioch, the nephew of Saint Patrick through his sister Darerca, is said to have established an episcopal see long before Colman’s time.] Inisboufinde, that is, “the island of the white calf.”

When he arrived there, he built a monastery and settled there the monks whom he had brought together from both peoples. Since they could not agree with one another—for the Scots, during the summer, when the crops were being gathered, would leave the monastery and scatter through places familiar to them, but, when winter came, would return and desire to share in common the things the English had prepared—Colman sought a remedy for this disagreement. Traveling throughout the surrounding region, near and far, he found in Ireland a place suitable for building a monastery. In the language of the Irish it is called [Note: [Col. 0180D] Mageo, Muigeo; commonly Maio. An episcopal see was established on the nearby mainland opposite Inisboufinde and is today attached to the archbishopric of Tuam; in 1559 Eugenius Mac Brenoan was the last bishop called Magonensis. Just as we have heard that in Bede’s time this place contained a large English monastery, so the compiler of the Book of Ballymote confirms that in the time of Saints Cormac and Adamnan it was a dwelling of one hundred Saxon saints. Ussher, *Primordia*, p. 499.] Mageo. He bought a small portion of it from the count whose property it was, in order to build a monastery there, adding the condition that the monks who settled there should offer prayers to the Lord also for the man who had granted them the place.

As soon as the monastery had been built, with the count and all the neighbors also assisting, he settled the English there [Al., placed them there], leaving the Scots on the aforementioned island. This monastery has remained under English inhabitants to the present day. It is the one that, having grown from something small into something great, is now commonly called Muigeo [Al., Maigeo; Al., Injugeo]. Since all its members long ago turned to better practices, it contains an excellent company of monks gathered there from the province of the English, who, following the example of the venerable Fathers, live under a rule and a canonical abbot in great self-restraint and sincerity, by the labor of their own hands [Al., live].

## CHAPTER V. On the deaths of Kings Osuiu and Ecgberct, and on the synod held at Herutford, presided over by Archbishop Theodore

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 670, the second year after Theodore came to Britain, King Osuiu of the Northumbrians was seized by an illness, of which he died in the fifty-eighth year of his age. At that time he was so deeply devoted to Roman and apostolic observance that, if he were saved from the illness, he intended even to go to Rome and end his life there at the holy places. He asked Bishop Uilfrid to become his guide on the journey, promising a considerable gift of money.

He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March and left his son Ecgfrid as heir to the kingdom. In the third year of Ecgfrid’s reign, Theodore summoned a council of bishops, together with several teachers of the Church who both loved and knew the canonical decrees of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0180D] “Teachers.” See Appendix no. 17]. When they had assembled together, he began carefully to teach them, in the spirit proper to a bishop, those things that were appropriate for the unity of ecclesiastical peace. The text of this synodical proceeding is as follows:

“In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, who reigns forever and governs his Church, it seemed good that we should assemble, according to the custom of the venerable canons, to deliberate on the necessary affairs of the Church. We assembled on the twenty-fourth day of September, in the first indiction [Note: [Col. 0181C] First. From this Wharton infers that the year of this synod was probably 672 rather than 673. But this conflicts with Bede’s own calculation in the Chronological Recapitulation [Col. 0181D] and with the actual sequence of the indictions], at the place called Herutford [Al., Herudford].

“I, Theodore, though unworthy, appointed by the apostolic see, bishop of the Church of Canterbury; and our most reverend fellow priest and brother Bisi, bishop of the East Angles; and our brother and fellow priest Uilfrid, bishop of the people of the Northumbrians, who was present through his own representatives. Also present were our brothers and fellow priests: Putta, bishop of the Kentish city called Rochester; Leutherius, bishop of the West Saxons; and Uynfrid [Col. 0181B], bishop of the province of the Mercians.

“When we had assembled and each had taken his seat according to his proper order, I said: ‘I ask you, dearest brothers, for the fear and love of our Redeemer, that we all deliberate together according to our faith, so that whatever has been decreed and defined by holy and approved Fathers may be observed uncorrupted by all of us.’ I continued with this and many other matters pertaining to charity and the preservation of the unity of the Church.

“When I had finished my opening address, I asked each of them in order whether they consented to observe what had long ago been canonically decreed by the Fathers. To this all our fellow priests replied: ‘It pleases us all exceedingly that whatever the holy canons of the Fathers have defined, we too should all preserve with eager and willing hearts.’ Immediately I produced for them the same book of canons [Note: [Col. 0181D] “The Book of Canons.” I do not think that this was some special book composed by Theodore, but the collection of the canons of the Church approved at the Council of Chalcedon, translated into Latin not long before by Dionysius Exiguus and received into the Western Church. For, after asking the agreement of the brothers, Theodore produced not new constitutions devised by himself, but the same book of canons, referring to what had long ago been canonically decreed by the Fathers, without mentioning any other book. From this same book he displayed the ten chapters he had marked as especially necessary in their circumstances. So far was he from composing a new book of canons that he scarcely even copied out the ancient canons from the Book of Canons], and from that same book I showed them, in their presence, the ten chapters that I had marked in various places, because I knew them to be especially necessary for us. I urged that all should receive them with greater care.”

**First chapter.** That we should all observe the holy day of Easter together on the Sunday after the fourteenth day of the first month’s moon.

**Second.** That no bishop should invade another’s parish, but should be content with governing the people entrusted to him.

**Third.** That no bishop should be permitted to disturb in any way monasteries consecrated to God or violently to take anything from their possessions.

**Fourth.** That the monks themselves [Al., bishops] should not move from place to place, that is, from monastery to monastery, except by the dismissal [Al., permission] of their own abbot; but should remain in the obedience that they promised at the time of their conversion [Al., manner of life].

**Fifth.** That no cleric, leaving his own bishop, should wander about indiscriminately, nor should anyone arriving anywhere be received without letters of recommendation from his bishop. If, once received, he refuses to return when invited, both the receiver and the one received shall be subject to excommunication.

**Sixth.** That visiting bishops and clerics should be content with the hospitality offered to them, and that none of them should perform any priestly office without the permission of the bishop in whose parish he is known to be.

**Seventh.** That a synod should assemble twice a year. But since various circumstances prevent this, it pleased everyone jointly that we should assemble once a year on the Kalends of August at the place called [Note: [Col. 0182C] Clofeshoch, commonly Cliff, near Rochester. Somner, however, in his Saxon Dictionary offers another opinion that seems not unworthy of consideration [Col. 0182D]. Camden had noted that the name of that place was formerly Sheovesham, and that a royal seat had been established there, with the people gathering there whenever serious matters of the kingdom were discussed. Somner therefore thought it not unlikely that the place-name had been written incorrectly as Sheofesham for Cleofesham, and that the sites bearing the two names were one and the same. The location itself seems to favor this opinion more than the sound of the names: it was not only in the very center of the island, but in the province in which Aedilbald, who sat as prince at the council of Clofeshoch and to whose kingdom the canons were adapted from Kent, held authority. Indeed, the councils held at that place that have survived took place when the kings of the Mercians exercised dominion over the upper provinces, while the kings of Kent had been reduced to the lowest condition, though formerly marked by supreme arrogance. But in all this there is nothing beyond conjecture, and that conjecture is certainly very unstable.] Clofeshoch.

**Eighth.** That no bishop should set himself above another through ambition, but that all should recognize the time and order of their assembly [Al., consecration].

**Ninth chapter.** The matter was discussed jointly: that, as the number of the faithful increased, more bishops should be appointed. But for the present we kept silent about this matter.

**Tenth chapter**, concerning marriages. That no one may have any marriage except a lawful one. No one shall commit incest; no one shall leave his own spouse except, as the holy Gospel teaches, on account of fornication. If anyone expels his own spouse, lawfully joined to him in marriage, then, if he wishes rightly to be a Christian, he shall not be joined to another, but shall remain as he is or be reconciled to his own spouse.

“After these chapters had thus been discussed and defined jointly, so that no scandal of contention might thereafter arise among any of us, or so that other things might be circulated in place of these, it pleased us that each of us should confirm whatever had been defined by the subscription of his own hand. I dictated this sentence of our definition to be written by the notary Titillo [Al., by the title]. It was enacted in the month and indiction written above [Al., written above].

“Therefore, whoever in any way attempts to act against this decision, confirmed according to the decrees of the canons by our common agreement and the subscription of our hands, and to violate it [Al., whoever attempted], shall know that he is separated from every priestly office and from our fellowship. May divine grace preserve us unharmed as we live in the unity of his holy Church.”

This synod was held in the year 673 from the Lord’s Incarnation. In that year Ecgberct, king of Kent, had died in July, and his brother Hlothere succeeded him in the kingdom, which he held for eleven years and seven months. [Note: [Col. 0183C] “Bisi.” He succeeded Boniface in 670; after the celebration of the council, in 673, Aecca was given him as coadjutor at Domnoc, and Beaduini at Helmham.]

Bisi, bishop of the East Angles, who is said to have been present at the aforementioned synod, was the successor of Boniface, whom we mentioned above, a man of great holiness and religious devotion. For after Boniface had died after seventeen years in his episcopate, Bisi himself was made bishop in his place by Theodore’s appointment. While Bisi was still alive, but prevented by a very serious illness from administering the episcopate, two bishops, Aecca and Baduvini, were chosen and consecrated in his place; from that time to the present, that province has customarily had two bishops.

## CHAPTER VI. How, after Uynfrid had been deposed, Saexuulf received his episcopate, and how Earconuald was appointed bishop of the East Saxons [Note: [Col. 0183C] Earconuald is omitted in Ed. C. I., incorrectly.]

[Col. 0183C]

Not long after these events had passed [674], Archbishop Theodore, offended by Uynfrid, bishop of the Mercians, because of a certain disobedience [Note: [Col. 0183C] “A certain disobedience.” Bede does not say what Uynfrid’s disobedience was. But if one considers the events and councils of that period, one will find that it happened for no other reason than that he refused to allow his see to be divided among several bishops. Although Theodore remained silent for the present in the council concerning the increase in the number of episcopates, both the ninth chapter proposed about it and the needs of the Church sufficiently show that he had fixed this intention in his mind. Since Uynfrid resisted, he could scarcely escape the archbishop’s censure, except by disturbing him in the see that he alone wished to occupy to the common detriment. According to Florence, this happened in 675], deposed him from the episcopate after he had held it for not many years. In his place he appointed as bishop Sexuulf, who was the founder [Note: [Col. 0183D] “Builder.” That is, through the generosity of the brothers Peada, Uulfheri, and Aedilthered, kings of Mercia, and of their sisters Kyneburga and Kynesuitha. Sexuulf was bishop of the Mercians from 675 to 691; before that he had been abbot of the monastery of Medhamsted from 664, the year in which, according to Uulfheri’s charter, it was founded.] and abbot of the monastery called [Note: [Col. 0183D] Medeshamstedi. The name is commonly derived from a deep whirlpool in the middle of the River Nene, which has now disappeared; but in reality it comes from the green meadows surrounding the river there, from which it means “dwelling-place in the meadows.” Because of the monastery dedicated to Saint Peter and endowed with papal privileges, it was called Saint Peter’s borough, and an episcopal see was established there by a most salutary council. After the Danish burnings, and the fury of the rebels, the church worthy of a bishop still remains as a notable monument of antiquity. In the windows of the monastic cloister was painted the legend of the martyrdom of Uulfhad and Rufin, sons of King Uulfheri, killed by their own father, who, moved by repentance for this crime, founded the monastery. Dugdale gives a fuller account in *Monasticon Anglicanum* II, p. 119. But Bede says nothing of this.] Medeshamstedi, in the region of the Gyrvii.

After his deposition, Uinfrid returned to his monastery called Ad Baruae, and there ended his life in an excellent manner of living.

At that time Theodore also appointed Earconuald bishop in the city of London for the East Saxons, over whom Sebbi and Sigheri ruled at that time, as we mentioned above. The life and conduct of this man, both during his episcopate and before it, are said to have been most holy, as even now the signs of heavenly powers provide evidence. For to this day his horse-litter, in which he used to be carried when ill, has been preserved by his disciples, and does not cease to heal many feverish people and others exhausted by any kind of illness. Not only are the sick cured who are placed beneath or laid upon this litter, but splinters cut from it and brought to the sick commonly bring them swift healing.

Before he became bishop, he had built two distinguished monasteries, one for himself and the other for his sister Aedilberga, and had excellently established both under regular discipline. For himself he built one in the region of Surrey, beside the River Thames, at a place called [Note: [Col. 0184C] Cerotaesei, now Chertsey. It is situated at the confluence of streams with the Thames and has an insular position, though it is not an island. Earconuald, with the assistance of Frithuold, who was a sub-king under Uulfheri, filled this monastery with wealth and monks. Its religious life flourished until the Danes, as elsewhere, destroyed the place, burning the church together with the monks [Col. 0184D] and abbot. King Eadgar, however, rebuilt it, searching everywhere for ancient charters by whose testimony he might restore to the place estates that certain nobles had seized, either by force or by appeal to the authority of antiquity. William of Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum* II, p. 134.] Cerotaesei, that is, “Ceroti’s island.”

For his sister he built one in the province of the East Saxons, at a place called [Note: [Col. 0184D] In Berecingum, now Barking, situated eight miles from London. There Earconuald’s sister Aedilberga had as companions in holiness and authority Hildelid, who succeeded her soon afterward and to whom the book of the blessed Aldhelm *On Virginity* was sent; see below, chapter 10; and Uulfilda, who lived a few years before the time of King Eadgar. Through their prayers that place, never entirely destroyed, even in the time of the Normans, was raised—as were many other places—to the highest rank in the number of its nuns and the beauty of its buildings. The same William of Malmesbury, in the same place. This Aedilberga was distinct from the queen of the West Saxons, wife of Ine, who later presided over the monastery of Barking after Hildelid and was numbered among the saints.] In Berecingum. There she herself could become the mother and nurse of women devoted to God.

After undertaking the governance of the monastery, she showed herself in every respect worthy of her bishop-brother, both by living rightly herself and by giving her subjects regular and devout counsel, as heavenly miracles also demonstrated.

## CHAPTER VII. How a heavenly light showed where the bodies of the holy women should be placed in the monastery of Barking

[676]

In this monastery many signs of miraculous power were performed. Many who knew of them have written them down for the remembrance and edification of those who came afterward; among these we too have decided to insert some into our ecclesiastical History.

When the storm of the aforesaid plague, ravaging everything far and wide, had also invaded that part of this monastery in which the men lived, and people were daily being carried off everywhere to the Lord, the anxious mother of the community began to ask more frequently in the assembly of the sisters where in the monastery they would wish their bodies to be placed and a cemetery made, if they too should be taken from the world by the same destruction as the others, whenever that plague reached the part of the monastery in which the company of God’s servants was separated from the men’s dwelling.

Although she repeatedly asked, she received no definite answer from the sisters. Yet she herself, together with them all, received a most certain answer from heavenly providence [Al., promise]. For one night, after the psalmody of the morning praises had been completed, the servants of Christ came out of the oratory and were singing their customary praises to the Lord at the graves of the brothers who had gone before them from this light. Suddenly, behold, a light sent from heaven, like a great linen cloth, came over them. It struck them with such astonishment that, trembling, they even interrupted the song they were singing.

The brilliance of the light that had been sent forth—beside which the noonday sun might appear dark—was soon lifted from that place and withdrew toward the southern part of the monastery, that is, toward the west of the oratory. After remaining there for some time and covering those places, it withdrew to the heights of heaven before the eyes of all. Thus no one could doubt that the very light which would lead or receive the souls of Christ’s servants in heaven was also showing the place for their bodies, where they would rest and await the day of resurrection.

The ray of light was so great that one of the older brothers, who at that very hour had been in their oratory with another younger brother, reported in the morning that the rays of light entering through the cracks of the doors or windows seemed to surpass every brilliance of daylight [Al., “which in the morning, when they entered…”].

## CHAPTER VIII. How, in the same monastery, a little boy dying called out to the virgin who was to follow him, and how another woman, about to leave the body, already saw a fragment of the future light

[676]

In the same monastery there was a boy of about three years, no more, named Aesica. Because of his still childish age, he was accustomed to be nourished and cared for in the cell of the virgins dedicated to God. When he was struck by the aforementioned plague and reached his final moments, he called three times [Al., three times in all] for one of the virgins consecrated to Christ, addressing her by her own name as though she were present: “Eadgyd, Eadgyd, Eadgyd.” Thus he ended his temporal life and entered the eternal one.

The virgin whom he called while dying was soon struck by the same illness where she was, and on the very day on which she had been called [Al., repeatedly called] she was taken from this light and followed into the heavenly kingdom the one who had called her.

Likewise, one of these servants of God, having been struck by the aforementioned disease and brought to the point of death, suddenly began around midnight to call out to those who were ministering to her, asking them to extinguish the lamp that had been lit there. When she repeated this request again and again, and no one obeyed her, she finally added:

“I know that you think I am speaking in madness; but now learn that this is not so. For I tell you truly that I see this house filled with such a great light that your lamp appears to me altogether dark.”

When no one yet replied or gave assent to such words, she said again:

“Then light that lamp for as long as you wish; nevertheless, know that it is not mine. For my light [Al., ‘my light: for’] will come to me when dawn begins.”

She began to relate that a certain man of God [Al., om. “of God”], who had died that same year, had appeared to her and said that, when dawn came, she would depart into everlasting light. The truth of this vision was soon proved by the girl’s death around sunrise.

## CHAPTER IX. What heavenly signs were shown when the mother of that community herself departed from the world

[Col. 0186C]

When Aedilburga, the pious mother of the community devoted to God, was herself about to be taken from the world, a wondrous vision appeared to one of the sisters named Torctgyd. She had lived in the same monastery for many years and had always striven to serve God in all humility and sincerity. She also sought to assist that mother in maintaining regular discipline by teaching and correcting the younger women.

So that her virtue might be perfected, in accordance with the Apostle, through weakness, she was suddenly struck by a very serious bodily illness and was greatly afflicted for nine years by the pious providence of our Redeemer. This happened so that, if anything defiling had remained in her among her virtues through ignorance or carelessness, the furnace of prolonged suffering might purify it all.

One night, then, as twilight was beginning, she left the room in which she lived and clearly saw what appeared to be a human body, brighter than the sun, wrapped in a shroud and carried upward. It had evidently been lifted from the house in which the sisters were accustomed to rest. As she looked more carefully to see what was drawing upward the bodily form she was contemplating, she saw that it was being lifted toward heaven by what seemed to be ropes brighter than gold. Once it had been introduced through the opened heavens, it could no longer be seen by her.

As she reflected on the vision, no doubt remained that someone from that community would soon die, whose soul, through the good works he or she had done, would be lifted to heaven as if by golden ropes. And so it truly happened. For after not many days had passed, the mother of that community, beloved by God, was led out from the prison of the flesh. Her life is known to have been such that no one who had known her ought to doubt that, as she departed this life, the entrance to the heavenly homeland was opened to her.

In the same monastery there was also a certain sanctimonious woman, noble in the dignity of this world and nobler in her love of the world to come. For many years she had been so deprived of the use of her entire body that she could not move even one limb herself. When she learned that the body of the venerable abbess had been carried into the church and was awaiting burial, she asked to be brought there and to be leaned against it in the posture of one praying.

While this was being done, she addressed her as though she were alive and asked her to obtain from the mercy of the compassionate Creator that she might be freed from such great and prolonged torments. She was heard without much delay. For twelve days later she too was led out from the flesh and exchanged temporal afflictions [Al., the temporal affliction] for an eternal reward.

But when the aforementioned servant of Christ, Torctgyd, remained in this life for three more years after the death of her mistress, she was so consumed by the illness we have described that she scarcely clung to her bones. At last, when the time of her release was already near, she lost not only the movement of her other limbs but also that of her tongue.

When this had continued for three days and as many nights, she was suddenly refreshed by a spiritual vision, opened her mouth and eyes, and, looking toward heaven, began to speak to the vision she was contemplating:

“Your coming is very welcome to me, and you have come well.”

After saying this, she was silent for a little while, as though waiting for the reply of the one whom she saw and to whom she was speaking. Then, as if mildly indignant, she added:

“I cannot at all bear this gladly.”

Again she was silent briefly, and then said a third time:

“If it absolutely cannot happen today, I beg that the interval not be long.”

She spoke; and, as before, after remaining silent for a little while, she concluded:

“If it has been decided in every respect that it must be so, and this decision may not be changed, I beg that no more than this coming night alone intervene.”

When she had said these things, the people sitting around her asked with whom she was speaking. She replied:

“With my dearest mother Aedilberge.”

From this they understood that Aedilburga herself had come to announce that the time of her departure was near. And just as Torctgyd had asked, after one day and night had passed, she was released from the bonds both of the flesh and of her illness and entered the joys of eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER X. How a blind woman received light while praying at the cemetery of the same monastery
