Aedilburga was succeeded in the office of abbess by a servant of God named Hildilid. For many years, that is, until extreme old age, she governed the same monastery most diligently, both in observing regular discipline and in providing for the things required for common use.

Since the place where the monastery had been built was too small, she decided that the bones of the servants of Christ, both male and female, who had been buried there should be taken up and all transferred to the church of the blessed Mother of God, so that they might be laid together in one place. Whoever reads the book from which we have extracted these accounts will find there how often the brilliance of heavenly light, how great a fragrance of wondrous odor, and what other signs appeared there.

I consider that the miracle of healing which the same little book reports as having occurred at the cemetery of that congregation dedicated to God must by no means be passed over. For there was a certain earl nearby whose wife, when sudden darkness fell upon her eyes, was afflicted by the same trouble, which increased day by day, until she could not see even the smallest particle of any light. While she remained shut up for some time in this night of blindness, it suddenly occurred to her that, if she were taken to the monastery [Al. adds: “were”] of the consecrated virgins and asked for light at the relics of the saints, she might recover the light she had lost. She did not delay, but immediately carried out what she had conceived in her mind. Taken by her maidservants to the monastery, since it was nearby, she declared that she had complete faith in her healing and was brought into [Al.: “to”] the cemetery. When she had prayed there for a long while on bended knees, she was heard without delay. For, rising from prayer, before she left the place she received the grace of the light she had requested; and she who had been led there by the hands of her servants returned home joyfully by the free movement of her own feet—as though she had lost temporal light for this one purpose alone, so that by her healing she might demonstrate how great is the light possessed by Christ’s saints in heaven and what grace of power they enjoy.

## CHAPTER XI. How Sebbi, king of that province, ended his life in monastic observance

At that time [A.D. 694], as the same little book also records, the kingdom of the East Saxons was ruled by a man greatly devoted to God, named Sebbi, whom we mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Above. See III.30.]

For he was exceedingly devoted to religious deeds, frequent prayers, and the pious fruits of almsgiving, preferring a private and monastic life to all the wealth and honors of the kingdom. He would have entered upon that life long before, had not his wife’s stubborn will refused a divorce, even though he would then have abandoned the kingdom. Hence it was thought by many, and often said, that it would be more fitting for a man of such character to be ordained a bishop than a king.

When he had spent thirty years in the kingdom as a soldier of the heavenly kingdom, he was seized by a very serious bodily illness, from which he also died. He urged his wife that, even then, they should devote themselves together to divine service, since they could no longer together embrace the world—or rather serve the world. Having obtained this from her only with difficulty, he went to the bishop of the city of London, named Ualdheri.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Ualdheri. The year of Earconwald’s death is uncertain, but it is clear that he died before King Sebbi’s retirement, that is, during the time of Ualdheri, who appears to have succeeded him in A.D. 694, although Savile, in his *Fasti*, assigns the date to A.D. 697, even though he had fixed Sebbi’s retirement at A.D. 694—something impossible. Earconwald’s body was buried in his own church of St. Paul, despite the futile resistance of the communities of Barking and Chertsey; his relics were raised into a shrine and solemnly placed for veneration in A.D. 1148. M. West. Earconwald’s day of death is recorded in the Martyrology on 30 April, and his translation on 14 November.]

Ualdheri, who had succeeded Erconwald. Through his blessing Sebbi received the religious habit which he had long desired [Al.: “had long desired previously”]. He also brought him a considerable sum of money to distribute to the poor, reserving nothing whatever for himself, but desiring rather to remain poor in spirit for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

When, as the aforementioned illness grew worse, he perceived that the day of his death was approaching, this man of royal spirit began to fear that, when he came to die under the pressure of such pain, he might utter something unworthy of his person or make some undignified movement with his limbs. Therefore he summoned to himself the aforesaid bishop of the city of London, where he was then staying, and asked that, when he died, no one more than the bishop and two of his attendants should be present.

[Col. 0189B]

When the bishop gladly promised that he would do this, not long afterward the man of God, as he had surrendered his limbs to sleep, saw a consoling vision which removed all the anxiety caused by this concern and also showed him on what day he would end this life. For, as he later reported, he saw three men come to him dressed in splendid garments. One of them sat before his bed, while the others who had come with him stood beside him; and when they asked about his condition, since they had come to visit him in his sickness, the seated man said that his soul would depart from his body both without any pain and with great splendor of light. He also indicated that he would die on the third day thereafter.

Both things were fulfilled just as he had learned them in the vision. For on the third day afterward, when the ninth hour had been completed, he suddenly gave up his spirit, as though gently falling asleep, without any sensation of pain.

For the burial of his body they had prepared a stone sarcophagus. But when they began to place the body in it, they found that the body was a palm’s breadth longer than the sarcophagus. Accordingly, sorrowfully, they added as much stone as they could to the length of the sarcophagus, approximately the measure of two fingers. Yet even then the sarcophagus could not contain the body. Since this created difficulty for the burial, they considered either looking for another coffin or, if they could, shortening the body by bending it at the knees until it could fit into the coffin.

But a wondrous event, accomplished only from heaven, prevented any of these things from having to be done. For suddenly, with the bishop present, together with the king’s son and monk Sighard—who afterward ruled with his brother Suefred—and a considerable crowd of people, that sarcophagus was found to be of suitable length for the body, so much so that even a pillow could be placed at the head; at the feet, however, the sarcophagus exceeded the body by the measure of four fingers.

He was buried in the church of the blessed Doctor of the Gentiles, by whose teachings he had learned to hope for heavenly things.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Doctor of the Gentiles. It is said that King Sebbi’s tomb remained visible there until the great conflagration of the church in A.D. 1666.]

## CHAPTER XII. How Haeddi received the bishopric of the West Saxons in place of Leutherius, Cuichelm that of the Church of Rochester in place of Putta, and Gefmund in Cuichelm’s place; and who were then the bishops of the Northumbrians

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Fourth. For the chronology of the bishops of the West Saxons down to Leutherius in A.D. 670, see III.7. He was succeeded by this Haeddi in A.D. 676.]

The fourth bishop of the West Saxons was Leutherius. The first was Birinus, the second Agilberct, and the third Uini. When Coinvalch died—in whose reign Leutherius had become bishop—the sub-kings received the kingdom of the people and held it divided among themselves for approximately ten years.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Sub-kings. After Coinvalch died without issue around A.D. 674, his wife Sexburga succeeded to the administration of the province for one year and did not relinquish power, as William of Malmesbury says, until death deprived her of it. Matthew of Westminster, however, writes that she was expelled from the kingdom when the nobles of the realm became indignant and refused to serve under a woman. The division of the kingdom among sub-kings supports this view. It should nevertheless be noted that, at the time when they are said to have ruled, the names of the kings Aescuini and Kentuini fill the annals down to Caedualla, while none of the sub-kings is mentioned. There was also another West Saxon queen: the wife of King Earconberct; see III.8 and IV.19.]

While they were ruling, Leutherius died, and Haeddi succeeded him in the episcopate. He was consecrated by Theodore in the city of London. During his episcopate, after the sub-kings had been defeated and removed, Caedualla assumed the government. After holding it for two years, he was finally moved by love of the heavenly kingdom to abandon it, while the same prelate still governed the Church; and he went to Rome, where he ended his life, as will be related more fully below.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 676,

[Note: [Col. 0190D] “Sixth.” Here Baronius was misled by the Cologne edition of Bede’s works, which reads “seventh” instead of “sixth,” contrary to the manuscripts and better editions. Writers attribute the cause of the invasion to an insolent reply made by King Hlotharius of Kent, but what the subject of that reply was is not recorded.]

when Aedilred, king of the Mercians, ravaged Kent with a hostile army which he had brought there and desecrated churches and monasteries without regard for piety [Al.: “love”] or fear of God, he also destroyed in the common disaster the city of Rochester, in which Putta was bishop, although he was absent at that time. When Putta learned that his church had been plundered and stripped of all its possessions, he went to Sexuulf, bishop of the Mercians, and, having received from him possession of a certain church and a small estate, ended his life there in peace. He did nothing at all to restore his bishopric, because, as we said above, he was more industrious in ecclesiastical than in worldly matters. He served God in that church alone and, wherever he was asked, went to teach the Church’s songs [Al.: “ecclesiastical” songs].

[Col. 0191A]

In his place Theodore consecrated Cuichelm bishop in the city of Rochester. But when Cuichelm, after not much time, withdrew from the episcopate because of lack of means and departed to other places, Theodore substituted Gebmund as bishop in his place.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 678,

[Note: [Col. 0191D] “Eighth.” The ancient manner of writing led less practiced readers into error, so that they read “seventh” and “ninth” instead of “eighth.”]

which was the eighth year of King Ecgfrid’s reign, a star called a comet appeared in August. It remained for three months and rose in the morning hours, displaying before it a tall column resembling a flame of radiance.

In that same year, when dissension arose between King Ecgfrid and the most reverend Bishop Uilfrid, that bishop was driven from the seat of his episcopate. Two bishops were appointed in his place to govern the people of the Northumbrians: Bosa, who governed Deira, and Eata, who governed the province of Bernicia. The latter held the episcopal see in the city of York, the former in the Church of Hagustald or of Lindisfarne. Both had been raised from the company of monks to the rank of bishop.

Along with them, Eadhaed was ordained bishop in the province of Lindsey, which King Ecgfrid had recently obtained after defeating and putting Uulfhere to flight. This province received him as its first proper bishop; its second was Aediluini, its third Eadgar, and its fourth Cyniberct, whom it has at present.

Before Eadhaed, the province had Sexuulf as bishop. He was also simultaneously bishop of the Mercians and of the Middle Angles. Thus, after being expelled from Lindsey, he remained in charge of those provinces.

Eadhaed, Bosa, and Eata were ordained at York by Archbishop Theodore. Three years after Uilfrid’s departure, Theodore also added two bishops to their number: Tunberct to the Church of Hagustald, with Eata remaining at Lindisfarne, and Trumvini to the province of the Picts, which at that time was subject to the rule of the Angles.

[Col. 0191C]

When Eadhaed returned from Lindsey because Aedilred had recovered the province, Theodore placed him in charge of the Church of Ripon.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Eadhaed. Together with the other bishops properly called bishops of Lindsey, he held his see at Sidnacester, near Gainsborough, through nine successions down to Brihtred. Concerning Eadhaed, see above, III.28.]

## CHAPTER XIII. How Bishop Uilfrid converted the province of the South Saxons to Christ

Uilfrid was driven from his bishopric. After wandering for a long time through many places, he went to Rome and returned to Britain.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] “And if on account of…” In the edition: “Yet, when he departed, because of the bitter oppression of the enemy, it was unable to have its own bishop.”]

Although, because of the hostility of the aforementioned king,

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Hostility. Its cause is attributed to prejudices conceived against Uilfrid by Ermenhurga. When Aedilthryde, the first wife of King Ecgfrid, who had supported Uilfrid, withdrew into a monastery, Ermenburga, who succeeded her in the king’s bed, turned the great favor shown him into hatred and hostility. The writers of his history intend this account, though whether rightly, see Appendix, no. 18.]

he could not be received in his homeland or in his own diocese, he nevertheless could not be restrained from the ministry of evangelization. For he went to the province of the South Saxons, which extends south and west from the Cantuwari as far as the West Saxons. It contained land of seven thousand households and, even at that time, was devoted to pagan worship. To this people he ministered the word of faith and the bath of salvation [A.D. 678].

The king of that people was Aedilualch, who had been baptized not long before in the province of the Mercians, in the presence and at the prompting of King Uulfehre. When he emerged from the font, Uulfehre received him as a son; as a sign of this adoption he gave him two provinces: the Isle of Wight and the province of the Meonware among the people of the West Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Meonware. The memory of this province remains in the county of Hampshire, in the hundreds of Meansborough, East Meon, West Meon, and Mansbridge.]

Accordingly, with the king’s permission—or rather, to the king’s great joy—the bishop washed the first leaders and soldiers of the province in the sacred font. The priests Eappa, Padda, Burghelm, and Oiddi [Al.: Burghelin, Oiddia] baptized the rest of the people, either at that time or afterward.

The queen, named Eabae [Al.: Eahae], had been baptized in her own province, that is, the province of the Hwiccas. She was the daughter of Eanfrid, the brother of Eanheri; both of them had been Christians together with their people. But the whole province of the South Saxons was ignorant of the divine name and of the faith.

There was also there a certain monk of the Scottish nation, named Dicul, who possessed a very small monastery [Al.: “monastery”] in a place called Bosanhamm,

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Bosenham and Selaeseu. From these monasteries, which still retain their site and name, arose Cissancaestir, today Chichester, when episcopal sees were transferred from obscure and less convenient places to cities. The church, founded shortly afterward by Bishop Radulph and rebuilt by the same man after a sudden conflagration with the help and generosity of King Henry I, presents a beautiful appearance to those who see it. Deriving the name of the place from Cissa, son of Aella, who first established the Saxon kingdom there, fits the rules of etymology reasonably well. But if it is true that antiquarians maintain that the Britons had their Caersei there, Cissa will have to be abandoned, and the origin of Chichester will appear more ancient.]

surrounded by woods and sea. Five or six brothers served the Lord there in humble and poor circumstances. None of the people of the province, however, cared either to imitate their life or to listen to their preaching.

As Bishop Uilfrid evangelized the people, he rescued them not only from the perpetual misery of damnation but also from the unspeakable disaster of temporal death. For during the three years before his arrival in the province, no rain had fallen in those regions. Consequently, an exceedingly severe famine attacked the people and struck them down in an impious death.

Indeed, it is said that as many as forty or fifty people at a time, weakened by hunger, would proceed to some precipice or seashore and, joining hands miserably, would all fall together, either to perish in the collapse or to be swallowed by the waves.

But on the very day on which that people received the baptism of faith, clear and abundant rain descended. The earth blossomed again, and a joyful and fruitful year returned with green fields. Thus, when their ancient superstition had been cast aside and idolatry had been blown away, everyone’s heart and everyone’s flesh rejoiced in the living God, understanding that he who is the true God had enriched them both with inward goods and with outward gifts through heavenly grace.

When the bishop came into the province and saw the great punishment of famine there, he taught them to seek their livelihood by fishing. For their sea and rivers abounded in fish, but the people possessed no skill in fishing except for eels.

[Col. 0193B]

So they gathered eel nets from everywhere, and the bishop’s men cast them into the sea. With divine grace assisting them, they soon caught three hundred fish of various kinds. Dividing them into three portions, they gave one hundred to the poor, one hundred to those from whom they had received the nets, and kept one hundred for their own use.

By this kindness the bishop turned everyone’s heart greatly toward his love, and they began more willingly to hope for heavenly things when he preached, since through his ministry they had received temporal goods.

At that time King Aedilualch gave the most reverend Bishop Uilfrid land of eighty-seven households, where he could receive his men who were wandering in exile. Its name was Selaeseu [Al.: Heleseu], which is called in Latin “Seal Island.” For that place is surrounded on all sides by the sea except on the west, where it has an entrance about the width of a sling’s cast. Such a place is called by the Latins a peninsula and by the Greeks a *chersonesos*.

When Bishop Uilfrid received this place, he founded a monastery there and established it in regular life, chiefly with the brothers whom he had brought with him. His successors are known to have held it down to the present day.

For five years—that is, until the death of King Ecgfrid—he himself was held in deserved honor by everyone in those regions and exercised the office of bishop both in word and in deed. Since the king had given him, together with possession of the aforesaid place, all the properties that were there, including fields and people, he washed all who were instructed in the faith of Christ in the water of baptism. Among them were two hundred and fifty male and female slaves.

[Col. 0193D]

By baptizing them all, he not only saved them from demonic slavery [Al. adds: “but”], but also, by granting them freedom, released them from the yoke of human servitude.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] CHAPTER XIV. There is great disagreement among the manuscripts in the numbering of the chapters. Neither this title nor the following one appears in the table of chapters of the Mori Codex, although Chapter 14 is found in the body of that codex. The same should be noted concerning Cottonian Codex II. In Cottonian Codex I, however, this Chapter 14 concerning Oswald is missing, and a very ancient hand notes in the margin: “Here a folio is missing.” Consequently, later manuscripts omit either the summaries of Chapters 14 and 15 or Chapter 14 itself, depending on which old codex they were copied from. But since the summaries and arrangement of the chapters agree well with the following text in the common manuscripts, and since one of the old manuscripts acknowledges that a folio is missing, while changing the received order creates some confusion for readers, I have followed the common arrangement despite the disagreement of the ancient codices.]

## CHAPTER XIV. How, through the intercession of King Oswald, the deadly pestilence was removed

In that monastery, therefore, several gifts of heavenly grace are said to have been specially [Al.: spiritually] manifested, since Christ had recently begun to reign there after the tyranny of the devil had been expelled. Of these, we have thought it worthwhile to commit one to memory. The most reverend [Al.: “most reverend and most religious”] Bishop Acca often related it to me and used to affirm that he had heard it from the most faithful brothers of that monastery.

At almost the same time when that province had received the name of Christ, a savage pestilence was attacking many provinces of Britain. When, by the will of divine providence, it reached the monastery just mentioned, which was then governed by a most religious priest of Christ named Eappa, many people were carried away indiscriminately from this life—both some of those who had come with that bishop and some of those who had recently been called to the faith from the same province of the Saxons.

The brothers therefore decided to undertake a three-day fast and earnestly [Al.: continually] beseech God’s mercy to deem it worthy to grant them compassion, either freeing those endangered by this disease from present death or preserving those carried away from the world from eternal condemnation of the soul.

At that time there was in the same monastery a certain little boy [Al.: “small boy”] of the Saxon nation, recently called to the faith. Struck by the same illness, he had lain for a considerable time on his bed. When the second day of the aforementioned fasting and prayers was being observed, it happened that, at about the second hour of the day, the boy was found alone in the place where he lay sick.

[Col. 0194C]

Then, by divine arrangement [Al.: dispensation], the most blessed leaders of the apostles graciously appeared to him. The boy was of an exceedingly simple and gentle disposition and preserved with sincere devotion the sacraments of the faith which he had received.

Greeting him with the most devout words, the apostles said:

“Do not fear, son, the death about which you are anxious. For today we are going to lead you to the heavenly kingdom. But first you must wait until Mass has been celebrated, and, after receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, you will then be lifted from both sickness and death to the eternal joys in heaven.

“Call the priest Eappa to you and tell him that the Lord has heard your prayers and mercifully looked upon your devotion and fasting. No one from this monastery, or from the little estates adjoining it, is going to die any longer from this plague. Rather, all those of your people who are suffering from this illness anywhere will rise from their sickness and recover their former health—except for you alone, who today are to be freed from death and led into heaven to behold the Lord Christ, whom you have faithfully served.

“This has been granted to you by divine mercy through the intercession of the religious and beloved king Oswald, who once ruled the people of the Northumbrians sublimely, both by the authority of temporal kingship and by the devotion of Christian piety that leads to the everlasting kingdom. For on this very day that king, though bodily slain by unbelievers in battle, was immediately taken up into heaven to the everlasting joys of souls and joined to the ranks of the elect.

“Let them search their books in which the deposition of the dead is recorded, and they will find that he was taken from the world on this day, as we have said. Let them therefore celebrate Masses in all the oratories of this monastery, both in thanksgiving for the hearing of their prayer and also in memory of the aforementioned King Oswald, who once ruled their people. For he used to pray humbly to the Lord for them as for the strangers of his own people.

“And when all the brothers have assembled at the church, let them all receive communion in the heavenly sacrifices; then, when the fast has been ended, let them also restore their bodies with food.”

[Col. 0195B]

After the boy had summoned the priest to himself and related all these words, the priest anxiously asked him what the men who had appeared to him were like in clothing and appearance.

He replied:

“They were altogether magnificent in clothing and appearance, exceedingly joyful and beautiful. I had never before seen such men, nor did I believe that any human beings could possess such beauty and loveliness. One was tonsured like a cleric; the other had a long beard. They said that one of them was called Peter and the other Paul, and that they themselves were ministers of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, sent by him from heaven for the protection of our monastery.”

The priest therefore believed the boy’s words. He immediately went out, consulted his annal, and found that King Oswald had been killed on that very day. He summoned the brothers and ordered that a meal be prepared, Masses celebrated, and that everyone receive communion according to custom. At the same time he ordered that a portion of the sacrifice of the Lord’s oblation be carried from the same offering to the sick boy.

When these things had been done, the boy died not long afterward, on that very day, and by his death proved that the words he had heard from Christ’s apostles were true. He also testified through his words that no one except himself was carried from that monastery out of the world at that time.

[Col. 0196A]

Through this vision, many who were able to hear of it were wonderfully inflamed both to implore divine mercy in adversity and to undertake the saving remedies of fasting. From that time, not only in that monastery but also in many other places, the birthday of that king and soldier of Christ began to be honored annually by the celebration of Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0195C] “From that time.” Learned men, observing that this chapter is absent from many ancient manuscripts and that its purpose seems so clearly directed toward the cult of Saint Oswald, have judged that it was appended to Bede. But since the chapter itself is found in the Mori and Cottonian II codices, and since the other Cottonian manuscript declares that it is missing a folio, adding that narratives of this kind are not unlike Bede’s, I did not consider it worthwhile to exercise excessively severe criticism here. It is certain that much popular devotion was directed toward Saint Oswald, as the solemn hymns composed for his feasts still testify. See Appendix, no. 19.]

[Note: [Col. 0195D] CHAPTER XV. Concerning the position of this chapter in the ancient manuscripts, see the note to the preceding chapter.]

## CHAPTER XV. How King Caedualla, after killing Aedilualch, king of the Geuissi, crushed that province with savage slaughter and devastation

Meanwhile Caedualla, a most vigorous young man of the royal family of the Geuissi,

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Of royal descent. This Caedualla was the son of Cynberct, grandson of Ceadda, great-grandson of Cutha or Cuthuin, and great-great-grandson of the great Ceaulin. For Cuthuin had three sons: Ceadda, the grandfather of Caedualla; Cutha, the great-grandfather of Ina; and Cynibald, the grandfather of Oswald the prince.]

while he was an exile from his homeland, invaded the province with an army, killed King Aedilualch, and crushed the province with savage slaughter and devastation [A.D. 685]. But he was soon expelled by the king’s commanders, Bercthuno and Andhuno,

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Commanders. They returned with a veteran army to Kent.]

who thereafter held the kingdom of the province. The former of these was later killed by Caedualla himself, when Caedualla was king of the Geuissi, and the province was reduced to a harsher servitude [A.D. 686].

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Andhuno. Florence calls him Aedilhun.]

Ini, who ruled after Caedualla, also subjected that province to a similar affliction for many years. Consequently, throughout that period it could not have its own bishop. When Uilfrid, its first bishop, was recalled home, the people of the province were subject to the bishop of the Geuissi—that is, of the West Saxons—who was in the city of Venta.

[Note: [Col. 0196C] In Venta. Haedda was bishop there at that time. Concerning him Theodore says in his *Decrees*: “We do not wish—indeed, it is not fitting for us—that, while our most holy brother Haedda survives, who so distinguished the Church of Venta by transferring, on the authority of the supreme pontiff Agatho, the body of the blessed Birinus, apostle of the West Saxons, from the town of Dorchester, where it had been buried, together with the see, into the city of Venta, and through whose labor and diligence, by apostolic mandate, the episcopal see was then first established in that city, we should injure or diminish his diocese in any respect.” For more concerning Caedualla, see IV.12 and V.7. SMITH. “In Venta.” Thus the Treves manuscript, with the Anglo-Saxon edition, instead of what all the other printed editions have: “found in the city.” CHIFFLET.]

## CHAPTER XVI. How the Isle of Wight received Christian inhabitants, and how its two royal boys were killed immediately after receiving baptism

[Note: [Col. 0196D] In the table of chapters of the Mori Codex this is the title of Chapter 14, although in the codex itself the two preceding chapters are placed under number 14, and this chapter concerning Wight is merely a continuation of number 14. The same should be noted concerning Cottonian Codex II. See above, the note to Chapter 14.]

After Caedualla had obtained the kingdom of the Geuissi [A.D. 686], he also seized the Isle of Wight, which until then [Al.: “up to that time”] had been wholly devoted to idolatry. He attempted to exterminate all the natives by tragic [Al.: “savage”] slaughter and to replace them with people from his own province. Although he had not yet, as they say [Al.: “as it is said”], been reborn in Christ, he bound himself by a vow that, if he captured the island, he would give a quarter of it, together with a quarter of the spoils, to the Lord.

He fulfilled this vow by offering that quarter to Bishop Uilfrid, who happened at that time to have arrived from his own people. According to the estimation of the Angles, the island contains land of twelve hundred households. The bishop therefore received possession of land of three hundred households.

The bishop entrusted the portion he had received to one of his clerics, named Bernuini, who was his sister’s son. He gave him a priest named Hiddila, who was to minister the word and the bath of life to all who wished to be saved.

I do not think that it should be silently passed over that, as the first fruits of those who were saved by believing from that island, two royal boys—the brothers of Aruald, king of the island—were crowned by the special grace of God.

When the enemies of the island were approaching, the boys fled from the island and were taken to the nearby province of the Jutes [Al.: “Vites”]. When they had been brought to a place called Ad Lapidem,

[Note: [Col. 0197D] “At the Stone.” Between Winchester and Southampton there is a village called Stoneham, which claims this place by its name.]

they believed that they could hide themselves from the victorious king, but they were betrayed and ordered to be killed.

When a certain abbot and priest named Cyniberct heard this—he had a monastery not far from there, in a place called Hreutford, that is, “Reed Ford”—

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Hreutford. Today Redbridge, where a bridge has been built at the site of the ford. In the Durham Calendar William, prior of Redeforda, is commemorated on 31 March.]

he came to the king, who was then secretly being treated in that region for wounds inflicted upon him while fighting on the Isle of Wight. Cyniberct asked him that, if it were necessary for the boys to be killed, they might first be instructed in the sacraments of the Christian faith.

The king consented, and Cyniberct instructed them in the word of truth, washed them in the saving [Al.: salutary] font, and assured them of their entrance into the eternal kingdom. Then, when the executioner was at hand, they gladly underwent temporal death, through which they had no doubt they would pass to the everlasting life of the soul.

In this manner, after all the provinces of Britain had received the faith of Christ, the Isle of Wight also received it. Yet, because of the misery of its perpetual subjection, no one there received the rank of episcopal ministry and see before Danihel, who is now bishop of the West Saxons [Al. adds: “and of the Geuissi”].

The island lies opposite the middle of the South Saxons and the Geuissi, separated from them by a sea three miles wide called Solvente.

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Solvente. Wormius, in his *Museum*, p. 4, observed remnants of this name in the chalk, or soapy earth, dug from the headlands of this strait, which the English usually call *erd*.]

In that sea, the twin tides of the Ocean which burst forth from the boundless northern Ocean around Britain meet each day and clash with one another beyond the mouth of the River Homelea,

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Homelea. Commonly Hamble.]

which enters the aforesaid sea through the lands of the Jutes belonging to the region of the Geuissi. When the conflict is ended, they flow back into the Ocean and return to the place from which they came.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the synod held at the field of Haethfelth [Al.: Hetfeld], under the presidency of Archbishop Theodore

At this time [A.D. 680], Theodore heard that the faith of the Church at Constantinople had been greatly disturbed by the heresy of Eutyches. Desiring the Churches of the Angles over which he presided to remain free from such contamination, he gathered an assembly of venerable priests and many learned men. He carefully inquired into the faith of each of them and found them all unanimous in their agreement in the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0197D] “Having heard.” While the sixth general synod was sitting at Constantinople against the heresy of Eutyches and the Monothelites, Pope Agatho held one at Rome to declare the faith of the Western Church. The metropolitans, having summoned the bishops of their respective provinces throughout Italy and Gaul, presented their votes to be sent to Constantinople. Theodore therefore performs here, on behalf of the English Church, what was done there. Uilfrid also, when he was at Rome in the case of his appeal before the synod, performed this on behalf of all the British Churches, from his own certain and direct knowledge. See V.20. Other causes have been assigned for this synod: the confirmation of the foundation of the monastery of Medeshamstede and the promulgation of the papal bull concerning it. Uilfrid was sent to Rome concerning these matters by Uulfhere, king of the Mercians, but Bede says nothing of them, nor does he declare anything there beyond the creeds of the faith. For the sequence of Uilfrid’s history, see also Appendix, no. 19.]

He took care to commit this agreement to writing in a synodal letter, for the instruction and remembrance of those who would come after, whose beginning is as follows:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, during the reigns of our most devout lords: Ecgfrid, king of the Northumbrians, in the tenth year of his reign, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September], in the eighth indiction; Aedilred, king of the Mercians, in the sixth year of his reign; Aldwulf [Al., Aduwulf], king of the East Angles [Al., Est Angles], in the seventeenth year of his reign; and Hlothere, king of the Kentish people, in the seventh year of his reign; with Theodore, by the grace of God archbishop of the island of Britain and of the city of Canterbury, presiding; together with the other venerable bishops of the island of Britain, the holy Gospels being placed before them, assembled in the place called by the Saxon name Hatfield [Al., Hetfeild], we jointly set forth the true and orthodox faith: as our Lord Jesus Christ [Al. omits: *Christ*], incarnate, delivered it to his disciples, who were present and saw and heard his words; as the holy Fathers’ creed delivered it; and as did all the holy and universal councils, and the entire chorus of approved teachers of the Catholic Church.

“Following these authorities piously and orthodoxly, we profess and believe in agreement with their divinely inspired teaching, and we confess according to the holy Fathers that the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is properly and truly consubstantial in unity, and unity in Trinity: that is, one God in three consubstantial subsistences or persons, [Col. 0198D] equal in glory and honor.”

After many further statements of this kind, pertaining to the confession of the true faith, this holy synod also added the following to its letter [Col. 0199A] [Al., added]:

> [Note: *We have received.* As a precaution of greater security, all the general councils against every heresy are received, as has been customary. Examples of such forms of confession made by bishops upon their arrival may be seen in the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, pp. 26–52.]

> “We have received [Al., we receive] the five holy and universal synods of the blessed and [Al. omits: *and*] God-pleasing Fathers: namely, that of the three hundred and eighteen who assembled at Nicaea against the most wicked Arius and his doctrines; that of the one hundred and fifty at Constantinople against the madness of Macedonius and Eudoxius and their doctrines; that of the two hundred at the first council at Ephesus against the most wicked Nestorius and his doctrines; that of the six hundred and thirty [Al., two hundred and thirty] at Chalcedon against Eutyches [Al., Eutychetes] and Nestorius and their doctrines; and again that of those assembled at Constantinople in the fifth council, in the time of Justinian the Younger, against Theodore [Al., Theodoret], and the letters of Theodoret and Ibas, and their doctrines [Col. 0199B] against Cyril.”

A little later:

> “And the synod held in the city of Rome in the time of [Note: *Martin.* This synod is added because it was expressly held against those who preached one operation and one will in Christ. See the following chapter.] Martin, the most blessed pope, in the eighth indiction, when the most devout Constantine was reigning in the ninth year: we have received and glorify our Lord Jesus, as [Al. adds: *also*] these men glorified him, adding nothing and taking nothing away; and we anathematize in heart and mouth those whom they anathematized, and those whom they received, we receive. We glorify God the Father without beginning, and his only-begotten Son, begotten from the Father before the ages, and the Holy Spirit proceeding ineffably from the Father and the Son, as those whom we have mentioned above—the holy apostles, prophets, and teachers—proclaimed. And we all subscribed [Al., *subscribe*], who together with Theodore the archbishop set forth the Catholic faith.””

## CHAPTER XVIII. John, the cantor of the Apostolic See, who came [Al., had come] to instruct Britain

[Col. 0199C]

The venerable John, chief cantor [Al., chief singer] of the church of the holy apostle Peter and abbot of the monastery of blessed Martin, was present at this synod and likewise confirmed the decrees of the Catholic faith [Note: *He confirmed the decrees.* See Appendix, no. 17]. He had recently come from Rome at the command of Pope Agatho, under the leadership of the most reverend Abbot Biscop [Al., Bishop Bisi], surnamed Benedict, whom we mentioned above [Al. omits: *whom we mentioned above*].

For when this same Benedict had built a monastery in Britain in honor of the most blessed chief of the apostles, near the mouth of the River Wear [Col. 0199D], he came to Rome with Ceolfrid, his collaborator and partner in that work, who afterward became abbot of the same monastery. He had been accustomed to do this frequently before, and he was honorably received by Pope Agatho of blessed memory [678]. He asked for and received from him, as a safeguard of the monastery’s liberty, a letter of privilege confirmed by apostolic authority for the monastery that he had built. He knew that King Ecgfrid had desired this and granted permission for it; with the king’s consent and gift of the land, he had built the monastery.

He also received the aforesaid abbot John to bring him to Britain, so that he might teach in his monastery the annual course of singing [Note: *The course of singing.* See Appendix, no. 12], as it was performed at Rome at Saint Peter’s. Abbot John (*abba*; Al., *abbas*) carried out the pontiff’s command. By teaching the singers of the aforesaid monastery orally the order and practice of singing and reading, and by committing to writing what the cycle of the entire year required for the celebration [Al., celebration of] feast days, he left instructions that have been preserved in that monastery to this day and have already been copied by many people throughout the surrounding region.

Nor did John teach only the brothers of that monastery. From nearly all the monasteries of the same province, those who were skilled in singing came together to hear him [Col. 0200B]. Many also sought to invite him to the places where he was to teach.

Besides the duties of singing and reading, he had received another commission from the apostolic pope: to learn carefully what faith the Church of the English held, and, on returning to Rome, to report it. For he brought with him the synod of the blessed Pope Martin, recently celebrated at Rome with the agreement of one hundred and five bishops, chiefly against those who preached one operation and one will in Christ. He entrusted it for copying to the monastery of the aforementioned most devout abbot Benedict.

At that time people of this kind had greatly troubled the faith of the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0200C]; but, by the Lord’s favor, they had already been exposed and defeated. Therefore Pope Agatho, wishing to learn—as in the other provinces—what the condition of the Church was in Britain and how free it was from the contamination of heretics, entrusted this task to the most reverend abbot John, who was being sent to Britain.

Accordingly, when the synod in Britain that we have mentioned was assembled for this purpose, the Catholic faith was found to be inviolable in every respect, and a copy of its acts was given to John to take to Rome.

But on his return to his homeland, not long after he had crossed the Ocean, he was seized by illness and died [681]. Because of the love of Saint Martin, whose monastery he governed, his friends carried his body to Tours and buried it there with honor. When he was traveling to Britain, he had been received with benevolent hospitality by that church; and the brothers had earnestly asked him, on his return to Rome, to come by that route and visit their church. Accordingly, he obtained there companions for his journey and for the work entrusted to him. Although he died on the journey, nevertheless the copy of the faith of the English was brought to Rome and received with the greatest gratitude by the apostolic pope and by all who heard or read it.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Queen Æthelthryth remained perpetually a virgin, and how even her body could not decay in the tomb

[Col. 0201A]

King Ecgfrid took as his wife a woman named Æthelthryth [660], daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, whom we have mentioned several times: a deeply religious man, outstanding in mind and conduct in every respect. Before her marriage to Ecgfrid, she had been the wife of another man, namely Tondberct, prince of the South Gyrwe. But after he died a short time after taking her as his wife, she was given to the king mentioned above. Although she remained in his companionship for twelve years, she nevertheless continued to be gloriously intact in perpetual virginity.

When I myself was asking about this, since some people had begun to doubt whether it was so, Bishop Wilfrid of blessed memory assured me, saying that he was the most certain witness of her purity [Al., virginity]. Indeed, Ecgfrid promised that he would give her many lands and much money if he could persuade the queen to consent to marital relations with him, because he knew that she loved no man more than him.

Nor should it be considered impossible that this could have occurred in our own age, since faithful histories relate that it happened several times in earlier times: the same Lord granting it, who promises to remain with us until the end of the age. The sign also of the divine miracle by which the buried flesh of this woman could not decay indicates that she had remained undefiled by contact with a man.

After repeatedly asking the king to permit her to abandon worldly concerns and serve only the heavenly King Christ in a monastery, she at last obtained permission and entered the monastery of Abbess Æbbe [Note: *Æbbe.* Æbbe was a virgin born of the royal Northumbrian line, daughter of Æthelfrith and sister of Oswiu and Oswald, and paternal aunt of Ecgfrid. Her first residence was above the River Derwent, in a settlement now bearing her name, commonly Ebchester. Later she moved to Coldingham, which Bede calls the city of Coludi. There was another abbess of the same name and monastery in 870 who escaped Danish violence after her nose and lip had been cut off, and who led the remaining sisters to follow her example. Bede’s Æbbe lived in the time of Saint Cuthbert and was close to him; see Bede, *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 10. She died in 684 and is commemorated in the English Martyrology on 25 August], who was King Ecgfrid’s aunt. This monastery was situated in the place called the city of Coludi [Note: *The city of Coludi.* Today a village in the territory of the Maeatae, or in the Scottish Marches, where Ptolemy’s Colana probably stood. The derivation recently proposed from the Colidei certainly never occurred to Bede. They were not Colidei but Celdei, and they gave places their names not from the worship practiced there but from the cells in which they lived. King Edgar of Scotland gave this place, out of reverence for God and Saint Cuthbert, to the monastery of Durham for the support of that monastery. In time, however, the prior and brothers decided to build a church there and install monks from the same monastery. See the manuscript codex of Wessington, p. 38. Several original charters of this settlement are printed in Appendix, no. 20.] She received from the aforesaid Bishop Wilfrid the veil of the religious habit [671].

After one year she herself became abbess in the region called Elge [Note: *Elge.* This was Æthelthryth’s homeland. There she had a brother, Aldwulf, king of the East Angles, and sisters of the highest reputation for piety; see III.8. Historians, however, give another reason for the transfer of the monastery: namely, that Ecgfrid, regretting the freedom he had granted her from marriage, tried to use force against the monastery of Coludi. A long legend is told there of a journey filled with dangers as well as miracles, by which she escaped from her husband; see the *History of the Church of Ely*, Cotton Library, Nero A.15, published in *Monasticum*, I, p. 87. In this place Æthelthryth deserved to be admitted to the canon of the saints under the name Saint Audrey, and she was included in the Roman Martyrology on 23 June. The day of her translation is observed as a feast in the English Martyrology on 17 October. On Æthelthryth, see further William of Malmesbury, *De pontificibus*, IV, pp. 273, 293; Thomas Walsingham in *Richard I*, p. 338. The church of Ely, built by Æthelthryth in 673, was burned by the pagans in 870. After several years it was partly repaired and entrusted to clerics; in about 970 Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester, filled it with monks, and in 1108 Henry I established the episcopal see there], where, after building a monastery of many virgins devoted to God, she began to be their virgin mother both by the example of heavenly life and by her instructions [672].

They say of her that, from the time she entered the monastery, she never wished to wear linen garments, but only woolen ones. Except before the principal approaching solemnities—for example, Easter, Pentecost, and Epiphany—she rarely wished to bathe in hot water, and then she bathed last of all, after all the other servants of Christ there had been washed through the service of herself and her attendants [Al., female attendants]. Except on the greater solemnities or in cases of pressing necessity, she rarely ate more than once a day. Whenever a more serious illness did not prevent her, she always remained in the church, intent on prayer, from the time of the morning synaxis until sunrise.

There are also those who say that, through the spirit of prophecy, she foretold the pestilence by which she would die and openly announced to all present the number of those from her monastery who would be taken from this world by it [Col. 0202B]. She was taken to the Lord in the midst of her people [679], seven years after she had assumed the rank of abbess. Just as she herself had ordered, she was buried nowhere else but among them, beside the others in the order in which they had died, in a wooden coffin.

Her sister Sexburh succeeded her in the ministry of abbess [695]. Sexburh had been married to Earconberht, king of Kent. When Æthelthryth had been buried for sixteen years, the same abbess decided to raise her bones, place them in a new coffin, and transfer them into the church. She ordered some of the brothers to search for a stone from which they could make such a coffin.

They boarded a ship—for the region of Ely is surrounded on every side by waters and marshes and has no larger stones—and came to a certain deserted little city, situated not far away, which in the language of the English is called Grantchester [Note: *Grantchester.* Grantchester near Cambridge is today in a worse condition]. At once they found near the city walls a coffin of white marble, beautifully made, with a lid of similar stone fitted perfectly over it. Understanding from this that the Lord had prospered their journey, they gave thanks and carried it back to the monastery.

When the body of the holy virgin and bride of Christ had been brought into the light from the opened tomb, it was found so incorrupt that one would have thought she had died or been buried that same day. The aforesaid Bishop Wilfrid and many others who knew her testify to this.

The physician Cynifrid, however, gave the most certain testimony, for he had been present both when she was dying and when she was raised from the tomb. He used to report that, when she had fallen ill, she had a very large swelling beneath her jaw.

> “They ordered me,” he said, “to cut open that swelling so that the harmful fluid within it might flow out. While I was doing this, she seemed to feel somewhat better for two days, so that many thought she might recover from her illness. On the third day, however, the pain became worse than before, and she was suddenly taken from the world; she exchanged all pain and death for perpetual health and life.

> “When, after so many [Al., so many more] years, her bones were to be raised from the tomb, and a canopy had been stretched above it, the whole congregation—brothers on one side and sisters on the other—stood around singing psalms. The abbess herself entered within with a few others to raise and wash the bones [Al., to raise and carry them away]. Suddenly we heard the abbess inside proclaim in a clear voice: ‘Glory be to the name of the Lord.’

> “Not long afterward they called me inside, after the door of the canopy had been opened [Al., from every side]. I saw the body of the holy virgin of God lifted from the tomb and placed on a bed, looking as though she were sleeping. When the cloth covering her face was removed, they also showed me the wound from the incision I had made; it had healed, so that, in a marvelous way, instead of the open and gaping wound with which she had been buried, only the faintest traces of a scar were then visible (*parerent*; Al., *appararent*).”

All the linen cloths in which the body had been wrapped were also found intact and so new that they seemed to have been placed around her chaste limbs that very day.

They say that when she was afflicted by the swelling and pain of her jaw or neck, she took great delight in this kind of illness and used to say:

> “I know with complete certainty that I deservedly bear the burden of illness in my neck, since I remember that, when I was a young woman, I wore around it the needless weight of necklaces. I believe that for this reason divine mercy wished me to be burdened with pain in my neck, so that I might thereby be released from the guilt of needless vanity. For now, instead of gold and pearls, the redness of a swelling and its burning heat project from my neck.”

It also happened several times that demons were driven from the bodies of the possessed by touching these garments, and that other illnesses were cured. They further report that the coffin in which she had first been buried brought healing to some who suffered from eye pain. After placing their heads against the coffin and praying, they immediately found the discomfort of pain or dimness removed from their eyes.

The virgins [Al., the virgin] therefore washed the body and, clothing it in new garments, carried it into the church and placed it in the sarcophagus that had been brought. There it is held in great veneration to this day. In a remarkable way, the sarcophagus was found so perfectly suited to the virgin’s body that it seemed to have been prepared for her in particular. The place for her head had also been fashioned separately and appeared to be shaped exactly to the measure of her head.

Ely is a region in the province of the East Angles comprising approximately six hundred households. It resembles an island, being surrounded, as we have said, either by marshes or by water. It received its name from the abundance of eels caught in those marshes. The aforesaid handmaid of Christ wished to have a monastery there because she, as we have already said, had derived her bodily origin from the province of the East Angles.

## CHAPTER XX. A hymn about Æthelthryth

It seems appropriate to insert into this History a hymn on virginity, which many years ago I composed in elegiac meter in praise and celebration of the same queen and bride of Christ [Note: *Bride of Christ.* Al. adds: “And therefore truly a queen, because she is the bride of Christ”]. I wished to imitate the practice of Sacred Scripture, into whose histories many poems have been inserted. This hymn is composed in meter and verse.

> Holy God, the Trinity, who govern all the ages,  
> Grant favor now to what I have begun, holy God, the Trinity.
>
> Let war resound in Maro; let us sing the gifts of peace:  
> Let Christ’s gifts be our theme; let war resound in Maro.
>
> Let chaste songs be mine, not the rape of foul Helen:  
> Let indulgence be for the wanton; let chaste songs be mine.
>
> I shall speak of heavenly gifts, not of wretched Troy’s battles—  
> Gifts in which the earth rejoices: I shall speak of heavenly gifts.
>
> Behold, the exalted God enters the womb of the venerable Virgin:  
> To free humankind, behold, the exalted God enters.
>
> A virgin woman, devoted to the world’s Parent, bears him:  
> Mary, the gate of God; a virgin woman bears him.
>
> The friendly company rejoices in the Virgin Mother of the Thunderer:  
> The friendly company rejoices, resplendent in virginity.
>
> Her honor has produced many from a chaste offspring:  
> Her honor has produced virginal flowers.
>
> The virgin Agatha, burned by savage fires, does not yield:  
> Eulalia too endures, burned by savage fires.
>
> Chaste Thecla overcomes wild beasts through the summit of her steadfast mind:  
> Holy Euphemia, chaste, overcomes wild beasts.
>
> Agnes laughs joyfully at swords, stronger than iron:  
> Cecilia joyfully laughs at hostile swords.
>
> A great triumph flourishes throughout the world through sober hearts:  
> The love of sobriety flourishes greatly throughout the world.
>
> Our own distinguished age has now been blessed by the virgin:  
> Our own distinguished Æthelthryth shines.
>
> Born of an excellent father, illustrious through royal lineage:  
> She is nobler in the Lord, born of an excellent father.
>
> From this she receives a queen’s honor and scepters beneath the stars:  
> Remaining above the stars, she receives greater honor from this.
>
> Why do you seek a husband, holy one, already given to the highest Bridegroom?  
> Christ the Bridegroom is present; why do you seek a husband, holy one?
>
> I believe that you now follow the mother of the heavenly King:  
> May you too be a mother of the heavenly King.
>
> The bride dedicated to God had reigned for twice six years:  
> And in the monastery she is the bride dedicated to God.
>
> Entirely consecrated to heaven, where she flourished in lofty deeds,  
> She gave back her soul, entirely consecrated to heaven.
>
> The blessed flesh of the virgin lay buried for twice eight Novembers:  
> Yet the blessed flesh of the virgin does not decay in the tomb.
>
> Christ, this is your work: for even her garment in the tomb  
> Shines inviolate. Christ, this is your work.
>
> Dropsy and the black disease depart in honor of the holy garment:  
> Illnesses flee; dropsy and the black disease depart.
>
> Rage burns in the enemy who once overcame Eve:  
> The virgin triumphs exultantly; rage burns in the enemy.
>
> See, bride of God, what glory is yours on earth:  
> What glory will remain for you in heaven; see, bride of God.
>
> You receive joyful gifts, radiant with festive torches:  
> Behold, the Bridegroom comes; you receive joyful gifts.
>
> And you modulate new songs with your sweet-sounding lyre:  
> The bride exults in a hymn, and in new sweet-sounding songs.
>
> No one separates from the company of the Lamb on the lofty throne her  
> Whom no one had carried away in affection from the Lamb on the lofty throne.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Bishop Theodore made peace between Kings Ecgfrid and Æthelred

In the ninth year of Ecgfrid’s reign [679], when a serious battle had been joined between him and Æthelred, king of the Mercians, beside the River Trent [Note: *Trent.* If this battle was fought south of the River Trent, it probably took place at Adwine’s Place, which the inhabitants derive from Edwin, who was killed there. The published manuscripts of Malmesbury support this view, in which the name of the royal youth is given as Edwin. It is certain, however, that Edwin was killed in the territory of York near Hatfield, and that Malmesbury’s Edwin arises from an error either of the battle or of the scribes. Editions of that author contain innumerable errors of this kind. Thus, despite the name of this town, the location of the battle remains uncertain], Ælfwine, the brother of King Ecgfrid, was killed [Note: *He was killed.* Wilfrid had foretold Ælfwine’s death when, after being expelled from York by King Ecgfrid, he was mocked by the king’s supporters, who burst out laughing and ridiculed him. It happened that, one year later, on the very day on which the bishop had suffered injustice at York, the body of the royal youth was brought into the city and proclaimed a long period of mourning].

He was about eighteen years old and greatly beloved by both provinces. King Æthelred had his sister, Osthryth, as his wife [Note: *His sister.* This relationship explains how, when Bishop Wilfrid was expelled from his bishopric and was not permitted to remain in the kingdom of the Mercians, he sought refuge among the Frisians during his exile and among the South Saxons on his return].

When the material for a more bitter war and a longer hostility between the kings and their fierce peoples seemed to have arisen, Theodore, the bishop beloved of God [Col. 0205C], relying on divine assistance, extinguished completely the fire of such great danger by a saving exhortation. The kings and peoples were reconciled with one another, and no human life was demanded in payment for the slain king’s brother; only the legally due fine of money was paid to the avenging king [Al., fine]. The treaty of peace then endured for a long time between those kings and their kingdoms.

## CHAPTER XXII. How the bonds of a certain captive were loosed while Masses were being sung for him

In the battle mentioned above, in which King Ælfwine was killed, a memorable event is known to have occurred. I believe it should by no means be passed over in silence, but that, if reported, it will prove beneficial to the salvation of many.

Among others killed there was a young man from the king’s army named Imma. He lay among the corpses of the slain, appearing dead, throughout that day and the following night. At last, having recovered his breath, he revived, sat up, and bound his wounds as best he could. After resting for a short while, he rose and began to leave, hoping to find somewhere friends who would care for him.

While he was doing this, he was discovered and captured by men of the enemy army and brought before their lord, the earl of King Æthelred. When the earl asked who he was, Imma was afraid to admit that he had been a soldier. Instead he replied that he was a peasant and a poor man, bound by marriage, and that he had come on the expedition with men like himself to bring food to the soldiers.

The earl took him in and cared for his wounds. When he began to recover, the earl ordered him to be bound at night so that he would not escape. Yet he could not be kept bound, for as soon as those who had tied him departed, his bonds were loosed.

He had a full brother named Tunna, a priest and abbot of a monastery in a city called Tunnacæster after him [Note: *Tunnacæster.* If Bede’s Tunnacæster is the modern Tynemouth, the name appears to have a different origin from its association with Abbot Tunna—namely, the monastery’s location at the mouth of the River Tyne. But Bede does not say that Tynemouth was named after Tunna; he says Tunnacæster, which readers assign to Tynemouth only because they find it similar in sound and have no other place to substitute for it. On the monastery of Tynemouth, see the note on Ingetlingum, III.14. In any case, the location of Tunnacæster remains uncertain. That Tunna was its abbot, however, is clear from Bede’s history. Since he was nearly contemporary with Bede, Bede could not have been ignorant of him].

When Tunna heard that his brother had been killed in battle, he came to see whether he might find his body. He found another man who resembled him in every respect and thought that it was his brother. He carried him to his monastery, buried him with honor, and frequently arranged for Masses to be celebrated for the release of his soul.

During the celebration of these Masses, what I have described occurred: no one could bind Imma without the bonds immediately coming loose. Meanwhile the earl who held him began to wonder and ask why he could not be bound—whether he perhaps possessed the so-called releasing letters of which tales are told [Note: *Releasing letters.* Among the ancients there were the *Ephesian letters* (*Ephesia grammata*, Greek Ἐφέσια γράμματα), that is, certain obscure incantations which they say Croesus also uttered while on the pyre. They relate that when the Milesian and Ephesian wrestlers competed at Olympia, the Milesian could not wrestle because the other had tied Ephesian letters to his ankle. When this was discovered and the letters had been removed, they say that the Ephesian was thrown thirty times. —Suidas].

Imma replied that he knew nothing of such arts:

> “But I have a brother,” he said, “a priest in my country, and I know that, thinking me dead, he celebrates frequent Masses for me. If I were now in the other life, my soul would there be released from punishment through his intercessions.”

While he was detained by the earl for some time, those who observed him more carefully noticed from his face, clothing, and speech that he was not of the poor common people, as he had claimed, but of noble birth. The earl then called him privately and questioned him more insistently about his origin, promising that he would do him no harm if he honestly revealed who he was.

When he did so, admitting that he had been one of the king’s officials, the earl replied:

> “From each of your answers I had realized that you were not a peasant. Now you are certainly worthy of death, since all my brothers and relatives were killed in that battle. Nevertheless, I shall not kill you, lest I violate my pledged word.”

When Imma had recovered, the earl sold him to a certain Frisian in London [Al., to a Frisian; alternatively, to a Frison]. But even when the Frisian was taking him there, he could not bind him in any way. The enemy placed upon him various kinds of bonds [Al. adds: “they were loosed”]. When the man who had bought him saw that bonds could not restrain him, he granted him permission to ransom himself if he could.

From the third hour, when Masses were customarily celebrated, his bonds were very often loosed. Imma swore that he would return or send him the money for his ransom. He then went to Kent, to King Hlothere, who was the son of the sister of Queen Æthelthryth mentioned above, and who himself had once been that queen’s official. He asked for and received from Hlothere the price of his ransom and sent it to his master on his behalf, as he had promised.

After this, when he had returned to his homeland and reached his brother, he recounted in order all the adversities that had befallen him and all the consolations that had arisen amid those adversities. From his brother’s account he learned that his bonds had been loosed especially at the times when the solemn celebrations of Masses had been performed for him.

He also understood that the other benefits and successes that had come to him in his danger had been granted from heaven through his brother’s intercession and the offering of the saving sacrifice. Many people who heard these things from the aforesaid man were inflamed with faith and devotion to piety, so that they prayed, gave alms, or offered the Lord sacrifices of sacred oblation for the deliverance of their own relatives who had departed from this world. They understood that the saving sacrifice avails for the eternal redemption of both soul and body [Col. 0207C].

Some of those who had heard this story from the man himself also related it to me. Since I learned that it was true, I considered it beyond doubt that it should be inserted into our Ecclesiastical History.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The life and death of Abbess Hild [Al. omits: “life and”]

In the following year, that is, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 680, the most devout handmaid of Christ, Hild, abbess of the monastery called Streaneshalch, as we related above [Note: *Above.* III.24–25], after the many heavenly works she performed on earth, passed from the earth to receive the rewards of heavenly life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December [17 November], when she was sixty-six years old.

Dividing these years into equal portions, she spent the first thirty-three in the world, conducting herself with the highest distinction, and consecrated the same number of subsequent years more nobly to the Lord in the monastic life. She was of noble birth, being the daughter of Hereric, the nephew of King Edwin. Together with that king, at the preaching of Paulinus of blessed memory, the first bishop of the Northumbrians, she received the faith and sacraments of Christ, and preserved them undefiled until she was worthy to attain his vision.

When she had resolved to abandon the secular habit and serve him alone, she withdrew to the province of the East Angles [648]. She was related to that king and desired from there, if she could somehow do so, to leave her homeland and everything she possessed, reach Gaul, and live as a stranger for the Lord in the monastery of Chelles, so that she might more easily merit her eternal homeland in heaven.

Her sister Hereswith [Note: *Hereswith.* Here Bede asserts that Hereswith, Hild’s sister and mother of Aldwulf, king of the East Angles, lived secluded under monastic discipline in the monastery at Chelles. For this reason many writers produce arguments by which they accuse Bede of error, particularly because, if Hild and her sister Hereswith entered the religious life together at Chelles in 648, the monastery of Chelles had not yet been founded by its founder Balthild. But the dates of the foundation of the monastery at Chelles are so uncertain that it is difficult to affirm that an author who lived not far from those times was mistaken, especially in so famous a history, in which English nuns played so large a part] was also in that monastery, awaiting the eternal crown under regular discipline. Hild imitated her example and, with the intention of making a pilgrimage, remained for a whole year in the province mentioned above [Note: *In the province mentioned above.* Namely, of the East Angles, as Bede expressly affirms in this very passage. Therefore the error of those who infer that Hild went from there to the monastery of Chelles to join her sister Hereswith is egregious. She certainly intended to do so, but she was detained in the province mentioned above and recalled by Bishop Aidan].

Then Bishop Aidan recalled her to her homeland [Al. omits “to”] and gave her a piece of land of one household on the northern side of the River Wear, where for one year she lived the monastic life with a very few companions [Note: *Northern.* This place seems to have disappeared, unless it refers to the church of Saint Hild, whose certain beginnings belong to a later period and which lies on the southern bank of the River Tyne rather than on the northern side of the Wear. It is nevertheless possible that, just as the monastery of the Gyrwe became united with Wearmouth despite the parallel distance between the places, so this church, although situated by the Tyne, received its name from the Wear. For I have nowhere been able to find a monastery on the northern side of the Wear except the one founded by Benedict Biscop].

After these events she became abbess of the monastery called [Note: [Col. 0208D] Heruteu. Today Hertlepool, almost an island at high tide. What remains there of the monastery is not of the original foundation but belongs to the order of the Friars Minor. The parish church of Hertensis, together with many other estates in that region, passed to the monks of Gisburn in Yorkshire through the donation of the founder, Lord Bruce.] Heruteu [DCL]. This monastery had in fact been founded not long before by the devout servant of Christ [Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209C] Heiu. Leland and others identify this woman with Bega, and construct for her a first residence in Copeland, commonly called St Bees; a second on the northern side of the river Uiur; a third at Heruteu; a fourth at Calcaria; and a final one at Hacanos, where she died. We shall find this opinion based on nothing except similarity of names. For the monastery in Copeland was not founded by Saint Bega but in her honor in the time of Henry I. And Heiu, who had a site on the northern side of the river Uiur, was plainly a different woman from the one said to have died at Hacanos, as is clear from what follows in this chapter.] Heiu, who is said to have been the first woman in the province of the Northumbrians to receive the resolve and habit of the monastic life, with Bishop Aidan consecrating her. But not long after the monastery had been founded, she withdrew to the town of Calcaria, which was called by the English Kaelcacaestir [Al.: Kalcacestir] [Note: [Col. 0209D] Kaelcacaestir. Camden identifies it with Tadcaster, Dodsworth and Gale with Newton Kyme; the manuscript reads Ingleby, Abberforth.], and there established a residence for herself.

When the servant of Christ Hild was placed in charge of that monastery, she immediately took care to order everything according to the rule of life, insofar as she could learn it from learned men. For Bishop Aidan and all the religious people who knew her, because of the wisdom naturally implanted in her and her love of divine service, regularly visited her, loved her devotedly, and diligently instructed her.

When, therefore, she had presided over this monastery for several years, devoting herself intensely to the ordering of the regular life [DCLVIII], [Col. 0209B] it happened that she was asked to undertake the construction or organization of a monastery at a place called [Note: [Col. 0209D] Streaneshalch. See III, 24 for the occasion of this transfer.] Streaneshalch. She carried out the task entrusted to her without sluggishness. For she established this monastery also according to the same disciplines of the regular life as the earlier one. Indeed, here too she taught the observance of justice, piety, chastity, and the other virtues, but especially of peace and charity, so that, following the example of the primitive Church, no one there was rich and no one needy; everything was held in common by all, since nothing appeared to belong to anyone as private property.

She herself was so prudent that not only ordinary people in their necessities, but even kings and rulers sometimes sought counsel from her and found it. She made her subjects devote themselves so fully to reading the divine [Col. 0209C] Scriptures and so earnestly exercise themselves in works of justice that it seemed very easy to find there many who could suitably undertake an ecclesiastical rank, that is, the ministry of the altar.

Finally, we later saw five bishops come from that same monastery, all men of singular merit and holiness. Their names were Bosa, Aetla, [Note: [Col. 0209D] Oftfor. In the *Monasticon*, I, p. 121, there is printed from the Register of Worcester in the Cotton manuscript Tiberius A. 13, fol. 10a, a charter of venerable antiquity granted by Ecgwine, the successor of Oftfor. In it he testifies that King Aethelred had donated the monastery of Fledanburg to Oftfor on the other side of the document. Thus the charter printed is only secondary, and that from a copy; the original charter of the king himself, placed on the front of the document, either was not in the Register or was omitted by the copyists. Both charters, among many others, were supplied to me with the greatest kindness by the highly honorable Lord Somers, not from the Register but from the autograph itself, which at first sight displays its antiquity and has been excellently preserved. It is a monument of the highest value and worthy of so great a possessor. See Appendix, no. 21.] Oftfor, John, and Wilfrid.

Of the first we stated above that he was consecrated bishop at York. Of the second it must briefly be reported that he was ordained to the episcopate of Dorchester [Al.: Dorchester]. Of the last two it will be said below that the first of them was ordained bishop of the church of Hagustald [Al.: Augustald], and the second bishop of the church of York.

Let us now speak of the middle one. After he had devoted himself to reading and observing the Scriptures in both monasteries of Abbess Hild, desiring at last more advanced instruction, he came to Kent, to Archbishop Theodore of blessed memory. After he had spent some time there in sacred studies, he also undertook to go to Rome, which at that time was considered a mark of great virtue. On returning from there, when he had entered Britain, he turned aside to the province of the Hwiccii [Al.: Huictii], which was then ruled by King Osric. There he remained for a long time, preaching the word of faith and at the same time displaying before those who saw and heard him an example of how to live.

At that time the bishop of that province, named Bosel, was so weakened by bodily illness that he could not discharge the episcopal office himself. Therefore, by the judgment of everyone, the aforementioned man was elected to the episcopate in his place and, at the command of King Aethelred, was ordained [DCXCI] by Bishop Wilfrid of blessed memory, who at that time held the episcopate of the Angles of the Midlands. Archbishop Theodore had already died, and no other bishop had yet been ordained in his place.

A little earlier, that is, before the aforementioned man of God Bosel, a very vigorous and learned man of outstanding intelligence, named [Note: [Col. 0210D] Tatfrid. Tatfrid was designated the first bishop of Worcester in the year 680. Since he died before his consecration, Bosel succeeded him until the year 691; Oftfor succeeded Bosel in his illness; when Oftfor died in 692, Ecgwine succeeded him. His charter concerning Fledanburg is found in the appendix to the preceding note.] Tatfrid, had been elected bishop of that province from the monastery of the same abbess [DCLXXX]. But before he could be ordained, he was taken away by an untimely death.

Nor did the aforementioned servant and abbess of Christ, Hild, whom all who knew her habitually called “mother” because of her outstanding piety and grace, provide an example of life only to those present in her monastery. She also offered an occasion for salvation and correction to many who lived far away, wherever the happy report of her industry and virtue had reached.

For the dream that her mother Bregusuid had seen in Hild’s infancy had to be fulfilled. When her husband [Note: [Col. 0210D] Hereric. From Edwin the Exile and Quoenburga, daughter of Creoda (Bede: Cearl), king of the Mercians, were born two sons, Osfrith and Eadfrith. Hereric, the son of Eadfrith, was the father by Beorsuitha (Bede: Bregusuid) of Saint Hild, abbess and founder of the monastery called Streaneshalch, and of Saint Hereswith, queen of the East Angles. *Florentius of Worcester, Genealogy.*] Hereric was living in exile under Cerdic, king of the Britons, where he also died by poison, she dreamed that he had suddenly been taken away and that she sought him with every care, but no trace of him appeared anywhere. Yet when she had searched for him most diligently, she suddenly found beneath her garment a precious necklace. As she examined it more closely, it seemed to shine with such a brilliance of light that, through the splendor of its radiance, it filled all the boundaries of Britain.

This dream was truly fulfilled in the daughter of whom we are speaking: her life offered examples of works of light not only to herself but to many who wished to live well.
