But when she had presided over this monastery for many years, it pleased the gracious guardian of our salvation that her holy soul should also be tested by a long illness of the flesh [DCLXXIV], so that, following the Apostle’s example, her virtue might be perfected in weakness. Struck by fevers, she began to be tormented by a severe burning, and for six continuous years she did not cease to suffer from the same affliction. Throughout that entire period she never failed either to give thanks to her Creator or to teach publicly and privately the flock entrusted to her.

Instructed by her own example, she warned everyone that, in bodily health received from the Lord, they must serve Him obediently, and that in adversity of circumstances or in illnesses of the body they must always give thanks faithfully to the Lord. In the seventh year of her illness, when the pain had turned inward, she reached her final day [Note: [Col. 0211D] She reached the final day. Saint Hilda died on 15 November. *Florence of Worcester*, under the year 680. King Edmund brought the bones of Abbess Hilda to Glastonbury while he was on a northern expedition. Manuscript of Wessington, p. 30.].

Toward cockcrow, after receiving the provision of the most holy Communion, she summoned the servants of Christ who were in the same monastery and exhorted them, amid words of instruction, to preserve peace with one another, indeed with all, according to the Gospel. She saw death joyfully in the midst of her exhortation—or rather, to use the words of the Lord, she passed from death to life.

That same night the almighty Lord deigned to reveal her death by a manifest vision in another monastery situated farther away, which she herself had built that same year and which was called [Note: [Col. 0212D] Hacanos. A place on Whitby Strand, thirteen miles from Whitby and three from Scarborough.] Hacanos.

In that monastery there was a certain religious woman named Begu, who had served God in the monastic life for more than thirty years, having dedicated her virginity to Him. As she was then resting in the sisters’ dormitory, she suddenly heard in the air the familiar sound of a bell, by which they were accustomed to be awakened or summoned to prayers whenever one of them had been called away from this world. When she opened her eyes, as it seemed to her, she saw the roof of the house removed and a light poured down from above, filling everything. As she gazed anxiously at that light, she saw the soul of the aforementioned servant of God being carried into heaven within the light, accompanied and led by angels.

When, roused from sleep, she saw the other sisters resting around her, she understood that what she had seen had been shown to her either in a dream or in a vision of the mind. Immediately she rose, terrified by great fear, and ran to the virgin who then presided over the monastery in place of the abbess, whose name was Frigyd. Covered with much weeping and tears and drawing long sighs, she announced that the mother of them all, Abbess Hild, had already departed from this world and that, as she watched, she had ascended with immense light and angelic guides to the threshold of eternal light and the company of the citizens above.

When Frigyd heard this, she awakened all the sisters and, having summoned them to the church, urged them to devote themselves to prayers and psalms for the soul of their mother. While they diligently did this for the remainder of the night, brothers arrived at first light to announce her death from the place where she had died. The sisters replied that they had learned the same thing beforehand. When they explained in order how and when they had learned it, it was discovered [Col. 0212B] that her passing had been shown to them by a vision at the very hour at which those brothers reported that she had left the world.

By this beautiful concordance of events, it was divinely arranged that, while the brothers saw her departure from this life, the sisters should then recognize her entrance into the everlasting life of souls. These monasteries are nearly thirteen miles apart.

They also report that, on that same night, in the very monastery where the aforementioned servant of God died, her death appeared in a vision to one of the virgins devoted to God, who loved her with immense affection. The virgin saw her soul go to heaven with the angels and, at the very hour when it happened, openly narrated this to the servants of Christ who were with her. She awakened them to pray for her soul even before the rest of the community had learned of her death. The matter was soon made known to the community at daybreak.

This woman had been set apart at that hour, together with several other servants of Christ, in a remote part of the monastery, where women who had recently come to the religious life [Al.: conversion] were accustomed to be tested until, once instructed according to the rule, they were received into the fellowship of the community.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### How a brother in her monastery was divinely granted the gift of singing

In the monastery of this abbess there was a certain brother specially distinguished by divine grace, because [Al.: who] he was accustomed to compose songs suited to religion and piety. Whatever he learned from the divine writings through interpreters, he soon expressed in poetic words composed with the greatest sweetness and compunction, in his own language, that is, the language of the English.

Through his songs the minds of many were often kindled to despise the world and [Al. adds: to] desire the heavenly life. Other religious people among the English later attempted to compose poems, but none could equal him. For he had not been taught the art of singing by human beings or through a human being; [Col. 0213A] rather, aided by God, he received the gift of singing freely.

Therefore he could never compose any frivolous or superfluous poem. Only those things that pertained to religion suited his religious tongue. Indeed, while he remained in secular clothing until the time of more advanced age, he had never learned any songs. Thus sometimes at a feast, when merriment required everyone in turn to sing, as soon as he saw the harp approaching him, he would rise from the middle of the meal, leave, and return to his house.

When he did this on one occasion, he left the house of the feast and went to the stalls of the animals, whose care had been assigned to him that night. At the proper hour he gave his limbs over to sleep, and in a dream someone stood beside him, greeted him, and called him by his name:

“[Note: [Col. 0213D] Caedmon. Most people conjecture that Caedmon died around the year 680, or somewhat later. William of Malmesbury speaks as follows of his remains and those of other saints, *De gestis pontificum*, book III, p. 154b, London edition: ‘Recently discovered—that is, before the beginning of the twelfth century—and brought to prominence were the bodies of the saints, Bishop Trumuini, King Oswiu, and his daughter Aelfled, who presided over the same monastery after Hild; and also that monk whom Bede reports to have received, by divine gift, knowledge of singing. That he possessed popular merit before God, many miracles, as they say sent down from above, now offer evidence.’ The feast day of this saint is recorded in the English Martyrology on 11 February, although Hugh Menard placed it on 10 February. Bale, century I, and Pits, age 7, count him among the illustrious writers of England. But both are mistaken in reporting that ‘he uttered divine songs while sleeping, which certain people wrote down from his mouth while he was awake.’ Bede does not write this.] Caedmon,” he said, “sing something to me.”

But he replied, “I do not know how to sing. That is why I left the feast and withdrew here: because I could not sing.”

Again the one who was speaking with him said, “Nevertheless, you must sing to me.”

“What,” he asked, “must I sing?”

The other replied, “Sing the beginning of created things.”

Upon receiving this answer, he immediately began to sing verses in praise of God the Creator, which he had never heard before. Their sense is this:

“Now we must praise the author of the heavenly kingdom, the power of the Creator, and his counsel, the deeds of the Father of glory. How he, being the eternal God, became the author of all wonders; how first, for the sons of men, he created heaven as the roof of the dwelling, and then the earth, the almighty guardian of the human race.”

This is the sense, but not the actual order of the words that he sang while asleep. For songs, however excellently composed, cannot be transferred word for word from one language into another without loss of their beauty and dignity.

Rising from sleep, he retained in memory everything that he had sung while sleeping, and immediately added to it many more words of worthy song to God, composed in the same manner.

In the morning he came to the steward who was in charge of him and reported what gift he had received. He was brought to the abbess and ordered, in the presence of many more learned men, to recount the dream and sing the song, so that by the judgment of all it might be established what the thing was and from where it came. Everyone judged that a heavenly grace had been granted to him by the Lord.

They explained to him some discourse from sacred history or doctrine and instructed him, if he could, to turn it into the melody of a song. He accepted the task, went away, and returned in the morning with an excellent song composed as he had been commanded.

Therefore the abbess, embracing the grace of God in the man, taught him to abandon his secular clothing and undertake the monastic way of life. Having received him into the monastery, she added him, together with all his own people, to the company of the brethren and ordered that the sequence of sacred history be taught to him.

He, for his part, turned everything he could learn by listening into the sweetest song, recalling it within himself and, as it were, ruminating like a clean animal. By singing it more sweetly, he in turn made his teachers his listeners.

He sang of the creation of the world, the origin of the human race, and the entire history of Genesis; of Israel’s departure from Egypt and entry into the promised land; of many other histories of sacred Scripture [Col. 0214B]; of the Lord’s incarnation [Al.: of the Lord and] passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; of the coming of the Holy Spirit and the teaching of the apostles.

He also composed many songs about the terror of the future judgment, the horror of the punishment of Gehenna, and the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom. He made many others as well concerning divine benefits and judgments. In all these he sought to draw people away from love of wickedness and to arouse them to love and diligently practice good works.

For he was a deeply religious man, humbly subject to the disciplines of the rule. Against those who wished to act otherwise, he was inflamed with the zeal of great fervor. Thus he also brought his life to a beautiful conclusion.

When the hour of his departure [Al.: death] was approaching, he was afflicted for fourteen days by bodily illness [DCLXXX]. Yet it was so moderate that throughout the entire period he was able both to speak and to walk. Nearby was a house into which the weaker brothers and those who appeared close to death were customarily brought.

As evening fell, on the night when he was to depart from the world, he asked his servant to prepare a place for him to rest there. The servant wondered why he made this request, since he did not appear at all likely to die yet, but nevertheless did what he had said.

When he had been placed there, he and those who had previously been in the house took turns speaking and joking with cheerful minds. After midnight had passed, he asked [Al. adds: everyone] whether they had the Eucharist inside. They replied:

“What need is there for the Eucharist? You are not about to die, since you are speaking with us so cheerfully, as though you were in good health.”

Again he said, “Nevertheless, bring me the Eucharist.”

After he had received it [Note: [Col. 0214D] In the hand. Baron discusses this rite of receiving the Eucharist—in the hand for men, on a clean cloth for women—in his notes on the *Martyrology*, 15 August, letter c. He shows that it remained in use for a long time in the West as well as in the East, even after persecution had ceased.], he asked whether they all had a peaceful disposition toward him and were free from complaint, dispute, and resentment. They all replied that their minds toward him were entirely peaceful and removed from all anger. In turn they asked him whether he had a peaceful disposition toward them [Al.: whether he would have one].

He immediately replied: “I bear a peaceful mind, my little sons, toward all the servants of God.”

Thus, fortifying himself with the heavenly viaticum, he prepared for entry into the other life. He asked how near the hour was when the brothers were to be awakened to sing the nocturnal praises of the Lord. They replied, “It is not far away.”

“Good,” he said, “then let us await that hour.”

Making the sign of the holy cross, he inclined his head upon the pillow and, falling asleep for a short while, quietly ended his life.

Thus it happened that, just as he had served the Lord with a simple and pure mind and tranquil devotion, so also, leaving the world in a peaceful death [Al.: mind], he came to behold Him. And that tongue which had composed so many saving words in praise of the Creator closed its life with its final words in His praise, signing himself and commending his spirit into His hands. From what we have related, he appears also to have foreknown his death.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### What sort of vision appeared to a man of God before the monastery of the city of Coludum was consumed by fire

At this time [DCLXXIX] the monastery of virgins called the city of Coludum, which we also mentioned above, was consumed by flames through the fault of negligence [Col. 0215C]. Yet all who knew the matter could easily perceive that this had happened because of the wickedness of those who lived there, and especially of those who appeared to be in positions of authority.

Nevertheless, a warning of divine mercy was not lacking for the punishment of the guilty, so that, once corrected, they might avert the anger of the just Judge from themselves, like the people of Nineveh, through fasting, weeping, and prayers.

In that monastery there was a man of Scottish origin named [Note: [Col. 0215D] Adamnanus. A priest named Adamnanus lived in the monastery of Coludum, whose holiness Bede praises in IV, 25. Henry Fitzsimon recorded his feast on this day in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Ireland*, calling him Adamnanus; but he incorrectly makes him an abbot and perhaps confused him with the abbot of Iona. John Wilson likewise includes him on this day in the earlier edition of his *English Martyrology*, but in the later edition of the same Martyrology he moved him to 16 March, for reasons unknown to us. In both places he calls him prefect of the monastery of Coludum; this is incorrect, for Aebba presided over both the men and the women. David Camerarius records him on 27 January: ‘On this same day Saint Adamnanus, abbot of Coludum, concerning whom see Westminster under the year 701.’ But this man was not an abbot, and Westminster is speaking of another Adamnanus. Hugh Menard, book II of the *Observations*, under 29 August, and Leflaeus, book IV of the *Deeds of the Scots*, assert that he was a monk. Nicholas Harpsfield also discusses him at length, section 7; Capgrave in the *Life of Saint Aebba*; and Trithemius, book III of *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 124.] Adamnanus. He led a life of chastity and [Al.: or] prayers, greatly devoted to God, so that he never took any food or drink except on Sunday and Thursday. Often he spent entire nights awake in prayer.

This strictness of a more rigorous life had first come to him out of necessity, for the correction of his wickedness. As time passed, however, he transformed necessity into custom.

In his youth he had committed some crime. When he came to his senses concerning what he had done, he recoiled from it with the greatest horror and feared that he would be punished for it by the strict Judge. He therefore approached a priest from whom he hoped to learn the path of salvation, confessed his guilt, and asked him to give advice by which he could flee from the coming [Al. adds: of God] wrath.

When the priest heard of his offense, he said: “A great wound requires the care of a greater remedy. Therefore devote yourself, as far as you are able, to fasts, psalms, and prayers, so that by anticipating the face of the Lord in confession you may deserve to find Him merciful.”

But the young man, held by the excessive pain of a guilty conscience and desiring to be released more quickly from the inward bonds of his sins, said: “I am young in age and vigorous in body. Whatever you impose upon me to do, provided that I may be saved on the day of the Lord, I shall easily endure—even if you command me to spend the whole night standing in prayer, or to pass an entire week abstaining from food.”

The priest replied: “It is too much to last an entire week without bodily nourishment. But it is sufficient to observe a fast of two or three days. Do this until I return to you after a short time and show you more fully what you ought to do and how long you must continue your penance.”

After saying this and prescribing for him the measure of his penance, the priest departed. When an unexpected circumstance arose, he withdrew to Ireland, from which he had originated [Al.: derived his origin], and did not return to him as they had agreed.

The man himself, mindful both of the priest’s command and of his own promise, devoted himself entirely to tears of repentance, holy vigils, and abstinence, so that he took nourishment only on Thursday and Sunday, as I have said, and remained fasting on the other days of the week.

When he heard that his priest had withdrawn to Ireland and died there, he continued from that time always to observe the prescribed measure of abstinence according to their agreement. What he had begun once out of remorse and fear of God because of his guilt, he now carried on tirelessly out of love of God, taking delight in its rewards.

While he diligently continued this for a long time, it happened one day that he had gone some distance from that monastery with one of the brothers and was returning after completing his journey. As they approached the monastery and saw its buildings raised high, the man of God broke into tears and displayed the sadness of his heart in his face.

His companion, observing this, asked why he was doing so. He replied: “All these buildings that you see, public and private, will shortly be reduced to ashes by consuming fire.”

When the companion heard this, as soon as they entered the monastery he took care to report it to the mother of the community, named Aebba. She was rightly disturbed by such a portent, summoned the man to her, and carefully questioned him about the matter and how he knew it.

He said: “Recently, while occupied at night with vigils and psalms, I suddenly saw someone standing beside me whose face was unknown. When his presence terrified me, he told me not to be afraid. Addressing me as though he were a familiar friend, he said: ‘You are doing well, since at this nocturnal hour, instead of giving yourself over to sleep, you have chosen to devote yourself to vigils and prayers.’”

“But I replied, ‘I know that it is greatly necessary for me to persist in saving vigils and to entreat the Lord diligently for my errors.’”

He continued: “‘You speak truly, because both you [Al.: because there] and many others need to redeem their sins by good works and, when they cease from the labors of temporal affairs, to labor more freely for the desire of eternal goods. But very few do this.

“‘For just now I passed through this entire monastery in order, inspecting the houses and beds of each person, and among them all I found no one occupied with the salvation of his soul except you. All of them, both men and women, either lie numbed in idle sleep or keep watch for sins.

“‘Even the little houses that had been built for prayer or reading have now been turned into chambers of feasting, drinking, talking, and other pleasures. The virgins dedicated to God, disregarding the reverence due to their profession, whenever they are free devote themselves to weaving delicate garments by which they either adorn themselves, as brides, for the peril of their condition, or seek to procure the friendship of men from outside.

“‘Therefore a severe vengeance from heaven, raging through flames, has rightly been prepared for this place and its inhabitants.’”

The abbess said: “Why did you not wish to reveal this discovery to me sooner?”

He replied: “I was afraid, out of reverence for you, that you might perhaps be excessively distressed. Nevertheless, take this consolation: this plague will not come during your days.”

When the vision had been publicized, the inhabitants of the place began for a few days to fear somewhat and to chastise themselves by interrupting their crimes. But after the death of the abbess they returned to their former filth, indeed committed even more wicked acts. And when they were saying, “Peace and security,” they were immediately punished by the penalty of the aforementioned vengeance.

[Col. 0217D] My most reverend fellow priest Aedgils related to me that all these things had happened in this way. At that time he was living in [Col. 0218A] that monastery. Later, when many of its inhabitants had departed because of its desolation, he lived for a long time in our monastery and died there.

We believed that these events should be inserted into our History so that we might warn the reader, through the works of the Lord, how terrible He is in His counsels concerning the sons of men. Otherwise, if at some time we serve the enticements of the flesh and fear God’s judgment too little, His sudden anger may seize us and either afflict us, in its just fury, with temporal losses or, examining us more strictly, carry us away to everlasting destruction.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the deaths of Kings Ecgfrid and Hlothere

In the year of our Lord’s incarnation 684, King Ecgfrid of the Northumbrians sent an army into Ireland under the commander Berct and miserably ravaged an innocent people, always most friendly to the English nation. The hostile hand spared not even churches or monasteries.

The islanders, however, as far as they were able, repelled arms with arms. Calling upon the help of divine mercy, they continually and for a long time asked that they might be avenged from heaven through imprecations [Al.: prayers]. Although those who utter curses cannot possess the kingdom of God, it was nevertheless believed that those who had been deservedly cursed because of their impiety would soon pay the penalties of their guilt, with the Lord as avenger.

Indeed, in the following year the same king, when he rashly led an army to devastate the province of the Picts, was induced—despite the strong opposition of his friends, and especially of Cuthbert of blessed memory, who had recently been ordained bishop [Note: [Col. 0217D] Cuthbert. See the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapters 24 and 27.]—into inaccessible mountain passes by enemies pretending to flee. There he was slain, together with the greater part of the forces he had brought with him, in the fortieth year of his age and the fifteenth of his reign, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

As I have said, his friends tried to prevent him from undertaking this war. But because, in the preceding year, he had refused to listen to the most reverend Father Ecgberct, so that he would not attack [Note: [Col. 0217D] Scotland. Since Scotland is mentioned here, modern Scottish historians transfer to their own country both the battle that Bede places in Ireland in the preceding year and the later battle in which Ecgfrid was killed, embellishing the entire matter with details of their own and placing it in Galloway. See H. Boece and Buchanan under Eugenius V. Undoubtedly this fatal battle for Ecgfrid took place in Scottish Albion. Simeon of Durham, p. 5, 3, identifies not only the region but the very site of the battle, saying that the king was killed at Nechtanesmere, “which is the lake of Nechtan,” and that his body was buried on the island of Iona. But that he did not invade Ireland in the strict sense cannot be asserted without excessive violence to Bede. Rather, it is clear that Scotland itself—the land which Ecgberct dissuaded the king from invading because it had harmed him in no way—is the same as the Ireland which Bede above described as “a people always most friendly to the English nation.” D. James Dalrymple candidly acknowledged this in his *Collections concerning Scottish History*, p. 34. Would that he had not implied that Bede was less candid—not only against the natural character of the man but also against the purpose of his own history, as will be evident to anyone who compares I, 34.] Scotland [Note: [Col. 0218D] That had harmed him in no way. Ecgberct rightly used this argument, because he had found the Irish people to be not only harmless but always most friendly. See III, 27.] that had harmed him in no way, it was granted him as punishment for that sin that he would not now listen to those who wished to save him from destruction.

[Additional variants omitted above: Streaneshalch, “much justice …” [Al.: “there seemed to be much”]; Hild’s dream, *expletum* [Al.: *impletum*, “fulfilled”]; Begu’s vision, *dum* [Al.: *cum*, “while/when”], and *famulis* [Al.: *famulabus*, “female servants”]; the Chapter XXIV heading has the alternative, “That the gift of singing was divinely granted to a certain brother”; Caedmon’s account has *ei* [Al.: *eum*, “him”], *hora competenti* [Al. adds: *jam*, “already”], *doctores suos … auditores sui* [Al.: *suos*, “his teachers … his listeners”], and *ex Aegypto* [Al.: *de Aegypto*, “out of/from Egypt”]; his death is *decessus* [Al.: *discessus*, “departure”], the nearby house is *proximo* [Al.: *proxima*], and the request concerning the brethren has [Al. adds: *an*, “whether”]; the final sentence has *ultima quoque* [Al.: *quaeque*, “also/final”] and *tranquilla morte* [Al.: *mente*, “mind”]. In Chapter XXV, *orationibus* has [Al.: *vel*, “or”], *excepta die* [Al.: *exceptis diebus*, “except on the days”], *reficeret* [Al.: *reficeretur*, “was refreshed/fed”], *lectos* [Al.: *lectulos*, “beds/little beds”], *nocturno quietis* [Al.: *nocturnae quietis*, “of the nocturnal rest”], and *maluisti* [Al.: *valuisti*, “you chose/were able”]. The closing reflection has [Al. adds: *sit*, “is”].]

From that time onward, the hope and strength of the kingdom of the English began to ebb and, slipping backward, to be carried away. For the Picts recovered the land of their own possession which the English and the Scots who were in Britain [Al. adds *est*, “are”] had held, together with a considerable part of the Britons [Al.: *plurimas gentes Anglorum*, “very many English peoples,” for *plurimos gentis Anglorum*]; and they have retained it to this day, for approximately forty-six years. Among the many from the English people who were either slain by the sword, reduced to servitude, or driven by flight from the land of the Picts, the most reverend man of God Trumwine, who had received the episcopate over them, also withdrew with his people who were in the monastery of Aebbercurnig [Note: [Col. 0219C] Aebbercurnig. See the note on this passage, I, 12.], situated indeed in the territory of the English but near the strait that separates the lands of the English and the Picts. Commending them wherever he could to friends in the monasteries, he himself chose a place of residence in the often-mentioned monastery of the servants and handmaids of God called Streanaeshalch. There, with a few of his own people, he led for many years a monastic life beneficial not only to himself [Al. omits *sibi*, “to himself”] but also to many. [Col. 0219B] When he died, he was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, in a manner worthy of his honor and life and rank [Al., *gratia*, “grace”] [Note: [Col. 0219D] He was buried. Concerning the relics of Trumwine, see G. of Malmesbury above, in the note on Caedmon, IV, 24.].

At that time the same monastery was governed by the royal virgin Aelbfled together with her mother Eanfled, both of whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0219D] Above, III, 15, 24.]. But when the bishop came there, the devoted teacher of God found in him both the greatest assistance in governing and consolation for her own life.

Alfrid succeeded Ecgfrid in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0219D] Alfrid. Because he was illegitimate, although older than Ecgfrid, he withdrew to Ireland during his brother’s reign, whether by force or through resentment. It is not impossible that the protection granted him by the Irish provided Ecgfrid with some pretext for the Irish war. He was buried at Driffeld in the eastern part of the territory of York, where his monument is still shown today.]. He was a man most learned in the Scriptures, and was said to be Ecgfrid’s brother and the son of King Osuiu; and, although within narrower boundaries, he nobly restored the shattered condition of the kingdom.

In that same year, which was 685 from the Lord’s incarnation, Hlother, king of the people of Kent, died on the eighth day before the Ides of February [Al., *Februarii*, “of February”]. After Ecgberct, his brother, who had reigned for nine years, Hlother himself had reigned for twelve years. He had been wounded in battle against the South Saxons, whom Eadric, the son of Ecgberct, had gathered against him, and he died while being treated. After him the same Eadric reigned for one year and six months. When he died, that kingdom was for some time destroyed by uncertain or foreign kings [Note: [Col. 0219D] For a period of time. On that occasion Caedualla, together with his brother Molo, invaded the province with all the force he could muster, believing that he would withdraw unopposed; but he did not encounter the provincials unprepared or lacking courage, as he had expected. After suffering many reverses, they put Caedualla to flight; and when his brother Molo had been driven into a certain hut, they set the hut itself on fire. Caedualla nevertheless did not cease to repair his loss by repeated devastation of the inhabitants, and to transfer revenge for the affair to his successor Ina, who granted peace after receiving 30,000 gold marks. See the Saxon Chronicle under the years 686, 687, and 694, compared with Malmesbury, I, 1, 2.]; until the rightful king Uictred—that is, the son of Ecgberct—strengthened in the kingdom, freed his people from foreign invasion through both religion and diligence.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the man of God Cudberct [Al., Cudberctus] became a bishop, and how, while still living the monastic life, he lived and taught.

[Col. 0220A]

In the same year in which King Ecgfrid ended his life, as we have said, he caused the holy and venerable man Cudberct to be ordained bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne. Cudberct had lived for many years in solitary life on the very small island called Farne [Note: [Col. 0220D] Farne. A place dedicated to retreat and meditation from the time of Aedan himself; see III, 16. Later Brother Bartholomew lived there and wrote the book of the *Farnese Meditations*, which is still preserved in the library at Durham.], situated in the Ocean nearly nine miles from that same church, with great discipline of body and mind.

From his earliest childhood he had always burned with zeal for a religious life; but at the beginning of adolescence he took upon himself both the monastic name and the monastic habit. He first [Al., *enim*, “for”] entered the monastery of Mailros [Note: [Col. 0220D] Mailros. It was situated in the valley of modern Scotland, twenty miles from Berwick, the last town of England. The ancient monastery, which had been destroyed, was restored by St David, king of the Scots, son of Malcolm the Pious and St Margaret, and was assigned, along with several others, to the Cistercian order. *Monasticon*, II, p. 1057. The abbey of St Mary of Mailros was founded on the Monday of Easter, and Richard was appointed its first abbot in 1136. *Chronicle of Mailros*, p. 165. A list of nineteen abbots through the year 1268 is found on p. 226.], which stood on the bank of the River Tweed and was then governed by Abbot Eata, a man of the greatest gentleness and simplicity. He later became bishop of Hexham, or of the Church of Lindisfarne, as we mentioned above. At that time Boisil was prior there, a priest of great virtues and prophetic spirit. Humbly subject to his discipleship, Cudberct received from him both knowledge of the Holy Scriptures [Al. adds “holy”] and examples of good works.

After Boisil had departed to the Lord, Cudberct was made [Al. omits *factus*, “made”] prior of the same monastery and instructed many in the regular life both through the authority of a teacher and through the example of his own conduct. He provided the monastery itself not only with counsels and examples of regular life, but also strove to turn the surrounding people far and wide from the life of foolish custom toward love of heavenly joys. Many profaned the faith they possessed by wicked deeds, while some, even in a time of plague, neglected the sacraments of the faith in which they had been instructed and ran to the wandering remedies of idolatry—as though they could restrain the scourge sent by God the Creator through incantations, amulets, or any other secrets of demonic art [Al., “daemonic art”].

To correct the error of both groups, he frequently went out from the monastery. Sometimes he rode a horse, but more often he traveled on foot [Al., “with his feet”], and came to the surrounding villages, preaching the way of truth to those who had gone astray; Boisil himself had also been accustomed to do this in his time. It was the custom of the peoples of the English at that time that, when a cleric or priest came to a village, everyone gathered at his command to hear the word. They willingly listened to what was said, and even more willingly followed in their actions what they could both hear and understand.

Cudberct possessed such skill in speaking, such power to persuade people of what he had begun [Al., “what he had taught”], and such a light in his angelic countenance that none of those present dared conceal from him the hidden places of his heart. All openly confessed what they had done, since they clearly thought [Al., *putarent*, “might think”] that these things could in no way be hidden from him; and, as he commanded, they cleansed their confessions through worthy fruits of repentance.

He was especially accustomed to travel through those places [Al. adds *et*, “and”] and preach in the hamlets that lay far away on steep and rugged mountains—places that others found frightening to visit and that, through their poverty as well as their rusticity, kept learned men from approaching them. Yet he devoted himself gladly to this pious labor and cultivated them with such diligent skill in teaching [Al., *tantum*, “so much,” for *tanta*] that, after leaving the monastery, he often did not return home for a full week [Al., *hebdomada*, for *ebdomade*], sometimes for two or three weeks, and occasionally for an entire month. Instead, remaining in the mountains, he called the rustic people to heavenly things through both the word of preaching and the work of virtue.

When the venerable servant of the Lord had lived for many years in the monastery of Mailros and shone forth through great signs of virtue [Al., “shone forth”], the most reverend abbot Eata transferred him to the island of Lindisfarne [Al. adds *et*, “also”], so that there too he might impress upon the brothers the guardianship of regular discipline by the authority of a prior and demonstrate it beforehand by his own conduct. For at that time the same most reverend Father himself governed the place by right of an abbot.

From ancient times it had been customary there for both a bishop with his clergy and an abbot with his monks to reside; nevertheless, the monks themselves also belonged familiarly to the bishop’s care. For Aedan, who was the first bishop of that place, came there with monks as a monk himself and established monastic life in it. It is known that blessed Father Augustine had earlier done the same in Kent, as the most reverend Pope Gregory wrote to him, and as we have also quoted above [Note: [Col. 0221D] Above. See Gregory’s response to Augustine’s first question, I, 27.]:

“But because your Fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to be separated from your clerics, in the Church of the English, which has recently been brought to the faith by God’s providence, you should establish the form of life that existed among our Fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church. Among them no one said that anything of what he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How, while living the anchoritic life, he brought forth a spring by prayer from dry [Al., “stony”] earth and obtained a crop through the labor of his hands beyond the proper season for sowing [Al., “reaping”].

[Col. 0222A]

Thereafter, as Cudberct’s merits in religious devotion increased, he reached the secluded silence of the anchoritic contemplation that we have mentioned [DCLXXVI]. But since many years ago we sufficiently described his life and virtues both in heroic verse and in simple prose, it is enough for the present to recall only this: when he was about to enter the island, he declared to the brothers, saying:

“If divine grace grants me in that place the ability to live by the work of my hands, I shall gladly remain there; otherwise, God willing, I shall return to you as quickly as possible.”

The place was completely without water, crops, or trees, and, because of the frequent presence of evil spirits, it was poorly suited to human habitation. But, according to the desire of the man of God, it became entirely habitable, for at his arrival the evil spirits withdrew [Al., *recesserunt*, “withdrew,” for *recessere*].

After he had driven away his enemies, enclosed a narrow dwelling there with a rampart, and, with the help of the brothers’ hands, built the necessary buildings within it—that is, an oratory and a common dwelling—he ordered the brothers to make a pit in the floor of that dwelling. The earth was extremely hard and stony, and there appeared to be no hope [Al., *species*, “appearance,” for *spes*] at all that a spring might be hidden within it. While they were doing this, however, through the faith and prayers of the servant of God, the pit was found full of water on the following day. To this day it supplies all who come there with a sufficient abundance of its heavenly grace [Al., *subministrat*, “furnishes,” for *ministrat*].

He also asked that agricultural tools and grain be brought to him. When he sowed the prepared [Al., “aforementioned”] earth at the appropriate time, absolutely nothing grew from it—not ears of grain, indeed, nor even a blade of grass—until the summer season. Therefore, when the brothers visited him as usual, he ordered barley to be brought, in case either the nature of that soil or the will of the heavenly Giver intended that a crop of that grain should arise there instead. When he sowed what had been brought to him in the same field, beyond all proper time for sowing and beyond all hope of fruitfulness, a plentiful crop immediately sprang up and provided the man of God with the desired nourishment from his own labor.

When he had served God there as a solitary for many years [DCLXXXIV], the rampart enclosing his dwelling was so high that from it he could see nothing but the sky, whose entrance he longed for. It happened that a fairly large synod was assembled in the presence of King Ecgfrid beside the River Alne [Al., “Alnae”], at a place called Adtuifyrdi [Note: [Col. 0221D] Adtuifyrdi. Everything Bede relates here about the synod of Twyford seems clearly to me to show that the synod was held at Twyford in Northumbria and was truly ecclesiastical: it was held in the presence of Ecgfrid, king of Northumbria, but presided over by Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. If anyone wonders that Theodore should exercise his functions so far from his see, let him consult IV, 2, with the accompanying note from G. of Malmesbury, *Gesta Pontificum*, I. Although there are several other Tuifords in other parts of England, Bede expressly distinguishes this one by its location beside the River Alne. And if the Life of St Cuthberct places this Tuiford beside the River Slu, that has no authority against Bede and proves nothing except a printer’s error, by which S was printed for A and u for n.], which signifies “at the double ford.” The archbishop Theodore, of blessed memory, presided over it. With one mind and unanimous agreement [Al., *unanimo omnium consensu*, “with the unanimous agreement of all”], all chose Cudberct as bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne.

Although many messengers and letters were sent to him beforehand, he could by no means be drawn from his monastery. At last the aforementioned king himself, together with the most holy bishop Trumwine [Al. omits *nec non*, “and also”] and other religious and powerful men, sailed to the island. Many of the brothers also came from Lindisfarne itself for this purpose. They all knelt, adjured him by the Lord, shed tears, and entreated him, until they drew him, also full of tears, from his hidden retreat and brought him to [Al., *in*, “into”] the synod.

When he arrived there, although he resisted strongly, he was overcome by the unanimous will of all and compelled to submit his neck to the office of the episcopate. He was especially conquered by the testimony that the servant of the Lord Boisil, when he disclosed to him [Al. omits *ei*, “to him”] through prophetic insight all that would happen to him, had also foretold that he would become a bishop [Note: [Col. 0223D] He had foretold it. See Bede’s *Life of St Cuthberct*, chapter 8.].

His ordination was not decreed immediately, however. After the winter that was approaching had passed, it was completed at the solemn feast of Easter in York [Note: [Col. 0223D] York. “King Ecgfrid and Archbishop Theodore gave St Cudberct in the city of York all the land from the wall of St Peter’s church as far as a large part toward the west, and from the wall of that church as far as the city wall toward the south.” Simeon of Durham, I, 9.], in the presence of the aforementioned [Al. omits *praefati*, “aforementioned”] King Ecgfrid. Seven bishops assembled for his consecration, among whom Theodore, of blessed memory, held primacy.

He had first been elected to the episcopate of the Church of Hexham in place of Tunberct [Note: [Col. 0223D] In place of Tunberct. See concerning him IV, 12. The reason for his deposition is unknown, but the deposition itself indicates Theodore’s presence, under whose direction ecclesiastical discipline was then in force.], who had been deposed from the episcopate [Al., “from the bishops”]. But because Cudberct preferred to be placed over the Church of Lindisfarne, in which he had lived, it was decided that Eata should return to the see of the Church of Hexham, for which he had first been ordained, and that Cudberct should take up the governance of the Church of Lindisfarne.

He adorned the episcopal office he had received by works of virtue in imitation of the blessed apostles. He protected the people entrusted to him with constant prayers and called them to heavenly things through salutary admonitions. And—as especially benefits teachers—he first demonstrated by doing himself the things he taught others to do.

Above all [Al. adds *et*, “and”], he was fervent with the fire of divine charity, restrained by the virtue of patience, most diligently devoted to prayer, and approachable to all who came to him for consolation. He even counted it as a form of prayer if he offered the sick brothers the help of his encouragement, knowing that the one who said, “You shall love the Lord your God,” also said, “You shall love your neighbor” [Al. adds, “as yourself”]. [Col. 0224A] He was distinguished by the discipline of abstinence and was always lifted toward heavenly things by the grace of heartfelt remorse. Finally, when he offered God the sacrifice of the saving victim, he commended his vows to the Lord not with a voice raised on high, but with tears poured forth from the depths of his heart.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Two. In the Mori manuscript, etc., chapter 27 begins here, and the title of the following chapter is assigned to it in the index; but, for the reasons given in the notes to chapter 14, Chifflet’s order and numbering are not changed.]

After completing two years in the episcopate, he returned to his island and monastery [DCLXXXVII], warned by a divine oracle that the day of his death—or rather of entering into that life which alone deserves to be called life—was already drawing near. At that same time he disclosed this to some people in his customary simplicity, though in more obscure words that were later clearly understood; to others he revealed the same thing openly.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How the same man, now a bishop, foretold to the anchorite Hereberct that his death was near.

[Col. 0224B]

There was [Al. adds *quidam*, “a certain”] a priest venerable for the uprightness of his life [Al. adds, “and character”], named Hereberct [Al., Heriberct], who had long been joined to the man of God by a bond of spiritual friendship. Living a solitary life on an island in that great lake from which the sources of the River Derwent emerge, he was accustomed to visit him every year and hear from him continual counsels concerning eternal salvation.

When he heard that Cudberct had come to the city of Lugubalia [Al., Leguraliam] [Note: [Col. 0223D] Lugubalia. In the presence of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, King Ecgfrid gave him at York the land mentioned above. “St Cudberct was given the village of Creca and three miles of land around that village, so that, when going to or returning from York, he might have a residence where he could rest; there he established a dwelling for monks. And because that land was insufficient, he received Lugubalia, called Luel, extending fifteen miles around, as an addition. There, having established a community of nuns, he consecrated the queen after she had received the religious habit, and founded schools for the advancement of divine service. Other landed possessions were also given to him, which it would be lengthy and unnecessary to list here; they are written in the church charters.” Simeon of Durham, I, 9. A charter of these donations copied from the Durham registers, with the names of Theodore and the seven bishops subscribed, is found in Appendix no. 22.], he came as usual, wishing to be kindled more and more toward heavenly desires by his salutary exhortations.

While they mutually intoxicated one another with the cups of heavenly life, the bishop said among other things:

“Remember, brother Hereberct, that now you should ask me whatever you need and speak with me. For after we have departed from one another, we shall no longer see each other face to face in this world of flesh. I am certain that the time of my release is near and that the laying down of my tent is imminent.”

When he heard this, Hereberct fell at his feet and, pouring forth tears with a groan, said:

“I beseech you by the Lord, do not abandon me, but remember your most faithful companion, and ask the heavenly mercy that, just as we have served him together on earth, so we may pass together into heaven to behold his grace. For you know that I have always striven to live at the command of your mouth, and whatever I have done wrong through ignorance or weakness, I have immediately sought to correct according to the test of your will.”

The bishop devoted himself to his prayers and was immediately instructed in spirit that he had obtained [Al. omits *se*, “that he”] from the Lord what he was asking:

“Rise, my brother,” he said, “and do not weep, but rejoice with joy, because the heavenly clemency has granted us what we asked.”

The subsequent course of events confirmed the truth of this promise and prophecy. After departing from one another, they did not see each other again in the body; but, on one and the same day—that is, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April—when they departed from the body, their spirits were immediately joined by a blessed vision of one another and were carried together by angelic ministry to the heavenly kingdom.

But Hereberct was first consumed by a divinely sent illness [Note: [Col. 0225D] Hereberct. See Bede’s *Life of St Cudberct*, chapter 28. On the island in the lake of the River Derwent near Keswick, where Hereberct established his solitary residence, a church was later built in honor of that holy anchorite, and devotion to the place was strengthened by episcopal indulgences. See Appendix no. 23.]. This was, as is credible, an arrangement of the Lord’s mercy, so that if he possessed any deficiency of merit compared with the blessed Cudberct, the pain of a long illness might supply it through the discipline of suffering. Thus, made equal in grace to his intercessor, he might deserve not only to depart from the body at the same time as he did, but also to be received with him into one and the same undivided seat of everlasting blessedness.

The most reverend Father died on the island of Farne, having earnestly asked the brothers that he be buried there, where he had served the Lord for no short time. At last, however, overcome by their prayers, he consented that he should be taken back to the island of Lindisfarne and buried in the church.

After this had been done, the venerable bishop Uilfrid governed the episcopate of that Church for one year, until someone could be chosen and ordained bishop in Cudberct’s place.

Afterward Eadberct was ordained [Al. omits *autem*, “however”] [DCLXXXVIII], a man distinguished both by knowledge of the divine Scriptures [Al. omits “divine”] and by observance of the heavenly commandments, and especially by his practice of almsgiving. In accordance with the Law, he gave the poor every year a tenth not only of his four-footed animals but also of all his crops and fruits, and even of his clothing.

## CHAPTER XXX. How, after eleven years of burial, his body was found free from corruption, and how, not long afterward, his episcopal successor departed from the world.

[DCXCVIII]

The divine dispensation wished to demonstrate more broadly how greatly the man of God Cudberct lived in glory after death, since even before his death his exalted life had been revealed by frequent signs of miracles. After eleven years had passed since his burial, it put into the mind [Al., *animos*, “minds”] of the brothers that they should raise his bones, which [Al., *qui*, “who”] they thought would be found dry after the rest of the body had been consumed and reduced to dust in the manner of the dead [Al., *corpore, reliqua*, “the body, the remaining things,” for *corpore reliquo*]; and they intended to place them in a new coffin, in the same place but above the floor, for the sake of due veneration.

When they reported to their bishop Eadberct that this was their wish, he approved their plan and ordered them to remember to do it on the anniversary of Cudberct’s deposition. They did so. Opening the grave, they found the entire body as though it were still alive: whole, with the joints of its limbs flexible, and much more like someone sleeping than someone dead. All the garments in which it had been clothed also appeared not merely untouched but remarkable for their original freshness and brightness [Al., “clarity”].

When the brothers saw this, they were immediately struck with overwhelming fear and hastened to report to the bishop what they had found. He happened at that time to be living alone in a more remote place, surrounded on every side by the returning waves of the sea. For he was always accustomed to spend the season of Lent there and to pass there the forty days before the Lord’s Nativity in great discipline, prayer, and devotion expressed through tears. In that place his venerable predecessor Cudberct had also served the Lord for some time in seclusion [Al., *secretius*, “more secretly”] before going to the island of Farne.

They brought him a portion of the garments that had surrounded the holy body. He gratefully accepted the gifts and gladly heard of the miracle; indeed, he kissed the garments themselves with wondrous affection, as though they still surrounded his father’s body.

“Put new garments on the body in place of those you have removed,” he said, “and then put it back in the coffin you have prepared. I know with complete certainty that the place will not remain empty for long, for it has been consecrated by such a great grace of heavenly miracle; and blessed is the one to whom the Lord, author and giver of all blessedness, will deign to grant the opportunity of resting there.”

When the bishop had finished these and many similar words with many tears and great remorse [Col. 0226C], speaking even with a trembling tongue, the brothers did as he had ordered. They wrapped the body in a new covering, placed it in a new coffin, and set it above the floor of the sanctuary.

Without delay, the bishop beloved of God, Eadberct, was struck by a severe illness. As the fever of his sickness increased day by day and grew exceedingly grievous, he himself soon afterward—that is, on the day before the Nones of May—departed to the Lord. They placed his body in the tomb of the blessed Father Cudberct and set above it the coffin in which they had placed the incorrupt remains of that same Father. At that place, signs of healings have also occurred several times, bearing witness to the merits of both men; some of them we once committed to memory in the book of his Life. But in this History too we have thought it useful to add one event [Al., *unum quod*, “one thing which”] that recently came to our attention.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How a certain man was healed of paralysis at his tomb [Al., “cured”].

There was in the same monastery a certain brother named Badudegn, who had served for a considerable time in caring for guests. He still survives today, and all the brothers and all the visiting guests testify that he was a man of great piety and religious devotion, submissive to the duty imposed upon him solely for the sake of heavenly reward.

One day, after washing in the sea the linen cloths or blankets that he used in the guesthouse, he was returning home when he was suddenly seized in the middle of the journey by a sudden affliction [Al. adds *corporali*, “bodily”]. He fell to the ground and lay face down for some time, scarcely managing at last to rise. When he did rise, he felt that one half of his body, from head to foot, was weighed down by the weakness of paralysis. Leaning on a staff with the greatest difficulty, he reached home.

The illness gradually increased, and when night came it became more severe, so that, when day returned, he could scarcely rise or walk by himself. Afflicted by this trouble, he formed in his mind a most useful plan: he would reach the church by whatever means he could, enter to the tomb of the most reverend Father Cudberct, and, kneeling there, humbly beseech heavenly mercy either to free him from such an illness, if that were useful for him, or, if divine providence required that he be disciplined longer by such an affliction, to endure the pain inflicted upon him patiently and with a tranquil mind.

He therefore did as he had resolved. Supporting his feeble limbs with a staff, he entered the church and prostrated himself before the body of the man of God. With pious intention he prayed that, through Cudberct’s help, the Lord might be favorable to him. During his prayers, as though released into sleep, he felt—as he was afterward accustomed to relate—that a great and broad hand touched his head on the side where he was suffering. Through that touch, the pain gradually departed from the entire part of his body that had been afflicted, and health followed it down to his feet [Al., “with health following it”].

When this had happened, he immediately awoke, rose completely well, and, again giving thanks to the Lord for his health, told the brothers what had been done for him. While everyone rejoiced with him, he returned to the service he had been accustomed to perform diligently, chastened as though by a scourge and made more careful.

The garments, too, with which the body of Cudberct, dedicated to God, had been clothed, whether while he was alive or afterward when he had died, were themselves not without the grace of healing, as anyone who reads the volume of his Life and Virtues will find.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How another man was recently cured of an eye ailment by his relics.

[Col. 0227D]

Nor should the event that occurred three years ago [Col. 0228A] through his relics [DCCXXVIII], and that has recently been reported to me by the brother on whom it occurred, be passed over in silence.

It happened in the monastery built beside the River Dacore [Note: [Col. 0227D] Dacore. A river flowing into the River Aymot, which rises somewhat higher up from Lake Hulswalter and separates the counties of Westmorland and Cumberland. A tradition still survives concerning an ancient monastery situated on the bank of this river; the village itself retains its name from the river.], from which it received its name. At that time a religious man named Suidberct [Note: [Col. 0228D] Suidberct. He should not rashly be confused with Suidberct, bishop of Werden, concerning whom Bede writes at length below, V, 12.] presided over it by right of an abbot.

There was in it a certain young man whose eyelid had been disfigured by a hideous swelling. As the swelling grew day by day and threatened the destruction of the eye, the physicians tried to soften it by applying medicinal poultices, but they were unsuccessful. Some said that it had to be cut out [Al., “taught/declared that it had to be cut out”]; others forbade this for fear of a greater danger. For a considerable time the aforementioned brother suffered from this affliction, and no human hand could cure the destruction threatening the eye; rather, it increased day by day. Then it happened that, through the grace of divine mercy, he was suddenly healed by the relics of the most holy Father Cudberct.

When the brothers had found [Al., *repererant*, “had found”] his body incorrupt after many years of burial, they had removed a portion of his hair, which, as is customary with relics, they could give or show to friends who requested it as a sign of the miracle.

At that time a certain priest of the same monastery, named Thruidred, possessed a small portion of these relics; he is now abbot of that monastery. One day, when he entered the church and opened the reliquary in order to give a portion of the relics to a friend who had requested it, the young man whose eye was diseased happened also to be in the church.

After the priest had given the friend as much of the relics as he wished, he gave the remainder to the young man so that he could put it back in its place. But the young man, prompted by a salutary inspiration, took the hairs from the holy head and applied them to his diseased eyelid. For some time he tried by this application to press down and soften the troublesome swelling. Having done so, he placed the relics back in their reliquary as he had been instructed, believing that his eye would quickly be healed by the hairs of the man of God which had touched it [Al., “which had been brought to it”].

Nor indeed [Al. adds *enim*, “for”] was his faith deceived. It was, as he was accustomed to relate, approximately the second hour of the day [Al., *horam . . . secundam*, “the second hour,” for *hora circiter secunda*]. But while he considered and carried out the other things that the day required, when the sixth hour of that day was approaching, he suddenly touched his eye and found it, together with the eyelid, so completely healed that it was as though no disfigurement or swelling had ever appeared there.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0229]

## CHAPTER ONE. How Oidiluald [Note: [Col. 0229D] Oidiluald. He succeeded St Cudberct in the solitary life in 697 and, having died after twelve years, in 699, was deemed worthy of a place in the Martyrology on 23 March and in the Benedictine tables on 8 Ides of March. See the final chapter of the prose Life of St Cudberct and chapter 45 of the metrical Life.] [Al., Oidilvaldus], Cudberct’s successor in the anchoritic life, calmed a storm by prayer when the brothers were in danger at sea.

[Col. 0229A]

[DCLXXXVII.] The venerable Oidiluald succeeded the man of God Cuthbert in the practice of the solitary life that Cuthbert had led on the island of Farne before his episcopate. Oidiluald had spent many years in the monastery called Inhrypum, and, having received the priestly office, himself consecrated it by deeds worthy of his rank. To make the nature of his merit and life clearer, I shall relate one of his miracles, told me by one of the brothers for whom and among whom it was performed—namely, Gudfrid, a venerable servant and priest of Christ, who later presided as abbot over the brothers of the same church of Lindisfarne in which he had been educated.

“I came,” he said, “with two other brothers to the island of Farne, wishing to speak with the most reverend Father Oidiluald. When, refreshed by his conversation and having sought his blessing, we were returning home, suddenly, while we were in the middle of the sea, the calm weather in which we had been sailing was broken. Such a great and savage storm arose that we could make no progress either by sail or by oar, and could hope for nothing but death.

“After struggling for a long time in vain against the wind and the sea, we finally looked behind us, wondering whether by some effort we might regain even the island from which we had set out. We found ourselves shut in on every side by an equally violent storm, with no hope of saving ourselves remaining. But when we raised our eyes farther away, we saw on the island of Farne the Father Oidiluald, most devoted to God, coming out of his hiding place and watching our journey. Having heard the crashing of the storm and the raging ocean, he had gone out to see what had happened to us. When he saw us in difficulty and despair, he bent his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to pray for our life and safety.

“When he completed his prayer, he simultaneously calmed the swelling waters, so completely that, when the violence of the storm had ceased everywhere, favorable winds escorted us across the level surface of the sea all the way to land. When we had escaped to shore and had also carried our little boat out of the waves, the same storm—which had been silent for a short while for our sake—soon returned and did not cease raging violently throughout the entire day. Thus it was plainly shown that the brief interval of calm that had occurred had been granted from heaven, through the prayers of the man of God, for the sake of our escape.”

The same man of God remained on the island of Farne for twelve years and died there. He was buried, however, on the island of Lindisfarne, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, beside the bodies of the bishops mentioned above. These events took place in the time of King Aldfrith [699], who ruled the people of Northumbria for nineteen years after his brother Ecgfrith.

## CHAPTER II. How Bishop John healed a mute and scabious man by blessing him

At the beginning of this reign, after Bishop Eata had died [685], the holy man John assumed the episcopate of the church of Hagustald. Those who knew him intimately are accustomed to relate many miracles of his virtues, especially the most reverend and truthful man Bercthun, formerly his deacon and now abbot of the monastery called Inderauuda—that is, “in the forest of the Deiri.” We have thought it useful to commit some of these to memory.

There was a secluded dwelling, surrounded by a sparse woodland within an enclosure, not far from the church of Hagustald—that is, separated from it by about a mile and a half, with the river Tyne flowing between. It possessed a cemetery of Saint Michael the Archangel. Whenever the season offered a suitable opportunity, and especially during Lent, the man of God used to stay there with a few companions and devote himself quietly to prayer and reading.

When, at the beginning of one Lent, he arrived there intending to stay, he ordered his attendants to look for some poor person burdened by especially serious illness or poverty, whom they could keep with them during those days in order to give alms. He always used to do this.

There was in a nearby village a certain mute young man known to the bishop, for he frequently used to come before him to receive alms. He could never utter even a single word. He also had such severe scabies and scaling on his head that no hair could ever grow on the upper part of his head; only rough hair seemed to stand around its circumference.

The bishop therefore ordered him to be brought and a small hut to be built for him within the enclosure of the dwelling, where he could live and receive his daily allowance from them. When one week of Lent had been completed, on the following Sunday he ordered the poor man to enter his presence. Once he had entered, he ordered him to put out his tongue from his mouth and show it to him. Taking him by the chin, he impressed the sign of the holy cross upon his tongue, then commanded him to draw the signed tongue back into his mouth and speak.

“Say some word,” he said. “Say *Gae* [or *Gea*; elsewhere *Gie*], which in the language of the English is a word of affirmation and assent—that is, ‘yes.’”

Immediately, when the bond of his tongue had been loosed, the man said what he had been commanded to say. The bishop added the names of the letters.

“Say A,” he said.

The man said A.

“Say B.”

The man said this too.

As he responded to each individual name of the letters spoken by the bishop, the bishop added syllables and words for him to say. When he answered every one of them in sequence, the bishop instructed him to speak longer sentences, and he did so. Nor did he cease throughout that entire day and the following night, for as long as he was able to remain awake, from speaking and showing others the secret thoughts and wishes that previously he had never been able to reveal.

He became like the man who had long been lame and was healed by the apostles Peter and John: leaping up, he stood and walked, and entered the temple with them, walking, leaping, and praising God—rejoicing, of course, in the use of his feet, of which he had been deprived for so long.

The bishop, rejoicing with him in his restored health, ordered a physician also to attend to healing the scabious condition of his head.

The physician did as he had been ordered. With the help of the bishop’s blessing and prayers, a handsome growth of hair appeared together with the healing of the skin. The young man, who had previously been deformed, poor, and mute, became clear-featured and ready in speech, with beautifully curling hair.

Rejoicing in the health he had received, and although the bishop offered him a place among his household, he preferred to return home.

## CHAPTER III. How he healed a sick girl by prayer

[DCLXXXVI.] The same Bercthun related another miracle of the aforementioned bishop. When the most reverend man Wilfrid had been restored to the episcopate of the church of Hagustald after a long exile, and the same John, after the death of Bosa, a man of great holiness and humility, had been substituted for him as bishop at York, John himself once came to a monastery of virgins at a place called Uetadun, where Heriburg was then abbess.

“When we arrived there,” he said, “and were received with great joy by everyone, the abbess informed us that one of the virgins, who was her own daughter, was suffering from a very serious illness. She had recently been bled in the arm, and while she was engaged in some activity she was struck by a sudden painful illness. As the pain quickly increased, the wounded arm became still more severely affected and turned into a swelling, so that it could scarcely be encircled by two hands. She lay in bed and, because of the extremity of the pain, appeared already to be dying.

“The abbess therefore asked the bishop to enter and deign to bless her, for she believed that the girl would immediately be better through his blessing or touch. He asked when the girl had been bled. When he learned that it had been during the fourth lunar phase, he said:

“‘You acted very foolishly and ignorantly in bleeding her during the fourth phase of the moon. I remember that Archbishop Theodore of blessed memory used to say that bleeding is quite dangerous at the time when both the light of the moon and the surge of the ocean are increasing. And what can I do for the girl if she is going to die?’

“But she entreated him more insistently on behalf of the daughter whom she dearly loved—for she had decided to make her abbess in her place—and at last she obtained permission for him to enter the sick girl.

“He therefore entered with me and went to the virgin, who was lying, as I have said, bound by great pain. Her arm had swollen so much that it had no flexion whatsoever at the elbow. Standing beside her, he said a prayer over her, blessed her, and went out.

“When afterward, at the proper hour, we sat down to table, someone came and called me outside, saying: ‘Quoenburg—for that was the virgin’s name—asks that you return to her as quickly as possible.’

“When I did so, I found her, as I entered, with a brighter face and looking like someone in good health. As I sat beside her, she said: ‘Shall we ask for something to drink?’

“‘Yes,’ I said, ‘I should like that very much, if you are able.’

“When a cup was brought, we both drank. Then she began to tell me that, from the moment the bishop had completed his prayer and blessing for her and had gone out, she had immediately begun to feel better. Although she had not yet recovered her former strength, all the pain—both that in her arm, where it had been more intense, and that throughout her body—had been completely removed, as though the bishop himself had carried it out with him, even though the swelling in her arm still appeared to remain.

“When we left, the disappearance of the dreadful swelling immediately followed the expulsion of the bodily pain. The virgin, rescued from death and suffering, together with all the others who were there, gave praise to the Lord and Savior and continued to do so.”

## CHAPTER IV. How he healed a count’s sick wife with blessed water

The same abbot also related another miracle of the aforementioned bishop, not very different from this one, saying:

“There was a village belonging to a certain count named Puch, not far from our monastery—that is, about two miles away. His wife had been confined by a most grievous illness for nearly forty days, so that for three weeks she could not be carried out of the room in which she lay.

“At that time it happened that the man of God was summoned there by the count to dedicate a church. When the church had been dedicated, the count asked him to enter his house for dinner. The bishop refused, saying that he ought to return to the monastery, which was nearby. But the count pressed his request more urgently and even vowed that he would give alms to the poor, provided that the bishop would deign to enter his house that day and break his fast.

“I too joined him in asking, promising that I would give alms for the nourishment of the needy, if he would enter the count’s house to dine and give his blessing. With difficulty and only after much delay, we obtained this from him, and entered to refresh ourselves.

“The bishop had sent to the sick woman some of the blessed water that he had consecrated for the dedication of the church, by one of the brothers who had come with me. He ordered him to give her some to taste and, wherever he learned that she was suffering the greatest pain, to wash her with that same water.

“When this had been done, the woman immediately rose healthy. She felt not only that she had been freed from her long illness but also that she had recovered the strength she had lost long before. She offered a cup to the bishop and to us. She continued to serve drink to all of us until the meal was finished, imitating the mother-in-law of blessed Peter the apostle, who, after being tormented by the burning of fever, rose at the touch of the Lord’s hand and, having received health and strength at once, ministered to them.”

## CHAPTER V. How he likewise recalled a count’s son from death by prayer

At another time, when he had been summoned to dedicate a church belonging to a count named Addi, and had completed the requested ministry, the same count asked him to enter and visit one of his sons, who was suffering from a very severe illness. Every function of his limbs had completely failed, and he appeared to be on the point of death. A coffin had already been prepared for him, in which his body was to be placed once he had died.

The man also added tears to his prayers, earnestly begging the bishop to enter and pray for the boy, because his life was very necessary to him. He believed, moreover, that if the bishop were willing to lay his hand upon him and bless him, he would immediately begin to improve.

The bishop therefore entered and saw the boy, surrounded by mourners, already close to death. The coffin in which he was to be buried had been placed beside him. The bishop said a prayer and blessed him. As he went out, he spoke the customary words of consolation:

“May you recover well, and quickly.”

After this, while they were sitting at table, the boy sent to his lord, asking him to send him a cup of wine because he was thirsty. The father rejoiced greatly that the boy was able to drink and sent him a cup of wine blessed by the bishop. As soon as the boy drank it, he immediately rose. When the stupor of his illness had been dispelled, he dressed himself in his own clothes, went out, entered among them, and greeted the bishop and his guests, saying that he too would be glad to eat and drink with them.

They ordered him to sit down with them for the meal, rejoicing greatly at his recovery. He sat, ate, drank, and rejoiced, conducting himself like one of the other guests. He lived for many years afterward and remained in the same state of health that he had received.

The aforementioned abbot says that this miracle did not occur in his own presence but was reported to him by those who had been present.

## CHAPTER VI. How he recalled his cleric, crushed by a fall, from death through prayer and blessing

Nor, I think, should this be passed over in silence: the servant of Christ Herebald [or Heritbald] is accustomed to relate a miracle performed by the bishop upon himself. At that time Herebald lived among the bishop’s clergy; now he presides as abbot over the monastery beside the mouth of the river Tyne.

“I found,” he said, “that his life, insofar as human beings are permitted to judge it—for I knew it very well from personal experience—was in every respect worthy of a bishop. I also learned through many other events, and especially through my own experience, what sort of merit he possessed before the eternal Witness [or Judge]. For he recalled me, so to speak, from the very threshold of death and restored me to the way of life by his prayer and blessing.

“When I was in the earliest period of my youth and lived among his clergy, assigned to the study of reading and singing but not yet restraining my mind completely from youthful pleasures, it happened one day that, traveling with him, we came upon a level, broad road suitable for racing horses. The young men who were with him, especially the laymen, began asking the bishop to allow them to test their horses against one another in a faster race.

“At first he refused, saying that what they desired was pointless. But at last, overcome by the unanimous insistence of many, he said: ‘Do it, if you wish, but let Herebald abstain entirely from that contest.’

“I myself begged more earnestly that I too might be allowed to compete with them—for I trusted the horse that he himself had given me, an excellent animal—but I could not obtain permission.

“Yet when, as I watched, they repeatedly raced back and forth before the bishop and returned with their horses urged into a gallop, I could not restrain myself, overcome by a reckless spirit. Although he had forbidden me, I joined those who were playing and began racing my horse with them.

“As I did so, I heard him behind me say with a groan: ‘Oh, what a great grief you are causing me by riding in this way!’ I heard him, but nevertheless persisted in what I had begun, despite his prohibition.

“Before long, as the spirited horse leaped with great force over a hollow in the road, I fell and immediately lost all sensation and movement, as though I were dying. At that place there was a stone level with the ground and covered by a thin layer of turf; no other stone could be found in the entire flat expanse of that field. By chance—or rather by divine providence, to punish the guilt of my disobedience—I struck this stone with my head and with the hand that I had thrust beneath my head as I fell. My thumb was broken, the joint of my skull was dislocated, and, as I said, I became entirely like a dead man.

“Since I could not move, they set up a tent there for me to lie in. It was about the seventh hour of the day. From then until evening I remained quiet and apparently dead. Then I revived slightly, was carried home by my companions, and remained silent throughout the night.

“I was vomiting blood, because my internal organs had been violently shaken by the fall. The bishop grieved deeply over my accident and death, for he loved me with special affection. That night he did not wish to stay with his clergy according to custom. Instead, he remained alone in prayer and passed the night in vigil, beseeching heavenly mercy, as I believe, for my recovery.

“Early in the morning he entered to see me. After saying a prayer over me, he called me by name and, as though waking me from a deep sleep, asked whether I knew who was speaking to me.

“I opened my eyes and said: ‘Yes, you are my beloved bishop.’

“‘Can you live?’ he asked.

“‘I can,’ I replied, ‘through your prayers, if the Lord wills.’

“He placed his hand upon my head and, speaking words of blessing, returned to prayer. After a short while he came back to see me and found me sitting up and already able to speak. He began to ask me—prompted, as soon became clear, by divine inspiration—whether I knew without doubt that I had been baptized.
