“I answered that I knew this without any doubt, because I had been washed in the saving font for the remission of sins. I also told him the name of the priest by whom I knew I had been baptized.

“‘If you were baptized by this priest,’ he said, ‘you were not properly baptized. I know him, and because, although he had been ordained a priest, he was wholly unable, owing to the slowness of his understanding, to learn the ministry of catechizing or baptizing, I ordered him entirely to cease presuming to exercise a ministry that he could not perform according to the rule.’

“After saying this, he himself immediately undertook to catechize me. When he breathed upon my face, I at once felt myself becoming better.

“He summoned a physician and ordered him to set and bind the dislocated joint of my skull. So quickly did I recover after receiving his blessing that the following day I mounted a horse and traveled with him to another place. Not long afterward I was completely healed and was also washed with the water of life.”

The same John remained in the episcopate for thirty-three years. Then, ascending to the heavenly kingdom, he was buried in the portico of Saint Peter, in his monastery called “In the Forest of the Deiri,” in the year 721 from the Lord’s incarnation. Since he had become less capable of administering the episcopate because of advanced old age, he withdrew to the aforementioned monastery after appointing his own priest Wilfrid to the episcopate of the church of York, and there completed his life in God by conduct worthy of him [718].

## CHAPTER VII. How Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, came to Rome to be baptized; and how his successor Ine also devoutly visited the thresholds of the blessed apostles

In the third year of King Aldfrith [688], Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, after ruling his people vigorously for two years, abandoned his authority for the sake of the Lord and the eternal kingdom and came to Rome. He desired to obtain this singular glory: that he might be washed in the font of baptism at the thresholds of the blessed apostles, for he had learned that through this alone the entrance to heavenly life was open to the human race.

At the same time, he hoped that, once baptized, he might immediately be freed from the flesh and pass, already purified, to eternal joys. Both things were fulfilled as he had determined in his mind, with the Lord’s assistance.

When he arrived there, while Sergius was serving as pope, he was baptized on Holy Saturday of Easter in the year 689 from the Lord’s incarnation. While he was still wearing the white baptismal garment, he was seized by illness and, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, was released from the flesh and joined to the kingdom [or fellowship] of the blessed in heaven.

At the time of his baptism, the aforementioned pope also gave him the name Peter, so that he might be joined even in name to the most blessed prince of the apostles, whose most sacred body he had come from the ends of the earth to venerate, instructed by devoted love. He was also buried in Peter’s church. At the pope’s command, an epitaph was written on his monument, so that the memory of his devotion might remain fixed through the ages and so that readers and hearers, seeing the example of his deed, might be kindled to religious devotion.

It was written in this manner:

> The heights, the wealth, the offspring, the powerful kingdoms, the triumphs,  
> Spoils, nobles, walls, fortresses, homes—  
> Whatever the virtue of his fathers, and whatever he himself had gathered,  
> Caedwalla, mighty in arms, left behind for the love of God,  
> That he might see Peter and, as a king, become a guest in Peter’s seat,  
> From whose font the gracious man might drink pure waters,  
> And from whose radiant stream drink in the splendid light,  
> From which life-giving brilliance flows everywhere.
>
> Receiving eagerly the rewards of renewed life,  
> He changed his barbarian fury—and hence his name—  
> And, converted, he joyfully changed his own name as well; Sergius the bishop  
> Ordered that he be called Peter, so that the father himself,  
> Cleansing him in the font of rebirth by Christ’s grace,  
> Might immediately bear him away to the citadel of heaven.
>
> Wonderful is the king’s faith! Most great is the mercy of Christ,  
> Whose purpose no one can approach!
>
> For he came safely from the farthest region of Britain,  
> Through various peoples, across straits and along roads;  
> He saw the city of Romulus and gazed upon the venerable temple,  
> Carrying the mystical gifts of Peter.
>
> White among the sheep of Christ, he will enter into their fellowship;  
> For in the body he possesses a tomb, but in mind he holds heaven.
>
> You may rather believe that he exchanged the insignia of his scepters,  
> Since you see that he earned the kingdom of Christ.

Here lies Caedwalla, also called Peter, king of the Saxons, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction. He lived approximately thirty years, during the reign of our most devout lord Justinian Augustus, in the fourth year of his consulship, while the apostolic man, our lord Pope Sergius, was pontiff in the second year of his pontificate.

When Caedwalla went to Rome [725], Ine, of royal descent, succeeded him in the kingdom. After holding authority over that people for thirty-seven years, he too abandoned his kingdom [or authority], entrusted it to younger men, and went to the thresholds of the blessed apostles while Gregory was serving as pontiff. He desired to spend some time as a pilgrim on earth near the holy places, so that he might deserve to be received more familiarly by the saints in heaven. During those times many from the English people—nobles and commoners, laymen and clergy, men and women—were accustomed to do the same eagerly.

## CHAPTER VIII. How, after Theodore’s death, Berctwald received the rank of archbishop and, among the many whom he ordained, made Tobias, a most learned man, bishop of the church of Rochester

In the year immediately following that in which Caedwalla died at Rome—that is, in the year 690 from the Lord’s incarnation—the archbishop Theodore, of blessed memory, an old man and full of days, died at the age of eighty-eight. He used to foretell to his people that he would live to that number of years, having learned it long before through the revelation of a dream.

He had remained in the episcopate for twenty-two years and was buried in the church of Saint Peter, where the bodies of all the bishops of Canterbury are deposited. Concerning him, as well as his companions of the same rank, it can rightly and truthfully be said that their bodies are buried in peace and that their name will live through generation after generation.

To speak briefly, during the time of his episcopate the English Church began to advance spiritually as it had never before been able to do. His person, life, age, and death are publicly and clearly revealed to all who come there by the thirty-four heroic verses of the epitaph on his monument. Its first verses are these:

> Here in the sacred tomb rests, with his body, the bishop  
> Whom the Greek tongue now calls Theodore.  
> Prince of pontiffs, blessed and supreme priest,  
> He explained clear teachings to his disciples.

Its final verses are these:

> For the nineteenth day of September had arrived,  
> When the spirit departed from the prison of the flesh,  
> Happily ascending to the fellowship of the new and blessed life,  
> Joined with the angelic citizens in the citadel of heaven.

### Editorial notes and textual apparatus

**[Col. 0229D] Berthun.** Berthun was for a long time deacon to St John the bishop, and was afterwards made by St John abbot of the monastery of Inderauuda. In extreme old age he died on the Ides of May, about A.D. 740 according to Capgrave, or 733 according to Leland’s *Collectanea*, and was buried in his monastery. In time his relics were translated and placed beside St John’s shrine at his altar in the church of Beverley. His name is written among the saints on 15 May in the Martyrology.

**[Col. 0230D] Dwelling.** This dwelling, with its oratory and cemetery, stood on a hill overhanging the bank of the river Tyne, called in English Erneshow and in Latin Eagle Hill, and was situated to the north. For more, see Richard, Prior of Hexham, *X Scriptores*, p. 291.

**[Col. 0231D] Uetadun.** Today Watton, that is, “wet town,” from the waters and marshes by which it is surrounded. It was an ancient monastery in the eastern part of the province of York, in which the miracle of this chapter was performed by Bishop John. Long ruined, it was restored for the use of the Gilbertines by Eustace, son of John, in King Stephen’s time. On this monastery see also *X Scriptores*, p. 415, together with the long account of a miracle of Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx.

**[Col. 0232D] Puch.** The estate of this count was called South Burton, two miles from Beverley. His daughter Yolfrid became a nun at Beverley; as this chapter shows, St John freed her mother from a most acute illness. Puch gave the manor of Walkington with his daughter. Yolfrid died on 13 March 742, and her bones were buried at Beverley. The manor of Walkington still belongs to the bishop of Durham.

**[Col. 0234D] Addi.** This count was of North Burton; in the time of St John the archbishop he gave that estate, together with the advowson of its church, to the church of Beverley.

**[Col. 0235D] “Remained.”** Historians maintain that John remained bishop of York for thirty-three years and, when age made him less equal to his office, retired to his monastery of Beverley, where he died three years later. Although Bede seems here to assert that John died immediately after the thirty-third year of his episcopate, this is not to be understood too strictly. When Wilfrid received the episcopate, that is, in 686, Bosa died and John was substituted in his place (V.3). Thus, reckoning the first year of the episcopate, the thirty-third must fall in 718, and three further years are allowed for his retirement, until 721, when he died.

**[Col. 0236D] Caedwalla.** Repenting of his raids in Kent and elsewhere, he went to Rome. Bromton, *X Scriptores*, p. 742. He is said to have made two charters: the earlier for Wilfrid in 680, granting Pagham with its appurtenances; the later for Theodore and the church of Christ, Canterbury, in 687, granting Geddinge and Wdetun. *Evidentiae Ecclesiae Christi Cantuariensis*, *X Scriptores*, p. 2207.

**[Col. 0236D] West Saxons.** They were formerly called Gewisse. See the note at III.7. Should anyone prefer another explanation, let him know that the Gewisse are also derived from Gewis, the great-grandfather of Cerdic. Cerdic was son of Elesa, grandson of Esla, and great-grandson of Gewis.

**[Col. 0237C] “Most sacred …”** Another reading has “most holy body”; another continues, “through long distances of places, instructed by devout love.” The following words have the variant, “might bear even his name.”

**[Col. 0237C] “Ablatum.”** The printed edition has *albatum* (“whitened”); another reading has *ablutum* (“washed”).

**[Col. 0237C] “Safe.”** Another reading is *hospes*, “a guest.”

**[Col. 0237C–D] “King of the Saxons.”** Sanderus thinks “king of the Britons” should be read, and Baronius supports him, adding three Caedwallas mentioned by Bede: the first, who killed Edwin (II.20); the second, who killed Æthelwealh (IV.15); and a third, who succeeded this Caedwalla, in the same place. But here he was misled by the error of manuscripts, which put *Is* in place of Ine, and Baronius took this to be a third Caedwalla. There were therefore only two Caedwallas: one king of the Britons (II.20), the other king of the Saxons. He was not a Saxon merely in title because, as Baronius supposes, he defeated the Saxons, but because he was descended from the royal house of the Gewisse, as Bede expressly states (IV.15). See also the note at the chapter just cited.

**[Col. 0237D] “Succeeded.”** The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, followed by Florence of Worcester, states that Ine went to Rome in 728; but both Bede and the Chronicle establish that Ine succeeded Caedwalla in 688 and set out for Rome after a reign of thirty-seven years. He must therefore have gone to Rome in 725.

**[Col. 0237D] “Of royal descent.”** Ine was son of Cenred; Cenred, of Ceolwald; Ceolwald, of Cuthwulf; Cuthwulf, of Cuthwine; Cuthwine, of Ceolma; Ceolma, of Cyneric; Cyneric, of Creoda; and Creoda, of Cerdic.

**[Col. 0237D–0238C] “He too, abandoning … to younger men.”** Æthelhard, Ine’s successor, and the atheling Oswald, against whom Æthelhard fought in that same year. The common editions here make a separate chapter and heading: “On the death of Archbishop Theodore.”

**[Col. 0238C] “Died.”** After recording Theodore’s death, Baronius adds that Abbot Hadrian died at the same time. Hadrian did indeed come to Britain with Theodore, but went to heaven much later: Bede testifies (V.21) that he died in the year following Wilfrid’s death, namely 710.

**[Col. 0238C–D] Theodore.** “He stirred the will of the faithful to build churches in cities and villages, to define parishes, and procured royal consent for these measures: so that those competent to build churches on their own land might enjoy their perpetual patronage; but if they built churches within the bounds of another’s lordship, the owners of that land should be recognized as patrons.” — Elmham.

**[Col. 0238D] “In which [the bodies] of all …”** The archbishops before Theodore were not buried in the church itself, but in its northern portico (II.3). Archbishops were buried in this church of St Peter until Archbishop Cuthbert obtained free burial in Christ Church from the Roman pontiff and King Eadberht in 758. He therefore built near Christ Church a basilica in honour of St John the Baptist, where he and his successors, except Lambert, were buried. *X Scriptores*, pp. 1295, 1772, 2210; Spelman, *Concilia*, I, p. 289.

**[Col. 0239B] “Tomb.”** The body of St Theodore, with St Augustine’s and other relics, was raised in 1091, on 6 September, according to the monk Goscelin, whose words in Book II of the *Translation*, ch. 27, are: “When the lid of the tomb of the most renowned Theodore was removed in the translation, its fragrance abundantly satisfied everyone, so that this delight even burst forth into the brothers’ cloister. He lay as he had been placed at the beginning, with the unbroken appearance of a metropolitan priest, clothed in a pall and only a monk’s cowl. Such was the grace that one would have thought the flesh still sound and living.”

**[Col. 0239C] “Prison.”** Another reading is *claustro*, “from the enclosure.”

**Alternative readings (Al.), in source order.** *ipse* for *ipsi*, “he himself”; *tempestas hiemis*, “a storm of winter,” for *tempestatis hiems*, “the winter-storm”; omission of *nobis*, “for us”; *deprecaturus*, “to entreat,” for *precaturus*, “to pray”; omission of *multum*, “violently”; *esset*, “was,” for *est*, “is”; *itaque*, “therefore,” for *autem*, “however”; addition of *est*, “died”; *Adfridi* for *Aldfridi*; “eight” for “nineteen” years; omission of *et scabiosum*, “and scabious,” in Chapter II; *Hujus*, “of this,” for *Cujus*, “of which”; addition of *autem*, “however”; *posset*, “might,” for *possent*, “might [plural]”; *proferre*, “utter,” for *profari*, “speak”; *eo*, “from him,” for *eis*, “from them”; “two miles” for “about two miles”; omission of *in*, “into”; *proximum*, “nearest” [OCR punctuation in the source is defective], for *proxime*, “nearby”; “of all the limbs” for “of every function of the limbs”; *mei cranii*, “of my skull,” with omission of *mihi*, “for me,” for *emicranii*, “of my skull”; *At*, “but,” for *Et*, “and”; *ad me revertens*, “returning to me,” for *me revisens*, “visiting me again”; *Cedualla* for *Caedualla*; “assisting” for “helping”; addition of *est*, “was released”; “fellowship” for “kingdom”; addition of *scriptum est, ut*, “it was written, so that”; *Cedual* for *Caedual*; *ejus*, “his,” for *et*, “and,” before “fourth year of the consulship”; *domino* for *domno*, both “lord”; *Hii* for *Ini*; “authority” for “kingdom”; *junioribus* for *juvenioribus*; *venientibus*, “coming,” for *advenientibus*, “arriving.”

[Col. 0240A] [Note: [Col. 0239C] “He succeeded.” The common manuscripts place here the ninth chapter with its heading, as above, chapter 8.] Berctuald succeeded Theodore in the bishopric. [Note: [Col. 0239C] “Berctuald.” The Saxon Chronicle, Polydore Vergil, and others call this man the first archbishop from among the English, making all his predecessors Italians or Romans; but this is contrary to Bede’s authority, who states at III.20 that Deusdedit was of the people of the West Saxons, and at IV.1 that Theodore was born at Tarsus in Cilicia. William of Malmesbury reports that Berctuald first held the abbacy of Glastonbury and afterward that of the monastery at Racuulf. Gale, *Scriptores*, XV, p. 308. He received the pallium from Pope Vitalian. *X Scriptores*, p. 1640. Ualdheri, bishop of London, sent this archbishop a letter concerning the disputes between the king of the West Saxons and the rulers of his own country. See it, copied from the Cottonian book entitled *Augustus II*, in Appendix no. 24. Another Berctuald, or Beorthuald, is mentioned by Heddie, chapter 39, as the son of King Ethelred’s brother.] He had been abbot in a monastery [Al.: “a certain monastery”] situated beside the northern mouth of the river [Note: [Col. 0239D] “Genlada.” Today, the Inlade.] Genlada [Al. adds: “which”], [Note: [Col. 0239D] “Racuulf.” A town once called Regulbium by the Romans, concerning which see John Battely’s *Antiquitates Rutupinae*; it was called Raculfminster by the Saxons and is now called Reculver. Around the same time that Æthelberht gave Augustine his court and built the palace of Racuulf for himself and his successors, a monastery was also built there; its last abbot was Wenred. *Monumenta Anglicana*, vol. I, p. 26. But according to the Saxon Chronicle, in the year 669 King Ecgberht gave Racuulf to the priest Bass, so that he might build a monastery there.] called Racuulf: a man himself learned in the knowledge of the Scriptures and also thoroughly instructed in ecclesiastical and monastic disciplines, although by no means comparable with his predecessor. He was indeed elected to the bishopric in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 692, [Note: [Col. 0240B] “Second.” The Lichfield Canon gives “first,” but incorrectly.] on the first day of July, while Uictred and [Note: [Col. 0240C] “Suaebhard.” Who this man was is uncertain. Thorn says that he violently seized the kingdom of Kent; but Matthew of Westminster reports that he was Uictred’s brother, and Florence of Worcester, after saying that Withred had been strengthened in the kingdom, adds that Suebheard held part of the kingdom with him. Yet if Suebheard held part of the realm by force, it is scarcely possible that the other was called “strengthened in the kingdom.” It is therefore probable that they were brothers and administered the government amicably with their combined strength. This man gave Abbess Eabba forty-four holdings at Insudaneye and twelve holdings at Sturreye; also land of two ploughlands at Sturie and of three ploughlands at Bodesham. *X Scriptores*, pp. 1770 and 2231.] Suaebhard ruling in Kent [Al.: “Uictred and Suebbard”]. He was ordained in the following year, on the third day before the Kalends of July, by Godwine, metropolitan bishop [Note: [Col. 0240D] “Of the Gauls.” Some read “of the Welsh” here incorrectly. For Bede expressly says at V.12 that Berctuald crossed the sea to be ordained, though not by Pope Sergius, as Baronius writes, but by Godwine, bishop of the Gauls.] of the Gauls; and he took his seat in his own see on the day before the Kalends of September, on a Sunday. Among the many bishops whom he ordained, he also consecrated Tobias in place of Gebmund, bishop of the Church of Rochester, who had died. [Note: [Col. 0240D] “Gebmund.” In what year he died is uncertain. The Saxon Chronicle, Florence of Worcester, Matthew of Westminster, and others declare that he died in 693, which seems true: for if Gebmund had survived at that time, Berctuald might perhaps not have crossed the sea, but would rather have received consecration from him. It is also certain that his successor Tobias attended the Council of Baccanceld in 694. On the other hand, Gebmund is said to have attended the Council of Berghamstede in 696, and a privilege of Uictred from 696 survives in which he is mentioned. Warthon, however, gives no weight to this council or privilege. *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I. For my part, I remain uncertain what judgment to make in this matter.]

[Col. 0241A] He was a man learned in Latin, Greek, and the Saxon language, and variously [Al.: “with varied”] equipped with learning.

## CHAPTER IX

How the holy man Ecgberct wished to come to Germany to preach but was unable; and how Uictberct did come there, but, since he too accomplished nothing, returned again to Ireland, from which he had come.

At that time [689] the venerable and in every way most honorably named servant and priest of Christ, Ecgberct, [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Ecgberct.” He is commemorated on 24 April, as can be seen in the Roman Martyrology and others. Around the year 689 he planned to go to Frisia. Suidberct was ordained in 693, V.11. Uilbrord and his companions came to Frisia in 692, V.10. Uictberct preached unsuccessfully in Frisia for two years, that is, in 690 and 691. A vision therefore prevented Ecgberct, who sent Uictberct, from going to Frisia around the year 689.] whom we have related as living the life of a pilgrim in the island of Ireland in order to attain his homeland in heaven [Note: [Col. 0241D] “We have related.” See III.27.], resolved in his mind to benefit many; that is, having undertaken an apostolic work, to commit the word of God by evangelizing to some of those nations which had not yet heard it. [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Which had not yet.” Yet in the year 603 a certain Englishman named Offo, descended from royal blood, preached the faith among the Germans. Spelman, *Councils*, I, 126. Wilfrid, deprived of his bishopric around 679 and on his way to Rome, was driven by a west wind into Frisia, where he preached Christ, V.20.] He knew that there were very many peoples in Germany from whom the English—or Saxons, who now inhabit Britain—were known to have derived their race and origin; hence they are still corruptly called Garmani [Al.: “Germani”] by the neighboring people, the Britons. They are the Frisians, Rugians, Danes, Huns [Al.: “Danes, Huns”], the ancient Saxons, and the Boructuarians. There are also many other peoples in those regions who still serve pagan rites. The aforesaid soldier of Christ intended to go to them by sailing around Britain, if perhaps he might rescue some of them from Satan and transfer them to Christ; or, if this could not be done, he considered going to Rome to see and venerate the thresholds of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ.

[Col. 0241C] But heavenly revelations and events alike prevented him from accomplishing any of these things. For when he had chosen very energetic companions, suitable for preaching the word, distinguished alike in action and learning, and had prepared everything that seemed necessary for travelers by sea, one morning a brother came to him—a former disciple in Britain and minister of God’s beloved priest Boisil [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Boisil.” “On 1 July: In Britain, the burial of the blessed Boisil, priest and confessor.” Durham Martyrology.]—who had been prior of the monastery of Mailros under Abbot Eata, as we related above [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Above.” See IV.27.], and reported a vision that had appeared to him that very night:

“When,” he said, “after completing the morning hymns I had laid my limbs down on my bed [Al.: “in bed”], and a light sleep had come upon me, my former master and most loving foster-father Boisil appeared and asked me whether I could recognize him. I replied: ‘Yes; you are Boisil.’ But he said: ‘I have come for this purpose, to bring Ecgberct the answer of the Lord and Savior; yet you must come to him as my messenger. Tell him, therefore, that he cannot fulfill the journey he has planned. For it is God’s will that he go instead to the monasteries of Columba to teach.’”

Columba was the first teacher of the Christian faith among the northern Picts beyond the mountains, and the first founder of the monastery on the island of Iona, which for a long time remained venerable among many peoples of the Scots and Picts. This Columba is now called Columcell by some, the name being formed from *cella* and *Columba*. [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Columba.” Concerning him and the conversion of the Picts, see III.4, where it is noted that, when he was seventy-seven years old, he was buried around the year 597; he was therefore born around 520. His nativity is celebrated on 5 June.]

When Ecgberct heard the words of the vision, he ordered the brother who had reported it not to tell anyone else, lest the vision perhaps prove deceptive. He himself, silently considering the matter, feared that it was true; yet he did not wish to cease preparing the journey by which he intended to go teach the nations.

A few days later the aforesaid brother came to him again, saying that Boisil had appeared to him in a vision that night after he had completed Matins [Al.: “after Matins had been completed”], and had said:

“Why did you tell Ecgberct so negligently and lukewarmly what I commanded you to tell him? Now go and say to him that, whether he wishes it or not, he must go to the monasteries of Columba, because their ploughs do not proceed rightly; but he must bring them back to the straight path.” [Note: [Col. 0242D] “The monasteries of Columba.” See V.22 concerning Ecgberct’s conversion of the people of Iona to the Catholic Easter.]

When he heard this, he again ordered the brother not to disclose it to anyone [Al.: “to anyone at all”]. Although he was now certain about the vision, nevertheless he attempted to begin the planned journey with the brothers already mentioned. When they had loaded onto the ship what the needs of so great a journey required and were waiting for favorable winds for several days [Al.: “on favorable days”], one night so violent a storm arose that, after destroying some of the things aboard, it left the ship lying on the shore amid the waves [Al.: “on its side”]. Yet everything belonging to Ecgberct and his companions was saved. Then he himself, as though saying something prophetic, remarked: “Because this storm is on my account,” and withdrew from that expedition, allowing himself to remain at home.

But one of his companions, named Uictberct, himself distinguished by contempt for the world and knowledge of doctrine—for he had spent many years as a pilgrim in Ireland, living the anchoritic life with great perfection [690]—boarded a ship and, reaching Frisia, preached the word of salvation for two continuous years to that people and its king Rathbedo [Al.: “Radhbedo”]. [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Rathbedo.” “Vincent relates in the *Historical Mirror* concerning the aforesaid king of the Frisians that, when the preaching of Bishop Wlfrann had induced him to be baptized, and he had dipped one foot into the bath, he withdrew the other and asked where the greater number of his ancestors were, in hell or in paradise. When he heard that more were in hell, he said: ‘It is more proper that I follow the greater number than the fewer.’” Capgrave, *Life of St. Willibrord*, where it is also related how the same Rathbedo was deceived by the devil, transformed into an angel and promising him golden houses.] Yet he found no fruit from so great a labor among the barbarian hearers. Then, returning to the place of his beloved pilgrimage [691], he began, as usual, to devote himself to the Lord in silence; and since he could not benefit outsiders in the faith, he took greater care to benefit his own people by the examples of his virtues.

## CHAPTER X

How Uilbrord, preaching in Frisia, converted many to Christ, and how his companions Hewald and Hewald suffered martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0243C–D] “Uilbrord.” He was born in the province of Northumbria; his father was called Wilgis. As a boy he was entrusted for upbringing at Hrypis; after leaving that monastery, drawn by Ecgberct’s fame, he set out for Ireland. Having remained there for twelve years, he finally made for Frisia with twelve companions to preach Christ. Capgrave, *Life of Willibrord*. There Pope Sergius made him bishop; he lived until old age and at last, weakened, appointed a co-bishop in his place to discharge the ministry. His commemoration is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of November.]

When the man of God Ecgberct saw that he himself was not permitted to come to preach to the nations—being detained for another benefit of the holy Church, about which he had been forewarned by the oracle—and that Uictberct, having gone to those regions, was accomplishing nothing, he nevertheless tried to send holy and industrious men to undertake the work of the word. Among them the outstanding Uilbrord excelled in priestly rank and merit.

When they arrived with him—there were twelve in number [Note: [Col. 0243D] “Twelve.” In Surius, under 1 March, their names are given by a certain Marcellinus, who pretends to have been one of them, in this order: Willibrord, Swibert, Acca, Wigbert, Willibald, Winibald, Lebuinus, the two Ewalds, Werenfrid, and Marcellinus; all these were priests. Finally, Adelbert, a deacon and son of the king of Deira. But this man, who calls himself Marcellinus and claims a share in the glory of this conversion, does not appear to be the person he pretends to be, but rather some recent and unskilled inventor of tales. For he counts two Hewalds among the twelve apostles, but it is clear from Bede that these two were distinct from the twelve: they are said to have followed the example of those twelve and to have reached the ancient Saxons, not Frisia, to which the twelve had turned. He also includes Uictberct among them and reports that he was killed by order of Rathbedo; but it is probable from this passage of Bede that Uictberct never returned to Frisia, but continued “to devote himself to the Lord in his customary silence” until his death, and that twelve other “holy men” were sent by Ecgberct. He also adds Acca, whom he foolishly says was later appointed bishop of Hagustald by Uilfrid. Yet it is clear from V.21 that Acca never left England except when he went to Rome with Uilfrid.]—they turned aside to Pippin, duke of the Franks, and were gladly received by him. Since he had recently captured Citerior Frisia, after expelling King Rathbedo from it, he sent them there to preach. He also assisted them with imperial authority, so that no one might inflict any harm on the preachers, and he encouraged by many benefits those who wished to accept the faith. Thus, with divine grace assisting, they converted many in a short time from idolatry to the faith of Christ [692]. [Note: [Col. 0244D] “Citerior Frisia.” Bede called this the territory taken from Rathbedo, or those lands now contained within the county of Holland, which are naturally nearer to the English, among whom Bede wrote, than the rest of Frisia beyond Lake Flevo. Or it may mean the nearer Frisia extending around the Meuse and Waal, the regions of Brabant, Gelderland, and Cleves on this side of the Rhine, which perhaps the Frisians had held after severing them from the Frankish kingdom. This is supported by the *Metz Annals*, published by Chesnaeus in volume III of the *Frankish Writers*, which state: “The blessed Pippin the Elder, grandfather of this man, governed by just laws the people dwelling in broad territories between the Carbonarian Forest and the river Meuse, and extending as far as the borders of the Frisians.” Thus, to the Franks, Citerior Frisia was the land reaching to the river Meuse; to the English, it was what is now Holland.]

Following their example, two priests of the English nation, who had lived for a long time in exile in Ireland for the sake of the eternal homeland, came to the province of the ancient Saxons, to see whether they could perhaps win some there for Christ by preaching. Both were alike in devotion and in name, for each was called Hewald. They were distinguished, however, by the different appearance of their hair: one was called Black Hewald and the other White Hewald. Both were imbued with religious piety, but Black Hewald was more thoroughly trained in knowledge of the sacred writings [Al.: “more instructed”].

When they came into the province, they entered the lodging of a certain steward and asked him to send them to the official who was over him, since they had a message and a useful matter [Al.: “a matter of usefulness”] that they ought to present to him. For these ancient Saxons have no king, but many officials placed over their people. When war threatens, they cast lots equally, and whichever man the lot indicates, all follow him as their leader during the war and obey him. When the war is over, all the officials again become equal in power. The steward therefore received them and, promising to send them to the official over him as they requested, kept them with him for several days.

When the barbarians learned that they belonged to another religion—for they were continually occupied with [Al. adds: “hymns”] psalms and prayers, and every day offered to God the sacrifice of the saving victim, carrying with them sacred vessels and a board consecrated for use as an altar—they regarded them with suspicion. They feared that, if the priests reached the official and spoke with him, they might turn him away from his gods and transfer him to the new religion of the Christian faith, and that thus their whole province might gradually be compelled to exchange its ancient worship for the new [Al.: “to change into the new worship”].

Therefore they suddenly seized and killed them: White Hewald by a swift sword-stroke, but Black Hewald through prolonged tortures and the dreadful tearing apart of all his limbs. After killing them, they threw them into the Rhine [Al.: “into the Rhine”]. When the official whom they had wished to see heard this, he was greatly angered that the foreigners who had wanted to come to him had not been permitted to do so. He sent men and killed all those villagers, and consumed the village by fire. [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Suffered.” The Gallican Martyrology reports that they suffered in Westphalia.]

The aforesaid priests and servants of Christ suffered on the fifth day before the Nones of October.

Nor were heavenly miracles lacking at their martyrdom. For when, as we have said, the pagans had thrown their slain bodies into the river, it happened that, against the current of the flowing stream, they were carried for nearly forty thousand paces to the very place where their companions were. Moreover, a very great ray of light, rising high to heaven, shone every night above the place wherever the bodies happened to have arrived; even the pagans who had killed them saw this.

One of the martyrs also appeared in a nocturnal vision to one of his companions, a distinguished and also worldly nobleman named Tilmon, who had been a soldier and had become a monk. He indicated that the bodies could be found at the place where Tilmon saw light shining from heaven upon the earth. This was fulfilled. For their bodies were found and buried with an honor worthy of martyrs, and the day of their passion or discovery is celebrated in those places with appropriate veneration.

Finally, when the most glorious Frankish duke Pippin learned of this, he sent for their bodies and, having had them brought to him [Al.: “when he learned this … having had them brought”], buried them with great glory in the church of the city of Cologne beside the Rhine. [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Church.” The collegiate church of St. Cunibert. Gallican Martyrology.] It is also reported that at the place where they were killed a spring welled up, and that at the same place it continues to pour forth the abundant gifts of its stream to this day [Al.: “to bathe it”].

## CHAPTER XI

How the venerable men Suidberct in Britain and Uilbrord at Rome were ordained bishops for Frisia.

[Col. 0245C]

In the earliest period of their arrival in Frisia [692], as soon as Uilbrord learned that the prince had granted him permission to preach there, he hastened to come to Rome. Pope Sergius then presided over the Apostolic See. Uilbrord wished to undertake the desired work of evangelizing the nations with the pope’s permission and blessing. At the same time he hoped to receive from him relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ, so that, while establishing churches among the people to whom he preached after destroying their idols, he would have the relics of the saints ready to introduce there; and, after depositing them there, he could dedicate each place in honor of the saints to whom the relics belonged [Al.: “in whose honor each place was to be dedicated”]. He also wished either to learn in Rome or to receive from there many other things required by the undertaking of so great a work. When all these wishes had been fulfilled, he returned to preaching.

At that time the brothers who were devoted to the ministry of the word in Frisia chose from their number a man modest in character and gentle in heart, Suidberct. [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Suidberct.” According to Pseudo-Marcellinus, Suidberct was born in the province of Northumbria to parents Sigeberct, count of Northumbria, and Bertha, countess. At the age of fifteen he entered the monastery of Beardaneu, and after spending nine years there received the priesthood. The same author records that he was imprisoned by pagans in Frisia and liberated by an angel, then gave sight to a blind man and restored life to a dead person; but scarcely any credence can be given to a history containing almost as many errors as lines.] They sent him to Britain at their request, and the most reverend Bishop Uilfrid ordained him. [Note: [Col. 0245D] “Ordained.” Suidberct was ordained in 693, before Berctuald had returned. But Marcellinus says that he was ordained in 695, and therefore states that he was consecrated by Uilfrid because Ecgberct, archbishop of York, was suffering from a serious illness. Baronius, however, not following Marcellinus here—though he copies him rather ineptly elsewhere—offers another explanation, namely, that Uilfrid was a legate of the Apostolic See. Marcellinus’ explanation is plainly false, because Ecgberct was not then archbishop of York; Baronius’ is not sufficiently clear either, for if Kent had a bishop at that time, if Berctuald had returned to his see, he would, as seems evident from this passage of Bede, have consecrated Suidberct.] At that time Uilfrid had perhaps been driven from his homeland and was living in exile in the regions of the Mercians. For at that time Kent had no bishop: Theodore had died, while Berctuald, his successor, had not yet returned to his episcopal see after crossing the sea to be ordained.

After receiving the episcopate and returning from Britain, Suidberct soon withdrew to the people of the Boructuarians and led many of them to the way of truth by his preaching. But not long afterward, when the Boructuarians were conquered by the people of the ancient Saxons, those who had received the word were scattered in every direction. The bishop himself, with some companions, sought Pippin. At the intercession of his wife Blithryda [Al.: “Blithrude”], Pippin gave him a place of residence on an island in the Rhine called in their language *In littore* (“On the Shore”). There he built a monastery [Note: [Col. 0246C] “Monastery.” He built it in a village on that island called Werda, in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]—which his heirs still possess—and for some time lived a most strict life. There [Note: [Col. 0246D] “He ended his days.” The brief Frankish Annals published by André du Chesne in volume II of the *Frankish Writers* have the following under the year 713: “The burial of Suitberct, bishop.” Pseudo-Marcellinus says that he died in 717, on the Kalends of March, a Friday, at the twelfth hour. But this is as unsuccessful as much else throughout that work. For in that year, with solar cycle 26 and Sunday letter C, the Kalends of March fell not on Friday but on Monday. The letter composed under the name of St. Ludger also contradicts it. For in chapter 1 it says that the year from the Nativity of the Lord 748 was the thirty-third after the celebrated passing of the most holy Suibert. It would therefore follow that he died in 715, when the solar cycle was 24 and the Sunday letter F; and in that year the Kalends of March did fall on Friday, as they did in 804. Suidberct was canonized by Leo III and is said to have been the first person solemnly enrolled among the saints. See St. Ludger’s letter in Surius, 1 March, and Cornelius à Lapide on Ecclesiastes, chapter XLIV.] he ended his final day.

After those who had arrived in Frisia had taught there for several years [696], Pippin, with the favorable agreement of all, sent the venerable Uilbrord to Rome. Sergius still held the pontificate. Pippin requested that Uilbrord be ordained archbishop for the people of the Frisians. This was carried out as he had requested in the year 696 from the Lord’s Incarnation. He was ordained in the church of the holy martyr Cecilia [Note: [Col. 0247D] “Cecilia.” St. Cecilia is commemorated on 22 November. Alcuin, in Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, third century, reports that Clement was consecrated in the Church of St. Peter.] on her feast day, and the pope mentioned above imposed on him the name Clement. He was immediately sent back to his episcopal see, only fourteen days after he had come to the City.

Pippin gave him the site of an episcopal chair in his illustrious fortress, which in the ancient language of those peoples was called Uiltaburg, that is, “the town of the Uilti” [Note: [Col. 0247D] “Uiltaburg.” Bede seems here to confuse two different places. It is probable that Uiltaburg was a place 3,600 paces from Traiectum, now called Uiltenburg. Cluverus, *German Antiquities*, II.36.], while in the Gallic language it was called Traiectum. There a church was built [Note: [Col. 0247D] “Church.” He consecrated it in honor of the holy Savior. Boniface, letter 97, in the *Library of the Fathers*, eighth century. He also built another church at Traiectum in honor of St. Martin.] and the most reverend pontiff preached the word of faith far and wide, recalling many from error. He also built several churches throughout those regions, as well as some monasteries [Note: [Col. 0247D] “Monasteries.” He is said to have founded one at Esternachus.].

Not long afterward he also appointed other bishops in those regions from among the brothers who had come there to preach either with him or after him. Some of these had already fallen asleep in the Lord. Uilbrord himself, surnamed Clement, still survives [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Still survives.” He did not die before the year 736. The Gallican Martyrology reports that he ruled the Church for forty years and was buried in the monastery of Esternachus in the diocese of Trier; this monastery became so famous through the miracles of the deceased that it was later distinguished by bearing his name. St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, says in letter 97 that he preached for fifty years, until extreme old age. Since he began his episcopate in 696, he must therefore have died around 745.] [731], venerable in advanced age, being in his thirty-sixth year in the episcopate, and after many struggles in the heavenly warfare sighing with his whole mind for the rewards of the heavenly recompense.

## CHAPTER XII

How a certain man in the province of Northumbria, rising from the dead, related many terrible and desirable things that he had seen.

In those times [696] a memorable miracle, like those of ancient times, occurred in Britain. For, to awaken the living from the death of the soul, a certain man who had been dead for some time rose again to bodily life and related many things worthy of remembrance. I have thought that some of these should be briefly set down here.

There was a householder in the region of Northumbria called Incuneningum [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Incuneningum.” Perhaps the province of Cunningham in Scotland.] who led a religious life with his household. Struck by bodily illness and brought by its daily increase to the point of death, he died at the beginning of the night. But at dawn he revived and suddenly sat up, driving all those who had been sitting beside the body and weeping into flight, struck by immense fear. Only his wife remained, although trembling and terrified, because she loved him more than the others. He consoled her, saying:

“Do not be afraid, for I have now truly risen from the death by which I was held, and have been permitted to live again among human beings. Yet from this time onward I must live not by the manner of life to which I was formerly accustomed, but by one very different from it.”

Immediately he rose and went to the little village’s oratory. Remaining in prayer until daybreak, he soon divided all the property he had possessed into three portions: one he gave to his wife, another to his children, and the third he kept for himself [Al.: “for himself personally”], immediately distributing it to the poor.

Not long afterward, freed from worldly concerns, he went to the monastery of Mailros [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Mailros.” Concerning this, see IV.27.], which is enclosed for the most part by the winding course of the river Tweed. Having received the tonsure, he entered the place of secluded residence that the abbot had foreseen for him. There he persevered until the day of his death in such great mortification of mind and body that, even if his tongue remained silent, his life declared that he had seen many things hidden from others, some dreadful and some desirable.

He related what he had seen in this way:

“He who led me was bright in appearance and splendid in clothing. We walked in silence, as it seemed to me, toward the rising of the summer sun. As we proceeded, we came to a valley of great breadth and depth, but of infinite length. It lay on our left, and one side displayed flames burning with a terrifying intensity, while the other, swept everywhere by raging hail and the cold of snow, was no less intolerable. Both sides were full of human souls, which appeared to be hurled alternately from one side to the other as though by the force of a storm. For when the wretched souls could not endure the violence of the immense heat, they leapt into the midst of the hostile cold; and when they could find no rest there either, they sprang back again, burning, into the midst of the unquenchable flames.

“As this unhappy alternation continued far and wide, as far as I could see, and an innumerable multitude of deformed spirits was tortured without any interval of repose, I began to think that perhaps this was hell, of whose intolerable torments I had often heard. My guide, who walked before me, answered my thought:

“‘Do not suppose that this is hell; for this is not that hell which you think it to be.’”

“[Col. 0248D] But as he gradually led me farther onward, while I was terrified by this most dreadful spectacle, I suddenly saw the places before us begin to grow dark and everything become filled with darkness. When we entered it, the darkness thickened for a short while to such an extent that I could see nothing except the appearance and clothing of the one who was leading me. As we proceeded alone beneath the night through the shadows, behold, suddenly there appeared before us numerous globes of hideous flame, rising as though from a great well and falling back into it again. When I had been brought to it, my guide suddenly disappeared and [Col. 0249A] left me alone in the midst of darkness and a horrid [Al., horrific] vision. But while those fiery globes continually sought the heights and then returned to the depths of the abyss, I saw that all the summits of the flames which rose up were filled with human spirits. Like sparks ascending with smoke, they were now hurled upward to greater heights, now, as the fiery vapors withdrew, sliding back into the depths [Al., the depth]. An incomparable stench, boiling up with those same vapors [Al., that same vapor], filled all those places of darkness. As I stood there trembling for some time, uncertain what to do, where to turn my steps, and what end awaited me, I heard behind me the sound of a sudden [Al., *subito*, “suddenly”] and most monstrous, pitiable wailing, together with a rattling [Col. 0249B] burst of laughter, like the jeering of an ignorant crowd insulting captured enemies.

“When the same sound, now louder, reached me, I observed a crowd of evil spirits dragging five [Al. omits: five] sorrowful and wailing human souls through the darkness. The spirits themselves were greatly [Al., truly] rejoicing and laughing. Among those human beings, as far as I could discern, one was tonsured like a cleric, one was a layman, and one was a woman. The evil spirits dragged them down into the midst [Al., the middle] of that burning abyss; and, when they had descended farther and I could no longer clearly distinguish the humans’ weeping from the demons’ laughter, I nevertheless still heard the confused sound in my ears. Meanwhile, some of the dark spirits rose from that fire-vomiting [Col. 0249C] abyss and, rushing up, surrounded me. With flaming eyes and breathing foul fire from their mouths and nostrils, they tormented me; they also threatened to seize me with the fiery pincers they held in their hands, though they could not touch me in any way, despite their attempts to terrify me.

“When I, enclosed on every side by enemies and by the blindness of darkness, turned my eyes here and there, hoping that some help might come from somewhere by which I could be saved, a path [Al., the path (*viam*)] appeared behind me—the path by which I had come—like the gleam of a star moving through the darkness. As it gradually grew and hastened more swiftly toward me, once it drew near, all the hostile spirits who had sought to snatch me with their pincers scattered and fled.

“The one who came and drove them away was the very one who had led me before. Then, turning to the right-hand road, he began to lead me as though toward the winter sunrise. Without delay he brought me out of the darkness into the clear air and serene light. As he led me through the open light, I saw before us an enormous wall, whose length in either direction and whose height seemed to have no limit. I began to wonder why we were approaching the wall, since I could see nowhere in it any door, window, or ascent. When we had reached the wall, at once, by I know not what means, we found ourselves at its summit.

“And behold, there was a very broad and most pleasant field, filled with such fragrance from blooming flowers that the sweetness of this wonderful scent immediately drove away all the stench of the dark furnace that had penetrated me [Col. 0250A]. Such light flooded the whole place that it seemed more splendid than all the brilliance of day, or than the rays of the noonday sun. In this field were innumerable gatherings of men clothed in white, and many seats for the ranks of the joyful. As he led me among the choirs of the blessed inhabitants, I began to think that this might perhaps be the kingdom of heaven, of which I had often heard preaching. He answered my thought: ‘No,’ he said, ‘this is not the kingdom of heaven that you suppose.’

“As we continued forward and passed through these dwellings of the blessed spirits, I saw before us a much greater abundance of light than before. There I also heard the sweetest voice of singers; and such a marvelous fragrance poured forth from that place that the odor which I had previously experienced and regarded as exceedingly great now seemed to me very slight. Likewise, in comparison with the light that had now appeared, the extraordinary light of the flowering field seemed altogether faint and small. When I hoped that we were about to enter the beauty of that place, my guide suddenly stopped; and, without delay, turning back, he led me by the very road through which we had come.

“When we had returned and reached those joyful dwellings of the spirits clothed in white, he said to me: ‘Do you know what all these things are that you have seen?’ I replied: ‘No.’ And he said: ‘That valley which you saw, dreadful with burning flames and rigid cold, is the place where the souls of those who delay confessing and correcting the sins they have committed are examined and punished. At the very moment of death they flee to repentance and thus depart from the body. Yet because they had confession and repentance even at death, they will all reach the kingdom of heaven on the day of judgment. Many are helped by the prayers, almsgiving, and fasting of the living, and especially by the celebration of Masses, so that they may be freed even before the day of judgment.

“‘Moreover, the fire-vomiting and foul well that you saw is the mouth of Gehenna, into which whoever has once fallen will never be freed for eternity. This flower-bearing place, where you see this most beautiful company of young people rejoicing and shining, is where the souls of those who depart from the body in good works [Col. 0250D] are received, though they are not so perfect that they immediately deserve to be admitted into the kingdom of heaven. Nevertheless, all of them will enter, on the day of judgment, into the sight of Christ and the joys of the heavenly kingdom. For whoever is perfect in every word, deed, and thought reaches the heavenly kingdom immediately after departing from the body. To its vicinity belongs that place where you heard the sound of sweet song together with the fragrance of sweetness and the splendor of light.

“‘But because you must now return to the body and live again among human beings, if you diligently examine your actions and strive to preserve your conduct and speech in uprightness and simplicity, you too will receive after death a dwelling-place among these joyful ranks of blessed spirits that you see. For when I withdrew from you for a time, I did so in order to learn what ought to become of you.’”

When he had said this to me, I greatly detested returning to the body, delighted as I was by the sweetness and beauty of the place I was looking upon and by the fellowship of those whom I saw in it [Al. adds: to be]. Yet I did not dare ask my guide anything; and suddenly, by I know not what means, I found myself living again among human beings.”

The same man of God did not wish to relate these and other things he had seen indiscriminately to all the idle and careless about their lives, but only to those who, either terrified by fear of torments or delighted by hope of everlasting joys, wished to draw spiritual improvement from his words [Col. 0251B]. Near his cell lived a certain monk named Haemgils, who also held the eminent rank of priest, which he matched with good works [Al., adorned it with good deeds]. He still survives and, as a solitary on the island of Ireland, supports the final period of his life with ordinary bread (*pane cibario*) and cold water.

This man often visited the same person and, by repeated questioning, heard from him what and what kind of things he had seen after being stripped of his body [Al., had seen]. Through his account, the things of which we have briefly spoken also came to our knowledge. He also related his visions to King Aldfrid, a man highly learned in every respect. The king listened to him so willingly and attentively that, at his request, he was admitted to the monastery mentioned above [Col. 0251C], crowned with the monastic tonsure, and, whenever he came into that region, frequently visited him to hear him.

At that time the abbot and priest of that monastery, a man of religious and modest life, was Aediluald [Note: [Col. 0251D] Aediluald. He was first a minister of Saint Cuthbert. *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, 30. Later he was abbot of Melrose, V, 12. Finally, having become a bishop around the year 724, he had a stone cross made which, many centuries later, acquired the greatest reputation for sanctity among the northern English. Simeon of Durham, *On the Church of Durham*, I, 12. He also ordered the book of the Gospels, which Bishop Eadfrid had written with his own hand in honor of the blessed Cuthbert, to be adorned with gold and jewels. Ibid., II, 12. Malmesbury says that he died in 738; Florence of Worcester, in 739; Simeon of Durham, in 740. He was buried in the church at Lindisfarne. After 135 years, his remains, together with those of Saint Cuthbert and other saints, were removed from there so that they would not be exposed to the fury of the Danes. After the monks had long carried that sacred treasure from place to place, the remains were finally transferred to Durham. Saint Aediluald is commemorated on 12 February.], who now worthily serves [Al., holds] the episcopal see of the Church of Lindisfarne.

He received in the same monastery a more secluded dwelling-place, where he could devote himself more freely to the uninterrupted service of his Creator in prayer. Because the place itself was situated on the bank of a river, he often entered it out of a great desire to chastise his body and frequently immersed himself in its flowing waters. There he would persist in psalms or prayers [Col. 0252A] for as long as he seemed able to endure it, standing motionless as the rising river [Al. adds: and] reached his loins, and sometimes his neck. Then, coming out onto the land, he never took off those garments, wet and cold, until they had been warmed and dried by his body.

In winter, when the broken crusts of ice floated around him—ice which he himself sometimes broke apart in order to make a place where he could stand or immerse himself [Al. adds: in the river]—those who saw him would say: “It is astonishing, brother Drycthelme—for that was the man’s name—that you can in any way endure such extreme cold!” He replied simply, for he was a man of simple character and moderate disposition: “I have seen colder things.” When they said: “It is astonishing that you should wish to maintain such severe [Col. 0252B] abstinence,” he replied: “I have seen more severe things.” Thus, until the day of his calling, he subdued his aged body amid daily fasts through an unwearied desire for heavenly goods, and by word and conduct he benefited many toward salvation [Al., for the sake of salvation].

## CHAPTER XIII. How, on the contrary, another man approaching death saw a book of his sins offered to him by demons

On the other hand, there was a certain man in the province of the Mercians whose visions and words, though not his conduct [Al., his words and conduct], benefited many, but not himself. He lived in the time of Coenred, who reigned after Aedilred [705] [Note: [Col. 0251D] Aedilred. Son of King Penda; in 675 he succeeded his brother Wulfhere. In 676 he ravaged Kent, IV, 12. In 680, at his petition, Pope Agatho confirmed by letter the privileges of Kings Peada and Wulfhere and of Sexwulf, by which they freed the monastery of Medeshamstede from every service owed either to king or bishop. *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*, years 675 and 679. In 679, Theodore made peace between him and Ecgfrid, IV, 21; and Aedilred recovered the province of Lindsey, which Ecgfrid had obtained after defeating Wulfhere, IV, 12. In 691, at Aedilred’s command, Wilfrid, who had been expelled from the episcopate and remained for a time with him, consecrated Oftfor, IV, 23. Aedilred also gave Evesham to Saint Ecgwine, where he built a monastery in 701. In 703 he gave him the castle of Chadbury and the old monastery of Stratford. *Monumenta Anglicana*, II, 851. In 704 he became a monk at the monastery of Beardaneu, mentioned in III, 11, which he had especially loved. *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*. He soon became abbot, V, 20. Malmesbury, *On the Kings*, book IV. He spent thirteen years there devoutly. *Monumenta Anglicana*, II, 851.]. He was a man placed in lay dress and military service; but, as much as he pleased the king by his outward industry, so much he was displeasing through his inner negligence.

The king therefore repeatedly urged him to confess, correct, and abandon his sins before the sudden arrival of death deprived him of all time for repentance and amendment. Yet, although frequently admonished, he despised words of salvation and promised that he would undertake repentance at a later time. While these things were happening, he was struck by illness, fell into bed, and [Col. 0253A] began to suffer severe pain. The king, who loved him greatly, visited him and urged him to repent of his offenses, at least then, before he died. But he replied [Al., was replying] that he did not wish to confess his sins at that time, but only when he rose from his illness, lest his companions reproach him for doing out of fear of death what he had refused to do while in good health. He spoke boldly, as it seemed to him, but miserably, as later became clear, deceived by demonic fraud [Al., demoniacal fraud].

As the illness grew worse, the king again entered to visit and instruct him. He immediately cried out in a pitiable voice: “What do you want now? Why have you come here? You can no longer bring me any benefit or salvation.”

The king replied: “Do not speak like that. See that you are of sound mind.”

“No,” he said, “I am not insane, but I clearly see the most dreadful knowledge before my eyes.”

“And what is that?” asked the king.

“A little while ago,” he said, “two most beautiful young men entered this house and sat beside me, one at my head and one at my feet. One of them brought forth a very handsome but exceedingly small book and [Col. 0253B] gave it to me to read. In it I found written all the good things I had ever done, and these were exceedingly few and slight. They took back the book and said nothing to me.

“Then suddenly an army of evil spirits, dreadful in appearance [Al., horrendous in appearance], arrived. They surrounded this house outside and, settling inside in great numbers, filled most of it. Then the one who seemed greater among them, both because of the darkness of his gloomy face and because of the precedence of his seat, brought forth a book of dreadful appearance, enormous size, and almost unbearable weight. He ordered one of his attendants to bring it to me to read [Al., to have it brought]. When I had read it, I found that all the sins I had committed—not only in deed or word, but even in the slightest thought—were [Col. 0253C] written in it most clearly in gloomy letters [Al., dark letters].

“He said to the white-clothed and splendid men who had been sitting beside me: ‘Why are you sitting here, knowing with absolute certainty that this man is ours [Al., that he himself is ours]?’ They replied: ‘You speak truly [Al., you speak]; take him and lead him into the accumulation of your condemnation.’ When they had said this, they immediately disappeared.

“Then two most wicked spirits rose up, holding plowshares in their hands [Al., knives; another reading, forks], and struck me—one on the head, the other on the foot. They are now creeping with great torment into the inner parts of my body [Al., my entrails]. As soon as they meet one another, I shall die, and the demons, prepared to seize me, will drag me into the prison of hell [Col. 0253D].”

Thus the wretched man spoke in despair. Not long afterward he died. The repentance which he had postponed for a short time, though he could have undertaken it with the fruit of pardon, he now performs eternally without benefit, subject to punishments. Concerning him it is clear that, as blessed Pope Gregory writes of certain others, he saw these things not for his own sake, since they did not benefit him, but for the sake of others who, learning of his death, might fear to defer the time of repentance while it was available, lest, overtaken by an unexpected moment of death, they should perish unrepentant.

The fact that he saw different books offered to him by good and evil spirits occurred by heavenly dispensation so that we might remember that our deeds and thoughts do not disperse into the air, but are all preserved for examination by the supreme Judge [Col. 0254A], whether they are to be shown to us at the end by friendly angels or by enemies. The fact that the angels first brought forth a white book and the demons afterward a black one; that the former was very small and the latter enormous: this should be understood to mean that in his first age he did some good things, but later, by acting wickedly as a young man, obscured them all. If, conversely, he had taken care in adolescence to correct the errors of childhood and to hide them from the eyes of God by doing good, he could have been numbered among those of whom the Psalm says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

I thought that this story, as I learned it from the venerable Bishop Pecthelm, should be told simply for the salvation of readers and hearers.

## CHAPTER XIV. How another man at the point of death saw the place of punishment appointed for him in hell

[Col. 0254B]

I myself knew a brother—would that I had not known him—whose name, if saying it would have helped, I could mention. He lived in a noble monastery, but himself lived ignobly. The brothers and superiors of the place repeatedly rebuked him and urged him to turn to a more disciplined life. Although he refused to listen to them, they nevertheless tolerated him patiently because of the necessity of his external work, for he was outstanding in the craft of a smith.

He was greatly devoted to drunkenness and the other allurements of a more dissolute life. He was accustomed to remain day and night in his workshop [Al., for a long time], rather than gather with the brothers in the church for psalmody, prayer, and hearing the word of life [Col. 0254C]. Thus what some people say happened to him: that whoever refuses to enter the church door voluntarily in humility must necessarily be brought unwillingly, as one condemned, to the door of hell.

Struck by illness and brought to the point of death, he summoned the brothers. Greatly sorrowful and resembling one already condemned, he began to say that he saw hell opened and Satan submerged [Al., plunged; another reading, immersed] in the depths of Tartarus [Al., the depth], and Caiaphas [Al., Caiaphas also] together with the others who had killed the Lord, delivered beside him to avenging flames. “Near them,” he said, “alas for wretched me, I see [Al., look upon] a place of eternal destruction prepared.”

When the brothers heard this, they began earnestly to exhort him to repent while he was still in the body [Col. 0254D]. He replied in despair: “I have no time now to change my life, since I myself have seen that my judgment has already been completed.”

Saying such things, he died without the saving viaticum. His body was buried in the most remote part of the monastery, and no one dared either celebrate Masses for him, sing psalms, or even pray for him.

O how greatly God has divided light from darkness! The blessed protomartyr Stephen, about to suffer death for the truth, saw the heavens opened; he saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. He sent the eyes of his mind before death to the place where he himself would be after death, so that he might die more joyfully.

But this smith, dark in mind and conduct, as death approached saw Tartarus opened; he saw the condemnation of the devil and his followers; he also saw his own wretched prison among them. Thus, with his hope of salvation lost, he might perish more miserably, but might leave to the living who learned of these things a cause of salvation through his destruction.

This happened recently in the province of Bernicia and, being widely reported, moved many to repent of their sins and not postpone repentance. Would that this might also happen henceforth through the reading of our writings!

## CHAPTER XV. How most of the Scottish Churches, at Adamnan’s urging, accepted the Catholic Easter; and how he wrote a book about the Holy Places

[Col. 0255B]

At that time [701], by the Lord’s gift, most of the Irish Scots, and also some of the Britons in Britain, accepted the reasonable and ecclesiastical time for observing Easter.

For Adamnan, a priest and abbot of the monks who were on the island of Iona, having been sent on an embassy by his people, came to Aldfrid, king of the English. After remaining for some time in that province, he saw the canonical rites of the Church, and was carefully admonished by several of the more learned not to presume to live, together with his very few companions in that remote corner of the world, contrary to the universal custom of the Church, whether in the observance of Easter or in [Note: [Col. 0255D] Others. Among these was the tonsure, V, 21, near the end.] any other decrees. His mind was changed, so that he gladly preferred what he had seen and heard in the Churches of the English to the custom of himself and his people [Col. 0255C]. He was indeed a good and wise man, most nobly instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures.

When he returned home, he tried to lead those who were on Iona, and those subject to that monastery, to the path of truth that he had learned and had embraced with all his heart, but he could not. He therefore sailed to Ireland, preaching to them and explaining by gentle exhortation the proper time of Easter. He corrected many of them, and nearly all who were free from the dominion of the people of Iona, from their ancestral error and brought them back to Catholic unity, teaching them thoroughly to observe the proper time of Easter [Note: [Col. 0255D] Corrected from the ancestral error. Al., “corrected from error,” omitting “ancestral”; another reading, “corrected from the error they held.”].

After celebrating the canonical Easter in Ireland, he returned to his own island and preached most earnestly in his monastery the Catholic observance of the time of Easter [Col. 0255D]. Yet he could not complete what he had undertaken. It happened that, before the cycle of the year was completed, he departed from this world [702]. Divine grace had arranged that a man most devoted to unity and peace should be snatched away to eternal life before, when Easter returned, he was forced into a more serious disagreement with those who did not wish to follow him to the truth [Col. 0256A].

[Note: [Col. 0255D] He wrote. He also wrote the *Life of Saint Columba*, which he arranged in three books.]

The same man wrote a book about the Holy Places [Note: [Col. 0255D] The book. This little work of Adamnan exists in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, third age, part II, p. 502 [Col. 0256D]. It is uncertain when Adamnan came as an envoy to Aldfrid or presented his book to him. It is certain, however, that he came to the king before 705, since the king died that year. Since Matthew of Westminster states that he was sent to Aldfrid in 701, I safely follow his authority in so obscure a matter. See *Patrologia Latina*, vol. LXXXVIII, col. 779.] that is highly useful to many readers. Its author, teaching and dictating it, was Arcuulfus, a bishop from Gaul, who had come to Jerusalem out of devotion to the holy places. After touring the whole Promised Land, he also visited Damascus, Constantinople, Alexandria, and many islands of the sea. While returning by ship to his homeland, he was driven by a storm to the western shores of Britain. After many further events, he came to the aforesaid servant of Christ, Adamnan. When Adamnan discovered that he was learned in the Scriptures and knowledgeable about the holy places, he welcomed him most gladly and listened to him even more eagerly. Thus, whatever Arcuulfus testified that he had seen in the Holy Places and that was worthy of remembrance, Adamnan immediately took care to commit it to writing [Col. 0256B].

He produced, as I have said, a very useful work, especially for those who live far from the places in which the patriarchs and apostles were buried and know about them only what they have learned by reading. Adamnan presented this book to King Aldfrid, and through the king’s generosity it was also made available for reading to lesser people. The author himself, having received many gifts from the king, was sent back to his homeland. I think it will be useful to readers to extract some things from his writings and insert them into this History of ours.

## CHAPTER XVI. What he recorded in the same book about the places of the Lord’s birth, Passion, and Resurrection

[Col. 0256C]

He wrote about the place of the Lord’s birth as follows:

“Bethlehem, the city of David, lies on a narrow ridge surrounded on every side by valleys. It is one thousand paces long from west to east, low-lying [Al., low], and without towers, with a wall built along the edges of the level summit. In its eastern corner there is a kind of natural half-cave, whose outer part is said to have been the place of the Lord’s birth; the inner part is called the Lord’s Manger. This cave, entirely covered within with precious marble, bears above the place where the Lord is more specifically said to have been born a great church dedicated to holy Mary.”

He likewise wrote in this manner about the place of His Passion and Resurrection:

“When one enters Jerusalem from the northern side, one must first, according to the arrangement of the streets, turn aside to the Constantinian church [Col. 0256D], which is called the Martyrium. The Emperor Constantine built it with magnificent and royal ornament because the Lord’s cross was found there by Helena, his mother [Al. adds: his].

“After this, to the west, the church of Golgotha is visible. In it appears the rock that once bore the cross itself, with the Lord’s body fastened to it [Al., the cross itself, with the Lord’s body fastened to it]. It now supports a very large silver cross, above which hangs a great bronze wheel with lamps. Beneath the very place of the Lord’s cross, a crypt has been cut into the rock. An offering for honored deceased persons is customarily made there upon an altar while the bodies are temporarily laid in the street.

“To the west of this church is the Anastasis—that is, the round church of the Lord’s Resurrection. Surrounded by three walls, it is supported by twelve columns. Between each wall it has a broad space like a roadway, containing three altars in three places of the middle wall: the southern, northern, and western sides. It has eight doors, that is, entrances, through the three walls facing one another; four of these face the southeast wind and four the east wind.

“In the middle of this church is the Lord’s round monument, cut out of rock [Col. 0257B]. Its interior height is such that a standing man can touch the ceiling with his hand. It has an entrance on the east, to which that great stone was fitted; inside, it still displays the marks of tools. On the outside it is entirely covered with marble up to the top of the vault. The summit, ornamented with gold, bears a large golden cross.

“On the northern side of this monument, the Lord’s burial place is cut into the same rock [Al. adds: it is]. It is seven feet long and rises three palms above the pavement. It has an entrance on the southern side, where twelve lamps burn day and night: four within the tomb and eight above on the right-hand edge.

“The stone that had been placed at the entrance of the monument is now split. Its smaller part stands before the entrance of the same monument as a square altar; the larger part stands in the eastern part of the same church as another square altar beneath coverings. The color of the monument and tomb appears to be a mixture of white and red.”

## CHAPTER XVII. What he likewise wrote about the place of the Lord’s Ascension and the tombs of the patriarchs

The aforesaid author also reports the following about the place of the Lord’s Ascension:

“The Mount of Olives is equal in height to Mount Zion, but surpasses it in breadth and length. Except for vines and olive trees, it is poor in trees, but fertile in wheat and barley. Its soil is not heathy [Col. 0257D], but grassy and covered with flowers.

“On its highest summit, where the Lord ascended into heaven, there is a large round church with three vaulted porticoes running around it and roofed above. The inner building could not be vaulted or roofed because of the passage of the Lord’s body. It has an altar toward the east, protected by a narrow and lofty roof [Al., a splendid roof]. In its center the Lord’s final footprints can be seen, beneath an opening in the sky where He ascended [Col. 0258A]. Although believers remove earth from them every day, they nevertheless remain and still preserve the same appearance, as though marked by impressed footprints [Al., marked as footprints].

“Around this earth lies a bronze wheel, high up to the neck, with an entrance on the west. Above it hangs from pulleys a large lamp, shining all day and night. On the western side of the same church are eight windows, and opposite them an equal number of lamps hanging on ropes. Their light shines through glass as far as Jerusalem; it is said to strike the hearts of those who look upon it with a certain gladness and compunction.

“Every year, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, after Mass has been completed, a violent blast of wind customarily comes from above and prostrates upon the ground all who are present in the church.”

He writes similarly about the location of Chebron [Al., Hebron] and the monuments of the Fathers:

“Chebron, once a city and the capital of David’s kingdom, now shows what it was only through its ruins. One stadion to the east, in a valley, it has a double cave where the tombs of the patriarchs are enclosed by a square wall, with their heads turned toward the north. Each is covered by a separate stone, hewn like a basilica. The tombs of the three patriarchs are made of white stone; Adam’s is darker and of poorer workmanship. He rests not far from them, at the northern and outermost part of that wall [Al., of that place]. The poorer and smaller memorials of three women can also be seen.

“From these monuments Mamre [Al., also called Mambre] is a thousand paces to the north [Col. 0258C]. It is very grassy and flower-covered, with a level plain on its summit. On its northern side stands the oak of Abraham, a trunk as high as two men, surrounded by a church.”

These excerpts from the writings of the aforesaid author, conveying the sense of his words but compressed into shorter and more concise language, I have thought it worthwhile to insert into our Histories for the benefit of readers. Whoever wishes to know more of that volume may seek it either in the volume itself or in the epitome from which we previously extracted a brief selection [Note: [Col. 0257D] In it. See the edition published below in its proper place.].

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the South Saxons received bishops, Eadberct and Eolla, and the West Saxons Daniel and Aldhelm; and concerning the writings of Aldhelm himself

[Col. 0258D]
