In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 705, Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, died before completing the twentieth year of his reign. His son Osred, a boy of about eight years, succeeded him and reigned for eleven years. At the beginning of this reign, Haeddi [variant: *Heddi*], bishop of the West Saxons, departed to heavenly life.

> **Note:** Departure. “Bishop Haeddi still rests in the upper cemetery of the monks, in a stone pyramid once nobly carved.” Usserius, *Antiquities*, p. 59. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that he died in 703, and Matthew of Westminster in 704; but this chapter shows that he did not die before 705. His feast is kept on the Nones of July.

> **Note:** Haeddi. There was a certain Aeddi who was a singing master (IV, 2) and who wrote the Life of Saint Wilfrid, published by Gale among the *Scriptores XV*. There was also another Haedda, who after the death of Sexwulf was placed over the diocese of Lichfield in 691, and also over Leicester after Wilfrid had been expelled. See Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus* IV, and *Anglia Sacra* I, 428. Our Haeddi, however, was first abbot at Streaneshalch (see the note on III, 7), and afterward was consecrated bishop in 676 (IV, 12). In 678: “He obtained from King Centwine the royal liberty of the island of Glastonbury for the ancient church, and secured from the same king free election for the brethren serving God there, so that they might have the right to elect and appoint their own ruler according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” Usserius, *Britannicarum Ecclesiarum Antiquitates*, p. 59; *Scriptores XV*, p. 308. With his consent and permission, King Baldred also gave the church of Glastonbury several hides and a fishery. Haeddi also, with the consent of the pagan Cædwalla, gave Lantokay to Glastonbury; Ina confirmed this gift in his great privilege made in 725. *Scriptores XV*, pp. 308, 311. He subscribed three charters made by Cædwalla, Baldred, and Ina for Aldhelm, abbot of Malmesbury. See the Life of Aldhelm in *Anglia Sacra* II, 11–12. He transferred the body of Saint Birinus to the city of Venta (III, 7).

Haeddi was a good and just man, and he practiced the episcopal life, or rather its teaching, having been formed more by the innate love of virtue in him than by reading.

> **Note:** Rather than by reading. William of Malmesbury is considerably perplexed on this point, since he had read Haeddi’s formal letters, composed with no little learning, and Aldhelm’s writings to him, “overflowing with the greatest force of eloquence and knowledge.” Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus* II.

Indeed, the most reverend bishop Pecthelm—of whom we shall speak in due place below—who for a long time remained a deacon or monk with his successor Aldhelm, was accustomed to report that at the place where Haeddi died, many miracles of healing were performed on account of his holiness [alternative reading omits “of healing”]. The people of that province were accustomed to take away dust from the place, put it into water for the sick, and by drinking or sprinkling this water bring healing to many ill people, both human beings and animals. Consequently, because the sacred dust was frequently removed—or, according to another reading, offered—a considerable pit was made there.

> **Note:** Deacon. He afterward became bishop of Candida Casa (V, 24).

After his death, the episcopate of that province was divided into two dioceses.

> **Note:** Divided. The bishop of Winchester was left with only two provinces, namely Hampshire and Surrey; the other province consisted of Wiltshire, Dorset, Berkshire, Somerset, Devon, and Cornwall. According to Matthew of Westminster, the division was made by synodal council in 704.

One was given to Daniel, which he governs to this day.

> **Note:** To Daniel. He is said to have been a disciple of Mailduf. He assisted Bede in composing his *History* (Preface to the *History*) and was the first to possess episcopal authority over the Isle of Wight (IV, 16). In 721 he went to Rome. According to Florence of Worcester, in 731 he consecrated Tatwine as archbishop. In 744 he resigned the episcopate. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that he exercised the monastic life at Malmesbury as long as he lived and was buried there, although the people of Winchester claim to possess him among themselves. Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus* II. He died in 745, although the Annals of Mailros and Matthew of Westminster defer his death to 746. In 745 King Cuthred of the Gewissae, with the consent and knowledge of Daniel and of the leading men, granted ten estates at Undecim to the monastery of Malmesbury. *Anglia Sacra* II, 25. Among the letters of Boniface, bishop of Mainz, we find a third letter addressed to this Daniel; and in Serarius’s notes on this letter of Boniface, Daniel’s reply is inserted. Among the same Bonifacian letters there are also three by Daniel himself: the thirty-third, addressed to all Christians; the sixty-sixth, to Bishop Forthere; and the sixty-seventh, to Boniface himself. *Bibliotheca Patrum* XIII, 71, 145, 82, 93.

The other was given to Aldhelm.

> **Note:** To Aldhelm, in the same place. His father was Kenter, a kinsman of King Ina. As a boy he had Adrian and Mailduf as teachers. First a monk at Malmesbury, he was then made abbot of Malmesbury in 675 by Bishop Leutherius. He enlarged and expanded the monastery which Mailduf had begun, and built there three churches: one to Saint Peter, another to the Blessed Mary, and a third to Saint Michael. Many estates were given to him and to his monastery by the kings and ealdormen of the Mercians and West Saxons: by the ealdorman Kenfrith, ten cassates; by King Æthelred, forty-five cassates; by the subking Berthwald, forty cassates; by King Cædwalla, 140 manentes; by Baldred, 100 manentes in place of 100 cassates; and by King Ina, forty-five cassates. He also founded a monastery beside the river Frome, where he consecrated a church to Saint John, and another at Bradford, where he dedicated a church to Saint Lawrence. While Sergius was pope, he went to Rome and obtained apostolic privileges for his monasteries. In 705 he became bishop of Sherborne. He intended to appoint abbots over his monasteries, but the monks resisted and would have no one but him as long as he lived. At Sherborne he also built a church, and through Ina’s charter he took abundant care for the liberties of all the churches and monasteries of the West Saxons. At last he died at Doulting, a village in Somerset, and was carried by Eguwin, bishop of Worcester, to Malmesbury, where he was buried in the church of Saint Michael in 709, on the vigil of Saint Augustine, 25 May. He lay in the earth for a long time, until, after 246 years, through the pious care of King Æthelstan, he was brought forth and placed in a shrine. See these and many further details in the Life of Saint Aldhelm in *Anglia Sacra* II. Ina is said to have built the monastery at Glastonbury on his advice. Indeed, in 704 Ina is reported to have granted by decree that the monastery of Glastonbury should be free from every burden of secular affairs and from tribute. *Scriptores XV*, p. 309. Aldhelm is commemorated on 25 May.

Aldhelm presided over it for four years with the utmost vigor. Both men were adequately instructed in ecclesiastical matters and in knowledge of the Scriptures.

Now Aldhelm, while still a priest and abbot of the monastery which they call the city of Mailduf, wrote, at the command of a synod of his people, an excellent book against the error of the Britons. They either celebrate Easter at the wrong time or practice many other things contrary to ecclesiastical chastity and peace. By reading this work he led many Britons subject to the West Saxons to the Catholic celebration of the Lord’s Easter.

> **Note:** Mailduf. “Mailduf, living the life of a hermit beneath the fortress of Bladon, which in Saxon is called Ingebbone Castle … Since the royal residence and its manor were not far from the fortress, near Brokenborough, the aforesaid hermit asked the castellan to build him a hut beneath the fortress, and obtained his request. When the necessities of life failed him, he gathered scholars around himself for instruction. Within a short time the scholars grew together into a small community. In their company Saint Aldhelm was thoroughly instructed and added dialectic to his studies. From there he fled and studied for some time at the feet of Abbot Adrian; sufficiently instructed, he returned to Malmesbury. Later he and his companions were tonsured under the monk Mailduf, who lived fourteen years after his tonsure.” Leland, *Collectanea* III, 158; *Monasticon Anglicanum* I, 50. Mailduf was Scottish by birth. Malmesbury, *Gesta Regum* I, 2. In Mailduf’s time his monastery possessed scarcely sixty cassates. The village of Brokenborough is reckoned at that number of cassates. *Anglia Sacra* II, 12.

> **Note:** An excellent book. He dedicated it to Geruntius, king of the Cornish Britons. See it in Boniface’s letters, *Bibliotheca Patrum* XIII, 86.

> **Note:** Other works. “Moreover, he published for King Aldfrith of the Northumbrians a book containing these chapters: *On the dignity of the number seven*, collected from passages of the Old and New Testaments and from the teachings of philosophers; *On the admonition of brotherly charity*; *On the nature of insensible things*, which are represented as speaking metaphorically; *On the rules of feet*; *On metaplasm*; *On synaloepha*; *On the scanning and elision of verses*; *On meter, alternating question and answer*. He also composed many letters.” *Anglia Sacra* II, 7. The following works survive in *Bibliotheca Patrum* XIII: the poem *On the Praise of Virgins*, *The Eight Principal Vices*, *The Book of Riddles*, several poetic works, and *The Book on the Praise of Virginity*.

He also wrote an outstanding book *On Virginity*, which, following Sedulius as a model, he composed in a double form, both in hexameter verse and in prose. He wrote several other works as well, being learned in every respect. For he was remarkable both for polished speech and, as I have said, for his knowledge of the Scriptures, both liberal and ecclesiastical.

After his death, Fort­here succeeded him in the pontificate—or episcopate—and survives to this day, himself a man very learned in the holy Scriptures.

> **Note:** Forthere. He is falsely said to have subscribed the council of Baccanceld held in 798. *Scriptores X*, 2211; Spelman, *Concilia* I, 317. From the appended names of Forthere, Daniel, and Acca, who had died long before, it is clear that these acts are spurious. Berhtwald sent him a letter, which is the fifty-eighth among the letters of Saint Boniface. In 737 he went to Rome with Frithogyth, queen of the West Saxons. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Westminster state that this occurred in 738.

While these men were administering the episcopate, it was established by synodal decree in 711 that the province of the South Saxons, which until then had belonged to the diocese of the city of Venta, over which Daniel was then presiding, should itself have an episcopal see and its own bishop.

> **Note:** Established. According to Matthew of Westminster, this was established in 711 while Daniel and Forthere, not Aldhelm, were administering the episcopate. Although Spelman seems to think otherwise (*Concilia* I, 209), Bede expressly testifies here that Aldhelm had already died.

> **Note:** It belonged. For the reason why it belonged to that diocese, see IV, 15.

Eadberct was consecrated their first bishop. He was abbot of the monastery of the late Bishop Wilfrid, called Selsey.

> **Note:** Selsey. See IV, 13.

After his death, Eolla—according to another reading, Ceolla—undertook the episcopal office. But after he too had been taken from this life several years later, the episcopate ceased until the present day.

## CHAPTER XIX

How Coinred of the Mercians and Offa, king of the East Saxons, ended their lives at Rome in the monastic habit; and concerning the life and death of Bishop Wilfrid

In the fourth year of Osred’s reign, Coinred, who had ruled the kingdom of the Mercians with great distinction for some time, relinquished the scepter of the kingdom with still greater distinction.

> **Note:** Coinred. The son of Wulfhere, following the example of his uncle Æthelred, went to Rome and became a monk, being especially moved by the pitiable death of a soldier; see V, 13. Malmesbury, *De Regibus* I, 4. In 708 he gave the monastery of Evesham land. Hampton, *Monasticon Anglicanum* II, 852. He also gave Saint Ecgwine eighty-four hides within the bounds of a place called Hetheholm, otherwise Aethemne. Leland, *Collectanea* I, 299.

For he came to Rome, was tonsured there while Constantine held the pontificate, and, having become a monk, remained at the threshold of the apostles in prayers, fasts, and almsgiving until his final day.

> **Note:** Constantine. A Syrian by nation, he was ordained on 25 March 708 and governed the Roman Church until 8 April 715.

Ceolred, the son of Æthelred, succeeded him in the kingdom; Æthelred had held that same kingdom before Coinred.

> **Note:** Ceolred. In 715 he and Ina fought at Wodnesbeorh, or at Bonebury, according to *Scriptores X*, p. 773; the outcome remained uncertain. Westminster says that he died in the following year and was buried at Lichfield. Malmesbury says that he suffered a pitiable premature death. Saint Boniface of Mainz, in Letter 19 to his successor Æthelbald, relates that “while Ceolred was feasting splendidly among his companions, an evil spirit seized him. It persuaded him to trust in the condemnation of God’s law and suddenly changed him, while drinking, into madness of mind, so that without repentance or confession, raging and insane, conversing with demons and abhorring God’s priests, he undoubtedly departed from this light to the infernal torments.” Spelman, *Concilia* I, 235.

The son of Sigehere, king of the East Saxons, whose name we mentioned above, also came with him.

> **Note:** Above. See III, 30.

His name was Offa.

> **Note:** Offa. He reigned over the kingdom of the East Saxons for a few years after Sigeheard and Swaefred. He went to Rome, together with King Coinred and Bishop Ecgwine, at the urging of Cyneswith, daughter of King Penda, whose hand he had sought. Malmesbury, *Gesta Regum* II, 6; Matthew of Westminster, under 705. Ecgwine returned home from Rome carrying with him a letter of privilege for the protection of his monastery at Evesham. See the charters of Kenred, Offa, and Ecgwine, and Constantine’s letter concerning the endowment of the monastery of Evesham, in Spelman, *Concilia* I, 209 and elsewhere. In 703 Offa is said to have given Offenham to the monastery of Evesham. *Monasticon Anglicanum* II, 851.

He was a young man of the most lovable age and appearance, and greatly desired by his entire people as the one to hold and preserve the scepter of the kingdom. Led by the same devotion of mind, he abandoned wife, lands, relatives, and homeland for Christ and for the Gospel, so that he might receive a hundredfold in this life and eternal life in the world to come.

> **Note:** His wife. If he had another wife besides Cyneswith, her name is unknown. Cyneswith cannot properly be called his wife, for she was only betrothed, not married. See Capgrave. It would more accurately be said that she abandoned him rather than he her; for it is clear that, out of regard for virginity, she rejected his marriage proposal.

When they reached Rome and the holy places, he too was tonsured, completed his life in the monastic habit, and attained the long-desired vision of the blessed apostles in heaven.

In the very year in which these men left Britain, the eminent bishop Wilfrid, after forty-five years from his reception of the episcopate, ended his life in the province called Oundle. His body was placed in a coffin and carried to his own monastery, called Ripon, where it was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, with the honor appropriate to so great a bishop.

> **Note:** Oundle. Oundle in Northamptonshire, near Stamford. The people of Peterborough claim that this monastery always belonged to them and was never Wilfrid’s monastery, but Haeddi, and Bede following him, say otherwise. Gale conjectures that it first belonged to Wilfrid and afterward passed to Peterborough.

Returning to the earlier stages of his life, let us briefly recall what he did. As a boy of good character, and surpassing his age in conduct, he behaved so modestly and prudently in all things that, deservedly, he was loved, honored, and embraced by his elders as one of themselves. When he reached his fourteenth year, he preferred the monastic life to the secular.

When he told this to his father—for his mother had already died—his father willingly assented to his heavenly vows and desires and ordered him to persevere in his salutary undertaking. He therefore came to the island of Lindisfarne and, giving himself over to the service of the monks, diligently sought both to learn and to practice the things belonging to monastic chastity and piety.

Because he possessed a keen intellect, he learned the psalms and several books very quickly. He was not yet tonsured, but he was already distinguished to no small degree by virtues greater than the tonsure, namely humility and obedience.

> **Note:** The reading “that is, humility and obedience” is added in one version.

For this reason he was honored with proper affection both by his elders and by his peers.

While he served God for several years in that monastery, the young man, whose mind was perceptive, gradually observed that the path of virtue taught by the Scots was far from perfect. He resolved to go to Rome and see what ecclesiastical and monastic customs were observed at the apostolic see.

When he reported this to the brothers, they praised his plan and urged him to carry out what he had decided in his mind—or, according to another reading, what he had decided. He immediately came to Queen Eanfled, since he was known to her and had been associated with the aforementioned monastery through her counsel and support, and told her that he desired to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles.

> **Note:** Eanfled. Daughter of King Edwin, she was the first of the Northumbrian nation to be baptized (II, 9). After her father was killed, she went to Kent with her mother (II, 20), and from there returned as wife to King Oswiu (III, 15). From him she requested a monastery at the place called Gilling in memory of King Oswine, who had been killed there (III, 24). She is said to have observed the true date of Easter (III, 25). At last she died and was buried at Streaneshalch (III, 24).

Delighted by the young man’s good purpose, she sent him to Kent to King Eorcenberht, her maternal uncle’s son, asking him to send Wilfrid honorably to Rome.

At that time the archbishopric was held by Honorius, one of the disciples of the blessed Pope Gregory, a man highly trained in ecclesiastical affairs.

> **Note:** Honorius. See II, 15, 16, 18, 20, and III, 14, 20.

While the lively-minded young man remained there for some time and diligently devoted himself to learning what he observed, another young man arrived, named Biscop and surnamed Benedict, of noble English birth, himself also wishing to go to Rome. We have mentioned him above.

The king therefore attached Wilfrid to Benedict’s company and ordered him to take Wilfrid with him to Rome. When they reached Lyon, Wilfrid was detained there by Dalfin, the bishop of the city, while Benedict vigorously completed the journey he had begun, traveling by ship all the way to Rome.

> **Note:** According to Chifflet, “he completed the journey begun by ship.”

The bishop delighted in the young man’s prudence in speech, the charm of his handsome appearance, his energetic conduct, and the steadiness and maturity of his judgment. He therefore gave him and his companions everything they needed in abundance for as long as they remained with him. He further offered, if Wilfrid wished, to entrust him with the government of a considerable part of Gaul, to give him his brother’s virgin daughter as a wife, and always to regard him as an adopted son.

But Wilfrid, thanking him for the kindness which, although he was a foreigner, the bishop had deigned to show him, replied that he had set his mind on another way of life and had therefore left his homeland and begun the journey to Rome.

On hearing this, the bishop sent him to Rome, giving him a guide for the journey and generously supplying everything the journey required. He earnestly begged him to remember to make the return journey through Lyon when he came back to his homeland.

On arriving in Rome, and devoting himself daily and constantly to prayer and to the study of ecclesiastical matters, as he had resolved in his mind—or, according to another reading, entirely resolved—he formed a friendship with the most learned and holy man Boniface, an archdeacon who was also a counselor of the apostolic pope.

Under Boniface’s instruction he learned, in order, the books of the four Gospels, the rational computation of Easter, and many other matters appropriate to ecclesiastical disciplines which he could not have learned in his homeland. After spending several months there happily occupied in study, he returned to Dalfin in Gaul and remained with him for three years. Dalfin tonsured him and held him in such affection that he had considered making him his heir.

> **Note:** Dalfin. No bishop named Dalfin ever governed the Church of Lyon. Everyone states that his true name was Annemundus. They hold Ebroin, mayor of the palace, responsible for the crime, carried out under the name of Baldhild, who was then administering the kingdom, rather than Baldhild herself. Anyone who reads the acts of this queen will immediately see how much she recoiled from inflicting death on pious and holy bishops. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, second century, p. 777.

But before this could happen, the bishop was taken by a cruel death, and Wilfrid was reserved instead for the episcopate of his own people, that is, of the English.

For Queen Baldhild sent soldiers and ordered the bishop to be killed. Wilfrid, his cleric, followed him to the place where he was to be beheaded, wishing to die together with him, although the bishop strongly opposed this. But when the executioners discovered that Wilfrid was a foreigner and belonged to the English nation, they spared him and refused to slaughter him together with their bishop.

> **Note:** Baldhild. Of Saxon birth, she was sold for a low price to Erchinoald, a nobleman among the Franks. Later she fled from his marriage proposal and was raised to the marriage-bed of King Chlodovech II. After his death she administered the kingdom for her son Chlothar. She built the monasteries of Chelles and Corbie and was generous to other monasteries. At last she withdrew to the monastery at Chelles, where she lived until her death. Ibid., Smith. The editions have Brunichild here, through a gross error. Brunichild was the wife of Sigibert, son of Chlothar and grandson of Chlodovech the Great; she was infamous for deceit and a terrible death. Baldhild entered the royal Frankish family nearly fifty years later; she was a woman distinguished for integrity of character and herself numbered among the saints. She was the wife of Chlodovech II, son of Dagobert, grandson of Chlothar II, and great-grandson of Chilperic, who was the brother of Sigibert, Brunichild’s husband. Bede, an Englishman less familiar with Frankish history, must be forgiven. For Queen Baldhild did not, as he says, send soldiers to order the Lyonnais bishop Dalfin to be killed, but only to bring him to the royal assembly so that he could clear himself in person of the charges brought by his adversaries. Fearing to do this, the accusers, in order to avert from themselves the punishment of retaliation that threatened them, did not behead the holy archbishop, as Bede adds, but impiously murdered him at night as he lay in bed, stabbing him with knives. All this is clear from the deeds of Dalfin, or Annemundus, which we have excerpted in various places from the records of the churches of Lyon. There he is venerated as a true martyr who suffered for justice on 28 September. Chifflet.

After coming to Britain, Wilfrid entered into the friendship of King Alhfrith, who had learned always to follow and love the Catholic rules of the Church.

> **Note:** Alhfrith. Authors confuse him with Aldfrith, but their names are plainly different. Alhfrith was also the legitimate son of Oswiu and died while his father was still alive; Aldfrith was illegitimate and reigned after his brother Ecgfrith. Alhfrith had Wilfrid as his teacher, whereas Aldfrith was educated by Irish scholars.

When Alhfrith discovered that Wilfrid was Catholic, he immediately gave him land for ten families at a place called Stamford.

> **Note:** Stamford. There is a town of this name in the southern part of Lincolnshire, but there is good reason to doubt whether it is the place Bede means. If we believe Henry of Huntingdon, the town is extremely ancient; in the second book of his *History*, the Saxons are said to have put the Scots and Picts to flight near it around 449. The Wessobrun manuscript, p. 38a, has the following: “At Stainforth there is a cell in honor of Saint Leonard, first established by Saint Wilfrid and later granted by King William the Conqueror to William of Durham, the prior, and the convent of Durham, for monks to inhabit.” But the cell cannot have been established by Saint Wilfrid there for this very reason: Stanford lies in Lindsey, which, when King Alhfrith gave Wilfrid land at that place, was not under the power of the Northumbrian king but of the Mercians. A place of this name must therefore be sought in the kingdom of the Northumbrians, and perhaps Stanford on the river Derwent in Yorkshire is the place we seek.

Not long afterward he gave him a monastery for thirty families at a place called Ripon.

> **Note:** Not long afterward. This was probably about 661. Wilfrid set out for Rome with Benedict, who, according to Florence of Worcester, left Britain in 653; after staying for a time with Dalfin in Gaul, he reached Rome in 654. After several months, as Eddius writes, he probably returned to Dalfin in the following year; having remained with him three years, he returned to Britain after Dalfin’s beheading in 658. After joining King Alhfrith’s friendship and remaining at his court three years, he became abbot of Ripon about 661. Eadmer, *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, in Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, century III, part I, p. 200.

> **Note:** Thirty. Forty, according to III, 25.

He had earlier given this place for the construction of a monastery to those who followed the Scots.

> **Note:** To those who followed the Scots. To Abbot Eata of Melrose, Saint Cuthbert, and the other monks of Melrose. See the Life of Cuthbert, 7–8.

But when they later had the choice, they preferred to withdraw from the place rather than accept the Catholic Easter and the other canonical rites according to the custom of the Roman and apostolic Church. He therefore gave it to Wilfrid, whom he saw to be imbued with better disciplines and customs.

At that time, in 664, Wilfrid was ordained priest in the same monastery by Agilbert, bishop of the Gewissae, whom we mentioned above. The king desired that a priest and teacher of such learning and religion should remain constantly in his personal company.

Not long afterward, after the sect of the Scots had been exposed and expelled, as we have shown above, the king sent him to Gaul and, with the counsel and consent of his father Oswiu, asked that he be ordained bishop.

> **Note:** Bishop. See III, 28 and IV, 2.

He was then about thirty years old. Agilbert was at that time governing the episcopate of the city of Paris—or, according to another reading, was exercising the episcopate in the city of Paris. Eleven other bishops assembled with him for the consecration of the bishop and carried out the ministry with great honor.

> **Note:** Honorably. “They raised him up, seated in a golden chair according to their custom, carrying him in their hands. Only the bishops touched him as they bore him into the oratories, while others sang hymns and chants in the choir.” Heddius, *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, 12.

While Wilfrid was still staying overseas, the holy Ceadda was consecrated bishop at York by order of King Oswiu, as mentioned above. He governed the Church with distinction for three years and then withdrew to take charge of his monastery at Lastingham.

> **Note:** He withdrew. See IV, 3.

Wilfrid then received the episcopate of the entire province of the Northumbrians.

Later, during the reign of Ecgfrith, he was expelled from the episcopate, and other bishops were consecrated in his place, as we mentioned above.

> **Note:** Expelled. Into the regions of the Mercians (IV, 13; V, 11).

He set out for Rome to state his case before the apostolic pope. When he boarded a ship, however, a west wind drove him to Frisia. He was honorably received by the Frisians and by their king Aldgisl. He preached Christ to them and instructed many thousands of them in the word of truth, washing them from the filth of their sins in the Savior’s font.

What the most reverend bishop of Christ, Willibrord, later completed with great devotion, Wilfrid himself first began there as an evangelical work.

> **Note:** Willibrord. See V, 11–12.

He spent the winter there successfully with the new people of God. Then he resumed his journey to Rome, and when his case was heard in the presence of Pope Agatho and many bishops, the judgment of all found that he had been accused without fault and that he was worthy of the episcopate.

In that same period Pope Agatho convened a synod of 125 bishops at Rome against those who taught that the Lord and Savior had one will and one operation. He ordered Wilfrid to be summoned and, seated among the bishops, to state both his own faith and that of the province or island from which he had come.

When he and his people were found to be Catholic in faith, it pleased the synod to insert this among its other acts. It was written as follows:

> “Wilfrid, the bishop beloved of God of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case, and acquitted by that authority of matters both certain and uncertain, and seated with 125 other bishops—or, according to another reading, fellow bishops—in the synod in the seat of judgment, confessed the true and Catholic faith on behalf of the whole northern region, and of the islands of Britain and Ireland inhabited by the peoples of the English, Britons, Scots, and Picts, and confirmed it with his subscription.”

After this he returned to Britain and converted the province of the South Saxons from the rites of idolatry to the faith of Christ.

> **Note:** Of the South Saxons. See IV, 13.

He also sent ministers of the word to the Isle of Wight.

> **Note:** Of the Isle of Wight. See IV, 16.

In the second year of Aldfrith, who reigned after Ecgfrith, he recovered his see and episcopate at the king’s insistence.

> **Note:** His see. The see of York (V, 3).

But after five years he was again accused and was expelled from the episcopate by that same king and by many bishops.

> **Note:** Expelled. Into the regions of the Mercians (IV, 13; V, 11).

He came to Rome, and when his accusers were present and he was given an opportunity to defend himself, several bishops sitting with the apostolic pope John, the judgment of all established that his accusers had contrived against him charges that were false in several respects. The aforesaid pope therefore wrote to the English kings Æthelred and Aldfrith that they should restore him to his episcopate, since he had been condemned unjustly.

The reading of the synod of the blessed Pope Agatho also aided the case for his acquittal. That synod had once been held in the city while Wilfrid was present and seated among the bishops in the same council, as we have said.

When the same synod, because the case required it, was read for several days before the nobles and a great crowd of people by order of the apostolic pope, they reached the passage where it was written:

> “Wilfrid, the bishop beloved of God of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case, and acquitted by that authority of matters both certain and uncertain,”

and the rest of the words quoted above.

When this was read, astonishment seized the listeners. While the reader was silent, they began asking one another who this Bishop Wilfrid was. Then Boniface, counselor of the apostolic pope, and many others who had seen him there in the time of Pope Agatho, said that he was the bishop who had recently come to Rome, accused by his own people and summoned to judgment before the apostolic see:

> “He came here long ago, equally accused. Once the case and the controversy of both parties had been heard and judged, he was declared by Pope Agatho of blessed memory to have been expelled from his episcopate contrary to law. He was held in such high regard by him that, in the council he had assembled, he ordered Wilfrid to sit among the bishops as a man of incorrupt faith and upright character.”

On hearing this, everyone, together with the bishop himself, declared that a man of such authority, who had exercised the episcopate for nearly forty years, ought by no means to be condemned. Instead, absolved completely from the charges brought against him, he should return to his homeland with honor.

> **Editorial chronological and textual-variant register:** The marginal chronological annotations omitted from the draft are: Forthere’s succession, 709; the South-Saxon decree, 711; Coinred’s departure, 709; Wilfrid at Lindisfarne, 648; his dispatch to Kent, 652; his attachment to Benedict’s party, `[CCLIII]` as printed; his arrival at Rome, 654; return to Dalfin, 655; Dalfin’s death, 658; Ripon, 661; Wilfrid’s priestly ordination, 664; his first expulsion, 678; his hearing before Agatho, 679; conversion of the South Saxons, 681; recovery of his see, 686; his second expulsion, 691; and the order for his restoration, 704.
>
> The remaining readings are as follows. In the division of Haeddi’s see, an alternative adds *est* (“was”) after *data* (“given”). Forthere’s office is *pontificatus*, with *episcopatus* (“episcopate”) as the alternative reading. Selsey is *Selaeseu*, alternatively *Selaeu*; the chapter heading reads singular *rex* (“king”), alternatively plural *reges* (“kings”). At Rome Offa is said to have arrived with the others (*pervenerunt*), alternatively alone (*pervenit*).
>
> Of Wilfrid, *transiens* (“surpassing [his age]”) is alternatively *transigens* (“spending [his age]”), and *gereret* (“he conducted himself”) alternatively *gerebat* (“was conducting himself”). Queen Eanfled knew him (*ei notus erat*); the alternative reverses the construction, *cui notus erat*, without changing the sense. At Lyon Wilfrid was *retentus* (“detained”); the alternative *retento* makes Dalfin the person detained. The king *jussit* (“ordered”) Benedict to take Wilfrid; alternatively the infinitive *perducere* (“to lead”) stands. The bishop was *obsecrans* (“earnestly begging”) Wilfrid to return through Lyon; alternatively *observans* (“observing”). One witness adds the name *Ulftridus* at Wilfrid’s arrival in Rome. Wilfrid remained with Dalfin three years, while Chifflet reads six. Dalfin offered to regard him as an adopted son “always”; one alternative omits “always.”
>
> In the account of Alhfrith’s gift, *ille* means “he” (Alhfrith), while the alternative *illi* means “to him” (Wilfrid). In the sentence on the Scottish party, one witness omits *et* (“and”) in “exposed and expelled.” In Frisia Wilfrid was *instituens* (“instructing”) many thousands, alternatively *instruens* (“teaching”). At Agatho’s hearing, one reading has *fuisset* (“had been accused”) rather than *fuisse* (“was accused”); one omits *fide* (“in faith”). In the synodal quotation York is *Eboracae*, alternatively *Eboracensis*; Wilfrid confirms the confession *cum subscriptione sua* (“with his subscription”), alternatively *cum conscriptione sua* (“with his written attestation”).
>
> Afterward Wilfrid is *reversus* (“having returned”), alternatively *veniens* (“having come”); one witness adds *veram* (“true”) before “faith.” In the later Roman judgment, one reading adds *est* after *scriptum* (“it was written”); *ergo* (“therefore”) is alternatively *enim* (“for”); those present in Agatho’s time had seen Wilfrid *ibi* (“there”), alternatively *ubi* (“where”); he had recently *advenerit* (“arrived”), alternatively *advenerat* (“had arrived”); Agatho had *probatus* (“declared/proved”) that he was unlawfully expelled, alternatively *prolatus* (“pronounced”); and the council consists of *episcoporum* (“bishops”), alternatively singular *episcopum* (“bishop”).

On his return from Britain, when he had reached the regions of Gaul, he was suddenly stricken with illness. As it grew worse, he was so afflicted that he could not even ride a horse, but had to be carried by his attendants on a litter [DCCV]. Thus conveyed [Al. adds: “was”] to the Gallic city of Meaux, he lay for four days and nights as though dead, showing that he lived only by his extremely faint breathing. When he had continued for four days without food or drink, voice or hearing, at last, as the fifth day dawned [Al., “advanced”], he rose as though awakening from a deep sleep and sat up. Opening his eyes, he saw around him groups of brothers singing psalms and weeping together. Sighing faintly, he asked where the priest Acca was. Acca was immediately summoned and entered; seeing him improved and already able to speak, he knelt and gave thanks to God with all the brothers who were present.

After they had sat together for a little while and, trembling at the prospect of heavenly judgments, had begun to converse about various matters [Al., “to converse for a while”], the bishop ordered the others to leave for an hour and began speaking to the priest Acca as follows:

“Just now a terrifying vision appeared to me. I want you to hear it and keep it secret until I know what God intends to be done with me. For someone splendid in a white garment stood before me and said that he was Michael the archangel. ‘For this reason,’ he said, ‘I have been sent: to call you back from death. The Lord has granted you life through the prayers and tears of your disciples and brothers, and through the intercession of his blessed mother, ever-virgin Mary. Therefore I tell you that you will indeed now be healed of this illness; but be prepared, for after four years I shall return and visit you. When you have reached your homeland, you will recover the greater part of your possessions that were taken from you, and you will end your life in tranquil peace.’”

Thus the bishop recovered, to the joy of all and with all giving thanks to God, and, having resumed his journey, he reached Britain.

When Archbishop Berctuald and Æthelred, formerly king but then abbot, had read the letters which he had brought from the apostolic pope, they gladly supported him. Æthelred summoned to himself Coenred, whom he had made king in his place, and asked him to become the bishop’s friend; he obtained his request. But Aldfrid, king of the Northumbrians, disdainfully refused to receive him, and did not long survive. Consequently, when his son Osred was reigning, a synod was soon held beside the river Nidd [Note: [Col. 0268D] “At the Synod.” See Hedd., 58, and Spelm., *Councils*, I, 203.]. After a considerable dispute between both parties, with everyone at last giving approval, he was restored to the episcopate of his own Church [Note: [Col. 0268D] “Of his own.” It is called “of Hagustald” because in the year 674 he himself built it in honor of the apostle Saint Andrew. Ric. Hag., chapter 3.]. Thus for four years, that is, until the day of his death, he lived in peace.

He died [Al. adds: “on the fourth day before the Ides of October”] in his monastery, which he possessed in the province of Oundle, under the rule of the abbot Cudwald; and, carried by the ministry of the brothers to his first monastery, called Ripon, he was placed [Al. adds: “-que”] in the church of the blessed apostle Peter beside the altar to the south (DCCIX), as we stated above [Al. omits “and”]; and this epitaph was written about him above [Al. omits “above”]:

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Wilfrid. See more about him in the appendix, no. 19.]

Here lies in body the great bishop Wilfrid,  
Who, led by love of piety toward the Lord, made this hall  
And consecrated it under the illustrious name of Peter,  
To whom Christ, arbiter of the world, gave the keys of heaven;  
And devotedly clothed it in gold and Tyrian purple.

Moreover, here he set up the lofty trophy of the cross,  
Radiant with metal; and he also ordered  
Four books of the Gospel to be written in gold;  
And fashioned for them a worthy chest of gleaming gold.

He corrected the Paschal seasons  
Of the Catholic cycle to the true rule of the canon  
Which the Fathers established; and, removing doubtful error,  
Displayed to his people the sure governing principles of the rite.

In these places he gathered large companies of monks  
And diligently guarded the precepts which the rule of the Fathers  
Had established; and, driven by many dangers  
At home and abroad for a very long time,  
After serving as bishop for fifteen times three years,  
He departed and joyfully sought the heavenly realms.

Grant, Jesus, that the flock may follow the shepherd’s path.

## CHAPTER XX. How Albinus succeeded the religious Abbot Hadrian, and Acca succeeded Wilfrid in the episcopate

[Col. 0269C]

In the year immediately following the death of the aforesaid Father [DCCX], that is, the fifth year of King Osred, the most reverend Father Hadrian, abbot—fellow-worker in the word of God with Theodore, bishop of blessed memory—died and was buried in his monastery, in the church of the blessed Mother of God (see Book IV, chapter 1; Book II, chapter 6). This was the forty-first year since he had been sent with Theodore by Pope Vitalian, and the thirty-ninth since he had come to Britain.

Among other testimonies to the learning both of Hadrian and of Theodore is the fact that Albinus, his disciple, who succeeded him in the governance of his monastery, was so thoroughly trained in the study of the Scriptures [Col. 0270A] that he knew Greek to a considerable extent, Latin no less than English, which was his native language.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Albinus. Bede was assisted by him in writing the history. See the preface to the *History*. He was blessed by Berctuald on the Sunday within the Octave of Easter, which was then the tenth day before the Kalends of May. Elm., W. Thorn, *Chronicle*, states that he was the first Englishman to govern that monastery, but this is incorrect, since Benedict Biscop, a noble Englishman, received the monastery’s governance from Theodore. Beda, *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow*, year 732. “Having completed his life in peace, he was buried in the church of the Mother of God beside the blessed Hadrian, his predecessor; but at the translation of Saint Augustine and his companions, that same Father Albinus, together with blessed Hadrian and the others buried there, was transferred from the aforesaid church of the Mother of God into the larger church and placed in the wall behind the altar of Saint Gregory.” Thorn. Quercetanus was therefore wrong when, in his preface to Alcuin’s works, he maintained that this man was the same as Alwin or Albinus who, as Matthew of Westminster reports, was bishop at Lichfield in the year 734 and died in 737. In the Roman Martyrology his anniversary is kept on the ninth day of January.]

The priest Acca succeeded Wilfrid in the bishopric of the Church of Hagustald [Note: [Col. 0270D] Acca. He was first an abbot before becoming a bishop; Bede addressed his *Hexaemeron* to Abbot Acca. He may have been abbot of Hagustald, for when Saint Wilfrid was dying he ordered the monastery at Hagustald to be given into the possession of the priest Acca. Hedd., 62. Bede also wrote for Acca his explanation of Luke and Mark and other works. In 732 he was expelled from the episcopate for some reason unknown to me. He died in 740, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. Ric. Hag., 14, 13: “His body was buried on the eastern side of the church of Hagustald, outside the wall. More than three hundred years after his burial, by divine revelation it was transferred from that place by a certain priest and placed in a coffin within the church.” Certain miracles concerning his relics are also reported. Sim. Dunelm., p. 101.], a man himself most energetic and distinguished both before God and among human beings. He enlarged the building of his own church, consecrated in honor of the apostle Saint Andrew, with manifold adornment and marvelous works.

For he took care—as he still does—that, after relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ had been acquired from every source, altars should be dedicated to their veneration, with separate porticoes constructed for this purpose within the walls of the same church. He also gathered with the greatest diligence accounts of their passions [Al., “passion”], together with other ecclesiastical volumes [Col. 0270B], and established there a most extensive and noble library. He likewise provided with the greatest care sacred vessels, lamps, and other things of this kind belonging to the adornment of the house of God.

He also summoned to himself an excellent cantor named Maban [Al., “by name”], who had been taught the melodies of singing by successors of the disciples of the blessed Pope Gregory in Kent, and kept him for twelve years to instruct himself and his people. In this way Maban could teach the ecclesiastical songs which they did not know, and, through his instruction, restore to their ancient condition those which, once known, had begun to grow old through long use or neglect [Al. omits “once”].

For Bishop Acca himself was also a most skilled singer, highly learned in the sacred writings, most pure in his confession of the Catholic faith, and most capable in the rules of ecclesiastical discipline. He does not cease to be such until he receives [Al. adds: “his”] the rewards of pious devotion [Al., “until he received them”; Al., “he ceased to be such”]. From childhood he had been raised and educated in the clergy of the most holy and God-beloved Bosa, bishop of York. He then came to Bishop Wilfrid in the hope of a better way of life and spent his entire life in his service until Wilfrid’s death. With him he also came to Rome [Note: [Col. 0270D] Rome. See V, 19.] and learned there many things useful to the institutions of the holy Church which he had been unable to learn in his homeland.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Abbot Ceolfrid sent the king of the Picts architects for a church, together with a letter concerning the Catholic Easter and the tonsure

[Col. 0271A]

At that time [DCCX], Naiton, king of the Picts who inhabit the northern regions of Britain, having been admonished by frequent meditation on the ecclesiastical Scriptures, renounced the error by which he and his people had until then been bound in their observance of Easter, and led himself and all his people to celebrate the Catholic season of the Lord’s Resurrection.

To accomplish this more easily and with greater authority, he sought assistance from the English, whom he knew long before to have ordered their religion according to the example of the holy Roman and apostolic Church. Accordingly, he sent envoys to the venerable man Ceolfrid, abbot [Note: [Col. 0271D] Ceolfrid. See the *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow* and Gyru.] of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which lies at the mouth of the river Wear and beside the river Tyne, in a place called Jarrow [Note: [Col. 0271D] “In Gyruum.” Today Jarrow in the county of Durham.]. After Benedict, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Above.” See IV, 18; V, 19.], Ceolfrid had most gloriously governed it.

Naiton asked him to send him an exhortatory letter [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Letters.” There is scarcely any doubt that Bede, living with Ceolfrid in the same monastery, assisted his abbot in explaining this difficult question. Both the style and the subject itself clearly indicate that the work is Bede’s. According to Baronius, the letter was written in 699; but I would rather say with Higden, in the *Polychronicon*, that it was written in 710, the same year in which the preceding chapter records the death of Abbot Hadrian. The timing of the conversion of the people of Iona to the canonical Easter also seems to support this conjecture, although Bede records in the following chapter that it occurred not long after these letters were written, even though it was not completed before 716.] by which he might more powerfully refute those who presumed to observe Easter at the wrong time. He also asked for instruction concerning the manner or form of the tonsure by which clerics ought to be marked, although he himself was already considerably instructed in these matters.

He further asked that architects be sent to him who could build a stone church among his people according to Roman custom. He promised that it would be dedicated in honor of the blessed chief of the apostles, and that he himself, together with all his people, would always imitate the custom of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, insofar as, being so far separated from the speech and nation of the Romans, they could learn it.

The most reverend Abbot Ceolfrid, favoring his pious vows and prayers, sent the architects who had been requested [Al., “who requested”], and also sent him a letter written as follows:

“Ceolfrid, abbot, sends greetings in the Lord to the most excellent and most glorious Lord King Naiton.

“We are most ready and willing, O king devoted to God, to explain according to your desire the Catholic observance of holy Easter, which you have sought from us with religious zeal, in accordance with what we have learned from the apostolic see. For we know that this has been granted from heaven to the holy Church whenever the very rulers of temporal affairs devote themselves to learning, teaching, and preserving the truth [Col. 0271D].

“Indeed, one of the secular writers truly said that the world would be governed in the happiest condition if either kings became philosophers or philosophers became kings. If a mortal man of this world could rightly understand the philosophy of this world—or [Chiffl. adds: “that is”] duly care for [Chiffl.: “speak of”] the condition of this world—how much more ought the citizens of the heavenly homeland, living as pilgrims in this world, to desire and implore with all the strength of their minds that, the more power each person possesses in the world, the more earnestly he should strive to heed the commands of the Judge who is above all things, and should train by example and authority those also who have been entrusted to him to observe them [Col. 0272A; Al. adds: “and”]?

“There are therefore three rules given in the sacred writings which establish for us the appointed time for celebrating Easter; no human authority may alter them in any way. Two of these were divinely established in the Law of Moses, and the third was added in the Gospel through the fulfillment of the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

“The Law commanded that Easter should take place in the first month of the year and in the third week of that month, that is, from the fifteenth day through the twenty-first. Through the apostolic institution derived from the Gospel, it was added that, in that third week, we must await the Lord’s Day and place the beginning of the Paschal season upon it. Whoever rightly observes this threefold rule will never err in determining the date of the Paschal feast.

“But if you desire to hear a fuller and more detailed explanation of each point, it is written in Exodus, where the people of Israel, about to be delivered from Egypt, are first commanded to celebrate the Passover. For the Lord said to Moses and Aaron:

“‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month each man shall take a lamb for his family and household.’

“And shortly afterward:

“‘You shall keep it until the fourteenth day [Al. adds: “day”] of this month. Then the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening.’

“From these words it is perfectly clear that, although the fourteenth day is mentioned in the Paschal observance, Easter is not commanded to take place on the fourteenth day itself. Rather, when the evening [Al., “in the evening”] of the fourteenth day arrives—that is, when the fifteenth moon, which begins the third week, appears in the face of heaven—the lamb is commanded to be sacrificed. This is the night of the fifteenth moon, on which, after the Egyptians had been struck down, Israel was redeemed from long slavery.

“‘For seven days,’ he says, ‘you shall eat unleavened bread.’

“By these words also the entire third week of the same first month is decreed to be solemn. But lest we should think that these seven days were to be counted [Al., “reckoned”] from the fourteenth through the twentieth, he immediately added:

“‘On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel. From the first day through the seventh day,’ and so on, until he says:

“‘For on this very day I shall bring your army out of the land of Egypt.’

“He therefore calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the day on which he was to bring their army out of Egypt. It is clear, however, that they did not leave Egypt on the fourteenth day, on whose evening the lamb was sacrificed and which is properly called Passover or Phase, but on the fifteenth day, as is stated most plainly in the Book of Numbers:

“‘They departed from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the following day [Al. adds: “they celebrated”] the children of Israel celebrated the Phase with uplifted hand.’

“The seven days of Unleavened Bread, the first of which saw the Lord’s people led out of Egypt, must therefore be counted, as we have said, from the beginning of the third week—that is, from the fifteenth day of the first month—through the completion of the twenty-first day of that month.

“The fourteenth day, moreover, is marked separately outside this number under the title of Passover, as the continuation of Exodus clearly teaches. After it had said, ‘For on this very day I shall bring your army out of the land of Egypt,’ it immediately added:

“‘You shall keep this day throughout your generations as a perpetual observance. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses.’

“For who does not see that, from the fourteenth through the twenty-first, there are not merely seven days but rather eight, if the fourteenth itself is counted? But if, as a more careful examination of the truth of Scripture shows, we count from the evening of the fourteenth day to the evening of the twenty-first, we shall plainly see that the fourteenth day extends its evening [Al. omits “in”] into the beginning of the Paschal feast in such a way that the entire sacred solemnity comprises no more than seven nights and as many days [Al. adds: “only”]. Thus our definition is proved true: the Paschal season is to be celebrated in the first month of the year and in its third week. It truly occurs in the third week, because it begins at the evening of the fourteenth day and ends at the evening of the twenty-first.

“After Christ our Passover was sacrificed and made the Lord’s Day—a day which among the ancients was called the first day of the week or of the Sabbaths—a solemn day through the joy of his resurrection, apostolic tradition inserted it [Al. adds: “now”] into the Paschal festivals in such a way that it determined that nothing should be anticipated or diminished in the timing of the legal Passover.

“Rather, it established that the first month of the year should be awaited according to the command of the Law, that its fourteenth day should be awaited, and that the evening of that day should be awaited. If this day should happen to fall on a Sabbath, each person should take a lamb for his family and household and sacrifice it in the evening [Al., ‘they should sacrifice it’]. That is, all the Churches throughout the world, which together form one Catholic Church, should prepare bread and wine as the mystery of the flesh and blood of the immaculate Lamb who took away the sins of the world. After the appropriate solemnity of Paschal readings, prayers, and ceremonies [Al. adds: ‘and’], they should offer these to the Lord in hope of their future redemption [Col. 0274A].

“For this is the same night on which the Israelite people were rescued from Egypt through the blood of the lamb; it is the same night on which, through Christ’s resurrection, all God’s people were freed from eternal death.

“But when the Lord’s Day dawned, they should celebrate the first day of the Paschal feast. For this is the day on which the Lord revealed the glory of his resurrection to his disciples through the joy of manifold holy manifestations.

“This is the first day of Unleavened Bread, about which it is written with great precision in Leviticus:

“‘In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month [Al. adds: “of this month”], at evening, it is the Lord’s Phase. And on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s Unleavened Bread. You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days. The first day shall be most celebrated and holy.’

“If it were possible for the Lord’s Day always to fall on the fifteenth day of the first month, that is, on the fifteenth moon, then we could always celebrate Easter at one and the same time with the ancient people of God, although with a different kind of sacrament, just as we share one and the same faith in celebrating Easter.

“But because the days of the week do not proceed in equal step with the moon, apostolic tradition—which was preached at Rome through blessed Peter and confirmed at Alexandria through Mark the Evangelist, Peter’s interpreter—decreed that, when the first month arrives and the evening of its fourteenth day arrives [Al. omits “in it”], the Lord’s Day should also be awaited from the fifteenth through the twenty-first day of that same month.

“On whichever of these days it is found, Easter should rightly be celebrated, because that day belongs to the number of those seven days on which the eating of unleavened bread is commanded. Thus it comes about that our Easter never departs in either direction from the third week of the first month. It embraces either the whole of it—that is, all seven of the legal days of Unleavened Bread—or at least some of them.

“For even if it should seize only one of them, namely the seventh itself, which Scripture commends so highly—‘The seventh day,’ it says, ‘shall be more celebrated and holier, and no servile work shall be done on it’—no one could accuse us of failing [Al., ‘accuse us of not’] to celebrate correctly the Lord’s Paschal day, which we have received from the Gospel, in the very third week of the first month established by the Law.

“Once the Catholic rationale for this observance has been disclosed, the unreasonable error of those who, without any compelling necessity, presume either to anticipate or to exceed the limits fixed in the Law becomes clear by contrast.

“Those who think that the Lord’s Paschal day must be observed from the fourteenth day of the first month through the twentieth [Al., “with the Lord’s Paschal day”] anticipate the time prescribed in the Law without any necessary reason. For when they begin celebrating the vigils of the holy night from the evening of the thirteenth day, it is clear that they establish as the beginning of their Easter the day of whose beginning they find no mention whatsoever in the decree of the Law [Al., “that”]. And when they refuse to celebrate the Lord’s Easter on the twenty-first day of the month, it is perfectly clear that they entirely exclude from their solemnity the day which the Law repeatedly commends as more memorable than the others because of its greater festivity.

“Thus, by a perverse ordering of the Paschal day, they sometimes complete it entirely in the second week and never place it on the seventh day of the third week.

“Again, those who think that Easter should be celebrated from the sixteenth day of the aforesaid month through the twenty-second depart from the straight path of truth with no less error, although on the opposite side; like those fleeing the shipwrecks of Scylla, they fall into the whirlpool of Charybdis and are swallowed up.

“For when they teach that Easter must begin at the rising of the sixteenth moon of the first month—that is, at the evening of the fifteenth day—it is plainly evident that they entirely exclude from the solemnity the fourteenth day of that month, which the Law first and chiefly commends. Thus they scarcely touch the evening of the fifteenth day, on which God’s people were redeemed from Egyptian slavery [Al., “Egyptian”], on which the Lord freed the world by his own blood from the darkness of sins, and on which, having been buried, he granted us hope of blessed rest after death.

“Receiving the punishment of their error upon themselves, when they establish the Lord’s Paschal day on the twenty-second day of the month, they openly violate the legitimate limits of Easter, since they begin Easter at the evening of the day on which the Law decreed that it should be completed and brought to an end. They designate as the first Paschal day one of which there is nowhere any mention in the Law: namely, the first day of the fourth week.

“Both groups, moreover, err not only in their definition and calculation of the age of the moon, but sometimes also in determining the first month.

“This discussion is too extensive either to be contained in this letter or to be appropriate to it. I will say only this: by means of the spring equinox it can always be determined without error which month, according to the lunar calculation, ought to be considered the first month of the year and which the last.

“According to the opinion of all Eastern peoples, and especially the Egyptians, who surpass other teachers in the art of calculation, the equinox customarily occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; we ourselves confirm this by observing the timepiece [Al., ‘have confirmed it’].

“Therefore, whatever full moon occurs before the equinox—whether it is the fourteenth or fifteenth moon—belongs to the final month of the preceding year and is consequently unsuitable for celebrating Easter.

“But whenever the full moon occurs after the equinox or on the equinox itself, it must be understood without any doubt that, since it belongs to the first month, the ancients were accustomed to celebrate Easter in it, and that we too ought to celebrate in it whenever the Lord’s Day arrives.

“The reason compelling us to do this is clearly that it is written in Genesis that God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night; or, as another edition reads, ‘the greater light for the beginning of the day and the lesser light for the beginning of the night.’

“Just as the Sun first proceeded from the middle of the East and established the spring equinox by its rising, and then the Moon, when the Sun was setting in the evening [Al., “toward evening”], followed from the middle of the East at its full phase, so in every year the first lunar month must necessarily be observed in the same order. Its full moon must not occur before the equinox, but either on the day of the equinox itself, as happened at the beginning, or after the equinox has passed.

“If the full moon precedes the time of the equinox by even one day, the stated reasoning proves that it must be assigned not to the first month of the beginning year but rather to the last month of the preceding year, and therefore is unsuitable for the Paschal festivals.

“If you are also pleased to hear the mystical meaning of these matters, we are commanded to celebrate Easter in the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, because, with the spirit of our mind renewed toward love of heavenly things, we ought to celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Resurrection and of our deliverance [Col. 0276B].

“We are commanded to celebrate in the third week of that month because Christ himself, who was to be sacrificed as our Passover, came with grace in the third age of the world, having been promised before the Law and under the Law. Rising from the dead on the third day after the sacrifice of his passion, he willed that this day should be called the Lord’s Day and that we should celebrate on it each year the festivals of his resurrection.

“For we too truly celebrate his solemnities only when, through faith, hope, and charity, we strive to make Passover with him—that is, the passage from this world to the Father.

“We are commanded to observe the full moon of the Paschal month after the spring equinox, so that first the sun may make the day longer than the night, and then the moon may present to the world the full circle of its light. For first the Sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing—that is, the Lord Jesus—overcame all the darkness of death through the triumph of his resurrection. Then, ascending into heaven and sending the Spirit from above, he filled his Church, which is often signified by the name ‘Moon,’ with the light of inward grace.

“Contemplating this order of our salvation, the Prophet said: ‘The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order.’

“Whoever maintains that the fullness of the Paschal moon can occur before the equinox is, in the celebration of the greatest mysteries, out of harmony with the teaching of the holy Scriptures. He agrees instead with those who trust that they can be saved without the grace of Christ preceding them. For even if the true Light had never overcome the darkness of the world by dying and rising again, they presume to teach that they can possess perfect righteousness [Al., “who”].

“Thus, after the sun’s equinoctial rising and after the full moon of the first month which follows it in due order—that is, after the completion of the fourteenth day of that month—we continue, as the Gospel admonishes us, to await the time of the Lord’s Day in the third week. Only then do we celebrate the desired festivals of our Easter.

“In this way we declare that we do not venerate merely the shaking off of the yoke of Egyptian slavery with the ancients, but that we honor with devoted faith and love the redemption of the whole world, which was prefigured in the deliverance of the ancient people of God and completed in Christ’s resurrection. We also signify that we rejoice with the surest hope in our own resurrection, which we believe will take place on that same Lord’s Day.

“The Easter Computus which we show you to follow is contained in a nineteen-year cycle. It had already begun to be observed in the Church long ago—that is, in the very times of the Apostles—especially at Rome and in Egypt, as we have already stated above.

“But through the diligence of Eusebius, who bears the surname derived from the blessed martyr Pamphilus, it was arranged more distinctly and systematically, so that what had previously been customarily sent each year by the bishop of Alexandria to all the Churches could thereafter, once the series of the fourteenth moons had been organized, be readily known by everyone [Col. 0277A].

“The Alexandrian bishop Theophilus composed a Paschal calculation for a period of one hundred years for the emperor Theodosius. His successor Cyril likewise contained a series of ninety-five years in five nineteen-year cycles. After him Dionysius Exiguus appended an equal number of additional years in the same orderly pattern, extending down to our own times.

“As these cycles approach their conclusion, such an abundance of calculators exists today that even in our Churches throughout Britain there are many who, equipped with those ancient Egyptian methods committed to memory, can very easily extend Paschal cycles across any span of time they wish, even up to five hundred and thirty-two years. When these have been completed, everything relating to the succession of the sun and moon, the month and the week, recurs in the same order as before.

“For this reason we have refrained from sending you the same cycles of the times to come: you sought instruction only concerning the calculation of the Paschal season, and you have proved that you possess an ample supply of Catholic Paschal cycles.”

«But since I have briefly and concisely recalled these matters concerning Easter, as you requested, I also urge you to take care that you maintain the tonsure that is ecclesiastical and fitting for the Christian faith, about which likewise you wished letters to be written to you. Indeed, we know that not all the apostles were tonsured in one and the same manner, nor does the Catholic Church now agree throughout the world upon one uniform and indistinguishable form of tonsure, just as it agrees in one faith, hope, and love of God. Finally, to look back to earlier times, [Col. 0277D] that is, to the patriarchs: Job, an example of patience, when the moment of tribulation came upon him, shaved his head, thereby clearly showing that in the time of prosperity he had been accustomed to grow his hair. Joseph, however, himself an outstanding practitioner and teacher of chastity, humility, piety, and the other virtues, is read to have been tonsured when he was to be released from slavery; it is plainly evident that during the time of his servitude he had usually remained in prison with uncut hair. Behold: each man of God outwardly displayed a different appearance from the other, yet inwardly their consciences agreed in an equal grace of virtue.

But although we may freely profess that the difference of tonsure does no harm to those whose faith in God is pure and whose love for their neighbor is sincere—especially since we never read that the Catholic Fathers had any controversy over the difference of tonsure, as they did over the diversity of Easter or of the faith—nevertheless, among all the tonsures that we find either in the Church or throughout the human race, I would rightly declare that none should be followed and embraced more than that which was worn upon his head by the one to whom the Lord said, when he confessed him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell [Al., of the lower world] shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18).

Nor would I believe that any tonsure ought rightly to be more abhorred and detested by all the faithful than that which was worn by the man to whom Peter himself said, when he wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit: “Your money be with you unto perdition, [Col. 0278B] because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money [Al., with money]. You have no part or share in this word” (Acts 8:20–21). Nor are we tonsured into a crown merely because Peter was tonsured in that way; rather, because Peter was tonsured in memory of the Lord’s Passion, therefore we too, who desire to be saved through that same Passion, wear with him upon the crown of our heads—that is, upon the highest part of our bodies—the sign of that Passion.

For just as the whole Church, because it became the Church through the death of its Life-giver, is accustomed to bear the sign of his holy cross upon its forehead, so that it may often be defended by the protection of this standard against the assaults of evil spirits, and may be taught by frequent reminder that it too must crucify its flesh with its vices and desires; [Col. 0278C] so also it is fitting that those who have either taken the monastic vow or hold the clerical rank, and who must necessarily bind themselves more strictly for the Lord with the reins of continence, should bear upon their heads through tonsure the form of the crown that he himself wore upon his head in his Passion—the crown of thorns that he bore in order to carry, that is, to bear away and remove from us, the thorns and thistles of our sins. Thus they may show even by their foreheads that they willingly and readily endure every mockery and insult for his sake, and signify that they always await the crown of eternal life which God promised to those who love him, and that, in order to receive it, they despise both the adversity and the prosperity of the world.

As for the tonsure that they say Simon Magus had, [Col. 0278D] what believer, I ask, would not immediately detest and rightly reject it at the first sight of it, together with the magic itself? It appears, indeed, on the surface of the forehead to present the appearance of a crown; but when, on examining it, you reach the nape of the neck, you will find the crown that you thought you saw shortened, so that you may rightly recognize such an appearance as fitting Simonian heretics, not Christians. In the present life, such men were thought by deceived people worthy of the crown of perpetual glory; but in the life that follows this one, they are not only deprived of every hope of a crown, but are also condemned to eternal punishment.

Nor should you think that I have pursued this matter as though I judged those who wear this tonsure to be condemned [Al., deserving condemnation], if they support the unity of the Catholic faith in faith and works. Rather, I confidently profess that many of them have proved themselves holy and worthy of God. Among them was Adamnan, the distinguished abbot and priest of the Columban community, [Note: [Col. 0279D] Adamnan. Concerning him, see V, 15.] who, having been sent as an envoy of his people to King Aldfrid and wishing to visit our monastery as well, displayed remarkable prudence, humility, and religious devotion in his conduct and speech. I said to him, among other things, in conversation:

“Holy brother, I beg you: since you believe that you are striving toward the crown of life that knows no end, why do you wear upon your head, in a manner contrary to your faith, an image of a crown that has been cut short? And if you seek fellowship with blessed Peter, why do you imitate the appearance of the tonsure of the one whom he anathematized? Why do you not rather show that even now, as far as you can, you cherish the appearance of him with whom you desire to live blessed forever?”

He replied:

“Know for certain, my beloved brother, that although by the custom of my people I have Simon’s tonsure, I nevertheless detest and reject Simonian treachery with all my mind. But I desire, insofar as my insignificance permits, to follow the footsteps of the most blessed prince of the apostles.”

Then I said:

“I truly believe that this is so. Yet it is made evident that you embrace in the secret of your heart the things that belong to the Apostle Peter if you also bear upon your face the things that you know to be his. For I think that your prudence can very easily judge that it is far more fitting to separate from your own face the appearance of the one whom you hate with all your heart and whose dreadful face you shrink from seeing, and to whom you have already dedicated yourself to God; and, conversely, just as you desire to follow the deeds and teachings of the one whom you seek to have as your patron before God, so it is fitting that you should imitate even now the custom of his appearance.”

This is what I said then to Adamnan. How greatly he had profited from seeing the ordinances of our churches, he demonstrated when, after returning to Scotland, he later corrected many crowds of his people through his preaching and brought them to the Catholic observance of the proper time of Easter—even though he was still unable to lead back to the path of a better rule the monks who lived on the island of Hii and over whom he presided by the special authority of their ruler. Had he possessed sufficient authority to do so, he would also have remembered to correct his tonsure.

But now I also admonish your prudence, O king, that you strive to preserve in every respect, together with the people over whom the King of kings and Lord of lords has set you, those things that accord with the unity of the Catholic and apostolic Church. For thus it comes about that, after receiving the power of a temporal kingdom, the most blessed prince of the apostles himself may gladly open for you and yours, together with the other elect, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. May the grace of the eternal King preserve you, reigning for a long time, safe and unharmed for the peace of us all, most beloved son in Christ.”

[Col. 0280A] When this letter had been read in the presence of King Naiton and of many learned men, and had been carefully translated by those who understood it into his own language, he is said to have rejoiced greatly at the exhortation. Rising from the midst of the assembly of his nobles, he bent his knees to the ground and gave thanks to God that he had been deemed worthy to receive such a little gift from the land of the English.

“Indeed,” he said, “I already knew before that this was the true celebration of Easter; but only now do I understand so fully the method of observing this season that I seem in every respect to have understood very little about these matters before. Therefore I openly profess, and declare in the presence of you who are sitting here, that I wish to observe this time of Easter perpetually with all my people; [Al. adds: and] I decree that all the clergy who are in my kingdom should receive this tonsure, which we hear to be wholly rational.”

Without delay, he completed by royal authority what he had said. Immediately, by public command, nineteen-year Easter cycles were sent throughout all the provinces of the Picts to be copied, learned, and observed, while the erroneous eighty-four-year cycles were everywhere erased. All the ministers of the altar and the monks were tonsured into a crown; and the corrected people rejoiced as though they had submitted themselves to a new discipleship under the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and were placed under his protection.

## CHAPTER XXII. How the monks of Hii, together with the monasteries subject to them, began to celebrate canonical Easter through the preaching of Ecgberct

[Col. 0280C]

Not long afterward, those monks of the Scottish nation who inhabited the island of Hii [Note: [Col. 0279D] Hii. Concerning the Hiienses, see III, 4; V, 15.], together with the monasteries subject to them, were also, through the Lord’s providence, brought to the canonical rite of Easter and tonsure. For in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 716, when Osred had been killed [Note: [Col. 0279D] Osred. He succeeded Aldfrid in 705, V, 18.
