Living a shameful life by sexually violating nuns, he was eventually killed through the plots of his relatives while fighting near the sea, close to the southern borders. Malmesbury, *De Gestis Regum* I, 3; Westminster, under the year 717; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, under the year 716.], and Coenred had taken up the government of the kingdom of the Northumbrians [Note: [Col. 0280D] Coenred. Son of Cuthwine. He and his successor Osric “had only this memorable distinction: that, though they thought they were avenging with due punishment the blood of their lord who had been killed, they polluted the air by a shameful end.” Malmesbury, *De Gestis Regum* I, 3.], Ecgberct came to them from Ireland. He was a man beloved of God and worthy to be named with every honor, a father and priest; we have often made mention of him above [Note: [Col. 0280D] More often. See III, 4 and 27; V, 10, 11.], and he was received by them with honor and great joy.

Since he was both a most gracious teacher and a most devoted practitioner of what he taught ought to be done, he was willingly heard by all. Through his pious and earnest exhortations, he changed that ancient tradition of their ancestors, concerning whom one may appropriately cite the apostolic saying: “They had a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” He thoroughly taught them, as we have said, to celebrate the chief solemnity in the Catholic and apostolic manner, under the figure of a perpetual crown.

[Col. 0281A] This is shown to have happened through the wondrous dispensation of divine mercy: because that people, which had learned the knowledge of God, had gladly and without envy taken care to communicate it to the peoples of the English, it too afterward, through the people of the English, reached the perfect rule of life in those matters in which it had been deficient. Conversely, the Britons, who were unwilling to reveal to the English the knowledge of the Christian faith that they possessed, now that the peoples of the English believe and are thoroughly instructed in the rule of the Catholic faith, still remain antiquated and limping along their own paths; they display heads without a crown and venerate the solemnities of Christ without fellowship with the Church of Christ.

The monks of Hii, under the instruction of Ecgberct, adopted Catholic ways of life under Abbot Duunchad, about eighty years after they had sent Bishop Aidan to preach to the English people. [Col. 0281B] The man of God Ecgberct remained for thirteen years on the aforesaid island, which he had consecrated to Christ as though through a new grace restoring ecclesiastical fellowship and peace. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 729 [Al., 728], when the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, after he had celebrated the solemn rites of Mass in memory of that same resurrection of the Lord, he himself also departed to the Lord on that day. The joy of the highest festival that he had begun with the brothers whom he had converted to the grace of unity, he completed with the Lord, the apostles, and the other citizens of heaven—or rather, he does not cease to celebrate that same festival without end.

[Col. 0281C] The dispensation of divine providence was wondrous: the venerable man not only passed from this world to the Father at Easter, but did so when Easter was being celebrated on a day on which it had never previously been accustomed to be celebrated in those places. The brothers rejoiced at their certain and Catholic knowledge of the proper time of Easter; they rejoiced in the protection of the Father who was departing to the Lord, through whom they had been corrected; and he rejoiced that he had been preserved in the flesh until he saw his hearers accept and celebrate with him the day of Easter, which they had always previously avoided. Thus the most reverend Father, certain of their correction, exulted that he might see the day of the Lord: “He saw it, and rejoiced.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. The present condition of the English people and of the whole of Britain

[Col. 0282A]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 725, which was the seventh year of Osric, king of the Northumbrians, who had succeeded Coenred, Uictred, son of Ecgberct, king of the Kentish people, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. Of the kingdom that he had held for thirty-four and a half years, he left as heirs three sons, Aedilberct, Eadberct, and Alric [Al., Aldric]. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Sons. “Eadberct, who held the paternal institutions for twenty-three years, Aedilberct for eleven, and Alric for thirty-four, did not stain their kingdoms by an ignoble end, except that Aedilberct greatly obscured the glory of his times through the accidental burning of a city, and Alric through an ill-fated battle against the Mercians.” Malmesbury, *De Gestis Regum* I, 1. Bromton, in the *Ten Writers*, p. 742, calls them Egfred, Edbrict, and Cuthred.]

In the following year Tobias, bishop of the Church of Rochester, died—a man, as we have mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0281D] Above. See V, 8.], of the greatest learning. For he had been a disciple of the revered teachers Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian. Therefore, as has been said, he learned Greek as well as Latin, together with the languages of ecclesiastical and secular learning, so that they were as familiar and well known to him as the speech of his native [Al., new] language. He was buried in the portico of the Apostle Saint Paul, which he himself had constructed inside the church of Saint Andrew as a place for his tomb. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Church. King Aedilberct constructed it, II, 3. Archbishop Lanfranc later renewed it, and Archbishop William dedicated it in the year 1130, on the third day before the Nones of May. See Gervase, *Acts of the Bishops of Canterbury*, under Lanfranc and William.] After him Alduulf received the office of bishop, being consecrated by Archbishop Berctuald. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Alduulf. He consecrated Tatwini. See below. In 732 he obtained from King Aedilbald of Mercia an annual rent of one ship for himself and his successors. From King Eadberct of Kent he likewise received a gift of ten ploughlands at Andscohesham, and obtained confirmation of the donation from Archbishop Nothelm in 738. Florentius says that he died in 741; Simeon of Durham, the *Mailros Chronicle*, and Pseudo-Asser in 739.]

[Note: [Col. 0282D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 729. Thus the Treves manuscript and the Anglo-Saxon version correctly read it, whereas the other printed editions falsely have 728. The reason is obvious: Bede says in the same place that the Lord’s Easter occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, which plainly corresponds to the year 729 according to the ancient computation. CHIFFLET.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 729, two comets appeared near the sun [Al., two], causing great terror to those who watched them. One preceded the sun as it rose in the morning; the other followed it as it set in the evening, as though foretelling dreadful calamity for both east and west. Or certainly, one preceded the rising of day and the other that of night, signifying that evils threatened mortals at both times. They carried a fiery torch toward the north, as though inclined to set it ablaze; and they appeared in January and remained for nearly two weeks.

At that time the most grievous plague of the Saracens was devastating Gaul with wretched destruction, [Note: [Col. 0282D] And they themselves. According to the testimony of almost all historians, the Saracens suffered two defeats at the hands of Charles Martel, besides the first one that Bede indicates here under the year 732. See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, section III, part I, p. 526, and Pagi under the year 732. But that this may not be the true year of this defeat seems to be obstructed by the fact that Bede completed his History in 731—unless we say with Pagi, whom see under the year 729, “that he later inserted into his History those words and the mention of this victory.”] and not long afterward they paid in that same province penalties worthy of their treachery.

In that year the holy man of God Ecgberct, as we mentioned above, departed to the Lord on the very day of Easter. [Col. 0283A] Immediately after Easter, that is, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, King Osric of the Northumbrians died. [Note: [Col. 0283B] Osric. Son of Alhfrid.] He had determined that Ceoluulf, the brother of King Coenred, who had reigned before him, would succeed him in the kingdom that he had governed for eleven years. [Note: [Col. 0283B] Ceoluulf. To him Bede dedicates his History. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, he began to reign in 731; according to Westminster, in 730; but according to Bede, in 729. In 733 he was captured, tonsured, and restored to the kingdom, according to Westminster. In 737 he became a monk at the monastery of Lindisfarne, conferring upon Saint Cuthbert’s monastery the royal treasures and lands—that is, Bregesne and Wereworde with their appurtenances—and also the church that he himself had built there. [Col. 0283C] He also gave four other estates: Wudecestre, Huuittingaham, Eadfingham, and Eaguulfigham. He was buried in the monastery of Lindisfarne in 760; “but later, as time passed, Bishop Ecgred of the same place transferred him to Norham, and after the course of many years his head was transferred to Durham together with the other relics of the saints.” Simeon of Durham, p. 9. When this king had become a monk, permission was given to the monks of Lindisfarne Church to drink wine or ale; before that time they drank only milk or water. Ibid., p. 139.]

The beginnings and course of whose reign were so full of the upheavals of adverse events that it is not yet possible to know what ought to be written about them or what end each of them will have. [Note: [Col. 0283C] End. They certainly had the worst possible end. For in the historians we scarcely read anything about the history of the province of Northumbria except either defeats or depositions of kings. See William of Malmesbury, *De Gestis Regum* I, 3; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, under the years 757, 759, 774, 778, 789, 790, 794, and elsewhere; Bromton, p. 795.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 731, Archbishop Berctuald, worn out by old age, died on the day of the Ides of January. He had held office for thirty-seven years, six months, and fourteen days. In his place, in that same year, Tatuini was made archbishop, [Note: [Col. 0283C] Berctuald. See V, 8.] a man from the province of Mercia, who had been a priest in the monastery called Briudun. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Tatuini. See the letter of Pope Gregory concerning Tatuini’s promotion to the primacy of all Britain in Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum* I, under the year 732. He blessed Nodbald, the successor of Albinus, as abbot. *Chronicle of Thorn*. He died in 734, on the third day before the Kalends of August according to Florentius; according to Birchington, on the Kalends of August; according to Thorn, in 735, on the last day of July. See his epitaph in Leland, *Collectanea* II, 116.] [Note: [Col. 0283D] Briudun. A monastery near the Bredon Hills in the county of Worcester, which Eanulf, grandfather of King Offa of Mercia, built in honor of Saint Peter, and which Offa later enriched with many estates in 780. *Monasticon Anglicanum* I, 122.]

He was consecrated in the city of Dorovernum by the venerable men Danihel of Winchester, Inguald of London, Alduino [Al., Adwaldo] of Lichfield, and Alduulf of Rochester, on the tenth day of June, a Sunday. He was a man distinguished in religion and prudence, and nobly instructed in sacred learning.

At present, therefore, Bishops Tatuini and Alduulf preside over the churches of the Kentish people. Inguald is bishop of the province of the East Saxons. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Inguald. He is falsely said to have subscribed the Croiland charter of 716 and the Council of Baccanceld in 798. Ingulf and the *Ten Writers*, p. 2212. Most historians testify that he died in 743; according to Hoveden and the *London Historical Summary*, in 744.]

Aldberct and Hadulac are bishops of the province of the East Angles. Danihel and Fortheri are bishops of the province of the West Saxons. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Danihel. Concerning Danihel and Fortheri, see V, 18.]

Alduini is bishop of the province of the Mercians. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Alduini. He is also called Wor; he succeeded Haedda when the latter died in 721. He died in 737. *Anglia Sacra* I, 428.]

Ualchstod is bishop of those peoples who live beyond the River Severn to the west. [Note: [Col. 0284B] Ualchstod. Bishop of Hereford, where Putta first presided, IV, 12. Concerning the cross begun by him for the adornment of the house of God, and concerning the epitaph of him and his predecessors inscribed upon the tomb constructed for them by Cuthberct, see Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum* IV.]

Uilfrid is bishop of the province of the Hwicce. [Note: [Col. 0284B] Uilfrid. He succeeded Ecgwine in 717. He died in 742 according to the *Worcester Ecclesiastical Annals*; in 743 according to Florentius.]

Cyniberct [Al., Cymberct] presides as bishop over the province of the Lindisfari. [Note: [Col. 0284B] Cyniberct. Concerning the succession of the bishops of Lindisfarne, see IV, 12. He died in 732. Simeon of Durham, p. 99.]

The episcopate of the island of Wight belongs to Danihel, bishop of the city of Winchester. [Note: [Col. 0284C] Wight. See IV, 16.]

The province of the South Saxons, having now remained for several years without a bishop, seeks episcopal ministry from the bishop of the West Saxons. [Col. 0284B] All these provinces, and the other southern ones as far as the boundary of the River Humber, together with their respective kings, are subject to the king of the Mercians, Aedilbald. [Note: [Col. 0284C] Aedilbald. He began to reign in 716. In 733 he conquered Sumurt. In 740 he was ravaging part of Northumbria through impious treachery. In the following year King Cuthred of the West Saxons waged a fierce war against him. In 743 he and Cuthred fought against the Britons. In 749 he granted a privilege to the churches and monasteries of Mercia. In 757 he was treacherously killed at Seccandune by his own guardians and buried at Hreopandune. See Boniface’s letter to him in Spelman, *Councils* I, 232.]

But in the province of the Northumbrians, over which King Ceoluulf presides, four bishops now hold the episcopal office: [Note: [Col. 0284C–D] Uilfrid. He succeeded Saint John (V, 6) and held office for fifteen years. Writers differ as to the date of his death: the continuator of Bede’s *Epitome* places it in 745, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in 744, Westminster in 743, Thomas Stubbs in 736, and Simeon of Durham in 735. It is especially attractive, because of their venerable antiquity, to follow the authority of the *Epitome* and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, notwithstanding that the former reports Ecgberct made bishop in 732 and the latter in 734—when Uilfrid had not yet died, but had perhaps voluntarily relinquished his see. Yet perhaps the opinion Pagi expressed under 731 should be followed. He judges that Uilfrid of York died in 732, according to Bede’s *Epitome*, and that authors who assign this Uilfrid’s death to 743 or later are mistaken, having interpreted the continuator of Bede’s *Epitome* under 745 as referring to Uilfrid of York, whereas it seems rather to be understood of Uilfrid, bishop of the Hwicce. “An inextricable dispute is maintained between Canterbury and York: the Canterbury men say that they possess the elder Uilfrid, while the York men contend that this younger one was transferred to Kent by Archbishop Odo.” Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum* III, 1.] Uilfrid in the Church of York, Ediluald in the Church of Lindisfarne [Al. adds: Church], Acca in that of Hexham, [Note: [Col. 0284D] Acca. Concerning him, see V, 20.] and Pecthelm in the church called Candida Casa. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Pecthelm. Deacon of Saint Aldhelm, the first bishop of Sherborne, V, 18. He died in 735. Florentius.] This church, recently added as an episcopal see because of the multiplying communities of the faithful, has him as its first bishop. [Note: [Col. 0285D] First. He was indeed the first bishop after the new foundation, but Ninia had once been bishop there, III, 4.]

At this time the nation of the Picts both has a treaty of peace with the English people and rejoices to share in the peace and truth of the Catholic faith with the universal Church. The Scots who inhabit Britain, content with their own territories, plot no ambushes or frauds against the English people. The Britons, although for the most part they attack the English people out of mutual hatred and, through their evil customs, oppose the observance of Easter and the condition of the whole Catholic Church, nevertheless, with divine and human power wholly resisting them, are unable to attain their desired purpose in either matter. For although they are partly independent, in some part they are subject to the servitude of the English.

With peace and the calm of the times smiling upon them, many among the Northumbrian people, both noble and common, lay aside their weapons and strive to enroll themselves and their children in monastic vows by receiving the tonsure, rather than to devote themselves to military pursuits. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Both nobles. See Bede’s fuller lament on this matter in the letter to Archbishop Ecgberct published below.] What end this matter will have, a later age will see.

This is the present condition of the whole of Britain, in approximately the 285th year after the arrival of the English in Britain, and in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 731. May the earth rejoice forever in his reign; and, with Britain rejoicing together in his faith, may the many islands be glad and confess the memory of his holiness.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A chronological recapitulation of the whole work, and concerning the person of the author

[Col. 0285C]

But since the matters that have been set out at greater length according to the divisions of time should be preserved in memory, it has seemed worthwhile to recapitulate them briefly.

In the sixtieth year before the Lord’s incarnation, Gaius Julius Caesar, [Note: [Col. 0285D] Julius. See I, 2.] the first of the Romans, attacked Britain in war and conquered it; yet he could not establish his rule there.

In the year 46 from the Lord’s incarnation, Claudius, [Note: [Col. 0285D] Claudius. See I, 3.] the second of the Romans, came to Britain, received the greater part of the island into submission, and also added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 167, [Note: [Col. 0285D] From the Lord’s incarnation.] Eleutherius became bishop of Rome and ruled the Church most gloriously for fifteen years. King Lucius of Britain [Note: [Col. 0285D] Lucius. See I, 4.] sent him a letter asking to be made a Christian, and obtained his request.

[Col. 0286A] In the year 189 from the Lord’s incarnation, the emperor Severus [Note: [Col. 0285D] Severus. See I, 5.] became emperor and reigned for seventeen years. He surrounded Britain with a wall from sea to sea.

In the year 381, Maximus [Note: [Col. 0285D] Maximus. See I, 9.] was proclaimed emperor in Britain, crossed into Gaul, and killed Gratian.

In the year 409, Rome was broken by the Goths [Note: [Col. 0285D] Goths. See I, 11.]; from that time the Romans ceased to rule in Britain.

In the year 430, Palladius [Note: [Col. 0286D] Palladius. See I, 13.] was sent by Pope Caelestine as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ.

In the year 449, Marcian, together with Valentinian, assumed the imperial power and held it for seven years. During their reign the English were summoned by the Britons and came to Britain.

[Col. 0286B] In the year 538, a solar eclipse occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, from the first hour until the third.

In the year 540, a solar eclipse occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [Al., of July], and stars appeared for nearly half an hour from the third hour of the day.

In the year 567, Ida began to reign. From him the royal lineage of the Northumbrians takes its origin, and he remained in the kingdom for twelve years.

In the year 565 [Al., 562], Columba, [Note: [Col. 0286D] Columba. See III, 4.] a priest from Scotland, came to Britain to teach the Picts and established a monastery on the island of Hii.

In the year 596, Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0286D] Gregory. See I, 23.] sent Augustine with monks to Britain, to evangelize the word of God to the English people.

In the year 597, the aforesaid teachers [Note: [Col. 0286D] Teachers. See I, 25.] came to Britain. [Col. 0286C] This was approximately the 150th year after the arrival of the English in Britain.

In the year 601, Pope Gregory sent the pallium [Note: [Col. 0286D] Pallium. See I, 29.] to Augustine, who had already been made bishop, and sent many ministers of the word, among them Paulinus.

In the year 603, battle was fought at Degsastan. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Degsastan. See I, 34.]

In the year 604, the East Saxons received the faith of Christ under King Saberct and Bishop Mellitus. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Mellitus. See II, 3.]

In the year 605, Gregory [Al. adds: the pope] died. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Died. See II, 1.]

In the year 616, King Aedilberct of the Kentish people died. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Aedilberct. See II, 5.]

In the year 625, Paulinus was ordained by Archbishop Justus as bishop of the Northumbrian people. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Paulinus. See II, 9.]

[Col. 0286D] In the year 626, Eanfled, daughter of King Aeduini, was baptized, together with twelve others, on the Saturday of Pentecost. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Eanfled. See II, 9.]

[Col. 0287A] In the year 627, King Aeduini was baptized with his people at Easter. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Aeduini. See II, 14.]

In the year 633, after King Aeduini had been killed, Paulinus returned to Kent. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Kent. See II, 20.]

In the year 640, King Eadbald of the Kentish people died. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Eadbald. See III, 8.]

In the year 642 [Al., 645], King Osuald was killed. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Osuald. See III, 9.]

In the year 644, Paulinus, formerly bishop of York but then bishop of the city of Rochester, departed to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Paulinus. See III, 14.]

In the year 651, King Osuini was killed, and Bishop Aidan died. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Osuini. See III, 14.]

In the year 653, the Middle Angles under Prince Penda were instructed in the mysteries of the faith. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Middle Angles. See III, 21.]

In the year 655, Penda perished [Al., King Penda of the Mercians was killed], and the Mercians became Christians. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Penda. See III, 24.]

[Col. 0287B] In the year 664, an eclipse occurred. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Eclipse. See III, 27.] King Earconberct of the Kentish people died, [Note: [Col. 0287D] Earconberct. See IV, 1.] and Colman [Note: [Col. 0287D] Colman. See III, 26.] returned with the Scots to his own people [Al., with his companions to the Scots; other reading omits “to his own people”]. A pestilence came; and Ceadda and Uilfrid were ordained bishops of the Northumbrians. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Of the Northumbrians. See III, 28.]

In the year 668, Theodorus was ordained bishop. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Theodorus. See IV, 1.]

In the year 670, King Osuiu of the Northumbrians died. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Osuiu. See IV, 5.]

In the year 673, Ecgberct, king of the Kentish people, died. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Ecgberct. See IV, 5.] A synod was held at Herutforda, [Note: [Col. 0287D] Herutforda. See IV, 5.] in the presence of King Ecgfrid and under the presidency of Archbishop Theodorus, a most useful synod of ten chapters.

In the year 675, Uulfheri, king of the Mercians, died after reigning for seventeen years and left the kingdom to his brother Aedilred.

In the year 676, Aedilred devastated Kent. [Note: [Col. 0287D] Aedilred. See IV, 12.]

In the year 678 [Chiffl., 677], a comet appeared. [Note: [Col. 0288D] The comet, and so forth. See IV, 12.] Bishop Uilfrid [Col. 0287C] was expelled from his see by King Ecgfrid; and in his place Bosa, Eata, and Eadhaeth were consecrated as bishops.

In the year 679, Aelfuini was killed. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Aelfuini. See IV, 20.]

In the year 680, a synod concerning the Catholic faith was held in the field of Haethfeltha, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Haethfeltha. See IV, 17.] under the presidency of Archbishop Theodorus. John, the Roman abbot, was present. [Note: [Col. 0288D] John. See IV, 18.] In that year Abbess Hild died at Streanaeshalch. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Hild. See IV, 23.]

In the year 685, King Ecgfrid of the Northumbrians was killed [Al., died]. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Ecgfrid … Hlotheri. See IV, 26.] In the same year King Hlotheri of the Kentish people died. [Note: [Col. 0288D] “In the same year … died” is omitted by one edition.]

In the year 688, King Caeduald of the West Saxons departed from Britain for Rome. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Caeduald. See V, 7.]

In the year 690, Archbishop Theodorus died. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Theodorus. See V, 8.]

[Col. 0288A] In the year 697, Queen Osthryd was killed by her own people, that is, by the leading men of the Mercians.

In the year 698 [Al., 699], Berctred, the royal commander of the Northumbrians, was killed by the Picts.

In the year 704, Aedilred, after ruling the Mercian people for thirty-one years [Al. omits “one”], became a monk and handed the kingdom over to Coenred. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Aedilred. See V, 9.]

In the year 705, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Aldfrid. See V, 18.] Aldfrid, king of the Northumbrians, died.

In the year 709, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Coenred. See V, 19.] Coenred, king of the Mercians, after reigning for five [Al., six] years, went to Rome.

In the year 711, the prefect Berctrid fought against the Picts.

In the year 716, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Osred. See V, 22.] Osred, king of the Northumbrians, was killed, and Ceolred, king of the Mercians, died; and the man of God [Note: [Col. 0288D] Ecgberct. See V, 22.] Ecgberct corrected the monks of Iona with regard to the Catholic Easter and ecclesiastical tonsure. [Col. 0288B]

In the year 725, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Wihtred. See V, 23.] Wihtred, king of the Kentishmen, died.

In the year 729, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Comets. . . Ecgberct. . . Osric. See V, 23.] comets appeared; Saint Ecgberct passed away. Osric died.

In the year 731, Archbishop Berctuald died. [Note: [Col. 0288D] He died. . . Tatuini. See V, 23.] In the same year Tatuini was consecrated the ninth archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, while Aedilbald was completing his fifteenth year as king of the Mercians.

These matters concerning the Ecclesiastical History of the Britons [Al., Britons], and especially of the English people, insofar as I have been able to learn them either from the writings of the ancients, from the tradition of our forebears, or from my own knowledge, I, Bede, servant of Christ [Al., servant of God] and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and [Col. 0288C] Jarrow, have arranged with the Lord’s help. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Bede. For more about this author of ours, see his Life published below.]

Born in the territory of that same monastery [679], when I was seven years old I was entrusted by my relatives for education to the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrid. From that time I have spent my entire life residing in the same monastery, devoting all my efforts to the study of Scripture. Between observing the rule of discipline and the daily responsibility of singing in the church, I have always found it pleasing either to learn, teach, or write.

In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate [691], and in my thirtieth year the priesthood [702], both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrid.

[Col. 0289A] From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my age [731], I have taken care to make these brief notes from the works of the venerable Fathers, or to add to them something in accordance with their meaning and interpretation, for the needs of myself and my brethren concerning Holy Scripture.

Four books on the beginning of Genesis, up to the birth of Isaac and the casting out [Al., expulsion, rejection, repudiation] of Ishmael [Al., three books].

Three books on the Tabernacle, its vessels, and the garments of the priests [Al., four].

Three books on the first part of Samuel, that is, up to the death of Saul.

Two books on the building of the Temple, with allegorical exposition, as also of the other matters.

[Col. 0289B] Also, thirty questions on the Book of Kings.

Three books on Solomon’s Proverbs.

Seven books on the Song of Songs [Al., eight; another, six].

On Isaiah, Daniel, the twelve prophets, and part of Jeremiah: divisions of the chapters excerpted from the treatise of Blessed Jerome.

Three books on Ezra [Al., Esdras] and Nehemiah.

One book on the Song of Habakkuk.

One book of allegorical exposition on the book of the blessed Father Tobit, concerning Christ and the Church.

Also, chapters of readings on the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, and Judges.

On the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

On the book of the blessed Father Job.

On the Parables, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

[Col. 0289C] On the prophet Isaiah, and also Ezra and Nehemiah.

Four books on the Gospel of Mark.

Six books on the Gospel of Luke.

Two books of Gospel homilies.

On the Apostle: I took care to transcribe in order everything that I found expounded in the works of Saint Augustine.

Two books on the Acts of the Apostles.

One book each on the seven [Al., six] Catholic Epistles.

Three books on the Apocalypse of Saint John.

Also, chapters of readings for the whole New Testament, except the Gospel.

[Col. 0290A] Also, a book of letters to various persons, of which there is one on the six ages of the world; one on the stages of the children of Israel; one on the passage in which Isaiah says, “And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited”; one on the calculation of the leap year; and one on the equinox, according to Anatolius.

Also, concerning the histories of the saints: I translated into prose the book of the life and passion of Saint Felix the Confessor from the metrical work of Paulinus.

I corrected, as far as I could, the book of the life and passion of Saint Anastasius, which had been badly translated from Greek and worse revised by some incompetent person, restoring it to the sense [Al., “as far as possible to the sense”].

I wrote the Life of the holy Father Cuthbert, monk and bishop, first in heroic meter and afterward in plain [Col. 0290B] prose.

The history of the abbots of this monastery, in which I rejoice to serve the heavenly mercy—Benedict, Ceolfrid, and Hwætberht—in two books.

The Ecclesiastical History of our island and people, in five books.

A Martyrology of the feast days of the holy martyrs, in which I have carefully tried to record all whom I was able to discover, noting not only on what day but also by what kind of contest, or under which judge, they conquered the world [Al., omits “carefully”].

A Book of Hymns, in various meters or rhythms.

A Book of Epigrams, in heroic or elegiac meter.

One book each on the Nature of Things and on Times.

[Col. 0290C] Also, one larger book on Times.

A book on Orthography, arranged in alphabetical order.

Also, a book on the Art of Meter, and appended to it another little book on Schemes or Tropes, that is, on the figures and modes of expression with which Holy Scripture is composed.

And I beseech you, good Jesus, that just as in your mercy you have granted me to drink sweetly from the words of your wisdom [Al., adds “or knowledge”], so you may graciously grant that I may one day come to you, the fountain of all wisdom, and always appear (parere; Al., apparere) before your face.

[Col. 0289]

# ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF THE CONTINUED CHRONOLOGY OF BEDE (C)

[Col. 0289D] In the year 731, King Ceolwulf was captured, tonsured, and restored to the kingdom, while Bishop Acca was driven from his see. [Note: [Col. 0289D] “In the year 731 . . . driven out” is omitted by the editor.]

In the year 732 [Al., adds “from the Incarnation of the Lord”], Ecgberct was made bishop in place of Wilfrid. [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Was made.” The edition reads: “was made. Bishop Cymbert of Lindisfarne died.”]

In the year 733, an eclipse of the sun occurred on the nineteenth [Al., eighteenth] day before the Kalends of September, around the third hour of the day, so that almost the whole orb of the sun appeared to be covered, as if by an exceedingly black and dreadful shield. [Col. 0290D] [Note: [Col. 0289D] “In the same year Tatuini, the archbishop, having received the pallium from the apostolic authority, ordained Aluic and Sigfrid as bishops” is added in the edition but is absent from the manuscript of Mori.]

In the year 734, the moon, suffused with a bloody redness, remained so for almost a full hour around the second day before the Kalends of February, about cockcrow; afterward, with darkness following, it returned to its proper light. [Note: [Col. 0290D] “Returned.” Thus far the Codex Mori and all manuscripts of better quality; but since what follows is found in the printed copies, I too may be permitted to add these chronological entries among the others.]

In the same year, Bishop Tatuini died.

[Col. 0291A] In the year 735, Nothelm was ordained archbishop; and Bishop Ecgberct, having received the pallium from the apostolic see, was confirmed as archbishop, the first after Paulinus. He ordained Fruidbert and Fruiduuald as bishops, and the priest Bede died.

In the year 737, excessive drought made the land barren; and Ceolwulf, having been tonsured of his own will, left the kingdom to Eadberct.

In the year 739, Æthelheard, king of the West Saxons, died, as did Archbishop Nothelm.

In the year 740, Cuthbert was consecrated in place of Nothelm. King Aethelbald of the Mercians was ravaging part of Northumbria by impious treachery; and their king, Eadberct, was occupied with his army against the Picts. Bishop Aethelwold also died, [Col. 0291B] and Cunwulf was ordained bishop in his place. Arwine and Eadberct were killed.

In the year 741, a great drought afflicted the land. Charles, king of the Franks, died; and his sons Carloman and Pippin received the kingdom in his place.

In the year 745, [Note: [Col. 0291] Wilfrid. Perhaps the bishop of the Hwicce, not the bishop of York.] Bishop Wilfrid and Ingwald, bishop of London, departed to the Lord.

In the year 747, Herefrid, a man of God, died.

In the year 750, Cuthred, king of the West Saxons, rose against King Aethelbald and Oengus. Theneor and Eanred died. Eadberct added Camp Cyil and other regions to his kingdom.

In the year 756, in the fifth year of Eadberct’s reign, on the Ides of January, an eclipse of the sun occurred. Later in the same year and month, that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, [Col. 0292A] the moon suffered an eclipse, like a dreadful and very black shield.

Boniface, also called Winfrid, bishop of the Franks, was crowned with martyrdom together with fifty-three others; and in his place Redger was consecrated archbishop by Pope Stephen.

In the year 757, Aethelbald, king of the Mercians, was miserably slain and fell by a fraudulent death at night at the hands of his own guardians; Beornred began to reign; Cynwulf, king of the West Saxons, died. In the same year Offa, having driven out Beornred, sought the kingdom of the Mercians with his bloodstained sword.

In the year 758, Eadberct, king of the Northumbrians, for the love of God and the heavenly homeland, having received the tonsure of Saint Peter by compulsion, left the kingdom to his son Oswulf.

[Col. 0292B] In the year 759, Oswulf was criminally killed by his own ministers; and in the same year Aethelwald, elected by his people, entered upon the kingdom. In his second year a great plague of mortality came and lasted for nearly two years, as severe and varied diseases ravaged the population, especially the affliction of dysentery.

In the year 761, Oengus, king of the Picts, died. He had carried his reign from beginning to end as a tyrant and butcher through bloody crime. Oswine was also killed.

In the year 765, Alhred was received into the kingdom.

In the year 766, Archbishop Ecgberct, endowed with royal lineage and imbued with divine knowledge, and Erihbert [Al., Frithbert], a truly faithful bishop, departed to the Lord. [Col. 0292C]

[Col. 0291]

# APPENDIX TO ALL THE WORKS OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, ESPECIALLY TO THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

*(Smith’s edition of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People)*

## NUMBER I [Smith, II]. On the Boundaries of the Provinces of the Heptarchy

[Col. 0291D]

Our Britain, greatly exhausted by the incursions of barbarians, summoned the Saxon people under King Vortigern to repel the violence and fury of the enemy. Under the leadership of the brothers Horsa and Hengist, they came here in great numbers from overseas regions. Nor did a single people flock to our island; rather, an enormous host from three of the stronger peoples of Germany came in rivalry: the Saxons, Angles, and Jutes.

From the Jutes came the Kentishmen; the Victuarii, who held the Isle of Wight; and those who were placed in the province of the West Saxons opposite the Isle of Wight, once called the nation of the Jutes. From the Saxons came the East Saxons, South Saxons, and West Saxons. From the Angles came the East Angles, Middle Angles, Mercians, and finally the entire stock of the Northumbrians.

We shall now show which regions or counties were included by the individual kingdoms after the Heptarchy had been established by the Saxons. [Col. 0292D] The province of the Kentishmen extends from the southern ocean as far as the River Thames and contains all Kent. The province of the South Saxons contains Sussex and Surrey. That of the East Saxons contains Essex, Middlesex, and part of Hertfordshire. That of the West Saxons contains Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, Hampshire, and Berkshire.

The province of the Meanwari is also situated among the West Saxons, namely in the district of Hampshire. The kingdom of the East Angles includes Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridge, and the Isle of Ely.

The kingdom of the Mercians includes Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, Worcestershire, Warwickshire, Leicestershire, Rutland, Northamptonshire, Lincolnshire, Huntingdonshire, Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Staffordshire, Shropshire, Nottinghamshire, Cheshire, and the other part of Hertfordshire.

Mercia is divided into Southern and Northern Mercia. The Southern Mercians number five thousand households and are separated by the River Trent from the Northern Mercians, whose territory contains seven thousand households. [Col. 0293A] This province also includes the Middle Angles, or Central Angles, such as the inhabitants of Warwickshire, Staffordshire, and other central regions of England; the Lindisfari, inhabitants of Lindsey; the Trans-Sabrinians; the Gyrvii, among whom the monastery of Peterborough is situated, and those who live beside or below the fen; the Hwiccii, today the people of Worcester; and finally the Mercians in the strict sense, who held the northern part of the kingdom as far as the River Mersey.

The last kingdom of the Heptarchy is the province of the Northumbrians, which, extending from the Firth of Forth, contained the remaining part of England. It was formerly divided into two kingdoms, the provinces of the Bernicians and the Deirans. The province of the Deirans had the River Tees, or the Tyne, as its boundary, not, as some say, the Tweed. The province of the Bernicians was bounded by the Scottish Sea.

## NUMBER II [Smith, III]. On the Twenty-Eight Cities of Britain

Britain was formerly distinguished by twenty-eight [Col. 0293B] very noble cities, besides countless forts, which were themselves equipped with the strongest walls, towers, gates, and bars. The names of the cities were as follows in the British language:

Cair Gurthigirn. Vortig. Guortigir. Guorthigirn. — Cair Municip. Muncip. Mincip. — Cair Meguod. Meguid. Meiguod. — Cair Ebroauc. Ebruc. Ebroanc. — Cair Caratauc. Taratauc. Cartauc. — Cair Mauchguid. Maguiod. Mauchguit. — Cair Caint. Taint. — Cair Peris. — Cair Legion. — Cair Segeint. Legeint. Regeint. — Kair Guent. Guerit. Gueint. — Cair Lerion. — Kair Pensavelcoith. Pentsavelcoit. Pensalvelcoit. — Cair Celemon. Celeimon. Celgimon. — Kair Guintuig. Gunituig, Guntuig. Guinting. — Cair Luadiit. Lualid. — Kair Colun. Colim. — Cair Custeint. Gusteint. — Cair Grauth. Granth. Grant. — Cair Lunden. — Kair Guoeirangon. — Kair Daun. Daim. Dauri. — Cair Guoricon. Guorion. — Cair Legion. Legion Guaruuic. Guarenic. — Cair Britto. [Col. 0293C] Brito. — Cair Droithan. Droithoi. — Kair Urnath. Urnach. Urnac. — Cair Luitcoith. Loitcoit.

To relieve the reader’s tedium somewhat, I thought it appropriate to add, besides these bare and barbarous names, the highly learned discussion once published about these cities by the most learned archbishop of Armagh, James Ussher.

1. **Cair Guorthigirn**, which Nennius confirms was built by Guorthigern, king of the Britons, in the region called Gwynedd, with this explanation added by an old scholiast: “Guasmoric built there, near Luguballia, a city which in English is called Palmecaster.” [Note: [Col. 0293] Luguballia: Carlisle. See below, no. 12, and Camden on Cumberland.] Geoffrey of Monmouth (*History of the Britons*, book VIII, chapter 2) suggests that it was situated “in the country of Hergin, above the River Wye” (that is the Wye, or Gwy, which flows between Monmouthshire and enters the Severn estuary), “on a mountain called Cloartius.” Others think it was situated in the region of Wales called Gwrtheyrnion, and that the Radnorshire stronghold of Gwrtheyrnion [Col. 0293D] arose from its ruins. See Lhuyd’s *Fragments*, folios 20–21, and Camden’s *Britain*, p. 479.

2. **Cair Mincip**, or Municip, incorrectly written *Mercipit* by Henry of Huntingdon. It is Verulamium, near the town of Saint Albans, which Tacitus establishes was a municipium in Roman times.

3. **Cair Meguaid**, otherwise Meiguod, commonly Meivod, situated in Montgomeryshire and formerly called Mediolanum by Ptolemy and Antoninus.

4. **Cair Ebrauc**, called by others Cair-Branc, is York [Alfred of Beverley and Henry of Huntingdon].

5. **Cair Caratauc**, incorrectly called Cair-Cucerat by Henry of Huntingdon. Humphrey Lhuyd shows in a fragment of a description of Britain that Cair-Caradoc was situated within the borders of Shropshire, between the rivers Teme and Clun. Geoffrey of Monmouth [Col. 0294A] (*History of the Britons*, book III, chapter 9; book VI, chapter 15), and Nennius’s glossator, interpret it as Salisbury.

6. **Cair Maunguid**, or Mauchguid. It is thought to be Antoninus’s Mancunium, that is, Manchester in Lancashire, or rather Manduessedum, that is, Manchester in Warwickshire. There is also Menegid in Anglesey, a place mentioned by Caradoc of Llancarvan in his history under the year 873.

7. **Cair Ceint**, otherwise Kent, that is, Canterbury [Alfred of Beverley and Henry of Huntingdon].

8. **Cair Peris**, that is, Portchester [the same authorities]. See Geoffrey of Monmouth, book V of his *History of the Britons*, chapter 8 [Heidelberg edition].

9. **Cair Legion**, which for William of Malmesbury (*Book I of the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, chapters 3 and 6) and Alfred of Beverley is Chester, or Westchester. It is the same city that in Bede’s *History*, book II, chapter 2, is called “the City of the Legions,” which by the English people is called Legacaester, but more correctly by the Britons Carlegion; likewise by Florence of Worcester under the year [according to Dionysius] [Col. 0294B] 894. Yet Matthew of Westminster, under the year 895, calls it Legecestria, in English Wirral, apparently from the Anglo-Saxon Annals appended to Bede, which seem not to have been properly understood. There we read: “They encamped in a deserted city in Wirral, which is called Legacaester.”

10. **Cair Segeint**, the city of the Segontiaci in the district of Hampshire, which stood above the Thames not far from Reading and is called Silchester, as Alfred of Beverley and Henry of Huntingdon note. Yet, in my opinion, they incorrectly placed the site of Silchester on the Thames. There is also Cair Seiont in Arfon, concerning which see no. 18. Geoffrey mentions the bishopric of Silchester, conferred upon a certain Maugan in King Arthur’s time, in book IX, chapter 15, of the *History of Britain*.

11. **Cair Guent**, which for Alfred of Beverley and Henry of Huntingdon is Winchester, or Winceaster; it was formerly called Venta Belgarum by the Romans. See no. 15. There is also Venta Silurum, situated in Monmouthshire not far from Caerleon, which still retains the ancient name Caer Went. The promotion of Diwanus, or Dwianus [thus the manuscript; elsewhere Duvianus], to the bishopric of Winchester in King Arthur’s time is mentioned in the *History of Britain*, book IX, chapter 15.

12. **Cair Lerion**, that is, Leicester [Alfred of Beverley and Henry of Huntingdon].

13. **Cair Pensauellcoit**. Geoffrey of Monmouth—and following him the author of *Eulogius*, in book V, as well as both Matthews of Paris and Westminster under the year of grace 52—interprets Kair Penheuelcoit as Exeter. In the Heidelberg edition of the *History of Britain* (book IV, chapter 16) and in the old Ascensian edition, Oxford was substituted for it by error.

Yet Exeter, which is called *Eaxan ceastre* in Saxon (more commonly, in contracted form, *Excester*), and which was called *Isca Danmoniorum* by the Romans, is known to have been called Cair Wisc, or Cair Isc, by the Britons, as Asser of Menevia also testifies in his *Deeds of King Alfred* under the year 876. Thus our Camden, rejecting this opinion, considers Geoffrey’s Pen Uchel coit, Ptolemy’s Uzella, and the Cornish Lestuthiell to be the same place; and Nennius’s Pontauel coit, Ptolemy’s Ischalis, and the Somerset Ivelchester to be another. He interprets the first British name as “high mountain in the forest,” and the second as “bridge at the Ivel in the forest.”

Nevertheless, it seems to me that Nennius’s Pensauelcoit was rather William of Poitiers’ Penvesellum (*Deeds*, I, p. 199), Orderic Vitalis’s Penvesellum (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ibid., p. 500), and William of Jumièges’ Penvesellum (*Norman History*, book VII, chapter 34, ibid., p. 286). Today it is called Pevensey and was famous at the first landing of William the Norman in England. The addition of the British word *coit* suits it well, since the Sussex region in which it lies was dense with wooded hedges.

14. **Cair Celemion**, which Camden conjectures to have been the Somerset Camalet.

[Col. 0295A] 15. **Cair-Guintguic**, which may have been Norwich, called Cair-Guntin by the Britons, or rather Winwick in Lancashire. To the old glossator of Nennius it is Winchester, or Wintonia.

16. **Cair Ligualid**, otherwise Legeuit and Lualid, that is, Luguballia, which Huntingdon calls Cair-Leil and which is commonly called Carlisle.

17. **Cair Colun**, or Colon, which for Geoffrey of Monmouth (*History of Britain*, book V, chapter 6) and Henry of Huntingdon is Colchester, situated on the River Colne and called Colonia by Antoninus in the *Itinerary*. Camden asserts in his account of Merionethshire that Harlech, a city of Meirionnydd situated on the Irish Sea, was also formerly called Cair Colun.

18. **Cair Custeint**, that is, the city of Constantius or Constantine. It is Cair-Seiont, near Caernarfon. Nennius reports that the tomb of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, was shown near the city called Cair Segeint: “as,” he says, “the letters on his tombstone indicate.” A British writer of the life of Gruffudd, son of Conan, prince of Gwynedd, places the ancient city of the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, in Arfon. Yet Matthew of Westminster relates that in the year of the Lord 1283 the body of the great prince, the father of the noble emperor Constantine, was found at Caernarfon near Snowdon and, by order of King Edward I, honorably placed in a church. These statements therefore appear to refer to Constantius, father of Constantine the Great, whom we read died at York in Britain, rather than to Constantius, son of Constantine, whom we read died at Mopsucrenae or Mopsuestia in Cilicia.

Consider whether the reference may not instead be to the tyrant Constantine; see Camden, p. 198, book XXVIII, with section 19. He was proclaimed emperor in Caer Segont in 407 and was killed in Gaul, not Britain, in 411.

19. **Cair Grauth**, otherwise Grant, that is, Grantecaester, now called Cambridge, says Henry of Huntingdon in book I of his *History*. The name was evidently derived from the River Granta, which he calls the river of Cambridge in book V. William of Ramsey, abbot of Crowland, mentions it in this way in the *Life of Guthlac*: [Col. 0295C]

> Among the English, from the River Granta, through a long  
> Circuit amid winding pools and rivers,  
> A marsh is spread around.

Before him Felix, the Crowland monk who wrote the life of Guthlac at the command of Aelfwald, king of the East Angles, wrote:

> “In the central regions of Britain there is a marsh of immense size and dreadful character, which begins at the banks of the River Granta, not far from a fort called by the name of Granta,” etc.

The Saxon translator rendered the river as *grantes ea* and the fort as *granteceaster*. Bede testifies in book IV, chapter 19, of his *History* that in his own time Grantacaester was a small, deserted city. Some think that Cambridge grew from its ruins. It is called Grantebricge and Grantanbricge by Asser of Menevia, Ethelwerd, the Anglo-Saxon Annals, [Col. 0295D] Florence of Worcester, Roger Hoveden, and Matthew of Florence in their accounts of the years 875 and 876. From it the surrounding county received the name Grantebridgeshire, in a charter of King Eadred dated 948 preserved by Ingulf, and Cantebrigesire in Henry of Huntingdon (folio 170 verso) and Roger Hoveden (folios 305 verso, 313 verso, and 337 recto, London edition). William of Malmesbury calls it the district of Grantebridge (*Deeds of the Kings of the English*, book I, chapter 6). Thus Alfred of Beverley also explains Cair Grant as Cantebrigge.

20. **Cair Lundein**, called by others Cair Lud. It is London, the capital of the kingdom.

21. **Cair Guiragon**, called by others Guorangon, that is, Worcester. It was called Cair Wrangon by the Britons and Worcester by the English. Rouse of Warwick says that it was founded by King Constantius; another declares that it was formerly the pride of the Romans in its walls. [Col. 0296A] See Camden on Worcestershire.

22. **Cair Daun**, Antoninus’s Danum, commonly Doncaster.

23. **Cair Guricon**, or Guorichon, which is either Warwick—for if one wishes to follow John Rous of Warwick, Saint Dubricius came there and had his episcopal seat where Warwick Castle now stands, and founded a church in honor of Blessed Mary, which remained visible down to our own day—or Ptolemy’s Viroconium, that is, Wroxeter in Shropshire.

24. **Cair Legion guar Usic**, called by the Britons Cair Leon ar Usk, that is, the city of the Legion on the River Usk, as it is still called.

25. **Cair Brithon**, which for Huntingdon and Camden (p. 175) is Cair Bristou, that is, Bristol. The former name, however, would more closely correspond to Dun-Britton, or Britannodunum, formerly called Alcluid, the ancient boundary of British and Pictish dominion. The British history reports that in King Arthur’s time a bishop named Eledanius, or Eldenius, was appointed there [Col. 0296B] (*History*, book IX, chapter 15).

26. **Cair Darithou**, or Draiton; for that is how it is read in Huntingdon, so that it may have been the Draiton of Shropshire.

27. **Cair Urnach**, which Camden thinks was Antoninus’s Uriconium, Ptolemy’s Virconium, and the Wroxeter of the people of Shropshire.

28. **Cair Luit coyt**, which for Geoffrey of Monmouth (*History of Britain*, book IX, chapter 3) [compared with Ranulph, book V of the *Polychronicon*, chapter 6, where he writes that Arthur’s seventh battle took place near Lincoln in the forest of Celidon], Alfred of Beverley, Henry of Huntingdon, and Ranulph of Chester (*Polychronicon*, book I, chapter 47) is Lincoln. Geoffrey of Monmouth writes:

> “Cair Lind-coit, situated in the province of Lindsey between two rivers upon a hill, is otherwise called Lindicolinum.” [Col. 0296C]

Thus he writes in book IX, chapter 3, of the *History of Britain*, where he recounts that after killing six thousand Saxons Arthur pursued them from there as far as the forest of Celidon. Hence Ranulph, in book V, chapter 6, of his *Polychronicon*, writes that the seventh battle [Note: [Col. 0295D] Battle of the Forest of Celidonia.] which Nennius reports Arthur fought against the Saxons in the forest of Celidon—that is, *Cath coit Celedon*—took place near Lincoln, so that no one may think it should be referred to the Caledonian forest in Albania, among the Scots, into which the Saxons never penetrated. *Lind coit* means “from the forests” according to Camden, p. 404.

In place of numbers 15, 18, 6, and 13, Henry of Huntingdon, in the first book of his histories, substitutes the following six:

1. **Cair Glou**, that is, Gloucester, concerning which Nennius writes: “Glovus built a great city on the bank of the River Severn, which in the British language is called Cair-Glovi and in Saxon Gloucester.” See William of Malmesbury, book IV of *On the Bishops* [toward the end of the catalogue of the bishops of Worcester, compared with the manuscript], and below at the end of chapter 6.

2. **Cair Cei**, that is, Chichester, commonly called Chichester.

3. **Cair Ceri**, that is, Cirencester, commonly Circester and Circiter, concerning which Asser of Menevia writes in the *Deeds of Alfred*, under the year 879: “He went to Cirencester, which in British is called Cair-Ceri and is in the southern part of the Hwicce.”

4. **Cair Dorm**, that is, Dormeceaster, which was situated in Huntingdonshire on the river called the Nen and has been completely destroyed. Today it is called Dornford.

5. **Cair Dauri**, or, as it appears in Alfred of Beverley, Cair Dorin, that is, Dorchester.

6. **Cair Merdin**, which is still called by that name.

[Col. 0297A] The word *Cair*, placed before all these names, means “city” or “fortress” among the Britons, as Giraldus Cambrensis notes, among others, in book I, chapter 5, of his *Itinerary through Wales*. John Caius (*On the Antiquity of Cambridge*, book I), following Gervase of Tilbury (*Otia Imperialia*, distinction II, chapter 47), adds that *Cair* means “city” in the Trojan language and that among the Welsh it also means “wall.”

Thus, just as the Hebrews call both a wall and a city [Note: [Col. 0297D] Hebrews. Numbers 35:4. Certainly Hermolaus the grammarian, citing Stephanus, says that among the Parthians the word signifies “city”], so the similar British word *Cair* denotes both walls and a city enclosed by walls. Some also observe the origin of this word in Great Cairo in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0297D] Some. See John Twyne’s *Commentaries on Britain*, book II, pp. 108–113] and likewise in Carthage, which Solinus writes was called *Carthada* [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Which.” Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 27, Salmasius edition, or chapter 30 in Delrio’s edition], because in the Phoenician language it expresses “new city.”

Hence it is known that both Carthage itself and the city of the same name built in Spain were called by the Greeks Καινὴ πόλις (*Kainē polis*, “New City”) [Note: [Col. 0297D] “It is known.” Stephanus of Byzantium, under Καρχηδών; Polybius, *History*, book II.] The twenty-eight cities in Britain were first counted, so far as I know, by Gildas; after Gildas, by Bede, Nennius, Henry of Huntingdon, Alfred of Beverley, Ranulph of Chester, Ralph of Maidstone, the author of *Eulogium*, and others. There are also others who add more to these [Col. 0298D]. Reptacestre, Cair Paladour, and Cair Badon may properly be added. Gildas and others say that these were famous cities in the times of the Britons and Romans. That there were many more in those times can easily be gathered from Antoninus, Marcian, and Ptolemy. Ptolemy designates thirty-seven cities south of the Pictish Sea, yet he omitted many equally ancient and noble ones, as are most of those he lists. Nor does the *Breviary* composed under Theodosius make us more certain about the number of cities. It lists forty-six stations; but who can guarantee that all these were cities? Moreover, nearly all these stations were frontier or border settlements, and few inland cities are mentioned.]

## NUMBER III [Smith, IV]. On the Time When Saint Alban, the British Protomartyr, and Other Christians Were Crowned with Martyrdom under Diocletian and Herculius, Enemies of the Christian Name

[Col. 0297B]

Among ecclesiastical writers there is much dispute about the year in which the Diocletian persecution began among the Britons. If any credence is to be given to the most ancient historians of our people, namely Gildas and Bede himself, this controversy can be settled with the greatest ease.

Gildas asserts that the Britons received Christ’s commandments, at least lukewarmly; among some, however, they remained intact until the nine-year persecution of the tyrant Diocletian. In that persecution churches were overthrown throughout the world; and while the same whirlwind of fury raged through all peoples, Saint Alban of Verulamium, Aaron and Julius, citizens of the City of the Legions, and others of both sexes in various places throughout Britain stood in the battle-line of Christ with the greatest courage, while the survivors concealed themselves in forests, deserts, and hidden caves, until, before the two-year period had been completely fulfilled, a new serenity of heaven and peaceful, tranquil times [Col. 0297C] returned, as after a long winter night.

Bede’s testimony also confirms Gildas’s account. In his *Chronicle* he writes:

> “In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, he in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the churches to be devastated and Christians to be afflicted and killed. In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian laid aside the purple at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan. . . . This persecution raged so cruelly and continuously that within one month seventeen thousand martyrs were found to have suffered for Christ; for it crossed even the borders of the Ocean and condemned Alban, Aaron, and Julius of Britain, together with many other men and women, in a blessed shedding of blood.”

We read nearly the same thing in the *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “Diocletian and Herculius ordered Christians to be killed in the tenth persecution after Nero; this persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those that had preceded it, for it continued without interruption for ten years. . . . Saint Alban suffered in it. . . .”

Thus both Gildas (*sections 7–8*) and Bede (*book I, chapters 6–7; Chronicle, under Diocletian*) confirm that Alban and his companions [Col. 0297D] were slaughtered in that persecution, which did not abate for nearly ten years and began in the nineteenth year of Diocletian. Therefore those waste their time in vain who, when assigning a year to the passion of these martyrs, attempt to force Bede unwillingly and against his own resistance to their side by placing it before Diocletian’s nineteenth year [Col. 0298A]. Nor do those who deny that these passages of Bede can be referred to a definite year of the emperor Diocletian seem to have fully perceived and understood them.

Alford, however (*Ecclesiastical Annals of Britain*, year 286), believing that he had sufficiently established his own opinion from other arguments—namely, that Alban suffered in the year 286—says that a manuscript copy of Bede came into his hands that clearly supported his view. For the closing sentence, which in printed copies reads, “For Saint Alban suffered in it . . .,” is found in his manuscript as follows: “For in that same year of the Lord’s Incarnation, 286, Saint Alban suffered.”

But I, who have seen more—and, I believe, older—manuscripts than Alford could have seen, do not find such a clause in even one of forty manuscripts of this kind. There is therefore no reason to rely upon the authority of a single manuscript, however ancient, [Col. 0298B] when the testimony of all the others declares it interpolated at this point.

But although Gildas and Bede most clearly testify that Saint Alban suffered martyrdom at the time stated above, certain details occur in other historical sources that make Bede’s chronology doubtful and difficult. For if the persecution did not arise in Britain before Diocletian’s nineteenth year, it is necessary that it broke out under the rule of Constantius Caesar. For from the time when Constantius was named Caesar, beginning, according to the calculation of the annals, in the year 292, the administration of Britain was entrusted to him, on the unanimous testimony of all the annals.

Eusebius, however (Hist. VIII.15; Supplement VIII; Life of Constantine I.13, etc.), writes that when the Roman Empire was governed by four emperors—Diocletian and Maximian as emperors, and Constantius and Galerius as Caesars—Constantius followed a course of life different from that of his colleagues; that he kept his hands pure and unstained by their wicked impiety; that he allowed his subjects, within the bounds of his empire, [Col. 0298C] to enjoy the deepest peace and to serve the worship of God without disturbance; and that he neither overthrew church buildings nor undertook anything against the Christians.

Lactantius likewise (On the Deaths of the Persecutors, §16) relates that the whole earth was afflicted and that, except in Gaul—that is, in those regions over which Constantius presided—three most savage beasts raged from East to West. Thus, while Constantius was still alive (Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History I.6), it did not appear unlawful either to the Gauls or to the Britons to profess the Christian religion, even while the churches in other regions were being tossed about by the storms of persecution.

I would not indeed wish to detract from Constantius’s reputation or in any way diminish the authority of the most distinguished historians. Yet since truth itself demands and insists that our Bede’s cause be defended, no one should be so carried away by his zeal to defend Constantius as to be angry or offended with me if I judge that those historians must be called to examination.

I admit that Constantius [Col. 0298D] was a man of the greatest gentleness and clemency and possessed neither Diocletian’s suspicious prudence nor Maximian’s bloodthirsty rashness. Yet, so long as he was adorned only with the rank of Caesar and did not himself hold supreme authority, [Col. 0299A] but served as an assistant to the emperor, who possessed supreme power, in administering the western provinces, he did not dare fail to show himself obedient to the imperial edicts.

And when letters had already been sent by Diocletian to Maximian and Constantius for the purpose of ordering them to lay waste the West also with the same most shameful destruction by which Diocletian was overthrowing the East, Lactantius (On the Deaths of the Persecutors, §15) acknowledges that Constantius, so as not to appear to dissent from the commands of his superiors, allowed the meeting places—that is, the walls that could be rebuilt—to be destroyed, but preserved the true temple of God, which is in human beings.

It is noteworthy that Eusebius—either because he was ignorant of what had been done in Gaul and entirely unfamiliar and foreign to the writing of its history, or because he wished to win the favor of Constantine for himself and for the Christians—places no mark of impiety upon Constantius. On the contrary, he asserts that Constantius was so kind, friendly, and gracious toward the Christians that he did not even destroy the churches. [Col. 0299B] In this matter he most plainly contradicts the author of the book On the Deaths of the Persecutors, who is nevertheless universally acknowledged to have known the condition of the Western Church better than Eusebius.

It must therefore be conceded that at least the churches of the Christians were destroyed with Constantius’s permission. Nor could that most merciful ruler have kept the Christians themselves entirely untouched by the common conflagration; we have Eusebius himself confessing as much. For he testifies that Gaul also (Eusebius, On the Martyrs of Palestine, ch. 13), together with all the regions stretching toward the setting sun—Spain, Mauretania, and Africa—experienced the fury of war during the first two years of the persecution.

This is further proved by certain inscriptions that Gruter inserted into his magnificent work (Inscriptions, vol. I, p. 280). At Clunia in Spain, on a beautiful column, we read the following inscription:

> DIOCLETIANUS JOVIUS ET MAXIMIAN. HERCULEUS CAES. AUGG. AMPLIFICATO PER ORIENTEM ET OCCIDENTEM IMP. ROM. ET NOMINE CHRISTIANORUM DELETO QUI REMPUBLICAM EVERTEBANT.

“Diocletian Jovius and Maximian Herculeus, Caesars and Augusti, after the Roman Empire had been enlarged in the East and West and the name of the Christians, who were overthrowing the state, had been destroyed.”

[Col. 0299C] There is another inscription in the same place:

> DIOCLETIAN. CAES. AUG. GALERIO IN ORIENTE ADOPT. SUPERSTITIONE CHRISTIANORUM DELETA, ET CULTU DEOR. PROPAGATO.

“Diocletian, Caesar and Augustus, adopted Galerius in the East, after the superstition of the Christians had been destroyed and the worship of the gods extended.”

These inscriptions are also read at Arevaci in Spain, on several columns. Baronius (year 304) believed that such trophies, erected over the destruction of the Christian religion, were set up not only in Spain but throughout the Roman world.

A splendid and truly remarkable coin of Maximian Herculeus points in the same direction (Spanheim, On the Excellence of Coins, vol. I, dissertation 5). On it Hercules is shown victorious over that many-headed Hydra with which he is fighting, together with the inscription:

> HERCULI DEBELLATORI.

“To Hercules, the Conqueror.”

By the reborn Hydra, after so many funerals, that new Hercules evidently intended to signify the Christian people; and, as though he had overthrown and triumphed over it together with his colleague Jovius, he wished this monument to endure among posterity.

It is rightly inferred from these inscriptions that Spain, which together with Gaul and Britain was under Constantius’s authority, [Col. 0299D] was flooded with Christian blood just as the other provinces were. Hence Prudentius rightly celebrates the courage of the martyrs of Caesaraugusta (Περὶ Στεφάνων, hymn 4), and asserts that their crowds were so immense that Carthage or Rome itself could scarcely surpass them either in the number of martyrs or in greatness of spirit. The immense slaughter also inflicted by Dacianus, the governor, throughout Spain is amply demonstrated by the Martyrologies and Acts of the Martyrs.

Someone may perhaps object that Spain was subject not to Constantius but to Maximian Herculius, whose savagery was native and innate, and that Lactantius teaches this in his book On the Deaths of the Persecutors (ch. 8):

> “For while he himself held Italy, the very seat of the empire, and the most prosperous provinces—Africa or Spain—were subject to him, he was not so diligent in guarding the wealth whose abundance was available to him.”

I believe that it can easily be proved that Lactantius must not be understood in such a way that we conclude, on his authority, that Spain was entrusted to Herculius.

[Col. 0300A] For the emperor Julian, who, I believe, was not entirely ignorant of which provinces had been entrusted to the governance of Constantius, his grandfather, expressly affirms in his Second Oration in Praise of the Emperor Constantius that Herculius possessed Rome and Italy, Libya, Sardinia, and Sicily, while Constantius, his grandfather, possessed the most warlike nations of Gaul, the western Iberians, and all the islands situated in the Ocean.

And unless we count Spain among Constantius’s territories, we cannot fully understand what is written in the Acts of Saint Marcellus the Centurion (Baronius, year 298, §5). At Tingitana, when Marcellus refused military service because he would not offer sacrifices to the gods, the governor Anastasius Fortunatus said:

> “I cannot overlook your rashness; therefore I shall report it to the emperors, and to Caesar himself.”

And in the same governor’s letter to Agricolaus, governor of Mauretania (§8):

> “This soldier”—namely, Marcellus—“has spoken many blasphemous things against the gods and against Caesar before the entire people.”

[Col. 0300B] The Acts therefore show that the place where Saint Marcellus suffered was under the rule of a certain Caesar—but not of Caesar Galerius, to whom historians assign Illyricum as the portion of the Roman world to govern, a region very far removed from the city of Tingitana.

Saint Marcellus was therefore crowned with martyrdom under Constantius Caesar, in Tingitanian Mauretania, which at that time was regarded as a province of Spain and was subject to the same vicariate.

Aurelius Victor writes that nothing was entrusted to Herculius except Italy and Africa, while Constantius received everything beyond the Alps that belonged to Gaul. I believe that, according to the customary manner of speaking in those times, these words include Spain, which certainly afterward always had the same rulers as Gaul. It was indeed subject to the prefect of Gaul, and without doubt the four prefectures—Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, and the East—arose from the division of the empire among four rulers.

An anonymous writer published by Valesius in his edition of Ammianus Marcellinus also writes that, after Constantius had been elevated to the supreme dignity of Augustus, [Col. 0300C] Severus took possession of Italy and everything that Herculius had held; yet he grants him nothing except Pannonia, Italy, and Africa.

Finally, Eutropius relates that Constantius, content with the provinces over which he already ruled, refused the administration of Africa and Italy, which Herculius had formerly governed. He says nothing about Spain because Constantius had long since assumed responsibility for that province.

If, therefore, we wish Lactantius to agree and correspond with these writers of the highest credibility, this passage must necessarily be understood in an entirely different sense. Lactantius perhaps spoke generally of the whole dominion of Herculius, which he held before Constantius attained the rank of Caesar. He made no mention of Gaul because those regions had been consumed by continual wars for fifty years and had been so stripped and plundered that they could not be counted among the provinces capable of supplying [Col. 0300D] abundant money to quench Herculius’s burning avarice and unrestrained desires.

Thus, although Spain must be counted among Constantius’s territories, a great force of persecution nevertheless fell upon it.

Leaving aside the evidence cited from Eusebius concerning the persecution experienced by Gaul for two years, I shall now bring forward another argument that will sufficiently establish that Gaul was not entirely free from the general calamity that afflicted the whole Roman world.

Constantius, a presbyter of Lyon and a serious as well as ancient writer, relates that Saint Peregrinus, the first bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and his lector Jovinianus earned the crown of martyrdom shortly before Constantine was proclaimed emperor (In the Life of Saint Germanus, in Surius, July 31):

> “Not long afterward an emperor was appointed, shining with Christian teaching. When the persecution had been removed, he opened the churches that had been closed and appointed Catholic superiors over them.”

This Christian emperor could have been no one other than Constantine. And since he received the empire shortly after the martyrdom of these men, [Col. 0301A] the Diocletianic persecution must necessarily be understood here.

It therefore seems certain that persecution also took place in those regions over which Constantius ruled. For so long as he possessed only the power of a Caesar and stood second to the emperor, although he was very well disposed toward the Christians, he nevertheless did not dare dissent so far from the emperors’ commands as to refuse to promulgate their edicts throughout all his provinces.

Once those edicts had been publicly disseminated, the ordinary judges and even the provincial governors, whether against Caesar’s wishes, in order to court the favor of the more powerful rulers, or to satisfy their own malevolence and cruelty, may have proceeded against the Christians.

If we also understand Lactantius’s words—that the whole earth was afflicted except Gaul—in the ordinary popular sense, and interpret them as referring specifically to Gaul properly so called, not to Constantius’s entire empire, it seems clear from this most diligent writer, who was by far the most skilled in matters occurring in the West, that this calamity struck the Christians in Spain and Britain. [Col. 0301B] For according to him:

> “The whole earth was afflicted, and except in Gaul three most savage beasts raged from East to West.”

In this passage Lactantius does not except Spain from the common disaster, nor Britain, but Gaul alone.

Thus, although Eusebius and the other Christian historians celebrate Constantius’s clemency and describe him as friendly from the beginning, he was considered merciful because he differed from the others and was not driven to every crime by the innate barbarity and savagery with which the other emperors were inflamed.

And since it was only after he had received the title of emperor that he revoked the edict of persecution, and since he left as his successor a son who not only restored the Christians to the worship of God and to their God but himself also embraced the faith of Christ, it is not surprising that those historians made every effort to erase completely the memory of all the injuries inflicted upon the Christians by Constantius.

The arguments drawn from the Christian historians are therefore not strong enough to overthrow Bede’s authority. Accordingly, [Col. 0301C] these British martyrs suffered in Diocletian’s nineteenth year, or at least his twentieth. Their martyrdom cannot in any way be assigned to Diocletian’s third or fourth year—that is, to the year of Christ 286 or the following year, as Alford wishes.

For in the year 286, on the first day of April, Maximian was proclaimed the new emperor in the West, according to Idatius. If we believe Alford, Maximian was appointed to serve Diocletian’s policy and was an energetic executor of his commands, and he sent an edict against the Christians into Britain.

But if we believe the historians of those times, Maximian was so heavily occupied with wars against the Bagaudae and other barbarian nations, even to the point of rebellion, that he had no leisure to persecute the Christians, except those who served under him in the army.

And after Carausius had arrogated to himself the title of Augustus in the year 287, we should not suppose that Maximian wished to send his edicts into Britain— which had defected from his rule—there to be neglected and trampled underfoot.

## NUMBER IV [Smith V]

### Concerning the frontier defenses and walls that the Romans built in Britain, and concerning the embassies that the Britons sent to Rome to request assistance when the Picts and Scots were invading the Roman province

[Col. 0301D]

When the Romans had brought infinite and immense regions far and wide under their power, so that they might more easily protect themselves and their frontiers and repel the injuries of barbarians, they enclosed the lands under their dominion with certain boundaries, some established by nature and others constructed by human skill.

The first kind consists of seas, mountains, and great rivers; the second of ditches, camps, fortresses, ramparts, stakes, and walls.

Thus, after the Romans had armed their way into Britain, the farther part was left to the barbarians, either because it was rough and unproductive or because its unconquered inhabitants bravely defended themselves and their country against the Romans’ futile assault. The nearer part was reduced to a province and, at different times, bounded by frontier defenses, concerning each of which I shall give my opinion in order.

[Col. 0302A]

When most of Britain had already been brought under Roman rule, Agricola established the first frontier defense. Whatever tract of land lay between the Bodotrian and Glottian estuaries was secured not by a wall or rampart but by garrisons (Tacitus, Life of Agricola), the enemy having been driven away as though into another island.

After Agricola returned to Rome, affairs in Britain declined in every respect. When Hadrian was administering the Roman Empire, the provincials could not be kept under his authority. The emperor therefore went to Britain, where he corrected many things and established a second frontier defense:

> “He was the first to draw a wall for eighty thousand paces, separating the barbarians from the Romans” (Spartianus, Life of Hadrian).

For it was his custom “in many places where barbarians were divided from the Romans not by rivers but by boundaries, to separate the barbarians by means of great stakes driven deep into the ground and joined together in the form of a wall-like hedge.”

That Scottish historian who wrote the *Wheel of Time* likewise says:

> “Hadrian was the first of all to draw a rampart of prodigious size, made of turf cut from the earth, as high as a mountain, with a deep ditch placed before it, from the mouths of the Tyne to the River Esk, from the German Sea to the Ocean.”

Hector Boethius gives the same account in the same words.

That this rampart ended at the mouth of the Esk is shown by the following inscription, reproduced by Camden in Cumberland:

> IMP. CAES. TRA HADRIANO AVG LEG. II. AVG F

It indicates that this work belonged to the Second Legion.

Associated with this wall were the Aelian bridge, the Aelian fleet, the Aelian cohort, and the Sabinian cavalry unit, all of which took their names from Aelius Hadrian and his wife Sabina.

But when Pius was emperor, the god Terminus once again yielded to the arms of Lollius Urbicus. When the barbarians were attempting revolution and harassing the allies of the Romans with war, Urbicus inflicted great defeats upon them and, according to Capitolinus (Life of Antoninus), “conquered the Britons by drawing another turf wall after driving back the barbarians.”

The historian calls it another wall because it was different from the one Hadrian had placed between the mouths of the rivers Ituna and Tina. Lollius therefore did not establish his boundary in that place but farther on, namely between the estuaries of the Glotta and the Bodotria, at the very place where Julius Agricola had fixed the limits of the Roman Empire.
