The Roman inscriptions carefully collected and published by Camden clearly establish this. To add some further support to the matter, I shall, with due respect to Thomas Hearne, that most learned and celebrated antiquary, bring forward another inscription discovered on the Scottish rampart and transcribed by him in his *Spicilegium* and Notes (p. 761), at the end of his splendid edition of William of Newburgh:

> IMP. C. T. AELIO HADRIANO. ANTO  
> NINO. AUG. P. P. VEX. LEG. VI. VIC. P. F. OPUS VALLI  
> P. C. XLI.

That this wall was also erected while Lollius Urbicus was governor in Britain is shown by a mutilated inscription which the learned and antiquarian scholar William Nicholson, bishop of Derry, had transferred from that place to the Glasgow library and most courteously communicated to my father:

> LEG. II. A LOLLIO. VR LEG. AUG. PR. P

The credit for the war completed in Britain and for the construction of this wall, set up to restrain the attacks of the enemy, must therefore be given to the emperor Antoninus and the governor Lollius.

After these disturbances had been settled, the Brigantes, who were troublesome to their neighbors and hostile to the Ordovices by land and sea, caused a disturbance. But the revolt was soon extinguished, and the Brigantes who had first kindled the flame were punished, [Col. 0303A] as Pausanias records in his *Arcadica*:

> Ἀπετέμνετο δὲ (sc., Antoninus Pius) τῶν ἐν Βριταννίᾳ Βριγάντων τὴν πολλὴν, ὅτι ἐπεσβαίνειν καὶ οὗτοι σὺν τοῖς ὅπλοις ἦρξαν τὴν Γενουνίαν μοῖραν ὑπηκόους Ῥωμαίων.

“That is, he cut off a large part of the Brigantes in Britain because they too, taking up arms, began to invade the Genounian district, which was subject to the Romans.”

What that province of Genounia was is entirely unknown unless we accept our Camden’s authority (On the Ordovices). He believes that Genouthia, or Gwynedd, is meant, where the seat of the Ordovices was located.

The distinguished Scottish scholar Robert Sibbald [Note: [Col. 0303] Sibbaldus. In a letter sent to my father, dated August 5, 1706.] interprets this passage of Pausanias differently and conjectures that the word ἀπετέμνετο should be understood as referring to a certain rampart constructed under the emperor Antoninus, by which he separated the Brigantes and the barbarians from the provincials.

This interpretation, however, does not greatly appeal to me. The Brigantes themselves, just like the Ordovices, had their settlement within the Roman province below Hadrian’s Wall. Antoninus therefore could not have deprived them of even the smallest piece of territory by drawing a wall between the Glotta and the Bodotria. Consequently, the word ἀπετέμνετο can be understood in no sense except that the Brigantes were deprived of a large part of their own territory because they had attacked their fellow provincials with hostile force.

[Col. 0303B] The Wall of Antoninus is called by the inhabitants *Gryme’s Ditch*, or *Gryme’s fosse*, and is said to have taken its name from a certain Gryme, a grandson of Eugenius, king of the Scots. But according to the distinguished Hearne (*Spicilegium* and Notes, p. 760), it is nothing other than *Grume’s Ditch*. For *grumae* or *gromae* were the boundaries of provinces. The Greeks called them γνῶμαι and γνώμονες, and eventually γρῶμαι; and although γνώμα is written in one passage of the *Suda*, γρώμα should more correctly be read.

After this, when the Caledonians were frequently fighting the Romans to preserve their freedom and avoid slavery, matters finally reached the point at which the emperor Severus received letters from the governor of Britain (Herodian III). These letters stated that the barbarians were stirring up rebellions there and devastating the entire region with raids and plundering, so that a larger force was needed to resist them, or even the presence of the emperor himself.

After hearing this, Severus immediately departed for Britain with a huge army. [Col. 0303C] Crossing the rivers and ramparts—namely, those of Hadrian and Antoninus—which had been placed to divide the Roman frontier from the barbarians (ibid.), he reached the farthest part of the island.

Finally, because of his weakness, he was carried in a covered litter through the entire hostile territory (Xiphilinus, epitome of Dio, Life of Severus) and returned to his allies after forcing the Britons to make a treaty. And, so that the barbarians would not invade the Roman province in the future,

> “He fortified Britain, which is the greatest glory of his reign, by a wall drawn across the island from sea to sea, extending on both sides to the limits of the Ocean. From this he also received the name ‘Britannicus.’ Finally, after a wall or rampart had been thrown up, he returned to Eburacum, not only victorious but also, as he believed, with peace established forever” (Spartianus, Life of Severus).

The place where Severus erected his wall against the barbarians is disputed by historians.

Buchanan maintains that this emperor drew a rampart from the estuary of the Glotta to the point where the Forth and the Avenni meet (*Book I*, p. 16; IV.116; V.135). Tillemont offers various arguments in support of his opinion (*History of the Emperors*, note 28 on the history of Severus).

Buchanan, however, calls Bede to his aid in vain, for Bede clearly distinguished Severus’s wall from the Scottish one between Aebercurnig and Penneltun (Ecclesiastical History I.12). [Col. 0303D]

When the Roman legion sent to destroy the enemy had driven them all across the sea, and was about to take leave of its allies, it did not repair the Scottish wall. Instead, it

> “placed a wall of solid stone from sea to sea, in a straight line between the cities that had been built there out of fear of the enemy, where Severus had once made a rampart. With the assistance of the Britons who accompanied them, they constructed this wall, still famous and conspicuous, at public and private expense. It was eight feet wide and twelve feet high, running in a straight line from east to west, as is evident to those who look upon it even today.”

[Col. 0304A] The width of the wall among the Northumbrians is here accurately noted, except that in the sloping and precipitous mountains, which seemed almost naturally enclosed and fortified against the fiercest rage of the enemy, it was only five or six feet wide.

The words of the Venerable Bede themselves clearly establish that Severus’s rampart was situated in this very place (Ecclesiastical History III.2). He describes the location of the Heavenly Field—or *Hefenfeld*—situated not far from the church of Hexham and the River Tyne:

> “It is a place beside that wall to the north, with which the Romans once enclosed all Britain from sea to sea in order to repel the attacks of the barbarians.”

So too do the words by which he identifies the wall as situated not far from the Tyne:

> “It is beside the wall with which the Romans once enclosed the island of Britain” (ibid., ch. 22).

Since that wall was placed in the spot where Severus had once made his rampart, Severus, if Bede may be believed, established his own wall not in Scotland but approximately in the same place where Hadrian had earlier constructed his turf wall.

[Col. 0304B]

Tillemont, thoroughly versed in both ecclesiastical and civil history, defends the opposite opinion. He asserts that it is certain that Agricola penetrated beyond the frontier of which we have spoken into the Scottish regions, and that Buchanan left no room for doubt that the Romans established a sufficiently secure city against barbarian attacks near Stirling.

This too, he argues, is a firm indication that they possessed that part of Britain for a long time. Since it is conceded that Antoninus placed his turf wall between the Glotta and the Bodotria, no one can say that the Romans ever yielded any part of their dominion to the barbarians.

And although, under Commodus, the enemy crossed the wall, it is nevertheless clear that Ulpius Marcellus, who was sent to destroy the Caledonians, confined them within their ancient boundaries. Finally, Severus forced the barbarians, who had again invaded the Roman province with hostile intent, to surrender a considerable part of their territory. For this reason, Tillemont argues, Severus built his wall not where Hadrian had formerly built his, but between the Glotta and the Bodotria.

He was also not deterred from this opinion by the fact that no historian ever speaks of new victories won in Britain after the time of Severus. What is asserted about Carausius, he says, rests on no authority; and if it has any appearance of truth, it is only said that Carausius strengthened Severus’s rampart.

He proceeds to show from Gildas as well as from Bede that it is certain that in the fifth century the barbarians were held beyond the estuaries of the Glotta and the Bodotria, while the Romans retained the rest of the province.

To answer so great a man more fully, I shall briefly review the history of Britain at that time.

Under the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, the northern Britons broke out into open rebellion. They disregarded the wall of Antoninus Pius and afflicted the province with the gravest disasters of war. Against them Calphurnius Agricola was sent as propraetor. [Col. 0304D] He confined the enemy within Hadrian’s rampart; for it is likely that he did not force them to retreat beyond the frontier of Antoninus because, farther within the rampart, at the territory of the Ottadini, a certain Aulus Licinius Clemens inscribed the name of Calphurnius Agricola on an altar (in Camden, On the Ottadini) that he had dedicated to the goddess Suria.

Under Commodus also, a very serious war was being waged in Britain. The Britons had crossed the wall that lay between them and the Roman camp—namely, Hadrian’s Wall—and had ravaged many places, killing the Roman commander and the soldiers who were with him (Dio, Life of Commodus).

Commodus sent Ulpius Marcellus against them, and he inflicted the greatest and most severe slaughter upon the barbarians. Although Commodus came close to killing him out of resentment for his excellence, he nevertheless dismissed him. Since the British war had not yet ended, Commodus placed men of the equestrian order, under Perennis, [Col. 0305A] in command of the soldiers, removing the senators (Lampridius, Life of Commodus).

The soldiers therefore became deeply angry with Perennis. When they were rebuked for causing a mutiny, they selected fifteen hundred men from their number and sent them to Italy. When these men had already reached Rome, they accused Perennis of aspiring to the throne and had him, brought before them, slaughtered as an enemy of the army and of Commodus.

After Perennis was killed, Pertinax went to Britain and suppressed the rebellions. Yet he encountered immense danger: during a mutiny of the legion he was nearly killed and was certainly left among the dead. Later he requested release from his command, saying that the legions were hostile to him because he had defended military discipline.

Commodus heard his request and designated Clodius Albinus as his successor (Capitolinus, Life of Albinus). Except for the brief period during which Junius Severus was governor of Britain under Commodus, Albinus administered the province vigorously after subduing the barbarian nations, until he was killed at Lyon in Gaul while contending with Severus for the empire.

Under Severus, while Virius Lupus was [Col. 0305B] propraetor in Britain, the Caledonians, although they had made a treaty with the Romans, did not fulfill their promises. They were ready to defend the Maeatae, who were devastating the province with raids, and Lupus was therefore compelled to buy peace from the Maeatae at a great price (Dio, Life of Severus).

Everything in Britain beyond the wall of Antoninus Pius is called Caledonia by Tacitus, and its inhabitants are called Caledonians. The Maeatae inhabit the region beside Hadrian’s Wall, which divides the island into two parts (ibid.).

When the Maeatae and their allies again began to rebel, Severus himself came to Britain and forced the enemy to make a treaty on the condition that “they yield a considerable part of their territory.” To protect his allies against future attacks, he fortified the frontier on both sides as far as the Ocean.

After these events, the Britons rebelled again (ibid.). Since the Caledonians and the Maeatae had both revolted, Severus was preparing to conduct the war there himself. But his death, which followed in the next year, delayed the war and restrained the angry hand of the emperor.

[Col. 0305C]

It is therefore plausible, from the history of those times, that the barbarians soon recovered their homeland and expelled the Romans from the whole region lying between the two walls—if not under Pius himself, then at least under Marcus Aurelius.

Under Commodus, it is also clear from Dio that Ulpius Marcellus defeated the Britons and confined them within Hadrian’s Wall, which they had crossed. But once the army had begun its mutinies, it cannot be believed that the barbarians were driven farther back for as long as Commodus ruled the Roman world.

Nor did Albinus extend the boundaries of the province. For when, after his death, Britain was brought under Severus’s power, Dio asserts that slightly less than half of the island belonged to the Romans (Xiphilinus, Life of Severus), and that the Maeatae, who lived beside the wall, took up arms against the Roman province.

Although Severus afterward compelled the Caledonians and Maeatae to surrender a considerable part of their own territory, he did not deprive either people of its entire region, nor did he bring those nations into the Roman [Col. 0305D] province.

He had not defeated the barbarians so thoroughly that he could fail to fear that they would not remain long in Roman allegiance and that, if they ever found an opportunity to revolt, they would have no respect for the faith of treaties but would burst into Roman territory.

This is indeed what they did, as we have said, and after Severus’s death they compelled Antoninus to restore to them, by treaty, that considerable region which his father had acquired by arms (Xiphilinus, Life of Antoninus).

It is therefore likely that the most prudent emperor Severus, knowing that the Maeatae were angry because they had lost the greater part of their homeland and would therefore seize the first opportunity to reclaim their former freedom, placed his wall where Hadrian had once drawn his.

Severus was not so foolish as to draw a rampart beyond the settlements of the Maeatae, whom he undoubtedly foresaw would invade the province as soon as the opportunity arose. To meet their attempts more promptly, we should therefore believe that this emperor repaired Hadrian’s Wall [Col. 0306A] so that it might defend the Romans against the incursions of the Maeatae, who lived beside it.

And if there is any authority for what the most learned translator of Camden notes (Edmund Gibson, note on the Pictish Wall), there will be no further room for doubt on this matter. It is said that a stone was recently found not far from Luguvallium, beside the wall, bearing this inscription:

> Sept. Severo Imp. qui murum hunc condidit.

“To the emperor Septimius Severus, who built this wall.”

As for what Tillemont says—that no victories were ever afterward won from the barbarians in Britain and that no new territories were added to the Roman Empire—I am not compelled by any force of argument to concede it.

Even if we admit that what Nennius relates about Carausius is false, it must nevertheless not be denied that Theodosius, in the time of Valentinian, recovered the whole region between the walls of Antoninus and Severus, protected it with watches and frontier defenses, and called it Valentia by the emperor’s authority.

Even granting that, according to Gildas and Bede, it is clear that in the fifth century the barbarians were prevented from invading Roman territory by the wall erected between the two estuaries—Dunbritannicus and Edinburgh—[Col. 0306B] Bede nevertheless makes clear that Severus’s rampart remained almost until those very times the boundary of the Roman province:

> “The Romans,” he says, “lived within the rampart which we have mentioned that Severus made across the island, toward the south. The cities, shrines, bridges, and paved roads constructed there testify to this even today. But they possessed by right of dominion the farther parts of Britain, and even the islands that lie beyond Britain” (Ecclesiastical History I.11).

Bede made this observation after speaking of Rome’s capture by the Goths in the year 411.

It is therefore certain that Severus’s rampart was drawn across the island from the mouth of the River Tyne. Consequently, those who defend the contrary opinion vainly attempt to find support in the fact that the commonly circulated manuscripts of Aurelius Victor and Eutropius state that Severus drew a rampart in Britain for thirty-two thousand paces [Col. 0306C] from sea to sea.

In the oldest copies of Eutropius, however, we infer from the ancient Latin writers who followed him—such as Saint Jerome in his Eusebian *Chronicle*, Paulus Orosius, Aurelius Cassiodorus in the *Consular Fasti*, and Bede himself in his *Chronicle*—that the sign for one hundred stood before this number.

The same conclusion follows from his Greek translator Paeanius, who rendered it as δύο καὶ τριάκοντα πρὸς τοῖς ἕκατον σημεῖα, “two and thirty with one hundred signs,” and from George Syncellus, who thought that Paeanius’s total should be expressed as one thousand stadia, assigning seven and a half stadia to each σημεῖον, or Italian mile.

Yet the location does not permit either a distance of thirty-two or of one hundred and thirty-two miles. The true reading seems to be eighty-two, so that it is reasonable to suspect that, through the error of scribes, the sign for fifty was entirely omitted in some manuscripts, while in others it was exchanged for the sign for one hundred—an error that could easily have occurred.

Another difficulty still remains to be removed: learned men dispute whether Severus’s wall [Col. 0306D] was made of turf or of stone. Bede, who thought it was made of turf, explains his view as follows:

> “He thought that the part of the island which he had recovered from the other unconquered peoples should be separated, not by a wall but by a rampart. For a wall is made of stones, whereas a rampart, by which camps are fortified to repel the enemy’s attack, is made of turves” (*Ecclesiastical History* I.15).

The very learned Ussher, however, adopted the contrary opinion (*British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 317), supposing that the learned presbyter was unaware that the Latin word *vallum* could mean the same as *murus*.

> “For even this very structure of Severus,” he says, “which Eutropius, and Jerome, Orosius, and Cassiodorus with him call a *vallum*, Spartian, older than all of them, calls a *murus* in his *Life of Severus*. He also shows that these terms were used interchangeably when, in the same Life of Severus, he adds: ‘After the wall or rampart had been sent to Britain.’ Hence what is written about Severus in the commonly circulated epitome of Aurelius Victor—‘He drew a rampart in Britain for thirty-two thousand paces from [Col. 0307A] sea to sea’—is expressed in Victor as edited by Andreas Schottus in this way: ‘Having undertaken greater things, he fortified Britain, so far as it was useful to him, with a wall, after the enemy had been driven out, drawing it across the island from one ocean coast to the other.’ Deceived, however, by this false distinction between wall and rampart, Bede believed that Severus’s work was not of stone but of turf.”

So much for Ussher. But, in my view, Bede was not led into any greater error by this distinction than was that eminent scholar himself, who uses two words—namely, *vallum* and *murus*—to designate one and the same thing. For by the examples which Ussher produced from Spartian and Victor, he did not prove that *vallum* means the same as a stone wall, but only that a *vallum* can be called a wall. Yet no one has ever denied this: the word *murus*, taken broadly, includes both a turf wall and a stone wall. Therefore, although Latin authors call a *vallum* by the alternative name *murus*, we should not rashly conclude that by *vallum* they meant a stone wall, especially [Col. 0307B] since it often happens in usage that a turf wall is called a *vallum*.

Bede is therefore mistaken in distinguishing so sharply and subtly between *murus* and *vallum* that he believed one word could in no way be taken for the other. Ussher, on the other hand, is equally mistaken (*ibid.*) in thinking that *vallum* signifies the same as a stone wall for the sole reason that it is called a wall by ancient authors.

Ussher continues and asserts that the stone wall finally constructed by the Roman legion was not placed where Severus had drawn his, but where shortly beforehand the Britons had erected their useless turf wall:

> “For no reason suggests that rational men would withdraw a hundred thousand paces backward and willingly surrender so much territory to the enemy, abandoning the narrowest part of the whole island, and one especially suited to fortification, and seeking another place where a wall almost three times longer than the former would necessarily have to be erected.”

But if the Britons’ turf wall was later, when the Romans bade farewell to [Col. 0307C] Britain, converted into stone, it follows that Severus made his wall not of turf but of stone.

Yet, in my judgment, this conclusion of the very learned Ussher is not sufficiently firm or certain. For, as was shown above, the most ancient authors who wrote anything about Severus’s work all say that Severus drew a *vallum* between the two seas, and that learned man has not at all proved that *vallum* means the same as a stone wall. If, therefore, Severus did not construct a stone wall, there can be no doubt that this wall was built by the Romans when they were returning home.

This is further confirmed by what John Fordun relates about the latest incursion of the Scots and Picts:

> “The victors,” he says, “suddenly calling together the rural populace, each with his sickles, mattocks, rakes, tridents, and digging tools, pierced the broad cracks and numerous openings in the wall, so that everywhere they might have a ready entrance and retreat. From those openings the structure afterward received its name, which in the English language sounds like *Thirle-Wall*, but in Latin is called *murus perforatus*, ‘the pierced wall’” (*Scots Chronicle* III.10).

The fortress of Thirle-Wall, as Ussher himself admits (*British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 318), can still be seen situated on the boundary between Northumberland and Cumberland, between the Tyne and the Irthing. There the barbarians wisely opened for themselves an entrance into the province, where a clear road, with no intervening river, lies open into the interior parts of England.

It is therefore likely that the Britons surrendered a large part of their country to the enemy, thinking that they would thereby make them well disposed and friendly. Nevertheless, the enemies, who could not be appeased, broke through the wall in Northumbria and inflicted dreadful slaughter.

Gildas himself adds no slight credibility and support to this argument. From him it is clear that the Scots and Picts possessed the whole stretch of territory beyond the gulfs of the Clota and Bodotria with full right of domination. The Roman legion sent to assist the Britons drove the enemy no farther than beyond the seas. Thus the wall of Antoninus was the boundary of both the British province and the tyranny of the barbarians; and the barbarians may properly be called the native inhabitants of those lands which they had already held for a long time, up to that wall.

Gildas, and Bede following him almost word for word, testify (Gildas, section 15; Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* I.12) that, when the Romans were returning to their own country, the Scots and Picts immediately returned and, having grown more confident than usual, “occupied the whole northernmost extremity of the land as natives, as far as the wall.”

Since, therefore, when the Romans were returning home, the Picts and Scots won new victories, they must have acquired new regions by force of arms beyond the wall of Antoninus. For they possessed the whole land as far as the wall of Antoninus when the Romans were already defending the province against their attacks. The wall of which Gildas speaks therefore cannot be any other than the one which we see placed between the mouths of the Irthing and the Tyne.

Some attempt to establish from Gildas and Bede that the Picts then first occupied the whole northern region as natives, as far as the wall of Antoninus, and thereafter remained there, sometimes making raids and engaging in conflicts. But this clause must not be explained in a manner that contradicts the testimony of all historians, who most certainly affirm that the Picts had an established dwelling-place there from ancient times.

The meaning of the clause will therefore rather be this: the Picts who had hitherto been in Britain, subject to the continual attacks of the Britons and Romans, harassed by their repeated skirmishes, assailed in war, and sometimes driven from their place and province—who had never until then lived peacefully in their own settlements for as long as the Romans had fought on behalf of the Britons—now rested for the first time, when the Romans openly refused assistance and the Britons no longer opposed them. Although they had inhabited the same part of the island for a long time, they had not previously been free from Roman attacks.

They therefore lived as far as the wall of Antoninus and, crossing the Scythian valley or strait of Bodotria in *curachs*—a kind of vessel—suddenly brought the whole island under their control as far as the wall of Severus.

Finally, Ussher (*British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 319), understands the clause in this way:

> “The Picts then first and thereafter dwelt in the northern part of the island, not indeed simply as inhabitants, but rested there—that is, they ceased from the devastation of British territory and from the most savage oppression which Gildas had described earlier. For although he adds that they sometimes made raids and inflicted destruction, nevertheless he clearly declares in the words immediately following that a truce had been granted to the devastated people and that the devastation had ceased—or, as Bede explains it (*Ecclesiastical History* I.14), that the hostile devastation had ceased.”

This interpretation clearly shows that the Picts were formerly inhabitants of Britain.

Ussher, however, wishing to give greater force to the arguments by which he had attempted to prove that Severus built a stone wall, adds that Gildas testifies that this final wall was laid out in a straight line from sea to sea [Col. 0308D], while the other one, between the mouths of the Tyne and the Esk, was drawn along a path that was not straight but oblique and curved, as the surviving traces still demonstrate to the eyes of those who inspect them.

But Bede’s authority forbids us to take the words “in a straight path” in such a strict sense. He declares (*ibid.* I.12) that the stone wall itself between the Tyne and the Irthing was drawn in a straight line.

Finally, it is argued that the magnificent praise which Spartian bestows upon Severus’s wall—when he asserts that it was the greatest glory of his reign—seems rather to require or demand that we believe Severus established a stone wall.

Yet, as it seems, the same reasoning could be used to say that the walls of Hadrian and Antoninus were also the greatest glory of their reigns, unless perhaps we suppose that their ramparts were not of such enormous size or height, or fortified with towers so strong and numerous, as Severus’s, and therefore were not commended to all posterity with such high praise.

This most illustrious monument of Britain’s conquest by that emperor is celebrated by Orosius (*History* VII.17), and by Bede, who copies his words (*Ecclesiastical History* I.5 and *Chronicle*), in the following manner:

> “Severus,” they say, “drew from sea to sea a great ditch and a very strong rampart, additionally fortified with numerous towers.”

But no historian confirms that the ramparts of Hadrian or Antoninus were fortified with numerous towers. Nevertheless, that they were not sufficiently strong or effective for resisting the enemy is abundantly demonstrated by the fact that Severus had to surround the province with a stronger embankment.

So much for Severus’s wall.

From that time onward, no historian anywhere spoke of a wall either constructed or repaired in Britain until Carausius, having assumed the imperial purple, occupied Britain. Regarding the restoration of Severus’s wall by Carausius, Nennius, the disciple of Elvodugus, writes as follows:

> “Severus constructed [a wall] from Pengaaul—which in Scottish is called Cenail and in English Penneltum—to the mouth of the river Clota and Cair-pentaloch, but it accomplished nothing. Later the emperor Carausius rebuilt it [Col. 0309B] and fortified it with seven castles between the two mouths. He also constructed a round house of polished stones beneath the bank of the river Carun, which received its name from his own name, raising a triumphal arch in memory of the victory” (*History of Britain*, ch. 19).

But anyone who delights in stories neither true nor plausible may believe Nennius when he writes about these events. If there is any credibility in his account, then:

> “Carausius, in vengeance for the killing of Severus, together with all the commanders of the Roman people who were with him in Britain, pierced through all the petty kings of the Britons and took mighty vengeance for Severus upon them” (*ibid.*, ch. 20).

Yet who does not see at first glance that all this is fabricated and fictitious? Carausius seized the empire a long time after Severus’s death. Severus was not killed by the petty kings of the Britons, but, already an old man, died at York from a very serious illness.

How, moreover, could Carausius have restored Severus’s wall between the Clota and Bodotria, when it is clearer than daylight that Severus built his wall not there but between the mouths of the Tyne and the Irthing? How absurdly he invented the claim that the river Carun received its name from Carausius! And, to make this seem more credible, how foolishly he changed the name *Carausius* into *Carutius*!

Furthermore, he asserts that the tyrant raised a round house of polished stones as a triumphal arch in memory of the victory, although it has nothing resembling a triumphal arch and seems instead to have been a shrine of some god, perhaps the god Terminus, as the very learned Buchanan and Camden conjecture (Buchanan, *History of Scotland* I.16; Camden, *Description of the Scottish Provinces*). I believe these men were far better antiquarians than Nennius, who collected scarcely anything but fables in his history of the Britons.

I now pass over the praises bestowed by Zosimus upon Diocletian (*History*, book II): that the Roman Empire, at its furthest boundaries, was everywhere fortified through his foresight with towns, forts, and burgs, and that all the military forces had their residences there, so that it would be impossible for the barbarians to cross, since troops everywhere advanced to repel the enemy.

Since Diocletian was never in Britain, however, and, after the division of the empire, governed its eastern regions, the historian must certainly be understood to be speaking of those boundaries.

I also pass over that final expedition of Constantius (*Panegyric of Constantius* by Eumenius), in which he subdued the Caledonians and other Picts. For there is no evidence that he either changed or repaired the boundaries.

I likewise disregard the accusation which Zosimus brought against Constantine (*ibid.*), whom he falsely asserts to have removed the frontier defenses, withdrawn most of the soldiers from the boundaries, stationed them in towns that needed no garrison, and left them exposed to the barbarians without protection. Victor, however, reports that Constantine conveniently placed camps and forts in several locations.

At last I come to the time of Valentinian I, when Theodosius hastened to Britain, which had been reduced to the utmost distress by a barbarian conspiracy. After defeating various peoples, he “restored cities and frontier camps, guarded the boundaries with watch-posts and outworks, and brought back the recovered province—which had fallen under the power of the enemy—to its former condition, so that, according to the same author, it had both a legitimate governor and, by the emperor’s decision, was afterward called Valentia” (Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, ch. 3).

This new province contained whatever lay from the Tyne to the ditch of Edinburgh. The rest of Britain had long before been divided into four parts.

Britannia Prima was the name given to the whole southern region bounded on one side by the British Sea and on the other by the Thames and the Severn Strait.

The second province contained the Silures, the Demetae, and the Ordovices.

Flavia Caesariensis comprised all the territory from the Thames to the Humber.

Maxima Caesariensis extended from the Humber to Severus’s Wall.

The fifth province, because it had formerly been under Roman allegiance during the reign of the emperor Antoninus and had afterward passed again into the power of the barbarians, is said to have been recovered by Theodosius and named Valentia after the emperor Valentinian. Since Theodosius fortified it with outworks, it is likely [Col. 0310B] that he renewed the wall of Antoninus.

Britain enjoyed peace for some time, until, while Gratian was administering the western empire, Maximus seized tyranny there, crossed into Gaul with a vast number of soldiers, stripped the province of every defense, and left it exposed to the incursions of the Scots and Picts.

Gildas the Wise, angered at Maximus, complains of this in the following terms:

> “The island, bearing the Roman name but not retaining Roman customs and law—in fact, casting away the seed of its bitter planting—sends Maximus to Gaul with a great accompanying host of followers, having been unlawfully, not properly, but in the manner of a tyrant, invested with the imperial insignia, which he never properly bore … From that time Britain, stripped of every armed soldier, of its military forces, and even of its rulers, however savage, and of its great youth, which accompanied the footsteps of the aforesaid tyrant and never afterward returned home, being wholly ignorant of every art of war, was trampled upon by two very savage overseas peoples—the Scots from the northwest and the Picts from the north—and for many years remained stunned and groaning.”

The first person said to have opposed the barbarians was Stilicho, before his consulship, which fell in the year 400. He earned this praise either from the poet Claudian (*Panegyric 2 on Stilicho*) or, in Claudian’s words, from this island:

> “Stilicho fortified me also, when I was perishing beneath neighboring peoples,
>
> when the Scot moved all Ireland,
>
> and the sea foamed with hostile oars.
>
> Through his care he made it possible for me not to fear Scottish weapons,
>
> nor tremble at the Pict,
>
> and to watch from a secure shore for the Saxon,
>
> who might come on uncertain winds.”

Stilicho fortified the island by placing a Roman legion at the frontier to repel the enemy’s attack. Of this same legion Claudian writes (*Book on the Getic War*):

> “And the legion stationed at the farthest Britons came,
>
> which keeps the savage Scot under control …”

Finally, the last outworks which the Romans placed to protect the province—one constructed not so much of stones as of turf, the other of stone, the former between the straits of the Clota and Bodotria, the latter in Northumbria—are accurately described by Gildas and Bede.

Since, however, it is obscure and uncertain at what time the Britons sent those three embassies to the Romans, imploring aid in a lamentable voice lest the northern peoples completely destroy the Roman province, I shall attempt, through a broad and extensive investigation, to distinguish their dates.

To make the truth clearer in this controversy, I shall first explain Bede’s opinion; then I shall attempt to refute and overturn the arguments of learned men who attack our author.

After saying that Rome was captured in the year 409 and Constantine killed in the year 411, Bede relates that Britain, stripped of every armed soldier and of all the young men who, through the rashness of the tyrants—first Maximus, afterward Constantine and his son Constans—had been taken away to Gaul, lay open to the plunder of the fiercest peoples.

In the *Chronicle* as well, under Honorius, after the seventh year of Honorius, in which the relics of Stephen were discovered—that is, after the year 414—he describes the construction of the walls and the first two embassies. He then mentions the twelfth year of Honorius, in which Jerome died.

We therefore possess definite chronological markers enclosing these events within a very narrow period. It follows that they occurred between the years 414 and 419—the seventh and twelfth years from the time when Honorius and Theodosius began to reign together.

A certain very learned man, however (Stillingfleet, *British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, book V), charges Bede with error because he related the miserable condition of the Britons and the aid obtained from the Romans after Constantine’s death, whereas Gildas seems clearly to assert that both events occurred shortly after Maximus had unlawfully assumed the purple and carried off with him to Gaul nearly all the forces that defended the island.

Accordingly, the first barbarian invasion followed Maximus’s downfall and preceded the time when Gratian Municeps seized the empire. When the Britons then earnestly demanded assistance, the Romans sent a very strong legion to their aid, perhaps under the command of Stilicho, who at that time was managing British affairs with the greatest care and dedication.

But let us grant that the history of these events immediately followed Maximus’s revolt in Gildas’s order of narration. It does not follow that Gildas intended us to believe that the dates of the events which he mingled together in one narrative should not be distinguished.

For he did not intend to write an exact and orderly history, but to touch upon the vices and misfortunes of his countrymen in a somewhat declamatory manner. Consequently, he joined together many things that, if we consider the chronology, are very far apart.

This can easily be proved from this very passage of his little history, if we observe how the time of Maximus and that of the three devastations and embassies—which culminated in the final embassy to Aetius, in his third consulship, in the year 446—are confused together.

Moreover, if the first aid sent to Britain drove back the invading barbarians shortly after Maximus’s death, then the second legion, which came to the assistance of the Britons when they were again in distress, must also have been brought there before Gratian’s time. It came to Britain in the very year in which the first legion returned home, or at least in the following year.

If Gildas is to be understood in this way, therefore, the eminent scholar is gravely mistaken in thinking that the second legion was sent at the beginning of Valentinian III’s reign.

The dates must therefore be distinguished, and the years in which each of the individual events related confusedly by Gildas occurred must be carefully noted.

There can be no doubt that Maximus, by carrying the British forces away to Gaul, was the original cause of all the disasters which this island afterward suffered. But after the barbarian nations had been driven back by Stilicho, the province recovered its former peace and power so completely that in the year 407 its soldiers had leisure to choose new tyrants: Marcus, Gratian, and, after those men had been killed, Constantine.

Having gathered forces from every quarter, Constantine exhausted whatever military strength Maximus had previously left behind (William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of England*, book I, ch. 1), and crossed into Gaul, leaving Britain without defense and without soldiers.

Since no one remained to resist, the Trans-Rhenane barbarians (Zosimus, book VI) and the ancient enemies of the province, invading everything at will in the year 409, reduced the inhabitants of Britain to such a condition that they defected from the Roman Empire and, no longer obeying Roman laws, lived according to their own will.

They did this, moreover, not without the authority and permission of the legitimate emperor himself. For Honorius, in letters written to the British cities, urged them to look after their own affairs.

From this time onward, therefore, the Romans ceased to rule in Britain, and the island, as Procopius states (*Vandalic War* I.2), could never afterward be recovered.

Although the Romans sent a legion twice to the Britons when they implored assistance, they did not send it in order to defend a region subject to themselves, but to aid their allies, who were suffering great calamities at the hands of the enemies of the Roman Empire.

The northern peoples therefore began to ravage the affairs of the islanders by plunder. The evil increased daily, and it became apparent that the whole island would soon be lost unless such attempts were promptly opposed.

Fearing this, and no longer able to endure the attacks of the Scots and Picts, the Britons sent to Rome in the year 414 or the following year. Honorius, worn down by their entreaties, sent a legion from Gaul which, according to Paul the Deacon (*History*, book XIV), slaughtered a great multitude of barbarians and drove the rest beyond the borders of Britain.

But as soon as the Romans departed, the enemies, arriving again by ship, trampled down and devoured everything in their path. The Romans flew to their aid once more, cut down the enemy, and drove them beyond the seas.

The most ancient writers therefore testify that the first two devastations, and consequently the first two embassies, occurred under the emperor Honorius. If they occurred under Honorius, they cannot better be assigned to any period than that in which the count Constantius freed Gaul from the tyrants and the Goths—precisely the period which Bede recorded in his *Chronicle*.

The very learned Stillingfleet, however, says that the condition of the empire was so obstructed and troubled at that time that the Romans could in no way assist the Britons in their danger. He says that the Alans, Suevi, and Vandals had occupied Spain; the Franks, Burgundians, and Goths, Gaul; that Jovinus and Sebastian, brothers, had seized the empire in Gaul after Constantine; and that, although the Goths, having entered Spain, had vigorously defeated the barbarians, Roman affairs in Gaul had nevertheless been reduced to such straits that Constantius, who then administered the empire there, was compelled to recall them from Spain and assign them the second province of Aquitania and certain cities of the neighboring provinces as places of settlement.

But let the reader forgive me for agreeing with Bede rather than with Stillingfleet, learned though he was.

In the year 414, as Orosius relates, the count Constantius, stationed at Arelate, a city of Gaul, drove the Goths from Narbonne through great energy in conducting affairs and compelled them to depart into Hispania Secunda.

In the following year, according to Hydatius, Ataulf, king of the Goths, was killed at Barcelona. Vallia succeeded him in the kingship and, at the beginning of the year 416, immediately made peace with Constantius. He then opposed the Alans and the Siling Vandals, who were settled in Lusitania and Baetica, and in the year 417, for the sake of the Roman name, inflicted great slaughter upon the barbarians within Spain.

For the treaty which Vallia, king of the Goths, made with Constantius contained the provision that the Goths should harass in war the barbarian nations occupying Spain, and that whatever territory was wrested from the enemy should pass to the Roman Empire, as may be gathered from Orosius.

After Vallia had therefore subdued the barbarian peoples, as the treaty required, he was recalled by Constantius to Gaul—not because he was needed to defend the Gallic province, which at that time was enjoying profound peace, but so that he might receive the reward of his valor.

For that reason he was enriched with possession of Aquitania, which occurred in the year 419.

Nor should Hydatius be followed regarding the year, since he writes that Vallia was recalled to Gaul in the preceding year:

> “It is scarcely credible that Honorius, in the same year in which he had restored the body of the Seven Provinces by an ordinance delivered on 17 April to Agricola, prefect of the Gauls (Historians of the Franks, edited by André du Chesne, vol. I, pp. 83–84), and had ordered that a council should be held each year in the city of Arles from 15 August to 15 September, should immediately dissolve that body and grant a large part of it to the Goths.”

It is therefore evident that the Alans, Suevi, Vandals, and Goths never disturbed the peace of the Gallic province from at least the beginning of the year 416 until the year 419.

As for the Franks and Burgundians, there is no evidence that they caused any disturbance after the tyrants were killed, and they either returned to their own country or, if they obtained part of Gaul through Roman generosity, conducted themselves in their new settlements in such a way as to demonstrate their loyalty and gratitude and their remembrance of the benefit.

Since, therefore, from the beginning of the year 416 until the year 419 the Western Empire enjoyed the greatest peace, no reason can be offered sufficient to overturn Bede’s opinion that the first two embassies took place during these years under Honorius.

What Sabellicus and Blondus say about legions sent by Aetius—the first around the year 422, the second under the command of Gallio of Ravenna around the year 426—does not move me (Sabellicus, *Enneads* VIII.1; Blondus, *Decade* I.2), since Bede’s testimony is too ancient to yield to the authority of historians so much later.

The third embassy to Aetius, under Valentinian III, is well known. When the Britons could no longer endure the attacks of the Picts and Scots, they implored Aetius’s assistance in the consulship of Aetius III and Symmachus, as is clear from their letter preserved by Bede (*Ecclesiastical History* I.13). They were unable, however, to obtain any assistance from him, since at that time he was occupied with the most serious wars against Attila, king of the Huns.

## NUM. V [Smith VII]

### § I. On the Gregorian Books

First of all, the library contains the Gregorian Bible in two volumes. The first has, on its first leaf, a rubric concerning the chapters of the Book of Genesis. The second volume begins with the prologue of blessed Jerome on the prophet Isaiah.

At the beginning of the books in these same volumes, certain leaves are inserted, some of which are purple and others rose-colored. When held up to the light, they display a marvelous reflection.

The same library also contains Augustine’s Psalter, which Gregory himself sent to him. On its first leaf begin certain devout meditations, written in this form: “Behold how far I have wandered through my memory,” and so forth, continuing to the fifth leaf, where begins: “All Scripture is divinely inspired.” On the other side of the same leaf are the Apostles’ Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, the *Gloria in excelsis*, and “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and so forth.

The Psalter begins on the sixth leaf. At the end of the same Psalter are hymns for both night and day:

- The first hymn, for midnight, is: “It is the hour of midnight.”
- The second, at cockcrow: “Eternal creator of all things.”
- At matins: “Splendor of the Father’s glory.”
- At prime: “Come quickly, brothers.”
- At terce: “Now the third hour rises.”
- At sext: “Completing twice three hours.”
- At none: “Three times the triple hour revolves.”
- At vespers: “God, creator of all things.”
- At compline: “We beseech you, Lord.”
- In Lent: “Christ, who are light and day.”
- The hymn for Sunday: “Eternal King and Lord.”
- The hymn for the Nativity of the Lord: “Attend, you who rule Israel, who sit upon the cherubim; before Ephraim, stir up your power and come.”

There follows, for the same feast, the hymn “Come, Redeemer of the nations,” continuing to the end.

At Easter the hymn is: “This is the true day of God.”

At the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul: “The passion of the apostles.”

Of Saint John the Evangelist: “Noble through the love of Christ.”

The vestment treasury also contains a Gospel text, at the beginning of which the ten canons are noted. It is called [Col. 0313D] the text of Saint Mildred because, according to report, a certain peasant swore falsely upon this text at Thanet and lost his eyes.

There is also another Psalter placed upon the table of the high altar. On its exterior is a flat silver image of Christ with the four Evangelists.

On the first leaf of this Psalter begins: “All Scripture is divinely inspired.”

On the third leaf begins the epistle of Pope Damasus to Jerome; at the end are the verses of that same Damasus, followed by Jerome’s epistle to Damasus with Jerome’s verses.

Then, on the fourth leaf, is a discussion of the origin of the psalms, at the end of which the Psalter is divided into five books.

The first book ends with Psalm XL, namely: “Blessed is he who understands,” and concludes with: “Let it be, let it be.”

The second book ends with Psalm LXXI, namely: “Give your judgment, O God,” and concludes with: “Let it be, let it be.”

The third book ends with Psalm LXXXVIII, namely: “The mercies of the Lord,” and concludes with: “Let it be, let it be.”

The fourth book ends with Psalm CV, namely: “Give thanks,” and concludes with: “Let it be, let it be.”

The fifth book ends with Psalm CL, namely: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and concludes with: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

On the fifth leaf of the same Psalter follows an explanation of *alleluia* according to the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Syrians, and Latins. There is also an interpretation of *Gloria* among the Chaldeans, and an interpretation of Psalm CXVIII according to each individual letter.

On the sixth leaf follows an account of when the psalms should be sung or read, as Jerome writes. There is also an arrangement of the psalms according to A, B, C, and D.

On the seventh leaf is a discussion of the Hebrew letters written in the Psalter.

On the eighth leaf is an interpretation of the psalms, continuing to the eleventh leaf, where the text of the Psalter begins with an image of the priest Samuel. At the end of the same Psalter are hymns for matins, vespers, and Sunday, as found in the other Psalter described above.

The library also contains another Gospel text, in which the ten canons are placed at the beginning, together with a prologue that begins: “Prologue of the Canons.”

There is also placed upon the table of the high altar a book with an upright silver image of Christ, whose right hand is blessing. It contains the conflict of the apostles Peter and Paul with Simon Magus and the passion of those same apostles; the passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle; the passion of Saint James; the passion of Saint Thomas the Apostle; the passion of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle; the passion of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist; the passion of the holy apostles Simon and Jude; and the life of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist.

There is also another book placed upon the same table of the high altar. On its exterior it bears a gilded silver image of the Divine Majesty, surrounded by crystal stones and beryls. It contains a passionary of the saints, beginning with Saint Apollinaris and ending with the passion of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice.

A book is also placed upon the same table at the high altar. Its exterior decoration has one large beryl in the middle, with numerous other crystal stones all around. It contains an exposition on the Epistles and Gospels, from the Third Sunday after the octave of Easter to the Fourth Sunday after the octave of Pentecost.

These are the first-fruits of the books of the whole English Church.

### § II. On the Donation of Vestments
Sacred vestments and priestly garments are still preserved in the vestment treasury: namely, one *cappa* of silk, sapphire-colored or azure, adorned with gold borders and with precious stones on the front in its upper part; two purple silk *cappae*, adorned with gold borders and with other similar ornaments; three purple silk *cappae*, woven throughout with variegated work of gold and milky-white color; and one purple silk chasuble, ornamented on its upper rear part with gold embroidery and precious stones. Nor are such numerous and distinguished tokens of the original endowment of our church to be contemplated without a mystical meaning. [Col. 0314D]

By the single sapphire- or azure-colored *cappa*, the unity and stability of the Christian faith may be understood. By the two *cappae* that are of the same purple color as the chasuble, it is signified that Christ, appointing seventy-two disciples, sent them in pairs ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come; and that he likewise says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” The identity of the purple color signifies that, through the power of Christ’s blood, if we follow his footsteps and each bear the burdens of the other, when he appears we shall be like him and shall see him as he is.

Thus, in order that we may preserve the fitting correspondence of the number two with unity, let the hope of forgiveness in contrition be followed by the hope of grace in confession, and let the hope of glory in satisfaction be present—this is signified by the purple color. This threefold hope proceeds from the unity and stability of faith, which is itself threefold: the first from faith in the commandments, the second from faith in the signs, and the third from faith in the promises. [Col. 0315A]

That there are three *cappae* of the same purple color, but woven throughout with variegated work of blue, or gold, and snowy-white color, is appropriately understood as charity, which, according to the Apostle, consists in three things: a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. By the milky or snowy-white color, therefore, understand purity of heart; by the blue or gold color, goodness of conscience; and by the purple, integrity of faith. In the variegated woven work throughout, observe the variety of virtues, which is founded upon charity.

That the purple color holds precedence in these three variegated *cappae* and in the other two is understood to signify that “no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid,” namely Christ Jesus, from whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. And note that the number of the *cappae* corresponds to the number of the legatees—namely, Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus, together with Laurence the priest and Peter the abbot. [Here *legatariorum* means “legates,” not beneficiaries.]

§ III.—On the golden and silver vessels given by Saint Augustine

[Col. 0315B]

As for the golden and silver vessels which Bede and other historians recount as having been sent and presented to this monastery by blessed Gregory to that same Augustine, what ought I now to write about them? I utterly do not know, except that I cannot mention the matter without a sigh. Some say that, at the time when the most impious Danes ravaged this land, everything had been hidden in secret places because of their frequent incursions into these regions, and that these things have not yet been brought to light. Others say that, in the time of King Richard I, the aforesaid gifts were removed from this monastery and handed over to the duke of Austria as ransom for release from captivity. Still others suppose that, when Abbot Egelsinus, out of fear of William the Conqueror, fled to Denmark in the year of the Lord 1070, and William confiscated this monastery together with everything belonging to it and appointed a certain monk named Scotlandus as abbot, objects of this kind, together with many others, were preserved in secret places, unknown to later generations. [Col. 0315C]

§ IV.—On the relics bestowed by Saint Augustine, which blessed Gregory sent to him

The relics which blessed Augustine is said to have first bestowed upon this monastery as a gift from Saint Gregory are still present in considerable number in the vestment treasury: namely, a doubled or two-branched cross, which Thomas Sprot and others record as being divided, made from the wood of the Lord’s Cross; and relics from the seamless tunic, from the hairs of blessed Mary, from Aaron’s rod, and from the relics of the apostles and martyrs, together with many others, which are reverently placed in the treasury.

As for the books, accept what the distinguished Udanleius writes about them in his extremely rich *Catalogue of Old Northern Books*, p. 173:

“Leading the procession of these venerable codices are Gregory’s Bibles, written in two volumes. [Col. 0315D] That these sacred Bibles existed in England not long ago is shown by the *Apologetic Petition of the Catholic—so they call themselves—Laymen to James I, King of Great Britain*, presented in July of the year of the Lord 1604. It contains these words: ‘Those very Bibles, precisely the same ones which Saint Gregory sent here with our apostle Saint Augustine, have until now been preserved by the special providence of God.’ These words are quoted by Doctor Doctor Sutcliffe in his *Response to the same Apologetic Petition*, p. 87.

“I have not yet examined the second codex, namely the Psalter, with sufficient care.

“I believe that the third and fifth codices—namely, the two Books of the Gospels—both still survive, although mutilated: one in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, the other, decorated with historical illustrations, in the Library of C. C. C. C. For each codex breathes the antiquity of early centuries; each is written in larger and more rounded Roman letters, which differ greatly from letters of that kind in Anglo-Saxon script; [Col. 0316A] in both, the parchment and the ink are of foreign workmanship. In each there were the ten Eusebian Canons, since notes and numbers referring to them are found here and there in the margins. The distinctions and corrections in the Bodleian Codex, written in an ancient Saxon hand, and Queen Ealhburg’s testament, made in the C. C. C. C. Codex around the year 850, demonstrate that both were brought to England eight hundred years ago. In that testament she lists the bequests which she herself gave to the abbey of Saint Augustine, to which this codex once belonged. Why, then, should I not affirm that both codices are those most ancient, venerable with age, which blessed Pope Gregory arranged to have sent to Saint Augustine at the beginnings of the Anglo-Saxon Church?

“The fourth codex, namely the Psalter, seems to have been lost. Nevertheless, in the Cottonian Library, Vespasian A. I., there exists the Roman Psalter of Saint Jerome, written in large Anglo-Saxon letters a thousand years ago. Before the Psalms it contains, in equally large but foreign letters, [Col. 0316B] everything, and in the same order, that is said to have been written in this Gregorian Codex. I therefore readily believe that one was a copy of the other.

“The sixth, seventh, and eighth codices have not yet come into my possession. Yet many ancient copies of them seem to survive in libraries. Indeed, that sixth codex appears to have been translated into Saxon in the course of time, since the same passions, and so forth, are found in Saxon homiliaries; and perhaps the same should be said of the seventh volume.

“The annalist calls these codices the first fruits of the books of the whole English Church. I will not dispute this, provided that the antiquarian reader remembers that Augustine brought with him to England Gregory the Great’s book *On Pastoral Care*, as the poetic preface prefixed to King Alfred’s translation of this work testifies.”

**No. VI [Smith VIII]. That Augustine baptized many thousands not in the vicinity of York, but in Kent**

[Col. 0316C]

In the year 597, through the work of Bishop Augustine and his companions, the Anglo-Saxons embraced the Christian faith in great numbers, and on the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity more than ten thousand were cleansed in the waters of baptism. This is evident from Gregory’s reply to Eulogius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, to whom that celebrated pontiff wrote the following year:

“While the nation of the English, situated in a corner of the world, remained until now faithless in the worship of wood and stone, it pleased me, with the assistance of your prayers, that, with God as my guide, I should send to it a monk from my monastery for the purpose of preaching. After I had granted him permission, he was made bishop by the bishops of the Germans, and, accompanied also by their support, he was brought to the aforesaid nation at the end of the world. And now reports have reached us concerning its salvation and his work: for he himself and those who were sent with him shine among that people through such great miracles that, in the signs they display, they seem to imitate the virtues of the apostles. On the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, which has just passed in this first indiction, more than ten thousand English, as we have been informed by that same brother and our fellow bishop, were baptized by him.” [Col. 0316D]

It is therefore established that many were baptized; but the place and province where they were baptized are disputed. It is commonly believed that the baptism took place near York, in the River Swale. Ranulphus in his *Polychronicon*, Birchington, Gotselinus in his *Life of Saint Augustine*, and others incline to this view. Yet it is difficult to suppose that immediately after his consecration Augustine quickly left Kent, where he had been received with the greatest kindness by King Æthelberht and undoubtedly had a rich harvest of souls, and then went abroad to baptize the people of York, among whom no one is recorded to have preached so soon. Bede himself explicitly confirms that Eanfled, daughter of Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, was the first of that people to be baptized, and that this occurred long after Augustine’s death (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 9). It therefore could not have happened that Augustine baptized so many thousands in the vicinity of York, if Eanfled was the first of that nation to be washed in baptismal water. [Col. 0317A]

What is said, then, about the River Swale and the many people baptized there should rather be attributed to Paulinus, bishop of York, than included among Augustine’s praises. For Bede mentions that river in the province of Deira, and says that Paulinus (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 14) was accustomed to remain there frequently and baptize very large numbers in that river. He also gives a good reason why the sacrament was administered in a river: “For,” he says, “at the very beginning of the Church as it was coming into being, oratories or baptisteries could not be built there.” Since this could also be said of Kent, Augustine could have baptized many thousands of people there in some river, and Gregory could have meant that event. Thus it happened that the baptisms of Paulinus and Augustine were confused with one another, although they ought rather to have been distinguished both by place and by time. [Col. 0317B]

**No. VII [Smith IX]. On the controversies that arose in the Church concerning the celebration of Easter**

In almost every age the controversy over the day of Easter was debated with enormous passion. Although it may seem to concern nothing pertaining to the integrity or purity of the Christian religion, but only discipline; although the question concerns an ecclesiastical rite and custom, which underwent change according to different places and times, rather than the faith itself, nevertheless the conflict was fought on both sides with such bitterness that each party accused the other of heresy, and the bond of concord and unity was torn apart.

This dispute concerning Easter first began under the pontificate of Anicetus. While he was administering the episcopate, the most holy Polycarp, who according to the custom of the churches of Asia celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day that might be, came to Rome on account of this question and held a discussion about it with Anicetus. [Col. 0317C] Yet neither could Anicetus persuade Polycarp to abandon his customary observance, nor Polycarp Anicetus to observe the Asian custom. They did not at all break the bonds of charity, but communicated with one another; and in Anicetus’s church he granted Polycarp permission to perform the rites customarily carried out in the Eucharist (*Irenaeus, Letter to Victor*). At last each departed from the other in peace, and all the churches—both those that observed the feast of Easter on the fourteenth day and those that did otherwise—remained at peace among themselves.

The Roman Church therefore celebrated Easter not with Polycarp on the fourteenth day of the first month, but on the Sunday immediately following it; yet no disagreement arose on that account. Under the pontificate of Victor, however, the controversy flared up much more fiercely between the Asian bishops and the Roman bishop. A council was held at Rome to suppress it, and various councils were convened in other churches, both in the East and in the West. With one accord and a common judgment, they issued the same decision concerning the observance of that feast. On the Roman side stood the bishops of Palestine, Alexandria, Pontus, Gaul, the province of Osrhoene, and Achaea; on the other side stood only the bishops of Asia, whereas all the remaining churches throughout the world followed another custom (*Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History* V, 23). [Col. 0317D]

Polycrates of Ephesus, who presided over the bishops of Asia, vigorously insisted that the custom handed down to him by his ancestors should be retained, and said that this tradition had been transmitted from the times of the apostles Philip and John down to his own day. [Col. 0318A] Victor, on the contrary, and the others who inhabited the various regions of the West, maintained that Peter and Paul had left them the custom which they observed (*Socrates*, V, 22). All the bishops of the Eastern Church who issued the same judgment as the Westerners on this matter likewise affirmed in their letters that this rite had passed from the apostles to them through continuous succession. Thus the churches contending on both sides possessed the same authority of custom; both presented their own practice as apostolic.

Since customs that had proceeded from the apostles themselves could neither be rejected nor condemned, it was necessary, because the customs were different, to conduct an examination of which of the two forms of discipline was more consonant with God’s law. This was done by the most solemn and holy synod held at Nicaea. Since the Syrians and Mesopotamians were deficient in the matter of the feast and celebrated the solemnity together with the Jews, the Fathers of Nicaea, judging the time opportune for correcting all that was amiss, established one catholic rule for observing Easter (*Athanasius, On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*).

It seemed wholly unworthy that Christians should celebrate this most sacred feast by imitating Jewish rite and custom (*Letter of Constantine* in *Eusebius, Life of Constantine* [Col. 0318B] III, 18–19); there was also a danger that Easter might be celebrated twice in the same year. Those who celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, without regard to the equinox, sometimes celebrated it one year after the equinox and another year before the equinox, because the fourteenth day of the moon fell at such a time. It also seemed especially incongruous and unbecoming that on so solemn a feast of our religion there should be disagreement, so that on the same days some devoted themselves to fasting while others held banquets.

Since Easter was observed with one unanimous judgment in Rome, Italy, all Africa, Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, all Greece, the Asian and Pontic dioceses, and finally Cilicia, it was just that the smaller number of churches should embrace the custom of the greater number, and that all should by common agreement approve the practice which had no connection with the perfidy of the Jews. Therefore it was established in this synod that the solemnity of Easter should be celebrated on the Sunday immediately following the fourteenth day of the first month of Easter. [Col. 0318C]

Before proceeding further, however, it must be noted that those writers (*Magdeburg Centuries*) are seriously mistaken who think that the Britons learned the Easter rite not from the Romans and Westerners but from the Easterners. Constantine explicitly testifies in the letter he wrote on this matter that Easter was customarily celebrated in Britain in the same way as at Rome. The same letter also makes clear that the Asian churches which, under Pope Victor, celebrated their feast with the Jews had, at least for the most part, acknowledged catholic Easter before the Council of Nicaea; and that the Syrians and Mesopotamians, who agreed with Victor, adopted the position of those writers.

After the day of the Easter celebration had been defined by this council, the whole Church obeyed the decree. The Syrians immediately showed themselves obedient to the command (*Athanasius*, cited above), and their council held at Antioch, confirming the Council of Nicaea (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 561), established in its [Col. 0318D] first canon that ecclesiastics who observed the Jewish Easter were to be deposed and laypeople excluded from communion. The Mesopotamians did the same: they cut off Audianus and his followers, the Quartodecimans, from the common unity of the Church (*Epiphanius*, *Heresies* 70). Those who stubbornly refused to conform to the authority and judgment of this ecumenical council were regarded as heretics and called Quartodecimans. Thus Saint Epiphanius (*Heresy* 50), Theodoret (*Heretical Fables* III, 4), and Augustine (*On Heresies* 29) list them among the heretics. The seventh canon of the First Council of Constantinople also counts them among those who, after renouncing their errors, were received into the Church through anointing.

To prevent any error from creeping into the celebration of Easter, the holy Fathers—if not the Council of Nicaea itself, at least the Fathers who sought to remove every opportunity for error (*Leo, Letter to Emperor Marcian*)—entrusted this entire responsibility to the bishop of Alexandria. For among [Col. 0319A] the Egyptians there seemed anciently to have been a transmitted expertise in this calculation, by which the date on which the solemnity of Easter would occur each year was reported to the apostolic see, so that the information contained in this document might generally be conveyed to the churches far away.

Once the Easter date had been learned from the letters of the Alexandrian bishop and proclaimed to all the churches by letters of the Roman pontiff, deacons customarily announced it in each church on the sacred day of Epiphany. That this custom of the Church—namely, that the Easter date should be announced by the Roman pontiff—was already in force before the Council of Nicaea is evident from the First Council of Arles, held in the year 314. Its first canon, addressed to Sylvester, the Roman pontiff, together with the others, reads:

“First, concerning the observance of the Lord’s Easter: that it be observed by us throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, and that you, according to custom, send letters to everyone.”

The Fathers of Nicaea also, if Saint Ambrose is to be trusted (*Ambrose, On Easter, to the Bishop of Emilia*, and *Dionysius Exiguus, On Easter*), so that no room at all might thereafter remain for uncertainty, assembled those most skilled in calculation concerning the feast just mentioned, worked out a cycle of nineteen years, and established, as it were, a circle from which a model could be generated for the remaining years. They called this circle the *Enneadecaeteris*.

But this is highly uncertain, and Jerome and Bede deserve greater credence, since they write that Eusebius of Caesarea composed the *Enneadecaeteris* somewhat after the Council of Nicaea, and that, as though it had been compiled in the council’s name, it acquired use and authority among some people. If the synod itself had created such a cycle, the Latins would certainly have rejected their erroneous cycle of eighty-four years altogether and embraced a new one instituted by Fathers so renowned for holiness and learning. I shall soon prove that they used no nineteen-year cycle until the pontificate of Leo the Great. [Col. 0319B]

[Col. 0319C] There is another matter which that celebrated assembly decreed should be observed, and which we confirm as having been defined either at this time or earlier by the canon counted among the Apostolic Canons, the Eighth: namely, that Easter may not be celebrated according to Jewish custom before the spring equinox. What the venerable Fathers thought about this matter is further evident from Constantine’s letter (*Eusebius, Life of Constantine* III, 18), which he wrote from that same council. It forbids Christians to have anything in common with the most hostile crowd of Jews and therefore forbids them to celebrate two Easters with them in the same year. This could happen in no other way than if the feast were celebrated one year after the equinox and another year before it.

This did in fact sometimes happen among the Jews, when their Easter month began on the fifth day of March and ended on the third day of April. As for the equinox itself, according to Theophilus, Ambrose, Cyril, and the others who wrote about the celebration of Easter, it was fixed on March 21. And if ecclesiastical tradition is to be trusted, the Fathers of Nicaea themselves established this day as the fixed and immovable point of the spring equinox. [Col. 0319D]

After such matters had been settled by so illustrious and venerable a synod, who would not have thought that all controversies concerning the proper celebration of the Easter feast had finally been brought to an end? Yet the matter turned out quite otherwise. Frequent disputes broke out after the conciliar decree between the churches of the East and the West.

For Saint Ambrose reports that a disagreement concerning the date of Easter occurred in the year of Christ 387. Writing to the bishops throughout Emilia, he says:

“Since, even after the calculations of the Egyptians and the decision of the Church of Alexandria, many bishops of the Roman Church are still awaiting my opinion in letters, it was necessary for me to write what I think concerning the day of Easter.”

Some Latins believed that the feast should be celebrated on the very day of the equinox, namely March 21. In an ancient Latin calendar preserved by Bucherius (*On the Cycle of Victor*, p. 262), Easter is marked on April 18; that date is also given in the canon of Victor of Aquitaine, on the sixteenth day of the moon, whose new moon both writers calculate from April 3. Finally, the Alexandrians, whom Ambrose follows and defends, celebrated Easter on April 25. Thus in that year the feast was celebrated differently at Rome, Alexandria, and Milan. [Col. 0320A]

After a short interval came the year 414, when Pope Innocent I, brought into doubt concerning the Easter date, wrote the following to Aurelius, primate of Carthage:

“Since on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the sixteenth day of the moon is almost calculated—for it is a little short of it—and likewise since on the fourth day before those same Kalends the twenty-third day occurs, I have judged that the Easter feasts should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the aforementioned Kalends, since we know that no Easter has previously been celebrated on the twenty-third day of the moon.”

The pontiff was uncertain whether to begin the Easter solemnity on March 22, when the sixteenth day of the moon began as that day was ending, or to postpone it until March 29, when the twenty-third day of the moon would begin, although that day lay outside the Easter limit. It is credible, however, that he restored that solemnity on March 22. [Col. 0320B]

Three years later, in the year of Christ 417, Easter was celebrated in the Roman Church on March 25, but by the Alexandrians on April 22, as Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily, writes to Pope Saint Leo:

“Then,” he says, “when it was being avoided that Easter should be held on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, it was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April”—as he also states there—“by order of Pope Zosimus.”

During the pontificate of Leo the Great there were also two controversies in the Christian Church concerning the date of Easter: the first in the year of Christ 444, the second in 455. Saint Leo, not wishing any diversity to arise in the observance of the principal feast, did not wait for the year 444 to arrive. While the preceding year, 443, was still passing, he first sought the opinion of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; then also [Col. 0320C] that of Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily.

Both replied that in the year of Christ 443 Easter in the following year, 444, should be celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, or April 23, although the Latins announced it for the seventh day before the Kalends of April, or March 26. Saint Leo accepted their opinion, as is clearly evident from Prosper’s *Chronicle* (*in Labbe*, vol. I, p. 453), where we read the following about Easter in that year:

“This year the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.”

But there was a greater dispute concerning Easter in the year 455. The Alexandrians announced their feast for the eighth day before the Kalends of May, or April 24; the Latins, however, announced it eight days earlier, namely on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, April 17. According to their respective rules, Easter had been legitimately assigned by both sides, and therefore the controversy seemed both more justified and more difficult.

Foreseeing this, Saint Leo, fearing a kind of schism in the Church, judged that it should be addressed in good time. In the year 453 he wrote two letters: the first to the emperor Marcian, the second to the empress Eudocia Augusta. He asked them amicably and earnestly to warn the Alexandrians not to permit Easter to be extended to the eighth day before the Kalends of May.
