Emperor Marcian did not fail to act on his behalf, but carefully asked the Egyptian and other Eastern bishops what they thought about the matter. Among those consulted, Proterius of Alexandria sent Leo an extended letter in which he showed that the Lord’s Easter ought to be postponed to the eighth day before the Kalends of May. After receiving this letter together with Marcian’s communication, which conveyed the same message, Leo, out of a desire for peace, though unwillingly, adopted the opinion of the Easterners. [Col. 0320D]

In Gregory of Tours we likewise read that there was some diversity in Gaul concerning the observance of Easter in the year 577:

“In that year,” he says, “there was uncertainty about Easter. In Gaul, however, we, together with many cities, celebrated holy Easter on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. Others, together with the Spaniards, observed this solemnity on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.”

There is another example of this kind of variation in the same Gregory of Tours, when he speaks of the fifteenth year of Childebert the [Col. 0321A] Younger, which is the commonly accepted year 590 of Christ:

“There was uncertainty about Easter because, in the cycle of Victorius, he wrote that Easter was to be celebrated on the fifteenth day of the moon. But lest Christians should celebrate these solemnities under that moon like the Jews, he added: ‘The Latins, however, [celebrate it] on the twenty-second.’”

Those who celebrated Easter with the Alexandrians on the fifteenth day of the moon held the feast on the seventh day before the Kalends of April; those who followed the twenty-second day of the moon held it on the fourth day before the Nones of April, eight days later.

Finally, a lengthy controversy was conducted with great passion between the Britons and Scots on one side and the Roman Church on the other. The Britons and Scots did indeed celebrate the day of Easter on a Sunday, but on the fourteenth day of the moon if Sunday fell on that day; and for a long time they stubbornly defended this manner of celebrating the solemnity against the Roman Church. But we shall recount these matters more fully later.

Now that these points have been properly set forth, we must ask what gave rise to such diversity in each age. From what else could it have arisen except from the variety of cycles that were once in use in different churches? [Col. 0321B] Until the pontificate of Leo the Great, the Latins used an eighty-four-year cycle in announcing the Easter feast, as Paschasinus testifies, designating this cycle by the name of the Roman calculation. The Alexandrians, and those who followed them, used the nineteen-year cycle in arranging Easter.

The cycles did not differ from one another alone; the canons observed in determining the feast also differed. Victor of Aquitaine (*Preface to the Easter Canon*), explaining the origin of the disagreements that repeatedly arose between the Latin and Alexandrian churches concerning the restoration of Easter at the proper time, enumerates the different Easter canons of each.

First, the Latins “judged that it should be observed especially from the third day before the Nones of March to the third day before the Nones of April—namely, over twenty-nine days—so that whichever of those days the moon was born would constitute the beginning of the first month.” Thus the Latins extended their Easter new moons from March 5, inclusively, to April 3, exclusively, over a period of twenty-nine days (*Noris, On the Latin Easter Cycle*). [Col. 0321C]

The Alexandrians, however, began their earliest new moon on March 8, and extended their latest to April 5. Thus, just as they differed from the Latins by three days at the beginning of the Easter month, so likewise they differed from them by three days at its end.

From this different rule of the two churches it followed, says Victor, that the Latins “maintained that the fourteenth moons of the same month [the Easter month] were to be observed from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May.” Thus the Easter fourteenth moons extended from March 18 to April 15, over an equal lunar month of twenty-nine days.

The Alexandrians, who placed their earliest new moon three days later, extended their fourteenth moons from March 21 to April 18, preserving the same number of twenty-nine days as the Latins.

Victor describes another Latin canon as follows: “They assigned no fewer than the sixteenth moon to the mystery of celebrating the Lord’s resurrection, and never accept more than the twenty-second moon.” The Alexandrians, however, celebrated Easter one day earlier than the Latins, namely also on the fifteenth moon, and did not carry it beyond the sixteenth moon.

Finally, the last Latin canon disclosed the beginning and end of the Sundays of Easter. For the earlier Latins assigned the earliest Easter Sunday to March 21 and the latest to April 21. Later, however, when the Latins accepted the Nicene equinox as fixed on March 21 (*Leo, Letter to Emperor Marcian*), they confined Easter Sundays between March 22 and April 21, so that the calculation of the lunar month might be preserved over a period of thirty days.

The Alexandrians, however, who in determining the new moons and the various fourteenth days of the moon did not overstep the limits of the lunar month, extended Easter Sundays from March 22 to April 25—namely, four days beyond the Latins. [Col. 0321D]

From these very different rules for arranging the Easter month it resulted that the Eastern Church, which had adopted the Alexandrian cycle, often disagreed with the Western Church in announcing the day, [Col. 0322A] and frequently even the month, of Easter. Indeed, the Latin bishops themselves did not at all agree among themselves, because some observed the Alexandrian canons, as I showed above concerning the Church of Milan under Saint Ambrose.

Hence the disagreement in the time of Ambrose in the year 387 arose because, according to the Latin rule, it was not permissible to extend Easter Sunday to April 23, whereas the Alexandrians judged that the feast should be moved to that date. Since that year was the sixth year of the eighty-four-year cycle, the fourth solar cycle, and the year marked by the letter C, and since the twenty-sixth moon was joined to the Kalends of January on a Friday, the next new moon fell on January 6, and from this the third day fell on March 6.

Since this latter was Easter according to the Latins, the fourteenth day of the moon was calculated as March 19, a Friday; and therefore Easter was to be celebrated on Sunday the 21st, on the sixteenth day of the moon. For according to the Latins, if the fourteenth day of the moon occurred on Friday, the following Sunday—that is, the sixteenth day of the moon—was assigned without doubt to the Easter feast, if Victor is to be believed.

The Alexandrians, however, omitting the March lunation, which for them was not Easter because it began before March 8, accepted the new moon of the Easter month on April 5. Since its fourteenth day fell on Sunday, April 18, they postponed Easter to the following Sunday, April 25. [Col. 0322B]

The Easter of the year 414, about which Pope Innocent was uncertain, shows how strongly the Latins recoiled from the custom of the Alexandrians, who celebrated the feast without scruple on the fifteenth moon. Because only a few hours were lacking before the sixteenth moon began on March 22, he doubted whether Easter should be postponed to the twenty-third moon, refusing to acknowledge a feast celebrated on the fifteenth moon.

The disagreement that occurred in the year 417 under Pope Zosimus clearly proves that, up to that year, Easter in the Roman Church had never exceeded April 21. For Zosimus, unwilling to cross this ancient limit of [Col. 0322C] Easter Sunday, refused to celebrate the feast on April 22 with the Alexandrians.

The year 417 was the thirty-sixth year of the eighty-four-year cycle, in which the twenty-eighth moon was marked on the Kalends of January. Therefore the next new moon fell on January 4, and from this the third day fell on March 4.

From this arose very serious difficulties. Since that lunation lay outside the beginning of the Easter month, an intercalary month had to be added. Since it consisted of thirty days, it ended on April 2; consequently the new moon of the Easter month had to begin on April 3. Yet according to the Latins this date lay beyond the limit of the Easter new moons, whose latest beginning was April 2.

But if they had exceptionally made the intercalary month hollow, since the fourteenth day of the moon—that is, April 15—or the fifteenth—that is, April 16—would have fallen on Sunday, Easter would have had to be transferred either to April 22, one day beyond the limit, or to April 23, two days beyond it.

The Roman Church of that time, therefore, so as not to move either the Easter new moon beyond its limit or the feast itself beyond its ancient boundary, preferred, when the twenty-eighth moon fell on the Kalends of January, either to advance the beginning of the Easter month by one day or, by changing one of the months from hollow to full, to calculate the new moon not from March 4 but from March 5. [Col. 0322D]

Hence the sixty-third year of the Latin cycle, the year of the Lord 444, marked on the Kalends of January by the same twenty-eighth moon and by the seventh day of the week, reduced the Western Church to exactly the same difficulties. It could not begin the Easter month with the new moon that began on April 2, because, since the fifteenth moon would fall on Sunday, April 16, the feast would have had to be postponed to April 23, two days beyond the limit.

Therefore, as the Latins had done on other occasions, they judged that the Easter month should begin on March 5. Its fifteenth moon then fell on Sunday the 19th, and Easter consequently had to be celebrated on March 26, which for them was the twenty-second moon.

When Paschasinus showed that the Latins refused to extend Easter beyond April 21—[Col. 0323A] truly refusing to cross the limit handed down by their ancestors, although they celebrated the feast on April 23—and when he suggested to Pope Leo that the Easter of the Passion should be celebrated within the ancient limit on April 21, even if the Easter of the Resurrection were postponed to April 23, Leo judged this interpretation legitimate and just. At that point, for the first time, he crossed the ancient boundary and agreed with the Alexandrians concerning the arrangement of Easter Sunday.

[Col. 0323B] Although Saint Leo thought that the celebration might in some sense be extended to the tenth or ninth day before the Kalends of May, he nevertheless judged it an excessively unusual and obvious transgression to carry the Paschal observance to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, the date assigned by the Alexandrians in the year 455. Therefore Leo held that the feast should be restored on 17 April, the sixteenth day of the moon, reckoning the new moon from 2 April, not from 4 April, to which the Neomenia had been assigned according to the Easterners—although, according to the Latins, that date lay outside the limit for the beginning of the Paschal month. Even though the pontiff declared that Easter ought rather to be observed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, he was overcome by the rescript and authority of Marcian, and decreed that in the Latin Church also it should be celebrated, in accordance with the Alexandrian opinion, on 24 April. Here it is worth noting, together with Cyril, a point confirmed by Saint Theophilus (*In Prologum Paschalem*): that the Latins called the new moon the third, sixteenth, or twenty-third day of the moon, and that they often began their new moons two days before the Alexandrians. This is most clearly shown by the new moon of the year 455.

[Col. 0323C] From the Council of Nicaea until the time of Leo the Great, the Latins used no nineteen-year cycle. During Leo’s pontificate, Victorius of Aquitaine, at the command of Hilary, Leo’s archdeacon, was the first, in the year 457, to transform the nineteen-year cycle into a period of 532 years. He adapted it in part to the Latin canons, carried it through twenty-eight solar cycles, and placed the nearest Paschal new moon on 7 March—two days beyond the Latin limit, but one day short of the Alexandrian limit. He did this in order to remove disagreements concerning the date of Easter, to discover the truth, and to eliminate the error of conflicting opinions. Yet although the Victorian period extinguished every disagreement concerning the Paschal month, it left intact the ancient disputes over the date of Easter. For since Victorius, in accordance with the Latin canons, excluded the fifteenth day of the moon from the Paschal solemnities whenever it fell on a Sunday in his cycle, he designated Easter one week later than the Alexandrians. Again, since he placed the limit for Paschal new moons on 3 April, two days before the Alexandrian limit, he sometimes announced Easter eight days earlier than the Alexandrians (*Bucherius, Commentary on the Victorian Canon*, ch. 8). Thus, throughout the entire cycle, he announced Easter on a date differing from the Alexandrian cycle thirty-two times.

[Col. 0323D] Indeed, as Gregory of Tours writes, in the year 577 Victorius announced Easter eight days earlier than the Alexandrians. The Gauls, who followed him, as I stated above, celebrated it on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 18 April, reckoning the new moon from 3 April. But among the Alexandrians in that year, which was the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the new moon was reckoned from 5 April; since the fourteenth day of the moon fell on Sunday, 18 April, Easter was transferred to 25 April. The Spaniards, however, differing from both groups, undoubtedly followed the opinions of the ancient Latins. They sometimes celebrated on the very day of the equinox, 21 March, and did not believe that they were violating the decree of the Nicene council if they admitted Easter on that day. They had persuaded themselves that the Nicene Fathers had sanctioned only this one rule: that Easter should not be celebrated before the equinox—not that it should not be celebrated on the equinox itself.

In the year 590, according to the same Gregory, Victorius and the Latins who agreed with him began the feast eight days later than the Alexandrians. The Alexandrians, and the Gauls who followed them, designated Easter in their second cycle on 26 March, the fifteenth day of the moon; but other Gauls, observing the canon of Victorius and therefore never admitting Easter before the sixteenth day of the moon, considered that their Easter had to be postponed to 2 April, the twenty-second day of their moon. We may also infer from the book of Victor, bishop of Capua, whose fragments Bede quotes (*On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 49, and in the short work *On the Vernal Equinox*), that in the year 550 different opinions concerning that year’s Easter existed in Italy, because Victorius delayed Easter by eight days. It was the nineteenth year of the Alexandrian cycle, and in it the fourteenth day of the moon was assigned to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, Easter to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, and the moon was reckoned as the twenty-first. It was likewise year 523 of the Victorian period, in which Easter was marked: “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—but for the Alexandrians, the eighth day before the Kalends of May—the sixteenth day of the moon.” For Victorius began the Paschal month according to the Alexandrian Golden Number 19 on 2 April, whereas the Egyptians delayed the new moon by two days.

The canon of Victorius was accepted only by the Latins and Westerners, and not even by all of them. In Italy, we can easily infer that it was not accepted at all by the Milanese from the fact that their bishop Ambrose had preferred the Alexandrian method to the Latin method as early as the year 386 and had introduced it into his church—or at least had preserved a practice introduced there before his time. [Col. 0324B] After Dionysius Exiguus published, in the year 525, a Paschal cycle of ninety-five years, the Roman Church, finally weary of the prolonged disputes over the proper restoration of the date of Easter which it had maintained for several centuries with the Alexandrian Church, indeed with the whole East, accepted the Dionysian cycle, which had been constructed according to the Egyptian canons.

The first to compose such a cycle was Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine (Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 42). Later, Pope Theophilus of Alexandria dedicated a cycle of one hundred years to the emperor Theodosius the Elder. After him, his successor Cyril comprised a series of ninety-five years in five nineteen-year cycles (Dionysius Exiguus, Letter 1, *On the Reckoning of Easter*); and following him, Dionysius Exiguus [Col. 0324C] appended an equal number of further years in the same orderly scheme.

This Dionysian cycle is divided into twelve common years, that is, years of 354 days, and seven embolismic years, that is, years of 384 days (Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 43). The first and second years are common; the third is embolismic; the fourth and fifth are common; the sixth is embolismic; the seventh is common; the eighth is embolismic; the ninth and tenth are common; the eleventh is embolismic; the twelfth and thirteenth are common; the fourteenth is embolismic; the fifteenth and sixteenth are common; the seventeenth is embolismic; the eighteenth is common; and the nineteenth is embolismic. Both kinds of year, common and embolismic, take their beginning from the beginning of the first month. Its beginning must be observed according to this rule: the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon must never precede the vernal equinox, but the legitimate date must fall either on the equinox itself—that is, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—or after it. Hence the beginnings of the lunar year must be sought from 8 March through the Nones of April (5 April). [Col. 0324D] The fourteenth day of the moon, occurring first on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and last on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, makes the date of the Paschal feast a matter to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

When Augustine, sent by Gregory the Great into Britain, had received this cycle from the Roman Church, he tried by every means to bring the Britons, who used another cycle, back into agreement with Roman practice (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 2). They, however, clinging tenaciously to their ancient custom, refused to depart from institutions once adopted. Their obstinacy finally reached such a point that it could not be broken or expiated even by the blood of twelve hundred monks. The Scots, too, who inhabited the island of Ireland, celebrated the Paschal solemnity at the same time as the Britons; and they hated Roman custom so much that Daganus, their bishop, when he came to Laurence, Augustine’s successor as the second bishop of Canterbury (*ibid.*, 41), was unwilling not only to eat with the Romans, but even to take food in the same lodging in which they ate. Laurence and his colleagues attempted to soothe their feelings by a sufficiently moderate letter [Col. 0325A], but accomplished nothing. Pope Honorius also sent them a letter (*ibid.*, 19), addressed to the bishops, priests, and abbots of Scotland; later John, who succeeded Severinus, the successor of that same Honorius, sent another (*ibid.*), full of great authority and learning, but with the same unfortunate result.

Yet even among these people there were some who exercised their zeal against their errors. For the beginning of the aforesaid letter of John clearly shows that not the entire Scottish people, but only certain individuals among them, had become entangled in that heresy. Bede likewise records that the people of the Scots who lived in the southern parts of the island of Ireland had long ago learned, at the admonition of the bishop of the apostolic see, to observe Easter according to the canonical rite. His letter survives among those from Ireland published by Usserius. There was also Cummianus, a monk from the Scottish people, who, having joined the Roman side, gave an account of his action to Segienus, abbot of Iona [Col. 0325B]. He mentions a synod held by his ancestors in the plain of Len, and the decision made there “that in the coming year they would celebrate Easter with the universal Church. But not long afterward a certain whitewashed wall arose, pretending to preserve the tradition of the elders. He did not make the two things one, but divided them, and in part nullified what had been promised.” Ronanus, a Scot by nation, also attacked the Lindisfarne monks, followers of Scottish rites (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 25). For when he disputed with Bishop Finan, he corrected many, but was wholly unable to correct Finan.

After Finan’s death, when Colman succeeded to the episcopate (*ibid.*), he too having been sent from Scotland, a more serious controversy arose over the observance of Easter and also over other disciplines of ecclesiastical life. Accordingly, when the question of Easter and the tonsure had been raised, a synod was convened in the monastery called Streaneshalch in the year 664. After a long dispute between Colman and Wilfrid [Col. 0325C], and after hearing the arguments of both sides, King Oswiu gave judgment in favor of Wilfrid. At that time Wilfrid was a priest in the monastery at Ripon, from which the Scots had shortly before been expelled; they “when given the choice, preferred to withdraw from the place rather than change their custom.” Seeing from their example that his own teaching had been rejected and his sect despised, Colman returned to Scotland, taking with him those who wished to follow him (*ibid.*, 26).

Around the year 700, through Adamnan, priest and abbot of the monks of Iona (*Ecclesiastical History* V, 15), who had been sent to England on a mission and had learned Roman practices there, a large part of the Scots in Ireland, and some of the Britons in Britain, adopted the ecclesiastical time of the Paschal observance. Nevertheless, he was unable to bring his own people on the island of Iona, or those subject to its monastery, to the path of truth. The same controversy was subsequently stirred up through the agency of Aldhelm (*ibid.*, 18), then abbot of Malmesbury, who, at the command of a certain synod, wrote a letter against the errors of the Britons [Col. 0325D]—the letter that stands as number 129 among the Bonifacian letters. After him, we must mention Ceolfrid, abbot of Jarrow and Wearmouth (*ibid.*, 21), whose learned letter to Naiton, king of the Picts, Bede commemorates. When the king read it, he rose from the midst of his nobles, bent his knees to the ground, and gave thanks to God that he had been deemed worthy to receive such a gift from the land of the English. He wished to observe the canonical date of Easter perpetually with all his people and to adopt the tonsure, which he had heard was fully reasonable.

Finally, in the following year, as Bede adds in the next chapter, the people of Iona and the monasteries subject to them were brought to the canonical rite of Easter and the canonical tonsure through the efforts of Ecgberht, an English monk who lived as a pilgrim in Ireland. This was ultimately the outcome of that long dispute, although Usserius states in his history of British antiquities that some remnants of the ingrained superstition remained among the Britons in Cambria [Col. 0326A]. The same is evident both from Bede’s fifth book, chapter 23, and from the 129th Bonifacian letter.

Among the Scots and Picts, therefore, the Paschal controversy had this fortunate outcome. It arose, as it once had, from a difference in cycles. The Church of the English accepted the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle, whereas the Scottish and British churches followed a certain computation contained within an eighty-four-year cycle (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 2; V, 21). Nor did they designate the Paschal Sundays, as the Roman Church did, from the fifteenth day of the moon to the twenty-first, but from the fourteenth to the twentieth. In one respect their cycle agreed with the computation formerly used by the Latins: both were eighty-four years long. In another respect it differed: they counted Paschal Sundays not, like the Latins, from the sixteenth day of the moon to the twenty-second, but from the fourteenth to the twentieth.

At the Synod of Pharæ in the year 664, Wilfrid, later bishop of York [Col. 0326B] (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 25), brought forward the authority of the apostle Peter against Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne. He asserted that when Peter preached at Rome, he established that Easter should be celebrated in such a way that its Sunday could be observed only from the fifteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first. Ceolfrid later wrote similarly to Naiton, king of the Picts, about the tradition attributed to Peter (*Ecclesiastical History* V, 21). He rejects not only the computation of the Scots and Britons, but also condemns those who maintained that Easter should be celebrated from the sixteenth day of the first month through the twenty-second. These good men did not doubt that what they saw observed at Rome in their own time should be referred to apostolic tradition and Peter’s institution, although it is certain that the Alexandrian Paschal computation was first adopted by the Romans only in the sixth century after Christ. We have shown above that their ancestors celebrated Easter from the sixteenth day of the moon to the twenty-second—that is, as Ceolfrid, ignorant of the matter, judged, they had fallen into the whirlpool of Charybdis and should be swallowed up.

[Col. 0326C] Colman also appealed in vain to the example of the holy apostle John to confirm his own rite. The blessed John and the Asiatics who followed his example celebrated their Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, regardless of the day of the week. Colman and his people, however, celebrated not on every day of the week, but always on Sunday, from the fourteenth day of the moon to the twentieth, “attempting to renew a new heresy from the old” (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 29). The old heresy, namely, was always to celebrate Easter with the Hebrews; the new heresy was to do so only sometimes, in those years in which Easter Sunday fell on the fourteenth day of the moon.

The Scots, however, quite correctly observed that Anatolius had written that Easter should be celebrated according to their custom from the fourteenth day of the moon to the twentieth. Wilfrid’s response is entirely inadequate when he says that Anatolius had reckoned the fourteenth day of the moon for Sunday Easter in such a way that he admitted it to be, on that very day, the fifteenth day of the moon toward evening, according to Egyptian practice; and that he had marked the twentieth day as Easter Sunday in such a way that, after the day had passed, he considered it the twenty-first [Col. 0326D] (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 25). For, beyond all doubt, Anatolius admitted Easter Sunday on the fourteenth Alexandrian day of the moon, together with the Quartodecimans (*Anatolius’s Canon*, in Bucherius), and never extended it beyond their twentieth day of the moon. In this, however, he plainly differed from the Scots: he established a nineteen-year cycle and expressly asserted that those who observe an eighty-four-year cycle never arrive at the true reckoning of Easter.

It must now be asked whether, according to this cycle of the Britons, Picts, and Irish, the beginning and end of the first month, and likewise the fourteenth and twentieth days of the moon, were the same as according to the Alexandrians. It seems very probable to me that all these matters differed in the two cycles. For Bede testifies that when Ecgberht taught the people of Iona to accept Catholic Easter, they celebrated Easter Sunday in the year 729 on the eighth day before the Kalends of May—a date on which Easter had never previously been celebrated in those regions [Col. 0327A], that is, among the Scots (*Ecclesiastical History* V, 21). The eighth day before the Kalends of May was the twentieth day of the Alexandrian moon. Therefore, if the Scots had observed the Alexandrian rules, they would certainly have celebrated their feast on that day. Since they did not, it is abundantly clear that they followed other principles in their computation. These words also show that the Paschal Sundays among the Scots were confined within narrower limits than among the Alexandrians. Among the Scots, Easter was never extended to the eighth day before the Kalends of May. From this it may appropriately be inferred that they followed, in part, the rules of the Latins, among whom the earlier authorities judged that Easter should never be extended beyond the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, while Leo and later writers extended it no farther than the ninth day before those Kalends.

It is further shown that their entire computation was very different from the Alexandrian one by Cummian’s letter to Segienus. He says that he had found the nineteen-year cycle of the Nicene Fathers to be contrary to the Scottish one, whose author, place, and time were unknown—in the Kalends, in the leap year, in the epact, in the fourteenth day of the moon, in the first month, and in the equinox. [Col. 0327B] He adds that the Scots made a common year embolismic and an embolismic year common, and that they were separated from the rest of the Church in celebrating Easter not merely by one week, but by an entire month.

Usserius (*British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 485) writes that in the year 630 the Irish, following an eighty-four-year cycle, observed Easter Sunday on the Kalends of April, one full week before the date prescribed in the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle, already accepted by the Romans. In the immediately following year, he says, a difference of four whole weeks intervened between the two computations: the Irish celebrated Easter on 21 April, while the Romans celebrated it on 24 March. That learned man had no doubt that this was the event to which Cummian’s account referred:

“We sent men whom we knew to be wise and humble; and, having come to Rome, in the third year they reached us . . . . . And in one lodging, with a Greek and a Hebrew, a Scythian and an Egyptian, they were together at Easter in the church of Saint Peter, in which month we are separated by a whole month.” [Col. 0327C]

The cycle of the Scots and Britons, therefore, differed greatly from that of the Alexandrians. But whether it was similar to that of the Latins, I confess that I do not know with sufficient certainty.

Bucherius, in his commentary on the Victorian canon (p. 171), thinks that Palladius, sent to the Scots in the year 431, introduced the Latin cycle together with the other rites of the Roman Church. This must certainly be acknowledged as probable. But when he asserts, on the authority of Bede (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 25), that the Scots sometimes celebrated Easter on the thirteenth day of the moon, this must not be understood in the same sense in Bede as in Bucherius. Bede means only that the Scots often began Easter on the evening of the thirteenth day of the moon, when, of course, the fourteenth day had already begun; for, if we believe the Jews, the fourteenth began on the evening of the thirteenth day.

The most learned cardinal Henry Noris, in his dissertation [Col. 0327D] on the Paschal cycle of Ravenna, a cycle of ninety-five years, inferred from Bede and from the ancient author of the books *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture* that the cycle of Victorius was in use in Ireland. But what he adduces from Bede concerning uncertain cycles does not prove this. And although the Irish author of the work *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture* may have used the cycle of Victorius, it does not follow that the Irish Church followed that period in determining Easter. Aldhelm, abbot of Malmesbury, plainly writes (*Letter to Geruntius*) that they did not decree that posterity should follow the course of Victor’s Paschal tables, which is contained in cycles of 522 years; rather, they celebrated the Paschal sacrament according to the rule of Sulpicius Severus—or Severus—who described an eighty-four-year cycle.

## NUM. VIII [Smith IX b]. On the Tonsure of Clerics

Besides the disagreement over the date of Easter, there was also a different form of tonsure in the churches of the English, [Col. 0328A] Britons, and Scots. The English, instructed by the Romans and imbued with the Christian faith, judged that tonsure should be preferred above all others—the tonsure which they had transferred from Roman custom for their own use and whose origin they attributed to the blessed apostle Peter. They judged that it ought to be borne by those who had either taken the monastic vow or received the clerical rank, fashioned and represented in the form of the crown of thorns which our Savior wore upon his head in his Passion. The Scots and Britons, imitating the rite of their fathers and predecessors, stubbornly rejected the Roman tonsure and defended their own, extending from ear to ear. The English attributed it to Simon Magus and branded it with that name, so that the new tonsure, which resembled a crown, might more easily be accepted.

Those who think that the complete shaving of the head, or the crown formed by shaving the head, was commanded by the apostles appear to have accommodated the language and customs of their own recent age to the primitive and apostolic period. [Col. 0328B] It seems to me much more probable that during at least the first four centuries clerics alone, as distinct from other believers, were instructed not to wear their hair excessively long; but that there was still no mention of a crown or of shaving the entire head.

The *Pontifical Book*, attributed to Damasus, testifies that what Saint Paul commanded all the faithful at Corinth was especially enjoined upon clerics, and claims that it was decreed by Pope Anicetus, who, according to that book, “established that a cleric should not grow his hair long, in accordance with the apostolic command” (*Labbe, Councils*, vol. I). It may therefore be inferred that before Anicetus’s decree clerics were accustomed to have longer hair and did not form crowns on their heads from their hair. Yet Anicetus did not institute a spherical tonsure, but only the tonsure consisting in the cutting of the hair; this ought to have been common to all the faithful, and even to unbelievers if any of them professed modesty. For there is no doubt that those who did not cut their hair close to the head, but let it fall somewhat longer, fulfilled this command, since the only thing forbidden was to let the hair hang down in a feminine manner and to keep it uncut. [Col. 0328C]

At the beginning of the sixth century, or certainly at the end of the fifth, but not before, the crown appears to have been openly introduced into the Church. For at that time, as Gregory of Tours reports, Nicetius, bishop of Trier, was born, and “when he had been delivered from the womb, his entire head was seen bare of hair, as is the custom with newborn infants; but around it a row of a few hairs appeared, so that you might think that a cleric’s crown had been marked out by them” (Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, ch. 17). Thus that clerical crown began in the fifth century. Nothing else seems to have provided its origin except the extremely strong desire then burning among bishops to imitate the life of monks, who by their holiness and every kind of virtue had won for themselves the esteem and respect of people everywhere.

That many of the earlier monks wore their hair long is taught by Jerome (*To Eustochium, On the Preservation of Virginity*), who angrily attacks certain men who grew their hair in a feminine fashion: “Flee men,” he says, “whose hair is feminine, contrary to the Apostle.” Augustine, rebuking monks who grew their hair, says: “They carry hypocrisy around for sale, fearing that holiness shorn may be considered less valuable than holiness with long hair, so that whoever sees them may think of those ancients whom we read about, Samuel and the others who were not shorn” (*On the Work of Monks*, ch. 31). Finally, Epiphanius, in heresy 80, censures the monks of Mesopotamia because they wore their hair long and uncut in the manner of women.

[Col. 0328D] That most monks were shorn in ancient times is clear both from this very criticism and from the fact that Julian, called the Apostate, before Constantius made him Caesar, had himself shorn down to the skin in order to imitate monastic life more effectively, as Sozomen testifies in book three, chapter one of his *History*. [Col. 0329A] Pachomius, too, who flourished in the fourth age, admits the tonsure in chapter 96 of his Rule, since he commands “that no one should cut his hair without the order of a superior.” Paulinus of Nola describes the monks of his time as follows: “Our fellow servants and fellow sufferers, humble in rough haircloth, clothed in little cloaks, girded with a rope, their hair cut to the skin in chaste ugliness, half-shorn unevenly, and their foreheads shaven bare” (*Letter* 7). Elsewhere he wishes that his sins might be cut away by his own hair “not by cutting it halfway, but as though by a razor’s tooth pressed down to the living flesh” (*Letter* 4).

Similarly, when Salvian depicts an African monk, he says that the man was cloaked and pale and shorn to the skin, with the flowing locks of his hair cut away. They cut their hair with such deformity to show that they took the greatest pleasure in being despised by human beings. Yet the more they wished to be despised, the greater honor they received. Hence many clerics, out of zeal for monastic and holier living, adopted the clothing, habit, and tonsure of ascetics. [Col. 0329B] For the short hair of clerics mentioned by Sidonius—which clerics shared with monks and penitents—is to be understood as such an *epikarsis* (ἐπίκαρσις), that is, a cutting or shortening of the hair. Sidonius did not know whether Maximus Palatinus was acting as a monk or a cleric, or as a penitent, because he had short hair but a long beard (*Letter* 24).

The tonsure of monks and clerics was therefore common at that time, probably for the reason that monks were frequently promoted to the highest clerical rank and honor without changing their habit, and that clerics adopted the monastic profession together with the corresponding habit and tonsure. They desired to imitate the harsher and humbler life of monks, and therefore rejected the empty splendor of clothing and worldly adornment.

Thus, slowly and gradually, the tonsure in the form of a crown was reached. During the first four centuries clerics wore their hair short and modest, but not closely shorn. [Col. 0329C] In the fifth century they cut their hair down to the skin; and only afterward were their heads marked with crowns. The tonsure that cuts the hair down to the skin therefore passed from monks to clerics, just as later the custom of wearing a crown of hair passed from clerics to monks. As time advanced—namely, in the age of Gregory of Tours, who died toward the end of the sixth century—monks and clerics were no longer distinguished, and to be shorn was the same as to become a cleric. Thus monks too were considered clerics because of the crown handed down by the hands of abbots. At the beginning of the eighth century, Ceolfrid, abbot of Jarrow, observes that not only clerics but also monks displayed upon their heads, by means of the tonsure, the form of the crown of thorns (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 21).

[Col. 0329D] Isidore, bishop of Seville, explains the shape of this tonsure extremely well in these words:

“But when, after the upper part of the head has been shorn, a circular crown is left below, I believe that the priesthood and the kingdom of the Church are represented in them. For among the ancients a tiara was placed upon the heads of priests. Made of linen, it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified by the shorn part of the head. The crown, however, is the breadth of the golden circle that encircles the heads of kings” (*On Ecclesiastical Offices* II, 4).

The clerical tonsure, therefore, was not formerly a small circle at the very top of the head, but a larger circle occupying most of the head. The comparison with the golden circle that surrounds the heads of kings, together with the words “after the upper part of the head has been shorn, a circular crown is left below,” clearly shows that this crown was once of considerable size. The part of the head around which the hair had been cut in a circle was the place of the crown. Beginning at the forehead, it ran around through the temples to the back of the head; passing above the ears, it encircled the whole head.

This was the form of clerical tonsure used throughout almost the whole of the West, though not everywhere. For from the Fourth Council of Toledo [Col. 0330A] it is certain that the crown had not yet been adopted in certain parts of Spain. The forty-first canon of that synod reads as follows:

“All clerics and readers, like Levites and priests, shall have the entire upper part of the head shorn, leaving below only the circular crown—not as readers in the regions of Galicia appear hitherto to have done, who, with long hair like laymen, cut only a small circle at the top of the head. For this rite has hitherto been the custom of heretics in Spain. Therefore, in order to remove a scandal from the Church, this sign of disgrace must be taken away, and there shall be one tonsure or habit, as is the custom throughout all Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.”

Here we are taught that before the year 633, when this synod was held, clerics throughout all the provinces of Spain used the crown-shaped tonsure, while those living in Galicia had not previously adopted it.

Gregory of Tours proves that the Gauls wore the crown. [Col. 0330B] It remains for me now to speak of Rome and Italy. That this kind of tonsure was also used there will be sufficiently clear from the painted image of Gregory the Great described by John the Deacon in the life of that pontiff (book IV, ch. 84). I shall mention here only what concerns the hair and beard:

“His beard was somewhat reddish and moderate, after the manner of his father; he was rather bald, so that in the middle of his forehead he had two thin, curling locks, sparse and turned toward the right; his crown was round and broad, with darkish hair neatly curled, hanging down to the middle of his ear.”

Thus, in the time of Gregory, when Augustine was sent into England, the crown was in use at Rome. Consequently, the apostolic legates introduced into Britain the same custom of cutting the hair that prevailed at Rome. Augustine first persuaded the English to adopt it; afterward the English persuaded the Scots and the other peoples of that island. These resisted for a long time and stubbornly, until at the beginning of the eighth century the Scots, at the urging of Adamnan and Ecgberht, and the Picts, when Ceolfrid, abbot of Jarrow, wrote to their king Naiton concerning this very matter, adopted the Roman tonsure together with Catholic Easter. [Col. 0330C] The Britons, still hardened in their old ways, continued to display heads without a crown (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 22).

Ceolfrid accurately depicts the tonsure of the Scots and Britons in the letter mentioned above. He admits that they used an *epikarsis* (ἐπίκαρσις) rounded over half the head, not very unlike Peter’s tonsure, except that it did not form a complete circle but ended behind as though interrupted and shortened. He describes it as follows:

“On the surface of the forehead it appears to present the form of a crown; but when, in examining it, you reach the neck, you will find that the crown you thought you saw has been shortened.”

It did not complete a full circle, but represented the shape of a semicircle, or of the moon with its horns joined together. This tonsure is said to extend from ear to ear in an ancient book of canons cited by the distinguished Usserius. It was abolished by the Roman tonsure, among other reasons, “so that it might distinguish Christians from Simon Magus, whose hair was cut from ear to ear on the front part, whereas previously magicians wore a lock of hair on the forehead” (*British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 479). According to this author, magicians customarily covered “only the entire front of the forehead.” [Col. 0330D] If we believe him, Simon Magus shaved one half—the part facing the forehead—while leaving untouched the other part, toward the back of the head. The Scots and the others imitated this form of tonsure instead of the Roman and English one. Although the front part of their heads was shorn, it was not completely shorn; hair was left on the forehead as far as the ears, so that a semicircle could be formed from it. For the Scottish tonsure had the form of a half-crown, or semicircle. It differed from the Catholic tonsure in this one respect: it did not extend around the entire head, but ran across the forehead to both ears, leaving the back of the head entirely untouched by the tonsure.

But why is Simon Magus said to have been the author of this tonsure? [Col. 0331A] Who before Abbot Ceolfrid ever taught that the Magus had instituted a half-crown? At that time it was a very common belief among the English that this kind of tonsure had begun with him; but they themselves do not explain where they had obtained this claim. Perhaps they assert it for this reason: since they proclaimed Saint Peter the author of the Roman tonsure that they embraced, they traced the tonsure of peoples whom they hated, which differed from Peter’s, to Simon Magus, Saint Peter’s chief enemy, in order to express their abhorrence of the disagreement more strongly.

But no other reason is given for saying that the crown originated with Saint Peter than the celebrated opinion of Jerome, according to which each church places its older and blameless customs within the succession of apostolic traditions. When the antiquity of a custom is such that its beginnings have escaped human memory, the common people are easily led to believe that it originated with those from whom the churches everywhere claim to have received their own traditions. [Col. 0331B] Therefore, if Saint Peter was not the author of any tonsure, no reason can be given why Simon Magus, his enemy, should have instituted one different from Peter’s tonsure. It is more probable, however, as is shown by that ancient Book of Canons preserved by Usserius, that its author was a certain swineherd of King Loiger, son of Nil, as Patrick himself asserted in a certain sermon.

Besides this Simoniac tonsure and Peter’s tonsure, there was also another practice concerning the cutting of the hair in Ireland. For in the catalogue of the saints of Ireland published by the most reverend archbishop of Armagh (*ibid.*, p. 474), which is divided into three orders of saints, certain members of the third order are said to have had *caesaries*, apparently the same as the ancient tonsure, in place of a crown:

“They had different rules and Masses, and a different tonsure. For some had a crown, while others had *caesaries*”—according to the ancient custom of clerics, who were not permitted to grow their hair long, but were permitted to have *caesaries*, that is, hair cut to a prescribed length. [Col. 0331C]

Columbanus, an Irishman established in Gaul, preferred the tonsure of the Scots and their other rites, as appears from the Council of Mâcon held in 624 and summoned on account of Agrestius. Agrestius, moreover, as Jonas records in the *Life of Eustasius* (Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century II), babbling against the rule of blessed Columbanus, adds among his other calumnies that the hair of the head was cut differently, marked by a different character, and that this departed from the custom of everyone—clearly referring to the Scottish tonsure, which produced a half-crown. Eustasius gave adequate answers to Agrestius’s other calumnies; but to the charge concerning the tonsure, because he could not conceal the matter and perhaps thought that it could not be approved by others, he made no reply. After returning from the Council of Mâcon, however, in order to remove the scandal arising from the unusual tonsure and from other customs foreign to the Roman Church, he joined the rule of Saint Benedict with the institutions of Columbanus. Hence the author of the book *On the Life of Blessed [Col. 0331D] Saleberga* states that, under the government of Waldebert, who succeeded Eustasius shortly after the council, several monasteries were built according solely to the rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus; and Orderic Vitalis expressly associates Eustasius with Benedictine institutions, affirming that he received the Benedictine standard from blessed Maurus (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII).

That same Bede, who declares Peter to be the author of the Roman tonsure and Simon the author of the Scottish, says that the Greeks derived their tonsure from blessed Paul. For he relates that Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, left his monastery in the East, came to Rome, and was eventually chosen by the pope to be elevated to the archbishopric of Canterbury. Having first been ordained subdeacon, he waited four months “until his hair grew, so that it could be cut into a crown. For he had possessed the tonsure of the Apostle Saint Paul, according to the custom of the Easterners” (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, 1). But I have shown above that Paul instituted no tonsure. It is extremely probable [Col. 0332A] that this Eastern tonsure, for which they sought authority from Paul, belonged not to clerics but to monks, who cut the entire head more closely, leaving no circle of hair—the circle that constituted the clerical crown. This emerges, unless I am mistaken, from Bede’s words. Theodore had embraced the monastic way of life; but monks cut off all their hair, as was shown above, with no crown ever mentioned. Since Theodore waited four months until his hair grew so that it could be cut into a crown, it necessarily follows that his entire head had previously been shaved; and therefore it seems certain that he had possessed the monastic tonsure. Germanus of Constantinople likewise confirms abundantly in his *Theory of Ecclesiastical Matters* that monks were shorn over the whole head. And the pseudonymous Dionysius the Areopagite mentions ἀποκάρσεως (*apokárseōs*), that is, the cutting off of all the hair, as a mark impressed upon the monastic head, without which the monk’s consecration would not proceed.

[Col. 0332B]

It is also probable that the clerical tonsure among the Greeks was not circular. Although the aforementioned Germanus speaks of a crown worn by Easterners, it was nevertheless not received in every part of the East. Nor should *τοῦ κλήρου σχῆμα* in canon 21 of the Council in Trullo be understood as referring to a crown, but rather to the equal shaving of the entire head, as Salmasius has proved at greater length (*Epistle on the Cutting of Hair and Beard*, p. 449). Ratramnus also affirms that among Greek clerics it was customary not to shave the beard, but to uncover the entire head by cutting away its hair.

These, then, are all the matters concerning the origin, antiquity, and diversity of the clerical tonsure that I thought ought to be noted. Nor can I refrain from wondering at the obstinacy of both the English and the Scots, who fought so fiercely on both sides over a matter so indifferent. Ceolfrid testifies that he had never read in the Catholic Fathers that there had been any controversy about the difference of tonsures, and that the distinction of tonsure does no harm to those whose faith in God is pure and whose charity toward their neighbor [Col. 0332C] is sincere; yet the dispute over this matter, trifling though it was, exceeded almost every limit. In such matters, just as no one may depart from the judgment of the Catholic Church, so it is fitting that the pastors of the Church should moderate their authority in such a way that they do not rashly provoke weak minds, excessively attached to their own opinions, into secession.

## IX [Smith, XII]. On Ecclesiastical Chant

The most learned Cardinal Bona has shown so clearly in his book *On Divine Psalmody* that the beginnings of ecclesiastical chant came from the apostles and apostolic men that nothing can be added to his learning. We must now inquire what manner of singing the Anglo-Saxon Church followed. We read in Bede that Augustine and his companions, as they approached the city of Canterbury, sang a litany in harmonious voice (*Ecclesiastical History* I, 25, 2 [lacuna]); [Col. 0332D] and that afterward, in the church of Saint Martin, Augustine was accustomed not only to pray and celebrate Masses but also to sing psalms. In what manner did they sing, unless in that which the Roman Church had, from which these apostles of the English people were sent? That they spread this method of singing throughout Britain is evident from the fact that James the Deacon, left by Paulinus in the Church of York and highly skilled in ecclesiastical singing, is said to have been the teacher of ecclesiastical chant in that province, according to the Roman or Canterbury custom, for many people (*Ecclesiastical History* II, 20). From this it is clear that the Roman and Canterbury customs were the same.

Bede expressly testifies elsewhere that all the English Churches learned the tones of ecclesiastical singing from the Canterbury Church (*Ecclesiastical History* IV, 1). There he also relates that the first teacher of singing in the Churches of Northumbria, apart from James, was Aeddi, surnamed Stephen, who had been invited from Kent by the most reverend Wilfrid, bishop of York. Benedict Biscop [Col. 0333A], too, on returning from Rome, taught his own monastery, near the mouth of the River Wear, the order of singing, psalmody, and ministry in the church according to the custom of the Roman institution (*Ecclesiastical History* IV, 18). He had received this instruction from John, archcantor of the church of the blessed Apostle Peter and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, whom Pope Agatho had sent so that Benedict might bring him to Britain as the future teacher of his monastery. John did not teach only the brethren of that monastery; from nearly all the monasteries of the same province those skilled in singing flocked to hear him.

After Wilfrid, Acca, bishop of Hexham, summoned to himself and to his people an excellent singer named Maban, who had been taught the tones of singing in Kent by successors of the disciples of blessed Pope Gregory. He kept him for twelve years, so that Maban might teach the ecclesiastical songs unknown to them and, through his instruction, restore to their former condition those which had once been known but had begun to grow old through long use or neglect (*Ecclesiastical History* V, 20). It is therefore plainly inferred [Col. 0333B] that all the Churches of the Anglo-Saxons had been taught the custom of psalmody that flourished among the Cantware and the Romans.

As for this Roman custom of singing, who else can be called its author than that great Gregory himself, who sent Augustine to Britain to preach and who himself established the method of singing? John the Deacon relates that, following the example of Solomon and because of the piercing sweetness of music, Gregory, being most devoted to singers, usefully compiled a cento *Antiphonary*, moved by the compunction produced by musical sweetness, and established a school of singers, which to this day sings in the holy Roman Church according to the same institutions. Hence, during Gregory’s time, when Augustine was entering Britain, singers trained in the Roman institution were also scattered throughout the West and taught the barbarians with distinction (*Life of Gregory* II, 6). Therefore Gregory’s disciples learned his method of singing and transmitted it widely throughout the Churches of the English.

[Col. 0333C]

Saint Gregory the Great instituted plainchant, which proceeds plainly and measures each note by an equal duration of short time (Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, p. 431). He did not observe a concordant discord of various voices or a harmonious melody produced by the distance between intervals; rather, he established only fixed limits and boundaries for each tone, together with definite transitions and progressions of the voices according to the natural arrangement of the diatonic genus. Franchinus observes (*Book I, chapter 8*) that Saint Gregory strongly and freely urges the sleepy to keep watch in the nocturnal responsories; that in the antiphons he sings plainly and sweetly; that in the Introits he summons the people to the divine office as though with a herald’s voice; that in the Alleluia and its verses he rejoices sweetly in divine jubilation; that in the tracts and graduals he proceeds at length and humbly; and that in the offertories and communions he preserves a certain moderation.

[Col. 0333D]

John the Deacon complains that the Gauls and Germans mixed certain elements of their own with the Gregorian chants, and he gives the following explanation:

> “For Alpine bodies, resounding loudly with the thunder of their voices, do not properly reproduce the sweetness of the melody they have received. The barbarous harshness of their wine-soaked throats, while attempting to produce a gentle song through inflections and repetitions, hurls out rigid voices with a kind of natural roar, like wagons sounding confusedly over steps; thus it disturbs [Col. 0334A] the minds of its hearers by irritating and clamoring at them, when it ought to have soothed them” (*Life of Gregory* II, 6).

He then relates how Charlemagne restored the chant of the Churches of Gaul to the prescribed sweetness of Rome, two singers having been sent into Gaul for that purpose by the most holy Pope Adrian. Henry of Knighton, canon of Leicester, writes in book II of *The Events of England* that around the year 1072 there was a certain disgraceful abbot named Thurstan who, among the other absurdities of his folly, despised the Gregorian chant in the liturgy and began to compel the monks to practice the chant of a certain William, a monk of Fécamp. From this it is clear how reluctantly the Western Churches endured even the slightest alteration of the Gregorian chant.

## X [Smith, XIII]. On the Place Where Ceadualla, King of the Britons, Was Killed by King Oswald

[Col. 0334B] Camden and others who follow him believe that the name of the place which Bede calls *Denisesburna*, that is, “Denisi’s stream,” was corrupted through the fault of copyists and should be read *Devilesburne*. They find traces of this name in the present-day Dilston, which is called Devilston in old books. But all the manuscript codices, in unanimous agreement, clearly give not *Devilesburn* but *Denisesburn*. Bede also testifies (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 2) that the site of the victory itself, Hefenfelth, lay beside the Pictish Wall, toward the north; but the town of Dilston lies not only south of the Wall but also on the River Tyne.

At that very place King Oswald erected a cross; afterward a church was built there, in which the brothers of the Church of Hexham used to keep vigils for the salvation of Saint Oswald. Since both the cross and the church of Saint Oswald are found on the northern side of the Wall, it seems to follow that Hefenfelth and Denisesburn must also be sought there. Camden writes that the place once called Hefenfelth, or “the heavenly field,” is now called by the same meaning [Col. 0334C] Haledon. There is indeed a town named Hallington, situated two or three miles north of Oswald’s church and cross, and which, as Thomas Errington, Esquire, the owner of that estate, testifies, is called Haledown in an old charter.

There is, however, a tradition that the village of Bingfield was called Hefenfelth in ancient times. Bingfield lies between Hallington and the Wall and is separated from Hallington by a stream called Erringburn. Since it lies beside the Wall to the north, it agrees sufficiently with Bede’s description. Perhaps, however, the entire region lying between Hallington and the Wall was once marked by the name Hefenfelth because of this victory.

According to an old tradition, the battle was fought in the fields of Cockley, a place situated below the church and cross of Oswald and between Erringburn and the Wall; perhaps the battle began in the Cockley fields and was then maintained with the greatest intensity near Erringburn as far as the fields of Hallington. But whether the engagement took place in the fields [Col. 0334D] of Cockley, Hallington, or Bingfield, Erringburn appears to have been the stream of Denisi, or Denisesburn, where Ceadualla was killed. It lies beside the Pictish Wall and the cross of Saint Oswald, to the north, precisely where Bede teaches that it must be sought.

So famous was that cross of Saint Oswald that the Convent of Durham once used it on its seal. On one side of the seal the head of Saint Oswald was displayed, and on the other his cross; this will become clearer from the accompanying plate (see the following page).

[Col. 0335]

## X [Smith, XIV]. On the School Established by Sigberct, King of the East Angles

[Col. 0335A]

For a long time there has been a major controversy, not easily decided, among learned men concerning this school of Sigberct. Some defend it with all their might as having flourished through the renown of the liberal arts; others, with equal zeal and fervor, assert that it was merely a grammatical school in which boys were instructed in the vernacular. Those who pleaded the cause of the University of Cambridge, and who devoted much effort—not so much labor, as they themselves seemed to think, as official duty—to proving it older than the University of Oxford, took pains to celebrate the praise of this school with extraordinary elegance, dignity, and fullness of expression. They declared that the liberal disciplines had there been established, if not renewed, by a pious king nobly inspired by love of good letters and learned men, and had thereby been placed, as it were, in safety.

The Oxonians, however, to whom the antiquity of the University of Cambridge is so troublesome [Col. 0335B] that whatever age is granted to it they regard as taken away from their own, spitefully strive with every effort to weaken its reputation, which is supported by the approval of many learned men. They rightly perceive that Sigberct’s school preceded the Alfredian school by many years. Since, then, this very question is debated between the most celebrated academies of the literary world and on both sides among men distinguished by learning and talent, I would not have involved myself in a dispute so great and so difficult to settle had not a certain necessity of explaining our author Bede, more than my own inclination, compelled me. Forced, therefore, to set forth what I think about the matter, and so that it may become clearer on which side the truth lies, let us examine Bede’s own passage, which reads as follows:

> “At this time, after Earpwald, the successor of Redwald, Sigberct his brother ruled the kingdom of the East Angles. He was a good and religious man. Long before, while living in exile in Gaul to escape the hostility of Redwald, [Col. 0335C] he had received the bath of baptism. After returning to his homeland and gaining possession of the kingdom, he soon wished to imitate the things he had seen well ordered in Gaul and established a school in which boys might be instructed in letters, aided by Bishop Felix, whom he had received from Kent and who supplied them with pedagogues and teachers according to the custom of the Cantware.”

[Col. 0336A] But are these words merely describing an ordinary school, where, apart from certain instructions shaping boys toward religion and virtue—which could also be given in the native language—we must admit that nothing else flourished? (*Antiquities of Oxford*, p. 35.) The most wise king plainly modeled his school on the standard of the schools in Gaul and appointed over it teachers like those placed in charge of the Canterbury schools.

Nothing, however, is more clearly established than that Gaul had always been filled with celebrated schools and teachers outstanding in the knowledge of the liberal disciplines. Jerome testifies that Gaul had always abounded in eloquent men and those learned in civil law (*Against Vigilantius*), and Juvenal testifies that it once supplied our countrymen with teachers of eloquence:

> “Eloquent Gaul taught the Britons to plead.”

Antoninus, also surnamed Pius, “bestowed both honors and salaries upon rhetoricians and philosophers throughout all the provinces, and therefore throughout Gaul” (Julius Capitolinus, *Life of Antoninus Pius*). Tacitus, speaking of Augustodunum (*Annals* III, 43), says that it was “the most noble offspring of Gaul, engaged there in liberal studies.” When that city was besieged by the brigandage of the Bagaudae rebellion and struck by the gravest disaster, [Col. 0336B] “that ancient seat of letters, the Maenian schools” (Eumenius, *On the Restoration of the Schools*), once distinguished by its splendid buildings and the number of its students, was destroyed by barbarian fury. Constantius, however, seeing “the most honorable youth of Gaul there trained in the liberal arts,” restored it to its former glory.

No less remarkable was the contest of Greek and Latin eloquence at the altar of Lugdunum; and Pliny notes (*Letters* IX, 11): “I had not thought there were booksellers at Lugdunum.” From this it is rightly inferred that under the early emperors this city flourished most abundantly in every kind of learning. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in his *Life of Maiolus*, calls the city of Lugdunum “the nurse and mother of philosophy, which, according to the ancient custom and ecclesiastical law of all Gaul, not undeservedly retains the citadel.” In the same author’s *Life of Adalheidis Augustus* we read: “All Burgundy rejoiced at his arrival; Lugdunum, once the mother and nurse of philosophy, exulted.” And in the *Book of Miracles [Col. 0336C] of Saint Aigulf, Abbot of Lérins*, who flourished in the age of Sigberct, we read that “a certain cleric said that he was a canon of the Church of Lugdunum and had come from the schools” (Mabillon, century II, p. 669).

Quintus Symmachus, too, who in the time of Valentinian and Theodosius surpassed the other men of his age in alert intelligence and genuine eloquence, admits (*Letters* IX, 88) that “whatever there is in him he owes to the Gallic sky; that, as an old pupil of the Garonne, he had imbibed the precepts of rhetoric into his breast; and that he had, through a learned teacher, a proper kinship with the schools of Gaul.”

[Col. 0337A] I pass over the schools of Massilia, most distinguished for antiquity and renown, and those highly learned professors (Ausonius, *Professors*) who were placed in charge of teaching the young at Narbonne, Toulouse, Bordeaux, and among the Pictones, as well as the municipal school at Vesontio (Ausonius, *Gratiarum Actio to Gratianus*). I also pass over what Jerome writes to the monk Rusticus concerning the studies of Gaul, which at that time were extremely celebrated, because the meaning of this passage is still disputed with great force and persistence between the patrons of the two academies.

I proceed to the Constitution of Gratian (*Theodosian Code* XIII, 3, 11), in which it is prescribed:

> “In each of the cities called metropolitan, let the very best men preside over the education of the young—namely, rhetoricians and grammarians learned in Attic and Roman doctrine.”

When we hear the word “grammarians,” however, we must not understand teachers of elementary letters. Their boundaries, rather, extended so widely that they embraced within their scope almost everything belonging to humane [Col. 0337B] learning; indeed, Ausonius calls certain Latin grammarians of Bordeaux philologists. Thus, in Gratian’s time, each archiepiscopal city in Gaul, and [Note: [Col. 0337] Some others: Augustodunum, Toulouse, Poitiers, Massilia.] some of the more distinguished cities even if they were not metropolises, had public professors. “Hence,” as Hospinianus observes concerning this law (*On Temples*, p. 419), “the study of the liberal arts and languages soon began to flourish there to such an extent that Saint Jerome, in a certain letter to Rusticus, called Gaul most flourishing in studies.”

As long, therefore, as Gaul was subject to Roman rule, it excelled in keen intellects, liberal studies, and the finest learning. But when barbarian nations burst in and for a long period devastated nearly all Europe with sword and flame, the face of affairs was so altered that both the arts and religion suffered the greatest loss. Although, while the fury of war raged everywhere, learning began everywhere to grow cold and collapse, it was not utterly trampled underfoot. [Col. 0337C] The Christian faith, though long and greatly harassed in Gaul by the invasions of the impious, always remained vigorous, and bishops educated at least in Latin letters always adorned the Gallican Church. It could not have happened that all learning and knowledge of the arts were completely extinguished while religion survived. Hence it does not seem far removed from the truth to suppose that the bishops of Gaul continued to observe, though without the abundant usefulness and benefit that had been possible under the favorable rule of the Romans, the wise system for educating the young that had once been established by the emperor Gratian, to the extent that they were able.

But after the kings of the Franks abandoned the worship of idols and joined themselves to the holy Church of Christ, and the arts and true religion likewise re-emerged, you will find clear traces of this custom in the historians of those times. Gregory of Tours was devoted to literary studies under Bishop Gallus (*Life of Gregory of Tours* in his works). Gregory the Great sharply rebuked Desiderius [Col. 0337D] of Vienne because he had taught grammar and studied secular letters (John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory* III, 33). Saint Germanus, abbot of Grandval, was also entrusted to Saint Modoaldus, bishop of Trier, who, recognizing the boy’s keen intelligence, instructed him in the liberal letters (Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, century II, p. 511).

Furthermore, the priests Cyprian and Messianus, together with the Deacon Stephen, who wrote the life, deeds, virtues, and miracles of Saint Caesarius of Arles, were disciples of that same Caesarius. Frodobert, abbot of Celle near the city of Troyes, was devoted, through his parents’ care, to the schools of Bishop Ragnesilus. Leodegarius, bishop of Augustodunum, was diligently nurtured by Dido of Poitiers and was thoroughly polished in every respect by the discipline of various studies in which the powerful of the world customarily took delight (ibid., p. 681). Finally, Praejectus, [Col. 0338A] bishop of Auvergne, was educated in letters at the school of the bishop of Issoire (ibid., p. 646).

But through the various storms of war that afflicted Gaul in the eighth century, since leisure and tranquility—friends of the Muses—had been taken away, the study of letters languished everywhere, until Charlemagne revived it once more and worked energetically to restore the public schools that had been established from ancient times in the episcopal cities. For this reason he sent a general letter to metropolitans, bishops, abbots, and others, so that “bishoprics and monasteries, in addition to the order of regular life, might devote effort to teaching through the study of letters.” Accordingly, the bishops and abbots assembled at the Second Council of Chalon, following the command of this most wise emperor, decreed: “They ought to establish schools in which both the skill of letters and discipline, and the instruction of Sacred Scripture, may be learned.”

His son, the emperor Louis Augustus, took the same care, as is evident [Col. 0338B] both from his *Life* and from the Second Council of Paris, as well as from Wandalbert, a monk of Prüm, in the preface to his *Life of Saint Goar*. There he writes that the study of letters had lain dormant in Gaul for many years, until, in his own time, through the generosity of princes and the diligence of excellent men, the study of the disciplines advanced.

Pope Eugene II and Pope Leo IV likewise established this in two councils held at Rome, the latter confirming the canons of the former. The canon relevant to this matter reads as follows:

> “It is reported to us concerning certain places that neither teachers nor care for the study of letters are to be found. Therefore, in all bishoprics and in the parishes subject to them, and in other places where necessity arises, every care and diligence must be taken that teachers and instructors be appointed who, possessing the studies of letters and the liberal arts together with the sacred doctrines, may teach them continually, because through these things the divine commandments are especially manifested and explained.”

A similar decree was also confirmed at the Third Council of Valence, held by order of the emperor Lothair in the case of Bishop Valentinus [Col. 0338C]. From these things it is clear that nothing was prescribed in the synods mentioned above that had not been instituted in ancient times, and that the schools in the individual bishoprics were not newly erected by these princes and prelates, but rather restored to their former splendor through their generosity and counsels.

Schools existed not only beside churches adorned with an episcopal see; in monasteries, too, the young were instructed in piety, religion, and good letters. How many great men, lights not merely of the Gallican Church but of the Catholic Church, were trained under the discipline and care of the men of Lérins? For as long as the praise and honor of Lupus of Troyes, Honoratus and Hilary of Arles, Maximus of Riez, Eucherius of Lugdunum, and Vincent of Lérins—which I believe will be perpetual and everlasting—are celebrated by both the Christian and literary commonwealth, so long will the fame and glory of that most illustrious monastery remain on the lips of all the most learned.

Illtud, too, a Briton by nation and one [Col. 0338D] of the disciples of Saint Germanus, taught geometry, rhetoric, grammar, and arithmetic in his monastery and was highly skilled in every art. From his school men of singular learning and remarkable knowledge went forth into Gaul, among them especially Gildas, abbot of Rhuys; Samson and Maglorius, bishops of Dol; and Paul, bishop of the Osismii. In the monasteries they founded, they undoubtedly established the same studies for cultivation that they had learned from their master.

Saint Columbanus, born in Ireland and instructed there in the liberal studies, later devoting himself to the practice of regular discipline in the monastery of Bangor, crossed into Gaul with twelve brothers. After founding two monasteries, he inflamed the minds of the Franks with such enthusiasm for knowledge of the liberal arts that within a short time his school at Luxeuil grew through the enormous number and multitude of its students (ibid., p. 8). [Col. 0339A] Under Eustasius, the teacher who succeeded Columbanus in governing the monastery of Luxeuil, very many were so well formed in moral purity and the liberal arts that, commended by the integrity of their lives and the reputation of their learning, they were elected abbots and bishops (ibid., p. 118).

Nor did Saint Benedict establish the foundations of his order at Subiaco before undertaking the education of boys. Maurus and Placidus, boys of senatorial family, together with others whom he educated from their earliest years, are witnesses to this; he instructed them in piety and literary studies. Maurus, coming to Gaul, built a monastery near Orléans, where many boys of noble birth were imbued with every kind of learning by him and by other teachers. Through his efforts, too, the rule of Benedict was introduced into Gaul, and monasteries began to arise everywhere in which humane letters and all the disciplines were taught. Finally, the schools of the Benedictines flourished so greatly that very many men distinguished not only for holiness of life but also for excellence in every field of study were raised to the [Col. 0339B] pontifical dignity.

Perhaps there were also other places in Gaul, apart from bishoprics and monasteries, in which every branch of learning flourished in the time of Sigberct. Apart from the fact that other places are mentioned in the two Roman councils referred to above, some people seem to have learned good letters elsewhere than in episcopal and monastic schools. We know that some were educated at the royal court and adorned with the disciplines by which the children of nobles ought to be instructed. We also read that others were entrusted to highly approved teachers to be imbued with the liberal disciplines, although it is not clear that they acquired this knowledge in bishoprics or monasteries.

Having shown, therefore, that Gaul plainly possessed schools for Sigberct to imitate—schools in which young men were polished in more refined letters and formed by the precepts of philosophy—we must next inquire what the school of the Cantware was like. [Col. 0339C] That among the Cantware, as in Gaul, young men devoted their greatest care to the pursuit and acquisition of these same arts is clear from this very passage of Bede. This provides no slight argument that the school established in Kent was likewise, as were those in Gaul, a home of the liberal arts.

This is also confirmed by the fact that Saint Livinus had Saint Augustine, the first bishop of Canterbury, as his instructor for five years, and, having been successfully educated by him in both sacred and humane letters, received from him the rank of priest (ibid., p. 455). Gotselinus likewise testifies in the *Life of Saint Augustine* that King Æthelberht founded bishoprics and monasteries, plainly for this purpose: that learned men sent by Gregory to Britain might teach letters there and instruct the English who had been converted to the faith of Christ in every ecclesiastical duty.

Thus, although at the beginnings of this Church its ecclesiastical offices necessarily had to be performed by foreigners, after the disciples of Saint Gregory had died, men were found among our own people who could be honored with episcopal [Col. 0339D] dignity and a see. “For when Paulinus of Rochester had departed this life, Archbishop Honorius ordained Ithamar in his place, a man indeed born of the people of Kent, but equal to his predecessors in life and learning. In him, as far as life was concerned, you would desire nothing of perfect holiness, and as far as knowledge was concerned, nothing of Roman refinement.
