Thus, he was the first Englishman in his homeland to bear the grace of pontifical honor, and he added a certain dignity to his countrymen” (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 14).

After Ithamar’s death, Deusdedit consecrated Damian (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 20), who was born of the race of the South Saxons. When the bishopric had remained vacant for a long time after Damian’s death, Theodore ordained Putta, who had been trained by disciples of blessed Pope Gregory both in ecclesiastical disciplines and in the art of singing according to the Roman custom. When Thomas, bishop of the East Angles, also died (ibid.), Honorius substituted in his place Berctgils, surnamed Boniface, from the province of Kent.

[Col. 0340A]

After Honorius had completed the course of his life, Deusdedit, from the people of the West Saxons, was elected archbishop of the Canterbury see. When he departed from this world, Kings Oswiu and Ecgberht, with the consent of the Church, appointed a good man and a priest suitable for the episcopate, named Wighard (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 29). He had been sufficiently instructed in every ecclesiastical discipline at Canterbury in Kent by the Roman disciples of blessed Pope Gregory—at Canterbury, that is, a city which, as Leland writes, then presented the appearance of a university. Finally, Erkenwald, bishop of London under Theodore the archbishop, was a disciple of the blessed pontiff Mellitus (Leland, *Collectanea*, vol. I, p. 20). From these examples it is proved clearly and abundantly that, before Archbishop Theodore, the Cantware had devoted the greatest care to the education of the young.

Nor is the mention made by our Bede of numerous books [Col. 0340B] an inadequate argument for this matter (*Ecclesiastical History* I, 29). After Gregory had heard how successfully everything had turned out in England, he sent them to Augustine so that the Saxon people might devote themselves to the study of every branch of learning. Benedict Biscop later imitated him and enriched his own monastery with a great abundance of books, acquired through the repeated journeys he made to Rome for that purpose. If we may conjecture about the books Gregory sent from those that Benedict brought back with him from Rome, they certainly embraced all the liberal arts and the most refined branches of learning. For Bede himself was nobly educated in this monastery, spending almost all his time reading the books that Benedict had collected from everywhere, and instructing himself in every discipline. Nor is it indeed likely that Benedict was more diligent in caring for his private monastery than Gregory was in caring for the entire Saxon Church.

Indeed, in many places beyond Kent the English youth devoted themselves to studies of letters and humane learning. When Aidan, a Scot by nation, was summoned to England [Col. 0340C] so that through his teaching and ministry the Northumbrian people might receive the grace of the Christian faith, King Oswald granted him “possessions and territories for the establishment of monasteries, and Scottish teachers instructed English children, together with their elders, in studies and in the observance of regular discipline” (Ecclesiastical History III, 3). From Aidan’s famous school emerged men of the greatest distinction, flourishing both in reputation for learning and in renown, whose teaching and industry yielded the richest fruits both to the ecclesiastical and to the literary commonwealth. Nor was the monastic school of the holy Hilda at Streaneshalch less deserving of the Church (Ecclesiastical History IV, 23), whose principal glory was that from it not a few were raised to the highest summit of ecclesiastical honor. If in other schools of our Britain the youth were cultivated in every branch of learning, there can be no room for doubt that the arts flourished most intensely at the seat of power above all others in the British world. Nor is this obscurely noted by the historians. For “after Saint Wilfrid had spent several years among the Lindisfarnians, he stayed for some time among the people of Kent, while Honorius held the rank of archbishop, and diligently applied himself to learning the things that he observed” (Ecclesiastical History V, 19). And “Oftfor, after devoting himself to reading and observing the Scriptures in both monasteries of the abbess Hilda, at length, desiring more advanced studies, came to Kent to the archbishop Theodore” (Ecclesiastical History IV, 23). From this it is abundantly clear that the Kentish school surpassed all others by far, at least in theological studies. Since, however, all other studies in those times were directed toward theology, and the more humane letters and liberal arts prepared the way for it—as Bede’s own books prove, embracing the whole compass of the liberal disciplines—it follows that the academy of the people of Kent must also have surpassed the others in the teaching of the arts.

The school therefore established at Canterbury was already sufficiently renowned even before Theodore became archbishop (Ecclesiastical History IV, 2). But when that most learned prelate [Col. 0341A] arrived in Britain with the abbot Hadrian, he made it far greater and more illustrious. “And because both were abundantly instructed in sacred and secular letters, gathering a company of students, they daily poured forth streams of saving knowledge to water their hearts, so that they also imparted to their pupils, amid the volumes of the sacred writings, the disciplines of metrical art, astronomy, and ecclesiastical arithmetic.” Their students were so learned that they knew the Latin and Greek languages equally as well as their own native tongue. Among them was Albinus, who succeeded Hadrian in the governance of the monastery (Ecclesiastical History V, 20), and Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne.

These considerations therefore plainly establish that both Gaul and Kent had long been renowned for their cultivation of the arts as well as of theology. Since two very learned men among the Oxford scholars, both of whom rendered the greatest service to antiquarian studies—one in his splendid History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford, the other in his choice Annotations with which he illustrated the Life of the great Alfred, written by the learned knight John Spelman and recently edited by himself—have, through their hostility toward the Sigberctine school, devoted much labor and diligence to overturning its renown, the nature of my undertaking requires that, if I have anything with which to answer their arguments, I should once again bring it forward.

Fuller, however, in the History of the British Church which he published in London, makes it sufficiently clear that, at least in his own judgment, the liberal arts flourished greatly among the Gauls, citing these words of Saint Jerome to the monk Rusticus: “I hear that you have a religious mother, who nourished you, who educated you as a child, and after the studies of Gaul—which are exceedingly flourishing—sent you to Rome, sparing no expense and enduring the absence of her son in hope of the future, so that Roman gravity might season the richness and polish of Gallic eloquence.”

Yet these most learned men [Col. 0341C] think that “nothing more can be gathered from this than that the monk was well instructed in the vernacular language, perhaps under the direction of a Gallic teacher and only in a grammatical school, and that at his mother’s urging he went to Rome to polish his intellect with arts suited to a man—that is, academic studies. This undertaking, they say, would not have been necessary if a university had already flourished in Gaul at that time” (Antiquities of Oxford, p. 35).

Nevertheless, if they cannot free themselves by any device or subtle interpretation from what we noted above concerning the schools of Gaul, they must do the greatest violence to the words of blessed Jerome. That most eloquent Father certainly means nothing other than that Rusticus’s mother sent him to Rome as though to the most distinguished academy in the whole Roman Empire. Young men from every province flocked there for the sake of study. Thus from Africa, although “there too were schools of the liberal arts, there were workshops of philosophers, and finally gymnasia of every kind, whether of languages or of morals” (Salvian, On the Government of God, book VII), the youth nevertheless went, eager to learn, to the teachers of the most powerful city. And although Africa had long been known as the nurse of advocates, “Saint Augustine proceeded to Rome in order to learn law” (Book VI of the Confessions, chapter 8). In the same way, scholars from Gaul travelled there in eager competition to study law.

Thus Paulinus of Nola (see his Life published together with his works) had Ausonius as his teacher at Bordeaux, under whom he made astonishing progress in poetic and rhetorical studies. But when Ausonius was summoned by Valentinian to court to oversee the studies of Gratian, his son, Paulinus left Bordeaux, went to Rome, and there practiced forensic advocacy with great success. Rutilius Namatianus likewise, speaking of a certain Gaul named Palladius (Journey I, lines 207–208), writes:

> An eloquent young man, recently sent from the fields of Gaul,  
> To learn the laws of the Roman forum.

And Saint Germanus (see his Life written by Constantius), [Col. 0342A] “so that a full course of literary study might flow toward him, after the Gallic lecture halls, within the city of Rome he added knowledge of law to the fullness of his perfection.” Likewise Quintus Symmachus, who as a young man devoted himself to learning eloquence among the Gauls, later writes that “in the dwelling-place of Latin eloquence he languished in leisure and study” (Book VIII, Letter 68).

Rusticus, therefore, following the custom of those times, went to Rome—not because the schools of Gaul were not exceedingly flourishing in the study of good letters, but so that he might season with the elegance and gravity innate in Roman minds the eloquence with which he had been imbued among his own people; so that he might dry up Gallic abundance with Roman salt, and adorn himself with the knowledge of law, which at that time flourished especially at Rome.

Finally, to make still clearer what sort of schools existed among the Gauls in Jerome’s century, it is evident that in those days Salonius (Eucherius of Lyon, Letter to Salonius, and Gennadius, Catalogue of Illustrious Men, under Salvian) and Veranus, on the island of Lérins under the teachers Honoratus and Hilary, were first nurtured and then [Col. 0342B] completed by the most learned men Salvian and Vincentius, who, instructed in both human and divine literature, excelled equally in eloquence and in the other studies. At the same time Sidonius Apollinaris (see his Life written by Savaron), a native of Auvergne, was entrusted to the celebrated schoolmasters Eusebius and Oenus. Under them he earnestly devoted himself to Greek and Latin letters; at length he gave himself wholly to philosophy, mathematics, and jurisprudence, by which studies he became more learned than others.

He also praises Hecticius, a nobleman of Auvergne (Sidonius Apollinaris, book III, letter 3), because “on account of the charm of his boyhood, studies of letters streamed toward Auvergne from every people”; and because to him was owed the fact that “the nobility, about to lay aside the scurf of Celtic speech, was now being imbued sometimes with oratorical style and sometimes even with poetic measures.” In the same manner Sidonius writes to a certain Asper, whose mother was from Auvergne (Letter 21, book IV):

> Here the flourishing studies of grammarians and rhetoricians, vying in counsel, fostered you while you were being imbued with the liberal disciplines; hence you did not emerge so moderately instructed that you could fail to love the people of Auvergne even on account of their letters.

Saint Remigius, too, was bishop of Reims and a man “of outstanding learning” (Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, book II), and among his own people he was “especially well instructed in rhetorical studies.” Finally, we read (Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines, in the Life of Caesarius of Arles) that Julianus Pomerius, a Moor by birth, went to Gaul and opened a school of rhetoric in the city of Arles.

Therefore, although—to avoid quibbling over the word—a university in the proper sense, consisting of four faculties and conferring fixed degrees of honor upon the learned according to solemn ritual, did not flourish in the age of blessed Jerome, there nevertheless certainly existed academies or schools in which the liberal studies were cultivated.

I hope, then, that in defending the schools of Gaul I have now fully discharged my obligation. What remains is to vindicate the distinguished academy of the people of Kent from the objections of the Oxford scholars. Fuller shows that Sigberct conformed his school in every respect to the model of the Kentish school. On the contrary, that most celebrated Oxford historian asserts (Antiquities of Oxford, p. 35) that Bede spoke nothing about the city of Canterbury itself, but “about the whole province,” in accordance with the custom of “having the people of Kent.” Let the Oxford scholars prove, if they can, that throughout his entire ecclesiastical work our author ever understood this expression to mean the whole province.

Moreover, it is highly probable that the province of Kent, in Sigberct’s time, was confined within the modest boundaries of the kingdom of Kent. For although the archbishops of Canterbury claimed metropolitan authority over other regions, it is nevertheless certain that none of them possessed so extensive a power with full authority before Theodore. But to answer this trivial objection fully, it is clear from this passage of Bede that “the people of Kent” must be understood either of Canterbury itself or, at most, of that diocese. For it is said that Sigberct was assisted by Bishop “Felix, whom he had received from Kent.”

That distinguished antiquary supplies no reason why we should suppose that the man who had come from Kent provided teachers according to some custom of the entire province of Kent, rather than according to what he had seen practiced in Kent, especially since nowhere, when noting praiseworthy customs of the people of Kent, had he stayed anywhere except at Canterbury with Archbishop Honorius (Ecclesiastical History II, 15). For after he had come from the regions of Burgundy to the archbishop and had declared his desire to him, he was certainly sent from Canterbury, the seat of Honorius, to preach the word of life to the East Angles.

At length the Oxford orator, thanks to his notably easy and generous disposition toward his opponents, deigned to concede that Bede “understood the custom of the people of Kent, and that Sigberct followed in their footsteps”; yet he vigorously contends that, “if we listen to all the writers, we must admit that, apart from an ordinary elementary school and certain instructions forming boys in religion, which were also customarily conveyed in the vernacular language, nothing else flourished there.”

I had not thought that anyone would be so bold and reckless as to appeal to all writers concerning the truth of some matter, while being unable to cite even one of them as a witness who supports his assertion. Since, therefore, what is freely asserted can be answered by a simple denial without danger, let the Oxford scholars either admit that no writers at all support them, or finally confirm their wholly denied assertion by some authority of witnesses.

The Oxford scholar continues in his usual manner, and, with a sufficiently arrogant and censorious style, calls Fuller, who reports that under Theodore, while he was seated among the people of Kent, lectures in geometry, arithmetic, and music were held at Canterbury according to Bede, “a most wicked falsifier.” But, my good sir, your mind is more agitated than is proper and seems almost to have lost both consistency and sanity. Is there nothing—“not even the slightest thing”—in Bede concerning the place where that Theodore and Hadrian opened schools? Does he not, in that very chapter in which Bede speaks of their school (Ecclesiastical History IV, 2), state most plainly [Col. 0343C] that ecclesiastical music had been known and celebrated in Kent up to that point—that is, from the time of the disciples of blessed Pope Gregory down to Theodore?

Once this is granted, is it believable that that most learned archbishop—who unquestionably not only protected the liberal sciences but wherever he found them established made them more flourishing—would, upon his arrival, have expelled from Kent, from his own Church and see, the art of music and the other disciplines in which we have proved above that youths trained by Gregory’s disciples in Kent were instructed? That would be the action of a barbarian, uncultivated and ignorant man—not of the wisest man, not of Theodore.

If, then, there was in Kent a school that was the home of the liberal disciplines, where shall we place it more suitably than at Canterbury, where Theodore had his archiepiscopal chair and Hadrian was in charge of the monastery, in which he could live appropriately with his companions and devote himself to the education of the youth with the greatest care? Finally, Bede himself, in his preface to his History, to remove every doubt about this matter completely, expressly testifies that “Albinus, a most reverend abbot and in every respect most learned man, was instructed in the Church of Canterbury by Theodore, archbishop of blessed memory, and by Hadrian, the abbot—venerable and most learned men.”

And above we showed from Bede that Oftfor, desiring more advanced studies, came to Kent to Archbishop Theodore. Berctuald, too (Leland, On Writers, under Berthowald), later archbishop, left the monastery at Glastonbury and moved to Kent with the same purpose as the rest of the noble Saxons, who flocked to Theodore and Hadrian as to the very fountains of good letters, with immense and ardent zeal for learning. He also had Aldhelm as his companion (William of Malmesbury, On the Bishops, book V), and studied letters together with him. Tobias, bishop of Rochester, was also educated at Canterbury among the people of Kent (Leland, under Tobias), and made use of these teachers, who were learned in every field.

William of Malmesbury likewise writes about Saint Aldhelm [Col. 0344A] that his parent entrusted his son for instruction in the first elements not to the school of some undistinguished teacher, but to Abbot Hadrian of Saint Augustine’s. “When he had grown somewhat older and had returned from Kent to the West Saxons, he added the liberal arts to the fullness of his knowledge at the monastery of Malmesbury; yet, in order that he might imbibe them to the marrow, he studied again in Kent at the feet of Hadrian.”

We therefore see that Theodore taught young men in his Church, and that Hadrian’s disciples in Kent studied at Hadrian’s feet, certainly in the school of the monastery of blessed Peter, over which the abbot of Canterbury presided, and that he was more learned in letters than almost all the learned men of his age. Let the Oxford scholars themselves judge upon whom that infamous mark of “falsifier” ought to be branded, with which Fuller is most unjustly stigmatized by their excessively angry and peevish orator.

For this reason it seems in no way appropriate to attribute to Greekeslada the glory of saying, on the authority of some anonymous writer, that Theodore once lectured there. Since we have shown above, from writers of unquestionable authority, that the English people had Theodore as their teacher in Kent, we have no regard for some uncertain author without a name, weight, or credibility. Nor does the account agree sufficiently even with those who praise him, for it differs in both person and time, asserting that Greekeslada was so named from the discipline of Theodore as its instructor, whereas in reality Theodore, as Twynus indeed asserts, came only as a restorer to those schools (Book II, section 8).

If the Oxford scholars hope, by means of what this anonymous writer wrote about Theodore holding schools at Greekeslade, to add any support to their cause, let them defend the whole of his testimony as genuine; for there is no reason why we should listen to a witness who mixes truth with falsehood. I do not think, however, that they will do so, lest they be forced to admit that the schools at Greeklade, established by Theodore, were later than the Sigberctine school.

The Oxford scholars object again that Bede calls the people for whose benefit Sigberct established the school “boys”—that is, such as had not yet withdrawn their hands from the schoolmaster’s rod—and that it is entirely clear from this that they did not assemble as academics, since he says that pedagogues were appointed over them. Who does not know that the word “pedagogues” applies to little boys who have not yet escaped rods and lashes? (Antiquities of Oxford, p. 39.)

But the objection made here is so slight, so foolish, that it seems scarcely worthy of any answer. I would say nothing more at all, were it not demanded by their triumphalism and unprecedented insolence. Who, however, would say that that distinguished Oxford antiquary did not know that both adolescents and boys properly so called, and even infants, are included under the name “boys,” especially among monastic authors? If anyone dared to say this, he would certainly pierce him with a heavier weapon than grammatical subtlety (ibid.).

That boys, indeed even infants, are to be understood in this sense can be demonstrated by the testimony of several authors who flourished in Bede’s age. How many people called boys do we read of as engaged both in philosophical and in theological studies? [Col. 0344D] It is well known that when Bishop Modoaldus saw Germanus, abbot of Grandval, to be a boy of acute intelligence, he instructed him in the liberal letters (Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines, century II, p. 511). Bishop Uulframnus of Sens, too, “when he was still in boyhood, was handed over to Catholic teachers to be imbued with the study of sacred letters; and throughout the whole period of his boyhood and adolescence, continuing his efforts up to manhood, he did not turn his mind away from this purpose” (ibid., century III, part I). Bercharius, too, after being instructed in the disciplines, is called a boy (ibid., century II, p. 833). Theodore of Canterbury likewise writes in his Capitula that the infants of the monastery should eat meat for fourteen years.

Similarly, in the Statutes of the Order of Saint Benedict, in Acher’s Spicilegium:

> We establish that infants who are received into monasteries should daily hear the Rule expounded and should not leave school until they have reached the legitimate age; then they should make profession and receive the blessing according to the form of the Rule.

These same persons are called “boys of the monastery” in Theodore, where the boys of the monastery are forbidden to be ordained before the age of twenty-five. Finally, Bede himself, as a very young child, was imbued with both sacred and secular learning (in his Life).

We have therefore shown, by no contemptible abundance of witnesses, that boys and even infants were formerly trained in the liberal disciplines. It is now necessary to correct their great dispute about pedagogues. Here, since the objection is so inept that it calls for no more extended or detailed investigation, it will be enough to say that *paedagogare* means the same as “to teach” (Surius, in the Life of Saints Severinus and Victorinus, no. 2), and that teachers of the liberal arts were also called pedagogues.

[Note: [Col. 0345] “Pedagogues.” Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines, century II, p. 517. “To the pedagogues of the liberal arts.” Ibid., p. 790.]

Our position is made entirely firm by the royal translator of Bede’s History, who rendered the word *pueri* as *geonge menn* and *paedagogos* as *lareowas*. The Oxford scholar now has nothing to offer except abuse. He calls the translator ignorant and declares, with complete authority, that the translation from the Latin exemplar was made with extreme incompetence and, given the blindness of that age, with sheer dull-wittedness [Col. 0345B]. See now how grateful the Oxford scholars are to the most learned founder of their academy! If only they can diminish the reputation of the University of Cambridge and weaken the glory of its antiquity, they are not ashamed to be liars, slanderers, and ingrates.

The most illustrious King Alfred was certainly neither so crude and barbarous nor so ignorant of the Latin language that he could not have made that Saxon translation accurately and learnedly. He had been educated with the greatest liberality; he knew the best Latin authors not merely in order to understand them, but also in order to translate and imitate them. In those times he was considered especially learned: a grammarian, orator, philosopher, historian, musician, prince of Saxon poetry, and also highly skilled in architecture and geometry. His translations were so solid, so elegant, and so vividly expressive that they delighted their readers in a remarkable fashion.

As for this particular translation, the most learned king rendered it word for word with such discernment and fidelity that he preserved perfectly even the precise force of every little word. In the words of the outstanding and universally learned Hickes—who himself knew Saxon literature exceptionally well and restored it to us, if not after many centuries of loss, at least after the most grievous neglect—nothing, I say, can be considered more perfect than the royal translations:

> “Good God! How native, easy, and simple is the language in them, especially in the paraphrase of Bede’s Ecclesiastical History! If you consider its most august author, whether the purity of its diction, the clarity of its style, or that marvelous vividness by which it places every event almost before the eyes of the reader, you will judge him equal to Caesar in expression” (Preface to the first edition of *A Saxon Grammar*, p. 12).

Nothing, therefore, appears honorable, modest, or decent in the Oxford historian. And since he has pursued the royal translator with such illiberal insults, he must either never have read his translation, or not read it completely, or at least have understood it most poorly.

But what if the word *paedagogos* is understood here in the sense the Oxford scholars wish? It must indeed be admitted that in the same schools which became famous for more advanced sciences, many devoted themselves from earliest childhood to learning the first rudiments of grammar, until they became capable of higher learning. For this reason perhaps our Bede mentioned both pedagogues, who taught the boys their first letters, and teachers, who instructed them in liberal studies.

Even if, then, we concede that the boys were handed over to teachers of the sort who ordinarily preside over grammar schools, since it nevertheless follows from Bede that teachers also presided in Sigberct’s school over the education of the youth, I do not see how this concession either benefits the Oxford cause or harms the people of Cambridge. The greatest credibility is lent to this conjecture by the similar method of educating boys among the people of Kent. We showed above that Saint Aldhelm learned his first letters among them and was later trained in every branch of learning.

Fuller continues, and, in order to prove that boys were capable of the arts and sciences, summons Asser of Menevia, who calls the scholars whom Alfred nurtured at Oxford “boys.” Here the most distinguished antiquary makes a remarkable reply (Antiquities of Oxford, p. 40). He demands to know from Fuller in what manuscript he found that word used of boys; he says that, among many other copies, he consulted those of Parker and Camden, and that the word appeared in none of them. He therefore again brands Fuller as a falsifier, and even dares to concede that boys—and not merely boys, but infants—studied at Oxford in ancient times, provided that this is confirmed by the testimony of Asser and by the words of some copy, however mutilated and fleeting, so long as it is not interpolated.

Take care, good sir, lest you be compelled, against your will, to fulfill what you have promised with so wide-open a mouth. What if I should show from your Cambdenian copy of Asser that infants themselves studied in Alfred’s school? Then surely the Oxford scholars must admit that their orator devoted himself above all to producing something that would make him ridiculous; for in this matter he has produced nothing that is not laughable.

Let us therefore hear Asser:

> “Aethelweard, the youngest of all, was handed over to the discipline of the literary school, by divine providence and the king’s admirable foresight, together with almost all the noble infants of the entire region, and also many of humble birth, under the diligent care of teachers.”

What could this mean less than “boys”? Indeed, the king most diligently gathered into his school a multitude not yet of boys, but of mere infants.

That King Sigberct established a school of the liberal arts has therefore, as I believe, been sufficiently demonstrated. I must now inquire most carefully what place that prudent king chose above all as the everlasting seat of philosophy and the Muses. Since men of outstanding talent and great renown have raised a serious and bitter dispute with one another on this matter—while the University of Cambridge affirms that the illustrious king was its founder and the Oxford scholars categorically deny it—I hope that my opinion, if only it rests upon sound arguments, will prove persuasive to both sides. I bring no prejudice to this case, since I was a student of both universities and am bound to both equally, not merely by some personal connection but also by inclination.

If, then, I may speak freely about what I think, I must admit that, at least to me, the cause of the people of Cambridge appears by far both the better and the more probable, and that the Oxford scholars act unjustly in attempting to detract from their antiquity. Let them themselves consider whether it must not necessarily be conceded that it can be proved by arguments equally strong that Sigberct established a school at Cambridge and Alfred his at Oxford.

For it is by no means certain from the most ancient histories that Alfred laid the foundations of the university itself. Asser, without doubt, who described Alfred’s life briefly in his Annals and at length in his book On His Deeds, nowhere mentions the University of Oxford, much less its foundation, although he was especially close to Alfred. It is plainly incredible that Asser would have wished to omit so splendid and memorable an undertaking, especially if a university of the sort presented to us by the Chronicle of the New Monastery of Winchester and by John Ross had been established there, where Alfred himself was one of the most celebrated professors.

Nor, throughout more than four hundred years of our historians—even though they narrated the other deeds of Alfred at length and had an especially opportune place for mentioning this matter—do I think that anyone can be found who recorded that public schools at Oxford had been either established or restored by him, before Ranulf of Chester. Those who followed in his footsteps generally proceed in the same manner, repeating the same account with equal confidence and showing little concern for the truth.

The Oxford scholars, however, answer those who assert that Asser said nothing about Oxford by appealing to a certain paragraph in that copy of Asser edited by Camden. It states that the worst and most dreadful discord arose at Oxford between Grimbald and those most learned men whom he had brought with him, on the one hand, and the old scholars whom he found there, on the other. These old scholars refused to embrace the laws and methods of reading instituted by Grimbald and stubbornly retained those formerly sanctioned by Gildas, Melkinus, Nennius, Kentigern, and others, and later approved by Saint Germanus.

From this, they claim, it is clear that Alfred established schools at Oxford, though not originally; rather, according to Asser’s testimony, he restored them.

But, with due respect to these most learned men, it rightly seems doubtful whether this paragraph was written by Asser himself or instead fraudulently stitched on by some recent forger. For in all manuscripts of the highest reliability this entire history of the Oxford dispute is absent—not only from the copy used by the most reverend Matthew, archbishop of Canterbury, but also from all those seen by Leland. Leland himself testifies that Asser wrote about the Ford of Isis only covertly, suppressing its name, and expressly states that he did not mention even by a shadow the names Graecolada, Lechelada, or Lathelada—purely Saxon words—nor the migration (Leland, Commentary on the Swan of Kent, under the words “Ford of Isis”).

If Asser had said anything about that dispute, the old scholars, Gildas, and the others, he would certainly have mentioned the migration at least by a shadow. For Gildas and the others named by this Pseudo-Asser, if any credence is to be given to the Oxford scholars who say that the school of the people of Greeklade flourished down to Theodore’s time, were supplying that school with laws of life and discipline long before the supposed migration could have taken place.

Finally, this paragraph is missing from the many copies which the Oxford antiquary himself says that he consulted. It is scarcely credible that so vigorous a defender of that academy, knowing how greatly the paragraph would contribute to increasing and strengthening the credibility of Camden’s copy, would knowingly have omitted it if he had found it in his manuscripts. And it is entirely incredible that those older historians—Aethelweard, Ingulph, Marianus Scotus, Florence of Worcester, William of Malmesbury, and the rest—should for more than four hundred years have universally and completely remained silent about Alfred’s restoration of the Oxford schools, or about this dispute, if they had read such a paragraph in copies of Asser.

From these facts it may be concluded that the truth is very close to this: no copy ever existed in which this paragraph was found other than the one mentioned by the illustrious Camden, and that the paragraph itself was perhaps inserted by some Oxford forger.

Moreover, before Asser mentioned the dispute, if he had observed the proper method of writing history, he would necessarily have mentioned the University of Oxford and either its celebrated foundation or its restoration. But as far as the Oxford schools are concerned, there is nothing at all in Asser—not even covertly—whatever Leland may say to the contrary.

The school in which Alfred arranged for his younger son Ethelweard, together with almost all the infants of the entire region, to be educated in the liberal arts was confined within the walls of the palace or royal hall, as is clear from Asser’s own account, in which he writes that the sons of nobles were brought up in the royal household. To this school, not to Oxford, Alfred assigned each year an eighth part of his annual revenues, according to Asser’s meaning and according to all the ancient historians who explain Asser.

If, then, the Oxford scholars will concede that the Menevian wrote neither ineptly nor foolishly, and that they knew him—not to say extremely well, but even moderately well—then, connecting what follows with what precedes, they must admit that this paragraph was not written by Asser, but was carelessly stitched into his history by some Oxford writer who, while foolishly believing the school mentioned by Asser to have been Oxford’s, was led into a most amusing error.

The illustrious Spelman also observed something that greatly diminishes the credibility of the paragraph inserted into Camden’s edition. He saw “an ancient manuscript of Asser, the very archetype from which, as some reasonably suppose, the archbishop first made this author known; reasonably, I say, whether one considers its character, akin to the Saxon script, or the small strokes and rubricated points with which that prelate was accustomed to mark the manuscripts he had read. In that manuscript, the paragraphs immediately preceding and following the account of the dispute appeared in a text of older and most indisputable writing, while other parts of the book were by a more recent hand and seemed spurious. Yet nowhere in the entire book did the learned knight detect this paragraph about the dispute, nor anything at all that differed from what the archbishop published.”

Whether, therefore, the archbishop made the Cottonian manuscript public, as Spelman believes, or the Lumleyan, as others maintain, we can safely affirm that either manuscript is far older than the one used by Camden. For this latter manuscript, according to Camden’s own judgment, is said at most to have been written in the time of Richard II, when scribes had long since ceased to use either the Saxon script or the script related to it in writing books. Twynus himself, in his letter to the illustrious Camden, admits that this copy is not the oldest.

Nor will the epilogue and the verses of Henry of Huntingdon in praise of Alfred, inserted at the end of the Parker manuscript, raise its antiquity even slightly. Anyone interested in antiquity knows very well what most often happens with manuscripts: extensive additions are written by a later hand at the end and in the margins. This will be sufficiently apparent from the Cottonian copy, which is written in Saxon letters and in which the epilogue and poems are also absent.

It can scarcely be believed that the ancient scholars, in their serious dispute with Grimbald, ever put forward those fictions concerning Gildas, Melchin, Nennius, Kentigern, and Germanus, since all of them can very easily be refuted from the histories of their lives and deeds. For not one of the entire company of historians has ever said that these men studied at Oxford, much less that they grew old there. What does still more to overthrow the authority of this clause is that it not only fails to cohere with the rest of the body of the history, but is not even internally consistent. This foolish forger confused and mingled things that cannot be joined or connected with one another. For, preserving no chronological order whatsoever, he says that Saint Germanus came to Oxford and, after spending half a year there, remarkably approved the orders and institutions mentioned above—that is, those of Gildas and the others. Yet this Germanus had departed from this life long before any of them was born.

> “Furthermore, this account does not agree with the arrival of Grimbald, which, as the Hyde book says, occurred in the year 885. For everyone agrees that Grimbald, having recently arrived in England, was retained for some time by Alfred at his own residence, so that Alfred himself might be privately instructed by Grimbald before Grimbald was sent to Oxford. Yet, according to the Winchester manuscript praised by Camden, the University began to be built in the second year after Grimbald’s arrival. Nevertheless, this article reports that Grimbald provided the occasion for the public dispute at Oxford, which broke out in the year 886, although the undertaking had gradually grown after being begun three years earlier—that is, one year before the University was founded and two years before Grimbald’s arrival.”

To this objection, drawn from the figures and chronological calculation, the Oxonians answer nothing except that chronological errors among our historians—and even in Asser himself—are obvious to any moderately attentive reader. As though there were not other extremely strong reasons for judging this article fabricated and fictitious! Although chronological error by itself may not be sufficient to abolish this clause’s credibility, it nevertheless greatly strengthens the other arguments devised to prove precisely that.

> “If we also compare the other circumstances that now emerge, how can we regard it as probable that Prince Alfred, who took so seriously the collapse of learning in his homeland and had undertaken its restoration by such remarkable means, would have permitted fraud to be done to a work so greatly and ardently desired by him through quarrels among a few scholars, of no importance whatsoever? And then, after he himself had departed from home and gone as far as Oxford to settle those disputes, would he have left the matter still so unresolved that his professors, wearied by the more obscure scholars, were compelled to abandon the work they had already undertaken? Certainly this was scarcely compatible with the king’s other dignity and discipline. Although gentle in disposition at other times, he was nevertheless severe and strict in enforcing what he had once wisely resolved.”

> “Nor does John Rossus, whom the *Apology* greatly celebrates, add any weight to this fiction of a dispute arising between Grimbald and the Oxonians. For he relates how wonderfully the learning restored by Grimbald flourished in these lands. Yet if the methods of teaching which he himself had established had been rejected, especially so quickly, this could certainly not have been done by Grimbald himself. Later, Rossus says, in his old age, after abandoning study, he went to Winchester.”

> “Let us inquire further where those ancient scholars were living when Alfred was beginning his reign. Although they were so ready to defend the supposed ancient institutions of the University, they were not present to assist the king, nor did they offer their services when, because of the scarcity of learned men, he was compelled to look abroad? As for the scholars, if there were any, quite apart from the fact that no mention is made anywhere of their assistance, we discover that they possessed very little learning, since the king himself tells us that at the beginning of his reign there were very few south of the Humber who knew how to render a Latin letter into the vernacular.”

However great Camden’s authority may be—and we willingly acknowledge him as a man of astonishing learning, whose most upright character and probity of life entirely remove every suspicion of artifice or fraud—it ought not therefore to be so great that it alone diminishes the credibility of all the manuscripts that have so far appeared, or weakens and dissolves the objections brought by Spelman against the *authenticity* (*Ἀυθεντία*) of this article, especially since those objections are of such a kind and possess such force and weight that no Oxonian has yet dared to offer any reply.

So much for the Pseudo-Asser. Let us now proceed to what Twyne cites from Malmesbury (*Apology*, book II, section 172). He introduces the historian as speaking in this manner:

> “King Alfred, servant of God, frequently visited Neot and sometimes made use of his counsels; for, on the advice of Neot the abbot, he was the first to establish at Oxford public schools of various arts.”

He also asserts that he found these words in Malmesbury’s little book on the antiquity of the monastery of Glastonbury. Malmesbury certainly wrote such a work, which the learned Gale published at Oxford. But let some Oxonian, however sharp-sighted, show me where throughout that entire little history the things cited by Twyne are to be found. Who, unless he had utterly cast away his reputation and standing, would ever resort to fables and fictitious records when he could not prove something from genuine histories?

But lest they seem to possess nothing except inventions with which to defend their cause, the Cantabrigians press an argument drawn from a certain and indisputable work of Malmesbury. They say that Malmesbury testifies that good learning flourished at Oxford before Alfred, though it was enlarged and promoted by him; that Grimbald was summoned from Gaul; and that the reason for summoning him was that, through his industry, he might revive the study of learning in England, which had fallen dormant and was almost dead (*Note on the Life of Alfred*, English edition, p. 178; *Antiquities of Oxford*, p. 15). They assert that this most diligent historian intended by the word *studium* the University of Oxford (Malmesbury, *On the Kings*, book II, chapter 4). From this premise, most shamefully begged, they then conclude that scholars studied there, though fewer than before the Danish invasion, and that Grimbald was to revive the interrupted study of learning at Oxford, not establish it anew.

But who, possessing a mind free from every prejudice, has ever conceived that this word referred to a crowd of students, or to a place in which literary studies were cultivated, rather than to learning itself? I certainly believe that when Malmesbury wrote these things he was thinking nothing at all about an Oxford academy, but wished only to show that in Alfred’s kingdom there had been no one skilled in letters, and that the pursuit of learning, long interrupted and nearly lost throughout England, had been revived through Grimbald’s efforts.

Another argument, not unlike this one, is drawn from Constantius’s *Life of Saint Germanus*, where the *universitas* of that region—that is, of Britain—is said to have readily adopted the opinion of Germanus and his companions. They contend that *universitas* in this passage means a company of people gathered into one place and joined by a fellowship of study (*Antiquities of Oxford*, p. 10). But it plainly means nothing other than that entire, whole, universal region.

No less ridiculous and absurd are the things the Oxonians babble about Saint Gildas while claiming him as their own. The author of this saint’s life says that, after taking leave of his pious teacher Iltutus, he proceeded to Iren in order to seek the opinions of other teachers both in philosophy and in sacred letters. Iren, therefore, means Ireland, which others call *Ierne* and *Iris*, and whose inhabitants are also called *Irenses*. At that time Ireland flourished under the disciples of Saint Patrick for both holiness and learning. The English themselves, once they had embraced the faith of Christ, frequently went to Ireland for the sake of learning.

The Oxonians, however, entirely deny that Iren is the same as Ireland, and ingeniously conjecture that Oxford is tacitly understood by that word. They merely change *Iren* into *Icen*, then into *Ichen* and *Ychen*, and finally into *Rydychen*, which in the British language means Oxford; and then they imagine that they have splendidly achieved everything they wish. But those who play such games with words must necessarily become the sport of everyone’s ridicule; and no one who has read these foolish trifles, however stern and naturally gloomy, can possibly restrain laughter.

Let us return to Alfred, whom the Oxonians proclaim the founder of their institution. The writers do not agree sufficiently about the time at which he accomplished this (*ibid.*, p. 14). Some assign the years 872, 873, or one nearby. But at that time the most illustrious king was so occupied with military affairs that he could in no way have devoted himself to promoting the liberal studies. Leland asserts that this glory belongs to the year 879, when, after the truce made between Alfred and Guthrum, the English were allowed to breathe for a while. The Pseudo-Asser places the event in the year 883, three years before that celebrated dispute. The annals of the monastery of Hyde name 886, and finally a chronicle by an unknown author names 895.

But if Saint Neot, as the Oxford historian writes (*ibid.*), played the chief role in restoring the academy and was a lecturer in sacred theology; or if Alfred, as Brompton testifies, first established at Oxford public schools of various arts at the advice of Blessed Neot the abbot, then Leland is plainly at fault through lateness, and so are all the others who assign a later year. For Saint Neot died in 877. After the author of his life has dealt with his death, he adds, in number 21:

> “At that time, namely, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, Guthrum, leader of the Danes, invaded England with a great fleet.”

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, century IV, part II.)

Thus Saint Neot’s death must be placed in that year or the preceding one. The same is also shown by the fact that Neot foretold that what he had predicted to King Alfred would soon be fulfilled as he approached the longed-for haven of letters—that is, death—according to number 18. Yet Alfred pursued Guthrum in 877, and Guthrum was defeated by Alfred after Easter of the following year, when Saint Neot appeared to Alfred during the fighting and aided him. Neot had previously encouraged Alfred, who was trembling before the battle, by appearing to him, according to number 26. He had therefore already departed this life.

Certainly, when Asser mentions the defeat inflicted on Alfred by Guthrum in 878 and foretold by Neot, he speaks of it as though Neot had already ceased to live:

> “The most blessed man Neot, who was still living in the flesh, who was his kinsman, grieved over this from the depths of his heart and, filled with the prophetic spirit, foretold that the greatest adversity would come upon him on account of it.”

Thus, by the year 878, when Alfred was compelled to yield to Guthrum, Neot had died; his death must therefore be assigned to 877 or the preceding year. Since Alfred was excessively occupied with wars during the earlier years of his reign, he could not, while Neot was alive, either establish or restore schools at Oxford. And since Neot died in 877, it necessarily follows that he did not lecture on theology in that academy, nor, at his urging, restore at Oxford the study of learning that had collapsed from its former condition.

Finally, since those writers who attribute the glory of this achievement to Alfred also acknowledge that a large share of the honor belongs to Neot, once it has been shown that Neot did not persuade the king to found Oxford’s schools, the Cantabrigians will immediately conclude that the king whom Neot is said to have advised had not been thinking at all about founding an academy.

But if the Oxonians still obstinately insist that their schools were established before the year in which Neot died, they will supply a new argument by which their opponents may overthrow that famous passage concerning the dispute in Asser. For the Pseudo-Asser reports that for three years after the new schools had been established by Alfred there was no serious disagreement between the old scholars and Grimbald and those most learned men whom he had brought with him; but in 886 the worst discord arose among them. From this it follows that Grimbald and his companions restored the Oxford academy to a better condition around 883.

If, however, it is said that the schools were repaired by Alfred before 877, while Neot was still alive, then without any doubt Asser—who was both Alfred’s contemporary and his intimate—never wrote this badly fabricated passage.

But to bury completely this fiction that the Academy was restored at Neot’s advice, it is clear that Asser omitted it, as did the anonymous author of Neot’s life [Note: [Col. 0351] He flourished in the twelfth century; see him in Mabillon, century IV, part II.]. Yet that author does mention the privileges of the English school at Rome granted by Pope Marinus at the request of King Alfred; Neot is said to have urged Alfred in this matter, though I find no mention in Asser that Neot did so, even though Asser records the privilege granted by Marinus.

Who does not see that the silence of a contemporary author who deliberately wrote about Alfred’s splendid achievements, and of the biographer who undertook to commit Saint Neot’s deeds to writing, ought among learned men to carry much greater weight than the false and deceitful testimony of short-sighted monks or writers who flourished long after Alfred’s age?

To Saint Neot the Oxford historian adds (p. 15) John Erigena, or Scotus, whom he says was a monk of the Church of Menevia and instructed the academics in logic, music, and arithmetic. He also confidently asserts that, contrary to all writers who deny it, John lectured on the arts at the same time as Neot and Asser. With due respect to this most learned man, who has made this assertion both confidently and boldly, I shall prove by no weak arguments that I must disagree with him on this matter.

John Erigena, or Scotus, who was a familiar of Charles the Bald and came to Gaul at the beginning of that king’s reign, was so far from being a monk of Menevia that he was not a monk at all. He is nowhere called a monk by contemporary authors of his age. Moreover, in the titles of his works, where authors customarily express their offices or dignities, he nowhere uses the name “monk,” as is clear from the preface to his book *On Divine Predestination*, which begins:

> “To the illustrious lords … Hincmar and Pardulus … John, your devoted servant in the Lord, sends greetings.”

The same is proved by his preface to the *Areopagitica*:

> “To the most glorious Charles, king of the Catholics, John, the least of the students of wisdom.”

Finally, to the Greek-Latin verses that he himself appended to a very ancient Greek-Latin Glossary he prefixed this title: “Verses of John.” Besides, if he had been a monk, he would at some point have withdrawn to a monastery; whereas, on the contrary, he was always at the court of Charles the Bald, as can be understood from the letter of Pardulus, bishop of Laon.

This John, therefore, was not a monk, nor was he from Menevia or, as the historian wishes, born at holy Menevia. He was by birth a Scot, as Pope Nicholas I chiefly testifies in his letter addressed to the elder King Charles:

> “It has been reported to our apostolate that a certain man named John, a Scot by birth, has recently translated into Latin the work of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite.”

Hincmar too, who was familiar with John, calls him *Johannes Scottigena* in chapter 31 of his later work *On Predestination*. Anastasius the Librarian likewise calls him *Scottigena* in his letter to Charles the Bald concerning the Areopagitic writings; in that letter he also calls him a barbarian, placed at the ends of the world. This is why authors of that age, in writings published on the subject of Gottschalk, regularly call him John the Scot, or, suppressing John’s name, “the Scot,” “that Scot,” or “a certain Scot.”

What is still more unfortunate is that John is said to have lectured at the same time as Neot and Asser. But if Asser did not come to Alfred until Neot had long been dead, it was impossible for them to instruct academics at Oxford at one and the same time. I have already shown sufficiently that Neot died in 877, and it is no less clear that Asser did not go to Alfred before 884.

Nor should we accept the claim made by some that there were two Assers: one who, according to the *Florilegus* and Florence, died as bishop of Sherborne in 883, whom the Oxonians claim as their own; and another from Menevia who wrote Alfred’s deeds. It is clear that those who assign his death to 883, and divide one man into two, have been led into a very serious error.

For it is established that Asser was summoned from Menevia to the king in 884. The king gave him two monasteries and, in the course of the following period, Exeter with the entire parish belonging to it in Saxony and Cornwall—that is, as it seems to me, the diocese of Sherborne, in which the city of Exeter and Cornwall are situated.

That he was bishop of Sherborne during the final years of Archbishop Athelred, before the year 889 in which that archbishop died, is plainly inferred from King Alfred’s will, in which the king gives one hundred marks, among others, to Asser, bishop of Sherborne. Ingulf also testifies that this same man, after his arrival in England, [Note: [Col. 0353] At Sherborne. See also Leland’s excerpts from the *Life of Grimbald*, in *Collectanea*, vol. II, p. 18.] occupied the see of Sherborne.

Alfred himself also mentions his bishop Asser in his preface to Gregory’s *Pastoral Care*, addressed to Bishop Wulfsige, who began to govern the Church of London around 898. Finally, the Saxon Chronicle and the Annals of Asser testify in the clearest terms that he died in 910.

There was therefore one and the same Asser, both of Menevia and of Sherborne, who succeeded Sighelm in that bishopric. For, according to the Saxon Chronicle and others, Sighelm carried Alfred’s alms to Rome and India in 883. Werstan succeeded Asser in 910, when Plegmund, as many bishops were then dying and the dioceses of Winchester and Sherborne were being divided into several parts, consecrated seven bishops in one day.

Malmesbury and those who follow him are therefore gravely mistaken when they say that Sighelm was later than Asser and insert between Asser and Werstan Sighelm, Ethelward, and a vacancy of the see lasting seven years. Nor should one trust those historians who write that seven bishops, among whom Werstan is found, were consecrated in one day in 904 or the following year by command of Pope Formosus, who had long since died, allegedly sending an order to that effect.

From all this, then, it is abundantly proved that John, Neot, and Asser did not teach the arts and theology at Oxford. Among the lecturers who flourished at Oxford at that time there was, however, another John, called a monk, who explained geometry and astronomy. Asser calls him an Ealdsaxon and the first head of the monastery of Etheling.

From this one man, three later defenders of the antiquity of the Oxford academy fabricated three Johns: namely, the Menevian, the Scot, and the Ethelingian. If any others besides this last had been summoned by Alfred to his palace, Asser, who carefully records the learned men employed by Alfred, would certainly not have passed them over in silence.

Those who labored so greatly to defend writers so stupid and recent—writers who made this most absurd assertion—therefore spent their efforts badly.

Nor did John Ealdsaxon ever lecture at Oxford. For Asser clearly indicates that Alfred’s school was not fixed at Oxford but established at the royal court, or *curtus*, to use Asser’s word. All the learned men whom Asser most diligently enumerates—Werferth of Worcester, Plegmund of Canterbury, the chaplains Athelstan and Werwulf, Grimbald and John, priests and monks invited from Gaul, and finally Asser himself—taught Alfred and the youth of that region in the royal household.

That Grimbald lectured at Oxford is allegedly proved by the fact that beneath the choir or chancel of the ancient church of Saint Peter in the eastern part of Oxford the underground chamber of Saint Grimbald is still shown.

But since this story rests solely on the authority of the Pseudo-Asser, and none of the ancient and unquestionably reliable writers makes the same assertion, while on the contrary it is abundantly clear from those writers that Grimbald was never at Oxford, this seems to me entirely worthy of being numbered among the Oxonians’ recent and ridiculous fabrications.

From John Rossus, the antiquary of Warwick, it is inferred that Alfred was the founder of the Oxford school because he records that the famous king built three halls, distinguished by the names of the University Halls: Great, Lesser, and Little. But everything Rossus wrote about the antiquity and foundation of the Oxford academy is so badly fabricated that it does not even bear the appearance of truth.

As for these halls, it is most certain that none of them existed in Alfred’s time. They all received that name because the University purchased them with the money of Master William of Durham.

The first to bear this name was called, at the time of its purchase, as the charters show, the Corner House. It had belonged to the hospital of Brackley, given by Master Robert of Preston, and was situated in the parish of Blessed Mary, nearer to the house once belonging to Galfrid Justet toward the north. The hospital sold this house to the University in 1253, and from that time it acquired the name University Hall in the Scholars’ Street.

Many years later, as the Oxford historian testifies (*Antiquities of Oxford*, part II, p. 57)—namely, in the sixth year of Edward III, that is, 1332—a very large tenement belonging to Richard of Tekene and others was purchased. At that time it was called Selvern Hall, commonly Selverne-Hall, and earlier Ludlow-Spicer’s Hall. Under Henry III it had been known as Durham Hall, commonly Durham-Hall, after a certain Andrew of Durham, a burgess of Oxford.

Having acquired this residence, the masters and scholars moved into it, intending it as the permanent dwelling of their fellowship. It then began to be called Great University Hall, taking its name from the academy under whose auspices it flourished. It was indeed larger than the two halls that were therefore called lesser.

The statutes of this Great University Hall still exist. It was purchased for the scholars of Master William of Durham, and the public seal of the academy, impressed in green wax, was attached to them. It is kept in the treasury of University College, in box A.A.

We therefore have this same historian refuting the fictions of Rossus and admitting that these halls were not called University halls because Alfred founded them, but because the University purchased them long afterward.

I have thus abundantly shown that everything the Oxonians have advanced about an academy founded at Oxford by Alfred is false and fictitious. If, therefore, they are granted that the illustrious king established the Oxford school, they must admit, by the same reasoning, that it can be shown that Sigberct founded his school, about which there has been so much dispute, at Cambridge.

The Oxonians object that no ancient writer testifies that Sigberct founded a school at Cambridge, and that Polydore Vergil was the first to assert this—not merely an outsider and a recent writer, but one whom almost everyone unanimously agrees to have been unreliable, or at least careless, in history.

It is especially worthy of notice that those who accuse Polydore of having written his history in bad faith nearly all become angry with him for that very reason: namely, because he rejected the British fables of Geoffrey. Among them is Leland, who nevertheless agrees with Polydore on this point.

It is also probable that Polydore was not the first author of this conjecture. For Leland, who wrote shortly after Vergil, says that the consensus of writers attributes to Sigberct and Felix the glory of establishing the Cambridge school, under the auspices of Christ (*Commentary on the Swan of Cambridge*, under “GRANTA”).

But Polydore’s opinion alone cannot in any way be called the consensus of writers. Moreover, if Polydore’s credibility is rightly called into question, Leland and the others who asserted the same thing should not be accused of fabricating fables. Their opinion and authority, as learned men, will, I believe, always carry more weight than the ridiculous and absurd errors of Brompton, Higden, and others who follow in their footsteps, asserting—whether through a faulty or rather wholly inadequate understanding of Asser—that Alfred was the founder of the Oxford academy.

But the Oxford historian (*Antiquities of Oxford*, p. 38) asks what indications Bede gave by which he showed that he intended Cambridge. The answer is very easy: Bede indicates that the site of Sigberct’s school was Cambridge by equally clear signs as Asser shows Oxford to have been the site of Alfred’s school.

Nor should anyone say that, if the academy was founded by Sigberct, it would claim Grantchester for itself. For it is clear from Bede that this little town was deserted in those times (*Ecclesiastical History* IV.17). It seems most certain that, when that place had failed—or rather, after its settlement had shifted to some extent—Cambridge arose from its ruins.

Without doubt, in Alfred’s time Cambridge was a very flourishing town, as is clear from Asser and the Saxon Chronicle (year 875). For there we read that it was sufficiently large for a great Danish army to winter there. It could scarcely have happened that so considerable a town, which gave its name to the entire province, suddenly arose from nothing.

After that city was devastated by the Danes in these times, if we believe John Rossus, King Edward, called the Elder,

> “in order to increase the clergy, just as his father had done at Oxford, restored Cambridge itself, together with all the other studies generally suspended, deserted, and destroyed from ancient times, to its former glory” (*History of the Kings of England*, p. 96).

If this is true, who else, I ask, can be named before Sigberct as the founder of a school in these regions?

The Oxonians must therefore admit that the authority of Rossus, an alumnus of the Oxford academy and a vigorous defender of its antiquity, has very great force in this matter—especially among those who, relying most heavily on his opinion, say that Alfred restored his school, founded three halls, and had teachers lecture there in the arts.

For if they deny Edward the glory of restoring Cambridge, the Cantabrigians may with equal right deny that this part of Rossus’s history is true when he speaks of Alfred restoring the University at Oxford.

But there is a strong argument that Sigberct did not establish a school at Cambridge: namely, that Malmesbury and others report that he established schools of learning in various places. Yet Bede’s authority completely breaks the force of this objection, since Bede mentions only a school.

I take no account of those who read *schools* in a certain manuscript of Bede. In all the manuscripts that I myself have seen, the word clearly reads *school*.

Thus far I have shown with sufficient success that Cambridge was the place where Sigberct established his school. There is, however, another extremely strong objection, which, as I think, will scarcely yield to any answer.

Peter of Blois, in his continuation of Ingulf, reports that Geoffrey, abbot of Crowland, in the time of Henry II, sent to his manor at Cottenham, near Cambridge, certain monks of his who were highly trained in philosophical theories and other sciences. They went daily to Cambridge and, having hired a public barn, taught their sciences there. In a short time they gathered a great number of students, which soon increased so greatly that neither the barn nor any church was sufficient to accommodate them.

> “From this source,” Blois continues, “small at first but grown now into a great river, we see the city of God made joyful, and all England made fruitful through the many masters and doctors who go forth from Cambridge, in the likeness of the most holy paradise.”

Here it must be admitted that the Cantabrigians will have absolutely nothing to answer unless the Oxonians themselves show them the way. When it is objected to them that Oxford was not a home of the arts before Alfred because the king himself tells us that at the beginning of his reign there were very few south of the Humber who knew how to render a Latin letter into the vernacular, they immediately reply that the scholars had then been driven out of Oxford by the violence of the Danes, and that for this reason the academy did not flourish in learned men during the first years of Alfred’s reign.

The Cantabrigians can use this very same reply. For after the academy had been restored by Edward the Elder, the Saxon Chronicle tells us that in 1010 the Danes occupied East Anglia, ravaged everything accessible for three months, carried off plunder, and burned villages; among them, as conquerors, they burned the city of Cambridge. As a result, the Sigberctine school was deserted by the Muses until, under the reign of Henry II, it returned to its former seat under the auspices of Abbot Geoffrey and his monks.

The entire controversy concerning the antiquity of the academies having now been treated, even if I have not shown that Sigberct’s school was at Cambridge, this much at least will be clear: either all the fables fabricated by Higden, Rossus, and others concerning an academy at Oxford founded by Alfred must be utterly rejected, or the Oxonians must admit, however unwillingly, that under Sigberct Cambridge was flourishing exceedingly in arts and sciences.

Let them accept whichever of these alternatives they prefer. For my part, I earnestly desire of both sides that all matters possessing either no authority or only doubtful authority be set aside, and that learned men no longer engage in so grave and bitter a dispute over fables or, at best, uncertain narratives.

Both academies will always possess the highest glory and the greatest renown, even if Alfred did not establish the one and Sigberct did not establish the other. In my opinion, Oxford will be sufficiently ancient if it is said to have arisen shortly before the time of Ingulf, who was sent there to be educated; and Cambridge will not be deprived of any substantial part of its honor if it is held not to have been established before Abbot Geoffrey.

Nothing, however, is clearer than that what historians report about the academies before these times is either plainly false or at least of doubtful and uncertain credibility.

Finally, if Sigberct’s school was not established at Granta, it is most probable that it was located either in the city of Domnoc, where Felix received his episcopal seat, or at Seham, where, after a church had been built and dedicated (*History of Ramsey*, Gale’s edition, p. 82), he had gathered a considerable community of monks. For it has already been sufficiently established above that schools were chiefly established in episcopal sees and monasteries.
