Memorandum: Robert [lacuna]odes of Newcastle upon Tyne, of revered and good memory, learned in the law of the kingdom of England and steward of the priory of Durham, and a constant and faithful friend of Saint Cuthbert, as well as a diligent helper and worker in recovering and preserving the rights and liberties of that same saint, and a spiritual confrater of the chapter of Durham, on the tenth day of January in the year of the Lord 1446, gave to the feretory of Saint Cuthbert a golden cross, hanging at the feet of that same saint on the eastern gable of the aforesaid feretory. On one side it had five precious stones: namely, at the center of the cross, one beautiful sapphire pleasing to the eye, and at each corner one precious red stone, together with small pearls circularly attached at the four extremities of the aforesaid cross. On the other side of the same cross were various relics, namely pieces from the stone column to which Christ was bound and scourged, and from a stone of his tomb, hewn from rock, enclosed in a beryl fashioned in the shape of a cross.

**No. XII [Smith XVI]. On the dwelling which Saint Ceadda had made for himself.**

From an old manuscript parchment belonging to the dean and chapter of Lichfield church, Dugdale, in the third volume of the *Monasticon* (p. 219), reports that there were two monasteries at Lichfield: one constructed on the western side in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary; the other, called Saint Ceadda’s Station, on the eastern side, where Saint Ceadda used to offer prayers and preach to the people, and which is now called Stowe. Wulfad and Ruffinus, sons of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, are said to have come to this dwelling or cell, as is clear from their passion (*Monumenta Anglicana* II, 119), while Saint Ceadda was bishop of Lichfield, and to have been baptized by him. Consequently, Wulfhere, thinking that they had embraced the Christian faith, killed both sons whom Ermenilda had borne him, if any credence is to be given to this historical account, in an impious slaughter.

But the whole story of these brothers’ death appears to be entirely fictitious. For King Wulfhere, whom the author of their passion calls a pagan, had accepted the Christian faith from the beginning of his reign; and, as soon as he became king, he began to promote Christianity and to found and enrich churches and monasteries. Thus William of Malmesbury wrote of him (*De Regibus* I.4) that Wulfhere “strongly aided by his favor the Christian faith, scarcely breathing in his kingdom and begun through his brother.” Indeed, it could not have happened that the king slaughtered his sons because they received baptism from Saint Ceadda. For he himself, after Jaruman’s death, asked Theodore to provide a bishop for himself and his people; and when Ceadda was given to them as bishop, he received him kindly and granted him land sufficient for fifty households to build a monastery in the place called Ad Baruae. Furthermore, they say that these men suffered martyrdom around the year 668, which is certainly entirely contrary to the truth. For in that year Ceadda had not yet occupied the see of Lichfield, since he did not administer that bishopric until the following year.

Alford, however (*Annals*, year 669, section X), thinks that this story should not be wholly rejected. He admits that it in no way agrees with what Bede relates about Wulfhere and Ceadda; but he says that, with a few alterations, everything could stand, and he judges that the men should be said to have been baptized earlier by some Mercian bishop, before Wulfhere began to reign, especially in the time of their father Penda, who, after several kings had been killed, labored to extinguish the Christian name.

But even so, the difficulties and contradictions in this narrative cannot be reconciled. For when Wulfhere was raised to the kingship, Bede testifies that he was a young man. It is therefore not likely that he had two adolescent sons in the time of his father Penda, who was killed three years or more before Wulfhere began to reign. Finally, Bede’s silence will carry the greatest weight with many people, for he certainly would not have passed over this matter in silence, especially since this impious deed of King Wulfhere is said to have been the reason for building the monastery at Stone in Staffordshire, where the repentant king was to wash away the enormity of his deed by a good work.

**No. XIII [Smith XVII]. On the Teachers of the Church.**

The Teachers of the Church, as it seems to me, were none other than the more learned clergy, well trained in ecclesiastical matters, who came to the synod together with their bishops. Such were Abbot Hadrian and Benedict Biscop, both thoroughly versed in the canonical institutions of the Fathers. They did not go to the council in order to make or confirm decrees by their own authority, but only to assist the bishops—who alone possessed the right to enact ecclesiastical laws—with their learning and counsel.

For it is clear from the synodal proceedings themselves, the text of which Bede inserted into his history, that the archbishop and his colleagues possessed full authority to make canons. Before the synod’s decrees, Theodore first wrote his own name, then the names of all the bishops who were present at that time; and everything was defined and established solely by their votes and consent. The council of Hatfield, held a few years later, was likewise celebrated under the presidency of Theodore, by the grace of God archbishop of the island of Britain and of the city of Canterbury, with the others of the island of Britain sitting with him.

It is entirely certain that before this time clergy of lower rank had obtained a place in synods. This is clear from canon 4 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633:

“On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, a synod is to be assembled in each province, because it is springtime, when the earth is clothed with grass and the food of young shoots is found. Therefore, at the first hour of the day, before sunrise, everyone is to be expelled from the church; and, after the doors have been closed, doorkeepers are to stand at the single entrance through which the priests must enter. Then all the bishops are to enter together and sit according to the times of their ordination. After all the bishops have entered and taken their seats, the presbyters whom the matter warrants admitting are then to be summoned. No deacon is to intrude among them. After these, suitable deacons whom the order of proceedings requires to be present are to enter; and, when a circle has been formed from the bishops’ seats, the presbyters are to sit behind them, while the deacons stand in the bishops’ sight. Then the laymen who have deserved to attend by the council’s election are to enter [lacuna]. No bishop is to withdraw from the common assembly before the appointed hour of general withdrawal arrives. Nor may anyone dare to dissolve the council until everything has been determined, so that whatever is concluded by common deliberation is subscribed by the hands of the individual bishops.”

The same point is shown by the Council of Clovesho, held under Archbishop Cuthbert in 747, where prelates of the sacred order from various provinces of Britain are said to have assembled at the synodal place together with many priests of the Lord and dignitaries of the lesser ecclesiastical orders. Hence it is clear that both presbyters and deacons were granted seats in councils. Nevertheless, the Toledan canon ascribes legislative right and authority to the bishops alone; and the canons of the Council of Clovesho prescribe solely by the authority of the prelates who, as teachers, have been placed by God above the others.

Finally, it may further be inferred from chapters 6 and 9 of the synod held at Celichyth in 816 under Archbishop Wulfred that only bishops possessed the power to enact ecclesiastical laws. Abbots, presbyters, and deacons were present there as well, but they discussed necessary matters and the welfare of the churches with the presiding bishops.

Nor can this be disproved on the grounds that John—who was not a bishop, but only chief cantor of Saint Peter’s church and abbot of the monastery of blessed Martin—subscribed to the Council of Hatfield and confirmed its decrees. For this John was a legate of Agatho, the Roman pontiff. This is clear both from Bede (*Ecclesiastical History* IV.18), who testifies that he “had received this commission from the apostolic pope, that he should carefully ascertain what faith the Church of the English held and report it on returning to Rome,” and from the Roman synod held in 679 (*Spelman, Councils*, vol. I, p. 160). By the authority, advice, and command of Agatho, John was sent to Britain; Agatho also gave him “the synod of blessed Pope Martin, written not long before at Reims with the agreement of 105 bishops, not only as testimony and confirmation of his legation, but so that whatever Saint Theodore the archbishop, together with wise, faithful, and religious men in the provinces of the English, might find more usefully and religiously in Christ for the churches of Christ and for all the people of God dwelling there, he might strengthen with the aforesaid authority.”

John therefore confirmed the decrees not by his own authority but by pontifical authority. Consequently, it does not follow from his subscription that other Teachers of the Church, who were not equipped with such a legation, possessed the same power.

**No. XIV [Smith XVIII]. On the cause of the disagreement that arose between King Ecgfrith and Bishop Wilfrid.**

The writers of Wilfrid’s Life make us certain that Ecgfrith was strongly bound to Wilfrid’s friendship during the first years of his reign. Indeed, as long as Æthelthryth was with Ecgfrith, Wilfrid prospered. But when she obtained a divorce from the king through Wilfrid’s advice and counsel and entered a monastery, the king, who bore the separation from his beloved bride with no small resentment, “did not cherish Wilfrid with the affection with which he had formerly honored him, but long concealed anger against him in his heart; and, when the opportunity was awaited, expelled him from the seat of his bishopric for this reason.” (*Life of Saint Æthelthryth*, in Mabillon, vol. II, p. 750.)

From this arose the king’s hatred of Wilfrid. When Ermenburga, whom the king later took in marriage, saw this, she inflamed his mind still further by introducing various causes of hostility. The queen was also inwardly offended because Wilfrid had often censured in her “womanly fickleness, the intemperance of slippery display, and the oppression and plunder of violent condemnation, which flourished in her with great swelling pride.”

Accordingly, when she perceived that the king’s mind was disturbed, she began, through deceitful speeches, to recount his glory to the king with admiring praise. After setting forth the abundance of his wealth, the multitude of his monasteries, the size of his buildings, and the crowd of subject princes, she added: “And what more does he himself possess for you than you possess for him? Your entire [Col. 0364C] kingdom is his bishopric.”

Moved by such words, and directing all his attention toward them as though his own advantage were being considered, the king thought that his affairs could not be better managed than by stripping Wilfrid of everything he possessed and dividing his bishopric among several bishops. The king’s mind was therefore alienated from Wilfrid because of Æthelthryth; nor was Ermenburga the first to incite Ecgfrith against him, although Eddius, Fridegodus, Eadmer, and others seem to have believed that their enmity originated with her.

**No. XV [Smith XIX].**

*(From the Cottonian Library, Aug. II.16.)*

**Charter of Hodilred, kinsman of Sebbi, king of the East Saxons.**

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. Whenever we seem to bring something to your holy and venerable places, we return to you what is yours; we do [Col. 0364D] not bestow what is ours. Therefore I, Hodilred, kinsman of Sebbi, of the province of the East Saxons, with his consent, of my own will, sound mind, and complete counsel, perpetually grant to you, Hedilurc, abbess, for the enlargement of your monastery called Beddanhaam, and transfer from my right to yours, the land called Bucingahaam, Budinhaam, Deccanhaam, and Ancenlabeshaam, and the field in the wood called Wuidmundesfelt, which together comprise forty hides, as far as the boundaries belonging to it, with everything pertaining to them—fields, woods, meadows, and marshes—so that both you and your successors may hold and possess them, and may have free power to do whatever you wish with that land.

Enacted in the month of March. I asked a suitable number of witnesses to subscribe. If anyone should attempt to oppose or corrupt this charter of donation, before almighty God, Jesus Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the undivided Trinity—let him know that he is condemned [Col. 0365A] and separated from all Christian fellowship [lacuna]. May this charter of donation nevertheless remain in its full force, and may the gift be firm and unshaken. The boundaries of this land by which it is enclosed are these: on the east, Writola Burna; on the north, Centices Triow and Hanchem Stede; on the south, the River Thames. But if anyone wishes to increase this donation, may God increase his goods in the land of the living with his saints without end. Amen.

+ I, Sebbi, king of the East Saxons, have subscribed in confirmation. I, Oedilred, the donor, have subscribed. + I, Ercnuwald, bishop, have consented and subscribed. I, Wilfrid, bishop, have consented and subscribed. + I, Haedde, bishop, have consented and subscribed. I, Guda, priest and abbot, consenting, have subscribed. + I, Egobald, priest and abbot, have consented and subscribed. + I, Hacona, priest and abbot, have consented and subscribed. + I, Hooc, priest and abbot, consenting, have subscribed. Sig+num manus Sebbi, king. Sig+num manus [Col. 0365B] Sigiheard, king. Sig+num manus Suaebred, king.

**Concerning the land of forty holdings (*manentia*) which Odilred gave.** [Note: [Col. 0365D] “Holdings.” Among the witnesses who subscribed this charter are listed Ercnuwald of London, Wilfrid of York, expelled from his see, and Huedde, bishop of Lichfield. Hence it is established that this charter was made [Col. 0366D] between the year 691, when Wilfrid was expelled again and Haedde was consecrated, and the year 694, when King Sebbi, Ercnuwald already being dead, received the religious habit from Waldhere.]

**Charter of King Sueabred of the East Saxons.**
In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior.

Although speech alone would suffice as testimony, nevertheless, for the precaution of future times, lest someone in the future should perhaps improperly incur the sinful offense of fraudulent ignorance, I therefore consider it necessary to append at least to humble documents something for the greater strengthening of their security.

Therefore I, Sueabraed, king of the East Saxons, and I, Paeogdhath, with the permission of King Aethelred, our kinsman, have decided to grant to Bishop Waldharius, in dominion, a certain portion of land for the remedy of our souls: namely, thirty hides, in the place called Tincahom, in the province called Middlesex.

This land is marked out by the following boundaries: on the east and south it is bounded by the River Thames; [Col. 0365C] on the north by a stream whose name is Fiscesburna. We have transferred possession of this land, as stated above, with its sown fields, pastures, meadows, marshes, fisheries, rivers, enclosures, and everything belonging to it, to be possessed in perpetuity by right of dominion by the aforesaid bishop; and let him have free power to do whatever he wishes.

Moreover, so that the generosity of this donation might continually be preserved more securely, we have also added witnesses, whose names are written below. If any of our successors should wish to increase and enlarge the munificence of this donation, may the Lord increase his portion in the book of life. But if anyone, God forbid, relying on tyrannical power, should attempt to violate it, let him know that he will tremble before the tribunal of Christ and render an account; nevertheless, this charter shall remain firm, written in the year 704 from the Incarnation of our Lord, in the second indiction, on the thirteenth day of June, that is, on the Ides of June.

+ I, Coenred, king of the Mercians, have decided to grant this land to Bishop Waldharius [Col. 0365D] in dominion, for the remedy of my soul, in the place called Tinccanham; and with willing heart I have impressed the cross with my own hand.

+ I, Ciolred, king of the Mercians, have confirmed this donation, previously granted by my kinsman King Coenraed, at the place called Arcencale, and have expressed the sign of the holy cross.

+ I, Headda, bishop, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Cotta, abbot, have consented and subscribed.  
+ Suebraed, king of the East Saxons, with his own hand.  
+ I, Peohthat, have placed my mark.

## Number XVI [Smith XX]

*(Charters preserved from the cell of Coldingham in the church of Durham.)*

## Charter of King Dunecan of the Scots

I, Dunecan, son of King Malcolm, hereditary and established king of Scotland, have given as an alms-gift to Saint Cuthbert and his servants Tiningeham, Aldeham, Scuchale, Cnolle, Hathermuth, and all the service which Bishop Fodan held from Broccesmuthe. I have given these with such quitclaim—with *saca* and *soca*—as Saint Cuthbert has ever had better from those from whom he holds his alms-gifts.

And I have given this for myself, for the soul of my father, for my brothers, for my wife, and for my children. And because I wished this gift to be stable for Saint Cuthbert, I secured the consent of my brothers. Whoever wishes to destroy this, or to take anything from it from the ministers of Saint Cuthbert, may he have the curse of God, of Saint Cuthbert, and of me. Amen.

The cross of Dun + ecan, king.  
Ead + gari.  
W + enton, the scribe.  
Ace + ard.  
Ul + f.  
Malco + lumb.  
Vui + get.  
Her + mer.  
Hem + ming.  
Aelf + ric.  
Feo + dbold.  
Ea + rnulf.

This charter is strengthened both by crosses and by a pendant seal. On the seal appears the figure of an armed man seated on a horse, around which is the inscription:

+ SEAL OF DUNECAN, KING OF THE SCOTS.

Dunecan reigned in the year 1093 and the following year.

## Charter of King Eadgar

Eadgar, king of the Scots, sends greetings to all his Scottish and English men.

Know that I give as an alms-gift to almighty God and to Saint Cuthbert, my lord, and to the church of Durham, and to the monks serving God in that church and destined to serve him there forever, for the souls of my father and mother, for the salvation of my body and soul, of my brothers and sisters, and for all my predecessors and successors, the estate of Coldingham, together with the following estates belonging to it: namely, Aldcambus, Lummesdene, Regnintum, Ristun, Swinewde, Farndun, Eitun, another Eitun, Prenegest, and Cramesmuthe.

I grant these aforesaid estates to God, to the said saint, and to his monks, with all lands, woods, waters, tolls, shipwreck dues, and all customs belonging to the aforesaid estates, and which my father held in them, quit and secure, to be freely disposed of forever according to their will.

## Another charter of the same king

Eadgar, king of the Scots, sends greetings to all Scots and English throughout his kingdom.

Know that I came to the dedication of the church of Saint Mary at Coldingham. That dedication, to the praise of God and to my pleasure, was suitably and honorably completed, pleasing and acceptable to all. I offered to that church upon the altar, as its endowment, and gave it the whole vill of Swintun with its boundaries, as Liulf held it, to be held forever free and quit from every claim and to be disposed of according to the will of the monks of Saint Cuthbert, for the souls of my father and mother and for the salvation of my soul, my brothers, and my sisters.

I also gave the monks twenty-four animals to restore that same land. I established the same peace at Coldingham while going, returning, and remaining there as is observed at Eilande and at Norham. Furthermore, I established for the men of Coldingamscire, as they themselves chose and confirmed in my hand, that [Col. 0367A] every year they should pay the monks half a mark of silver from each ploughland.

Witnesses: Aelfwoter; Thor Long; Aelfric the butler; Algar the priest; Osbern the priest; Cnut the churl; Ogga; Lesing; Swein Ulfkill’s son; Ligulf of Bamburgh; Uhtred, Eilan’s son; Uuiaet the White; Tigerne.

The seal shows a crowned king seated on a throne, holding a scepter in his right hand and a sword in his left. The inscription on the seal is:

+ IMAGE OF EDGAR, BASILEUS OF THE SCOTS.

Eadgar reigned from 1097 to 1107.

## Another charter of the same king

Eadgar, king of the Scots, sends greetings to all Scots and English in his kingdom.

Know that I grant and give to my lord Saint Cuthbert and his monks Paxtun, just as I held it, with its men, lands, and waters. Let the monks possess it as freely and quietly as Coldingham, according to their will.

Farewell.

## Another charter of the same king

[Col. 0367B]

Eadgar, by the grace of God king of the Scots, sends greetings to all his faithful Scots and English throughout his kingdom.

Know that I give as an alms-gift to God and Saint Cuthbert and his monks Fiscwic, in lands and waters and with everything adjacent to it, specifically the land lying between Horverdene and Cnapadene, for the soul of my father and mother and for the salvation of my soul, my brothers, and my sisters, to be held and possessed freely and quit, and to be disposed of according to the will of the monks of Saint Cuthbert, my lord.

Farewell.

## Charters of Alexander I

Alexander, by the grace of God king of the Scots, sends greetings to all Scots and English throughout his kingdom.

Know that I give to God and Saint Cuthbert, my lord, and his monks everything they possessed in lands and waters on the day when my brother King Eadgar was alive and when he died, as freely and quietly, with all customs, as the aforesaid monks held that same land most freely and quietly on that very day; specifically, the land lying between Horevoredane and Cnapedane, as my brother Eadgar’s writ bears witness to them.

### Writ to Prior Algar and the convent of Durham concerning Swintun

Alexander, by the grace of God king of the Scots, sends greetings to Prior A. and the whole convent of the church of Saint Cuthbert.

I command and order you in no way to enter into a plea or any legal proceeding concerning the land of Swintun before it comes before me. I also make known to you, lord prior, that I have many matters to discuss privately with you as soon as this can be done.

Farewell.

## Another charter of the same king

Alexander, by the grace of God king of the Scots, sends greetings to A., prior, and the whole congregation of Saint Cuthbert.

Know that I give and grant on my behalf to God and Saint Cuthbert, and to you, his monks, the whole of Swintun, free and quit to be held and entirely possessed, as the writ of my brother King Eadgar bears witness that he gave it to you.

Furthermore, I command and forbid that any of you should in any way plead concerning that same Swintun or answer any man concerning it, unless I myself order it face to face or by my letters. For my brother David and I will secure for the aforesaid saint and for you monks both the alms-gift of our brother Eadgar and our own likewise.

Alexander reigned from 1107 to 1124. On the obverse of his seal appears a king seated on a throne, wearing a crown and royal clothing, holding a sword in his right hand and an orb in his left. The inscription is:

+ ALEXANDER, KING OF THE SCOTS, WITH GOD AS HIS GUIDE.

On the reverse is an armed horseman with the same inscription.

## Charters of David the earl

[Note: [Col. 0367D] David, later when he was king, gave the canons of Saint Andrew’s the island of Lochleven by this charter, which is still preserved in the archives of Durham: “David, king of the Scots, sends greetings to bishops, abbots, earls, sheriffs, and all good men of his entire land. Know that I have granted and given to the canons of Saint Andrew’s the island of Lochleven, so that they may establish there the canonical order, and that the *Keledei* found there may remain in peace with them and under them, if they wish to live according to the rule; [Col. 0368D] and if any of them wishes to resist this, I wish and command that he be expelled from the island. Witnesses: Robert, bishop of Saint Andrew’s; Andrew, bishop of Katen.; Walter the chancellor; Nicholas the clerk; Hugh de Moreville; Walter, son of Alan. At Berwick.” David’s seal, with only the name changed, was the same as that of Alexander I.]

David, earl, sends greetings to Bishop John, Colban, Cospatric, and all his faithful men.

You yourselves know that judgment was given before me between the monks of Saint Cuthbert and my *drengs* concerning the land of Horevoredane: namely, that if those monks had lawful witnesses or my brother’s writ, the aforesaid land would remain quit to them.

Therefore I wish you to know that I myself saw the writ and gift of my brother King Eadgar, which I have also sent to you, and whatever that writ bears witness to them, I wish and grant that they should hold freely and quietly.

Witnesses: William, my nephew; Osbern the chaplain; Hugh de Moreville.

## Another charter of the same earl

David, earl, sends greetings to Algar, prior, and his other brothers at Durham.

Know that on my behalf I give and grant Swinton to you, free and quit, to do with it according to your will, just as my brother King Eadgar gave it to you and offered it upon the altar, and as his writ bears witness that it belongs to your use.

And know for certain that I do not wish henceforth to allow anyone in any way to inflict injury or trouble upon you concerning it.

Witnesses: Queen Matilda and her son William.

On the seal of David the earl appears an armed horseman, with the inscription:

+ SEAL OF DAVID, EARL OF THE ENGLISH, BROTHER OF THE QUEEN.

His sister Matilda married Henry I, king of England.

## Charters of Henry the earl

[Col. 0368C]

Henry, earl, son of the king of Scotland, sends greetings to his justices, barons, sheriffs, reeves, ministers, and all his good men throughout his entire county of Northumberland, French and English.

Know that the lands and possessions of the monks of Durham are in my peace and under my protection. Therefore I firmly command all my officials to maintain their men and property, and I forbid anyone to wrongfully dispossess them, on pain of incurring my full forfeiture.

Witnesses: Eng., chancellor, and Gill de Umfraville. At Newcastle.

## Another charter of the same earl

Henry, earl, son of the king of Scotland, sends greetings to Gisl. de Umfraville, his constable, and to all his other barons and men.

Know that the land and possessions of the monks of Durham are in my own hand, under my own protection, and in my peace. Therefore I command you all, and order you, to preserve peace for all their lands and possessions and to have it preserved by all your men, steadfastly and everywhere, as you love me.

Witnesses: Osbert, prior of Jedburgh, and Richard, prior of Hestoldesham. At Jedburgh.

Henry was the son of David I, king of Scotland, and died during his father’s lifetime in 1152. His seal is almost the same as that of his father David when he was earl, but bears this inscription:

+ SEAL OF HENRY, EARL OF NORTHUMBERLAND, SON OF THE KING OF SCOTLAND.

## Charter of Count Gospatric

[Note: In 1139 King David confirmed this donation of Gospatric. He renewed his confirmation in 1167, “except for the thirty shillings which the monks shall give to his son Gospatric and his heirs every year as the king’s *conredium*, and except for the king’s army, for which the monks shall attend the king, while Gospatric shall be quit of military service.”]

### Charter of Gospatric, earl of Dunbar

To all the sons of God’s holy Church, both high and low, ordained and lay, Gospatric, earl and brother of Dolfini, sends greetings.

Know that I have granted and given to God and Saint Cuthbert and his monks, as an alms-gift, the vill of Edrom and its church with all its chapels, and another vill called Nesbit, free and quit to be possessed forever, with everything belonging to those vills in lands and waters, meadows, and pastures, for the soul of King Malcolm and his sons, Kings Eadgar and Alexander, and for King David and his son Henry, and for myself, my wife, and my sons, and for the souls of all my parents.

If anyone wishes to contradict this alms-gift of mine, let the matter be between him and God.

Witnesses: William, son of Dun.; Gospatric, his son; Ulkil, son of Meld.; Raud, son of Lind.; S., priest; John, chaplain; Gospatric, son of Crin.; Aldan, his brother; Lambert the steward.

Farewell.

Whoever takes this away, may God take away from him both this life and the kingdom of heaven.

## Charter of Gospatric’s son

Gospatric, earl, sends greetings to all the sons of holy Church.

Know that I have granted and confirmed by this charter of mine to God and to the brothers of the church of Saint Cuthbert at Durham, serving God there, the alms-gift which my father gave them and I have given them—namely, Edrom and Nesbit, and the church of Edrom with all the appurtenances which my father gave them and confirmed by his charter.

Witnesses: Andrew, archdeacon; Adam, his brother; Nigel, chaplain; Ketel, son of Dolfini; Ernald; Alden, steward; Adam, son of Alden; Adam, son of Gospatric.

## Charter of Thor Long

To all the sons of holy mother Church, Thor Long sends greetings in the Lord.

Know that Eadgar, my lord, king of the Scots, gave me Ednam, which was deserted. With his help and my own money I inhabited it and built a church in honor of Saint Cuthbert.

I gave that church, together with one ploughland, to God and Saint Cuthbert and his monks to possess forever. I made this donation for the soul of my lord King Eadgar, for the souls of his father and mother, for the salvation of his brothers and sisters, for the redemption of Lefwin, my dearest brother, and for the salvation of my own body and soul.

If anyone should presume by force or cunning to take this donation of mine away from the aforesaid saint and the monks serving him, may almighty God take from him the life of the heavenly kingdom, and may he suffer eternal punishments with the devil and his angels.

Amen.

## Another charter of the same man

To his most beloved lord David, earl, Thor, wholly yours, sends greetings.

Know, my lord, that King Eadgar, your brother, gave me Ednam, which was deserted. With his help and my money I inhabited it and built a church from the foundations. Your brother the king caused it to be dedicated in honor of Saint Cuthbert and endowed it with one ploughland.

I gave this same church to the aforesaid saint and his monks for the soul of that same lord of mine, King Eadgar, and for the souls of your father and mother, and for your salvation and that of King Alexander and Queen Matilda.

Therefore I ask you, as my most beloved lord, that for the souls of your parents and for the salvation of the living you grant this donation to Saint Cuthbert and to the monks who will serve him forever.

The seal of Thor Long shows the figure of a seated man, bareheaded, holding the hilt of a sword in his right hand and its blade in his left. The inscription of the seal is:

THOR SENDS ME TO A FRIEND.

David the earl confirmed this donation.

## Charter of Bishop Robert of Saint Andrew’s

[Note: King David confirmed this charter; Alexander and Pope Urban later examined that confirmation together with Robert’s charter. When a dispute arose concerning procurations between Hugh, bishop of Saint Andrew’s, and the convent of Durham, Bernard, prior of Newburgh; William, abbot of Alnwick; Geoffrey, prior of Brinkburn; and Master Bernard sent to Pope Urban a certificate of all these instruments. From him they received, together with J., archdeacon of Dunkeld, the authority to settle this dispute. The document sent to the lord pope still survives in the archives of Durham, containing the allegations of both parties under the seals of these men, except for the archdeacon of Dunkeld, who withdrew.]

To all the faithful of holy mother Church, clerical and lay, present and future, Robert, by the grace of God bishop of Saint Andrew’s, sends greetings.

Let it be known to you all that, in the presence of our lord King David, Turstin, archbishop of York, Ranulf, bishop of Durham, John, bishop of Glasgow, Geoffrey, abbot of Saint Albans, and many other persons, we summoned Algar, prior of Saint Cuthbert at Durham, before the door of the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Roxburgh.

There, insofar as episcopal authority is concerned, by the attestation and protection of this present charter, we publicly declared, granted, and confirmed the church of Collingham, free and quit forever, both from us and from our successors, from every claim, custom, *cana* and *cunevethe*, and from every service belonging to us or to our successors.

Therefore we wish, and by episcopal authority confirm, that the church of Collingham and every church or chapel which from now on shall canonically belong to the church of Saint Cuthbert shall be free and quit forever from every episcopal aid, *cana*, and *cunevethe*, so that they shall be freer and quieter than any other churches in Lothian.

And I forbid any bishop, archdeacon, or dean from now on to demand any custom or aid from them, unless they should perhaps wish to give it freely.

We did all this at the request and on the advice of our lord King David and the aforesaid bishops, our brothers, for love of Saint Cuthbert and in fellowship with the monks of Durham, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, on the feast of Saint Kenelm the martyr, in the year 1127 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

Present as witnesses: Robert, my brother; Blahan, priest of Linton; Aldulf, priest of Aldenhansoc; Henry, priest of Lemhale; and others; Godwin, priest and steward; Godwin, chamberlain; and many other religious persons, both clerical and lay.

# Number XVII [Smith XXI]

*(Certain charters made before the Conquest, all recently in the possession of the most honorable D. D. Somers.)*

## Charter of King Aethelred to Bishop Oftfor

The Apostle Paul, speaking most explicitly about the Lord’s final judgment, says:

“For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, [Col. 0370D] whether good or evil.”

But what the Apostle affirms that each person will receive according to his merits, the Lord himself reveals in his Gospel, saying:

“The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

I, Aethelred, king, by Christ’s gift, continually [Col. 0371A] dread this truly fearful and terrible judgment of almighty God with all the fear of my heart. Therefore, so that there I may deserve to obtain pardon in the presence of the gracious Judge for the absolution of crimes, whether my own or those of my former wife Osthryth, I have transferred to Bishop Oftfor the land called Fledanburg, containing forty-four hides, to be possessed by him, so that, just as it was originally transferred, through his diligence the most honorable religious life of the monks dwelling there under an abbot might be restored.

If any obstinate person should attempt to oppose this donation with a spirit of violation and should try to break it, let him know that he will suffer the due penalties under the fearful judgment.

+ I, Aethelred, confirming my own donation, have subscribed under the title of the holy cross.  
+ I, Headda, bishop, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Torchctuald, the king’s earl, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Eadwald, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Cille, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Osfrith, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Ecfrith, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Tuddul, have consented and [Col. 0371B] subscribed.  
+ I, Gudhlac, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Sigivald, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Folchere, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Berhttred, have consented and subscribed.  
+ I, Oftfor, bishop, confirming with my own hand the donation which I received from the king, have subscribed below.

[Note: This charter was made around the year 692.]

## On the back: the charter of Bishop Ecguine

I, Ecguine, by God’s dispensation successor to the most reverend Bishop Oftfor, have become his successor in the episcopate.

The monastery called Fledanburg, which is preserved in this same charter, on its other side, as having been transferred to the aforesaid predecessor of mine by royal subscription, I grant in possession, as far as I am able, to this venerable secular prince, Aethilhaeard. This is on the condition, however, that the regulations of monastic life should always be observed there.

In exchange for this donation of ours, I have received from him, for ecclesiastical right, twenty hides of land in the place called Aet Stretford. It should nevertheless be known that I wished to do this for a reasonable cause: namely, that he should receive forty-four hides of land in exchange for the twenty hides, on the condition that after his death this land should be given, without anyone’s contradiction, to the church of Uuegern, under the jurisdiction of the episcopal see, as an eternal alms-gift to me and to my predecessor Oftfor.

Peace be upon those who confirm and preserve this. May eternal dispersion come upon those who diminish or contradict it.

Aethelric, Aethelvueard, Aethelberht, Omoling, abbot: these are the confirmers and witnesses.

## Charter of Aldred, sub-king of the Hwicce

+ Reigning Lord throughout the ages of ages.

I, Aldred, sub-king of the Hwicce, with the permission of the venerable Bishop Tilhere, give that monastery at Flaedanbyrg to Aethelburg, my kinswoman, before the witnesses named below, on the condition that she possess it for as long as she lives, and after she goes the way of her fathers, return it to the church of Uuegern, under the jurisdiction of the episcopal see.

And I command her, in the holy name of the Ruler above the heavens, that she have neither God’s nor my permission to change this into anything else, but that she fulfill it just as it was commanded by Aelfred, Aethelheard, and Bishop Ecguuine, who previously held this land and handed it over to us.

Let her complete and fulfill this our alms-gift.

I, Aldred, shall confirm this donation of mine with the sign of the holy cross.

+ I, Tilhere, bishop, shall confirm this petition of mine by subscribing.  
+ I, Aethelburg, abbess, have subscribed, consenting most willingly.  
+ I, Creda, abbess.  
+ I, Bacola, abbess.  
+ I, Tadhere.  
+ I, Guthheard.  
+ I, Humberlit, priest.  
+ I, Cyneberht.  
+ I, Cuthred.  
+ I, Dudda.  
+ I, Ceobba.

We have all subscribed and confirmed our testimony by consenting.

## Charter of Offa, king of the Mercians, and Aldred, sub-king of the Hwicce

[Col. 0372A]

+ In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who continually governs all ages with pious direction.

It is therefore established and plainly evident as unquestionable truth that all things seen here by human strength are vain, fleeting, and transitory, while those things hidden from human eyes remain forever and endure steadfastly through the ages without end.

It is also most certainly known, on the authority of the testimonies of the sacred books, that through these fugitive worldly things they may purchase the eternal kingdoms of heaven.

Therefore I, Offa, king of the Mercians, by the free grace granted by God the Father, imitating the example of my ancestors, considered in my heart how, from these worldly royal scepters and kingdoms received from the Creator and giver of all good things, I might give something, however unworthy, for the remedy of my soul and for gaining the rewards of heaven, for the uses of monastic generosity and to the churches.

Accordingly, I and Aldred, sub-kings of the Hwicce, jointly, for almighty God and for the eternal salvation of our souls, freely grant to the monastery called Aet Wiogorna Ceastre and to the church of blessed Mary, mother of the Lord, founded there, in ecclesiastical possession, land comprising ten hides twice over—that is, the estate called Oetgeate—with the same freedom in every respect under the right of that church with which King Aedhilbald wrote it to my grandfather Eanulf.

That is, in all cases, great and small, it shall remain free and undisturbed forever, for as long as the faith of Christ remains strong among the English in Britain . . . Let it be free from every power of kings and princes and their subjects.

In the highest name of God we command this.

And so that this munificence of ours, granted for Christ, may remain perpetually with the stronger stability, we have caused the signs and names of the witnesses, consenting bishops, abbots, and princes to be written below in this charter as testimony.

+ I, Offa, by the Lord’s permission king of the Mercians, have impressed the banner of Christ’s cross with my own hand upon this donation of ours for greater security.  
+ I, Aldred, by God’s gift sub-king of the Hwicce, place upon this donation of ours the sign of the saving cross before all peoples.  
+ I, Eadberht, bishop, by the permission of Christ the Lord, have consented to and subscribed these words.  
+ I, Berhthun, prelate, by the gift of the Lord and Father, have consented to and subscribed these provisions.  
+ I, Ceolulf, bishop, by God’s grace permitting it, have consented to and subscribed these matters.  
+ I, Tilhere, priest, by the gift of predestination, have consented to and subscribed these affairs.  
+ I, Alberht, bishop of the church, by the Lord’s grant, have consented to and subscribed these gifts.

+ Mark of the hand of Botwin, abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Folcberht, [Col. 0372D] abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Brordani, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Beorhtwald, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Esne, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Eadbald, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Eadbald, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Brordan, prefect.

## Charter of Uhtred, sub-king of the Hwicce

+ In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I, Uhtred, with God’s predestining permission, holding some authority over my own people, the Hwicce, and following the examples of my fathers, have considered how from the portion of this worldly government I might generously give something into ecclesiastical freedom for the redemption of my soul.

Therefore, with the permission and consent of the most pious king of the Mercians, Offa, I shall give to my beloved and faithful servant Ceolmund eight hides, with everything belonging to them . . . . . . in Habene Homme . . . . . . of ecclesiastical right [Col. 0373A] forever, for almighty God, so that while he lives he may have and possess it, and after him may leave it by hereditary right to whichever man he wishes, to be possessed with the same freedom with which it was granted to him.

That estate lies on the southern side of the hill called Breodun, on the northern side of the stream called Carent. It extends from that river Carent, rising up to the summit of the aforesaid hill Breodun, on whose summit there is a city called by the ancient name Baenintesburg. There is the boundary of that estate, again on the hill; and from the south the River Carent descends through the plain.

Therefore, so that this donation of mine, granted for the deliverance of my soul, may remain all the more firmly . . . I write below the signs and names of the witnesses and consenters.

+ I, Offa, king of the Mercians, consenting to this donation of my sub-king, have impressed the sign of the holy cross for greater security.  
+ I, Aldred, ruler, strengthening my munificence, have placed the venerable sign of Christ’s cross.  
+ I, Eadberht, by the grace of the Lord bishop, have consented and subscribed.  
+ Mark of the hand of Curan, abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Uvillan, abbot.  
+ I, Berthun, by God’s gift prelate, have consented and subscribed.  
+ Mark of the hand of Tredan, abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Bacolan, abbot.  
+ I, Tilhere, by God’s gift prelate, have consented and subscribed.  
+ Mark of the hand of Uvillan, abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Tilberht, abbot.  
+ Mark of the hand of Brordan, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Esne, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Cudred, prefect.  
+ Mark of the hand of Beorhtwald, prince.
