+ Mark of the hand of Dudda, butler.

+ These things are certain in the year 756 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the third year of the reign of Offa, king of the Mercians.

## Charter of King Offa

+ Seeing before our eyes the momentary and perishable existence of all this unstable life [Col. 0373C] and the departure of those presently near us, we must hasten with the greatest urgency to work for everyone, as the truthful assertion of apostolic teaching proves, and especially for those who are members of the household of faith.

Therefore I, Offa, king of the Mercians and also of the other surrounding peoples, supported by heavenly mercy, give to the church which my grandfather Eanulf built in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, at the place called Aet Breodune, for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors, land of twenty hides at the places called Aet Wersdhille and Aet Coftune, together with the wood adjoining that land.

It is to remain for the use of the bishop of the church of Worcester, with its meadows, pastures, streams of water, and without any obstacle of contradiction from my future princes or dukes.

Let that land be free from every exaction of kings, princes, and their subjects, except the repair of bridges and fortresses and military expedition.

In the year 780 from the Lord’s Incarnation this grant of land was written by me and by my bishops and princes, whose names I shall record below.

+ I, Offa, by God’s gift king, protect this donation of mine with the sign of the holy cross.  
+ I, Cynethryth, by the grace of God queen of the Mercians, have consented to and subscribed this donation of the king.

+ I, Joanberht, archbishop.  
+ I, Eadberht, bishop.  
+ I, Ciolwulf, bishop.  
+ I, Tilhere, bishop.  
+ Mark of the hand of Brordan, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Berhtrud, duke.  
+ Mark of the hand of Eadbald, prince.  
+ Mark of the hand of Eadbald, duke.

## Council at Clofesho, in the time of Biornwulf, king of the Mercians

In the name of the triune God, who is blessed forever. Amen.

“The year since Christ’s birth had passed eight hundred and twenty-five, and the latter indiction was in its course; and it was the reign of Biornwulf, king of the Mercians. [Col. 0374A]

Then there was a synodal assembly at the famous place called Clofesho; and there King Biornwulf himself, his bishops, his chief men, and all the councillors of this people were gathered.

Then there was much discussion about the wood-pasture at Sutton, opposite Scirhylte to the west. The swine-reeves wished to drive the pasture further and improve the wood, because these were ancient rights.

Then the bishop and their councillors said that they would not concede to him more than had been ordained in Aethelbald’s day: three hundred swine for mast, and that the bishop was then to have two-thirds of the wood and of the mast.

Then Archbishop Wulfred and all the councillors decreed that the bishop and his household might establish on oath that it had been so ordained in Aethelbald’s day and that he had demanded no more. The bishop immediately pledged Eadwulf the alderman to that oath before all the councillors, and a term of thirty nights was allowed him to come to the episcopal seat at Worcester. [Col. 0374B]

At that time Hama was swine-reeve at Sutton, and he rode until he was at the city; he saw and examined the oath, as his lord Eadwulf had commanded him, but nevertheless did not greet him.

These are the names and designations of those who were assembled at the synodal council:”

+ Sign of the hand of Biornwulf, king of the Mercians. + Wulfred, archbishop, have consented to this agreement. + Oethelwald, bishop, have consented. + Hraethun, bishop, have consented. + Heaberht, bishop, have consented. + Bionna, bishop, have consented. + Eadwulf, bishop, have consented. + Wilred, bishop, have consented. + Wigthgn, bishop, have consented. + Albstan, bishop, have consented. + Humberht, bishop. + Ceolberht, bishop. + Cynred, bishop. + Torhthelm, prior. + Eanmund, abbot. + Wihtred, abbot. + Cuthwulf, abbot. + Eanmund, abbot. + Eathberht, ealdorman. + Biornoth, ealdorman. + Sigred, ealdorman. + Cudthred, ealdorman. + Eadwulf, ealdorman. + Mucel, ealdorman. + Uhtred, ealdorman. + Allhheard [Col. 0374C], ealdorman. + Bolom. + Aldran. + Bynna. + Wighelm. + Heaberht, bishop. + Eadgar, priest. + Wigberht, priest. + Heahstaef, priest. + Brada, priest. + Cuthbald, priest. + Regngar, priest. + Cuthbert, priest. + Ecgmund, priest. + Heahferhth, deacon. + Wighelm, deacon. + Cyneberht, deacon.

With all the other priests, apart from these mass-priests: likewise sixty.

## Chirograph of Alhwine, bishop of the Hwiccas, and Aethelwulf, ealdorman

+ In the name of the Lord. Certainly, those things which are composed by wise and prudent men, and also by bishops and [lacuna] as wholesome and necessary, ought to be written and marked with lettered characters and with the established signs of documents, lest perhaps the learning of the philosophers and Stoics be handed over to oblivion.

Therefore I, Alhwine, by the grace of God bishop of the province of the Hwiccas, and my community, at Worcester, have granted to Aethelwulf, ealdorman, and his wife Wulfthryth, eleven cassates in two places, namely at Codes Wellan and at Sture. We have written these lands to them for their lifetime under this condition: that they shall possess themselves, both while living and afterward, reconciled and joined to Worcester, with their bodies and all their best goods, whatever they may possess, if God should provide that they rest in this land on this side of the sea.

For this matter they have also agreed that the aforesaid prince Aethelwulf shall preserve the liberties of that church at Worcester and of the monasteries belonging to it, with true friendship and good devotion, without fraud, for as long as life remains to him here. He shall never break or diminish this arrangement, nor consent to any of his successors doing so.

And Aethelwulf, ealdorman, shall have this matter fixed for the bishop and his community in the four books of the Gospels of Christ, with its charter, and under God’s surety of bread, so that he may keep it firmly.

After he or his wife has gone along the way of the fathers, let the aforesaid lands return to the church at Worcester [Col. 0375A] without any obstacle, together with all the goods then found there.

If what we do not wish should happen—if anyone should presume, through devilish teaching, to break this arrangement—then let the bishop and his community be free to enjoy their own land as they please. Let peace and happiness be granted to those who consent to and preserve this decree of ours, here and in the future. But let eternal vengeance or destruction come upon those who oppose or diminish it, unless they make amends here before God and men with satisfaction.

This charter of donation is dated in the year of the Incarnation of Christ 855, in the third indiction, in the metropolitan place called Worcester.

+ These are the witnesses and confirmers of this donation, whose names are written below.

+ I, Aethelwulf, ealdorman, have consented and subscribed. + I, Ahlwine, bishop, have consented and subscribed to this donation of mine.

+ I, Cuthheard, priest and provost, have consented [Col. 0375B]. + I, Ahlmund, priest, have consented. + I, Wulfheard, priest, have consented. + I, Ecgberht, priest, have consented. + I, Ciolberht, priest, have consented. + I, Daehheh, priest, have consented. + Baldred, deacon. + Eueferth, deacon. + Wuihhere, deacon. + Putta. + Leofmon.

## Agreement between Burgred, king of the Mercians, and Wulferd

+ With God and our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 866, in the tenth indiction, I, Burgred, king of the Mercians, with the consent and permission of my elders, willingly grant and give to Wulferd a part of the land of the kingdom given to me by God: two hides at Soeges Lea, belonging to the place which the country people call Wulfferdinleh, so that he may possess and enjoy it well as an eternal inheritance and may leave it after himself to whomever he wishes [Col. 0375C], in perpetual right, with all the goods belonging to this land, anciently and formerly established, in fields and pastures and parts and woods, and whatever belongs to this land.

I, Burgred, king of the Mercians, shall augment this gift of mine to Wulferd. I shall assign to him seventy fattened swine from that common woodland assessment which the country people call Wulfferdinleh, and five loads of good rods, and every year one oak for building, together with other necessary timber, and an abundance of firewood as he needs it. I shall also give him the woodland assessment belonging to him on the other side, in field and wood, just as it belongs to the land of the two hides.

I, Wulferd, in purchase and exchange for this little parcel of land, Wulferdinlea, have given to Burgred, king of the Mercians, land of five hides, free for the lifetime of this man, and four hundred shillings in pure silver, and two horses with all their equipment, and eight oxen, and fifty swine, and two hundred crops with all their grass, and thirty measures [Col. 0375D] of threshed barley, without tribute and without suburban dues.

This aforementioned little parcel of land, Wulfferdinlea, is encircled by these boundaries:

“Here is the land-boundary at Wulfferdinlea: from Sture to Honey Brook; then along the brook to the old hedge; along the hedge to the old way; along the way to the great street; along the street to the four-boundary houses; from there to Caleb Brook; along the brook to Horse Brook; along the brook to the ditch; along the ditch to Sture; again from Sture to the ditch; along the ditch to the place called Cuth’s Thorn-tree; along the ditch to Heasecan’s Barrow; from Heasecan’s Barrow to the ditch; along the ditch to Wenferth; along Wenferth again to Sture.”

If anyone wishes to preserve this donation of mine, may heavenly mercy preserve him here and in heaven. But if anyone attempts to diminish or break it, let him know that he is accursed before the highest God, unless he makes worthy amends here before God and men. Here were present the witnesses whose names are set out below.

[Col. 0376A] + I, Burgred, king of the Mercians, shall strengthen this donation of mine with the sign of Christ’s holy cross. + I, Aethelswith, queen, have consented and subscribed. + I, Ceolworth, have consented and subscribed. + I, Wulfsig, bishop, have consented and subscribed. + I, Eadbald, bishop, have consented and subscribed. + I, Ceored, bishop, have consented. + I, Alhhun, bishop, have consented. + I, Deorlaf, have consented and subscribed. + I, Aldred, abbot. Humberht, ealdorman. Beornoth, ealdorman. Beornard, ealdorman. Eamberht, ealdorman. Mucel, ealdorman. + I, Aethelwulf, ealdorman. Aethelheard. Berhtferth. Aethelred. Berhtric. Ceolmund. Boldred. Eadgar. Mucel.

## Charter of Aethelred, ealdorman of the Mercians, which Wanley rightly suspects to be of doubtful antiquity and authenticity

+ With our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the year of his Incarnation 884, in the second indiction, I, Aethelred, supported by divine grace in the principate and dominion of the people of the Mercians, grant to Aedhelwulf land of five hides at the place called Hymeltun.

I grant the aforesaid land with everything belonging to it: woods, meadows, pastures, and salt-boiling places—that is, where six vessels may be prepared—free from any tribute imposed by the ruler of the aforesaid people, or by ealdormen, judges, or officials, whether in stationing or in the loading of carts, except by the one who is lord of the aforesaid land of Hymeltun.

With the testimony and consent of those whose names are written below, this is granted. Under the governance of Aethelred, ealdorman, of the aforesaid noble people of the Mercians, it was enacted at Hrisbyri, where their public assembly was then held, as they discussed among themselves the necessary ordinances of the aforesaid people.

O you men of every age to come, I beseech you, by the words of the fearsome, discerning, and just Judge, that this grant, whether in the aforesaid land or in the salt-village, remain perpetually free from every census and tribute. If anyone—what we do not wish—should corrupt and violate the agreement, let him know that he will have to render an account on the day of judgment before God and his angels, unless he first takes care to make amends with worthy satisfaction.

The names of the third group of those consenting and writing are these:

I, Aethelred, governing the dukedom of the people of the Mercians, have taken care to confirm and subscribe. Wulfred, bishop, have consented and subscribed. I, Werfrith, bishop, have consented and subscribed. Deorlaf, bishop, have consented. Athelwald, ealdorman. Aedulf, ealdorman. Beornath, ealdorman. Aethelferth, ealdorman. Alhhelm, ealdorman. Eardwalf. Elfwald. Eadnoth. Aelfred. Aethelmund.

“These are the land-boundaries: first to the black pool; from the pool to the [uncertain: ‘how upon how eathland’], all the way until the ox turns; then it comes to the boundary hedge toward Grafton; then to Aesebed; from Aesebed along three furrows to the hollow way; from the way to the bishop’s wood; from there to the ditch-way; from the way into the little grave, then into the old ditch; then [uncertain] into Grobb’s valley; then [Col. 0376D] to the port-street; from the way into Maerford; from the ford into Hnutfen; from the fen into the old cottage; then to Graf Ridge; from the ridge into the dwelling-way; from the way onto Uffan Lea; from that lea to the little brook; then to Hymel Brook; along the brook upward to Egcbyrht’s croft; then upward toward the two crofts to the street at Ipwael Hill; along the street into Hennuc; then into Rugan Meadow; from Rugan Meadow again to the black pool.”

## Charter of Bishop Uuerfrith

+ In the name of our Lord, the saving Christ, I, Uuerfrith, bishop, with the consent of all the community, at Worcester, young and old, grant to Cyneswith, my kinswoman, three hides of land at Alhmundingtun, the life-hides which the community had previously chartered to me for the lifetime of three men.

Now I write it again for her, with their consent: three hides of land for the lifetime of three men, and she shall have the right to exploit the wood in the wood which the ceorls use. I also grant her separately the ceorls’ grove. In addition, the two hides of land, the ceorls, and the Alhmunding woodcutting shall belong to the three boroughs for as long as it remains unbroken.

Cyneswith shall not grant it to any other man for as long as it remains unbroken, except to one of her children, whichever one she wishes, if she lives then. If she does not live then, she shall grant it to whichever of her kinsmen she wishes, according to what she has earned.

And I, Uuerfrith, bishop, ask and beseech that these three hides of land, and also the wood, when it reverts, be given to Clive, to the bishopric, without any contradiction. And I, Uuerfrith, bishop, and all the community beseech our successors that none of them should alienate this gift before it reverts, as it stands in this writing.

All the community went to my dwelling at Worcester and gave me their hands in pledge for this agreement. Their names are written below [Col. 0377B]. They shall have it freely in every respect, except that each year they shall give three measures of wheat as church-scot to Clive.

At the lower part of this charter are half-letters forming this word, namely: chirograph.

+ Werfrit, bishop. + Cynhel, abbot. + Werfridh, priest. + Ecfrith, priest. + Wighard. + Berhthelm. + Eardwulf. + Wulfred. + Berhthelm. + Cynah. + Eamberht. + Wullaf. + Cynhelm. + Cenfrith. + Cynhelm. + Heahred. + Wulfgar. + Eardwulf. + Cynelaf. + Wigfrid. + Wulfric. + Ceolhelm.

## Charter of King Eadred

+ By the gracious will of God, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 946, after the death of King Edmund, who had ruled royally for seven years over the kingdoms of the Angles, Saxons, and Northumbrians, and over the pagans and Britons, it happened that his uterine brother Eadred, chosen in succession by the leading men, was consecrated that same year as king and ruler in Catholic fashion, by pontifical authority, for the kingdoms under the fourfold administration.

This king, finally, in the estate called King’s Town—where his consecration was also performed—perpetually bestowed many gifts upon many people. This Wulfric, his eager foot-servant, can certainly praise with joy; the same king honors and enriches him with generous largesse, granting him land of seven hides to enjoy in perpetual right, bounded by definite paths, as is said below, at Wurcingtun, with great and small appurtenances, except the fortress and bridge and the service of the army which had been appropriated.

This appropriation, moreover, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 846 and in the first cycle-year in which the scepters of the crowned Angles and Northumbrians, and of the pagans with the Britons, were governing, was carried out in this manner, with the following witnesses writing their names.

+ Eadred, king, with the archbishop and the other bishops, appropriated this land with the trophy of victory.

+ Oda, archbishop. + Wulfstan, archbishop. + Dheodred, bishop. + Aelfhaeh, bishop. + Wulfgar, bishop. + Koenwald, bishop. + Aelfric, bishop. + Wulfhelm, bishop. + Wulfsige, bishop. + Aelfred, bishop. + Aethelgar, bishop. + Aethelwald, bishop. + Hopael, sub-king. + Marcant; Cadmo. + Aethelmund, ealdorman. + Alhhelm, ealdorman. + Aethelstan, count. + Eadric, prince. + Osulf, high-reeve. + Urin, Imorcer, earl. + Grim; and Coll, earl. + Eadred, abbot. + Wigstan, abbot. + Dunstan, abbot. + Uhtred.

May those who increase the royal inscription receive an increase of the blessed reward of the eternal king. Amen.

## Charter of Bishop Oswold

[Col. 0378A]

+ I, Oswold, consecrated bishop by the abundant grace of Christ, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962, with the assent of Eadgar, king of the English, and of his leading men of both orders, grant perpetually a certain parcel of land—three cassates—which a certain matron named Alhdhrydh formerly possessed, in the place commonly called Cungle, to a certain royal minister named Alfwold, so that he may hold it with all its equipment for as long as he lives, and after his death his mother, if she survives, may receive it.

If not, after his death let it return for the use of the bishop at Worcester, free from obligation. Let the church’s due and the bishop’s burial at Worcester come under its jurisdiction. Let the other [holder] rejoice in complete freedom, except for military service and the established obligations of bridge or fortress construction.

But if anyone wishes to transfer this donation of ours to something other than what we have established, let him be deprived of fellowship with God’s holy church and be punished continually, mournfully, in the eternal fires of the abyss with Judas, the betrayer of Christ, and his accomplices, unless he makes proper amends for our decree which he has violated.

### The same

+ By the wondrous generosity of the Creator, humanity, possessing whatever temporal things it may possess, has been granted the opportunity, out of regard for piety, to offer solace reverently to all, and especially to those who, presenting worship to God, are bound to one another by the unity of their temporal bond.

Therefore I, Oswald, as the prelate of the Worcester diocese, with the power of Christ, ruler of heaven, favoring me, judged that I should act from such devotion of mind. At the command and exhortation of Eadgar, emperor of the English people, and also with the consent of Aelthere, ealdorman of the Mercians, I have granted to you, my brother Osulf, possession of five and a half hides, divided into three separate places.

First, at the place called Grimanleah, four hides, with everything properly belonging to them; secondly, at Mosleage, one hide, with all that belongs to it; thirdly, at Wican, half a hide. I have granted all these to you as a perpetual inheritance, with all the customary advantages properly attached to that land: lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting, and fisheries, so that you may hold and enjoy them throughout all your life.

Finally, when you die, leave them to whichever two heirs you prefer to possess them perpetually; and when they too have passed from this age, let the property be restored to the authority of the holy see of Mary.

May almighty God preserve in his heavenly glory, without punitive fear, those who increase and preserve this gift. Let those who diminish or despoil it know that at the last judgment they will have to render an account before God himself, the just judge of all.

“These are the boundaries of the land at Grimanleah, which they have given to the bishop. First, from the hall, by the community boundary, to Sceaccan-hall; then by the boundary of the whole enclosure to the new ditch; then upward and along the new ditch until the old hedge-row; afterward along the old hedge-row to the falc-path; then upward along the path to Christ’s mark; from Christ’s mark downward and along the old ditch, westward and northward, to Maler Brook; then onward, as Alr Brook lies upward, to the boundary of Mossetena; then by the boundary of Mossetena over Sihtferth to the old king’s enclosure; then along the old king’s enclosure northward to the old stockade; from the old stockade by the boundary of Beonetsetena to Sihtferth; and along Sihtferth into Baele, and along Baele into the fern-covered place.””

“These are the boundaries of the land at Masleage: from the old settlement westward to Gearnec; then along the brook to the boundary enclosure; along the enclosure over the field-stream to Timber Ridge; from there to Beastinc Ridge; then eastward to the black bridge; from there again to the old field.”

“These are the boundaries of the half-hide of land at Wican: first from Turtling Ford to Horse Croft; from Horse Croft by Wulfric’s boundary into the pool; from the pool upward by the spring to the lane; along the lane northward to Atling’s grassland; into the hedge, along the hedge eastward to Lawarn; along Lawarn to Streon-hall; by Streon-hall into Temede, upward against the stream; along Temede again into Turtling Ford.

And the salt spring which belongs to Grimanleah, at Broad Settlement, and the other to Niosleah, in the same settlement.”

“I, Oswold, bishop, say all this which is declared here in this book to my brother Osulf for the lifetime of three men. Whoever changes it for unjust reasons, may God blot out his name from the book of life, unless he turns to repentance beforehand.”

This charter was written with the consent of its witnesses, whose names are noted below [Col. 0379B]. Let this land be free from every king except ecclesiastical dues.

+ I, Oswald, bishop, have consented. + Wulfric, priest.

+ Eadgar, priest. + Wistan, priest. + Aelfred, cleric. + Wulfhun, cleric. + Aelfstan, cleric. + Eadwine, cleric. + Aelfgar, cleric. + Wulfheah, cleric. + Tuna, cleric. + Eadweard, cleric. + Aethelstan, priest. + Brihtan, cleric. + Wulgar, cleric. + Wenstan, cleric. + Ufic, cleric. + Leofwine, cleric. + Wulfnodh, cleric.

### Another charter of the same man

+ In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967, I, Oswald, bishop of the city of Worcester, freely grant to my kinsman Osulf two hides, at Bradanbeorh and at Holenfesten, and to two heirs after him whom he chooses. Thereafter let it return for the use of the bishop of the aforesaid city.

For the clerics of that city have received three hides at Speclea in exchange for what is called Bradanbeorh and Holenfesten, so that as long as the breath of life remains in any one of them, they may have and possess it [Col. 0379C], and thereafter let it return to the use of the bishop according to the aforesaid order.

This was done on the condition that every year, when the season of pasturing arrives, one hundred swine necessary for their use may feed there without anyone’s contradiction.

May holy Mary, holy Michael, holy Peter, and all God’s saints forgive those who preserve this arrangement. If anyone wishes to break it without just cause, may God himself turn him toward rightful repentance. If he will not, may he have God against him at the common judgment on the last day of this life.

These are the witnesses of this reconciliation, whose names are written below.

+ Wulfric, mass-priest. + Aelfred, cleric. + Byrhstan, cleric. + Ufic, cleric. + Eadgar, mass-priest. + Wulfun, cleric. + Wulfgar, cleric. + Wulfeh, cleric. + Aethelstan, mass-priest. + Aelfstan, cleric. + Aelfgar, cleric. + Leofwine, cleric.

## Charter of King Eadgar

+ In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Every generous munificence of kings ought indeed to be strengthened by a written document, lest the succession of posterity, ignorant of it, should unhappily fall into the frivolity of wickedness.

Therefore I, Eadgar, by the favor of divine grace king and first officer of all Albion, grant in eternal inheritance a certain parcel of land—ten cassates—in the place commonly called Cygtun, to my faithful minister, known by the name Alfwold throughout this island of the Gnostics [uncertain reading], so that while life accompanies him he may possess it with all its appurtenances, namely meadows, pastures, and woods, having obtained his desire; and after the end of his life he may leave it free to whichever heirs he wishes.

Let the aforesaid land be free from every earthly service, except three established obligations: military service, and the repair of bridges or fortresses. If anyone therefore wishes to transfer this donation of ours to something other than what we have established, let him be deprived of fellowship with God’s holy church and be punished continually, mournfully, in the eternal fires of the abyss with Judas, the betrayer of Christ, and his accomplices, unless he makes proper satisfaction for what he has done against our decree.

The aforesaid land is surrounded on every side by these boundaries:

“These are the land-boundaries into Cyngtun: from Weles Burn to the [uncertain: ‘how sic’]; from that stream to the ditch; from the ditch to the mere; from the mere to the street; from the street to Morthhlaw; from Morthhlaw to Thorndune eastward; from Thorndune to Hüybban’s barrow; from the barrow to the foul pool; from the foul pool to [lacuna]; from the spring to the Mercians’ mere; from the Mercians’ mere to Succan’s pool; from Succan’s pool to Grundling Brook; along the stream from that brook to Fidestan; from Fidestan to the stone; from the stone to the rough thorn; from the rough thorn again to Weles Burn.”

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 969, the chirograph of this donation was written, with the consent of the following witnesses, whose names are written below.

+ I, Eadgar, king of the English, have strengthened this with the sign of the holy cross, with the consent of my learned men.

+ I, Dunstan, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, have possessed and subscribed. + I, Oscitel, archbishop, have promptly consented.

+ I, Aelfstan, bishop, have signed. + I, Aethelwold, bishop, have consented. + I, Osulf, bishop, have confirmed. + I, Wynsige, bishop, have consolidated. + I, Oswold, bishop, have strengthened. + I, Wulfric, bishop, have consented. + I, Aescwig, abbot. + I, Osgar, abbot. + I, Aelfstan, abbot. [Col. 0380C] + I, Aethelgar, abbot. + I, Aelfric, abbot. + I, Cyneward, abbot. + I, Aelfere, ealdorman. + I, Aelfeh, ealdorman. + I, Ordgar, ealdorman. [Col. 0380B] + I, Aethelstan, ealdorman. + I, Aethelwine, ealdorman. + I, Byrhtnodh, ealdorman. + I, Byrhtferdh, minister. + I, Aelfwine, minister. + I, Wulfston, minister. + I, Aethelward, minister. + I, Eanulf, minister. + I, Osulf, minister. + I, Wulfstan, minister. + I, Leofwine, minister. + I, Aelfward, minister. + I, Aethelmund, minister. + I, Osward, minister. + I, Leofwine, minister.

### The same

We are very frequently instructed by the admonition of orthodox ecclesiastical strength that, being most subject to him and supplying what is needed, we should serve him who, arranging the structure of the whole world in wondrous and ineffable order, first fashioned the microcosm—Adam—from fourfold material, breathed into him a living spirit in its gracious likeness, and formed all things below, setting over them, for the purpose of testing, one forbidden exception. He placed him beside the delight of paradise, with Eve as his most fitting companion.

But, alas, seduced by a larval deception, enticed by the shifting and persuasive evasions of the deceitful woman [Col. 0380D], he bit the forbidden apple of the curse, and, cast down into this troubled age, earned perpetual death for himself and his descendants.

When the prophets had foretold these things, and the heavenly angel had long secretly announced the prophecies of the supreme King in orthodox teaching to pure minds, bringing a blessing from above—not as the seditious tongue of the Jews declares, but embracing the most graceful eloquence of the ancients and the moderns, overthrowing the ravings of Arius and Sabellius, frustrating them with an allegorical discourse, and calling us from the dull blindness of shadow into the joy of the heavenly inheritance—the heavenly angel, descending from the lights of heaven to the ear of the undefiled virgin, as the evangelical writings proclaim, seems to have sung wondrous songs.

To her the whole Catholic Church cries out with harmonious voice:

“Blessed are you, Virgin Mary, because you believed; the things that were spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled in you.”

Wonderful to say, the Word becomes incarnate and is embodied—that Word of whom the evangelist, rising above all the height of human understanding, says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,”

and so forth.

When that incarnation was taken from the Virgin, the crime of the ancient virgin was removed, and honor was bestowed upon all women, surpassing them in bright wonders. Thus, with the divinity of Christ remaining untouched and his humanity having suffered, freedom mercifully came to enslaved servants.

For this reason I, Eadgar, king of the English and of the other nations dwelling round about, with the high-throned one favoring me, so that I may deserve to obtain a share in the mercy of the ruler of the highest throne, grant eternal monastic privilege and freedom to the monks living according to the rule in the renowned monastery situated in the place called by the inhabitants of this region by the noble name WIGORNA [lacuna], dedicated to Mary, ever-virgin mother of our Lord, and also to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his fellow apostle Paul.

After the death of N. [lacuna], the distinguished man in whose time this restoration of freedom was granted with Christ’s assistance, let the whole congregation of the prepared monastery choose for itself, by suitable counsel, whoever it shall elect as abbot from the same brotherhood, and appoint him justly according to the regular institutions of blessed Benedict.

Let the freedom of this privilege thereafter be held perpetually by all Catholics. Let no outsider, relying on tyrannical arrogance, seize authority and exercise power in the aforesaid monastery. Let the community of that monastery, as I have said, rejoice in the privilege of perpetual freedom.

Let the aforesaid monastery be free from every earthly service under the same terms by which, as is contained in an ancient privilege, it had been freed by our predecessor, King Coenwulf, a most zealous defender of orthodox faith, while Beornod, ealdorman, held authority.

The lands which, in ancient and modern times, kings and religious men and women, and I myself, have restored by rightful grant for the use of the monks, our Lord Jesus Christ, and his mother Mary, are the following.

At the time when the property which I granted with devoted mind to the Lord had been unjustly taken away from God’s holy church, certain treacherous men, seizing new hereditary charters for themselves, issued them. But in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit we command that no Catholic person receive those documents; rejected by all the faithful, let them be counted accursed, while the ancient privilege remains continually in force.

These are the names of the lands belonging to Worcester.

In addition, I command that a quantity of three acres and two estates in the famous city which its inhabitants call Worcester be held perpetually in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ under the same condition of freedom. Also, for the making of salt, eighteen vats in two places—ten at Middlewich and eight at Nethamestwich—and a station for two furnaces at Wittun, and the vessel called Westrincge, with one hide and a half-hide at the place called Nortun, and half a hide at the place called East Westwood, shall likewise remain perpetually free [Col. 0381D].

But if anyone—what we do not wish—seduced by the madness of avarice, like an epileptic, should rashly attempt to violate the generosity of this munificence of ours, let him be alienated from fellowship with God’s holy church and from participation in the most holy body and blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, through whom the whole world was freed from the ancient enemy of the human race. Let him be assigned to the left hand with Judas, the betrayer of Christ, unless he humbly repents here with worthy satisfaction for what he has rebelliously presumed to do against God’s holy church.

Let the apostate obtain neither practical forgiveness in this life nor theoretical rest, but let him be thrust into the eternal fires of the abyss and be tortured continually in utmost misery with Ananias and Sapphira.

Written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 972, this chirograph of the munificence was made with the consent of the witnesses whose names, arranged below according to the dignity of each person in both orders, are written by the Lord’s disposition.

I, Eadgar, monarch of the English of Britain, have strengthened this miraculous gift with the holy cross. I, Dunstan, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, have confirmed the benevolence of the same king. I, Oswold, primate of the basilica of York, have given my assent to this royal gift. I, Aethelwold, bishop of Winchester, have drawn this out with my own hand in canonical subscription. I, Aelfstan, bishop of the see of London, have gladly impressed the sign of the holy cross. I, Aelfwold, bishop of the see of Sherborne, have fearlessly strengthened this gift. I, Brihwelm, servant of God’s people, have applauded this king’s generosity with joy. I, Alfwold, observer of God’s law, have impressed the figure of the holy cross at the king’s command. I, Alftan, archimandrite of the see of Rochester, have cheerfully placed the miracle of the holy cross. I, Eadelm, overseer of the entrusted peoples, have joyfully confirmed this blessing. I, Wynsige, shepherd of the spiritual fold, with God’s grace favoring me, have consolidated this grant. I, Adhulf, with the Lord’s assistance, have confirmed this gift with the trophy of the holy cross. I, Alfdhrydh, companion of the aforesaid king, have subscribed this composition with the seal of the holy cross.

I, Aelfric, abbot, have subscribed. I, Aesewig, abbot, have consented. I, Osgar, abbot, have dictated. I, Aedhelgar, abbot, have impressed. I, Cineweard, abbot, have drawn it. I, Foldbriht, abbot, have copied it. I, Aelfaeh, abbot, have confirmed. I, Sideman, abbot, have strengthened. I, Osweard, abbot, have consented. I, Brihteah, abbot, have impressed. I, Godunine, abbot, have consented. I, Brihnoth, abbot, have assented. I, German, abbot, have confirmed. I, Aelfere, ealdorman. I, Orlac, ealdorman. I, Aelhelwine, ealdorman. I, Brihnoth, ealdorman.

“This is the charter of freedom and of the lands which King Eadgar granted to God, for the praise of God, at Worcester, to Saint Mary and Saint Benedict.”

## Charter of Osuuald, archbishop

[Col. 0382C]

+ With our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, in the year of the Incarnation of the same Lord 984, and in the fifth year of the reign of our king Aethelred, I, Osuualdus, by the mercy granted by God archbishop of the church of York, having also obtained the episcopal see which is at the monastery of Worcester in the region of the Mercians, grant in possession and enjoyment to a certain kinsman of mine named Eadwig, for his most humble obedience, and to his wife named Wulfgyuu, land of three hides at the place called Wulfrintun, for the days of their lives.

If the course of the man’s life should outlast the term of his wife, let he himself be the first possessor of that land. But if she should outlive her husband, let she herself remain the first heir of the same land; and afterward, if they have offspring, let them leave it to their descendants. If they have no children, let them leave it to two heirs whom they choose, whoever remains longer after them.

Let that land be free from every secular obligation except the repair of bridges and fortresses and military service against enemies.

This charter was written and confirmed with the names of men, which are seen marked below with the sign of Christ’s cross.

+ I, Oswold, archbishop. + I, Wynsige, priest. + I, Aethelstan, priest. + I, Aelfsige, priest. + I, Eadgar, priest. + I, Wistan, priest. + I, Eadward, priest. + I, Aethelsige, priest. + I, Wulfward, deacon. + I, Aethelric, deacon. + I, Godinge, deacon. + I, Leofstan, deacon. + I, Wulfhun, cleric. + I, Cynethegn, cleric. + I, Wulfgar, cleric. + I, Leofwine, cleric. + I, Ulfic, cleric. + I, Aelfnodh, cleric. + I, Athelwold, cleric. + I, Wulfnodh, cleric.

## Agreement between Wulfric and Wulfstan, archbishop
+ Here is revealed in this document how the agreement was made which Wulfric and the archbishop drew up when he obtained the archbishop’s sister as his wife: how he promised her [uncertain: “as much”] land at Eolre-tūn and at Ribbeford for her lifetime; and he promised her [uncertain: “as much”] land at Cnihtwic. He wished to acquire it for her for the lifetime of three men, at the estate at Wincelcumbe. And he gave her [uncertain: “as much”] land at Eanulfingtūn, to give and sell to whomever she most loved during her lifetime and after her lifetime, to whomever she most loved. [Col. 0383B] And he promised her 50 mancuses of gold, and 30 men, and 30 horses.

Now Wulfstan the archbishop, Leofwine the ealdorman, Aethelstan the bishop, Aelfword the abbot, Brihteh the monk, and many good men besides them were witnesses that these agreements had thus been made, each both agreeing and consenting. Now there are two documents for these agreements: one with the archbishop at Worcester, and the other with Bishop Aethelstan at Hereford.

At the foot of the page: half of the word (a divided chirograph).

## Charter of Bishop Leofsige

+ With Christ, the disposer of all kingdoms, uniquely arranging his own creatures in weight and measure. The principal cultivators of the holy Scriptures established this by their teachings, so that whatever mortals wished to add for their needs might be fastened by the written letters, lest in later generations carefully composed arrangements should be destroyed by forgetfulness—or rather by the treacherous fraud of successors.

[Col. 0383C] Therefore I, Leofsige, bishop and pontiff by the providence of almighty God, freely and willingly grant to my faithful servant Godric, for his diligence, humble service, and worthy payment, a certain part of land, namely one hide, at the place commonly called Bishop’s Hill, with all that properly belongs to that place: pastures, fields, meadows, and, separately, fifteen acres of meadowland along the river-bank, four furlongs before Tidlington; and half an acre at Scott Hom; and twelve acres of arable land between the river and the ditch at the stone-quarry; and the enclosure at Waringwic; and the ley of the hay-yard; and the third acre of bean-land at Bishop’s Hill, so that he may possess and enjoy it safely for as long as he lives.

When his lifetime has ended, he shall leave it to any two heirs whom he chooses, still within his own family. Thereafter it shall be restored to the holy mother church of Worcester. Let the aforesaid land therefore remain free from every worldly service and tribute, except the needs of the holy church of God, or the common military expedition, or the repair of a bridge or fortification.

[Col. 0383D] These are the boundaries of the land at Bishop’s Hill: first, at the foul spring; from the spring along the boundary to Clopton’s boundary; along the boundary to the old street; from the street to the pit; from the pit to the headland; along the headlands to the middle of the high mere; from the mere along the stream to Aelfric’s bridge; from the bridge along the furrow to Slough Hill; then from there to the headland in the salt street; from the street into Scott Brook; along the brook to the outside of the croft which Wynstan built there, upon the ditch which he dug, to Scott Rife’s boundary. Along that boundary to Wilmund’s ditch-[lacuna]-boundary; along that boundary to Berland’s headland; along that boundary to Shield’s headland; along those headlands to Aelfled’s boundary; from Aelfled’s boundary to Gren’s [Col. 0384A] mere; from there to the green way; along the way back to the foul spring.

This charter too was written in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1016, in the fourteenth indiction. The aforesaid land was enclosed by these boundaries. These are the witnesses who assented, whose names are written below.

+ I, Wulfstan, archbishop of the Church of York, confirmed this. + I, Leofsige, bishop, strengthened this gift of mine with the sign of the cross. + I, Aethelstan, bishop, subscribed.

+ I, Godwine, priest. + I, Wulfwine, priest. + I, Aelmaer, priest. + I, Wulfwi, priest. + I, Aeglwine, deacon. + I, Byrhtmaer, deacon. + I, Wilstan, deacon. + I, Berhtwine, deacon.

## Charter of Bishop Lyfing

+ In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038, in the sixth indiction, I, Lyfing, supported by the help of the heavenly Ruler, with the permission of King Harold, and of Leofric, duke of the Mercians, freely and willingly grant to my faithful man, known by the name Aedhelr-[lacuna]-nuncupated, for his faithful service, a certain part of land, namely five hides, at the place which the inhabitants of that land call Hylcromba and Bocctūn, with all that properly belongs to it, so that he may faithfully enjoy it for as long as he lives and, after the end of his life, leave it to two heirs whom he chooses. ## Charter of Bishop Ealdred

+ Here it is made known in this document how Bishop Ealdred has granted Wulfgeat a certain portion of land, namely half a hide at the estate called Dictort, to hold and use for the lifetime of three men and after their lifetime. Let that land go back to whoever then wishes to govern the bishopric at Worcester, and let them thereafter be subject and obedient and follow the lordship of whoever is bishop then. And if they withdraw from any of this, let them lose the grant.

The whole community at Worcester, the community at Evesham, and the community at Pershore are witnesses to this, as are Earl Leofric, Earl Odda, Aeltric his brother, Berhtric son of Aelfgar, Owine, Wagan, Aeglric the bishop’s brother, Ceolmaer, Atsur, Esebearn, Ordwig, Aethelstan the Fat, Aelfweard at Longdon, and all the leading thegns in the shire of Worcester, both Danish and English. ## No. XVIII (Smith IX). Charter of King Eadbald concerning Northbourne

[Col. 0386B] In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Eadbald, king, son of the glorious King Aethelberht—whom Augustine, first teacher and apostle of the English, rescued with his kingdom from the eternal torments of hell and, washed clean in the font of baptism, joined to the company of the saints—having at last been cleansed from the mire of sins and led to knowledge of the Creator of all creatures through the venerable Laurence, blessed Augustine’s disciple, whom that father had ordained as his successor in the archbishopric of the still-new Church of the English, by continual sermons and by signs, as well as by the wounds which he himself endured and displayed for my sake, acknowledge and worship the Lord my God.

Therefore I, Eadbald, established upon my father’s throne, imitating my father’s footsteps, and increasing and confirming the churches of God which my father Augustine founded by his vigorous zeal and enriched with lands and many honours, gratefully grant and amicably give, for the honour of God, the holy apostles, and Saint Augustine, and for the remedy of my father’s soul and of my own and my parents’ souls, to the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul founded in the suburb of the city of Canterbury, endowed with the privilege of ecclesiastical liberty and enriched with lands and various honours, a certain part of my kingdom, thirty ploughlands called Northbourne, for the use of the monks serving God there. There lie Father Augustine and my father; there also they have decreed that archbishops and kings succeeding one another should rest; and there I command that my body be buried.

I give and endow this aforesaid land, with everything belonging to it—pastures, marshes, meadows, woods, and sea-coasts—as free and quiet in every respect as my father or I ever held any land more freely. I have confirmed this gift with the trophy of the holy cross and sealed it with my royal charter, while the archbishop, namely my baptizer Laurence, sat in attendance and commended it, and while my queen Emma and my sons Egfrid and Ercumbert subscribed, together with the two bishops Mellitus of London and Justus of Rochester, and many other counts and nobles of mine, who agreed and subscribed, wishing eternal life for the supporters and authors of this gift, but a terrible curse from almighty God, the holy apostles, and our father Augustine upon those who envy or diminish it.

I, Laurence, archbishop by the grace of God, confirm this gift with the sign of the holy cross, as I have seen the king do. I, Emma, daughter of the king of the Franks and wife of King Eadbald, have armed it with the banner of the venerable cross. I, Mellitus, bishop of London, attest to what I have seen with the sign of the holy cross. I, Justus, bishop of Rochester, approve and subscribe. I, Egbert, willingly strengthen it with the sign of the cross. I, Ercumbert, attesting by the venerable [cross], gladly grant, attest, and subscribe. I, Sueard, consented. I, Guthard, subscribe.

This was enacted in the year from the incarnation of our Saviour Jesus Christ 618, in the sixth indiction.

## No. XIX [Smith XXII]. Copy from Register III of Durham, p. 137. The election of blessed Father Cuthbert and the gift made to him of Creec

[Col. 0387A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 685, a synod having been assembled beside the River Alne, at a place called Twyforth, over which Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, presided, and since Cuthbert could in no way be drawn from his island despite many messengers and letters sent to him, I, Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians, together with Bishop Trumwine and other religious men, sailed to the island and brought him unwillingly to the synod. There, by the command of all, he was compelled to undertake the office of bishop.

To him and to all his successors, with the counsel of Archbishop Theodore, Trumwine, and the whole council, for the salvation of my soul and of my successors, I gave the estate called Creec, together with three miles around that estate. I also gave the city called Lugubalia, with fifteen miles around it, so that both he and his successors might possess these in perpetuity for the service of God, free and quiet as I possessed them, and to dispose of them according to their will.

I, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, subscribed. I, Bosa, bishop, subscribed. I, Cedde, bishop of the East Saxons, subscribed. [Note: This charter is plainly fictitious: Cedde died in the year 664; Sexwulf likewise did not become bishop of the Mercians until after the death of Ceadda, who is said to have subscribed this charter, but who nevertheless died in 672.] I, Sexwulf, bishop of the Mercians, subscribed. I, Eata, bishop of Hexham, subscribed. I, Trumwine, bishop of the Picts, subscribed. I, Ceadda, bishop of Lichfield, subscribed. I, Eadhed, bishop of Lindsey, subscribed.

This gift was written in the time of Pope Agatho, in the fortieth year of King Egfrid’s age, but in the fifteenth year of his reign.

Lord John de Kingston and Lord Richard de Castro Bernardi received the original of this copy by indenture from Roger de Alverton, by order of the lord prior.

## No. XX [Smith XXIII]. Indulgence of Thomas Appleby, bishop of Carlisle, granted in 1374 to those who travelled to the island of Saint Herbert for devotion

Thomas, by divine permission bishop of Carlisle, to his beloved son, the vicar of Crosthwaite, and so forth. We judge it worthy and just that we, who by the duty of our office are bound to be witnesses of the truth, should bear testimony to the truth.

Indeed, when we were recently reading the sacred pages, among other things we found that the venerable priest Bede, the most renowned teacher, wrote in his book on the Deeds of the English, and bore witness, that Herbert the priest was a disciple of Saint Cuthbert. He led a solitary and holy life on an island in the River Derwent, but used to visit Saint Cuthbert once every year and receive salutary instructions from him.

[Col. 0387D] It happened that Saint Cuthbert came to the city of Lugubalia, now called Carlisle. When Herbert heard this, he approached him in his customary manner. Among other things Saint Cuthbert told him that the dissolution of his body was soon to come and that this had been divinely revealed to him. Hearing this, Lord Herbert cast himself with tears at the feet of the holy bishop, beseeching and praying him to obtain from the Lord that, just as they had served the Lord in life with one and the same spirit, so they might depart from this world at one and the same time, death coming upon them together.

The aforesaid Bishop Cuthbert, reclining for a little while upon his elbow, soon raised himself and said to the priest Herbert: “Brother Herbert, rejoice with great joy, because what we asked of the Lord we have obtained.” This was fulfilled not long afterward. For on the thirteenth day of April the aforesaid bishop died on the island of Farne, and Herbert died on the island mentioned above.

And because we believe that this holy event is unknown to many, indeed almost to everyone, and because it does not seem good that what the Lord has deigned to reveal for the glory of his saints should remain hidden from people, we firmly command and enjoin you to go on the said thirteenth day of April to the aforesaid island of Herbert and have a Mass of Saint Cuthbert celebrated, even with chant, and to publish these letters of ours to your parishioners. In addition, we grant by these presents forty days of indulgence to all and each of those who on that day come to the aforesaid place out of devotion, in honour of Saint Cuthbert and in memory of the said Herbert.

[Col. 0388B] Written at Rose.

## No. XXI [Smith XXIV]. Letter of Waldhere, bishop of London, to Berctuald, archbishop of Canterbury

To the most reverend Berctuald, blessed in the praises of the Catholic Fathers and governing the whole of Britain, Waldhere, your reverence’s suppliant and humble servant, sends greetings.

For I have always had a devoted desire to seek the counsel of your holiness when affairs prospered and to serve your most wise commands. How much more, amid adverse and difficult circumstances, does voluntary necessity drive my ignorant smallness to consult the diligence of your prudent consideration. Since necessity now presses, I think it worthwhile to inquire earnestly of your benevolence what ought to be done.

I do not think it can have escaped your notice how great and serious were the quarrels of discord that for some time sprang up between the king of the West Saxons and the rulers of our country; and, more unhappily still, how the ecclesiastics who, willingly or unwillingly, share in the government under them became involved on both sides in this same dissension. Yet at the meetings of both parties they often confirmed peace in words and proposed an agreement, so that exiles might be removed from among us and they themselves might not attempt to inflict upon us as great an evil as they threatened in their speeches. None of these things, however, had yet been fulfilled in practice.

A few days ago they agreed by common consent that on the Ides of October all the kings of both parties, the bishops, abbots, judges, and the rest should assemble at a place called Breguntford. There, when a council of all had been gathered, the causes of all their disagreements would be determined, and whoever was convicted of having offended would make satisfaction to the other by a proper correction.

Since they have asked me, our people have urged me, and the particular needs of our church compel me, it is fitting that I be present at this council. This is especially so because both sides promise to observe the condition of the agreement which I and their bishop were peacefully and unanimously arranging.

Therefore, by the almighty Creator of all things, I beg the privilege of your holiness: deign to make known to me what I ought to do in this matter. For I cannot in any way reconcile them and become, as it were, a hostage of peace unless a very close fellowship of communion is established between us. I neither wish nor dare to do this unless your permission and will are granted, because I remember how it was decreed at last year’s synod that they were not to be admitted to communion if they did not hasten to fulfil your judgment concerning the ordination of bishops; yet, still neglecting this, they did not carry it out.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Ordination. From this letter it is clear that, during the reign of Coenred, so serious a dispute arose between the archbishop and the bishop of the West Saxons concerning the ordination of bishops that the bond of communion was severed. In the year 704 Coenred succeeded Aethelred, who had already become a monk; and since it is highly probable that the controversy concerning the ordination of bishops arose because the bishop of the West Saxons would not permit his very extensive diocese to be divided into several dioceses, it is credible that Haeddi, who died in the year 705, was at that time bishop of the East Saxons. These letters were therefore written either in 704 or in the following year.]

Therefore, although they invite me and our people entreat me, I am now more prepared to obey the command of your mouth. And you, excellent father, use prudent counsel, so that I may either agree to the voice of those who entreat me, if that pleases you, or evade it and withdraw myself from the discussions of this council, if you judge that just. Only let me remain in every way of the same mind with you.

For this reason, although I had been summoned, I did not come to the recent meeting of King Coenred, his bishops, and his other nobles, which they held concerning the reconciliation of Aelfdryth, because I did not know what your religious authority wished to decide on this matter, so that, after learning it, I might consent more freely, rather than involve myself beforehand through the initiative of others. What more? I choose what you choose, reject what you reject, and in all things share your judgment.

I have taken care to make this known to you by letter, lest it become public knowledge among many. May the divine Trinity graciously preserve your reverence, who pray for us.

## No. XXII [Smith XXV]. Charter of King Hlothar, made in the year 679

In the name of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. I, Hlothar, king of the people of Kent, seeking the remedy of my soul, give to you, Berctuald, and to your monastery, the land at Thanet called Westana, with all that belongs to it—fields, pastures, marshes, woods, small springs, and fisheries—all, as has been said, belonging to that land. As it is now possessed, I show it by the well-known boundaries, and in the same manner I grant it to you and to your monastery through my agents. You and your successors shall hold and possess it forever and defend it; no one shall contradict this, with the consent of Archbishop Theodore, Edrico son of my brother, and all the princes. As it has been given to you, so hold it, and so shall your successors.

Whoever attempts to act against this gift shall be separated from all Christianity and suspended from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. I have caused this charter of gift to remain firm in its strength, and for its confirmation I have made the sign of the holy cross with my own hand and asked the witnesses to subscribe.

Enacted in the city of Reculver, in the month of May, in the seventh indiction.

On the same day mentioned above I added another piece of land at the Stour, according to the well-known boundaries which I and my agents have shown, with fields, woods, and meadows, just as we mentioned the aforesaid land. Let this also be given by me in the same manner, with everything belonging to it, and let it remain forever in the power of the abbot. No one shall contradict it, God forbid—not I, nor my relatives, nor anyone else. If anyone acts otherwise, let him know that he is condemned by God and will render an account to God for his soul on the day of judgment.

+ Sign of the hand of Hlothar, the donating king. + Sign of the hand of Cumberct. + Sign of the hand of Cebred. + Sign of the hand of Osfrid. + Sign of the hand of Irminfrid. + Sign of the hand of Aethelmaer. + Sign of the hand of Hacan. + Sign of the hand of Ealdred. + Sign of the hand of Aldhod. + Sign of the hand of Cudhard. + Sign of the hand of Bernhard. + Sign of the hand of Uuelhisci.

## No. XXIII [Smith XXVI]. Indulgence of William, bishop of Dunblane, granted to visitors of the incorrupt body of Saint Cuthbert

To all the faithful of Christ to whom this present writing shall come, William, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Dunblane, eternal salvation in the Lord.

Among the illustrious confessors of Christ whose bodily presence protects the English Church, blessed Cuthbert is known to possess no ordinary renown for holiness. Nor is he undeservedly raised up by human praises, since through his merits the infirm obtain the grace of health. His flesh, free from decay and remaining entirely intact, seems to present him as sleeping rather than dead.

The incorrupt condition of the blessed man’s limbs is attested not only by the writing of the Venerable Bede, but also by very many testimonies of the saints, and was most clearly proved by the translation of that most sacred body.

Therefore, considering the distinction of so great a confessor, and trusting in the mercy of the highest and undivided Trinity, almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of Saint Cuthbert the confessor, and of all God’s saints, we mercifully release forty days of the penance imposed upon them to all our parishioners and to others whose diocesan bishops approve this indulgence, provided that their sins are truly repented and confessed, and that they come to his shrine for devotion and prayer and bring something with devotion from the goods granted to them by God.

Given at Durham, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1284. From the original document in the church of Durham.

## No. XXIV [Smith XXVII]. Charter of King Wihtred of Kent

+ In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ. I, Wihtred, king of the people of Kent, providing for my future, have decided to give something to Him who gives me everything. Having taken counsel, it seemed good to me to grant to the basilica of blessed Mary, Mother of God, situated at the place called Lyminge, four ploughlands called Pleghelmestun, with everything belonging to that land according to its well-known boundaries, namely Bereweg, Megwine’s road, and Stretleg.

I also grant forever to the same blessed Mary, Mother of God, a part of the little estate called Numining-seta, for the pasture of three hundred sheep, on the southern side of the river called Liminaea. We do not set out the boundaries of this little estate because they have been enclosed on every side by the inhabitants.

I wish this gift of mine to remain firm forever, so that neither I nor my heirs may presume to diminish anything from it. If anyone attempts otherwise, whoever he may be, let him know that he is transgressing under the ban of anathema. For its confirmation, because of my ignorance of letters, I have made the sign of the holy cross and asked suitable witnesses to subscribe, namely the venerable man Berctuald, archbishop.

+ I, Berctuald, bishop, consented and subscribed when asked. + Sign of the hand of Wihtred, king. + Sign of the hand of Aethelburh, queen. + Sign of the hand of Enfrid. + Sign of the hand of Aethelfrid. + Sign of the hand of Hagan. + Sign of the hand of Botta. + Sign of the hand of Bernhaend. + Sign of the hand of Theabul. + Sign of the hand of Frodi. + Sign of the hand of Aehcha. + Sign of the hand of Aesica. + Sign of the hand of Adda. + Sign of the hand of Egisberht.

Enacted in the month of July, in the thirteenth indiction. [That is, in the year 700 or 715.]

## Charter of King Aethelbald of the Mercians

I, Aethelbald, by God’s gift king not only of the Mercians but also of all the provinces generally called the southern English, for the remedy of my soul and the release of my sins, graciously give and transfer into ecclesiastical possession to my venerable companion Cyniberht, for the construction of a monastery in the province anciently called Housmere beside the river named Stour, a certain piece of land, namely ten cassati, with everything necessary belonging to it, including fields, woods, fisheries, and meadows.

He shall have the power, for as long as he lives, to hold and possess it, or to leave it to whomever he wishes, either during his lifetime or after his death. The aforesaid field lies on both sides of the aforesaid river, having on the northern side a wood called Cynibre, and on the western side another called Moereb, most of which belongs to the aforesaid field.

If anyone attempts to violate this gift, let him know that at the dreadful judgment he will have to render a terrible account to God for his tyranny and presumption.

This charter was written in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 736, in the fourth indiction.

+ I, Aethelbald, king of Britain, confirming my own gift, subscribed. + I, Wær, bishop, consented and subscribed. + I, Winfrid, bishop, by order of King Aethelbald, subscribed. + I, Aethelric, sub-king and count of the most glorious prince Aethelbald-[lacuna], consented and subscribed to this gift. + I, Ibe, although unworthy, abbot, consented and subscribed. + I, Beardberht, brother and duke of the aforesaid king, consented and subscribed. + I, Ebbella, giving my consent, subscribed. + I, Onoc, count, subscribed. + I, Oba, consented and subscribed. + I, Sigibed, consented and subscribed. + I, Bercol, consented and subscribed. + Ealduuft, consented and subscribed. + I, Cusa, consented and subscribed. + I, Dede, consented and subscribed.

## No. XXV. Commentary on Boethius’ Book on the Trinity

[Note: If you please, see the text of the Book on the Trinity among Boethius’ works, in Patrologia, vol. LXIV, col. 1247. Editor.]
of the Christian religion, etc. Wishing to descend to the treatment of the question proposed, the Philosopher first sets forth a commendation of the catholic faith, since he intends to instruct us in it. In this commendation he refutes Amrius, Sabellius, and Vigilantius, [Col. 0391C] together with those who attend to the distinction of the persons only in their names, as the following text will make clear.

He therefore commends this faith by its author, when he says “Christian,” since Christ is its author; by its practice, when he says “religion,” since its practice is the exercise of religion; by its dignity, when he says “reverence,” for only what is worthy is to be revered; by its effect, when he says “salutary,” for it produces in the believer that which confers salvation; and by its suitability, when he says “the precepts of the universal”—that is, precepts spoken universally, because they concern no one group in particular. For the Gospel rejects neither sex nor age, nor was it given to one nation, as the Law was, but was offered to all. In the Law it is said: “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob”; here, however, grace offers itself to all.

Again, he commends the faith by its worship, when he says that “its worship has spread through every quarter of the world”: it is worshiped in the South, the East, the West, and the North. He calls the Christian religion the catholic faith, through which Christians are religious—[the text is corrupt: “plures usui, re Christi”]; [Col. 0391D] that is, many wish to be regarded as religious through the catholic faith, while nevertheless thinking wrongly about it. Yet although they try, so far as lies in them, to deform it, it does not lose its own brightness. Hence he adds: “But that faith,” etc.

Since, however, faith is understood in several ways, we must determine which faith is meant here. Faith is sometimes understood as belief—for example, that we believe Christ to have been born of a virgin, to have died and been crucified, to have risen on the third day, and to be going to judge the living and the dead. But this faith does not distinguish between the faithful and the unfaithful, since the demons also possess it. Hence James says: “The demons believe and tremble.”

Faith is also called a virtue, as the Apostle defines it: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.” But this definition is given more according to the effect of faith than according to its nature. It is called “the substance of things hoped for” because through faith the things hoped for subsist in us: it makes us hope for things that are not seen. It is not called “the substance of things hoped for” because it concerns only those things about which there is hope, since hope concerns only future and good things. Faith, however, concerns future, present, and past things, and both good and evil things.

Through faith we believe that God created all things in the beginning, that Christ assumed flesh from the Virgin, and other such things that have already passed. We also believe that Christ’s true body is upon the altar while Mass is being celebrated. Again, we believe future things, such as the resurrection of the dead and the like; and we believe that the good will receive rewards, while the wicked will receive punishments. Thus faith concerns both good and evil things.

Faith, therefore, is broader than hope; nevertheless, it is called “the substance of things hoped for” in order to indicate that, just as hope concerns only things that are not seen, so also does faith. It follows: “The proof of things not seen.” [Col. 0392B] Thus we believe that the Son was begotten from the Father, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, and that the dead will rise. We cannot prove these things by any arguments; faith alone takes the place of proof.

If someone were to ask, “How do you know about the Virgin’s childbirth, or about the future state of the elect?” I have no other proof than that I firmly believe what the prophets and others who spoke through the Holy Spirit said about these things—namely, that God could in no way deceive when he spoke through them and performed miracles, and so forth. I see that most of what they said has been fulfilled, and I do not doubt that the rest will be fulfilled.

In these matters, therefore, faith alone serves as proof, because “faith has no merit when human reason supplies the evidence”; or it is “the proof of things not seen,” because faith is based solely on things that are not apparent. But it is certain that faith exists; therefore it is certain that things not apparent exist. Thus faith is the proof of things not seen—that is, it proves that things not apparent exist.

Without this faith there is no virtue and no merit. What is this? It is the first grace, [Col. 0392C] which precedes every virtue, at least by nature if not in action. This is the faith by which we believe what is called catholic. Hence in the Creed: “This is the catholic faith, which unless each person believes, etc.” It is one among all. Hence the Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism.”

If this is said of the faith by which we believe, then it is not one numerically but generically, as is found in the commentary on the Epistles. For the virtue of faith that is in me cannot be in anyone else; nevertheless, it appears to be the same as that which is in another because it is similar to it.

Here, therefore, he is discussing the virtue of faith, or rather the faith by which we believe. He says, then, that this faith is supremely powerful, and no other, and is salutary—that is, it alone confers salvation. Or “solitary,” because only this faith is powerful, not the sects of heretics. I mean that faith which is called catholic, or universal; “or” is used disjunctively. For catholic and universal are the same.

Catholic means fitting together or uniting. The faith is therefore catholic because it unites; or universal because, just as every universal contains many things and unites them in the same nature, so the catholic faith unites all people in the same sacraments, in the same hope, and in the same charity. What more need be said? It unites everyone without distinction in one new man.

Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul.” And the Apostle says: “In Christ there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither male nor female.” For there is no acceptance of persons with God. It is as if he said: Being a Jew or a man contributes nothing to salvation, nor does being a Gentile or a woman contribute anything to salvation.

Elsewhere: “Faith is the first union of the mind with God.” Here he also gives two reasons why it is called catholic or universal; but one of them seems to be the etymology of what is called universal—namely, that it has spread through all boundaries.

Rules are so called from “ruling,” because they govern us by teaching what we ought to avoid and what we ought to do. It is called universal because it embraces everyone. “Authority” is understood as something great, for it confers salvation. It has “spread,” that is, it has flowed gradually from one region to another, since perhaps there is some place where it is not practiced.

Why does he say this? Having commended the catholic faith, he adds what he thinks about the distinction of the three persons in the same essence. He himself thinks one thing, while the sects of heretics think another. They are called heretics—that is, divided—because they are separated from the unity of the Church. Here, therefore, the foundation of our faith must be laid.

The foundation of our faith is that we believe there to be one divine essence and three distinct persons: distinct, indeed, but not separated; undivided, but not conjoined. Likewise, that the Father begot the Son consubstantial with himself, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Likewise, that the three persons are subject—[the text is corrupt: “quam ex parte”]. The New and Old Testaments bear witness to this part of the faith.

The Old Testament invokes the unity of essence when it says: “Israel, your God is one God.” And: “There shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship foreign gods.” Likewise, the Truth says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.” “Whoever sees me sees the Father”—words that openly declare both the simplicity of the essence and the distinction of the persons, referring “one” to the substance and “I and the Father” to the persons.

The authority of the Old Testament also reveals this distinction of persons, namely where it says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Since God was not speaking to an angel or to any creature when he said this, he openly demonstrated a plurality of persons, which philosophers also recognized from creatures, such as Plato and others.

They understood thought and νοῦς [nous, intellect], but the magicians of Pharaoh failed with regard to the third sign. Although they understood thought and νοῦς through philosophical inquiry, they were utterly unable to comprehend the person of the Holy Spirit.

That the Father begot the Son from eternity is manifest from these words: “Today I have begotten you.” Through “today,” which signifies the present time, eternity is indicated, since eternity knows neither past nor future. Through “begotten” perfection is indicated, so that the Son is not an imperfect God, but coeternal and consubstantial with the Father.

The Greeks say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, but not from the Son, because this is not found in the Creed published at the Council of Nicaea. For this reason it was also promulgated that whoever said otherwise should be anathema. Therefore they say that we are under anathema. This is false, because we do not say something different—that is, something contrary—but rather they themselves openly speak against the Apostle. For he says: “Because he sends the Spirit of his Son, crying in our hearts, ‘Abba, Father.’” Many other authorities agree with this.

There were certain disgraceful men, whose names now offend the ears of Catholics, who, on the basis of the subject, would not concede that one God is three persons. They confused or mocked themselves with this argument: “Nothing is what it belongs to; but the divine essence belongs to three persons; therefore there are not three persons.”

Against them Augustine speaks openly in his book On the Trinity: “We say that there are three persons of the same substance.” But lest this seem to deny that the three persons are one and the same essence, he adds, as if correcting himself: “Or we say that the three persons are the same essence, not from the same essence, as though nature were one thing and person another.”

See how he professes nature and person to be the same, and therefore one nature to be three persons and three persons to be one nature.

The Incarnation of the Word also pertains to the foundation of our faith: namely, that we believe the Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin and in the Virgin. He both assumed this flesh by creating it and created it by assuming it—not by creating or forming flesh for himself in the Virgin’s womb from nothing, as certain heretics believed, but rather by assuming flesh from the substance of the Virgin, which he created by assuming it—that is, purified it. It was not conceived according to the lustful law of conception, and therefore was free from every sin, though not from the penalty of sin. [Col. 0394A] He endured this penalty not by necessity, as other human beings do, but solely by his will.

One and the same is God and man, man and God, and one and the same person. There are two natures in him, namely divine and human; three substances: flesh, soul, and divinity. Thus we must believe these and other things pertaining to the Incarnation, as well as the resurrection of the dead; all these things pertain to the foundation of our faith.

In what he says about the Trinity, he refutes Sabellius, who, on account of the simplicity of the substance, impiously confused the Trinity of persons, together with those who qualify God or attend to the Trinity only in names. In what he says about unity, he refutes Arius, who, on account of the distinction of the persons, wickedly tore apart the simplicity of the substance, as we have shown above.

“According to the Catholics,” they say, “the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.” From this arose the Vigilantian heresy. For Vigilantius transferred the principles of natural things to theology and asserted three gods.

He said that this argument was necessary: “Socrates is a man, Plato is a man, Cicero is a man; therefore there are three men and not one man.” Likewise: “Socrates is white, Plato is white, Cicero is white; therefore there are three white men and not one white man.” Therefore, if the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, there will be three gods and not one God.

He was deceived because he thought that, just as in natural things, when there is a plurality of persons, the plurality of the name of the nature and of the nature itself enters in, so that one can say “three men,” likewise in God, when there is a plurality of persons, the plurality of the name of the nature and of the nature itself enters in, so that one could say “three gods” [read ut, “so that,” for non].

It is consequently reported that blessed Ambrose, a man of remarkable simplicity, replied: “God does not save the world through dialectic.” He is also said to have prescribed that the litany should say: “From the dialecticians, deliver us, O Lord.”

Augustine, however, whom God had reserved to oppose the heresies, disproved Vigilantius’s argument in this way: “Your combination, Vigilantius, is invalid. Socrates is a man from one humanity, Plato from another, and Cicero from another; therefore it follows: ‘There are three men.’ But the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God from one and the same Deity; therefore it does not follow: ‘There are three gods.’”

When Augustine says that “Socrates is a man from one humanity, Plato from another,” he seems by these words to indicate that each human being has one nature—“one,” I mean, by the singularity of essence—as some wrongly interpret this passage.

For no nature is one by singularity of essence except the nature of the three persons. Humanity is not called one by singularity of essence, but rather by union; nor is Socrates’ unity one by singularity, but rather by union—namely, because it unites the spirit with something else.

The nature of all human beings is the same. Augustine clearly demonstrates this in his commentary on Genesis, where he says that “God created all the natures of all things in six days.” He created, therefore, diverse causes within the natures themselves, not different natures.

There is therefore not one nature of Socrates and another of Plato, nor is this so in the case of other things.

What, then, does Augustine mean? He did not say “by another singularity of essence,” but “by another alternation.” Because alternation enters into human nature through the multitude of accidents, the plurality of the name of nature and of nature itself also enters in, so that one may say: “This is one man, and that is another man,” and also: “These are two, or three, or more men.”

But because the divine nature is one and the same by singularity of essence, and alternation cannot enter into it—for there is no variety of accidents there—the divine nature and the name of the divine nature cannot receive plurality. Therefore one cannot say “two gods” or “three gods.”
