The foregoing authority of blessed Augustine must therefore be understood in this way: it dissolves Vigilantius’s argument. He is also said to have attacked him as follows: “You will no longer be called Vigilantius, but Dormitantius.”

These, then, are the beginnings of the arguments that Boethius has for dissolving the question. Some nevertheless say that Augustine produced the aforesaid argument of the heretic before he was converted.

“Where the Father”—Continuation. The catholic faith holds that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. It is also certain that there is only one God. Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, not three gods.

In saying “the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,” distinguishing three persons, he refutes Sabellius, whose heresy was that the same person was Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For he said that the Father proceeding into the Virgin was the Son. Hence he was also called a Patripassian.

In order to avoid him, the almost-libertine Semi-Arians became such: they agreed with the Catholics concerning the predicate, but concerning the subject they did not dissent from Arius, as will become clear in its proper place.

In saying “one,” he refutes Arius, Vigilantius, and their followers. Jerome openly reproves all of them when he says in his letter On the Explanation of the Faith to Pope Damasus: “Confounding Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same essence; avoiding the peculiarity of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressly according to their own properties.” Again: “For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of names—that is, persons—or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences.”

Thus Jerome speaks against them.

“What conjunction”—that is, what they derive in this way from the foregoing: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, not three gods”—is an argument of indifference, and it is one composite part.

But here, in order to understand indifference, the authorities of Augustine and Hilary must first be set forth [the printed text has praetermittendae, “must be passed over”; read praemittendae, “must be prefaced”]. Through them they wished to distinguish the Trinity of persons in the same substance, insofar as it can be known in this world.

To explain this according to the measure of our capacity, Augustine says: “In the Father there is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the connection, or harmony, of unity and equality.”

As can be gathered from the form of the words, Augustine, wishing somehow to suggest what was ineffable and incomprehensible, resorted to mathematics. Arithmeticians establish unity as the principle of numbers, since all numbers are generated from it; but unity itself is simple and is generated from no [number].

Numbers are indeed generated one from another, but generation in numbers is nothing other than their multiplication, whether by the same number or by another. By the same number, as when two multiplied by itself generates four: twice two are four. By another, as when two multiplied by three generates six: twice three, or three times two, produces six.

Since unity is the principle of numbers, generation in numbers is nothing other than multiplication. The first generation in numbers therefore occurs through multiplication by unity.

Unity itself is also multiplied by itself, in this way: “one one,” if the expression “one” were in use. But because it is not in use, we say instead: “Once one generates unity from itself,” though it does not generate itself or another, but something equal to itself.

It does not generate itself, because it is not multiplied in order to become unity, since unity already exists. Nor does it generate another, because in this multiplication there is no division of the simple essence of unity; rather, through its multiplication it generates unity in the same singularity of essence.

Hence the heretic’s argument is shown to be false: “God begot God; therefore he begot either himself or another God.” We prove by what has been said that this is false. Unity multiplied by itself generates unity, neither itself nor another.

But since saying “once one” amounts to saying “one,” or since equality is evident—[the text is uncertain here: “or a note of equality”]—we say that, when unity is multiplied, it generates equality in the same essence.

Since, however, something is always said to be equal in relation to that to which it is equal, and that to which it is equal is understood in relation to what is equal to it, from unity and equality proceeds the connection of unity and equality in the same singularity of essence.

Yet unity truly generates the connection, because it is not multiplied in order to become connection; rather, from unity and equality proceeds the connection attributed to the three persons.

For just as unity generates equality from itself in the same essence and does not generate connection, but connection proceeds from unity and equality, so, if it is permissible to compare the least things with the greatest, the Father generates from himself the Son consubstantial with him, not another God. He did not generate the Holy Spirit; rather, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son in the simplicity of his essence.

For this reason equality is also attributed to the Son. It is said that God creates all things in the Son, and not in the Holy Spirit, although the works of the Trinity are undivided.

God creates all things in equality because as much as the substantial form attributes to each thing, so much God creates in it. For as much humanity attributes to a man, so much—and neither more nor less—God creates in the man. That a man is sometimes born goitrous, or one-eyed, or possessing something of this sort, comes from contingency, not from creation; and so it is with other things.

Again, because the Son is called equality, it is said that God creates forms in the Son. This can sufficiently be explained, but it must be explained more deeply for those who understand these matters more profoundly.

Just as unity is the principle of number, so, as Boethius says in his On Music, equality is the principle of multiplicity. Where there is multiplicity, there is greater and lesser, and therefore inequality.

Equality is therefore the principle of inequality, while inequality in forms consists entirely in forms; for things are separated and distinguished from one another by forms alone. God created everything in matter.

Since the Son is called equality, as has been shown above, and equality is the principle of inequality, which consists in forms, the Son—or the Father in the Son—is rightly said to create forms.

Hilary, wishing again to explain the distinction of the persons, resorts to likenesses. He says:

“Let a lamp be kindled, and let another lamp of the same length and size be taken, whether in wax or in wood, and let it be kindled from the other. It necessarily receives the whole light from it. If the light were divided, its whole would not remain, but the whole light remains. Therefore it is not part of the light, but the whole light that has been received. The received light, therefore, is entirely of the same substance as the light from which it is received.

“But from the light from which it is received and from the light received proceeds a radiance that is wholly in the received light and wholly in the light from which it is received—that is, it is entirely of the same substance as those lights.”

Note that when fire is mentioned here, the reference is not to a coal or a flame, but to radiance, since fire is spoken of in these three ways, as Chalcidius explains in his commentary on Plato’s Timaeus.

Since radiance is an accident, how can it be said to have a substance? The substance of light is being meant; its being is spoken of as one might speak of the substance of whiteness, or rather of a form. Such things are truly said to exist, but this may be discussed elsewhere.

Although, therefore, the substance of the things mentioned is entirely the same, they are nevertheless distinguished by such a wondrous law of nature that one cannot truthfully say: “The light from which light is received is the received light,” or “the proceeding light,” or conversely. Rather, the radiance from which it is received is different from the received radiance, and the received radiance is different from the proceeding radiance.

Thus, if it is permissible to compare the least things with the greatest, the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds are entirely of one and the same substance. The whole divinity is in the Father, the whole in the Son, and the whole in the Holy Spirit. Yet the Father is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the Son; rather, the Father is one person distinct from the Son, and the Son is one person distinct from the Holy Spirit.

This likeness nevertheless lacks perfection because it concerns corporeal things, and therefore involves local separation, which cannot in any way exist among the three persons.

Let the radiance therefore be abstracted from the flame, but in such a way that there is no confusion or massing together of the lights.

This is evident in the soul. The soul generates its wisdom from itself and within itself; from the soul and from wisdom proceeds love, by which the soul loves its wisdom and wisdom loves the soul. There is no local distinction there, nor any confusion of substances.

Thus the Father begot the Son from himself, not outside himself, but in the same essence; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both in the same substance. There is no local distinction or confusion or massing together of substance.

Thus blessed Hilary resorted to likenesses, wishing to suggest the distinction of the three persons insofar as it can be known in this world.

From the first likeness, therefore, let the distinction of the three persons in the same essence be understood, together with the fact that God begot God, neither himself nor another God. From the second, let the identity of essence in the three persons be understood. From the third, let it be understood that there is therefore no local distinction, nor any massing together or confusion of substance.

It must also be known that these likenesses are useful for explaining the Apostle’s words: “Figure and radiance.” What he called “figure” he referred to the fact that the Son is called the equality of unity—that is, the first tetragon.

For “once one” is the first tetragon, which for the reasons stated above is attributed to the Son of God. Hence the Spanish Sibyl says: “When you have reached,” she says, “the ribs of the first tetragon sitting beside the ribs of the standing eternal tetragons,” etc.—thus designating the Son of God by the first tetragon and the angels by the tetragons.

She therefore affirms that this one is sitting and those are standing, as though it were proper to this one to reign, while it is proper to those, as useful servants, to stand in attendance.

What he called “radiance” he referred to the fact that the Son is called “light from light.”

Hilary, descending again more deeply, distinguishes the Trinity of persons in the same essence in theological language, saying: “In the eternal, infinity; in the image, form; in the gift, use.”

Some person, either not understanding these words or wishing, as was his custom, to discover something new, altered them: “In the eternal, infinity,” he said instead, “in the Father, eternity; in the image, form,” and so forth. But I am not concerned with this.

No one should doubt that what Hilary says—“in the eternal, infinity”—is spoken theologically. “Infinite” is a name of negation, whereas “eternal” is a name of affirmation.

Theology, however, is partly affirmative and partly negative, as blessed Dionysius makes clear by using both kinds well.

Affirmative theology is that by which we affirm of God things that may properly be said of God, such as: “God is life,” “God is truth,” and other things of this sort.

According to affirmative theology, the philosopher Parmenides gave the following description of God, which someone among the saints might even have given [perhaps read ultro, “of his own accord”]: “God,” he says, “is that for which whatever being is, is the being of everything that is.”

What did the philosopher intend? Did he establish plurality in God through “everything” and “whatever”? Far from it. Rather, he embraced only a plurality of names.

He understood, therefore, that for God to be just is nothing other than for God to be; or that for God to be great, strong, pious, and so forth, is nothing other than for God to be God. None of these things introduces any plurality into God.

Augustine says this: “Whatever is in God is God.” That is, strength in God is God, wisdom in God is God, and truth in God is God—something that cannot be true of any creatures.

Negative theology consists in denying of God, through all the names of things, what those names signify, as blessed Dionysius does in his Hierarchy, saying: “God is not truth, he is not wisdom, he is not virtue.”

Not long afterward, however, he affirms of God all the names that he had denied through affirmative theology, saying: “God is life, God is truth, wisdom, and virtue.” He was not contradicting himself, nor affirming now what he had previously denied. Far from it.

When he affirms that God is life, he affirms that God is God; but when he denies that God is life, or something similar, he does not deny that God is God. Rather, he denies to God the proper meaning of names and the distinction of states.

All names follow forms, since names are given to things from their forms. The name “man” is given from humanity, and the name “stone” from stoneness.

Because names follow forms, and because things are distinguished from one another by forms, names accordingly distinguish states. When we hear the name “man,” we distinguish intellectually the thing that is man from a stone and from other things, though we do not thereby comprehend any individual man distinctly.

Likewise, the name “just” is given from justice, while the name “strong” is given from another quality, namely strength; these names distinguish different states when applied to a human being.

For it is one thing for a man to be just, another for him to be strong, and yet another for him to be a man; being a man is different from being just or strong.

But this is not so in God. When names are transferred to God, they cannot in any way distinguish states. If states transferred to God did distinguish him, God could not be called both just and strong, since God is simple. “Just” would establish one state and “strong” another.

When Dionysius therefore denied the aforementioned proper meaning of names and the distinction of states in God, he was attending to this point. [Note: Col. 0397. Perhaps read: “he attended to the distinction of states.” Ed.]

When it is said, “God is justice,” or “just,” or “truth,” and so forth—things that may properly be said of God—there is no distinction of states, nor is a quality or quantity predicated, but substance above substance, that is, hyperousia, as Boethius will likewise say.

For there are no states in God by which he can be distinguished from other things—if I may call them ‘other’—nor can he be comprehended.

Hence Basil, commenting on the Hierarchy where it says “God is not life,” says: “When I understand God, my intellect approaches nothing rather than something,” that is, the removal of all things.

It is as if he said: “When I consider God, I understand rather what he is not than what he is.” Yet he did not say “toward nothing,” but rather “toward no-thing.” When all things are removed, God is understood in some manner, as when we say: “God is that which is neither sun, nor moon, nor heaven, nor world.”

We know what he is not, but we do not fully understand what he is; nevertheless, he is in some manner intimated.

Hence Augustine says: “What God is, I can neither understand nor encompass in the mind.” When we hear the name “man,” we understand a thing of that sort—that is, we encompass it in the mind. When we hear the name “God,” we encompass nothing in the mind.

For this name was not given from any form that informs God and distinguishes him from other things.

But lest we linger too long, let us return to the matter at hand.

“Infinity,” therefore, is a name belonging to negative theology. When we remove all things from God, we understand God in the obscurity of his infinity.

Since “infinite” is a name of negation, it asserts nothing. Indeed, if the force of the word is considered, insofar as God is called infinite, generation, emission, or procession cannot be considered in God; only the removal of all things from God is understood.

“Eternal,” however, is a name of affirmative theology and does assert something. For that is eternal which, although it is the limit of all things, has no limit of its own. The eternal, not the coeternal, simply implies a beginning.

Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same eternal being, and therefore “eternal” is a name of the substance, nevertheless, because the Son is a beginning from a beginning, while eternity simply includes a beginning, the name “eternal” reaches the person of the Father.

“Infinity” is added. Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same infinite being, the Father is a beginning not from a beginning, the Son is a beginning from a beginning, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son.

In the Father, I say, there is authority. To him alone it belongs not to be from another, and infinity is thereby especially applicable to him.

Since eternity indicates a beginning, while infinity indicates that which is without a beginning, these two together express the person of the Father. Thus, by saying “in the eternal, infinity,” Hilary intimated the person of the Father.

To distinguish the person of the Son, he rightly said: “Form in the image.” The Son is the likeness of the Father, expressed in every respect.

Likewise, by saying “use in the gift,” he rightly intimated the person of the Holy Spirit. Since the persons must be referred to one another, so that the Father is called the Father of the Son and the Son the Son of the Father, it was necessarily appropriate, as blessed Augustine says, that the name “Holy Spirit” should be assigned to the one who is referred to the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds in likeness.

He could not be called “the Spirit of the Father,” for then there would already be two Sons. Nor could he be called “the Father of the Spirit” or “the Son of the Spirit,” for then there would already be two Fathers.

Therefore the name “gift” was given to the Holy Spirit, so that we may say “the gift of the giver,” “the gift of the giver,” and “the giver of the gift.”

If, then, by saying “in the gift” he intimated the person of the Holy Spirit, he rightly added “use,” because through the gifts of the Holy Spirit we make use of God.

Thus Hilary distinguished the persons when he said: “In the eternal, infinity; in the image, form; in the gift, use.”

Having explained these matters, before proceeding to what follows, we must guard against the Arian heresy.

For Arius, wickedly detracting from the truth of the divine substance, maintained that the three persons were not homousion but homeusion—that is, not of one substance but of similar substance.

HOMO means “one,” USIA means “substance,” and HOME is interpreted as “similar.” To prove this, he used the following arguments:

“Christ,” he says, “is true God, but he was made and established before the ages by the will of the Father.”

He tried to prove this by the following argument: “The Father begot the Son. Therefore he begot him either willingly or unwillingly. But he did not beget him unwillingly, because no one could compel him. Therefore he begot him willingly. Thus the will of the Father existed before the Son, and therefore,” he says, “they are not of the same substance. For if they were of the same substance, they would also be of the same will; therefore, if they are not of the same will, neither are they of the same substance.”

Augustine responds to this argument:

“The heretic asks whether God is unwilling or willing, so that the same fault may rebound upon him. If he is willing, then according to the heretic he will not be of the same substance as himself; but if he is unwilling, he is not God, because no one compels him. Therefore the man lies when he says that the Son is not of the same substance as the Father.”

Again Augustine, against Arius:

“What the heretic has said is inconsistent, when he says that Christ is true God. For in the law that he himself accepts it is written: ‘Israel, your God is one God.’ But this was said either of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, or of two, or of all three.

“If it was said of the Father alone, then the Son is not God, which he himself admits. If it was said of the Son alone, then the Father is not [Col. 0399C]

God, which he himself does not deny. If it is said of the Holy Spirit alone, then neither the Father nor the Son is God, although he concedes this. If it is said of the Father and the Son alone, then the Holy Spirit is not God, which he affirms. Therefore he must concede that the three persons are one God, since he accepts a law that says that there is only one God, and he says that this God is the true God.” Augustine likewise against Arius, concerning the claim that Christ was made before the ages and therefore is not coeternal with the Father:

“Let it be asked,” he says, “whether he was made from nothing or from something. If from something, then from the Father, since nothing existed except the Father. Therefore he is of the same nature as the Father. For just as one thing begets another thing of the same nature—human being begets human being, lion lion, ox ox—so God necessarily begot God, of precisely the same nature.”

See how directly Augustine contradicts those who say that Socrates has one humanity and Plato another, and that each human being possesses humanity through the singularity of essence, while, not finding it to be the same, they explain it in this way, that is, as “similar.” Augustine is not, in fact, arguing against Arius, but interprets Arius’s position as though he were a heretic who understood the Father and the Son to be *homoiousioi*, that is, of similar substance—which in God is the same as nature.

“But if he concedes that Christ was made from nothing,” Augustine says, “I ask through whom he was made. For he himself says that this Christ, by the Father’s spoken command and will, made both invisible and visible things from things that did not exist. Therefore, since he says that all things were made through the Son while conceding that the Son was made, he will necessarily say that the Son was made through himself, although he did not exist before he was made.

“Again, if he concedes that Christ was made before time, then Christ is eternal, since nothing existed before time except what is eternal. But if he says that some time was created before the ages in which Christ was made, through whom was that time created, since Christ did not yet exist, although he concedes that all things were made through him?”

Arius further wishes to prove by this argument that the Father is of a substance different from the Son: “The Father sent the Son, and the Son was sent; but the one who was sent is different from the one who sent. Therefore the Father and the Son are not of the same substance.”

“ This is false,” Augustine says, “because a human being sends a human being, although the sender and the one sent are of the same nature. But because separation can occur there, let us transfer the example to fire. Fire sends forth its radiance, yet the substance of the radiance and of the fire is the same. Nevertheless, the likeness must not be pressed in every respect. For radiance, if it could speak, which is on a wall, could not truthfully say, ‘Where I am, my Father is with me.’”

It should also be noted that when he says above that the human sender and the one sent are of the same nature, he is likewise arguing against those who say that Socrates has one humanity and Plato another. This is not to be understood as arising from a different singularity of essence, but rather from something different—that is, something altered—as we carefully explained above.

The Incarnation of the Son likewise compelled Arius, above all, to say that the Father’s substance was one thing and the Son’s another. The heretic thought that if the substance of the three persons were one and simple, then, since it is established that the Son was incarnate without the divine substance being absent, the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit would necessarily have to be incarnate. For this reason, he thought that the substance which is the Father—and thus the three persons—had become incarnate. The heretic was deceived.

The Catholic faith understands the matter otherwise. It confesses that the substance of the three persons is one and undivided, and yet that the Son was so incarnate that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was incarnate, although the persons are undivided; and wherever the Son is, there too are the Father and the Holy Spirit. How this is so cannot be known, but it can be suggested to some extent through a certain likeness involving three pronouns: *hoc* (“this”), *id* (“that”), and *idem* (“the same”).

When I say *hoc* (“this”), I indicate what I wish simply to discuss, in such a way that I do not signal that the utterance depends on something previously said. When, however, I utter *id* (“that”), I speak of the same substance as before, but not simply: the utterance remains dependent on what preceded it. Since *id* is said relatively, it always carries with it that to which it refers. When I afterward utter *idem* (“the same”), I indicate that the utterance concerns the very same substance referred to by *id* and by *hoc*, but in such a way that *idem* is referred equally to *id* and to *hoc*.

Thus *hoc* expresses the person of the Father. Just as *hoc*, in making the first cognition, does not show that the utterance depends on what preceded it, so the Father exists from himself and not from another. *Id* suits the Son, because through *id* the utterance concerns the same substance as through *hoc*, though not simply. For *id* carries *hoc* with it when it refers to *hoc*. Thus the Son is of the same substance as the Father, and must be referred to him, from whom he also has his being. *Idem*, finally, at least retains the property of the Holy Spirit, because through *idem* the utterance concerns precisely the same substance as through *id* and *hoc*; yet *idem* does not simply draw *id* toward *hoc*, since it is related equally to both. Thus the Holy Spirit is precisely of the same substance, and is the same substance, as the Father and the Son. He does not have being from himself, but proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is referred equally to both. [Col. 0400D]

Let us now strive altogether to investigate, if it can be done, the Incarnation of the Word through some kind of likeness. When *hoc* (“this”) is uttered, the mind conceives *hoc*, but nothing else—only *hoc*. Afterward, when *id* (“that”) is uttered, the mind conceives *id*, but not without *hoc*, for *id* carries *hoc* with it when it refers to it. Yet the mind does not conceive *hoc* and *hoc* in such a way that the same substance is expressed through both pronouns.

Thus, if it is permissible to compare the smallest things with the greatest, the Virgin conceived the Son, but not without the Father or the Holy Spirit. Yet she did not conceive the Father or the Holy Spirit; rather, the one undivided substance of the three persons remained. Note that when I said, “The Virgin conceived the Son, but not without the Father,” I did not relate “without” to “conceived.” For she conceived the Son in such a way that she did not conceive the Father or the Holy Spirit. Rather, I related “without” to the Son, because from eternity the Son is in the Father, and the Father is in him.

Arius also established another heresy. He says that the Son assumed only a spirit, not a soul. He thinks that this is what the Evangelist meant when he said, “The Word became flesh.” For he did not say, “It became a soul.” He explains the passage as follows: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”—that is, my divinity.

Augustine responds to this:

“I ask,” he says, “how he will explain what Christ himself says: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death’; and: ‘I have power to lay down my soul, and to take it again’; and: ‘You will not abandon my soul in hell.’ For how can divinity be sorrowful? Or how could God lay down himself? Or how could he abandon himself in hell, except insofar as he is present in all things through essence? In no way.”

The Evangelist’s statement is therefore to be understood as follows. He used “flesh” for the whole by synecdoche—that is, “flesh” for “human being.” Arius therefore lied when he asserted that Christ assumed only flesh, that Christ was not coeternal with God the Father, and that he was not of the same substance as the Father. And because he wickedly divided the simplicity of the essence of the three persons, when he was going to Constantine and wished, as usual, to make his heresy known, he turned aside to the customary places of nature; there his entrails were destroyed, to the condemnation of his life [the text reads *vitae damnationem*]. Constantine too, having fallen into this heresy, is said to have ended his life. [Col. 0401B]

Now, with the unity of the divine substance preserved, let us turn to the inquiries in which the poison might lie. Why, then, should the word “person” posit something common in the three persons, something that each person is?

We reply that the word “person” posits nothing common in the three persons insofar as it is given from personal distinction, not from an underlying union. Indeed, from the fact that someone is called a person, he is more clearly distinguished from the Son, even though he is shown to have something in common with the Son. But we must begin from a higher point.

Among words said of the good, some are said according to relation; others denote a relation among the persons; others denote God’s relation to creatures. Among the persons are “Father,” “Son,” “gift,” and “counsels”; in relation to creatures are “Lord,” “Creator,” and “principle.” As Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*, “He was not Lord before he had a servant.” Thus he began temporally to be Lord when the creature, made in time, began to serve him. Similarly, God began to be Creator in time, from the moment at which he made creatures. For he did not create them [the text reads *creavit*, apparently corrupt in context], nor are they coeternal with the Creator.

Augustine shows by an analogy involving something that begins to be a price without undergoing change that certain things are said of God temporally, without objection, in Book IV of *On the Trinity*:

“A coin,” he says, “when it is called a price, is called so relatively, yet it is not changed when it begins to be a price, nor when it is called a pledge, nor in similar cases. If, therefore, a coin can be called relatively without any change in itself, how much more readily should we understand this of the unchangeable substance of God: although it begins to be called something temporally, this does not mean or imply that anything has happened to God’s substance, but only to the creature to which the term is applied. When something begins to be called temporally what it was not called before, it is plainly being called relatively—not according to an accident by which something has happened to it, but according to an accident belonging to that to which it is related.” [Col. 0401D]

Therefore the Father is temporally God, Lord, and Creator [Note: “[Col. 0401] This clause seems to convey a heretical meaning. Perhaps it should read: ‘Therefore the Father is God; temporally he is Lord and Creator.’ EDITOR.”]. Yet it is true that he is Lord of all from eternity and Creator from eternity, but not that he is eternally Lord or eternally Creator. It should not seem strange that something is said to belong to him temporally. For it belongs temporally to the Son of God to have assumed flesh, and likewise to be called “Christ,” although Christ is eternal.

Thus these names, which belong to God temporally, indicate a relation to creatures. More generally, a name that denotes a relation to creatures, when uttered by itself, does not establish personal distinction, but rather signifies the unity of essence. For that reason plurality cannot enter into the name itself; it is said in the singular of the three persons: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three lords or three creators, but “three [who are] one Lord, one Creator, one principle.” [Col. 0402A]

Some, however, say that these three names sometimes denote relation and sometimes substance. They wish to establish that “Lord” is a name of essence from the passage: “He who ascended above the sunset—the Lord is his name,” and from the commentators: “NAME,” that is, an essential name.

Likewise, they wish to establish that “principle” is a name given from the union of substance from John’s statement: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.” There the commentator says that “to be the principle itself” is the same as “to be itself.” They also say that “creator” is understood in two ways: creator in act and creator by nature. A creator in act has being temporally and denotes a relation to creatures. A creator by nature—that is, one possessing the power to create—has being eternally, and in this sense the name is substantial.

Otherwise, if creatures did not exist, the Holy Spirit would not be a principle. The Father is indeed the principle of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son is also, of course, the principle of the Spirit from eternity, but the Holy Spirit would be the principle of nothing.

Note, however, that although “principle,” taken absolutely, denotes a relation to creatures, an accompanying expression establishes personal distinction. Thus, when I say “principle not from a principle,” I express the person of the Father; when I say “principle from a principle,” the person of the Son; and when I say “principle from the Father and the Son,” the person of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the following argument is invalid: “The Father is principle not from a principle; the Son is principle from the first; but the first, not from the first, is not principle from the first. Therefore the Father and the Son are not the same principle, or else they are two principles.” For the first expression, which establishes personal distinction by what accompanies it, although uttered in relation to creatures, nevertheless declares the unity of substance.

The same point can be falsified by a similar example: “The Father is God not from God; the Son is God from God. But God not from God is not God from God. Therefore the Father and the Son are not the same God, or else they are two gods.” This too is false for the same reason as the preceding argument. Although “God” is a name of substance, when accompanied by “not from God” it denotes the person of the Father; when accompanied by “from God,” the person of the Son. [Col. 0402C]

It follows that, since the three persons are one principle, we must ask whether they are principle without principle. It is clear concerning the Father that he is both principle and principle not from a principle. We must therefore ask whether the Son and the Holy Spirit are principle without principle.

I say that there are two questions here. If the meaning is, “The Son is principle without principle,” that is, “He is principle in such a way that he never began,” then it is true. If, therefore, the meaning is “principle without principle,” that is, “principle not from a principle,” then it is true—but in that case the Son would be the Father. I say the same concerning the Holy Spirit. It may also be asked whether he is principle from a principle. But we neither affirm nor deny this. We do not affirm it, lest we appear to confuse the persons; for usage already reverts to the expression mentioned above, so that their pluralization (*horum complurationem*; the text is corrupt) designates the person of the Son. We do not deny it, lest we appear to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from no one, especially since we find neither position in authoritative texts.

Let this, then, suffice concerning names signifying a relation to creatures. Names designating the relation of one person to another always establish personal distinction, such as “Father” and similar terms.

Of names said according to substance—that is, according to themselves, not in relation—some are given from the union of substance, others from personal distinction. From identity come terms such as “God,” “just,” and “almighty”; plurality does not enter into these. From distinction comes “person.” For because the Father is distinguished from the Son by a certain property, and the Son from the Father, the Father is called “Father” and is a person, while the Son is another person.

When Augustine says, “Person is said from itself,” this must be understood to mean that it is not said relatively. It is not called “from itself” because the name is given from the identity of essence.

Someone may object: Even if the Father were never Father and the Son were never Son—which is impossible—would the Father nevertheless be a person, and the Son likewise? This is clear in natural things. Adam in paradise was neither father nor son, unless he is called the son of God by creation; yet at that time he was a person. It therefore does not appear that the name “person” belongs to the Father or the Son through some distinction.

I reply that although Adam was neither father nor son, he nevertheless had being as a person through distinction. For he is called a person, as it were, because he is one through himself when he is rational, distinct and separate from every other thing. Thus the name “person” is given from personal distinction and signifies one possessing personal distinction.

Some, however, say that in the singular the name is one of essence and posits something common in the three persons, as does “God.” When I say, “The Father is a person” and “the Son is a person,” I have not said one thing of the Father and another of the Son. But if another term is added—if one says, “The Father is another person from the Son,” or of the Holy Spirit, “He is the third person,” or in the plural, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons”—then it establishes a plural distinction.

Augustine likewise says:

“This is the one name which, although said according to itself of each of the persons, is not taken individually in the totality, but plurally. Augustine says that the name ‘person’ was devised so that, when it was asked what the three or what the three things were, one name could be given in reply: namely, ‘three persons.’ Apart from the terms mentioned above, there is only one name, ‘Trinity,’ which is not said individually of any person, but equally of all; it is now substantial and denotes plurality.” [Col. 0403B]

Note that when I said that the name “God” and similar names posit something common in the three persons, I used “common” improperly, though not without authority. Fulgentius, in *To Ferrandus the Deacon*, says that many things are common to the three persons and others proper to them. Common are such things as that God is wise, just, and pious. Yet Fulgentius himself also misused the word “common.”

When it is said that this name is common to the three persons, it must be understood to mean that it is not given from personal distinction but from the unity of substance. Otherwise the statement is false. If the proper force of the word is considered, absolutely nothing is common to the three persons. For if something were common to them, it would be either substantial or accidental—and neither can be considered in God.

Again, if “being God” were common to the three persons, they would participate in it. But neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is God by participation in divinity; rather, each is God by nature. Therefore nothing is common to the three persons if the force of the word is considered.

Someone may object: “Is God God from deity? Is God good from goodness?” I concede this. Therefore goodness is something from which God is good, and yet goodness is not God. This is false.

From this point arose the heresy of those who denied that goodness, wisdom, and deity are God, so that these would be posited as something partial—unless the statement is understood as follows: “Deity is God,” that is, “the one who is deity is God.” Thus these terms always overflow on the side of the Father. They were deceived by agreeing with Arius and observing in the Creator what belongs to creatures.

When one says, “God is good from goodness,” or “a human being is human from humanity,” the added expression, beneath which poison lies concealed, signifies cause and participation. But when one says, “God is from deity,” or “God is good from goodness,” the proposition does not signify cause or participation, as the semi-Arians understood it; rather, it signifies essence. Its meaning is: “God is God from deity,” that is, “he is God in such a way that he is deity itself.” Thus unity is one, and goodness is good; and each expression said of God in this manner must be understood accordingly.

For all these constructions—“God is from deity,” “the three persons are of one essence,” “of one nature,” and similar expressions—are intransitive, as was decreed at the Council of Rheims. The archbishop asked this of the man who led those who perhaps thought that such constructions were transitive. [Col. 0404A]

It must still be asked what that sect means when it says: “Nothing that belongs to Christ is to be worshiped.” If they mean Christ’s possession or part, they speak truly. But if they mean the divinity which is Christ’s nature, then to say that it is not to be worshiped is damnable. In that case the construction is intransitive, and the meaning is: “The nature of the three persons”—that is, “the nature which is the three persons”—or “the nature of the Son,” or “the nature of Christ,” which is the Son or Christ.

Someone may also say: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one deity, one God. Are they the same? For if they are the same, then they are the same either generically, specifically, or numerically.” For just as whatever things differ—the text also has *differentia* (“difference”)—differ by genus, species, or number, so whatever things are the same are the same by genus, species, or number.

We reply that the three persons are not the same in genus or in species, since nothing substantial is common to them. We do not concede that they are the same numerically, lest we fall into the Sabellian heresy. For if they are numerically the same, then the very same God who is the Father is the Son, just as the same person who is Tullius is Cicero; and thus there would be confusion of the persons.

We therefore say that the expression “to be the same in essence” is taken from natural things and must now be transferred to divine things. Likewise, we say that the three persons do not differ, if “differ” is taken properly. They do not differ by genus or species, since they do not participate in contrary qualities. Nor do they differ numerically, if the proper force of the word is considered. In logic, to differ numerically means to differ through a plurality of accidents, and no such thing can be conceived in God. [Col. 0404B]

Therefore there is no difference in the three persons. This is what Boethius says: “The principle of whose conjunction is indistinction.”

Someone may object: “The person of the Father is other than the person of the Son, and the person of the Holy Spirit is another; therefore the three persons differ.” This is false. “Other” there is not a name of difference but of negation. The meaning is: “The person of the Father is not the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit.”

To guard ourselves entirely against expressions asking whether the three persons differ, we must distinguish the question as follows. If the meaning is “They differ,” that is, “They are distinguished or separate,” then the statement is true. If the meaning is “They differ,” that is, “They participate in contrary qualities,” then it is false.

Again, if someone asks, “Do they differ numerically?”—that is, by a plurality of accidents, as the term is used in logic—the answer is false. But if one says, “They differ numerically,” meaning “by number,” in such a way that one can say of the Father, “He is one person,” of the Son, “He is another,” and of the Holy Spirit, “He is the third person,” then the statement is true.

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are therefore one God; and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

But caution is necessary here. They will say: “The Father is God—we concede this. The same God is the Son.” This must be distinguished. If the whole expression “the same God” is supplied, it must not be conceded, lest we fall into the Sabellian heresy; for “the same” is then referred to the Father.

When we say, “A human being runs; the same person argues,” “the same” is referred to the human being, about whom the discourse has already occurred. The meaning is: “The same running human being argues.” Similarly, when it is said, “The Father is God; the same God is the Son,” if the whole expression “the same God” is supplied, “the same” is necessarily referred to God, about whom the discourse has already occurred. The meaning is: “God the Father is God the Son,” which is what the Sabellians say.

The expression must therefore be distinguished as follows: “The Father is God; the same God is the Son.” If the whole expression “the same God” is supplied, the statement is false. But if “the same” is not supplied as part of the subject, but is predicated of God, and “the Son” is predicated of God, so that the meaning is “The Father is God; God is the same Son”—that is, “God the Son is the same God as the Father”—then the statement is true. Otherwise it is false.

God the Father is not the same God as the Son, although he is the same God with the Son. This is well attested by the brief gloss on John, which says “whose God,” as if it said: “the God of the Father, the God of the Son, and the God of the Holy Spirit.” And so that the three persons may be completely distinguished in the same essence, one must say: “The Father is God; another, the same God, is the Son” [Note: “[Col. 0403] The phrase is incomplete and ought to be restored as follows: ‘So that by “another” personal property may be indicated, and by “the same,” etc.’ EDITOR.”], so that personal property may be indicated by “another,” while the simplicity of essence is signified by “the same God.” [Col. 0405A]

It is asked again whether the nature of the three persons is to be worshiped, and whether, since the persons are of the same nature, it is permissible to say, “The three persons are one nature.”

The semi-Arians say that the three persons are one nature, using the ablative, or “through one nature.” Thus they say that the Father is not nature and that God is not nature. For “nature” is a name of abstraction. In natural things there are therefore three things: the name of person, which in some way underlies; the name of union; and the name of nature, which in some way supervenes—such as Socrates, human being, humanity. So in God there are person, God, and nature.

Just as “human being,” the name of union, is predicated of the person, while “humanity,” the name of nature, is not predicated of the person, so we say, “Socrates is a human being,” but we do not say, “Socrates is humanity.” Likewise, God is predicated of the person “Father,” but nature is not predicated of the person. Thus we say, “The Father is God,” but not, using the nominative, “The Father is nature” or “God is nature.”

They likewise say that the divine nature is not to be worshiped, but that God and the person are to be worshiped. Thus they say that nothing belonging to Christ is to be worshiped—that is, no nature, whether divine or human. They wish to establish this from the authority of blessed Augustine, where he says: “Nature did not assume nature, but a person.”

“Therefore,” they say, “the one who assumed is to be worshiped, namely, the person; not the one who did not assume, namely, nature.”

But whether the three persons are one nature or not, we shall explain by first showing whether it must be conceded that nature is to be worshiped.

We say, then, that “nature” is a name of abstraction. Although, when transferred to God, it signifies no abstraction, the word “nature,” when uttered, always suggests abstraction because of its original coinage. But there is no abstraction of nature from the three persons.

Therefore, to someone asking simply, “Is the divine nature to be worshiped?” I will answer: “Yes”; and whoever denies it is a heretic, because the word “nature,” transferred to God, does not signify abstraction.

But to a learned person who asks the same question after the discussion has been properly developed, I answer by denying only the property of the expression: “It is not to be worshiped,” because the word “nature” always suggests abstraction. But if the meaning and truth of the thing are considered, I affirm that it is to be worshiped.

For just as, when speaking of someone who has drunk water, we deny that he has drunk “substance”—not denying the truth of the matter, but only the proper force of the expression—so, when a learned person asks whether the divine nature is to be worshiped, if only the property of the expression is being denied and not the truth of the matter, we say, “No.” But if only the truth of the matter is being affirmed and not the property of the expression, we say, “Yes.”

Why is this? So that the property of the expression may be observed and no abstraction of nature from the three persons be made. For two things are considered in disputation: the property of the expression and the truth of the matter.

For truth to be present in an utterance, three things are necessary: the thing, the utterance, and the speaker’s opinion. If the utterance and the opinion are present, truth is present in the utterance even if the third element—the thing itself—is absent. For even if the matter is not as it is said to be, the speaker does not lie if he believes what he says; he is truthful. To lie is to speak against one’s conscience.

Therefore, if the opinion is absent while the other two are present—the thing and the utterance—the speaker nevertheless lies in saying it; and so forth. Someone may sometimes lie by means of a true proposition, because he speaks against his conscience; conversely, by uttering a false proposition, someone does not lie if he believes that things are as he asserts.

When the Jew said of Christ, “You are the King of the Jews,” although he spoke the truth, he nevertheless lied, because the relevant opinion was absent. Yet he did not tell a lie, since for that it would have been necessary for him to say something false, as a lie is a false signification of speech with the intention of deceiving.

Thus everyone who says a lie lies, but not everyone who lies says a lie, as is clear from the example just given. Accordingly, when the Jew said to Christ, “You are the King of the Jews,” the property of the expression was present and what he said was true, but the truth of his intention was absent. Similarly, when it is said, “Nature is to be worshiped,” the property of distinction is absent, yet the truth of the thing and of the intention is present.

Augustine, attending only to the property of the expression and not to the truth of the matter, said, “Nature did not assume nature.” He was not denying the truth of the matter, but the property of the expression, although other reasons for his statement may also be found—namely, that he was speaking against certain heretics who said that one nature was mingled with another. Nevertheless, I have neither seen nor found anyone who dared claim that he had seen this authority in Augustine. [Col. 0406A]

Note that when it is said, “God is the name of nature, not of person,” these genitives do not signify a possessor but a creature. It is not denied that the name “God” likewise names a person as well as nature; rather, the causal meaning is: “God is a name given from the union of substance, not from personal distinction.”

Once it has been settled whether it must be conceded that nature is to be worshiped, it remains to ask whether, since the three persons are of the same nature, it must be conceded that the three persons are one nature, just as this is conceded with the genitive, and whether it should also be conceded with the nominative.

Augustine makes this sufficiently clear in his book *On the Trinity*:

“We say that the three persons are of the same essence, or we say that the three persons are the same essence; not as though one thing were nature and another person.”

See how Augustine, lest the statement that the three persons are of the same substance seem to exclude the statement that they are the same substance, added: “Or we say that the three persons are the same essence.”

Following Augustine, therefore, we say that the three persons are of the same nature and that the three persons are one nature, using the nominative.

We can also prove this to one who contradicts us as follows: “The three persons are of the same nature, and not by participation; therefore the three persons are one nature.”

And yet it is not said: “The three persons are of the same nature.” The property of the expression is observed because the names “nature” and “person” have been transferred from these created things to God. In created things, however, “nature” is a name of abstraction and supervenes, while “person” underlies. Therefore we say that someone is of a certain nature, but not that he is a certain nature.

When, therefore, we say that the three persons are of the same nature, both the property of the expression and the truth of the matter are observed. But when we say that the three persons are the same nature, because “nature” is a name of abstraction, although there is no abstraction in God, we do not observe the property of the expression, but we do observe the truth of the matter.

Note also that we must not say that the Father and the Son are “from the same essence,” that is, “of the same essence.” The Son is from the essence of the Father, but the Father is from no one; otherwise he would already be begotten or proceeding. [Col. 0406C]

It is asked again whether, since the Father is nature, the Son is of the same nature, and the Holy Spirit is the same nature—and conversely—one may concede the following: “Nature begot nature,” or “Nature [begot] a person,” or “A person [begot] nature.”

I reply that I neither affirm nor deny any of these statements, because such words could introduce error. It would then seem that the same persons had begotten themselves. For in both cases “nature” would be a name of essence. Why would it be more a name of person when one says “Nature begot” than when one says “Nature is Father”?

No Catholic, however, denies that when I say “Deity is the Father” and “Deity is the Son,” I am speaking of the same thing; but this is true of nothing except the divine essence. Therefore even the argument “God begot God” could not be falsified, since in that expression “God” denotes a person.

I do not deny this, lest I seem to make nature diverse in the three persons—to say, namely, that the Son’s nature is one thing and the Father’s another. But when I say “Deity is the Father,” I am speaking through this name of the divine nature. Likewise, when I say “Deity is the Son,” I am speaking of the divine nature.

Since I therefore attribute being Father and being Son to the divine nature, why should I not also attribute to it having a Son or a Father, or even having been begotten or begetting? It appears that having a son and having a father are the same, though perhaps they are not entirely the same.

Although it is true that whoever is a father has a son, or has begotten one, it is not true of everything in such a way that a universal comprehension is produced through either expression. Begetting belongs to the whole person, not to the nature. Nevertheless, I have not stated this assertively, but as a question; conditionally, however, I would concede all the foregoing. For the one who is nature and person begot the one who is either nature or person. [Col. 0407A]

It is also asked how the three persons are said to be one God—whether “one” is derived from union or from unity. For in logic “one” is used in this way.

We reply that it is not “one” from union, as a species or genus is said to be one. God does not unite several things that participate in him substantially or accidentally. The three persons are not one God by participation.

But how are they one? Is it by singularity, so that “one God” means “a singular God”? God forbid, for this is the position of the Sabellian heresy. If God is singular, then only one person is God.

Against this Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “God is not singular, but one.”

How, then, are they one? By identity of essence or substance.

Again, when someone asks, “Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one sole God?” the statement must be distinguished as follows. If “sole” removes the distinction of persons, so that the whole expression “one sole God” means “they are God the Father and not God the Son,” or “God the Son and not God the Holy Spirit,” or “God the Son,” or “God the Holy Spirit,” then the statement is false. This is what the Sabellian heresy means.

But if “sole” removes the plurality of gods, so that “God” is predicated of the three persons, while “one” and “sole” are predicated of God, and the meaning is “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one sole God,” that is, “They are God, and not several gods but one sole God,” then the statement is true.

Likewise, if the statement is reversed as follows—“One sole Father is God, is the Son, and is the Holy Spirit”—it is false, unless “God” alone is made the subject. But “one” and “sole” must be predicated of God, as we said above: “God the Father is God; the same God is the Son.” Otherwise the statement is false.

For if the whole expression “one sole God” is made the subject, it is false. Its meaning would then be: “God the Father is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit”; or, “God the Son is—”

Pater and Son and Holy Spirit; or, God the Holy Spirit is Father and Son and Holy Spirit. For greater clarity, therefore, one should say as follows: It is not the case that one sole God (if the whole expression is taken as the subject) is Father and Son and Holy Spirit; nor are three gods Father and Son and Holy Spirit; rather, the three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are one sole God, so that the distinction of persons may be maintained, while the simplicity of essence is preserved through the one sole God.

Again, to someone who says, “There is one God who is Father and Son and Holy Spirit,” the distinction must be made in this way: If “who” establishes a personal relation, the statement is false; but if it refers to the simplicity of substance, it is true.

But let us now proceed. That person who is the Son was made man; but to be a man is to be something; therefore that person who is the Son was made something that is not from eternity. Therefore that person was made, and something that is a person—or something that is not a person—was made. This is false. One must therefore explain in how many ways something is said to “become.”

Something is said to become in five ways: either something comes to be through transformation of substance, through transmutation, through the joining of parts, through participation—which occurs in many ways—or through union, which likewise occurs in many ways.

Transformation of substance occurs in two ways: either through a change of matter or through a change of substantial form. Through a change of substantial form, for example, water becomes stone, and Lot’s wife became a statue. For in this case the substance’s substantial form was changed: the very same body remains, but its species was changed, not its genus. Through transmutation, however, something of a substance comes to be, as bread becomes Christ’s body. The substance of the bread passes into Christ’s body—not its form; rather, these forms subsist in the air or without substance. If something impossible elsewhere occurs in this case, that is not surprising, since Christ’s body itself was conceived in an ineffable manner and the whole Incarnation proceeded in a wondrous manner.

Some, however, say that nothing passes into Christ’s body. They hold that, beneath the accidents under which the substance of bread previously existed, Christ’s body exists after consecration. Thus they explain the statement: “The invisible priest changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood by his word and by a hidden power,” namely, that he causes it to exist beneath the same accidents.

When asked what becomes of the substance of bread, which had previously been beneath those accidents, they say that it returns to primordial matter or perishes completely. For they do not regard it as objectionable if a creature perishes through transfusion, as water mixed with wine does through the transfusion—that is, through the mingling—of wine and water.

Through the joining of parts, something comes to be as a body is formed from limbs, and a house from walls, roof, and foundation.

Through participation, either by informing, indwelling, or in a third manner.

Informing may be substantial or accidental. It is substantial when matter, through being informed by humanity, becomes a man; it is accidental when Socrates, through being informed by whiteness, becomes white. Through indwelling, a just man becomes God—not by nature, but through participation.

How so? Not substantially or accidentally, but through indwelling—that is, because God dwells within him.

There is also a third way in which something comes to be through participation: an unbeliever becomes a Christian by receiving baptism, not because he is [a Christian], but because he participates in the sacrament. Accordingly, this mode is called sacramental.

Union may be spiritual or personal. It is spiritual when the heart and soul of the multitude of believers became one, because they were spiritually united in one ardor of charity. It is personal union when the Son of the Father became man.

None of the aforementioned modes applies to him. He did not come to be through transformation of substance, because he did not cease to be God when he became man, nor did he possess being through some substantial form that was transformed. Nor did he come to be through transfusion, for the divine nature was not mixed with the human nature, as the Eutychian heresy maintains. It says that Christ consists of two natures, but not in two natures, since it teaches that one was mixed into the other.

Nor did he come to be through the joining of parts, because Christ does not consist of integral parts. Nor through participation, because humanity is neither substantial nor accidental to Christ. Even if I were perhaps to grant that humanity was substantial to that man, as it is to me—for he was a true man, just as I am—I would not therefore grant that something was substantial to Christ, because “Christ” is the name of a person. Nothing substantial or accidental belongs to that person in the way that a true body or soul is a part of that man; they are not, however, parts of Christ.

Hence Augustine says: “Let us by no means say that there are parts in Christ.”

Nor do I say this by distinguishing between man and God as though they were governed by different rules. For the same one is God and man, and man and God are one person. Rather, the saints speak about Christ in different ways according to the different natures in him.

Thus Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*: “Insofar as he is man, Christ is less than himself; insofar as he is God, he is greater than himself.” And concerning the passage, “Therefore he gave him the name that is above every name,” and so forth, one says: “He gave it to God, not to man”; another says: “He gave it to man, not to God.”

Why should I pursue each formulation? No mode can be fitted to him except personal union, which until Christ’s time had been unheard of. No greater miracle was ever heard of than that the third person assumed humanity by uniting it in the same person.

Nor is it sufficient to say simply, “He became man,” as though the expression meant merely “he was humanized.” For the soul is said to be incorporated, yet it is not a body or corporeal. In Christ, however, it is not true that he was humanized without being man. Therefore the expression must be explained as follows: The person became man, and he is God and man; that is, the person was humanized in such a way that that person is God and man, and God and man are that person.

Thus we say that the following inference is invalid: “God became man; therefore he became something.” He did not become something for that reason; rather, he assumed humanity by uniting it to himself in personal union.

Or we may reasonably grant that he became something—namely, man—in accordance with Augustine, who says: “One thing from the Father, another from the mother, but not another person.” If he is something else from his mother, then he is something from his mother, and that something is not from eternity; therefore he became something that is not from eternity.

It does not follow from this: “Therefore he became something that is a person,” as though a person had become a person; nor does it follow that he became something that is not a person, for then there would already be two things, which is false. Rather, he became something—that is, man—and he himself is a person.

Again, Christ is God, and not merely God as a consequence of that which he is because he is man. Therefore it is false to say that he is God and that another person is God, since the very reason for which he is said to be not merely God but man and God is that he is man.

Or we may distinguish the expressions in this way: “He is something else,” that is, a human person, and to be a man is not to be God—this is true. But “he is something else,” meaning something belonging to him that is not God—this is false.

Someone might object in this way: “Christ is other than God; Christ is two things.” This is false, because, since being man means assuming humanity through personal union, this does not mean being two things.

Again, the question is raised: Since the person who became man is the divine nature, may one concede the statement, “The divine nature became man”?

We answer that, since “nature” is a term of abstraction, although it produces no division in God, if one says, “The nature became man,” the expression appears to indicate the convertibility of one nature into another. That is false; and because the propriety of the expression is lacking, it should not be conceded without qualification. Nevertheless, the truth underlying the statement should not be denied, since Pope Leo says: “Humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by eternity, immortality by power, and the inviolable nature was united to the passible nature.” Gregory says the same: “Divinity came to us shod”—that is, clothed in humanity.

Again, the question is raised whether the three persons are one simple God.

We answer that if “simple” is set against the plurality of gods, so that it is taken to mean simplicity of essence, the statement is true. But if it means singularity, it is false. For then they would be saying that the three persons are one person—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.

Again, one asks why it is said, “The Father begot the Son,” “The Son was begotten by the Father,” and “the Spirit proceeds,” and whether one may say, “The Father begets” or “will beget the Son,” or “the Spirit will proceed.”

We answer that no verb transferred for speaking about God signifies time in the ordinary way. The statement “The Father begot the Son” is not used because “begot” signifies something past, but because it signifies completion—namely, the perfection of the Son’s generation from the Father.

Holy Church therefore chose to say, “The Father begot the Son,” so that the perfection of generation might be indicated by the perfect preterite. It does not say “begets” or “will beget,” lest an imperfection of generation be suggested by the present or future tense.

Thus Gregory, commenting on Job, says: “The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before the ages; or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased to be born, let us more truly say: he is always born.”

We cannot say, “He is always being born,” lest he appear to be imperfect. But so that he may be designated eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born,” since “born” pertains to perfection and “always” to eternity. Yet even in calling this “perfect,” we depart greatly from expressing that truth, because what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Nevertheless, in the language of our weakness, we speak by condescension: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

The Psalm likewise says: “Today I have begotten you.” It says “today” because that generation does not pass away; it says “I have begotten” because it has no beginning.

Concerning the Holy Spirit, however, the Church chose to say “proceeding,” using the present tense, because God gives him to us continually.

But the question now arises: When the Son said, “I proceeded from the Father,” are the Son and the Holy Spirit one proceeding person or two proceeding persons?

We answer that if “one” refers to substance, or if “proceeding” is predicated of substance, the statement is true. But if “one” refers to person, or if “proceeding” is joined to it so that the meaning is, “The Son and the Holy Spirit are one proceeding,” that is, “They are the proceeding Son” or “the proceeding Holy Spirit,” the statement is false.

Similarly, if “two” refers to substance, the statement is false; if it refers to person, it is true.

Note also that both the Son and the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father. There is nevertheless this difference: the Son proceeds as one born, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds as one given.

Since we have very frequently mentioned the divine substance, we must now consider how “substance,” which is understood in several ways, is understood in God.

The Greeks grant that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three *hypostases*, or *prosopa*, and are of the same *ousiosis* and the same *ousia*. But first let us see in how many ways the term “substance” is understood.

In the book on natures, “substance” is said either from *substare* (“to stand beneath”), from *subsistere* (“to subsist”), or from both.

When it is derived from *substare*, the Greeks call it *hypostasis*, while we properly call it “substance”; in this sense it belongs to matter, which has the property of standing beneath.

For **ὑπό** (*hypo*) means “under”; hence *hypostasis* means “that which stands beneath.”

When it is derived from *subsistere*, it is called by the Greeks *ousiosis*, while we properly call it “subsistence.” In this sense it belongs to form, which is truly subsistence, because it subsists independently of the flux of matter.

When it is determined by both—that is, by standing beneath and by subsisting—it is called by the Greeks *ousia*, and by others “essence.” In this sense it belongs to what is composed of both, namely matter and form, or to what retains the property of a composite of both. Since a composite consists of essence and subsistence, it is therefore said to stand beneath and to subsist—not by virtue of “substance” or “subsistence” as such.

It is called that which stands beneath because it retains the property of matter, from which it derives the perfection of having essence; for it is something distinct or discrete.

The soul, however, is called a substance, not because it is matter, form, or a composite of both, but because it retains the property of a composite of both. It stands beneath accidents, such as vices and virtues, and it subsists, or is something distinct and determinate.

Boethius distinguishes this well in his book *On Two Natures and One Person of Christ*. He also touched upon it in his commentary *super cath. R.* [the abbreviated title is uncertain], saying: “When it signifies three substances—matter, form, and composite—here he is dealing with the composite,” and so forth.

In God, however, the Greeks use the terms mentioned above. They say that the three persons are of the same *ousia* and the same *ousiosis*, but are three *hypostases* and three persons. They do not simply say *ousia*, however, but *hyperousia*, that is, “supersubstance,” as the same Boethius teaches below.

Since this distinction is made among the Greeks in all these matters, the reason for it must be explained.

The three persons are said by the Greeks to be of one *ousia*, or to be one *ousia*, because, as Boethius says elsewhere, they are—that is, they have being. For *ousia* has been transferred from created things to God. In created things it means essence: that which consists of matter and form, and is what it is, retains the property of essence. Such things have being in this way. Matter or form, taken by itself, is not said to “be,” according to Augustine.

The term has therefore been transferred to God, who truly is. Yet, according to the theology of negation, we can say, “God is not”—namely, he does not participate in eternity. According to the theology of affirmation, however, we say, “God is,” that is, he is being itself.

But because *ousia* in created things implies a subject capable of contraries, since it signifies a composite of both matter and form, the Greeks, lest the transferred term imply the same thing in God, say *hyperousia*, that is, “supersubstance.” We do not, however, deny that God is *ousia*.

Since the three persons have one being, they are said to be of one *ousia*, because the term *ousia* applies to them insofar as they are.

The three persons are said to be of one *ousiosis* because, as the same Boethius says elsewhere, they require nothing in order to be; and in this way the propriety of the transfer is preserved.

Among created things, *ousiosis* signifies the form that brings matter into being, yet does not itself require anything in order to be, according to Plato.

Thus the three persons are said to have one *ousiosis*, because, they say, God is simple form, conferring being upon all things while requiring nothing for his own being.

Because in created things *hypostasis* properly means that which stands beneath, and because each thing stands beneath accidents, the term, when transferred to God, indicates personal distinction but not the reception of any accidents. Hence the three persons are called three *hypostases*, that is, three persons.

For *prosopa* is taken from actors. *Prosopa* and *prosopopoeia* are terms of the same kind. *Prosopopoeia* means transformation. Hence *prosopa* came to mean three persons: actors represented persons and transformed themselves at one time into a boy, at another into a young man, and at another into an old man, producing different voices according to each person’s age and according to the size of the openings in their masks.

Thus they are called *prosopa*, that is, three persons.

But we must now consider briefly what a person is—whether the definition given by Boethius can apply to the three persons. It is as follows: “An individual substance of a rational nature.”

Some, misunderstanding Boethius, said that this definition had not been given in a Catholic manner, arguing in this way: “If a person is an individual substance of a rational nature, then the three persons are individual substances”—which is false. For there is one undivided substance of the three persons.

Against them we say that this definition was not given according to the sense in which “substance” means *ousia* or *ousiosis*, but according to the sense in which “substance” means *hypostasis*.

According to this meaning, it could also rightly be said that the three persons are three substances, unless Holy Church rejected this way of speaking, as Boethius says in his book *On Two Natures and One Person of Christ*, lest a division of the divine essence appear to result.

To satisfy ordinary usage, therefore, we can reasonably describe a person as follows: “A person is an individual *hypostasis* of a rational nature.”

But does not *hypostasis* mean the same as person? Indeed, when one says, “A person is an individual *hypostasis* of a rational nature,” it is the same as saying, “A person is an individual person of a rational nature.” In that case, the same thing is being described by the same thing.

I therefore say that “substance” contains a determination—“individual of a rational nature”—and is restricted by it to the meaning of person. Thus, although “substance” is understood in several ways, with this determination it has the force of *hypostasis*. Consequently, *hypostasis* need not be added when one is making the predication in order to complete the description of person.

Boethius’ description is sufficient according to the explanation we have given: the term “substance” is restricted by the expressions included in the description of all the genera to the meaning of *hypostasis*. Nevertheless, that description cannot be applied to the three persons, because ecclesiastical usage forbids it; that usage has already narrowed the meaning of the term “substance.”

Some, however, say that this definition was given concerning natural things.

Note also that this person or that person is not a part of God. The old women’s heresy must be rooted out—the heresy of those who swear by “the three parts of God.” Rather, as Augustine says, one person is no less than two, nor two less than three; nor are three less than two, nor two less than one.

Perhaps, however, when the old women swear by the three parts of God, they intend to speak of the body of Christ. Otherwise, the oath expresses heresy.

Again, someone might ask: “Are the three persons coeternal? Is the Son coequal with the Father? Is the Father coeternal with the Son?”

I neither affirm nor deny this. I do not affirm it, lest I appear to assign authority to the Son or to the Holy Spirit. Nor do I dare deny it, lest I appear to say that the Father is not of the same eternity as the Son, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one eternal being.

If the expression “three eternal beings” is found in any authoritative text, it must be explained rather than proclaimed, because contemporary usage has now abolished it. Explain it in this way: There are three, each one of whom is eternal, and the three are found to be one eternal being.
