# No. XXVI. THE CUCKOO, OR THE CONFLICT BETWEEN SPRING AND WINTER

*(Gilles, vol. II.)*

## SPRING, WINTER, PALAEMON

Suddenly all the shepherds of sheep came together from the high mountains,

[Col. 0412A] beneath the shade of trees in the springtime light,

to celebrate together the joyful Muses.

Daphnis, too, was present, and the elder Palaemon.

All these were preparing to sing praises to the cuckoo.

Spring also came, girded with a garland of flowers;

icy Winter came, shaggy with stiff hair.

For these there was a great contest over the cuckoo’s song.

Spring was the first to strike up three verses in melody:

### SPRING

I wish my cuckoo would come, that dearest of birds.

He usually becomes a most welcome guest to everyone,

singing good songs in the houses with his bright-red beak.

Then glacial Winter replied in a stern voice.

### WINTER

Let the cuckoo not come, but sleep in black caves;

he is accustomed always to carry hunger with him.

### SPRING

[Col. 0412B] I wish my cuckoo would come with joyful budding,

and drive away the cold, the nourishing companion of Phoebus forever;

Phoebus loves the cuckoo as he grows in the serene light.

### WINTER

Let the cuckoo not come, since perhaps he produces hardships,

multiplies battles, separates cherished rest,

disturbs everything; sea and land suffer.

### SPRING

Why, sluggish Winter, do you sing insults against the cuckoo?

You who, heavy with torpor and covered in dark caves,

[lie there] after Venus’s feasts, after the cups of foolish Bacchus.

### WINTER

I have riches, and joyful banquets as well;

there is sweet rest, and a warm fire in the house.

The cuckoo knows these things [Al.: “does not know them”]; but that treacherous fellow labors.

### SPRING

[Col. 0412C] The cuckoo bears flowers in his beak and supplies honey,

builds houses, and sails peaceful waters,

and produces offspring and clothes the fields in joy.

### WINTER

These things are hostile to me, although they seem joyful to you.

But it is pleasant to count the desired treasures through the chests,

and to rejoice in food while also resting forever.

### SPRING

Who, sluggish Winter, always ready to sleep,

will heap up riches for you or gather any treasures,

if neither Spring nor Summer labors beforehand for you?

### WINTER

You speak truly: since they labor much for me,

they are also servants subdued under my authority,

now serving me as their master whatever they labor to produce.

### SPRING

You are no master to them, but poor and needy—*superbis* (“for/among the proud”; Al. *superbus*, “proud”),

[Col. 0412D] nor will you now be able to feed yourself entirely by your own efforts,

unless the cuckoo who will come supplies you with nourishment [Al.: “provision”].

Then Palaemon replied joyfully from his lofty seat,

and Daphnis likewise, together with the faithful band of shepherds.

### PALAEMON

Cease speaking further, Winter, you cruel squanderer of things;

and let the cuckoo come, the shepherds’ sweet friend.

Let joyful shoots burst forth on our hills;

let there be pastures for the flock, and rest sweet in the fields;

let green branches provide shade for the weary;

and let the she-goats come to the milking-pails with full udders,

while the birds salute Phoebus beneath varied song.

Therefore, come more quickly now, cuckoo, behold!

You who are already sweet love, a most welcome guest to all,

everything awaits you—the sea, the earth, and the sky.

Hail, sweet glory, cuckoo; hail through the ages.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 784. PAULUS WINFRIDUS THE DEACON, SON OF WARNEFRIDUS

[Col. 0413]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis.)*

[Col. 0413A] Paulus Winfridus, son of Warnefridus, a deacon of the patriarchate of Forum Julii or Aquileia, was secretary or chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. After Desiderius was captured by Charlemagne in the year 774, Paulus himself was taken captive; thereafter, because of his steadfast loyalty and affection toward Desiderius, he became an object of dislike and an exile. Soon afterward he became a monk of Monte Cassino and, because of his talent and learning, was also loved and honored by Charlemagne, as Charlemagne’s poems to Paulus, preserved by Leo of Ostia in book I, chapter 15, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, sufficiently and abundantly testify.

Concerning this Paulus, besides Leo, one should consult Peter the Deacon, book 8 of *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, illustrated with the learned notes of Giovanni Battista Mari; and, among more recent writers, Daniel Wilhelm Moller, *Dissertation on Paul the Deacon*, Altdorf, 1686, quarto. I pass over our own Johann Hübner, second century of the *Historical Library*, Hamburg, p. 63 and following, as well as Vossius, Labbe, vol. II, pp. 170 and 778 and following, Cave, and others.

Paulus’s writings are these: an epitome of the twenty books of Verrius Flaccus, [Note: [Col. 0413B] Suetonius, *On Grammarians*, chapter 17, where he indicates that Verrius was chosen as tutor to the grandsons of Augustus.] the famous ancient grammarian’s work *On the Meaning of Words*, already reduced by Sextus Pompeius Festus to a briefer form. Paulus dedicated this epitome to Charlemagne, prefacing it with a letter bearing this title:

“To the lord King Charles, resplendent with the gift of generosity, wisdom, and power, most exalted of kings: Paulus, the least little servant.”

As for editions of this epitome and of the remains of Festus and Verrius, I do not intend to repeat what I said in book IV, chapter 6, of the *Latin Library*. The Anonymous of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 67, says:

“Paulus, a learned man, wrote among other works a very useful book entitled *On the Meaning of Words*.”

A considerable part of the *Miscellaneous History* also belongs to this Paulus. For the first eleven books are the same as the ten books of Eutropius, except that Paulus occasionally adds something of his own. He then continues Eutropius; the five following books are his, [Note: [Col. 0413C] Leo of Ostia, book I, chapter 15, where two books, rather than five little books, are attributed to Paulus.] extending from the time of Julian the Apostate to the time of Justinian I. The remainder, namely book seventeen and those that follow, were added by Landulfus Sagax, chiefly from Theophanes, or from Anastasius the Librarian, who translated Theophanes from Greek into Latin.

I discussed editions of the *Miscellaneous History*, including the one that also exists in Canisius’s recension, in volume XIII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 201 and following, in book III, chapter 9, of the *Latin Library*. I have discussed Landulfus and Anastasius above, in their proper place.

The *Homiliary* [Note: [Col. 0413C] See Du Cange under this word.] has improperly been attributed by some to Alcuin [Note: [Col. 0413C] As in the Spanish version published at Valencia in 1552, folio: “The Homiliary compiled by Alcuin.”], but it should be attributed to Paulus [Note: [Col. 0413C] Sigebert of Gembloux in his *Chronicle*, and also Alberic, monk of the Three Fountains, under the year 807, p. 152 of vol. II of Leibniz’s *Historical Additions*: “Emperor Charles, selecting the best passages from the writings of the Catholic Fathers through the hands of Paul the Deacon, had readings suitable for each feast compiled for reading in the Church throughout the course of the year.” Florus, deacon of Lyons, in his book of homilies for the entire year, arranged from the treatises of various Fathers, in the *Thesaurus of Anecdotes* of Edmund Martene and Ursinus Durandus, vol. V, p. 612.

“O prudent reader, whose concern is the unceasing life,

read through this present book with a studious heart,” etc. For more on this work and its old German translation, see, among others, Johann Heinrich von Seelen, *Select Literary Works*, p. 252 and following; Johann David Köhler, *On the Library of Charlemagne*, Altdorf, 1727, quarto, § 6. A similar work, containing readings for the epistles appointed in the Church on Sundays and feast days, collected and published from the ancient doctors of the Church, was compiled by Laurentius Surius, Cologne, 1596, folio.] The work comprises homilies on the Sunday and annual Gospel readings, selected from the writings of approved doctors of the Church at Charlemagne’s command for the use of the churches.

It survived into later ages and appeared in various places: Speyer, 1482; Basel, 1493 and 1505; Cologne, 1517, 1525, 1530, and 1539; Lyons, 1520 and 1525; Paris, 1537 and 1569, all in folio. Nor do I think that the work differs from the one which the very learned writers of the *Literary Itinerary*, published in French in 1717, quarto, Edmund Martene and Ursinus Durandus, report that they found in the library of Auxerre, p. 56. Although that manuscript codex bears the name of Ebrardus and is entitled *Homiliary of the Fathers, arranged at the command of Charlemagne*, I would rather believe that it was the work of the copyist than of the compiler.

“Ebrardus, your suppliant, presented this book

to the Lord and to you, Germanus;

remember the suppliant.

Let no one remove it, whose heart Christ

possesses, lest he provoke Him to anger.

Indeed, approving his brother’s gift and vow,

he will persist in whatever he can accomplish

with equal love.

For he asks that it be solemnly read

among the company of the brethren,

to the praise of the Lord, night and day.”

The names of those whose homilies are read in this *synagogue* (συναγωγή, “collection”) are these:

Alcuin, whose three books *On the Faith* are found on p. 118 and following of the Basel edition; they were also printed separately at Frankfurt in 1555 and included among his works.

Ambrose, frequently.

Anselm, vol. II, p. 36b.

Augustine, frequently.

John Chrysostom.

Fulgentius of Carthage, p. 21b, vol. II, pp. 53b and 67.

Gregory the Great, frequently.

Haymo, p. 31b, vol. II, pp. 43b, 68b, and 73b.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] This is Eric of Auxerre, who wrote the life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre for Charles the Bald in six books of verse between the years 875 and 877. His homilies must have been inserted after the time of Paul the Deacon, as must Haymo’s; this Eric was a disciple both of Haymo and of Lupus of Ferrières. See Charles Le Cointe, under the year 839, no. 19, vol. VIII of the *Annals of France*, p. 586, and the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, June 25, p. 829 and following.]

Henricus, pp. 20b, 5b, 126b, 133b, 140b, 142b, 145, 147b, 152, 160b, 163b, and vol. II, p. 21b.

Jerome, frequently.

Hilary, vol. II, p. 60.

John Chrysostom, frequently.

Isidore, p. 17b.

Leo the Great, frequently.

Maximus, frequently.

Saint Severianus of Gabala, p. 27.

Johann Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book I, chapter 11, § 15:

“In the writing of charters and also of books, after the golden age, when individual words were distinguished by individual points, almost no separation of words was made by scribes until Charlemagne, who, through the efforts of Alcuin (*Letter* 15), restored the distinctions or subdivisions of points. In this undertaking the most pious prince employed Paulus Warnefridus and Alcuin, highly skilled deacons. The former illuminated with punctuation the homilies customarily read throughout the year and several letters of Augustine; the latter illuminated with punctuation the book called the *Comes*. Nevertheless, this use of punctuation became established in charters only later, etc.”

“Let them distinguish proper cola and commas by lines,

and place the points in their proper order.”

## History of the Winnili [Al.: Vinnuli], Later Called Lombards, Down to the Destruction of Their Kingdom in 773

This outstanding work in six books, after the old editions—the Ascensian edition, the Augsburg edition of 1515, published with Jordanes, and the Basel edition of Sigismund Gelenius of 1532, published with Suetonius and others—was revised with exceptional care by Bonaventure Vulcanius and published with Jordanes and other writers on Gothic affairs [Note: [Col. 0416D] Compare, if you please, what is said in the *Latin Library*, book III, chapter 17.] at Leiden in 1597 and 1618, octavo. It was later published by Hugo Grotius at Amsterdam in 1655, octavo, and by Janus Gruter in *Lesser Latin Writers of Augustan History*, Hanover, 1611, folio. [Note: [Col. 0416D] The illustrious Sparwenfeld, according to Leibniz, wished to publish, in Leibniz’s writings, p. 167, *The Criticisms of Foreigners on the Goths*, as a supplement to Grotius’s collection.]

About the same time, Friedrich Lindenbrog also examined these books of Paulus against manuscript codices and illustrated them with notes, adding a notable supplement to the final chapters of book VI, chapters 59–61. This was later included in Freher’s *French Historians*, from the Palatine manuscript, and in the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIII, where the books appear on p. 161 and the supplement is reprinted on p. 332.

The excellent Lindenbrog edition appeared at Hamburg in 1611, quarto, under this title:

*Three Writers of Ancient Histories of Various Peoples:*

*Jordanes, bishop, on the succession of kingdoms and times;*

*the same author’s History of the Origin of the Goths;*

*Isidore of Seville on the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi;*

*the same author’s Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings;*

*Paul Warnefrid F., deacon, on the Deeds of the Lombards, six books.*

Finally, the books of Paulus, with various readings from the Ambrosian and Modoetian (Monza) codices [Col. 0415D] and with notes by the distinguished Horatius Blancus, were published by the highly praised Muratori in volume I of the *Thesaurus of Writers of Italy*, p. 395, Milan, 1723, folio.

## Life of Saint Gregory I, Pope

This work, in four books, was praised by Sigebert and published by Johann Mabillon in the first century of the Benedictines, p. 385, and thereafter in the most recent edition of Saint Gregory’s works, vol. IV, Paris, 1706, folio. See also the new edition of the praised Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 498 and following. Paulus himself mentions it in book III, chapter 24, of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*.

[Col. 0416A] A little book on the number or order of the bishops who succeeded one another in the city of Metz from the very beginning of preaching until the year 777, written at the request of Bishop Angilramnus. It is found in Freher’s *Corpus of Frankish History*, p. 171; in the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIII, p. 329; and most recently in Augustine Calmet’s *Civil and Ecclesiastical History of Lorraine*, published in French at Nancy in 1728, folio.

From this little book comes the fragment concerning the ancestors and children of Charlemagne, in volume II of André du Chesne’s *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, p. 201; and the passage concerning Blessed Arnulf, successor of Pappolus, in Peter Pithoeus’s *Twelve Writers*, p. 288. Paulus himself mentions it in book VI, chapter 16, of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, as does Sigebert, chapter 80, who calls it the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*.

From this little book was taken the epitaph of Arigisus [Al.: Anchisi], prince of Benevento, found in the *History of the Lombard Princes* by Peregrinus, in the celebrated Muratori’s *Thesaurus of Writers of Italy*, vol. I, p. 395; and the epitaph of Saint [Col. 0416B] Hildegard, vol. III of the *Acts of the Saints*, April, p. 789, which Baronius improperly attributed to Alcuin.

## Miracles of Saint Arnulf

Saint Arnulf was first mayor of the palace of the king of the Franks and later bishop of Metz. According to Sigebert, he sought an eremitical life and died in the year 632. The work was published in volume III of the works of Bede the Venerable and afterward attributed to Paulus by Surius, under August 24. Paulus himself mentions it in book VI, chapter 15, of the *History of the Lombards*.

## Martyrdom of Saint Cyprian of Carthage

This was published in the editions of Cyprian by Jacobus Pamelius and John Fell of Oxford, among others; the martyrdom was omitted from Ruinart’s *Selected Acts*. In the judgment of Tillemont as well (*Memoirs of Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 638, Paris edition), it seems to be attributable to a later Paulus, who wrote in the time of Charles the Bald.

## Lives of Saints Benedict, Maurus, and Scholastica

The lives of Saint Benedict, who died in 543; Saint Maurus, who died in 584; and the virgin Saint Scholastica, sister of Saint Benedict, who died about the year 542, were published at Rome [Col. 0416C] in 1590, quarto, in the third part of the poems of T. Prosper Martinengo, and in Mabillon’s first century of the Benedictines. But I see that they have been omitted from the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III, March 21, p. 275; vol. I, January 15, p. 1039; and vol. II, February 10, p. 393.

Leo of Ostia calls Paulus a truthful and distinguished historian in his account of the deeds of Saint Benedict, II, 44. The reciprocal elegiac verses on the miracles of Saint Benedict, in which the first half of a hexameter is repeated in the second half of a pentameter, are mentioned by the same Leo in book I, chapter 15. They begin:

“From where shall I begin, holy Benedict, to tell your triumphs?”

They are found in book I, chapter 26, of Paulus’s *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, and in Aimoinus’s sermon on Saint Benedict in the *Library of Fleury*, p. 284.

Similar reciprocal verses on Saint Scholastica, in Arnold Wion’s third book of the *Tree of Life*, under February 10, vol. II, p. 47, begin:

“O blessed sister of Benedict, blessed in Christ’s name,

O blessed sister of the exceptional father.”

In this poem Paulus testifies that he also sang the praises of the same virgin in heroic verse:

“Formerly, most chaste one, we wrote other praises for you

in heroic verses—behold, in heroic verses.”

Baronius’s opinion is less credible, since he attributes the work to Saint Bertharius; nor could I persuade myself that Bede was its author, although in Bede’s works there are also eight distichs, and more extensive ones, in vol. VII, p. 350 and following.

Among several of his letters there is a *Letter on the Rule of Saint Benedict* [Note: [Col. 0417C] The fragments of letters to Charlemagne published by Baluzius, vol. I of the *Miscellany*, p. 362 and following, are not by Paulus the Deacon but by Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia. This should therefore be corrected in the excellent Cave’s *Literary History*. Nor should the verses of Paulus on the miracles of Saint Benedict, whose editions were mentioned above as lost, be attributed to him.] written to Charlemagne in the name of Theodamarus, abbot of Monte Cassino; it is found in Angelus della Noce’s notes to Leo of Ostia, book VII, chapter 12.

The same Angelus states that he read, under Paulus’s name, an *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*, although he denies that it is by him. Leo, however, testifies that the rule was expounded by Paulus, book I, chapter 15; Hugo Menard preferred to attribute it to the monk Ruthardus, a pupil of Rabanus and Strabo.

An epitaph on Venantius Fortunatus is found in book II, chapter 23, of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*.

A sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary is found in volume IX of Edmund Martene’s *Ancient Monuments*, p. 266.

A hymn to Saint John the Baptist, beginning “That they may sing with loosened voices,” is found in the Roman Breviary, June 24, and elsewhere.

You may read in Leo of Ostia, book I, chapter 15—or, as it appears in Peter the Deacon, chapter 8 of *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*—that Paulus composed rhythmically almost all the short readings of the annual calendar. According to Peter, he “composed rhythmically all the short readings from the beginning of the world to his own age, together with the annual calendar.”

Peter adds that Paulus wrote verses to Emperor Charlemagne and to Arichis, prince of Benevento and son-in-law of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. The verses to Arichis are found in Camillus Peregrinus’s *History of the Lombard Princes*, Naples, 1643, quarto, p. 235.

Of the fifty homilies of Paulus mentioned by the same Peter, some survive, according to Giovanni Battista Mari, in manuscripts in the Medicean and Cassinese libraries. One was also printed among the little works of several holy Fathers, Lyons, 1615, p. 450, on Matthew XVIII, 23: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king.” It begins: “The present reading from the holy Gospel.”

[Col. 0417C] Some attribute to Paulus a chronological collection with a brief historical narrative, under the name of an unknown monk of Monte Cassino, extending from the year 840 to 875. It was published by Camillus Peregrinus in the *History of the Lombard Princes* and reprinted in volume II of Muratori’s *Thesaurus* and in the ninth volume of Burmann’s collection.

No one has yet published the *Book of the Deeds of the Bishops of Pavia*, which Galesinius testified that he had seen.

A hymn on the passion of Saint Mercury, whose martyrdom is commemorated on November 25, was published by Peter Piperno of Benevento in book V, chapter 20, of *On Magical Effects*, Naples, 1647, quarto. He either found no second hymn on the translation of the body of Saint Mercury to Benevento, or omitted it after finding it.

A hymn for the feast of the Assumption of the Holy Virgin, August 15, beginning “Who could, with abundant speech, mighty one,” is found in the Beneventan breviary.

A *Life of Saint Maurus* in reciprocal verse, beginning:

“Leader, way, life to your own, honor and praise, glory, virtue,

Jesus, light of light, leader, way, life to your own.”

See the notes of Giovanni Battista Mari on Peter the Deacon, p. 168. He says:

“Moreover, we preserve some manuscript fragments under the name of Paulus the Deacon, though mutilated and fragmentary, namely a *Life of Germanus, most holy Patriarch of Constantinople*; an *Oration on the Death of Peter Damian and His Renunciation of the Episcopate*, in which Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, is mentioned; a *Life of Saint Peter of Damascus, bishop*; and also [a life] of another Peter, likewise a martyr.”

According to Peter the Deacon, chapter 9:

“Hilderic, a pupil of this Paulus, composed exceptionally lucid verses on the origin of his teacher, his life, education, learning, religion, and appearance.”

This is the work which the praised Marus, in his notes to chapter 8, published from the Cassinese Library under the title *Epitaph*. It consists of forty-one verses and begins:

“Your bright fame is exceedingly renowned throughout the ages.”

Paulus the Deacon, in addition to the sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary, also composed a homily on the passage, “Jesus entered into a certain village.” P. Martene published it together with the sermon on the Assumption in *Ancient Monuments*, vol. IX, p. 270.

The verses, or epitaph, placed by Ailderic to Paulus, published from a Cassinese manuscript much more accurately than by Miraeus, were edited by P. Gattula in *Cassinese History*, vol. I, part I, p. 26. Here is the beginning:

“When clear fame makes [you] exceedingly renowned throughout the world.” [Note: [Col. 0418C] Miraeus reads: *tua* (“your”).]

The Reverend Abbot Le Beuf, in his *Dissertation on the Ecclesiastical and Civil History of Paris*, vol. I, p. 411 and following, published several verses of this Paulus, namely:

On p. 411, a hexameter poem to Peter of Pisa, Charlemagne’s teacher in grammar. It begins: “Candide Lumbifido.”

On p. 412, “Verses of Paulus Sent to the King.” It begins: “Cinthius occiduas,” etc.

On p. 414, there is a supplicatory work in verse by Paulus to Charlemagne, imploring liberty for his brother, who had been captured in war and held captive for seven years. His letter to Theudemarus, abbot of Monte Cassino, follows, in which he declares that he is held by an ardent desire to free himself from the court and join the Cassinese community.

# HISTORICAL WORKS OF PAULUS WINFRIDUS THE DEACON, OR THE FIRST PART OF HIS COMPLETE WORKS

## [HISTORY OF THE LOMBARDS]

[Col. 0419]

# PROLEGOMENA TO THE LOMBARD HISTORY OF PAULUS THE DEACON

*(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*.) Preface of L. A. Muratori.*

[Col. 0419A] Paulus, whom learned men commonly call the Deacon, was a Lombard by nation and had Warnefridus for his father. This is why he is also given the surname Warnefridus, as he himself states in book IV, chapter 39, of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*.

His great-great-grandfather Leuphis came to Italy with the Lombards, being himself of Lombard descent. His great-grandfather Lupicis had established his home in the fortress of Forum Julii, in the province of Venetia; from there he was led into captivity by the Avars. At length he returned to Forum Julii and restored his property and family there.

“The latter,” Paulus says, “begot my grandfather Arichis; Arichis in turn begot my father Warnefrid; Warnefrid, from his wife Theudelinda, begot me, Paulus, and my brother Arichis, who took our grandfather’s name.”

Herkempertus, who lived only one century after Paulus, affirms that Paulus himself was born at Forum Julii in his fuller *History of the Lombards*, preserved by Camillus Peregrinus. There he praises the Deacon Paulus as “one who was born in the city of Forum Julii.”

In Paulus’s epitaph, however, Hilderic, once his disciple and abbot, says that he was born “where the shining river Timavus often has its courses.” These words seem rather to designate Aquileia as Paulus’s homeland. Hence it came about that Paulus is commonly called the Aquileian Deacon. That name may perhaps indicate not his birthplace but the church whose clergy he joined; for Forum Julii, like Aquileia, was subject to one bishop, or patriarch.

As a young man he went to Pavia and was educated at the royal court. He devoted himself entirely to literary study and was consequently dear to the Lombard kings Ratchis, Cunipert, and Desiderius.

If we trust Leo Marsicanus in the *Cassinese Chronicle*, book I, chapter 15, after Pavia had been captured by Charlemagne and the strength of the Lombards had been utterly broken, Paulus was taken to France and became a very close associate of King Charles. But afterward, when rivals had stirred up a charge that he had participated in a conspiracy against Charles, and because of his steadfast loyalty to Desiderius, formerly king of his people, he was exiled by Charles’s command to the island of Diomedes.

After several years of exile he fled from there and lived in great honor with Arichis, duke of Benevento. When that prince finally died, Paulus became a monk in the holy solitude of Monte Cassino, where [Col. 0420A] he most devoutly completed the remainder of his life.

Later writers have repeated this account, following Leo Marsicanus, with their eyes closed. The celebrated Mabillon, however, in the *Benedictine Annals*, under the year 777, considers this exile of Paulus to belong among old fables. What lies beyond doubt is that the Deacon joined the monks of Monte Cassino and, in that monastery, died on the Ides of April, approximately in the year 799 of the Christian era.

Paulus the Deacon extended his reputation among posterity through various writings. He left an appendix to the histories of Eutropius, carried from the emperors Valentinian and Valens down to Justinian; we have already discussed it above in the preface to the *Miscellaneous History*. He also wrote, at the request of Angilramnus, bishop of Metz, a little book, or *History of the Bishops of Metz*. Then he wrote the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great, Pope* and, in addition to a *Homily on Saint Benedict*, published separately, he composed an extensive *Homiliary* at Charlemagne’s command, arranged for the feasts of the entire year [Col. 0420B] and excerpted from the homilies of Saints Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Origen, Leo, Bede, and others.

All these works have been published in print, as have certain fragments of letters issued by Baluzius. Paulus is also credited with the *Life*, or *Passion*, of Saint Cyprian; the lives of Saints Benedict, Maurus, and the virgin Scholastica; a poem on Saint Scholastica; and certain hymns, among them the celebrated hymn in honor of Saint John the Baptist, “That they may sing with loosened voices,” and others. But these attributions are uncertain.

The *Life of Saint Arnulf* attributed to Paulus the Deacon in Bede is none other than the work read in the *History of the Bishops of Metz*. Paulus is also said to have committed to writing a commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, which occurs in certain manuscript codices; but the distinguished Mabillon maintains that this work should rather be attributed to Hildemar.

If we believe Galesinius, Paulus also left a *History of the Bishops of Pavia*. I do not value Galesinius so highly that I consider him a competent judge in this matter. Certainly no one else has seen this work, either before or since—not even the people of Pavia, although it was in their interest either to preserve or to redeem a little work so dear to them. [Col. 0421A] Giovanni Battista Marus hints at other fragments of Paulus the Deacon’s works in his notes to Peter the Deacon’s *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*.

As for the *History*, or six books *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, which we are now reprinting, it has our Paulus as its unquestionably certain author, and he wrote it after adopting the monastic life. It is truly an outstanding work; if it were removed, the history of the Lombard kingdom and people among the Italians would be exceedingly meager and incomplete.

Some think that Paulus narrated nothing but fables concerning the origin and migration of the Lombards, and Cluverius in particular does not hesitate entirely to discredit Paulus the Deacon’s reliability on this point. Indeed, there is scarcely any people or family whose origin is not teeming with fables, and Paulus himself is not free from such wares. Nevertheless, his authority should not be attacked with so harsh and sweeping a judgment. Even in these matters it seems not to be despised, since, apart from the fact that he could have learned much about his own people, among whom he flourished, he also shows himself elsewhere to be extremely accurate and learned. He also had before his eyes a *History of the Lombards* written by Secundus of Trent in the same century in which the Lombards burst into Italy.

This history was published at Augsburg in 1515, then at Basel in 1532, and afterward at Leiden in 1595. In these editions the work ended with the words: “guarding the peace of the Franks and Avars.” Friedrich Lindenbrog, however, added to his Hamburg edition of 1611 a fragment which Freher also published among the *Frankish Historians* issued at Hanover in 1613 from the Palatine manuscript.

I too shall append that same fragment in this edition, together with other additions [Col. 0422A] made by an ancient anonymous author and published by Freher. Nevertheless, since that fragment is absent from other manuscripts of the *History of the Lombards*, I would not wish to attribute it without hesitation to our Paulus as well.

Certainly Gruterus, discussing this supplement, says that it exists in only one manuscript, “to which each person may attach as much weight as is permitted by the testimony of a single witness.” Indeed, the very learned Pagius, in his *Criticism of Baronius*, under the year 774, no. 7, says:

“I do not doubt that this addition belongs to some later author.”

Pagius proves this from the fact that the author of the addition places the defeat of Pavia, the capture of King Desiderius, and the end of the Lombard kingdom “in the year 773 from the Lord’s Incarnation,” although the common reckoning of the ancient historians and monuments establishes that these events occurred only in the following year, namely 774.

Paulus the Deacon was a contemporary of those events—indeed, an eyewitness to the overthrow of his own people—and therefore could not have been mistaken in assigning the year of so memorable a disaster. [Col. 0422B] Moreover, Paulus always speaks copiously, affectionately, and honorably of his kings; the writer of the fragment, on the other hand, writes of the last kings with hostility and excessive brevity, and calls Desiderius “a certain duke of the Lombards,” as though he were an unknown man, although he had been duke of Tuscany and was the last to rule the Lombard kingdom.

Finally, to mention this point, this Lombard history is printed in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. X, as well as at the end of Grotius’s *History of the Goths*, published at Amsterdam in 1655, although the Freherian fragment is omitted.

[Col. 0421]

# NOTICE TO THE READER BY HORATIUS BLANCUS OF ROME

[Col. 0421C] Since a new edition of Paulus the Deacon was, according to the plan of dates set out above, to be added to this collection, whose author is the learned Muratori, and since our Palatine superiors had placed upon me the burden of demonstrating, to the best of my ability, my respect and obedience toward men distinguished by learning and excellence of character and in many ways most beneficent toward me, as well as my diligence in the work itself, I began to consider which copy of the celebrated author I should select from among the published editions.

For several copies circulate that differ from one another in no slight degree, as will be evident to anyone who compares them together. I intended to provide as corrected an edition as possible and to accomplish for Paulus Warnefridus what we have undertaken in reprinting other authors.

For this man, a member of the Lombard nation, preserved the affairs of that once very extensive kingdom from the arrival of his people in Italy. He is the sole writer of the unlettered age, and, considering the misfortune of those times, not an inelegant one. If he were lost, the greatest gap would arise in Italian history, and this illustrious city would suffer a loss—the city that, raised to the majesty of a royal seat, ruled over almost all Italy, and, as the ancient Roman Empire declined and the fortunes of the Goths were torn away, took upon itself and strengthened the glory of Italian power.

Indeed, if our Paulus is removed, what darkness will not descend upon the affairs of the Lombard kingdom? What splendor will not have vanished from the world, when almost all the other writers remain silent and scarcely utter a word or two while hastening on to other subjects? What obscurity would finally be cast upon our law if the laws of the fiefs, derived from the Lombards and preserved down to this day, were not assisted by the reading of Paulus?

For these reasons Paulus demanded more accurate care, and to apply that care as far as I could, I obtained the example of Friedrich Lindenbrog, published in the Plantinian press. I again offer my thanks to the most learned man, Don Giovanni Gaspare Berretta, a Cassinese monk, who supplied me with the use of this book, long sought in vain, since scruples prevent us from moving the other Ambrosian copy from its place.

I preferred the Lindenbrog edition to the others chiefly because that man of great reputation, highly praised for his knowledge of antiquities, had added various readings from manuscript codices and illustrated them with learned notes. He designated his name only by its initial letters, which led Angelus della Noce, abbot of Monte Cassino, into error in his notes to Leo of Ostia, when he attributed this edition, approved by himself, to Bonaventure Vulcanius. It must be restored to its true author, Lindenbrog.

I also thought it would be more acceptable to learned men if the genuine reading could be known from a new collation of my own with other ancient codices. For this reason, through the favor of the most learned Joseph Anthony Saxius, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, I used an old manuscript of excellent quality, bound in the same volume after the *Miscellaneous History*. I wished to have a specimen of its script engraved in the following plate, to demonstrate the reliability of the ancient codex.

Another codex also came to light when the learned Count Donatus Sylva and I, with the assistance of the most courteous canon Brenno, were investigating among fragments of papers in the archive of the basilica of Monza for ancient monuments relating to our Lombards. Yet my spirit recoiled from the unhappy condition, the wasted labor, and the calamity or negligence of the ancients.

I say that, among the many manuscript codices preserved there, the *History* of our Paulus appeared, fuller than the others in matters relating to that same basilica. These additions are read with only a few variants in the Ascensian edition, as I have noted in its proper place. I also supplied a specimen of this manuscript in the following plate.

Someone may perhaps argue with me that a more certain indication of the age in which this codex was written is provided by the following clause, which the same scribe inserted, in one and the same form of script and in an unbroken series, amid the description of Italy near the end of book II, in a place sufficiently inappropriate, on manuscript folio 23. The words there are these.

“Under the reign of the emperor Otto the Younger, in the month of August, a comet-star appeared traversing [the sky], in the third indiction [Col. 0423A]. In that very year this occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. The moon lost its light for about an hour, and a great earthquake occurred, at cockcrow. For the fourth indiction.

“Likewise, while Otto the emperor, father of the aforesaid Otto the Younger, was reigning, in the fourteenth indiction: this occurred on the day before the Kalends of November. A sign appeared in the sky. Truly, toward the north, around cockcrow, the sky was seen to brighten like dawn. In that brightness a very white column appeared standing upright from the earth, its top reaching to the northern star. On either side of it the sky was fiery like flame, and there appeared dark, sulfurous clouds full of rain. All this was seen at approximately the fourth hour.”

Since the third indiction occurred only once during the reign of Otto the Younger—for although he had a double epoch, he did not prolong it beyond the sixteenth year of his reign, in which, after his disastrous battle with the Greeks, while he was eager to seize the part of Italy beyond the Tiber, he returned by right of restoration and died at Rome in the year of Christ 983, as the more accurate historians record—it follows that the third indiction must be assigned to the year 975, in which the comet appeared, and the following year, 976, in which the lunar eclipse and the earthquake occurred, to the fourth indiction. Yet this scribe, whoever he was, asserts that these two consecutive years, which our method of reckoning distinguishes, were only one year; for in his time the period of years was reckoned not from the Nativity but from the Incarnation. For that reason, the month of February of the fourth indiction is counted in the same year in which the third indiction had elapsed.

Moreover, I have recorded this eclipse, the earthquake, and the other phenomena all the more willingly because I have so far encountered no mention of them in writers of that age; and from this I believe it may be asserted that this Modoetian Codex was written under Otto the Younger. Its very script agrees with this, as experts will recognize, and among the ancients it was common to consign the more notable events of their times to memory through such notices and to insert them into the books of others, as Mabillon and many others have observed. But I return to the edition of Paul.

I retained the Lindenbrogian text and added at the foot the variant readings published by him, together with my own variants from both of the aforementioned Codices, marking them with the initial letters A. M. and L. Thus the Ambrosian, Modoetian, and Lindenbrogian Codices are each identified in their proper place whenever any of them differs even slightly from the text set before it. Learned men approve this scrupulous diligence, by which passages of authors often corrupted are restored to their purity. Nor did I shrink from adding this arduous labor to the continual reading of so many other writers. In it I had as assistant our most exacting Philippus Argelatus, so that, most courteous reader, a fuller supply of material might be available to you and you might more conveniently investigate Paul’s meaning amid the very abundance of copies, especially with the aid of the Ambrosian Codex, which is older than the other and approaches Paul’s own age more closely, and which in many places has a distinctive reading [Col. 0423D], generally the more corrected.

I also appended Lindenbrog’s notes, in which that most learned man illuminated and adorned much in our author from the deeper antiquity of Greek and Latin learning, with the greatest elegance and erudition. When reading through them, I noticed that this highly praised man had not willingly abstained from matters relating to history, as he openly professes in his letter. I therefore thought I ought to undertake this labor myself: rashly indeed, if I had intended to enter the public arena on a contrived occasion with a man so celebrated for the fame of his published works, though virtually invited by him and taking advantage of an appropriate opportunity, I seem rather to have complied with his wishes after his death—which was my sole desire.

For the keen-eyed Lindenbrog knew that our Paul deviated from the truth in more than one place, especially in matters preceding his own age, or failed to indicate the sequence of events adequately, and at times even plainly reversed it. Moreover, since Paul drew three histories together on a single thread—Greek, Frankish, and Lombard—and since many events occurred among these three most powerful nations, he interwove the separate histories so that they do not always correspond with one another without exposing him to the charge of error. This was why stricter critics attacked him so harshly. More equitable minds, however, have long been persuaded that this history deserves the highest esteem once whatever may have been drawn from impure sources has been cleansed away. Lindenbrog wished for this, and on suitable occasions the observations of very celebrated men accomplished it—especially Baronius, the foremost author of sacred history, when he reviewed the sequence of Lombard times according to his own method. Following the torch of so great a man, I too attempted to complete the work with continuous notes, so that readers might have at hand, while reading Paul himself, the evidence by which the order of the events he narrates could either be corrected or explained [Col. 0424B].

The authority of outstanding men induced me to undertake this work—namely, that of the most excellent Count Carlo Archinto and the Marquis Theodor Alexander Trivulzio. Judging the matter by their learning and expertise, not by my own inadequacy, they so bound me to them by their advice and by the abundance of learned conversation they regularly held with me about literary affairs that I would already have been ashamed to depart from their opinion, fearing that my prolonged excuse might be attributed to laziness.

I therefore thought it better to be overcome by the judgment of my patrons. Taking up my pen, I first took care to arrange the chronology of the Lombard kings from Alboin’s arrival in Italy—namely, from the year 568—up to the death of Liutprand, with which Paul concluded his history, so that the years of each king enumerated by our author would be recorded in their proper place in continuous sequence. Learned men have devoted great labor to this matter. In investigating it myself, I wished to admit no conjectures except those drawn from the testimony of writers of the same age, wherever such testimony happened to exist, or from the dates of royal diplomas. If only a greater number of these were made publicly available, we could establish a more certain chronological system, since some of those already published have been corrupted in their numerical indications either by the ravages of time or by the negligence of copyists.

In this endeavor I sometimes departed from the chronology of more recent historians, especially Sigonius; but I appended the arguments by which I thought the authority of the others should by no means be followed. In a similar manner I traversed the periods of the Lombard dukes, reviewing the opinions of Camillus Peregrinus and other men of this kind.

In those passages where our author is supported by the testimony of other ancient writers, I likewise noted this, so that greater credibility might accrue to him. At the very beginning of the History I deliberately revisited the celebrated controversy over the origin of the Lombard people, following the learned men Cluverius and Grotius. They have treated the matter so thoroughly with their learning that scarcely anything new can be brought forward; and it will be useful, at the very entrance of the history, to trace the matter back to its deeper source [Col. 0424D].

I thought by this means, most courteous reader, to win your favor. If you approve, I shall rejoice; if you detect an error, I shall gain from your correction.

Finally, I wish to warn you that in this edition of ours, as in those of Lindenbrog and Grotius, the summaries of the chapters have not been correctly placed. Chapter 48 actually begins above, at the beginning of chapter 47, with the words “Apud Beneventum,” etc.; its summary should therefore have been moved back. Nevertheless, lest we introduce a division of the chapters different from that of the printed editions and thereby create a greater inconvenience, we have concealed the error. Farewell.

[Col. 0427]

## CATALOGUE OF THE LOMBARD KINGS

**I. AGELMUND.** From the family of the Gunginci, after the dukes Ibor and Aio had died, he was acclaimed king of the Lombards. Paul, col. 452. He was killed by the Bulgars, leaving a daughter captive, col. 454.

**II. LAMISSIO.** Agelmund’s foster-son; he fought with an Amazon, col. 453. He received the kingship and avenged Agelmund’s death. He died, col. 454.

**III. LETHU.** He reigned for forty years. He left the kingdom to his son, col. 456.

**IV. HILDEHOC.**

**V. GUDEHOC.** He led the Lombards into the territory of the Rugii, col. 456.

**VI. CLAFFO.** Son of Gudehoc, col. 458.

**VII. TATO.** Son of Claffo. He destroyed the kingdom of the Heruli, col. 458. He was deprived of life and kingdom by Wacho, the son of his brother Zuchilo, col. 462.

**WACHO.** Not counted by Paul in the royal lists, nor by King Rothari in the prologue to his laws, because he seized the kingdom by force, col. 462.

**VIII. WALTARI.** Son of Wacho, of the Lithingian stock like the preceding kings. He reigned for seven years, col. 464.

**IX. AUDOIN.** He led the Lombards into Pannonia and defeated the Gepids, col. 464. He had Rodelinda as wife and Alboin as son, col. 465.

**X. (I. [Note: [Col. 0427] From the time when the Lombards gained possession of Italy.]) ALBOIN.** He killed Cunimund, king of the Gepids, and took his daughter Rosemund as wife after Clotsuinda’s death, col. 475. He led the Lombards into Italy, col. 483. He was killed by Helmichis at the counsel of his wife Rosemund and reigned for three years, col. 498.

**XI. (II.) CLEPH.** He had Massana as wife. He reigned one year and six months and was murdered by one of his retainers, col. 501.

**XII. (III.) AUTHARI.** Cleph’s son, first called Flavius. He stormed Brescello, col. 519. He married Theodolinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians, col. 532. He was carried off by poison; he reigned six years, col. 540.

**XIII. (IV.) AGILULF.** Duke of Turin, Theodolinda’s second husband, elevated to the kingship by the Lombards, col. 540. He had daughters—one, unnamed, the wife of Godescalch of Parma, col. 552—and Gundiberga, col. 566; and a son, Adaloald, whom he made his associate in the kingdom, col. 566. He reigned for twenty-five years, col. 578.

**XIV. (V.) ADALOALD.** He fell into insanity and was expelled from the kingdom after he had reigned ten years with his mother, col. 579.

**XV. (VI.) ARIOALD.** He succeeded Adaloald and reigned twelve years, col. 579. He had Gundiberga as wife, I believe.

**XVI. (VII.) ROTHARI.** By family, an Arodus. He promulgated laws, ibid. He reigned sixteen years and four months, col. 585.

**XVII. (VIII.) RODOALD.** Son of Rothari. Paul gave him Gundiberga as wife; perhaps she had married Rothari after Arioald, col. 586. He was killed by a Lombard whose wife he had violated. He reigned seven years and five days, col. 588.

**XVIII. (IX.) ARIPERT.** Son of Gunduald, Theodolinda’s brother. He reigned nine years, col. 590.

**XIX. (X.) BERTARID AND GODEBERT.** Sons of Aripert. They reigned one year and three months, col. 612. Because of their mutual discord, Grimoald, duke of Benevento, seized the kingdom: Godebert was killed and Bertarid put to flight, col. 590.

**XX. (XI.) GRIMOALD.** Having secured the kingdom, he married the daughter of King Aripert, col. 591. While attempting to strike a dove with an arrow, he died on the ninth day after being bled, when a vein ruptured, col. 612. He reigned nine years, leaving a son, Garibald. Ibid.

**XXI. (XII.) BERTARID.** He was recalled to the kingdom, not without a miracle, col. 613. He made his son Cunibert his associate in the kingdom, col. 614. He died after reigning alone and with his son for eighteen years, col. 615.

**XXII. (XIII.) CUNIBERT ALONE.** He had Hermelinda as wife, descended from the Saxon people of England, col. 616. He fought against the rebel Alachis and defeated him, col. 617. He reigned alone for twelve years, col. 636.

**XXIII. (XIV.) LIUTPERT.** Cunibert’s very young son. Under the guardianship of Ansprand, he was driven from the kingdom by Ragunbert, duke of Turin, son of King Godebert, col. 637.

**XXIV. (XV.) RAGUNBERT.** He died in the same year. Ibid.

**XXV. (XVI.) ARIPERT.** Son of Ragunbert. He killed King Liutpert, whom he had captured in battle. He drove his guardian Ansprand into exile and cruelly treated Ansprand’s wife and daughter, col. 639. He was drowned in the river Ticino, col. 646. He reigned with his father and alone until the twelfth year, col. 647.

**XXVI. (XVII.) ANSPRAND.** With the aid of the Bavarians, among whom he had taken refuge, he defeated Aripert. After his victory he held the kingdom for only three months. Ibid.

**XXVII. (XVIII.) LIUTPRAND.** Son of Ansprand, proclaimed king shortly before his father’s death. Ibid. He accomplished many distinguished deeds. He succumbed to illness. He reigned thirty-one years and seven months, col. 670.

**XXVIII. (XIX.) SAINT RACHIS.**

**XXIX. (XX.) AISTULF.**

**XXX. (XXI.) DESIDERIUS.** Under him the kingdom of the Lombards was overthrown by Charlemagne.

[Col. 0429]

## EPITAPH OF PAUL THE DEACON, WRITTEN BY HILDERIC, ABBOT AND HIS DISCIPLE

Since clear and exceedingly illustrious fame throughout the ages  
joins you with the stars in blessed assemblies,  
who, O deacon, could adequately proclaim  
your truthful triumphs, supreme Paul, in words pouring forth light?

So that the reader hurrying here, and the visitor, may know  
that your limbs rest beneath this sacred tomb,  
it is fitting to unlock in song,  
in a poem worthy of it, the nourishing deeds  
of your beloved praise.

Long ago, you drew your lineage from the distinguished stock of the Bardic people,  
a race then renowned throughout the world  
for its strength, arms, and wealth.

So worthy is that race: you were born of its offspring  
where the river Timavus often has shining courses  
[the transmitted wording is uncertain].

At once the royal court took you in for upbringing,  
at the prompting of divine inspiration,  
because of your glory and because you were the light of your fatherland.

When, beyond the Tiber, peaceful life and learning  
then remained for all peoples and lofty kings [the printed *tua* is uncertain],  
you began fittingly to penetrate  
all the heights of sacred wisdom,  
with the pious king Ratchis giving guidance.

When you had worthily grasped very many doctrines,  
you, shining upon all like Phoebus  
from the heavenly stars,  
adorned the northern peoples with radiant light.

And thus, when the glory of the fleeting age  
was already enriching you abundantly  
with fitting treasures,  
you, devoted to the eternal Lord,  
boldly despised the honors of this world  
for the sake of a blessed life without end.

Trusting in the piety of the immense King of heaven,  
you hastened here with a heart blossoming  
for the Lord Christ,  
to bow your neck beneath the enclosures  
of blessed Benedict.

Soon the sacred assembly, adorned by your example,  
began to shine with brilliant radiance.

For in you piety continually remained,  
along with sweet affection,  
the nectarous love of peace, victorious patience,  
exceedingly skillful simplicity, supreme concord,  
and every good thing together,  
always worthy of reverence.

Therefore the jewel-studded realms of heaven now retain you,  
while through the ages you likewise retain  
a starry crown.

May this sacred song of honor be pleasing to you,  
which I, Hilderic, your disciple, have sung through tears.  
By your sacred prayers, please make me,  
your ever-beloved Father, obtain perpetual rest.

[Col. 0429]

## TO THE MOST NOBLE AND DISTINGUISHED MEN, LORD OTTO A DURING, DEAN OF THE CHURCH OF BREMEN AND PROVOST OF VALLE-LILIORUM; LORD VITO ORTELIUS WINSEMIUS, JURIST, COUNSELOR OF THE MOST SERENE KING OF DENMARK AND DEAN OF THE CHURCH OF HAMBURG. F. L. B. DEDICATES THIS

Most distinguished men, noble through antiquity and fortunate through nobility: the saying of the ancient poet Lucilius has always seemed to me excellent, when he warns that above all we ought to consider

> our fatherland’s welfare first,  
> then that of our parents,  
> and finally, last of all, our own.

With the greatest justice and right, therefore, the land that gave us birth, nourished us, educated us, and drew out, fanned, and fostered the hidden sparks of the divine mind within us demands the first place for itself [Col. 0430]. I freely acknowledge that this was done for me; and, wishing to offer some return, I decided to bring this History of Paul once more into the light.

Although it deals chiefly with the Lombards, it nevertheless often mentions other peoples of Germany. I truly do not know what more useful thing than History I could offer: from it one may learn how the urn of worldly fortunes has varied, and, as though from a citadel,

> to look down from afar upon the errors of men  
> spread widely throughout the world;

and it nevertheless outweighs [other works] by its own merit, however uncultivated and barbarous its style may be. This should be borne with equanimity in this book. Such were the times then: rarely did anyone sacrifice to the graces of Mercury; learning was so deserted, and a single general sluggishness had so oppressed minds everywhere, that no beginner was kindled by the pursuit of emulation.

How great would the admiration of this work be—good heavens!—if it had appeared in those times when eloquence supplied what events lacked. Now the greatest deeds lie buried beneath the baseness of their words. What prevents us from thinking that these were the greatest deeds, performed by men who were a terror even to the most warlike peoples, men against whom Mars himself would scarcely dare, as the Comic poet says, to open his mouth? These are the men whom Alexander declared must be avoided, whom Pyrrhus feared, and whom Caesar was terrified of; these, finally, are the peoples among whom the peace of the Romans and of others came to an end.

But lest, by loving my Germans too much, I myself become hateful, let my speech turn rather to you, most distinguished men. Since you belong to a noble people and are yourselves foremost among the noble, I have chosen you as the men to whom I would especially offer this book, following in this the custom of our ancestors. Just as they used to offer the first fruits and other gifts as libations to their gods, so I offer you these first fruits of my studies. Receive them kindly, as befits your dignity and humanity, and regard me as commended to you.

Lyon in Belgium, on the day before the Ides of July, 1595.

[Col. 0431B]

## PREFACE OF F. LINDENBROGIUS

A single and wholly honorable motive moved me to publish this History of the Lombards: love of our common fatherland, that is, Germany. When I saw that very few people had committed the excellent deeds of our ancestors to writing, and that the best of those writers had, by the will of the gods, gone to the common abode, I judged that this evil had to be resisted, lest this work suffer a similar fate.

Although our Paul must be placed among proletarian writers and those of the lowest bench, nevertheless, if we seriously love what is right, it must be admitted that one can learn from him certain things that one would seek in vain from others. Here one may rightly apply the saying of Varro:

> “Just as there is no field of good grain without some worthless ear, so there is none so bad that it does not contain something good.”

For this reason I prepared this new edition. Nor could I be deterred from my undertaking by the style of a writer who does not threaten us with those

> grand words of untamed Cicero;

indeed, in some places he is barbarous. Hence it happens that many read books of this kind with the greatest annoyance, especially those who can tolerate nothing except what is polished and scholastic.

To reconcile these tedious people somewhat, I had to set snares for their ears; therefore I added certain notes, like an afterpiece following a play, in which I wished to explain matters relating to ancient customs and other passages that seemed unlikely to be understood by the common reader. Whether this has turned out successfully is for the judgment of the truly learned [Col. 0432B]. As for those mushrooms, and those who judge more by their noses than by reason, I pay them no attention.

I took care deliberately not to heap up too many examples in support of the subject I wish to teach, although this would not have been difficult for me. I preferred to leave this field to those who may exercise themselves in it and seek the palm from such activity. Nor was it my intention to note matters bearing upon history, lest I offend those who may perhaps have long since labored over them.

To make it clear whose authority this edition follows, understand it thus. I used a manuscript copy supplied to me by the distinguished and greatly learned Abraham Ortelius. I also used two printed editions, one printed by Ascensius in 1514, the other at Augsburg in 1515; my friend Franciscus Raphelengius was the intermediary who procured the latter for me.

I followed chiefly the manuscript and the Augsburg edition, because they agreed in almost everything; indeed, they seemed to possess somewhat more of the genuine text—*γνήσιον*, “authentic.” The Ascensian edition differed in a thousand places, but I wished to extract only those variant readings that were of some importance; for what purpose would it serve to record them all?

With these words, whoever you may be, reader—and you above all, enjoy the happy condition of Germany and favor my studies.

[Col. 0431]

## JOHN TRITEMIUS, ABBOT OF SPANHEIM, IN HIS *CATALOGUE OF ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*

[Col. 0431A] Paul, a monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the Order of Saint Benedict, an Italian by nationality, a man exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly educated in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, was held in great esteem by the emperor Charles because of his learning.

Formerly, before his conversion, he was a deacon of the Church of Aquileia and chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. He was captured with Desiderius by Charles and taken to Gaul; afterward he became a monk. He wrote quite a number of volumes both in verse and in prose, of which I have found only the following.

[Note: [Col. 0431A] Paul does not mention this Desiderius, nor Aistulf, who reigned before him in the year 753, as Regino writes. Anyone wishing to read more about these two kings may consult Book II of Regino.]

At the request of Adelberga, daughter of King Desiderius, he added:

[Col. 0432A]

Two books added to the *Chronicle* of Eutropius.

One book of *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*.

One book of the *Life of Pope Gregory I*.

One book of the *Life of Saint Arnulf*.

One book, in verse, of the *Life of Saint Benedict*.

Six books of the *Deeds of the Lombards*.

One book of several hymns in different meters.

One book of letters to various persons.

At Charles’s command he arranged histories and readings for the entire year, appropriate to the individual feasts of the saints. He also compiled and wrote many other works. He flourished in the time of that same Charlemagne, in the year 780.

[Col. 0433]

## PAUL WARNEFRID [Note: [Col. 0433A] He himself writes in this history, Book IV, chapter 39, that this is the author’s true name. Most call him a deacon; others also call him a monk, as does the manuscript copy of Paul, monk of Cassino. He seems, however, to have first been from Atria; for in ancient glosses, where fragments of Festus are cited under his name—Festus whom our author mutilated, alas, to the great harm of the republic of letters—Paul of Athens is named. A great man considers this corrupt and thinks that it should be written “Paul of Atria”; he may, as one might suspect, have been from Atria at that time, later a deacon, and finally a monk. Saxo Grammaticus calls him simply Paul, adding no further name; if desired, see Lindenbrog’s Book VIII. Our manuscript Codices from which we have noted the variant readings are titled as follows: the Ambrosian: “Here begins the first book of the History of the Lombards”; the Modoetian: “Paul the Deacon’s account of the Deeds of the Lombards.”] DEACON OF FORUM JULII, ON THE DEEDS OF THE LOMBARDS. (C)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE. On Germany, which nourishes many peoples and therefore gives rise to many nations.

[Col. 0433A]

The more the northern region is removed from the sun’s heat and chilled by snowy cold, the healthier it is for human bodies and the more suited to the propagation of peoples [Note: [Col. 0433B] Another copy omits *magis*, “more.” Lindenbrog. Thus in the Ambrosian.] ; conversely, the nearer every southern region is to the sun’s heat, the more it always abounds in diseases and the less suited it is to sustaining mortals [Note: [Col. 0433B] Another copy reads: “the more it abounds in diseases.” Lindenbrog.].

[Note: [Col. 0433B] Paul attributes the excellence of the northern region chiefly to its cold and snows, which perhaps inspire horror in us, so that he may assert that his Lombards, whom he leads forth from there, were distinguished by this benefit of nature—and not without reason. For, both according to the testimony of the ancients and in view of the commerce of modern peoples, who could now wrest this distinction from a region so well known? We know that the Macrobians, Μακρόβιοι—“long-lived people,” celebrated among the ancients—were located beneath the northern sky. Hence Plutarch says in *Natural Questions*, chapter 30:

> “Asclepiades says that Ethiopians grow old more quickly, namely in their thirtieth year, because their bodies are scorched by the excessive heat of the sun. In Britain, on the contrary, old age begins in the one hundred and twentieth year, because, owing to the coldness of those regions, bodies retain within themselves a fiery nature; and because the bodies of Ethiopians are more porous, since they are relaxed by the heat of the sun, whereas in the northern regions bodies are denser and therefore more vigorous as well.”

For these reasons Hippocrates, in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, says of the Μακρόβιοι: “It is reasonable that these people should be longer-lived than others,” and that their customs are “rather wild than tame.”]

Thus it happens that such great multitudes of peoples arise beneath the northern axis that not without reason the whole region, as far as the Tanais and westward—even though its individual places are also designated by proper names—is called by the general name Germany [Note: [Col. 0434A] The Modoetian reads: “the whole region as far as the western shore, although individual places are designated by their proper names, is nevertheless called by a general name,” etc. Both readings may perhaps be defective, since they do not sufficiently indicate the greatest division of Germany, the part extending toward the north. I believe one should not depart from the received text, since it indicates several boundaries, and the meaning is that the whole part of Europe bordering Asia, from the northern axis to the Tanais and to the western shore, is called by the general name Germany. Thus no small portion of the Muscovite and Polish kingdoms, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway would be assigned to Germany—though by the greatest geographical division, not by that with which the Romans distinguished Germany, as Paul himself observes.

For the Tanais, whose source and course were not sufficiently known to the ancients, since they falsely led it away from the Rhiphaean Mountains along a winding route, was regarded as separating Europe from Asia. Lucan, Book III:

> Where the Halys, fatal to Croesus, flows,  
> where the Tanais, descending from the summit  
> of the Rhiphaean Mountains, placed upon its banks  
> the names of a different world,  
> and was likewise the boundary of Asia  
> and of Europe, dividing the confines  
> of the middle earth.

Tacitus, in Book I of *On the Customs of the Romans*, describes Germany in a more exact style:

> “All Germany is separated from the Gauls, the Raetians, and the Pannonians by the Rhine and Danube rivers; from the Sarmatians and Dacians, by mutual fear or by mountains. The remaining sides are surrounded by Ocean, which embraces broad bays and immense expanses of islands, together with certain peoples and kings recently made known by war.”

Nevertheless, you can easily adapt this passage of Paul to Tacitus’s words if, following the ancients, you derive the Tanais from the Rhiphaean Mountains—which Tacitus appears to suggest. Paul knew these mountains very well from his Pliny, Book IV, chapter 13:

> “Next we must proceed so that the regions beyond Europe may be described; and, having crossed the Rhiphaean Mountains, the northern shore of Ocean is on the left until one reaches Gades,” etc.]

The Romans, after occupying those regions, called the two provinces beyond the Rhine Upper and Lower Germany [Note: [Col. 0435A] This division of Germany into Lower and Upper is frequent among historians and geographers and should be referred approximately to the time of Augustus, as Cellarius proves from Dio Cassius, Tacitus, and others in *Ancient Geography*, Book II, chapter 3, p. 369.]. [Note: [Col. 0434C] I would not confidently assert what is meant by the words “so that not without reason,” etc., “Germany,” unless perhaps Paul was referring to the well-known etymology of *Germania* and intended to indicate the number of its armies by the name itself.]

From this populous Germany, innumerable bands of captives are often carried away and sold for a price to southern peoples. Many nations have also often emerged from it, because it produces so many mortals that it scarcely suffices to sustain them, and these nations have afflicted not only parts of Asia but especially the neighboring part of Europe [Note: [Col. 0435A] “Because it produces such multitudes of mortals as it scarcely suffices to sustain,” Lindenbrog and the Modoetian.].

Cities destroyed throughout Illyricum and Gaul bear witness to this everywhere; but above all wretched Italy [Note: [Col. 0435A] “Throughout miserable Italy,” Lindenbrog; “Miserable Italy,” Modoetian.], which has experienced the savagery of almost all those peoples [Note: [Col. 0435B] “The Huns, Heruli, Thuringians,” Lindenbrog; “the Goths indeed, the Vandals, the quarrelsome Heruli, and the Turgilingi,” etc., Modoetian.]: the Goths, the Vandals, the Rugii, the Heruli, and the Turcilingi, as well as other fierce and barbarous nations from Germany [Note: [Col. 0435B] ... ]

An almost inexplicable difficulty will confront us at the very threshold if we wish to recount the origins of the peoples whom Paul here lists and to investigate their ancient settlements with any certainty amid such obscurity of affairs. Indeed, very learned men, highly distinguished for their knowledge of antiquity, have diligently attempted these difficult provinces; among them Philippus Cluverius was perhaps the most painstaking in his *Germania antiqua*. Yet in more than one place he endeavored to uproot the credibility of our Paul entirely. For he maintained, on the authority of Strabo, Tacitus, and Velleius Paterculus (*History*, book III, chapter 26), that the Lombards had not migrated from Scandinavia but had dwelt adjacent to the Semnones; and he argued the same concerning the other peoples mentioned here, in book III, chapter 46. Therefore, for a fuller elucidation of our Paul, I have thought it not inappropriate to append his words here.

Having restored the genuine name *Vandals*, he writes:

> “We must now consider which nations were of Vandalic stock. Pliny names only the Burgundiones, Varini, Carini, and Gutones. Of these, the Gutones held settlements by the river Vistula, the Varini in the duchy of Mecklenburg, not far from the river Elbe. Within these boundaries many other peoples also dwelt along the Codanian Gulf.
>
> “But this is not surprising. Pliny does not enumerate all the peoples of every stock, but only one or two, as it seemed appropriate to him; consequently, the rest must be supplied from other authors. To the Vandals, therefore, I add the Lemovii, or Heruli, the Rugii, Tidini, Suardones, Eudoses, Angles, Caviones, Thuringians, Nuitones, and Lombards. Since the Burgundiones, Gutones, Varini, and Lombards were of Vandalic stock, there can be no doubt about the others situated among them.
>
> “Pliny explicitly bears witness concerning those three nations. Concerning the Lombards, Paul the Deacon is indeed a fabulous but, for the purpose of proving this point, suitable witness: in his *History of the Lombards*, through sheer ignorance of nations and names, he makes the Vandals different from the Winili and narrates wars between these two names as though between entirely alien peoples. His words in book I, chapter 1, are these: ‘The Goths, therefore, etc.’; and immediately in chapter 2: ‘In the same manner, etc.’
>
> “That this account of Scandinavia is false I have demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently above, in the discussion of the Lombards. I believe that Jornandes too held the same opinion as the Deacon. In his account of Scanzia he mentions a people called the *Vinoviloth*, a name which I suspect arose from the genuine designation of the Vandals, *Vindoli*. For in Jornandes the *Finnaithae* and the *Svethidi* are likewise the Finns and the Swedes, as I have shown above.
>
> “The Deacon continues in chapter 7 as follows:

> ‘The Winili, therefore, having left Scandinavia with Ibor and Ayo as their leaders, came to the region called Scoringia and settled there for several years. At that time Ambri and Assi, leaders of the Vandals, were oppressing all the neighboring provinces by war. Having been exalted by many victories, they sent messengers to the Winili, ordering them either to pay tribute to the Vandals or to prepare themselves for the trials of war.’

> “And in chapter 9:

> ‘It is certain, however, that the Lombards, originally called Winili, were afterward so named from the length of their beards, untouched by the razor; for in their language *lang* means “long,” and *bart* means “beard.”’

> “Sigebert likewise relates this and adds that a battle was fought between the Winili and the Vandals. The account of a war between the Lombards and their neighbors may be true, as may the account of the name *Winili*; but the story of their origin in Scandinavia is entirely false. For these Vandals—the Goths, Rugii, Turcilingi, and others—came from Scandinavia no more than did the rest, although Jornandes also led the Goths, Rugii, and Heruli out of Scandinavia.
>
> “This varied and almost inexplicable error arose in the crude and ignorant age of Jornandes and the Deacon because the designation of one and the same Vandal people was altered in many ways according to differences of dialect. The Lombards, therefore, were called by another name, *Vinili*, that is, *Vindili* or Vandals—not by a proper and peculiar name, but by the common name of all the nations inhabiting the Codanian Gulf between the Vistula, the Elbe, and the Chalusus.
>
> “I believe chiefly that they fought the other Vandals between the Elbe and the Viadrus because they themselves were afterward separated from the common designation of those peoples in foreign regions, just as were the Gothones, Burgundiones, Heruli, and Rugii, concerning all of whom I shall say more shortly.

> “That the word *Vinili*, or *Vinnuli*, *Winili*, and *Winuli*, was the proper designation of the Vandals, virtually *Vindili* and *Vinduli*, is especially clear from Helmold’s *Slavic History*. He writes in book I, chapter 11:

> ‘Where Poland comes to an end, one reaches the most extensive province of the Slavs, those who in ancient times were called Vandals but are now called Vinithi, or Vinuli. The first among them are the Pomeranians, whose settlements extend as far as the Oder. Then another river, namely the Oder, flowing northward, passes through the midst of the Vinuli peoples, dividing the Pomeranians from the Wiltzi.’

> “And afterward:

> ‘After the Oder’s gentle course and the various peoples of Pomerania, the province of the Vinuli appears toward the west; these are called the Tholenzes, or Redarii.’

> “No more, by my muse’s good favor, Helmold, was *Vinuli* the proper name of the Vinithi, or Vindi, that is, the Slavs, than it was of the Vandals. I have indeed proved above by sufficiently strong and certain arguments that the Vinidi, or Venedi, were Slavs, that is, Sarmatians. But that the Vandals, or Vindeli, were Germans dwelling on this side of the Vistula was attested approximately four hundred years before the migration of the Venedi, or Slavs, into Germany by the most illustrious authors, Pliny and Tacitus. The latter even indicates that the name was already so ancient and established that some believed one of the sons of the god Tuiton himself had been called by it.
>
> “I therefore restore the word *Vinuli*, and likewise *Vinili*, which the Deacon, with a lesser error, assigns exclusively to the Lombards, to the name of the Vandili, or Vanduli, and Vindeli. But the reason why the Venedi, or Vinedi—that is, the Slavs—were called Vindeli and Vandals was no other than the reason that caused the Marcomanni and Suebi, and later also the Slavs or Venedi, who are said to call themselves and the other Slavs Czechs, to be called Bohemi. For the Bohemi were properly the Gallic Boii who, before the Marcomanni, inhabited the region enclosed by the Hercynian Forest, which consequently received the name Bohemia. Thus the Marcomanni, and later the Czechs, because they occupied Bohemia, were called Bohemi; in the same way the Vinidi, who were Sarmatians, because they occupied the lands of the Vandals, were called Vandals. The fact that the names *Vinidi* and *Vindili* were not wholly unlike each other contributed considerably to this designation, etc.”

Against this Hugo Grotius, in his *Prolegomena* to the *Gothic, Vandalic, and Lombard History*, although suppressing Cluverius’s name, inveighs—perhaps more harshly than was fitting—while seeking to restore those peoples, and the others mentioned by Paul, to Scandinavia. He was inflamed by his love for Swedish affairs, or rather by a certain passion common to nearly all writers of the recent age in this matter: each fiercely contends that our riches have been wrested by his own people and that our empire has been overthrown, stubbornly claiming eternal fame for himself from our spoils.

After Grotius had traced the origins of the Goths, against Cluverius’s opinion, back to Scandinavia and even to the Swedes, he discusses the Vandals and Lombards with great learning:

> “What more certain account of the Vandals could anyone today imagine presenting than what Procopius brought forward a thousand years ago? He spoke frequently with the Vandals in Africa; moreover, he knew Gelimer, king of the Vandals, and the Vandal nobles brought to Constantinople through daily familiarity. Is it believable that a man so eager to inquire into everything ancient either did not chiefly ask where those Vandals who occupied Spain and Africa came from, or that Gelimer and the other leading men of that people had nothing certain to answer, based on ancient tradition and songs handed down in perpetual memory?
>
> “Procopius says, in the first book of his Vandalic history, that the Vandals were no less Gothic peoples than the Ostrogoths, Visigoths, and Gepids, distinct in name but agreeing in origin and customs. He further says that they had the Gothic language and that he did not doubt they had once been a single people. And lest anyone think that he said this rashly, in the fourth book of his Gothic history he again counts the Vandals among the Gothic peoples and records that they came with the Goths from their ancestral settlement to Lake Maeotis.
>
> “Add to this Jornandes. When he lists the peoples of Scanzia, he includes the *Vinoviloth*, a word signifying the possession of the Winili. For *ot* is also ‘possession’ among the ancient Saxons, whence *feot*, or *feudum*, a fiduciary possession of fruits.
>
> “Those whom the Greeks call *Vandili*, others *Vandalii*, *Vandali*, or *Wandali*, and the old Table calls *Vanduli*, are called *Winili* by Paul Warnefrid, *Vinuli* by Adam of Bremen, and *Winuli* by others, with the vowels changed and the letter D either added or removed—a common occurrence among Germans, as we have already noted.
>
> “I shall soon add Paul Warnefrid as a witness concerning the origin of the Vandals, when I come to the Lombards. That man of extensive reading was not ignorant of most of these matters, but, trusting to his own ingenuity, as he often did elsewhere, he refused to yield to them. What, then, drove him away in this matter, as earlier in the case of the Goths, from the most ancient opinion? A certain passion. Let us see what he alleges.
>
> “Pliny includes the Burgundiones, Varini, Carrini, and Gutones among the Vindelici in Germany, where he wishes *Vindeli* to be read in the manuscripts. I readily grant that it is one and the same word in its ending, which was open to foreigners; I do not unwillingly acknowledge the difference. But how does this injure my case, when I believe that the Vandals reached Germany long ago—indeed, among the earliest peoples, as Jornandes leads me to think—and left there some peoples of their blood and name, just as I do not deny that the Goths did?
>
> “This is sufficient to dispose of the objection. But, to say what I think and to shed as much light as I can on matters obscured by antiquity, I do not believe that either *Vandals* or *Swedes* was the name of a single people.
