Just as certain Iazyges were called Metanastae and, in Latin, wandering Sarmatians, so I believe that certain Germans were called not by themselves but by those who first experienced their force—just as the German name arose from the Tungri—sometimes Suebi and sometimes Vandals.
>
> “Why some used one name and others the other, I consider accidental, according to the impression made upon the peoples whom they encountered. For everyone familiar with the German language knows that both words signified people who did not remain in fixed settlements but moved now here, now there, etc.”

And below:

> “We must not, therefore, ask how widely the name of the Vandals extended. It could extend as widely as their habit of wandering and occupying the possessions of others; but from whom did those Vandals who held Spain and afterward Africa arise and claim that they had arisen? For these are the people we are now discussing. It is no more credible that they were deceived in this matter than if someone wished to suspect the Batavi of making the same claim, when they declared to Tacitus and to certain Roman writers several centuries later that they had sprung from the Catti.
>
> “To this may be added the testimony of the ancient historian Dexippus. He wrote in the time of Gallienus, as we learn from Trebellius and Eunapius. He says that the people of whom we are speaking came as Vandals not from inner Germany, where Tacitus places the Vandals, but from the coast of the Ocean. I mean those Lombards whose power was then great in various places and finally in Italy.
>
> “Whom should I believe rather than Paul Warnefrid the Lombard? For what can be held more certain concerning matters so remote from our memory than what the songs of each people and the perpetual tradition passed down from ancestors to descendants have preserved? These are his words in the *Lombard History*: ‘In the same manner, etc.’
>
> “He rightly calls the Lombards *Winuli*, that is, ‘wanderers’; yet shortly afterward he says that they fought with the Vandals, because the pronunciation of the same word had changed over time and caused it to be thought a different name. Since the historian of Germany correctly observed this, I willingly grant him the praise he deserves. Paul of Bremen followed him and likewise says that they were called Vandals through the Winuli.
>
> “Another passage must be added to the well-known passages of that Paul, from his lesser-known *Miscellaneous History*. For when he reaches the time of the sons of Theodosius, he says, as I have related, himself a Lombard:

> ‘At that time there were Goths and many other peoples, especially those living beyond the Danube. Of these, the four more distinguished were the Goths, the Huisigoths—for *Hypogoths* is printed incorrectly, as is proved by other passages of the same writer; the letters H.U. were commonly used for W.—the Gepids, and the Vandals. They changed only their name and nothing else; all, however, were of the malignant Arian faith. Under Arcadius and Honorius, these peoples crossed the Danube and settled in Roman territory. The Gepids, from whom the Lombards and Avars were afterward divided, inhabited the villages around Singidunum and Sirmium.’

> “From unpublished Greek books our most learned Salmasius extracted this for us:

> Γήπαιδες οἱ λεγόμενοι Λογγοβάρδοι  
> *Gepids, who are called Lombards.*

> “Likewise Constantine Porphyrogenitus, emperor of Constantinople, transcribed from the history of Theophanes:

> Γήπαιδες ἐξ ὧν ὕστερον διῃρέθησαν Λογγοβάρδοι  
> *Gepids, from whom, after a division had taken place, the Lombards arose.*

> “If those Lombards whom Paul mentions came from the Gepids, then they certainly came originally from the Goths. For the Gepids undoubtedly derive their origin from the stock of the Goths; these are the words of Jornandes. He also does not allow us to remain ignorant of where they received their proper name. When the Goths first departed from Scanzia in three ships, those who traveled more slowly in one ship, becoming separated in counsel from the rest of their people, occupied an island in the river Vistula and afterward moved into more distant regions. Jornandes derives the origin of the name Gepids from their delay. In his text *Gepanta* is now incorrectly read for *Gepaita*; for *Gepait* in German means one who has delayed. The sound is heard even more clearly in the same name as it is pronounced by the Greeks, Γήπαιδες.
>
> “Procopius too, when he describes those related peoples as connected with the Goths—namely, the Ostrogoths, Visigoths, and Vandals in customs and language—adds the Gepids and says that the ruler of the Gepids was named Ostrogotha.
>
> “Nor was Paul Warnefrid the first to assign this origin to his Lombards. Before him Prosper of Aquitaine, a man of excellent reliability and bishop of Reggio, had written the same. When he reaches the time of Theodosius, these are his words:

> ‘The Lombards, having departed from the remotest borders of Germany and immediately from the coast of the Ocean, and from the great island of Scandia, eager for new settlements, first defeated the Vandals under the leaders Ibo and Ayo.’

> “Following these authorities, Otto of Freising likewise assigns to the Lombards, no less than to the Goths, an origin in Scandia.
>
> “But what does this man, who is by no means without eloquence, have to say in opposition to these authorities? He has something, certainly; but, if I see correctly, it is very slight. He says that Strabo, Tacitus, and Ptolemy place the Lombards in inner Germany long before the time of this departure. They do indeed place them there, and not in a single passage: Tacitus by the Viadrus, Strabo on this side of the Elbe, and Ptolemy after Tacitus.
>
> “The knot is easily untied if one considers that this name signifies nothing other than men with long beards, as all Germans know and that Paul himself acknowledges. Names derived from appearance are commonly given by those whom people approach, at different places and times, now to one group of men, now to another.
>
> “According to Tacitus, it was customary among the Germans ‘to let the hair and beard grow and not to remove, until an enemy had been slain, the facial appearance vowed and pledged to valor.’ We have an example of this in the civil war of the Batavi, in the same author.
>
> “But whenever a great host approached with one and the same appearance, it is not surprising that this novelty gave rise to a new name, now here and now there. What have Domitius Ahenobarbus, Frederick Barbarossa, and another pirate of the same name in common with the *Macropogones* and Lombards? Nothing, except that they had the same facial appearance, from which the same designation arose.
>
> “All that we have discussed thus far is confirmed when taken together by the emperor of Constantinople whom I have just mentioned, Constantine Porphyrometer [Porphyrogenitus], who cites as his authority Theophanes, whom the Greeks have placed in the catalogue of saints. For he says that they were all of one Gothic origin, and that the Goths were properly so called, as were the Gepids and Vandals; and that the Lombards came from the Gepids.
>
> “Let us therefore believe the ancient writers, since these recent writers have offered nothing more worthy of belief: that the Vandals, Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Gepids, and Lombards all owe their origin to Scanzia, specifically to that part occupied by the Sueones. The Sueones, or at least the greater part of them, are afterward included under the name of Northmen.”

I have copied these passages from Cluverius and Grotius at greater length than the plan assigned to our notes perhaps required; readers may nevertheless find them useful. They will serve in place of a complete dissertation for learning the origin of the Lombards, after Cluverius departed from Paul and the other writers of the Middle Ages and led many of the moderns over to his own opinion, setting aside the authority of the ancients. The remaining arguments brought forward by Bodinus, by which he derived the Lombards from his Gaul—namely, from the Langones and Bardi—have been rejected by nearly all writers.

For the rest, I willingly add my vote to Grotius’s side, indeed to that of our Paul, if my vote is worth enough to add to the number. I place the greatest weight on the constant tradition of that very enduring people, which alone preserved the memory of its deeds amid wars, frequent migrations, and, more importantly, fierce and unlettered customs, and which, after the Lombards had become civilized in Italy, entered history only late, chiefly through the agency of our Paul.

King Authari himself openly acknowledges this tradition as the Lombards’ sole monument of antiquity in the preface to his laws. There he recounts the names of the other kings from the memory of the elders. It is therefore not surprising if an anachronism has crept in or if the sequence of events is incomplete and less than exact.

The testimony of the most holy pope Gregory, surnamed the Great, also contributes to strengthening Paul’s credibility and, in my judgment, deserves the greatest weight. He himself conducted so many affairs with the Lombards, in peace and war, precisely at the time of the people’s arrival in Italy, that he must have known their origin and observed the account faithfully narrated by Jornandes—for in that unhappy age he was highly learned in both divine and human affairs.

Thus, in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 38, he writes:

> “Soon those terrible signs from heaven followed, so that spears and fiery battle lines seemed to appear from the North. Soon the savage race of the Lombards, drawn from the sheath of its habitation, rushed upon our neck.”

He had evidently copied the words “from the sheath of its habitation” from Jornandes, book I, chapter 4 of our edition, page 193.

Finally, what Albertus Krantius says at the beginning of his *Denmark* is not irrelevant to this passage:

> “It seemed worthwhile,” he says, “to set aside the affairs of each kingdom so that each might receive its own distinction and it might be separately recognized what Denmark, what Sweden—which is also Gothia—and what Norway accomplished. For the kingdom of the Lombards established in Italy—which the ancient Italians called Cisalpine Gaul—is a glory of the Danes who departed from Scania. The glory of the Goths, however, is that they conquered Italy, devastated the city of Rome, and long held a kingdom in Italy, as well as for a long time in Gaul and Spain. The Norwegians, for their part, have claimed as their own the fact that the maritime region of France was called Normandy after their name; from there they penetrated as far as Mediterranean Italy and first established a duchy in Apulia and Calabria and a county in Sicily, and afterward founded a noble kingdom in both Sicilies, which endures to this day.”

They came forth.

## Chapter II. On the island of Scandinavia, and that the people of the Winili, that is, the Lombards, departed from it

[Col. 0437A]

In the same way, the people of the Winili, that is, the Lombards, who afterward ruled prosperously in Italy, derived their origin from the peoples of Germany—[Note: [Col. 0438B] Lindenbrog reads: “Deriving its origin from Scandinavia, an island of the Baltic or Baltic Sea, it departed in search of new settlements because of its multitude, although other causes of their departure are also asserted. Of this, etc.” It would be tedious here to repeat the ancient fables and errors concerning the island of Scandinavia, especially those of Pliny, from whom our Paul drew not a little, because the Latins and Greeks, as Ziegler wrote in his special treatise, had Scandinavia almost entirely unknown. Evidence of this is that they commonly described that region as a cold zone condemned to perpetual snow and incapable of supporting any living creature, etc. Thus it is called by Pliny and Solinus *Scandia*, by Jornandes *Scanzia*, and by the ancients *Baltia* and *Basilia*, as Cluverius, Grotius, Cellarius, and others prove by the testimonies they cite in their descriptions. Ziegler calls it *Schondia* and writes the following concerning the etymology of that name: “It retained the name Schondia, which signifies pleasantness, as I said—or, to render word for word, beauty—because, through the blessing of the sky, the responsiveness of the earth, the convenience of its harbors and markets, its maritime resources, the fishing of its lakes and rivers, the hunting of noble wild animals, its inexhaustible veins of gold, silver, bronze, and lead, the industry of its settlers in cultivating the soil, the frequency of its towns, and its civic institutions, it yields to no blessed region.” But this etymology of the name has been rejected by the consensus of the learned, and the explanation has prevailed among others which Grotius derives from Jornandes in the cited *Prolegomena*, page 3: “Because all the peoples of that land used hewn rocks—as he himself reads—as fortresses, and called those very defenses *Scantzen*. Hence *Scandia*, and with the addition of *au*, a word meaning land, *Scandinavia*.” Its description, in summary, is taken from Ziegler, who includes maps: “It is bounded on the west by the Hyperborean Ocean, on the north by an unknown land, on the east by part of White Russia and the Baltic Sea, and on the south by the Gulf of Gothia and part of Denmark. It includes three royal kingdoms: Norway, Sweden, and Gothia. It also includes thirty-seven dynasties subject to kings.” More truly a peninsula than an island, and of such vast size that the ancients called it another world, as in Pliny, book IV, chapter 16.]—although other causes of their departure are also asserted, they came from the island called Scandinavia. Pliny Secundus (the Elder) also mentions this island in the books he composed on the nature of things.

This island, therefore, as those who explored it reported to us, is not so much situated in the sea as it is surrounded by sea waves that encircle the land—[Note: [Col. 0440D] Because of the flatness of the shores, sea waves surround the lands. This is absent from the Ascensian edition: Lindenbrog.]—because of the flatness—[Note: [Col. 0440D] “Of the shores”; another reading: “of the seas.” Lindenbrog.]—of its shores.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] Hear Cluverius at this point: “What, I ask, does this mean: ‘It is not situated in the sea but surrounded by marine waves’? I see what misled the man. He had heard from someone about the island of Zealand, which has level shores; he understood this to be the largest of the Scandian islands. He had also heard that immense Scandinavia was rather a peninsula than an island. Later, I believe, confusing these two accounts through forgetfulness, he made one small island out of them—not so much situated in the sea as surrounded by marine waves. By these words he intended to indicate a peninsula. Such nonsense, therefore, whether in Ptolemy, the Deacon, or any others, must be rejected, lest by embracing it we do injury to the credibility of more authoritative writers.]

The peoples settled within it, therefore, having multiplied to such a degree—[Note: [Col. 0441D] “After they had sprouted forth.” Modoet reads “after they had populated it.”]—that they could no longer live together, divided the entire multitude, as the story goes, into three parts and determined by lot which of them should leave their homeland and seek new settlements—[Note: [Col. 0441D] Modoet reads: “A certain part of them leaving their homeland in order to seek new lands, etc.” Lindenbrog: “They determine by lot which of them should leave their homeland and seek new settlements.”]

## Chapter III. That Ibor and Ayo were the first leaders of the Winili, together with their mother Gambara

The portion to which the lot had assigned the task of leaving its native soil and seeking foreign fields—[Note: [Col. 0441D] “Pursuing fields and seeking lands.” Lindenbrog.]—having appointed over itself two leaders, namely Ibor and Ayo—[Note: [Col. 0441D] Another reading: “Aione”; another: “Agione,” and likewise below, according to Lindenbrog; thus manuscript M. Here what Prosper of Aquitaine wrote about the departure of the Lombards under these leaders, in the passage cited by Grotius, should certainly be restored.]—who were brothers, still flourishing in youthful age, and superior to the others. Having said farewell both to their people and to their homeland, they set out to seek lands where they might settle.

The mother of these leaders was named Gambara—[Note: [Col. 0441D] Saxo Grammaticus, *History of Denmark*, book VIII, calls her Gambaruc.]—a woman who, among her own people, was both sharp in intellect—[Note: [Col. 0441D] Another reading: “as far as was possible among barbarians.” Lindenbrog.]—and prudent in counsel—[Note: [Col. 0441D] Another reading: “prudent together with her sons.” Lindenbrog.]—and they placed no small confidence in her wisdom in difficult circumstances.

## Chapter IV. On the seven men sleeping in Germany

I think it will not be out of place to interrupt the order of our narrative for a little while and, since our pen is still occupied with Germany, briefly relate a marvel celebrated there by everyone, together with certain other matters.

At the farthest limits of Germany toward the northwest—[Note: [Col. 0441D] So the Augsburg edition reads. Manuscript: “surrounded.” Others: “surrounded at the farthest limits of Germany.” Lindenbrog. The reading *Circium* must certainly be retained.]—on the very shore of the Ocean, a cave is seen beneath a lofty rock. In it seven men, asleep in a long sleep from an uncertain time, lie at rest. Not only their bodies but also their clothing remain so intact that, because they have endured all these years without any corruption, they are held in reverence by those same untutored and barbarous nations.

In appearance they are plainly seen to be Romans. When one person, driven by curiosity, wished to strip one of them, his arms, as the story goes, immediately withered; this punishment terrified the others, so that no one dared to touch them again.

[Note: [Col. 0442B] Baronius relates the history of the seven holy martyrs, the Sleepers, crowned at Ephesus under Decius, from Metaphrastes, Cedrenus, and other Greek authors, in his annals under A.D. 254 and in the *Roman Martyrology* on July 27. He also relates another group of seven from Gregory of Tours and Sigebert, whom he thinks to be the same as those whom Paul mentions here. He may have reached this conclusion because our author inserted almost word for word into his history the *Acts of Saint Hospitius* by the same Saint Gregory, as well as many other passages, as we shall note below. But Saint Gregory places the Sleepers in the Major Monastery, commonly called Marmoutiers, near Tours, whereas Paul places them at the farthest limits of Germany toward the northwest, that is, on the very shore of the Ocean. I am therefore more easily persuaded that they were different men, although I am not unaware that the letter of Saint Gregory of Tours cited by the learned Baronius has been relegated by modern writers among the spurious works. In any case, whether Paul is to be believed is a matter each person may decide as he wishes.]

You may see to what end divine Providence has preserved them for so many ages. Perhaps one day those peoples will be saved through their preaching, since they are thought to be Christians and could not otherwise be so.

## Chapter V. On the people of the Scritobini

Near this place—[Note: [Col. 0442C] Other readings: *Scrictofinni*, Lindenbrog; *Scrittobini*, Ambrosian manuscript; *Scriptobini*, Modoetius. He writes that they were called by this name from jumping. The word still exists among the Germans today: *scriten* means “to spread apart” or “to separate the feet,” or, as Paul prefers, “to jump”; in this he agrees with the Greeks, who call it σκίρτᾶν, “to leap.” The name differs from that used by Procopius, who in book II of his *Gothic War* calls them Σκριτιφίκοι; other writers call them *Scritofini*. Lindenbrog. Concerning them Cluverius writes in book III of his *Germania antiqua*, chapter 38: “At the extremities of this island of Scandinavia, toward the northwest, on the very shore of the Ocean, Paul the Deacon places the Scritofinni in book I, chapters 4 and 5. Even today, on the far northern shore of Finnmark, they are said to be called *the Scricfinder* near the Rubeas promontory.” And below, page 175: “Their name is cited by Procopius in book II of his *Gothic Affairs* as Σκριθιφίκοι, a corrupted form of Σκριθιφίννοι, *Schritifinni*. Even today this whole people is called *Finnem* or *Fennem*. Nor is the ill-timed judgment acceptable of those who recently maintained that in both the Deacon and Jornandes one ought to read *Scritobini*, as though their name were derived from the word *bein*, meaning foot or leg, because the Deacon says that it was formed in the German language from jumping. If the unanimous agreement of so many authors who write F or Φ did not persuade us that they were Finns by name as well as by race, it should at least have moved us that even today they are called by the Danes, Norwegians, and Swedes, and by themselves, *Skrikfinner*, or, in their spelling, *Skrikfinder*.” Grotius does not disagree with Cluverius on these points in his *Prolegomena*; he also adduces other names for this people from the testimonies of ancient writers. For the rest, Adam of Bremen writes the following about their location in his *Description of Denmark*: “On the northern frontier of the Swedes, or Northmen, dwell the Scritfinni, who, they say, outrun wild animals. Their greatest city is Halsingaland, and Halsingaland is a region, etc.”]

The Scritobini, for that is what this people is called, live nearby. Even in summer they are not without snow—[Note: [Col. 0443C] Another reading: “Nor can it be otherwise than that they feed on the raw flesh of wild animals, etc.” Lindenbrog.]—and, being no different in reason from the wild beasts themselves—[Note: [Col. 0443C] Ambrosian manuscript and Modoetius: “nor anything else.”]—they feed on raw flesh of wild animals. They also make garments for themselves from their shaggy skins—[Note: [Col. 0443C] Modoetius: “hairy skins.”]

They derive their name etymologically from jumping, according to the barbarian language. For by leaping, using a certain contrivance of curved wood resembling a bow—[Note: [Col. 0443C] Procopius describes the customs of the Scritofinni somewhat differently in his *Gothic War*, although with a very serious error he relegates them to the farthest Thule; book II, chapter 15 of our edition, page 287.]—they catch wild animals.

Among them there is an animal—[Note: [Col. 0443C]

In some copies the word *non*, “not,” is absent. Lindenbrog.

Perhaps one should read “not very unlike a stag.” For concerning the wild animal Paul describes here, the often-mentioned Cluverius writes in book I of his *Germania antiqua*, page 135: “Even today in those lands there is an animal not unlike a stag in size and horns. Its common name is *een rhene*, from which there is no doubt that the name of the garment just mentioned was derived—the *rheno* mentioned by Caesar and Sallust, which Isidore describes in book XIX, chapter 23—which Paul saw in Italy or Gaul. For the claim made by certain grammarians today that *rheno* was so called ἀπὸ τῶν ῥηννῶν, that is, from lambskins, is false, as Varro attests in book IV of his *Latin Language*. Varro, who was not ignorant of Greek, says that it is a foreign and Gallic word; Isidore likewise says that it is Germanic.”

Paul uses *non satis* for “not much” below in chapter VI, as do Anastasius the Librarian and other writers of this kind. Let them judge for themselves how elegant this expression is.]

—not very unlike a stag. I saw a garment made from its hide, which was bristling with hair and fitted in the manner of a tunic down to the knees, just as, according to the report, the Scritobini use—[Note: [Col. 0443D] Modoetius: “with which, as was reported, the Scriptobini, etc.” Lindenbrog: “with which, as was said, the Scritofinni, etc.”]

In those regions, around the summer solstice, for several days the brightest light is seen even at night—[Note: [Col. 0443D] These words, from “around the summer solstice” through “although daylight,” are absent from the Ascensian edition. Lindenbrog.]—and the days there are much longer than elsewhere. Conversely, around the winter solstice—[Note: [Col. 0443D] Modoetius reads *pruinale* instead of *brumale*.]—although daylight is present, the sun is not seen there, and the days are shorter than anywhere else, while the nights are also longer.

For the farther one withdraws from the sun, the nearer the sun itself appears to the earth, and the longer the shadows grow—[Note: [Col. 0444B] The word *longius*, “farther,” is absent in some copies. Lindenbrog.]—.

Finally, in Italy, as the ancients also wrote, around the day of the Lord’s birth, nine feet are measured in the shadow of a human stature at the sixth hour. But I, in Belgic Gaul, in a place called—[Note: [Col. 0444B] Another reading: “the village of Tours.” Lindenbrog.]

The name Totonis must absolutely be retained in its contracted form. Theotonis is a very well-known town in the histories of the Franks; for there, under the Merovingian and Carolingian kings, a most celebrated palace stood for a long time. In it Charlemagne, after convening the nobles and summoning his sons Pippin and Louis, divided the kingdom and drew up his testament, strengthened by a new provision for preserving peace and by other solemnities. *Annals of Deeds*, under Charlemagne, years 805 and 806. Michael the German, in Mabilon’s *De Re Diplomatica*, book IV, chapter 141. His ordinance still exists under the title *Capitulary of Charlemagne given at the town of Theotonis*, in the fifth year of his imperial reign. Today the French call it Thionville, on the Moselle River, not far from the city of Metz, concerning which our Paul rendered an excellent service in his *History of the Bishops* of that city.]

At the town of Totonis, standing and measuring the shadow cast by my height, I found it to be nineteen and a half feet. In the opposite direction likewise, the nearer one proceeds southward toward the sun, the shorter the shadows always appear, [Note: Others read: “so that, around the summer solstice, for one looking toward the sun from the middle of the sky in Egypt, at Syene, and in the neighboring regions, no shadows are seen,” etc. Lindenbrog.] to such an extent that, at the summer solstice, when the sun looks down from the middle of the sky, no shadows are visible in Egypt, Jerusalem, and places situated in their vicinity. In Arabia, however, at this very time the sun is seen above the middle of the sky toward the north, and, conversely, the shadows are seen pointing southward. [Note: Paul perhaps took this from Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, chapter 75. The very familiar terms from the sphere are ἄσκιοι (*askioi*), ἀμφίσκιοι (*amphiskioi*), ἑτερόσκιοι (*heteroskii*), περίσκιοι (*periskioi*), that is, those who have no shadows, shadows on both sides, shadows on one side, and shadows all around. Concerning the Arabs, the following is especially well known:

> You have come, Arabs, into a world unknown to you,
>
> amazed that the shadows of the groves do not go to the left.

]

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the two navel-points of the Ocean Sea, which lie on either side of Britain

Not very far from the shore about which we have just spoken, toward the western region, where the boundless expanse of the Ocean opens, lies that exceedingly deep chasm of waters which by the customary name we call the navel of the sea. It is said to swallow the waves twice a day and to vomit them forth again, just as along that entire coast it is clearly observed that the tides advance and retreat with extraordinary speed. Such a chasm, [Note: Or “whirlpool”; absent in others. Lindenbrog. The same in Modoet.] or whirlpool, is called Charybdis by the poet Virgil, [Note: *Aeneid*, book III; others nevertheless also attribute it to Thule, as does Statius, book V, *Silvae* 1:

> Thule, resounding all around with the receding whirlpool.

The additional claim that ships are swallowed there and vomited forth again is likewise touched upon by Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XIII, fable 8:

> Scylla attacks the right side, and unappeased Charybdis the left;
>
> she swallows the ships snatched away and vomits them back.

Lindenbrog.]

which he says in his poems is situated in the Sicilian strait, speaking in this manner:

> On the right Scylla, on the left unappeased Charybdis
>
> keeps watch, and three times from the bottom of the abyss
>
> swallows enormous waves into the depths,
>
> then raises them again beneath the open sky,
>
> and the alternating surge lashes the stars.

From this whirlpool, of which we have spoken, [Note: “Whirlpool”; others read “chasm.” Lindenbrog.] ships are often said to be dragged away suddenly and swiftly, with such speed that they seem to imitate arrows gliding through the air; and sometimes they perish in that exceedingly dreadful abyss. [Note: “Exit”; Modoet. reads *exitus*, “destruction.”] Often, when they are already on the point of sinking, they are driven backward by sudden masses of water and then carried away from it again with as much speed as that with which they had previously been drawn in. [Note: Concerning this chasm, Cluverius writes: “Now, toward the borders of Norway and Finnmark, no one acquainted with these regions is unaware that there is, in the common tongue, a place called Maelstroom, or, as others call it, Muskestroom, among the islands of Lofoten and Værøy.” Ziegler, in his map of Norway, adds: “The sea between the islands and Norway is called Tyalleslund, the Euripus, or the narrows of the island of Stafwen, etc.; Lofoth, etc.; Langanas, etc.; Vastral, etc. Between these three islands the sea is called Muskostrom, that is, ‘tide.’ Here the sea is swallowed into caverns when the tide advances and is poured back out at the ebb; the currents rush along with the greatest possible force. This sea is navigable until it reaches the lower mouths among the cliffs, and those who encounter it at an unfavorable time are carried headlong into the chasm. The remains of shipwrecks are very rarely returned; and if they are ever returned, they are found worn down by collision with the rocks, so that they appear almost covered with down. This is a power of nature surpassing the fabled Symplegades, the dreaded Malea, the Sicilian Charybdis, and every other marvel known to mortals that nature can produce in the rest of the sea.”]

They affirm that there is another chasm of this kind between the island of Britain and the province of Gaul, [Note: Ambrosius reads “between Britain and Galicia.”] and the shores of Sequania and Aquitaine likewise support this claim. [Note: Others read “the Sequanian and Aquitanian shores.” Lindenbrog; likewise Modoet.] Twice a day these shores are filled by such sudden inundations that a person who happened to be caught even a little way inland from the shore might scarcely escape. You may see the rivers of those regions flow back with the greatest speed toward their source, and for many miles the sweet waters of the rivers turn bitter. An island called Evodia lies about thirty miles from the Sequanian shore. [Note: More commonly called Ebodia, popularly Ornay and Aldernay. William Camden, in his *Britannia*, writes: “Alderney lies nearest to the shore of Normandy, or of the Lexobii; in the royal archives it is called Aureney and Aurigney, so that it appears to be the Aurica mentioned by Antoninus among the islands of the Britannic Sea. It is scarcely seven miles from the Norman promontory of La Hague, etc. From there, toward the west, a rocky ridge extends, dangerous to sailors, called the Casquettes.”]

Its inhabitants assert that from it one can hear the gurgling of the waters descending toward the same Charybdis. [Note: Others omit *auditur*, “is heard.” Lindenbrog.] I heard a very distinguished Gaul relate that several ships, first battered by a storm, were afterward swallowed by this same Charybdis. Of all the men who had been aboard those ships, only one survived. While he was still breathing and floating above the waves, he was carried by the force of the flowing waters [Note: Others omit “of the flowing waters.” Lindenbrog.] all the way to the edge of that monstrous abyss. [Note: Modoet. reads: “all the way to the edge of that most monstrous abyss,” etc.] When he saw the deepest chaos, open without end, and, already half dead with terror, expected that he would be hurled into it, suddenly—something he could not have hoped for—he was thrown upon a certain rock and settled there. For, when all the waters that were to be swallowed had already run down, the margins of the chasm had been left bare. [Note: Others read: “the edge of that chasm had been left exposed.” Lindenbrog; likewise Modoet.] While he sat there, trembling with fear amid such straits and scarcely able to remain still, and nevertheless awaited the delayed moment of death, he suddenly saw what looked like great mountains of water leap back from the depths, and the ships that had been swallowed emerge first. When one of them came close to him, he seized it, approaching as best he could. [Note: Lindenbrog and Modoet. read: “approaching as he was able, he seized it.”] Without delay he was carried in swift flight almost to the shore and escaped the danger of the dreaded death; afterward he became the narrator of his own peril.

It is credible that our own sea, that is, the Adriatic, [Note: Although unlike the Ocean, it nevertheless washes the shores of Venice and Istria. Lindenbrog.] though smaller, nevertheless similarly washing the shores of Venice and Istria, has little hidden channels of this kind, through which the retreating waters are swallowed and then vomited back as they advance to inundate the shores. [Note: Others read: “vomited back after inundating the shore”; Lindenbrog: “return after inundating the shore”; Modoet.] Having thus briefly considered these matters, let us return to the narrative we began.

## CHAPTER VII  
### How the Winili came to Scoringa, and how the leaders of the Vandals, Ambri and Assi, ordered them to pay tribute

[Col. 0446B]

Accordingly, the Winili, having departed from Scandinavia [Note: Some add: “or the island of Scandia.” Lindenbrog.] with their leaders Ibor and Ayo, came to the region called Scoringa and settled there for several years. At that time Ambri and Assi, leaders of the Vandals, were oppressing all the neighboring provinces by war. Having already been elated by many victories, they sent messengers to the Winili, ordering them either to pay tribute to the Vandals or to prepare themselves for the trials of war. Then Ibor and Ayo, with their mother Gambara urging them on, decided that it was better to defend their freedom by arms [Note: Others read: “than to disgrace it by paying tribute.” Lindenbrog. Modoet. reads: “than to disgrace them by the payment of tribute.”] than to disgrace that same freedom by the payment of tribute. Through ambassadors they informed the Vandals that they would fight rather than serve.

At that time all the Winili were in the flower of youthful age, but few in number, since they occupied only a third part of a single island of no great size. [Note: From this one may infer either that Paul had forgotten the account of Scandinavia which he had read in Pliny—“of immense size, only a portion of it being known, inhabited by the nation of the Hilleviones in five hundred villages, and called another world”—or that he had learned that the Winili had emigrated from one of the neighboring islands of Scandinavia, which was not very large, in order to seize new settlements by the sword because of the narrowness of their territory, and that, using only the name of the better-known region, he has handed down to us a matter entirely enveloped in darkness.]

## CHAPTER VIII  
### On Wodan and Frea: a ridiculous tale

[Col. 0447A]

Antiquity relates here a ridiculous tale: that the Vandals, approaching Wodan, asked him for victory over the Winili, and that he replied that he would grant victory to those whom he first saw at sunrise. [Note: Others read “whom he saw first.” Lindenbrog.] [Note: Modoet. reads: “And when this had happened, and Godan was intently looking at them as the sun rose, he said:”] Then Gambara is said to have approached Frea, the wife of Wodan, and asked her for victory for the Winili. Frea advised that the women of the Winili should arrange their loosened hair before their faces [Note: Others read “let it hang down.” Lindenbrog.] in the likeness of a beard, and should appear early in the morning with the men. They were to place themselves where Wodan could see them all together, opposite the window through which he was accustomed to look toward the east. And so it was done. When Wodan saw them at sunrise, he said: “Who are these Langobards?” [Note: Ambrosius reads “Longobards?”] Then Frea added that, since he had given them their name, he should also grant them victory. Thus Wodan granted victory to the Winili.

[Note: I do not think that an older writer of this tale than Paul is extant. Saxo Grammaticus, in book VIII, also mentions it from Paul, although for Frea he has Frig. His words are: “Having first sailed to Blekinge and then passed along Moringa, they landed at Gotland, where, according to Paul, they are said to have received the name of the Langobards, whose nation they afterward founded, through the agency of the goddess Frig.” Lindenbrog. Frea in Paul and Frig in Saxo Grammaticus are the wife of that other ridiculous Wodan; in Adam of Bremen she is Fricco, that most shameful associate of his, with the gender changed, as will be discussed below.]

These things deserve laughter and should be regarded as nothing. Victory is not attributed to human power but is rather granted from heaven.

## CHAPTER IX  
### Why the Winili were called Langobards, and that Wota himself is the one whom the Romans call Mercury

It is certain that the Langobards, although at first called Winili, were afterward given this name because of the length of their beards, untouched by the sword. [Note: Otto of Freising also writes in book II, chapter 13 of his *Deeds of Emperor Frederick* that they were called Langobards for this reason, as does Gunter in book II:

> Langobardia is named from its long beards.

Others disagree with them and assert that they were named after the Bardi, peoples of Saxony. Lindenbrog. Among those who disagree with Paul, Bodin must especially be counted. In his *Method of History* he wished them to have originated from the Langones and Bardi, as I noted above, and to have been called by that name. Erycius Puteanus, however, responds to him in *History of Insubria*, book I, chapter II, no. 7: “These are trifles of ingenuity. No nation had more Bardi in its intellectual character, and Bodin wrongly trusted Festus, who was wandering in error concerning the word *Bardus*, although the prophets and singers of the Gauls were called Bardi. The Langones, however, were the Lingones in Gaul; so, in the ancient usage, they would properly have been called Lingobardi, whom everyone calls Longobards, while some call them Langobards in the German tongue,” etc.]

For in their language *lang* means “long,” and *Baert* means “beard.” [Note:

Godan; Modoet. reads Gwodan.

Ambrosius says that, with the additional letter *d*, they called him Goddan.]

Wodan, whom they called Gwodan with the addition of the letter *g*, is the very one whom the Romans call Mercury, and is worshiped as a god by all the peoples of Germany. [Note: Ambrosius reads “was worshiped.” Another Wodan was the god of the Swedes, concerning whom Adam of Bremen writes well in his *History of the Northern Peoples*, recently published from the library of the most noble Lord Henry Rantzau:

“In this temple, called Ubsola in the native language, which is entirely constructed of gold, the people worship images of three gods. The most powerful of them, Thor, has the central seat; Wodan and Fricco occupy the places on either side. Their meanings are said to be as follows. Thor presides over the air; he governs thunder and lightning, winds and rains, and directs the crops. The other, Wodan—that is, the stronger one—rules wars and supplies men with strength against their enemies. The third is Fricco, who grants peace and pleasure to mortals; they fashion his image as an enormous Priapus, while they carve Wodan armed, as our people commonly carve Mars. Thor, however, with his scepter, appears to represent Jupiter.”

Thus far Adam. From our Wodan, whom Paul identifies with the Roman Mercury, the Belgians even today corruptly call Wednesday *Woensdag* instead of *Wodensdag*. Likewise, I think that *Freidag*—*Fredag* among the Danes—meaning Friday, is derived from Wodan’s wife Frea, although I would not dare assert this with certainty. P. Nannius erred and misunderstood the native language when he thought that *Woensdag* derived from profit, because the Roman Mercury was famous as the patron of gain. Nor does it seem plausible to me that *Freidag* means something like “day of liberation,” because Venus was the goddess of liberty. Instead of Wodan, the distinguished J. Lipsius, in his commentary on Tacitus, thinks that one should read *Wonstam* or *Wondam*, derived from a word for profit; if anyone prefers this, let him read it so. Lindenbrog. Cluverius does not approve this etymology of Lipsius. His words in book I of *Ancient Germany*, page 226, are:

“By no means, my Lipsius, may I be so fortunate as to agree with you: the day of Mercury was not named by your ancestors from profit, as though from the native word *Wonnen*, meaning gain or acquisition, itself derived from the verb *Winnen*, meaning to gain or acquire. Rather it was named from the word of Mercury himself, Trismegistus, *Godan*. Hence even today in Westphalia the same day is called *Godensdach*, and among some of your countrymen, by contraction—as in most words among you, where one of two vowels in the middle is elided—*Goensdach*; among others, *Woensdach*, likewise contracted from *Wodensdach*, which comes from Wodan,” etc.

And farther on:

“From what has already been said it is also sufficiently clear that in the manuscripts of the Deacon and of Gothofredus, *Godan*, *Wodan*, and *Gotan* have been wrongly and incompetently written as *Godam*, *Wodam*, and *Gotam*, as though they were accusative forms from nominatives *Goda*, *Woda*, *Gota*, and *Wota,” etc.*

Yet Cluverius himself was not free from correction by Grotius, in the prolegomena cited to his own history. After rejecting what Cluverius had assembled to demonstrate that *Theut* and *Dan* were the same word, and after explaining their genuine meanings, Grotius writes:

“Wodan, from *Woden*, meaning ‘to rage,’ was believed by the ancient Germans to preside as a god over peace and wars. Because of his twofold power, some Latins preferred to call him Mercury, others Mars. He is the same whom others write Othinus, omitting the harsher letter, and so forth.”]

[Note: Others read: “who was not only around these times,” etc. Lindenbrog.] It is said that he existed not at this period, but much earlier, and not in Germany but in Greece.

## CHAPTER X  
### How the Langobards conquered the Vandals, and concerning the famine of the Langobards

[Col. 0449A]

The Winili, therefore—who are also the Langobards—engaged the Vandals in battle and, fighting fiercely as men contending for the glory of freedom, gained the victory. Later they suffered severe want from famine [Note: Others read: “famine and scarcity of provisions.” Lindenbrog.] in that same province of Scoringa, and were greatly disheartened.

[Note: To designate precise boundaries for Mauringia, as also for the Scoringa mentioned above, would scarcely be possible for anyone without a lengthy dissertation amid such a diversity of writers, much less in this brief excursion of ours. The distinguished Leibniz, among more recent scholars, writes the following in his little book on the *Origin of the Franks*:

“It is clear from Paul Warnefrid, commonly called the Deacon, who describes the journey of the Langobards—although fictitiously—that Maurungania, or rather Mauringavia, or Mauringia, was situated by the Baltic Sea, apart from the fact that this is indicated by the word itself. For Mauringia is a maritime region, like the Morini and Armorica; and today nearly the same region is called Pomerania. The Pomerani are situated by the sea in the Slavic tongue, just as the Polabi are situated by the Elbe, for *lube* is the Slavic name for the Elbe.”

To clarify this, Johann Georg Eccard adds his own etymology of the name and, on its basis, assigns more definite boundaries—although in this respect he differs even from Leibniz, whom he is defending:

“Paul the Deacon,” he says, “calls the same region Mauringia and indicates that it was near Scoringa, or the coastal region of the Cimbric Chersonese facing the Danish islands. After Moringia, this same author places Golanda, or the land of the Goths—not because the Gothic region itself lay immediately adjacent to Mauringia, but because the intervening peoples were then ruled by the Goths. With complete justification, however, Wagria and the neighboring provinces, together with the lands of Lauenburg and Mecklenburg, could be called Mauringia from their *morae*, or marshes, and their lakes. Nowhere else will you find such frequent marshes as in this region. It appears that the Slavs, invading from there, called the adjacent region Pomerania, or, as they themselves say, *Pomorze*, not so much because it lay by the sea—for in that case the name Pomerania would suit the entire coast—as because it was near ancient Mauringia,” etc.

The matters which chiefly French writers have assembled against Leibniz are not to be reported here. It will suffice to have brought a little light to our Paul from this distinguished man; although his reliability, especially at this point, is suspect, we have already set down from Grotius considerations which perhaps advise against wholly rejecting it.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### How the Langobards, wishing to cross into Mauringia, were prevented by the Assipitti

When they departed from there and planned to cross into Mauringia, the Assipitti blocked their route, refusing to allow them passage through their territory in any way. [Note: Of these the aforementioned Eccard writes to Leibniz in *On the Origin of the Franks*: “The Assipitti, whom Paul mentions above Mauringia, differ completely from the Usipetes who lived on the lower Rhine, and signify the remaining Assi, who had not gone north with Odin.”] [Note: Ambrosius reads “in every manner.”] The Langobards, however, when they saw the enemy’s great forces and did not dare to engage them because of the smallness of their army, deliberated about what they should do, and at last necessity discovered a plan. [Note: Modoet. reads: “while they were considering what they ought to do, at last,” etc.; Lindenbrog, instead of *decernerent*, has “were seeking.”]

They pretended to have cynocephali in their camp—that is, men with dogs’ heads. [Note: Lucian, swallowed long ago with a ship in the belly of that monstrous beast, likewise feared cynocephali, crab-clawed men, and other monsters of that kind in book I of the *True History*.] They spread among the enemy the report that these beings waged war with exceptional ferocity, drank human blood, and, if they could not catch an enemy, drank their own blood. To make this claim credible, they enlarged their tents and lit very many fires in the camp. [Note: Agathias, book V, describes a similar stratagem of Belisarius:

“Then, when night came on, he kindled many signal fires spread widely across the plain, so that the enemy, seeing them, might suppose the army to be enormous by counting the fires.”

Nor was this stratagem useless, for Caesar likewise indicates in book II of *The Gallic War* that the size of an enemy force was customarily judged from the fires lit in its camp: “The camp, as was shown by the smoke and fires, extended over more than eight miles in width.” Lindenbrog.]

When the enemy heard and saw these things, they became credulous and no longer dared attempt the war they had threatened. [Note: Absent in some copies. Lindenbrog; likewise in Modoet.]

## CHAPTER XII  
### On the single combat of two brave men, one of whom was a Langobard and the other an Assipittus

[Col. 0450A]

They nevertheless had among them a very brave man, whose strength they trusted and who, without doubt, could obtain whatever they wished. They set this man forward alone to fight above all others. They ordered the Langobards to send one of their own choosing to meet him in single combat, on the condition that, if their champion won the victory, the Langobards would depart by the route by which they had come; [Note: Modoet. reads: “by which they had arrived.”] but if he were defeated by the other, they would no longer prevent the Langobards from crossing their territory.

While the Langobards were uncertain whom they should send against so warlike a man, someone of servile condition voluntarily offered himself. He promised to engage the enemy who challenged him, on the condition that, if he gained victory over the enemy, they would remove the mark of slavery from him and his descendants. [Note: Others read “the bond.” Lindenbrog.] What more is there to say? They gladly promised to do what he had requested. [Note: Ambrosius and Modoet. read: “They promised that they would do,” etc.] He attacked the enemy, overcame him, and won. Thus he secured for the Langobards the opportunity to cross, and for himself and his descendants, as he had wished, the rights of freedom. [Note: Modoet. reads: “He gave the Langobards an opportunity to cross and obtained for himself and his descendants the rights he had desired”; Ambrosius: “having obtained them.”]

## CHAPTER XIII  
### How the Langobards crossed into Mauringia and afterward advanced to farther regions

The Langobards, therefore, at last reached Mauringia. In order to increase the number of their warriors, they rescued many from the yoke of slavery [Note: Ambrosius reads “from servile condition.”] and brought them into a state of freedom. To ensure that their freedom might be regarded as legally established, [Note: Ambrosius and Modoet. read *ingenuitas*, “freedom.” The manumission rite deserves notice. For the forms of manumission found in the title on manumissions in the laws of the Langobards belong to another category. Lindenbrog. Perhaps among the ancient Langobards it was customary to manumit slaves by the handing over or casting of a spear, a practice that had fallen out of use in later times. Several forms of manumission are indeed listed by King Rothari in book II of the Laws, title 35, as Lindenbrog observes. The more solemn form was that by which someone was said to have made a *fulfreal*, the formula of which is:

“Whoever makes him *fulfreal*—Lindenbrog interprets this as ‘free,’ from the German *fulfrey*—and makes him an outsider to himself, that is, *amund*, or outside his power, as Grotius explains in his *Nomenclator*, in our edition, page 370B, must proceed as follows: first let him hand him over into the hands of another free man, and let him confirm him by *garanthinx*, that is, by cession, according to Grotius; then let the second hand him over into the hands of a third in the same manner, and the third into the hands of a fourth. Let the fourth lead him to a crossroads and release him from the obligation by *thinging* him with a pledge, and let witnesses be present there and say: ‘At the four roads, wherever you wish to walk, you shall have free power,’ etc.”

Thus, through the crossroads and the four regions of the world, complete freedom to wander is appropriately signified. There was also a manumission by which a slave was released through *impans*, that is, by a royal declaration, and in the most holy churches through the priest’s leading him around the altar. Finally, there was another form by which, as I infer from the law itself, a slave acquired a lesser degree of freedom; by this form a person was said to have made him an *aldio*. Grotius noted in the cited passage that *aldio* corresponds to our Latin *libertus*, “freedman.” Another method of manumission also became established among us through the Salic Law, by shaking a coin from the slave’s hand, as may be seen in the compact of that law, title 30.]

they solemnly established it in the customary manner by means of an arrow, nevertheless muttering certain words in their native language for the validity of the act.

The Langobards then departed from Mauringia and came to Golanda, where they are said to have remained for some time. [Note: Others read: “They settled in Regulandia.” Lindenbrog. Modoet. reads *Rogulandam*, through a scribal error, instead of *Rugulandiam*, the land of the Rugii. This has in common with Golanda that the Rugii too were a Gothic nation, as Procopius asserts in book III of his *Gothic History*.]

After this they are said to have possessed Anthabet, Bathaib, and likewise Vurgundaib for several years. We may suppose these to be names of districts or of places of whatever kind. [Note: Rather, regions. For the illustration of our Paul at this point, the most learned Eccard writes to Leibniz in *On the Origin of the Franks*, page 253:

“After crossing Mauringia, Paul says that the Langobards came to Golanda, that is, the land of the Goths. Jornandes clearly indicates that the Goths ruled, especially under Hermaneric, over the entire coast of the Baltic Sea, even on this side of the Vistula. From the Gothic homeland he reports that they went into Anthaib, that is, the land of the Antes, or Poland, and then descended into Bathaib. Bathaib is without doubt the land of the Gepids, namely ancient Dacia. The Gepids were so called as the remnants of the Goths, from *beiten* or *biden*, ‘to remain’ or ‘to be left over’; and *pide*, *beite*, or *bathe* can regularly mean ‘remnant,’ especially if, according to the ancient custom, the *e* is pronounced. Bathaib, therefore, is the region of the Bathi, or remnants—namely, of the Goths, who are the same as the Gepids. Burgundaib is the land of the Burgundians, which the Gepids held nearby before entering Gaul,” etc.]

## CHAPTER XIV  
### How, after the deaths of the leaders Ibor and Ayo, the Langobards had Agilmund as their first king

[Col. 0452A]

Meanwhile Ibor and Ayo died. They had led the Langobards out of Scandinavia [Note: Others read “from Scandinavia, or, as I have said, Scandavia.” Lindenbrog.] and had ruled them up to this time. The Langobards no longer wished to remain under leaders and established a king for themselves, after the manner of the other nations.

Thus Agelmund, the first, ruled over them. [Note: Modoet. reads *Algemundus*. The succession of the Langobard kings, which Paul begins here with Agelmund, does not agree well after the seventh king, Tato, with the preface to the laws issued by King Rothari. Charles Sigonius appended part of this preface to his history under the year A.D. 643. I have thought it appropriate to record the whole of it here from his manuscript papers, as a supplement to our author. Lest I seem to wrong a man of proven reliability, however, I wish readers to know that it was copied by a later hand, and not without errors, by one or another of his scribes, with no additional testimony from the manuscript in which these words were found. I must also acknowledge the kindness of the distinguished Joseph Anthony Saxius, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, through whose courtesy all the manuscripts are available, as well as—what is especially pleasing to me—his generous store of deeper learning.]

### IN THE NAME OF THE LORD

“Here begins the edict which I, Rothari, most excellent king and seventeenth king of the Lombard race, in the name of God, renewed with my chief judges, in the eighth year of my reign, by God’s favor, in the thirty-eighth year of my life, in the second indiction, and happily in the seventy-sixth year after the arrival of the Lombards in the province of Italy, when Alboin was then king, through the operation of divine power. Given at Ticinum in the Palace.

The rule written below declares how great our concern and care have been, and still are, for our subjects, especially because of the continual afflictions of the poor and also because of the excessive exactions of those who possess greater power, whom we have recognized as suffering violence. Considering this, we have judged it necessary, through the grace of almighty God, to correct and arrange the present law: to renew and amend all the earlier laws, to add what is lacking, and to cut away what is excessive. We have provided that all these matters be gathered into a single volume, so that each person may live quietly with law and justice intact, and may labor even against his enemies and defend his own boundaries.

Although these matters stand thus, we have nevertheless judged it useful, for the memory of future times, to have written on this parchment the names of our predecessor kings, from the time when kings began to be remembered among the people of the Langobards, insofar as we have learned it from ancient men. It was as follows:

The first was Agelmund; II, Lamissio; III, Lethe; IV, Gildech; V, Gudeoch, son of Gildehoc. [Note: The Laws read: “Hugo de hoc.”] VI, Caffo, son of Gudehoc. [Note: The Laws read: “Daffo fil. de hoc.”] VII, Tato, son of Caffo; and VIII, Unichis, son of Tato; IX, Unabo, son of Unichis, grandson of Tato; X, Valamir; XI, Alboin, who, as stated above, led the army into Italy; XII, Clepes, of the lineage of Belleos; XIII, Aginulfus Turingus; XIV, Autari, son of Depex, of the lineage of Aravad; XV, Audofal, son of Aginulfi; XVI, Aruand, of the lineage of Caupus; XVII, I, who in the name of God am called King Rothari, son of Nandigus, of the lineage of Arodus.

Naudigus, son of Nocton; Nocton, son of Alamannus, son of Chilzon; Chilzon, son of Weo, son of Fronco; Fronco, son of Faco; Faco, son of Mamo; Mamo, son of Obthora.

Rothari gave the laws which the reader will see first.”

Concerning the kings Unichis and Unabo, the eighth and ninth in the present catalogue, whose numbers we have distinguished by correcting those in Sigonius’s manuscript, our author is completely silent, as though, if this reading of the preface is genuine, Paul’s succession of kings were incomplete. Conversely, the memory of Andoin, Alboin’s predecessor, has escaped Rothari, so that, if he is added to the royal lists, Rothari himself must be counted as the eighteenth king. If Unichis and Unabo are removed, as they are in Paul, Rothari would have reigned not in the seventeenth but in the sixteenth place. I am surprised that our exceptionally observant Sigonius did not notice this; for if, as he says in book I of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Wechel edition, page 4, Alboin, son of Andoin, ruled the Langobards as the tenth king, then, once Rothari is reached, both accounts are demonstrably erroneous.

This reading of the preface also differs from our Paul concerning the date of the Langobards’ arrival, although in chapter 21 Paul sends us back to the same point with complete confidence. But more on this below. Meanwhile, it is useful to learn from other records as well who the first Langobard kings were, together with Paul.]

Agelmund, son of Ayo, descended from the lineage of the Gunginci, which was regarded among them as the nobler one. [Note: Others read: “tracing both his family and his origin from the Gungingi.” Lindenbrog and Modoet. have *Gungingos*, or *Guningos*. Grotius interprets this as “the Benevolent,” and by this name the family of King Agelmund was called, just as another was called that of the Adelingi, discussed below.] As tradition has handed down from his ancestors, he held the kingdom of the Langobards for thirty-three years.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the harlot who gave birth to seven infants, one of whom was Lamissio, and on his single combat with an Amazon
In those times a certain prostitute, having given birth to seven boys at a single delivery—more savage than all beasts—threw them into a pool to be killed. If this seems impossible to anyone, let him read the histories of the ancients, and he will find that not only seven infants, but even nine, were born at once by a single woman [Note: Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts: “at one time.”]. It is especially certain that this happens among the Egyptians. [Note: Paul extracted this from his Pliny, Book VII, chapter 3, concerning extraordinary births: “It is certain that triplets are born, as the example of the Horatii and Curiatii demonstrates. Among the portents mentioned above, there is an exception in Egypt, where the Nile, fertile in drink, and so forth.”]

It happened, therefore, that King Agelmund, while making his journey, came to that same pool. When, reining in his horse, he gazed in wonder at the pitiable infants, and with the spear that he carried in his hand turned them this way and that, one of them seized the royal spear by thrusting out his hand. Moved by compassion and struck with deeper wonder at the event, the king declared that he would become a great man. Immediately he ordered him to be lifted from the pool and, after handing him over to a nurse, commanded that he be raised with every care [Note: Another reading: “with every guardianship.”].

And because he had taken him from the pool which in their language is called *lama* [Note: You will also find the word in Festus. *Lacuna*, “a collection of water,” is derived from *lacus*; others call it *lama*, others *lustrum*. Beatus Rhenanus thinks that *Qualama* should be read, from a spring. For in the German language *quellen* means “to gush forth.”], he gave him the name Lamissio [Note: “Lamissio,” as though *Lamis-sohn*, “son of the pool,” according to Grotius]. When he had grown up, he became so vigorous a young man that he proved both exceedingly warlike and, after Agelmund’s death, ruled the kingdom [Note: Modoetian manuscript: “undertook.”].

They relate that, when the Lombards, journeying with their king, reached a certain river and were prevented by the Amazons from crossing farther, he fought their strongest woman in the river by swimming and killed her, thereby securing glory for himself and passage for the Lombards [Note: Another reading: “and prepared a crossing between the two armies,” and so forth; Modoetian manuscript]. For this had first been agreed between the two armies: if that same Amazon defeated Lamissio, the Lombards would withdraw from the river; but if she were defeated by Lamissio, as in fact happened, the Lombards would be granted the opportunity to cross the waters [Note: Another reading: “if the Amazon defeated Lamissio.”]. It is certainly evident that the sequence of this account is supported by little truth [Note: Another reading: “but it is evident that the sequence of this account is less supported by truth.”].

For it is clear to all who know the histories of antiquity that the race of the Amazons had been destroyed long before these events could have occurred [Note: See Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 8, and the material that P. Petitus collected in a separate little book], unless perhaps the places where these events are said to have taken place were not sufficiently known to historians, and their existence was scarcely reported by any of them; in that case it might have happened that some such race of women existed there down to that time. For I too have heard from certain people that, even to this day, a race of such women exists in the innermost regions of Germany [Note: Another reading: “in the remotest regions.”].

## CHAPTER XVI. How the Bulgars, attacking the Lombards’ camp by night, killed King Agelmund and carried off his daughter captive

Accordingly, after the Lombards had crossed the river of which we spoke, when they had reached the farther lands, they remained there for some time. Meanwhile, since they suspected nothing adverse and were at rest, excessive security—which is always the mother of disasters—brought them no slight ruin [Note: Another reading: “and, being completely untroubled during a long period of rest, their security,” and so forth. Another manuscript: “and, being deeply at rest for a long time,” and so forth.]. Finally, while all were sleeping, relaxed by negligence, the Bulgars suddenly attacked them [Note: Another reading: “the Bulgars,” and so throughout]. They wounded many of them, struck down many, and ravaged their camp so savagely that they killed Agelmund himself, the king, and carried away his only daughter as a captive [Note: Another reading: “ravaging their camp for so long and so cruelly,” and so forth. Another manuscript: “they raged about for a long time, until they themselves,” and so forth.].

## CHAPTER XVII. How Lamissio became king and how he overcame the Bulgars

Nevertheless, after these disasters the Lombards recovered their strength and made Lamissio, of whom we spoke above, their king. Since he was ardent in youthful age and sufficiently ready for the trials of war, desiring nothing except to avenge the death of Agelmund, he turned his arms against the Bulgars [Note: Another reading: “of his protector Agelmund.” Another: “of his foster father Agelmund,” as in the Modoetian manuscript.].

As soon as the first battle was joined, the Lombards, turning their backs on the enemy, fled back to the camp. Then King Lamissio, seeing this, began to shout in a loud voice to the entire army that they should remember the disgrace they had suffered [Note: Modoetian manuscript: “so that they might remember the disgrace they had endured”], and recall before their eyes the dishonor they had received [Note: Another reading: “the dishonor received before their mind’s eyes, so that they might remember how,” according to Lindenbrog], how the enemy had slain their king and how pitifully they had carried away captive his daughter, whom they had hoped would become their queen.

Finally, he urged them to defend themselves and their people with weapons, saying that it was better to lay down one’s life in war than, as worthless slaves, to be exposed to the mockery of the enemy. As he shouted these and similar words, strengthening their spirits for enduring the trials of war, now by threats and now by promises, he declared that if he saw anyone of servile status fighting, he would grant him freedom together with rewards.

At last, fired by the exhortation and example of their leader, who had been the first to leap into battle, they rushed upon the enemy, fought fiercely, and struck down their adversaries with a great slaughter. Finally, taking victory from the victorious, they avenged both the king’s death and their own injuries. Then, having gained rich booty from the spoils of the enemy, they became from that time forward bolder in undertaking and enduring the labors of war [Note: Another reading: “in seeking and undertaking.” Another reading in the Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts: “bolder.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. How, after Lamissio’s death, Lethu assumed the kingdom, and after him his son Hildehoc, and thereafter Bodeac reigned

After Lamissio, who had reigned second, died, Lethu ascended as the third to the direction of the kingdom [Note: Other manuscripts: “Leth.”]. When he had reigned for nearly forty years, he left Hildehoc his son—who was fourth in the succession [Note: Another reading: “who was fourth in the numbering of the kingdom, as successor to the kingdom.”]—as his successor. When he too had died, Gedehoc, the fifth [Note: Other reading: “Gedeochis.” Another: “Gudeoc.” Ambrosian manuscript], assumed the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XIX. The war between Edoagar, king of the Torcilingi, and Felecheus, king of the Rugians; and how, after Odoacer had defeated the Rugians, the Lombards occupied their province

[Note: Up to this point we have wandered as though through a labyrinth among the various fortunes and regions of the Lombards and the territories they occupied, deprived of a chronological thread. Paul, or any other writer, provides none; unless we prefer, by an effort of weak conjecture, to guess the order of the times rather than investigate it. From here onward, let us be permitted to follow the footsteps of our historian with a more secure stride. We have from Cassiodorus the definite date of the overthrow of the Rugian kingdom, which our author indicates here. His words, excerpted from the *Chronicle*, are these: “Boethius, an illustrious man, consul. In this consulship Odoacer, having defeated and captured Phoeba, king of the Rugians, took possession of the kingdom.” The anonymous Cuspinianus, cited by Pagi, adds: “In the consulship of that same man”—namely Boethius—“a battle was fought between Odoacer, king, and Febanus, king of the Rugians; Odoacer won and brought King Febanus captive on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.” The consulship of Boethius, according to the more common reckoning, falls in the year 487 of our Lord Jesus Christ and the twelfth year of Odoacer’s reign in Italy.]

In those times war broke out between Odoacer, who had already been reigning in Italy for several years [Note: Another reading: “had reigned”], and Feletheus, also called Feva, king of the Rugians [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “Fleba.” Cassiodorus: “Phoeba.” The anonymous Cuspinianus: “Febanus”; other authorities have “Faba,” “Favia,” “Favianus,” “Feuba,” and “Fethia.” Eugippius, in the *Life of Saint Severinus*, has “Feletheus” and “Felecteus”; others have “Filetus,” “Feletrus,” “Seva,” and “Selettus,” as the most learned Fathers of the Bollandist continuation to the *Acts of Saint Severinus* have noted.], the cause of great hostility [Note: Eugippius, chapter 12, relates the cause of the war between Odoacer and Feletheus: “When Frederick”—he was Feletheus’ brother—“learned of the blessed Severinus’ death, he was poor and, in his impious barbarian greed, ever more savage. He believed that the garments assigned to the poor and several other things ought to be taken away. Joining sacrilege to this crime, he ordered that a silver chalice and the other furnishings of the altar be removed,” and so forth. “After stripping away all the monastery’s possessions, he left only the walls, which he could not transport across the Danube; but soon the announced vengeance reached him. For within a month he was killed by Frederick, his brother’s son, and lost both his plunder and his life. Therefore King Odoacer made war upon the Rugians; after defeating them and driving Frederick into exile, and capturing his father Fava, he migrated with him and the harmful wife mentioned above, namely Gisa, to Italy.”].

Feletheus at that time lived on the farther bank of the Danube, which that same river separates from the borders of Noricum [Note: Another reading: “which the Danube separates from the territory of Onericus.”]. In these Norican territories [Note: Another reading: “of the Onerici”] there was then a monastery of the blessed Severinus [Note: Eugippius, in the passage cited above: “At that time, then, the most holy servant of God Severinus, coming from the regions of the East, lived in the neighboring parts of Riparian Noricum and the regions of Pannonia, in the town called Asturis,” which, as he had foretold, was destroyed by the barbarians. “Later, as Aventinus says in the *Annals of Bavaria*, faithfully preserving Eugippius’ account, he lived at Batavia, Quintiana”—Quintana is a colony of the Quintani—“in Vindelicia, and at Vienna in Noricum.” At Batavia, on the bank of the river, a church dedicated to him still stands, and there is a parish called by his name. Three miles from Vienna there is a village called Severinus, still retaining the name. In his notes on Eugippius, Lazius testifies that the ruins of the cell remain in the village of Siferinga, and that the village received its name from Saint Severinus. Cuspinianus states that he purchased there a house where traces of Severinus’ cell remained in his memory. It is a great mile from Vienna. Lazius says, however, that the larger monastery stood in a place called Heyligstat—that is, “Holy Place”—from the dwelling of the saints there. Saint Leopold removed stones from there for the construction of the cloister at Neuburg, and so forth.], and Severinus, endowed with the holiness of complete self-restraint and already renowned for many virtues [Note: Another reading: “endowed with every knowledge and distinction of holiness.” Another: “with every knowledge and holiness.”], lived in those same places until the end of his life. Yet now his body is preserved at Naples [Note: Another reading: “his little body at Naples.” The Modoetian manuscript has the same. Saint Severinus, the apostle of Noricum, was transferred in the sixth year after his burial, according to Eugippius, when the Romans, migrating to Italy, had been freed from the Rugians’ domination: first to Montefeltro, then, by the authority of Pope Gelasius and at the request of the distinguished woman Barbaria, to the fortress of Lucullanum, and finally, when the Saracens began ravaging the shores of Campania, in the year 910 of the Christian era, to Naples. There it was solemnly buried by John the abbot in the famous monastery of Saint Severinus, where it is still reverently preserved. *Acts of the Saints*, Bollandists.].

Here he often admonished the Feletheus of whom we have spoken, and his wife, whose name was Gisa [Note: Another reading: “Gila,” as above], in heavenly words, urging them to cease from wickedness. When they scorned his pious words, he foretold long beforehand what would later happen to them.

Accordingly, Odoacer assembled the peoples who obeyed his authority—namely, the Torcilingi, or Turingi, the Heruli, and that part of the Rugians which he had long possessed, as well as the peoples of Italy [Note: Another reading: “Then Odoacer, having gathered the peoples under his authority, namely the Turgilingi, or Turingi, the Heruli, and the part of the Rugians that he had long possessed, together with the peoples of Italy, came into Rugiland and fought with the Rugians,” and so forth.]—and came into Rugiland. He fought the Rugians and, crushing them in a final disaster, also destroyed Feletheus, their king [Note: All the other authorities assert that Feletheus was captured with his wife Gisa and carried off to Italy; among them is the anonymous Cuspinianus cited above, who adds the date of Odoacer’s triumph in the city of Rome. Feletheus may perhaps have been killed after that triumph.].

After laying waste the entire province [Note: Another reading: “and then returning to Italy by force”], he returned to Italy and carried away with him a great multitude of captives. Then the Lombards left their own territories and came to Rugiland [Note: Another reading: “Rugulanda”], which in Latin is called the homeland of the Rugians [Note: Another reading: “the region of the Rugians.”]. Because it was fertile soil, they remained there for some years [Note: The number of years during which the Lombards inhabited the region of the Rugians can be deduced from Procopius, Book II, chapter 14. “When Anastasius assumed the Roman empire, the Heruli, having no longer any people whom they might attack, laid down their arms and remained at peace, and a period of three years passed for them in this very peace. Becoming exceedingly weary of it, they reviled Rodulf, their leader, whenever they visited him, calling him soft and womanish; and while taunting him with other such names, they abused him without any restraint. Rodulf, unable to bear the insult, marched against the Lombards, who had done them no wrong; without bringing any charge against them or considering any dissolution of their agreements, he brought against them a war without cause.” Thus, in the third year of Anastasius’ reign, Rodulf brought arms against the Lombards; this was the year 493 of the Christian era. Yet they had come from the region of the Rugians to the open fields three years earlier, as Paul says in the following chapter. It follows that they inhabited the region of the Rugians from the notable victory of Odoacer in 487, or shortly afterward, until 491, the first year of Anastasius. I observe nothing in our Paul that conflicts with this calculation of the times. It should also be noted from this passage of Procopius that the Lombards were already Christians at that time, though infected with the Arian perfidy.”].

## CHAPTER XX. After Gedehoc’s death, Claffo reigned, and after him Tato, who destroyed the kingdom of the Heruli

Meanwhile Gudehoc died [Note: Another reading: “Gedeochus.”], and his son Claffo succeeded him [Note: Another reading: “his son.”]. When Claffo too had died, Tato, his son [Note: Another reading: “Tudo,” and likewise below], ascended as the seventh to the kingdom. The Lombards also left Rugiland and settled in the broad open fields which in the barbarian language are called *feld* [Note: Other manuscripts: “filden.” Almost all German scholars read *felden* in the plural, according to grammatical usage, from *feld*. The sense is that not only the fields of which Paul speaks here, but any other fields, are called *feld* in the German language. Wolfgang Lazius identifies them in Book XII of *On the Migrations of Peoples*, where he discusses the Lombards’ seventh settlement: “Finally, heading toward the interior and in the direction of the Danube, they received the open plains under the tribute of the king of the Heruli, which are now seen extending broadly in Moravia,” and so forth.].

While they remained in that place for a period of three years, war arose between Tato and Rodulf, king of the Heruli. Although at first they had formed treaties, the cause of discord between them was this.

A brother of King Rodulf came to Tato to negotiate peace. When, after completing his embassy, he was returning to his homeland, it happened that he had to pass before the house of the king’s daughter, whose name was Rumetruda.

Seeing the crowd of men and the noble retinue, she asked who the man might be who possessed so distinguished an escort. She was told that he was the brother of King Rodulf, returning home after completing his embassy [Note: Other manuscripts: “after completing the embassy.”].

The girl sent someone to invite him to accept a cup of wine [Note: Another reading: “The girl sent someone who,” and so forth. Other manuscripts omit “of wine.”]. He came with a simple heart, just as he had been invited. But because he was short in stature, the girl despised him in arrogant pride and addressed mocking words to him. He, flushed equally with shame and indignation, replied with words that brought the girl still greater embarrassment.

Then, inflamed with feminine fury and unable to restrain the pain in her heart, she endeavored to carry out the crime that she had conceived in her mind [Note: Modoetian manuscript: “the evil.”]. She pretended patience, brightened her expression, and, soothing him with pleasanter words, invited him to sit down. She arranged for him to sit in such a place that a window in the wall was behind his shoulders.
