She had covered the window with a costly curtain, ostensibly to honor the guest, but in reality so that no suspicion might strike him [Note: “Ordering her servants to perform a most atrocious deed,” according to Lindebrog], and she commanded her own servants, while she herself spoke as though to the cupbearer and said, “Mix,” to pierce him from behind with spears [Note: “And so it happened; for immediately the cruel woman,” and so forth, according to another manuscript]. And so it was done. At once the cruel woman gave the signal [Note: Another reading: “and they carry out her commands,” and so forth], and her wicked orders were fulfilled. Pierced through with wounds, he fell to the ground and died.

When this was reported to King Rodulf, he mourned the cruel death of his brother, and, unable to bear his grief, burned to avenge his brother’s death. Breaking the treaty he had made with Tato, he declared war upon him [Note: These words are absent from some manuscripts.].

What more is there to say? The armies of both sides met on the open plains. Rodulf sent his men into battle while he himself remained in the camp, entirely confident of victory, playing at a board game [Note: Other manuscripts: “At that time the Heruli were renowned for their skill in war and for the slaughter of many.” Another reading: “experienced in wars, or in the practices of armies, and renowned for the slaughter of many,” and so forth.].

For at that time the Heruli were practiced in warfare and already famous for the slaughter of many. Whether to wage war more swiftly or to show their contempt for the wound inflicted by the enemy [Note: Another reading: “to indicate that they despised it.”], they fought naked, covering only the private parts of their bodies [Note: The learned Cluverius proves by many testimonies of the ancients that this custom existed among certain peoples of Germany and even among the Gauls, *Ancient Germany*, Book I, chapter 44. To these testimonies should be added Procopius, who reports the same concerning the Antes, in the history cited above, Book III, chapter 14, in our edition, page 313, column 1.].

Trusting confidently in their strength, while he himself played securely at the board, the king ordered one of his men to climb a tree that happened to be nearby, so that he might report to him more quickly the victory of his own men [Note: Another reading: “the victory of his own people”], threatening to cut off his head if he reported that the Herulian line was fleeing [Note: Another reading: “or said that the Herulian line had been broken and that he saw the Lombards overpowering them.”].

When he saw that the Herulian line was being broken and that they were being overwhelmed by the Lombards, the king repeatedly asked him what the Heruli were doing. He replied that they were fighting excellently [Note: The Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts: “not daring to say”]. He did not dare to disclose the evil that he saw until the entire army had turned its back to the enemy [Note: “Then, although late, bursting into speech,” according to Lindebrog.].

Finally breaking into words, he said: “Woe to you, wretched Herulia [Note: Another reading: “Herolia”], who are being chastised by the heavenly Lord’s anger” [Note: Another reading: “are being punished by the heavenly Lord’s anger.”].

At these words the king, troubled, said: “Are my Heruli fleeing?” He replied: “It is not I who have said this, but you yourself, O king.”

Then, as commonly happens in such circumstances, the king and all the others were thrown into confusion, uncertain what to do; and when the Lombards arrived, they were severely slaughtered. The king himself, though fighting bravely to no purpose, was killed.

As the Herulian army scattered here and there, such a heavenly anger came upon them that, seeing the green flax of the fields, they thought it was water deep enough for swimming [Note: The following story is more plausible if one considers that the Heruli, caught in fields of flax, were so impeded that, in opening a path for flight, they bent the flax aside with outstretched arms and, being naked, presented to their pursuers the appearance of swimmers.].

While they stretched out their arms as though about to swim, they were cruelly struck down by the swords of the enemy. Then, after the Lombards had achieved victory, they divided among themselves the enormous booty they had found in Rodulf’s camp [Note: Another reading: “They divided among themselves the enormous booty that they had found in Rodulf’s camp.”].

Tato carried away Rodulf’s standard, which they call a *bandum*, and his helmet, which he had been accustomed to wear in battle [Note: Suidas: “The Romans call *bandon* the standard carried in war.” The Latin–Greek Glossary has “*bandum*, λίγνον”—which should be corrected to “σίγνον.” Constantine the Great, writing to Pope Sylvester, says: “Likewise the imperial scepters, and all the standards, and the *banda*, and the other ornaments of imperial majesty.” Hence *bandophoros* means “the one who carries the standard of the *bandum*.” Thus the excellent Gesner long ago edited and corrected the passage; there was no need for others to repeat it. O old age! O manners!].

From that time onward the entire strength of the Heruli declined, so that they never again had a king ruling over them [Note: Procopius likewise relates that the kingdom of the Heruli was destroyed in the chapter cited above, chapter 14. He continues the history of that people and says that, after the disastrous battle, part of them remained in the region of the Rugians and, driven by hunger, fled from there to the territory of the Gepids. Finally, after crossing the Danube, they settled with the Romans in Illyricum under the emperor Anastasius. Soon afterward, when they became troublesome to our people, they were restrained by Justinian VI and, through his kindness, received lands and were instructed in the Christian religion. He says that another part migrated to the island of Thule—by which Scandinavia must be understood, as noted elsewhere—and that from there Aordus, a man of royal blood, was summoned by the remaining Heruli living in Illyricum to rule them. Contrary to Paul’s account, he says that, because Aordus was delayed on the long journey and was awaited for a long time, the impatient Heruli asked Justinian for another king, and he gave them Suartua; but when Aordus arrived, they revolted from Suartua and soon afterward from the emperor.].

From then on the Lombards became richer, and, their army enlarged by the various peoples whom they had conquered [Note: Increased by the many different peoples whom they had overcome], they began voluntarily to seek out wars and extend the glory of their valor in every direction [Note: Another reading: “to spread it abroad.”].

## CHAPTER XXI. The death of Tato, the reign of Wacho, how Wacho defeated the Suebi, his wives and daughters, and the reign of his son Waltari

But Tato did not long enjoy the triumph of war [Note: Another reading: “after this triumph of war.”]. [Note: In the Modoetian manuscript, “Walcho.” He is by no means to be included in the royal lists according to Paul’s view—a view not understood by his epitomizer in the summary prefixed to the present Chapter 21. For, after Tato, whom he had called the seventh king of the Lombards, he counts Waltari as eighth, excluding—as in the prologue to the laws issued by King Rothari—Wacho, who had seized the kingdom not by ancestral laws but by force, after killing his uncle Tato and driving Hidelchis, Tato’s son, or rather grandson, into flight among the Gepids. For this reason Rothari had put Hidelchis—or Unichis, as our reading has it, perhaps corrupted in Lombard names—in Wacho’s place as number eight, and assigned him as successor a son Unabo, of whom our Paul says not a word.] For Wacho, the son of his brother Zuchilo [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “Luchilo.” Modoetian manuscript: “Zachilo.”], attacked him and deprived him of life.

Hildechis, the son of Tato [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “Hilchis.” Modoetian manuscript: “Tato’s son.”], also fought against Wacho; but when Wacho prevailed, he was defeated and fled to the Gepids [Note: Another manuscript: “to the Gepids,” and likewise below], where he remained in exile until the end of his life.

[Note: Here it is also useful to reconstruct Wacho’s fortunes from Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book III, chapter 35: “When Waces ruled the Lombards, he had a brother’s son named Risiulf, whom the law called to the leadership after Waces should die. Waces, therefore, taking precautions that the authority might pass to his own son, brought a charge against Risiulf and, without cause, punished the man with exile. He immediately fled from his homeland with a few companions to the Varni, leaving two sons behind. By means of money Waces persuaded those barbarians to kill Risiulf. Of Risiulf’s sons, one died of illness; the other, named Ildisgus, fled to the Sclaveni. Not long afterward Waces died of illness, and the leadership of the Lombards passed to Valdalus, the son of Waces. Since he was still a very young child, Auduinus was appointed guardian and administered the government. Having acquired great power through him, Auduinus soon obtained the government for himself, when the child suddenly died of illness.”

“From this account, Warnefrid’s history must be supplemented, and I think the reading of the prologue should be approved, although Procopius assigns the kingdom to Wacho—or, as he pronounces the name in Greek dialect, Vaces—which after his death was exclusively due to his brother’s son. This may perhaps have escaped him through his less precise knowledge of Lombard affairs. It should nevertheless be recognized that a writer of the same period mentions a son and a grandson of Tato, calling the first Risiulf and the second Ildisgus. King Rotharis also listed both of them, though under different names; according to the ancestral laws, he numbered not so much those who had reigned as those who ought to have reigned, excluding those who had seized the kingdom by force. Hence, if in our Paul you read ‘Hildechis, Tato’s grandson,’ rather than ‘son,’ as he himself has it, and if Hildechis is certainly Procopius’ Ildisgus, we shall have complete agreement—unless my opinion is about to yield immediately to better arguments. For the present, I am willing that our account should yield to Procopius. From the same Greek author, in the chapter cited, we possess a definite chronological indication of the time when Hildechis fled to the Gepids: namely, while Justinian was emperor and Vigilius was residing at Constantinople as supreme pontiff, in the fourteenth year of the Gothic war, which learned reckoning places in the year 548 of the Christian era.”]

[Note: The outcome of this war between the Lombards and the Gepids is related by the same Procopius, in the chapter cited. I reproduce here what he writes about Hildechis, referring it to the fuller account of Lombard history:

“When war broke out between the Gepids and the Lombards, as I have said, Ildisgus immediately came to the Gepids, bringing with him those Lombards who followed him and a large number of Sclaveni. The Gepids hoped that they would restore him to the kingdom. When peace had been made between the Lombards and the Gepids, Auduinus at once demanded Ildisgus from the Gepids, as from friends. They refused in every way to surrender the man, but ordered him, once he had left that place, to save himself wherever he wished. Accordingly, without delay, he returned to the Sclaveni with his followers and with some Gepids who volunteered to accompany him. From there he went to Totila and the Goths, having with him an army of no fewer than six thousand men. When he reached Venetia and encountered some Romans led by Lazarus, he engaged them, defeated them, and killed many. He did not, however, join the Goths; but after crossing the Danube, he withdrew again to the Sclaveni.”

Afterward he also fled to the Greeks at Constantinople, where Justinian received him with the greatest kindness and placed him in command of a military regiment. But, persuaded by a Goth named Goar, he fled again to the Gepids. There, because he was hostile to the emperor, he soon lost his life through Auduinus’ stratagem.” — Procopius, Book IV, chapter 27.]

### Separate translations of the supplied Latin Procopius renderings

[Col. 0453B; source anchors also retained through Col. 0454B, 0455B, 0456B, 0457B]

**Rugiland; Procopius, Book II, chapter 14 (Latin rendering).** “When Anastasius had assumed the reins of the Roman empire, the Heruli, having no people left to attack, laid down their arms and kept quiet. That peace lasted three years. Thoroughly weary of it, they abused their king Rodulf; when they came to him, they called him soft and effeminate, and with other insults of that kind struck at him with the greatest disgrace. Moved by the affront, Rodulf undertook an expedition against the entirely innocent Lombards, alleging no offence and not pleading any broken treaty, but bringing war from mere inclination of mind.”

[Col. 0458B–0459B]

**Rodulf and the Heruli; Procopius, Book II, chapter 14 (Latin rendering).** “When the Lombards heard this, they sent men to Rodulf himself, humbly to ask the cause for which the Heruli were discussing war against them. If they had been defrauded of any part of the tribute, they promised to repay it at once with great interest; if they complained that the tribute assessed was too small, the Lombards would not find it burdensome to make it greater. Rodulf dismissed these envoys with threats and pressed on. The same people sent a second embassy with the same earnest requests; when it too was repulsed, they sent a third, declaring that the Heruli ought not to bring arms against them without cause. If the Heruli came upon them with such a purpose, they would oppose the attack, not willingly but under the greatest necessity, calling God to witness: at his nod even a slight vapor could withstand all human strength. It was fitting that he who had been led by the causes of war should decide the outcome of the fight for both peoples. They said this, thinking the aggressors would be frightened. But the Heruli, fearing nothing, persisted in their plan to fight the Lombards. When the armies stood near each other, a thick black cloud covered the part of heaven above the Lombards, while it was especially clear above the Heruli. From this one might have inferred that the Heruli were going into a battle fatal to themselves; no omen could be more grievous for barbarians entering battle. Yet the Heruli paid no attention, and with complete confidence and most arrogant contempt attacked the enemy, judging the event of war from the multitude of armed men. When they came to blows, there was a great slaughter of the Heruli, in which Rodulf himself was involved. All the rest were thrown into flight; forgetting their valor, most were killed on the spot by the pursuing enemy, and very few escaped.”

[Col. 0460B–0462B]

**Wacho and Risiulf; Procopius, Book III, chapter 35 (Latin rendering).** “When Waces ruled the Lombards, he had a nephew—more exactly, a brother’s son, preserving the proper force of *anepsios*—named Risiulf, whom the law called to the kingship after Waces had departed this life. Waces, however, providing that he should leave the rule to his own son, accused Risiulf without cause and punished him with exile. Risiulf immediately fled from his homeland to the Varni with a few companions, leaving two sons there. Waces induced these barbarians with money to kill Risiulf. One of Risiulf’s sons died of illness; the other, named Ildisgus, escaped to the Sclaveni. Not long afterwards Waces died of illness, and the Lombard leadership fell to Waces’ son Waldalo. Since he was a very small boy, Auduin was appointed guardian and administered the kingdom. Then, strengthened by much power, Auduin himself soon obtained the kingdom when the boy was suddenly struck down by disease.”

[Col. 0463B]

**Ildisgus; Procopius, Book IV, chapter 27 (Latin rendering).** “When war at last broke out between the Gepids and Lombards, Ildisgus immediately went over to the Gepids with Lombards who had joined him and a large force of Sclaveni. The Gepids hoped to place him in the kingdom. But when peace had been made with the Lombards, Auduin at once demanded Ildisgus from the Gepids as from friends. They refused to surrender him and advised him to escape wherever he wished. Without delay, with his own men and some Gepids who volunteered, he returned to the Sclaveni. From there he set out to visit Totila and the Goths, taking with him no fewer than six thousand armed men. Entering Venetian territory, he fought a Roman force led by Lazarus; he put it to flight and killed many. He did not, however, join the Goths; but after crossing the river he withdrew again to the Sclaveni.”

### Remaining source-column anchors

[Col. 0453B] [Col. 0454B] [Col. 0455B] [Col. 0456B] [Col. 0457B] [Col. 0458B] [Col. 0459B] [Col. 0460B] [Col. 0461B] [Col. 0462B] [Col. 0463B]

The Gepids from that time entered into hostilities with the Lombards. At the same period Wacho invaded the Suebi and subjected them to his rule. If anyone considers this false, and [Note: Modoet.: “does not regard it as true.” Lind.: “and does not consider it true.”] does not acknowledge the truth of the matter, let him reread the preface to the edict which King Rothari composed concerning the laws of the Lombards; he will find this written in nearly all the manuscripts, just as we have inserted it in this little history. [Note: In some copies the word τὸ is absent. Lind.: If the genuine reading of the preface quoted in Sigonius’s manuscripts is that one, it is certainly strange that our Paul should appeal to the same source, since he differs from it so greatly, as we have observed above. Moreover, when I carefully examined both the published Lombard laws available to me and the manuscripts preserved in this Ambrosian library in the excellent codex O, no. 53, 4, I nowhere found this preface. Hence I suspect that even in Warnefrid’s time it did not precede every copy of the laws. A portion of it is extremely common in Sigonius and many others.]

Wacho had three wives. The first was Ranicunda, daughter of the king of the Thuringians. [Note: Al.: “a daughter named Ravicunda,” etc.; Lind.] Then he married Austrigosa, daughter of the king of the Gepids, by whom he had two daughters. [Note: Amb.: *Aurigosa*; Modoet.: *Hastrigosa*; Lind.: *Hostricosa*.] One was named Wisegarda, whom he gave in marriage to Theodebert, king of the Franks. [Note: Al.: *Theudebert*, and it varies in this name throughout; Lind.] The second was called Walderada; she was joined to Cuswald, another king of the Franks, but because he hated her, he gave her in marriage to one of his own men, named Garipald. [Note: Modoet.: *Chusupald*; Lind.: *Supald*. Al. omits the words from “but because he hated her” to “The third.” Lind. Saint Gregory of Tours mentions both Frankish queens in his *History*, but, calling one of them the daughter of a certain king, he offers no evidence of Lombard descent, which must be sought from our author. Here, however, “two errors must be corrected,” as Pagius writes in his *Historical-Critical Chronicle* under the year 536, no. 16: one was made by the copyist, the other by Paul himself, who was often poorly informed about the affairs of the Frankish kings. In place of Cuswald, one should read Teuwald, that is, Theodobald. Gruter’s edition is still more corrupt, for it has Cusupald, following the Palatine manuscript. Paul must be corrected from Gregory of Tours: he says that Theodovald gave Waldrada in marriage to one of his own men, named Garipald. This was in fact done by Chlothar, not Theodovald, and Garivald was not a royal domestic but a tributary duke and prefect of Bavaria. See the rest in the same author.]

Wacho’s third wife was Salinga, daughter of the king of the Heruli. [Note: Al.: *Saliga*; Lind.] By her he had a son whom he named Waltari. [Note: Ambrosian and Modoetian: *Waltari*; Lind.: *Waltaritus*.] When Wacho died, Waltari reigned over the Lombards as the eighth king. [Note: Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts read “the ninth”; this was perhaps a copyist’s license, since he himself did not understand Paul’s meaning. I judge the editors’ reading, based on the observations above, to be retained. For our author had passed over the unfortunate son and grandson of Tato; if these are restored in accordance with Procopius and Rothari, Waltari becomes the tenth king.]

All these men were Lithingi. [Note: Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts read *Adalingi*; Lind. *Adelingi*. On the meaning of this name Cluverius writes in *Germanic Antiquities*, book I, p. 12: “Noble men, as even now in Germany they are commonly called in the native language *die Aedeleute* and *die Adelen*, and in another dialect *Eddelüde* and *Eddelen*; and nobility itself is called *der Adel*. Thus formerly nobles were called, according to the variety of dialects, *thi Adalinge*, *Athalinge*, *Aethelinge*, *Eddelinge*, doubtless from the primitive word for nobility, *Adal*, or *Athal*, *Athe*, and *Adel*. The Adalingi are mentioned in the old poem addressed to King Louis and by Paul the Deacon; after enumerating eight Lombard kings, he adds: ‘All these were Adalingi,’ for so among them a certain noble lineage was called.” “Not, by Hercules, merely among the Lombards, but among all the nations of Germany,” and so forth. Yet, with due respect to so great a man, this generic name for nobility could also have been bestowed, because of its exceptional ancient nobility, upon the single lineage of Gudehoc, which ended in the boy Waitari, just as the name Gungings, of the same kind, was bestowed on the lineage of Agelmund. It would be superfluous to seek examples from the other nations as well.] For that was the name among them of a certain noble lineage.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### After Waltari’s death Audoin reigned, and he led the Lombards into Pannonia.

[Note: Paul gives Waltari a place in the royal lists, as does King Rothari, after eliminating Wacho from the succession. I think the only reason was that this little boy was the chief of Claffo’s royal lineage and, although his father had seized the kingdom by force, he administered it under Audoin’s guardianship, while Hildich was still alive, as Procopius reports in the cited chapter 35, in accordance with ancestral right and law, though only for a short time.]

After Waltari had held the kingdom for seven years, he was taken from this life. [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “four.”] After him the ninth king, Audoin, obtained the kingdom. [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “the tenth,” a continuation of the copyist’s error noted above.] Not long afterward he led the Lombards into Pannonia. [Note: The same Paul explains below, book II, chapter 7, when Audoin led the Lombards into Pannonia; accordingly the Lombards’ migration into Pannonia must be assigned to the year of Christ 526, as Sigebert also testifies in his *Chronicle*. Procopius, book III of the Gothic War, chapter 32, where he traces more fully the affairs of the barbarians who were tearing apart the Western Empire, speaks of this migration and asserts that the Lombards came into Pannonia by Justinian’s gift:

“King Justinian gave to the Lombards the city of Noricum, the fortifications of Pannonia and many other places, and very large sums of money. For this reason the Lombards left their ancestral homes and settled here on the far side of the river Ister, not far from the Gepids.”

“Now when Justinian Augustus had given the Lombards the city of Noricum, the fortifications of Pannonia, other places, and in addition a very large sum of money, they for that reason abandoned their ancestral settlements and established themselves on the opposite bank of the river, not far from the Gepids.”

He then relates in the following chapter, 34, that war arose between the Gepids and the Lombards, and that each people’s king sent an embassy to the emperor to obtain assistance. He adds:

“At that time Thorisin was ruling the Gepids, and Auduin the other people.”

“At that time Thorisin ruled the Gepids; Auduin, the Lombards.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### The war between the Gepids and the Lombards, in which Alboin killed the son of the king of the Gepids.

The Gepids and the Lombards at last brought into the open the quarrel that had long been conceived, and war was prepared on both sides. [Note: Some copies read: “The quarrel conceived long before at last burst into open war, which both sides prepared according to their resources.” Lind.: “Rather, Procopius, cited above, book III, chapter 34, and book IV, chapter 18, states that war had repeatedly been waged between the Gepids and the Lombards. In his account, events preceding this Lombard victory, which Paul’s narrative here supplements, must be reviewed; perhaps the war was the one related by Procopius in book IV, chapter 25. Audoin sent the joyful news of it to Constantinople in the seventeenth year of the Gothic War, that is, in the year 551 of the Christian era.”]

When battle had been joined, while both armies fought bravely and neither gave way to the other, it happened that in the very midst of the struggle Alboin, son of Audoin, and Turismodus, son of Turisind, encountered one another. [Note: Some copies read “Alboin’s son Audoin.” Lind.: This reading is corrupt, for Procopius and the other writers clearly establish that Audoin preceded Alboin.]

Alboin struck him with his sword, threw him from his horse, and killed him. [Note: Procopius likewise asserts that Turisind, or Thorisin, was king of the Gepids at the time when Audoin ruled the Lombards. He records a similar fate for Wacho: Ustrigotho, son of King Elemund, was driven from the Gepid kingdom; he fled to Audoin, as Ildisgus fled to the Gepids, and was impiously killed by Audoin. This became the price for Ildisgus, who was likewise killed by Thorisin, or Hildich, in the eighteenth year of the Gothic War. See Procopius, book IV, chapter 27.]

When the Gepids saw that the king’s son, through whom the war had been fought to a great extent, had died, they immediately lost heart and took flight. [Note: “Upon whose side the greater part of the war had depended.” Modoetian and Lind.] The Lombards pursued them fiercely, cut them down, and, after killing very many, returned to strip the dead.

When the Lombards had completed their victory and returned to their own settlements, they suggested to their king Audoin that Alboin should become the guest of the king whose valor had won them victory in battle, so that, just as he had been his father’s companion in danger, he might also be his companion at the feast. [Note: Some copies read “so that he might be his companion”; Lind. and Modoetian: “so that he might be a common companion.”]

Audoin replied that he could by no means do this, lest he violate the custom of the people. “You know,” he said, “that it is not our custom for the son of a king to dine with his father unless he has first received arms from the king of a foreign people.” [Note: See what Petrus Pithoeus, jurist, noted in *Adversaria*, book I, chapter 1. Lindenbrog.]

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### How Alboin went with forty men to Turisind, whose son he had killed, asking him for arms so that he might sit at table with his own father, and how he received arms from Turisind.

After Alboin had heard this from his father, he took with him only forty young men and went to Turisind, king of the Gepids, with whom he had long before waged war. [Note: Al.: *Turisind*; Lind. Al.: “with whom he had fought shortly before.” Lind.] He explained the reason for his coming.

Turisind received him kindly, invited him to his own banquet, and placed him at his right hand, where his son Turismodus had once been accustomed to sit. Meanwhile, as they partook of the various dishes set before them, Turisind, recalling his son’s former place and bringing his son’s death back to mind, saw the man who had killed him sitting in that place. Drawing deep sighs, he could not contain himself; at last his grief burst into speech.

“This place is dear to me,” he said, “but the person sitting in it is exceedingly painful to behold.”

Then another son of the king who was present, provoked by his father’s words, began to insult the Lombards. Since they wore white bands below the shins, he asserted that they resembled mares whose feet were white up to the legs. [Note: Modoetian and Lind.: “on the shins.” Some copies add: “He also said that the mares they brought or pretended to bring were gentle.”]

“They are fruitful little mares,” he said, “the ones you resemble.” [Note: Ambrosian and Modoetian: “They are stinking mares, he said, whom you imitate.” Lind.: “Fertile mares.”]

Then one of the Lombards replied: “Go to the field of Asfeld, and there you will certainly be able to test how vigorously these creatures whom you call mares can kick—there, where the bones of your brother lie scattered like those of a worthless beast in the middle of the meadows.” [Note: Ambrosian: *Feld*. In German this means the same as *campus* in Latin; here Paul uses it for a designated place of battle.]

When the Gepids heard this, unable to bear the humiliation they had suffered from the Lombards, they were violently enraged and attempted to avenge the manifest insults. The Lombards, on the other hand, ready for battle, all laid their hands upon the hilts of their swords. [Note: Some copies: “they place their hands”; the manuscript: “they send them.” Lind.]

Then the king sprang up from the table, placed himself between them, and restrained his men from anger and battle. He threatened that the first person to begin the fight would be punished first, saying that a victory could not please God when someone killed an enemy in his own house. [Note: Modoetian and Lind.: “a guest.”]

Thus the quarrel was finally suppressed, and thereafter they completed the feast with cheerful hearts. Turisind took the arms of his son Turismodus and handed them to Alboin, then sent him back safely and peacefully to his father’s kingdom. [Note: Some copies add: “and allowed him to return safely to his father’s kingdom.” Lind.]

When Alboin returned to his father, he thereby became his father’s guest. [Note: Some copies: “Alboin, distinguished by such splendid arms, immediately became his guest.” Lind.] While he happily enjoyed the royal delicacies with his father, he related everything in order that had happened to him in the palace of Turisind among the Gepids. Those present marveled at and praised Alboin’s courage, and they extolled Turisind’s great loyalty no less highly.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### On the reign and victories of Justinian.

At this time Augustus Justinian ruled the Roman Empire with fortunate success. He conducted wars successfully and proved extraordinary in civil affairs. Through the patrician Belisarius he decisively defeated the Persians; through that same Belisarius, after capturing their king Gelimer, he destroyed the nation of the Vandals almost to annihilation, and restored all Africa to the Roman Empire after ninety-six years. [Note: Modoetian: “ninety-seven.” Others read: “after ninety years, and rightly, under Roman law and force.” Nevertheless Regino also gives ninety-six years; others, ninety-seven. Lind.]

Again, by the strength of Belisarius, he overcame the Gothic nation in Italy after capturing their king Witigis. [Note: Some copies: “Witichis.” Lind.] Afterward, through the ex-consul John, he crushed with remarkable valor the Moors who were troubling Africa and their king Antalas. [Note: Manuscript: “Antalam”; others: “Attalam” or “Anitalan.” Lind.] In the same way he subdued other peoples by the right of war.

For all these victories he deserved to bear the additional names Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Wandalicus, and Africanus. [Note: Modoetian: “Atticus, Albaricus.” Some copies contain only “Alamannicus, Amicus, Alanicus, Wandalicus.” I have restored the text as written here from the corrupt Ascensian edition. Agathias, book I, and Justinian himself in several places confirm that this is correct.]

He also corrected the laws of the Romans, whose excessive length and useless inconsistency had become burdensome, with remarkable brevity. He compressed all the imperial constitutions, which had been contained in many volumes, into twelve books, and ordered the same volume to be called the Justinian Code.

Again, he reduced the laws of the individual magistrates—or judges and legal scholars—which had extended to nearly two thousand books, to a total of fifty books, and gave that Code the name *Digest*, or *Pandects*. He also newly composed four books of the *Institutes*, in which the text of all the laws is briefly contained. He decreed that the new laws which he himself had established, gathered into a single volume, should be called the Code of the *Novels*. [Note: Some copies: *Novella*. Lind.]

The same emperor also built within the city of Constantinople a church for Christ the Lord, who is the Wisdom of God the Father. In Greek he named it **ΑΓΙΑΝ ΣΟΦΙΑΝ**, that is, “Holy Wisdom.” [Note: See Procopius, *On the Buildings of Caesar Justinian*, book I, Lind.] Its construction surpasses all other buildings so greatly that nothing like it can be found throughout the whole extent of the earth.

[Note: Although several historians and jurists have poured out praises of the most sacred emperor Justinian, some also reproached him with the heresy of the Aphthartodocetes, that is, the “Incorruptibles,” as well as with other matters unworthy of remembrance. But the most eminent Baronius and others prove from the testimony of the ancients that he repented of that error. Pope Agatho and Odilbert, archbishop of Milan, also praised Justinian, as our Paul does.]

For this emperor was Catholic in faith, upright in his works, and just in his judgments; therefore everything came together for his good.

[Note: In the year of Christ 514.]

In his time Cassiodorus flourished at Rome in both secular and divine knowledge. Among the many noble works he wrote, he especially disclosed with great power the hidden meanings of the Psalms. [Note: He wrote this book on the Psalms in the same year in which he devoted himself to the monastic life in his celebrated monastery at Vivarium near Squillace, where he had been born. It is certain that he died more than ninety years old; the year is uncertain.]

He was first consul, then senator, and finally became a monk. [Note: Rather, he became praetorian prefect through the generosity of Athalaric, to whom he was very dear; for many infer the surname “Senator” given to Cassiodorus from his own books.]

At this same time [Note: In the year 525 of the Christian era.] Dionysius the abbot, established in the city of Rome, composed the Paschal calculation with wonderful ingenuity. [Note: Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus, a Scythian by birth and highly skilled in Greek and Latin, author of the Paschal cycle and celebrated collector of the sacred canons. To Paul and Bede, in the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, he is called abbot of the city of Rome. He was Cassiodorus’s friend and associate; Cassiodorus calls him only a monk, as Pagius notes in his *Historical Criticism* under the year 527, no. 10.]

At that time Priscian of Caesarea also, at Constantinople, explored, so to speak, the profound depths of the grammatical art. [Note: Some copies: “profound investigations.” Lind. On Priscian, see Cassiodorus, *On Orthography*, chapter 12.]

At that time, likewise, Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church, a remarkable poet, composed the *Acts of the Apostles* in hexameter verse. [Note: He dedicated them to Pope Vigilius on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the third year after the consulship of the illustrious Basil, in indiction 7, which by common reckoning falls in 544. He recited them before the clergy and people in the presence of the blessed Peter with immense applause.]

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On blessed Benedict, his miracles, and his praises.

In these days the most blessed Father Benedict, devout and holy, shone forth in the place called Sublacus, forty miles from the city of Rome, and afterward in the fortress of Cassinum, which is called [Note: Some copies: “at Cassinum.” Lind.] Harum. [Note: Ambrosian: “Arum”; Lind. and other copies: “Aurum,” “Clarum,” or “Bacrum.” Modoetian: “The fortress,” a reading superior to all the others and more consistent with the ancient descriptions of Mount Cassinum, as in the poet Marcus and others.] He excelled in the merits of a great life and in apostolic virtues. As is well known, blessed Pope Gregory composed his Life in his *Dialogues* in graceful language. I too, according to the smallness of my talent, have woven together each of his miracles in individual distichs in elegiac meter, as follows:

[Note: All these verses, through chapter 27, are absent from the Ascensian edition. Lind. They are found in our manuscripts.]

I shall begin where, holy Benedict, your triumphs—

Where shall I begin the heaps of your virtues?

Hail, blessed Father, whose merit appears in your name—

Radiant light of the age, hail, blessed Father.

Nursia, exalted by so great a fosterling, rejoice greatly—

Bearing the stars to the world, Nursia, rejoice greatly.

O youthful glory, surpassing your years in character—

Surpassing the old, O youthful glory.

Your flower, your paradise, despised the world’s flowers—

Your flower, your paradise, scorned Rome’s riches.

The nurse carried the vessel torn from its breast in sorrow—

The nurse carried back the vessel, restored, in joy.

[Note: He calls the nurse of Saint Benedict his *paedagoga*. As Saint Gregory writes, she followed him when he fled from Rome and lamented the broken sieve (*capisterium*), a vessel for cleaning wheat; I remember that this word is still heard among the Sabines.]

A man bearing the name of Rome concealed the novice among the crags—

He brought the aid of piety, bearing the name of Rome.

[Note: Saint Romanus, a monk whose name came from Rome, “when he learned Saint Benedict’s desire, kept the secret and supplied assistance; he gave him the habit of holy life and ministered to him insofar as he could.” Saint Gregory.]

Caves hidden from all mortals resound with praises—

The caves known to you, Christ, resound with praises.

You endure cold, winds, and snow, indefatigable, for three years—

For love of God you scorn cold, winds, and snow.

[Note: Al.: “you endure”; Lind., and so the Ambrosian manuscript.]

A revered deception is pleasing; thefts committed for piety are approved—

Where the holy man was hidden, a revered deception is pleasing.

He signals that the agapes are ready, but the livid one obstructs them—

Yet kindly faith signals that food is present.

[Note: The ancient Christians used *agapes* to indicate banquets to which the poor were invited. Tertullian discusses them well, among other places, in *Apology*, chapter 39: “Our supper explains its name; it is called *agape*, which among the Greeks means love. However great the expense, it is gain to spend in the name of piety, since we also aid the needy with this refreshment.” See Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book III; Cassian, *Conferences*, 24.12. There is much about Christian agapes elsewhere, beyond what Lindenbrog has noted. Here, however, Paul explains by the word *agapes* the affection of Saint Romanus, who daily lowered bread to Saint Benedict on a cord with a little bell tied to it; the bell was broken when the devil rolled down a stone.]

[Note: In Greek fashion, he calls sacred rites *orgia*, though with no very happy inspiration; for *orgia* were rites of Bacchus, so called from anger, and are not well suited to Christian Easter celebrations, at which a priest, instructed long ago by Christ, placed food before Saint Benedict.]

He properly celebrates the sacred rites, because he lends his ear to Christ—

Feeding the abstainer, he properly celebrates the sacred rites.

[Note: “When shepherds brought food for the body, they carried away nourishment for life from his mouth into their own breasts.” Saint Gregory.]

The eager swineherds bring welcome food to the caves—

With joyful hearts they bring welcome food.

Fire is destroyed by fire, while thorns tear the flesh—

The bodily fire is destroyed by fire from heaven.

[Note: The evil demon, troubling Saint Benedict in the form of a black blackbird, is put to flight by the sign of the cross.]

The hidden evil is detected from afar by the wise man—

The hidden evil cannot withstand the weapons of the cross.

[Note: A monk, gently beaten with a rod, perseveres in prayer.]

Gentle blows restrain the wandering mind—

Gentle blows drive away the wandering evil.

A perpetual stream flows from the natural marble—

A perpetual stream moistens dry hearts.

[Note: The sickle, as Saint Gregory writes, had fallen into the lake from the hand of a Goth who had come for conversion. Saint Benedict took hold of its handle, which remained in the monk’s hand, and cast it into the lake; immediately the iron returned from the depths and entered the handle.]

You sought the iron from the bottom of the whirlpool, torn from its handle—

Leaving the depths, the iron sought the handle.

[Note: Saint Maurus, on Saint Benedict’s command, ran across the lake with dry feet and rescued Saint Placid.]

Carrying out the father’s command, he runs across the waters—

Borne over the waves, he runs, carrying out the father’s command.

The water opened a path for the eager executor of his master’s order—

For the inexperienced runner the water opened a path.

You too, little boy, are carried away by the waves but do not perish—

You stand as a truthful witness, you too, little boy.

The treacherous hearts, stirred by malignant goads, lament in infernal flames—

The treacherous hearts lament in infernal flames.

[Note: Florentius the priest, driven by envy, sent Saint Benedict bread infected with poison; a raven carried it away.]

The raven bears away the food offered by kindly hands—

Commanded to take the dreadful thing far off, the raven bears away the food.

[Note: Florentius, having been unable to remove him by poison, sent girls into the garden and drove Benedict into flight by the danger of temptation. When the disciples joyfully announced to Benedict that the priest had fallen headlong from a balcony and died, he wept.]

The holy heart grieves that its enemy has been destroyed by sin—

The holy heart grieves at his death, O disciples.

[Note: He came to Mount Cassino, where the river Liris flows at its foot.]

Seeking lovely Liris, you are attended by noble leaders—

Drawn from heaven, you seek lovely Liris.

The wicked serpent rages, stripped of its place and altars—

The wicked serpent rages, deprived of its peoples.

Away, wicked rider; let marble be given to the walls—

You are compelled by command: away, wicked rider.

[Note: By the sign of the cross he drives the enemy out of a stone weighed down by the devil sitting upon it; the monks then easily lift it to build the cells.]

A devouring fire is seen to rise in deceptive flames—

No gleaming jewel is seen by you in the devouring fire.

A brother’s limbs are torn while a wall is being built—

The brother is present safe and sound while a wall is being built.

[Note: Though absent, he knew the supper prepared for monks outside the cell and, recounting the foods and the number of drinking-cups, rebuked the gluttons.]

Hidden deeds lie open; the open gluttons are exposed—

The hidden deeds of the gift received lie open.

[Note: The very well-known deception of King Totila, and Saint Benedict’s prophecy of his life.]

Cruel tyrant, the nets of your deceit are frustrated—

You receive the bridle of your life, cruel tyrant.

Numa’s lofty walls will not be overthrown by any enemy—

A grievous multitude will overthrow Numa’s lofty walls.

[Note: Ambrosian: “will be overthrown”; “a storm, he says, will overthrow,” etc.]

You are punished by a grievous foe, lest you bring the gift of strife to the altar—

You bring gifts to the altars; you are punished by a grievous foe.

[Note: He foretells to the monk Theoprobus the destruction of the monastery of Cassino, which occurred when the Lombards broke in. Since this pertains to the history of that people, see what the most learned Mabillon noted in Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues* about the date of that incursion. But our Paul the Lombard, perhaps also from affection for his own people, adds: “The same people restore all the folds of the flock”—which is certainly true, for the later Lombard princes deserved exceedingly well of the monastery of Cassino and of the whole Benedictine family.]

All the folds of the flock, foreknown, are handed over to a people—

The same people restore all the folds of the flock.

Boy, friend of deceit, Hydra’s persuasion ensnares you—

You are not ensnared by Hydra, boy, friend of deceit.

[Note: Exhilaratus by name, who, warned, found a serpent hidden in a vessel of wine.]

Be silent, swelling mind; be still, and do not attack the seer—

All things lie open to the prophet: be silent, swelling mind.

[Note: Ambrosian: “be silent”; a monk, son of Defensor, puffed up by pride while serving Saint Benedict.]

Black hunger is driven away by food brought from heaven—

Black hunger of mind is nevertheless driven away.

[Note: These two verses are absent in some witnesses. Lind.]

All hearts are astonished because you were present without a body—

All hearts are astonished at what you warn, having seen it through.

[Note: Ambrosian: “having foreseen.”]

At the command of his voice they are not permitted to be absent from the sacred rites—

At the command of his voice they attend the sacred rites.

[Note: Ambrosian: “At the command of his voice they scorn to put a bridle on their speech.” Ambrosian and Lind.: “They flee from the tombs at the command of his voice.” These are consecrated women who, after death, were seen to withdraw from the sacred rites and then, when the most holy Father blessed them, to attend them again.]

[Note: The body of a boy monk who had left the monastery for his father without a blessing.]

The gaping earth thrusts forth the buried body—

The earth holds the body’s command in its gaping breast.

The treacherous dragon soothes the fugitive into hastening—

The treacherous dragon halts the forbidden journey.

The fatal evil struck down the honor of the head—

The fatal evil goes far away at the commands.

The pious man promises golden metal to the needy, though he does not possess it—

The pious man received golden metal from heaven.

[Note: Some copies: “You, pitiable one, whose skin has been changed with the varied skin of a serpent.” The manuscript has “to whom the serpent’s gall is varied.” Lind. and the Ambrosian manuscript have the latter reading.]

You, pitiable one, whose skin is changed by the serpent’s variegated hide—

You receive your skin unharmed, pitiable one.

The rough rocks seize the glass but cannot break it—

The rough rocks preserve the glass uninjured.

Why do you fear to bring forth and conceal a drop of oil?

The jars certainly flow; why do you fear to bring it forth and conceal it? [Note: Some copies: “See, they flow.” Lind. and Ambrosian.]

From where do you hope for healing, when there is no hope of health—

You who always fear? From where is healing for you? [Note: Ambrosian and Lind.: “You who always destroy.”]

Ah, pitiable old man! You fall beneath a hostile blow—

Yet by the blow you recover, ah, pitiable old man! [Note: Ambrosian: “O weeping one.”]

Barbarian reins restrain hands ignorant of crime—

The barbarian reins flee of their own accord from the hands.

That proud man thunders on horseback with threatening cry—

That proud man lies stretched upon the ground beside his horse.

A father’s neck bears the body of his dead son—

A father’s neck bears his living son. [Note: Some copies: “the son who is to be seen.” Lind.]

Love conquers all; the sister bound the blessed man with rain—

Sleep is absent from his eyes; love conquers all. [Note: Ambrosian: “Love conquered.”]

Pleasing in simplicity, like a dove, he seeks the heights—

Pleasing in simplicity, he enters the kingdoms of heaven.

O one most fitting for God, to whom the whole world is opened—

You who explore hidden things, O one most fitting for God.

A fiery sphere bears the just man swimming above the heavens—

Whom holy love has set aflame: the fiery sphere bears him.

[Note: In the Ambrosian manuscript these two verses are absent.]

He appears when called three times, a witness fit to attest the miracle—

Dear in the father’s love, he appears when called three times.

Good leader, warning of battles, you strengthen hearts by your examples—

You are the first to rush into arms, good leader warning of battles.

He gave fitting signs as he left the fellowship of life—

Hastening toward life, he gave fitting signs.

Constantly singing psalms, he never gave his plectrum rest—

Singing sacred things, he died, constant singer of psalms.

Those whose minds were one are held in the same tomb—

Equal glory holds those whose minds were one.

A radiant road appeared, bordered by gleaming torches—

The radiant road by which the holy man ascended appeared.

Seeking the rocky enclosure, she found salvation through error—

She escaped error by seeking the rocky enclosure.

The servant, an exile, poor and insignificant, offered small poems as a humble gift—

He offered small poems.

I pray that they may be suitable guides for you on the heavenly path—

O Father Benedict, I pray that they may be suitable for you. [Note: Paul also praised Saint Scholastica and Abbot Maurus in a similar poem and meter.]

We have also woven a hymn containing the individual miracles of the same Father in Archilochian iambic meter:

Brothers, with joyful hearts,

Come with equal song,

Let us enjoy the joys

Of this illustrious feast.

[Col. 0473A]

Here Benedict, revealer

Of the narrow path,

The Father ascended to the kingdoms,

Seeking the rewards of his labors.

He shone like a new star,

Driving away the world’s clouds.

At the very threshold of life,

He despised the flowers of the age.

All-powerful in miracles,

Inspired by the breath of heaven,

He shone with wonders,

Foretelling the coming age.

About to bring food to many,

He restored the vessel of bread,

Seeking the narrow prison,

He extinguished fires with fires.

He shattered the cup carrying poison

By the weapons of the cross,

He restrained the wandering mind

With a gentle bodily scourge.

Rivers pour forth from rocks.

The iron returns from the whirlpool,

Runs obediently through the waves,

And the boy escapes death with his cloak.

The hidden poison is revealed,

The swift executor fulfills commands,

And a collapse crushes the enemy.

The roaring lion yields, roaring fiercely.

[Note: Ambrosian: “It becomes light at the bottom.”]

At the bottom the mass becomes light.

The phantom pyre moves away,

Health returns to the broken,

The transgression of the absent is revealed.

The cunning ruler is detected;

The unjust possessor flees.

Future things are foreknown.

No secret reaches the heart.

Buildings are founded through visions,

The earth vomits up corpses,

The fugitive is curbed by the dragon,

Heaven rains down coins.

Glass resists the rocks,

Jars pour forth oil,

A vision releases the bound,

The dead recover life.

The power of such great light

Is conquered by a sister’s prayer;

The more one loves, the more powerful one becomes.

The heaven that he beholds—

Unknown in earlier ages—

Shines with radiance by night,

By which the whole world is seen,

And the holy man is borne upward amid flames.

Among these things, like nectar,

</source>
Miranda plectro claruit.  
He shone forth wonderfully on the lyre.

For he aptly traced the lines  
for the followers of the sacred life,  
now a sufficiently powerful guide of the pupil.  
Be present to the sighs of the flock;  
may he grow in goodness, avoiding the water-snake,  
and may he be a follower of your path.

I would like briefly to relate what blessed Pope Gregory did not at all describe in this saintly Father’s Life. Accordingly, when, by divine admonition, he was approaching from Subiaco toward this place where he rests—a journey of nearly fifty miles—three ravens, which he was accustomed to feed, followed him as they flew around him. At every [Col. 0474B] fork in the road, until he arrived here, two angels appearing in the form of young men showed him which route he ought to take.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Ambrosianus and Modoetensis read “at every fork in the road, until he arrived here”; this reading is also confirmed in the sermon of Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who incorporated into his lesson Paul’s text from “I would like” to “composed in his praise.”]

At this place, moreover, a certain servant of God then had his dwelling; to him it was divinely said:

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Verses by the poet Marcus; read the remainder in the cited Martinengius.]

“Spare these places; another friend is present.”

When he arrived here—that is, at the fortress of Cassino—he always constrained himself by great abstinence; but especially during Lent he remained shut away and withdrawn from the tumult of the world. I have taken all this from the poem of the poet Marcus, who, on coming here to the same Father, composed several verses in his praise, which I have deliberately not transcribed in these little books, to avoid excessive length. Nevertheless, it is certain that this outstanding Father was divinely summoned to this fertile place, beneath which lies a rich valley, so that here an assembly of many monks might be formed, as indeed has now happened under God’s governance [Note: [Col. 0473D] Amb., “has been done.”]. Having related in passing these matters that ought not to be omitted, let us return to the course of our history.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the death of Audoin, the reign of Alboin, and how Alboin defeated Cunimund, king of the Gepids, and married his daughter Rosemund

Accordingly, Audoin, whom we mentioned earlier, [Note: [Col. 0473D] Al.: “The ninth king of the Lombards, who, after accomplishing many distinguished deeds, departed this life. From his wife Radelinda he had Alboin, about whom we have already written at some length. After his funeral and the proper rites had been completed, the often-mentioned Alboin, the tenth king, assumed the government of the entire Lombard people, etc.” L.] king of the Lombards, had Rodelinda as his wife [Col. 0474D], and she bore him Alboin, a man suited to war and exceptionally energetic in every respect.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] From Procopius, book IV, chapter 25, we learn who Rodelinda was: “And Amalafrid, a Goth, grandson through a daughter of Amalafrida, the sister of Theoderic, king of the Goths, and son of Hermenefrid, ruler of the Thuringians—whom Belisarius took with Witigis to Byzantium, and whom the emperor of the Romans appointed commander—gave his sister in marriage to Audoin, ruler of the Lombards.” “And Amalafrid (he was among the commanders), a Gothic man, was grandson through a daughter of Amalafrida, sister of Theoderic, king of the Goths, and son of Hermenefrid, king of the Thuringians. Belisarius conveyed Amalafrid, together with Witigis, to Byzantium; the emperor of the Romans made him a commander and gave his sister to Audoin, king of the Lombards, in marriage.”]

Audoin therefore died, and afterward Alboin, already the tenth king, came forward to govern his homeland with the wishes of all in his favor. Since he possessed a most celebrated [Col. 0475A] and powerful name [Note: [Col. 0475B] The name of King Alboin is celebrated at length by Nicetius, bishop of Trier, in the edition published by the most learned Sirmond, volume I of the Councils of Gaul: “We are astonished,” he says, “when nations tremble before him, when kings offer him reverence, when rulers praise him without ceasing, and when the emperor himself sets him before others; why does he not hasten to seek the remedy of his soul?” And below: “Such an ornament, such a man, such as King Alboin is said to be, such is the fame whom the world so exalts—why is he not converted, or why does he appear slow to seek the way of salvation?” For Nicetius wrote around A.D. 563 to Queen Clodosinda, urging her to make every effort to recall her husband from the Arian error.] renowned everywhere, Clotarius, king of the Franks, gave him his daughter Clotsiunda in marriage [Note: [Col. 0475C] Amb., Clotsuindam; Clodsuinda. Lind. Through this marriage Alboin became the son-in-law of the most powerful king and the kinsman of four Frankish kings. See Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, book IV, chapter 35.]. From her he had only one daughter, named Alpsiunda.

Meanwhile Turisendus, king of the Gepids, died, and Cunimund succeeded him in the kingdom. Wishing to avenge the ancient injuries of the Gepids, he broke the treaty with the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0475C] Al., “the treaty struck with the Lombards by his father.” Lind.] and chose war rather than peace.

Alboin, however, entered into a perpetual alliance with the Avars, who had first been called Huns and were later called Avars after the name of their own king [Note: [Col. 0475C] Modoet., “Abbars.”] [Note: [Col. 0475C] Theophylact, book VII, chapter 8.], and then set out for the war prepared by the Gepids. When the Gepids were advancing against him from the opposite direction [Note: [Col. 0475C] Al., “were preparing themselves.” Lind.], the Avars, as they had agreed with Alboin, invaded their homeland.

A sorrowful messenger came to Cunimund and announced that the Avars had invaded his territory. Although he was disheartened and placed in difficulties on both sides [Note: [Col. 0475C] Amb., “on both sides.” Modoet., “and sorrowful, and thus …” Lind.], he nevertheless urged his men first to engage the Lombards. If they could overcome them, they could then drive the army of the Huns from their homeland.

Battle was therefore joined, and the fighting was carried on with all their strength. The Lombards emerged victorious, raging against the Gepids with such fury that they destroyed them utterly, so that out of their great multitude scarcely a messenger survived [Col. 0476A].

In that battle Alboin killed Cunimund, and, having taken his head, made from it a drinking vessel [Note: [Col. 0475C] This custom was known among barbarians; concerning the Scythians Strabo writes, book VII: “Especially since the Scythians sacrifice strangers, eat human flesh, and use skulls as drinking cups.” Pliny, book VII, chapter 11: “The first anthropophagi, whom we have said to live toward the north, ten days’ journey above the Borysthenes River, drink from human skulls and use the skins, with the hair, as coverings before their breasts.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII: “The Scordisci, now far removed from those same provinces, once savage and fierce, as antiquity records, appeasing Bellona with the victims of captives, and drinking human blood more eagerly from human skulls.” Lind.]—a kind of cup that among them is called a *scala*, but in the Latin language is called a *patera* [Note: [Col. 0475D] This word has not yet fallen out of common use, not only among Germans but also among other peoples. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 5: “Cups, bowls, and *scalae* are kinds of drinking vessels formerly made of wood, whence they received their names. The Greeks called every kind of wood *kala*.” Lind.].

He led away as a captive his daughter, named Rosimunda, together with a great multitude of people of different sexes and ages. Since Clotsiunda had died, he took Rosimunda as his wife, as later became clear, to his own destruction.

Then the Lombards acquired such great booty that they now reached the utmost wealth. The race of the Gepids, however, was so diminished that from that time onward they no longer had a king. All who had survived the war either became subject to the Lombards or, while the Huns possessed their homeland, groaned under their harsh rule down to the present day [Col. 0476B].

[Note: [Col. 0475D] This passage is absent from other copies. Lind. Lazius writes the following on this passage of Paul: “Thus far the Deacon: these words clearly reveal the destruction of a most noble people, so that we need not henceforth investigate other settlements of the Gepids. For those who had survived the disaster, concealed in the mountain ravines above the Jazyges, were subjected to the service of the Avars and Huns, and even today are recognized as subject to the Hungarians, the descendants of the Avars and Huns, in those places and territories of which we have spoken above.” I would not rashly assign the date of the overthrow of the Gepid kingdom, since the writers disagree. Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, assigns it to the year 547; the abbot of Biclaro assigns it to the seventh year of Justin, which according to the reckoning of scholars is A.D. 571. The very learned Pagi, in his *Critica*, attempts to derive a more certain date from Procopius. After reporting what we transcribed above from book IV, chapter 25, he maintains that these events occurred in A.D. 551. I would not follow so highly authoritative a man, because I think that the war narrated by Procopius was a different war from this final and fatal war against the Gepids: the first was truly between Audoin and Thorisinus, the last between their sons Alboin and Cunimund. I am led to this conclusion by the fact that Procopius reports that in the following year Ildisgus fled to the Gepids and Ustrigothus to the Lombards, and that both were killed there by agreement—something that could not have happened after the kingdom had been overthrown. Therefore I follow the Biclarian and believe that these events occurred under the emperor Justin, though in the earlier years of his reign, since in the seventh year Alboin had already come into Italy.]

The name of Alboin, however, spread so widely and became so illustrious that even to this day, among the people of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0476D] Al., “of the Bavarians.” Lind.], among the Saxons, and among other peoples of the same language, his generosity, glory, success in war, and valor are celebrated in their songs [Note: [Col. 0476D] Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*: “They celebrate in ancient songs, which among them is the only kind of memory and annals”; on this passage see the note of the very learned Lipsius. I think that the songs which the Bards sang were similar to these; concerning them Ammianus Marcellinus writes, book XV: “The Bards sang the brave deeds of illustrious men, composed in heroic verse, to the sweet measures of the lyre.” Athenaeus, book VI, citing Posidonius: “The Celts,” he says, “take with them, when they go to war, companions who share their life, whom they call parasites. These men speak their praises before assembled crowds and before each of those individuals who listen separately; their recitations are the men called Bards. They prove to be poets who, with song, utter praises.”]. It is also widely reported that especially fine weapons were manufactured under him.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0477]

## CHAPTER I. How the Lombards, led by Narses the *chartularius*, gave him assistance against the Goths

[Col. 0477A]

Accordingly, when victories of the Lombards were being proclaimed everywhere in abundance, Narses [Note: [Col. 0477B] The glossary gives *χαρτοφύλαξ* (*chartophylax*), *chartularius*; but others do not approve this, distinguishing between *chartophylax* and *chartularius*. Suidas says that he was the same as a *scriniarius*: “*Scriniarius*, the *chartularius* of the prefect, the man who carries the *scrinium*, that is, the chest.” The author of the *Etymologicum* also calls the *chartophylax* a *scrik[i]arius*, so that the interpretation of the glossary might in some way be defended. His office can be inferred almost entirely from the words of Leo and Anthemius, book III, title *On the Regular Distributions*, where it is written: “The *chartularii*, who are appointed to review the titles of distributions from the cohortal offices of each province.” They also issued *σύμβολα*, that is, memoranda, as D. Cujacius has shown. They were under the authority of the *praepositus sacri cubiculi*; therefore an old scholiast on the fifteenth constitution of Julian Patricius, title 60, interprets *cubicularii* as *chartularii*. Thus Narses, whom others call a *chartularius*, is called a *cubicularius* by George Cedrenus: “In the twenty-fourth year Narses the *cubicularius* was sent to Rome to fight the Goths.” There is also mention of a *great chartularius* in the *Curopalates*, as well as of a *chartularius* who was master of the cavalry and infantry. See the Theodosian Code, book V, *On Various Offices and Attendants*, to which Zonaras, book III, pertains: “And the Roman language knows how to call Paul, the overseer of the imperial grooms, a *chartularius*.” Similarly Nicetas writes: “Theodore Chumnus, being *chartularius* of the horse-stations.”] the imperial *chartularius*, who at that time was in charge of Italy, was preparing war against Totila, king of the Goths. Since he had long possessed the Lombards as allies [Note: [Col. 0477C] Al., “as his confederates.” Lind.], he sent envoys to Alboin [Note: [Col. 0477C] Al., “to Alboin.” Lind.] asking him to provide assistance while he fought against the Goths.

Alboin then sent him a picked force from his own men [Note: [Col. 0477C] Al., “a selected band of warriors.” Lind.]. [Note: [Col. 0477C–D] Procopius, book IV, chapter 26, describing Narses’ forces and preparations against Totila, writes: “Audoin, ruler of the Lombards, persuaded by the emperor Justinian with much money and by the compact of their alliance, selected two thousand five hundred men from among his followers, skilled in war, and sent them to his aid; and he also provided them with an attendant force of more than three thousand fighting men.”] They were sent to support the Romans against the Goths [Note: [Col. 0477D] Al., “Getae.” Lind.]. These men were transported across the gulf of the Adriatic Sea into Italy, joined the Romans, and entered battle with the Goths. After the Goths, together with their king Totila, had been destroyed to the last man, the Lombards returned victorious to their homeland, honored with many gifts [Col. 0478A].

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Our author suppresses the savagery of the Lombards and the impious acts of his own people when they first came into Italy, which was bound to them by an alliance. These matters must again be taken from Procopius, book IV, chapter 33: “Narses, delighted by what had occurred, attributed everything to God (as was indeed true) and managed the affairs at hand. First, he tried to redeem with a great payment the Lombards whom he had brought with him from their outrageous conduct—for, in addition to their other abominable offenses, they burned the buildings they encountered and used shameful violence against women who had taken refuge in sacred places. After presenting them with a large sum of money, he allowed them to return to their ancestral customs and ordered Valerian and his nephew Damian, together with their followers, to lead them as far as the Roman frontier, so that they would harm no one on their return journey.” [Col. 0478C] These events occurred in the twenty-sixth year of Justinian’s reign and the eighteenth year of the Gothic war, that is, A.D. 552.]

Throughout the entire period during which the Lombards possessed Pannonia, they were auxiliaries of the Roman state against its rivals.

## CHAPTER II. How Narses defeated Buccellinus and Amingus, commanders of the Franks, and on the death of Leutharius, the third commander

At this time Narses also waged war against the commander Buccellinus [Note: [Col. 0478C] Al. reads *Bucilinus*, and does so consistently. Lind.] [Note: [Col. 0478C] That Buccellinus was killed by Narses in A.D. 554 is established with great probability from Procopius and his continuator Agathias by Valesius and other writers of Frankish history, although most of the old chroniclers disagree among themselves about the date. From both Greek writers we learn of the Franks’ expedition into Italy under King Theudebert; from Agathias we learn of its unfortunate outcome and of the destruction of Buccellinus and Leutharius, who paid to God, their avenger, the penalty for the crimes they had committed in Italy. Concerning Buccellinus, see St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I.], whom King Theudebert of the Franks, after entering Italy, had left behind with another commander, Hamingus, when he returned to Gaul, so that they might bring Italy under subjection.

When Buccellinus was laying waste almost all Italy by plundering and presenting abundant gifts from the spoils of Italy to his king Theudebert, he decided to winter in Campania [Note: [Col. 0478C] Agathias reports that Buccellinus established his camp in Campania, while Leutharius, inflamed by the vain hope of restoring the Gothic kingdom, was hastening back to Gaul.]. At last, at a place called Tannetum [Col. 0479A], he was defeated by Narses in a severe battle and killed [Note: [Col. 0478C] Al., Tanneta. Lind. and Modoet. It is certain from the cited Agathias, book II, that the battle was fought on the banks of the Casilinus River, also called the Vulturnus. The place is celebrated in verses inscribed there, as Constantine Porphyrogenitus records in *On the Themes of the Eastern Empire*, book II, theme XI: “Narses defeated Buccellinus in battle beside the Casilinus River”; so also Gregory of Tours and many others. I frankly confess that I cannot identify the place called Tannetum by Paul, unless I wish to guess that it was the same place mentioned by Porphyrogenitus in *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 27: “Capua was a very great city; it was captured and destroyed by the Vandals, that is, the Africans, and, since it lay deserted, the Lombards inhabited it. When the Africans again attacked it, the bishop Landulf built a fortress at the river bridge and called it Capanten.” Cluverius declares that the town of Tannetum near Parma is unknown to him.] [Note: [Col. 0479C] The Gallic writers mentioned above maintain that Hamingus, commander of the Frankish army in Italy, was defeated and killed in the year after Buccellinus and Leutharius. His hatred of Narses and the Romans is reported by Menander Protector, book I.]

When Hamingus attempted to bring assistance to Widin [Note: [Col. 0479C] Al. reads *Widinus*. Lind.], count of the Goths, who had rebelled against Narses, both were defeated by Narses. Widin was captured and sent into exile at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0479C] Al., “went into exile.” Lind.]. Hamingus, who had provided him assistance, was killed by the sword of Narses.

A third Frankish commander, named Leutharius [Note: [Col. 0479C] Al., Leuthardus. Lind.], the brother of Buccellinus [Note: [Col. 0479C] By birth an Alemannian.], while wishing to return to his homeland laden with much booty, died a natural death between Verona and Tridentum, beside Lake Benacus [Note: [Col. 0479C] Near the city of Ceneda, or, as Agathias writes, Cenesia.] [Note: [Col. 0479C] His death was disgraceful: in a frenzied fit, he tore his own flesh with his teeth, died howling, and, overcome by the force of the disease, destroyed his entire army.].

## CHAPTER III. How Narses destroyed Sinduald, petty king of the Heruli, who had rebelled against him

Narses nevertheless also fought against Sinduald [Note: [Col. 0479D] Al. reads *Sindualdus*; another Al. reads *Ilduald*. Lind.] [Col. 0479B] [Note: [Col. 0479D] Amb., “king of the Brentians.” Modoet., “of the Bretons.” Lind. Elsewhere he reads “Bretons,” “Brions,” “Bentians,” or “Britons.”], king of the Brebtorans, who was still left from the stock of the Heruli and whom Odoacer had brought with him into Italy [Note: [Col. 0479D] This is absent from other copies. Lind.].

Narses had first bestowed many benefits upon him, since he had faithfully adhered to him [Note: [Col. 0479D] Agathias, book I, page 387, recounts Narses’ favors toward Sinduald. He had promoted him over Aruth and appointed him commander of the Heruli. The same author also praises Sinduald for his proven loyalty to the Romans and his military valor, by which he fought vigorously against Buccellinus. See page 391, column 2.]. But when Sinduald finally rebelled arrogantly and desired to reign, Narses defeated him in war and, after capturing him, suspended him from a lofty beam [Note: [Col. 0479D] Sigebert, year 549.].

At that time Narses the patrician also gained control of the whole of Italy through Dagisteus, the master of soldiers, a warlike and courageous man [Note: [Col. 0479D] It was chiefly through the valor of Dagisteus that Rome was recovered from the Goths and restored to its own people in the twenty-sixth year of Justinian’s reign, as Procopius reports, book IV, chapter 33, page 367. This made possible the recovery of all Italy as well. I think that Paul must be understood in this sense here.].

Narses had first been a *chartularius*, but afterward, on account of his merits in valor, he earned the dignity of the patriciate [Note: [Col. 0480B] Justinian calls this honor a supreme dignity in the *Institutes*, book I, title 12, one that can be ended only by death. “For,” as Cassiodorus writes, book VI, letter 2, “as soon as it has been bestowed, this honor becomes coeval with the rest of a man’s life, a faithful and inseparable girdle of distinction, which does not know how to leave him before he departs from the world,” and so forth. See the entire passage, for it is highly relevant here. Lind.].

He was also a very devout man, Catholic in religion, generous toward the poor, and diligent in restoring basilicas [Note: [Col. 0480C] Al., “in recovering.” Lind. and Amb.]. He devoted himself so earnestly to vigils and prayers that he obtained victory more through his supplications poured out before God than through military arms [Note: [Col. 0480C] Narses has distinguished eulogists in Nicephorus, Procopius, Agathias, and other Greek historians; but more eminent than all of them is Evagrius, book IV, chapter 23, quoted by Baronius: “Those who lived with him on intimate terms testify concerning Narses that he so depended upon the divine power and honored it with every kind of piety, and that he venerated the Virgin, who is also the Mother of God, so greatly that she visibly appeared to him and instructed him when battle ought to be joined. Nor did he readily enter the field before learning from her that the proper time had arrived.”].

## CHAPTER IV. On the signs of the pestilence and the mortality that devastated Italy in the time of Narses

In his time a very great pestilence arose, especially in the province of Liguria [Note: [Col. 0480C] Baronius, the foremost historian of the Church, correctly observed from this chapter of our Paul that bubonic plague spread through Italy in the final year of the emperor Justinian, A.D. 565. For our author writes a little below, “while Justinian was emperor, he departed this life.” The testimony of St. Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 26, also supports this.].

Suddenly certain marks appeared on houses, doors, vessels, or clothing; and if anyone tried to wash them away, they appeared more and more strongly. After a full year had passed, glands began to arise in the groins of human beings or in other more delicate parts, in the form of a nut or a date [Note: [Col. 0480D] Suidas: “Among many peoples, the dates of Phoenicia are called fingers.” They were also called *Nicolaus* dates. Isidore’s glossary: “The *Nicolaus* date, a name given to them by Augustus Caesar, to whom such dates were frequently sent from Syria by Nicolaus of Damascus.” Nevertheless, Hesychius of Alexandria in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, and Suidas after him in his account of Nicolaus of Damascus, write that these were not dates but cakes. Serenus Sammonicus likewise uses the term for cakes:

“Break five grains of foreign pepper  
into soft Nicolaus cakes,  
which, inserted in the morning, you will take.”

Lind.] These were followed immediately by an intolerable feverish heat, so that a person died within three days. If someone survived three days, however, he had hope of living.

Everywhere there was mourning, everywhere tears. For, as popular rumor had it, those who fled in order to escape the disaster left their houses deserted, with only the little dogs guarding them; the livestock alone remained in the pastures, with no shepherd present [Note: [Col. 0480D] Al., “the herds.” Al., “the cattle.” Lind.]. You could see estates or fortresses formerly filled with crowds of people, and then, on the following day, after everyone had fled, everything plunged into the deepest silence [Note: [Col. 0480D] Al., “in utter desolation and silence.” Lind.].

Sons fled, leaving their parents’ corpses unburied. Parents, forgetting natural affection, abandoned their children in the fever. If some person was touched by ancient piety and wished to bury a neighbor, he himself remained unburied; while performing the service, he was killed. As he paid the last respects to a corpse, his own corpse remained without anyone to perform the rites [Note: [Col. 0481C] Modoet., “while he was planning to render burial service, he himself became a corpse, etc.” Lind., “while he was preparing beforehand to render service to the dead, he himself remained a future corpse without burial.”].

You could see the world reduced to its ancient silence [Note: [Col. 0481C] Al., “no voice was heard except that of those groaning in death; no voice of shepherds, etc.” Lind.]. No voice sounded in the countryside, no shepherd’s whistle, no ambushes by wild beasts against the sheep, no losses among domestic birds. Crops, past the time for harvesting, awaited the reaper untouched. The vineyard, having lost its leaves, remained unharmed, shining with grapes. As winter approached, by night and by day the trumpet of combatants resounded; many heard what seemed to be the murmur of an army. There were no traces of travelers, no killer could be seen, and yet the corpses of the dead surpassed the power of sight.

Pastoral places had been turned into burial grounds for human beings [Col. 0481B], and human dwellings had become refuges for wild beasts. These evils occurred only within Italy, as far as the territories of the Alamanni and Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0481C] This statement by our Paul is difficult to reconcile with what St. Gregory of Tours reports about the people of Rheims being saved from the plague through the intercession of St. Remigius, the people of Auvergne through the help of St. Gallus, and the people of Trier through that of St. Nicetius—unless one assigns this dreadful calamity in those regions to the following years.].

Meanwhile, while Justinian was emperor, he departed this life, and Justin the Younger assumed the government of the state at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0481C] Justin the Younger, the son of Dulcissimus and Vigilantia, Justinian’s sister, was crowned by John the Scholastic, patriarch, in November of that same year, 565, and assumed the empire.].
