At this time also Narses the patrician, whose diligence was vigilant in every matter, captured Vitalis, bishop of the city of Altinum, [Note: [Col. 0481C–D] His city had been destroyed by the barbarian invasion; after Rothari’s victory its episcopal see was transferred by Bishop Paul to Torcello on the Scultenna. Vitalis fled because of the schism mentioned below, and perhaps he was one of the bishops who had cursed Narses. This Narses, despite Baronius’s doubt, was none other than the eunuch and patrician.] who many years earlier had fled to the kingdom of the Franks—that is, to the city of Agonthia [Note: [Col. 0481D] Modoet., Magothiensem. Magontiensem. Lind.]—and condemned him to exile in Sicily [Note: [Col. 0481D] Baronius writes concerning these words: “Moreover, no one should suppose that the pious man Narses arrogated so much to himself as to lay hands upon bishops, except when this was ordered for him in several letters by Pope Pelagius, the predecessor of this John, as the letters of Pelagius quoted above readily demonstrate,” namely, those quoted in the year 556, number 4 and following.].

## CHAPTER V. On the Romans’ envy toward Narses

Accordingly, after Narses had, as stated, destroyed or overcome the entire Gothic people [Col. 0481C], and had likewise defeated the Huns of whom we spoke [Note: [Col. 0481D] Al., “these also.” Lind. and Amb.], he acquired great wealth in gold, silver, and other kinds of property. The Romans, for whom he had labored greatly against their enemies, consequently became envious of him [Note: [Col. 0481D] Al., “he incurred [their envy].” Lind.]. They made the following complaint against him to the emperor Justin and his wife Sophia:

“It would have been better for the Romans to serve the Goths than the Greeks, when a eunuch named Narses rules and oppresses us with servitude, while our most pious ruler knows nothing of it. Either free us from his hand, or else we shall hand over both the city of Rome and ourselves to foreign peoples.”

When Narses heard this, he briefly replied: “If I have done evil to the Romans, may I meet with evil.”

The emperor then became so angry with Narses [Note: [Col. 0481D] Al. reads “the emperor Justin.” Lind.] that he immediately sent Longinus to Italy as prefect, to take Narses’ place [Col. 0482B]. When Narses learned of this, he was greatly afraid. He was especially terrified by the same empress Sophia, and he did not dare return to Constantinople. Among other things, she is said to have sent him this message: since he was a eunuch, he should divide out wool-work among the girls in the women’s quarters [Note: [Col. 0481D] Manuscript, *gynecetum*. Lind.].

To this Narses is said to have replied: “I shall weave for her a web such as, while she lives, she will not be able to put away and unravel” [Note: [Col. 0481D] Al., “to lay aside and unwind.” Lind.].

Thus, driven by hatred and fear, he withdrew to the city of Naples [Note: [Col. 0482C] Amb., “Naples, a city of Campania.” Lind., “he withdrew to Naples, a city of Campania, and soon sent envoys.” Modoet., “he withdrew to Naples, a city of Campania, and immediately sent envoys.”]. He then sent envoys to the Lombard people, instructing them to abandon the poor [Note: [Col. 0482C] Modoetensis reads “very poor.”] fields of Pannonia and come to Italy, filled with every kind of wealth, to possess it. At the same time he sent them many varieties of fruit and other kinds of produce for which Italy is fertile, so that he might entice their minds to come there [Col. 0483A] [Note: [Col. 0482C] Against this account, by several arguments—arguments too lengthy to enumerate here—the eminent Baronius endeavors to prove, chiefly from a poem of Corippus, that Narses could not have incurred the displeasure of the Romans, because, having already been recalled to Constantinople by Justinian, he had attended the inauguration of the emperor Justin and had not returned from there. But learned men have established that three Narseses were famous at one and the same time. One was our eunuch, the patrician and prefect of Italy, one of the brothers of Aratius; Procopius discusses him in *The Gothic War*, book II, chapter 13. A second, likewise a brother of Aratius, fell in the Persian war under Justinian, as Procopius writes, book II, chapter 25. The third is perhaps the same man mentioned in the *Miscellany*, book XVII, who was burned by Phocas, and to whom the letters of St. Gregory the Great, book I, were addressed; Corippus’ poems also concern him, for they agree very well with what Theophanes reports in the cited passage. Thus Narses was in Italy under Justin and, after being recalled unjustly from there, could have summoned the Lombards, even though the Greek writers have passed over the matter in silence; several Latin writers, however, affirm it along with our Paul: Anastasius the Librarian in the *Life of John III*, the *Miscellany*, book XVII, Mellitus, Isidore of Seville, Marius of Avenches, Sigebert, and many others. Against Baronius’ view, therefore, we must yield to the testimony of the Latins, who in this matter could have known Narses’ rebellion better, and whose friendship with the barbarians was widely known among the Greeks and especially reported by Procopius. Indeed, our own people had seen the Lombards shortly before presented with enormous rewards by Narses and led outside Italy under the pretext of official service by his nephew, as I noted above. Hence, when the Lombards invaded again, the widespread Italian rumor concerning Narses’ rebellion may have arisen once more. Although this was perhaps concealed at Constantinople after his death, it did not prevent his corpse from being received into the imperial city—a meaningless reward for his victories and military valor. Nor does the praised piety of the man prove that Narses did not yield to justifiable grief: Boniface the Count, who had St. Augustine as his eulogist, also stirred up the Vandals to occupy Africa. The one point in which I would by no means approve our Paul is his claim that Narses sent the Lombards fruits and various products for which Italy is fertile; for, as allies of the Romans in the Gothic war, they had already tasted these things and satisfied their hunger and appetite in Italy.].

The Lombards [Note: [Col. 0483C] Ambrosianus reads “rejoicing at the news.”] received the joyful news, and what they themselves had long desired, with gratitude; they raised their hopes in anticipation of future advantages. Immediately terrifying signs appeared by night over Italy: fiery battle-lines appeared in the sky, flashing forth the blood that was later poured out [Note: [Col. 0483C]

Al., “stretching forth with such a flash.” Lind.

St. Gregory the Great testifies that these signs preceded the Lombards’ invasion, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 38: “Soon those terrifying signs in the sky followed, so that spears and fiery battle-lines seemed to be seen from the northern region. Soon the savage nation of the Lombards, drawn from the sheath of its dwelling, rushed upon our neck.” Likewise, in the first homily on the Gospels: “Before Italy was handed over to be struck by the sword of the gentiles, we saw fiery battle-lines in the sky, flashing forth the blood of the human race that was afterward poured out.”]

## CHAPTER VI. How Alboin summoned the Saxons to his assistance

Alboin, preparing to set out for Italy with the Lombards, requested aid from his old friends, the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0483C] The manuscript reads “enemies.” Lind.], so that he might enter spacious Italy [Note: [Col. 0483D] Al. reads “a spacious region.” Lind.] with a large force and possess it. More than twenty thousand men came to him with their wives and children, intending to go with him to Italy according to his wishes.

When Clotarius and Sigisbertus, kings of the Franks, heard this [Col. 0483B], they settled the Suebi [Note: [Col. 0483D] Al. reads *Suavi*, and Modoetensis does so consistently. Lind.] and other peoples in the places from which those same Saxons had departed [Note: [Col. 0483D] Amb., “they introduced them.”].

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Here Paul is mistaken, unless perhaps a copyist substituted Clotarius, the father, for Guntram or one of Sigebert’s other brothers; Clotarius did not survive until the Lombards’ expedition was being prepared, for he had died in A.D. 561, as Marius records in his *Chronicle*. I noted above that Alboin married Clodosinda, daughter of King Clotarius.]

## CHAPTER VII. How Alboin, leaving Pannonia, came to Italy with the Lombards

Then Alboin granted his own settlements—that is, Pannonia—to his friends the Huns, on the condition that, if at any time the Lombards should need to return, they would receive their fields back again [Col. 0484A] [Note: [Col. 0483D] Al., “would recover them.” Lind.

The very learned Pagi, in his *Critica*, writes concerning these words of Paul under the year 569: “The emperor Marcian had assigned Dacia, which we now call Transylvania, to the Huns, as we saw under the year 454; but after the departure of the Lombards they extended their settlements as far as the Anisus River, and from there inflicted the greatest suffering on Bavaria, etc.”]
repeterent. Therefore the Lombards, leaving Pannonia with their wives, children, and all their possessions, hastened to take possession of Italy. They had lived in Pannonia for forty-two years; they departed from it in April, during the first indiction, on the day after Holy Easter, whose festival that year, according to the calendar, fell on the Kalends of April, when 568 years had already elapsed since the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Most scholars, relying on the authority of Marius of Aventicum, who connected the Lombards’ invasion of Italy with the third year of Justin’s consulship, reject in the year 569, contrary to Paul’s testimony, this notable chronological date. I, however, would side with those who affirm the reliability of our author, since several arguments make it clear from the letters of Saint Gregory the Great, the preface to Rothari’s laws, and the testimony of Sigebert, with Procopius offering no resistance. Saint Gregory wrote, in the thirteenth indiction, Book V of the latest edition by the learned Benedictines of Saint-Maur, to the Empress Constantina: “We have now lived for twenty-seven years amid the swords of the Lombards in this city”; and to the Emperor Phocas, Book XIII, indiction 6: “For how we are oppressed by daily swords and by how many incursions of the Lombards for a period of thirty-five years already, we cannot adequately express in any words of petition.” Since the first letter was written in the year 595 of the Christian era, subtracting twenty-seven years brings us back to 568; and the same calculation applies to the second, which was written in 603. It seems plausible to me that the most holy pontiff reckoned the period of calamities from the very beginning of the nation’s incursions rather than from the establishment of its domination—contrary to Theophanes’ chronology. He says: “The Lombards departed from Pannonia on the very Kalends of April, and in the second indiction they began to plunder Italy; but in the third indiction they began to rule in Italy.” For who could persuade himself that the Lombards, coming from Pannonia into Italy, spent so much time on the journey? Or, if they had arrived in the first indiction, that they restrained their hands until the following year? Paul’s chronology is also confirmed by the cited preface to Rothari’s laws. It was issued in the second indiction—which falls in the year 643—“after the Lombards’ arrival in the province of Italy, from which Alboin, then king, arrived in the seventy-sixth year.” This very plainly indicates the year 568. Since our Paul contradicts this reading in Book IV, chapter 44, where “seventy-seventh” is read, it seems preferable to regard the reading in that chapter as requiring correction rather than to overturn the chronology. Finally, Procopius is by no means opposed to our account; although, as I noted above, he places the Lombards’ migration into Pannonia in the fourteenth year of the Gothic war, the matter must nevertheless be traced further back and referred to the first years of Justinian, so that they lived in that region for forty-two years.]

## CHAPTER VIII. How Alboin, coming to the borders of Italy, climbed the King’s Mountain, and concerning the wild bison

[Col. 0484B] Accordingly, when King Alboin had reached the farthest borders of Italy with his entire army and a mixed multitude of common people [Note: [Col. 0484D] Ambrosian manuscript: “a multitude of both sexes,” etc.], he climbed the mountain that rises prominently in that region. From there, as far as he was able to see [Note: [Col. 0484D] Descending from Pannonia into Italy, Alboin perhaps traveled through the neighboring Julian Alps, by which the Gothic king Alaric had come. See Cluverius, *Italia antiqua*, Book I.], he gazed upon part of Italy. It is said that, for this reason, the mountain was from that time called the King’s Mountain. [Note: [Col. 0484D] On this matter see Cluverius, *Germania antiqua*, Book III, chapter 47.] They say that wild bison are raised on this mountain [Col. 0485A]—and this is not surprising [Note: [Col. 0485B] Modern edition: “since Pannonia reaches as far as this place.”], since it extends as far as Pannonia, which is rich in these animals. Finally, a thoroughly trustworthy old man told me that on this mountain he had seen the hide of a bison killed there, on which, he said, fifteen men could have lain side by side.

## CHAPTER IX. How Alboin entered the territory of Venetia and appointed his nephew Gisulf duke in Friuli

From there, when Alboin had entered without any obstacle the territory of Venetia, which is the first province of Italy—that is, the boundaries of the city, or rather fortress, of Forum Julii—he began to consider whom he ought preferably to entrust with the first of the provinces he had begun to occupy. For all Italy that extends toward the south, or rather [Col. 0485B] toward the east [Note: [Col. 0485B] The manuscripts of Lind. read “toward the Corus”; Ambrosian manuscript, “Etruria.”], is surrounded by the waves of the Tyrrhenian [Note: [Col. 0485B] “Of the Adriatic Sea.” Lind.] or Adriatic Sea; on the west and north, however, it is so enclosed by the ridges of the Alps that it can be entered only through narrow passes and over the highest mountain ranges. On its eastern side, where it joins Pannonia, it has a broader and [Note: [Col. 0485C] Some copies: “most ample.” Lind.] very level entrance. Accordingly, as we have said, while Alboin was considering whom he ought to appoint duke in this region, he resolved to place over the city of Forum Julii and the whole of its region his nephew Gisulf, as the story goes [Note: [Col. 0485C] These words are not found in the Ambrosian manuscript.], a man altogether suitable for the position, who had been his *strator*, whom they call in their own language [Note: [Col. 0485C] Ambrosian manuscript: “Machedonas.”] *Marpahis*.

[Note: [Col. 0485C] Suidas: “*Strator* is a kind of rank.” The office was such that he lifted his lord onto a horse and led the horse. Spartianus: “As his *strator* was lifting him onto the horse, he pierced his side with a dagger.” Constantine the Great: “And, holding the bridle of his horse, we performed the office of a *strator*.” Hence they were also called *equistratores* and *protostratores*. The author of the *Life of Cyprian*: “Two officials came to him: one, a *strator* from the staff of Galerius Maximus, proconsul, who had succeeded Aspasius Paternus; and the other, an *equistrator* from the guards of that same staff, etc.” Consult Curopalates on the *protostratores*. These men were also called *statores*, as the previously cited example shows, and as this ancient inscription does:

[Col. 0485D] “To the divine Manes. M. Antonius Heutucas made this for Antonius Fortunatus, an imperial *stator* (attendant), fosterling of the emperors, most deserving.”]

[Col. 0485D] What *Marpahis* means I cannot clearly determine. I consider the reading of the manuscript more reliable, in which *Marbais* occurs; he was so called because he had authority and command over horses, just as a *sculthais* had authority over those who transgressed the laws. Few are unaware that *mar* means a female horse; hence also *Marscalk*, “servant of mares.” For *scalk* means “servant,” not only among the Germans but also among the Goths, who certainly used the Germanic language. In their books it is read thus, in the Canticle of Simeon, which I saw in the possession of the illustrious Joseph Scaliger: “*Fra leitais scalk theinana*”—“Now you dismiss your servant.” Our Paul’s *strator* was thought by a distinguished man to be the same person whom the Gauls call *grand écuyer* [“grand equerry”]; I have thought it worthwhile to insert his opinion here. Lind. In the Salic Law, *marescalcus* is distinguished from *strator*, so that the former was entrusted with the care of horses, while the latter concerned himself only with saddling the horses and bringing them to his master.

[Col. 0486B] This Gisulf declared that he would not undertake the government of that city and people unless the king granted him the Lombard [Note: [Col. 0486C] The word *fara* also occurs in Lombard law, title 64, §1: “Concerning permission to migrate with a *fara*,” etc. Lind. Other copies: *pharas*, that is, “lineages”; “he granted them for settlement.” Accordingly, with the king’s consent, he received the Lombards whom he had chosen, etc. Lind. and Mod.] *faras* he himself wished to select—that is, families or lineages—to settle there. And it was done: with the king’s consent, he received the principal Lombard families he had chosen, so that they might dwell with him; and only then did he obtain the honor of leadership. [Note: [Col. 0486C] Hence many derive the institution of the exceptional dignity later established in Italy, and they assert that Gisulf was the first duke, in the sense in which we commonly use the term.] He also asked the king for herds of noble mares, and in this matter too his request was granted through the prince’s generosity.

## CHAPTER X. Which kings ruled the Franks at that time, and concerning Pope Benedict

[Col. 0486B] In those days when the Lombards invaded Italy, the kingdom of the Franks, King Chlotar having already died, was ruled in four divisions by his sons. The first of them [Note: [Col. 0486C] Other copies: “Charibertus.” Lind.] Aripert held his seat at Paris; the second, Guntramnus, governed the city of Orléans; the third, [Note: [Col. 0486C] Other copies: “Chilpericus.” Lind.] Hilpericus, held his throne at Soissons [Note: [Col. 0486C] Other copies: “Sens,” and so also Mod.] in place of his father Chlotar; and the fourth, [Note: [Col. 0486C] Other copies: “Sigibertus.” Lind. *Sichipertus*. Mod.] Sigisbertus, nevertheless, ruled at the city of Metz [Note: [Col. 0486C] I discussed Chlotar’s year of death in chapter 6 of this book. Concerning his sons, Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 22, has the following, which Paul excerpted: “Thus these four among themselves—namely Charibert, Guntchramn, Chilperic, [Col. 0486D] and Sigibert—made a lawful division. The lot gave Charibert the kingdom of Childebert and Paris as his seat; to Guntchramn, the kingdom of Chlodomer and the seat of Orléans; to Chilperic, the kingdom of his father Chlotar and Soissons as his throne; and to Sigibert, the kingdom of Theodoric and Rheims as his seat.” These words are recorded in the Forbenian edition. Gregory of Tours gives a different account of the division of the kingdom in Book IV, chapter 24, where he says not Sens but Soissons, not Metz but Rheims, and not Aripert but Charibert, the first of Chlotar’s sons. Sabellicus, *Enneads* 8, Book V, says that Arithpert, the eldest, ruled at Paris, Guntramnus at Orléans, Chilperic at Soissons, and Sigebert at Metz.].

At this same time, the most holy man Benedict was governing the Roman Church as pope. [Note: [Col. 0486D] In the year 568, when the Lombards came into Italy, John III of that name was pope; his successor, Benedict I, surnamed Bonosus, was elected in the year 573. Anastasius led Paul into error, for he says: “Benedict, a Roman by birth, son of Boniface, sat for four years, two months, and fifteen days. During his time the nation of the Lombards invaded all Italy, and there was also a great famine, so that even a multitude of fortified places surrendered themselves to the Lombards, in order to alleviate the scarcity caused by the famine.” These words must be understood not of the time of their arrival, as Paul has it, but of their broader domination, as the words “all Italy” indicate.]

The blessed Paul was also in charge of the city of Aquileia and its people as patriarch. Fearing the barbarity of the Lombards, he fled from Aquileia to the island of Grado [Note: [Col. 0487B] Modern and Lind. editions: “from Aquileia” throughout.], carrying away with him the entire treasury of his church. [Note: [Col. 0487B] The most eminent Norisius proves with the greatest precision in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod* that it was Paulinus, archbishop of Aquileia—not Paul—who, fearing the Lombards, migrated from Aquileia to the island of Grado after exporting the church’s treasure. He also proves that this was the same man who, according to the letter of Pope Pelagius I to Narses, and after Probinus, his successor Helias, transferred the see to the island as well, by the authority of Pelagius II; this was also confirmed by the synod of Grado. Today the most distinguished patriarch resides at Udine; formerly his jurisdiction was extremely extensive, for it included the whole region from Pannonia to the river Adda and Rhaetia II. Baronius, Norisius, and other writers on sacred history have written much concerning the patriarchate of Aquileia.]

That year [Note: [Col. 0487C] The words from here through “But in the following” are absent from some copies. They stood thus in the Modoetian manuscript, but were added in a more recent hand.] during the preceding winter, so much snow fell on the plain as ordinarily falls on the highest Alps. But in the following summer there was such abundant fertility that no age is said to remember anything comparable. At that time the Huns—also called Avars—having learned of the death of King Chlotar, attacked his son Sigisbert. Meeting them in Thuringia, he utterly defeated them beside the river [Note: [Col. 0487C] *Alpen*; other copies: *Alben*. Lind.; *Albem*. Mod.] Elbe, and granted them peace when they requested it. [Note: [Col. 0487C] Saint Gregory of Tours reports Sigisbert’s Hunnic war in Book IV, chapter 26.]

Brunichildis, coming from Spain, was then joined in marriage to Sigisbert; [Note: [Col. 0487C] She was the daughter of Athanagild; see Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 28. Fortunatus composed a poem on her marriage. But Paul confuses the chronology, which is corrected by the Gallic writers.] by her he had a son named Childebert. Again the Avars fought against Sigisbert in the same places as before, defeated the Frankish army, and won the victory.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the death of Narses

Narses, having returned from Campania to Rome [Note: [Col. 0487C] The manuscript reads “from Samnium”; Lind., “from Campania”; the Ambrosian manuscript has *Cannia*, plainly corrupt, since Anastasius makes clear that Narses returned from Campania. He writes: “When Pope John learned that the Romans had sent a petition against the senator Narses to the emperor, he hastened to Naples. Pope John began to ask him to return to Rome. Then Narses said to him: ‘Tell me, most holy pope, what evil have I done to the Romans? I shall go to the feet of the one who sent me, so that Italy may know how I labored with all my strength on its behalf.’ Pope John replied: ‘I shall go sooner than you leave this land.’ Thus Narses returned with the most holy Pope John. The holy pope then remained in the cemetery of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian and lived there for a long time, even consecrating bishops there. Narses, however, entered Rome and died not long afterward.” According to the common scholarly conjecture, this occurred as the year 568 was ending or in the following year, since the history of King Alboin is entirely silent about Narses. Thus far concerning Narses are the ancient testimonies that had long been publicly available; now there must also be added what, shortly before, we read in Agnellus, or the *Ravennate Pontifical*, through the kindness of the distinguished Benedict Bacchinius. This testimony is of great importance and is something one would search for in vain elsewhere. The *Pontifical*, in the *Life of Saint Agnellus*, the twenty-seventh bishop of Ravenna, says: “In his days the Franks were expelled from Italy by the patrician Narses. After this a comet appeared in August and remained until the Kalends of October. The Emperor Justinian died at Constantinople in the fortieth year of his reign, and there was great mourning everywhere and exceedingly great sorrow for such an orthodox man. Red signs appeared in the sky, the city of Fano was consumed by fire, a multitude of people were destroyed by flame, and the fortress of Cesena was devoured by fire. But in the third year of the Emperor Justin the Younger, the patrician Narses was summoned from Ravenna; he departed with all the wealth of Italy, was governor for sixteen years, defeated two Gothic kings, and slaughtered the Frankish dukes with the sword.” In the *Life of Peter the Elder*, chapter 28, it continues: “In that year—that is, in the second indiction in which Peter had been consecrated at Rome—Venetia was occupied and invaded by the Lombards, and they were expelled without a battle. In the fifth year of the Emperor Justin II there was pestilence among cattle and death everywhere; afterward, when Tuscany had been plundered by the Lombards, they besieged Ticinum, which is called Pavia.” Soon afterward: “At that time, at Caesarea near Ravenna, by the prefect Longinus, a *palocopiam* [or, as the distinguished Muratorius reads it, *palorum copia*, ‘an abundance of stakes’] was constructed in the manner of a wall out of fear of the nation. Then the Roman Senate gradually declined, and afterward Roman liberty was taken away with triumph. For from the time when Basilius was serving as consul until the patrician Narses, the Roman provincials were reduced to nothing. After this the Lombards went out and crossed Tuscany as far as Rome; setting fires, they burned Petra Pertusa. Those Lombards built Forum Cornelii, and the city was completed by them. In those days the nation of the Avars arose, and they came into Pannonia. The patrician Narses died at Rome, after winning many victories in Italy amid the stripping bare of all the Romans; he rested in the Palace of Italy and died in the ninety-fifth year of his life.” Behold, then, another outstanding testimony concerning Narses, his hostility toward the Romans, and his death, from a writer who—as our Muratorius proves in his most careful preface, which will accompany this edition—lived in the year 839. He had seen not this History of Paul, as Bacchinius believed, but the common records of Lombard affairs, as I persuade myself from the differing form of the narrative, as will be noted below. It is therefore clear that the year of Narses’ death preceded the siege of Ticinum, while the Lombards were plundering Tuscany. For Agnellus, with the words “from the time of Basilius,” traces Narses’ affairs and the fortunes of the Romans farther back; these had entirely collapsed under that same Patrician and provided just grounds for hostility. Thus Anastasius and Agnellus agree very well: Narses could have withdrawn from Ravenna, from which he had been recalled, into Campania, and soon afterward to Rome, where he died almost a centenarian, at the advanced age which the learned Baronius, after making his calculation, assigned to him. There is only one point in Agnellus that I do not understand well: “He rested in the palace of Italy,” which must be understood of his tomb, unless *Italiae* has intruded in place of *Constantinopoli*.]

he was removed from this life not long afterward. His body, placed in a leaden coffin together with all his riches, was carried to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Felix, bishop of Tarvisium

Accordingly, when Alboin had come to the river [Note: [Col. 0489C] Other copies: *Blavem*, *Plavem*. Lind.; *Plabem*. Ambrosian manuscript: *Plavem*, which reading is superior to the others. Cluverius: “Beyond the river Sile and the towns of Altinum and Tarvisium is the river Plavis, one of the chief rivers of Italy, now commonly called *la Piave* by the Italians living there and *die Pleif* by the Germans.”] Plavis, Bishop Felix of the Tarvisian church came to meet him. [Note: [Col. 0489C] Modoetian manuscript: “of the Tharvisian church.” Concerning this Felix, Fortunatus, who held him especially dear, wrote in his poem:

“Where my Tarvisium sits, if you enter gently,  
Please seek the illustrious companion Felix,  
With whom Martin once restored my sight.”]

Since the king was exceedingly generous, he granted Felix all the possessions of his church that he requested and confirmed what had been asked through his *pragmaticus*. [Note: [Col. 0489C] That is, by a written rescript; see Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 19; Du Chesne’s *Glossary* under this word. The king’s graciousness is also noteworthy, for perhaps by it he was attempting, at his very arrival, to draw the hearts of the Italians to himself.]

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning this same Felix and the most learned man Fortunatus

Since we have mentioned this Felix, it is fitting also to relate a few things about the venerable and most learned man Fortunatus, who asserts that Felix was his companion. The Fortunatus of whom we speak was born in a place called [Note: [Col. 0489C] This village, also called Duplavelis, beside the river Plavis between Tarvisium and Ceneta, is mentioned by Regino in *Chronicle*, Book I; Cluverius maintains that it was also the birthplace of the poet Fortunatus, on an elevated hill on the left bank of the river, where there is now a village commonly called San Salvadore.] Duplavilis, a place not far from the fortress of Ceneta or the city of Tarvisium. Nevertheless, he was brought up and educated at Ravenna and became highly distinguished in grammar, rhetoric, and also [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “geometry.” Lind. and Mod.] metrical composition.

When he was suffering from extremely severe pain in his eyes, and Felix likewise, his companion, was afflicted with pain in his eyes [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “was likewise suffering from pain in the same eyes.” Lind.], the two of them went to the basilica of the blessed Paul and John, which is situated within that same city. Near it there was an altar constructed in honor of the blessed confessor Martin, and beside the altar was a window in which a lamp had been placed to provide light. As soon as these two men, Fortunatus and Felix, touched their aching eyes with the oil from it [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “after these brothers.” Lind. and Mod.], the pain immediately fled and they obtained the health they desired.

For this reason Fortunatus venerated Saint Martin so greatly that, after leaving his homeland, shortly before the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “were to invade Italy, he decided to visit his most holy relics, which were located in Gaul. He himself clearly describes this journey through rivers, mountains, valleys, towns, and villages in his poems. After he had …” Lind.] invaded Italy, he hastened to Tours to the tomb of that blessed man. He relates in his own poems that the route by which he hastened there led through [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “the streams of the Tilavem and the Reunia.” Other copies: “the Reuniam”; Mod.: “through other streams of the Menta and the Reunia, by Osopum.” Ambrosian manuscript: “hastening to the Reunia”; the remainder is not found.] the little streams of the Menta and Reunia, through Osopum and the Julian Alps, through [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “Aguntum.” Lind.] the fortress of Aguntum, and across the rivers Dravus and Byrrus, as well as Briones and the city of Augusta, through which the Virdo and [Note: [Col. 0489D] Other copies: “Lecha.” Lind.] Lech flow. [Note: [Col. 0489D] All these details should be restored from Cluverius’s reading, *Italia antiqua*, p. 199: “Through the streams of the Tilavem [Col. 0490B] and Reunia, through Osopum and the Julian Alps, through the fortress of Aguntum, and across the rivers Dravus and Byrrus, as well as Briones and the city of Augusta, through which the Virdo and Lech flow.” The restored reading is taken from Fortunatus, Book IV, *On the Life of Saint Martin*:

“You go to Augusta, which the Virdo and Lycus water;  
There you will venerate the bones of the holy martyr Afra.  
If you have leisure to travel and the Bavarian does not bar your way,  
Proceed through the neighboring places where the Breones dwell, across the Alps,  
Entering where the swift-flowing river Oenus rolls.  
Then seek the temples of blessed Valentinus,  
Making for the Noric countryside, where the Byrrus turns its waters.  
The road leads across the Dravus, where the hilltop fortresses rise;  
Here Aguntum, seated upon a mountain ridge, proudly dominates.  
From there seek the steep paths where the Julian Alps extend,  
Rising higher until the mountain reaches the clouds.  
Then leave by the road to Forum Julii, named after its prince,  
Through your cliffs, Osope, where the water flows,  
And above the waters Reunia towers over the Tilavem.”

“Here Augusta” means Augusta Vindelicorum, Augsburg, near which two rivers, the Licus and Virdo—now commonly called the Lech and the Wertach—flow. The town of Vipitenum is now Sterzing; the river Byrrus is now the Aicha, which flows into the Eisack near the village of Pyrbak; Littamum, Loncium, and Aguntum are now Luttach, Lienz, and Innichen. The river Tilavem, or Tilavemptus, is now commonly called the Tagliamento. The fortress of Reunia is now Ragogna on the left bank of the Tilavemptus. Osopum, or Osupum, is another fortress on a prominent rock beside the same river, retaining the name Osopo. The cited Cluverius argues at length that Paul incorrectly called the Noric Alps the Julian Alps here.] After he had reached Tours [Col. 0490B] in accordance with his wish [Note: [Col. 0490D] Other copies: “Tours.” Lind.], he passed through Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0490D] Ambrosian manuscript: “having arrived”; Lind.: “he lived there.”] and settled there. He composed there the deeds of many saints, partly in prose and partly in metrical language. Finally, in that same city he was first ordained a priest and then [Note: [Col. 0490D] Some have denied, contrary to Paul’s testimony, that Venantius Fortunatus was bishop of Poitiers; but it is clearly established from the material cited by Pagius in the year 568, no. 4, in his critique of Baronius, that he was indeed invoked in the litanies of the monastery of Saint Cyprian outside the walls of Poitiers. The learned scholar dates his journey through Gaul to the year 565.] a bishop, and there he now rests, buried with fitting honor.

He composed the Life of Saint Martin in four books in heroic verse, as well as many other works, especially hymns for individual festivals and, above all, little verses addressed to individual friends. In sweet and eloquent speech he composed them as a poet second to none. When I had come to his tomb to pray, I composed the following epitaph at the request of Aper, abbot of that place [Note: [Col. 0491C] Thus the manuscript; other copies: “at the request of the presbyter.” Lind. In Mod.: “at the request of Ab—of that place.”]:

[Note: [Col. 0491C] These verses are absent from the Ascensian edition. Lind. In Mod. they were added by a more recent hand.]

“Renowned for genius, swift in understanding, sweet in speech,  
Whose delightful melody many a page sings;  
Fortunatus, the summit of poets, venerable in conduct,  
Born in Ausonia, is buried in this soil.  

From whose sacred mouth we learn the deeds of the saints of old;  
These show us how to walk the path of light.  
Happy Gaul, adorned with such great jewels:  
By whose radiance the dense night flees from you.  

I have brought forth these modest verses in plebeian song,  
So that your holy honor might not lie hidden among the peoples.  
Return a kindness to the wretched, lest I be rejected by a just judge;  
Distinguished in merit, blessed one, I beg you, ask that I not be despised.”

We have given this brief account of so great a man so that his fellow citizens might not be utterly ignorant of his life. Now let us return to the sequence of the history.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Alboin captured the province of Venetia

Accordingly, Alboin captured Vicentia, Verona, and the remaining cities of Venetia, except Padua, Monte Silicis, and Mantua. [Note: [Col. 0491C] The manuscript and the Augustan edition read: “Except Padua, Monte Silicis, and Mantua.” Lind. The reading is corrupt, as will be evident below.]

For Venetia does not consist only of the few islands that we now call the Venetias; its boundary extends from the borders of Pannonia as far as the river Adda [Note: [Col. 0491C] Other copies: “as far as the Dua.” Lind.]. This is proved by the annalistic books, in which Pergamum is said to be a city of Venetia. For in the histories we also read the following about Lake Benacus: [Note: [Col. 0491C] These are the words of Servius and Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XIII, chapter 19. Benacus is now Lake Garda.] “Lake Benacus of Venetia, from which the river Mincius flows.”

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Other copies: “For although among the Latins aspiration is changed into *u*, the Greeks call them praiseworthy.” Lind. Another version: “For although among the Latins a single letter is added, the Greeks call them praiseworthy.” Mod.

Cluverius, *Italia antiqua*, Book I, p. 129, after citing Servius’s words—“Then a certain king Aenetus came, who held Venetia; after his name later generations called it Aenetia and then Venetia”—adds: “I still doubt whether Servius wrote *Aenetus* the king and *Aenetia*, and I could easily suspect that, just as the people of Gaul beyond the Alps are variously named by authors—sometimes Aedui, sometimes Hedui—so too in Servius these words *Henetus* and *Henetia* were later changed by copyists into *Aenetus* and *Aenetia*. Unless Paul the Deacon was a poor grammarian rather than a good historian when he wrote: ‘The Eneti, although one letter is added among the Latins, are called praiseworthy in Greek,’ etc. By the one letter he means *u*, because among the Latins they were called *Veneti*, whereas among the Greeks they were called Ἐνέτοι. Yet “praiseworthy,” or “commendable,” was not expressed in Greek by ἐνέτος but by αἰνετός, from the root αἶνος, which signifies praise and encomium.” This is indeed correct, but it is harsh in the manner of grammarians; nor will examples be lacking elsewhere of words in which a diphthong was altered contrary to grammatical reasoning merely because of similarity in pronunciation. But what is the point of this?]

For the *Eneti*, although one letter is added among the Latins, are called “praiseworthy” in Greek. Venetia is also joined to Histria, and the two are regarded as a single province. Histria is named from the river Hister; according to Roman history, it is said to have been more extensive than it is now. [Note: [Col. 0492C] Cluverius proves and praises this, marking out the ancient boundaries of Histria, as is his custom, with numerous testimonies from earlier writers.] The city of Aquileia was the capital of this Venetia; in its place Forum Julii is now regarded as the chief city, so called because Julius Caesar established a market there for commerce.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Liguria, the second province of Italy

[Col. 0492A]

I think it not irrelevant to touch briefly upon the remaining provinces of Italy as well. The second province is Liguria [Note: [Col. 0492C] Other copies: “Thus Liguria is the second province after Venetia.” [Col. 0492D] Lind.], so called from the gathering—that is, the collecting—of legumes, for it is very fertile in them [Note: [Col. 0492D] Cluverius again mocks these words: “As for the rest, I have little knowledge of where that name was given to the people; for the fables and foul nonsense that the grammarians of the barbarous age recorded about it, including Paul the Deacon, are mere trifles.” See the remainder in Book I, chapter 7.]. In it are Mediolanum and [Note: [Col. 0492D] Other copies: “Ticinum.” Lind. and Mod.] Ticinus, which is otherwise called Papia. It extends as far as the territory of the Gauls. Between it and [Note: [Col. 0492D] Mod.: “Suavia.”] Suavia—that is, the homeland of the Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0492D] Other copies: “the province.” Lind. and Mod.]—which lies toward the north, two provinces, Rhaetia Prima and Rhaetia Secunda, lie between the Alps; the Rhaetians are known to inhabit these regions in particular.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the fifth province of Italy, called the Cottian Alps, and the sixth, called Tuscany

[Col. 0492B]

The fifth province is called the Cottian Alps [Note: [Col. 0492D] Other copies: *Cocciae*, *Coccio*, and so throughout. Lind.]. They were named after King Cottius, who lived in Nero’s time. This province extends from Liguria toward the east as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea; on the west it is joined to the territory of the Gauls. In it are the cities of Aquae, where there are hot springs, Dertona, and the monastery of Bobium; also Genua and [Note: [Col. 0492D] Other copies: “Savona.” Lind.] Saona.

The sixth province is Tuscany, which was so called from incense (*thus*), which its people used superstitiously to burn in the sacrifices of their gods. [Note: [Col. 0492D] As though from the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν, “from sacrificing.”] Within it, toward Circius, lies Aurelia; on its eastern side lies Umbria. In this province is situated Rome, which was once the capital of the whole world. In Umbria, which is placed in part of this province, are Perusium, Lake Clitorius, and [Col. 0492C] Spoletum [Note: [Col. 0492D] The manuscript reads *Spoletium*; other copies *Spoletinum*. Lind. The same form occurs in Pliny, Book III, chapter 14; Solinus, chapter 8; Servius on Virgil XII; and Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book IX, chapter 2.]. Umbria was so called because it survived the rains, when a watery disaster once devastated its peoples.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Campania, the seventh province of Italy, and Lucania, or Brittia, which is the eighth

The seventh province, Campania, extends from the city of Rome [Col. 0493A] as far as the river Siler of Lucania [Note: [Col. 0493C] Other copies: *Silerum*. Lind.; *Silerem*. Mod.]. In it are situated the extremely wealthy cities of Capua, [Note: [Col. 0493C] Mod.: “Neapolis.”] Naples, and [Note: [Col. 0493C] Other copies: “Salernum.” Lind.] Salernus. It was called Campania on account of the exceedingly fertile plain of Capua; otherwise, for the most part, it is mountainous.

The eighth province, Lucania, which received its name from a certain grove, begins at the river Siler together with [Note: [Col. 0493C] Ambrosian manuscript: “Briccia, which was so called from the region.” Paul may have taken the etymology of the name from Jordanes; but see the better account in the geographers.] Brittia, which was so named after the name of a former queen. It extends as far as the Sicilian Strait along the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea, holding the right-hand horn of Italy, just as the two provinces above it do. In it are situated the cities of Pestus and Lanius [Note: [Col. 0493D] Other copies: “Pestum and Lamum.” Lind.], Cassianum, Consentia, and Rhegium.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Apennine Alps, which are the ninth province of Italy, and Aemilia, which is the tenth

[Col. 0493B]

Finally, the ninth province is called the Apennine Alps. They begin at the point where the Cottian Alps end. Proceeding through the middle of Italy, these Apennine Alps divide Tuscany from Emilia and Umbria from Flaminia. In this province are the cities of Ferronianus [Note: Another reading is “Ferromanum.”], Montepellium [Note: Manuscript reading: “Monsbellium”; another reading: “Monsbellus”; “Montebellum.”], Bobium, and Urbinum, as well as the town called Verona. The Apennine Alps, however, are said to have received their name from the Punic peoples—that is, Hannibal and his army—who, advancing toward Rome, made their way through them [Note: After adducing passages from Isidore and Servius, from which Paul perhaps copied this account, Cluverius rightly exclaims: “Would you say that these men had any knowledge of Italy? Would you believe that they had ever read the Roman histories concerning the Hannibalic War? I scarcely think so, since no one could be so uncultivated and ignorant of Roman affairs as not to know through what region the Pennine—or, as others have written, the Pennine Alps—run. Hannibal is said to have broken through them with his Punic army by iron, fire, and vinegar. They are, of course, what is now called Mons Jovis, or by another name Mons D. Bernhardi.”]. Some say that the Cottian Alps and the Apennine Alps constitute a single province; [Note: The manuscript and Lind. read “Victor’s,” and so does Amb.; other copies read: “But such writers are refuted by history.” The printed editions have this latter reading. Yet in Victor’s manuscript one reads: “It is Sextus Aurelius Victor, whose words occur in the *Excerpts of the Roman Emperors*, under Nero: ‘He reduced Pontus to the status of a province with the permission of Polemo the client-king, from whom it was called Polemonian Pontus; likewise the Cottian Alps, after King Cottius had died.’”] but Victor’s history refutes them, calling the Cottian Alps a province in their own right.

The tenth province, Emilia, begins at Liguria and proceeds toward Ravenna between the Apennine Alps and the waters of the Po. It is adorned with wealthy cities, namely Placentia and Parma, Regium and Bononia, and the Forum of Cornelius, whose fortress is called Imolas [Note: Elsewhere, “Imola.”]. There were also those who said that Emilia, Valeria, and Nursia were a single province; [Note: Another reading is: “But that their opinion is false in many respects is proved.”] but their opinion cannot stand, because Tuscany and Umbria lie between Emilia and Valeria and Nursia.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Flaminia, the eleventh province of Italy, and Picenum, which is reckoned the twelfth

The eleventh of the provinces is Flaminia, situated between the Apennine Alps and the Adriatic Sea. In it stand the most distinguished city of Ravenna and five other cities, called by the Greek name Pentapolis [Note: The manuscript and other copies read: “Which are called Pentapolis by a Greek name.”]. It is agreed that Aurelia, Emilia, and Flaminia received such names from the paved roads that come from the city of Rome [Note: Another reading: “which lead to the city of Rome”] and from the names of those by whom they were paved.

After Flaminia comes Picenum, the twelfth province [Note: Another reading: “Picenum.”]. On its southern side it has the Apennine Mountains, and on the other the Adriatic Sea. It extends as far as the river Piscarius [Note: Another reading: “Piscaria.”], and contains the cities Firmus, Asculus, [Col. 0494B] Pinnis, and Adria, which has been consumed by age [Note: Cluverius contends that the Adriatic Sea received its name not from this Adria of Picenum, but from the other Adria at the mouths of the Po.]. The inhabitants of this region, when they were hastening there from the Sabines, had a woodpecker settle upon their standard; [Note: So report Festus and Strabo. Others derive the name from Picus, son of Saturn.] for this reason it received the name Picenum.

## CHAPTER XX. On Valeria and Nursia, which is set down as the thirteenth, and Samnium, which is the fourteenth

The thirteenth province is Valeria, to which Nursia is attached. It lies between Umbria, Campania, and Picenum, and on the east reaches the territory of the Samnites. [Note: These words are absent in some copies.] Its western part, which begins at the city of Rome, was formerly called Etruria, after the people of the Etruscans. It contains the cities of Tibur, Carsilis [Note: Another reading: “Carsulos,” or “Carsiolis”; “Carsiolis.”], Reate, Furcona [Note: Another reading: “Furcanum,” or “Furconium.”], and Amiternum, as well as the territory of the Marsi and their lake, which is called Fucinus.

I therefore judge that the territory of the Marsi should be reckoned within the province of Valeria, because in the catalogue of the provinces of Italy it was not described separately by the ancients. But if anyone should prove by sound reasoning that this was a province in its own right, his reasonable opinion must in every respect be upheld.

The fourteenth province is Samnium. It lies within Campania and between the Adriatic Sea and Apulia, beginning at Piscaria. In it are the cities of Theate [Note: Another reading: “Theata.”], Aufidena, Hisernia [Note: Another reading: “Esernia, which has been destroyed by age.”], and Samnium, itself worn away by antiquity, from which the whole province takes its name, as well as its exceedingly wealthy capital, Beneventus [Note: Another reading: “Beneventum.”].

The Samnites, moreover, are said to have formerly received their name from the spears they were accustomed to carry [Note: So the manuscript and the Augsburg edition. Nevertheless, I think one should read: “which the Greeks call *saunia*.” Hesychius: “*Saunion*: a barbarian spear,” a reading confirmed by Pliny, Book III, chapter 12: “The Samnites, whom the Sabelli and the Greeks called Saunitae, had old Bovianum as a colony,” and so forth. Lind. From these words of Pliny, and from other ancient historians, Cluverius argues that the Samnites were not named from spears but from the Sabines. See Book III of *Italia Antiqua*, p. 648.], which the Greeks call *saunia*.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Calabria, Apulia, and Salento, which is called the fifteenth province

The fifteenth of the provinces is Apulia, together with Calabria joined to it, within which lies the region of Salento. On the west, or southwest, it has Samnium and Lucania; on the east, toward the rising sun, it is bounded by the Adriatic Sea. It contains sufficiently wealthy cities: Luceria, Sepontum [Note: Other readings: “Sipontum”; “Carvisium.”], Canusium, Agerentia, Brundisium, and Tarentum, and, on the left horn of Italy—which extends for fifty thousand [paces]—Hydruntum, well suited to commerce.

Apulia, however, is named from destruction, for there the earth’s green growth is more quickly destroyed by the heat of the sun.

## CHAPTER XXII. Sicily is the sixteenth province of Italy; Corsica the seventeenth; Sardinia the eighteenth

The island of Sicily is reckoned the sixteenth province. It is washed by the Tyrrhenian Sea, or the Ionian [Note: Ambrose has “is washed.”] and is called by the personal name of the Sicilian leader [Note: Later writers derive the name of this most celebrated island from better ancient authorities and everyone knows the most widely accepted account.].

Corsica is the seventeenth. Sardinia is placed as the eighteenth; both are surrounded by Tyrrhenian waves. Corsica is named from its leader, Corsus; Sardinia from Sardus [Note: Another reading: “Sardo.”], son of Hercules.

## CHAPTER XXIII. For what reason a part of Italy is called Cisalpine Gaul

It is nevertheless certain that the ancient historians called Liguria, part of Venetia, Emilia, and Flaminia Cisalpine Gaul. Hence the grammarian Donatus, in his exposition of Virgil, said that Mantua was in Gaul. Hence also it is read in Roman history that Ariminum was situated in Gaul.

For in the most ancient period Brennus, king of the Gauls, who ruled over the city among the Senones, came to Italy with three hundred thousand Gauls of the Senones and occupied it as far as Sena Gallica, which was named by the Gauls, the Senones. The reason why the Gauls came to Italy is described as follows. When they had tasted wine brought from Italy, enticed by their desire for wine they crossed over into Italy.

One hundred thousand of them, hastening not far from the island of Delphi, were destroyed by Greek swords. Another hundred thousand entered Galatia [Note: Other readings: “Galactia”; “Galitia.”]; at first they were called Gallo-Greeks, and afterward Galatians. These are the people to whom Paul, the Doctor of the Nations, wrote his Epistle.

The remaining one hundred thousand Gauls in Italy, founding Ticinum, Mediolanum, Bergamum, and Brexia, gave their name to the region of Cisalpine Gaul. These are the Gauls of the Senones who once invaded the city of Romulus. Just as we call that Gaul which lies beyond the Alps Transalpine Gaul, so we call the Gaul on this side, below the Alps, Cisalpine Gaul.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Why Italy is so called, and why it is also called Ausonia or Latium

Italy, which contains these provinces, received its name from Italus, the leader of the Siculi, who invaded it in ancient times. Or Italy is so called [Note: Taken from Festus.] because large cattle—that is, *itali*—are found there. For from the word *italus*, by diminution, with one letter added and another changed, the word *vitulus* is formed.

Italy is also called Ausonia, from Auson, the son of Ulysses. At first, however, the region of Beneventum was called by this name; afterward all Italy began to be called so.

Italy is also called Latium, because Saturn, fleeing from his son Jupiter, found a hiding place within it. [Note: I know that the division of all Italy set out by Paul in the preceding chapters has been rejected by many, since it does not correspond in every place to the ancient divisions of the provinces. Yet no one well versed in antiquity will deny that Italy had different provinces at different times, and that an almost immense gap opened in its history as the Roman Empire declined. From this I have drawn an argument in favor of our author, a native of that same region, who ought to have known the state of affairs nearer to his own time. I would have this account challenged only by arguments supported by the testimony of the ancients. Several learned men have long debated these matters; to report their observations in detail would have been extremely laborious and would have burdened readers hastening toward the history. For that reason I have deliberately omitted them.]

Since we have now said enough about the provinces of Italy and about the name of the country in which the events we are recounting took place, let us return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Alboin entered Mediolanum

Alboin, therefore, entering Liguria in the third indiction, entered Mediolanum on the third day before the Nones of September [Note: Another reading: “on the Nones of September.”], during the episcopate of Archbishop Honoratus. Afterward he captured all the cities of Liguria except those situated on the seacoast.

Archbishop Honoratus, abandoning Mediolanum, fled to the city of Genoa [Note: The Milanese annals report that Saint Honoratus fled to Genoa, driven by grief because he had been responsible for surrendering the city to Alboin, which the most savage king plundered contrary to the agreement.].

Paul the patriarch, after holding the priesthood for twelve years, was taken from this life and left the governance of the Church to Probinus.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the city of Ticinum was besieged for three years, and how the Lombards invaded Tuscany

At that time the city of Ticinum, enduring a siege for more than three years, held out bravely, while the Lombard army remained not far away on its western side.

[Note: Bernardus Saccus, in his *History of Ticinum*, understood Paul’s meaning very well at this point: “It is agreed by all writers that Pavia was besieged for three years; Platina too testifies to this in the *Life of John III*. While King Alboin, with part of his army, was pressing the city most fiercely and harassing it long, day and night, and so that neither Longinus nor the emperor might be able to consider freeing the city, Alboin ordered the other part of the army to cross the Po and turn its arms against the peoples of Emilia and Tuscany. Thus, at one and the same time, Italy was ravaged by one people in three regions, with no commander or army opposing a camp to Lombard fury.”]

Meanwhile Alboin, having expelled the soldiers, invaded everything as far as Tuscany, except Rome and Ravenna, as well as certain fortresses situated on the seacoast. At that time the Romans had no strength to resist, because the pestilence that arose under Narses [Note: Another reading: “the bubonic plague.”] had killed very many people in Liguria and Venetia, and because, after the year of abundance mentioned above, an extreme famine broke out and devastated all Italy.

It is certain that Alboin then brought with him to Italy many people from various nations, whether captured by other kings or by himself. Hence, even to this day, we call the villages in which they live by their names: Gepids, Bulgars, Sarmatians, Pannonians, Suebi, Noricans, and other such names.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Alboin entered Ticinum

After enduring the siege for three years and several months, the city of Ticinum finally surrendered to Alboin and the besieging Lombards. When Alboin entered it through the gate called Saint John’s, on the eastern side of the city, his horse collapsed in the middle of the gate. Although urged by spurs and beaten on both sides [Note: Ambrose: “although beaten on both sides with blows from spears.”] by the groom [Note: Another reading: “by a stable attendant.”], it could not be raised.

Then one of the Lombards addressed the king in these words: “Remember, my lord king, what vow you made. Break so harsh a vow, and you will enter the city. For this is truly a Christian people within the city.” Alboin had indeed vowed that he would destroy with the sword the entire population because they had refused to surrender to him.

After he broke this vow and promised forgiveness to the citizens, his horse immediately rose, and he entered the city. He harmed no one and remained faithful to his promise.

Then all the people ran to the palace that King Theuderic had once built [Note: Agnellus gives a fuller account of Theuderic’s palace in the *Life of Saint Peter the Elder*, chapter 28.]. After such great sufferings, now confident in hope for the future, they began to lift their spirits [Note: The Ascensian edition reads: “After such great misery, already trusting in hope, he began to raise his spirit toward better things.” The Augsburg edition has *revelare* instead of *relevare*, apparently in place of the Greek term.].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How Alboin, after reigning for three years, was killed by Helmechis at the counsel of his wife

After this king had reigned in Italy for three years and six months [Note: These words—“after he had reigned for three years and six months”—gave Baronius, Camillo Peregrini, and several others difficulty in determining the year of King Alboin’s death. The highly esteemed Peregrini, in his *History of the Lombard Princes*, dissertation on the years of Zotto’s duchy, attacks Carlo Sigonio over his distinction between two separate dates, one for the Lombards’ arrival in Italy and another for the establishment of their kingdom. Nevertheless, Sigonio must still be followed; the distinguished Bacchinius defended him in his chronological historical dissertation on the *Life of Peter the Elder*, bishop of Ravenna. The meaning is that Paul counts the years of the Lombard kingdom from the capture of Pavia by Alboin, which is also confirmed by the testimony of others, especially Sigebert and Herman the Lame. As Pagius notes, Herman writes in his fuller chronicle that Alboin, after occupying Pavia and establishing the seat of his kingdom there, “reigned in Italy for three years and six months.” In this sense Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 35, must also be understood and should not be corrected with Baronius.], he was killed by a plot devised by his wife.

The cause of his killing was as follows. While he was sitting at a banquet in Verona, more cheerful than was proper, he ordered wine to be given to the queen in a cup he had made from the skull of King Cunimund, his father-in-law, and invited her to drink merrily with her father.

Lest anyone think this impossible, I speak the truth in Christ: I myself saw this cup on a certain feast day, held in his hand by Prince Ratchis [Note: Another reading: “Ratichis.”] so that he might display it to his guests.

When Rosemunda noticed what had happened, she conceived a deep grief in her heart. Unable to restrain it, she immediately burned with a desire to kill her husband and avenge her father’s death. She soon entered into a plot with Helmichis [Note: Other readings: “Helmiges”; “Helmigis.”], who was the king’s *schilpor*, that is, his armiger and foster-brother, to kill the king.

[Note: This was the office of great men. Corippus writes that Narses was the armiger of Justin, Book II:

“Meanwhile Narses, the lord’s armiger,  
surveying his master’s footsteps,  
rises tall above the ranks.”

The *Curopalates* calls such men *skouterioi* [Greek: σκουτερίους]; Procopius, I think, calls them *doryphoroi* [Greek: δορυφόρους]. Thus, concerning Odoacer, Book I of the Gothic War, from the manuscript of the illustrious Joseph Scaliger: “There was among them a certain man named Odoacer, belonging to the king’s *doryphoroi*.” Unless one prefers to interpret *doryphoroi* there as “household guards,” for that is what they were called. Socrates, Book I, chapter 13: “One of the *doryphoroi*, whom the emperor calls household members.” Concerning these, see Book XII of the *Code*, title 17, and there the jurist Jacques Cujas. The *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Roman Empire also mentions armigers: “Senior armiger protectors, junior armiger protectors.” But those were different from these, as also in Gunter, Book VII. I think ordinary armigers were merely soldiers or guards, since the ancient grammarians interpret *armigeri* in that way. In our Paul, however, I would rather read *schilpor*, or *schilphor*, in place of the word meaning “armiger”; this is a word commonly used by the Germans.]

Helmichis persuaded the queen to enlist Peredeus, who was a very powerful man, in the plot. [Note: Another reading: “Peredeus, who was a very powerful man, should be drawn into this plot. Peredeus,” and so throughout.] Since Peredeus was unwilling to consent to the queen’s proposal for so great a crime, she secretly placed herself at night in the bed of her wardrobe attendant, with whom Peredeus was accustomed to commit adultery. Peredeus, unaware of what had happened, came and lay with the queen.

After the crime had been committed, she asked him whom he thought she was. When he named the woman he supposed his mistress to be, the queen replied: “Not at all as you think—I am Rosemunda.” “You have now committed such a deed, Peredeus, that either you must kill Alboin, or he will destroy you with his sword.”

Then he understood the evil he had done. Though he had not been willing before, he was compelled by this means to consent to the king’s murder. [Note: Another reading: “Then he understood what he had done; and although he had not been willing of his own accord, he consented to the king’s murder under such compulsion.”]

At midday, while Alboin had given himself over to sleep, Rosemunda ordered a profound silence to be maintained throughout the palace. Removing all the other weapons, she firmly fastened his sword to the head of the bed so that it could neither be taken up nor drawn. Then, in accordance with Helmichis’s plan, she introduced Peredeus, the murderer [Note: Another reading: “Peredeus and Helmichis, the murderers, according to the plan.”], more savage than any beast.

Alboin suddenly awoke from sleep and, understanding the danger that threatened, quickly reached for his sword. Since he could not draw it, fastened as it was, he nevertheless seized a footstool and defended himself with it for some time.

But alas, what sorrow! That most warlike and extraordinarily courageous man, unable to prevail against his enemy, was killed like an unarmed man [Note: The manuscript reads “one of the incestuous”; another reading: “one of the feeble.”]. He who had become famous in war through the slaughter of so many enemies perished by the counsel of a single little woman [Note: Another reading: “most fortunate in war.”].

[Note: Agnellus, in the *Ravennate Pontifical* and the *Life of Peter the Elder*, gives a somewhat different account of Alboin’s killing. He does not know of Peredeus as an accomplice, as Paul does, and says that Alboin was killed by Helmichis himself, who had been driven into so great a crime by Queen Rosmunda out of fear of the adultery he had committed. In other respects he agrees with our Paul and adds: “The king was overcome and killed. The Lombards wished to kill the murderer and the queen with him, but, learning of the plot, she came to Verona until the people’s fury subsided. Yet the Lombards quarreled violently against her; after the palace had been plundered by a multitude of Gepids and Lombards, she came to Ravenna in August and was honorably received by the prefect Longinus with all royal assistance.” From this it appears that Agnellus does not agree with Paul about the place where the tragedy occurred, unless Alboin was killed at a villa near Verona. Nor does he agree concerning the flight, which in our account, as in the following chapter in Agnellus, was made easy for Rosmunda by the support of Longinus and the faction of her Gepids and Lombards.

Marius writes: “In the fourth year of the consulship of Justin the Younger Augustus, in the fifth indiction, Albuenus, king of the Lombards, was killed by his own men—that is, by Helmechis and the others—with the consent of his wife, at Verona. The aforementioned Helmechis, together with his wife, whom he had taken in marriage, and with all the treasure, both what he had brought from Pannonia and what he had gathered from Italy, surrendered himself and part of the army to the state at Ravenna.”]

His body was buried amid the greatest weeping and lamentation of the Lombards beneath the ascent of a certain staircase adjoining the palace.

He was tall in stature and, in every part of his body, well formed for the conduct of war. In our own times Giselbertus, who had been duke of the Veronese [Note: The manuscript reads “Gislepert.”], opened his tomb and removed his sword and whatever was found among his ornaments. For this reason, with his customary vanity, he boasted among uneducated people that he had seen Alboin [Note: Another reading: “he boasted among uneducated people, maintaining that Alboin had ordered it.”].

## CHAPTER XXIX. How Helmichis wished to reign but could not

After Alboin had been killed, Helmichis attempted to seize his kingdom, but he could not, because the Lombards, grieving excessively over Alboin’s death, sought to kill him.

Rosemunda immediately sent word to Longinus, the prefect of Ravenna, asking him to dispatch a ship quickly that could receive them [Note: Another reading: “that could receive her and Helmichis.”]. Delighted by this message, Longinus hastened to send a ship. Helmichis and Rosemunda, now his wife, boarded it by night as fugitives, taking with them Albsuinda, the king’s daughter [Note: Other readings: “Albisinda”; “Albsuinda.”], and all the Lombard treasure. They reached Ravenna swiftly.

Then the prefect Longinus began to urge Rosemunda to kill Helmichis and unite herself to him in marriage. Since she was inclined toward every kind of wickedness and desired to become mistress of Ravenna, she consented to undertake so great a crime.

While Helmichis was washing in the bath, she offered him, as he came out of the bath, a cup of poison, claiming that it was health-giving [Note: Another reading: “she gave him, as he came out, a cup of death, which she asserted was health-giving.”].

When he realized that he had drunk the cup of death, he drew his sword against Rosemunda and forced her to drink what remained. Thus, by the judgment of almighty God, the most wicked murderers perished in a single moment.

## CHAPTER XXX. How Longinus, after their deaths, sent Albsuinda with the Lombard treasure to the emperor, and how Peredeus killed a lion in Constantinople

After these people had been killed, the prefect Longinus sent Albsuinda with the Lombard treasures to the emperor Tiberius in Constantinople [Note: Ambrose reads: “sent her to the emperor.” Agnellus, in the passage cited, says: “Then the prefect Longinus took all the Lombard treasures and all the royal riches that Rosmunda had brought from the Lombard kingdom and sent them, together with Rosmunda and the daughter of King Alboin, to the emperor Justin in Constantinople. The emperor rejoiced and greatly enriched the prefect.” All the others assert that Alboin was removed from the living under the emperor Justin, not under his successor Tiberius; the chronology noted above supports this. Paul’s reading should therefore be corrected here.].

Some also assert that Peredeus came to Ravenna together with Helmichis and Rosemunda, and that from there he was sent with Albsuinda to Constantinople. There, in a public spectacle before the emperor [Note: Ambrose: “in the presence of the people.”], he killed a lion of extraordinary size.

According to their account, because he was a brave man and might attempt some evil in the imperial city, the emperor ordered that his eyes be torn out [Note: Another reading: “because he was a man of great courage.”].

After some time he fitted himself with two knives. Concealing them in his sleeves, he went to the palace and promised that, if he were admitted to the emperor, he would tell him something useful.

The emperor sent two patricians, his close associates, to receive Peredeus’s message. When they came to Peredeus, he approached them more closely as if he were about to tell them something secret. Then, drawing the knives from his sleeves, he severely wounded both men, so that they immediately fell to the ground and died [Note: “He wounded both of them so severely with the knives drawn from his sleeve that they immediately fell to the ground and died.”].

Thus, in some measure resembling that most courageous Samson, he avenged his injuries and, in return for the loss of his two eyes, killed two men most useful to the emperor.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the reign of Cleph, who reigned second

The Lombards in Italy, by common agreement, chose Cleph [Note: Other readings: “Cleh”; “Clohem,” or “Cleph.”], a most noble man from among their own people, as their king in the city of Ticinum.

[Note: After Alboin had been killed, and with him his royal line, the Lombards established Cleph as their king in the thirteenth position. The catalogue of Rothari must be supplemented, since it omitted Andoin, or Audoin; or, as I myself am persuaded, his name does not appear in the learned Sigonio’s cited papers because of a copyist’s error.]

[Note: The evils inflicted upon Italy under the kings Alboin and Cleph and the thirty dukes can be seen in the books of the *Dialogues* and letters of Saint Gregory the Great, Gregory of Tours, and other writers of that age. Baronius collected these monuments of cruelty under the year 573.]

Cleph killed many powerful Romans, some with the sword and others by driving them out of Italy. After he had held the kingdom for one year and six months with his wife Massana [Note: Another reading: “Asane”; “Messona,” or “Ansare.”], he was stabbed to death by a boy from his own retinue [Note: His cruelty had provoked hatred and rebellion against him; the intervening details of the tragedy have been lost.].

## CHAPTER XXXII. How the Lombard dukes lived without a king for ten years, during which Italy was subjugated

After Cleph’s death, the Lombards remained under dukes for ten years without having a king. Each of the dukes held his own city.

Zaban held Ticinum, Uvaillari Bergamum, Alachis Brixia, Evin Tridentum, and Gisulf Forum Julii [Note: Other readings: “Zaban, Ticinum; Alboin, Mediolanum; Wallari, Bergamum; Alachis, Brixia; Eoin, Trentum.” Another: “Zabanus, Ticinum; Alboinus, Mediolanum; Vallarus, Bergamum; Comus, Trentum, or Tridentum.”]. In addition to these, there were thirty other dukes in their own cities.

[Note: Another Lombard duke, Gummarith, is mentioned by Saint Gregory the Great at Populonium in Etruria, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 2.]

During those days many distinguished Romans were killed through greed [Note: Another reading: “because of the greed of the dukes.”]; the rest were divided among the enemies [Note: Another reading: “among their hosts.”] and were made tributaries, so that they paid the Lombards one-third of their crops [Note: Another reading: “so that they paid one-third of their produce to the Lombards.”].

[Note: In the manuscript the whole chapter read as follows: “Therefore, after Cleph died, the Lombards were without a king for ten years; only dukes ruled over them.”]

Through these Lombard dukes, in the seventh year after the arrival of Alboin and the entire people, Italy was captured for the most part and subjugated by the Lombards: churches were plundered, priests killed, cities demolished, and peoples who had multiplied like crops were destroyed, except in those regions that Alboin had captured [Note: It was not in the seventh year after the arrival of Audoin that the Lombards ravaged Italy, but after a considerably longer period, as the cited testimonies demonstrate. Paul transferred this account from Gregory of Tours into his history, but misunderstood Gregory’s words.].

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. How the Lombard dukes were sent to plunder Gaul

Accordingly, some of the Lombard dukes entered Gaul with a powerful army.

[Note: Pagius, in his usual meticulous fashion, carefully distinguishes the various Lombard incursions into Gaul before the death of King Sigebert, in his critical notes on Baronius under the year 575. He asserts that the first occurred while Mummulus held the patriciate of the province, having succeeded Amatus, a man of the same rank who had been defeated and killed by the Lombards, as Saint Gregory of Tours reports in Books IV, chapters 36 and 37. In that incursion the Lombards [were defeated] at the city of Ebredunum, and afterward the Saxons, allies of the Lombards, in the territory of the city of Reggio, at the village of Stablon, while Alboin was reigning.

The second incursion is reported by Fredegar in the *Epitome*, chapter 68, and by Marius in his *Chronicle*. The Lombard dukes Talaord and Nuccio were defeated by Wiolichus and Theudofredus, dukes of Guntram. Marius marks the year with these words: “King Cleph was killed by his own boy, and in that same year the Lombards again entered the valley, seized the Cluses, and stayed for many days in the monastery of the holy Acaunenses. Afterward they fought a battle at Baccis against the Frankish army, where almost all of them were killed and a few escaped by flight.” Although Marius assigns this to the eighth year of Justin’s consulship and the seventh indiction, the distinguished scholar restored it very appropriately to the year 576 by correcting the chronology.

Paul makes no mention of this incursion. The final incursion followed the earlier one under the leadership of Amo, Zaban, and Rhodanus. At that time the events occurred which Saint Gregory of Tours and our Paul recount concerning Saint Hospitius, who had foretold the Lombard invasion. Everything Paul copied from Saint Gregory concerning the Lombards’ invasion of Gaul should therefore be restored in this order.]

The man of God Hospitius, who was confined at Nicea [Note: Saint Gregory gives “Nicea.”], foresaw their arrival long beforehand, because the Holy Spirit revealed it to him, and he foretold to the citizens of that same city the evils that threatened them.

He was a man of great abstinence and exemplary life. Bound with iron chains to his flesh and wearing a hair shirt over them [Note: Ambrose: “with chains fastened to his flesh”; Modoetius: “bound away from the flesh.”], he lived on bread alone, with a few dates. During the days of Lent he was nourished by the roots of Egyptian herbs, which hermits use and which merchants supplied to him [Note: Ambrose: “which Egyptians use”; Modoetius: “which hermits use.”]. [Note: From these words of Saint Gregory, Ruinart and Mabillon infer that there were very frequent commercial contacts at that time between the Gauls and the Egyptians.]

Through this man the Lord deigned to perform great miracles, which are recorded in the books of the venerable Gregory, bishop of Tours [Note: *History of the Franks*, Book VI, chapter 6.].

This holy man therefore foretold the arrival of the Lombards in Gaul as follows:

“The Lombards will come into Gaul and devastate seven cities, because their wickedness has increased in the sight of the Lord. For the whole people is devoted to perjuries, subject to thefts, intent on robbery, and ready for murder; among them there is no fruit of justice. Tithes are not given; the poor are not fed; the naked are not clothed; the stranger is not received in hospitality. Therefore this plague will come upon this people.”

He also instructed his monks, saying: “Leave this place, taking with you what you possess. For behold, the nation I foretold is approaching” [Note: Ambrose: “is hastening.”].

When they said to him, “We will not leave you, most holy Father,” he replied: “Do not fear for me. It will happen that they will inflict injuries upon me, but they will not harm me unto death.”

## CHAPTER II. On the Lombard who wished to kill the blessed Hospitius
As the monks were departing, the army of the Lombards arrived. [Note: Modoet.: “While they were devastating everything they had found, they came to the place where the holy man was confined.”] While it was devastating everything it had found, it reached the place where the holy man was confined. But he showed himself to them through the window of the tower. They, meanwhile, went around the tower, seeking an entrance through which they could reach him, but could not find one. Then two of them climbed onto the roof and uncovered it. Seeing him [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “bound.”] bound with chains and clothed in sackcloth, they said: “This is a criminal; he has committed murder, and that is why he is kept bound in these fetters.” [Note: Another reading: “They summoned him aside and questioned him.” Lind. “They summon an interpreter and inquire.” Mod.] After calling an interpreter, they asked him what evil he had done that he should be confined under such punishment. He confessed that he was a murderer and guilty of every crime. Then one of them, drawing his sword in order to cut off his head, [Note: Al.: “raised his right hand to cut it off, but his right hand immediately,” etc. Lind.] immediately had his right arm [Note: Mod.: “hung suspended and stiffened in the very stroke.”] stiffen in the very act of striking, and he could not draw it back to himself.
