He dropped the abandoned sword to the ground. When his companions saw this, they raised a cry to heaven [Note: Mod.: “to the sky.”], begging the holy man mercifully to tell them what they should do. He, however, making the sign of salvation, restored the withered arm to health. The Lombard who had been healed [Note: Manuscript: “reborn.” Lind.] and converted to the faith of Christ immediately became a cleric, then a monk, and remained in the service of God in that same place until the end of his life. While the blessed Hospitius was speaking the word of God to the Lombards, two commanders who had listened to him reverently were returned unharmed to their homeland [Note: Mod.: “restored.”]; but certain others who had despised his words perished miserably in that very province.

## CHAPTER III. How the patrician Amatus brought war upon the Lombard army, and how he was captured and killed by them

Accordingly, while the Lombards were devastating Gaul, Amatus, [Note: He had recently been the successor of Celsus, says the blessed Gregory, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 42.] [Note: Al.: “patrician of the Alemannic province.” Lind.] the patrician of the province who obeyed Guntram, king of the Franks, led an army against them. When battle had been joined, he turned his back and was killed there. The Lombards then inflicted such slaughter upon the Burgundians that the number of those killed could not be reckoned. Enriched by immeasurable booty, they returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER IV. How the Lombards, after entering Gaul, were defeated by the patrician Mummulus

After they had departed, [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “Emius.” Mod.: “Eunius,” as it is read in the blessed Gregory.] Eunius, also called Mummulus, was summoned by the king and obtained the dignity of patrician. When the Lombards again rushed into Gaul and advanced as far as Mustiascalmes, [Note: Other readings: “Mustias Scalmes” or “Muscias Scalmes.” Lind.: “Muscias Scalmes.” Ambrosian manuscript. Ruinart noted various readings in the Codex Corbeiensis of the blessed Gregory: “Musticascalmes.” Bec.: “Musciascalmes.”] a place adjacent to the city of Embrun, Mummulus moved his army and set out there with the Burgundians. [Note: Al.: “with the Franks.” Lind. The first reading is to be retained, as it is found in the blessed Gregory.] Having surrounded the Lombards with his army, [Note: Gregory of Tours, book IV, chapter 22: “Having cut roads through the forest paths.” Lind.] and having also cut passages through the remote parts of the forests, he rushed upon them and killed many of them. He captured some others and sent them to his king, Guntram. After accomplishing this, the Lombards returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER V. How the Saxons came into Italy with the Lombards

After this, the Saxons who had come into Italy with the Lombards broke into Gaul [Note: “They break into Gaul” is absent in the Ambrosian manuscript.] and established a camp within the territory of Riez, that is, at the village of Stablon, [Note: Other reading: “Stalbon.” Lind.] moving through the villages of the neighboring cities, seizing booty, carrying off captives, and even laying waste to everything. When Mummulus learned of this, he rushed upon them with an army, killed many of them, and did not cease striking them until night brought the fighting to an end. For he had found them unaware and supposing nothing of what had happened. At daybreak the Saxons drew up their army and prepared themselves bravely for battle, but messengers intervened and they made peace. After giving gifts to Mummulus, abandoning the captives and all their booty, they returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER VI. How the Saxons entered Gaul again with their wives and children

Accordingly, after the Saxons had returned to Italy, they took with them their wives and children and all their household possessions, [Note: Mod.: “to return.”] and decided to come again to Gaul, evidently so that, after being received by King Sigebert, they might return to their homeland with his assistance. It is certain that these Saxons had come to Italy with their wives and children in order to settle there. But, as can be understood, they did not wish to remain subject to the authority of the Lombards. Nor were they permitted by the Lombards to remain under their own law; for that reason they are thought to have gone back to their homeland.

As they were about to enter Gaul, they formed two divisions. One division entered by way of the city of Nice, while the other entered through Embrun, returning by the road they had taken the previous year. Since it was the time of the harvest, [Note: Al.: “because it was the time for gathering the harvest, they reaped and threshed the grain and ate it.” Lind., and similarly Mod.] they gathered and threshed grain, eating it and supplying it as food to their animals. They plundered livestock and did not refrain from setting fires. When they reached the Rhône River [Note: Al. omits this. Lind.], intending, after crossing it, to present themselves to Sigebert in his kingdom, Mummulus met them with a large force. Then, seeing him, they became very afraid and, after giving many gold coins as their ransom, were permitted to cross the Rhône.

As they proceeded toward King Sigebert, they deceived many people along the way by their trade, selling copper rods [Note: Other reading: “bronze plates and sheets in place of gold; for they had been colored in some way, I do not know how, so that they imitated the appearance of tested and assayed gold.” Lind.] which had somehow been colored so as to imitate the appearance of tested and assayed gold. As a result, some, deceived by this trick, gave gold and received copper, and were reduced to poverty. At last, when they reached King Sigebert, they were permitted to return to the place from which they had previously set out.

## CHAPTER VII. How the Saxons expelled the Suebi and other peoples who lived in their homeland

[Col. 0506A]

When they had reached their homeland, they found it occupied by the Suebi [Note: Other reading: “by the Suavi.” Lind. and Mod.] and by other peoples, as we mentioned above. Rising against them, they attempted to destroy [Note: Mod.: *extradere* (“hand over” or “deliver up”; reading uncertain).] and wipe them out. But the others offered them one-third of the region, saying: “We can live together and dwell in common without conflict.” When they would in no way agree, the others then offered them half; after that, two-thirds, reserving only one-third for themselves. [Note: Other reading: “When the Saxons refused.” Lind.] When they still refused, the others offered them, together with the land, all their livestock, provided only that they cease from war. But the Saxons did not agree even to this [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “even to this.”]; they sought battle and, before the conflict, decided among themselves how they would divide the wives of the Suebi.

But matters did not turn out for them as they expected. For when battle was joined, twenty thousand of them were killed. Four hundred and eighty of the Suebi fell, while the survivors won the victory. The six thousand Saxons who had survived the battle also vowed that they would cut neither their beards nor their hair until they had avenged themselves upon the Suebi. When they again engaged in battle, they were severely beaten, and thus ceased from war.

[Note: Tacitus did not omit this custom in his account of the practices of the Germans. His words are: “Among other German peoples this is an individual and rarely practiced act of daring, but among the Catti it has become a shared obligation: to let the hair and beard grow, and not remove that vowed and virtue-bound appearance of the face until an enemy has been slain.” A similar vow also appears in the narrative concerning Apollonius of Tyre, which anyone who considers it worth the trouble may read there. Lind.]

## CHAPTER VIII. How three Lombard commanders—Amo, Zaban, and Rhodanus—were defeated by Mummulus

After this, three commanders of the Lombards, namely Amo, [Col. 0506C] Zaban, [Note: Other reading: “Laban”; and so Gregory of Tours always calls him Raban. Lind.] and Rhodanus, invaded Gaul. Amo, taking the road to Embrun, advanced as far as Machovilla, [Note: Other reading: “the village of Macho.” Lind.: “Machaovilla.” Mod. observes that this reading occurs in the old Codex Corbeiensis and in the *History of the Franks* of the blessed Gregory, as Ruinart notes here.] which Mummulus had received as a royal benefice, and there pitched his tents.

Zaban, [Note: Ruinart approves this reading in his notes on the blessed Gregory, adding: “Others have ‘the city of Dea,’ which is the same thing. For Dia or Dea, a city of the Vocontii, is an episcopal city still celebrated even now. Bellovacensis, however, has ‘Verdun,’ and Corbeiensis ‘Virdun,’ although ‘Vinsun’ had been written in the first hand; but the correction is of the same age as the manuscript codex. Freherus indeed notes in the margin that the Palatine manuscript has ‘Virdun’; hence Valesius thinks that this city had two names, one Latin, namely Dea, the other Gallic, Virdunum,” etc.] descending through the city of Die, came as far as Valence. Rhodanus attacked Grenoble. Amo, for his part, subdued the province of Arles together with the cities surrounding it. Advancing as far as the very Stone Field, which lies beside the city of Marseille, he laid waste everything he could find. [Note: Other reading: “the people of Aix.” Lind.] When he was preparing to besiege Aix, he accepted twenty-two pounds of silver and withdrew from that place.

Rhodanus and Zaban likewise devastated by fire and plunder the places to which they had come. When this was reported to the patrician Mummulus, he came with a strong force and first engaged Rhodanus, who was attacking Grenoble. He killed many of his army and forced Rhodanus himself, wounded by a spear, to flee to the heights of the mountains.

From there, breaking through the remote forest paths with the five hundred men who remained to him, Rhodanus reached Zaban, who was then besieging the city of Valence, and reported to him everything that had happened. When they came together to the city of Embrun, plundering everything, Mummulus met them there with an innumerable army, and after battle had been joined, defeated them. [Note: Other reading: “They found Mummulus with an army confronting them, and, when battle was joined, were defeated by him.” Lind.]

Then Zaban and Rhodanus, returning toward Italy, reached Susa. [Note: Other reading: “Segusium.” Lind. Commonly Suze, on the Dora River.] At that time the city was held on the emperor’s side by Sisinnius, the master of the soldiers. [Note: A boy sent by Mummulus brought him a letter announcing that Mummulus was approaching. Lind. The word “boy” as used here by writers of later periods denotes nothing other than a servant. Sidonius uses it in this sense, book I, letter 11: “If he sets out when a hunt has been announced, he considers it beneath royal dignity to fasten a bow at his side. Yet if, while hunting, you point out a wild bird or beast close at hand, or if God presents one to him while he is traveling—as I read from a manuscript once used by me, *sceda*; commonly, ‘if while hunting you point out a bird or beast, or while traveling’—a boy places it in his hand, which is turned behind his back, with the cords or thong hanging loose.” Lind.] A servant of Mummulus arrived and handed Sisinnius a letter addressed to him by Mummulus, saying that Mummulus was approaching quickly. When they learned this, Zaban and Rhodanus immediately departed from there for their own territory.

When Amo heard this, he gathered all his booty and set out to return to Italy. But, impeded by the snows and abandoning most of his booty, he could scarcely break through the Alpine pass with his men, and so reached his homeland.

## CHAPTER IX. How the Franks captured the Lombard fortress of Anagnis, and how Count Ragilo was killed by the Frankish commander Chramnichis

In those days, when the Franks arrived, the fortress of Anagnis, situated above Trent on the frontier of Italy, surrendered to them. For this reason the Lombard count Ragilo, [Note: Other reading: “Largare Rugilo.” The manuscript likewise reads: “For this reason the Lombard count, wishing . . .” Lind.] by name, coming from Lagare to Anagnis, plundered it. [Note: Other reading: “to Magnos,” and likewise below. Lind.]

As he was returning from the plunder, he was killed in the field of Rotilian by the Frankish commander Chramnichis, who encountered him, together with many of his men. Not long afterward Chramnichis came to Trent and devastated it. Evin, duke of Trent, pursuing him, killed him with his companions at a place called Salurnis, and recovered all the booty he had taken. [Note: Sigonius rightly records this Frankish expedition into Italy against the Lombards under the year 577. Concerning the places mentioned in this chapter, see Cluverius in his *Italy*.]

After expelling the Franks, he recovered the territory of Trent.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the death of Sigebert, king of the Franks, and the marriage of Duke Evin

At this time Sigebert, king of the Franks, was killed through the treachery of his brother Chilperic, with whom he had entered into war. His kingdom was assumed by his son Childebert, still a very young child, together with his mother Brunhild, [Note: Lind. and Mod.: “Brunichilde.”] who undertook its government. [Note: Paul also received this account from Gregory of Tours, and for the war between Sigebert, Guntram, and Chilperic, see book IV. Sigebert was killed by two assassins with knives smeared with poison, through the agency of Fredegund, the wife of King Chilperic. The holy Germanus had also foretold this to Sigebert, warning him not to fall into the pit he had prepared by attempting to arrange the death of his brother Chilperic. By the common judgment of scholars, the year of Sigebert’s death is reckoned as 575.]

Evin, duke of the people of Trent, whom we mentioned earlier, took as his wife a daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians. [Note: John Aventinus gives a fuller account in the *Annals of Bavaria*: “Through the treachery of Fredegund, the wife of Chilperic, Sigebert—fearing nothing less from two deserters, since he had learned from them the counsels of his brother—was stabbed. The army, left without a commander, scattered in flight wherever fear carried each man. Brunhild was captured, while the underage Childebert was rescued from the imminent danger and taken into Germany by the commander Gundovald; in the city of Metz he was hailed as king.” And below: “Then Garibald, son of Theudebert, spread the report of Sigebert’s death, claiming at the same time that Thessalon had also perished. Next he seized the dukedom of Bavaria and compelled the Bavarians to swear allegiance to him. And, to make himself more august—despising Childebert’s childhood and the incompetence of the Frankish kings Chilperic and Guntram, who, given over to sexual excesses and luxury, were moreover destroying one another with mutual wounds—he called himself king. Then, to strengthen his power, he joined the Lombard nobles to himself by marriage alliances: he gave his daughter in marriage to Evin, duke of Trent, and betrothed another, named Theodelinda, to Authari, king of the Lombards.”]

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the death of Justin the Younger

At this time, as was stated above, Justin the Younger was reigning at Constantinople. [Note: I noted in book II, chapter 4, that Justin the Younger assumed the imperial power in 565, following the conjecture of the eminent Noris in his learned dissertation on the Fifth Synod.] He was wholly devoted to greed, a despiser of the poor, and a despoiler of senators. [Note: This is stated in nearly the same words in the *Miscellaneous History*, book XVI, which may perhaps have been inserted by the same Paul.] His greed was so fierce that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could heap up the talents of gold he had seized. [Note: Paul had read this in the blessed Gregory of Tours, who alone charged Justin with heresy.] He is also said to have fallen into the Pelagian heresy.

When he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, by the just judgment of God he lost the understanding of reason and became insane. [Note: Greek and Latin writers of that age relate that Justin fell into madness after suffering several disasters. Evagrius, book V, chapter 12, adds that the empress Sophia sent an embassy to Chosroes, king of the Persians, complaining of her husband’s calamity and asking the victor for a truce. Inflamed by illness, Justin attacked his brother-in-law Baduarius and provoked him with insults; but, recovering his senses afterward, he again treated him honorably. The abbot of Biclaro, who was then living at Constantinople, writes in his *Chronicle*: “The emperor Justin is shaken by a serious illness; this illness was thought by some to be a movement of the brain and by others a torment inflicted by demons.” I would support Baronius’s view that these reports refer to this Justin II, since the blessed Gregory of Tours relates in his book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 6, that the emperor Justin was freed from demonic illusions through the power of Saint Ferreolus, now the greatest ornament and protection of this most fortunate metropolis.]

[Col. 0509A]

He appointed Tiberius Caesar, who was to govern his palace or the individual provinces; a just, useful, energetic, wise, charitable man, equitable in judgments, renowned in victories, and—what surpasses all these qualities—a most genuine Christian. When this man distributed to the poor much of the treasure Justin had accumulated, the empress Sophia frequently rebuked him for having reduced the state to poverty, saying: “What I gathered over many years, you scatter prodigally in a short time.” He replied: “I trust in the Lord, because money will not be lacking for our treasury, provided that the poor receive alms and captives are ransomed. For this is to make a great treasure, as the Lord says: ‘Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth corrupts, and where thieves do not break in and steal.’ Therefore, from what the Lord has given, let us gather treasures in heaven, and the Lord will deem us worthy to increase them in this world.” [Note: Other reading: “in heaven.” Lind. This too occurs nearly word for word in Gregory of Tours and in the *Miscellaneous History.]

After Justin had reigned for eleven years, [Note: Other reading: “twelve.” Lind. and so Mod. This reading is more accurate, since Justin did not reign only eleven years but, according to the common judgment of scholars, twelve years and ten months; he was deposed on 5 October 578, as follows from Noris and more recent authorities.] he ended his life together with the madness he had incurred. [Note: Other reading: “He finally ended his life in the madness he had incurred.” Lind. and Mod.] The wars that, as we said above by anticipation, were waged by the patrician Narses against the Goths and Franks took place during his reign. Finally, when Rome, in the time of Pope Benedict, was suffering from famine because the Lombards were laying waste everything around it, Tiberius, sending many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt, relieved it through his devoted mercy. [Note: Other reading: “Tiberius, sending it.” Lind.]

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the rule of Tiberius Constantine and his good deeds

After Justin’s death, Tiberius Constantine, the fiftieth of the Roman rulers, assumed the imperial power. As we said above, while he was still Caesar under Justin, he governed the palace and gave many alms each day. [Note: Hence they were called *curatores palatii* in book I of the *Code*, under “Counts and Tribunes of the Scholae.” Corippus gives a good account of them in book I of *On the Praises of Justin*:

“When you governed the divine palace of your mighty father,

Equal in responsibilities, differing only in the diadem,

You were called *Curopalates* according to the order of affairs.”

Agathias says that they were simply called curators, book V: “A man honored with the dignity of consul and appointed to exercise care and supervision over the imperial dwellings and possessions. The Romans call such men curators.” See their official formula in Cassiodorus, book VII. Lind.]

The Lord supplied him with a great abundance of gold. For, while walking through the palace, he saw on the pavement of the house a marble slab on which the Lord’s cross had been carved, and he said: “Behold, we trample under our feet the cross of the Lord, by which we ought to protect our foreheads and breasts.” He immediately ordered the same slab to be removed. When the slab had been dug up and raised, they found another beneath it bearing the same sign; he ordered that one removed as well. When it had been taken away, they found a third. After this too had been removed at his command, they discovered a great treasure containing more than one thousand hundredweights of gold. After the gold had been taken up, he distributed it to the poor even more abundantly than was his custom. [Note: All this is found in Gregory of Tours and in the *Miscellaneous History*.]

The patrician Narses of Italy, when he had a large house in a certain city within Italy, came to the aforementioned city with many treasures. There, secretly in his own house, he dug a large cistern and deposited in it many thousands of hundredweights of gold and silver. After killing all who knew of it, he entrusted the matter to one old man alone, binding him by an oath. [Note: Other reading: “to a young boy, whom he bound by oath.” Lind. and Mod.]

After Narses had died, [Note: Al.: “the aforesaid boy, now grown old.” Lind.] the old man mentioned above, now coming to Caesar Tiberius, said: “If it is of any use to me, Caesar, I will tell you of a great matter.” He replied: “Tell me; whatever you wish will benefit you, if you report something that will benefit us.” The man said: “I possess a hidden treasure of Narses, which, now that I am at the end of my life, I can no longer conceal.”

Then Caesar Tiberius rejoiced and sent his own servants to the place; the astonished old man went before them. [Note: The words “sent his own servants” are absent from other manuscripts. Lind.] When they reached the cistern, they uncovered it and entered. So much gold and silver was found there that the bearers could scarcely have emptied it over many days. He distributed almost all of it to the needy with his customary lavish generosity. [Note: Paul took this entire account of Narses’ treasure from the blessed Gregory of Tours, and perhaps the author of the *Miscellaneous History* and Anastasius the Librarian did so as well. There is not a word of it in the Greek historians, and for that reason it is commonly counted among fables. In my judgment, however, whatever one may think about the treasure, Pagius used the better argument to prove that our Paul was in error when he wrote: “Second, it is fabulous that the same Paul, book II, chapter 11, reports that Narses was taken from this life at Rome, and that his body was placed in a lead coffin with all his riches and carried to Constantinople. For if Narses, as Paul later reports in book III, chapter 12, came to Constantinople with many treasures, secretly dug a large cistern there, placed his treasure in it, and died in that city, how could he have died at Rome and all his riches have been carried from Rome to Constantinople?” But, with all respect for so great a man, our Paul in no way contradicts himself. For if I correctly understand the meaning of his account, he does not say that the treasure was hidden at Constantinople, but “in a certain city within Italy”; and, as the Ambrosian manuscript reads, “in Italy.” From there, after Narses’ death, it was later brought to Constantinople. Gregory of Tours must be understood in the same sense, since his wording is almost identical. Moreover, it must be said that the slaughter of the servants attributed to the piety of the praised Narses is inconsistent with it, even though Latin writers brand so great a man with the stigma of greed.]

When Tiberius was about to receive the imperial crown, and the people were awaiting him at the Circus according to custom, his enemies prepared an ambush for him. They intended to raise Justinian, the grandson of Justin, to the imperial dignity. [Note: Justinian, son of Germanus, was appointed commander of the Roman army by Tiberius.]

But Tiberius, first proceeding through the holy places, then summoned the bishop of the city and entered the palace with the consuls and prefects. Clothed in purple, crowned with a diadem, and placed upon the imperial throne, he was confirmed in the glory of the kingdom amid immense acclamations. [Note: Concerning this ritual, Curopalates gives an excellent account: “After this, the new emperor, seated upon the shield, is raised aloft and appears to all the crowds standing below. The front of the shield is held by the emperor himself and, if he is alive, by the father who is being proclaimed, together with the patriarch. The sides and rear are held by those superior in rank, namely despots and sebastocrators, if there are any; otherwise by the more distinguished and noble magistrates. If there is no father, the front of the shield is held by the most honored of the dignitaries or magistrates, together with the patriarch, while the rear is held by those who follow.” Corippus, book II:

“Four chosen young men raise a great circle

Higher than the shields; and, lifted by their hands,

He himself stood above the attendants.”

See more in Peter Pithoeus, jurist, *Adversaria*, book II, chapter 6. After the elevation, he was anointed by the patriarch. Curopalates: “After this, the new emperor is raised, whatever he may wear upon his head. Immediately all who are in the church uncover their heads and stand. The patriarch anoints the emperor’s head in the form of a cross with the holy chrism, loudly pronouncing the word ‘Holy.’” Luitprand, book VI: “Received by the same supreme pontiff with wondrous ornament and wondrous ceremony, he received the anointing of the empire.” Thus you will very often see these expressions joined together: “raised to the kingship and anointed.” Lind.]

When his adversaries heard this and were unable to harm him, who had placed his hope in God, they were covered with great shame and confusion. After a few days had passed, Justinian arrived and threw himself at the emperor’s feet, bringing him fifteen hundredweights of gold in gratitude for his favor. Tiberius, accepting him according to his customary patience, ordered him to attend him in the palace. [Note: Paul transferred this account, like almost everything else narrated in the present chapter, nearly word for word from the blessed Gregory of Tours.]

But the empress Sophia, forgetful of the promise she had once made to Tiberius, attempted to lay a plot against him. [Note: Mod.: “deceitful.”] When he went out to the estate so that, according to imperial custom, he might enjoy the vintage festival for thirty days, she summoned Justinian secretly and wished to raise him to the throne. [Note: It was not unusual for historians, especially those who wrote the lives of emperors, to record this practice. There were holidays not only during the vintage but also during the harvest. The *Theodosian Code*, under “Holidays,” book II, says: “We order all days to be legal days; only those days may remain holidays which the indulgent year has granted to the two seasons for the rest of labor, to temper the heats of summer and gather the fruits of autumn.” At that time it was not lawful to plead a case or write a legal summons. Statius also touches on this in book IV of the *Silvae*:

“Surely now the laws of Latium do not mingle quarrels,

And the sluggish year keeps peace; the returning harvests

Have dismissed the forum, nor does a crowd of defendants

Now ask you to depart from the vestibule, nor complaining clients.”

Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “For the vintage, holidays had relaxed judicial business.” It was also customary to keep a holiday after the election of an emperor. Curopalates: “For ten successive days, or more, or somewhat fewer—for no fixed number of days is prescribed, but only as the emperor may wish—they celebrate completely.”]

When Tiberius learned this, he returned to Constantinople at full speed, seized the empress, and stripped her of all her treasures, leaving her only enough food for her daily sustenance. [Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “at the greatest speed”; and immediately afterward, “having been stripped,” instead of “stripped.”] He separated her servants from her and placed others of his own faithful people in their place, ordering that absolutely no one from her former household should have access to her. [Note: The reason why the empress Sophia became hostile to Tiberius after her husband’s death is related somewhat differently in the *Miscellaneous History*, book XVII, perhaps from Zonaras: “When the acclamation was made, ‘Empress Anastasia, may you conquer; Lord, preserve those whom you have ordered to rule,’ she was angered by this unexpected event, because she had lost the hope of being empress and Tiberius’s wife; for she did not know of his marriage, which is scarcely credible in an emperor.”] [Note: Leaving her only daily food and clothing. L. and M.]

Although he rebuked Justinian with words alone, he afterward loved him with such affection that he promised his own daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son. [Note: The accounts given by Greek authors concerning Justinian cast doubt upon this supreme example of Tiberius’ clemency. It is certain that Tiberius, after removing Justinian from command because he was no longer as successful against the Persians as before, replaced him with Maurice. Since the chronology is scarcely clear—Simocatta, book III, chapter 15, places the event while Justin was still alive, while Evagrius, book V, chapter 19, and the Biclarian among the Latins say: “After Justin’s death, when Tiberius was already wearing the imperial crown, he removed Justinian from power”—I would more readily believe that Maurice was substituted for Justinian for both reasons, namely conspiracy and inactivity.]

But for some reason unknown to me this arrangement did not come to fruition. His army, sent against the Persians, defeated them with the greatest force. [Note: Other reading: “sent into Persia, he waged war against the Persians with the greatest force.” Lind.] Returning victorious, he brought back so great a mass of booty, including twenty elephants, that it was thought capable of satisfying human greed.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the gold that he sent to the emperor Chilperic, and concerning the blessed Gregory
To him [Note: Alternatively, Chilperic. Lind.] Hilperic, king of the Franks, sending his envoys, received from him many ornaments [Note: Alternatively, coins. Lind.], including gold pieces each weighing a pound [Note: In Ambrosianus, bearing a quadriga, etc.], bearing on one side the emperor’s likeness and, inscribed in a circle: “TIBERIUS CONSTANTINUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS”; and on the other side a quadriga and its driver, with the inscription: “GLORY OF THE ROMANS” [Note: What Menander Protector writes should be assigned to this period, Royal Paris edition, p. 124:

“About the fourth year of the reign of Tiberius Constantine Caesar, the people of the Slavs invaded Thrace, numbering nearly one hundred thousand, etc. He [the Caesar] sent a large quantity of gold to Italy, as much as thirty centenaria, which a certain Pamphronius, a man of patrician rank, had brought from Old Rome to the emperor. Having then arrived at the imperial city for this purpose, he came to request the Caesar to aid Italy, exhausted by the incursions of the Lombards. But the Caesar, since the Persian war occupied all his attention and he was wholly absorbed in it, was unable to send an army there. Nor did he think it possible for him to wage war simultaneously in the East and the West. Instead, he gave money to Pamphronius so that, if he could somehow manage it, he might persuade some of the leaders of the Lombard people, desirous of profit, to change sides and become Romans, together with the forces under their command, and thereby cease harassing Italy. If the Lombards refused, as was likely, he was to take the other course: to make war against them and to enlist some of the Frankish leaders as allies by means of the payment of money, and thus weaken and destroy the power of the Lombards.”

“About the fourth year of the reign of Tiberius Constantine, nearly one hundred thousand Slavs invaded Thrace, etc. The Caesar sent a great quantity of gold to Italy, up to one hundred and thirty pounds, which Pamphronius—by name, a patrician in rank—had brought from Old Rome to the emperor. He had then come to the imperial city to ask the Caesar to rescue Italy, oppressed by the incursions of the Lombards, and restore it to freedom. But the Caesar, for whom everything was of no account beside the Persian war, since he was wholly devoted to it, could not send an army; nor did he decide that he himself should wage war in the East and West at the same time. Rather, he gave money to Pamphronius, with which, if he could, he might persuade some of the leaders of the Lombard nation to cross over to the Romans, together with the forces under their command, and not trouble Italy at all. If the Lombards refused, as was probable, he was to take the field against them and enlist some Frankish leaders as partners through the payment of money, and by this means weaken and break the power of the Lombards.”].

In his days the blessed [Note: 

Scholars have debated under which pope Saint Gregory the Great was sent to Constantinople as apocrisarius of the Apostolic See. The better-supported conjecture is that of the eminent Noris, who maintains that Pelagius II entrusted him with this office and enrolled him as cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church at the beginning of his pontificate and of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. The office of apocrisarius frequently appears in writers on Greek affairs, and its principal function was to attend to the Church’s business before the emperor, as is also recorded in glossaries.

The distinguished Bacchinius, in his *Pontificale Ravennate*, in the Life of John of Rome, observed from a letter of that same Saint Gregory to Castorius that, after imperial authority had been delegated to the exarchs, the Roman pontiffs also sent their apocrisarii to Ravenna. There survives a letter of Pelagius II to Saint Gregory, written on 4 October, in the third indiction, in the year of Christ 585, while Gregory was serving as apocrisarius at Constantinople. It is particularly suitable for establishing knowledge of Lombard affairs at this time; I have excerpted it as a supplement to our Paul’s account of Baronius:

“Pelagius, bishop, to his beloved son Gregory, venerable deacon.

“Everything necessary has been conveyed to you through the notary Honoratus, whom we have sent to your affection with our brother and fellow bishop Sebastian. Since he has until now been at Ravenna with the glorious lord Decius, patrician, he should by his own report inform you about everything; or, if you deem it necessary, you may bring it to the emperor’s attention. For the Lombards’ treachery has inflicted such calamities and tribulations upon us, contrary to their own oath, that no one could adequately report them. You will be able to learn from the report of our aforementioned brother Sebastian how we received him and with what affection, at your urging, he was received among us. He has also promised us that he will report to our most pious lord the emperor the needs and dangers of all Italy.

“Therefore speak and deliberate together about how you may quickly come to the aid of our dangers, for the commonwealth here has been so constricted that, unless God inspires the heart of our most pious ruler to bestow upon his servants the mercy innate in him, and deigns to grant us that *diacopsis*, or one master of soldiers and one duke, we shall be left in utter distress. For the Roman territories especially appear to have been deprived of every defense. The exarch also writes that he can provide us no remedy, since he declares that he is not even sufficient to guard those regions. May God therefore command him to hasten to aid our dangers before the army of that most wicked people, with God opposing them—which may He avert!—can prevail and seize the places held by the commonwealth, etc.”

I would believe that the events mentioned above, which I have reported from Menander, were brought about by the urgings of this letter and the efforts of Saint Gregory, were I not accused of chronological error.].

Gregory the deacon, who later became pope, while serving as apocrisarius in that same imperial city, composed the *Moralia* [Note: More accurately, he would have said that he began writing them, since he completed the books of the *Moralia* after returning from Constantinople.] and defeated Eutychius, bishop of that city, who was in error concerning the resurrection [Note: Concerning the error of Saint Eutychius, Saint Gregory himself says in his commentary on Job, at the words “and again I shall be clothed with my skin,” after recounting what the patriarch had written about the resurrection—namely, that it would occur without tangible flesh:

“Then, having been drawn into a long dispute on this matter, we began to withdraw from one another in the most serious hostility. When Tiberius Constantine, emperor of blessed memory, secretly received both him and me and learned what disagreement existed between us, weighing the arguments of both sides and refuting with his own arguments the very book that Eutychius had written about the resurrection, he decided that it ought to be burned in the flames. After we had departed from him, a severe illness immediately followed me, while illness and death followed that same Eutychius, etc.”

From this it is easy to infer the year in which the dispute took place—namely, the final year of Saint Eutychius, which was also fatal to Tiberius.].

At this same time [Note: Alternatively, Pharoald. Lind.] Faroald, the first duke of the Spoletans, invaded Classis with a Lombard army and left the wealthy city stripped and emptied of all its riches [Note: Here what Mabillon reports in volume II of the *Veterum Analectorum* should be inserted, from the subscription at the end of the *Collectaneum* excerpted from the books of Saint Augustine by Eugippius, priest and abbot of Lucullanum. It reads as follows, namely: “To Reducus, bishop of the Neapolitan city. ‘And at his command I, Peter, notary of the holy Catholic Church of Naples, corrected it as best I could, on the day before the Ides of December, under our lord the emperor Tiberius Augustus of Constantinople, in the seventh year of his reign, in the third year after the consulship of that same Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction, while the Lombards were besieging the city of Naples.’”

Paul makes no mention of the Lombard invasion of the Transtiberine region of Italy or of the siege of Naples under the thirty-six dukes. Yet below, in chapter 33, he writes: “About this time is thought to have occurred what is related about King Authari. For it is said that this same king then passed through Spoleto to Benevento, seized that region, and traveled as far as Rhegium, the farthest city of Italy, near Sicily.” He reports below, in book IV, chapter 35, that the famous city was invaded only by John Consinus.

But, unless I am mistaken, it is possible to detect testimony consistent with the evidence cited in Constantine Porphyrogenitus, so vigorously attacked by Peregrinius in his dissertation on the date of the establishment of the duchy of Benevento; and Paul himself openly admits that he had not investigated this matter as thoroughly as he should have. From this we may demonstrate that his History is defective, though we cannot supplement it in the absence of fuller monuments of ancient affairs.

Sigonius likewise assigned to the time of Tiberius, on the authority of Anastasius the Librarian and other Latin writers, the Lombard attack upon Rome itself. He writes:

“‘In the following year’—that is, 579—‘the Lombards resolved by common agreement to invade Etruria, which had remained under Roman rule, and, if matters went well, finally to attack Rome itself. Accordingly, having gathered forces from everywhere, they invaded the borders in hostile array, and, after extensive devastation and laying waste the fields far and wide with fire and sword, attacked the towns under Roman authority. In that assault Sutrium, Polimartium, Orte, Todi, Amelia, Perugia, Luceoli, and other places were brought to the point of siege with scarcely any display of military effort.’”

And below:

“‘The Lombards, encouraged by firmer hope, whether of booty or of victory, advanced into Roman territory, drove away the livestock they could seize, and savagely vented their fury even upon the people, trees, crops, and buildings they encountered. At last they brought their camp up to the city itself. The city was not only without a garrison but also without a commander; and what increased the city’s calamity was that it did not even possess an adequate supply of grain if the siege had to be endured for long. The Lombards’ continual raids prevented the peasants from working the fields safely; that summer they had produced no harvest, and the poverty of preceding years had nearly emptied the Church’s granaries.

“When Pope Benedict perceived this with his customary prudence, he immediately sent a letter to Tiberius, asking that, if he could not confront the devastation of the fields and the siege of the City because of the great distance across seas and lands, he should at least rescue him from the danger of the impending shortage and famine and send a large quantity of grain by sea to the City. When Tiberius received this, he immediately ordered cargo ships to sail to Egypt to purchase grain and then hasten from there to Rome.

“Meanwhile, after repeatedly attempting to assault the City and being repulsed from the walls by the courage of the Romans, the Lombards had achieved less than they expected and had surrounded the City with a siege, etc.” When the grain had finally been brought to the harbor of Ostia and transported from there to Rome, despite the Lombards’ efforts to prevent it, they considered abandoning the siege, “and, when the Romans requested it, granted a truce.”].

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the death of Patriarch Probinius

When Probinius, patriarch at Aquileia [Note: Other authorities omit the name Probinius. Lind. The ancient designation “patriarch” is noteworthy.], died after ruling the Church for one year, the priest Helias was appointed over that same Church.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the death of Tiberius Constantine Augustus and the reign of Maurice

Tiberius Constantine, therefore, after ruling the empire for seven years [Note: Namely, four years, ten months, and the same number of days as sole ruler; the remaining period he ruled jointly with his father Justin.], sensing that the day of his death was near, on the advice of Sophia Augusta [Note: It is entirely unreported how Sophia Augusta, whom Paul above had called rebellious, was restored to the emperor’s favor.], chose Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth [Note: Maurice was a Roman by descent and had Arabissus in Cappadocia as his birthplace.], a vigorous man, for the empire; and, having adorned his daughter with royal ornaments [Note: Alternatively, he gave her in marriage to him. Lind. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*: “Tiberius, the new Constantine, gave him—namely Maurice—his daughter Constantina in marriage on 14 August.” Zonaras, *Annals* 14, Royal Paris edition, fol. 72, adds that Tiberius, perceiving that death from consumption was near, gave his daughter Charito to Germanus and Constantina to Maurice in marriage, and named both of them Caesars. He then ordered Maurice to be crowned emperor.], he handed her over to him [Note: Because of his illness, Tiberius himself did not deliver the speech; instead, at his command, John the rhetorician, who held the office of quaestor, delivered it. Zonaras gives it at greater length in book XVIII, chapter 6: a highly elegant speech, and one worthy of a pious emperor. Saint Gregory of Tours, from whom Paul took this account, and several others also preserve it.], saying:

“Let my empire be granted to you together with this girl. Use it happily, always remembering to take delight in equity and justice.”

After saying this, he departed from this light for his eternal homeland [Note: On the day after the speech.], leaving the peoples in great mourning at his death [Note: These are the words of Saint Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 30.]. For he was of the greatest goodness: prompt in almsgiving, just in judgment, most cautious in judging, despising no one but embracing everyone with goodwill; he loved all, and was himself loved by all.

After his death, Maurice, clothed in purple and crowned with a diadem, proceeded to the Circus. When the people had acclaimed him [Note: Alternatively, with praises and applause. Lind. Examples of this are abundant in the *Lives of the Emperors*. Corippus writes:

“With countless praises they exalt the names of rulers;
With three hundred voices they pray for life to Justin.
The entire people cries out as many praises to Augusta Sophia;
A thousand voices sing a thousand praises, each distinct.
They proclaim Justin and Sophia to be two equal lights of the world:
‘Reign as equals forever,’ they say.
They pray for happy years for happy rulers.
That voice resounded long, and at last fell silent.” Lind.], he distributed gifts among the people and was the first of Greek descent to be confirmed in the imperial office [Note: Alternatively, confirmed in the empire of the Greeks. Lind.].

[Note: In the election of an emperor this occurred twice, performed by a man of senatorial rank; such gifts were called *epikombia*. [Col. 0517D] Curopalates says: “They throw into the crowd what they call *epikombia*. It is done as follows: cutting pieces from cloths, they tie to each piece three gold coins, as many silver coins, and three obols, and throw them into the multitude.” Lind.]

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the reign of Authari and the security that existed in his time

[Col. 0517B]

The Lombards, however, after having been under the authority of dukes for ten years, finally by common agreement established as their king Authari, son of the aforementioned prince Clephus [Col. 0518A] [Note: I assign Authari’s election, together with Pagius, to the year 586, although several authorities adopt a different view. To preserve the chronology of subsequent events, they are forced, contrary to Paul’s testimony, either to compress the years of the dukes into a smaller number or, as Sigonius and Baronius maintain, to move the election back to an earlier year.

The abbot of Biclaro writes in his *Chronicle*: “In the thirteenth year of Leovigild, the Lombards chose for themselves a king from their own people, named Autharic; during his reign the Roman soldiers were also completely slaughtered.” But the thirteenth year of Leovigild, 586, does not fit at all if it is counted, as Pagius counts it, with the rest. The most eminent Baronius, drawing from Saint Gregory, relates immediately after Authari’s election the miracle of Saint Peter’s key, which perhaps occurred in the following years.], as their king. Because of his rank they also called him Flavius, a forename which all the Lombard kings who followed him happily used.

In his days, in order to restore the kingdom, the dukes who then existed contributed half of all their property for royal purposes, so that there might be resources from which the king himself, or those who adhered to him [Note: Alternatively, those who were present with him. Lind. and Mod.], and who were devoted to his service in various offices, could be maintained. The burdened peoples, however, were distributed among Lombard hosts [Note: In Ambrosianus, “lodgings for the Lombards.”].

There was indeed something remarkable in the Lombard kingdom: there was no violence, no ambushes were laid. No one unjustly oppressed anyone; no one despoiled anyone [Note: Neither did anyone unjustly impose compulsory service upon another, nor despoil anyone. Modoet.: *angaria*, “forced, involuntary labour”; hence the verb *angariare*, “to impose compulsory service,” and *angarianus*, one who leases land in order to receive such service, as the ancient glossaries state. I do not compile what learned men have written on *angariae* and *parangariae*, but refer readers to their books. Lind.] [Note: Against this the most eminent Baronius writes, under the year 585:

“This is what Paul says; but he too was a Lombard and favored his own people too much. Others who lived at this time tell a different story, especially Pope Gregory, who often, because of the enormous crimes committed by them, calls the Lombards a most wicked nation and reports many things about them that are plainly contrary to what Paul relates.”

I would not, however, deny that under Authari the Lombards’ ferocity was moderated by the new structure of the kingdom. Earlier plundering may have ceased, and precautions may have been taken so that a Lombard would not, as before, molest an Italian by exercising the freer law of war—especially since the Lombards were now thinking of retaining Italy, and, having captured its more strongly fortified cities and afflicted the whole people, had good reason for hope.

Unless, perhaps, alarmed by the report of Childebert’s coming to Italy, they had created for themselves a new defense under a single king and, having become gentler, had attempted to turn the Italians away from the Franks.].

There were no thefts and no robberies; everyone traveled wherever he wished in safety and without fear.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### How Childebert entered Italy but departed after making peace

[Col. 0518B]

At this time the emperor Maurice sent fifty thousand solidi to Childebert, king of the Franks, through his envoys [Note: Baronius, on the authority of Cedrenus, places this embassy from Maurice to Childebert, king of the Franks, and Childebert’s expedition into Italy, in the third year of Maurice’s reign, corresponding, he says, to 588. Gregory of Tours, however, places it in the ninth year of King Childebert, which corresponds, according to Pagius, to 584.

In Duchesne’s collection of Frankish writers there are letters addressed to King Childebert on the occasion of this expedition and of another mentioned below by our author. I judge the first two to belong to this expedition and the other to the later one, discussed in chapter 30. They contain several events omitted by our author concerning Greek operations against the Lombards: namely, the capture of Modena, Altinum, and Mantua, as well as the surrender of Parma, Reggio, and Piacenza while the Greeks were marching to besiege them.], so that he might invade the Lombards with an army [Col. 0519A] and drive them from Italy. Childebert suddenly entered Italy with an innumerable multitude of Franks. The Lombards, however, fortifying themselves in the cities, negotiated through envoys, offered gifts, and made peace with Childebert.

When he had returned to Gaul, the emperor Maurice learned that he had made a treaty with the Lombards and began to demand back the solidi which he had given him for the harm to be inflicted upon the Lombards [Note: Alternatively, for the expulsion of the Lombards. Lind.]. But Childebert, relying on the strength of his own forces, did not even wish to give him an answer on the matter [Note: Alternatively, *solidorum*. Lind.].

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the capture of Brescello and the flight of Duke Droctulf

After these events, King Authari undertook to besiege the city of Brescello, situated on the bank of the Po [Col. 0519B]. Duke Droctulf had fled there from the Lombards [Note: Alternatively, Droctrulfus. Lind. and Modoet.], and, handing himself over to the emperor’s side, was resisting the Lombard army valiantly in association with the imperial soldiers.

This man, born among the Suebi—that is, the Alemanni—had grown up among the Lombards and, because he was handsome in appearance, had obtained the honor of the dukedom. But when he found an opportunity to avenge his captivity [Note: These words are absent from one witness. The following also read: “He was of suitable appearance; he had earned the honor of the dukedom; but when …” Lind.], he immediately took up arms against the Lombards [Note: Modoet. reads: “He immediately rose in arms against the Lombards.”]. The Lombards waged severe wars against him, and at last, being superior to him and the soldiers he commanded, compelled him to withdraw to Ravenna.

Brescello was captured [Note: Modoet. reads: “Brescello was captured by force.”], and its walls were also destroyed down to their foundations.

[Note: The existence of a peace between King Authari and the patrician Smaragdus before the year 586 is demonstrated by a letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria, which is generally said to have been written in that year. It contains the following:

“Pelagius, etc., to his most beloved brothers Helias and the other bishops, etc.

“Let it not be thought, most beloved brothers and sons, that our letters have been sent to your affection later than they should through ill will, dissimulation, or negligence. Rather, as you know, the circumstances of the times and the necessity imposed by the enemy have prevented this until now. For, as the Lord says through the prophet: ‘Can a woman forget the son of her womb?’ Let it not therefore be thought that we have not mourned the separation from our own flesh with deep weeping and lamentation. But would that, beloved, the Lord enlighten the eyes of your hearts so that you could see the groans of our heart on your behalf. For who, as the blessed Apostle says, is weak and I am not weak? Who is scandalized and I am not inflamed? And elsewhere: ‘If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.’

“After almighty God, for the happiness of our most Christian rulers, through the labors and solicitude of our son, the most excellent Smaragdus, exarch and chartulary of the sacred palace, deigned meanwhile to grant us peace or at least quiet, we hasten with every care to send these present letters to you, etc.”

[Col. 0520B] There is also another letter of the same pontiff concerning Lombard affairs, addressed to Aunarius, or Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, as Sirmondus asserts in his *Collection of Gallican Councils*. In it he asked that bishop to detach the Frankish kings from their alliance with the Lombards [Col. 0520C]. It should be assigned to the earlier period of the thirty-six dukes, since it was given in the year 580 or the following year, according to Sirmondus’s reading.

From this and the other matters noted here and there, it will be clear that our Paul, as the saying goes, tasted Lombard history only with his fingertips, and passed over in silence the most important events. This is even more evident from another notable monument of the ancient Greeks, which should be inserted into the account of the times of Maurice, drawn from Theophylact and Theophanes. After the famous Roman victory over the Persians at Martyropolis, they record another victory over the Lombards at Old Rome, as Greek writers of later times call it.

Theophylact writes, book III, chapter 4:

“Old Rome [Ῥώμη δή] repulsed the attacks of the Lombards.”

And Theophanes, under the year 580 according to the Alexandrian reckoning, writes:

“In this year, in the month of September, in the sixth indiction, the Lombards began war against the Romans.”

It is perhaps a plausible conjecture that the Roman victory preceded the truce mentioned in this chapter, even though the Greek chronological indications do not fit this period very well.]

After this, King Authari made peace with the patrician Smaragdus, who was then in charge at Ravenna, lasting until the third year.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the death of Droctulf and the epitaph with which he was honored

With the assistance of this Droctulf, whom we mentioned earlier, the soldiers of Ravenna often fought against the Lombards. With his help they also built a fleet and drove out the Lombards who held the city with their fleet [Note: Ambrosianus: “the fleet.”].

When he had completed the term of his life, they granted him an honorable tomb before the threshold of the blessed martyr Vitalis and exalted his praises in the following epitaph:

> In this tomb lies Droctulf [Note: Alternatively, “Droctulf lies here only in body.” Lind.; Ambrosianus reads *Doctron* for *Droctulf*.], though only in body;
>
> Through his merits he lives throughout the whole city [Note: Alternatively, “throughout the world.” Lind.].
>
> He was indeed among the Bards [i.e. Lombards], but by race a Sueve [Note: Alternatively: “He was indeed from the *validi* [reading uncertain], for of Suevian stock; / born, while still a young man, he was captured by the enemy.” Lind.; Ambrosianus reads “Sueve.”];
>
> Yet from that origin he was pleasing to every people.
>
> Terrible was his face to behold, but gentle was his mind [Note: Alternatively, “but his heart was kindly.” Lind.],
>
> And his robust breast bore a long beard.
>
> Here he was always a lover of the Roman and public standards [Note: Alternatively, “always following Roman arms.” Lind.];
>
> He himself became the destroyer of his own people.
>
> He despised [Note: Ambrosianus reads “he despises.”] his beloved parents while he loved us,
>
> Considering Ravenna his fatherland.
>
> His first glory was the capture of Brescello [Note: Ambrosianus reads “of Brexellus.”],
>
> Where, dwelling, he was a terror to all his enemies.
>
> Powerful beneath the Roman standards [Note: Alternatively, “beneath the foremost standards.” Lind.], he was able to help;
>
> Christ granted him the first banner to possess.
>
> Hence also, while Faroald by treachery [Note: Alternatively:
>
> “... the fleet, with fleets he opposed arms;
>
> For a long time he set arms against our walls.” Lind. and Mod.]
>
> sought to avenge the fleet, he prepared arms against fleets.
>
> Fighting with little ships on the river Badrinus [Note: Modoet. reads *Brandinus*; alternatively: “Here he crushed the forces and wealth of the Longobards, / made renowned to the stars by the honors bestowed upon him, / with the martyr’s aid, etc.” Lind.],
>
> He himself defeated the countless forces of the Lombard Bardic people.
>
> Again, in the eastern lands, he overcame Avar,
>
> Winning the greatest palm of victory for his lords.
>
> Strengthened by the aid of the martyr Vitalis,
>
> He came to these places, often triumphing as a victorious man.
>
> He also asked that his remains lie in the churches of that martyr;
>
> He gladly desired these places as his tomb after death [Note: Alternatively, “thinking that these places would be blessed in the future.” Lind.].
>
> Dying, he himself asked these things of the priest John [Note: Alternatively:
>
> “... dying, he asked for these gifts,
>
> And, happy, went to the stars when they had been inscribed.” Lind.],
>
> Through whose pious love he returned to these earthly regions.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the priesthood of Pope Pelagius and the error of Helias the patriarch

[Col. 0522A]

Finally, after Pope Benedict, Pelagius was ordained pontiff of the Roman Church without the emperor’s command [Note: In the year 577 Pelagius ascended to the pontificate. Anastasius gives the following account of his election, which Paul perhaps follows: “He was ordained without the emperor’s command because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome on every side, and great devastation was being caused by them.”], because the Lombards were besieging Rome all around and no one could depart from Rome.

[Note: The history of the Aquileian schism, which our Paul has woven into his account of Lombard affairs, must be traced back to a purer source and from a greater depth, lest, together with him, I fall into the greatest errors—errors that I shall point out below in their proper places in the writings of men distinguished both by learning and by the purple, namely Baronius and Noris.

After Origen, the leader of the Pelagians, was condemned—Origen, who had in the West the Aquileian monk Rufinus as a defender of his errors—a new succession of disturbances and calamities began. Theodore, metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia, surnamed Ascidas, a most vigorous defender of Origen, deceived Justinian by the greatest fraud, persuading him that the Acephalites could be induced to subscribe to the Council of Chalcedon if he corrected only the three chapters by which they were offended.

The Acephalite sect “was born at Alexandria,” writes Noris; “for many, rebelling against the Alexandrian bishop because he had accepted the Council of Chalcedon, and dogmatizing without a head, were called Acephalites.”

The three chapters proposed by Theodore were these:

First: “That Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, the teacher of Nestorius, should be condemned, although his praises are contained in the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, which was read at the Council of Chalcedon.”

Next: “That the books of Theodoret against the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril, approved at the Council of Ephesus, should be prohibited—books which the Fathers of Chalcedon had not condemned, content as they were with the anathema pronounced against Nestorius by Theodoret, who was present.”

Finally: “That the aforementioned letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian should be rejected, since in it Ibas praises Theodore, accuses Saint Cyril, and charges the Council of Ephesus with having issued, without examination, a rash sentence against Nestorius.”

The empress Theodora, who openly favored the Acephalites, pressed the same point upon Justinian: “But with the intention that, once a correction had been made in some matters of the Council of Chalcedon, the authority of that council as a whole might then collapse.”

The emperor agreed and, in the year 543, as Noris argues, issued the first edict against the three chapters. The patriarchs subscribed to it, while Stephen, the deacon and apocrisarius of Pope Vigilius, refused. Hence disputes and quarrels arose, and soon “the Church was divided into parties: the East had accepted Justinian’s edict, while the Westerners—Illyrians, Italians, Gauls, Spaniards, and Africans—were fighting for the three chapters.”

Moved by enormous disturbances, the emperor arranged for the question to be decided in a full synod in the imperial city. Under the pretext of reconciling the sect of the Acephalites, he gathered the bishops in the imperial palace for a sacred council and summoned Pope Vigilius to him. Vigilius sailed from Rome to Sicily and from there to Constantinople. Received with the greatest honor by Justinian, he immediately promulgated a decree against the Acephalites and suspended Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, from communion because he had compelled many bishops to sign Justinian’s decree.

Soon, however, changing his mind, Vigilius wrote his *Judicatum* to Menas and condemned the three chapters he had previously defended. The emperor, pleased, published these matters again in a new edict. But when the Western Churches were in uproar, it became clear too late that Vigilius’s judgment had increased the disputes, and that there was no hope except in an ecumenical council, to which the bishops were ordered to come.

Meanwhile, Vigilius recovered his judgment from the hands of Menas, so that the matter might remain intact for the Fathers at the council and a kind of truce might be made concerning the question of the three chapters. But Theodore, impatient of this delay, published a book against the three chapters and persuaded the emperor that, since the Westerners refused to attend the council, he should himself publish an edict against the three chapters. He did so, rewarding the Eastern bishops of his faction and punishing with exile the others who refused to subscribe to the condemnation of the chapters.

Vigilius, rising against this as was proper, incurred the emperor’s anger. To avoid it, he fled from the Placidian palace to the church of Saint Peter at Hormisdas; then, after receiving an oath of security, he returned to the Placidian palace. But when he learned day by day that the pledge had been violated, he crossed over to Chalcedon. After once again receiving a pledge, he was recalled to Constantinople by Justinian, who treated him more gently, and he received a profession of faith from the patriarch Menas, Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, and others who had returned to the right path. The emperor’s edicts were also revoked, so that the matter might be brought intact before the council.

That council was finally held at Constantinople in the year 553, with 165 Fathers sitting in it. Vigilius refused to attend and, in a written document called the *Constitutum*, invalidated the acts of the council, arguing that an equal number of Fathers from the East and the West ought to have been assembled. But with Justinian’s support everything was completed in the Fifth Council, and, among other matters too lengthy to recount here, the three chapters were condemned. Changing his mind once again, Vigilius approved the council, withdrew the *Constitutum* and his other writings previously composed in defense of the three chapters, and afterward, while returning to Rome, died on the journey.]

Vigilius’s successor was Pelagius, the first of that name. At Justinian’s persuasion he condemned the Three Chapters and thereby incurred the Italians’ hatred, as had the memory of Vigilius. since many had already persuaded themselves that the authority of the sacred Council of Chalcedon was being undermined by this new decree. The bishops of Venetia and Istria resisted more than the others and, having created a schism, withdrew into separate factions, to such an extent that Pelagius attempted, through the patrician and prefect Narses, to compel the dissenters by force to accept the council. But they cursed Narses himself with dire imprecations, as I noted above; and, at the instigation of Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, according to Paul, they held a provincial assembly. At it they maintained that no one could proscribe the Three Chapters, which had not been condemned by the Fathers of Chalcedon.

Meanwhile Justinian died and Justin was his successor. Seeing the provinces torn apart by schism and new controversies arising daily, he published an edict concerning the faith—a policy of excellent intention but futile outcome. When Narses was recalled from Italy, the schismatic Venetians became more emboldened and, when the Lombards arrived, immediately joined them, so that with this further protection of arms they might rise up more insolently. They could not be recalled to sound judgment by any admonitions of John III, who had succeeded Pelagius I, nor of Benedict, nor of Pelagius II, although the last of these was extremely benevolent toward them because he transferred the episcopal seat to the island of Grado, as Paul also relates. Norisius proves that at the same synod of Grado at which Pelagius was acclaimed, the schismatic bishops again swore against the Fifth Council.

After this, when a truce had been arranged between the Lombards and Smaragdus, Pelagius turned to the schismatics and attempted by every means to restore them to the Church. He sent several letters to Elias, the first of which I noted above; Baronius also recited others. Paul, our author, testifies that these were written by Saint Gregory, although the pontiff, in his letters, where he mentions the letters noted by Pelagius, suppressed the matter out of modesty.

Noris writes that, after Pelagius had sent the letters to Elias mentioned above, “understanding that he was singing to the deaf, he cast aside his pen and judged that the schismatics must be dealt with by armed force,” and incited the patrician Smaragdus against them. They, however, by petitions addressed to the Emperor Maurice, obtained through letters sent to Smaragdus “that he should in no way presume to disturb any priest on account of the cause of communion.” These are the words of the petition transmitted to the emperor under Gregory. In it we read: “While the glorious chartularius Smaragdus was repeatedly distressing our father, Elias, archbishop of the Church of Aquileia, of holy memory, for that very cause …” From this it is clear that our author is in manifest error when, concerning Elias, he writes that he was “unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon,” since Elias himself fostered the schism in order to defend the Three Chapters.

Pelagius sent Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon, a very useful letter, which blessed Gregory composed while he was still a deacon.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Childebert’s war against the Spaniards

Meanwhile Childebert, king of the Franks, was waging war against the Spaniards and defeated them in battle. The cause of this conflict was as follows. King Childebert had given his sister Ingund in marriage to Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Spaniards. Hermenegild had been converted from the Arian heresy, in which his father languished, to the Catholic faith through the preaching of Leander, bishop of Seville, and the exhortations of his wife. But his impious father killed him with an axe on the very sacred Easter day.

[Note: Ambrosius reads “day.”]

[Note: Another reading has “Heleandri” instead of “Leandri.”]

[Note: Another reading has “bishop of Spain.”]

[Note: The divine Gregory, called the Great, also relates this in Book III, chapter 31, of the Dialogues, as does the other Gregory of Tours in Book V, chapter 39, of his History of the Franks. The latter writes the following about Ingund, the wife of Saint Hermenegild:

“Ingund, daughter of King Sigebert, was sent into Spain with great splendor. She was received with great joy by her grandmother Goisvintha—for she was the mother of Brunichild, wife of King Sigebert, whom she had had by King Athanagild, her former husband. But Goisvintha did not allow her to remain long in the Catholic religion. Rather, she began with flattering words to entice her into the Arian heresy, so that she might be rebaptized. But Ingund bravely resisted and began to say: ‘It is enough that I have once been washed clean from original sin by the saving baptism, and that I have confessed the most holy Trinity to exist in one equality,’ and so forth.

“When Goisvintha heard this, she was inflamed with the fury of anger. Seizing the girl by the hair, she dashed her to the ground, beat her for a long time with kicks, covered her with blood, ordered her stripped, and had her plunged into a pool. Yet, as many assert, she never turned her mind away from our faith.”]

Ingund, however, after the death and martyrdom of her husband, fled from Spain and, while attempting to return to Gaul, fell into the hands of soldiers who were stationed on the frontier against the Spaniards and the Goths. She was captured with her young son and taken to Sicily, where she died.

[Note: Another reading has: “who protected the Spanish frontier against the Goths.”]

[Note: The cited Gregory of Tours writes that Ingund died in Africa, which does not agree with Paul’s account of her flight. He writes: “Therefore, as we said above, Ingund, abandoned by her husband with the emperor’s army, was being led with her little son to the emperor himself when she died in Africa and was buried there.”

In my judgment, the account of the divine Gregory is closer to the truth. For it is established that Saint Leander was sent by Saint Hermenegild to Constantinople to Emperor Maurice, in order to obtain assistance against the persecution raised by the Arians, and that there this bishop formed a friendship with the divine Gregory the Great. The other Gregory of Tours likewise relates that the arms of the Greeks were allied with Saint Hermenegild. In Book V, chapter 39, he adds:

“But he”—that is, Leovigild—“having given the imperial prefect thirty thousand solidi so that he might withdraw his support from him, came against him with an army. Hermenegild, however, summoned the Greeks and went out against his father, leaving his wife in the city. When Leovigild came against him from the opposite side, and Hermenegild, abandoned by his support, saw that he could accomplish nothing, he sought the church that was nearby,” and so forth.

Moreover, against Baronius’s opinion, more recent writers assign the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild, which occurred when the Easter festival was approaching, to the year 585, relying especially on the testimony of the abbot of Biclaro. He writes:

“In the third year of Maurice, which was the seventeenth year of Leovigild, Hermenegild was killed at Tarragona by Sisbert. The Franks, wishing to seize Narbonese Gaul, entered it with an army,” and so forth.

The same expedition is also mentioned by the divine Gregory of Tours in the cited Book VIII, chapter 28:

“Leovigild handed over his son Hermenegild, whom the woman mentioned above had borne, to death. Moved by these events, King Gunthram sent an army into Spain,” and so forth.

At that place it should be noted that the expedition which Paul attributes to Childebert was assigned by Gregory to Gunthram, his uncle—unless perhaps both invaded Spain, and, as Valesius maintains, there were two Frankish wars against the Spaniards after the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild. Concerning Leovigild’s Arian persecution, see Isidore’s Chronicle of the Goths, year 608.]

His son, however, was sent to Emperor Maurice at Constantinople.

[Note: See, in the appendix to the History of the Franks by the divine Gregory of Tours, the various letters sent by Childebert and Brunichild to Athanagild, the son of Saint Hermenegild, and to the emperor and others while Athanagild was living at Constantinople. The highly learned Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur illustrated their edition with these materials.]

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Frankish army that came into Italy

Again the Emperor Maurice sent envoys to Childebert and persuaded him to send an army into Italy against the Lombards.

[Note: One edition has “to him.”]

Childebert, believing that his own sister was still alive at Constantinople,

[Note: Modius has “sister.”]

listened to Maurice’s envoys and, so that he might recover his sister, once again sent a Frankish army into Italy against the Lombards. While the Lombard forces were hastening to meet them, the Franks and Alamanni, being at odds among themselves, returned to their homeland without gaining any advantage.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the flood and the miracle that occurred in the basilica of Saint Zeno

At that time there was a flood in the territory of Venetia and Liguria, as well as in the other regions of Italy, such as is believed not to have occurred since the time of Noah. Landslides devastated estates and villages, and there was likewise a great destruction of human beings and animals. Roads were destroyed and highways scattered. The river Athesis rose so greatly that around the basilica of blessed Zeno the martyr, situated outside the walls of Verona, the water reached the upper windows.

[Note: Modius has “Adexis.”]

[Note: Modius adds “and confessor.”]

[Note: Another reading has “ponds.” Lindanus adds: Isidore’s Glosses explain *lavina* as “a fall that brings ruin”; the word is also found in the divine Jerome. In the Deacon’s continuation of the History of Eutropius, Book XVIII, we likewise read: “There were *lacunae* of estates and villages”; this should be read: “There were *lavinae* of estates and villages.” The transmitted reading is plainly corrupt.]

[Note: Ambrosius has “although, just as blessed Gregory …”]

Blessed Gregory, later pope, nevertheless wrote that the water did not enter that basilica at all.

[Note: Another reading has “the water did not enter at all.”]

Some portions of the walls of Verona were also overthrown by the same inundation. This flood occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

[Note: Another reading has “the inundation occurred on the Kalends of November.” Lindanus and Modius. The divine Gregory the Great discusses both the flooding of the Tiber and that of the Athesis in Book III, chapter 19, of the Dialogues. He asserts that the miracle of the waters overflowing the basilica of Saint Zeno occurred in the presence of King Authari. The year may be inferred from the other Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 1. He writes:

“In the fifteenth year of King Childebert”—which is the year of Christ 589—“our deacon, returning from the city of Rome with relics of the saints, reported that in the preceding year, in the ninth month, the river Tiber rose in such a great flood over the city of Rome that ancient buildings collapsed, and even the granaries of the Church were overturned; several thousand measures of grain perished in them. A multitude of snakes, together with a dragon as large as a beam, descended through the bed of this river into the sea,” and so forth.

The most eminent Baronius thinks that the dragon was one of the creeping beasts of extraordinary size that Pliny calls *boa*, which were sometimes seen in the regions near the Tiber.]

There were also such flashes of lightning and peals of thunder as scarcely occur even in summer. Two months later, much of the same city of Verona was consumed by fire.

During this outpouring of the flood, the river Tiber rose so high at Rome that its waters flowed over the city walls and occupied its largest districts. Then, through the bed of that river, a dragon of extraordinary size, passing through the city together with a great multitude of snakes, descended as far as the sea.

Immediately after this inundation there followed an extremely severe pestilence, which they call the groin-plague. It devastated the people with such slaughter that scarcely a few remained from the immeasurable multitude. It first struck Pelagius, the venerable pope, and killed him without delay. Then, after the shepherd had been taken away, it spread among the peoples.

[Note: Paul took this account from Gregory of Tours, who continues at the cited passage:

“Immediately there followed a disaster which they call the groin-plague. For, arriving in the middle of the eleventh month, it first struck Pope Pelagius, in accordance with what is read in the prophet Ezekiel: ‘Begin from my sanctuary.’ When he had died, a great slaughter of the people occurred from this disease.”

Learned writers establish the death of Pope Pelagius in the year 590. Pagius, in his *Critica*, is for me an unfailing guide in chronology, unless manifest reason dictates otherwise.]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the pontificate of blessed Gregory and the calamity that then occurred at Rome

In this great tribulation, blessed Gregory, who was then a deacon, was unanimously elected pope. When he had ordered a sevenfold litany to be held, within the space of one hour, while the people were praying to the Lord, eighty of them suddenly fell to the ground and breathed out their spirits.
