[Note: In the year 590, on September 3, the divine Gregory was consecrated pontiff, while the groin-plague that had carried off Pelagius was raging. What our Paul relates about the litanies he copied from the other Gregory of Tours, as is shown by the order of the persons and places from which the sevenfold litany proceeded. That order does not correspond at all to the other arrangement made by Gregory the Great himself in his sermon delivered at that time, whose beginning is “It was necessary, most beloved brothers,” as the most eminent Baronius noted. Baronius thought that the litanies had been repeated in varying order, and that for this reason different orders were also recorded by the two Gregorys.]

The litany was called “sevenfold” because blessed Gregory divided the entire population of the city into seven groups to pray to the Lord. In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all the abbots with their monks; in the third, all the abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all the children; in the fifth, all the laymen; in the sixth, all the widows; and in the seventh, all married women.

We omit saying more about blessed Gregory because, several years ago, with God’s help, we composed his Life. In it we set down, according to the limits of our ability, everything that ought to be said.

[Note: The Life of the divine Gregory the Great, written by our Paul, still exists. It is placed before the writings of that holy pontiff in the latest and more carefully corrected edition of the Benedictine Fathers of Saint Maur.]

## CHAPTER XXV. How blessed Gregory converted the English

At this time the same blessed Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with several other monks who feared the Lord, into Britain, and through their preaching converted the English to Christ.

[Note: The divine Gregory did not send Augustine and Mellitus to England at one and the same time. Several letters of the divine Gregory survive in Book VI of the Register of Letters, indiction 14, in the year of Christ 596, in which he commends Augustine to Theoderic and Theodebert, kings of the Franks, and to Queen Brunichild, as well as to various bishops and abbots of Gaul. At the same time he also sent another letter to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, in which he lamented the calamities suffered from the Lombards in these words:

“As for how much we suffer from the swords of the Lombards in the daily plundering, mutilation, and slaughter of our citizens, we refuse to relate it, lest, while speaking of our own sorrows, we should increase yours through the sympathy you show us.”

In Book XI, indiction 4, he commends Mellitus and the presbyter Laurence, who had been sent to Augustine. On the occasion of these letters the matter has been discussed at length, especially among writers of Frankish history; but the difficulties have been very satisfactorily resolved in the notes appended to the same letters in the celebrated edition of the Benedictine Fathers. See also Pagius under the year 596.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the death of the patriarch Elias and the priesthood of Severus

In these days Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, died after having held the priesthood for fifteen years.

[Note: After Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, died, Severus succeeded him, as Paul relates. Severus fought most fiercely for the Three Chapters. When Smaragdus came to Grado, he seized him in the church and, with military violence, abused and beat him, then led him to Ravenna. There, before the archbishop, Severus was compelled to condemn the Three Chapters. Together with Severus, John of Parentium, Severus of Tergeste, and Vindemius, bishop of Ceneta, were also captured and compelled to condemn the Three Chapters.

For a fuller explanation of the present chapter, I shall add the words of the learned Norisius:

“Paul the Deacon’s text here requires correction. For although he says that three bishops were led to Ravenna with Severus, later, at the end of the chapter in Grotius’s edition, he lists them as though there were five, in this form: ‘Severus, Parentinus, John Patricius, Vindemius, and John.’ The passage must instead be read exactly as follows: ‘Severus of Tergeste, John of Parentium, and Vendemius.’ The same writer says in the same place that Smaragdus forced them by violence to accept the judgment of John of Ravenna, threatening them, he says, with exile, and so forth. Thus, through ignorance of history, he invents a Catholic bishop and defender of the Roman faith as a rebel against the apostolic see.

“Concerning this captivity of Severus, the schismatics wrote the following to Maurice:

‘After our blessed archbishop Severus had been ordained in the holy Church of Aquileia, the insults inflicted upon him, the injuries and bodily beating with clubs, the violence by which he was led to the city of Ravenna and reduced to custody, and the necessities by which he was oppressed and crushed could certainly have reached the merciful ears of our Lord.’

“From this it is clear that Sigonius is mistaken when he writes that Smaragdus, because he had captured and mistreated Severus, was recalled from Italy by Maurice, and that Romanus the patrician was given to him as successor. The schismatics would certainly not have concealed this, nor would they have expressed doubt as to whether the event had come to the emperor’s attention.

“The Aquileian manuscripts imagine that Smaragdus was possessed by a demon as a sacrilege, for the schismatics published such statements in order to keep the people in error, and so forth.

“Meanwhile, when it became known throughout Istria and Venetia that Severus and his colleagues had condemned the Three Chapters at Ravenna, everyone avoided their presence. They were not admitted to ecclesiastical communion until they had again given a pledge on oath in favor of the Three Chapters at a synod.

“The synod was convened at Marano, now a strongly fortified town of the Venetians, almost surrounded by the lagoons of the Adriatic Sea and situated on the shore of the Friulian region near the river Stella. Paul writes that ten bishops gathered there, and so forth.

“In the printed books the names of the bishops are listed as follows: Peter of Altinum, ‘the illustrious,’ Ingenuinus, and so forth, as above. But if ten gathered, why are only nine names of schismatics given? This error also entered the manuscript. ‘The illustrious’ has wrongly been placed as an epithet of Peter of Altinum; it is the name of a bishop of Concordia who took part in another synod in the year 529. The passage should therefore be read as follows: ‘Peter of Altinum; Clarissimus of Concordia.’

“Laurentius should also be called Bellunensis. The bishop of Luna in Liguria near the river Magra was not a suffragan of the metropolitan of Aquileia, whereas in the other synod held shortly afterward Laurentius is called Bellunensis. Bellunum is a city of Venetia.

“Almost all those bishops had subscribed to the synod of 529. The bishops of Treviso and Vicenza, however, were not present at that time, and Junior had been substituted for Solarius of Verona.”]

Severus succeeded him and assumed the governance of the Church. Smaragdus the patrician came from Ravenna to Grado, personally dragged Severus out of the basilica, and led him to Ravenna with violence, together with three other bishops from Istria—John of Parentium, Severus, and Vindemius—and also Antonius, an elderly defender of the Church.

[Note: The remainder, up to the full stop, is absent from other manuscripts.]

Threatening them with exile and inflicting violence upon them, Smaragdus compelled them to communicate with John, bishop of Ravenna, who had condemned the Three Chapters and who, in the time of Pope Vigilius or Pelagius, had withdrawn from communion with the Roman Church. After a year had passed, they returned from Ravenna to Grado. Neither the people wished to communicate with them nor did the other bishops receive them.

The patrician Smaragdus, justly struck down by a demon, took Romanus the patrician as his successor and returned to Constantinople.

[Note: Modius has “justly chastised by the Lord.” Another reading has: “But the patrician Smaragdus, justly chastised,” and so forth.]

After this a synod of ten bishops was held at Marano.

[Note: In Modius, the Greek word for “ten” is not found.]

[Note: Modius has “at Mariano.”]

There they received Severus, patriarch of Aquileia, after he had given a statement of his error, because he had communicated at Ravenna with those who condemned the Three Chapters. The names of the bishops who refrained from this schism are as follows: Peter of Altinum, Clarissimus; Ingenuinus of Sabione; Agnellus of Trent; Junior of Verona; Horuntinus of Vicenza;

[Note: Ambrosius has “Horocius”; Modius, “Horontius”; Lindanus, “Herentius.”]

Rusticus of Treviso; Fonteius of Feltre; Agnellus of Asolo; Laurentius of Luna.

[Note: Ambrosius has: “Beldunensis, Maxentius of Julia, and Adrianus of Pola.” Modius has: “Velunensis, Maxentius of Villia, and Adrianus of Pola.” Lindanus has: “Velunensis, Maxentius of Julia, and Adrianus of Pola.”]

The following bishops, however, communicated with the patriarch: Severus, Parentinus, John Patricius, Vindemius, and John.

[Note: Ambrosius adds: “namely Severus,” and so forth.]

At this time King Authari sent an army into Istria, commanded by Euin, duke of Trent.

[Note: Another reading has “Eoinus.”]

After plundering and burning, they made peace for one year and brought a large sum of money to the king.

Other Lombards were besieging Francio, commander of the troops, on the island of Amacina. He had still belonged to the faction of Narses and had maintained himself there for twenty years.

[Note: Ambrosius has “the island of Amencina”; other manuscripts have “Amacina” or “Comacina,” as in Modius. The latter is the more carefully corrected reading, since the passage concerns the island in Lake Lario, twenty miles from the city of Como.]

After six months of the siege Francio handed the same island over to the Lombards. He himself, released by the king as he had wished, hastened to Ravenna with his wife and possessions. Many riches were found on the island, which had been entrusted there from the individual cities.

[Note: Charles Sigonius relates all these events under the year 587. If the false synod at Marano followed afterward, as Paul seems to suggest, these events should be assigned to the subsequent years.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. How King Authari took Childebert’s sister in marriage

King Flavius Authari sent envoys to Childebert, asking that Childebert’s sister be joined to him in marriage. When Childebert, after receiving gifts from the Lombard envoys, had promised to give his sister to their king,

[Note: Another reading has: “he promised her to their king and sent an embassy to the emperor,” and so forth. In the year 587 Authari received an embassy from King Childebert, who was asking him to give his sister Clodosuinda in marriage. Another embassy came from Reccared, king of the Goths and brother of Saint Hermenegild, who had succeeded his father Leovigild and, under the instruction of Saint Leander, had cleansed the kingdom of the Arian plague. Saint Gregory of Tours mentions this embassy in Book IX, chapters 16, 25, and 28. From this one may explain the difficulties arising from the death of Ingund, who was also being imposed upon Reccared, and which the envoys resolved by giving ten thousand solidi to Brunichild and Childebert.

It is not entirely clear whether Clodosuinda was Reccared’s wife. Queen Baddo, his wife, subscribed to the Third Council of Toledo, unless perhaps, as Marianus asserts in Book VI, chapter 1, of his History of Spain, after her death Reccared married Clodosuinda. The chronological evidence of that council, however, conflicts with this, as Pagius observed.]

when envoys from the Goths in Spain arrived, he promised the same sister to them instead, because he learned that that people had been converted to the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How the Franks entered Italy and were defeated by the Lombards

In the meantime Childebert sent an embassy to the Emperor Maurice, asking him to undertake against the Lombard people the war that he had not undertaken previously and, with the emperor’s assistance, drive them from Italy.

[Note: Ambrosius has: “and with his counsel remove them from Italy,” and so forth.]

Maurice delayed no longer and sent his army into Italy to defeat the Lombards. King Authari and the Lombard forces boldly advanced to meet it and fought bravely for their freedom.

In that battle the Lombards won the victory. The Franks were severely slaughtered; some were captured, many escaped by flight, and barely returned to their homeland.

[Note: Another reading has: “so that the Lombards conquered them all. The Gauls were severely afflicted; although many were captured, very many nevertheless escaped by flight.”]

[Note: Gregory of Tours, frequently cited above, also relates that Childebert was planning an expedition into Italy. In Book IX, chapter 20, he adds that Childebert instructed Felix, the envoy whom he was sending to Gunthram, his uncle, to deliberate about the proposed marriage, also to obtain from Gunthram assistance for the expedition he was preparing against Italy. Gunthram replied:

“‘I cannot,’ he said, ‘send my army into Italy in order to hand them over to death voluntarily, for a very severe plague is now devastating Italy.’”

Nevertheless, he could not restrain the young man, who was inflamed by age and desire, since he longed to recover his father’s dominion.

The same Gregory describes the destruction of that army in Book IX, chapter 25:

“After the commanders had been mobilized, they met in battle with the army that was going there. But when our men had been severely slaughtered, many were struck down, some captured, and very many escaped by flight; they barely returned to their homeland. So great was the slaughter of the Frankish army there that no similar one is remembered.”

This disaster is commonly assigned to the year 588.]

So great was the slaughter of the Frankish army there that none is remembered as greater elsewhere. It is truly remarkable that Secundus, who wrote something about the deeds of the Lombards, passed over this great victory of theirs, since the events related above concerning the destruction of the Franks are recorded in his history in almost these very words.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How King Authari went to Bavaria to see his betrothed

After this King Flavius Authari sent envoys to Bavaria to ask Garibald, their king, for his daughter in marriage. Garibald received them kindly and promised to give his daughter Theudelinda to Authari.

[Note: Ambrosius has “Teulinda.”]

When the envoys returned and reported this to Authari, he himself, wishing to see his betrothed, took with him a few but well-equipped Lombards, and also one man whom he trusted above all others and who was, as it were, his elder. Without delay he went to Bavaria.

When they had been brought before King Garibald according to the custom of envoys, the man who had come with Authari as though he were his elder, after the greeting, spoke the customary words. Since no one of that people recognized Authari, he approached King Garibald more closely and said:

“My lord King Authari has sent me for this specific purpose: I am to look upon your daughter, his betrothed, who is to become our lady, so that I may be able to report more certainly to my lord what her appearance is like.”

When the king heard this, he ordered his daughter to come. Authari silently observed her, and since she was of quite elegant appearance, she pleased him in every respect. He said to the king:

“Since we see that your daughter has such a person that we rightly desire her to become our queen, if it pleases your authority, we would prefer to receive a cup of wine from her hand, as she will later do for us.”

When the king had agreed that this should be done, she took the cup of wine and first offered it to the man who appeared to be the elder. Then she extended it to Authari, not knowing that he was her betrothed. After he had drunk and returned the cup, he touched her hand with his finger without anyone noticing, and drew his right hand from his forehead down over his nose and face.

She reported this to her nurse, blushing. Her nurse said to her:

“If he were not the king himself and your betrothed, he would certainly not dare to touch you. But let us keep silent for now, lest your father learn of this. For in truth he is a worthy man, one who ought to hold a kingdom and be joined to you in marriage.”

At that time Authari was in the bloom of youthful age, of becoming stature, covered with fair hair, and very handsome in appearance.

[Note: Another reading has “with blond hair.”]

Soon, after receiving provisions from the king, they set out on the journey back to their homeland and hastily departed from the territory of the Noricans.

[Note: Another reading has: “he returned to Italy with his men, hastily departing from the territory of the Noricans.”]

The province of the Noricans, inhabited by the people of Bavaria, has Pannonia to the east, Suavia to the west, Italy to the south, and the waters of the Danube to the north.

When Authari had already come near the borders of Italy and still had the Bavarians who had escorted him with him, he rose as high as he could upon the horse he was riding. With all his strength he drove into the nearest tree the small axe that he carried in his hand, left it fixed there, and added these words:

“Authari is accustomed to deliver such a blow.”

[Note: Another reading has “such a stroke” or “such a wound.” Lindanus has “such a blow”; Ambrosius explains that *ferita* means a wound or blow. The word is so explained in the Lombard laws, Title III, section V, and Title X, section III.]

When he had said this, the Bavarians who were accompanying him then understood that he himself was King Authari.

After some time, when trouble had come upon King Garibald because of the arrival of the Franks,

[Note: Childebert feared that the Bavarians, who were his tributaries, might defect to the Lombards through this royal relationship. It is established that Garibald was succeeded by Tassilo; it is uncertain whether Garibald fled to Authari when Childebert arrived or perished in the war.]

his daughter Theudelinda fled to Italy with her brother Gundoald and sent word to her betrothed Authari that she was approaching. He immediately went to meet her with great magnificence, intending to celebrate the wedding, and encountered her in the field of Sardis above Verona. Amid universal rejoicing, he took her in marriage on the Ides of May.

[Note: In the year 589.]

Among the other Lombard leaders who were there was Agilulf, duke of the city of Turin. At that place, when the air had become disturbed, a certain tree located within the royal enclosure was struck by a bolt of lightning with a great crash of thunder.

At that time Agilulf had among his men a boy skilled in divination. Through the devilish art he understood what the lightning strikes portended for the future. While he was sitting privately with Agilulf to attend to the necessities of nature, he said to him:

“This woman who has just married our king will shortly become your wife.”

When Agilulf heard this, he threatened to cut off the boy’s head if he said anything more about the matter. The boy replied:

“I can indeed be killed, but the fates cannot be changed. For it is certain that this woman has come to this country so that she may be joined in marriage to you.”

This was later fulfilled.

[Note: The words “But the fates cannot be changed” are absent from some manuscripts.]

At this time, for a reason unknown, Ansul, a kinsman of King Authari, was killed near Verona.

## CHAPTER XXX. How the Frankish army came into Italy again
At this time as well, Grippo, Childebert’s envoy, returned from Constantinople and reported to his king how honorably he had been received by the emperor Maurice, and that the emperor had promised to avenge, according to King Childebert’s wishes, the injuries he had suffered at Carthage. Childebert immediately sent a Frankish army into Italy for a second time, with twenty commanders, to destroy the Lombard nation. Among these commanders, Anduald, Olo, and Cedinus were the more prominent.

**Notes [Cols. 0531C–0532D].** Ambrosianus reads “from Constantinople”; other copies read: “after completing an embassy at Constantinople, he returned to the same king,” and so forth. Modœtiensis reads “that he would avenge [them].” Paul, in his usual manner, relates these matters in an abbreviated form; they should be set out more fully. Childebert had sent Bodegisil, Evantius, and Grippo as envoys to Maurice. They arrived at Carthage, where one of Evantius’s servants stole a necklace from a merchant. When the merchant could not recover his property by entreaties, he forcibly detained the servant and was killed by him with a sword. When the prefect learned of the killing, he immediately came with a band of soldiers to the envoys; a quarrel arose, and the envoys Bodegisil and Evantius were killed by the soldiers. Then Grippo, seeking redress for the violation of the law of nations and of peace treaties, came to Maurice, who promised to avenge Childebert’s envoys. There are many further records in Greek and Frankish histories concerning Childebert’s frequent embassies to Maurice.

Other copies read *Aldoaldus* and *Holo*; Lindanus and Modœtiensis regularly do so. Gregory of Tours has *Chedinus*.

The manuscript reads *Libitionis*. Philip Cluverius, in Book I, chapter 14 of his *Ancient Italy*, repeats from Gregory of Tours the following matters relevant to elucidating our Paul:

“After these things had been reported to Childebert by Grippo—that is, the matters I noted above—he immediately ordered an army to move into Italy and sent twenty commanders to subdue the Lombard nation. As they approached the frontier of Italy, Andovald, with six commanders, took the right-hand route and came to the city of Milan; there they pitched camp at a distance on the plain. But Duke Olo, rashly approaching the fortress of Bilitio, situated in the Canine Fields, was struck beneath the breast by a javelin, fell, and died. When these men had gone out on a foraging expedition to obtain provisions, they were everywhere struck down by the attacking Lombards.

“There was in the territory of the city of Milan a lake called Ceresium, from which a small but deep river issues. They had heard that the Lombards were encamped on the shore of this lake. When they approached it, before they had crossed the river mentioned above from that shore, one of the Lombards, standing protected by a cuirass and helmet and holding a spear in his hand, cried out against the Frankish army: ‘Today it will appear to whom the Divinity grants victory.’ Then a few men crossed over against this Lombard and, fighting, struck him down; and behold, the entire Lombard army turned to flight and passed away. Having crossed the river, they found none of them, but only recognized the arrangement of the camp, where they had had fires and pitched tents. Since they had caught none of them, they returned to their camp. But Chedinus, entering the left side of Italy with thirteen commanders, captured five fortresses,” and so forth, as Paul has it from the same author.

Cluverius adds:

“Thus this author more clearly indicates the location of the Canine Fields. For Bilitio, a fort or small fortress, still lies today at the foot of the Rhaetian Alps above Lake Verbanus—commonly called by its inhabitants Lago Maggiore—beside the river Ticino; with the name slightly altered, it is called Belizona or Bellinzona. Andovald, therefore, one of King Childebert’s commanders who had set out from Gaul with the army, came by the right-hand route, still the most frequented, from Switzerland through Mount Saint Gotthard and the Lepontine valley along the bank of the Ticino to the town or fortress of Bilitio, and thence to Milan. Chedinus, however, came by the left-hand route through the towns of the Grisons, as they are called—Chur and Chiavenna—and thence through Lake Larius and the town of Como into the territory of that same city of Milan,” and so forth.

Olo, however, when he rashly approached the fortress of Bilitio [Col. 0533A], was wounded by a javelin beneath the breast and fell dead. The other Franks, when they had gone out to plunder, were overthrown in every place by the attacking Lombards. Anduald and six other Frankish commanders, meanwhile, arrived at the city of Milan and pitched their camp in the open country at some distance from it.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Ambrosianus reads “all.”

At that place envoys of the emperor came to them, announcing that an army was approaching to support them and saying: “After three days we shall come with it. This will be your sign: when you see the houses of that village, which lies on the mountain, being consumed by fire, and the smoke of the conflagration rising to the heavens, know that we are approaching with the army we have promised.”

The Frankish commanders waited six days beside the village, according to the agreement, but saw none of those whom the emperor’s envoys had promised would come. Cedinus, entering Italy on the left with thirteen commanders, captured five fortresses and exacted oaths from them.

**Notes [Col. 0533C].** Ambrosianus reads: “The commanders waited for the army for six days,” and so forth. The manuscript reads “with thirteen thousand [men].” Ambrosianus continues: “The Frankish army also reached Verona, and they pitched,” and so forth.

The Frankish army came by way of Piacenza as far as Verona, and after oaths had been given they established many camps in peace. Those who had surrendered to them, supposing that they intended no treachery, were then killed.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Other copies read: “But after the oaths had been given, the peoples who had entrusted themselves to them were killed, suspecting no treachery from them.” Lindanus and Modœtiensis.

The names of the fortresses that they destroyed in the territory of Trent are these: Tesana, Maletum, Semiana, Appianum, Fagitana, Cimbra, Vitianum, Brentonicum, Volenes, Ennemase, two in Alsuca, and one in Verona.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Other copies read *Maletunum* and *Sermosanum*.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Modœtiensis reads *Sermosana*; Ambrosianus has *Sermiana*.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Ambrosianus reads *Api panii*.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Other copies read *Cumbra* and *Britianum* or *Brixianum*; Lindanus and Modœtiensis have *Britianum*.

**Note [Col. 0533C].** Other copies have *Belones*; others *Balonesene* and *Mase*. Lindanus and Modœtiensis have *Volaernes*.

To this Cluverius adds, in Book I, chapter 15 of his *Ancient Italy*:

“Most of these places lie beyond the Adige in the territory of the Rhaetians, as will become clear in the following chapter. For the readings *Volenes* and *Ennemase*, other copies have *Balenefene* and *Mase*. I would almost conjecture that the text originally read *Volenes* and *Malsesene*. The former I shall later show to lie beyond the Adige, midway along the shore of Lake Benacus, between Brentinus and Brentonicum; it is still called the town of Malsesene.”

And below, in the following chapter:

“Nothing at all is clear about Cimbra. Tesana is now commonly called Tessina, between Feltre and Trent. Midway between these lies Vivianum, situated on a high hill beside the Brenta; from its name I conclude that Paul the Deacon’s reading *Vitianum* is corrupt, for other copies have the still more corrupt *Brixianum*—unless the shape of the letter X more closely resembles U than T. Appianum, above Trent, is now commonly called Altiano. Semiana, now lying between Alsuca and Feltre near the Cismon River, is called Mean. Between it and Feltre is a village commonly called Faian; this may have been Facitana. From there, Volenes is undoubtedly the village now called Volagne or Volargne, near the Adige above Verona, close to Clusa. As for the final place, which in the common copies of Paul is called *in Ferruge*, I wonder whether the name may not be corrupt, and whether the true reading was *Verruca*”—which Cluverius identifies with Castel della Pietra.

When all these fortresses had been destroyed by the Franks, all their inhabitants were led away captive. In the case of the fortress of Ferruge, however, through the intervention of the bishops Ingenuinus of Savio and Agnellus of Trent, a ransom of six hundred solidi was paid for each man.

**Note [Col. 0534D].** Other copies read: “one solidus, up to six hundred solidi”; Modœtiensis, Ambrosianus, and Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0534C].** Ambrosianus reads *Femigero*.

**Note [Col. 0534C].** Other copies add “of Salvone,” and “Agnellus of Trent.” Modœtiensis likewise has *Agnellus*; Ambrosianus has *Savianus*. Cluverius, in the cited chapter, writes:

“The location of Sublabione, or Sublavione, can be determined from the route and the distance: it lay near the town of Brixen, on the nearer side of the Alps, beside the Eisack River, and is mentioned as an episcopal see by Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 26. In this region an episcopal town called Sabio is mentioned; in chapter 32 below its name is Savio. It is today a small town about ten miles from Brixen, commonly called Saben. The annals of these regions testify that the episcopal seat was transferred from there to Brixen. That place, therefore, is unquestionably the ancient town of Sabio, or Savio.”

Meanwhile, since it was summer, the Frankish army began to suffer severely from dysentery because of the unaccustomed climate, and many of them died from the disease.

What more is there to say? After the Frankish army had ravaged Italy for three months without accomplishing anything and without being able to take vengeance on its enemies—because they had withdrawn into the strongest positions—nor to reach the king, against whom vengeance was intended, since he had fortified himself within the city of Ticinum, as we have said, the army, weakened by the unhealthy climate and constrained by hunger, resolved to return home.

As they returned to their country, they suffered such a shortage of food that, before they reached their native soil, they offered first their own clothing and even their weapons in exchange for food.

**Notes [Col. 0534D].** Other copies read “the violence of famine”; the manuscript reads “for eating.”

**Note [Col. 0534D].** Other copies read: “the army, as I have said, weakened by the unhealthy climate.”

**Note [Col. 0534D].** Modœtiensis reads: “the army, constrained by hunger,” and so forth.

**Note [Col. 0534D].** This passage is taken almost word for word from Saint Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 3.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How King Authari proceeded to Beneventum

It is thought that what is reported about King Authari occurred around this time. For it is said that the same king reached Beneventum by way of Spoleto, captured that region, and even traveled as far as Rhegium, the city at the extreme end of Italy, near Sicily.

**Note [Col. 0534D].** Other copies read *Spoletum*; Lindanus has *Spoletinum*.

Because it is said that a certain column stood there amid the waves of the sea, he is reported to have ridden on horseback as far as it and touched it with the tip of his spear, saying: “As far as this will be the boundaries of the Lombards.”

That column is said to remain to this day and to be called Authari’s Column.

**Note [Col. 0534D].** This reading is absent from some copies.

Camillus Peregrinius, in his dissertation *When the Duchy of Beneventum Was Established*, comments as follows:

“No one is unaware that writers, whenever they happen to narrate matters that they have investigated little or not at all, usually attribute them to common report and disclaim responsibility for their accuracy. That Paul followed this practice—leaving aside for the moment another purpose of his, which I shall discuss shortly—is readily inferred by a sound conjecture. For he certainly did not wish to affirm as an established fact what the people of Beneventum commonly babbled about Authari’s Column: a fiction that they dreamed up when the column, by whatever circumstance, had acquired its name from the king or some other man. They found an appropriate occasion for such a tale because, although the Lombards possessed nearly all Italy, they never crossed the strait into Sicily, and they marked the boundaries of their dominions with columns; at some point, a column placed near Rhegium was said to have defined the limits of the region.”

Yet, however the matter may stand, these considerations by no means diminish Paul’s credibility, whose judgment was excellent. Indeed, beginning from the time of Authari I would rather repeatedly retrace the Lombards’ frontier boundaries.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Zotto, the first duke of Beneventum

The first Lombard duke in Beneventum was named Zotto. He held that principality for a period of twenty years.

**Note [Col. 0535C].** This passage is absent from Modœtiensis.

No passage in our Paul has caused learned men greater difficulty than the present chapter. Investigating from it the beginnings of the duchy of Beneventum, they have reached widely divergent conclusions.

The first to pose this question was Antonius Caracciolus, in his *Propylaeum to the Four Chronologists* edited by him. He found grounds for doubt in Herchempertus’s catalogue of the dukes of Beneventum, which plainly states that the duchy of Zotto began in the very year 568, when the Lombards entered Italy with King Alboin. He also relied on Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book I, chapter 48, who, recounting that the city was captured by the Greek patrician Symbatius in the year 891, adds that the duchy of Beneventum had lasted 320 years. Subtracting that number from 891 leads back to the year 571.

Caracciolus chiefly confirms this opinion by the argument of a letter of Saint Gregory the Great to John, bishop of Ravenna, written in indiction 10 and therefore belonging to the year 592. In it, Aroges—whom Paul calls Arichis, Zotto’s successor in the duchy—is mentioned. From Paul it is clear, as Caracciolus conjectures, that Arichis was appointed by King Agilulf “not long after he entered upon the kingship, namely in the same year 591, or at the latest in the following year, 592.” He therefore concludes that “Zotto’s twenty years cannot be assigned, as they certainly must be, unless we reckon backward from the year 592 to 571.”

Camillus Peregrinius did not accept this reasoning in his aforementioned dissertation on the time when the duchy of Beneventum was established. In order to overturn Caracciolus’s foundations, he cast doubt on Leo of Ostia’s reading from the Monte Cassino manuscript and asserted that the manuscript reads not 320, nor 318, but 330, as do the Venetian and Paris editions.

Then, citing the words of Constantine Porphyrogenitus in Book 27 of *On the Administration of the Empire*, he pursued the matter at greater length and scarcely dared to place the establishment of the duchy before Alboin’s arrival in Italy. He suggested that its founders were those first Lombards whom Procopius mentions as allies of the Romans in Narses’s army.

I am surprised that this conjecture imposed so greatly upon a man of such sharp judgment. For Procopius himself shows that their number was small; and, more importantly, the same author states that Narses sent them out of Italy under the pretext of honoring them, so that they would not continue to intrude upon the possessions of their allies.

However the matter may stand, my inclination is toward Caracciolus’s argument based on the letter of Saint Gregory, the writer of that age, whatever reading may be found in Leo of Ostia. Nor are the arguments persuasive that the most learned man adds to his *Chronicle of the Dukes of Beneventum* in his comparison of the years assigned to those dukes with the Christian era. For Saint Benedict Bachinius had already resolved all the difficulties in his *Ravenna Pontifical*, in the dissertation on the age of Peter the Elder, and elsewhere, in his new comparison with Camillus Peregrinius, which should be consulted.

I am also inclined toward Caracciolus’s argument from the siege of Naples, which I mentioned above as having taken place during the reign of the Emperor Tiberius, since we know that the Lombards made incursions into the Trans-Tiberine region of Italy long before our Paul persuaded himself of the contrary from popular report.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How King Authari sent envoys to Guntram, and concerning his marvelous vision

Meanwhile King Authari had sent an embassy with peaceful words to Guntram, king of the Franks and specifically the uncle of King Childebert. The envoys were received kindly by him, but were then sent on to Childebert, who was his nephew on his brother’s side, so that peace with the Lombard nation might be established through his decision.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** “Received and then sent on to Childebert.” Ambrosianus and Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** Other copies read *votum*, “wish.”

**Note [Col. 0536D].** See Saint Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 3.

This Guntram, whom we have mentioned, was a peaceful king and distinguished by every virtue. One of his highly remarkable deeds deserves to be briefly inserted into our history, especially since we know that it is not contained in the history of the Franks.

Once, when he had gone hunting in a forest, and his companions—as commonly happens—had scattered here and there, he remained alone with one exceptionally faithful servant. Overcome by very deep sleep, he laid his head in the servant’s lap and fell asleep.

From his mouth a small animal, shaped like a reptile, emerged and ran alongside a narrow brook, trying to cross it.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** Modœtiensis reads “which was nearby.”

The servant in whose lap he rested drew his sword from its sheath and placed it across the stream. The reptile crossed over it to the other side.

After it had entered a hole in the mountain not far away, and then returned after some time, it crossed the stream again over the same sword and reentered Guntram’s mouth, from which it had emerged.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** Modœtiensis adds: “Afterward, having awoken from sleep.”

When Guntram awoke, he said that he had seen a marvelous vision. He reported that in a dream it had appeared to him that he had crossed a certain river over an iron bridge and entered beneath a mountain, where he had seen many masses of gold.

The man in whose lap he had rested his head while sleeping then told him in order everything that he had seen happen to him.

What more is there to say? The place was excavated, and priceless treasures that had been deposited there in ancient times were found.

From that gold the king later made a solid *ciborium* of marvelous size and great weight and wished to send it, decorated with many precious gems, to the Lord’s Sepulchre at Jerusalem. But when he was unable to do so, he had it placed over the body of the blessed martyr Marcellus, which was buried in the city of Cavallonnus, where his royal seat was; and it remains there to the present day.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** Ambrosianus reads *Cabiliono*; Modœtiensis, *Cabillomno*; Lindanus, *Cabillonensi*, adding that the church was founded by King Guntram himself.

Nowhere is there any work made of gold that can be compared with it.

**Note [Col. 0536D].** A *ciborium* is a type of cup shaped like the leaves of the colocasia, as the scholiast Porphyrio explains in his commentary on Horace, *Satires* II.7:

“Fill the forgetful smooth bowls with Massic wine.”

Hesychius explains *ciborium* as follows: “*kibōrion* [κιβώριον], an Egyptian name for a drinking vessel.”

But let us return to our history, having briefly touched upon these matters that deserved to be reported.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the death of King Authari and the reign of Agilulf

Meanwhile, while the envoys of King Authari were staying in Francia, King Authari died at Ticinum on the Nones of September, reportedly after taking poison, having reigned for six years.

**Note [Col. 0537B].** King Authari died in the year 590, when Saint Gregory the Great was raised to the pontificate. There survives a letter of his to all the bishops of Italy, written in indiction 9, from which we learn of the impious edict of King Authari shortly before his death. It reads:

“Because the most wicked Authari forbade the sons of the Lombards to be baptized in the Catholic faith during the Easter solemnity that has recently been completed, for this offense the Divine Majesty destroyed him, so that he would not see another Easter solemnity,” and so forth.

Immediately an embassy was sent by the Lombards to Childebert, king of the Franks, to announce to him the death of King Authari and to request peace from him. When he heard this, he received the envoys but promised that he would grant peace later. Nevertheless, after several days he dismissed the envoys with the peace he had promised.

They allowed Queen Theudelinda, who was highly esteemed by the Lombards, to remain in her royal dignity, advising her to choose for herself from among all the Lombards whichever man she wished—one, naturally, who could usefully govern the kingdom.

After consulting with prudent men, she chose Agilulf, duke of Turin, both as her husband and as king of the Lombard nation. He was a vigorous and warlike man, suited to the governance of the kingdom both in appearance and in character.

The queen immediately sent for him and hurried to meet him at the town of Laumellum. When he came to her, she had wine poured for herself after a few words had passed between them. After she had drunk first, she gave the remainder to Agilulf.

Having received the cup, he honorably kissed the queen’s hand. The queen, smiling with embarrassment, said that he ought not to kiss her hand, but her mouth, and that he should join his lips to hers. She then raised him to her kiss and disclosed to him her intentions concerning their marriage and the royal dignity.

What more is there to say? The marriage was celebrated with great rejoicing. Agilulf, who was related to King Authari, assumed the royal dignity at the beginning of November.

**Note [Col. 0538B].** The queen immediately hurried to meet him at the town of Laumellum when he came to her at her command, and, after receiving a cup, had wine served. Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0538B].** She made him sit beside her and, after a few words, wine was served, and so forth. Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0538B].** She should be kissed not on the hand but on the mouth. Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0538B].** Other copies read: “and she disclosed her decision that he should undertake the royal dignity.” Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0538B].** Modœtiensis has *fuit*, “was”; Ambrosianus has *fuerat*, “had been.”

**Note [Col. 0538B].** Other copies read: “but at that time only a few Lombards had assembled; afterward, in May,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, after the Lombards had assembled together, he was raised by all to the kingship at Milan in the following May.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER I. How King Agilulf sent envoys to Francia on behalf of the captives

After Agilulf’s royal dignity had been confirmed—he was also called Ago—he sent Bishop Agnellus of Trent to Francia on behalf of those who had been led captive by the Franks from the Tridentine fortresses.

**Note [Col. 0537C].** Saint Gregory of Tours also calls him Ago in Book X, chapter 3:

“Envoys came,” he says, “announcing that King Authari was dead and that Paul had been appointed in his place.”

The most eminent Baronius thinks that this explains the change of name: when Agilulf came over to the Catholics, as related below, he assumed this new name.

**Note [Col. 0537D].** Other copies read: “to recover those who had been taken captive from Trent,” and so forth. Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0537D].** Agnellus, the bishop of Trent, opposed the Roman Pontiff and the Catholics with the schismatics in the controversy over the Three Chapters. He subscribed to the pseudo-synods of Grado and Marano and supported the schismatics’ appeal to the emperor Maurice, as the most eminent Norisius noted.

When he returned from there, he brought back some captives whom Brunihildis, queen of the Franks, had redeemed at her own expense.

**Note [Col. 0538C].** Other copies have *Brunechildis*. Lindanus.

Duke Evin of Trent also went to Gaul to obtain peace and returned after securing it.

**Note [Col. 0538C].** Other copies have *Eoinus* or *Ennius*.

## CHAPTER II. On the drought that occurred in the same year and on the locusts

That year there was an exceptionally severe drought from January through September, and a great shortage of food and severe famine resulted.

**Note [Col. 0538C].** Other copies read: “a great shortage of grain and severe famine,” and so forth. Lindanus.

A great multitude of locusts also came into the territory of Trent. They were larger than other locusts. Strangely enough, they consumed the grasses and marsh plants but touched the crops of the fields only slightly.

**Note [Col. 0538C].** Other copies read: “the shrubs as well.”

The following year they came again in no less similar fashion.

**Note [Col. 0538D].** Paul’s history must be supplemented at this point from the *Register of Letters* of Saint Gregory the Great. Among the letters written in indiction 10 are several in which the most holy pontiff laments Duke Ariulf’s attacks upon the Romans and attempts by every means to oppose him.

The third letter in the order of the Benedictine Fathers of Saint Maur, addressed to Velox, master of the soldiers, says:

“We have previously made clear to Your Glory that soldiers were ready to come there; but since your letter reported that enemies had gathered and were making incursions here, this circumstance detained them here. Now, however, it has seemed useful to send some soldiers there. Your Glory should strive to admonish and encourage them to be ready for the work. When the opportunity arises, speak with our illustrious sons Maurilius and Vitalianus, and whatever, with God’s help, they decide for the welfare of the republic, carry out.

“And if you learn that Ariulf is making incursions either here or in the direction of Ravenna—and it is not necessary to say that he is making incursions—work against him from the rear as befits brave men, so that your reputation in the republic may, with God’s help, advance still further in proportion to the quality of your labor,” and so forth.

Another letter, number 29 in the order, addressed to Maurilius and Vitalianus themselves, says that Gregory had been informed that Ariulf was making an incursion toward the city of Rome and urges them to press him from behind. In the following letter, number 30, addressed to the same men, he carefully warns them about the doubtful loyalty of the people of Suana, whose defection to Ariulf was indicated by the letters of the Lombard duke. He invites them, if they learn that Ariulf’s army is preparing to march against the City, to ravage the duke’s territories.

In the forty-sixth letter, addressed to John, bishop of Ravenna, he repeats the same matter with tears:

“Do not attribute the fact that I have not replied sufficiently to the many letters of Your Blessedness to my sluggishness, but to my illness. For, because of my sins, at the time when Ariulf came against the Roman city, killed some and mutilated others, I was so afflicted with grief that I fell into a colic.”

Nor was the cruelty of Duke Ariulf the only thing that caused the holy pontiff the deepest sorrow. In the same letter, which above all others reveals the condition of Roman affairs at that time, he continues:

“I was greatly surprised that the well-known concern of Your Holiness did nothing for this city or for my needs. But as your letters circulated, I learned that you were indeed acting with concern, yet had no one before whom you could act.

“I therefore attribute this to my sins, because the man who is now in office both pretends not to fight against our enemies and prevents us from making peace. He means the Roman patrician. Even if he now wished to make peace, we could not do so at all, because Ariulf, who has the army of Authari and Nordulf, demands that those troops be assigned to him as a benefice before he will consent to discuss peace with us,” and so forth.

And below:

“If there is ever any opportunity to obtain something from him”—that is, from the Roman patrician—“let Your Fraternity act upon him so that we may make peace with Ariulf, if we can accomplish even a little, since the soldiers have been removed from the Roman city, as he himself knows.

“The Theodosiaci who remained here, receiving no military pay, scarcely even apply themselves to guarding the walls. With the city abandoned by everyone, if it does not have peace, how will it endure?”

And below:

“We inform Your Excellency, the Exarch, with urgent insistence concerning the city of Naples, because, as we have learned, Arigis has joined Ariulf, has violated his allegiance to the republic, and is lying in wait for that city. Unless a duke is sent there quickly, it must already be counted among the lost.”

I believe there can be no doubt that this Ariulf was the same duke of the people of Spoleto whom Paul mentions in the following chapter, chapter 27, and that his victory at Camerinum followed all these events.

## CHAPTER III. How King Agilulf killed Minulf, and concerning the rebellions of Gaidulf and Ulfari

In those days King Agilulf killed Minulf, duke of the island of Saint Julian, because at an earlier time he had surrendered himself to the Frankish commanders.

**Note [Col. 0540B].** Other copies have *Menulfum*. Lindanus.

**Note [Col. 0540B].** Other copies read “of the island of Saint Julius.” Lindanus.

Gaidulf, duke of Bergamo, rebelled in his city of Bergamo and fortified himself against the king; but after giving hostages he made peace with him.

**Note [Col. 0540B].** Other copies read: “Gandulf, duke of Bergamo, in his city of Bergamo.”

**Note [Col. 0540C].** Other copies add: “with the king.”

Again Gaidulf withdrew to the island of Comacina. King Agilulf entered that same island of Comacina, expelled Gaidulf’s men from it, and transferred to Ticinum a treasure that he found there, deposited by the Romans.

**Note [Col. 0540C].** Other copies read: “Gaidulf’s auxiliaries.” The word *homines* is to be understood here in the sense in which it is used by the jurists. Thus, in Capitolinus’s *Life of Pertinax*: “He was so eager for profit that at the Sabatian fords, although emperor, he conducted trade through his own men, just as he had been accustomed to do as a private citizen.” Likewise in Symmachus, *Letters* III.27 and V.54. See Cujacius, *Observations* VIII.14. Lindanus.

Gaidulf, however, fled again to Bergamo and was there captured by King Agilulf, who once more received him into favor.

**Note [Col. 0539B].** Other copies read: “was captured.” Lindanus.

Duke Ulfari also rebelled against King Agilulf at Treviso, but Agilulf besieged and captured him.

**Note [Col. 0540C].** Other copies read: “Duke Ulfari of Treviso against Agon, or Agilulf.” Lindanus.

## CHAPTER IV. On the plague at Ravenna and on Childebert’s war with Hilperic’s son

That year the bubonic plague was again exceedingly severe at Ravenna, Grado, and in Istria, just as it had been thirty years earlier.

**Note [Col. 0540C].** From our Paul and from other historians of our affairs it is clearly established that bubonic plague repeatedly spread through various regions of Italy.

At this time King Agilulf also made peace with the Avars.

**Note [Col. 0540C].** Other copies have *Abaribus*, and likewise below. Lindanus.

Childebert also waged war against his cousin, the son of Hilperic. In that battle as many as thirty thousand men were killed.

**Note [Col. 0540C].** Other copies have *Chilperic*. Lindanus.

There was then an exceptionally cold winter, such as scarcely anyone could remember having occurred before. In the region of Briones, blood flowed from the clouds.

**Note [Col. 0540D].** Other copies read: “And within the waters of the Rhine a stream of blood flowed”; others: “and a stream of bloody water issued from the inner river”; others: “and from the waters of the Maternus River,” and so forth. Lindanus.

Meanwhile, streams flowed as though they were rivulets of blood.

## CHAPTER V. How the blessed Gregory sent his book of the *Dialogue* to Queen Theudelinda

In those days the most wise and blessed Pope Gregory of the city of Rome, after writing many other works for the benefit of the holy Church, also composed four books on the lives of the saints. He called the work the *Book of the Dialogue*, that is, “the speech of two,” because he had produced it as a conversation with his deacon Peter.

**Note [Col. 0540D].** That is, in the year 593 or 594 of the Christian era, as can be inferred from the book of the *Dialogues* itself. In Book III, chapter 19, we read: “About five years ago, when the Tiber left its bed near this city of Rome.” In Book IV, chapter 26: “During that mortality which three years ago devastated this city with the most violent destruction.”

I assigned the flood, from Saint Gregory of Tours, to the year 589, and the bubonic plague to 590. These various chronological indications cannot easily be reconciled unless one supposes that the plague continued longer and that the holy pontiff had its final period in mind. We have another chronological indication in a letter of the same holy pontiff to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse. In that letter Gregory writes of “some miracles of the Fathers that occurred in Italy” and asks Maximian to report the ones he remembers. Since the letter was written in indiction 11, it is reasonably conjectured that the *Dialogues* were published the following year.

These books the aforementioned pope sent to Queen Theudelinda, whom he knew to be devoted to the faith of Christ and outstanding in good works.

**Note [Col. 0541C].** Other copies read: “in good practices.” Lindanus.

## CHAPTER VI. On the good works of the same Queen Theudelinda
Through this queen also the Church of God gained much benefit. For while they were still held fast in the error of paganism, the Lombards had seized nearly all the property [Note: [Col. 0541C] Mod., “the dignities.”] of the churches; but, moved by her salutary entreaty, the king both adhered to the Catholic faith and bestowed many estates upon the Church of Christ [Note: [Col. 0541C] A charter of King Agilulf still exists in volume V of the *Bullarium Cassinense*, and in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra*, by which he ceded to Saint Columbanus the abbot and his companions residing at the basilica of Saint Peter in the Bobbio valley, for their possession, four miles in every direction, whether cultivated or uncultivated: “Given at Milan, in the palace, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighth year of our most fortunate reign, in the fifth indiction.” Yet it must be said that an error has entered these chronological indications. For if Agilulf, as our Paul writes above in the final chapter of Book III, assumed royal power when the month of November had already begun, but nevertheless, after the Lombards had been assembled together, was raised by all to the kingship at Milan in the month of May, then, regardless of whether the beginning of his reign is reckoned from the commencement or from the confirmation of his royal authority, the eighth year of his reign could not have fallen in the fifth indiction. For it is plainly established from a letter of Saint Gregory that the last Easter celebrated while Authari was alive must be assigned to the year 590, and in that year the eighth indiction was in progress. Therefore Agilulf both assumed the kingship after September, when the ninth indiction had already begun, and was confirmed in it; and from that point, if the number of years of his reign is carried to the eighth, we arrive at the first indiction, not the fifth, as it is read in the printed editions. Other charters of King Adaloald also survive, by which this is confirmed concerning Agilulf; we shall note them below.] and restored the bishops, who had been reduced and cast down, to the honor of their customary dignity.

## CHAPTER VII. That Tassilo was appointed king by Childebert, king of the Franks

In those days Tassilo [Note: [Col. 0541D] Mod., “Taxillo.”] was appointed king by Childebert, king of the Franks, among the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0541D] The word “king” is not read in Ambrosianus.] [Note: [Col. 0541D] Namely, in the year 595, according to Sigebert and Hermannus Contractus in the *Chronicle*.]. Soon afterward, entering the province of the Slavs with an army and winning a victory, he returned to his own land with very great booty.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the patrician Romanus seized the cities held by the Lombards; that King Agilulf killed the duke Maurisio; and that he made peace with Saint Gregory and the Romans

At this time also Romanus, the patrician and [Col. 0542A] [Note: [Col. 0541D] The *Glossarium Graecolatinum* gives ἔξαρχοι as “nobles, princes.” Lind. Learned men explain *exarchus* almost as ἔκ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, “from the ruler.” It was the title of the highest magistrate, who exercised the emperor’s functions in the provinces; we read of the exarchs of Italy, Africa, and so forth. The exarch of Italy resided at Ravenna, from which he was also named. Longinus, sent against the Lombards by the emperor Justin, was the first to bear this title and authority in Italy.] exarch of Ravenna, hurried to Rome. While returning to Ravenna, he recovered [Note: [Col. 0542C] Mod., “he retained.”] the cities that were held by the Lombards, whose names are these: Sutrium, Polimartium, [Note: [Col. 0542C] Manuscript: “Hortestuder.” Another reading: “Hortam Faider.” Lind.] Horta, Tuder, Ameria, [Note: [Col. 0542C] Another reading: “Perusium.” Lind.] Perusia, Luceoli, and certain other cities.

When this deed was reported to King Agilulf, he immediately left Ticinum with a powerful army and made for the city of Perusia. There, for several days, he besieged Maurisio, the duke of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0542C] Another reading: “Mauritionem.” Lind. and Mod.], who had surrendered himself to the Roman side; and without delay, after capturing him, he deprived him of life.

At the arrival of this king, blessed Pope Gregory was so terrified that he abandoned his exposition of the temple of which we read in Ezekiel, as he himself also relates in his homilies [Note: [Col. 0542C] The words of Saint Gregory, at the beginning of Book II on Ezekiel: “Because, pressed by many cares, I was not able to examine the book of the prophet Ezekiel in its entirety and order before your Charity, it pleased me to comply with your good desires, so that at least his final vision—which was shown to him concerning the building situated on the mountain, and which is more obscure than all his other visions—might be expounded. Indeed, I must obey your will. But there are two things that disturb my mind in this matter: one, that this same vision is covered by such clouds of obscurity that scarcely anything can be seen in it through the light of understanding; the other, that we have learned that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, has already crossed the Po and is hastening with all speed to besiege us. Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, what the wretched mind, occupied by the disturbances of its fear, can accomplish in penetrating obscure and mystical meanings, etc.”

“But let no one blame me,” he says after Homily 22, “if I cease after this discourse, because, as you all see, our tribulations have increased. We are surrounded on every side by swords; on every side we fear the danger of imminent death. Some return to us with their hands cut off; others are reported captured, others killed. I am now compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition, because my soul is weary of my life, etc.”]. King Agilulf, therefore, having settled matters [Note: [Col. 0542D] Another reading: “after Maurisio had been killed.” Lind. and Mod.], returned to Ticinum.

Not long afterward, chiefly at the urging of Theudelinda, his wife, as blessed Gregory frequently exhorted her in his letters, he made a very firm peace with the same holy Pope Gregory and with the Romans. In acknowledgment of this, that same venerable priest sent the queen the following letter.

## CHAPTER IX. Letter of blessed Gregory to Queen Theudelinda

“Gregory to Theudelinda, queen of the Lombards.

“Because, as our son Abbot Probus has reported, we have learned that Your Excellency has devoted herself more earnestly and kindly than usual to making peace. For we could not have expected otherwise of your Christianity than that, in the cause of peace, you would show your labor and goodness to all. Therefore we give thanks to Almighty God, who by his mercy so governs your heart that, just as he has granted you right faith, so also he permits you always to perform what pleases him. For, most excellent daughter, you should not think that you have gained a small reward from the blood that was destined to be shed on both sides.

Therefore, returning thanks for your goodwill, we beseech the mercy of our God to repay you for your good deeds in body and soul, here and in the future. We also greet you with fatherly affection and urge you to act with your most excellent husband in such a way that he may not reject fellowship with the Christian commonwealth. For, as we believe you know, it would be useful in many ways if he wished to place himself in its friendship.

You, therefore, as is your custom, continue diligently to do whatever pertains to the reconciliation of the parties; and whenever an opportunity for reward presents itself, strive so to act that your good deeds may commend you all the more before the eyes of Almighty God.”

## CHAPTER X. Another letter of the same man to King Agilulf

“Gregory to Agilulf, king of the Lombards.

“I give thanks to Your Excellency [Note: [Col. 0543C] Mod., “we give thanks.”] because, having heard our petition, you established the peace that we believed would benefit both parties, just as we had confidence in you [Note: [Col. 0543C] Mod., “the peace that would benefit both parties, etc.”]. For this reason we greatly praise the prudence and goodness of Your Excellency [Note: [Col. 0543C] Another reading: “truth.” Lind.], because, by loving peace, you have shown that you love God, who is its author.

For if—God forbid—it had not been made, what [Note: [Col. 0543C] Another reading: “had happened.” Lind.] ought to have happened except that, amid sin and danger to both parties, the blood of the wretched peasants, whose labor benefits both sides, would have been shed? But so that we may experience the benefit of this peace in the manner in which it was made by us, we greet you with fatherly affection and ask that, whenever the opportunity arises, you instruct your dukes in the various regions, and especially those established in these territories, by your own examples, to preserve this peace purely, as was promised [Note: [Col. 0543C] Amb., “especially.”] [Note: [Col. 0543C] Lind. and Mod., “by your letters.”], and not to seek any opportunities from which either some quarrel or [Note: [Col. 0543C] Another reading: “sedition.” Lind.] ingratitude might arise, so that we may be able to give thanks for your will [Note: [Col. 0543C] Mod., “ought to give thanks.”].

As for the bearers of this letter, we received them, as truly your men, with the affection that was proper, because it was right that we should both receive and dismiss with charity wise men who, by God’s favor, had announced that peace had been made [Note: [Col. 0543C] From the register of the letters of Saint Gregory it appears that these were sent in the second indiction. But if a comet appeared in the following month of January, and John, archbishop of Ravenna, died—and if he died in the year 595, as Baronius and, following Agnellus, Bacchinius maintain—then the peace between the Lombards and Romans must be assigned to earlier years. I would by no means overturn this chronology, chiefly on the basis of another letter of the same holy pontiff to Innocentius, prefect of Africa, in Book X, sent in the following third indiction. There he writes: “Since, then, we have learned what zeal you have shown in preparing the dromons, we relieve your anxiety with the news you desired, informing you that, with God’s favor, we have reached an agreement concerning peace with the king of the Lombards until the month of March of the coming fourth indiction. Whether this agreement will hold, we do not know, because it was later reported that the same king had died, although this still remains uncertain.”

Since it is plainly established from this letter that peace had been ratified until the next fourth indiction, it must necessarily be said, given the shortness of the interval during which the king’s illness was not yet known, that the congratulatory letters to Agilulf and Theudelinda were sent in the preceding second indiction. From that letter we also learn the conditions of the peace, which Paul did not mention at all; and anyone can easily infer from the same Book of Letters that peace had been purchased at a price. Perhaps the following words addressed to the empress Constantia also refer to this: “For twenty-seven years now we have lived in this city amid the swords of the Lombards. How much is distributed among them daily by this Church so that we may be able to live among them need not be explained. But I shall state it briefly: just as in the regions of Ravenna Your Lords’ piety has a treasurer with the first army of Italy who provides the daily expenses arising from such matters, so in this city I am their treasurer for such causes. And yet this Church—which at one and the same time spends so much without ceasing on clergy, monasteries, the poor, the people, and, in addition, the Lombards—behold, is still burdened by the affliction of all the churches, etc.”

How much labor and effort the holy pontiff devoted to purchasing this peace, despite the resistance of the Greeks, is shown by several other letters, which it would be too lengthy to recite here.]”

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the comet, the death of John the bishop and of the duke Evin, and the Bavarians

[Col. 0544B]

Meanwhile, in the following month of January, a comet appeared morning and evening throughout the entire month [Note: [Col. 0544D] Ambrosianus, “at that same time.”]. In that same month John, archbishop of Ravenna, died; in his place Marianus, a Roman citizen, was substituted [Note: [Col. 0544D] He is likewise called this in Gratian’s *Decree*; in other sources he is Marianus. He was the nephew of the deceased John the Roman. Several letters of Saint Gregory to both men survive; all of them were carefully reviewed by the distinguished Bacchinius, in his work on the bishops of Ravenna.].

When Duke Evin also died at Trent, Gaidoaldus, a good man and Catholic in faith, was appointed duke in the same place. During these very days the Bavarians, numbering as many as two thousand men, attacked the Slavs; but when Cacanus arrived, they were all killed [Note: [Col. 0544D] Ambrosianus, “with King Cacanus arriving.”]. At that time wild horses and buffaloes were first brought into Italy, and they were wonders to the peoples of Italy.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the death of Childebert, king of the Franks, the war of the Avars with the Franks, and the death of King Guntram

[Col. 0544C]

At this time Childebert, king of the Franks, in the twenty-fifth year of his age, was extinguished by the force of poison, as is said, together with his own wife [Note: [Col. 0544D] Namely, in the course of the year 596, as Baronius correctly inferred from Saint Gregory’s letters to his sons Theuderic and Theudebert. Hermannus Contractus reports his death quite differently from our author: “Childebert,” he says, “a strong and energetic king of the Franks, son of Sigebert, died in the twenty-first year of his reign and the twenty-fifth year of his age, having, as they say, received poison from his wife.” According to our author, his sons were entrusted to the guardianship of their grandmother Brunichildis. See Fredegarius, chapter 16.].

The Huns also, who are called Avars, entering Thuringia from Pannonia, waged very severe wars with the Franks. Queen Brunichildis then ruled Gaul with her still very young grandsons, Theudebert and Theuderic [Note: [Col. 0545C] Mod., always “Theudebert and Theuderic.”], from whom the Huns received money and returned to their own lands.

King Guntram also died [Note: [Col. 0545C] Ambrosianus, “king of the Burgundians.” Contrary to Baronius’s opinion, it is now clearly established that Childebert outlived Guntram, king of Burgundy. For we read in Fredegarius: “Childebert assumed his kingdom”; and in Gregory of Tours, *Miracles of Saint Martin*, Book IV, chapter 37: “At the time when, after the death of the most glorious King Guntram, Childebert, king of the Orléanais, entered the city, etc.” Concerning his death, Fredegarius, chapter 13, says: “In the thirty-third year of Guntram’s reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the king himself died and was buried in the church of Saint Marcellus, in the monastery which he himself had built.” From these facts, and from the solar eclipse related by the same Fredegarius under the preceding year, the distinguished successors of the Bollandists, Henschenius and Papebrochius, in their preliminary examination concerning the genealogy of the Dagobertine kings, in volume III for the month of March, established 593 as the year of Guntram’s death.

Moreover, the virtues of this most pious king shone so brightly that he was enrolled among the saints, and 28 March was dedicated to him, as may be seen in the cited *Acts of the Saints* of Bollandus.

As for what concerns our Lombards, there is another matter not fully reported by Paul that occurred at this time and must by no means be passed over in silence: the capture of the city of Cotrone and the removal of a great number of captives in the year 596, as we can gather from a letter of Saint Gregory the Great. It was addressed to the patrician Theotista, who, like several others, had donated a large quantity of gold to the holy pontiff for the redemption of captives. See Book VII, indiction 15.] and Brunichildis, queen, assumed his kingdom together with his still young grandsons, the sons of Childebert.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Cacanus sent envoys to Agilulf, and concerning the peace with the patrician Gallicinus

At that time King Cacanus of the Huns sent envoys to Agilulf at Milan and made peace with him. The patrician Romanus also died, and Gallicinus succeeded him and entered into a peaceful agreement with King Agilulf [Col. 0545B].

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Agilulf’s peace with the Franks, and the deaths of Zangrulfus and Warnecautius

[Note: [Col. 0545D] “At this time also.” Mod.]

At this time Agilulf made a perpetual peace with Theuderic, king of the Franks. After this, King Agilulf killed Zangrulfus, duke of the Veronese, who had rebelled against him. He also killed Gaidulfus, duke of Bergamo, whom he had already spared twice [Note: [Col. 0545D] Another reading: “Gandulfus, also of Bergamo.” Lind.]; and in the same manner he killed Warnecautius at Ticinum [Note: [Col. 0546B] Another reading: “Wernecausus.” Lind. and Mod. “Warnecantius.” [Col. 0546C] A.].

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the plague at Ravenna and the mortality at Verona

At a later time a very severe plague again devastated Ravenna and those who lived along the seacoast [Col. 0546A]. In the following year a severe mortality consumed the people of Verona [Note: [Col. 0546C] Nearly the same account is given by the bishop of Ravenna in the *Life of Saint Marianus*, XXX, chapter 2: “In his time, those dwelling around the seacoast, and especially in this city of Ravenna, were devastated by a very severe plague; and when a year had elapsed, the citizens of Verona were consumed by a powerful death. After this, a terrible sign appeared in the sky, and, as though bloodstained enemies were fighting throughout the entire night, a very bright light shone.”].

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the bloody sign in the sky and the war among the Franks

At that time a bloody sign also appeared in the sky, as it seemed, together with blood-red spears, and a very bright light throughout the entire night. At that time Theudebert, king of the Franks, waging war with his cousin Clotarius [Note: [Col. 0546C] The manuscript reads “Lotharius”; Lind. likewise preserves this below. The reading of the printed editions should be retained by the editor.] [Note: [Col. 0546C] Fredegarius in his *Chronicle*, chapter 20, and Aimoinus, Book III, chapter 88, relate the war between Theudebert, king of Austrasia, and Theuderic, king of Burgundy, against Clotarius II, king of Neustria. They make the meteorological apparition reported by Paul correspond to this event and commonly establish it as having occurred in the year 600.

The unfortunate outcome for Clotarius was brought about chiefly at the instigation of Brunichildis, the grandmother of Theudebert and Theuderic. The battle was fought in the territory of Sens, at the little river Aroane, not far from the village of Dromello. “There,” writes Fredegarius in the cited chapter 20, “the army of Clotarius was slaughtered most severely. When he himself and those who remained had been put to flight, they plundered and devastated the districts and cities along the bank of the Seine that had surrendered to Clotarius. The cities were broken open with great violence, and a great multitude of captives was led away from there by the army of Theuderic and Theudebert.

Clotarius, overcome, whether willingly or unwillingly, confirmed by treaty that between the Saône and the Loire, as far as the Ocean Sea and the Breton frontier, the territory should belong to Theuderic; and that through the Saône and the Isère, the entire duchy of Dentelinus as far as the Ocean Sea should be received by Theudebert. Only twelve districts between the Isère, the Saône, and the coast of the Ocean Sea remained to Clotarius.”], severely defeated his army.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the death of Ariulfus, duke of Spoleto, and the duchy of Theudelapius

In the following year Ariulfus, the duke who had succeeded Faroald at Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0546D] Another reading: “Farualdus.” Lind.], died.

After Ariulfus had waged war against the Romans at Camerinum and won a victory, he began asking his men who that man had been whom he himself had seen fighting so bravely in the battle he had fought. When his men replied that they had seen no one there fighting more courageously than the duke himself, he said:

“Certainly I saw another man there who was much and in every respect better than I, who, whenever anyone from the opposing side wished to strike me, always protected me with his shield.”

When the duke himself had come near Spoleto, where the basilica of the blessed martyr Sabinus is situated, in which his venerable body rests [Note: [Col. 0546D] Mod., “Sabinus the bishop.”], he asked whose such a spacious house was. Faithful men replied that the martyr Sabinus rested there, whom Christians, whenever they went to war against their enemies, were accustomed to invoke for their aid [Note: [Col. 0547B] Another reading: “that they might have his protection, and therefore called upon him for their assistance.” Lind.].

But Ariulfus, who was still a pagan, replied:

“How can it be that a dead man can provide any assistance to the living?”

Having said this, he dismounted from his horse and entered to inspect the same basilica. While the others were praying, he began to admire the paintings of the basilica. When he saw the image of the blessed martyr Sabinus depicted there, he immediately declared under oath:

“This man certainly had exactly the appearance and clothing of the man who protected me in battle.”

Then it was understood that the blessed martyr Sabinus had brought him assistance in the battle.

After Ariulfus died, the two sons of the former duke Faroald contended with one another for the duchy [Col. 0547B]; one of them, named Theudelapius, having gained the victory, assumed the duchy [Note: [Col. 0547B] Another reading: “one of them, Theudelapius by name, gained the victory and assumed the duchy.” Lind.].

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the plundering carried out by the Lombards at the monastery of Saint Benedict

[Note: [Col. 0547B] “The effort of learned writers,” says Bacchinius in his historical-chronological dissertation on the age of Peter the Elder, addressed to the bishop of Ravenna, “is well known: they attempt to reconcile Paul Warnefridus with Leo of Ostia, and Leo of Ostia himself with the Ostian tradition, where they discuss the destruction of the monastery of Cassino by the Lombards and the length of time that elapsed between its desolation and its restoration by Petronax.”

This matter has been debated at length by Camillus Peregrinus in his chronology of the dukes of Benevento; by Abbot Angelo della Noce; by Bollandus, Mabillon, Bacchinius, and other most distinguished men. It would be too lengthy to list all their arguments here. From them, for the correction rather than the elucidation of our Paul, it is enough to extract the older records of this matter, from which it is proved that this notable destruction of the celebrated monastery must be assigned to earlier times, contrary to Paul’s testimony.

Gregory the Great, who lived nearer to the age and was in fact a witness of the tragedy itself, has the following in Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 17, when speaking of Saint Benedict’s prediction:

“A certain nobleman named Theoprobus had been converted by the admonition of the same Father Benedict, etc. One day, when he had entered his cell, he found him weeping bitterly. When he had remained there for a long time and saw that his tears did not cease, and yet that the man of God was not weeping as he was accustomed to do in prayer but in grief, he asked what was the cause of so great a sorrow. The man of God immediately replied: ‘This entire monastery which I have built, and everything that I have prepared for the brothers, have been handed over to the nations by the judgment of Almighty God. Yet I could scarcely obtain that souls might be granted to me from this place.’ Theoprobus then heard his words; but we see their fulfillment, since we know that his monastery has now been destroyed by the nation of the Lombards. For recently, during the night, while the brothers were resting, the Lombards entered there; and after plundering everything, they were unable to keep even one person there, etc.”
