Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Pelagius II*, says: “The brothers, fleeing from the monastery, went to Rome . . . . . and, by the permission of Saint Pelagius II, pope, and of the emperor Tiberius Maurice, they built a monastery beside the Lateran patriarchate.” Perhaps from this Leo of Ostia, in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, Book I, chapter 2: “The brothers went to Rome and, by permission of the Roman pontiff Pelagius, who at that time presided over the apostolic see, built a monastery beside the Lateran patriarchate; and there they lived for one hundred and thirty years, during which the monastery of Cassino remained destroyed.”

For a clear explanation of these matters, I shall cite in full the words of the most learned Mabillon in the Benedictine *Annals*, Book VII:

“Bonitus was then in charge of Cassino. He obtained as his successor in governing the Cassinese community at the Lateran Valentinian, who, according to Gregory, presided over the Lateran monastery for many years. This one fact is sufficient to correct the common opinion of our writers, who place this destruction in the year 589. For Gregory began to write his *Dialogues* in the year 593. Valentinian had already ceased to live at that time; he had presided over the Lateran monastery for many years—at least ten years. Therefore the monastery of Cassino had been destroyed, and the monks driven from it, more than ten years earlier; Pelagius had granted them a place beside the Lateran basilica for building a monastery, certainly around the year 580, which was the fourth year of his pontificate.

Nor does it matter that Gregory, writing the second book of the *Dialogues* to Valentinian’s successor, calls this destruction recent. For Gregory does not use ‘recent’ only once to mean a period of ten, or even twenty, years, as two passages quoted by me elsewhere in the notes on this passage of Gregory plainly demonstrate, etc.”

Concerning Leo’s testimony he writes the following in chapter 3:

“The aforementioned author must be corrected in saying that the Cassinese monks remained at the Lateran for one hundred and ten years, during which the monastery of Cassino remained destroyed. Another manuscript reads one hundred and thirty years; but in both cases the interval of time is too short. For between Pelagius II, during whose pontificate this destruction occurred, and Gregory II, under whom, according to Leo, the sacred monastery was restored by Petronax, nearly 140 years elapsed. In place of Gregory III, however, Gregory II must be substituted. Since he began his pontificate in the year 715, the ruin of the monastery of Cassino lasted at least 135 years, etc.”]

Around this time the monastery of the blessed Father Benedict, situated in the fortress of Cassino, was invaded by the Lombards at night [Col. 0548A]. After plundering everything, they were unable to keep even one of the monks there, so that the prophecy of the venerable Father Benedict, which he had foreseen long before, might be fulfilled. He had said:

“I could scarcely obtain from God that souls might be granted to me from this place.”

The monks fleeing from that place also made for Rome, carrying with them the book of the holy Rule that the aforesaid Father had composed, along with certain other writings, as well as a quantity of bread and a measure of wine [Note: [Col. 0548D] These are discussed in chapters 39 and 40 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. The *hemina* is called a measure of wine; many curious details have been written about it, but they do not belong here.], and whatever they were able to carry away from the furnishings.

After the blessed Benedict, Constantinus governed the congregation; after him Simplicius; after Simplicius Vitalis; and finally Bonitus. Under Bonitus this destruction took place.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the death of Zotton and the duchy of Arichis

When Zotto, duke of the Beneventans, had died [Note: [Col. 0548D] Another reading: “Arichis.” Lind. and Mod. give “Arigis.” From the subsequent succession of the dukes of Benevento this chronology of the years of the established duchy of Benevento is also confirmed—the chronology that I presented above in Book III, chapter 32, together with Caracciolus. For if Zoto held the principate at Benevento for a period of twenty years and had as his successor Arigis, as our author calls him; or Archis, as the *Chronicle of the Dukes of Benevento* has it; or Arichis, as the anonymous Cassinese author has it; or finally Arogis, as Saint Gregory the Great calls him, it is now plainly established from the letter of the said holy pontiff to John, bishop of Ravenna, whose words I quoted, that in the tenth indiction—namely, in the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ 591, when the letter was sent—Arichis had already been elevated to the principate of Benevento and had plotted with another duke, Ariulfus, against the city of Naples.

Since our Paul writes that he received the principate through the favor of King Agilulf, it must necessarily be said that this occurred shortly after the king’s inauguration. Thus, if one counts backward twenty years, one arrives at the time of Caracciolus, as far as is possible amid such great obscurity concerning events.

Nor do the arguments that the learned Peregrinus draws from more recent chroniclers disturb this conclusion. Greater faith must be placed in writers of the same age, and there is no force in the argument drawn by Peregrinus from our Paul himself—namely, that the beginning of Zotto’s duchy must be placed in the time of King Authari because, while narrating the deeds of this king, our author mentions Zotto. It was very common for him to report many matters by anticipation, as he himself admits in more than one place.] Arigis was sent by King Agilulf to succeed him in his place. He had been born in Friuli and had raised the sons of Gisulf, duke of Friuli; he was also related by blood to that same Gisulf.

A letter of blessed Pope Gregory to Arigis survives, addressed as follows [Note: [Col. 0549C] It was sent in the fifth indiction; see Book XII, number 23, in the edition of the Benedictine Fathers of Saint-Maur.].

## CHAPTER XX. Letter of blessed Pope Gregory to the same Arichis

“Gregory to Duke Arigis [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus, “Arichis.”].

“Because we have confidence in your glory just as we truly have confidence in our son, we are encouraged to ask you for certain things with confidence, judging that you will by no means allow us to suffer grief [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus, “you”; Manuscript L., “that you allow no one.”]—especially in a matter by which your soul may be greatly assisted.

We inform you that, for the churches of the blessed Peter and Paul, we require a considerable number of beams. For this reason we have instructed our subdeacon Sabinus to cut a number of them in the region of the Bricci [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus and Mod., “Briciorum.” Lind. has “Brixiorum”; another reading, “Brictonum.”] and to drag them as far as the sea to a suitable place [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus, “to transport them”; the verb *debeat* is not read and should not be supplied.].

Since he needs assistance in this matter, we greet Your Glory with fatherly affection and ask that you assign your agents [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus, “actionaries.”] who are in that place [Note: [Col. 0549D] Mod., “that you command.”], so that the men under their authority may send him assistance with their oxen, in order that, with your cooperation, he may better accomplish what we have entrusted to him.

For our part, we promise that, when the work has been completed, we shall send you a suitable gift [Note: [Col. 0549D] Mod., “a gift.”], one that will not be insulting [Note: [Col. 0549D] Ambrosianus, “unworthy.”]. For we know how to take account of such matters and to respond to our sons who show us goodwill.

Therefore once again we ask you, glorious son, to act in such a way that we may become your debtors for the favor you have granted, and that you may receive a reward for the churches of the saints.”

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the captivity of King Agilulf’s daughter, and that King Agilulf sent an artisan to Cacanus

In those days the daughter of King Agilulf, together with her husband named Godescalchus, was captured from the city of Parma by the army of the patrician Gallicinus and was led to the city of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0549D] The bishop of Ravenna, in the *Life of Marianus*, bishop XXX, perhaps repeats this account from Paul: “Meanwhile Agilulf’s daughter was captured, together with her husband Gudelschalchus, by the army of the patrician Callinicus from the city of Parma, and the captives were brought to this city of Ravenna”; and below: “Thus, as we have said, there was always war between the Ravennates and the Lombards, and there was great discord on account of his daughter, who had been captured by the Ravennates. Because of her, the city of Cremona was captured and destroyed by the aforesaid king, and Mantua was severely harassed and broken apart.”].

At this time also King Agilulf sent artisans to Cacanus, king of the Avars, to build ships; with these, Cacanus captured a certain island in Thrace.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the basilica of the blessed John at Modicia, which Queen Theudelinda built

At about the same time Queen Theudelinda built the basilica of the blessed John the Baptist, which she [Note: [Col. 0550B]

Ambrosianus has “Modica”; another reading, “Modoetia,” and likewise elsewhere. L. Tristanus Calchus, *History of Milan*, Book IV, writes: “The common people call it Modoetia; nevertheless this word is used by Paul. We, however, rely on the inscription of a stone carved there in very ancient letters in the following form:

C. SERTORIUS L. F. OUF. VETERANUS LEG. XVI. CURATOR. CIVIUM. OMN. OR. MOGUNTIACI.

“It is a wealthy town, watered by the Lambro. He argues from this stone that the town was called Moguntiacum. Yet the stone has a noteworthy variant reading, *Romanor.* for *omn. or.*; and Apianus, from whom Gruter had copied it, read the same inscription here at Milan, at Saint Victor’s.

“Balthasar Fidelis, archpriest of the basilica of Modoetia, thinks in a book that he wrote to Leo X, Supreme Pontiff, that Modicia was so called from the modest size of its revenue, and he agrees with Calchus concerning the ancient name Moguntiacum. Whatever the truth may be, Ennodius calls it Moditia in Book VI, Letter 10, as the learned Fontanini noted in his dissertation on the Iron Crown.

“I myself have read Modicia and Modica indiscriminately in all the old charters of the ninth and tenth centuries belonging to the distinguished patron of antiquity and good letters, Count Donatus de Sylva, and in the archive of the basilica of Modoetia itself.]

Modicia [Note: [Col. 0550D] The following passage is found only in the Ascensian edition:

“She built it for herself, for her husband, and for her sons and daughters, and for all the Italian Lombards, so that Saint John himself might be an intercessor for us with the Lord our God Jesus Christ. We all unanimously promise him that every year, on the day of his Nativity—that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of July—we will honorably send from our resources to his shrine, so that through his intercession we may obtain the help of our Lord Jesus Christ both in war and in every other place to which we may go. From that day onward, in all their undertakings, they began to invoke Saint John, asking him to provide them assistance through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ; and they all remained unharmed and proved victorious over all their adversaries.

That place lies twelve miles above Milan. The queen arranged for it to be dedicated and wonderfully adorned it with many ornaments of gold and silver; she enriched it with estates and assigned to the same place many households and properties in honor of Saint John the Baptist. Let us relate the text of the donation-charter that Queen Theodelinda, together with her son King Adalwald, made to Saint John, her patron, as a gift from God and as part of her dowry; she had it written in the presence of her people. If anyone at any time should violate this testimony of her will, let him be condemned with Judas the traitor on the day of the final judgment.

Its regulation was as follows: No one is in any way to interfere with the property of Saint John, except the priests who serve there day and night, as servants; the menservants and maidservants subject to that place are to live there together in common.”

Since these words were absent from the manuscript and from the Augustan edition, I did not wish to admit them into the text. Lind. In the Modena manuscript the following words are found, with only a few variants. At the place where the text reads “so that Saint John himself,” it continues: “Let him be an intercessor for all the Lombards with the Lord; and they unanimously vowed among themselves—the nobles together with their king and with Queen Theodelinda—and said: ‘If Saint John, etc.’” Where the text reads “their adversaries,” it continues: “That place, situated twelve miles above Milan, he dedicated and wonderfully adorned with many ornaments of gold and silver; he enriched it with estates and subjected many households and properties to the same place in honor of Saint John the Baptist. Let us relate the offering-charter of Queen Theodelinda, etc.”]

had built, and she dedicated that place, which lies twelve miles above Milan, and adorned it with many ornaments of gold and silver [Col. 0551A] and sufficiently enriched it with estates [Note: [Col. 0551C]

“As Fidelis himself writes, the very great devotion with which the Lombards honored this church is still attested by the cups, crowns, crosses, and golden panels adorned with emeralds, jacinths, electrum, carbuncles, pearls, and countless other little gems; by the great altar frontal, both golden and silver; by that remarkable vessel of excellent sapphire; and by the other royal ornaments that were left there.” All these things are still preserved in the distinguished treasury of that basilica, enduring monuments of Lombard piety. Through the kindness of the reverend canons I have often viewed them carefully, with immense pleasure. I think it appropriate here to display, on the facing page, the royal crowns reproduced from their originals.

The first is adorned not so much with gold as with an iron plate. The inhabitants of this place firmly maintain that it was made from one of the nails of the Lord’s Passion, and every year they place it solemnly upon the cross and expose it for the pious veneration of the people. Concerning it Sigonius writes in Book I of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 591:

“Milanese authors, following their native annals, assert that a crown was placed upon him—that is, upon Agilulf—by Queen Theodelinda. It was indeed golden, but woven around an inner iron circlet; hence the name ‘iron crown’ arose in the Italian Lombard kingdom.”

The second belonged to King Agilulf. It bears a figure of our Lord Jesus Christ holding his right hand raised in the sign of the cross and an open book in his left, marked with the mystical Greek letters Α and Ω. On either side of the figure are angels and the twelve apostles, separated by intervals marked with columns. The upper edge is decorated all around with sixty-five pyropes and emeralds, without any rays or pendants. It weighs twenty-one ounces and twenty-two denarii, as Mabillon also recorded in his *Italian Journey*, p. 212. On the lower part is inscribed the following legend:

“AGILULF, BY THE GRACE OF GOD, GLORIOUS KING OF ALL ITALY, OFFERED [THIS] TO SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST IN THE CHURCH OF MODICIA.”

This is indeed a very grand title, since in his time the Greek emperors still ruled in Italy through their exarchs, and their territories extended over the Roman Duchy, the Exarchate of Ravenna, and the borders of Naples. From this crown hangs a golden cross decorated with gems and pearls, weighing twenty-four ounces and fourteen denarii.

The last crown is called Theodelinda’s, although it bears no inscription. It too is of gold, decorated with emeralds, and weighs fourteen ounces and nineteen denarii. A second cross also hangs from it, weighing fifteen ounces and seven denarii and shining with gems on both sides.

These crowns, with their crosses and the other more notable gifts, are likewise represented on a marble tablet above the principal door of the basilica. It was carved in a barbarous age, as the shapeless figures sufficiently indicate—especially the river Jordan, seeming to descend from the breast of Christ the Lord, by which the most unfortunate artist wished to represent the water drawn for the baptism of Saint John the Baptist. Three crowns are carved on the side, with an equal number of crosses hanging from them. For this reason I have by no means approved the statement in the distinguished Fontanini’s dissertation, chapter 9, § 4, that the iron crown had always been without its cross. On the Modicia stone I see it accompanied by a cross just like the other two. Nor should this be counted as a fault in that very keen-eyed man, since, while writing in Rome, he had not visited the basilica at Modicia. It will nevertheless be useful now to record the observation, lest the force of his argument ever offend the sensibilities of certain tiresome mockers when set against the sight of the ancient stone.

On the same tablet there can also be seen a golden hen with her chicks and several vessels, gifts of the same royal Theodelinda and of Lombard munificence. They display precisely the form that each of them still possesses in reality in the treasury, so that there can be no doubt that they were drawn from the originals at that time.]

[Note: [Col. 0552C] Mod., “a great palace.”] In that place Theuderic, once king of the Goths, also built a palace, because in summer the place itself, being near the Alps, is temperate and healthy.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the palace that she built

There too the aforementioned queen [Note: [Col. 0552C] Mod., “for herself.”] founded her palace, in which she had something [Note: [Col. 0552C] The words “and had something from the deeds of the Lombards painted” are found in some copies. “In which painting” is absent from Lind. and Mod.; they read, “in which something from the deeds of the Lombards is clearly displayed.”] from the deeds of the Lombards painted. In that painting it is clearly shown how the Lombards at that time cut the hair of their heads, what sort of clothing they wore, and what their appearance was [Col. 0552A].

They shaved the back of the neck as far as the nape and left it bare, while allowing the hair to hang down from the face to the mouth [Note: [Col. 0552D] This was also customary among the Goths. Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Letter 2: “The little flaps of the ears, as is the custom of the people, are covered by the lashes of the overlying hair,” where “lashes of hair” means curls, a common ornament of the Germans. Hence they are also called *cirrigeri*—“curl-bearers”—as the most distinguished Justus Lipsius, whose name should never be mentioned without praise, has shown excellently in his notes on Tacitus’ *Germania*. There he also adds some information about German clothing that is well worth reading. Lind.]. They divided this hair toward either side along the parting of the forehead.

Their garments were loose, and chiefly of linen, like those customarily worn by the English Saxons, decorated with broad bands woven in various colors. Their shoes were almost open as far as the very tip of the great toe [Note: [Col. 0552D] Mod. and Lind., “open as far as the great toe.”] and were held in place alternately by thong-laces. Later they began [Note: [Col. 0552D] Clearly a German word, Lind.; in Latin, “leg-warmers.” See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.] to use *hoses*, over which, when riding, they put reddish-brown *tubrugi* [Note: [Col. 0552D] Τὸ, “the,” is not read in Mod.] [Note: [Col. 0552D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XIX, chapter 22: “They say that *tubruci* are so called because they cover the shins and breeches.” Lind. in the *Glossary*: “a woolen greave, customarily put over greaves or leather shoes.” Byrreus: “of a reddish color.”], but they adopted this practice from Roman custom [Note: [Col. 0552D] Amb., “from Roman, not from their own, custom.”].

[Col. 0553] [Col. 0555] [Col. 0557] [Col. 0559]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the destruction of the city of Padua

[Col. 0561A]

Down to these times the city of Padua had resisted the Lombards with the utmost courage, its soldiers continuing the struggle. But at last, when fire had been set to it, the whole city was consumed by devouring flames, and by order of King Agilulf it was destroyed down to the ground. The soldiers who had been in it, however, were permitted to return to Ravenna.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the peace made with the Avars, and on the Lombards’ entry into Istria

At this time Agilulf’s envoys returned from the Khan and announced that a perpetual peace had been made with the Avars [Note: [Col. 0561B] Another copy: “with the Hunnic Avars.” Lind.]. An envoy of the Khan also arrived with them and proceeded to Gaul, announcing to the Frankish kings that, just as they had peace with the Avars, so they should have peace with the Lombards. Meanwhile the Lombards, together with the Avars and the Slavs, entered the territories of Istria and laid everything waste with fire and plunder.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the birth of Adaloald, son of Agilulf, and the capture of Mount Silicis

At that time a son was born to King Agilulf by Queen Theodelinda, in the palace at Modicia [Note: [Col. 0561B] Amb. always has “at Modicia”; Mod., “at Modicia.”], and he was named Adaloald [Note: [Col. 0561B] Other copies: “Adaloald”; others, “Adalualdus,” and likewise below. Lind.]. In the following period the Lombards attacked the fortress of Mount Silicis. At about the same time, after Gallicinus had been repulsed at Ravenna, Smaragdus returned; he had previously been patrician at Ravenna.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the death of the emperor Maurice

Thus Augustus Maurice, after ruling the empire for twenty-one years with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine [Note: [Col. 0561B] Al.: “Constantine and Avorans, who was a *strator* [groom], etc.” Lind.], was killed by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus [Note: [Col. 0561B]

It is thoroughly established among learned men that Maurice ruled for twenty years, three months, and several days, and likewise that among many ancient writers incomplete years were counted as complete, as our Paul does here. Zonaras, in his *Annals*, took no account of the year in which Maurice’s reign began, for he writes:

Ἔθανε δὲ Μαυρίκιος ἐτῶν ἑξήκοντα καὶ τριῶν, εἴκοσι βασιλεύσας ἐνιαυτούς.

“Maurice died at the age of sixty-three, having reigned twenty years.”

That was evidently at the end of November in the year 602, when the sixth indiction had already begun.

We reproduce the horrible death of the unfortunate emperor, which several Greek writers relate, from the *Alexandrian Chronicle*:

Ἐκρατήθη δὲ Μαυρίκιος Τιβέριος μετὰ τῆς γυναικὸς καὶ ὀκτὼ τήκνων αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν ἅγιον Αὐτένομον πλησίον Πραινέτου, καὶ τῇ κζʹ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μηνὸς ἡμέρᾳ τρίτῃ ἐσφάγη πλησίον Χαλκηδόνος αὐτὸς Μαυρίκιος Τιβέριος· καὶ Πέτρος, Ἰουστῖνος, καὶ Ἰουστινιανὸς, καὶ Πέτρος δὲ ὁ ἀδελφὸς Μαυρικίου κουροπαλάτης ὤν, συσχεθεὶς καὶ αὐτὸς· ἐσφάγησαν δὲ εἰς Διαδρόμους πλησίον τοῦ Ἀκρίτα. Κωνσταντῖνος ὁ Λάρδις ἀπὸ ἐπάρχων γενόμενος πραιτωρίων, καὶ λογοθέτης, καὶ κουράτωρ τῶν Ὁρμίσδου, καὶ Θεοδόσιος ὁ υἱὸς Μαυρικίου, καὶ Κομεντίολος ὁ πατρίκιος, καὶ στρατηλάτης, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐσφάγη πέραν πλησίου τοῦ ἁγίου Κώνωνος πρὸς θάλασσαν, καὶ τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο κυνόβρωτον.

“Now Maurice Tiberius was arrested with his wife and his eight children in the church of Saint Autonomus near Praenetum. On the twenty-seventh day of the same month, a Tuesday, Maurice Tiberius himself was slaughtered near Chalcedon, together with Peter, Justin, and Justinian. Peter, the brother of Maurice, who was *curopalates*, was also captured and killed. They were killed at the Diadromoi near Acritas. Constantine Lardis, who had been made prefect of the praetorium after serving as governor, and was logothete and curator of the Hormisdus; Theodosius, the son of Maurice; and the patrician Commentiolus, who was also commander of the army, were likewise slaughtered beyond the city near Saint Conon, by the sea.”

He was compelled to behold the deaths of his sons; and when, at the last, the nurse had secretly substituted her own son in the place of one of them to be handed over to death, the emperor could not bear it and exposed the deception, repeatedly uttering these words: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.” See Theophylact, who relates that the spectacle of the corpses cast into the sea and repeatedly driven by the waves onto the shore formed the final scene of the tragedy. Maurice receives very frequent praises from the Greek historians, who nevertheless charge him with avarice because he refused to give the Khan the half-gold payment requested for each captive soldier; for this reason the Khan, in barbarous ferocity, killed them all, twelve thousand in number.]

was killed.

He was, however, useful to the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0562C] Amb., “useful to the state, but excessively devoted to avarice.”]. For he often gained victory while fighting against the enemy. The Huns, who are also called Avars, were likewise defeated by his prowess [Note: [Col. 0562C] Several Greek writers give a fuller account of the wars between Maurice and Cacanus, king of the Avars: Theophylact, Nicephorus, Zonaras, Manasses, Cedrenus, and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*; among Latin writers, the *Miscellaneous History*, Book XVII, based on Theophanes.].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the dukes Gaidoald and Gisulf, and on the baptism of Adaloald

[Col. 0562B]

In this year Duke Gaidoald of Trent and Gisulf of Friuli, who had previously been at odds with King Agilulf’s alliance, were received by him into peace [Note: [Col. 0562C] Another copy: “Gandoaldus.” Lind.]. At that time the aforesaid boy Adaloald, son of King Agilulf, was also baptized at Saint John’s in Modicia [Note: [Col. 0562C] Other copies: “in the church of Saint John.” Lind. and Mod.], and was lifted from the font by Secundus [Note: [Col. 0562C] Baronius, the father of the *Annals*, thinks that this Secundus was the same as Secundinus the abbot, to whom many letters of Saint Gregory were addressed.

“He was,” he says, “an abbot of great renown among the Lombards, as appears from other letters of Gregory himself addressed to Queen Theodelinda. We find this same man named in Paul the Deacon—not, I think, without scribal error—not Secundinus but Secundus, and the same author states that Queen Theodelinda’s son Adaloald was baptized by him, calling him by no other title than ‘servant of God’ and identifying his homeland as Trent, where he discusses his death. He frequently cites him, for he reports that a history of the Lombards was written by him, and so forth.”

But in Saint Gregory’s own letter to Theodelinda, Book XIV, indiction 7, in the recent edition, Gussanvillaeus notes that he found *Secundum* in all the manuscripts. From that letter we learn that Secundus had written a book concerning the Three Chapters, and that the queen had asked Gregory to answer it more fully. Pleading illness, Gregory meanwhile sent her the synod held under Justinian as a reply, so that she might learn the sequence of the events. Afterward he also sent various gifts, “by which he attempted to win over so great a man, whom he knew could keep the Lombards within Catholic communion,” as the cited Baronius writes under the year 599, nos. 15 and 16. He is said to have died at Trent around the year 615. See Vossius, *On Latin History*, etc.]

a servant of Christ from Trent, whom we have often mentioned. It was then the day of the Paschal festival [Col. 0563A] [Note: [Col. 0563B]

“The seventh day before the Ides of April” is not found in Mod. or the other copies.

That is, in the year 603, when Easter was celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of April, with the sixth indiction in progress. Saint Gregory congratulated Theodelinda on the birth of Adaloald in the letter cited above, writing as follows and adding gifts:

“The letter that you recently sent to us from the region of Genoa made us sharers in your joy, because by the grace of almighty God we know that both a son has been given to you and—what is highly praiseworthy in your Excellency—that he has been joined to the Catholic faith. For nothing else could have been expected from your Christianity than that you should strive to fortify, with the assistance of Catholic rectitude, him whom you received by divine gift, so that our Redeemer might recognize you as his familiar handmaid and might bring up the Lombard people happily under his fear as their new king. Therefore we pray almighty God both to preserve you in the way of his commandments and to make our most excellent son Adaloald advance in his love, so that, just as he is already great among human beings, he may likewise be glorious before the eyes of our God through good deeds.”

And below, after the remarks I have cited concerning Secundus:

“For our most excellent son, King Adaloald, we have arranged to send amulets—that is, a cross containing a piece of the wood of the Lord’s holy cross, and a reading from the holy Gospel enclosed in a Persian case. I have also sent three rings to my daughter, his sister: two with jacinths and one with a white stone. I ask you to give them to them, so that through your Excellency our affection may be treasured with them. In addition, while fulfilling the duty of greeting with paternal affection, we ask you to convey our thanks to your husband, our most excellent son the king, for the peace that has been made, and, as you are accustomed to do, urge his mind in every way toward future peace, so that you may find before God the reward of an innocent people—which might have perished through scandal—among the many good works that you perform.”]

the seventh day before the Ides of April.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the capture of Cremona and Mantua, the death of the king’s daughter, and the war with the Franks

In those days there was still hostility between the Lombards and the Romans because of the king’s daughter’s captivity. For this reason King Agilulf left Milan in July and besieged the city of Cremona with the Slavs whom Cacanus, king of the Avars, had sent him as auxiliary troops. He captured it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September and destroyed it down to the ground.

In the same way he stormed Mantua. After breaching its walls with battering rams [Note: [Col. 0563D] Amb., “with the Avars.”], he granted the soldiers who were in it permission [Note: [Col. 0563D] Ms., *viam* (“a way”). Lind.] to return to Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0563D] Amb. and Mod.: “He entered it on the Ides of September.”], and entered it on the day of the September Ides. [Col. 0563B] At that time a fortress also surrendered to the Lombard side [Col. 0564A], one called Vulturina [Note: [Col. 0563D] Other copy: “Vulturnia.” Lind. Cluverius, commenting on these words of our Paul, writes:

“Since he counts Vulturina among the places listed with Padua, Mount Silicis, Milan, Cremona, Mantua, and Brescello, I am amazed at what entered the minds of Blondus and others, that they should have drawn it to the place where the Adda flows into Lake Larius, and then maintained that the valley at the beginning called Vulturina was there, although it derives that name from the fortress of Tellius. But that fortress of the Deacon—whether it is called Vulturnia, as some copies have it, or Vulturina, as others, or, perhaps more correctly, Vulturia—is no other place than the present small village between Cremona and Brescello, situated on the left bank of the Po opposite Caneto, commonly called Valdoria.”].

The soldiers, however, set fire to the town of Brescello [Note: [Col. 0564B] Other copy: “Brixellum.” Lind.] and fled.

When these events had been accomplished, the king’s daughter was returned by the patrician Smaragdus, together with her husband, her children, and all her possessions. Peace was made in the ninth month, lasting until the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction [Note: [Col. 0564B] That is, the year 605. This agrees with the date given in the cited letter of Saint Gregory, indiction 7, namely after September of the year 603. In November of that same year—called the ninth month by Saint Gregory of Tours and others who begin the year in March—peace was made with the Lombards for approximately a year and a half.].

The king’s daughter soon returned from Ravenna to Parma [Note: [Col. 0564B] Amb.: “returning because of the difficulty, etc.” Mod.: “She returned to Parma, which because of the difficulty, etc.”], but, endangered by the difficulty of childbirth, she died immediately [Note: [Col. 0564B] The word “immediately” is absent from Amb.]. In this year Theudebert and Theuderic, kings of the Franks, fought against their uncle Chlothar. Many thousands fell on both sides in that battle.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the passing of blessed Pope Gregory and his holiness

At that time blessed Gregory also departed to Christ, while Phocas was already reigning in his second year [Col. 0564B] [Note: [Col. 0564B] Paul incorrectly connected the second year of Phocas’ reign with the death of Saint Gregory by the eighth indiction. It is established that Phocas began to rule toward the end of the year 602, during the sixth indiction, from these words of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*:

Καὶ τῷ Νοεμβρίῳ μηνὶ τῆς αὐτῆς Ἰνδικτιῶνος, ἐπανάστασις γέγονε Μαυρικίῳ παρὰ Φωκᾶ στρατιώτου, μετὰ τοῦ στρατοῦ, καὶ Μαυρικίος μὲν Τιβέριος σὺν τῇ γυναικὶ Κωνσταντίνῃ καὶ παισὶν θʹ, τουτέστιν ϛʹ μὲν ἄρρεσι, Θεοδοσίῳ, Τιβερίῳ, Πέτρῳ, Παύλῳ, Ἰουστίνῳ, καὶ Ἰουστινιανῷ, καὶ τρισὶ θηλείαις, Ἀναστασίᾳ, Θεοκτίστῃ καὶ Κλεοπάτρᾳ φεύγων τῇ κβʹ τοῦ Δίου μηνός, κατὰ Ῥωμαίους Νοεμβρίου τῇ νυκτὶ τῇ ἐπὶ κγʹ, διαφαινούσης παρασκευῆς. Φωκᾶς δὲ τῇ κγʹ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μηνὸς ἡμέρᾳ ϛʹ στεφεὶς ὑπὸ Κυριακοῦ πατριάρχου Κωνσταντινουπόλεως εἰς τὸν σεβάσμιον οἶκον τοῦ ἁγίου Ἰωάννου ἐν τῷ Ἑβδόμῳ, τῇ κεʹ τοῦ ῥηθέντος μηνὸς, ἡμέρᾳ κυριακῇ εἰσῆλθεν ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει κατεσθεὶς εἰς ὄχημα ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἑβδόμου εἰσελθὼν διὰ τῆς χρυσῆς πόρτας, καὶ τῶν Τρωαδησίων ἐμβόλων, καὶ τῆς μέσης ὅλης ἕως τοῦ παλατίου, μηδενὸς ὅλως ἀντιστάντος, ἀλλὰ πάντων εὐφημούντων.

“In November of that same indiction—namely, the sixth—Phocas raised a revolt with his army against Maurice. Maurice Tiberius, with his wife Constantina and nine children, six males—Theodosius, Tiberius, Peter, Paul, Justin, and Justinian—and three daughters—Anastasia, Theoctiste, and Cleopatra—fled on the twenty-second day of the month Dios, which is November according to the Romans, during the night leading into the twenty-third, as Friday was dawning. On the twenty-third day of the same month, a Friday, Phocas was crowned by Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople, in the venerable church of Saint John at the Hebdomon. On the twenty-fifth day of that month, a Sunday, he entered Constantinople from the Hebdomon, riding in a chariot through the Golden Gate, along the porticoes of the Troadesians, and through the entire central city as far as the Palace, with no one resisting at all, but everyone acclaiming him.”

Saint Gregory, however, “died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, before the sanctuary, on March 12,” as Anastasius records: in the year 604, during the seventh indiction. Since the second year of Phocas’ reign was completed in November of that same year, 604, the eighth indiction was indeed in progress, but it does not correspond to the year of Saint Gregory’s death.]

Sabinianus was appointed in his place to the office of the apostolate [Col. 0565A]. At that time the winter was exceedingly cold, and the vines died in almost every place. The crops too were partly ravaged by mice [Note: [Col. 0565B] The words “were partly ravaged by mice” are absent in some copies. Lind.], and partly withered after being struck by blight [Note: [Col. 0565B] Anastasius, in his account of Sabinianus, writes: “At the same time there was a severe famine in the city of Rome. After peace had been made with the Lombard people, he ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened and grain to be sold to the people, etc.” From this it is clearer that the cold and crop failure, followed by the great famine, should be assigned to the year 605, since the first winter after Gregory’s death occurred while Sabinianus was seated.]

For the world ought then to have suffered hunger and thirst, when, with so great a teacher departing, lack of spiritual nourishment and the aridity of thirst invaded human souls [Note: [Col. 0565C] Amb., “to perish from hunger and thirst.”].

I should like to insert here into this little work a brief passage from a letter of the same blessed Pope Gregory, so that it may be more clearly understood how humble this man was, and of how great an innocence and holiness. When he had been accused before Augustus Maurice and his sons of having killed a certain bishop named Malchus while he was in custody, in exchange for solidi, he wrote a letter concerning the matter to his own *apocrisiarius* Sabinianus [Note: [Col. 0565C] Amb. reads “Savinianus,” but the editors’ reading should be retained; the letter is certainly addressed to the deacon Sabinianus, the same man who succeeded Gregory in the papacy.], who was in Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0565C] Isidore in the *Glosses*: “An *apocrisiarius* is a confidential minister of the Roman Church, a confidential envoy.” They are very frequently mentioned in the books of the jurists. They were also called *adresponsi*. *Novella* 25, chapter 1: “Let him likewise have an *adresponsus*, or *apocrisiarius*.”], and among other things said:

“Tell our most serene lords one thing briefly: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, today the Lombard people would have neither king, nor dukes, nor counts, but would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I shrink from involving myself in the death of any human being. As for the same bishop Malchus, he was neither in custody nor under any affliction. On the day when he pleaded his case, and was led away, he was taken—without my knowledge—by Boniface the notary to his house; there he dined and was honored by him, and suddenly died during the night.” [Col. 0566A]

Behold what a man of humility he was [Note: [Col. 0565C] Amb., “of innocence.”]: although he was the supreme pontiff of God, he called himself the servant of human beings [Note: [Col. 0565C–D] Al., “he called himself a servant.” Lind. Mod.: “Although he was the supreme pontiff, he called himself a servant,” etc.]. Behold what a man of innocence he was [Note: [Col. 0565D] Amb., “what a man of innocence he was.”]: although the Lombards were unbelieving and laid everything waste, he did not wish to involve himself in their death [Note: [Col. 0565D] Amb., “he had not wished to involve himself.”].

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the reign of Adaloald and the peace made with the Franks

Thus [Note: [Col. 0565D] In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 605, during the eighth indiction.] in the following summer, in the month of July, Adaloald was raised as king over the Lombards at Milan, in the Circus [Col. 0566B], in the presence of his father, King Agilulf. Envoys of Theudebert [Note: [Col. 0565D] It can also be inferred from the age of King Theudebert’s daughter that she was betrothed to Adaloald while still a child and before reaching the age of three. At that time Theudebert himself had scarcely reached his twentieth year, as can be gathered from the Frankish Annals.] king of the Franks were present, and the daughter of King Theudebert was betrothed to the royal boy [Note: [Col. 0565D] The words “king of the Franks, and the daughter of King Theudebert was betrothed to the royal boy” are absent from other copies. Lind.]. A perpetual peace was established with the Franks [Note: [Col. 0565D] The following words written by Fredegar in his *Chronicle*—no. 45—relate to this passage and are highly useful for illustrating our history:

“I shall relate how the Lombard people paid an annual tribute of twelve thousand solidi to the Frankish dominion, and I shall not conceal the manner in which they ceded two cities, Augusta and Siusium, with their territories, to the Frankish side. After Cleph, the supreme prince, died, twelve Lombard dukes passed twelve years without kings. During that time, as is written above, they broke into various places in the Frankish kingdom. As a settlement for this presumption, they handed over the cities of Augusta and Siusium, with their entire territory and people, to Guntchramn’s side.

“After this they sent an embassy to the emperor Maurice. These twelve dukes each sent an envoy, seeking the protection and patronage of the empire. They also sent twelve other envoys to Guntchramn and Childebert, so that, having the protection and defense of the Franks, they might pay twelve thousand solidi annually in tribute to the two kings; and, by ceding the valley called Ametegis to Guntchramn’s side, they secured their protection wherever it was more suitable. After this they chose the patronage of the Franks with complete devotion. Soon, with Guntchramn’s and Childebert’s permission, the Lombards raised Authari the duke to kingship over themselves. Another Authari, himself a duke with his entire duchy, surrendered to imperial rule and remained there. King Authari paid annually the tribute that the Lombards had promised to the Frankish side. After his departure, his son Ago was raised to the kingship and is known to have fulfilled the same obligation.

“In the thirty-fifth year of Chlothar’s reign, three noble envoys of Lombard descent—Agilulf, Pompegius, and Gauto, or Guto—were sent by King Ago to King Chlothar. They asked that the twelve thousand solidi which they paid every year to the Frankish treasury be canceled, and cleverly presented three thousand solidi in secret: of these, Warnacharius received one thousand, Gundealdus one thousand, and Chucus one thousand. They presented Chlothar with thirty-five thousand solidi altogether. On the advice of those mentioned above, who had secretly received the gifts, Chlothar accepted the money, canceled the tribute owed by the Lombards, and confirmed perpetual friendship with the Lombards by oaths and treaties.”

Several things in Fredegar’s account here require correction, since he was not well informed about Lombard affairs: namely, that Agilulf was the son of Authari and that only twelve dukes ruled the Lombards after Cleph’s death, during the time of Maurice. I will not deny, however, that he knew what had happened in Gaul.]

## CHAPTER XXXII. The war of the Franks with the Saxons

At the same time, while the Franks were fighting the Saxons, a great slaughter took place on both sides. At Pavia, too, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, the cantor Peter was struck by lightning [Col. 0567A].

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the peace made with the patrician Smaragdus and the capture of the Tuscan cities

Then, in the following month of November, King Agilulf made a one-year truce with the patrician Smaragdus [Note: [Col. 0567B] Other copy: “a truce.” Lind.], receiving twelve thousand solidi from the Romans. The cities of Tuscany—namely the King’s Bath [Note: [Col. 0567B] Mod., “the King’s Bath.”] and the Old City—were also invaded by the Lombards. Then, in April and May, a star appeared in the sky, which they call a comet. Afterward King Agilulf again made peace with the Romans for three years [Note: [Col. 0567B] That is, in the year 606.].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the death of Severus the patriarch and the priesthoods of John and Candidianus

[Col. 0567B]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Death of Patriarch Severus, and the Ordination of John and Candidianus

[Col. 0567B]

In these days, after Patriarch Severus had died, [Note: [Col. 0567B] Mod.: “John was ordained in his place,” etc.] John the abbot was ordained patriarch at Old Aquileia, with [Col. 0568A] the consent of the king and Duke Gisulf. At Grado also Candidianus [Note: [Col. 0567B] Mod. and Lind.: Romanus.] Romanus was ordained bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0567B] Having removed the errors that our author had accumulated in several places in Book III, chapter 26, I shall follow the learned Norisius, drawing on no other source than the books themselves of the schismatics, in relating what happened after the false synod of Marano. I shall review the acts of the blessed Gregory in this same affair—Gregory who succeeded Pelagius and devoted no less care to bringing the schismatics back to the Church.

At the beginning, he summoned Severus, bishop of Aquileia, to Rome, together with the other schismatic bishops, because Severus had violated the faith which he had professed before John, archbishop of Ravenna, [Col. 0567C] as is stated in Book I of the letters, together with the imperial commands that he had obtained. After receiving these, Severus called his colleagues together. A disorderly synod was held by those who were subject to Lombard rule, and its decision was that no one should go to Rome. Letters were sent to Maurice, and it was resolved to reject the judgment of the Roman See.

Meanwhile, after Severus had assembled the bishops of Istria, they jointly adopted the decision to appeal from the pope to Caesar. By the letters they sent, they so influenced Maurice with their fabrications that he wrote to Gregory and to the Roman exarch, ordering that no molestation be inflicted upon them; for he feared that, if force were used, the Istrians—who still adhered to their own party—might be made more favorable to the Lombards.

As long as Romanus held the exarchate, Gregory had no hope of correcting the schismatics; nor was there any while Callinicus remained in the same office. But after Callinicus was recalled to Constantinople, Smaragdus came to Italy again. Remembering his earlier successful conduct of affairs, Gregory once more provoked him by letters against Severus and the schismatics. In the meantime Maurice was killed. Gregory had never found him favorable to his cause, but under the emperor Phocas he had already conceived better hopes, when shortly afterward he departed to heaven.

Severus of Aquileia, however, did not long survive. He too died in the year 605. “And because,” as John the Deacon writes, quoted by Norisius in The Life of Saint Gregory, chapter 38, “he did not deserve to return to the unity of the holy universal Church, by his own madness he also stirred up the Roman pontiff to divide the unity of his own diocese, so that from the time of his death the diocese of Aquileia was divided between two metropolitans, namely, the Catholic and the schismatic. Nor afterward, although all in general returned from the schism to unity, could it be restored to its former union down to the present time.”

For when the people of Grado sought a Catholic bishop and the people of Aquileia a schismatic bishop, each side obtained its own: Candidianus of Ariminum for the Catholics, and John the abbot for the schismatics. [Col. 0568B] The exarch supported Candidianus, while Agilulf supported John. It is clear from the register of the letters of the blessed Gregory how welcome the schismatics were at Agilulf’s court. Indeed, there was already a rumor that Queen Theodelinda had gone over to them. For this reason Gregory sent her many letters, including those in Book III of the Register and another which I quoted above, when he congratulated her on the birth of Adalwald.

Our author’s further statement here, that the schismatic John was ordained at Old Aquileia with the consent of King Agilulf and Duke Gisulf, is also found in the Chronicle of Dandulus, reported by Ughellus. From this source, as Norisius and others note, Martianus must be rejected, since he makes him Severus’s successor.

“After Marcian,” writes Dandulus, “Candidianus succeeded as patriarch in the aforesaid metropolitan see of Grado. During his time, with the consent of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, Duke Gisulf forcibly ordained John the abbot bishop at Forum Julii. Three bishops consented to this, with God opposed to them, and they ordained him, etc. He sat for five years.”]

Again, in November and December, a comet appeared. After Candidianus had died at Grado, the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0568C]

Others: “Epiphanius.” Lind.

In the year 615, as Ughellus generally reckons it. Dandulus says the following about him: “This man, by nationality an Istrian from the town of Humag, was a Catholic man and sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures. He was made a presbyter and notary of this see by Patriarch Elias, and at the Council of Grado competently carried out the office entrusted to him. Later, Patriarch Severus appointed him first of the notaries. Now, by the bishops, clergy, and people who remained devoted to the Romans, he was elected and consecrated patriarch at Grado, and for this reason was afterward called the Gradan.”]

Epiphanius, who had been [Note: [Col. 0568C] “First of the notaries” means nothing other than leader or chief: just as there was a first of the accountants and a first of the record-keepers, so there was also a second and a third. In the time of Nicephorus Gregoras this title fell out of use, and they called the first official “lord.” Thus he himself writes in Roman History, Book VII, p. 109: “They now call the leader of Boeotia and Thebes ‘great lord’ instead of ‘great first official’” (Τῆς Βοιωτίας καὶ τῶν Θηβῶν ἀρχηγὸν, ἀντὶ μεγάλου πριμμικερίου, μέγαν κύριον ὀνομάζουσι νῦν). Different people have different opinions about the origin of the name. Some think they were called that as though they were “first wax,” that is, inscribed first on a white tablet or register; others think that τὸ cerius is merely an extension of the word, signifying nothing further. Lind.]

the first of the notaries, was ordained patriarch by the bishops who were under Roman rule; and from that time two patriarchs began to exist.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Invasion of the City of Naples, and the Death of the False Emperor Eleutherius

At this time John Compsinus invaded Naples. A few days later, Eleutherius the patrician expelled him from that city [Note: [Col. 0568D] Amb.: “Eleutherius the eunuch patrician assumed the imperial authority.”] and killed him. After this the same Eleutherius, the eunuch patrician, assumed the imperial authority.

[Col. 0568B] While he was traveling from Ravenna to Rome, he was killed by soldiers at the fortress of Luceoli, and his head was carried to Constantinople to the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Anastasius the Librarian, in his Life of the Holy Deusdedit, writes: “At the same time Eleutherius the patrician and chamberlain came to Ravenna and killed all who had been involved in the murder of John, exarch and judge of the state. He came to Rome and was received by the most holy Pope Deusdedit with great honor. When he had left Rome, he came to Naples, which was held by John Compsinus Intarta—or, as others read, Antarta. Eleutherius the patrician entered Naples by fighting and killed the tyrant. He then returned to Ravenna, and after a gift had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout all Italy.”

And in the Life of Boniface V, the successor of Saint Deusdedit: “At the same time, before the days of his ordination, Eleutherius the patrician and eunuch, having become Intarta, seized the kingdom. When he came to the Roman city, he was killed there by the soldiers of Ravenna in the fortress called Luceoli. His head was taken to Constantinople to the most pious emperor.”

From these accounts we clearly learn the sequence of events, and indeed that the event occurred somewhat later than our author states. For while the see was vacant, before the ordination of Boniface, Eleutherius, himself a rebel like John Compsinus, had been killed—namely, in the year 618. See what Camillus Peregrinius noted in his Dissertation on the Boundaries of the Duchy of Benevento toward the South, p. 33.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Peace Made with the Emperor

[Col. 0569A]

At this time also King Agilulf sent his notary Stabilicianus to Constantinople, to [Note: [Col. 0569B] Others: “Stablicianus.” Lind.] the emperor Phocas [Note: [Col. 0569C] Anib.: “Phocas.”]. When he returned with the emperor’s ambassadors, peace having been made for one year, the same ambassadors presented imperial gifts to King Agilulf.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Phocas Augustus, His Death, and the Empire of Heraclius

Phocas, therefore, as has been stated above, after Maurice and his sons had been killed, invaded the Roman kingdom and ruled for the course of eight years. [Note: [Col. 0569C] Not quite complete: for he had been crowned on 23 November 602, and, according to the common reckoning of learned men, Heraclius was inaugurated emperor in October of the year of Christ 610, on a Monday, as I noted above and as the Alexandrian Chronicle likewise records.]

At the request of Pope Boniface, Phocas decreed that the Roman and apostolic See should be the head of all the Churches, because the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0570A] was styling itself the first of all the Churches. [Note: [Col. 0569C] Anastasius, in his Life of Boniface III, from whom Paul perhaps took this passage: “He obtained from Phocas, the ruler, that the apostolic See of blessed Peter the apostle should be the head of all the Churches, that is, the Roman Church, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was first of all the Churches.”

This celebrated question in ecclesiastical annals concerns the title “ecumenical,” or “universal,” which John, surnamed the Faster, bishop of Constantinople, had tried with the greatest ambition to arrogate to himself in the time of the blessed Gregory the Great. This innovation, whose roots reached deeper—namely, the repeated attempts to establish primacy in the see of Constantinople despite the opposition of the Roman pontiffs—offended the holy pontiff as was fitting. Yet he scarcely refrained from ecclesiastical censure against John himself, although John was otherwise a religious man.

Several letters on this matter remain in Gregory’s register, addressed to his own representative, to John himself, to the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, to the empress, and to the emperor Maurice. Among them, the twentieth letter of Book V of the cited edition contains many arguments by which he attacked this new title, though his efforts were fruitless so long as Maurice reigned, since Bishop John enjoyed great influence with him.

After all these men had been removed from this life by various fates, Boniface III, who succeeded Gregory after Sabinianus, finally obtained this from Phocas, the successor of Maurice, while Cyriacus occupied the see of Constantinople. Phocas confirmed it by an edict, declaring that “such a title was fitting for the Roman Church alone and belonged exclusively to the Roman pontiff, who should be called universal, but not the bishop of Constantinople,” as the eminent Baronius reports. Under the year 606, see there the renewed disputes between Phocas and Cyriacus, taken from Theophanes, which the famous author thinks provoked the emperor to issue this decree out of hatred for Cyriacus.]

That same emperor, at the request of another Pope Boniface, ordered that the old shrine called the Pantheon [Note: [Col. 0570B] Amb.: “which had previously been called.”] be cleansed of the filth of idolatry and made into a church of the blessed perpetual Virgin Mary and of all the martyrs, so that where once the worship of all—not gods, but demons—had been carried on [Note: [Col. 0570B] Mod.: “was practiced.”], there afterward the memory of all the saints might be celebrated. [Note: [Col. 0570B] Anastasius likewise writes, in his Life of Saint Boniface IV: “At the same time he asked the ruler Phocas for the temple called the Pantheon, in which he made a church of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, and of all the martyrs.” Concerning the dedication of this celebrated temple, which is still seen at Rome under the popular name Santa Maria della Rotonda, see Papebrochius, in the Life of Saint Boniface IV, under 25 May, and Pagi, under the year 607, no. 3.]

In his time the Prasini and Veneti [Note: [Col. 0570B] These were the factions of the charioteers. See Pliny, Book VII, chapter 33; Suetonius, Life of Domitian, chapter 7; Tertullian, On Spectacles, chapter 9; Cassiodorus, Book III of the Variæ, letter 13; Suidas, Isidore, and Cedrenus, at the beginning of the Roman Empire. Lind.] waged civil war throughout the East and Egypt, and slaughtered one another. [Note: [Col. 0570C] Others: “on their own.” Lind.] The Persians also, waging the most serious wars against the Roman state, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself. [Note: [Col. 0570C] “And destroying the holy churches and profaning the sacred things among them,” etc. Amb.]

They destroyed the churches and profaned the holy things. [Note: [Col. 0570C] Others: “They carried away the ancient ornaments of the holy places and fortified them, and also carried off the holy banner of the Lord’s cross.” Lind., and likewise Mod. and Amb.; but τὼ veterum is not found. Paul is mistaken here in connecting the capture of Jerusalem by King Chosroes with the years of Phocas’s reign. For it is clear from Theophanes and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle that this notable calamity occurred under Heraclius, in the second indiction, which falls in the year 614. Nowhere is it related at greater length than in the Alexandrian Chronicle, whose words we reproduce:

“Indiction 2, year 4 after the consulship of Heraclius Augustus, III. From 22 January is recorded the second year of the reign of Heraclius the younger Constantine. In this year, around the month of June, a calamity worthy of unending lamentation befell us. For, together with many cities of the East, Jerusalem too was captured by the Persians, and many thousands of clergy, monks, and virgin nuns were slaughtered in it. The Lord’s tomb and the famous temples of God were burned. In short, all precious things were destroyed. The venerable wood of the Cross, together with the innumerable sacred vessels, was taken by the Persians, and Patriarch Zacharias was also taken captive.

These events did not occur over a long period or during an entire month, but within a few days. On the fourteenth of the month Gorpiæus, which the Romans call September, in the third indiction, at the third exaltation of the life-giving Cross, the venerable sponge was received and, together with the life-giving Cross, was elevated in the great church, having been sent by the patrician Nicetas. On the twenty-eighth of Hyperberetæus, which the Romans call October, on the seventh day, during the night preceding Sunday, the venerable lance was brought from the holy places. One of those who attended the accursed Sarbaras, after receiving it from them, gave it to the aforementioned Nicetas. Immediately, on that Sunday, it was proclaimed in the great and most holy church as soon as it had been brought in. On Tuesday and Wednesday it was venerated by men, and on Thursday and Friday by women.”]

They also carried away the banner of the Lord’s cross from among the ornaments of the holy places. [Col. 0571A] Against this Phocas, Heraclianus, who governed Africa, rebelled. Coming with an army, he deprived him of both kingdom and life, and his son Heraclius [Note: [Col. 0571D] He is also called the father of the emperor Heraclius in the Alexandrian Chronicle.] assumed the government of the Roman state. [Note: [Col. 0571D] In the year 610.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Death of Duke Gisulf, the Plundering of the City of Forum Julii, and the Other Calamities Suffered by the Lombards from the Huns

Around this time the king of the Avars, whom in their own language they call the Chagan, [Note: [Col. 0571D] Historians commonly attest that the kings of the Avars were called Chagans.] came with an innumerable multitude and entered the territory of Venetia. Duke Gisulf of Forum Julii boldly went to meet him with as many Lombards as he could gather. But although with courageous determination he fought with a few men against an immense multitude, he was nevertheless surrounded on every side and almost entirely destroyed with all his men.

The wife of Gisulf, Romilda by name, fortified herself within the enclosure of the walls of the fortress of Forum Julii, together with the Lombards who had escaped and with the wives and children of those who had perished in the battle. [Note: [Col. 0571D] Mod.: “She was enclosed within the walls of the fortress of Forum Julii.”]

She had sons named Taso and [Note: [Col. 0571D] Others: “Caco,” and so below. Lind.] Cacco, already youths, while Radoaldus and Grimoaldus were still children. She also had four daughters, one of whom was called [Note: [Col. 0572C] Others: “Pappa.” Lind. and Mod.] Appa, and another Gaila; we do not know the names of the other two.

The Lombards also fortified themselves in the other neighboring fortresses, namely at [Note: [Col. 0572C] Others: “Cormones.” Lind.] Cormons, [Note: [Col. 0572C] Mod.: “Nemasapo.” Amb.: “Hemas Osopo.” Others: “Nemas”; others: “Memaso Osopio.” Lind.] Nomaso, Osopo, Artenia, [Note: [Col. 0572C] Others: “Reumari.” Lind.] Reunia, [Note: [Col. 0572C] Manuscript: “Glemonia.” Lind.] Glemona, and also [Note: [Col. 0572C] Others: “at Bilige.” Lind. and Mod. Others: “Mibligine.” Cluverius, in Ancient Italy, on this passage of Paul the Deacon: “Osopum, a fortress, also called Osopium or Osupum—for Paul the Deacon’s manuscripts vary this name in this way—is situated on the same river and is still commonly called Osopo. It is conspicuous above Reunia on a natural and elevated rock surrounded by the neighboring fields. Artenia and Glemona are nearby fortresses: the inhabitants now call the former Artegna in their native language, and the latter Ghiemona, or, more corruptly, Gemona, etc.

“I infer from the proximity of the places already described that the Nemasus of Paul the Deacon is the village which is now commonly called Mazo, on the Fella River, not far from the confluence with the Tagliamento and from the town of Venzone. But the manuscripts of the Deacon vary greatly here: some have Nemaso, others Nomaso, others Hemas, some Nemas, and several Memaso, though most have the first syllable Ne. It is mentioned again in Book V, chapter 22: ‘At the fortress of Nemas, not far from Forum Julii, he was killed.’

“The remaining fortress, Ibiligo in some manuscripts, Ibligo in others, and Biligo in still others, seems to be the village which, below the town of Tercentum, divided by the right bank of the river, opposite the fortresses mentioned above, is now commonly called Biliris.”]

Ibligine, whose position is wholly impregnable. In the same way, they fortified themselves in the remaining fortresses, so that they would not become prey to the Huns, that is, [Note: [Col. 0572D] Others: “Avars,” or “Bavarians.” Lind.] the Avars.

The Avars, however, ranging throughout the territory of Forum Julii, devastating everything with fire and plunder, shut up the town of Forum Julii under siege and attempted to storm it with all their strength. Their king, that is, [Note: [Col. 0572D] Others: “the aforesaid Chagan.” Lind.] the Chagan, while he went armed around the walls [Note: [Col. 0572D] Mod.: “was walking around armed with an army.”] with a large cavalry force, seeking the side from which he might more easily capture the city, was observed by Romilda from the walls. When she saw that he was flourishing in youthful age, the wicked harlot desired him, and immediately sent him word that, if he would take her in marriage, she would surrender to him the city together with all who were in it.

When the barbarian king heard this, he promised, through the deceit of his own wickedness, that he would do what she had requested, and pledged to take her in marriage. She, without delay, opened the gates of the fortress of Forum Julii and admitted the enemy to her own destruction and that of all who were there. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Mod.: “him.”]

When the Avars entered Forum Julii with their king, they plundered everything they could find. They burned the city itself with fire and carried away captive everyone they found, falsely promising that they would settle them in the territories of Pannonia from which they had come.

When they were returning to their homeland and had reached a field which they call Sacred, they decided to kill with the sword all the Lombards who had reached mature age, while dividing the women [Note: [Col. 0572D] The words “and the children” are absent. Taso is also not found in some manuscripts. Lind.] and children by lot as slaves.

Taso and Cacco, or [Col. 0573A] Rodoaldus, the sons of Gisulf and Romilda, when they learned of this wickedness of the Avars, immediately mounted horses and took flight. One of them wished to kill their young brother Grimoaldus, thinking that, being so small, he could not keep himself on a running horse, and judging it better to kill him with the sword than to let him endure the yoke of captivity.

When he had raised his spear in order to strike him, the weeping boy cried out, saying: [Note: [Col. 0573D] Amb.: “Do not stab me, my brother,” etc.] “Do not stab me, for I can keep myself on the horse.” Then, reaching out his hand, he seized him by the arm and placed him on the bare back of the horse, and encouraged him to hold on. The boy grasped the horse’s bridle with his hand and followed his fleeing brothers.

When the Avars discovered this, they immediately mounted their horses and pursued them. The others escaped by swift flight, but the boy Grimoaldus was seized by one of them who had ridden faster. [Note: [Col. 0573D] Others read *tamen eum comprehensum* (“yet [him] captured”). Lind.] Nevertheless, his captor did not think it worthy of him to strike the boy with the sword because of his tender age, but kept him instead to serve him. [Note: [Col. 0573D] Others: “Although the enemy, returning to the camp, was leading him back by grasping the bridle of his horse, he rejoiced at such a great…” Lind.]

As he was leading him back to the camp, holding the horse’s bridle, and exulting in such noble spoil—for the boy was of elegant appearance, with shining eyes and hair as white as milk—the captive, grieved to be dragged away, summoned great courage in his narrow breast. He drew from its sheath the sword that he could possess at that age [Note: [Col. 0573D] τὼ “narrow” is not found in Amb. Likewise, “sheath.”], and struck the Avar who was dragging him at the back of the head with as much force as he could muster. [Note: [Col. 0573D] Others: “And he struck the head of the enemy going before him with whatever small effort he could.” Lind.] The blow reached the brain, and the enemy was thrown from his horse. But the boy Grimoaldus, [Note: [Col. 0573D] Mod. does not contain “having turned.”] turning his horse, joyfully took flight [Col. 0573C] and at last rejoined his brothers. When he announced his own escape to them, he also gave them immeasurable joy by reporting the enemy’s death.

The Avars killed with the sword all the Lombards who had reached manhood, while they carried away the women and children under the yoke of captivity.

As for Romilda, who had been the source of all this wickedness, the king of the Avars, in accordance with the oath he had sworn to her, kept her for one night as though in marriage. Finally, he handed her over to twelve Avars, who tormented her with lust throughout the entire night, taking turns among themselves.

Afterward he ordered a stake to be fixed in the middle of the field and commanded that she be impaled upon its point [Note: [Col. 0573D] Mod.: “upon its summit.” Receptum etiam hoc genus supplicii Sclavis fuit. Helmoldus Historiae Slavorum cap. 53: “Quanta enim mortium genera Christicolis intulerint, relatu difficile est, cum his quidem viscera extorserint palo circumducentes, hos cruci affixerunt irridentes signum Redemptionis nostrae.” Lind. Tunc primum hoc tormenti genus in Italia visum plures notaverunt.] [This type of punishment was also customary among the Slavs. Helmold, *History of the Slavs*, ch. 53: “It is difficult to relate how many kinds of death they inflicted on Christians: from some they tore out the entrails, winding them about a stake; others they fastened to a cross, mocking the sign of our Redemption.” Lind. Many have observed that this form of torture was then first seen in Italy.], adding this reproach: “Such a husband is what you deserve to have.” Thus the dreadful betrayer of her country perished by such a death. She had cared more for her own lust than for the safety of her fellow citizens and relatives.

Her daughters, however, did not follow their mother’s lust but devoted themselves to the love of chastity. So that they would not be defiled by the Avars, they placed the flesh of raw chickens beneath a band around their breasts. The flesh, putrefying from the heat, gave off a foul smell. When the Avars wished to touch them, they could not endure the stench. They thought that the girls naturally smelled that way, and withdrew from them in disgust, saying that all Lombard women were foul-smelling.

By this device the noble girls escaped the lust of the Avars and remained chaste, while they also left women a useful example for preserving chastity, should anything of that kind happen to them. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Others: “a useful model.” Lind.] Later, having been sold in various [Note: [Col. 0574D] Amb.: “provinces.”] regions, they obtained marriages worthy of their nobility. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Amb.: “were sought in marriage.”] One of them, they say, married the king of the Alamanni, and another the ruler of the Bavarians. [Note: [Col. 0574D] John Aventinus writes in the Annals of that people that Gaila married Gariobald, ruler of the Bavarians.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Genealogy of Paul the Son of Arnefrid

[Col. 0574B]

[Note: [Col. 0574D] Amb.: “But the occasion now requires,” etc.] The occasion now requires that, setting aside general history, I should also relate briefly and privately the genealogy of myself, [Note: [Col. 0574D] The words “I who write this” are absent in Amb.] who am writing this, and, since circumstances demand it, repeat the course of the narrative somewhat earlier.

At the time when the nation of the Lombards came from Pannonia to Italy, my great-grandfather Leuphis [Note: [Col. 0574D] Amb. and Mod.: “Leupchis”; others: “Leuchis.” Lind.] came with them as one of the same Lombard people.

After he had lived in Italy for several years, he died, leaving behind five sons whom he had fathered, still little boys. This disaster of captivity, of which we have just spoken, seized them and led them all from the fortress of Forum Julii into exile in the land of the Avars. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Mod.: “this period.”] [Note: [Col. 0574D] Mod.: “seizing them.”]

After they had endured the misery of captivity in that region for many years and had reached manhood, four of them—whose names we do not retain—remained in the distress of captivity. Their fifth brother, named [Note: [Col. 0574D] Mod.: “Leuphis.” A.: “Leupigis.” L.: “Leuchis,” or “Leupchis.”] Lupicis, who afterward became my great-grandfather, determined, with the inspiration—as we believe—of the Author of mercy, to cast off the yoke of captivity. He sought to make his way to Italy, where he remembered that the Lombard people dwelt, and to return to the rights of freedom.

When he had undertaken the journey and begun his flight, carrying only a quiver, a bow, and a small amount of food for the road, and not knowing at all where he should go, a wolf came to him and became his companion and guide. It went ahead of him, frequently looked back, stopped when he stopped, and preceded him when he moved forward. He understood that it had been divinely given to him to show him the road that he did not know.

After they had traveled in this way for several days through the wilderness of the mountains, the bread that the traveler had possessed, though it had been little, ran out completely. As he continued his journey fasting and grew weak from hunger [Note: [Col. 0575C] The word *fame* (“hunger”) is not found in Mod.], he stretched his bow and wished to kill the wolf with an arrow so that he might eat it. But the wolf anticipated the attacker’s blow and escaped from his sight.

When the wolf had gone away, he did not know where to go. Moreover, he had become exceedingly weak from lack of food. As he was already despairing of life, he threw himself upon the ground and fell asleep. In his sleep he saw a certain man speaking these words to him:

“Rise, you who sleep. Take the road in the direction opposite to where your feet are pointing; for Italy, to which you are traveling, lies that way.”

He immediately rose and began to go in the direction he had heard indicated in his dream. Before long he reached a human dwelling. There was in fact a settlement of Slavs in those places.

When an old woman saw him, she immediately understood that he was a fugitive and suffering from lack of food. Moved by compassion for him, she hid him in her house and secretly supplied him with food little by little, lest, if she provided nourishment to the point of satiety, she should extinguish his life altogether. [Note: [Col. 0575C] Others: “And thus she provided him with an adequate amount of food until he recovered his strength.” Lind.]

In the end she gave him food in moderation until he had recovered and was able to regain his strength. When she saw that he was strong enough to undertake the journey, she gave him provisions and instructed him in which direction he should go. [Note: [Col. 0575C] Amb.: “encouraged him.”]

After traveling for several days, he entered Italy and reached the house in which he had been born. It was so deserted that it had not only no roof but was also full of brambles and thorns. After cutting these down, [Note: [Col. 0575C] Amb.: “finding a spear within those same walls,”] he found a great ash tree within the same walls and hung his quiver on it.

Later, enriched by gifts from his relatives and friends, he rebuilt the house and took a wife. But he could recover nothing of the property that his father had possessed, since those who had seized it had excluded him through their long and continuous possession.

As I have already stated above, he was my great-grandfather. He fathered my grandfather Arichis; Arichis in turn fathered my father Warnefrid; and Warnefrid, by his wife Theudelinda, fathered me, Paul, and my brother Arichis, who bore the name of our grandfather.

Having given this brief account of the sequence of my own genealogy, let us now return to the path of general history.

## CHAPTER LX. The Duchy and the Death of Taso and Saco
After the death, as we have said, of Gisulf, duke of Friuli, his sons Taso and Cacco undertook the government of the same duchy. In their time they possessed the region of the Slavs called Zellia [Col. 0576B] [Note: [Col. 0575C] Ambrosian and Modenese: “Cagellia”; Lindanus: “Aglia.” A region of Upper Pannonia, now called the county of Cilli, or Zemplén county after the town of Zemplín, is part of the Upper Kingdom of Hungary.], as far as the place called Medaria. From there until the time of Duke Ratchis [Note: [Col. 0575D] Ambrosian: “Ratigis.”], these same Slavs paid tribute to the dukes of Friuli.

The Roman patrician Gregory treacherously killed these two brothers in the city of Opitergium.

> [Note: [Col. 0575D] Al.: “For when he promised that he would cut Taso’s beard as was customary, and declared him his son,” etc. Lind. The custom of the ancients is explained with great learning by Adrian Valesius in his notes on Berengarius. After indicating by several examples what it meant among the Romans to celebrate a *barbatoria*, he adds: “Traces of the ancient custom also remained among Christians. Parents, relatives, and friends would lead a youth to be shaved in church, and through the ministry of a priest or even a bishop they would offer good wishes for him whose first down was about to be removed. In the Book of Sacraments of Pope Gregory there is found, together with the prayer for the cutting of the hair, also a prayer for cutting the beard, which is as follows: ‘O God, by whose Spirit every creature rejoices when it grows to maturity, hear our prayers for this servant of yours, N., who rejoices in the beauty of youthful age and is to be shorn at its first beginning, so that, protected in all things by the help of your protection, he may receive heavenly blessing and rejoice in the safeguards both of the present life and of the eternal one.’ The nobles, moreover, chose some man of great dignity by whose hand their first beard would be removed. Thus the Lombard Taso, duke of the men of Friuli, had chosen the Roman patrician and exarch of Ravenna, Gregory, for this purpose; but through fraud and treachery he was killed by him. For Gregory had promised under oath that he would cut Taso’s beard as was customary and make him his son, etc., as Paul relates in Book IV of *The History of the Lombards*. From this it is clear that the person whose first beard had been removed by another’s hand stood to that other in the position of an adopted son. The cutting of the first beard, together with the preparation of the festive banquet that was customarily given to relatives and friends, and even the day itself on which the beard was removed, was called a *barbatoria*. See more on this subject in the same author.”]

For when he promised Taso that he would cut his beard as was customary and make him his son, Taso himself, together with his brother Cacco and selected young men, entered Opitergium and came to Gregory, suspecting no evil.

> [Note: [Col. 0576D] Al.: “Having entered the same Opitergium with his chosen retainers,” etc. Lind.]

As soon as the patrician had seen that he had entered Opitergium with his companions, he ordered the city gates to be closed and sent armed soldiers against Taso and his companions.

> [Note: [Col. 0576D] Amb.: “Suspecting nothing.”]

When Taso and his men learned this, they boldly prepared themselves for battle; and, bidding one another farewell after peace had been granted them, they scattered here and there through the several streets of the city, killing everyone they could find in their way.

> [Note: [Col. 0576D] Mod.: “Through the several streets of the city, as best they could, and elsewhere, killing those who attacked them in the several streets of the city, when they had inflicted a great slaughter,” etc. Lind.]

After they had inflicted a great slaughter on the Romans, they too were finally killed. Patrician Gregory, however, because of the oath he had given, ordered Taso’s head to be brought to him and, perjuring himself, cut off his beard as he had promised.

> [Note: [Col. 0576D–0577B] Fredegarius relates the matter differently in his *Chronicle*, under the ninth year of King Dagobert, corresponding to 631—or, if he himself reckoned differently, perhaps to 630. He had indicated that Arioald, immediately after receiving the kingdom, had planned to kill Taso, not the duke of Friuli but the duke of Tuscany.
