He then continues: “In that year Charoald, king of the Lombards, secretly sent envoys to the patrician Isaac and asked him by whatever means he could to kill Taso, duke of the province of Tuscany. In return for this service, he promised that the three hundred measures of gold which the Lombards received annually from the public treasury—that is, from the imperial treasury—would be reduced by one hundred measures of gold, which King Charoald would cancel for the imperial side. When the patrician Isaac heard this, he considered by what devices he might accomplish it. He sent an ingenious message to Taso, who was then in disgrace with King Charoald, asking him to enter into friendship with him, while he himself would provide him assistance against King Charoald. Deceived by this stratagem, Taso went to Ravenna. Isaac sent word to meet him, but, through fear of the emperor, did not dare to admit Taso and his armed followers within the walls of Ravenna. When Taso, believing this, left the weapons of his men outside the city and entered Ravenna, the men who had been prepared immediately attacked him and killed both him and all his companions who had come with him. King Charoald then cancelled one hundred measures of gold for the imperial side, as he had promised Isaac; thereafter only two hundred measures were paid annually by the Lombards to the Roman patrician. One measure contains one hundred pounds of gold. Immediately afterward King Charoald died.” Although Aimoinus usually copies Fredegarius in his *History of the Franks*, in Book IV, chapter 32, when he relates Taso’s death, he agrees with our Paul.]

## CHAPTER XLI  
### On Grasulf, Duke of Friuli, and on the arrival of Radoald and Grimoald in Benevento

After these men had been killed, Grasulf, brother of Gisulf, was appointed duke of Friuli.

Radoald and Grimoald, however, considering it beneath them to live under the authority of their uncle Grasulf, and already approaching youthful maturity, boarded a small boat and, rowing, reached the territory of Benevento. From there they hastened to Arichis, duke of the Beneventans and formerly their tutor. He received them most warmly and treated them as his sons.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] Al.: “Raichis”; manuscript of Lindanus: “Archis”; Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts: “Arichis.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] Amb.: “Under his rule”; Al.: “Under the authority of their uncle,” and do not read “Grasulf.” Lind.]

At this time, after Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, had died, his son Garibaldus was defeated by the Slavs at Aguntum, and the territories of the Bavarians were plundered.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] Al.: “At Maguntia.” Lind.]

Nevertheless, after the Bavarians had recovered their strength, they both wrested the plunder from the enemy and drove the enemy from their own borders.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] We owe to Paul information about the Slavs and other peoples who occupied various regions at this time—information that we read nowhere else. Aguntum was a town of Noricum, ninety Roman miles from Aquileia and sixty from Julium Carnicum. See the *Itinerary of Antoninus*.]

## CHAPTER XLII  
### On the peace made with the emperor and with the Franks, the devastation of Istria, and the death of Gunduald

King Agilulf made peace with the emperor for one year and then for another, and likewise renewed peace with the Franks.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] Amb.: “Renewed the harmony of peace.”]

In that same year the Slavs, after killing the soldiers, disastrously plundered Istria.

In the following month of March, Secundus, servant of Christ, died at Trent. We have already often spoken of him; he composed, down to his own time, a brief history of the deeds of the Lombards.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] See what I noted above, chapter 28, note 99.]

At that time King Agilulf again established peace with the emperor. In those days Theudebert, king of the Franks, was also killed, and an exceedingly fierce battle was fought between them.

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] Al.: “Between the Franks.” Lind.]

> [Note: [Col. 0577D–0578B] Fredegarius testifies in his *Chronicle* that this final war between Theudebert, Chlothar, and Theuderic was fought in the seventeenth year of Theuderic’s reign, and therefore belongs to the year 613 of the Lord. The battle was fought at Tolbiacum, and Theudebert, after being defeated, withdrew to Cologne. Theuderic pursued him, captured him through the treachery of his own men, and sent him to his grandmother Brunechild. “She asked that he be made a cleric. But not many days later, in great wickedness, she ordered him to be killed after his clerical ordination,” as Jonas writes in the *Life of Saint Columbanus*. After him his two sons, Chlothar and the boy Meroveus, were killed, their brains being dashed out against a rock.]

Gunduald also, the brother of Queen Theudelinda, who was duke in the city of Asti, died at this very time, struck by an arrow, although no one knew who had caused his death.

> [Note: [Col. 0578B–0579A] Fredegarius gives a fuller account of this matter. In relating Theodolinda’s second marriage with King Ago, he either did not know of her first marriage with Antharius or deliberately passed over it as having lasted only a short time: “Ago, he writes, king of the Lombards, took as his wife Theudelinda, sister of Grimoald and Gundoald, of Frankish stock—elsewhere he says Bavarian stock—whom Childebert had previously betrothed. After he had set her aside on the advice of Brunechild, Gundoald transferred himself and all his possessions to Italy with his sister Theudelinda and gave Theudelinda in marriage to Ago. Gundoald took a wife from a noble Lombard family, by whom he had two sons, named Gundebert and Haribert. King Ago, son of King Authari, had by Theudelinda a son named Odoald and a daughter named Gundeberga. While Gundoald was greatly loved by the Lombards, King Ago and Theudelinda, already jealous of him, arranged his death. While he was sitting on a *faldaone* to relieve his bowels, he was wounded by an arrow and died.” Much in this agrees with our Paul. But whether one should believe Fredegarius when he seems to suggest that Theodolinda, praised for her remarkable piety, consented to so savage a crime against her brother is another question—unless Gundobald’s desire to reign had grown so great that he rose against his kinsman the king and against his own sister, and thus deservedly paid the penalty. It should also be noted that he says Childebert, on the advice of Brunechild, withdrew from the marriage arrangement with Theodolinda. Our author gives this history differently, and the others follow him.]

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### On the death of Agilulf, the reign of Adaloald, his expulsion, and the reign of Arioald

King Agilulf, also called Ago, after reigning for twenty-five years, died, leaving his son Adaloald, still a very young boy, as king, together with his mother Theudelinda.

> [Note: [Col. 0578D] Al.: “Adalvald,” and so throughout. Lind.]

> [Note: [Col. 0578D] Adaloald was born in the year 603, and at that time Easter fell on the seventh day before the Ides of April, as Paul says; thus he was already thirteen years old.]

> [Note: [Col. 0578D–0579A] That is, in the year 616. For he was raised to the kingship in 591, and if he reigned for twenty-five years, his death must be assigned to this year, not to the following year, as Sigebertus does in his *Chronicle*. The learned Pagius also confirms this by a charter of King Adaloald, his son and successor, in favor of the monastery of Bobbio, preserved by Ughelli in volume IV. It reads: “Given at Ticinum, in the palace, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the sixth year of our most fortunate reign, in the ninth indiction, prosperously.” “For,” he writes, “if in the year 621, marked by the ninth indiction, he was reckoning the sixth year of his reign, he had certainly assumed the kingdom before the twenty-sixth of July in that year.”]

Under him churches were restored and many gifts were bestowed upon holy places.

> [Note: [Col. 0579A] Amb.: “Donations.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0579A] This should be attributed to the devout queen. There is also another charter of the same King Adaloald in favor of the monastery of Bobbio, preserved by Ughelli in the place cited, volume IV.]

But when Adaloald became insane through a derangement of mind, after he had reigned for ten years with his mother, he was expelled from the kingdom, and the Lombards substituted Arioald in his place.

> [Note: [Col. 0579A–0579D] Fredegarius gives more information than our Paul about Adaloald: “In that same fortieth year,” he says, “of Chlothar, Adaloald, king of the Lombards, son of King Ago, succeeded his father in the kingdom. He kindly received the envoy of the emperor Maurice, named Eusebius, who had cleverly come to him. After being anointed in a bath with certain ointments, he was persuaded by Eusebius; and after the anointing he could do nothing except what Eusebius urged him to do. He was persuaded by him to arrange that all the more distinguished nobles in the Lombard kingdom should be killed. When he had already slain twelve of them with the sword, although they had committed no offense, the survivors, seeing that their lives were in danger—”

> “All the elders and the most noble men of the Lombard nation, acting in concert, chose and raised to the kingship Charoald, duke of Turin, who had as his wife Gundeberga, sister of King Adaloald. King Adaloald died after taking poison. Charoald immediately seized the kingdom.”

> The eminent Baronius had inferred from the parallel fate of Arichis’s son, which Paul relates below, that this derangement of Adaloald’s mind had been produced by magical poisoning; Fredegarius confirms this and gives us the means of correcting Paul. Fredegarius himself, however, must be corrected where he joins the empire of Maurice with the fortieth year of the reign of Chlothar II; Heraclius must be substituted there. We have already noted that Maurice was killed by Phocas, his successor, in 602, while Chlothar’s fortieth year falls in the year of Christ 624, according to Fredegarius’s own reckoning. He assigns him forty-five years of reign from the death of his father Chilperic, although, as Pagius observes from Aimoinus, these were incomplete years, since Aimoinus says that he reigned only forty-four years from that time.

> As for our Lombards, I believe that Paul and Fredegarius agree very well regarding the time when Adaloald fell in mind and kingdom. For if, with our author, ten years are counted from the death of Agilulf, we arrive at 626, two years after Eusebius had infected Adaloald with the ointment. It is a plausible conjecture that this much time elapsed before the remaining Lombards, fearing for themselves after twelve dukes had already been murdered, removed Arioald—whom Fredegarius calls Charioald—by poison.

> It is more difficult, however, to determine the beginning of Arioald’s reign. The cited Pagius, in his *Criticism* under the year 626, argues against all more recent chronologers, and even against our Paul, that Arioald reigned while Adaloald was still alive. His argument is based on a letter of Pope Honorius to Isaac, exarch of Ravenna, assigned to an uncertain year, as Baronius says, who quotes it as follows: “It has been reported to us that the bishops beyond the Po tried to persuade Peter, son of Paul, to abandon King Adalvald and attach himself to the tyrant Ariovald. Therefore, because Peter refused to obey their wicked counsels and wishes faithfully to preserve the oaths sworn to King Ago, father of Adaloald—that is, when Adaloald was raised to the kingship while his father was alive, at Milan in the Circus—and because it is displeasing both to God and to men that those who ought to avenge such a crime should themselves prove its instigators, we ask you, after you have restored Adalvald to the kingdom by divine assistance, as we hope, to send the aforesaid bishops to Rome, so that we may not leave such a crime unpunished.”

> Pagius adds: “Moreover, Jonas, who lived at this time, relates in the *Life of Saint Bertulf*, who succeeded Saint Attala as abbot of Bobbio in the year 627, chapter 11, that Bidulf, a monk of the monastery of Bobbio, was sent by Saint Attala, abbot of Bobbio, to the city of Ticinum, and there encountered Ariovald, king of the Lombards. He says further that Bertulf, after succeeding Saint Attala in the abbacy of Bobbio, came to Rome to Honorius while Arioald was reigning.”

> From this Pagius returns to Adaloald and argues that he was restored to the kingdom, on the evidence of charters by which he confirmed to the monastery of Bobbio the possessions donated by his father Agilulf. The first was given to Abbot Attala at Ticinum, in the palace, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the sixteenth year of our most fortunate reign, in the fifteenth indiction. The second was given to Abbot Bertulf at Pavia, on the sixteenth day of August, in the seventeenth year of our fortunate reign, in the first indiction. See these documents in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra* and in volume II of the *Cassinese Bullary*.

> For my part, although I have agreed with this most learned man where he asserts that Arioald occupied the kingdom while Adaloald was still alive, and although I have understood Fredegarius in that sense when he writes that all the elders and most noble men of the Lombard nation, acting in concert, chose him to be raised to the kingship and afterward relates Adaloald’s death, I cannot accept the restoration of Adaloald to the kingdom, contrary to the history of Paul and Fredegarius. According to those two witnesses, the king’s madness was followed by his death. Nor should we rely on the dates of the charters, since they do not at all agree in their reckoning of Adaloald’s reign, as the most discerning scholar and several others have observed. Moreover, if Adaloald were restored to the kingdom with Pagius, the entire chronology would be thrown into confusion and would not agree with the years of King Rothari, which we shall find more securely established below from his preface.

> I therefore assign the beginning of Arioald’s reign to after 624, the fortieth year of Chlothar; counting twelve years of his reign with Paul, and understanding those years as incomplete, as he himself counted them in more than one place, I arrive at approximately 636. I assign Rothari to the beginning of the following year of the Christian era, and shall gladly accept from more skilled men a better chronological arrangement.

> This much I would certainly affirm: our Paul gave Arioald’s wife, Gundeberga, to Rodoald. This is proved not only by the testimony of Fredegarius but also by the words of Jonas in the *Life of Saint Bertulf*, chapter 12. He writes: “Ariowald, son-in-law of Agilulf, kinsman of Adalwald, credulous in the Arian sect, undertook the kingdom of the Lombards after Adalwald’s death.” Indeed, Paul’s own history proves him plainly mistaken, as will be shown below in chapter 49.]

Of the deeds of this king nothing at all has come to our knowledge.

> [Note: [Col. 0580D] Although Paul openly admits that he knows nothing of King Arioald’s deeds, the learned Baronius collected certain information, chiefly from the book of Jonas; see it under the year 626. There he rightly observes that no mention of Queen Theodolinda occurs thereafter and argues that the famous queen had already died before her son Arioald suffered his mental derangement. In the basilica at Monza, anniversary prayers for the expiation of her sins are still recited with solemn ceremony on the eleventh day before the Ides of January. This may have been the day of her death, although such identifications are often not demonstrable.]

About this time the blessed Columbanus, born of the race of the Scots,

> [Note: [Col. 0580D] Mod.: “Of the Goths,” and Lindanus also reads it thus.]

after he had built a monastery in Gaul at a place called Luxovius,

> [Note: [Col. 0580D] Al.: “Luxovium.” Ambrosian, Modenese, and Lindanian manuscripts have “Lexovium.”]

came to Italy and was gladly received by the king of the Lombards. He built the monastery called Bobbio in the Cottian Alps, forty miles from the city of Ticinum. At that place many estates were donated by individual princes, whether Lombard or others, and a great community of monks was established there.

> [Note: [Col. 0581B–0581D] Our Paul frankly admits that he did not possess a sufficiently clear understanding of the Lombard history of this period, and in fact disturbed its chronological order. The arrival in Italy of Saint Columbanus, abbot, must be assigned to the time of Agilulf, not to the reign of King Arioald. It is clear from Jonas’s *Life of Saint Columbanus* that, after Theudebert had been defeated and killed—by whose authority Columbanus had been driven into exile at the instigation of Queen Brunechild—Columbanus, after traversing Germany with preaching and miracles, where he had withdrawn with his companions, hastened to Italy in order to convert to the truth of the Christian religion the Slavs who occupied the region of Venetia.

> He had foretold the death of that most unfortunate king while he was still leaving Gaul and, having openly threatened it three years in advance, could not restrain the king’s raging spirit. These events occurred in 612, and therefore Columbanus came to Italy while Agilulf was reigning. At Agilulf’s command he also sent a very long letter to Boniface IV, supreme pontiff, concerning the schism of the Three Chapters, shortly after his arrival, as I gather from the letter itself. The schism was still seething after the time of Saint Gregory, and the king therefore feared less favorable outcomes for his kingdom.

> I have already mentioned the donations of Agilulf and Adaloald to this distinguished monastery; the generosity of the kings who followed was no less, especially that of Liutprand. Many ancient documents are still preserved in its archives, as I remember hearing more than once from Dom Celestine Lorefice, a Cassinese monk. Would that this most learned man, so highly experienced in antiquities, might one day publish them for the benefit of scholars.]

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### On the death of Arioald, the reign of Rothari, and the fact that Duke Arichis sent his son Aio to the king

After Arioald had ruled over the Lombards for twelve years, he was taken from this life. Rothari, by descent an Arodus,

> [Note: [Col. 0581D] Al.: “Harodus.” Lind. Rothari himself also calls himself an Arodus in the preface to his laws, where he lists his ancestors as well. See Book I, chapter 14.]

assumed the kingdom of the Lombards.

> [Note: [Col. 0581D–0582C] I believe that Paul counted the twelve years of Arioald’s reign not from Adaloald’s death but from Arioald’s acclamation while Adaloald was still alive. Thus, from the fortieth year of Chlothar, when Adaloald lost the use of his mind through poison, we descend to the year of Christ 636, to which Rothari’s accession must be assigned, according to Rothari’s own testimony.

> In the preface to his laws he states that he issued them in the eighth year of his reign, in the second indiction, and in the seventy-sixth year after Alboin’s arrival. This plainly indicates the year 644, when the second indiction was in progress and when the seventy-sixth year was counted from 568, the year in which the Lombards came to Italy—not the seventy-seventh year, as the scribal error in this chapter reads. I correct the text on the basis of the wording of the edict itself, both in our edition and in the manuscript of the monastery of Cava, as Camillus Peregrinius noted in the appendix to Book I of his *History of the Lombard Princes*, p. 229; indeed, the calculation itself requires this, since the seventy-seventh year does not fall within the second indiction.

> Deducting eight years from 644, I return to 636. Nor do I approve the view of those who suppose that an error has entered into the numbers of Rothari’s regnal years and replace them by conjecture. The reading of the manuscripts and printed editions is consistent; if such freedom were permitted, now that histories have been returned to their ancient chaos, we should need to use the pen to correct every third line. I know that neither Sigebertus nor others agree with my chronology, but testimonies from the same period always have greater weight for me, unless I depart from them for a known reason.]

He was a man strong in bodily power and one who followed the path of justice; nevertheless, he did not hold to the straight line of the Christian faith but was stained by the treachery of the Arian heresy. For the Arians say, to their own destruction, that the Son is less than the Father, and likewise that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father and the Son. We Catholics, however, confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one true God in three persons, equal in power and possessing the same glory.

During his reign, in nearly every city of his kingdom there were two bishops, one Catholic and the other Arian. In the city of Ticinum it is still shown where the Arian bishop, residing at the basilica of Saint Eusebius, had a baptistery, although another bishop presided over the Catholic church.

> [Note: [Col. 0582C] From this point through the word “presided,” the other manuscripts do not read the passage. Lind.]

That Arian bishop, who was named Anastasius and had been in that same city,

> [Note: [Col. 0582C] Al.: “Who presided in that same city, was,” etc. Lind.]

was converted to the Catholic faith and afterward governed the Church of Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 0582C] This was evidently Anastasius II, entered in the catalogue of the saints, whose memory is celebrated on May 30. He subscribed to the general synod of 679 under Pope Agatho and rested in the Lord on May 30, 680. He was buried in the old cathedral church at Ticinum. See the *Acts of the Saints* of the Bollandists and Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*.]

This King Rothari composed the laws of the Lombards, which they had preserved only by memory and customary practice, in written form, and ordered the written code itself to be called the Edict.

> [Note: [Col. 0582C–0582D] For this reason King Rothari says in the conclusion of the Lombard laws: “Inquiring into and recalling the ancient laws of our fathers.” The Lombard laws were called *Auricabeones*, just as those of the Goths were called *Bellagines*. The glosses of Isidore—which I possess through the kindness of the most illustrious Lord Joseph Scaliger, the only patron of my studies, if I may say so without ill omen—read: “Anclabeo, or Auricabeo: the law of the Lombards.” Concerning the Getae, Jordanes writes in his history: “By teaching them physics, he made them live according to their own laws,” which laws, “written down even to the present day, they call Bellagines.” But what these words mean still remains, in my opinion, to be investigated. Lind.]

It was already the seventy-seventh year since the Lombards had come to Italy, as the same king testified in the preface to his Edict.

## CHAPTER XLV  
### On the death of Arichis, duke of Benevento, and the duchy of Aio

Duke Arichis of Benevento sent his son Aio to this king. When Aio came to Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0582D] Manuscript: “Caunum.” Lind.], and proceeded toward Ticinum, the Romans gave him there a potion of such a kind that it caused him to lose his mind; from that time onward he never possessed a sound and fully rational understanding.

Therefore, when Duke Arichis, the father of the man just mentioned, had reached advanced old age and was approaching his final day, knowing that his son Aio was not of sound mind, he commended Radoald and Grimoald, who were already in the flower of youth,

> [Note: [Col. 0582D–0583B] The learned Peregrinius raises serious difficulties here against our Paul. He writes: “Paul himself must explain how Arichis, before becoming duke, was tutor to Radoald and Grimoald; and how, after having lived fifty years in the duchy, he appointed them, while they were still in the flower of youth, as his own and his son’s successors in the duchy, as he relates in the following chapter.” Unless we understand Paul’s expression in the same sense in which Peregrinius himself thinks that the word “boy” could be applied to a young man of more advanced age, on the evidence of his Casapullan inscription: “Here lies Secundus the boy, who lived twenty-two years.”]

as though they were his own sons, to the Lombards who were present, and told them that these men would be able to govern them better than his son Aio could.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### On the death of Aio and the duchy of Radoald

After Arichis had died, having held the duchy for fifty years,

> [Note: [Col. 0583B] Manuscript reading: “five.” Lind. Our manuscripts read as in the printed edition.]

his son Aio was made leader of the Samnites.

> [Note: [Col. 0583B–0583C] I connected the death of Zotto, duke of Benevento, with the year 611 of the Christian era above, chapter 19, note 64. From that point, counting the fifty years during which Arichis, his successor, held the principate, I arrive, together with Camillus Peregrinius, at the year 661.]

Nevertheless, Radoald and Grimoald obeyed him in all things as their elder brother and lord.

> [Note: [Col. 0583C] Yet they were partners in the principate, as our author indicates here not obscurely.]

When Aio had governed the duchy of Benevento for one year and five months, the Slavs came with a multitude of ships and pitched camp far from the city of Sipontum.

> [Note: [Col. 0583C] Perhaps *non longe* should be read. Since the ancient Apulian city of Sipontum was near the Adriatic Sea, the Slavs could easily have sailed from the territory of Venetia and landed there.]

They dug hidden pits around their camp. When Aio came against them, in the absence of Radoald and Grimoald, intending to defeat them, his horse fell into one of these pits.

> [Note: [Col. 0583C] Another reading: “He fell into a pit, where he was killed and perished at the hands of the Slavs. When Rodoald arrived and spoke with one of the same Slavs in their own language, and when he saw that they had become more savage in battle because of this deed, he immediately attacked them,” etc. Lind.]

As the Slavs rushed upon him, he was killed together with several of his men.

> [Note: [Col. 0583C] Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts: “Together with some others,” etc.]

When this was reported to Radoald, he came quickly and spoke to the same Slavs in their own language.

> [Note: [Col. 0583C–0583D] The Slavs had formerly been neighbors of the men of Friuli, from whose duchy Radoald and Grimoald had come; therefore they could have learned the Slavs’ language from childhood.]

By doing this he made them less eager for battle. Then he immediately attacked them, struck them down in a great slaughter, avenged the death of Aio, and forced the surviving enemies to flee from that territory.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### On the cities captured by Rothari

[Col. 0584A]

Therefore King Rothari captured all the Roman cities situated on the coast, from the Tuscan city of Luna onward as far as the borders of the Franks.

[Note: Alternatively, “from the city of Luna in Tuscia.” Lind.]

He likewise conquered and destroyed the city of Opitergium, situated between Tarvisium and Forum Julii.

[Note: Fredegarius, in his Chronicle, assigns these events to the time of King Clovis, after the acquittal of Gundeberga, about which more below. He writes: “Chrotharius, marching with an army, took from the Empire and devastated the maritime cities of Genava, Albinganum, Varicottim, Saona, Ubitergium, and Luna; he broke them, consumed them with fire, plundered and stripped the people, condemned them to captivity, and, destroying their walls down to the foundations, ordered that these cities be called villages.” But he incorrectly numbers Opitergium among the cities on the Ligurian Sea, whereas our author describes its location very accurately. It is certain that it lay between the rivers Plavis and Liquentia, in the territory of Venetia; today it is called Oderzo. The passage may, however, be corrupt, as the word *Varicottim* indicates, the meaning of which, so far as I know, no one has yet been able to determine.]

He waged war against the people of Ravenna and the Romans at the river of Emilia, which is called the Scultenna.

[Note: Alternatively, “the Sculteria.” Lind.]

In that battle eight thousand fell when the remaining Romans openly turned their backs and fled.

[Note: Alternatively: “while the rest of the Romans openly turned their backs.” Lind.]

At that time a great earthquake occurred at Rome, and there was a great inundation of waters. After this came the plague of the scabies,

[Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “of scabs.”]

[Note: Inappropriately, Paulus extends this event to the time of Rothari, although it must be referred to an earlier period, according to the testimony of Anastasius in his account of Pope Deusdedit. Anastasius immediately relates these dreadful disasters after the killing of John of Compsa, in the following words: “At the same time a great earthquake occurred in the month of August, in the eleventh indiction”—or, as the more accurate manuscripts read, “in the sixth indiction,” since no year of Pope Deusdedit’s pontificate fell within the eleventh indiction. “After this a plague came upon the people, an affliction of scabies, so that no one could recognize his dead.”]

so severe that no one could recognize his dead because of the excessive swelling of the inflammation.

At Beneventum, meanwhile, after Duke Radoaldus had died—he had governed the duchy for five years—

[Note: In some copies the words “who had governed the duchy for five years” are absent. Lind.]

his brother Grimoaldus became duke and governed the duchy of the Samnites for twenty-five years. By a captive girl, though one of noble birth, whose name was Itta,

[Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “It.”]

he fathered a son, Romuald, and two daughters.

Since he was a most warlike and distinguished man everywhere, when the Greeks came at that time to plunder the sanctuary of the holy archangel Michael situated on Mount Garganus, Grimoaldus came against them with an army and struck them down in a final slaughter.

[Note: Alternatively, “the Saracens.” Lind.; likewise Mod.]

[Note: On this passage of Paulus, Camillus Peregrinius, in his dissertation *On the Northern Boundaries of the Duchy of Beneventum*, writes: “Since Paulus attributes this sacrilege to the Greeks, I fear that our author—whose reliability I have always regarded as suspect in matters that might diminish the glory of his own Lombards—is imposing upon us. Why should I not rather believe that such things were committed by those whom we know to have plundered the monastery of Cassino in earlier years, and to have followed idolatry or the Arian heresy—for authors disagree on this—up to the year 663, namely the Lombards of the duchy of Beneventum? It is otherwise clear that the Greeks, following an ancient custom with devoted zeal, honored the name of Saint Michael.”

“And further,” he writes, “I shall therefore believe that at that time the Greeks frequently fought with the Lombards at Garganus for possession of that place, as elsewhere for other places, and that the latter, having gained the victory, plundered the sacred cave of the archangel.”

That sharp-minded man confirms his conjecture with several arguments, above all by the reading of the *Acts of Saint Barbatus*, which Bollandus and Henschenius incorporated into their celebrated collection. There it is stated that, after the Emperor Constantius had departed from the city of Beneventum—an event discussed below—Duke Romuald, offering immense gifts to the supreme pontiff, through whose prayers the Beneventans had stood unharmed against their enemies, heard the following from him:

“If you wish to offer a gift for your salvation, strive to make one sacrifice: submit entirely to the blessed seat of the Mother of God, which I, unworthy though I am, now govern, the house of blessed Michael situated on Garganus and everything subject to the jurisdiction of the bishopric of Sipontum. Since all things are corrupted when they lack guardians, and consequently a continual sacrifice cannot be offered there, what we have better arranged for you will prove more beneficial to your salvation.”

Since those same *Acts* make it entirely clear that Lombard idolatry continued down to the time when, at the exhortation of Saint Barbatus, they abandoned the worship of a serpent and of a hide hanging from a tree, Peregrinius suspects that they themselves caused the desolation of the sacred crypt. He adds the testimony of the anonymous Cassinensian and of Erchempert, who compare the victory of the Campanians—that is, the Lombards—over the Neapolitans in the year 860, who had come under the name of Greeks, with another victory “when, long ago, while the festival of the blessed archangel Michael was being celebrated on Garganus, they fell.” Hence he persuades himself that the opportunity for plunder belonged rather to the victors than to the defeated.

However the matter may stand, in my judgment his arguments do not make the case so clear that we can prove our Paulus to be in error, especially since he does not actually write that the Greeks committed the deed, but only that they attempted it. The Lombards of Sipontum, who were more distinguished than the others in religious devotion and held the sacred crypt in the highest veneration, perhaps persuaded themselves of this from popular rumor. Since the crypt had already been consecrated with solemn rites, they may have turned the Greeks’ arrival into a worse charge, accusing their rivals through partisan zeal.

In any event, even before Romuald’s conversion there were many Christian, and specifically Catholic, Lombards in Transtiberine Italy. This is proved by a single letter of Saint Gregory to Duke Arichis: he calls him “son” and promises him the future grace of good works—something he certainly would not have written to an Arian or pagan.

The reading of the Modoetian and other manuscripts, which have *Saracenis* here instead of *Graecis*, would cut through all these difficulties. Yet I find it no less difficult to establish from other historians that the Saracens came into Apulia at this period.]

# CHAPTER XLVIII. On the death of Duke Radoaldus and the succession of his brother Grimoaldus to the duchy

But King Rothari, after he had held the kingdom for sixteen years and four months,

[Note: Alternatively, “fifteen years.” Lind.]

departed this life and left the kingdom of the Lombards to Rodoaldus, his son.

[Note: I assign the death of King Rothari to the beginning of the year 653 on the basis of the dates in his own edict. Yet, with Benedict Bacchinius, I am compelled to place the beginning of the reign of his son Rodoaldus while his father was still alive, so that we may arrive at the period of Grimoaldus and at the edict in which Rothari enlarged and explained the Lombard laws, as will be related below.]

He was buried beside the basilica of blessed John the Baptist. After some time, a man inflamed by wicked greed

[Note: The *τὸ iniqua*—“the wicked [word]”—does not occur in the Modoetian manuscript.]

opened his tomb at night and carried away whatever he found among the ornaments of his body. Blessed John appeared to him in a vision, terrified him greatly, and said:

“Why did you dare to touch this man’s body? Although he may not have been a true believer, he entrusted himself to me. Since, therefore, you presumed to do this, you shall never again have entry into my basilica.”

And so it happened. For whenever he wished to enter the sanctuary of blessed John, his throat was immediately struck as if by a very powerful

[Note: Ambrosian manuscript: “fist.”]

boxer, and he was suddenly hurled backward as though pushed. I speak the truth in Christ: the man who saw this happen with his own eyes reported it to me himself.

# CHAPTER XLIX. On the death of King Rothari and the reign of Rodoaldus

Rodoaldus, therefore, after his father’s funeral, assumed the kingdom of the Lombards and married Gundiberga, the daughter of Agilulfus and Theudelinda.

[Note: From the beginning of this chapter down to this word, the passage is absent from the Ambrosian manuscript. I noted above that Gundeberga was not the wife of Rodoaldus but of Arioaldus, on the testimony of Jonas in the *Life of Saint Bertulfus*, which deserves the greatest confidence, since he was a writer of that age. Fredegarius also supports this: in his *Chronicle* he writes not only that she was the wife of King Arioaldus, but also of his successor Rothari—or, as he calls him, Chrotnarius—with whom she suffered cruelty not unlike that which she had endured with her former husband because of Adaulfus’s slander. He writes as follows:

“Queen Gundeberga, because all the Lombards had confirmed their loyalty to her with oaths, ordered a certain Chrotharius [alternatively, Chrothacharius], one of the dukes from the territory of Brissia, to come to her. She compelled him to leave the wife he had and to take her in marriage, promising that through her all the Lombards would raise him to the kingship. Chrotharius willingly consented, confirming by oaths at the holy places that he would never set Gundeberga aside, diminish anything of her rank or honor, and, loving her with exclusive affection, would show her every fitting honor. At Gundeberga’s urging, all the Lombard nobles raised Chrotharius to the kingship.

“When Chrotharius began to reign, he killed many Lombard nobles whom he perceived to be rebellious against him. Seeking peace, he established the strictest discipline and fear throughout the Lombard kingdom. Forgetting the oaths he had sworn to Gundeberga, Chrotharius shut her in a chamber at Ticinum, in the palace hall, and forced her to live as a private woman. She was kept under this confinement for five years.

“Chrotharius continually indulged himself with concubines. But Gundeberga, because she was a Christian, blessed almighty God in this tribulation and devoted herself constantly to fasting and prayer. When it pleased God, Aubedo, sent as an envoy by King Clovis [alternatively, Chlotharius], arrived at the Italian city of Pavia, also called Ticinum, on an embassy to Chrotharius, king of the Lombards. Seeing that the queen, whom he had often seen when he came on embassies and by whom he had always been kindly received, had been imprisoned, he represented to King Chrotharius, among other matters—as though this had been included in his instructions—that he ought not to humiliate the kinswoman of the Franks, whom he had held as queen and through whom he had even obtained the kingdom. In this matter the Frankish kings and Franks would show themselves most ungrateful.

“Out of respect for the Franks, Chrotharius ordered her to come out. After approximately five years, Gundeberga proceeded throughout the city and outside it, in royal fashion, to the holy places for prayer. Chrotharius ordered the estates and fiscal resources that he had possessed to be restored to her. Enriched until the day of her death both in rank and in many possessions, she thereafter retained them happily with royal dignity. Aubedo, for his part, was richly rewarded by Queen Gundeberga.”

Pagius reasonably explains, from Saint Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 9, why Aubedo, the envoy of the king of the Franks, calls Gundeberga a kinswoman or relative of the Frankish kings. Theudelinda was the daughter of Garibaldus, duke of Bavaria, who had married Valdetrada, or Walderada, queen of the Franks and widow of Theudobald, king of Austrasia. After Theudobald’s death, Chlotharius “took her to his bed; but, rebuked by the priests, he left her, giving her to Duke Garibaldus.” Pagius adds that Theudelinda was also a niece of Theudebert, king of the Franks, who had married Wisegarda, the sister of Walderada’s mother.

Others write that Theudelinda was the daughter of Ragintrudis, sister of Theudobald, king of Austrasia, and derive the relationship from that connection. But the testimony just cited proves them to be in error.

The remarkably perceptive Baronius had already noted, under the year 659, no. 5, that Paulus’s error is exposed by his own history. If Theudelinda ruled for ten years with her son Adaloaldus after the death of her husband Agilulfus, and Arioaldus succeeded him, ruling for twelve years, and Rothari then ruled for sixteen years and four months, Gundeberga must have been at least over forty years old by that time. Indeed, if we reckon from the year 603, when Saint Gregory the Great sent her rings, as in the letter quoted above in chapter 28, we shall find her almost sixty. One might nevertheless doubt whether the gifts of the supreme pontiff were sent to Gundeberga or to another daughter of Agilulfus, the wife of Codescalchus of Parma, since the name is not expressly given in the aforementioned letter. Even granting this possibility, however, the first chronological calculation proceeds far enough to make Gundeberga entirely innocent of adultery without the assistance of Carellus.]

This Queen Gundiberga, following the example of her mother, built a basilica in honor of blessed John the Baptist within the city of Ticinum, just as her mother had built one at Modicia.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has the column reference at this point.]

She wondrously adorned it with gold, silver, and curtains, enriched it abundantly with every kind of possession, and was herself buried and now rests there.

When she had been accused by her husband of the crime of adultery, her own servant, named Carellus, asked the king that he might fight in single combat with the man who had brought the accusation against the queen, for the chastity of his mistress.

[Note: Alternatively, “to defend his mistress’s chastity.” Lind.]

[Note: This reprehensible judgment, and other practices of the same kind—trials of fortune rather than of truth, or, as a Christian should say, rash attempts by which the profound judgments of God are tested—long prevailed above all in our Italy under the Lombard laws. There are so many examples that anyone who attempted to list them all would undertake a futile task.]

When he entered single combat with that accuser, he defeated him before the assembled people. After this event the queen returned to her former dignity.

[Note: Fredegarius gives a fuller account, and for that reason I transcribe his words:

“Queen Gundeberga, beautiful in appearance, kind to all, most abundant in compassion, Christian, generous in almsgiving, and distinguished for her goodness, was loved by everyone. A certain man named Adaulfus, of Lombard stock, habitually attended at the royal palace in the king’s service. On one occasion he came to the queen and, standing in her presence, Queen Gundeberga, loving him as she loved the others, said that Adaulfus had been well formed in stature. Hearing this, he said: ‘You have deigned to praise the form of my stature; command me to lie beside you.’ She firmly refused him and, despising him, spat in his face.

“Adaulfus, realizing that his life was in danger, immediately ran to King Charoaldus and asked for a private place in which he might make his accusation. Having obtained one, he said to the king: ‘My queen Gundeberga has secretly spoken with Duke Taso of Tuscia—whom he had earlier described as living in the Tuscan province—for three days, so that she might kill you with poison and raise him, a married man, to the kingship.’

“Believing these lies, King Charoaldus drove Gundeberga into exile in a tower of the fortress of Caumellum

[Alternatively, Camellum; but perhaps Laumellum should be read, as in Aimoinus.]

“Clotarius sent envoys to King Charoaldus, asking why he had humiliated Gundeberga, queen and kinswoman of the Franks, by shutting her away in exile.” Charoaldus replied with these lying words as though they were true.

“Then one of the envoys, named Ansoaldus, said to Charoaldus—not as though he had been instructed to do so, but on his own initiative: ‘You could clear this matter of blasphemy. Order the man who reported such words to you to arm himself, and let another man from Queen Gundeberga’s side come forward. Let the two armed men engage in single combat, so that by God’s judgment it may be known, through their struggle, whether Gundeberga is innocent of the charge or perhaps guilty.’

“When this proposal pleased King Charoaldus and all the nobles of his palace, he ordered Adaulfus to enter the armed contest. From Gundeberga’s side, her cousins came forward, and a man named Pitto, armed against Adaulfus, undertook the combat on her behalf. When they had fought, Adaulfus was killed by Pitto. Gundeberga immediately returned from exile after three years and was restored to the kingship.”

See Aimoinus, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 10.]

# CHAPTER L. On the death of King Rodoaldus and the reign of Aripertus

Rodoaldus likewise, as the story goes, violated the wife of a certain Lombard and was killed by him after he had reigned for five years and seven days.

[Note: With Bacchinius, I believe that Rodoaldus did not survive the year 654, lest I be led onto still more difficult ground with the others who depart from this chronology. Those who contend that Paulus’s intention contradicts this may judge how much credence should be given to a chronologist of this kind. For my part, I have noted what I could with such ability as I possess; I openly declare that I shall be most grateful to those who point out a more accurate path.]

Aripertus succeeded him in governing the kingdom. He was the son of Gundualdus, who had been the brother of Queen Theudelinda. He founded at Ticinum a sanctuary of the Lord and Savior outside the western gate called Marenca. He adorned it with various ornaments and endowed it sufficiently with property.

# CHAPTER LI. On the death of the Emperor Heraclius, the succession of Constantine, and the reign of the second Constantine

[Note: The Emperor Heraclius died in the year 641, on the eleventh day of February, as Pagius has established very well in his *Historical and Chronological Criticism*, by comparing the Eastern Chronicle with Nicephorus. Paulus therefore confuses the succession of the emperors that follow. It is certain that, after Heraclius’s death, Constantine, his son, and not Heraclonas, assumed the empire. After 103 days, according to Nicephorus, Constantine died of illness—or, according to another account, was poisoned through the agency of Martina, his stepmother, and Pyrrhus the patriarch. Heraclonas, Martina’s son, then obtained power with his mother and held it for six months. When those months had elapsed, the senate expelled Heraclonas, his mother, and Valentinus, through whose agency the disturbance had arisen, from the administration of the empire. Martina’s tongue was cut out, Heraclonas’s nose was amputated, and both were sent into exile. The senate then raised Constans, the son of Constantine and grandson of Heraclius, to the imperial throne, as Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Zonaras relate. He ruled the empire for thirty-seven years, according to the usual reckoning.]

In those days, after the Emperor Heraclius Augustus had died at Constantinople, his son Heraclonas assumed the imperial authority with his mother Martina and ruled the empire for two years. When he died, his brother Constantine, another son of Heraclius, succeeded him

[Note: Alternatively, “for seven months. Then Constantine …” Lind.]

and reigned for six months. After his death, his son Constantine ascended to the imperial dignity and held the kingdom for twenty-eight years.

# CHAPTER LII. On Caesar, queen of the Persians

About this time the wife of the king of the Persians, named Caesar,

[Note: Alternatively, “Caesarea, queen of the Persians.” Lind; and likewise the Modoetian manuscript, which is followed by a few others.]

departed from Persia with a few of her faithful attendants and came to Constantinople in private attire, out of love for the Christian faith. The emperor received her honorably. After several days she obtained baptism as she desired, and the Augusta lifted her from the sacred font.

When her husband, the king of the Persians, heard this, he sent envoys to Constantinople to the emperor, asking that he return his wife to him.

[Note: Alternatively, “to the emperor.” Lind.]

When they came to the emperor, they announced the words of the king of the Persians, who was demanding his queen.

[Note: The Modoetian manuscript has “his wife.”]

The emperor heard this. Completely unaware of the matter, he answered them:

“As for the queen whom you seek, we confess that we know nothing, except that some woman came here in private attire.”

The envoys replied:

“If it pleases Your Presence, we wish to see this woman of whom you speak.”

When she came at the emperor’s command, as soon as the envoys saw her,

[Note: The Ambrosian and Modoetian manuscripts read: “as soon as the envoys saw her.”]

they fell at her feet and reverently informed her that her husband was seeking her. She answered them:

“Go and report to your king and lord

[Note: Alternatively, “to your former husband and mine.” Lind.]

that, unless he also believes in Christ as I have now believed,

[Note: Alternatively, “unless he now believes in Christ.” Lind.]

he will never again be able to have me as the companion of his bed.”

Why say more? The envoys returned to their homeland and reported to the king everything they had heard. Without delay, he came peacefully to Constantinople with sixty thousand men

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “twelve.”]

to the emperor, who received him gladly and with sufficient honor.

[Note: Alternatively, “with great honor.” Lind.]

Believing in the Lord Christ together with all his people, he was baptized with them in the water of the sacred font, was lifted from the font by the emperor, and was confirmed in the Catholic faith. After the emperor had honored him with many gifts, he joyfully and gladly returned to his homeland with his wife.

[Note: This story, which also entered the *Miscellaneous History*, perhaps arose from the account preserved by Theophylact Simocatta and the abbot of Biclarum, writers of the same age, to whom it had come through popular report. Chosroes II, whether by strategy or mindful of the favor he had received from the martyr Saint Sergius, to whom he had made a vow in return for restoration to his kingdom, showed goodwill toward the Christian religion; but he did not renounce his errors, as is clearly established by a letter of Pope Saint Gregory to Saint Domitian, bishop of Melitene, cited by Baronius and others. Fredegarius wrote still more fabulous material about this matter in his *Chronicle*.

In any event, while the Emperor Heraclius was still alive, Chosroes was pierced with arrows and killed at the command of his son Siroes in the year 627. Thus all these events should be connected not with the reign of Constans but with that of Heraclius.]

About this time, when Grasulfus, duke of Forum Julii, had died at Forum Julii, Ago assumed the government of the duchy. At Spoletum also, after Theudelapius had died,

[Note: Alternatively, “Theodelapius.” Lind.]

Atto became ruler of that city.

# CHAPTER LIII. On the death of Aripertus, his son Godebertus who succeeded him, the reign of Grimoaldus, and the death of Duke Garibaldus

Accordingly Aripertus,

[Note: Alternatively, “Aribertus.” Lind.]

after he had ruled the Lombards at Ticinum for nine years, died and left the kingdom to be governed by his two sons, still young men, Bertaridus and Godebertus.

[Note: Alternatively, “Bertharidus”; alternatively, “Partharitus”; this is consistent throughout in Lind and the Modoetian manuscript.]

Godebertus indeed had the royal seat at Ticinum, while Bertaridus was at the city of Mediolanum.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript consistently has “Godibertus.”]

Between these brothers, through the agency of wicked men, a source of discord and hatred arose, to such an extent that each attempted to invade the other’s kingdom.

[Note: Sigebertus, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 660, writes: “After Ariperth, king of the Lombards, had died, his sons Godebertus and Bertharith spent the year not so much arranging the kingdom as contending over it. In the following year Grimoaldus, duke of Turin, treacherously killed Godebertus, son of Ariperth, king of the Lombards, and seized his kingdom.”

This agrees with the order of events narrated by Paulus after the death of Aripertus: there was an interval of one year before Grimoaldus gained power. Since there is scarcely room for doubt about assigning this date, for Grimoaldus himself states in his legal edict that in July of the eleventh indiction he was entering the sixth year of his reign—and that year was 668 of the Lord’s incarnation—counting backward brings us to 661, to which the death of Aripertus must be assigned.

Peregrinius did not notice this. He allows no interval between the death of Aripertus and the beginning of Grimoaldus’s reign, and, assigning the latter to a later date in his own comparison, wrongly accuses Paulus of chronological inversion in his cited dissertation *On the Northern Boundaries of the Duchy of Beneventum*.]

For this reason Godebertus sent Garibaldus, duke of Turin, to Grimoaldus, the energetic duke of the Beneventans, inviting him to come as quickly as possible and provide assistance against his brother Bertaridus. He promised that he would give him the king’s daughter, his own sister, in marriage.

But the envoy himself, acting treacherously against his lord, urged Grimoaldus to come and seize the kingdom of the Lombards, which the two young brothers were dissipating, since he was mature in age, prudent in counsel, and strong in power.

When Grimoaldus heard this, he immediately directed his mind toward obtaining the kingdom of the Lombards. He appointed his son Romuald duke at Beneventum, then set out with a chosen force on the road to Ticinum. Through every city he encountered,

[Note: The Modoetian manuscript reads, “through which he made his way.”]

he enlisted friends and supporters to help him obtain the kingdom. He sent Trasemundus, count of Capua, through Spoletum and Tuscia, so that he might attach the Lombards of those regions to his alliance. Trasemundus diligently carried out his instructions and met him on the road at Emilia with many auxiliaries.

[Note: Alternatively, “on the Aemilian Way.” Lind.]

Accordingly, when Grimoaldus had arrived near Placentia with a strong multitude of men, he sent Garibaldus, who had been dispatched to him by Godebertus as an envoy, ahead to Ticinum, so that he might announce his arrival to Godebertus.

When Garibaldus came to Godebertus, he said that Grimoaldus would soon arrive. When Godebertus asked him where he should prepare lodging for Grimoaldus, Garibaldus replied that it was fitting for Grimoaldus, who had come for his sake and was to receive his sister, to have lodging inside the palace.

And so it was done. When Grimoaldus arrived, he received lodging inside the palace.

[Note: After “and so it was done,” this is absent from some copies. Linden. The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “he received a residence.”]

That same Garibaldus, the seed of every wickedness, persuaded Godebertus to come to speak with Grimoaldus wearing a cuirass beneath his clothing and claiming that Grimoaldus wished to kill him.

[Note: Alternatively, “asserting that he suspected Grimoaldus wished to kill him.” Lind.]

Again, that master of deception came to Grimoaldus and told him that unless he prepared himself carefully, Godebertus would kill him with his sword. He insisted that when Godebertus came to speak with him, he would be wearing a cuirass beneath his clothing.

What more is there to say? When they came to meet on the following day and, after the greeting, Grimoaldus embraced Godebertus, he immediately perceived that he was wearing a cuirass beneath his clothing.

[Note: Alternatively, “claiming that he had put it on for the purpose of killing him, he immediately drew his sword.” Lind.]

Without delay he drew his sword, deprived him of life, seized his kingdom and all his power, and subjected them to his own authority.

At that time Godebertus had a little son named Reginbertus.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “Raginbertus”; the Modoetian manuscript, “Raunpertus”; Lind has “Raginpertus”; alternatively, “Rambertus.”]

Godebertus’s loyal followers rescued the boy and secretly raised him. Grimoaldus did not trouble to pursue him, since he was still an infant.

When Bertaridus, who was reigning at Mediolanum, heard that his brother had been killed,

[Note: The words “that his brother had been killed” are absent from some copies. Lind.]

he fled as quickly as he could and reached Cacanus, king of the Avars,

[Note: Alternatively, “of the Avars or Huns.” Lind; Ambrosian manuscript, “of the Avars.”]

leaving behind his wife Rodelinda and his little son Cunibertus. Grimoaldus sent them into exile at Beneventum.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “Grimoaldus sent them into exile.”]

After these events, Garibaldus—at whose instigation and through whose efforts and struggle these deeds had been accomplished, and who had not only done this but had also acted fraudulently in his embassy by failing to deliver intact the gifts he ought to have carried to Beneventum—did not long enjoy the fruits of such deeds.

[Note: Alternatively, “effort.” Lind.]

There was a certain short little man, descended from Godebertus’s own household, in the city of Turin.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “in the city of Turin. He …”]

Knowing that Duke Garibaldus would come to the basilica of blessed John to pray on the very sacred day of Easter, he climbed onto the sacred baptismal font and, holding himself with his left hand against a column of the hut,

[Note: Alternatively, “a little column.” Lind; the Ambrosian manuscript has “a small column.”]

beneath which Garibaldus would pass, held a drawn sword under his cloak. When Garibaldus came near and passed by, he raised the sword and, striking with all his strength, struck him in the neck,

[Note: The words “and immediately cut off his head” are absent from the Ambrosian manuscript.]

and immediately cut off his head. Those who had come with Garibaldus rushed upon the attacker and killed him with many blows.

Although he himself fell, he nevertheless took notable vengeance for the wrong done to his lord Godebertus.

[Note: The Modoetian manuscript adds: “Grimoaldus took the king’s daughter as his wife and likewise sent the army back to its own territory.”]

# BOOK FIVE

# CHAPTER I. How Grimoaldus, after securing the kingdom, married the daughter of King Aripertus

[Note: Alternatively, “Grimoaldus thereafter secured in the kingdom.” Linden. and Ambrosian manuscript.]

After Grimoaldus had secured the kingdom at Ticinum,

[Note: That is, in the year 662, as I noted above on the basis of the date of the edict. I have read its chronological markers not only in the printed editions but also in the cited manuscript of Lombard laws, a manuscript of excellent quality in the Ambrosian Library.]

not long afterward he married the daughter of King Aripertus, who had long before been promised to him and whose brother Godebertus he had killed.

[Note: Alternatively, “Gundebertus.” Lind.]

He dismissed to their homes, enriched with many gifts, the Beneventan army by whose assistance he had obtained the kingdom. He nevertheless retained some of them to live with him, granting them very generous estates.

# CHAPTER II. On the flight of Bertaridus, how he returned to Grimoaldus, and how he fled again to Francia
After he learned that Bertarid had fled and gone to Scythia, and was staying with Cacan, he sent word through envoys to Cacan, king of the Avars, that, if he kept Bertarid in his kingdom, he could not thereafter continue to enjoy the peace which he had hitherto maintained with the Lombards and with himself. [Col. 0592D–0593C] When the king of the Avars heard this, he summoned Bertarid and told him to go wherever he wished, lest, on his account, the Avars should incur hostility with the Lombards.

[Note: We recognize Cacan’s firmer loyalty toward Bertharid from Eddius, in his *Life of Saint Wilfrid I*, archbishop of York, a writer of that age, in Mabillon’s appendix to volume IV of the Benedictine century. Adrian Valesius, as the same Mabillon reports in his preliminary observation, was the first to notice that Eddius was speaking there of Bertharid, whom Eddius calls Berchter, king of Campania:

“Thus, writes Eddius, the holy bishops—namely Wilfrid and Theodatus—proceeded, the Lord directing their way, and came to Berchter, king of Campania” [Col. 0593D]—that is, of the Lombards, as is certainly evident from the same writer, although Bollandus, in his treatment of the life of that pontiff written by Eadmer, does not understand the matter correctly; for, describing the return of that same holy Wilfrid from Rome, Eddius says: “Crossing through Campania and the mountains, he came into the region of the Franks”—“a humble and quiet man, trembling at the words of God. Receiving the pilgrims kindly, according to the Lord’s command, he told our holy pontiff:

“‘From Britain, messengers of your enemies came to me, greeting me in their words and promising me the greatest gifts if I would, as they said, constrain you, a fugitive bishop, and detain you as you made your way to the apostolic see. I refused so wicked a deed and said to them: “At some time in my youth I was an exile, driven from my homeland, living under a pagan king of the Huns. He made a covenant with me by his idol-god that he would never betray or surrender me to my enemies. After some time, messengers of my enemies came to the pagan king with a message, promising under oath to give him a full bushel of gold coins if he would hand me over to them for destruction. Refusing them, he said: ‘Without doubt may the gods cut short my life if I commit this sacrilege and violate the covenant of my gods.’ But I, all the more because I know the true God, will not give my soul over to destruction for the gain of the whole world!”’

“‘Then our holy pontiff and his companions, with honor and guides, just as the Lord magnified him by protecting him everywhere in his pilgrimage, he sent back in thanksgiving to the Apostolic See, which he had long desired.’”]

[Col. 0593A] [Note: Amb. reads: “He returns to Grimoald.”]

When Bertarid heard this, he returned to Italy and sought out Grimoald, for he had heard that Grimoald was most merciful. When he had reached the city of Lodi, he sent ahead to King Grimoald Hunulf, a man utterly faithful to him, to announce his arrival.

[Note: Other readings have *Unulfum* and *Anulfo*; Lind. reads “to flee to his protection.”]

Hunulf came to the king and reported that Bertarid was approaching under his protection. On hearing this, Grimoald confidently promised that Bertarid, coming under his protection, would suffer no harm. [Col. 0593B]

Meanwhile Bertarid arrived and entered Grimoald’s presence. When he attempted to throw himself at the king’s feet, the king mercifully restrained him and raised him to his face and to a kiss.

[Note: Amb. reads: “and raised him to a kiss.”]

Bertarid said to him: “I am your servant. Knowing that you are most Christian and pious, although I could live among pagans, I have come to your feet, relying upon your mercy.”

The king, as was his custom, confirmed his promise by oath, saying: “By him who caused me to be born, after you have come to me under my protection, you shall suffer no harm in any respect. Rather, I shall arrange matters for you so that you may live honorably.”

Then, providing him lodging in a spacious house, he ordered that, after the hardships of his life, he should have rest, and commanded that food from the public stores and whatever else was necessary should be supplied to him generously.

[Note: Amb. adds: “Providing this, he ordered them to have rest after so great a labor.”]

When Bertarid came to the lodging prepared for him by the king, crowds of citizens of Ticinum immediately began flocking to him, either to see him or to greet him as one known to them from former days.

But what cannot an evil tongue bring about? Certain malicious flatterers soon came to the king and reported that, unless Bertarid were speedily deprived of life, the king himself would immediately lose both his life and his kingdom. They insisted that the whole city was flocking to Bertarid for this reason. [Col. 0593C]

When Grimoald heard this, he became excessively credulous, forgot what he had promised, and was immediately inflamed with the desire to kill innocent Bertarid. He devised a plan for depriving him of life the following day, since it was already late.

Accordingly, toward evening he sent him various foods, as well as excellent wines and different kinds of drink, so that he might make him drunk and, once weakened by heavy drinking throughout the night and buried in wine, render him incapable of giving any thought to his safety. [Col. 0594A]

[Note: Another reading: “buried in wine and sleep.”]

Then one of the men who had formerly served Bertarid’s father brought Bertarid a royal dish.

[Note: The Lind. manuscript reads “a cup.”]

As though coming to greet him, he thrust his head beneath the table and secretly informed him that the king intended to kill him.

Bertarid immediately ordered his cupbearer to pour him nothing but a little water into a silver bowl. When those who were bringing him drinks of various kinds at the king’s command urged him to drink the entire bowl, he promised that, in honor of the king, he would drink it all, but merely sipped a little water from the silver cup.

When the servants reported to the king that Bertarid was drinking most eagerly, the king answered happily: “Let that drunkard drink! Tomorrow he will pour out those same wines mixed with blood.” [Col. 0594B]

Bertarid immediately summoned Hunulf to him and told him of the king’s plan for his death. Hunulf at once sent a boy to his own house to bring him bedding, and ordered that a bed be made for him beside Bertarid’s bed.

Without delay, King Grimoald sent his guards to watch the house in which Bertarid was resting, so that he could not escape in any way.

When dinner was over and everyone else had gone out, only Bertarid, Hunulf, and Bertarid’s wardrobe-keeper remained.

[Note: Another reading: “Partharith and his wardrobe-keeper remained.”]

The latter was entirely faithful to him. Bertarid revealed the plan to him and begged him to pretend that, while Bertarid fled, he himself was resting in the same chamber for as long as he could, even until the following day.

[Note: Mod. reads “that Bertarid should flee with Hunulf,” and, for the latter clause, “within [the chamber] beyond the day for as long as he could,” etc.]

When the man promised to do this, Hunulf placed his own bedclothes, mattress, and bearskin across Bertarid’s back and neck.

[Note: The variants for *pannos lecticarios* are *lectaricios* (Al., Amb., M.) and *lectarios* (Lind.).]

Acting on the plan, he began pushing him out through the door as though he were a rustic slave. He heaped many insults upon him, struck him from above with a stick, and continued driving him forward, so that, pushed and beaten, Bertarid repeatedly fell to the ground.

When the king’s guards, who had been stationed there to keep watch, asked Hunulf what was happening, he replied: “This worthless slave made my bed in the chamber of that drunken Bertarid, who is so full of wine that he lies there like a dead man.

[Note: Mod. reads “set up” for “made.”]

It is enough that I have followed his madness this far; from now on I shall remain in my own house for the duration of my lord king’s life.” [Col. 0595A]

When the guards heard this and believed that what they had heard was true, they became cheerful. Giving them room to pass, they allowed Hunulf—and Bertarid, whom they thought was a slave because he had covered his head so that he would not be recognized—to depart together.

After they had gone, that utterly faithful wardrobe-keeper carefully bolted the door and remained alone inside.

Hunulf lowered Bertarid by a rope from a corner of the wall on the side facing the river Ticino, and joined to him as companions as many men as he could. Taking horses which they had found grazing, they hurried that same night to the city of Asti [Col. 0595B],

[Note: And men who still remained rebellious toward Grimoald.]

where Bertarid’s friends were staying. From there Bertarid made for the city of Turin as quickly as possible and, after crossing the passes of Italy, reached the homeland of the Franks.

Thus almighty God, in his merciful providence, both rescued an innocent man from death and preserved from guilt the king who sincerely desired to do good.

[Note: Amb. reads: “and preserved from offence the king who desired from his heart to do good.”] [Col. 0595D]

## CHAPTER III. Grimoald’s mercy toward Hunulf and Bertarid’s wardrobe-keeper

King Grimoald, meanwhile, thinking that Bertarid was resting in his lodging, had a line of men stationed on both sides from that lodging all the way to his palace, so that Bertarid could be escorted between them and have no possibility of escape.

When messengers sent by the king came to summon Bertarid to the palace and knocked at the door where they thought he was resting, the wardrobe-keeper inside asked them, saying: “Have mercy on him and let him rest a little longer, for he is still exhausted from the journey and is overcome by very deep sleep.”

When they agreed to this, they reported to the king that Bertarid was still resting in deep sleep. Then the king said: “Did he fill himself so completely with wine yesterday evening that he is still unable to wake?”

[Note: Another reading has “at yesterday’s dinner.”]

Nevertheless, he ordered them to awaken him at once and escort him to the palace.

They came to the door of the chamber in which they hoped Bertarid was resting and began knocking more forcefully. Then the wardrobe-keeper again began asking them to allow Bertarid to sleep a little longer.

Angrily shouting that the drunken man had now slept long enough, they immediately broke down the door of the chamber with their heels and entered to look for Bertarid in the bed.

When they did not find him,

[Note: They suspected that he had gone to relieve himself. The words “When they did not find him there either” are absent from Amb. and the other L manuscripts.]

they suspected that he had gone to attend to a bodily necessity. When they did not find him there either, they asked the wardrobe-keeper what had happened to Bertarid.

[Note: Another reading: “what had happened, and, once he had understood the whole matter, he immediately went to him,” etc.]

He answered that Bertarid had fled.

They immediately seized him by the hair in fury, brought him before the king, and said that he was an accomplice in Bertarid’s flight and therefore deserved death above all.

The king ordered him to be released and questioned him in detail about how Bertarid had escaped. He reported everything to the king just as it had happened.

Then the king asked those standing around him: “What do you think of this man, who has carried out such a deed?”

They all answered with one voice that he deserved to be tortured with many punishments and put to death.

[Note: Mod. adds “and torments.”]

But the king said: “By him who caused me to be born, this man deserves to prosper, since he did not refuse to give himself over to death for loyalty to his master.”

He immediately ordered that the man be placed among his own wardrobe-keepers, warning him to preserve toward himself the same loyalty that he had shown toward Bertarid, and promising that he would grant him many benefits.

When the king asked what had happened to Hunulf, it was reported to him that Hunulf had taken refuge in the basilica of the blessed archangel Michael.

[Note: This is very frequently found in historians and other writers. See the Code, title *On Those Who Take Refuge in Churches*. The custom was first introduced by the Athenians, among whom there stood—as is now commonly known—an altar of mercy. The laws forbade violence against those who embraced it; consequently that place was always crowded with suppliants, as Statius elegantly writes in *Thebaid*, book XII:

“Always it holds the frightened; always the place bristles with needy crowds;  
the altar, unknown to the fortunate alone.”

People likewise fled to the statues of emperors, *Codex*, single law, *On Those Who Take Refuge at the Statues of Emperors*, and this was the safest refuge, as the most learned men have already shown. Those who fled to military standards were also safe from every injury. I think the reason was that images of emperors and rulers were usually attached to them. Tacitus, *Annals*, book I: “He had no other support in his danger than the camp of the First Legion. There he embraced the standards and the eagle and protected himself by religious awe; and if the standard-bearer Calpurnius had not warded off the final violence, etc.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXV: “Conscious of his fraud and guilt, he took refuge at the military standards.”] [Col. 0596B–D]

The king immediately sent word to him, promising voluntarily that he would suffer no harm, provided only that he came under the king’s protection.

When Hunulf heard this royal promise, he immediately came to the palace and threw himself at the king’s feet. The king asked him how and by what means Bertarid had been able to escape.

When Hunulf had related everything to him in order, the king praised his loyalty and prudence and mercifully granted him all his property and everything he possessed. [Col. 0596C]

## CHAPTER IV. How Grimoald sent Hunulf and Bertarid’s wardrobe-keeper to Bertarid

After some time, the king asked Hunulf whether he wished in those days to be with Bertarid. Hunulf answered under oath that he would rather die with Bertarid than live anywhere else amid the greatest pleasures.

Then the king questioned the wardrobe-keeper, asking whether it would be better for him to remain with the king in the palace or to live with Bertarid in exile.

When he gave him an answer similar to Hunulf’s, the king kindly accepted their words and praised their loyalty. He ordered Hunulf to take whatever he wished from his house—boys, horses, and various furnishings—and to hasten unharmed to Bertarid.

He released the wardrobe-keeper in the same way. Taking all their possessions in sufficient quantity, according to the king’s kindness, and with the same king’s assistance, they set out for the homeland of the Franks and their beloved Bertarid. [Col. 0597A]

## CHAPTER V. Grimoald’s war against the Franks and his victory

At this time an army of the Franks left the province [Col. 0597B]

[Note: Mod. reads: “Leaving the province of Gaul and entering Italy,” etc.]

and entered Italy. Grimoald advanced against them with the Lombards and deceived them by the following stratagem.

Pretending that he was fleeing their attack, he withdrew his men and left his camp entirely empty, together with the tents and the various goods stored there, especially an abundant supply of excellent wine.

When the Frankish army arrived, supposing that Grimoald and the Lombards, overcome by fear, had abandoned an intact camp, they immediately became delighted

[Note: Amb. reads “immediately.”]

and eagerly seized everything, preparing a lavish dinner.

While they were resting, weighed down by various foods and much wine, and overcome by sleep, Grimoald attacked them after midnight. He cut them down in such a massacre that scarcely a few of them were able to escape and return to their homeland.

The place where this battle of the Franks was fought is still called the River, and it is not far from the walls of the city of Asti.

[Note: Mod. reads *Rivulus* (“Little River”); for the final phrase Mod. reads “from the city of Asti.”] [Col. 0598A]

## CHAPTER VI. How Constans Augustus came to Italy and besieged Beneventum

In those days Constantine Augustus, also called Constans,

[Note: He had already conceived the plan of transferring the seat of the empire from Constantinople to Rome, since he saw that he was hated by the citizens because of the murder of his brother Theodosius, the crimes committed against the holy pope Martin and Maximus, and the Monothelite heresy, as Zonaras, Theophanes, Cedrenus, and other Greek writers affirm. In any event, they contain no mention of the subsequent Lombard war, nor does Anastasius the Librarian. Yet one may infer it from the necessity of the case, if he intended to transfer the empire from Greece to Italy, for he could not have carried this out without removing the Lombards. We owe the preservation of this sequence of events to our Paul, confirmed by the Latin testimonies cited below. We learn that these events took place as the year 662 was ending from the aforementioned Anastasius the Librarian, who states that the emperor came to Italy in the sixth indiction, during the pontificate of the holy Vitalian, and later “entered Rome on the fifth day of the month of July, Wednesday, in the aforesaid indiction.” These chronological markers certainly correspond to the year 663 and also agree well with the epoch of Grimoald’s reign.] [Col. 0597C–D]

desiring to wrest Italy from the hands of the Lombards, departed from Constantinople, traveled along the coast, and came to Athens. From there he crossed the sea and landed at Tarentum.

[Note: Mod. reads “at the city of Tarentum,” etc.]

Beforehand, however, he went to a certain solitary who was said to possess the spirit of prophecy, and diligently questioned him about whether he could conquer and subdue the nation of the Lombards who lived in Italy. [Col. 0598B]

The servant of God asked for a period of one night

[Note: In the Ascensian edition the passage reads as follows:

“In order to consult the Lord God about this matter”—Mod. reads “to beseech God”—“he faithfully offered prayers to the Lord with a ready heart, saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings and true light, who sent the Holy Spirit in the form of fire upon your apostles, send the Holy Spirit of your consolation into my mouth, so that I may be able to give sound counsel to these men who have come to me in your name.’

“At that same hour three spiritual persons appeared to him: one was the archangel Michael, the second John the Baptist, and the third the apostle Peter. Then one of them said to the solitary: ‘Tell the emperor Constans that, regarding the matter which he has arranged in his heart, the Lord’s will is not yet [that it should happen]. The nation of the Lombards who live in Italy cannot now be conquered by anyone, because a certain queen who came from another province built a basilica in honor of God and Saint John the Baptist within the territory of the Lombards, adorned it with honorable possessions, and arranged that male and female servants and the other dependents there should serve God, while priests should serve God faithfully in that oratory’—Mod. reads *oraculo* (“oracle”) for *oratorio* (“oratory”)—‘and for this reason Saint John continually intercedes for the Lombard nation.
