“‘That nation itself, humbly and devoutly, offers every year from its possessions gifts to the Lord in honor of God and Saint John the Baptist on the day of the Baptist’s birth, for the preservation of that oratory. The place is called Modicia.

“‘Yet we shall tell you truly in God: a time and day will come when all the inhabitants of this land will hold the aforementioned oratory in contempt, drive away all its possessions, and often oppress the male and female servants who are subject to it because of its possessions. The priests who now serve God there day and night will be greatly disturbed, and their property will be taken away. Because of this, their life will be led in bitterness.

“‘When these things begin and you see them happening, then certainly that nation will perish with everything belonging to it, and it will stand as a reproach to all the nations around it.’

“Then the solitary said to them: ‘I beg your clemency: if they turn back to the foregoing promise and way of life, will they not find mercy?’

“They replied: ‘You know what the Truth said: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you.”’

“At that same hour they vanished from his sight”—Mod. reads “they appeared nowhere thereafter.”

“When morning came, he carefully revealed everything to the same Constans Augustus in the order given above. Then the emperor gladly received his words. And we have found that this came to pass,” etc.

[Note: The omitted Mod. variants within this quotation are: “Constans has such a matter” for “the matter which he has arranged”; “at all times, on the day of his birth, [it] offers [gifts] to that oracle”; *Vere tamen* (“But truly”) for *Verumtamen*; *subjecti* for *subacti* (“subjected”); and, for the question concerning conversion, “If they have turned to their former promise, will they find pardon?”]

so that he might pray to the Lord about the matter. In the morning he answered the emperor as follows:

“The nation of the Lombards cannot now be conquered by anyone, because a certain queen who came from another province built the basilica of the blessed John the Baptist within the territory of the Lombards, and for this reason blessed John himself continually intercedes for the Lombard nation. But a time will come when that sanctuary will be held in contempt, and then the nation itself will perish.”

We have found that this came to pass, because, before the destruction of the Lombards, we saw that the same basilica of blessed John the Baptist—which is situated in a place called Modicia—was being administered by worthless people, so that the venerable place was being granted to unworthy and adulterous men, not for the merit of their lives but in exchange for payment. [Col. 0599A]


## CHAPTER VII. How Grimoald came to Beneventum at the invitation of his son Romoald

As we have said, when Constans Augustus arrived at Tarentum, he departed from there and invaded the territory of the Beneventans. He captured nearly all the Lombard cities through which he passed. [Col. 0599B]

[Note: Amb. reads “Lucerna”; another reading is “Luceria as well, a wealthy city, and Apulia attacked more vigorously.” Lindenb. reads “wealthy Apulegia,” as does Mod.]

He attacked and stormed Luceria, a wealthy city of Apulia, with great force, destroyed it, and laid it completely level with the ground.

[Note: Another reading is “Acherontia,” or “Agerentia.” Lind. reports that this is also found in Amb. and Mod.]

He was unable to capture Arentia, however, because of the exceptionally fortified position of the place.

Then, with his entire army, he surrounded Beneventum and began to attack it vigorously. At that time Romoald, the son of Grimoald, still a young man, held the duchy there.

As soon as he learned of the emperor’s arrival,

[Note: Glossary: *Nutricius*, τροφεύς, “nurse,” “foster-father,” or “guardian.” An ancient inscription reads:

“Memmia Tertulla to her deserving *nutricius* and mother, and to her descendants and herself.”

Ulpian, in his book *On the Office of the Proconsul*, calls such persons *educatores*, “educators,” law 33, *Digest*, *On Manumission by the Rod*. Justinian, book I of the *Institutes*, title 6, §5, mentions “a pedagogue, or a *nutricius*, or an educator, or an alumnus.” Theophilus expressed the passage as follows: “And to say, ‘He is my pedagogue, or nurse, or foster-father, or foster-child’” (Καὶ τὸ εἰπεῖν, ὅτι παιδαγωγός μου ἐστὶν, ἢ τροφὸς, ἢ τροφεὺς, ἢ ἀλοῦμνος).

In another inscription such persons are called *tatae*:

“To Titus Claudius Epaphroditus, his deserving *tata*, he made this.”

The word is also found in the Court Historian, where mention is made of τοῦ τατᾶ τῆς αὐλῆς, “the *tata* of the court.” But whether it is identical with the present term I cannot easily say.]

he sent his foster-father, named Sesuald, across the Po to his father Grimoald, begging him to come as quickly as possible and powerfully rescue his son and the Beneventans whom he himself had raised.

When King Grimoald heard this, he immediately began going to Beneventum with his army to bring aid to his son.

Many of the Lombards, however, left him on the journey and returned to their own homes, saying that he had plundered the palace and was returning to Beneventum never to come back.

Meanwhile the emperor’s army was violently attacking Beneventum with various engines of war. [Col. 0600A]

[Note: Another reading: “Although Romoald did not dare to attack the entire army together with his Lombards in equal battle, nevertheless he frequently,” etc.]

Romoald, on the other hand, resisted bravely with his Lombards. Although, because of the smallness of his army, he did not dare to engage such a multitude in hand-to-hand combat, he nevertheless frequently burst into the enemy camp with lightly armed young men and inflicted great losses on them everywhere.

[Note: The ancient author of the *Acts of Saint Barbatus* likewise relates the siege of Beneventum:

“At that time Constantine, also called Constans, ruled the empire of Constantinople. Desiring to recover Italy from the hands of the Lombards and bring it back under his authority, just as it had formerly been under the power of his predecessors, he crossed the sea with an immense multitude of his men and entered Tarentum. From there he set out and ravaged nearly all the cities of Apulia. Proceeding to the exceedingly wealthy city of Luceria, he captured it in very severe battles and, turning all the hands of the plunderers against it, laid it completely level with the ground. Rejoicing at its destruction, Augustus quickly moved his camp and placed it beside the walls of Beneventum.

“Without delay, having amassed an army for attacking the city with various engines of war, he appointed his nobles to conduct the assault. In that city was Romoald, whom we mentioned above, with a few but very strong Lombards; and Saint Barbatus the Father was staying there with them. After the city had been surrounded in terrifying fashion, they fought for a very long time in unprecedented battles to capture it.

“Romoald, however, being magnanimous and undaunted, resisted him bravely, now from the walls, now by sudden sallies, and crushed a very large part of his enemies. Because of the smallness of his army, he was afraid to draw up a battle line against them in the open. Nevertheless, with lightly armed men he repeatedly struck down the enemy’s troops by sudden attacks from one side and the other. But the aforementioned Augustus, the more attentively he saw Romoald resisting him, the more fiercely he brought new battles against him,” etc.

These acts contain no mention, however, of Grimoald the father being summoned to aid him.]

While Grimoald, his father, was hastening with all speed, he sent to his son the same foster-father whom we mentioned above, so that he might announce his arrival.

When Sesuald had come near Beneventum, he was captured by the Greeks and brought before the emperor. [Col. 0600B]

The emperor asked him where he came from. He replied that he came from King Grimoald

[Note: Amb. and Mod. read “he said that he came.”]

and announced that the king himself was approaching quickly.

The emperor was immediately terrified and took counsel with his men about making peace with Romoald, so that he might be able to return to Naples. [Col. 0600D]

## CHAPTER VIII. How the emperor, having taken Romoald’s sister as a hostage, departed from Beneventum

Having taken Romoald’s sister, whose name was Gisa, as a hostage, he made peace with Romoald.

[Note: Peregrinius notes an apparent contradiction here in the dissertation cited above, *On the Boundaries of the Principality of Beneventum*: namely, that the account says that Gisa was handed over as a hostage to the emperor by Duke Romoald after he had received news that his father, King Grimoald, was already at hand with a powerful army. The learned man did not understand Paul’s meaning correctly. On the contrary, after reporting that the hostage had been given, our author says that Sesuald, who had been sent ahead by the king to announce his arrival, was brought to the walls so as to deprive Romoald of hope of aid. The Greeks had evidently made an agreement with the Lombards that, unless Grimoald brought help within a fixed period, Romoald would surrender himself and his men. Therefore the Greeks who had captured Sesuald threatened him with death, as was their customary deceit, and brought him to the walls so that, being known to his own people, he might affirm that the king could not come. Sesuald, however, refused to do this, thereby making himself worthy of everlasting praise through this remarkable example of courage.]

He ordered Sesuald, his foster-father, to be brought to the walls and threatened him with death if he told Romoald or the citizens anything about Grimoald’s arrival. Instead, he was to affirm that Grimoald could not come at all.

Sesuald promised that he would do as ordered.

[Note: He said that he wished to see Romoald. In Mod. the words “When Romoald came quickly” are absent; the same form is noted in another manuscript by Lind. Amb. reads “he said that he wished Romoald to come. When he had arrived,” etc.]

But when he came near the walls, he said that he wished to see Romoald. When Romoald came quickly, Sesuald addressed him as follows: [Col. 0601A]

“Be courageous, Lord Romoald, and have confidence; do not be troubled, for your father will soon be here to bring you aid. Know that he is staying tonight beside the river Sangro with a powerful army. I ask only that you show mercy to my wife and children, because this treacherous people will not allow me to live.”

[Note: Amb. reads: “with my wife and children.”]

When he had said this, the emperor ordered his head to be cut off. It was thrown into the city together with the war engine called a *petraria*.

[Note: This was the name used in later times; earlier it was called a *scorpio* or *onager*. Anyone wishing to know its form should read Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII, for the passage is too long to reproduce here. Nicetas Choniates calls them πετροβόλα ὄργανα, “stone-throwing engines,” and writes that the barbarians used them especially, in book III of *The Deeds of Alexius Angelus*: Ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ πετροβόλα μηχανήματα, οἷς ἐχρωντο οἱ βάρβαροι, “and also the stone-throwing engines which the barbarians used.”] [Col. 0601D]

Romoald ordered Sesuald’s head to be brought to him, kissed it in tears, and ordered it to be buried in a worthy little coffin.

## CHAPTER IX. How Count Micola of Capua afflicted the emperor’s army

Fearing the sudden arrival of King Grimoald, the emperor abandoned the siege of Beneventum and departed for Naples. [Col. 0601B]

His army, however, was severely defeated by Count Mittola of Capua beside the waters of the river Calor, at a place that is still called Pugna.

[Note: Another reading is “Calbris.” Concerning this passage of Paul, Camil. Peregrinius writes in the work cited:

“I have no doubt that the river Calor is called by Paul the Sabato; Peter the Deacon recognizes it nearby in *Additions to the Ostian History*, book IV, chapter 16, where this place is called Pugna.”

This is an admirable argument, though Peregrinius adds a criticism that is too severe:

“But for Constans to have turned off from the direct road while retreating straight and hastily toward Naples, as Paul relates, is the usual confusion of places and events.”

I certainly do not see how Peregrinius could have inferred this precipitous retreat of the emperor and his direct route toward Naples except from his own conjecture. Although it may be probable, I have not considered it so important that it should cause us to withdraw our trust from Paul, especially since I have noted the position of both rivers as I once saw it in person; on account of this, no one could say that Constans, retreating from Beneventum to Naples, made an excessive detour.] [Col. 0602C–D]

## CHAPTER X. How Romoald defeated Saburrus, sent by the emperor, with twenty thousand men

After the emperor reached Naples, one of his nobles, named Saburrus,

[Note: Another reading: “from him.”]

is said to have requested twenty thousand soldiers from Augustus and promised that he would fight Romoald and emerge victorious.

When he had received the army and arrived at a place called Forinus,

[Note: Another reading is “Foranus”; another, “Formiae.”]

and had pitched his camp there, Grimoald, who had already arrived at Beneventum, heard of this and wished to march against him.

His son Romoald said to him:

[Note: Another reading: “There is no need, excellent father, for you to march.” Lindenb.]

“There is no need. Give us only a portion of your army. With God’s favor I shall fight him, and when I have conquered, the greater glory will certainly be attributed to your power.”

This was done. With the king’s approval,

[Note: Another reading: “And so, with the king’s consent, he went out against Saburrus with part of the army.”]

Romoald received part of his father’s army and set out with his own men against Saburrus.

Before engaging him in battle, he ordered trumpets to sound on all four sides, and then boldly charged upon them.

When both lines were fighting with fierce determination, one of the king’s soldiers named Amalongus,

[Note: Another reading: “Amelongus.” Lind. and Mod.]

who was accustomed to carry the royal lance, struck a certain Greek soldier forcefully with both hands using that same lance. He lifted him from the saddle on which he was riding and raised him into the air above his head.

When the Greek army saw this, it was immediately terrified by immense fear and turned to flight. It was slaughtered in the greatest disaster, and by fleeing it brought death upon itself while providing victory to Romoald and the Lombards.

Thus Saburrus, who had promised his emperor that he would win a victory and erect a trophy over the Lombards, returned to him with only a few men and brought back disgrace.

Romoald, having achieved victory over the enemy, returned triumphantly to Beneventum and brought joy to his father and security to everyone by removing the fear of the enemy.

## CHAPTER XI. The evils inflicted by Constans Augustus upon the Romans and the plunderings he carried out in the various regions; and how he was killed
At that time, however, the Emperor Constans, realizing that he had accomplished nothing against the Lombards, turned all the threats of his savagery against his own people—that is, against the Romans. For, departing from Naples, he proceeded to Rome. At the sixth milestone from the city, Pope Vitalian, together with the clergy and the Roman people, met him. When the emperor had reached the threshold of blessed Peter, he presented him with a pallium [Note: Ambrosius has “presented it there”; another reading has “a pallium woven with gold”; Lindanus: “but he remained in Rome for twelve days.”] woven with gold. Remaining among the Romans for twelve days, he removed all the ancient bronze fittings that had been installed as ornaments of the city, to such an extent that he even stripped the basilica of blessed Mary—which had once been called the Pantheon and had been built in honor of all the gods, but which by then, through the grant of earlier emperors [Note: Namely, the Emperor Phocas, as our author wrote above.], had become a place dedicated to all the martyrs—and took away its bronze roof tiles [Note: Modestus reads: “and from there removed the bronze tiles together with the other items, etc.”], sending them, together with all the other ornaments, to Constantinople.

Then the emperor returned to Naples and proceeded by land to the city of Rhegium [Note: Another reading has “Regia”; the manuscript has “the city of citizens”; Lindanus.]. Entering Sicily in the seventh indiction, he settled in Syracuse and imposed upon the people—or inhabitants and landowners—of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia afflictions such as had never before been heard of, so that even wives were separated from their husbands and children from their parents. The peoples of those regions also endured many other unheard-of sufferings, so that no one retained any hope of life [Note: Ambrosius: “so that no hope of life remained for anyone.”]. For vessels and the treasures of the holy churches of God were also removed by imperial command and through Greek avarice.

[Note: The Greek term *κειμήλιον* means “treasure” or “treasure-vessel.” Hesychius explains: “*Κειμήλια*: vessels, gifts, and deposited wealth.” Learned men understand the former sense in the following verse of Homer, *Iliad* 6:

> And receive worthy ransom;
>
> Many treasures lie stored in the house of a wealthy father,
>
> Bronze, gold, and finely wrought iron.

Triphiodorus proves the latter sense in his account of the destruction of Ilium:

> And they plundered many treasures
>
> From the deserted chambers.

Cassiodorus calls deposited funds *depositivae pecuniae* in Book VI, Letter 8: “Deposited monies also, which through long antiquity have lost their rightful owners, are, upon your investigation, assigned to our treasury.” Lindanus.]

The emperor remained in Sicily from the seventh indiction until the twelfth. At last, however, he paid the penalty for such great injustices [Note: Modestus: “he paid the penalty for such great calamities and injustices.”]; and while he was bathing, he was killed by his own men [Note: The Greek and Latin writers say that at Syracuse, in the bath, Constans was killed by Andrew, son of Troilus, who struck him violently on the head with the vessel in which hot water was being poured. Anastasius says that he was killed in the church of Saint Vitalian on 15 July, in the eleventh indiction. More recent scholars place the event in the twelfth indiction, as it is read in our Warnefridus and in several manuscripts of Anastasius. This is supported by the proceedings of the Sixth Synod, in which the thirteenth year of the consulship of Constantine Pogonatus is counted—an excellent indication that Constans died after the beginning of the twelfth indiction. Since our author wrote above that Constans ruled for eighteen years, he counted both terminal years incompletely, as he often does elsewhere.].

## CHAPTER XII. On the reign of Mecetius and his death

After the Emperor Constans had been killed at Syracuse, Mecetius seized the imperial power in Sicily, but without the consent of the army of the East [Note: The manuscript praises Mezentius for the distinction of his appearance.]. Against him, the soldiers of the Italian army—some coming through Istria, others through the regions of Campania, and still others from the regions of Africa and Sardinia [Note: Another reading: “coming to Syracuse from Sardinia”; Lindanus and Modestus.]—made a violent assault upon Syracuse and deprived him of life. Many of his judges were mutilated, and many were brought to Constantinople; together with them, the head of the false emperor was also carried away [Note: See Anastasius the Librarian, in the Life of Pope Adeodatus.].

## CHAPTER XIII. How the Saracens, coming from Alexandria, devastated Sicily and plundered whatever the Emperor Constans had removed from Rome

When the Saracen nation heard this—having already overrun Alexandria [Note: Ambrosius and Modestus: “which had already overrun Alexandria,” etc.] and Egypt [Note: This occurred under the Emperor Heraclius and Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria. In their time, in the year 635, Egypt was taken from Roman rule and submitted its neck to the yoke of the Saracens.]—they suddenly came with many ships, invaded Sicily, entered Syracuse, and inflicted a great slaughter upon the inhabitants, with scarcely a few escaping by taking refuge in very strongly fortified camps and on the mountain ridges. They also carried off immense booty, including all the bronze ornament and various objects that the Emperor Constans had removed from Rome, and thus returned to Alexandria [Note: Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Adeodatus, also records this devastation of Sicily by the Saracens. He connects it with the pontificate of Adeodatus, who succeeded Saint Vitalian, and with the death of Mecetius. But, since the Greek writers, including Theophanes, agree that it occurred in the year 661 according to the Alexandrian reckoning—beginning on 1 September of the year 669 according to the Latin reckoning—it is commonly assigned to the time of Saint Vitalian.].

## CHAPTER XIV. On the death of Gisa, the sister of Romoald

The king’s daughter, Gisa by name, whom we said had been taken from Benevento as a hostage [Note: Another reading: “we said that she had been taken away by the emperor”; Lindanus.], came to Sicily and ended her days.

## CHAPTER XV. On the excessive rains and thunder that occurred at that time

At that time there were rains and thunderstorms so great as no human being had previously remembered [Note: Ambrosius: “as no human being had remembered.”], so that countless thousands of people and animals were killed by lightning. That year the legumes, which could not be gathered because of the rains, grew again and were brought to maturity [Note: Anastasius says that this occurred after the death of Adeodatus.].

## CHAPTER XVI. How King Grimoald appointed Trasemund duke at Spoleto and gave him his daughter in marriage

But Grimoald, having rescued the people of Benevento and their provinces from the Greeks [Note: Another reading: “the first fruits of the Greeks.” Lindanus. The first reading should be retained, and its meaning considered; see Camillus Peregrinius, *Whether the Duchy of Benevento Was Tributary to the Ancient Provinces*, p. 75.], was preparing to return to his palace at Ticinum [Note: Another reading: “he returned after making arrangements concerning Trasemund, who had formerly been count of Capua,” etc.; Lindanus]. He had Trasemund, who had formerly been count of Capua [Note: Here “count” means a governor, as in the *Notitia Imperii*: “Count of Egypt, count of Isauria, of Africa, of Italy,” etc., where more is said about his dignity. For the dignity and office of counts among the Lombards, see the same Peregrinius, in the dissertation cited above.], and who had served him most energetically in acquiring the kingdom [Note: Another reading: “had rendered him vigorous assistance”; Lindanus], marry his daughter, the other sister of Romoald. After Atto, whom we mentioned above, he appointed Trasemund commander at Spoleto, and from there returned to Ticinum.

## CHAPTER XVII. That after Grasulf, Ago held the duchy of Forum Julii, and that after him Lupus became their commander

Indeed, as we had stated above, after Grasulf, duke of the people of Forum Julii, had died, Ago was appointed his successor in the duchy [Note: Ambrosius: “Adgadus was appointed his successor in the duchy, concerning whom,” etc. Modestus: “Ago was appointed his successor in the duchy.”]. From his name, a house situated within Forum Julii is still called the House of Ago. After Ago’s death, Lupus became commander of the people of Forum Julii.

This Lupus entered the island of Grado, which is not far from Aquileia, with a cavalry army, by way of the *strata*—a road that had formerly been constructed across the sea [Note: *Strata* means “road.” Victor of Vita, *On the Persecution of the Vandals*, Book III: “The roads, or paths, filled with the corpses of the dead exhaling stench, killed the living travelers on every side.” It is still especially common among the Germans. Lindanus.]. After plundering the city itself, he carried away the treasures of the Church of Aquileia [Note: After the treasure of the Church had been transferred from Aquileia to the island of Grado out of fear of the Lombards, the first to lay sacrilegious hands upon it was Fortunatus, bishop of Grado, who had defected from the Catholics and taken refuge with the Arians in the fortress of Cormons above Aquileia, under Pope Honorius. At the urging of Primigenius, a Catholic bishop and successor to Fortunatus, the Emperor Heraclius sent back more gold and silver than had been taken, as Dandulus writes in Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*.]. When Grimoald went to Benevento, he entrusted his palace to this Lupus.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Duke Lupus rebelled against Grimoald

While King Grimoald was absent, Lupus had behaved arrogantly in many matters at Ticinum, since he did not expect the king to return [Note: Ambrosius: “since he did not expect him to return,” etc.]. When the king did return, Lupus knew that the things he had done improperly displeased him. Therefore, conscious of his wickedness, he went to Forum Julii and rebelled against that same king.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the duke himself waged war against the Avars

Then Grimoald, unwilling to stir up civil war among the Lombards, sent word to Cacan, king of the Avars, to come with an army to Forum Julii against Duke Lupus and overthrow him in battle [Note: Modestus: “to crush him.”]. And so it happened.

For when Cacan came with a great army to a place called Fluvius [Note: Another reading: Flovius; Lindanus.], as older men who had been present at that very battle told us, Duke Lupus fought against Cacan’s army with the people of Forum Julii for three days [Note: Ambrosius: “within” three days]. On the first day he defeated Cacan’s powerful army, with only a few of his own men wounded. On the second day, after a number of his men had already been wounded and killed, he likewise destroyed many of the Avars. On the third day, although still more of his own men had been wounded or killed, he nevertheless destroyed a large part of Cacan’s army and seized abundant booty. But on the fourth day they saw such a multitude advancing against them that they could scarcely escape by flight.

## CHAPTER XX. On the death of Duke Lupus and how the Avars plundered the territory of Forum Julii

There, then, after Duke Lupus had been killed, the survivors fortified themselves in the castles. But the Avars ranged throughout all their territory, attacking everything with raids or setting it on fire. After they had done this for several days, Grimoald sent them orders to cease their devastation. They sent messengers to Grimoald, saying that they would by no means abandon Forum Julii, which they had conquered by their own arms [Note: The manuscript of Lindanus and another reading have: “They would by no means leave Forum Julii, so that whatever they had conquered by their own arms,” etc.].

## CHAPTER XXI. How the Avars, unwilling to leave Forum Julii, were expelled by Grimoald’s cunning

Then Grimoald, compelled by necessity, ordered an army to be assembled [Note: Ambrosius: “he began to assemble”; Lindanus: “he began to gather”], so that he might drive the Avars from his territory. In the middle of the plain he established his camp opposite the Avar enemy [Note: Ambrosius and Modestus: “establishing his camp opposite the Avar encampment.”]. Since he had only a small part of his army, and Cacan was sending messengers to him [Note: The words “and Cacan was sending messengers to him” are absent from Ambrosius.], he repeatedly made the very men he had—dressed differently and equipped with various weapons—pass before the eyes of the envoys for several days, as though a new army were continually arriving.

When the Avar envoys saw the same army passing by in different clothing and with different weapons [Note: Another reading: “When they saw it passing by equipped with different clothing and weapons, they thought them to be different men and believed that there was an immense multitude of Lombards,” etc.; Lindanus.], they believed it to be an immense multitude of Lombards. Grimoald therefore said to them: “With the whole multitude of the army that you have seen, I shall immediately attack Cacan and destroy the army of the Avars [Note: Ambrosius: “and destroy the Avars”], unless they quickly leave the territory of Forum Julii.”

After seeing and hearing this, the Avar envoys reported it to their king, who immediately returned with his entire army to his own kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Warnefridus, the son of Lupus

Finally, after Lupus had been killed in the manner we have described, his son Warnefridus wished to obtain the duchy at Forum Julii in his father’s place [Note: Ambrosius has *Arnefrit*; the manuscript of Lindanus, *Arnefridus*.]. But, fearing the power of King Grimoald, he fled to the people of the Sclaveni at Carnuntum, which they corruptly call Carantanum. Later, when he came with the Sclaveni, intending—as though—to recover the duchy by their power, the people of Forum Julii attacked him at the fortress of Nemas [Note: Another reading: Neumasum; Lindanus. See what I noted above, Book IV, chapter 38, no. 162.], which is not far from Forum Julii, and killed him.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Wectari, duke of the people of Forum Julii, and his victory

Next Wectari was appointed duke at Forum Julii [Note: The manuscript of Lindanus has *Juvectari*, and likewise below.]. He was a native of the city of Vicentia [Note: Another reading: “Vincentina”; Lindanus], a kindly man who governed the people gently.

When the people of the Sclaveni heard that he had gone to Ticinum [Note: Another reading: “had gone to the king at Ticinum”; Lindanus], they gathered a powerful multitude and wished to attack the fortress of the people of Forum Julii. Coming there, they made camp at a place called Broxas [Note: Cluverius, *Ancient Italy*, Book I, p. 201: “It is uncertain where this place, whose name is plural, Broxae, was situated along the Natiso River. It is nevertheless likely to have been above Forum Julii, toward Carantanum, the region of the Sclaveni now called Carinthia.”], not far from Forum Julii.

By divine providence it happened that Duke Wectari returned from Ticinum the previous evening, without the Sclaveni’s knowledge. His companions had returned home, as normally happens, but when he himself heard this news about the Sclaveni, he advanced against them with a few men—namely, twenty-five [Note: Modestus has twenty-two; Lindanus, twenty-six.].

When the Sclaveni saw him coming with so few men, they mocked him, saying that a patriarch was coming against them with his clergy [Note: Modestus: “that a patriarch was coming with a procession of clerics.”]. When he drew near the bridge of the Natiso River [Note: Ambrosius has “of the Nasicus.” Cluverius has collected extensive information about the Natiso River, its course, and its distinction from another river called the Natissa, in *Ancient Italy*, Book I, p. 185. There he writes: “The bridge of the Natiso was near the village of Tertium, where a flour mill can be seen placed upon the river.” He supports this conjecture with excellent arguments, which would be burdensome to reproduce here.], which was located where the Sclaveni were stationed, he removed his helmet from his head and showed his face to the Sclaveni, for he was bald.

When the Sclaveni recognized that he was Wectari, they were immediately thrown into confusion and shouted that Wectari was present. As God terrified them, they thought more about flight than battle. Then Wectari attacked them with the few men he had and struck them down in so great a slaughter that, out of five thousand men, scarcely a few survivors remained [Note: I am more inclined to believe that this passage of our Paulus is defective than that he wrote something so incredible. For twenty-five very brave men could scarcely have been sufficient in one assault to slaughter five thousand goats.].

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the death of Wectari, how Laudaris succeeded him, and on Rodoald, who held the duchy after him

After Wectari, Laudaris held the duchy at Forum Julii [Note: Another reading: Landheri; Lindanus.]. When he died, Rodoald succeeded him in the duchy [Note: Another reading: Radoaldus; Lindanus.].

## CHAPTER XXV. How Grimoald joined the daughter of Duke Lupus in marriage to his son Romoald

After Duke Lupus had died, as we have said, King Grimoald gave Lupus’s daughter, named Theuderada, in marriage to his son Romoald, who ruled Benevento [Note: The author of the Life of Saint Barbatus, bishop, in the Bollandists, writes that Theoderada had already been given to Romoald, duke of Benevento, before Constans’s arrival, and that, at the urging of the holy bishop, when Benevento was being besieged by the emperor, she stole the idols from her husband. These details do not agree with our author, who asserts that the marriage took place at least in the year following the siege. Another anonymous author of the eighth-century Life of Saint Sabinus, also published by the Bollandists on 9 February, seems to support the author of Saint Barbatus’s Life. In chapter 5 he writes: “At that same time Grimoalt governed the kingdom of the Lombards. He appointed his son Romoalt prince of Benevento and gave him in marriage the daughter of Lupus, who was of noble lineage, named Theoderada, whom we have just mentioned. When Romoalt died, he left her to govern the Samnite people with a young son.” From this it can readily be inferred that, at the same time that Grimoald appointed his son duke of the Beneventans, he also gave him a wife. The piety of Theoderada is also praised: after being warned by a vision and miracle, she built a church in honor of Saint Canusinus and placed his body in a marble tomb, adorning the altar coverings with gold and gems.].

By her Romoald fathered three sons: Grimoald, Gisulf [Note: Modestus: Agisulfus.], and Arichis [Note: Modestus: Arichit; another reading: Arichitum; Lindanus.].

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Grimoald avenged himself on those who despised him

King Grimoald also avenged himself for the injuries inflicted by all those who had deserted him when he had gone to Benevento.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Grimoald conquered and destroyed Forum Popilii

He also destroyed Forum Popilii, a Roman city whose citizens had inflicted certain injuries upon him when he was setting out for Benevento and had repeatedly harmed the messengers who went back and forth from Benevento [Note: “Messengers were sent”; compare the Frankish history, Book IV, chapter 7, Book IV, chapter 12, and elsewhere. Lindanus.]. He entered Tuscany by the Bardonian Alps during Lent [Note: Cluverius discusses the Bardonian Alps and Berceto below, Book VI, chapter 58, in the work cited, Book I, p. 293. From Book I, chapter 9, of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, and Book I, chapter 2, of Liutprand, he argues where both names were situated, stating: “There is no other passage through the mountain than the route by which, even today, travelers proceed from the valley of the Magra River, from the towns of Sarzana, Aulla, Villafranca, and Pontremoli, to Berceto; from there the road continues through Forum Novum to the city of Parma. I have shown above that Roman commanders once led armies from this route toward the fortress of Mutilum of the Boii; but at that time the Ligurian Apuani held this Bardonian mountain.”], entirely unbeknownst to the Romans. On the very holy Saturday of Easter, at the hour when baptism was being administered, he unexpectedly attacked the same city and inflicted such a slaughter that he even killed the deacons who were baptizing infants at the sacred font. Thus he overthrew that city, so that even to this day only a very few inhabitants remain there.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the hatred Grimoald held against the Romans

Grimoald indeed had no small hatred of the Romans, because they had once deceived his brothers Tasso and Cacco [Note: Another reading: Tassonem and Catonem; Lindanus and Modestus.] under a pledge of good faith. For this reason he utterly destroyed the city of Opitergium, where they had been killed, and divided its surrounding territory among the people of Forum Julii, the people of Tarvisium, and the people of Ceneta [Note: Another reading: “where they had lived”; another: “where they had been.” Lindanus.].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Alzecon, duke of the Bulgars, and how he was settled with his people in Benevento

At this time Alzecon, a duke of the Bulgars, for a reason unknown, departed from his people and entered Italy peacefully with the entire army of his duchy. He came to King Grimoald, promising that he would serve him and dwell in his country. Grimoald sent him to his son Romoald at Benevento and ordered Romoald to grant him and his people places in which to live [Note: The word τό—“places”—is not found in Ambrosius.].

Romoald welcomed them gladly and assigned them spacious places to inhabit, which until that time had been deserted—namely, Sepianum [Note: Ambrosius: Sepinum; another reading: Sepia; Lindanus.], Bovianum, Isernia [Note: Another reading: Esernia; Lindanus.], and other cities with their territories [Note: Camillus Peregrinius correctly observed that the account in the *Miscellaneous History* does not agree with Paulus concerning the arrival of the Bulgars in Italy. The following passage appears in Book XIX of that work: “In the time of Constantine, who ruled in the West, when Orbatus, lord of the aforesaid region of Bulgaria, or of the Contragors, changed his life and left five sons, he charged them not to separate from one another in any way through mutual dwelling, and not to serve any other nation. But shortly after his death, when they fell into division, his five sons were separated from one another, together with the people whom each had under his authority. The first son, called Buthajas, obeying his father’s command, remained in the land of his ancestors, etc.” After enumerating the other four and their migrations, he says of the fifth, whose name he omits: “The other, coming not far from the city of Ravenna into the Pentapolis, was placed under Christian rule.” Peregrinius agrees with Paulus by citing an anonymous author of Cassino, published by him, who, narrating several histories in continuous sequence, writes in section 3: “Alzecon the Bulgar was received with his people for habitation; the Lombards, overcoming the peoples of the Greeks and Romans, took possession together of the whole territory of Benevento.” Peregrinius suspects that the anonymous author brought together in one place the arrival of Alzecon and the great victory of the Lombards over the Greeks and Romans, by which they obtained the Beneventan region so extensively—at the time of Constans, as our author explicitly asserts. He therefore conjectures that Alzecon and his people were summoned by the duke of Benevento and his father, King Grimoald, as auxiliaries against the Greeks, and that they were brought from the fields of Ravenna, where they had first been received as guests, to new settlements, where they remained through royal favor. Nevertheless, I would not depart from our author, placing little confidence in the anonymous writer, who gathers many events separated by a long period into a single bundle. However plausible the conjecture may be that the Bulgars migrated from Ravenna to the Beneventan region in order to restore a land perhaps devastated by Greek violence, I retain our author’s account.].

He ordered Alzecon himself to be called a *gastaldium*, changing the name of his dignity from duke [Note: Another reading: “a gastald instead of a duke,” etc. It has often been noted by others what this term means in the Lombard laws. Peregrinius, praised above all others, treats the matter more precisely in his dissertation *Whether the Duchy of Benevento Was Tributary to the Ancient Provinces*. There, after explaining the civil power of the gastalds and turning to their military authority, he corrects Jacobus Cujacius, Book I, *On Fiefs*, section “If, however, the gastalds,” who maintains that the cities mentioned by our author were given to Alzecon by right of gastaldship—not as a permanent and proper fief, but temporarily and almost in the capacity of an agent. Peregrinius writes: “I cannot agree with this very learned man. For the prerogative of the gastalds was not simple and single, but multiple and mixed, as has been said. Moreover, Alzecon does not seem to have relinquished either the cities and towns received for habitation or the care of his people after the completion of his year as gastald, just as he had laid aside the dignity and name of duke. For Paulus plainly asserts that the Bulgars inhabited the settlements assigned to them down to his own age. Although they spoke Latin as well, they did not at all lose the use of their own language—and, I would add, that they had a gastald from their own people. In my judgment, therefore, King Grimoald refused Alzecon the name of duke, not because he was unwilling to grant him a permanent gastaldship, but because, once established under the duke of Benevento, Alzecon could not retain his original dignity. Since he was an immigrant, he ought to receive a temporary dynasty in places that he and his people would inhabit permanently.” I myself, although I do not depart from Cujacius in matters relating to the rights of this kind of gastaldship, think that Alzecon’s position was of a different kind and that he had nothing in common with the other gastalds except the name. In truth, I believe that he held his fief by perpetual right, having laid aside the name of duke so that he could not be regarded as the equal of Romoald, his lord, from whom he had received the benefice.].

Those who inhabit these places to this day, as we have said, although they also speak Latin [Note: That is, the common and popular Italian language, as Peregrinius interprets this passage. For “to speak Latin” in Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio was said of those who used not ancient and Latian speech but the language then in use among the Italians. Otto of Freising also uses the expression in this sense in *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick II*, chapter 13, when he praises the Lombards as Italians for the elegance of their Latin speech.], have nevertheless not lost the use of their own language.

## CHAPTER XXX. How, after the tyrant Mecetius was killed, Constantine became ruler of the Romans in place of the Emperor Constans

After Constans Augustus had been killed in Sicily, as we have said, and the tyrant Mecetius, who had succeeded him, had been punished [Note: Modestus: Constantine. Another reading: Meretius; another: Mozentius; Lindanus: Mezotius; Ambrosius.], Constantine, son of the Emperor Constantius Augustus, assumed the rule of the Roman Empire, and he held the principate over the Romans for seventeen years [Note: Modestus has eighteen; Ambrosius, nineteen—both corrupt readings, and the editors’ reading should be retained here. Greek and Latin historians agree that Constantine Pogonatus ruled for seventeen years. He died at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction, according to Anastasius in his Life of John V.].

In Constantine’s time, the archbishop Theodore [Note: Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning whom Bede writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 1: “He was ordained by Pope Vitalian in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 668, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, and together with Adrian he was sent to Britain on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.”] and the abbot Adrian [Note: Of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury. Concerning him the cited Bede writes, Book IV, chapter 2: “Theodore’s co-worker in the word of God; and because both were abundantly instructed in sacred and secular letters, they gathered a crowd of disciples, and every day rivers of saving knowledge flowed forth to water their hearts. Thus, among the volumes of sacred writings, they also taught their hearers the disciplines of meter, astronomy, arithmetic, and ecclesiastical learning.” Abbot Adrian is included among the saints, and the churches of England celebrate his memory on 9 January. See the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists for that day.]—men equally learned, sent by Pope Vitalian to Britain—enriched many churches of the English with the fruits of ecclesiastical teaching. Among them, Bishop Theodore composed a penitential concerning the judgments of sinners, specifying, with admirable and careful discernment, for how many years a person should repent for each sin [Note: This book is called the *Penitential*, and Spelman reports its principal contents in his *Collection of the Councils of England*. A manuscript is preserved in the Library of Saint Benedict at Cambridge. He also published other writings, which Labbe printed in volume VI of his *Collection of Councils*. Theodore held a council against the Monothelites. Mabillon presents his Life in volume II of the Benedictine century. According to Bede, Book V, chapter 8, he passed to heaven on 19 September 690.].

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the comet and the works of Pope Donus

In the following period, in the month of August [Note: Another reading: “In the second following year”; Lindanus.], a comet appeared in the eastern sky, with exceedingly bright rays [Note: Another reading: “with rays of diminished brightness, which later scattered in different directions”; Lindanus.]. Afterward it turned back upon itself and disappeared [Note: Bede discusses this comet in Book IV, chapter 12. Anastasius, in his Life of Donus, writes: “While he had been elected, during the month of August, a star appeared in the east, from cockcrow until morning, for three months. Its rays penetrated the heavens. At its appearance all the provinces and peoples rose in wonder; afterward it turned back upon itself and disappeared. Following this event, a very great mortality also came from the east.” Since the election of Donus is assigned by the more accurate calculations of recent scholars to the year 676, the comet’s appearance falls in the following year, although nearly all chronologists disagree among themselves.].

Soon afterward, a severe pestilence followed from that same eastern region and devastated the Roman people. In those days Pope Donus wonderfully paved with large white marble stones the area belonging to the Roman Church called Paradise, in front of the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter [Note: Anastasius likewise writes in his Life of Donus: “He paved the upper court of the blessed Apostle Peter, which is in front of the church and enclosed by a four-sided portico, with large marble stones.” Paradise was the middle portion of the court, lying below the steps of the basilica and surrounded by the four-sided portico, as Valesius observes, citing ancient testimony, in his notes on the panegyric poem *On the Praises of Berengar*].

## CHAPTER XXXII. How Bertaridus decided to go to the kingdom of the Saxons in Britain

At this time Dagobert ruled the kingdom of the Franks in Gaul [Note: This passage of Paulus gave Mabillon material, in the preface to Part I of the fourth Benedictine century, for investigating the restoration of Dagobert II to the kingdom of Austrasia, a matter over which nearly all historians of Frankish affairs have struggled greatly. It is established that, after his father Saint Sigebert, king of Austrasia, had been called to heaven, Dagobert was, through the wickedness of Grimoald—who, holding the dignity of mayor of the palace, had been appointed guardian of the orphan—driven into exile in Ireland so that Grimoald might give the kingdom to his own son. Dagobert was later recalled, chiefly through the efforts of Saint Wilfrid, archbishop of York. The year of his restoration is uncertain. Mabillon, noting that our author assigns Dagobert the kingdom before Grimoald’s death—which he likewise assigns to the year 671 on the basis of Grimoald’s edict—supposes that Dagobert was restored before that year. Others deny that Paulus is reliable here and substitute Clotaire III or Childeric for Dagobert, relying on numerous arguments that cannot be discussed here, both because of their number and because of their variety, since nearly every writer proceeds according to his own judgment and conjecture. Valesius, Comtius, Henschenius, and several others have treated the matter more fully in their exegesis and dissertations *On the Three Dagoberts*. It is enough for me to have noted these matters in passing.], with whom King Grimoald had entered into a firm treaty of peace.

Fearing Grimoald’s power even while he remained in the Frankish realm, Bertaridus departed from Gaul and prepared to hasten to the island of Britain and to the king of the Saxons.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the death of King Grimoald, the return of Bertaridus, and his reign
But Grimoald, when, on the ninth day after the bloodletting, he was staying in his palace [Note: Col. 0612D. Flebotomum; Lindau manuscript: Flevotomum; Amb.], attempted, after taking up a bow, to strike a dove with an arrow, a vein in his arm ruptured. His physicians, so it is said, applied poisonous medicines to the wound and thereby deprived him utterly of this light [Note: Col. 0612D. Amb., *life*]. He also added to the edict composed by King Rothari certain chapters of the law which seemed useful to him [Note: Col. 0612D. I have spoken of these above. See the Lombard laws]. He was a man of exceptionally powerful physique, foremost in courage, bald-headed, with a prominent beard, adorned no less with prudence than with strength [Note: Col. 0612D. Mod., *well suited*]. His body was buried in the basilica of the blessed confessor Ambrose, which he himself had formerly built within the city of Ticinum.

After the death of King Aripert, when one year and three months had already elapsed, he seized the kingdom of the Lombards and himself ruled for nine years [Note: Col. 0612D. He died in the year 671, as is clear from the prologue to his own edict and from this testimony of Paul, to which Sigebert in his *Chronicle* also contributes, assigning Grimoald nine years of reign], leaving his son Garibald as king. Garibald had been born to him by the daughter of King Aripert and was still of childish age.

Therefore, as we had begun to say, Bertarid departed from Gaul and boarded a ship in order to cross to the island of Britain, to the kingdom of the Saxons. When he had sailed some distance across the sea, a voice was heard from the shore asking whether Bertarid was aboard that ship. When he was told that Bertarid was there, the one who was shouting added: “Tell him to return to his own country, because today is the third day since Grimoald was taken from this life” [Note: Col. 0613C. Amb.: “that he should return,” and so forth].

When he heard this, Bertarid immediately turned back. On reaching the shore, however, he was unable to find the person who had announced Grimoald’s death. He therefore concluded that this had not been a human being but a divine messenger. From there, returning to his homeland, when he reached the passes into Italy, he found that all the palace services and the entire royal dignity had already been prepared for him, together with a great multitude of Lombards [Note: Col. 0613C. Amb. and Modoet.: “He found himself expected, with everything prepared. Thus, returning to Ticinum,” and so forth].

Accordingly Bertarid returned to Ticinum, expelled the child Garibald from the kingdom [Note: Col. 0613C. Another manuscript: “having expelled the child Grimoald from the kingdom.” Lind. and Amb.: “the child,” and so forth], and was raised to the kingship by all the Lombards in the third month after Grimoald’s death. He was a pious man, Catholic in faith, steadfast in justice, and an exceedingly generous provider for the poor. He immediately sent to Beneventum and recalled from there his wife Rodelinda and his son Cunibert [Note: Col. 0613C. Amb.: Cunibert].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the monastery which he built, or which his queen constructed

When he had assumed the rights of kingship, in that place on the bank of the river Ticinum from which he had once fled, he built a monastery called “New” for the Lord, his deliverer, in honor of the holy virgin and martyr Agatha [Note: Col. 0613C.

The writers of the history of Ticinum say that this church was built by Bertarid and consecrated to the holy virgin Agatha for the following reason: on the night preceding the feast of that holy virgin, he avoided Grimoald’s fury by being lowered from the city walls on a rope opposite the church. There still exists a notable monastery of holy virgins, commonly called, after the neighboring hill, Saint Agatha in the Mountain. It formerly belonged to the Order of Saint Benedict and now to the Conventual Sisters of Saint Clare. For its varied fortunes, see *Sacred Pavia* by P. Romuald of Saint Mary. On the front of this church the following inscription is read: “Pertharid, king of the Lombards, dedicated this church to Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr, in the year of Christ 673.” In this sacred convent Cuniperga, daughter of King Cunibert and granddaughter of Bertharid, achieved distinction in the dignity of abbess, as is read in a fragment of the inscription on her tomb:

“Learn, if you wish to know . . . what this tomb conceals, a woman . . . what kind of image she was, enclosed beneath precious stone; toward those for whom . . . here, like snow, her honored limbs are dissolved. Whoever . . . Cuniberga, handmaid of the Mother of God, . . . This gentle lady was . . . She was beautiful in appearance . . . beautiful among women. To widows and orphans, with serene face and truly shining eyes, she was ignorant of the cloud of this world; from her lips flowed honey. She presided over the virgins . . . truly the daughter of the father, Cunibert, the excellent king. This daughter bore in herself the entire likeness of him whose . . . and in whom her father’s sweetness flourished in spirit. And let the sacred college of virgins, dedicated to Christ, declare what this attests . . .”]

He gathered many virgins there and enriched the same place with various possessions and ornaments [Note: Col. 0614C. Another manuscript: “possessions.” Lind.].

His queen and wife, Rodelinda, built outside the walls of that same city of Ticinum a basilica of the holy Mother of God, called “at the Poles,” with marvelous workmanship, and adorned it with wondrous ornaments. The place itself is called “at the Poles” because once upon a time poles—that is, beams—stood erected there, which for this reason were customarily set up according to Lombard usage [Note: Col. 0614C.

Consult the sources concerning this rite in which, to use the words of Septimius, “the ancient tenor of memory” remains from the former literature. I know of nothing similar. Lind.

A more recent testimony, in addition to Paul’s, is also supplied by Aulicus of Ticinum in his *History of Gaul*, in these words: “Among other things there are three most ancient cemeteries, venerable throughout the whole world, which were formerly much larger than they are now: namely, the cemetery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which extends as far as the third wall and the ditches of the city; the cemetery of Saint John at Rurgo; and the cemetery of Saint Mary at the Poles, in the middle of which is the chapel of Saint Adrian, where the kings of the Lombards and many other nobles were buried. This cemetery is said to have been one of the four principal cemeteries of the world, and therefore nobles from distant regions chose burial there, having individual poles planted above their graves with some sign by which each person could recognize his own burial place. Hence it is still commonly called the church of Saint Mary at the Poles.” Concerning the location of this cemetery and church, see what the cited author has discussed in *Sacred Pavia*.]

For if someone had been killed in some place—whether in battle or in any other manner—his relatives fixed a pole within his tomb, placing at its top a dove made of wood, turned toward the place where their beloved one had died, so that it might be known in which direction the deceased rested [Note: Col. 0614D. The words that follow, through “they placed,” are absent from other manuscripts. Lind.].

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning Bertarid and the reign of his son Cunibert

[Col. 0614B]

Bertarid therefore ruled alone for seven years. In the eighth year he made his son Cunibert his associate in the kingship, and together they ruled for ten years.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning Alachis’s first rebellion and how he was restored to favor

While they were living in great peace and enjoying tranquility on every side, there arose against them a son of iniquity named Alachis [Note: Col. 0614D. Amb. and Mod.: *always*, Alabis]. Through him, after peace had been disturbed in the Lombard kingdom, enormous slaughter of the people took place.

When he was duke in the city of Tridentum, he fought with the count of the Bavarians—whom they call a *gravio* [Note: Col. 0614D. Another manuscript: *gravium*. See the Salic Laws. Lind. Our Paul rightly makes the rank and office of the *graviones* equivalent to those of Lombard counts. They are mentioned repeatedly in the Salic Laws, as the learned Lindenbrog observed. Among later writers, D. Eccard, in his notes on those laws and on the Teutonic Catechism, investigated the origin of this word and derived it from *ragen*, which he explains as “to stand out”; hence *graviones* are provincial judges. Others derive it from *grau canus* (“gray-haired man”); yet both etymologies converge upon the same conception of the office. From this passage of our Paul it should further be observed that the *graviones* possessed military as well as civil authority. Col. 0615C. Ambros.: Bauganum. This is the well-known market town at the confluence of the Athesis and Atagis, now Bolzano.]—who governed Bauzanum and the other fortresses. Alachis defeated him decisively. Elated by this success, he also raised his hand against his own king, Bertarid, and, rebelling, fortified himself within the fortress of Tridentum.

King Bertarid advanced against him and laid siege to him from outside. Suddenly and unexpectedly, Alachis emerged from the city with his men [Note: Col. 0615C. Amb.: “from the city”], routed the king’s camp, and forced the king himself to flee. Later, however, through the intervention of Cunibert, the king’s son, who had long loved him, he returned to the favor of King Bertarid. Although the king had wished several times to kill him, his son Cunibert always prevented this, considering that Alachis would henceforth remain faithful.

Nor did Cunibert cease pleading with his father until he obtained for Alachis the duchy of Brixia [Note: Col. 0615C. Mod.: “to obtain this through prayers.” Another manuscript: “to burden his father with prayers.” Lind.]. His father repeatedly protested that Cunibert was doing this to his own ruin, since he was giving his enemy the strength to seek the kingship. The city of Brexiana had always possessed a large multitude of Lombard nobles, and Bertarid feared that with their help Alachis would become more powerful.

During these days King Bertarid constructed, with marvelous workmanship, a gate adjoining the palace in the city of Ticinum, which is also called the Palatine Gate [Note: Col. 0615C. Amb. and Mod.: Platinensis. Another manuscript: Placensis. Lind.].

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the death of Bertarid and the reign of Cunibert

After he had held the kingdom for eighteen years—first alone and afterward with his son—he was taken from this life [Note: Col. 0615D. Amb.: “he was succeeded.” Paul is not consistent in his enumeration of King Bertarid’s years: in the preceding chapter, 35, he assigns him seventeen; here, eighteen. I think this is a scribal error, unless perhaps the final year here was incomplete. Sigebert in his *Chronicle* assigns him seventeen, although he places the beginning of Bertarid’s reign one year earlier; since it must be assigned to the year 671, his death must have occurred in 688]. His body was buried beside the basilica of the Lord Savior, which his father Aripert had built.

He was of pleasing stature, full-bodied, gentle in every respect, and gracious. King Cunibert took as his wife Hermelinda, of the Saxon-English race. When she saw in a bathhouse a girl named Theodote, born of a very noble Roman family, possessing an elegant body and adorned with blond, flowing hair reaching almost to her feet [Note: Col. 0615D. Amb.: “flowing”], she praised the girl’s beauty to her husband, King Cunibert. He pretended not to be pleased to hear this from his wife, but nevertheless burned with a great love for the girl.

Without delay he went hunting in the forest called the Urbs and ordered his wife Hermelinda to accompany him. From there he departed by night and returned to Ticinum. He had the girl Theodote brought to him and slept with her. Later, however, he sent her to a monastery which, after her name, is called Theodote within Ticinum [Note: Col. 0615D. The monastery of Saint Mary called Theodote, commonly della Posteria. It still preserves the memory of a certain Theodote, indeed also an ancient funerary stone of another virgin consecrated to God by that name in the same church, which reads as follows:

“I shall finally recount the lineage of the heavenly maiden . . .

Her mother lived for many years among the virgins,

feeding the little sheep of Christ in the Lord’s flock;

cherishing them, she taught, rebuked, corrected, and loved them.

Lest the envious man deprive her of one of his sheep, although

he wore a wrinkled brow, her heart was pure toward them,

and her gentle hands abstained from scourging.

In giving food, she was generous in feeding the needy.

Adorned with character, gracious and honorable,

patient, great-hearted, and charitable in action,

she was fittingly such, since she came from such a stock.

B. . . . growing from a new shoot, like a river from its source,

. . . beyond the coverings, there was a great parent.

If the speech is directed toward the course of events and the concerns of the present age,

there are many things that we can say.

Through you the beautiful shrine of the Virgin is always cherished.

Removing what is old, you restore all that is mean.

For the dwellings situated in the convent smile,

the ancient walls surpassing the faces of those who look upon them,

nor are there such things anywhere in the world, except the palaces of kings.

Nor the holy churches, which gleam with a splendid foundation

and which are equaled in piety by . . . All are honored.

Therefore this Theodota, for the pupils of her Theodota,

to whom you left the name, dignity, and chair,

the lady, afflicted in heart with many tears,

I adorned and embellished with beautiful sarcophagus stones,

living for approximately twenty-two years . . .

She closed the remarkable portals of life . . .

on the . . . day of April, in the third indiction. Nor do I approve the author of *Sacred Pavia’s* explanation of the letters, referring them to the year 926, since that year was marked by the fourteenth indiction, not the third. In a purer age I would read *de pecunia sua* (“from her own money”); but, frankly, I cannot easily disentangle the Lombardic form. Let others more skilled judge.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How Alachis invaded Cunibert’s palace

Alachis, long pregnant with the iniquity he had conceived, was supported by Aldo and Grauso, citizens of Brexiana, as well as by many other Lombards. Forgetful of the great benefits King Cunibert had bestowed upon him, and also forgetful of the oath by which he had promised to be completely faithful to him, he invaded Cunibert’s kingdom and palace within Ticinum while Cunibert was absent.

When Cunibert heard this [Note: Col. 0616D. Amb.: “hearing this, he immediately fled to the island,” and so forth], he fled to an island situated in Lake Larius, not far from Como [Note: Col. 0616D. Another manuscript: “He took refuge on an island not far from Lake Comacinus.” Lind.], and there strongly fortified himself.

Great distress arose among all who loved him, especially the priests and clerics, whom Alachis hated. At that time the bishop of the Church of Ticinum was a man named Damian, distinguished in holiness and adequately trained in the liberal arts. When he saw that Alachis had invaded the palace, he sent his deacon Thomas to him, a wise and religious man, so that neither he nor his Church might suffer any harm at Alachis’s hands. Through Thomas he sent Alachis the blessing of his holy Church.

Alachis was informed that the deacon Thomas was standing before the doors and had brought a blessing from the bishop. Then Alachis, who, as we have said, hated all clerics, said to his men: “Go and tell him: If he has clean underclothes, let him enter; otherwise, let him keep his foot outside.”

When Thomas heard these words, he replied: “Tell him that I have clean underclothes, since I am wearing ones that I washed today” [Note: Col. 0617D. The word *lota* is not read in Amb.].

Alachis then said to Thomas: “Go again and tell him that I am not speaking of the underclothes, but of what is contained within the underclothes” [Note: Col. 0617D. Amb. and Mod.: “Alachis again ordered him: ‘I am not speaking,’” and so forth].

Thomas replied: “Go and tell him: God alone can find fault with me in these matters; that man certainly cannot.”

Alachis then had the same deacon brought inside and spoke with him harshly and abusively. Fear and hatred of the tyrant seized all the clerics and priests, who thought that they would be wholly unable to endure his savagery [Note: Col. 0617D. Mod omits the word “him” after “endure”]. They began to desire Cunibert all the more because they held the proud usurper of the kingdom in greater detestation [Note: Col. 0617D. Another manuscript: “the perverse one”; another: “since they held the proud invader of the kingdom in greater execration.” Lind.]. But his savagery and barbarous cruelty did not retain the kingdom he had seized for long.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How Cunibert again entered his palace

One day, while Alachis was counting solidi on a table, a tremissis fell from the table. The son of Aldo, still a small boy, picked it up from the ground and returned it to Alachis [Note: Col. 0617D. One tremissis, according to Amb. and Mod. Another manuscript: a third; the Lindau manuscript: a tremensis. A tremissis is a type of coin. It also occurs in the Lombard laws, title 101, § 62; the Bavarian laws, title III, § 1; and elsewhere. Lind.].

Thinking that the boy understood little, Alachis said to him: “Your father possesses many of these, which, if God wills, he will soon give me.”

When the boy returned home to his father in the evening, his father asked him whether the king had said anything during the day. He reported everything to his father exactly as it had happened, including what the king had said to him [Note: Col. 0618D. Mod.: “He made known what had happened. When he heard this,” and so forth; likewise Lind.].

When Aldo heard this, he was greatly frightened. He summoned his brother Grauso and told him everything the king had maliciously said [Note: Col. 0618D. “He addressed his brother Grauso and told him everything,” and so forth]. They immediately took counsel with their friends and with those whom they could trust about how they might deprive the tyrant Alachis of the kingdom [Note: Col. 0618D. Another manuscript: “of kingdom and life.” Lind.] before he could inflict some injury upon them.

They set out promptly for the palace and said to Alachis: “Why do you deign to remain in the city? Look, the entire city and all the people are faithful to you, while that drunken Cunibert is so weakened and dissolute that he can no longer possess any strength. Go out and go hunting; amuse yourself with your young men. We, together with your other faithful supporters, will defend this city for you. We also promise you that shortly we shall bring you the head of your enemy Cunibert.”

Persuaded by their words, Alachis left the city and proceeded to the enormous forest called the Urbs, where he began to occupy himself with games and hunting [Note: Col. 0618A. Mod.: “desolate”; another manuscript: “deserted and abandoned.” Lind.].

Aldo and Grauso, meanwhile, went to Lake Comacinus, boarded a ship, and traveled to Cunibert. When they reached him, they fell at his feet and confessed that they had acted wickedly against him. They told him what Alachis had maliciously said against them and what counsel they themselves had given Alachis for Cunibert’s destruction.

Why say more? They wept together and exchanged oaths, setting a day on which Cunibert would come and they would hand over the city of Ticinum to him. And so it happened. On the appointed day Cunibert came to Ticinum, was received by them with the greatest eagerness, and entered his palace.

Then all the citizens—and especially the bishop, as well as the priests and clerics, the young and the old—ran eagerly to meet him. Embracing him with tears, they shouted their thanks to God, filled with immeasurable joy at his return. He kissed them all and comforted them as best he could.

A messenger suddenly reached Alachis, informing him that Aldo and Grauso had fulfilled what they had promised him, had brought Cunibert’s head—and not merely his head but his whole body—and that Cunibert was sitting in the palace. Hearing this, Alachis was overwhelmed with anguish. Furiously gnashing his teeth, he uttered many threats against Aldo and Grauso. He then departed and returned through Placentia to Austria [Note: Col. 0618D. Amb. and Mod. always read *Istria*, and Lindenbrog reads it that way elsewhere as well. It seems clear that *Istria* should be restored on the basis of what follows].

He enrolled the individual cities as his allies, partly by persuasion and partly by force [Note: Col. 0618D. Mod.: “joining and associating them with himself”]. When he came to Vincentia, its citizens marched out against him and prepared for battle, but were soon defeated and became his allies. From there he departed and seized Tarvisium, and in the same manner also the remaining cities [Note: Col. 0618D. Another manuscript: “the other cities, so that he might gather an army against Cunibert and so that the people of Friuli might come to his aid,” and so forth].

While Cunibert was gathering an army against him, and the people of Friuli wished, in accordance with their loyalty, to march to his aid, Alachis hid himself at the bridge of the river Liquentia, forty-eight miles from Forojulium and on the road taken by those traveling to Ticinum, in a forest called Capulanus. As the army of the people of Friuli came in scattered groups, he compelled them all, as they arrived, to swear allegiance to him, carefully taking precautions lest anyone who had turned back after coming should inform the others. Thus all those coming from Forojulium were bound by oaths to him [Note: Col. 0618D. Another manuscript: “What more? Alachis and all Istria came with their men against Cunibert into the field,” and so forth. Mod. and Amb. likewise have *Istria* here].

What more? With all Austria on Alachis’s side, Cunibert, on the other, came with his men into the field called Coronata and pitched camp there [Note: Col. 0619D. It was situated on the banks of the river Adda, as is made perfectly clear by the following chapter].

## CHAPTER XL. Alachis’s war against Cunibert

Cunibert sent a messenger to Alachis, ordering him to enter into single combat with him, since there was no need to weary both armies. Alachis did not agree to this proposal.

One of his men, a Tuscan by birth, a warlike and courageous man, tried to persuade him, calling him brave and urging him to come out boldly against Cunibert. Alachis replied: “Although Cunibert is a drunkard and dull of heart, he is nevertheless sufficiently bold and of extraordinary strength. For in the time of his father, when we were young men, there were in the palace sheep of remarkable size [Note: Col. 0619D. Glossary: πρόβατον ἀρνίον, “sheep, lamb.” *Verbella*, a sheep. It is written in this form in Licinius Rufinus, under the title *On Cattle-Rustlers*, in the Frankish laws, book II, chapter 75, and frequently in those laws. Lind.]. Grasping the wool on their backs, he could lift them from the ground with his arm extended—something I could not do.”

When the Tuscan heard this, he said to Alachis: “If you do not dare to engage Cunibert in single combat, you shall no longer have me as your companion and helper.” Saying this, he rushed away, immediately fled to Cunibert, and reported these words to him [Note: Col. 0619D. Amb.: “he himself reported this to him.”].

Thus, as we have said, both armies assembled in the field of Coronata. When they were already near enough to come into contact, Zeno, a deacon of the Church of Ticinum and custodian of the basilica of the blessed John the Baptist, which stood within that same city and had once been built by Queen Gundiberga, loved the king greatly and feared that he might perish in battle. He therefore said to the king:

“My lord king, our entire life depends upon your safety. If you perish in battle, this tyrant Alachis will destroy us all by various punishments. Therefore, be pleased to accept my counsel. Give me your armor, and I will go and fight this tyrant. If I go, you will recover your cause; but if I win, greater glory will be attributed to you, because you will have won through your servant” [Note: Col. 0619D. Mod.: “because your servant has won,” and so forth].

When the king refused to do this, the few faithful men who were present began with tears to beg him to assent to what the deacon had said [Note: Col. 0619D. The word *eum* is absent from Mod.]. At last, overcome—as was fitting for a man of pious heart—by their prayers and tears, he gave the deacon his cuirass, helmet, greaves, and other weapons, and sent him into battle in his own person.

The deacon was of the same stature and appearance as the king, so that when he emerged armed from the tent everyone thought that he was King Cunibert [Note: Col. 0619D.].

Battle was therefore joined, and the forces fought with all their strength. Alachis concentrated his efforts wherever he thought the king was. Believing that he had killed Cunibert, he killed the deacon Zeno. When he ordered that his head be cut off so that, having raised it on a spear, they might shout praises to God, he removed the helmet and recognized that he had killed a cleric.

Then, raging, he cried out: “Alas for me! We have accomplished nothing, since we entered this battle only to kill a cleric.” He therefore made the following vow: “If God grants me victory again, I shall fill a well with the testicles of clerics.”

## CHAPTER XLI. Again concerning the war between Cunibert and Alachis, Cunibert’s victory, and how he entered Ticinum in triumph

Cunibert, seeing that his men had been defeated and were almost turning to flight [Note: Col. 0619D. Another manuscript: “seeing his men, almost painted, looking toward flight.” Lind.], immediately showed himself to them. Once their fear had been removed, he strengthened the hearts of them all to hope for victory.

The armies were drawn up again, and Cunibert on one side and Alachis on the other prepared for battle [Note: Col. 0619D. Another manuscript: “When the armies were already near and both sides were joining battle,” and so forth. Lind. Amb. reads *conjungentur* (“were joined”) rather than *contingerent* (“came into contact”)].

When the two armies were near enough to engage, Cunibert again sent the following message to Alachis:

“Look at how great a multitude stands on either side. Why should so many people perish? Let me and him join in single combat, and let whichever of us the Lord chooses to grant victory possess this entire people safe and unharmed.”

When Alachis’s men urged him to do what Cunibert had proposed [Note: Col. 0619D. Amb. and Mod.: “When Alachis’s men begged him,” and so forth], he replied:

“I cannot do this, because among his spears I see the image of the holy archangel Michael, to whom I swore allegiance” [Note: Col. 0620D. This passage should be noted as evidence that the ancient Lombards used to paint the patrons of their nation upon their spears. Their particular devotion to Saint Michael the archangel is attested not only by the churches erected in his honor and by numerous historical monuments, but also by coins struck by that people bearing his sacred image carrying a spear and a lance. Recently the most learned Jerome Anthony Reyna, royal financial officer, outstanding in his expertise and office in monetary matters, showed me two gold coins of the same type; we shall describe them under King Liutprand. Camillus Peregrinius also possessed silver coins of the same type and claims that both kinds were struck by the dukes of Beneventum, perhaps because the neighboring devotion of Mount Garganus caused Saint Michael to be worshiped more frequently among them].

Then one of them said: “Through fear you see what is not there, and now it is too late for you to think about such things.”

The armies then engaged amid the blaring of trumpets. Neither side gave ground, and the greatest slaughter of the people took place. At last the cruel tyrant Alachis died, and Cunibert, with the Lord’s help, won the victory.

When Alachis’s army learned of his death, it sought refuge in flight. Those whom the sword did not strike down were killed by the river Adda. Alachis’s head was severed and his legs were cut off; only a shapeless and mutilated corpse remained.

The army of the people of Friuli was not present in this battle. Since Alachis had compelled them unwillingly to swear allegiance, they therefore gave assistance neither to King Cunibert nor to Alachis; when the two sides joined battle, they returned to their own territories.

After Alachis had died in this manner, King Cunibert ordered the body of the deacon Zeno to be buried magnificently before the doors of the basilica of the blessed John, which he himself had erected. He himself, destined to reign amid every kind of exultation and the triumph of victory, returned to Ticinum [Note: Col. 0621A. Amb.: “the ruler.”].

# BOOK SIX

## CHAPTER I. How Romoald captured Tarentum, and how Theuderada built the monastery of Saint Peter

While these events were taking place among the Lombards beyond the Po, Romoald, duke of the Beneventans, assembled a large army, attacked Tarentum, and captured it. In the same manner he subdued Brundusium and the entire extensive region surrounding it to his authority.

His wife, Theuderada [Note: Col. 0621C. Mod.: Theodorata], at the same time built outside the walls of the city of Beneventum a basilica in honor of the blessed apostle Peter. In that place she established a convent of many handmaids of God [Note: Col. 0621C. Mod.: “founded”].

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the death of Romoald and how the body of Saint Benedict was carried to Gaul
