After Romoald had governed the duchy for sixteen years [Note: Col. 0621C. “These years,” writes Bollandus correctly in his preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint Sabinus, Bishop of Canusium*, “seem to be counted from the death of his father, not from the time when his father seized the kingdom. For if Romoald’s wife was given to him only in the year 664 or 665, after the Greeks had been driven from the siege of Beneventum, Lupus had been killed through the agency of the Huns, and the people of Friuli had been expelled—when he was already in his second or third year of rule—how can it plausibly be supposed that Wigilinda, daughter of Bertarid, was married to a son who survived his father by only three years while Bertarid was still almost a child, as Paul relates below? Furthermore, the chronology of the succeeding dukes will be perfectly consistent if we place Romoald’s accession in the year 671, when his father died, or in 672; otherwise it becomes unstable. Thus, after Grimoald’s death in the year of Christ 671, he succeeded him and ruled for sixteen years.”], he was taken from this life. After him his son Grimoald ruled the Samnite peoples for three years [Note: Col. 0621D. Bollandus continues: “He was succeeded in the year 687 by Grimoald, his still adolescent son, under the guardianship of his mother Theodorada, as is said in the *Life of Saint Sabinus*, chapter 5, section 16, and so forth.” Since he lived three years as duke, his death must be assigned to the year 690.].

Wigilinda, sister of Cunibert and daughter of King Bertarid [Note: Col. 0621D. Another manuscript: Winilinda. Lind. Winiolenda. Mod.], was joined to him in marriage [Note: Col. 0621D. Another manuscript: Parthariti. Mod. does not read “king”]. After Grimoald’s death, his own brother Gusulf became duke [Note: Col. 0622A. Gusulf, brother of the deceased duke and grandson of King Grimoald, succeeded him in the year 690 mentioned above. This agrees with the chronology established by Bollandus and with what Anastasius writes about Gusulf under John VI, as well as with what our author writes below in chapter 27. From there it follows that Gusulf’s death occurred in 707, after seventeen years as duke. I have recorded these matters more precisely so that the chronology of what follows may emerge more clearly.], and he ruled Beneventum for seventeen years.

Winiberta was joined to him [Note: Col. 0621D. Another manuscript: Winniperga; another: Winiperga. Lind. Our manuscripts: Winiperga], and she bore him Romoald.

Around this time, when there had already been a lapse of several years, a vast solitude existed in the fortress of Cassinum [Note: Col. 0621D. Another manuscript: “on the mountain.” Lind. Col. 0622C. Amb.: Cassinum], where the sacred body of the most blessed Benedict rested [Note: Col. 0622C. Amb. and Mod.: “had rested for some time,” and so forth].

Franks from the region of the Cenomanni or the Aureliani [Note: Col. 0622C. Other manuscripts: Ceromannorum or Aurianensium. Lind. Amb.: Celmanicorum or Aurelianensium. Mod.: Celimanicorum or Aurianensium.], having pretended to spend the night near the venerable body [Note: Col. 0622C. Among ancient Christians this word very frequently means nocturnal prayers and psalmody, as in Saint Jerome, Tertullian, and others.], carried away the bones of that same venerable Father and also of his revered sister Scholastica and transported them to their own country [Note: Col. 0622C. Amb.: “pretended”].

There, two monasteries were built individually in honor of the blessed Benedict and Saint Scholastica [Note: Col. 0622C. Amb.: “in honor of both, that is, of the blessed …”].

But we know for certain that that venerable mouth, sweeter than every kind of nectar, and the eyes that had always gazed upon heavenly things, together with the other members, although they had dissolved into ashes, remained [Note: Col. 0622C. Another manuscript does not read “into ashes.” The Lindau manuscript: “the rest of the members remained incorrupt.” Mod.: “the other members, although decayed, remained.”].

For only the body of the Lord, uniquely, did not see corruption. The bodies of all the saints, however, destined to be restored afterward to eternal glory, were subject to corruption, except those which, through divine miracles, are preserved without blemish [Note: Col. 0622C.].

The very famous controversy arising from this passage of our Paul [Col. 0622D] concerning the translation of the body of the holy abbot Benedict and of his sister Scholastica, repeatedly revived between the monks of Monte Cassino and those of Fleury—in fact, between our Italians and the French—has long been treated by outstanding scholars. Nevertheless, this passage, which each side endeavors to draw to its own position, calls for some observation of my own, however inadequate, in accordance with my purpose. Therefore, granting myself only what is strictly necessary here, I gladly leave the remainder of the controversy—raised from the records of subsequent historians, or from papal bulls, and from the diplomas of emperors and kings, as well as from whatever else bears upon the matter—to be explained by those more skilled amid so great a conflict of assertions. “For,” as Baronius—whom I am not worthy to call my teacher—had previously written on this same matter, “the mind shrinks—shrinks, I say—from entering so dense a thicket of this controversy.”

Our Italians, on the authority of Leo of Ostia, insist that Paul’s meaning should be explained in such a way that in the first part of the sentence he reports what was then being circulated among the common people concerning the translation of the body of Saint Benedict, but in the second what he himself had learned from the truth. Leo of Ostia writes in his *Cassinese Chronicle*, chapter 44:

> “Those, however, who think that they are supported in this matter—namely, concerning the translation of the body of Saint Benedict and of Scholastica—by the testimony of Paul the Deacon, certainly a truthful and distinguished historian, should know that it is customary among writers of history to follow popular opinion in their narrative. Thus, in Luke, blessed Mary calls Joseph the Lord’s father, saying: ‘I and your father were sorrowfully seeking you’; and in Mark, Herod is said to have been grieved because the girl had asked for the head of the Baptist—although no one who knows the facts can doubt that neither statement was literally true.””

Laurentius of Cassino adds to this, in his little work *On the True Existence of the Body of Saint Benedict in the Cassinese Church*, several arguments to strengthen Leo of Ostia’s explanation. Since Nuceus gathered the more substantial of these into Appendices 2 and 3 to Leo himself, printed in Rome, I shall quote his words:

> “It may seem remarkable,” writes Nuceus, “as Laurentius observed, that the opponents rely upon the authority of Paul Warnefrid. For after Paul had inserted the account of the translation—or theft—in his historical work, he immediately adds: ‘But it is certain for us that that venerable mouth, sweeter than every nectar, and the eyes that always gazed upon heavenly things, together with the other members, remained, although they had dissolved into ash.’ Who does not see from this circumlocution that Paul plainly corrected and refuted the account which he had first copied from the records of others—for the event did not occur in his own age? Perhaps he had written and published it before he could be more accurately informed among the Cassinese about the truth of the matter; hence he later retracted it, adding that it was certain to him and to the Cassinese that Benedict’s body had remained intact at Cassino. For he says not merely ashes, but ‘the mouth and the eyes and the rest,’ that is, the limbs. Therefore they were not stolen.”

In the third appendix he argues again:

> “For whatever is brought forward from the testimony of Paul the Deacon has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently rejected in our preceding dissertation. What could Paul have understood by ‘the mouth’ and ‘the eyes that always gazed upon heavenly things,’ unless the skull, which still retained the hollows of the eyes? What by ‘the other members,’ unless the whole structure of the body? For when he adds ‘although they had dissolved into ash,’ he speaks not by asserting this, but by conceding it, and speaks from the standpoint of the French, as though he said: ‘Although I grant you that the limbs dissolved into ashes, this is the common condition of mortals; for the Holy of holies alone did not see corruption.’ By the force of this comparison he plainly indicates that by ‘ashy limbs’ he wished to understand nothing other than limbs that were not incorrupt, but gradually passing into ashes—something which the learned know is not infrequently meant by the designation ‘ashes,’ and so forth.”

The French, on the other hand, on whose behalf the most learned men have hitherto fought most fiercely—men whom their latest champion, Mabillon, has reviewed in his dissertation, in the second Benedictine century—explain this passage in approximately the following sense, in Mabillon’s own words:

> “Paul concedes Saint Benedict’s bones to the French, but vindicates the limbs that had dissolved into ashes for the Cassinese. Which limbs? ‘The mouth and the eyes, and the rest’—that is, fleshly members—‘although they had dissolved into ash.’ ‘The rest,’ I say, apart from the bones, which he had previously assigned to the French. For he concedes no limbs to the Cassinese except those that had ‘dissolved into ash.’ Therefore they are not bones, which do not readily resolve into ash. Hence, when Paul says in Book VI, chapter 40, that Petronax reached the sacred body [Col. 0624A] of blessed Father Benedict, he either understands synecdochically the limbs dissolved into dust, or rather the tomb itself, by that figurative manner of speaking in which the container is taken for the thing contained.”

“But even if this is so, and Paul later withdrew his earlier opinion, nevertheless the members which he says remained at Cassino he asserts had ‘dissolved into ash,’ and so forth.”

And further:

> “Finally, it is certain that Paul, not while still a layman but already a monk, undertook to write his history in the monastery of Cassino. This is evident both from this passage, where he says, ‘But it is certain for us that that mouth, and so forth, remained,’ and from Book I, chapter 26, where, after commending at length Saint Benedict, whom he repeatedly calls his own Father, he writes the following about Marcus the poet and monk:
>
> “‘Coming here—that is, to Mount Cassino—he constrained himself to great continence throughout. I have taken all this from the poem of Marcus the poet, who, coming here to the same Father, and so forth.’
>
> “And shortly afterward:
>
> “‘It is certain that this outstanding Father was called from heaven to this fertile place for this purpose: that here an assembly of many monks should be formed, as has happened even now under God’s protection, and so forth.’”

Mabillon finally concludes:

> “Let it therefore remain established that Paul spoke not from popular opinion, nor from ignorance, but from the opinion then received by himself and by his fellow Cassinese, when he assigned Saint Benedict’s bones to the French and the ashes to the Cassinese; nor did he ever retract his opinion.”

I have reported almost in full these arguments concerning our Paul, lest I should appear to be swayed by partisan zeal. Yet the reading of our manuscript codices must by no means be concealed [Col. 0624C]. In place of the editors’ *requiescebat* (“was resting”), they clearly and without any suspicion of corrupt writing have *requiescit* (“rests”); and this reading agrees with another passage of the same Paul, namely Book I, chapter 26, where we read:

> “Finally, when, at the divine prompting, he came from Subiaco to this place, where he rests, after traveling almost fifty miles, and so forth.”

If this reading is genuine—as I might reasonably persuade myself from the ancient Ambrosian Codex in particular, a specimen of which we have displayed in this edition—we should now have our Paul favoring the Italians and his fellow Cassinese. Indeed, the arguments of the French would collapse, weakened by another reading found in our codices, if Paul truly wrote, as he did in the Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts:

> “But it is certain for us that that venerable mouth, sweeter than every nectar, and the eyes that always gazed upon heavenly things, together with the other members, remained, although they had dissolved.”

For the sense would be—unless I am perhaps mistaken—that Paul regarded it as certain that the body of Saint Benedict was preserved at Cassino, namely “the mouth, the eyes, and the other members, although dissolved,” that is, loosened from their structure. He therefore designated those more notable members in order to magnify the sacred pledge; for it contained “that mouth, sweeter than every nectar, and the eyes that always gazed upon heavenly things.”

Nor do I think that what Mabillon absolutely asserted has been sufficiently established: namely, that our Paul wrote this history of the Lombards on Mount Cassino after he had become a monk. Although the most learned man employs a conjecture worthy of his intellect, a doubt still remains from chapter 15 of Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle*. There, speaking of Paul after his accusation, he says that King Charles, moved by compassion toward a most learned man, addressed his nobles as follows:

> “Tell me what you think should be done about this matter.”
>
> They replied: “Order that his eyes be torn out, lest at some time he send some writings against you to someone.”
>
> And the king said: “Where and when shall we be able to find so distinguished a historian or poet?”

Therefore, according to Leo’s testimony—he was nearer in time to Warnefrid’s age and knew him well, preserving for us much about his life and deeds which we should seek in vain elsewhere—Paul had written the history before he was accused. Paul had indeed written a history of the bishops of Metz; but what man, especially what Frenchman, would have valued him so highly as to be drawn into admiration and, because of him, provoked to anger?

There is also an older and by no means obscure piece of evidence from Abbot Hilderic, in the epitaph by which he celebrated the life and memory of his master. We read there:

> By divine prompting the royal palace straightway  
> Took you in to be nurtured, for the honor and light of your fatherland;  
> When beyond the Tiber your peaceful life and learning  
> Then won the approval of all peoples and lofty kings,  
> You grasped every summit of sacred wisdom,  
> Worthily penetrating, at the urging of the pious King Ratchis,  
> The many doctrines which you had fittingly mastered;  
> Thereby shining upon all, as Phoebus from the stars above,  
> You adorned the northern peoples  
> With radiant light.

By these lines, unless my judgment deceives me, he alludes to the *History of the Lombards*. He then proceeds to describe Paul’s monastic life:

> “Let these things now suffice, together with the glory of this all-too-fleeting age,” and so forth.

He enumerates the things accomplished by Paul in that condition, as appears in the complete reading of his epitaph before our edition. From this I might conjecture that, encouraged by King Ratchis himself, Paul first laid his hand to the writing of the *History*, although he may perhaps have completed it on Mount Cassino after the fortunes of the Lombards had been shattered. But further discussion would now be burdensome.]

---

## Chapter III. Concerning Rodoald, Duke of Friuli, and Ansfrit, who usurped his duchy

[Col. 0623A]

Rodoald, whom we previously stated to have held the duchy at Forum Julii [Col. 0624A], being absent from that city, Ansfrit seized his duchy from the fortress of Reunia without the king’s authorization.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Another reading has *Aufridus*. Lind.]

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Another reading has *Reuma*. Lind. But the first reading should be retained, as I noted elsewhere.]

When Rodoald learned of this, he fled into Istria and then by ship, passing through Ravenna [Col. 0625A], reached King Cunibert at Ticinum. Ansfrit, not content to govern the duchy of Friuli, rebelled against King Cunibert as well and wished to invade his kingdom. But he was captured at Verona, brought before the king, blinded, and confined in exile. After this, Ado, the brother of Rodoald, governed the duchy of Friuli for one year and seven months under the title of *loci servator*.

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Another reading has *servationis*. Lind. *Loci servatores* are those sent by prefects of the praetorium, counts, or governors for the purpose of administering justice, as D. Cujacius explains in *Observationes*, Book III, chapter 14. Lind.]

## Chapter IV. Concerning the synod held at Constantinople and the letter of Bishop Damian

While these things were taking place in Italy,

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The Monothelite heresy did not begin in the East at this time, as our author asserts, but, according to many investigations by learned scholars, either as early as the year of Christ 616 or thereabouts. At this time, namely in the year 680, the Sixth Synod was convened to eradicate it, under Pope Agatho and the emperor Constantine Pogonatus. Its Acts survive; Baronius argues that they should be supplemented by the writings of Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of that pontiff.]

a heresy arose at Constantinople which asserted that there was one will and one operation in our Lord Jesus Christ. This heresy was stirred up by Gregory, patriarch of Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The Modenese manuscript has *Georgius*, and likewise below; this is the genuine reading. For it is established that George, patriarch of Constantinople, attended the Sixth Synod with Macarius, the two principal leaders of the Monothelites. George, one of those two principal leaders together with Macarius, later repented of his error, following better counsel, as Paul also relates below.]

Macarius,

[Note: [Col. 0625B] The Antiochene bishop, that great falsifier, who, when the synod had pronounced its judgment, fell from the honor of the episcopate. [Col. 0626B]]

Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0626B] These too were patriarchs of Constantinople. See Zonaras and Theophanes.]

For this reason the Emperor Constantine Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0626B] “The number of bishops said to have attended the synod,” writes Baronius, “is given differently by different authors. The Greek annals, both in Cedrenus and in Theophanes, have two hundred and eighty-nine. Photius, in his letter or treatise *On Synods*, numbers one hundred and seventy; Paul the Deacon, one hundred and fifty. Theodore Balsamon gives one hundred and seventy-one. In the final session of the same synod, all the bishops who signed, together with the legates, priests, and deacons, number one hundred and sixty-six. At the very beginning of the synod, however, the number is much smaller, since all the bishops could not possibly have reached Constantinople in so short a time.” I add Anastasius, who in his account of Saint Leo II numbers one hundred and fifty Fathers, including the pope himself.]

caused one hundred and fifty bishops to assemble. Among them were also the legates of the Holy Roman Church, sent by Pope Agatho: John the Deacon and John, bishop of Porto.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] Another reading: “the bishop of Tulle.” Lind. Anastasius names the papal legates sent by Agatho to Constantinople for the celebration of the synod, after they had received the imperial letters sent to his predecessor Donus, as follows: “And he sent Abundantius, bishop of Paternus, John, bishop of Reggio, and John, bishop of Porto; Theodore and George, priests; John the Deacon and Constantine; Theodore, priest of Ravenna; and devout monks, servants of God, and so forth.” They were received by the emperor with the highest honor and, when dismissed, exposed Macarius’s fraud at the synod and most ably defended the orthodox faith of the Roman pontiffs.]

They all condemned the same heresy. At that moment such a mass of spiders’ webs fell in the midst of the people that everyone marveled. By this it was signified that the filth of heretical depravity had been driven away.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] Anastasius and the *Miscellaneous History* likewise relate this from our countrymen.]

Gregory the patriarch was corrected, but the others, persisting in their own defense,

[Note: [Col. 0626C] The Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts have: “persisting in their dissension.”]

were struck down by the punishment of anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] The Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts: “persisting, they were anathematized and struck by divine vengeance.”]

At that time Damian, bishop of the Church of Ticinum,

[Note: [Col. 0626C] The most eminent Baronius, in his notes to the *Martyrology*, accuses our Paul of error here because he says that Saint Damian, bishop of Pavia, wrote a letter in the name of Mansuetus, archbishop of Milan, to the Constantinopolitan synod against the Monothelites, whereas in the Roman council under Agatho one Magnus is found among the signatories, not Damian, bishop of Pavia:

> “But,” replies Ughellus, generally approved, “if that most learned man had reckoned more accurately on ecclesiastical matters on this occasion, and had noticed that Magnus had signed as bishop of Popilia, not of Pavia, and that Anastasius, who had attended that council, preceded our Damian, bishop of Pavia, he would not have been so surprised at Paul the Deacon, who attributes the letter to Damian, a bishop who at that time was only a priest and who had dictated the letter one year before succeeding Anastasius, who himself is also found to have signed the decrees of the Roman council. Nor should Paul the Deacon be blamed if he thought it of little importance whether one said that Damian, as a priest or as a bishop, had composed the letter; for a serious historian could easily disregard the interval of one year between the writing of the letter and his episcopal succession.”]

composed, in the name of Mansuetus, archbishop of Milan, a letter on this matter that was highly useful and of sound faith, and it carried considerable weight at the aforesaid synod.

The orthodox and true faith is this: just as there are two natures in our Lord Jesus Christ, namely, divine and human, so also there are believed to be two wills, or operations. Do you wish to hear what belongs to his divinity? “I and the Father are one,” he says. Do you wish to hear what belongs to his humanity? “The Father is greater than I.” Observe him sleeping in the boat according to his humanity; observe his divinity when the Evangelist says: “Then he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.”

This is the Sixth Universal Synod, held at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, in the time of Pope Agatho, while the Emperor Constantine presided and carried out its proceedings within the enclosure

[Note: [Col. 0627C] This was commonly called the *Trullus* or *Trulla*; others write *Tholus*, from the shape of the vault placed above it.]

of his palace.

## Chapter V. Concerning the eclipse of the moon and sun, and the pestilence that occurred at Rome and Ticinum

[Col. 0627C]

At this time, in the eighth indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse.

[Note: [Col. 0627C] Anastasius also mentions this lunar eclipse in his account of Agatho, in these words: “In the eighth indiction, the moon underwent an eclipse in the month of June, on the twenty-eighth day.” But Pagius, in his chronological criticism, following Calvisius in his *Chronological Work*, restores the date to the eighteenth, at the beginning of Monday, only half an hour after midnight, in the year of Christ 680, to which the eighth indiction belongs. As for the solar eclipse narrated here by Paul, Calvisius proves that it preceded the lunar eclipse, occurring in the previous year, on July 13, a Wednesday, four hours after midday.]

An eclipse of the sun also occurred at almost the same time, around the tenth hour of the day, on the fifth day before the Nones of May. Immediately afterward there followed a most severe pestilence

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Anastasius, in his account of Saint Agatho, gives almost word for word a similar account of the plague that ravaged Rome, its suburbs, and the military camps at this time. Paul adds that Ticinum, the royal city of the Lombards, was also devastated by the same calamity, until, after relics of the blessed martyr Sebastian had been brought from the city of Rome and an altar had been erected in the basilica of Saint Peter *ad Vincula*, the dreadful disease ceased. I think that the learned Baronius and others interpreted the designation Saint Peter *ad Vincula*, common to both the Roman and Ticinese basilicas, in the sense that the dedication of an altar in honor of Saint Sebastian in the Roman basilica of Saint Peter *ad Vincula* should be inferred from this passage of Paul. This was supported chiefly by a variant reading which he had noted in the margin at the words *ab urbe Roma* (“from the city of Rome”), in whose place he wrote *ad urbem Romam* (“to the city of Rome”), so that the sense would be that the body of Saint Sebastian had been brought from the catacombs into the City, as Sigonius interprets it in Book II of *On the Kingdom of Italy*. Yet that reading occurs neither in the Lindebrogian manuscripts nor in our own manuscripts. The historians of Ticinum unanimously assert that Saint Damian, the bishop whom our author mentioned shortly before, obtained the martyr’s relics from the Roman pontiff and placed them, with solemn ceremony and an altar erected in his honor, in the Church of Saint Peter *ad Vincula*. He added a vow by which he bound himself and his clergy to go there to perform sacred rites in solemn processions for three days before the feast and on the feast day itself. Baronius also asserts that an image of the same saint, made in mosaic, still exists in the Roman basilica, as may indeed be seen in our own day, with a full beard—an indication of the common error of painters. Although I would not dare to dispute the antiquity of the Roman altar, for it could easily have been dedicated shortly before the Ticinese one during that calamity, I would readily believe that Paul was speaking here of the Ticinese altar, and I agree with the conjecture of that most learned man: from that time onward devotion was transmitted to later generations, so that in time of plague the name of the holy martyr might be invoked to drive it away.]

for three months, namely July, August, and September. So great was the number of those dying that even parents with their children and brothers with their sisters were placed two by two on biers and carried to burial near the city of Rome.

In the same way this pestilence also devastated Ticinum, so that, when all the citizens were fleeing over the mountain passes or to various [Col. 0627C] places, grass and shrubs grew in the forum and through the streets of the city. At that time many people visibly saw a good angel and an evil angel passing through the city at night. At the command of the good angel, the evil angel, who appeared to carry a hunting spear in his hand, struck the door of any house with the spear; and as many people as there were strikes against a door, so many would die from that house on the following day.

Then it was revealed to someone that the pestilence itself would not cease until an altar of the blessed martyr Sebastian was set up in the basilica called Saint Peter *ad Vincula*. This was done. When the relics of the blessed martyr Sebastian had been brought from the city of Rome, as soon as an altar had been erected in the aforesaid basilica, the pestilence itself ceased.

## Chapter VI. How the ancient enemy announced to Aldo and Grauso that Cunibert intended to kill them

King Cunibert was taking counsel in the city of Ticinum with his *strator*, who in his native language is called a *marpahis*, about how he should deprive Aldo and [Col. 0628B] Grauso of their lives. Suddenly a large fly settled on the window beside which they were standing.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Another reading has: “one of the little birds.” Lind.]

Cunibert wished to kill it by striking it with a knife, but succeeded only in cutting off one of its feet.

Meanwhile Aldo and Grauso, unaware of the king’s plan, were coming to the royal palace. When they approached the basilica of the holy martyr Romanus,

[Note: [Col. 0628D] The words “which is situated near the palace” are absent from the Ambrosian manuscript.]

which is situated near the palace, a certain lame man suddenly came toward them, with one foot cut off. He told them that Cunibert intended to kill them if they went to him. On hearing this, they were seized with great fear and took refuge behind the altar of the same basilica.

Soon King Cunibert was informed that Aldo and Grauso had taken refuge in the basilica of the blessed martyr Romanus. The king then began to rebuke his *strator*, asking why he had betrayed his plan.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Another reading: “had dared to betray it.” Lind.]

His *strator* replied:

> “My lord king, you know that after we took this counsel I have not left your presence. How, then, could I have told it to anyone?”

The king then sent to Aldo and Grauso, asking them why they had fled to the holy place.

They replied:

> “Because it was announced to us that our lord the king intended to kill us.”

He sent to them again, asking who had announced this to them, and ordering that, unless they revealed the messenger, they could not obtain his favor. Then they told the king what had happened,

[Note: [Col. 0629C] The Ambrosian manuscript has: “they reported.”]

saying that a lame man had come toward them, with one foot cut off, and that he used a wooden leg up to the knee; he had been the messenger of their impending death.

Then the king understood that the fly whose foot he had cut off had been an evil spirit and that it had revealed the secrets of his plan.

[Note: [Col. 0629C] The Ambrosian manuscript has: “had been the messenger of the secret of his plan.”]

He immediately received Aldo and Grauso from the same basilica under his protection, pardoned their offense, and thereafter kept them in the place of [Col. 0629B]

[Note: [Col. 0629C] The Ambrosian and Modenese manuscripts have: “faithful.”]

sons.

## Chapter VII. Concerning Felix, the grammarian and deacon

At this time Felix flourished in the art of grammar. He was the paternal uncle of Flavian, my teacher. The king loved him so greatly that, among his other gifts of generosity, he presented him with a staff decorated with silver and gold.

## Chapter VIII. Concerning John, bishop of Bergamo

At about the same time,

[Note: [Col. 0629C] Saint John, bishop of Bergamo, attended the Roman council against the Monothelites under Pope Agatho. “And because he was exceedingly dear,” writes Ughellus, “to Cunibert, king of the Lombards, and to Duke Grimoald, whom he converted from the Arian sect to Christ, and because he obtained from them many privileges in favor of his Church, he eventually went to war with Cunibert against Alachis, duke of Trent and a follower of the Arian sect. After suffering an irreparable misfortune together with the king through the unfavorable outcome of fortune, he was, not far from Bergamo, after undergoing exquisite tortures and the squalor of prison, killed for the Catholic faith by the proud and impious victor in the very church of Saint Alexander, and buried there, and so forth.”]

John, bishop of the Church of Bergamo, was a man of remarkable holiness. Once, while conversing at a banquet, he offended King Cunibert. As the bishop was returning to his lodging, the king had a fierce and untamed horse prepared for him, one that habitually threw its riders to the ground with an enormous roar.

When the bishop mounted it, the animal became so gentle that it carried him with a mild gait all the way to his own house. When the king heard this, from that day onward he honored the bishop with the respect due to him, and gave him the very horse that had been consecrated by his mounting it.

## Chapter IX. Concerning the dark star that then appeared and the eruption of Mount Vesuvius

[Col. 0630A]

At this time, during the night, a star appeared near the Pleiades,

[Note: [Col. 0629D] The Ambrosian manuscript has *vigiliae*, as do the printed editions of Anastasius. The first reading is preferable, for the very well-known stars called Πλειάδες (*Pleiades*) by the Greeks and *Vergiliae* by the Latins are meant.]

with the sky clear, between the Nativity of the Lord and the Epiphany. It was completely darkened, as when the moon is covered by a cloud.

After this, in the month of February,

[Note: [Col. 0629D] Anastasius adds the day, namely “after the feast of Saint Valentine.”]

in the middle of the day, a star rose in the west and, with great brilliance, moved toward the regions of the East.

Then, in the month of March,

[Note: [Col. 0629D] The Modenese manuscript has: “Vesuvius erupted with fire for,” and so forth. Another reading has: “Bebius erupted.” Thus in Lindenbrog’s text and in the printed *Lives of the Pontiffs* by Anastasius. Since that author reports that these events occurred under Benedict II, the only year of his pontificate, namely the year of Christ 684, must be intended. But Paul does not connect this correctly with the invasion of Africa by the Saracens, which he discusses in the following chapter.]

the fire of Vesuvius erupted for several days, and all the vegetation round about was destroyed by its dust and ash.

## Chapter X. How the Saracen people captured Africa and destroyed Carthage

[Col. 0630B]

Then the unbelieving and God-hostile people of the Saracens,

[Note: [Col. 0630C] From Egypt into Africa. Modenese and Lind.]

advancing from Egypt into Africa with a very large force,

[Note: [Col. 0630C] The caliph Abdul-Malik, after subjugating Arabia, sent Hasan the Felician on this expedition and honored him with the title of commander of the West. He besieged Carthage, captured it by assault, and destroyed the walls of the most illustrious city down to their foundations in the year of Christ 696, as Pagius establishes from the Arab Noweiri in that year.]

captured Carthage after besieging it, cruelly ravaged the captured city, and leveled it to the ground.

## Chapter XI. Concerning the death of Constantine, the reign of Justinian, and his victory over the Saracens

Meanwhile the Emperor Constantine died at Constantinople, and his younger son Justinian took up the rule of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] Constantine Pogonatus, according to the testimony of Anastasius in his account of John V, died at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction, which had begun in that month, in the year of Christ 685. He left as his successor in the empire Justinian, the second of that name, scarcely sixteen years old, as Theophanes, Zonaras, and Nicephorus write. Paul calls him “younger” for no other reason, unless the reading should be: “and his son Justinian the younger,” and so forth.]

He held the reins of government for ten years. He took Africa away from the Saracens and made peace with them by land and sea.

[Note: [Col. 0630D] The Modenese and Lindenbrogian texts read: “across the seas.”]

[Note: [Col. 0630D] All the Byzantine writers, especially Theophanes, condemn this peace as highly damaging to the Roman state, because Justinian, by dismissing the Mardaites, weakened the strength of the empire.]

Because Pope Sergius refused to favor and subscribe to that synod of error which Justinian had held at Constantinople, Justinian sent his own *protospatharius*, Zacharias,

[Note: [Col. 0630D] *Spatharii* were bodyguards. Cedrenus writes: “A *spatharius* is a bodyguard.” Hence *protospatharius*. Curopalates writes: “He is called *protospatharius* because formerly he was first among the *spatharii* in attendance; now he has no official service.” Lind.]

and ordered that Sergius be brought to Constantinople.

But the soldiery of Ravenna and the neighboring regions, scorning the emperor’s wicked command, drove the same Zacharias out of the city of Rome with insults and injuries.

[Note: [Col. 0630D] Anastasius gives a fuller account of this in his life of Sergius. This Trullan synod, also called the Quinisext, was held a few years later in the Trullus of the great palace at Constantinople. Its purpose was, as the Greeks maintained, to supplement the Fifth and Sixth Synods, at which no canons had been issued for the restoration of discipline and reform of morals. There is great disagreement among scholars concerning the year in which it was held, but most assign it to the year of Christ 691. See Baronius under the following year, where he gives all the reasons why Sergius refused to subscribe to the synod.]

## Chapter XII. How Leo seized the imperial dignity and drove Justinian into exile

[Col. 0631A]

Leo, seizing the imperial dignity against this Justinian, deprived him of the kingdom. After ruling the Roman Empire for three years,

[Note: [Col. 0631B] At the completion of the tenth year of his reign, as Nicephorus writes, Justinian II was expelled from the empire by Leontius the patrician, whom our author calls Leo. Justinian had deprived him of his honor as commander of the eastern forces and had kept him under guard for a full three years; then, after releasing him, he placed him in command of Greece. Remembering these injuries, Leontius, aided by Callinicus the patriarch—whom the emperor had shortly before ordered to be killed—rose against Justinian and easily deposed him, since he was hated by the people for his excessive cruelty. He sent him, mutilated in tongue and nose, to the city of Cherson. From this calamity Justinian received the Greek surname *Rhinotmetus*.]

he kept Justinian in exile in Pontus.

## Chapter XIII. How Tiberius defeated Leo, cast him into prison, and became emperor

Again Tiberius rose against this Leo

[Note: [Col. 0631C] The Ambrosian manuscript has “rebelling.”]

and invaded his kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0631C] Apsimarus, raised to the imperial dignity by the favor of the army and taking the name Tiberius, came to Constantinople with a naval fleet that was returning from Africa, having accomplished nothing after the Saracens had occupied it. In the third year of Leontius’s reign he captured Leontius and, after mutilating his nose, entrusted him to soldiers to be kept in the Monastery of Dalmatus, as Theophanes and Zonaras relate.]

He kept him under guard in that same city throughout the entire period of his own reign.

## Chapter XIV. How Pope Sergius corrected the Aquileian synod when it refused to accept the holy Fifth Synod

[Col. 0631B]

At this time a synod was held at Aquileia which, through ignorance of the faith, was reluctant to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council [Note: Another reading: “which was then the universal council.”], until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to agree with the other Churches of Christ. [Note: Paul has reproduced this word for word from Bede, *Book VI on the Ages of the World*, and Anastasius confirms it in his account of Sergius, writing: “In his time the archbishop of the Church of Aquileia, and the synod assembled under him, who had hesitated to accept the holy Fifth Ecumenical Council, being themselves in error, were instructed by the admonitions and teachings of that most blessed pope and were converted. They then accepted the venerable council with satisfaction. Those who had previously been held under the charge of error, enlightened by the teaching of the Apostolic See, consonant with the truth in peace, were released to return to their own homes” — or, as it is read elsewhere, “returned.” The most distinguished Norisius explains more fully how this happened; from him, in the preceding Book IV, chapter 34, I have traced the history of the schism down to the division of the diocese of Aquileia. The highly praised author continues in chapter 1, section 6, with the events carried out by the schismatics after Agilulf’s death, when Queen Theodelinda, having received the Fifth Synod from the holy Gregory the Great and having been sufficiently instructed by Catholic admonitions, openly adhered to it. Consequently Firminus, Petrus, Providentius, and other bishops of Istria came over to us; following their example, several bishops of Venetia who were under Lombard rule did likewise, while only the Aquileians persisted in rebellion—especially at a time when very few people throughout the world refused to accept the Fifth Synod. Shortly afterward, under King Adaloald, the schismatics were joined by that monk Agrestinus of the monastery of Luxeuil, who did not hesitate to send a letter through Aureus, the king’s notary, to the holy Attala, abbot of Bobbio, in an attempt to incite him to detest the schism. Finally there was Bishop Fortunatus of Grado, whom I mentioned above as having fled to the schismatics after removing the treasure of the Church of Grado. These facts indisputably show that the schism continued until approximately the time noted for Sergius. Yet each of the two cardinals cited observes that, under Pope Martin, the bishop of Aquileia attended the Lateran Synod in 649 and likewise, under Saint Agatho, subscribed the letter sent to the emperor, together with several of his suffragan bishops. But this is not the only difficulty: another emerges from the words of our Paul, or rather of Bede, whom Paul copied—namely, whether the synod said in this chapter of Paul to have been held at Aquileia was that same synod held during the time of Pope Pelagius I, or another synod convened again in the time of Sergius. Baronius and Norisius followed the former opinion, the latter relying especially on the conjecture “that it may be gathered clearly enough from the adverb *until* that the error and the wrong judgment concerning the Fifth Synod had prevailed among the Aquileians for a long time before Sergius.” Bollandus, in his notes to the *Life of Saint Honoratus*, Pagius in his *Critical Chronology* under the year of Christ 699, and many others followed the latter opinion. The younger Palladius, in his vernacular history of Forum Julii, corrects the reading of Bede and our Paul and substitutes Pelagius for Sergius, thus joining the first opinion; but the manuscripts of Bede and of our Paul oppose him. Bollandus thought it incongruous to say that Sergius had corrected a synod held more than 150 years earlier, while Pagius supposes that Paul preserved Bede’s meaning more closely, especially since the words of Anastasius cited above say that a synod was convened under the Aquileian bishop who held office in Sergius’s time. The chronology also agrees with Paul’s account, which places this in the time of Tiberius Absimarus. Everyone agrees that the schism begun under Pope Vigilius finally came to an end under Sergius, with God’s help.]

This synod, however, was held at Constantinople in the time of Pope Vigilius, under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics who maintained that blessed Mary had given birth to a mere human being, not to God and man. In this synod it was established in accordance with Catholic teaching that blessed Mary should always be called *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”), because, as the Catholic faith holds, she truly gave birth not to a human being alone but to God and man. [Note: Lindau manuscript: “Ever-virgin, not as Theodore said, but as the Catholic [faith says],” etc.]

## CHAPTER XV  
### How Theodald, king of the Angles, came to Rome, was baptized, and died immediately afterward

In those days Cedoald, king of the Anglo-Saxons, who had waged many wars in his homeland, was converted to Christ and hastened to Rome. [Note: Our author calls him Cedoald; Bede calls him Cedvald, Cedvalla, or Ceadvalla; and the English writers cited by Baronius under the year 689 call him Cedvaldradus. Some maintain that he was a king of the Britons, not of the Saxons; among them is Sanderus, cited by the same cardinal, who charges Paul with error. If the error were real, however, it should be imputed to Bede, from whom our author copied these facts about King Cedvalla, as he copied many others. To correct this, they rely on the authority of Geoffrey; but Baronius, to extricate himself, enumerates from Bede three Cedvallas living at one time: first, a king of the Britons in 633; second, one mentioned by Bede in 678, distinct from ours, who had as successor the last Cedvalla. “But Alfordus,” as Pagius noted in his Critical Chronology for 687, no. 10, “shows that the most learned cardinal was mistaken in the number, country, and lineage of the Cedvallas. There were only two Cedvallas; the successor of the second Cedvalla was not Cedvalla but Ina, or Ine. Of the two Cedvallas, one was indeed a Briton and the other a Saxon; nor was the latter king of the Saxons merely in title because, as Baronius supposes, he defeated the Saxons, but because he was born of the royal Saxon line, as English writers consistently affirm.” Bede gives the year of Cedvalla’s baptism as follows: “While Sergius held the pontificate, he was baptized on the holy Saturday of Easter in the year 689 from the Lord’s Incarnation; and, still wearing the white garments, he was seized by illness and released from the flesh on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May,” etc. The English Martyrology records the name of King Cedvalla and counts him among the saints.] When he came to King Cunibert, he was received by him with great honor. After he reached Rome, he was baptized by Pope Sergius and given the name Peter. [Note: The reason for this custom is explained in *Distinction* 4, under the title “Why the white garment is given to the baptized Christian”: “After baptism a white garment is given to Christians, signifying the Christian innocence and purity which, after the removal of the former stains, they must preserve undefiled through the practice of holy conduct, in order to present it before the tribunal of Christ. All who are reborn are clothed in white garments for the service of the Church’s resurrection. Those who have been baptized also use white garments so that, whereas the cloth of ancient error had darkened the face of their first birth, the clothing of their second regeneration may display the glory of their new condition. After the sacred anointing, his head is covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he possesses the diadem of royal power and priestly dignity.” Relevant here too are these words in Book V of the Theodosian Code, concerning spectacles: “During the fifty days, as long as the garments that imitate the heavenly light of the bath bear witness to the new light of holy baptism.”]

While still clothed in white, he departed to the heavenly kingdom. His body was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter, and this epitaph was inscribed above him:

> The height, wealth, offspring, mighty kingdoms, triumphs,  
> Spoils, nobles, walls, camps, and homes—  
> All that his fathers’ valour and he himself had amassed—  
> Mighty Cedoald left for love of God,  
> [Note: Baronius observed that the English, who call Cedoald Cedvaldradus, read this verse: “King Cedvaldradus left [them] for love of God.”]  
> So that, a royal guest, he might behold Peter and Peter’s see,  
> And from his font receive nourishing waters.  
> [Alternative reading: “From whose font he might receive sacred waters, white-clad.”]  
> And might receive the splendid light in a radiant draught,  
> From which life-giving brightness shone everywhere.  
> [Ambrosian reading: “From which life-giving brilliance flows everywhere.”]  
> And, joyfully discerning the rewards of renewed life,  
> Changed his barbarian ferocity and thence also his name.  
> Converted, he joyfully made the change; and Bishop Sergius,  
> Himself a father, ordered that he be called Peter.  
> Christ’s grace at the font, cleansing him as he was reborn,  
> Immediately bore him, white-robed, to heaven’s lofty citadel.  
> [Alternative reading: “The wave cleansing the reborn man—which is Christ’s grace.”]  
> [Alternative reading: “Carried him at once to the heights of heaven.”]  
> Wonderful was the king’s faith; supreme the mercy of Christ,  
> Whose counsel no one can penetrate.  
> Safe in coming from Britain’s farthest world,  
> Through diverse peoples, straits, and roads,  
> He saw the Romulean city and beheld Peter’s venerable shrine,  
> Bearing mystical gifts.  
> [Note: “Coming as a guest from the farthest city of Britain.”]  
> White among Christ’s sheep, he will go in fellowship with them;  
> For in body he has a tomb, but in mind the things above.  
> You would think that he had exchanged the insignia of scepters,  
> Seeing that he won the kingdom of Christ.  
> [Note: After these verses, whose author is said to have been Saint Benedict, archbishop of Milan, concerning whom Bede reports below in chapter 29, Bede gives another inscription in prose: “Here lies Ceadvalla, also called Peter, king of the Saxons, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction. He lived approximately thirty years, during the reign of our lord Justinian, most pious Augustus, in the fourth year of his consulship, while the apostolic man, our lord Pope Sergius, was pontiff in the second year of his pontificate.”]

## CHAPTER XVI  
### How the kingdom of the Franks in Gaul began to be governed by the mayors of the royal palace

At this time in Gaul, as the kings of the Franks degenerated from their customary strength and intelligence, those who appeared to be the mayors of the royal palace began to administer the power of the kingdom and to do everything that it was customary for kings to do, since it had been ordained from heaven that the kingdom of the Franks should pass to their descendants. [Note: Isidore’s glosses: “*Architriclinius*: mayor of the palace”; he is also called the overseer of the king’s court or prefect of the palace. Cedrenus calls him *prooikos* (πρόοικος); because the passage is uniquely relevant, I shall transcribe it entire. In Leo the Iconoclast, p. 373: “It is recorded that it was customary for the king of Francia to rule by hereditary right and to administer nothing except to eat and drink without reason. But in the month of May he sat before the whole nation; they did obeisance to him and received his obeisance in return; customary gifts were brought to him, and he gave gifts back to them. He had an overseer, acting on his and the nation’s judgment, to administer every affair.” The Frankish Annals edited by P. Pithoeus, jurisconsult, state: “They were indeed called kings, but the entire royal power was held by the mayor of the palace, except that charters and privileges were written in the king’s name, and that the person called king was carried in a wagon drawn by oxen to the Field of March, where, seated in an elevated place and seen by the people once a year, he solemnly received the public gifts offered to him. The mayor of the palace stood before him and announced to the people what was to be done during the ensuing year. When the king thus returned home, the mayor of the palace administered the remaining affairs of the kingdom.” After the battle of Textricia, Frankish historians observe, royal authority was transferred to the mayors of the palace, so that “from then on,” as Erchanbert writes, “the kings began to possess the name but not the honour. Yet where it had been determined that they should live, abundant sustenance was supplied and continual guard was maintained over them, lest they might exercise anything by right of power.” In that battle, commonly assigned to 687, King Theodoric was defeated, Berthar, author of the worst counsel, was overthrown, and Pippin, grandson of Saint Arnulf, was raised to greater power. Hence one may observe the chronology confused by our author: he joins the times of Saint Arnulf with the death of King Cedvalla, who died in 689, when Pippin of Herstal was mayor of the palace and remained in office until his death in 714. Saint Arnulf, however, had already before 614, when raised to the episcopate, flourished at the Frankish court—perhaps with the dignity of mayor of the palace, which Fredegarius assigns to Pippin, although he makes the holy bishop a participant in his counsels. I shall concede Paul only this: that from that time the Frankish kings gradually lapsed into idleness, as Eginhard also writes in his *Life of Charlemagne*: “The Merovingian family, from which the Franks were accustomed to create kings, is said to have endured down to King Childeric, who, by order of Stephen, Roman pontiff, was deposed, tonsured, and thrust into a monastery. Although it may seem to have ended with him, it had long possessed no vigour and displayed in itself nothing illustrious save the empty title of king,” and the rest, in which, like Erchanbert, he describes the unhappy condition of kings at that time.] [Note: Here Paul refers to what he had written in his book on the bishops of Metz, tracing the lineage of Charlemagne to this holy bishop; he makes Charlemagne the great-great-grandson of Arnulf through Anchises, the younger son of Saint Arnulf, Pippin of Herstal, Charles Martel, and Pippin the Short, Charlemagne’s father. In the same book he writes that Pippin “had twice already defeated the people of the Lombards through his father, capturing one of their kings, whose name was Desiderius, and driving into Constantinople the other, who was called Aldegisus, together with his father [perhaps, ‘who was reigning with his father’]. He brought all Italy under his power without a serious battle and—something that rarely happens—tempered victory with merciful restraint.” These facts concerning the sons and grandsons of Saint Arnulf are thoroughly established, although some assign to him a third son, named Waltchisus, the father of Saint Wandregisilus, abbot. There is great controversy among learned men concerning Arnulf’s parents; on this see Mabillon, *Benedictine Centuries*, century II, in the *Life* of the same saint, and his genealogical tree at the beginning of that volume.]

At that time Arnulf was mayor of the palace. As later became clear, he was a man beloved by God and of extraordinary holiness. After the glory of the world, he submitted himself to the service of Christ, proved remarkable in his episcopate, and finally chose the eremitical life, giving every kind of service to lepers and living with the strictest continence. A book exists at the Church of Metz, where he had exercised the episcopate, containing accounts of his miracles and of his abstinence. I too, in the book I composed concerning the bishops of that city, at the request of Angilramnus, a most gentle man distinguished for holiness and archbishop of the aforementioned Church, composed certain accounts of the wonders of this most holy man Arnulf. I have now judged it superfluous to repeat them. [Note: Other readings: Angelramnus; Ageltramnus; in the modern edition, Angeliamnus; in the Ambrosian manuscript, Angelrannus.] [Alternative reading: “his miracles.”]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### The death of King Cunibert and the kingdom of his son Liutbert

[Column 0636A]

[Note: The Ambrosian and modern editions read: “beloved by all, after,” etc.] Meanwhile Cunibert, a prince beloved by all, after ruling the kingdom of the Lombards alone for twelve years after his father, was finally taken from this life. [Note: I noted in Book V, chapter 37, no. 155, that the death of Bertarid, King Cunibert’s father, occurred in the year of Christ 688; since our author says that Cunibert reigned twelve years after his father’s death, his own death must be assigned to the year of Christ 700.]

At the field of Coronata, where he had fought against Alachis, he built a monastery in honor of the martyr Saint Gregory. [Note: Another reading: Alahis.] [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “George,” as do certain other editions used by Baronius. He noted concerning this passage of Paul that the monastery built by King Cunibert was believed to have stood in the suburbs of Ferrara, the famous and very ancient monastery under the name of Saint George; Mabillon followed him in the Benedictine century, page 600, volume I. But these very learned men failed to notice Paul’s statement concerning the field of Coronata, where he says, plainly enough, that the monastery was built. In Book V, chapter 40, he locates it in such a way that there can be no doubt that it stood by the river Adda, on the route followed by travelers coming from Istria to Pavia, and was therefore far from Ferrara. A village called Coronata still exists near the Aureolus Bridge, popularly called Cornate through a slight corruption of the name, in the broad fields along the Adda. The inhabitants still preserve the memory of the Lombard victory, and devotion to Saint George is common among them. Why should I not believe that a monastery was once founded there?]

He was an elegant man, distinguished by every virtue and a bold warrior. He was buried amid many tears of the Lombards beside the basilica of the Lord Savior, which his grandfather Aripert had once built. [Note: In the royal city of Pavia, where a fragment of the epitaph placed on his tomb can still be read in the same basilica among the Cassinese monks. Our very learned Muratori reports it in his *Antiquities of Este*, first part, chapter 10, page 73:

> From the golden spring the kings rest in ordered succession:  
> Here the grandfather, father, and lamented son are held.  
> Cunibert, most flourishing and powerful king,  
> Whom Italy, now widowed, will mourn as lord, father, and shepherd,  
> And thereafter as a grieving husband.  
> If you seek his ancestry on the other side,  
> His grandfather was a king; his mother held the kingdom’s reins.  
> Wonderful was he in appearance, pious; and if you ask about his mind,  
> It too was wonderful. [lacuna]

Another epitaph, for Queen Raginthruda, exists at Pavia in the atrium of Saint Mary at the Perticae; but I have found no mention of her in our Paul. Leo of Ostia, chapter 8, mentions Rattruda, daughter of Saint Rachis, who with her mother Tasia founded a nunnery not far from Monte Cassino. I would not confidently claim that the inscription belongs to her, and still less would I attempt to determine which king’s wife she was, since Paul omitted the names of the wives of Adaloald, Arioald, Rothari, Aripert I, Grimoald, Liutbert, and Aripert II. The stone is inscribed as follows:

> Buried among the ancestors,  
> Raginthruda, always to be remembered  
> In pious little utterances,  
> From the life of all whom  
> Death, as the years arose,  
> Suddenly removed while she occupied the royal throne,  
> Although she completed her rule in only a few days,  
> Thus adorned the beginnings of the kingdom entrusted to her:  
> Revering the temples of God and honoring priests, ministers of the Church,  
> Devoted to them with holy reverence.  
> How often she laid aside her purple garments and diadem,  
> Serving Christ in the poverty of the poor;  
> And thus, fasting, ministered to the needy with her own hands,  
> So that she exchanged royal splendor for a lowly garment,  
> “Das mis… restored the empty …” [uncertain, as the inscription breaks off]

]

He left the kingdom of the Lombards to his son Liutbert, still of childish age, and appointed as his guardian Ansprand, a wise and distinguished man. [Note: The modern edition reads “appointed him.” Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 699, writes with our Paul: “When Cunipert, king of the Lombards, died, his son Luitpert, a boy, succeeded to the kingdom, having Ansprand as his guardian.” But that author places the beginning of Liutbert’s reign, as with the preceding kings, one year too early. Hermannus Contractus correctly agrees with our chronology in assigning Cunibert’s death to the year 700.]

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Ragunbert, duke of Turin, overcomes Liutbert, seizes the kingdom, and dies in the same year

After eight months had passed, Ragunbert, duke of Turin—whom King Godebert, when he was being extinguished by Grimoald, had left as a small child, as we also said above—came with a strong force against Ansprand and Rothari, duke of Bergamo. He engaged them at Novara, defeated them in the field, and seized the kingdom of the Lombards; but he died that same year. [Note: Sigebert likewise supports Paul, under the year 700: “Ragunbert, duke of Turin, defeated Ansprand, guardian of King Liutpert, in war and reigned for one year.” This must be understood as an incomplete year, so that both authors assign Ragunbert’s death to 701, with the only contradiction being Sigebert’s error in counting one continuous year.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### How Aripert seized the kingdom, captured Liutbert alive, and later killed him

[Note: Alternative reading: “Then the son of King Godebert, named Aribert, was made king and again prepared for war.” The Lindau and modern editions consistently read *Aripert* for *Aribert*.] Then his son Aripert, preparing for war once more, fought King Liutbert at Pavia, together with Ansprand, Ottone, Tazo, Rothari, and Faro. [Note: Other readings: Totone; Zotone and Tarzone.] [Note: Other readings: Pharao or Pharo.] Having defeated all of them in battle, he captured the child Liutbert alive. [Note: This battle of Aripert, the second king of that name among the Lombards, and his victory over King Liutpert are illuminated by what the learned Baronius excerpted from the *Life of Saint Bonitus*, former bishop of Clermont. I transcribe it here to provide a fuller account of the history: “Finally, after entering Italy, Saint Bonitus was received by the king of the Lombards both reverently and affectionately. While the king was enjoying conversation with the man of God, he heard that the city [Pavia] was being besieged by an army. Immediately leaping up, he ordered his men to take up arms and prepare to fight the enemy with him. Then, humbly turning to the man of God, he said: ‘I ask you, Father, to offer prayers to the Lord for me. I am engaged with my enemies. May I, through your intercession, carry away the palm of victory from them.’ He soon left the city and joined battle with the enemy. Victory favored the side of Aripert—for that was the name of the Lombard king—so completely that, after many had been killed and thrown down, and after the king himself had been wounded in the groin and captured, he returned with great rejoicing to the man of God, thanked him for the support of his prayers, commended himself again to his prayers with great humility, and arranged that the necessities of life should be supplied to him in his kingdom.”]

Ansprand, meanwhile, fled and fortified himself on the island of Comacina.

## CHAPTER XX  
### How Rothari, reigning at Bergamo, was captured by Aripert and deprived of his life

But Duke Rothari returned to his city of Bergamo and seized the kingdom. Against him King Aripert set out with a large army. After first storming and capturing Lodi, he besieged Bergamo and attacked it with battering rams and various engines of war, without any difficulty. [Note: Alternative readings: “after storming Laude Pompeia”; and “Pergamum” or “Bergomum” for Bergamo. The Ambrosian manuscript consistently has *Pergamum* and *Pergamensem*.] [Note: The names of these machines varied. There were machines called *lesae*. Cedrenus mentions them on page 644: “He himself had wicker shelters woven from willow branches, carefully covered above with ox hides and fitted with wheels beneath the bases of the poles carried by the bearers—such machines are called *lesae*—and he filled them with men carrying mattocks, hoes, and other agricultural tools, so that they might gradually bring the *lesae* forward and attach them to the walls,” and so forth. There were also machines called *clitae*. The author of the *Life of Charlemagne*, edited by P. Pithoeus, writes: “They prepared *clitae* for subduing the fortress by force.” Turpinus lists other kinds in chapter 9: “In the seventh month, after placing stone-throwers, mangonels, and *troiae* beside the wall.” A learned man thought that *mangonels* referred to the machines which the French call *mantels* or *mantellettes*, that is, covered siege galleries. Let the reader judge concerning the rest.]

He soon captured it, seized the false king Rothari, shaved off his head and beard, and confined him in exile at Turin; he was killed there several days later. [Note: Other reading: “Rotharius and King Freodo.”] [Note: It was an ancient custom to shave captives and those defeated in war, a custom also touched upon by Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 9:

> Thus the old Sicambrian, with shorn head,  
> After you have been defeated, draws backward  
> His neck toward the old hair, the new hair.

Elsewhere in the same author I understand Ovid’s verse in this way:

> Now Germany will send you captive hair;  
> You will be adorned with the gift of the conquered people.

I think this custom had also been common among other peoples many centuries earlier, judging from Deuteronomy 21, where concerning a captive girl it says: “She shall shave her head, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured,” and so forth. Shaving the head was also a form of punishment; hence the expressions “to be shorn bald and flogged” are read very frequently. Cedrenus, in his account of Justin, page 320, writes: “After striking him and shaving his head, he mounted him naked on a donkey and led him in triumph through the middle of the city.” Here too one sees him placed on a donkey; in antiquity it was customary to place those about to suffer punishment on donkeys or other animals and lead them through the streets as a spectacle. Agathias, concerning the killers of Gabara, Book IV: “Some sat upon the mules and were carried along the highways, becoming a great spectacle to the Colchians and deserving the greatest fear.” Thus Nicetas Choniates, in Book II, tells how Andronicus was placed upon a camel: “After a few days one of his eyes was also torn out, and, having been placed upon a mangy camel, he was led in triumph through the marketplace.” But these matters belong elsewhere.]

As for Liutbert, whom he had captured, he deprived him of life in the same way in a bath.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### How Ansprand, fleeing to Bavaria, remained with Theudebert, its duke

He also sent an army against Ansprand on the island of Comacina. [Note: Another reading: “He came to him through Chur, the city of the Rhaetians.”] When Ansprand learned this, he fled to Chiavenna and then, through Chur, a city of the Rhaetians, came to Theudebert, duke of the Bavarians, and remained with him for nine years. [Note: From these words of Paul, and from others in the following chapter 35, where he connects the ninth year after Ansprand’s flight with the tenth year of Theudebert, Pagius, in his *Critical History*, under the year 712, infers that the beginning of Theudebert’s tetrarchy should be placed at the beginning of 702 and Ansprand’s flight at its end. Thus Aripert’s second victory over Liutbert is properly assigned to the beginning of the same year.]

The army of Aripert invaded the island to which Ansprand had fled and destroyed his fortress.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### How Aripert disfigured Ansprand’s wife, son, and daughter in different ways, and how he allowed Liutprand to go to his father in Bavaria

King Aripert, therefore, after consolidating his kingdom, deprived Sigibrand, Ansprand’s son, of his eyes and afflicted in various ways all those related to him by blood. He also kept Ansprand’s younger son Liutprand in custody. [Note: Another reading: “Because he regarded him as an insignificant person and saw that he was still an adolescent, he not only did not rage against his body,” and so forth.] Since he perceived him to be an insignificant person and still a mere boy, he not only inflicted no bodily punishment upon him but allowed him to depart and go to his father. There is no doubt that this happened by the will of almighty God, who was preparing him to govern the kingdom.

Liutprand therefore set out to his father in Bavaria and brought him immeasurable joy by his arrival. King Aripert, however, had Ansprand’s wife, named Theuderada, arrested. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “Theodorata.”] Because she boasted, with feminine confidence, that she would become queen, her face was disfigured by having her nose and ears cut off. In the same way Liutprand’s sister, named Aurona, was made deformed. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “Arona”; the modern edition, “Auruna”; the Lindau manuscript, “Aurora.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### How Anchis, son of Arnulf, was then mayor of the palace in Gaul

At this time in Gaul, within the kingdom of the Franks, Anchis, son of Arnulf—so called, it is believed, from Anchises, the ancient Trojan—held the chief power under the title of mayor of the palace. [Note: These words too are found in the book on the bishops of Metz written by our Paul. Perhaps he had also read in the histories of that people that the Franks were descended from Troy, and, delighted with the lineage of Charlemagne, repeated the claim everywhere. One should nevertheless note the continuing error in the present chapter, arising from the faulty chronology previously given for Saint Arnulf: Anchis, or Ansegisus as he is called elsewhere, must be moved back to an earlier period, before his son Pippin.]

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### The death of Aldo at Forum Julii and the duchy of Ferdulf, who was killed by the Slavs

When Aldo also died at Forum Julii—he whom we had said was the guardian of the place [Note: Another reading: Ado; the modern and Ambrosian editions likewise have this form]—Ferdulf assumed the duchy. [Note: Lindau manuscript: “who [won] praise from the regions of Liguria,” etc.; the surviving variant is a fragment.] He was a slippery and arrogant man from the region of Liguria. While seeking the glory of victory over the Slavs, he brought great losses upon himself and the people of Forum Julii. He gave rewards to certain Slavs so that, through their persuasion, they would bring the Slavic army into the same province. This was indeed accomplished.

The cause of the great disaster in the province of Forum Julii was as follows. Slavic brigands attacked a flock and the shepherds of the sheep grazing in their vicinity and carried away booty from them. The local governor pursued them—a nobleman, powerful in spirit and strength, whom in their own language they call a *sculdahis*—but nevertheless he could not overtake those brigands. [Note: The Lindau manuscript has *schuldaizo*; other copies have *sculdabem*; the modern edition has *sculdabus*. This word occurs frequently in the Lombard laws: title 115, section “If anyone kills a *schulthais* or royal officer”; and in the laws of King Liutprand, title 20, section 1, and elsewhere. It is still preserved in many parts of Germany. The additions to the Salic Law, section 14, also read: “And if a *gastaldius*, or *sculdhais*, or prefect of the place …” The learned Eccard explains: “*Heischen* means to seek or demand, and *Schuld* means debt. Hence the compound *sculdahus*, *scultetus*, Dutch *schout*, German *Schultheis* and *Schultze*, properly designates a collector or exactor. The old glosses read: *SCULDASIUS*, a subordinate judge.”]

As he was returning, Duke Ferdulf met him. When he asked what had happened to the brigands, Argaid—for that was his name—replied that they had escaped. [Note: The Lindau manuscript reads: “Arga said to him—for that was his name—‘Have you pursued the Slavs in vain?’ He replied that they had fled.” The Ambrosian and modern editions consistently have “Slavs.”]

Then Ferdulf, indignant with him, said: “When will you ever be able to do anything bravely, since you have the name *arga* derived from Argaid?” [Note: The Lombard Laws, title 120, section 1, read: “Concerning one who calls another *arga*: If anyone, in anger, calls another *arga* and cannot deny it, but says that he said it in anger, then, under oath, he shall say that he did not know him to be *arga*. This word has not yet fallen out of use among the Germans. I think it derives from the Greek, since the Greeks call a lazy and heedless person *argos* (ἀργός).]

The other man, provoked to the greatest anger, replied, being a most courageous man: “So may God will it that you and I, Duke Ferdulf, do not leave this life before others learn which of us is more *arga*.” [Note: The Ambrosian and modern editions read: “I and you, Duke Ferdulf.”]

After they had exchanged these vulgar words, it happened only a few days later that the army of the Slavs—for whose arrival Duke Ferdulf had given the rewards—came with great force. After they had placed their camp on the summit of a mountain, and it was difficult to approach them from almost every side, Duke Ferdulf came with his army and began to circle the mountain, so that he might attack them from the flatter places.

Then Argaid, whom we mentioned earlier, said to Ferdulf: “Remember, Duke Ferdulf, that you called me sluggish and useless and used the common word *arga* of me. Now let the wrath of God come upon the one of us who is the last to approach these Slavs.” Saying this, he turned his horse and began to hasten toward the Slavic camp over the rugged slope where the ascent was difficult.

Ferdulf, considering it disgraceful not to attack the Slavs himself through the same difficult places, followed him over every rough, difficult, and inaccessible path. His army, considering it shameful not to follow its duke, began to follow him as well.

When the Slavs saw them approaching from the steep and varied slopes, they prepared themselves bravely. [Note: The modern edition reads “various.”] Fighting them more with stones and axes than with weapons, they killed nearly all who had been thrown from their horses, and thus gained the victory not by strength but by chance.

There the entire nobility of Forum Julii perished; there Duke Ferdulf fell; and there too the man who had provoked him was killed. So many brave men were defeated there through the evil of rivalry and [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “and imprudence.”] imprudence—men who, had they acted with a single mind and sound counsel, could have laid low many thousands of enemies.

Yet one Lombard, named Munichis, who afterward became the father of Peter, duke of Forum Julii, and of Ursus, duke of Ceneda, acted alone with courage and bravery. After he had been thrown from his horse, one of the Slavs suddenly attacked him and bound his hands with a rope. But with his hands tied, he pulled a spear from the right hand of that Slav and struck him with it; then, still bound, he threw himself down through the rugged places and escaped.

We have included this account above all so that nothing similar may happen to anyone through the evil of rivalry.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning Corvulus’s duchy at Forum Julii, who was blinded by the king

After Duke Ferdulf had died in this manner, Corvulus was appointed in his place. Holding the duchy for only a short time, he offended the king and lived dishonorably after his eyes had been torn out.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Pemmo, duke of the Forojulians, and the birth of his three sons

After this Pemmo obtained the duchy. He was an ingenious man and useful to his country. His father was Billo of Belluno, who, because of the rebellion he had caused there, later came to Forum Julii and lived there peacefully.

Pemmo had a wife named Ratberga. Since she had a rustic appearance, she often begged her husband to put her away and marry another woman who would be worthy to be the wife of so great a duke. But he, being a wise man, said that he valued her character, humility, and modest chastity more than bodily beauty.

By this wife Pemmo fathered three vigorous sons, namely Ratchis, Ratchait, and Ahistulf. Their birth raised their mother’s humility to glory. The duke gathered together all the sons of the nobles who had died in the war mentioned above and raised them together with his own children, as though they too had been begotten by him.

> **Note [Col. 0641C].** Another reading has *Billione*: he was not from Belluno, but because of …, etc. — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** Another reading has *diligence* or *energy* (*gnavitas*). — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** Another reading has *Ahistulf*; another, *Aistulf*. — Lind.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning Gisulf, duke of the Beneventans, and how he invaded Sura and other fortresses

At this time Gisulf, leader of the Beneventans, captured Sura, a Roman city, Hirpini, and Arx, taking these towns in the same manner.

When this Gisulf came into Campania with all his forces during the pontificate of Pope John, he caused fires and carried out much plundering. He captured many prisoners and encamped as far as the place called Horrea; no one was able to resist him. The pontiff sent priests to him with apostolic gifts and redeemed all the prisoners from his hands. He also made the duke himself return to his own territory with his army.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** Another reading has “Duke Orsurus.” — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** Another reading has “the Hirpine [city] and Auxinium.” — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** Baronius restored the corrupted readings of these names, replacing *Sura* with *Sora*, *Hirpinos* with *Arpinum*, and *Arcon* with *Arcanum*: places that, as he himself—a native of Sora—says, are not far apart and are still very well known.

> Anastasius relates this plundering by Duke Gisulf in his account of John VI: “Gisulf, duke of the Langobard people at Benevento, came into Campania with all his might, causing fires and carrying out much plundering. After taking not a few captives, he dug a trench as far as the place called Horrea, and since no one was found who could resist him, the pontiff, having sent priests with apostolic gifts, redeemed all the captives from their hands and made him return to his own territory with his army.” The distinguished cardinal thought that these events occurred in the year 702; I too would not dare to alter his chronology concerning this expedition of Gisulf, in view of Anastasius’s continuous narrative.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the donation that King Aripert made to the Roman Church, and concerning two English kings

At this time Aripert, king of the Langobards, restored the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged by right to the Apostolic See but had long been taken away by the Langobards. He sent this donation to Rome, written in letters of gold.

In those same days two kings of the Saxons came to Rome to the threshold of the apostles and, as they wished, soon died.

> **Note [Col. 0642D].** Ambrose has *of the Guttian Alps*. See Anastasius, in his account of John VII; Bede; Ado of Vienne; and Hermannus Contractus, who connects this notable donation with the year 707.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning Benedict, archbishop of Milan

At that time Benedict, archbishop of Milan, also came to Rome and pleaded the case of the Church of Ticinum. But he was defeated because, from ancient times, the bishops of Ticinum had been consecrated by the Roman Church.
