This same venerable Archbishop Benedict was a man of outstanding holiness, whose reputation for goodness was celebrated throughout all Italy.

> **Note [Col. 0642D].** The Lindau manuscript reads: “The episcopate of Ticinum had been consecrated at Rome by the Church.” The reasons for this most ancient controversy—by which the archbishops of Milan, claiming metropolitan rights over the bishops of Ticinum, repeatedly and unsuccessfully asserted their authority, while the people of Ticinum insisted upon their complete liberty—were collected with the greatest care by our distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori in his excellent dissertation, which he appended to volume I of the *Anecdota*. In it, that highly learned and devoted student of antiquity and lover of the public good assembled deeper evidence from ancient records, which serves as a commentary on this passage of Paul. There is also another separate booklet by P. Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo. Let the reader consult both works; the method of notes adopted here does not permit more.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the death of Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, and the duchy of his son Faroald

After Trasemund, duke of the Spoletans, had died, his son Faroald was substituted in his father’s place.

Wachilapus was Trasemund’s brother, and he governed the same duchy jointly with his brother.

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** Another reading has *Trasimund*. — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** The Modena manuscript has *Wolchilla*; another has: “with him his brother Wolchila governed the same duchy.” — Lind.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the emperor Justinian, how he again seized the empire and killed his rebellious subjects

Justinian, who, after losing the imperial power, was living in exile in Pontus, recovered the kingdom with the aid of Terebellus, king of the Bulgars, and killed the patricians who had expelled him.

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** The Modena manuscript has “had been in exile.”

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** Another reading has *Trebellius*. — Lind.

He also seized Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them beheaded in the middle of the circus before the entire people.

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** Another reading has *Leontius*. — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0643B].** By Leo is meant Leontius, who had expelled Justinian; by Tiberius, the man who had expelled Leontius. With them were Heraclius, the brother of Tiberius, and many other leading men of the city. See Cedrenus, Zonaras, Theophanes, and other Greek writers; among the Latins, Anastasius, in his account of John VII, and the *Miscellaneous History*, book XX, where the following is read:

> “In the seventh year of the reign of Absimarus, etc., Justinian came to the imperial city together with Terebellus, encamped with the Bulgars under his command at the Gate of Carsus, as far as Blachernae. For three days he addressed those who were in the city, but was insulted by them, since they would not admit even a word from him. Justinian, however, entering through the aqueduct with a few kinsmen, after engaging in battle, raised a tumult and took the city by digging; shortly afterward he pitched his tent in the palace of Blachernae.
>
> “Therefore, in the first year of his empire—that is, in the year in which Justinian recovered his empire—he gave Terebellus many gifts, including royal vessels, and dismissed him in peace. Absimarus, meanwhile, fled to Apollonia; but after suffering pursuit, he was captured and brought to Justinian. Heraclius was brought in chains from Thrace, together with all who had supported him, and Justinian hanged them all on the wall. When he had set out for the Mediterranean districts, he likewise killed many of those whom he found there, both officials and private persons.
>
> “He had Absimarus and Leontius, bound in chains, publicly dishonored in procession throughout the city. While the horse races were being held and Justinian himself sat on the throne, they were dragged publicly and thrown prostrate at his feet. He trampled their necks until the first prize had been awarded, while the entire populace shouted: ‘You have walked upon the asp and basilisk, and trampled the lion and the dragon.’ He then punished these men, who had been condemned to death, in the beasts’ enclosure, etc.”

> **Note [Col. 0643D].** Another reading has *Callinicus*, and likewise below. — Lind.

Gallicinus, patriarch of Constantinople, had his eyes torn out and was sent to Rome. Cyrus, the abbot who had supported Justinian while he was in exile in Pontus, was appointed bishop in Gallicinus’s place.

Justinian summoned Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and then sent him back. Justinian prostrated himself on the ground and begged the pope to intercede for his sins; he renewed all the privileges of the pope’s Church.

When Justinian sent an army into Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the same venerable pope strongly urged him not to do this. Nevertheless, he could not prevent him.

> **Note [Col. 0643D–0644D].** The word *sent him back* (*remisit*) is absent from the Modena manuscript. We learn the date of Pope Constantine’s journey to Constantinople from Anastasius. In his *Life* of Constantine he writes: “At that same time the aforesaid emperor sent a sacred letter to Pope Constantine, ordering him to ascend to the imperial city. The most holy man, obeying the imperial commands, immediately prepared ships so that he might undertake the sea journey, and he departed from the Roman port on the fifth day of October, in the ninth indiction, etc.” This indiction had begun toward the end of the year 710.

> The reason Justinian was moved against the people of Cherson was that they had plotted against him while he was in exile. Since he was of a most savage disposition, he prepared a fleet against them and ordered all of them to be slaughtered by the sword. This was done without resistance, except that the infants were spared for captivity. On its return, the fleet was wrecked by a storm near Byzantium. Thereafter the emperor raged most cruelly against the leaders of that wretched people and against the innocent children, as the Greek writers Theophanes, Cedrenus, and others relate. Not content with this, in the following year he prepared another fleet to level all the buildings of the Chersonese to the ground and plow them up with a furrow.
>
> “Struck with fear, the Chersonesites who had survived the massacre, relying on the aid of Chagan, prince of the Khazars, openly rebelled against the emperor. With them were Elias Spatharius and Bardanes of Pergamum, son of Nicephorus, who, changing his name, was called Philippicus and seized the empire. Justinian had previously had this man beaten, tonsured, bound in iron chains, and exiled to the island of Cephalenia because, foolishly relying on a pseudo-monk’s prophecy, he had promised himself supreme power. He had soon recalled both men and placed them in command of the fleet.
>
> “When they approached the Chersonesites, Justinian, hearing of the rebellion, first vented his anger upon the family of Elias. He then sent the fleet to capture Bardanes. But when Bardanes could not be delivered into the soldiers’ hands, they either feared returning to the emperor with their mission unfinished or, as is recorded in the peroration of the deacon Agatho, became deranged in a fanatical tumult. Hailing Philippicus, they turned that same fleet against Justinian under Philippicus’s command.
>
> “We easily infer from the unanimous agreement of the writers that these events occurred while Constantine was staying in the imperial city. Our author says that Constantine recommended milder counsels; Anastasius’s account in the *Life* of that pontiff should therefore be supplemented here.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. How Philippicus killed Justinian and seized the imperial dignity

The army that had been sent against Philippicus went over to his side and made him emperor. Coming against Justinian at Constantinople, Philippicus fought him twelve miles from the city, defeated and killed him, and obtained his kingdom.

Justinian had ruled with his son Tiberius for six years during this second reign. Leo mutilated him by cutting off his nose when he expelled him.

After Justinian had again assumed the empire, whenever he wiped away a dripping discharge of rheum with his hand, he ordered almost as many of those who had opposed him to be beheaded.

> **Note [Col. 0644D].** Another reading has “whenever he wiped away with his hand a drop that was flowing out.” — Lind. and Mod.

> **Note [Col. 0644D].** The Modena manuscript has “seven years”; nevertheless the editors’ reading should be retained, although Baronius assigns Justinian eight years after his recovery of the empire. The error is disproved by Anastasius. After writing that Pope Constantine returned to the city on October 24, in the tenth indiction, he continues: “After three months a mournful message sounded forth: Justinian, the most Christian and orthodox emperor, had been slaughtered.” Thus Justinian was killed before the year 711 had ended, in the tenth indiction, which had begun in September of that year. Since he had been restored in 705, he ruled again for only six years.

> **Note [Col. 0645B–C].** Theophanes adds that whenever the most savage emperor rose from lunch or dinner, he handed someone over to death, so that he stained the reputation of the Catholic faith with innumerable massacres.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the death of Peter the archbishop and the priesthood of Serenus

At last, in these days, Patriarch Peter died, and Serenus assumed the governance of the Church of Aquileia. He was a man endowed with simplicity and inclined toward the service of Christ.

> **Note [Col. 0645C–D].** This chapter of Paul requires a correction to Ughellus’s chronology of the patriarchs of Aquileia. There Peter is not carried beyond the year 694, whereas our author plainly states that he died in 711. I would therefore place Agatho entirely before him and remove from Peter the charge of schism, which was wrongly attributed to him. For if the schism ended while Sergius was Roman pontiff, as historians agree, how can Peter—who sat under Constantine, the successor of Sergius, after both John VI and John VII and Sisinnius—be said to have remained in schism? The praise given to Serenus is even less appropriate, since it belongs to his predecessor, or perhaps to this Peter, if he truly began to hold office in 670 after renouncing his error.
>
> Nor did Serenus attend the synod held at Aquileia—if this is indeed sufficiently certain, as I noted above—since, “instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius,” that Church of Aquileia “consented and agreed to assent with the other Churches of Christ.”
>
> What the same Ughellus reports concerning the pallium sent to Serenus by Saint Gregory II at the request of King Liutprand, together with a letter of exhortation warning him not to attempt to invade the rights of the Church of Grado, does agree with Serenus. On this matter see what the most learned Lucentius noted in his remarks on Ughellus.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How Philippicus was defeated by Anastasius

Philippicus, also called Bardanes, after being confirmed in the imperial dignity, expelled Cyrus, whom we have mentioned, from the episcopate and ordered him to return to govern his monastery in Pontus.

Philippicus sent Pope Constantine letters containing an erroneous doctrine. Constantine rejected them with the counsel of the Apostolic See. For this reason he had paintings made in the portico of Saint Peter depicting the acts of the six holy universal synods.

When such paintings had existed in the imperial city, Philippicus had ordered them removed. The Roman people therefore decreed that no one should receive the name, letters, or image on a coin of the heretical emperor. Accordingly, his likeness was not brought into the church, nor was his name recited during the solemn celebrations of Mass.

After Philippicus had held the empire for one year and six months, Anastasius, also called Artemius, rose against him, expelled him from the empire, and deprived him of his eyes, but did not kill him.

Anastasius sent letters to Pope Constantine in Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Council.

> **Note [Col. 0645D].** Another manuscript omits the word *Pontum* (“Pontus”). In Bede, book VI of *On the Ages of the World*, the passage reads likewise, and perhaps our author copied it from there. After expelling Cyrus, Theophanes writes in his *Chronicle*, Philippicus “promoted a certain John, a companion in wickedness and erroneous opinion, in his place.”
>
> Philippicus, a disciple of the abbot Stephen, who had been a disciple of Macarius, had scarcely been raised to the empire when he began to profess a heresy opposed to the Sixth Council. He became so mad that he ordered the image of that same Sixth Council, which had been displayed for several years near the Fourth and Sixth Schools in the vestibule of the imperial palace, to be thrown down, saying that otherwise he could not endure entering an imperial residence that was not his own, etc. This is recorded in the peroration of the deacon Agatho, published by Combefisius. It explains the events related below concerning the synods painted by Constantine in the portico of Saint Peter.

> **Note [Col. 0646C].** Another reading has: “He ordered the statues of the saints to be destroyed and the images to be scraped from all the churches, and he ordered the Roman clergy to agree with the Church of Constantinople concerning the *homoousios*—‘of the same substance.’ For this reason the Roman people took their stand with the pope.” — Lind.
>
> Nothing should be changed in the first reading, however. I believe this alteration was made by some inexperienced person, since our manuscripts oppose it and the chronology of the well-known history does not permit it.

> **Note [Col. 0646C].** Bede also records this in the place cited. Anastasius, in his account of Constantine, adds that a civil war arose from this Roman decree, since many refused to accept Peter, whom the emperor had appointed duke; but the conflict was immediately settled through the pope’s efforts. Shortly afterward, when Philippicus’s death was announced, the civil war was completely extinguished.

> **Note [Col. 0646C–D].** Theophanes, Zonaras, and others disagree with our Paul and assign Philippicus a reign of two years. But learned men had already demonstrated from other historical records that Paul should not be abandoned. Baronius presented the clearest evidence in public records concerning the miraculous healing of a possessed girl through an image of Saint Anastasius. Pagius adds another testimony from the cited peroration of the deacon Agatho, from which we learn that Philippicus was captured and blinded on the very Saturday of Pentecost, the eleventh indiction (the year 713). Counting backward from that event, we discover the truth of Paul’s account.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How Ansprand, aided by Theudebert, defeated Aripert with the Bavarians; concerning Aripert’s death in the river; the flight of his brother Guntbert; and the reigns of Ansprand and his son Liutprand

After Ansprand had spent nine full years in exile among the Bavarians, Theudebert was at last raised as leader of the Bavarians in the tenth year. Ansprand then came to Italy with an army, fought Aripert, and a great slaughter of people took place on both sides.

Although night eventually separated the combatants, it is certain that the Bavarians turned their backs and that Aripert’s victorious army returned to camp. But Aripert did not wish to remain in the camp; instead, he entered the city of Ticinum, thereby giving his own men despair and his enemies courage.

After he had entered the city and realized that his army was offended by this action, he immediately resolved to flee to Francia and took as much gold as he thought would be useful from the palace. While, weighed down by gold, he attempted to swim across the river Ticinum, he fell there, was suffocated by the waters, and died.

His body was found the next day, dressed in the palace. It was then carried to the Basilica of the Lord Savior, which Aripert had built in ancient times, and buried there.

> **Note [Col. 0646D].** Ambrose always has *Bavaria*.

> **Note [Col. 0646D].** Another reading has *having accepted the plan*. — Ambrose.

> **Note [Col. 0646D–0647D].** The year 712 is clearly established as the year of Aripert’s death by the length of his reign and by the beginning of Liutprand’s reign. Liutprand began to reign in the same year in which Aripert died, as Paul and others write, although Sigebert assigns this to the year 710 while agreeing with Paul in the other details.
>
> “Ansprand,” he says, “returned to Italy with the Bavarians; he fought Aripert, who fled and was drowned in the river, and he recovered the kingdom of the Langobards. Ansprand died after three months, and his son Liutprand reigned for thirty-two years.”
>
> Baronius says here that Paul was mistaken and that Aripert reigned not twelve years but only eight. But the learned cardinal had displaced the beginning of Aripert’s reign and thereby shortened it. The beginning of Liutprand’s reign is demonstrated for this year by the dates in a charter reported by Margarino in volume II of the *Bullarium Cassinense*. It is dated “in the nineteenth year of his reign, on the first day of December, in the twelfth indiction,” by which the year 731 is marked from the Kalends of September.
>
> I add another donation made by Senator, son of Albinus, and Theodolinda, his wife, to the monastery of nuns established within the city of Ticinum, in the donors’ own house. God willing, we shall publish it in full in the *Collection of Diplomas*. It reads: “In the reign of our lord Liutprand, the most excellent king, in the third year, in the name of God, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.” Since the thirteenth indiction marks the year 715, Liutprand’s first year is likewise shown here to have been 712.
>
> Similar chronological notices appear in a charter of Liutprand in Ughellus, volume I, page 411.

During the days in which he held the kingdom, he would go out at night and travel here and there, investigating for himself what each city was saying about him. He carefully examined what sort of justice each judge was administering to his people.

When envoys from foreign peoples came to him, he wore cheap clothing or furs in their presence. So that they would be less inclined to plot against Italy, he never served them expensive wines or delicacies of other kinds.

> **Note [Col. 0647D].** The Modena manuscript has “a precious dinner.”

He reigned with his father Ragunpert and then alone, up to the twelfth year.

> **Note [Col. 0647D].** Another reading has *Ragimbert*, and Ambrose has it likewise; another has *Godibert* or *Tangibert*, whom Lind. alone reads, etc. He was a pious man, devoted to almsgiving and a lover of justice. In his time the fertility of the land was excessive, but the age was barbarous.

His brother Guntbert fled to Francia at that time and remained there until the day of his death.

> **Note [Col. 0647D].** The Modena manuscript has *Gunipertus*.

He had three sons. The eldest, named Raginbert, governed the city of Orléans in our own day.

After Aripert’s funeral, Ansprand took possession of the kingdom of the Langobards and reigned for only three months. He was an outstanding man in every respect, and few could equal his wisdom.

Seeing that Ansprand was dying, the Langobards placed his son Liutprand upon the royal throne. When Ansprand heard this while he was still alive, he was greatly rejoiced.

> **Note [Col. 0647D–0648C].** Another reading has *Lansprand*, and likewise below. — Lind.
>
> While Ansprand was still alive, the Langobards gave his son Liutprand as his successor in the kingdom, recognizing that his death was approaching and thereby rendering this final service to an excellent king. Ansprand was buried at Ticinum in the chapel of Saint Adrian the martyr, which he is said to have built himself. The following inscription was placed on his tomb:

> Ansprand, honorable in character, strong in prudence,  
> Wise, modest, patient, eloquent in speech,  
> Before those standing by, he brought forth from his heart  
> Words as sweet as honey from the comb.  
> When his spirit was journeying toward the heavenly vault,  
> Having lived approximately eleven times five years,  
> He left the summit of the kingdom to his excellent son,  
> The illustrious Liutprand, and the governance of the people.
>
> Given at Pavia, on the Ides of June, in the tenth indiction.

> This further confirms the date of the beginning of Liutprand’s reign, which agrees with the dates cited above and indeed with the preface to his edict in the laws of the Langobards, as the most eminent Baronius observed.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How Theodosius defeated Anastasius, seized the kingdom, and concerning the flooding of the Tiber

At this time the emperor Anastasius sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens. But his army, changing its plan, returned from the middle of its journey toward Constantinople. Seeking Theodosius the Orthodox, it elected him emperor and installed him, though under compulsion, upon the imperial throne.

Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a severe battle at the city of Ares [reading uncertain], and, after Anastasius had given his oath, made him a cleric and ordained him a priest.

As soon as Theodosius received the kingdom, he restored to its former place in the imperial city the venerable image depicting the holy synod, which Philippicus had removed.

In those days the river Tiber flooded so greatly that, overflowing its bed, it caused much destruction to the city of Rome. It rose on the Via Lata to a height of one and a half *statura*, and the waters extended from the Gate of Saint Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge.

> **Note [Col. 0648C].** Another reading has: “Changing his plan against him, he returned from the middle of his journey,” etc. Ambrose has: “Coming to another decision,” etc.

> **Note [Col. 0648C–D].** Ambrose and the Modena manuscript have *Nicaea*, and Lind likewise; this reading is more correct. Greek and Latin writers establish that Anastasius fled to the city of Nicaea and unsuccessfully fortified himself there against Theodosius, as Theophanes relates under the Alexandrian year of the Incarnation 707, together with Nicephorus, Cedrenus, the *Miscellaneous History*, and Anastasius in his account of Gregory II.
>
> The year in which Theodosius became emperor is still scarcely clear. I find Pagius’s opinion persuasive: Paul connected all these events—the flooding of the Tiber and the beginning of Theodosius’s reign—with the same period, and compelling arguments assign them to the year 716.

> **Note [Col. 0648D].** Ambrose has: “In which the holy synods were depicted, and which Philippicus had removed.” Anastasius, in the passage cited, has: “In which the six holy synods had been depicted,” etc.

> **Note [Col. 0648D].** Ambrose has *the Lateran [road]*, but the first reading should be retained, since anyone familiar with the regions of the city will know the place.

> **Note [Col. 0648D].** Ambrose has *the Molvian [Bridge]*.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the English people, Pippin king of the Franks, his wars, and how his son Charles succeeded him

In those times many nobles and commoners of the English people, men and women, dukes and leading men, regularly came to Rome, moved by divine love.

At that time Pippin held the chief authority in the Frankish kingdom. He was a man of astonishing boldness, who immediately crushed his enemies when he attacked them.

For example, after crossing the Rhine against a certain adversary, he rushed upon him with only one companion and slaughtered him together with his men while he was seated in his chamber.

He also waged many wars against the Saxons, especially against Rathod, king of the Frisians. He had other sons as well, but among them Charles was the foremost; he later succeeded his father in the chief authority.

> **Note [Col. 0648D–0649C].** Ambrose has “dukes and commoners,” and likewise in other passages. — Lind.

> Pagius observed that this Pippin of Herstal occupied the leadership of all Francia after the battle of Tertry and was mayor of the palace of the three kingdoms. From that point, namely from the year 687, he traced the origin of Pippin’s power down to the year 714, when Pippin died not long after his son Grimoald had been killed.

> **Note [Col. 0649C].** The Modena manuscript has: “After crossing the river Heino, which flows near the Danube,” etc., and the others likewise. — Lind.

> **Note [Col. 0649C].** Ambrose has *Rathpodo*; another reading has *Raboto*. The Mettensian Annalist calls him Radbod, and Bede calls him Radhbedus. He was defeated by Pippin around the year 690 and gave his daughter, named Theudsinda, in marriage to Grimoald, Pippin’s son.

> **Note [Col. 0649C].** Pippin’s sons were Drogo and Grimoald by Plectrude, and Charles and Childebrand by Alpaida. Charles, surnamed Martel, took control of affairs after his father, since Drogo and Grimoald had already died.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How King Liutprand killed Rotharit, his rebel, and concerning that king’s boldness

When King Liutprand had been firmly established in the kingdom, his kinsman Rotharit wished to kill him. Rotharit prepared a banquet for him in his house at Ticinum and hid armed men of great courage in the house to kill the king while he was dining.

When this was reported to Liutprand, he ordered Rotharit to be summoned to his palace. There, as he had been told, he himself examined him by hand and found that he was wearing a coat of mail beneath his clothing.

When Rotharit realized that he had been discovered, he immediately leapt backward and drew his sword to strike the king. The king, for his part, drew his own sword from its scabbard.

Then one of the king’s attendants, named Subo, seized Rotharit from behind but was wounded by him in the forehead. Rotharit and the others then leapt upon him and killed him there. His four sons, who had not been present, were killed wherever they were found.

King Liutprand was a man of great boldness. When two of his armed men were planning to kill him and this had been reported to him, he went alone with them into a very deep forest. He immediately held his drawn sword against them and reproached them for having planned to kill him. He urged them to do what they had intended.

They at once fell at his feet and confessed everything they had plotted. He dealt similarly with others as well. Nevertheless, he spared those who had confessed the guilt of so great a crime.

> **Note [Col. 0649C].** Ambrose has “he entered.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the death of Gisulf, duke of Benevento, and the duchy of his son Romoald

After Gisulf, duke of the Beneventans, had died, the people of the Samnites elevated his son Romoald to govern them.

> **Note [Col. 0649C–D].** Ambrose and the Modena manuscript have: “Romoald, his son, undertook to govern the people.” Another reading has *undertook*, instead of *elevated*.

> The passages that Paul wrote about Gisulf I in chapter 2 of this book should be restored to this place. He gives the years of Gisulf’s duchy, which, if they began after Grimoald’s three-year period, must be counted from the year 690 through 707, so that Gisulf did not live to see King Liutprand. Paul’s historical order is confused: he links Gisulf’s death with the events performed by Liutprand, but anyone who examines his history will notice that this happens repeatedly.

## CHAPTER XL. How blessed Petronax restored the monastery of the holy Father Benedict at Cassino, and concerning the monastery of Saint Vincent
[Col. 0650B] About this time, Petronax, a citizen of the city of Brescia, moved by divine love, came to Rome and, at the urging then of [Note: [Col. 0649D] Leo of Ostia, in Book I, chapter 4 of his *Chronicle*, identifies this Gregory as Gregory III; but, as I noted above, Book IV, chapter 18, no. 62, Gregory II must be restored in place of Gregory III. The basis is the *Life of Saint Willibald*, bishop of Eichstätt, which Camillus Peregrinius was the first to adduce for this matter in his series of the abbots of Cassino; Bollandus, in his treatment of Saint Gregory II, Angelus a Nuce in his chronological excursus to Leo of Ostia, no. 481 and following, Mabillon [Col. 0650C] in the *Annales*, Bacchinius in his dissertation on the age of Peter the Elder, and others agreed with him. Peter the Deacon assigns Petronax’s arrival at Cassino to the time of Pope Zacharias, but our author clearly contradicts him. To Peregrinius’s argument Mabillon adds the Cassinese cult of Saint Gregory II, not Gregory III, and the chronological calculation: Petronax governed the restored monastery of Cassino for thirty-two years, and, counting backward from the time of Optatus, Petronax’s successor, who in 752 was sent as an envoy by Stephen II to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, Petronax arrived around 720, when Saint Gregory II occupied the papal throne.] Pope Gregory, sought the fortress of Cassino. When he reached the sacred body of blessed Father Benedict, he began to live there with certain [Note: [Col. 0650C] Nuceus interprets “simple men” as hermits in these words, which Leo copied almost word for word into his *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 4, adding only that Petronax’s companions were given to him by Gregory as “several brothers from the Lateran congregation,” namely that community which, after the monks had been driven from Cassino, had formed beside the Lateran with the permission of Pope Pelagius II and the emperor Tiberius Maurice.] simple men already dwelling there. [Note: [Col. 0650D] Leo writes that these same brothers elected him abbot, cited chapter.] They appointed that same venerable man Petronax as their senior.

After not much time had passed, through the cooperation of mercy and with the support of the merits of blessed Father Benedict, and when nearly [Note: [Col. 0650D] Nuceus reads the number 110 also in a manuscript of Leo of Ostia, marked B. A shorter number was likewise recorded by Adrevaldus of Fleury, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, Book I, chapter 113, and by Abbo of Ursperg in his *Chronicle*. Leo’s other manuscript, marked A, the Venetian edition, and Nuceus’s Paris edition itself have 130; Peter’s register, which he himself cites, has 120. Yet in all cases at least 135 must be restored with Mabillon. Bacchinius, in the work cited, attempts to excuse Paul for an anachronism, but, not entirely trusting himself, he too adopts the opinion of the others.] one hundred and ten years had elapsed since that place had been deprived of human habitation, he became father to the many monks—noble and of ordinary rank—who flocked to him. Under the holy yoke of the Rule and the instruction of blessed Benedict, he began to live there after restoring the dwellings, and he raised this holy monastery to the condition in which it is now seen.

Later, the distinguished priest and God-beloved bishop Zacharias [Col. 0651A] bestowed many forms of assistance on this venerable man Petronax: books [Note: [Col. 0651B] Ambrosian manuscript: “also.”] of Holy Scripture and other things pertaining to the monastery’s usefulness. Moreover, with paternal devotion, he granted him the Rule which blessed Father Benedict had written with his own holy hands. [Note: [Col. 0651B] Leo states that this sacred copy of the Rule was burned in a fire in 896, together with the monastery at Teano. The monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent, situated beside the source of the river Volturno and now flourishing with a great community, had already been built by three noble brothers—Tato, [Note: [Col. 0651B] The names Tato, Taso, and Paldo are not found in Ambrosian manuscript; the Modoetian manuscript has Tassone, Catone, and Tato; [Col. 0651C] Lindenbrog has Rhasone, and so forth, as in the Modena manuscript. But nothing should be changed from the editors’ reading; for it is established that these illustrious brothers were so called on account of the nobility of their birth and the splendor of their conduct. “They were born of noble stock and were related by blood, being descended from two brothers: Paldo from one, while Taso and Tato were born of the other,” as Saint Autpert, abbot, relates in the *Life of Saint Paldo*. Leaving the city of Benevento and their paternal wealth, they took refuge with Saint Thomas, the restorer of the monastery of Farfa; on his advice they built the monastery of Saint Vincent beside the bank of the river Volturno, not without a miracle. Saint Paldo was its first abbot; he had assumed governance of the sacred monastery in the year 707 from the Incarnation of the Lord, under Pope Sisinnius; Taso was second, and Tato last. More about them may be found in the cited *Life* in Ughelli, Bollandus, and Mabillon.] Taso, and Paldo—as the writings of the very learned Autpert, abbot of that same monastery, [Note: [Col. 0651C] Paul alludes to the *Life of Saint Paldo*, written by Saint Autpert, abbot of that same monastery of Saint Vincent. Ferdinand Ughelli made it public in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*. Concerning the distinguished monastery of Saint Vincent, Nuceus writes the following to Leo of Ostia, no. 495: “This monastery is situated approximately twelve miles from Cassino; it grew into the greatest wealth and holiness. Now it breathes solitude and horror on every side, deprived of all monastic observance and entrusted only to an abbot of the sort they call commendatory, etc.”] in the volume he composed about this matter, make clear.

While blessed Pope Gregory of the Roman See was still alive, the fortress of Cuma was seized by the Beneventan Lombards; but when the Neapolitan duke arrived by night, some of the Lombards were captured and some killed, and the fortress itself was recovered by the Romans. For the redemption of this fortress, the pope gave seventy pounds of gold, as he had originally promised. [Note: [Col. 0651D] See Anastasius, in his account of Saint Gregory II, and Baronius, under the year of Christ 715.]

## CHAPTER XLI. How, after the death of the emperor Theodosius, Leo succeeded him in the kingdom

Meanwhile, [Note: [Col. 0651D] Not “after the death of Theodosius,” as the text says. He did indeed reign for one year, as our author states, but while still alive and willingly he abdicated the empire. “Theodosius, however, together with his son, having become members of the clergy, spent the remaining time of their lives in peace,” says Theophanes. Nicephorus traces the occasion to the corrupted state of the government, when the empire was being attacked with impunity by wars on every side, as the Saracens assailed the imperial city by land and sea. “When these things became known, both the military commanders and the civil magistrates, observing Theodosius’s inexperience and knowing that he was unequal to resisting such powerful enemies, began to press and urge him to abdicate the empire and to allow himself to be safely compelled to enter the clergy. He did not reject the proposal, but when the year of his reign had ended, he voluntarily abdicated, etc.”] when the emperor Theodosius had died, after ruling the empire for only one year, Leo Augustus was appointed in his place. [Col. 0652A]

## CHAPTER XLII. How Charles, prince of the Franks, defeated Reginfrid

Among the Frankish people also, after Pippin had been taken from life, his son Charles [Note: [Col. 0652C] Nicknamed Martel, son of Pippin of Herstal.]—the Charles of whom we spoke earlier—although through many wars and battles, wrested the principality from Reginfrid’s hands. For while he was being held in custody, [Note: [Col. 0652C] The Continuator of Fredegar, chapter 104: “In those days Duke Charles, detained in custody by the aforementioned woman Plectrude, was freed by the help of God.” She, at the same time, was Pippin’s wife by a double marriage with Alpaida, the mother of Charles Martel; she protected Theudoald, Pippin’s grandson by his son Grimoald, mayor of the palace, with the support and authority of the Austrasians, and was hostile to Charles. After Theudoald died shortly after the battle of the Cottean Forest, Ragenfrid was made mayor of the palace among the Neustrians; this was the cause of the war with Charles.] he escaped by divine providence and first engaged Reginfrid [Note: [Col. 0652C] The first battle between Charles and Ragenfrid was fought at a place called Amblava, from the river Amblava, commonly Ambles, in 716. The second was fought at “the place called Vinciacum in the district of Cambrai,” in the following year, on 21 March, according to the Continuator of Fredegar, chapter 106. Finally, in the district of Soissons, in 719, according to the same author, chapter 107.] two or three times with a few men, and at last defeated him in a great battle at [Note: [Col. 0652D] Other manuscripts: Provence. The Lindenbrog and Modena manuscripts: Vincentiacum. Ambrosian manuscript.] Vinciacum. [Note: [Col. 0652D] The words “to whom he granted one city, namely Angers, as a residence” are absent from some manuscripts, including Lindenbrog.] Nevertheless, he granted him one city, namely Angers, as a residence. He himself undertook the government of the entire Frankish people. [Col. 0652B] [Note: [Col. 0652D] Pagius, in his *Chronological Criticism of Baronius*, under 719: “Paul correctly writes that Charles wrested the Frankish principality from Raginfrid in three battles, but incorrectly says: ‘At last he defeated him at Vinciacum,’ etc. For the battle at Vinciacum was the second, not the third. Moreover, Charles did not grant the city of Angers to Raginfrid until 724.” He proves this most firmly from the Annalist of Metz and other writers of Frankish history, etc.]

## CHAPTER XLIII. How King Liutprand confirmed the donation to the Church and took the daughter of Theudebert in marriage

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Anastasius, in his account of Saint Gregory II: “At that time King Liutprand, at the admonition or rebuke of so great a man, confirmed the restored donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps which King Aripert had made and this man had recovered.” After this come the account of a lunar eclipse and the arrival of Theudo, king of the Bavarians, discussed in the following chapter; therefore, according to the same author, this donation must be placed before 716.]

At that time King Liutprand confirmed the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church. [Col. 0653A] Not long afterward, the same ruler married Guntruda, [Note: [Col. 0653C] Other manuscript: daughter of Theodebert. Lindenbrog and Ambrosian manuscripts: daughter of Theutpert. Modena manuscript: daughter of Theopert.] daughter of the duke of the Bavarians, with whom he had lived in exile. By her he had only one daughter.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How Faroald attacked the fleet, and how Theudo, duke of the Bavarians, came to Rome to the threshold of the apostles

At this time Faroald, leader of the Spoletans, with a fleet [Note: [Col. 0653C] Other manuscript: fleet. It can easily be inferred from the following chapter, chapter 49, and from Anastasius—who makes no mention of Faroald’s attack—that Ravenna was attacked by Lombard arms more than once under King Liutprand. Yet since both our author and Anastasius transmit these events in a style more concise than the matter warranted, it is impossible, in my view, to restore the complete sequence of events.], invaded the city of Ravenna; but by order of King Liutprand it was restored to the Romans.

Against this duke Faroald, [Note: [Col. 0653D] During the time of this duke Faroald, the monastery of Farfa, previously destroyed by the Lombards, was restored through the work of Saint Thomas, a priest of Maurienne; and in the history of the nine hundred monks beheaded by the Saracens, this Faroald is said to have granted many possessions to that monastery.] his son Trasemund rose up, made him a cleric, and seized his position.

In those days Theudo, duke of the Bavarian people, came to Rome for the sake of prayer, to the footsteps of the blessed apostles. [Col. 0653B] [Note: [Col. 0653D] Other manuscript: vestibules. The pilgrimage of Theudo II, duke of the Bavarians, should, according to Anastasius, be assigned to the year 716; he connects it with the lunar eclipse of that same year, as I noted above. It occurred on 13 January, a Monday, after the fifth hour from midday, as Calvisius writes in his chronological work. This Theudo is the man whom Saint Rupert, bishop of Salzburg, converted to the Christian faith.]

## CHAPTER XLV. How, after Patriarch Serenus died, Callistus assumed the government of the Church, and concerning Pemmo’s war against the Slavs

At Forum Julii, therefore, after Patriarch Serenus had been taken from this world, Callistus, an outstanding man who had been archdeacon of the Church of Tarvisium, undertook the governance of the Church of Aquileia with the support of Liutprand, the prince. [Note: [Col. 0653D] Around the year 730, according to Ughelli. Letters of Saint Gregory II to him are reported by Baronius from the chronicle of Dandolo [Col. 0654C] under the year 729.]

At that time, as we said, Pemmo ruled the Langobards of Forum Julii. [Note: [Col. 0654C] Ambrosian manuscript: “and the Lombards.”] When he had brought the sons of the nobles whom he had raised together with their own children to youthful age, a messenger suddenly came to him announcing that an immense multitude of Slavs had arrived at a place called [Note: [Col. 0654C] Other manuscript: Lauriana. Lindenbrog.] Lauriana.

With these young men he attacked those same Slavs three times and struck them down with great slaughter. No one on the Lombard side fell there except Siguald, [Note: [Col. 0654C] Other manuscript: Sivaldus. Lindenbrog: Sicualdus. Modena manuscript.] who was already advanced in age. In the earlier battle fought under Ferdulf, he had lost two sons. After he had avenged himself on the Slavs twice, according to his own desire, he could not be restrained from doing so a third time, although the duke and the other Lombards forbade him. He replied to them: “I have now sufficiently avenged the death of my sons; even if death comes, I shall receive it gladly.” And so it happened: he alone was killed in that battle.

Pemmo, however, after striking down many of the enemy and fearing that he might lose more of his own men in war, made a treaty of peace with those same Slavs in that place. From that time onward, the Slavs increasingly began to fear the arms of the men of Forum Julii.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the arrival of the Saracens in Spain, and how Charles and Eudo defeated them in Gaul

At that time the people of the Saracens, crossing from Africa at the place called [Note: [Col. 0654C] Other manuscript: Septa. Anastasius the Librarian, in the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, has: “The people of the Hagarenes, crossing over from Africa from the place called Ceuta, entered Spain,” almost word for word as in our text. He adds only that Eudo’s victory was granted not without a miracle: Saint Gregory had sent sponges with a blessing the previous year, and these were divided among the soldiers. [Col. 0654D] Florus also speaks of this in his book *On the Roman Pontiffs.*] Septem (Ceuta), invaded the whole of Spain. Then, ten years later, they came with their wives and little children and entered the province of Aquitaine in Gaul, as if intending [Note: [Col. 0654D] Other manuscript: “they entered as permanent inhabitants.” Lindenbrog.] to settle there.

At that time Charles was at odds with Eudo, prince of Aquitaine. Nevertheless, joining forces, they fought against those same Saracens with a common strategy. For when the Franks attacked them, they killed 375,000 Saracens. On the Frankish side, only 1,500 fell there. Eudo too, attacking their camp with his men and killing many in the same manner, laid everything waste. [Note: [Col. 0654D] Baronius, drawing on the Chronicle of Pithou—or, as it is commonly called, the Annals of Fulda—and on the Continuator of Fredegar, together with the Annalist of Metz and other more recent writers, says that the Saracens were summoned into Gaul from Spain by Eudo himself out of hatred for Charles, and unanimously assigns their notable defeat, in which Abdirama, king of that wicked people, was killed, to the year 725. Pagius, however, under 732, no. 1 and following, thinks that the Continuator of Fredegar—who had written the history at the command of Childebrand, Charles’s brother—because hostility between Charles and Eudo had resumed after the victory, wrote out of animus against Eudo that the Saracens had been summoned by that same Eudo. After citing several writers of that period, he points out an error both in Baronius himself and in Paul and Anastasius: they confuse different battles with the Saracens and wrongly attach the victory that occurred in 732 to the year 725.]

## CHAPTER XLVII. How the Saracens besieged Constantinople and were defeated by the Bulgars

[Col. 0654C]

At this same time, that people of the Saracens came with an immense army, surrounded Constantinople, and besieged it continuously for three years, until, while the citizens cried out to God with great persistence, many of the Saracens perished from hunger and cold, war and pestilence. [Col. 0655A] [Note: [Col. 0655B] Other manuscript: “and so, as though during the time of the siege,” etc.; another: “as though terrified by the siege.” Lindenbrog: “as though from their side of the siege.” Ambrosian manuscript. Bede, whom Paul copied word for word, has the reading found in the printed edition; our author adds only the reference to the plague in the city of Constantinople. From Theophanes we infer that the Saracens besieged the imperial city in 717, but, having accomplished nothing and suffered many disasters, departed in the following year. Thus both Bede and our author must be corrected at this point. Baronius recorded the memory of the city’s liberation from the Greek *Menologion*. A historical oration also exists in volume II of the *Auctarium of the Library of the Fathers.*] and, wearied by the siege, withdrew.

After leaving there, they attacked in war the Bulgar people, which is situated [Note: [Col. 0655B] Ambrosian manuscript: “located above the Danube.”] above the Danube. Defeated by them as well, they fled back to their ships. As they were making for the open sea, a sudden storm arose, and many perished, their ships either sinking or being shattered. Within Constantinople itself, 300,000 people died of the plague.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How King Liutprand brought the body of blessed Augustine to Ticinum

When Liutprand heard that the Saracens, after ravaging Sardinia, were also defiling the places where the bones of Bishop Augustine had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the devastation of the barbarians, he sent there, paid a great price, acquired them, [Note: [Col. 0655C] Bede supports Paul’s account in his book *On the Six Ages*, stating that King Liutprand transferred the body of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, from Sardinia to Ticinum. Several people have searched in vain for the year of the translation. In volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, Mabillon, on the basis of a charter of the same king reported in a manuscript chronicle of the archive of the Church of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, thought that this happened in the first year of the king’s reign. But in the *Annales* he observed that the basilica was counted among the buildings constructed by this king, and therefore, given the short time available, it is scarcely credible that so magnificent a work was completed and the body of Saint Augustine deposited there. Baronius uses another conjecture and assigned the event to 725, because Bede had ended his book with the account of the translation in that year. He recounts the sequence of events from a letter of Peter Oldradus, but that letter has long since been relegated among the spurious. No less extensive have been the efforts of learned men, after the discovery of the sacred relic on 1 October 1695, concerning its identity, as they say. Our most learned Saxius collected several dissertations on the subject through his own diligence and deposited them in the Ambrosian Library, with the pens of thirty-four different authors arguing on both sides. Among them was Dom John Gaspar Berretta of Cassino, to whom I owe the Lindenbrog edition of Paul, and who possesses an abundance of profound learning. In a special booklet he thoroughly investigated the entire matter.] and transferred them to the city of Ticinum, where he buried them with the honor due to so great a Father. In those days the city of Narnia was seized by the Lombards. [Note: [Col. 0655D] In some manuscripts these words, “the city of Narnia,” through the end of the chapter are absent. They are found in the Lindenbrog, Ambrosian, and Modena manuscripts; in the Ambrosian manuscript the reading is Narina rather than Narnia. Anastasius, in his account of Saint Gregory II, where he joins this event with the siege of Ravenna discussed in the following chapter, correctly has Narnia.]

## CHAPTER XLIX. Which cities of the Romans King Liutprand invaded, and concerning the worsening actions of Leo Augustus

[Col. 0656A]

At that time King Liutprand besieged Ravenna, attacked and destroyed its fleet. [Note: [Col. 0655D] Other manuscript: “besieged it with a fleet and destroyed it”; but the reading has been corrupted, as in the cited passage of Anastasius. There it should read: “Seizing the fortress, he took away many captives and carried off immeasurable wealth.” Ravenna is generally said to have been occupied by Liutprand in 726. We learn the manner of the event from only one source, Agnellus, in his account of Saint John, thirty-ninth bishop of Ravenna: “During the reign of King Liutprand, who ruled the Lombards”—he uses the genitive in the Greek manner in place of an ablative absolute—“the aforementioned city was surrounded and ravaged by his army, having been betrayed by its own citizens through a fraudulent trick at the gate called the Healthful Village, which stood beside the river Pantheus. All the citizens ran there, but one of them, hostile to his fellow citizens, after promising money and bringing the keys, secretly opened the gates of the gate leading to the Leper’s Village, where there is a bridge made of beams. After the barriers had been unfastened and all the gates opened, the enemies entered the city and overturned it. For by God’s judgment, the very man who had plotted against his fellow citizens and opened the barriers of the gate was immediately pierced through by the trunk of a beam and died, etc.” After the city was captured, Pope Gregory sent the duke of Venice the letter which Baronius reports under that year; our author below, chapter 54, indicates that through their efforts it was restored once more to the Greeks. [Col. 0656B]]

Then the patrician Paul sent from Ravenna men who were to kill the pope. [Note: [Col. 0656C] Paul the patrician was not the only one who plotted against the supreme pontiff, nor did he do so only once; Leo the Isaurian was urging him on with his commands because the pope resisted the emperor’s fury against the holy images with apostolic courage.] But when the Lombards resisted in defense of the pope, the Spoletans at the Salarian Bridge [Note: [Col. 0656C] Other manuscript: Solariopara. Lindenbrog.] and Lombards from the Tuscan regions in other places resisted as well, and the plan of the people of Ravenna was thwarted.

At this time the emperor Leo burned in Constantinople the images of the saints after they had been taken down. He also ordered the Roman pontiff to do the same if he wished to retain imperial favor, but the pontiff refused to do so. [Note: [Col. 0656C] The events that occurred in Italy on the occasion of Leo’s orders are recounted at greater length by Anastasius: the killing of distinguished men, “both in Campania and in the regions of Ravenna”; some took the emperor’s impiety as their side, while others held with the pontiff and the faithful, and the people divided into factions. The destroyers of the sacred images tried to win the Lombards over to their side with gifts, but the Lombards, in religious zeal, “bound themselves together with the Romans as if by one chain of faith, all desiring to endure a glorious death in defense of the pontiff.” Hence the frequent hostilities and reconciliations at this time between the Romans and the Lombards, for no other reason, as I am persuaded, than that they might resist their common Greek enemies as the circumstances of the time required; once the Greeks’ strength had been broken, the Lombards again took up arms against the Romans.]

The entire army of Ravenna, and likewise that of Venice, [Col. 0656B] resisted such commands with one accord. Had the pontiff not prevented them, they would have attempted to set up an emperor over themselves. [Note: [Col. 0656D] Greek writers unjustly accuse the Roman pontiffs of inciting the peoples of Italy against the emperor Leo, so that they would defect from the empire. But these words of Paul, which agree with Anastasius, demonstrate precisely the opposite, as we say.]

King Liutprand also invaded the fortresses of Aemilia, Foronianum, [Note: [Col. 0656D] Fenonianum. Ambrosian and Modena manuscripts. Other manuscript: Fenoriarum. Lindenbrog.] Montem Bellium, [Note: [Col. 0656D] Modena manuscript: Mount Vellum. Lindenbrog: Pellium.] Buxeta and Persiceta, Bologna and the Pentapolis, [Note: [Col. 0656D] Ambrosian and Modena manuscripts: “and Auximum.” On these places Cluverius writes in *Ancient Italy*, Book I: “The town of Buxeta, whose name is in the plural, lies in the region of Aemilia itself, near the Po around Cremona; it is now commonly called Busseto. The town or fortress of Persiceta likewise preserves the memory of its ancient name and is now commonly called San Giovanni in Persiceto, on the same side of the Aemilian Way, about nine miles from Modena. The Cassinese Chronicle also mentions it, Book I, chapter 57, in these words: ‘In the county of Modena, at the estate called Persiceta.’ On the other side of the road, toward the Apennines, not far from the towns of Bazzano and Savignano, is the fortress of Mons Pellius, now commonly called Monteveglio or Vejo. I am uncertain whether the fortress of Foronianum was the place now commonly called Fugliano or Fuliniano, a village on the Nure River above Piacenza; and I strongly suspect that Paul the Deacon himself wrote Foronovanum, a fortress whose town was anciently called Forum Novum and is now commonly called Fornovo, situated at the confluence of the Taro and Ceno rivers, ten miles from Parma, etc.” [Col. 0657D]] and Auximum. [Col. 0657A]

He invaded Sutrium in the same manner at that time. [Note: [Col. 0657D] The Modena manuscript reads: “Likewise at that time he invaded Sutrium.”] But after a few days it was restored to the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Anastasius, in his account of Saint Gregory II, relates more fully the capture and restoration of Sutrium: “At that time, in the eleventh indiction, the fortress of Sutrium was seized by the Lombards through treachery. It was held by those same Lombards for 140 days. But after the pontiff had sent many continuous letters and admonitions to the king, although he had given many gifts and had at least been stripped of all his own resources, the king of the Lombards restored and donated the fortress, sending the aforesaid donation to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.” From this we learn the year of the event, namely 728, in which the eleventh indiction was in progress. After this our author must be supplemented from the same Anastasius, who narrates the events of the twelfth indiction, perhaps deliberately omitted by Paul. A treaty was made between Eutychius the patrician and Liutprand: “that, after the armies had been assembled, the king would subjugate the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, while the exarch would subjugate Rome and carry out what had earlier been commanded concerning the person of the pontiff”—namely, that he should be killed. “The king came to Spoleto, received oaths and hostages from both dukes, and with his entire company advanced into Nero’s Field. The pontiff came out to meet him and, when presented before him, tried as best he could to soften the king’s spirit through pious admonition, so that he fell at his feet and promised not to inflict harm on anyone. Thus, moved by pious exhortations to such deep remorse, he removed the garments he was wearing and placed before the apostle’s body his cloak, bracelets, and silver cross. After the prayer had been made, he begged the pontiff to deign to receive the aforesaid exarch into a reconciliation of peace, and this was done.”]

During the same period Leo Augustus advanced to worse deeds, compelling all who lived in Constantinople, by force and by persuasion alike, to remove wherever they were found the images both of the Savior and of his holy Mother, as well as those of all the saints, and he had them burned in the middle of the city.

Because many of the people tried to prevent such a crime from being committed, some of them were beheaded and others mutilated in part of their bodies. [Note: [Col. 0658C] Ambrosian manuscript: “were hindering it.”] Since the patriarch Germanus did not consent to this error, he was expelled from his own see, and the presbyter Anastasius was ordained in his place.

## CHAPTER L. Concerning Romoald, duke of Benevento, and his son Gisulf

Finally, Romoald, duke of Benevento, took as his wife a woman named Guntberga, who was the daughter of Aurona, the sister of King Liutprand. By her he fathered a son, whom he named Gisulf after his own father.

After her, he took another wife, named Ravigunda, daughter of Galdoald, [Note: [Col. 0658D] Other manuscript: duke of Brescia. Lindenbrog: Brixiani.] duke of Brescia.

## CHAPTER LI. Concerning Pemmo’s hostility toward Patriarch Callistus

At that time a serious quarrel of discord arose between Duke Pemmo and Patriarch Callistus. The cause of this discord was as follows. [Note: [Col. 0658D] Other manuscript: “The cause of the discord was Fidentius, bishop of Forum Julii. At an earlier time he had lived within the walls of the fortress of Forum Julii with the permission of the preceding dukes.” Lindenbrog.]

At an earlier time Bishop Fidentius, coming from the fortress of [Col. 0657C] [Note: [Col. 0658D] Ambrosian manuscript: Julianum. Modena manuscript: Forum Julii.] Julianum, had lived within the walls of the fortress of Forum Julii with the permission of the preceding dukes, and there established the see of his bishopric. When he died, Amator was ordained in his place. [Note: [Col. 0658D] Modena manuscript: “as bishop.”]

Until that same day, the earlier patriarchs, because they could not live in Aquileia on account of the incursions of the Romans, had their see not at Forum Julii but at Cormons. [Note: [Col. 0658D] Norisius, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 4, restored the ancient see of the bishops of Julianum—now commonly called Zuglio—from this chapter of Paul, against Baronius’s opinion. With compelling arguments he showed that Forum Julii did not have a bishop of its own, but that the bishop of Julianum resided there provisionally. Ughelli also failed to notice this, but the error has been removed in the addition concerning the ancient bishoprics; see it there.]

This greatly displeased Callistus, who was distinguished by nobility: a bishop lived in his diocese with the duke and the Lombards, while he himself was forced to live merely among the common people. What more need be said? He proceeded against that same bishop Amator, expelled him from Forum Julii, and established his own residence in Amator’s house.

For this reason Duke Pemmo, together with many noble Lombards, formed a plan against the same patriarch. He seized him, led him to the fortress of Pontium, [Note: [Col. 0658D] Ambrosian manuscript: Notium.] which stands above the sea, and wished to throw him from there into the sea. But, because God restrained him, he did not do so; nevertheless, he kept him imprisoned and sustained him on the bread of affliction.

When King Liutprand heard this, he burst into great anger. He took the duchy away from Pemmo and appointed his son Ratchis in his place. Pemmo then planned to flee with his followers to the land of the Slavs. But his son Ratchis obtained forgiveness for his father from the king by pleading with him and restored him to the king’s favor.

Having gained confidence that no harm would come to him, Pemmo went to the king together with all the Lombards with whom he had formed the plan. The king then sat in judgment and, yielding to Ratchis, ordered Pemmo and his two sons, Ratchait and Ahistulf, to stand behind his seat. The king, raising his voice, ordered all those who had supported Pemmo to be seized by name.

Then Ahistulf, unable to bear the pain, having nearly drawn his sword, wished to strike the king, had not his brother Ratchis restrained him. When these Lombards had been seized in this way, Hersemar, who had been one of them, drew his sword and, while many pursued him, defended himself bravely and fled into the basilica of Saint Michael. Thereafter he alone obtained impunity through the king’s clemency, while the others were tortured in chains for a long time.

## CHAPTER LII. Ratchis’s war against the Slavs

Ratchis, having at last become duke at Forum Julii, as we had said, entered Carniola, the homeland of the Slavs, with his men. He killed a great multitude of Slavs and devastated all their possessions. When the Slavs suddenly attacked him there, while he had not yet taken his spear from his armorer, he struck down with the club he was carrying in his hand the first man who came against him and ended his life. [Note: [Col. 0659C] Other manuscript: “raising the axe which he held in his hand,” etc. Lindenbrog.]

## CHAPTER LIII. How King Liutprand cut the hair of Pippin, son of King Charles

About this time Charles, [Note: [Col. 0659C] Modena manuscript: king.] prince of the Franks, sent his son Pippin to Liutprand so that, according to custom, he might receive his hair. Liutprand cut his hair, thereby becoming his father, and, after enriching him with many royal gifts, sent him back to his father. [Note: [Col. 0659C] I noted above, Book IV, chapter 40, no. 198, that this ancient custom of cutting the hair was illuminated by Adrien de Valois. Mabillon should be added to him here, in the preface to the first part of the third century of the Benedictine era. He observes that this custom was also practiced among the Greeks: Constantine Pogonatus sent the *mallones*—that is, locks or curls of hair, from the Greek μαλλός—of the sons of Justinian and Heraclius to Pope Benedict II, as Anastasius testifies. He observes, I say, that this custom may perhaps first have been introduced among the Frankish kings by Pippin, and that thereafter they wore their hair arranged in a circle, as the hair in the wax images of the Carolingians appears evenly rounded down to the shoulders. Before that time, according to the testimony of Agathias, who lived in the preceding century, it was customary for these kings to keep their hair uncut from childhood.]

## CHAPTER LIV. The Saracens, returning once more to Gaul, are defeated by the Franks, and how Liutprand went to aid the Franks

[Col. 0659C]

At the same time the army of the Saracens, entering Gaul again, [Col. 0660A] caused great devastation. Charles engaged them in battle not far from Narbonne and, as before, [Note: [Col. 0659D] The fighting between Charles Martel and the Saracens did not occur in only these three battles—namely, in Aquitaine, at Narbonne, and in Provence—but also in other parts of Gaul and at various times, as is evident from the writers of Frankish history. Our author records the more notable victories. Einhard, speaking of Charles Martel in his Life of Charlemagne, likewise relates the first two in these words: “Charles, etc., defeated the Saracens, who were attempting to occupy Gaul, in two great battles: one in Aquitaine near Poitiers, the other near Narbonne by the River Berre, so completely that he compelled them to return to Spain.” The battle at Narbonne, fought in the year 737, [Col. 0660C] is described at length by the Continuator of Fredegar in his appendix. The final battle in Provence, omitted by Einhard, is related by the Annalist of Metz, the same Continuator of Fredegar, and the Nazarian Annals under the year 739. All agree that King Liutprand took part in it, and his epitaph reads:

> Thereafter the fierce  
> Saracens trembled, whom he, tireless, drove away,  
> When they were pressing the Gauls, at Charles’s request for aid.

he struck them down in a great slaughter. The Saracens, entering the territory of Gaul a second time, advanced as far as Provence, [Note: [Col. 0660C] Everything that follows up to the words “When Gisulf, because of his age,” is lacking in A.] and, after capturing Arles, destroyed everything around it. Charles then sent ambassadors with gifts to King Liutprand and asked him for assistance against the Saracens. Without delay, Liutprand hastened to his aid with the entire Lombard army. When the Saracens learned this, they immediately fled from those regions. Liutprand, however, returned to Italy with his entire army.

The same ruler waged many wars against the Romans, in which he was always victorious, except that once, at Rimini, while he was absent, his army was defeated; and on another occasion, when the king was staying in the Pentapolis near the village of Pilleus, a great number of those who were carrying gifts, presents, or offerings of the individual churches [Note: [Col. 0660D] Modena reads “blessings.”] to the king were killed or captured by the Romans who attacked them. Again, while Ravenna was held by Hildebrand, the king’s nephew, and Peredeo, duke of Vicenza, the Venetians suddenly attacked them: Hildebrand was captured by them, while Peredeo fell fighting bravely.

At a later time also, the Romans, swollen with their customary pride, gathered in full force under the leadership of Agatho, duke of Perugia, and came to seize Bologna, [Note: [Col. 0660D] A and others read “to capture it.” Lind.] where Walcari, Peredeo, and Rothari were then encamped. They attacked the Romans, inflicted great slaughter upon them, and compelled the rest to flee. [Note: [Col. 0660D] Paul has sampled so little from the events in which the Romans were successful that scarcely anything can be turned to historical use; and, what is more regrettable, we cannot at all supplement him from other writers, since, so far as I know, none has spoken of these matters. Anastasius does indeed provide much that is relevant to Lombard affairs, but he too passes over in silence the events mentioned in this chapter.]

## CHAPTER LV

Concerning Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, and Gisulf of Benevento, and Gregory and the reign of Hilprand.

[Col. 0660C]

In those days [Note: [Col. 0660D] Anastasius wrote more fully than our author about the rebellion of Duke Trasemund against King Liutprand. Describing the final events of Saint Gregory III, he relates them under Saint Zacharias, Gregory’s successor:

“Here he found the whole province of Italy greatly disturbed, while Liutprand, king of the Lombards, was persecuting Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, who, while that same king was pursuing him, had taken refuge in this Roman city. And since the aforesaid Trasemund had not been restored by his predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory, and by Stephen, formerly patrician [Col. 0661A] and duke, or by the entire Roman army, after a siege had been undertaken, the same king took four cities from the Roman duchy on his account: Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera. Thus the king returned to his palace in the month of August, in the seventh indiction. Duke Trasemund, however, after conferring with the Romans and assembling the general army of the Roman duchy, entered the territory of the duchy of Spoleto from two directions. The Marsicans, Forconians, and Balvenses, or Prinenses, immediately, seized with fear because of the great size of the Roman army, submitted to Trasemund. Then, entering through the Sabine territory, they came to the city of Rieti. The people of Rieti likewise immediately submitted. Proceeding from there, they entered Spoleto in the month of December of the aforesaid indiction.”

Paul adds below that Hilderic, whom Liutprand had appointed in his place, was then killed by Trasemund.

“There was great turmoil between the Romans and the Lombards, since the Beneventans and Spoletans were also holding with the Romans. But because Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, refused to fulfill what he had promised jointly to the aforesaid pontiff, the patrician, and the Romans concerning the recovery of the four cities that had been lost on his account, and of the other cities which he had promised in his articles of agreement, and because the aforementioned king was preparing to move against the Roman duchy, the aforesaid Pope Gregory of blessed memory was removed from this life by divine summons, and by divine will the most holy Zacharias was elected to the pontificate, etc. An embassy was therefore sent to the aforementioned king of the Lombards, and the pope preached salutary admonitions to him. Inclined by the exhortations of this holy man, he promised to return the aforesaid four cities which he had taken from the Roman duchy. When he had set his army in motion to seize Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, the Roman army, at the exhortation of the holy man, went out to assist the aforementioned king. When Trasemund saw that he had been deceived, he left the city of Spoleto and surrendered himself to the aforementioned king.”

The king made him a cleric, as Paul adds in the following chapter, 57.

Yet an error has entered into Anastasius’s numerical indications. For if, in the month of August of the seventh indiction—which was the year 739—Liutprand returned from the Roman duchy to his palace, then, in the second month, namely April of that same year, when Charles, according to the Continuator of Fredegar, hastened to Provence, he could not have been present at this battle unless one supposes—which is scarcely possible—that he completed both wars within so short a time, returning first from the war against the Saracens and then from the Roman war to Pavia. Moreover, in December, when Trasemund entered Spoleto, the seventh indiction was not in progress but the eighth, as several writers have correctly observed. I therefore correct the passage from Anastasius himself and put the eighth indiction in place of the seventh. For he proceeds to narrate the later events under the tenth indiction:

“And he returned the aforesaid four cities, which he himself had taken two years earlier, after a siege undertaken on behalf of the aforesaid Trasemund, duke of Spoleto, etc.”

I therefore assign the siege of the city to the year 740, and to the following year, 741, the death of Hilderic, the restoration of Trasemund to the duchy, the rebellion of the Beneventans, and the embassy sent by Saint Gregory III to Charles, so that he might assist the Romans against the Lombards. For then, as our author writes in the following chapter, “when Liutprand heard such things concerning Spoleto or Benevento, he again sought Spoleto with an army.” Finally, I assign to the year 742 the surrender of Trasemund, the conference of Zacharias with Liutprand, and the restoration of the cities, as Anastasius continues to relate in the cited passage.]

Trasemund rebelled against the king. [Col. 0661A] The king came against him with an army, and Trasemund fled to Rome. In his place Hilderic was appointed.

When Romuald the Younger, duke of the Beneventans, had died—he had held the duchy for twenty-six [Note: [Col. 0662B] Modena reads “twenty-seven.”] years— [Note: [Col. 0662B] Above, in chapter 2, no. 8, I assigned the beginning of his rule to the year 707; therefore Romuald died around 733.] his son Gisulf remained, still a small child. Certain men rose up against him and attempted to destroy him. But the people of Benevento, who had always remained faithful to their rulers, killed them and preserved the life of their duke.

When Gisulf, because of his childish age, was not fit to govern so large a people, King Liutprand came then to Benevento, removed him from there, and appointed his own nephew Gregory duke at Benevento. A wife named Giselberga was joined to him in marriage. Thus King Liutprand, [Note: [Col. 0662B] Others read “having settled the affairs of Benevento.” Lind.] having arranged matters, returned to his throne.

He educated his nephew Gisulf with paternal affection and joined him in marriage to Coniberg, born of noble lineage. [Note: [Col. 0662B] Ambrose reads “Scauniperga.” Thus the bishop of Ostia calls her in book I, chapter 5, and praises the piety of this devout woman, by which she dedicated to blessed Peter the temple of idols constructed in the fortress of Cassino.]

At that time King Liutprand fell ill and approached death. The Lombards, thinking that he was about to die, raised his nephew Hildeprand outside [Note: [Col. 0662B] Others read “outside the walls of the city of Pavia.” Lind.] the walls of the city, at the church of the holy Mother of God called Ad Perticas, as king. [Note: [Col. 0662B] The year in which Hildeprand was summoned to share the kingdom with Liutprand is indicated by a document in the Lucca archives, reported by Fiorentinius in his Commentary on Matters Concerning Countess Matilda, book III, by Ughelli in Italia sacra, and by others, with these chronological details:

“During the reign of the lord Liutprand, most excellent king, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and in the first year of his most excellent nephew, Lord Hilprand, king, in the month of March, in the fourth indiction”—which was the year 736 of Christ.

Mabillon, in the Museo Italico and in volume II of the Benedictine Annals, presents a diploma of that same King Hildeprand: “Enacted at Pavia in the palace, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year of our fortunate reign, in the twelfth indiction”—that is, in the year 744, when Liutprand died. From the agreement of these dates, I think there can be no doubt that Paul has reported several matters in a confused chronological order. For the illness of Liutprand and Hildeprand’s association in the kingdom preceded Trasemund’s rebellion, with which he has joined all the events in this chapter. In his defense, however, I interpret his intention as follows: when, in this chapter, he speaks of Romuald of Benevento, the narrative must be referred back to earlier times, as he himself indicates at the end in these words: “After several years had passed, Trasemund, etc.” He then returns to the continuation of the history he had begun and later completes it in chapter 57, without departing from the chronology of Anastasius, since both place the end of Trasemund shortly before the death of Liutprand.]

When they handed him the staff, as is customary, a cuckoo came flying and settled on the top of the staff. [Note: [Col. 0662D] Concerning the spear or staff mentioned here—the ancient sign by which the Lombard kingdom was conferred—those who maintain the antiquity of the Monza crown from the time of Gregory and its imposition upon the Lombard kings before Charlemagne’s successors contend most vigorously, citing this passage as evidence that royal inauguration consisted in the mere delivery of the spear. Distinguished scholars have brought forward the treasures of deeper antiquity in dissertations on both sides of the question: our Muratori, in volume II of the Anecdota, and Fontanini in a separate booklet, weighing the judgments of Biondo, Sigonius, Cointius, Mabillon, and others. This is not the place to repeat their arguments, nor do I wish to take a side. For the benefit of learned readers, I have arranged for publication of an image of a stone set in the same basilica at Monza [Col. 0667C], on the rear of the ambo; it depicts the coronation of a seated king, with clerics and nobles of the people standing by.] [Col. 0663] [Col. 0665] [Col. 0667A] [Note: [Col. 0667C] Ambrose: “Then this portent seemed to certain prudent men to signify something. Everything else to the end of the chapter is lacking.”]

Then certain prudent men thought that this portent signified that his rule would be fruitless. When King Liutprand learned of it, he did not take it calmly; nevertheless, after recovering from his illness, he kept him as his partner in the kingdom.

After several years had passed, Trasemund, who had fled to Rome, returned to Spoleto, killed Hilderic, and again ventured to rebel against the king.

## CHAPTER LVI

How, after Gregory’s death, Gothschalcus became duke in Benevento; and how King Liutprand waged war in the Pentapolis.

Now Gregory, after governing the duchy at Benevento for seven years, was removed from this life. After his death, [Col. 0667B] Godeschalcus became duke and governed the Beneventans for three years; a wife named Anna was joined to him in marriage. [Note: [Col. 0667D] Leo of Ostia also mentions this Godeschalcus, duke of Benevento, who was succeeded by Gisulf II. In book I, chapter 5, and again in chapter 8, he did not list him between Gregory and the said Gisulf, since in that passage he noted only the final pontiffs and dukes, as Nuceus correctly observed there. I do not at all approve, however, of his chronology for the period during which these dukes ruled the Beneventans. Since I have assigned the beginning of Romuald’s rule to the year 707, counting his twenty-six years brings me to 733, when I believe Gisulf II was removed from the duchy while still a child. Counting Gregory’s seven years from that point, as our author states, I assign the beginning of Godeschalcus’s rule to 740, and, after his three years had been completed, I place the restoration of Gisulf II shortly before 744, when King Liutprand died. I think my chronology agrees with Paul chiefly because he narrates Gisulf’s restoration near the end of Liutprand’s reign.]

When King Liutprand heard such things concerning Spoleto or Benevento, he again marched toward Spoleto with an army. Proceeding into the Pentapolis, [Note: [Col. 0667D] Others read: “while he was proceeding from Fanum Fortunae toward Forum Sempronii.” [Col. 0668C] Lind.] as he traveled from the city of Fanum to Forum Sempronii, in the forest lying between them the Spoletans, joining forces with the Romans, inflicted great damage on the king’s army.

In the rearmost position the king stationed Ratchis and his brother Ahistulf with the men of Friuli. [Note: [Col. 0668C] Both brothers were later raised to the Lombard throne after Liutprand’s death; but Ratchis, after abdicating the kingdom, earned the crown of sanctity in the monastery of Cassino.] The Spoletans and Romans attacked them and wounded some of them.
