Nevertheless, Ratchis, with his brother and some very courageous men, sustaining the whole burden of the battle and fighting bravely, killed many and withdrew himself and his men, except for the few wounded whom I have mentioned.

There a particularly brave Spoletan named Berto, shouting aloud to Ratchis by name, came against him fully armed. Ratchis suddenly struck him and threw him from his horse. When his companions wanted to kill him, Ratchis, in his customary compassion, allowed him to escape. Crawling into the forest on hands and feet, he got away.

Against Ahistulf, however, two very courageous Spoletans came upon him from behind on a certain bridge. Striking one of them with the reverse side of his spear, he threw him from the bridge; then, turning suddenly against the other, [Note: [Col. 0668C] Others read: “he deprived him of life and plunged him into the river.” Lind.] he killed him and sank him after his companion.

## CHAPTER LVII

What Liutprand did at Spoleto; and how Godeschalcus, hearing of his arrival at Benevento, was killed by the Beneventans.

Now Liutprand arrived at Spoleto, expelled Trasemund from the duchy, and made him a cleric. In his place he appointed his nephew Agibrand. [Note: [Col. 0668C] Others read “Ansprand.” Lind.]

When he was hastening toward Benevento, Godeschalcus, hearing of his arrival, attempted to board a ship and flee to Greece. After placing his wife and all his possessions aboard the ship, and when he himself was about to go up last, the Beneventans, loyal to Gisulf, attacked and killed him. His wife, together with everything she possessed, was carried to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER LVIII

What he did at Benevento; concerning Baodolino, a man of extraordinary holiness; and concerning his equal, Theudelapius, and Peter, bishop of Pavia.

Then King Liutprand arrived at Benevento and again appointed his nephew Gisulf duke in his own [Note: [Col. 0668D] Others read “former.” Lind.] place. Having thus settled matters, he returned to his palace.

This most glorious king built many basilicas in honor of Christ in the various places where he used to reside. He founded the monastery of blessed Peter, situated outside the walls of the city of Pavia, which is called the Golden Heaven (*Coelo Aureo*). On the summit of Mount Bardon he also built the monastery called Bercetum. [Note: [Col. 0668D] Mabillon very properly proves from the deeds of Moderamnus, bishop of Rennes, narrated by Frodoard in book I, chapter 20, and from the Annals, volume II, year 718, that King Liutprand was not the founder but the benefactor of the monastery of Bercetum on Mount Bardon. It had previously been built in honor of Saint Abundius the martyr and later in honor of Saint Remigius, whose relics Moderamnus had brought from the monastery of Rheims into Italy and, warned by a miracle, deposited there. Liutprand enriched it with possessions and buildings through his royal generosity, so that our author regards him as its founder.]

In Olonna also, in his suburb (*prohastium*), [Note: [Col. 0668D] The words *suo prohastio* are absent elsewhere. They are written according to a usage common in that century: thus they said *hostium* where we say *ostium*, and *harenam* instead of *arenam*. *Prohastium* is therefore Greek προάστειον (*proasteion*), that is, Latin *suburbanum*, “a suburb.” The passage is to be understood in no other way. Lind.] he established for Christ, with remarkable workmanship, a dwelling in honor of Saint Anastasius the martyr, and also founded a monastery there. Likewise, in many individual places he established divine temples.

Within his palace too he built a shrine of the Lord and Savior, and—a thing no other king had possessed—appointed priests and clerics to chant the divine offices for him daily.

In the place called Forum, beside the River Tanaro, there lived in the time of this king a man of extraordinary holiness named Baodolinus, [Note: [Col. 0669C] Others read “Bandolinus.” Lind.] who shone forth through many miracles, with the grace of Christ assisting him. He often foretold the future and announced things occurring in his absence as though they were present.

Finally, when King Liutprand had gone into the forest called Urbem to hunt, one of his companions, attempting to strike a stag with an arrow, unintentionally wounded the king’s nephew, that is, the son of his sister, named Aufusus. When the king saw this—for he loved the boy very much—he began to lament his injury with tears. He immediately sent one of his horsemen to hurry to the man of God Baodolinus and ask him to pray to Christ for the boy’s life.

While the messenger was going to the servant of God, the boy died. When the messenger reached him, Christ’s servant said: “I know why you have come, but what you have been sent to ask [Note: [Col. 0669C] Modena reads “what you were sent to request.”] can no longer be done, because that boy has died.”

When the man who had been sent reported to the king what he had heard from the servant of God, the king, although grieved that he could not obtain the result of his prayer, nevertheless clearly recognized that the man of the Lord, Baodolinus, possessed the spirit of prophecy.

There was also, near the city of Verona, [Col. 0670A] a man named Theudelapius, [Note: [Col. 0669C] Others read “Theolapius.” Lind.] not unlike him. Among the wonders he performed, he too foretold many future events through a prophetic spirit.

At that same time Peter, bishop of the Church of Pavia, also flourished in life [Note: [Col. 0669C] Others read “in his life-giving deeds.” Lind.] and conduct. Because he was related to the king, he had once been confined in exile at Spoleto by King Aripert. While he was frequently attending the church of blessed Sabinus the martyr, that same venerable martyr foretold to him that he would become bishop at Pavia. After this had occurred, he built a basilica for the same blessed martyr Sabinus on his own land near that city.

Among the other virtues of the excellent life he possessed, he also shone adorned with the flower of virginity. We shall place in its proper location a certain miracle of his, which occurred at a later time. [Note: [Col. 0669C] Others: “We shall place it in its proper location in the lives of the bishops.” Lind. Henschenius gives further information about Saint Peter, bishop of Pavia, on 7 May. In his account he also prints, from Gruter, an epitaph in which the following concerning his royal kinship is likewise found:

> Illustrious in lineage, touching the stock of kings,  
> Noble in speech, nobler still in character.]

Now Liutprand, after holding the principate for thirty-one years and seven months, [Note: [Col. 0669C] Modena reads “the kingdom.”] completed the course of this life at an advanced age. [Note: [Col. 0669C] All authorities mark the death of King Liutprand as occurring in 744, so that no labor is needed on this point. Anastasius, under Saint Zacharias, clearly indicates that he ceased to live before the Kalends of June; from him Paul’s account must be supplemented. Our author omitted Liutprand’s final efforts against the city of Ravenna and the occupation of the fortress of Cesena. These events moved Eutychius the exarch and John the archbishop, by their appeals, to induce the supreme pontiff to provide aid, so that he left Rome and hastened to Ravenna and from there to Pavia to meet Liutprand. The pope was kindly received by him, as was proper, during the vigil of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and by paternal admonitions finally obtained from him that he cease from war:

“And the aforementioned king, after much resistance, was persuaded to extend the boundaries of the city of Ravenna as they had previously been held. He restored two parts of the territory of the fortress of Cesena to the commonwealth. He retained the third part of the same fortress under pretext, having made an agreement that, until the Kalends of June, when his envoys returned from the royal city, he would restore to the commonwealth both the fortress and the third part which he held as a pledge.”

Anastasius writes that these events occurred in the eleventh indiction, that is, in the year 743 of Christ. He then continues:

“Saint Zacharias returned to the Roman city with all those who were with him. Giving thanks to God, he again celebrated the feast of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul with all the people, and devoted himself to prayer, asking almighty God to grant mercy and consolation to the people of Ravenna and Rome against that ambushing and persecuting king, Liutprand. Divine mercy did not disregard his prayers, but removed that same king from this life before the appointed day, etc.”]

His body was buried in the basilica of blessed Adrian the martyr, where his father also rests. [Note: [Col. 0670C] In our own time the tomb of King Liutprand is not in the basilica of Saint Adrian the martyr, as Paul writes here, but in the other basilica of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven. The writers of Pavia believe that it was transferred there; indeed, they say that it was moved again within the same basilica of Saint Peter. Formerly it could be seen at the entrance to the confession, placed upon four columns; now, however, by decree of the sacred Council of Trent, it lies on the ground before the nearby altar dedicated to Saint Severinus Boethius. The following inscription is read there:

[Col. 0670D]

> In this tomb lies Flavius Lymprandus, once  
> The illustrious king of the Lombards, fierce in arms  
> And victorious in war. Sutrium and Bologna attest this,  
> As does Rimini, and likewise the unwilling walls  
> Of Spoleto; for by stronger arms he subjected these to himself.  
> Rome, long besieged by this great soldier,  
> Dreaded his power; thereafter the fierce  
> Saracens trembled, whom he, tireless, drove away,  
> When they were pressing the Gauls, at Charles’s request for aid.  
> The Hungarian, aided by this man alone, the Frank, and all  
> The neighboring peoples lived in grateful peace throughout.  
> Under this king flourished—wondrously—holy and abundant  
> Religion, as the Alps testify, whose Church  
> He possessed after conquering them, and the vast temples  
> Which he built while alive, by which, famous throughout the world,  
> He will forever illumine all the ages,  
> Especially that dedicated to heavenly Peter,  
> The Key-Bearer. In this Golden Heaven, with provident care,  
> He established it; Augustine, brought here from elsewhere,  
> Lies there under the same king, whose teaching makes the Church shine.]

He was a man of great wisdom, shrewd in counsel, exceedingly pious, and a lover of peace; powerful in war, merciful toward offenders, chaste, modest, constantly vigilant in prayer, generous in almsgiving, ignorant indeed of letters but the equal of philosophers, and nourisher of his people, [Col. 0671A] an augmenter of the laws.

The following laws still survive in the collection of Lombard laws, added by King Liutprand to the edicts of the earlier kings. Indeed, the measure still in use in this city is called the Liutprand foot and is employed in settling disputes concerning rain gutters. It would be lengthy to recount individually all the monuments of piety which the illustrious king left to posterity and through the generosity of his donations by which he deserved so well of monasteries and churches. Among these, the church of Como displays royal diplomas by which it received very extensive estates as gifts.

Liutprand is also praised in an inscribed poem on the stone of the tomb of blessed Cumianus, bishop, of the family of Saint Columbanus, in the monastery of Bobbio, where the following is read:

> Here the sacred remains of blessed Cumianus lie at rest,  
> Whose soul, entering heaven, rejoices with the angels.  
> He was great in dignity,  
> In lineage and form;  
> Scotland sent this old man  
> To the Italian shores.  
> At Ebovium he was placed, bound by love  
> Of the Lord,  
> There, vigilantly preserving the venerable teaching  
> Of Columbanus,  
> Keeping watch, fasting, tireless,  
> Constantly praying.  
> For four Olympiads  
> And the cycle of one year  
> He lived so happily  
> That he is now believed blessed.  
> Gentle, prudent, pious,  
> Peaceful toward all the brethren,  
> He had ninety years of age,  
> One lustrum besides, and four months together.  
> [Col. 0672A] But, excellent and mighty Father,  
> Show yourself an intercessor  
> For the most glorious King Liutprand,  
> Who devotedly adorned  
> Your tomb with precious stone,  
> So that it might be manifest where  
> Your blessed body lies buried.

> The lord Cumianus, bishop, was buried here  
> On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.  
> John the Master made this.

Finally, I shall add a gold coin bearing his image, concerning which I spoke earlier, following the conjecture of Camillus Peregrinus, engraved in the preceding bronze table, column 663.

As for our Paul, who did not extend his history to the succeeding kings—Hildeprand, Ratchis, Aistulf, and finally Desiderius of that people—I repeat the words of Erchempert at the very beginning of his History of the Lombards, [Col. 0672B] where, in a crude style, he explains the reason for the mutilation of the narrative:

“Paul, a very learned man, composed in a concise though brief account, with prudent arrangement, the succession of the Lombards, their departure, and the situation of their kingdom—that is, their origin, how they came out from the island of Scandinavia to Pannonia, and again migrated from Pannonia to Italy and assumed the kingdom. Nevertheless, extending the history from Gammara and his two children almost to the reign of Ratchis, he did not without reason exclude the later age from narration, because in it the kingdom of the Lombards came to an end. For it is the custom of a learned historiographer, especially one discussing his own people, to recount only those things which are recognized as contributing to the accumulation of praise.”

If anything should have slipped from me imprudently in these notes that is alien to Catholic truth—which I abhor and have taken the greatest care to avoid—I wish all of it to be invalid, void, unwritten, unspoken, and of no effect.]

At the beginning of his reign he captured many fortresses of the Bavarians, placing greater reliance always upon prayers [Col. 0672A] than upon arms, and always taking the greatest care to preserve peace with the Franks and the Avars.

[Col. 0673]

# LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, BY PAUL THE DEACON, MONK OF CASSINO

(See *Patrologia*, volume LXXV, columns 42–62.)

# BOOKLET ON THE SUCCESSION OF THE BISHOPS OF METZ

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0673]

# Dissertation on the Apostolic Origin of the Church of Metz, by Mr. Chaussier, Superior of the Minor Seminary of This City

[Col. 0673A]

The Church of Metz, relying on an ancient and constant tradition, had always believed that its origin went back to apostolic times, and that Saint Clement, its founder and first bishop, had received his mission from the prince of the apostles himself. During the last century, however, this ancient tradition was challenged by scholars whose works and opinions no longer permitted the beginnings of Christianity at Metz to be placed earlier than the middle of the third century.

Modern criticism, whose zeal had been aroused by the apocryphal narratives that centuries of ignorance had mingled with the indisputable facts of earlier ages, was then undertaking a complete revision of history, in order to free it, through the examination of monuments, from all the errors that [Col. 0674A] obscured and often even distorted the truth of events.

But it ordinarily happens in periods of vigorous reaction that the application of a sound principle does not remain within the limits that calm reason would have set. There is always reason to fear enthusiasm and, consequently, excesses, which the future must evaluate and repair. Today people are beginning to understand that the criticism of the eighteenth century may also have had its excesses, and that questions settled by it may legitimately be reopened for discussion. It seemed to us that the question of the apostolic origin of the Church of Metz might be one of them. [Note: [Col. 0673A] The history of religion, while recognizing the indisputable services rendered to it by the work of modern criticism, has also had to reproach it for exaggerations. The origins of the churches were treated by scholars with preconceptions which, in many cases, it is true, were not without foundation, but which in many others ought to have yielded to respect. The most ancient and constant traditions, whenever they were not supported by monuments as indisputable and as ancient as the traditions themselves, were treated as nonexistent and lumped together, under a common condemnation, with the most fabricated opinions and those most lacking in authority.

But it was especially in regard to the miracles of the saints that criticism displayed an excessive and profoundly unjust distrust. It would seem that, in its view, it was no longer true that God takes pleasure in glorifying his saints through miracles, and that one ought to doubt all wonders not recorded in the pages of the Gospel. Certainly, not all the miraculous events reported in [Col. 0674B] the histories of the saints are certain to the same degree as the articles of faith; often they do not possess all the marks of certainty that could place them beyond every discussion in the eyes of unbelief. But when they are supported by a tradition and by monuments respected in the Church, and especially when they are received into its liturgy, they provide sufficient grounds for credibility to edify the faithful children of the Church.

Moreover, this proscription of the miracles of the saints did not fail to provoke protests from distinguished scholars. Baronius, in a dissertation placed at the beginning of the Roman Martyrology published by him, shows that the Acts of the [Col. 0675C] martyrs, whose miracles have been so generally scorned by certain critics, possess marks of authenticity and truth sufficient for minds free from prejudice. The Bollandists, not only [Col. 0675D] wisely discuss and respectfully collect the miracles of the saints in their immense work, but often reproach critics for their partiality and sometimes even for their bad faith. To give one example, here is how they protest against the silence of our hagiographer concerning the miracle that occurred in the church of Saint Stephen of Metz, when Saint Glossindis, having taken refuge there, received the religious veil from the hands of a heavenly messenger:

> “A recent Gallic hagiographer conceals and almost denies this miracle in the Life of Saint Glodesindis. Shall I say, from ignorance or from very bad faith? Certainly, he found the passage nowhere written in the form in which he himself presents it. See the Acts of Saint John Gualbert, on 12 July, page 314, where we chastised his more serious offense of this kind.”

(*Acta Sanctorum*, July 25, under the Life of Saint Glodesindis, page 205, B.)]

We therefore propose to submit the matter here to a new examination, with the aim of defending the ancient traditions of the Church of Metz and showing that all the attacks of modern criticism are insufficient to strip them of the high probability that, for so many centuries, has won them the rightful respect of our ancestors.

We do not conceal from ourselves that there is some boldness on our part in entering into a discussion in which we encounter as opponents scholars of the first rank, such as Dom Calmet, Dom Cajot, and the learned authors of the *History of Metz* [Note: [Col. 0675D] …]

D. Calmet, dissertation on the bishops of Metz, at the beginning of his *History of Lorraine*.—D. Cajot, *Antiquities of Metz* [Col. 0676C].—*History of Metz*, by the Benedictines of Saint-Vanne, vol. I.

Mr. Clouet, abbé and librarian of the city of Verdun, began publishing an *Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 0676D] of the province of Trier, in which he undertakes to reproduce, concerning the origin of the churches of this province, the opinions of the learned Benedictines, without submitting their arguments to any discussion and, consequently, without advancing the question one step further. It is greatly to be regretted that Mr. Clouet’s otherwise remarkable labors remained outside the movement of revision and restoration manifested in our own time.]

But fortunately we shall not be left to our own resources: we shall have powerful support from other scholars no less distinguished, and especially from the Bollandists, who for a long time have defended our ancient traditions in their immortal work, the *Acta Sanctorum* [Note: [Col. 0676D] See, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, the articles on Saint Patient, January 8; Saint Servatius, May 13; Saint Autor, August 10; Saint Adelphus, August 29; and so forth. Our task would have been less difficult and less laborious if these scholars had already treated the article on Saint Clement, first bishop of Metz.].

Father Longueval, in his dissertation on the time when the Christian religion was established in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0676D] *History of the Gallican Church*, vol. I, p. 45.], laid down several principles that will [Col. 0675B] serve us as a point of departure. He proves, first, that it appears certain that the Christian religion was established in Gaul from the first century by the disciples of the apostles; second, that although established in Gaul from its beginnings, the Christian religion made little progress there during the first two centuries. These propositions, which seem to us an exact consequence of an impartial study of the monuments of tradition, already answer a considerable number of the general objections raised against our thesis by our adversaries. We shall therefore refer to Father Longueval’s dissertation for this part of our discussion and shall proceed at once to the entirely specific question of the antiquity of the Church of Metz.

For Father Longueval’s first principle to be true, we must recognize that some cities of Gaul received preachers sent to them by the apostles. Can one really conceive that Saint [Col. 0675C] Peter, who during the first years of his apostolate traveled through part of Asia and Greece in order to sow the Gospel there, after establishing at the center of the Empire the seat of his spiritual government, remained in Rome for twenty-five years without concerning himself with the provinces of the West? Hardly had he settled in that city when he hastened to send Saint Mark to Egypt with the title of bishop of Alexandria; and would he have neglected Gaul, one of the nearest and most important regions by virtue of its extent and population? How, likewise, can one suppose that Saint Paul, who, after evangelizing so many different peoples, intended to extend his evangelical conquests as far as Spain (Rom. 15:24), [Col. 0676A] suddenly allowed his zeal to cool in the capital of the world, to the point of no longer thinking of sending at least preachers to the provinces of the West, which he could not evangelize personally? These suppositions are evidently inadmissible, and Father Longueval’s first proposition, even if it had no other proof than these considerations, would still seem to us incontestable. [Col. 0676B] The question therefore comes down to determining whether the Church of Metz was not one of those churches in Gaul that had the honor of being founded by the disciples of the apostles.

Father Longueval accepts as almost certain the mission of Saint Trophimus to Arles around the middle of the first century. Among the multitude of churches claiming the same antiquity of origin, he further distinguishes three that can boast of it with greater probability than the others. “There are scarcely any cities,” he says, “other than Trier, Cologne, and Metz, where one finds enough bishops to continue this succession from the time of the apostles. But,” he adds, “the catalogues of these churches and of several others do not possess all the authority necessary to reassure us” (p. 54). If this last observation applies truly to the churches of Trier and Cologne, whose catalogues in fact contain fairly lengthy gaps and many uncertainties, the same is not true of the Church of Metz. The chronological difficulties that have served chiefly as the foundation for the critics’ attacks on the tradition of this Church, and that were the source of the uncertainties which held Father Longueval back, can receive a satisfactory solution, as we shall soon see. Let us first set out the reasons we have for believing that, among the ancient churches of Gaul which, according to Father Longueval’s doctrine, must have enjoyed the privilege of being founded by the disciples of the apostles, the Church of Metz is one of those with the strongest claims to assert this ancient origin.

[Col. 0676C] The Benedictines of Saint-Vanne, in their *History of Metz*, and more particularly D. Cajot, a Benedictine of Saint-Arnoul of Metz, in his work entitled *The Antiquities of Metz*, after showing what the cities of Belgic Gaul were like at the time of the Roman invasion, how rare they were, and how little they deserved the name of cities, nevertheless acknowledge and prove that ancient Metz, the capital city of the Mediomatrici, which Ptolemy in his *Geography* calls *Divodurum Mediomatricorum* [Note: Μεδιομάτρικες, ὧν πόλις Διουοδούρον (“The Mediomatrici, whose city is Divodurum”) (Ptolemy, *Cosmography*, book XI, chap. 9)], nevertheless stood out among all the other cities of the province, both because of its antiquity—as one of the principal and oldest Celtic settlements in this part of Gaul—and because of its size and population, being the chief center of the great nation of the Mediomatrici.

After the first clashes between Caesar’s legions and the peoples of Gaul, the Mediomatrici, having understood that they could not long resist the conqueror’s arms, preferred voluntarily to submit to the Roman yoke rather than allow themselves to be compelled by force. They offered their alliance to Caesar, who accepted it. Amid the difficulties caused him by other tribes, he doubtless preferred to have this powerful nation as an ally rather than as an enemy. The constant and loyal fidelity of the Mediomatrici, together with the extent and population of their city, induced the Romans to make it one of the principal seats of their power. Thus Divodurum, having become their ally, far from losing anything of its original status, had acquired, by the first century, a new and greater importance as the central point of Roman domination in Belgic Gaul. [Col. 0677B] Various facts attest this. First, Roman roads converged on Divodurum from different points. Second, from the first century the Romans adorned it with remarkable monuments. One may mention a palace within the city, and in the suburbs an amphitheater and a naumachia supplied by the waters of Gorze. These waters were brought there by an aqueduct twenty-two kilometers long, which at Jouy passed over the Moselle on arches of prodigious height and workmanship attesting the finest days of Roman power [Note: The Benedictines also cite a great number of Roman bas-reliefs, inscriptions, and funerary stones found at Metz and in the [Col. 0677D] surrounding area (see the *History of Metz*, vol. I, and *The Antiquities of Metz*).]. Third, Tacitus tells us that it was in this city that the Roman legions came from the region around Trier to seek refuge after the misfortunes they suffered during the war against Civilis [Note: *Legiones in Mediomatricorum sociam civitatem abscessere* (“The legions withdrew into the allied city of the Mediomatrici”) (Tacitus, *Histories*, book VI, chap. 70).]. Fourth, the same author tells us that when Vitellius’s legions had been received there with every kindness, *omni comitate*, they were suddenly seized one evening by a panic, on the basis of false rumors, which drove them to take up arms; in their fury they attacked the peaceful and harmless inhabitants and slaughtered four thousand of them [Note: “At Divodurum, the town of the Mediomatrici, although they had been received with every kindness, a sudden panic terrified them; they abruptly seized their weapons to massacre an innocent population—not from a desire for plunder or spoil, but through fury, madness, and unknown causes, and therefore causes all the more difficult to remedy—until, calmed by the commander’s pleas, they refrained from destroying the city. Nevertheless, about four thousand people were killed” (Tacitus, *Histories*, book I, chap. 63).]. A city that could suffer so great a loss among its inhabitants without declining in importance must certainly have had a considerable population. Fifth, the Romans had established at Divodurum their military warehouses and their cloth manufactures for the legions. The emperors had had the stores of furniture and clothing intended for their use transported there and kept there whenever the affairs of the country made their presence in the province necessary [Note: See the *History of Metz*, vol. I, and *The Antiquities of Metz*.].

It is therefore certain that in the first century Metz was a central point of Roman operations in Belgic Gaul, and that from then on the city must, for that very reason, have been in continual communication with the capital of the Empire. If Trier rivaled Metz in this respect and became the metropolis of the province, that occurred only later, when the emperors judged it necessary to establish themselves closer to the Rhine in order to oppose more effectively the increasingly threatening invasions by the Germanic peoples [Note: The Latin name of Trier, *Augusta Trevirorum*, even proves that this city owed its true foundation to the Roman emperors; and indeed, at the time of Caesar, Trier was so insignificant that when Indutiomarus, chief of the Treveri, was preparing for war against the Romans, he did not think it possible to defend it. He even had the old men and children removed from it and sought to place them in safety in the depths of the great forest of the Ardennes.].

All these circumstances, as can be seen, allow us to conclude, with no little probability, that when Saint Peter sent preachers into Gaul, Metz must have been one of the first—and perhaps the very first in Belgic Gaul—to share in so great a benefit.

But let us turn to the positive evidence for this event. We find it in the tradition of the Church of Metz and in the monuments supporting that tradition. Beginning with the last century, when modern criticism cast doubt on the date of Saint Clement’s mission, and going back to the most remote times, we find in the Church of Metz a firm belief, an ancient, constant, uninterrupted tradition, recorded in its liturgy, which teaches us that Saint Clement, its first bishop, was sent to it around the middle of the first century by the apostle Saint Peter, who had established his see at Rome in the year 47 of Jesus Christ; that, on arriving at Metz, he sowed among the Mediomatrici the first seeds of the faith and succeeded in forming there a fairly numerous flock [Note: This flock, although fairly numerous in itself, may not have been very conspicuous to unbelievers, since it was not concentrated in Divodurum; it belonged to the entire nation of the Mediomatrici, as is proved by the ancient boundaries of the diocese of Metz. This nation extended east of the Treveri as far as the Triboci, the Nemetes, and the Vangiones, who inhabited the banks of the Rhine and the regions around Speyer, Worms, and Strasbourg. Such was also the original extent of the diocese of Metz, which advanced through Vic, Dieuze, and Blâmont as far as Sarrebourg and Saverne. Saint Clement and his successors therefore extended their preaching throughout the entire nation of the Mediomatrici and were regarded as its pastors at a time when the Mediomatrici had not yet lost their character as a distinct people, separate from the neighboring nations.]; that he was succeeded in the see of Metz first by Saint Caelestis and afterward by Saint Felix, both of whom had been his collaborators in carrying out his apostolic mission; and finally, that from these first preachers onward, the succession of our bishops has experienced no interruption to the present day. In support of this tradition, the Church of Metz displays the catalogue of all the pontiffs who governed it from the first century to the nineteenth and who succeeded one another with no interruptions other than rare and brief vacancies. Here are several observations that will enable us to appreciate the value of this tradition and of the monuments that establish it.

1. It was fixed in an authentic work that we possess and that predates the centuries conventionally called the ages of ignorance. We have a *History of the Bishops of Metz* written around the year 778 by Paul Warnefrid, a deacon of Aquileia known in literature as Paul the Deacon. This writer, one of the most distinguished men of the age of Charlemagne and the author of several esteemed works that we possess, was the minister and secretary of state of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, when Charlemagne defeated and dethroned that prince. The learned conqueror knew how to appreciate Warnefrid’s merit and attract him to his court. He placed him for some time at Metz to establish a school there, and it was there that Paul, at the request of Saint Angelram, wrote his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, using documents supplied to him and exercising a critical judgment not subsequently imitated by the chroniclers who treated the same subject. It is evident that, in working on this book, Paul the Deacon had before him: first, the diptychs of the Church of Metz, in order to establish the order of succession of the bishops; second, ancient documents, which he designates in his book by the terms *relatio prisca* and *relatio antiqua*; and third, everything that the general history of the Church could provide him, as far as possible, in order to complete the particular history he had undertaken. Thus he follows Gregory of Tours step by step in everything he relates about Saint Autor and the sack of Metz. It would therefore be an obvious error to say, as some authors have sought to imply, that this tradition of the Church of Metz dates from Paul the Deacon. Warnefrid’s criticism and integrity, his care to remain silent and to warn us when his documents provide him with no details, and the state of learning at the time and in the country where he lived assure us that he collected only facts attested to him by serious authorities or facts that the Church of Metz had possessed for a long time. Appended to Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Bishops of Metz* is a catalogue giving the duration of each bishop’s episcopate. This catalogue is plainly nothing other than a copy of the diptychs of the Church of Metz, which Paul the Deacon had before him when composing this short work. Since he wrote his little treatise in an elevated style and wished to present Saint Bishop Angelram with an edifying rather than a scholarly work, he doubtless did not wish to scatter it with figures, which, moreover, the Church of Metz already possessed. But in order that everything might be gathered into a single body, he had the catalogue found there extracted from the diptychs and transcribed after his manuscript; consequently, it must possess the authority of an authentic document [Note: [Col. 0679B]

Paul the Deacon’s little work *De Episcopis Metensis Ecclesiae* is printed, together with the other works of this author that survive, in volume XIII of the *Maxima Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, published at Lyon in 1677. The manuscript from which this edition was made was from the ninth century, or at least conformed to a ninth-century manuscript, since the catalogue appended to it ends with Walla, the fourth successor of Saint Angelram, who died in 883.

In the first volume of his *History of Lorraine*, D. Calmet gives, from a manuscript of the convent of Saint-Arnoul of Metz, a text of this little work that differs considerably, with regard to the history of Saint Clement, from the text reproduced in the *Maxima Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*. But the Saint-Arnoul manuscript has clearly undergone a massive interpolation, which introduced into Paul the Deacon’s work, following what he wrote about Saint Clement, a passage containing a large part of the apocryphal narratives that circulated in the tenth and eleventh centuries concerning the life of the apostle of Metz. The proofs are as follows.

1. According to D. Calmet, the Saint-Arnoul manuscript dates only from the eleventh century or, at most, the tenth; yet that was precisely the period when such alterations were made. They were often, one might say, the work of men more pious than enlightened, who thought they were completing an older author’s work by inserting the popular narratives current in their own time. The *Gesta Trevirorum*, edited by D. Calmet in the same volume, underwent similar interpolations, by that scholar’s own admission.

2. The much older manuscript from which the edition published in the *Maxima Bibliotheca veterum Patrum* was made contains none of these apocryphal narratives. Now, while it is easy to explain their insertion into the Saint-Arnoul manuscript, it would be difficult to explain their omission from a ninth-century manuscript if they had been present in Paul the Deacon’s autograph.

3. Paul the Deacon mentions the opinion of certain persons concerning the absence of snakes in the place where Saint Clement first established his dwelling; but he does so only cautiously, leaving to others responsibility for an assertion that did not seem to him to possess all the desirable grounds for credibility: “They affirm,” he says, “who have knowledge of that place, that where he first lived not even a snake can remain, and that all harmful pests entirely shun that place from which the signs of true salvation once emanated.” This is all that we find in Paul the Deacon that might have any connection with the supposed marvels recounted in the Saint-Arnoul manuscript [Col. 0680B] after the passage just quoted. But how far this cautious passage is from the ridiculous story of the snakes inserted in the Saint-Arnoul manuscript! In the former, the cause of a phenomenon asserted by persons who know the place is not even sought in Saint Clement’s personal acts. There is even a real contradiction between the skeptical spirit of the preceding passage and the affirmative tone of the interpolated fragment. The same author—and Paul the Deacon above all—cannot have written such disparate things on the same page.

4. The style of the interpolated fragment is not Paul the Deacon’s: it displays neither his taste nor his rational manner; its ideas are exaggerated, [Col. 0680C] its superlatives and epithets are piled up; finally, it frequently contains expressions such as *praefatam urbem* (“the aforesaid city”), *amphitheatrum superius dictum* (“the amphitheater mentioned above”), or *jam crebro nominatum* (“already frequently mentioned”), *inibi* (“there”), *parvissimus* (“very tiny”), and so forth. These expressions, which are by no means familiar to Paul the Deacon, indicate a degeneration that at least has the flavor of the tenth century. Let the reader judge from the beginning of the passage, which we reproduce here:

“For our elders report that the following immense miracle of this most holy prelate and apostolic man—a miracle that ought not to be concealed—was handed down to them in a most truthful account, through the succession of the ages, by ancient elders greatly devoted to the practice of holy religion. For at the time when that venerable pontiff arrived at the aforesaid city, a very great calamity was ravaging the people of that district. For the amphitheater mentioned above was filled with so great a multitude of snakes, etc.”

The remainder is in the same style.

5. Finally, one can even observe that the alteration of Paul the Deacon’s work was progressive and increased over time. This was acknowledged by the Benedictines of Saint-Vanne (*History of Metz*, vol. I, p. 263, note), when they compared the manuscripts of the convents of Saint-Arnoul, Saint-Symphorien, and Saint-Clement of Metz.

All these reasons therefore demonstrate that the Saint-Arnoul manuscript was genuinely interpolated, and that in order to obtain Paul the Deacon’s authentic work, one must consult the edition published in the *Maxima Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*. It is astonishing that the Benedictines of Saint-Vanne, who suspected the alteration of the Saint-Arnoul manuscript, were no more familiar than D. Calmet with Paul the Deacon’s true text. At least, these scholars reason only from the altered text of Saint-Arnoul, without supposing that another text exists. This observation is important for the subject we have undertaken to discuss.]

In addition to Paul the Deacon’s work and the catalogue appended to it, we also possess a history of our bishops entitled *Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz*. This [Col. 0681A] chronicle likewise gives the duration of each bishop’s episcopate, but it dates only from the twelfth century [Note: This *Chronicle* was printed in d’Achéry’s *Spicilegium* (folio edition, vol. II, p. 224).]. Finally, we possess other catalogues of the same kind, but all of them are later than Paul the Deacon’s [Note: See the *Monitum* of d’Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, placed at the head of the *Chronicle* cited above. See also the Bollandists (*Acta Sanctorum*, vol. XXXVII, August 29, article on Saint Adelphus).].

2. This succession of bishops cannot be attacked in its entirety. Most of those from the early centuries, concerning whom criticism might have sought to raise difficulties, are honored as saints in the Church; their tombs were venerated, and their relics were transferred and honored in various places until the end of the last century. Accordingly, the scholars whose opinion we are contesting have never called the existence of any of these bishops into doubt [Note: Saint Clement was buried in the crypt of the oratory he had built for himself near the amphitheater. This oratory later became a sacred place for the Christians of Metz, and most of our ancient bishops were buried there beside Saint Clement. Later, a large church was built over this oratory under the title of Saint Felix; in the eleventh century it was rebuilt [Col. 0681D] and took the name of Saint Clement. Around Saint Clement, in the part of the Sablon adjoining the city, between the Seille and the Moselle, stood several other magnificent churches. The most celebrated was the one originally dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist, which later took the name of Saint-Arnoul when the holy bishop of that name was buried and honored there. Hence this place was designated by the words *ad Basilicas*. In 1552 all these beautiful churches were razed by order of the Duke of Guise, and fortifications were built in their place in order to put Metz in a state of defense against the aggression of Charles V. The relics of Saint Clement, together with those of the holy bishops Victor I and II, Sambace, Phronimus, Legontius, and Explentius, were then transferred *intra muros* and later deposited in a church that took the name of Saint Clement. The relics of Saint Simeon had been given in 770 to the abbey of Senones [Col. 0682C] by Saint Angelram. In the ninth century, Bishop Drogo had likewise removed from Saint Clement the relics of Saint Ruffus, which he granted to the abbey of Otternheim near Worms; those of Saint Adelphus, which he gave to the abbey of Neuwiller in the diocese of Strasbourg; and those of Saint Caelestis and Saint Autor, with which he enriched the abbey of Marmoutier. The church of Many, near Faulquemont, has possessed from time immemorial relics of Saint Caelestis and Saint Autor, which were doubtless given to it at the time of their translation to Marmoutier. Finally, at the beginning of the eleventh century, the holy emperor Henry transferred the relics of Saint Felix to Germany [Col. 0682D]. The body of Saint Patient had been buried in the church of Saint John *ad Basilicas* and was transferred in 1552 *intra muros* to the church of Saint-Arnoul. The body of Saint Urbicius was first deposited in the church of Saint-Maximin beyond the Seille, then in a chapel built in his honor outside the city near the Porte des Allemands; from there, in 1552, it was transferred to the parish church of Saint-Eucaire. Most of these relics were lost during the Revolution of 1793. The church of Saint-Martin at Pont-à-Mousson still preserves some bones of Saint Clement, which had long ago been given to it and of which it has recently returned several fragments to Metz Cathedral. Such is the history of the relics of our first fifteen bishops. Since the existence of the subsequent bishops cannot in any way be called into question, we shall not pursue these indications further.].

3. Nor can the duration assigned to each of these bishops’ episcopates in the various catalogues cited above be attacked by direct arguments. For all these catalogues generally [Col. 0681B] agree on the duration of the episcopates; the differences found among them result either from scribal errors or from the fact that some use round numbers, whereas others add months and days to the years.

During the first centuries, when it appears suspect to our adversaries, the duration of these episcopates is entirely consistent with the ordinary pattern of succession throughout the whole series of our bishops. For during the five centuries extending from the middle of the first century to the year 550, when Saint Villicus occupied the see, twenty-four bishops ascended the see of Metz; and during the following five centuries—that is, from Saint Villicus to Adalbero III, who was raised to the see of Metz in 1047—there were twenty-five. The difference of one or two bishops over the same period of five hundred years on either side could even be explained, without resorting to the fortuitous combination of the ages at ordination and the unequal duration of human life, by the absence of immediate succession, which must have occurred more frequently during the first centuries, when the administration of the churches could not have been as regular as it later became, once the religion had become dominant in the state.

[Col. 0682A] Now, by adding together all these episcopates, beginning with that of Saint Hesperius, who certainly occupied the see at Metz in 535, the duration assigned in our catalogues to each bishop’s episcopate leads us back to the middle of the first century for the beginning of Saint Clement’s episcopate—a result that completely confirms the ancient tradition of the Church of Metz.

Here, then, is a tradition supported by monuments which, according to sound criticism, certainly cannot be despised. One must be careful not to confuse it with those traditions and documents lacking authority that scholars have too often, we admit, had to combat and eliminate. It seems to us that to shake so ancient and imposing a tradition, so solidly supported by authentic monuments and so fully in harmony with the condition of our homeland during the first centuries of Roman domination in Gaul, requires powerful and strictly positive arguments. Let us therefore examine [Col. 0682B] our adversaries’ proofs. If we succeed, as we hope, in showing that they are in no way conclusive, our thesis will remain standing with all the authority we have just claimed for it.

Our adversaries’ arguments concern different headings. We shall set them out in succession and gather them into a single body, so that no one can suspect us of concealing their force. We shall then answer them one by one.

I. Saint Victor I, the fifth bishop of Metz, attended a council held at Cologne in 345, or at least subscribed to the Council of Sardica held in 347, as appears from the Acts of those councils. Now, if twenty years of episcopate are assigned to each of his four predecessors, one arrives only around the middle of the third century for the mission of Saint Clement and the beginnings of the Church of [Col. 0682C] Metz. Moreover, according to Gregory of Tours, followed by Paul the Deacon, Saint Autor, the thirteenth bishop of Metz, was taken captive by Attila when that barbarian prince came to sack Metz in 451. Here, then, are two dates that place the beginnings of the Church of [Col. 0683A] Metz at least two centuries later than our catalogues do.

II. We possess a letter from Saint Ruffus, the ninth bishop of Metz, to Saint Nicetius, archbishop of Trier and his metropolitan. Now Saint Nicetius occupied the see of Trier only around 532, whereas Saint Ruffus, according to our catalogues, should have lived at the beginning of the third century: another chronological difficulty [Note: See these chronological difficulties proposed by D. Calmet in his dissertation on the bishops [Col. 0683D] of Metz (*History of Lorraine*, vol. I, p. 18 ff.). We do not discuss Saint Firmin, or Phronimus, whom an anachronism by Baronius in the Roman Martyrology has attending the Council of Agde in 566. This error can only be regarded as the result of an oversight, for the Acts of that council read: *Firminus presbyter, missus a domino meo Pappalo episcopo, subscripsi* (“I, Firminus the priest, sent by my lord Bishop Pappalus, have subscribed”). As can be seen, this subscription is not even that of a bishop.].

III. It appears that the duration of the episcopates of several ancient bishops of Metz was extended in order to reach apostolic times; for the duration of the episcopates of the following bishops, selected from among the oldest, must be regarded as excessive and highly improbable: Saint Clement, who occupied the see for twenty-three years; Saint Felix, forty-two years; Saint Simeon, thirty years; Saint Ruffus, twenty-nine years; Saint Firmin, forty-five years; Saint Legontius, thirty-four years; Saint Autor, forty-nine years; and Saint Urbicius, twenty-nine years [Note: See D. Calmet at the place cited above, and Abbé Clouet (*Ecclesiastical History of the Province of Trier*, p. 55, note).].

[Col. 0683B] IV. It is also reasonable to believe that, again with the aim of reaching this antiquity, names taken from the catalogues of neighboring churches were entered into the catalogue of the bishops of Metz. Saint Clement, Saint Legontius, and Saint Autor are named in the catalogue of the bishops of Trier, and Saint Firmin in that of the bishops of Verdun.

V. The history of Saint Clement is filled with apocryphal details that deserve no credence. How can one accept that, arriving at Metz around the year 50, he established himself in the caves of the amphitheater, which at that time could not have been abandoned, still less in ruins, since it must have been built only about twenty years earlier? How can one accept that Metz, which was so populous at that time, and its newly built amphitheater were lairs of dragons and snakes, which Saint Clement supposedly led like a herd to drown in the Seille? How can one accept that he dedicated an altar to Saint Peter while that apostle was still alive, that he had several churches built at a time when Christians were not yet building them, and so forth?

VI. The cult of Saint Clement was unknown at Metz before Bishop Heriman, who, in 1090, raised his relics, enclosed them in a reliquary, and had them honored in a church that he caused to be built and dedicated in honor of Saint Clement [Note: [Col. 0683D] *History of Metz* by the Benedictines of Saint-Vanne, vol. I, p. 210.].

VII. How can we believe that Saint Patient, the fourth bishop of Metz, was Greek by origin and was sent by Saint John the Evangelist, given that his very name is Latin? And is not the story of Saint John’s tooth, which Saint Patient supposedly received from this Apostle and caused to be honored as a relic, fabricated?

VIII. No councils are seen to have been held at Metz before the sixth century, “which clearly shows that [Col. 0684A] this Church is very recent, since everywhere we see the celebration of councils closely follow the establishment of the great Churches (*History of Metz*, vol. I, p. 199).”

IX. Finally, if the Gospel was preached and had adherents at Metz as early as the first century, how can we suppose that this remained unknown to the city’s authorities, who, being pagans, ought to have taken an interest in it? How can we persuade ourselves that the Romans permitted a religion contrary to the state religion and prohibited by the emperors’ edicts to be practiced publicly and peacefully in their midst, in the city of Metz? For no martyrs or confessors of the faith are cited at Metz during the persecutions that produced so many elsewhere, particularly at Trier. Yet the emperor Maximian Herculius, to whom the Christian name was so hateful, certainly visited Metz. This is attested by the inscription on a monument found in that city [Note: [Col. 0683D] See D. Cajot (*Antiquities of Metz*, p. 167).—We are not speaking of the absence of monumental antiquities, such as gravestones, building remains, and so forth, that would indicate the presence of Christianity at Metz during these early centuries. [Col. 0684C] No scholar advances this negative argument. For it is known that churches were not yet being built [Col. 0684D] during the early centuries, and that the Mediomatrici were scarcely accustomed to erect monuments over the tombs of their dead. Indeed, all the gravestones dating from this period bear the stamp of Roman paganism, which Christians could not imitate. Besides, this argument would prove too much, for no monument of Christian origin in the diocese is known to date back to the sixth century; yet, by everyone’s admission, Christianity was established there at least from the beginning of the fourth century.].

[Col. 0684B] These are the objections. We have neither concealed nor weakened them; let us now take them up successively in order to answer them.

I. We shall say first, with the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 0684D] On this first difficulty, see *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. XIV, article on Saint Servatius, 13 May; vol. XXXVII, article on Saint Autor, 10 August, and article on Saint Adelphus, 29 August.], that if we had to follow the chronology assigned by our adversaries to the episcopate of Saint Victor and that of Saint Autor, we would encounter serious difficulties. Let us first seek, in the chronology of our ancient bishops, a secure date that can serve as our point of departure. The episcopate of Saint Hesperius provides it. This bishop attended and subscribed the First Council of Clermont, held in 535 [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Hesperius, bishop of the Church of Metz, in the name of Christ, have assented and subscribed” (*In the Acts of the First Council of Arverne*, in Sirmond, *Councils of Gaul*, vol. I, under the year 535).], and we must regard as accurate the documents that place his accession to the episcopal see in 531.

Now, first, if Saint Autor, the thirteenth bishop of Metz, is made to attend the sack of that city by Attila in 451, and Saint Hesperius, the twenty-third, to attend the Council of Clermont in 535, there are only eighty-four years between Saint Autor and Saint Hesperius. This leaves, on average, only about eight years of episcopate for each of the [Col. 0684C] ten bishops who occupy this interval, whereas, during the following five centuries—as throughout the entire succession of our bishops—the average duration of episcopates is approximately twenty years. This irregularity in the succession of our bishops certainly indicates an error in the first of these two dates, since the second is indisputable.

Second, according to our catalogues, the bishops from Saint Victor to Saint Autor must have occupied the see for nearly two hundred years, whereas only 104 years separate the Council of Cologne from Attila’s invasion. The same catalogues assign at least 225 years to the combined episcopates of Saint Autor and Saint Hesperius, whereas only eighty-four years separate the sack of Metz by Attila from the First Council of Clermont. We must therefore, on the one hand, treat as nonexistent an ancient and constant tradition, as well as documents dating from the eighth century that bear within themselves no sign of falsity or fabrication, and, on the other hand, acknowledge, for a succession of ten bishops, an interruption of the historical law governing episcopal successions. These are serious consequences in historical criticism, and, in order to be accepted, they require the support of entirely incontestable evidence. Let us therefore see whether the monuments cited by our adversaries possess such authority.

First, the Acts of the Council of Cologne, which Saint Victor is said to have attended, cannot be presented as a document of unimpeachable value. The Benedictines of Saint-Vanne (*History of Metz*, vol. I, p. 216), together with Baronius, Tillemont, and other scholars, regard them instead as fabricated, since, they say, the names of the Fathers who subscribed them are evidently copied from the Acts of the Council of Sardica, held the following year; and Euphratas, bishop of Cologne, against whom this council was supposedly convened and who was supposedly deposed and condemned there, nevertheless [Col. 0685B] attended the Council of Sardica the following year and was even sent by that council to the emperor Constantius.

Father Henschenius, in his learned dissertation on Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, while accepting the existence of this council as genuine, nevertheless regards its Acts as seriously corrupted, at least as regards the proper names. Thus, first, following Father Sirmond, he points out that the word *Laticlavo* has been substituted for *Articlavo*, the ancient name of the city of Verdun. Second, he cites as improperly inserted into these Acts the subscription of Simplicius, bishop of Autun, who lived only in the following century, whereas in 346 it seems to him that Saint Cassianus must have occupied the see of Autun. Third, he likewise thinks that some half-learned person, or some ignorant copyist, wrongly inserted there—or at least produced there through the corruption of another name—the name of Euphratas, a bishop distinguished for his learning and virtue, whom he believes to have been the immediate successor of the man who was deposed at the council. The Fathers of the council may have suppressed the latter’s name so as not to impose too solemn a disgrace upon his memory; or perhaps the name of the deposed bishop bore some resemblance to that of Euphratas, which the incompetent corrector or restorer thought he ought to substitute. These are the principal corruptions that Henschenius observes in the Acts of this council [Note: [Col. 0685D] Here is an extract from Father Henschenius’s own words:

“Simplicius is assigned the episcopate of Autun, although it appears that Saint Cassianus was then seated there, and after him Egemonius, and then, in the following century, Simplicius, as we stated in the Life of Saint Amator, 1 May. Let us therefore, with the reader’s permission, point out that we believe another name as well to have slipped into the same text, either falsely inserted by some half-learned person or badly distorted by an unskilled copyist—namely, that of the bishop of Agrippina [Cologne], although the other bishops at the council may have enveloped it in profound silence in order to spare his reputation, or it may have been distorted from the name of Euphrasius, Euprasius, or some similar name: Euphratas, I say, [Col. 0686D] a man both most learned and utterly upright, as will soon become clear; indeed, we believe that he exposed the wickedness of the other and was substituted in place of the one who had been deposed.” (*Acta Sanctorum*, on Saint Servatius, 13 May, p. 210, C.)].

Certainly, the authority of such a document is far from unimpeachable, whatever opinion one may adopt concerning the existence of the Council of Cologne.

The second monument set against our catalogues is the text of the Acts of the Council of Sardica, held in 347, to which Saint Victor is also said to have subscribed. But the subscriptions of the bishops in the Acts of this council—including, indeed, the name of Victor, twice even—are given without any indication of the episcopal city of each signatory. It is only by a rather gratuitous supposition that one claims that one of these subscriptions, “Victor,” belongs to the bishop of Metz. Would such a conjectural inference suffice [Col. 0686A] to destroy the authority of our positive evidence?

Third, the testimony of Gregory of Tours offers no stronger argument, for this historian plainly contradicts himself concerning the matter before us, and the most reasonable meaning that can be assigned to his text favors our catalogues, as we shall soon see.

Finally, the letter of Saint Ruffus, the fourth document cited, has absolutely no value, except against our adversaries, as we shall likewise undertake to demonstrate below.

These, then, are the most compelling arguments of our adversaries, and they prove to rest only upon apocryphal or falsified monuments, upon contradictory monuments, or upon monuments of purely conjectural authority. Consequently, sound criticism must regard them as entirely powerless against the tradition of the Church of Metz, the authority of our catalogues, and the regular law governing [Col. 0686B] episcopal successions.

If, however, one insists that the bishop of Metz truly subscribed the Council of Cologne, we shall see that this bishop must have been Saint Autor, not Saint Victor.

Indeed, in his account of the sack of Metz and the captivity of Saint Autor under Attila, Gregory of Tours—followed on this point by Paul the Deacon—makes Saint Autor a contemporary of Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren. He relates how Saint Autor was warned by Saint Servatius of the barbarians’ imminent arrival and of the impending destruction of his episcopal city (*History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 5). Now Saint Servatius is one of the Fathers of the Council of Cologne, held in 346, and probably also of the Council of Sardica, held in 347. He therefore lived a century before Attila.

On the other hand, following the catalogues of our bishops, Saint Autor would have occupied the see of Metz from approximately 326 until approximately 375. It is therefore he who [Col. 0686C] would have subscribed the Council of Cologne together with his contemporary and friend Saint Servatius; and in the Acts of this council that we possess, *Autor* should be read instead of *Victor*. A copyist’s error would thus have substituted the latter name for the true name in the subscriptions of the council’s Fathers.

After the other falsifications or corrections identified in the Acts of this council by Father Sirmond and Father Henschenius, and which we mentioned above, the Bollandists do not hesitate to admit here an error of the same kind, which must have introduced the name of Victor into these Acts in place of that of Autor; they even cite earlier authors who have no doubt whatever about this alteration [Note: [Col. 0686D] “Here Autor sat with Saint Servatius in the Council of Agrippina; but, with a single letter changed through the inadvertence of copyists, the Acts read *Victor*: this error had already been observed by Meurissius, bishop, in the *History of the Bishops of Metz*; by Aegidius Gelenius, book I of *The Greatness of Agrippina-Cologne*, section 6, note 3; by Claude Robert, in *Gallia Christiana*, and others” (*Acta Sanctorum*, May, 13 May, on Saint Servatius, p. 214, E).].

D. Cajot does indeed protest; but, in order to reject this correction of a faulty text, he is forced to make a similar hypothesis, entirely gratuitous and much more difficult to explain, by reading *Aravatius* or *Arvatius* for *Servatius* in the text [Col. 0686D] of Gregory of Tours. Between the names *Autor* and *Victor* the difference is not great, especially in ancient scripts. They consist of approximately the same number of strokes, almost identical; and it is easy to understand how, probably having before him a manuscript six or seven hundred years old, deteriorated by age—as the Acts of the Council of Cologne must have been in the tenth or eleventh century—a manuscript in which the characters of the signatures were doubtless poorly formed, as is customary, a copyist could easily have been led to read *Victor* instead of *Autor*, a proper name rare in the Church and perhaps unknown to him. Moreover, this word occurred only once in his manuscript, whereas in Gregory of Tours’ work the word *Servatius* occurs so many times that one cannot admit the possibility of a copyist’s error by which it was substituted for *Arvatius*.

As for the Acts of the Council of Sardica, the subscriptions found there bear so close a resemblance to the subscriptions of the Council of Cologne that, once the latter had been corrupted, one can readily understand how this supposed correction passed into the Acts of the Council of Sardica—if, indeed, one wishes to admit that the bishop of Metz subscribed it. In any case, nothing proves this conclusively, as we said above.

To complete our explanations concerning this first argument of our adversaries, it remains for us, first, to account for Saint Autor’s captivity by some means other than Attila’s invasion, and, second, to show that the most reasonable meaning of Gregory of Tours’ text accords with the chronology of our catalogues.

1. At the period to which our catalogues assign Saint Autor’s episcopate, history records a great invasion by the barbarians of Germania into the northern provinces of Gaul. The emperor Constantine had just died; these barbarians, whom fear of his name had until then kept in check, soon crossed the Rhine to carry their devastation into the provinces of Gaul. Caesar Julian was sent to the West to fight them, and [Col. 0687C] after winning a famous victory over them in 357, he succeeded in driving them back beyond the river and freeing the provinces of the Empire. During this invasion, Metz and its territory were sacked, and the holy bishop Autor was carried away captive to a place called Decempagi, which is believed to have been the city of Dieuze.

2. Since Gregory of Tours makes Saint Autor at once a contemporary of Saint Servatius and of Attila, there is an obvious anachronism in his account, whatever period one assigns to Saint Autor’s episcopate. It is true that D. Calmet, in order to avoid the anachronism of making Saint Servatius contemporary with Attila, accepts a second Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, invented by Pagi; but this Saint Servatius II, entirely unknown to history, is rejected by the other critics. We have just seen that the hypothesis substituting *Arvatius* for *Servatius* is likewise inadmissible. We may add that the word *Arvatius* has not occurred in any manuscript of Gregory of Tours, and that Paul the Deacon was already reading *Servatius* in the eighth century. It is therefore truly Saint Servatius, contemporary with the Councils of Cologne and Sardica, whom Gregory of Tours designates in chapter five of the second book of his *History of the Franks*.

In interpreting an author, when faced with two hypotheses each containing an anachronism, criticism requires us to accept the one demanded by the greater authorities and whose anachronism is more easily explained by the ideas of the author being interpreted. Now, on the one hand, we have our catalogues, [Col. 0688A] which make Saint Autor a contemporary of Saint Servatius, not of Attila; and, on the other, we have only Gregory of Tours’ contradictory account. Moreover, Gregory of Tours’ error is easily explained in the direction indicated by our catalogues. The Bollandists [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Acta Sanctorum*, August, 10 August, on Saint Auctor, no. 5.] find nothing strange in supposing that this author confused various devastations that Metz suffered at the hands of barbarians from beyond the Rhine and attributed Saint Autor’s captivity to Attila, although it occurred during an earlier invasion. In this he would merely have yielded to the ideas of his time and to the impression of terror that Attila’s ravages still left behind.

“Attila’s invasion,” says the author of the *Annals of the Middle Ages*, “was a prodigious event that powerfully struck the imagination of contemporaries and posterity, so much so that its memory could not be erased. It even seems that the desolation of several provinces and the sack of a multitude [Col. 0688B] of cities—perhaps ruined at another time and by other invasions—was attached to it [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Annals of the Middle Ages*, vol. II, book V, p. 212, octavo edition, Paris, 1825.].”

Gregory of Tours is not, moreover, so accurate as to rule out this supposition, especially with regard to events that he did not verify personally or gather from reliable documents. Thus, in his *History of the Franks*, he reverses and confuses the order of succession of the Vandal kings, even attributing to one what belongs to another [Note: [Col. 0687D] See *Acta Sanctorum*, 13 May, on Saint Servatius, p. 213, no. 14, and Gregory of Tours’ *History of the Franks* in the collection of memoirs relating to the History of France, published by M. Guizot.]. Nothing, therefore, is more natural in his account than the anachronism by which he makes Saint Autor a contemporary of Attila.

Thus everything is explained. Once Gregory of Tours’ error is recognized and the correction of the Acts of the Council of Cologne admitted, events and persons resume their natural places in the chronology. But one document still remains for us to discuss: the letter of Saint Ruffus to Saint Nicetius, his metropolitan.

[Col. 0688C] II. We confess that we are astonished that the learned abbot of Senones judged this alleged letter of Saint Ruffus worthy of appearing among the documents in the case he brings against the antiquity of the Church of Metz. For, to accept and defend such a document, one must plunge into the most palpable contradictions. How, indeed, could Saint Ruffus, the ninth bishop of Metz, have existed in 532 if, as D. Calmet maintains, Saint Autor, the thirteenth bishop of Metz and the fourth successor of Saint Ruffus, had lived seventy years earlier and had been carried captive by Attila in 451? What, moreover, are we to make of the thirteen bishops intervening between Saint Ruffus and Saint Hesperius, if the former wrote to Saint Nicetius in 532 and the latter attended the Council of Clermont in 535?

The fact is that nothing in this letter proves that it was written by Saint Ruffus, bishop of Metz. It is entitled *Epistola Rufi episcopi ad Nicetium papam*—“Letter of Bishop Ruffus to Pope Nicetius”—without any indication of date or place [Note: [Col. 0688D] See Duchesne’s *History of France*, where this letter is reproduced, vol. I, p. 863.]. If history reveals no other Ruffus than the bishop of Metz to whom it can be attributed, or any other Nicetius, pope or archbishop, than the one who governed the Church of Trier in the sixth century and to whom our holy bishop could have addressed it, we must conclude either that this is a fabricated document or that not all the persons in the history are known. For it is perfectly evident that, under no hypothesis, could this letter have been written in 532 by Saint Ruffus, bishop of Metz, to Saint Nicetius, archbishop of Trier.

We now see how little value the documents invoked by our adversaries against [Col. 0689A] the apostolic origin of the Church of Metz possess, and into what confusion, contradictions, and inextricable difficulties one is led by accepting them. Accordingly, none of our adversaries has attempted to coordinate the chronology of our bishops according to these documents; that would have been impossible. By following, instead, the chronology of our catalogues, together with the very simple explanations we have just given, everything becomes intelligible, clear, coordinated, and perfectly consistent.

It was not Saint Victor who attended the Council of Cologne, but Saint Autor, a contemporary not of Attila but of Saint Servatius, who, like him, subscribed the same council. It was Saint Servatius who warned him of the invasion of the barbarians who sacked Metz around the middle of the fourth century and carried him away captive. Finally, the historical law governing the duration of episcopates holds throughout the entire series of our bishops, and we are not forced to trample underfoot ancient and worthy monuments [Col. 0689B] of respect.

Once the matter of chronology has been clarified and settled, the remaining difficulties being only negative evidence or obscurities of detail, they are too secondary to shake our thesis. Nevertheless, we shall answer them.

III. We may say with the Bollandists that it is entirely gratuitous to regard the duration of the episcopates of several of our ancient bishops as excessive and improbable, and for D. Calmet to suppose that the episcopates of several of them were lengthened in order to reach the apostolic age. We have already shown that, during the first five centuries of our catalogues, to which this accusation applies, the average duration of episcopates is the same as during the following five centuries, when the episcopal successions are entirely certain.

The inspection of our catalogues would in any case suffice to invalidate D. Calmet’s supposition. For would a forger of this kind have left episcopates of three years and two months, three years and six months, and so forth, such as those of Saint Victor II and Saint Bonnolus, alongside episcopates of forty-two years and six months, thirty-four years, and so forth, such as those of Saint Firminus and Saint Legontius? Would he not have distributed his additions in a less unequal and more plausible manner?

Finally, why should we suppose that what occurred later could not have existed in the earlier centuries? From the eighth to the eleventh century, without going beyond our catalogues, we find that Saint Sigisbaud occupied the see for twenty-four years; Saint Chrodegang, twenty-three years; Saint Angelram, twenty-three years; Drogo, thirty-three years; Robert, thirty-four years; Saint Adalbero I, thirty-five years; Thierry II, forty-three years; Adalbero III, twenty-six years; and Stephen, forty-four years. The latter was consecrated in 1021, more than a year after his election, by Pope Callixtus II, his uncle, and died on 29 December 1063.

Our last four bishops before the Revolution of 1793 were bishops for the following lengths of time: M. de Feuillade, twenty-eight years; M. de Coislin, thirty-six years; M. de Saint-Simon, twenty-seven years; and M. de Montmorency, fifty-five years. The latter was made bishop of Orléans in 1753, of Condom in 1757, and of Metz in 1760; he lived until 1808 [Note: [Col. 0689D] Contemporary history offers examples of long episcopates no less remarkable. Cardinal de La Tour d’Auvergne, currently bishop of Arras, was appointed under the Concordat in 1802 and has consequently already completed forty-five years as a bishop. Bishop Droste de Vischering, bishop of Münster and brother of the illustrious archbishop of Cologne, [Col. 0690D] came in 1844 to venerate the Holy Robe at Trier in the forty-ninth year of his episcopate; in 1845 he celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of his consecration, and died in 1846 after fifty-one years as a bishop.].

D. Calmet and his disciples therefore have no grounds for bringing an accusation of falsity against our catalogues because they present several lengthy episcopates during the early centuries, since this difficulty does not exist for the later centuries.

IV. Must we conclude, from the fact that the names of some of our ancient bishops are found in the catalogues of other Churches, that our catalogues were falsified by the introduction of bishops foreign to the Church of Metz? We do not think so. Could the same name not have been borne by different persons during those ancient centuries, just as happened later and still happens today? Will it be said that Saint Abbo, who occupied the see of Metz at the beginning of the eighth century, was wrongly inserted into our catalogues because, at approximately the same period, a bishop also named Abbo occupied the see of Verdun? The certainty of the history of those times argues against it.

Let us therefore acknowledge that this identity of name proves nothing against the authority of our catalogues. This is made especially clear by the fact that it concerns precisely persons who are well known and whose existence as bishops of Metz is beyond doubt. No one, indeed, can question that Saint Clement was the first bishop of Metz; Saint Autor’s episcopate is connected with the history of Metz by incontestable facts; Saint Firminus is mentioned [Col. 0690B] as bishop of Metz in the Roman Martyrology; and, finally, the relics of all these holy bishops were preserved until recent times at Metz or in the churches to which they had been given [Note: [Col. 0690D] See above, the note to column 681.].

If one were to insist upon the reality of borrowings of this kind, they would have to be attributed not to the Church of Metz, whose succession of bishops is too secure to be attacked, but to the neighboring Churches, whose catalogues are entirely inadequate for reaching back to apostolic times and are, moreover, far from offering the same certainty as that of the Church of Metz.

Perhaps, too, the care given by some of our bishops to neighboring peoples whose Churches were deprived of pastors caused their names to be inserted in the diptychs of those Churches. This conjecture is not entirely improbable when one recalls the fairly common practice among the first bishops of Gaul of considering themselves missionaries to an entire province when that province lacked other pastors. [Col. 0690C] The objection we are refuting can therefore provide no serious argument against the authority of the catalogues of the Church of Metz.

V. But here is another objection that appears weightier to our adversaries and upon which they insist at length. The history of Saint Clement is filled with apocryphal details that deserve no credence.

Historical truths can, we do not deny, be encumbered and obscured by apocryphal accounts. The duty of sound criticism is then not to abandon the truth together with the error, but to separate one from the other, preserving the truth and rejecting the error. In recognizing marks of truth in our ancient traditions, we are far from wishing to grant equal authority to everything that popular narratives, welcomed by credulous authors, may have added to them.

For the history of Saint Clement, we adhere to the authentic work of Paul the Deacon—that is, to the work as reproduced in the *Maxima Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*. We reject the corrupted text of the Saint-Arnoul manuscript and of the other tenth-century manuscripts, whose interpolation we have demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0690D] See above, the note to column 679.]. It is in these falsified manuscripts that all the incredible, often ridiculous legends accumulated during the tenth and eleventh centuries—legends to which our adversaries resort in order to attack the truth of Saint Clement’s history.

Paul the Deacon’s genuine text is serious, reasonable, [Col. 0691A] and free from these fabricated stories, which we willingly leave to all the rigors of criticism.
