Thus this fifth objection collapses of itself, without our needing to dwell upon it. We shall discuss only a few circumstances in Paul the Deacon’s account that appear obscure.

Since the amphitheater was of recent construction, how could Paul the Deacon have said that Saint Clement made his dwelling and an oratory there? This author expresses the circumstance only by leaving responsibility for it to others: *In cavernis, ut ferunt, amphitheatri hospitium habuit*—“In the caverns of the amphitheater, as they say, he had his lodging.” Those are his words. If they are weighed carefully, one will see that they in no way imply that the amphitheater was in ruins, and that the words *in cavernis* have clearly been abused in order to arrive at that supposition.

What, in fact, should we understand by these caverns of the amphitheater? Were they not chambers constructed beneath the tiers of seats, some of which were reserved for the animals used in [Col. 0691B] the spectacles, while others served as dwellings for guards or other persons to whom Saint Clement, on departing from Rome, might well have been directed and commended? Or were these caverns perhaps a kind of stalls built against the amphitheater, or, finally, other hollows or neighboring structures that derived their names from this monument? In any case, nothing in these expressions implies that Saint Clement took up residence inside the amphitheater itself, still less that the monument was in ruins.

Another circumstance raised as an objection is Saint Clement’s consecration of his oratory under the name of Saint Peter, although that Apostle was still alive. This astonishes us because we attach [Col. 0692A] to the words *praeceptoris sui nomine consecravit*—“he consecrated it in the name of his teacher”—the idea of a cult rendered to Saint Peter, as is practiced today in the Church with respect to the saints to whom temples are dedicated.

But is it certain that Saint Clement had the same thought, and that this dedication under the name of Saint Peter did not merely consist in giving his oratory the name of his revered teacher, whose memory he wished to make present to his flock as a means of maintaining Catholic unity? Later, no doubt—and perhaps even during Saint Clement’s lifetime, since he survived Saint Peter—this remembrance of unity and filial devotion was transformed into a true cult, which tradition has transmitted to us. In any event, greater or lesser obscurity concerning these secondary circumstances cannot invalidate the truth of the principal fact as we have established it.

VI. Let us suppose that the cult of Saint Clement was, before the eleventh century, as unknown at Metz as is claimed. What would follow from this with regard to the question [Col. 0692B] before us? Obviously, nothing. For the issue here is not the cult rendered to Saint Clement, but his existence and the period in which he lived.

Now, from this alleged absence of a cult, one could at most infer that his sainthood had not been authentically attested by the Church—not that he did not exist, or that he existed only in the third or fourth century. The period in which a person flourished is in no way what determines the cult rendered to him; and supposing that Saint Clement lived in the fourth century, he could have been honored as a saint after his death, if the Church had judged him worthy of it, just as if he had lived in the first century.

Thus this objection misses its mark, and we do not need to resolve it in order to defend our thesis [Note: [Col. 0691B]

Although this is not the place to discuss the foundations of the cult of Saint Clement, since the objection we have just refuted directly attacks that cult, we shall briefly make the following observations.

From the fact that, before Bishop Hériman’s elevation and translation of Saint Clement’s relics, no other event is found in history so prominent as to attest the cult rendered by the Church of Metz to its first bishop, to conclude that this cult did not exist and to date its origin from that event is a false way of reasoning, rightly reproached to eighteenth-century criticism. Indeed, it is very much its method to exclude from the annals of the Church everything that it does not find authorized and supported by material monuments, without regard for the testimony of the ancient traditions of the Churches. And yet, when it comes to worship, and especially to supporting the cult of the saints of the early centuries, what can the Churches produce other than their traditions, their usages, and their immemorial practices? Does it not seem [Col. 0691D] that, in the eyes of criticism, the traditions, usages, and worship of the Churches could be destroyed, altered, or suddenly created according to the caprice or ill-understood piety of a bishop? Has anyone ever seen a bishop in the Church one day undertake to establish the previously unknown cult of a person who had died centuries earlier? To bring such an accusation without proof, as is done here, against a bishop as enlightened and zealous as Hériman was—is that not to offer a very great and wholly gratuitous insult to his memory? And if, impossibly, such an attempt had been made, how could one admit that all the clergy and all the faithful of a diocese, at the mere word of a bishop, had bowed without protest and rendered solemn worship to a person previously unknown in the catalogue of the saints and in the liturgy of their Church? On the contrary, it seems to us that one would reason entirely correctly by taking the objection’s opposite position and saying: Hériman raised the [Col. 0692B] relics of Saint Clement and placed them upon the altars, where thereafter they never ceased to be objects of the [Col. 0692C] worship of the clergy and faithful of the diocese; therefore the cult of Saint Clement was in use and immemorially accepted in the Church of Metz at the time of Hériman. Otherwise, the honor rendered to these relics would have been, in that Church, a very strange innovation, for which it would be impossible to give an account.

Indeed, we find the cult of Saint Clement, like that of most of our other holy bishops, established in the most ancient monuments of our liturgy. It is true that these monuments are later than Hériman; but the office of Saint Clement bears in them the same marks of antiquity as that of the other bishops, and there can be no doubt that, had some documents come down to us revealing the state of the liturgy in our diocese during the preceding centuries, we should find the name of Saint Clement at the head of the catalogue of the holy bishops of Metz honored in the liturgy of this [Col. 0692D] Church. Everything that history teaches us about the honors rendered to our holy bishops shows them gathered around Saint Clement.

Indeed, was not the crypt in which Saint Clement was buried the first sacred place of the Christians of Metz? Was it not continuously the object of their veneration for centuries, because of the holy relics it contained? Was it not in this crypt, as in a separate sanctuary, that the relics of his holy successors—some of whom are named in the Roman Martyrology—were deposited, to be honored by a cult shared with those of Saint Clement? These latter men, who certainly had a right to the public worship of the Church, were honored no differently from Saint Clement in that ancient burial place, and Paul the Deacon praises the holiness of the apostle of Metz no less than that of our other pontiffs. If later, when the miracles of Saint Felix of Nola made so much [Col. 0693B] noise in the Church and made his cult so popular, a church under the invocation of the Thaumaturge of Campania was added to Saint Clement’s crypt, this was without prejudice to the worship rendered to our holy bishops whom that ever-venerated crypt contained. From there, indeed, as from a sacred treasury, holy bodies were taken at different times to enrich other Churches with these precious [Col. 0693C] relics; and Saint Clement’s own body was finally removed as well, in order to be placed upon the altars.

But why wait so long to render to Saint Clement’s relics the honor accorded them only in the eleventh century by Bishop Hériman? Why were they not raised earlier from the ground and exposed upon the altars? The answer to this question is evident to those who know the profound respect with which the Western Church was imbued for the relics of the saints. This respect went so far that people did not dare touch those sacred bones. Thus they took great care not to disturb them from the place where they had originally been deposited. We see an example of this respect in the discovery of the relics of Saint Saturnin, apostle of Toulouse. When, in the fourth century, Hilary, bishop of that city, discovered the place of Saint Saturnin’s burial, he took great care not to touch those [Col. 0693D] precious bones; he contented himself with having the foundations of the small chapel that was to contain them dug around them. Pope Saint Gregory the Great, in the sixth century, expresses the full extent of this veneration in his reply to the empress Constantine, who had asked him for relics of Saint Paul in order to enrich the church she was building in honor of the Apostle of the Nations. Saint Gregory categorically refuses to send sacred bones to this pious princess: “because,” he says, “it is not the custom at Rome, when relics of the saints are given, ever to presume to touch anything of the body; one contents oneself with placing in the reliquary a piece of the cloth in which they are wrapped. For,” he adds, “in Rome and throughout the West it is altogether intolerable and even sacrilegious if anyone should perhaps wish merely to touch the bodies of the saints.”

> “It is not the Roman custom, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything of the body; only a piece of the cloth is placed in the reliquary.… For in Rome, or throughout the regions of the West, it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should perhaps wish to touch the bodies of the saints.”

(Saint Gregory the Great, Letter 30 to the Empress Augusta Constantine; in his works, vol. II, p. 708.)

It was scarcely before the eighth century that this religious respect for the [Col. 0694C] bodies of the saints began to yield to the benefit which the piety of the faithful was to derive from their solemn exposition in the churches. We read in the history of Saint Chrodegang (eighth century) that, having been sent by Pepin the Short to Pope Saint Stephen to persuade him to come to France and thereby escape the tyranny of Astolf, king of the Lombards, that pontiff gave our pious bishop the bodies of the martyrs Saint Gorgon, Saint Nazarius, and Saint Nabor—a favor extremely rare at that time. It was doubtless in imitation of Pope Stephen that Saint Angelram, a few years later, allowed himself to remove the body of Saint Simeon from Saint Clement’s crypt and give it to the abbey of Senones; that Drogon, around the middle of the ninth century, also dared to remove four bodies from it—those of Saint Rufus, Saint Adelphus, Saint Caelestis, and Saint Autor—in order to bestow them upon other abbeys; that, in the middle of the eleventh century, Saint Felix’s body was likewise removed from it and given to [Col. 0694D] the Emperor Saint Henry; and that finally Bishop Hériman, toward the end of the same century, thought it more fitting to exhume the body of Saint Clement himself, together with those of the other holy bishops buried beside him, in order to give them a place of honor upon the altars, according to the practice that had prevailed in the Church. His piety then inspired him to replace Saint Clement’s modest crypt with a basilica dedicated to him. Is there anything in all this that proves that the cult of Saint Clement had previously been unknown at Metz? Is it not rather the exact opposite conclusion that must be accepted?

[Note: [Col. 0693A] In this place, Codices 2 and 4 insert a longer account of Saint Clement’s miracles, which, since it is of very uncertain authority and of no importance for the history of Germany, I have decided to omit.]

[Col. 0693A] **VII. Let us come to Saint Patient.** For his history we do not possess the authority of Paul the Deacon, who merely names him, giving him a share in a sentence of praise common to several successors of Saint Clement. Our chronicles make him Greek by origin, sent by Saint John the Evangelist at a time when the Church of Metz, after having been successively governed by Saint Clement’s two companions, Saint Caelestis and Saint Felix, had finally been left without a shepherd. This mission of Saint Patient from Saint John the Evangelist is, in the history of this holy bishop, the only fact which we believe should not be abandoned, although we attach no importance to it with regard to our general thesis. His Latin name presents no real difficulty, for Asia Minor had long since become a province of the empire, so that Roman families could have settled there while retaining their Latin names. The greatest difficulty, [Col. 0693B] raised by the Bollandists themselves [Note: [Col. 0694D] *Acta Sanctorum*, month of February, day 21, on Saint Felix, p. 236, E.], concerns the chronology.

Following our catalogues, one can scarcely date the beginning of Saint Patient’s episcopate earlier than the year 130. How, then, could he have been sent by Saint John, who had ceased to live in the third year of Trajan’s reign—that is, in the year 100?

We are inclined to believe that a numerical error has crept into the duration of the episcopate of Saint Felix, Saint Patient’s predecessor. The catalogues assign him forty-two years and six months of episcopate, which, though not impossible, appears unlikely. For if we suppose him to have been twenty-five or thirty years old when he came among the Mediomatrici with Saint Clement and Saint Caelestis, his forty-two years of episcopate, added to Saint Clement’s twenty-three years and Saint Caelestis’s fifteen, assign him a life of 105 to 110 years. If, on the contrary, we suppose that he occupied the see for thirteen years instead of forty-two, and that a copyist mistakenly wrote XLII for XIII, everything falls into place and becomes easy [Note: [Col. 0694D] The use of Roman numerals made such errors easy and common, and the Benedictines of Saint-Vanne admit several corrections of this kind in their *History of Metz*. See vol. I, pp. 121, 178.]. This holy bishop would have held the see until about the year 100; and, in his old age, encountering difficulty in receiving a successor from Rome, he would have appealed to Saint John, who was still living. The apostle would have sent him Saint Patient, who would then have occupied the see longer than our catalogues indicate. If one were permitted to suppose a second error or an inept correction, one would see that it would not have been difficult for a copyist to assign fourteen years of episcopate [Col. 0694B] to Saint Patient instead of forty-five, by writing XIV for XLV; thus it would have been the latter, not Saint Felix, who had an episcopate of more than forty years. The age of the manuscripts may have placed the copyists in uncertainties that caused these errors in the dates.

The difficulty can also be resolved in another way, by admitting that Saint Felix, being old and infirm, asked Saint John for a coadjutor toward the end of the first century, and then lived for a long time after [Col. 0695A] entrusting this coadjutor with the care of his flock, which he could no longer govern himself; and that his death, finally occurring around the year 130, caused the kind of contradiction we find between the figures in our catalogues and the tradition that tells us Saint Patient received his mission from the Apostle Saint John. But, once again, these are merely details obscured by difficulties that may remain without shaking our general thesis. As for the fact of Saint Patient’s mission from Saint John the Evangelist, the tradition attesting it may well have become altered in its circumstances; but it seems to us that it must have originated in the reality of the principal fact. We do not think that it should be abandoned as false on this point because of a chronological uncertainty which, as we have just seen, is not without a solution. Among the circumstances with which the fact of this mission has been encumbered, some seem to us to deserve little [Col. 0695B] confidence, while others appear to us altogether inadmissible [Note: [Col. 0695D] The fragment of the *Life of Saint Caelestis* collected by the Bollandists (*Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. I, p. 469) seems to us almost an amplification [Col. 0696D] made by its author in order to exercise his imagination on a pious subject, rather than with the aim of writing the life of a saint.].

**VIII.** No councils were held at Metz before the year 538, in which a manuscript chronicle cited by Meurisse (*History of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 76) mentions one that appears to have been the first held in that city. This evidently shows, it is said, that this Church was very recent, since everywhere we see the celebration of councils closely follow the establishment of the great Churches.

For our part, this evidence does not strike us at all. On the contrary, we see quite clearly that the authors of this argument recognized its weakness, since, in order to make it more plausible, they deemed it necessary to make the Church of Metz a great Church and to generalize a fact that is not established for all great Churches. It is indeed very difficult to persuade oneself that the Church of Metz was very recent in the sixth century, when one sees its twenty-third bishop, [Col. 0695C] Saint Hesperius, attending the Council of Clermont in 535. Moreover, this objection would prove too much; for if it were indisputable that the holding of councils had always closely followed the establishment of great Churches, and if one granted the Church of Metz the title of great Church that is here willingly bestowed upon it, one could not even place the origin of this Church as early as the fourth century, since it was not until around the middle of the sixth century that it was honored for the first time by the presence of a council.

But let us answer directly with the following observations:

1. The scholars of Saint-Vanne will surely not demand, as proof of the apostolic origin of our Church, that councils should have been held at Metz during the first three centuries. The state of oppression in which the Christian religion found itself did not permit these striking manifestations of the Church’s government. In Gaul above all, the Churches were still too few and too little flourishing for anyone to think of celebrating councils there.

2. During the fourth and fifth centuries, the provinces of northern Gaul were so frequently ravaged by barbarians from beyond the Rhine that the holding of councils there still encountered very great obstacles. In those times of disorder and public calamity, travel was dangerous and communications extremely difficult. On the other hand, the heresies that agitated the central provinces of the empire did not reach the episcopal body in northern Gaul; and these heresies, as is well known, were in those ancient centuries the ordinary cause for holding councils. Thus history teaches us that, just as these assemblies were then frequent in the provinces close to the center of the empire, they were rare in our remote provinces.

3. In establishing the apostolic origin of the Church of Metz, we did not claim to present it as a great Church or as a mother Church of other Churches, since, on the contrary, it is well known that it remained a Church of secondary rank, while its neighbor Trier became the metropolitan see of the province. If, therefore, the need for a provincial council had arisen, it would have had to be convened at Trier, the seat of the province’s spiritual and temporal authority, unless the necessity of investigating the case of an accused person on the spot had required the assembly to be held elsewhere, as happened in 346 for the Church of Cologne. The Church of Metz was spared the misfortune of seeing such a necessity arise for it.

Let us conclude, then, that if no councils were [Col. 0696B] held at Metz before the sixth century, it was not at all because the Church of Metz was very recent; rather, given the difficulty and rarity of holding councils in our provinces before that period, no sufficiently grave circumstances arose to justify convening any of these holy assemblies at Metz.

**IX.** Finally, there remains the question of the absence of persecutions stirred up by the pagans in the Church of Metz. We acknowledge that our annals contain no document attesting that the Christians of Metz were persecuted for their religion, either by their pagan fellow citizens or by the Romans who elsewhere produced so many generous martyrs. And although one might perhaps say that documents of this kind were destroyed along with many others amid the ruins of which Metz was so often the scene during the first five centuries of our era, we willingly admit at once that there were no persecutions of Christians in [Col. 0696C] the Church of Metz. But it will be conceded that this argument is entirely without force in the question before us, if the following considerations are properly weighed.

1. At Metz, as in the rest of Gaul, the progress of Christianity was slow and inconspicuous, as Father Longueval proves.

2. Since Metz was a large and populous city, Christianity could spread there and form a community sizeable in itself, but small in relation to the population, and consequently unlikely to attract the authorities’ attention.

3. The Mediomatrici, who remained attached to the worship of idols, had seen introduced among them, with the Roman armies, such a great variety of gods and cults unknown to their ancestors that they must have become fairly indifferent in religious matters and, for a long time, seen Christianity merely as one more god and one more rite.

4. The Romans were not all persecutors of Christians. There were often Christians in the armies, even among the commanders; the execution of decrees depended greatly upon the particular governors of the cities and upon the tranquillity and unity of the inhabitants; and in a great many cities humane governors always found a way to silence informers and conceal the presence of Christians by temporarily removing whatever was conspicuous in their worship.

5. Since Metz was an allied city, it possessed a greater share of authority in its administration than cities such as Trier, which, having been reduced by force of arms, had become [Col. 0697A] almost entirely Roman [Note: [Col. 0697C] Suetonius assures us that allied cities—and, according to Tacitus, Metz was one of them (see note b, col. 677)—were not reduced to Roman provinces like the other cities conquered by Caesar: “He reduced all Gaul, except the allied cities, to the form of a province” (Suetonius, *Julius Caesar*, chap. 25).].

6. The inhabitants of Metz, whether pagan or Christian, naturally peaceful [Note: [Col. 0697C] One proof of the peaceful and humane character [Col. 0698C] of the Mediomatrici is that, notwithstanding their well-known martial valor, they had the wisdom to remain constantly outside all the revolts of neighboring peoples, which so often caused blood to flow on Gallic soil during the first period of Roman rule.], humane, and composed of a single indigenous nation, were united among themselves by social relations and often by family ties. Consequently, all must have joined in avoiding anything that could lead to the shedding of their fellow citizens’ blood, especially after they had been warned by Trier’s cruel example of the terrible excesses to which imprudent denunciations could lead.

7. It is impossible to admit the existence of a large and flourishing Church at Trier at the end of the third century without conceding the same fact for Metz, both because of the reciprocal commerce between the two cities and because relations with Rome were at least as easy and as frequent for Metz as for Trier.

8. Most of our adversaries admit that Metz had Christians and bishops around the middle of the third century. It is therefore for them as much as for us to say why the emperor Maximian Herculius and his minister Rictius Varus did not produce martyrs there as they did at Trier.

9. Finally, Metz is not the only example that can be cited of a city which, although containing a Church within it, nevertheless passed through the early centuries without martyrs, despite the publication of persecuting edicts and the presence of persecuting princes. The Church of Arles, which Father Longueval regards as founded by the disciples of the apostles, likewise had no martyr, except Saint Genesius, who, being a clerk when Maximian Herculius came to Arles, was beheaded on that emperor’s orders for refusing to transcribe the edict of persecution that this deadly enemy of the Christian name had ordered to be published.

It is therefore not impossible that, surrounded by particular circumstances, a local Church might pass through periods of pagan persecution without seeing the blood of its children flow. This final objection, like those preceding it, thus remains powerless [Col. 0697C] to shake the traditions of the Church of Metz concerning its apostolic origin.

Let us finally summarize and conclude. Father Longueval has proved the general fact that Christianity was established in Gaul from the time of the apostles; he counts the Church of Metz among those that can, with the greatest reason, claim this antiquity. The condition of Metz from the earliest period of Roman rule makes this assertion plausible; and the tradition of this Church, supported by monuments respectable for their antiquity and authenticity, claims this honor for it with great force of reason. Modern criticism has indeed expressed the contrary opinion; but, after submitting its arguments to impartial discussion, we believe that we have left none unanswered in a manner that, if not always conclusive, has always been plausible and sufficient to show their ineffectiveness against our positive evidence.

We have shown, in fact, that the monuments alleged against the chronology resulting from our catalogues do not possess, in the present question, the value attributed to them; that the text of Gregory of Tours, insofar as it concerns Saint Autor, must be interpreted in favor of our opinion; and that the apocryphal details concerning the history of Saint Clement, which came into circulation in the tenth century, cannot shake the historical truth as Paul the Deacon had recorded it as early as the eighth century. We have shown [Col. 0698B] that the cult of the apostle of Metz is not as recent as people would have us believe, although this circumstance has no weight in determining the period of his preaching; that the succession of our bishops could not have been lengthened by the insertion of any name foreign to it; and finally that no solid argument against the thesis we defend can be drawn either from Saint Patient’s mission from Saint John the Evangelist, from the absence of persecution against Christians in the region of Metz during the early centuries, or from the absence of councils held in the city of Metz during the two following centuries.

The tradition attesting the apostolic origin of the Church of Metz therefore remains invested with all the marks of a high degree of probability. Notwithstanding the obscurities that may still remain concerning certain circumstances of a fact so difficult to elucidate because of its antiquity and the lack of detailed documents, we are entitled to conclude that one is [Col. 0698C] closer to historical truth by accepting the tradition of the Church of Metz than one would be by rejecting it in order to follow the opposing teachings of eighteenth-century criticism. In two words, this tradition presents itself to us with an imposing authority, which all the attacks of modern scholarship have been unable to shake, and which should make it dear and worthy of respect to all the children of this ancient Church.

[Col. 0697]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOKLET

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*.)

[Col. 0697D] Paul Warnefrid, deacon of the Church of Aquileia, a man among the foremost of his age, whose *History of the Lombards* we are about to publish, while living in Francia as a survivor of his people, wrote, in the year 784, at the request of Angilram, bishop of Metz and archchaplain of King Charles (*History of the Lombards* VI, 16), apparently at Metz, a booklet on the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] Fastrada was already Charles’s wife, but no children had been born to her; therefore after the year 783, before Angilram’s death in 791, and—if the Anonymous of Salerno is to be trusted—occasionally before Charles’s war against Arichis, duke of Benevento, conducted in 786.]

In it he imitated the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, already famous for a long time, and embellished the meager catalogues of the bishops of Metz from the ancient traditions of the Fathers, Gregory of Tours, the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, the chronicle of Fredegar, and the narratives of King Charles himself, in such a way that the work deserves to occupy a place among the sources of the eighth century. We have used it in preparing this edition.

1. The Chesnian fragment, inserted in 1636 in volume II of the *Francic Writers*, pp. 201–206, begins with Bishop Agiulf. Chesne had used a codex of excellent quality and complete, though it appeared difficult to read in several places. I have therefore retained its readings in general, but have corrected some of them with the aid of—

2. A codex formerly belonging to Saint Symphorian of Metz, and supplied the verses that had fallen out. I used it in Paris, where it is preserved in the Royal Library under number 5294 (Colbert 2509; formerly Royal 4187, 5, 5). It is a parchment folio manuscript, written toward the end of the eleventh or at the beginning of the twelfth century, by order of Constantine, “with Betto’s reed”; it had already been examined by Labbe, who published from it the *Lives of Adelbero, bishop of Metz; Adelphius, abbot; and Saint Romaric*. Its readings already reveal a hand different from Warnefrid’s in the fact that German proper names—Rotheid, Adelheid, Hildegard—have been given Roman endings. On the other hand—

[Col. 0700A] 3. The first edition, prepared in 1613 by Marquard Freher in the *Corpus of Frankish History*, pp. 171–177, had been published from a codex close to the Chesnian one, but differing from it in that it did not contain the epitaphs inserted into the work. It appends a catalogue of the bishops of Metz extending to the death of Wala.

4. The codex of Saint Arnulf of Metz, which Calmet reproduced in the *Proofs of the History of Lorraine*, cols. 51–60, lacks the epitaphs and presents several very poor readings; otherwise, it comes very close to the other Metz manuscript.

Accordingly, in the first part of the work, which contributes very little to history, I compared Freher’s edition with Calmet’s. In the second, I attempted to correct the Chesnian text, chiefly with the aid of the codex of Saint Symphorian, and to restore it to the ancient manner of writing. Only a few explanatory notes were needed.

[Col. 0699]

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Thus in 3: “The Life of Blessed Clement, first pontiff of the people of Metz, begins.”]

## THE BOOKLET BEGINS: ON THE SUCCESSION OF THE BISHOPS WHO, FROM THE VERY BEGINNING OF HIS PREACHING, SUCCEEDED HIM IN THE CITY OF METZ

(C)

### First Text

(From Pertz, in the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*.)

[Col. 0699B] After Christ the Lord, having accomplished everything that he had ordained to be done with the Father for the salvation of the world, had departed to heaven, and as soon as the blessed apostles had received and been strengthened by the promised gift of the Holy Spirit, they immediately determined by common counsel, in accordance with divine providence, by lot which province or region each of them should undertake to evangelize.

As each therefore departed for the place assigned to him, blessed Peter, who was first among them and stood out like a most valiant leader, hastened with complete eagerness to the city that was then the capital of the whole world—that is, the city of Romulus—after first founding a church at Antioch and dedicating it in the name of his see.

When he had reached Rome, he immediately sent from his company excellent and learned men who would subjugate to Christ the Lord, by the word of faith, the chief cities situated in the West. Thus he sent Apollinaris to Ravenna, Lucius to Brundisium, and Anatolius to Milan. But Mark, who was regarded as foremost among his disciples, he assigned to Aquileia. After Mark had placed his companion Hermagoras in charge there, he returned to blessed Peter and was nevertheless sent by him to Alexandria.

At that time, when in Belgian Gaul there flourished the city of the Mediomatrici, also called Metz, situated on the very bank of the Moselle and abounding in crowds of people, the blessed apostle Peter sent to that same city [Col. 0700B] a man named Clement, distinguished and proven in merit, elevated to episcopal dignity. With him, as ancient tradition relates, other devout teachers were likewise sent by that prince of the apostles to conquer by the word of faith the principal cities of Gaul.

When blessed Clement arrived in the city of the Mediomatrici, he took up residence, as they relate, in the caves of the amphitheater situated outside the same city. In that place he also built an oratory for the Lord, established an altar there, and consecrated it in the name of blessed Peter the apostle, his teacher. This venerable priest, while preaching assiduously to the people of that city, with divine mercy cooperating with him, led a very great multitude of them—delivered from the filthy worship of idols and the blindness of error—to the splendor of the true faith; and he shone forth as the first proclaimer of righteousness and herald of truth in those regions.

Finally, those who know that place affirm that in the amphitheater where he first lived after his arrival, to the present day [Note: [Col. 0699C] At this point, Codices 2 and 4 insert a more extensive account of Saint Clement’s miracles [Col. 0700C], which, since it is of highly uncertain authority and of no importance for the history of Germany, I have decided to omit.] no serpent is able to remain, and harmful creatures of every kind flee that place, from which the signs of true salvation once issued.

A man full of God, named Caelestis, succeeded him. Leading a heavenly life while proclaiming the kingdom of heaven, he enlarged the number of believers equally by his example and his teaching.

After him, finally, Felix undertook the government of the Church. Then Patient. After these came Victor, fifth in the succession. Then another Victor. Afterward Simeon, the seventh. After him Sambatus [Note: [Col. 0701] *Sambatius* in manuscript 4], the eighth. It is certain that through the zeal of all these men the Church of God grew, although their individual deeds are hidden from us [Note: [Col. 0701] *sint* in manuscript 4].

Rufus [Note: [Col. 0701] *ruffus* in 3.] and Adolfus, who are numbered ninth and tenth, must undoubtedly be believed to have shone with great merits in life, since they shone by such a miracle even after death. When their bodies had been buried in the basilica of blessed Felix the martyr, as the report has come down to us, there was a certain religious man, solicitous for the care of his soul, who at night used to go around with unremitting devotion all the oratories situated outside the walls of that city, in order to commend himself to the Lord through private prayers. When he had reached the aforesaid basilica of blessed Felix the martyr, but had not been granted permission to enter it [Note: [Col. 0701] *deest* in 3.], he approached the outer wall beside that part where the bodies of the aforesaid priests were resting, and there prostrated himself in prayer with the whole concentration of his mind. After pouring out his prayers, when he had risen from prayer and was reciting, in honor of those saints at whose tombs opposite he had prayed, the verse of a psalm, namely, “The saints shall exult in glory,” he immediately heard from within the voice of one adding: “They shall rejoice in their resting places.”

[Col. 0701C] Firminus succeeded these holy men, and then Legontius; concerning whose lives, apart from their names, no ancient report has conveyed anything to us.

Then the thirteenth venerable bishop, Auctor, received the governance of the Church, at a time when not only Gaul but almost the whole of the West suffered the savagery of raging barbarians. Although other distinguished deeds are also believed to have been performed by this man, only two of his miracles have been widely transmitted to our memory. At that time, then, while this revered bishop was leading a life adorned with every virtue, Attila, king of the Huns, more savage than all beasts, having many barbarian nations subjected to his rule, after he had crushed Gundigarius, [Col. 0701D] king of the Burgundians, who had come to meet him, loosened the reins of his savagery against the whole of Gaul.

When blessed Servatius [Note: [Col. 0701] *servasius* in 3.], bishop of Tongeren, had foreseen his arrival [Note: [Col. 0701D] From Gregory of Tours, *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 5.], he went to Rome to the most sacred bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that through their eminent merit he might especially obtain from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0701] *quatenus*; the remaining apparatus is abbreviated/uncertain: *i. s. i. a.*] that he turn away the indignation of His wrath and free the people of the city of Tongeren from so great a disaster. Then it was divinely revealed to him through that same blessed apostle Peter [Col. 0702A] that heavenly judgment had decreed that all Gaul should be delivered over to the ravaging of the barbarians, except for the shrine of blessed Stephen the deacon and proto-martyr situated at Metz, where his precious blood had been stored without any taint of corruption.

When these things had been revealed to Saint Servatius, he hastened back to Gaul and found the swarms of Huns already raging throughout the whole country. When they had withdrawn from the siege of the people of Metz [Note: [Col. 0701] 4 lacks *de obsidione*; 3 has *ad obsidionem*.], because they saw that the city was impregnable on account of the strength of its walls, it happened that blessed Servatius, returning from Rome at that very time, arrived at Metz. After he had related to his fellow bishop Auctor everything he had learned through the revelation, he returned to his own city, that is, Tongeren. Immediately afterward [Col. 0702B] the wall of the city of Metz collapsed [Note: [Col. 0701D] Compare Fredegar, *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 11.] and, by heavenly design, opened access to the enemy.

When blessed Auctor noticed that the city had been delivered to the swords of the enemy, he ordered all the little children who had not yet received the washing of the sacred font to be baptized. When the Huns therefore heard that the walls of the city of Metz had collapsed, they returned to it with swift haste from the camp situated twelve miles away, which is called Scarponna [Note: [Col. 0702D] Charpeigne, or Sampeigne, on the Moselle.]. As they ravaged everything with fire and plunder, they killed many of the citizens, including the little ones who had been baptized; the rest who could survive the slaughter they led away into captivity together with the holy bishop Auctor.

Indeed, what had previously been foretold by blessed Peter to Servatius, the servant of Christ, concerning the dwelling of blessed Stephen the deacon and proto-martyr, was fulfilled. For when the raging barbarians saw that basilica from a distance, they hurried toward it as if to seize rich spoils; but as they came nearer, it appeared to their eyes like an enormous rock and solid mass. Though, blinded in mind, they felt it all around with their hands and sought an entrance, nothing at all appeared to them except the hardness of natural stone. Finally, withdrawing several times and returning again, when they saw that they were accomplishing nothing, they departed at last, exhausted, frustrated in the outcome of their wickedness.

I shall not be silent, moreover, about what blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours, related in his books concerning this oratory [Note: [Col. 0702D] Book II, chapter 6.]. For he reports:

“Before these enemies arrived, a faithful man saw in a vision blessed Stephen the Levite conferring with the holy apostles Peter and Paul concerning this destruction, and saying: ‘I beg you, my lords, do not permit the city of Metz to be burned by its enemies for your sake, because there is in it a place in which the relics of my smallness are contained; rather, let them learn that I can accomplish something for its people before the Lord. But if the people’s crime has grown so great that nothing else can be done except that the city be handed over to the flames, at least let this oratory not be burned.’

“They answered him: ‘Go in peace, dearest brother; your oratory alone shall be spared the fire. But we cannot obtain this for the city, because the sentence of the Lord’s decree has already gone forth against it. For the people’s sin has prevailed, and the outcry of their wickedness has risen before the Lord. Therefore this city shall be burned with fire.’

“From this it is beyond doubt that, through their intercession, while the city was laid waste, the oratory remained unharmed.”

When the enemy had thereafter reached the town called Decempagos [Note: [Col. 0703D] Duose, or Dieuze, twelve Roman miles distant from Metz.], which is thirty miles from the city of Metz, because our God always cares for His servants and, as the Psalmist says, “in anger does not withhold mercy,” such darkness suddenly surrounded those same Huns [Col. 0703B] that they had no idea what to do or where to turn. Then, carefully seeking the cause of so great a calamity, as the circumstances required, they heard from one of the captives [Note: [Col. 0703] *captis* in 3.] whom they were leading that they were suffering such things because of the servant of the heavenly Lord, Bishop Auctor, whom he said he had seen among the captives.

After an inquiry had immediately been made, they found blessed Auctor. When they asked him what gift he wished to receive in order to free them from so great a danger, he replied that no other gift could be offered to him more pleasing than their allowing all the captives whom they were leading to return to their homes. If they did this, he promised that he would undoubtedly ask his Lord to rescue them from the darkness by which they were held [Col. 0703C]. And it happened. Immediately, searching throughout the entire Hunnic army for the captives they were leading, they returned them to blessed Auctor; and, as had been promised them, the darkness ceased for them, light was restored, and they were freed from their distress.

Thus the venerable servant of Christ, though for a short while he was counted among the captives, released many from captivity at the same time. O how much more glorious was the triumph he achieved over the citizens he brought back than the cruel barbarians could have triumphed when they had previously carried them away as victors!

Let us come also to another miracle, accomplished by heavenly power through his merits. At a certain time, in the oratory of blessed Stephen the proto-martyr, which we mentioned above, a beam, loosened from the very summit of the roof, fell and broke the marble of the altar, which was of exceptional whiteness, so that it divided it completely into two parts. Blessed Auctor was present, and while all who were there were saddened by the damage that had been inflicted, he himself, trusting in the Lord, ordered the broken pieces to be joined to one another and the necessary implements to be prepared for him, so that he might offer upon it, in the customary manner, the gift of the divine sacrifice [Col. 0704A].

While they were astonished and watching to see what he would do, he immediately offered the saving offering to God. At once all that fracture was so solidly restored that it seemed not to have been divided before at all. There is, however, something in that marble that can still be admired to no small degree. For to those who look at it attentively it appears even now as though divided, but when carefully handled with the fingers [Note: [Col. 0704D] Paul himself appears to have inspected it.], it proves so solid that no sign of any division in it can be perceived.

There is no doubt that he performed many more marvelous deeds, but how great and what sort of man he was can be fully recognized from what has been reported [Note: [Col. 0703] *revelata* in 3.] here [Note: [Col. 0703] *plenius* in 4.].

Aepletius succeeded him as the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 0703] *aeplitius* in 4.]. Then came Urbicius as the fifteenth; Bonolus as the sixteenth [Col. 0704B]; Terentius as the seventeenth; Gunsolinus as the eighteenth [Note: [Col. 0703] *gonsolonus* in 4.]. After him came Romanus; finally Fronimus as the twentieth. After him came Cromatius [Note: [Col. 0703] *grammatius* in 4.]. Then Agathander [Note: [Col. 0703] *agathimber* in 4.]. These three whom we have just mentioned are, as can be observed in their names, to be believed to have arisen from Greek origin [Note: [Col. 0703] *manare* in 3.].

After these, Sperus governed the Church. Then came Villicus [Note: [Col. 0703] *vilicus* in 4.]. Next, Petrus as the twenty-fifth. Agiulfus as the twenty-sixth [Note: [Col. 0703] *aigulfus* in 2.], who is said to have been born of a father descended from a noble senatorial family [Note: [Col. 0703] *ortus* in 1 and 4; *ortu* in 3.] and from the daughter of Clovis, king of the Franks. After him came his nephew [Note: [Col. 0703] *istius* in 4.], named Arnoaldus. Pappolus followed him.

After these, the most blessed Arnulfus was chosen to govern the Church [Note: [Col. 0703] *rigimen* in 2.], a man distinguished in every respect by the light of holiness and the splendor of his lineage. Born from the most noble and powerful stock of the Franks [Col. 0704C] [Note: [Col. 0703] *stemate* in 2.], he governed the Church of God in such a way that he also became administrator of the palace [Note: [Col. 0703] 1 has “under the dignity of the office of mayor of the palace.”]. Indeed, both while he remained in the body and after his departure from this life, he performed many marvelous deeds [Note: [Col. 0703] *patravat* in 2.]. Anyone who wishes to know them should read the little book specially written about his deeds.

I shall nevertheless relate one of his remarkable deeds, and I have often wondered in what manner the one who compiled his Life passed it over [Note: [Col. 0704D] It is found in the Viennese manuscript of the *Life of Saint Arnulfus.*]. Once, while he was doing penance for certain excesses, it happened that he was crossing the bridge over the Moselle River. When he saw the deep and impenetrable whirlpools of the waters flowing beneath him, carrying in his mind a confidence in a hope that could not be doubted, he removed a ring from his finger and threw it into the depth of the water, saying:

“Then I shall consider myself released from the bonds of my faults when I have recovered this ring that I am throwing away.”

After several years, when he had risen to the office of bishop, a fisherman brought him a fish. Since he abstained from meat, he ordered it to be prepared for his evening meal. When his servant had gutted it in the customary manner [Note: [Col. 0703] *exinterasset* in 2.], he found the same ring inside the fish’s intestine [Note: [Col. 0703] 2 lacks *eum*.]. Astonished at the event but unaware of its significance, he brought it to blessed Arnulfus. As soon as Arnulfus saw it, he immediately recognized it and, now confident of the remission of his sins, gave thanks to almighty God. From then on he did not lead his life less strictly, but rather constrained himself with still greater abstinence.

This venerable father likewise asked a sign from the Lord, as once that Gideon did. Gideon wished to obtain an indication through the fleece placed on the threshing floor as to whether he could gain victory over his enemies; Arnulfus, throwing the ring into the deepest whirlpool of the river, wished to discover whether he had already won victory over his enemies. The men whom Gideon had defeated were indeed strong, but those whom Arnulfus overcame were stronger.

I learned this not from some ordinary person [Note: [Col. 0705] *quolibet* in 2.], but came to know it from the very guarantor of all truth, the exalted King Charles, who, descended from the lineage of that blessed Arnulfus, stood three generations below him in the line of descent. For, to return to what came before, this venerable man, during his youth, fathered two sons through a lawful marriage, namely Anschisus [Note: [Col. 0705] *anchisum* in 4.] and Chlodulfus [Note: [Col. 0705] *clodulfum* in 2 and 4.]. The name Anschisus [Note: [Col. 0705] *anchisi* in 2 and 4.] is believed to have been derived from Anchises, the father of Aeneas, who once came from Troy to Italy. For the Frankish people, as has been handed down by the ancients [Note: [Col. 0705] *ab autoribis* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0706D] That is, Fredegar.], traces its origin to Trojan descent.

When the venerable Arnulfus had these two sons of whom we have spoken, since he was merciful and always intent upon works of piety, he began to urge both his sons to give him their assent, so that he might distribute all his possessions for the use of the poor [Col. 0705C]. Then the elder son, Chlodulfus, utterly refused to do this—that is, to grant his father the portion owed to himself [Note: [Col. 0705] *pater* in 1.]. But the younger son, Anschisus, trusting that through Christ’s mercy more would be granted to him, willingly promised to obey everything his father wished.

The venerable father thanked his son and foretold that he would possess more than he had left him; moreover, he blessed him and all the offspring who would be born from him in the future. And so it happened. For greater riches came to Anschisus than those he had left him, and his father’s blessing was so firmly established in him [Note: [Col. 0705] *sunt* in c.; *beneficia* in 2.] that men so vigorous and brave were born from his lineage that the kingdom of the Franks was not undeservedly transferred to his family [Col. 0705D].

And so that you may recognize this, pay attention briefly [Note: [Col. 0705] *animadvertens* in 2; *animadverte* in 4.]; I shall explain it. Anschisus fathered Pippinus, than whom nothing more daring could ever have existed. Pippinus fathered Charles, a man to be compared with the very bravest, who, among the great wars he waged, so thoroughly crushed the Saracens that even to this day that fierce and treacherous people fears the arms of the Franks.

This man in turn fathered Pippinus, no less distinguished for wisdom and courage, who, among his other deeds, with remarkable success defeated and subdued the Wascones, who had long been rebellious against Frankish rule, together with their prince Waifarius [Note: [Col. 0705] *facilitate* in 1 and 3.]. His son in turn was the great King Charles, who expanded the kingdom of the Franks as it had never before been expanded [Note: [Col. 0705] *antea* in 4.].

Finally, among the many remarkable deeds he accomplished, he brought the people of the Lombards, already twice defeated by his father, entirely under his rule without a serious battle. He captured one of their kings, named Desiderius, and drove the other, called Adelgisus, who had been reigning together with his father, into Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0705] *graecorum* in 4.], [Note: [Col. 0705] *alterumque* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0705] *ut* in 1 and 3.]—and, something that rarely happens, tempered his victory with merciful moderation.

Moreover, rescuing the Romans and Rome itself—the city of Romulus, which had long desired his presence [Note: [Col. 0705] *desideratam* in 2.], once mistress of the whole world and then groaning under the oppression of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0705] *languobardis* in 2.]—from harsh distress, he added them to his scepters; and he likewise gained possession of all Italy through a mild rule. Concerning this man, one cannot know whether one should admire more in him his military valor, the brilliance of his wisdom, or his mastery of all the liberal arts.

By his wife Hildegard he fathered four sons and five daughters. Before his lawful marriage [Note: [Col. 0705] *conubium* in 2.], however, he had a son named Pippinus by Himiltrude [Note: [Col. 0705] *himiltruda* in 2.], a noble girl.

The names of the children whom Hildegard bore him [Note: [Col. 0705] *hildegardis* in 2, and so throughout thereafter, plainly contrary to Paul’s usage.] are as follows: the first was called Charles, named after his father and great-grandfather; the second likewise Pippinus, sharing the name of his brother and grandfather; the third was Lodobich [Note: [Col. 0705] *lodohic* in 4, *lodowicus* in 1, *ludonuicus* in 2.], who was born in the same birth as Illotharius [Note: [Col. 0705] *lothario* in 2.], who died at the age of two. Of these, by God’s favor, the younger Pippinus holds the kingdom of Italy, and Lodobich that of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0705] *tenet* in 1; *tenuit* in 2.].

After Hildegard died, the most excellent King Charles took Frastrada as his wife. Hildegard rests near the city of Metz, in the oratory of blessed Arnulfus [Note: [Col. 0705] *oratorium* in 2.]. Because the aforesaid kings traced their origin to blessed Arnulfus, they placed there the bodies of their deceased loved ones [Note: [Col. 0705] 2 lacks *suorum charorum defuncta*.].

There were buried there two daughters of King Pippinus [Col. 0706D] [Note: [Col. 0706D] Father of Charles the Great.], one called Rodthaid [Note: [Col. 0705] *rothaidis* in 2.], the other Adelaid [Note: [Col. 0705] *adhelaidis* in 2.]. There also were buried two daughters of the younger King Charles, namely Adelaid and Hildigard. Hildigard, who was named after her mother, followed her dying mother all too soon [Note: [Col. 0705] 4 lacks *est*. But the middle portion is missing.].

I have taken care to append below the epitaphs of all these women, composed by us at the command of the glorious King Charles [Note: [Col. 0705] 2 lacks *a nobis*.] [Note: [Col. 0705] *composita sunt*; the epitaph of Rohaidis in 2; the middle portion is missing.], so that the reader might be fully informed about them.

### Epitaph of Rothaidis [Note: [Col. 0707] *rohaidis* in 2.], daughter of King Pippinus

Here I, Rothaid, who lie here, am called by that name [Note: [Col. 0707] “Rotaith by name” in 1; “Rothaidis” in Meurisse, *History of the Bishops of Metz*, from the manuscript of Saint Arnulfus at Metz.],

And I derive my lineage from an exceedingly exalted stock;

For my brother is Charles, who by arms subdued

The Italian peoples, relying upon the power of the Thunderer.

Pippinus is my father, begotten from the prince Charles [Note: [Col. 0707] *ortus* in 2.],

Who struck down the Agarenian tyrant in a great slaughter [Note: [Col. 0707] *clade* is Ch.’s conjecture.].

Pippinus was my great-grandfather, than whom no one was more daring;

But my great-great-grandfather was the powerful Anschises [Note: [Col. 0707] *anschisa* in 2.], who derives

His name, after a long passage of time, from that Trojan Anchises [Note: [Col. 0707] *anschisa* in 2.].

This holy father and blessed bishop Arnulfus begot him,

Arnulfus, who shines everywhere through his wondrous deeds.

My parents placed me here, trusting in the hope of this man.

### Epitaph of Adheleidis, the daughter mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0707] Also, “of the other daughter A.” in 1.]

Perpetual love and the reason for attaining salvation,

Which makes him hasten here with an attentive heart,

Do you wish to know why this sacred place contains

So many tombs, where the hall of the star-bearing heaven is revealed?

This holy man, who afterward guarded the Lord’s flock,

Was formerly the father of a legitimate offspring;

His descendants, trusting in their great-grandfather as patron,

Desire to place their limbs in this holy place.

Here rests Adheleid, the pious virgin, daughter of Pippinus;

Holy father, protect both her and the others.

### Epitaph of Queen Hildegard

The golden elements that gleam with shining figures

Show how splendid were the limbs buried here.

Here lies Queen Hildegard, exalted consort

Of the mighty king Charles, to whom she was well married.

She surpassed the offspring of her illustrious lineage

As far as the Indian gem surpasses the soil from which it was born.

So great was the grace of her flourishing beauty

That no woman in the West was more beautiful.

Neither sardonyx nor Parian marble [Note: [Col. 0707] *patrio* in 2.] mingled with lilies and roses

Could equal the tender beauty of her.

Yet the lights of her heart surpassed this appearance,

As did the simplicity of her soul and her inward beauty.

You were gentle, wise, skillful [Note: [Col. 0707] *solers* in 2.], and delightful,

Generous and adorned with every virtue.

But why should I say more, since no praise for you is greater

Than that you pleased so great a man?

And when the mighty warrior had joined to his ancestral scepters

The swan-bearing Po and the Roman Tiber [Note: [Col. 0707] *tybrum* in 2.],

You alone were found worthy to hold

The golden scepters of a manifold kingdom in your hand [Note: [Col. 0707] I supplied the next two verses from the manuscript; they are absent in Ch.].

The twelfth year had now received you,

When honey-sweet love joined you together;

In the twelfth year again he took you from us,

Alas, mother of kings! Alas, glory and grief!

The Frank, the Swabian, the German, and the Briton himself [Note: [Col. 0707] “And you, B.” in 2; “and also B.” in Meurisse.],

And the Iberian host mourns you together with the fierce Getae [Note: [Col. 0707] *gentis* in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0707] 2 lacks *duris*.].

The inhabitant of the Loire mourns you, and the land of Italy mourns you,

And anxious Rome itself groans at your death.

You moved even the courageous hearts of men to tears,

And tears fell amid shields and weapons.

Alas, with how many fires you, wise woman, and always firm in strength,

Burned the manly breast of the steadfast warrior!

This certain hope comforts all who grieve:

That for your worthy deeds you now possess the sacred kingdoms.

Now, Arnulfus, pray to Jesus [Note: [Col. 0707] One verse is absent in 1; in 2 only “Jesus …” is found, followed by a long lacuna; *exores* is read; I have attempted to restore the remainder.]

That she, O gracious father, may become a participant in them with you.

### Epitaph of Adelaidis, daughter of King Charles, who was born in Italy when he himself subdued it [Note: [Col. 0707] “Epitaph of the daughter of the great Charles, born from his marriage when he had subdued Italy” in 1.]

Here lies buried in this little tomb a tiny girl,

Called Adelaid after the sacred river.

Her father is Charles, mighty with a double diadem,

Noble in character [Note: [Col. 0707] *mobilis* in 1.] and sufficiently brave in arms.

She first saw the light near the lofty walls of Pavia,

When her powerful father seized the Italian kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0707] *petens* in 1.].

But, hastening toward the Rhône, she was snatched from the threshold [Note: [Col. 0707] 1 lacks *rapta est*.] of life [Note: [Col. 0707] *lumine* in 1.],

And her mother’s heart was struck far away by grief.

She passed away without seeing her father’s triumphs;

Now she holds the blessed kingdoms of the eternal Father.

### Epitaph of Hildigard, the daughter mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0707] “Of that same Charles” in 1.]

Hildegard, a bitter death suddenly snatched you away,

As Boreas snatches privet in early spring.

The circle of a year had not yet been completed for you,

Nor had the annual light come to you twice [Note: [Col. 0707] *genuina* in 2.].

Tiny girl, though small, you leave behind no small grief,

Piercing the royal heart of your father with a dart,

And, bearing your mother’s name, you renew the grief of her death [Note: [Col. 0707] “Renewing grief from your mother” in 2; “from the heart” in Meurisse.]

After you had lived scarcely forty days.

With sorrowful hearts we pour out rivers of tears,

While you, too fortunate, seek lasting joys [Note: [Col. 0707] *petis*. “Copy of the grant of the pallium: John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [and so forth], to Walo (corrected to Walon), venerable bishop of the Mediomatrici, [and so forth], September, indiction 12. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September … in the sixth year of the pontificate … indiction 12. + Farewell in the Lord. But these words are inserted in the text in manuscript 2.”].

Having thus briefly touched upon these matters that ought not to be passed over [Note: [Col. 0707] 1, 3, and 4 lack this phrase.], let us return to the course of our narrative.

After the most blessed Arnulfus, Goericus, the thirtieth bishop, who was also called Abbo, presided over the Church of Metz [Note: [Col. 0707] *mettensis* in 2.].

Then Godo was the thirty-first to undertake the care of the episcopal office [Note: [Col. 0707] “Godo, the first”; *p. a. t. Godo* in 2.].

When he had departed from the world [Note: [Col. 0708D] 2 has “when he had withdrawn from this world”], Chlodulfus, whom we mentioned above, the natural son of the blessed father Arnulfus and the brother of Anschisus, from whom the royal seed was propagated, ascended to the episcopal dignity as the thirty-second bishop on account of the glory of his father’s holiness [Col. 0708D]. Beyond the fact that he arose from such a root, fame has conveyed nothing further about him to us.

When he had died [Note: [Col. 0709] *decidente* in 2.], Abbo was chosen as the thirty-third bishop to govern the faithful people.

After him came Aptatus, and then Felix; they served as pastors of the Lord’s flock with happy success [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 has “after whom, finally.”].

Next, Sigebaldus, born of noble parents, became bishop over the religious community, a man wholly devoted to the interests of the Church and a most diligent restorer of sacred buildings. Concerned for the condition of souls, he founded two monasteries. One is called Eleriacum [Note: [Col. 0709] *elanacum* in 1 and 3; *hiliriacum* in 4.] or also Nova-cella [Col. 0709C] [Note: [Col. 0709C] Saint-Avold.]; the other is called Novum-Villare [Note: [Col. 0709] *nova villa* in 1 and 3; *novum villare* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0709C] Neuviller.]. A dreadful pain of gout afflicted him severely; but, fixing his mind upon eternal joys, he endured bodily pains with the greatest patience [Col. 0709B].

At this point the distinguished man, worthy to be celebrated with every praise, Chrodegangus, was chosen bishop. He was born in the district of Hasbania, of Sigramnus as father and Landrada as mother, descended from the first nobility of the Frankish race. Raised by Charles the Great himself in the palace, he became that king’s referendary [Note: [Col. 0709] 4 has “he himself, likewise.”], and finally, in the time of King Pippinus, earned the episcopal dignity.

He was altogether renowned and radiant with every nobility, handsome in appearance, most eloquent in speech, versed both in his native language and in Latin, a nourisher of the servants of God, and not only a provider [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 lacks *altor*.] but also a most merciful guardian of orphans and widows. Though he was wealthy in every respect, he was chosen uniquely by King Pippinus and the entire assembly of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 lacks *a*.], sent to Rome [Col. 0709C], and summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul, as everyone’s wishes earnestly desired.

He gathered the clergy together and made them live within the enclosure of the cloister like a monastic community. He established a rule for them concerning how they ought to serve in the Church, and generously supplied them with provisions and the necessities of life [Note: [Col. 0709] 4 has *necessaria*.], so that, not needing to attend to perishable business, they might devote themselves solely to the divine offices. He ordered that the clergy, thoroughly instructed in divine law and in Roman chant, should observe the custom and order of the Roman Church, something that had by no means been done in the Church of Metz up to that time.

Together with the assistance of King Pippinus, he ordered the construction of the bier-cover (*reba*) [Note: [Col. 0709] *sedem* in 1 and 3.] [Col. 0710C] [Note: [Col. 0710C] The cover or canopy of a bier.] of Saint Stephen the proto-martyr, together with his altar and screens, the presbytery, and the arches around it. Likewise, he ordered a presbytery to be made in the greater church of blessed Peter. He also constructed an ambo decorated with gold and silver, together with arches around the throne before that altar.

Moreover, he built a monastery in the parish of Saint Stephen, in the district of the Moselle, in honor of the most blessed apostle Peter; he endowed it with great resources, established monks there [Note: [Col. 0709] *instituit* in 2 and 4.], and joined them together in one charity under the rule of the holy Father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 lacks this phrase.]. He also built another monastery called Gorzia [Note: [Col. 0709] *gorgia* in 4 throughout thereafter.] [Col. 0710C] [Note: [Col. 0710C] Gorze, in the district of Scarponna.], where in the same way he gathered a considerable multitude of monks [Note: [Col. 0709] *vocatur* in 2 and 4.].

Finally, he requested from Paul, the Roman pontiff, the bodies of three holy martyrs: that of blessed Gorgonius, which rests at Gorze; that of blessed Nabor, which was buried in the monastery of Hilariacum; and that of blessed Nazarius [Note: [Col. 0709] “And of blessed Nazarius” in 2.], which he placed beyond the river Rhine [Note: [Col. 0709] *reni* in 2.] in the monastery called Lorishaim [Note: [Col. 0709] *lorsan* in 2; *lorsam* in 4.], where a basilica of marvelous beauty had been built in honor of that martyr.

This estate had once been given to the same Bishop Chrodegangus, for the benefit of Saint Stephen, by Chilliswindis, a religious woman, and her son Cancro [Note: [Col. 0709] *cangro* in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0709] *tradiderunt* in 2 and 4.]. This blessed man was generous in almsgiving, utterly pure in charity, and a host to visitors and pilgrims. But since it would be lengthy to recount in order all the good deeds he performed, let it suffice to have briefly touched upon these few out of the many.

He consecrated very many bishops in various cities, as well as priests, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical orders, according to the custom of the Roman Church, on the Saturdays of the four seasons of the year. He ruled the Church of Metz for twenty-three years, five months, and five days [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 has *r. quoque*.]. He died on the day before the Nones of March, in the time of King Pippinus [Note: [Col. 0709] 2 has *obiitque*.]. He rests in the monastery of Gorze, which he built from its foundations.

Now, most holy Father Angilramnus [Note: [Col. 0709] *angelramne* in 2; *angilramme* in 4.], the course of the narrative awaits your blessedness. But, mindful of my own inadequacy, I do not dare to undertake unworthily what ought to be set forth in a more accomplished style concerning the praiseworthy course of your life [Note: [Col. 0709] “Here ends the brief account of the deeds of the bishops” in 2. What follows was transcribed from the same manuscript.].

# Deeds of the Bishops of Metz. Second Text [Note: [Col. 0709C] We reprint the two texts of the same little work written by Paul the Deacon because they differ in many places. [Col. 0710C] From Pertz’s Preface the reader will judge which one has been interpolated. EDITOR.]

*(From D. Calmet, in the* History of Lorraine, *vol. II.)*

[Col. 0709]

[Col. 0709C] After the Lord Christ had migrated to heaven, having completed everything He had determined to accomplish with the Father for the salvation of the world [Col. 0710C] [Col. 0711A], as soon as the blessed apostles had received and been strengthened by the promised gift of the Holy Spirit, they immediately decided by common counsel, according to divine providence, by lot which province or region each of them should undertake to preach.

As each of them went to the place assigned to him, blessed Peter, who was first among them, stood out like a most powerful leader. With complete eagerness he hastened to the city that was then the capital of the whole world, namely, the city of Romulus, after first founding the Church at Antioch and dedicating it in the name of his own see.

When he reached Rome, he immediately sent from his company excellent and learned men who would subjugate to Christ the principal cities situated in the West through the word of faith. Thus he sent Apollinaris to Ravenna, Leucius to Brundisium, and Anatolius to Milan. Mark, who was considered foremost among his disciples, he assigned to Aquileia. When Mark had appointed his companion Hermagoras over that people, he returned to blessed Peter and was likewise sent by him to Alexandria.

At that time, when in Belgic Gaul the city of the Mediomatrici, also called Metz, situated on the very bank of the Moselle River, abounded in populous tribes, blessed Peter the apostle sent to it a man named Clement, outstanding and proven by his merits, elevated to episcopal dignity. Together with him, as ancient tradition relates, other religious teachers were also sent by that prince of the apostles [Col. 0711C] to conquer through the word of faith the principal cities of Gaul.

When blessed Clement reached the city of the Mediomatrici, he took lodging, as they say, in the caves of the amphitheater situated outside the same city. In that place he also built an oratory for the Lord, set up an altar in it, and consecrated it in the name of blessed Peter the apostle, his teacher.

While this venerable priest preached to the people of that city with assiduous exhortation, divine mercy cooperating with him, he led a very great multitude of them, freed from the filthy worship of idols and the blindness of error, to the splendor of the true faith. He was the first in those regions to shine forth as a teacher of righteousness and a herald of truth.

[Col. 0711D] Finally, those who know the history of that place assert that in the amphitheatre where he first lived upon arriving, not even a serpent can remain to the present day; indeed, harmful pests of every kind shun that place, from which long ago the tokens of true salvation proceeded in such a manner. For they say that our elders learned from ancient seniors, deeply devoted to the worship of holy religion, and that the report was handed down with complete truthfulness through successive ages: namely, that this most holy bishop and apostolic man performed a miracle so great that it ought not to be concealed.

At the time when this venerable pontiff arrived at the aforesaid city, a terrible plague was devastating the people of that district. The amphitheatre mentioned above was so full of serpents [Col. 0712A] that no one dared either to enter or even to approach the place. For from their poisonous breath a deadly pestilence had arisen, cruelly afflicting not only human beings but also horses, oxen, sheep, and all other animals.

When the most blessed Clement was approaching the walls of that city, the plague had spread so widely that no one could safely go out or return. If anyone, compelled by extreme necessity, wished to leave through its gates or even to approach them, he immediately died most miserably, struck by the force of the poison. Nor is it surprising that the slippery serpent was bringing down the bodies of those whom it loved through its chosen vessels, since from their minds it had not yet entirely lost its rightful power through [Col. 0712B] the water of sacred baptism [lacuna].

After the worshipper of the divine and wondrous Trinity had begun to fulfil the preaching entrusted to him with every effort of his mind, an innumerable multitude of the sick soon hastened to him for help, hearing him preach the true Lord. They recognized from the mouth of the outstanding shepherd that they had rightly been infected with serpentine poison. When he saw their unspeakable misery, he did not delay in giving them the most health-giving medicine. He promised that the mercy of the true God would soon be present to them if they did not refuse to abandon the detestable worship of idols. At last, therefore, not only the sick but also the few who remained, having adopted a salutary resolution, promised that they would renounce all images and idols and remain safe, provided they were not deprived of the benefits promised by the bishop of the Most High God [Col. 0712C].

Hearing these words, so long desired by him, the man of God, ready to endure every danger on their behalf, immediately offered special praises to the Creator on behalf of all. Then, gathering a few brothers around him, he presented the sacrificial offering which Christ the Lord commanded the faithful devoutly to perform in remembrance of him. After he had fortified himself and his companions with the sacred nourishment, he did not hesitate to engage the ancient enemy in combat. Entrusting his hope to the Lord of heaven and earth, he fearlessly entered the caverns of the theatre to fight the ancient serpent, namely, the devil.

When the serpents sensed the sound of approaching footsteps, they immediately began to emerge from the caverns [Col. 0712D], eagerly striving to devour the man of God. But he, having made the sign of the cross, advanced toward them without fear from a distance. Unable to resist his power any longer, they immediately lowered their swollen necks.

According to ancient tradition, the man of God at once removed the stole that he wore around his neck, bound the largest of the serpents with it before the eyes of the entire people, and led it with his own hands, bound, to the river Salia, which flows nearby. There he released it and said:

“In the name of the most holy and undivided Trinity, whom through the preaching of my most blessed master Peter, prince of the apostles, I have recognized as the true God, I command you: harming neither human beings nor animals, cross this river immediately, together with all the pestilential multitude attached to you [Col. 0713A], and go to those regions where no human habitation can exist.”

The holy priest had scarcely finished speaking when the enormous serpent, together with all the others, began to depart swiftly, as the distinguished bishop had commanded. From that day onward, the place was so cleansed of every impurity of serpents that, as has been reported above, scarcely even the smallest worm is ever found there.

Then, seeing so great a display of power fulfilled by God through his man, the entire people eagerly sought to hear the word of truth from his mouth, desiring to fulfil their pledged promise. The most blessed Clement, seeing such devotion in the people, gave the Giver of all good things the greatest thanks. Instructing them according to ecclesiastical custom, he urged them to prepare themselves with the utmost devotion to receive the gift of holy baptism [Col. 0713B]. Obedient to his commands in all things, they were deemed worthy to become members of the one holy mother Church.

Finally, renouncing all the impurities of idols, they were washed by his holy hands through water and the Holy Spirit, and were freed not only from every bodily sickness but also—and this is the greater thing—from the maladies of their souls. Then that most noble jewel among bishops, striving daily, in the words of the Psalmist, to advance from virtue to virtue until he might be worthy to behold the vision of the Lord of hosts, built, after the church of the blessed apostle Peter mentioned above, another basilica, as is reported, in honour of the most holy Baptist John. There he drew many souls away from the devil and acquired them for God [Col. 0713C], and established it as a baptistery for the faithful people throughout the passing years. There, too, the practice of holy religion grew so greatly that later, for a considerable period, a community of monks served Christ there under the regular discipline.

He is likewise said to have built a third church. In its foundations he made a crypt of extraordinary beauty and arranged below it a remarkable spring, suitable not only for drinking but also highly health-giving, if anyone drank from it with faith, for driving away every disease. Before the entrance to that spring he consecrated an altar in honour of his frequently mentioned master, the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles. There the venerable bishop made a tomb for himself, as it may still be seen to this day [Col. 0713D], and in it he lay buried for a considerable time.

We ought, therefore, not only to believe the things we have briefly recalled but also not to doubt many other matters, almost innumerable, since the savage and untamed necks of the pagans could never have been subjected to Christ unless he himself, who said, “Without me you can do nothing,” had cooperated. Thus, just as we have frequently heard in the deeds of the holy apostles, the leaders of the holy Church of God, and of their apostolic successors, this distinguished and apostolic man too should be believed to have performed wondrous and magnificent deeds.

For our Author and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, is read in the Gospel to have said to all his faithful [Col. 0714A]: “Amen, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these.” To encourage the hearts of the faithful to believe the things we are recounting, we have thought it worthwhile to insert here a vision of a certain faithful man. Since he is still alive, we believe it better to withhold his name.

After completing a long period of service and pouring out his prayers to the Lord with the utmost devotion, this man wished to give himself over to sleep. At that moment a memory of the most blessed Clement came into his mind. He began to be deeply troubled in his heart about the bishop just mentioned: how could one who, with the Lord’s permission, had been able to subject so many thousands of people to Christ shine with scarcely any radiance of miracles?

As he reflected on these matters, he could scarcely be overcome by sleep that night [Col. 0714B]. While he was not yet asleep, though not entirely awake either, a man of extraordinary brightness stood before him and said:

“Why, dearest brother, do you appear throughout this long night, like an unbeliever, to doubt the powers of the holy bishop Clement? Know without any uncertainty that he was mighty in the flesh through the greatest miracles, so much so that the fame of his powers spread even to the Roman citadels. It reached not only the other faithful but also the very first of the apostles, who marvelled at the grace of God in him.
