“But because of the sins of the Christian people, the Lord, Creator of all things, often permitted a fierce barbarian nation to come upon them and destroy them and the churches in which they heard and despised his commandments, together with the volumes of Holy Scripture. For this reason the deeds of this man, as well as those of many saints [Col. 0714C], have been almost entirely handed over to oblivion.

“But what wonder is it if he shone with great powers while he lived, when even now, if the faith of sinners has not failed, the place of his relics gleams with no ordinary miracles? In our own times we ourselves saw, with our own eyes and with immense wonder, one lame man, wholly disabled in body, healed before his most holy body, and three possessed men cleansed.”

On the ninth day before the Kalends of December, the greatest prince and priest passed from this wretched and unstable life to the blessed and angelic homeland. United with the great princes of the priests, he now stands before the Lord of heaven, ready to intercede with him for the sins of faithful peoples, and there he rejoices happily with him for ever and ever. Amen.

Coelestis, a man full of God, succeeded him. Living a heavenly life while proclaiming the kingdom of heaven, he increased the number of believers alike by his example and by his teaching. After him Felix assumed the governance of the Church, and then Patiens. After these came Victor, fifth in order, followed by another Victor. After them came Simeon, the seventh; after him Sambatius, the eighth. It is certain that through the efforts of all these men the Church of God grew, although their individual deeds are hidden from us.

Rufus and Adelphus, who are ninth and tenth in number, must without doubt be believed to have shone with great merits during their lives, since they also shone after death through such a miracle. When their bodies had been buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Felix, as the report handed down to us relates, there was a devout man concerned for the care of his soul. At night, so that he might commend himself to the Lord in private prayers, he was accustomed to make the rounds with unceasing devotion of all the oratories situated outside the walls of that city.

When he had reached the aforesaid basilica of the blessed martyr Felix, but had not been granted the opportunity to enter, he approached the outer wall, at the point where the bodies of the aforementioned priests rested, and there prostrated himself in prayer with all the concentration of his mind. When, after pouring out his prayers, he rose from prayer and recited, in honour of the saints opposite whose tombs he had prayed, a verse from the Psalms—namely, “The saints shall exult in glory” [Col. 0715B]—he immediately heard from within a voice adding: “They shall rejoice in their resting-places.”

Firminus succeeded these holy men, followed by Legontius. Apart from their names, no account of their lives has come down to us from antiquity. Then the thirteenth venerable bishop, Auctor, assumed the governance of the Church at a time when not only Gaul but almost the whole of the West suffered the violence of raging barbarians. Although other distinguished deeds are also believed to have been performed by this man, two miracles in particular have been widely transmitted to our memory.

At that time, while this reverend bishop was leading a life adorned with every virtue, Attila, king of the Huns, more savage than every beast, having many barbarian nations subject to his rule, after crushing Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians, who had come out to meet him, gave free rein to his savagery against all Gaul [Col. 0715C].

Having foreseen his arrival, the blessed Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, went to Rome to the most sacred bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that through their sublime merits he might specially obtain from the Lord the deliverance of the people of Tongeren from so great a destruction. There it was divinely revealed to him through the same blessed apostle Peter that heavenly judgment had decreed that all Gaul should be handed over to the ravaging of the barbarians, except for the shrine of the blessed levite and protomartyr Stephen situated at Metz, where his precious blood was preserved without any stain of corruption.

When these things had been revealed to Saint Servatius, he hurried back to Gaul and found the swarms of Huns already raging throughout the country. They had withdrawn from the siege of Metz because they saw that the city was impregnable through the strength of its walls. At that very time, while returning from Rome, the blessed Servatius happened to arrive at Metz. After reporting to his holy fellow bishop Auctor all that he had learned through the revelation, he returned to his own city, namely Tongeren.

No sooner had he departed than the wall of the city of Metz collapsed, opening an entrance to the enemies by heavenly providence. As soon as the blessed Auctor noticed that the city had been handed over to the swords of the enemy, he ordered all the children who had not yet received the washing of the sacred font to be baptized [Col. 0716A].

When the Huns, who were besieging a fortress twelve miles from there called Scarponna, heard that the walls of Metz had collapsed, they returned to it again with great haste. They laid waste to everything with fire and plunder, killed many of the citizens, including the children who had been baptized, and carried away as captives the survivors who had escaped destruction together with the bishop, Saint Auctor.

What had been foretold by the blessed Peter, the servant of Christ, to Servatius concerning the shrine of the levite and protomartyr Saint Stephen was indeed fulfilled. When the raging barbarians saw that basilica from a distance, they hurried toward it as though to seize the finest booty [Col. 0716B]. As they approached more closely, it appeared to their eyes like an enormous rock, solid yet movable. Blinded in mind, they felt around it with their hands, seeking an entrance, but nothing at all appeared to them except the natural hardness of stone. Finally, withdrawing repeatedly and then returning, and seeing that they accomplished nothing, they departed in exhaustion, frustrated in the fulfilment of their wickedness.

Nor will I be silent about what the blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours, related in his books concerning this oratory. He reports that, before these enemies came, a faithful man saw in a vision the blessed levite Stephen conferring with the holy apostles Peter and Paul concerning this destruction and saying:

“I beseech you, my lords, do not allow the city of Metz to be burned by its enemies under the protection of your patronage, because it is my place, in which the pledges of my littleness are contained. Rather, let the people learn that I can accomplish something with God. But if the people’s wickedness has grown so great that nothing else can be done except that the city be handed over to the flames, at least let this oratory not be burned.”

They replied to him:

“Go in peace, dearest brother. Your oratory alone will escape the fire. But we shall not obtain this for the city, because the sentence of the Lord’s decree has already gone forth against it. The sin of the people has prevailed, and the outcry of their wickedness has risen before the Lord. Therefore this city will be consumed by fire.”

Hence there is no doubt that, through their intercession, the oratory remained unharmed after the city had been laid waste.

When the king and the enemy had reached the town called Decempagi, thirty miles from the city of Metz [Col. 0716D], the Lord—who always cares for his servants and, in wondrous mercy, does not restrain himself, as the Psalmist says—suddenly surrounded those same Huns with such darkness that they had no idea what to do or where to turn.

They carefully sought the cause of so great a calamity, as the circumstances required, and heard from one of the captives whom they were leading away that they were suffering such things because of Auctor, the bishop of the heavenly God, whom he said he had seen among the captives. They immediately made an investigation and found the blessed Auctor. When they asked him what reward he wished to receive in order to free them from so great a danger, he replied that no other gift could be offered to him more pleasing than the release of all the captives whom they were carrying away, allowing them to return to their own homes. If they did this, he promised that he would certainly obtain from his Lord that they be delivered from the darkness in which they were held.

It was done. The Huns then searched throughout their entire army for the captives whom they had been leading away and returned them to the blessed Auctor. Immediately, as had been promised them, the darkness ceased, light was restored, and they were freed from their distress. Thus the venerable servant of Christ, although assigned for a short time to the lot of the captives, released many from captivity. How much more glorious was his triumph over the citizens whom he brought back than the triumph the cruel barbarians could have celebrated when they had previously carried them away as victors!

I shall now turn to another miracle accomplished through his merits by heavenly power [Col. 0717B]. At a certain time, in the oratory of the blessed protomartyr Stephen mentioned above, a beam became detached from the very summit of the roof and fell down. It shattered the marble, of remarkable whiteness, that was on the altar, splitting it entirely into two parts.

The blessed Auctor arrived. While all who were present were saddened by the damage that had been inflicted, he himself, trusting in the Lord, ordered the two fractures to be joined together and instructed that the necessary implements be prepared for him so that he might offer the divine sacrifice above it in the customary manner. While they stood amazed and watched to see what he would do, he immediately offered the saving host to God. At once the entire fracture was so solidified that it seemed not to have been divided before.

Nevertheless, something remains in that marble which can still be admired to no small degree [Col. 0717C]. To those who look at it, it still appears divided; but when it is carefully handled with the fingers, it proves to be so solid that no sign of any division can be perceived in it. There is no doubt that he performed many more wondrous deeds, but from those that have been related his character and greatness can be more fully recognized.

The fourteenth to succeed him was Aeplitius; then came Urbicius, the fifteenth; Bonolus, the sixteenth; Terentius, the seventeenth; and Gonsolonus, the eighteenth. After him came Romanus; then, twentieth in order, Fronimus; after whom came Grammatius, followed by Agathimber.

These three whom we have mentioned above are believed, as their names indicate, to have come from Greek origin. After them Sperus governed the Church, followed by Vilicus; then came Peter, the twenty-fifth; and Agiulphus, the twenty-sixth, who is said to have been born of a father from a noble senatorial family and to have been descended through his mother from a daughter of Clovis, king of the Franks.

After him came his nephew, named Arnoaldus, followed by Pappolus. After these the most blessed Arnulphus was appointed to govern the Church, a man distinguished in every respect by the light of holiness and the splendour of his lineage. Born from the most noble and valiant stock of the Franks, he governed the Church of God in such a way that he also became administrator of the palace.

While remaining in the body and likewise after his departure from this life, he performed many wondrous deeds. Anyone who wishes to know them should read the little book composed specifically about his deeds.

[Col. 0718A] I shall nevertheless relate one of his remarkable deeds, and I have been sufficiently astonished at the manner in which the man who compiled his Life passed it over. While he was doing penance for certain offences, it happened that he was crossing the bridge over the river Moselle. When he saw the deep and impenetrable whirlpools of the waters flowing beneath him, he carried in his mind a confidence born of unquestioning hope. Extending a finger, he threw a ring into the depths of the water.

“Then,” he said, “I shall consider myself freed from the bonds of my sins when I recover this ring that I am throwing away.”

Several years later, after he had risen to the office of bishop, a certain fisherman brought him a fish. Because Arnulphus abstained from meat, he ordered it to be prepared for his evening meal. When his servant, according to custom, had gutted it [Col. 0718B], he found the same ring inside the fish’s entrails.

Astonished at the event but unaware of its significance, he brought it to the blessed Arnulphus. As soon as Arnulphus saw it, he immediately recognized it, and, now confident of the forgiveness of his sins, gave thanks to almighty God. From then onward he did not lead his life less strictly; rather, he constrained himself to still greater abstinence.

This venerable Father likewise sought a sign from the Lord, as once that Gideon did. Gideon wished to obtain a true indication, through the fleece placed on the threshing floor, whether he would be able to gain victory over his enemies. Arnulphus, throwing a ring into the deepest whirlpool of the river, wished to test whether he had already gained victory over his enemies. Those whom Gideon defeated were indeed strong, but those whom Arnulphus overcame were stronger.

I learned this not from some insignificant person [Col. 0718C], but from the eminent king Charles himself, the champion of all truth, who descended from the lineage of that blessed Arnulphus and stood three generations removed from him in the line of descent.

To return to the earlier narrative: this venerable man, in the time of his youth, fathered two sons through a lawful marriage, namely Anchisus and Clodulphus. The name Anchisus is believed to have been derived from Anchises, the father of Aeneas, who once came from Troy to Italy. For the nation of the Franks, as its historians have handed down, traces its beginnings to Trojan ancestry.

When the venerable Arnulphus had these two sons whom we have mentioned, he was merciful and always devoted to works of piety. He began to urge both sons to agree that he should distribute all his possessions for the use of the poor [Col. 0718D]. The elder son, Clodulphus, absolutely refused to allow this to be done—that is, to give his father the portion owed to him. But the younger son, Anchisus, trusting that Christ’s mercy would grant him more, willingly promised to obey everything his father wished.

The venerable father thanked his son and foretold that he would possess more than he had left behind. He also blessed him and all the offspring who would be born from him in the future. And so it happened: more wealth accrued to Anchisus than he had left behind, and his father’s blessing was so firmly established in him that from his descendants were born men so vigorous and strong that, not undeservedly, the kingdom of the Franks was transferred to his lineage. I shall teach you how you may recognize this by noting a few things.

Anchisus fathered Pippin, than whom no one could ever have been more daring. Pippin fathered Charles, a man to be ranked among the very bravest, who, among the many great wars he waged, so thoroughly crushed the Saracens that to this day that fierce and treacherous people fears the arms of the Franks.

This Charles fathered Pippin, likewise distinguished for wisdom and courage. Among his other achievements, he defeated and subdued the Basques, who had long been rebellious against Frankish rule, together with their prince Waisarius, with remarkable success.

His son in turn was the great king Charles, who expanded the kingdom of the Franks as it had never been expanded before [Col. 0719B]. Among the many remarkable deeds he accomplished, he twice conquered the nation of the Lombards: he captured one of their kings, whose name was Desiderius, and drove the other, called Adelgisus, together with his ruling father, into Constantinople. He brought the whole nation under his rule without a difficult battle and, something that rarely happens, tempered victory with merciful moderation.

He also rescued the Romans and the city of Romulus itself—which had long desired his presence, had once been mistress of the whole world, and was then groaning under Lombard oppression—from harsh distress, and added them to his sceptre. He likewise took possession of all Italy with gentle rule. Of this man, one could not know whether to admire more his military valour, his brilliance of wisdom, or his mastery of all the liberal arts [Col. 0719C].

By his wife Hildegard he fathered four sons and five daughters. Before his lawful marriage, however, he had a son named Pippin by Dimiltruda, a noble girl. The names of the children whom Hildegard bore him are as follows: the first was called Charles, after his father and great-grandfather; the second was likewise Pippin, sharing the name of his uncle and grandfather; the third was Lodohic, who was born in the same birth as Lothair, who died at the age of two.

Of these, by God’s favour, the younger Pippin now holds the kingdom of Italy, and Lodohic holds Aquitaine. After Queen Hildegard died, the most excellent king Charles married Fastrada, while Hildegard rests at the city of Metz in the oratory of the blessed Arnulphus. Because the kings just mentioned derived their origin from the blessed Arnulphus [Col. 0719D], they placed there the bodies of their loved ones who had died.

Two daughters of King Pippin were buried there: one named Rotald, the other Adelaid. There were also buried the two daughters of the younger King Charles, namely Adelaid and Hildegard. Hildegard, who was named after her mother, soon followed her mother in death.

Having briefly touched upon these matters that ought not to be passed over, let us return to the course of the narrative. After the most blessed Arnulphus, Goericus, the thirtieth bishop of Metz, who was also called Abbo, governed the church of Metz. Then Godo, the thirty-first, discharged the duties of the episcopal office.

When he departed from the world, Clodulphus, whom we mentioned above, the biological son of the blessed Arnulphus and brother of Anchisus, from whom the royal seed was propagated, rose to the episcopal dignity as the thirty-second bishop, on account of the glory of his father’s holiness. Beyond the fact that he sprang from such a root, no further report about him has reached us.

After his death, Abbo, the thirty-third bishop, was appointed to govern the faithful people. After him Aptatus and then Felix became happy shepherds of the Lord’s flock. Next, Sigibaldus, born of noble parents, became bishop of the religious community. In every respect he was devoted to the interests of the Church and a most diligent restorer of sacred foundations.

Concerned for the condition of souls, he founded two monasteries. One of them is called Hilariacum, or Nova-Cella; the other is called Novum-Villare. A dreadful pain of gout afflicted him severely. But fixing his mind on inward joys, he endured his bodily pains with the greatest patience.

Then the distinguished man, worthy to be praised in every respect, Chrodegangus, bishop, was chosen. He was born in the district of Hasbania, to his father Sigranus and his mother Landrada, and descended from the first nobility of the Frankish race.

He was raised in the palace by Charles the Elder himself and became his referendary. Finally, in the time of King Pippin, he merited the pontifical dignity. He was altogether illustrious and radiant with every form of nobility, handsome in appearance and most eloquent in speech. He was learned both in his native language and in Latin [Col. 0720C].

He nourished the servants of God and was not only a provider for orphans and widows but also their most compassionate protector. Since he was wealthy in every respect, he was chosen in a singular manner by King Pippin and by the entire community of the Franks, and was sent to Rome. As all desired, he summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul.

He united the clergy and made them live within the enclosure of the cloister, after the manner of a monastery. He established a rule for them concerning how they ought to serve in the Church and supplied them sufficiently with food and the necessities of life, so that, not needing to occupy themselves with perishable affairs, they might devote themselves solely to the divine offices.

He also instructed the clergy abundantly in divine law and Roman chant and commanded them to observe the custom and order of the Roman Church, something that had not previously been done at all in the Church of Metz [Col. 0720D].

Together with the assistance of King Pippin, he ordered the construction of the *reba* of the protomartyr Saint Stephen, together with his altar, screens, presbytery, and arches all around.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Alternatively, *repam* (see the Life of Saint Eligius, book II, chapter 39, at the end of volume V of the *Spicilegium*). *Repa*, or *reba*, means a canopy, a *dais*, or a covering placed over altars and the tombs of saints (Du Cange, “REPA”).]

Likewise, in the church of the blessed Peter, he ordered a presbytery to be constructed. He also built an ambo decorated with gold and silver and erected arches around the throne before the altar.

Moreover, in the parish of Saint Stephen, in the district of Moselle, he founded a monastery in honour of the most blessed apostle Peter. He enriched it with great resources and established monks there, uniting them in one charity under the rule of the holy Father Benedict [Col. 0721A].

He also built another monastery called Gorgia, where in the same way he gathered a considerable number of monks. Finally, he requested from Paul, the Roman pontiff, the bodies of three holy martyrs: that of the blessed Gorgonius, which rests at Gorgia; that of the blessed Nabor, which was buried in the monastery of Hilariacum; and that of the blessed Nazarius, which he placed beyond the river Rhine, in a monastery called Lorsam, where a basilica of extraordinary beauty had been built in honour of that martyr.

The estate called Chillisiundis had formerly been handed over to the same Bishop Chrodegang, for the benefit of Saint Stephen, by a devout woman named Chillisiundis and her son Cangro. This blessed man was generous in almsgiving, pure in charity, and a gracious receiver of guests and pilgrims [Col. 0721B].

But since it would take too long to recount in order all the good deeds he performed, let it be enough to have briefly sampled these few from among the many. He consecrated numerous bishops in various cities, as well as priests and deacons and the other ecclesiastical orders, according to the custom of the Roman Church on the Saturdays of the four seasons of the year.

He governed the Church of Metz for twenty-three years, five months, and five days. He died on the sixth day before the Nones of March, during the reign of King Pippin. He rests in the monastery of Gorgia, which he built from its foundations.

Here, most holy father Angilramnus, the place in the sequence of the narrative now awaits your blessedness. But, mindful of my own insignificance, I do not dare inadequately to attempt what ought to be brought forth in a grander style concerning the praiseworthy course of your life [Col. 0722B].

## On the Order of the Bishops of Metz

### Metrical Text

*(From D. Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*

[Col. 0721]

[Col. 0721B] You who visit the sacred dwellings with lively zeal,

if the love of knowing touches your hearts—whose labour

acquired these leaders for Christ, this splendid city

of men, or whoever first brought to these shores

the light that dispelled ancient error—

read carefully what follows, a poem

skilfully composed concerning the true faith from the life-giving East,

and you will be instructed briefly.

When Peter, supreme leader of the eternal King, had come to the walls of Rome,

which was the head of the world, from the eastern lands,

full of every pattern of virtue [Col. 0711C],

he sent distinguished men, armed with heavenly weapons,

to capture strongholds and bring them to the joys of life.

Among their number, one called Clement [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.]—

the one who had succeeded Peter at Rome—

brought the light into this city

which the ancient settlers once called Metz.

An outstanding bishop, through the divine word he brought salvation,

and here, first of all, founded the Lord’s sheepfold worthily,

sending golden examples of the people to future generations.

Coelestis succeeded him by merit, receiving his name from his life and strong in heavenly doctrine.

Felix, the third [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the second day before the Ides of October.], happily enlarged the Church.

The fourth, Patiens [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.], is present, whom patience adorned well.

Then Victor [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the sixth day before the Ides of January.] shone forth, for victory gives him his name.

After him comes the sixth bishop [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.], with the same name.

The seventh is Simeon [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.], sprung from Hebrew blood.

Sambatus, the eighth [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.], faithfully observes the mystical Sabbaths.

After them you come, Rufus [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the seventh day before the Ides of November.], ruddy with the flames of love.

Adelphus, the tenth [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.], an excellent lover of the brethren.

Then came Firminus [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.], whose breast was firm with strength.

You, gracious Legontius [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.], follow these as the twelfth.

Then Auctor [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the fourth day before the Ides of August.] flourished, enriched with heavenly gifts.

Epletus [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the third day before the Kalends of August.] held this chair as the fourteenth.

Urbicius [Note: [Col. 0721D] Died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.], the fifteenth, was renowned in this city.

After him Bonulus [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the seventh day before the Ides of October.] performed the work of goodness according to custom.

Terentius [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.], you continually trod the holy thresholds.

The eighteenth is said to be Lamgunsolon [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the second day before the Kalends of August.].

From there you receive, Romanus [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the Ides of April.], the honour of the venerable court.

After him Fronimus [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.] wisely ruled the holy fold.

Grammatus [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.] generously instructed the people in grammar.

Danaus Agatimber [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the fourth day before the Ides of May.] shines in the Church’s sanctuary.

After these came [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.] Sperus, whom hope supported from on high.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.] Villicus preserves the inner estates under his governance.

The twenty-fifth, [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the fifth day before the Kalends of October.] Peter gives utterances to the people.

Both lineage and a radiant [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.] life adorn Agiulf.

From here came Arnoald, descending from the Sicambrian stock.

Afterward you take up the enclosure of Chrifaculus, [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the second day before the Kalends of December.] Papulus, which must be preserved.

[Col. 0722D] Then [Note: [Col. 0722D] Died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.] the blessed Arnulf shone forth with splendid radiance.

[Col. 0723A] Next [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October.] Goericus presides, also called Abbo.

After him [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the eighth day before the Ides of May.] Godo, the thirty-first, first maintains the sacred high office.

The holy [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the eighth day before the Ides of May.] Chlodulphus, sprung from noble stock, follows.

Another venerable bishop, [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.] Abbo, appears again.

Aptatus governs the clergy with fitting reins, [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.]

Felix displays fortunate realms to the peoples, [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.]

The eminent [Note: [Col. 0723A] Died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.] Sigibald shines through his excellent deeds.

The noble pope [Note: [Col. 0724A] Died on the second day before the Nones of March.] Chrodegangus is held in honor by all.

[Col. 0724A] Now, the thirty-eighth shepherd, supported by his lord’s

Aid, led the sheep to the holy pastures of life:

[Note: [Col. 0724A] Died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.] Angelramnus; at that time the greatest in arms,

King Charles, distinguished in judgment, appearance, and courage,

Received the scepter of Italy as a gift from Christ.

May the right hand of the Most High, at the request of blessed Stephen,

Protect and govern them, happy, forever [Note: [Col. 0724A] These five are to be added: Gundulphus, who died on the seventh day before the Ides of September; Drogo, archbishop, on the sixth day before the Ides of December; Adventius, on the day before the Kalends of September; Wala, on the third day before the Ides of April; Ruotpertus, who was ordained bishop on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.].

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0723]

## CATALOGUE OF THE BISHOPS OF METZ

*(Chaussier, superior of the minor seminary.)*

[Col. 0723B] In this catalogue, for our ancient bishops we shall follow the chronology of Meurisse in his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, although it is open to correction on several points, which it is not our intention to discuss here.—A great many of our ancient bishops are honored with the title of saint. For most of them, this title rests upon the greatest authority that particular Churches can provide when the persons in question lived in the earliest centuries: their cult has been admitted from time immemorial into the liturgy of the Church of Metz [Note: [Col. 0723C] In the library of the diocesan major seminary there is a manuscript Breviary of Metz from the beginning of the fourteenth century, around 1325; another [Col. 0723D] Breviary of Metz, printed in 1546; and a supplement for the saints of Metz, to be added to the Roman Breviary when that Breviary was adopted in the diocese of Metz in 1610. The library of that city also possesses six or seven Missals and other liturgical books of the diocese or of religious houses in the city of Metz. These manuscripts are from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries: two of the oldest [Col. 0724C] bear the date 1324, another that of 1348, and one of the more recent the date 1458.—These are the various monuments that served us to establish [Col. 0724D] which of our bishops were honored as saints in our former liturgy.]; indeed, for some of them it passed, already in antiquity, into the liturgy of neighboring dioceses; and the names of several are found with the title of saint in the Roman Martyrology.

For a certain number of these ancient pontiffs, the title of saint is not founded upon authorities equally respectable. No trace of their cult is found in the monuments of our former liturgy: only their names are entered in the Martyrology of Metz, or in the Gallican Martyrology [Col. 0723C] of Du Saussay, which, because of its lack of critical judgment, carries little weight when it is a matter of assigning the title of saint to any person.—In the catalogue that we give here, beside each name of a saint we shall indicate the most authoritative source that assigns him this title. The letter L means ancient liturgy; R, Roman Martyrology; M, Martyrology of Metz; and G, Gallican Martyrology.

[Col. 0725]

## THE PASSION OF SAINT CYPRIAN, ATTRIBUTED TO PAUL THE DEACON

*(From the edition of the works of Saint Cyprian by Fell, Oxford.)* (C,S)

[Col. 0725C] [Note: [Col. 0725D] Under the emperor Valerian. The account of Cyprian’s passion, according to the editions of Manutius and Morellius, places before it, as a sort of prologue, an excellent fiction that sufficiently reveals the age in which it originated, and which runs as follows: “When the glorious name of Christ, hated by the Gentiles, was being attacked with the greatest determination in an attempt to erase it, and persecution was taking place in the city of Rome, the most blessed Cornelius, who was endowed with the highest virtues, was then governing the pontificate of that city. Having been arrested by the governor and afflicted with prolonged tortures, he ended his temporal life by the sword, destined to receive from God eternal life without end. But when this hatred had also been inflicted in the regions of Libya, many Christian peoples, preferring to lose their transitory life and attain what had been promised by God, were brought to completion through various torments. They say that at that time the governor had a lime-kiln kindled, and that burning coals with incense were presented at its mouth; the governor said to the Christians: ‘Choose one of these two things: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or be thrown into the lime.’ Then three hundred men, armed with faith, professing Christ the Son of God to be God, cast themselves with swift violence into the fire and were submerged amid the vapors of the powdered lime; Christ consecrated them to himself. In those days, while such things were being done, the blessed bishop Cyprian was governing the Church of Carthage. Having been arrested by the Gentiles, he was presented before unjust tribunals in the city while Paternus was proconsul.” In the old Martyrology it begins, “In the secretariat, under the consuls Tuscus and Bassus,” as the Sarisburian and Gallican codices read. Evidently, when the accounts of exile and passion were joined together for ecclesiastical use and annual commemoration, the chronological heading that properly belonged only to the passion was prefixed to both. FELL.] In the consulship of the emperor Valerian for the fourth time and Gallienus for the third [Col. 0726C] [Note: [Col. 0725C] “In the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.” Old Martyrologies: Sarisburian, Gallican, Fossian. “The writings of the noble emperors have come to me, ordering that those who reject the ceremonies be compelled, against their will, to sacrifice to the gods and to perform sacrifice.” *Acts of the Passion*.], on the third day before the Kalends of September, [Col. 0727A] at Carthage [Note: [Col. 0727D] “In the secretariat.” Greek glossary: *σέκρετον*—tribunal, archive; *σέκρετον*—council. Hesychius. ID.], in the secretariat, the proconsul Paternus said to Bishop Cyprian:

“The most sacred emperors Valerian and Gallienus have deigned to send me letters in which they ordered that those who [Note: [Col. 0727B] “Practice the Roman religion.”] do not practice the Roman religion must recognize the Roman ceremonies. So I have inquired about your name; what do you answer me?” [Note: [Col. 0727B] “I inquire from you, concerning your name, what answer you give me.” Codex of Conches.]

Bishop Cyprian said: “I am a Christian and a bishop.”

“I know no other gods except the one true God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them. We Christians serve this God; we entreat him day and night [Note: [Col. 0727C] “For us and for their safety.” Sarisburian, Gallican.] for ourselves, for all human beings, and for the safety of the emperors themselves.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “So you persist in this resolve [Note: [Col. 0727C] “That you will not sacrifice.” *Acts of the Passion*]?”

Bishop Cyprian replied: “A good resolve, which knows God, [Col. 0727B] cannot be changed.” [Note: [Col. 0727C] “It cannot be changed. Not only concerning bishops.” Gallican, Sarisburian, *Acts of the Passion*.]

The proconsul Paternus said: “Then, in accordance with the command of Valerian and Gallienus, will you be able to depart into exile to the city of Curubis?”

Bishop Cyprian said: “I will depart.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “They have deigned to write to me not only concerning bishops but also concerning presbyters. I therefore want to know from you who the presbyters are who reside in this city.”

Bishop Cyprian replied: “You have judged according to your laws, rightly and beneficially, [Note: [Col. 0727C] Thus: “That we are not informers.” *Acts of the Passion*.] [Note: [Col. 0727D] “That there should be no informers.” Those banished from the city by imperial rescripts and driven from the tribunals were informers. Hence an informer had the basis for the exile he procured. Cyprian therefore rightly appeals to the laws, whereas “we are not informers” would be a feeble statement. ID.] that there should be no informers.”

[Note: [Col. 0727C] “Therefore we cannot produce them; nor do they offer themselves to you voluntarily, since holy Scripture forbids this. For when sought by you they will be found.”] “Therefore they cannot be exposed and denounced by me; but they will be found in their own cities.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “Today I am seeking them here.”

Cyprian said: “Since discipline forbids anyone [Note: [Col. 0727D] “To offer himself voluntarily.” In his last letter Cyprian says, “The Lord wished us rather to confess than to profess.” FELL.] to offer himself voluntarily, and since this would also displease your own authority [Note: [Col. 0727D] “May this also displease your authority.” Thus Arrius Antoninus said to Christians who were, as it were, demanding death in a body, *ὦ δειλοί, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνήσκειν, κρεμνοὺς ἤ βρύχους ἔχετε*—“O cowards, if you wish to die, you have cliffs or nooses.” Tertullian, *To Scapula*. ID.], they cannot offer themselves; but when sought by you they will be found.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “They will be found by me.” [Note: [Col. 0728B] “They will be found in their own cities.” The proconsul Paternus said: “They will be found by me.” Sarisburian, Gallican.]

And he added: “They have also ordered that no assemblies be held in any places and that no one enter cemeteries. Therefore, if anyone does not observe this most salutary command, he shall be punished with death.”

Bishop Cyprian replied [Note: [Col. 0728C] “That they enter cemeteries, and whoever is caught doing so shall be punished with death. Saint Cyprian replied: ‘Do what has been commanded you.’ After this, the blessed martyr was led into exile, by order of the proconsul Aspasius, to the city of Curubis. After many days he came forth.” *Acts of the Passion*.]: “Do what has been commanded you.” [Note: [Col. 0728C] “Do what has been commanded you. And when Cyprian, chosen by God, had been taken from the city of Curubis.” Sarisburian, Gallican.]

Then the proconsul Paternus ordered the blessed Bishop Cyprian to be taken into exile.

After he had remained there for a long time, Galerius Maximus succeeded Aspasius Paternus as proconsul. He ordered that the holy Bishop Cyprian, recalled from exile, be brought before him.

When the holy martyr Cyprian, chosen by God, had returned from the city of Curubis, where he had been sent into exile by order of Aspasius Paternus, then proconsul, he remained in his gardens in accordance with the sacred ordinance. From there he daily expected that they would come to him, as had been revealed to him.

While he was staying there, suddenly, on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, two officials came to him [Note: [Col. 0728C] “Two officials from the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus; and lifting him up.” *Acts of the Passion*.]: one [Note: [Col. 0728C] “An official escort.” It makes no difference whether one says *stratorem* or *statorem*, for the manuscripts recognize both; one word is of Greek origin, the other Latin. They seem generally to have been those later called *commentarienses*. An excellent law of Constantine addressed to Florentius, the *rationalis*, to be written in golden letters, vividly depicts the character of these men. The reader will pardon me if I give the entire passage, since it must by no means be mutilated. Cod. I.IX, title 4, *On the Custody of Accused Persons*: “Whenever an accused person has been brought forward in any case, whether an accuser is present or public concern has brought him there, inquiry must immediately be made, so that the guilty may be punished and the innocent acquitted. If the accuser is temporarily absent, or the presence of associates seems necessary, this must indeed be arranged as quickly as possible. Meanwhile, the person who has been brought forward must not be put into iron handcuffs that cling to the bones, but into longer chains, so that torture may be absent while faithful custody remains. Nor should the prisoner suffer the darkness of the innermost cell, but should be invigorated by being allowed to use the light; and when night has doubled the need for custody, he should be received in the vestibules of the prisons and in healthy places, and when day returns, at the first rising of the sun, should immediately be brought out into the public light, lest he perish from the punishments of prison—which is recognized as wretched for the innocent and not severe enough for the guilty. It shall also be observed that neither those who perform the duty of official escorts nor their assistants may sell their cruelty to accusers, put the innocent to death within the prison walls, or, after removing them from the hearing, consume them through prolonged wasting. For fear of both loss of reputation and danger will threaten the judge if any official escort exhausts someone beyond the proper time through hunger or by any other means, and he does not immediately subject to capital punishment the person in charge of the custody and his assistants.” ID.] an official escort of the staff of Galerius Maximus, the proconsul [Col. 0729A] who had succeeded Aspasius Paternus, and another [Note: [Col. 0729D] “Mounted escort.” *Ἀναβολεύς*, a *mareschalcus* among Latin-barbarian writers: one who lifts an armed emperor or commander onto a horse. Manilius speaks of their birth: “He will go higher than the chariot, / Or load horses with weapons, or lead them into battle.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXX, chapter 5, calls him a mounted soldier. ID.] mounted escort [Note: [Col. 0729C] “A mounted official of the proconsul,” Gallican; “sequestrator,” Sarisburian; “aequestrator,” an old manuscript cited by Gothofredus.] from the guards of the same staff [Note: [Col. 0729C] “And also guards of the same staff, and both of them.” Sarisburian.],

who lifted him into their carriage, placed him in the middle, and brought him to Sextus, where the same proconsul Galerius Maximus had withdrawn for the sake of recovering his health.

Thus the same proconsul Galerius Maximus ordered that Cyprian be kept for another day.

At that time the blessed Cyprian was brought to the official escort and mounted escort of the same staff of the most illustrious proconsul Galerius Maximus. He withdrew to the escort’s lodging and stayed there with him in the district called Saturnus, [Note: [Col. 0729D] “Between Venerea and Salutaria.” Perhaps the shrines of Venus and Salus. FELL.] between Venerea and Salutaria [Note: [Col. 0729C] “Between Venerea and Salutaria,” Collection of Montbrison; “between the two streets Venerea and Salutaria,” German manuscript 1; Gallican: *salaria*; an incorrect reading, *saltuaria*, in other manuscripts. “Returning from exile, he was staying in his gardens. While he remained there, two officials from the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus came to him and lifted him into their carriage; they brought him to the proconsul, to the place where he was staying to restore his health. Taken in charge by the official escort, he withdrew to his lodging, into the district called Saturnus, and stayed there; all the people of the brethren came to him.” *Acts of the Passion*.], and all the people of the brethren gathered there.

When holy Cyprian learned of this, he ordered the young women to be kept under guard [Note: [Col. 0729D] “To admonish the young women.” Rigaltus says: “To discipline them, that is, he warned them to conduct themselves with the greatest chastity, mindful of chastity, holiness, and modesty.” ID.] [Note: [Col. 0729C] “That the young women be admonished.” Gallican, Sarisburian. “In the district, praying, they had come to hear your word, because they were staying before the door of the official’s lodging out of love for the glorious martyr.”], since they had all remained in the district before the door of the official’s lodging. [Col. 0729B]

And so, on the following day, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, [Note: [Col. 0730C] “When morning came.” *Acts of the Passion*. “Very early.” Gallican. “When morning came, the blessed Cyprian was brought before the proconsul, who looked at him and said: ‘Are you Thascius Cyprian, who have offered yourself as pope to men of sacrilegious mind? The most sacred emperors have ordered you to sacrifice. Take thought for yourself, lest you perish.’ Then the angry proconsul said: ‘For a long time.’” *Acts of the Passion*.] in the morning, a great crowd gathered at Sextus, in accordance with the order of the proconsul Galerius Maximus.

The same proconsul Galerius Maximus then ordered Cyprian to be brought before him that day, while he was seated in the courtyard of Sauciolus.

When he had been brought forward, the proconsul Galerius Maximus said to Bishop Cyprian: “Are you Thascius Cyprian?”

Bishop Cyprian replied: “I am.”

The proconsul Galerius Maximus said: “You have offered yourself as pope to men of sacrilegious mind?”

Bishop Cyprian replied: “I have.”

The proconsul Galerius Maximus said: “The most sacred emperors have ordered you to perform the ceremonies.”

Bishop Cyprian said: “I will not do so.”

Galerius Maximus said: “Take thought for yourself.”

Bishop Cyprian replied: “Do what has been commanded you; in so just a matter there is no deliberation.”

Galerius Maximus [Note: [Col. 0730D] “Having consulted with the council.” As was customary among Roman governors, they consulted, behind a curtain, with the advisers seated there about the sentence to be pronounced. See Acts 25:12. ID.] having consulted with the council, pronounced sentence, scarcely and reluctantly, in words of this kind:

“For a long time you have lived with a sacrilegious mind, and you have gathered many men into your wicked conspiracy, and you have made yourself an enemy of the Roman gods and sacred laws. Nor have the devout and most sacred rulers, the Augusti Valerian and Gallienus, and [Note: [Col. 0730D] “Valerian, the most noble Caesar.” His father, when setting out for Persia, declared him Caesar; there the most wretched old man paid for this persecution of the Christians through a most miserable captivity and, if possible, an even more miserable death. ID.] Valerian, the most noble Caesar, been able to recall you to the practice of their ceremonies. Therefore, since you have been discovered to be the author and standard-bearer of the most wicked crimes, you yourself shall be an example to those whom you have joined to yourself through your crime; your blood shall ratify the discipline.”

After saying this, he read the decree from the tablet: “It is our pleasure that Thascius Cyprian be punished by the sword.”

Bishop Cyprian said: [Note: [Col. 0730C] “I give thanks to almighty God, who deigns to release me from the bonds of this body.” Gallican, *Acts of the Passion*.] “Thanks be to God.”

[Note: [Col. 0730C] “As he was being led away, the people, weeping and wailing, said: ‘Let us also be beheaded with him.’” *Acts of the Passion*.] After this sentence, the crowd of the brethren said: “Let us also be beheaded with him.”

For this reason a disturbance arose among the brethren, and a great crowd followed him.

Thus Cyprian was led out [Note: [Col. 0730D] “Into the field of Sextus.” The Roman Martyrology: “The field of Sextus,” six miles from Carthage near the sea, “was exchanged.” ID.] into the field of Sextus. There he [Note: [Col. 0730D] “His cloak, a *birrus*.” A *lacerna* or *birrus*; one of the two words must be regarded as an explanatory addition. The most eminent Cardinal Baronius labors greatly to demonstrate from this passage “what the dress of bishops was”; and indeed that sharp-sighted man showed us that the linen garment in which Cyprian stood, “the linen garment common to all bishops, which some call an ephod and which in Italian is called a rochet,” was such a garment. But the *birrus* “was red in color and a [Col. 0731B] silken clerical garment.” Thus we are supposedly shown “the ancient dress of bishops,” so that over the undergarment they would put a linen garment, over that a loose tunic, and finally a *birrus* cloak covering only the shoulders—the type of garment that we now see worn by the cardinals of the holy Roman Church and by those bishops who have been advanced to that dignity from religious orders. We thus learn that Cyprian was either a cardinal of the Roman Church or had been promoted to the episcopal dignity from a religious order. Certainly there is nothing that partisan zealots cannot persuade themselves of, and even hope to persuade others of. Is this how the clerics of the Roman Church, conspicuous in their dress, go out in public when they are in regions where they fear for themselves—girded with swords and, to use the words of our countryman Campianus, dressed in the most demented attire? The proconsul would foolishly have been concerned to uncover bishops and presbyters if they were conspicuous to everyone by their clothing. His nose must be extremely dull who does not detect in what follows interpolations by copyists, worthy of their [Col. 0731C] centuries and their wits. They, thinking that a tunic did not sufficiently suit episcopal dignity, obligingly supplied a dalmatic. FELL.] stripped off his cloak and *birrus* [Note: [Col. 0730C] “But when the glorious martyr had been brought forward, he took off the cloak and *birrus* that he was wearing, folded it, and laid it at his knees; then he took off his tunic and handed it to the deacons.” *Acts of the Passion*. “He took off his tunic.” Sarisburian.],

bent his knee to the ground, and prostrated himself in prayer before the Lord.

When he had stripped off his dalmatic and handed it to the deacons, he stood in linen [Note: [Col. 0730C] “To the linen garment,” Sarisburian; “standing in linen,” *Acts of the Passion*; “in linen clothes,” Gallican.] and began to await the swordsman.

When the swordsman arrived, he ordered his men to give the swordsman twenty-five gold pieces [Note: [Col. 0731C] “They should give the swordsman twenty-five gold pieces.” This generosity seems to have arisen from the copyists’ munificence. But if each gold piece were worth five shillings of our currency, the small sum given would amount to six pounds and five shillings of the money we call sterling. ID.] [Note: [Col. 0731A] “He ordered them to give.” Sarisburian.].

The brethren, meanwhile, spread linen cloths and handkerchiefs before him [Note: [Col. 0731A] “The brethren, weeping, placed linen cloths and handkerchiefs before him, so that the holy blood flowing down might not be absorbed by the earth.” *Acts of the Passion*.].

Then the blessed Cyprian covered his eyes with his own hand. Since he was unable to tie the strips of cloth around himself, the presbyter Julian and the subdeacon Julian tied them for him.

And thus the blessed Cyprian suffered martyrdom.

Because of the curiosity of the Gentiles, his body was placed nearby [Note: [Col. 0732B] “With candles and twisted torches.” Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 261, no. 36, says: “Here the ancient custom of burying Christians is disclosed: the clergy of various ranks and orders preceded, each carrying a lighted torch, in a truly great procession.” Thus, while Valerian held the empire, Christians had various ranks and orders, and they celebrated the funerals of martyrs in ordered procession, in a manner resembling the supplications of today. Here, as so often elsewhere, we miss the reliability and dignity of ecclesiastical history. Rigaltus says: “In the copies it reads, ‘To the candles and *scolaces*.’ Most correctly. *Scolaces*, a word of Greek origin, means twisted rushes or cords, from which waxed torches were made for nighttime illumination. *Funales* and *scolaces* were candles that tightly bound the book-chest of Numa in every direction. They were made of pliant material suitable for binding and, when placed underground, did not rot because they were packed with cedar and wax.” The brethren had gone to remove the body in the dead of night [Col. 0732C] so that the African Gentiles might not attempt against Cyprian what the Asian Gentiles had perpetrated against Polycarp. On this matter see Eusebius, book IV, chapter 15. The Jews in John 18 are said to have come *μετὰ φανῶν καὶ λαμπάδων*—“with lanterns and torches.” ID.] with candles and *scolaces*, in the courtyards of Macrobius [Col. 0732A] Candidus, the procurator, which are on the Mappalian Way beside the fishponds, with great rejoicing and triumph.

A few days later the proconsul Galerius Maximus died.

The most blessed martyr Cyprian suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus: [Note: [Col. 0732C] “While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns.” Learned men know well that this formula was introduced into the Church at a later time. ID.] “while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”

[Col. 0731]

## THE LIFE AND MIRACLES OF SAINT ARNULF, BISHOP, WRITTEN BY PAUL THE DEACON ACCORDING TO SURIUS

*(From the Cologne edition of the works of the Venerable Bede.)* (C,S)

[Col. 0731D] Blessed Arnolfus, bishop, was of sufficiently high and noble Frankish birth, and extremely wealthy in worldly possessions; but afterward he was nobler and more exalted in faith. Since I learned some of his praiseworthy deeds from those close to him who related them, and most of them through my own knowledge, I consider it worthwhile to begin my account from the very origin of his birth.

There was, then, a certain pilgrim, a servant of God named Stephanus, who came from the regions of Italy and settled in a place adjoining the parents of this blessed man. When the child’s birth had been revealed to this pilgrim by the Spirit, after a brief silence he at last began to speak prophetically in these words: “Know that this child who [Col. 0732D] has been born will be exalted to the highest honors and will be great before God and men”—as the outcome of events proved.

For the boy, of praiseworthy character and preceded by the grace of God, was handed over to be instructed in literary studies. He surpassed all his fellow-students in keen intelligence and retentive memory, and, advancing by degrees in the virtues, progressed from day to day. When, already well educated, he had reached mature age, he was entrusted for training in virtuous conduct to Gundolfus, the sub-king and counselor of the king. After testing him through many trials, Gundolfus deemed him worthy of service to King Theodebert. While remaining in that king’s service, who would be capable of recounting how greatly he surpassed everyone in the power of waging war, especially since he had often bravely driven back the enemy phalanxes with his own sword? Thus within a short time he became first among all, so that six provinces—which then and now are administered by an equal number of officials—were governed under his sole authority.

Meanwhile, while this energetic soldier diligently rendered to God the things that are God’s—namely, in prayer, fasts, and almsgiving—and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s—being strong in war and prudent in counsel—he was prevailed upon by friends and relatives to take as his wife a girl of the noblest family, adorned with distinguished character.

In this matter the Lord bestowed upon that man a special gift of his grace: from that excellent woman he was deemed worthy to receive the joy of two sons, who, like the splendid adornment of two jewels, afterward began to shine in the world. [Col. 0733A]

In those days there was at the king’s court an excellent man named Romaricus, joined to blessed Arnolfus by intimate affection. Having learned, through living continually with him, of the blessed man’s desire—a constant meditation concerning monasteries and holy places—they took counsel together and resolved, in accordance with the Gospel’s command, to leave all their possessions and become pilgrims for the love of Christ. But the Lord’s will opposed the plan of both in this matter. For Christ’s providence did not judge it right that these two men, who would one day shine in the world like two lamps, should be hidden beneath a bushel, but rather that, placed upon a lampstand, they should give light to all through their faithful works.

In those days it happened that the city of Metz, deprived of its pastor, with one voice [Col. 0733B] and equal agreement requested that Arnolfus, the king’s household officer and counselor, be ordained their bishop. Although he wept and resisted greatly, he was finally compelled, since this was pleasing to God, to undertake the governance of the aforementioned city. Yet he was not permitted to abandon the high office he held at the palace.

After he had thus been elevated to episcopal dignity, he revealed the need of the poor with such great and perfect generosity [Al., “relieved”] that, when the fame of the blessed man was heard even in distant regions, an innumerable crowd of men and women hastened to him to be refreshed. Who could recount the rule of his abstinence, when at times, after fasts prolonged for three days or even longer, he lived on barley bread or a drink of water? He also constantly wore, hidden beneath his tunic, a hair shirt [Col. 0733C], which imposed a double torment upon his limbs, already severely worn down by vigils and fasts.

Amid these continual bodily afflictions, by which blessed Arnolfus voluntarily chastised himself for the love of his heavenly homeland, the Lord deigned to display through him many works of miraculous power. I shall undertake to relate some of them here.

When the man of God was staying in the neighboring regions of the Vosges, specifically on the estates of Saint Stephen, patron of the church of Metz, a certain woman named Becila, possessed by a demon, was being gravely tormented before his presence. Since he was supported by every form of compassion, he said with deep sighs: “Alas, wretched human nature, in which the enemy has gained such power that what Christ ought rather to inhabit has become his dwelling!” Saying this, he gave himself over in tears to prayer. When the prayer was finished, the demon was driven out, and he immediately restored the woman to health.

At the time when the universal Church customarily observed a three-day fast, the holy man went outside the city, according to the city’s custom, with crosses and a mixed multitude of people, for the sake of prayer. And behold, a woman from the midst of the crowds raised her voices toward heaven. When the man of God heard this and recognized that she had been seized by a demon, he opposed the hostile spirit with the banner of the cross and freed her from the evil enemy.

At another time, when he had gone within the city to the basilica of the Holy Cross for the sake of prayer, he found there a girl raging wickedly. Moved by compassion, he said to his archdeacon: “Brother, let us keep vigil tonight for this poor little woman, so that, if she is healed through God’s grace, we may return home tomorrow rejoicing.” And so it happened.

In the time of King Dagobert, while blessed Arnolfus was staying at his palace, a certain leper cried out to him, asking for food or clothing. Arnolfus immediately ordered him to be brought to his lodging. There, while showing the sick man his customary fatherly compassion, he asked him whether he had been washed with the sacred water of baptism.

“Not at all, my lord,” he replied, “for who would grant this grace to me, wretched and cast off by the people?”

The holy bishop said: “Now, beloved brother, believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and immediately you will receive healing of body and soul.”

The leper therefore received the sacrament of baptism from the blessed man and was freed from every bodily affliction. From then on he became healthy in both substances—he who had previously been sinful and defiled. [Col. 0734A]

After this, when the holy bishop had come into the territory of the Thuringians in the company of the aforesaid king, it happened that one of the nobles, named Nutilo, was mourning with great lamentation for his son, whom he dearly loved and who was already drawing his final breath. Blessed Arnolfus sympathized with his grief. The father, despairing of the beloved boy’s recovery, was thinking of nothing except having his head cut off and his corpse handed over to the flames, in the manner of the pagans.

Arnolfus approached the sickbed and, after praying, addressed him in these words: “Repent, son, if you have done anything wrong, and you will immediately be restored to your former health.”

What more is there to say? He brought forth a confession of each of his transgressions, more through sobs than words; then he was anointed with blessed oil by the hands of Christ’s priest [Col. 0734B], and in that same hour he recovered so completely that he seemed never to have suffered any illness at all.

A wicked man named Notto dared, together with his accomplices, to inflict an insult upon the holy bishop, claiming that he was not a worshiper of God but rather a man devoted to pleasure. In the nighttime, not only the king but also the queen would sometimes hurry to his bedchamber as though seeking his counsel.

One day, then, when that man had gone to bed with his belly full of wine, together with his companion in slander, the Lord commanded that all their garments be surrounded on every side by flame. They immediately leapt up with an enormous outcry and threw water around their buttocks and genital areas, where their shirts were burning most fiercely [Col. 0734C]; but they could not extinguish the divinely sent flame. At last they both rolled themselves in the mud like pigs in a wallow. There they cried out for a long time and only at last barely escaped the punishment they deserved.

In them, without doubt, was fulfilled what is written in the Psalm: “The one who slanders his neighbor secretly, him I will pursue.” We should not doubt that this too was accomplished by divine judgment: these slanderers were burned most violently in those parts where the lust with which they accused the righteous man was unquestionably dominant.

Not long afterward, the author of this slander, the aforementioned Notto, was himself denounced to the king for such crimes, so that the royal sword might cut off both his offenses and his life, and his son likewise might be subjected to the same sentence. [Col. 0735A]

At about the same time, when blessed Arnolfus had already distributed nearly all the Church’s treasures for the use of the poor, there still remained a silver dish weighing seventy-two pounds. A certain Hugo, first among the nobles, purchased it for a price; but almighty God did not permit a layman to enjoy an object that had long ago been consecrated in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

When the aforementioned Hugo had been struck down by a sudden death, the dish was brought to King Lotharius. When, through the report of certain persons, he learned that blessed Arnolfus had sold it for the sustenance of the poor, he immediately, as though inspired from heaven, ordered that it be swiftly brought to the holy pontiff in the city of Metz, with one hundred gold pieces placed upon it.

When many miracles had begun to increase through the blessed man, he desired to devote himself to God alone and sought some more remote places near the Vosges. There, shut away in a little cell, he struck heaven day and night with his most holy prayers.

Meanwhile, he began to be concerned that the people entrusted to him by the Lord, with him removed, might receive less of the nourishment of eternal life. He therefore sent letters through messengers to the king, earnestly asking that he appoint another bishop in his place, one who might instruct Christ’s people more worthily by the word of preaching.

When Lotharius received this message, he was filled with no small anguish. Complaining that he would be deprived of all counsel if blessed Arnolfus were removed from the palace’s company, he wrote back to him as follows:

“Regarding what you wished to ask through your letter, lord Father—that another bishop be substituted in your place—our presumption in no way dares to do this. Rather, with all devotion, we ask that, if you have resolved to spend your life somewhere in the practice of good works, you remain among the people entrusted to you, as you began, conducting yourself as an example to them by which they may obtain salvation.”

It is not surprising that King Lotharius embraced the blessed man with such affection, since he entrusted his son Dagobert, elevated to the principate, to him for instruction as though he were his own offspring. As long as he lived, he considered it highly beneficial to arrange all the affairs of the kingdom through Arnolfus’s counsel and foresight.

After King Lotharius died, blessed Bishop Arnolfus still burned with the same desire as before—namely, to live in the wilderness—and again and again requested permission for this from Prince Dagobert, whom he himself had carefully raised. The king, stirred against him by the devil, became so angered one day when Arnolfus was overly insistent in his request that he seized a sword and wished to drive him away wounded.

Then Arnolfus, making light of the anger of the king who was about to die, said firmly: “What are you doing, wretched man? Do you wish to repay me evil for good? Now, since this is your pleasure, rage against me as much as you wish. I do not hesitate to die for the love of him who gave me life and died for me.”

As he spoke, one of the nobles standing nearby reproved the king’s rashness in gentle words. His fury was calmed, and by the intervention of God’s grace his criminal intention was prevented from taking effect.

Meanwhile, when the queen arrived and heard of the agitation that had flared up without cause against the man of God, she threw herself, together with the king, at his feet. With tears they asked him to have mercy on them by forgiving the injury they had inflicted, saying:

“Go, lord, to the wilderness as you desire; only let us have you appeased, whom we have unjustly offended.”

After granting them forgiveness, blessed Bishop Arnolfus was leaving the palace when, behold, a multitude of the lame, the blind, and all the poor stood before the doors, crying out to him with raised voices:

“O holy shepherd, why are you abandoning us wretched people? Who will have mercy on us, or who will give us food or clothing?”

To these and similar tearful cries the compassionate Father replied, himself weeping as he said:

“Do not grieve, my little children. God will give you a shepherd who will feed you in compassion and mercy. Be at peace with one another, kind and merciful, so that, while you are oppressed in this present life by poverty and misery, you may deserve to reign happily with Christ in the life to come.”

Having said this, he immediately went forth to the contests of prayer. [Col. 0736C]

After a short time had passed, Saint Goericus, surnamed Appo, was chosen as his successor. He was admirable in the holiness of his life and beloved by all those entrusted to him.

When the excellent man Romaricus heard that blessed Arnolfus had chosen the solitary life, he departed from the region of the Vosges and went to him. By mutual agreement, within the vast solitude of the wilderness they prepared a suitable place for themselves.

But before they left the city to go into the wilderness, I must not be silent about the miracle performed by blessed Arnolfus in that same city.

It happened by chance that, one night, a fire consuming the king’s storeroom raged there, and the flame, belching forth, licked the house threateningly on every side. Suddenly the whole city arose; when the people saw their destruction, they broke into lamentation and cries.

When we heard this, we hurried with rapid steps to the house of the man of God and found him, as was his constant custom, engaged in psalmody. Romaricus immediately took him by the hand and said:

“Come out, lord. Behold, our horses are at the doors. Come out, I say, lest—God forbid—that fire consume you in this city.”

To this he replied: “By no means, beloved. Rather, lead me there and place me near the fire, so that we may see this wicked conflagration that is raging. If God wills me to burn, behold, I am in his hand.”

We therefore held his hands and came to the burning dwelling. At his command, we immediately prostrated ourselves in prayer. When the appointed chapter had been recited, we all rose. Then he raised his hand and opposed the sign of the cross to the flames. At once, marvelously, as though struck from heaven, the fire, harming nothing elsewhere, was wholly turned back within the walls and died out. [Col. 0737A]

When we saw this, we gave thanks to God and, after Matins had been said, returned to our beds.

At that same hour, one of the brothers had the following vision. Looking toward heaven, he saw something like a sign of the cross depicted in a flame of fire, and a voice came from heaven saying: “Do you see this sign? On this night Bishop Arnolfus has, through it, delivered this whole city from the fire.”

While we were all marveling at the power we had seen, by which he had extinguished the fire above, that brother related the vision and led us all into still greater wonder.

After these events, blessed Arnolfus abandoned all worldly possessions, distributed his resources among the poor, and, now faithful and secure in the treasure stored up in heaven, became poor in the world for Christ’s sake but already rich in the power of God. Like a new Elijah, he hastened to the wilderness, and among beasts and wild animals he daily resounded with praises to God.

He took with him several monks, to whom he continually rendered the most faithful service with his own hands: removing and cleaning their shoes from their feet, frequently washing their heads and feet, and also diligently arranging their beds each day. He did not reject kitchen service either; often hungry himself, he cooked for his fellow-monks.

He also adorned the bed on which he lay—with a hair shirt: the bed was mean in the eyes of men but most beautiful in the sight of angels—and rejected soft and costly clothing. [Col. 0737B]

While he was thus leading an angelic life amid these and countless other good works, almighty God wished to call his athlete to the appointed prize. The chosen pontiff, with the religious man Romaricus, his companion, and the other monks standing around him and awaiting his glorious departure from this world, addressed them in these words:

“Beloved lords, entreat Christ for me. For the day is already at hand on which I shall appear to be presented before my Judge. What shall I do? I have done nothing good in this world. I am hemmed in and constrained, surrounded by every crime and sin. Pray for me, then, that I may deserve forgiveness from the Lord.”

Meanwhile the hour came when that holy soul was carried by the hands of angels to Christ. Immediately there was great joy among the heavenly powers, but immense mourning among Christ’s poor and the monks in this world.

When the venerable Bishop Goericus heard of the death of blessed Pontiff Arnolfus, he took with him two other bishops, gathered a great crowd of clergy and laity, and went to the wilderness. With great reverence they lifted up the body of the man of God and returned to the city.

When they came to a certain river whose banks, worn away into soft earth, offered a slippery passage to those traveling along them, the men at the rear who were carrying the bier slipped and fell. But, as I believe, angels were immediately present there. For those in front continued freely on their way without being delayed, until those who had fallen visibly rose before everyone and, placing themselves once more beneath the bier, fulfilled their part in the service as before.

Another miracle also occurred on that journey. In the district of Calvomont, there was a certain incestuous man named Centa. While blessed Arnolfus was still alive, he had often wished to lead him to reform but had been unable to do so; he therefore left him without repentance.

When those carrying the blessed man’s funeral bier reached the boundaries of this incestuous man’s property, suddenly the limbs of the bearers stiffened, so that they could not proceed any farther in any way.

When the priests and all the people saw this, they began to be greatly distressed and wondered what they should do and where they should turn, especially since the day was already declining toward evening. Duke Notto, who was one of those walking with them, said:

“It is evident that this holy man disdains to enter the land of this incestuous man. Therefore, if we could reach my residence, which is some distance from here, before night begins, I would provide what necessities I have at hand—even though I fear I am no longer able to refresh such a great multitude, since you have arrived unexpectedly and have found me wholly unprepared.”

When they heard this, all the people set out toward the town of that same duke. The bearers of the bier were given such speed that, arriving at the appointed place before daylight ended, they seemed rather to feel themselves being carried than to be carrying the body themselves.

Then Notto said: “Since we have very little prepared, let Saint Arnolfus provide for us this night.” The effectiveness of events followed these words of faith. For such an abundance of food and drink appeared that, after everyone had been sufficiently fed, half of it still remained for the following day.

After this they reached the city with great prosperity and joy. Stirred by the report, the citizens ran out to meet them with crosses and candles, in immense joy and wonder. They received their shepherd, whom they had lost earlier when he fled by God’s judgment, now reigning in heaven, and they reverently laid his sacred body in the basilica of the holy apostles.

When he had been buried, he demonstrated by miracles what he had obtained from Christ in the wilderness for his fellow citizens.

A certain woman named Julia, who had long been blinded in her eyes, approached the man of God’s tomb and prayed with confidence. Without delay she received the sight she had desired for so long. She then saw with her own eyes the paths along which she had previously been accustomed to walk only with the help of another’s hand, and returned joyfully to her lodging.

I must not be silent about another miracle, which I recently learned through the account of the religious man Arnegaudus, the abbot.

At about the same time, a certain woman living in the suburb had dared to work on the Lord’s Day. Struck by God’s judgment, both her hands became contracted. Overwhelmed by great anguish, she went to the aforementioned abbot and tearfully begged his mercy.

He immediately instructed her to hurry in faith to the tomb of the holy bishop. When she arrived there, she found the monastery doors closed. She gave herself over to prayer with tears, asking Saint Arnolfus to heal her. After she had long entreated the Lord, through the intercession of the blessed pontiff’s merits her contracted fingers were loosened, and the desired remedy followed with great speed.

At about the same time, a little man named Cero, whose feet were so contracted that, supported by crutches on either side, he could move forward only with a pitiful, halting gait, was healed at the man of God’s tomb. He returned to his home with the natural soles of his feet made firm—he who had come there without feet naturally formed for him. [Col. 0740A]

These few accounts, out of the many manifestations of miracles by this blessed pontiff, we have inserted in writing as best we could. If we had decided to set down in writing all that he did, our pen would have produced an enormous and excessively tedious volume.

For the present, let these things suffice for the benevolent reader, who, for the benefits displayed through the merits of the holy bishop for the salvation of many, should bless the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong power and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# MISCELLANEOUS HISTORY, COMPILED BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR, INCLUDING THE HISTORY OF EUTROPIUS, WHICH PAUL THE DEACON EXTENDED WITH MANY ADDITIONS AT THE REQUEST OF ADELBERGA [Al., ADHILBERGA], DUCHESS OF BENEVENTO. HE BROUGHT IT DOWN FROM THE REIGN OF VALENTINIAN TO THE TIMES OF JUSTINIAN. AND LANDULPHUS SAGAX, OR SOMEONE ELSE, CONTINUED IT TO THE YEAR OF CHRIST 816.

*(From Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0739]

# MURATORIUS’S PREFACE

I have thought it appropriate to give first place in our Collection to the History commonly called the Miscellany. Since my plan has been to assemble those writers who, from approximately the five-hundredth year after the birth of Christ, pursued the history of Italy, this author seemed able, so to speak, to prepare the way for the others, since he continues to narrate events in Italy from the foundation of the City and brings them down to the end of the eighth century of the Christian era.

Thus readers will have, joined to the ancient history of the Romans, the deeds of the following centuries, collected by an ancient author. The sequence of events will thereby become more orderly, being contained in a single thread of narration, and the readers’ progress from ancient times to more recent ones will be easier and more pleasant.

The learned called it Miscellaneous History because it was excerpted from various authors, their narratives being mixed together into a single body.

But who was the author of this Miscellany? Let us hear Vossius, book II, chapter 30, of *On Latin Historians*:

“The first eleven books,” he says, “are the same as the ten books of Eutropius, except that Paul [namely, the deacon] occasionally adds something of his own.
