This was done at the command of Adelberga, or Adhilberga, duchess of Benevento, whose husband was Arichis, father of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. Paul then continues Eutropius; the next five books are his. The remaining books—namely the seventeenth and those that follow—were added by Landulphus Sagax, chiefly from Theophanes or Anastasius the Librarian, who translated Theophanes.”

Cave makes a similar statement.

Dupin, however, in volume VI of *Ecclesiastical Authors in the Library*, writing about Paul the Deacon, says:

“The abridgment of Roman History drawn from several writers is also wrongly attributed to him. For although he added to the *Breviary of Roman History* composed by Eutropius, he is not the author of this Collection, which rather had Anastasius the Librarian as its author.”

On the other hand, the great father of the *Annals*, Baronius, under the year 719, cites:

“The Annals of the Greeks, by Theophanes, who wrote in Greek that History entitled the Miscellany, which is circulated under the title of Paul the Deacon through an error.”

Yet such eminent men ought to have proceeded more cautiously or accurately in investigating the author of the Miscellany.

Baronius, in fact, departed far from the truth by attributing the entire Miscellany to Theophanes. Vossius attempts to absolve him from this opinion by saying that Baronius, following Fronto Ducaeus, did not mean to attribute the whole Miscellaneous History to Theophanes or Anastasius, but only “the final books.”

Yet Baronius’s words under the year 719, which we cited above, are clear. There exists Theophanes’ Greek *Chronography*, together with its translation, and also an Ecclesiastical History translated from Greek by Anastasius. [Col. 0741]

It is clearer than midday that the Miscellany, especially in its final books, was composed from the same Theophanes and Anastasius, while the earlier books were compiled from other sources.

As for Dupin’s view that Anastasius was rather the author of this Collection, I see that too asserted without evidence. Although the later books of the Miscellany are derived from the History Anastasius translated from Greek, and are often reproduced word for word, we have no ancient writer or manuscript testifying that the Miscellaneous History is owed to the work of Anastasius the Librarian.

But should Paul the Deacon be called its author, as many have thought? This too cannot be maintained if we are speaking of the complete work. For that History extends to the year 813, namely to the first year of the reign of the emperor Leo the Armenian, not to 806, as Canisius wrote, failing to notice that the Dionysian era differs by seven years from the Alexandrian era used by Theophanes.

Paul the Deacon is believed to have died around the year 799 after Christ; consequently, we understand that the structure of the Miscellany must be attributed to a more recent author. Moreover, from book XVII through book XXIV almost everything is taken from the translation of the Greek History which, beyond all doubt, was composed by Anastasius the Librarian—that is, by an author who lived and wrote more than a century and a half after Paul the Deacon’s death.

Who, then, would attribute the compilation of the entire Miscellany to Paul? I have said too little. Even in those books which, by the consensus of scholars, are believed to have Paul as their source—namely book XII and the following books—many passages occur which, as I have learned by comparison, are taken from Anastasius’s celebrated translation. Therefore not even that portion of the Miscellany which scholars call an appendix to Eutropius and ascribe to Paul the Deacon seems attributable to his name and work.

Amid these difficulties, let the learned accept the opinion that seems most convincing to me.

First, it must in no way be denied that Paul Warnefridus, or Paul the Deacon, contributed certain additions to Eutropius’s *Breviary*. Leo Marsicanus, bishop of Ostia, a thoroughly ancient and learned writer, scarcely allows us to doubt this. He writes as follows in book I, chapter 15, of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, speaking of Paul the Deacon:

“At the request of that same Adelperga—whom above he had called the daughter of King Desiderius—he added here and there to the Roman History which Eutropius had briefly composed a great deal from Ecclesiastical Histories. Finally, he attached to it two little books, extending from the time of Julian the Apostate, at which Eutropius had ended that History, to the time of the first emperor Justinian.”

Second, since even in those same books which are said to have been added by Paul from his own resources there occur certain fragments drawn from Anastasius’s translation, it seems certain to me that this Miscellaneous History was compiled not by Paul the Deacon and not by Anastasius the Librarian, but by some author—certainly a very ancient one, though later than they—who, after extracting material from the works of Eutropius, Paul, Anastasius, and other ancient books, completed the framework of the entire Miscellany.

Indeed, allow me to say that I am surprised scholars have not yet noticed how greatly the commonly circulated books of the Miscellany depart from those which Paul added to Eutropius.

I possess the *Breviary of Eutropius* restored to its integrity by Elias Vinetus and published at Amsterdam in 1625 together with other abbreviators of Roman History. There, after the ten books of Eutropius—which lack much of what is read elsewhere in the Miscellany—there follows Paul the Deacon’s book XI, added to Eutropius’s History concerning the deeds of the Romans.

Paul proceeds to book XVII, which he concludes as follows:

“Since there still remain matters to be said concerning the felicity of Augustus Justinian, they must be brought forth in the following little book, God presiding.”

The subsequent book XVIII extends its narrative to Leo the Isaurian. Yet it offers nothing that does not occur here and there, scattered through the *History of the Lombards*. Thus it may be doubted whether Paul himself wrote these things and also inserted them into his *History of the Lombards*, or whether someone else, extracting them from that work, composed book XVIII of the Miscellany.

Nevertheless, since in the most ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library the following words are read at the end of book XVII—the words I quoted earlier, clearly indicating that a book was to follow—although that book is missing from the same manuscript, it may be conjectured that Paul composed it and that it is the book published by Vinetus. Paul himself, or someone else, may later have divided it into fragments and reproduced it once more in the *History of the Lombards*.

Therefore Vinetus’s edition contains Paul’s genuine and original appendix to Eutropius, which the author of the Miscellany subsequently enlarged with other additions. Consequently, the great difference between the edition of Paul’s appendix prepared by Vinetus and the books of the Miscellany attributed by scholars to Paul the Deacon finally proves that not even any portion of the Miscellany can be attributed exclusively to Paul the Deacon.

To investigate this matter more certainly, I took care to consult the aforementioned Ambrosian manuscript through the learned Saxius, prefect of the library. He wrote to me that the additions to Eutropius there agree with Vinetus’s edition, but not with the printed books of the Miscellany, and that book XI begins as follows:

“In the year 1118 from the foundation of the City [Vinetus has 1119], Valentinian, the thirty-eighth, born at Cibalae in Pannonia, etc.”

Finally, then, I think it should be established as the more probable view that the Miscellaneous History was composed, under the direction of someone, after the time of Anastasius the Librarian, from various authors—namely from the books of Eutropius, Florus, Suetonius, Victor, Eusebius, Rufinus, Orosius, Jordanes, and others—and above all from the Ecclesiastical History which the aforementioned Anastasius translated from Greek and handed down to posterity.

Some write that this compiler was Landulphus, surnamed Sagax, perhaps relying upon the authority of some manuscript. Ciacconius, on the other hand, in his *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, calls the author of the Miscellany Paul, or rather John the Deacon.

But whoever he was—whether Landulphus Sagax or John the Deacon—nothing further can be said about such an author, since the monuments of antiquity have left us nothing about him beyond his bare name.

It is useful only to note that, in the time of the aforementioned Anastasius, that is, around the year 875, there flourished John the Deacon of the Roman Church, counted among ecclesiastical writers. Through his work we possess the Life of Saint Gregory the Great in four books, which has often been reprinted.

He may have been the author of the Miscellany; but whether he was, I consider uncertain. Therefore, perhaps it will be wiser in future, when occasion arises to use this History, to omit the name and cite only “the author of the Miscellany.”

As we indicated above, the Ambrosian Library possesses a parchment manuscript of great importance. Unless my conjecture deceives me, it appears to have been written eight hundred years ago, or at least seven hundred, in small, rounded characters.

It begins with the *History of the English*, by Bede the priest; then follows Dictys Cretensis on the Trojan War, without the letter to Rufinus that appears in the printed editions.

Next follows book I of the Roman History:

“In Italy, according to some, Janus was the first to reign, etc.”

These words concern Eutropius, whose name is not mentioned there. Afterward are attached the books added by Paul the Deacon, which differ from the text of the Miscellany; Paul’s own name is also omitted.

From these materials joined together, sixteen books are formed, ending with the death of Justin I Augustus. After him Paul promises that he will speak about the reign of Justinian I Augustus, but this book is missing there.

After this one reads Paul’s *History of the Lombards*, ending at chapter 55 of book VI. Then begins a prologue to the *History of the Goths*, but without mentioning the name of Jordanes, or Jornandes; the distinguished man Puricellius nevertheless added that name in a recent hand.

At the end are found, besides Seneca’s fictitious letters to the Apostle Paul, the [Col. 0743] *Deeds of Apollonius of Tyre*, which should be counted among Roman tales. These were written by a different hand from the preceding materials and are consequently less ancient.

But there is no need to recommend further the dignity and usefulness of the *Miscella*. In it the republic of scholars possesses a continuous sequence of universal history—especially Roman and Italian history—collected into one whole: material which must otherwise be sought laboriously, and sometimes unsuccessfully, from other authors. Nor should this Collection be thought insignificant because its author lived too far removed from the flourishing Roman republic. He himself is exceedingly ancient, and wrote in times when many histories still survived, whose irreparable destruction we, born later, lament with fruitless complaint. Certainly so many books of Livy, Tacitus, Trogus Pompeius, and other chroniclers have perished; but perhaps they had not all disappeared when this writer undertook to compose the *Miscella*. Therefore, whenever the excellent monuments of antiquity fail us, it is useful to turn to those who, although they flourished several centuries later, were nevertheless able to handle the books of the ancients more fortunately than we can. Thus the *Miscella* too will have its own honor, and it will be the mark of a learned and at the same time prudent critic to summon it as a witness and make use of its assistance wherever the older histories are either silent or disagree among themselves.

This History was published at Paris in 1531, and then at Basel in 1569. It subsequently appeared at Ingolstadt under the care of Heinrich Canisius, with variant readings, in 1603, and at Hanover, with emendations and notes by Jan Gruter, in 1611. It was also included in volume XIII of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1677.

[Col. 0743]

## NOTICE TO THE READER

We have never learned more clearly how many additions were made to this History, which they called the *Miscella*, over the course of time than when this new edition had to be prepared. For we had at our disposal five ancient parchment codices preserved in the very rich Ambrosian Library, and, after examining them all carefully, we found them written in almost one continuous text and containing that immense sequence of events, excerpted chiefly from Greek authors, which appears for the most part in the printed editions.

For this reason, in our collation we selected the older and most trustworthy codex praised by the very learned Muratori in his preface to this History. We believed that we would thereby earn the gratitude of scholars by presenting its complete reading, so that the reader might recognize, almost at a single glance, whatever had been added to this *Miscella* in later times. We arranged the matter as follows: what is read in our codex was printed in the old, as it is called, common type, while the remainder was printed in italics, commonly called cursive type.

If anything had been omitted from the printed editions but was found in our codex, we inserted all of it in the notes at the foot of each page, together with the variant readings, wherever appropriate. In this way the entire Ambrosian codex has been published, its reading being continued through our notes and through the old form of type.

Since, however, in another of the Ambrosian codices we found the section attributed to Landulfus Sagax, and observed that it was altogether different from the printed version, we decided to place it at the end of the History, so that readers would not be wearied by a long series of notes. It should not be passed over in silence that Landulfus Sagax—or anyone else responsible for such an addition—did nothing other than repeat, in abbreviated form, the History of Paul the Deacon, generally using his very words.

The initial letters preceding the notes are distributed as follows: the letter A designates the Ambrosian Codex; B, the various readings of Bongarsius Bodryaeus; H, the Hersfeld manuscript edited by Canisius. We reproduce here the preface to its variant readings:

> “The distinguished Jacobus Bongarsius Bodryaeus noted variant readings in the *Miscella* from a manuscript of Paul the Deacon, and likewise from the manuscript of Pithoeus and from others. We obtained these variant readings. And since I also possessed the parchment manuscript of Paul the Deacon from the monastery of Hersfeld, I collated that one as well.
>
> “So that anyone might see what the final author added to the *Miscella*, we therefore indicate in the variant readings how Eutropius, Paul the Deacon, and our *Miscella* differ; this is done especially as far as the point at which Eutropius ends. For the remaining books of Paul the Deacon, by which he continues Eutropius, are readily available there.
>
> “For Paul the Deacon was the first to assemble the History of the *Miscella*, and he copied Eutropius almost entirely, adding from time to time certain material from other authors; afterward Landulfus Sagax enlarged it. The Hersfeld manuscript has the following about Paul the Deacon:
>
> “‘This Paul was a monk of Monte Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict. He also composed the Life of Saint Gregory the pope, as he himself says in his book on the Lombards. He also composed the hymn “*Ut queant laxis*,” and certain other useful works.’”

[Col. 0743]

[Note: The Ambrosian Codex bears the title: *The Breviary of Roman History by Eutropius*.]

# MISCELLANEOUS HISTORY

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0743D] According to some authorities, Janus was the first to reign in Italy. Saturn followed him. Fleeing from Greece to escape Jupiter, his son, Saturn hid himself in a city called Saturnia after his name; its ruins can still be seen in the territory of Tuscany, not far from Rome. Because Saturn hid in Italy, the region was called Latium from his hiding place. He himself first taught the still-uncivilized peoples to build houses, cultivate the land, plant vineyards, and live according to human customs, whereas previously they had supported life only on acorns, being half-wild, and had lived either in caves or in huts woven from branches and foliage. He also first introduced bronze coins among them. For these services he was called a god by the rustic multitude of the inhabitants.

[Note: A. and H. read *ab indocili et rust.* (“by the untaught and rustic [multitude]”); B. reads *ab indocili inc.* (“by the untaught, un…,” abbreviated).]

These words, up to “After him came his son Faunus,” are absent from the Hersfeld manuscript of Paul the Deacon.

After him came Picus, his son. It is related in myth that, because he rejected the love of a certain very famous sorceress named Circe, he was changed into a bird bearing his name. After him came his son Faunus, who was the father of Latinus. His mother, Carmentis Nicostrata, is believed to have discovered the Latin letters. During their reigns, one hundred and fifty years are said to have elapsed.

While Latinus was reigning—he corrected the Latin language and gave the Latins their name—Troy was captured by the Greeks. At that time Labdon was in the third year of his rule among the Hebrews; Teutanes was reigning among the Assyrians; and Thoos was reigning among the Egyptians.

[Note: A., B., and H. read *Tautanes*.]

[Note: B. and H. read *Thous*.]

This occurred after four thousand and nineteen years from the beginning of the world; one thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven years from the Flood;

[Note: H. reads: 1,782 years from the Flood.]

eight hundred and five years from the birth of Abraham and in the forty-third year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians;

[Note: A. and H. read: “in the eight hundred and thirty-fifth year from the birth of Abraham and in the forty-third year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians.”]

four hundred and ten years from the birth of Moses; four hundred and four years before the founding of Rome; and four hundred and six years before the first Olympiad.

After Troy had been captured, Aeneas, son of Venus and Anchises, came to Italy in the third year after the destruction of Troy. He fought Turnus, son of Daunus, king of the Tuscans, and killed him; he took Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, as his wife, and after her name called Lavinium the town he had built. Aeneas therefore reigned over the Latins for three years.

When he died, Ascanius, also called Iulus, his son, succeeded to the kingdom. Aeneas had begotten him at Troy by his wife Creusa, daughter of King Priam, and had brought him with him to Italy.

[Note: This is not found in the cited manuscripts A., B., and H.]

Ascanius, leaving the kingdom to his stepmother Lavinia, founded Alba Longa. With great devotion he raised his brother Silvius Postumus, who later reigned after him, the son of Aeneas and Lavinia. He also transferred the household gods of his father Aeneas from Lavinium to Alba Longa. The statues, however, returned to Lavinium of their own accord. When they were again carried to Alba Longa, they once more sought out the older shrines.

[Note: Likewise, all this is marked in a different typeface.]

Ascanius then fathered a son, Iulus, from whom the family of the Julians arose.

[Note: B. reads: “his own Iulus.”]

[Note: A. reads: “a little child, and one who was not yet fit to govern citizens.” B. and H. read: “A little child, because he was not yet fit to govern citizens.” A further reading in the manuscripts is: “Ascanius, after thirty-eight years.”]

He was a little child and was not yet fit for the civic responsibilities of government. After Ascanius had reigned for thirty-eight years,

[Note: A. reads thirty-nine.]

he left his brother Silvius Postumus as heir to the kingdom.

Silvius Postumus therefore reigned for twenty-nine years.

[Note: A., B., and H. likewise read twenty-nine.]

He was called Postumus because he was born after his father’s death; Silvius because he had been raised in the countryside. From him all the Alban kings were called Silvii. After him Aeneas Silvius reigned for thirty-one years. Then Latinus Silvius reigned for fifty years; during his reign David was also reigning among the Hebrews. After his death Alba Silvius reigned for thirty-nine years.

[Note: “He reigned.” I correct the text from B. and H. The common text, followed by Canisius, reads corruptly: “he undertook the kingdom.”]

After him came Aegyptus, or Atvs, his son, for twenty-four years. Then Capis Silvius, son of the preceding king, reigned for twenty-eight years; he founded Capua in Campania. Likewise Capetus Silvius, son of Capis, reigned for thirteen years.

[Note: A., B., and H. read *Carpentus*.]

Tiberinus, son of Capetus, followed for nine years. The river Tiber was named after him because he fell into it and died; previously it had been called the Albula.

Agrippa Silvius succeeded him and reigned for forty years. Homer is said to have lived in Greece during his reign. After him Remus Silvius, son of the earlier king Agrippa, reigned for nineteen years. He established a fortress for the Albans among the hills where Rome now stands; because of his impiety he was struck by lightning and died.

After him Aventinus Silvius reigned for thirty-seven years. He was the son of Remus, the earlier king, and, having died and been buried on the hill that is now part of the city, gave the place its enduring name.

[Note: A. and B. read *Aremuli*; H. reads *Remuli*.]

His successor was Procas Silvius, son of the same Aventinus. He reigned for twenty-two years.

[Note: A. reads twenty-three. B. reads: “son of Aventinus, who reigned for twenty-three years.” H. agrees with A.]

While he was reigning, Phidon of Argos discovered measures and weights.

[Note: B. reads *Sidon*; H. reads *Fidon*.]

At that time Aza was reigning in Judaea and Jerusalem.

[Note: A., B., and H. read: “Azarias in Judah and Jeroboam in Israel [or Jerusalem] were reigning.”]

Amulius, his younger son, succeeded him and reigned for forty-three years. Numitor, the elder son of King Procas, was driven from the kingdom by his brother Amulius and lived on his estate. His daughter was selected as a Vestal virgin so that she might be prevented from bearing children, and so forth.

[Note: From these words onward, the passage is absent from the Hersfeld manuscript of Paul the Deacon.]

When Procas died, he left his will to his two sons, Amulius and Numitor, stipulating that one should immediately receive the money and the other the kingdom. Amulius, however, gave his brother Numitor the choice of what he wished to receive. Numitor took the money, while Amulius obtained the kingdom, in which he reigned for forty-three years.

While he held the kingdom, he consulted the gods, and received the response that he would be killed by his brother’s offspring and lose the kingdom. He immediately drove Numitor from the kingdom. Numitor, departing, lived on his estate.

He had two children, Sergestus and Rhea, who was also called Ilia. Fearing the oracle, King Amulius took Sergestus hunting with him and killed him in the forest. He made Rhea, also called Ilia, a Vestal virgin, so that she might be prevented from bearing children.

When, in the seventh year of her uncle’s reign, she gave birth to twin infants, she was buried alive in the ground according to the law. But Faustulus, the royal herdsman, carried the infants, who had been exposed near the bank of the Tiber,

[Note: A. reads “of the river.”]

to his wife Acca Laurentia. Because of her beauty and her bodily appetite, she had been called by her neighbors a money-making she-wolf.

[Note: A. reads: “Because of their beauty and their bodily rapacity, they were called she-wolves by their neighbors.” B. reads: “she was called a she-wolf by her neighbors.”]

For this reason, even to our own day, the cells of prostitutes are called *lupanaria*, “wolf-dens.” When the boys had grown up, they gathered a band of shepherds and robbers, killed Amulius at Alba,

[Note: A. reads: “after Amulius had been killed at Alba.”]

and restored their grandfather Numitor to the kingdom.

[Note: From these words the longer history of Eutropius begins. It is therefore clear that the preceding material was added by Paul the Deacon. —Canisius.]

The Roman Empire—which, as far as human memory can recall, was scarcely anywhere smaller at its beginning, nor anywhere greater in its expansion throughout the whole world—takes its origin from Romulus. He was, as has been stated above, the son of the Vestal virgin Rhea Silvia and, as was believed, of Mars; he was born together with his brother Remus in a single birth.

When he was eighteen years old and was engaging in brigandage among shepherds, he established a small city on the Palatine hill on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad,

[Note: The Pithoeus manuscript has the reading found in the common edition. The manuscript of François Fabrus reads 414. Manuscripts A., B., and H. also agree with the common edition, except that they do not contain the word “fourth.” Eutropius, in Merula’s edition, reads: “the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the third year of the sixth Olympiad, 394 years after the destruction of Troy,” according to those who give the highest and lowest figures.]

419 years after the destruction of Troy, or, as Orosius preferred, 404 years after it, six years before the ten tribes of Israel were transferred by Sennacherib, king of the Chaldeans, to the mountains of the Medes.

After founding the city, which he called Rome after his own name, and from which the Romans also received their name, he did approximately the following. Having built a temple which he called the Asylum, he promised immunity to all who fled to him. For this reason he received into the city a multitude of neighboring people who had incurred some offense among their own fellow citizens and had fled to him.

[Note: This is not found in H. A. reads: “Finally, Latins and Tuscans who were shepherds, and even the Phrygians from overseas who had come with Aeneas, and the Arcadians who had arrived under the leadership of Evander, flowed together. Thus he gathered them, as it were, from various elements into a single body and made them one Roman people.”]

Finally, Latins and Tuscan shepherds, as well as Phrygians from overseas who had come with Aeneas and Arcadians who had arrived under the leadership of Evander, flowed together. Thus, as it were from various elements, he gathered them into one body and made them a single Roman people.

He selected one hundred elders, by whose counsel he would conduct everything. He called them senators because of their old age, and fathers because of the similarity of their care. He also selected one thousand fighting men, whom he called soldiers from their number.

Since neither he nor his people had wives, he invited the nations of the neighboring cities to a spectacle of games and carried off their maidens in the fourth year from the founding of Rome.

[Note: H. reads “the third year.” Dionysius, Book II, says that this occurred in the fourth year of Romulus and that the number of maidens was 683. —Canisius.]

Then the most beautiful of the maidens, amid the acclamation of all the abductors, was awarded to Thalassius, the commander of Romulus.

[Col. 0747C]

Hence, even today, at wedding ceremonies people commonly shout “Thalassius,” meaning that the bride is of such a kind that she deserves to have Thalassius.

[Note: This word is absent from manuscripts B. and H.]

When wars were stirred up because of the outrage committed against the abducted women, he defeated the Caeninenses,

[Note: A. reads “Cecinenses.”]

the Antemnates, the Crustumini, the Sabines, and the Fidenates.

[Note: B. and H. read “the Fidenates and Bicentes.” Our A. likewise has this reading. Canisius reads “the Veientes,” as does Eutropius.]

All these towns surround the city. At that time the maiden Tarpeia was crushed beneath the shields of the Sabines on the hill that, after her name, was called the Tarpeian Hill; the Capitol was later built there.

The Romans nevertheless made a treaty of friendship with the Sabines, whose daughters they had carried off, to such an extent that the elderly Sabine king Titus Tatius reigned alongside Romulus.

[Note: A. reads: “reigned with Romulus, and the Sabines…” B. and H. read: “reigned equally with Romulus, and the Sabines…”]

As soon as Romulus had admitted him into a partnership of kingship, he killed him. The Sabines and Romans also became one people.

At that time, in order to strengthen their union, the Romans placed the Sabines’ names before their own names, and the Sabines did the same with Roman names. From that time the custom continued that no Roman should be without a personal name.

Because of this same association, when Romulus carried a long spear in the Sabine manner—a spear called *quiris* in their language—he was called Quirinus.

[Note: A. reads *Ciris* and *Cirinus*. B. and H. read: “It was called *Cyris*, and he was called Quirinus.” B. nevertheless has *Cirinius*.]

The Romans, whether from *quirites*, meaning long spears, or from Quirinus, began to be called Quirites.

Finally, Remus was killed by Fabius, the commander of his brother Romulus, with, as is said, Romulus’ consent, by a shepherd’s mattock.

[Note: A. and B. read: “it is uncertain whether with his brother’s consent, by a mattock…”]

The reason for his death was this: he had scolded them for saying that the rampart which they had built for the protection of the new city would not be sufficient, and he had leapt across its narrow limits.

[Note: These two words are absent from B. and H., as well as from A.; the following words, beginning “with the Veientines,” are also absent up to “Romulus, however.”]

A battle was still being waged against the Veientine peoples, insignificant in name but great in strength; the town of the Caeninenses had been captured and destroyed. Once they had taken up arms, there was never any rest for them, since at home they feared disgraceful poverty and shameful hunger if ever they settled down to peace or a treaty.

But when Romulus, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, had been struck by lightning at the Goat Marsh and had disappeared, he was believed to have passed to the gods in the thirty-ninth year of his reign and was consecrated under the name Quirinus.

[Note: B. and H. read: “When Romulus had disappeared at the Goat Marsh…” See Dionysius, Book II, and Valerius, Book V, chapter 3.]

Then the senators ruled at Rome for five days at a time, and under their rule one year was completed.

Afterward Numa Pompilius was made king, while Hezekiah was reigning among the Hebrews. He waged no war, but benefited the state no less than Romulus. For he established the worship of the gods, laws, and customs among the Romans, who by their habitual warfare now seemed brigands and half-barbarians.

[Note: This is not found in the cited manuscripts.]

He also organized the year into ten months, which had previously been confused and without any calculation, and established countless rites and temples at Rome. He died of illness in the forty-first year of his reign.

[Note: Vineto placed faulty punctuation at this point, although he acknowledges it in Bongarsius’ manuscript. H. reads: “He divided it into ten months. Previously it had been confused, without any reckoning, and limitless, etc.” Eutropius, and Paul after him, attribute to Numa what all attribute to Romulus. Romulus divided the year into ten months; Numa added two. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* 1.1.]

While Numa was reigning, Glaucus first devised the method of joining iron by welding.

Tullus Hostilius succeeded him. He was the first among the Romans to use purple and the fasces, while Manasseh was reigning in Judaea. He renewed the wars, relying on a youth well trained in arms, and made war upon the Albans, who are now called Albans and live twelve miles from Rome. He defeated them in the sixth engagement, with a disastrous slaughter.

[Note: In A. and H., after the word “renewed,” the following is read: “He defeated the Albans, who are twelve miles from the city of Rome; he overcame the Veientes and Fidenates in war, of whom some are seven miles from the city of Rome and others eighteen miles away. He enlarged the city, etc.” B. reads *Vogentes* instead of *Veientes*.]

He also defeated the Veientes and Fidenates in war; some were six miles from Rome and others eighteen miles away.

[Note: In B. and H., as in Eutropius, the passage from this point through “he enlarged the city” is absent.]

When peace was again broken, Mettius Fufetius, planning a deceit in the war against Fidenae, had been summoned by the Romans after a temporary peace had been arranged. He treacherously deserted and deceived them so completely that, in the midst of the battle, he sat with his army on a nearby hill.

The Roman king Tullus Hostilius then used his ingenuity and said that Mettius had withdrawn on his advice, so that, once the signal had been given, he might fall upon the enemy columns from the rear. Thus he revived the spirits of his own men, who had already despaired because their support had withdrawn, and terrified the Albans; he defeated the Fidenates.

He had Mettius Fufetius tied to chariots and torn apart because of his treachery.

He enlarged the city by adding the Caelian Hill. After reigning for thirty-two years, he was struck by lightning and burned together with his house.

During these times the city of Byzantium was founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans; it was later called Constantinople.

[Note: This is absent from A., B., and H., as is the passage shortly afterward: “he defeated all the neighboring peoples as far as the Aventine.”]

After him Ancus Marcius, grandson of Numa through his daughter, assumed the power. At that time Josiah was also reigning among the Hebrews.

He fought against the Latins, defeated all the neighboring peoples, and, through countless engagements, crushed the twelve powerful peoples of Tuscany. He added the Aventine Hill and the Janiculum to the city.

[Note: B. and H. read: “He founded the city of Ostia beside the sea, sixteen miles from the city of Rome.” A. reads: “likewise in the twenty-third year.”]

He founded the city of Ostia beside the sea, sixteen miles from Rome. He died of illness in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. During his reign Epidamnus was founded, which was later called Dyrrachium.

[Note: B. reads: “During his reign Epidaurus was founded, which was later called Dyrrachium.” H. reads: “Epidamnus was founded, which was later called Dyrrhachium.” A. reads *Duratium*.]

Then Priscus Tarquinius assumed the kingdom. He doubled the number of senators and built the Circus at Rome. He established the Roman Games, which continue to our own day.

[Note: These are the words of Eutropius.]

He also defeated the Sabines and joined to the territory of the city of Rome a considerable amount of land that he had taken from them.

[Note: B., H., and Eutropius read “the same land.”]

He was the first to enter Rome in triumph. He built walls and sewers and began the Capitol. In the thirty-seventh year of his reign he was killed by the sons of Ancus, the king whom he had succeeded.

While Tarquinius was reigning, Arion of Methymna is said to have been transported by a dolphin to Taenarum.

[Note: A. reads “between the seas”; B., “into a warm bath”; H., “of the inner regions.”]

At that time Massilia was also founded. In that period Jerusalem was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans.

After him Servius Tullius assumed the power. He was born of a noble woman who was nevertheless a captive and a slave, and he reigned for thirty-four years.

[Note: The remainder is not found in A. or in the cited manuscripts.]

While he was sleeping in the lap of Tarquinius Priscus, his head appeared to burn. When Tanaquil, the king’s wife, saw this portent, she raised him among her own children; for this reason he attained the kingdom.

While he was reigning, Belshazzar ruled the Chaldeans. Under him Daniel read and interpreted the mysterious writing on the wall.

[Note: B. reads “the Chaldean”; A. reads “Chaldaean.”]

Servius also subdued the Sabines, defeated the Veientes in battle and broke their power, though he did not subdue them, and added the three hills—the Quirinal, Viminal, and Esquiline—to the city. He dug a ditch around the walls.

[Note: B. reads: “He subdued the Sabines and the three hills, the Quirinal, Viminal, and Erculian.” H. reads: “He subdued the Sabines and the three hills, the Quirinal, Viminal, and Esquiline.” A. reads *Culinum* for *Esquilinum*, and shortly afterward *citra* for *circum*.]

He was the first of all to organize a census, which until then had been unknown throughout the world. Under him, after everyone at Rome had been registered, the city had 84,000 Roman citizens, including those who lived in the countryside.

He was killed by the crime of his son-in-law Tarquinius Superbus, the son of the king whom Servius had succeeded, and of the daughter whom Tarquinius had as his wife.

[Note: The remainder is not found in the manuscript or in Eutropius.]

At the same time Claudia Quinta, a Vestal virgin, was accused of sexual misconduct. But she, unwilling to clear herself by ordinary means, went to the ship in the shallows of the Tiber and climbed aboard it. She tied the prow with her girdle and said: “If I am a virgin, follow me.” Immediately the ship moved and entered Rome.

Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh and last king, then seized the power. At that time 42,400 Jews returned to Jerusalem at the release granted by Cyrus, king of the Persians.

[Note: A. reads: “42,000 Jews returned to Jerusalem, etc.”]

He was the first to devise fetters, bull-hide whips, clubs and plates,

[Note: A., B., and H. read *lautumias* instead of *laminas*.]

shackles, chains, exile, the mines, and prisons.

He defeated the Volscians, a people not far from Rome for those traveling toward Campania.

[Note: A. adds afterward: “He defeated and subdued the cities of Gabii, Suessa, and Pometia.” H. likewise has this addition.]

He subdued the strong towns in Latium, namely Ocriculum, Gabii, Suessa, and Pometia. He made peace with the Tuscans and built a temple to Jupiter on the Capitol.

Later, while besieging Ardea, a city situated eighteen miles from Rome, he lost the power. For when his son Sextus Tarquinius, armed at night, had violently violated the noble Lucretia, daughter of Lucretius Tricipitinus and wife of Collatinus, she summoned her husband, father, and friends from the camp. Weeping and ashamed, she complained of the violence she had suffered.

[Note: A., B., H., and Eutropius read: “When his son, himself the younger Tarquinius, had violated the most noble wife of Collatinus, and she had complained of the outrage to her husband, father, and friends, she killed herself in the sight of all. For this reason Brutus, a relative and himself a Tarquin, etc.” A. consistently reads *Conlatinus*.]

They tried to console her by saying that the guilt of violence inflicted by another did not touch her chastity: it was not her honorable mind but only her body that had been violated. “No unchaste woman,” she said, “shall henceforth defend herself by the example of Lucretia.” Then she suddenly plunged into her entrails the sword that she had concealed beneath her clothing.

For this reason Brutus, himself a relative of Tarquinius, also roused the people and deprived Tarquinius of the power.

[Note: A. reads: “Soon the army too, which was besieging the city of Ardea together with the king, abandoned him.” H. reads: “which had attacked it.”]

The army also soon abandoned him; it had been attacking the city of Ardea together with the king. The king came to the city, but was shut out when the gates were closed. After he had reigned for thirty-five years, he fled with his wife and children.

Thus Rome was ruled by seven kings for 243 years, although at that time Rome possessed, at its greatest extent, scarcely as much as fifteen miles of territory.

In the time of the Tarquins, the most chaste Judith killed Holofernes. In those same years the philosopher Pythagoras flourished. Born on Samos, he lived at Croton and finally went to Metapontum, where he was buried.

[Note: A. and B. add: “He lived at Croton and finally went to Metapontum, where he was buried. From this point the consuls began to be appointed: two in place of one king, for this reason…”]

But the great evils the Romans endured during those 243 years of uninterrupted royal domination are shown not only by the expulsion of a single king, but also by their rejection of the royal name and power. For if the fault had rested with the arrogance of only one man, he alone ought to have been expelled, while the dignity of the better rulers was preserved.

[Col. 0751B] Therefore, after the kings had been driven from the City, the Romans, deeming it necessary to consult their own interests rather than to rule over anyone’s liberty, created consuls. For this reason two were created in place of one king: so that, if one wished to be wicked, the other, possessing equal power, might restrain him. It was also decided that they should not hold command for longer than a year, lest prolonged authority make them more arrogant; instead, they should always be fellow citizens who knew that after a year they would be deprived of office [Note: [Col. 0751D] H. and Eutropius: “private citizens.”]. Thus, in the first year after the kings had been expelled [Note: [Col. 0751D] A. reads *consules* after *regibus*.], the consuls were L. Junius Brutus, who had worked most vigorously for Tarquin’s expulsion, and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia’s husband. But Tarquinius Collatinus was immediately deprived of his dignity. For it had been decided that absolutely no one should remain in the City who was called Tarquinius. Therefore, after taking all his property, he emigrated from the City [Col. 0751C], and in his place P. Valerius Publicola was made consul [Note: [Col. 0751D] A., B., and H.: Lucius Valerius.].

Nevertheless, the expelled king Tarquin stirred up war against the city of Rome. Gathering many peoples, especially the Etruscans and Veientes, he fought in order to be restored to the kingship. In the first battle the consul Brutus and Arruns, Tarquin’s son, killed one another; nevertheless, the Romans withdrew victorious from that battle [Note: [Col. 0751D] A., B., H., and Eutropius: “They withdrew victorious from that battle. They buried Brutus at Rome.”]. Since one more Etruscan had fallen, the Roman victor departed. The Roman matrons mourned Brutus, the defender of their chastity, as their common father, for a year.

Valerius Publicola made Spurius Lucretius Tricipitinus, Lucretia’s father, his colleague. When the latter died of illness, he again took Horatius Pulvillus as his colleague. Thus the first year had five consuls, since Tarquinius Collatinus had withdrawn from the City because of his name, Brutus had perished in battle, and Spurius Lucretius had died of illness.

In the second year, Tarquin again brought war upon the Romans in order to recover the kingship, with Porsenna, king of Etruria, bringing him aid [Note: [Col. 0751D] A., B., H., and Eutropius: “Porsenna, king of Tuscany, and he nearly captured Rome, but on that occasion too he was defeated. In the third year after the expulsion of the kings, Tarquin…” The intervening material is absent.]. For three continuous years he terrified, confined, and besieged the trembling City. Unless Mucius—who had gone to Porsenna’s camp and tent to strike him, killed his subordinate instead, who was distributing the soldiers’ pay and was wearing purple, mistaking him for the king, and, after being immediately captured, explained why he had come, then finally placed the hand that had made the mistake upon the fire burning on the altar—or the maiden Cloelia, who, after a short interval, broke her bonds and crossed the river Tiber in an astonishing passage, had shaken the enemy by their boldness, the Romans would certainly have been forced either to endure defeat, overcome by the enemy’s attack, or to submit to slavery after the king had been restored.

That same Cloelia had been given to Porsenna as a hostage. She deceived the guards, mounted a horse, crossed the Tiber, and returned to Rome. By decree of the Senate, an equestrian statue was given to her [Col. 0752B].

One day, when the Etruscans were rushing into Rome across the Sublician Bridge over the Tiber, a certain Horatius Cocles alone opposed them at the head of the bridge, until the bridge was broken up and part of it collapsed. Immediately afterward, still armed, he threw himself into the Tiber and, victorious alike over the enemy and the river, avoided the weapons cast upon him by the Etruscans.

In the third year after the expulsion of the kings, when Tarquin could not be received back into the kingship and Porsenna, who had made peace with the Romans, offered him no aid, Tarquin withdrew to Tusculum, a city not far from the City, and there lived out fourteen years in private life, growing old with his wife.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] A., H., and Eutropius: “When the Sabines brought war upon the Romans [Col. 0752D], they were defeated and a triumph was celebrated over them. In the fifth year, that Lucius Valerius…”]

In the fourth year after the expulsion of the kings, the Sabines, having gathered forces from every direction and making a great display of military preparation, advanced against Rome. Terrified by this threat, the Romans prepared for war, and a triumph was celebrated over them [Col. 0752C].

In the fifth year after the expulsion of the kings, that P. Valerius, Brutus’s colleague and four times consul, died a fateful death. He was so poor that, when money had been collected from the people, he had the expense of his burial provided. The matrons mourned him for a year, just as they had mourned Brutus.

In the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings, when Tarquin’s son-in-law had gathered a huge army to avenge the injury done to his father-in-law, a new office was created at Rome, called the Dictatorship, greater than the consulship. In the same year a master of the cavalry was also appointed to obey the dictator. Nothing can be said to resemble that ancient dictatorship more closely than the imperial power which your Serenity now possesses, especially since Augustus Octavian, whom we shall discuss later, and before him Gaius Caesar, ruled under the name and authority of dictator [Col. 0752D].

The first dictator at Rome was M. Valerius [Note: [Col. 0752D] A., H., and B.: “Largus was the first”; Eutropius: “Largius.”]; the first master of the cavalry was Sp. Cassius.

In the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings [Note: [Col. 0752D] A. has: “The Roman people created a revolt; and when it was being suppressed by the Senate and the consuls, it then created tribunes of the plebs for itself.” B. and H. agree, changing *cumque* to *tanquam*.], there followed the secession of the plebs from the patricians. While M. Valerius the dictator was conducting a levy of soldiers, the people, goaded by various injuries and thinking that they were being oppressed by the Senate and the consuls, occupied the Sacred Mount under arms [Col. 0753A]. What could be more terrible than such a disaster? It was as though the body, cut off from the head, was plotting the destruction of the head by which it breathed. Then the people created tribunes of the plebs for themselves, as their own judges and defenders, through whom they might be safe against the Senate and the consuls.

At the same time Nehemiah, with the permission of Xerxes, king of the Persians, came to Judaea and restored the walls and the city.

In the following year the Volscians prepared war against the Romans and, defeated in battle, also lost the city of Corioli, which they had regarded as their finest possession [Note: [Col. 0753D] A.: “They rebuilt.”].

In the eighteenth year after the kings had been expelled, the Roman commander Gaius Marcius, who had captured Corioli, a Volscian city, was driven from the City. In anger he went to the Volscians themselves and received their assistance against the Romans. He often defeated the Romans and advanced to within five miles of the City, intending to attack even his own country. He rejected envoys who sought peace, until his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia came to him from the City. By their entreaties they turned back the army, which Rome had been unable to repel by force. He was the second after Tarquin to become a commander against his own country. At the place where they had pleaded with him, his husband [i.e. Marcius] built an altar to Fortuna Muliebris.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] A. has: “overcome by entreaty,” as does Hersfeld. The remainder is lacking in both, down to “C. Flavius and L. Virginius, consuls.” Then follows: “Three hundred noblemen of the Fabian family alone undertook war against the Veientes, promising the Senate and people that they would complete the entire contest by themselves. Thus all the nobles set out—men who individually ought to have been commanders of great armies—and fell in battle. Only one survived from so great a family, because, on account of his childish age, he could not be led into battle.” Herodotus, Book VII, relates something similar concerning Leonidas, king of the Lacedaemonians; note well that the author here follows Livy, whom Dionysius nevertheless refutes in Book IX.]

When T. Geganius and P. Minucius were consuls, two of the greatest and most dreadful scourges of all evils—famine and pestilence—seized the exhausted City. The fighting ceased for a little while, but deaths did not. The Veientes and Etruscans, formidable enemies, rising for war after adding the forces of neighboring peoples to their own, were met by the consuls M. Fabius and Cn. Manlius [Col. 0753C]. After the oath by which the Romans had sworn that they would not return to camp until victory, the battle was so savage, and fortune so equal for the defeated and the victors alike, that, after a very large part of the army had been lost and the consul Manlius had been killed in battle, the consul M. Fabius refused to accept the triumph offered him by the Senate, because his brother had fallen while fighting bravely in that battle. He said: “Because, in view of such great losses to the state, mourning is due rather than a triumph.”

When C. Fabius and L. Virginius were consuls, the glorious Fabian family, so remarkable in number and strength, undertook the war against Veii assigned to it. How great a bereavement it brought upon the state by its destruction is still attested by names of ill omen: the river Cremera, which destroyed them, and the gate which sent them forth [Col. 0753D]. For when 306 Fabii, truly the brightest lights of the Roman state, had sought for themselves a separate ten-year war against the Veientine enemy, promising the Senate and the people that they alone would complete the entire struggle, all the nobles set out—men who individually ought to have been commanders of great armies. Then, led into an ambush and surrounded by the enemy, they were all slaughtered there, with only one spared to announce the disaster; because of his childish age, he could not be led into battle [Col. 0754A].

After this a census was held in the City, and the census found there 117,318 citizens [Note: [Col. 0754D] A. reads: “117,319 citizens were found.” In the following year, however, when the Roman army was besieged on Mount Algidus, almost twelve miles from the City, L. Quintius Cincinnatus was made dictator; he possessed and cultivated with his own hands a farm of four *jugera*. H. has “117,319.” The rest agrees with Ambrose.].

At the same time the Vestal virgin Porphyria was buried alive for the crime of sexual misconduct.

Thus, 359 years after the founding of the City, when warfare had been suspended for a short time, a severe pestilence— which always either interrupted truces made there or compelled them to be made—spread violently through the entire state [Col. 0754B]. It was fitting that, after the monstrous omen which had preceded it, the sky should have seemed to burn, when the capital of the nations was aflame with such a fire of diseases. For that year pestilence consumed both consuls, Ebutius and Servilius; it destroyed most of the military forces and wiped out many nobles, especially the plebs, with a loathsome wasting disease, although a plague that had arisen in the preceding fourth year had already devastated the same people.

In the following year exiled citizens and fugitive slaves, led by Herdonius, a Sabine, invaded Rome and set fire to the Capitol. The younger men bravely resisted them under the consul and commander Valerius, but the battle was so savage and serious that the consul Valerius himself was killed there, and, by his own death, further stained a victory over slaves that was unworthy of Rome.

The following year was one in which a consul was besieged with his army defeated. For the Aequi and Volscians engaged the consul Minucius in battle, overcame him, and surrounded him as he fled on Mount Algidus, which lies about twelve miles from the City, with hunger and the sword. The situation would have ended disastrously had not Quintius Cincinnatus, that outstanding dictator, broken the siege after crushing the enemy. He had been found in the countryside, possessing and cultivating with his own hands a four-*jugerum* farm. When he was found at work, even plowing, he wiped away his sweat and, summoned from the plow to the fasces, received the bordered toga [Note: [Col. 0754D] H. has “the bordered toga,” and follows A.: “He accepted it, slew the enemy, and freed the army; he placed the yoke of oxen upon horses, and, holding victory like a plow-handle, was the first to drive the conquered enemy before him.”].

Then, having assumed office and organized an army, he became victorious after killing the enemy and freed the army. He placed the yoke of oxen upon horses and, holding victory as though it were a plow-handle, was the first to drive the conquered enemy before him.

In the year immediately preceding the three-hundredth year from the founding of the City, while envoys sent by the Athenians were awaited to bring the laws of Solon, Roman arms were checked by famine and pestilence [Col. 0755A].

In the three-hundred-and-second year from the founding of the City, consular government came to an end, and ten men were appointed in place of the two consuls, to possess supreme power for establishing the Attic laws. They were called the Decemvirs from their number. This arrangement brought great ruin upon the state. For the first of the Decemvirs, Appius Claudius, when the others yielded, continued the authority for himself alone. Immediately afterward a conspiracy of the others followed, so that, having disregarded the established custom by which the insignia of power belonged to one man but authority was shared by all, they might conduct everything according to their own desires. Thus, among the many things all of them arrogantly presumed to do, they suddenly proceeded individually with twelve fasces and the other imperial insignia [Col. 0755B].

With this new and shameful arrangement begun, a procession of tyrants emerged under the pretext of an embassy from the consuls. They added two tables of laws to the original ten and acted with the greatest arrogance. On the day when it was customary to lay down their magistracies, they proceeded with the same insignia.

In the second year, Appius Claudius violated a virgin named Virginia, the daughter of a certain Virginius [Note: [Col. 0755D] H., for *Virginii*, has *viri*.]. Her father was already serving honorably against the Latins on Mount Algidus. Driven by grief over the loss of liberty and by shame at the dishonor, Virginius the father dragged his daughter, who had been claimed for slavery, forward and, as a pious killer of his own child, struck her down in the sight of the people [Note: [Col. 0755D] A. and H., instead of *stupravit*, have “he wished to violate her,” and omit the rest of the following material: “Her father killed her so that she would not suffer violation at the hands of the Decemvirs, and, departing for the soldiers, stirred up a revolt. Thus power was taken from the Decemvirs…”].

Moved by the horror of this necessity and warned by the danger to their liberty, the people occupied the Aventine under arms. They did not cease defending their liberty by force until power had been taken from the Decemvirs and they themselves had been condemned.

In the year 315 from the founding of the City, earthquakes throughout almost the whole year were so frequent and severe in Italy that Rome was wearied by continual reports of countless shocks and the collapse of farms and towns. After this there was such unbroken and scorching drought that it denied the hope of both the present and the coming year of producing crops from the earth. Finally, in these times, the Fidenates rebelled against the Romans, supported by a mass of the greatest auxiliary forces. The Veientes and Tolumnius, king of the Veientes, provided them assistance. Both cities were so close to the City that Fidenae and Veii were eighteen miles from Rome. The Volscians also joined them. But they were defeated by M. Aemilius the dictator and L. Quintius Cincinnatus the master of the cavalry, and they lost their king as well. Fidenae was captured [Col. 0756A] and destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] From this point the remainder is not found in A., H., B., or Eutropius, down to “After twenty years.”]

There was such a conflict of disasters and hostile passions within Fidenae itself that domestic disasters, overwhelmed by wars pouring in from abroad, were either obliterated, or, after the losses of war had brought a relaxation of hostilities, different plagues, blazing forth in heaven and on earth, corrupted everything with unceasing assault.

At that time the island of Sicily, shaken by a most severe earthquake, was devastated, with the deadly fires of Etna boiling over and hot ashes falling, to the great destruction of fields and farms. At that time also the city of Atlante, attached to Locris, was suddenly torn away from the mainland by an unexpected rush of the sea and laid waste as an island. The city of the Athenians too was seized by a wretched pestilence and long ravaged.

After twenty years, the same Veientines rebelled. Furius Camillus was sent as dictator against them. He first defeated them in battle; then, besieging their city for a long time, he captured it secretly through tunnels. It was the most ancient and richest city in Italy. When he found there a statue of Juno Moneta, he ordered it to be transferred to Rome. One of the soldiers, joking, asked the image whether it wished to go to Rome. It replied: “I do.”

Afterward he also captured the Faliscans, a city no less noble. But envy arose against him at home, as though he had divided the spoils improperly, and for this reason he was condemned [Note: [Col. 0755D] B. and H. agree word for word with Eutropius: “He was expelled from the state. Immediately afterward the Senonian Gauls came to the City. Having defeated the Romans eleven miles from Rome near the river Allia, they pursued them and also occupied the City; nothing could be defended except the Capitol. After they had besieged it for a long time, and the Romans were already suffering from hunger, Camillus, who was living in exile in a neighboring city, came upon the Gauls, and they were utterly defeated. Nevertheless, after receiving one thousand pounds of gold so that they would not besiege the Capitol, they withdrew. Camillus followed them and slaughtered them so completely that he recovered both the gold which had been given to them and all the military standards they had captured. Thus he entered the City in triumph for the third time and was called a second Romulus, as though he too had founded his country. Around this time the history of Esther is thought to have been written. The philosopher Plato is also said to have lived at this time.” Eutropius, however, ends the first book with these words: “the founder of his country.” He has nothing further. CANIS.

Ambrose agrees with these manuscripts.

In the Hersfeld manuscript: “Here ends the first book of Roman History.”]

and was expelled from the state.

After this came an incursion of the Belgic Gauls and the burning of the City. Who, if possible, could dare to compare the calamity of that time with this disaster, although the fable of the former evil does not weigh equally with the injury of the present?

The Senonian Gauls, therefore, under the leadership of Brennus, relying on a large and exceedingly powerful army, were besieging the city of Clusium. Abandoning the siege, they advanced toward Rome with all their strength. Fabius the consul met them as they rushed in with such fury, but he could not withstand them. Rather, that enemy assault cut down, overthrew, and swept through the Romans like dry crops. The river Allia bears witness to this disaster of the Fabii, just as the Cremera bears witness to the destruction of the Fabii. No one could easily recount a similar collapse of the Roman army, even if Rome had not additionally been burned.

The Gauls entered the exposed City, slaughtered the senators, who sat rigid in their seats like statues, and, after the senators had been burned by the fire of their homes, buried them all beneath the collapse of their roofs. When human strength could no longer resist them at all, they consulted Apollo of Delphi. He replied that the gods and fair-haired maidens would fight alongside them against the Gauls. Then Brennus, overwhelmed by snow in the Alps, was destroyed along with his entire army.

They therefore confined the remaining young men—who, it is agreed, then numbered scarcely a thousand—hidden in the citadel of Capitoline Hill, enclosing them there under siege. They wore down those unfortunate remnants with hunger and pestilence, despair and fear. The Capitol would immediately have been captured had Manlius not been awakened by the cackling of a goose and resisted.

When the Gauls had besieged them for a long time and the Romans were already suffering from hunger, the Gauls threw fragments of bread in place of stones. Consequently, after receiving one thousand pounds of gold so that they would not besiege the Capitol, they withdrew from the City. Camillus followed them and slaughtered them so completely that he recovered both the gold that had been given to them and all the military standards they had captured, although he had already inflicted a most severe defeat upon them.

Thus Camillus entered the City in triumph for the third time and was called a second Romulus, as though he too had founded his country.

While those same Gauls were besieging the Capitol, C. Fabius Dorsuo, the Flamen Quirinalis, carried out the sacred rites on the appointed day and made his way to the Quirinal Hill through the enemy camp. After performing the sacrifice, he returned.

Around this time the history of Ezra is thought to have been written. The philosopher Plato is also said to have lived at this time.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757B] In the year 365 from the founding of the City, all Achaea was shaken by a most violent earthquake, and two cities, Bura and Helice, were swallowed up when the ground split open [Note: [Col. 0757D] Another reading: “Hebra.”].

Thus, after the capture of the City, the offices were changed for the first time, and military tribunes with consular authority were appointed in place of two consuls. From this point the Roman state began to grow. For in that year Camillus defeated the city of the Volscians, which had waged war for seventy years; he also captured the city of the Aequi and that of the Sutrini, destroying their armies, and celebrated three triumphs at once.

Titus Quintius Cincinnatus also defeated the Praenestines, who had advanced with war as far as the gates of the city of Rome, pursuing them to the river Allia. He added to the Romans eight cities that had been under their rule and, attacking Praeneste itself, accepted its surrender. All this he accomplished in twenty days; a triumph was decreed for him [Col. 0757C].

The office of military tribune, however, did not last long. For after a short time it was decided that none should be appointed, and four years passed in the City without any higher magistracies there. Nevertheless, the military tribunes with consular authority again assumed the office, and continued in it for three years. Then consuls were again appointed.

When L. Genutius and Q. Servilius were consuls, Camillus died, and the honor of a second place after Romulus was bestowed upon him [Note: [Col. 0757D] A., B., and H.: “was conferred upon him. At this time an immense pestilence afflicted the Romans continuously for two years, and in the following year a sufficiently grievous portent occurred.” The remainder is absent.].

In the year 384 from the founding of the City, an immense pestilence seized the whole of Rome. It was not, as usually happens, a disturbance of the atmosphere lasting more or less than its customary period—that is, the untimely dryness of winter, the sudden heat of spring, the unsuitable moisture of summer, or the rich, thick, and undigested excess of autumn, together with the foul air exhaled from the forests of Calabria, whose passage commonly brings sudden acute illnesses. Rather, it was severe and prolonged, affecting no sex differently from another and no age differently from another; for two full years it continually consumed everyone with a general wasting disease [Col. 0758B], leaving even those whom it did not drive to death exhausted and afflicted by shameful emaciation.

In the following year a sufficiently grievous portent occurred. In the middle of the City [Note: [Col. 0757D] A. does not have “in the forum.”] the earth split open, and, after a vast chasm had suddenly been torn apart, the underworld yawned visibly. Since this remained open for a long time and terrified everyone, the soothsayers finally explained that the depth of the chasm could be closed if what was most precious in Rome were thrown into it. The matrons’ jewelry was thrown in vain for a long time. Then the Roman knight M. Curtius, distinguished by his family, took up his military equipment, mounted his horse, and hurled himself into the chasm, thus [Note: [Col. 0758D] In the same manuscripts, after “thus it was closed,” the following is found: “Meanwhile the dictator T. Quintius was sent against the Gauls who had come into Italy. They had settled four miles beyond the river Anio, away from the City. There the most noble young senator L. Manlius advanced against a Gaul who had challenged him … and soon acquired his surname. The Gauls were routed, and shortly afterward defeated by the dictator C. Sulpicius. Not long afterward they were defeated by C. Marcius the Tuscan; eight thousand of them were led captive in triumph.”].

After him, those performing sacrifices threw grain into the same place, and soon the earth returned to its natural condition.

In the year 388 from the founding of the City, another terrifying flood of Gauls settled beside the river Anio, at the fourth milestone from the City. They would certainly have seized the City, already thrown into confusion, both because of the weight of their numbers and because of the vigor of their courage, had they not grown sluggish through their own inactivity and gentleness. There he began a most savage single combat. L. Manlius, a most noble young man from the senatorial order, advanced against a Gaul who had challenged him to single combat and killed him. He took the golden torque and placed it around his own neck, thereby acquiring for himself and his descendants forever the surname Torquatus.

Immediately afterward the dictator Quintius destroyed them in an exceedingly bloody engagement. Many Gauls, routed from this battle, gathered their forces again and rushed into war, but were defeated by the dictator C. Sulpicius. A little later a battle against the Etruscans also took place under C. Marcius. From this one may infer how many people were killed, since eight thousand Etruscans were captured.

A census was held again.

In the third year, during those same days, the Gauls spread themselves through the coastal regions and the plains below the Alban Mountains, seeking plunder. Since the Latins, who had been subdued by the Romans, refused to provide soldiers [Col. 0759A], the Romans conducted a new levy and selected recruits [Note: [Col. 0759D] A., B., and H.: “after the Romans had selected only recruits, and so forth.”]. Ten legions were formed. This number amounted to sixty thousand armed men or more, and they advanced against the Gauls. Although Roman affairs were still small, such was their excellence in military matters [Note: [Col. 0759D] Thus, clearly, the manuscript of Paul the Deacon consistently retains Eutropius’s wording more closely. CANIS.].

When they had set out against the Gauls under the leadership of L. Furius, one of the Gauls challenged the best of the Romans to single combat. Then M. Valerius, a military tribune, offered himself. When he advanced armed, a raven settled upon his right arm. As soon as the battle against the Gaul began, that same raven struck the Gaul’s eyes with its wings and claws, preventing him from looking straight ahead. Thus the Gaul was killed by the tribune Valerius, and the raven gave him not only victory but also a name. For afterward he was called Corvinus, and, because of this merit, he was made consul for thirteen years [Note: [Col. 0759D] A. has twenty-three; so also B. and H.].

After the Gaul who had issued the challenge was killed, all the others were terrified and, fleeing in scattered groups, were slaughtered with great loss. At that time night appeared to be prolonged until a very large part of the day. At that time stones mixed with hail fell from the clouds [Note: [Col. 0759D] A.: “stones from the clouds,” and so forth.]. At the same time Alexander the Great was born—that great chasm of misery and most savage whirlwind of the entire East.

In the year 409 from the founding of the City, the Latins who had refused to provide soldiers also began to demand from the Romans that one consul should be elected from their people and the other from the Roman people. When this was denied, they brought war against the Romans [Note: [Col. 0759D] A. has: “War was undertaken against them, and they were defeated in a great battle; a triumph was celebrated over them after their subjugation.” B. and H. agree, except that instead of *his* they have *suis*, “after their own subjugation,” and so forth.], under the consuls Manlius Torquatus and Decius Mus. In that war one consul was killed and the other became an impious killer.

For Manlius Torquatus killed his young son, who had been victorious and had killed Decius, a noble Tusculan knight and an especially challenging and taunting enemy [Col. 0759C]. The other consul, when he saw that the wing under his command was being cut down and afflicted in a renewed clash, deliberately threw himself among the densest ranks of the enemy and died.

Although Manlius was victorious, he did not deserve the customary procession of noble Roman youths in his triumph, since he was a parricide. Statues of the consuls were set up on the Rostra in recognition of their victory.

In that year Alexandria was also founded by Alexander of Macedon.

In the following year Minutia, a Vestal virgin, was condemned for incest and buried alive in the field that is now called the Wicked Field [Note: [Col. 0759D] Everything from here through the words “Now the Romans” is inserted; it is not found in the manuscripts or in Eutropius.].

After an interval of time, there occurred something that I shudder to recount. For when Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Flaccus were consuls, the Roman matrons were inflamed by incredible madness and a love of crimes. It was a foul and pestilential year; everywhere the air was already infected, and heaps of corpses were being carried out. Yet everyone still held the simple belief that the deaths were caused by corrupted air, when a certain slave woman came forward as an informer and proved the matter. First, many matrons were compelled to drink the poisons they had prepared; then all those who had swallowed them perished together. So great was the number of matrons implicated in these crimes that 370 are reported to have been condemned at the same time.

In the year 442 from the founding of the City, King Alexander of the Epirotes, the uncle of that Alexander the Great, crossed into Italy with his forces. As he prepared war against the Romans and strengthened his army around the neighboring cities of Rome, seeking through warfare either to acquire auxiliaries for himself or to deprive his enemies of them, he was defeated and killed in Lucania in a great battle by the Samnites, who were supporting the Lucanian people [Col. 0760B].

In the year 426 from the founding of the City, the Romans had already begun to be powerful. For war was being waged about 130 miles from the City among the Samnites, a people situated between Picenum, Campania, and Apulia. If one asks about their wealth, they were adorned with gold and silver weapons and multicolored clothing, even to the point of extravagance; if about their deceitfulness in ambushes, they attacked chiefly through forests and by the treachery of mountains; if about their rage and fury, they were driven to the destruction of the City by sacrilegious and human sacrifices; if about their stubbornness, they had broken their treaty with the same enemies six times [Note: [Col. 0759D] A.: “of the world.”].

[Note: [Col. 0759D] H. is considerably fuller here through a notable addition: “More emboldened: finally, before they engaged the Romans, they defeated in Lucania King Alexander of the Epirotes, the brother of Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great. He had crossed into Italy with his forces and was preparing war against the Romans; while the Samnites were supporting the Lucanians, they defeated him in a great battle in Lucania. In that battle Alexander of Epirus himself was also killed. Therefore the Romans against the Samnites, and so forth.

A. agrees with H. as far as ‘with his forces into Italy, preparing war’; from there it continues: ‘they defeated him in Lucania, and in that battle…’”]
more spirited. Therefore the Romans undertook war against the Samnites on behalf of the Campani and Sidicini. For Campania is the most beautiful region of all—not only of Italy, but almost of the whole world. [Col. 0760C] [Note: [Col. 0760D] A., B., and H.: “No sea is more welcoming.”] No sea is more welcoming to ships. Here are those famous harbors: Caieta, [Note: [Col. 0760D] In all copies: “Misenus, Baiae warm with springs, Lucrinus,” etc.] Misenus, Lucrinus, and Avernus, a kind of mouths of the sea. Here are mountains clothed [Note: [Col. 0760D] A., instead of *amicti*, has *amici*.] with vines: [Note: [Col. 0760D] A., *Caurus*. B. and H., *Laurus*.] Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus, and the most beautiful of them all, Vesuvius. The cities by the sea are Formiae, Cumae, Puteoli, [Note: [Col. 0760D] *Hyrcolanum*. B. and H., *Hircolanium*.] Herculaneum, Pompeii, and Capua itself, the capital of cities, once counted among the three greatest—Rome, Carthage, and Capua. For this city [Note: [Col. 0760D] These two words are absent from B. and H.] and for these regions the Roman people attacked the Samnites.

L. Papirius Cursor set out for that war with the authority of dictator. When he returned to Rome, he ordered Q. Fabius Maximus, master of the cavalry, whom he had left with the army, not to fight in his absence. Fabius, finding an opportunity, fought very successfully [Note: [Col. 0760D] A., B., H., and Eutropius: “fought and destroyed the Samnites.”] and destroyed twenty thousand [Col. 0760D] Samnites. For this reason the dictator condemned him to death, because he had fought against his orders; but, amid the immense enthusiasm of the soldiers and the people, he was freed, and such a mutiny was aroused against Papirius that he himself was almost killed.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Later the Samnites, when the Romans were trapped by the narrowness of the terrain at the Caudine Forks under the consuls T. Veturius and Sp. Postumius, defeated them with great disgrace, etc.]

After this the Samnites, equipped with more careful preparation and greater resources, took up position at the Caudine Forks under the consuls T. Veturius and Sp. Postumius. They defeated all the Roman forces there, confined by the narrowness of the terrain and by their weapons, with immense disgrace. Their commander Pontius so abused the security born of victory that he thought it necessary to consult his father Herennius as to whether he should kill the trapped Romans or spare them—yet, if he spared them, preserve them alive for humiliation. He chose the latter course. [Note: [Col. 0761D] A., B., and H. omit the rest, beginning “for it was universally known…”] For it was universally known that the Romans had often before been defeated and killed, but had never been captured or forced into destruction.

Thus the Samnites, having won the victory, ordered the entire Roman army, shamefully captured, stripped of its weapons and clothing, and granted only a single cheap covering to protect the modesty of each man’s body, to be sent beneath the yoke and subjected to servitude, in a long procession of humiliation. They took six hundred Roman cavalrymen as hostages, then sent back the consuls, loaded with disgrace but deprived of everything else, under such conditions of peace as the Samnites chose to impose. But if the Romans had kept faith with the Samnites, their subjects, as they themselves wish their subjects to keep faith with them, they would either not exist today at all, or would serve under Samnite rule.

In the following year, at the command of the Senate, [Note: [Col. 0761D] After “at the command of the Senate,” all copies have: “the peace concluded with the Samnites was broken. Lucius Papirius was sent as consul against them. He was then held in such high esteem among the Romans for his warlike ability that, when it was said that Alexander was crossing into Italy, the Romans chose him above all the other commanders to withstand Alexander’s assault. The Samnites therefore engaged Papirius and were defeated; seven thousand of them were sent beneath the yoke. B. and H.: “beneath the yoke”; “Papirius triumphed over the Samnites.” At that time Appius Claudius the Censor brought in the Claudian water supply, etc.] the Romans broke the pact concluded with the Samnites and forced them into war. Since the consul Papirius pressed the matter, the conflict produced great slaughter on both sides, as the anger of recent disgrace on one side and the glory of the recent victory on the other spurred the combatants on.
