At last the Romans won through stubborn endurance in dying: they did not cease either to be cut down or to cut down their enemies until, after the Samnites had been defeated and their commander captured, they imposed the yoke on seven thousand of them.

Then Papirius stormed and captured Satricum after expelling its Samnite garrison. At that time Papirius was considered by the Romans so warlike and energetic that, when it was said that Alexander the Great was planning to descend from the East, conquer Africa by force, and then cross into Italy, the Romans—who at that time had among their commanders men of the highest distinction in public affairs—judged that Papirius above all others would be able to withstand Alexander’s power.

At that time Appius Claudius the Censor brought in the great Claudian aqueduct and paved the Appian Way. Around this period Jioaddus was high priest at Jerusalem, [Col. 0761D] and his brother Manasses built a temple on Mount Gerizim. [Note: [Col. 0762D] From this point the manuscripts, except for the words “P. Cornelius, Rufinus,” follow Eutropius: “The Samnites, having renewed the war, defeated Q. Fabius Maximus and killed three thousand men. Later, when his father, Fabius Maximus, had been assigned to him as legate, he both defeated the Samnites and captured many of their towns. Then Publius Cornelius,” etc.]

In the year 450 from the founding of the City, when Fabius Maximus was consul for the fifth time and Decius Mus for the fourth, four flourishing and very courageous peoples of Italy united in a single army and alliance. For the Etruscans, Umbrians, Samnites, and Gauls, conspiring in one army, attempted to destroy the Romans. The courage of the Romans was shaken by this war, and their confidence was weakened. Since they did not dare to rely entirely on their strength, they divided the enemy by strategy, considering it safer to involve them in several wars than in one serious war.

Accordingly, after sending some of their own forces ahead to ravage the enemy’s fields and forcing the Umbrian and Etruscan armies to return to defend their own territories, they hastened to engage the Samnites and Gauls. In this war, when the Romans were being pressed by the attack of the Gauls, the consul Decius was killed; Fabius nevertheless, after inflicting great slaughter on Decius’s contingent, finally won. In that battle eleven thousand Samnites or Gauls are reported to have been killed, while seven thousand Romans were destroyed from Decius’s contingent alone, including Decius himself, who was killed.

Livy reports that, apart from the Etruscans and Umbrians, whom the Romans had drawn away from the war by a stratagem, the Gallic and Samnite infantry numbered 140,330, their cavalry 47,000, and that one thousand charioteers stood armed against the Roman line. But, as has often been said, the Romans were always either burdened by domestic peace disturbed by foreign wars or by foreign successes aggravated by internal diseases, so that their immense courage was oppressed from every direction. Pestilence burdened this bloody and sorrowful victory of theirs, and the funeral processions of the dead that met them polluted the triumphal celebrations. There was no one to whom joy in the triumph could be recommended, since the entire state was either sighing for the sick or mourning the dead.

The following year, when the Samnites renewed the battle, they were defeated and fled into their camp. Later the Samnites assumed new courage and a new appearance—that is, with their weapons and garments silver-plated—and, resolved to die unless they won, offered themselves for battle. Against them the consul Papirius was sent with an army. When the augurs, interpreting omens, forbade him to engage, he mocked them, seized the war with as much good fortune as determination, and brought it to an end. For in this battle twelve thousand of the enemy are reported to have been killed and three thousand captured.

But sudden diseases spoiled this victory as well—a victory truly deserving of praise, which the haruspices had been unable to prevent. For so great and intolerable a pestilence seized the state for three years that, in order to calm it by whatever means they could, they consulted the Sibylline Books, which ordered that Aesculapius be brought from Epidaurus. Envoys were sent to the Greek city, and the Epidaurians received them willingly and courteously.

There a serpent appeared to the envoys, an animal rarely seen by the inhabitants except as a favorable sign. After appearing familiarly for three days, it climbed aboard the Roman trireme in full view of everyone and, coiled in the cabin of the envoy Q. Burgonius, rested there. The Romans departed from the city, and the serpent was always visible on the ship. When they reached Antium, the serpent descended at the threshold of the temple of Aesculapius and hid among the myrtles for three days, without coming out for its customary food. Then it returned to the ship.

When they reached the Tiber, it swam to the island, where a temple was established for it, and immediately health was restored to the Romans.

Two years later Fabius Gurges, as consul, fought unsuccessfully against the Samnites. For, after losing his army and three thousand men, he was defeated and fled back to Rome. When the Senate was therefore deliberating about removing him, his father Fabius Maximus pleaded against his son’s disgrace and voluntarily offered to go as his son’s legate, if his son were granted the opportunity to remove the disgrace and wage war again.

After this request was granted and battle had been joined, the old and devoted father saw his son, the consul, suddenly surrounded by the Samnite commander Pontius and the enemy’s hostile weapons. Riding on horseback, he thrust himself into the middle of the battle line. Moved by this act, the Romans pressed forward with their entire line until they defeated and captured the commander Pontius himself, after destroying the enemy army. Twenty thousand were killed in that battle, while four thousand, together with their king, were captured, as well as very many towns.

Then P. Cornelius Ruffinus and M. Curius Dentatus, both consuls, were sent against the Samnites. They finished them off in immense battles, tearing down the very ruins of their cities, so that today Samnium must be sought within Samnium itself and can scarcely be found.

The war with the Samnites, waged for forty-nine years with great slaughter of the Romans, ended with the removal of their captured commander. [Note: [Col. 0764D] A. has *sublatum* (“removed”) instead of *finitum* (“ended”). A continues: “After some years, the forces of the Gauls again joined the Etruscans and Samnites against the Romans; but, as they advanced toward Rome, they were destroyed under the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Labella. At the same time war was declared against the Tarentines, who dwell at the farthest extremity of Italy, because they had insulted Roman envoys. They sought assistance against the Romans from Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, because he traced his origin from the line of Achilles. He soon came into Italy; then,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0763D] From this point the Hersfeld manuscript agrees word for word with Eutropius, as published by Merula, up to the words in Eutropius, fol. 20, column 7: “they occupied with arms.” After those words the manuscript differs slightly, as follows: “occupied. Cyneas, the envoy, on the day after he had entered Rome, greeted both the equestrian order and the Senate by their individual names. Nevertheless, the peace he offered was displeasing. The Senate sent back word that he could not have peace with the Romans unless he withdrew from Italy, etc.” The following material likewise agrees word for word with Eutropius in the manuscript, up to the words in Merula’s edition of Eutropius, fol. 21, line 15: “he was killed at Argos, a city of Greece.” After these words manuscript H. adds: “At this time Simeon, the high priest among the Jews, son of Onias, was distinguished; his surname was Justus. Then, when the Tarentines learned of Pyrrhus’s death,” etc. CANIS.] No enemy within Italy had ever wearied Roman courage more.

In the following year war was waged against the Sabines by the consul, who himself reported how many thousands of men had been killed and how many captured. When he wished to report to the Senate the extent of the Sabine territory acquired and the number of prisoners, he was unable to state the number.

In the year 463 from the founding of the City, when the Lucani, Bruttii, and Samnites, having formed an alliance with the Etruscans and Senonian Gauls, were preparing to renew the war against the Romans, the Romans sent envoys to appease the Gauls. When the Gauls killed these envoys, the praetor Caecilius was sent with an army to avenge the envoys’ death and suppress the enemy’s uprising; he was overwhelmed by the Etruscans and Gauls and perished. In addition, seven military tribunes were killed in that battle, many noblemen were slaughtered there, and fourteen thousand Roman soldiers were also struck down in that war.

[Col. 0763D] In the year 464 from the founding of the City, the Tarentines, who occupy the farthest point of Italy, attacked a Roman fleet that happened to be passing by and that they had viewed from the theater as a spectacle. Only five ships barely escaped by flight; the rest of the fleet was dragged back into the harbor and destroyed, the naval commanders were slaughtered, all those fit for war were killed, and the remainder were sold for a price.

The Romans immediately sent envoys to Tarentum to complain about the injuries inflicted upon them. The Tarentines beat them and sent them back with their injuries increased. For these reasons a great war broke out. The Romans, considering what and how many enemies were clamoring around them, were driven by extreme necessity to compel even the proletarians to take up arms—that is, to enroll in military service those who in the City had always remained free for the purpose of producing offspring, since concern for offspring is useless unless present circumstances are secured.

Accordingly, the Roman army, under the consul Aemilius, burst into the entire territory of the Tarentines, ravaged everything with fire and sword, stormed many [Col. 0764B] towns, and cruelly avenged the insult it had insolently received.

Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, greatly strengthened the Tarentines, who were supported by numerous garrisons of neighboring peoples. He traced his descent from the line of Achilles and, because of the greatness of his strength and the supreme importance of his counsels in war, transferred that name to himself as well. For he wished to vindicate Tarentum, a city founded by Lacedaemonians and related to Greece. He first brought into Italy the entire strength of Epirus, Thessaly, and Macedonia, and also twenty elephants, which until that time had been unknown to the Romans. He was terrifying by land, sea, men, horses, weapons, beasts, and, finally, by his own strength and stratagems—except that, deceived by the response of that Delphic spirit, whom they themselves call a great prophet, he made ambiguous the outcome of the man who had not consulted him.

It was then that the Romans first fought an overseas enemy. The consul P. Valerius Levinus was sent against him. When he captured some of Pyrrhus’s scouts, he ordered them to be led through the camp and shown the entire army, and then released, so that they might report to Pyrrhus what was being done with the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0764D] A. adds after “what was being done”: “Soon, when battle had been joined and Pyrrhus was already fleeing, he won with the aid of the elephants, whom the Romans, unfamiliar with them, feared; but night brought the battle to an end. Levinus nevertheless fled during the night. Pyrrhus captured 1,800 Romans and,” etc.]

Thus the first battle between King Pyrrhus and the consul Levinus was fought at Heraclea, a city of Lucania, and by the river Uri. The day was consumed in a very fierce struggle, with all on both sides intent on dying and ignorant of flight. When the elephants were brought among the running battle lines, fierce in appearance, oppressive in smell, and terrifying in bulk, the Romans, seeing them and surrounded and frightened by this new kind of warfare, scattered in panic, especially because their horses were terrified.

But after Minutius, a centurion of the Fourth Legion and its first spearman, cut off with his sword the hook extended toward him by so fierce a beast—the appendage they call the hand—[Col. 0764D] and, having wounded it, forced the animal in confusion to turn away from the battle and rage fiercely among its own men, the battle lines began to be thrown into disorder and mixed together by its uncontrolled movements. The battle was finally brought to an end, helped by the night.

Levinus nevertheless fled during the night. The Romans were ruined by the shameful flight that followed their defeat. It is reported that fourteen thousand eight hundred twenty infantrymen fell, while 246 cavalrymen were killed, 712 were captured, and twenty-two standards were lost.

Pyrrhus treated the Romans he had captured with the highest honor and buried those who had been killed. When he saw them lying dead with wounds in front and fierce expressions on their faces, he is said to have raised his hands to heaven and uttered these words: “I could have been master of the whole world, if I had obtained soldiers such as these.”

The number of Pyrrhus’s allies who were killed is not recorded, especially since it is the custom of all ancient writers not to report the number of the slain on the side that won, lest the losses of the victor stain the glory of the victory—unless, perhaps, so few have fallen that the smallness of the losses increases admiration and fear of their courage. This was the case in the first encounter of the Persian war under Alexander the Great, when, among almost four hundred thousand enemy dead, only 120 cavalrymen and nine infantrymen in his army are reported to have been lost.

But Pyrrhus bore witness before all his gods to the severity of the disaster that he had suffered in this war, affixing an inscription in the temple of Tarentine Jupiter, in which he wrote:

> These men, who once were unconquered, best father of Olympus,  
> I defeated in battle—and was defeated by the same men.

When his allies reproached him for calling himself defeated when he had won, he is said to have replied: “Indeed, if I win in the same way a second time, I shall return to Epirus without a single soldier.”

Meanwhile, after the Roman army had secretly fled from the camp following its defeat, it perceived that the wretched disaster of the war had been increased and compounded by more terrible portents. For some foragers who had happened to disperse were seized, as though by a sudden hostile storm, amid a horrific crash of the sky, and consumed by terrible lightning. The same whirlwind struck down thirty-four of them; twenty-two were left half-dead; pack animals were killed, and very many were captured. Thus the event should rightly be regarded not as a sign of future devastation but as devastation itself.

After this, Pyrrhus, having joined the Samnites, Lucani, and Bruttii to himself, marched toward Rome. He ravaged everything with sword and fire, laid waste Campania, and came to within eighteen miles of the City at Praeneste. Soon, intimidated by the army that was following him with the consuls, he withdrew into Campania.

Envoys were sent to Pyrrhus to ransom the captives. Pyrrhus ordered Lyco and Molossus to go out to meet them. He himself advanced to the gate with his soldiers splendidly arrayed and, after receiving the envoys honorably, sent the captives back to Rome without ransom.

He so admired one of the Roman envoys, Fabricius, after discovering that he was poor, that he tried to induce him to come over to his side by promising him a quarter of his kingdom. Fabricius rejected him. [Note: [Col. 0765D] A.: “For this reason, when Pyrrhus was filled with great admiration for the Romans, he sent an envoy,” etc.]

Since Pyrrhus was consequently filled with great admiration for the Roman envoys, he sent with them an envoy named Cyneas to request peace on equal terms, so that Pyrrhus might retain that part of Italy which he had already occupied by his arms.

On the day after Cyneas had entered Rome, he greeted both the equestrian order and the Senate by their individual names. Nevertheless, the peace he offered was displeasing. The Senate sent word back to Pyrrhus that he could not have peace with the Romans unless he withdrew from Italy.

The Romans then ordered all the captives whom Pyrrhus had returned to be considered disgraced, because they had allowed themselves to be captured while armed, and declared that they would not return to their former status until they had brought back the spoils of enemies known to them whom they had killed. [Note: [Col. 0765D] A., “truly,” instead.]

Thus Pyrrhus’s envoy returned. When Pyrrhus asked him what sort of Rome he had found, Cyneas replied that he had seen the homeland of kings—meaning, evidently, that nearly all the men there were of the sort that Pyrrhus alone was thought to be among the Epirotes and the rest of Greece. [Note: [Col. 0765D] A. omits the rest and has: “Publius Sulpicius and Decius were sent as consuls against Pyrrhus. When battle was joined, Pyrrhus was wounded, the elephants were killed, twenty thousand of the enemy were slain, and only five thousand Romans. Pyrrhus [returned] to Tarentum,” etc.]

The second battle between Pyrrhus and the Romans took place on the borders of Apulia, under the consuls P. Sulpicius and Decius. The losses of war were suffered by both sides, but chiefly by Pyrrhus, while the victory belonged to the Romans. For when, after a long time, with all rushing vigorously toward mutual slaughter, the outcome of the war hung in the balance, Pyrrhus, wounded by a spear through the arm, was the first to withdraw from the battle. Fabricius, too, the legate, was wounded at that time.

The elephants, wounded in the first battle and shown capable of being driven into flight, were later harried by fires placed beneath their hindquarters and softer parts. Moreover, carrying burning machines around in frantic fury, they became a destruction to their own side. Five thousand Romans were killed in that battle; twenty thousand from Pyrrhus’s army were struck down. Fifty-three of the king’s standards were taken, and eleven Roman standards were lost. Pyrrhus was driven back to Tarentum.

A year later Fabricius was sent against Pyrrhus, the man who earlier could not be induced, even among the envoys, by the promise of a quarter of the kingdom. At that time, when he and the king had neighboring camps, Pyrrhus’s physician came to him by night, promising that he would kill Pyrrhus with poison if Fabricius promised him something in return. Fabricius ordered the physician to be bound and taken back to his own home, and ordered that Pyrrhus be told what the physician had promised against his life.

The king, astonished, is said to have remarked: [Note: [Col. 0766D] A.: “He,” instead of “This man.”] “This is Fabricius, who can be turned from honesty with greater difficulty than the sun from its course.” [Note: [Col. 0766D] A.: “can be.” Then: “The king departed for Sicily. Fabricius won,” etc.]

Pyrrhus, however, [Col. 0766D] broken by war, went to Sicily after the death of Agathocles, king of Syracuse, having been summoned to take command there, and entered Syracuse. Fabricius triumphed after defeating the Lucani and Samnites.

But the misery of the Romans ceased for no truce. The interval between wars was consumed by the evils of disease; and when fighting ceased abroad, anger from heaven was enacted within. For under the consuls Fabius Gurges for the second time and C. Genucius Clepsina, a severe pestilence invaded Rome and its territory. It seized everyone, especially women and animals, and, killing the fetuses in the womb, emptied future generations of offspring; premature births were expelled as miscarriages, endangering the mothers. The succession and the race of living creatures were believed to be destined to fail, since the proper order of life-giving birth had been taken away.

Then the consuls Curius Dentatus and Cornelius Lentulus were sent against Pyrrhus. [Note: [Col. 0767D] A. omits the rest and has: “They were sent. Curius fought against him, destroyed his army, drove him back to Tarentum, and captured his camp. Twenty-three thousand of the enemy were killed that day. Curius,” etc.]

Meanwhile Pyrrhus returned from Sicily, and the consul Curius Dentatus confronted him. A third war against the Epirotes was fought in Lucania, on the Arusian plain. At the first encounter, when Pyrrhus’s soldiers were thrown into confusion by the Roman assault and, looking about for a means of escape, were preparing to withdraw from the battle, Pyrrhus ordered the elephants to be brought forward from the reserves.

The Romans, now accustomed to fighting beasts, had prepared small missiles wrapped in tow and smeared with pitch, with barbs attached to their hooks. They hurled these, burning, at the backs and towers of the animals and easily turned the raging, burning beasts back upon those whose support they had been.

They say that the king had eighty thousand infantry in that battle and six thousand cavalry. Of these, twenty-three thousand are reported to have been killed, while four hundred were captured. Pyrrhus himself was driven from Tarentum, and his camp was captured. Curius triumphed during his consulship and was the first at Rome to bring in four elephants. [Note: [Col. 0767D] A.: “Soon Pyrrhus also withdrew from Tarentum and was killed at Argos, a city of Greece. At this time among the Jews,” etc.]

Fifteen years after he had come to Italy, Pyrrhus fled in defeat. After many and very serious wars fought in Greece, he was led astray by his desire for the Spartan kingdom and died at Argos, the most flourishing city of Achaea, struck by a stone.

His big toe was said to be a remedy if it touched the swollen kidneys of someone suffering from that condition. When Antigonus, the victor, ordered it to be burned, it burned in such a way that the same toe was found untouched by the fire. The digit was enclosed in a golden casket and buried in the very ancient temple of Dodonaean Jupiter.

At this time Simon, son of Onias, was distinguished among the Jews as high priest; his surname was [Note: [Col. 0767D] A.: “He was Justus.”] Justus.

At that time as well, among the Romans, the Vestal virgin Sextilia, convicted and condemned for incest, was buried alive at the Colline Gate.

In the year 470 from the founding of the City, the Tarentines, having learned of Pyrrhus’s death, again sought to stir up new arms against the Romans. They requested the assistance of the Carthaginians through envoys and [Note: [Col. 0767D] A. adds: “afterward received it: the Carthaginians were defeated by the Romans, although,” etc.] received it. When battle was joined, the Romans won. There the Carthaginians, although not yet declared enemies, realized that they too could be defeated by the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0767D] The remainder through “C. Fab.” is absent from A. and [Col. 0768D] from two other manuscripts, B. and H.; A. nevertheless has *superari* (“be overcome”) instead of *vinci* (“be defeated”).]

In the following year, Roman severity cut down a great part of its own vitals. For, when Pyrrhus had long since been approaching, the Eighth Legion, losing confidence in Roman hopes, dared a new crime: it killed all the Reginenses, whom it was then assigned to support, seized all their possessions for itself, and claimed the town itself.

Genucius the consul was ordered to punish this crime and such criminals. After besieging the city of the Reginenses and capturing them all, he inflicted deserved punishments on the remaining deserters and brigands, but sent the Roman soldiers of the intact legion to Rome. By order of the people, they were beaten with rods in the middle of the Forum and struck down with the axe. Then Rome seemed to itself to be victorious, when it killed its own entire legion—although that legion would certainly and without doubt have been defeated if it had been destroyed by the enemy’s sword.

Under the consuls C. Fabricius Luscinus and C. Claudius Canina, envoys from Alexandria, sent by Ptolemy, came to Rome and obtained from the Romans the friendship they had requested.

In the year 471 from the founding of the City, obscene and dreadful prodigies were either seen at Rome or reported. The temple of Salus was shattered by a lightning strike, and part of the wall at the same place was likewise, as they say, struck from heaven. Three wolves entered the City before dawn carrying a half-eaten corpse; frightened by the noise of the people, they left it dismembered in the Forum.

At Formiae, the walls were scorched and shattered on every side by many lightning strikes. In the territory of Cales, a flame suddenly erupted through a fissure in the earth and, raging terribly for three days and three nights, reduced five *jugera* of farmland to ashes, completely draining away its fertile substance. It is reported that it consumed not only the crops but also the trees, roots and all.

In the following year, under the consuls Quintius Gulō and Fabius Pictor, the Picentes began a war. [Note: [Col. 0768D] A. and H.: “They began a war and were defeated by the following consuls, P. Sempronius and Appius Claudius; a triumph was celebrated over them,” etc.] The consuls P. Sempronius and Appius Claudius led an army against the Picentes. When the two lines had taken position opposite one another within the range of a missile, the earth suddenly shook so monstrously and with such a great and dreadful crash that both armies, stunned by the wonder, were paralyzed with fear.

For a long time both peoples remained thunderstruck, held back by a foreboding awareness of what they had begun. At last, with an impetuous advance, they entered the battle. That war was so grievous that one may rightly say that the earth, destined then to receive so much human blood, also trembled with a terrible groan.

The few Romans who survived that battle nevertheless won, and a triumph was celebrated over them. The Romans founded the cities of Ariminum in Gaul and Beneventum in Samnium. At that time the Romans also attacked [Note: [Col. 0768D] One copy has *Cothrona* instead of *Croton*. “At this time blood flowed from springs in several places, and milk descended from the clouds in the form of rain. Marc,” etc.] Croton.

In the year 467 from the founding of the City, amid many prodigies, blood was seen flowing from the earth and milk from the sky. For blood also poured forth, gushing from many springs, and milk fell drop by drop from the clouds like rain; dreadful showers, as they appeared to the observers, watered the earth.

Under the consuls M. Atilius Regulus and L. Julius Libo, war was declared against the Sallentines in Apulia. The Brundisians were captured together with their city, and a triumph was celebrated over them.

[Col. 0768D] [Note: [Col. 0768D] A., B., H., and Eutropius: “In the year 477, when the name of the city of Rome had already become famous,” etc.]

Although the name of the city of Rome had now become famous, no arms had yet been carried outside Italy. Therefore, so that the strength of the Roman forces might be known, a census was held. It was then found that there were 290,334 male citizens, [Note: [Col. 0768D] A. has 92,000.] although wars had never ceased since the founding of the City.

[Note: [Col. 0769D]

After “wars had never ceased,” A. has: “and war was undertaken against the Africans. First, under the consuls Appius Claudius and Q. Fulvius, the Romans fought against them in Sicily, and Appius,” etc.

Manuscripts B. and H. agree word for word in what follows with the edition of Eutropius published by Merula, except for a few variant readings. Manuscript H. calls him *Duillum*, whereas Eutropius has *Duillium*. H. has *primam clipeam Africae civitatis*; Eutropius has *primam Clypeam Africae civitatem* (“Clypea, the first city of Africa”). Everything else is Eutropian up to the words “he received seventy-four cities into allegiance,” which occur in Merula’s Eutropian edition, fol. 23, line 17. After those words manuscripts B. and H. continue as follows:

“Meanwhile, at the river Bagradas, Regulus killed a serpent of extraordinary size, whose skin measured 120 feet in length and was brought to Rome, where for some time it was a marvel to everyone. Then the Carthaginians, defeated, sought peace from the Romans. Since Regulus refused to grant it except on the harshest conditions, the Africans sought aid from the Lacedaemonians. The Roman commander Regulus was defeated by Xanthippus, who had been sent by the Lacedaemonians, with the most disastrous consequences. For only two men escaped from the entire Roman army; five hundred, together with the commander Regulus, were captured; thirty thousand were killed. Regulus himself was thrown into chains. At this time Ptolemy Philadelphus,” etc.]

At that time the Carthaginians, having given aid to the Tarentines against the Romans, when they were reproached by envoys of the Senate, added to the disgrace of having broken their treaty the still more shameful stain of anticipated perjury.

At that time also the Vulsinians, the most prosperous of the Etruscans, perished as punishment for their luxury. For when, under a license that had become customary, they indiscriminately made their slaves free, admitted them to banquets, and honored them with marriages, the freedmen, having been admitted to a share in power, planned by crime to usurp its fullness. Freed from the yoke of slavery, they burned with ambition for domination; and those whom, while subjects, they had loved as masters with equanimity, they now, as free men, execrated—those whom they remembered to have been their masters. Therefore the freedmen, conspiring in crime, were so numerous that they would plainly have been superior; they seized the city for their own class alone, criminally appropriated their masters’ property and marriages, and drove their masters far away into exile. Those wretched and impoverished exiles were brought to Rome. There, after their misery had been displayed and their complaint lamented, they were both avenged and restored through the severity of the Romans.

In the year 481 from the founding of the City, a great pestilence ravaged Rome. I shall be content merely to indicate its severity, since I cannot explain it in words. If one considers the length of time during which it lasted, it extended beyond two years in its devastation. If one considers the depopulation it produced, a census was taken that inquired not how many people had perished, but how many had survived. If one considers the violence with which it afflicted the population, the Sibylline Books bear witness: they declared that it had been imposed by heavenly wrath. But lest anyone be offended by a captious interpretation, as though, because the Sibyl spoke of angry gods, we too seem to have spoken of heavenly anger, let him hear and understand that although such things are often brought about through aerial powers, they absolutely do not occur without the will of almighty God.

At the same time the Vestal Virgin Caparronia, accused of incest, perished by hanging; her seducer and the slaves who shared the secret were punished.

In the year 483 from the founding of the City, when Appius Claudius and Quintus Fulvius were consuls, the Romans sent the consul Appius Claudius with an army to the Mamertines—Messana was their famous city in Sicily—who had requested both aid against Hiero, king of Syracuse, and assistance against the Carthaginian forces joined to Hiero. When battle had been joined, Appius Claudius celebrated a triumph over the Carthaginians and Hiero, king of Sicily.

In the following year, when Marcus Valerius and Titus Otacilius were consuls, great achievements were performed by the Romans in Sicily. Tauromenium, Catana, and fifty additional cities were received into allegiance.

In the third year war was prepared in Sicily against Hiero, king of the Sicilians, and the Carthaginians, by the consul Appius Claudius. He defeated the Syracusans and Carthaginians so quickly that the king himself, terrified by the magnitude of the events, declared that he had been defeated before he had even engaged in battle. Then, with his strength broken and his confidence lost, he humbly begged the Romans for peace together with all the Syracusan nobility, and, by order of the consuls, gave two hundred talents of silver.

**Note:** A omits everything after “talents”; the other manuscripts continue: “The Africans were defeated in Sicily, and a triumph was celebrated over them. Quintus …”

The consuls, having received the silver, proceeded to Agrigentum, a city of Sicily, and there surrounded the Carthaginian garrisons with fortifications and a rampart. When the elder Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians, shut in by that siege, had been reduced to extreme want, Hanno, a new Carthaginian commander, intervened unexpectedly with 1,500 cavalry, 30,000 infantry, and also thirty elephants. He delayed the capture of the city for a short time, but the city was soon taken. The Carthaginians were defeated and routed in a great battle; eleven elephants were captured; all the Agrigentines were sold under the auctioneer’s crown, and a second triumph over them was celebrated at Rome. The elder Hannibal then made a sortie and escaped with a few men.

In the fifth year of the Punic War, which was being waged against the Africans—

**Note:** A begins here as follows: “First, when Gaius Duilius and Gnaeus Cornelius Asina were consuls, the Romans fought at sea, having prepared beaked ships, which they call Liburnians. The consul Cornelius was deceived; Duilius, having joined battle, defeated the Carthaginian commander, captured thirty-one ships, sank fourteen, captured 7,000 of the enemy, and killed 3,000. Nor did …”

When Gnaeus Cornelius Asina and Gaius Duilius were consuls, and the elder Hannibal was ravaging the Italian coast with a fleet of seventy ships, the Romans likewise ordered a fleet to be built and equipped. The consul Duilius promptly accomplished this. For within sixty days of the trees being felled, a fleet of 130 ships was launched and stood at anchor.

The other consul, Cornelius Asina, set out for the island of Lipara with sixteen beaked ships, which they call Liburnians. There, summoned by Hannibal as if to a peace conference, he was captured by Punic treachery and killed in chains. When the other consul Duilius soon heard this, he too set out against Hannibal with thirty beaked ships, which they call Liburnians. When a naval battle was joined, Hannibal, after losing the ship on which he was traveling, escaped in a boat. Thirty-one of his ships are reported captured, thirteen sunk, 3,000 men killed, and 7,000 captured. No victory was ever more welcome to the Romans, since they had been invincible on land and now also possessed great power at sea.

Afterward, when Gaius Aquilius Florus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio were consuls, the Carthaginians placed Hanno, appointed in Hannibal’s place, in command of a naval battle for the defense of Sardinia and Corsica. He was defeated by the consul Scipio; after losing his army, he threw himself into the thick of the enemy and was killed there. Scipio ravaged Corsica and Sardinia, led away many thousands of captives from there, and celebrated a triumph.

In the same year 3,000 slaves and 3,000 naval allies conspired to destroy the city of Rome. Had treachery not been hastened and forestalled their plan, the city, deprived of a garrison, would have perished by the hands of slaves.

In the following year the consul Calatinus, while attacking Camerina, a city of Sicily, rashly led his army into defiles that the Carthaginian forces had long since fortified. Since he had absolutely no opportunity either to resist or to escape, he was saved by the courage and service of Calpurnius Flamma. He selected a band of 300 men, seized a hill occupied by the enemy, and turned all the Carthaginians against himself in battle until the Roman army, with the enemy no longer pressing them, passed through the blocked defiles. All the men in that battle were killed; Calpurnius alone, although pierced by wounds and covered with corpses, escaped.

The elder Hannibal, again placed in command of the Carthaginian fleet, engaged the Romans in a naval battle unsuccessfully and was defeated. When a mutiny arose in his army, he died, even being covered with stones.

When Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus were consuls, the war was transferred to Africa against Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander.

**Note:** A continues: “He fought at sea and was defeated; for, after losing sixty-four ships, he withdrew.”

The consul Atilius ravaged the famous Sicilian islands of Lipara and Melita. Ordered to transfer the war to Africa, the consuls set out for Sicily with 330 ships. Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, and Hanno, commander of the fleet, met them. When a naval battle was joined, the Carthaginians were put to flight and lost sixty-four ships; the Romans lost twenty-two.

The victorious consuls crossed over to Africa and first of all received the city of Clypea into surrender. Proceeding from there toward Carthage, they ravaged 300 forts, or somewhat more, and carried their hostile standards around the territory of Carthage.

**Note:** A: “Manlius returned victorious to Rome and brought back 27,000 captives. Atilius …”

The consul Manlius departed Africa with the victorious fleet and brought back to Rome 27,000 captives together with immense spoils.

The consul Atilius Regulus remained in Africa and organized the war against the Carthaginians. Fighting against three Carthaginian commanders—that is, two Hasdrubals and Hamilcar, summoned from Sicily—he waged an exceedingly fierce war against them. In it 18,000 Carthaginians were killed, 5,000 were captured, eighteen elephants were taken, and eighty-two cities were received into surrender.

**Note:** A after “remained” continues: “He drew up his line against the Africans, fought victoriously against three Carthaginian commanders, killed 18,000 of the enemy, captured 5,000 together with eighteen elephants, and received seventy-four cities into allegiance. Meanwhile, at the river Bagradas, Regulus killed a serpent of extraordinary size, whose hide was 120 feet long; when brought to Rome, it was for some time a wonder to everyone, and so forth.”

As he was marching with the army, he pitched camp not far from the river Bagradas. There, when a serpent of extraordinary size was devouring many soldiers who had descended to the river to fetch water, Regulus went out with the army to destroy the beast. But the javelins hurled at its back accomplished nothing, and every cast of a weapon was ineffective: the missiles slipped across the dreadful lattice of its scales as though across an oblique tortoise-formation of shields and, astonishingly, were repelled by its own body so as not to wound it. When he saw that a great multitude were being crushed by its bites and that others were being killed by its exceedingly poisonous breath, he ordered ballistae to be brought up. By these, a stone of wall-like size was driven into its spine, loosening the framework of its entire body; soon, surrounded by weapons, it was easily overcome.

Its hide was carried to Rome. They say that it measured 120 feet in length, and for some time it was a wonder to everyone.

Therefore the Carthaginians, broken by wars and exhausted by disasters, asked Regulus for peace. But when they heard that the conditions of peace were intolerable and harsh, they judged it safer to die armed than to live in misery. They decided to purchase not only the aid of the Spaniards and Gauls, whom they had already long possessed in great numbers, but also that of the Greeks. Accordingly they summoned Xanthippus, king of the Lacedaemonians, with auxiliary forces, and appointed him commander in the war.

Xanthippus, having inspected the Carthaginian forces and led them out onto the plain, greatly improved their arrangements and joined battle with the Romans. A vast multitude of Roman soldiers was there. For 30,000 Roman soldiers were struck down in that engagement. That famous commander Regulus was captured with 500 men and thrown into chains. At last, in the tenth year of the Punic War, he afforded the Carthaginians a glorious triumph.

Xanthippus, conscious of so audacious an act and fearing the changing fortunes of unstable affairs, immediately left Africa for Greece.

At this time Ptolemy Philadelphus permitted the Jews who were in Egypt to be free. He sent votive vessels to Eleazar, the high priest of Jerusalem, and arranged for the divine Scriptures to be translated from the Hebrew language into Greek by the seventy interpreters. He kept them in the Alexandrian library, which he had assembled for himself from every kind of literature.

**Note:** The Hersfeld manuscript reads: “When Marcus Aemilius Paulus and Servius Fulvius Nobilior were consuls, both Roman consuls set out for Africa, and so forth,” and continues with other material in which it agrees word for word with Eutropius, except that the manuscript reads “from 460 ships,” where Eutropius has 464. Likewise, where Eutropius and H. read “15,000 of the enemy, either killed or captured,” the Bongarsian manuscript reads: “the fifteenth of the enemy.” A, like C, omits the particle *praeterea* (“in addition”).

When Marcus Aemilius Paulus and Servius Fulvius Nobilior were consuls, after hearing of Regulus’s capture and the defeat of the Roman army, they were ordered to cross into Africa with a fleet of 300 ships and set out for Clypea. The Carthaginians immediately came there with an equal fleet, and a naval battle could not be postponed. The consul Aemilius sank 104 Carthaginian ships, captured thirty together with their crews, and in addition killed or captured 35,000 of the enemy; he enriched his soldiers with immense booty.

But nine Roman ships were sunk, and 1,100 soldiers perished. The consuls pitched camp near Clypea. The two Carthaginian commanders named Hanno came there again with a large army. When battle was joined, they lost 9,000 men; and Africa would then have been subdued had not the famine been so great that the army could not remain longer.

As the consuls and their victorious fleets were returning to Italy laden with spoils, they suffered a dreadful shipwreck near Sicily. For of the 460 ships, scarcely eighty could be saved after their cargoes had been thrown overboard; nor had so great a storm at sea ever been heard of at any time.

Nevertheless, the Romans immediately repaired 200 ships, and the disaster did not make their courage any weaker.

**Note:** A has *infractus* (“unbroken”) instead of *infractior* (“less broken”).

At this time the first silver coin was struck in the City.

**Note:** The same manuscript has *figuratus est* (“was fashioned”) instead of *signatus est* (“was struck”), and omits the remainder beginning “Servilius, and so forth.” B and H likewise agree with Eutropius.

Then Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was sent with an army into Numidia and Mauretania. After acting savagely and bloodily against all the inhabitants, who were said to have welcomed Regulus gladly, he condemned the survivors to pay 1,000 talents of silver and 20,000 cattle; he crucified the leaders of all the peoples.

In the third year, as always happens when untamed fury quickly forgets danger, the consuls Servilius Caepio and Sempronius Blaesus crossed into Africa with 260 ships. They ravaged the entire coast lying around the Syrtes and, advancing inland, captured and destroyed many cities and brought immense booty back to the fleet.

**Note:** A after “260 ships” adds: “they set out for Africa and suffered shipwreck. Therefore …”

As they were returning to Italy, they struck the rocks near the promontory of Palinurus, which projects into the sea from the Lucanian mountains, and disastrously lost 150 cargo ships and the celebrated booty cruelly acquired.

Since the continuous disasters displeased the Romans, the Senate decreed that naval warfare should be abandoned, and that only sixty ships should remain for the defense of Italy.

**Note:** A: “retreating from naval battles,” and so forth.

Yet, driven by their unconquered desire, they immediately violated this decree. Moreover, the consul Cotta crossed into Sicily and fought the Carthaginians and Sicilians in many battles by land and sea, leaving throughout Sicily massacres of both enemies and, in part, allies unburied.

When Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Gaius Furius Placitus were consuls—

**Note:** Eutropius has “Gaius Furius Pacillus”; A and H have “Gaius Furius Placitus.”

Hasdrubal, the new Carthaginian commander, came from Africa to Lilybaeum with 130 elephants and more than 30,000 cavalry and infantry, and immediately joined battle with the consul Metellus near Panormus. But Metellus, fearing the great force of the beasts, first, by a very skillful plan, drove them either into flight or to their death, and thus easily defeated the great force of the enemy.

Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed in that battle. Twenty-six elephants were also killed; he captured 104 that were wandering about through the Numidians whom he had as auxiliaries, and led them through Italy. They provided the Italian peoples with a most impressive spectacle.

Hasdrubal fled to Lilybaeum with a few men and, while absent, was condemned to death by the Carthaginians.

After this, exhausted by so many burdens, the Carthaginians decided that peace should be requested from the Romans and that prisoners should be exchanged. For this purpose they judged that Atilius Regulus, formerly the Roman commander whom they had held captive for five years, should be sent among the other envoys under a particularly solemn oath.

When he came to Rome and was brought into the Senate, he did nothing as though he were a Roman. He declared that from the day on which he had fallen into the power of the Africans he had ceased to be a Roman. Therefore he even kept his wife away from his embrace, and persuaded the Senate not to make peace with the Carthaginians. They were broken by so many disasters and had no hope; they were not worth returning so many thousands of captives on account of one old man—himself—and the few Romans who had been captured. Thus he prevailed. For no one admitted the Africans when they requested peace.

Regulus himself returned to Carthage. When the Romans offered to keep him in Rome, he refused to remain in that city in which, after he had served the Africans, he could no longer possess the dignity of an honorable citizen.

**Note:** A and H continue: “Therefore, when he had returned to Africa, they cut off his eyelids so that he would remain awake until death amid intolerable torture and pain, and at last they killed him by every form of torment. After Claudius Pulcher and Gaius Junius were consuls—H nevertheless does not have ‘Gaius’—Claudius fought against the auspices and was defeated by the Carthaginians. For of 220 ships, he fled with thirty; ninety were captured or sunk together with their crews. The other consul also lost his fleet in a shipwreck, but kept his army safe because the shores were nearby. And so forth.”

Therefore, after returning to Africa, they cut off his eyelids so that he would remain awake until death in intolerable torture and pain, and so that he would always stand gazing at the sun’s rays; they bound him to a contrivance and killed him.

Then the other Atilius Regulus and Manlius Vulso, both twice consuls, set out for Lilybaeum with a fleet of 200 ships and four legions. The Romans attempted to besiege that town, situated on a promontory, but Hannibal, the son of Hamilcar, arrived; they were defeated, lost most of their army, and barely escaped themselves.

After them the consul Claudius set out with a fleet of 220 ships against the enemy at the harbor of Drepanum. There, when he was soon intercepted by the Carthaginian fleet, he was immediately defeated because he had fought against the auspices. He himself fled with thirty ships to the camp at Lilybaeum; all the rest—that is, eighty together with their crews—were captured, and the others were sunk. It is reported that 9,000 soldiers were killed and 20,000 captured.

The consul Gaius Junius, Claudius Pulcher’s colleague, also lost his entire fleet in a shipwreck, but kept his army safe because the shores were nearby.

In the following year as well, the Punic fleet crossed into Italy and ravaged large parts of it far and wide.

While these events were taking place, Manasses, his uncle, succeeded Eleazar as high priest in Judaea.

**Note:** A continues: “When Gaius Lutatius Catulus and Aulus Postumius Albinus were consuls, in the twelfth year of the Punic War Catulus began a war against the Africans. He set out for Sicily with 300 ships; the Africans prepared 300 ships against him. Never had such great forces fought at sea. Lutatius Catulus boarded his ship while ill, for he had been wounded in the previous battle. A battle was fought against the city of Lilybaeum in Sicily with great Roman courage. Seventy-three Carthaginian ships were captured, twenty-five sunk, 32,000 of the enemy captured, 13,000 killed, and an immeasurable amount of gold, silver, and booty brought under Roman control. Twenty Roman ships were sunk. The battle was fought on the sixth day before the Ides of March. The Carthaginians immediately requested peace, and peace was granted to them. The captives …” H agrees with the Ambrosian manuscript, and both agree with Eutropius, as Canisius noted, except in the number of ships sunk and enemies killed.

Meanwhile Lutatius Catulus crossed into Sicily with a fleet of 300 ships. There, while battle was being joined near the aforementioned city of Drepanum, he was fighting among the foremost men and was pierced through the thigh. He was rescued only with great difficulty when he was already being overwhelmed.

The Carthaginians, however, came against Sicily with 400 ships and great forces under the command of Hanno. Lutatius was no less energetic; rather, with astonishing speed he anticipated the Carthaginians’ plans. After the fleets of both sides had remained close together near the Aegates Islands, opposite the Sicilian city of Lilybaeum, for the entire night, with their anchors almost interwoven, at daybreak Lutatius first gave the signal for battle.

As the battle grew fiercer, Hanno was defeated, turned his ship around, and was the first to flee. Some part of his army went with him toward Africa; others took refuge in Lilybaeum. Seventy-three Punic ships were captured; 130 were sunk; 32,000 of the enemy were captured, and 14,000 killed. Never had such great forces fought at sea. An immeasurable amount of gold and silver booty was brought under Roman control. Twelve Roman ships were sunk.

The battle was fought on the sixth day before the Ides of March. Lutatius then came to the city of Eryx, which the Carthaginians held, and there killed 2,000 Carthaginians in battle.

Then the Carthaginians, in urgent haste, sent first to the consul Lutatius and afterward to Rome; they begged for peace and immediately obtained it. The Roman captives held by the Carthaginians were returned. The Carthaginians also requested permission to redeem the captives whom the Romans held from among the Africans.

The Senate ordered that those in public custody should be given back without payment; those held privately, however, were to return to Carthage after their owners had been paid a price, and that price was to be paid from the treasury rather than by the Carthaginians.

The Carthaginians made peace with the Romans on this condition: that they withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia and pay them 3,000 talents of refined silver over twenty consecutive years.

In those days Onias, the Jewish high priest, the distinguished son of Simon the Just, was in office.

**Note:** A and H after “was in office” continue: “At that time also the poet Quintus Ennius was born at Tarentum; later he taught at Rome, content with the service of a single maidservant. Quintus Lutatius and Aulus Mallius were appointed consuls; they made war on the Faliscans—a city that had once been wealthy in Italy—which both consuls concluded within six days of their arrival. Fifteen thousand of the enemy were killed; peace was granted to the rest, although half their land was taken away.” With these words Eutropius also ends Book II.

In the year 507 from the founding of the City, a sudden destruction of Rome itself preceded the Romans’ triumph. I would not recklessly say how a sudden event that brought even a modest joy to Rome was immediately overwhelmed by the gravest mourning.

For when Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Aulus Manlius were consuls, disasters of fire and water nearly consumed the City. The Tiber, swollen by unusual rains and overflowing beyond expectation in duration and magnitude, destroyed all the buildings of Rome situated on level ground. Different kinds of terrain combined for a single disaster: what the slower floodwaters held, they dissolved by soaking; whatever the torrent’s current encountered, it knocked down by force.

The devastation of the waters was followed by an even more serious destruction by fire. The fire—its origin unknown—spread through many parts of the city and caused a pitiable slaughter of people and houses; it also consumed in a single conflagration as much wealth as many foreign victories could not provide. Then, when it was ravaging everything around the Forum, it seized the temple of Vesta. Metellus, while rescuing the gods that were about to burn, escaped only after half his arm had been scorched.

When Titus Sempronius Gracchus and Gaius Valerius Flaccus were consuls, they made war on the Faliscans. This city had once been wealthy in Italy; both consuls defeated it within six days of their arrival, killing 15,000 of the enemy, granting peace to the rest, but taking half their land.

In the same year the Alpine Gauls also became new enemies of the Romans, and the war against them had varying results. In the first conflict, 3,000 Romans fell under the consul Valerius; in the second, 14,000 Gauls were killed and 2,000 captured.

But because of the earlier defeat—

**Note:** In Canisius’s edition, *triumphans* (“triumphing”) is printed erroneously.

—triumph was denied to the consul.

# BOOK THREE

**Note:** A and H add: “which lasted twenty-two years.” The Romans, now famous for the highest glory, sent envoys to Ptolemy, and so forth. Eutropius also has twenty-two years.

When the Punic War had ended—a war that lasted twenty-three years—the Romans, now renowned for the greatest glory, sent envoys to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, when Lucius Cornelius Lentulus and Fulvius Flaccus were consuls, promising assistance because Antiochus, king of Syria, had made war against him. Ptolemy thanked the Romans but accepted no assistance, for the battle had already been concluded.

At the same time Hiero, the most powerful king of Sicily, came to Rome for the games and gave the people 200,000 *modii* of grain as a gift.

**Note:** A has *exhibuit* (“presented”) instead of *dedit* (“gave”). A continues: “When Lucius Cornelius Lentulus and Fulvius Flaccus were consuls, in whose consulship Hiero had come to Rome, war was also waged against the Ligurians within Italy. For those same consuls were the first to lead Roman legions across the Po. There battle was fought against the Insubrians and Ligurians; 23,000 of them were killed, 5,000 captured, and a triumph was celebrated over them. In the following year blood flowed in the river of Picenum, the sky appeared to burn among the Tuscans, and at Ariminum three moons appeared simultaneously during a night shining with much light. Nevertheless the Carthaginians were attempting to renew the war, urging the Sardinians, who were required by the terms of peace to obey the Romans, to rebel. A Carthaginian embassy nevertheless came to Rome and obtained peace. When Titus Mallius Torquatus and Gaius Attilius were commonly called consuls, a triumph was celebrated over the Sardinians; peace was made everywhere, and the Romans had no war. This had happened only once since the founding of Rome, under King Numa Pompilius. Lucius Postumius, and so forth.”

**Note:** H agrees with Ambrosianus with a few exceptions. In place of 200,000 it has 200,000 as well; in “against the Ligurians” it reads “also Ligurians.” In “in the river of Picenum” it has “into the river of Picenum,” and so forth.

Sardinia rebelled under Carthaginian instigation when Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gaius Attilius Balbus were consuls. Therefore the Sardinians were soon subdued and crushed; and it was decreed that war should be brought against the Carthaginians, violators of the peace that they themselves had requested.

The Carthaginians, on the contrary, humbly begged for peace. After twice sending envoys and achieving nothing, and after ten of their leading men had likewise twice made humble appeals without obtaining anything, they finally succeeded through the speech of Hanno, the man of humblest standing among the envoys.

In this year the gate of Janus Geminus was closed, because there was no war anywhere that year; this had occurred under King Numa Pompilius.

In the year 517 from the founding of the City, Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was killed by the Spaniards in battle while secretly preparing another war against the Romans.

In the following year, when Lucius Postumius Albinus and Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus were consuls, they waged war against the Illyrians because Roman envoys had been killed by the Illyrians.

**Note:** A continues: “After many cities had also been captured, they received even kings into surrender; and then for the first time a triumph was celebrated over them. When Aemilius was consul, immense forces of Gauls crossed the Alps. The historian Fabius, who took part in that war, reported that 700,000 men had been assembled for it. But the consuls successfully accomplished only 40,000, and so forth.”

**Note:** H has 70,000 instead of 700,000; in the rest it agrees with our text.

Afterward an exceedingly savage war was waged against the Illyrians themselves. Many towns and smaller settlements were destroyed, and the survivors surrendered to the consuls Fulvius and Postumius. Then for the first time a triumph was celebrated over the Illyrians.

Three years later the pontiffs brought grief upon the wretched city by their sacrilegious sacrifices. For the decemvirs, going beyond the custom of ancient superstition, buried alive in the Forum Boarium a Gallic man and woman together with a Greek woman.

But this magical binding immediately turned against them. They atoned for the dreadful deaths they had inflicted upon foreigners through the most shameful slaughter of their own people. For when Lucius Aemilius Paulus and Gaius Attilius Regulus were consuls, the Senate was thrown into great terror by the revolt of Cisalpine Gaul, especially because it was reported that a huge army was approaching from farther Gaul, chiefly the Gaesatae—a name not for an ethnic people, but for Gallic mercenaries.

Therefore the consuls, alarmed, assembled the forces of all Italy for the defense of the empire. After this had been done, 800,000 armed men are said to have been present in the armies of both consuls, as the historian Fabius wrote, who took part in this war. Of these, 348,200 were Roman and Campanian infantry, and 26,600 cavalry; the remaining multitude consisted of allies.

When battle was joined near Arretium, the consul Attilius was killed. The 800,000 Romans fled, though not even such a number were killed as ought to have terrified them. Historians report that only 3,000 of them were then killed. This is all the more disgraceful and shameful because such enormous forces fled after losing so few men, thereby showing that in their other victories they had prevailed not through courage of spirit but through the outcomes of war. For who, I ask, would believe that this number had existed in the Roman army, much less that it had fled?

After this a second battle was fought with the Gauls, in which fully 40,000 Gauls were slaughtered, and a triumph was decreed for Aemilius. The Gauls certainly had fierce spirits and bodies more than human in size; but experience proved that their courage, just as it is greater than that of men in the first assault, is afterward less than that of women.

For Alpine bodies, raised under a damp sky, possess something resembling their own snows: as soon as they grow hot from the heat of battle, they immediately break into sweat and, with slight exertion, melt as though beneath the sun.

Under their leader Brittomarus, these men swore that they would not lay aside their belts until they had climbed the Capitol at Rome.

**Note:** A and H have “until they had burned the Capitol.”

And this was done. For after defeating them, Aemilius stripped them of their belts on the Capitol. Because their leader had vowed a golden torque to his Mars from a Roman soldier, Aemilius erected for Jupiter a golden trophy made from the torques of Ariobistus himself—

**Note:** A: “Ariobistus”; H: “Ariobistus.”

—and of the other Gauls.

**Note:** A continues: “Several years afterward war was fought against the Gauls in Italy. When the war had ended, with Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio as consuls, Marcellus then, with the commander …” H: “war was fought, and the war ended.”

In the following year the consuls Manlius Torquatus and Fulvius Flaccus were the first to lead Roman legions across the Po against the Ligurians. There battle was fought against the Insubrian Gauls; 23,000 were killed and 5,000 captured.

In the year immediately following this one, dreadful prodigies terrified the City. Blood flowed in the river of Picenum; at Falerii the sky appeared to burn; and at Ariminum the night shone bright with much light. Three moons appeared to rise in different regions of the sky. At Rome, a cow belonging to Gnaeus Domitius spoke, saying: “Beware, Rome.” Meat also fell from the sky; birds seized part of it, while part lay uncorrupted for a long time.

At that time Caria and the island of Rhodes were also shaken by a great earthquake, so violently that, as roofs generally collapsed, that famous colossus too fell.

In the same year the consul Flaminius, disregarding the auspices that forbade him to fight, engaged the Gauls and defeated them. In that battle 9,000 Gauls were killed and 17,000 captured.

After this Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio fought against the Gauls. Then the consul Marcellus, having unexpectedly fallen into the hands of the Gauls and seeing everything hostile, with no possibility of escape, broke into the midst of the enemy. Struck by his unexpected boldness, they were thrown into confusion, and he also killed their king, named Virdomarus.

**Note:** A and H have “Virdomarus.”

Where scarcely any hope of safety had existed, he carried away the king’s splendid spoils. Later, together with his colleague, he destroyed the great forces of the Gauls and, among the many towns of the Insubrians whom he had forced to surrender, stormed and captured Mediolanum as well, a most prosperous city. He brought great booty to Rome, and, in his triumph, Marcellus carried on his shoulders the spoils of the Gallic king, set upon a stake.

**Note:** A: “the Gallic spoil of Stipicius”; H: “the Gallic spoil of Stipicius.”

When Minucius Rufus and Publius Cornelius were consuls, war was brought against the Istrians because they had plundered Roman ships carrying grain. They were subdued after much Roman blood had been shed.

At this time Simon, son of Onias, became high priest of the Jews.

**Note:** A and H continue: “In the same year the Punic War …”

Here there briefly reappears that ancient Roman appetite for infamous glory, even through presumed acts of parricide. For Fabius Censorius killed his son Fabius Buteo, who had been accused of theft—a deed, certainly, which a father judged worthy of punishment even by parricide, although the laws did not even deem it deserving of a monetary penalty or of the harshest exile in the case of any human crime.

In the year 534 from the founding of the City, the Second Punic War was brought upon the Romans by Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians. When he was still nine years old, he had already sworn at the altars to his father Hamilcar that, as soon as he was able, he would fight against the Romans. He had also foreseen this dream: he seemed to see a young man, more august than human form, urging him to follow him, at Jupiter’s command, toward the destruction of Italy. Then, looking behind him, he seemed to behold a huge serpent ravaging everything, and to hear the crashing of heaven; he also saw storm clouds with a baleful brightness in the sky. He asked the young man going before him what would follow. To this the other replied: “You see the destruction of Italy; leave the rest to the fates.”

Hannibal therefore began to attack Saguntum, a flourishing city of Spain and a friend of the Romans, when he was in his twentieth year.

[Note: A and H, after “twentieth,” have “with 150,000 forces assembled.” To him, etc.]

The Romans warned him through ambassadors to refrain from war.

[Note: Both [A and H] have: “He refused to admit the ambassadors.” Rome.]

He most outrageously refused even to allow the Roman ambassadors sent to him to appear before him. The Romans also sent ambassadors to Carthage, so that Hannibal might be ordered not to wage war against the allies of the Roman people. The Carthaginians gave a harsh reply.

Meanwhile the Saguntines were overcome by hunger and, finally captured by Hannibal in the eighth month, were subjected to the most extreme punishments. A grim portent had foretold this great disaster to them. For when a woman had almost given birth, the infant returned into the womb, signifying the destruction of the city.

Hannibal was demanded as the author of so great a calamity. While the Carthaginians evaded the issue, Fabius, the leader of the embassy, said: “What delay is there? In the fold of this robe I carry war and peace; which do you choose?” When they shouted back, “War,” he said: “Then accept it.” And, shaking out the lap of his toga in the middle of the Senate house, he poured it out—not without horror, as though he truly carried war in his lap.

Then Publius Cornelius Scipio set out with an army for Spain, and Tiberius Sempronius for Sicily.

[Note: After “Sicily,” both have: “war was declared against the Carthaginians. Hannibal,” etc.]

Hannibal, leaving his brother Hasdrubal in Spain, crossed the Pyrenees Mountains, opening a way with the sword through the fiercest Gallic tribes. Only on the ninth day did he finally reach the Alps.

[Note: The same [manuscripts] add after “crossed”: “He then opened the Alps to himself in that region.” It is reported that he brought into Italy 80,000 infantry, 10,000 cavalry, seven and thirty [elephants], etc.]

There, while he overcame in battle the mountain Gauls who resisted his ascent, and cut through impassable rocks with fire, vinegar, and iron, he remained for four days; only on the fifth day, with the greatest exertion, did he reach the level ground. He is said to have brought into Italy 100,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, and 37 elephants.

Meanwhile many Ligurians and Gauls joined Hannibal. Sempronius Gracchus, learning of Hannibal’s arrival in Italy, transported his army from Sicily to Ariminum.

Publius Cornelius Scipio was the first to meet Hannibal at the Ticinus. When battle had been joined, his men were routed and almost all destroyed; he himself was saved from death by his son Scipio, still wearing the boy’s bordered toga, who was later surnamed Africanus and had scarcely passed out of childhood. Nevertheless, wounded, he returned to the camp.

Then, in the same consulship, battle was fought at the river Trebia, and again the Romans were defeated with equal disaster. Sempronius Gracchus also engaged Hannibal at the same river and, after losing his army, escaped almost alone. Hannibal too was wounded in that battle.

At that time many Italians surrendered to Hannibal. After he had crossed into Etruria, he was caught by a storm on the summit of the Apennines and remained there for two days; immediately afterward he and his army were confined immovably by the snow. A great number of men, a very large number of pack animals, and nearly all the elephants perished from the cold.

The Romans were then also terrified by dreadful portents. For the disk of the sun seemed to grow smaller, and shields were seen in the sky at Arpi.

[Note: A and H have “palms.”]

[Note: A and H have “palms.”]

The sun too seemed to have fought with the moon. At Capena two moons rose during the day.

[Note: In both [accounts], two moons rose. In Sardinia, etc.]

The region of Picenum was struck by a rain of stones. In Gaul, at the same time, a wolf drew a sword from its sheath before a sentry. In Sardinia, two shields sweated blood. To the Falisci, the sky seemed to split open as though by a great chasm. At Antium, too, while the reapers were harvesting, bloody ears of grain were thought to have fallen into the basket, and bloody rain fell.

Therefore Hannibal, coming into Etruria, knew that the consul Flaminius was alone in the camp and sought to seize the nearer, though marshy, route, so that he might overwhelm him unprepared as quickly as possible. At that time the river Sarnus, swollen with mud, had left behind hanging and unstable plains, of which it was said:

And the Sarnus, which waters the plain.

When Hannibal advanced against them with his army, the mists—especially those rising from the marsh—blotting out the view, he lost a large number of allies and pack animals. He himself, riding upon the one elephant that alone had survived, barely escaped the difficulty. But he lost the eye that had already been diseased in the Alps, through the violence of the cold, sleeplessness, and toil.

When he had come near the camp of the consul Flaminius, he provoked Flaminius to battle by ravaging the surrounding territory. This battle was fought at Lake Trasimene, where the Roman army, surrounded through Hannibal’s extremely skillful strategy, was utterly slaughtered. The consul himself was also killed; twenty-five thousand Romans were cut down in that battle, six thousand are reported to have been captured, and the rest fled. Two thousand of Hannibal’s army fell, despite the Romans’ enormous disaster—especially since their ardor for fighting had become so intense that they did not notice at all the extremely violent earthquake that happened at that very time and is reported to have demolished cities, shifted mountains, split rocks, and forced rivers to flow backward.

A certain Roman soldier was wounded so severely that he could no longer use his hands. When a Numidian tried to strip him of his armor, the soldier seized the enemy’s neck with his arms and bit off his nose and ears.

Meanwhile, the Romans later sent Quintus Fabius Maximus against Hannibal. By delaying battle, he broke Hannibal’s momentum. For he placed his camp along the highest mountain ridges and in the hidden passes of the woods, and so evaded Hannibal’s ardor. [Note: A. and H. add after “evaded”: “and soon, when an opportunity had been found, defeated him. After he had been defeated…”] Since Hannibal could not draw him into battle, he ravaged the fields of Italy but spared the villa of Maximus the Delayer, so that he might thereby arouse suspicion of treachery against Maximus among the Romans. But Fabius’s well-known loyalty made Hannibal’s cunning fruitless for the Romans. Meanwhile Maximus, having found an opportunity, fought and won.

Even after his defeat, Hannibal is said to have spoken to his men about Fabius as follows: “Did I not tell you that this enormous mountain cloud would overwhelm us on the plain by the violence of the storm?”

In the year 540 from the founding of the City, the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paulus and Publius Terentius Varro were sent against Hannibal and succeeded Fabius. Fabius warned both consuls that they could defeat Hannibal, a cunning and impatient commander, in no other way than by delaying battle.

But when, because of the impatience of the consul Varro, and despite the opposition of the other consul, Aemilius Paulus, battle was joined near the village called Cannae in Apulia, both consuls were defeated by Hannibal. For Hannibal had learned that in the morning the Aufidus River blew up powerful gusts of wind, driving whirlwinds of sand and dust. He therefore arranged his battle line so that the whole force of the wind would strike his own men from behind but the Romans in the face and eyes. For this reason he routed the Roman army. [Note: A. reads “Fidem” (“faith/loyalty”).]

For in that battle forty-four thousand Romans were killed. [Note: A. and H. continue from this point: “In that battle three thousand Africans perished, and a large part of Hannibal’s army was wounded. Nevertheless…” H. reads “None.”] Three thousand of Hannibal’s army were killed, and a large part was wounded. Yet in no Punic war were the Romans ever driven so close to total destruction.

The consul Aemilius Paulus perished in that battle. Although wounded, he had sat down upon a certain rock, and when Lentulus offered him a horse on which he might flee and survive the disaster, he refused; he remained there until he was killed by the enemy. Twenty men of consular or praetorian rank also perished; thirty senators were captured or killed; three hundred men of the nobility; forty thousand infantrymen; and three thousand five hundred cavalrymen. [Note: H. reads: “three hundred noble men, forty thousand soldiers.”] The consul Varro fled to Venusia with fifty horsemen. [Note: A. reads “Venusium.”]

There is no doubt that that day would have been the final day of the Roman state if Hannibal had immediately hastened to invade the City. But he became so elated by the success of the war that he admitted none of his fellow citizens into his camp, but gave them his replies through interpreters. He even repeatedly despised the Lacedaemonian Maharbal, who very often promised him that he would soon be dining in the Capitol if only his plan were followed in every respect.

Meanwhile Varro returned to Rome, and thanks were given him by the Senate and the people because he had not despaired of the commonwealth. [Note: A. and H. read “had not despaired,” and immediately afterward, “for honors, honors.”] He showed for the rest of his life that he had survived not from desire for life but from love of the commonwealth. For he let his beard and hair grow, and afterward never again took food while reclining. When offices were offered him by the people, he also declined them, saying that the commonwealth needed more fortunate magistrates. [Note: A. and H. read after this, “was in need of work.” They continue: “Yet amid all these disasters no Roman thought it worthy even to mention peace. Slaves were manumitted, something never done before, and made soldiers. After that battle many Italian cities that had obeyed the Romans transferred their allegiance to Hannibal. Hannibal [and the Romans]…”]

Hannibal therefore offered the Romans the opportunity to ransom their prisoners. The Senate replied that those citizens were unnecessary who, although armed, had allowed themselves to be captured. He afterward killed them all by various punishments. He cut off the soles of some men’s feet; he compelled others, especially brothers or blood relatives, to fight one another in pairs in the camp. The spectacle did not end until one had survived the slaughter—but he too was then to be slaughtered. As proof of his victory, Hannibal also sent three modii of gold rings to Carthage, which he had removed from the hands of the Roman cavalrymen, senators, and soldiers whom the others had killed.

So great was the Romans’ final despair concerning the commonwealth that the senators thought they ought to deliberate about abandoning Italy and seeking new homes. This would have been approved on the authority of Caecilius Metellus had not Cornelius Scipio, then a military tribune—the same man who afterward was called Africanus—deterred them with drawn sword, threatening to kill each of them. Instead, he compelled them all to swear allegiance to his words for the defense of their country.

The Romans, daring as though to breathe again from the underworld and return to hope of life, created Decius Junius dictator. After conducting a levy, he gathered four legions from every source, including men seventeen years old, for immature and unorganized military service. At that time, too, he compelled slaves of proven strength and willingness—whether volunteers or, if necessary, purchased at public expense—to take the military oath under the designation of freedom. They removed the missing weapons from the temples, and private wealth was poured into the impoverished treasury. Thus the equestrian order and the trembling plebs, forgetting their personal interests, took counsel together for the common good.

Junius the dictator, recalling an ancient response to Roman misery, opened what was virtually an asylum by edict. He promised immunity to all men who were burdened by crimes and debts and consigned them to military service. Their number amounted to six thousand men.

Campania—or rather all Italy—defected to Hannibal, since the possibility of restoring the Roman state had been utterly abandoned. After this, the praetor Lucius Postumius was sent to fight the Gauls, but he was killed together with his army.

Then, when Sempronius Gracchus and Quintus Fabius Maximus were consuls, Claudius Marcellus, designated proconsul after his praetorship, was the first to rout Hannibal’s army in battle. After the commonwealth had suffered such ruin, he gave hope that Hannibal could be defeated.

Meanwhile in Spain, where Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal had remained with a large army in order to subject the whole country to the Africans, he was defeated by the two Roman commanders, the brothers Scipio. He lost thirty-five thousand men in that battle; ten thousand of these were captured, and twenty-five thousand were killed. The Carthaginians sent him twenty-two thousand infantrymen, four thousand cavalrymen, and twenty elephants to restore the strength of his forces. [Note: A., H., and E. read “twelve thousand.”]

The Romans, having lured the Celtiberian soldiers—the first foreign troops they had begun to keep in their camp—with money, brought them from the enemy’s alliance into their own camp.

The proconsul Sempronius Gracchus was led into an ambush by a certain Lucanian who was his guest and was killed. [Note: H. reads: “Centurius Penula, a centurion, sought a war against Hannibal on his own initiative.” A. has “Centerius,” and so forth.] The centurion Centenius Penula voluntarily requested a campaign against Hannibal. He was killed with the eight thousand soldiers whom he had led into battle.

After this, the praetor Gnaeus Fulvius was defeated by Hannibal. Having lost his army, he barely escaped.
