[Note: From this point onward, the remainder is missing in manuscript H. as far as the words “he dismissed the Spaniards.” Manuscript A. continues: “In the fourth year after Hannibal came to Italy, he killed the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius, eleven tribunes besides, and seventeen thousand soldiers. The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal continuously for three days at Nola. On the first day they withdrew after an evenly matched battle; on the following day the consul was defeated; on the third day, victorious, he killed eight thousand of the enemy and forced Hannibal himself, with the rest, to flee into camp. Hannibal…”]

Hannibal occupied many Roman cities throughout Apulia, Calabria, and Bruttium. At that time King Philip of Macedonia also sent ambassadors to him, promising assistance against the Romans on the condition that, once the Romans had been destroyed, Hannibal would in turn provide him with assistance against the Greeks.

When Philip’s ambassadors were captured and the matter became known, the Romans ordered Marcus Valerius Laevinus to go to Macedonia and the proconsul Titus Manlius Torquatus to Sardinia. For Sardinia, too, had been stirred up by Hannibal and had abandoned the Romans.

Thus, at one time, battles were being fought in four places: in Italy against Hannibal, in Spain against his brother Hasdrubal, in Macedonia against Philip, and in Sardinia against the Sardinians and the other Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian. This Hasdrubal was captured alive by the proconsul Titus Manlius, who had been sent to Sardinia; twelve thousand were killed with him and fifteen hundred were captured. Thus Sardinia was subdued by the Romans. Manlius, victorious, brought Hasdrubal and the prisoners back to Rome.

Meanwhile Philip was also defeated by Laevinus in Macedonia, and in Spain Hasdrubal and Mago, Hannibal’s third brother, were defeated by the Scipios.

I am ashamed to recall it. What shall I say? Was it rather the wickedness or the misery of the Romans? Or, more truly, wicked misery or miserable wickedness? Who would believe that at a time when the treasury of the Roman people was begging for a poor contribution from private citizens, when the soldier in the camp was scarcely fit even in number and was nothing but a boy, a slave, a criminal, or a debtor, when the entire Senate in the Curia seemed almost wholly composed of newcomers, and finally when all resources had been so diminished and broken that deliberation was being undertaken about abandoning Italy—at that time, when they could not possibly sustain even one domestic war, three overseas wars had additionally been undertaken: one in Macedonia against Philip, the most powerful king of Macedonia; another in Spain against Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother; a third in Sardinia against the Sardinians and the other Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians; besides the fourth war against Hannibal, by which they were being crushed in Italy?

And yet their courageous despair against one another advanced toward better things. For amid all these circumstances they fought in despair and conquered by fighting. From this it is clearly shown that the times were not then more peaceful for leisure, but that miserable men were more courageous.

In the year 543 from the founding of the City, Claudius Marcellus barely captured Syracuse, the wealthiest city of Sicily, in a second assault. Although he had long besieged it, he could not take it by force because he was repelled by the machines of Archimedes, a Syracusan citizen endowed with marvelous ingenuity.

In the tenth year after Hannibal had come to Italy, when Gnaeus Fulvius and Publius Sulpicius were consuls, Hannibal moved his army out of Campania. After inflicting enormous devastation throughout the territory of Sedicinum and Suessula, he proceeded along the Via Latina and encamped at the Anio River, three miles from the City. The whole population was seized by incredible fear: the Senate and people were trembling with different anxieties, and even the matrons, crazed with terror, ran along the battlements, carried stones onto the walls, and eagerly desired to fight before the walls.

Hannibal himself advanced threateningly with his light cavalry as far as the Colline Gate and then drew up all his forces for battle. The consuls and the proconsul Fulvius did not refuse the fight. But when the battle lines of both sides had been deployed and stood in view of Rome—the prize that would belong to the future victor—such a great storm suddenly poured down from the clouds, mixed with hail, that the disordered ranks could scarcely gather in their own camps while holding on to their weapons.

Then, when clear weather returned and the forces had gone back onto the plain and into battle formation, a second storm, more violent than the first, broke out. Because of the greater fear it caused, it restrained their boldness and compelled the terrified armies to retreat into their tents. Hannibal then, turning his thoughts toward religious omens, is said to have remarked: “The will to seize Rome is granted to me, but the opportunity is not; or the opportunity is granted, but the power is lacking.” [Note: A. reads “turning toward the region.”]

But in Spain the two brothers Scipio, who had been victorious for many years, were killed by Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother. Their army, however, remained intact. They had been deceived more by chance than by valor.

In Campania, Capua was captured by the proconsul Quintus Fulvius. The leading men of Campania took their own lives by poison. Fulvius killed the entire Senate of Capua with punishments, even though the Roman Senate opposed it.

Two women from the Campanian side—that is, Vescia Oppia, a respectable married woman, and Clivia Facula, a prostitute—had acted kindly toward the Roman cause. One of them had always prayed to the gods for the safety of the Roman people; the other had provided food for Roman soldiers who were prisoners. For these services they retained both their freedom and their property during the destruction of Capua, and they obtained the privilege of choosing their reward. [Note: Another manuscript reads “Falcula.”]

At that time the consul Marcellus also captured a large part of Sicily, which the Africans had begun to hold, including Syracuse, the most noble city, as I have said. Enormous booty was brought to Rome.

Laevinus made an alliance in Macedonia with Philip, many peoples of Greece, and King Attalus of Asia, and then departed for Sicily. There he captured at Agrigentum a certain Hanno, an African commander, together with the city itself, and sent him to Rome with the noblest prisoners. He received forty cities into surrender and stormed twenty-six. Thus, after recovering all Sicily and breaking Macedonia, he returned to Rome with immense glory.

Hannibal then suddenly attacked the consul Gnaeus Fulvius in Italy and killed nine thousand men.

[Note: A. reads: “Meanwhile, in Spain, where, after the two Scipios had been killed, Mallius was the Roman commander, Publius Cornelius Scipio was sent, the son of Publius Scipio, who had waged war there, at the age of [lacuna]…”]

Meanwhile, after the two brothers Scipio had been killed in Spain and everyone had been struck with fear and hesitation, Scipio, still a very young man, voluntarily offered himself for the command. Although there was a shortage of money in the treasury, on the initiative of Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Laevinus, who were then consuls, all the senators openly contributed coined gold and silver to the quaestors for public use. They retained for themselves, their sons, and thereafter their daughters and wives nothing except their rings and amulets, and for each person no more than a single ounce of gold and a single pound of silver.

Scipio was twenty-four years old, the foremost of all Romans both in his own generation and, for the most part, in the generations that followed. This is the man who, when the senators were deliberating—as I have said—out of fear of Hannibal about abandoning Italy, forbade it with drawn sword. [Note: A. reads: “were deliberating; when he was a military tribune, with drawn sword…” It adds later: “He forbade it, and, swearing first that he would stand as the defender of his country, compelled everyone likewise to swear. He restored the Romans to hope of life as though from the underworld.”]

He received the proconsular command in Spain and, intent above all upon avenging his father and uncle, crossed the Pyrenees and at his first assault captured New Carthage in Spain. There the Carthaginians had stored their greatest pay funds, strong garrisons, large supplies of gold and silver, and the noblest hostages whom they had received from the Spaniards. There he also captured Mago, Hannibal’s brother, and sent him to Rome with the others.

There was immense joy at Rome afterward. Scipio restored the Spanish hostages to their parents. Finally, when a remarkably beautiful young woman in the bloom of adulthood had been captured by him, he preserved her with fatherly compassion, allowing her parents to ransom her. He also persuaded the girl’s fiancé, a man of the noblest birth, to come to him; like a compassionate father, he gave the girl to him in marriage and, as her dowry, forgave the price he had received from her parents. Because of these actions, with the girl’s fiancé and his parents especially urging it, almost all Spain transferred its allegiance to him.

After this he defeated and drove away Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal and seized enormous booty. [Note: From this point manuscript A. continues: “Meanwhile in Italy the consul Publius Fabius Maximus recovered Tarentum, where enormous forces of Hannibal were stationed, and there also killed the Carthaginian commander Carthalo. Thirty…”]

Moreover, he brought eighty cities under his power, either through surrender or by war. After selling the Africans under the auctioneer’s crown, he dismissed the Spaniards without payment.

[Note: H.: “In the fourth year after Hannibal came to Italy, Gnaeus Fulvius the proconsul…”]

In Italy Hannibal killed the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius, eleven tribunes besides, and seventeen thousand men. The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal continuously for three days at Nola. On the first day they withdrew after an evenly matched battle; on the second day the consul was defeated; on the third, victorious, he killed eight thousand of the enemy. He forced Hannibal himself, with the rest, to flee into camp. [Note: The Hersfeld manuscript has: “He forced him into camp.” It then continues: “Hannibal occupied many Roman cities throughout Apulia…” This agrees word for word with Eutropius, Merula, folio 31 through folio 33, except that where Eutropius reads “with Publius Sulpicius and Gnaeus Fulvius as consuls, Hannibal advanced as far as the fourth milestone of the City,” manuscript H. has more fully: “When Gnaeus Fulvius was consul, Hannibal moved his army from Campania and, after enormous devastation of the whole region, advanced along the Via Latina through the territory of Sedicinum and Suessula as far as the fourth milestone of the City; his cavalry reached the gate…” A little later, where Eutropius, folio 33, reads “for the most part the foremost of his age,” manuscript H. is fuller and reads: “for the most part. This man, then, when the senators were deliberating, out of fear of Hannibal, about abandoning Italy, and when he was a military tribune, forbade it with drawn sword; and, swearing first that he would stand as the defender of his country, compelled everyone likewise to swear. He restored the Romans to hope of life as though from the underworld. He captured Carthage in Spain, where the Africans had all their gold, and so forth.”]

Meanwhile the consul Quintus Fabius Maximus again stormed and captured Tarentum, which had revolted from the Romans. There he destroyed Hannibal’s enormous forces together with their commander Carthalo. [Note: A. reads “thirty-five thousand.”] He sold thirty thousand prisoners, distributed the booty among the soldiers, and deposited the money obtained from the sale of the men in the treasury. Then many cities that had transferred themselves to Hannibal again submitted to Fabius Maximus. [Note: “Submitted” is added. A. reads “surrendered,” omitting the rest and continuing: “In the following year Scipio performed remarkable deeds in Spain, both personally and through his brother Lucius Scipio; they recovered seventy cities. In Italy, however, they fought badly. For the consul Claudius Marcellus was killed by Hannibal. In the third year after Scipio had departed for Spain, he again performed glorious deeds. He defeated the king of the Spaniards in a great battle, accepted him into friendship, and was the first of all not to demand hostages from a defeated enemy. Despairing…”]

Hannibal ambushed and killed both consuls, Marcellus and Crispinus, together with their army.

In the third year after Scipio had departed for Spain, he again performed glorious deeds. He defeated the king of the Spaniards in a great battle, accepted him into friendship, and was the first of all men not to demand hostages from a defeated enemy.

Then, despairing that Spain could be held for long against Scipio, Hannibal summoned his brother Hasdrubal to Italy with all his forces. [Note: A. reads: “When he came, the consuls Appius Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator…”]

Hasdrubal, coming from Spain through Gaul to Italy while Appius Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator were consuls, brought with him substantial auxiliary forces of Spaniards and Gauls. When, after he had already descended from the Alps in his haste to arrive, he had been betrayed to the consuls, he fell into an ambush prepared by the Roman army near the Metaurus River, while Hannibal remained unaware. Nevertheless, he was killed while fighting bravely. [Note: A. adds: “Fifty-eight thousand from his army were killed, five thousand were captured, and forty-four Roman citizens were found among them and recovered. A great quantity of gold and silver was brought to Rome. In the year…”]

The outcome of the battle remained uncertain for a long time, especially because the elephants were greatly harassing the Roman battle line. The Romans called the soldiers who harassed them from a distance *velites*, from *velitare*, because this form of military service had recently been devised: selected young men of agile build sat behind the cavalrymen with their weapons; when they came near the enemy, they leapt down from the horses and immediately fought on foot, while the cavalrymen who had transported them fought from another side and threw the enemy into confusion.

The elephants were driven backward by these *velites*. When their own men could no longer control them, they were killed with a smith’s iron tool—that is, a chisel driven between the ears. The commander Hasdrubal himself had first devised this method of killing the beasts when necessary.

This battle was fought near the Metaurus River, where Hasdrubal was defeated—like Lake Trasimene, where the Roman army [was defeated], the Picenian city of Cesena, and that village of Cannae. For fifty-nine thousand of Hasdrubal’s army were killed there in a great slaughter. Five thousand four hundred were captured. Four thousand Roman citizens were found among them and recovered, which brought consolation to the victorious consuls. For eight thousand of their own army also fell. [Note: H. reads: “Fifty-eight thousand of his army were captured; four hundred and four Roman citizens were found among them and recovered. A great quantity of gold and silver…” These words agree exactly with Eutropius until the end, except that near the end of the third book Eutropius reads “two hundred thousand pounds,” whereas this manuscript reads “a quantity of twenty thousand,” and in the final line Eutropius reads “after the seventeenth year,” while the manuscript reads “after the nineteenth year.”]

A great quantity of gold and silver was brought back to Rome. The head of Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal was thrown before Hannibal’s camp. When he saw it and learned at the same time of the Carthaginians’ defeat, in the thirteenth year after he had come to Italy he fled into Bruttium. [Note: A. reads “Britain” instead of “Bruttium,” and omits the rest: “After this…”]

After this, for a whole year, a period of rest from the disturbances of war seemed to intervene between Hannibal and the Romans, because disease was raging in the camps and a very severe pestilence was afflicting both armies.

After this Hannibal began to lose confidence in the outcome of the war, while the Romans gained immense courage. Therefore they themselves summoned Publius Cornelius Scipio from Spain, who had already reduced the whole of Spain, from the Pyrenees to the Ocean, to the form of a province. [Note: A. adds after “Scipio”: “He [came] to Rome, etc.”] He accordingly came to Rome with immense glory.

At the same time, Onias, son of Simon, was high priest in Jerusalem.

When Quintus Caecilius and Lucius Valerius were consuls, all the cities in Bruttium that Hannibal held surrendered to the Romans.

In the fourteenth year after Hannibal had come to Italy, Scipio, who had accomplished many successes in Spain, was elected consul with Licinius Crassus and sent to Africa. [Note: A. reads “was made consul”: “to this man…”] People believed that there was something divine in this man, to such an extent that he was even thought to converse with the gods. Indeed, he never undertook either public or private business before spending a very long time in the shrine of Capitoline Jupiter, before he was seen by anyone.

In Africa he fought Hanno, son of Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander, killed him, destroyed part of his army by slaughter and part by capture, and seized his camp. For in that battle he killed eleven thousand Carthaginians with four thousand five hundred soldiers.

[Note: A. continues: “He captured Syphax, king of Numidia, who had joined the Africans, and invaded his camp. Scipio sent Syphax to Rome with the noble Numidians and immense booty. When this had happened…”]

The consul Sempronius, having engaged Hannibal and been defeated, fled to Rome.

Scipio attacked the winter quarters of the Carthaginians and the camps of the Numidians in Africa, both of which were not far from Utica, and set them on fire at the dead of night. The Carthaginians, terrified, thinking that the fire had started accidentally, ran unarmed to extinguish it. For this reason they were easily overwhelmed by armed troops. In both camps forty thousand Carthaginians and Numidians were consumed by fire and sword; five thousand were captured. The commanders themselves were horribly burned and barely escaped.

The commander Hasdrubal fled to Carthage. Thus Syphax and Hasdrubal soon rebuilt a very large army, engaged Scipio again, and were defeated and fled. Laelius and Massinissa captured Syphax as he fled. The rest of the multitude fled to Cirta, which Massinissa accepted into surrender after besieging it. He led Syphax to Scipio in chains. Scipio entrusted him to Laelius to be taken to Rome with enormous spoils and very many prisoners. When Syphax died while in custody at Tibur, the Senate ordered that he be honorably buried at public expense.

When this became known, almost all Italy abandoned Hannibal. The Carthaginians ordered him to return to Africa, which Scipio was ravaging. Thus, in the seventeenth year, Italy was freed from Hannibal. He is said to have left it in tears, after killing all the soldiers of Italian origin who were unwilling to follow him.

The ambassadors of the Carthaginians asked Scipio for peace. He sent them from there to the Senate at Rome, and they were granted a truce of forty-five days, long enough for them to go to Rome and return. Thirty thousand pounds of silver were accepted from them.

The Senate ordered peace to be made with the Carthaginians according to Scipio’s decision. Scipio imposed these conditions upon them: that they should possess no more than thirty ships, pay fifty thousand pounds of silver, and return the prisoners and deserters. [Note: A. adds after “return”: “Meanwhile, when Hannibal was approaching Africa, peace…”]

Meanwhile, as Hannibal drew near the African coast, he ordered one of the sailors to climb the mast of the ship and look out from there to determine what region they held. The sailor replied that he had seen a ruined tomb. Hannibal, abhorring the omen, altered his course and landed his forces at the town of Leptis.

He immediately came to Carthage after restoring his forces, and the peace was disturbed. The Africans committed many hostile acts. Nevertheless, when their ambassadors came from the City, the Romans captured them but released them at Scipio’s command.

Hannibal, having been defeated by Scipio in frequent battles, also began to seek peace and a conference with Scipio. When the two most illustrious commanders had stared fiercely at one another for a long time, stunned by mutual admiration, and a conference had been arranged between them, the Carthaginians were displeased with the conditions because five hundred thousand pounds of silver and one hundred thousand pounds had been added to the previous terms on account of their recent treachery. They ordered Hannibal to fight. [Note: A. adds after “peace”: “When they had come to a conference, peace was granted on the same conditions as before, with an additional five hundred thousand pounds of silver and one hundred thousand pounds because of the new treachery. The Carthaginians were displeased with the conditions and ordered…”]

Hannibal sent three scouts to Scipio’s camp. Scipio captured them, ordered them to be led around the camp, and showed them the entire army, without asking them anything about the enemy. He then ordered lunch to be given them and, after they had eaten and their horses had been refreshed, allowed them to return, so that they might report to Hannibal what they had seen among the Romans.

Meanwhile a battle was joined by both commanders. It was arranged for a long time through the great skill of the commanders and fought with vast masses of troops—a battle such as scarcely any age had witnessed, since, as we have said, the most experienced men had led their forces into war. [Note: A. reads “a battle was drawn up, such as scarcely any…”]

Scipio returned victorious. [Note: A. reads “withdrew” for “returned” and continues: “with Hannibal himself almost captured; he escaped first with many horsemen, then with twenty, and finally with four.”] Eighty elephants were either captured or killed there. Twenty thousand five hundred Carthaginian soldiers were killed.

Hannibal, having experienced everything both before and during the battle, escaped amid the confusion, first with many horsemen, then with twenty, and finally barely with four, and fled to Hadrumetum. After thirty-six years, he came to Carthage—the same city from which he had departed as a small boy. Twenty thousand pounds of silver and eighty pounds of gold were found in Hannibal’s camp, together with an abundance of other furnishings. [Note: A. reads “abundant equipment,” and then continues: “After that battle peace was made with the Carthaginians. Scipio returned to Rome, triumphed with immense glory, and from that time began to be called Africanus. The Second Punic War ended in the nineteenth year after it had begun.”]

Let Rome boast, if it wishes, of its victories: Hannibal, however, was overcome by the luxuries of Campania while lingering in that delightful province. While he floated in the waters, while he was everywhere saturated with fish and oysters, while he smelled sweetly, drank, and slept, the relaxation of the waters softened Punic ferocity. Seplasia, a town of Campania, weakened and dissolved the man whom other hardships had hardened, with its fragrant perfumes.

After that battle, therefore, the Carthaginians, convinced that no hope remained except in seeking peace, again begged that peace be granted. When Gaius Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Aelius Paetus were consuls, peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, with the consent of the Senate and the people. More than five hundred ships were even brought out to sea and burned in full view of the city.

Scipio, already called Africanus, entered the City in triumph with immense glory. Terence, who afterward became a comic poet, had been captured among the noble citizens of the Carthaginians who had been subjugated. Wearing the cap, which was a sign of granted freedom, he followed behind the triumphal chariot. [Note: A. has “The man Terence…”]

In the five hundred and forty-fifth year from the founding of the City, the Second Punic War ended, in the nineteenth year after it had begun.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789D] When the Punic War had therefore ended, the Macedonian War against King Philip followed. In the five hundred and fifty-first year from the founding of the City, Titus Quintius Flaminius [Note: H. and Eutropius read: “conducted the war successfully against King Philip, and peace was granted to him on these terms…” A. continues after “was sent”: “He conducted the war successfully, and peace was granted to him on these terms…”]
sent against Philip, king of the Macedonians. After many very serious battles, in which he defeated the Macedonians, he granted Philip peace on these terms: that he should not make war upon the Greek cities whom the Romans had defended against him; that he should return the prisoners and deserters; that he should retain only fifty ships and surrender the rest to the Romans; that for ten years he should pay four thousand pounds of silver each year; and that he should surrender his son Demetrius as a hostage. [Note: A. adds after this: “Titus Quinctius also made war upon the Lacedaemonians, likewise defeated their commander, and to those whom…”]

Then he fought against the Lacedaemonians. After defeating their commander Nabis, he received them into allegiance on whatever terms he wished and celebrated a magnificent triumph. Before his chariot he led the most distinguished hostages: Demetrius, the son of Philip, and Armenes, a Roman captive of Nabis. These men had been sold throughout Greece under Hannibal; all were recovered, and, with their heads shaved because their servitude had been removed, they followed the triumphal chariot.

At the same time the Insubres [Note: H.: “the Insubres and Boii”] and the Boii, by whom Ticinum was founded, together with the Cenomani, having joined their forces under Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander who had remained in Italy, ravaged the cities of Cremona and Placentia. They were defeated by the praetor L. Fulvius in a very difficult war. The consul Marcellus was overwhelmed by the Boii in Etruria and lost a large part of his army. Furius, another consul, later came to his aid, and together they ravaged the entire nation of the Boii with fire and sword, almost annihilating it.

[Note: From this point onward, the remainder is not read in A. or H. until the words “the Macedonian war having ended.”]

Later the proconsul Flaminius subdued King Philip in war, together with the Thracians, Macedonians, Illyrians, and many other peoples who had come to his aid. The Macedonians were defeated and lost their camp. Polybius writes that eight thousand of the enemy were killed that day and five thousand captured. Valerius says that forty thousand were slaughtered, while Claudius records that thirty-two thousand were killed.

But this discrepancy among the writers is certainly falsehood. The cause of the falsehood is plainly flattery: they strive either to heap praise upon the victor and exalt the valor of their country, for the benefit of those living or of posterity. Otherwise, if the number had not been investigated, it would not have been stated, however inaccurately. If it is glorious for a commander and his country to have killed the greatest possible number of enemies, how much more joyful for the country and honorable for its commanders must it seem to have lost either none or very few of their own?

Thus it is perfectly clear that, with the same shamelessness in lying by which the number of slain enemies is increased, the losses of allies who have been lost are diminished or even entirely concealed. Accordingly, Sempronius Tuditanus was overwhelmed in Nearer Spain and killed together with his entire Roman army.

After the Macedonian war had ended, the Syrian war followed.

[Note: H. and Eutropius, Book IV: “During the consulship of P. Cornelius Scipio and M. Attilius Glabrio. Hannibal had joined Antiochus, abandoning his native Carthage lest it be surrendered to the Romans,” and so forth. In these matters manuscript H agrees word for word with Eutropius, except that where Eutropius, folio 38, reads “thirty thousand infantry and four thousand cavalry were killed on the king’s side in that engagement,” H. reads “fifty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry.” Likewise, Eutropius calls Scipio “Asiaticus,” whereas H. calls him “Asiagenus.”]

[Col. 0792D] A. also agrees with Hersfeld. Here, however, we record the variant reading of our C. after the word “abandoning,” so that, unlike Canisius, we do not send readers to another task: “abandoning.” Aulius Glabrio fought successfully in Achaea; the camp of King Antigonus was captured in a night battle, and he himself was put to flight. “Since Philip…”]

During the consulship of L. Valerius Flaccus and M. Porcius Cato, King Antiochus of Syria, preparing war against the Roman people, crossed from Asia into Europe. At that time Hannibal, because rumors about him were being circulated among the Romans as a means of provoking war, was ordered by the senate to be handed over to the Romans. He secretly fled from Africa out of fear that he would be surrendered to the Romans and went to Antiochus. Finding Antiochus hesitating at Ephesus, he soon drove him into war.

At that time the law proposed by the tribune of the plebs Oppius—under which no woman was to possess more than half an ounce of gold, wear a multicolored garment, or use a carriage within the city or beyond it for more than a thousand paces, unless she did so for religious purposes—was repealed after twenty years. Once this decree had been abolished, what need is there to describe the extent to which the matrons indulged themselves, since they began to live in luxury just like men?

During the consulship of P. Cornelius Scipio and M. Acilius Glabrio, Antiochus, although he had occupied Thermopylae, whose defenses would have made him safer in view of the uncertain outcome of war, was nevertheless defeated in battle in Achaea by the consul Glabrio. His camp was captured in a night engagement; the commander himself barely escaped from the battle with a few men and reached Ephesus. He is reported to have had sixty thousand armed men, of whom forty thousand were killed and more than five thousand fled.

The other consul, Scipio, engaged the nation of the Boii and killed twenty thousand in that battle. Because Philip had aided the Romans against Antiochus, his son Demetrius was returned to him.

Then, during the second consulship of P. Scipio Africanus and the consulship of T. Sempronius Longus, ten thousand Gauls were killed near Milan. In the following battle eleven thousand Gauls were killed, while five thousand Romans were slain. Minucius, driven into extreme danger by the Ligurians and surrounded by an enemy ambush, was scarcely rescued through the efforts of the Numidian cavalry. [Note: A. adds: “and was liberated. L. Cornelius…”]

After this the praetor Digitius defeated the Celtiberians together with their neighboring peoples and captured their king. In both Spains, the praetors Flaminius and Fulvius fought wars that were extremely fierce and bloody for both peoples.

During the consulship of L. Cornelius Scipio and C. Laelius, Scipio Africanus went as legate to his brother, the consul L. Cornelius Scipio, against Antiochus. He held a friendly conference with Hannibal, who was with Antiochus, but, having accomplished nothing in the matter of peace, withdrew from Antiochus.

In the following year Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal, who was with Antiochus, in a naval battle. Antiochus himself was later crushed in a great battle near Sipylum, at Magnesia, a city of Asia, by the consul L. Cornelius Scipio. The Romans were aided in that battle by Eumenes, the brother of King Attalus, who founded Eumenia in Phrygia.

Fifty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry on the king’s side were killed in that engagement. Then the king sought peace and voluntarily sent back the son of Africanus, although it is uncertain whether he had captured him while reconnoitering or in the battle. The senate granted peace on the same terms that had previously been offered to him, although he had been defeated: he was to withdraw from Europe and Asia and remain within the Taurus; he was to provide ten thousand talents and twenty hostages; and he was to surrender Hannibal, the instigator of the war.

The senate gave King Eumenes all the cities of Asia that Antiochus had lost in the war. To the Rhodians, who had brought aid to the Romans against King Antiochus, they granted many concessions. Scipio returned to Rome and celebrated a magnificent triumph. He too received the name “Asiaticus,” in imitation of his brother, because he had conquered Asia, just as his brother was called “Africanus” because of Africa.

[Note: A. also has “Asiagenus.”]

[Note: From this sentence through “Then L. Baebius,” these words are absent from H. From that point the manuscript H agrees with the Miscellany through “[those who] took care.”]

Meanwhile, in the farther province of Spain, the proconsul L. Aemilius was killed and perished together with his entire army at the hands of the Lusitanians. Then L. Baebius, setting out for Spain, was surrounded by the Ligurians and killed with his entire army. It is consequently clear that not even a messenger survived, so completely were they annihilated, that the people of Massilia had to report the very destruction at Rome.

[Note: From this sentence through “the consul Marcius,” everything is absent from H. and A.]

The consul Fulvius crossed from Greece into Gallograecia, which is now called Galatia, and reached Mount Olympus, to which all the Gallograecians had fled with their wives and children. There he fought a most bitter war. For the Romans, crushed by arrows, huge stones, and other weapons hurled from the high ground, at last broke through to close combat with the enemy. Forty thousand Gallograecians are reported to have been killed in that battle.

[Note: H.: “The consul Marcius set out against the Ligurians, was defeated, and lost four thousand soldiers. During the consulship of Spurius Postumius Albinus and Marcus Philippus, Marcus Philippus celebrated a triumph over the Aetolians,” and what follows; H. agrees with Eutropius through “was buried.” A. has “Alvinus” instead of “Albinus.”]

The consul Marcius set out against the Ligurians, was defeated, and lost four thousand soldiers. Had he not quickly retreated into the camp after his defeat, he would have suffered the same disaster of annihilation that Baebius had earlier suffered from those same enemies.

During the consulship of M. Claudius Marcellus, King Philip, who had killed Roman envoys, had earned pardon because of the most modest entreaties of his son Demetrius, whom he had sent as an envoy. Philip then immediately poisoned the same son, regarding him as a friend of the Romans and a traitor to himself, while that son’s brother perpetrated the parricide, making an instrument of their father, who suspected no unhappy evil from either of them.

During the consulship of Sp. Postumius Albinus and Q. Marcius Philippus, M. Fulvius celebrated a triumph over the Aetolians. [Note: A.: “celebrated a triumph. Hannibal, who, after Antiochus had been defeated, fled to Prusias, king of Bithynia, lest he be handed over to the Romans. He requested…”]

In those same days Hannibal, after Antiochus had been defeated by the Romans, fled to Prusias, king of Bithynia, lest he be handed over to the Romans. He was demanded from Prusias by Q. Flaminius. When he was about to be surrendered to the Romans, he drank poison and was buried at Libyssa in the territory of the Nicomedians.

[Note: The remainder through “in the same year” is absent from A. and H.]

Philopoemen, commander of the Achaeans, was captured and killed by the Messenians. In the same year Scipio Africanus, after living for a long time in exile from the ungrateful City, died of illness at the town of Liternum.

[Note: A. continues after “died”: “Then Vulcan…” H.: “at the town of Amiternum he died of illness. Then an island of Vulcan, which had not existed before, suddenly emerged from the sea. In those days also occurred what the history in the Book of Maccabees relates about Heliodorus. When King Philip of Macedonia died—he had both waged war against the Romans and later brought aid to the Romans against Antiochus—his son Perseus rebelled in Macedonia, with immense forces prepared for war. For he had as allies…” In these matters H. agrees word for word with Eutropius through “he commended Nicomedes to the senate.” Compare here what has been inserted and added here and there in the Miscellany. CANIS.]

He ordered the following inscription to be placed on his tomb: “Ungrateful fatherland, you do not even possess my bones.”

At that time in Sicily an island of Vulcan, which had not existed before, suddenly emerged from the sea amid everyone’s amazement and has remained there down to the present. In those days also occurred what the history in the Book of Maccabees relates about Heliodorus. [Note: A. omits the rest; after the word “history” it continues: “Accordingly, when Philip…”]

The praetor Q. Fulvius Flaccus routed twenty-three thousand men in a great battle in Nearer Spain and captured four thousand. Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in Farther Spain compelled one hundred and five towns, emptied and battered by wars, to surrender. At the same time L. Postumius routed forty thousand enemies in battle in Nearer Spain, while the praetor Gracchus, again in that region, stormed and captured two hundred towns.

Accordingly, after Philip, king of Macedonia, had died—he had waged war against the Romans and had afterward provided aid to the Romans against Antiochus—his son Perseus rebelled in Macedonia, having assembled immense forces.

[Note: A. has “having gathered them together.” He had as allies the king of Thrace and the king of Illyria, whose name was Gentius. The Romans, however, had as auxiliaries Eumenes, king of Asia; Ariarathes of Cappadocia; Antiochus of Syria; Ptolemy of Egypt; and Massinissa of Numidia. But Prusias…]

For the exceedingly savage nation of the Bastarnae, during the consulship of Lepidus and Mutius, was destroyed without any battle, lured by the hope of plunder and by the opportunity to cross the river Ister. At that time the Danube, which is also called the Ister, happened to be covered with thick ice, allowing an easy passage on foot.

Accordingly, when an immeasurable multitude of people and animals imprudently crossed in one enormous column all at once, the ice, creaking under the immense weight and the shock of those walking across it, split apart. The frozen crust, finally overcome and shattered beneath the entire column that it had long supported, abandoned it in the midst of the whirlpools; then, obstructed by the same fragments and covered over again, it submerged them. Only a few from the whole people barely escaped to either bank, their entrails torn open.

During the consulship of P. Licinius Crassus and C. Cassius Longinus, the Macedonian war was conducted, and deservedly ranks among the greatest wars. At first all Italy was on the side of the Romans; then Ptolemy, king of Egypt; Ariarathes of Cappadocia; Eumenes, king of Asia; and Massinissa of Numidia joined them.

Prusias, king of Bithynia, although he had Perseus’s sister as his wife, nevertheless maintained an impartial stance toward both sides. [Note: A. adds after “he presented himself”: “Publius Licinius, consul and commander of the Romans, was sent against him and was defeated by the king in a serious battle. Nevertheless, although the Romans had been defeated, they refused to grant peace when the king requested it, except on these terms: that he surrender himself and his people to the senate and the Roman people.”]

Accordingly, when the consul Licinius Crassus arrived, Perseus came to meet him with Cotys, king of Thrace, and Gentius, king of Illyria, whom he had as allies. Battle was joined, and the Romans were disastrously defeated and fled. In the following battle, after both sides had suffered equal losses, they withdrew to their winter quarters.

Then Perseus, after routing the Roman army in many battles, crossed into Illyria and captured by fighting the town of Uscana, which was defended by Roman garrisons. There he captured a large number of Roman troops: some he killed, some he sold at auction, and some he led with him into Macedonia.

Soon L. Aemilius Paulus, the consul, was sent against him, and the praetor C. Anicius against Gentius in Illyria. [Note: H.: “Gajonicius.”] Gentius was easily defeated in a single battle and soon surrendered himself. His mother, wife, two sons, and brother likewise came into Roman power. The war was completed within thirty days; it was learned that Gentius had been defeated before news arrived that the war had begun.

With Perseus, however, the consul Aemilius Paulus fought on the third day before the Nones of September and defeated him. Twenty thousand of his infantry were killed, while the cavalry fled with the king. The Roman army lost one hundred soldiers, whereas the Macedonians surrendered themselves to the Romans.

The king himself, when he was abandoned by his friends, came into Paulus’s power. Yet the consul Aemilius Paulus treated him with honor, not as a defeated man. He did not even permit Perseus, who wished to fall at his feet, to do so, but seated him beside himself on his chair.

Moreover, P. Vacienus, traveling by night toward the city of Rome, saw two young men seated upon white horses. They ordered him to report to the senate the following day that Perseus, king of the Macedonians, had been captured by Paulus. Vacienus duly delivered the joyful news, but by order of the senate he was sent to prison as a rash speaker of uncertain things. Soon, when Paulus’s letter arrived, the truth of the day and the victory became clear. Vacienus was immediately released from custody and received a farm as a gift.

Later the same twins appeared to Vacienus at the lake of Juturna, where they were washing the sweat from themselves and their horses.

Meanwhile the Romans imposed these terms upon the Macedonians and Illyrians: that they should be free and should pay half of the tribute that they had previously paid to their kings, so that it might be evident that the Roman people fought more for justice than for greed.

Accordingly, at an assembly of neighboring peoples, Paulus announced this and entertained the embassies of many nations that had come to him at a most magnificent banquet, saying that the same man ought both to conquer in war and to be elegant in the arrangements of a feast.

Soon he captured seventy cities of Epirus that had rebelled against him, distributed the plunder among the soldiers, and returned to Rome with great pomp on Perseus’s ship, which is said to have been of extraordinarily unusual size, so that it reportedly had sixteen banks of oars. He celebrated a magnificent triumph in a golden chariot, with his two sons standing on either side.

Before the chariot were led the king’s two sons and King Perseus himself, forty-five years old.

[Note: From here the remainder is not read in A. through the words “After him.”]

Later he died in confinement at Alba. The senate sent a quaestor to his funeral, who buried him royally at the expense of the Roman people. His younger son learned the craft of bronze-working at Rome in order to endure poverty and died there.

After him Anicius also celebrated a triumph over the Illyrians. King Gentius was led before his chariot together with his brother and sons. Kings of many nations came to Rome for this spectacle, including Attalus and Eumenes, kings of Asia. Prusias of Bithynia also came to offer congratulations, and they were received with great honor.

[Note: A. reads “they were welcomed” instead of “they were received,” and continues: “and with permission…”]

The senate ordered the quaestor P. Cornelius Scipio to meet Prusias at Capua and provided him with lodging at Rome and very generous funds, so that, while some had been subjected by arms, others, captivated by their manners, might submit.

Accordingly, with the permission of the senate, they placed in the Capitol the gifts that the kings had brought. Prusias also commended his son Nicomedes to the senate.

In addition, many wars of very diverse outcomes were fought everywhere among many nations, which I have omitted for the sake of brevity.

In the year 600 from the City’s foundation, during the consulship of Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Aulus Postumius Albinus, when a great fear of the Celtiberians had seized all the Romans and there was no one among them who dared go to Spain either as a soldier or as a legate, P. Scipio—who would later be called the Younger Africanus—voluntarily offered to serve in Spain, although he had already been assigned by lot to Macedonia.

[Note: H. adds “later.”]

Accordingly, he went to Spain and inflicted great slaughter upon the nations, often performing the duty of a soldier more than that of a commander. He even met and killed in single combat a barbarian who challenged him.

The praetor Sergius Galba, however, was defeated by the Lusitanians in a great battle. After losing his entire army, he himself barely escaped with a few men.

In the following year L. Minucius fought successfully in Lusitania. Later the consul Marcellus achieved favorable results there as well.

[Note: A. and H. continue after “achieved”: “The third war against Carthage was then undertaken, in the six hundred and first year from the City’s foundation, during the consulship of Lucius Mallius Censorinus and M. Mallius, fifty-one years after the conclusion of the Second Punic War. They set out for Carthage. The Carthaginians…”]

At the same time the censor Messala was the first to propose that a theater be built in the City. Scipio, called Nasica, opposed this with a very forceful speech, saying that such a project would be most hostile to a warlike people because it was intended to nurture idleness and licentiousness. He so moved the senate that it ordered not only the removal of all the materials prepared for the theater, but also that benches not be set up for the games, so that neither townsmen nor those living within a thousand paces outside the city could sit while watching them, lest their courage become softened.

Accordingly, in Spain, the praetor Sergius Galba received the Lusitanians living on this side of the Tagus River into surrender as volunteers, but then treacherously killed them. For, pretending that he would act for their benefit, he surrounded them with soldiers and killed them all while they were unarmed and unsuspecting. This event afterward became the cause of a great uprising throughout Spain because of the Romans’ treachery.

At the same time Tucia, a Vestal virgin, was accused of incest. But she scorned clearing herself by human evidence and carried a sieve to the Tiber. There she submerged it, adding this prayer: “O Vesta,” she said, “if I am dutiful and chaste, I shall carry this water from the Tiber to your temple.” And she did carry it.

In the year 602 from the City’s foundation, during the consulship of L. Manlius Censorinus and M. Manlius, the Third Punic War broke out. Accordingly, when the senate had resolved that Carthage should be destroyed, the consuls set out for Africa, and Scipio, then a military tribune, encamped near Utica at the camp of the elder Africanus.

There the Carthaginians were summoned and ordered to surrender their weapons and ships. [Note: A. and H. add: “and, after they had surrendered them: So great was the quantity of weapons suddenly handed over that all Africa could easily have been armed from it. After they had surrendered their weapons to the Romans, they were ordered to leave the city and withdraw ten thousand paces from the sea. The Carthaginians turned their grief into desperation…”]

They surrendered such a great quantity of weapons all at once that all Africa could easily have been armed from them. But after the Carthaginians had handed over their weapons and had been ordered to abandon the city and withdraw ten thousand paces from the sea, they turned their grief into desperation, determined either to defend their state or to be buried with it and within it.

Soon they appointed two commanders, both named Hasdrubal, and began to manufacture weapons. When bronze and iron ran out, they made weapons of gold and silver. After the consuls had demolished part of the wall with siege engines, the Carthaginians nevertheless defeated and overwhelmed them.

[Note: H.: “defeated and repulsed.” A.: “were defeated and repulsed.”]

When the consuls fled, Scipio, then a military tribune, defended them by driving the enemy back inside the walls.

[Note: A. has “Fameas” instead of “Phameas.” This is also the reading in H. and Eutropius.]

Another commander, Phameas, was in charge of the Carthaginian cavalry. Scipio, the grandson of Scipio Africanus, was then serving there as military tribune, as has been said.

[Note: A. and H. add: “He was greatly feared by all…”]

Among all nations he inspired fear and reverence. He was regarded as both extremely ready for battle and exceptionally prudent. Accordingly, the consuls accomplished many things through him, and neither Phameas nor Hasdrubal avoided anything more carefully than engaging that part of the Roman army where Scipio was fighting.

At about the same time Massinissa, king of the Numidians, who for nearly sixty years had been a friend of the Roman people, died in the ninety-seventh year of his life.

[Note: A. and H. add: “He died leaving forty-four sons,” and after the word “ordered” they omit the remainder and read: “When it had therefore become clear…”]

He remained vigorous in body throughout his life. He was the man who never covered his head in rain, however heavy, or in cold weather. He could stand in one spot so long that young men first gave way from weariness before he moved from the place where he had stood. If he was standing, he would not move even a limb for the entire day. If he had begun a journey on horseback, he would not dismount; if on foot, he would not mount.

He would often join day to night while riding and entrusted his protection and security to the fiercest dogs. [Note: In the Canisian edition: “in the rain.”]

After the age of eighty-six he fathered a son named Mechinia, and in the last period of his life he omitted nothing that he had done as a young man.

Accordingly, when Massinissa died, leaving forty-four sons, he ordered Scipio to divide his kingdom among his sons. After Scipio had divided the kingdom of Numidia among the sons of Massinissa, he returned to Carthage.

Manlius stormed and plundered the city of Thegala. Twelve thousand Africans were killed there and six thousand captured. Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian commander and grandson of Massinissa, was killed by his own men in the senate house with fragments of benches, because of Scipio’s betrayal.

In the year 606 from the City’s foundation—that is, fifty-one years after the Second Punic War—during the consulship of Cn. Cornelius Lentulus and L. Memmius, since Scipio’s name had become famous, he was made consul while still a young man and attempted to destroy Carthage *suppocte* [the passage is corrupt and mutilated; perhaps read *sub noctem*, “toward nightfall”].

[Note: “Made consul after the fifth year,” according to both A. and H.; “and was sent against Carthage. While he had fought against it for six days and nights…”]

He entered Cothon, where, after fighting for six days and nights, the final desperation of the Carthaginians drove them to surrender, asking that those whom the disasters of war had left alive might at least be permitted to live in servitude.

[Note: A. and H.: “First a sufficiently pitiful procession of women descended; afterward came the men, more wretched still. For it is handed down that there were twenty-five thousand women…”]

First, therefore, a very pitiful procession of women came down; afterward the men descended, presenting an even more wretched sight. It is handed down that there were thirty-five thousand women and thirty thousand men.

King Hasdrubal voluntarily surrendered himself.

[Note: A.: “surrendered himself. The deserters…”]

He obtained only his own safety. The deserters who had occupied the temple of Aesculapius threw themselves down voluntarily and were consumed by fire.

[Note: A. and H.: “were consumed. Hasdrubal’s wife, together with her sons, in womanly madness threw herself into the midst of the flames. The city itself burned continuously for sixteen days,” and so forth.]

All the Roman deserters whom he could find, Scipio afflicted with crucifixion; the Latins he beheaded with the axe.

When Hasdrubal’s wife saw Carthage burning, she ran toward her husband with her two children and said to him: “Live, you who are able to survive Carthage. For you pleaded for us in vain.”

Then, with her children willing, in manly grief and womanly madness, she threw herself into the midst of the flames. Thus, as the last queen of Carthage, she met the same end in death that the first queen had once met. The city itself burned continuously for seventeen days and offered its victors a miserable spectacle of the changing conditions of human life.

[Note: After the word “offered,” both A. and H. read: “The whole multitude of captives, except for a few nobles, was sold. Destroyed…”]

Carthage was destroyed, every stone of its walls being crushed into dust. Its site is said to have been as follows. It enclosed twenty-two thousand paces within its walls and was almost entirely surrounded by the sea, except at the entrance, which opened for three thousand paces.

[Note: H.: “which opened for three…” A. likewise has this reading.]

That place had a wall thirty feet thick, built of squared stone, forty cubits high.

[Note: A. adds after “forty”: “A stone called Byrsa.”]

The citadel called Byrsa extended for somewhat more than two thousand paces. On one side there had been a wall common to the city and to Byrsa, overlooking the sea. That sea is said to have been a lagoon, because the projecting tongue of land extending before it calmed it.

[Note: A.: “is constricted.”]

The spoils found there, which Carthage had collected from the destruction of various cities, and the ornaments of cities, were returned to the cities of Sicily, Italy, and Africa that recognized them as their own.

Thus Carthage was destroyed seven hundred years after it had been founded.

[Note: A. reads from here: “Thus, in the fourth year after the Third War had begun…”]

The entire multitude of captives, except for a few nobles, was sold. In the fourth year after it had begun, the Third Punic War was brought to an end.

Scipio earned the name that his grandfather had received—namely, that because of his valor he too should be called Africanus.

[Note: A.: “the Younger.”]

[Note: A. and H. omit the remainder after “should be called” and immediately continue: “Meanwhile…”]

After Carthage had been captured by the Romans, certain persons stripped Apollo of a golden garment. Later the hands of those who had taken it were found together with fragments of the tunic.

Meanwhile, in Macedonia, a certain Pseudo-Philip took up arms and defeated the Roman praetor Publius Juventius, who had been sent against him, annihilating him. After him Q. Caecilius Metellus was sent by the Romans as commander against Pseudo-Philip. After twenty thousand had been killed, he recovered Macedonia and also brought Pseudo-Philip himself under his power.

[Note: A. has twenty-five thousand instead of twenty thousand.]

In the year 606 from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0799D] These words are absent in A. and H., which briefly have, after the words “brought him under his power”: “War was also declared against Corinth, the most distinguished city of Greece, on account of an injury done to Roman envoys. The consul Mummius captured and destroyed it. Thus three triumphs were celebrated at Rome simultaneously, etc.”], that is, in the same year in which Carthage was destroyed, during the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, the overthrow of Corinth followed the ruin of Carthage; and the miserable conflagration of two exceedingly powerful cities, in different parts of the world and at a short interval of time, shone forth.

For when the praetor Metellus had defeated the Achaeans and Boeotians in two wars—first at Thermopylae, and afterward in Phocis—Claudius the historian reports that twenty thousand were killed in the first war and seven thousand in the second. Valerius Antias likewise confirms that a battle was fought in Achaia, and that twenty thousand Achaeans, together with their commander Dieus, fell. Polybius of Achaia, however, although he had been in Africa with Scipio, nevertheless, since he could not have been unaware of his country’s disaster, asserts that there was only one battle in Achaia, under the command of Critolaus. He says that Dieus, who was bringing soldiers from Arcadia, was overwhelmed by Metellus together with his army.

But we have already said something about the diversity of conflicting historians. It is enough that this exposed and notorious mark of falsehood plainly shows how little credence should be given to the rest: for even in matters they themselves witnessed, they disagree.

Accordingly, while Metellus the praetor was planning the overthrow of the cities whose defenses throughout Achaia had been destroyed, the consul Mummius suddenly arrived in the camp with a few men. Immediately dismissing Metellus, he attacked and captured Corinth, the most distinguished city of Greece, without delay, on account of the injury done to the Roman envoys. At that time it was by far the most renowned city in the whole world. For over many previous centuries it had been the workshop of every kind of artisan and every craft, and the common market of Asia and Europe.

Permission was therefore cruelly granted to plunder the captives; and everything was so consumed by slaughter and fire that the conflagration poured out from the circuit of the walls as though from a furnace, narrowed into a single peak. Thus, after a very large part of the population had been consumed by sword and flame, the survivors [Col. 0799D] were sold under the crown. Once the city had been burned, its walls were utterly demolished, and the masonry of the walls was reduced to dust; but an immense quantity of booty was carried away.

Indeed, because of the multitude and variety of the statues and images, when gold, silver, bronze, and all the metals had been mingled together and had flowed together in that conflagration of the city, a new kind of metal was produced. Hence, down to the present day [Col. 0800A], whether made from that metal itself or in imitation of it, bronze is called “Corinthian bronze,” and vessels are called “Corinthian vessels,” as tradition has handed down.

At the same time, three very celebrated triumphs were held at Rome: that of Africanus, from Africa, with Hasdrubal led before his chariot; that of Metellus, from Macedonia, preceded by Andriscus [Note: [Col. 0799D] A. has “Andaristus”; H., “Andariscus.”], the same man who was also called Pseudophilippus; and that of Mummius, from Corinth, before whom bronze statues, painted panels, and other celebrated ornaments of the city were carried.

Again in Macedonia, Pseudoperseus [Note: [Col. 0799D] A., “Pseudoperses.”], who claimed to be the son of Perseus, gathered slaves and rebelled. When he already had sixteen thousand armed men, he was defeated by the quaestor Tremellius [Note: [Col. 0799D] A. and H., after the words “was defeated,” omit the remainder and immediately read: “In those days Androgynus, etc.”; [Col. 0800D].].

Meanwhile, during the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, Viriatus in Spain—a Lusitanian by birth, a shepherd and brigand—first by attacking the roads, then by ravaging the provinces, and finally by defeating, routing, and subduing the armies of the Roman praetors and consuls, became a source of the greatest terror to all the Romans.

As he was crossing and ranging widely over the Iberus and the Tagus, the greatest rivers of regions utterly unlike one another, the praetor Gaius Vetilius confronted him. After almost his entire army had immediately been destroyed, Vetilius himself, the praetor, barely escaped by fleeing with a few men. Then the same Viriatus routed the praetor Gaius Plancius, after breaking him in many battles. Later Claudius Unimanus, sent against Viriatus with a great military force—as though to erase the stain of the earlier defeat—increased the disgrace by making it worse. For when he engaged Viriatus, he lost all the forces he had brought with him, together with the greatest strength of the Roman army. Viriatus fastened up on the mountains the military cloaks, fasces, and other Roman insignia as a trophy.

At the same time, three hundred Lusitanians engaged one thousand Romans in a certain wooded pass. Claudius reports that seventy Lusitanians, but three hundred and twenty Romans, were killed in the battle. As the victorious Lusitanians departed scattered and off their guard, one of them, separated far from the others, was caught on foot after horsemen had surrounded him. He pierced one of their horses with his spear, then severed its rider’s head with a single stroke of the rider’s own sword. He struck them all with such fear that, while everyone looked on, he himself went away free and unhurried.

During the consulship of Appius Claudius and Quintus Caecilius Metellus, Appius Claudius engaged the Salassi, a Gallic people, and, being defeated, lost five thousand soldiers; in the following battle he killed five thousand of the enemy. But since a law had established that anyone who had killed five thousand enemies should have the right to celebrate a triumph, he too sought a triumph. Because he had not obtained one on account of his earlier losses, however, he resorted to disgraceful folly and ambition and celebrated a triumph at his own private expense.

During the consulship of Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus, among other prodigies, an androgyne seen at Rome was, by order of the haruspices, plunged into the sea. [Note: [Col. 0800D] From this point A. and H. read: “At the same time Metellus was sent into Celtiberia and performed distinguished deeds among the Spaniards. Quintus Pompeius succeeded him, and not long afterward Quintus Caepio too was sent to the same war, which Viriatus was waging against the Romans in Lusitania. Because of this fear, Viriatus was killed by his own men, after he had stirred up Spain against the Romans for fourteen years. At first he was a shepherd, then a leader of brigands, and finally he incited such great peoples to war that he was regarded as Spain’s champion against the Romans. For first Sextus Vetilius—H. has Vecilius—the praetor, confronted him; after his entire army had been slain, he barely escaped by fleeing. Then the same Viriatus routed Gaius Plautius, the praetor, after breaking him. After this he defeated Claudius Unimannus—H., Unimammium; others, Unimanum—with his entire army. Finally, when his killers sought a reward from Caepio, the consul (Eutropius has Scipio), the answer was given that the Romans had never approved of commanders being killed by their own soldiers. These words agree almost verbatim with Eutropius, except that several manuscripts contain more material inserted, as you see, than Eutropius does. CANIS.”]

But the performance of that impious expiation accomplished nothing. For such a great pestilence suddenly arose that the attendants responsible for burying the dead first proved insufficient and then disappeared altogether. By now even the great houses remained empty of the living and full of the dead: extensive inheritances within, and no heirs at all. Finally, people were denied the ability not only to live in the City but even to approach it; such foul odors were exhaled throughout the City from the corpses of those wasting away beneath their roofs and on their beds.

At last, amid their sufferings, the Romans came to recognize how wretched and futile that cruel expiation had been—an expiation that opened the way to the death of men by instituting the death of a human being. It had first been undertaken as a means of forestalling the impending disaster, and the pestilence followed. Yet the disease subsided without any satisfaction rendered by sacrifices, once the affliction had been completed according to the measure of the hidden judgment.

If those craftsmen of evasions, the haruspices, had happened to celebrate the rite precisely when illnesses, as usual, began to decline, they would undoubtedly have claimed for themselves, their gods, and their rituals the glory of restored health.

Accordingly, the consul Metellus, fighting in Celtiberia against the Lusitanians and Viriatus, drove off the enemy and liberated the town of Bacia, which Viriatus was besieging; he also received it, together with several other forts, into surrender. But he committed an act execrable even to the most barbarous peoples of Scythia, let alone to Roman fidelity and moderation. For he cut off the hands of five hundred of their chiefs, whom he had received after inviting them to an alliance and accepting their surrender under the terms of capitulation.

Q. Pompeius, consul of the following year, entered the territory of the Numantines and withdrew after suffering a very great defeat—not only with his army almost destroyed, but also with very many of the nobles who had accompanied that campaign killed. Viriatus, after wearing down Roman commanders and armies for fourteen years, was killed through the treachery of his own men. In this single matter the Romans acted courageously toward him: they judged his assassins unworthy of reward, saying that the Romans had never approved of commanders being killed by their own soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] The remainder, up to the words “the boy at Rome,” is absent from H. and A.]

But I could now, and indeed often, insert those tangled wars of the East, which rarely begin or even end except through crimes; yet the wars of the Romans, with whom our present concern lies, are so numerous that foreign affairs may rightly be regarded with disgust. At that time Mithridates, sixth king of the Parthians after Arsaces, defeated Demetrius’ commander and victoriously invaded the city of Babylon and all its territory. He also subdued all the peoples who live between the river Hydaspes and the Indus, and extended his bloody rule as far as India. He defeated and captured Demetrius himself when he encountered him in a second war. After Demetrius had been captured, a certain Diodotus usurped his kingdom and royal title together with his son Alexander. Later, so that he would not have Alexander—whom he had made his partner in the danger of invading the kingdom—as his partner in possessing it, he killed his own son Alexander.

Under the consuls M. Aemilius Lepidus and C. Hostilius Mancinus, various prodigies appeared, and, insofar as it lay within their power, they were treated according to custom. But favorable outcomes do not always support soothsayers who hunt for omens of events and augurs who construct deceptions. For the consul Mancinus, after receiving the army from Pompeius at Numantia, conducted all his battles so unsuccessfully, and was driven to such utter desperation, that he was forced to make a most disgraceful treaty with the Numantines. Pompeius, too, had shortly before concluded an equally dishonorable treaty with those same Numantines; nevertheless, the senate ordered that the treaty be dissolved and Mancinus surrendered to the Numantines. He was exposed before the Numantines’ gates with his body naked and his hands bound behind his back. Remaining there until evening, abandoned by his own people and not received by the enemy, he presented a spectacle that moved both sides to tears.

When he was about to wage war against the Numantines and sacrifice to Lavinium, the keeper of the sacred chickens released the chickens from their cage. They flew into a forest and were not found for a long time, despite much searching. The same man, when he was about to sail from the harbor of Hercules, heard a voice without seeing its source: “Mancinus, remain.” When he had boarded a small boat, he was horrified to see there an enormous snake. Three unhappy events were announced by these three prodigies: battle, treaty, and surrender.

Meanwhile, in Further Spain, Brutus defeated by an exceedingly harsh and difficult war 60,000 Gallaecians who had come to the aid of the Lusitanians, although he had taken them by surprise. Forty thousand of them are reported to have been killed in that battle, six thousand captured, and only a few to have escaped by flight.

In Hither Spain, the proconsul Lepidus persistently attempted to conquer the Vaccaei, an innocent and suppliant people, even though the senate forbade it. Soon, however, after suffering a very serious defeat, he paid the penalty for his wicked obstinacy. Six thousand Romans, previously considered unconquerable, were killed in this unjust war; the rest escaped after their camp had been burned and even their weapons lost. This defeat under Metellus was no less disgraceful than that under Mancinus.

Under the consuls Ser. Fulvius Flaccus and Q. Calpurnius Piso, a boy was born at Rome—

[Note: [Col. 0801D] The manuscripts H. and A. have what follows, up to the words “Then Scipio consulted Tyresius,” in a different and much shorter form, in these words: “At that time a four-footed, four-handed boy was born at Rome from a slave woman, with four eyes, the same number of ears, and a double male nature. In the territory of Bononia, crops grew on trees. Then Q. Pompeius, consul, having been defeated by the Numantines, who were the wealthiest people in Spain, made a dishonorable peace. After him, the consul C. Hostilius Mancinus again made an infamous peace with the Numantines; the people and senate ordered that it be broken and Mancinus himself handed over to the enemy, so that in his person they might punish, as it were, the author of the treaty. And since for fourteen successive years four consuls had worn down 40,000 Romans—H. reads ‘with only 4,000’—after such disgrace, whereby Roman armies had twice been subjected by the Numantines, Publius Scipio Africanus was made consul for the second time and sent to Numantia. He first corrected the vicious and inactive soldier by training him rather than punishing him, without any harshness. Soon, when battle had been joined with the Numantines, the Roman army, and so forth.”]

from a slave woman, four-footed and four-handed, with four eyes and the same number of ears, possessing a double male nature. In Sicily Mount Etna belched forth and poured out enormous fires. Like torrents, they rushed headlong down the slopes, and their flames consumed everything nearby; farther away they scorched the land with hot ashes flying broadly through the air together with dense vapor. This kind of portent, always native to Sicily, is not usually a prediction of evil but an infliction of it. In the territory of Bononia, crops grew on trees.

Then a slave war arose in Sicily. It was so savage and serious, so equipped with a multitude of slaves and so great in the size of its forces and strength, that it terrified not only the Roman praetors, whom it completely routed, but even the consuls. For 70,000 slaves are reported to have conspired at that time to take up arms, excluding the city of Messana, which kept its kindly treated slaves in peace.

In this respect alone Sicily was more wretched: because it is an island and never sufficiently capable of remaining under its own law, it was now subjected to tyrants, now to slaves—either the former imposing slavery through wicked domination, or the latter perversely exchanging freedom for it. This was especially so because, closed in on every side by the sea, it cannot easily cast out what is within it. It nurtured an internal evil, even a viperous conception of its own destruction, increased by its own lust and destined to survive through its own death.

The uprising of a slave disturbance is rarer than that of other peoples and therefore more savage, because the free multitude is moved with the intention of enlarging its country, whereas the slave multitude is moved with the intention of destroying it.

In the year 620 from the founding of the City, when the disgrace produced by the treaty made at Numantia weighed upon the Roman face almost more heavily than the disgrace once suffered at the Caudine Forks, Scipio Africanus was elected consul for the second time with the consent of all the tribes and sent with an army to besiege Numantia.

Numantia was situated in Hither Spain, not far from the Vaccaei and Cantabri, at the head of Gallaecia; it was the last stronghold of the Celtiberians. For fourteen years, with only four thousand of its own men, it not only withstood 40,000 Romans but also defeated them and forced them into shameful treaties. After such disgrace, whereby Roman armies had twice been subjugated by the Numantines, P. Scipio Africanus was sent, as we have said, to destroy Numantia.

After entering Spain, he did not immediately attack the enemy, as though he might catch them off guard, knowing that this kind of people never lies so idle and sluggish in spirit that, by the very character of its condition and equipment, it does not surpass the preparations of others. Instead, for some time he trained his vicious and inactive soldiers in the camp as though in schools, correcting them by exercise rather than punishment and without any harshness. Then he ordered by a severe edict that everything kept in the camp for pleasure be removed. Finally, two thousand prostitutes, together with the camp-followers, were expelled from his military camp.

Under a strict commander the army made such sudden progress that the Romans soon leveled Numantia, which had long been most destructive to them. Yet although he spent part of the summer and the whole winter without even obtaining a battle, this diligence accomplished almost too little. For when an opportunity for fighting arose, the Roman army, overwhelmed by the Numantines’ attack, turned its back and fled. But when the consul reproached them and threatened them, throwing himself in their way and holding them back with his hand, they at last became indignant, returned against the enemy, and forced the men whom they had been fleeing to flee.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] Afterwards he compelled them. In the cited manuscripts A. and H.: “Therefore, although …,” with the remainder omitted, which we have marked in a different type.]

It is difficult to make credible what then occurred: the Numantines were fleeing, and the Romans saw them fleeing. Although Scipio rejoiced and boasted because it had happened beyond expectation, he nevertheless declared that no further war ought to be undertaken against them. Accordingly, he enclosed the city with a siege and surrounded it with a ditch ten feet wide and twenty feet deep.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] Afterwards he closed it in; they read the same: “He surrounded it with a rampart. And when, shut in for a long time, they were suffering from hunger and asking for an opportunity to fight, so that they might be permitted to die like men, at last, after first being warmed by a large quantity of the drink customarily made from moistened grain, they suddenly burst upon the Romans. A fierce struggle for a long time …”]

He then strengthened the rampart, which had been constructed with stakes, by means of frequent towers. Numantia, situated on a hill not far from the river Durius, enclosed three miles within the circuit of its walls, although some maintain that it occupied only a small site and had no wall. It is therefore credible that, pressed by the Roman war, they enclosed this space for the convenience of feeding and guarding their cattle, or even of cultivating the land, while themselves holding a small citadel naturally fortified. Otherwise, given the smallness of their population, so extensive a circuit of walls seemed more likely to betray than to protect them.

After being enclosed for a long time and slaughtered by hunger, the Numantines offered to surrender themselves if tolerable terms were ordered. For, having often asked for the opportunity of a fair fight, so that they might be allowed to die like men, they all suddenly burst out at the end through two gates, after first taking a large quantity of drink—not wine, for that region is not productive of wine, but juice made by a skillful process from wheat. They call this juice, because it is heated, *caelia*.

The fiery power of the germinated grain is first aroused after the grain has been moistened; it is then dried, ground into flour, and mixed with a soft liquid. Through fermentation, this drink acquires a sharp flavor and the heat of intoxication. Thus, warmed by this drink after their long hunger, they offered themselves for battle.

The fierce struggle lasted a long time and reached the point of danger for the Romans. The Numantines would once again have proved to Rome, by fleeing, that they could fight against them, had they not fought under Scipio. After their bravest men had been killed, the Numantines withdrew from the battle, but with their ranks arranged, and they did not return to the city like fugitives.

[Note: [Col. 0804D] A. reads “they yield.”]

They refused to receive the bodies of the slain when they were offered for burial.

[Note: [Col. 0804D] Afterwards both manuscripts read: “They refused; and, with the city closed, all together …”]

With their final hope reduced to despair and all resolved upon death, they set fire to the city from within. All of them together perished by the sword, poison, and fire.

[Note: [Col. 0804D] The Romans gained nothing else from these people except security for themselves. They said that they had escaped the Numantines more than they had conquered them. Not one Numantine was held by the victor’s chain, whatever follows. Compare this, reader, with Eutropius, and you will see what Paulus Diaconus added to Eutropius and what the author of the *Miscellany* added to Paulus Diaconus. CANIS.]

The Romans gained absolutely nothing from the defeated except their own security. Even after Numantia had been destroyed, they said that they had escaped the Numantines rather than conquered them. Not one Numantine was held by the victor’s chain; hence Rome saw a triumph, although fire consumed whatever household goods there were.

At that time, while these events were taking place at Numantia, the seditions of the Gracchi were being stirred up at Rome.
