Scipio then consulted a certain Celtic leader, Tyresius, asking why Numantia, previously unconquered, had endured so long and afterward been destroyed. Tyresius replied: “Concord provided victory; discord destruction.” The Romans accepted this as an example, as though it had been said about themselves and to themselves, since news was being brought to them of the whole City in discord because of seditions.

At this time, among the Jews, after Judas Maccabaeus had been killed, his brother Jonathan was recognized as high priest. At the same time Pacuvius, the writer of tragedies, became famous at Brundisium.

Scipio then captured some cities of Spain and received others into surrender. He razed Numantia to the ground and received the rest of the province into allegiance.

At the same time King Attalus of Syria, the brother of Eumenes, died and left the Roman people as his heir.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “of Asia.”]

Thus Asia came to the Roman Empire by testament.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Ambrosianus and Hersfeldensis read from here: “Soon Decius Junius Brutus also celebrated a triumph with great glory over the Gallaecians and Lusitanians, and afterward Scipio Africanus celebrated a second triumph over the Numantines, fourteen years after he had celebrated one over Africa. Meanwhile a slave war broke out in Sicily, and more than 20,000 slaves were then slaughtered by Fulvius and Rutilius. At Minturnae 450 slaves were crucified. At Sinuessa, 4,000 slaves are reported to have been crushed by Q. Metellus and Cn. Servilius. Meanwhile the disturbance …”]

After Carthage and Numantia had been destroyed, a useful debate arose among the Romans concerning foresight, and a disgraceful contest concerning ambition. Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, angry with the nobility because he had been marked down among the authors of the Numantine treaty, decided that land hitherto held by private individuals should be distributed among the people.

He removed the authority of Octavius, the tribune of the plebs who opposed him, and appointed Minucius as his successor. For these reasons anger seized the senate and arrogance seized the people. Gracchus, seeking popular favor by means of bribery, introduced an envious law that the money which had belonged to Attalus should be distributed among the people.

When Nasica opposed him, Pompeius also promised that he would prosecute Gracchus as soon as he had left office. Gracchus, striving to remain tribune of the plebs in the following year, consulted the keeper of the sacred chickens at home and was forbidden by him to go out into the Campus. But when he persisted in going, he struck his foot against the threshold outside the door so violently that a joint was torn off.

Then, as he was going out, three ravens flew at him with hostile cries, and, fighting one another, knocked a roof tile down before his feet. When he consulted the auspices on the Capitol, he heard similar omens. On the day of the elections, when he was inflaming the people to sedition, the nobility, stirred up by Nasica, drove the plebs away with fragments of benches.

Gracchus fled down the steps above the arch of Calpurnius, having thrown off his cloak, and collapsed after being struck by a fragment of a bench. Rising again, he was killed by a second blow, when a nail was driven into his brain.

Two hundred more were killed in that sedition, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. Gracchus’ own unburied corpse also wasted away.

Meanwhile, the contagion of the slave war that had arisen in Sicily spread widely and infected many provinces. At Minturnae, 450 slaves were crucified; at Sinuessa, as many as 7,000 slaves were crushed by Q. Metellus and Cn. Servilius Caepio. In the mines of Athens the same slave disturbance was dispersed by the praetor Heraclitus. At Delos, too, slaves swelling with a new uprising were suppressed when the townspeople anticipated them. Apart from that first source of the Sicilian evil, these events were like glittering sparks that sowed separate fires.

In Sicily, after the consul Fulvius, the consul Piso captured the town of Mamertium, where he killed 8,000 fugitives; those whom he could capture he fastened to the gallows. When the consul Rutilius succeeded him, he too recovered Tauromenium and Enna by war, the strongest refuges of the fugitives. More than 20,000 slaves are reported to have been slaughtered at that time.

The cause of such a wretched and inextricable war would certainly have meant death for the masters, unless the slaves’ insolence had been met with the sword. Yet even in the most unhappy losses of the battle and the still more unhappy gains of victory, as many of the defeated perished, so many of the victors were destroyed.

In the year 622 from the founding of the City, a war was stirred up in Asia by Aristonicus, the son of Eumenes, who had been born from a concubine. Eumenes himself had been the brother of Attalus.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Ambrosianus reads “of Eumenes.”]

An extremely well-equipped army was sent against him under P. Licinius Crassus, consul and chief pontiff, who also had boundless royal auxiliaries. For Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, aided the Romans, as did Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, with whom there was afterward a very serious war, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, and Pylaemenes of Paphlagonia.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] Ambrosianus, Hersfeldensis, and Eutropius read “Polemenes.”]

Supported by their enormous forces, Crassus nevertheless was defeated in the battle that followed. After the army had been driven into flight with very great slaughter, he himself was captured by the enemy. Choosing death rather than being led away by a barbarian, he thrust the stick with which he was driving his horse into the eye of the man who was holding him.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] A. adds: “then thrust it into him, and he was immediately stabbed by him.”]

The barbarian, inflamed with anger and grief, pierced Crassus’ side with a sword. Thus, having devised a manner of death, he escaped the disgrace of slavery. Aristonicus took his head; his body was buried at Smyrna.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] The remainder, marked in a different type, is not read in Ambrosianus or Hersfeldensis.]

He had learned Greek so quickly during military expeditions in the camps that he answered Aristonicus’ companions in every part of their language without an interpreter.

[Col. 0806D]

Afterward the Roman consul Perpenna, who was coming as Crassus’ successor, hurried to Asia when he heard the outcome of the war.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] A. adds: “and, having defeated Aristonicus in battle near the city of the Stratoniceans, to which he had fled, he compelled him by hunger to surrender. Aristonicus …”]

Aristonicus, resting after his recent victory, was attacked by an unexpected war and, stripped of all his forces, was put to flight. When Perpenna had surrounded the city of Stratonice, to which Aristonicus had fled, he compelled him, exhausted by hunger, to surrender. Aristonicus was strangled in prison by order of the senate. A triumph could not be celebrated over him, because the consul Perpenna died at Pergamum while returning to Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] From here Ambrosianus and Hersfeldensis read: “In those days such a multitude of locusts increased throughout Africa that they gnawed away at crops, grasses, leaves, and even the bark of trees. Carried up by a sudden wind, they were sunk in the African Sea. When the waves had carried their heaps along the extended shores, the rotting mass gave off a pestilential odor. Hence a plague of all living creatures—birds, livestock, and wild beasts—arose, and the corruption was increased. Through this pestilence 800,000 people perished in Numidia and more than 200,000 around Carthage. Thirty thousand Roman soldiers who were stationed there for the garrison were also killed. Under the consuls Lucius Metellus Caecilius and T. Q. Flamininus (H. reads L. Caecilius Metellus).”]

In the same year, the wretched life of Ptolemy, king of the Alexandrians, met an even more wretched end. He had first become notorious through sexual relations with his sister, then taken her in marriage, and finally cast her off more disgracefully than he had married her. He took his own stepdaughter—that is, the daughter of his sister and wife—as his wife. He killed his own son, whom he had fathered by his sister, as well as the son of his brother. Therefore, detestable because of such incest and parricides, he was driven from the kingdom by the Alexandrians.

At the same time Antiochus, not content with Babylonia, Ecbatana, and rule over all Media, engaged Phraates, king of the Parthians, in battle and was defeated. Although he seemed to have 100,000 armed men in his army, he dragged along more than 200,000 camp-servants and sutlers, mixed together with prostitutes and stage performers. Thus he was easily overwhelmed by the strength of the Parthians together with his whole army and perished.

Under the consuls C. Sempronius Tuditanus and M. Acilius, I would not recklessly count among the greatest Roman disasters the fact that P. Scipio Africanus, after publicly warning the day before of the danger to his life—for he had learned that danger was being announced against him by wicked and ungrateful men while he was laboring for his country—was found lifeless in his bedroom early the next morning. This is especially so since Africanus’ vigor and moderation carried such weight in that city that, while he lived, it was easily believed that neither a social nor a civil war could arise.

Some say that he was killed through the treachery of his wife Sempronia, the sister of the Gracchi, lest that wicked family, born—as I believe—for the destruction of its country amid the impious seditions of men, should be still more monstrous through the crimes of women. The cause of his death was this: C. Carbo, tribune of the plebs, wishing to avenge the killing of the Gracchi and revive the suppressed sedition, asked P. Scipio Africanus, who was returning after destroying Numantia, during a public assembly what he thought about the death of Gracchus. Africanus replied that Gracchus seemed to have been justly killed.

Under the consuls M. Aemilius and L. Orestes, Mount Etna, shaken by a great tremor, overflowed with fiery globes. On the following day the island of Lipara and the sea around it became so violently boiling that it dissolved even scorched rocks, tore the ships’ decking away with wax melted by the heat, and cooked dead fish and those floating on the surface. It also suffocated human beings, except those who could flee farther away, by the repeated inhalation of hot air, burning their vital organs internally.

Under the consuls M. Plautius Hypsaeus and M. Fulvius Flaccus, while Africa had scarcely yet become quiet after the devastation of its wars, a horrible and unprecedented destruction followed. Immense swarms of locusts had multiplied throughout Africa. They had not merely stripped away all hope of crops and consumed every kind of grass together with part of its roots and the leaves of trees together with the tender parts of their branches; they also gnawed at bitter bark and dry wood. Suddenly seized by the wind, compressed into masses, and carried for a long time through the air, they were plunged into the African Sea.

When the waves, driving their enormous heaps, pushed them far along the widely extended shores, the decaying and putrefying mass exhaled an exceedingly foul and, beyond all expectation, pestilential odor. Hence such a plague followed among all living creatures alike that, as the air was corrupted and birds, livestock, and wild beasts wasted away, their rotting corpses scattered everywhere increased the infection.

But how great the human pestilence was, I shudder throughout my body even as I recount it. In Numidia, where King Micipsa then ruled, 800,000 people are said to have perished. Along the seacoast, especially near the shores of Carthage and Utica, more than 200,000 died. At Utica itself, 30,000 Roman soldiers, who had been stationed to garrison all Africa, were destroyed and wiped out.

The disaster struck so suddenly and violently that it is reported that, at Utica itself, on a single day, through a single gate, more than 1,500 of the younger men were carried out dead.

Nevertheless, with peace and by the grace of almighty God, in whose mercy and trust I speak these words, I would say this: although in our own times locusts sometimes arise in different parts of the earth and often cause damage, though tolerable, never in Christian times has such an inextricable force of evil occurred that the destruction caused by locusts, which could in no way have been endured while they were alive, would have caused greater harm after their death. While they were alive, everything was destined to perish; once they had perished, it would have been preferable that they themselves had not perished, since everything else was perishing more completely.

In the year 627 from the founding of the City, under the consuls L. Aemilius Caecilius Metellus and T. Quintius Flamininus, Carthage in Africa was ordered to be restored. At last, in the twenty-second year after it had been destroyed, it was restored and filled with families of Roman citizens who were to inhabit it.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] A. and Hersfeldensis have the following, differing slightly from one another: “Carthage was restored by order of the senate. It remains”—Hersfeldensis: “now remains”—after twenty-two years had elapsed since it had been destroyed by Scipio. Roman citizens were settled there. In the year 627 from the founding of the City, under the consuls Caius Cassius Longinus and Sextus Domitius Calvinus—H. reads “Calvus”—they made war upon the Transalpine Gauls and killed an immense multitude beside the Rhône, including the Arverni—H. reads “the Arbennorum”—at that time the most distinguished nation, and their leader Bituitus. Finally, when Bituitus boasted that the small number of Romans could scarcely provide food for the dogs he had with the army, although he himself had 180,000 armed men, he was defeated in battle by the Romans. From his army 150,000 perished, some in battle and some drowned together with the bridge that they had constructed over the Rhône from joined boats. An enormous quantity of gold torques belonging to the Gauls was brought to Rome as booty. Bituitus surrendered himself to Domitius—H. reads “gave himself up”—and was led by him to Rome; both consuls celebrated a triumph with great glory. Under the consuls M. Porcius Cato and Q. Marcius Rex—H. reads “Martius”—in the year 633 from the founding of the City, a colony was established at Narbo in Gaul; and in the following year, under the consuls Licinius Metellus and Q. Mucius Scaevola, a triumph was celebrated over Dalmatia. In the year 635 from the founding of the City, under C. Cato, and so forth.”]

A great portent preceded the restoration. When surveyors had been sent to mark out the territory of Carthage, they found that the boundary stakes, which had been fixed as markers, had been torn out during the night by wolves, bitten and gnawed away. For some time it was debated whether it was advantageous for Roman peace that Carthage be restored.

In the same year, Caius Gracchus, brother of that Gracchus who had already been killed in the sedition, was created tribune of the plebs amid an uprising and became a great disaster to the Republic. For after repeatedly stirring up the Roman people to the most bitter seditions by distributions and excessive promises, especially on account of the agrarian law for which his brother Gracchus had also been killed, he finally withdrew from the tribunate, Minucius succeeding him.

When Minucius, tribune of the plebs, had for the most part overturned the decrees of his predecessor Gracchus and repealed his laws, Gracchus, accompanied by an immense crowd together with Fulvius Flaccus, ascended the Capitol, where an assembly was being held. There a herald was killed by the Gracchians amid the greatest tumult, as though it were a signal for war.

Flaccus, surrounded by his two armed sons, with Gracchus also accompanying him in civilian dress and concealing a short sword beneath his left arm, occupied the Dianium as a citadel, although he had first unsuccessfully sent forward a herald to summon the slaves to freedom.

On the opposite side, Decius Brutus, a consular man, charged in with C. Publius amid a great struggle. Flaccus fought there for a long time with the greatest determination. Gracchus, after withdrawing into the temple of Minerva, wished to fall upon his sword but was restrained by the intervention of Letorius.

Thus, while the war remained for a long time uncertain, archers sent by Opimius scattered the densely packed multitude. The two Flacci, father and son, having leapt from the temple of Luna into a certain private house and barred the doors, were stabbed after the latticework wall had been broken through.

Gracchus, while his friends fought and died for him for a long time, with difficulty reached the Sublician Bridge. There, so that he would not be captured alive, he offered his neck to his slave.

Gracchus’ severed head was brought to the consul, while his body was carried to his mother Cornelia at the town of Misenum. This Cornelia, the daughter of the elder Africanus, had withdrawn to Misenum, as I have said, after the death of her first son. Gracchus’ property was confiscated. The younger Flaccus was killed in the strength of his youth. Two hundred and fifty from Gracchus’ faction are reported to have been killed on the Aventine Hill.

The consul Opimius was as harsh in the investigation as he had been brave in war. He killed more than 3,000 people by punishments, many of them innocent and not even given a hearing.

At the same time Metellus overran and subdued the Balearic Islands by war, suppressing with a great slaughter of their inhabitants the pirate raids that were then arising from them. The proconsul Cn. Domitius also defeated the Gallic Allobroges in a very serious battle near the town of Vindalium, especially because the unfamiliar appearance of the elephants terrified the enemy’s horses, and the enemy fled in confusion. Twenty thousand Allobroges are reported to have been killed there and 3,000 captured.

At the same time Mount Etna erupted with more than its customary violence. Fiery torrents poured over the land and flowed widely around it, overwhelming the city of Catina and its territory, so that the roofs of the buildings, scorched and weighed down by hot ashes, collapsed. To alleviate this disaster, the senate remitted ten years of taxes to the people of Catina.

In the year 628 from the founding of the City, the consul Fabius met Bituitus, king of the Arverni, who was preparing for war with the greatest equipment, with so small an army that Bituitus boasted that the Romans were scarcely sufficient to provide food for the dogs he had with his army.

When Bituitus realized that one bridge over the river Rhône was insufficient for transferring his forces, he built another from boats joined together and connected by chains, with planks laid and fastened upon it. When battle was joined and the Gauls had fought fiercely for a long time, they were defeated and turned to flight. As each man sought his own safety, their columns were piled together without order; in their hurried crossing they broke the bridge’s fastenings and soon were drowned together with the boats themselves.

Bituitus’ army is said to have contained 158,000 armed men, of whom 150,000 were either killed or drowned. The consul Q. Marcius attacked in war a Gallic people situated at the foot of the Alps. When they saw themselves surrounded by Roman forces and understood that they would be unequal to the war, they killed their wives and children and threw themselves into the flames.

Those whom the Romans had forestalled, so that they had no opportunity then to carry out their intended death, consumed themselves after being captured—some by the sword, some by hanging, and some by denying themselves food. Not one at all, not even a little child, survived who was willing, for love of life, to endure the condition of slavery. A Roman colony was established at Narbo, and a triumph was celebrated over these peoples.

In the year 635 from the founding of the City, the consul C. Cato made war upon the Scordisci and fought disgracefully.

[Note: [Col. 0810D] A. reads “the Cordisci.”]

Under the consuls C. Caecilius Metellus and Cn. Carbo, the two Metellus brothers celebrated triumphs on the same day, one over Thrace and the other over Sardinia.

[Note: [Col. 0810D] A. adds after “celebrated a triumph”: “and news was brought to Rome that the Cimbri had crossed from Gaul into Italy. After Scipio Nasica, etc.” At this point H. again agrees with the *Miscella* for only a few lines; it agrees, however, word for word with Eutropius down to the end of Book IV, which it concludes with the words: “he was led away in chains.” After these words the manuscript H. adds: “and soon afterward, by order of the consul, he was strangled in prison.” In these days at Jerusalem John, leader and high priest of the Jews, flourished; because he had defeated the Hyrcanians in war, he received the name Hyrcanus. At about the same time Cicero was born at Arpinum, his mother named Helvia and his father of equestrian rank, from a royal stock of the Volscians. At the same time a certain Roman maiden, traveling to Apulia, was killed by a thunderbolt. All her clothing was stripped off without any rent, the fastenings of modesty and of her feet were undone, and even her necklaces and rings shattered; though her body was unharmed, she lay naked. Her horse likewise lay dead, with its bridle and straps undone. Canisius records these matters from his Hersfeld manuscript; they also agree with the Ambrosian manuscript. But we continue our own reading, lest we inconvenience readers by referring them to Eutropius.]

With Publius Scipio Nasica and Lucius Calpurnius Bestia as consuls, war was declared by the agreement of the Roman people and Senate against Jugurtha, king of the Numidians. [Note: The same source adds after “war was declared”: “because he had killed his brothers Adherbal and Hiempsal, the sons of Micipsa, kings and friends of the Roman people. The consul Calpurnius Bestia was sent against him; corrupted by the king’s money, he made with him a most disgraceful peace, and it was rejected by the Senate. Afterwards, in the following year, Spurius Postumius Albinus went against him. He too, through his brother, fought disgracefully against the Numidians. Third, Quintus Caecilius Metellus was sent as consul. He …”]

Jugurtha, the adopted heir of Micipsa, king of the Numidians, having been made co-heir with his natural sons, first killed his fellow heir Hiempsal, and, after defeating Adherbal in war, drove him from Africa. Then he corrupted with money the consul Calpurnius Bestia, who had been sent against him, and induced him to accept the most shameful terms of peace; these the Senate rejected. Moreover, when Jugurtha himself came to Rome, after corrupting or attempting to corrupt everyone with money, he wickedly embroiled the whole city in seditions and disputes. As he was leaving it, he branded the city with a sufficiently infamous saying, declaring: “O venal city, destined soon to perish if it finds a buyer.”

In the following year, he defeated Spurius Postumius Albinus, the brother of the other consul Postumius, whom the latter had placed in command of an army of forty thousand armed men, near the city of Calama, while he was greedily pursuing the treasures of the king stored there. He imposed upon the defeated man a disgraceful treaty, and joined to his own kingdom almost all Africa, which had defected from the Romans. Afterwards Quintus Caecilius Metellus was sent as consul. He restored the army, corrected with immense severity and restraint, to Roman discipline, while committing no bloody act against anyone. He [Note: A.: “with various [readings].”] defeated Jugurtha in two battles, killed or captured his elephants, [Note: Our manuscript reads: “He captured many of his cities, and when he was already about to bring the war to an end, Gaius Marius succeeded him. He defeated both Jugurtha and Bocchus, king of Mauretania, who had begun to bring aid to Jugurtha; he killed ninety thousand armed men to the last man, captured several towns of Numidia as well, and brought the war to an end when Jugurtha was captured by his quaestor Cornelius Sulla, a great man, after Bocchus surrendered Jugurtha, who had previously fought on his behalf. By Marcus Junius Silanus, colleague of Quintus Metellus, the Cimbri were defeated in Gaul; and by Minucius Rufus, etc.”]

He overthrew many of Jugurtha’s cities. When he saw that, in his presence, his Numidian kingdom was being ravaged and could not be defended, he compelled him to surrender. Jugurtha gave three hundred hostages and promised in addition to supply grain and other provisions; he also surrendered more than three thousand deserters.

Thereafter, when the precarious peace did not restrain his wicked raids, Jugurtha was broken by the consul Gaius Marius, who was endowed with almost as much cunning as Metellus himself, and by Roman strength—especially after Marius had surrounded by stratagem and captured the city of Capsa, said to have been founded by Hercules the Phoenician and exceedingly full of royal treasures. Then, distrusting his own resources and strength, Jugurtha made an alliance with Bocchus, king of the Moors; increased enormously by his cavalry, he wearied Marius’s army with very frequent incursions.

At last, near the ancient city of Cirta, the royal seat of Masinissa, Jugurtha met the Romans, who were preparing to storm it, with sixty thousand horsemen. Never had any battle been more tumultuous or more terrifying for a Roman soldier. The dust raised by the rushing to and fro, the shouting, and the attacks of the circling cavalry covered the sky, robbed the day of its light, and spread night over it. So great was the cloud of missiles that no part of the body was safe from blows. The soldiers had neither clear vision for looking ahead, because of the darkness, nor freedom of movement for avoiding danger, because of the press of the multitude.

The Moorish and Numidian horsemen did not trouble themselves to seek out a well-positioned enemy with a well-aimed attack; rather, they hurled their weapons at random, certain that the wounds would not be random. Thus the Roman cavalry, forced together into one mass, and the infantry into another, became densely packed. The intervention of night, providing a pause in such danger, brought the battle to an end.

On the following day the armies again broke forth against the enemy with the same aspect of danger. Although the soldiers could not strike with drawn swords, they were driven back from a distance by javelins; they could not flee, for cavalry everywhere swifter in pursuit had enclosed them. Now it was the third day, and no aid appeared from anywhere; everywhere the terrible image of death presented itself.

At last the consul Marius, through a bold despair that opened a path to hope, burst out all at once from the rampart with his entire column and gave himself simultaneously to the plain and to the battle. When the surrounding enemy not only tore at the rear of the column but also struck the middle of it from a distance after their weapons had been discharged, and when the disturbed Romans were exhausted to the very limit of despair by the heat of the sun, the intolerable thirst, and the presence of death on every side, suddenly that familiar aid of the Romans against Africans—rain and storm—was sent from heaven and became an unexpected salvation.

For a sudden rain gave the thirsty Romans refreshment and drink and cooled those burning with heat. It also made the Numidians’ spear shafts slippery and therefore useless, since they were accustomed to hurl them by hand without thongs. Their shields, made serviceable and protective by stretched and hardened elephant hide, have the property of drinking in rain like a sponge and thereby becoming unwieldy through their sudden weight. Since the shields could no longer be carried about, they could not provide protection. Thus, when the Moors and Numidians were unexpectedly thrown into confusion and abandoned, Bocchus and Jugurtha fled.

After this, in the final war, those same kings brought ninety thousand armed men into the field against the Romans. The Romans defeated them, and these troops too are reported to have been slaughtered to the last man. At this point Bocchus, abandoning hope of continuing the war, sought peace. As the price of peace, he treacherously captured Jugurtha, loaded him with chains, and sent him to Marius through Cornelius Sulla, quaestor and lieutenant of Marius.

Meanwhile it was announced at Rome that the Cimbri were planning to cross from Gaul into Italy. They were defeated in Gaul by Marcus Junius Silanus, consul and colleague of Quintus Metellus. At the same time, the Scordisci and Triballi in Macedonia were defeated by Minucius Rufus, and the Lusitani in Spain by Servilius Caepio. Two triumphs were celebrated over Jugurtha: the first by Metellus, the second by Marius.

Nevertheless, Jugurtha was led in chains before Marius’s triumphal chariot with his two sons, and shortly afterward, by order of the consul, he was strangled in prison. During these days, John was leader and high priest of the Jews at Jerusalem. Because he had defeated the Hyrcani in war, he received the name Hyrcanus.

At about the same time Cicero was born at Arpinum, of his mother Helvia and his father, a member of the equestrian order from the royal Volscian family. [Note: A. continues: “At the same time a certain virgin …,” as Canisius noted in the Hersfeld manuscript above, p. 29, n. 70; in our manuscript the book ends with the same words.]

At the same time an obscene and grievous portent was seen. The Roman equestrian Lucius Cluvius, returning with his wife and daughter from Rome to Apulia, was caught in a storm. When he saw that his daughter was terrified, he wished to reach nearby shelter more quickly. He abandoned the vehicles, seized horses, and took his virgin daughter, riding on horseback, into the middle of the column.

The girl was killed instantly by a stroke of lightning. Yet all her clothing had been removed without any tearing, the fastenings on her breast and feet had been undone, and even her necklaces and rings had been scattered. Her body itself was unharmed, except that she lay naked in an obscene manner with her tongue slightly protruding. The horse on which she had been riding also lay dead at a distance. Its saddle coverings, bridle, and girths had been undone, and its trappings had been torn and scattered in every direction.

A short time later, the Roman equestrian Lucius Veturius violated the Vestal virgin Aemilia through a secret sexual crime. Aemilia also persuaded two other Vestal virgins to participate in the incest and handed them over to the companions of her corrupter. [Col. 0813B] When the matter was disclosed by a slave, punishment was inflicted on them all.

During the same period of the Jugurthine War, the consul Lucius Cassius pursued the Tigurini in Gaul as far as the Ocean. He was again surrounded by the same enemy through an ambush and was killed. Lucius Piso, Cassius’s lieutenant and a former consul, was also killed. Gaius Publius, the other lieutenant, so that the remaining portion of the army—which had taken refuge in the camp—would not be destroyed, gave the Tigurini hostages and half of all his possessions under a very firm treaty. When he returned to Rome, he was summoned before the people by Caelius, tribune of the plebs, because he had given hostages to the Tigurini, and fled into exile.

The proconsul Caepio removed one hundred thousand pounds of gold and one hundred and ten thousand pounds of silver from the temple of Apollo in the captured Gallic city called Tolosa. When he had sent it with guards to Massilia, a city friendly to the Roman people, it is reported—some witnesses so testify—that, after secretly killing those to whom he had entrusted its protection and transport, he stole the whole amount criminally. Hence a major investigation was later held at Rome.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0813]

[Note: In H., the beginning of Book V agrees word for word with Eutropius as far as “Catulus’s army XXI” [as printed]. Our A. has variant readings in certain places from both, which we note. It then proceeds: “The Roman consuls Marcus Manlius and Quintus Caepio were defeated by the Cimbri, Teutones, Tigurini, and Ambrones, peoples of Germans and Gauls, near the river Rhône; with enormous slaughter they also lost their camp and a great part of their army. Fear at Rome was great, scarcely less than, etc.”]

While the war in Numidia against Jugurtha was being waged, in the year 642 from the founding of the City, Marcus Manlius, consul, and Quintus Caepio, proconsul, were sent against the Cimbri, Teutones, Tigurini, and Ambrones, peoples of Gaul and Germany who had then conspired to destroy Roman power. They divided the provinces between themselves along the river Rhône.

While they disagreed among themselves in the bitterest jealousy and rivalry, the Romans were defeated with great disgrace and danger to the Roman name. In that battle the consul Marcus Manlius was captured and killed, and his two sons were also slain. Antias writes that eighty thousand Romans and allies were slaughtered at that time, and forty thousand camp servants and sutlers were killed.

Thus, it is reported, only ten men survived from the entire army, merely to carry back the wretched news and increase the misery. The enemy gained possession of two camps and enormous booty, but, with a novel and unheard-of curse, destroyed everything they had captured. Clothing was torn, gold and silver were thrown into the river, the men’s breastplates were cut to pieces, the horses’ trappings were scattered, the horses themselves were plunged into the depths, and men were hanged from trees with nooses placed around their necks. Thus the victor recognized neither booty nor the defeated man any mercy.

At that time Rome experienced not only the greatest mourning but also the greatest fear—almost as great as in the time of Hannibal during the Punic wars—lest the Cimbri immediately cross the Alps and ravage Italy. [Note: A. and Eutropius have “lest the Gauls should again come to Rome. Therefore, after his victory, Marius …”]

During the same period Quintus Fabius Maximus killed his young son, who had been relegated to the countryside, together with two slaves who had assisted in the parricide; immediately afterward he manumitted the slaves themselves as a reward for their crime. When the case was brought before the people, he was convicted, with Gnaeus Pompeius as accuser.

After his victory over Jugurtha, Marius was made consul for a second time, and the war against the Cimbri and Teutones was assigned to him. The consulship was also conferred upon him for a third and a fourth time, because the Cimbrian war was prolonged. In his fourth consulship he had Quintus Lutatius Catulus as colleague. [Note: After “Catulus”: “He engaged the Cimbri and killed two hundred thousand of the enemy in two battles, captured eighty thousand, and forced their leader Teutobod to flee. Because of this achievement, he was made consul while absent. Meanwhile the Cimbri and Teutones, whose numbers were still infinite, crossed into Italy. Gaius Marius and Quintus Catulus fought against them again, but the victory was greater on Catulus’s side. In the battle which they both fought together, one hundred and eleven thousand were killed either in battle or flight, and sixty thousand were captured. The Romans …”]

The Teutones, Cimbri, Tigurini, and Ambrones had set up camp near the rivers Isère and Rhône, where they flow together. After fighting for three continuous days around the Roman camp, seeking some way to drive the Romans from the rampart and pour them out into the open, they decided to make for Italy in three columns.

After the enemy had departed, Marius moved his camp and occupied a hill overlooking both the plain and the river where the enemy had spread out. When his army lacked water for drinking and he was reproached by everyone’s complaints, he replied that water was indeed in sight, but that it had to be won by the sword.

The camp servants first rushed into battle with a shout, and the army followed. Soon the battle was fought with the ranks drawn up in proper order, and the Romans won. On the fourth day the lines on both sides were again led out onto the plain, and they fought with almost equal danger until nearly midday. Later, when the day grew hot and the loose bodies of the Gauls melted like snow, the slaughter rather than the battle continued until night.

Two hundred thousand armed Gauls were killed in that war, eighty thousand were captured, and scarcely three thousand are reported to have escaped. Their leader, Theutobodus, was also killed.

Their women, with greater courage than if they had been victorious, negotiated with the consuls that, if their virginity remained inviolate and they were to serve the sacred gods, their lives should be spared. When they failed to obtain what they requested, they dashed their children against rocks and killed themselves with the sword and by hanging.

This was what happened to the Tigurini and Ambrones. The Teutones and Cimbri, however, with their forces intact, crossed the snowy Alps and spread through the plains of Italy. Their savagery was so great that, although they rejoiced to die in battle and lamented in illness, they considered it disgraceful to live after losing their leader.

When they had spread through the plains of Italy, and their harsh nature had been softened for a long time by gentler breezes, cups, food, and baths, Marius, consul for the fifth time, and Quintus Catulus were sent against them. When the day and the plain had been assigned for battle, they followed Hannibal’s strategy: they arranged the battle in mist but fought in sunlight.

The first confusion among the Gauls arose because they sensed too late that the Roman line had been arranged to attack them before they realized that it was present. When the wounded cavalrymen were immediately forced back upon their own men and confused the whole mass, which was still approaching in disorder, the sun rose with the wind. The dust from the opposite direction filled their view, and the brightness of the sun was dimmed.

Thus it happened that so great and terrifying a multitude was slaughtered with minimal Roman loss but with their own complete destruction. One hundred and forty thousand of them are said to have been killed in that battle, and eleven thousand captured. Three hundred Roman soldiers from both armies perished.

Thirty-three Cimbrian standards were taken. Of these, Marius’s army carried off two, and Catulus’s army thirty-one. [Note: A. has thirty-six thousand.]

The Romans experienced an even more serious battle from their women than from the men themselves. For the women, having arranged their wagons in the manner of a camp [Note: These details are also in the Hersfeld manuscript.] and fighting from above them, long resisted the Romans. But when they were terrified by a new kind of slaughter—for their hair and the crowns of their heads were cut off [Note: A. and Eutropius: “their necks.”], leaving them disfigured by a sufficiently shameful wound—they turned against themselves and their own people the weapons they had taken up against the enemy.

[Note: A.: “others.”] Some were strangled in mutual combat; others, seizing one another by the throat [Note: A. and Eutropius: “faces.”], were strangled; others, having fastened ropes around the legs of horses and then immediately goading the horses, placed their necks into the same ropes with which they had bound the horses’ legs and were dragged away and killed [Note: A.: “They died after fastening ropes to their own necks and being drawn by the horses’ legs.”]; others hung by a noose from the raised poles of the wagons. [Note: A. reads “hung.” One woman, while hanging herself, tied two sons by their necks to her feet with ropes passed around their necks. Thus, etc.]

Another woman was found who had tied two sons by their necks to her feet with ropes passed around their necks; when she had let herself go to die by hanging, she dragged them with her to their deaths.

Amid these many and pitiable forms of death, two Regulus brothers are also reported to have rushed together with drawn swords. The kings Lucius and Boiorix fell in battle. Clondicus and Cesorix were captured.

Thus, in these two battles, three hundred and forty thousand Gauls were killed and one hundred and forty thousand captured, apart from the countless multitude of women who, with feminine fury but masculine force, killed themselves and their little children. [Note: A. has the shorter reading: “This was the end of the war.”]

These wars ended here. A triumph was decreed for both commanders. [Note: A. begins here: “When Sextus Julius Caesar and Lucius Marcius Philippus were consuls, in the year 659 from the founding of the City, etc.” These words are absent from H. up to “In the year 649 from the founding of the City.” From that point H. agrees with Eutropius, except that where Eutropius reads “only in the fifth year,” H. reads “in the fifteenth year it reached its end.”]

After such a triumph for Marius and such a Roman victory, an incredible and previously unheard-of crime was committed at Rome, one which turned joy throughout the City into horror and mourning. A certain Publius Malleolus, assisted by slaves, killed his mother. Condemned for parricide, he was sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea. Thus the Romans completed both the crime and the punishment. Even the Athenian Solon had not dared to establish such a penalty, since he did not believe that the crime could occur. But the Romans, who knew that they were descended from Romulus, understood that even this could happen and established this unique punishment.

In the year 645 from the founding of the City, after the Cimbrian and Teutonic war and Marius’s fifth consulship—by which the stability of Roman power is rightly judged to have been preserved—the sixth consulship of the same Gaius Marius was so undermined that the state almost collapsed through internal disaster.

To unfold and traverse the complications of the disputes and the inextricable causes of the seditions would be both inconvenient and lengthy. It is enough that I speak briefly: the first author of the disturbance was Lucius Apuleius Saturninus, a most bitter enemy of Quintus Metellus Numidicus, a truly eminent man. When Metellus was elected censor, Saturninus had him dragged from his house and, as he fled to the Capitol, besieged him with an armed multitude. He was driven away by the indignation of the Roman knights, after a great slaughter had taken place before the Capitol.

Then Saturninus and Glaucia, through the treachery of the consul Gaius Marius, killed Aulus Numius, their competitor. In the following year Marius, consul for the sixth time, Glaucia, praetor, and Saturninus, tribune of the plebs, conspired to drive Metellus Numidicus into exile by any means.

When the case was brought before the people, Metellus, innocent but with the same judges corruptly appointed, was condemned and departed into exile amid the grief of the entire City. Saturninus, fearing that Memmius, a vigorous and upright man, would become consul, raised a sudden riot and killed him as he fled, smashing him with a crude club wielded by the henchman Publius Metius.

While the Senate and Roman people raged against such great disasters to the Republic, the consul Marius, adapting his character to the moment, joined himself to the consensus of the respectable citizens and calmed the aroused plebs with a gentle speech.

Saturninus, emboldened by infamous attempts, held an assembly in his own house, where some called him king and others commander. Marius enrolled the plebs by maniples, stationed another consul with garrisons on the hill, and fortified the gates himself. Battle was joined in the Forum.

Driven from the Forum by Marius’s troops, Saturninus fled to the Capitol. Marius cut the pipes by which water was brought there. A sufficiently dreadful battle was then fought in the Capitol’s courtyard. Many were killed around Saufeius and Saturninus. Saturninus openly shouted and declared that Marius was the author of all his plans.

When Saturninus, Saufeius, and Labienus, compelled by Marius, had taken refuge in the Senate house, the Roman knights broke down the doors and killed them. Gaius Glaucia was dragged from the house of Claudius and butchered. Furius, tribune of the plebs, decreed that everyone’s property should be confiscated. Gnaeus Dolabella, Saturninus’s brother, was killed with Lucius Geganius while fleeing through the vegetable market.

Thus, when the authors of so great a sedition had been killed, peace returned to the people. Then Cato and Pompeius proposed a bill concerning the return of Metellus Numidicus, to the joy of the entire City. But the consul Marius and the tribunes of the plebs, Furius and his faction, intervened so that it would not be carried through.

Rutilius was a man of the utmost integrity. He showed such steadfastness in faithfulness and innocence that, when the day of his trial was announced by his accusers, he neither let his hair or beard grow until the hearing, nor tried to win supporters by shabby clothing or humble appearance, nor placate his enemies, nor attempt to influence the judges. He delivered even the speech granted to him by the praetor with no more submissive spirit. Although he was attacked by evident slander and was rightly thought deserving of acquittal in the judgment of all good men, he was condemned by the perjury of the judges. He moved to Smyrna, where he grew old, content with literary studies.

In the year 649 from the founding of the City, with Sextus Julius Caesar and Lucius Marcius Philippus as consuls, although almost all other wars had ceased, internal causes stirred up the Social War throughout Italy. [Note: A. and Eutropius read: “Although the wars had ceased, the Picentes, Marsi, and Paeligni raised a most serious war in Italy. When they …”]

Although these peoples had for many years obeyed the Roman people, they then began to assert for themselves an equal freedom. This war was exceedingly destructive. The consul Rutilius was killed in it, as were Caepio, a noble young man, and another consul, Porcius Cato. [Note: A. adds after “consul”: “The leaders against the Romans from among the Picentes and Marsi were Titus Vettius, Hierius, Asianus, Titus Legennius, and Albus Duentius. The Romans fought well against them. Gaius Marius, who had been consul six times, and Gnaeus Pompeius fought against them, but especially Lucius Cornelius Sulla, who, among his other distinguished achievements, routed the enemy commander Duentius with a large force so completely that he lost only one of his own men. Although the war continued for four years with severe losses, it ended in the fifteenth year through the consul Lucius Cornelius Sulla, who had previously performed many brave deeds in the same war as praetor. At that very time dreadful portents appeared. For under …”]

Meanwhile Livius, tribune of the plebs, stirred up all the Latins to arms, having enticed them with the hope of freedom but being unable to fulfill what had been agreed. [Note: H.: “At that very time dreadful portents appeared. For at sunrise …”]

To this was added the terror caused by dreadful portents that afflicted the grieving city. At sunrise a fiery globe flashed from the northern region with an immense crash of the sky. Among the people of Arretium, when loaves of bread were being broken at a banquet, blood flowed from the middle of the loaves as though from wounds in human bodies.

Moreover, for seven continuous days a hail of stones, mixed also with fragments of potsherds, battered the earth over a very wide area. Among the Samnites, flames burst forth from an enormous cleft in the earth and seemed to extend all the way to heaven. [Note: After “was seen,” A. and H. omit the remainder and read: “Then also animals of every kind, etc.”]

Many Romans also saw, while traveling, a golden-colored sphere roll down from heaven to earth, grow larger, and then, with the sun rising, be carried upward from earth into the heights and cover the sun itself with its size.

Drusus, troubled by such disasters in his own house, was killed, though the author is uncertain. Thus the Picentes, Vestini, Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Samnites, and Lucani, while still secretly contemplating defection, killed at Asculum Gaius Servius, a praetor sent to them as lieutenant. They immediately closed the city and slaughtered all the Roman citizens in a declared massacre.

The most atrocious destruction was immediately preceded by unspeakable portents. Animals of every kind, accustomed to endure the touch of human hands gently and to live among humans, abandoned their stalls and pastures and fled to the forests and mountains with pitiful bleating, neighing, and lowing. Even dogs, whose nature is to be unable to exist outside human society, wandered about with tearful howls like wolves.

There was no delay: after these grave portents came the civil wars. At that time, among the Jews, Aristobulus was the first to assume the insignia of the diadem as both king and high priest. [Note: A. adds: “king and high priest alike, with the diadem, etc.”] [Note: A. and H. continue after “insignia”: “In the year 662 from the founding of the City, for the first time at Rome …”]

The praetor Gnaeus Pompeius therefore waged war against the Picentes by order of the Senate, and was defeated. After this, the Samnites appointed Papias Mutilius as their commander. The Marsi, however, chose Agamemnon, the chief pirate, as their preferred leader.

Julius Caesar, defeated in battle against the Samnites, fled with his army slaughtered. The consul Rutilius chose his kinsman Marius as his lieutenant. Marius continually warned him that delay would be useful in the war and that the inexperienced soldiers ought to be exercised for a while in camp. Rutilius, thinking that Marius was acting deceitfully, despised the advice and carelessly led his entire army into an ambush of the Marsi. There the consul himself was killed, many nobles were slain, and eight thousand Roman soldiers were cut down.

The river Tolenus carried the arms and bodies of the slain into the sight of Marius the lieutenant and raised them up as testimony to the disaster. Marius immediately seized his forces and unexpectedly overwhelmed the victorious enemy; he too killed eight thousand of the Marsi.

Caepio, led into an ambush by the Vestini and Marsi, was killed together with his army. Lucius Julius Caesar, after fleeing when defeated near Aesernia, gathered forces from every side and, fighting against the Samnites and Lucani, killed many thousands of the enemy. When the army acclaimed him commander and he sent messengers to Rome with news of the victory, the Senate put aside the *saga*—that is, the mourning garment it had assumed when the Social War began—and, with hope of victory shining, recovered the ancient dignity of the toga.

Marius then killed six thousand Marsi and stripped seven thousand of their weapons. The same Marius kept in his camp a woman named Syra, a sacred minister, on whose authority he claimed that he undertook everything.

Meanwhile the praetor Lucius Cornelius Sulla was sent with twenty-four cohorts to Aesernia, where Roman citizens and soldiers were being hard pressed by a very close siege. By a great battle and a massive slaughter of the enemy, he saved the city and its allies.

Gnaeus Pompeius routed the Picentes in a severe battle. As a result of this victory, the Senate resumed the broad-striped *laticlaves* and the other insignia of rank, although at the first hopeful turn of Caesar’s victory it had assumed only the togas. Porcius Cato, the praetor, defeated the Etruscans, and Plotius, the lieutenant, defeated the Umbrians, at the cost of much blood and with the greatest difficulty.

After fighting a battle, Sulla reverently prayed before his soldiers to the image of Apollo taken from Delphi, asking it to fulfill its promises; he seemed confident as he entered the war.

When Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Porcius Cato were consuls, Pompeius besieged the city of Asculum for a long time. He would not have captured it, however, unless he had defeated the people who burst forth into the open with overwhelming force.

Eighteen thousand Marsi, with their leader Franco, were killed in that battle, and three thousand were captured. Four thousand Italian men who escaped from that slaughter had climbed, gathered into a single column, onto a mountain ridge. There they were exhausted and crushed by snow and stiffened in a pitiable death.

For when they stood stunned by fear of the enemy, some leaning against stakes or rocks, others resting upon their own weapons, all appeared with their eyes open and their teeth bared, as though alive. To those looking from a distance there was no indication of death except the prolonged immobility that no living human body can endure for long.

On the same day the Picentes joined battle and were defeated. Their leader Judacilius summoned his commanders and, after magnificent banquets and abundant drinking, challenged them all to imitate him. Having drunk poison, he died. Everyone praised his deed, but no one followed his example.

In the year 661 from the founding of the City, when the Roman army had gone to besiege Pompeii, Postumius Albinus, a former consul and then lieutenant of Lucius Sulla, aroused the hatred of all the soldiers against himself through intolerable arrogance and was killed with stones.

Sulla, the consul, declared that civil blood could be expiated only by the blood of enemies. Moved by awareness of this matter, the army undertook the battle in such a way that each man saw that he must die unless he won. Eighteen thousand Samnites were killed in that battle. He also pursued and killed the Italian commander Juventius and a great number of his people.

The consul Porcius Cato, commanding Marius’s forces, had performed several brave deeds and boasted that Gaius Marius had accomplished nothing greater. For this reason, while he was waging war against the Marsi near Lake Fucinus, he was struck down amid the confusion of battle by the son of Gaius Marius, as though by an unknown assailant.

Gaius Gabinius, a lieutenant, was killed while storming the enemy camp. The Marrucini and Vestini were ravaged while Pompeius’s lieutenant Sulpicius pursued them. Propedius and Obsidius, Italian commanders, were overwhelmed and killed by the same Sulpicius near the river Tifernus in a dreadful battle.

After entering Asculum, Pompeius beat their prefects, centurions, and all their leading men with rods and struck them with the axe. He sold the slaves and all the booty at auction under the spear. He ordered the remaining people, free but naked and destitute, to depart. Although he hoped that this booty would provide some relief for public military pay, Pompeius contributed nothing from it to the impoverished treasury.

At the same time, when the treasury had been completely exhausted and there was no money for the pay and grain allowance, the public lands around the Capitol that had been assigned for possession to the pontiffs, augurs, decemvirs, and flamens were sold under the pressure of poverty. A sufficient sum of money was accepted to provide temporary relief in the time of want.

Indeed, at that time the wealth stripped from all the ruined cities and denuded lands was being poured from every side into the lap of the city itself, while Rome, driven by shameful poverty, was auctioning off its own principal parts. Let anyone therefore consider the character of those times: Rome was like an insatiable belly, consuming everything and always hungry, more miserable than all the cities it had made miserable. Leaving nothing, it possessed nothing, and was driven by the spur of domestic hunger to continue the unrest of war.

At the same time King Sothimus entered Greece with great Thracian auxiliaries and ravaged the entire territory of Macedonia. At last he was defeated by the praetor Gaius Sentius and compelled to return to his own kingdom.

In the year 662 from the founding of the City, while the Social War, which had lasted five years, had not yet ended, the first civil war was stirred up at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0819D] A. adds: “It arose at the same time, etc.”] In that same year the Mithridatic War also began. Gaius Marius [Note: [Col. 0819D] A.: “Six times consul”] provided the occasion for the civil war in his sixth consulship. For when Sulla, as consul, was sent to wage war against Mithridates, who had occupied Asia and Achaea, and while Sulla was holding his army for a short time in Campania so that the remnants of the Social War, of which we have spoken, which had been fought within Italy, might be removed, Marius sought a seventh consulship and sought to have himself sent to the Mithridatic War. [Note: [Col. 0819D] A. adds: “Therefore, angered, Sulla came to the City with his army and fought there against Marius and Sulpicius. He first entered the City under arms; he killed Sulpicius, drove Marius into flight, and, after arranging Gnaeus Octavius and Cornelius Cinna as consuls for the following year, departed for Asia. From this point the Hersfeld manuscript agrees word for word not with Miscella but with Eutropius up to the words ‘against the younger Marius,’ where H. reads: ‘he fought against the younger Marius, and after killing fifteen thousand of his men, lost four hundred of his own,’ and so on to the end. Hersfeld is fuller than Eutropius, but nevertheless more abridged than Miscella.”]

On learning this, Sulla—truly impatient, obstinate, and driven by unrestrained anger—first took up position with four legions before the City. There he killed Gratidius, Marius’s lieutenant, as though the first victim of the civil war. Soon he burst into the City with his army, demanded torches in order to set the City ablaze, and, with everyone concealed by fear, marched at speed along the Sacred Way into the Forum. Marius had tried in vain to stir up the nobility, inflame the plebs, and finally arm the equestrian order; at last, after enticing slaves to arms with the hope of freedom and plunder, he did not dare to fight at all, but withdrew to the Capitol. When Sullan cohorts rushed against him, however, he fled after a great slaughter of his followers. There Sulpicius, Marius’s colleague, was struck down after being betrayed by his slave. The consuls decreed that the slave himself should be freed because he had revealed an enemy, but thrown from the Tarpeian Rock because he had betrayed his master.

As Marius fled, surrounded by the madness of his pursuers, he hid himself in the marshes of Minturnae. From there, smeared with mud, he was unhappily and shamefully dragged out and brought to Minturnae as a disgraceful spectacle; when he was thrust into prison, he terrified the executioner sent to him by his mere expression. Then, slipping free of his bonds, he fled to Africa. After summoning his son from Utica, where he was being held under guard, he immediately returned to Rome and joined himself to the consul Cornelius Cinna in a partnership of crimes.

Sulla therefore departed for Asia. Mithridates, king of Pontus, who also held Lesser Armenia and the whole Pontic Sea around it, together with the Bosporus [Note: [Col. 0821D] A.: “in”], first wished to drive Nicomedes, a friend of the Roman people, out of Bithynia. He sent word to the Senate and the Roman people that he would make war upon Nicomedes because of the injuries he had suffered. The Senate replied to Mithridates that, if he did this, he too would suffer war from the Romans. Angered, therefore, he immediately occupied Cappadocia and drove from it Ariobarzanes, its king and a friend of the Roman people. Soon he also invaded Bithynia and Paphlagonia, expelling from the latter the friendly kings of the Roman people, Pylaemenes and Nicomedes.

From there he hurried to Ephesus and sent letters throughout Asia ordering that, wherever Roman citizens were found, they should all be killed on a single day. This was done. For eighty thousand Roman citizens living throughout the kingdom are said to have been killed on one day. What mourning there was among so many provinces, what groaning among both those being killed and those killing, when each individual was forced either to betray innocent hosts and friends or himself to face the punishment of his guests!

Meanwhile, the city of Methone in Achaea [Note: [Col. 0821D] A.: “Matone”] was handed over to Mithridates by Aristion the Athenian. Mithridates had already sent Archelaus, his commander, to Achaea with one hundred and thirty thousand cavalry and infantry [Note: [Col. 0821D] A.: “one hundred and twenty thousand”]. Through him Athens and the rest of Greece were also occupied.

Sulla, to whom the Mithridatic War had fallen after his consulship, besieged Archelaus at the Piraeus, the port of the Athenians, which was fortified with seven walls, and captured Athens itself by force. [Note: [Col. 0821D] A.: “He besieged the Piraeus, not far from Athens, and captured Athens itself. Afterwards, having engaged Archelaus in battle, he defeated him so completely that, out of one hundred and twenty thousand men, scarcely ten thousand remained to Archelaus. Only fourteen men were killed from Sulla’s army. When Mithridates learned of this battle, he sent seventy thousand of the finest troops from Asia to Archelaus. Sulla engaged him again. In the first battle fifteen thousand of the enemy were killed, as was Archelaus’s son Diogenes; in the second, all of Mithridates’ forces were destroyed, and Archelaus himself hid naked in the marshes. When Mithridates heard this, he ordered, etc.”]

Afterwards he engaged Archelaus in a regular battle. One hundred and ten thousand of Archelaus’s army are reported to have been killed, with scarcely ten thousand remaining. From Sulla’s army—an astonishing thing—only thirteen men were killed. When Mithridates learned of the defeat, he sent from Asia seventy thousand chosen soldiers to Archelaus as reinforcements. In the second battle fifty thousand of these were killed, and there Diogenes, Archelaus’s son, was slaughtered. In the third engagement all the troops Archelaus had were destroyed. For twenty thousand of his soldiers, driven into a marsh, implored Sulla’s mercy, but were killed by the victor’s insatiable anger; another twenty thousand were forced into a river and killed, while the rest of the wretched men were slaughtered everywhere.

Moreover, Mithridates intended to kill the leading men of the most distinguished cities in Asia and confiscate their property. After he had already killed sixteen hundred in this manner, the Ephesians, fearing their example, expelled his garrison and shut their gates. The Smyrnaeans, Sardians, Colophonians, and Trallians did likewise. Alarmed, Mithridates ordered negotiations for peace with Sulla.

Meanwhile, at that same time, Sulla defeated some of the Dardani, Scordisci, Dalmatians, and Moesians, and received others into his allegiance. But when envoys came from King Mithridates requesting peace, Sulla replied that he would grant it only if the king, abandoning the cities he had occupied, returned to his own kingdom.

Afterwards, however, both came to a conference, and peace was arranged between them, so that Sulla, hastening to the civil war, would not have danger at his back. [Note: [Col. 0822D] A.: “He would not have it. For while Sulla defeated Mithridates in Achaea and Asia, Marius, who had been driven into flight, and Cornelius Cinna, one of the consuls, renewed the war in Italy and entered the city of Rome, the most distinguished men, etc.”]

Therefore Marius and Cinna, while Sulla was fighting in Asia and defeating Mithridates, divided their army into four parts in order to overthrow the entire state. Three legions were given to Marius; Gnaeus Carbo was placed over one division of the forces; Sertorius received another—that Sertorius, namely, who had already been the instigator and participant in this civil war and who, when this was over, later stirred up another war in Spain, prolonging it for many years amid the greatest Roman disasters. The remaining portion of the army followed Cinna.

Gnaeus Pompeius, who had been summoned by the Senate with an army to aid the state and had long been kept in suspense by his pursuit of revolutionary schemes, was despised by Marius or Cinna and therefore went over to the other consul, Gnaeus Octavius. Soon he engaged Sertorius. The unfortunate battle was broken off by the coming of night. Six hundred soldiers were slaughtered on each side. The next day, when the mingled bodies were being separated for burial, a Pompeian soldier recognized, while stripping it, the body of his brother, whom he himself had killed. Cursing the gods, he carried off the body and placed it on a pyre beneath the Pompeian camp; then, piercing his own breast with a sword, pouring out tears and blood together, he cast himself upon the fire over his brother’s corpse.

Marius then entered the colony of Ostia by force and practiced there every kind of lust, greed, and cruelty. Pompey perished after being struck by lightning, while his army was attacked by pestilence and almost entirely consumed. For eleven thousand men from Pompey’s camp died, while six thousand from Octavius’s side were lost.

Marius stormed the cities of Antium and Aricia as an enemy and killed everyone in them except the traitors; he allowed their property to be plundered by his own men. Afterwards the consul Cinna with his legions and Marius with fugitives entered the City. They killed the most distinguished men and many former consuls from the Senate, proscribed many others, and, after destroying Sulla’s house, forced his sons and wife to flee. [Note: [Col. 0822D] A.: “They compelled them. The entire remainder of the Senate, fleeing from the City, came to Sulla in Greece, begging him to aid his country. He, etc.”]

Marius then brought together the heads of murdered citizens, carrying them to banquets, displaying them on the Capitol, and piling them up at the Rostra as a spectacle and ornament. In particular, he handled at the very banquet the severed head of Marcus Antonius, the outstanding orator, while corruption was oozing from it; he insulted it, mocked it with abuse, and embraced Publius Annius, who had brought the bloody head.

When he had forced his way into his seventh consulship with Cinna as consul for the third time, he was finally carried off by an untimely death at the beginning of his consular power. Who would not rightly marvel at his seven consulships and two triumphs? Who would not deservedly be astonished by Scipio’s most eminent testimony concerning him? For when Scipio was asked at dinner whether anything fateful had happened concerning that Scipio himself, whom the state was destined to have as a great commander, he looked around and said: “Perhaps this man here.” For he had looked with all his attention toward Marius.

Meanwhile Cinna made up for the slaughter of the good by the massacre of the wicked. When a leading band of fugitives had been brought in and was insatiable in its greed for plunder, but was giving no share to the consuls, the instigators of the plunder, it was summoned into the Forum as though for military pay and, surrounded by soldiers, was destroyed while unarmed. Eight thousand fugitives were killed in the Forum of the City that day. Cinna himself, consul for the fourth time, was also killed by his own army.

The remaining senators, who had escaped the power of Cinna, the savagery of Marius, the madness of Fimbria, and the audacity of Sertorius, were transported to Greece. By their entreaties they compelled Sulla to bring aid to his country, which was in peril—indeed, almost ruined. He crossed into Italy to wage civil war against the consuls Norbanus and Scipio.

As soon as he reached the Campanian coast, he fought his first battle against Norbanus not far from Capua. [Note: [Col. 0823D] A.: “Then he killed six thousand of Norbanus’s men, captured six, and lost twenty-four of his own. From there, etc.”] Then Romans killed seven thousand Romans, and six thousand of the same side were captured by them. Sulla lost one hundred and twenty-four of his own men.

From there he turned against Scipio and, before a battle, received his entire army into surrender without bloodshed. But when the consuls at Rome had changed, and Marius, the son of Marius, and Papirius Carbo had assumed the consulship, [Note: [Col. 0823D] A.: “Sulla fought against the younger Marius and, after killing fifteen thousand of his men, lost three hundred of his own. Sulla then engaged with the commander of Campania and the remaining forces at the Colline Gate; he killed eighty thousand men. Soon afterwards, having entered the City, he treacherously killed three thousand men contrary to the pledge given. And when they were raging with great cruelty against guilty and innocent alike, Quintus Catulus said openly to Sulla: ‘With whom, then, shall we finally be victorious, if in war we kill armed men and in peace unarmed men?’ Sulla then ordered Marcus Marius, dragged from a goat-herd’s hut, to be bound, taken across the Tiber, and slaughtered after his eyes had been gouged out and his limbs cut apart or broken piece by piece. He pursued Marius, Marius’s son, to Praeneste, besieged him, and drove him to death. Again he fought a most severe battle against Lamponius and Cecrinates, commanders of the Marian faction, at the Colline Gate. Seventy thousand enemies are said to have been against Sulla in that battle; twelve thousand surrendered to Sulla, while the rest were consumed by the victor’s insatiable anger. Gaius Carbo also, the other consul, fled from Ariminum to Sicily and was killed there by Gnaeus Pompeius. Recognizing the ability of this young man, twenty-one years old, Sulla set him over armies so great that, etc.”] Sulla’s commanders fought several battles against the Marian faction, with the most disastrous success. Quintus Metellus killed Carrinas’s forces and broke into his camp, while Gnaeus Pompeius inflicted a severe slaughter on Carbo’s cavalry.

The praetor Damasippus, at the instigation of the consul Marius, summoned Quintus Scaevola, Gaius Carbo, Lucius Domitius, and Publius Antistius into the senate house as though for consultation, and brutally killed them. The bodies of those murdered were dragged by executioners with hooks and thrown into the Tiber.

Sulla then fought against the younger Marius. In that battle, according to Claudius, twenty-five thousand of Marius’s army were killed, while four hundred perished on Sulla’s side. Pompeius also drove Carbo from his camp and pursued him, now slaughtering his men, now forcing them to surrender, thereby depriving him of much of his army. Metellus crushed Norbanus’s column, where nine thousand of the Marian faction were killed.

When Lucullus was being besieged by Quintius, he broke out and, by a sudden attack, destroyed the besieger’s army. More than ten thousand are reported to have been killed there.

Fabius Arianus, who held command as propraetor and was seeking to seize the kingdom of Africa through the agency of slaves, was burned alive with his entire household by their masters, who cast bundles of brushwood upon him at Utica.

Sulla then drew up his standards against Lamponius, the Samnite commander, and Carrinas with his remaining forces, before the very City and the Colline Gate at the ninth hour of the day, and at last won after a most severe battle. Eighty thousand men are said to have been scattered there; twelve thousand surrendered themselves, while the insatiable anger of the victorious citizens consumed the remaining multitude as it fled.

When Sulla entered the City as victor, he killed three thousand men who had surrendered through envoys, unarmed and secure, contrary to law and to the pledge given. Many others were killed at that time—not merely innocent men, but even men of Sulla’s own faction. They are said to have numbered more than nine thousand.

Thus, while free slaughter raged throughout the City and executioners wandered everywhere, Quintus Catulus said openly to Sulla: “Against whom, then, shall we finally be victorious, if in war we kill armed men and in peace unarmed men?”

Then Lucius Sulla, on the advice of Furfidius, a first-rank centurion, was the first to introduce that infamous list of proscription. The first proscription contained eighty names, among them four former consuls: Carbo, Marius, Norbanus, and Scipio; Sertorius was also among them, at that time especially to be feared. Another list was posted containing five hundred men.

When Lollius, believing himself safe and conscious of no wrongdoing, was reading it and suddenly encountered his own name, he tried to withdraw from the Forum in agitation with his head covered, but was killed. Yet even the lists themselves did not seem to guarantee safety or an end to misfortune. Some they slaughtered after proscribing them; others, after they had slaughtered them, they proscribed. Nor was there a single or uniform method of death, so that at least the law of enemies might be observed in the killing of citizens—enemies who demand nothing from the defeated except life.

Sulla ordered Marcus Marius to be dragged from a goatherd’s hut, bound, taken across the Tiber to the tomb of the Lutatii, and killed after his eyes had been gouged out and his limbs broken apart piece by piece. After him, the senator Publius Letorius and the triumvir Venuleius were killed. The head of Marcus Marius was sent to Praeneste.

When Gaius Marius saw it, seized by utter despair while Lucretius was besieging him, he rushed into a mutual death with Telesinus so as not to fall into the hands of his enemies. Since he himself struck more violently at the man rushing against him, the hand of the attacker was weakened around his own wound. Thus, after Telesinus had been killed and he himself lightly wounded, Marius offered his neck to his slave.

Sulla slaughtered the praetor Carrinas. Then he went to Praeneste and ordered all the leaders of the Marian army—that is, the legates, quaestors, prefects, and tribunes—to be killed.

Again he fought a most severe battle against Lamponius and Carrinas, commanders of the Marian faction, at the Colline Gate. Seventy thousand enemy troops are said to have stood against Sulla in that battle. Twelve thousand surrendered to Sulla; the rest were consumed by the victor’s insatiable anger in the battle line, in the camps, and in flight.

Gnaeus Pompeius captured Carbo, the other consul, as he fled from Ariminum and tried to escape to the island of Cossura. He brought him back to Sicily and killed him along with several of his associates. Sulla, recognizing the ability of the young Pompeius, who was twenty-one years old, placed him over such great armies that he was regarded as second only to Sulla.

After Carbo was killed, Pompeius recovered Sicily. [Note: [Col. 0825B] A. adds: “Crossing thence into Africa, he killed Domitius, commander of the Marian faction, and Jerdam, king of Mauretania, who was bringing aid to Domitius.”] He crossed over to Africa and, after making a sortie near Utica, killed eighteen thousand men. In that war Domitius, the Marian commander, was killed while fighting among the foremost.

The same Pompeius pursued the Numidian king Iarbas as he fled and had him stripped of all his forces by Bogud, son of Bocchus, king of the Moors. When Iarbas soon returned to Bulla, after the town had been surrendered to Pompeius, Pompeius killed him.

After these events, Sulla celebrated a triumph over Mithridates with immense glory. Gnaeus Pompeius also triumphed over Africa at the age of twenty-four, something that had been granted to no Roman. [Note: [Col. 0825B] A. adds: “Afterwards he triumphed. Thus the two … came to an end.”]

Sulla was created dictator, so that the lust for domination and cruelty might be both armed and veiled by the respectability and prestige of an honorable and distinguished title; at last, he appeared as a private citizen.

Thus, when Publius Servilius and Appius Claudius were consuls, these two most disastrous wars came to an end: the Italian Social War and Sulla’s civil war. [Note: [Col. 0825B–C] A.: “The Italian war, which is also called the Social War, and the Civil War; both were prolonged for ten years.”]

They lasted ten years. They consumed more than one hundred and fifty thousand Romans [Note: [Col. 0826B] A. adds: “men”], thirty-three former consuls [Note: [Col. 0826B] A.: “twenty-three”], seven former praetors, sixty former aediles, and approximately two hundred senators [Note: [Col. 0826B] A.: “approximately”], apart from the countless peoples throughout Italy who were destroyed without discrimination.

Afterwards, however, when Sulla had died, Lepidus, rising as an advocate of the Marian faction against Catulus, the Sullan commander, renewed the war and stirred up the ashes of the wars back to life. [Note: [Col. 0826B] A. adds: “rising up, renewed the war.”] The armies then fought twice in the field, and many Romans were killed—the wretched survivors already few in number [Note: [Col. 0826B] A.: “Romans were destroyed”] and still raging with that madness.

The city of Alba was besieged and assaulted because Scipio, the son of Lepidus, had fled there. [Note: [Col. 0826B] A. adds: “It was stormed and captured.”] It was preserved only by the final, pitiable surrender of its starving remnants. Brutus, fleeing into Cisalpine Gaul and pursued by Pompeius, was killed near Regium.

Thus this civil war vanished with the same speed with which it had arisen, like fire in straw, brought to an end no less by Catulus’s mercy than by weariness with Sulla’s cruelty.

At this time Alexandra, the wife of Alexander, was reigning in Jerusalem; during her reign the Jews were oppressed by disorder and various disasters.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0825]

[Col. 0825C] [Note: [Col. 0825D] The Hersfeld manuscript agrees word for word with Eutropius from the beginning up to folio 38, at the words “for the gladiators”; and so on. In these passages it differs both from Miscella and from Eutropius. But immediately afterwards it returns and agrees word for word with Eutropius up to “he penetrated to the Danube.”]

When Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Quintus Catulus were consuls, in the year 673 from the founding of the City, [Note: [Col. 0825D] A.: “After the consuls had settled the state with Sulla, new wars broke out.”] while the din of new wars resounded everywhere—one in Spain, another in Pamphylia and Cilicia, a third in Macedonia, and a fourth in Dalmatia—Sertorius, a man powerful through deceit and audacity, who had belonged to the Marian faction [Note: [Col. 0825D] A.: “Sertorius, who had belonged to the Marian faction”] and feared the fate of the others who had been killed, fled from Africa and slipped into Spain, where he stirred the most warlike peoples of Spain to arms.
