[Note: [Col. 0826D] A. adds: “fearing the fate of the others who had been killed, he stirred Spain to war.”]

Against him, to state the matter briefly, two commanders were sent: Quintus Caecilius Metellus, the son of the man who defeated King Jugurtha, and Lucius Domitius, the praetor. [Note: [Col. 0826D] A.: “Caecilius and Metellus, etc.”] [Note: [Col. 0826D] A. adds: “The praetor was killed while asleep by Hirtaleius, Sertorius’s commander. Metellus fought Sertorius with varying success. Afterwards, when Metellus alone was thought unequal to the contest, Gnaeus Pompeius was sent to Spain. Thus Sertorius, opposed by two commanders, often fought with varying fortune. In the eighteenth year he was killed by his own men, and the end, etc.”] Domitius was crushed with his army by Hirtuleius, the commander of Sertorius. Manlius, the proconsul, crossed from Gaul into Spain with three legions and one thousand five hundred cavalry and joined battle with Hirtuleius on unfavorable terms. Stripped by him of his camp and forces, Manlius fled almost alone into the town of Ilerda.

Afterwards, when Metellus alone was fighting because he was thought unequal to the battle, Gnaeus Pompeius was sent to Spain. Metellus, worn down by many battles and wandering through remote places, exhausted the enemy by delay until he joined Pompeius’s camp. Thus, with two commanders opposing him, Sertorius often fought with varying fortune.

Pompeius, having gathered an army near Palentia, took the city of Lauron. Sertorius then defeated and routed Pompeius, captured Lauron, and cruelly devastated it. He led the rest of the Lauronian column, which had survived the slaughter, into Lusitania in a wretched captivity.

He boasted that Pompeius—the Roman commander whom he had defeated—had been sent from Rome to this war with great confidence, not as proconsul but in place of consuls. Galba writes that Pompeius then had thirty thousand infantry and one thousand cavalry; he records that Sertorius had seventy thousand infantry and eight thousand cavalry.

Afterwards Hirtuleius engaged Metellus near Italica, a city of Baetica, lost twenty thousand soldiers, and, defeated, fled with a few men into Lusitania. Pompeius captured Belgida, a city of Celtiberia.

Sertorius then engaged Pompeius and killed ten thousand of his soldiers; but on the other wing, where Pompeius was victorious, Sertorius himself lost the same number. Many other battles were fought between them. Memmius, Pompeius’s quaestor and also the husband of his sister, was killed; the brothers of Hirtuleius were killed. Perpenna, who had joined Sertorius, was crushed.

Finally Sertorius himself was killed in the eighteenth year after the beginning of the war through the treachery of his own men, by the same means as Viriatus. The war was ended by the young Gnaeus Pompeius and Quintus Metellus Pius, and almost all the cities of Spain were brought into submission to the Roman people. [Note: [Col. 0827D] A.: “Were brought into submission. Appius Claudius was sent to Macedonia after his consulship.”] They gave the Romans a victory without glory.

Although afterwards part of his army followed Perpenna, it was defeated by Pompeius, and Perpenna was killed with his entire army. Since all the cities had voluntarily and without delay been received into surrender, only two remained: Uxama and Calagurris. Pompeius destroyed Uxama; Afranius, after Calagurris had been exhausted by a prolonged siege and driven by pitiable want to the infamous food of making meals from the corpses of wives and children, destroyed it in a final massacre and conflagration.

The assassins of Sertorius did not even consider it necessary to ask the Romans for a reward, remembering that the assassins of Viriatus had previously been denied one.

Meanwhile Appius Claudius, to whom the Macedonian War had fallen, fought minor battles against the various peoples who inhabited Rhodope [Note: [Col. 0827D] A. adds: “and there died of illness”] and were devastating Macedonia with extreme cruelty. Among the other things horrible to tell and hear that they inflicted upon their captives, when a drinking vessel was needed they used the bloody bones of human heads, still covered with hair and smeared within their cavities with poorly drained brains. The most bloodthirsty and savage of them were the Scordisci.

As I have said, Claudius thought that these peoples should be driven from the boundaries of Macedonia by war, and he placed himself against great masses of evils. When, distressed in spirit and surrounded by cares, he was also seized by illness, he died.

Gaius Scribonius Curio was sent as his successor after his consulship. [Note: [Col. 0827D] A.: “He defeated the Dardani and advanced as far as …”] Avoiding the force of the peoples attacked in the previous war, Curio turned his arms against Dardania, overcame it, and advanced as far as the Danube. [Note: [Col. 0827D] A.: “He penetrated to the Danube, earned a triumph, and within three years, etc.”] Within three years he brought the war to an end.

Publius Servilius, an energetic former consul, was sent to Cilicia and Pamphylia. [Note: [Col. 0827D] A.: “Afterwards.”] [Note: [Col. 0827D] A.: “An energetic man. He subdued Sicily, attacked and captured the most famous cities of Lycia; among them Phaselis, Olympus, and Corycus of Cilicia. He also attacked the Isaurians and brought them to surrender, and within …”] He therefore attacked Cilicia and Pamphylia with extreme cruelty and, in striving to subdue them, almost destroyed them. He captured Cilicia and its cities after besieging and crushing them.

He also ranged over Mount Olympus, destroyed Phaselis, and demolished Corycus. He traversed the slopes of the Taurus Mountains facing Cilicia, broke the Isaurians by war, and brought them into surrender; within three years he ended the war.

He was the first of all the Romans to lead an army across the Taurus and establish a route through it. [Note: [Col. 0828D] A.: “Of the Romans, he crossed the Taurus. Returning from there, etc.”] On his return he received a triumph and earned the name Isauricus.

Gaius Cosconius was sent to Illyricum as proconsul. [Note: [Col. 0828D] A.: “As proconsul. He subdued much of Dalmatia, captured Salonae, and, after bringing the war to completion, returned to Rome after two years.”] After crushing and subduing Dalmatia, he finally stormed and captured Salonae, a flourishing city, after two years, and returned to Rome once the war had been settled.

At the same time the consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Catulus’s colleague, wished to stir up a civil war; his movement was nevertheless crushed within a single summer.

Thus several triumphs took place at the same time: those of Metellus from Spain, Pompeius’s second from Spain, Curio’s from Macedonia, and Servilius’s from Isauria.

In the year 676 from the founding of the City, while Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Marcus Aurelius Cotta were consuls, King Nicomedes of Bithynia died and made the Roman people his heir by his will. [Note: [Col. 0828D] From here A. omits the rest; what follows begins: “Mithridates …”]

Meanwhile Fimbria, an attendant of Marian crimes and the boldest of all men, killed the consul Flaccus, whose lieutenant he was, at Nicomedia. Soon, after seizing the army, he drove Mithridates’ son out of Asia to Nicopolis, attacked Mithridates’ position, expelled Mithridates himself from Pergamum, and pursued him as he fled, besieging him in Bithynia.

He would certainly have captured him if Lucius Lucullus had put concern for the state before civil dissensions and had wished to hem him in by sea with a fleet stationed against him.

Then Fimbria, angry with the Ilians, who seemed to have repelled him by shutting their gates out of devotion to Sulla’s faction, destroyed the city of Ilium itself—ancient mother of Rome—utterly by slaughter and fire. Sulla immediately rebuilt it.

Fimbria was then at Thyatira with his army. Fimbria’s fugitives joined Mithridates, and at their urging Mithridates concluded an agreement with Sertorius through envoys sent to Spain. Sertorius sent Marcus Marius to him to strengthen the alliance; the king detained Marius and soon made him commander in place of Archelaus, who had already gone over to Sulla with his wife and children.

Meanwhile Mithridates, breaking the peace, again wished to invade Bithynia and Asia. [Note: [Col. 0828D] A.: “To invade them; both consuls were sent against him, not one, etc.”] He sent his commanders Marius and Eumachus against the consuls Lucullus and Cotta with a large army.

The two consuls, however, did not have the same fortune against them. Cotta was defeated by them in battle at Chalcedon, suffering very heavy losses, and was forced inside the town, where he was besieged. [Note: [Col. 0828D] A.: “Besieged. But when Mithridates moved from there to Cyzicus in order to …”]

Mithridates surrounded Cyzicus with a ditch while besieging it, intending, once Cyzicus had been captured, to invade all Asia. [Note: [Col. 0828D] A.: “Lucullus, the other consul, confronted him; while Mithridates remained for a long time in the siege of Cyzicus, Lucullus attacked him from the rear, etc.”] Lucullus, the other consul, besieged him from the rear, defeated him in many battles, and exhausted him by hunger, compelling him to suffer what he had inflicted.

He sent a messenger to the Cyzicenes themselves, telling them to be of good courage: one of the soldiers, skilled at swimming, crossed seven thousand paces by hanging from two inflated skins, holding a short staff in his hands and paddling with his feet. Mithridates, suffering from scarcity, ordered part of his fleet, equipped with weapons and troops, to return home. Lucullus intercepted it and destroyed the whole force. For he is said to have killed more than fifteen thousand men at that time.

At that time Fannius, who had joined Mithridates, and Metrophanes, the royal praetor, were defeated by Mamercius. With two thousand cavalry they fled into Moesia, but, leaving the road and entering the plains, they came upon sandy fields and hills. There not only are vast mountains and rocks visible, darkened as though by a kind of soot, but the desolate ground also lies charred, and for fifty thousand paces the plains are decayed beneath ashes hanging over the depths, without any burning by fire or furnace.

In three places there are also displays of scorched chasms, which the Greeks call *Pisae*. After wandering there for a long time, they were finally rescued from unexpected dangers and secretly reached the king’s camp.

King Deiotarus of Galatia killed the king’s commanders in battle.

Meanwhile Mithridates, at Cyzicus, was besieged at the very hour when he was besieging the city, and reduced his army to great want and pestilence. For he is said to have lost more than three hundred thousand men to hunger and disease during that same siege. He himself seized a ship and secretly fled from the camp with a few men.

Lucullus, with his soldiers unbloodied, a spectator of another’s disaster, gained a new kind of victory. Soon he attacked Marius, defeated him, and put him to flight. In that battle more than eleven thousand Marian soldiers are reported to have been killed.

Afterwards Lucullus engaged the same Marius in a naval battle and either captured or sank thirty-two royal ships and a considerable number of cargo vessels. Many of those whom Sulla had proscribed were killed there. The next day Marius was dragged from the cave where he had been hiding and paid the deserved penalty for an enemy’s spirit.

In the same advance Lucullus devastated Apamea and, beneath Mount Olympus, destroyed Prusias, a very strongly fortified city, after capturing and storming it.

Mithridates, sailing toward Byzantium with a fleet prepared for battle, was caught by a storm and lost eighty beaked ships. When he himself was already sinking with his shattered vessel, he leapt into the *myoparo*, a pirate ship belonging to Seleucus, with the pirate’s own assistance. From there he reached Sinope, and afterwards Amisus, with great difficulty.

In that same year at Rome, Catiline, accused of incest—which he was alleged to have committed with Fabia, a Vestal Virgin—escaped conviction, supported by Catulus’s influence.

In the year 678 from the founding of the City, M. Licinius Lucullus received the province of Macedonia—the cousin of the Lucullus who had waged war against Mithridates—and a new war suddenly broke out in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] A., Mallius. A.: “For seventy-four gladiators, under the leaders Spartacus, Crixus, and Oenomaus, escaped after breaking out of the gladiatorial school at Capua.”]

Seventy-four gladiators escaped from the school of Cn. Lentulus at Capua after breaking through its entrance. Immediately afterward, under their leaders Crixus and Oenomaus, Gauls, and Spartacus, a Thracian, they occupied Mount Vesuvius. From there they burst out and stormed the camp of the praetor Clodius, who had surrounded them with a siege; after putting him to flight, they turned all his possessions into plunder. Then, being led around through Consentia and Metapontum, they quickly gathered enormous forces. Crixus is said to have had a multitude of ten thousand, while Spartacus had three times that number. For Oenomaus had already been killed in an earlier engagement.

Thus, while they mingled everything with slaughter, fires, plunder, and sexual violence—

[Note: [Col. 0830D] A.: “And many married women killed themselves because of the pain of violated modesty. They stirred up a war against Italy scarcely less serious than Hannibal’s. For after defeating many commanders, including two Roman consuls at once, they gathered an army of nearly sixty thousand armed men. They were defeated in Apulia by M. Licinius Crassus, proconsul.”]

—at the funeral of a captive married woman who had killed herself in grief over her violated modesty, they presented a gladiatorial spectacle as a gift, using four hundred captives, and themselves intending to watch the spectacle—since their leaders were, so to speak, trainers of gladiators rather than commanders of soldiers.

[Col. 0830B]

Then the consuls Gellius and Lentulus were sent against them with an army. Gellius overwhelmed Crixus, who was fighting with the utmost ferocity, in battle; Lentulus, defeated by Spartacus, their leader, fled. Later, after both consuls had unsuccessfully joined their forces, they fled after suffering defeat. Next, Spartacus defeated and killed C. Cassius, the proconsul, in battle. Therefore, when the state was terrified and trembled with almost no less fear than it had trembled under Hannibal, who was roaring around the gates, the Senate sent M. Licinius Crassus with the consuls’ legions and a new reinforcement of soldiers.

As soon as he engaged the fugitives in battle, he killed six thousand of them and captured eight thousand. Then, before attacking Spartacus himself, who was making camp at the headwaters of the river Silarus, he defeated his Gallic and German auxiliaries—

[Col. 0830C]

—of whom thirty thousand men, together with their leaders, were killed. Finally, he engaged Spartacus himself in Apulia, where he had drawn up his battle line, and routed the largest forces of fugitives with him. For sixty thousand of them are reported to have been killed, six thousand captured, and three thousand Roman citizens recovered. The rest, who had escaped from this war and were wandering about, were worn down through persistent pursuit by several commanders. After many disasters had befallen Italy, the war was brought to an end in its third year.

In the year 681 from the founding of the City—

[Note: [Col. 0830D] A.: “Under P. Cornelius there were only serious …”]

—there were only two serious wars in the Roman empire: the Mithridatic and the Macedonian. These two wars were being conducted by the two Luculli, L. Lucullus and M. Lucullus.

L. Lucullus, after the battle of Cyzicus—

[Note: [Col. 0830D] A.: “after the flight.”]

—because he had defeated Mithridates, and after the naval battle in which he had overpowered his commanders—

[Note: [Col. 0830D] A.: “in which.”]

—pursued him. After recovering Paphlagonia and Bithynia, he also invaded his kingdom. He captured Sinope and Amisus, the most distinguished cities of Pontus.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] A.: “Afterward he captured them”; the rest omitted: “In a second battle …”]

But at Sinope, Seleucus the arch-pirate and the eunuch Leochares, who were in command there for the purpose of defending the city, left it plundered and burned. Lucullus, moved by the internal disaster of his wretched enemies—

[Col. 0831A]

—extinguished the fire that had been set by arriving swiftly. Thus the wretched city, by a reversal of its fortunes, was destroyed where it ought to have been defended and saved where it ought to have been destroyed, alternately becoming the enemy’s and the ally’s.

Moreover, Lucullus crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris. In a successful battle near the city of Cabira, belonging to Tigranes—

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A., Gavera; H., Gavera; Eutropius, Gabira.]

—where Mithridates had brought together immense forces from his entire kingdom, Lucullus engaged Mithridates and Tigranes with a very small force of his own and killed a great number of the enemy. For he killed thirty thousand men in that war. Mithridates fled accompanied by scarcely six hundred horsemen. His camp was plundered; he threw away his diadem and tiara so that he would not be recognized. Lesser Armenia also, which he had held, was taken from him.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A.: “Mithridates, with thirty thousand of the king’s finest troops, while five thousand Romans had been ravaged. Mithridates was routed and his camp plundered. Armenia also …”]

Nevertheless Mithridates was received after his flight by Tigranes, king of Armenia, who at that time ruled with immense glory and had often defeated the Persians; he had occupied Mesopotamia, Syria, and part of Phoenicia.

Therefore Lucullus, pursuing the fleeing enemy, entered—even though winter was approaching—the kingdom of Tigranes, who ruled the Armenians. He captured Tigranocerta, the most distinguished city of Arziana in the Armenian kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A., “Arzianen.” Eutropius: “He captured Tigranocerta, the most distinguished city of Armenia.” H.: “He took Tigranocerta, the most distinguished city of Yrzianena in the Armenian kingdom, and defeated the king himself with seven hundred clibanarii.”]

He defeated the king himself, who was approaching with seven thousand five hundred clibanarii and one hundred thousand archers and armed troops, with eighteen thousand soldiers, so that he destroyed a large part of the Armenians. From there he set out for Nisibis and captured that city as well, together with the king’s brother.

But those whom Lucullus had left in Pontus with part of the army, so that they might protect the conquered regions for the Romans, conducted themselves carelessly and greedily and gave Mithridates an opportunity to invade Pontus again. Thus the war was renewed.

When Lucullus was preparing an expedition against the Persians after the capture of Nisibis, a successor was sent to replace him.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A.: “Afterward he was sent”; followed by: “Another …”]

At the same time Metellus, praetor of Sicily, had found Sicily afflicted by that most disgraceful praetorship of C. Verres. Pirganion, the arch-pirate, was especially ravaging it with wicked slaughter; after driving away the Roman fleet, he had taken possession of the harbor of Syracuse. Metellus soon compelled him to leave Sicily after crushing him in a land and naval battle.

The other Lucullus, who had succeeded Curio, was the first of the Romans to wage war against the Bessi, and defeated them in a great battle on Mount Haemus. He conquered the town of Uscudama, inhabited by the Bessi, on the very day on which he attacked it.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A.: “Muscumada.”]

He captured Cabulen and penetrated as far as the Danube. He also stormed the peoples who were surrounded by the Rhodope Mountains—

[Note: [Col. 0831D] A.: “Surrounded by mountains, they committed deeds among their other horrors, terrible to tell and hear. When they needed a cup, they eagerly and without horror used the bones of human heads, still bloody and hairy, smeared inside with badly scraped-out brains, as though they were ordinary cups. Afterward …” H., together with A., has *circumfusae* instead of *circumfugae*.]

[Col. 0832A]

—whom Claudius had already thought to drive from the borders of Macedonia. From there he attacked many cities situated above Pontus. He destroyed Apollonia; he captured Calatis, Parthenopolis—

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A., Galathia.]

—Thomos—

[Note: [Col. 0832D] H., Tonos.]

—Istrus, and Burchaon—

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A., Burziaonem; H., Burtiaonem.]

—and, after completing the war, returned to Rome.

Both consuls celebrated magnificent triumphs, but Lucullus, who had fought against Mithridates, did so with greater glory, having returned victorious over such great kingdoms.

After the Macedonian war had been completed, while the Mithridatic war continued—the king having renewed it by gathering auxiliary forces after Lucullus’s withdrawal—the Cretan war broke out. Caecilius Metellus was sent against it. After great battles, within three years he captured the whole island—

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A.: “the whole province.”]

—and exchanged the laws of Minos for Roman laws. He was called Creticus and celebrated a triumph from the island of Crete.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] The remainder, up to the words “and he was called,” is not read in A. and H.]

At that time Libya also came under Roman rule by the will of Appion, who had been its king. It contained famous cities—

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A., Vernica.]

—Berenice, Ptolemais, and Cyrene.

While these events were taking place, pirates, scattered throughout all the seas, were already intercepting the transport of ships and even ravaging islands and provinces. Through the impunity afforded by their crimes and their desire for plunder, people commonly joined them, and their numbers grew enormously.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A.: “They infested every sea, so that, although the Romans were victorious throughout the world, navigation alone was unsafe. Therefore …”]

For this reason the war was assigned to Cn. Pompey, who, after the pirates had long carried out extensive devastation by land and sea, completed the war within a few months, with immense success and remarkable speed.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A. adds after “completed”: “Soon afterward he was also entrusted with the war against King Mithridates in Lesser Armenia. In a night battle he defeated him, plundered his camp, killed forty-five thousand of his men, and lost only twenty of his own army and two centurions. Mithridates fled with his wife and two companions. Not long afterward, when he was raging against his own people and had slaughtered many of his friends, as well as his sons Exipodras and Magaras, Pharnaces …”]

Later, having become Lucullus’s successor, he enclosed Mithridates’s camp in a siege in Lesser Armenia near Mount Dastracus. The king, making a breakout by night with all his forces and deciding to repel even his pursuer in battle, was nevertheless pursued by Pompey as he fled. Thus the battle was joined at night.

The moon had then risen behind the Romans, and Mithridates’s soldiers, mistaking the nearness of the enemy for the length of their shadows, cast all their missiles in vain. The Romans afterward attacked as though unarmed and won without difficulty, capturing the camp. For forty thousand of Mithridates’s army were killed or captured. The Romans had one thousand wounded, but scarcely forty killed, together with two centurions.

Mithridates slipped away in the confusion of battle, helped also by the benefit of the faint moonlight. Abandoned by all his friends, philosophers, writers of history or poetry, and physicians, he went alone through remote places, leading his horse by the hand and trembling at every nocturnal sound. He turned aside into a certain fortress and from there proceeded into Armenia.

Pompey pursued Mithridates and, between two rivers that rise from one mountain through different caverns—that is, the Euphrates and the Araxes—founded the city of Nicopolis for veterans, camp-followers, and the sick who wished to settle there.

He defeated Horodis, king of the Albanians, and his commanders in battle three times. Later, he gladly accepted letters and gifts from Horodis seeking to renew peace with the Albanians, and granted him pardon and peace.

He routed Artaces, king of Iberia, in battle and received all Iberia into submission. He gave Lesser Armenia to Deiotarus, king of Galatia, because he had been an ally in the Mithridatic war. He restored Paphlagonia to Attalus and Polemon. He appointed Aristarchus over Colchis.

Then, advancing from Pontus, he reached Ecbatana, the capital of the Parthian kingdom, on the fiftieth day.

In the Bosporus, while Mithridates was celebrating the Cerealian rites, an earthquake suddenly arose with such force that, it is said, a great destruction of cities and villages followed from it.

At the same time Castor, Mithridates’s commander, who was in charge at Phanagoria, killed the king’s friends, occupied the citadel, and sent four of Mithridates’s sons to the Roman garrisons.

Mithridates, inflamed with anger, erupted into crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0833C] From the words “Then he attacked many cities above Pontus” to “when he was raging against his own people,” H. agrees word for word with Eutropius; from that point onward, however, it differs and reads as follows: “When he was raging against his own people and had slaughtered many of his friends, Pharnaces, another of his sons, terrified by the example of his brothers, won over to himself the army that had been sent to pursue him and soon led it against his father. Mithridates, after pleading in vain for a long time with his son from a very high wall, when he saw that he was unrelenting, is said to have exclaimed: ‘Since Pharnaces orders me to die, you, ancestral gods, if you exist, I beg you to make him one day hear this same voice from his own children.’ Then, descending immediately to his wives, concubines, and daughters, he gave poison to them all. When he himself had drunk last of all, yet could not be destroyed by the poison because of the antidotes with which he had fortified himself, he invited a certain Gaul, Vitigis’s soldier, and offered him his throat. Such was the end of Mithridates. He died in the Bosporus, a man of immense energy and judgment. He reigned sixty years; he lived seventy-two; he waged war against the Romans for forty years. Pompey then waged war against Tigranes, and so forth; there Miscella continues. Ambrose, together with Hersfeld, agrees with this, as we have also noted in its proper place.”]

For after he had killed several of his friends at that time, including his own son Hypodran—having already earlier slaughtered another son, Machares, in a parricide—Pharnaces, another of his sons, terrified by the example of his brothers, won over the army that had been sent to pursue him and soon led it against his father. This happened by a just judgment, because he had contended with his father over the right to the kingdom.

Meanwhile Mithridates, after pleading in vain for a long time with his son from a very high wall, when he saw that he was unrelenting, is said, as he was about to die, to have exclaimed:

“Since Pharnaces,” he said, “orders me to die, you, ancestral gods, if you exist, I beg you to make him one day hear this same voice from his own sons.”

[Col. 0833C]

Then he immediately descended to his wives, concubines, and daughters and gave poison to them all. When he himself had drunk last of all, yet could not be destroyed by the poison because of the antidotes with which he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful substances, he struggled in vain, seeking by some means for the poison that had entered him to be driven through his veins by the body’s movement. He invited a certain Gallic soldier, who was running about after the wall had been breached, and offered him his throat.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] A.: “Yet because of the antidotes with which he had fortified his vital organs, he could not be destroyed by the poison …”]

Such was the end of Mithridates’s life. He left us a most powerful proof of his learning—

[Col. 0834A]

—being, as is reported, the most studious of all men. He spoke the languages of the twenty-two peoples whom he ruled, so that he never heard embassies through interpreters.

He died in the Bosporus, a man of immense energy and judgment. He reigned for forty years—

[Note: [Col. 0834C] A., sixty.]

—though others say thirty—

[Note: [Col. 0834C] Ambrose: “He lived seventy-two years. He waged war against the Romans for forty years. Pompey then waged war against Tigranes, and so forth.”]

In the year 689 from the founding of the City, when M. Tullius Cicero was the orator and C. Antonius the consul, Pompey, having received news of Mithridates’s death, waged war against Tigranes. But Tigranes immediately surrendered to him and came into Pompey’s camp at the sixteenth milestone from Artaxata. After falling at Pompey’s knees, he placed his diadem in Pompey’s hands.

Pompey placed it back on his head—

[Note: [Col. 0834C] A.: “placed it back on him.”]

—and treated him magnificently, though he deprived him of part of his kingdom and imposed a large payment. Syria, Coele Syria, Phoenicia, and Sophene were taken from him.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A. and H.: “Syria, Phoenicia, and Sophene”; the word “Coele” is also absent in Eutropius.]

Moreover, he gave the Roman people six thousand talents of gold and silver—

[Col. 0834B]

—

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A.: “of gold and silver, which he was to give to the Roman people.”]

—because he had provoked a war against the Romans without cause.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A.: “had provoked.” Pompey soon afterward also waged war against the Albanians and prudently defeated their king. Finally, when he was asked by letters and gifts, he granted him pardon and peace. He also defeated the king of Iberia in battle and received him into submission. He gave Lesser Armenia to Deiotarus, king of Galatia, who had been an ally in the Mithridatic war. He restored Paphlagonia to Attalus and Polemon and appointed Aristarchus king over Colchis. Then he attacked the Ituraeans, and so forth. Hersfeld, also together with our text, is fuller here and agrees word for word with Eutropius up to “Then to Judaea,” except that where Eutropius has “to the people of Daphne,” H. has “to the people of Damascus.”]

Soon afterward he defeated the Ituraeans and Arabs and captured their city, which is called Petra. When he came into Syria, he granted freedom to Seleucia, a city near Antioch, because it had not accepted King Tigranes. He returned the hostages to the Antiochenes. He gave the people of Damascus a small amount of land, so that the place might be more spacious for him, being delighted by the beauty of the location and the abundance of its waters.

From there he crossed into Judaea—

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A.: “Having crossed over, he besieged Jerusalem, the capital of the nation, not only …”]

—where Aristobulus ruled, having expelled his brother Hyrcanus, and was the first king from the priestly line. Pompey sent Gabinius with an army to Jerusalem, their city. He himself immediately followed, and, after being received by the leading men of the city but driven away by the populace from the wall of the Temple, intensified the siege.

Because of the natural strength of the place, and because it was fortified by a massive wall and a very large ditch, he ordered the legions to relieve one another at different times, day and night, without respite. With difficulty he stormed it in the third month. Fourteen thousand Jews were killed—

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Eutropius, twelve thousand; Hersfeld, twenty-two thousand.]

—and the rest of the multitude surrendered.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A.: “He received the rest into submission, and so forth.”]

He ordered the walls of the city to be destroyed and leveled to the ground; its circuit is said to have been four thousand paces. After striking several of the Jewish leaders with the axe, he restored the priesthood to Hyrcanus and brought Aristobulus, a captive, to Rome.

Pompey himself declared before the assembly that he had conducted this war in the East against twenty-two kings.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] A. adds afterward: “After accomplishing these things, he withdrew into Asia and brought an end to a very ancient war. In the year 689 from the founding of the City, when M. Tullius Cicero was orator and Cn. Antonius consul, Lucius Sergius …”]

[Col. 0835A]

Meanwhile L. Sergius Catiline, of the noblest family but of the most depraved character, conspired with certain men who were indeed distinguished but reckless, intending to destroy his fatherland. His conspiracy, which had been formed in the City during those same days, was exposed; in Etruria it was extinguished by civil war. Catiline was expelled from the City by Cicero, while his associates were arrested and strangled in prison. Catiline himself was defeated and killed in war by the other consul, Antonius.

But since this history, conducted by Cicero and described by Sallust, is sufficiently known to everyone, it is enough for us now merely to have touched upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0835C] This passage, from here to “avenged,” is absent from H., which agrees word for word with Eutropius in what follows, up to “advanced to the British Ocean”: “For in that region he stormed the Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobriges, Rauraci, and Boii, of whom forty-seven thousand were killed; the rest fled. Then he compelled King Ariovistus, whom the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Edues, and Suevi were helping, to flee; he captured his two wives and two daughters and slaughtered his entire army relentlessly over fifty thousand paces. After this he defeated the people of the Belgae, joined by the Bellovaci [otherwise Bellovagui], with sixty thousand armed men, and crushed the Suessiones, numbering fifty thousand. The Imbervi (I correct: Nervii), moreover, whose savagery was so untamed that they never allowed merchants to come to them, nevertheless had fifty thousand armed men. The Atrebates, Ambiani, Menapii, Caleti, Velocasses, Veromandi, Aduatuci, Condrusi, Eburones, Cerosicemanes—who are all called Germans by one name—are reported, together with those mentioned above, to have numbered two hundred seventy-two thousand. When they suddenly burst from the forests and threw Caesar’s terrified army into flight, at last, through Caesar’s exhortations, the army recovered and almost destroyed them all. Then Titurius Albinus, Caesar’s commander, destroyed the Alberci, Eburovices, and Lixovii with incredible slaughter. Publius Crassus, another commander, killed thirty-eight thousand among the Aquitani and Cantabri. Caesar again attacked the Germans who had crossed the Rhine and were preparing to subject all Gaul to themselves, and so forth, in the passages where H. agrees with Miscella, fol. 42, column 2 B. From this point, reader, you will note the variant readings; so that you may compare them, I will add these also from another manuscript. CANIS.”]

A disturbance also arose among the Peligni, instigated by Marcellus father and son and exposed through L. Betius. Once Catiline’s conspiracy had been exposed, it was suppressed as though cut off at the root. Both matters were avenged: the one among the Peligni by Bibulus, the other among the Bruttii by Cicero.

In the year 690 from the founding of the City, when D. Junius Silanus and L. Muraena were consuls, Metellus celebrated a triumph over Crete, and Pompey one over the pirate and Mithridatic wars.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] A.: “over the pirate war and the Mithridatic war.”]

No triumphal procession had ever been comparable to it. The sons of Mithridates were led before his chariot—

[Note: [Col. 0836D] A.: “the son of Mithridates.”]

—as were the son of Tigranes and Aristobulus, king of the Jews. An immense amount of money was displayed, together with an unlimited quantity of gold and silver. At that time there was no serious war anywhere in the world.

In the year 693 from the founding of the City, C. Julius Caesar, who afterward became emperor, was made consul with L. Bibulus. Gaul beyond the Alps, Cisalpine Gaul, and Illyricum were assigned to him, together with ten legions granted for five years.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] A.: “with ten [legions]. He first defeated the Helvetii, who are now called Squadi. Then, by winning very serious wars, he advanced as far as the British Ocean. For he stormed the Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobriges, Rauraci, and Boii, as Canis reads in Hersfeld; see note 55 above.”]

The Senate later added Transalpine Gaul, or Gallia Comata, to his command. Suetonius Tranquillus has explained this history in the fullest detail; we have excerpted from him the portions appropriate to our purpose.

The Helvetii, the bravest people among all the Gallic tribes, had been incited to arms by a certain nobleman of their nation, Orgetorix, who hoped to invade all Gaul. The chief reason for their exceptional courage was that they were almost continually engaged in war with the Germans, from whom they were separated only by the Rhine. When the other nobles seized Orgetorix and forced him to face death, they were nevertheless unable to restrain the common people, once their minds had been inflamed by the prospect of plunder.

After forming a conspiracy and setting a date, they burned their villages and houses so that no desire or hope of returning might remain, and set out. Caesar encountered them at the river Rhône and defeated them twice in a great and difficult war, forcing the defeated people to surrender.

When the entire multitude first set out, the forces of the Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobriges, Rauraci, and Boii, including both sexes, numbered approximately one hundred fifty-seven thousand. Forty-seven thousand of them fell in the war; the rest were sent back to their native lands.

Later Caesar fought against King Ariovistus, who was stirring up and bringing with him incredible German forces. He had recently boasted that he had subdued all the peoples of Gaul. Caesar compelled him to flee near the Sequani. When Caesar’s army, terrified for a long time by the Germans’ numbers and courage, refused to engage in battle, Ariovistus escaped into Germany by crossing the Rhine in a small boat.

His two wives and two daughters were captured. Ariovistus’s army included the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes—

[Note: [Col. 0836D] Another reading: Edures, Eudeses. CANIS.]

—the Sebusii, and the Suevi.

The most difficult part of the battle was the German phalanx. They had formed themselves into a single mass and interwoven their shields above their heads, thereby protecting themselves as they advanced against the Roman line. But when some Roman soldiers, distinguished by agility and courage, leapt onto the covering testudo and, tearing away the shields one by one as though they were scales, pierced from above the exposed shoulders of the men whom they had uncovered, the enemy, terrified by this new danger of death, broke apart their formidable formation.

Then they turned to flight and were slaughtered relentlessly for fifty thousand paces. It was impossible to determine the number of Germans, either how many had taken part in the battle or how many had been killed.

After this, the people of the Belgae, who constitute a third part of Gaul, rose up against Caesar. Their forces were distributed as follows. The Bellovaci, who seemed to surpass the others in numbers and courage, had sixty thousand picked armed men—

[Col. 0836C]

—the Suessiones, from twelve towns, fifty thousand; the Nervii, whose savagery was said to be so great that they never allowed merchants to approach them or wine and other merchandise to be brought to them, lest the resulting pleasure produce weakness in their courage, likewise had fifty thousand.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] Another reading: Atuacii.]

The Atrebates and Ambiani had ten thousand; the Morini twenty-five thousand; the Menapii ten thousand; the Caleti ten thousand; the Velocasses and Veromandi ten thousand; the Atuatici seventeen thousand; the Condrusi, Eburones, and—

[Note: [Col. 0836D] Another reading: Ceroceromani.]

—the Cercesi and Pemani, who are called Germans by one name, forty thousand.

[Col. 0837A]

Thus all together are reported to have numbered two hundred eighty—

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: seventy.]

—two thousand of the finest armed troops.

When these people suddenly burst from the forests, Caesar’s army was thrown into confusion and driven into flight, suffering the loss of many of its men. Nevertheless, through the encouragement of its commander, it recovered, attacked the victors, and almost destroyed them all.

Thus, after accomplishing great deeds in Gaul, Caesar decided to set out for Italy and sent Galba with the Twelfth Legion against the Veragri and Seduni. Galba had settled for the winter in a village of the Veragri called Octodurus and had allotted to the inhabitants the middle part of the town, which was divided by a torrent. One day he saw that they had all withdrawn during the night and occupied the nearby hill.

They had scornfully regarded the smallness of scarcely half a legion and thought that victory, which would require no effort, was voluntarily presenting itself to them. They had invited their neighbors to share in the slaughter and plunder.

Galba, therefore, surrounded by such immediate and serious dangers, anxious and uncertain of a definite plan amid different counsels, suddenly saw the Gauls pour down from the mountain. They surrounded the unfinished camp and overwhelmed the few defenders along the rampart with stones and missiles.

When the camp was already being breached, on the advice of Pacuvius, the chief centurion, and Volusenus, the tribune, all the Romans burst out through the gates. They suddenly attacked the unwary enemy and first threw them into confusion; then, when the enemy had turned to flight, they routed them in a lamentable slaughter. For more than thirty thousand barbarians are reported to have been killed then.

Caesar had thought that all the peoples of Gaul were now pacified, but he was drawn into a new and very great war. For while the young P. Crassus was wintering near the Ocean among the Andegavi with the Seventh Legion—

[Col. 0837C]

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: Oceatenus; Andegavos, another reading Caudicavos.]

—the Veneti and the other neighboring peoples suddenly conspired to take up arms. They bound the Roman envoys and informed the Romans that they would return them only if they received back their own hostages.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: Deditiani.]

They brought the Osismii, Lexovii, Nannetes, Ambibariti, Morini, Diablintes, and Menapii into the war as allies.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: Osismi, Namnetes, Deditiani.]

They also summoned auxiliary forces from Britain.

When Crassus informed Caesar of the revolt of the subject peoples, Caesar understood how difficult it would be to undertake the war. Nevertheless, he judged that so important a matter must not be neglected, lest the other peoples be given license to attempt similar things.

Accordingly, he pursued the enemy and unsuccessfully tried to attack them by land, since the enemy was protected by the tidal inlets flowing in from the Ocean and by inaccessible recesses secured by the natural boundaries of the land. He ordered longships to be built on the river Loire so that they could be sent into the Ocean.

As soon as these ships were seen by the enemy, their two hundred twenty ships, prepared and fully equipped with every kind of weapon, immediately advanced and took up position opposite them at the harbor.

Brutus, looking around and realizing that the naval contest was overwhelmingly unequal—for the barbarians’ ships were constructed of solid timber and, like rocks, blunted the blows of the rams driven against them—had prepared this first means of assistance: extremely sharp hooks, not fixed rigidly to poles but attached to ropes. When necessary, these hooks could seize the ropes of the enemy from a distance; after the poles had been pulled down, the hooks could be drawn back along the ropes and cut them.

After this had been quickly arranged, Brutus ordered the rigging of the enemy ships’ masts to be cut. When the masts fell, he immediately rendered several ships motionless, as though they had been captured.

Others, terrified by this danger, tried to flee with their sails hoisted in the direction in which the wind was blowing. But when the wind ceased, they became objects of ridicule for the Romans.

Therefore, after all the ships had been burned and those who had fought had been killed, the remaining Gauls surrendered. But Caesar, chiefly because of the wrong done to the envoys and so that he might brand this people, quick to every kind of scheme, with the mark of a terrifying example, had all the chiefs killed by torture and sold the rest under the crown.

During these days Titurius—

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: Albinus, Caesar’s commander, destroyed the Alverni, Eburovices, and Lixovii.]

—the commander of Caesar, after making a sortie, destroyed the Aulerci, Eburovices, and Lexovii with incredible slaughter. They had killed their own leading men because those men were unwilling to revive the war or to be its instigators.

P. Crassus, however, when he had arrived in Aquitania, was met by war. The Sociates attacked the Romans with a large cavalry force and very strong infantry and for a long time threw them into serious confusion. Later they were defeated, driven into the town of the Sociates, and besieged. When they saw that the town was about to be stormed, they surrendered their arms and were received into submission.

The Aquitani, shaken by this defeat, gathered an army from every direction and summoned auxiliaries from Further Spain as well. They appointed as their commanders men who had served with Sertorius.

While all these people were preparing to lay siege to Crassus, Crassus overwhelmed and destroyed them in their camp. For of the Aquitani and Cantabri, who had then come to their aid in a force of fifty thousand, thirty-eight thousand are reported to have been killed.

Caesar attacked the Germans who had crossed the Rhine with immense forces and were preparing to subject all Gaul to themselves, and slaughtered them almost to the last man. Their number is said to have been approximately four hundred forty thousand.

Then Caesar built a bridge, crossed the Rhine into Germany, and freed the Sicambri and Ubii from siege.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Another reading: “the Sugambri and Ubii.”]

He terrified all Germany by his arrival, including the Suevi, the largest and most savage nation. Many writers have stated that they consisted of one hundred districts and peoples.

Soon afterward he dismantled the bridge and withdrew into Gaul.

For nine years he subdued all Gaul, which lies between the Alps, the Rhône, the Rhine, and the Ocean, and extends around a circuit of six million paces.

[Col. 0838D]

From there he came to the Morini, from whom the nearest and shortest crossing to Britain is made. Having prepared approximately eighty cargo and transport ships, he crossed into Britain and waged war against the Britons, who before him had not even known the name of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0838D]

From this point the Hersfeld manuscript agrees word for word with Eutropius, except that where Eutropius reads “in the year 699 from the founding of the City, M. Licinius Crassus,” H. reads 697; where Eutropius has “Surena of King Orodes,” H. has “of Herodes”; and where Eutropius reads “with the armies dismissed, he returned to the City, and because of this insult, from Ariminum …,” H. has the fuller version: “he returned to the City, and on the authority of Marcellus, the consul, Pompey was sent with imperium to the legions that were at Luceria. Because of this insult, from Ariminum …”

[Col. 0839C]

Likewise, where Eutropius has “at Pharsalus,” H. has “at Paleopharsacus, after the troops had been drawn up,” and so forth. Eutropius reads: “seven thousand cavalry on the left wing”; H.: “six hundred cavalry on the left wing and five hundred on the right.” Eutropius: “with great determination.” H. reads more fully: “with great determination, and although for a long time the outcome on both sides remained uncertain, Pompey, on one side, kept urging them, saying, ‘Spare the citizens,’ though he did not do so, while Caesar, on the other, did what he was urging, saying, ‘Strike the soldiers in the face.’ At last Pompey’s entire army fled and his camp was plundered.”

Here again H. agrees with Eutropius down to the words “having followed his friendship, he ordered Pompey to be killed after sending eunuchs, and his head and ring were sent to Caesar.” When he saw them, Caesar is said to have shed tears as he looked upon the head of so great a man and of his once son-in-law.

Soon afterward Caesar came to Alexandria, where Ptolemy himself also plotted against him. Pressed by the force of his attacking enemies, Caesar boarded a small boat. When it soon became overloaded by the weight of those following him and sank, he swam two hundred paces to a ship with one hand raised above the water, holding the documents—

[Col. 0840C]

(correct from Miscella, fol. 46, column 2 B: *charts*).

[Col. 0840D]

Soon afterward there was a naval battle, and so forth. In these matters H. agrees with Miscella, fol. 46, at the same place, up to the words “Caesar took possession of Alexandria.” From those words H. agrees with Eutropius almost word for word to the end, except that after the final word of Book VI of Eutropius, “he was stabbed,” H. adds: “A man than whom no one ever …,” which is found in Miscella, fol. 47, column 2 B, to the end.]

These matters are from the Hersfeld manuscript. Canisius continues our Ambrosian reading with continuous notes; therefore, after the words “the name of the Romans had been known,” we append our own text as well:

He also made them, after they had been defeated and had given hostages, tributaries. From Gaul he imposed an annual payment of sestertii as tribute, and, attacking the Germans beyond the Rhine, defeated them in the most savage battles.

Amid so many successes, he fought badly three times against the Averni: once while present and twice while absent.

About the same time, in the year 697 from the founding of the City, and so forth.]

There, after first being exhausted by a bitter battle, [Col. 0839A] he was then caught by contrary weather and lost most of his fleet, along with no small number of soldiers and almost all his cavalry. Returning to Gaul, he sent the legions into winter quarters and ordered six hundred ships of both types to be built. With these he was transported back to Britain at the beginning of spring. While he himself advanced against the enemy with the army, the ships lying at anchor were caught by a storm: some collided with one another, others were driven onto the sands and broken apart. Forty of them perished; the rest were repaired only with great difficulty.

Meanwhile, Caesar’s soldier Sceva, having crossed ahead in a small boat with four comrades to a rock near the island, was stranded there when the ocean receded. A great number of Britons attacked the few Romans; nevertheless, the others, who had been his very few companions, returned by boat. [Col. 0839B] Sceva remained undaunted, overwhelmed by missiles from every side. At first he held his ground with his spear; finally, alone against many, he fought with his sword. When he had become exhausted and wounded, and had lost his helmet and shield through the blows, he swam to Caesar’s camp wearing two cuirasses and asked the commander’s pardon for his rashness. Caesar rewarded him by raising him to the rank of centurion.

Accordingly, Caesar’s cavalry was defeated by the Britons at the first encounter, and there Labienus the tribune was killed. In the second battle he defeated the Britons, though at great cost to his own men, and put them to flight. From there he advanced to the river Thames, which, they say, can be crossed at only one place. On the farther bank of the river, an immense multitude of the enemy, under their leader Cassobellaunus, took up position and had fortified the riverbank—and almost the entire ford beneath the water—with extremely sharp stakes. When this was discovered by the Romans [Col. 0839C] and avoided, the barbarians, unable to withstand the assault of the legions, hid themselves in the forests; from there, by frequent sallies, they severely and repeatedly harassed the Romans.

Meanwhile Trinovantum, a very powerful city, together with its leader Androgorius, surrendered to Caesar after giving forty hostages. Following this example, many other cities entered into alliance with the Romans; after giving hostages, they became tributary. At their direction Caesar seized the stronghold of the leader Cassobellaunus, situated between two marshes, fortified by the protection of the forests, and crowded with provisions and every other resource, after a hard-fought battle.

Thereafter Caesar returned from Britain to Gaul. Once he had sent the legions into winter quarters, he was surrounded and harassed on every side by sudden outbreaks and upheavals of war. [Col. 0840A] For Ambiorix, conspiring with the Eburones and the Atuatuci and encouraged by the advice of the Treveri, ambushed and killed the legates Titurius Sabinus and Arunculeius Cotta among the Eburones, together with their entire legion. Elated by this victory, Ambiorix hastily gathered the Atuatuci, the Nervii, and many others to arms, and marched against the legate Cicero, who at that time was likewise in command of a legion in winter quarters.

The size of the enemy force could be inferred from the following: when Roman captives told them that a rampart had to be built around the camp for the siege, and they had no agricultural tools, they cut up the earth with their swords and carried it away in their cloaks. In barely three hours they completed, over a circuit of fifteen miles, a rampart ten feet high and a ditch fifteen feet deep. In addition, they had built one hundred and twenty towers of astonishing height. And [Col. 0840B] when, for seven successive days and nights, the enemy’s wedges continued fighting, and a very strong wind suddenly arose, they hurled red-hot pots with slings, together with weapons set alight at the hearths and soon glowing with fire, into the camp. Once this had been done, the wind, rushing over the tops of the buildings, quickly fanned the scattered flames.

Yet even then the Romans did not yield, though they were overwhelmed on every side by wounds, hardships, fasting, sleeplessness, and fires. At last Caesar was informed that one legion had been destroyed and another was already almost exhausted. As Caesar approached with two legions, the enemy abandoned the siege and, gathering all their forces, rushed against him. Caesar deliberately shut himself up in a very small camp and ordered the cavalry to be sent ahead to pretend flight, so that, by contempt for him, the enemy might be lured toward the passage of the valley, which lay in the middle and seemed dangerous to him. When they approached, he ordered the gates to be additionally blocked.

Seeing this, the Gauls, as though they had already won, turned to build up the rampart on the outside. Caesar suddenly poured out his prepared army through all the gates and fought them fiercely. At last he saw one of his soldiers fighting too sluggishly, seized his shield, and rushed against the enemy. At this, the army was ashamed, and, having driven the Gauls into flight, slaughtered them in an immense massacre. For they are said to have numbered sixty thousand at that time, of whom only a few escaped through the impassable marshes.

Induciomarus, leader of the Treveri, possessing a large armed force, after learning of the agreement of all Gaul, decided to destroy Labienus and the legion he commanded, believing this would be easy to accomplish; afterward, joined by the Eburones and Nervii, he intended to march against Caesar and crush him. Labienus, using whatever stratagems he could, feigned fear and thus, by a sudden sally, overthrew Induciomarus, who had become careless and was roaming before the rampart with his attacking forces. By this victory Labienus checked the remaining efforts of the Gauls, and Caesar enjoyed somewhat greater quiet during the rest of the winter.

But, understanding that greater tasks of war still lay before him—especially since, after losing a very large part of his army and suffering serious injuries to others, he seemed not even adequate to sustain himself, much less to suppress the attack of the Gauls—he had Cn. Pompeius, the proconsul, enlist legions and send them to him as reinforcements. Thus, before winter had ended, three legions came to his camp.

Accordingly, before the enemy forces could unite, Caesar prepared, at the beginning of spring, to attack the frightened and crush them while scattered within their own territories. First, therefore, he ravaged the territory of the Nervii, but handed over the very abundant booty to the army. Then he invaded the Menapii, who seemed to him especially well fortified by their immense marshes and extremely dense forests, with three columns; after great slaughter had been spread everywhere, he accepted the remaining suppliants into surrender.

In the battle that followed, Labienus killed all the forces of the Treveri, whom he had skillfully provoked into war before they could join the approaching Germans, and immediately captured the city itself.

Caesar, wishing to avenge the deaths of the legates Sabinus and Cotta, learned that Ambiorix and the Eburones, the authors of the legion’s destruction, had fled into the forest of Arduenna. This forest is the largest in all Gaul: it extends from the banks of the Rhine and the borders of the Treveri as far as the Nervii and stretches for more than fifty miles in length. Caesar, calculating that it would be extremely dangerous for his men to divide themselves through the broad, obstructed forests and search for an enemy thoroughly familiar with the region, invited all Gaul by messengers to seek out and plunder, each according to his own preference, the booty hidden in the forest of Arduenna.

By this means, while Gauls were dying on both sides, he avenged the greatest injuries inflicted on the Romans without endangering a single Roman. Thus, secure in this very safe method of victory, he returned to Italy.

Accordingly, when Caesar had returned to Italy, Gaul again conspired to take up arms, and many peoples joined together. Their leader was Vercingetorix, at whose advice all the Gauls immediately set fire to their own cities of their own accord, Bituricum being the first city to be burned by its own people. From there they attacked Caesar, who had secretly hurried back to his army by forced marches through the province of Narbonensis.

Caesar had then enclosed the town called Cenapium in a siege. After it had long been attacked, it was finally captured and destroyed, following many Roman losses, on a rainy day, when the great mass of the enemy’s siege equipment and their sinews were weakened. Forty thousand people are said to have been there; of these, scarcely eighty escaped by flight and reached the nearest Gallic camp.

Furthermore, the Arverni and the neighboring peoples, having also won over the Aedui to their side, fought many battles against Caesar. When they, exhausted by fighting, had withdrawn into a certain town, the soldiers, greedy for booty, turned their attention to storming it, despite Caesar’s useless protest that the terrain was unfavorable. [Col. 0842A] Accordingly, while Caesar was hard pressed there by enemies bursting down from above, he was defeated and fled after losing a large part of his army.

While these events were taking place at Halesta, Vercingetorix, whom all had unanimously preferred as king, urged that from all Gaul everyone capable of bearing arms should be present for this war. For, he said, this was the one war through which they would obtain either perpetual freedom, or eternal slavery, or the death of all. Thus, in addition to the numberless force he had previously gathered, approximately eight thousand cavalry and two hundred and fifty thousand infantry were assembled.

Then the Romans and Gauls occupied two hills facing one another. After fighting there through many repeated sallies and with varying outcomes, the Romans at last prevailed through the valor of the foremost German cavalry, whom they had long since made their friends and now summoned to their aid.

On the following day, after gathering all who had escaped by flight, Vercingetorix said that he had honestly been the instigator of defending freedom and breaking the treaty. And now, whether they should all offer themselves to the Romans unto death, or whether he alone should be surrendered on behalf of all, he was ready in spirit. Accordingly, the Gauls took up the wish they had for some time concealed through shame as though it were the king’s proposal, and immediately, while begging pardon for themselves, surrendered him alone as the author of a great crime.

The Bellovaci were considered, in their own opinion, stronger than all the Gallic peoples. Under the leadership of Correus they renewed the war and joined to themselves, in the alliance of the war they had undertaken, the Ambiani, Aulerci, Caleti, Bellocasi, and Atrebates. They seized a certain place enclosed and obstructed on every side by marshes.

When battle was joined, they slaughtered a large force of the Remi that had come to the Romans’ aid. Then, after occupying a place they themselves had prepared as suitable for an ambush, and after the Romans, having discovered this, had come equipped and drawn up in battle order to the site of the ambush, battle was joined. The Romans enclosed the fleeing Gauls within the same fortifications of the terrain by which they had themselves been enclosed and killed them all. There Correus, refusing either flight or surrender, killed Romans who pressed upon him so that he might be taken alive, and forced them to kill him.

Accordingly, when Caesar believed that all Gaul had been pacified and would not dare to attempt any further disturbances, he sent the legions into winter quarters. He himself, however, devastated the territory of Ambiorix, who had provoked so many wars, with a dreadful slaughter of its inhabitants.

But C. Caninius the legate encountered a war among the Pictones, where a large enemy force surrounded his legion, obstructed by the terrain, and brought it to the utmost danger. The legate Fabius, after receiving Caninius’s letter, marched against the Pictones. There, informed by captives about the advantageous features of the region, he surprised the unsuspecting enemy and, inflicting great slaughter, carried off very abundant booty.

Then, after giving Caninius a signal of his arrival, Caninius suddenly rushed into the enemy’s camp and threw himself against them. Thus, while Fabius pressed them on one side and Caninius on the other, countless Gallic forces were slaughtered in a great and prolonged battle.

From there Fabius marched against the Carnutes. For he knew that Deonacus, the ancient leader and instigator of the entire rebellion, had escaped from this war and, if he joined the Aremorican peoples, would again stir up the greatest disturbances in Gaul. But he subdued them, still trembling from the novelty of the situation, with remarkable courage [Col. 0843A] and speed.

Meanwhile Draptes and Literius, seeing that Caninius and the legions had arrived in their territory, gathered forces from every side and occupied the town of Lugdunum. This town hung upon the highest summit of a mountain fortress; on two sides it was surrounded by steep slopes and a considerable river. Farther down, a broad spring made it secure, while its abundant supply of grain within made it safe; from afar it looked down upon the enemy’s futile movements.

Caninius did what Roman foresight alone could accomplish: he drew both leaders, together with most of their forces, out onto the plain and defeated them in a very great battle. For, when one of the leaders had been killed, the other fled with only a very few men, and no one returned to the town.

Yet Caesar was needed for its siege. Accordingly, informed by messengers, Caesar arrived. After examining everything, he saw that, if he attempted to take the town by force, his army would be destroyed as a spectacle and mockery for the enemy. There was only one means of defense: to cut the enemy off from water by whatever method he could.

But even this could not have been accomplished without Caesar. The spring from which they obtained drinking water issued from the middle of the mountain’s sloping side. Caesar ordered a covered approach to be brought up near the spring and a tower to be built.

Immediately a great sortie came from the town. Though they fought without danger to themselves, the Romans, despite resisting stubbornly and advancing in increasingly large numbers, were nevertheless slaughtered in considerable numbers. Accordingly, a ramp was constructed, along with a sixty-foot tower whose summit could reach the level of the spring, so that missiles could either be thrown from equal height or the danger of rocks hurled down from above could be avoided.

But when the townspeople saw that not only their livestock but also the weaker classes of human beings were being exhausted by thirst, they filled barrels with pitch, tallow, and shingles [Col. 0843C], set them alight, and sent them tumbling down the slope; they themselves, spread throughout the entire town, followed after them.

When Caesar saw that the burning siege engines made the battle dangerous and burdensome for his men, he ordered the cohorts to move rapidly around the town by a concealed route and suddenly raise a vast uproar on every side. At this, the terrified townspeople, while wishing to run back to defend the town, withdrew from attacking the tower and destroying the ramp.

Nevertheless, those who, under the protection of the ramp, were digging tunnels to cut the channels of the spring caused the watercourses they found hidden underground to be divided repeatedly, weakened, and consumed within themselves.

When the spring had dried up, the townspeople, seized by utter desperation, surrendered themselves. Caesar, however, cut off the hands of all who had borne arms, but left them alive, so that the punishment of the wicked might be made more evident even to posterity. For the proposed example of punishment is highly effective in restraining boldness: the very visible condition of the living wretch both reminds those who know of it and compels the ignorant to inquire.

Thus, when the Gauls had been exhausted and subdued, Caesar returned safely to Italy with the legions, fearing no further Gallic uprising behind him, since he knew for certain that he had left behind no one who either dared to stir up trouble or, if trouble were stirred, needed to be feared.

In the year 697 from the founding of the City, M. Licinius Crassus, colleague of Cn. Pompeius Magnus in his second consulship [Note: [Col. 0843D] A.: He was sent against the Parthians. When he fought near Carrhae against the omen and the auspices, he was defeated by Surena, commander of Orodes the king, and was finally killed together with his son, a most distinguished and outstanding young man. The remnants of the army were saved by Cassius the quaestor. With exceptional courage he restored the ruined situation with such valor that, on his return across the Euphrates, he defeated the Persians in repeated battles. From this point the civil war followed, accursed and tearful, [Col. 0844D] in which, besides the lamentable disasters that occurred in the battles, the fortune of the Roman people also changed.] having obtained by lot the province against the Parthians, a man of insatiable greed, heard of the wealth of the temple in Jerusalem, which Pompey had left untouched. He turned aside into Palestine, approached Jerusalem, entered the temple, and plundered its riches.

From there, advancing through Mesopotamia toward Parthia, wherever he passed he demanded assistance from allied cities and exacted payments. As soon as he crossed the Euphrates, he immediately encountered Bajeses, sent to meet him by Herod, king of the Parthians. Bajeses sharply rebuked him for crossing the Euphrates, impelled by greed, contrary to the treaty of Lucullus and Pompey. Therefore, he said, it would soon happen that, in place of Parthian gold, he would be loaded with Seric iron.

[Col. 0844B] When they had reached the vicinity of Carrhae contrary to the omens and auspices, the Parthians suddenly attacked, with Surena and Syllaces as commanders, and overwhelmed the Romans with arrows. Many senators fell there, as well as several former consuls and men of praetorian rank. Crassus’s son, too, a most excellent young man, was killed in the battle line. In addition, four cohorts, caught in the open fields with the legate Vargunteius, were destroyed.

Surena then set out to pursue Crassus rapidly with cavalry. He surrounded him, captured him when he was vainly seeking a conference, led him into the camp, and finally killed him by pouring gold into his mouth. A few, rescued by the protection of night, fled to Carrhae.

When the Roman disaster became known, many eastern provinces would have abandoned the alliance or loyalty of the Roman people, had not the quaestor Cassius, gathering a few soldiers from the rout, checked the swelling power of Syria with outstanding courage and moderation. He defeated and killed Antiochus and his immense forces in battle; he also drove from Syria the Parthians sent there by Herod, who had already entered Antioch, and killed their leader Hosagen.

Thus the condition of the Roman state is always subject to alternating change, like the character of the Ocean Sea, which differs every day: now it is raised by increasing tides for seven successive days, now during the following seven days it is withdrawn through natural loss and inward ebb.

In the year 700 from the founding of the City, an uncertain fire, whose origin is unknown, seized a very large part of the city. They say that the city had never before been seized and devastated by so great a conflagration. For tradition records that fourteen districts, together with the Jugarius district, were consumed.

From this point the civil war began, which had long been prepared by great disagreements and efforts. For Caesar, returning victorious from Gaul, demanded that a second consulship be decreed for him in his absence [Note: [Col. 0844D] A. after the word “demanded” adds, with Eutropius, “and, when it was without any doubt being offered to him, it was opposed,” etc.]. The consul Marcellus opposed him, as did [Note: [Col. 0844D] A. “Pompey, Cato”; he was ordered to return to the City after disbanding his armies.] Bibulus and Cato, with Pompey pressing the opposition.

Then the senate decreed that Caesar should not enter the City unless he had dismissed his army. And by the authority of Marcellus, the consul, [Col. 0845A] Cn. Pompeius was sent with military command to the legions stationed at Luceria [Note: [Col. 0845D] A. “He was sent”; because of this injustice, he came from Ariminum, where he had soldiers gathered, against his country with an army. “The consuls,” etc.]. Caesar withdrew to Ravenna.

M. Antonius and P. Cassius, tribunes of the plebs, intervening on Caesar’s behalf, were barred from the senate house and the forum by the consul Lentulus and went to Caesar, accompanied by Curio and Caelius.

After crossing the river Rubicon, Caesar soon reached Ariminum. He had only five cohorts at that time; with these, as Livy says, he attacked the whole world. He explained what needed to be done, lamented his injuries, and declared that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their country.

From there, through Antonius, he received from Lucretius the seven cohorts that were stationed at Sulmo. He brought over to his side the three legions that were stationed with Domitius at Corfinium.

The consuls, together with Cn. Pompeius, the entire senate, and all the nobility, fled from the City and crossed into Greece. At Dyrrhachium, in Epirus, Macedonia, and Achaea, the senate, under the leadership of Cn. Pompeius, prepared for war against Caesar.

Caesar entered the deserted city, made himself dictator [Note: [Col. 0845D] A., after “made himself dictator”: “Then he made for Spain; there he overcame Pompeius’ very powerful and brave armies, under the three commanders L. Afranius, M. Petreius, and M. Varro. Returning from there, he crossed into Greece, fought against Pompeius, was defeated and routed in the first battle. He escaped, etc.”], and, when the money from the treasury was refused him, broke down the doors, seized it, and brought out from it 4,135 pounds of gold and nearly [Note: [Col. 0846D] Perhaps read “ninety thousand.”] 900,000 pounds of silver. From there he departed for Ariminum to join the legions, then crossed the Alps and came to Massilia. Because he was not admitted, he left Trebonius there with three legions to besiege it. During that war, a soldier of the Twelfth Legion, fighting for Caesar against them in a naval engagement, seized an enemy ship with his right hand. When that hand was cut off, he grasped it with his left and did not release it until he was drowned.

[Col. 0845C] Caesar then hastened to Spain, which the Pompeian commanders L. Afranius, M. Petreius, and M. Varro held with their legions. There, after defeating Petreius and Afranius in many battles, he dismissed them once an agreement had been arranged. In Further Spain he received two legions from M. Varro. Likewise, his commanders acted similarly: Curio expelled Cato from Sicily; Valerius expelled Cotta from Sardinia; and Varus drove Tubero from Africa.

On his return Caesar reduced Massilia, which had been subdued by siege, granting only life and freedom and stripping it of everything else. But Dolabella, a supporter of Caesar’s faction, was defeated in Illyricum by Octavius and Libo and, deprived of his forces, fled to Antonius. Basilus and Sallustius, each commanding a legion over which he had authority, and likewise Antonius, as well as Hortensius, who was approaching from the lower sea with a fleet, all advanced together against Octavius and Libo and were defeated. When Antonius had surrendered himself to Octavius with fifteen cohorts, Libo led them all away to Pompeius.

Curio crossed from Sicily into Africa with an army. King Juba immediately engaged him with all his forces and massacred him. Octavius attempted to besiege Salonae but lost all the forces he had brought. Caelius defected from Caesar and joined the exile Milo. When the two of them attempted to attack Capua with the aid of slaves, they were killed.

Bibulus, at Corcyra, overcome by shame because the enemy had mocked the guard-line that he had extended across the sea and before the town, exhausted himself by hunger and sleeplessness. Appius Claudius Censorinus, who by Pompeius’ order was guarding Greece, wished to test the already discredited trustworthiness of the Pythian oracle. For, when the prophetess had been compelled by him to descend into the cavern, she is said to have replied, when consulted about the war:

“Nothing in this war concerns you, Roman; you shall possess Euboean Coela.”

They call the Euboean Gulf “Coela.” Thus Appius departed, perplexed and uncertain because of the ambiguous oracle.

Meanwhile, at Dyrrhachium, many kings of the East came to Gnaeus Pompeius with auxiliaries. When Caesar had arrived there, he unsuccessfully surrounded Gnaeus Pompeius with a siege, enclosing the land with a ditch fifteen miles long, while Pompeius had the sea open to him. Pompeius destroyed a certain fortification near the sea, which Marcellinus was defending, and killed Caesar’s garrisons that were stationed there.

Caesar attacked Torquatus and one legion in an attempt to storm them. When Pompeius learned of the danger to his allies, he drew all his forces there; and, as he moved the standards in that direction, opposing thunderbolts came against them. Bees also settled upon the standards. At this sight sudden grief overwhelmed the army: the sacrificial victims fled in the temples, statues turned around, some wept, and others sweated. So great was the clamor of weapons in the air that at Antioch they rushed to the walls as though enemies were arriving.

Meanwhile Caesar abandoned the siege and turned against Pompeius. Torquatus, bursting forth immediately, pursued him as he retreated. Thus Caesar’s soldiers, terrified by the danger on both sides, fled, although Caesar himself vainly tried to stop them. Caesar nevertheless escaped because night intervened and Pompeius was unwilling to pursue him. Caesar said that Pompeius did not know how to win and that, on that one day, he himself had merely been able to be defeated. [Note: [Col. 0846D] After “be defeated”: “Then in Thessaly, at Palaeopharsalus, they fought with immense forces drawn up on both sides. Pompeius’ line had 40,000 infantry, cavalry, etc.”]

In that battle 4,000 of Caesar’s soldiers, twenty-two centurions, and several Roman knights were killed. Sceva, Caesar’s bravest soldier, was also killed in the battle. When Pompeius’ soldiers urged him to surrender, he is said to have replied that he was tired. One man ran up as though to receive his weapons; Sceva struck him, and several others were brought down at the same time. He himself, however, received wounds in the head, shoulder, and thigh, and lost an eye. His shield was found to have been struck by 120 blows.

Then Caesar proceeded in silent formation through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompeius followed with his greatest forces, and battle was joined. Accordingly, the lines were drawn up on both sides. Pompeius placed eighty-eight cohorts in three ranks. His infantry numbered more than 40,000; there were 600 cavalry on the left wing and 500 on the right, besides many kings, senators, and very numerous Roman knights, together with a large force of light-armed troops. [Note: [Col. 0846D] A reads “500”; besides this, there were auxiliaries from the whole East, the entire nobility, countless senators, and men already victorious in great wars. Caesar had in his line not a full 30,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry. [Col. 0847D] Never before had Roman forces, neither greater nor commanded by better leaders, assembled in one body, destined to subdue the whole world if they had been led against barbarians. The battle was fought with immense exertion. And when for a long time, etc.]

Caesar likewise arranged eighty cohorts in three ranks. He had fewer than 40,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry. It was a sight to behold—and to lament—that the combined strength of the Romans had assembled on the fields of Pharsalus for mutual slaughter. If concord had directed those forces, no peoples and no kings could have withstood them.

At the first clash Pompeius’ cavalry was driven back and exposed his left flank.
