Then, after the fighting had long remained uncertain on both sides, while Pompeius, on one side, said, “Spare the citizens,” [Note: Pompeius was saying this while urging his men on.] but did not do so, Caesar, on the other hand, did what he was urging when he said, “Soldier, strike the face.” At last the entire army of Pompeius fled, and his camp [Note: “was then plundered” follows in the source: “He himself …”] was plundered.

In that battle 15,000 Pompeian soldiers and thirty-three centurions were killed. Such was the outcome of the battle at Palaeopharsalus.

Pompeius, fleeing, found a merchant ship at the mouth of the Peneius River and crossed to Asia. From there, driven onward through Cyprus, he made for Alexandria, intending to receive assistance from the king of Egypt, to whom the senate had assigned a guardian because of his youth. But the king followed fortune rather than friendship: he killed Pompeius and sent his head and ring to Caesar.

When Caesar saw it, he is said even to have shed tears as he looked upon the head of so great a man and of his once son-in-law, and ordered it to be burned after being drenched with perfumes. [Note: “and of his own” follows in the source. Soon afterward Caesar came to Alexandria; Ptolemy himself also laid a trap for him. Caesar, pressed by the attack of the enemies who were beginning hostilities, …]

Pompeius’ wife and sons fled, while the rest of the Pompeian fleet was plundered and everyone aboard it was cruelly massacred. Pompeius of Bithynia was also killed there. Lentulus, a former consul, was killed at Pelusium.

Caesar, after settling affairs in Thessaly, came to Alexandria. When he had withdrawn into the royal palace, the guardians kept him from receiving money, cunningly stripping their own temples so that they might make the royal treasuries appear empty and stir up the people’s hatred against Caesar. Moreover, Achillas, the royal commander, once stained with Pompeius’ blood, was also plotting Caesar’s death. Ordered to disband the army under his command—20,000 armed men—he not only disregarded the order but also drew up a battle line.

In the battle itself, the royal fleet was ordered to be hauled ashore and burned. When the flames spread also to part of the city, they consumed 40,000 books stored by chance in nearby buildings: truly a singular monument to the zeal and care of our ancestors, who had gathered so many and such great works of illustrious minds.

Hence, although even today there exist in the temples—some of which we ourselves have seen—bookcases whose emptiness, after they were plundered by our people in our own time, commemorates that event, and although this is indeed true, it is more honorably believed that other books had been sought out to rival the earlier care devoted to learning than that there was at that time any other library which is thought to have contained more than 400,000 books and therefore to have escaped.

Afterward Caesar captured the island where the lighthouse is. Achillas came there with Gabinian soldiers, and a great battle was joined. A large number of Caesar’s soldiers fell there; all the murderers of Pompeius were also killed. Caesar himself, pressed by the force of the attacking enemy, climbed into a small boat. When it was soon weighed down and sunk by the mass of those following him, he swam 200 paces to a ship, holding one hand above the water because it held his papers.

Soon afterward, defeated in a naval engagement, he nevertheless, with great good fortune, either sank or captured the royal fleet. At the request of the Alexandrians he restored their king to them and advised them to strive to test Roman friendship rather than Roman arms. Yet, as soon as he was free, the king immediately made war on Caesar; but he himself was destroyed at once, together with his entire army. For it is reported that 20,000 men were killed in that war, 12,000 surrendered with [Note: The source has “60.”] seventy long ships, and 500 of the victors are said to have fallen.

The young king himself, picked up in a small boat as he tried to flee, was drowned and killed when many others leapt into it. His body, washed ashore, was recognized by the evidence of its golden breastplate. [Note: [Col. 0848D] A, after “was”: “Having taken possession of Alexandria, Caesar assigned the kingdom to Cleopatra, etc.”] Caesar sent the breastplate ahead to Alexandria, compelled all the Alexandrians to surrender and despair, and gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra, the sister of Ptolemy, with whom he had maintained a sexual relationship. She afterward entered the city with royal retinue. [Note: [Col. 0848D] A: “entered. Returning from there, Caesar [dealt with] Pharnaces, etc.”]

From there Caesar traversed Syria and defeated in battle Pharnaces, son of Mithridates the Great, who had assisted Pompeius at Thessaly and was rebelling in Pontus and occupying many provinces of the Roman people; afterward he forced him to his death.

Returning from there to Rome, he made himself dictator for the third time and consul together with M. Aemilius Lepidus, who had been master of the horse for the dictator’s office a year earlier. [Note: [Col. 0848D] A: “who had previously been his master of the horse for the dictator, etc.”]

From there he went to Africa, where the immense body of Roman nobility had renewed the war together with Juba, king of Mauretania. The Roman commanders were P. Cornelius Scipio, of the ancient family of Scipio Africanus—and he had also been the father-in-law of Pompeius the Great—M. Petreius, Varro, M. Porcius Cato, and L. Cornelius Faustus, son of the dictator Sulla.

When war was joined against them, after many engagements and the slaughter of a very large number of men, Caesar was victorious. [Note: The source adds: “Caesar: Cato, Scipio, and Petreius killed themselves on the way; Faustus Sulla, formerly the son of the dictator, and son-in-law of Pompeius, was killed by Caesar. Afterward …”] The camps of both sides were plundered, and sixty elephants were captured.

Cato killed himself at Utica. Juba offered his throat to the executioner after paying him. Petreius pierced himself with the same sword. Scipio, attempting to flee to Spain in a ship but driven back to Africa by the wind, cut his own throat on that ship. T. Torquatus was killed on the same vessel.

Caesar ordered Faustus Sulla, once the son of the dictator Sulla and son-in-law of Pompeius, together with his grandsons, his daughter Pompeia, Afranius, and Petreius’ son, to be killed.

After a year Caesar entered Rome with four triumphs. [Note: The source adds: “He made himself consul for the fourth time and immediately set out for Spain, where the sons of Pompeius, Gnaeus and Sextus, had prepared a massive war. There were many battles. The last was near the town of Munda, in which Caesar was so nearly defeated that, when his men were fleeing, he wished to …”]

He was appointed dictator for the fourth time and consul. After arranging and restoring the state of the Republic, he immediately set out for Spain against the Pompeii, the sons of Pompeius. On the seventeenth day after he had departed from Rome, he reached Saguntum. He then fought many wars of varying outcome against the two Pompeii, Labienus, and Accius Varus.

The final war was fought near the river Munda. There the battle was waged with such forces and such slaughter occurred that Caesar himself, when he saw his line being forced back and cut down, although his veterans did not blush even to yield, wished to kill himself, lest, after so much military glory, he should fall into the power of young men, at the age of fifty-six.

Finally, after restoring his troops, the Pompeian army suddenly turned and fled. [Note: [Col. 0850C] A: “He defeated his own men, and the elder son of Sextus Pompeius was killed; the younger fled. From there Caesar, etc.”] Indeed, that war was fought on the very day on which Pompeius the father had fled from Rome to wage war.

For four years this civil war thundered without interruption throughout the entire world. T. Labienus and Accius Varus were killed in battle. Sextus Pompeius fled with 100 cavalrymen. His brother Gnaeus, having quickly gathered a considerable force of Lusitanians, engaged Caeson​​ius, was defeated, and, while fleeing, was killed. The town of Munda was captured only with difficulty, amid immense slaughter, while Caesar attacked it.

From there Caesar returned to Rome, after settling the civil wars throughout the world, and began to act too arrogantly, contrary to the custom of Roman liberty. Since he bestowed honors according to his own will, although previously they had been conferred by the people, did not rise for the senate when it came to him, and performed other royal and almost tyrannical acts, a conspiracy was formed against him by 260 or more senators and Roman knights.

The chief conspirators were the two Brutuses, descendants of that Brutus who had first been consul at Rome and expelled the kings; C. Cassius; and Servilius Casca.

Accordingly, when Caesar had come one day among the other senators to the senate-house, he was dispatched with twenty-three senatorial daggers and died pierced by wounds. [Note: The source adds: “The man was stabbed through …”] After this deed the senators withdrew to the Capitol with drawn daggers. For a long time they deliberated whether the Capitol ought to be burned together with the authors of the murder.

The people, provoked by grief, carried off his body and burned it in the Forum with fragments of the tribunal platforms and benches.

That same night Calpurnia, his wife, saw him in a dream lying in her lap, pierced with wounds. She begged Caesar not to leave for the senate that morning. But he, often heedless of omens, disregarded the dream, though the outcome confirmed it.

Accordingly, a few days before Caesar was killed, after an ox had been sacrificed in the senate-house according to custom, no heart was found among the entrails. When the haruspex Spurinna declared that this concerned a danger to his life, Caesar, recalling his own firmness, said: “Are you surprised that an ox has no heart?” But soon afterward his life came to an end.

The same Spurinna had told Caesar a few days earlier that he should beware the Ides of March. On that day, when he saw Spurinna, Caesar said: “The Ides of March have come.” He replied: “But they have not yet passed.”

On that same day Caesar was stabbed—the man who had distinguished himself in wars more than any other human being. Under his command 1,192,000 enemies were killed. For how many he slaughtered in the civil wars, he did not wish to record.

He fought with standards joined in battle fifty times, surpassing M. Marcellus alone, who had fought in the same manner thirty-nine times. Moreover, no one wrote more quickly, no one read more quickly, and he dictated even four letters at once.

He was of such great kindness that those whom he had subdued by arms he conquered even more by clemency.

At the same time, three suns appeared at Rome; gradually they came together into a single circle. Among the other portents that occurred throughout the world, an ox in the suburbs of Rome spoke to a man plowing, saying that it was being driven forward in vain: not grain, but men, would shortly be lacking. [Note: [Col. 0850C] A: “shortly.”]

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849D] In approximately the seven hundredth and ninth year from the founding of the City, after Julius Caesar had been killed, civil wars broke out again. For the Senate favored Caesar’s assassins [Note: [Col. 0849D] A.: “It favored them. But Antony, consul, etc.” H. and Eutropius, together with the Ambrosian manuscript.] and was attempting to crush Antony, consul and leader of Caesar’s faction, through civil war. Thus, while the state was in turmoil amid the many crimes Antony was committing [Note: [Col. 0849D] A.: “With the Republic in confusion, while Antony was committing many crimes, by the Senate, etc.”], he had shut Decimus Brutus up under siege at Mutina; for this reason he was declared an enemy by the Senate.

Two consuls, Hirtius and Pansa, were sent to assault Antony and rescue Brutus [Note: [Col. 0849D] A.: “Two consuls to pursue him.”] [Col. 0850D], and with them went Octavius, a young man seventeen years old, born to the senator Octavius, descended on his mother’s side from Aeneas through the Julian family, Caesar’s nephew and the son of his sister Accia. Caesar had left him his heir by will and had ordered him to bear his name. This is the man who was later called Augustus and who gained control of affairs [Note: [Col. 0850D] A.: “He gained supreme power. Therefore the three commanders who marched against Antony defeated him at Mutina, yet it happened that both consuls died as victors. Thus three armies obeyed Caesar Augustus. ‘Antony, having been driven away,’ etc.”]. [Note: [Col. 0850D] This material, up to “Antony was driven away,” is absent from the Hersfeld manuscript.]

To explain briefly the accumulation of disasters, he fought five civil wars: the Mutinensian, Philippian, Perusian, Sicilian, and Actian. Of these, two—the first and the last—were against Marcus Antony; the second against Brutus and Cassius; the third against Lucius Antony; and the fourth against Sextus Pompey, son of Gnaeus Pompey.

Pansa, arriving first, was caught in an ambush; amid the slaughter of his men he himself was severely wounded by a javelin and died several days later from the same wound. Hirtius, bringing aid to his colleague, destroyed Antony’s great forces in a vast slaughter. Caesar meanwhile guarded the camp. In the second battle against Antony there was great slaughter on both sides. For Hirtius, the consul, was then killed there, while Caesar won the victory. Decimus Brutus, who had taken part in the conspiracy that killed Julius Caesar, poured out prayers of repentance before him.

Antony, driven away after losing his army [Col. 0851B], fled to Lepidus, who had formerly been Caesar’s master of the cavalry and at that time possessed large forces of soldiers; he was received by him [Note: [Col. 0851D] A.: “He was taken in. Soon, with Lepidus’ assistance, Caesar made peace with Antony, and as though he intended to avenge …”].

Dolabella killed Trebonius, one of Caesar’s assassins, at Smyrna. The armies of both slain consuls obeyed Caesar. Later Decimus Brutus was captured and killed in Gaul by the Sequani. Basilus, a Roman knight and one of Caesar’s assassins, was killed by the hands of his own slaves.

Meanwhile, with Lepidus giving sufficient assistance, Caesar restored Antony to favor and was reconciled with him through the favor of his daughter Dina, whom he took in marriage; and, as though he intended to avenge the death of his father, by whom he had been adopted through a will, he set out for Rome with an army [Note: [Col. 0851D] A.: “He set out and began to act so that a consulship would be granted to him in his twentieth year. He proscribed the Senate and began, with Antony and Lepidus, to hold the Republic by force of arms. Through them the orator Cicero and many other nobles were also killed. Meanwhile, etc.”].

When a rumor arose in the City that a proscription was impending, Gaius Toranius, a former praetor, fearing no such thing, was killed by an attack of soldiers in his own house [Col. 0851C], and many others were slaughtered. Through these men the orator Cicero and many other nobles were also killed; and Caesar, together with Antony and Lepidus, began to hold the Republic by armed force.

Therefore, so that unrestrained slaughter might not spread more widely and wildly, the names of one hundred and thirty-two senators were posted on a tablet: first at Lepidus’ command and under his name, then under Antony’s, and third under Caesar’s. There Antony proscribed Tullius Cicero, his enemy; there Lepidus cast his own brother Paulus into the same group of the proscribed. Later thirty Roman knights were added to the number of the proscribed. Many prolonged and varied massacres were carried out, and the houses of the proscribed were destroyed after everything had been plundered.

In Syria, Dolabella fought many wars against Cassius, the assassin of Julius Caesar; when defeated by him, he killed himself.

Meanwhile Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Caesar, having assembled large armies [Note: [Col. 0851D] A.: “They stirred up a great war against Caesar. For many armies had occupied Macedonia and the East. They set out, etc.”] throughout Macedonia and the East, met at Athens and laid waste all Greece. Cassius attacked the Rhodians by land and sea and forced them to surrender, leaving them nothing except their lives [Col. 0852A].

Accordingly Caesar Octavianus Augustus and Marcus Antony marched against them. Lepidus had remained behind to defend Italy. At Philippi, a city of Macedonia, they fought them with great preparations for war [Note: [Col. 0851D] A.: “They fought. In the first battle Antony was defeated, and Caesar was defeated; nevertheless Cassius, the leader of the nobility, perished. In the second they killed Brutus and the countless nobility that had fought with him. Thus the Republic was divided between them, so that Augustus, etc.”], pursued them, and forced them to die, although it was then most evident that the battle had been won not through the valor of Antony’s party but through Caesar’s good fortune.

For Caesar was ill at the time. He had decided to remain in the camp at Pharsalus in order to obtain rest, while at Philippi, with daylight approaching, the Roman forces were about to engage one another in civil war. But at the urging and entreaties of his physician Antonius, who declared that Minerva had warned him in a dream to lead Caesar out of the camp that day for the sake of his health, Caesar, with difficulty, left the midst of the troops in a litter.

But while he was intent upon the outcome of the victory [Col. 0852B], Brutus, one of Caesar’s assassins, captured his camp. Yet the Caesarian soldiers in turn captured the camps of Brutus and Cassius. Driven to despair by this, Brutus and Cassius inflicted premature death upon themselves before the war had ended. For when the assassins were summoned, Cassius offered his head and Brutus his side.

During that war, which was fought at Philippi, Lucius Cassius saw Julius Caesar, his uncle, dressed in purple, rushing upon him at full speed on horseback; and he soon cried out with a groan: “Let us yield, since killing has not profited us.”

Meanwhile the Republic was divided between Augustus and Antony in such a way that Augustus held Spain, Gaul, and Italy, while Antony held Asia, Pontus, and the East.

But in Italy Lucius Antony, consul, stirred up civil war; he was the brother of the man who had fought with Caesar against Brutus and Cassius [Col. 0852C]. He was defeated and captured at Perusia, a city of Etruria, and was killed [Note: [Col. 0852D] A.: “Nor was he killed. Meanwhile, Sextus Pompey, son of Gnaeus Pompey, stirred up a great war in Sicily. With these matters, etc.”].

At Rome, meanwhile, Antony’s wife Fulvia, Caesar’s mother-in-law, was behaving like a woman exercising dominion. In this transformation of consular and royal eminence, it is uncertain whether she should be called the final stage of declining power or the first of power beginning; certainly she was insolent even toward those through whom she was being enabled to become insolent. For she attacked Caesar, who had returned to Brundisium, with insults, factions, and plots. Driven back by him, she withdrew to Antony in Greece.

Sextus Pompey, son of Gnaeus Pompey, after learning that he had been included among the proscribed, turned to brigandage and ravaged the entire coast of Italy with slaughter and plunder. He also stirred up a great war in Sicily with those who remained from the party of Brutus and Cassius and who had flocked to him [Note: [Col. 0852D] A.: “They flocked to him. War was waged by Caesar Augustus Octavianus and Marcus Antony against Sextus Pompey; at last peace was arranged.”]. By obstructing the grain supply, he afflicted Rome with famine.

Then he was defeated in war by Caesar Octavianus and Marcus Antony. Soon the Triumvirs—if I may not call them tyrants—namely Lepidus, Caesar, and Antony, made peace with him. But immediately afterward, when Pompey took fugitive slaves into his forces contrary to the agreement, he was treated as an enemy.

Menas, Pompey’s freedman, defected to Caesar with a fleet of sixty ships, and by Caesar’s order himself took command of that fleet. At once, together with Statilius Taurus, he fought a naval battle against Menecrates, Pompey’s commander. Then Caesar himself concluded a most bloody war against the same Pompeians.

But immediately afterward he lost almost the entire victorious fleet in a shipwreck near Scyllaceum. At the same time Marcus Agrippa conducted operations successfully in Aquitania. Lucius Ventidius Bassus defeated the Persians and Parthians, who were invading Syria, in three major wars, and killed their king Pacorus, son of King Orodes, in battle—on the very day on which King Orodes had once killed Crassus through the commanders Surena and Sulaces [Note: [Col. 0853D] A.: “Ventidius Bassus defeated the Persians as they invaded Syria in three battles. Pacorus, the king’s [son], etc.”] [Note: [Col. 0853D] A.: “Through the commander Surena, Crassus, etc.”].

He was the first to celebrate at Rome a properly deserved triumph over the Parthians [Col. 0853B] [Note: [Col. 0853D] A.: “He celebrated it. Meanwhile Pompey broke the peace, was defeated in a naval battle, and, fleeing into Asia, was killed. Antony, who held Asia and the East, repudiated Octavia, the sister of Caesar Augustus, and married Cleopatra, queen of Egypt. He also fought against the Persians, defeating them in his first battles. Yet while returning he suffered from hunger and pestilence; and when the Parthians pressed upon him as he fled, he withdrew as though defeated. At this time a great war, etc.”].

Meanwhile Antony, after capturing scarcely one fortress, made peace with Antiochus, so that he might appear to have completed so great an undertaking. He appointed Ventidius governor of Syria and ordered him to make war upon Antigonus, who at that time had conquered the Jews, captured Jerusalem, and given the kingdom to Herod. Ventidius immediately defeated him and received his surrender.

Menas the freedman, with sixty ships, returned to Pompey, who received him mercifully; and Menas burned Caesar’s fleet, although Caesar had recently lost another fleet in a second shipwreck. Later Menas was surrounded by Agrippa in a naval battle and defected to Caesar with six triremes. But Caesar, regarding him as a deserter for the third time, left him inactive, granting him only his life.

Then Agrippa fought and won a naval battle between Mylae and the island of Lipara against Demochares and Pompey [Col. 0853C]. There he either sank or captured thirty ships, and Pompey, with the rest of his ships damaged, fled to Messana.

Meanwhile Caesar had crossed to Tauromenium, and Pompey overwhelmed him with a sudden attack. Therefore, after many of his ships had been sunk and a great multitude of his soldiers lost, Caesar fled to Italy. Without delay he returned to Sicily, where he encountered Lepidus, arriving from Africa and claiming the supreme position for himself through terror, threats, and arrogance.

A few days later, Agrippa, by Caesar’s order, engaged Pompey in a most savage naval battle and defeated him, while Caesar watched from the shore with his battle line drawn up. For he either sank or captured one hundred and sixty-three ships. Pompey escaped with difficulty in only seventeen ships.

Lepidus, swollen with the arrogance of his twenty legions, had plundered Messana after allowing it to be given over to the soldiers. When Caesar himself came to him, Lepidus twice spurned him and instead ordered that he be attacked with weapons. Caesar avoided them by protecting himself with a cloak wrapped around his left arm.

Then, mounting his horse, he returned to his men; and, advancing with his army formed against Lepidus, he compelled most of Lepidus’ legions to cross over to his own side, with only a few men being killed.

At last Lepidus understood where his vanity was leading [Col. 0854A]. He laid aside his military cloak, put on a dark garment, and, becoming a suppliant before Caesar, obtained his life and property, though he was condemned to perpetual exile.

Taurus, Caesar’s prefect, received into allegiance almost the whole of Sicily, which had been ravaged and crushed by the sword. At that time forty-four legions were under the sole command of Caesar.

The soldiers, rendered more ferocious by their numbers, had stirred up disturbances in order to receive lands. But Caesar, great in spirit, discharged twenty thousand soldiers, restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters, and crucified six thousand whose masters could not be found.

The Senate decreed that he should enter the City in an ovation and possess tribunician power in perpetuity.

In those days, across the Tiber, a fountain of oil flowed from the ground out of an inn for travelers and ran throughout the entire day in a most abundant stream.

Antony, meanwhile, having set out against the Parthians and crossed the Araxes [Col. 0854B], was surrounded by every kind of misfortune and at last barely returned to Antioch with a few men. For he had attempted many battles, and whenever he escaped from them he had always been defeated by the large numbers of cavalry and archers. In addition, he was hindered in uncertain and unknown regions and was driven by extreme hunger to consume unholy food. Many of the soldiers surrendered themselves to the enemy.

From there he crossed into Greece and ordered Pompey, who had been defeated by Caesar and was restoring his army and war, to come to him with a few men.

Pompey, fleeing from the Antonian commanders Titus and Furnius, was repeatedly defeated by land and sea, captured, and killed.

Caesar subdued and conquered Illyricum, Pannonia, and part of Italy through war. Antony captured Artabazes, king of Armenia, by treachery and deceit; bound with a silver chain, he forced him to reveal the royal treasures [Col. 0854C]. After storming the stronghold where Artabazes had said they were hidden, Antony carried away a great quantity of gold and silver.

Elated by this money, he ordered war to be declared against Caesar and commanded that a divorce be announced to Octavia, Caesar’s sister and his own wife; he also ordered Cleopatra to meet him from Alexandria.

He himself set out for Actium, where he had built a fleet. When he found that nearly a third of the sailors had been consumed by hunger, he was unmoved and said: “Let the oarsmen only be safe; for there will be no lack of rowers as long as Greece has men.”

He himself fought against the Persians and Parthians and defeated them in his first battles. Yet while returning he suffered from hunger and pestilence, and when the Parthians pressed upon him as he fled, he withdrew as though defeated.

He also stirred up a great civil war, compelled by his wife Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, who in womanly desire wished to rule even in the City [Col. 0854D] [Note: [Col. 0854D] A.: “To rule; he was defeated by Augustus in a naval battle, a famous and illustrious one at Actium, a place in Epirus. From there he fled to Egypt; when his affairs were desperate and everyone was defecting to Augustus, he killed himself. Cleopatra, etc.”].

Therefore Caesar set out from Brundisium for Epirus with two hundred and thirty ships equipped with rams.

Agrippa, sent ahead by Caesar, captured many cargo ships, heavily laden with grain and weapons, which were coming from Egypt, Syria, and Asia to support Antony. After traversing the Gulf of the Peloponnese, he stormed Methone, a city fortified by a very strong Antonian garrison. From there he captured Corcyra [Col. 0855A], pursued the fugitives in a naval battle, routed them, and, after carrying out many bloody operations, came to Caesar.

Antony, moved by the shortage and hunger of his soldiers, began to hasten the war. He suddenly drew up his forces and advanced to Caesar’s camp, but was defeated.

On the third day after the battle Antony moved his camp to Actium, prepared to decide the matter in a naval battle. Caesar had two hundred and thirty ships equipped with rams and thirty triremes without rams, equal in speed, together with eight legions stationed aboard the fleet, excluding five praetorian cohorts.

Antony’s fleet consisted of one hundred and seventy ships. Though inferior in number, it surpassed Caesar’s fleet in size. For its ships rose ten feet above the sea.

This was a famous and great war at Actium, a place in Epirus. From the fifth hour until the seventh, with victory uncertain, there was extremely heavy slaughter on both sides [Col. 0855B]. The rest of the day, together with the following night, turned toward Caesar’s victory.

Queen Cleopatra fled first with sixty of her fastest ships. Antony too, having removed the insignia from his flagship, followed his fleeing wife.

At daybreak Caesar completed the victory. It is reported that twelve thousand of the defeated fell; six thousand were wounded, of whom one thousand died while receiving treatment.

Antony and Cleopatra also decided to send their children, together with part of the royal treasury, ahead to the Red Sea. They themselves, having stationed garrisons around the two horns of Egypt, Pelusium and Paraetonium, prepared a fleet and forces for renewed war.

[Col. 0856A] Caesar, proclaimed imperator for the sixth time and consul for the fourth time with Marcus Licinius Crassus, came to Brundisium. There he organized the defenses of the world by distributing the legions.

From there he set out for Syria and soon approached Pelusium, where he was voluntarily received by the Antonian garrisons.

Meanwhile Cornelius Gallus, sent ahead by Caesar, received into allegiance the four legions that Antony had stationed at Cyrene as a garrison. From there he defeated and captured Paraetonium, the first city of Egypt on the Libyan side, and immediately defeated Antony himself at Pharos.

Antony undertook a cavalry battle against Caesar; he was miserably defeated in that encounter as well and fled.

On the Kalends of Sextilis, at first light, Antony went down to the harbor to arrange his fleet. Suddenly all the ships defected to Caesar.

When he had been stripped of his single remaining support, Antony, terrified, withdrew with a few men into the palace [Col. 0856B].

Then, as Caesar approached and the city was thrown into confusion, Antony stabbed himself with a sword. Still half alive, he was carried to Cleopatra, into the monument in which she had shut herself up, determined to die.

[Note: [Col. 0855B] H., together with Eutropius, agrees word for word from the beginning up to Eutropius’ words “he killed himself.” At that point H. varies as follows [Col. 0855C]: “He killed himself; Cleopatra, adorned with various ornaments, came to Caesar, hoping, by her appearance, to entice him to desire her, as she had enticed the others. But he restrained himself on behalf of chastity and was not at all moved toward her desire; he soon ordered her to be guarded. She escaped from custody and, placing herself beside her Antony in the precious tomb, admitted an asp to herself, and the rest,” in which he again agrees with Eutropius up to the words “had held with Antony and Lepidus,” where he varies as follows: “had held with Lepidus. Finally, when he had returned victorious from the East and entered the City in a triple triumph, Augustus was then first hailed as such because he had enlarged the Republic; from that time he obtained supreme power over affairs, which the Greeks call monarchy. In those days, across the Tiber, a fountain of oil poured forth from the ground at an inn for travelers and flowed throughout the entire day in a most abundant stream, signifying the grace of Christ among the nations. At that time also a circle resembling a heavenly rainbow appeared around the sun. Therefore, when in the forty-second year Caesar had established the firmest and truest peace, the Lord Christ was born in Bethlehem, and this peace served his coming. At no time before Caesar did the Roman state flourish more. For, excepting, etc.” In these matters H. again agrees with Eutropius, except that H. reads “the Vindelici and the Talassi in the Alps, all the maritime cities of Pontus. Among these, the most renowned were the Bosporus and Cappadocia of Pontus.” In the other matters, I say, H. agrees with Eutropius up to the words “ran beside his chariot,” where H. varies as follows: “ran beside it. Finally, he so detested disturbances, wars, and quarrels that he never declared war against any people except for just reasons. He used to say that it was the mark of a boastful and frivolous character, in the ardor of triumphing and for the sake of a laurel crown—that is, unproductive leaves—to cast the safety of citizens into danger through the uncertain outcomes of battles; and that nothing was less suited to a good commander than rashness; that whatever was done advantageously was accomplished quickly enough; and that arms should never be taken up without hope of a greater benefit, lest a victory sought at slight profit resemble fishing with a golden hook, whose loss, if it breaks off and is lost, cannot be repaid by any gain from the catch [Col. 0856B]. He also strongly criticized an invention of his uncle, who, by calling soldiers ‘fellow-soldiers’ in a new and flattering manner, had softened the authority of the ruler while trying to make himself more beloved. Finally, he treated citizens with the greatest clemency; toward his friends he proved loyal. The chief among them were Maecenas, for his silence, and Agrippa, for his endurance of labor and his modesty. He also loved the poets Virgil and Flaccus. Though slow to accept friendships, he was extremely constant in preserving them. He devoted himself so greatly to liberal studies, especially eloquence, that no day passed—even when on campaign—without his reading, writing, or declaiming. He enlarged and adorned Rome with many buildings, boasting in this saying: ‘I found Rome built of brick; I leave it clothed in marble.’ He was mild, gracious, of civic disposition, and handsome in his whole body; but especially in his eyes, whose gaze, flashing like the brightest stars, readily accepted that those who looked intently at him turned away as from the rays of the sun. When a certain soldier turned his eyes away from his face and Augustus asked him why he did so, he replied: ‘Because I cannot bear the lightning of your eyes’ [Col. 0856D]. Yet so great a man was not without vices. For he was somewhat impatient, mildly quick-tempered, secretly envious, and openly criminal. Moreover, he was more desirous of domination than can be estimated and an ardent gambler. Although he abstained greatly from food and wine and to some extent from sleep, he nevertheless served lust to the point of public disgrace; for he was accustomed to recline among twelve catamites and an equal number of girls. After putting away his wife Scribonia, seized by love for another man’s wife, he took Livia to himself, as though her husband were consenting. Livia already had sons, Tiberius and Drusus. And although he was devoted to luxury, he was nevertheless a most severe avenger of that same vice, like those who are harsh in punishing vices to which they themselves are greatly indulgent. Having entered his seventy-seventh year, he died at Nola from illness, etc. folio 52, column 2, C.”]

Cleopatra, adorned with various ornaments, came to Caesar, hoping that, as she had done with others, she might entice him to desire her by her appearance. But he restrained himself within himself on behalf of chastity and was not at all moved toward her desire; he soon ordered her to be guarded [Note: [Col. 0856D] A.: “On behalf of chastity, for his own sake.”].

[Note: [Col. 0856D] A.: “who, having escaped that custody.”] But after she realized that she was being kept for the triumph, she escaped from custody and, placing herself beside her Antony in her precious tomb, admitted an asp to her left arm and was killed by its poison [Col. 0857A] [Note: [Col. 0857D] A.: “She died. Egypt was added to the Roman Empire by Octavian Augustus, and Gnaeus Cornelius Gallus was placed over it. Egypt thus first had a Roman governor. With wars throughout the world completed, Octavian Augustus returned to Rome in the twelfth year after he had been consul and thereafter held the Republic alone for fourteen years. Before that he had held it for twelve years with Antony and Lepidus. Finally, etc., as Canisius reads in II, no. 17, up to the words ‘At no time,’ after which the Ambrosian manuscript has: ‘Rome flourished more than before Caesar. For, excepting the civil wars in which he was victorious, he added to the Roman Empire Egypt, Cantabria, Dalmatia, often conquered before but then thoroughly subdued, Pannonia, Aquitania, Illyricum, Rhaetia, the Vindelici and Thalassi in the Alps, all the maritime cities of Pontus’ [Col. 0858D]. Among these were the most renowned Bosporus and Cappadocia of Pontus. He conquered the Dacians in battle, slaughtered great forces of Germans, and drove them beyond the river Elbe, which in barbarian territory lies far beyond the Rhine. He conducted this war, however, through his stepson Drusus, just as he conducted the Pannonian war through his other stepson Tiberius. In that war he transferred four hundred thousand captives from Germany and settled them along the bank of the Rhine in Gaul. He recovered Armenia from the Parthians; the Persians surrendered hostages to him, something no one before him had achieved. The Scythians and Indians, to whom the Roman name had previously been unknown, sent him gifts and ambassadors. Galatia, etc.”].

Caesar took possession as victor of Alexandria, by far the richest and largest of all cities, together with the whole region of Egypt, and Gnaeus Cornelius Gallus was appointed over it. Rome’s wealth increased so greatly through Egypt that, because of the abundance of money, the prices of estates and other saleable goods were set at twice what they had been until that time.

To provide the City with an abundant grain supply, Caesar opened channels that had been blocked with mud through the neglect of age, using the labor of soldiers; and twenty million measures of grain were brought annually from Egypt into the City.

Meanwhile, by Caesar’s order, Antony’s elder son was killed, as were Publius Canidius, a most hostile enemy of Caesar but also disloyal to Antony; Cassius Parmensis, the final victim in vengeance for the violation of Caesar, his adoptive father; and Quintus Ovinius, chiefly notorious because, as a Roman senator, he had not blushed to supervise the queen’s most obscene woolworking and weaving establishment.

Afterward Caesar came with infantry forces to Syria, then withdrew into Asia for the winter, and later traveled through Greece to Brundisium.

# AUGUSTUS.

In the year 725 from the founding of the City, when the emperor Caesar Augustus was consul for the fifth time and L. Apuleius was consul, Caesar, returning victorious from the East, entered the City in a triple triumph on 6 January. The Sun and Moon, Cleopatra’s children, were led before his chariot. Then, for the first time, he himself closed the gates of Janus, all the civil wars having been put to rest and brought to an end.

On that day he was first hailed as Augustus because he had increased the state: a name previously inviolate for everyone, and until then unassumed by others, legitimately used only by the lords of the world. It signified the summit of imperial power, and from that same day supreme control of affairs and authority began to reside in one man—and remained there—in what the Greeks call μοναρχίαν, “monarchy.” Nor at any earlier time, before Caesar Augustus, did the Roman state flourish more greatly.

For when, after his uncle Gaius Caesar had been killed, he was returning from Apollonia and entering the City, around the third hour, a circle resembling a heavenly rainbow suddenly surrounded the disk of the sun in a clear and cloudless sky—as though it were showing that one man, supreme and most powerful in this world, and alone the brightest in the universe, was about to come, in whose time one would arise who alone would both make and govern that very sun and the whole world.

Then, on a second occasion, after he had received the legions from Pompey and Lepidus in Sicily, restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters, and distributed forty-four legions under his sole command for the protection of the world, he entered the City in an ovation and decreed that all debts owed to the Roman people should be remitted, with even the written records of them erased.

In the year 726 from the founding of the City, when the emperor Caesar Augustus was consul for the sixth time and M. Agrippa for the second time, Caesar, realizing that two hundred years of activity in Spain had accomplished little if he allowed the Cantabrians and Asturians—two of the strongest peoples of Spain—to live under their own laws, opened the gates of Janus and himself set out with an army for the Spains.

The Cantabrians and Asturians are part of the province of Gallaecia, where the extended range of the Pyrenees descends northward not far from the nearer ocean. They were prepared not only to defend their own liberty but also dared to seize that of their neighbors; by continual raids they ravaged the Vaccaei, Turmodigi, and Aurigones.

Accordingly, Caesar established a camp near Segisama, embracing almost the whole of Cantabria in three columns. After the army had long been exhausted without success and repeatedly brought into danger, he finally ordered a fleet to be brought against the unsuspecting enemy by way of the Aquitanian Gulf and the Ocean, and the troops to be disembarked. Only then did the Cantabrians, engaging in a great battle beneath the walls of Attica and being defeated, flee to Mount Vinnius, naturally an extremely secure position, where they were nearly destroyed to the last man by the hunger of the siege.

Next, the town of Tracilium, which had resisted with great force and for a long time, was finally captured and destroyed. In addition, Antistius and Firmius, the legates, subdued the more distant parts of Gallaecia, planted with mountains and forests and bounded by the Ocean, through great and arduous wars.

They also surrounded Mount Medullius, which towers above the river Minio and on which a large multitude of people had taken refuge, with a siege after enclosing it with a ditch fifteen thousand paces in length. Thus, when that naturally savage and fierce people realized that it was neither capable of enduring a siege nor equal to undertaking a war, they rushed to voluntary death through fear of slavery. Almost all of them killed themselves by fire, sword, or poison.

The Asturians, however, having established their camp by the river Astura, would have overwhelmed the Romans with great planning and force had they not been anticipated and forestalled. They attempted suddenly to crush the three legates, divided with their legions among three camps, by attacking them with three equally large columns, but their plan was exposed by the treachery of their own people.

Carusius later met them in battle and defeated them, though not without considerable loss among the Roman soldiers. Some of them, escaping from the battle, fled to Lancia. When the soldiers prepared to attack the surrounded city with fire, their commander Carusius both obtained from his own men a suspension of the burning and compelled the barbarians to consent to surrender. For he was earnestly striving to leave the city intact and unharmed as a witness to his victory.

Caesar paid this honor to the Cantabrian victory: he ordered the gates of war to be closed at that time as well. Thus Janus was closed for the second time by Caesar, and for the fourth time since the founding of the City.

After this, Claudius Drusus, Caesar’s stepson, having received Gaul and Raetia as his provinces, subdued by arms the greatest and strongest peoples of Germany. For at that time, as though they were hastening toward an appointed day of peace, all the peoples were stirred up in successive waves toward an encounter with war or the conclusion of a treaty—either to accept the conditions of peace if defeated or to enjoy quiet liberty if victorious.

The Norici, Illyrians, Pannonians, Dalmatians, Maesi, Thracians, Dacians, Sarmatians, and many other great peoples of Germany were, under different commanders, either defeated, checked, or shut off by the barrier of the greatest rivers, the Rhine and the Danube.

In Germany Drusus first subdued the Usipetes, then the Tencteri, and then the Chatti. He also drove them back beyond the river Elbe, where they are far within barbarian territory, well beyond the Rhine. He nearly annihilated the Marcomanni as well.

Afterward he defeated in a single war, though it was harsh even for his own men, the strongest nations, those to whom nature had given strength and custom experience in using it: the Cherusci, Suebi, and Sicambri alike. Their courage and savagery can be judged from the fact that their women too, whenever they were enclosed among their wagons by a sudden Roman attack, when their weapons had run out—or when they lacked anything else that fury could use as a weapon—would throw their little sons, crushed against the ground, into the faces of the enemy. In each killing of a son they were twice guilty of parricide.

At that same time, in Africa, Cossus, Caesar’s commander, restrained the Massylians and the more widely wandering Gaetulians within their borders by skill [Note: [Col. 0859D] Perhaps the reading should be *arctis*, “confined” or “restricted.”], and compelled them through fear to keep away from the Roman frontiers.

Meanwhile, at Tarraco in Hither Spain, envoys of the Indians and Scythians, having crossed the whole world, finally found Caesar there, beyond which they could no longer continue their search. They thus transferred to Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great. Just as a delegation of Spaniards and Gauls had approached Alexander in the middle of the East, near Babylon, to seek peace, so here, at the farthest limits of the West, the Eastern man, the Indian, and the Northern Scythian humbly addressed Caesar, bringing gifts characteristic of their peoples.

After the Cantabrian war had lasted five years, and all Spain, with a kind of sigh of exhaustion, had settled down and been restored to everlasting peace, Caesar returned to Rome. During those same days he conducted many wars in person and many others through commanders and legates. Among the rest, Piso was sent against the Vindelici. After subduing them, he came victorious to Caesar at Lugdunum.

Tiberius, Caesar’s stepson, wiped out the Pannonians, who were swelling with a renewed revolt, in a most bloody slaughter. Immediately afterward he took up war against the Germans and brought back forty thousand captives in victory. This was truly a great and most terrifying war, conducted with fifteen legions over three years; as Suetonius attests, scarcely any greater war had occurred after the Punic War.

At the same time, however, Quintilius Varus, propraetor, was utterly destroyed beyond the Rhine by rebellious Germans, together with his tribunes and quaestors, while he was treating his subjects with extraordinary arrogance and greed. Caesar Augustus bore this disaster of the state so heavily that, disfigured by his clothing, his hair, and the other signs of mourning, and often striking his head against a wall in the force of his grief, he cried out: “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”

Agrippa defeated the Bosporans and, having recovered in war the Roman standards which they had once taken under Mithridates, compelled them to surrender. He recovered Armenia from the Parthians.

The Parthians, as though they were being marked out before the eyes of all because the whole world had either been conquered or pacified and all the strength of the Roman Empire was now destined to be turned against them alone—for they were tormented by the memory of their former duty to avenge the slaughter of Crassus—voluntarily sent back to Caesar the standards they had taken from Crassus. After handing over royal hostages, they earned a firm treaty through an extremely loyal petition.

Galatia too was made a province under him, although previously it had been a kingdom, and M. Lollius was the first to administer it as propraetor.

He was held in such affection even among barbarians that kings who were friends of the Roman people founded cities in his honor and named them Caesareas: one in Mauretania, founded by King Juba, and another in Palestine, which is now a very famous city.

Many kings came from their kingdoms to pay him homage, and, dressed in Roman clothing—wearing the toga, that is—they ran beside his carriage or horse.

Finally, he so detested crowds, wars, and quarrels that, except for just causes, he never made war upon any people. He used to say that it was the mark of a boastful and frivolous character to endanger the security of citizens through the passion for triumphing and for a laurel crown—that is, fruitless leaves—by exposing it to the uncertain outcomes of battles. Nothing was less fitting for a good commander than rashness; anything that could be done advantageously was done quickly enough; and arms should not be taken up unless there were hope of a greater benefit, lest victory resemble that of fishermen using a golden hook, whose loss through its breaking away cannot be balanced by any profit from the catch.

He also strongly criticized an invention of his uncle, who, while calling soldiers “fellow soldiers” in a new and flattering manner and trying to make himself more beloved, had softened the authority of the ruler. [Note: [Col. 0859D] These words are not found in A., H., or Eutropius Merula; instead, after *emolliverat*, they have “Finally,” etc. [Col. 0860D]]

Once established in power, he personally exercised the tribunician authority. Finally, he treated his citizens with the greatest clemency and proved faithful to his friends. The chief among them were Maecenas, distinguished by silence, and Agrippa, by endurance of labor and moderation.

He also loved the poets Virgil and Flaccus. He was slow to enter friendships but extremely constant in preserving them. He devoted himself so intensely to liberal studies, especially eloquence, that no day passed—even when he was on campaign—without his reading, writing, or declaiming.

He issued some new laws and revised others in his own name. He enlarged and adorned Rome with many buildings, boasting in the saying: “I found a city of brick and leave behind a city of marble.”

He was gentle, agreeable, civil in character, and witty; handsome in his entire body, but especially in his eyes [Note: [Col. 0860D] Ambrosius has “large”]. His gaze flashed like that of the brightest stars, and he gladly accepted it when those who looked at him yielded, as though before the rays of the sun.

When a certain soldier turned his eyes away from his gaze and was asked why he did so, he replied: “Because I cannot endure the thunderbolt of your eyes.”

Yet so great a man could not be without faults [Note: [Col. 0861D] A. has “he was not without vices”]. He was somewhat impatient, mildly irascible, secretly envious, and openly factional. Moreover, he was more desirous of ruling than can be estimated, and devoted to gambling.

Although he consumed much wine and food, while abstaining to some extent from sleep, he nevertheless served lust to the point of bringing disgrace upon common reputation. For he was accustomed to sleep with twelve catamites and an equal number of girls.

After dismissing his wife Scribonia, he became obsessed with love for another man’s wife and joined Livia to himself, as though her husband had granted her to him. Livia already had two sons, Tiberius and Drusus.

Although he was enslaved to luxury, he was nevertheless a very strict avenger of that same vice, like those people who are harsh in punishing vices to which they themselves are especially indulgent [Note: [Col. 0861D] A., with H., reads *acres sunt* after this: “Having entered his seventy-seventh year, he died of illness at Nola, although …”].

For the poet Ovid, also called Naso, because he had written three books of *The Art of Love*, he condemned to irrevocable exile.

Because he had a cheerful or agreeable disposition, he delighted in every kind of spectacle, especially wild animals of unfamiliar appearance and in enormous numbers.

Although in gaining supreme power he had been regarded as an oppressor of liberty, in exercising it he loved the citizens so much that once, when he saw only three days’ supply of grain in the storehouses, he had decided to die by poison if fleets did not meanwhile arrive from the provinces. When they did arrive, his safety was attributed to the good fortune of the state.

Thus, in the year 752 from the founding of the City, Caesar Augustus, after peace had been established among all peoples from East to West, from North to South, and throughout the entire circuit of the Ocean, closed the gates of Janus himself for the third time. Thereafter they remained shut for nearly twelve years in the most tranquil peace, until even rust marked them.

They opened only in Augustus’s old age, when an uprising of the Athenians and a movement among the Dacians disturbed the peace.

With the gates of Janus closed, he strove to nourish and enlarge by peace the state he had acquired by war. He established many laws through which the human race might practice, in free reverence, the discipline of civilized conduct. He avoided the title “lord” as though it were an insult.

For when, while he was watching the games, the following line was spoken in a mime—“O fair and good lord!”—and everyone, as though it had been said about him, applauded enthusiastically, he immediately restrained the disgraceful flattery with his hand and expression. On the following day he rebuked it in a very severe edict and thereafter did not allow himself to be called “lord,” not even by his children or grandchildren, whether seriously or jokingly.

In his time the distinguished wise men at Rome were Virgil, Flaccus, Sallust, Livy, Hortensius, Terence, Horace, Athenodorus of Tarsus, and Sotion of Alexandria.

Augustus also discovered, by counting the inhabitants of the City of Rome according to their districts, that the number of men living there was 131,037.

Therefore, at that time—that is, in the forty-second year of his reign—when, by God’s ordering, Caesar established the firmest and truest peace, Christ was born, and peace served his coming. At his birth, in the hearing of human beings, the rejoicing angels sang:

> Glory to God in the highest,  
> and on earth peace to people of good will.

In the year 760 from the founding of the City, fire consumed fourteen of its districts; it is uncertain where the blaze began. Nor, as Livy says, was it ever devastated by a greater fire, so much so that several years later Caesar Augustus distributed a large amount of money from the public treasury for the restoration of what had then been burned.

After the Redeemer of the world, the Lord Jesus Christ, came to earth and was registered as a Roman citizen in Caesar’s census, while, as I have said, the gates of war had remained closed for twelve years in the most blessed tranquility of peace, Caesar Augustus sent his grandson Gaius to organize the provinces of Egypt and Syria.

As he passed from Egypt through the territory of Palestine, Gaius refused to worship at Jerusalem in the temple of God, which was then holy and renowned, as Suetonius Tranquillus reports. When Augustus learned of this through him, he used faulty judgment and wisely praised Gaius for having acted correctly.

Thus, in the forty-eighth year of Caesar’s reign, such a dreadful famine followed upon the Romans that Caesar ordered the families of gladiators, all foreigners, and also the largest groups of slaves to be driven out of the City, except for physicians and teachers. Thus, while the ruler sinned against the holy sanctuary of God and the people were corrected through famine, the character of the punishment displayed the magnitude of the offense.

Then, to speak in the words of Cornelius Tacitus, once Janus had been opened in the old age of Augustus, while new peoples at the ends of the earth were repeatedly sought for reasons of advantage and sometimes at a cost, it remained open through the reign of Vespasian.

Meanwhile, Caesar Augustus, seventy-eight years old, entered Nola and died of illness, although others write that he was killed through Livia’s treachery, since she feared that, if Agrippa—his stepson, whom she had banished to an island out of stepmotherly hatred—were brought back, he would exact punishment from her after gaining supreme power [Note: [Col. 0861D] A.: “Lest, because she had discovered that Agrippa, the son of Scribonia, her stepson, …”].

He was buried at Rome in the Campus Martius.

Accordingly, the Senate decreed that he, whether dead or murdered, should be honored with many new distinctions. For, besides having previously called him “Father of his Country,” it consecrated temples to him both at Rome and throughout the most famous cities. Everyone commonly exclaimed: “Would that such a man had either never been born or had never died—one who was not undeservedly thought, in large part, like a god.”

For scarcely anyone was more fortunate than he in war or more moderate in peace. During the forty-four years in which he alone exercised supreme authority, he lived in a most civil manner, extremely generous toward everyone and most faithful to his friends, whom he had raised to such great honors that he nearly made them equal to his own rank.

He ruled for fifty-six years: twelve with Antony and Lepidus, and forty-four alone [Note: [Col. 0862D] II. has: “He held power for forty-six years, twelve with Antony and thirty-four alone”; but an anonymous corrector’s hand in the manuscript has made fifty-six out of forty-six.]. Certainly he would never have drawn the power of the state to himself, nor have retained possession of it for so long, unless he had abounded in great natural gifts and cultivated abilities.

He left the state in the greatest happiness to his successor Tiberius [Note: [Col. 0862D] A., after *reliquit*, adds: “immediately ruled it, he who was his stepson,” etc.].

# TIBERIUS

In the year 767 from the founding of the City, Tiberius Caesar, the second son of Livia, assumed the imperial power. He had been Caesar’s stepson, then his son-in-law, and finally his adopted son.

Because he was called Claudius Tiberius Nero, the wits cleverly named him “Caldius Biberius Mero” because of his love of wine [Note: [Col. 0863D] A. has *joculatoribus*, “jesters,” instead of *jocularibus*, “witty men”].

Before assuming power, under Augustus, he had been sufficiently prudent in warfare and sufficiently fortunate that the government of the state could not unjustly be entrusted to him.

He possessed considerable literary knowledge and was more distinguished in expression, but his character was extremely bad: savage, greedy, treacherous. He pretended to want what he did not want, appearing hostile to those for whom he desired to provide, and benevolent toward those whom he hated.

He was better at sudden replies or decisions than at those that had been sought or prepared [Note: [Col. 0863D] A. has “considered and deliberated,” and omits the remainder; it then continues: “Nowhere,” etc.].

Finally, when the principate had been offered to him by the senators—a result he had achieved through cunning—he pretended to refuse it, while harshly probing what each individual said or thought. This brought ruin upon all the better men. For, believing that he was sincerely trying, through a long speech, to avoid the burden of imperial office, they expressed their opinions according to his wishes and fell into the ultimate disasters.

He himself never fought, nor did he conduct any serious wars even through legates, except that, whenever rumors of disturbances among peoples were discovered in certain places, they were quickly suppressed. [Note: [Col. 0863D] Hersfeld has: “He fought; he waged wars through his own legates. Having summoned certain kings to himself by blandishments, he never sent them back,” etc.; in these passages it agrees with Eutropius down to the words “he died in Campania.” In the fifteenth year of this reign the Lord Jesus Christ began his preaching. Also in the eighteenth year of the same reign Jesus Christ, Son of God, offering himself to death for us, was crucified. Gaius Caesar, surnamed Caligula, succeeded Tiberius: the most wicked descendant of Drusus, Augustus’s stepson, and of Tiberius himself, and one who even purged Tiberius’s disgraces. “War against the Germans,” etc.; in these passages it agrees with Eutropius down to the words “he died at the age of thirty-two,” where H. has: “he died at the age of thirty-one, in the fourteenth year of his reign, and in him all Augustus’s family was extinguished.” Finally, to all his crimes he added this also: that he slaughtered the holy apostles of God, Peter and Paul. Servius Galba succeeded him, etc.; in these passages H. again agrees with Eutropius down to the end of Book VII. Ambrosius has in some places divergent readings from Hersfeld and Eutropius Merula; we shall note them in their places. Here, however, after *remisit* (“sent them back”), it agrees with both down to the words “which is now called Caesarea,” etc.].

In the fourth year of his reign, Germanicus, son of Drusus and father of Caligula, celebrated a triumph over the Germans against whom he had been sent by the aged Augustus.

He summoned certain kings to himself by flattering promises and never sent them back, among them Archelaus of Cappadocia. He reduced Archelaus’s kingdom to the form of a province and ordered its chief city to be called by his own name; it is now called Caesarea, though previously it was called Mazaca [Note: [Col. 0864D] A. has “Mazaga.”].

He suppressed the brigandage of the Gaetulians. He craftily trapped Maroboduus, king of the Suebi.

For most of his reign he governed the state with great and serious moderation. Thus, when governors in certain provinces advised increasing the taxes, he wrote that it was the duty of a good shepherd to shear his sheep, not flay them.

After the Lord Jesus Christ had suffered, risen from the dead, and sent his disciples to preach, Pontius Pilate, governor of the province of Palestine, reported to the emperor Tiberius and to the Senate concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, and the miracles that had openly been performed either by Christ himself or by his disciples in his name. He also reported that, as the faith of very many people was eagerly growing, Christ was believed to be God.

Tiberius, with the support of great favor, proposed to the Senate that Christ should be regarded as a god. The Senate, moved by indignation because the matter had not first been referred to it according to custom, so that it might itself decide first whether worship should be accepted, refused to consecrate Christ. By an edict it decreed that Christians should be expelled from the City, especially because Sejanus, Tiberius’s prefect, obstinately opposed the adoption of this religion.

Nevertheless, Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death by an edict.

He also proscribed and forced to death very many senators. He had selected twenty patrician men as an advisory council, and scarcely left two of them unharmed; he killed the rest for various reasons.

He killed his prefect Sejanus when Sejanus was plotting revolution. He destroyed his sons Drusus and Germanicus, who were his adopted sons, by unmistakable signs of poisoning. He killed the sons of his son Germanicus.

In the twenty-third year of his reign, and in the seventy-eighth year and fourth month of his life, while he punished the innocent and the guilty alike—his own people and foreigners, as we have said—with savage fury, military discipline having collapsed, Armenia was ravaged by the Parthians, Moesia by the Dacians, Pannonia by the Sarmatians, and Gaul by neighboring peoples.

He himself was killed in Campania, to the immense joy of everyone, through the plots of Caligula [Note: [Col. 0864D] A. has: “He died in Campania,” and omits the rest; it continues: “In the fifteenth year of his reign John began his preaching. In the eighteenth year of the same reign Jesus Christ, the Son of God, offered himself to death for us and was crucified. Gaius Caesar, surnamed Caligula, succeeded Tiberius. Drusus …”].

In the twelfth year of this reign a new and incredible disaster occurred at the city of Fidenae. The seating structure of the amphitheater collapsed while the people were watching a gladiatorial performance, killing more than twenty thousand people.

Then, in the seventeenth year of the same reign, when the Lord Jesus Christ voluntarily gave himself over to suffering but was impiously seized by the Jews and fastened to the cross, a tremendous earthquake occurred throughout the world. Rocks were split in the mountains, and many parts of the greatest cities collapsed after being shaken more violently than usual.

On that same day, from the sixth hour of the day until the ninth hour, the sun was completely darkened, and a dreadful night suddenly covered the earth. As it is said:

> And the impious ages feared everlasting night.

It is clear that neither the moon obscured the sun’s light nor clouds intervened, since it is reported that, on that day, the fourteenth-day moon, positioned across the whole region of the sky, had been far removed from the sun’s sight, and that the stars shone throughout the entire sky during the daylight hours—or rather, during that dreadful night.

This is attested not only by the faith of the holy Gospels but also by several Greek books, although these events are reported as having occurred in the nineteenth year of Tiberius.

Among others, Phlegon also writes about them. He numbers the Olympiads concerning these events and, in the thirteenth book, asserts the following in the same words:

> In the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad there occurred the greatest eclipse of the sun, and night came upon the earth at the sixth hour of the day, so that even the stars appeared in the sky. A great earthquake also occurred in Bithynia and overturned a large part of the city of Nicaea.

# C. CALIGULA

In the year 790 from the founding of the City, Gaius, the third ruler after Augustus, surnamed Caligula, began to reign. He was the son of Germanicus, grandson of Drusus, Augustus’s stepson, and nephew of Tiberius himself [Note: [Col. 0865C] A. has “son”]. Because he had been born in the army, he received the nickname Caligula, “little military boot.”

He was the most wicked man of all who had preceded him [Note: [Col. 0865C] A. adds: “the most wicked, and one who …”], and one who even cleansed away Tiberius’s disgrace [Note: [Col. 0865C] A. has *purgaret*, “would cleanse,” instead of *purgaverit*, “cleansed.” The note continues: “War against …”].

Before becoming ruler he was dear and welcome to everyone. In power, however, he was such that it was rightly said that there had never been a more cruel master.

To state briefly the magnitude of his cruelty, he is said to have exclaimed: “Would that the Roman people had a single neck!” He often complained about the conditions of his time, because they were marked by no public calamities.

He himself undertook war against the Germans, and, entering Suebi territory, did nothing of consequence.

He committed incest with his three sisters; with one of them he even fathered a daughter.

He walked about in the clothing of his gods, declaring himself Jupiter because of the incest, and, in the Bacchic chorus, Liber [Bacchus].

I do not know whether it was appropriate to hand this down to memory, except perhaps because it is useful to know everything about rulers, so that wicked people may at least avoid such conduct through fear of their reputation.

In the palace he subjected noble married women to public lust.

He was the first to put on a diadem and order himself to be called “lord.”

Across the three-mile stretch lying within the Bay of Puteoli by the mole, he laid ships in two rows, solidified a roadway by piling up sand until it resembled land, and, conspicuous on a decorated horse, wearing an oak crown as though celebrating a triumph and dressed in a golden military cloak, rode along it in a two-horse chariot.

During those same days the Jews, who were already being harassed everywhere by deserved disasters because of Christ’s passion, were defeated and driven out of Alexandria after a revolt had arisen there. To present their complaints, they had sent to Caesar as envoy, for the second time, a certain Philo, a man exceptionally learned in every respect.

When he came to Rome, he spoke with the apostle Peter and is said to have enjoyed his friendship.

But Caligula, hostile to all people and especially to the Jews, rejected Philo’s embassy. He ordered all the sacred buildings of the Jews, and above all that ancient sanctuary at Jerusalem, to be profaned with pagan sacrifices and filled with statues and images. He also ordered that he himself be worshiped as a god.

Pilate, the governor who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, after encountering and provoking many disturbances at Jerusalem, was so constricted by the anxieties inflicted by Gaius that, stabbing himself with his own hand, he sought an end to his troubles through the speed of death.

Accordingly, when Gaius raged against everyone with enormous greed, lust, and cruelty, he was killed by soldiers in the palace in the thirty-eighth year of his life, in the third year of his reign, in the tenth month and on the eighth day [Note: [Col. 0866C] A.: “Twenty-nine years old, in the fourth year of his reign, in the tenth month and on the seventh day. After these words Book VII continues up to ‘was buried ignobly.’”].

After he had been killed, two little books were found in his private rooms. One had the title *The Dagger*, the other *The Sword*. Both contained the names and identifying marks of highly distinguished men of both orders, namely the senatorial and equestrian orders, who had been designated for death.

A huge chest of various poisons was also found. When these were thrown into the sea at the command of Caesar Claudius, the waters are said to have been polluted, not without great destruction of fish, whose dead bodies the tide cast everywhere along the neighboring shores.

# BOOK EIGHT

## CLAUDIUS

[Col. 0865]

[Note: [Col. 0865D] A.: After him came Claudius, Caligula’s uncle, the son of Drusus, who has a monument at Mainz, and whose nephew was Caligula. Here Modia the empress, etc. Eutropius: “Claudius, Caligula’s uncle, the son of Drusus, who has a monument at Mainz together with his son, and whose nephew Caligula also was, his brother.” Hersfeld, together with Ambrose, where it is noted that neither Eutropius nor the manuscripts begin a new book here, but continue this material in Book VII.]

In the year 795 from the founding of the City, Claudius, the fourth ruler after Augustus, attained the kingdom. He was Caligula’s uncle, the son of Drusus, the stepson of Caesar Augustus, of whom Caligula was the grandson; Drusus has a monument at Mainz. When the Senate had decreed that the family of the Caesars should be exterminated, Claudius was found hiding in a disgraceful hiding place. Because he was foolish and seemed to the inexperienced to be very gentle, the soldiers made him emperor.

He shamefully obeyed his belly, wine, and lust. Foolish and almost dull-witted, cowardly and fearful, he was subject to the commands of his freedmen and his wife. During his reign Scribonianus Camillus was proclaimed emperor in Dalmatia but was immediately killed. The Moors were expelled from the provinces by Caesar, and a division of the Musulanians was massacred. The Aqua Claudia was brought into Rome.

At the beginning of his reign, therefore, Peter, the apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, came to Rome and taught the saving faith to all believers by his faithful word, confirming it most powerfully by miracles; from that time Christians began to exist in Rome. Rome perceived the benefit conferred upon its faith. For at that same time a great miracle of God’s present grace occurred.

Furius Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, was plotting civil war and had persuaded many very brave legions to change their oath. Accordingly, a day was appointed for all to assemble from every direction around the new emperor. Yet neither could the standards be adorned, nor could the insignia be removed or moved in any way. The army, shaken by faith in so great and unprecedented a miracle and converted to repentance, immediately killed Scribonianus, who had been abandoned on the fifth day, and kept its former military oath.

Claudius therefore ruled moderately, doing many things calmly and temperately, but some cruelly and rashly. He killed thirty-five senators and three hundred Roman knights for the slightest reasons. He made war on the Britons, whom no Roman had attacked after Gaius Caesar, and, having conquered them through the distinguished and noble men Gnaeus Sentius and Aulus Plautius, celebrated a notable triumph. He also added to Roman rule certain islands lying in the ocean beyond Britain, which are called the Orkneys, and gave his son the name Britannicus.

He was so courteous toward certain friends that he himself escorted the nobleman Plautius, who had performed many distinguished deeds in the British expedition, when he was celebrating his triumph; and as Plautius climbed the Capitol, Claudius walked on his left.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] A. reads “walked behind.”]

His wife Messalina at first openly used adulterers as though she had a legal right to them; because of this many men, abstaining through fear, were destroyed. Then, inflamed more violently, she planned to have the noblest married women and virgins brought to her in the manner of prostitutes, with the men compelled to attend. If anyone recoiled from such acts, she attacked him and his entire household by fabricating a charge, so that she seemed rather to rule her husband than to be married to an emperor.

Thus her freedmen gained supreme power and polluted everything with adultery, exile, murder, and proscriptions. Among them he appointed Felix over the legions of Judaea. After the British triumph he gave the eunuch Posidonius, who ranked among the bravest soldiers, distinguished arms as a gift, as though he had shared in the victory. He made Polybius walk midway among the consuls.

Narcissus, his secretary, preceded all these men, behaving as master of the master himself and openly elevated by praetorian honors. He was so wealthy that, when he complained of the poverty of the treasury, a famously witty saying was circulated: he would have money in abundance if he were admitted into partnership by two freedmen.

While conducting a census of the citizens of Rome, he found 6,000,941.

In the fifth year of Claudius’s reign, an island emerged from the depths of the Aegean Sea between Thera and Therasia, extending for a distance of thirty stadia. In his seventh year, under the procurator of Judaea, Cumanus, such a great riot arose in Jerusalem during the Days of Unleavened Bread that, when the people were crushed together at the exit of the gates, thirty thousand Jews are said to have been slaughtered and suffocated in the crush.

At that time also the altar “To the Unknown God” was erected among the Athenians.

Nevertheless, in his eighth year there was such a great famine at Rome that the emperor, seized by the people in the middle of the Forum, was shamefully assailed with insults and pieces of bread. He escaped the fury of the aroused populace only with difficulty, fleeing into the palace through a private entrance.

In Claudius’s time a phoenix was seen in Egypt. This bird is said to fly from Arabia to the mentioned place in the six hundred and fifty-fourth year. Apollonius of Tyana, born in Italy, a Pythagorean philosopher, was then influential at Rome, so much so that Philostratus and others describe him as having been of keener intellect even than Pythagoras himself.

Claudius married Agrippina, the daughter of his brother Germanicus. Seeking to secure the empire for her son, she first attacked her stepson Britannicus in the palace by various forms of treachery and then killed her own husband with poison.

He lived sixty-four years and ruled for fourteen years. After his death he was deified and called “the Divine.”

[Note: [Col. 0867D] A. adds “after being called”: “Nero succeeded him, very much like his uncle Caligula, who …”]

His funeral, as once in the case of Tarquinius Priscus, was long concealed, while guards were bribed by feminine cunning and pretended that he was ill. His stepson Nero assumed the authority of the empire.

## NERO

In the year 808 from the founding of the City, Domitius Nero, born to Domitius Ahenobarbus, the fifth ruler after Augustus, attained the principate. He was tolerable for five years; hence some writers report that Trajan used to say that all emperors were far inferior to Nero’s five-year period. Afterward he became in every respect very much like his uncle Caligula, who both disfigured and diminished the Roman Empire.

He was guilty of unheard-of luxury and extravagance. Following Caligula’s example, he bathed in hot and cold ointments and fished with golden nets, which he hauled in with purple cords.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] A. reads “scarlet-colored.”]

[Note: [Col. 0868D] A.: “He killed a countless part of the Senate and deprived them of their property,” etc.]

He deprived very many senators of their property without any charge existing. On a single day he wiped out the entire census of all those he killed, even applying torture. Driven wild by an unbridled rage for cruelty, he killed a large part of the Senate and nearly destroyed the equestrian order. He was an enemy to all good men.

He was also so tormented by lust that he is reported to have refrained neither from his mother nor from his sister, nor from any respect for blood relationship. He took a man as his wife; then, dressed by a man in the appearance of a bride, he was received as a wife, with the Senate publicly summoned, the dowry declared, and everyone attending the celebration according to the custom.

At last he prostituted himself with such disgrace that he toured nearly all the theaters of Italy and Greece, taking upon himself the shame of various costumes, dancing and singing on stage in the dress of a lyre-player or tragic actor.

He committed many parricides, killing his brother, his mother, and his sister.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] A. reads “in place of his sister, his wife.”]

He burned the city of Rome for six days and seven nights so that, gazing upon the spectacle, he might see what Troy had once looked like when captured and burning. He himself watched from the summit of the lofty Maecenatian tower and, delighted by the beauty of the flames, sang the Iliad in tragic costume.
