The granaries built of squared stone and those great apartment blocks of the ancients, which the spreading fire could not reach, were shaken and set alight by great machines once prepared for foreign wars.

His greed was so extreme that after the fire he allowed no one to approach the remains of his property. He himself carried away everything that had survived the flames in any way. He ordered the Senate to contribute to him annually 10 million sesterces for expenses.

He married Octavia and Sabina, surnamed Poppaea, after their husbands had been murdered.

He accomplished absolutely nothing in military affairs.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] A. reads “he dared nothing.”]

He almost lost Britain. For under him two of its most distinguished towns were captured and destroyed. The Parthians seized Armenia and sent Roman legions under the yoke.

Nevertheless, two provinces were created under him: Pontus Polemoniacus, when King Polemon ceded it, and the Cottian Alps, after King Cottius had died.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] A. reads “Cottius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0869D] A. adds “after he had died”: “For this reason he became hateful to the city of Rome, was abandoned by everyone at once, and was declared an enemy by the Senate. When he was sought for punishment—a punishment of this kind: that he should be led naked …”]

Then Galba, praetor of Spain, and Gaius Julius seized the imperial power.

When Nero learned that Galba was approaching and that the Senate had decreed that he should be led naked through the public streets, with a fork inserted around his neck, beaten with rods until death, and then hurled from a cliff, he was abandoned on every side and fled from the palace. At midnight he left the city, accompanied by Phaon, Epaphroditus, Neophytus, and the eunuch Sporus, whom he had once castrated and attempted to fashion into a woman.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] A. adds: “and in the suburban estate of his freedman, which is …”]

At his freedman’s suburban estate, situated between the Salarian and Nomentan roads at the fourth milestone from the City, he pierced himself with a sword. The impure eunuch mentioned above assisted his trembling hand.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] A. adds “after the fourth milestone”: “he killed himself.”]

Since no one could be found to strike him, he had first cried out: “So then, I have neither a friend nor an enemy? I have lived disgracefully; let me die still more shamefully.”

He built at Rome the baths that were formerly called Neronian and are now called Alexandrian. He died in the thirty-first year of his life and had ruled for twenty-four years. With him the entire family of Augustus came to an end.

In his time the poets Lucan, Juvenal, and Persius flourished at Rome, as did Seneca the tragedian, Musonius, and the philosophers Plutarch.

The Persians had loved Nero so greatly that they sent ambassadors asking permission to build a monument to him.

Yet all the provinces and the whole of Rome rejoiced so greatly at his death that the plebs, wearing the caps of manumission as though freed from a cruel master, celebrated a triumph.

Finally, to all his acts of depravity he added this: he was the first at Rome to inflict punishments and death upon Christians and ordered them to be tortured throughout all the provinces in a similar persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] A.: “That he slaughtered the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Servius Galba succeeded him, a senator of ancient nobility, when …”]

In an attempt to eradicate the very name, he fastened the most blessed Apostle Peter to a cross and cut off Paul’s head with a sword.

Soon afterward, calamities arising on every side overwhelmed the wretched city in heaps. For in the following autumn such a plague settled upon the city that thirty thousand deaths were entered in the records of Libitina.

## GALBA

In the year 822 from the founding of the City, Servius Galba arose from Spain and, the sixth ruler after Augustus, attained the principate. He was a senator of the most ancient nobility, descended from the family of the Sulpicii. He was seventy-three years old when he was chosen emperor by the Spaniards and Gauls and was soon willingly accepted by the entire army.

As soon as he learned of Nero’s death, he came to Rome and adopted Piso, a noble and energetic young man, as his son and successor to the throne.

[Col. 0870A]

In his youth Galba had been infamous and intemperate in eating. He arranged everything according to the counsel of three friends—Junius, Cornelius, and Icelus—to such an extent that they lived together within the Palatine residence and were commonly called “pedagogues.”

His private life had been distinguished by military and civil achievements. He was often consul, often proconsul, and frequently a commander. In the most serious wars he treated his soldiers with such extreme severity that, as soon as he entered the camp, this saying immediately became current: “Learn to be a soldier, soldier: it is Galba, not Getulicus.”

His reign was brief. It would have had a good beginning, had he not seemed too inclined toward severity. He was killed through Otho’s plot, his throat cut in the seventh month of his reign in the Forum at Rome. He was buried in his own gardens, on the Aurelian Way, not far from the city of Rome.

## OTHO

Lucius Salvius Otho, after Galba and Piso had been killed, seized the empire as the seventh ruler after Augustus. He was born to distinguished ancestors from the town of Ferentum.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] A. reads: “After Galba had been killed, he seized the empire,” etc.]

On his mother’s side he was nobler than on his father’s, though neither side was obscure. In private life he was soft, especially in youth, when he was wholly disgraceful, and he was a companion of Nero. In his reign he was unable to provide any proof of his abilities.

For at the same time that Otho had killed Galba, Vitellius had also been made emperor by the Germanic armies. Civil war was undertaken against him. Otho first fought victoriously against the Vitellian commanders in three minor battles: one near the Alps, another around Placentia, and a third near a place called Castores.

In the fourth battle, however, he was defeated in a light engagement at Bebriacum in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Eutropius calls it this. H. has “Betriacum,” as does the Ambrosian manuscript.]

Although he still had immense forces available for the war, he voluntarily killed himself. The soldiers begged him not to despair so quickly of the outcome of the war, but he said that he was not worth so much that a civil war should arise on his account. Thus he died by his own hand in the thirty-eighth year of his life.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] A. adds “after one day”: “Then Vitellius …”]

He died on the ninety-fifth day of his reign. He was so beloved by his own soldiers that many of them, when they saw his body, killed themselves with their own hands.

## VITELLIUS

Next Vitellius, the eighth ruler after Augustus, obtained the empire. His family was more honored than noble. His father, Lucius Vitellius, was not born to particular distinction, but he had held three ordinary consulships.

Vitellius himself was arrogant, cruel, and avaricious, with extravagant habits, and he ruled with great disgrace. He was conspicuous for savage behavior, especially for gluttony and voraciousness, since he is said often to have feasted for four or even five days at a time.

One banquet in particular has been committed to memory: his brother Vitellius gave it for him, and it is said that, in addition to other expenses, two thousand fish and seven thousand birds were served.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] A. and Eutropius read “in a single day.”]

He wished to resemble Nero and displayed this so openly that he even honored Nero’s remains, which had been humbly buried.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] A.: “He honored Nero’s funeral, which had been conducted humbly. He was killed by Vespasian’s commanders, after Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, had first been killed in the City; Vitellius burned the Capitol together with him. He was killed with great disgrace: dragged publicly naked through the city of Rome, with his hair standing up, his head bent back, a sword placed beneath his chin and wrapped in filth, and his chest assailed by everyone who passed by. Finally he was slaughtered and thrown into the Tiber, and even …”]

For this reason he was hated by everyone.

After learning of Vespasian, he first attempted to lay down the imperial power. Then, encouraged by certain men, he drove Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, who suspected no evil at that time, into the Capitol together with the other Flavians. He set fire to the temple and, mingling flames with ruin, delivered them all alike to a common death and burial.

But after Vespasian had been proclaimed emperor in Palestine, he came to Greece. As the Greeks themselves admit, he was delighted by what he heard from Apollonius of Tyana concerning the timing of his reign and his other great and favorable prospects. Apollonius was returning from the Indians, Brahmans, and Gymnosophists who lived there.

Vitellius was defeated by Vespasian’s soldiers in a battle fought beneath the walls of the City and was abandoned by his own army. As the enemy approached, he was already terrified. He withdrew into a small room near the palace, but was dragged out from there most disgracefully, his hands bound behind his back, and led around for the amusement of the crowd.

As he was led naked through the Sacred Way, so that even at the end of his evils he might not, through shame at the crimes he had committed, lower his face in embarrassment, his hair was held upright and his head bent back, with a sword placed beneath his chin. Half naked and covered about the mouth and chest with much mud, dung, and other filth too shameful to mention, he was brought into the Forum.

He was dragged down the Gemonian Steps, where he had permitted Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, to be killed. There he was flayed by repeated blows of innumerable small strikes. Then he was dragged with a hook and plunged into the Tiber; he was not even granted an ordinary burial.

He died in the fifty-seventh year of his life, in the eighth month and first day of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 0872B] Eutropius has “in the eighteenth month and one day.” H. has “in the eighth month and one day,” together with Ambrose.]

For many days Vespasian’s soldiers raged with indiscriminate slaughter against the Senate and the Roman people, in many wicked and impious ways.

[Col. 0872B]

Vespasian succeeded him, the ninth ruler after Augustus.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0871]

## VESPASIAN

[Col. 0871B]

[Note: [Col. 0871D] In A. these words cannot be read as far as “obscure,” and a new book does not begin. Instead, after the word “one,” it reads: “Vespasian succeeded him, having been made emperor in Palestine; obscurely, etc.”]

In the year 815 from the founding of the City, after that brief but troubled darkness of tyrants had been dispelled, peaceful serenity returned under Vespasian.

He was indeed obscurely born, but comparable with the best. His private life was distinguished: sent by Claudius to Germany and then to Britain, he fought the enemy thirty-two times, added two very powerful peoples, twenty towns, and the Isle of Wight, lying near Britain, to Roman rule.

[Note: [Col. 0872D] A. adds “he had added,” omitting the intervening words and immediately reading “he had renewed Rome,” etc.]

To return to the matter somewhat earlier: after the passion of Christ, the Jews, wholly abandoned by God’s grace, were surrounded on every side by every kind of evil. Some of them, led astray on Mount Carmel by lots that foretold that leaders arising from Judaea would gain possession of the world, drew the prophecy to themselves and broke out in rebellion. After destroying the Roman garrisons, they also put to flight the governor of Syria—whose province is called Palestine—who had come to their aid, having seized the eagle and massacred his forces.

Nero sent Vespasian against them, and Vespasian took his elder son Titus with him on the journey. He transported twenty-eight large and powerful legions with him into Syria.

After capturing many of the Jews’ towns, he shut them up under siege in the city of Jerusalem, where they had gathered especially for the festival. When Nero’s death became known, and at the urging of many kings and commanders—above all Josephus, the commander of the Jews, who, after being captured and placed in chains, had steadfastly said, as Suetonius reports, that he would soon be released by the same man, but as emperor—Vespasian obtained the empire.

He left his son Titus in the camp to conduct the siege of Jerusalem and departed for Rome. When he learned of Vitellius’s death, however, he stopped for a short time at Alexandria.

Titus, meanwhile, pressing the Jews with a great and prolonged siege, at last broke through the city walls with engines and every kind of military apparatus, though not without a great loss of his own men.

To capture the inner fortification of the Temple, which the multitude of priests and leaders defended after it had been opened, required greater force and delay. It was captured within twenty days.

After it had been brought under his power, Titus gazed upon the structure, remarkable in its workmanship and venerable in its antiquity, and deliberated for a long time whether to burn it as an encouragement to the enemy or preserve it as a testimony to his victory.

When word was brought to him from Rome that his father had gained the empire, his right calf was seized by an excessive swelling of flesh, so that he could not put on a shoe. This was restored, like other things, on the counsel of Josephus, the Jewish commander, who had ordered [him] to pass before the man whom he hated most.

Titus, therefore, having been proclaimed emperor by the army, burned and destroyed the Temple at Jerusalem. It had stood from the day of its first construction until the day of its final destruction for 1,102 years.

He leveled all the walls of the city to the ground. Cornelius and Suetonius report that six hundred thousand Jews were killed in that war.

Josephus, however, the Jewish commander who was in charge at that time and who had earned pardon and favor with Vespasian on account of the aforementioned prophecy of empire, writes that 1,100,000 perished by the sword and famine, while the survivors, driven into various conditions, were scattered throughout the entire world. Their number is said to have been 90,000.

Before these events, obscene and terrible omens, as Josephus himself says, were either seen or reported.

A bright star resembling a sword was seen hanging over the city from above, and a comet also appeared to burn throughout the entire year with deadly flames.

Before the time of the destruction and the war, when the people were gathering for the festival of Unleavened Bread, on the eighth day of the month of April, at the ninth hour of the night, such a great radiance of light surrounded the altar and the Temple that everyone thought broad daylight had appeared. It lasted for half an hour.

To the unskilled and ignorant this seemed favorable, but the learned in the law and all sound teachers recognized the deadly portent.

At the same festival, a victim brought for sacrifice and standing beside the altars gave birth to a lamb in the very hands of the attendants.

The inner door of the Temple, facing east, was covered with solid bronze and was of immense weight. It could scarcely be closed even by twenty men pushing with all their strength. It was also secured with iron bars and bolts, held fast by locks lowered from above. Yet at the sixth hour of the night it suddenly appeared to have opened.

A few days after the festival had ended, on the twenty-first day of the month of May, another prodigious and almost incredible vision appeared—one that would truly have been thought false had the testimony of the eyes not confirmed it.

Near sunset, chariots and four-horse teams were seen moving through the air over the whole region, while companies of armed men appeared to mingle with the clouds and surround the city with unexpected ranks.

On another festival, called Pentecost, priests entered the Temple at night to perform the customary services. At first they felt certain movements and heard noises; then they suddenly heard voices saying: “Let us depart from here.”

Another event, even more terrible, was added to these.

A certain man named Jesus, son of Ananias, a common and rustic man, began suddenly to cry out during the festival of Tabernacles, seven years before the war, while the city still enjoyed abundance:

“A voice from the East, a voice from the West, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the Temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against the people.”

Day and night he continually went around all the streets proclaiming this, until certain leading men of the people, moved as though by indignation at an unfavorable portent, seized him and inflicted many blows upon him.

But he said nothing at all in his own defense, nor did he plead with those surrounding him. With equal persistence and shouting he repeated the same words.

Then the leaders, understanding that there was something divine in the man—as indeed there was—brought him before the Roman governor. There he was scourged until his bones were laid bare. He shed neither prayers nor tears, but uttered the same voice miserably and with a kind of wailing, repeating it after almost every blow and adding this as well:

“Woe, woe to Jerusalem!”

Vespasian and Titus, therefore, celebrating a magnificent triumph over the Jews, entered the City.

Among the three hundred and twenty triumphs celebrated up to that time, this spectacle was beautiful and previously unknown to all mortals: father and son, borne together in one triumphal chariot, carrying away a most glorious victory from those who had offended father and son.

Vespasian conducted himself at Rome with the greatest moderation. He was only rather eager for money, so much so that he unjustly took it from certain people. Yet, although he gathered it with every careful provision, he distributed it with great zeal, especially to those in need.

Before him it was scarcely known that any ruler had been either more generous or more just.

He was of exceptionally gentle temper. He did not readily punish those whose offenses against his majesty were especially severe beyond the penalty of exile.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] A. adds after “majesty,” “who had offended against it”; and after “penalty,” it reads: “Under him Judaea was added to the Roman Empire, as was Jerusalem, the most famous city of Palestine; Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, and Samos, which had previously been free; likewise Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, which had been under friendly kings. He reduced these to the form of provinces, after they had committed offenses, etc.”]

Among his other virtues, he had this singular quality: he forgot enmities. Thus he gave the daughter of Vitellius, his enemy, a very rich dowry and married her to a highly distinguished man.

He patiently endured the agitation of his friends and, being very witty, answered their insults with humorous remarks. Licinius Mucianus, by whose assistance he had attained the empire, became insolent through confidence in his services. Vespasian amusingly restrained him by bringing in someone familiar to them both and saying only this:

“You know that I am a man, don’t you?”

But why be surprised that he behaved so toward friends, when he was even forgetful of offenses and enmities?

[Note: [Col. 0874D] A. adds “he was forgetful. He gently endured the oblique remarks of advocates and the insolence of philosophers directed against him,” etc.]

He gently endured the indirect remarks of advocates and the insolence of philosophers directed against him, yet he was a diligent enforcer of military discipline.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] A. adds “military”: “He celebrated a triumph over Jerusalem with his son Titus. Through these deeds, and because he had …”]

He restored the world, which had long been bloodless and exhausted, in a short time, judging very wisely that wicked services are often performed out of fear.

Moreover, by admonishing people with very equitable laws and—what is more powerful—by the example of his life, he had eliminated many vices. He was, however, weak, as some wrongly think, in relation to money, although it is sufficiently clear that, because of the poverty of the treasury and the destruction of the cities, he devised new levies of tribute that had not previously been imposed.

He restored Rome, disfigured by earlier fires and ruins, allowing those who wished to build to do so if the owners were absent. He repaired the Capitol, the Temple of Peace, and the monuments of Claudius, and established many new structures.

Throughout all the lands where Roman law prevailed, cities were renewed with splendid adornment, and roads were strengthened by immense works.

Mountains were then cut through along the Flaminian Way for a level passage at the place commonly called the Pierced Rock.

He brought a thousand peoples under order, having found scarcely two hundred organized before, after most had been destroyed by the savagery of tyrants.

The Parthian king Vologeses was compelled to make peace by fear alone.

Then, without any disturbance of war, the Roman state advanced to immense greatness.

Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, and Samos, which had previously been free, and likewise Trachean Cilicia and Commagene—which we now call Augustofratensis and which had been under friendly kings—were then first reduced to the form of provinces and obeyed Roman governors and laws.

In the ninth year of his reign, three cities of Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake, and there was a great plague at Rome.

When his friends warned him to beware of Mettius Pomposianus, about whom widespread talk claimed that he would become emperor, Vespasian made him consul, alluding to the matter with this jest:

“One day he will remember so great a favor.”

He maintained the same routine throughout the whole empire: he kept watch at night; after public business was completed, he admitted his friends while being greeted, taking up his shoes and royal clothing.

After hearing whatever matters had arisen, he exercised by riding and then rested. Finally, after bathing, he arranged a dinner in a more relaxed frame of mind.

My subject has compelled me to say more about a good emperor whom the Roman state, drained by the savagery of tyrants, obtained fifty-six years after the death of Augustus, as though by a kind of fate lest it collapse completely.

After this, when he had become beloved and agreeable to the Senate, the people, and finally everyone, mixing serious matters with jokes, which delighted him, he died.

When a long-haired star appeared—the Greeks call it κομήτης, “comet”—he said: “This concerns the king of the Persians, whose hair is more abundant.”

Then, exhausted by diarrhea,

[Note: [Col. 0875D] A. reads “after becoming exhausted.”]

he died in his own villa near the Sabines. Rising, he said:

“An emperor ought to depart standing from the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0875D] A. adds: “at the age of sixty-nine, in the ninth year of his reign and on the seventh day, and he was enrolled among the gods.”]

He understood the horoscope of his sons so well that, although many conspiracies were formed against him, and although he contemptuously ignored their exposure with great pretense of indifference, he said in the Senate that either his sons would succeed him or no one would.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] A. after the word “no one” reads: “His son Titus succeeded him, who was also called Vespasian, a man remarkable for every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called the love and delight of the human race. Most eloquent, etc.”]

## TITUS VESPASIANus
In the year 828 from the founding of the City, Titus, son of Vespasian and the freedwoman Domitilla, the tenth emperor after Augustus, succeeded his father after his death; he too was called Vespasian. From childhood he was devoted with the greatest zeal to distinguished pursuits of uprightness, military service, and literature, and he showed by the gifts of mind and body what he had striven for. When he assumed responsibility for the state, it is incredible how far he surpassed his father, whom he imitated—especially in clemency, generosity, honor, [Col. 0875C] and contempt for money. These qualities were all the more welcome because, on account of certain acts committed while he was still a private citizen, he had been believed likely to become harsher and fond of luxury and avarice.

For when he obtained the prefecture of the praetorian guard during his father’s reign, he crushed anyone whom he suspected or who opposed him, sending men through the theaters and military camps to demand their punishment by spreading hateful accusations, as though they had been convicted of a crime. Among these was the former consul Caecina, whom he invited to dinner and ordered to be murdered, scarcely after he had left the dining room, on suspicion of having violated Berenice, his wife. He had also sold quarrels under his father and was greedy for plunder. Hence, when everyone thought of him and called him a Nero, they were deeply distressed that he had obtained supreme power.

But these qualities were transformed for the better, and they brought him such immortal glory that he was called “the delight and love of the human race.” Finally, when he assumed the royal burden, [Col. 0875D] he ordered Berenice, who hoped to marry him, to return home, and the troops of eunuchs to depart. By this act he gave, as it were, a sign that his former intemperance had changed.

While succeeding emperors were accustomed to confirm gifts and concessions made by earlier rulers, as soon as he began to reign he voluntarily provided by an edict for those who possessed such grants. He was extremely eloquent, warlike, and self-controlled. He pleaded cases in Latin and composed poems and tragedies in Greek. While serving under his father in the siege of Jerusalem, he transfixed twelve defenders with twelve arrows.

He showed such piety toward the Jews that, as he went around Jerusalem and saw the ditches filled with corpses and the land of their country drenched with the corruption of human bodies, he raised his hands to heaven and, with a great groan, called God as witness that this deed was not his own.

At Rome he displayed such civility in his rule that he punished no one at all. He carried his clemency so far that he released men convicted of conspiring against him and kept them in the same intimacy in which he had formerly held them.

[Note: A. reads *habuerit*.]

To state his clemency briefly: when two men of the highest rank had conspired against him and could not deny the crime they had planned, he first warned them; then, after they had been brought into the amphitheater, he ordered them to sit beside him on either side. He requested a gladiator’s sword from the equipment of the *mirmillones*, whose combat was being displayed, and, as though testing the blade, handed it to each of the two men in turn. When they were struck with terror and marveled at his composure, he said:

“Do you see that power is granted by fate, and that an attempt at crime is useless, whether one hopes to obtain power or fears to lose it?”

He also repeatedly entreated his brother Domitian, who was plotting ambushes and stirring up the soldiers, with tears, not to desire to attain by parricide what would come to him even with Titus’s consent, and what he already possessed, since he shared in the imperial power.

He was so easygoing and generous that, although he denied nothing to anyone and was reproached by his friends, he replied that no one ought to leave the emperor sad. Moreover, when one day at dinner he remembered that he had given nothing to anyone that day, [Col. 0876C] he said in a reverent and almost heavenly utterance: “My friends, we have wasted this day.”

[Note: A. adds after *praestitisse*: “he said to his friends, ‘Today I have wasted the day.’” Eutropius has: “Friends, today I have wasted the day.” H. reads *amicis*: “Today I have wasted the day.”]

He built an amphitheater at Rome and killed five thousand wild beasts at its dedication.

[Note: A. adds after *occidit*: “Through these things, etc.”]

During his reign a sudden fire burned at Rome for three days and nights without respite, and many public buildings were destroyed. At that time, they say, the summit of Mount Vesuvius in Campania also burst open, pouring out great fires; neighboring districts, with their cities and inhabitants, were destroyed by torrents of flame.

A plague also struck Rome, scarcely ever previously so severe. Yet, amid these disasters, he helped everyone at his own expense, employing every kind of remedy: sometimes restoring the sick himself, sometimes comforting those afflicted by the deaths of their relatives.

After this, beloved with extraordinary popular favor, he died of illness in the same villa in which his father had died, after he had ruled for two years, eight months, and twenty days following his father, in the forty-second year of his age.

[Note: A. adds after *viginti*: “after he had become emperor.”]

[Note: A. adds after *quadragesimo*: “Such was the public mourning at his death that all, etc.”]

It is scarcely possible to believe how much mourning his death brought upon the City and the provinces, so deeply did everyone grieve as though bereaved in his own household. When his death was announced toward evening, the Senate rushed into the curia during the night and heaped upon him, though dead, such praises and thanks as it had never bestowed while he was alive; and he was enrolled among the gods.

[Note: A. reads *congessit* and, after *egerat*: “Nor was he enrolled among the gods while present.” It adds: “Domitian, his younger brother, immediately received the imperial power; he was more like Nero…”]

## FLAVIUS DOMITIAN

In the year 830 from the founding of the City, Domitian, son of Vespasian and the freedwoman Domitilla, the full brother and younger brother of Titus, the eleventh emperor after Augustus, assumed power.

He was more like Nero, Caligula, or Tiberius than like his father or brother. During his first years, however, he was moderate in his rule; soon, plunging into enormous vices, lust, anger, cruelty, and avarice,

[Note: A. reads *progressus* (“having advanced”).]

 he aroused such hatred against himself that he obliterated the merits of his brother and father. He killed the noblest men of the Senate and was the first to order himself to be called, written of, and worshiped as “lord and god.”

When all others had been removed, he idly and ridiculously pursued swarms of flies, raging with the lust whose foul exercise the Greeks called *κλινοπάλη* (*klinopálē*, “bed-wrestling”). Hence, when someone asked whether anyone was in the palace, the answer was: “Not even a fly.”

He permitted no statue of himself to be erected on the Capitol except one of gold or silver. He killed his cousins. His pride, too, was execrable. Among the Romans he ordered men to be castrated so that he might keep them in the palace, and he ordered his wife to be called Augusta.

He conducted four campaigns: one against the Sarmatians, another against the Chatti, and two against the Dacians. I would set out at length how great were the battles between Diurpaneus, king of the Dacians, and the commander Fuscus, and how great was the Roman disaster—when the former consul Oppius Sabinus and Cornelius Fuscus, prefect of the praetorian guard, were killed with large armies—if Cornelius Tacitus, who composed this history with the greatest care, had not said that he had bound himself, as had Sallustius Crispus and many other authors, to suppress the number of those killed, and had not himself especially chosen to do the same.

Domitian, however, carried away by the most depraved boastfulness, celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Chatti in the name of conquered enemies, although his own legions had been destroyed.

[Note: A. reads: “He celebrated a double triumph over the Dacians and Chatti.”]

Against the Sarmatians he claimed only a laurel crown, although there his legion and its commander had been killed.

[Note: A. adds: “Nevertheless, he suffered many disasters in those same wars; for in Sarmatia a legion…”]

[Note: A. adds: “The legion was killed along with its commander. And Oppius Sabinus, former consul, and Cornelius Fuscus, prefect of the praetorian guard, were killed by the Dacians with large armies.”]

But when he had become hated by everyone because of his crimes, Antonius, especially enraged by the insult in Domitian’s words—for he was distressed at being called a prostitute—seized power while governing Upper Germany. Domitian defeated him in battle through Norbanus and Appius.

At Rome he also began or rebuilt from the foundations many buildings.

[Note: A. reads: “He constructed many works, among them, etc.”]

Among them were the Pantheon, the Capitol, the Forum Transitorium, an odeon, porticoes,

[Note: A. reads: “the portico of the gods, etc.”]

the Iseum and Serapeum, and the stadium; he restored the pepper warehouses, the temple of Vespasian, Minerva Chalcidica, the Matutine School, the Golden Mile, the Sweating Meta, and the libraries consumed by fire, obtaining copies from everywhere, especially Alexandria.

[Note: A. adds: “and the stadium.” It continues: “But when he had begun to be hated by everyone because of his crimes, he was killed by a conspiracy of his own people in the palace, in the thirty-fifth year of his life and the fifteenth of his reign. His funeral was carried out with great disgrace by undertakers and he was buried ignobly.”]

He was so skilled with the bow that arrows shot toward a man standing at a distance passed between the fingers of his extended hand.

He was the second after Nero to order a persecution of the Christians, in which many were crowned with martyrdom, as Orosius writes. Among them was Flavia Domitilla, niece through her sister of Flavius Clemens, who had been consul; she was exiled to the island of Pontia for bearing witness to the faith.

[Col. 0878B] At that time the most blessed apostle John was also banished to the island of Patmos.

Among the Jews, too, he ordered that the descendants of David be sought out and killed through the harshness of tortures and the bloodiest investigation, as though someone from the seed of David were still destined to come, while the holy prophets were both envied and believed to possess the power to obtain the kingdom.

Thus Domitian, struck by fear of his cruelty and by the consciousness of his own crimes, was overwhelmed. Many conspired against him, led by Parthenius, superintendent of the bedchamber; Stephanus; and Clodianus, who at that time was under suspicion and awaiting punishment for fraud involving embezzled money. His wife Domitia was also brought into the plot, because she feared torture from the emperor on account of her love for the actor Paris.

They stabbed Domitian with many wounds after the forty-fifth year of his life and the fifteenth of his reign.

[Note: Eutropius gives “the forty-fifth year of his life”; H. gives “the thirty-fifth year.”]

The Senate, however, ordered his funeral to be carried out disgracefully and ignominiously by undertakers, like that of a gladiator; it decreed that his name should be erased, and he was buried without honor.

During his reign the secular games were celebrated.

Up to this point, those born at Rome or in Italy ruled the empire. From here onward came outsiders. Thus it became clear that the city of Rome grew through the excellence of foreigners. For what was wiser or more moderate than Nerva? What was more godlike than Trajan? What was more outstanding than Hadrian?

## BOOK TEN

[Note: In A. this book is numbered VIII, since up to this point it continues Book VII.]

## NERVA

In the year 846 from the founding of the City, under the consulship of Vetus and Valens, the state returned to its most prosperous condition, having been entrusted with extraordinary good fortune to worthy rulers.

[Note: Eutropius, Book VIII. H.: “In the eight hundred and fiftieth year from the founding of the City, under the consulship of Vetus and Valens.” Elsewhere H. agrees word for word with Eutropius from the beginning, except for a few variant readings, which I note. *Canis.* A. also reads 850.]

After the destructive tyrant Domitian had been killed, Cocceius Nerva, born at Narnia, was elected the twelfth emperor after Augustus.

[Note: A. reads: “Nerva succeeded while still in private life…”]

In private life he had been moderate and energetic, of middling nobility,

[Note: A. adds after *mediae*: “who …”]

and already quite old. Through the efforts of Petronius Secundus, prefect of the praetorian guard, and likewise Parthenius, Domitian’s murderer, he was made emperor and showed himself most just and civil.

[Note: A. adds: “He became emperor. Aequis., etc.”]

[Note: A. adds after *praebuit*: “By divine provision for the state, etc.”]

When he had assumed power, a rumor soon arose that Domitian was alive and about to appear. Nerva was so terrified that his color changed, he lost the power of speech, and could scarcely remain standing. But Parthenius restored his confidence, and he returned to his customary composure.

When he was received gratefully by the Senate in the curia, only Arius Antoninus, an energetic man and Nerva’s close friend, prudently expressing the condition of rulers, embraced him and said that he congratulated the Senate, the people, and the provinces, but by no means Nerva himself. It would have been better for Nerva always to elude bad emperors than, while bearing the weight of so great a burden, to be subjected not only to troubles and dangers but also to the hostility of enemies and friends alike—friends who presume that they deserve everything and, if they have extorted anything at all, are more savage even than enemies.

Nerva forgave whatever had been added to the taxes under the name of punishment, restored oppressed cities, and ordered that girls and boys born to impoverished parents be supported at public expense throughout the towns of Italy.

In his first edict he recalled all exiles. Through this general clemency the apostle John too was released and returned to Ephesus.

To prevent himself from being frightened by the approach of malicious men, he was warned by a saying of Junius Mauricus, a steadfast man. Mauricus had been invited to a private dinner and, seeing Veiento present—Veiento had held consular honors under Domitian but had prosecuted many people through secret accusations—heard Nerva mention Catullus, a notorious informer. Nerva asked what Veiento would do if he had outlived Domitian. Mauricus replied: “He would be dining with us.”

[Note: Another reading is *Maturicius*.]

Nerva was a very frequent and highly knowledgeable arbiter of quarrels. When Calpurnius Crassus, discovered and confessing, tested the soldiers’ loyalty with extravagant promises, Nerva removed him with his wife to Tarentum, although the senators criticized his leniency.

When Domitian’s murderers were demanded for execution, he was so overcome that he could neither restrain vomiting nor a bowel movement; nevertheless, he resisted vehemently, repeatedly declaring that it was more just to die than to stain the authority of the empire by betraying the men who had made it possible for power to be seized.

But the soldiers disregarded the emperor: they killed Petronius with a single blow and Parthenius after first removing his genitals and thrusting them into his mouth. They ransomed Casperius at great expense; because he had become more insolent through such a savage crime, he compelled Nerva to give public thanks to the soldiers for having killed the worst and most wicked of all human beings.

Nerva provided for the state by divine providence and adopted Trajan in place of a son and as a partner in power.

[Note: A. adds after *adoptando*: “He died at Rome after one year…”]

While, prompted by anger, he was shouting at the top of his voice against a certain man named Regulus, he was seized by sweating. When the sweating subsided, an excessive chill set the beginning of a fever, and not long afterward he ended his life, after one year, four months, and eight days of imperial rule, in the seventy-second year of his age. He was enrolled among the gods.

[Note: A. reads: “He was enrolled among the gods. Ulpius Crinitus Trajan succeeded him, born at Italica in Spain, of a family…”]

The Senate carried his body on its shoulders, as it had once carried Augustus’, and buried it in Augustus’ tomb on the Campus Martius. On the day of his death there was an eclipse of the sun.

## TRAJAN

In the year 847 from the founding of the City, Ulpius Crinitus Trajan, from the city of Tudertum, called Ulpius after his grandfather and Trajan after Traius, the founder of his paternal family—or so called from the name of his father Trajan—became the thirteenth emperor after Augustus. He was born in Spain, of a family more ancient than distinguished. His father had first been consul.

[Col. 0880B] He was made emperor at Agrippina, a famous city of Gaul.

[Note: “At Agrippina in Gaul.”]

He possessed diligence in military affairs, gentleness in civil matters, and generosity in relieving cities. Since two qualities are expected of excellent rulers—uprightness at home and courage in war, with prudence in both—his moderation in the greatest affairs was such that he seemed to have blended his virtues by some kind of balance, except that he was somewhat devoted to food and wine.

He administered the state in such a way that he deservedly surpassed all emperors, in extraordinary civility and courage. He extended the boundaries of the Roman Empire far and wide; after Augustus, the empire had been more defended than nobly enlarged. He restored the cities beyond the Rhine in Germany. He subdued Dacia after defeating Decebalus and made it a province beyond the Danube, in the lands now inhabited by the Taiphali, now by the Victophali, and by the Tervingi.

[Note: The form in A. is *Victophali*; Eutropius has the same, while H. has *Victoali*. A. has *Victohali*.]

That province occupied a circuit of one million paces. He recovered Armenia, which the Parthians had occupied, after killing Pharmatasiris, who held it.

[Note: A. reads *Farmatosiriae*.]

He gave a king to the Albani. He received into his allegiance the kings of the Iberians, the Sarmatians, the Bosporans, the Arabs, the Osrhoenians, and the Colchians. He seized the Cardueni and the Mardomedi.

[Note: A. reads *Corduenos*. Eutropius reads *Marchomedes*; H. and A. read *Marcomedes*.]

He defeated and held Antemusium, a large region of Persia, as well as Seleucia, Ctesiphon, Babylon, and Edessa.

[Note: A. reads: “Babylon; he defeated the Messenii…”]

He advanced as far as the borders of India and the Red Sea, and there established three provinces: Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia, together with the peoples who reach as far as Madena. Later he reduced Arabia to the form of a province and established a fleet on the Red Sea so that through it he might ravage the borders of India.

Yet he surpassed his military glory by his civility and moderation. At Rome and throughout the provinces he showed himself equal to everyone. He frequently visited his friends to greet them, whether they were ill or were celebrating feast days, and regularly held unceremonious banquets with them, sometimes sitting in their vehicles. He harmed none of the senators and did nothing unjust to enlarge the treasury. He was generous toward everyone, enriching all publicly and privately and increasing the honors of anyone whom he had known even with moderate familiarity.

He built throughout the world and granted many immunities to cities. He did nothing that was not tranquil and peaceful, so that throughout his entire reign only one senator was condemned—and even that was done by the Senate without Trajan’s knowledge.

For these qualities, throughout the world he deserved every kind of veneration, as one who was close to the gods, both living and dead. Among his sayings this one is reported as especially distinguished. When his friends blamed him for being too open and accessible to everyone, he replied that he was such an emperor to private citizens as he, while a private citizen, would have wished an emperor to be.

He built baths in honor of Sura, through whose efforts he had obtained the imperial power. It seems superfluous to wish to list all his achievements by name, since it is enough to say that he embellished and restored everything.

He endured toil, devoted himself to every excellent and warlike man, and preferred simpler characters to the most learned—since he himself possessed limited knowledge and was moderately eloquent. In justice and in human and divine law he was equally an innovator and a guardian of ancient tradition.

All these qualities seemed the greater because, after the Roman state had been ruined and prostrated by many savage tyrants, he was believed to have been providentially granted at the proper moment as a remedy for such great evils. Indeed, at his arrival many marvelous omens were reported. Among them was a crow which, from the summit of the Capitol, uttered in Attic speech: *ἔσται καλῶς*—“It will be well.”

While he was indeed deceived by error in persecuting Christians, being the third after Nero to do so, he ordered that those found everywhere should be compelled to sacrifice to idols and that those who refused should be killed. Many were consequently put to death.

Pliny Secundus, who, as Tertullian reports, had been appointed a persecutor among the other judges, informed him that these people were guilty of nothing deserving death except that they did not sacrifice to the gods and, rising before dawn, praised Christ as though he were a god while abstaining from every evil.

Trajan wrote back to him that Christians were not to be sought out in any way on account of their faith.

Nevertheless, soon afterward Nero’s Golden House at Rome, built at the expense of all private and public resources, was suddenly consumed by fire. It was thereby understood that a persecution sent by another had fallen chiefly upon the monuments of the very man from whom it had first arisen, and that it was punished in its own author.

An earthquake destroyed four cities of Asia: Elaea, Myrina, Pitane, and Cyme; and two Greek cities, those of the Opuntians and the Oricians. Three cities of Galatia were destroyed by the same earthquake. The Pantheon at Rome, built by Domitian, was burned by lightning. An earthquake at Antioch nearly demolished the entire city.

Then, in an incredible upheaval, the Jews, as though driven mad by frenzy, broke out at the same time in various parts of the world. Throughout Libya they rose against the inhabitants and waged the most savage wars. The region was so devastated after its inhabitants had been killed that, unless the emperor Hadrian had later brought in colonists gathered from elsewhere, the land would have remained completely empty, its inhabitants wiped out.

They threw all Egypt, Cyrene, and the Thebaid into turmoil through bloody uprisings. At Alexandria they were defeated and crushed in a battle that was then fought. In Mesopotamia too, when they rebelled, war was waged against them by order of the emperor. Thus many thousands of them were destroyed in a vast slaughter.

They also destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus after killing all its inhabitants.

After achieving immense glory in war and at home, Trajan, returning from Persia, died at Seleucia in Isauria from an intestinal discharge.

[Note: Eutropius: “He died in the sixty-second year of his age, in the ninth month and fourth day, and was enrolled among the gods.” H.: “He died in the sixty-third year of his age, in June, on the fourth day, in the nineteenth year of his reign, in the sixth month and fifteenth day, and was enrolled among the gods.”]

He died in the sixty-third year of his age, after one month and four days, in the nineteenth year of his reign, in the sixth month and fifteenth day. He was enrolled among the gods.

[Note: A. reads: “He was enrolled among the gods. He alone of all was buried within the City. His ashes were placed in a golden urn in the forum he built, beneath the column, whose…”]

The ashes of his burned body were brought to Rome in a golden urn and buried in Trajan’s Forum beneath his column, whose height is 140 feet. His image was placed on top, as is customary with triumphal figures, and was carried into the City, with the Senate and army leading the procession.

At that time the Tiber flooded much more destructively than under Nerva, causing great devastation to the neighboring buildings. A severe earthquake occurred in many provinces, as well as a savage pestilence, famine, and fires. Trajan assisted in all these disasters through carefully devised remedies of many kinds. He decreed that the height of buildings should not exceed sixty feet, because of the ease of their collapse and the ruinous expense involved whenever such events occurred.

Hence he was deservedly called Father of his Country.

Such honor was paid to his memory that even down to our own age emperors were hailed in the Senate only with the words: “More fortunate than Augustus, better than Trajan.”

[Note: “Down to our own age.” These are the words of Eutropius, which Paul the Deacon, Manuscript H., and the *Miscella* also preserved. *Canis.*]

The glory of his goodness prevailed so completely in him that, whether flatterers or sincere praisers, all found in him an opportunity for the most magnificent example.

[Note: A. reads: “an example.”]

## HADRIAN

In the year 867 from the founding of the City, Aelius Hadrian, of Italian stock from Spain, born to Aelius Hadrianus, Trajan’s cousin, and descended from the town of Adria—which gave its name also to the Adriatic Sea—was made the fourteenth emperor after Augustus.

Hadrian became emperor without any intention on Trajan’s part, although Trajan’s wife Plotina worked to bring it about. For while alive Trajan had refused to adopt him, although he was the son of his cousin.

[Note: Spartianus, Eutropius, Hersfeld, and Ambrosius read: “the son of his cousin.”]

Envious of Trajan’s glory, Hadrian immediately surrendered the three provinces.

[Note: A. reads: “He too was born at Italica in Spain.”]

 that Trajan had added—that is, he recalled the armies from Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Armenia, and decided that the Euphrates should be the boundary of the empire.

[Note: A. reads *reliquit* (“he relinquished”).]

He also tried to do the same with Dacia, but his friends frightened him away from the plan, lest many Roman citizens be handed over to the barbarians, because Trajan, after conquering Dacia, had transferred countless forces there from the entire Roman world to cultivate its fields and cities. The strength of Dacia had been exhausted by the long war against Decebalus.

[Note: A. instead of *Decibali* has *civili re*—the reading is uncertain.]

Throughout his entire reign, however, he kept the peace. Only once did he fight against the Sarmatians through his governor, and he won.

He traveled around the Roman world and built many things.

Instructed and educated through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom, and the envoy Serenus Granianus, who had composed books on the Christian religion, he ordered—by a letter sent to Minutius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia—that no one should be permitted to condemn Christians without an accusation of a crime or proof.

At the same time, he was called Father of his Country in the Senate, with honors surpassing those of his ancestors even after his death; and his wife was called Augusta.

The text of the letter is as follows:

“I have received a letter written to me by your predecessor, Serenius [Note: Another reading is *Granianus*. See Zonaras.] Germanus, a most distinguished man, and I do not wish to pass over his report in silence, lest innocent people be disturbed and an opportunity for plundering be given to informers.

Therefore, if the provincials are able to support their petition against the Christians with clear evidence, so that they may accuse them before the tribunal of some offense, I do not prohibit them from pursuing the matter. But I do not permit them to use only petitions and acclamations for this purpose. For it is much more just that, if anyone wishes to accuse them, you should investigate the charges.

If, therefore, anyone accuses them and proves that the persons mentioned are doing anything contrary to the laws, you shall impose punishments according to the merit of their offenses. But you will take the greatest care that, if anyone brings a charge against one of these people out of a desire to slander, you punish that person with harsher penalties in proportion to his wickedness.”

Thus Hadrian organized the state under the fairest laws.

He completely subdued the Jews, who had been driven into turmoil by the disorders caused by their crimes and were laying waste to the province of Palestine, through a final slaughter. Jerusalem was finally destroyed so utterly that, in accordance with the divine saying, not one stone was left upon another.

He also avenged the Christians whom the Jews, under the leadership of Chozeba, had tortured because they would not join them against the Romans.

[Note: Eusebius’s *Chronicle* reads *Chorebas*.]

He ordered that no Jew should have permission to enter Jerusalem, while the city was permitted only to Christians. He restored it by constructing walls, giving it the status of a town, and ordered it to be called Aelia, from his own name.

At the same time, the distinguished rhetors Favorinus and Palaemon were active at Rome, as were Herodes of Athens and Marcus.

Hadrian was extremely eloquent in Latin and highly learned in Greek letters, so that many called him “the little Greek.” He increased the intellectual pursuits and customs of the Athenians. Skilled not only in language but also in the other disciplines, he knew how to sing, play the lyre, and practice medicine; he was a musician, geometrician, painter, and sculptor in bronze and marble, second only to Polyclitus and Euphranor.

Accordingly, he seemed wholly fashioned for such accomplishments, so that human affairs appear never to have produced anything more elegant.

His memory was beyond what anyone can readily believe: he could recall and name places, business, soldiers, and even absent persons. This was a task of immense labor, since he had traveled through all the provinces on foot, preceding the accompanying procession while restoring every town and enlarging its institutions.

For the appearance of military legions, he had organized into centuries the smiths, surveyors, architects, and every kind of worker involved in constructing or decorating walls.

He was varied, complex, and many-sided, apparently born as an arbiter between vices and virtues. He controlled the impulses of his mind by a certain artifice. He skillfully concealed an envious, gloomy, lustful, and boastfully insolent character by pretending to self-restraint, clemency, and affability, while concealing the passion for glory with which he burned.

He was extremely sharp in provoking others and answering serious remarks with jokes and insults. You would have thought that he had prepared in advance a reply to everything—a poem for a poem, a saying for a saying.

His wife Sabina, treated almost with the insults appropriate to a slave, was driven to voluntary death. She openly declared that, because she had recognized and endured his monstrous character, she had taken care not to become pregnant by him, lest she bear offspring for the destruction of the human race.

Defeated by an internal disease that he had long endured calmly, but now burning with pain and unable to bear it, he killed several senators. Having obtained peace from many kings by secret gifts, he openly boasted that he had achieved more in leisure than the others had achieved by arms.

He organized the public offices, the Palatine offices, and military service in the form that, with only a few alterations, still exists today.

Finally, he was consumed by a pitiable end, worn down by torment in every limb, to such an extent that he repeatedly begged his most trusted servants to offer him death, and he was kept under the guard of his dearest attendants so that he would not do violence to himself.

He did not win great glory for clemency, although he was extremely diligent concerning the treasury and military discipline.

He died in Campania at Baiae, in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the tenth month and twentieth day, at the age of sixty-two.

[Note: A. reads: “In Campania at Baiae, being more than sixty years old, in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the tenth month and twenty-second day. The Senate was unwilling to grant him…” Eutropius has the twenty-ninth day.]

The Senate refused to grant him divine honors. Nevertheless, when his successor, Titus Aurelius Antoninus Fulvius, strongly demanded this, and all the senators openly resisted, he finally prevailed.

## ANTONINUS PIUS
Therefore Hadrian was succeeded by M. Antoninus Fulvius Bojonius, the fifteenth from Augustus, later also called Pius, of distinguished but not very ancient lineage. Adopted by Hadrian as his son—whose son-in-law he had been—he was a remarkable man, who may rightly be compared with Numa Pompilius, just as Trajan might be equated with Romulus. He lived with immense [Col. 0884D] [Note: A.: “honesty,” privately, greater in private life than in the imperial office.] integrity, greater as a private citizen than in imperial power; harsh toward no one and benevolent toward all. In military affairs he sought moderate glory, preferring to defend the provinces rather than enlarge them. He sought the most upright men to administer the state, honored the good, and detested the wicked without any harshness [Note: A.: “Venerable, no less than fearsome, to friendly kings, so much so that many nations of barbarians, laying down their arms, brought their disputes and lawsuits to him and obeyed his judgment. He…”]. He strove to be a friend to kings. For twenty-three years he ruled the whole world by authority alone, without a single war, and all kings, nations, and peoples feared and loved him so greatly that they regarded him more as a parent or patron than as their lord or emperor; all, as though wishing him favorable like one of the heavenly powers, asked him to judge their disputes.

Indeed, the Indians, Bactrians, and Hyrcanians sent ambassadors after learning of the justice of so great an emperor, which he adorned with [Note: Bongarsius: “an unconquered, serene, and beautiful expression.”] a beautiful, composed face. He was tall in body and properly robust. Before coming out to be greeted, he tasted a little bread, lest, with the blood around his vital organs growing cold and his strength exhausted through fasting, he should collapse and thus be unable to perform the public duty that he carried out with extraordinary diligence, as though he were the model of an excellent head of household. He lacked any appetite for glory or display. He was so gentle that, when the senators pressed him to pursue those who had conspired against him, he restrained the investigation, knowing perfectly well that men eager to commit a crime against themselves did not need to be searched out too persistently; for if more were discovered, it would become clear how hateful he was to them.

This man had been extremely wealthy before becoming emperor, but by generously distributing all his possessions in soldiers’ pay and among [Note: A.: “reducing them through gifts to his friends.”] his friends, he diminished them. Nevertheless, he left behind a wealthy treasury. He was called Pius because of his clemency [Note: A.: “He was called so afterward. He died at his own estate near Orium, twelve miles from the City, in the seventy-seventh year of his life and the twenty-third of his reign, and so forth.”].

During his reign, the philosopher Justin presented Antoninus with a book composed in defense of the Christian religion and made him favorably disposed toward Christians. Not long afterward, when persecution against them was stirred up and intensified, he wrote a letter to all the peoples of Asia in these words:

> “I certainly do not doubt that even the gods themselves are concerned that no guilty person should remain hidden; for it is much more fitting for them to punish those who refuse to sacrifice to them than for you to do so. Yet you confirm the opinion that those whom you persecute hold concerning you, when they say that you are impious and without a god [Col. 0885C]. Hence they consider it preferable to lay down their lives for their God and willingly embrace death rather than submit to you and yield to the laws of your religion.
>
> “Concerning earthquakes, whether those that have occurred or those that are now occurring, it will not be absurd to console your grief with a fitting admonition. For I have learned that in such matters you transfer common disasters to the discredit of those people. In this respect, they gain greater confidence before God. You, however, whenever you are ignorant of such things, neglect the other gods, while expelling and driving out the worship of the immortal God whom the Christians worship, persecuting the adherents of that observance even to death. Concerning them, many governors of the provinces had also written to our revered father. He replied that they were to suffer no such harassment unless they were accused of attempting something against the condition of the Roman Empire.
>
> “Many others have also reported these matters to me, and, following my father’s judgment, I have replied with equal moderation. If anyone persists in bringing charges against such people without any crime having been committed, let the person reported on account of this name be acquitted, even if it should be proved that he is a Christian and that the charge brought against him is true. But let the person who brings the accusation be liable to the penalty he attempted to impose.”

This was publicly posted at Ephesus during the assembly of Asia.

At the same time, in Rome, the philosopher Arianus of Nicomedia was prominent as praetor, as were Maximus of Tyre, Apollonius the Stoic of Chalcedon, and Basilides [Note: Eusebius’s manuscript reads “Syropolitanus”; the printed text has “Cytopolitanus.”], the Cytopolitan. These men also became the emperor’s most genuine teachers.

Antoninus, therefore, was consumed by a fever lasting several days at his own villa near Lorias, twelve miles from the City, after completing the seventy-seventh year of his life and the twenty-third year of his reign [Note: Eutropius and Eusebius: “He died at his own villa near Lorias.” H. has “near Orium.”]. He was enrolled among the gods and deservedly consecrated [Note: A. omits the remainder: “After him M. Antoninus Verus reigned.”], so that temples, priests, and countless other honors were decreed in his name. He was so gentle that, when the Roman people pelted him with stones on suspicion of a shortage of grain, he preferred to calm the disturbance by explaining the situation rather than avenge the uprising.

## M. AURELIUS

In the year 911 from the founding of the City, M. Aurelius Antoninus Verus, the sixteenth from Augustus, obtained the imperial power. He was unquestionably of the noblest lineage, since his paternal descent went back to Numa Pompilius and his maternal descent to the king of Salentum. With him ruled L. Annius Antoninus Verus [Note: Thus also Eutropius. But H. has “L. Annius Antonius Severus.”]. Then for the first time the Roman Republic obeyed two men administering the empire with equal authority, whereas until that time it had always had only one Augustus [Note: A.: “Then for the first time the Roman…”].

The two were related both by descent and by marriage. Verus was Antoninus Pius’s grandson, while Antoninus was Antoninus Pius’s son-in-law through his wife, Galeria Faustina the Younger, his cousin [Note: Thus also the Hersfeld manuscript. But Eutropius has “Valeria.” See Orosius, the epitome of Victor, and Capitolinus, from whom the compiler of the *Miscellany* drew this passage. From this point, as almost always elsewhere, Paul the Deacon has somewhat more than Eutropius, while the author of the *Miscellany* sometimes adds more than the Deacon, as will be evident to anyone comparing them individually. CANIS.].

They waged war against Vologeses, king of the Parthians, who had rebelled for the first time after Trajan’s victory [Note: A.: “They had rebelled against Trajan. Verus Antoninus went there. He, while at Antioch…”] and was devastating Armenia, Cappadocia, and Syria in a violent invasion. L. Verus Antoninus went out to that war. While he was sacrificing at Athens, a fire was seen in the sky being carried from west to east. While he was operating at Antioch and around Armenia, he accomplished many great things through his generals. He captured Seleucia, the most famous city of Assyria, situated on the river Hydaspes, together with four hundred [Col. 0886D] thousand inhabitants. He brought back a Parthian triumph [Note: A.: “Afterward he brought it back: he celebrated a triumph with his brother and father-in-law. He died…”].

Nevertheless, he died in Venetia between Altinum and the city of Concordia, while traveling and sitting in a carriage with his brother, suddenly struck by blood in an attack of the disease that the Greeks call ἀπόπληξις [apoplexy] [Note: A.: “which they call it. A man of little civic character.”]. He was especially devoted to tragic poetry, of harsh and dissolute character, but, out of respect for his brother, never dared anything atrocious. He died in the eleventh year of his reign and was enrolled among the gods.

After him Marcus Antoninus Verus held the state alone. Anyone could more easily admire him than praise him. From the beginning of his life he was utterly tranquil, so much so that even from infancy he altered his expression neither from joy nor from sorrow [Note: A.: “did not change it.”]. He was devoted to Stoic philosophy. He himself was a philosopher not only in the habits of his life but also in learning, and while still a young man was so remarkable that Hadrian prepared to leave him as his successor. After adopting Antoninus Pius, however, Hadrian wished him to be Pius’s son-in-law [Note: A.: “his son-in-law. For this reason…”], so that in this order he might reach the imperial power.

He was trained in philosophy by Apollonius of Chalcedon and in knowledge of Greek literature [Note: A.: “by Sextus of Chaeronea, and so forth.”] by Sextus of Chaeronea, the grandson of Plutarch. Fronto, the most distinguished orator, taught him Latin literature.

He dealt with everyone in Rome on equal terms and was elevated by no arrogance [Note: A.: “He was not elated by the height of imperial power. He was most ready in generosity. The provinces…”]. He used the height of imperial power generously and with great readiness. He governed the provinces with immense benevolence and moderation. Under this emperor, affairs were successfully conducted against the Germans.

He possessed every virtue and a heavenly intellect, and was placed, as it were, as a defender against public calamities. For if he had not been born for those times, surely everything in the Roman state would have collapsed as in a single fall. There was never peace in arms; wars raged throughout the entire East, Illyricum, and Italy [Col. 0887C]. Earthquakes, not without the destruction of cities; floods of rivers; frequent plagues; armies of locusts ravaging the fields—in short, scarcely anything that mortals are accustomed to call or imagine as capable of wearing them down through the greatest anguish failed to rage during his reign. I believe that this was divinely assigned, so that while the law or nature of the world gives birth to something unknown to human beings, it might be softened by the counsels of rulers as by medicinal remedies.

He allowed distinguished men to hold banquets with the same furnishings and similar servants as he himself used.

During these days, in the course of the Parthian war, he ordered the fourth persecution of Christians since Nero to be carried out. It became so severe at his command that many saints in Asia and Gaul were crowned with martyrdom.

He himself waged one war, against the Marcomanni, but it was of such magnitude that no memory records anything comparable, so that it may be compared with the Punic Wars. It was made more serious because entire Roman armies had perished. Under him the plague was so great that, after the Persian victory, a very large part of the population in Rome, throughout Italy, and in the provinces, and almost all the military forces, were weakened by disease.

Thus, after he had persisted for three continuous years at Carnuntum with immense labor and moderation, he brought the Marcomannic War to an end [Note: A.: “which the Quadi were waging.”]. The Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Suebi, and almost all Germania were waging it with them [Note: A.: “all the barbarians joined in, killed many thousands of men, and [did so] to the Pannonians…”]. The army advanced as far as the territory of the Quadi, but was surrounded by the enemy. Because of the lack of water, it faced both the danger of thirst and the danger posed by the enemy. Then, at the invocation of the name of Christ, which certain soldiers publicly uttered as they poured themselves into prayer with great steadfastness of faith, such a force of rain poured down that it restored the Romans most abundantly and without harm. The barbarians, however, terrified by repeated lightning strikes—especially since many of them were killed—were forced to flee.

The Romans pursued them, slaughtering them to annihilation, and won a most glorious victory, one to be preferred to almost all the triumphs of antiquity, with a small and untrained number of soldiers but with the most powerful aid of Christ. Many thousands of men were therefore killed, and the Pannonians were freed from slavery [Note: A.: “He returned to Rome.”]. He again celebrated a triumph at Rome with his son Commodus Antoninus, whom he had made Caesar.

To finance this war, when the treasury had been exhausted and he had no gifts left to distribute to the soldiers, and when he was unwilling to impose anything upon the Senate or the provincials, he sold the articles of imperial luxury after they had been displayed for a long time in Trajan’s Forum: golden vessels, crystal and myrrhine cups, his wife’s and his own silk and golden garments, and many jeweled ornaments. The sale continued for two uninterrupted months, and a great deal of gold was raised.

After the victory, however, he returned the purchase price to those buyers who wished to return what they had bought. He troubled no one who preferred to retain what had once been purchased [Note: A.: “to retain it. He allowed distinguished men to hold banquets with the same furnishings as himself and with similar servants. In the edition…”].

At the presentation of public entertainments he was so magnificent [Note: A.: “in the presentation of entertainments after the victory, so much so…”] that he is said to have exhibited one hundred [Note: A.: “at one time.”] lions at once.

During his reign Cassius, having seized tyranny, was killed. He also remitted the taxes imposed in earlier times throughout all the provinces and ordered all the defamatory records of fiscal proceedings to be gathered together and burned in the Forum. He moderated the harsher laws with new enactments.

At the same time Galen, the excellent physician of Pergamene origin, was prominent at Rome. Salvius Julianus was publishing laws at Rome; the rhetor Fronto, the sophist Aristides of Smyrna, the poet Oppian, and the Platonic philosopher Atticus were also at Rome.

After restoring the state to prosperity through virtue and gentleness, he died in Campania near the town of Vendobona, in the eighteenth year of his reign and the sixty-first year of his life [Note: A.: “and, with everyone striving eagerly, he was enrolled among the gods.”].

When news of his death reached Rome, the City was thrown into public mourning. The Senate assembled in the curia dressed in gloomy clothing, and everyone, with one accord, anticipated what had scarcely been believed even of Romulus: that Marcus had been received into heaven. In his honor temples, columns, and many other memorials were decreed.

## COMMODUS

[Col. 0889A]

His successor was L. Aurelius Commodus, his son, who was himself also called Antoninus and was made the seventeenth emperor from Augustus. From the very beginning he showed what he would become. When his father, near death, warned him not to allow the barbarians, already worn down, to recover their strength, he replied: “An undertaking can be completed by the living, even if gradually; from the dead, nothing.”

He possessed nothing of his father except that he too fought successfully against the Germans. He attempted to transfer the month of September to his own name, so that it would be called Commodus. But he was corrupted by the greatest disgrace of luxury and obscenity [Note: A.: “by the obscenity of his wife.”], and he very frequently fought in gladiatorial contests in the arena. Later he also fought in the amphitheater against men of this kind [Note: A.: “He fought against such men. He died a sudden death, so that he is thought to have been strangled or killed by poison, after ruling twelve years and eight months following his father, amid such universal execration that he was judged an enemy of the human race even after death.”], and against wild beasts.

He also killed many senators, especially those whom he observed to excel in nobility and ability, as though they were a reproach to the king’s crimes [Note: The passage is displaced and should be restored from Orosius. CANIS.]. Among them he killed Salvius Julianus, the legislator.

Punishment overtook the City. The Capitol was struck by lightning, and the resulting fire, driven by a ravenous whirlwind, burned the library that had been assembled through the care and diligence of the ancestors, along with other nearby buildings. Later another fire broke out at Rome and leveled the temple of Vesta, the palace, and a large part of the City.

His wife was Martia, of freedman origin, though endowed with beauty and the arts of a courtesan. After she had completely bound his mind to her, she offered him a cup of poison as he came out of the bath. Finally, after a very strong wrestler sent in for the purpose compressed his throat, he expired in the house of Vestilianus, having ruled twelve years and eight months after his father, in the twenty-second year of his life.

## PERTINAX

He was succeeded by Helvius Pertinax, who obtained the imperial power as the eighteenth from Augustus. He was an old man, having reached the age of seventy [Note: Thus Eusebius, Capitolinus, and Victor have “sixty.”], and was then serving as prefect of the City. By a decree of the Senate [Note: A.: “By decree of the Senate he was ordered to rule on the eightieth day of the reign.”] he was compelled, against his will, to accept the imperial power. Hence he acquired that surname.

On the eighty-first day of his reign he was butchered with many wounds in a mutiny of the praetorian soldiers and through the crime of Salvius Julianus [Note: A.: “He was killed by the crime of Salvius Julianus.”]. His head was carried throughout the City.

He died in this manner—a man who, as an example of human advancement, rose through every kind of labor to the highest honors, so much so that he was called Fortune’s ball. He was of humble origin, for he was born to a freedman father. He had been a teacher of the literature taught by grammarians on the barren estate of Lollius Gentianus among the Ligurians; even while serving as prefect, he most generously acknowledged himself to be that man’s client.

He was more affable than beneficent. Hence they called him by the Greek name χρηστόλογος (*chrestologos*, “speaker of gracious words”). He was never moved to revenge an injury he had received. He loved simplicity. In speech, at table, and in his manner of walking, he presented himself as an ordinary man.

After his death, the title of divine was decreed for him. In praise of him, applause was repeatedly raised until their voices failed:

> “While Pertinax ruled, we lived in safety; we feared no one! Father of the pious, Father of the Senate, Father of all good men!”

## DIDIUS JULIANUS

After him Didius [Note: A.: “Sabinus.”] Salvius Julianus, a native of Milan, seized control of the state as the nineteenth from Augustus. He was a nobleman and highly skilled in law, the grandson of Salvius Julianus, who under the deified [Note: A.: “Hadrian.”] Antoninus composed the perpetual edict [Note: A.: “After the edict.”]. He was factious, rash, and greedy for power.

At this time Pescennius Niger was created Augustus at Antioch, and Septimius Severus at the town of Sabaria in Pannonia [Note: Victor has “in Sabatia Pannonia.”]. Julianus was defeated by Severus in the civil war at the Milvian Bridge. While fleeing, he was captured in the palace, led into a secluded palace bath, and, with his neck extended like a condemned man’s, was beheaded. His head was placed on the Rostra, seven months after he had begun to rule [Note: A.: “He was defeated and killed by Severus at the Milvian Bridge and in the palace. He lived seven months after…”].

## SEPT. SEVERUS

In the year 947 from the founding of the City [Note: Orosius has 844.], Septimius Severus, the twentieth after Augustus, assumed the administration of the Roman Empire [Note: A. reads: “From this point Septimius Severus, a Roman…”].

He was from Africa, from the province of Tripolitania, from the town of Lepcis. He alone, in all recorded memory, both before and afterward, was an emperor from Africa [Note: A.: “The only one of all.”]. At first he was an advocate of the treasury, then a military tribune, and afterward, through many different offices and honors, rose to the administration of the entire state [Col. 0890C] [Note: A.: “He came. He wished to be called Pertinax in honor of that Pertinax who had been killed by Julianus. He was exceedingly frugal, naturally harsh. Many things…”].

He waged many wars successfully. He killed Pescennius Niger, a man of every kind of depravity who had rebelled in Egypt and Syria, at Cyzicus [Note: A. has “Fescennius”; Victor has “Pescennius.”]. He defeated the Parthians, the interior Arabs, and the Adiabenes [Note: A.: “Azabenes.”]. He overcame the Arabs so completely that he even established a province there. For this reason he was called Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus [Note: Likewise, “Azabenicus.”].

He restored many things throughout the Roman world. Under him Clodius Albinus, who had been Julianus’s accomplice in killing Pertinax, made himself Caesar in Gaul. He was defeated and killed at Lugdunum.
