Severus was the most warlike of all who had preceded him: harsh in character and persevering to the end in everything he undertook, while in benevolence he was astonishing [Col. 0890D] and constant wherever he inclined. He was diligent in acquiring and generous in giving, equally forceful toward friends and enemies. Thus he enriched Lateranus Cilo, Anulinus Bassus [Note: Victor has “Amulinus.”], and many others, also with houses worthy of mention, chief among them those we see called the Parthian and the Lateran.

He allowed no honors to be sold under his rule. He restrained the Jews and Samaritans, who were attempting to rebel, by force of arms. He subjected Christians to the fifth persecution since Nero, and many saints in various provinces were crowned with martyrdom.

Therefore Severus was distinguished not only for military glory but also for civil pursuits. He was learned in Latin literature, fully accomplished in philosophy, educated in Greek speech, and more fluent in Punic eloquence.

His final war was in Britain [Note: A.: “And so that…”]. He fortified the recovered provinces with complete security [Note: A.: “He fortified them with a wall twenty-two thousand paces long, and so forth.”]. Thus he constructed a great ditch and a very strong wall, strengthened further by frequent towers, for 132,000 paces [Col. 0891B] from sea to sea [Note: A.: “He extended it. He died at Eboracum in extreme old age, in the sixteenth year of his reign and the third month, and was made divine, and so forth.”].

There, at the town of Eboracum, when he could no longer endure the pain in all his limbs, especially his feet, he greedily attacked heavy foods and large quantities of meat as a substitute for the poison that had been denied him. Since he could not digest them, he died under the pressure of indigestion in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the tenth month, at the age of sixty-five, and was called divine.

He left two sons as successors, Bassianus and Geta. Bassianus asked the Senate to impose upon him the name Antoninus [Note: A.: “He wished it.”].

## CARACALLA

Thus he was called M. Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus Caracalla [Note: A.: “Bassianus, also called Caracalla because of his character…”], and he succeeded his father. He was born at Lugdunum.

This Bassianus was so called from the name of his maternal grandfather. But when he had brought a large quantity of clothing from Gaul and had made long, ankle-length garments called *caracallae* [Col. 0891C], and had compelled the common people to enter dressed in such garments in order to greet him, he received the surname Caracalla from the name of this sort of clothing.

He killed his brother Geta, for which crime he paid the penalty in madness, being pursued by the avenging Furies, rightly called the *Ultrices*, from whose madness he later recovered.

When he saw the body of Alexander of Macedon, he ordered himself to be called Alexander the Great. He was led so far by the deceptions of flatterers that, with a grim expression and his neck turned toward his left shoulder—imitating what he had noticed in Alexander’s face—he walked about trying to convince himself that his appearance was extremely similar.

He was generally like his father in character, though somewhat harsher and more threatening. At Rome he built an excellent work, the baths called the Antonine Baths [Note: A.: “the bathhouse called Antoninian.”], but nothing else memorable.

He was a man of uncontrolled lust who married his stepmother Julia [Note: A.: “He took her as his wife. He died in Osrhoene near Edessa while preparing an expedition against the Parthians in the year…”].

While preparing and setting out on an expedition against the Parthians, he was traveling toward Carrhae. At Edessa in Osrhoene, he withdrew to attend to natural needs and was killed by a soldier who was following him as though to guard him. This occurred in the sixth year of his reign, in the second month, when he had scarcely passed his forty-third year of life [Note: A.: “of his age.”]. His body was carried to Rome in a public funeral [Note: A.: “was carried out.”].

## MACRINUS

Next, Opilius Macrinus, who had been prefect of the praetorian guard, and his son Diadumenus were created emperors by the army. Because of the brevity of their time, they accomplished nothing memorable. Their rule lasted two months and one year [Note: A.: “It lasted. Both were killed together in a military mutiny.”]. Both were cut down by the same army at Archelais because Macrinus was restraining military luxury and excessive pay.

## HELIOGABALUS

In the year 972 from the founding of the City, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Varius was created emperor, the twenty-third from Augustus. He was believed to be the son of Antoninus Caracalla by Semea, his secretly violated cousin [Note: A.: “He was believed to be his son.”]. He was a priest of the temple of Heliogabalus, and therefore was called Heliogabalus.

The grandfather of his mother Semea had been named Bassianus. He was a priest of the Sun, whom the Phoenicians, from whom he came, called Heliogabalus. From him this man was called Heliogabalus.

When he came to Rome amid enormous expectation from both soldiers and Senate, he polluted himself with every disgrace and lived most shamefully and obscenely. Turning upon himself the desire for sexual intercourse that, because of a defect of nature, he could not satisfy, he ordered himself to be called Bassiana instead of Bassianus.

He joined a Vestal virgin to himself as though in marriage, and, after cutting off his genitals, consecrated himself to the Great Mother. He made his cousin Marcellus, who afterward was called Alexander, Caesar.

Two years and eight months after he had begun to rule [Col. 0892C], he was killed at Rome in a military disturbance, in the sixteenth year of his life, and with him his wretched mother [Note: A.: “Suriasera.”].

The soldiers dragged his body through the streets of the City like a dog’s corpse, calling him, in a military jest, the whelp of an untamed and rabid lust. Finally, when the narrow opening of a sewer could not receive the body, they carried it as far as the Tiber, attached a weight so that it would never rise, and threw it into the river. From these events the Tiber was called *Tractitius*.

## ALEX. SEVERUS

In the year 975 from the founding of the City, he was succeeded by Aurelius Severus Alexander, the twenty-fourth from Augustus, called Caesar by the army and Augustus by the Senate, while still a very young man [Note: A.: “Aurelianus.”].

After undertaking a war against the Persians, he most gloriously defeated their king Xerxes [Note: Lampridius has “Artaxerxes.”]. He governed military discipline with the greatest severity and discharged whole legions that had begun disturbances. He had Ulpian, the founder of jurisprudence, as his assessor or master of the offices [Note: A.: “the founder. He was also popular at Rome. He perished in Gaul in a military disturbance in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the day…”].

His mother Mammea arranged to hear the Christian presbyter Origen. He was also good for the state, though troubled in himself.

During his reign Taurinus was made Augustus in the East, but, out of fear, threw himself into the river Euphrates. At that time Julius Maximinus also seized power in Gaul, after corrupting many of the army.

When Alexander saw that his guards were abandoning him near Mainz, he exclaimed that his mother had been the cause of his death. When an attacker rushed upon him, he wrapped his head, offered his neck, and presented it to be violently compressed by the man’s hands. This occurred in the twenty-sixth year of his life, the thirteenth year of his reign, and the eighth day of the month.

He was exceptionally dutiful toward his mother Mammea, and for this reason beloved by everyone. She had compelled her son to ensure that even the small leftovers from the table and meal, though already partly eaten, were set aside for another banquet.

## MAXIMINUS

[Col. 0893B]

After him [Note: These are the words with which Eutropius, Paul the Deacon in Book IX, and our A. begin; A. has “Maximianus, the first to attain the imperial power from the military association alone,” and so forth.] Julius Maximinus, a Thracian by origin, came to power as the twenty-fifth from Augustus, in the year 988 from the founding of the City.

He was the first emperor to be made from the military ranks, solely by the soldiers’ will, with no authority of the Senate intervening; nor was he himself a senator. After successfully waging war against the Germans [Note: A.: “After the war had been conducted, when he had been proclaimed emperor by the soldiers, he was killed at Aquileia by Pupienus, after they had handed him over…”], he was killed at Aquileia by Pupienus while persecuting both innocent and guilty wealthy men. His soldiers deserted him, together with his son Diadumenus, still a boy, with whom he had ruled for three years and a few days. Everyone shouted in military jest: “Not even a puppy should be kept from the worst stock.”

He carried out the sixth persecution of Christians after Nero. During his reign, the two Gordians, father and son, seized the principate and died one after the other.

## GORDIANUS

[Col. 0893C]

Next Gordianus, the grandson of Gordianus through his son, was made emperor, the twenty-sixth from Augustus. He was born at Rome to a most distinguished father, who, by the consent of the soldiers, was chosen leader while serving as proconsul of Africa during the reign of Maximinus [Note: A.: “had been elected.”].

When Gordianus therefore came to Rome, Balbinus and Pupienus [Note: A.: “were killed in the palace; only Gordianus was reserved for the imperial power. Gordianus…”]—brothers—were killed.

Gordianus was still very young. After marrying Tranquillina at Rome, he opened the gates of the Temple of Janus, which I do not recall anyone having written were opened after Vespasian and Titus. He then set out for the East and brought war against the Parthians, who were already preparing to break out. He conducted the war successfully and inflicted great defeats upon the Persians.

On his return, not far from the Roman frontier, he was killed near the Persian city of Ctesiphon through the treachery of Philip, the prefect of the praetorian guard, who ruled after him. Philip had stirred the soldiers to revolt. This occurred in the twentieth year of Gordianus’s life and the sixth year of his reign.

The soldiers built him a tomb at the twentieth milestone from Circesium [Note: A.: “Circessus.”], a fortress that is now Roman and overlooks the Euphrates, and gave the place the name Tomb of Gordianus. They carried his remains to Rome and called him divine.

During his reign, Porphyry, the student of the Platonic philosopher Plotinus, was esteemed at Rome; the philosopher Theopompus was prominent at Chaeronea, and the sophist Nicanor at Athens.

## PHILIPPUS

[Note: A.: “There were two Philips, son and father. After Gordianus was killed, they seized the imperial power and the army…”]

In the year 997 from the founding of the City, M. Julius Philippus, the twenty-seventh from Augustus, together with his son Gaius Julius Saturninus Philippus [Note: Victor has “Gallus.”], seized the imperial power. They departed from Syria and brought the army back safely to Italy.

They were the first of all emperors to become Christians at Rome. On the day of Easter, that is, during the very vigil, when they wished to be present and share in the mysteries, the Roman bishop Fabian did not permit them to do so until the emperor confessed his sins and stood among the penitents. He was not to have access to the mysteries in any way unless, through penance, he first washed away the many offenses reported against him.

It is therefore said that he willingly accepted what the priest had commanded him, demonstrating by his actions and deeds that he possessed divine fear and the fullest faith in the religion.

In the third year of their reign, the thousandth year of the city of Rome was celebrated with an immense display of games and spectacles.

Both were later killed by the army: the elder Philippus at Verona, with the middle of his head cut off above the rows of teeth; the younger at Rome, after they had ruled for five years. Nevertheless, both were enrolled among the gods.

The younger Philippus was twelve years old when he was killed [Col. 0894C]. He had such a severe and gloomy disposition that, even then, from the age of five, no joke whatsoever could make him laugh. He noticed his father laughing too loudly at the secular games, although he was still a tender child, and marked it with an averted expression.

This Philippus was born in the humblest station, the son of a highly distinguished father who had been a leader of brigands.

## DECIUS
[Note: A.: After these, Decius, etc.] In the year 1003 from the founding of the City, Decius, from Lower Pannonia and born at Bubalia, the twenty-eighth after Augustus, seized the empire after Philip had been killed. [Note: A.: assumed it.] He was the seventh after Nero to issue deadly edicts for persecuting and killing Christians, and he sent very many of the saints from their torments to the crowns of Christ. [Col. 0894D] He suppressed the civil war that had arisen in Gaul and made his son Decius Caesar. He built a bath at Rome. [Note: A.: He built it. When he and his son had ruled for two years, both were killed in a war against the barbarians; of them the elder was swallowed up in a whirlpool, etc.] A man equipped with skill and every virtue, he was calm and approachable at home, and most energetic in arms. During his reign, when very many Goths had crossed the river Ister, devastating the cities of the Romans, [Col. 0895A] they captured and ravaged Misa and Nicopolis. Decius, however, attacked them in war together with his son and, at Abritus—a place called Foroterebronium—killed thirty thousand barbarians, while losing very many of his own men, especially Thracians. He himself too was drowned in the same war amid the confused crowds, in a swamp’s whirlpool, so that even his body could not be found. [Note: A.: be found; condemned by a fitting judgment, since, having initiated persecution against the Christians, he also destroyed among others the most blessed Lawrence, deacon and martyr.] His son too was killed in the war, in the second year of his reign. The Scythians, however, returned with very much booty and many captives, leaving behind Philippopolis, a city of Macedonia, deserted. In his time Valens Licinianus was made emperor and immediately killed.

## GALLUS

[Note: A.: Soon the emperors Gallus Hostilianus and Gallus’s son Volusianus were created. Under them Aemilianus attempted a revolution in Moesia; when both had set out to suppress him, they were killed at Interamna, before completing two years. Nothing, etc.] Soon the army created as emperors Virius Gallus and Gallus’s son Volusianus. During their reign [Col. 0895B] Hostilianus Perpenna was made emperor by the senate, but not long afterward was carried off by the plague. Under them Aemilianus too was made emperor in Moesia. Both emperors marched against him and, while preparing a civil war near Interamna, were cut down by their own army, in approximately the forty-seventh year of the father’s life and the second year of his reign; they had been born on the island of Meninge, which is now called Girba. Their rule achieved nothing at all that was noteworthy; it was known only for plague, diseases, and illnesses. [Note: A.: their reign was known for this.] For scarcely any Roman province, city, or household existed that was not afflicted and devastated by that general pestilence.

## AEMILIANUS

[Note: Aemilianus, born in the greatest obscurity, ruled in still greater obscurity; for he had been a Moor and was killed in the third month.] Aemilianus, a Moor by origin and born in the greatest obscurity, ruled in still greater obscurity. For he was greedy and, in the fourth month, was condemned at Spoletium—or at the bridge which, they say, received the name Sanguinarius from his killing, between Otriculi and Narnia, situated midway by region between Spoletium and the city of Rome—and was killed in the forty-seventh year of his life. [Col. 0895C]

## VALERIANUS

[Note: A.: Hence Licinius Valerianus in Raetia, etc.] In the year 1008 from the founding of the City, Licinius Valerianus, surnamed Colobius, the thirtieth after Augustus, while residing in Raetia and Noricum, was made emperor by the army and soon Augustus. His son Gallienus too was called Caesar at Rome by the senate. [Note: A.: was called. Their rule was harmful and almost fatal to the Roman name, so that, whether because of the emperors’ misfortune or their cowardice, the Germans came as far as Ravenna. Valerianus, etc.] He was born to very illustrious parents, yet was stupid and extremely sluggish, and suited neither by judgment nor by deeds to any practical conduct of public affairs. He made Cornelius Valerianus, his son Gallienus’s son, Caesar. During their reign the Germans also reached Ravenna. While they were ruling, Regilianus in Moesia and Cassius Labienus Posthumus in Gaul, after Gallienus’s son had been killed, became emperors. In the same way [Note: Victor: Aelianus.] Lolianus at Mainz, [Col. 0896A] Aemilianus in Egypt, Valens among the Macedonians, and Aureolus at Milan seized power.

Then the Goths again crossed the Ister and ravaged Thessalonica, a city of Illyricum; loaded with booty, they returned to their own country. At that time the Heruli too, sailing in five hundred ships through the Maeotian marshes toward the Pontus, captured Byzantium and Chrysopolis. Valerianus, therefore, while waging war in Mesopotamia, was defeated by Sapor, king of the Persians. Soon afterward he was captured and grew old among the Parthians in disgraceful slavery. For as long as he lived, the king of that province used to mount his horse by bending him down and placing his foot upon his neck. He, the eighth after Nero, as soon as he seized power, compelled Christians by tortures to sacrifice to idols and ordered those who refused to be killed; the blood of the saints was poured out across the whole breadth of the Roman realm.

## GALIENUS

[Col. 0896B]

Gallienus, his son, therefore substituted another son, Salonianus, in place of Cornelius, his son’s son. He was devoted to the diverse love of mistresses: Salonina, his wife, and a concubine named Pipa, whom he had received from her father, the king of the Marcomanni, under the appearance of marriage, after granting him part of Upper Pannonia. [Note: Pollio: Pipara.]

Meanwhile Gallienus, when he had become a young Augustus, at first conducted the empire successfully, then tolerably, and finally disastrously. [Note: A.: at first ruled successfully, etc.] For as a young man he performed many energetic deeds in Gaul and Illyricum: he killed Ingenuus at Mursa, who had assumed the purple, and Regillianus; for a long time he was calm and tranquil, but then, dissolving into every kind of licentiousness, loosened the reins of government through disgraceful indolence and despair. The Alemanni, after devastating Gaul, penetrated into Italy. [Col. 0896C] Dacia, which Trajan had added beyond the Danube, was then lost. Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were ravaged by the Goths; Pannonia was devastated by the Sarmatians and Quadi. The Germans penetrated as far as Spain. After occupying Mesopotamia, the Parthians began to claim Syria for themselves.

When affairs were already desperate and the Roman empire had almost been destroyed, Posthumus, born in the greatest obscurity in Gaul, assumed the purple and ruled for ten years in such a way that he restored the nearly exhausted provinces with immense courage and moderation. He was killed in a mutiny of the soldiers because he had refused to hand over Mainz, which had rebelled against him while Lolianus was attempting a revolution, to be plundered by the troops. After him Marius, a most worthless craftsman, received the purple and was killed on the second day. Victorinus afterward received the government of Gaul, a most energetic man. But because he was excessively lustful and corrupted other men’s marriages, he was killed at Agrippina. [Note: A.: Octoarius.] A certain staff officer, Octoarius, had contrived the plot, in the second year of his reign. [Col. 0897A]

Tetricus, a senator, succeeded him. While administering Aquitania with the rank of governor, he was elected emperor in his absence by the soldiers and assumed the purple at Bordeaux, but endured many mutinies of the troops. While these events were taking place in Gaul, in the East the Persians were defeated by Odenathus: Syria was defended, Mesopotamia recovered, and Odenathus advanced as far as Ctesiphon. [Note: A.: He always calls him Odenachus.]

Thus, when Gallienus had abandoned the state, the Roman empire was preserved in the West by Posthumus and in the East by Odenathus. Meanwhile Gallienus marched against Aureolus. After he had driven him into Milan and besieged him at the bridge which, from his name, is called Aureolus, he was killed by his own men, together with his brother Valerianus, through a stratagem of that same commander, Aureolus. [Note: A.: Meanwhile Gallienus was killed at Milan, together with his brother Valerianus, through the treachery of his commander Aureolus, in the ninth year of his reign.] He ruled for fifteen years—six with his father and nine alone. He lived fifty years.

## CLAUDIUS

In the year 1024 from the founding of the City, Claudius, the thirty-first after Augustus, succeeded him. Chosen by the soldiers, he was proclaimed Augustus by the senate. Many think that he was descended from Gordianus, while, as a young man, he was being educated for marriage by a mature woman. This Claudius was designated emperor by the dying Gallienus, who, while stationed at Ticinum, had sent him the imperial garments through Gallonius Basilius.

He destroyed in a great battle and with an incredible slaughter the Goths who, scattered throughout Illyricum and Macedonia under Decius, had ravaged them for fifteen years. [Note: A.: whom he defeated in a great battle after they had ravaged Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years.] He was a frugal and modest man, steadfast in justice, and suitable for administering the state. After Aureolus had been killed by his own men and the legions recovered, he fought near Lake Benacus against three hundred thousand Alemanni. [Note: A.: at Lake Benacus, fighting in a forest called Ligana, etc.] He routed so great a multitude [Note: A.: he routed such a multitude of armies, etc.] that scarcely half survived.

Claudius, however, having learned from the prophetic books which he had ordered to be consulted that the plague required the death of the chief man in the senate as its remedy, though Pomponius Bassus, who was then the leading senator, offered himself. Claudius gave his own life to the state, so that the oracle should not prove false. Nevertheless, within two years of his reign he died of illness at Sirmium and was proclaimed a god. [Note: A.: He was proclaimed one. The senate honored him greatly, namely, by ordering that a golden shield be placed for him in the senate house and likewise a golden statue on the Capitol.] He had declared beforehand that no man of such rank should be regarded as superior to the emperor. Since this act was pleasing to all, the nobles consecrated for him not only the divine title but also a golden statue near the image of Jupiter himself on the Capitol, as well as a golden shield in the senate house.

## QUINTILIUS

[Col. 0897D]

After him Quintilius, Claudius’s brother, was elected emperor by the agreement of the soldiers. A man of exceptional moderation and civility, equal or superior to his brother, he was proclaimed Augustus with the consent of the senate and was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign.

## AURELIANUS

[Col. 0898A]

[Note: A.: After him Aurelianus took up the empire.] In the year 1027 from the founding of the City, Aurelianus, the thirty-second after Augustus, was made emperor. Born to a father of modest station and, as some report, a tenant of the famous senator Aurelius, he was a native of Dacia Ripensis, which lies between Dacia and Macedonia. He was a powerful man in war, though immoderate in spirit and rather inclined to cruelty. He defeated the Goths most energetically on the Danube and restored Roman dominion to its ancient boundaries.

He was not unlike Alexander the Great or Caesar the dictator. For he recovered the Roman world from its invaders in three years, whereas Alexander reached India through immense victories in thirteen years and Gaius Caesar subdued the Gauls in ten years, while fighting against his fellow citizens for four. Aurelianus was victorious in three battles in Italy: at Placentia, near the river Metaurus, and at Fanum Fortunae, and finally on the fields of Ticinum.

During his reign Septimius was made emperor among the Dalmatians [Note: A.: Septiminus.] and soon was slaughtered by his own men. Aurelianus was the first among the Romans to fasten a diadem to his head and to use gems and an entirely golden garment, something that had previously seemed almost unknown in Roman custom. He enclosed the City with stronger and broader walls and built a temple of the Sun, in which he amassed an immeasurable quantity of gold and gems. He instituted the use of pork for the people.

In Gaul he defeated Tetricus at Châlons, after Tetricus had betrayed his own army, whose constant mutinies he could not endure. Indeed, in secret letters he had begged Aurelianus so earnestly that, among other things, he used a verse of Virgil:

> Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one.

Aurelianus promoted him to be governor of Lucania. [Note: A.: Claudius, the corrector.] He accompanied the promotion with an elegant jest: “It is better to govern some part of Italy than to rule beyond the Alps.”

He also captured Zenobia, after the killing of her husband Odenathus, who held the East, not far from Antioch, more through the terror of battle than through battle itself. [Note: A.: He defeated her near Antioch without a serious battle.] Entering Rome, he celebrated a magnificent triumph as the restorer of East and West, with Tetricus and Zenobia preceding his chariot.

During his reign the moneyers in the City also rebelled, debasing the currency and killing Felicissimus, the financial administrator. [Note: A.: the rationalis.] [Note: Vopiscus says: at the instigation of.] Aurelianus suppressed them with the utmost cruelty after their defeat and condemned many nobles to death. He was savage and bloodthirsty, and in some respects necessary [Note: A.: than in war.] but in none a lovable emperor, grim at all times, even after killing his sister’s son. [Note: A.: the killer of his sister’s son.] Nevertheless, he was to a great extent a corrector of military discipline and dissolute morals.

He abandoned the province of Dacia which Trajan had established beyond the Danube, despairing of being able to retain it after all Illyricum [Col. 0899A] and Moesia had been devastated. He transferred the Romans removed from the cities and fields of Dacia to central Moesia and called that region Dacia; it now divides the two Moesias and lies on the right bank of the Danube as it flows into the sea, whereas previously it had been on the left.

When he, the ninth after Nero, decreed that persecution should be carried out against the Christians, lightning struck before him, greatly terrifying those standing around. Not long afterward he was killed on the road through the treachery of his slave, who carried to certain military men, his master’s friends, a written list of their names, falsely imitating Aurelianus’s hand, as though Aurelianus were preparing to kill them. Thus, to forestall him, they killed him themselves midway along the road between Byzantium and Heraclea, at a place on the old highway called Cenophrurium. His death, however, did not go unavenged, and he also deserved to be numbered among the gods. He ruled for five years and six months.

## TACITUS

After him Tacitus, the thirty-third after Augustus, assumed the empire. He was a man of exceptionally good character and suitable for administering the state, but he was able to display nothing. [Note: A.: He was overtaken by death within the sixth month of his reign.] For within the two hundredth day of his reign he died of fever at Tarsus.

## FLORIANUS

Florianus, who had succeeded Tacitus, remained in power for two months and twenty days. [Note: A.: and achieved nothing worthy of remembrance.] But when the greater part of the army chose Probus, experienced in military affairs, Florianus, having treated the empire as though in play, brought about his own death by cutting his veins and bleeding to death.

## PROBUS

[Col. 0899C]

[Note: A.: After him Probus, a man illustrious for glory, etc.] In the year 1033 from the founding of the City, Probus, the thirty-fifth after Augustus, attained the empire. Born to a rustic father devoted to gardening, a Dalmatian by name [Note: Victor: by blood.], he entered the administration of the state with military glory. He restored the Gauls, occupied by barbarians, with extraordinary success in battle. [Note: A.: He restored them. Certain men who attempted to usurp the empire—namely Saturninus in the East, Proculus, etc.]

He then fought two civil wars, and indeed with much bloodshed, against certain emperors created by the army: one in the East against Saturninus, the other against Proculus and Bonosus of Agrippina, whom he crushed in great struggles. He permitted the Gauls and Pannonians to possess vineyards. By military labor he planted Mount Alma near Sirmium and Mount Aureus in Upper Moesia with vines, and gave them to the provincials to cultivate.

After waging countless wars and restoring peace, he said that soldiers would soon no longer be necessary. He was a keen, energetic, and just man, equal to Aurelianus in military glory and superior to him in civilized conduct. Nevertheless, he was killed at Sirmium in a mutiny of the soldiers, in an iron-plated tower. He ruled for six years and four months.

## CARUS

[Note: A.: After him Carus was made Augustus at Narbo.] In the year 1040 from the founding of the City, Carus, born at Narbo in Gaul, the thirty-sixth after Augustus, ruled. He immediately made his sons Carinus and Numerianus Caesars, and ruled with them for two years.

While he was waging war against the Sarmatians, news arrived of disturbances among the Persians, and he set out for the East. While he was staying at Antioch, his son Numerianus wished to enter a church to investigate the mysteries of the Christians. But Saint Babylas prevented him, saying: “It is not permitted for you to see the divine mysteries of the Christians, since you are polluted by sacrifices to idols.” Enraged, he killed him.

Carus performed notable deeds against the Persians, defeated them in battle, and captured the most famous cities of Seleucia and Ctesiphon. [Note: A.: Sohonem; others, Sohenem. Orosius: Cochen. C. manuscript of Fabri: Sohaenen.] When he had his camp above the Tigris, he perished by the force of a divine thunderbolt.

His son Numerianus, whom he had taken with him as Caesar against the Persians, was a young man of excellent promise. When he was being carried on a litter because he was suffering from pain in his eyes, he was treacherously killed at the instigation of Aper, who had been his father-in-law. [Note: Victor: in a small bed. A. likewise.] His death was concealed by deceit until Aper could seize the empire, but the crime was exposed by the stench of the corpse. For the soldiers who followed him, disturbed by the foul odor, drew back the coverings of the litter and, after several days, were able to recognize that he was dead. [Note: A.: his death was exposed.]

Meanwhile Carinus, whom Carus, when departing for the Parthians, had left in Italy, Illyricum, and Gaul, killed Sabinus Julianus, who was attempting to seize the empire, in the Veronese fields, and polluted himself with every crime. He killed very many innocent people on fabricated charges and corrupted noble marriages. He was also destructive to his fellow students, who in the lecture hall had mocked him with clever verbal teasing. [Note: Victor: of a word. A. likewise.] He was hated by all good men. Not long afterward he paid the penalty. [Note: A.: Not long afterward he was punished.] He was killed chiefly by the hand of his own tribune, whose wife he was said to have polluted.

For when the victorious army returning from Persia had lost Augustus Carus to a thunderbolt and Caesar Numerianus to treachery, it made Diocletian emperor.

## DIOCLETIANUS

In the year 1042 from the founding of the City, Diocletianus, the thirty-seventh after Augustus, was made emperor. He was a native of Dalmatia. [Note: A.: of Dalmatian origin, a man born in the greatest obscurity.] Born in the greatest obscurity, he was believed by many to be the son of a scribe and by some to be the freedman of the senator Anulinus. His mother’s name, as well as the name of the town, was Dioclea; from these names he was called Diocles until he assumed the empire.

When he acquired power over the Roman world, he converted a Greek name into Roman usage. First, in an assembly, he swore to the army that Numerianus had been killed without any deceit on his part. Aper, who had plotted against Numerianus, was standing beside him, and Diocletianus struck him with a sword in the sight of the army.

Afterward he defeated Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Illyricum, at Murgum, while Carinus was living under the hatred and execration of everyone. [Note: A.: and detestation.] He had been betrayed by his own army, which he had considered the stronger—or certainly had been abandoned—between Viminacium and Mount Aureus. [Note: A.: Murgum. Vopiscus: Martium.]

Having thus gained control of Roman affairs, when the Rusticani had stirred up a revolt in Gaul and given the name Bagaudae to their faction, while they had Amandus and Aelianus as leaders, he sent Maximianus Herculius as Caesar to subdue them. Maximianus subdued the peasants in minor battles and restored part of Gaul.

At about this time Carausius, who was born in the lowest condition but had acquired an excellent reputation through the ranks of an honorable military career, had been assigned at Boulogne, in the region of Belgica and Armorica, to patrol the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were infesting. After he had often captured many barbarians, but had neither returned the booty intact to the provincials nor sent it to the emperors, instead claiming it for himself alone, suspicion arose that he was deliberately allowing the barbarians to pass so that he could intercept them with their booty and enrich himself by this opportunity. Maximianus ordered him to be killed. He seized the purple and occupied Britain. [Note: Manuscript of François Pithou: Severae.]

Thus, when affairs were in turmoil throughout the whole world, Carausius in Britain, [Note: A.: was in revolt.] Achilleus in Egypt, and Julianus in Italy became emperors, but perished by different ends. Julianus, after a dagger had been driven through his ribs, threw himself into a fire. Narseus, king of the Persians, was waging war against the East. The Quinquegentiani were ravaging Africa. [Note: A.: were infesting it. Narseus was carrying war into the East.]

Soon Diocletianus made Aurelius Maximianus, surnamed Herculius, Augustus instead of Caesar. He created Constantius and Galerius Maximianus, surnamed Armentarius, Caesars. Constantius is said to have been the grandson through his daughter of the emperor Claudius. [Note: A.: It is reported that Maximianus Galerius, so that he might also be joined by kinship, etc.] He had joined Maximianus Galerius to himself by marriage. Constantius took Theodora, Herculius’s stepdaughter, as wife; by her he later had six children, the brothers of Constantine. Galerius took Valeria, Diocletianus’s daughter, as his faithful wife. Both had previously had wives, but Diocletianus compelled them to repudiate them. [Note: A.: Both had previously had wives, but he compelled them to repudiate those wives.]

Although wars against Carausius had been attempted without success against a man highly skilled in military affairs, peace was finally arranged. After seven years, his associate Allectus killed him, and himself held Britain for three years; he was overthrown by the treachery of Asclepiodotus, the prefect of the praetorium. Thus Britain was recovered in the tenth year. [Note: A.: Although wars had been attempted unsuccessfully against him.]

At the same time Constantius Caesar fought successfully in Gaul near Lingones. In a single day he experienced both adverse and favorable fortune. For when the barbarians suddenly attacked, he was forced inside the city with such desperate urgency that, after the gates had been closed, he had to be lifted onto the wall by ropes. [Note: A.: by means of ropes.] Yet scarcely five hours later, when the army arrived, he killed nearly sixty thousand Alemanni.

Maximianus Augustus also brought the war in Africa to an end, having subdued and brought to peace the Quinquegentiani. Diocletianus conquered Achilleus, who was under siege at Alexandria, in the ninth month and killed him. He used the victory harshly, staining all Egypt with severe proscriptions and massacres. On that occasion, however, he also organized and arranged many matters that remain down to our own age.

Constantine, the son of Constantius, was with him. Although still very young, he acted bravely in battles and sympathized with the Christians. Diocletianus, observing that he was advancing in understanding, bodily strength, and intellectual ability toward education, and recognizing that he would become the destroyer of his tyranny and its doctrine, was driven by envy to attempt to kill him by deceit. But God unexpectedly saved him and restored him to his father. [Note: In the edition of Canisius: *indutuens*; perhaps *intuens* should be read, or the word may be understood otherwise.]

Meanwhile Diocletianus in the East and Maximianus Herculius in the West ordered churches to be devastated and Christians to be afflicted and killed, in the tenth persecution after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those previously recorded. For ten years it continued without interruption through the burning of churches, the proscription of innocents, and the massacres of martyrs.

An earthquake followed in Syria, by which, as buildings collapsed everywhere at Tyre and Sidon, many thousands of people were crushed. Galerius Maximianus at first fought an unsuccessful battle against Narseus. Then, engaging between Callinicum and Carrhae, he fought imprudently rather than cowardly—for he joined battle with a very small force against an extremely numerous enemy—and was driven back. He set out for Diocletianus and met him on the road. Diocletianus is said to have received him with such insolence that, wearing the purple, he reportedly ran before Diocletianus’s carriage for several miles.

Soon afterward, having gathered forces throughout Illyricum and Moesia, he fought Narseus, the grandfather of Hormisdas and Sapor, in Lesser Armenia, with great success and no less strategy and courage. Indeed, he even performed the duty of a scout together with a second and a third horseman. After routing Narseus, he plundered his camp, captured his wives, sisters, and children, led away an immeasurable number of Persian nobles from the interior, and drove the king himself into the most remote deserts. [Note: A.: he drove him, in the extremities of the kingdom, into the deserts, etc.]

For this reason he returned in triumph to Diocletianus, who was staying in Mesopotamia with his garrisons, and was received with great honor. Thereafter they waged various wars, together and separately, subduing the Carpi and Basternae and defeating the Sarmatians. They settled immense numbers of captives from these nations within Roman territory.

Diocletianus was cleverly compliant, moreover shrewd and extremely subtle in intelligence. He wished to conceal his own severity beneath the unpopularity of another. Nevertheless, he was a most diligent and capable ruler. Although he was the first to introduce into the Roman empire more of the form of royal custom than of Roman liberty, and ordered that he himself be worshiped—whereas before him all emperors had been greeted as judges—he also added jeweled ornament to clothing and footwear. Previously the insignia of the empire had consisted only in the purple cloak, while everything else was ordinary.

Herculius, on the other hand, was openly savage and uncivil, revealing the harshness of his character in the terror of his expression. Indulging his own nature, he obeyed Diocletianus in all his harsher counsels. When, however, Diocletianus, as age grew heavier upon him, realized that he was no longer sufficiently capable of directing the empire, he urged Herculius to withdraw into private life and entrust the guardianship of the state to younger and more vigorous men.

His colleague obeyed reluctantly. Nevertheless, on the same day each of them exchanged the imperial insignia for private dress: Diocletianus at Nicomedia and Herculius at Milan, after the famous triumph that they had celebrated at Rome over numerous nations, with an impressive procession of dishes. [Note: A.: They made a procession of dishes.] The wives, sisters, and children of Narseus were led before the chariot.

They withdrew: one to Salona, the other to Lucania. Diocletianus grew old as a private citizen in splendid leisure at a villa not far from Salona. When Herculius and Galerius asked him to resume the empire, he detested it as though it were some kind of plague and replied as follows:

> If only you could see the vegetables cultivated by our hands at Salona; surely you would never judge that this should be attempted.

He lived sixty-eight years, of which he spent nearly nine after the empire in private dress. He died, as became sufficiently clear, by voluntary death through fear. When he had excused himself from attending the wedding festivities to which Constantine and Licinius had summoned him, on the grounds of old age preventing him from attending, he received threatening letters rebuking him for having favored Maxentius and for favoring Maximianus. Fearing a dishonorable death, he is said to have swallowed poison, displaying an extraordinary resolve, so that alone among all men after the foundation of the Roman empire he might voluntarily return from so great a height to the condition and civility of private life. Thus what had happened to no one since the human race was born happened to him: although he died a private citizen, he was nevertheless numbered among the gods.

# BOOK ELEVEN

## CONSTANTINE AND GALERIUS

[Col. 0903B] [Note: Thus Eutropius and Paul the Deacon begin Book Ten, which is Eutropius’s last.]

When these men had died, Constantine and Galerius were created Augusti for the administration of the state. [Note: A.: Constantius also.] The Roman world was divided between them [Col. 0903C] [Note: A.: among them in this way: the Roman world, etc.] so that Constantius held Gaul, Italy, and Africa, while Galerius held Illyricum, Asia, and the East. Two Caesars were appointed: Severus for Italy, and Maximus, Galerius’s sister’s son, for the East. At the same time Constantine was made Caesar.

Constantius, however, content with the dignity of Augustus, declined responsibility for administering Italy and Africa. He was an outstanding man of exceptional civility, concerned for the wealth of provincials and private citizens and not greatly interested in the advantages of the treasury. He used to say that it was better for public resources to be held by private individuals than locked away within a single enclosure.

He was so modest in his habits that, on holidays, if a meal had to be given for a larger number of friends, dining rooms were furnished with silver borrowed door to door from private citizens. He was not merely lovable but venerable. He was especially beloved by the Gauls because they had escaped under his rule the suspect prudence of Diocletianus and the bloodthirsty rashness of Maximianus.

He died in Britain, at York, in the thirteenth year of his reign, and was numbered among the gods. Galerius was a man of good character and outstanding in military affairs. When he realized that, with Constantius’s permission, Italy had also been added to his administration, he sent Maximus Caesar to the East and left Severus in Italy. He himself remained in Illyricum. [Note: A.: Maximianus, whom he appointed over the East, and Severus, to whom he gave Italy; he himself, etc.]

## CONSTANTINUS

In the year 1061 from the founding of the City, after Constantius had died, [Col. 0904B] Constantine, his son by a less distinguished marriage, the thirty-eighth after Augustus, was made emperor in Britain. On the sixth day before the Kalends of August, he entered as his father’s most desired successor and ruler. [Col. 0904C]

While still a young man, he was being held by Galerius in the city of Rome under the pretext of religion, as a kind of hostage. He seized the opportunity to flee and, in order to frustrate those pursuing him, killed the public post-horses wherever he passed along the route. He reached his father in Britain. By chance, at those same days, fate was pressing Constantius, his father, toward his final hour.

After Constantius died, with everyone around him striving to secure the succession, but especially Crocus, king of the Alemanni, who had accompanied Constantine as an ally, Constantine seized the empire. [Note: Manuscript of Crocus.] He joined his sister Constantia to Licinius, whom he had summoned to Milan, and made his own son, Crispus by name, born to his concubine Minerva and born in the town of Arles during those same days, Caesar; he also made Licinianus, Licinius’s son, who was about twenty months old, Caesar.

## MAXENTIUS
Meanwhile at Rome the praetorians, having stirred up a revolt, proclaimed Augustus Maxentius, the son of Herculius, who was staying at a public estate [Note: [Col. 0904D] A., not far from the City], six miles from the City along the Lavican Way. At this news Maximianus Herculius, encouraged by the hope of recovering the rank that he had unwillingly lost, hastened to Rome from Lucania, which he had chosen as his private residence, growing old amid very pleasant fields. He also urged Diocletian by letter [Col. 0905A] to resume the powers that he had laid down [Note: [Col. 0905D] A., “the authority he had relinquished”], but Diocletian treated the proposal as void.

Against the movement of the praetorians and Maxentius, Severus Caesar was sent to Rome by Galerius. He arrived with an army and besieged the City, but, deserted through the treachery of his own soldiers [Note: [Col. 0905D] A., “he was deserted. Maxentius’s forces increased, etc.”], he was killed by Herculius at the Three Taverns. His funeral was brought into Gallienus’s tomb, which lies nine miles from the City along the Appian Way.

After this Herculius Maximianus, with the support of the armies, attempted to strip his son Maxentius of imperial power, but endured the soldiers’ revolt and insults. Maxentius’s resources increased, and his imperial position was confirmed. [Note: [Col. 0905D] A.: “And the empire was strengthened. Severus, fleeing to Ravenna, was killed. Nevertheless Herculius Maximianus afterward attempted, in an assembly of the armies, to strip his son Maxentius, but endured the soldiers’ revolt and insults.”] Herculius departed for Gaul, with a scheme contrived as though he had been expelled by his son, so that he might join Constantine as his son-in-law; yet he was plotting to kill Constantine when an opportunity arose. Constantine was then reigning in Gaul with the immense favor of the soldiers and provincials, after slaughtering the Franks and Alamanni and capturing their kings, whom he also exposed to wild beasts when he had prepared a magnificent spectacle for the public.

When the plot was therefore discovered through Fausta [Note: [Col. 0905D] A., “through his daughter Fausta”], who had disclosed the deception to her husband, Herculius fled, but was overtaken by Constantine at Massilia. He had been preparing to sail from there to his son, but, captured by Constantine, he paid the penalty in a most fitting end [Note: [Col. 0906D] A., “he paid the penalty in a most just death. A man…”]: in the final manner of death, with his neck broken by a noose. He was a man inclined to every harshness and cruelty, treacherous, troublesome, utterly devoid of civility, dull-witted, of rustic and Pannonian origin—for even now, not far from Sirmium, a place rises prominently with a palace built there by him, where his parents practiced wage labor.

He died at the age of sixty, after twenty years as emperor. By Eutropia, a Syrian woman, he fathered Maxentius and Fausta, Constantine’s wife; to her father Constantius he had given his stepdaughter Theodora.

## LICINIUS

At this time Licinius was made emperor by Galerius. He was born in Dacia, known to Galerius through an old association, vigorous in the exertions of the war he had waged against Narseus, and acceptable in his services. [Note: [Col. 0906D] A.: “He was acceptable. Galerius’s death immediately followed. Thus the *Respublica*, etc.”]

Meanwhile Galerius himself intensified with harsher edicts the persecution against the Christians that had been launched by Diocletian and Maximian. After exhausting the provinces for ten years through every kind of oppression, with his chest rotting inwardly and his vital organs dissolving, he even vomited worms, beyond the horror of human misery. The physicians, unable any longer to endure the stench, were repeatedly killed at his command. Then a certain physician, taking courage from desperation, rebuked him, saying that his suffering was the punishment of God and that for this reason he could not be cured by physicians. After widely issued edicts, Galerius recalled the Christians from exile; but, unable to endure his torments, he brought his life to an end.

Although his justice was uncultivated and rustic, it was sufficiently praiseworthy. He was handsome in body, an outstanding and successful warrior, born to farming parents and a herdsman of cattle, from which he received the surname *Armentarius*. He was born in Ripensian Dacia and buried there, naming the place Romuliana after his mother Romula. He dared insolently to assert that his mother, like Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, had conceived him after being penetrated by a dragon.

Meanwhile the state was held by four new emperors: Constantine and Maxentius, sons of Augusti, and Licinius and Maximinus, men newly risen to power. In the fifth year of his reign, however, Constantine began a civil war against Maxentius [Note: [Col. 0906D] A.: “He began it; he routed his forces in many battles and finally defeated him at the Milvian Bridge near Rome, where Maxentius was raging with every kind of destruction against the nobles, and he gained possession of Italy. They say that Maxentius was kept in place by an artifice of women, which had been employed to hold the husband’s mind, through the auspices of a most welcome birth begun in childhood. Not long afterward, etc.”], because Maxentius ordered the wives of senators, and especially of the nobles, to be publicly seized and brought to satisfy his lust, and afterward returned to their husbands—not because his adulterous desire had been satisfied, but because it had been transformed.

Such fear had overwhelmed the senators and the common people that they did not dare even to show openly that they were afraid. They endured their unprecedented slavery with groans, and fear prevented them from thinking of anything on behalf of liberty, while he was driven not by anger alone but by a lust for slaughter. Finally, one day he ordered his soldiers to go through the streets of the entire city and cut down with their swords everyone they encountered, of whatever age or sex. Innumerable crowds of Roman citizens, not enemies but fellow citizens, were struck down by weapons.

The senators, especially those who appeared conspicuous in the senate either through office or wealth, were punished and proscribed on fabricated charges as though they were guilty. He also cultivated the practice of magic with the greatest zeal. To carry out these rites, noble pregnant women were sought out; when they had been brought in, they were cut open, infants were seized and torn from the womb, and their entrails were extracted and examined. Lions too were slaughtered, and by certain unspeakable formulas and prayers composed through demonic magic it was said—and believed—that wars could thereby be averted and that the law of gods and men governing the kingdom could be preserved by impiety.

To all these evils was added the fact that those who had been terrified by tyrannical cruelty throughout the other cities and countryside, believing that nothing concerning their lives was safe, abandoned their fields and fled into hiding in remote places. Since all labor in plowing and sowing ceased, such hunger invaded the City and every region that nothing remained for the support of life.

Constantine therefore routed his forces in many battles, yet because of his magical practices he feared him greatly. While he remained in much hesitation, turning over in his mind many thoughts about the necessity of the impending war, and as he traveled repeatedly raising his eyes toward heaven and praying there for divine help, he saw in sleep, in the eastern part of the sky, the sign of a cross shining with fiery brightness.

Terrified by so great a vision and disturbed by the novel sight, he saw angels standing beside him and saying: “ΕΝ ΤΟΥΤΩ ΝΙΚΑ, Constantine”—that is, “In this conquer.” It is also said that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and commanded him to make a similar figure and to have this aid in battle, by which he might obtain the rights of victory.

Eusebius Pamphilus reports that he heard Constantine himself declare under oath that, around midday, when the sun was already declining, he himself and the soldiers who were then with him had seen a sign of the cross formed from light, together with an inscription joined to it saying: “In this conquer.” He says that this miracle was shown to him while he was traveling with part of his army in a certain place. While he was considering what it might be, night came on, and as he slept Christ appeared with the sign that he had seen in the sky and ordered him to make an image of that sign, which would be an aid in the clashes of battle.

Then, made joyful and already confident of victory, he transformed the sign of the cross that he had seen in the sky into military standards. He also fashioned the so-called *labarum* [Note: [Col. 0907D] Ms., “lebarum”] from gold and precious stones in the form of the Lord’s cross. This military standard was more precious than the others because it preceded the emperor and because it was customary for the soldiers to worship it.

For this reason, I think Constantine changed the most noble distinction of the Roman Empire into the sign of the cross, so that through frequent sight of it and attention to it they would gradually abandon their former custom of subjection and would believe that the only God was the one whom the emperor worshiped, or under whose leadership and protection he advanced against his enemies.

This sign was always displayed before all the ranks, and he ordered it especially to be present with the battle lines when they were hard-pressed in combat. He therefore appointed designated standard-bearers to serve it. Their duty was to carry it on their shoulders in rotation and to pass through all the battle lines in this way.

It is said that on one occasion a certain man carrying the standard suddenly became afraid when the enemy attacked and handed it over to another to carry. When he withdrew from the battle and avoided the missiles, he was suddenly struck and died. The man who had accepted the sacred trophy, however, remained unharmed despite the many missiles directed at him. For, by a marvelous operation of divine power, the enemy arrows lodged in the standard, while the standard-bearer immediately pulled them out amid the dangers.

It is also said that no other servant of this kind ever died of a wound, as commonly happens in war, or suffered the disaster of captivity.

When Constantine had already pitched his camp not far from the Milvian Bridge, Maxentius was suddenly driven to meet him. Rushing out of the City of Rome, he ordered the rest of his army to follow him and himself went ahead, armed. He had ordered the river to be covered with ships arranged as a trap and leveled with bridges laid over them.

Constantine then ordered the golden cross that he had fashioned to be carried before him. When the engagement took place, those who were with Maxentius were defeated, and many of them were killed. Maxentius, fleeing, hurried to enter from the side onto a bridge made of ships a little above the Milvian Bridge, but when his horse slipped he was plunged into the depths. His body, swallowed by the mud because of the weight of his breastplate, was found only with difficulty.

This was the seventh year of Constantine’s reign. During this period Diocletian died at Salona.

It is said that Maxentius was kept in power by a woman’s artifice, which worked to hold the husband’s mind, through the auspices of a most welcome birth begun in childhood (so the text reads). This Maxentius was never dear to anyone, not even to his father or to his father-in-law Galerius.

Meanwhile the Roman citizens who had appealed to Constantine to rise to their aid, now liberated from the tyranny of wicked Maxentius, crowned the City and received the victorious Constantine with joy together with the life-giving cross. They praised God aloud, worshiped him for seven days, and magnified Constantine the victor with their praises.

## MAXIMINUS

Not long afterward in the East as well, Maximinus Caesar attempted a revolt against Licinius, but an accidental and uncomplicated death at Tarsus in Cilicia forestalled his imminent ruin [Note: [Col. 0907D] A., “forestalled it. Constantine, however, a great man and one who strove to accomplish everything he had prepared in his mind, at the same time aspiring to rule the whole world, made war on Licinius, although there was a relationship and affinity between them—for his sister Constantia was married to Licinius—and first unexpectedly overwhelmed him in Pannonia, and then, when he was preparing a war with great resources at Cibalae, …”].

Born from a sister of Armentarius and called Daza by his true name before becoming emperor, after his accession he was called Galerius Maximinus. He was Caesar for four years, then Augustus in the East for three. In origin and upbringing he was a shepherd, but a devotee of every wise man and of literature. His character was quiet, though he was excessively fond of wine; when drunk, he ordered certain harsh acts with a corrupted mind. Later, regretting what he had done, he decreed that the orders he had issued should be postponed until a sober and morning hour.

## VALENS

Meanwhile Valens was proclaimed emperor in the East by the army, and by that same Licinius he was put to death.

## ALEXANDER

Then Alexander, who had been made emperor at Carthage, was slaughtered by Constantine’s army. He was a Phrygian by origin, timid in character, and, because of the weakness of old age, unequal to hardship.

Thus, in the fourteenth year of his reign, Constantine became *Monocrator*—sole ruler—of the entire Roman Empire. He transferred all his care to divine matters, erecting churches and generously endowing them from the public treasury according to a regular plan.

He wrote the first law ordering that the temples of idols be handed over to those devoted to Christ; together with him his son Crispus issued laws. The second law ordered that Christians alone should serve in the army and command peoples and armies. The third required two Paschal weeks—one before and the other after the Resurrection—to be celebrated without the labor of any occupation.

When these things had been done, profound peace and tranquility prevailed throughout the world. The faithful rejoiced, as all nations continually flocked to the faith of Christ, received baptism, and at the same time shattered the images of their ancestral cults.

But, in truth, since empires scarcely preserve harmony, Constantine, a great man who strove to accomplish everything he had prepared in his mind and who at the same time aspired to rule the whole world, made war on Licinius, although there was a relationship and affinity between them. He first defeated him in Pannonia. In a second engagement at Cibalae, beside a marsh called Hiulca, Constantine broke into Licinius’s camp at night, and Licinius fled. In his swift flight he reached Byzantium, where he made Martinianus, master of the offices, Caesar.

Constantine took possession of all Dardania, Moesia, and Macedonia, and occupied numerous provinces. There were then various wars between them, and peace was restored and broken. [Note: [Col. 0909D] A.: “At last Licinius was defeated in a naval and land battle at Nicomedia, surrendered, and was killed at Thessalonica, contrary to the sanctity of his oath. This man…”] [Note: [Col. 0909D] A.: “At last Licinius was defeated in a naval and land battle at Nicomedia, surrendered, and was killed at Thessalonica, contrary to the sanctity of his oath. This man…”]

When Licinius was about to fight Constantine again, he placed his hope of victory in divinations and sacrifices. Finally, the Greeks also say that he then consulted the divination of the Delphic and Twin Apollo, and that when he asked about the war the demon replied:

“O old man, young warriors are watching you closely; your life has been released, and savage old age will receive you.”

Meanwhile Constantine, superior in battle, defeated Licinius in a naval and land engagement. At Nicomedia, a city of Bithynia, he captured him wearing the imperial garments and surrendering. He sent him into custody at Thessalonica and ordered him, together with Martinianus, to be killed contrary to the sanctity of his oath, fearing—after the removal of his father-in-law Herculius Maximianus—that Licinius might again take up the purple, which he had laid down, to the ruin of the state.

Licinius was killed after nearly fourteen years of rule and at almost sixty years of age. In his greed for every form of wealth he was the worst of men, and he was not free from sexual luxury. He was extremely harsh, considerably impatient, hostile to literature, which in his excessive ignorance he called a poison and public pest—especially forensic learning.

He was, however, quite useful to farmers and country people, since he had been born and raised among them [Note: [Col. 0909D] A., “since he had been born and reared from that class”], and in military matters he was a most severe guardian of the ancient discipline. He was a vigorous tamer of eunuchs and all courtiers, calling them the moths and mice of the palace.

At the same time the Roman state was under one Augustus and three Caesars, something that had never happened before, since Constantine’s sons governed Gaul, the East, and Italy.

But the arrogance of worldly success [Note: [Col. 0909D] A., “of favorable circumstances”] changed Constantine from the former teachable gentleness of his character. First he persecuted his relatives: he killed an excellent man and youth of good character, his sister’s son Commodus [Note: [Col. 0910D] A., “Commodus”]. Soon afterward he ordered Crispus to be killed, as is believed, at the prompting of his wife Fausta. Then he killed his wife Fausta by throwing her into overheated baths, when his mother Helena reproached him in deep grief for the death of her grandson. Later he killed numerous friends.

In the first period of his reign he was comparable to the best emperors; in the last, to mediocre ones. Innumerable virtues of mind and body shone in him. He was extremely eager for military glory, and fortune favored him in wars, though in such a way that it did not surpass his own exertion.

After the civil war he also defeated the Goths, the strongest and most numerous peoples, in various engagements on that most barbarous soil, namely, in the region of the Sarmatians [Note: [Col. 0910D] Ms., “in the barbarian gulf of the sun”]. At last he granted them peace and established a great gratitude toward himself among the barbarian peoples. [Note: [Col. 0910D] A.: “He secured it.”]

He suppressed a certain Calocerus, who was attempting revolution in Cyprus. At his tricennalia he appointed as Caesar Dalmatius, the son of his brother Dalmatius.

He was more eager for praise than can be estimated. He was accustomed to call Trajan “the wallflower,” because inscriptions bearing his name appeared on many buildings. He built a bridge over the Danube, adorned his royal clothing with gems, and wore a head continually decorated with a diadem.

Nevertheless, he was highly advantageous in many matters: he quieted calumnies through very strict laws; he cultivated civil arts, especially literary studies; he himself read, wrote, reflected, received embassies, and heard the complaints of the provinces. He was a seeker after the love of justice, which he won for himself through both generosity and teachability. Although uncertain toward some friends, he was outstanding toward the rest, neglecting no opportunity to make them wealthier and more distinguished.

He promulgated many laws [Note: [Col. 0910D] A., “he imposed many laws”]: some good and equitable, most unnecessary, and several severe.

He was the first to attempt to raise the city bearing his name to such grandeur that it might rival Rome. Since everything was succeeding for him, he wanted to possess a city of his own. Coming to the plain situated before Ilium beside the Hellespont, above the tomb of Ajax [Note: [Col. 0910D] Ms., “Aiantas”], where the Achaeans had their camp while fighting against Troy, he marked out a city and built gates that are still visible to sailors.

While he was carrying out these plans, God appeared to him during the night and warned him to seek another place. He instructed him to proceed to Byzantium in Thrace and to dwell there. Constantine enlarged Byzantium, which had originally been called by that name, surrounded it with a massive wall, and adorned it with buildings of various kinds. He established it equal to imperial Rome and legally decreed that, after being renamed Constantinople, it should be called the second Rome. The law itself is known to have been inscribed on a marble tablet and set up beside his equestrian statue in the Strategium.

Having bestowed this city with the greatest generosity, he settled in its distinguished houses men of means from the city of Rome, selected others from different places according to their rank, and distributed large houses among them so that the city would be inhabited.

At that time the God-loving emperor also built the temples of Saint Sophia, Saint Irene, the Apostles, Saint Mocius, and the Archangel. After the temple of Asclepius near Aegae and that of Venus at Aphaca had been utterly destroyed, along with many others, he gave their revenues to the churches.

He placed decorated images on public display in the city of Constantinople and set up Delphic tripods in the circus for public spectacle. Since they can be seen with one's own eyes, they are said to overflow abundantly.

At that time many peoples came to baptism, moved by the miracles performed by captive priests who had been taken captive under Gallienus.

Meanwhile the emperor’s mother, Helena by name, having been warned in a dream, hurried to Jerusalem. She found Christ’s tomb, although only with difficulty, covered with filth, and a temple of Venus built above it, where they insulted the place with songs sung by virgins. She ordered the most wicked temple to be destroyed, its dust, polluted by unholy sacrifices, to be removed, and to be scattered far from the city.

Then, having ordered the place to be cleansed, she immediately saw the Lord’s monument appear openly. Around it three crosses were also discovered, buried beneath the ground, together with the nails and a title written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: “JESUS THE NAZARENE, KING OF THE JEWS.”

It is said that a dead man rose again when touched by the cross. Concerning this wood the Sibyl said among the pagans:

“O thrice-blessed wood, upon which God was stretched.”

Then they began to wonder which cross belonged to the Lord and which to the thieves. Accordingly, Macarius, bishop of the city, resolved the doubt by the following procedure. He brought one of those crosses, with fervent prayer, to a woman of distinguished birth who had been worn down by a long illness, and he recognized the power of the Savior. As soon as the cross touched the woman, it drove away the affliction of her most grievous illness and restored her health.

Of the nails with which Christ’s hands had been pierced, the emperor placed some in his helmet, taking care for the protection of his son’s head so that they might ward off weapons of war. He mixed others into a horse’s bridle, acting with foresight for the emperor and fulfilling the ancient philosophy. For long ago the prophet Zechariah had cried out, saying: “And what is in the bridle shall be holy to the Lord Almighty.”

He gave part of the Savior’s cross to his son. Constantine received it and, believing that the city in which this fragment was preserved would be kept safe, devoutly enclosed it, as is said, in his statue, which had been erected in the Forum of Constantine on a porphyry column.

He left the remaining part, enclosed in a silver reliquary, to Macarius, the priest of the city. He gathered craftsmen from every direction and built there enormous and splendid churches.

After this the emperor, taking the greatest care for the Christians, rejected pagan superstition. He removed the gladiatorial combats, ordered his own images to be placed in the temples, and decreed that the cubit by which the Nile is measured should no longer each year be carried to the temple of Serapis, but to the churches.

Constantine was preparing for war against the Parthians, who were already harassing Mesopotamia [Note: [Col. 0911D] A.: “They were harassing it. In the thirty-first year of his reign, at the age of sixty-six, he died near Nicomedia at a public estate. Death, etc.”]. In the thirty-second year of his reign and the sixty-sixth year of his life, he was seized by illness and left Constantinople for Nicomedia, as though going to warm baths. He was consumed by disease at a public estate, having made a will for his three sons, in the consulship of Felicianus and Tacianus, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.

He was more a mocker than a flatterer, and for this reason was called *Trachala* in a common proverb. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Ms., “Trochela.”] For ten years he was pre-eminent; for the following twelve, a brigand; for the final ten, a ward—so called because of his immoderate extravagances.

His death had also been announced two years beforehand by a comet, which shone for some time with extraordinary size. The Greeks call it κομήτης, “comet.” [Col. 0911D] He deserved to be numbered among the gods [Note: [Col. 0911D] A., “to be enrolled among them”].

His body was placed in a golden coffin, carried to Constantinople, and deposited in a high place of the palace. It was held in great honor and veneration, as though he were still alive, until one of his sons should be present. Later, when Constantius came from the East, his body was buried with imperial rites in the Church of the Apostles, in a porphyry sarcophagus.

He left as successors his sons and one son of his brother Dalmatius. Each of them received the government of the following regions.

He made his first son Constantine ruler over everything beyond the Alps at his own decennalia. At his vicennalia he established Constantius in the East, from the strait of the Propontis into Asia and the East. At his tricennalia he appointed the younger Constans over Illyricum, Italy, and Africa. He appointed Dalmatius over Thrace, Macedonia, and Achaea. He appointed Hannibalianus, a kinsman of Dalmatius Caesar, over Armenia and the nations surrounding the allied territories.

Dalmatius Caesar, however, a man of the most promising character and not unlike his uncle, was not long afterward overthrown by a military faction [Note: [Col. 0911D] A., “by a crime”], with the consent, rather than the command [Note: [Col. 0911D] A., “by the order”], of his cousin Constantius.

Constantine, while striving to invade the territory of his younger brother, began a war against him. When he rashly engaged in battle at Aquileia, he was killed by the generals of Constans and thrown into a river called the Alpha, not far from Aquileia, in the consulship of Acindinus and Proclus.

As a result, rule of the Roman Empire in the western regions came to Constans, while that of the East came to Constantius.

At the same time the Roman state was also greatly disturbed. The nation of the Franks, established around Gaul, was hostile to the Romans; Constans crushed it and subjected it to the Roman Empire. At that time a great earthquake also occurred in the East, especially at Antioch, which was shaken continuously for a year, and the city of Neocaesarea in Pontus fell.

## CONSTANTIUS

Constantius and Constans issued laws forbidding a Jew to purchase a slave; otherwise the slave was to be confiscated and handed over to the public treasury. Moreover, if anyone dared to circumcise a slave, the one who presumed to do such a thing was to be punished with the sword.

## CONSTANS

For a while the reign of Constans was vigorous and just. Soon, however, when he was afflicted with poor health and had more burdensome friends [Note: [Col. 0912D] A., “more depraved friends”], he turned to serious vices. Since he was intolerable to the provincials and unpleasant to the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0912D] A., “since he was so”], and since he wandered through the forests and wooded valleys around Gaul from a desire to hunt, several military men conspired to kill him, with Crestius and Marcellinus as the instigators, and Magnentius also involved.

When the day for carrying out the plan had been chosen, Marcellinus invited many people to dinner, pretending that it was his son’s birthday. After the banquet had continued late into the night, Magnentius, withdrawing as though to attend to the ordinary needs of the stomach, assumed imperial dress at Augustodunum. [Note: [Col. 0912D] See Victor.]

When Constans learned of this, he attempted to flee, but at the town of Helena, near the Pyrenees and not far from Spain, he was killed by Gaiso, who had been sent with the choicest troops. This occurred in the seventeenth year of his reign and the thirtieth year of his life. He had been Caesar for three years.

He was weak in his feet and hands because of pain in his joints. He was fortunate in the mildness of the climate and the abundance of crops, and throughout his entire period there was no fear of the barbarians. He was formidable without excessive cruelty.

The fortunes of Constantius were different. He suffered many grievous reverses at the hands of the Persians: towns were often captured, cities besieged, armies slaughtered, and no battle against Sapor was successful for him, except that at Singara, where he lost an unquestionable victory [Note: [Col. 0913D] A., “a doubtful victory”] through the ferocity of his soldiers, who, in a seditious and foolish manner contrary to the principles of warfare, demanded battle when the day was already declining.

During the same period Dyrrachium in Dalmatia collapsed in an earthquake. Meanwhile, when a great earthquake occurred in the Phoenician city of Berytus, a very large part of it fell, so that many pagans entered the church, promising that they would observe the Christian rite.

After the death of Constans, when Magnentius controlled Italy, Africa, and Gaul, Illyricum also underwent a change of regime [Note: [Col. 0913D] A., “it acquired one, when Vetranio was elected emperor with the consent of the soldiers.”]. Vetranio, master of the soldiers, was elected emperor at Mursa in Pannonia with the agreement of the troops.

They made him, already an old man and beloved by all because of the length and success of his military service, ruler for the defense of Illyricum: an honest man, of the old morality, and of pleasant civility, but entirely unacquainted with the liberal arts, so much so that he did not learn even the elements of the first letters until he was an old man and already emperor [Note: [Col. 0913D] A., “until he had received them.”].

Then the emperor Constantius made his cousin Gallus Caesar. Giving him his own name, he assigned Syria and Antioch as his residence, so that through him the eastern regions might be protected.

When Gallus came to Antioch, a sign appeared in the sky over the East on the day of Pentecost. A column in the form of a cross was seen in heaven, displaying an extended appearance of light from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives. Around it there was a crown resembling a rainbow. Constantius Gallus also saw this.

Meanwhile Constantius Augustus had begun a civil war to avenge his brother’s death [Note: [Col. 0913D] A.: “He had begun it; Vetranio’s authority was abolished, and by a new and unprecedented custom he was compelled, with the consent of the soldiers, to lay down the insignia.”] He set out for Illyricum and established a military camp. Vengeance for his brother’s death compelled him, especially vengeance against Vetranio, who had been made Augustus by the soldiers.

When he reached Sirmium, he met Vetranio after mutual treaties had been made. It happened that the soldiers who had appointed Vetranio transferred their support to Constantius. Then they all proclaimed Constantius alone emperor and Augustus with a single shout.

When no mention was made of Vetranio, he suddenly realized that he had been betrayed and threw himself at the emperor’s feet. Constantius removed his crown and purple garment and spoke to him mercifully, advising him to rest in the guise of a private citizen, which was more suitable for his age than bearing a title burdened with anxieties.

He ordered that abundant expenses be supplied to him from public revenues, for Vetranio was almost foolishly simple-minded. While Vetranio was staying at Prusa in Bithynia, Constantius wrote to him, saying that he had been the cause of many benefits to Vetranio, since he had freed him from so many anxieties and evils that would otherwise have come upon him; and that he himself had not acted well, because he had spent on Vetranio what he ought to have provided for himself.

In these days at Rome Nepotianus, the son of Eutropia, Constantius’s sister, seized the title of Augustus at the urging of criminals. On the twenty-eighth day Magnentius crushed him. His head was carried through the City on a spear, and there were extremely severe proscriptions and massacres of nobles [Note: [Col. 0914D] A.: “They occurred.
