Not long afterward Magnentius was routed in battle at Nursa and almost captured. Great, etc.”]

## MAGNENTIUS
At this time Constantius fought against Magnentius at Mursa and won. In that battle the Roman forces were almost entirely exhausted, and the fortunes of the whole empire were [Col. 0914B] thrown into ruin. Thereafter, when Magnentius had withdrawn into Italy, he routed many at Ticinum and, as victory commonly does, made his pursuers more audacious. Coming to Rome, he killed many senators and members of the populace. There, recognizing that the soldiers of Constantius were close at hand against him, he advanced toward the western regions of Gaul.

When many very serious battles were fought there between the two sides, now one, now the other seemed to be victorious. At last Magnentius was defeated and fled. Seeing the soldiers, as though saddened by their own destruction, he tried to encourage them while standing on higher ground, following his customary manner of addressing them. Then they, prepared to show Magnentius their customary loyalty, but against their will and unwillingly, all cried out with one voice: “Constantius Augustus, may you win!” Magnentius interpreted this omen as applying to himself, as though imperial power had been divinely granted to him, and for that reason [Col. 0914C] he continued farther.

When an engagement subsequently took place with the soldiers of Constantius near Mount Seleucus, Magnentius alone fled to the city of Lugdunum. There he seized and killed his own mother and his elder brother, whom he had appointed Caesar to defend Gaul. Not long afterward, being hemmed in there by the soldiers of Constantius, he secretly prepared a sword and, piercing his side, assisted the blow by striking against a wall. Since he was of enormous stature, blood poured from his nostrils and mouth. In the forty-second month of his imperial power, at nearly fifty years of age, he died— in the sixth year of Constantius’s reign, and in the second year of the consulship of Constantius Gallus, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

He was born to barbarian parents who inhabited Gaul. Ready in the pursuit of learning, sharp in speech, proud and immoderate in spirit, and fearful, he was nevertheless skilled at concealing his fear beneath the appearance of boldness. [Col. 0914D]

When his death was heard of, his brother Decentius ended his life with a noose made by fastening together a band.

Thus, in these battles, the immense forces of the Roman Empire were exhausted [Note: [Col. 0914D] A.: “Its forces were consumed in that struggle, etc.”]—forces suitable for any external war, capable of bringing many triumphs and much security [Note: [Col. 0914D] A.: “To contribute. Soon afterward Constantius appointed Gallus, the son of his paternal uncle, Caesar in the East; and Magnentius, defeated in various battles, took his own life at Lugdunum in the third year and seventh month of his reign. His brother likewise [died] at Senones; he had sent him out as Caesar to defend Gaul. During this period Gallus Caesar was also killed by Constantius in many civil wars. The man was, etc.”] to the empire.

But even then no rest came to the state. For shortly afterward, in western Gaul, a certain Silvanus, plotting revolution, arose as a usurper; the commanders of Constantius killed him on the twenty-eighth day. He was of a very pleasing disposition. Although born to a barbarian father, he was nevertheless sufficiently polished by Roman education and was patient.

Moreover, the Jews living at Diocaesarea in Palestine were disturbing the neighboring regions. Taking up arms, they attempted to resist the Romans. Thereafter, while Gallus Caesar was residing at Antioch, he sent an army against them, killed them, and devastated the city.

When he believed that he had acted successfully, unable to endure his good fortune, he moved toward tyranny. Revealing his intention to the emperor, he killed the quaestor Magnus and Domitian, prefect of the East. For this reason Constantius, angered, summoned him. Since he could not dare to disregard the summons, he proceeded to the emperor. When he had come opposite the island of Falconense, Constantius ordered him to be killed there, in the seventh year of his reign and in the third year of the consulship of Gallus.

He was a man naturally savage and inclined toward tyranny [Note: [Col. 0915D] A.: “More prone”], if he had been permitted to rule by his own right [Note: [Col. 0915D] A.: “Had been permitted. Silvanus too, having plotted revolution in Gaul, was killed before the thirtieth day. And he alone, [Col. 0916D] etc.”].

At that time Constantius alone was ruler and Augustus in the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0916D] A.: “Was. Soon afterward he sent Julian, his cousin and Gallus’s brother, as Caesar to Gaul, giving him his own sister in marriage, after the barbarians had captured many towns and were besieging others. Everywhere, etc.”].

Now, therefore, a few things must be said about Claudius Julian, his family, his education, and how he came to imperial power.

Constantine, who called Byzantium Constantinople after his own name, had two brothers by the same father but not by the same mother. One was called Dalmatius, the other Constantius. Constantius had two sons, Gallus and Julian.

After the death of Constantine, founder of the city of Constantinople, when the soldiers had killed the younger Dalmatius, these two also, their father already dead, nearly suffered the danger of death along with Dalmatius. Gallus was spared by an illness thought to be incurable, while Julian was spared by his infancy, for he was eight years old.

When the emperor’s fury against them had subsided, Gallus was near Ephesus among teachers, where he also possessed estates inherited from his forebears. Julian, meanwhile, as he grew up in the lecture halls of Constantinople, was trained in the basilica where the teachers were. He appeared in private dress and had as his tutor a eunuch named Mardonius; he studied grammar under Nicocles of Lacedaemon, and rhetoric under the sophist Ecebolius [Note: [Col. 0916D] Manuscript: “Ecybolum”].

Julian had been a Christian from the beginning. As he advanced in his studies, a report also spread among the people that he might be able to govern the state. When this became more widely known, it aroused agitation in the emperor Constantius. For this reason he kept Julian away from the imperial city and sent him to Nicomedia, ordering that he should not meet with the sophist Libanius the Syrian.

At that time Libanius, having been expelled from Constantinople by the tutors, was living at Nicomedia. Julian was therefore forbidden to study under Libanius because he was a pagan; nevertheless, Julian made use of his books. While he was making progress in rhetoric, the philosopher Maximus came to Nicomedia—not the Byzantine Maximus, the father of Euclid, but the Ephesian, whom the emperor Valentinian later ordered to be killed for practicing what were regarded as magical arts.

He had come to Nicomedia for no other reason than that he had been drawn by Julian’s reputation. When Julian had tasted his philosophical discourse, he began also to imitate his teacher’s religion. Maximus had likewise implanted in Julian’s mind a desire for imperial power.

When these things did not escape the emperor’s ears, Julian, placed between fear and hope and wishing to conceal his suspicion—that one who had recently been an upright Christian had later become a traitor—shaved his head and pretended to lead a monastic life. In secret he practiced philosophy, but publicly he read the sacred books of the Christians. Finally, he was appointed a reader in the church of Nicomedia, and in the presence of the assembled people he read the divine Scriptures in the church.

Under this appearance he escaped the emperor’s anger. He did these things out of fear, but he did not at all abandon the hope he had conceived in his mind. He used to say to many of his friends that the times would be happy when he himself held power.

Not long afterward, when Gallus had been killed, Julian suddenly became suspect to the emperor, who also ordered that he be kept under guard. When he had slipped away in flight, he saved himself by moving from place to place. Only with difficulty, and at a late hour, did the emperor’s wife Eusebia discover where he was concealed. She pleaded with the emperor that he should suffer no harm, but rather be sent to Athens to study philosophy.

Julian therefore began to desire the imperial scepter. For this reason, traveling throughout all Hellas, he sought prophets who would give responses, asking whether he would attain his own imperial power. He found a man who claimed that he could tell him what he desired to hear.

This man led him to a certain place of idols and brought him into the inner sanctuary. He summoned deceptive demons, and when they appeared in solemn fashion, Julian was compelled by terror to make the sign of the cross on his forehead. Then, looking upon the figure of the Lord’s trophy, the demons suddenly disappeared.

Recognizing what had happened, the magician began to blame Julian. Julian explained that he had been terrified and said that he had been struck with amazement at the power of the cross, since the demons had vanished when they saw that sign.

The magician replied: “Do not suppose this, good man, that they were afraid, as you say; rather, they withdrew because they detested this sign.” Thus, having deceived the wretched man, he filled Julian with hatred of the Christian sign.

After this Constantius summoned Julian and appointed him Caesar on the seventh day before the Ides of November. He gave him his sister Helena in marriage—she was called Constantia—and sent him to Gaul against the barbarians.

These barbarians were the very ones for whose assistance the emperor Constantius had appealed against Magnentius. Since they had accomplished nothing against the tyrant, they were devastating Roman cities and capturing others. Everywhere there was shameful destruction [Note: [Col. 0916D] A.: “There was”], and the Roman Empire was already tottering amid unmistakable disaster [Col. 0917A] [Note: [Col. 0917D] A.: “Was wavering. From whom, with small forces at Argentoratum, a city of Gaul, enormous forces of the Alamanni were destroyed. Their most noble king was captured, and Gaul was restored. Many other remarkable deeds were later accomplished by the same Julian against the barbarians: the Germans were driven back beyond the Rhine, and the Roman Empire was restored to its own borders. Not long afterward, when the Germanic army was being withdrawn from the defense of Gaul, Julian was made Augustus by the agreement of the soldiers. A year having intervened, he set out to take possession of Illyricum, while Constantius was occupied in wars against the Parthians. When Constantius learned of these events, he turned toward civil war, but died on the journey between Cilicia and Cappadocia, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign and at the age of forty-five; he deserved to be counted among the gods. The man was, etc.”].

When Julian was still a young man, the emperor ordered him to undertake nothing except on the advice of the commanders. But when the commanders, having received authority, neglected their duties, and the barbarians therefore prevailed, Julian allowed the commanders to devote themselves to their pleasures. Taking the soldiers, however, and promising them the spoils of the enemies they killed, he made a beginning in defeating the barbarians and won their affection for himself.

It is therefore reported that, when he had entered a certain city, a laurel crown of the kind with which cities are customarily decorated, hanging between columns, fell upon his head when its cord broke and crowned him most appropriately. When this had happened, everyone cried out that it was a sign that he would receive imperial power.

Meanwhile, when Julian complained to the emperor about the negligence of the commanders, another master of the soldiers was sent to him, one suited to his energy. With this man’s assistance he engaged the barbarians confidently. When they showed the emperor’s letters to the barbarians through envoys, inviting them to come into the provinces, that commander sent their envoys into chains.

Then, in an engagement at Argentoratum, a city of Gaul, he destroyed the enemy’s immense forces with a small Roman army. Bodies stood in heaps like mountains; blood flowed like rivers. The noble king Chonodamarus was captured [Note: [Col. 0918D] Manuscript: “Nodomarus”] and sent to Constantius. All the nobles were routed, and the frontier of Roman possession was restored.

Later, fighting against the Alamanni who were settled along the Rhine River, he captured their most powerful king, Bodomarius. Adorned with this celebrated victory, and governing the soldiers with moderation of life and gentleness, he was proclaimed Augustus by them.

Since an imperial crown was lacking, one of the standard-bearers took the torc that he wore around his neck and placed it around Julian’s head.

## JULIAN

In this way Julian became emperor. After this, thinking nothing of Constantius, he courted with honors the judges appointed by him and circulated letters designed to arouse hatred against him. These letters showed that Constantius, because of the war he had waged against Magnentius, had brought barbarians into Roman territory.

Constantius pressed him through embassies to return to his former rank and title. Julian, replying in gentler terms, stated that under the name of supreme imperial power he would obey much more dutifully.

Then Julian, suddenly changing his religion, although he had previously been thought to be a Christian, called himself chief priest. He went to the temples of the pagans and sacrificed there. He urged his subjects to worship such things and strove to wash away and renounce the Christian profession through sacrifices, rites of renewal—which the pagans call expiations—and the blood of victims [Col. 0918A].

While Constantius was staying at Antioch because of the Persian war, Julian, hoping that he could retain Illyricum without war, was making his way toward them. He said that he wished to make satisfaction to Constantius, as though he had accepted the imperial insignia not of his own will but at the will of the soldiers.

It is said that, when he had reached those regions, after the grape harvest had already been gathered and around the setting of the Pleiades, grapes were brought forth again. Moreover, rain descending from the sky formed, upon his garment and likewise upon the garments of the others, individual drops in the shape of crosses.

Because of this, it seemed to him and to others that the grapes produced out of season offered him a favorable sign, while the rain falling upon the garment strengthened the garment on which it fell. Others, however, said that the out-of-season grapes signified the emperor’s destruction, after the manner of such clusters, and that his reign would be brief.

Regarding the cross, they said that this sign foretold the fact that it was the heavenly teaching of the Christians and that everyone ought to be marked with the sign of the cross.

When Constantius heard that Julian was coming against him, he abandoned preparations for the Parthian war and made his way toward Constantinople. As he traveled, growing more and more inflamed with grief and, as was his nature in such matters, impatient, he hurried fiercely. At the foot of Mount Taurus, near the town of Mopsocrene, between Cilicia and Cappadocia, he died of a severe fever, which excessive indignation and sleeplessness intensified, on the third day before the Nones of November, in the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign and at the age of sixty-five.

Of these years, he reigned thirteen with his father, twenty-four after his father, that is, seven alone, and sixteen with his brothers and Magnentius. He deserved to be counted among the gods.

At the same time, part of Constantinople was destroyed by a great earthquake.

He was a man of remarkable tranquility, calm, and excessively trusting toward friends and intimates; soon afterward he became more devoted to his wives. Nevertheless, in the early years of his reign he had conducted himself with great restraint. He also enriched his associates, without dishonoring those whose laborious services he had experienced [Note: [Col. 0918D] A.: “Not leaving them without honor”].

He was nevertheless inclined toward severity whenever his imperial position was under suspicion [Note: [Col. 0918D] A.: “Otherwise gentle, and one whose fortune in civil wars, more than in external wars, ought to be praised. After this Julian took possession of power and brought war against the Parthians with a great army. I too took part in that expedition. He received some towns and forts of the Persians into surrender, or captured them by force, ravaged Assyria, and for some time maintained a stationary camp near Ctesiphon. Returning as a victor, he imprudently entered into battle and was killed by the enemy’s hand on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventh year of his reign and at the age of thirty-one; he too was counted among the gods. The man was remarkable, etc.”].

Otherwise he was gentle, successful in civil wars but pitiable in foreign wars, extraordinarily skilled with arrows, and highly temperate in food, wine, and sleep. He endured labor, desired eloquence, and, because he was unable to attain it owing to the slowness of his intellect, envied others. He was devoted to the affection of eunuchs, courtiers, and household servants, and also to his wives. Content with them, he was not defiled by any misplaced or unjust lust [Col. 0918D].

Of the wives he had in great number, he especially loved Eusebia. She was attractive, but through Adamantias, Gorgonias, and other troublesome attendants [Col. 0919A], she damaged her husband’s reputation, contrary to the custom of more modest women, whose advice often benefits their husbands.

For, to say nothing of the others, it is incredible to relate how greatly Pompeia Plotina increased Trajan’s glory. When his procurators were harassing the provinces with accusations, so that one of them was said to approach every wealthy person in this manner: “What do you have? Where did you get it?” and then, thirdly, “Put down what you have,” she rebuked and reproached her husband for being careless of his own good name. As a result, he later became such a man that, detesting unjust exactions, he called the treasury a spleen, because as it grows the remaining limbs waste away.

Therefore, when Constantius had died, Julian was already in possession of Thrace, and thereafter, coming to Constantinople, he was proclaimed Augustus. Meanwhile, when he had entered Constantinople [Col. 0919B], he began to consider how he might please the people and suitably win their favor. He accomplished this by the following stratagem.

For he knew well that Constantius was hated by all the peoples who embraced the doctrine of consubstantiality; for this reason they appeared to have been excluded from the churches, and their bishops had been confiscated and sent into exile. At the same time, he also knew that the pagans had been distressed by the prohibition of sacrifices and desired to attain a time when their temples would be opened, so that they might have permission to sacrifice to their idols.

Thus, recognizing that both peoples had been wounded with grief by the deceased Constantius, and that all alike were lamenting the violence of the eunuchs—especially the plunderings of Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, who had abandoned his own see and invaded that of Constantinople—Julian commended himself to everyone by such an artful disguise. [Col. 0919C] To some Christians he pretended to show affection; to other pagans he was lavish through empty display; yet to all alike he revealed what sort of religion he held in common.

First, disparaging Constantius’s cruelty toward his subjects and rebuking it before the entire people, he ordered the bishops who had been carried into exile to be recalled and their confiscated possessions restored. He also quickly ordered the temples of the pagans to be opened to their attendants, and decreed that those who had been oppressed by the eunuchs should be received again and recover what had wrongly been taken from them.

But he condemned Eusebius, who presided over the imperial bedchamber, to death—not only because he had oppressed many people, but also because he had heard that, on his advice, Julian’s brother Gallus had been killed. He buried Constantius’s body with royal honors. He expelled from the palace the eunuchs, barbers, and cooks: [Col. 0919D] the eunuchs because his wife had died and he had married no other woman after her; the cooks because he used simple foods; and the barbers because, as he said, one barber was sufficient for many men. Restoring many writers to their former standing, he ordered that the others be given payment for their writing. He also abolished the public transport service of mules and horses.

Few praise these actions of his; many condemn them. For he even kept vigil at night composing books, and, descending into the senate, recited them publicly. He was the only emperor after Julius Caesar to recite speeches in the senate-house. He honored those devoted to the disciplines, especially philosophers. Yet he possessed in great measure the fault of empty glory, and in the work he had written about the Caesars he tore to pieces all the emperors who had preceded him. [Col. 0920A]

Moved, therefore, by this arrogance, he also composed books against the Christians. In expelling cooks and barbers he acted as a philosopher, though not as an emperor; but in disparaging and attacking others he acted neither as a philosopher nor as a ruler.

Thus Julian, who had long been striving to spread paganism throughout all his dominion and to exterminate Christianity, first ordered the sons of the Galilaeans—for that is what he called the worshipers of our Savior—not to study the disciplines of poets or philosophers. “We are wounded by our own feathers,” he said, according to the proverb; “for, armed with writings produced by us, they wage war against us.”

The pagan temples were indeed open, and the sacrifices of the pagans proceeded throughout the cities according to his will; but he was tormented by the fear that his zeal would be frustrated by the abundance of Christians. He was particularly troubled because many of his priests had Christian wives, children, and servants.

Believing that the condition of Christianity consisted in a good life and manner of conduct, he took pains everywhere to adorn pagan temples with seats and processions modeled on the instruction and order of the Christian religion. He established readers of his superstition according to pagan doctrines and admonitions, after the manner of clerics, so that they might solemnly observe fixed hours, days, and prayers. He likewise ordered them to appoint persons capable of philosophizing to care for men and women, to provide lodging for travelers and the poor, and to offer other forms of provision for the needy, thereby organizing the pagan religion and giving it the name of piety.

If anyone sinned, whether willingly or unwillingly, he established, according to the Christian tradition, that the offender should undergo correction after an appointed period of moderate repentance. [Col. 0920C]

He is said especially to have envied the letters of the bishops—those documents by which, when writing to one another, they customarily commended travelers and indicated by every means where they were going and from whom they came, so that they might obtain assistance as though they were known and trusted friends, supported by the testimony of an official seal. Considering these things, he hastened to accustom the pagans to the practices of the Christians.

For he wrote a letter to Arsabius, the high priest of Galatia, in the following terms:

“The rites of the pagans are not yet being conducted according to our intention, because their worshipers have been placed in a state of negligence. For the splendor, greatness, and sublimity of the gods are greater than every reason and every hope. But may the gods be gracious to our souls because of the negligence in which we remain, since, through their providence, such a great change has been accomplished in so short a time—one that no one would initially have dared even to pray for.

“Why, then, do we believe that this is sufficient, and why do we not observe how the Christians’ care for travelers has increased their superstition, as well as the many services they provide around graves and the dead, and their honorable zeal for a way of life—not genuine, but pretended? I think that such practices ought to be carried out among us in accordance with truth.

“It is therefore not right that you alone should be such a man; rather, all the priests throughout Galatia must be so. Entreat them, bend them by prayer, or at least remove them swiftly from the priestly ministry unless they bow their necks to the gods together with their wives, children, and servants. They must no longer tolerate their servants or children doing otherwise, but must despise the Galilaeans, who impiously act against the gods and place impieties before pieties.

“Next, admonish them all that a priest must neither go to spectacles nor drink in taverns, nor preside over any trade, disgraceful occupation, or indecent undertaking. Honor those who obey; expel those who disobey.

“Establish hostels in every city, so that travelers may enjoy our benevolence—not only our own people, but also strangers in need of money. To provide you with the means for this, I have meanwhile decreed that thirty thousand measures of grain and sixty thousand sextarii of wine be distributed annually throughout Galatia. One-fifth of these supplies should be spent on the poor who attend the temples; the remainder should be distributed to travelers and the needy.

“For it is disgraceful that the Jews are not rejected, but rather nourished by the impious Galilaeans, who support both their own people and ours, while our own people are deprived of the assistance of their own. Therefore, also teach the pagans to make contributions for such services, and instruct the villages of the pagans to offer the first fruits of their crops to the gods. Teach them by such benefactions, explaining that this practice was formerly ours. Homer proves this, for he introduces Eumenes doing such things.

“We, then, neither imitate the good practices of our own people, but leave them to others, nor are we ashamed of our negligence; rather, we reject reverence for the gods even more. If, therefore, I learn that you are doing these things, I shall be filled with joy.

“Receive the governors of the provinces at your home less often, and send them written communications frequently. When they enter the city, let none of the priests go out to meet them. When they come to the temples of the gods, let no soldier, or any member of the official entourage who happens to precede them, go in before them; whoever wishes may follow afterward. When the governor reaches the very threshold of the temple, let him be a private citizen. For you, as you know, are the judge within. This too appears to be required by the sacred ordinance.

“Therefore let those who obey be pious for the sake of truth, and let those who resist be restrained from empty glory. For what punishment would he suffer, or what assistance would he deserve, who refused to have the mother of the gods favorable to him? Those who neglect her will not only be without complaint against them, but will also endure the force of our indignation. For it is not right to spare one who has the gods as enemies. Persuade them, then, that if they wish to enjoy my protection, they must all strive to offer worship to the mother of the gods.”

While the emperor was doing these things for the destruction of the Christians, he did not prevail over his subjects, and he was ashamed to prepare open violence against the Christians.

Meanwhile, in order to accustom the soldiers to paganism, he attempted to restore to its former form the elevated standard of the Romans, the labarum, which Constantine, as has been stated above, had changed into the form of a cross. In public images, however, he depicted Jupiter as bringing him a crown and purple robe from heaven, while Mercury and Mars looked toward him, as though testifying that he was wise and brave. He did this with the images so that, under the pretext of imperial authority, the gods might secretly be worshiped, and his subjects deceived in this manner without realizing it.

For he thought that, if he imposed this upon them willingly, he could afterward accomplish whatever he wished; but if he recognized that they rejected it, he would remove pardon and torture them, as though they had resisted the traditional ceremonies around Rome and had committed an offense against the state and the empire itself.

A few, even after being subjected to punishment, recognized the trick, because, as was customary, they refused to worship. The crowd, however, as usually happens, worshiped the images simply through ignorance. Yet this brought no advantage to the emperor.

When he was devising many means by which to exalt the rites of the pagans, he found a way that bestowed upon many Christian soldiers the radiant crown of virtue. The time arrived when soldiers customarily received imperial gifts—for this was usually done on the Kalends of January, on the birthdays of emperors, and on the birthdays of royal cities. He investigated how he might deceive them simply by means of the ancient custom.

He ordered that each person approaching the emperor’s hands, after being instructed by the officials, should first offer incense; for incense and an altar had been placed before him, according to the ancient Roman custom.

Some then freely displayed their courage and would neither offer incense nor accept the gift. Others, because of the pretext of the law and antiquity, did not realize in their minds what sin they had committed. Still others, seized by greed or disturbed by fear, or trapped by the sudden command, were unable to avoid paganism even though they understood what they were doing.

Many, deceived through ignorance, were later invoking Christ among one another over food and drink, as is customary. One man replied: “Why do you suffer while invoking Christ, whom you denied a little earlier, when, as you received a gift from the emperor, you threw incense into the fire?”

When the soldiers heard this and recognized what they had done, they immediately leaped up and ran publicly. In a sudden rush they cried out, calling God and all people to witness that they were Christians, that they would remain in that name, and that they had acted through ignorance; if such a thing could be said, only their hand had been pagan, while their conscience had taken no part in the deed.

When they came before the emperor, they threw down the gold they had received and demanded in a loud voice [Col. 0922C] that he take back what he had given and kill them. In this way they confessed that they were doing penance because their right hands had sinned thoughtlessly, and that, for Christ’s sake, they wished to surrender their whole bodies to punishment.

When Julian heard this, he was aroused to fury and ordered their heads to be cut off. As they were being led to their death, followed by the people, who marveled at their courage undertaken for piety, they came to the place where criminals were customarily punished.

Then the eldest of them asked the executioner to cut off, before all the rest, the head of a certain Roman, who was still a young man, so that he would not be broken by seeing the deaths of the others. When the young man had knelt on the ground and the executioner had drawn his sword, a messenger suddenly arrived, shouting that the killing must be stopped.

But the young man, deprived of death, said: “Roman was not deemed worthy to be called a martyr of Christ.”

Although the wicked emperor, driven by envy, had forbidden their blood to be shed, he nevertheless did not permit them to live in the cities, but sent them into exile in the remotest regions of the Roman world. Afterward he ordered that those who refused to sacrifice should not enter the palace, and commanded that they should share neither in the council, the forum, the courts, any dignity, nor any form of public association.

Meanwhile, while Julian was sacrificing at Constantinople before Fortuna, Mares, bishop of Chalcedon, approached him and publicly called him impious, godless, and an apostate. Julian is said to have reproached him only for his blindness. He was an old man and, because of the weakness of his eyes, was led by another’s hand.

Moreover, wishing to insult him, Julian customarily said: “Your Galilaean god cannot heal you either.”

Mares replied: “I give thanks to my God for my blindness, because this has happened to me so that I might not see you stripped of piety.”

The emperor made no reply and withdrew. For he thought that paganism would be strengthened if he showed himself patient and gentle toward Christians.

When the Persians learned that Constantius had died, they gained confidence and came to the borders of the Romans, announcing war. For this reason Julian gathered the Roman forces from every direction and brought them with him toward the destruction appointed for him. He sent to Delphi, Delos, and Dodona to obtain oracles about whether it would be expedient for him to undertake the war.

Then all the prophets gave him confidence for battle and promised him victory. It will not be burdensome to insert one response as an example of falsehood or deception. It was as follows: [Col. 0923B]

“Now we all advance, carrying the trophies of the god’s victory, around the river Tigris. I shall be their leader, the warrior Mars.”

It is appropriate to publish the absurdity of these verses, given that they call the rational lord and ruler of the Muses “the Pythian.” But when I discover that falsehood has been inserted into his deceptions, I lament. For he wished to call the river “Tigrem,” although *Tigris* is its nominative form, and it flows across the fields of Assyria before descending into the Persian Gulf.

Deceived by these oracles, the unhappy man dreamed of victory in his mind and prepared, after a triumph over the Parthians, to bring war against the Galilaeans.

He seized many villages and camps, and by then was also capturing cities. After ravaging Assyria, he established his camp near the city of Ctesiphon. There he besieged the king so closely that the king repeatedly sent embassies, offering to surrender part of his homeland if Julian would withdraw once the war had ended. Julian refused, showed no mercy to the supplicants, and did not understand that although victory is good, excessive victory is deeply odious.

He placed particular confidence in the magical arts that the philosopher Maximus displayed for him, and imagined that he would attain the glory of Alexander of Macedon—or even surpass it. For, according to the doctrine of Pythagoras and Plato, he believed that he possessed the soul of Alexander, transferred through the changing of bodies, or at least that another Alexander existed in another body.

For this reason he refused to accept the prayers of the Persian king.

Meanwhile, after he had first appointed a guide for the captives in a deserted region, an elderly deserter later undertook, under the guise of a traitor, to show him a shortcut. When they had traveled for three days and reached an even greater wilderness, they fell into an ambush.

They immediately killed the old man with clubs. He confessed that he had done this for the freedom of his homeland and that he was willing to endure every torture. When the Parthians began pressing him from every side, he ran out from the already established camp, carrying only a shield.

While he was thus striving, in an ill-considered burst of zeal, to arrange the ranks for battle, he was struck by a spear from one of the enemy—and indeed by a man who was fleeing. He was carried back to his tent, but came out again to encourage his men. Gradually drained of blood, he collapsed around midnight.

Some say that a javelin, suddenly hurled, passed through his arm and entered his side. But who inflicted the deadly wound remains unknown to this day. Some say that it was one of the invisible powers; others, one of the shepherds of the Ishmaelites; others, a soldier exhausted by hunger and travel. But whether it was a man or an angel, it is evident that he served divine commands.

Callistus, who at that time served among the emperor’s companions and wrote his history in heroic verse, says that Julian was wounded by a demon. Libanius, the Syrian sophist, among the other praises he wrote of his life, says at the end of his book:

“O fosterling of demons, disciple of demons, and observer of demons!”

Julian died during his fourth consulship, which he held with Sallustius, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the third year of his reign and the seventh after Constantius had appointed him Caesar, at the age of thirty-one.

After his death, his magical practices at Carrhae were discovered. Because he had refused to pass through Edessa on account of the worship of the true religion, he had entered a temple honored by the pagans. There, after celebrating certain sacrilegious rites with his companions, he arranged doors and locks and ordered some soldiers to keep watch there, so that no one might enter within until he returned.

When Julian had died and the pious Jovian had succeeded him, those who entered the temple found a woman hanging by her hair, with her hands stretched out. Her abdomen had been opened so that the victory of the Persians might be examined in her liver.

When his death was announced in that city, everyone held a public celebration. They rejoiced not only in the churches and at the tombs of the martyrs, but also proclaimed the victory in the theaters, rejoicing together with the priests. For all cried out together:

“Most foolish Maximus, where are your prophecies? God lives, and his Christ.”

He was otherwise an excellent man and would have governed the state with distinction, if the fates had permitted it. He was highly educated in the liberal disciplines [Note: [Col. 0923D] A.: Learned, more educated in Greek, and so much so that, although his Latin learning corresponded with his Greek knowledge, his eloquence, etc.]. For he had equaled the philosophers and the wisest of the Greeks, possessing immense eloquence, being especially ready in practice [Note: [Col. 0923D] A.: “and prompt”], and having an extremely tenacious memory [Note: [Col. 0923D] A.: “and very extensive.” “In certain philosophers he was more nearly comparable” [Col. 0924D] “Toward friends, etc.”]. He was generous toward his friends, but less attentive than was fitting for a ruler [Note: [Col. 0924D] “It was fitting. For there were some who inflicted wounds upon his glory. Toward the provincials, etc.”].

He was physically strong, though short in stature, with a long beard and eyes that darted here and there. Toward the provincials he was extremely just and, insofar as possible, restrained the taxes. He was civil toward everyone, took only moderate care of the treasury, was eager for glory and, through it, usually excessive in spirit. He was an excessive persecutor of the Christian religion, though in such a way that he refrained from bloodshed. [Note: [Col. 0924D] A.: “Marcius Antonius.”]

He resembled Marcus Antoninus, whom he also strove to imitate [Note: [Col. 0924D] A.: “Jovian was born, etc.”], and was superstitious in the worship of the gods.

He had deliberately declared beforehand that he would make no disposition concerning the empire, lest—as commonly happens amid the conflicting ambitions of friends—envy of sovereign power, through discord, should bring danger upon the army. He was bolder than was fitting for an emperor, whose own safety must always be preserved for the security of all, and especially in wartime. So fiercely had his desire for glory prevailed over him that neither an earthquake nor the many omens by which he was forbidden to march against Persia could induce him to put an end to his ardor. Not even the sight, during the night before the day of battle, of a huge globe falling from the sky served as a warning to him.

# JOVIANUS

Therefore, on the following day, without any delay, they placed the imperial fillets upon Jovian. He was a brave and noble man and at that time a *millenarius*, when Julian had laid before the soldiers the legal choice either to sacrifice or to leave the army. Jovian chose rather to surrender his military belt than to obey the emperor’s impious commands.

Julian therefore kept him at that time among the military men because of the necessities of the war. When the soldiers forcibly dragged him toward the imperial office, he shouted that he did not wish to rule pagan men, since he himself was a Christian.

When the entire army cried out together that they too were Christians, he accepted the empire.

Because the army was suffering from deprivation in Persia, he made peace with Sapor, king of the Persians—a peace indeed necessary, but dishonorable—by altering the boundaries and handing over some part of the Roman Empire. Nothing of this kind had ever happened before him since the Roman Empire was founded.

Indeed, our legions had been sent under the yoke at Caudium by Pontius, the Samnite commander, and in Spain at Numantia, and in Numidia, although no territory was nevertheless surrendered. That peace agreement would not have been wholly blameworthy if, when it was still possible, he had wished to alter the necessity of the treaty, as the Romans had done in all the wars I have mentioned. For war was immediately brought upon the Samnites, the Numantines, and the Numidians, and the peace was not maintained.

But, fearing a rival to his own empire and remaining in the East, he gave little thought to his glory.

Then the emperor departed from Antioch and came to Tarsus in Cilicia, where he buried Julian’s body honorably. After performing all the customary rites for his funeral, he was designated consul together with his son Varronianus.

While he was hastening to Constantinople, he came to an estate called Dadasta, between Galatia and Bithynia. There the philosopher Themistius, meeting him with other senators, recited a consular speech.

At the aforementioned estate, during the winter, he was overcome by illness and died a sudden death. Many believe that he was rendered lifeless by excessive gluttony [Note: [Col. 0925C] A.: “lifeless from excessive crudity,” etc.], for he had indulged too greatly in food while dining. Others attribute it to the smell of his chamber, which was oppressive to those resting there because of the recently applied lime plaster [Col. 0926B]; some to the excessive number of burning coals that he had ordered to be lit because of the severe cold.

He died in the seventh month of his reign, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0925C] A.: “the fourteenth day before the Kalends”], at the age of thirty-three, according to those who give the highest or lowest figure; and, through the kindness of the emperors who succeeded him, he was enrolled among the gods.

He was born to his father Varronianus, a resident of the territory of Singidunum in the province of Pannonia. Since his father repeatedly lost children, he was instructed in a dream to name the child who was about to be born, when his wife’s labor was already imminent, Jovian [Note: [Col. 0925C] A.: “Jovianus. This distinguished man, etc.”].

He was remarkable in body, cheerful in disposition, and devoted to letters [Note: [Col. 0925C] A.: “He was elected to obtain the empire by the agreement of the army. He was better known to the soldiers through his father’s recommendation than through his own. When affairs had already been thrown into confusion, and the army was also suffering from deprivation, he had been defeated in one battle by the Persians and in another, and made peace with Sapor, necessary indeed but dishonorable, after being fined in territory and surrendering a considerable part of the Roman Empire—something that had never happened before him in the three hundred and twenty-two years since the Roman Empire had been founded. Moreover, our legions had been sent under the yoke at Samnium under Pontius Telesinus, in Spain at Numantia, and in Numidia, although no territory was nevertheless surrendered. That peace agreement would not have been wholly blameworthy if he had wished to alter the necessity of the treaty when it was still possible, as the Romans had done in all the wars I have mentioned [Col. 0925D]. For war was immediately brought upon the Samnites, Numantines, and Numidians, and the peace was not maintained; but, fearing a rival to the empire and remaining in the East, he gave little thought to his glory. He then set out and, heading toward Illyricum, died a sudden death on the borders of Galatia. In other respects he was neither sluggish nor imprudent.” The words “Many, etc.,” as read above, through “was enrolled among the gods,” are placed later in the Ambrosian manuscript and the following manuscripts; they immediately add: “For he was both inclined toward civic affability and by nature exceedingly generous.” Such was the state of the Roman commonwealth under the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus, in the year 1118 from the founding of the City. But since we have come to illustrious and venerable emperors, we shall for the present set a limit to the work. For what remains must be related in a more elevated style; we do not so much omit it now as reserve it for more careful writing.”]

He was devoted to civic life, and by nature extremely generous; among his other virtues, he was neither imprudent nor sluggish. When the army had come to Nicaea in Bithynia, he appointed Valentinian emperor on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, an excellent man [Col. 0926C] and fully worthy of the imperial dignity [Note: [Col. 0926C] In A.: “Here ends Book X. Thus far Eutropius composed the history, to which Paul the Deacon nevertheless added certain material. This is the tenth and final book of Eutropius, which Paul the Deacon made his own, adding certain things at various points. In the manuscript of Hersfeld, the following had been appended: ‘Thus far Eutropius composed the history; although Paul the Deacon added certain material at the command of the most Christian lady Adelperga, ruler of Benevento, wife of the lord Arichis, the wisest and Catholic prince. What follows Paul himself joined together in his own style from various authors.’ This is found in the manuscript. Paul the Deacon, continuing Eutropius, is available; you, reader, may compare him and see how much the author of the *Miscella* added. CANISIUS.”]

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0925]

# VALENTINIAN

[Col. 0925D]

In the year 1118 from the founding of the City, Valentinian was proclaimed emperor, the forty-second after Augustus. [Note: A.: “Thirty-eight, born at Cibala in Pannonia; when he was tribune of the Scutarii at Nicaea, he was proclaimed Augustus and summoned his brother Valens from Constantinople into partnership, etc.”] He was Pannonian by birth, from the city of Cibala. [Note: Ms.: “Paulus, from Pannonian Cibala.” Common edition: “from Cibala.”] [Col. 0927A] When he was tribune of the Scutarii, military command was entrusted to him, because he knew military discipline most thoroughly. He was a great-hearted man and always appeared better than his present circumstances; he excelled not only in courage but also in prudence, self-control, and justice, and was distinguished by the greatness of his physique.

He was so kingly and courteous that, when the army had attempted to associate another partner with him, he replied with what is sung by everyone: “It was your responsibility, soldiers, when there was no emperor, to give me command of the empire; but once I have undertaken it, it is now my responsibility, not yours, to consider the common affairs.” The soldiers, astonished at his words, followed his will.

When he came to Constantinople thirty days after his accession, he admitted his brother Valens to a partnership in the empire, [Col. 0927B] granting him the Eastern provinces while retaining the Western for himself.

His father Gratianus, born of humble stock at Cibala, was called Funarius because five soldiers had been unable to wrest from him a rope that he was carrying for sale. For this achievement he was enrolled in the army and rose as high as the power of the praetorian prefecture. Because of his reputation among the soldiers, the empire was offered to Valentinian. [Note: A.: “The empire was imposed upon him, though he resisted, etc.”]

While under the emperor Julian he maintained the integrity of the Christian faith, and, as has been said, was tribune of the Scutarii. [Note: A.: “When he was tribune, the sacrilegious emperor ordered him either to sacrifice to idols or to leave the army; voluntarily, etc.”] He entered the temple of Fortuna with Julian. The temple attendants stood on both sides of the doors and purified those entering by sprinkling them with water, as they themselves claimed. Valentinian, walking ahead of the emperor, saw a drop of the sprinkling on his cloak and, indignant, struck the temple attendant with his fist, saying that he had been polluted rather than purified.

When Julian saw this, he ordered Valentinian to be confined, saying: “Either sacrifice to the idols or leave the army.” Valentinian departed voluntarily. Before long, after Julian had been killed and Jovian had died, the man who had lost his tribunate for the name of Christ received the empire in place of his persecutor.

When he had already ruled the empire for three years together with his brother Valens, Valentinian, at the urging of his mother-in-law and wife, created his son Gratianus, who was not yet fully mature, Augustus.

Thus, when Valentinian was at the beginning of his reign and was traveling from Constantinople through Thrace toward Rome, the bishops of the Hellespont and Bithynia, and all who proclaimed the Father and the Son consubstantial, sent Hypatius, bishop of Heraclea Perinthus, as an envoy to him, so that he might deign to take part in correcting the doctrine.

When Hypatius approached the emperor and announced the bishops’ embassy, Valentinian replied: “It is not lawful for me, together with the people subject to me, to concern myself closely with matters of this kind. Therefore, priests, do what seems right to you.” They then came to Lampsacus, remained there for two months, and finally annulled what had been enacted at Constantinople by Eudoxius and Acacius; they decreed that the faith set forth at Seleucia should be maintained.

But the impious Valens overturned what had been done at Lampsacus and sent the bishops who had assembled there into exile.

Meanwhile, Valens remained for a long time at Antioch and granted everyone permission to celebrate his own sacred rites: pagans, Jews, and all heretics alike. The pagans even held festivals while ministering to demons. After Jovian had extinguished the vanities of idolatry following Julian, Valens again allowed them to flourish. The worship of Jupiter and Dionysus, and the rites of Ceres, were no longer celebrated secretly, as though under a pious emperor; instead, revelers ran everywhere through the middle of the streets. At that time the prince was hostile only to those who appeared to preach the apostolic doctrine.

In the same year, at Atrebates, true wool mixed with rainwater flowed down from the clouds. At Constantinople, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, hail of extraordinary size fell and killed some people. [Note: A.: “He destroyed them. In those days Procopius, seizing tyranny at Constantinople, was destroyed in Phrygia Salutaris, and many of his faction were killed and proscribed. About this time there was an earthquake, etc.”]

Some indeed say of Valens that his wife Dominica persuaded him to depart from the orthodox faith held by his own brother and to follow the teaching of Arius so zealously. Others, however, write that after he had become emperor and had been rebaptized by Eudoxius, he confirmed by oath at that very baptism that he would share Arius’s belief and would in no way accept the *Homoousion*.”

Meanwhile, while Valens was staying in Syria, a tyrant named Procopius arose at Constantinople. Having quickly gathered a large military force, he hastened against the emperor; when this was reported to him, he held back his advance for a little while.

While the outcome of the war was still coming to birth, an earthquake occurred throughout the whole world, [Col. 0928C] so that the cities of Sicily and many islands were shaken and overthrown, and countless peoples were crushed beneath the ruins. [Note: A.: “The sea so went beyond its shore that Sicily’s …”] [Note: A.: “They crushed them. Meanwhile Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, bishop of the Arian heresy, lapsed into a most savage heresy and attempted to persecute Catholics, but was restrained by his brother’s authority. At that time Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted Christians most cruelly among his people and raised them to the crown of martyrdom. Valentinian, etc.”]

Around Bithynia it was so great that it overthrew the city of Nicaea. The sea also altered its boundaries: in some places it rushed in with such force that it watered regions where people had previously been able to walk; in other places it withdrew so far that dry land was exposed.

In the following year, during the consulship of Gratianus and Dagalaifus, wars were prepared. When the tyrant Procopius had left Constantinople and was moving his camp against the emperor, Valens, hearing of it, came from Antioch and engaged him near the Phrygian city of Nacolia. In the first battle he was defeated. Shortly afterward, however, he captured Procopius, when the soldiers Agelo and Gomarius handed him over. Later he ordered them also to be executed by certain unexpected punishments.

For, disregarding the oath he had given them, he cruelly killed them by having them cut apart with saws. As for the tyrant, he bent two neighboring trees toward one another, had one of Procopius’s feet tied to each, and then released the trees; springing back into the air, they tore Procopius apart.

At the same time, a certain errant demon, taking advantage of Valens’s cruelty, persuaded him to investigate who would assume the empire after him. For this reason he practiced necromancy. When these arts had been completed, the demon put many people to death, delivering responses—not openly, but by crooked deception. When consulted about the empire, it displayed the four letters ΘΕΟΔ and said that a man bearing this name would take the summit of imperial power after Valens.

When this reached the emperor’s ears, he was driven by jealousy to kill many whom he judged likely to seize the tyranny. Thus Theodorus, Theodulus, Theodotus, and anyone who had these letters at the beginning of his name were put to death. Among them Theodosius was also killed, a brave man descended from the province of Spain and the father of Theodosius, who later ruled the empire.

Because of this fear, many changed the names they had previously borne and denied them under oath, in order to avoid danger.

Meanwhile, after Auxentius, the Arian bishop of Milan, had died, Valentinian summoned the bishops and addressed them as follows:

“You know clearly—for you are learned in the divine words—what a bishop ought to be, because it is not fitting for him to govern those subject to him by word alone, but also by his manner of life, and to show himself an imitator of every virtue, possessing a good life as a witness to his teaching. Choose such a man, therefore, and establish him in the episcopal seat, so that we also, who govern the empire, may sincerely bow our heads to him and, whenever we have sinned as human beings, necessarily receive his admonitions like medicines from a physician.”

When the emperor had said this, the synod asked that he himself make the decision, since he was wise and pious. But he replied: “Such an election lies above you. You, endowed with divine grace and shining with that splendor, will be better able to choose.”

Then the priests assembled and deliberated about the episcopal see. The inhabitants of the city, however, as commonly happens, created a disturbance, each group wishing one man or another to be ordained. Those who belonged to the sect of the Arian Auxentius struggled to have someone like themselves appointed, while the orthodox strove to obtain a bishop of their own doctrine.

When Ambrose, who at that time had been entrusted with the civil administration, learned of this sedition and feared that something might erupt in the city, he immediately went to the church. Then, when the sedition had ceased, they gave a unanimous voice, asking that Ambrose be ordained shepherd of the flock, although he had not yet been baptized.

When the emperor learned this, he immediately ordered him to be baptized and ordained bishop as a worthy man. For he knew that Ambrose’s will was more reliable than any weight of evidence and that he understood the decrees of the entire rule of faith with greater subtlety. He also judged that divine judgment was present in him, since even the opposing party had agreed in his election.

Thus, after receiving the gift of holy baptism, Ambrose simultaneously received the grace of the episcopate.

After this had happened, it is said that the excellent emperor offered the following hymn to the Savior and Lord: “I give thanks to you, almighty Lord and our Savior, because to this man I entrusted bodies, but you entrusted souls, and you have shown that my choice accords with justice.”

A few days later, when Saint Ambrose complained with great confidence before the emperor that the judges were acting unjustly, the emperor said: “I have long known this confidence of yours. Since I clearly approved it, I not only did not resist, but also shared in the choice of your ordination. Hurry, therefore, to heal, as divine law commands, the sins of our souls.”

Meanwhile, Valentinian crushed the Saxons, a people situated along the shores and impassable marshes of the Ocean, terrifying in courage and agility and dangerous to the Roman frontiers, as they were planning a massive incursion in the very territories of the Franks.

The new enemy, the Burgundians, also began to be known by a new name. More than eighty thousand armed men, it is said, occupied the bank of the Rhine. The people of Gaul, where they now remain in their presumed possession, still testify that these men had once been gathered into a great nation after Drusus and Tiberius, the adoptive sons of Caesar, had subdued Inner Germany and distributed its inhabitants through military camps. They are also said to have taken their name from their work, because the frequent settlements established along the frontier are commonly called *burgi*—“forts”—and because their force was exceedingly powerful and destructive. Nevertheless, not long afterward they became Christians.

Valentinus was overcome before he seized the tyranny. [Note: A.: “Meanwhile in Britain, before he seized the tyranny, etc.”]

In the eleventh year of his reign, when the people of the Sarmatians, a small and insignificant nation, rose against him and spread through the provinces of Pannonia, ravaging them, Valentinian prepared war against them and defeated them. At the town of Brigetio, when envoys of the Quadi had been sent to request peace, [Note: A.: “When he was answering the embassy of the Quadi, in the fifty-fifth year of his life, by a sudden outpouring of blood, which in Greek is called *apoplexis*, etc.”] he asked their envoys whether all the Sarmatians were such men and of such contemptible bodily stature.

When they replied to the emperor, “You have their better men here, and you see them,” he cried out with great force: “The Roman Empire is enduring terrible things, reaching even to Valentinian, if men such as these Sarmatians, though they are what they are, rise against the Romans.”

Then, from excessive agitation and the clapping of his hands, a bodily vein ruptured and a great quantity of blood burst forth. This condition is called in Greek ἀπόπληξις (*apoplexis*, “stroke” or “apoplexy”). He lost his voice but remained conscious and died. Some attributed this to immoderate eating and security. [Note: A.: “Satiety.”] He was fifty-five years old, in the consulship of Gratianus and Equitius, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.

He was an outstanding emperor: handsome in appearance, [Note: A.: “Decent in appearance.”] capable in intellect, serious in character, [Note: A.: “Grave, like Aurelian, etc.”] highly polished in speech, although sparing in speaking, severe, forceful, hostile to vices, and extremely avaricious. [Perhaps read *maxime*, “extremely.”] [Note: Ms.: “Infected.”] Some, however, interpreted his excessive severity and frugality as cruelty and avarice.

He was sharp in the matters I am about to recount, close to Hadrian in character; he painted most beautifully, remembered things, devised new weapons, fashioned images in wax or clay, and made prudent use of places, times, and speech. To conclude briefly: if he had been permitted to rid himself of the unfaithful men to whom he had entrusted himself as though they were most faithful and prudent, or to use tested and learned advisers, he would undoubtedly have shone forth as a perfect prince. [Note: A.: “Foul.”] [Note: A.: “Afterward he would have excelled. In the year, etc.”]

Accordingly, after his death, on the sixth day following it, the soldiers of Italy created his four-year-old son, the boy Valentinian, emperor. Equitius and Merobaudes were responsible; the child had been brought from a nearby place where he had been staying with his mother.

His brother and uncle subsequently accepted his rule, although unwillingly, since it had been done without their knowledge.

## VALENS

In the year 1128 from the founding of the City, Valens, the forty-third emperor after Augustus, held the empire of the East for four years after Valentinian’s death, while Gratianus, Valentinian’s son, ruled in the West together with Valentinian, his very young brother. [Note: A.: “While Gratianus was reigning, he made his very young brother Valentinian his associate in the empire.”]

This Valentinian had been born to Justina, the second wife of Valentinian. [Note: A.: “He was born thus: Valentinian the elder, after his wife had long praised Justina’s beauty, joined her to himself in marriage and granted laws on her account, etc.”]

It is said that Valentinian married her in the following way, at the command of his earlier wife Severa. Justus, Justina’s father, was a judge in Picenum during the time of Constantius. He dreamed that an imperial purple garment had been born from his right thigh. When the vision was being repeated by many people, it reached the ears of Constantius. Considering the dream as indicating that an emperor would be born from him, Constantius sent and killed Justus. His daughter Justina remained a virgin.

Later the matter came to Severa’s attention. Justina visited her frequently and was loved by her, so much so that she even bathed with her. When Severa had looked for a long time at Justina bathing beside her, she was delighted by the virgin’s beauty and captivated by affection. She told the emperor that the virgin Justina was so beautiful that she herself was worthy to be the emperor’s wife.

Valentinian, taking her words to heart, considered marrying Justina, but did not wish to cast Severa aside, by whom Gratianus had been born. He therefore publicly issued a law throughout the city that anyone who wished might lawfully enter two marriages. For this reason, it was said, nations would be populous, because the practice was customary among them. [Note: A.: “It is customary. Accordingly, as we have said, Valentinian took Justina and had four children by her: Valentinian, whom Gratianus, as stated above, associated with himself in the kingdom, and Gratam, Justam, and Gallam.”]

Once the law had been promulgated, Valentinian himself was united to Justina. She bore him this Valentinian and three daughters: Justa, Grata, and Galla. Two of them remained virgins. The elder Theodosius, however, later took Galla as his wife; their daughter Placidia was born from this marriage. She later received the surname Galla from her mother’s name.

Meanwhile, Valens, carrying out in deeds the impiety he had long contemplated, issued a law requiring monks to serve in the army and ordered those who refused to be killed with clubs by tribunes and soldiers. Their number was immense. They lived throughout the vast deserts of Egypt, spread across sandy regions where, because of thirst, barrenness, and the dangerous abundance of serpents, human habitation was absent; nevertheless, a great multitude of monks had filled those places with inhabitants. In particular, a large number obtained the palm of martyrdom at Nitria.

Throughout the individual provinces, various hardships were inflicted upon the Catholic churches and upon peoples of the true faith.

Meanwhile, in Africa, a certain Firmus, having stirred up the Moorish peoples and made himself king, devastated Africa and Mauretania. By treachery he captured the distinguished city of Caesarea in Mauretania and handed it over to the barbarians as plunder.

Against him Theodosius, the father of the Theodosius who later ruled the empire, was sent by the elder Valentinian as a commander. [Note: Ms. of François Pithou: “With the assistance of the *comitatenses*, Theodosius, master of the cavalry.”] He defeated the Moorish peoples, who had spread out, in many battles, and drove the stricken and overwhelmed Firmus to his death. After he had restored all Africa together with Mauretania through his exceptionally experienced foresight, he was ordered by Valens to be killed. He chose to be baptized at Carthage for the remission of sins. [Note: A.: “He preferred this, and finally, dying a glorious death, willingly offered his throat to the executioner, etc.”] After he had obtained the sacrament of Christ that he had sought, and after a glorious life in this world, secure of eternal life, he voluntarily presented his neck to the executioner.

Around this time the Goths, established beyond the Ister, began a civil war between two factions. Fridigernus commanded one side and Athalaricus the other. Fridigernus and all his followers were Arians, while Athalaricus and his followers were pagans.

When Athalaricus prevailed, Fridigernus asked Valens for assistance through his own Arian bishop, Ulfila. Ulfila had lived under Constantius with the Arians Eudoxius and Acacius. He was also the first to devise Gothic letters and translated the divine Scriptures into that language.

Valens immediately ordered the soldiers of Thrace to provide assistance to Fridigernus. With this support Athalaricus was defeated and put to flight. Not long afterward, when the Goths had again come to terms with one another, Ulfila instructed not only Fridigernus’s Goths but also Athalaricus’s.

Athalaricus, grieved that his own religion was being violated, handed over to punishment many of his people who had become Arians. The Arians call them martyrs to this day. For this reason Fridigernus and his people sought the western regions, while Athalaricus remained there with his army.

Those who had gone west with Fridigernus were called Visigoths in the western language of their homeland—that is, “Western Goths.” Those who remained with Athalaricus in their native settlements were called Ostrogoths—that is, “Eastern Goths.”

At that time the people of the Huns, long enclosed among their own inaccessible mountains, suddenly erupted in a frenzy against the Goths and drove them, once thrown into confusion, from their ancient settlements.

For we have learned from antiquity that their origin was as follows. Filimer, king of the Goths and son of the great Godaric, the fifth ruler of the Getae after their departure from the island of Scandia, entered the Scythian lands with his people. There he discovered among his people certain magical women, whom they call *Alyrumnas* in the Gothic language. Suspecting them, he expelled them from his midst and drove them far from his army, forcing them to wander in the wilderness.

When wild men, whom some call “fig fauns” (*fauni phicarii*), saw them wandering through the desert, they mingled with them in intercourse and produced this exceedingly savage race. At first it lived among the Maeotian marshes, small, hideous, and feeble, almost an inhuman race, known by no other voice except that it displayed some likeness to human speech.

From such a stock, therefore, the Huns were born and came to the borders of the Goths. Even those whom they perhaps could not defeat in war were overwhelmed by the terror of their appearance and put to flight by their fearsome aspect.

Their appearance was of a frightening blackness, like a deformed mass—if it is permissible to say so—rather than a face. They had points rather than eyes, whose grim gaze revealed the courage of their minds. They even rage against their newborn offspring on the first day. They cut the cheeks of male children with iron, so that before they receive the nourishment of milk they are forced to undergo the suffering of a wound.

Thus they grow old without beards, and their young men lack beauty, because faces furrowed by iron consume the proper grace of hair in scars. They were small in stature but swift in their sharp movements and exceedingly ready for riding, broad-shouldered and prepared for bows and arrows, with strong necks always held erect in pride.

They lived under human form with the savage ferocity of beasts. When the Goths saw this extremely mobile race, marauding among many nations, crossing the Danube in flight, they were received by Valens without any treaty of alliance. [Note: A.: “They were received. Then, driven by hunger because of the intolerable greed of the commander Maximus, they rose to arms; after defeating Valens’s army, they poured through Thrace, devastating everything with slaughter and fire. When Valens learned this, he left Antioch and prepared his army against the Goths too late, etc.”]

Valens granted them lands in Thrace for settlement, thinking that he had acquired from them a prepared source of assistance against all barbarians. For this reason he thereafter neglected the soldiers and despised those who had previously labored against the enemy.

He also ordered his tax collectors throughout the province, in villages and cities, to exact eighty solidi from each soldier.

This, then, was the beginning of the time when the Roman state was subjected to calamities. For when the barbarians had occupied Thrace, they freely ravaged the Roman provinces and devastated the neighboring cities.

Meanwhile Valens was coming from Antioch to Constantinople. At the Bosporus he learned that the Gothic people had risen for war, and immediately sent to his brother Valentinian, asking for assistance. Valentinian wrote back that it was neither religious nor just for such a man to govern the imperial laws while he was in rebellion against God; rather, it was just that his arrogance should be subdued and that he should not exercise the rights of imperial power.

When the wretched man learned this, although constrained by greater necessity, he nevertheless did not cease from his excesses but remained rebellious against the truth.

Meanwhile Terentius returned victorious from Armenia, an excellent man, appropriately adorned with piety. Valens ordered him to ask for whatever gift he wished. He replied, as a pious man ought to think: “I ask neither gold, silver, an estate, a belt, nor a house, but only that one church be granted to those who have endured dangers for the apostolic doctrine.”

When Valens received the written petition and read it, he tore it apart and ordered Terentius to ask for something else. But Terentius replied: “Receive the words of my prayer, emperor, and I have my gift; I ask for nothing else. The Judge of all is the judge of my intention.”

After Valens crossed the Bosporus and came to Thrace, he first remained at Constantinople, preparing for war. He then sent the general Trajan with lightly equipped troops against the Goths. Trajan was defeated and returned in disgrace. When Valens reproached him for softness, Trajan replied:

“I was not defeated, emperor, but you were, because you fight against God and secure his favour for the barbarians.” Do you not know whom you expelled from the churches and to whom you handed them over?”

Meanwhile the barbarians ranged throughout Thrace and devastated even the suburbs of Constantinople with fire and slaughter, since no one was able to resist them forcefully.

When they reached the city walls, the afflicted city murmured against the emperor. Stimulated at last by repentance for his sin, he ordered the bishops and the other holy men to be recalled from exile. [Note: A.: “He commanded it. Finally, after a lamentable war had been waged with the Goths, at the first …”]

The circus games were being held, and there they heaped insults upon Valens, calling him weak and a deserter from wars. They shouted: “Give us weapons, and we will fight.”

Inflamed by anger, the emperor left Constantinople on the third day before the Ides of June, threatening that, when he returned, he would exact penalties from the citizens of Constantinople for their injuries, since they had initially appeared to give assistance to Procopius. He even threatened to plow the city under.

The holy monk Isacius, holding the bridle of King Valens’s horse as Valens finally departed for battle, said to him: “Where are you going, emperor, fighting against God and having God as your adversary?”

In anger Valens handed Isacius over to prison and threatened him with death if he returned, just as Micaiah had once been treated by Ahab.

After Valens’s engagement, some of his own men confessed that he had ordered divinations to be performed concerning the battle that threatened him.

He led the people of Constantinople as far as the city of Adrianople, which lies on the border of Macedonia. In the fifteenth year of his reign he finally fought a lamentable war with the Goths.

At the first attack of the Goths, the Roman cavalry squadrons were thrown into confusion and abandoned the exposed infantry. The infantry were immediately surrounded by the enemy cavalry and overwhelmed by clouds of arrows. Fleeing madly in every direction from fear, they were completely cut down and perished beneath the swords and spears of their pursuers. [Note: A.: “They perished utterly. The emperor himself, etc.”]

The emperor himself, wounded by an arrow, [Note: A.: “He was wounded.”] turned to flight. Because of the severity of his pain, he fell from his horse and was carried into a very humble hut. [Note: A.: “Very severe; often [from] a horse, etc.”] When the Goths arrived, they set fire beneath it, and he was burned in the conflagration. [Col. 0935A] [Note: A.: “He was burned. Finally, when the Goths asked him to send them bishops from whom they might receive the rudiments of the faith, Valens sent them teachers of the Arian doctrine, and thus that entire people became Arian. Justly, etc.”]

This occurred on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the fiftieth year of his life and the thirteenth year of his reign with his brother Valentinian; after Valentinian’s death, he had ruled for two years, five months, and thirteen days.

The following qualities are to be approved in him: he was good to landowners and farmers, rarely changed judges, was faithful to his friends, and became angry without harm or danger to anyone. He was, however, very fearful.

Some say that, while the divine Isacius was in prison and Valens was being burned, Isacius discerned through divine grace and purity of spirit the stench of Valens’s body and foretold his destruction to those who were with him, before the messengers arrived to report the events of the battle.

By the just judgment of God, therefore, he was burned by those whom he had inflamed with the fire of treachery. For when the Goths asked him to send them bishops from whom they might receive the rudiments of the faith, he sent them teachers of the Arian doctrine. [Col. 0935B] Thus the whole people became Arian.

After the emperor had been killed, the Goths, now secure, came again as far as the walls of Constantinople and devastated its suburbs. [Note: A.: “Secure, they hastened toward the city of Constantinople, where Dominica Augusta, the wife of Valens, then gave large sums of money to the populace and turned the enemy away from ravaging the city; she faithfully and courageously preserved the kingdom for her relatives. In the year, etc.”]

Therefore the citizens who had taken up arms, and who were able to carry whatever weapons they found, resisted the enemy as best they could. Dominica, the wife of Valens, supplied rewards from the public treasury to those who fought well, according to military custom. The Saracens also provided assistance; their queen, named Mavia, who was allied with the Romans, had sent them.

## GRATIANUS.

In the year 1132 from the founding of the City, Gratian, the forty-fourth emperor after Augustus, held the empire for six years after Valens’s death. [Note: A., XL. Note A: “He held it, although he had already long before reigned together with his uncle Valens and his brother Valentinian. Accordingly, etc.”]

Accordingly, when Gratian was still very young and saw an immeasurable multitude of enemies pour into the Roman territories, relying on the power of Christ he threw himself against the enemy with a military force vastly inferior in number. Immediately, near Argentoratum, a most terrifying town of Gaul, he brought an extraordinarily successful war to an end. For more than thirty thousand Alamanni are reported to have been killed in that battle, with scarcely any loss to the Romans. [Note: A., Argentaria.] [Note: A.: “They are reported. Ultimately, the cultivation of the true faith brought this to him. For while Italy had until that time languished under the disease of Arian perfidy, after the late death of Auxentius, when Ambrose, formerly a pagan judge, had suddenly been elected bishop at Milan by divine providence and had soon afterward been baptized with Catholic baptism and ordained bishop, and when he had presented books on the Catholic faith to the emperor Gratian and had been received with the veneration due to him, all Italy immediately returned to the true faith. At that time, etc.”]

At that time, in Gaul, near Tours, the most blessed Martin was shining forth through many virtues; and throughout the whole world, illustrious in teaching and knowledge, Jerome the presbyter was radiant at Bethlehem, a city of Palestine, while Augustine, bishop of the city of Hippo in Numidia, was likewise radiant.
