[Note: A.: “Renowned for teachings and knowledge.”] [Note: A.: “Jerome, situated at Bethlehem in Palestine, was radiant. Moreover, etc.”]

But when Gratian realized that the greatest danger to the entire Roman empire was impending, since Thrace and Dacia were held as native lands by the Goths and Taifali, and by the Huns and Alans, more destructive than every other calamity, he left Italy and came to Pannonia. [Note: A.: “The final danger to the whole Roman empire.”] At that time Theodosius was held in very great renown, both because of the nobility of his parents and because of his own courage. For this reason, having been harassed by the envy of his fellow judges, he was living in Spain, where he had been born and raised.

When the emperor was hesitating about what he should do—for the barbarians, exalted by victory, seemed invincible—he himself also summoned Theodosius from Spain, trusting that the barbarians could be overcome under his command, just as Nerva had once chosen the Spaniard Trajan, through whom the commonwealth was restored. For, suddenly declaring him master of the soldiers, he sent him with an army against the barbarians.

Thus Theodosius believed that the commonwealth, afflicted by the anger of God, could be restored by the mercy of God. Placing all his confidence in the help of Christ, he boldly attacked those great Scythian nations, feared by all earlier peoples and, as Pompey and Cornelius testified, avoided even by that great Alexander; nations then equipped with Roman arms and horses after the Roman army had been destroyed—that is, the Alans, Huns, and Goths. [Note: A.: “Then, etc.”] [Note: A.: “He attacked them and defeated them in great and numerous battles. He entered Constantinople as victor.”]

The barbarians, unable to withstand the assault, abandoned their battle lines. Some fled, others pursued, and an immense slaughter of barbarians took place. The few who escaped secretly crossed the river Ister. Immediately the excellent commander, having dispersed his army among the neighboring cities, returned swiftly to the emperor, so that he himself became the messenger of his own victories; yet this seemed incredible to the emperor himself, who was astonished by what had happened. For the envious were saying that he too had fled and had lost his army.

But he asked that those who disparaged him be sent to see the multitude of enemies who had been slain. Persuaded by these words, the emperor sent men to inspect what had happened and report to him.

Meanwhile the excellent commander saw a divine vision and clearly recognized that it had been shown to him by God, the source of all things. For in a dream he had seen that Saint Meletius, bishop of the city of Antioch, was clothing him in the imperial cloak and placing a crown upon his head. Having seen this during the night, he told one of his friends in the morning. The man said that the dream was clear and contained nothing enigmatic or doubtful.

After a few days, those who had been sent to inspect the victory returned and reported that many thousands of the enemy had been killed. Therefore the emperor Gratian, rejoicing and with everyone’s approval, clothed Theodosius in the purple at Sirmium, while he was thirty-three years old, and placed him in command of the East and Thrace together, in the consulship of Ausonius and Olibrium, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Accordingly, Theodosius entered the city of Constantinople in triumph. And so that he might not frighten that small Roman army by constant warfare, he made a treaty with Athalaric, king of the Goths. [Note: A.: “With Athanaric, whom he always calls by that name.”]

Athalaric came to Constantinople to Theodosius, who received him with extraordinary warmth and affection. When Athalaric had entered the city and saw both the city’s buildings and the crowds of people adorned as though for a festival, and when he fixed each thing in his mind and afterward entered the emperor’s palace and observed the various services and duties there, he said:

“Without doubt the emperor is an earthly god. Whoever attempts to raise a hand against him will himself be guilty of his own blood.”

Nevertheless, before long, when illness came upon him, he departed this life. The emperor himself went before his funeral procession and honorably committed him to burial. But all the Gothic peoples, after the death of their king, observing Theodosius’s courage and kindness, surrendered themselves to the Roman empire.

In those days the Parthians, who after Julian’s death and the frequent defeats of other emperors, and now also after Valens had been overcome, had been spewing forth the satisfaction of their most recent victory with savage mockery, voluntarily sent ambassadors to Theodosius at Constantinople, humbly asked for peace, and entered into a treaty with him. [Note: A.: “The Parthians and the other barbarian nations, previously hostile to the Roman name, voluntarily sent ambassadors to Theodosius at Constantinople and humbly asked for peace, and a treaty was made with them. Meanwhile, when Theodosius in the East had subdued the barbarian peoples and at last restored Thrace, freed from the enemy, and had made his son Arcadius his colleague in the empire, Maximus, a man, etc.”]

Meanwhile Theodosius, having received hostages from the Goths on account of the treaty, came to Thessalonica. There, after falling ill and wishing to be baptized, he summoned Acolius, the bishop of that city, and asked what faith he held. When Acolius replied that the Arian plague had not been able to enter Illyricum, but that they had preserved inviolate from the beginning the faith of the Council of Nicaea, Theodosius gladly accepted his words, was baptized, and was freed from his illness.

During this period the emperor Theodosius designated his son Arcadius Augustus, in the second consulship of Merobaudes and that of Saturninus, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.

In Italy, while Valentinian was still a sufficiently young boy, Probus, formerly consul, exercised the administration of affairs. His mother Justina, however, since she was an Arian, had not dared to injure the orthodox while her husband was alive. After his death, when her son was very young, she came to Milan and was hostile to Ambrose, to the point of ordering that he be sent into exile.

When he was ordered to leave the church, Ambrose said:

“I do not do this willingly, lest I seem to surrender the fold to wolves and to those who blaspheme God. If it pleases you, kill me here; I shall willingly accept death in this place.”

At that time Maximus was a vigorous man, brave and worthy of the imperial dignity—unless he had risen through tyranny against his oath of allegiance. In Britain he was unwillingly proclaimed emperor by the army and crossed into Gaul. [Note: A.: “Vigorous, upright, and worthy of Augustus.”]

But Gratian, while neglecting the army and preferring to the old Roman soldiers a few Alans whom he had transferred to his side at enormous expense, had become so attached to the company and almost the friendship of the barbarians that he sometimes traveled in the same dress as they. Thus he aroused the soldiers’ hatred against himself.

Accordingly, Maximus was welcomed by the soldiers and legions hostile to Gratian. He suddenly attacked Gratian, who was terrified and wished to cross into Italy, and killed him after ensnaring him by deceit. [Note: A.: “He outwitted and killed him at the age of twenty-nine, and expelled his brother Valentinian Augustus from Italy. Valentinian, fleeing to the East, [was received] by Theodosius with paternal affection, etc.”]

The reason for his murder was this: Maximus spread a rumor among the people that Gratian’s wife was hurrying to meet her husband at the city of Lyon in Gaul as he crossed the river. Gratian, believing that his wife Creusa—whom he had recently married—was coming, failed to take precautions against the ambush and, as though blind, fell into the pit of a savage enemy. When Gratian had therefore arrived as if at his wife’s carriage, Andragathius suddenly sprang out and killed him.

He died in the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus, in the fifteenth year of his reign and the twenty-ninth year of his life. Immediately Maximus expelled Valentinian Augustus and his mother Justina from Italy into Illyricum. Then he came to Constantinople, where Theodosius received him with paternal affection and soon restored him to the empire.

Gratian was born at Sirmium and was educated in literature to no ordinary degree. He could compose verse, speak elegantly, and explain rhetorical controversies in the manner of the rhetoricians. He did nothing else day and night except meditate on arrows, [Note: A.: “Than to meditate on little arrows.”] believing it to be the greatest pleasure and a divine art to strike what had been aimed at. He was sparing in food, sleep, and wine, and victorious over lust. He would have been full of every virtue if he had directed his mind toward learning the art of governing the commonwealth; but from this he was almost entirely alienated, not only in inclination but also in practice—that is, he was generally more cheerful than was appropriate and more modest than the interests of the commonwealth allowed.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0937]

## THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0937D]

In the year 1139 from the founding of the City, [Note: A., 38. The same is found in the manuscript of Paul and in the vulgate editions.] Theodosius, born of Theodosius his father and Thermantia his mother, the forty-fifth emperor after Augustus, obtained sole possession of the Roman world after Gratian had been killed by Maximus and remained in power for eleven years, although he had already reigned for six years in the East while Gratian, by his favor, was reigning jointly with him. [Note: A.: “Had reigned while Gratian was alive. Accordingly, for just and necessary reasons, etc.”] [Note: A.: “His father, Honorius.”] [Note: A.: “Forty-one of the emperors, after Gratian had been killed, etc.”]

Moved by necessary causes to civil war, as he sought both to avenge the death of one of the two Augusti brothers and to restore the other, he advanced against the tyrant Maximus, superior in faith alone, for he was far inferior in the comparison of the entire military apparatus. Maximus was then established at Aquileia. His companion Andragathius directed the whole war. By an artful plan he had fortified all the approaches through the Alps and across the rivers with very large forces of soldiers; but while preparing to anticipate and overwhelm the unsuspecting enemy by a naval expedition, he voluntarily abandoned the very barriers that he had blocked.

Thus Theodosius entered the undefended Alps without anyone noticing and, arriving unexpectedly at Aquileia, shut in the great and savage enemy Maximus, who by the mere terror of his name exacted tribute and military payments even from the most savage German peoples. [Note: A.: “He shut him in, captured him, and killed him. This, etc.”]

When Maximus’s soldiers were unable to withstand the emperor’s assault, they seized the tyrant, bound him, and immediately presented him to the emperor. He was killed by them on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. The blessed Martin had foretold this destruction of Maximus.

Valentinian, having recovered Italy, gained possession of the empire. Andragathius, the commander who had killed Gratian, learned of Maximus’s death, threw himself headlong from a ship into the nearby river, and was drowned. [Note: A.: “He threw himself headlong from the ship into the waves and was suffocated, etc.”] Theodosius received a bloodless victory through God’s providence.

He also destroyed Victor, Maximus’s son, whom his father had left as emperor in Gaul while he was still a child. [Note: A.: “He put him to death. Then the younger Valentinian, after he had crossed into Gaul and was living there in the peaceful security of the commonwealth, was strangled at Vienne by the treachery of his commander Arbogast, and so that, etc.”]

Then the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius came to Rome after completing the victory. Honorius was with them, still a boy; after the victory won against Maximus, his father had summoned him from the city of Constantinople.

The emperor Theodosius, therefore, residing in the City of Rome, greatly benefited the city, providing some things and beneficially taking away others. Yet he prohibited two practices worthy of shame.

From the beginning there had been in the city of Rome a house built on an immense scale, in which bread was made and distributed to the entire city. In the course of time, the managers of these establishments turned the public bakeries into dens of robbery. Since mills had been installed in underground locations, they established shops along every side of those buildings and made prostitutes stand in them, so that through them they might receive many people: some who came for bread, and others who hurried there for the shameful purpose of lust.

By mechanical devices people were made to fall from the shop into the mill, and this happened especially to foreigners. They were so concealed and shut in that many who labored there were not permitted to leave until old age, while their relatives thought that they had died.

One of Theodosius’s soldiers fell into such a trap. When he had been shut in at the mill and was not allowed to leave, he drew his sword and killed those who were preventing him. Terrified, they then let the soldier go. When the emperor learned of this, he had the managers put to death by punishment and ordered the bakery itself to be utterly destroyed.

He abolished another practice of the same kind. If a woman had been caught in adultery, the matter was not corrected; rather, she was handed over to an increase of sin. They confined her in a narrow brothel and admitted men who fornicated with her. At the hour when they were committing the shameful act, they struck little bells, so that by that sound her dishonor might be made known. [Note: Cedrenus, κώδων, “bell.”]

When the emperor heard of this, he did not permit it to continue but ordered the brothels themselves to be destroyed.

After these acts, he left Valentinian at Rome and returned with Honorius to Constantinople, in the consulship of Dacianus and Symmachus, on the fourth day before the Ides of November. [Note: Marcellinus, Tatianus.]

The emperor Theodosius, however, also experienced emotional disturbances and, mixing immense cruelty with a rage that had some just basis, committed an unjust act of passion. It is necessary to recount this, both for the benefit of readers and because of the memorable reputation of his virtues.

Thessalonica is a large and populous city. When a sedition had arisen there, some judges were stoned and dragged away. Theodosius, angered by this, did not restrain the weakness of his wrath. Instead, he ordered the citizens to be invited to the circus games and commanded swords to be unsheathed unjustly against everyone, and the innocent to be killed together with the guilty. [Note: Ἄδικα ξίφει κατὰ πάντων ἐγύμνωσε: “He unjustly bared the sword against all.” Cedrenus, see the passage.] Seven thousand people, as is reported, were killed all together, without a prior trial, like a harvest. [Note: Zonaras, fifteen thousand.]

When Ambrose heard of this disaster, filled with groans, and the emperor had come to Milan and wished solemnly to enter the sacred church, Ambrose met him outside at the doors and prevented him from entering the sacred threshold, addressing him as follows:

“Do you not know, emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter that has been committed? Does your mind, after the cause of such great fury, fail to recognize the weight of your presumption? Perhaps the power of the empire prevents recognition of sin. Yet reason ought to prevail here over power.

“You must know human nature, its mortality and dissolution, and the dust of your ancestors, from which we were made and to which we shall be reduced. You must not, trusting in the purple flower, remain ignorant of the weaknesses hidden beneath the body’s covering. [Note: Ὁμαλίζων βασιλεύεις: “You rule as one equal among equals.”]

“You are emperor over people equal to yourself and over fellow servants. For there is one Lord, King, and Creator of all. With what eyes, then, will you look upon the temple of our common Lord? With what feet will you tread his holy pavement? How will you extend hands from which unjust blood still drips? How will you receive the Lord’s body with such hands? With what presumption will you take the cup of precious blood into your mouth, when so much blood has been unjustly poured out in the fury of your words?

“Withdraw, then; withdraw, lest by a second sin you attempt to increase your former wickedness. Accept the bond with which the Lord of all has now bound you. For it is the greatest medicine of health.”

Obeying these words—for he had been nourished by divine instruction—and clearly knowing what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings, the emperor returned to the palace groaning and weeping.

When eight continuous months had passed, the Nativity of our Savior approached. The emperor, sitting in the palace amid continual lamentations, incessantly shed tears.

Rufinus the magister entered. He enjoyed exceptional confidence with the emperor, and when he saw him prostrated in grief, he approached to ask the cause of his tears. But the emperor groaned most bitterly and shed tears still more abundantly:

“You are playing, Rufinus,” he said, “and you do not feel my troubles. I lament and mourn my calamity, because the temples of God are open to beggars who are his servants, and they freely entreat their own Lord, but I have no entrance to him. Moreover, the heavens too are closed.”

As he said this, he broke off each word with sobs.

Rufinus replied: “If it pleases you, I shall run and persuade the bishop by my prayers to release the bond with which he has bound you.”

But the emperor said: “You will not persuade Ambrose. I know that his decree is just, and that he will not respect imperial power so as to violate the divine law.”

When Rufinus used many words to promise that Ambrose could be softened, the emperor ordered him to go immediately. He himself followed shortly afterward, encouraged by the hope Rufinus had given him.

But the admirable Ambrose, as soon as he saw Rufinus, said:

“You have imitated the shamelessness of dogs, Rufinus. You are the author of so great a slaughter, yet you wipe shame from your forehead. You are neither ashamed nor afraid to bark against the divine image.”

When Rufinus pleaded and said that the emperor was coming, Ambrose, inflamed by heavenly zeal, said:

“I declare to you, Rufinus, that I shall prevent him from entering the threshold. But if he has changed imperial authority into tyranny, I shall gladly accept death.”

Rufinus heard these and other words and reported the bishop’s resolve to the emperor, warning him not to leave the palace. But the emperor, already in the middle of the street and having learned what had happened, said:

“I am going, and I shall accept just reproaches to my face.”

When he reached the sacred threshold, he did not dare to enter the holy basilica. Instead, he came to the bishop and found him sitting in the reception room. [Note: Ἐν τῷ ἀσπαστικῷ οἴκῳ: “In the reception room.” Pith.] He pleaded with him to release his bonds.

But Ambrose said that his presence was tyrannical and that Theodosius was raging against God and trampling upon his laws.

The emperor replied:

“I am not rising up against ecclesiastical decrees, nor am I trying to enter the sacred threshold unjustly. Rather, I ask you to release my bonds and to entreat the mercy of our common Lord on my behalf, so that the door may not be closed to me—a door that our Lord has opened to all who practice repentance.”

Then the bishop said:

“What repentance have you shown after such great crimes? By what medicines have you healed incurable wounds and injuries?”

The emperor replied:

“It is your task to teach and prepare the medicines; mine is to accept what is offered.”

Then Saint Ambrose said:

“How did you entrust your judgment to fury? Why did reason not deliver the sentence, but rather anger? Write a law that will annul the law of fury. Let the sentence of death and proscription remain only in writing for thirty days and await the judgment of reason.

“After these days have passed, when anger has subsided, reason can judge the case within itself and establish what it recognizes according to truth. During these days it will become clear whether the sentence you have issued is just or unjust. If reason proves that what was issued is unjust, it will annul it; if just, it will confirm it. The number of days will be sufficient for examining these matters.”

The emperor accepted this admonition with a willing mind and, confident that it was an excellent law, immediately ordered it to be written down and confirmed it in writing with his own hand. When this had been done, Ambrose released his bonds.

This law is observed to the present day. It is as follows:

“Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Flavianus, praetorian prefect of Illyricum. If we should order that some persons be punished more severely than is our custom, after considering the case, we do not wish them immediately either to undergo punishment or to receive sentence; rather, for thirty days their lot and fortune shall remain suspended concerning what has been decreed against them. Let the guilty receive bonds, and let them be vigilantly guarded under custody and by diligent watches.”

Thus the most sacred emperor, daring to enter the threshold, did not stand and plead with the Lord, nor did he bend his knees, but lay prone upon the pavement and cried out in the words of David:

“My soul clung to the pavement; revive me according to your word.” [Note: Cedrenus, ἐκολλήθη τῷ ἐδάφει, etc.: “My soul clung to the pavement,” etc.]

Tearing out his beard and hair with his hands, striking his forehead, and sprinkling drops of tears upon the pavement, he begged to obtain pardon.

When the time approached at which he was accustomed to offer the sacrifice at the altar, he rose and entered with tears. After he had made the offering, as he was accustomed to do, he stood inside the chancel screen. [Note: Κιγκλίδων: “of the rails” or “chancel screen.”]

But Ambrose did not remain silent. He explained again the distinction between the places. First he asked what the emperor was waiting for there. When the emperor said that he was waiting to receive the sacred mysteries, Ambrose sent word through the archdeacon:

“Emperor, the inner places have been assigned only to priests; the others are permitted neither to touch nor to enter them. Go out, then, and share this waiting with the others. For the purple makes emperors, not priests.” [Note: Ἀλουργίς: “purple.”]

Then the most faithful emperor, accepting this instruction also with a grateful spirit, sent back this reply:

“I did not stand inside the screen out of audacity; I learned that this was the custom in the city of Constantinople. Therefore I give thanks for such a remedy.”

So great was the power of virtue possessed by the bishop and the emperor. I admire the conduct of both: the confidence of the one, the obedience of the other; the fervor of the one’s zeal, the purity of the other’s faith.

Moreover, the rules of piety that he had received from his priestly teacher he also observed after returning to Constantinople. For when he had gone to church during a festival and had placed gifts upon the altar, he immediately went out.

When Nectarius, then bishop of the Church, sent to ask why he had not wished to remain inside, the emperor sent back this reply:

“Only with difficulty could I learn what distinction there is between emperor and priest. Only with difficulty did I find a teacher of truth. I know only Ambrose to be worthy of being called a bishop.”

The emperor also had another opportunity and occasion through which he might triumph in good works. His wife, whose name was Placilla, [Note: Σύζυγος ᾗ Πλακίλλα ὄνομα: “His wife, whose name was Placilla.” Cedrenus.] often reminded him of the divine laws, while first instructing herself perfectly.

She was not exalted by the heights of royal power but was rather inflamed by divine love. The greatness of the benefit increased her desire for the benefactor. As soon as she came to the purple, she took the greatest care of the lame and weak, using neither servants, maids, nor other attendants. She acted personally, going to their dwellings and providing each person with whatever was needed. [Note: Cedrenus, λελωβημένων καὶ πεπηρωμένων: “of the maimed and crippled.”]

Thus she hurried through the churches and the guest-houses for the sick belonging to the churches, ministering to the ill with her own hands: wiping their pots, tasting their broth, offering spoons, breaking bread, distributing food, rinsing their cups, and doing all the other things that servants and attendants customarily perform.

To those who tried to prevent her from such activities she would say:

“To distribute gold is the work of imperial power. But I offer this service on behalf of that very imperial power, to him who has bestowed every good thing upon me.”

She often said to her husband:

“You must always consider, husband, who you once were and who you are now. If you always recognize this, you will not prove ungrateful to the Creator and benefactor; rather, you will govern the empire you have received lawfully and appease the author of these blessings.”

By such words she offered her husband a kind of excellent benefit and an abundance of virtue.

Now a certain grammarian named Eugenius, a teacher of Latin literature, abandoned the schools and served at the palace. He was Valentinian’s secretary and was honored by many because of his eloquence.

At that time, it is said, after careful thought, he took Arbogast as his associate. Arbogast was born among the lesser Gauls, was a commander in the military order, a savage man prepared for slaughter, and a most filthy worshiper of idols. [Note: Other accounts are given by Zonaras and Cedrenus. See shortly afterward Marcellinus Comes, from whom the Miscella is derived.]

Having done this, he turned toward tyranny and plotted Valentinian’s death, corrupting eunuch chamberlains at the Gallic city of Vienne. They strangled the sleeping emperor and then suspended him by a noose, so that it might be believed that he had inflicted a voluntary death upon himself.

After he had been killed, Arbogast made Eugenius a tyrant, choosing a man upon whom he could impose the title of emperor while he himself exercised imperial power—a barbarian excessive in spirit, counsel, action, boldness, and strength.

He gathered innumerable and unconquerable forces from every direction, relying on Roman garrisons and barbarian auxiliaries, and supported by some through authority and by others through kinship. [Note: A.: “Supported. In fact, he was a Frank by birth and a most filthy worshiper of idols. Accordingly Eugenius, etc.”]

When the emperor Theodosius heard this, he was again bound by anxieties and prepared a second war after that against Maximus. Gathering military strength and designating his son Honorius as emperor in his own consulship and that of Abundantius, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, he hastened once more with great energy toward the West.

Meanwhile, considering the outcome of the war, he sent to the Thebaid for John, a monk who had insight into hidden things. He sent to him the eunuch Eutropius, who was exceptionally loyal to him, so that he might either bring John back if he wished to come, or ask him, if he refused, about the outcome of the war.

Eutropius was unable to bring John back, but he reported his message: Theodosius would conquer and kill the tyrant, and after the victory he would die in Italy.

Accordingly, when Theodosius was setting out to fight against Eugenius, leaving both his sons in the city of Constantinople, many barbarians from beyond the river Ister followed him to fight against the tyrant. In a short time he arrived in Gaul with a very large force. There he prepared for war, and already had many thousands of soldiers.

Eugenius and Arbogast, therefore, held the Alpine passes with their entire army drawn up, while Theodosius stood on the highest mountains. Without food or sleep, he devoted himself to prayer with tears. [Note: A.: “Devoting himself to prayer, he spent the whole night awake, although he knew that he had been abandoned by his own men, etc.”]

Around cockcrow, overcome by drowsiness, he saw in a dream that he was lying in a field and that two men in white garments, seated upon white horses, stood beside him. They ordered him to have confidence and to arm his soldiers at dawn for victory, saying that they had been sent to give him comfort. One of them said that he was John the Evangelist, the other that he was the apostle Philip.

After learning of this vision, Theodosius did not cease praying but shed still more abundant tears. The vision was also revealed to one of the soldiers and reached the emperor through various persons.

The emperor said:

“He did not see this on my account, but so that no one would believe that I had fabricated what I saw, it was therefore also shown to him. For the common Lord first showed it to me.”

Although he knew that he was separated from his own men, he did not know that he was surrounded by enemies. He confidently seized his weapons, gave the signal for battle with the sign of the cross, and entered the battle even if no one should follow him, destined to be victorious. [Note: A.: “He entered it destined to be victorious. For John the Anchorite, when consulted, had promised him victory. When Arbitio, the commander of the enemy forces, had surrounded him unknowingly with ambushes, etc.”]

Arbitio, commander of the enemy forces, was the first means of salvation. When he had trapped the unsuspecting emperor in a surrounding ambush, he immediately turned to reverence for the emperor. He not only freed him from danger but also strengthened him with assistance. [Note: A.: “He equipped him. When the battle was joined, a violent whirlwind, etc.”]

The battle was therefore joined near a river called the Frigidus. On the side where Romans were fighting Romans, the fighting was evenly matched. But because the emperor’s barbarians were serving as auxiliaries, the side of Eugenius seemed the stronger.

When the emperor saw the barbarians being destroyed, he was overcome by the greatest distress. He stood upon a high rock, from which he could both see and be seen by either army. Casting aside his weapons, he turned to his customary aid, threw himself upon the ground, and invoked God as his helper, saying:

“Almighty God, you know that I have undertaken these battles in the name of Christ your Son and for the sake of just vengeance. If you are wrathful, take vengeance on me; but if I have come here with a credible cause and trusting in you, extend your right hand to your servants, ‘lest the nations perhaps say: Where is their God?’”

Immediately his request was not frustrated. A certain man named Barbarius, his master of the soldiers, a man distinguished by faith, piety, and strength of spirit, was suddenly so encouraged that he rushed with the foremost commanders toward the place where the barbarians were fighting. By doing this he broke the battle line and immediately put the enemy to flight.

Then another miracle occurred. A violent whirlwind from Theodosius’s side rushed into the faces of the enemy and struck their chests with great force against their shields. At one moment it pressed their shields tightly against them; at another, violently tearing them away, it left them exposed; at another, continually driving against them, it thrust them backward. The weapons that they themselves had hurled with great force were caught by the winds, their force reversed and driven back, and struck them disastrously. The darts launched from Theodosius’s side were carried through the vast air beyond the range of a human throw and firmly fixed in the enemy.

Thus, when the battle had been brought to an end, the tyrant ran to the emperor’s feet and begged to be granted his life. But he was beheaded by the soldiers at the emperor’s feet on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the third consulship of Arcadius and the second of Honorius.

Arbogast, the cause of so many evils, fled two days after the battle. When he realized that he could not live, he killed himself with his own sword.

Before this, Theodosius had sent ten thousand Gothic auxiliaries, and the commander Arbogast had utterly destroyed them. Yet for Theodosius to have lost them was more a gain than a loss.

In praise of this remarkable victory, a certain poet named Claudianus, an outstanding but pagan man, sang the following testimony to God and to the emperor, among other verses: [Note: A.: “These verses.”]

> O greatly beloved of God, for you heaven itself wages war,
And the conspirators come to the sound of the trumpets of the winds. [Note: [Col. 0945D] This passage is taken from Cedrenus.]

At that time, in the regions of the East, in the province of Palestine, in the fortress of Emmaus, a child was born, complete as far as the navel and divided above it, so that he had two chests and two heads, each with his own faculties: one ate and drank, while the other did not eat; one slept while the other kept watch, although sometimes they slept together. They also played together with one another, and each wept, and they struck one another. They lived for nearly two years. One of them then died, while the other survived him by four days.

Accordingly, the emperor Theodosius, exhausted in body after public labor, fell ill. Expecting that he would die of the illness, he thought rather about the commonwealth, considering what usually happens to people when an emperor dies. He therefore summoned his son Honorius from Constantinople and invested him as emperor at Rome. When Honorius had come to Milan, Theodosius, having recovered somewhat from his illness, celebrated the victory in the Circus. Before dinner he put on a spectacle as though he were well; after dinner he was suddenly weighed down by illness and could not come to the spectacle, but he ordered his son to attend the games. When night came, he died, in the consulship of Olibrius and Probinus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventeenth year of his reign and the fiftieth of his life. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Aurelius Victor, 60.]

It is said that his parents, warned by a dream, consecrated to him the name which in Latin can be understood as “given by God.” [Note: [Col. 0945D] A.: “can be understood.” Concerning this oracle it was also circulated in Asia that he would succeed Valens, and that his name would begin with the letters Θ and Δ. Deceived by this correspondence of the beginning, Theodorus, presuming that the empire was owed to him, paid the penalties of his criminal ambition. Theodosius, however, was its propagator.]

He was a distinguished promoter and defender of the commonwealth, resembling Trajan in character and bodily appearance, as the writings of the ancients and their portraits show; from Trajan, moreover, he derived his origin. He had the same imposing stature, the same limbs, comparable hair and face, except that his cheeks were somewhat less hollow and he did not have such enormous eyes. I do not know whether he possessed as much charm and such a bloom of youth in his face, or such dignity in his bearing. [Note: [Col. 0945D] A.: “a bloom of youth.”] [Note: [Col. 0946D] A.: “in his bearing.”]

His mind, however, was altogether similar, so much so that nothing can be said of Trajan that does not seem transferable from the books to this man: a kind disposition, merciful and sociable, thinking that he differed from others only in his clothing. [Note: [Col. 0946D] A.: “a kindly disposition … He thought that he differed from the rest only in his dress. Toward everyone…”] He was respectful toward all people, but especially generous toward the good. He loved simple characters and admired the learned. [Note: [Col. 0946D] A.: “but harmless. To bestow great gifts with a great spirit, to love citizens, even those known through private companionship, and to reward them with honors, money, and other benefits, especially…”] This was particularly true of those whose services toward him he had tested even in a not very severe crisis. [Note: [Col. 0946D] “Otherwise, as a father.” Francisci Pithoeus’s manuscript: “or as a father.”]

Yet he detested to such a degree the vices with which Trajan was stained—namely drunkenness and the desire for triumph—that he did not initiate wars but found them already begun. By law he prohibited lascivious entertainments and female flute-players from being brought into banquets. He attributed so much importance to modesty and continence that he forbade the marriages of cousins as though they were marriages between sisters.

If we compare him with the most perfect men, he was moderately educated in letters, plainly shrewd, and very diligent in learning the deeds of his ancestors. [Note: [Col. 0946D] A.: “of his forebears. When he read of the arrogance of rulers, especially of the treacherous and ungrateful, he cursed them.”] Among these he never ceased cursing those whose proud and cruel deeds, hostile to liberty, he read about—Cinna, Marius, Sulla, and all rulers, but especially the ungrateful and factious.

He certainly became angry at unworthy things, but was quickly moved to relent. Hence, after a brief delay, he sometimes softened his severe commands. [Note: [Col. 0946D] A.: “was softened. At times he issued severe orders which were contrary to the natural gift in which Augustus excelled. Hence he was once reproved by a certain teacher of philosophy who…”] He possessed from nature the gift which Augustus had received from a teacher of philosophy. When this teacher saw that he was easily stirred, he warned him, so that he would not decree anything harsh, that whenever he began to grow angry he should count the twenty-four Greek letters from memory. In this way, by diverting the agitation—which lasts only a moment—to another mental activity, he would allow it to fade after a short interval.

He was unquestionably better after his royal power had been increased by years, and still more so after his civil victory—an exceedingly rare virtue. For he attended with greater concern to the grain supply and restored from his own resources the great weight of gold and silver that had been taken away and spent by tyrants. [Note: [Col. 0947D] A.: “restored. Even kindly emperors scarcely used to grant anything but bare estates and ruined properties.”]

There are also the smaller matters, those, as the saying goes, within the palace, which, because they are hidden, draw the eyes and ears of human curiosity more strongly toward themselves. He possessed an exceptional concern for filial devotion: he honored his paternal uncle as a father, regarded the children of his deceased brother and sister as his own, and embraced relatives, connections, and parents with a parent’s affection, [Note: [Col. 0947D] A.: “and relatives and in-laws with a parent’s affection…”] and gave elegant and cheerful banquets rather than extravagant ones. He mingled conversation according to the rank, interests, and dignities of his guests, speaking with a gravity that was nevertheless pleasant.

He was a gentle father and a harmonious husband. He exercised himself neither for sensual pleasure nor to the point of weariness. [Note: [Col. 0947D] A.: “when he had leisure, by walking. Refreshing his mind, he maintained his health through moderation in eating. His gentleness toward men and the extent of his devotion toward God are shown by this one example. When at Milan he wished to enter a church to take part in the solemn celebration of the Mass, and the blessed Ambrose said that he would not admit him on account of a certain crime unless he publicly repented, he humbly endured the prohibition and, without shame, accepted with devotion the form of penance imposed by the bishop. Flacilla was joined to him in marriage, by whom he begot Arcadius and Honorius. After she died, he married Galla, daughter of Valentinian the Elder and Justina, and sister of Valentinian the Younger; she bore him Placidia, who later acquired the surname Galla from her mother. Thus Theodosius, in his fiftieth year, departed human life peacefully at Milan, leaving both commonwealths secure to his two sons Arcadius and Honorius. His body was transferred and buried at Constantinople in the same year. And so on.”] When he had leisure, he refreshed his mind more by walking and maintained his health through moderation in eating.

Flacilla was joined to him in marriage, and by her he fathered Arcadius and Honorius. After her death he married Galla, the daughter of Valentinian the elder and Justina, and sister of Valentinian the younger. She bore him Placidia, who later acquired the surname Galla from her mother. Thus, at the age of fifty, Theodosius departed this life in peace at Milan, leaving both commonwealths secure to his two sons, Arcadius and Honorius. His body was transferred to Constantinople that same year and buried there. [Note: [Col. 0947D] A.: “And so on.”]

In the same year, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, the body of Theodosius was brought to Constantinople with solemn honor and was committed to burial by his son Arcadius. A few days later, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, the army that had been with the emperor Theodosius against the tyrant also returned. When the emperor Arcadius, according to custom, had gone out to meet the returning army at the gates, the soldiers killed Rufinus, the emperor’s prefect. For he was suspected of plotting to seize tyrannical power. It was also said that he himself had summoned the Huns into the Roman provinces; they were then devastating Armenia and the eastern regions.

## ARCADIUS, HONORIUS

In the year 1146 from the founding of the City, [Note: [Col. 0948D] A.: 1149.] Arcadius, son of Theodosius, in the East, and his brother Honorius, in the West, began to hold the common empire with their seats divided, being forty-sixth in succession from Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0948D] A.: “42.”]

Their father had entrusted its administration to very powerful men: Rufinus, who was in charge of the eastern court and was killed by the army, and Stilicho, who held the empire of the West. [Note: [Col. 0948D] A.: “the Western Empire. Arcadius lived twelve years after his father’s death and, dying, handed over the supreme power of the empire to his very young son Theodosius. Meanwhile, Gildo…”]

When Honorius assumed the empire of the West, he abolished the gladiatorial games, which had long been celebrated at Rome, for the following reason. A certain Telemachus, living as a monk, came to Rome for this purpose. While that impious spectacle was being performed, he entered the arena and, going down into it, tried to separate the gladiators who were fighting each other with swords. When the spectators raged against him and pressed on with the shedding of blood, they killed the promoter of peace with stones. The remarkable emperor, learning of this, counted him among the victorious martyrs and utterly abolished the impious spectacle.

At that time the Huns, crossing the river Ister, were devastating Thrace. The brigands of Isauria also gathered in very great numbers, came as far as Carenae and Phoenicia, and plundered the cities and villages lying between.

At the same time Stilicho, the Patrician and master of the army under Honorius, endowed with great power and having many Romans and foreigners under his command, had entered into conflict with the leaders of Arcadius and was thinking of engaging them. Accordingly, acting with Honorius, he arranged for Alaric, king of the Goths, to be appointed master of the soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0948D] “He calls him a Gothic exarch of the Vandals. Cedrenus.”] Stilicho advanced against Illyricum and appointed Jovius prefect there, so that he might raise arms against the Romans and subject the provinces of Honorius to his authority.

When Alaric had gathered the barbarians under him who lived throughout Dalmatia, he came to Epirus. After remaining there for a long time, he returned to Italy. When he wished to depart, he was detained by letters from Honorius, as he himself admitted.

Meanwhile, a great earthquake occurred at Constantinople, so that the earth trembled beneath and a flame poured down from heaven hung above. It continued until God, entreated by the prayers of Prince Arcadius and the Christian people, turned away the destruction that threatened them, demonstrating that he alone is the protector of the humble and the punisher of the wicked.

The emperor Arcadius was a gentle and tranquil man, and toward the end of his life he was considered venerable for the following reason. In the city of Constantinople there is a very large house called Caryae, that is, “of the walnut.” In the vestibule of this house stands a walnut tree on which, as the story goes, the martyr Acacius had been hanged and died. For this reason a chapel was also built there.

Wishing to see it, Arcadius came to pray and, having completed his vow, was returning. Therefore all the people living around the chapel ran together, wanting to see the emperor. Some had gone ahead outside the house so that they might have a better view of the emperor and observe the order of the procession; others followed. When everyone—women, children, and slaves alike—had gone out of the house, the great building adjoining the chapel suddenly collapsed entirely. A cry of amazement followed, as people wondered how the emperor’s prayer had delivered so many from the danger of the impending ruin.

Meanwhile Gildo, count of Africa, learning of the death of Theodosius and judging that there was little hope in the young heirs, began to usurp Africa as his own possession. His brother Macezil, abhorring his brother’s treachery, returned to Italy. Gildo, however, deceitfully entrapped and killed two adolescent sons of Macezil, whom their father had left in military service in Africa. Macezil, his brother, was then sent to pursue Gildo as an enemy in war.

Macezil, who had already learned from Theodosius how much a man’s prayer through faith in Christ could obtain God’s mercy in the most desperate circumstances, went to the island of Capraria. From there he brought with him certain servants of God, joining them to his prayers, and continued with them for several days in prayer and fasting, [Note: [Col. 0949D] A.: “and nights. Three days before, when he was about to come close to the enemy, he saw in the night the blessed Ambrose, who had recently died, indicating to him the day and place where he would win the victory, and on the third…”] and nights. For this reason he earned victory without battle and vengeance without slaughter.

The name of a river is Ardealio; it flows between the cities of Tevestes and Amedara. There, having encamped with a small force—that is, with five thousand soldiers, as they say—against seventy thousand enemies, Macezil wished, after a delay, to withdraw from the place and cross the narrow defiles formed by the valley lying before him. As night fell, he seemed in a dream to see the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who had recently died. Ambrose gestured with his hand and, striking the ground three times with his staff, said: “Here, here, here.”

Macezil understood this by prudent interpretation as a message from one who deservedly announced victory: the word indicated the place, the number indicated the day. He therefore remained where he was. On the third day, after a night spent in vigil with prayers and hymns, [Note: [Col. 0949D] A.: “keeping vigil, he proceeded with only five thousand against eighty thousand enemies and, by God’s command, received them into submission without battle. At this sight…”] he advanced against the enemy as though surrounded by the sacraments of heavenly mysteries. When he spoke words of holy peace to those who first met him, he struck a standard-bearer who insolently resisted with his sword on the arm, and by the wound forced him, his hand disabled, to lower the standard.

At this sight Gildo’s barbarian auxiliaries immediately turned their backs. Gildo himself fled, boarded a ship, and, having returned to Africa, was strangled and died several days later.

But Macezil, puffed up by the insolence of success, abandoned the company of the holy men with whom he had previously conquered while serving God. He even dared to violate God’s Church and did not hesitate to drag certain people out of it. Punishment quickly followed his sacrilege. For after those whom he had dragged from the Church for punishment had survived and mocked him, after some time he alone was punished. [Note: [Col. 0949D] A.: “was punished. Meanwhile Rufinus, to whom Theodosius had entrusted the administration of the eastern court, corrupted by the evil of treachery, attempted to invade the kingdom with the aid of barbarians and paid the penalty by a most just death. Stilicho also, of the West…”]

In him alone it was proved that divine judgment is always watchful in both directions: when he hoped, he was helped; when he despised, he was killed.

When Arcadius saw that he was dying, and saw that his son Theodosius was still a child—for he was eight years old—and considered that the boy might be attacked by treachery, he declared him emperor and appointed King Isdigerd of the Persians to be his guardian by testament.

Isdigerd accepted Arcadius’ testament and, maintaining peace toward the Romans without envy, preserved the empire for Theodosius. He also sent him a certain Antiochus, a remarkable and reasonable man, as guardian and tutor, and wrote the following to the Roman Senate:

“While Arcadius sleeps, having appointed me guardian of his son, I have sent one who may take my place. Therefore let no one attempt treachery against the child, lest an intolerable war without treaty [Greek: Ἄσπονδον, “without a truce”] arise against the Romans.”

When Antiochus came to Constantinople, he was gladly received by the emperor Honorius. There was peace between the Romans and the Persians, and Antiochus himself wrote many things especially on behalf of the Christians. Thus Christianity was extended in Persia through the mediation of Maruntha, bishop of Mesopotamia.

Arcadius died on the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, in the thirty-first year of his life, after thirteen years of imperial rule with his father and fourteen years as sole emperor. [Note: [Col. 0950D] Marcellinus: thirteen.]

Meanwhile Stilicho, Patrician of the West and guardian of the empire, forgetful of the benefits conferred upon him and forgetful of his relationship—for he was the father-in-law of Honorius—also sought the kingdom for his son Eucherius and inflicted enormous evils upon the commonwealth. [Note: [Col. 0950D] A.: “he favored them; he often defeated Alaric with the Goths, and so on.”] Although he could often have destroyed the barbarians, he favored them; he defeated the king of the Scythians with his Goths and often shut them in, yet always released them. What end he met will be told more appropriately in its own place.

In the midst of these events, Radagaisus, by far the most savage of all the ancient and contemporary enemies, [Note: [Col. 0950D] A.: “Ragodaisus,” always.] suddenly inundated all Italy with an attack. They say that more than two hundred thousand Goths were among his people. Besides this incredible multitude and untamed courage, he was a barbarian and a Scythian who had vowed to offer all Roman blood as a libation to his gods.

Immediately boundless fear seized Rome. All the pagans in the city gathered together, and everyone cried out that they were suffering these things because the rites of the great gods had been neglected. Great complaints were heard everywhere, and people continually demanded that the rites be restored. Blasphemies raged throughout the city. The name of Christ was assailed by the common people with insults as though it were some kind of plague.

The Romans hired two pagan leaders against Radagaisus, king of the Goths: Sarus and Uldin of the Huns. [Note: [Col. 0950D] A.: “two commanders, Sarus of the Goths and …”] [Note: [Col. 0950D] Manuscript: “Huldin and Saurus.” Paul the Deacon: “Sarus and Viridinus.”]

But God did not permit the power of the unbelievers to appear equal to his own. Radagaisus was crushed by divine power on the rugged ridge of Mount Fesulae. Fear pressed in upon him from every side, and the troops for whom Italy had previously seemed too narrow for their numbers were driven by the hope of hiding into one small summit. [Note: [Col. 0950D] A.: “When he had come there…”] As they were consumed by hunger and thirst, King Radagaisus alone, taking hope of flight, was captured by the Romans and thrown into chains. Detained for a short time, he was put to death.

So great, it is said, was the multitude of captive Goths that whole groups of people were sold everywhere for a single gold coin, like the cheapest animals. [Note: [Col. 0951D] A.: “were sold. Meanwhile Alaric was invading Italy…”]

At that time Alaric, king of the Goths, who had been subject to Roman authority and to the emperor Theodosius and had supplied assistance against the tyrant Eugenius, and had consequently been honored with Roman dignities, could not endure his own good fortune. He did not choose to rule, but, departing from the city of Constantinople, came to the regions of the West.

When he arrived in Illyricum, he overturned everything. Crossing Thessaly, he engaged in battle near the river Peneus. At Nicopolis in Epirus the Thessalians killed nearly three thousand of his men. [Note: [Col. 0951D] Manuscript: “Peneum.”]

After this, when he had entered Italy and requested from Honorius a place where he could settle with his army, Honorius, after deliberation, granted the Goths Gaul. While Alaric was proceeding to Gaul, he halted for a time at Pollentia to recover his pack animals. [Note: [Col. 0951D] A.: “he had halted at Pollentia for a little while. Stilicho the count…”] Stilicho the Patrician, seeking the destruction of the commonwealth and attempting to attack the Goths by ambush, entrusted the main conduct of the war to the pagan commander Saul.

On the very sacred day of Easter, while the Goths were praying and expecting nothing of the sort, Saul fell upon them and overthrew a large part of them. For the Goths, at first thrown into confusion and yielding out of religious reverence, eventually seized their weapons, encouraged one another in their customary manner, [Note: [Col. 0951D] A.: “encouraged one another and, with superior courage, defeated the army…”] and, with greater courage, defeated the army.

Then, aroused to a frenzy of rage, they abandoned the route they had begun and hastened toward Rome, laying waste by fire and sword everything through which they had passed. Without delay they reached the city, captured it, and devastated it. They burned many of its marvels and subjected many members of the senatorial order to various punishments. Beforehand, however, they had issued an order that if anyone had fled to holy places, especially to the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, those people were to be left inviolate and safe above all; thereafter, insofar as they could, those greedy for plunder were to refrain from bloodshed.

Nevertheless, mocking the Roman empire, they made a certain man named Athalus emperor. One day they made him appear as an emperor; the next, they made him serve in the guise of a slave. [Note: [Col. 0951D] Cedrenus and Marcellinus differ.]

Rome was captured on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 1164 of its foundation. On the approach of the third day, the Goths voluntarily withdrew from the city. [Note: [Col. 0951D] A.: “from the city, after setting fire to several houses, though not even to as many as Caesar once burned. Then…”]

It is reported that when Alaric was marching toward Rome, a venerable man living as a monk warned him not to dare to commit such evils or to rejoice in killings and bloodshed. But Alaric replied: “I am not going willingly to Rome; someone troublesome visits me every day, tormenting me and saying: ‘Go and destroy the city of Rome.’”

Then, raging with similar devastation through Campania, Lucania, and Bruttium, the Goths reached Rhegium, wishing to cross over to Sicily. When they tried to cross in ships, they suffered shipwreck and lost many of their men there.

While Alaric was deliberating what to do, he died suddenly at Consentia. The Goths diverted the river Busentus from its bed through the labor of captives and buried Alaric in the middle of the riverbed with many treasures. Restoring the river to its course so that no one could discover the place, they killed the captives who had taken part in the burial.

The Goths then made Athaulf, a relation of Alaric, their king and returned to Rome. Like locusts, they stripped away whatever remained, carrying off Galla Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of Honorius, whom Athaulf married at Forum Cornelii. She later proved greatly beneficial to the commonwealth.

For by her keen intelligence and subtle persuasion she bent her husband’s mind so that he voluntarily sought peace from the Romans. As he was proceeding to Gaul, he was later killed at Barcelona through the treachery of his own people. [Note: [Col. 0952D] A.: “at Barcinona.”]

After him, Segeric seized the kingdom. While he was preparing to preserve peace with the Romans, he too was killed by his own people.

Then Vallia assumed the rights of kingship. He was chosen by the Goths to break the peace, but appointed by God to confirm it. [Note: [Col. 0952D] A.: “Gaul”; it always calls it this.]

Meanwhile Stilicho the Patrician, born of the treacherous and deceitful nation of the Vandals, had, as stated, a son named Eucherius, who from childhood had plotted the persecution of Christians. Two years before the Roman invasion, in order to place Eucherius on the imperial throne, Stilicho voluntarily stirred up peoples intolerable in numbers and strength—the Alans, Suebi, Vandals, Burgundians, and many other nations with them—and urged them to take up arms. [Note: [Col. 0952D] A.: “stirred them up and wanted them to attack Gaul, so that under this…”]

They soon crossed the Rhine and sought to drive out the Franks from Gaul. Advancing in a straight line, they reached the Pyrenees, so that, under this emergency, Stilicho might be able to wrest the empire from his son-in-law for his own son.

At last, when these enormous disasters became known to the emperor Honorius and the Roman army, the army was justly aroused and Stilicho was killed. In order to clothe one boy in purple, he had shed the blood of almost the entire human race. His son Eucherius was also killed, and a few of their attendants were punished for such vast schemes.

At the same time, the most distinguished places in the City were destroyed by lightning—places which the enemy had been unable to set on fire.

Meanwhile in Britain, Gratian, a townsman of that island, was created a tyrant and soon killed. In his place Constantine was chosen from the lowest military ranks, solely because of the hope attached to his name and without any merit of courage. Crossing to Gaul, he was repeatedly deceived by the barbarians through an uncertain alliance and proved more a detriment than an advantage to the commonwealth.

At that time two wealthy young men, Didymus and Viridianus, took household slaves and native servants and attempted to defend themselves and their homeland against the barbarians and the tyrant. Against them Constantine sent his son Constans, made Caesar from a monk, together with certain allied barbarians, into Spain.

Supported by the barbarians’ assistance, Constans killed them in the first battle. When the passes of the Pyrenees had been entrusted to these barbarians, they allowed all the ferocity of the peoples that had been raging through Gaul to enter the provinces of Spain.

Thus, after many massacres, fires, and acts of plunder, the barbarians, eventually settled in different places and turned to the plow, began to cherish the surviving Romans as allies and friends. [Note: [Col. 0954D] A.: “divided among different settlements. End of Book XII. Book XIII begins. Therefore…”]

# BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 0953]

In the year 1165 from the founding of the City, Theodosius the Younger was emperor in the East. In the second year of his reign, Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, is said to have advanced in accordance with God by admonishing, persuading, and baptizing a certain Jewish paralytic, whom he brought forth healthy from the bath.

Accordingly, when the emperor Honorius saw the strength of the commonwealth weakened daily by misfortunes, he sent the brave and warlike Constantius with an army to Gaul. [Note: [Col. 0953D] A.: “Count Constantius, when, and so on.”] As soon as he entered Gaul, he immediately destroyed the tyrant Constantine at Arles.

His son Constans was killed at Vienne by his own count Gerontius. In his place Gerontius appointed a certain Maximus, but he himself was slaughtered by his own soldiers. Maximus was then stripped of the purple and died in exile and poverty in Spain.

Afterward Jovinus arose in Gaul and soon fell. His brother Sebastianus was immediately created tyrant and killed. The consul Tertullus, who had boasted in the Senate that he would become emperor, likewise perished by a similar end. [Note: [Col. 0953D] Orosius VII, chapter 42: “pontiff.”]

Athalus, whom the Goths had made emperor, was captured by Constantius and sent to Honorius. His hand was cut off, but he was left alive.

Heraclianus was also appointed count of Africa; while that same Athalus still bore the shadow of imperial power, he energetically defended Africa against the judges sent by Athalus and obtained the consulship. [Note: [Col. 0953D] A.: “With his son-in-law Sabinus, and with three thousand seven hundred ships, he set out from Africa toward Rome, but at the encounter with the count…”]

Inflated by this pride, he chose as his son-in-law a certain Sabinus, his household officer, a man strong in intellect, skilled in action, and worthy to be called wise if he had applied his mental powers to peaceful pursuits. While he endured suspicions of certain dangers with Sabinus, he acted accordingly; after holding back the African grain supply for some time, he finally hastened toward Rome with an immense and almost incredible fleet of ships.

For it is said that he possessed three thousand seven hundred ships—a number which history records as having belonged neither to Xerxes, that famous king of the Persians, nor to Alexander the Great, nor to any other king. As soon as he had landed with his troop of soldiers while proceeding along the coast toward the City, he was terrified by the appearance of the count Marinus and put to flight. Seizing a ship, he returned alone to Carthage, where he was immediately killed by soldiers.

Honorius overcame all these men with the greatest religious devotion and through the great diligence of Constantius. Rightly so. For in those days, at the command of Honorius and with the support of Constantius, the heretics in Africa were brought to submission and peace was restored to the Church. At that time the most illustrious teacher of the whole Church, Augustine, flourished at royal Hippo.

Meanwhile Vallia, king of the Goths, terrified by God’s judgment, returned to her brother Honorius, at Constantius’ demand, Galla Placidia, whom he had treated honorably in his custody. He made peace with him, giving selected hostages, and promised that he would fight on behalf of the Romans against the barbarians who had invaded Spain.

In reply, the kings of the Vandals, Alans, and Suebi sent an embassy to the emperor Honorius in these words:

“Keep peace with everyone and accept hostages from everyone. We fight for ourselves; for ourselves we die; for you we win. It will be gain for your commonwealth if both sides perish.”

When these enormous troubles had been settled, with God’s favor, Honorius gave his sister Galla Placidia, long promised, in marriage to his count Constantius, a man of unimpeachable loyalty and great strength. Constantius fathered by her a son, Valentinian, who later ruled the empire of the commonwealth.

At this time he made a very firm treaty with Vallia, king of the Goths, granting him the province of Aquitaine in Gaul for habitation, together with certain neighboring cities of that same province. [Note: [Col. 0954D] A.: “the province of Aquitaine in Gaul, and so on.”]

Since Honorius saw that everywhere he was protected by Constantius’ courage and intelligence, whether through war or through the moderation of peace, he admitted him at Ravenna into partnership in the kingdom with the unanimous support of all. Before seven months had passed, however, Constantius was taken from this life.

In those days, at Bethlehem in Palestine, the blessed Jerome migrated to Christ after completing ninety-one years of life. [Note: [Col. 0954D] A.: “ninety-one years of life, and so on.”]

Afterward Maximus assumed the tyranny in Spain, through the faction of Jovian, who was then considered distinguished in military affairs. [Note: [Col. 0954D] A.: “seized it.”] Not long afterward both men were defeated and captured by Honorius’ army and were presented to him while he was celebrating his thirtieth anniversary at Ravenna.

At this time the Britons, unable to endure the attacks of the Scots and Picts, sent to Rome. Promising their submission, they requested assistance against their enemies. Honorius immediately sent them a legion of soldiers, which defeated a great multitude of barbarians and drove the rest from the borders of Britain.

But as soon as the Romans departed, the enemies arrived again by ship and trampled down and devoured everything in their path. Once more the Romans hastened there, defeated the enemy, and drove them across the sea.

At this time, while the Vandals and Alans were ravaging Spain, Honorius sent the commander Castinus with an army to defend it. Castinus, however, turned the distinguished man Boniface, experienced in military affairs, away from participation in his expedition through inept and unjust authority.

Boniface, judging it dangerous and unworthy to follow a man whom he had found to be discordant and arrogant, quickly made his way to the harbor of the City and from there broke into Africa. Later this caused great damage to the commonwealth and became the cause of the destruction of all Africa.

Castinus, deprived of such a colleague, achieved nothing worthy in Spain. [Note: [Col. 0955D] A.: “deprived of his colleague because of his intemperance, and so on.”]

Meanwhile the Augusta Placidia, driven out by her brother Honorius, departed for the East with her sons Honorius and Valentinian. She was received honorably and gladly by the Augustus Theodosius, son of Arcadius, her other brother. [Note: [Col. 0955D] A.: “Honorius, after he had ruled for years with the younger Theodosius, son of his brother Arcadius, as mentioned above, and so on.”]

After Honorius had reigned for fifteen years—having already ruled thirteen years with his brother and two years under his father—he left the commonwealth peaceful, as he had wished, and died at Rome. His body was buried near the shrine of the blessed apostle Peter. [Note: [Col. 0955D] A.: “the shrine of the Apostle.”]

He had no offspring. For the two daughters of Stilicho, Maria and Thermantia, were married to him one after the other, but both, by God’s judgment, were overtaken by unexpected death and departed this life as virgins. [Note: [Col. 0955D] A.: “departed this life as virgins, and so on.”]

Honorius was not greatly unlike his father Theodosius in character and religion. Although many foreign and civil wars arose in his time, they were brought to an end with either no bloodshed or very little.

After Honorius had departed from human affairs, a certain John, one of the imperial secretaries, supported by the assistance of Castinus, master of the soldiers, seized the empire.

In the year 1177 from the founding of the City, Theodosius, son of Arcadius, [Note: [Col. 0955D] “Forty-third.”] the forty-seventh Roman ruler from Augustus, governed the Eastern Empire. [Note: A.: “Emperor. When he learned of the death of his uncle Honorius, he immediately [appointed] Valentinian, etc.”] John sent an embassy to him, begging to be accepted as emperor and also asking him to reclaim Africa by force of arms from Boniface, since he had become too weak to defend himself.

But Theodosius thrust John’s envoys into prison and sent the praetorian prefect Ardaburius against him; the usurper attacked and imprisoned him at Ravenna. When Theodosius learned this, he made Valentinian, the son of his aunt Placidia, Caesar and sent him with his mother, the Augusta, to recover the Western Empire. [Note: A.: “He sent him. At that time, while John was demanding by war the Africa which Boniface held, he had become too weak to defend himself. Finally, when Placidia Augusta and Valentinian Caesar arrived, they immediately overthrew him with remarkable success and, victorious, seized the reins of government. Their soldiers then cruelly plundered Ravenna, etc.”] He also sent Aspar, son of Ardaburius, ahead of Valentinian against John.

An angel of the Lord, appearing in the guise of a shepherd, guided Aspar and those who were with him, leading them through an impassable marsh beside Ravenna, which God had made passable. After they crossed over by a dry route and found the city gates open, they killed the usurper, released Ardaburius from his chains, and cruelly plundered Ravenna, because its citizens had been especially favorable to the usurper’s party.

They condemned Castinus, the master of the soldiers, to exile; John was believed to have seized the tyranny through his faction. Aetius was pardoned because the Huns, whom John had received through his agency as auxiliaries, had returned to their own country through Aetius’ efforts. Valentinian was therefore made emperor with the consent of all Italy and, by decree of Theodosius, was likewise called Augustus.

While these events were taking place, a Gallic town named Achilas [Note: A.: “A noble town”; P., Pith.: “Aurelia.”] was besieged by the Goths with military force, until, when Aetius approached, they withdrew without escaping punishment. [Note: A.: “they withdrew.” Boniface meanwhile was increasing in power and glory in Africa. Against him Mavortius and Gallio were sent, etc.]

In the following year, that is, the sixteenth year of Theodosius’ reign, the bishop Maruthas of Mesopotamia healed the son of the Persian king Yazdegerd, who was afflicted by a demon. Meanwhile the emperor Theodosius, moved by great kindness, although he had defeated the most powerful Persians, nevertheless spared the Christians living in Persia and embraced peace. For this purpose he sent the patrician Helion, whom he said should be greatly honored, and Anatolius, praetorian prefect of the East.

Vararanes, recognizing his defeat, received the embassy, and so the persecution that had been directed against the Christians ceased. Since victory over the Persians had been granted through God’s aid, many Romans distinguished for eloquence composed praises of the emperor. His wife also composed many poems in heroic verse. She was eloquent, the daughter of the Athenian sophist Leontius, and had been instructed by her father in every branch of learning. When the emperor was about to marry her, Bishop Atticus made her a Christian; although she had previously been called Athenais, he gave her the name Eudoxia at baptism.

At the same time there were Goths and many other great peoples living beyond the Danube in the northern regions. Of these, four were the more civilized: the Goths, the Hypogoths, the Gepids, and the Vandals. They changed only their name and nothing else, and all used one language; but all belonged to the malignity of the Arian faith.

Crossing the Danube under Arcadius and Honorius, these peoples settled in Roman territory. The Gepids—of whom the Lombards and Avars were later divided off—lived in the villages around Singidunum [Col. 0956D] and Sirmium. The Hypogoths, after plundering Rome under Alaric, went into Gaul and took possession of what was there. The Goths first held Pannonia; then, in the eighteenth year of the younger emperor Theodosius, they occupied the villages of Thrace. After dwelling in Thrace for fifty-eight years, they also seized the Empire of the West.

The Vandals, having joined themselves to the Alans and taken in the Germans who are now called Franks, crossed the Rhine under the leadership of Modogisclus and settled in Spain, which is the first of the provinces of Europe from the western ocean.

Meanwhile Valentinian was unable to save not only Britain, Gaul, and Spain, but also lost western Libya, the region called Africa, in the following manner. There were two praetorian prefects whom we have mentioned, Aetius and Boniface, whom Theodosius had sent to Rome at Valentinian’s request.

When Boniface had received authority over western Libya and was increasing in power and glory in Africa, Aetius, inflamed by envy, brought an accusation against Boniface, as though he were plotting rebellion and striving to retain Libya. He disclosed this to Placidia, who was Valentinian’s mother. But he wrote to Boniface:

“If you are summoned, do not come; for you have been accused, and the emperors are calling you deceitfully.”

Boniface accepted this message and, trusting Aetius as though he were his own servant, delayed coming when summoned. Then the emperors received Aetius as though he were loyal, and sent Mavortius and Gallio against Boniface. While they were preparing to besiege Boniface, he killed them. [Note: A.: “they were killed. From that time, while peoples who did not know how to use ships were being called upon for aid by the combatants, the sea was made passable. Again, etc.”]

Again Count Suuldus was sent against Boniface. [Note: A.: “Sigisvuldus”; thus in the French manuscript and in Pith.] Boniface therefore realized that he could not safely hold Africa, and saw that danger threatened him. Burning with rage to the ruin of the whole state, he crossed from Libya to Spain and went to the Vandals and Alans. [Note: A.: “increasing in fury, he summoned the nation of the Vandals and Alans, together with their king Geiseric, from Spain and brought them into Africa; they devastated almost all Africa with the sword, etc.”]

When he found Modogisclus dead and his sons Guntharius and Genseric governing, he urged them to divide Spain and Libya into three parts. They promised that each party would rule together with him, but that all would take vengeance jointly against any enemy. With such assurances, the Vandals and Alans crossed the strait and settled in Libya. They devastated almost all Africa with the sword, fire, and the most savage plundering; moreover, they overthrew the Catholic faith through Arian impiety.

Amid this storm the most blessed Augustine, previously mentioned, bishop of Hippo, so as not to witness the ruin of his city, went to Christ in the third month of the same siege, having completed seventy-six years of life, forty of which he had spent in the clerical or episcopal office. [Note: A.: “went to Christ. At the same time, when there was peace throughout the world and remarkable agreement, Boniface returned from Africa to Italy through Rome, having received the rank of master, etc.”]

At the same time, certain members of the Roman senate who were friends of Boniface informed Placidia of Aetius’ false accusation. They also showed her the letter previously sent by Aetius to Boniface, which Boniface himself had forwarded to them. Placidia was astonished, but did Aetius no harm. To Boniface, however, she sent an encouraging message accompanied by oaths.

After Guntharius died, Genseric became emperor of the Alans and Vandals. Boniface therefore took up arms against the Vandals in response to the message he had received, with a large army coming to him both from Rome and from Constantinople, where Aspar was master of the soldiers. When battle was joined against Genseric, the Roman army was defeated.

Thus Boniface came to Rome with Aspar and dispelled the suspicion by demonstrating the truth of the matter; he received from the emperor the rank of master of the soldiers. After defeating Aetius, who resisted him, in battle, he died of illness a few days later. In this manner Africa was conquered by the Vandals.

At that time Martianus, who later became emperor, was captured alive by Genseric while he was still a soldier and serving Aspar. Aetius, after laying down his office, was living on his estate. When a rival attempted to overwhelm him there by a sudden attack, he fled to Rome, and from there went to Dalmatia, then to Pannonia, to the Huns. Using their friendship and assistance, Aetius obtained peace from the rulers, together with the recovery of his interrupted power. [Note: A.: “the rights of the rulers, and the right of the interrupted [authority].”] Not long afterward he also attained the dignity of the patriciate.

After the African disaster mentioned above, a peace with the Vandals—more necessary than beneficial—was established when a portion of Africa was granted to them for settlement through Trigetius. [Note: “For three years,” an error in Prosper.] In these same times Aetius, the patrician, crushed Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians living within Gaul, in war, and granted peace to him when he begged for it.

Meanwhile the Goths disturbed the terms of peace and occupied many townships near their settlements. Since they were especially hostile to the people of Narni, and were afflicting its citizens with a prolonged siege and famine, Count Litorius arrived, put the enemy to flight, and freed the city from hunger by bringing an abundant supply of grain. [Note: A.: “of Narbonne.”] [Note: A.: “a long [siege].”]

Then, in the following year, war was waged against the Goths with the aid of the Huns. At that time Genseric, within the bounds of his settlement in Africa, wishing to overthrow the Catholic faith through Arian impiety, persecuted certain of our bishops so severely that he expelled them from the cities as well as depriving them of their lawful basilicas. Their steadfastness did not yield at all to the threats of the most arrogant king. [Note: A.: “to no threats.”] [Note: A.: “yield.”]

In those days Valentinian Augustus went to Constantinople to his cousin and lord, the emperor Theodosius, and married his daughter. [Note: A.: “At the same time, etc.”]

Around the same period many Jews in Crete became Christians because of the following occurrence. A certain Jewish deceiver pretended that he was Moses, sent from heaven to lead the Jews living on that island across the sea. He claimed to be the very man who had once led the children of Israel through the Red Sea.
