Throughout the year he went around each city of the island, persuading the Jews to believe him and urging them to leave behind all their money and possessions. Once led by him across the dry seabed, they would reach the joys of the Promised Land. Captured by this hope, they neglected all their own work, despised their possessions, and handed them over to various persons.

When the day appointed by the Jewish deceiver arrived, everyone followed him with their wives and children. He led them to a certain cliff that sloped sharply downward and ordered them to wrap themselves in the form of their hair. The leaders did so, and when they came to the cliffs they suddenly died, torn apart by the sharp rocks or drowned in the water.

Even more would have died if, by God’s providence, certain Christian fishermen and merchants had not arrived. They rescued and revived some while they were being killed; then, realizing the evil resulting from their folly, they restrained others from throwing themselves to their deaths and announced the death of those who had fallen first.

When they recognized the deception, they blamed themselves for having so readily believed him. They wished to kill the deceiver, but could not seize him, for he suddenly disappeared. This gave rise to the suspicion that he had formerly been a wandering demon disguised in human form. Because of this event and calamity, many of the Jews of Crete were then converted to the Christian faith.

Meanwhile a fire broke out in the city of Constantinople and gradually reached the baths called the Achillean Baths, then the place called Pelargus, so that the church of the Novatians was engulfed. [Note: Nicephorus Callistus, Book XIV, chapter 41; Socrates, Book VII, chapter 39: “The public building that was named after Achilles.”]

It is said that Paul, their bishop, remained amid the flames of the church, praying to God that the church too might not be burned. That place was saved, and to this day, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, a gathering is held there among the Novatians. This place is venerated not only by Christians but also by pagans.

The present occasion requires an account of the origin of this heresy. Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, who because of the persecution that had occurred under Decius wished to make himself bishop and expel Cornelius, used to make offerings, distribute a portion to each person, and, while holding both hands of the recipient, compel miserable people to swear this oath as a blessing. He would not release them until the person swearing had said:

“Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never at any time abandon me and return to Cornelius.”

The wretched man would not taste the food until he had first cursed himself. Instead of saying “Amen” after receiving the bread, he said:

“May I never return again to Cornelius.”

Because of this doctrine, the emperor Constantine, wishing to reconcile the Churches, summoned Bishop Acesius to the Council of Nicaea. After the definition of the faith, he asked whether Acesius also agreed with the faith and with the decree concerning the celebration of Easter.

Acesius replied: “There is nothing new, emperor, in what the synod has defined. For long ago, and from the times of the apostles, I myself received both the rule of faith and the date of the Easter celebration.”

When the emperor asked again, “Why then do you separate yourself from communion?” Acesius repeated what had occurred under Decius and brought forward the severity of the most bitter rule. He said that those who sin after baptism with a sin that divine Scripture declares to be unto death ought not to be made worthy of communion in the sacraments. Rather, they should indeed be invited to repentance, but they should await the hope of remission not from priests but from God alone, who has the power to forgive sins.

When Acesius had said this, the emperor replied: “Acesius, set up a ladder; and if you can climb into heaven alone, climb.”

Valentinian Augustus, son of Constantius and Galla, then went to Constantinople to his cousin and lord, the emperor Theodosius, and married his daughter, named Eudoxia, whom Eudoxia had borne to him. [Note: Cedrenus and Marcellinus: “Eudocia.”] He returned to Rome during the consulship of Isidore and Senator.

In the following year the emperor Theodosius sent his wife Eudoxia to Jerusalem to offer hymns of thanksgiving to God. She presented many gifts to the churches, worshiped both the holy cross and the places worthy of veneration, and returned to the imperial palace.

In the thirtieth year of Theodosius’ reign, great earthquakes occurred in Constantinople for four months, so that the frightened Byzantines remained outside the city in the place called the Campus, crying out to God in prayers and litanies together with the bishop.

One day, while the earth was shaking and the entire people were crying out more intensely, “Κύριε ἐλέησον” (“Lord, have mercy”), around the third hour, everyone saw a certain young man lifted into the air by divine power. A divine voice was heard instructing him to tell the bishop and the people to conduct the litany and say:

“Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us,”

adding nothing else.

Bishop Proclus, having received this litany, ordered the people to follow it, and immediately the earthquake ceased. The blessed Pulcheria, greatly astonished at the miracle together with her brother, decreed that this divine hymn should be sung throughout the world. From that time all the Churches adopted the practice of singing it to God every day.

At the same time pirates ravaged many islands, especially Sicily.

Meanwhile Litorius, who held the second position of authority after Aetius and was in command with the aid of the Huns, sought to surpass Aetius’ glory. Trusting the answers of the haruspices and the signs of demons, he imprudently engaged the Goths in battle. At first he inflicted a great slaughter on the enemy; afterward, when almost all his own men had been killed, he himself was disgracefully captured by the Goths.

Finally peace was made with them, after the Romans had requested it more humbly than ever before, following the disaster of this tearful war. While Aetius was occupied in Gaul with arranging affairs, Genseric—whose friendship no one suspected—seized Carthage by a trick under the pretext of peace. After torturing its citizens by various forms of torment, he converted all its wealth to his own use. He did not refrain from plundering the churches either: after emptying them of their sacred vessels and depriving them of the ministry of priests, he ordered them no longer to be places of divine worship but dwellings for his own people.

He raged against the captive population as a whole, but was especially hostile to the nobility and to religion, so that it could not at all be discerned whether he had waged war more against human beings or against God.

Thus Carthage was captured by the Vandals after 585 years had passed since it had begun to obey Roman rule.

In the following year Genseric crossed over to Sicily and afflicted it with great calamities. But when he received news about Sebastian, who was making his way from Spain to Africa, he quickly returned to Carthage, believing that it would be dangerous for himself and his people if a man experienced in warfare settled down to recover Carthage. Sebastian, however, wishing to appear more a friend than an enemy, and rashly presuming upon the friendship of the barbarian king, was killed by an unhappy death. [Note: A.: “Sebastian.”]

After this the emperor Theodosius launched a war against the Vandals, sending a large fleet under the commanders Ariovindus, Ansila, and Germanus. [Note: A.: “Ariovindus.”] By delaying the undertaking through prolonged hesitation, they proved more a burden to Sicily than a defense of Africa.

During this period Attila, king of the Huns, a brave and arrogant man, while ruling over the Huns together with his brother Bleda, devastated Thrace and Illyricum with savage destruction. He reduced all the forts and cities to servitude, except Adrianople and Heraclea, which had formerly been called Perinthus.

The Roman army that had been staying in Sicily then returned to defend the eastern provinces. Theodosius was therefore compelled to send an embassy to Attila. He offered him six thousand pounds for his withdrawal and promised to pay an annual tribute of one thousand pounds.

Around these same days Rome was shaken by an earthquake so terrible that many of its houses and buildings collapsed. [Note: A.: “the first.”]

The Britons mentioned earlier, when they were again oppressed by the incursions of the Scots and Picts, sent Aetius a letter full of tears and troubles and urgently begged his assistance. Aetius did not grant their request, since he was occupied against neighboring enemies. Some of the Britons nevertheless resisted bravely and drove the enemy away; others were forced to submit.

Finally, after the Picts had conquered the farthest part of the same island, they made it their dwelling and have not been expelled from it to this day. The remaining Britons, continually fearing the attacks of the Scots and no longer trusting in Roman protection, invited the people of the Angles, with their king Vortigern, to defend their homeland. They received them in friendly alliance, but when circumstances changed they found in them enemies and attackers instead of helpers.

Thereafter the people of the Angles, or Saxons, arrived in Britain in three longships. When news of their successful journey had reached their homeland, a large army was nevertheless sent. Joining the earlier arrivals, it first drove away the enemies for whose sake it had been summoned; then it turned its weapons against the Britons, inventing the excuse that the Britons had provided insufficient pay for those who were fighting on their behalf. By fire or sword it subjugated almost the whole island, from its eastern region to the western.

Theodosius, after ruling the Empire for twenty-seven years—apart from the twenty-one preceding years during which he had reigned with his uncle Honorius, and including twenty-five years spent with his son-in-law Valentinian—died of illness at Constantinople and was buried there. [Note: Ambrose, in these words: “Book XIII ends here. The remainder is not read.”]

Theodosius was so wise that, when people conversed together, he was believed to possess knowledge of every subject. He endured cold and heat alike, often fasted, and especially on Wednesday and Friday, out of Christian devotion. His imperial residence appeared no different from a monastery.

Each morning he went to his sisters and recited the divine praises. For this reason he could also recite the sacred writings without a book. When bishops spoke, he answered from the divine reading as though he had once been made a priest. He collected sacred books and studied whatever their interpreters or commentators appeared to have written, more diligently than Ptolemy Philadelphus had studied.

He surpassed all people in patience and clemency. The emperor Julian, although he had been a philosopher, did not bear the injury inflicted by the people of Antioch but, in great anger, imposed tortures on Theodore. Theodosius, however, taking great delight in the syllogisms of Aristotle, practiced philosophy through his actions, overcoming anger, grief, and lust, and desiring to avenge himself on no one.

When one of his attendants asked why he subjected none of those who injured him to death, he replied: “Would that it were possible for me to restore the dead to life!”

He was so merciful that whenever someone committed an offense deserving death, the condemned person did not reach the city gates before being recalled through the emperor’s clemency.

Once, while he was watching in the amphitheater at Constantinople, the people began to shout: “Let the trainer of the cruel beast fight by means of riddles!” He replied: “Do you not know that we are accustomed to watch mercifully?”

He was distinguished by such great piety that he honored all who were consecrated to God, especially those whom he heard to excel in venerable conduct. It is said that when the bishop of Chebron in Constantinople had died, Theodosius searched for his extremely filthy cloak and wrapped himself in it, believing that he would gain something from the holiness of the deceased.

On one occasion the weather became stormy while he was watching the people. A violent storm arose in the full circus, with heavy rain pouring down. The emperor then put aside his own desire and ordered the herald to proclaim that it would be better to disregard the spectacle and ask God to preserve everyone unharmed from the threatening storm.

At these words the entire people prayed with great joy and offered hymns in harmony; the whole city sang as though it were a single Church. The emperor, standing among them, hurried away in ordinary clothing and was not disappointed in his hope. Suddenly the weather returned to calm, recalled by divine mercy, and the year proved exceedingly fruitful for all crops. [Col. 0963A]

Whenever wars arose, he took refuge in God, following David, knowing that God is the author of battles, and overcame his enemies through prayers. [Note: Thus far Socrates, Book VII, chapter 2.]

Yet this emperor was not free from faults. He was changeable and surrounded by every wind; hence he even signed documents that he had not read.

Meanwhile the blessed Pulcheria, before anyone else had learned of the death of her brother, the emperor Theodosius, summoned Martianus, who was living in religious devotion and chastity—a mature and suitable man—and said to him:

“Since the emperor has died, and I have chosen you as pleasing above all the senate, give me your word that you will preserve my virginity, which I have entrusted to God, and I will proclaim you emperor.”

When he promised this under oath, she summoned the patriarch Anatolius and the senate and proclaimed him emperor of the Romans.

# BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0963]

In the year 1204 from the founding of the City, after Theodosius had died, Martianus, the forty-eighth ruler from Augustus, was appointed emperor of the Eastern court. [Note: A.: “Martianus, forty-fourth in the Eastern succession, etc.”] The period of Valentinian, however, is reckoned among the years of this emperor or of the preceding one.

Valentinian, ruler of the Western Empire, at that time established a treaty of peace with Genseric, king of the Vandals, and Africa was divided between them according to fixed boundaries. Genseric, puffed up by the success of his affairs and becoming arrogant even among his own people, was subjected to a powerful conspiracy. When their plot was discovered, they perished after being tortured by him with various punishments. In their deaths he lost no less of his strength than he would have lost if he had been defeated in battle. [Note: A.: “a conspiracy of his own people, etc.”]

Meanwhile Attila, king of the Huns, while ruling together with his brother Bleda within Pannonia and Dacia, devastated Macedonia, Moesia, and Achaea, as well as both the provinces of Greece, with the most savage fury, as has been said. [Note: A.: “Moesia.”] He killed his own brother Bleda, his fellow ruler, and compelled the peoples to obey him. [Note: A.: “Thrace”; thus Pith.]

Supported by the strength of the fiercest nations that he had subjugated, he turned his mind toward destroying the Western Empire. His army was said to number nearly seven hundred thousand men. He was a man born for the upheaval of the world, the terror of all lands, as common report declared.

He was arrogant in his bearing, carrying himself to and fro so that his pride in power appeared even in the movement of his body. He was indeed a lover of war, but personally restrained in action; powerful in counsel; open to the entreaties of petitioners; gracious toward those once received into his allegiance; short in stature, broad-chested, with a large head, small eyes, a sparse beard sprinkled with gray, a flat nose, and a dark complexion, displaying the marks of his origin.

Under his dominion were the famous king of the Gepids, Andaricus [Note: A.: “Ardaricus”], and Walamir, ruler of the Goths, who was more noble than the very king whom he then served. There were likewise the strongest peoples: the Marcomanni, Suevi, and Quadi; moreover the Heruli, Turcilingi, or Rugi, with their own petty kings; and other barbarian nations dwelling in the northern regions. [Note: A.: “Turcilingi.”]

Arrogant in command of all these peoples, Attila believed that he could easily obtain whatever he desired through the strength of his forces. [Note: A.: “although in the strength of his forces, etc.”] Nevertheless, he endeavored to attack his enemies through the cunning of strategy no less than through the power of arms; for, foreseeing with the sagacity with which [Note: A.: “he desired; nevertheless, with no less …”] [Note: A.: “through strategic skill.”]

A.: pretending [to do so], he asserts that he will fight against the Romans, while, conversely, claiming to seek the Romans’ friendship, he promises to take up arms against the Goths, their particular enemies. Thus this crafty barbarian acted so that, if he could separate these peoples from one another’s alliance, he might more easily crush both in separate engagements. Aetius, foreseeing his stratagems with no less shrewdness, sent envoys to Theodoric, who at that time ruled the Goths at Toulouse, to establish a peace treaty with him. Theodoric agreed to the Roman envoys’ proposal, joined with them in a very firm alliance, taking no less thought for his own interests, and promised to fight alongside them.

Meanwhile, the Romans were aided by the Burgundians; the Alans, with their king Sangiban; the Franks, Saxons, Riparioli, Bariones, Sarmatians, Armoricans, Lutetians, and nearly all the peoples of the West. Aetius had enlisted all of them in the alliance for war, lest he meet Attila with an inferior force. Both sides assembled on the Catalaunian Plains, which are said to extend one hundred leagues in length and seventy leagues in breadth, according to the Gallic method of measurement.

Thus, as soon as Attila had entered Gaul, on his first advance he crushed Gundicarius, the king of the Burgundians, who had come out to meet him. Then, when they had reached the place of battle, he consulted a haruspex to learn whether he could foretell what outcome the war would bring him. The haruspex, examining the entrails of animals by demonic art, announced an unfavorable result to Attila, but added this small consolation: that the chief commander of the opposing side would fall in the battle. Attila, however, believing that this prediction concerned Aetius’s death—whose destruction he thirsted for—did not hesitate to commit himself to battle, even at the cost of his own men’s ruin, provided that he could kill Aetius, who was stoutly resisting his designs.

He therefore joined battle when the day was already declining toward evening, so that, if he were defeated by the enemy, he might conceal himself in the darkness of the approaching night. The bravest nations assembled on both sides; the battle lines engaged; and a fierce and stubborn fight began, such as scarcely any history records. They did not cease in the ardor of battle until the arrival of night deprived them of the will to fight. In that battle, 180,000 men are reported to have been killed. So much blood was shed that a little stream flowing there suddenly became an enormous torrent and carried the corpses of the slain along with it.

Attila’s suspicion concerning Aetius’s death had deceived him. For while Aetius remained unharmed, Theodoric, king of the Goths, fell there. Although neither army had yielded in that battle, it is nevertheless certain that Attila had been defeated. On the following day he confined himself within the defenses of his wagons and did not dare to break out, yet he continued to make a din with trumpets and shouting. Thorismund, son of King Theodoric, grieving over his father’s death, decided to hem Attila in by siege, so that he might destroy him and his army utterly. [Col. 0965A]

Then Attila, already despairing of his life, built a huge pyre from saddles in the cavalry camp, intending to burn himself there if the Goths pressed their attack, so that no one might rejoice over his injury and so that the king of so many nations might not fall into the hands of his enemies.

But Aetius, recklessly considering that the Romans would be weakened by the Goths if Attila were killed, and that thereafter they would have assistance against the Goths should necessity arise, persuaded Thorismund—as though advising him for his own interests—to return home and seize his father’s kingdom. Otherwise, if his brothers invaded it, it would be more bitter for him to fight with his own people than with his enemies. Thorismund willingly accepted this counsel as having been offered for his safety, returned home, and took possession of his father’s kingdom.

In fact, Aetius had devised this plan in order to withdraw Attila from Thorismund’s attack. Alas for the ignorance of human beings! In trying to avert the danger, he brought such ruin upon his country through this precaution.

When Attila saw that he had returned to his own country after the enemy had been left behind, his spirits rose and his hope of survival was strengthened. He returned to Pannonia, gathered a much stronger army, and entered Italy in fury. First he attacked Aquileia, a city situated at the very beginning of Italy. After besieging it continuously for three years, he accomplished nothing against it because the citizens resisted vigorously. Then, when he heard the murmuring of his army, which could no longer endure the shortage of food, he made a circuit of the city one day to discover from which side it could most easily be captured.

Suddenly he saw birds accustomed to nesting on the gables of buildings—the birds called storks—leaving the city all at once and carrying their young away across the countryside in their beaks. “Look,” he said, “at these birds, who know the future: they are abandoning the city because it is doomed.” He immediately brought up engines and artillery, encouraged his men, and attacked the city fiercely. Without delay, he captured it. Its wealth was plundered; its citizens were taken captive or slaughtered; and, after the plundering, flames consumed what remained when fire was set to it. [Col. 0965C]

There was in that city a woman of the highest nobility named Digna. Her beauty was extraordinary, but she was adorned even more greatly by the radiance of her chastity. Her dwelling stood above the city wall, and a tall tower rose over her house, beneath which the river Natissa flowed in crystal-clear streams. As soon as she sensed the enemy’s entry and the city’s capture, she threw herself headfirst from the top of that same tower, her head wrapped in a covering, lest she become a spectacle for the filthiest enemies and lest the beauty of her soul be defiled by lust imposed upon her by force. Thus, through a memorable death, she ended her fear of losing her chastity.

The savage enemy also burned and demolished many fortresses in the same region, killing or taking captive their citizens. He destroyed Concordia, Altinum, and Patavium, neighboring cities of Aquileia, leveling them to the ground in the same manner. From there the Huns raged through all the cities of Venetia—that is, Vicentia, Verona, Brixia, Bergomum, and the rest—with no one resisting. They likewise plundered Mediolanum and Ticinum, but refrained from burning them, though they did not refrain from the sword. Then, after the cities of Emilia had been similarly stripped, they finally made camp at the place where the river Mincius flows into the Po.

There Attila remained, wavering in mind over whether he should march on Rome or abandon the attempt. He was not concerned for the city, against which he was hostile, but feared the example of Alaric, who did not long survive the capture of the city. While he recalled these anxieties in his mind, a most peaceful embassy suddenly arrived from Rome. For the most holy man, Pope Leo, went to him in person. When he had entered the barbarian king’s presence, he obtained everything he desired and brought back the safety not only of Rome but of all Italy. Attila had been terrified by a sign from God and was able to say nothing to Christ’s priest except what the priest himself preferred.

It is therefore reported that, after the pope’s departure, Attila was asked by his men why he had shown such extraordinary respect to the Roman pope, obeying almost everything that the pope had commanded. The king replied that he had not reverenced the person of the man who had come, but had seen another man standing beside him in priestly dress, more august in appearance and venerable with white hair. That man, with a drawn sword, had threateningly promised Attila death unless he fulfilled everything the pope requested. [Col. 0966A]

Thus restrained from his savagery, Attila left Italy and returned to Pannonia. Honoria, the sister of the emperor Valentinian, who was being kept under strict guard by her brother for the sake of her chastity, sent her eunuch to him to demand that her brother give her to Attila in marriage. Attila received this message after he had already passed beyond the borders of Italy and could not immediately return with his exhausted army. He therefore sent word to the emperor Valentinian, threatening to inflict still worse harm upon Italy soon unless Valentinian immediately sent him his sister together with the portion of the kingdom due to her.

After returning to his own quarters, Attila took as his wife a very beautiful girl named Ildico, in addition to the many wives he already possessed. While celebrating lavish wedding banquets and drinking an amount of wine greater than he had ever before consumed at one time, he lay back to rest and was suffocated by a sudden flow of blood, which customarily also ran from his nostrils. Thus he died.

That same night at Constantinople, the Lord appeared in a dream to the emperor Marcian and showed him Attila’s broken bow—the weapon on which that people chiefly relies in war.

While these events were taking place, adherents of the Pelagian heresy were attempting to subvert the faith in Britain. The Britons sought help from the bishops of Gaul and received, for the defense of the true faith, the most holy man Germanus, bishop of the church of Auxerre, already renowned for many virtues, together with Lupus, bishop of Troyes, a man of apostolic grace. Through miracles no less than through words of teaching, they brought everyone back to the confession of sound faith.

But while the holy bishops were still remaining there, a powerful force of Saxons and Picts came to Britain. Nevertheless, the Britons immediately seized their weapons and went out to meet the enemy. Blessed Germanus voluntarily joined them and went with them to the battle. When he had taken his position as commander of the army before the joined battle lines, and the massed enemy was already approaching, the holy bishop trusted neither the shouting of the crowd nor swords. He merely ordered that, when he first cried out, all the others should answer him with the same words in a single voice.

Then, with a great voice raised, “Alleluia” rang out. When the entire army responded “Alleluia” with a shout lifted to the stars, and all the surrounding places echoed with it, such terror immediately seized the enemy that, breaking their line and taking flight as though a sword were hanging over each man’s neck, they fled trembling to their own country.

Since virtue always produces envy, the emperor Valentinian—as events made clear—feared Aetius’s successful achievements, as mentioned above. He therefore killed both Aetius and the most noble senator Bostius with the sword. Thus the very warlike Aetius, once the terror of King Attila, fell; and with him the Western Empire and the safety of the Roman state also collapsed, never thereafter recovering its former strength. [Col. 0966D]

But Aetius’s death did not go unpunished for Valentinian. In the following year he too was stabbed and killed by Aetius’s soldier Transila, after having ruled the empire for thirty years. Of these years, he ruled twenty-five with Theodosius, his father-in-law, and five with Marcian.

After Valentinian’s death, Maximus seized the authority of the kingdom at Rome. Before two full months had passed, however, he was killed by the Romans. Immediately Geiseric arrived with ships from Africa and a very powerful army of his people, supported in addition by an auxiliary force of Moors, while the most blessed Leo was still serving as pontiff of the Roman Church.

The Romans were struck by this terrible news, and the nobles and common people alike fled from the city. Geiseric took possession of Rome, which had been left without any defense. The same holy bishop Leo met him outside the gate, and his supplication, with God’s help, so softened Geiseric that, although everything had been handed over to his authority, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and punishment.

For fourteen days Rome was emptied of all its wealth through unrestricted and unimpeded plunder. Many thousands of captives were carried off to Carthage, each according to the age or skill that pleased their captors, together with Queen Eudoxia, who had invited Geiseric to undertake this deed, and her two daughters.

In this way Rome was captured by Geiseric, after Alaric had first invaded it. This was the second capture, forty-four years after the first, and 1,208 years after the city’s foundation.

After Rome had been abandoned, the Vandals and Moors poured through Campania, consuming everything with sword and flame and plundering whatever could survive. They captured the most noble city of Capua, razed it to the ground, and took its inhabitants captive and its possessions as plunder. They likewise overthrew the very wealthy city of Nola and many others in a similar ruin. They also left Naples, and other cities that they could not capture because of their strength, stripped of their agricultural resources. All who had survived the sword were subjected to the yoke of captivity. [Col. 0967B]

Amid these storms, the most pious man Paulinus, bishop of Nola, after spending everything he could possess on the redemption of captives, finally had nothing left except himself. Unable in his compassionate heart to bear the motherly tears of a certain widow for her son, he went with her to Africa, from which the enemy had already departed, and surrendered himself into the service of a barbarian as a substitute for the young man. Once his holiness became known among that barbarian people by God’s will, he eventually returned to his own city together with all his fellow citizens.

Geiseric, after being enriched by the wealth of Italy, returned to Africa. He gave in marriage to his son Trasamund the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, whom he had carried away from Rome as a captive. From her, evidently, Hilderic was born, who later became the fourth ruler of the Vandals in Africa after Geiseric.

After Geiseric withdrew from Rome, the Romans, in the following month, appointed Avitus emperor over the impoverished Roman state. Around this time the Visigoths also, with their king Theodoric, son of Theodoric, crossed the Pyrenees and invaded Spain.

Meanwhile, after ruling the empire at Constantinople for seven years, the emperor Marcian was killed through a conspiracy of his own people.

## BOOK FIFTEEN

In the year 1211 from the foundation of the City, after the death of the emperor Marcian, Leo the forty-fifth of the Roman rulers obtained the imperial dignity at Constantinople. In due course he made his son Leo his associate in the empire.

After Avitus had been removed from human affairs in Italy, Majorian seized the empire at Ravenna. He held it for nearly four years and was then killed not far from the city of Dertona, beside the river Ira. Immediately afterward Severus was made emperor at Ravenna and was called Augustus.

In the third year of his reign, Biorgor, king of the Alans, arrived with an army. The patrician Ricimer met him and defeated him not far from the city of Bergomum in Venetia, killing him. Severus, after reigning for four years, died a natural death at Rome.

At the same time, a fire that broke out unexpectedly consumed much of Constantinople, destroying its buildings. Then, by the unanimous agreement of the army, Anthemius assumed the authority of the empire after Severus’s death. In the following year Servandus, prefect of Gaul, attempted to seize the empire and was driven into exile by order of the emperor Anthemius. Again, after a year had passed, the Roman patrician Romanus, deceitfully striving to seize the imperial dignity, was beheaded by order of Anthemius.

In those days Geiseric once more wished to sail to Italy, but Basiliscus, the patrician, defeated him in a naval battle, and he returned ingloriously to Carthage. In the East, however, the patrician Aspar plotted against Leo Augustus and made his own son Caesar. Leo immediately summoned the victorious army from Sicily and inflicted a deserved death upon the patrician Aspar, the newly appointed Caesar, and another son of Aspar, his brother. [Col. 0968A]

At this very time a great source of discord arose between the emperor Anthemius and his son-in-law, the patrician Ricimer, who was then stationed at Milan and governed Liguria. Epiphanius, the distinguished bishop of Ticinum, intervened between them and first restored harmony. Then Ricimer, breaking the treaty with barbarian treachery—for he was of Gothic descent—soon marched against Rome with a powerful force and established his camp at the Anician Bridge.

Rome was thus divided: some favored Anthemius, while others followed Ricimer’s treachery. During these events Olybrius, sent by Leo Augustus, came to Rome and obtained royal authority while Anthemius was still alive.

Bilimer, governor of Gaul, learned of Ricimer’s conspiracy against Anthemius and wished to bring assistance to Anthemius, so he hurried to Rome. He engaged Ricimer in battle at Hadrian’s Bridge, but was immediately defeated and killed by him. After Bilimer’s death, the victorious Ricimer invaded Rome and, in the fourth year of Anthemius’s reign, slaughtered him with the sword.

In addition to the shortage of food and the epidemic that afflicted Rome at that time, the city was also grievously plundered. Except for two districts, where Ricimer and his men remained, every other part was devastated by the greed of the plunderers. But Ricimer did not long rejoice in his treachery. Three months later, after being tortured by illnesses, he too died. After Ricimer’s death, the emperor Olybrius made his nephew Gundobad patrician.

Olybrius himself died a natural death at Rome after ruling the empire for seven months. After his funeral, Licerius, a member of the household guard, was made emperor at Ravenna by the patrician Gundobad, with the consent also of the entire army. In the following year, the patrician Nepos suddenly arrived with an army, stripped Licerius of royal authority, and ordained him bishop at Salona, a city of Dalmatia.

At that time Euric ruled the Visigothic peoples at Toulouse. The causes of dispute between Nepos and Euric had grown throughout Italy and Gaul, and both sides were preparing for war against the other. But through the intervention of Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, who has already been mentioned, the terms of a treaty between them were confirmed.

Not long after these events, Theodoric, surnamed Strabo, son of Triarius, arrived armed with a great multitude of Ostrogoths, advancing as far as the fourth milestone from the City. He harmed none of the Romans, however, and soon returned to Illyricum, where he died.

The present point requires an explanation of why some of the Goths are called Ostrogoths and others Visigoths. It is appropriate to go back somewhat to earlier times so that the origin of these names may be explained.

In the time of the earlier Valentinian Augustus, when the Gothic peoples then lived together within the borders of Thrace, [the wording is corrupt here]; those from the western regions, in a division associated with Alaric, were called Visigoths—that is, Western Goths. [Col. 0968D]

After Leo Augustus had ruled the Eastern Empire for seventeen years, he died.

After Leo’s death, Zeno immediately obtained the imperial dignity. The Leo mentioned above, whom his father Leo had associated with him in power, was feared by his mother because of Zeno’s attack. She secretly made him a cleric. When Zeno pressed her strongly to reveal her son, she presented another boy of similar appearance in his place. That Leo thereafter lived in the clerical state until the time of Justinian.

In that same year, Augustulus arrived in Italy with an army against Nepos. After driving him away, he seized control of the empire. When another year had passed, the patrician Orestes concluded a treaty with Geiseric, king of the Vandals.

While these things were happening among the Romans, Odoacer hastened toward Italy from the farthest borders of Pannonia with a very powerful multitude of Heruli, supported in addition by the aid of the Turcilingi, or Sciri. While he was still leading his army through the countryside of Noricum, he learned of the reputation of Severinus, the servant of Christ who was then living in those regions. Odoacer approached him to seek his blessing.

After receiving the blessing, he wished to leave the man’s cell. Because he was tall, he bent his head so that he would not strike it against the lintel of the doorway. The man of God, who knew the future, immediately said to him: “Go now to Italy, go, Odoacer, though for the present clothed in the poorest skins of animals; soon you will give much more to many.”

The outcome of events confirmed these words. For a few years later he exercised authority over all Italy and, in addition, over the City.

When Odoacer entered Italy, the patrician Orestes immediately met him at the borders of Liguria. Seeing that he could accomplish nothing against such a powerful multitude, especially since some of his own men had already deserted him, Orestes, trembling with fear, shut himself inside Ticinum, trusting in its fortifications.

Odoacer soon arrived with his army and entered the city after capturing it by force. Everything was devastated by plunder; the sword raged everywhere; and fire consumed both sacred and private buildings. At last Orestes was captured by the enemy, taken as far as Placentia, and beheaded there.

From there the same barbarians spread through all the cities and, without delay, subjected all Italy to their own authority. Many cities that were preparing to resist were completely overthrown after their inhabitants had been killed. Odoacer, seeing his successes increase, immediately seized royal authority.

Augustulus, who had presumed to exercise imperial power, saw all Italy being subjected to Odoacer’s strength. Terrified by unprecedented fear, he voluntarily and pitiably laid aside the purple. After having held the Roman state for scarcely eleven months, he surrendered the imperial majesty.

Thus the Roman Empire at Rome, venerable throughout the entire world, and that imperial elevation which had begun with Augustus Octavian, perished with this Augustulus, in the year 1209 from the foundation of the City; in the 517th year from Gaius Caesar, who first seized singular power; and in the 475th year from the Incarnation of the Lord. [Col. 0969C]

After Augustulus had been removed from the imperial dignity, Odoacer entered Rome and obtained the kingdom of all Italy. He held it for fourteen years without disturbance. Then Theodoric, king of the Goths, came from the East and entered Italy to take possession of it.

To make fully clear why and from where he came, it is necessary to return for a while to earlier events. Walamir, king of the Ostrogoths, whom the preceding book mentioned as having been subject to Attila, king of the Huns, immediately after Attila’s death shook off the domination of the Huns over himself and his people, remembering their ancestral freedom. King Ardaric of the Gepids and the other subject nations did the same.

The Huns were angered that Walamir and his army had not only shaken off the yoke of their authority but had also encouraged the other nations to do likewise. They therefore pursued them like runaway slaves and immediately took up arms to restore them to their former servitude. Walamir gathered his people and attacked the Huns. He inflicted such slaughter upon them that thereafter the surviving Huns feared the arms of the Ostrogoths.

After this, the emperor Leo made a treaty with the Goths, who were ravaging Illyricum, and accepted as a hostage Theodoric, son of Theodemir and born of the concubine Erelieva, from Walamir, his paternal uncle.

After Walamir was killed by the Sciri, his brother Theodemir assumed the royal authority. When the kingdom was subsequently divided, Theodemir received the eastern portion, while Windimir received the western empire, which was to be ravaged. But as soon as he entered Italy, he died, leaving his son Windemer as successor to the kingdom.

Windemer, after receiving gifts from Licerius, then emperor, went to Gaul, joined himself to his kinsmen the Visigoths, and became one people with them.

Meanwhile, after achieving a pleasing victory, Windemer was returning home. He gladly received Theodoric, son of Theodemir, who had been sent back by the emperor Leo. When Theodoric was already eighteen years old, he secretly took some attendants with him without his father’s knowledge, invaded the neighboring people of the Sarmatians, and brought back to his father rich spoils and abundant booty taken from them.

When Theodemir died, everyone supporting Theodoric, he ascended to the government of the kingdom. When this event was reported to Zeno Augustus, he received the news gladly. He summoned Theodoric back to Constantinople and honored him with great distinction and wealth, elevating him even to the consul’s fasces—the first dignity after the imperial rank—and placing a bronze equestrian statue of him before his palace.

But while Theodoric enjoyed such luxuries at Constantinople, his people, the Ostrogoths, were suffering severe want. Because the terms of the treaty prevented them from making their customary raids, and the subsidies offered by the emperor were insufficient, they began to endure no small shortage of necessities. They cursed the treaty that had been arranged and denounced the useless agreement. They immediately sent messengers to Theodoric to tell him that, while he was enjoying the banquets of the Greeks, they were enduring the misery of poverty.

They urged him, if he wished to look after himself and his people, to return quickly, so that they might seek new lands in which to settle before the entire nation perished.

When Theodoric learned this, he approached Augustus Zeno, complained, and explained his people’s poverty. He asked that Italy be given to him and begged to be released from his obligations. He added that, if he could overcome Odoacer and obtain Italy, the glory would accrue to the emperor by whom he had been sent; if he were defeated in war, the emperor’s gains would nevertheless increase, since he would no longer have to pay the collectors of the daily subsidies.

Zeno was saddened to hear this, because he did not wish to lose Theodoric. Nevertheless, after deliberation and with the interests of the Roman state in mind, he granted Theodoric’s requests. He assigned Italy to him by an official imperial instrument, confirmed the grant with the gift of the sacred vestment, commended the Roman Senate and people to him, and allowed him to depart.

Theodoric therefore left Constantinople, returned to the Ostrogoths, and immediately urged them to be ready to set out as soon as possible to take possession of Italy.

Before reaching Italy, however, he defeated in battle and killed Triopstila, king of the Gepids, who was plotting against him. He also overthrew Busa, king of the Vulgares, together with a great part of his forces, inflicting a massive slaughter.

Theodoric therefore left Moesia with the entire multitude of the Ostrogoths and all their possessions. Traveling through Sirmium and Pannonia, he came to Italy. First, he established his camp beside the river Sontius, which flows not far from Aquileia. While the animals, exhausted by the length of the journey, were recovering somewhat in the exceptionally rich pastures found there, Odoacer met him with a large army and with all the forces of Italy.

Theodoric met him boldly, defeated him in a great battle, and finally put him to flight. From there Theodoric marched toward Verona. Odoacer again opposed him with no less preparation for war than before. Theodoric engaged him not far from Verona and crushed his army in a tremendous slaughter, forcing Odoacer and all his forces to turn their backs.

As they plunged headlong into the river Adige in fear of the flight, many were caught in its swift whirlpools and drowned. Theodoric followed the fugitives in the same advance and immediately invaded Verona while the terrified citizens were panic-stricken.

Odoacer, fleeing with those who had escaped, made for Rome. But when the gates were immediately closed, he was shut out. Seeing that entry was denied him, he consumed with sword and fire everything he could reach. Leaving that place as well, he entered Ravenna, where he began preparing defensive fortifications by which he might protect himself against his enemies. [Col. 0971B]

Theodoric, departing from Verona, reached Milan. While he was staying there, a great multitude of soldiers and many of the Italian peoples gathered to him. But a few days later, the army that had surrendered to him defected again to Odoacer’s side at the instigation of a certain man named Tuffa.

This event terrified Theodoric so greatly that he fortified himself and his army at Ticinum. Seeing these changing circumstances, Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, entered Liguria with an immense army, plundered everything he could find at will, and carried an immeasurable multitude of captives with him to Gaul.

Theodoric kept his army inside the fortifications for some time. Finally, leaving his mother, sisters, and the multitude of the common people there, and having complete confidence in the faithfulness of Epiphanius, that most holy man, he went with lightly equipped bands of soldiers to besiege Odoacer at Ravenna.

When he had set up camp at a place called the Pine Grove, not far from the city, he besieged Odoacer for almost three continuous years. Odoacer frequently came out of the city with his men and harassed Theodoric’s army. At last, attacking the camp by night, he inflicted a great defeat upon Theodoric’s army. Finally overcome, while the Goths resisted with the utmost courage, Odoacer fled into the city.

Not long afterward Theodoric received him into his allegiance and then treacherously killed him.

After the Goths left Ticinum three years later, the Rugians immediately invaded the same city. For two continuous years they devastated all the surrounding places, as well as the city itself, by plunder. The most blessed Epiphanius was still alive, and the citizens, afflicted amid such dangers, were strengthened by his holiness.

Theodoric sent him to Gaul to Gundobad to redeem captives. In addition to the countless multitude for whom he paid a price, he brought back with him six thousand captives who had been granted solely out of reverence for his holiness.

Thus, after killing Odoacer at Ravenna, Theodoric obtained control of all Italy. Not long afterward he went to Rome and was received by the Romans with great joy. He granted them 120,000 measures of grain each year for their support.

While these events were taking place in Italy, the Bulgars cruelly devastated all Thrace. Constantinople also suffered a great conflagration at that time.

In Africa, Himeric, who had succeeded Geiseric in the kingdom after Geiseric’s death, followed the Arian treachery. He drove more than 334 Catholic bishops into exile, closed their churches, and afflicted the people with various punishments. He cut off the hands of countless people and severed their tongues, yet he could not take away their ability to speak the Catholic confession.

In Britain, Ambrosius Aurelianus—perhaps the only survivor of the slaughter of the Roman people by the Saxons—also assumed the purple. Leading an army of Britons, he often defeated the victorious Saxons. From that time, now one side and now the other held the advantage, until the Saxons became more powerful and took possession of the entire island over its full extent. [Col. 0972B]

Meanwhile, to strengthen the power of his kingdom, Theodoric married Audefleda, daughter of Jodoin, king of the Franks. He gave his sister Amalafrida in marriage to Huneric, king of the Vandals; the daughter of that same Amalafrida, Malaberga, to Ermenfred, king of the Thuringians; and two daughters born of a concubine, Theodicoda and Ostrogotho, one to Alaric, king of the Visigoths, and the other to Sigismund, king of the Burgundians.

He gave his third daughter, Amalasuntha, to Eutharic, who came from the stock of the Amals and had been summoned from Spain. There was no people in Italy that was not joined to Theodoric either by marriage alliance or by treaty.

After Zeno Augustus had governed the Roman state for seventeen years, he died at Constantinople.

## BOOK SIXTEEN

Since the rule of the Roman city had now come to an end, it seems more useful and appropriate to me to draw the line of calculation from the years of the Lord’s Incarnation, so that it may be known what happened and at what time.

In the year 492 from the Lord’s Incarnation, after Zeno’s death, Anastasius put on the purple. He was the forty-seventh in the succession of kings. He stained the glory of the Roman Empire with the filth of the Eutychian heresy.

During his reign such great discord arose at Rome over the election of Symmachus and Laurentius that Festus, the most noble of the senators and a former consul, together with Probinus, also a former consul, supporting the party of Laurentius, made war against Faustus, the former consul, and the others who adhered to Symmachus. They committed many slaughters and murders in the middle of the City, killing many of the priestly order, many clerics, and a great number of Roman citizens.

At that time Trasamundus, who had succeeded his brother Huneric in the Vandal kingdom in Africa, followed the treachery of his brother and of his father Geiseric. He closed the churches of the Catholics and sent 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia. Blessed Pope Symmachus did not cease supplying them with daily assistance.

Amid these storms, blessed Fulgentius flourished in the confession of the faith and in knowledge.

In those same days in Africa, while a certain Arian named Olympius was washing his body in the waters of a bath and uttering disgraceful and blasphemous words concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity, a fiery dart suddenly came down from heaven and visibly burned him.

A certain Arian bishop named Barbas, wishing to assert, contrary to the rule of faith, that the Son and the Holy Spirit were lesser than the Father, was baptizing someone. He said: “I baptize you, Barbas, in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately the water that had been brought for the baptism disappeared completely. When the person who was to be baptized saw this, he immediately fled to the Catholic Church and, according to the custom of the faith, received the baptism of Christ.

…he knew that it would not be safe for him if the Goths who were dwelling within Gaul should join the Romans [Col. 0965A] in alliance. Pretending to be a friend of the Goths, he hastened toward the city of Aurelianum, attempting to persuade the king of the Visigoths [Col. 0966A] to invade the Roman Empire together with him and possess it on equal terms.

But he sent an embassy to the emperor Valentinian [Col. 0967A], pretending peace, and deceitfully announced that he was going to avenge the Romans upon the Goths and restore the Roman provinces [Col. 0968A] of Gaul and Spain. The emperor, however, was by no means unaware of his deceit. Therefore [Col. 0969A], through the patrician Aetius, he very quickly approached Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, won him over to his own side [Col. 0970A], and together with that patrician sent him against Attila, who, after laying waste almost all of Gaul, was already besieging Aurelianum [Col. 0971A].

Without delay, Aetius, having gathered warriors from every quarter, advanced most bravely to meet the Huns, together with King Theodoric and his son Thorismund. There, when an incredible battle had been joined—scarcely any similar battle is found in memory of mankind—the Romans prevailed, Attila was put to flight, and the king of the Goths was killed. This engagement, begun around the ninth hour of the day, resulted in the death of one hundred and eighty thousand men from both sides.

But shortly afterward the emperor Valentinian Augustus killed Aetius, the singular hope of the Roman people, with his own hands and through the treachery of others. Together with him, all the fortune and strength of the West collapsed. For Attila, immediately recovering his confidence, bloodstained, made for Italy; he captured Aquileia and utterly obliterated it. He destroyed Ticinum and Mediolanum, royal cities. From there, after laying waste the surrounding regions [Col. 0971B], when he was also preparing to break into Rome, Pope Leo the Great approached him, sent by the emperor Valentinian [Col. 0972A]. He rendered him so mild that, having at once secured a very firm promise of peace, Attila departed, never to return beyond the Danube.

For he soon passed from human affairs and, even in death, at last brought an end to the long affliction of the human race. The Goths, not content with the province which they had earlier received from the Romans for habitation near Gaul, invaded Arverni and Narbonne with their territories after capturing them, encouraged, as it were, by the ruin of the Roman state and by the frequent changes of emperors.

For the emperor Valentinian was killed by friends of Aetius, whom he had chosen as his bodyguards, and a certain Maximus, through whose deceit this had been carried out, was created emperor. When he had compelled Eudoxia, his widow, against her will to enter into marriage with him, she invited Genseric, as is said, king of Africa, to come as the avenger of her husband.

At his arrival [Col. 0972B], Maximus, scarcely having completed the second month of his reign [Note: [Col. 0972D] Perhaps: “having completed”], when the nobility was fleeing throughout the city because of his license and groups of the populace [Col. 0973A] were escaping from Rome, was himself also preparing to flee in fear. But he was immediately torn apart by the royal servants, dismembered limb by limb, and thrown into the Tiber.

Genseric immediately captured the city, which was without a garrison, and, softened by Pope Leo’s meeting with him, preserved Rome from fire, slaughter, and torture. Nevertheless, after taking away all its wealth, he carried many thousands of captives back to Carthage, together with the empress Eudoxia and her daughters.

Through the authority of this Pope Leo and by order of the emperor Marcian, the Council of Chalcedon was held. At Rome, after the death of Maximus, Avitus assumed the empire; shortly afterward he laid it down and was ordained bishop of Placentia. At Constantinople, however, the emperor Marcian died in the sixth year of his reign, after the completion of six months.

## LEO

[Col. 0973B]

In the year 1210 from the founding of the City, Leo, the forty-ninth after Augustus, obtained the empire. At Rome, after Avitus, Majorian was made Caesar. In the fourth year of his reign he was killed near Dertona, a city of Spain, through the treachery of Severianus, who died at Rome in the third year of his reign.

In his place, Arthemius, sent by the emperor Leo, was killed in the sixth year of his reign, with the Roman city suffering the greatest calamity. Olybrius succeeded him; Glycerius removed Olybrius after taking power at Ravenna, and he himself was soon deprived of power by Nepos and ordained bishop of Porto.

Leo, emperor of the East, died in the sixteenth year of his reign and left the empire to Zeno.

## ZENO

In the year 1226 from the founding of the City, Zeno, the fiftieth [Col. 0973C] after Augustus, ruled. The patrician Orestes deprived Nepos Caesar of the empire and made his own son Augustulus emperor.

But immediately Odoacer, king of the Turcilingi and Rugians, after overrunning Italy, captured Rome—the fourth time since its foundation—and, after sending the emperor Augustulus into exile, himself ruled tyrannically at Rome. Theodoric, king of the Goths, sent by Zeno, besieged, captured, and killed him; then, with the consent of the emperor Zeno, he himself ruled at Rome.

## ANASTASIUS

After Zeno died sixteen years later, Anastasius succeeded him. Favoring the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, he persecuted the Orthodox.

At the same time, Symmachus and Laurentius were elected at Rome while the citizens were divided against one another, and innumerable massacres and acts of plunder [Col. 0973D] were committed by both sides. For approximately three years, many of the priestly order, many clerics, and still more Roman citizens were killed, until Theodoric, the ruler who then held Rome, came and, although he was an Arian, confirmed Symmachus as bishop of Rome after a synod had been held. He ordered Laurentius, however, to be installed as bishop in the city of Nuceria.

Laurentius nevertheless did not rest in any way, but stirred up riots. He was deposed by Symmachus and sent into exile in Dalmatia, and thus the conflict ceased.

At the same time, Trasamundus, who had succeeded his brother [Note: [Col. 0973D] Huneric] Honorius in the Vandal kingdom of Africa, followed the impiety of his brother or father Genseric [Col. 0974A]. After closing the Catholic churches, he sent two hundred and twenty bishops into exile [Note: [Col. 0973D] A.: “in Sardinia”]. Blessed Pope Symmachus did not cease to provide them with daily assistance.

Amid these storms, blessed Fulgentius flourished in confession of the faith and in learning. During those same days in Africa, when a certain Arian named Olympius was bathing in the bathhouse of the Elyans and was uttering shameful and blasphemous words concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, a fiery dart suddenly came down from above [Note: [Col. 0974D] “From heaven.”] and visibly burned him.

Moreover, when Deuterius, the Arian bishop of Byzantium, was baptizing a certain man named Barban, wishing, contrary to the rule of faith, to assert that the Son and the Holy Spirit were lesser than the Father, he said while about to baptize him: “I baptize you, Barbas, in the name of the Father [Col. 0974B], through the Son in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately the water that had been brought for the baptism disappeared completely.

When the man who was to be baptized saw this, he fled at once to the Catholic Church and, according to the custom of the faith, received Christ’s baptism, making the miracle known to everyone.

Meanwhile, while Theodoric was ruling peacefully in Italy, he constructed royal residences for himself in each of the more distinguished places. At that time, after the death of Agarus, an incursion of the Saracens into Phoenicia and Syria took place again, with his brother Vadicarimus ranging through the regions like a whirlwind, and even more swiftly.

In that same year—that is, the eleventh year of Anastasius’s reign—the Bulgars roamed through Illyricum and Thrace before they were recognized and cruelly devastated them. Constantinople also suffered a great conflagration during those days.

Then, at Neocaesarea, where an earthquake was about to occur, a soldier traveling through the region saw two soldiers above it and another soldier shouting behind him: “Preserve the house in which the tomb of Gregory is.” When the earthquake occurred, a large part of the city collapsed, except for the house of Gregory Thaumaturgus—that is, “the worker of miracles.”

Meanwhile, Juliana, a most illustrious woman who had built a church of the Mother of God at Honoratae, labored greatly on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon. Even the emperor, although devising many schemes against her, could not persuade her to communicate with Timothy; nor could Timothy himself, though he frequently went to her, persuade her to do so.

The emperor Augustus also harassed her cousin Pompeius and his wife, a distinguished woman [Col. 0974D], in many ways, in order to banish the venerators of the council and those who supplied Bishop Macedonius with what was necessary while he was in exile.

Then he ordered certain leading men to admit upon the ambo in the church of Saint Theodore the Sparotian an addition to the Trisagion, namely: “Who was crucified for us.” As a result, the crowds, indignant, went out from there during the litanies throughout the day. Timothy also ordered all the churches, through a written memorandum [Note: [Col. 0974D] “Memorandum” (*commonitorium*)], to say the Trisagion in the litanies with the addition; many, out of fear, did so.

But the monks came singing another psalm. When the people saw them, they shouted: “The Orthodox have come well!” [That is, “Welcome to the Orthodox!”]

Much conflict also arose, as well as the burning of many houses and ten thousand murders, while the crowd shouted against Anastasius and demanded the emperor Vitalianus. Anastasius fled and hid, and even Ariadne herself tore him apart with insults, as having become, so to speak, the cause of many evils for Christians.

When Alamundarus, ruler of the Saracen people, had been baptized, Severus sent two bishops infected with the stain of his depravity to establish communion with him. By God’s providence, however, Alamundarus had been baptized by Orthodox Christians who accepted the council.

When the bishops of Severus hastened to turn the ruler away from the true doctrine, Alamundarus refuted them marvelously with the following story. He said to them:

“Today I received a letter saying that the archangel Michael had died.”

When they said that this was impossible, the ruler replied:

“Then, according to you, how [Col. 0975B] could God have been crucified naked, unless Christ had two natures, since surely not even an angel can die?”

Thus the bishops departed in confusion, to the shame of Severus.

Therefore Vitalianus, whom the people had demanded as emperor, having the Bulgars and a multitude of Huns with him, captured Anchialus and Odyssopolis, excepting the whole of Thrace, Scythia, and Moesia. He also seized Cyril, master of the soldiers of Thrace, and advanced toward Byzantium carrying his spoils.

Sparing the city, he encamped at Sosthenium. Anastasius, overwhelmed by despair, sent certain men from the senate to ask him to negotiate and to swear, together with the senate, that he would recall the bishops who were at Heraclea in Thrace from exile.

Vitalianus added that the leaders of each military corps should also swear to this; that Macedonius and Flavianus, who had been wickedly expelled, should recover their thrones; that all the other bishops likewise should be restored; and that a Roman synod should be held, at which all the bishops would assemble and, by common judgment, reject the measures undertaken against the Orthodox.

Thus, when the emperor, the senate, the other leaders, and the people had sworn and confirmed that this should be done, peace was made, and Vitalianus returned to his own territory.

Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, wearied by Theodoric, with Vitalianus supporting him, sent Bishop Evodius [Note: [Col. 0975D] A.: “Ennodius”] and the archdeacon Vitalianus to hold the synod at Heraclea. Almost two hundred bishops also came from various places. But, deceived by the emperor and Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, they departed without accomplishing anything.

For the impious emperor, violating the agreements, secretly informed the Roman pope not to come. He had sent a sacred letter to Vitalianus, so that he might transmit it to Rome and the pope might set out to hold the synod at Heraclea. But the entire people and senate publicly cursed Anastasius as a perjurer.

Vitalianus, indignant with Anastasius because of his perjury, inflicted much harm upon the armies of Anastasius and upon the rest of the state: killing, plundering, stripping them of their weapons, and finally selling each soldier for one bronze coin as an insult to Anastasius.

Meanwhile, the Huns called Sabers, crossing the Caspian [Col. 0976A] Gates, laid waste Armenia, Cappadocia, Galatia, and Pontus, so that they nearly reached Euchaita. Macedonius, fleeing from there, almost perished but was saved at Gangra [Note: [Col. 0975D] A.: “Grangas”].

When Anastasius learned this, he ordered him to be kept under careful guard there and, as they say, sent men to kill him. After dying at Gangra, Macedonius was placed in the church of Saint Callinicus the Martyr, beside his relics, and brought about many cures.

When he lay lifeless, he is said to have made the sign of the cross upon himself with his hand. Theodore, one of those who were with him, saw him in a dream saying to him:

“Receive this message; go and say to Anastasius: ‘I am going to my fathers, whose faith I have preserved. But I shall not cease to increase in the Lord until you come, and we enter into judgment.’”

In that same year at Alexandria [Col. 0976B], many men, women, and children, cruelly possessed by demons, suddenly began to bark. In a dream, someone saw a figure saying that these people were suffering because of the anathemas of the Council of Chalcedon.

Then, in the twenty-seventh year of Anastasius’s reign, the same emperor saw in a vision a terrifying man carrying a book. When he opened it and found the emperor’s name, he said to him: “Behold, because of your evil faith I erase fourteen.” And he erased them.

After waking, Anastasius summoned the prefect Adamantius and told him the vision. “I too,” said Adamantius, “saw this same thing last night: while your empire was standing before me, a huge pig came, seized my robe, threw me to the ground, and killed me.”

Accordingly, Proclus the interpreter of dreams was summoned, and Anastasius told him what they had seen. Proclus predicted that both of them would die shortly afterward [Col. 0976C].

Since Anastasius continued in the heresy into which he had fallen and, following the heresiarch Eutyches, denied that there were two natures in Christ—namely, divinity and humanity—Pope Hormisdas, who had succeeded Symmachus, sent Evodius, bishop of Ticinum, and others with him as envoys to Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0975D] A.: “to Constantinople as envoys, etc.”], carrying a written statement of the Catholic faith, so that they might restore Anastasius to the bosom of the Church.

He not only rejected their salutary exhortations but also expelled them from his presence with abuse and, after placing them on a fragile ship, ordered that they should not approach any city anywhere throughout Greece.

Divine vengeance immediately followed his impious violence. For when he was completing the twenty-seventh year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0976D] A.: “was engaged in it; struck by a thunderbolt, he died. In the year, etc.”], he died, and the pious Justin, an elderly and highly experienced man, ruled in his place. He had risen from the ranks of the soldiers to the senate.

Some say that Anastasius perished after being struck by a divine thunderbolt.

## JUSTIN

In the year 511 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0976D] A.: “In 518, Anastasius the heretic having been punished, Justin the Catholic…”], Justin Curopalates, an Illyrian by birth and a Catholic man, obtained the imperial throne.

To him, for the restoration of the faith, Germanus, a man distinguished for holiness and bishop of the city of Capua [Col. 0977A], was sent by Pope Hormisdas. He was received with due honor and strengthened the uncertain hearts of many in the faith.

At that time in Africa, after Transmundus, king of the Vandals and adherent of the Arian perfidy, had died [Note: [Col. 0977D] A.: “Trasamundus”], Childeric, his son by the captive Eudoxia, daughter of the emperor Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0977D] A.: “Hildericus”], obtained the Vandal kingdom. Following not the counsels of his heretical father but those of his Catholic mother, he showed himself a devotee of the true faith.

As his father Transmundus approached death, because he saw that Childeric favored the Catholic party [Note: [Col. 0977D] A.: “he perceived”], he tried to bind him by the obligations of an oath, so that he would never favor or assist the Catholics in his kingdom.

As soon as his father had died, however, and even before he assumed the rights of kingship, Childeric caused all the bishops whom Transmundus had forced into exile to return, and ordered their churches to be restored. Seventy-four [Col. 0977B] years had now passed since the churches in Africa had first been destroyed by their grandfather Genseric.

In the third year of the emperor Justin, when war broke out between the Romans and the Persians, Justin sent envoys and gifts to Zeliobes, king of the Huns [Note: [Col. 0977D] Manuscript: “Zelioche”], and Zeliobes promised under oath that he would provide the emperor assistance against the Persians.

Later, however, when the king of the Persians sent to him, Zeliobes received the envoy and promised that he would provide the same assistance against the Romans. When Justin learned this, he was greatly distressed.

Zeliobes then sent twenty thousand men against the Persians to attack the Romans. Justin, for his part, sent an embassy to Chuades, king of the Persians, seeking peace. In a letter written as though about another matter, he also mentioned Zeliobes, saying that Zeliobes had oaths of assistance [Col. 0977C] with the Romans, had received many gifts, and wanted to become a traitor to the Persians; and that, since “we are brothers,” it was necessary for them to come to friendship and not be deceived by “those dogs.”

Then Chuades secretly summoned Zeliobes and asked whether he had received gifts from the Romans and encouraged them against the Persians. Zeliobes replied: “Yes.”

Chuades, angered, killed him. During the night he sent a multitude of Persians and killed Zeliobes’ people, suspecting that they had come to him through treachery. All who were able to escape returned to their own territory.

In the fifth year of Justin’s reign, Zatus, king of the Laz, withdrew from the Persian kingdom. Cabades was reigning, and he loved Zatus, having himself elevated him as king of the Laz. Zatus came to Byzantium to Justin and asked him to become a Christian and to be called by him the emperor of the Laz.

The emperor received him with great joy, enlightened him through baptism, and called him his son. When the emperor of the Laz departed from Justin, he carried a crown and a white imperial cloak [Note: [Col. 0977D] Greek: *χλαμίδα βασιλικὴν ἄσπρην*, “a white imperial chlamys”].

When Cabades, king of the Persians, learned this, he informed Justin, saying:

“Although friendship and peace exist between us, you are doing what belongs to enemies, and you are taking up those who have always been under Persian authority.”

Justin replied:

“We have neither taken up nor subverted anyone subject to your rule [Col. 0978A]. Rather, Zatus came up to our imperial power, fell down, and begged to be freed from wicked and pagan doctrine, from impious sacrifices, and from the error of demons; to approach the Lord, the creator of all things; and to become a Christian. We baptized him, released him, and sent him back to his own region.”

From that time friendship was established between the Romans and the Persians.

In the eastern regions, however, since the Arian heresy was still strong everywhere at that time, Justin, in the sixth year of his reign, began to strive in every way out of zeal for the orthodox faith to extinguish the name of the heretics. He decreed that their churches everywhere should be consecrated for Catholic worship.

When Theodoric, king of Italy, polluted by the Arian plague, heard this, he sent Pope John to the emperor Justin at Constantinople, together with Theodore [Note: [Col. 0977D] A.: “Importunus”], the consular man Hypatius, and Agapitus, a consular man, as well as Agapitus the patrician [Note: [Col. 0977D] A.: “and another Agapitus”].

Through them he also sent a warning, threatening that unless Justin immediately returned their churches to the heretics and allowed them to live in peace, Theodoric himself would destroy all the people of Italy by the sword.

When they reached the emperor and had been received by him as was fitting, they earnestly begged him, with great tears and deep concern for their own safety and that of their people, to receive willingly the substance of their embassy, even though it was unjust, and to take thought for Italy, which was destined to perish.

Moved by their tears, Justin granted what they requested and left the Arians in possession of their rights.

While these envoys were delayed on their journey, Theodoric, driven by the fury of his wickedness, killed with the sword Symmachus, an ex-consul and patrician, and Boethius, a senator and ex-consul, both Catholic men.

During those days, after Alaric, king of the Visigoths, had been killed by the Franks, Theodoric sent his commander Ibba [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “Ibbas”], who killed more than thirty thousand Franks. After Alaric’s death, he appointed his own armor-bearer Theodem [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “Theodem”], the son-in-law of his nephew [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “of his grandson”], guardian of Athalaric.

Pope John, returning from Constantinople, came to Ravenna with those with whom he had departed, and with whom he had gone to Theodoric. Theodoric, angered by malice because Justin, the defender of Catholic piety, had received John honorably, killed him together with his companions by the suffering of imprisonment.

Divine punishment soon followed this most savage cruelty. For on the ninety-ninth day after this crime he died a sudden death [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “on the ninety-eighth day”].

A solitary, a man of great virtue, saw his soul being led between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus and plunged into the cauldron of Vulcan, which was near that place [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “was there”].

Thus, after Theodoric had been punished in this manner, the Goths placed Athalaric in the kingdom, the one mentioned above, born from the daughter of King Theodoric, together with his mother Amalasuntha [Note: [Col. 0978D] A.: “placed him in the kingdom. But when Justinian…”].

Meanwhile, Cabades, king of the Persians and son of Peroz, killed many thousands of Manichaeans, together with their bishop Indagarus [Note: [Col. 0979B] A.: “Indazarus”], in a single day, along with the Persian nobles who were in agreement with them.

For the Manichaeans had instructed his son, named Phatuarsan, from childhood and promised him, saying:

“Your father has grown old, and if it should happen that he dies, the leaders of the magicians will make one of your brothers emperor, because he holds their doctrine. But we can persuade your father through our prayers to renounce the empire and promote you, so that everywhere you may confirm the doctrines of the Manichaeans.”

Phatuarsan promised that he would do this if he became emperor.

When Cabades learned of this, he ordered an assembly to be held, as though he intended to make his son emperor. He ordered all the Manichaeans, together with their bishop, their women, and their children, to attend the assembly. He likewise ordered Glonazes, chief of the magicians, and the magicians, as well as Boazanes, the Christian bishop beloved by Cabades as an excellent physician, to attend.

After the Manichaeans had assembled, Cabades said:

“I rejoice over your doctrine, and while I am still alive I wish to give you my son Phatuarsan, so that he may be one of you. But separate yourselves to receive him.”

They, trusting in their confidence, separated themselves.

Cabades then ordered his army to enter, and they killed them all with the sword, together with their bishop, in the presence of the chief of the magicians and the Christian bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0979B] A.: “In the year 6017 of the world, 518 from the divine Incarnation, an earthquake at Antioch.”]

While an earthquake was still occurring at Antioch, Bishop Euphrasius was buried and killed by the earthquake. Every house and church collapsed, and the beauty of the city was destroyed. No such divine vengeance had occurred in any other city throughout all generations.

The most pious emperor Justin, when he learned this, grieved deeply in his heart. He removed the diadem from his head and the purple from his body, mourned in sackcloth, and sat for many days. Even on a feast day, when he went out to the church, he would not permit himself to wear a crown or a chlamys.

Then, in April of the same indiction [Note: [Col. 0979B] A.: “of the fifth indiction”], the emperor Justin became ill. While he was still alive, he advanced Justinian, his sister’s son, as emperor [Col. 0980B], and Justinian ruled jointly with him for four months.

In August of the fifth indiction [Note: [Col. 0980B] “I think ‘of the fifth’ should be read”], Justin died at Constantinople, after having administered the imperial dignity for eleven years [Note: [Col. 0980B] A.: “Having administered it, he rested in peace at Constantinople”].

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 0979]

## JUSTINIAN

[Col. 0979C]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 521 [Note: [Col. 0979D] A.: 329; Justinian, son of Justin’s sister, ninth among the Roman emperors and forty-fourth to hold the imperial dignity, etc.], Justinian alone assumed the imperial rule of the Romans. As soon as he had received the authority of the empire, he turned his attention to restoring the condition of the state. First, through the patrician Belisarius [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Belisarius” throughout Ambrosianus], a man of great ability, he attacked the Persians, who, after crossing the Roman frontier, were devastating their territories severely. Belisarius routed them in great battles and entered Constantinople in triumph, in accordance with the emperor’s wish.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Ms. of Pithoeus: “In the same year the singular emperor Justinian obtained the imperial dignity; but the king of the Heruli, named Gretes,” etc. ]

Meanwhile, the king of the Heruli, named Gethes, came to Constantinople with his people and asked the emperor to make him a Christian. The emperor received him from the baptismal font at the Epiphany, and he promised to assist him in whatever matters he wished.

In the same year [Col. 0979D] a certain woman from the Huns called Sabers, named Boazer, a widow, joined the Romans; she had with her one hundred thousand Huns.
