At that time also the king of the Huns who live beside the Bosporus, named Gorda, approached the emperor, became a Christian, and was received by him. After granting him many gifts, the emperor sent him back to his own country to guard Roman interests and the city of Bosporus. The city was called Bosporus because every year it supplied oxen to the Romans in exchange for money.

He also stationed a body of Roman soldiers and tribunes to guard the city on account of the Huns and to collect the ox-tax. He issued a regulation concerning bishops, stewards, orphanages, and guest-houses: they were not to possess anything by inheritance except what they could prove they had owned before their promotion, and concerning such property they could make a will. From the moment of their promotion, however, no one was to have the right to dispose of anything; everything was to pass by inheritance to that venerable household.

The emperor promulgated strict laws against the lustful. Many were punished, and great fear and caution arose. He also renewed the conflicting laws, producing a separate Code and calling it the *Novella Constitutions*. In these he forbade a ruler to purchase property, build a house, or inherit the property of an outsider in places under his authority, unless that person were related to him.

In the same year Antioch again suffered divine retribution, two years after its earlier disaster. There was a great earthquake and a most violent storm. Those who survived performed litanies, all barefoot and crying out, “Κύριε ἐλέησον” (“Lord, have mercy”) [Note: Fr. and Pithoeus: “and throwing themselves upon the snow”]. A vision appeared to a man who worshiped God, instructing him to tell all the survivors to write upon their lintels: “Christ is with us; stand firm.” When this had been done, God’s anger ceased. Once again the emperor and the empress gave large sums of money for the restoration and rebuilding of the city of Antioch, which he renamed Theopolis.

Moreover, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction, Alamundarus, a petty king of the Saracens, invaded and plundered First Syria as far as the boundaries of Antioch, to a place called Litargum. He killed many people and burned the outskirts of Chalcedon. When the leading Romans heard this, they went out against them. Upon learning of their approach, the Saracens, together with the Persians, fled with their captives and plunder.

Furthermore, the Samaritans and Jews in Palestine crowned a certain Julian emperor and took up arms against the Christians, committing acts of robbery, murder, and arson. God delivered them into Justinian’s hands, and he killed them and beheaded Julian the tyrant.

In the third year of his reign, the emperor Justinian promulgated a law that there were to be neither pagans nor heretics [Note: [Col. 0981D] Ms.: “They were not to serve in the army.” See this constitution, *Codex*, “On Heretics,” law XVIII, Contius’s edition], but only orthodox Christians, granting the others a period of three months for conversion.

Meanwhile, Athalaric, king of the Goths, though he had not yet completed the years of childhood [Note: [Col. 0981D] A.: “four years, instead of ‘the years of childhood’”], was carried off by an untimely death. His mother, Almasuinta [Note: [Col. 0981D] A.: Malasvinta], after his death, associated Theodatus with herself in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0981D] A.: “as her colleague”]. But Theodatus, forgetful of the favor bestowed upon him, after a few days ordered her to be strangled in a bath.

Because she had commended herself and her son to the emperor while she was still alive, the emperor Justinian, upon hearing of her death, immediately burned with deep anger against Theodatus. Realizing that the emperor was hostile to him, Theodatus sent the blessed Pope Agapitus to Constantinople, so that he might obtain from Justinian pardon for the deed.

When that holy pontiff approached the emperor Justinian and discussed the faith with him, he discovered that Justinian had fallen into the doctrine of Eutyches. From him the blessed bishop had previously suffered serious threats. But when Justinian saw the bishop’s unshaken steadfastness in the Catholic faith—for he had gone so far as to hear such words from the bishop: “I wished to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor, but now I have found Diocletian”—he finally, by God’s will, yielded to the bishop’s admonitions and returned, together with many others who were likewise in error, to the confession of the Catholic faith.

He also publicly deprived Anthimus, bishop of that same royal city and defender of the aforesaid heresy, of communion after convicting him; and, having persuaded the emperor, he compelled him to go into exile. Not long afterward, that same pontiff died in the same city [Note: [Col. 0981D] A.: “died there. Meanwhile, Belisarius was sent by Justinian with an army to Africa, which the Vandals had possessed for many years. Soon, after engaging the Vandals in battle, he routed their great forces and captured their king Gelimer alive, sending him to Constantinople. Carthage too was recovered ninety-six years after its destruction. But while Agapitus,” etc.].

In the seventh year of Justinian’s reign the Vandalic wars began. A certain bishop of the eastern regions alarmed the emperor Justinian after receiving a vision from God commanding him to approach the emperor and request that the Christians in Libya be freed from their tyrants. When the emperor heard this, he could no longer keep his resolve in check. He armed both the army and the ships, prepared provisions, and ordered Belisarius to be ready. He appointed him as commander to be sent to Libya, and the emperor made him supreme governor in all matters. Procopius, the historian of these events, was also with him.

They departed from the city of Pegia and crossed to Abydos. Belisarius took care that the entire fleet should sail together and turn toward battle as one. When they reached Sicily, he sent the historian Procopius to Syracuse to see whether he might find anyone who would guide them to Libya. Belisarius himself, taking the fleet, hurried to Caucanum, a village two hundred stades distant from Syracuse.

Procopius entered Syracuse and bought provisions. Unexpectedly, he also met a man who had been his friend since childhood. This man knew the places in Libya and the sea route; only three days had passed since he had come from Carthage. He assured Procopius that they were entirely safe and need fear no one who might bring an army against them, since Gelimer was only four days’ journey away [Note: [Col. 0982D] Ms. Pithoeus: Segilbum]. [Note: [Col. 0982D] A.: “When Belisarius learned these things, he crossed over.”]

Procopius took this man with him and, arriving at Caucanum, presented him to Belisarius. They went out to a certain estate, built an embankment and a deep ditch, and encamped there. Although the place lacked water, when the ditch was dug the earth produced enough water for the needs of the animals and the armies.

On the following day the soldiers rushed out to plunder. The commander summoned them and addressed them as follows:

“To use violence and feed upon what belongs to others is injustice at all times, and especially for us, who are placed in danger. Trusting in this, I transported you to this land: so that by justice and good works we might both please God and strive to draw the Africans to ourselves. Your present lack of restraint will turn against us and cause the Africans to assist the Vandals. Therefore obey my words: buy provisions and bring them back. Let yourselves appear neither unjust nor people who turn the friendship of the Africans into hostility. Rather, strive to please God; stop attacking what belongs to others and extracting profit at the cost of danger.”

Belisarius then sent a chosen army and captured the city without difficulty. They approached it by night and entered together with the carts coming in from the countryside; thus they gained possession of it. At daybreak they captured both the priest and the leading men of the city and sent them to the commander.

After capturing Carthage, Belisarius reminded his soldiers, saying:

“See, fellow soldiers, how favorably things have turned out for us. Let us show moderation toward the Africans. See that you preserve good conduct in Carthage. Let no one oppress anyone or steal anything belonging to another. After suffering many evils at the hands of the barbarous Vandals, our emperor has sent us to grant them freedom.”

With these words he entered Carthage and, ascending the palace, sat upon Gelimer’s throne. The merchants of Carthage and all who lived near the sea came to him, complaining that they had suffered robbery at the hands of the fleets. He bound Caloninus, commander of the ships, by oath to bring back everything that had been stolen and restore it to its rightful owners. But after defrauding some of them and violating his oath, he soon paid the penalty. For, having lost his senses, he died eating his own tongue.

The commander held the city so peacefully that he injured no one, nor did anyone in the marketplace need to keep watch over his house; the soldiers ate what they bought. He released the Vandals who had taken refuge in sacred places, after giving them a guarantee of safety. He also carefully repaired the city walls, which had previously collapsed through neglect.

People also repeated in Carthage an old saying: “Gamma pursued Beta; now Beta pursues Gamma,” which seemed to have reached its fulfillment. Formerly, Genseric had pursued Boniface; now Belisarius pursued Gelimer.

Moreover, the multitude discovered so much money that no place had ever been known to contain so much. The Vandals had carried immense wealth into Libya after plundering the Roman dominion. Since the city and region themselves were excellent and fertile, they yielded great revenues of money. The Vandals had held Libya for ninety-five years. But after gathering great riches, on that day all their wealth returned to Roman hands.

For within three months, during which Belisarius fought—from the Kalends of September to the Kalends of December—he subjected the whole of Libya. He sent John the Armenian with two hundred chosen men to pursue Gelimer until they captured him alive or dead. John was about to overtake and capture Gelimer, had the following event not occurred.

A certain Uliares, one of Belisarius’s armor-bearers, was with John. Having become drunk, he fell into a depraved state of mind. Seeing a bird sitting in a tree, he drew his bow and shot at it. He failed to hit the bird but struck John from behind in the neck. Wounded, John died, leaving great grief to the emperor Justinian, to Belisarius, and to all the Romans and Carthaginians.

Thus Gelimer fled that day toward the Maurusii. Belisarius pursued him and enclosed him on a small mountain at the farthest edge of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0983D] Ms. Pithoeus: Pappua], besieging him there through the winter, when all necessities failed him. The Maurusii have no bread, wine, or oil; they eat meal and unripe barley as irrational animals do.

In this distress Gelimer wrote to Pharas, whom Belisarius had left to guard him, asking him to send a lyre, one loaf of bread, and a sponge. Pharas wondered what this meant until the man who had carried the letter explained that Gelimer wished to see bread, since he had not seen bread since ascending the mountain; that he wanted the sponge because his unwashed eyes had been injured, so that the sponge might restore them to clarity; and that he wanted the lyre to lament and weep over his misfortune.

When Pharas heard this, he felt compassion and lamented the lot of humanity. He followed Gelimer’s requests and sent him many things of which he was in need.

After the winter had passed, Gelimer feared the Roman siege and, out of pity for his relatives and sons, who had become infested with worms amid the siege and misery, lost courage. He wrote to Pharas that, once he had received a guarantee of good faith, he and those who were with him would proceed to Belisarius. Pharas confirmed this by a binding oath; Gelimer then took everyone with him and came to Carthage. Belisarius received him gladly.

Gelimer entered Belisarius’s presence laughing. Some thought that, because of the excess of his suffering, he had gone beyond the limits of nature and had become delirious. His friends, however, thought that he was a clever man, and they reflected that although he had been a king of royal descent, possessed great strength and vast wealth, he had been driven into flight, endured many evils, and was now led away as a captive, with nothing said of him except that he displayed much laughter and behavior that people considered worthy of his condition.

Belisarius kept him, together with all the Vandal nobles, without dishonor, intending to take them to the emperor Justinian at Byzantium.

Belisarius immediately sent Cyrillus with the head of Zatinon, Gelimer’s brother [Note: [Col. 0984D] Ms. Pithoeus: Lazonis], to the island of Sardinia, which was called Kirnus, and first subjected it to the Romans. He sent another John to Caesarea, which lies in Mauretania thirty days’ journey from Carthage, near Gades and toward the setting sun. He also sent another John, one of the imperial guards, to the strait at Gades and to the fortress called Septum.

He sent Apollinarius, a good man, to the islands near the Ocean, namely Majorca and Minorca. He also sent some Africans to Sicily and ordered them to seize a Vandal fortress. The Goths who were guarding it informed Athalaric’s mother. She wrote to Belisarius asking him not to besiege that fortress tyrannically until the emperor Justinian knew of the matter and did what seemed appropriate to him.

Thus the Vandalic war came to an end. But envy, as often happens amid great prosperity, also fell upon Belisarius. Some denounced him to the emperor, alleging that he was plotting tyranny. The emperor sent Solomon to test Belisarius’s intentions: whether he would come with Gelimer and the Vandals or remain there and send them onward.

Belisarius departed for Byzantium, leaving the commander Solomon in Libya. When Belisarius arrived with Gelimer and the Vandals, he deserved to receive great rewards, such as in former times were granted to Romans worthy of the highest victories. For in the six hundred years that had passed, no one had attained such honor except Titus, Trajan, and the other emperors who, holding commands against barbarian nations, had triumphed magnificently.

After displaying the spoils and the captives taken in the war, he published them in the middle of the city in the procession that the Romans call a triumph. He proceeded in the ancient manner, but on foot, to his own house and as far as the Hippodrome.

The spoils consisted of everything that belonged to the ruler’s administrative order: golden thrones, chariots in which the wives of kings were carried, ornaments made of precious stones, many thousands of talents of silver, and various imperial vessels. Genseric had taken these to Africa after plundering the Roman palace. Among them were also the vessels of the Jews, which Titus, son of Vespasian, had brought to Rome after capturing Jerusalem.

The captives in the triumph included Gelimer himself, wearing a certain purple garment, and all his relatives. There were also Vandals who were exceptionally tall and well-built.

When Gelimer reached the Hippodrome and saw both the emperor seated upon the tribunal and the crowd standing on either side, he continually cried out: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” When he reached the emperor’s tribunal, they removed his purple garment, forced him to fall prostrate, and compelled him to worship the emperor.

The emperor then granted Gelimer many pleasant and fertile estates in Galatia and permitted him to live there with all his relatives. He did not, however, promote him to the rank of patrician, because Gelimer refused to abandon the sect of Arius.

While Solomon was administering the state, the Maurusii took up arms against the Africans. The Maurusii descended from the peoples whom Jesus son of Nave drove out from the land of the Phoenicians, who lived from Sidon all the way to Egypt. When they reached Egypt and were not received there, they came to Libya and inhabited it. At a later time, when the Roman emperors possessed the land, they called it Hoen.

They set up two hollowed stones above a great spring, bearing Phoenician letters that said: “We are those who fled from the face of Jesus the robber, son of Nave.”

There were also other peoples, originally native to Africa, who had a king named Asclepius, reigning jointly with Hercules. They asserted that he was a son of the earth and that he founded Carthage.

Solomon took an army from Carthage and marched against the Maurusii. They fled and threw themselves over precipices, killing themselves. Fifty thousand Maurusii died in this war [Note: [Col. 0985D] Ms. Pithoeus: five hundred thousand], while not a single Roman died. Indeed, none of them received even a wound; all won the victory entirely unharmed.

Many of the Maurusian leaders joined the Romans. The Romans captured such a multitude of men, women, and children that they sold a Maurusian slave to anyone who wished to buy one for the price of a single sheep.

Then an old saying of a certain prophetic woman came true for them. She had cursed them, saying: “Their multitude shall perish at the hands of a beardless man.” Solomon had been made a eunuch against his will in childhood, losing his genital organs because of an injury.

After recovering the whole of Libya, Solomon returned to Carthage.

Furthermore, at the beginning of spring Belisarius was sent to make Sicily tributary to the Romans. While he was wintering there, the Roman soldiers in Libya revolted against Solomon in the following manner. They had taken the wives of the Vandals who had been killed, possessed their fields as their own, and refused to pay the emperor’s taxes for them.

Solomon warned them not to oppose the emperor, but to restore to him everything that had been decreed. Some of them, especially the Goths, fell into the sect of Arius. The priests of the Church excluded them and refused even to baptize their children. Thus a quarrel arose on a feast day.

The soldiers conspired to kill Solomon in the church. When he heard of this, he urged them to withdraw from the revolt. After a short time he succeeded.

But when the Roman pontiff Agapitus, who had asked the emperor Justinian to make peace with Theodatus, died at Constantinople, Justinian sent the patrician Belisarius, already renowned for many victories, against Theodatus, so that he might also free Italy from the domination of the Goths.

While Belisarius was spending some time in Sicily, Theodatus, king of the Goths, was killed. Vithegis succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0985D] A.: Vitigis; thus throughout]. As soon as he seized the kingdom, he went to Ravenna, forcibly took away the daughter of Queen Amalasuinta, and joined her to himself in marriage.

Belisarius therefore turned against Vithegis the forces he had gathered for the war against Theodatus. Departing from Sicily for Campania, he approached Naples. The citizens of Naples refused to receive him. Enraged, he exerted all his strength to attack the city. After besieging it vigorously for several days, he finally captured it by force and entered. He raged with such anger not only against the Goths who lived there but also against the citizens that he spared neither age nor sex, nor finally even religious women or priests.

He killed men before the eyes of their wives—a pitiful sight—and led the surviving mothers and children away under the yoke of captivity [Note: [Col. 0985D] A.: “he subjected them”]. He plundered everything and did not refrain from stripping the most sacred churches.

From there he departed and hastened to Rome. When he entered Rome, the Goths who were living in the city went out by night, left the gates open, and fled to Ravenna. As soon as Vithegis learned this, he came against Belisarius at Rome with a huge army.

Belisarius, judging that the time was not suitable for battle, shut himself within the walls of the city and surrounded it with fortifications. The Goths, besieging Rome, consumed everything around it through plunder and fire. Wherever they found Romans, they killed them with the sword. They stripped all sacred places and laid impious hands even upon the tombs of the venerable martyrs. They attacked the city continually, but the careful skill of Belisarius defended it.

In addition to the pressure of war, Rome was oppressed by a shortage of food. A famine had grown so severe throughout the world that year, especially in Liguria, that, as the blessed Dacius, bishop of Milan, reported, many mothers ate the limbs of their unfortunate children.

After the Goths had besieged Rome for a full year, they were finally frightened and returned to Ravenna. Belisarius, however, was repeatedly and severely rebuked by Pope Silverius for having committed such great and terrible murders at Naples. At last he was corrected and repented. He set out for Naples again, and, seeing the houses of the city plundered [Note: [Col. 0986D] A.: “and laid waste”] and empty, eventually devised a plan for restoring its population.

He gathered men and women from the various villages of the territory of Naples and settled them in the houses: people from Cumae, Puteoli, and many others living in Liguria, as well as from Playa, Sola, Piscinula, Locotroccla, Summa, and other villages. He also brought people from Melanos, Surrentum, and the village called Stabiae, adding men and women; likewise, he added people from the settlements of Cimiterium.

Not long afterward he went to Africa to fight the Vandals again and gained a victory over them. Gathering survivors and captives from Africa, as well as people from Sicily and the city of Syracuse, from the cities of Calabria—namely Malita and Consentia—and their villages, and from the whole of Apulia, he repopulated the devastated city.

Nevertheless, during the collection of people arriving from the individual cities, foolish talk usually increased greatly. For that reason the governor of Sicily annually sent them a noble and wise man to judge and distinguish matters of which they themselves had little knowledge.

Belisarius left Naples in good order and entered Rome [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “returned”]. Immediately an order was brought to him from the empress Theodora that he should send Pope Silverius into exile after convicting him on the accusation of false witnesses, because he had refused to accept Anthimus, the heretical bishop of Constantinople, back into office [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “had refused to restore him”].

Although unwilling, Belisarius carried this out without delay. Pope Silverius was finally driven to the island of Pontia, where he died in exile.

Vithegis, meanwhile, again gathered a large Gothic army into one force and engaged Belisarius. After a great slaughter of his men, he was put to flight. John, the military commander surnamed “the Bloodthirsty,” pursued him as he fled by night, captured him alive, and brought him to Rome to Belisarius.

After completing his victory, Belisarius returned to Constantinople, bringing Vithegis with him. Justinian was very pleased when he saw him, and soon afterward, having made Vithegis a patrician, he assigned him the administration of the Persian frontier [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “he assigned him the regions beside the Persian frontier, and there,” etc.]. Vithegis lived there and ended his life.

Belisarius, having been raised to honors worthy of him, was sent once more to Africa against Vintarith, who had again stirred up the Vandals and ruled among them [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “He had seized the kingship among them. Belisarius, to Africa against Guntharith,” etc.]. As soon as Belisarius reached Africa, he treacherously killed Vintarith under the pretext of peace and subjected the remaining Vandals to the authority of the state.

Afterward Belisarius returned to Rome in triumph and offered to blessed Peter, through the hands of Pope Vigilius, a golden cross weighing one hundred pounds and decorated with the most precious gems, on which he had inscribed his victories.

At this same time, blessed Benedict, a wondrous man and no less prescient of future events, was shining with virtues at Cassinum, where he was living in a monastery after a solitary life [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “Father Benedict”].

In this period also the nation of the Lombards was living in Pannonia, then friendly to the Roman people. Audoin was in charge of its kingdom. At that time, when he fought Turisind, king of the Gepids, he gained the victory through his son Alboin, a vigorous young man.

Indeed, while the two armies were engaged, Alboin boldly attacked Thurismod, the son of King Turisind, and killed him. The Gepids were thrown into confusion by this event, and Alboin secured victory for his own people.

At Rome, meanwhile, Pope Vigilius, because of the same cause of the empress’s anger that had affected his predecessor, was taken to Constantinople by Anthimus the *scribo* and from there driven into exile.

After Vithegis was captured, the Goths north of the Po [Note: [Col. 0987D] Fr. Pithoeus: Elpebadus; A.: Heldebadus] appointed Ildebald as their king. He was killed in the same year, and Eutarius succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: Erarius]. He too was slaughtered before the year had ended.

Afterward they appointed Badvila, also called Totila, as king. He immediately gathered an army from every direction and invaded all Italy [Note: [Col. 0987D] A.: “They again invaded Italy”].

As he was passing through Campania and the monastery of the man of God, Father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0988D] A.: “They made their way through it; then, proceeding through the territories of Lucania and Bruttium, they went to Rhegium; soon afterward they crossed the Sicilian strait and invaded Sicily. From there they returned and marched upon Rome, surrounding it with sieges. Rome,” etc.], he deserved to hear these words from him:

“You commit many evils; you have committed many evils. Now cease from iniquity. You will cross the sea, enter Rome, reign for nine years, and die in the tenth.”

Then, descending from the monastery, he proceeded through the territories of Lucania and Bruttium toward Rhegium. Soon afterward he crossed the Sicilian strait and invaded Sicily. From there he returned and marched upon Rome, surrounding it with sieges.

Rome suffered such a great famine that, because of the enormity of the shortage, people wished to eat the flesh of their children. When the Romans were utterly exhausted and unable to defend the walls, Totila entered the city through the Ostian Gate.

Wishing to spare the Romans, he ordered the trumpets to sound throughout the whole night, so that they might protect themselves from Gothic swords either in the churches or by hiding in whatever ways they could. He lived for some time among the Romans as a father among his children. As may reasonably be inferred, the admonition of blessed Father Benedict, whom he had once visited, brought about this kindness of spirit in one who had previously been excessively cruel.

Some of the senators, in distress, hastened to Constantinople and told the emperor what calamities had befallen Rome [Note: [Col. 0988D] A.: “They told the emperor”]. He immediately made Narses, his eunuch chamberlain, Exarch of Italy and sent him to Rome with a strong force, so that he might quickly assist the afflicted city.

When Narses came to Italy [Note: [Col. 0988D] A.: “He came and fought a great battle with the Goths. After they had been,” etc.], he made an alliance with the Lombards and sent envoys to Alboin, asking him to provide assistance in the war he was about to wage against the Goths.

Alboin then sent a chosen force of his men to support the Romans against the Goths. They crossed the Adriatic Gulf, joined the Romans, and engaged the Goths in a great battle. When the Goths had been almost annihilated, Narses killed King Totila, who had already reigned for more than ten years. He sent Totila’s bloodstained garments, together with his crown decorated with precious stones, to the imperial city, and they were cast at the emperor’s feet before the senate.

Then he captured their two fortified cities, Verona and Brescia, and restored the Roman city and all Italy to the authority of the state [Note: [Col. 0989D] A.: “He restored them”]. He sent the Lombards, honored with many gifts, back to their own country. Throughout the entire period during which the Lombards possessed Pannonia, they served as allies of the Roman state against its enemies.

Meanwhile, Solomon, living in Libya, fortified all the walls of that city. Since the Maurusii had departed from Numidia in defeat, he made the region of Zaben, Mauretania, and Sitifis, its metropolis [Note: [Col. 0990D] Fr. Pithoeus: Japhin], tributary to the Romans. Caesarea is the first metropolis of the other Mauretania.

Meanwhile, the king of Iberia, named Zamanardus, went up to Constantinople to the emperor Justinian with his wife and senators. He asked Justinian to be a champion and brotherly friend of the Romans. The emperor accepted his proposal and honored him and his senators with many gifts. Likewise, the empress gave his wife ornaments varied with jewels, and they dismissed them peacefully to their kingdom.

In the eighth year of Justinian’s reign, Pompeiopolis in Mysia suffered divine retribution. The earth split open in an earthquake, and the middle of the city, together with its inhabitants, was buried. They were beneath the earth, and their voices could be heard crying out for mercy. The emperor gave much money to bring them out and assist them, and he generously helped those who were still alive.

In the same year Justinian instituted in the church the singing of what is called “The Only-Begotten Son and Word of God.”

In the twelfth year of Justinian’s reign, two Bulgar kings, Vulger and Droggo, moved with a multitude into Scythia and Mysia. Justin was then military commander of Mysia, and Blandarius of Scythia. When they came out, they engaged the Bulgars in battle, and the military commander Justin was killed in the fighting. Constantine, son of Florentius, was appointed in his place.

The Bulgars came as far as the regions of Thrace. The military commander Williriacus went out against them with the Huns [Note: [Col. 0990D] Another source: “from Illyricum with the Huns”]. The emperor had received him as his godson at holy baptism. He attacked the Bulgars in the center, cut them down, and killed great numbers. He recovered all the plunder and gained a powerful victory, killing two of their kings.

In the same year Chosdroes, king of the Persians, captured great Antioch in Syria.

In the thirteenth year of Justinian’s reign, Mundus, descended from the Gepid people, joined the Romans.

In the fourteenth year of Justinian’s reign, Chosdroes, king of the Persians, made his fourth invasion of Roman territory. Belisarius, coming from the west, compelled him by his wisdom to return ineffectually to his own land.

In the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign, in the month of October, a pestilence occurred at Byzantium. In the same year, at the Hypapante of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0990D] In the Roman Church, the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary; in the Greek and Ambrosian Churches, the Lord’s feast. For more on its institution, see the learned Saxius, *Apologetic Dissertation on Saints Gervasius and Protasius*, no. 14], the feast began to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.

In the sixteenth year of Justinian’s reign, the kings of the Azumites, the Indians, and the Jews came to war with one another for the following reason.

The king of the Azumites rules beyond Egypt. Roman merchants enter the territory of the Azumites through the Homerites and proceed to the interior regions of the Indians and Ethiopians. The merchants, following their customary practice, entered the territory of the Homerites. Their king Damianus killed them and seized all their possessions, saying: “The Romans mistreat the Jews who are in their country, and they kill—”
them, and as a result the Azumites broke off trade with the inland Indians. The king of the Azumites, Adad, became indignant and sent word to the Homerite: “Because you have harmed my kingdom and the interior of India, preventing merchants from entering to us.” They came into bitter enmity and began war against one another.

When they were about to fight, Adad, king of the Azumites, made a vow, saying: “If I conquer the Homerite, I will become a Christian, since I am fighting on behalf of the Christians.” Through God’s action he won a most decisive victory, captured their king Damian alive, and took possession of their land and kingdoms. Giving thanks, Adad, king of the Azumites, sent to the emperor Justinian, asking him to provide a bishop and clergy so that he might be instructed and become a Christian.

[Col. 0990C] Justinian was exceedingly glad about this and ordered them to be given whomever they wished. After making careful inquiries, the envoys chose the venerable John, a virgin and mansionarius of Saint John the Great at Alexandria, who was sixty-two years old. Having received him, they departed for their own country, to their king Adad. Thus they believed in Christ and were enlightened.

In the seventeenth year of Justinian’s reign, a great earthquake occurred throughout the entire world. In that same year a certain man from the region of Italy appeared, going about through the villages. His name was Andrew, and he had with him a red and blind dog, which performed miracles at his command. When he himself stood in the marketplace, with a crowd gathered around, the gold, silver, and iron rings of those standing there were secretly brought away by the same dog and placed on the pavement. Andrew covered them, gave orders to the dog, and then took them up and gave each person his own. Likewise, he handed out mixed coins of various emperors, identifying them by name. Moreover, while a crowd of men and women stood present, he revealed which among them were pregnant, fornicators, adulterers, misers, and magnanimous people; he disclosed everyone truthfully. Therefore they said that he possessed the spirit of Python.

In the eighteenth year of Justinian’s reign, the sea spread over Thrace for four miles and covered the land around the regions of Odessus and Dionysiopolis. Many people perished in the waters, and then, at a command, that same sea was restored to its proper places.

In the nineteenth year of Justinian’s reign, there was a shortage of grain, wine, and oil, together with heavy rain. A great earthquake and destruction occurred at Constantinople on Holy Easter. The populace began abstaining from meat on February 4; but the emperor ordered meat to be put on sale the following week. All the meat sellers slaughtered and displayed meat, yet no one bought or ate it. Easter, however, was celebrated as the emperor had ordered, and the people were found to have fasted an additional week.

In the twenty-first year of his reign, great earthquakes and rains occurred, and the empress Theodora died. Likewise, in the following year there were flashes of lightning and thunderclaps so violent that sleepers were injured by the thunder, and fires broke out near Byzantium.

In the twenty-third year of Justinian’s reign, an envoy from India came to Constantinople bringing an elephant, and entered the Hippodrome. In March the elephant broke out of its stable at night, killing many people and injuring others. In June, the dedication of the Church of the Holy Apostles took place at Constantinople. The relics (*λείψανα*) of the apostles Andrew and Luke were deposited there, and Bishop Menas passed by with the holy relics (*λειψάνοις*), seated in an imperial golden carriage decorated with precious stones and holding three reliquaries of the holy apostles on his knees; thus he celebrated the dedication.

In the twenty-seventh year of Justinian’s reign, a terrible earthquake occurred at Constantinople and in other cities, lasting forty days. Gradually the people were moved to repentance, conducting litanies, attending them frequently, and remaining in the churches. But after God’s great mercy had been manifested, the people fell back into worse behavior. The memory of this earthquake is observed every year, with the people conducting a litany in the field.

In the twenty-eighth year of Justinian’s reign, there were dreadful thunderclaps and flashes of lightning, together with a terrifying south wind, so that the cross standing inside the Gate of Rhesius fell.

[Note: Col. 0991D. Cedrenus has: “inside the Golden Gate.”]

In the twenty-ninth year of Justinian’s reign, the Jews and Samaritans of Caesarea in Palestine stirred up a revolt. Having formed themselves, as it were, into the factions of the Green and the Blue, they attacked the Christians of that city, killed many of them, burned the churches, killed Stephen, the prefect of that city, in the praetorium, and plundered his property. His wife, fleeing to the city, went to the emperor, who ordered Adamantius, the master of the soldiers, to go down to Palestine and exact vengeance for Stephen’s killing. When he arrived, he hanged some of those whom he found, beheaded others, mutilated others, and confiscated their property. Great fear arose throughout all the eastern regions.

In the thirtieth year of Justinian’s reign, a fiery comet appeared in the sky, shaped like a spear, extending from the north to the west.

In the thirty-first year of Justinian’s reign, there was an exceedingly terrifying earthquake, such as no one in that generation remembered ever having occurred on earth. The earth shook day and night for ten days, and afterward the shaking ceased. The emperor, however, did not wear the crown for ten days. On the holy feast of Christ’s Nativity, he likewise proceeded into the church without it. He even caused the customary banquets held at nineteen couches to cease and distributed their expenses to the poor.

[Note: Col. 0991D. Suidas has: “banquets.”]

In that same year, an unexpected people entered Byzantium, those called the Avars, and the entire city ran to see them, as though no one had ever seen such a people. Their hair was extremely long at the back, very tangled, and fastened with ribbons; the rest of their clothing was like that of the other Huns. Fleeing from their own country, they came into the regions of Scythia and Moesia and sent envoys to Justinian, asking to be received.

In the thirty-second year of Justinian’s reign, the great dome of the Church of Constantinople was built and raised more than twenty feet above the upper part of the building that had previously stood there.

In the thirty-third year of his reign, the emperor began building a bridge over the river Agoreas, diverting the same river into another channel. He turned five remarkable arches over it and made it passable, although previously it had been wooden.

[Note: Another reading has: Sangarios.]

In the thirty-fourth year of Justinian’s reign, a report spread through Constantinople that the emperor had died. He had come from Thrace and was seeing no one. The common people therefore suddenly seized the loaves from the places where they were made and sold, and around the third hour no bread could be found anywhere in the city. The workshops were also closed, and the palace whispered that no one from the Senate was seeing the emperor because he was suffering from a headache. Consequently, they believed that the emperor had died.

Meanwhile, around evening, the Senate held a council, sent the prefect, and caused lights to be lit throughout the city, since the emperor had recovered. In this way the city was rescued from the disturbance.

After the emperor had recovered, Eugenius, who had been prefect, denounced the curators George and Etherius, alleging that they had wished to make Theodore, the son of the master Peter, emperor. When the matter was investigated and in no way substantiated, Eugenius incurred the emperor’s anger, and his house was transferred to the public treasury.

There was also a devastating plague in Cilicia, Anazarbus, and great Antioch, as well as an earthquake. The Orthodox and the Severians clashed with one another, and many killings took place. The emperor sent Zimarchus, count of the East, who suppressed the disorders, sent many into exile, confiscated their property, and mutilated them.

In the thirty-fifth year of Justinian’s reign, on the twenty-fifth day of November, some men secretly plotted to kill the emperor. They were Ablavius and Marcellus, money-changers, and Sergius. Their plot was as follows: when the emperor was seated in the dining hall in the evening, before permission to depart was given, they would kill him, with men cooperating with them hidden inside in the silentiary and in a corner of the *incurium* [reading uncertain], so that, once the plot had been carried out, they could create a disturbance.

[Note: Another reading has: “with his men cooperating with him, hidden in a corner and in the carriage.”]

Ablavius had also received fifty pounds of gold from Marcellus, the silver-dealer, so that he would cooperate with him. But, trusting in God’s will, Ablavius confided in Eusebius, the former consul and count of the federates, and in John the Logothete, saying: “This evening we intend to attack the emperor.” When they reported this to the emperor, he arrested them and found that they were carrying concealed swords.

Marcellus, the silver-dealer, frustrated in his hopes, drew the sword he was carrying and, after being seized in the dining hall, struck himself three times; he died.

[Note: Another reading has: “they were given [the blows].”]

Sergius, however, fled to Blachernae. After he had been brought out—

[Note: Another reading has: “after he had been brought out of the church.”]

—and questioned, he was persuaded to confess that Isaac, the silver-dealer, and the most glorious patrician Bilisarius had been accomplices in this plot, and that Vitus, the money-changer, and Paul, the curator, had known of the plan of that same Bilisarius.

[Note: Another reading has: Hisaucius.]

When they were arrested and handed over to Procopius, the prefect, they confessed and spoke about Bilisarius, who immediately fell under the emperor’s displeasure. Many others also resorted to flight.

Meanwhile, on the fifth day of December, the emperor convened a silent session, bringing in Eutychius the patriarch, and ordered their confessions to be read aloud. When this was heard, Bilisarius was weighed down by immense grief. The emperor sent out men, arrested all his household, and ordered Bilisarius himself to remain seated at home under guard.

Meanwhile, on the twentieth day of December, certain places in Africa were captured by the Moors who had risen against Africa, as follows. A certain man named Chutinas, an exarch of the Moors from that very people, had been accustomed to receiving from the ruler of Africa who was then in office a fixed amount of gold.

[Note: Another reading has: “from the proconsul.”]

When he came to receive it, John, the ruler of Africa, killed him. The sons of Chutinas then rose up to avenge their father’s payment and, having taken up arms against him, began plundering parts of his territory.

[Note: Another reading has: Cuatinas; another, Cutzinus.]

When the emperor learned of this, he sent his nephew Martianus, master of the soldiers, with an army to pacify the Moors, and they came over to him. Thus Africa obtained peace.

In that same year, when certain disturbers were stirring up Constantinople, the emperor had the thumbs cut off those alone who had fought with swords.

On the nineteenth day of March, the patrician Bilisarius was released, having recovered all his dignities.

In that same year, envoys of Ascelti, king of the Hormetionites, came to Constantinople.

[Note: Another reading has: Ermechionites.]

In the thirty-seventh year of his reign, Justinian went on a mission of prayer to Mirangula—that is, Germanicia, a city of Galatia.

[Note: Other readings have: “Mirianglos, that is, Germanias”; “Mariangelos, that is, Germias”; and “Mariangelos, that is, Gernias.”]

In November, Arethas the patrician and ruler of the Saracens entered Byzantium to pay the emperor what was owed by his sons and, by reason of that obligation, to secure that after his death they would hold the leadership of their tribe.

[Note: Another reading has: “the ruler of the tribe.”]

In the thirty-eighth year of his reign, Justinian, advocating the doctrine of the corruptible and the incorruptible, issued everywhere an edict contrary to piety. God intervening first, he died, having reigned thirty-eight years, seven months, and ten days; such was his successor, Justin the Curopalates.

# JUSTIN II

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 558, Justin, emperor and nephew of Justinian, was crowned by Eutychius the patriarch. [Note: Another version: “crowned by John.” So too Cedrenus.] He was a Thracian by nationality, magnanimous, and successful in all things. He also had a wife named Sophia, whom he crowned Augusta.

Although he was devout, he adorned the churches that Justinian had built—namely, both the great church and the Church of the Holy Apostles, as well as other churches and monasteries—giving them treasures and all their revenues. He was also exceedingly orthodox, and he sent the monk Photinus, stepson of Bilisarius Patricius, granting him authority against every cause and person, to reconcile all the churches of Egypt and Alexandria.

In the second year of Justin’s reign, Etherius and Avitus, together with a physician who was with them, plotted against the same Emperor Justin. When their plot was discovered, they were killed by the sword. [Note: Another version: “Audius.” Evagrius, Book V, chapter 3: “Addeus.”]

In the third year of Justin’s reign, the most devout Augusta Sophia summoned the dealers in money and the notaries, ordered the debt bonds and registers to be brought to her, gave them to the debtors, and returned them to their owners. For this she was greatly praised by the entire city.

In the seventh year of Emperor Justin’s reign, the Romans and Persians violated the peace, and the Persian war was renewed. This happened because the Homerites [Note: Another version: “the Indians sent a legion.”] had sent a message of affection to the Romans, and the emperor had sent Julianus the Master [Note: Another version: “Magistrianus, with the imperial letter, to Arethas.”] with an imperial letter to Archetas, king of the Ethiopians, by way of the Nile River from Alexandria and the Indian Sea.

Archetas, king of the Ethiopians, received him with great joy, since he eagerly desired the friendship of the Roman emperor. When Julianus returned, he related that, when King Archetas received him, the king was naked, wearing only a girdle, and around his loins a linen garment woven with gold. Around his belly he wore torn clothing with precious pearls, and on his arms five bracelets each, while on his hands he wore golden armlets.

On his head was a jeweled cloth, having on each side four braided bands; around his neck was a golden torque. He stood upon four elephants, which were standing and bore a yoke and four wheels. Above them was a covered chariot with golden petals, such as the chariots of princes [Note: Another version: “of provincial governors.”]. Standing upon them, he carried a very small round shield and two golden lances. His entire senate was with him, armed and singing musical melodies.

When the Roman envoy had been brought in and had prostrated himself, he was ordered to rise and was brought before the king. When the king had received the emperor’s imperial letter, he kissed the seal that was attached to the emperor’s breast. After receiving the gifts as well, he was very pleased.

When he read the imperial letter, however, he found that he was instructed to arm himself against the Persian king, ravage the territory of the Persians nearest to him, and enter into no further treaties with the Persians.

Immediately, therefore, King Archetas assembled his army and, in the presence of the Roman envoy, began battle against the Persians, sending the Saracens subject to him ahead of him. He himself then advanced into the Persian territory and devastated everything that was in those regions.

King Archetas took Julianus by the head, gave him the kiss of peace, and dismissed him with great goodwill and many gifts.

Another event also occurred that disturbed Chosroes. For at that time the Huns—whom we customarily call Turks—sent an embassy to Justin, dispatching it through the territory of the Alans. Fearing this, Chosroes put forward as an excuse the rebellion of the Armenians against him, which had arisen because they had joined Justin. He also demanded the return of the refugees.

For the Roman emperor was paying the Persians five hundred pounds of gold every year, so that they would guard the forts nearest that region, lest invading peoples destroy both states; and the fortresses were maintained at common expense.

Justin, however, dissolved the peace, declaring that it was a disgrace for Romans to pay tribute to the Persians. Consequently, a great war arose between the Persians and the Romans in that region.

Justin appointed Martinus Patricius, his kinsman, commander of the East, and sent him against the Persians.

In the eighth year of his reign, Justin fell ill and became angry with his brother Biduarius, whom he assailed with insults. Finally, he ordered the chamberlains to bring him out, beaten with fists, before the assembly of senators. For Biduarius was the count of the imperial stables.

When Sophia learned of this, she was distressed and complained to the emperor. He repented, went down to the stable, and suddenly entered with the chief of the chamberlains.

When Biduarius saw the emperor, he fled from place to place through the upper parts of the stable, out of fear of the emperor. But the emperor cried out:

“I adjure you by God, my brother; wait for me.”

When he had run after him, he seized him, embraced and kissed him, saying:

“I have sinned against you, my brother; but receive me as your former brother and as your emperor. For I know that this happened through the operation of the devil.”

He fell at the emperor’s feet and, weeping, said:

“Truly, my lord, although you possess authority, you have disgraced your servant in the presence of the senate. Now, my lord, give me an account of these things.”

And he showed him the horses. The emperor then asked him to eat with him, and they were reconciled.

In that same year a great war took place near Sagarthon between the Romans and the Persians, and the Romans were victorious.

In the ninth year of Justin’s reign, Hormizd, king of the Persians, appointed Arimardan as commander of the Persians and sent him into Roman territory to ravage it. He returned after taking much booty.

When Justin learned this, he was overwhelmed by the weight of the disaster, lost the use of his senses, and fell into an illness. He asked Hormizd to make a treaty, and Hormizd agreed that it should be an annual payment.

Emperor Justin made Tiberius his own count of the excubitors [Note: Another version: “his son”] and named him Caesar, appointing him his associate both in the hippodromes [Note: Another version: “in the hippodromes and on feast days”] and in the imperial residences. For the emperor was disabled in his feet and therefore spent most of his time lying on a couch.

In the eleventh year of his reign, Justin constructed the great aqueduct of Valens and abundantly supplied the city with water.

In the twelfth year of his reign, Emperor Justin took possession of the synagogue of the Jews that was in Constantinople, in Chalco [Note: Another version: “in the Chalcoprateia”], paying them its price, and made it a church of Our Lady, the holy Mother of God, which is near the great church.

But when the emperor fell ill and was given a brief respite from his illness, he summoned Eutychius the pontiff, the senate, all the priests, and the citizens. Tiberius Caesar was brought before them all, and Justin proclaimed him emperor, using these words:

“Behold God, who has done good to you and given you this position; it was not I. Honor him, so that you too may be honored by him.

“Honor your mother, who was once your mistress. You know that at first you were her servant, but now you are her son.

“Do not rejoice in bloodshed; do not share in murder; do not repay evil with evil, lest in evil you become like me in enmity. For I, as a man, have sinned. Indeed, I have become guilty and have received according to my sins; but I shall have a case against those who did this to me before the tribunal of Christ.

“Do not let the imperial position exalt you as it exalted me. Pay attention to everything as you would to yourself. Know who you were, and who you now are. Do not become proud, and you will not sin.

“You know who I was and what I have become—who I was, and who I am. All these people are your sons and servants. You know that I honored you as my own child. When you see all these men, you see the affairs of the state.

“Pay attention to your army [Note: Another version: “Do not receive soft men into the army, lest some say…”], and do not admit soldiers to your banquets, lest certain people say to you, ‘Your predecessor behaved in this way.’ For I say these things because of what I have suffered.

“Let those who possess property enjoy it. But give gifts to those who have none.”

After the patriarch had offered a prayer and everyone had said “Amen,” Caesar fell at the emperor’s feet and said to him:

“If you wish, I am not [Note: Another version: “If you wish, I am; if you wish, I am not.”]”

And the emperor said:

“May God, who made heaven and earth, himself place in your heart all that I have forgotten to say.”

While the emperor continued speaking these things, he filled the entire assembly with tears. When the assembly had been dismissed, he distributed gifts to his subjects and performed all the customary acts associated with the proclamation of an emperor.

This Justin was good at the beginning of his reign, but afterward fell into every form of avarice: that is, he became a despoiler of the poor and a plunderer of senators. [Col. 0998A] So great was the madness of his greed that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could gather whatever talents of gold he seized.

In the eleventh year of his reign—which was the year of the divine Incarnation 568, in the first indiction—the Lombards departed from Pannonia. In the second indiction they began to plunder Italy, and in the third indiction they began to rule in Italy.

[Note: In what follows, the Miscella follows Theophanes for the most part, often word for word. We have seen the Greek manuscript of Theophanes. We have also seen the Roman manuscript of Anastasius Bibliothecarius, the translator of Theophanes. Jacobus Bongarsius also noted various readings from the Greek manuscript of Theophanes. We have selected some of them. Perhaps the complete Greek Theophanes, together with Anastasius, will soon come to light. Therefore, whenever we cite Greek various readings hereafter, even without adding the name, you should understand them to be those of Theophanes. Canisius.]

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

## TIBERIUS II

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 571 [Note: Theophanes: “in the month of October, in the second indiction”], Tiberius began to reign, having been crowned by Eutychius the patriarch. He too was of Thracian descent.

When he had begun to reign, the factions cried out: “Augusta Anastasia, may you conquer! Save, Lord, those whom you have ordered to reign.” [Note: Theophanes reads: “Τὰ μέρη Α . Α. τοῦ βήκας .” (a corrupt or uncertain factional acclamation).] Hearing this, Sophia, Justin’s wife, was struck with alarm.

For she wanted to marry Tiberius so that she might remain Augusta; she did not know that he had a wife. Some, however, said that she had also been intimate with him during Justin’s lifetime, and that she herself had persuaded Justin to make him Caesar.

But Tiberius, fearing her, took Anastasia as his wife, crowned her Augusta, and distributed a large donative [Note: Ὑπατίαν, “the consular donative.”]

Tiberius was just, useful, energetic, wise, generous in almsgiving, just in judgment, renowned in victory, despising no one, but embracing everyone with goodwill.

When he distributed generously to the poor much of the treasure that Justin had accumulated, Augusta Sophia frequently rebuked him because he had reduced the state to poverty, saying:

“What I gathered over many years, you are scattering in a short time.”

He replied:

“I trust in the Lord that money will not be lacking in our treasury, provided only that the poor receive alms and captives are ransomed. This is the great treasure, as the Lord says: ‘Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth corrupts, and where thieves do not break in and steal.’ Therefore, from what the Lord has granted, let us give to the poor and gather treasures in heaven, and the Lord will deem it worthy to increase them for us in this world.”

One day, while walking through the palace, he saw on the floor of a room a marble slab on which the cross of the Lord had been carved. He said:

“We ought to fortify our foreheads and our breasts with the cross of our Lord, and behold, we are treading upon it.”

Having said this, he immediately ordered the slab to be removed. When the slab had been dug up and raised, they found another beneath it bearing the same sign. He ordered that one removed as well. When it had been taken away, they found a third.

When this too had been removed at his command, they found beneath it a great treasure containing more than one thousand hundredweights of gold. He distributed the gold to the poor even more abundantly than he had been accustomed to do.

Narses Patricius of Italy also came from Italy to the city mentioned above with many treasures. There, in his own house, he secretly dug a large cistern, into which he placed many thousands of hundredweights of gold and silver.

After killing everyone who knew of it, he entrusted the matter to only one old man, exacting an oath from him. After Narses had died, the old man came to Tiberius Caesar and said:

“If it is of any benefit to me, Caesar, I shall tell you something of great importance.”

He replied:

“What do you want? It will benefit you if you tell us something that will benefit us.”

The old man said:

“I possess the hidden treasure of Narses, which, now that I am at the end of my life, I can no longer conceal.”

Then Tiberius rejoiced and sent his own men to the place. The old man went ahead, while they followed in astonishment. When they reached the cistern, they opened it and entered. So much gold and silver was found there that it could scarcely be emptied by those carrying it away even over many days.

Tiberius distributed nearly all of it to the needy in accordance with his customary lavish generosity.

Finally, when Rome was suffering from famine during the time of Pope Benedict, while the Lombards were devastating everything around it, Tiberius sent many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt and relieved the city through his zeal for almsgiving.

When he was about to receive the imperial crown and the people, according to custom, were awaiting him at the spectacle of the Circus, certain opponents prepared a plot against him in order to raise Justinian, Justin’s nephew, to imperial rank.

Tiberius was proceeding through the holy places. Then, having summoned the city’s pontiff, he entered the palace with the consuls and prefects. Clad in purple, crowned with the diadem, and placed upon the imperial throne, he was confirmed in the glory of the kingdom with immense acclamations.

When his opponents heard this, and were unable to harm him because he had placed his hope in God, they were covered with great confusion and shame.

After a few days had passed, Justinian arrived and threw himself at the emperor’s feet, bringing fifteen hundredweights of gold as a token of gratitude for the favor he had received. Tiberius, accepting him according to his customary patience, ordered him to remain at his side in the palace.

Augusta Sophia, meanwhile, forgetful of the promise she had once made concerning Tiberius, attempted to lay a plot against him.

When Tiberius had gone out to the country to enjoy thirty days of the grape harvest according to imperial custom, Sophia secretly summoned Justinian and wished to raise him to the throne.

When Tiberius learned of this, he hastened back to Constantinople, seized Sophia, and stripped her of all her treasures, leaving her only the food necessary for her daily sustenance. He separated her attendants from her and placed others of his own trusted men to serve her. He also ordered absolutely that none of her former attendants should have access to her.

As for Justinian, Tiberius merely rebuked him with words, but afterward loved him so greatly that he promised his own daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son. This matter, however, for some reason did not reach fulfillment.

In the second year of his reign, King Tiberius sent to the Persian king according to custom, announcing his accession. Since the Persian king did not accept peace, Tiberius assembled great forces and, distributing the royal treasures, raised many armies. He appointed the aforementioned Justinian Master of the East.

In the third year of his reign, the Persian king took up his forces and hastened into Armenia. When the Roman commander heard that the Persian king himself was about to enter the battle, he prepared for it.

Fear had entered the Roman people, and therefore Justinian, addressing the troops, restrained their fear of battle.

When the battle took place and the Persians had discharged a great shower of arrows—so great that even the rays of the sun were hidden—they then endeavored to hurl continuously with their shields the missiles that were being shot from the bows.

But when the Roman line stood firm, the Persians could not endure it. The Babylonian host was put to flight, and great multitudes perished.

Meanwhile, the Romans seized the Persians’ equipment, the royal tent, and the entire splendid array. They also captured elephants and sent the notable animals and those royal spoils to Tiberius.

Therefore, unable to endure the humiliation, the Persian king imposed a law that no Persian king should ever again go out to battle.

The Roman army, however, after the Persian disasters, advanced even into the interior of Persia, inflicted great destruction there, and took captives, reaching even to the middle of the Hyrcanian Sea.

When winter arrived, the Romans did not return to their own country, but spent the winter in Persia.

In that same year Tiberius began to build the public baths of Blachernae, restored many churches, hospices, and homes for the elderly, and ordered himself to be recorded in Phoenician letters as “Tiberius Constantine.”

Meanwhile, Emperor Tiberius purchased the bodies of pagans and formed them into a military unit under his own name, clothing and arming them to the number of fifteen thousand. He gave them as commander Mauricius, count of the foederati, and as subcommander Narses, and sent them against the Persians.

When a very great battle had taken place, the Romans became victorious and took from the Persians the cities and regions that they had captured under Justinian and Justin.

Mauricius departed for Constantinople and was received by the emperor with immense honor. Tiberius made Mauricius’s victories public and gave him his daughter Constantina in marriage, naming both of them Caesars.

In the month of August, after eating in the morning a mulberry that was pleasing in appearance but spoiled, he contracted phthisis (φθίσιν).

When he was near death, the patriarch John and the senate were summoned, and he was carried into the tribunal in a litter. Since he could not speak, he made known to the people, through an epagnosticus [an uncertain term in the text], what was useful for Roman affairs. Together with the advice of Augusta Sophia, he proclaimed his son-in-law Mauricius emperor.

When everyone had applauded the emperor’s decision and Mauricius as emperor, Tiberius turned in his bed and died, having reigned six years, ten months, and eight days.

# MAURICIUS

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 577, Mauricius became emperor. He was of Cappadocian descent.

In that same year the Avars served as ambassadors to Emperor Mauricius. Shortly before, they had conquered Sirmium, a notable city of Europe. They demanded eighty thousand pieces of gold, which they received annually from the Romans, and asked that another twenty thousand be added.

The emperor, seeking peace, accepted this.

Chagan [Note: Χαγάνος, “the khagan”] asked that an elephant, an Indian animal, be sent to him for his inspection. The emperor sent him the largest of all. After seeing it, he sent it back to the emperor.

He likewise requested that a golden bed be sent to him, and the emperor sent it. He too, after looking at it, sent it back to him.

He then demanded that another twenty thousand be added beyond the previous amount. When the emperor refused, Chagan destroyed the city of Sigidon and captured many other cities subject to Illyricum.

The emperor then sent Helpidius Patricius and Commentiolus as ambassadors to Chagan. The barbarian, however, claimed that he was acting in accordance with the pledges of the treaties and professed that he desired peace.

In the East, Mauricius appointed John Mystacon commander of Armenia. When John came to the Nymphius River, where it is known that the Tigris joins it, he engaged in battle with Cartharigas, the Persian commander [Note: Μετὰ Καρδαρήγαν στρατηγοῦ, “with Cardarigas the commander.”] The Romans prevailed over the barbarians.

Cardarigas, however, is not a personal name but a very high rank among the Persians.

In the second year of his reign, Mauricius was named consul and donated many treasures to the city. He promoted Philippicus to commander of the East and gave him Gordia [Note: Τὴν ἰδίαν ἀδελφήν, “his own sister.”], his daughter, in marriage.

Philippicus then seized the Persian side, approached Nisibis, suddenly entered Persia, and took a great deal of booty. Leading it safely through the mountains, he transferred it into the region of the Medes. After devastating many villages there, he returned to Roman territory.

Chagan, king of the Avars, was eager to break the peace. For he armed the tribes of the Sclaveni against Thrace, and they reached as far as the Long Walls, causing great destruction.

The emperor brought troops and commoners out from the palace and the city and ordered the Long Walls to be guarded. He appointed Commentiolus commander, armed him, and sent him against the barbarians. Commentiolus unexpectedly fell upon the barbarians, killed great multitudes, and drove them back.

When he had reached Adrianople, he encountered a multitude of Sclaveni carrying booty for Andragastus; charging them, he rescued the captives, but was deprived of victory.

In the third year of Emperor Mauricius, Philippicus took up his armies and set out for the Persian region. After capturing Arscennene, he obtained great booty and caused fear among the Persian armies.

Meanwhile, he returned to Constantinople suffering from illness, while the soldiers returned to their own country without injury.

In the fourth year of the reign of Maurice, Philippicus left the imperial city, took up his military equipment, and hastened toward the city of Amida. After assembling the armed forces, he asked them whether they were ready to march to war. When the Romans, by their oaths, had persuaded him that they would fight eagerly, he came to Anazarbus [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ἄρξαβον, “Arxabon.”].

When Cardarigas learned of this, he consigned the report to ridicule, supposing that what was being said was a dream. He summoned the Magi and asked them further: “Who will be master of victory?” The demon-appeasers declared that the Persians would receive victory from the gods.

The Persians therefore consulted together, made joyful by the promises of their ancestors, and immediately prepared wooden-and-iron fetters [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ξυλοπόδας, “wooden-footed” or “wooden fetters”; [Col. 1001C]] with which to bind the Romans in chains. The commander, however, warned the Romans not to destroy the labor of the fields, lest the justice of God, which hates evil [Note: [Col. 1001D] Μισοπόνηρος, “hating evil”], transfer the victory to the barbarians.

On the following day the commander sent out two phylarchs of the Saracens. They captured some Persians alive, through whom they learned the movements of the enemy. These men asserted that God wished the barbarians to attack the Romans every day [Note: [Col. 1001D] Τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ, “on the Lord’s Day.”].

At dawn Philippicus took leave of the Romans and advanced to battle with three phalanxes. Taking upon himself a divine and manly form [Note: [Col. 1001D] Θεανδρικὴν μορφήν, “divine-human form”]—which the Romans declare to be ἀχειροποίητον, that is, “not made by human hands”—he moved through the lines and bestowed divine strength upon the armed men. Standing behind the battle line, while retaining this equipment, he appeased God with many tears, for God had taken the rulers of the heavenly orders as auxiliaries [Col. 1001D].

While the battle was being fought, Vitalianus, commander of the battle line, moved more boldly than all the others, broke through the Persian phalanx, and carried off its baggage. The Romans, however, began to occupy themselves with the spoils. When Philippicus saw this, he feared that the others might return to the booty as well, forget the battle, and be destroyed when the barbarians turned upon them. He therefore placed his own helmet on Theodore of Illyricum and sent him to strike with the sword those who were occupied with the spoils [Col. 1002A]. When they saw him and supposed that he was Philippicus, they abandoned the spoils and hastened back to the battle.

When the fighting had continued for many hours, the commander gave the order to strike the Persian horses with spears. This was done, and the Persian army was put to flight. The Romans gained a great triumph, killed many of the Persians, and stripped them of their possessions.

On the following day Cardarigas again armed himself for battle, having gathered his forces. After a second engagement, the Romans again won, and many Persians were killed. Two thousand were also captured alive and sent to Byzantium. Cardarigas fled as well, and the Persians rejected him with insults.

Philippicus sent Heraclius, the father of Heraclius who later became emperor, as subcommander and investigator of the barbarians [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ὑποστράτηγον ἐπὶ κατασκοπῇ, “subcommander for reconnaissance.”]. After taking the troops, Heraclius entered Babylonia and besieged the fortress of Clomannus [Note: [Col. 1001D] Χλωμάρον; [Col. 1002B]].

Cardarigas, however, selected untrained soldiers together with pack animals [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ἱπποζυγίων, “pack animals.”]. After gathering a crowd, he boasted that he was moving the army, and by night, through fortified and obscure places, they reached the rear of the Romans, not at all confident that they would be able to engage them hand to hand.

An untimely fear fell upon Philippicus, and he made use of an astonishing flight [Note: [Col. 1002D] Ἀλόγως, “irrationally” or “without reason.”]. When the Romans learned of this, they too were turned to flight through places difficult to traverse, encountering many dangers. When the sun had risen, they were freed from the disaster, since no one pursued them. Reaching the commander, they reviled him with the harshest insults. The Persians, however, thinking that the flight was feigned, did not dare to pursue them.

Heraclius crossed the Tigris and set fire to the notable settlements and strongholds of the Median region [Note: [Col. 1002D] Χωρία, “settlements” or “districts”; [Col. 1002C]]; then he returned to Philippicus with much booty.

In the fifth year of the reign of Maurice [Note: [Col. 1002D] Alternatively: “the Avar Chagan,” throughout; “by treaty.”], Chajanus, having dissolved the treaty, savagely attacked Moesia and Scythia, overthrowing Ratiaria, Bonomia, Aquae, Dorostolum, Zandapa, and Marcianopolis [Note: [Col. 1002D] Κωνωνίαν καὶ Ἄκυς, “Cononia and Aquae.”].

Commentiolus came to the coastal region. Having divided his army, he distinguished the unreliable from the best. He ordered forty thousand useless men to guard the rampart, while taking six thousand chosen men: of these he gave two thousand to Castus, two thousand to Martinus, and with two thousand himself hastened against the barbarians.

Castus came to Zardapa and Haemus [Note: [Col. 1002D] Ἐπὶ τὰ Τζαπάρδα καὶ Αἶμον, “to Zardapa and Haemus.”]. Finding the barbarians settled in idleness, he destroyed many of them. After obtaining much booty, he entrusted it to an armed escort for safekeeping.

Martinus, having reached the region around the city of Nean [Note: [Col. 1002D] Εἰς τὰ περὶ Τομαῖαν, “to the region around Tomi.”], unexpectedly fell upon Chajanus and killed many of his men, so that Chajanus purchased his own safety by flight. Martinus, glorious in victory, returned to the commander, where he had promised to await them.

Commentiolus, however, overcome by fear, returned to Marcianopolis. When they did not find him there, they gathered their armies and encamped in the narrow passes of Haemus [Note: [Col. 1002D] Ἐπὶ τοὺς στενωποὺς τοῦ Αἴμου στρατοπεδεύονται, “they encamp in the narrow passes of Haemus.”].

Martinus, seeing Chajanus crossing the river, returned to the commander. Castus, having crossed the river and approaching those Avars who had gone ahead, defeated them in battle. But Castus, deceived by the promises of a certain commander [Note: [Col. 1003D] Alternatively: “of a certain vain demon.”], did not return to the commander. On the following day Chajanus seized the crossings and hemmed him in.

The people were therefore divided, and each man fled through the forests as best he could. Some were captured by the barbarians and revealed where Castus was hiding. After capturing him, the barbarians rejoiced.

Chajanus, proceeding at midday, hastened toward Thrace and reached the Long Walls. Commentiolus, however, who was hiding in the forests of Haemus, came out with Martinus. Reaching Chajanus, they found him unprepared, because the Avar multitude had spread throughout Thrace. During the first watch of the night [Col. 1003B] he hastened against him, and a great deed would certainly have been accomplished if a certain accident had not frustrated his effort.

When one pack animal overturned its load, someone called out to the animal’s master to lift the load, saying in the language of his homeland: “Turn back, turn back, brother” [Note: [Col. 1003D] Τόρνα, τόρνα, φράτρε, “Turn back, turn back, brother.”]. The master did not hear the many calls at all. But the people, hearing this, thought that the enemy was approaching, and they turned to flight, shouting at the loudest volume, “Turn back, turn back!”

Chajanus, clothed in immense fear, fled completely. Romans and barbarians appeared to be fleeing from one another, with no one pursuing.

Moreover, Chajanus, having gathered his forces, besieged the city of Aperia. He attempted to kill Busan, the Manganar of the city [Note: [Col. 1003D] Μάγγαναρ; alternatively, “Manganarium.”], when he was discovered. Busan begged him to spare his life in return for giving him a large amount of money. But Chajanus [Col. 1003C] had him bound and presented him to the city.

Busan himself appealed to the inhabitants of the city to ransom him, explaining how often he had fought for the city. A certain citizen persuaded the crowd that this should not be done. Since Busan was despised, he promised to hand the city over to Chajanus. After a siege instrument had been made—the device they call a “ram” [Note: [Col. 1003D] Πολιορκητικὸν ὄργανον, “siege instrument.”]—he captured the city.

The barbarians departed by their ingenious stratagem, reduced other cities to slavery as well, and returned with many captives.

When the Byzantines heard that Castus had been captured by the barbarians, they turned against Maurice with great abuse and openly assailed him with insults.

At the same time Heraclius, the father of Heraclius, attacked a Persian fortress and captured it. Likewise Theodore captured the fortress of Mazarus [Note: [Col. 1003D] Τὸ μάζαρον φρούριον, “the fortress of Mazarus.”], and both men came to Bavides [Note: [Col. 1003D] Εἰς τὸ βεϊοῦδες, “to Bavides.”].

Although the fortress was extremely well fortified, a soldier named Saphires, using goads and driving them against the joints of the stones, made an entrance through them. When that brave man had climbed to the crown of the wall, a Persian drove him off. Saphires fell downward, but the Romans caught him on their shields. He courageously undertook the task again, and once more was driven back from the fortification.

Again the Romans caught him on their shields, and for a third time he attempted the assault. When he had climbed to the top of the wall, he killed the Persian. Then, presenting his head to the Romans, he filled them with great confidence. Many imitated the brave man and climbed the wall by means of poles. The fortress was surrendered to the Romans. They killed some of the Persians, took others captive, and set fire to the fortress together with its furnishings.

Meanwhile Philippicus again traveled to Byzantium, leaving Heraclius as commander of the Romans. When he reached Tarsus and learned that the emperor had appointed Priscus commander of the East and sent him there, he wrote to Heraclius, ordering him to dismiss the army and come to Armenia to Narses, and to make Priscus’s arrival known to him.

The emperor had ordered Philippicus to deprive the army of a quarter of its pay. Philippicus, however, fearing that this would provide an opportunity for tyranny, did not obey the emperor concerning this matter. Consequently, he was removed from his command.

Priscus, arriving at Antioch, ordered the soldiers to assemble at Monocarton [Note: [Col. 1003D] P. Pith., “Monocertum collected”; Franc. Pith., “Monocartum [Col. 1004D] collected.” Greek manuscript: Μονόκαρτον.]. They also summoned Germanus, to whom the command of the Edessenes had been entrusted, together with the bishop; and he went with them to the army, intending to celebrate the feast of Easter with them.

The commanders of the army came to meet him with two bandon standards at some distance from the army [Note: [Col. 1004D] Μετὰ τῶν βάνδων· ἀπὸ δύο σημείων τοῦ στρατοπέδου, “with the bandon standards, from two points of the camp.”]. But Priscus, following custom, did not dismount from his horse or use the customary greetings. This was the beginning of the hostility, for crowds endure common insults with greater severity.
