After the feast day, the emperor’s grim letters were displayed [Col. 1004C]. The crowds therefore converged upon the commander’s tent, some carrying swords and others throwing stones or pieces of wood. Priscus became afraid and, mounting his horse, escaped the danger by flight.

They tore down his fixed tent and plundered everything that belonged to him. He reached Constantia, where physicians treated him for the blows inflicted by stones and for his wounds. He sent the city’s bishop to make a settlement and promised that he would persuade the emperor not to deprive them of any share in the customary distributions.

But the army rejected the bishop with insults. They declared Germanus commander, unwilling though he was, by lifting him upon a shield. They overturned the imperial statue and demolished its images. They were about to break out into tyranny and plunder the cities [Note: [Col. 1004D] Διαχωρεῖν ἤμελλον καὶ τὰς πόλεις κυκλεύειν; perhaps σκυλεύειν, “to plunder the cities.”], unless Germanus had prevented them from doing so by many threats and exhortations.

Priscus made these events known to the emperor, and the emperor once again appointed Philippicus commander of the East. Priscus returned to Byzantium.

The army, however, affirmed by oaths that it would in no way be governed by Maurice. The barbarians rejoiced in the Romans’ calamities [Note: [Col. 1004D] Ταῖς βαρβαρικαῖς, “barbarian.”].

The emperor sent Aristobulus, curator of the imperial residences [Note: [Col. 1005D] Τὸν κουράτωρα τῶν βασιλικῶν οἴκων, “the curator of the imperial residences.”], to the army, so that by oaths and gifts he might dissolve the tyranny; and he did so.

After the tyranny had been overthrown, a great war arose between the Persians and Romans around Martyropolis. The Romans, attacking the Persians with their power and the valor of their commanders, killed Maruzas, the Persian commander [Note: [Col. 1005D] Βάροζας, “Barozas.”]. Three thousand were also captured alive, including commanders of Persian forces [Note: [Col. 1005D] Alternatively: “the commanders of the Persian units,” τῶν περσικῶν ταγμάτων ταξίαρχοι.]; only one thousand returned to Persia.

The Romans sent many Persian spoils from Persia to the emperor, together with all the captives and the bandon standards.

In the month of December, in the sixth indiction, the Lombards brought war against the Romans, severely ravaging the Roman territory and plundering the exarchate of Ravenna. The peoples of the Maurusians also inflicted great disturbances upon Africa [Col. 1005B].

In Persia there is a prison called Lethe. The king of the Persians confined many people from different nations there, together with the captives from the city of Dara. These men, in despair, rose against their guards. They killed Marusa and brought his head to Byzantium [Note: [Col. 1005D] Μανουσᾶν καὶ τὴν τούτου ἀδελφὴν λαβόντες εἰς τὸ Βυζάντιον ἧκαν, “having killed Manousas and taken his sister, they came to Byzantium.”].

The emperor received them with great joy, and the army scarcely received Philippicus again as commander. When war arose between the Persians and Romans around Martyropolis, the Romans were defeated. The emperor removed Philippicus from the command once more and sent Commentiolus as commander of the East.

Heraclius, however, prospering in the war, killed the Persian commander. After Asarthatus had been killed [Note: [Col. 1006D] Alternatively: “Asrathatus.”], the Persians fled and the Romans pursued them. After great slaughter had been inflicted upon them, the Romans also captured the garrison and sent many spoils to Byzantium.

Finally, the emperor made the city splendid with cavalry reconnaissance and commercial activity.

Hormizd, king of the Persians, sent the commander Bara, who had been promoted, together with many powerful men, against Suania. Unexpectedly attacking him at the Araxes River, he moved his camp.

After the Turks had been conquered, Hormizd’s power among the Persians increased so greatly that he even received forty thousand gold pieces in tribute from the Turks, although previously he himself had paid an equal amount to the Turks.

When Maurice learned of this, he advanced Romanus to the command and sent him with a powerful force into Suania. When Romanus reached Lazica [Note: [Col. 1006D] Alternatively, Jazicen.] and approached the Phasis River [Col. 1005D], he moved the army into Albania.

When Bara heard that Romanus had set out, he mocked the affair. He also wished to capture the Roman battle line by hand, for he had not entered into war against the Romans.

Romanus, however, divided the Roman forces, leaving the untested men with the baggage. Taking ten thousand with him, he hastened against the barbarians and ordered two thousand to precede the army. When they encountered the Persians who had advanced before them, they put them to flight [Col. 1006A] and killed them all.

When flight ensued, all the Persians, hemmed in by an estate blocking their way, perished [Note: [Col. 1006D] Alternatively: “a ravine,” κρημνοῦ.]. The Romans advanced as far as the barbarians’ rampart, so that Bara was astonished at it.

When Romanus heard this, he began to encourage the army, and they prepared to fight in the plain of Albania. Bara attempted to steal the battle, but his plan was frustrated. Romanus rose and prepared himself with great elegance.

When the armies engaged one another and many of the barbarians had been killed, a great victory came to the Romans. The barbarians were stripped, and, deprived of burial, became food for the beasts.

When Hormizd, king of the Persians, heard this, he could not bear the disgrace. He sent Bara a woman’s garment and deprived him of his command.

Bara, in turn, prepared a rebellion, advanced [Col. 1006B] into tyranny, and provoked Hormizd by reciprocal insults in letters. He wrote this superscription on the letter: “Bara sends this to Hormizd, son of Chosroes.” [Note: [Col. 1006D] Ὁρμίσδᾳ τῇ θυγατρὶ Χοσρόου ὁ βαραᾶμ ταῦτα: “Bara [sends] this to Hormizd, daughter of Chosroes.” The wording differs from the Latin.]

After assembling the troops, he asserted that Hormizd was angry with the army because it had been defeated by the Romans. He displayed forged letters, supposedly sent by Hormizd, concerning the reduction of the soldiers’ pay. He reminded them of Hormizd’s savagery, cruelty, greed, and violence; of how he delighted in murders and was hostile to peace; of how he had handed nobles over to chains, killing some with the sword and others with a tiger; and of how he forced the Persians to divide their forces in great battles so that they might be destroyed and not rebel against him.

With such words Bara addressed the army and kindled a great tyranny against Hormizd. They all fortified Bara with oaths and jointly resolved to depose Hormizd.

Hormizd sent his armed master Ferrochan with a force against Bara [Note: [Col. 1006D] Φερογάνην τὸν μάγειρον αὐτοῦ, “Ferrochan, his cook.”].

Bara, however, told Ferrochan that it was not fitting for Persians to bring arms against Persians. He reminded them of Hormizd’s harshness, injustice, delight in bloodshed, love of murder, faithlessness, arrogance, and violence.

The people around Ferrochan, recognizing that Bara had spoken the truth, killed Ferrochan, joined Bara, and went toward Ctesiphon.

Hormizd was holding Byndoes, a man of great dignity, in chains. While affairs were in a state of great confusion, Besta [Note: [Col. 1006D] βεσδᾶν, “Besta.”], the brother of Byndoes, rushed into the prison, brought out his brother Byndoes, and, having gathered a rustic or civic crowd, entered the palace at the third hour of the day.

They found Hormizd seated upon the royal throne according to royal custom and subjected him to many insults. Byndoes seized Hormizd, removed the diadem from his head, and handed him over to prison. They asked that Chosroes be given the ancestral throne.

Moreover, Hormizd sent his messenger from his prison to the Persians, asking to speak with the commander concerning what was expedient [Note: [Col. 1007D] Alternatively: “to the Persian woman”; Greek manuscript, τῇ Περσίδι, “to the Persian woman.”].

On the following day the Persian senate assembled in the palace together with the crowd. They brought Hormizd out in chains. Hormizd reminded the Persians that such things ought not to be done against kings. He recounted how many trophies he had won since becoming king, what good deeds he had performed for the Persians, how he had compelled the Turks to pay tribute to Persia, forced the Romans to love peace, and captured Martyropolis; he also recounted the benefits he had received from his father.

He asked that Chosroes be removed from the kingship as a friend of strife, ambitious, a lover of blood, arrogant, injurious, and eager for battles. He declared that he had another son, whom he begged them to advance as king.

Byndoes answered Hormizd [Col. 1007B], bringing his transgressions into the open and rousing everyone against him. They brought Hormizd’s wife and son into the midst, and cut them in two with a saw, dividing them in the middle before Hormizd’s eyes [Note: [Col. 1007D] Ἐδιχοτόμησαν, “they split in two.”].

They also deprived Hormizd of his eyes and placed him in prison. Chosroes treated his father somewhat kindly in confinement, giving him every kind of food. Hormizd, however, abused him in return and trampled upon what was sent by the king.

Therefore Chosroes became angry and ordered him to be beaten across the loins with clubs from the forest until he died. This deed made the Persians sorrowful and increased their hatred of Chosroes.

Chosroes gathered the forces of his kingdoms, went out against Bara, and came to the plain of the Zab River, where Bara had a rampart. Suspecting that some of the nobles were attached to Bara [Col. 1007C], Chosroes killed them.

When the people became disturbed, Chosroes fled with a few men, and all who had been with Chosroes went over to Bara. Chosroes hesitated about what he should do. Some advised him to withdraw to the Turks, others to the Romans.

Chosroes mounted his horse, loosened its bridle, and ordered everyone to follow wherever the horse moved. The horse directed its course toward the Roman side. Chosroes was found at Ceresium [Note: [Col. 1007D] Κερκέσιον] and sent his ambassadors, making his arrival known.

It happened that the patrician Probus, who was there, received him and informed the emperor about him by letter. Bara sent ambassadors to Maurice, asking him not to assist Chosroes.

The emperor Maurice ordered the commander Commentiolus to receive Chosroes at Hierapolis and honor him with imperial service.

In the same year the emperor ordered a litany to be performed at Blachernae in memory of the Mother of God, and ordered praises to be sung to Our Lady, naming the observance the Panegyris.

Maurice made Chosroes king of the Persians and sent to him Domitian, bishop of Melitene and his relative, together with Narses, to whom he entrusted command of the war.

When they came to Chosroes, they led all the Roman forces into Persia [Col. 1008A]. When Bara learned this, he gathered his forces and encamped at a place called Alexandrines, intending to prevent the troops coming from Armenia from joining Narses.

Maurice had ordered Musticon, commander of the Armenian army, to receive the troops and join Narses in arranging the war against Bara. During the night the Roman forces united and drew up their battle line against Bara.

Bara, held by fear, had encamped on a mountain. When a dreadful battle was fought, Narses, disregarding the elephants, broke the center of the barbarian phalanx. As a result, Bara’s other phalanxes also weakened, and the tyrant’s forces fell into a great flight.

Narses pursued the Persians without restraint, strewing them with slaughter, and brought six thousand captives to Chosroes [Col. 1008B]. Chosroes killed all of them with the sword. But he sent all those who were Turks to the emperor in Byzantium.

The Turks had a sign on their foreheads, a cross marked in black [Note: [Col. 1007D] Τοῦ σταυροῦ κεντιτοῦ διὰ μέλανος, “a cross marked in black”; alternatively, “with their foreheads scarred.” [Col. 1008D] P. Pith.: “with their foreheads scratched.”]. The emperor asked them how they came to bear this sign on their foreheads.

The Turks replied that many years earlier a plague had occurred in Turkey, and that some Christians had devised this sign; from that time, salvation had come to their homeland.

The Roman army took Bara’s tent and furnishings, together with the elephants, and brought them to Chosroes. Bara fled into the interior of Persia, and thus their war was brought to an end.

Chosroes, therefore, surrounded by great victory, recovered his throne. As Narses was returning to his own country, he said to Chosroes: “Remember, Chosroes, this present day: the Romans are giving you the kingdom.”

Fearing a treacherous assassination, Chosroes asked Maurice for one thousand Romans to guard him. Maurice, who felt affection for Barbarus [Note: [Col. 1008D] Βάρμαδον, “Barmadus.”], granted his extensive request. Thus the war between the Persians and the Romans came to an end.

Meanwhile, when the Easter festival arrived, Theodosius, the son of Maurice, was crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople. In the same year the emperor Maurice completed the church of the Forty Holy Martyrs, which Tiberius had begun to build.

Meanwhile, although profound peace had occupied the East, an Avar war weighed upon Europe [Note: [Col. 1008D] The reading appears to be “Avar”; the passage in Theophanes is corrupt.]. Therefore the emperor transferred forces from the East into Thrace.

In the ninth year of his reign, when spring was beginning and the armies had reached Thrace, Maurice went out with them to see what had been destroyed by the barbarians. The Augusta, the patriarch, and the senate begged the emperor not to enter the war in person but rather to entrust it to the commander.

The emperor did not consent. As he was going out to Septimium, a solar eclipse occurred. When he was at Rhegium, he encouraged the crowds with money.

While he was going hunting, a very large wild boar charged against Caesar. Because of the miraculous terror, the horse tried to throw Caesar off. After causing a long disturbance, however, it could not throw Caesar. Thus the boar departed, driven away by no one [Note: [Col. 1009D] Conjecturally “wounded”; τρωθείς].

Moreover, while traveling by ship toward Perinthus, amid violent winds and rain, when the sailors had given up hope, the emperor’s boat was carried away, so that he scarcely reached the place called Daonium and was unexpectedly saved.

That night a little woman gave birth and uttered pitiable cries. When morning came, the emperor sent someone to see what had happened. They found a child who had been born without eyes or eyelids, whose hands did not extend to the arms, and whose lower back naturally had something attached to it like a fish’s tail.

When he saw this, the emperor ordered that it be killed. On that same day the emperor’s horse, which was surrounded by golden ornament, suddenly split apart as it fell. The emperor was saddened, taking all these things as omens.

On the following day three men of Sclavinian origin were detained by the Romans. They carried nothing made of iron, but only lyres. The emperor asked them both where they came from and where their dwelling was located.

They said that by origin they were Sclavinians, but that they lived near the end of the western Ocean. They reported that Chajanus had sent an embassy to them, with gifts for the leaders of their people, seeking their assistance against the Romans.

They said that they had sent their own taxiarchs to give Chajanus an explanation, because they could not send him auxiliary forces owing to the length of the journey. They claimed to have spent eighteen months on the road and thus to have come to the Romans.

They carried lyres because they had seen none of their countrymen armed and because their region did not know what iron was [Col. 1009C].

The emperor, admiring both their age and the great size of their bodies, sent them to Heraclea. When he came to the coast and learned that ambassadors of the Persians and the Franks had arrived, he returned to the palace.

In the tenth year of the reign of Maurice, Chajanus sought to receive an increase in the terms of the agreements. The emperor, however, did not accept the barbarian’s proposals. Therefore Chajanus again made war, devastated Sigidon, and moved his camp against Sirmium.

The emperor ordered Priscus, commander of Europe, to go. Priscus ordered Sylvianus, appointed subcommander, to go ahead [Note: [Col. 1009D] Σαλβιανὸν ὑποστράτηγον, “Sylvianus, subcommander.”]. They advanced against the barbarians, engaged them in battle, and the Romans won.

When Chajanus heard this, he gathered his forces and hastened to war [Col. 1009D]. But when Sylvianus saw the multitudes, he was astonished and withdrew to Priscus.

When Chajanus learned of the Romans’ withdrawal, he went to the coast, then to Saint Alexander, and handed everything there over to the all-devouring fire.

Crossing into Drizipera [Note: [Col. 1009D] Alternatively: Dirizipera; Greek manuscript, Δριζήπερα], he attempted to destroy the state, employing instruments of devastation. The inhabitants of Drizipera, however, drew up their battle line against him for a long time.

They surrounded the gates and threatened to defeat the barbarians, although they were in great fear. Then a certain divine power came to their aid. At midday the barbarians thought they saw Roman forces coming out of the city, and they supposed that they would have to engage them in battle. Struck with terror, they fled in tireless flight and reached Perinthus.

Priscus, unable even to endure the sight of the barbarian multitudes, entered the fortress of Zurulus and fortified it. The barbarian attempted to besiege Priscus.

When Maurice heard this, he was uncertain what should be done. Then, after adopting an excellent plan, he armed himself against the countless number of barbarians. He persuaded one of the excubitors, by means of great gifts and promises, to attack the barbarians voluntarily, and he gave him a letter for Priscus containing the following:

“To the most glorious commander Priscus:

Do not fear the harmful undertaking of the barbarians, for this has been done for their destruction. Know that Chajanus will return with great confusion to his own country, which has been assigned to him by the Romans. Therefore let Your Glory remain near Zurulus, leading them around there. We shall send ships by sea and capture their families, and he will be forced to return to his own country, filled with confusion and loss.”

When Chajanus received and read the letter, he became afraid. He sent peaceful proposals to Priscus with a few gifts, poor and unworthy ones, and returned in powerful flight to his own land.

In the eleventh year of the reign of Maurice, the same emperor sent Priscus with all the Roman forces to the Ister River, to prevent the Sclavinian peoples from crossing.

When Chajanus learned that Priscus was at Dorostolum, he sent ambassadors to him and brought an accusation, claiming that the Romans had initiated the war. Priscus excused himself, saying that he had not come to wage war against the barbarians but had been sent by the emperor against the Sclavinian peoples.

When Priscus heard that Ardagastus had scattered the Sclavinian forces for plundering, he crossed the Ister at midnight and unexpectedly attacked Ardagastus [Note: [Col. 1009D] Alternatively: “he joined Ardagastus.”].

When Ardagastus sensed the danger, he scarcely escaped alive, having not yet mounted his horse [Note: [Col. 1010D] Conjecture: “having mounted a bare horse”; Greek ἵππου τε γυμνοῦ ἐπιβάς.]. The Romans killed many Sclavinians, devastated Ardagastus’s territory, captured abundant booty, and sent it to Byzantium through Tatemer.

But while Tatemer was traveling lightly equipped, he gave himself over to drunkenness and luxury, and the Sclavinians attacked him [Note: [Col. 1010D] Τατίμερ ἐκλύτως, “Tatemer unencumbered” or “lightly equipped.”]. Overcome by fear, he came to Byzantium in flight.

The Romans who appeared to have been with him, however, being exceedingly hostile to the Sclavinians, gained a most glorious victory over the barbarians and presented the emperor with the captives unharmed. The emperor rejoiced and, together with the whole city, offered grateful hymns to God.

Priscus, relying on his confidence, advanced into the interior of the Sclavinian territories. Gipes, a man of the Christian religion, defected to the Romans, showed the Romans an entrance, and held the barbarians in check [Note: [Col. 1010D] Γήπαις, “Gipes.”].

By Gipes’s treachery, therefore, the river having been crossed, Priscus discovered at midnight Musacius, king of the barbarians [Note: [Col. 1010D] Μουσούγιον τὸν ῥῆγα τῶν βαρβάρων, “Musacius, king of the barbarians”; [Col. 1011A]], corrupted by drunkenness. He was celebrating the funeral feast of his own brother.

After capturing him alive, Priscus inflicted slaughter upon the barbarians. Having captured much and abundant booty, the Romans gave themselves over to drunkenness and gluttony. Then the barbarians, gathering together, threatened the victors. There would have been a reciprocal exchange, more savage than the earlier valor, had not Genzo, standing firm with the Roman infantry, prevented the barbarians’ attack by a brave battle.

In the twelfth year of the reign of Maurice, when Priscus had again reached the Ister and had plundered the Sclavinian peoples, he brought the emperor no small amount of booty.

The emperor sent Tatemer to Priscus and ordered the Romans to remain there throughout the winter. When the Romans learned of this, they objected, asserting that it could not be done because of the barbarian forces and because the region was quite unfavorable to them [Col. 1011B].

Priscus, however, won them over by persuasive words to winter there and fulfill the emperor’s command.

In the thirteenth year of the reign of Maurice, prodigies were born in the suburbs of Byzantium: one child, namely, with four feet, and another with two heads. Those who write histories with diligent care say that such things do not signify good fortune for the cities in which they are born.

The emperor deprived Priscus of the command and made his brother Peter commander of the Roman forces. Priscus, therefore, after gathering his forces and before Peter had arrived, crossed the river.

When Chajanus heard of the Roman army’s crossing, he was greatly astonished. He sent to Priscus to ask the reason and to demand a share of the booty, allowing the Romans on those terms to cross the river. For he was exceedingly enraged at the prosperity of the Romans.

Priscus therefore sent him an ambassador concerning this matter, namely Theodore the physician, richly endowed with shrewdness and intelligence.

Theodore saw that Chajanus was a great boaster, making arrogant replies, uttering threats, and claiming to be lord of all nations. He therefore softened the barbarian’s pride with an ancient story, saying:

“Listen, Chajanus, to a profitable tale. Sesostris, king of the Egyptians, illustrious, exceedingly fortunate, renowned for his wealth and his unconquerable power, reduced very many great nations to slavery.

“Falling into arrogance, he sat upon a chariot constructed of the gold and precious stones attached to it, and subjected four conquered kings to the yoke, making them draw the chariot.

“When this was taking place during a splendid festival, one of the four kings repeatedly turned his eyes backward and watched as the wheel revolved. Sesostris questioned him, saying: ‘Why do you fix your eyes behind you?’

“He replied: ‘I marvel at this wheel, which is unstable and moves in such a way—now lowering the lofty, and again raising up those who have been brought low.’

“Sesostris, understanding the parable intelligently, then established a law that kings should no longer draw the chariot.”

When Chajanus heard this, he smiled and said that he sought peace. Priscus returned the booty to Chajanus for the crossing and, after taking all the spoils, without [source ends incomplete].

He crossed the river with loss. Moreover, Chajanus was highly praised for having accepted these things. Priscus came to Byzantium, and Peter assumed the praetorship.

[Col. 1012A] In the fourteenth year of the reign of Maurice, the emperor ordered the praetor Peter that the Romans should receive one third of their pay (roga) in gold, one third in weapons, and another third in various garments. When the Romans heard this, they turned toward rebellion. But the praetor, fearing the consequences, assured the soldiers that this was not true and displayed other letters to the armies, ordering that those who had performed brave deeds and triumphed over dangers should enjoy the greatest repose in the city, be supported among the veterans at public expense, and that the soldiers’ sons should be enrolled in the places of their parents. By such persuasion he pacified the people, and they praised Caesar with an encomium of good repute.

Peter reported these events to the emperor. When he came to Marcianopolis, he sent ahead one thousand men. They encountered Sclavini carrying off a great deal of Roman [Col. 1012B] booty; pursuing them, they killed them, recovered much booty, and restored the Roman property to the countryside.

In the same year the emperor built a round solarium at Manaura, set up his own statue in the middle of its courtyard, and placed weapons there.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Maurice, while Peter was engaged in hunting, a wild boar suddenly encountered him and crushed his foot against a tree; he suffered for a long time from unbearable pain. Nevertheless, when the emperor heard that many peoples of the Sclavini had risen against Byzantium, he denounced him in extremely harsh letters and with severe reproaches.

Peter, however, was compelled to reach Novas. The inhabitants of the city, together with common soldiers and the bishop, came out to meet him. When the praetor saw them, their weapons, and their fear, [Col. 1012C] he ordered them to abandon the city and join the Roman force. But the soldiers assigned to guard the city refused to do this. Then the praetor, overcome with rage, sent Genzon with a multitude of soldiers.

When the inhabitants realized what was happening, they took refuge in the church and remained there with the doors of the temple shut. Genzon, out of reverence for the temple, withdrew without accomplishing anything. Peter, however, angered, removed Genzon from the praetorship and sent Scribo, ordering that the bishop be brought to him in disgrace. The assembled citizens, for their part, drove Scribo from the city with dishonor.

After closing the gates, they extolled the emperor Maurice with praises, but heaped insults upon the praetor; thus Peter withdrew from there in disgrace.

[Col. 1012D] Moreover, he sent one thousand men ahead to reconnoiter. They caught up with one thousand Bulgars. The Bulgars, relying confidently upon Chajanus’s peace, proceeded without fear. The Romans attacked the Bulgars. The latter sent seven men to warn them that the peace must in no way be broken.

When those who had gone ahead heard this, they reported it to the praetor. He said: “Even if the emperor himself should come, I will not spare these men.” When the battle was joined, the Romans were routed; but the barbarians did not pursue them, lest, though victorious, they should expose themselves to danger.

The praetor then flogged the taxiarch of the advance guard. When Chajanus learned of this, he sent envoys to Peter, accusing him of initiating the affair and of the Romans’ having broken a just peace without cause. Peter, however, using deceptive language, declared that he had been unaware of the movement, but nevertheless arranged to give double the booty.

[Col. 1013A] Thus, after the barbarians had lost their plunder and recovered twice as much in return, they took measures to preserve the peace. Peter then hastened against the exarch Ardagastus. The barbarians encountered him near the riverbank and prevented him from crossing. But the Romans, shooting arrows from the straits, routed them. As they turned in flight, Ardagastus was immediately struck and died.

The Romans crossed, seized much booty, and were returning to their own territory. But when their guides lost their way and led them into waterless places, the army was placed in danger. As they continued their journey, they came by night to a river called the Helicium. Once the Romans were across the river, barbarians hidden along the banks shot at those who were drawing water. The Roman troops were thereby subjected to great distress, and, defeated by the barbarians, were put to flight.

When Maurice heard this, he deprived Peter of the praetorship [Col. 1013B] and sent Priscus once again as praetor of Thrace.

In the sixteenth year of the reign of Maurice, the general Priscus went forth into Thrace, reviewed the army’s forces, and found that a great number of them had been destroyed. Having assembled these forces, he came to the River Ister and to Novae. When Chagan learned this, he sent envoys to inquire into the reason for his arrival. Priscus admitted that he had come for the purpose of hunting. But Chagan said: “It is not right to hunt in another’s territory.” Priscus, on the contrary, said that it was his own territory, and reproached him with having fled from the East.

The barbarian, after destroying the wall of Sigidon, advanced toward Roman territory. When Priscus learned this, he came to the island of the Ister and, taking dromons, came to Chagan at Constantiola, wishing to speak with him. When Chagan came to the bank of the river [Col. 1013C], Priscus addressed him sadly. Chagan said to him: “What have you to do, Priscus, with me and my land? Do you intend to take this [Note: [Col. 1013D] Another reading: ‘by deceit, and from’] from my hands? Let God judge between me and the emperor Maurice, and let him require from his hands the blood of the Roman army and of my army.”

Priscus replied: “Restore the city of Sigidon to the Romans.”

He said: “Are you trying to take one city from us? Before long you will see fifty Roman cities reduced to servitude under the Avars.”

Priscus, however, brought ships up the river to Sigidon, plundered it, and drove the Bulgars out of it.

In the seventeenth year of the reign of Maurice, Chagan, gathering his forces, hastened into Dalmatia. When he reached Balcha, he plundered all forty cities situated around it. When Priscus learned this, he sent Gudon to investigate the situation. Gudon concealed himself in a small valley and, at daybreak, fell upon their rear, immediately killing them all and bringing the captured booty to Priscus. When Chagan learned of the disaster, he returned to his own country, and Priscus returned to his own quarters.

In the eighteenth year of the reign of Maurice, Priscus took his forces and came to Sigidon. Chagan, having gathered his own power, suddenly appeared in Moesia and attempted to capture the city of Comea. Therefore Priscus, leaving Sigidon, came close to him.

When the festival of Easter was being celebrated and the Romans were wasting away from hunger [Col. 1014A], Chagan, hearing of this, informed Priscus that he should send him wagons to carry food to the Romans, so that they might celebrate their festival with rejoicing. Accordingly, Priscus sent him forty wagons filled with provisions. In the same way, Priscus also sent the barbarian certain Indian spices—namely, pepper, Indian leaf, costus, cassia, and other things of this kind that are sought after—while Chagan was staying at Sirmium. When Chagan received these gifts, he rejoiced greatly over them, and until the festival had ended Romans and barbarians lived together, with no fear between the two armies.

When the festival had ended, the barbarians separated from the Romans, came to the city of Dirizipera, and plundered it. They set fire to the church of Saint Alexander and stripped his tomb, which was covered with a silver roof. They also inflicted insults upon the martyr’s body, and, after taking great booty in Thrace, they feasted magnificently, exulting over the Romans [Col. 1014B].

When Commentiolus came to Byzantium, the city was overwhelmed by the greatest agitation and distress, so that, seized by fear, the inhabitants resolved to abandon Europe and migrate to Asia and Chalcedon. The emperor also, taking the guards and an armed, selected troop, fortified the wall. The populace guarded the city and urged the senate to advise the emperor to send an embassy to Chagan.

But God, taking vengeance for the martyr Alexander, brought a plague of sickness upon the barbarians. In a single day fever and bubonic disease killed seven of Chagan’s sons, together with many other [Note: [Col. 1013D] Another reading: ‘crowds’] disgraceful persons. Thus, after the joy of triumph with songs and [Col. 1014C] hymns, lamentations, tears, and inconsolable mourning took possession of the barbarians.

The senate, however, urged Caesar to send an embassy to Chagan. The emperor sent Armazo to Chagan, together with many women from Dirizipera, so that he might soften the soldiers with conciliatory words. But Chagan did not wish to accept the gifts, overcome by unbearable lamentation for the death of his sons. He said to the envoy:

“Let God judge between me and the emperor Maurice. I will return his captives, receiving from him one coin for each person” [Note: [Col. 1014D] Nicephorus: ‘two’].

Maurice absolutely refused to give this. Chagan again asked to receive one coin for each person. But the emperor would not agree even then—[Note: [Col. 1014D] Greek: Ἀνὰ κεράτια δʹ, ‘four keratia apiece’] not even four siliquae.

Then Chagan, stirred by rage [Col. 1014D], killed them all and returned to his own country, having imposed upon the Romans an agreement to pay fifty thousand gold pieces. He also declared that he would not cross the River Ister.

From this point a great hatred against the emperor Maurice arose, and people began to subject him to curses. Likewise, the people in Thrace were stirred up against the emperor with insults. The army sent representatives to the emperor against Commentiolus, alleging that he had committed treason in battle. Among them was Phocas, who addressed the emperor with particular severity and contradicted him in the council, so that one of the patricians struck him on the face and pulled out his beard.

The emperor, however, did not accept the people’s complaint against Commentiolus [Col. 1015A], but dismissed them as ineffective. For this reason the beginning of a conspiracy against the ruler was set in motion.

Moreover, at about this same time in Egypt, on the River Nile, while the prefect Menas was walking with the people in a place called Delta (Δέλτα), at sunrise creatures in human form appeared in the river—namely, a man and a woman.

The man had a broad chest and a terrifying face, reddish hair mingled with white, and he exposed his nakedness down to the loins; he was seen naked by everyone, while the remaining parts of his body were covered by the water. The prefect bound him by oaths not to destroy the spectacle before everyone had been satisfied with this unexpected sight.

The woman had breasts and a feminine face [Col. 1015B], long hair, and, until the ninth hour, the whole people marveled at these creatures. At the ninth hour they sank into the river.

Menas duly wrote these things to the emperor Maurice.

In the nineteenth year of the reign of Maurice, on Easter Day, the Augusta Sophia, wife of Justin, together with Constantina, the wife of Maurice, brought a crown that had been fashioned and presented it to the emperor. After examining it, he went into the church and offered it to God, hanging it above the holy table on triple little chains woven with stones and gold.

When the Augustae learned this, they were greatly distressed, and Constantina, in a quarrel with the emperor, made the festival day an occasion of contention.

Since the emperor paid no attention to the complaints of the troops stationed in Thrace, Commentiolus again took armed men, came to the Ister, and joined Priscus at Sigidon [Col. 1015C]. The peace that had existed with the Avars was dissolved. After it was dissolved, they came to Viminacium, which is a large island in the Ister.

When Chagan heard this, he gathered his forces and advanced into the Roman countryside. He therefore assigned four of his sons, together with other forces, to guard the crossings of the Ister. But the Romans, having constructed rafts, crossed the river and, under the general Priscus, engaged Chagan’s sons in battle.

Commentiolus, having fallen ill, remained seated on the island of Viminacium. When the battle had lasted many hours and the sun had set, after three hundred Romans had already been killed, four thousand barbarians perished. Likewise, on the third day, when they were fighting, the Romans approached the barbarians from higher ground, drove them toward the lake, and, routing the Avars, killed many of them. Among these, Chagan’s sons were also killed, and the Romans won a glorious victory [Col. 1015D].

Chagan, however, gathering a large force, advanced against the Romans. While the battle continued, the Romans routed the barbarians and won a victory more distinguished than all the others.

Meanwhile Priscus sent four thousand men ahead, ordering them, after crossing the River Tyrso, to investigate the movements of the barbarians. But the barbarians, knowing nothing of what had happened, celebrated a festival and feasted together. The Romans fell upon them secretly and inflicted the greatest terror. They killed thirty thousand Gepids and other barbarians, and, after securing abundant booty, returned to Priscus.

Chagan, once more gathering his forces, came to the Ister. When battle was joined [Col. 1016A], the barbarians were defeated and drowned in the currents of the river; many of the Sclavini also perished with them. The Romans took alive three thousand Avars, eight hundred Sclavini, three thousand two hundred Gepids, and also two thousand other barbarians.

Chagan then sent envoys to the emperor Maurice, attempting to recover the captives. But the emperor, not yet having learned of the Romans’ glorious victory, wrote to Priscus ordering him to return only the Avars to Chagan.

In the same year, a certain man, clothed all around in monastic dress and distinguished in religion, ran with a drawn sword from the marketplace to the bronze statue of the gladiator. He foretold that the emperor would die by the sword in a universal slaughter.

Likewise, Herodian openly foretold to Maurice the things that were going to happen to him.

While the emperor, barefoot at night, was conducting a litany with the entire city and proceeding toward the Carpian districts, certain men from the crowd, rioting against the emperor, threw stones at him, so that the emperor barely escaped with his son Theodosius and completed his prayers at Blachernae [Col. 1016B].

In the twentieth year of his reign, Maurice came to his senses. Knowing that nothing is hidden from God, but that he repays everyone according to his works, and reflecting upon the crime he had committed in the matter of the captive woman, whom he had not redeemed, he judged it better to receive punishment for his sin in this life rather than in the future. He therefore sent written prayers to all the patriarchal sees, to all the cities subject to him, and to the monasteries in the desert and in Jerusalem, and sent money, candles, and incense to the laurae, asking them to pray for him, so that he might receive punishment here [Col. 1016C] and not in the age to come.

He was also scandalized by his son-in-law Philippicus, because he was called a *philiter* [the term is uncertain]. Philippicus, however, repeatedly swore to the emperor that he was pure in his service and harbored no deceit against him.

When Maurice was entreating God to grant mercy to his soul, one night, while sleeping, he saw himself in a vision standing before the bronze gate of the palace, before an image of the Savior, with a great crowd standing there as well. Then a voice came from the inscription of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, saying: “Deliver Maurice.”

The ministers of judgment seized him and brought him before a purple navel-like object that stood there. The voice said to him in its own words: “Where do you wish me to repay you—here or in the age to come?”

When he heard this, he replied: “Lover of mankind, Lord [Col. 1016D], and righteous judge, here rather, and not in that age.”

The divine voice then ordered that Maurice, his wife Constantina, his sons, and all the members of his household be handed over to the soldier Phocas.

When Maurice awoke, he summoned the man who had been sleeping before him and sent him to his son-in-law Philippicus, ordering him to bring Philippicus quickly to him. When the man had gone, Maurice summoned Philippicus. Philippicus rose, called his wife Gordia, kissed her, and said: “Farewell; you will not see me again.”

She cried out loudly through her tears to the *parakoimomenus*: “I adjure you by God: what is this matter, for which he is summoning him at this hour?”

The man swore that he did not know, since the emperor had suddenly risen from sleep and sent him.

Philippicus therefore asked to receive the body of Christ [Col. 1017A], and then to hasten to the emperor. His wife lay on the ground, rolling about, weeping, and entreating God.

When Philippicus entered the imperial chamber, he threw himself at the emperor’s feet. The emperor said to him:

“Forgive me for the Lord’s sake, because I have sinned against you. Until now I have been offended by you.”

Then, ordering the *parakoimomenus* to leave, he rose and fell at Philippicus’ feet, saying:

“Forgive me, for now I know with certainty that you have done me no wrong. But tell me: do you know of a soldier named Phocas among our troops?”

Philippicus, reflecting, said to him:

“I know one man who, a short time ago, was sent from the army as an officer and opposed your rule.”

The emperor said: “What sort of man is he?”

He replied: “Young and reckless, but nevertheless timid” [Col. 1017B].

Then Maurice said: “If he is timid, he is certainly also a murderer.”

He related to Philippicus the revelation of his dream.

That night a star appeared in the sky, called a comet.

On the following day Magistrianus arrived. He had been sent to the holy Fathers of the desert and brought back the following answer from them:

“God, having received your repentance, will save your soul and establish you with the saints, together with your entire household. But you will depart from the imperial office with disgrace and danger.”

When Maurice heard this, he glorified God magnificently.

As autumn approached, the emperor Maurice ordered Peter that the army should winter in the region of the Sclavini. The Romans refused and would not consent to do this, both because their horses would be weakened and because they would have to transport a great quantity of booty [Col. 1017C]; they also feared the multitudes of barbarians known to be scattered throughout the region, and began to plot a revolt.

The general, angered against the people, dismissed them in anger [Note: [Col. 1017D] Pithoean fragment: “into madness”; Pithoean edition: “into a state of dementia”]. Heavy rains then fell upon the people, together with severe cold.

Peter was staying twenty miles away from the army. Maurice, however, troubled Peter by letter, ordering him to cross the Ister and obtain the army’s winter provisions from the region of the Sclavini, so that he would not be forced to provide public supplies to the Romans.

The general summoned Gadimus and said:

“The emperor’s orders seem exceedingly harsh to me, ordering the Romans to winter in a foreign land. For it is cruel not to obey him, and again it is most cruel to obey him. Avarice prepares no good; it is the mother of all evils. As the emperor languishes under its influence, he is, because of it, bringing these greatest evils upon the Romans.”

He summoned the army’s *taxiarchs* and explained the emperor’s intention to them.

When the people heard this, they stirred up riots, and certain distinguished leaders among them fled and came to the general. The crowds, gathered together, brought forward Phocas the centurion as their commander; they raised him upon a shield and acclaimed him as commander with praises.

When Peter heard this, he fled and reported everything to the emperor. But the emperor, hearing of these difficulties, tried to conceal them from the crowds. On the second day he held an equestrian spectacle [Col. 1018A], concealing the misfortunes of the crisis.

The people of the Greens cried out, saying:

“Constantine and Commentiolus, thrice Augustus of the Romans, bring troubles upon your people, so that crosses may be set up for them because of the sins we possess. May God, who created all things, subject to you every enemy and foe, both internal and external, without bloodshed.”

The emperor said to the factions:

“Let the excess and restlessness of the irrational soldiers not disturb you.”

The Blues replied:

“May God, who permitted you to rule, subject to you everyone who attacks your rule. And if it is a Roman who, having broken faith, turns his back on you, may he reduce that man to servitude under you without bloodshed.”

The emperor armed these men and restrained them with conciliatory speeches. Together with the *demarchs*, he ordered them to guard the city walls [Col. 1018B].

Moreover, while the emperor’s son Theodosius was hunting at Callicratia with his father-in-law Germanus, the Romans sent Theodosius a letter asking that he be made emperor. If that could not be done, they asked at least that Germanus be proclaimed emperor. “For,” they said, “we will no longer tolerate being ruled by Maurice.”

When Maurice learned this, he summoned his son. He ordered Commentiolus to watch the walls, while he accused Germanus and Germanus’ son of having been the cause of these calamities.

When Germanus attempted to defend himself, Maurice said:

“O Germanus, there are two grounds for my suspicion: the people’s letter to you, and the fact that, although they have consumed everything, they spared no one except your own people. Spare me, Germanus, the trouble of making a long speech [Col. 1018C]. Nothing is sweeter than to die by the sword.”

Germanus fled to the temple of the Mother of God called Cyri. When the emperor learned this, he sent the eunuch Stephen to bring Germanus out of the church. When Stephen attempted to drag him out by force, Germanus’ supporters resisted and expelled Stephen; then, taking Germanus, they fled into the great church.

The emperor beat his son Theodosius with rods, asserting that Germanus had escaped because of him. He sent guards to bring Germanus out of the great church. At this, great commotion arose in the city.

Germanus wished to leave and surrender himself. But the crowds would not allow him to leave and attacked the emperor with great insults, saying:

“May he who loves you have no skin, Marcionite” [Col. 1018D] [Note: [Col. 1018D] Another reading: “Maurice”].

When those who were guarding the walls learned this, they betrayed their post through negligence.

At midnight Maurice removed his imperial robe, clothed himself in a private garment, entered a dromon with his wife, his sons, and Constantinus, and fled. Throughout the entire night the forces assailed the emperor with the worst insults and also reproached the patriarch Cyriacus.

When a great storm raged, Maurice was saved amid enormous dangers at the shrine of Saint Autonomus. During the night he was also seized by arthritic pains—what are called pains of the hands and feet.

He sent his son Theodosius with Constantinus to Chosroes, king of the Persians, asking him to remember the things that had been done to him by Maurice and to repay his former benefaction by helping his son.

Germanus, meanwhile, sent to Sergius, the demarch of the Green faction, asking him to assist him in obtaining the imperial power. He promised to honor the Green faction and to elevate Sergius himself to great dignities.

Sergius disclosed this to the distinguished men of the populace, who absolutely rejected it, admitting that Germanus had never abandoned his affection for the Blues.

The Greens went out and acclaimed the tyrant Phocas with great praise. They persuaded him to come to Septimium. Phocas therefore sent Theodore, the *a secretis*, who entered the great church and read before the people that the patriarch, the senate, and the populace should come to Septimium [Col. 1019B].

When this had been done and everyone had assembled at Septimium, the patriarch Cyriacus extracted from the tyrant a profession of the orthodox faith and an undertaking that he would preserve the Church without disturbance.

The tyrant appeared to urge Germanus on. When Germanus pretended that he was unwilling, and the populace praised the tyrant, he was proclaimed evil, and the tyrant was advanced as lord of the scepters. Calamity prevailed over prosperity, and great misfortunes for the Romans began.

The tyrant’s proclamation took place in the church of Saint John the Baptist. After remaining there for two days, on the third day he entered the imperial palace and sat upon the imperial carriage.

On the fifth day he crowned his wife Leontia as Augusta.

On that day [Col. 1019C] the factions rioted against one another over the stations assigned to them. The tyrant sent his fellow demarch Alexander to restrain the factions. Alexander laid hands on Cosmas, the demarch of the Blues, drove him away, and tore him apart with insults.

The Blues, angered, cried out:

“Go and learn order! Maurice has not died.”

When the tyrant heard this, he was stirred to kill Maurice. He sent soldiers, who took him to Chalcedon, to the harbor of Eutropius. First he tortured him by slaughtering his sons, and then punished the emperor himself. For his five male sons were killed one after another before his eyes.

Maurice, however, patiently enduring his misfortune, invoked God in all things and repeatedly said:

“You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is upright” [Col. 1019D].

Thus the death of the sons became the father’s epitaph, displaying virtue amid the mass of calamity.

When a nurse stole one of the emperor’s children and offered her own child to be killed in his place, Maurice did not consent, but demanded his own child.

Some say that, after the child was killed, milk flowed together with blood, so that all who looked upon it lamented bitterly.

Thus the emperor, rising even above the laws of nature, exchanged this life for another.

From that time onward, various and immense afflictions did not cease to beset the empire. Finally, Chosroes, king of the Persians, dissolved the peace, the Avars devastated Thrace, and both Roman armies were destroyed [Col. 1020A]. Thus, when Heraclius was reigning and conducted a most diligent inquiry into the armed forces, he could find no one from the whole multitude that had been present in the tyranny of Maurice and Phocas, except two men.

# PHOCAS

In the year 595 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the tyrant Phocas killed Maurice, as has been related, together with his five male children. He ordered their heads to be placed [Note: [Col. 1019D] Greek: Ἐν τῷ κάμπῳ τοῦ τριβουναλίου, “in the field of the tribunal”] in the tribunal field for many days. He went out of the city and gazed at them until they began to stink.

His brother Peter was also killed, together with many other leading men.

A report, however, holds that his son Theodosius had escaped and was thus found safe.

Moreover, Chosroes, king of the Persians, magnified this report [Col. 1020B], lying about it in one way and another, and saying that Theodosius was with him, as though he were protecting him, while hoping to obtain the Roman empire. He was convicted in many ways, especially because he suddenly began wars and greatly devastated Roman affairs.

Meanwhile, a certain Calligraphus of Alexandria, a venerable man, was going home from the morning vigil at midnight. He saw bronze statues [Note: [Col. 1019D] See Nicephorus XVIII, chapter 41, and Cedrenus. Manuscript: “from altars”; Pithoeus’ manuscript: “from bronze, brass”] being torn away and saying in a loud voice that Maurice and his sons had been killed, together with all the events that had taken place at Byzantium.

When morning came, he went and reported these things to the Augustal [Note: [Col. 1020D] Greek: Ἀυγουσταλίῳ, “to the Augustal”]. The Augustal ordered him to disclose them to no one and, having written, awaited the outcome. When the ninth day had passed, behold, a messenger arrived announcing the killing of Maurice. Then the Augustal published the demons’ prophecy before the people [Col. 1020C].

Narses, formerly a Roman general, prepared a rebellion against the tyrant and seized Edessa. Phocas therefore wrote to Germanus, the general who was besieging Edessa.

Narses wrote to Chosroes, king of the Persians, urging him to gather his forces and establish a war against the Romans.

Phocas made his brother Domentiolus *magister* and Priscus commander of the guards.

In the second year of Phocas’ reign, Chosroes, king of the Persians, sent a large force against the Romans. Germanus was afraid, but was compelled to engage in battle. When he was wounded in it, his attendants carried him as far as the city of Constantia, and the Romans were defeated. Germanus also breathed his last on the eleventh day.

Phocas transferred his forces from Europe to Asia and, after adding agreements with Chagan, supposed that he would quiet the nations of the Avars. Having divided these forces, he sent some against the Persians, and others, together with Leontius the eunuch and his chief officer, to besiege Edessa against Narses.

Chosroes, having gathered his forces, took up position at Dara. Narses, however, went out from Edessa and fled to Hierapolis.

Meanwhile, Chosroes engaged the Romans at Ardumum. Having constructed a fortification from elephants, he entered battle and won a great victory. He captured many Romans and punished them by beheading.

After these events Chosroes returned to his own country [Col. 1021A], leaving Zongoi with the forces.

When Phocas learned this, he raged against Leontius, brought him to Byzantium in iron shackles and with disgrace, appointed his nephew Domentiolus general, and made him overseer of the palace.

In the third year of Phocas’ reign, Chosroes sent Cardariga and Rusmaysan, who plundered Roman territory.

Domentiolus, having given Narses his word and persuaded him by many oaths to trust him that he would suffer no injury from Phocas, sent him to Phocas. But Phocas did not keep his word and burned Narses alive.

The Romans were therefore deeply saddened, because Narses inspired great fear in the Persians, to such an extent that the sons of the Persians trembled when they heard his name. The Persians, however, rejoiced with great joy.

In the fourth year of Phocas’ reign [Col. 1021B], the eunuch Scholasticus, a distinguished man of the palace, took the lady Constantina and her three daughters and fled to the great church, on the advice of the patrician Germanus, who desired the imperial power.

A great sedition therefore arose in the city. Germanus sent a talent of gold to the demarch of the Greens so that he might cooperate with him, but the leading men of the populace refused to accept it.

The tyrant sent men to the church to drag out the women. The patriarch Cyriacus resisted the tyrant and absolutely refused to allow the women to be taken from the church by force. But after Phocas had sworn to him with certainty that he would not harm them, they were brought out of the church and shut up in a monastery.

Moreover, in the same year the Persians captured Dara together with all Mesopotamia and Syria, inflicting a great but uncounted captivity [Col. 1021C].

In the fifth year of his reign, Phocas joined his daughter Domentia to Priscus, the patrician and commander of the guards. When the wedding had taken place in the palace of Marnas, he ordered an equestrian spectacle to be held.

The demarchs of both factions placed the insignia of Priscus and Domentia beside the four columns, with imperial emblems. When the emperor heard of this, he became angry and sent for the demarchs—Theophanes and Pamphilus. He had them stand naked and ordered them to be beheaded.

When he sent the *protocursor* to ask them on whose orders they had done this, they replied that they had done it according to the custom of the *lineator* [Note: [Col. 1021D] Another reading: *linealirae*].

The *lineatores*, or surveyors, were asked why they had done this. They replied that, since the emperors had been named by everyone, they had done it on their own initiative [Col. 1021D].

Priscus, meanwhile, was overcome with fear, lest he should incur the emperor’s anger. When the crowds cried out that pardon should be granted them, Phocas granted the pardon.

From that time onward Priscus was disgruntled and was not on good terms with Phocas.

Meanwhile, a certain woman named Petronia became a servant of the empress Constantina and carried messages to Germanus.

When the report spread that Theodosius, the son of Maurice, was alive, both Constantina and Germanus entertained good hope. But the wicked Petronia disclosed these matters to the tyrant.

The tyrant handed Constantina over to the commander Theoprepius [Note: [Col. 1021D] Another reading: “Theodore”] to be tortured. While she was being tortured, she confessed that she knew the patrician Romanus and his conversations. Romanus was arrested and interrogated, and he stated that others were also his accomplices in a conspiracy against the tyranny.

The prefect of the East, Theodorus, was arrested, and the tyrant killed him. He cut off the feet of Helpidius [Note: [Col. 1022D] Another reading: “beating his hands and feet”] and handed him over to the fire, while Romanus was beheaded.

He slaughtered Constantina and her three daughters with the sword at the place where Maurice had been killed.

He killed Germanus and his daughter by the sword.

Likewise, he killed John Gizan, the patrician; Theodosius, who was distinguished by the rank of *Subdiva* [Note: [Col. 1022D] Another reading: “Subadiuvae”]; Andrew Sanctocroben [Note: [Col. 1022D] Another reading: “Scombra”; another: “Scombrum”]; and David, the *chartophylax* of Hormisdas.

In the same year the Persians crossed the Euphrates and devastated the whole of Syria, Palestine, and Phoenicia, inflicting a great slaughter upon the Romans [Col. 1022B].

In the sixth year of Phocas’ reign, Priscus, unable to endure both the unjust murders and the other evils perpetrated by Phocas, wrote to Heraclius the patrician and general of Africa, asking him to send his son Heraclius and Nicetas, the son of the patrician Gregoras, his subordinate general, so that they might come against the tyrant Phocas.

For he had heard that Heraclius was contemplating rebellion in Africa, and therefore no ships had sailed to Constantinople that year.

Phocas killed all of Maurice’s relatives, as well as Commentiolus, the general of Thrace, and many others.

A mortality also occurred in that year, together with a shortage of every kind of commodity.

Moreover, the Persians, advancing with Cardariga, captured Armenia and Cappadocia. In battle they routed the Roman forces, captured Galatia and Paphlagonia, and came as far as Chalcedon, devastating every age-group without mercy.

These men were imposing tyranny upon the Romans from outside the gates, while Phocas was committing worse acts within, killing and taking captives [Col. 1022C].

In the seventh year of Phocas’ reign, the Jews of Antioch, after a violent quarrel had arisen against the Christians, killed Anastasius the Great, patriarch of Antioch. They thrust his entrails into his mouth and afterward dragged him through the streets of the city. They also killed many of the citizens and burned them.

Phocas appointed Bonosus commander of the East and Chotin *magister militum*, and sent them against the Jews [Col. 1022D]. But they were unable to calm their disturbance.

Gathering their armies, they attacked them, killed very many, and drove some of them into exile from the city after cutting off their limbs.

Phocas held an equestrian spectacle, and the Greens provoked him with insults, shouting:

“Have you drunk again in the *gabasta*?” [Note: [Col. 1022D] Nicephorus XVIII, chapter 43: “Gabatha.”] “Have you lost your senses again?”

At Phocas’ command, Comas, the prefect of the city, cut down many of them, beheaded some, and killed others by putting them into sacks and throwing them into the sea.

The Greens, gathering together, set fire to the praetorium. They burned the senate house [Col. 1023A], the archives, and the prisons; the prisoners escaped from them in chains.

Phocas, angered by this, ordered that they should not serve in the army [Note: [Col. 1023B] Another reading: “he ordered the Greens not to serve as soldiers”].

Meanwhile, Heraclius, the general of Africa, suffering harassment from the senate, summoned his son Heraclius to be sent against the tyrant Phocas. His subordinate general Gregoras likewise sent his son Nicetas by the overland route, arranging that whichever of them arrived first and overcame the tyrant should receive the empire.

That year the winter became extraordinarily severe, so that the softness of the sea was turned into the hardness of ice.

Phocas then ordered Macrobius [Note: [Col. 1023B] Another reading: “Scribonius”] Scribonius to be shot at Septimium, hanging from a lance of the kind on which recruits were trained, as though he had been privy to the conspiracy against him.

For Theodorus, the Cappadocian prefect, Helpidius, the *praepositus* of the armament, and various others had formed a plan to kill Phocas in the hippodrome [Col. 1023B].

After the meal, Theodorus [Note: [Col. 1024B] Pithoeus: “the praetorian prefect”], the *praepositus praetorio*, began to unfold his plan to them [Col. 1024A].

It happened that Anastasius, the *comes largitionum*, was also present there. After the meal, when the matters concerning the conspiracy had been recounted, Anastasius regretted having been found there. He did not say what was in his heart, but remained silent.

Helpidius, however, persisted, saying:

“Do you not want me, when he has taken his seat on the throne above the hippodrome, to seize him, tear out his eyes, and then kill him?”

He promised to provide them with chariots.

When the matter became known to Phocas through Anastasius’ betrayal, he ordered the prefect, Helpidius, and the leading men who had known of the affair to be investigated with the utmost care.

When they were interrogated, they confessed the details of the conspiracy and that they had intended to make Theodorus emperor.

Phocas therefore ordered Theodorus, Helpidius, Anastasius, and the others who had known of his conspiracy to be beheaded.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

[Col. 1023]

# HERACLIUS

[Col. 1023B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 602, Heraclius was proclaimed emperor in Africa. He came with ships furnished like fortresses, containing within them little chests and images of the Mother of God, like reliquary boxes. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Another reading: as George also relates.] George also is said to have come from Africa and Mauretania, leading a large army. Likewise Nicetas, son of the patrician Gregora, came through Alexandria and the Pentapolis, bringing with him a great number of infantry.

Heraclius had been betrothed to Eudocia, daughter of Rogatus the African, who at that time was in Constantinople together with Epiphania, Heraclius’s mother. When Phocas heard that Heraclius’s mother was in the city, as well as Eudocia, who had been betrothed to him, he seized them and kept them under guard in the imperial monastery called the Monastery of the New Repentance.

When Heraclius had gone to Abydos, he found Theodore, the count of Abydos, and, questioning him, learned what was happening in Constantinople. Phocas, however, sent his brother Domentiolus, the master of the soldiers, to guard the Long Walls. When he learned that Heraclius had left Abydos, he abandoned the walls, fled, and entered Constantinople.

Heraclius, meanwhile, at Abydos received all the exiled nobles whom Phocas had banished there, and with them went up to Heraclea. Stephen, metropolitan of Cyzicus, took the image of the holy Mother of God Mary from the church and brought it to Heraclius.

When he subsequently reached Constantinople, Heraclius put in at the harbor of Sophia and, joining battle, defeated the tyrant through the grace of Christ. The populace seized him, killed him, and burned him at the Taurus. Heraclius then entered the imperial palace and was crowned by Sergius, the patriarch, in the oratory of Saint Stephen located in the palace. On the same day his bride Eudocia was crowned Augusta [Col. 1024B], and both received wedding crowns from Sergius the patriarch; on that one and the same day he was presented both as emperor and as bridegroom.

In the month of May the Persians marched against Syria, and [Note: [Col. 1024D] Another reading: they captured Apamea.] they captured Capessa and Edessa and came as far as Antioch. [Col. 1024C] The Romans, meeting them, were defeated, and the entire Roman population perished, so that very few of them escaped.

In the second year of Heraclius’s reign, the Persians captured Caesarea in Cappadocia and led away many thousands of its inhabitants as captives. The emperor Heraclius found the affairs of the state in disarray. For the Avars had made Europe deserted, while the Persians had devastated all Asia, laid its cities waste, and destroyed the Roman army in battle. On seeing this, he began to hesitate about what he should do. Searching the army to see whether anyone might have survived, he found only two among all those who had served in the tyranny with Phocas against Maurice.

In the same year a son was born to the emperor by Eudocia, Heraclius the Younger, who was also called New Constantine, and the Augusta died in the same fifteenth indiction. In the third year of Heraclius’s reign, Epiphania, Heraclius’s daughter, was crowned Augusta by the patriarch Sergius in the palace oratory. In the same year, during the first indiction, Heraclius the Younger, son of Heraclius, who was also called Constantine, was crowned by the aforementioned patriarch. In that same year the Saracens also drew up their battle line against Syria, and, after devastating several villages, returned.

In the fourth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Persians captured Damascus and led away a great multitude as captives. The emperor Heraclius sent ambassadors to Chosdroes, asking him to cease shedding human blood without mercy, to fix the tribute, and to accept an agreement. He dismissed the ambassadors without result and gave them no explanation, hoping by every means to seize the Roman imperial power. [Col. 1025A]

In the same year Heraclius, acting incestuously, took his niece Martina as his wife and proclaimed her crowned by the patriarch Sergius.

In the fifth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Persians captured the Jordan by force of arms, as well as Palestine and the holy city, and through the agency of the Jews killed many people there—ninety thousand, as some say. For these Jews bought Christians, as many as each person could afford, and killed them. They seized Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, and brought him to Persia, together with the precious and life-giving wood and much booty.

In the same year another Constantine was born to the emperor, and he was baptized at Blachernae by the patriarch Sergius.

In the sixth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Persians captured all Egypt, Alexandria, and Libya as far as Ethiopia. After carrying off much booty, very many spoils, and money, they returned to their own country. They were entirely unable to capture Carthage; leaving a guard, they withdrew from besieging it.

In the seventh year of Heraclius’s reign, the Persians encamped against Carthage, which they also captured by force of arms. In the same year the younger Constantine, who was also Heraclius, son of Heraclius, became consul. He also promoted his younger brother Constantine, born to Heraclius and Martina, to the rank of Caesar.

In the eighth year of his reign, Heraclius again sent ambassadors to Chosdroes in Persia, requesting peace. Chosdroes again rejected them, declaring: “I will not spare you until you renounce the Crucified One, whom you confess to be God, and worship the Sun.”

In the ninth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Avars drew up their battle line against Thrace. Heraclius sent ambassadors to them and requested peace. When the Chagan had promised that he would make peace, the emperor went outside the Long Wall with all the royal ceremonial and many gifts to receive the Chagan, intending to obtain from him oaths and mutual pledges of peace.

But that barbarian, despising both his pledges and the things he had sworn, suddenly advanced tyrannically against the emperor. The emperor, astonished at this unexpected undertaking, escaped by flight and returned to the city. The barbarian, having obtained all the royal equipment and furnishings, overturned many villages and unexpectedly plundered those whom the hope of peace had deceived, carrying off as many people as he could capture.

In the tenth year of his reign, Heraclius sent ambassadors to the Avar Chagan [Col. 1025D], complaining about the wicked deeds he had committed and urging peace. Since he was preparing battle lines to send against Persia, he wished to make an agreement with the Chagan. The latter, out of respect for the emperor’s affection, declared that he had repented and promised that peace would be made. The ambassadors concluded treaties and returned in peace. In the same year the Persians captured Ancyra in Galatia.

In the eleventh year of Heraclius’s reign, the harsh Chosdroes imposed his yoke upon all people through the shedding of blood and the exaction of tribute. Elated by his triumph, he was in no way able to remain steady. Then Heraclius, having taken up the zeal of God and believing that he had made peace with the Avars, transferred [Col. 1026A] the forces of Europe into Asia and intended, with God’s cooperation, to hasten against Persia.

In the twelfth year of Heraclius’s reign, in April, on the fourth day, in the tenth indiction, the emperor Heraclius, having celebrated the Paschal solemnity, set out against Persia at once, on Monday evening. Since he was constrained by lack of funds after borrowing money from the venerable houses, he also took many candle-bearing vessels from the Great Church, together with other liturgical vessels. Having melted these down, he had gold and very many silver coins struck from them [Note: [Col. 1025D] Νομίσματα, καὶ μιλιαρίσια—“coins and miliarensia.”]

He left his son in the city with the patriarch Sergius to administer affairs, together with Bonosus, a patrician, an astute man who was wise and experienced in every matter. He also wrote to the Avar Chagan, asking him to take care of Roman affairs, as one who had made an agreement of friendship with him, appealing to him as guardian of his son.

Departing from the imperial city, he went out by the place called the Gates and traveled by ship. From there he proceeded through the other regions subject to him and selected a new army. He began to train these men and instructed them in the practices of war. Dividing the army into two parts, he ordered them to conduct mock battles and engagements with one another without bloodshed. He taught them the war cry and the charge against one another, so that when they encountered battle they would be astonished at nothing but would advance confidently against the enemy.

The emperor received in his hands a male figure of God, one not painted by human hands, but which, “in the word of the εἰκών” [image], which establishes and orders all things, brought forth a form without painting, as it were a birth without seed. Trusting in this image painted by God, [Col. 1026C] he began the contests, giving the people his oath that he would fight together with them unto death and cling to them as to his own sons. For he wished to possess authority through love no less than through fear.

When he found the army sunk in great indolence, fear, disorder, and disgrace, and scattered through many parts of the land, he immediately gathered it together. All together, as if with one voice, praised the authority and courage of the ruler. He strengthened them with words, saying:

“See, brothers and sons, how the enemies of God have trampled our land underfoot, devastated our cities, burned our altars, and filled the tables of the bloodless sacrifices with blood and murder; and how they have filled the churches, which admit no disgraceful practices, with the most disgraceful pleasures.”

Then, arming the ranks again for military training, arranging two armed divisions, setting up trumpets, and forming phalanxes of shields, the people stood clad in breastplates. For when he had more cautiously drawn up the battle line, he ordered them to engage one another. Violent thrusts and blows were exchanged, and the appearance of war was displayed. It was a terrifying spectacle to behold: danger without fear, and an advance toward slaughter without bloodshed, so that, when necessity came, each person might remain safer after seizing an opportunity for harmless killing.

After arming them all in this manner, he commanded them to abstain completely from injustice [Col. 1027A] and to pursue piety.

When he reached the regions of Armenia, he ordered chosen men to advance ahead. A multitude of cavalry from among the Saracens, who at that time were under Persian treaties, were secretly planning to attack the emperor. The emperor’s men who had gone ahead met them, captured their commander, and brought him bound to Heraclius; when the others were put to flight, they killed many of them.

Because winter was approaching, the emperor withdrew to the climate of Pontus. The barbarians thought that they could besiege him while he wintered there. But he eluded the Persians, turned aside, and hastened into Persia. When the barbarians learned this, they became embittered because of the unexpected report.

Sarbarus, the Persian commander, relying on his authority, came into Cilicia so that, after entering Roman territory, he might compel Heraclius to turn his back and flee. Fearing that the emperor might enter through Armenia and throw Persia into confusion, he was forced to follow the Roman army, intending to steal a battle and attack by night in darkness.

But, because the full moon shone with light throughout the entire night, he was thwarted in his deception. He reviled the moon, which had previously been an object of his worship, alleging that it had suffered an eclipse by some accidental occurrence. From that time Sarbarus feared to engage the emperor in battle. He took to a mountain like a gazelle and, looking down from above, observed the Roman army, well ordered and arranged with wise skill.

When the emperor learned of their fear, he remained in places suitable for rest, provoking Sarbarus to battle. The Persians often came down secretly from the mountain and stirred up engagements, but the Romans held the advantage in every respect [Col. 1027C], and their army’s confidence grew as they saw the emperor leaping forward and fighting in every encounter.

A certain Persian who had recently defected was enrolled in the emperor’s army. He fled back to the Persians, believing that they would destroy the Roman army. When he saw their fear, however, he returned to the emperor after ten days and clearly reported the entire terror of the barbarians.

Sarbarus could no longer endure remaining on the mountain and was forced to proceed to battle. Dividing his army into three parts, he suddenly descended at daybreak, prepared for battle before sunrise. The emperor, foreseeing this, arranged his army in three equally formed phalanxes for combat.

When the sun rose and the emperor was facing east [Col. 1027D], its rays blinded the Persians, since they worshiped the sun as a god. The emperor pretended that his people had been put to flight. The Persians, loosening their phalanxes, thought that they could pursue them without restraint.

The Romans then turned and calmly routed them, killing many of them. Pursuing them up the mountain, they drove them into precipices and trackless places, crushing them all there. Among those precipices they had taken up positions like wild goats. They captured many of them alive. They also seized their camp and all their equipment.

The Romans, raising their hands toward heaven, gave thanks to God and prayed without ceasing for the emperor, who had proved himself worthy. Those who previously had not dared even to look upon Persian dust now found their tents standing unmoved and stripped them of their belongings. Who could have expected the unconquerable race of the Persians to turn its back on the Romans?

The emperor therefore left the army with its commander to winter in Armenia and himself returned to Byzantium.

In the thirteenth year of his reign, Heraclius departed swiftly from the imperial city and hastened to Armenia. Chosdroes, king of the Persians, sent Sarmanzarim with his army to enter Roman territory. Heraclius wrote to Chosdroes, telling him either to embrace peace or to understand that he would enter Persia with his army.

Chosdroes neither embraced peace nor considered Heraclius’s message truthful. He thought that Heraclius would not dare approach Persia. But the emperor entered Persia on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

When Chosdroes learned this, he ordered Sarmanzarim to return. He gathered his forces from throughout Persia and, having entrusted them to Sathin, ordered Sarmanzarim to assemble them quickly and then advance against the emperor.

Heraclius summoned his army and encouraged them with exhortatory words, saying:

“Men, brothers, let us take the love of God into our minds and strive to avenge this injury. Let us therefore stand bravely against our enemies, for they have done many terrible things against Christians. Let us honor the Roman empire, which belongs to the Lord himself and not to another, and let us stand against enemies armed with impious weapons.

“Let us put on faith and not fear slaughter or the slaughtering nation. Let us reflect that we stand within Persian territory, where a great flight carries danger. Let us avenge the violation of virgins. When we see the limbs of our fellow soldiers torn apart, let us grieve in our hearts. These things do not bring any reward, but the prizes of everlasting life.

“Let us stand courageously, and the Lord God will cooperate with us and destroy our enemies.”

When the emperor had encouraged the people with these and many other exhortations, one man answered him on behalf of all:
