“You have expanded the narrowness of our hearts, Lord, enlarging your mouth in admonition. Your words have sharpened our swords and produced spirits that cannot be conquered. Through your words you have made us ready for action. We are ashamed, when we see you leading us in battle, and we follow your commands in every respect.”

The emperor then took his forces and immediately advanced into inner Persia [Col. 1028D], burning its cities and camps.

A certain terrifying miracle also occurred there. At the summer solstice the air became drenched with moisture, refreshing the spirits of the Roman army, so that they drew from this the greatest hope.

Heraclius further heard that Chosdroes was in the city of Gazaca with forty thousand fighting men. He advanced against him with great force. Some Saracens whom he had subdued and sent ahead encountered the guards of Chosdroes. They killed some of them and brought others, bound in fetters together with their commander, before the emperor.

When Chosdroes learned this, he abandoned both the city and the army and resorted to flight. Heraclius pursued him [Col. 1029A] and killed some who had been overtaken; the rest scattered here and there in disarray.

When the emperor reached the city of the Gazacenians, he rested his army in its suburbs. The Persians who had taken refuge with him reported that Chosdroes, while fleeing, had consumed all the crops in those regions with fire and had reached the city of Thebarma, situated in the east. There was a temple of fire there, as well as the wealth [Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: of Croesus, king of the Lydians.] of King Erisilidor, and the delusion of the coals. Having taken these things, he had proceeded toward the region [Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: he made his way toward Dastarger.]

The emperor departed from the city of the Gazacenians and reached [Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: Thebarmeson.] Thebarma. Entering it, he consumed the Temple of Fire with flames, burned the entire city, and pursued Chosdroes into the narrow regions of Media.

Chosdroes wandered from place to place and hid in these two regions [Col. 1029B]. Pursuing him, Heraclius laid waste many cities and regions. When winter approached, he deliberated where he should winter with his people. Some advised him to remain in Albania; others said that Chosdroes was advancing against him.

The emperor ordered the people to await the divine oracle for three days, conducting themselves chastely and purely. After receiving the response, he decided to winter in Albania.

As he was departing and traveling there, carrying with him a great amount of Persian booty, he suffered no small number of attacks from Persian divisions. By divine cooperation he gained the victory over them all.

Moreover, when a violent storm fell upon him on the way and frost overtook him in Albania, and he had fifty thousand prisoners [Col. 1029C], he took pity on them with a compassionate heart, broke their bonds, granted them pardon, and gave them rest. As a result, they all entreated him with tears to become Persia’s liberator from Chosdroes, the destroyer and butcher of the world.

In the fourteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, Chosroes appointed Sarrablagas prefect, a criminal man, greatly puffed up with pride. He entrusted him with an army—namely, those called [Note: [Col. 1029D] Alternatively, Chosdrogetae.] Chosdrogetae and Perozitae—and sent him into Albania against Heraclius. When they had entered the borders of Albania, they did not dare stand and fight before the emperor; instead, they held the passes leading into Persia, intending to lie in ambush while conducting a siege.

But Heraclius, as soon as spring arrived, departed from Albania across open country, rich in abundant provisions, and made his way into Persia, although the great length of the journey consumed much time. Sarrablagas, however, tried to take the shorter route, as being more direct, so that he might overtake him in Persian territory.

Heraclius therefore exhorted the people, saying:

> We know, brothers, that the Persian army, wandering through pathless places, both wears out their horses and weakens the men themselves. Let us hasten and proceed against Chosroes with all speed, so that, falling upon him unexpectedly, we may throw him into confusion [Col. 1030A].

But the people rejected this advice, especially the leaders of the Lazans, Abasgians, and Iberians. Thus they fell into trouble.

Sarbaras also arrived with his people, whom Chosroes had armed with every resource and sent through Armenia against Heraclius. Sarrablagas followed behind Heraclius, but did not engage him in battle, waiting to unite with Sarbaras and then arrange the fight. When the Romans learned of Sarbaras’s advance, they were seized with fear and fell at the emperor’s feet with tears, knowing how great an evil it is for a servant not to yield to his master’s wishes. Repenting of their disobedience, which they had wickedly committed, they said:

> Extend your hand to us, lord, before we perish [Col. 1030B]. We yield ourselves to you in whatever you command.

Then the emperor hastened to engage Sarrablagas before he could unite with Sarbaras’s forces. By making many attacks against him by night and by day, he drove him into fear; leaving both of them behind, he quickly pursued Chosroes.

Two Romans went over to the Persians and persuaded them to believe that the Romans were fleeing in terror. It happened, however, that they also heard another report [Note: [Col. 1030D] Alternatively, “rumor.”], namely that Sathin, the Persian prefect, was approaching with another army as reinforcements. When Sarrablagas and Sarbaras learned this, they strove to provoke Heraclius into battle before Sathin arrived and transferred the glory of victory to himself. Believing the deserters, they hastened against Heraclius and, approaching him, encamped, wishing to attack him all at once.

But Heraclius departed in the evening and traveled throughout the night. After moving away from them, he found a grassy field and encamped there. The barbarians, thinking that he was fleeing in fear, followed him in disorder in order to overtake him. He, however, met them and joined battle. Seizing a wooded hill and gathering his troops upon it, by God’s cooperation he routed the barbarians and, pursuing them through the defiles, killed a great multitude.

Sarrablagas also fell, wounded in the back by a sword. While they were engaged in the struggle, Sarbaras arrived with his army. The emperor turned upon him as well, killed many of his men, and scattered the rest in flight. He also captured their baggage [Note: [Col. 1030D] Greek: Τοῦλδον, *touldon*, “baggage.”]

Sarbaras, having joined with Sathin [Note: [Col. 1030D] Alternatively, Sain.], gathered the barbarians who had survived, and they again prepared to advance against Heraclius. But the emperor hurried into the territory of the Huns, through their difficult country, in rough and trackless places. The barbarians followed him.

The Lazans, however, together with the Abasgians, grew afraid and withdrew from the Roman alliance, returning to their own country. When Sathin noticed this, he pursued Heraclius with great fury together with Sarbaras.

The emperor gathered his army and encouraged them with words, strengthening them by his protection, saying [Col. 1031A]:

> Let the multitude of our enemies, brothers, not trouble you. For if God wills it, one man will pursue a thousand. Let us therefore give ourselves for the salvation of our brothers and receive the crown of martyrdom, so that the future may praise us and God may repay us with rewards.

By these and many other words he inspired courage in the army. With cheerful countenance he drew up the battle line. Although the two sides stood only a short distance apart, they did not attack one another from morning until evening.

In the evening the emperor took the road and proceeded. The barbarians again followed behind him [Note: [Col. 1031D] Alternatively, “and changing direction.”], accompanying him along the route and wishing to overtake him. They fell into marshy ground, however, and, wandering about, came into great danger.

The emperor crossed the borders of Persia and traveled through Armenia. Since that land was held by the Persians, many joined Sarbaras, and his forces thereby increased. When winter approached, he dispersed the multitude among their own districts so that they might rest in their houses.

When Heraclius learned this, he planned a night attack. A violent storm was raging, and Sarbaras had no suspicion. The emperor selected the strongest horses and the most powerful men in the army, armed the latter doubly, and ordered some of them to advance ahead against Sarbaras, while he himself followed with the others.

As they hurried through the night and reached an estate called Lasbanum at the ninth hour of the night, the Persians who were there, having learned of the attack, rose against them. The Romans killed all of them except one, who reported the matter to Sarbaras.

Sarbaras mounted a horse naked and barefoot and purchased his safety by flight. The emperor put to fire the women of Sarbaras and the entire Persian elite, together with the chiefs, satraps, and picked soldiers who had climbed onto the roofs of the houses and prepared to fight. Some he killed, others he consumed with fire, and still others were bound with handcuffs and fetters, so that almost none of those belonging to Sarbaras escaped.

They also seized Sarbaras’s weapons: his golden shield, his sword, his equally golden spear, his belt adorned with precious stones, and his footwear. After taking all these things, they advanced against those dispersed through the villages. When these people learned of Sarbaras’s flight, they fled without restraint. The emperor pursued and killed many of them, taking others captive, while the rest returned to Persia in confusion.

The emperor then gathered his army and wintered fearlessly in those regions with joy.

In the fifteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, Muhammad was regarded as prince of the Arabs. Heraclius gathered his army and deliberated by which route he should proceed. Two narrow and difficult roads lay before him: one led toward Tarentum, while the other led into the land of the Syrians.

The road leading toward Tarentum was indeed more distant, but it lacked provisions of every kind. The road leading into the land of the Syrians crossed the Taurus and offered abundant and plentiful food [Col. 1032A]. Everyone preferred this route, although it was steeper and more severe because of the great quantity of snow.

After crossing it with great labor in seven days, they reached the river Tigris. Having crossed it, they came to Martyropolis and Amida, where both the army and the captives rested. From there the emperor was also able to send letters to Byzantium, report everything concerning himself, and bring great joy to the city.

Sarbaras, having gathered his dispersed people, rose against him. The emperor sent a picked division of soldiers to guard the passes leading toward him and the approaches that lay toward the East. He himself moved about and came face to face with Sarbaras.

After crossing the river Nymphion, he reached the Euphrates, where there was a bridge joined together from ropes and boats. Sarbaras, however, cut the ropes of the bridge and moved the entire bridge from one bank to the other. When the emperor arrived and could not cross by the bridge, he moved about, found a ford, crossed it unexpectedly and without danger in the month of March, and reached Samosata.

After crossing the Taurus again, he proceeded to Germanicia. Having crossed Adana, he reached the river Saros. Sarbaras restored the bridge to its former place, crossed the Euphrates without hindrance, and followed after him.

But after the emperor crossed the bridge of Saros, he found a resting place for both the army and the animals and encamped nearby, refreshing them. Sarbaras also reached the opposite side. Having found the bridge and taken possession of the fortifications that the Romans had built upon it, he encamped.

Many Romans made disorderly sorties across the bridge and engaged the Persians, with great slaughter occurring among them. The emperor, however, forbade them to rush about in disorder, lest the adversaries should find a way to meet them at the bridge and cross over together.

The people did not heed the emperor. Sarbaras secretly stationed some of his forces in hidden places, then displayed himself as though fleeing. In this way he drew many Romans, against the emperor’s wishes, across the bridge in pursuit of him.

When they turned back and the Persians put them to flight, Sarbaras killed all whom he caught outside the bridge, making them suffer punishment for their disobedience. When the emperor saw that the barbarians had broken their ranks in pursuit [Col. 1032D], and that many of the Romans standing on the outworks had been killed, he pursued them.

A gigantic Persian man met the emperor and attacked him in the middle of the bridge. The emperor struck him and threw him into the river. When he fell, the barbarians turned to flight. Because the bridge was narrow [Note: [Col. 1032D] Alternatively, “like frogs.”], they threw themselves into the river on both sides, while others were cut down by swords.

A multitude of barbarians shot arrows from the riverbanks and resisted, preventing the Romans from crossing. But the emperor crossed and bravely resisted the barbarians with a few of his companions, fighting with extraordinary courage. Sarbaras himself was astonished at this and said to a certain Roman named Cosmas who stood beside him [Note: [Col. 1033D] They called him a deserter, Margarites.]:

> Do you see, Cosmas, how boldly Caesar stands for battle, fighting alone against such a multitude and rejecting the missiles like an anvil?

For he was recognized by his red boots [Note: [Col. 1033D] Greek: Ἐκ τῶν βασιλικῶν παρασήμων, “from the imperial insignia.”]. He inflicted many blows, although he received no dangerous wound in this battle.

They fought throughout the entire day. As evening approached, they separated from one another, and Sarbaras, fearing the night, withdrew. The emperor gathered his people and hurried toward the city of Sebastia. After crossing the river Alon, he remained there throughout the winter in great joy.

Chosroes, enraged, sent for and carried away the treasures of all the churches in the region subject to the Persians. He also compelled Christians to become followers of Nestorius [Col. 1033B], intending to humiliate or crush the emperor.

In the sixteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, Chosroes, king of the Persians, raised a new army for battle, gathering selected men from every nation—foreigners, citizens, and slaves. He handed this levy over to the prefect Sathin. He also took another fifty thousand selected from Sarbaras’s phalanx, joined them to Sathin, and named them [Note: [Col. 1033D] Greek: Χρυσολόχας, “Golden Companies” or “Golden Regiments.”]. He sent them against the emperor.

He sent Sarbaras with the remainder of his army to Constantinople, so that they might ally themselves with the Huns in the West, whom they call Avars, together with the Bulgars, Sclaveni, and Gepids, and then advance against the city and besiege it with united forces.

When the emperor learned this, he divided his army into three parts and sent them to guard the city [Col. 1033C]. He entrusted one part to his brother Theodore and ordered him to fight against Sathin. Taking the smaller division for himself, he hurried into Lazica and, while there, summoned the Turks from the East—whom they call Khazars—to his aid.

Sathin, arriving with the newly chosen army, reached Theodore, the emperor’s brother, and fought against him. But, through the aid of God and the intercessions of the greatly praised Mother of God, when the battle was joined, hail of extraordinary size fell upon the barbarians and struck many of them. The Roman battle line, however, remained unharmed.

The Romans routed the Persians and killed a great multitude. When Chosroes learned this, he became angry with Sathin. Sathin, overcome by severe weakness of spirit and falling ill, died. By Chosroes’s order, his salted body was brought to him, and Chosroes, though he was dead, had it beaten repeatedly.

The Khazars then broke through the Caspian Gates and entered Persia in the region of Adragia, together with their prefect Zeibil, who was second in rank to the Khagan. Wherever they traveled, they both plundered the Persians and committed cities and villages to fire.

The emperor also set out from Lazica to meet them. When Zeibil saw him, he hurried forward, embraced his neck, and bowed before him while the Persians of the city watched. The entire Turkish people fell prostrate upon the ground, stretched out upon their faces, and honored the emperor with a gesture that is foreign among the gentiles [Col. 1034A]. Their princes likewise climbed upon the rocks and fell down in the same manner.

Zeibil also offered his firstborn son to the emperor. Delighted by the young man’s words, Heraclius admired both his appearance and his wisdom. Zeibil selected forty thousand brave men and gave them to the emperor as auxiliaries. He himself then returned to his own country.

After receiving these forces, the emperor immediately advanced against Chosroes.

Sarbaras hurried toward Chalcedon, while the Avars approached the Thracian city and prepared to devastate it. They brought many engines against it and filled the bay with an infinite, or innumerable, multitude of carved ships brought from the Danube [Note: [Col. 1034D] Alternatively, “the left wing.”].

For ten days they besieged the city and waged war by land and sea. But through the power and cooperation of the Lord, and through the intercessions of the undefiled Mother of God and virgin Mary, they were defeated. A great multitude of their men having been laid low both on land and at sea, they returned to their own regions in great confusion.

Sarbaras, however, while besieging Chalcedon, did not depart. He wintered there, making raids, plundering the neighboring districts, and destroying cities by fire.

In the seventeenth year of his reign, Heraclius entered Persia in September together with the Turks. When Chosroes learned this, he was unexpectedly thrown into confusion because of the winter. But when the Turks observed both the winter and the frequent Persian attacks, they could not endure sharing them with the emperor. They gradually dispersed and all abandoned him [Col. 1034C], returning home.

The emperor addressed his people, saying:

> Know, brothers, that no one wishes to help us except God alone, and the Mother who bore him without seed, to show his power. For salvation does not lie in the multitude of peoples or weapons; rather, he sends his aid to those who hope in his mercy.

Chosroes, however, gathered his forces, promoted a warlike and exceptionally brave man named Razates to command them, and sent him against Heraclius.

The emperor committed the Persian cities and fortresses to fire, and as the Persians approached, he consumed them with his sword. On the seventh day before the Ides of October, he reached the region of Chamaita and refreshed his people for an entire week.

Razates arrived at Ganza and followed after him. As the Romans continued onward and consumed their provisions, Razates followed behind like a dog suffering from hunger and was scarcely nourished by a tenth of their supplies [Note: [Col. 1034D] Alternatively, “from crumbs.”]. When he found no provisions, many of the animals were consumed.

On the Kalends of December the emperor came to the great river Zaban. After crossing it, he encamped beside the city of Nineveh. Razates arrived and followed him near the ford. When he had come within three miles, he found another ford and crossed.

The emperor sent Bathanas, master of the soldiers, with a few picked men. Bathanas found the Persian prefect’s standard and, after killing his companion, brought back his head and his entirely golden sword. Having killed several others, he led twenty-six men alive to the emperor. Among them was Razates’ sword-bearer, who informed the emperor that Razates intended to fight against him, as Chosroes had ordered him, and that Chosroes had sent him three thousand armed men as reinforcements, who had not yet arrived.

When the emperor learned this, he sent the baggage ahead of him and followed after it, considering how he might find a place where he should fight before those three thousand could unite with them. Having found a field suitable for battle, he addressed the people and arranged the battle.

When Razates arrived there, he too drew up the battle line and advanced against the emperor in three divisions. The battle took place on the day before the Ides of December. The emperor rushed forward before everyone else and met the Persian commander. By divine power and through the assistance of the Mother of God, he struck him down, and those who were with him fled headlong.

Again another man confronted the emperor, and he too struck him down. A third also rushed against him and struck him on the lip with the point of his sword, inflicting this wound upon him. But the emperor killed him as well. When the trumpets sounded, the two armies engaged one another.

As a fierce battle was being fought, the emperor’s horse, called Dorcon, was severely wounded in the thigh by a spear-thrust from the infantry [Note: [Col. 1035D] Alternatively, “the horse Phalba.”]. The emperor also received many blows from swords to the face, but because he wore a covering woven from sinews, he did not receive a mortal wound.

Razates fell in this battle, as did three Persian commanders, almost all the chiefs, and the greater part of their army. Fifty Romans were also killed, and some were wounded; ten of the wounded later died.

The battle lasted from morning until the ninth hour. The Romans captured twenty-eight Persian standards, apart from those that had been broken. From the stripped corpses they took their cuirasses and helmets, as well as all their wagons. They remained separated from one another by a distance twice the range of an arrow. There was no flight.

Nevertheless, during the night the Romans watered and recovered their animals. The cavalry who were farther away remained until the seventh hour of the night, then moved back to their camps. After taking these spoils, the Romans departed and encamped at the foot of a rugged mountain, being cautious.

They also took many swords encased in gold, golden belts set with jewels, and Razates’ shield, entirely covered with gold, bearing a *petala* of one hundred and twenty [units unspecified]. They took his cuirass woven with gold and his *scaramaggin* [Note: [Col. 1035D] P. Pith., *charrure*; alternatively, *chamare*; Cedrenus, *scaramangium*.], bringing it together with his head, as well as a led horse and his saddle made entirely of gold.

One man was also captured, Barsumes, a chief of the Iberians living under Persian rule.

No one remembers a battle of this kind between Rome and Persia, one that continued throughout the entire day and in which the Romans were victorious. Yet this was accomplished solely through God’s help [Col. 1036A].

The emperor then led his assembled army against Chosroes in order to terrify him. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, the emperor learned that Razates’ forces—the men who had escaped from the battle—had united with the three thousand sent by Chosroes and were following behind him. He immediately captured Nineveh.

After crossing the great Zaban, he sent George, a commander of a thousand, with a thousand soldiers to hurry and seize the bridges of the Lesser Zaban before Chosroes learned of it. George traveled forty-eight miles during the night, seized the four bridges of the Lesser Zaban, and gained possession of the Persians found in the fortresses.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of January, the emperor reached the bridges, crossed over, and turned aside to the houses of Hyesdem. There he refreshed both the army and the animals and celebrated the feast of the Nativity of Christ.

When Chosroes learned that the Romans held the bridges of the Lesser Zaban, he sent word to the Persian army commanded by Razates that they should hasten, get ahead of the emperor, and proceed against him. They hurried on, crossed the Lesser Zaban, and got ahead of the emperor by other routes.

When the emperor captured the palace called Dezeridan, he destroyed and burned it. The Persians, after crossing the bridge of the river Torna, encamped there. The emperor then seized another palace of Chosroes called Rusa and overturned it.

He feared [Note: [Col. 1035D] Alternatively, “he considered.”] that the enemy would fight against him at the bridge of the river Torna. But when the Persians learned this, they abandoned the bridge and fled [Col. 1036C].

The emperor crossed without hindrance and seized another palace called Beibal [Note: [Col. 1036D] Alternatively, Berlam.]. Chosroes had also built a hippodrome there, but the emperor likewise destroyed it.

Some Armenians who were with the Persians came to the emperor by night and said:

> Chosroes is encamped with his elephants and his army, five thousand men, near his palace called Damastager, in a place named Bastaroth. He has ordered the entire army to assemble there in order to fight against you. There is also a river there without a ford, with a narrow bridge, many constrictions caused by dwellings, and foul streams.

The emperor therefore took counsel with the chiefs and remained with the army in the palace of Bechal. In one of the porticoes he found three hundred fattened birds [Col. 1036D], and in another portico five hundred fattened does. In yet another he found one hundred fattened wild asses. He gave all these to the entire people, and they celebrated the Kalends of January there.

Finally, having found sheep, pigs, and cattle beyond number, the entire people rested, feasting and glorifying God.

Moreover, after capturing those who had been responsible for bringing these animals, they learned from them more clearly that Chosroes, on the twenty-third day of December, when he learned that the emperor had crossed the bridge of the Torna, had immediately departed from the palace at Damastager, intending to go to Ctesiphon and fight. He loaded all the wealth he possessed in the palace onto elephants, camels, and pack animals, and wrote to his servants and to Razates’ people that they should enter the palace and the houses of the chiefs and carry away whatever was found in them.

Accordingly, the emperor sent half of his army to Damastager, while he himself departed by another road toward another palace called Beddarach. After giving these places over to destruction and fire, they gave thanks to God, who through the intercessions of the Mother of God performs such miracles.

For who ever hoped that Chosroes would flee from the face of the Roman ruler from his own palaces at Damastager and make for Ctesiphon, when for twenty-four years he had not dared to look upon Ctesiphon, and his royal residence had been at Damastager [Col. 1037B]?

The Roman forces found in his palaces at Damastager three hundred *robanda*, accumulated at different times. They also found many remaining spices: a great quantity of aloe, large pieces of aloe wood, each weighing seventy or eighty pounds; abundant silk; pepper; many *calbasiae camisias* [Note: [Col. 1037D] Greek: Μετάξαν καρβάσια καμίσια, “silken garments and shirts.”]; sugar; ginger; and other spices beyond number.

Some also found silver, clothing of cloth of gold, bed coverings, or woven carpets, in great abundance. All these goods were very valuable, but because they were heavy, they burned them completely. They also burned Chosroes’ tents and curtains, which he used like porticoes when he encamped in the field, as well as many statues [Col. 1037C].

In these palaces they also found a menagerie containing deer, gazelles, wild asses, peacocks, and pheasants in innumerable numbers. In his animal enclosure they found lions and tigers of astonishing size alive.

Furthermore, very many captives took refuge with the emperor, including Edessenes and Alexandrians, as well as numerous other groups.

Meanwhile the emperor celebrated the feast of lights near Damastager, rejoicing and refreshing both the people and the animals. He also destroyed Chosroes’ palaces—exquisitely decorated and astonishing buildings, magnificent houses—which he demolished down to their floors, so that Chosroes might learn how deeply the Romans had grieved over the cities he had laid waste and burned.

Many of the palace courtiers were captured. When questioned about when Chosroes had departed from Damastager, they said that nine days before the Romans arrived, having heard of their approach, he secretly pierced the city wall beside the palace and boldly went out through the lattices [Note: [Col. 1037D] Alternatively, “through the gardens”], together with his wife and children, so that no disturbance would arise in the city. Neither his army nor his chiefs knew of it until he had traveled five miles.

Only then did he order them to follow toward Ctesiphon. A man who could not travel five miles a day, fleeing, traveled twenty-five. His wives and children, who previously had not seen one another, then fled together, jostling one another.

When night came, Chosroes entered the house of a worthless peasant, in whose lodging he could scarcely remain. Heraclius later learned this and was astonished. After three days, Chosroes reached Ctesiphon.

Chosroes had received an answer from sorcerers and astrologers twenty-four years earlier, when Dara was devastated during the reign of the Roman emperor Phocas: he had been told that he would die at the time when he went to Ctesiphon. For this reason, from that time onward he had not dared to travel even one mile from Damastager in that direction; instead, fleeing from there, he went elsewhere.

But he did not dare remain there either. After crossing the bridge over the Tigris, he went to the city situated beyond it, called Seleucia among us [Note: [Col. 1038D] P. Pith., Gueserseleucia.], but called Gueser by the Persians. There he deposited all his money and settled with his wife Syra and three other women who were his daughters.

He sent his remaining wives and many of his children forty thousand [paces/miles] farther into the interior of the East, to a very strongly fortified place.

Some Persians accused Sarbaras before Chosroes, saying that he sympathized with the Romans and spoke against Chosroes. Chosroes therefore sent his sword-bearer with an order to Cardarigas, Sarbaras’s subordinate commander at Chalcedon, writing that he should kill Sarbaras and, after taking command of the Persian people himself, hasten into Persia to aid Chosroes.

The man carrying the letter was captured by the Romans near Galatia. After capturing him, they secretly brought him to Byzantium and handed him over to the emperor’s son.

When the emperor learned the truth, he immediately summoned Sarbaras. When Sarbaras entered, he stood before the emperor. The emperor handed him the letter that Chosroes had sent to Cardarigas, and, having shown him the messenger who had been sent, he read the letter aloud.

When Sarbaras became certain of the truth, he immediately changed sides and made treaties with the emperor’s son and the patriarch. He prepared a false letter from Chosroes, adding to it the names of another four hundred satraps, tribunes, and centurions who were supposedly to be killed.

Having devised a method and affixed a seal, he gathered the commanders, including Cardarigas himself. After the letter had been read, he said to Cardarigas:

> Do you see that you must carry this out?

The chiefs, enraged, renounced Chosroes and made peace with the emperor. After taking counsel together, they decided to depart from Chalcedon and return to their own territories without destroying anything.

Heraclius also wrote to Chosroes:

> I am pursuing you, and I am hastening toward peace. I do not burn Persia willingly, but because I have suffered violence from you. Let us therefore at least now throw down our weapons and embrace peace. Let us extinguish the fire before it sets everything ablaze.

When Chosroes refused this proposal, the hatred of the Persian people against him increased greatly.

Chosroes therefore mobilized the dependents of his chiefs, all his household servants, and those of his women. He armed them and sent them to unite with Razates’ army and take their stand at the river Narba, twelve miles from Ctesiphon. He ordered them, while the emperor was crossing the river, to cut the bridges.

On the seventh day before the Ides of January, the emperor departed from Damastager. After traveling for three days, he encamped twelve miles from the river Narba, where the Persian army was stationed, including two hundred elephants.

The emperor sent George, commander of the Armeniac troops, to go as far as the river and find out whether the Narba had a ford. When George discovered that the Persians had cut the bridges and that there was no ford, he returned to the emperor.

The emperor then moved on to Zituron, burning the regions and cities throughout the month of February.

In March, when he reached an estate called Barsan, they remained there for seven days. He sent Mezetius, the prefect, on a reconnaissance mission. Gundabundas, a chiliarch in Sarbaras’s army, joined him with five others—three counts and two officers—and brought them to the emperor.

Gundabundas reported the following essential information to the emperor:

> When Chosroes fled from Damastager and went to Ctesiphon and then to Seleucia, he was struck by dysentery. He wished to crown his son Merdasan, whom he had fathered by Syra. Then he crossed the river again on his return, bringing with him Merdasan, Sere, and another son of his, Adar. But he left his firstborn son Syroes, his brothers, and his women on the far side of the river.

> When Syroes learned that Chosroes wished to crown his brother Merdasan, he was disturbed. He sent his foster-brother to Gundabundas with the message: “Come across the river, and I will speak with you.”

> Gundabundas feared Chosroes and did not cross, but sent him this reply: “Write to me through my foster-brother whatever you wish.”

> Syroes wrote to him:

> “Do you not know how the Persian state is perishing under this wicked man Chosroes? He wishes to crown Merdasan and has despised his firstborn son. If you speak to the army so that they receive me, I will increase their pay and make peace with the Roman emperor and the Turks, and we shall live well. Work with your people so that I may reign, and I will promote all of you, assist you, and especially assist you.”

> Gundabundas sent him this reply through his foster-brother:

> “I will say whatever I can to the prefect. I have been diligent and have spoken with twenty-two counts, persuading them to support my will, as well as many other chiefs.”

> Gundabundas reported these matters to Syroes. Syroes replied that on the tenth day before the Kalends of April he should take the younger men and meet him at the Bridge of the Tigris [Col. 1039D], where they should receive him into the army and advance against Chosroes.

> He reported that two sons of Sarbaras were with Syroes, as well as the son of Hyesdem and many other sons of chiefs, together with the son of Aram, all chosen men. If they were able to kill Chosroes, all would be well; but if not, they would all come with Syroes to the emperor.

Gundabundas came to the emperor and said:

> Syroes has sent me to you, lord. For he fears the Roman empire, which once preserved Chosroes, although the land of the Romans suffered many evils from him in return. Because of Chosroes’ ingratitude, the emperor may not even trust me.

The emperor nevertheless sent him back to Syroes, ordering him to open the prisons, bring out the Romans held there, give them weapons, and advance against Chosroes.

Syroes obeyed the emperor [Note: [Col. 1039D] Alternatively: “After bringing out those who had been confined, he hastened against his father, the parricide.”]. The prisoners were brought out, and Syroes advanced against his father, namely Chosroes.

When Chosroes attempted to flee but was unable to do so, he was captured and tightly bound with iron fetters. They also placed iron weights around his neck and sent him into the house of darkness, which he himself had newly built as a storehouse for money. They gave him only a little bread and water and killed him by starvation.

For Syroes said:

> Let him eat the gold that he gathered uselessly, for the sake of which he also starved many people and destroyed the world.

Syroes then sent satraps to insult and spit upon him. They brought Merdasan, the son whom Chosroes had wished to crown, before him and killed him in his presence. They also killed his other sons before his eyes. Syroes sent every enemy of Chosroes to heap insults upon him, strike him, and spit upon him.

After this had continued for five days, Syroes ordered him to be killed with bows. Thus, little by little, amid sufferings…
...surrendered his utterly wicked soul. Then Syroes wrote to Heraclius, announcing to him the death of the wicked Chosdroes, and concluded with him a perpetual and most firm peace, releasing to him all the Christians who were being held captive in the prisons and throughout Persia, together with Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, and the precious and life-giving wood that had been taken away by Sarbaras when he captured Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, Syroes was recognized as [Col. 1040C] king of the Persians. He reigned for one year; at that time Muhammath, prince of the Arabs, or Saracens, who was living under the Persians, was completing his sixth year and approaching his ninth. Meanwhile, after peace had been made between the Persians and Romans, the emperor sent his brother Theodore with letters and with men of Syroes, king of the Persians, so that the Persians who were in Palestine, Jerusalem, Edessa, and the other Roman cities might return peacefully to Persia and pass harmlessly through Roman territory.

Finally, after the emperor had waged war against Persia for six years, in the seventh year, peace having been restored, he returned to Constantinople with immense joy, fulfilling in this a certain mystical *theōria* (θεωρία). For in six days God created all things, and He called the seventh [Col. 1040D] day the day of rest; so he too, after six years spent in many labors, returned to the city in the seventh year and rested in peace and rejoicing.

When the people of the city heard of his arrival, all, driven by an unbearable longing to meet him, went out to [Note: [Col. 1040D] Alternatively, “Jeriam.”] Leriam, together with the patriarch and Constantine, his son and the emperor, carrying olive branches and lamps, and praising him with thanksgiving and tears. His son approached, fell at his feet, and, after embracing him, they both drenched the earth with their tears. When the people saw this, they all offered grateful hymns to God, and at last, having received the emperor, entered the city in jubilation.

In the nineteenth [Col. 1041A] year of Heraclius’s reign, Adhesyr ruled the Persians for seven months. The emperor, setting out from the imperial city as soon as spring arrived, proceeded to Jerusalem, carrying back there the precious and life-giving wood, in order to give thanks to God. When he had reached Tiberias, the Christians accused a certain Hebrew named Benjamin of doing them harm. He was exceedingly wealthy and had received the emperor and his army. The emperor, however, condemned him, saying: “For this reason you are troublesome to the Christians and to my faith.” Then, after admonishing him and persuading him to believe, the emperor baptized him in the house of Eustachius of Naples, who, himself being a Christian, had also received the emperor.

Thus the emperor entered Jerusalem and restored both Zacharias the bishop and the venerable precious and life-giving [Col. 1041B] wood of the cross to their proper place. He gave abundant thanks to God, and, having driven the Hebrews from the holy city, ordered that they should not have permission to approach the venerable city more closely than three miles.

When he reached Edessa, he restored to the Orthodox the church that had been held by the Nestorians from the time of Chosdroes. When he came to Hierapolis, he heard that Syroes, king of the Persians, had died, and that Adhesyr, his son, had succeeded him in the government of the kingdom. After he had held the sovereignty for seven months, Sarbaras revolted against him. Having struck him down, Sarbaras ruled the Persians for six months. After the Persians had killed him, they elevated [Note: [Col. 1041D] Alternatively, Boranim; alternatively, Baraman; P. Pith., Doram.] Bornaim, the son of Chosdroes, as king. He held the Persian kingdom for seven months. Hormisdas succeeded him; when he was expelled by the Saracens, the Persian kingdom [Col. 1041C] came under the Arabs [Note: [Col. 1041D] Alternatively, “under Michammath.”] and has remained so to the present day.

In the twentieth year of Heraclius’s reign, Hormisdas was reigning over the Persians. While Heraclius was at Hierapolis, Athanasius, patriarch of the Jacobites, came to him—a sharp and evil-minded man, possessing the characteristic cunning of the Syrians. When the matter of faith was brought before the emperor, Heraclius promised him that, if he accepted the Council of Chalcedon, he would make him patriarch of Antioch.

Athanasius pretended to accept the council, confessing two united natures in Christ. He then asked the emperor about operation and will: how ought these to be spoken of in Christ, as double or as single? The emperor, startled by this novel expression, wrote to Sergius, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 1041D]. He also summoned Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, and, having questioned him, found him in agreement with Sergius concerning one will and one operation. For Sergius, being Syrian by birth and descended from Jacobite parents, wrote back and confessed one natural will and one operation in Christ. The emperor accepted the advice of both and found Athanasius also agreeing with them. For he knew that where one nature is acknowledged, there too one operation is found.

Having become certain of this, the emperor wrote to John, pope of Rome, reporting the opinion of the aforementioned men; but John by no means accepted their sect. After George of Alexandria died, Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, was [Col. 1042A] sent to succeed him. United with Theodore, bishop of Pharan, he produced that discolored hydra—rather, that vanity—of “unity,” writing with him that there was one operation in Christ.

As they pursued these things, the Catholic Church fell into great disgrace, together with the Council of Chalcedon. For the Jacobites and Theodosians exulted, declaring: “It is not we who have communicated with the Council of Chalcedon; rather, the Council of Chalcedon has communicated with us, confessing one nature of Christ through one operation.”

Meanwhile, Sophronius was consecrated bishop of Jerusalem. Having gathered the bishops living under his authority, he struck the impious doctrine of the Monothelites with the sword of anathema, and sent a synodical letter to Sergius of Constantinople and to John, pope of Rome. When Heraclius [Col. 1042B] heard this, he was confused: he did not wish to destroy what was his own, yet he could not endure the reproaches.

Then Heraclius, thinking that he was doing something significant, published that document which is called Zeno’s edict. It professed neither one nor two operations in Christ. When it was read, those who are followers of Severus and hold such views also began, in taverns and baths, to disparage the Catholic Church, declaring:

“First, those who held the opinions of Nestorius, the Chalcedonians, repented, were converted to the truth, and were united with us through one operation into one nature of Christ. But now, repenting of this and having no understanding, they have lost both: they confess neither one nor two operations in Christ.”

After the death of Sergius, Pyrrhus assumed the Constantinopolitan throne [Col. 1042C] and impiously confirmed what had been taught by Sergius and Cyrus. When Heraclius died and his son Constantine became emperor, Pyrrhus, together with Martina, killed him with poison, and Heraclonas, Martina’s son, became emperor.

But the senate and the entire city expelled Pyrrhus as an impious man, together with Martina and her son. Constans, the son of Constantine, became emperor, and Paul was consecrated bishop of Constantinople; he too was a heretic. John, bishop of Rome, however, gathered a council of bishops and anathematized the Monothelite heresy. Likewise, in Africa, at Byzantium [Note: [Col. 1042D] Alternatively, “Byzacium.”], Numidia, and Mauretania, various bishops assembled and struck the Monothelites with anathema.

When John fell asleep in the Lord, Theodore was appointed pope in his place. When Pyrrhus reached Africa, he appeared in mutual encounter with the most holy Maximus [Col. 1042D]—namely, the most devout Abba, distinguished in monastic discipline—and also before the assembled bishops who were present there. After they had reproved and persuaded him, they sent him to Rome to Pope Theodore. Having delivered a written confession of orthodoxy to the pope, he was received by him.

Meanwhile, after he had departed from Rome and reached Ravenna, he returned like a dog to his own vomit. When Pope Theodore learned of this, he summoned the full Church and went to the tomb at the summit of the apostles. After requesting the divine chalice, he let drops of the life-giving blood fall into ink, and with his own hand caused Pyrrhus’s deposition to be written and his excommunication to be carried out [Col. 1043A].

Moreover, when Pyrrhus reached Constantinople, Paul died, and the audacious heretics once again installed Pyrrhus on the Constantinopolitan throne. After Pope Theodore died, the most holy Martin was consecrated bishop of Rome. When Maximus reached Rome and stirred Pope Martin to zeal, they gathered a synod of one hundred and ten bishops. They anathematized Sergius, Pyrrhus, Cyrus, and Paul, and more explicitly proclaimed and affirmed two wills and two operations in Christ our God.

In the ninth year of his reign, Constans, the grandson of Heraclius, in the eighth indiction, became enraged when he learned these things. He had Saint Martin and Maximus taken to Constantinople, tortured at Cherson, and banished into exile in other regions [Col. 1043B]. He also punished many people in the western provinces. Moved by zeal for God, they too convened a holy synod, renounced the Monothelite heresy, and explained the two wills and operations.

Thus, while the Church was being troubled by emperors and impious priests, Amalek the destroyer rose up, persecuting the people of Christ. There followed the first terrible downfall of the Roman army—namely, that which occurred at Gabatha, Hermuchas, and Demithas, with the shedding of blood—after the devastations of Palestine, Caesarea, and Jerusalem; then came the Egyptian destruction, followed thereafter by the capture of the Mediterranean regions and islands and of all Romania, as well as the complete destruction of the Roman army and fleet in Phoenicia, together with the destruction of all Christian peoples and places. This did not cease until the persecutor of the Church was killed in Sicily.

In the twenty-first year of Heraclius’s reign, Muhammat [Col. 1043C], the Saracen and Arab prince and false prophet, died, having advanced his kinsman Ebubezer to his own position of authority. At that time news of his death arrived, and everyone was afraid. But the deluded Hebrews, at the beginning of his advent, thought that he was the Christ whom they awaited. Thus some of those who attended him approached him and accepted his religion, abandoning the Law of Moses, the beholder of God. There were ten in number who did this; they also remained with him until his slaughter.

But when they saw him eating camel, they realized that he was not the one they had supposed him to be. They hesitated about what they should do and whether they should abandon his religion. In their misery and fear, however, they taught him unlawful things against us Christians, and in this way they continued to associate with him.

I think it necessary to recount his lineage. He came from the great tribe of Ishmael, the son of Abraham. Nizar, the great-grandson of Ishmael, is said to have been the father of them all. He fathered two sons: Muhdar and Rabian. Muhdar fathered Iliez, Ziason, Theominen, Asydus, and others whose names are unknown. All these dwelt in the wilderness of Midian, where they raised livestock and lived in tents.

There are also [Col. 1044A] those more remote from them who are not of their tribe but come from Getham—namely, those who are called Ammonites, who are also called Homerites. Some of them conduct trade with their camels.

When the aforementioned Muhammat was poor and an orphan, it seemed good to him to enter the service of a certain wealthy woman, his kinswoman, named [Note: [Col. 1043D] Alternatively, Chaldi.] Eadiga, as a hired agent to conduct trade with her camels in Egypt and Palestine. Gradually gaining her confidence—for she was a widow—he took her as his wife and acquired possession of her camels and property.

When he came to Palestine, he associated with Jews and Christians and obtained certain writings from them. He also suffered from epilepsy. When his wife discovered this, she was deeply distressed, being a noblewoman [Col. 1044B] who had joined herself to such a man—one who was poor and epileptic.

He himself tried to console her, saying: “I behold a certain vision of the angel named Gabriel; unable to endure his appearance, I lose consciousness in my mind and fall.” Since she had another monk as a friend, an exile living there because of his infidelity, she told him everything, including the angel’s name. Wishing to assure her, he said: “He has spoken the truth. For this angel is sent to all the prophets.”

Having first accepted the word of the false monk, she believed him and proclaimed to the other women of her tribe that he was a prophet. In this way the report passed from the women to the men, first of all to [Note: [Col. 1044D] Alternatively, Abubachar.] Ebubezer, whom he left as his successor.

His heresy [Col. 1044C] occupied part of the wilderness, eventually by force of war. At first it spread secretly for ten years; then it continued in war for ten years as well, and openly for nine. He taught his hearers that whoever killed an enemy, or was killed by an enemy, would enter Paradise.

He described Paradise as consisting of bodily food, drink, and intercourse with women, with rivers of wine, honey, and milk, and with the intercourse of women who were not those present now but others, to be enjoyed in the future for many years, together with overflowing pleasure and other things filled with luxury and folly. Nevertheless, he taught them to have compassion on one another and to assist the suffering.

In that same year, his son David was born in the East; on the same day Heraclius, the son of the younger Heraclius—also called Constantine—was born [Col. 1044D], and he was baptized by the patriarch Sergius.

In the twenty-second year of Heraclius’s reign, Eububezer is recorded as leader of the Arabs; he held the principate for three years. The Persians, however, rose up against one another and fought each other. At the same time, the king of the Indians sent Heraclius gifts of congratulation for his victory over the Persians—pearls, that is, and many precious stones.

Muhammad died. He had appointed four amirs to conquer the Christians who were of Arab descent. These came against the fortress of Mucheas, where Theodore [Note: [Col. 1044D] Alternatively, Bligarius, that is, chamberlain.] Begarius was stationed, intending to attack the Arabs on the day when they were going to sacrifice to idols. When Begarius learned of this, he gathered all their soldiers who were guarding the desert and, carefully inquiring from an Arab the day and hour at which they were going to attack them, himself fell upon them in the battle called *mothos* (μόθως). He killed three amirs and a very large crowd of the people.

One amir escaped, named Chalegus—that is, the one whom they call “the Sword of God”. Among the Arabs who lived nearby were certain men who received small military payments from the emperors to guard the entrance of the desert. At that time a certain eunuch came to distribute the soldiers’ payments. When the Arabs came, as usual, to receive their payments, the eunuch provoked them to anger, saying: “Since the master scarcely gives payments to soldiers, how much less to these dogs?” Seeing this, the Arabs went away to the men of their own race, and those men led them into the region of Gaza, which was a very wealthy entrance to the desert opposite Mount Sida.

In the twenty-third year of Heraclius’s reign, when Eububezer had sent four commanders who, as I have said, had been led by the Arabs, they came and seized Ran and the whole region of Gaza. At last, when a commander from Caesarea of Palestine arrived with a few soldiers, he entered battle and was killed, together with his army, which consisted of three hundred men. After taking many captives and very extensive spoils, they returned with a splendid victory.

In the same year an earthquake occurred in Palestine, and a sign appeared in the sky, toward the south, called *dokētēs* (δοκήτης), announcing the power of the Arabs. It remained for thirty days, extending from Mesembria to Arcturus; it was shaped like a sword.

In the twenty-fourth year of Heraclius’s reign [Col. 1045C], Ebubezer died. He had held the principate for two and a half years. Haumar then assumed the principate. He sent an army against Arabia and captured the city of Bostra together with other cities. They advanced as far as Gabata.

Theodore, the brother of the emperor Heraclius, engaged them in battle, was defeated, and came to the emperor at Edessa. The emperor then appointed another commander, named Bahan [Note: [Col. 1045D] Alternatively, Bahantem; alternatively, Bohanem.], and sent him, together with Theodore the treasurer and Roman forces, against the Arabs.

When he reached Emesa, a multitude of Saracens met him. After killing them, together with those who commanded them, he drove the survivors as far as Damascus. There they took refuge near the river of the Bardanenses. Heraclius, however, abandoning Syria and falling into despair, took the precious wood from Jerusalem and went to Constantinople [Col. 1045D].

Bahanes returned from Damascus to Emesa together with Theodore the treasurer, having an army of forty thousand men. They pursued the Arabs from Hesma to Damascus.

In the twenty-fifth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Saracens drew up their battle line in Arabia against Damascus, being beyond number. When Bahanes learned this, he sent to the imperial treasurer, asking him to come with his army to help him, since the Arab forces were extremely numerous.

The treasurer therefore came to Bahanes. They set out from Emesa to meet the Arabs, and after an engagement, on the first day—which was Tuesday, the twenty-third day of August—those who were with the treasurer were defeated [Col. 1046A]. When a dispute arose, those who were with Bahanes proclaimed Bahanes emperor and rejected Heraclius. Then those who were with the treasurer withdrew, and the Saracens, finding an opening, began the battle.

Meanwhile, as a south wind was blowing against the Romans, they were unable to face the enemy because of the dust and were defeated. They threw themselves into a narrow pass of the Hermucta River and perished there utterly. The two commanders together had forty thousand men.

The Saracens then came in splendid triumph against Damascus, captured it, and captured the regions of Phoenicia. They settled there and directed their battle line toward Egypt.

When Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, learned of their advance, he took action and, after making agreements, promised—fearing their greed—that Egypt would pay them two hundred thousand denarii each year. He also promised to send them gold for the truces that had been agreed with them. After these payments had been made for three years, he secured Egypt against devastation.

Meanwhile, Cyrus was accused before the emperor of giving Egypt’s gold to the Saracens. The emperor, angered, sent for him. He appointed a certain Manuel, an Armenian by birth, as Augustal prefect. When the year had been completed, the Saracens’ agents came to receive the gold. But Manuel drove them away, saying: “I am not Cyrus, unarmed, to pay tribute to you; I am armed.”

When they had departed, the Saracens immediately armed themselves against Egypt. After making war on Manuel, they drove him away. He himself, with a few others, was received alone in Alexandria [Col. 1046C]. The Saracens then placed Egypt under tribute.

When the emperor heard what had happened, he sent Cyrus to persuade them to withdraw from Egypt under the former agreement. Cyrus went to the Saracens’ camp and gave an account, declaring that he was liable for breach of faith and affirming with oaths that he would restore the former agreement if they wished it.

The Saracens, however, would not agree to this in any way. They said to the bishop: “Can you swallow this enormous column?” He replied: “That cannot be done.” They answered: “Nor is it possible for us to withdraw any further from Egypt.”

In the twenty-sixth year of Heraclius’s reign, Haumar directed his battle line against Palestine and, after besieging the holy city for two years, captured it by a word [Col. 1046D]. Sophronius, the chief priest of Jerusalem, had received a word concerning the security of all Palestine.

When Haumar entered the holy city, clothed in camel hair and filthy garments and displaying a satanic pretence, he sought the temple that Solomon had built, intending it as a place of worship for his blasphemy. When Sophronius observed this, he said: “In truth, this is the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place.” With many tears, this defender of piety mourned the Christian people there.

While Haumar was staying there, the bishop asked him to accept a linen garment with clothing and put it on. He refused to wear them. Only with difficulty did he persuade him to put them on until his own clothes had been washed [Col. 1047A]. He then returned them to Sophronius and put on his own garments.

Meanwhile Sophronius died. By word and deed he had adorned the Church of Jerusalem and had opposed the error of Heraclius and his Monothelite supporters, namely Sergius and Pyrrhus.

In the same year Haumar sent forces into Syria and subjugated the whole of Syria to the Saracens.

In the twenty-seventh year of Heraclius’s reign, John, surnamed Chatheas [Note: [Col. 1047C] Alternatively, Catzas. The Greek manuscript has Καττᾶς.], procurator of Osrhoene, came to Hyaidus at Chalcedon and promised to give him one hundred thousand *nomismata* each year, so that he would not cross the Euphrates, either armed for peace or armed for war, until the amount of gold had been paid.

Moreover, John went to Edessa and sent Hyaidus the annual tribute that had been delivered. When Heraclius heard this, he judged John liable, because he had done it without the emperor’s knowledge [Col. 1047B], and, after summoning him, condemned him to exile. In his place they appointed a certain Ptolemy, commander of the soldiers.

In the twenty-eighth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Arabs captured Antioch. Haumar sent Muhavias as commander and amir of the entire region that was under the Saracens, from Egypt, that is, to the Euphrates.

In the twenty-ninth year of Heraclius’s reign, Hyaidus crossed the Euphrates with his entire army and came to Edessa. The Edessenes opened the gates and received him, together with the region, the commander of the soldiers, and the Romans who were with him.

They then departed for Constantia. After devastating it, they captured it by battle and killed three hundred Romans. From there they went to Daras, captured it by battle, and lost many men there. Thus Hyaidus captured Mesopotamia [Col. 1048A].

In the thirtieth year of Heraclius’s reign, the Saracens directed their battle line against Persia and engaged the Persians in war. Prevailing powerfully, they made all the Persians subject to themselves. Hormisdas, who ruled the Persians, escaped by flight to the inner regions of Persia and abandoned the royal insignia.

The Saracens, however, took captive the daughters of Chosroes with all the royal equipment and brought them to Haumar.

In the same year Haumar ordered the entire world that was under him to be registered. A census was made both of human beings and of animals and crops.

## CONSTANTINE

In the thirty-first year of his reign, the emperor Heraclius died, having become dropsical, after ruling for thirty years [Col. 1048B]. His son Constantine ruled after him for four months. He was given poison by his stepmother Martina and the patriarch Pyrrhus, and died. Heraclonas, the son of Martina, ruled with his mother Martina.

## HERACLONAS

In the first year of Heraclonas’s reign, Muhavias captured Caesarea of Palestine after besieging it for seven years and killed seven thousand Romans there.

In the same year the senate rejected Heraclonas together with his mother Martina and Valentinus, Martina’s spokesman. Heraclonas’s nose was cut off. After they had been sent into exile, they elevated to the principate Constans, the son of Constantine and grandson of Heraclius, who ruled for twenty-seven years.

## BOOK NINETEEN

[Col. 1047]

## CONSTANS

[Col. 1047C]

In the year 634 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Constans began to reign. When he had begun to rule in the first year of his reign, he said to the senate:

“My father Constantine, who begot me and who, during the lifetime of his own father—namely, my grandfather Heraclius—ruled with him for a sufficient time, but afterward for a far too short time, was deprived of life by the envious destruction of the sweetest hope of his stepmother Martina; and this was because of Heraclonas, who was wickedly born of her and Heraclius. By your resolution with God, your exceedingly provident, noble, and magnificent body rightly expelled Martina together with her son from the imperial power, lest they violate so wretched an empire of the Romans [Col. 1047D].

“Therefore I ask you to take as advisers men experienced in the common service of your subjects.”

Having said this, he dismissed the senate, honoring it with lavish gifts.

In the second year of Constans’s reign, Haumar began to build a temple in Jerusalem. The structure did not stand but collapsed. When he inquired about the cause, the Jews told him that unless the cross above the temple on the Mount of Olives was removed, the structure would not stand. For this reason the cross was taken away from there [Col. 1048C], and thus the building stood.

For this same reason, those who worship Christ made many crosses [Note: [Col. 1047D] Alternatively, those who hated Christ removed the crosses.].

In the third year of Constans’s reign, the patrician Valentinian raised a revolt. The emperor sent against him and killed him, thereby restoring the people to his favor.

In the fourth year of Constans’s reign, Haumar, the leader of the Saracens, was murdered by treachery by a certain Persian named Margarita. Finally, finding him while he was worshiping, he stabbed him in the belly with a sword fixed in it, and thus Haumar ceased to live. He had been amir for twelve years. Hoamen, his kinsman and the son of Tufan, was appointed after him.

In the fifth year of Constans’s reign, Hoamen was recognized as prince of the Arabs. Gregory, the patrician of Africa, together with the Africans, fomented a dispute.

In the sixth year of Constans’s reign [Col. 1048D], a violent wind arose on the earth. It tore up many plants, uprooted enormous trees, and overturned many columns and a choir of monks.

In the same year the Saracens attacked Africa with hostile intent. After battle had been joined against the tyrant Gregory, they put him to flight, killed those who were with him, drove him from Africa, and, after arranging tribute and agreements with the Africans, returned.

In the seventh year of Constans’s reign [Col. 1049A], Muhavias moved an army by sea against Cyprus. He had seventeen hundred boats and captured Constantia together with the whole island. After capturing it, he devastated it.

When he heard that Carcorizus the chamberlain was coming against him with a very large Roman force, he sailed against Aradus. Having landed with his fleet near the town of the island, he attempted to capture the fortress, using various engines.

When he was unable to accomplish anything, he sent a certain bishop named Thomaricus to intimidate them, so that they would surrender the city, accept his treaty, and leave the island. When the bishop had entered among them, they detained him.

The people of Muhavias refused to surrender. Therefore, when the siege that he had established against Aradus had proved fruitless [Col. 1049B], because they refused to yield to Muhavia, he returned to Damascus, for winter had arrived.

In the eighth year of Constans’s reign, Muhavia moved an army forcefully against Aradus to fight it and obtained it by a word, allowing the inhabitants to settle wherever they wished. He dismantled and burned the city walls and rendered the island uninhabitable to the present day.

In the ninth year of Constans’s reign, Busur, commander of the army, together with the Arabs, directed his battle line against Isauria. After killing many and taking five thousand captives, he returned.

The emperor Constans sent a certain Procopius to Muhavia seeking peace. Peace was made for two years, with Muhavia taking Gregory, the son of Theodore, as a pledge in Damascus.

In the tenth year of Constans’s reign [Col. 1049C], the patrician Fasagnates of the Armenians fomented a dispute against the emperor and made treaties with Muhavia, giving him his son.

When the emperor heard this, he came as far as Caesarea in Cappadocia and, despairing of Armenia, returned.

In the eleventh year of Constans’s reign, ashes fell from the sky, and great fear fell upon all human beings.

In the twelfth year of Constans’s reign, Muhavias, returning from Rhodes, destroyed its Colossus after it had stood for one thousand three hundred and sixty years. When a Jewish merchant from Emesa purchased it, he loaded nine hundred camels with its bronze.

In the same year Avidus, an Arab commander, moved against Armenia. After overtaking the commander Maurianus, he pursued him as far as the Caucasian mountains and ravaged the region.

In the thirteenth year of Constans’s reign [Col. 1049D], Muhavias ordered a great fleet to be built, so that their fleet might sail against the imperial city. All their equipment was stationed at Tripoli in Phoenicia.

When two brothers who were friends of Christ, living at Tripoli and sons of a certain trumpeter, saw this, they were wounded by zeal for God. They rushed impetuously to the city prison, which held a multitude of imprisoned Romans. After breaking open the gates and releasing the prisoners, they attacked the amir.

After killing him and those who were with him, and consigning all the preparations to fire, they crossed by ship into Roman territory.

Nevertheless, even then they did not abandon the same preparations. Muhavias was campaigning against Caesarea in Cappadocia. He appointed Ablulathar as master of the naval construction. Ablulathar came to the place called Phoenix in Lycia, where the emperor Constans and the Roman fleet were stationed, prepared to fight him at sea [Col. 1050A].

When the emperor was about to engage him in a naval battle, he dreamed that he was in Thessalonica. After awakening, he recounted the vision to a certain interpreter of dreams. The man said: “O emperor, if only you had neither slept nor seen the dream! For being in Thessalonica suggests *thes allō nikēn* (θές ἄλλῳ νίκην), which means: ‘Give victory to another’; that is, victory will pass to your enemy.”

Nevertheless, finding nothing to do for the naval engagement, the emperor arranged the Roman fleets for combat. When the fleets rushed against one another, the Romans were defeated, and the sea was filled with Roman blood [Col. 1050B].

The emperor dressed another man in his own clothing. Then the aforementioned son of the trumpeter leapt into the imperial boat, seized the emperor, and unexpectedly saved him by transferring him to another ship.

The man himself, a very brave and manly soldier, fought fiercely on the imperial ship, killed many, and gave himself over to death in place of the emperor. The enemies surrounded him and held him in their midst, supposing that he was the emperor. After he had killed many, the enemies killed him too, together with those who were wearing the imperial clothing.

The emperor thus escaped and was saved. Abandoning everything, he sailed to Constantinople.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, Hoamen, the leader of the Arabs, was killed by treachery. He had been amir for ten years. Meanwhile, civil war arose among them [Col. 1050C]. For all those who were near the desert wanted one man—the former Muhammad’s cousin—while those who were in Syria and Egypt favored Muhavia. Muhavia prevailed and held power for twenty-four years.

In the fifth year of Constans’s reign, Muhavias was recognized as prince of the Arabs. He gathered an army against Halim, and the two engaged each other in the land of Balissum, near the Euphrates.

Those who were with Muhavia, being the stronger, gained control of the water. As a result, those who were with Halim, overcome by thirst, gave way. Muhavias did not wish to fight, but won the victory without effort.

In the sixteenth year of Constans’s reign, the emperor moved an army against Sclavinia. He took many captives and subjugated the region.

In the seventeenth year of Constans’s reign [Col. 1050D], an agreement was made between the Romans and the Arabs. Muhavia sent an embassy because of the rebellion, so that the Arabs would give the Romans one thousand *nomismata* each day, together with a horse and a slave.

In the same year Martin, the most holy Roman pope, was led into exile. He had fought bravely for the truth, became a confessor, and died in the regions of the East.

In the eighteenth year of Constans’s reign, Constans killed his own brother Theodosius.

While the Arabs were at Saphin, the aforementioned Hali was killed by treachery, and Muhavias ruled alone, inhabiting Damascus in royal fashion and storing up treasures of money there.

In the nineteenth year of Constans’s reign, the heresy of the Arabians appeared—namely, those who are called the Caururgites [Col. 1051A]. Muhavias attacked them. Those who were in Persia he humbled, but those who were in Syria he exalted. Some he called Hisamites, and others Heraclites. He raised the gifts of the Hisamites as high as two hundred *nomismata*, but reduced those of the Heraclites to thirty.

In the twenty-first year of his reign, the Arabs moved an army against Roman territory. They plundered many places and devastated several regions.

In the twenty-second year of Constans’s reign, part of Cilicia was opened to plunder, and they settled at Damascus at their own discretion.

In the twenty-third year of Constans’s reign, the error of the Fastings arose. Habdinarramen the Chaldaean [Note: [Col. 1051D] Alternatively, Chaledi.] moved an army against Roman territory, wintered there, and demolished many regions [Col. 1051B].

The Sclavini, meanwhile, gathered to him and descended with him into Syria, numbering five thousand. They settled in the region of Apamea, in the fortress of Seleucobri.

In the twenty-fourth year, Busur moved an army into Roman territory. Thomaricus, bishop of Apamea, died, and the bishop of Emesa was burned.

In the twenty-fifth year of Constans’s reign, Busur again moved an army into Roman territory. He devastated the regions of the Hexapolis and of Phadala and wintered there.

In the twenty-sixth year of Constans’s reign, Saporius, commander of the Armeniacs and Persian by birth, rebelled against the emperor Constans. He sent Sergius, the commander of the soldiers, to Muhavia, promising that he would subjugate Roman territory to Muhavia if Muhavia would assist him against the emperor [Col. 1051C].

When Constantine, the emperor’s son, learned of this, he too sent Andrew the chamberlain to Muhavia with gifts, so that Muhavia would not support the rebel.

When Andrew came to Damascus, he found that Sergius had arrived first [Note: [Col. 1051D] P. Pith.: “had forestalled him.” But Mauchias pretended to sympathize with the emperor. Sergius was sitting.]. When Andrew entered, Sergius saw him and stood up.

Muhavia then rebuked Sergius, saying: “Why were you afraid?” Sergius replied that he had acted according to custom.

Muhavia then turned to Andrew and said: “What do you seek?”

Andrew replied: “That you give assistance against the rebel.”

Muhavia said: “You are both enemies, but I will give it to the one who has offered more.” Andrew replied: “Do not hesitate, amir. How can the emperor’s offer be better for you than the rebel’s greater offer?”

“Nevertheless, do what is more pleasing to you.” With these words Andrew fell silent.

Muhavias said: “I will consider the matter.” He ordered both men to leave [Col. 1051D].

Muhavias then secretly summoned Sergius and said to him: “Do not pay homage to Andrew any longer; otherwise you will accomplish nothing.”

The next day Sergius arrived and was sitting before Muhavia. When Andrew entered, Sergius did not rise for him as he had the day before.

Andrew, seeing Sergius, attacked him with insults. He became angry and said to him: “If I live, I will show you who I am.”

Sergius replied: “I do not rise for you, because you are neither man nor woman.”

Muhavia restrained them both and said to Andrew: “Agree to give what Sergius gives.”

“And how much is that?” Andrew asked.

Muhavia replied: “To provide the Arabs with the public revenues” [Col. 1052A].

Andrew said: “Woe to you, Muhavia, who advise giving away the body while retaining only the shadow. Agree with Sergius in whatever way you wish; I will certainly not do this. Nevertheless, leaving you to God, who is more powerful than you, we take refuge in him so that he may help the Romans, and in him we have placed our hope.”

Having said this to Muhavia, he said: “Farewell.” He left the city of Damascus and went to Melitene, because a tyrant was in the regions to which Sergius was going.

When he reached Arabissus, he encountered the keeper of the fortifications, who did not support the tyrant. He therefore ordered him to watch for Sergius’s return and bring him to Andrew. Andrew himself continued on, without forgetting the matter, waiting for Sergius. He reported what had happened to the emperor.

Meanwhile Sergius, negotiating with Muhavia about what had taken place [Col. 1052B], obtained Phadalam, the Arab commander, to fight with barbarian assistance and aid Saporius.

When Sergius went ahead of Phadalam and was traveling gladly toward Sare, he came to the fortifications and fell in with Andrew’s forces. They seized him, bound him, and brought him to Andrew.

When Sergius saw Andrew, he threw himself at his feet and begged him to spare him.

Andrew said to him: “You are Sergius, who boasted of your manhood before Muhavia and called me a little woman. Behold, from now on your manhood will be of no help to you; rather, it will bring you death.”

With these words he ordered Sergius’s genitals to be cut off and him to be hung on a piece of wood.

When Constantine learned that Phadalam had come to assist Saporius, he sent the patrician Nicephorus [Col. 1052C] with a Roman force to resist Saporius.

Sapor was staying at Adrianople. When he learned that Nicephorus was coming against him, he prepared himself for battle.

One day, as was customary, he left the city seated on a horse. When he approached the city gate, he struck the horse with a whip. The horse leapt violently, struck Sapor’s head against the gate, and deprived him of life in a miserable manner. Thus God granted the emperor the victory.

Phadalam came to the Hexapolis. When he learned all these things, he was troubled and sent to Muhavia requesting assistance, because the Romans had come to an agreement.

Muhavias sent his son Gizid, arming him against the Roman forces. The two sides met at Chalcedon [Col. 1052D] and took many captives [Note: [Col. 1052D] Alternatively, “they took Arab captives.】.

They also captured Amorium in Phrygia. After leaving five thousand armed men behind as a garrison, they withdrew into Syria.

When winter arrived, the emperor sent the same Andrew the chamberlain. Although there was much snow, he came by night, climbed the wall by means of a piece of wood, and entered Amorium. They killed all the Arabs, so that not one of those five thousand remained at all.

In the twenty-seventh year of his reign, Constans was killed by treachery in Sicily at Syracuse, in a bath called Daphne. The cause was this: after the murder of his brother Theodosius, he was hated by the Byzantines, especially because he had brought Martin, the most holy pope, dishonorably to Constantinople and exiled him to the regions of Cherson, and because he had cut off the tongue and hand of the great and most wise confessor Maximus. He had condemned many of the Orthodox to beatings, exile, and confiscation of property because they would in no way agree with his heresy.

Indeed, he also handed over to torture and exile the two Anastasii, who had been disciples of Maximus the confessor and martyr. Because of such deeds he became hated.

Since he was very much afraid, he wished to transfer the empire to the city of Rome. For this reason he wanted to take the empress and his three sons away from Byzantium, unless Andrew the chamberlain and Theodore the patrician of Colonia had prevented this plan.

He had spent six years in Sicily [Col. 1053B]. When he entered the aforementioned bath, a certain Andrew, the son of Troilus, entered with him to attend him. When the emperor had begun to be rubbed with Gallic soap [Note: [Col. 1053D] Alternatively, “with soap.”], Andrew took a bucket, struck it against the emperor’s head, and immediately fled.

Since the emperor remained in the bath, those who were outside rushed in and found him dead.

After he was buried, they made a certain Armenian named Mitium emperor, compelling him by force. He was very handsome and attractive.

When Constantine heard of his father’s death, he came to Sicily with a large fleet, attacked Mitium, and killed him together with his father’s murderers. After setting the western regions in order, he returned to Constantinople and ruled the Romans together with his brothers Tiberius and Heraclius.

## CONSTANTINE

[Col. 1053C]
