In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 660, Constantine reigned. The Saracens moved an army into Africa and, as they say, led away eighty thousand captives. Meanwhile, those from the eastern regions came to Chrysopolis, saying: “If we believe in the Trinity, let us crown all three.” Constantine was therefore disturbed because he alone was crowned, while his brothers possessed no dignity. He sent Theodore Patricius of Colonia to calm them, praising them highly; he also asked them to take the elder men with them when they entered the city and to join the Senate in deliberation, so that their will might be fulfilled. But the emperor immediately hanged these deceived men on a gallows across the strait at Syce. When the others saw this, they departed in confusion and sorrow to their own homes [Col. 1053D]. Constantine therefore cut off his brothers’ noses.

In the second year of Constantine’s reign [Note: [Col. 1053D] Alternatively, “a storm,” or “Bozor, a storm.”] a great storm arose, and many people and animals were endangered. Phadalas spent the winter at Cyzicus.

In the third year of Constantine’s reign he set out with hostile equipment, and they returned after taking very many captives.

In the fourth year of Constantine, a rainbow appeared in the sky in the month of March, and all flesh trembled, so that everyone said that the consummation had come. In the same year, after constructing a great fleet, the enemies of Christ—namely, Muhammad and Caysus—sailed to Cilicia [Note: [Col. 1053D] And Lycia; they wintered near Smyrna.] and Lycia, and a pestilence arose in Egypt. Saevus Amires was sent with another fleet to assist them, since he was particularly suitable and bold in battle. When Constantine, who had been appointed emperor, learned of this movement against Constantinople by those who opposed God, he too built triremes of extraordinary size carrying fire, as well as dromons.

In the fifth year of Constantine’s reign, the aforesaid fleet of those who opposed God sailed up and arrived in the Thracian regions, specifically from the summit of Septimius, which faces west—that is, from the building called Magnaura—and again as far as the fortress called Cyclobium, which faces east. Battle was therefore joined throughout the day, from morning until evening, from the Golden Gate’s brachialion [Col. 1054B] as far as Cyclobium, both sides pressing against each other in the same dust.

They remained there from the month of April until September. Then they returned and went to Cyzicus; after capturing it, they wintered there, and every spring they sailed up and similarly fought against the Christians. After seven years of such actions, having lost a multitude of fighting men through the help of God and the Mother of God, and having suffered very severe wounds, they were thrown into confusion and returned in immense sorrow. When this fleet, which God had destined for destruction, had departed and was caught by winter’s violence and the force of storms near the region of Scylla, it was utterly crushed and completely perished.

Suphian, son of Aruph and the second brother, engaged in battle with Florus, Petrona, and Cyprian, who possessed Roman strength [Col. 1054C], and thirty thousand were killed. Then Callinicus, an architect who had fled from Heliopolis in Syria to the Romans, arrived. With the marine fire he had prepared, he burned the Arabs’ vessels and set them afire together with the animals;” thus the Romans returned in triumph, after the invention of marine fire.

In the sixth year of Constantine’s reign, Cadallus, son of Chaisi, and Phadalles spent the winter in Crete.

In the seventh year of Constantine’s reign, a sign appeared in the sky on a Saturday.

In the eighth year of Constantine’s reign, a great swarm of locusts appeared throughout Syria and Mesopotamia.

In the ninth year of Constantine’s reign, the Mardaites entered Lebanon [Note: [Col. 1054D] In an old codex of Dionysius of Fleury, the following was written in the margin: “The Greeks call pirates ‘Mardaites.’”] and held the territory from Mount Maurus to the holy city. They seized the summits of Lebanon, and many captives, slaves, and natives fled to them, so that within a short time they became many thousands.

When Muʿawiya and his counselors learned of this, they were greatly afraid, concluding that the Roman Empire was being divinely protected. He sent envoys to the emperor Constantine, asking for peace and promising to deliver the agreed annual payments to the emperor. When the emperor received their proposals and heard their request, he sent with them John Patricius, surnamed Pitzigaudin, a man of ancient lineage, experienced in public affairs and many kinds of business, and endowed with great prudence [Col. 1055A]. He was especially well suited to debate with the Arabs and to establish appropriately whatever concerned peace.

When John arrived in Syria, Muʿawiya gathered both Amirs and [Note: [Col. 1055D] Alternatively, Corasins.] Girasins and received him with great honor. After many peaceful words had been exchanged between them, it was agreed that a written treaty of peace should be made under oath concerning the annual payment, namely, that the Hagarenes should provide the Roman state with three thousand pounds of gold, fifty captive men, and fifty noble horses.

After these terms had been jointly confirmed by both parties, and both sides had mutually promised to observe them for thirty years, a very extensive peace was established between the Romans and the Arabs. Thus, after two general written documents had been sworn and exchanged between them [Col. 1055B], the aforesaid renowned man returned to the emperor with many gifts.

When those inhabiting the western regions learned of this—namely Chagan the Avar, the more distant kings, the Exarchs and Castaldi, and also the princes of the nations situated in the West—they sent envoys bearing gifts to the emperor and asked that peaceful goodwill toward them be confirmed. The emperor granted their requests and likewise confirmed a beneficent peace with them. Great security was thus established both in the East and in the West.

In the tenth year of Constantine’s reign, a great earthquake occurred throughout Mesopotamia. The ascent of Edessa and the dome of the church collapsed [Col. 1055C], and Muʿawiya rebuilt it out of respect for the Christians.

In the eleventh year of Constantine’s reign, Muʿawiya, chief counselor of the Saracens, died. He had been praetor for twenty years and had held the office of emir for twenty-four years. His son Gizid began to rule. In that same year, the people of the Bulgars invaded Thrace.

At this point it is necessary also to speak about the antiquity of the Onogundur Bulgars and the Contragians. In the northern regions of the Euxine Sea that are navigable, and in the marshes called Maeotis, a very great river flows into them from the Ocean, passing through the land of the Sarmatians. Its name is Atel. The river Tanais joins it; that river itself emerges from the Iberian Gates, which are said to lie in the Caucasus Mountains, and flows into the same Atel.

Above the Maeotian marshes, where the Tanais and Atel mingle, the Atel divides. From it the river called Eucthis flows into the Maeotian marshes and returns to the boundary of the sea near Necropela and the acroma called “the ram’s face” [Note: [Col. 1055D] Alternatively, “nacroma.”]. From the aforementioned marshes a similar river flows toward the sea, and through the land of the Cimmerian Bosporus it is carried into the sea of the Euxine. From this river comes what is called Murzilin and things similar to it. In the regions adjoining the marshes and facing east, as far as Phanagoria and the Iberians who live there, many nations dwell.

From the same marshes as far as the river called Cuphis, where the Xyxtus is caught—the fish called the Bulgar fish—there has been, from ancient times, Great Bulgaria. Those called Contragians are also of the same tribe as the Bulgars.

In the time of Constantine, who ruled in the West, when Orbatus [Note: [Col. 1056D] Alternatively, Crobatus.]—the lord of the aforementioned Bulgar or Contragian host—was changing his life and leaving five sons, he charged them not to separate from one another’s common dwelling in any way and not to serve any other nation. But shortly after his death, the five sons came to division, and they were separated from one another together with the people whom each held subject to his authority.

His first son, called Buthajas, obeying his father’s command, remained in the land of his ancestors down to the present day [Col. 1056B]. His second son, his brother Contaragus, crossed the Tanais and settled opposite his brother. The fourth and fifth crossed the Ister—that is, the Danube. One of them submitted himself in Avarian Pannonia to Chagan the Avar and remained there with his own authority; the other came near the city of Ravenna into the Pentapolis and was placed under Christian rule.

Their third son, called Hasparuch, crossed the Danapris and Danastris and went to Honglon. He settled among the northern rivers within the Danube, between it and those rivers, observing that the place was secure and difficult of access on both sides. Since it was marshy and surrounded by rivers here and there, it provided the people with abundant quiet through the protection of their enemies.

After the five had thus been divided and reduced in number, a great people of the Khazars came out of the inner depths of Berzilia, the first Sarmatia. They ruled all the accessible land as far as the Pontic Sea and first installed Buthajas as ruler of First Bulgaria, establishing the tribute that is still carried to them from him.

When the emperor Constantine learned that an unclean and sordid people from Triplo had pitched its tents beyond the Danube at Honglon, and that, approaching the Danube, it was ranging through the region now held by them but then possessed by Christians, he was deeply distressed and ordered all the armies to cross into Thrace. He assembled a fleet by land and sea and moved against them, wishing to pursue them in war. He sent infantry into battle through Epirus against Honglon and the Danube, and, approaching the shore, ordered that ships be brought up.

When the Bulgars saw this rapid advance and the immense multitude, they despaired of their safety, fled to the aforementioned stronghold, and fortified themselves on every side. For three or four days, they did not dare to come out of their fortification, while the Romans, because of the neighboring marshes, could not bring on a battle. The impure people observed that the Romans had relaxed their efforts; they recovered courage and became more energetic.

When the emperor was suffering increasingly from pain in his feet and was compelled, at midday, to go away for the use of the baths [Col. 1057A], he returned with five dromons and his own men, abandoning the commanders and the army. He ordered them to exercise with their spears and to attack the enemy if they should come out; otherwise, they were to besiege them and block them within their fortifications.

But the cavalrymen, spreading the report that the emperor had fled, and overcome by fear, likewise used this pretext to withdraw, with no one pursuing them. When the Bulgars saw this, they followed after them, killing many with the sword and wounding many others, pursuing them as far as the Danube.

After crossing the Danube, they came as far as the place called Barnan near the end of Odessus. There they observed that the inland position was extremely secure: the Danube lay behind it, while in front and on the sides there were fortifications and the Pontic Sea. They also dominated the neighboring Sclavinian tribes, which were called the Seven.

They settled the Severians from the forward fortification of the Veregabori toward the eastern regions. In the places to the south and west, extending as far as Avaria, they settled the remaining seven tribes, which were under treaty.

When they had spread throughout these regions, they grew proud and began to destroy and plunder the Roman camps and estates. Consequently, the emperor was compelled by force to make peace with them, promising to provide them with annual payments, to the shame of the Romans because of the multitude of their sins.

It was astonishing even to hear, for those who lived far away and those who lived nearby, that the man who had made all peoples tributary to himself—those dwelling in the East and West, in the North and in Mesembria—had been overcome by this detestable people.

The emperor, however, believed that this had happened to the Christians through God’s providence. Interpreting the matter evangelically, he made peace, and he remained at peace with all enemies until his death. His chief concern was to unite all the churches of God, which had been divided everywhere since the time of his great-grandfather Heraclius and of the madmen Sergius and Pyrrhus, who had unworthily ruled the throne of Constantinople and dogmatized that there was one will and one operation in the Lord God our Savior.

This most Christian emperor condemned their wicked opinions at the universal council summoned at Constantinople, attended by 289 bishop-fathers, and confirmed the doctrines that had been established in the preceding five holy and universal councils [Note: [Col. 1057D] The Pithaean codices read “six.”]. Through that same holy, precise synod of the universal council, he decreed that the pious doctrine of two wills and two operations should be proclaimed. The council was presided over both by the most pious emperor Constantine himself and by the pious priests.

At that time Gizid became ruler of the Arabs and ruled them for three years.

In the twelfth year of Constantine’s reign, the holy and universal Sixth Synod was assembled at Constantinople, consisting of 289 holy fathers, at the command of the pious father Constantine [Col. 1058A].

In the thirteenth year of his reign, Constantine removed his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius from the imperial government and ruled alone with his son Tiberius.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, Muctar the Liar, while exercising tyranny, gained control of Persia. He called himself a prophet, and the Arabs were thrown into confusion.

In the fifteenth year of Constantine’s reign, Marwan became ruler of the Arabs. After Gizid had died, the Arabs were disturbed, and the Theriexteri [Note: [Col. 1057D] Alternatively, Etherii.] rose up. They appointed as their leader a certain Habdallas, son of Zubedir, and the Phoenicians and Palestinians gathered together. They came to Damascus and also as far as Gabatha, Asan, and Amiran of Palestine. They gave their right hands to Marwan [Note: [Col. 1057D] Alternatively, Marzuan.] and made him their leader; he administered the emirate for nine months.

After he died, his son Habdimelich assumed the leadership. Having held the emirate for twenty-one and a half years, he attacked the tyrants and killed Habdallas, son of Zubedir [Note: [Col. 1058D] Alternatively, Zudebir.], as well as Dadacus.

In the sixteenth year of Constantine’s reign, there was a great famine and pestilence in Syria, and Habdimelich’s people gained control. When the Mardaites were pressing upon the regions of Lebanon, and pestilence and famine prevailed, Habdimelich sought the peace that had been requested by Muʿawiya. He sent envoys to the emperor, promising to provide 365,000 gold coins, 365 noble slaves, and an equal number of horses.

In the seventeenth year of his reign, the pious emperor Constantine died after having ruled for seventeen years, and his son Justinian became emperor [Col. 1058C].

## JUSTINIAN

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 678, Justinian ruled the Romans, while Habdimelich ruled the Arabs; he governed them for twenty-two years. In that year Habdimelich sent to Justinian to confirm the peace. The following peace was agreed between them: the emperor would withdraw the Mardaites’ forces from Lebanon and prohibit their raids, while Habdimelich would provide the Romans each day with one thousand gold coins, one horse, and one slave. They would also share equally the revenues from Cyprus, Armenia, and Iberia.

The emperor sent Paul the magister to Habdimelich to confirm what had been agreed. A written guarantee was made under the attestation of witnesses, and Paul, having been generously honored, returned. The emperor then sent for and took twelve thousand Mardaites, having cut off their Roman military service.

All the cities now inhabited by Arabs along the frontier, from Mopsuestia [Note: [Col. 1058D] Alternatively, Amonpseustia.] as far as Fourth Armenia, were weak and uninhabitable because of the attacks of the Mardaites. Once they had been restrained, Romania suffered every kind of calamity up to the present day.

In the same year Habdimelich sent Ziphien, the brother of Muʿawiya [Col. 1059A], into Persia against Muctar the Liar and the tyrant. Muctar killed Ziphien. When Habdimelich heard this, he came into Mesopotamia and suffered tyranny at the hands of Saʿid. Having overcome him by argument, he compelled him to open Damascus, which Saʿid had occupied in advance, and afterward he treacherously killed him.

Justinian was still young, about sixteen years old, and was managing everything thoughtlessly. He sent Leontius the praetor into Armenia with Roman forces. After the Saracens who were there had been killed, Leontius subjected Armenia to the Romans. Likewise, after bringing Iberia, Albania [Note: [Col. 1059D] Alternatively, Bucania.], Hyrcania, and Media under tribute, he sent very large sums of money to the emperor.

When Habdimelich learned of this, he went to Cercesium and subdued Eupolis.

In the second year of Justinian’s reign, there was a famine in Syria, and many Romans entered Romania because of it. The emperor came into Armenia and there received the Mardaites who had been in Lebanon, after the bronze wall had been destroyed.

He also destroyed the peace established with the Bulgars, disrupting the arrangements that had been properly made by his father. He ordered the cavalry forces to cross into Thrace, wishing to plunder both the Bulgars and the Sclavinians.

In the third year of his reign, Justinian moved his army against Sclavinia and Bulgaria. He repelled the Bulgars when they met him for the time being. Then, rising up against Thessalonica, he killed large numbers of Sclavinians in battle; others, when they fled to him in the region of Obsicium [Note: [Col. 1059D] Alternatively, “of service”; alternatively, “of obedience.”], he settled there after crossing the strait at Abydos [Col. 1059C].

When he was returning, he was hindered on the march by the Bulgars in the narrow part of a fortification. After the slaughter of his own people and much bloodshed, he scarcely managed to escape.

In the same year, Habdalla Zubir [Note: [Col. 1059D] Alternatively, Habdallan Zubin.] sent his brother Musab against Muctar [Note: [Col. 1059D] Alternatively, “Muctar turned against him as soon as the battle began.”]. Muctar fled into Syria, but Habdimelich intercepted and killed him. Habdimelich then made war against Musab, defeated and killed him, and subdued all Persia.

In the fourth year of Justinian’s reign, Habdimelich sent Chagan against Zubir in Macha. Chagan killed him there. After the region had been subjected to Chagan, who had opposed him, Chagan burned Zubir’s idol-temple together with its priest. For this reason, Habdimelich advanced Chagan to be praetor of Persia. Persia, Mesopotamia, Great Armenia, and the Hirii [Note: [Col. 1060D] Alternatively, Hyrii; alternatively, Ethrii.] were subjected to Habdimelich, and consequently the internal wars ceased.

In the fifth year of Justinian’s reign, the discord came to an end. The Arab principate was freed from every war, and Habdimelich obtained peace after all had been subjected to him.

In the sixth year of his reign, Justinian foolishly dissolved the peace he had made with Habdimelich. He irrationally wished to transfer the entire island of Cyprus and its population. He also refused to accept the coinage that had been sent by Habdimelich, although it had only recently appeared and had never previously been produced.

Many Cypriots were drowned while attempting to cross, and others died from illness. The survivors returned to Cyprus. When Habdimelich heard this, he was satanically provoked and asked that the peace not be broken, but that his coinage be accepted, since the Arabs did not accept the Romans’ engraved design on their coins. After weighing out gold, he said: “No harm will come to the Romans because the Arabs mint new coins.”

But Justinian regarded the request as having been made out of fear and did not consider that their aim was first to restrain the incursions of the Mardaites. Thus, by means of an apparently reasonable pretext, he dissolved the peace.

This came to pass, and Habdimelich sent men to build the temple of Muchan. He wished to remove the columns of holy Gethsemane, but a certain most Christian man named Sergius, who was general and logothete of Mansur and very close to Habdimelich, and the patrician who was his associate among the Christians, who was in charge in Palestine and was surnamed Clausus, asked him not to do this. Instead, they urged him, through their supplications, to persuade Justinian to send him others in their place. This was done.

In the seventh year of his reign, Justinian selected thirty thousand men from among the Sclavinians who, at his command, were to migrate and serve as soldiers. After arming them, he called them the “Acceptable People” and appointed a man named Nebulus as their prince.

Trusting in them, he wrote to the Arabs that he would not remain in the peace that had been established in writing. Taking the Acceptable People and all the cavalry forces, he went to maritime Sebastopolis.

The Arabs, however, concealed their intentions and had no desire to break the peace. Yet, compelled by the emperor’s transgression and insolence, they came armed to Sebastopolis and declared that the emperor must not break what had been agreed between them under oath and in harmony; otherwise, God, the avenging judge, would punish the offense.

Since the emperor could not endure even hearing such words, they broke the written treaty of peace and the agreement, and hung it in a high place before them as a standard [Note: [Col. 1060D] Paul the Deacon and Cedrenus read “a spear.”]. Then they charged against the Romans, having Muhammad as their leader, and began the battle in this manner.

At first the Arabs were defeated. Meanwhile, Muhammad sent a purse full of coins to the leader of the Sclavinians who were assisting the Romans [Note: [Col. 1060D] Κούκερον: “Koukeron.”]. By seducing him with many promises, he persuaded him to flee to his side with twenty thousand Sclavinians, and thus he secured the flight of the Romans.

Then the emperor killed the survivors of these men, together with their children and wives, beyond the place of the precipice called Leucatius, which lay on the sea within the territory of Nicomedia [Note: [Col. 1060D] Alternatively, “a bay”; the Pithaean manuscript reads “sinīn.”].

In the eighth year of Justinian’s reign, Sabbis, the patrician of Armenia, having learned of the Romans’ defeat, handed Armenia over to the Arabs. The interior Persian territory called Cerasa was also subjected to them. There a rebel named Sabinus arose and killed many Arabs. He himself had nearly killed Chagan in the river by every means.

At that point the Hagarenes became even more reckless and ravaged Romania.

In the ninth year of Justinian’s reign, an eclipse of the sun occurred at the third hour of the day, so that some stars appeared clearly. Muhammad moved his army against Romania, taking with him Sclavinian refugees who were familiar with Romania, and led away many captives.

Justinian, meanwhile, occupied himself with the affairs of the palace and built a dining hall called Justinian’s. He appointed Stephen the Persian as his sacellarius and chief master of the eunuchs and as judge. Stephen was exceedingly treacherous and cruel toward bloodshed; he never ceased mercilessly beating and even stoning outsiders, as well as their superiors.

One day, when the emperor had gone out, that savage beast dared to whip even his mother, Anastasia Augusta, with reins, like a child. By displaying many such evils in public affairs as well, he made the emperor hated by everyone.

Similarly, in the affairs of the general logothesium [Note: [Col. 1061D] Γενικὸς λογοθέτα: “general logothete.”], he appointed a certain monk named Theodotus. This man had first been confined in the Augustan regions of Thrace. He was himself extremely savage and forced many officials and distinguished men of the state—not only those among the administrators but also inhabitants of the city—to pay exactions, services, and assessments without cause, pointlessly, and without excuse. He also had them hanged with ropes and afflicted with smoke from straw.

Moreover, by imperial command, the prefect handed many men over to prison and ordered that they be kept there for several years [Col. 1061C]. All these things increased the people’s hatred of the emperor.

The emperor also demanded from Callinicus the patriarch a prayer to destroy the church of the holy Mother of God, called Metropolite, situated beside the palace. He wished to install a basin in its place and construct bases for the people [Note: [Col. 1061D] Δήμου Venetorum: “of the Venetian people.”], so that they might receive the emperor there.

But the patriarch said: “We have a prayer for establishing a church, but we do not accept the destruction of a church.” When the emperor compelled him and demanded the prayer in every way, the patriarch said: “Glory to God, who continually sustains us and bears with us, now and forever, unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

When they heard this, they destroyed the church and made the basin. They built the aforesaid church of Metropolite near Petrion [Col. 1061D].

In the tenth year of Justinian’s reign, Muhammad led an army against Fourth Armenia and returned after taking many captives.

In the same year Justinian was expelled from the kingdom, as follows. He ordered Stephen Patricius and the praetor surnamed Rufus to kill the people of Constantinople at night, beginning with the patriarch.

Leontius, a patrician and former master of the soldiers of the East, who had often conducted himself honorably in wars and had spent three years in confinement, was recalled from Triplo [Note: [Col. 1062D] Alternatively, “immediately.”] and promoted as praetor of Hellas. He was ordered to embark on three dromons and to depart from the city that same day.

At night, near the harbor of the Julianians at Sophia, beside the place called Maurus, he fixed his station to begin the journey from the city. He bade farewell to the friends who came to him. Among them were his relatives and companions: Paul the monk of Callistratus, who was also an astronomer; Gregory the Cappadocian, who had been a keeper of the gates but later became a monk; and the abbot of Florus. They had frequently visited him in confinement and assured him that he would become emperor of the Romans.

Leontius said to them: “You made me certain in prison that I would become emperor, and now my life is ending in misfortune. Soon I will be awaiting death hour by hour.” They replied: “Do not delay.” And this was immediately fulfilled.

Leontius took as many of his men and weapons as he had and ascended in great silence to the praetorium. They knocked at the door and pretended that the emperor had arrived to arrange matters concerning certain men known to be there.

When this was reported to the prefect then in office, he came quickly and opened the doors. Leontius seized him, struck him on the face, and bound his hands and feet.

Leontius entered, opened the prisons, and released many strong men who had been confined for six or eight years, most of them soldiers. He armed them and went out with them into the forum, shouting. Sending word to all Christians at Holy Wisdom and throughout the entire region, he began to cry out in his own voice.

The city’s multitude quickly gathered in tumult at the laver of the church. Leontius himself, together with his two monk companions and several of the more distinguished men who had come out of confinement, went up to the patriarchate to the patriarch.

He found the patriarch himself disturbed because of what had been ordered concerning the patrician Stephen Rufus. Leontius persuaded him to descend to the laver and cry out: “This is the day which the Lord has made.”

The entire multitude raised its voice: “Let Justinian’s bones be dug up!” Thus all the people ran to the hippodrome.

When day had come, they led Justinian into the hippodrome. They cut off his nose and tongue and sent him into exile at Cherson.

The crowd seized the monk Theodotus, the general logothete, and Stephen the Persian sacellarius. They bound them with ropes from behind, dragged them through the middle of the street, led them to the Taurus [Note: [Col. 1062D] Alternatively, Vaurus.], and burned them.

Thus they acclaimed Leontius as emperor.

## BOOK TWENTY

[Col. 1061]

[Col. 1061D] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 688, Leontius ruled the Romans. When he began to reign, he remained at peace on every side [Col. 1062D] and governed the empire for three years.

In the second year of Leontius’ reign, Senalidus moved an army against Romania and returned after taking many captives. When a revolt had been stirred up, Sergius, the patrician of Lazica, handed it over to the Arabs.

In the third year of Leontius’ reign, the Arabs moved their army into Africa and gained control of it. They established there certain regular troops from their own army [Note: [Col. 1063D] Ταξεῶται: “regular soldiers.”].

When Leontius learned this, he sent John Patricius, a capable man, with all the Roman fleets. When John reached Carthage and opened its harbor by breaking the chain in battle, he put the enemies to flight and courageously pursued them. He liberated all the African camps, left behind garrison troops [Note: [Col. 1063D] Alternatively, “his own guards.”], reported the matter to the emperor, and wintered there while awaiting his orders.

When the chief counselor learned this, he sent against them a large and more powerful force. It drove the aforesaid John and his fleet from the harbor in battle and encamped outside in hostile fashion.

The aforesaid John returned to Romania, wishing to receive a larger force from the emperor, and came as far as Crete to approach the Prince.

But the army, unwilling to go to the emperor through its commanders—for fear and confusion had seized them—adopted a most wicked plan and cursed the emperor. They chose as emperor Absimarus, the drungarius of the Cibyrrhaeots, who was stationed at Curiositas, and named him Tiberius.

While Leontius remained at Constantinople and was cleansing the harbor of Neorion, bubonic plague fell upon the city and consumed a multitude of its people in four months.

Absimarus came with the army that was with him and landed opposite the city at Syce.

For some time Leontius refused to surrender the city. Then a betrayal was carried out through a particular wall at Blachernae by foreign leaders to whom the keys of the land wall had been entrusted under a dreadful oath. Through treachery these men handed over the city.

When the fleet’s soldiers entered the houses of the citizens, they stripped the inhabitants naked.

Absimarus ordered that Leontius, after his nose had been cut off, be held under guard in the monastery of Dalmatios. He sent the leaders and friends who had remained with Leontius into exile, after beating and condemning them to proscription.

He promoted his own brother Heraclius, a highly capable man, as sole general [Note: [Col. 1063D] Μονοστράτηγον: “sole commander.”] of all the cavalry forces abroad and sent him into the regions of Cappadocia to range through the fortifications and take charge of affairs and arrangements against the enemies.

## ABSIMARUS

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 691, Absimarus was made emperor of the Romans. He reigned for seven years, revolted against Abdarron [Note: [Col. 1063D] Alternatively, “Abderachman in Persia.”], gained mastery over him, and Abipsa Chagan pursued him.

In the second year of Absimarus’s reign, the Romans traversed Syria, reached as far as Samosata, and plundered the surrounding region. They killed, it is said, two hundred thousand Arabs [Col. 1064A], seized very large amounts of booty, and captured many Arabs; then they returned, having inflicted great fear upon them.

In the third year of Absimarus’s reign, Habdella moved his army into Roman territory. He attacked Tarentum but accomplished nothing and returned. He rebuilt Mopsuestia and stationed guards there.

In the fourth year of Absimarus’s reign, Baanes, surnamed Heptadaemon, subjugated the Fourth Armenia [Note: [Col. 1064D] Another reading: “Armenia,” and “he subjugated it to the Arabs, as though acting out a dream of rule.” Greek: Ὡς ὀννειροπολούμενον, “as though dreaming.” Another manuscript, Pith.: ὡς ὀνειροπολέμενον, “as though warring in a dream.”]. Absimarus, for his part, sent Philippicus, son of the patrician Nicephorus, into exile in Cephalonian territory, having him sold entirely by imperial command. For he claimed that he had seen in a dream that an eagle protected and overshadowed his head. When the emperor heard this, he immediately banished him into exile.

In the fifth year of Absimarus’s reign, the Armenian nobles stirred up a revolt against the Saracens. They killed those who were in Armenia and again brought Absimarus and the Romans into their country. But Muhammad, having drawn up his army against them, killed many of them, subjected Armenia to the Saracens, and burned the leading Armenians, who had been gathered together and were living in one place.

At the same time, Azar moved his army into Cilicia with ten thousand men. When Heraclius, the emperor’s brother, had encountered him, he killed very many of them and sent the survivors bound to the emperor.

In the sixth year of Absimarus’s reign, Azidus moved his battle line against Cilicia and was attacking the fortress of Sisium. Heraclius, the emperor’s brother, captured it and, engaging the Arabs there in battle, killed ten thousand of them.

Meanwhile, Justinian, while living near Cherson and publicly declaring that he would again become emperor, caused the inhabitants of those regions to fear that danger to them would come from the imperial government. They therefore took counsel to kill him or, at any rate, send him to the emperor. But when he perceived this, he fled and came to Dara, asking to be presented to the khan of the Khazars. When the khan learned the circumstances of the affair, he received him with great honor and gave him his sister Theodora as a wife.

After a short time, at the khan’s request, he went down to Phanagoria and lived there with Theodora. When Absimarus heard this, he sent to the khan, promising to give him many gifts if he would send Justinian to him alive and, if not, at least send his head.

The khan yielded to this request and sent him a guard, supposedly so that Justinian might not suffer treachery from his own people. He instructed Fazin, who had been appointed there as his representative, and Blagizin, prince of Bosporus, that when he gave the signal they should murder Justinian.

When Theodora learned this from one of the khan’s servants and revealed it to Justinian, he summoned the aforementioned princes, Facin and Blagizin, as though for a private conversation, and had their necks strangled.

He immediately sent Theodorus into Khazaria. He himself fled from Phanagoria, went down to Men, found a ship ready, boarded it, and sailing along the coast came as far as Symbolum, near Cherson [Col. 1065A]. From there he secretly sent for and brought away Barisbacurius and his brother Salibas, Stephen, and Moropaulus, together with Theophilus. When Theophilus had sailed with them to Cherson, he crossed the Pharos.

At last, while they were crossing Necropolis—or the mouths of the Dnieper and Dniester—and a storm arose, they all despaired of their safety. Majaces, one of his household, said to him:

“Look, lord, we are dying. Vow to God for your safety that, if God restores your empire to you, you will take vengeance on none of your enemies.”

But he answered angrily:

“If I spare any one of them, may God sink me in this very place.”

He escaped from that storm without harm and entered the river Danube.

When he had sent Stephen to Trebellis, lord of Bulgaria [Col. 1065B], asking him to provide aid for recovering his ancestral empire, he promised under oath that he would give him very many gifts, take his daughter as his wife, and obey and assist him in everything.

Trebellis received him with great honor, roused the entire Bulgarian people subject to him, and in the following year they came to the imperial city.

In the seventh year of Absimarus’s reign, Habdimelich, prince of the Arabs, died, and his son Ulid, son of Abdalharis, assumed his rule.

In that same year, Justinian came to the imperial city with Trebellis and, together with the Bulgarians under his command, encamped at the Gate of Carsius and as far as Blachernae. For three days he addressed those who were in the city, but they responded by insulting him [Col. 1065C] and would not admit even a word from him.

Then Justinian, with a few of his own people, entered through the aqueduct, raised a tumult, and gained possession of the city by digging through it. Shortly afterward he pitched his tents in the palace of Blachernae.

## JUSTINIAN II

Therefore, in the first year of his reign—that is, when Justinian recovered his empire—he gave Trebellis many gifts, including royal vessels, and dismissed him in peace.

Absimarus, meanwhile, fled to the city of Apolloniades, but, pursued and captured, was brought to Justinian. Heraclius was brought in chains from Thrace, together with all who had supported him; Justinian killed them all by hanging [Note: [Col. 1065D] Greek: Ἐφούλκισεν, “he hanged them.”].

When he later went to the Mediterranean regions, he likewise killed many of those whom he found there, both officials and private persons.

He had Absimarus and Leontius, bound in chains, publicly disgraced in procession throughout the city. While the horse races were being held and he himself was seated on the throne, they were dragged publicly and thrown face down at his feet. He trampled their necks until the first race [Note: [Col. 1065D] Greek: Βαίου, “of the race” or “of the course”] had been completed, while the entire populace shouted:

“You have walked upon the asp and the basilisk, and you have trampled the lion and the dragon.”

Thus he punished these condemned men with execution in the animal arena. He sent Callinicus, the patriarch, into exile at Rome after having his eyes removed. Cyrus, who had been confined on the island of Amastris [Note: [Col. 1066D] Another reading: Protocyrus; another reading in his place: Cyrus], because he had foretold Justinian’s restoration to the empire, he advanced and installed in his place.

He destroyed an innumerable multitude from both the civil and military rolls. Many he caused to be killed by a bitter death after being put into sacks; others, whenever he reclined at lunch or dinner, he destroyed as soon as he rose, some by hanging and others by mutilation. Thus great fear came upon everyone.

Meanwhile, he sent a fleet to bring his wife from Khazaria, and many boats sank together with their crews. When the khan heard this, he sent him the following message:

“Madman, was it not enough to bring your wife in two or three boats, instead of killing so great a multitude? Or do you think you can deceive her by some trick as well? Look: she has borne you a son. Send for them and receive them.”

He sent Theophylact, the chamberlain, and brought Theodora and her son Tiberius back. He crowned them, and they ruled together with him.

In the second year of Justinian’s reign, Ulid seized the Catholic Church of Damascus, driven by a diseased envy against the Christians because of the temple’s extraordinary beauty. He prohibited the public registers of the logothetes from being written in Greek and ordered that they be recorded in Arabic without calculation, because it is impossible to write in their language the monad, duality, or trinity, or eight and a half, or three. For this reason, Christian notaries are still employed by them to this day.

In the third year of his reign, Justinian broke the peace between the Romans and the Bulgarians. He made the cavalry cross into Thrace and, having built a fleet, hastened against the Bulgarians and Trebellis.

When he arrived at the riverbank, he ordered the boats to be brought in front of the fortress. While the people, scattered through the fields like sheep to gather hay, were dispersed, Bulgarian scouts observed the Romans’ careless arrangement. They gathered like wild beasts, suddenly attacked, and utterly consumed the Roman flock, taking much booty, horses, and weapons, apart from those who were killed.

Justinian fled to the fortress with those who had escaped and kept the gates closed and barred for three days. When he saw that the Bulgarians persisted, he was the first to cut the tendons of his own horse and ordered everyone else to do the same. Having placed the weapons of war on the wall, he boarded boats secretly by night and sailed away. In confusion [Col. 1066D] he reached the city.

In the fourth year of his reign, Masalmas moved his army against the tyrant, because of the army’s indignation at the killing of Mavinia by Marinianus. He besieged the place and wintered there.

The emperor sent against them two commanders, Theodore Cartherucas and Theophylact Saliban, with an army and with the rural population, which was to perform the labor of fighting and pursuing them. When they came to battle with one another and attacked the enemy in disorder, they immediately turned and fled; many thousands perished, and many were taken captive.

The enemy took their baggage and provisions and besieged them [Col. 1067A] until they captured the city. Their provisions had run out, and for that reason they were preparing to withdraw.

The men of the tyrant’s city, despairing at these words, accepted the promise of immunity, went out to them, and the city was abandoned and has remained deserted to the present day.

But the Romans did not keep their word. They sent these men into exile in the wilderness and retained many of them as slaves.

In the fifth year of Justinian’s reign, Abas moved his army against Roman territory. After taking many captives, he returned and began to build Garis in the region of Eupoleos.

In the sixth year of Justinian’s reign, Muctam moved his army against Cilicia and took many fortresses by agreement. Camachum, together with the neighboring places, was also betrayed to them.

Meanwhile, Justinian sent the patrician Maurus to Cherson with a large fleet [Col. 1067B], together with the patrician Stephen, surnamed Asmictus. He was inflamed by the memory of past evils and of the plots that the people of Cherson, the people of Bosporus, and the inhabitants of the other districts had made against him.

He gathered all the ships—dromons, triremes, boats, chimaeras, and skiffs—as far as the chelandia [Note: [Col. 1067D] Greek: Ἀπὸ μικροῦ ἕως μεγάλης, “from the smallest to the largest”] by contribution from every inhabitant of the city, namely senators, artisans, commoners, and members of every guild.

Having sent these ships, he ordered them to kill with the sword everyone living in those fortresses and to spare no one. He also entrusted them with Elias the spatharius, who was to be appointed commander of Cherson.

When they came to Cherson, no one resisted them. They captured the fortresses and killed everyone with the sword, except the little children, whom they spared and kept for themselves as slaves.

They brought before the emperor Tudun, prince of Cherson, who was also the khan’s representative; Zelus, who was of his lineage and family and was regarded as the foremost of the citizens; and forty other distinguished and leading men of Cherson, together with their families, all bound.

They roasted seven other leading men of Cherson, having fastened them to wooden spits and placed them over the fire. They also bound twenty others by the arms behind their backs, tied them to the ship’s prow, filled the ship with stones, and threw them into the deep.

When Justinian heard this, he raged over the children’s survival and ordered them to come to him as quickly as possible.

When the fleet set out in October and was caught in the open sea at the rising of the star called Taurus [Note: [Col. 1067D] Another reading: Arcturus], almost the entire fleet sank. It was reliably reported that seventy-three thousand of them were drowned [Col. 1067D].

When Justinian learned this, he was not saddened; rather, he was filled with joy. Still devoted to such madness, he threatened them with a loud cry and sent another fleet, ordering Cherson to be plowed down to its very pavement and all the children who remained to be dashed against the wall.

Those who were in those fortresses heard this, fortified themselves, and, compelled to turn against the emperor, sent to the khan in Khazaria, asking him to provide a people to guard them.

Meanwhile Elias the spatharius rose up, together with Bardanes the exile, who had then been recalled from Cephalonian territory and was with the fleet at Cherson [Col. 1068A].

When the emperor learned this, he sent with a few dromons the patrician Gregory, surnamed the Syrian, the general logothete; John, the prefect; and Christopher, commander of the Thracian turmarchs, with three hundred armed men.

He entrusted them with Tudun and Zelus, who were to be restored to Cherson as they had previously been, in order to give an account to the khan through an envoy; and he ordered them to bring Elias and Bardanes to him.

When they crossed over to Cherson, the people of Cherson deigned to give them this account: on the following day they urged only these citizens to enter and then closed the gates. They slaughtered the general logothete and the prefect with the sword.

They handed over Tudun, together with Zelus and the turmarch who had been brought in, to the Khazars, along with the three hundred soldiers, and arranged for them to be sent to the khan.

When Tudun died on the journey, the Khazars killed the turmarch together with the three hundred soldiers when they received him.

Then those who were in Cherson and in the other fortresses cursed Justinian. They also acclaimed Bardanes Philippicus, who had been sent there into exile, as emperor.

When Justinian learned this, he became even more insane. He killed the sons of Elias the spatharius in their mother’s lap. He compelled their mother to marry a cook who was an Indian by race.

After building another ship, he sent the patrician Maurus Besus, giving him siege engines, a battering ram, and every instrument for destroying the city. He ordered them to raze the walls of Cherson and the entire city to the ground and to spare no living soul [Col. 1068C], and instructed them to report repeatedly on what they were doing.

When he crossed over and brought down with the battering ram the tower called Centinarisia, together with the neighboring tower called Syagrium, the Khazars arrived, and a truce in the war was made.

Bardanes fled and went to the khan. Since the unsuccessful fleet did not dare return to the emperor, its members cursed Justinian and acclaimed Bardanes as emperor.

Moreover, they asked the khan to give them Philippicus. The khan required from them an assurance that Philippicus would not be betrayed by them and demanded that each man deliver one coin to him. When they immediately gave these, he handed Philippicus over to them as emperor.

While the fleet delayed and no report arrived, Justinian realized the reason. Taking with him those of the Obsequian forces who were present, together with part of the Thracians, he went as far as Sinope to learn what had happened at Cherson.

When he looked toward the farther regions, he saw the fleet [Note: [Col. 1067D] Another reading: “the fleet setting sail toward the city”; and, gnashing his teeth like a lion, he himself went toward the city] and showed his intention of attacking as he prepared to return to the city.

But Philippicus arrived first and encamped as far as Amastris [Note: [Col. 1068D] Another reading: Damastris].

Philippicus immediately sent Maurus the patrician and John the spatharius, surnamed Strutus, against Tiberius; Elias, with a military detachment, against Justinian at Damastris; and another force against Barisbacurius, who had taken flight.

Maurus, together with the aforementioned Strutus, went to Blachernae and found Tiberius holding in one hand a column of the holy table of God and of the altar of the Mother of God, and in the other the precious wood, with phylacteries around his neck.

Outside the tribunal sat Anastasia, his father’s mother. She fell at Maurus’s feet and begged him not to kill her grandson Tiberius, since he had done nothing wrong.

While Tiberius held Maurus’s feet and begged him with tears, Strutus entered the tribunal, seized him by force, took the precious wood from him and placed it upon the table, and hung the phylacteries around his own neck.

After taking the boy outside and stripping him, they stretched him across the threshold, cut his throat like a sheep, and ordered him to be buried in the church of the Holy Unmercenaries [Note: [Col. 1069D] That is, the saints Cosmas and Damian, because they practiced medicine without payment], called Paulina’s [Col. 1069B].

Barisbacurius, the first patrician and count of the Obsequians, was also captured and killed.

When Elias, together with the man who was with him, went up to Damastris, the army there came out to converse with him. He offered the people who were with Justinian a promise of immunity. All were therefore separated from Justinian and abandoned him, joining the party of Philippicus.

Then the aforementioned Elias, filled with rage, ran up, seized Justinian by the neck, cut off his head with the dagger he wore at his side, and sent it to Philippicus through the Roman spatharius.

Philippicus sent it through the same spatharius to the western regions, as far as Rome.

Before Philippicus became emperor, a certain man was confined in the monastery of Callistratus [Col. 1069C], a seer and a heretic [Note: [Col. 1069D] Greek: Ἀστρόνομος, “astrologer”]. When Philippicus came to him, he said:

“The empire has been reserved for you.”

Philippicus was troubled, and the confined man said:

“If God commands it, why do you resist? I say this because the Sixth Council was wrongly conducted. If you become emperor, reject it, and the empire will become strong and long-lasting for you.”

Philippicus swore that he would do this.

When Leontius had succeeded Justinian, Philippicus went up to the confined man, who said to him:

“Do not hurry; it will happen to you.”

When Absimarus became emperor, Philippicus again went up to him, and the man said again:

“Do not hasten; that event is awaiting you.”

Philippicus confidently confessed this to some of his friends. They reported it to Absimarus, who had Philippicus beaten, tonsured, bound in iron chains, and sent into exile in Cephalonia [Col. 1069D].

When Justinian [Note: [Col. 1069D] Another reading: Philippicus] recovered the empire, he recalled him. Once he was reigning, he held a false synod of bishops, in accordance with the speech of the false monk and the confined man, and rejected the holy and universal Sixth Council.

In that same year, that worthless man suffered blindness.

During those days, while Justinian lived in great security, he discovered a vast amount of money and splendid property that had been gathered there over many years by earlier emperors through proscriptions [Col. 1070A] and various means, especially by the aforementioned Justinian. He squandered all of it uselessly, in vain, and without regret.

In his arguments he was considered reasonable and prudent; but in his actions and conduct he proved himself everywhere unworthy and reprehensible. He was also a heretic and an adulterer.

## PHILIPPICUS

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 704, Philippicus ruled the Romans. He reigned for two years. Ulid ruled the Arabs and held the command for nine years.

In the first year of his reign, Philippicus expelled the Armenians from their own land and compelled them to live in Fourth Armenia and Melitene.

But he did not succeed in moving more violently against the holy and universal Sixth Council or in overthrowing it; rather, the divine doctrines were confirmed by him [Col. 1070B].

He found John to be of like mind and made him bishop of Constantinople, deposing the bishop Cyrus, whom he also sent into exile at the monastery of Chora. He made the deacon Nicholas, surnamed Calix, a sophist trained in medicine, quaestor, as he was then.

He also promoted Algepidus, a deacon of the Great Church [Note: [Col. 1070D] Another reading: “a deacon’s cup”], and Antiochus the chartophylax, together with others of the same character; they too anathematized the holy Sixth Council in writing.

Meanwhile the Bulgarians secretly entered through Aphilea, fell into a narrow passage, and, after causing great slaughter, ravaged as far as the city. They carried away many people and found abundant wedding celebrations and lavish banquets, with various silver vessels and other furnishings. They advanced as far as the Golden Gate, emptied all Thrace of its booty [Col. 1070C], and returned unharmed to their own country with countless flocks.

Likewise, the Arabs captured Misthea and other fortresses, taking much booty consisting of the households of many people and innumerable livestock.

In the second year of Philippicus’s reign, Abas moved his army against Roman territory, captured Antioch of Pisidia with much booty, and returned.

An earthquake occurred in Syria.

When the two years of Philippicus’s reign had passed, and at the birthday games, after the Greens had won, the emperor decided on the Saturday of Pentecost to enter on horseback with a reception and musical instruments, bathe in the public bath of Zeuxippus, and dine with citizens of ancient lineage.

While he was resting at midday, Ruffus [Note: [Col. 1070D] Greek: Πρωτοστράτηγος τοῦ Ὀφικίου, “first general of the Office”; another reading: “of the imperial service”], the first of the stratores of the Obsequians, surnamed Buramphus, and [Note: [Col. 1070D] Another reading: “with Theodore the patrician of Myacesium”] Theodore, patrician of Myacesium, together with the soldiers of his theme whom he had in Thrace, entered through the Golden Gate.

Hurrying to the palace, they found Philippicus resting at midday, seized him, and led him to the oratory of the Greens [Note: [Col. 1070D] Greek: Ἀρματώριον τῶν Πρασίνων, “the armory of the Greens”]. There they gouged out his eyes, without anyone knowing.

On the following day, that is, Pentecost, when the people had gathered in the Great Church, Artemius, the chief secretary, was crowned and changed his name to Anastasius.

On the Saturday after Pentecost, Theodore of Myacesium was deprived of his eyes. On the second Saturday, Gregory Buramphus suffered the same fate [Col. 1071A]. They were sent into exile at Thessalonica.

## ARTEMIUS

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 706, Artemius ruled the Romans.

Masalmas therefore made incursions against Roman territory and, after plundering Galatia, returned with booty and much spoil.

Artemius, meanwhile, had appointed capable men to the cavalry commands and reasonable men to civil offices, and now lived in peace.

When the Arabs and the Maurophoroi armed themselves against Roman territory [Note: [Col. 1071D] Another reading: “by land and sea”], the emperor sent leaders to Syria, to Ulid, ostensibly to discuss matters relating to peace—Daniel, and among others the patrician Sinopites and the prefect of the city. He ordered them carefully to investigate their movements and the force they were preparing against Roman territory.

When they had heard what was happening and returned, they reported to the emperor that the Arabs possessed a great force, by land and sea, against the imperial city [Col. 1071B].

He then ordered everyone carefully to prepare provisions sufficient for a period of three years. “Whoever does not possess this,” he said, “must depart from the city.”

He appointed supervisors for the construction of ships and began to build dromons, fire-bearing triremes, and very large triremes. He renewed the sea walls and likewise the land walls, setting up crossbows, large engines in the towers, and other ingenious machines. As far as possible, he fortified the city and stored a very great quantity of grain in the imperial granaries, where he kept it under the strongest security.

In the second year of Artemius’s reign, who was also called Anastasius, Ulid, the Arab commander, died [Col. 1071C]. Zulcimin, son of Habdimelich, succeeded him in the command and held it for three years [Note: [Col. 1071D] Another reading: Hanalid. “The Arab leader and Suliman.”].

In that same year Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan city of Cyzicus to Constantinople. At that time the following memorandum of transfer [Note: [Col. 1071D] Greek: Κοιτατώριον, “memorandum” or “official record”] was pronounced, containing these words:

“By the election and approval of the most religious presbyters and deacons of the entire venerable clergy, the sacred senate, and the Christ-loving people of this imperial city, preserved by God; by divine grace, which always heals the weak and completes what does not exist, Germanus, the most holy bishop of the metropolitan see of Cyzicus, has been transferred as bishop of this city, preserved by God and imperial in character.

“This transfer has taken place in the presence of Michael, the most holy presbyter and envoy of the apostolic see, and of the remaining priests and bishops, under the emperor Artemius.”

When Artemius learned that the Saracen fleet was sailing from Alexandria to Phoenice in order to cut cypress timber, he selected swift boats from his own fleet and sent selected troops from the Obsequian theme, ordering them all to assemble at the river Rhodes. He placed over them as commander and head John, a servant of the Great Church called Pope Joannaces, who at that time was the general logothete.

When he had reached Rhodes and gathered the ships, he addressed the leaders concerning their defenses, their voyage to Phoenice to burn the timber, and the preparations that the Hagarenes were found to have made.

Although everyone readily obeyed, the Obsequians refused absolutely. They detested the emperor and killed the deacon John with spears [Note: [Col. 1072D] Another reading: “Then, dividing from the fleet…”].

Those foolish men sailed back to their own places. But the wicked officers sailed against the imperial city.

When they reached Adramyttium, they found themselves without a leader. There they found a local man named Theodosius, who was a collector of public taxes [Note: [Col. 1072D] Greek: Διοικήτης πράκτως τῶν δημοσίων, “administrator and collector of the public revenues”], an idle and ignorant man. They urged him to become emperor.

He fled and hid in the mountains, but when they found him, they acclaimed him as emperor and compelled him by force [Col. 1072B].

When Artemius learned this, he placed his own household officials in command of the city, together with the fleet he had built. Having armed them, he himself entered Nicaea and withdrew into the city, where he fortified himself.

The rebels advanced, mobilized the entire Obsequian theme, gathered the Goths and Greeks, and, with many small and large merchant boats, came by land and sea to Chrysopolis.

When the city’s fleet had anchored in the harbor of Saint Mamas [Note: [Col. 1072D] Another reading: “of Saint Menas”], they fought one another day after day for six months.

When the city’s fleet had gone to the city harbor of Neorion and taken up position there, Theodosius crossed over and gained control of the Thracian districts.

After a betrayal had opened the gate of the isolated wall of Blachernae, he captured the city.

The wicked Obsequian populace, together with the Goths and Greeks, ran through the citizens’ houses by night, sparing no one, and carried out an immense slaughter [Col. 1072C].

They seized the leaders who were there, together with Artemius and Germanus, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, and brought them to the hut of Artemius and those who were with him.

When Artemius saw this and acknowledged his own despair, he surrendered himself. Having received a promise of immunity, he put on monastic clothing.

Theodosius preserved him unharmed but sent him into exile at Thessalonica.

Philippicus had ruled for two years and nine months; Artemius for one year and three months.

Leo, moreover, who was commander of the Eastern forces, did not submit to Theodosius because he had supported Artemius. Artabasdus the Armenian, commander of the Armeniac theme, was conspiring and cooperating with him. Leo promised him his daughter in marriage, and he fulfilled that promise.

## THEODOSIUS
In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 708, Theodosius reigned for one year. During his reign, Masalmas directed an army against Constantinople, and sent Zulcimin with an army by land and Haumar by sea. [Note: Col. 1072D. Another reading: Suseliman; P. Pith.: Suheliman.] He himself came after them with a great hostile force. When Zulcimin and Bacarius reached Amorium, they wrote to Leo, commander of the Eastern forces, as follows:

> We know that the Roman Empire is suited to you. Come, therefore, to us, and let us discuss matters of peace.  
> [Note: Col. 1073D. Another reading: intuens, “observing.”]

Zulcimin, however, perceiving that Amorium had no army and that hostility lay with the commander because he was aiding Artemius, besieged it, while waiting for Masalmas. As soon as he approached the city, the Saracens began publicly praising the commander Leo as emperor and asking those inside to do the same. The people of Amorium, seeing that the Saracens were praising him with affection, praised him as well.

When the commander realized that Amorium would be attacked because the tax-assessors and the leading officials were absent, he sent word to Zulcimin:

> If you want me to come to you and discuss matters of peace, why are you besieging the city?

He replied:

> Come, and I will withdraw.

Accepting this assurance from him, the commander came to him with three hundred horsemen. The Hagarenes, seeing him, came out to meet him wearing their coats of mail, for he was remaining a mile and a half from their camp.

For three days, as he advanced toward them, they discussed with him the matters relating to peace and their withdrawal from the city. They, however, maintained:

> Promise peace, and we will withdraw.

When the commander discovered that they intended to detain him, he invited many distinguished Saracens to dinner. When they had come down, Zulcimin sent three thousand armored soldiers to surround him so that he could not escape and to guard him. When they learned of the guard, they reported to him:

> A multitude of Saracen cavalry is standing around us.

Then one of them, a horseman named Zubeir, came and stood in his presence, saying:

> A slave who stole a large sum of money has fled, and because of him we have mounted our horses.

When the commander recognized their deception, he said to him:

> Do not be troubled, for wherever he has gone, we shall find him in our camps.

But he was saddened and wished secretly, through one of his men, to make known to the people of Amorium:

> Fear God, lest you betray yourselves. For Masalmas is also approaching, and the bishop has already gone out to him and is telling him these very things.

When Zulcimin learned that the bishop had gone out to him, he sent to the commander, saying:

> Give us the bishop.

The commander, distressed, hid him. Instructing one of his men, he said:

> While we are speaking together, dress him in other garments and, as though he had been sent for wood or water, let him go into the mountains.

When the Saracens persisted in demanding him, the commander said:

> Is he not here?  
> [Note: Another reading: “He is not here.”]  
> Nevertheless, go to the amir, and I myself will come, and we shall discuss everything.

They, however, thinking that once he had entered the amir’s presence they would hold him in their midst, let him go. He mounted his horse and, intending to depart with two hundred men, turned toward the left as though he were going hunting.

The Saracens who were with him said:

> Where are you going?

He replied:

> I want to stay in the meadows.

They said to him:

> Your plan is not good, and we are not coming with you.

Then the commander said to his men:

> They intended to hold us by the promise they had given us, and because of us to destroy the Christians. But of these men—or living creatures—who have remained, they retain none.

When ten thousand had gone away, he stayed behind. On the following day he sent his chamberlain, the commander of his household troops, and conveyed this message to them:

> Since you gave me your word and wished to detain me by deceit, for that reason I withdrew.

Masalmas, however, was holding the fortified positions and had crossed over. Zulcimin did not know this. The amir’s men and Zulcimin’s people became tumultuous, asking:

> Why are we besieging the walls and not making incursions?

They struck their tents and departed.

The commander introduced Nicetas the turmarch into Amorium with eight hundred soldiers,

[Note: Another reading: “Niceas.”]

after sending out many women and children, and departed for Pisidia.

When Masalmas came into Cappadocia, the Cappadocians came out to him,

[Note: “The Cappadocians, despairing of their situation, came out to him.”]

begging him to receive them. When Masalmas heard of the hostility that Theodosius held toward the commander, wishing to deceive him, make an agreement with him, and through him bring the Roman realm under his authority, he said to them:

> Are you the commander’s men?

They replied:

> Yes.

He said:

> Do you do whatever he does?

They replied:

> Yes.

Then he said to them:

> Go to your camps, and do not fear anyone.

He ordered his own people not to plunder throughout all the provinces.

When the commander learned this and understood that Zulcimin would report to Masalmas that he had released him and withdrawn, he sent a letter to Masalmas, saying:

> I wanted to come to you, but when I arrived at Zulcimin, he wished to detain me; therefore I am afraid to come to you.

Masalmas therefore said to the commander’s man:

> I know that the commander is deceiving me, so that he may not utterly plunder his provinces.

The commander’s man said to him:

> It is not so; he is writing to you truthfully.

Then Masalmas asked:

> What is Amorium’s attitude toward him?

He replied:

> It is favorable, and it is subject to him.

Angered, Masalmas insulted him, saying:

> Why are you lying?

But he replied:

> It is as I have said.

Then Masalmas sent troops against it together with the turmarch and led out the wealthier families. Masalmas, therefore, deeply distressed by this, drove him away in fury.

For he had planned to capture the city in the summer, await the fleet, then descend into Asia and winter there. Accordingly, he summoned the commander’s man again and questioned him. He, however, swore to him:

> Everything I am telling you is true; moreover, many troops entered it with the turmarch, and he carried off from there all the property of its inhabitants and the impoverished families.

After hearing this, Masalmas wrote to the commander:

> Come to me, and I will make an agreement with you and arrange everything according to your wishes.

The commander, therefore, considering that Masalmas had come near and would cross through his provinces within another five days, sent two envoys to him and conveyed this message:

> I have received your letter and accepted your proposal. Look: I am coming to you. But, as you know, I am a commander, and money, silver, and a population will follow me. Allow me, therefore, to make a statement concerning each of these matters. If, as I request, my case is settled by you, all will be well, indeed excellent. But if not, at least let me depart unharmed and exempt from harassment.

When the envoys from Theodosius reached him, Masalmas said to them:

> I knew that the commander was truly deceiving me.

They replied:

> Far from it.

Then, after granting them the assurance he had requested, he released them until the envoys returned to the commander with the written agreement.

Masalmas, however, possessing vast forces and unable to remain anywhere, went to Acroenum. Moreover, when the commander saw that Masalmas had crossed through his provinces, he went to Nicomedia, caught up with Theodosius’ son, and captured him together with all the imperial equipment and the leading men of the palace.

Masalmas, meanwhile, descended into Asia and wintered there, while Haumar wintered in Cilicia. The commander, taking the emperor’s son and consulting with those who were with him, came to Chrysopolis.

When Theodosius learned what had happened, he received from Leo, through the patriarch Germanus and the senate, a pledge of security and of the undisturbed preservation of the Church; and thus they entrusted the empire to Leo.

Theodosius and his son became clerics together and passed the remainder of their lives in peace. Masalmas, however, coming to Pergamum, besieged it and, by God’s permission, obtained it through a diabolical operation and the instruction of a certain magician. For they took a woman of that city who was pregnant and already about to give birth, cut her open, and, taking the infant, boiled it in a cauldron. In this detestable sacrifice to God, all those who wished to fight dipped the sleeves of their right hands. For that reason they were delivered into the hands of their enemies.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

[Col. 1075]

## LEO

[Col. 1075B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 709, Leo was raised to be emperor of the Romans, and he ruled for twenty-four years. Zulcimin is recorded as commander of the Arabs; he held office for three years.

In this year, then, Leo began to reign. He was descended from Germanicia and was Syrian by birth. Justinian, when he was previously reigning, transferred him to Mesembria in Thrace. Later, during his reign, when he came with the Bulgars, he was met with gifts of five hundred sheep. Justinian was appeased, immediately made him a *spatharius*, and treated him as a close friend.

Moreover, certain men, driven by envy, disparaged him as though he were aspiring to the imperial power. When an inquiry was held concerning this, they were confounded as accusers. Certainly, from that time onward, many began to speak in this manner about him. Although Justinian [Note: Another reading: “plainly did not wish to injure him.”] wished to harm him, he was nevertheless seized by weariness and resentment toward him, and sent him to Alania with money to stir up the Alans against Abasgia, while the Saracens held both Abasgia and Lazica and Iberia.

As he proceeded into Lazica, he deposited the money at Phasis and, taking only a very few natives with him at Apsilia, crossed the Caucasus Mountains and came to Alania. Justinian, wishing to destroy him, sent men who took the money from Phasis. The Alans, however, receiving the *spatharius* with every honor and listening to his words, entered Abasgia and plundered it.

Then the lord of the Abasgi addressed the Alans, saying:

“How shall I find another such chamberlain [Note: Another reading: “another chamberlain, not this one,”] as Justinian had and should have sent to stir you up against us, your neighbors, except this man? For he deceived you, including concerning the promised money: Justinian sent it, but then took it away. Give him to us, and we will give you three thousand gold coins, so that our ancient friendship may not be dissolved.”

The Alans replied:

“We did not obey him for the sake of money, but because of our affection for the emperor.”

Again the Abasgi sent to them, saying:

“Give him to us, and we will give you six thousand gold coins.”

The Alans, wishing to learn the Abasgian territory, promised to accept the six thousand coins and to hand over the *spatharius*. They then confessed everything to the *spatharius* and said:

“As you see, the road leading into Romania is closed, and you have no way to cross. Instead, let us act craftily: we shall promise to hand you over to them, send our men with them, learn the locations of their defenses, attack them, and destroy their territory.”

The Alan envoys went to Abasgia, promising to betray the *spatharius*. They received many gifts from the Abasgi, who then sent further messengers, together with a quantity of gold, to receive the *spatharius*.

The Alans said to the *spatharius*:

“These men, as we foretold, have come to receive you, and Abasgia awaits you. Since we are near them and merchants going to them are continually passing back and forth, do not disclose our plan. We shall hand you over openly; when we have departed, pretending to have been moved elsewhere, we shall secretly send men behind them. We shall kill them and hide you until our people have gathered in sufficient numbers. Then we shall enter their land together. And so it happened.

When the *spatharius* and his men had been seized, the Abasgian envoys departed, having bound him. Afterwards the Alans, returning with their lord Lotax, killed the Abasgi while concealing the *spatharius*. Then, choosing soldiers, they marched against Abasgia, entered its defenses unexpectedly, and plundered and devastated much of the country.

When Justinian heard this and learned that his orders had been carried out even without the money, he sent a letter to the Abasgi:

“If you have kept our *spatharius* safe and allowed him to pass through your territory unharmed, we forgive you all your offenses.”

They received this with joy and again sent to Alania, declaring:

“We will give you our sons as hostages. Give us the *spatharius*, so that we may send him to Justinian.”

The *spatharius*, however, refused to accept this, saying:

“God is able to open a door for my departure. I shall not leave through Abasgia.”

After some time, when the Roman and Armenian armies had entered Lazica and were attacking Archeopolis, they withdrew after hearing of the Saracens’ arrival. About two hundred of them, however, separated from the rest, went into the region of Apsilia, and plundered the Caucasus Mountains.

When the Saracens came to Lazica, the Roman and Armenian people fled and returned to Phasis. Those two hundred men, returning to the Caucasus, remained in the mountains and lived as brigands, suffering the despair of their own people.

When the Alans learned this, they supposed that a large number of Romans were in the Caucasus Mountains. Rejoicing, they said to the *spatharius*:

“The Romans are approaching. Go to them.”

The *spatharius*, therefore, took fifty Alans and crossed the Caucasus Mountains with the Cyclopes in the month of May. He found the Romans there and, greatly rejoicing, asked where the army was. They replied:

“When the Saracens invaded Romania, the Romans returned. We ourselves, unable to go into Romania, came to Alania.”

He said to them:

“What shall we do now? It is impossible for us to cross this territory.”

The *spatharius* replied:

“It is not possible to cross by any other route.”

There was a fortress there called Siderium. [Note: Another reading: “At that place a garrison was maintained by a certain Pharasmavius.” Another manuscript reads *Pharasmavius*.] A certain Manius, who was under Saracen authority and at peace with the Armenians, was stationed there.

The *spatharius* sent word to him, saying:

“As long as you are at peace with the Armenians, make an agreement with me also. Place yourself under my rule, and give us assistance in descending to the sea and crossing to the territory of Trebizond.”

Since he was unwilling to do this, the *spatharius* sent some of his men to the Armenians and ordered them to prepare an ambush.

“When they go out of the fortress to work,” he said, “seize as many of them as you can, and hold the gates against those who are outside until we arrive.”

They departed and prepared the ambush. When the people had gone out to work, they suddenly attacked, seized the gates, and captured many men.

When Pharasmavius came to the camp with a few men, the *spatharius* also arrived. He negotiated with Pharasmavius and asked him to open the gates peacefully. Pharasmavius refused and prepared for battle. Since the fortress was fortified, however, they were entirely unable to capture it.

Marinus, chief of the Apsilians, learned that the fortress was under attack and was seized by fear, supposing that the *spatharius* had a very large force with him. Taking three hundred men, he went to the *spatharius* and said:

“I will lead you safely as far as the coast.”

Pharasmavius, seeing the necessity, said to the *spatharius*:

“Take my son as a hostage, and I declare that I will serve the empire.”

When he had received his son, the *spatharius* said to him:

“What sort of servant do you claim to be, when, although you are shut in, you speak to us? It is impossible for us to depart until we capture the fortress.”

Then Pharasmavius said:

“Give me your word.”

The *spatharius* gave him his word that he would do him no harm. But with the thirty men who entered with him, he ordered:

“As soon as we have entered, hold the gates and let everyone come in.”

Having done this, he returned to set fire to the camp. When a great conflagration had begun, they went out, carrying away whatever of their possessions they could bear. After another thirty days, he destroyed the walls down to the ground and marched down into Dapsilia with Marinus, their chief. The Dapsilians received him with immense honor.

From there he departed, reached the coast, and returned to Justinian.

After Justinian had been killed and Philippicus had been blinded, Artemius became emperor. He promoted Leo to be commander of the Eastern forces. When Theodosius became emperor and Artemius had been expelled, the Roman commonwealth was thrown into confusion by the incursions of the barbarians, the murders committed by Justinian, and the criminal acts of Philippicus. Leo was therefore stirred up. He fought on behalf of Artemius and opposed Theodosius; indeed, to speak the truth, he struggled to transfer the empire to himself—and he did so.

He had as his ally and collaborator Artabasdus, commander of the Armeniac theme. After he became emperor, Leo made Artabasdus his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter Anna, promoted him, and appointed him *curopalates*.

Meanwhile Masalmas, having wintered in Asia, awaited Leo’s promises.
