When he received nothing from Leo and learned that he had been deceived by him, he departed and once more transported a large army across the Hellespont from Abydos into Thrace. He marched against the imperial city and wrote to Zulcimin, the *protosymbolus*, asking him to come with the fleets that had been prepared.

On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, Masalmas began to besiege the city and also plundered the fortresses of Thrace. After surrounding it with an earthen wall, they dug a long and extensive ditch around it and placed a dry-stone wall above it.

On the Kalends of September, in the first indiction, the enemy of Christ, Zulcimin [Note: Another reading: “Suhetiman.”] came with the fleet and his *amirs*. He had boats of extraordinary size, ships carrying supplies, and eight hundred *dromons*. He established his station from Magnaura to Cyclobium.

Two days later, with the south wind blowing, they departed by sea and came to the city. Some of them crossed to the places called Eutropius and Anthemius; others reached the parts of Thrace from the fortress of Galathus as far as Clydium.

Because the great ships were weighed down and slowed by their cargo, as many as twenty boats remained behind under the guard of the Dorsini, each carrying one hundred armored men to guard them. When calm weather had enclosed them in the current and the south wind blew gently, they were driven outward.

The emperor immediately sent fire-bearing ships against them from Acropolis [Note: Another reading: “Atropolis.”] and, by divine assistance, consumed them with fire. Some were driven against the walls of the shore; others, together with their crews, sank into the depths; still others were carried as far as the sharp and broad island, where they were consumed.

The people in the city gained confidence, while the enemy was struck with great terror when they witnessed the extraordinary power of the fire. They had intended that same evening to bring their fleet to the walls of the shore and place gangways above the battlements, but the Almighty destroyed their plan through the intercession of His most pure Mother, Mary.

That same night the emperor secretly removed the chain from the region of Galathus. The enemy, supposing that the emperor had moved it in order to deceive them, did not dare to enter as far as Galathus or to bring their ships there. Instead, they sailed to the Gulf of Sosthenium and fortified their fleet there.

On the eighth day before the Ides of October, Zulcimin, their commander, died, and Haumar, son of Habdimazid, assumed the office of *amir*.

When a very severe winter came upon Thrace, so severe that the earth seemed unable to produce anything and appeared to have been turned into crystal, a multitude of the enemy’s horses, camels, and other animals died.

In spring, Suphian arrived with the fleet that had been built in Egypt. He had four hundred grain ships, together with *dromons*. When he learned the effectiveness of the Roman fire, he crossed into Bithynia and then, crossing back, brought his ships into the harbor of Boniagrus.

A little later Gizid arrived with another fleet, which had been built in Africa. He too had three hundred and sixty ships, together with equipment and supplies. Having likewise learned about the liquid fire, he brought his ships to Saturon and Brian, as far as the harbor of Chorta.

The Egyptians of these two fleets took counsel together during the night. Removing the small boats from the grain ships, they fled to the city, praising the emperor, so that from Heria to the city the sea appeared to be on fire.

The emperor learned from them that two ships were concealed in the gulf. He had fire-producing siphons fitted to the *dromons*, put them aboard the triremes, and sent them against the two fleets. With God’s assistance, through the intercession of the undefiled Mother of God, the enemy were immediately sunk. Our men seized their spoils and supplies and returned with joy.

At the same time Mardasan again advanced from the gates with an Arab army, ranging as far as Nicaea and Nicomedia. The commanders of the empire who were concealed in Libyssa and Sophon, in the manner of the Mardaites, together with infantry who suddenly attacked them and inflicted various losses, forced them to flee from that region.

Afterwards, finding a passage across the strait that could be traversed with some difficulty, the men who departed from the city of Chelandia carried away a great quantity of supplies.

Moreover, a severe famine fell upon the Arabs. They were all dying and ate their own animals—horses, asses, and camels. Some also say that they ate dead human beings and even their own excrement, placed in an oven and baked.

A pestilential disease also fell upon them, and countless numbers of them perished.

The Bulgarian people then made war upon them, and, according to those who know the matter more accurately, killed twenty-two thousand Arabs.

At that time many terrible things happened to them, so that by experience they learned that God and the most holy Virgin, Mary the Mother of God, protect this city and the Christian emperor. They also learned that God’s forgiveness is not wholly withdrawn from those who call upon Him in truth, although we are chastised to some degree because of our sins.

## The Second Year of Leo’s Reign

Haumar was recognized as commander of the Arabs, and ruled them for two years.

In this same year Sergius, the *protospatarius* and commander of Sicily, heard that the Saracens were besieging the imperial city. He crowned there as emperor a Constantinopolitan from among his own men, Basil, the son of Gregory Onomagulus, whom he called Tiberius after changing his name. He made appointments and established his own commanders on the advice of Sergius.

When the emperor heard this, he sent Paul, his own *chartularius*, whom he appointed *patricius* and commander of Sicily. He gave him two *spatharii* as assistants, a very small number of men for his service, and instructions for the commanders of the West, as well as sacred messages to be read to the people.

They entered a swift *dromon* by night and departed for the region of Cyzicus. Traveling from place to place by land and sea, they suddenly arrived in Sicily.

When they had entered Syracuse, Sergius heard of it and was astonished. Reflecting on his own offense, he fled to the neighboring Lombards of Calabria.

The people assembled, and, after the sacred message had been read and they had been assured that the empire still stood and that the city was ready to resist the nations, and after the messengers had recounted what had happened concerning the two fleets, they praised Leo the emperor. They handed over Basil Onomagulus and the commanders who had gone out from him, bound, to the prefect.

The prefect beheaded Basil together with his own special prefect, preserved their heads in brine, and sent them to the emperor by the *spatharii*. Of the others, he sent some into exile after flogging or tonsuring them; others he sent into exile after having their noses cut off.

Thus a great corrective settlement was established throughout the West.

Sergius, having received from the prefect a promise of pardon, came out to meet him, and so all the regions of the West obtained peace.

Meanwhile Haumar, having gained control of the Arabs, ordered Masalmas to return. The Saracens therefore departed and returned in great confusion on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of August.

As their fleet was making its journey, a storm sent by God, through the intercession of the Mother of God, fell upon them and scattered them. Some were destroyed near Proconnesus and the other islands; others were caught in whirlpools, and the rest were submerged in the sea.

Those who survived and crossed the Aegean Sea were immediately struck by the terrible wrath of God. Fiery hail descended upon them and caused the sea water to boil. As the pitch melted, the ships, together with their crews, were drawn into the depths. Only ten of them survived, by the providence of God the Savior, so that they might report to us—and also to the Arabs—the great things that God had done among them.

Our people were able to find these ships and capture five of them. The other five were brought safely to Syria to proclaim the power of God.

In the same year, after a great earthquake, Haumar prohibited wine in the cities and compelled Christians to apostatize. Those who apostatized he exempted from tribute, but he killed those who refused to consent, thereby producing many martyrs.

He also decreed that the testimony of a Christian against a Saracen should not be accepted.

He also composed a doctrinal letter to the emperor Leo, impiously thinking to persuade him to abandon his faith.

## The Third Year of Leo’s Reign

A son, Constantine, was born to Leo the emperor. He was more impious than his father and the forerunner of Antichrist.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Maria, Leo’s wife, was crowned Augusta in the Triclinium. She proceeded alone, with solemn attendance and without her husband, to the Great Church. After offering a prayer before entering the altar, she went to the great baptistery, while her husband had already entered with a few attendants.

There, when Germanus the high priest was baptizing Constantine, the successor to their wickedness and empire, the infant Constantine displayed a dreadful and foul sign foreshadowing what he would be. He defecated in the sacred font, as those who carefully witnessed the event report. Germanus the most holy patriarch prophetically said:

“This is clearly destined to be a sign of the great evil that he will bring upon Christians and the Church.”

After the divine services, Augusta Maria returned again with solemn attendance, together with her baptized son, distributing gifts from the Church as far as the Gate of Aenea.

In the same year Nicetas Xylinites wrote to Artemius, who was staying in Thessalonica, telling him to go to Terbellis. He gave him an army and fifty hundredweights of gold. After receiving these, Artemius came to Constantinople.

Since the city refused to admit him, the Bulgars handed him over to Leo and returned after receiving generous honors.

The emperor killed Artemius together with Xylinites and confiscated the property of Xylinites for the public treasury, for Xylinites, while serving as *magister*, had possessed great wealth.

The Bulgars executed the *patricius* Sisinnius, surnamed Rendacius, because he had been associated with Artemius. They handed over the archbishop of Thessalonica to the prince Leo, and he was beheaded together with Artemius.

Likewise, Leo killed the *patricius* Hisoen, the count of the Opsikion, Teoctistus the chief secretary, and Nicetas the *autarches* and count of Titiacum, as their friends and allies. He sent the others into exile after mutilating their noses and condemning them to confiscation.

## The Fourth Year of Leo’s Reign

Gizid, son of Habdimelich, was recognized as commander of the Arabs, and ruled them for four years.

In the same year, on Easter Day of the third indiction, Constantine was crowned by his father Leo in the tribunal of the nineteen couches, with Patriarch Germanus performing the prayers according to custom.

That year Haumar, commander of the Arabs, died. A tyrant arose from Persia, also named Gizid Mohabe, and many Persians went over to him. When Gizid was sent against him, Masalma killed him and subdued Persia.

## The Fifth Year of Leo’s Reign

A certain Syrian false Christ appeared and deceived the Hebrews, saying that he was Christ.

## The Sixth Year of Leo’s Reign

Leo compelled the Hebrews and the Montanists to be baptized. The baptized Jews, however, contrary to their own intention, washed away their baptism, ate and participated in the holy sacrament, and defiled the faith.

The Montanists, prophesying about themselves and defining the faith, entered houses assigned to their error and burned themselves.

## The Seventh Year of Leo’s Reign

A certain Jew from Laodicea on the Phoenician coast, a magician, came to Gizid and promised that he would preserve his rule over the Arabs for forty years if he removed the venerable images honored in the churches throughout his dominion.

The foolish Gizid believed him and issued a general edict against the holy images. But, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and through the intercessions of His Mother and of all the saints, Gizid died, while many still refused even to hear his satanic edict.

Having received this bitter, unlawful, and wicked doctrine, the emperor Leo became for us the cause of many evils.

When he found a certain man named Beser who agreed with this lack of discipline—although Beser had been born of Christians, he had been taken captive and brought to Syria, where he was found to have deserted the faith that is in Christ and to follow the doctrines of the Arabs—Leo honored him when he returned to the Roman commonwealth, shortly after being freed from their slavery, because of his bodily strength and his agreement with the perverse opinion.

Leo thereby made him a supporter and accomplice in the guilt of this great evil.

The bishop of Nacolia also agreed with him. Devoting himself to the same lack of discipline, he lived a similar life with him.

## The Eighth Year of Leo’s Reign

Gizid, commander of the Arabs, died. His son Evelid succeeded him. Evelid began to build palaces throughout the cities and regions, to lay out new gardens, establish parks, and bring out watercourses.

He also marched against Romania and returned after losing many of those who were with him.

## The Ninth Year of Leo’s Reign

The impious emperor Leo began to speak against the holy and venerable images.

When Pope Gregory of Rome learned this, he prohibited the payment of tribute by the city of Rome and Italy. He wrote a doctrinal letter to Leo, saying that an emperor ought not to make pronouncements concerning the faith or violate the ancient doctrines of the Catholic Church, which had been proclaimed by the holy Fathers. [Note: See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book VI, chapter 49.]

## The Tenth Year of Leo’s Reign

Masalmas marched with an army against Romania and captured Caesarea of Cappadocia. Muhavias, son of Evelid, also marched against Romania and, after ranging through the country, returned.

In that same year, during the summer, a vapor appeared to boil up from the depths of the sea between the islands of Thera and Therasia, as though from a fiery furnace, and continued for several days. As it gradually thickened and spread, the entire smoke appeared as a fiery blaze.

Because of the density of the earthly substance, it sent great pumice stones, like heaps, throughout Asia Minor, to Lesbos, Abydos, and the coasts of Macedonia, so that the entire surface of the sea was filled with these pumice stones.

In the midst of this immense fire, an island formed from an accumulation of earth and joined itself to the island called Hiera, although it had not previously existed.

Just as the aforesaid islands of Thera and Therasia once boiled up, so this island too arose in the time of Leo, the enemy of God. He supposed that divine wrath directed against him would be on his side, yet he more insolently stirred up war against the holy and venerable images. He had as his colleague and helper Beser, the denier of God, who was like him in irrationality.

Both men were uneducated and undisciplined, and from this many kinds of evil arise.

The crowds in the imperial city were very distressed by the new doctrines and planned to rise against him. They killed certain imperial officials who were removing the icon of God that could be seen placed above the great bronze gate. Many of them were punished for the truth by mutilation of their limbs, scourging, exile, and confiscation of property, especially those who appeared distinguished by nobility and eloquence.

Leo even extinguished the schools of learning and the pious education preserved from the time of Constantine the Great of blessed memory. Leo became the destroyer of this and many other good things belonging to Constantine, since he also possessed the mentality of the Saracens.

Moved by divine zeal, naval forces rose against him in a great uprising, both those of Hellas and those from the Cycladic islands.

Agallianus, the *turmarch* of the Helladic forces, was commander of the army, together with Stephen. As they approached the imperial city, they were defeated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction, after engaging the Byzantines. Their ships were burned by fire. Some of them were drowned, among them Agallianus, who, fully armed, threw himself into the sea.

The survivors came over to the emperor, and Cosmas and Stephen were executed.

The wickedness of the impious Leo and his accomplice therefore increased, as he extended persecution against piety.

During the summer solstice of this tenth indiction, after they had received their wicked victory over their fellow believers, two Arab *amirs* prepared an attack against Nicaea in Bithynia: Amer, leading fifteen thousand light-armed troops, went ahead and unexpectedly surrounded the city, while Muhavias followed with another eighty-five thousand.

After a long siege and the partial destruction of the walls, they nevertheless failed to capture the city. The prayers of the holy Fathers, which had been faithfully directed to God, were graciously received, and the sanctification of the venerable church prevailed—the church in which their sacred images are raised for veneration and are honored to this day by those who share their mentality.

Moreover, a certain Constantine, a *strator* of Artabasdus, saw an image of the Mother of God standing. He seized a stone, threw it at her, shattered it, and, when it had fallen, trampled on it.

In a dream he saw Our Lady standing before him and saying:

“Do you know what a powerful case you have brought against me? In truth, you have done this against your own head.”

Afterwards, when the Saracens were attacking the wall and the battle was raging, that wretched man ran to the wall like a brave soldier. He was struck by a stone hurled from a siege engine; his head and face were crushed, and he received a fitting recompense for his impiety.

The Saracens collected much booty and spoil and returned. God thereby showed even this impious man that he had not triumphed because of the piety he had falsely proclaimed concerning his fellow believers, but because of a divine and ineffable judgment that blunted and removed such Arab strength from the city of the holy Fathers. Through their intercessions, because of the carefully honored images preserved there, this served as a rebuke and an unassailable judgment against the tyrant, as well as a confirmation of those who act piously.

The impious man was not mistaken only concerning prayer before the venerable images, but also concerning the intercessions of the most pure Mother of God and of all the saints. He abhorred their relics as wickedly as his Arab teachers did.

From that time onward he shamelessly disparaged the blessed Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, accusing all his imperial and episcopal predecessors, as well as the Christian peoples, of having been idolaters because of their prayer before the holy and venerable icons. In his ignorant unbelief, he could not understand the language concerning affective prayer.

## The Eleventh Year of Leo’s Reign

In the same year Muhavias captured the fortress of Atheus and returned.

## The Twelfth Year of Leo’s Reign

The son of Chajani, ruler of the Khazars, marched against Media and Armenia. He found Gradacus, the Arab commander, in Arabia, killed him and the multitude that was with him, devastated the lands of the Armenians and Medes, and returned, striking great fear into the Arabs.

## The Thirteenth Year of Leo’s Reign

Masalmas moved his camp against the land of the Turks. They engaged one another, and men fell in battle on both sides. Terrified, Masalmas fled into the mountains of the Khazars and returned.

In the same year the emperor Leo, raging against the right faith, brought the blessed Germanus before him and began to coax him with flattering words.

The blessed high priest said to him:

“We have heard that the removal of the holy images will occur, but not during your reign.”

When Leo compelled him to say under whose reign it would occur, Germanus replied:

“Under Conon’s.”

Leo said:

“Indeed, my name from baptism is Conon.”

Germanus replied:

“God forbid, lord, that this evil should be accomplished through your reign. The one who will bring it to completion is the forerunner of Antichrist and the destroyer of the divine Incarnation.”

The savage tyrant raged at this and threatened the blessed man, like Herod the executioner.

The patriarch recalled to him the promises he had made before becoming emperor, how he had given God as guarantor that he would not disturb the Church in any way from its apostolic and divinely transmitted rites.

But the wretch was not even then confounded. He watched and secretly planted certain words, striving to find him acting against the emperor, so that he might depose him from the throne as a conspirator rather than as a confessor.

In this he had as his accomplice Anastasius, his disciple and *syncellus*, to whom he had promised, as one who agreed with his impiety, that he would become the adulterous successor to the throne.

The blessed Germanus, not unaware of Anastasius and seeing him so ill-disposed, imitated his God and, as though addressing another Judas Iscariot, wisely and gently reminded him of the things connected with betrayal.

Since he saw Leo to be unchangeable, he one day turned to Anastasius, who was treading on the back of his robe as he was going in to the emperor, and said:

“You will not escape the time of entering.” [Note: The Greek expression is δίϊππον (*disippon*), rendered here as “Duppin.”]

Anastasius was distressed by these words. Together with the others who had heard them, he did not understand the prophecy. But when he experienced its fulfillment at the end of fifteen years—in the third year of the reign of the emperor Constantine, the persecutor, in the twelfth indiction—everyone was persuaded by divine grace that the words had been prophetically spoken to the ungrateful man.

After Constantine had obtained the empire following the rebellion of his kinsman Artabasdus, he entered through Duppin. [Note: “This Anastasius was killed and, together with the other enemies, paraded in the hippodrome.”] He exhibited Anastasius, naked and seated backward on an ass, because he had cursed Constantine together with the other enemies and had crowned Artabasdus, as will be related in its proper place.

In Byzantium this sacred and outstanding Germanus, defender of the pious doctrines, prevailed as a champion, fighting against the beasts—against this Leo, the “Pheronymus” [Note: Another reading: “Pheronymus.” Cedrenus has Φερώνυμον.]—and his supporters.

In elder Rome, Gregory, the most holy apostolic man and confessor of Peter, chief of the apostles, shone in word and deed. He removed Rome and Italy, together with all the rights of the commonwealth and of the Church in the West, from obedience to Leo and to the empire established under him.

In Syria, near Damascus, John the presbyter and monk, surnamed Chrysorrhoas, an excellent teacher, shone forth in life and word. [Note: Another reading: “John Mansur.” See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book VI, chapter 39.]

Leo expelled Germanus from the throne, although Germanus had been appointed under him. Gregory openly rebuked Leo in letters that are known to many, and John, together with the bishops of the East, subjected him to anathemas.

On the seventh day before the Ides of January, on a Tuesday of the thirteenth indiction, the impious Leo held a silence concerning the holy and venerable icons in the tribunal of the nineteen couches. He summoned Germanus, the most holy patriarch, thinking that he could persuade him to sign against the holy icons.

The strong servant of Christ did not in any way consent to his detestable false doctrine. After rightly setting forth the word of truth, he renounced the high priesthood, handed over the pallium, and, after many didactic discourses, said:

“If I am Jonah, throw me into the sea. For without a universal synod it is impossible for me, according to apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers, to innovate concerning the faith, O emperor.”

He departed to the place called Platanium and devoted himself to quiet in his ancestral house. He had served as high priest for fourteen years, five months, and seven days.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, they appointed as patriarch Anastasius, falsely so named, the disciple and *syncellus* of the blessed Germanus, who agreed with Leo’s impiety because of his love of worldly power.

They promoted him to be bishop of Constantinople.

As I have said, Gregory, the most holy bishop of Rome, rejected Anastasius together with his writings. He rebuked Leo in letters as one acting impiously and caused Rome and all Italy to withdraw from his rule.

The tyrant, therefore, raged against the venerable images and extended his persecution.

Many clerics, monks, and devout laypeople suffered danger for speaking rightly.

In the fourteenth year of Leo’s reign, this year Masalmas moved an army against Romania and, when he had entered Cappadocia, captured the fortress of Cursianus by treachery. In the fifteenth year of Leo’s reign, Masalmas moved his camp against Turkey and, when he had reached as far as the Caspian Gates, turned back from there in fear [Col. 1086B]. In the sixteenth year of his reign, the emperor Leo married the daughter of Chajani, the khagan of the Khazars, to his son Constantine, after making her a Christian. He named her Irene. After learning the sacred writings, she became distinguished by her devotion and reproved these men for their impiety. Muhavias, son of Evelid, meanwhile drew up his forces against Romania and, coming as far as Paphlagonia, returned with much booty.

But the emperor raged against the pope and against the revolt of Rome and Italy; he assembled a large fleet and sent it against him, appointing Manes, the praetor of the Cibyrrhaeots, as its commander. Then the enemy of God, raging still more fiercely and being possessed by an Arab mentality, imposed head-taxes upon the Thracian territories, Sicily, and Calabria. He ordered that what are called the patrimonies of the holy chief apostles—estates which formerly contributed half a gold piece and three talents to the churches—be paid into the public treasury. He also ordered that male children be counted and registered, just as Pharaoh once did with those among the Hebrews, although even his Arab teachers are known not to have done this to the Christians living in their lands [Col. 1086C].

In the seventeenth year of Leo’s reign, a mortality occurred in Syria, and many perished. In the eighteenth year of Leo’s reign, Zacharias was recognized as Roman bishop. In the same year Theodore Mansur was sent into exile in the regions of the desert. A fiery, shining sign appeared in the sky, and Muhavias ravaged Asia.

In the nineteenth year of Leo’s reign, Zulcimin moved an army against the region of Armenia and accomplished nothing [Col. 1086D]. In the twentieth year of Leo’s reign, Zulcimin led many captives away from Asia and also took captive a certain Pergamene who claimed to be Tiberius, the son of Justinian. Evelid sent him to Jerusalem in honor of his son and to inspire imperial fear, with imperial and appropriate honors, soldiers, and scepters; he ordered him to be led throughout Syria with great honor, for all to see.

In the twenty-first year of the emperor Leo, Zulcimin moved an army against Romania and ravaged the fortress called Siderum [Col. 1087A]; he also led away captive Eutychius, son of the patrician Marianus.

In the twenty-second year of Leo’s reign, in the month of May, in the eighth indiction, Zulcimin moved against Romania with eighty thousand men and four commanders. Gamer was their general, lying in ambush with ten thousand brigands in the Asian district. His associates were Melich and Bathal, who with twenty thousand cavalrymen were ravaging the area around Acronium. After them came Zulcimin with sixty thousand men, advancing around Cappadocia and Tyana. Some of these, after inflicting extensive slaughter upon men, women, and beasts throughout Asia and Cappadocia, returned unharmed.

Those who were with Melich and Bathal at Acronium were attacked and defeated by Leo, or Constantine. Many of them perished in the fighting itself together with the two commanders. Eight hundred warriors, who had stood against them with as many as six thousand men, fled to Sinada; remaining alive, they joined Zulcimin and returned toward Syria without glory [Col. 1087B]. In the same year, many in Africa were given over to destruction by them together with the praetor, a Damascene by name.

In the twenty-third year of Leo’s reign, the markets of Damascus were burned by the Raticeni, the most wicked Syrians, who were affixed to the gallows. In the same year a great and terrifying earthquake occurred at Constantinople, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth indiction, on the fourth day of the week, at the eighth hour. Churches and monasteries collapsed, and a great number of people perished.

The statue that stood above the Gate of Attalus of the Great Constantine also fell, together with Attalus himself; so did the inscription of Arcadius that stood above the column of Xerophilus, and the statue of the elder Theodosius that was seen above the Golden Gate. Parts of the city walls also fell, as did cities and villages in Thrace, Nicomedia in Bithynia, Praenetus, and Nicaea, where only one church remained standing. In certain places the sea also fled beyond its boundaries, and the earthquake continued for twelve months.

The emperor addressed the people, saying: “You are unable to build the walls, but we shall order the administrators to do so, and they will collect from each person one silver coin for every gold coin.” Having received this money, the emperor rebuilt the walls. Thus arose the custom of giving the administrators two siliquae [Note: [Col. 1087] Twenty-three denarii; φόχος (*phóchos*, an uncertain term) on each coin.]

The year from the creation of the world was, according to the Romans, the six thousand forty-eighth from Adam; according to the Egyptians, or Alexandrians [Col. 1087D], the six thousand two hundred thirty-second; according to the Macedonians, from Philip, the one thousand sixty-third [Col. 1088A].

Leo reigned from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction, until the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth indiction, having reigned twenty-four years, two months, and twenty-two days. Likewise, his son Constantine, his successor in empire and impiety, reigned from that same fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth indiction, and himself reigned thirty-four years, three months, and two days.

Thus, as we have said, Leo died in that same year, by a death both of soul and of body, and his son Constantine became emperor. Whatever happened to Christians under the impious Leo—whether concerning the Orthodox faith, civil administration, the pursuit of shameful profit and avarice, the impositions devised and levied throughout Sicily, Calabria, and Crete, the apostasy of Italy on account of this cacodoxy, famine, pestilence, and the oppression of the nations, to say nothing of particular matters—is shown in the preceding chapters.

It is, however, fitting henceforth to set forth, for the benefit of posterity and of the wretched people now deceived by his cacodoxy, the mockeries perpetrated by his son’s reign, as by the God who sees all things, truthfully and not needlessly: what he impiously did from the tenth indiction, the first year of his reign, until the fourteenth indiction, the year of his death.

This most pernicious, uncivilized, savage man, who exercised power tyrannically and unlawfully, first abandoned God, his undefiled Mother, and all the saints. He delighted in magical sorceries, debauchery, bloody sacrifices, horse dung [Col. 1088C], and urine; he rejoiced in effeminacies and invocations of demons, and from his earliest age lived among every invention that corrupts souls.

Since he had received his father’s imperial power together with wickedness, he displayed no small amount of depravity in a short time, so that all immediately hated him for his shamelessness. Pressure was therefore brought to bear upon Artabasdus the curopalates and count of the Opsikion, who had married his sister Anna, to assume the empire.

In the same year Evelid killed Christian captives in every city. Among them Eutychius, son of the patrician Marianus, was revealed as a true martyr at Carrhae in Mesopotamia, where his relics also work healings by the grace of God; many others likewise were brought to perfection through their blood.

# BOOK TWENTY-TWO

[Col. 1087]

## CONSTANTINE

[Col. 1087D]

In the year 733 from the incarnation of the Lord, Constantine, persecutor of the laws handed down by the Fathers, reigned by divine judgments and because of the multitude of our sins. When he had set out toward the district of the Opsikion on the fifth day before the Kalends of July against the Arabs, he came to the city called Crasus [Col. 1088D].

When the aforementioned Artabasdus of Dorylaeum was with the people of the Opsikion, they became mutually suspicious. Constantine sent to him asking that his sons be sent to him, since he desired to see them as though they were his grandsons. His intention, however, was to seize them and imprison them.

When Artabasdus understood the fraud, knowing his immeasurable wickedness, he fell into despair for himself. Addressing and persuading the people, he rushed against Constantine with the entire multitude. They killed with swords Beser the patrician, who was a follower of the Saracen religion and had gone ahead of them.

Constantine, however, happened to find a wretched horse lying there. Mounting it, he fled to Amorium. When he had hurried to the theme of the Orientals, whose praetor was Lacinus, those men surrounded him. He encouraged them with great promises and sent them to Sisinnius, who was praetor of the Thracesian themes, and persuaded them to help him.

From this arose most savage battles and conflicts among his subjects, since each man was called emperor. Artabasdus also wrote to Theophanes the patrician and magister, who had remained in the city as the emperor’s representative. Through Athanasius the Silentiary, who favored Artabasdus, he gathered the people at the catechumenia of the Great Church and, by letters and through the aforesaid Athanasius, persuaded everyone to believe that the emperor had died [Col. 1089B].

Artabasdus was proclaimed emperor by the themes. Then all the people, together with Athanasius the false-named patriarch, subjected Constantine to anathema and condemnation as an arrogant man and an adversary of God. They gladly approved his death, as though liberated from the greatest evil. They proclaimed Artabasdus emperor as an Orthodox man and champion of the divine doctrines.

Immediately Monotes sent word into the Thracian districts to Nicephorus, Artabasdus’s son and praetor of the Thracesians, that he should strengthen the city’s guard and establish an army there. After closing the gates of the walls and setting guards, he seized Constantine’s sons, beat them, tonsured them, and placed them under guard.

When Artabasdus had entered the city with the Opsikians, Constantine reached Chrysopolis with two themes, namely those of the Thracesians and the Orientals. Unable to accomplish anything, he returned and wintered at Amorium.

Artabasdus raised sacred images throughout the city. Meanwhile the barbarians, perceiving their quarrel with one another, inflicted much plunder upon Romania, under the leadership of the praetor Zulcimin.

The false patriarch Anastasius, holding the venerable and life-giving wood, swore to the people, saying: “By him who was affixed to it, Constantine the emperor spoke to me in these words, affirming: ‘Do not suppose that the Son of God is the one whom Mary bore and who is called Christ, but a mere man. Mary bore him just as my mother bore me.’” Then all the people cursed him.

In the second year of Constantine’s reign—he held the Roman empire for thirty-five years—the Arab commander Evelid died. Since the holy Church of Antioch had remained widowed for forty years, the Arabs forbidding a patriarch to be appointed there, it had a certain very devout Syrian monk named Stephen, uncultivated indeed but religious.

The most holy Church of Antioch instructed the Christians living in the East that, if they wished to be permitted to have a patriarch, they should choose this Stephen. Believing that this had been divinely arranged, they consecrated him to the see of Theoupolis. From that time until now, such appointments have proceeded without hindrance.

In the same year Gizid, son of Habdimelich, obtained the Arab leadership [Note: [Col. 1089D] Another reading: Hualid, son of Hisam.]. Constantine sent Andrew the spatharius to him, while Artabasdus sent Gregory the logothete, each seeking assistance.

There was also a lack of rain and earthquakes in various places, so that mountains were joined to one another in the desert of Saba and fortresses sank into the earth and were swallowed up.

In the same year Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, together with the entire city, returned from the cacodoxy of the Monothelites to orthodoxy, having remained under Cyrus, who was patriarch of Alexandria under Heraclius.

The commander Gamer also moved against Romania with a multitude of Arabs and returned after leading many into captivity. A sign appeared in the sky toward the north in the month of June.

Hali ordered that the most holy metropolitan of Damascus have his tongue mutilated, on the grounds that he openly denounced the kinship of the Arabs and the Manichaeans. He sent him into exile to Eudaemon Arabia, where he died a martyr, having received death for Christ’s name. According to the narrators of this event, he celebrated the divine liturgies with particular clarity; they testify that they themselves were fully convinced of this from what they heard.

His imitator and namesake Peter was revealed in those same times at Mavima as a voluntary martyr for Christ [Col. 1090C]. While suffering from illness, he summoned the leading Arabs, since they were accustomed to him when he had been a chartularius and had rendered the public taxes after the accounts had been made up. He said to them:

“May you receive from God a reward for visiting me, although you are unbelieving friends. I want you to be witnesses of my testament, which is as follows: Everyone who does not believe in the Father, the Son, and the consubstantial Holy Spirit, and in the Trinity of the Godhead in the unity, is dead in soul and worthy of eternal torment. Such is your false prophet Muhammat, the forerunner of the Antichrist. Therefore, if you believe my testimony to you concerning heaven and earth, depart from his fable. I advise you not to be tormented together with him.”

While he reasoned and discoursed with them about God in this and many other ways, they listened in astonishment—or perhaps madness—and appeared to endure it patiently, supposing that because of his illness he was out of his senses. But when he recovered from his infirmity, he began to cry out in a louder voice: “Anathema to Muhammat, to his fabulous writing, and to all who obey and believe him!”

Then he suffered punishment by the sword and was revealed as a martyr.

Our holy Father John, rightly surnamed Chrysorrhoas—“Golden-streaming”—because of the golden and radiant grace of the Holy Spirit that blossomed in him both in word and in the conduct of his life, honored him with encomiastic discourses. The impious emperor Constantine annually subjected this John to anathema because of his eminent orthodoxy. Instead of Mansur, which was his ancestral name and which, in the Jewish sense, means “redeemed,” Constantine called him Manseron, changing his name, as a new teacher of the Church [Col. 1091A].

In the same year Gizid transferred the Cyrii to Syria. Artabasdus sent his son Nicetas, a monostrategos promoted to command, to the Armenian theme. He likewise crowned his son Nicephorus through the patriarch Anastasius.

In the month of May, when Artabasdus had gone into the district of the Opsikion and had chosen soldiers, he seized all Asia and ravaged it. When Constantine learned this, he moved against him. When he reached him in the district of the Sardeans, as Celbianus was returning, he engaged him in battle, routed him, and pursued them as far as Cyzicus.

When Artabasdus reached Cyzicus, he boarded a dromon and was saved in the city [Col. 1091B].

Moreover, in August of the same tenth indiction, Nicetas the monostrategos, Artabasdus’s son, brought battle against Constantine at Modrimen and Cysseum. Turning his back, he fled, and killed the Armenian Tridates, a most courageous soldier and cousin of Artabasdus, together with many other commanders.

The losses of both sides were considerable: the Armenians and the Armenian forces fighting against the Orientals and the Thracesians, who supported Constantine.

Meanwhile the ancient enemy, the devil, aroused such savagery and mutual slaughter against Christians in those times that even sons rose against fathers and brothers against brothers, sparing no one in the slaughter. The opposing positions and houses were burned without mercy [Col. 1091C].

Amid these events, Pope Stephen of Rome, after suffering many evils at the hands of Astulf, king of the Lombards, fled to the Franks under Pippin, who was mayor of the palace and first in the entire administration of the affairs of the Frankish people.

It had formerly been their custom for a lord—that is, a king—to rule according to hereditary succession and to do nothing or arrange nothing except to eat and drink irrationally, remain at home, preside on the Kalends of May before the whole nation, greet them and be greeted by them, receive the customary services, bestow gifts upon them, and thus live with them until the next May. He had the mayor of the palace as his adviser, arranging all the affairs of the nation.

Those who belonged to that lineage were said to descend from the [Note: [Col. 1091D] Another reading: “the descendants, Cristatae.”] Cristati [Col. 1091D], which is interpreted as Trichorachati. For they had hair growing along their backs like pigs.

The aforementioned Pope Stephen, compelled by force and driven by Astulf’s cruelty, was also urged by him to go to Francia and do whatever he could. When he arrived, he advanced Pippin as king, a man of proven worth, who at that time also governed affairs after the king. Pippin had defeated the Arabs who had crossed from Africa into Spain and who still hold that same Spain; they had also hastened to fight against the Franks.

Pippin, resisting them with a multitude, killed their commander Habdirracines, son of Muhavia [Note: [Col. 1091D] Another reading: “and also their commander Habdorracmen.”] [Col. 1092A], who held the leadership of that people. At the same time he killed an almost uncountable multitude beside the River Rhône.

He is admired and loved by the people not only for this but also for other outstanding deeds. He was made their first leader, and not ignobly [Note: [Col. 1092D] Another reading: “not without distinction.”]. The same Stephen released him from the perjury committed in making him king; he also tonsured Pippin’s predecessor as king and enclosed him honorably and peacefully in a monastery.

This Pippin had two sons, Charles and his brother Carloman.

In the third year of Constantine’s reign, a sign appeared in the north, and ash descended in various places. A great earthquake also occurred at the Caspian Gates.

Gizid was killed by the Arabs. He had ruled for one year, and his son Hyces now held the leadership [Note: [Col. 1092D] Another reading: Hizidlipsos.]. This man, after distributing much money, obtained Damascus from Habdimelich and received pledges that he should rule.

In September of the twelfth indiction, Constantine descended to the district of Chalcedon and returned to the Thracian districts, since Sisinnius, praetor of the Thracesians, had already returned through Abydos and was besieging the landward wall of the city.

When the emperor came to the Gate of Carsius, he went as far as the Golden Gate, displaying himself to the crowds; then he returned again and made camp at Saint Mamas.

The citizens began to suffer because supplies were running out. Accordingly, Artabasdus sent Anastasius, a secretary, and Artabasdus his domesticus to carry provisions to the Caspian Gates. The fleet of the Cibyrrhaeots and the fleet of Abydos encountered them, seized them, and brought them to the emperor. He gave the grain to his people but immediately deprived Anastasius and Artabasdus of their eyes [Col. 1092C].

After this Artabasdus attempted to open the gates from the landward side and engage Constantine in battle. When the clash occurred, Artabasdus’s army was routed, and many died, among them Monotes.

Artabasdus constructed triremes carrying cauldrons of fire and sent some of them to Saint Mamas against the fleet of the Cibyrrhaeots. When they reached Saint Mamas, the Cibyrrhaeots came out and drove them back.

A severe famine arose in the city, so that a measure of barley was sold for twelve coins, legumes for fifteen, millet and lupins for eight, five pounds of oil for one coin, and a sextarius of wine for half a coin.

As the people were being killed by hunger, Artabasdus was compelled to allow them to leave the city. But after closing the gates, he prevented some of them from leaving. Some therefore washed their faces and wrapped themselves in women’s clothing; others concealed themselves in monastic habit and haircloth garments. In this way they were able to hide and get out.

Nicetas the monostrategos, having gathered his people after their dispersal from Odrina, came as far as Chrysopolis. When he was returning, the emperor crossed over and pursued them from behind. When he reached Nicomedia, he captured Nicetas by force together with the curator who had formerly been bishop of the Marcellians; he immediately ordered the latter to be beheaded. He ordered that the monostrategos, bound, be displayed upon the wall [Col. 1093A].

On the fourth day before the Nones of November, he suddenly fought in the afternoon and seized the city by means of the landward wall.

Artabasdus, however, together with the patrician [Note: [Col. 1093D] Another reading: Bagtango.] Bagranus, entered a ship and appeared for the moment to have escaped to Mopsuestia. He then went to the fortress of Puzanes and shut himself inside.

When the emperor captured them by force, he blinded Arabasdum together with his two sons. He beheaded Bagranus in the vivarium and hung his head on the Milion for three days.

Thirty years later, remembering the evil and showing no mercy, the emperor ordered Bagranus’s wife to go to the monastery of Chora—for he had been buried there—and to dig up his bones, carry them in her cloak to the tombs called those of Pelagius, and lay them there together with the dead who had died by violence.

O inhumanity! He also killed many other leading men who had assisted Artabasdus, and crippled countless others by removing their eyes, hands, or feet. He ordered the foreign soldiers who had entered with him to go into the houses and seize the possessions of the citizens’ families.

He displayed many other evils, indeed innumerable ones, to the city. When he celebrated the hippodrome games, he brought Artabasdus, bound, into the circus through the Dippion together with his sons and friends, along with Anastasius the false-named patriarch, who had been publicly beaten and was sitting backward on a donkey. He paraded them all through the Dippion into the circus.

He restored Anastasius, since he was his associate, to the priestly throne, but intimidated him and subjected him to servitude. Sisinnius the patrician and praetor of the Thracesians, who had accompanied him extensively and fought on his behalf, and was known to be his cousin, he blinded after eleven days [Col. 1093C].

In the fourth year of Constantine’s reign, Maruan is known as the Arab commander; he held the leadership over them for six years. In this year a great comet was seen in Syria. Trebith also incited a revolt against Maruan, as did Datach of Arur. Maruan captured and killed them at the borders of Emesa with a multitude of warriors, namely ten thousand.

In the same year, at the request of the Christians of the East, Maruan permitted Theophylact, a presbyter of Edessa, to be consecrated patriarch of Antioch, while Stephen was sleeping [i.e. had died]; he ordered him to be honored by the Arabs with letters [Note: [Col. 1094D] Another reading: “with catholic letters.”]. He was adorned with spiritual gifts, especially chastity.

Abas, who had shed much Christian blood and ravaged many places [Col. 1093D], was killed in prison. At Cithium he had hanged one hundred twenty Calbenians on a tree. A certain Ethiopian sent by Maruan came to him and, after filling a sack with quicklime, entered and suffocated him by placing the sack over his entire head and nostrils. Thus the evil-doer Abas received a just punishment.

For through magical deceptions and invocations of demons he had devised many evils against Christians. He had also taken part with Gizid in bloodshed.

In the fifth year of the reign of Constantine, Zulcimin, having gathered troops, again undertook war against Marwan; after losing seven thousand men, he was defeated and escaped to the vicinity of Palmyra, and thereafter into Persia. [Col. 1094A] The inhabitants of Emesa, Heliopolis, and Damascus also stirred up a revolt against Marwan, who, while sending his son against Datach, himself came with a force to Emethsa, which he captured in four months. Datach, meanwhile, was coming from Persia with a very large army. Marwan attacked him in Mesopotamia, and after killing many of his associates, seized and killed him.

At this time Constantine captured Germanicia, directing his army against Syria, and Dulichium, having found an entrance because of the Arabs’ mutual conflict; he dismissed the unarmed Arabs who were there. He also took with him his maternal relatives and settled them in Byzantium, together with many Syrian Monophysite heretics. Many of these still live in Thrace, and, following Peter the Fuller, crucify the Trinity in the Trisagion.

Moreover, from the fourth day before the Ides of August until the Kalends of October, dark obscurity occurred. Then Marwan, victorious after capturing Emesa, killed all the relatives and children of Hiscen, and stormed the walls of Heliopolis, Damascus, and Jerusalem, slaughtering many prominent men and mutilating the remainder.

In the sixth year of Constantine’s reign, a great earthquake occurred in Palestine, around the Jordan, and throughout Syria, in January, at the fourth hour. Many thousands, indeed countless people, died; churches and monasteries collapsed, especially near the desert of the holy city.

That same year a pestilential death, beginning in Sicily and Calabria and consuming everything like a fire, reached Monobasia, Hellas, and the intervening [Col. 1094C] islands. It scourged the impious Constantine throughout the entire fourteenth indiction and restrained him from the madness that he was directing against the holy churches and the holy and venerable images. Yet he remained uncorrected, like Pharaoh of old.

This bubonic plague continued to spread and reached the imperial city in the fifteenth indiction. Suddenly, on human clothing, on the sacred vestments of the churches, and on the curtains, many little crosses appeared, as though marked with oil. Great sadness and loss of courage consequently arose because of the uncertainty of this sign.

Nevertheless, divine anger also came, continually destroying not only the citizens of the city but also those living in all its suburbs. Visions likewise appeared to many people, who, falling into ecstasy, thought that they were accompanying certain foreigners, as they supposed, with savage faces; they greeted and conversed with people encountered on the road as though with friends. After noting what these figures said, they later reported it. They also saw them entering houses, leaving some people in the houses and wounding others. Much of what they said was subsequently seen to happen.

Furthermore, in the spring of the first indiction the plague spread more widely, but in summer it burned with such force that entire houses were completely shut up, and there was no one who did not have to bury the dead. Necessity therefore devised the expedient of laying boards over animals and carrying the dead upon them. Others likewise were transported piled onto wagons.

When all the tombs—both in the city and in the suburbs—had been filled, and the cisterns without water, the pools, many vineyards, and even the inner gardens within the old walls had been dug up for such burials, scarcely were all these places sufficient for so great a necessity.

When every house had been filled with calamity because of the deposition that the rulers had impiously made against the holy images, the fleet of the Agarenes immediately came from Alexandria to Cyprus, where the Roman fleet also was. But when the commander of the Cibyrrhaeots attacked them, and they were trapped in the harbor of Cirama, the mouth of the harbor being held, they admit that, although there were thirty dromons, only three escaped.

In the seventh year of Constantine’s reign, Gregory was killed by the Aruritae, and Marwan was victorious, as I have related above.

In the eighth year of Constantine’s reign, the people of the eastern regions of Persia, called the Chorosanitae Maurophori, rose up against Marwan and all his kindred who had ruled from the false prophet Muhammad up to Marwan himself, and against those called the sons of Muhata.

After the killing of Gizid, these groups fought and constrained one another. Those called the sons of Hiscem, together with the relatives of Halim—and the false prophet’s own descendants, though concealed and fugitive—gathered in Arabia Minor, with Hybraim, son of Evelid, holding the chief position among them. They sent one of their freedmen, named Amussim, to Chorosan, to certain prominent men there, asking them to support them against Marwan.

These men gathered at the house of a certain Cactaban, took counsel, and incited slaves against their own masters. They killed many in a single night and, enriched with their arms, horses, and money, became more powerful.

They divided into two tribes, namely the Caismians and the Lamonites. When Amussim saw that the more powerful were the Lamonites [Note: [Col. 1095D] Another reading: Hiamanites], he stirred them up against the Caismians. After killing the latter, he came into Persia with Cactaban, attacked Hibin, son of Halbaren, and, after defeating him, captured nearly one hundred thousand men.

When he came to Hibin, where the enemy was, and Hibin was advancing with two hundred thousand men, Amussim defeated him. Then, coming to Marwan at the Zaban River, where Marwan had three hundred thousand men, he defeated him and killed an innumerable multitude of them. It was a sight worthy of wonder: in accordance with Scripture, one pursued a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight.

When Marwan saw that they were winning such powerful victories, he went to Carrhae. After crossing the river, he encountered a bridge made of boats, and, taking money with him, fled to Egypt with his household and four thousand native troops.

In the ninth year of Constantine’s reign, Marwan suffered persecution from the Maurophori and, after a very severe battle, was captured and killed by them. Their leader was Salim, son of Halim, one of the fugitive dignitaries and one of those who had sent Amussim.

The rest, having gathered against Samaria and the region called Thraconitis, distributed the leadership by lot: Abubalas first, then his brother Habdalla, son of Muhammad, and after him Hyse. They assigned Habdalla, son of Halim and brother of Salim, the supreme command of Syria; Salim himself was to govern Egypt.

They decreed that Habdalla, the brother of Abubalas, should receive by lot the principate over Mesopotamia. Abubalas himself, who also held the foremost position of all in Persia, transferred to himself the Persian principate, together with those Persians who had supported him from Damascus.

Those who had escaped—namely, the sons and relatives of Marwan—came from Egypt into Africa and, crossing the narrow strait of the sea toward the Ocean, located at what is called the Seven, which forms the boundary between Libya and Europe, settled in Hispanic Europe, where they remain to the present day. They had with them certain people known to have lived there previously, having been transported there by ship from Muhavia, since they were his relatives and shared his religion.

The destruction under Muhavia lasted six years.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the same third indiction, a son was born to the emperor Constantine. He named him Leo; his mother was the daughter of Chajani of Khazaria.

That same year an earthquake occurred in Syria, a vast and terrible catastrophe. Some cities were completely destroyed; others only partially; while others, together with their walls and dwellings intact, moved from the mountainous regions into the lower plains and remained safe at a distance of about six miles, or a little more.

Finally, those who had seen the land of Mesopotamia with their own eyes asserted that it had been split open for a length of two miles, and that from its depths another earth, exceedingly white and sandy, had risen. From its midst, they said, an unblemished mule-like animal emerged, speaking with a human voice and announcing an invasion of the nation from the desert against the Arabs. This also came to pass.

In the following year, the fourth indiction, on the feast of holy Pentecost, the emperor Constantine crowned his son Leo emperor through Anastasius, his associate patriarch.

In the tenth year of Constantine’s reign, Muhammad became leader of the Arabs and ruled them for five years. That same year the Chalcedonians stirred up hostilities against the Maurophori Persians, and four thousand of the latter were killed by them in the mountains of Emesa. The same thing also happened in Arabia, where the same Persians fought against the Caismians.

When Marwan’s head, embalmed with myrrh, was brought, many ceased their hostilities.

In the eleventh year of his reign, Constantine captured Theodosiopolis and Melitene and led away Armenian captives. Theodore, son of Bigarius and a native of Arabia Minor, was appointed patriarch of Antioch after the death of the most holy Theophylact. He governed the church for six years.

In the twelfth year of his reign, the impious emperor Constantine, swollen with pride, devised many things against the Church and the orthodox faith. By remaining silent day after day, he unfortunately bent the people to follow his own opinion, becoming a forerunner of the impiety that was to come.

In the thirteenth year of Constantine’s reign, Anastasius, who had wickedly ruled the Constantinopolitan throne, died in body and soul, exhausted by the miserable illness called *cordapsus*. Excrement poured out through his mouth, and he paid a fitting penalty for the audacity that he had displayed against God and against his own master.

That same year the impious Constantine convened an unlawful council of thirty-eight bishops against the holy and venerable images in the palace of Hieria. Its leaders were Ephesius, son of Absimarus, and Pastillas of Perge. They formulated as doctrine whatever seemed right to them, with no one present from the Catholic sees—namely Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, or Jerusalem. Beginning on the fourth day before the Ides of February, they continued until the sixth day before the Ides of August of the same seventh indiction.

When they had assembled at Blachernae as enemies of the Mother of God, the emperor Constantine ascended the ambo holding Constantine the monk, who had been bishop of Syleion. After praying, he proclaimed in a loud voice:

“Many years to Constantine, the universal patriarch.”

Then the emperor ascended the tribunal with Constantine the wicked prelate and the other bishops, and they shouted, publicly proclaiming their cacodox faith before the entire populace. They anathematized Germanus, the most holy patriarch, Gregory of Cyprus, and John Chrysorrhoas of Damascus, nephew of Mansur—holy and venerable men and teachers.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, Muhammad, also called Abubalas, died after ruling for five years. His brother Habdalla was at Macha, the place of their blasphemy.

Amussim, who was in Persia, therefore wrote that he should retain the principate, as it had been assigned to him by lot. When he learned that Habdalla, son of Halim, while his brother Salim was supreme governor of Syria, was aspiring to the principate and coming to obtain Persia, opposing the Persians and favoring those in Syria who were supporting him, he gathered his armies and attacked him near Nisibis. Amussim prevailed and killed many of them. Most of these were Slavs and Antiochenes.

Habdallas alone escaped. After a few days he sent a message to the other Habdalla, Muhammad’s brother, who had come from Macha to Persia with great eagerness. He shut him up in a decaying little house, ordered its foundations to be dug out, and secretly killed him.

Amussim, meanwhile, was raging against the Arabs of Syria because they had risen against the Maurophori and had captured many people in Palestine, Emesa, and the coastal regions. He was planning to attack them, but Habdalla restrained him with his armies. Enraged, Amussim hurried into inner Persia with a multitude.

Habdalla greatly feared him, and so summoned him with persuasive words and prayers, sending him the accursed insignia of their ruler—the rod and sandals of the false prophet Muhammad—and asking him to turn aside to him by a day’s journey so that he might offer him suitable thanksgiving.

Deceived, Amussim came with one hundred thousand horsemen. After joining Habdalla, he was killed by him with his own hands. Thus the principate was conferred upon Habdalla, who ruled the Arabs for twenty-one years.

In the fifteenth year of his reign, Constantine moved the Syrians and Armenians whom he had brought from Theodosiopolis and Melitene into Thrace. From these the heresy of the Publicans [Note: [Col. 1097D] Another reading: Paulicians] also spread.

Likewise, since only a few inhabitants remained in the city because of the plague, he brought in families from the islands and from Hellas, as well as from the lower regions, and in this way repopulated the city, making it densely inhabited.

That same year the Bulgarians sought terms because of the forts that had been built. But when the emperor intended to dishonor their *apocrisiarius*, they went out hostilely, reached the Long Wall, inflicted great destruction, and returned unharmed.

In the sixteenth year of Constantine’s reign, a considerable earthquake occurred in Palestine and Syria, on the seventh day before the Ides of March. Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, was exiled because the Arabs envied him, since he frequently reported their actions to the emperor Constantine by letter. Thereafter Halim sent this exile to his native region, Moabitis, and ordered that no new churches be built there, that the cross not be seen, and that no Christian discuss doctrine with the Arabs.

He also moved against Romania with eighty thousand men. When he reached Cappadocia, he heard that Constantine was advancing against him in arms. Terrified, he returned without accomplishing anything, except that he took with him a few Armenians who had come over to him.

In the seventeenth year of Constantine’s reign, Habdalla increased the tribute imposed on Christians so greatly that he subjected to taxation all monks, recluses, and Cionites known to be pleasing God.

He also marked the *cimilia* of the churches [Note: [Col. 1098D] Another reading: *cimiliarchia*] and brought Jews to sell them; they bought them freely.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, Constantine captured the Sclavini settled near Macedonia and subdued the remainder.

That same year certain Maurophori Persians, being adherents of a magical religion and held fast by diabolical deception, sold their possessions. They climbed naked onto the walls and threw themselves down, believing that they would fly into heaven. Having done nothing worthy of such a fate, they shattered their limbs as they plunged downward. Habdallas, through Halim, killed sixteen of them—specifically those who were leaders in the error—in Beroea and Chalcis.

In the nineteenth year of Constantine’s reign, the Arabs prevented the Christians from using the public writing offices for a short time. But, compelled once again, they entered into the same business with them, since they themselves were unable to write the calculations. They also drew up many armies, engaged Paul, the commander of the Armeniacs, in battle near Melan, and killed him. They likewise took forty-two distinguished men captive, together with many heads.

The emperor moved his army into Bulgaria. When he came to Verebegan, the Bulgarians met him at the barrier and slaughtered many of his troops. Among those captured were Leo the patrician, commander of the Thracesians, and Leo the *logothete* of Tudromium. They also captured their arms and a large number of people, and so returned dishonorably.

In the twentieth year of Constantine’s reign, there was an error concerning Easter. The orthodox in the East celebrated Easter on the eighth day before the Ides of April, whereas the erroneous heretics celebrated it on the Ides of April.

That same year the head of Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist was transferred from the monastery of Spelei to his own church in the city of the Emesenians. It was a celebrated place, and a descent had been built there. At that place it is honored and worshiped by the faithful to this day; it is honored with every fragrant odor, bodily and spiritual, and pours forth healing for all who approach with burning faith.

That same year a very bright comet appeared in the East for ten days and then again in the West for twenty-one days.

A certain Syrian named Theodore, a Libanite from the region of Heliopolis near Lebanon, rose up against the Arabs. When he made war upon them, many fell on both sides. Finally, he himself turned his back and fled, while all the Libanites who were with him were killed.

Revolts and wars also occurred in Africa, during a solar eclipse on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, a Friday, at the tenth hour.

Certain Maurophori rose up at Dabecho, declaring the son of the chief insignia-bearer to be God, as their nourisher. They put forward doctrines of this kind, entered the house of the Maurophorus who held this error, and killed sixty key-bearers. Some went out toward Barrasson and took many captives and innumerable sums of money.

In the twenty-first year of Constantine’s reign, the Cassiotae stirred up a revolt against the Maurophori because of women. Some of the Maurophori had remained in a house where three brothers lived, and they wished to throw the brothers’ wives into the sea. The three brothers rose up, killed them, and overpowered them. The others then gathered and killed the remaining men as well.

When Salimus sent troops, they came upon the brothers by treachery, seized them, and hanged them on a gallows; they also killed many others.

During the Paschal festival he entered the holy assembly in the Catholic church. While the metropolitan bishop stood there and cried out in the customary manner, saying to God, “Your people and Your Church entreat You,” they took him and shut him in prison. Another man completed the holy assembly, and great fear arose. Unless the metropolitan had calmed him by prudent and humble words, a terrible deed would certainly have been committed at that hour. This man was the blessed Anastasius.

That same year Constantine the persecutor killed the notable monk Andrew, called the Calybite, at Blachernae, with blows in the hippodrome of Saint Mamas. Andrew had rebuked his impiety and called him a Valentinianist and a Civilianus [Note: [Col. 1100D] Another reading: Julian]. Constantine ordered him to be thrown into the sea’s current; but his sisters snatched him away and buried him in the marketplace of Leucadia.

In the twenty-second year of Constantine’s reign, a comet appeared in the East, and the son of Phatnia was killed.

The Bulgarians rose up, killed their masters, and appointed a man named Zeletin to the council; he was thirty years old. Many Slavs, moreover, fled to the emperor, and he placed them over Arthan.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, the emperor went out into Thrace, sending a fleet through the Euxine Sea consisting of as many as eighty *chelandia*, each carrying twelve horses.

When Zeletis heard that a movement had been made against him by land and sea, he enlisted twenty thousand men from the neighboring nations. Having stationed them in the fortifications, he made himself secure and fearless.

When the emperor arrived, he encamped on the plain of Anchialus. On the day before the Kalends of July, in the first indiction, a Thursday, Zeletis appeared with a multitude of peoples. They entered battle and continued killing one another for a long time. Finally Zeletis turned his back and fled.

The battle lasted from the fifth hour until evening. Large numbers of Bulgarians were killed, many were captured, and many submitted to the emperor.

The emperor, elated by this victory, publicly celebrated it by entering the city with armed armies and being acclaimed with the loudest praises of the people. He dragged the captured Bulgarians, bound in *hylopandurae*, through the city [Col. 1100C] and ordered them to be beheaded outside the Golden Gate.

The Bulgarians, meanwhile, killed Zeletis together with his princes and appointed Sabinus, the son-in-law of their former lord Comersius. Sabinus immediately sent to the emperor and sought peace. But when the Bulgarians assembled, they firmly resisted, saying to him:

“Bulgaria, as we see, is being reduced through you to servitude under the Romans.”

Sabinus therefore, having provoked their hostility, fled to the fortress of Mesembria and went over to the emperor. The Bulgarians appointed another lord for themselves, named Paganus.

In the twenty-third year of Constantine’s reign, the Turks came out through the Caspian Gates, killed many people in Armenia, seized considerable booty, and returned.

A certain Cosmas was bishop of Epiphaneia, a city of Apamea in Syria. When some citizens of Epiphaneia brought an accusation against this same Cosmas before Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, concerning the diminution of the sacred vessels, and Cosmas was unable to restore them, he abandoned the orthodox faith, joined Constantine in heresy, and opposed the sacred images.

By common decision, Theodore, patriarch of Antioch; Theodore of Jerusalem; and Cosmas of Alexandria, together with the bishops subject to them, anathematized him unanimously, each in his own city, on the day of holy Pentecost, after the reading of the holy Gospel.

That same year, beginning with the Kalends of October, a great and bitter frost occurred—not only in our land but also in the East, and still more severely in the northern regions. Because of the intensity of the ice, the Pontic Sea was turned into stone-like hardness for a distance of as much as one hundred miles. On its surface the ice reached a depth of thirty cubits. All the regions from Lycia to the Danube and the Euphrates, as well as the Dniester, the Dnieper, and Necropela, and the remaining shores as far as Mesembria and Moesia, suffered in the same way.

When this frost had been covered with snow, it increased by another twenty cubits, so that the sea resembled dry land. People and wild and domesticated animals walked upon the surface of the ice from Khazaria and Bulgaria, including the neighboring islands.

In February of the second indiction, by God’s command, this ice descended into the Danubian region and Hieron, breaking into many different pieces shaped like mountains. They traveled through the strait to the city, as far as the Propontis and the islands, filling all the coastal regions and shores.

We ourselves saw these pieces and descended upon one of them with about thirty companions of our own age. It carried both wild and tame animals, alive and dead.

Anyone who wished could travel on dry ground from the Sophian districts to the city, and from Chrysopolis to Saint Mamas and to the places called Galatians, without hindrance. One of the ice masses broke against the staircase of the Acropolis and shattered it; another, of enormous size, struck the wall and shook it with such force that even the inner houses were inundated by the sea.

The ice broke into three pieces and surrounded the city from Manganes to the Bosphorus; its height exceeded the walls.

All the people—men, women, and children—continued ceaselessly to gaze upon the spectacle, then returned home in tears, not knowing what they could say about it.

Moreover, in March of that same year, stars appeared falling from heaven, so that everyone who saw them thought that the consummation of the present age was imminent. There was also great drought, so severe that even springs dried up.

The emperor summoned the patriarch and said to him:

“Now, what would harm you if we said *theotokon* (θεοτόκον, ‘God-bearer’) and *Christotokon* (χριστότοκον, ‘Christ-bearer’)?”

But the patriarch embraced him and said:

“Have mercy, Lord. May this speech not lead to your contagion. Do you not see how Nestorius is proclaimed and anathematized by the whole Church?”

He replied:

“I asked because I wanted to learn—but let the matter go no further than you.”

In the twenty-fourth year of Constantine’s reign, the Turks again came out through the Caspian Gates and into Iberia. When the Arabs engaged them in battle [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: the Avars], many on both sides perished.

Habdallas, through such a stratagem, removed Hyse, son of Muza, from the principate, upon whom, as stated above, the third lot of succession after him had fallen.

Seeing that Hyse was suffering from a headache, a hemicrania, and an attack of *scotoma* [Col. 1102A], Habdallas persuaded him that he could be cured if his physician, Moses, a deacon of the church of the Antiochenes, blew some sneezing compound into his nostrils. Habdallas had already, by gifts, induced Moses to prepare a drug of the utmost potency, which was also strongly narcotic.

When Moses had obeyed Habdallas, Hyse inhaled the compound through his nose and became filled with it throughout his head and all his senses. Deprived even of his governing faculties, he lay speechless.

Habdallas then summoned the commanders and leading men of the nation and said:

“What do you think about the future king?”

They unanimously rejected Hyse and gave their right hands to his son Habdalla Muhammad, who was called Madi.

They carried Hyse home without consciousness. After the third day, when he recovered, Habdallas consoled him with fabricated excuses and recompensed his injuries with one hundred talents of gold.

That same year Paganus, lord of Bulgaria, sent to the emperor, asking to meet him face to face. Having received a promise, he came down with his *boilades*. When the emperor was seated together with Sabinus, he received them, reproached them for their disorder and their hatred of Sabinus, and they made peace, as they supposed.

But the emperor secretly sent men into Bulgaria and captured the prince of the Severi, a Slav who had committed many evils in Thrace.

A Christian was also captured—among Christians he was called Margarites—and he was made the first of the Scauri. At Saint Thomas they cut off his hands and feet, then summoned physicians, who cut him open alive from the chest to the pubic region in order to examine the position and structure of the human body. They then handed him over to the fire.

The emperor immediately left the city. Finding Bulgaria without guards because of the deceptive peace, he entered through the fortifications and proceeded as far as Zitas [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: Turahani]. He sent fire into the enclosures [Note: [Col. 1102D] Cedrenus: αὐλάς, “courtyards”] and returned, having accomplished nothing of consequence.

In the twenty-fifth year of his reign, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the fourth indiction, the raging, impious, and wicked emperor ordered Stephen the Protomartyr, called the New, to be dragged out. Stephen had been confined at Saint Auxentius on the nearby mountain of Amastris.

Those who had received the fruit of his instruction and shared his single and like-minded purpose—students and men assigned to the other orders—seized his foot, tied it with a rope, and dragged him as far as the seaward parts of the palace. There they tore him apart and threw his honorable relics into the place of those who had died by violence, because he had admonished many, led them to the monastic life, and persuaded them to despise royal dignities and wealth.

The venerable man was honored by everyone because he had spent nearly sixty years in monasteries and had shone with many virtues.

He also accused many rulers and soldiers of worshiping images and subjected them to various punishments and bitter scourging. He exacted a general oath from everyone living under his rule that no one should worship an icon. He also made Constantine, the false-named patriarch, ascend the ambo, raise the precious wood, and swear that he was not one of those who worshiped images.

He soon persuaded him to become a Stephanite instead of a monk, to eat meat, and to allow lyre-players to be admitted to the imperial table. But vengeance was not long delayed, and it delivered this murderer to the punishments he deserved.

Finally, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth indiction, he marched against the Bulgarians and sent 2,600 *chelandia* to Achelon, having built and armed them from all the military provinces. When they had anchored at Thoris, the north wind blew and nearly all of them were wrecked, and many of the people perished. The emperor ordered nets to be stretched out, the dead to be recovered, and them to be buried.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September of the same fourth indiction, he publicly denounced and dishonored the monastic habit in the hippodrome, ordering every monk to hold a woman by the hand and pass through the hippodrome in that manner, receiving insults heaped upon them by the entire people.
