Likewise, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, nineteen distinguished princes were brought to the Circus games and paraded as though they had plotted evil against the emperor. They had not been truthfully accused; the emperor envied them because they were handsome, vigorous, and praised by everyone.

Some of them were also accused because of their religion, since they had visited the aforementioned recluse and publicly spread accounts of his sufferings. The emperor killed these men. The principal ones were:

Constantine the patrician and former *logothete of the course*, whom he had nicknamed Podopagurus, and his brother Strateius, *spatharius* and commander of the guards;

Antiochus, made *logothete of the course* and governor of Sicily;

David, *spatharius* and count of the Opsikion;

Theophylact, *protospatarius* and chief of the imperial strators, son of the patrician Bardanes;

Theophylact the *candidatus*;

and others.

After having them publicly led into the hippodrome for the games, spat upon, and cursed by the whole people, he pronounced sentence. He punished the two brothers Constantine and Strateius by beheading inside the hunting enclosure. The entire populace lamented loudly over them.

When the emperor learned this, he became angry, beat Procopius the prefect, and removed him from office, as though he had allowed it to happen. He sent the others, after blinding them, into exile. Sending them one by one, and being filled with every cruelty, he ordered them to be beaten with a hundred lashes at the places where they lived.

On the third day before the Kalends of September of the same fourth indiction, the same mad and malicious emperor acted against his namesake and associate, the patriarch. He found certain clerics and monks and instructed them to say:

“We heard the patriarch speaking against the emperor with Podopagurus.”

He sent them to the patriarch to accuse him. When the patriarch swore that this was false, the emperor made them swear upon the precious wood, and they declared:

“We heard these curses from the patriarch.”

Then he sent an order and sealed it with a bull, and exiled the patriarch to Iberia [Note: [Col. 1103D] Another reading: Hieria], and again to the island of the prince.

In the twenty-sixth year of Constantine’s reign, Habdallas son of Hali died when a tower in which he was being guarded collapsed upon him. Habdallas, while holding the office of amir, displayed many evils toward the Christians living under his rule. For he also removed the crosses from the churches and prohibited the celebration of night vigils, as well as the learning of letters. Those among them who are called *aruritae*, which means “emulators,” rose up against the wilderness of Palmyra.

But the man who ruled the Christians by the ineffable judgments of God—perhaps like Jezebel of old, or the mad Ahab—displayed under his rule, over orthodox bishops, monks, laypeople, prelates, and subjects, things far worse than the madness of the Arabs. Everywhere he rejected as useless and unwritten the written intercessions of the holy Virgin and Mother of God and of all the saints, through which every aid flows to us; he also cast out their holy relics and made them objects of hatred. Thus, whenever someone distinguished was heard to be honored for the healing of souls and bodies, or—as is customary—venerated by pious people, he immediately threatened such persons with death, as though they were acting impiously. Otherwise, he imposed confiscations, exiles, and tortures. A relic pleasing to God—regarded by its possessors as a kind of treasure—was taken away and thereafter made an object of hatred.

The profane emperor did something of this sort also to the most precious relic of the praiseworthy mother Euphemia. He threw it, together with its casket, into a deep place, unable to endure the fact that it emitted from itself throughout the whole people the sweetness of ointment and reproved his madness concerning the intercessions of the saints. But God, who preserves the bones of those who please him, according to the divine words, kept it unharmed, intending again to display it on the island of Lemnos. Therefore, appearing in a nocturnal vision, she commanded that it be raised up and preserved.

Under the pious emperors Constantine and Eirene, in the fourth indiction, it returned with fitting honor to its own church. He himself, like an enemy of the churches, had made it a common armory and decreed that it should become a dung heap; but they cleansed it and consecrated it again, both to refute his impiety and to display their own piety. We ourselves saw this astonishing miracle, worthy of being committed to writing, twenty-two years after the death of the wicked ruler, together with the most pious emperors and the most holy patriarch Thrasios; and, although unworthy, we embraced it with them and received great grace.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December of the same fifth indiction, by imperial decree, Nicetas, a eunuch of Slav origin, was irregularly advanced as patriarch of Constantinople. Then a drought occurred, so that not even dew fell from heaven. Water completely failed in the city, and the cisterns, baths, and springs—which had previously flowed continually—remained unused. Seeing this, the emperor began to restore the aqueduct of Valentinian, which had lasted as far as Heraclea but had been destroyed by the Avars.

Accordingly, having selected craftsmen from various places, he brought from Asia and Pontus one thousand builders and two hundred plasterers; from Greece and the islands, five hundred brickmakers; and from Thrace itself, five thousand laborers and two hundred makers of measuring rods. He placed over them commanders and supervisors of the works, as well as one patrician. When the work was completed, water entered the city.

On the same day, in the fifth indiction, he promoted magistrates and workmen worthy of his wickedness: namely, Michael of Edessa [Note: [Col. 1105D] Alternatively, Melissenus, στρατηγὸν τῶν ἀνατολικῶν, “commander of the eastern forces.”] in the theme of the Orientals; Michael Lachanodracon in the Thracesians; and over the Buccellarians, Manes, named from *mania*, that is, madness [Note: [Col. 1105D] Εἰς τὸ βουκελλάριον, “to the Buccellarian [theme].”]. But who is capable of recounting the criminal abominations of these men, some of which are briefly treated by us in their proper places? For if all their deeds were written down—the deeds carried out at the command of the ruler [Note: [Col. 1105D] Alternatively, “for the cure.”]—I do not think, to speak properly with the Evangelist, that even the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written about them.

In the twenty-seventh year of Constantine’s reign, Constantine, the patriarch in name only, was brought from the Prince’s Island on the ninth of October, in the sixth indiction; and the tyrant had him beaten because he could not escape. He ordered preparations to be made in the Forum and made him sit in the lap of the Great Church. A secretary was with him, carrying a volume of writing in which his offenses had been recorded.

When the entire people had assembled there at the king’s command, and were watching, the document was read aloud in the hearing of the whole people. At each chapter the secretary struck him in the face, while Nicetas the patriarch sat in the sanctuary and looked on. Afterward, when they had placed him on the ambo and made him stand upright, Nicetas took the document and sent it to the bishops. They removed his shoulder-covering, anathematized him, and, calling him “the companion of Absin” [Note: [Col. 1105D] *Scotiopsit*.], expelled him from the church [Note: [Col. 1106D] They removed him while he walked backward.].

On the following day, while the Circus games were being held, they shaved his face and stripped his beard bare, removing the hair from his head and eyebrows. They dressed him in a short woolen garment without sleeves, made him sit upon a donkey carrying a pack, and made him hold its tail. They led him through the Dippium into the Hippodrome, while the whole people called down evils upon him and spat at him.

Constantine, his nephew, was leading the donkey, his nose having been cut off. When they came before the crowd, they descended and spat upon him and threw dust over him. When they had brought him to the tribunal, they threw him from the donkey, trampled upon his neck, and set him facing the crowd, where he heard their mocking words until the equestrian games were concluded.

In the same month, the impious emperor sent patricians to him with this message: “What do you say about our faith and the council that we have held?” He, with his understanding turned toward vanity, answered, “Well,” he said, “you believe rightly, and you have conducted the council well,” thinking that by this he would placate him. But they immediately replied: “We do not wish to hear these things from your polluted mouth. Therefore go from here into darkness.” Thus, after sentence had been pronounced, he went down to the enclosures of the wild beasts and was beheaded. They tied his head by the ears and hung it for three days at the Milion, for the people to see. They tied the body by one foot to a rope and dragged it through the streets as far as the places by the sea, where they threw it to be associated with those who had died violent deaths. In the same way, after three days they carried his head there and threw it away.

O the irrationality, cruelty, and mercilessness of the most savage beast! The wretch did not fear the holy baptismal font. For Constantine had received into his arms two sons of the emperor by the latter’s third wife. He had always been shown to be savage and uncivilized in character.

From this year onward he exercised even greater madness. For he deposed Peter, the noble *stilicen* from Metra. When that man [Note: [Col. 1106D] Alternatively, “alive.”] refused to yield, together with his doctrines, he bound his feet and shut him up in the aforementioned place of the palace [Note: [Col. 1106D] Alternatively, *palagii*.]. He also ordered him to be dragged through the streets and cast away. He bound others in sacks, weighted them down with stones, tore out their eyes, and ordered them thrown into the sea; he cut off their noses, flayed them with whips, and devised every kind of torture against those who lived piously.

In the city he carried these things out himself, together with his associates, the patrician Antony, the domestic of the Schools, and Peter the magistrate, over the people of each order—men whom he had personally trained for such deeds. In the foreign provinces he acted through the aforementioned magistrates.

For he delighted in the sound of the lyre and in banquets, and he ceaselessly trained those who adhered to him in shameful speech and dancing. Thus, whenever someone, falling or suffering pain, uttered the customary Christian cry, saying, “Mother of God, help,” or was caught keeping vigils, or was accustomed to churches, or lived religiously, or did not use oaths indiscriminately, he was condemned as an enemy of the emperor and declared to be one whose memory must be erased.

As for the monasteries, which were established for the glory of God and as a refuge for those being saved, he decreed that they should become common houses for his military supporters. Finally, he gave the monastery of Dalmatius—which was among the finest monasteries of Byzantium—as a dwelling for soldiers. Those called the monasteries of Calistratus, Dii, and Maximus, as well as other sacred houses of monks and virgins, he destroyed from their foundations.

Those who, from among distinguished soldiers [Note: [Col. 1106D] Alternatively, “from among soldiers or senators.”], had chosen to undertake the monastic life—especially those who had adhered to him and had been accomplices in his lusts and impious deeds—he handed over to death, fearing the disgrace that would come upon him through the public declarations of those who denounced him.

Hence he also took Strateius, the brother of Podopagurus, who was handsome in appearance. For he loved to have such men attached to him because of his lusts. But when he realized with displeasure that Strateius had been distressed by his unspeakable madness toward men and had made it known to the enclosed blessed Stephen of Saint Auxentius, and had received remedies for salvation, he spread the accusation that Strateius was plotting against him and killed him together with the enclosed man, as has been said.

He caused decorated images to abound in the city [Note: [Col. 1107D] P. Pithoeus: *horno*. Alternatively, *horto*.]. For, having become a new Midas, he amassed gold and stripped the farmers. Because of the exaction of taxes, people were forced to sell the abundant gifts of God’s produce at an easy or very low price.

In the same year, Nicetas, the patriarch in name only, erased the images made of mosaic [Note: [Col. 1107D] Διὰ ψηφίδων, “by means of tesserae.”] that were in the patriarchal smaller secret chamber. He removed the images of the great secret chamber, which had been carved in wood, and smeared over the faces of the remaining images. He did the same in Abramios.

In the twenty-eighth year of his reign, the emperor crowned his wife Eudoxia, although he was a third-married man and she was his third wife, in the tribunal of the nineteen couches. On the Kalends of April, on the day after holy Easter had been celebrated, he appointed the sons born to him by her—namely Christopher and Nicephorus—as Caesars. The patriarch delivered an address, and the emperors placed upon them the chlamys and the helmets appropriate to Caesars.

In the same manner he made their youngest brother Nicetas a nobleman, placing upon him a chlamys and a golden crown. Thus they proceeded, while the emperors scattered *bypatia*, *trimisia*, *nemisia*, and new coins, as far as the Great Church.

In the twenty-ninth year of Constantine’s reign, Eirene entered the city, coming from Athens with dromons and many chelandia adorned with silken coverings. The city’s leading men, with their wives, came out to meet her and preceded her. When the patriarch had come to the palace, to the church of the Pharos, the betrothal of the emperor Leo to that same Eirene was celebrated. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, Eirene was crowned Augusta and empress in the dining hall.

In this year also there was an exchange in Syria: man for man, woman for woman, and child for child. Habdallas ordered them to shave their beards and to make *calamauci* one cubit and a half long [Note: [Col. 1108D] Alternatively, *amelancos*. Alternatively, *cammelancos*.].

In the thirtieth year of Constantine’s reign, Banacas moved his army against Romania and carried away many captives. The Romans entered the Fourth Armenia and plundered it. Moreover, Salem died, and Germanicia was transferred to Palestine.

In the same year, Lachanodracon, imitating his master, gathered at Ephesus every monk and nun living in the theme of the Thracesians. He led them out into the plain and said: “Whoever wishes to obey the emperor and us must put on white clothing and take a wife at this very hour. But whoever thinks this unimportant will be deprived of his sight and condemned to exile in Cyprus.” Then the deed was completed together with the word. Many were revealed as martyrs, while many others, weakened and failing, perished; and the Dragon made those people his associates.

Moreover, in the ninth indiction, in the month of January, a son was born to the emperor Leo and Eirene while Constantine, his grandfather, was still alive.

In the thirty-first year of Constantine’s reign, Banacas moved his army against Romania. When he had descended from Isauria to the fortress of Scices, he besieged it. When the emperor heard this, he wrote to Michael, magistrate of the Orientals; to Manes [Note: [Col. 1108D] Alternatively, “of the Buccellarians.” P. Pithoeus: “of the Buccellarii.”], magistrate of the Buccellarians; and to Bardan, magistrate of the Armeniacs. When they arrived, they held the enemy’s exit, because the passage was extremely difficult to traverse.

The fleet of the Cibyrrhaeots, arriving with Praecona, its magistrate and *spatharius*, docked in the harbor of the aforementioned fortress. When Banacas saw this, he despaired of his own side, but then recovered confidence and restored courage to his men. Ascending toward the infantry forces, with great and sudden shouts he raised a cry together with all his men. Thus he put them to flight in terror, killed many, plundered the whole surrounding region, and returned with much booty.

In the same year, Lachanodracon, the magistrate of the Thracesians, together with his secretary Leo and Leo the former monk, sold all the monasteries of men and women, all the sacred vessels, books, livestock, and whatever properties belonged to them, and brought the proceeds to the ruler. All monastic and patristic books that he found he burned in the fire. Whenever someone appeared to possess a relic of a saint for safekeeping, he likewise committed it to the fire; and he punished its possessor as one acting impiously. He killed many monks by flogging and slaughtered some with swords.

Moreover, he deprived countless people of their sight. He smeared the beards of some with wax and oil, set them alight, and thus burned both their faces and their heads. He subjected others to many tortures and then sent them into exile. Finally, throughout the entire theme subject to him, he left not a single man wearing the monastic habit.

When the emperor learned of this—he who always hated what was good—he wrote to him in thanks, saying: “I have found you to be a man after my own heart, one who carries out all my wishes.” Imitating him, the others likewise perpetrated similar deeds.

In the thirty-second year of Constantine’s reign, Habdallas sent Mualabicus into Africa with a large army. Alfadalbadinar entered Romania and captured five hundred prisoners. But the people of Mopsuestia, meeting them and engaging them in battle, killed one thousand Arabs.

Habdallas, however, went to Jerusalem and fasted. He ordered Christians and Hebrews to be branded on their hands. For this reason many Christians fled to Romania.

In the thirty-third year of his reign, in the month of March and the twelfth indiction, Constantine moved a fleet of two thousand chelandia against Bulgaria. He himself entered a red chelandion and set out to enter the river Danube, leaving the magistrates of the cavalry themes outside the enclosures, in case they might be able to enter Bulgaria while the Bulgarians were directing their attention toward him.

When he reached Barnas, he became afraid and considered turning back. But the Bulgarians, fearing in the same way and envying him, sent Hoylam and Zigaton to request peace. When the emperor saw them, he rejoiced and made peace, each side giving an oath that the Bulgarians would not go out against Romania, nor would the emperor attempt to enter Bulgaria.

After written agreements had been exchanged concerning this, the emperor returned and entered the city, leaving the themes in the camps he had established.

In October, in the eleventh indiction, he received word from Bulgaria through secret friends that the lord of Bulgaria was sending twelve thousand men from the people, together with Boyladen, to capture Berzitia and bring its inhabitants into Bulgaria. Envoys of the lord of Bulgaria had come to him while these men were still in the city. The emperor pretended that he was moving an army against the Arabs, and both the standards and the royal equipment and supplies crossed over.

After he had dismissed the envoys and learned through their scouts that they had departed, he took up his army and set out in haste. Gathering the Taxatae and the Thracesians and uniting the ranks of the nobles, he made them number eight hundred thousand. Proceeding to the place called Lithsoria, they fell upon the enemy without the sound of any trumpet. He routed them and won a great victory. He returned with much spoil and many captives, displaying the triumph of his trophy near the city and marching in astonishment at the spoils. He called this war glorious because no one had resisted him and no Christian blood had been slaughtered or shed in it.

In the thirty-fourth year of Constantine’s reign, Constantine, breaking the peace with the Bulgarians, again constructed a great fleet. He placed twelve thousand cavalrymen in it and dispatched all the magistrates of the fleets with the force. He himself, however, remained behind with the cavalry, being afraid.

When they had reached Mesembria and entered it, the north wind blew violently, nearly everything was wrecked, and many perished. He returned without having achieved any benefit.

Teleric, the lord of Bulgaria, having learned that the emperor was discovering his plans through his associates, wrote to him, saying: “I wish to flee and come to you. Therefore send me a guarantee of safety, and tell me which friends you have here, so that I may trust them and they may come to meet me.” The emperor, acting thoughtlessly, wrote to him. When Teleric learned this, he cut those men down through the middle. When Constantine heard of it, he tore out his gray hairs for some time.

In the thirty-fifth year of his reign, in the month of August and the thirteenth indiction, the emperor went out against the Bulgarians. There he was struck by a divinely inflicted disease in the legs, called in Greek ἄνθραξ, “carbuncle.” Then, seized by a very severe fever, he returned to Arcadiopolis, carried on a bed on the shoulders of his subjects. Reaching Selymbria, he boarded a ship.

When he reached the round fortress, he died miserably in the chelandion, crying out and saying: “While still alive I have been handed over to an unquenchable fire.” He demanded that the holy Virgin and Mother of God be praised, although he had been her enemy without reconciliation.

After the death of his father he had reigned for thirty-five years, two months, and twenty-six days. Thus he ended his life, stained with much blood, invocations of demons and sacrifices, persecutions of the holy churches, of the true and undefiled faith, and of monks, as well as violations of monasteries and various evils—growing beyond measure, no less than Diocletian or any of the tyrants.

Moreover, in the same year and month, Habdallas, leader of the Arabs, died. Since these two men, like the fiercest beasts, had long ravaged the human race through their cruelty, they died by the providence of God, and Leo and Mady, their sons, obtained the rule.

Moreover, in the same year Adalgis, king of the Lombards, came to the imperial city and placed himself as a fugitive under the emperor’s protection.

## BOOK TWENTY-THREE

[Col. 1109]

In the year 768 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Leo, son of Constantine, was emperor, and Mady was regarded as leader of the Arabs. He ruled over them for nine years. The emperor Leo began to spend the money that had been left to him by his father. He pleased both the nobles and the people and appeared, for a short time, to be pious and a friend of the holy Mother of God and of the monks. Accordingly, he placed metropolitan monks in the highest offices, created many military units from the themes, and enlarged the ranks in the city.

For this reason the commanders of the themes were moved to action. They all entered with a great multitude of people, requesting Constantine, his son, as emperor. But he, as is customary with rulers, replied to them: “He is my only son, and therefore I fear to do this, lest something human should happen to me and, while he is still a child, you hand him over to death and promote another.”

But they declared under oath that they would satisfy him and that no one would reign except his son, even if God should wish him to die. From the Lord’s Day on which the solemnity of Palm Sunday is celebrated until the fifth day of Holy Week, while the people were gathered in the Hippodrome and making this request, he ordered them to swear on Holy Friday.

All the people swore upon the honorable and life-giving wood: those from the themes and the Senate, those of the exterior orders, all the citizens, and the workers in the workshops. They swore not to accept any emperor except Leo or Constantine and their descendants. They produced written declarations of the oath they had sworn, in their own hands.

On the following day, Holy Saturday, the emperor went out into the tribunal of the nineteen couches and promoted his most noble brother Eudoxius; for their father had promoted Anthimus while he was still alive. The emperor proceeded with the remaining Caesars, the three most noble men, and the new Constantine to the Great Church.

After changing his clothing, as is customary for emperors, he ascended the ambo together with his son and the patriarch. When all the people had entered, they placed their written declarations upon the holy table. Then the emperor addressed the people as follows:

“Behold, brothers, I fulfill your requests and give you my son as emperor. Behold, you receive him from the Church and from the hand of Christ.”

They cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Be our guarantor, Son of God, because from your hand we receive our lord Constantine as emperor, to guard him and to die with him.”

On the following day, when the great and Lord’s Day of Easter was celebrated—on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourteenth indiction—at the dawn twilight, the emperor went out together with the patriarch into the Hippodrome, an altar being carried before him and the whole people watching. The patriarch delivered a prayer and crowned the emperor’s son. Thus both emperors proceeded to the Great Church, together with two Caesars and three most noble men.

The empress Eirene also proceeded, after the emperors had gone before her. Scepters were carried in front by the Schools in attendance, and they ascended by the staircase of the bronze gate into the church of the catechumens [Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, “the catechumenia of the church.” P. Pithoeus: “the catechumena of the church.”], without going out into the street of the Embolos.

In May of the same indiction, Nicephorus Caesar, the emperor’s brother, was accused of having plotted against him with certain *spatharii*, *stratores*, and other imperial officials. The emperor held silence at the Magnaura and explained to the people what had been said about him.

They unanimously shouted that both men should withdraw from their midst, forgetting—always perjurers—that they had sworn to their father that after his death they would not permit injury to be inflicted upon his sons. But the emperor condemned the rebels, after having them beaten and tonsured, to exile. He ordered them to be deported to Cherson and that those districts be preserved under guard and protection.

In the second year of Leo’s reign, Teleric, lord of Bulgaria, fled to the emperor. The emperor made him a patrician and joined to him Eirene, his wife’s cousin. When he received him from the holy baptismal font, he honored and loved him magnificently.

In the third year of Leo’s reign, Ithumas took his seat at Dabechus and stirred up a rebellion. Leo sent out the Roman forces, and one hundred thousand entered Syria. Their commanders were Michael Lachanodracon, magistrate of the Thracesians; Artavadus the Armenian, magistrate of the Orientals [Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, *Artanasdus*.]; Tazates, magistrate of the Buccellarians; Basterotes, magistrate of the Armeniacs; and Gregory, magistrate of the Opsicians.

They surrounded Germanicia, where Isbal, son of Mady, was stationed. They seized all his camels, and they would also have captured Germanicia if Isbal had not persuaded Lachanodracon with gifts. Lachanodracon withdrew from the fortress, went out to plunder the region, captured the heretical Syrian Jacobites, and returned again to the camp.

Ithumas, having sent an army from Debechus and the Amirates, engaged the Romans in battle. Five of the Amirates and six thousand Arabs fell, and on Friday they returned. They had gone out on Sunday.

Moreover, after a *maïoma* [Greek: μαὶωμα] had taken place, the emperor sat on a throne at Sophianus with his son, and the magistrates thus proclaimed the triumphs they had won. He transferred the heretical Syrians to Thrace and settled them there.

In the fourth year of Leo’s reign, Mady, leader of the Arabs, inflamed with fury, sent Asach with a large force—namely, the Maurophoroi of Syria and Mesopotamia. He descended as far as Dorileum.

The emperor, however, ordered the magistrates not to fight them in open battle but to fortify the cities and bring the people inside, appointing great commanders over each city for its defense. They themselves were to take three thousand selected soldiers each and pursue the enemy, preventing them from scattering their movements. The Romans first burned both the fodder for the horses and the food wherever they found it.

When the Arabs had remained at Dorileum for fifteen days and their provisions had failed, their animals became useless, and much plunder was taken from them. They returned and besieged Amorium for one day. When they saw that it was fortified and possessed a large supply of weapons, they returned without accomplishing anything.

In the fifth year of Leo’s reign, Mady, leader of the Arabs, came to Dabechus with much equipment and military power. After sending his son into Romania, he himself returned to the holy city. He sent Thesian, who was called the Zealot, and gave him authority to make apostates of Christian slaves and to lay waste the holy churches. He came to Emesa and promised that he would not compel people to undergo *menzerizing* [Note: [Col. 1112D] Alternatively, *Magariz*.], except those who had formerly been unbelievers, until the Hebrews and Christians were exposed. Immediately he began to torture them impiously, as neither Lysias of old nor Agricola had done, and he destroyed many.

But the women, through the grace of Christ our God, overcame his madness. They were the wives of the archdeacon of Emesa and of the son of Isaiah. After being greatly tortured, they did not yield to impiety. They received a thousand lashes each and were subjected to many other tortures, yet they received from Christ the crown of victory.

He also reached as far as Damascus and left many churches desolate, paying no attention to the guarantee given to the Christians by the Arabs.

Moreover, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, after the death of Nicetas, the bishop of Constantinople mentioned above, during the second week of the fast, on Sunday, Paul, an honorable man of Cypriot birth, shining in word and deed, was consecrated patriarch of Constantinople by great force after making extensive excuses on account of the heresy he had held.

In the middle of the week of the fast, James the *protospatarius*, Papias, Strateius, and Theophanes, the *cubicularii*, together with other religious men, were arrested because they worshiped the images. Then Leo, the son of the persecutor, revealing his hidden wickedness, had these men mercilessly beaten, tonsured, and paraded in chains through the middle of the city. He ordered them to be confined in the praetorium. Among them, the aforementioned Theophanes died, becoming a confessor and attaining the crown of martyrdom. After his death, all the others were found to be proven monks.

Aaron, meanwhile, entered the Armenian theme and besieged the fortress of Semaluos throughout the summer. In September he captured it by capitulation. He had sent Ithuman into Asia with fifty thousand men. Michael Lachanodracon met him with a small force, defeated him, and slaughtered Ithuman’s brother.

In the same month, in the fourth indiction, Leo, son of Constantine, died in the following manner. When he had become mad about stones [Note: [Col. 1113D] Λιθομανής, “stone-mad” or “mad for stones.”], he became excessively fond of the crown of the Great Church. He took it and carried it away. Carbuncles broke out on his head, and, seized by a violent fever, he died after reigning for five years and six days.

## CONSTANTINE AND EIRENE

In the year 774 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the most pious Eirene, together with her son Constantine, gloriously received the empire from God on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the fourth indiction. God was proclaimed wondrous even in this: through a widowed woman and an orphaned boy, the immense impiety that had been raised against him and his servants was overthrown—the tyranny of Constantine, the enemy of God, which had been directed against all the Churches, against the former fisherman of the devil, and against the weakness of the uneducated.

After forty days of her reign, while her son was ten years old, certain senators took counsel and wished to bring out Nicephorus Caesar and establish him as emperor. When this became known to her, Gregory, *logothete of the course*; Bardas, formerly magistrate of the Armeniacs; Constantine, *spatharius* of the vicarius and domestic of the Excubitors; Theophylactus Rangabe, *drungarius* of the Twelfth Island; and many others were arrested. She had them beaten and tonsured and sent into exile in various places.

She had her husband’s brothers, the Caesars and the most noble men, tonsured and serve as priests, and made them distribute communion to the people at the feast of the Nativity of Christ. At that feast she proceeded publicly in imperial fashion with the boy and restored to the Church the *stemma* that had been taken away by her husband, beautifully fashioned and adorned with precious stones.

She promoted Helpidius as magistrate in Sicily; he had previously been magistrate there as well. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, the same Helpidius was accused of siding with the Caesars. She sent Theophilus the *spatharius* and ordered him to seize and bring Helpidius by a short route. When he went there, the Sicilians did not surrender Helpidius. But she sent his wife and sons, after having them beaten and tonsured, to the magistrate to be kept under guard.

In June she assigned all the interior parts of the theme to guard the enclosures and watch for the Arabs’ departure. She placed over it John the *sacellarius*, who was a eunuch and her domestic. Mady, however, sent Cebir with a large force. They met at the place called the Milion, and, engaging in battle, defeated the Arabs. Many of them were killed, and they returned in confusion.

Meanwhile, the most pious rulers began to act boldly, spread the word of the Lord, allow those who wished to be saved to renounce the world without hindrance, exalt the glorification of God, restore monasteries, and make every good thing manifest.

In this same year, at the long walls of Thrace, a man digging found a stone coffin [Note: [Col. 1114D] Λάρνακα, “stone coffin” or “chest.”]. After he had cleaned and lifted it, he found a man lying within it. The letters fastened to the coffin contained the following words:

“Christ will be born from the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Eirene, O sun, you will see me again.”

In the second year of Constantine and Eirene, Eirene sent Constantine the sacellarius and Mamalus the primicerius to Charles, king of the Franks, in order that he might give his daughter in marriage to Constantine, her son, the emperor. After an agreement and oath had been made between the two parties, they left Helisaeus, a eunuch and notary, to teach her the letters and language of the Greeks, and also to instruct her according to the customs of the Roman Empire.

After many ships had been built and peoples from the themes selected, together with sufficient commanders, she promoted Theodore, a patrician and eunuch, an energetic man, and sent him against Helpidius in Sicily. When many battles had been fought, those who were with Theodore prevailed. Seeing this, Helpidius was afraid; taking with him all the money he possessed, he crossed over with Nicephorus into Africa. Having received from the Arabs a pledge of security, he joined them. They received him as though he were emperor of the Romans, crowned him uselessly, and clothed him in boots and imperial dress.

While the Roman people were occupied with these matters, Mady, son of Aaron, came forth with a large force and abundant equipment from Maurophorion, all Mesopotamia, Syria, and the Desert. He came to Chrysopolis, leaving Binusus behind to besiege Nacolia and guard his rear. He also sent Burnice into Asia with thirty thousand men. After Burnice had defeated Lachanodracon with the army of the Thracesian theme at a place called Darinus, although the opposing force numbered thirty thousand, he killed five thousand of them.

The empress, however, sent her domesticus Antonius with the regiments; he seized Baris and enclosed them. Tazates, governor of the Bucellarians, took refuge with them because of the hatred he bore toward Stauratius the patrician [Col. 1114D] and Tudromius the eunuch logothete, who at that time appeared superior to everyone and disposed of everything. Having given them counsel, he urged them to seek peace.

When Stauratius, Peter the magister, and Antonius the domesticus went out for this purpose, they did not act with sufficient care to receive their proposal cautiously and secure the sons of the leading men. Instead, they went out rashly, were seized by the others, and bound in fetters. Both sides were compelled to make peace, and the Augusta and Aaron exchanged many gifts, the agreement being confirmed on the condition that she would pay them tribute every year. After peace had been made, they departed and also abandoned the city of Nacolia. Tazates, moreover, took away his wife and all his property.

In the third year of her reign, after peace had been made with the Arabs and access had been secured, Eirene sent Stauratius the patrician and logothete of the dromos with a large force against the tribes of the Sclaveni. When he had descended into Thessaly and Greece, he subjected them all and made them tributary to the Empire. He also entered the Peloponnese and brought much booty and plunder to the Roman Empire.

In the fourth year of Constantine and Eirene, Stauratius, of whom mention has been made above, returned from the Sclaveni and displayed the trophies of his triumph in the Hippodrome. In May of the same seventh indiction, the empress Eirene went out with her son and a great force into Thrace, carrying instruments and other kinds of musical equipment. She came as far as Beroea, ordered it to be rebuilt, and named it Eirenopolis. She also reached Philippopolis in complete security and returned, having likewise built Anchialus.

In the same year, the Arab commander Mady, also called Muhammat, died, and his son Moses assumed the leadership.

On the first day of the Kalends of September of the same seventh indiction, Paul, the most holy patriarch, fell ill, left the throne, and withdrew to the monastery of Flori, where he assumed the monastic habit, without the imperial government’s knowledge. When the empress learned this, she came with her son in grief and cried out, “Why have you done this?”

He answered her with lamentation: “Would that I had never sat upon the priestly throne while the Church was suffering tyranny—especially since it has been torn from the other universal sees and anathematized.”

Then she sent patricians and the leading members of the Senate whom she had summoned to hear what he said. He told them: “Unless a universal synod is held and the error that exists among you is corrected, you have no salvation.”

They said to him: “Why, when you were consecrated, did you subscribe to the icon?” [Note: [Col. 1115] Alternatively, “when you were consecrated, [you subscribed] to the icon, [saying] that you would not consecrate icons”—the printed reading is uncertain.]

He answered: “That is why I am afflicted with lamentation and have hastened to repentance, imploring God not to judge and punish me as a priest because I have remained silent until now and, through fear of your fury, have not proclaimed the truth.”

With these words he fell asleep in peace, leaving behind much lamentation among pious and impious people and among the religious men of the state. He was indeed a man worthy of honor, exceedingly merciful, and deserving of every reverence; both the commonwealth and the Empire placed great trust in him. From that time, therefore, discussion and controversy began concerning the holy images.

In the fifth year of the reign of Eirene with her son, Moses was advanced as commander of the Arabs; he ruled them for one year. In this same year, after gathering the entire people at Magnaura, Eirene said to them:

“Do you know, brothers, what Paul the patriarch did? If he were still alive, we certainly would not have allowed him to leave the priestly throne, even though he had assumed the monastic habit. But since, as it pleased God, he has departed this life, let us provide a man who can shepherd us wisely and preserve the Church of God through instructive teaching.”

They all declared that there should be no one else but Tharasius, the confidential secretary (a secretis).

She replied: “We too have chosen him, but he objects and says that he will not accept the election of the emperor and the whole people.”

Then he answered the people:

“Our orthodox emperors, guardians of the immaculate faith of us Christians, faithful imitators of those who are in the glory of God, caring for our welfare and especially now diligently considering ecclesiastical affairs, have taken me into the intention of their piety, so that a high priest might be established in this royal city, and they ordered that what they had resolved should be made known to me.

“When I declared myself unworthy of this and gave no consent, since I could neither bear nor sustain the yoke of such a burden, they ordered me to be brought before you because you had become unanimous in this counsel and its supporters.

“And now, men who fear God and always keep him in your hearts, you who are called Christians by the invocation of Christ, the true God, hear a very brief speech from my insignificance and humility.

“Whatever answer I have given to our pious and entirely orthodox emperors, I shall also offer before you as an apology for my prayer. I am weighed down by fear when consenting to this election, and I fear that I may run from the face of God in such a manner, heedless and without due caution, that I may fall under a terrible condemnation.

“For if the divine apostle Paul, who heard the voices of God, who had heaven educating him, who became a beholder of paradise, who heard ineffable words, and who carried the name of the Lord before nations and kings, said, ‘Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified,’ how then can I, who have lived in the world, been numbered among the laymen, and served in the administrations of the emperor, leap without judgment or circumspection into the greatness of the priesthood? It is a dreadful undertaking for my insignificance and a rash ambition.

“This is the reason for my fear: I see and behold the Church, which has been built and founded upon Christ God, the rock, now torn apart and divided. We speak one way and another, while the Christians in the East who share one faith with us speak differently; and although the Westerners agree with them, we have been alienated from them all and are anathematized by them day after day.

“Anathema is a dreadful punishment: to be cast far from the kingdom of heaven and sent away by God, being led into the outer darkness. The law of the Church knows neither sect nor dispute as its proper boundary; just as it knows how to confess one God, one baptism, and one faith, so it also knows one concord in every ecclesiastical matter.

“For nothing is so acceptable and pleasing in the sight of God as that we should be one and that the one catholic Church should be made one, just as we confess in the creed of our sincere faith.

“And we ask, brothers—for I believe that you also do so, since I know that you fear God—that your pious and orthodox emperors summon a universal synod, so that we, who belong to one God, may become one; we, who worship the Trinity, may become united and unanimous companions; we, who belong to Christ our Head, may become one body, joined and knit together; we, who belong to the Holy Spirit, may become not against one another but for one another; and we, who belong to the truth, may become wise, speaking what is true. Let there be no strife or dissension among us, so that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard us all.

“If the orthodox and defending emperors consent to your request and mine, I too give my consent. Otherwise, it is impossible for me to do this, lest I be subjected to anathema and be found condemned on the day of our Lord and righteous Judge, when neither emperor nor priest, neither rulers nor any multitude of human beings, will be able to rescue me.

“Whatever pleases you, brothers, give as your answer to my apology—or rather, to your own declaration—and respond to my petition.”

Everyone gladly listened to what had been said and gave their assent that a synod should be held.

But Tharasius, speaking again to the people, said:

“Leo the emperor overturned the images. When the synod was held, it found them overturned; and because they had been overturned by imperial authority, the same matter again requires investigation: how they presumed, as it pleased them, to abolish the ancient custom handed down in the Church. But the truth of God, to speak apostolically, is not bound.”

Accordingly, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January of that eighth indiction, our blessed father Tharasius was consecrated patriarch of Constantinople. After he had sent synodical letters to Rome together with men and a statement of his faith, he was received by Adrian the pope.

“The empress also sent a request that he dispatch her letters and distinguished men who might be present at the synod. He sent Peter, vicedonus of the Church, and Peter, abbot of Saint Sabas, honorable men adorned with every virtue.

“Both the empress and the patriarch also sent to Antioch and Alexandria. For the peace that had been made with the Arabs had not yet been broken, and from Antioch they brought John the Great, renowned in word and deed and sharing in holiness, who had been syncellus of the patriarch of Antioch; and Thomas of Alexandria, a zealous and most religious man, who also became distinguished as archbishop of the great city of Thessalonica in Illyricum.

Meanwhile, after Moses had died, Aaron became commander of the Arabs. He ruled them for twenty-three years and inflicted many evils upon the Christians.

In the sixth year of her reign, the emperors sent orders and summoned all the bishops under their authority. Those sent from Rome by Adrian, with his letters and men, arrived, as we have said, as did those from Antioch and Alexandria. On the seventh day before the Ides of August, in the ninth indiction, they presided in the church of the holy apostles in the royal city and began to reread the holy Scriptures and to bring accusations against one another, while the emperors and catechumens looked on.

But the people of the Scholarii, the Excubitors, and the other regiments, brought together by their commanders, also had as their leader Constantine, the God-hated former emperor. They rushed upon them with drawn swords, threatening to kill both the high priest and the orthodox bishops and abbots.

Although the imperial authorities tried through the men standing near them, their associates, to calm them, they did not comply; rather, they reproached them. When the patriarch rose and entered the tribunal with the bishops and monks, those bishops who shared their evil purpose went out to them shouting and saying: “We have won!” By God’s grace, those furious and inhuman men harmed no one, and when the synod had been dissolved in this way, each person returned to his own place.

In the seventh year of her reign, Eirene sent Stauratius the patrician and logothete into Thrace, in September, at the beginning of the tenth indiction, to the farther themes. He persuaded them to become his collaborators and to drive from the city the impious people whom the utterly wicked Constantine had organized.

Pretending that she was about to move the entire army against the eastern regions because the Arabs had gone forth, she sent out all the imperial equipment and baggage as far as Malagma. Then those from the outer themes entered and seized the city.

She sent word to them, saying: “Send me your weapons. I have no need of you.”

Those fools, rendered senseless by God, gave up their weapons. Then, placing their households on ships, she sent their exiles from the city into their own regions, ordering each to go to the place where he had been born.

After forming her own army and establishing commanders obedient to her, she again sent orders in May throughout every place, summoning all the bishops to assemble in the city of Nicaea in order to hold a council there. Throughout the entire summer all of them gathered at Nicaea. She had not dismissed those who had come on behalf of the Roman see and the Eastern churches, but kept them with her.

In the eighth year of the reign of Eirene and Constantine, Tharasius, archbishop of Constantinople, went out to the city of Nicaea. The holy and universal seventh synod of the bishops was held, and the catholic Church recovered its ancient adornments. It proclaimed nothing new, but preserved unchanged the dogmas of the holy Fathers, rejected the new heresy, and anathematized the three falsely named patriarchs—namely, Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas—and all who agreed with them.

The first gathering and session of the bishops took place in the catholic church of Saint Sophia in the city of Nicaea. On the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the eleventh indiction, in the month of November, they all entered the royal city. While the emperors presided together with the bishops at Magnaura, the document was read, and both the emperor and his mother subscribed to it, confirming their piety according to the ancient doctrines and works of the priests. They dismissed them with honor, and the catholic Church of God obtained peace, although the enemy did not cease to sow his tares in his works; nevertheless, the Church of God, though always attacked, triumphs.

In the ninth year of her reign, the empress Eirene, after peace with the Franks had been broken on account of the marriage agreement, sent Theophanes the protospatharius and brought from the Armeniac theme a girl named Maria from Amnia. She joined her to Constantine, her son, although he was deeply grieved and unwilling because of the affection he felt for the daughter of Charles, king of the Franks, to whom he had previously been betrothed. He consummated the marriage in November of the twelfth indiction.

Meanwhile, Eirene sent John the sacellarius and logothete into Longobardia, together with Adelgis, formerly king of greater Longobardia, whom they called Theodatus [Note: [Col. 1119D] Alternatively, “Theodore.”], in order, if possible, to take vengeance upon Charles and to detach certain people from him.

They went down with Theodore, the eunuch patrician and governor of Sicily. After a battle had been joined, Adelgis was captured by the Franks and put to death cruelly.

In the tenth year of Eirene’s reign, the devil, envious of the emperors’ piety, moved certain men to incite the mother against her son and the son against his mother. They bent her will, claiming that they had become certain through prophetic foreknowledge of future events, and said to her:

“It is not predestined by God that your son should retain the imperial power; it is yours, given to you by God.”

She, like a deceived woman, especially since she also possessed a love of rule, believed that this was so and did not recognize that the men who wished to control affairs were advancing this claim under a pretext.

When the emperor was already twenty years old, physically strong and capable, he saw that he exercised no authority and was grieved. On the other hand, he saw that Stauratius the patrician and logothete possessed everything, that everyone went to him, and that no one dared visit himself. Therefore, after taking counsel with a very few of his intimate associates, with his magister Peter, the patrician Theodore, and the patrician Damian, he likewise resolved to seize Stauratius, send him into exile in Sicily, and hold the Empire himself together with his mother.

On the sixth day before the Ides of February, a terrible earthquake occurred, so that no one dared sleep at home. Everyone lived in gardens and under the open sky, after making shelters and tents.

The empress went out with her son to Saint Mamas. When the matter was reported to Stauratius and the plan became known, he stirred the Augusta against her son. She seized all the emperor’s men, struck and tonsured them, including John the protospatharius and his baiulus, and sent them into exile in the lower regions as far as Sicily. She subjected Peter the magister to humiliations and ordered him to sit in her house, and did the same with Theodore the patrician.

She had the patrician Damian beaten and tonsured and sent into exile at the fortress of Apolloniades. She also beat her son, assailing him with many insults, and prevented him from appearing for many days.

She began to bind the army by oaths, saying: “As long as you live, we will not allow your son to rule.” Everyone swore this, and no one dared contradict her.

Meanwhile, the fleet of the Arabs went out against Cyprus. When the empress learned this, she too gathered all the Roman ships and sent them against them. When both commanders had reached Myra, the Arab commander turned from the Chelidonian promontory and entered the Gulf of Attalia.

The Arabs, moving away from Cyprus, were caught by calm weather and drifted about on the sea. When they were seen to be near the land, the commanders saw them and prepared for battle after drawing up their line.

Theophilus, commander of the Cibyrrhaeots, being a strong man, boldly went out ahead of everyone. He was captured by them and then led to Aaron to be seen by him. Aaron urged him to become a betrayer of the faith and accept temporal gifts. Since he absolutely refused and, though compelled still more strongly, would not yield in any way, he suffered execution by the sword and was shown to be an excellent martyr.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 783, Eirene, in the first year of her reign, in September, in the fourteenth indiction, sent messengers, and they came to the Armeniac theme to administer oaths. The people utterly refused to swear, saying:

“We will not be ruled by your son during your lifetime, nor will we place Eirene before the name of Constantine. Rather, we shall name Constantine and Eirene, as we accepted them from the beginning.”

She again sent Alexius the spatharius and drungarius of the Vigla to persuade them. But they seized him and advanced him as their commander. They consigned the patrician Nicephorus to custody, praised their own prince and emperor Constantine, and acclaimed him.

When the populations of the remaining themes learned this, they expelled their commanders and likewise proclaimed Constantine alone emperor.

O the wicked devices of the devil! How he strives by many schemes to destroy the human race! Those who fifteen years earlier had sworn a terrible oath and deposited written declarations made with their own hands upon the holy altar now swore again that they would not be ruled by her son during her lifetime. Then, forgetting this, they exalted Constantine the emperor with praises of good repute, miserable men not considering that an oath must not be reversed. Necessarily, every reciprocal oath is followed by perjury, and perjury is a denial of God.

In October, in the fourteenth indiction, those from the themes who had gathered at Acroas [Note: [Col. 1119D] Alternatively, “Tynea.”] unanimously sought Constantine, the emperor, who was in his twentieth year [Note: [Col. 1120D] Alternatively, “twenty-fifth”; alternatively, “thirtieth.”]. Fearing the people’s attack, Eirene released him. They confirmed him as emperor but rejected his mother.

Moreover, the emperor sent Michael Lachanodracon and John, his baiulus and protospatharius, and bound the Armeniacs by oaths not to receive Eirene, his mother, as empress. He confirmed Alexius as his commander.

When he returned to the city in December, he had Stauratius beaten and tonsured and sent into exile among the Armeniacs, to satisfy them. He also sent Aetius the eunuch protospatharius, his intimate associate, and all the eunuch’s household servants into exile. He settled his mother, with her customary gentleness and abundance, in the palace of Eleutherius, which she herself had built and in which she had hidden much money.

In the same month a fire broke out, and the patriarch’s dining hall, called the Thomaites, the quaestorium, and other houses as far as Milium were burned. [Note: [Col. 1121] Alternatively, “Theophilus, their turmarch, and Gregory.”]

In April, Constantine moved his camp against the Bulgars and came to the fortress called Probati, at the stream of Saint Gregory. He encountered Cardam, lord of Bulgaria. After a small battle toward evening, those on the Roman side became afraid and fled during the night, returning without glory; the Bulgars too, fearing them, withdrew.

In the second year of Constantine’s reign, in September, he moved his camp against the Arabs. Departing from Amorium, he went to Tarsus in Cilicia.

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, at the request of his own mother and many nobles, the emperor declared her empress once again. She was elevated together with him by acclamation, so that the formula became “Constantine and Eirene,” as at the beginning, and everyone obeyed.

The Armeniac theme, however, remained obstinate, still resisting. It demanded Alexius, who had shortly before been their commander and, after being summoned by the emperor and elevated to the dignity of patrician, appeared to be living with him.

Because of this demand and certain things said about Alexius—namely, that he would become emperor—the emperor had him beaten and tonsured and placed in the praetorium.

In July he moved the army against the Bulgars and built the fortress of Marcellus. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, Cardam, lord of Bulgaria, came out with all his forces and took up position among the fortifications.

Relying on his confidence, and persuaded by false prophets that victory would be his, the emperor rashly and disorderly engaged in battle. He was decisively defeated and, having been put to flight, returned to the city. He had lost many men, not only from the common people but also from the leading ranks, among them Michael the magister Lachanodracon and Bardas the patrician; Stephen the protospatharius; Nicetas and Theognostes, who had become commanders; many imperial men; and also Pancratius, the false prophet and astrologer who had foretold that the emperor would win.

The Bulgars also carried off the baggage, money, horses, and curtains, together with the entire imperial equipment.

When the regiments had gathered in the city, they resolved to bring out Nicephorus and make him Caesar and emperor. When Constantine learned this, he sent for and brought both sons of his grandfather Constantine to Saint Mamas. He deprived Nicephorus of his eyes, and Christophorus, Nicetas, Anthimus, and Eudoxius of their tongues. Along with them he also deprived the patrician Alexius mentioned above of his sight, obeying the counsels of his mother and of the leading Stauratius, who assured him that unless he blinded Alexius, they would elect him emperor.

This punishment for these evils took place in August, on a Saturday, in the fifteenth indiction, at the ninth hour. Nevertheless, God’s justice did not leave this unjust vengeance unpunished for long. For after five years, in the same month and on the same Saturday, Constantine himself was deprived of his eyes by his own mother.

In the third year of Constantine’s reign, when the Armeniacs heard that the patrician Alexius had been blinded, they placed their commander, namely the patrician Theodore Camulianus, under guard.

When the emperor learned this, he first sent several men to them. After holy Easter, however, he himself moved the army against the Armeniacs, together with the other themes, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the first indiction, on the holy day of Pentecost.

After defeating them when, through the treachery of the Armenians who were with them, they had been betrayed, he captured them. He killed Andronicus the spatharius and turmarch, and Gregory, bishop of Sinope; the rest he afflicted with the loss of their property, expenses, and confiscations.

He brought one thousand of their bound soldiers into the city through the Blachernae Gate. On their faces he wrote in ink and by punctures: “Armeniac conspirator.” He then dispersed them both into Sicily and among the other islands.

The Armenian traitors received from the emperor neither honor nor freedom, and therefore handed over the fortress of Amachan to the Arabs.

In the fourth year of Constantine’s reign, the Arabs captured the fortress of Sebasan under a pledge of security; for this reason its commanders also returned to their own lands.

In the fifth year of his reign, Constantine, hating his wife Maria at the prompting of his mother, who sought the Empire, and pursuing a course judged blameworthy by everyone, compelled her to become a nun. After persuading her, he tonsured her in January.

In April he moved the army against the Arabs. In May, entering battle with one of their raiding forces at a place called Amusan, he defeated and routed them and pursued them as far as the river. When he came to Ephesus and had offered prayers at the holy place, he granted the market-trading privilege, worth one hundred pounds of gold, for the service of Saint John the Apostle.

In August the emperor crowned Theodate, a chamberlain, as Augusta and married her.

In the sixth year of his reign, in the first indiction, the emperor Constantine celebrated the beginning of his marriage with Theodate in the palace of Saint Mamas for forty days.

In April of the same indiction, during the night, a very terrible earthquake occurred in Sicily and Crete. In May a very dreadful earthquake occurred at Constantinople.

Cardam, lord of Bulgaria, sent word to the emperor, saying: “Either grant me the terms of the agreement, or I shall come as far as the Golden Gate and lay waste to Thrace.”

The emperor put horse dung in a purse and sent it to him, saying: “I have sent you the sort of terms I judged suitable for you. But since you are old, I do not wish you to weary yourself by coming to these places. I shall come as far as Marcella; you come out, and do whatever God judges.”

After sending to the outer themes, the emperor assembled his people and came as far as Versicinia. Cardam came as far as the grove of Abroleva, but, being afraid, remained in the forest.

The emperor, however, having encouraged his people, went as far as Abroleva and invited Cardam for seventeen days. Cardam did not dare to come out, but retreated in flight to his own lands.

In the same year the Arabs came to Amorium. Since they accomplished nothing, they returned after plundering the surrounding regions.

In the same year, Plato, abbot of the monastery of Sakkudion, withdrew from communion with Tharasius the patriarch because he had admitted the emperor to communion, allowed him to tonsure his wife Maria, and ordered Joseph, a monk and abbot of the monastery called Concarata, to crown him in marriage to Theodate.

When the emperor learned this, he sent the patrician Bardanius, domesticus of the Schools, together with John, count of the Opsikion, brought Plato into the city, and shut him up within the cloister of the church of the commander of the army, which was in the palace.

He struck the remaining monks, together with Plato’s nephews, and sent them into exile at Thessalonica. The emperor’s mother supported them because they resisted and disgraced her son.

In the seventh year of his reign, in September, the emperor went out with his mother to take the baths at Prusa.

In October a son was born to the emperor, whom he named Leo. When the emperor learned this, he left his mother at the baths, together with the entire imperial retinue and the commanders, and hurried back to the city.

Therefore his mother, finding an opportunity, won over the commanders of the forces by gifts and promises so that her son might be deposed and she might rule alone. By flattering some herself and others through her agents, she drew them all to her side and waited to find a suitable day.

Meanwhile, when Adrian the pope died at Rome, Leo, a most honorable and altogether reverend man, was consecrated.

In March the emperor went out against the Arabs, taking with him Stauratius the patrician and the other friends of his mother, as well as a chosen troop of twenty thousand expeditionary soldiers from both themes.

When those who were with Stauratius saw the enthusiasm of the people and the emperor, they feared that, if battle were joined, he might win and they might be frustrated in the plots they had devised against him. They therefore bribed the guards and persuaded them to lie, reporting that the Saracens had fled.

The emperor, consequently, entered the city in great grief and without accomplishing anything. On the first day of May his son Leo died, and he mourned him deeply.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, as he was making his way from the equestrian games to Saint Mamas, those from the regiments came to seize him. The emperor’s mother addressed them. When he learned of this, he entered his chelandion and crossed over to Pylas, intending to take refuge in the Eastern theme.

The friends of his mother were also with him, though he did not know that they were there. He himself and his wife went as far as Triton.

After taking counsel, his mother’s friends said to one another: “If the people gather around him, he will no longer be held under our control; we shall no longer be able to remain hidden from him, and he will destroy us.”

His mother gathered in the palace of Eleutherius those who belonged to the regiments and stationed them there. She entered the palace, and when she learned that the people were flocking to the emperor, she became extremely afraid. She considered how she might send bishops to him, receive his response, and sit in a corner.

But she secretly wrote to the friends who were with him: “Unless you find some way to act and hand him over, I shall tell the emperor what you have said to me.”

They, fearing her, seized him despite his pleas. They brought him into a chelandion, arrived at the city on Saturday morning, and shut him in the Purple Chamber, in which he had also been born. Around the ninth hour they cruelly and irreparably tore out his eyes, so that death immediately followed and ended him, through the counsel of his mother and her advisers.

The sun was darkened for seventeen days and did not give its rays, so that ships at sea lost their way. Everyone said that, because the emperor had been blinded, the sun too had been blinded and had withdrawn its rays. In this manner Eirene, his mother, ruled the Empire thereafter.

In the same year, at Rome, the relatives of Adrian, the blessed pope of revered memory, stirred up the people and rioted against Leo the pope. They seized him and blinded him, although they were unable to extinguish his sight completely.

He fled to Charles, king of the Franks, who took severe vengeance upon his enemies and restored him to his see. In return for this favor to Charles, he crowned him emperor in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, anointing him with oil from head to foot, clothing him in imperial robes, and placing the crown upon him on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth indiction.

Thus Eirene ruled the Romans for five years.

EIRENE.

[Col. 1124C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 791, when Eirene had begun to reign for the second time, she immediately sent Dorotheus, the hegumen of Chrysopolis, and Constantine, the chartophylax of the Great Church, to Habdimelich, who was ravaging parts of Cappadocia and Galatia, to intercede for peace; but this was not accomplished.

In the month of October, certain rebels persuaded the sons of Tuterapiu [Note: [Col. 1123D] Alternatively, Tonterapiu]—of Constantine, namely, the enemy of God—who had been placed under guard in the palace, to flee to the Great Church, as though seeking security for their subsequent immunity, so that by this opportunity they might acclaim one of them emperor. When a great multitude of people had gathered at the church, the eunuch patrician Aetius entered and led them out by persuasion, with no one paying attention to them; and they condemned them to exile at Athens.

The two patricians Stauratius and Aetius, who were known to be the empress’s favorites, became enemies of one another, so that they openly displayed their hostility. Both intended, after her death, to secure the empire for their own relatives.

In the second year of Eirene’s reign, Habdimelich set out against Romania. Having sent thousands of swift troops on a raid, he descended as far as Malagma. After seizing Stauratius’s horses in the stables and capturing the imperial cavalry, he returned without suffering injury; the rest descended as far as Lilia [Note: [Col. 1124D] Alternatively, Lidia] and obtained much booty.

In the month of March, in the seventh indiction, Achamirus, prince of the Sclavini of Belzitia, being harassed by the inhabitants of Hellas, wished to bring out Constantine’s sons and promote one of them as emperor. When the empress Eirene learned of this, she sent against the patrician Constantine Serentapicus [Note: [Col. 1125D] Alternatively, Tesseracondapechus], his son Theophylact, who was a spatharius, and his nephew. She put out the eyes of all of them and scattered their wickedly devised plot against her.

On the Monday of the Paschal festival, Eirene proceeded from the Church of the Holy Apostles, borne in a golden chariot drawn by four white horses and held by four patricians: namely, Bardanius, prefect of the Thracesians; Sisinnius, prefect of Thrace; Nicetas, Domestic of the Schools; and Constantine Boyla. She scattered *hypatian* liberally.

In the month of May the empress fell ill, almost to the point of death, and the rivalry between the eunuchs Aetius and Stauratius was extended. Aetius assisted the patrician Nicetas, Domestic of the Schools, and they pursued Stauratius severely, making the empress believe that he was seeking the empire. She became violently angry with him and, ascending to the palace called Tenthierium [Note: [Col. 1125D] Alternatively, Tontiera], told him that he was concerned with rebellion and faction and was acquiring guilt for her. In answer to this, he offered a defense and fortified himself. He was raging against Aetius, Nicetas, and the aforementioned patricians.

In the third year of Eirene’s reign, in the month of February, in the eighth indiction, the aforementioned patrician Stauratius was organizing tyranny and faction in the imperial city. He won over and appeased with money and gifts the scholarii who were there, together with the excubitors and their commanders. But the pious empress Eirene, after a *silentium* had been held in the triclinium of Justinian [Col. 1125C], forbade every serving soldier to join Stauratius. Thus affairs obtained a modest tranquillity.

Aetius and Nicetas, however, together with certain others, competed in opposing Stauratius. Struck in the heart, he discharged foaming blood through his mouth from the region of the chest and lungs. When the physicians saw this, they declared it fatal. But flatterers and ignorant men—not only physicians, but also false monks and diviners—persuaded him by oaths to believe, right up to the day of his death, that he would live and reign. Relying on them, he organized a sedition in Cappadocia to be raised against Aetius, which he did not live to hear about.

For two days after his death, a messenger came with news of this; those who had been seized in the sedition were sent into exile and subjected to punishments.

In the fourth year of Eirene’s reign, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth indiction, Charles, king of the Franks, was crowned by Pope Leo. When he had wished to wage war against Sicily with fleets, he repented and instead desired to be joined in marriage with Eirene; envoys were sent for this purpose in the following year, in the tenth indiction.

In the month of March, in the ninth indiction, the pious empress Eirene remitted the civic taxes of the Byzantines and relieved Habd and Hieria of the imposts called *commercia*, relying upon great expressions of thanks for these and many other benefits [Col. 1126A].

In the fifth year of Eirene’s reign, the patrician Aetius, freed from Stauratius and therefore enjoying security, was striving to transfer the empire to his own brother. He also made him *Monostrategus* in Thrace and Macedonia, while he himself held the more distant themes, namely the East and the Opsikion.

When he had become swollen with pride, he dishonored and considered worthless those commanders who were superior to him. They became deeply distressed and, plotting faction against the empress, put this plan into action.

Meanwhile, envoys sent by Charles and Pope Leo arrived before the most pious Eirene, requesting that she be joined to him in marriage and come to the West. She certainly would have complied had the aforementioned Aetius not prevented it by his power, usurping the empire for his own brother [Col. 1126B].

In the following year, which was the first year of Nicephorus, on the day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, at the fourth hour of the night, which dawns on Monday, that same Nicephorus, while he was patrician and general logothete, stirred up a tyranny against the most pious Eirene. God, in his ineffable judgments, was permitting this because of the multitude of our sins; Nicetas the patrician and Domestic of the Schools cooperated with him, as did his brother Sisinnius the patrician, [Note: [Col. 1125D] Alternatively, “men full of perjuries and frauds, the Triphylii.” [Col. 1126D] There were also with him Leo the patrician Tesseracontapechis, Gregory the patrician Musulatius]—a man full of perjuries and frauds—and Nicetas Triphylius.

With him were also Leo the patrician Musulatius, Theoctistus the patrician, and Peter the patrician and quaestor. They led astray certain members of the populace who belonged to the official orders. When they came to the gate called the Chalce and had suddenly deceived the guards by false statements, they persuaded them to believe that they had been sent by the empress herself, so that they might acclaim that same Nicephorus as emperor. They claimed that the patrician Aetius was using force against her in order to proclaim his brother Leo emperor. Believing this great lie, the guards together proclaimed as emperor the man who was a tyrant.

Thus those patricians came to the Great Palace and entered it. From there they sent lowborn slaves throughout the city, making an acclamation before midnight. They placed guards in the middle of the palace called Tueleutherium, where the empress happened to be.

At dawn they summoned her, shut her in the greater palace, and then proceeded to the Great Church to crown the criminal [Col. 1126D].

Meanwhile the entire population of the city gathered, and, deeply displeased at what was being done, cursed both the one who was crowning and the one being crowned, even while everyone was congratulating him.

Indeed, those who lived with religion and reason marveled at the divine judgment: how it had permitted her, who had contended for the true faith like a martyr, to be expelled by a swineherd—especially since her most devoted servants had resolved to cling chiefly to her because of their avarice: namely, Leo the patrician eunuch; the *sacellarius* of Sinope; and the three sons of the men hated by God [Note: [Col. 1126D] Alternatively, “the three sons hated by the gods”; alternatively, “the hated sons”], as well as the patricians mentioned above [Col. 1127A]. She had enriched them with countless gifts, often dining with them; and by flatteries accompanied by dreadful oaths they had made her certain, claiming that they considered themselves more necessary to her than all the things of the world and affirming how much goodwill they bore toward her.

Others, as though fallen into a trance, perceived nothing clearly of what had happened and thought they had seen a dream. Others, who knew how to discern matters accurately, blessed the happiness that had passed and mourned the misery that would come through the tyranny—especially those who had already experienced something of the tyrant’s evil-minded ambition.

A darkness and collapse of mind possessed everyone alike, without consolation. Rather than prolonging the account by writing out one by one the shameful events of that pitiable day, I shall pass over them.

Finally, on the following day [Col. 1127B], taking certain patricians with him, he went up to the empress, who had been committed to custody. As was his custom, he pretended a false kindness, by which he also deceived many, and excused himself, saying that he had ascended to the principate unwillingly and had never desired it.

He cursed those who had advanced him and had attacked her by treachery, comparing them to the betrayer of the Lord, who betrayed those with whom he had dined. He also displayed black shoes and claimed that he loved wearing such things contrary to the imperial laws. He deceitfully urged her to have confidence, even swearing concerning every bodily comfort that it was fitting for a mistress to obtain from a servant, and encouraging her not to regard her misfortune as any hardship.

Finally, he urged her to conceal nothing from him of the imperial treasures. He condemned the vice of avarice and could not endure that she possessed these treasures [Col. 1127C]. For he was consumed by it, devouring everything and placing all his hope and confidence in gold.

But the God-beloved Eirene, although it would have been fitting for a woman to be overcome by the emotion of such a sudden reversal, perhaps wisely said to him:

“Yesterday you were a perjured servant; today you are regarded as an able, seditious, and shameless tyrant. As for me, O man, I reckon that it was God who raised me up when I was once an orphan and then advanced me to the throne when I was unworthy. I attribute the cause of my deposition to myself and ascribe it to my sins; yet in all things and in every way, blessed be the name of the Lord.

“As for the manner of your advancement, I attribute it to God.
