Nevertheless, I was not unaware of the reports brought to me concerning the dignity with which you are now surrounded; the outcome of events has shown that they were true. Had I taken them badly, it would have been easy for me to have you killed.

“But now, at one time trusting your oaths and at another sparing you, I have thought little of many who were devoted to me, giving to God what is his, through whom kings reign and the powerful possess the earth.

“Even now, since you are pious and have proceeded from him, I worship you, and I ask you to spare my weakness. Grant me the House of Eleutherius, which I built as a place of refreshment for my incomparable calamity.”

He replied: “If you wish this to be done for you, swear to me by every divine power that you will conceal nothing from me of the imperial treasures. I shall fulfill your requests and grant you every satisfaction.”

She swore to him by the precious and life-giving Wood: “I will not move from you a single obol”—and she did so.

But once he had obtained what he desired, he immediately banished her into exile on the island of Principus, to the monastery that she herself had built, while Charles’s envoys were still in the city and observing what was taking place.

## BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 795, the voracious Nicephorus, having obtained power over everything, did not even wish to conceal his hypocrisy to any small degree. As though he were about to cut off justice, he established a wicked and unjust tribunal in the Magnaura [Col. 1127D].

The tyrant’s intention, as events themselves showed, was not to distribute rights to the poor, but by this means to dishonor all who were eminent, imprison them, and transfer to himself what belonged to everyone. This he also did.

Seeing that everyone was distressed against him, and fearing that, remembering Eirene’s benefactions, they might call her back to the empire, in the month of November, with an exceedingly severe winter approaching, that pitiless man did not pity her. He ordered her to be carried into exile on the island of Lesbos and guarded with the greatest care, so that no one might even see her.

On the day before the Kalends of May, Nicetas Tryphilius died, as they say, destroyed by poison administered by Nicephorus. On the Nones of May, a Thursday, when Nicephorus had gone out to the suburbs of Chalcedon and mounted a very tame horse, the animal, by God’s providence, threw him off and crushed his right foot [Col. 1128C].

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, a Wednesday, at the first hour, Bardanes the patrician and prefect of the Easterners, who was surnamed the Turk, was proclaimed emperor by all the inhabitants of his themes of their own accord. He resisted them greatly, wishing to escape from them, but was entirely unable to do so.

He descended as far as Chrysopolis and, after circling about for eight days without being received, returned as far as Malagma. Fearing God and reflecting that perhaps through him the slaughter of Christians would occur, he took pity and sent to Nicephorus. After receiving a written undertaking in Nicephorus’s own hand—also signed by the most holy patriarch Tharasius and all the patricians—that he and all who were with him would be preserved unharmed and uninjured, on the sixth of the Ides of September he secretly fled and descended into the Bithynian city, to the monastery of Heraclius.

There he found a *chelandium* that had been sent by the emperor for this purpose. He was tonsured, clothed in a monastic robe, and entered it. He then departed for the island called Prima, where he had built a monastery, supposing that contemptible Nicephorus would respect the terrible pledge he had given him and that he would suffer no harm.

But Nicephorus first stripped him of his property. Then, taking this as a pretext, he captured all the commanders of the themes and their inhabitants, and some from the imperial city as well. He abandoned the army’s private pay. Yet what account could adequately relate all the other things he did in those days, through God’s indulgence for our offenses?

On the ninth day, in the month of August of the eleventh indiction, the empress Eirene died in exile on the island of Lesbos. Her body was transferred to the island of Principus, to the monastery that she had built.

[Col. 1129B] In the second year of his reign, Nicephorus crowned his son Stauratius emperor through the most holy patriarch Tharasius, on the ambo of the Great Church. He was utterly unfit for such a dignity, both in appearance and in strength and understanding.

Moreover, Nicephorus, who had never preserved the truth anywhere, sent certain Lycaonians—or rather, like-minded and consenting werewolves—to the island of Prota. He ordered them to depart and, as though without his knowledge, to deprive Bardanes of his sight, and after the deed to flee to the church.

When this had been done, both the patriarch and the senate, as well as all who feared God, grieved bitterly. But the most wicked emperor Nicephorus, with oaths, pretended to seek all the leading Lycaonians, as though he intended to avenge himself upon them, doing everything according to outward display and nothing according to God [Col. 1129C].

For, in addition to his other acts of transgression, he possessed especially this peculiarity of mind, by which he had also deceived many before becoming emperor. Nevertheless, those who clearly knew his inclination regarded it as ridiculous. His shameless, darkened, and polluted face then became inaccessible for seven days, while he deceitfully wailed inside the imperial bedchamber.

His womanish tears were also natural to him; it is beyond doubt that such tears occur in many wicked men and false prophets, although this did not escape the notice of very many people.

In the month of August, when he had set out against the Arabs, he met them at Crasus in Phrygia. Battle was joined, and he was defeated. After losing many men and almost being captured alive himself, he was barely saved by certain exceptionally brave commanders [Col. 1129D].

In the third year of his reign, when faction had arisen in Persia, the Arab commander descended in order to pacify them. Nicephorus, however, finding the opportunity, built Ancyra in Galatia, as well as Thebasan and Analatrasum. He also sent a raiding force, but those who returned accomplished nothing and instead lost many men.

In the fourth year of Nicephorus’s reign, Aaron, commander of the Arabs, moved against Romania with a great force: three hundred thousand men, namely, both Black-clad troops and forces gathered from Syria and Palestine.

When he came to Tyana, he built a house of his blasphemy. Besieging and capturing Heraclius, then a very strongly fortified castle, he also captured Thebasan, Malacopan, Sideropelum, and Andrasum.

He also sent a raiding force of sixty thousand warriors, which descended as far as Ancyra. After seeing this, he returned [Col. 1130A].

The emperor Nicephorus, held back by fear and inability, also went out, in desperation, to display the strength of his misfortune. After winning many victories, he sent to Aaron the metropolitan of Synada, Peter the hegumen of Gylei, and Gregory the steward. After they had engaged in extensive negotiations, they established peace: each year he was to pay them thirty thousand *nomismata*, together with three *nomismata* as the emperor’s head-tax and three for his son.

Having received these payments, Aaron rejoiced and exulted more than if he had received ten thousand talents, as though he had subdued the Roman Empire.

They also agreed that the camps that had been destroyed should not be rebuilt. But when the Arabs had withdrawn, he immediately rebuilt and fortified those same camps. When Aaron learned of this, he sent again and recaptured Thebasan. He also sent a fleet to Cyprus, destroyed the churches, forced the Cypriots to emigrate, and, after causing great destruction, dissolved the peace [Col. 1130B].

In the fifth year of his reign, Nicephorus moved the army against the Bulgars. When he reached Adrianople and perceived that the imperial officials and certain members of the orders were plotting faction against him, he turned back ineffectually, accomplishing nothing except that he inflicted vengeance upon his own tribesmen, subjecting many of them to slaughter and confiscation of their property.

In the sixth year of Nicephorus’s reign, in the month of September, Aaron, commander of the Arabs, sent Chumeid with a fleet against Rhodes. When he had crossed over unexpectedly and reached Rhodes, he inflicted great destruction there. Nevertheless, the fortified town that was on the island remained unassailed. When he himself had begun his return, he was manifestly attacked by Saint Nicholas, worker of miracles. For when he had come to Myra and attempted to crush its sacred shrine, he crushed another in its place; and immediately the fleet was caught in a violent disturbance of many winds, sea-waves, thunder, and lightning, so that very many boats were smashed. Chumeid himself, the attacker, recognized the saint’s power and escaped the danger beyond all expectation.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, Nicephorus, after making a wide selection of virgins from every province subject to him in order to provide a wife for his son Stauracius, separated Theophania of Athens, a kinswoman of the blessed Eirene, from the man to whom she had been betrothed, and joined her to the wretched Stauracius. In this, as in other matters, he acted imprudently and proved himself a transgressor. But the other two women whom he had selected with her, and who were more beautiful than she, he openly corrupted during those same wedding celebrations; and everyone mocked him for this obscenity.

Finally, in the month of February, when many of the leading men were contriving hostility against him, they chose Arsabir, the quaestor and patrician, a pious and most reasonable man. When the many-sided Nicephorus learned of this, he had Arsabir beaten, tonsured, and made a monk, and sent him into exile in Bithynia. The others he subjected to beatings and tonsures, as well as confiscations and exiles: not only the leaders of secular life, but also bishops and monks, and likewise the *syncellus*, *sacellarius*, and *chartophylax* of the Great Church—reasonable men worthy of reverence.

In the seventh year of Nicephorus’s reign, the commander of the Arabs died in inner Persia, in the region called Khurasan, and his son Muhammad assumed the leadership. He was troublesome in every respect. Against him his brother Abdallah raised a rebellion and became the author of civil war. Consequently, those who were in Syria, Egypt, and Libya were divided among various governments and overturned both public affairs and one another, in confusion, through slaughter, plunder, and various outrages, against one another and against their Christian subjects.

As a result, the churches in the holy city of our God were abandoned, as were the monasteries of the two great [Note: [Col. 1131D] Others read *librarum* (“of pounds”); others *baurarum*; P. Pith. reads *laurarum*.] laurae—namely, those of the holy Chariton, of Cyriacus, and of Saba—as well as the other monasteries of the saints Euthymius and Theodosius.

Theodore, abbot of the Studion, and his brother Joseph, archbishop of Thessalonica, together with Plato the recluse and their other monks, withdrew from communion with the most holy patriarch Tarasius because of Joseph the *vicedominus*, who had unlawfully crowned Constantine and Theodote. Then the emperor Nicephorus, seizing the opportunity, assembled bishops and abbots and ordered a synod to be held against them. By its decision they were expelled from the monastery and the city and assigned to exile, in the month of January, in the second indiction.

In that same year, while the *roga* was being distributed to the people beside the river Strymon, the Bulgarians attacked and seized it—one thousand one hundred pounds of gold—and killed a great many people, together with the *praetor* and the commanders. Several commanders of the other themes had also been assessed there; all of them perished on the spot. The Bulgarians also seized the entire baggage train and returned in this manner.

In the same year, before the solemnity of Easter, Crummus, the Bulgarian commander, having drawn up his battle line against Sardica, captured it by treachery. Of the Roman soldiers he killed six thousand, besides a multitude of civilians.

Nicephorus went out against him on the Tuesday of Holy Passion Week, but accomplished nothing worthy of mention. When the commanders who had survived the Bulgarian slaughter begged him for a word of salvation, he refused to grant it and thus lost them. Among them was Cumatius the *spatharius*, skilled in mechanical arts.

Nicephorus, however, with great disgrace and by means of solemn oaths, tried to persuade the royal city that they should believe he had celebrated the Easter festival in Crummus’s palace. Moreover, when he wished to rebuild the city of Sardica, which had been destroyed, he feared the resistance of the populace. He therefore began demanding money from them for the construction, on the pretext that they had to persuade the emperor to undertake the building.

But they, with sound judgment, provoked by the arguments supplied by that wicked man, rioted against him and against their own commanders for six hours. Then they attacked and tore apart the commanders’ tents. When they came as far as the emperor, they overwhelmed him with insults and curses, swearing that they could no longer endure his boundless greed and wicked purpose.

Pretending to be suddenly terrified, he rose from the table. At first, through the patricians Nicephorus and Peter, he tried to calm the army with oaths and persuasive words. But after gaining a brief respite, the people seized a certain hill. Because they held it in their own hands, they forgot their grievance and cried out, “Κύριε ἐλέησον” (“Lord, have mercy”), as though because of some earthquake or failure of the rains.

But he, always ready for every evil, secretly won over many commanders during the night with gifts. On the following day he came in person among them and addressed the crowds with complete calm, assuring them with terrible oaths that he was equally concerned for their children. Then he reached the royal city without delay, abandoning the patrician and *primiscrinius* Theodosius, surnamed Salibara, in order to learn from one another which of them had carried out the rebellion.

When the crowds were returning, he pretended that he would distribute *roga* to them at Saint Mamas. After punishing many of them with executions, tonsures, and exiles, he led the rest across to Chrysopolis, trampling underfoot oaths so great and so terrible. On account of their misery they called the crossing “the fiery river.”

In the eighth year of his reign, Nicephorus, after many impious punishments, turned his attention to completely humiliating the army. He ordered Christian exiles from every theme to be transported to the Slavic lands, while their property was sold. This affair was no less than captivity. Many, driven mad, blasphemed and called down the advance of their enemies; others mourned around the tombs of their parents and declared the dead blessed. Some even resorted to hanging themselves, so that they might be rescued from such evils.

They could not carry away with them the immovable property that they possessed, and they saw the wealth acquired through their parents’ labors being lost. A sense of utter impossibility seized everyone. This began in the month of September and ended around Easter.

As a second affliction alongside this one, he ordered the poor to be enrolled for military service and armed against their fellow countrymen. He also ordered each person to contribute eighteen and a half *nomismata* to the treasury, together with all the customary public taxes.

As a third evil, he ordered the assessments of their taxes to be weighed and increased, and ordered two *siliquae* to be paid on account of the [Note: [Col. 1132D] Others read *Cariaticorum*; others *Chartiatis*.] Cariacites.

As a fourth wickedness, he ordered all remaining revenues to be increased.

As a fifth affliction, he ordered a tax to be collected from the tenants of venerable institutions—namely, orphanages, hospitals and gerontocomia, churches, and monasteries governed by rules—according to every hearth, from the first year of his tyranny. He also ordered that the more valuable possessions be brought to the imperial treasury.

As a sixth affliction, he ordered the *praetors* to investigate those who had suddenly risen from poverty and to exact money from them, as though they were discoverers of hidden treasures.

As a seventh invention, he ordered those who had found a jar, or any vessel, twenty years earlier and had retained it until that time to be deprived of all their own money.

As an eighth measure, he ordered those who had inherited from grandfathers or fathers and had become poor after dividing the property to pay twenty shekels to the public treasury, dating from those same years. He also ordered those who had purchased slaves outside Abydos to pay two *nomismata* as a tax, especially those who were in the Dodecaschoinos.

As a ninth measure, he compelled shipowners who lived along the coast, especially those who made their living by agricultural labor in Asia Minor, to purchase goods from the property he had seized, at whatever valuation he himself assigned.

As a tenth measure, after gathering the distinguished shipowners of Constantinople, he lent them four *siliquae* per *nomisma* at interest, while they simultaneously paid twelve pounds of gold, as well as carrying on their customary commerce.

These matters, selected from many, have been described only briefly, indicating the manifold schemes he devised for every form of greed. The evils that he inflicted in the royal city on men of high, middling, and low rank cannot be written down. He investigated how some lived at home and sent certain wicked slaves to denounce their masters. At first he appeared to doubt what they reported; then he confirmed their accusations. He did the same with men of lowly status, judging those who made accusations worthy of honors.

Moreover, he overthrew the households of many inhabitants from the first generation to the third, relying on the hope that the sooner they collapsed, the sooner he himself would possess them by inheritance.

It is worthwhile to commit this episode also to memory, for pleasure and as an example. A certain Cerularius was wealthy in the marketplace through his own labor and did nothing wrong. When he had been summoned, the voracious emperor said to him:

“Place your hand on my head and swear how much gold you possess.”

When he modestly refused as though unworthy, he was compelled to do so by the emperor and said that he had one hundred pounds. The emperor ordered them to be taken away at that very hour, saying:

“What need have you to trouble yourself? Dine with me, take ten pounds, and be content with them.”

In the ninth year of his reign, Nicephorus extended his schemes against the Christians: godless inspections in the purchase of animals, unjust valuations of various fruits, extortions from commanders, and loans at interest on ships. He imposed a law on everyone that nothing should be lent at interest, along with ten thousand other inventions of evil, whose detailed history would burden those who seek to learn only a concise account of events.

On the Kalends of October, a Tuesday, a certain dissolute man dressed as a monk drew a sword and ran into the palace, seeking to kill Nicephorus. Two of those standing nearby rushed at him, but he severely wounded them. After he was captured and subjected to many punishments, he excused himself by pretending to be possessed by a demon and accusing no one at all. Nevertheless, the emperor fastened him to a piece of wood together with those undergoing punishment.

Many thereafter prophesied that this would prove to be a portent of an enormous miracle, declaring that it would happen to rulers and subjects alike, just as it had happened to the impious Nestorius.

He was also an exceedingly fervent friend of the Manichaeans, now called Paulicians and Athingani, who were established in Phrygia and Lycaonia and regarded as his neighbors. He continually rejoiced in their responses and sacrifices. When the patrician Bardanius rebelled against him, Nicephorus summoned these men and overcame Bardanius through their machinations.

For he tied a bull by its horns to an iron stake in a certain place, bent it down toward the ground, and had it killed while it bellowed and rolled about. Then, grinding its garment in a mill in the opposite direction and using incantations, he won the victory—God permitting it on account of the multitude of our sins.

These people obtained under his reign a place where they could live without fear. Consequently many of the more frivolous were corrupted by their unspeakable sects.

During the tax collection, a false hermit named Nicholas and certain blasphemers with him had also become enemies of right doctrine and opponents of the venerable images. Nicephorus defended them and caused both the high priest and all who lived according to God to grieve on this account.

Often, when people cried out against them, he became angry, rejoicing when they stirred up hostilities against one another. He mocked every Christian who loved his neighbor, as an overturner of the divine commandments. His concern was to bring rational and irrational judgments against every person to punitive proceedings in the Magnaura, so that no one would have leisure to act against his impieties.

Finally, he ordered military commanders to use bishops and lower-ranking clergy like servants, sending them to visit bishoprics and monasteries and to abuse with authority those under their control. He reproached those who, from the time of the world, had contributed golden or silver vessels to divine services, and he declared that it was right for everything consecrated in the churches to be treated as common property—like Judas, who decrees such a thing concerning the Lord’s ointment.

He also accused all his imperial predecessors of being improvident, generally removing all foresight from them. At the same time he said that no one could deceive a ruler if the ruler wished to hold the principate vigorously. But he became vain in his thoughts and was destined to be slain by divine judgment.

Meanwhile, in the month of February of that same fourteenth indiction, on the first Saturday of the fast, Saracens encountered Leo the *praetor* of the Armeniac theme near Euchaita, while he was carrying the theme’s *roga*. They seized it together with a great multitude of people. It amounted to sixteen talents and one thousand three hundred pounds. Even after this, Nicephorus was not rebuked in such a way as to abandon his greed.

Thus the new Ahab, uneducated by signs and, on the contrary, more ambitious than Phalaris and Midas, prepared for war against the Bulgarians together with his son Stauracius. In July he departed from the royal city and ordered Nicetas, the patrician and general *logothete*, to impose public taxes on churches and monasteries and to exact from the houses of the commanders the payments owed for the preceding eight years. There was great lamentation.

When he heard a complaint from one of his own servants—namely, the patrician Theodosius Salibara, who said to him, “Everyone, my lord, is crying out against us, and at the time of trial they will rejoice at our fall”—he replied:

“If God, hardening my heart as Pharaoh’s, has hardened it, what good will come to those under my hand from Nicephorus?”

Theodosius, do not expect anything beyond what you see. The Lord knows these things. I, the writer of this account, heard them from Theodosius himself, spoken aloud.

Having gathered the armies, not only from Thrace but also from the more distant themes, he threatened even the poor infantrymen, armed with slings and sticks and supplied with their own pay, and blaspheming, to march against the Bulgarians.

But Crummus, fearing the multitudes, sought peace while they were at Marcellae. He was prevented from granting it by wicked counsels and by the persuasion of those who shared his counsel. After many circuitous movements through trackless regions, he entered Bulgaria headlong, reckless and at the same time afraid, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, while Sirius appeared to be consuming everything. He repeatedly said:

“Who will go and deceive Ahab? For whether God or the adversary is leading me, I go unwillingly.”

Before he had entered Bulgaria, Bizantius, this emperor’s beloved servant, fled to Crummus at Marcellae, secretly taking with him an imperial garment and one hundred pounds of gold. Many interpreted this flight as an omen of Nicephorus’s ruin.

For three days, believing himself to be prospering after the first engagements, he attributed the victory not to God, who grants success, but proclaimed only the good fortune and good counsel of Stauracius. He threatened the commanders who had tried to prevent his entry, and ordered irrational animals, infants, and people of every age to be killed without mercy. He left the dead bodies of his fellow countrymen unburied, caring only about collecting plunder.

He placed keys and seals over the inner chambers of Crummus, thereby securing them as his own property for the future. He also cut off, from Christians who had so much as touched anything of the spoils, their ears and other limbs. He burned the palace called Crummus’s Court. When he had been brought very low, Crummus sent a message saying:

“Behold, you have conquered. Take, therefore, whatever pleases you, and depart in peace.”

But since he was an enemy of peace, Nicephorus refused to accept it.

Then Crummus, raging, placed wooden defenses at the entrances and exits of the region and surrounded and fortified it with a wall.

When Nicephorus learned of this, he was immediately struck with terror and, wandering about, did not know what to do. He foretold coming destruction to those who were with him, declaring:

“Even if we had wings, let no one hope to escape ruin.”

These operations lasted for two days, Thursday and Friday. On Saturday night, the confusion of armed crowds around Nicephorus and those with him was heard, and all the battle lines were thrown into disorder.

Before the beginning of day, the barbarians came upon Nicephorus’s tent and miserably killed him and the nobles who were with him. Among them were the patricians Aetius Peter and Sisinnius Triphyles; the patrician Theodosius Salibara, who had grieved the blessed Eirene and shown her many evils; the patrician Eparchus; the *praetor* of the East; many *protospatarii* and *spatharii*; the domestic of the *excubitores*; the commander of the regiments; the imperial *drungarius* of the guard; the *praetor* of Thrace; and many commanders of the themes with countless people. Every hope of the Christians was destroyed, and all the weapons and imperial vessels were lost.

May Christians never again see the shameful events of such a day, since they surpass every lamentation.

Crummus cut off Nicephorus’s head and hung it on a wooden frame for many days, to display it to the nations coming to him and to the disgrace of us all. Afterwards he took it down, stripped it, and covered it externally with silver; then, boasting, he made the princes of the Slavs drink from it.

Although many women were widowed and many children orphaned in a single day, and the lamentation was unbearable, his death nevertheless became a consolation to many.

None of those who survived gave a clear account of the manner of his death. Some also report that Christians attacked him with stones as he was falling. But among the effeminate men—namely, his servants, with whom he also had sexual relations—some perished in the fire of the enclosure and others by the sword together with him.

Under this man’s rule the Christians never experienced a worse one. He surpassed all who had ruled before him in ambition, luxury, and barbarian cruelty. To recount these matters individually would be unbelievable to posterity and burdensome to us.

Stauracius was also dangerously wounded on the right side of his neck. He escaped from the battle only with difficulty and came to Adrianople, having been brutally struck by blows.

But the patrician Stephen, domestic of the schools, with Theoctistus the *magister* also present, proclaimed Stauracius emperor and addressed the people who had survived against his father. They were very pleased.

Michael Europalates, having escaped unharmed, was strongly urged by his friends to accept the title of emperor. He refused because of the oaths he had sworn to Nicephorus and Stauracius. Stephen, the domestic, resisted him because he hoped that Stauracius would live.

But Stauracius, as an immense quantity of blood burst forth through his urine, wasted away in his thighs and shins, so that he came to Byzantium in a litter.

The patriarch Nicephorus, who loved him with deep affection, advised him to appease God and to console those whom his father had oppressed through greed. To him, the true heir of his father’s disposition said that he could restore no more than three talents to them.

These were only part of his injustice in those matters. Nevertheless, even in this he was reluctant, not trusting that he would survive.

Since he preserved an unbroken alliance with no one, in the manner of his father’s disposition, he repeatedly subjected the *magister* Theoctistus, the domestic Stephen, and Michael Europalates to disgrace. He also turned against his sister Procopia, treating her as though she were plotting against the Augusta Theophania.

For the wretched woman hoped to obtain the empire through imitation of the blessed Eirene, since she was childless.

But Stauracius, seeing that he was becoming incurably ill, hastened to acquire the empire for his wife and to incite the Bulgarians against the Christians, adding evils upon the former evils. Because of this, the frightened patriarch Nicephorus, the *magister* Theoctistus, and the domestic Stephen, after much hostility, entered into mutual friendship with Michael Europalates.

Around the end of September, in the fifth indiction, on the evening of the Kalends of October, Stauracius questioned Stephen the domestic, who had been summoned, asking how he could bring Michael, his sister’s husband, from his own house before him in order to put out his eyes.

Stephen replied that this would be impossible at that hour because of the power surrounding Michael and the fortification of his house and location. He asked that what had been said be made known to no one.

But Stephen, after bending him with persuasive words so that he would not be anxious, gathered throughout the entire night the soldiers of the regiments who remained, together with his own commanders, in the Hippodrome, in order to proclaim Michael emperor, as will be related below.

The patriarch Nicephorus required from Michael a document written in his own hand concerning the orthodox faith, and requiring him to keep his hands free of Christian blood, as well as concerning sacred persons—that is, monks and the entire ecclesiastical order—so that they would not be struck by him.

## MICHAEL
In the year 804 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Nones of October, Michael Europalates, called “the Most Gentle,” was proclaimed Roman emperor in the Hippodrome by the entire senate and the military ranks. He reigned for two years. When Stauratius heard the acclamation, he immediately cut off his hair and put on monastic clothing. Through Simeon the monk, his kinsman, he earnestly implored the patriarch. The patriarch came to the palace together with Emperor Michael and urged Stauratius not to grieve over what had happened, asserting that it had been done not through treachery but because of despair over Stauratius’s life. But Stauratius, raging with his father’s wicked fury, did not yield, saying to him: “You will never have a better friend than me.”

At the fourth hour Michael was crowned by Patriarch Nicephorus on the ambo of the Great Church. Great rejoicing took place, and he gave the patriarch one pound of gold and twenty-five pounds to the clergy. For he was a magnanimous and not greedy man, and he consoled all who had been harmed by Nicephorus’s wickedness; he also restored the senate and the army with gifts.

On the fourth day before the Ides of October, Procopia was crowned Augusta in the Triclinium, and he enriched the senate with many generous gifts. To the wives of the thematic soldiers who had been killed in Bulgaria he gave five talents of gold. He also enriched Theophania, the wife of Stauratius, who had embraced the solitary life, and her relatives, who had lived miserably under Nicephorus. Among other gifts, he granted her a distinguished house and the monastery called Thebraica, where Stauratius was buried.

He likewise enriched all the patricians and senators, priests and high priests, military monks, and the poor, both those living in the imperial city and those dwelling in the themes. Thus, within a few days, the immeasurable avarice of Nicephorus—for which he had also perished miserably—appeared to have vanished.

In addition to his many excellent virtues, since he was most devout and orthodox, he grieved over those who were separated from the holy Church for whatever reason or pretext. He persistently entreated the most holy patriarch and those who could work for the common peace. Among these were Theodore, abbot of the Studion, Plato, and Joseph, archbishop of Thessalonica and Theodore’s brother, who were being held under harsh conditions in the Studion. He labored to reconcile them with the leaders of their monastery, and he succeeded.

He also sent to Charles, king of the Franks, concerning peace and a marriage agreement involving his son Theophylact. The most holy patriarch Nicephorus likewise sent synodical letters to Leo, the holy pope of Rome; previously, Nicephorus had been forbidden to do this.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth indiction, the most tranquil Emperor Michael crowned his son Theophylact emperor. Patriarch Nicephorus performed the coronation on the ambo of the Greater Church, on Thursday. Michael offered the most precious crown at the holy altar, together with golden vessels, beautiful stones, and quadrangular curtains, anciently woven with gold and bright purple and adorned with wonderful holy images. He also gave the patriarch twenty-five pounds of gold and one hundred pounds to the venerable clergy, making the holy festival and the proclamation of his son splendid.

The most devout emperor, moved by great divine zeal against the Manichaeans—now called Paulicians—and the Athingani living in Phrygia and Lycaonia, promulgated, in accordance with the pronouncements of the most holy patriarch Nicephorus and other devout men, the death penalty against them. But certain other wicked counselors opposed this under the pretext of repentance, although it was impossible for those deceived by their error to perform repentance.

They ignorantly maintained that priests were not permitted to proclaim death against the impious, in every respect contradicting the divine Scriptures on this matter. For if Peter, the chief of the apostles, put Ananias and Sapphira to death for only one lie, and Paul cries out, saying, “Those who do such things are worthy of death”—and this concerns only bodily sin—how could they not be opposed, since these people serve demons through every kind of spiritual and bodily impurity?

Stauratius, consumed by an ulcer arising from a mortal wound inflicted around the region of the spine, so that no one could approach him because of the great stench, died on the third day before the Ides of January, in the fifth indiction. He had reigned, as is believed, two months and six days.

On the fifth day before the Ides of May, Thursday, a great solar eclipse occurred. On the seventh day before the Ides of June, Emperor Michael set out against the Bulgarians, and Procopia went with him as far as Zerulum.

Crunnus, duke of the Bulgarians, had captured Debeltum by siege and had transported elsewhere its inhabitants together with their bishop. The forces that had gathered around him because of the evil and frequent counsels of the emperor’s wicked advisers turned especially against the Opsicians and Thracians, inflicting ambushes and injuries upon them. Michael restrained them and, by gifts and admonitions, imposed silence and brought them to reconciliation.

When the Bulgarians learned of the divisions within the army and realized that the Romans feared battle, they were greatly encouraged and prevailed against Thrace and Macedonia. Then the Christians abandoned Anchialus and Beroe and fled, although no one pursued them. The inhabitants of Nicetas, the fortress of Probatus, and certain other strongholds, as well as those of Philippopolis, Philippoi, and Strymon, likewise took the opportunity to flee and returned to their own homes.

This was caused by divine indignation, which exposed the madness of Nicephorus. His supposed reforms, in which he had gloried, quickly collapsed; it also exposed the wicked opinions of many who, while attacking God, had ceased to condemn the widespread heresies of the Paulicians, Athingani, Iconoclasts, and Tetradites.

I pass over the adulteries, fornications, lusts, perjuries, fraternal hatreds, and avarice, as well as the remaining transgressions against the holy and venerable images and against the holy monastic habit. They were moving their tongues, calling blessed before God the abominable Constantine because he had fought vigorously against the Bulgarians on account of the piety that those wretched men impiously confessed him to have possessed.

But those who were in the imperial city armed themselves after the universal synod in order to overthrow the orthodox faith. They wished, without God, to rule as blind men over the sons of Constantine, the enemy of God, who had been confined under guard on the island of Banormus. They intended to steal them away by night and bring them to the army. But the Lord confounded them, raising up the most devout Michael in defense of the truth.

After the assembled peoples had discussed the faith, Michael returned to the imperial city. Wisely considering the matter, he deterred many from rebellion by a few blows and ordered the sons of Constantine, who were seen to have been deprived of their eyes, to be carried into exile at Aphusia.

One of the seducers mentioned above—a false hermit, an associate of Nicholas in the practice of sorcery, who had removed the icon of the most holy Mother of God—he mutilated by cutting out his tongue. That man died both in body and in soul. But he publicly exposed his associate Nicholas, who promised that he would repent, and, after Nicholas confessed his own crimes, he handed him over to be confined in a monastery, lest he abuse his monastic habit by living freely according to his own will.

He also exposed the Athingani and sent them into exile through Leo, the governor of the East.

In the month of August, in the fifth indiction, Thebid raised an army against the Christians. Leo engaged him in battle and prospered, killing two thousand men and capturing horses and weapons.

Muhammad, the eldest son of Aaron, who held the leadership of the people, entered into war in inner Persia with his brother Abdallah, was defeated, and, fleeing to Gabda, gained possession of it. Another tyrant divided Damascus, Egypt, and Africa between them, while another ravaged Palestine like a bandit.

In the second year of Michael’s reign, Crunnus, duke of the Bulgarians, again sent an embassy to Emperor Michael through Dragomir, seeking the treaties that had been promised under Theodosius of Adramyttium and Patriarch Germanus to Cormesius, who at that time was lord of Bulgaria. Those treaties included the territories extending to Amelon of Thrace; garments or scarlet skins up to the value of fifty pounds of gold; the return of fugitives of either side to the other if they had happened to plot against their superiors; and the protection of merchants in both regions by official orders and seals. If anyone were found without a seal, whatever he possessed was to be seized and deposited in the public treasury.

He wrote to the emperor: “Unless you hasten to peace by your own decision, I will wage war against Mesembria.”

After receiving these proposals, the emperor, influenced by the advice of his wicked counselors, did not accept peace. Under the pretext of false piety and a concern for the ruin of the state, the wicked counselors argued that fugitives ought not to be returned. As evidence they cited the Lord’s Gospel saying: “The one who comes to me I will never cast out.”

In the middle of October, Crunnus drew up his forces against Mesembria with siege-engines, mangonels, and battering rams, which he had learned to use because of Nicephorus, the destroyer of the Christians. An Arab who had fled to the Christians after baptism was highly skilled in mechanical arts. He stationed him at Adrianople. Instead of granting him any reward, he reduced his pay and, when the man complained bitterly, struck him. Grieving over this, the man fled to the Bulgarians and taught them all the mechanical arts involved in such operations.

Applying this knowledge, and meeting no resistance because of the Romans’ great stupidity, Crunnus captured Mesembria after a month.

On the Kalends of November, when he was in distress, the emperor summoned the patriarch and took counsel concerning peace. The metropolitans were also present—namely, the metropolitan of Nicaea and that of Cyzicus—together with the wicked counselors and Theodore, abbot of the Studion. The patriarch and the metropolitan bishops supported peace with the emperor, but the wicked counselors, together with Theodore, abbot of the Studion, overturned it, declaring:

“No one accepts peace at the expense of violating the divine command. The Lord says: ‘The one who comes to me I will never cast out.’ First, since none of them fled to us, how did we betray those who were within the Court, when we were able to save them in peace? Second, even if they did flee, though only rarely to us, nevertheless, for the sake of the salvation of many, it was necessary to strive rather than to enrich ourselves through uncertain and invisible things. For it is more pleasing to God to save many rather than a few. To suffer loss in many things for the sake of a small profit is the height of folly.”

These things took place on the Kalends of November.

On the Nones of November, a comet appeared in the form of two shining moons, joining and separating into different shapes, so that they formed the appearance of a headless man. On the following day, a wretched report arrived concerning the destruction of Mesembria, alarming everyone because of the expectation of still greater evils.

The enemy found Mesembria full of all the things ordinarily needed for human habitation and took possession of it, together with Debeltum. There they also found thirty-six bronze siphons, through which liquid fire was discharged, as well as a considerable supply of silver and gold.

In the same year many Christians came from Palestine and Syria to Cyprus, fleeing the immense oppression of the Arabs. Since Syria, Egypt, Africa, and every principality subject to them lacked a general ruler, murders, robberies, adulteries, and every action hateful to God were being perpetrated in the cities and villages, as though the people were divinely destined to perish. In the holy city of our God, the places venerated there—the sanctuaries of the holy Mother of God, the Resurrection, Calvary, and the others—were profaned.

Likewise, the most renowned lauras of the desert, those of Saint Chariton and Saint Sabas, together with the other monasteries and churches, were left deserted. Some were killed after suffering martyrdom; others hastened to Cyprus and from there to Byzantium. The devout Emperor Michael and the most holy Patriarch Nicephorus received them with gracious generosity.

To those who came to the city he gave a distinguished monastery. To the monks and laypeople who remained in Cyprus he sent a talent of gold and consoled them in various ways.

Michael was indeed gentle and merciful toward everyone, but he was sluggish in administering affairs, having been reduced to servitude under the master Theoctistus and the other leaders.

Moreover, in the month of February two Christians fleeing from Bulgaria announced to the emperor that Crunnus was suddenly hastening to plunder those who were in Thrace. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March the emperor left the city, but by God’s providence he returned without accomplishing anything. He ascended to the monastery of Saint Tarasius, the holy patriarch, and, after celebrating his memorial together with Augusta Procopia, covered his sacred tomb with a silver covering weighing ninety-five pounds.

After Mesembria had been captured, and Crunnus had refused peace, the emperor ordered selected troops from all the themes to cross into Thrace before spring. Everyone found this burdensome, especially the Cappadocians and Armeniacs.

When the emperor went out with the military forces in May, his wife Procopia again went with him as far as the aqueduct near Heraclea. But the crowds, taking this harshly, turned against Michael with insults and curses.

On the fourth day before the Ides of May, an eclipse occurred near the twelfth part of Taurus, according to the clock, at sunrise, and great fear fell upon the crowds.

The emperor, however, went around Thrace with the governors and armies, neither advancing against Mesembria nor accomplishing any of the other things that ought to be done for the destruction of the enemy. He merely followed the empty speeches of his counselors, who had no experience of war and therefore insisted that the enemy would not dare come against him while he sat in his own territory.

The gathering of fellow citizens, deficient in necessities and destroying their compatriots through plunder and invasions, was more burdensome than the barbarian assault.

Around the beginning of June, Crunnus, duke of the Bulgarians, went out with his armies, fearing that there were many Christians. When he moved his army to Versinicia, about thirty standards from the imperial camp, Leo the patrician and governor of the East, and John the patrician and governor of Macedonia, surnamed Aplaces, were eager to defeat them, but the wicked counselors prevented them from doing so by order of the emperor.

While the city was celebrating litanies with the high priest in the Church of the Holy Apostles, certain impious men, hateful to God and devoted to the heresy of Constantine, closed the gate of the imperial tombs. Since no one was paying attention because of the crowd, they suddenly forced the gate open with a certain noise, as though by some supernatural operation. They rushed inside and fell before the tomb of the seducer, invoking him rather than God.

“Arise,” they said, “and help the ruined state.”

They spread the report that Constantine had risen, mounted on a horse, and was going to defeat the Bulgarians—though he, on the contrary, inhabits Tartarus with the demons.

The city prefect arrested them. At first they lied, saying that the gates of the tombs had opened spontaneously by divine power. When brought before the prefect’s tribunal and wavering in their testimony, however, they confessed before any punishment that they had perpetrated the fraud of forcing them open. The prefect deservedly subjected them to the public spectacle, while they cried out the reason for their public punishment.

Thus the devil, the inventor of wickedness, instructed his soldiers not to accuse their own sins but the orthodox faith handed down by the Fathers and the sacred habit of monks, which is the gymnasium of divine philosophy.

Many who blasphemed in these matters were Christians only in outward habit but were Paulicians in truth. Unable to reveal their detestable deeds, they corrupted the uneducated on such occasions, calling Constantine—who was Judaic in outlook—blessed as a prophet and victor, and embracing his heresy, which overturned the incarnate dispensation of our Lord.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of June, when the armies engaged in battle not far from Adrianople, the Christians conducted themselves very badly in the war, but the enemy won the battle. So many of the Romans did not even look upon the engagement but fled at full speed. Crunnus, astonished, thought that what had happened was some indication of an ambush and held his men back somewhat from pursuit. But when he saw them fleeing without any restraint, he pursued and killed great numbers, and, coming upon the baggage, carried it off together with the spoils.

The emperor fled and returned to the city with the crowds. After summoning their leaders, he also promised to abdicate the empire, swearing to this. Among them was Leo the patrician and governor of the East. The emperor wished to take him as a partner in holding the empire, as a devout, courageous, and altogether energetic man.

Leo did not agree in any way. The emperor therefore left him in charge of the themes, intending on the eighth day before the Kalends of June to abdicate the empire and promote another ruler. His wife and sons, however, together with those who had wickedly gained power, did not permit this.

The most holy Patriarch Nicephorus agreed with this plan, saying: “He and his sons will be saved if such a man is promoted.”

When the governors descended into the city with the crowds and heard that the emperor had fled, they despaired of ever again being ruled by him. They took counsel among themselves and implored Leo to assist the commonwealth and support the religion of the Christians.

For some time he strongly hesitated, considering the difficulty of the circumstances, the intolerable invasion of the barbarians, and his own proper and guileless conduct toward emperors. But when he saw that the enemy was hastening toward the city, he wrote to Patriarch Nicephorus, affirming the correctness of his faith and asking that, with the patriarch’s prayer and assent, he might assume the empire.

He came to the tribunal set up before the city together with the governors and armies, and was shown to be the most legitimate Roman emperor. At midday he entered Constantinople through the Gate of Carsius and reached the imperial palace.

When Michael heard the acclamation, he hurried to the oratory of the Pharos together with Procopia and his children. Having had their hair cut, they put on monastic clothing on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the sixth indiction, on Monday.

**LEO**

[Col. 1143B]

On the following day Leo was crowned by Patriarch Nicephorus on the ambo of the Greater Church. He ordered the city gates to be guarded and, by day and night, personally went around the walls, encouraging everyone and urging them to maintain good confidence and hope, since God would quickly and unexpectedly accomplish what was needed through the intercessions of the undefiled Mother of God and all the saints. He would certainly not permit us to be utterly confounded because of the multitude of our sins.

Meanwhile, the new Sennacherib—namely, Crunnus—left his own brother with his forces to attack Adrianople. Six days after Leo’s accession, he arrived with his forces and horses and surrounded the imperial city beside the walls, from Blachernae to the Golden Gate, displaying his power.

After performing a polluted demonic sacrifice in a meadow beside the sea, he asked the emperor to allow him to plant his spear in the same Golden Gate. When this was not permitted, he returned to his tent.

When he had admired the city walls and the emperor’s well-ordered battle line, and had become discouraged about the siege he had hoped for, he turned to negotiations and, before peace, made exploratory statements.

The emperor took the opportunity and attempted to ambush him, but was prevented from bringing this to completion by the multitude of our sins. Those administering the plan acted with rustic incompetence: they wounded Crunnus but did not inflict a mortal blow.

Furious at this, the wicked man sent a force to Saint Mamas, burned the palace there, and returned with the bronze statue of Leo from the Hippodrome, together with a bear and a little dragon, all placed on a wagon with selected bricks and marble. He then captured Adrianople, which had been under siege.

[Note: [Col. 1143B] Thus far Anastasius the Librarian, from Theophanes. In the Greek exemplar there follows certain material from the chronicle of Leo the Grammarian concerning the later emperors up to Constantine, the son-in-law of Romanus. [Col. 1144B] In Anastasius P. Pith. there follows: “This is the collection of years, as is added below: Adam, year 230,” etc. In the Brissian exemplar there follows Bosina, wife of King Bissinus, and the narrative concerning Theodoricus. Canisius.]

[Col. 1143]

# LANDULPH THE WISE’S ADDITION TO THE MISCELLANEOUS HISTORY

## NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME FROM A MANUSCRIPT OF THE AMBROSIAN LIBRARY

[Col. 1143C]

When, as has been stated above, the Roman Empire had already ceased among the Italians, and very many peoples were rushing against them, it had passed as far as the Pelasgum [uncertain reading]. At this time Justinian Augustus was ruling the Roman Empire by a fortunate destiny. He conducted wars successfully and proved extraordinary in civil affairs.

Through the patrician Belisarius he courageously defeated the Persians; and through that same Belisarius he destroyed the nation of the Vandals, capturing their king Gelimer, and restored all Africa to the Roman Empire after ninety-six years. By the forces of Belisarius alone he also overcame the nation of the Goths in Italy, capturing their king Witigis.

Afterward, through John the former consul, he struck down the Moors who were troubling Africa, together with their king Attila, by remarkable valor. In the same way he subdued other peoples by the right of war. For this reason, on account of all these victories, he earned the right to be called Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, and Africanus.

He also corrected the laws of the Romans, whose length was excessive and whose useless contradictions were many, with marvelous brevity. He gathered all the imperial constitutions, which were contained in many volumes, into twelve books, and ordered that this same work be called the Code of Justinian.

Again, he reduced the laws of the individual magistrates and judges, which had extended to nearly two thousand books, to a total of fifty books, and called this Code the Digest or Pandects.

He also newly composed four books of Institutes, in which the text of all the laws is briefly contained. The new laws that he himself had established he gathered into a single volume and decreed that it be called the Code of Novels.

Within Constantinople the same emperor also built a temple to Christ the Lord, who is the Wisdom of God the Father. In Greek he named it *Hagia Sophia*, that is, “Holy Wisdom.” Its work surpasses all other buildings to such a degree that nothing like it can be found throughout the whole extent of the earth.

The emperor was Catholic in faith, upright in his deeds, and just in his judgments; therefore everything worked together for his good.

In his time Cassiodorus flourished in the city of Rome in both secular and divine learning. Among the many noble works he wrote, he most powerfully unlocked the hidden meanings of the Psalms. He was first consul, then senator, and finally a monk.

At this time [Note: [Col. 1145D] Paul the Deacon reads “Dionysius.”] Dionysius, an abbot established in the city of Rome, composed the paschal computation with admirable skill.

At that time also Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church and a remarkable poet, wrote the Acts of the Apostles in hexameter verse.

In those days blessed Father Benedict also shone forth, first in the place called Subiaco, forty miles from the city of Rome, and afterward in the fortress of Cassinum, called Claris [reading uncertain], both through the merits of his great life and through apostolic virtues.

Since victories of the Lombards were frequently resounding on every side, Narses, the imperial *chartularius*, who was then governing Italy, prepared war against Totila, king of the Goths. Since he had long had the Lombards as allies, he sent envoys to Alboin so that he might provide assistance when Narses went to fight the Goths.

Alboin then sent a chosen force from his people to support the Romans against the Goths. They crossed into Italy through the Gulf of the Adriatic Sea, joined the Romans, and entered battle with the Goths. After the Goths had been destroyed to the last man, the Lombards, honored by Totila their king with many gifts, returned victoriously to their own country. Throughout the period in which the Lombards possessed Pannonia, they were helpers of the Roman state against its enemies.

At this time Narses also waged war against the duke Buccellinus. When King Theudebert of the Franks had entered Italy, he had left Buccellinus there with another duke, Hamingus, to subjugate Italy, while Theudebert returned to Gaul.

At that time also Priscian of Caesarea investigated the profound depths of grammatical art, so to speak, at Constantinople.

When Buccellinus had devastated nearly all Italy through plunder and had presented his king Theudebert with abundant gifts from the spoils of Italy, he decided to winter in Campania. At length, however, he was defeated and killed by Narses in a severe battle at a place called Tannecum.

Hamingus, while attempting to bring assistance to Widin, count of the Goths, who had rebelled against Narses, was defeated together with him by Narses. Widin was captured and sent into exile at Constantinople. Hamingus, who had assisted him, was killed by the sword of Narses.

A third Frankish duke, named Leutharius, Buccellinus’s brother, wished to return to his homeland laden with much booty. Between Verona and Trent, near Lake Benacus, he died a natural death.

Narses also fought against Sindual, king of the Heruli who still remained from that stock. Odoacer alone had brought these men with him into Italy. At first Sindual adhered faithfully to Narses, who bestowed many benefits upon him. But when Sindual finally rebelled arrogantly and desired to reign, Narses defeated and captured him in war and hanged him from a high beam.

At the same time, the patrician Narses, through Dagisteus, a military commander who was warlike and brave, gained control of all the boundaries of Italy.

This Narses had first been a *chartularius*; afterward, because of his valor, he deservedly earned the dignity of the patriciate. He was a most devout man, Catholic in religion, generous toward the poor, and highly devoted to restoring basilicas. He gave himself so fully to vigils and prayers that he obtained victory more through the supplications poured out to God than through weapons of war.

Meanwhile, when the Emperor Justinian departed this life, Justin the Younger assumed the government of the state at Constantinople.

During these times the patrician Narses, whose diligence was watchful in all matters, captured Vitalis, bishop of the city of Altinum, who many years earlier had fled to the king of the Franks—that is, to the Gothic city—and condemned him to exile in Sicily.

After, as has been said, Narses had destroyed or defeated the entire Gothic nation, and had likewise conquered those whom I have mentioned, he acquired much wealth in gold, silver, and other goods. He consequently incurred great hatred from those on whose behalf he had labored so much against their enemies.

They made the following accusation against him before Justin Augustus and his wife Sophia:

“It would have been better for the Romans to serve the Goths rather than the Greeks, where the eunuch Narses rules, oppresses us with servitude, and our most devout prince knows nothing of it. Either free us from his hand, or else we will hand ourselves and the Roman city over to foreign peoples.”

When Narses heard this, he briefly replied: “If I have done evil to the Romans, may I find evil.”

The emperor was so angered against Narses that he immediately sent Longinus, the prefect, to Italy to take Narses’s place.

When Narses learned of this, he was greatly terrified. He was especially frightened by Augusta Sophia, to such a degree that he did not dare return to Constantinople. Among other things, she is said to have sent him this message: since he was a eunuch, he should go and divide spinning tasks with the girls in the women’s quarters.

In response to these words, Narses is said to have replied: “I shall weave for her a web such as she will be unable to put down while she lives.”

Thus driven by hatred and fear, he withdrew to Naples, a city of Campania, and immediately sent envoys to the Lombard people, instructing them to abandon the poor fields of Pannonia and come to possess Italy, which was filled with every kind of wealth.

At the same time he sent many kinds of fruit and other products for which Italy is fertile, so that he might entice their minds to come. The Lombards gladly received the welcome news and what they themselves most desired; finally, they raised their spirits in anticipation of future advantages.

At once terrifying signs appeared by night in Italy: fiery armies were seen in the sky, glittering with the blood that was afterward poured out.

Narses returned from Campania to Rome and, not long afterward, was taken from this life there. His body was placed in a lead coffin and carried to Constantinople together with all his wealth.

During this period, as was stated above, Justin the Younger was reigning at Constantinople. He was devoted to every kind of avarice and despised the poor; he despoiled the senators. His greed was so violent that he ordered iron chests to be made in which to pile up the talents of gold he extorted. He is also said to have fallen into the Pelagian heresy.

When he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, he became deranged by the just judgment of God, having lost his understanding.

He appointed Tiberius Caesar, a just, useful, energetic, wise, charitable man, fair in judgment, distinguished in victories, and—surpassing all these qualities—the truest of Christians, to govern the palace and the individual provinces for him.

When Tiberius distributed to the poor much of the treasure that Justin had amassed, Augusta Sophia frequently rebuked him for reducing the state to poverty, saying: “What I gathered over many years, you are scattering prodigally in a short time.”

He replied: “I trust in the Lord that money will not be lacking in our treasury, provided only that the poor receive alms or captives are redeemed. This is to make a great treasure, as the Lord says: ‘Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth corrupts, and where thieves do not break in or steal.’ Therefore, from what the Lord has given us, let us gather treasures in heaven, and the Lord will deem us worthy to increase us in this age.”

After Justin had reigned for eleven years, he finally ended his life together with the madness he had incurred.

The wars waged by the patrician Narses against the Goths and Franks, which we mentioned above by anticipation, took place during Justin’s reign.

Finally, when Rome in the time of Pope Benedict was suffering from famine because the Lombards were devastating everything around it, Justin relieved it by sending many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt, in a work of mercy.

After Justin’s death, Tiberius Constantine, the fiftieth of the Roman rulers, assumed the empire. While, as we said above, he was administering the palace when Justin was still Caesar and was giving many alms every day, the Lord supplied him with a great abundance of gold. For, as he was walking through the palace, he saw on the pavement of a room a marble slab on which the Lord’s cross had been carved, and he said: “Behold, we trample under our feet the Cross of the Lord, with which we ought to fortify our foreheads and breasts.” He immediately ordered that the same slab be removed from the ground. When it had been lifted and stood upright, they found another beneath it bearing this sign +, and he ordered that it too be removed. When it had been taken away, they found a third; and when, by his order, this too had been removed, they discovered a great treasure, containing more than a thousand hundredweights of gold. After the gold had been removed, he distributed it to the poor even more abundantly than had been his custom.

The patrician Narses, too, who possessed a large house in a certain city within Italy, came to the city mentioned above and there secretly dug a great cistern in his house, in which he deposited many thousands of hundredweights of gold and silver. After killing all who knew of it, he entrusted the secret to only one old man, exacting an oath from him. After Narses had died, the old man came to Caesar Tiberius and said: “If it is of any benefit to me, Caesar, I will tell you something important.” He replied: “Tell me. Whatever you report that may benefit us will benefit you.”

“I have,” said the old man, “a treasure belonging to Narses hidden away, which, now that I am at the end of my life, I cannot conceal.” Caesar Tiberius was delighted and sent his own men to the place. The old man went before them, while they followed attentively. When they reached the cistern, uncovered it, and entered, so much gold and silver was found there that those carrying it away could scarcely remove it in many days. He distributed almost all of it to the needy with his customary extreme generosity.

When he was about to receive the imperial crown, and the people were waiting according to custom for the spectacle in the Circus, Augusta Sophia prepared a plot against him in order to raise Justinian, Justin’s nephew, to imperial dignity. But Tiberius first proceeded through the holy places; then, after summoning the bishop of the city, he entered the palace with the consuls and prefects. Clothed in purple, crowned with the diadem, and seated upon the imperial throne, he was confirmed in the glory of the kingdom amid immense acclamations. When his adversaries heard this and were unable to harm him, since he had placed his hope in the Lord, they were covered with great shame and confusion.

A few days later, Justinian threw himself at the emperor’s feet and, in recognition of the favor he had received, presented him with fifteen hundredweights of gold. Tiberius accepted him according to the measure of his own patience and ordered him to remain at his side in the palace. But Augusta Sophia, forgetting the promise she had once made to Tiberius, attempted to lay snares for him. When he had gone to the estate where, according to imperial custom, he was to enjoy himself for thirty days during the grape harvest, she secretly summoned Justinian and wished to raise him to the throne. When Tiberius learned of this, he hurried back to Constantinople, seized the Augusta, stripped her of all her treasures, and left her only her daily food. He separated her attendants from her and put others of his faithful servants in their place, ordering absolutely that none of the former attendants should have access to her.

As for Justinian, although he was rebuked only in words, Tiberius afterward loved him so greatly that he promised his own daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son. But for some reason unknown to me this matter never came to completion.

An army sent by Tiberius defeated the Persians with great force. Returning victorious, it brought back such a vast quantity of booty, together with twenty elephants, that it seemed sufficient to satisfy human greed.

Thus Tiberius Constantine, after ruling for seven years, sensing that the day of his death was near, chose Mauricius, a Cappadocian by birth and a brave man, to be emperor, with the advice of Augusta Sophia. He adorned his daughter with royal ornaments and handed her over to Mauricius, saying: “If my empire has been granted to you together with this girl, use it happily, always remembering to delight in equity and justice.” After saying this, he departed from this light to his eternal homeland, leaving the people in great mourning at his death. For he was of the greatest goodness, ready in almsgiving, just in judgment, and extremely cautious in judging; he despised no one but embraced everyone with good will, and loved all—while he himself was also loved by everyone.

When he had died, Mauricius, clothed in purple and crowned with the diadem, proceeded to the Circus. After the people had acclaimed him and he had distributed gifts among them, he was the first of Greek origin to be confirmed in the empire.

At this time the emperor Mauricius sent fifty thousand solidi through his envoys to Childepert, king of the Franks, so that he might invade the Lombards with an army and drive them out of Italy. Childepert suddenly entered Italy with an immeasurable multitude of Franks. The Lombards, however, fortifying themselves in the cities, made peace with Childepert through the exchange of envoys and the offering of gifts. When he had returned to Gaul, the emperor Mauricius learned that he had made a treaty with the Lombards, thereby causing him loss at the hands of the Lombards, and he wished to demand it back. But Childepert, relying on the strength of his own forces, did not even wish to give him a reply on the matter.

After these events, King Authari attempted to capture the city of Brexillus, situated on the bank of the Po. The Lombard duke Dotrulf had taken refuge there, having transferred his allegiance to the emperor’s side, and, supported by soldiers, was resisting the Lombard army bravely. He was of the Suavian—that is, Alamannic—people, but had grown up among the Lombards. Because he was handsome and capable, he had earned the honor of the dukedom. But when he found an opportunity to avenge his captivity, he immediately took up arms against the Lombards. The Lombards waged fierce wars against him and finally, overcoming him and the soldiers he supported, forced him to withdraw to Ravenna. Brexillus was captured, and its walls were destroyed down to the ground.

Afterward King Authari made peace for three years with the patrician Smaragdus, who at that time governed Ravenna.

Finally, after Pope Benedict, Pelagius was ordained bishop of the Roman Church without the prince’s authorization, because the Lombards were besieging Rome on every side and no one could leave the city. Pelagius sent a very useful letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. Blessed Gregory, while still a deacon, composed this letter.

Again, the emperor Mauricius sent envoys to Childepert and persuaded him to send an army into Italy against the Lombards. Childepert believed that his sister was still living at Constantinople. Yielding to the envoys of Mauricius so that he might recover his sister, he once more sent a Frankish army against the Lombards in Italy. When the Lombard forces hurried against them, the Franks and Alamanni, being at odds with one another, returned to their homeland without gaining any advantage.

At that time there was a flood in the territories of Venetia and Liguria, as well as in the other regions of Italy, such as is not believed to have occurred since the days of Noah. Lakes were formed over estates and farms, and there was a great destruction of human beings and animals alike. Roads were destroyed and highways broken up. The river Athesis rose so high that, around the basilica of blessed Zeno the martyr, situated outside the walls of Verona, the water reached the upper windows, although, as blessed Gregory later wrote when he was pope, the water did not enter the basilica itself. Some portion of the walls of Verona was also brought down by the same flood. This inundation occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [17 October]. There were also such flashes of lightning and peals of thunder as scarcely occur even in summer.

Two months later the city of Verona was largely consumed by fire.

During this outpouring of the flood, the river Tiber rose so high at Rome that its waters flowed over the city walls and especially occupied its districts. Then, traveling through the bed of that same river together with a great multitude of serpents, a dragon of enormous and wondrous size passed through the city and descended as far as the sea.

Immediately after this inundation there followed an extremely severe pestilence, called the inguinal plague. It devastated the people with such slaughter that, from an immeasurable multitude, scarcely a few remained. It first struck Pope Pelagius, a venerable man, and killed him without delay. Then, after the shepherd had been slain, it spread through the people.

In the midst of this great tribulation, blessed Gregory, who at that time was a deacon, was unanimously elected pope. When he ordered a sevenfold litany to be held, within the space of one hour, while the people were beseeching the Lord, eighty of them suddenly fell to the ground and breathed out their spirits. The litany was called “sevenfold” because blessed Gregory divided the entire population of the city into seven groups to pray to the Lord. In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all the abbots with their monks; in the third, all the abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all the children; in the fifth, all the laypeople; in the sixth, all the widows; and in the seventh, all married women.

We omit saying more about blessed Gregory because, several years earlier, with God’s help, we had already composed his Life. In it we described everything that needed to be said, insofar as our limited abilities allowed.

At this time the same blessed Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with several other God-fearing monks, to Britain, and through their preaching converted the Angles to Christ.

In these days Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, died after having held the priesthood for fifteen years. Severus succeeded him and assumed responsibility for governing the church. When the patrician Smaragdus came from Ravenna to Grado, he himself dragged Severus from the basilica and took him to Ravenna by force, together with three other bishops from Istria—namely John of Parentium, Severus, and Vindemius—and also Antony, now an old man and Defender of the Church. Threatening them with exile and subjecting them to violence, he compelled them to communicate with John, bishop of Ravenna, who condemned the Three Chapters, because during the time of Pope Vigilius or Pelagius he had withdrawn from communion with the Roman Church.

After a year had passed, they returned from Ravenna to Grado. Neither the people wished to communicate with them, nor did the other bishops receive them. The patrician Smaragdus, not unjustly seized by a demon, accepted a Roman successor to the patriciate and returned to Constantinople.

After this, a synod of ten bishops was held at Marano. There they received Severus, patriarch of Aquileia, who offered a written confession of his error because he had communicated at Ravenna with the condemners of the Three Chapters.

The names of the bishops who abstained from this schism are these: Peter of Altinum, the most illustrious; Ingemutius of Sabiona; Angelus of Tridentum; Junior of Verona; Horontius of Vicenza; Rusticus of Treviso; Fonteius of Feltre; Angellus of Altinum; Laurentius of Belluno; Maxentius of Zuglio; and Adrian of Pola.

The following bishops, however, communicated with the patriarch: Severus, Parentinus, John the patrician, Vindemius, and John.

Thus the emperor Mauricius, after ruling the empire for twenty-one years together with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, was killed by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus. He had been useful to the state; for he often fought against its enemies and won victories. The Huns, who are also called Avars, were likewise defeated by his valor.

In these days, after the death of Severus the patriarch, John, an abbot, was ordained patriarch in Old Aquileia in his place, with the consent of the king and Duke Ghisulf. At Grado, Candidianus was ordained bishop by the Romans. Again, in November and December, a comet appeared. After Candidianus died, Epiphanius was ordained patriarch at Grado. He had been chief of the notaries under the bishops who were subject to the Romans. From that time there began to be two patriarchs.

Phocas, therefore, as has been stated, after killing Mauricius and his sons and invading the Roman empire, ruled for eight years. At the request of Pope Boniface, he decreed that the see of the Roman Church should be the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was first among all the churches.

At the request of another Pope Boniface, he also ordered that the old temple called the Pantheon, after its idolatrous filth had been removed, should become a church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of all the holy martyrs. Thus, where once the worship and service of not gods but demons had been carried on, the memory of all the saints would henceforth be celebrated.

During his reign the Prasini and Veneti waged civil war throughout the East and Egypt, slaughtering one another in mutual carnage. The Persians also waged extremely severe wars against the state, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself, destroyed churches, profaned holy things, and carried away, among the ornaments of holy and public places, even the standard of the Lord’s cross.

Against this Phocas, Heraclius, who governed Africa, rebelled. Coming with an army, he deprived him of both life and kingdom. Heraclius, his son, then assumed the administration of the Roman state.

In these days, after the death of the emperor Heraclius at Constantinople, his son Heracleoneus assumed the rights of the kingdom together with his mother Martina and ruled the empire for two years.

When he died, his kinsman Constantine, the son of Heraclius, succeeded him and ruled for six months.

After Constantine too had died, his son Constantine ascended to the dignity of the kingdom and held it for twenty-eight years.

Around this time, the wife of the king of the Persians, named Caesara, left Persia with a few faithful attendants and came to Constantinople in ordinary clothing out of love for the Christian faith. The emperor received her honorably. After several days she received the baptism she desired and was lifted from the sacred font by the Augusta.
