When her husband, the king of the Persians, heard this, he sent envoys to the emperor at Constantinople, asking him to return his wife to him. The envoys came to the emperor and reported the words of the Persian king, who was demanding his queen.

The emperor, hearing this and knowing nothing of the matter, replied: “As for the queen whom you seek, we confess that we know nothing, except that a certain woman came here in ordinary clothing.”

The envoys replied: “If it pleases Your Presence, we should like to see the woman you mention.”

When she came at the emperor’s command, as soon as the envoys saw her, they fell at her feet and respectfully conveyed to her what her husband was demanding. She answered them: “Go and report to your king and lord that, unless he believes in Christ as I have now believed, he will never again be able to have me as his wife.”

Why say more? The envoys returned to their homeland and reported everything they had heard to the king. Without delay, he came peacefully to the emperor at Constantinople with sixty thousand men. The emperor received him gladly and with fitting honor. Believing in Christ the Lord together with all his people, he was washed with them in the water of holy baptism, was lifted from the font by the emperor, and was confirmed in the catholic faith. After being honored by the emperor with many gifts and receiving his wife, he returned joyfully and happily to his homeland.

In these days Constantine, who was also called Constans, wishing to free Italy from the power of the Lombards, departed from Constantinople. Traveling along the coast, he came to Athens; crossing the sea from there, he landed at Tarentum. Before this, however, he visited a certain solitary said to possess the spirit of prophecy and carefully asked him whether he could overcome and subdue the Lombard people living in Italy.

The servant of God asked for the interval of one night so that he might entreat the Lord about this matter. In the morning he replied to the emperor: “The Lombard people cannot now be overcome by anyone, because a certain queen, coming from another province, built a basilica of blessed John the Baptist in Lombard territory, and for this reason blessed John himself intercedes for the Lombard people. A time will come when that sanctuary will be held in contempt, and then that people will perish.”

We have proved that this was indeed fulfilled, because before the destruction of the Lombards we saw that the same basilica of blessed John—which is certainly situated in a place called Modicia—was placed in the charge of worthless persons, so that it was bestowed upon unworthy and adulterous men, not for the merit of their lives but in exchange for payments.

Thus, when, as we have said, the emperor Constans had come to Tarentum, he departed from there, invaded the territory of Benevento, and captured almost all the Lombard cities through which he passed. He also stormed Luceria, a wealthy city of Apulia, attacking it with great force, and destroyed it, leveling it to the ground. He was unable to capture Agerentia, however, because of the exceptionally fortified position of the site.

Then, with his entire army, he surrounded Benevento and began to attack it fiercely. At that time Grimoald’s son, still a young man, held the dukedom there. As soon as he learned of the emperor’s arrival, he sent his tutor, Gesuald by name, across the Po to his father Grimoald, begging him to come as quickly as possible and powerfully aid his son and the Beneventans whom he had raised. When King Grimoald heard this, he immediately began to march toward Benevento with an army to bring aid to his son.

Many Lombards abandoned him on the way because he had stripped the palace and was returning to Benevento with no intention of coming back. He was attacking it fiercely with various engines, while Romoald, on the other side, resisted bravely with the Lombards. Although, because his army was small, he did not dare engage such a great multitude in open combat, he frequently burst into the enemy camp with lightly armed young men and inflicted great losses on them everywhere.

As his father Grimoald was now hastening toward him, he sent the tutor mentioned above to his son to announce his arrival. When the tutor came near Benevento, he was captured by the Greeks and brought before the emperor. The emperor asked him where he had come from. He said that he had come from King Grimoald and announced that the king would arrive very soon.

The emperor was immediately terrified and took counsel with his men about making peace with Romoald so that he could return to Naples. He took Romoald’s sister, whose name was Gisa, as a hostage and made peace with him.

He ordered that Romoald’s tutor Jesuald be led to the walls and threatened him with death if he told Romoald or the citizens anything about Grimoald’s arrival. Instead, he was to insist that Grimoald could not come at all. Jesuald promised that he would do as commanded. But when he came near the walls, he said that he wished to see Romoald.

When Romoald quickly came to him, Jesuald addressed him as follows: “Be steadfast, Lord Romoald, and, placing your trust in God, do not be troubled, because your father will soon be here to bring you aid. Know that he is staying this night near the river Satricus with a strong army. I ask only that you show mercy to my wife and children, because this treacherous people will not allow me to live.”

After he had said this, the emperor ordered that his head be cut off and, with a war engine called a stone-thrower, be hurled into the city. Romoald ordered that the head be brought to him, kissed it in tears, and commanded that it be buried in a worthy place.

Fearing the sudden arrival of King Grimoald, the emperor abandoned the siege of Benevento and departed for Naples. His army, however, was severely defeated by the Capuan count Micola near the waters of the river Calor, at a place called to this day Pugna.

After the emperor reached Naples, one of his leading men, named Saburrus, reportedly asked the emperor for twenty thousand soldiers, promising that he would fight Romoald and emerge victorious. When he had received the army and reached a place called Forinus, where he set up camp, Grimoald, who had already arrived at Benevento, heard this and wished to march against him.

His son Romoald said to him: “There is no need. Give us only a portion of your army. With God’s favor I will fight him, and when I win, the greater glory will certainly be attributed to your power.”

And so, after receiving part of his father’s army, he marched against Saburrus together with his own men. Before engaging him in battle, he ordered trumpets to sound from the four sides. While both lines were fighting with fierce determination, one of the king’s soldiers named Amangus, who customarily carried the royal spear, struck a certain little Greek with that spear using both hands, lifted him from the saddle on which he was riding, and raised him into the air above his head.

When the Greek army saw this, it was struck with immense terror and turned to flight. It was slaughtered in a final disaster, and, by fleeing, escaped death only to grant victory to Romoald and the Lombards. Thus Saburrus, who had promised the emperor that he would win a trophy of victory over the Lombards, returned to him with only a few men and brought back disgrace.

Romoald, having won the victory over his enemies, returned triumphantly to Benevento and brought joy to his father and security to everyone by removing the fear of the enemy.

But the emperor Constans, seeing that the Lombards had done nothing against him, turned all the threats of his savagery against his own people, that is, the Romans. Departing from Naples, he went to Rome. Pope Vitalianus, together with the priests and the Roman people, met him at the sixth milestone from the city.

When the emperor reached the threshold of blessed Peter, he offered there a pallium woven with gold. He remained at Rome for twelve days and removed everything that had formerly been fashioned from bronze as an ornament of the city. He even stripped the basilica of the blessed Mary—once called the Pantheon and built in honor of all the gods, but which by the concession of earlier rulers had already become a place dedicated to all the martyrs—of its bronze roof tiles, carrying them away and sending them to Constantinople together with all the other ornaments.

Then the emperor returned to Naples and traveled by land to the city of Rhegium. Entering Sicily during the seventh indiction, he settled at Syracuse. There he inflicted upon his people—or upon the inhabitants and landowners of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia—such sufferings as had never before been heard of, even separating wives from husbands and children from parents. The peoples of those regions endured many such unheard-of evils, so that no one retained any hope of life. Even the sacred vessels and treasures of the holy churches of God were taken away by imperial command and through the greed of the Greeks.

He remained in Sicily from the seventh through the twelfth indiction. At last, however, he paid the penalty for such great wickedness: while washing in the bath, he was killed by his own men.

After the emperor Constans had been killed at Syracuse, Mezentius seized the kingdom in Sicily, but without the consent of the eastern army. Against him, soldiers from Italy came to Syracuse—some through Istria, some through Campania, and others from Africa and Sardinia—and deprived him of life. Many of his judges were mutilated and brought to Constantinople, and with them the head of the false emperor was also carried away.

Hearing this, the Saracen people, who had already overrun Alexandria and Egypt, suddenly came with many ships and invaded Sicily. They entered Syracuse and inflicted a great slaughter upon the people, with scarcely a few escaping; these fled to strongly fortified camps and the ridges of the mountains. They also carried away immense booty, including all the bronze and other ornaments that the emperor Constans had removed from Rome, and then returned to Alexandria.

The king’s daughter, whom we said had been taken from Benevento as a hostage, came to Sicily and there ended her days.

Thus, after Constans had been killed in Sicily, as we have said, and Mezentius the tyrant who had succeeded him had been punished, Constantine, the son of the emperor Constantius, assumed the government of the Roman empire and ruled the Romans for seventeen years.

During the reign of Constantius, the archbishop Theodore and the abbot Adrian, a most learned man, were sent by Pope Vitalianus to Britain. Through ecclesiastical teaching they made many churches of the Angles fruitful. Archbishop Theodore composed judgments for sinners, specifying, with marvelous and discerning care, how much each person ought to repent for each sin.

While these things were happening, a heresy arose at Constantinople that asserted that there was one will and one operation in our Lord Jesus Christ. This heresy was promoted by George, patriarch of Constantinople, and by Macarius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter.

For this reason the emperor Constantine caused one hundred and fifty bishops to assemble. Among them were envoys of the holy Roman Church, sent by Pope Agatho: John the Deacon and John, bishop of Portus. All of them condemned the same heresy.

At that hour such a quantity of spiders’ webs fell in the midst of the people that everyone marveled. By this it was signified that the filth of heretical depravity had been driven away.

The patriarch George was indeed corrected, but the others, persisting in their defense, were struck by the punishment of anathema. At that time Damian, bishop of the Church of Tieni, composed, under the name of Mansuetus, archbishop of Milan, a very useful letter in defense of the right faith. It made a significant contribution at the aforementioned synod.

The right and true faith is this: just as there are two natures in our Lord Jesus Christ, namely, God and man, so there are also two wills, or operations. Do you wish to hear what belongs to his deity? “I and the Father are one,” he says. Do you wish to hear what belongs to his humanity? “The Father is greater than I.” Observe him sleeping in the boat according to his humanity; observe his divinity, as the evangelist says: “Then he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about.”

This was the sixth universal synod, celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, during the time of Pope Agatho, with the emperor Constantine following and presiding within the enclosure of his palace.

Afterward the emperor Constantine died at Constantinople, and his younger son Justinian assumed the government of the Roman empire, holding its reins for ten years. He took Africa from the Saracens and made peace with them on land and sea.

He ordered Sergius the bishop to be brought to Constantinople by his protospatharius Zacharias because Sergius had refused to favor and subscribe to the error of that synod which he had held at Constantinople. But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions, scorning the wicked command of the rulers, drove the same Zacharias from Rome with insults and abuse.

Against this Justinian, Leo seized the imperial dignity and deprived him of the kingdom. He ruled the Roman empire for three years and kept Justinian, an exile, in Pontus.

Again Tiberius rose up against Leo and invaded his kingdom. He also kept Leo in custody in the same city for the entire period during which he himself reigned.

At this time a synod was held at Aquileia. Because of its knowledge of the faith, it hesitated to accept the fifth universal council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to agree with that council and with the other churches of Christ.

This synod was held at Constantinople during the time of Pope Julius, under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics who asserted that blessed Mary had given birth to a mere human being, not to God and man. At that synod it was established in accordance with catholic doctrine that blessed Mary, ever virgin, should be called Theotokos—“Mother of God”—because, as the catholic faith teaches, she gave birth not merely to a human being but truly to God and man.

At this time in Gaul, within the kingdom of the Franks, Anschis, the son of Arnulf—believed to have been named from Anchises, the Trojan of old—held power under the title of mayor of the palace.

But Justinian, who had been exiled in Pontus after losing the imperial power, recovered the kingdom with the aid of Terebellus, king of the Bulgars, and killed the patricians who had expelled him. He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his place, and ordered them to be slaughtered in the middle of the Circus before the entire people.

He sent the patriarch of Constantinople, Gallicinus, to Rome after having his eyes torn out, and appointed Cyrus, the abbot who had cared for him in his exile in Pontus, bishop in Gallicinus’s place.

He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and sent him back. Prostrating himself on the ground, he asked the pope to intercede for his sins and renewed all the privileges of his Church.

When he sent an army to Pontus to capture Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the same venerable pope strongly urged him not to do so, but was unable to prevent him. The army sent against Philippicus went over to Philippicus’s side and made him emperor.

Philippicus came against Justinian at Constantinople, fought him at the twelfth milestone from the city, defeated and killed him, and acquired his kingdom. Justinian had ruled for six years on this second occasion together with his son Tiberius; Leo had mutilated his nostrils when expelling him. Afterward, when Justinian had once more recovered the empire, whenever he wiped away a discharge of rheum with his hand, he ordered almost as many of those who had opposed him to be slaughtered.

But Philippicus, also called Bardanis, after being confirmed in imperial dignity, expelled Cyrus, whom we mentioned, from the patriarchate and ordered him to return to Pontus to govern his monastery.

Philippicus sent Pope Constantine a letter containing a false doctrine. The pope, with the counsel of the apostolic see, rejected it. For this reason he had paintings made in the portico of Saint Peter depicting the acts of the six holy universal synods. For when such paintings had existed in the royal city, Philippicus had ordered them removed.

The people decreed that no one should accept the name, documents, or image of the heretical emperor on solidi. Consequently, neither was his image brought into the church nor was his name pronounced during the solemn celebration of Mass.

After Philippicus had ruled for one year and six months, Anastasius, also called Artemius, rose up against him, expelled him from the kingdom, and deprived him of his eyes, though he did not kill him.

Anastasius sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, the patrician and exarch of Italy. In them he declared himself a supporter of the catholic faith and a defender of the holy sixth synod, or council.

At this time the emperor Anastasius sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens. His army, turning to another plan, returned from the middle of its journey to Constantinople, sought out Theodosius the Orthodox, elected him emperor, and compelled him to take his seat upon the imperial throne. Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a serious battle near the city of Nicaea. After Anastasius had given him an oath, he made him a cleric and had him ordained priest.

[Col. 1158A] As soon as he had received the kingdom, he restored in the royal city to its former place the venerable image depicting the holy synod, which Philippicus had cast down.

In these days the river Tiber flooded so greatly that, overflowing its channel, it caused much destruction to the Roman city. The water rose to a height of one and a half times the stature of a man, and the waters flowing from the gate of Saint Peter reached as far as the Milvian Bridge. It remained so for seven days, until, after the citizens had held frequent litanies, the waters finally receded on the eighth day.

Meanwhile, after the emperor Theodosius had died—he had ruled the empire for only one year—Leo Augustus was installed in his place. At this time also that same Saracen people, coming with an immense army, surrounded Constantinople [Col. 1158B] and besieged it continuously for three years, until, while the citizens were crying out to God with many acts of justice, very many of the Saracens perished from hunger and cold, war and pestilence, and so, wearied by the siege, withdrew. After leaving there, they attacked in war the Bulgarian people, who live beyond the Danube; defeated by them as well, they fled back to their ships. When they were making for the open sea, a sudden storm arose, and very many of their ships were sunk or shattered, so that they perished. Within Constantinople itself, three hundred thousand died of pestilence.

At that time the emperor Leo burned the images of the saints that had been removed at Constantinople. He also commanded the Roman pontiff to do likewise if he wished to retain the imperial favor. But the pontiff refused to do this. The entire army of Ravenna, and likewise that of Venice, unanimously resisted such orders, and, had the pontiff not prevented them, would have undertaken to set up an emperor over themselves [Note: [Col. 1157D] It should read “they would have undertaken”]. At that time the king of the Lombards, Liutprand, besieged Ravenna, attacked the fleet, and destroyed it [Note: [Col. 1158D] It should read “destroyed”]. Then the patrician Paul sent men outside Ravenna to kill the pontiff. But when the Lombards resisted in defense of the pontiff, the Spoletans came to his assistance, and Lombards from Tuscany and other regions offered resistance; thus the plan of the people of Ravenna was brought to nothing.

Again, when Hildebrand, the king’s nephew, and Peredeo, duke of Vicenza, held Ravenna, a sudden attack was made upon them, and Peredeo fell while fighting bravely. At about the same time Leo Augustus proceeded to worse measures, compelling all who lived in Constantinople, by force as well as by persuasion, to take down wherever they were found the images both of the Savior and of his holy Mother, as well as of all the saints; he then had them burned in the middle of the city. Since many of the people tried to prevent such a crime, some of them were beheaded and others mutilated in parts of their bodies. Germanus the patriarch, refusing to consent to this error, was expelled from his own see, and the presbyter Anastasius was ordained in his place.

# The Second Part of the Complete Works of Paul Winfrid the Deacon—Ascetical Works. Homiliary, That Is, Sermons or Addresses to the People by the Most Distinguished Fathers of the Church, First Collected into One by Paul the Deacon at the Command of Charlemagne

[Note: [Col. 1159] We reprint it according to the Cologne edition of Eucharius Cervicornus, 1539.]

[Col. 1159]

## Charles, Relying on the Help of God, King of the Franks and Lombards and Patrician of the Romans, to the Religious Readers Subject to Our Rule (S)

Although divine mercy always protects us at home and abroad, both in the fortunes of war and in the tranquility of peace, and although human frailty cannot repay any of its benefits—for our God is immeasurable in mercy—he graciously approves the devout intentions of those devoted to his service.

Therefore, because we are concerned that the condition of our churches should always advance toward what is better, we labor with vigilant zeal in the study of letters to restore the workshop of learning, almost obliterated by the negligence of our forebears, and we invite others, as far as we can, to the study of the liberal arts by our own example as well.

Among these works, some time ago, with God assisting us in everything, we carefully corrected all the books of the Old and New Testament, which had been corrupted through the incompetence of scribes. Moreover, stirred by the examples of the venerable memory of our father Pippin, who through his own efforts adorned all the churches of Gaul with the singing of the Roman tradition, we likewise take care, with diligent attention, to distinguish those churches by a notable series of readings.

Finally, when we found that certain readings had been joined to the nocturnal office through the fruitless labor of some men—although undertaken with a proper intention, it was nevertheless inadequate—we discovered that these readings had been set down without the names of their authors and were riddled with countless winding faults. We have therefore not allowed, in our days, incongruous solecisms to resound among the divine readings during the sacred offices. We have turned our attention to reforming the course of those same readings for the better, and we entrusted the work of polishing it to Paul the Deacon, our familiar and devoted servant.

Our instruction was that, carefully reviewing the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, he should select certain flowers from their very broad meadows and arrange whatever was useful into a single garland. Desiring devotedly to obey our highness, he read through the treatises and sermons of various Catholic Fathers, selecting the very best, and presented to us, in two volumes covering the entire cycle of the year, readings appropriately assigned to each feast, arranged distinctly and free from defects.

Having examined the text of all these readings with our own discernment, we confirm these same volumes by our authority and hand them over to your religious care to be read in the churches of Christ.

[Col. 1159]

## Dedication Verses of Paul the Deacon

May you use happily  
The gift of Christ  
For many years,  
And may you be  
The light and glory  
Of your people,  
O Prince Charles,  
And ruler  
Of the Roman world,  
And glory  
Of the Dardanian race.

[Col. 1159]

## Homily XVII: On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

*(From Origen.)*

“At that time, when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit,” etc. (Matthew I).

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph. What necessity was there for Mary to be betrothed to Joseph, unless it was so that this mystery might be concealed from the devil, and that wicked one might find no opportunity at all for devising fraud against the betrothed virgin? [Col. 1163A] Or she had been betrothed to Joseph so that, once the child was born, Joseph might appear to care for the infant or for Mary herself, whether when he went to Egypt or when he returned from there. For this reason she was betrothed to Joseph, although she was not joined to him in desire.

“‘His mother,’ he says. A spotless mother, an incorrupt mother, an untouched mother. ‘His mother’: whose mother? The mother of the only-begotten God, of the Lord and king of all, the fashioner and creator of everything; of him who is without a mother in heaven and without a father on earth; of him who, in heaven according to his divinity, is in the bosom of the Father, and on earth, according to the assumption of a body, is in the bosom of his mother.

“O grace worthy of great wonder! O unspeakable sweetness! O ineffable and great mystery! The very same woman is virgin and mother of the Lord, mother and the one who bore him, his handmaid and his own created work—the very one who gave birth to him. Who has ever heard such things? Who has seen them? Who could have conceived that a mother might be a virgin and give birth untouched, remaining a virgin even as she gave birth?

“For just as once the bush appeared to be burning, yet the fire did not touch it (Exodus III), and just as the three boys were enclosed in the furnace, yet the flames did not harm them and there was not even the smell of smoke upon them; or as happened with Daniel, who, enclosed in the lions’ den with its barriers unopened, received a meal brought to him by Habakkuk (Daniel III, VI, XV), so this holy virgin gave birth to the Lord but remained untouched. She became a mother but did not lose her virginity. She gave birth to an infant and, as has been said, remained a virgin. A virgin, therefore, she gave birth and a virgin she remained. She became the mother of a son and did not lose the seal of chastity.

“Why? Because this was not merely the man who appeared, but the only-begotten God who had come in the flesh. Nor was he suddenly begotten carnally; perfect divinity came in a body. This whole and undivided God therefore came or was born in a human body, and he who was both God and Lord took the form of a servant. For no part of the only-begotten came in a body, nor did he divide himself so that half would be with the Father and half in the Virgin. Rather, he was wholly with the Father and wholly in the Virgin, wholly in the Father’s bosom and wholly in the human body. He did not abandon the things above when he came to seek the things below; preserving what is in heaven, he saved what is on earth. Everywhere omnipotent, undivided and indivisible, here is the holy only-begotten God.

“For if this human and bodily word, when uttered into the ears of many, is not divided among individuals so that part is in one and part in another, but is possessed whole and complete by all, so that it is wholly in each person, how much more is the only-begotten Word of God wholly everywhere—in heaven and on earth, with the Father and in the Virgin? It is not divided, as has been said, nor cut apart, nor made into parts; rather, whole, it holds all, fills all, illumines all, and possesses all.

“Thus this virgin Mary is called the mother of this only-begotten God: worthy of the Worthy, spotless mother of the Holy, one mother of the One, unique mother of the Unique. For no other only-begotten came upon earth, nor did another virgin give birth to the only-begotten.

“In all these things that have been said, his mother Mary is read to have been betrothed. And he says: ‘She was found to be with child.’ To whom was she found, or by whom was she found? First, by the angels who guarded her, protected her, and preserved her, and who guarded her most blessed soul in honor of him who was to be born from her. [Col. 1163B] Next, she was not improperly thought to have been found by the blessed Joseph himself, holy and just, who, with almost marital permission—although he did not touch her—knew everything about his future wife, as she was thought to be.

“‘Joseph her husband,’ he says, ‘being a just man, and unwilling to expose her.’ He calls him ‘husband’ against the perversity of the Jews, so that they would not rage against the virgin. For this reason also she was betrothed to Joseph, as was said above. If she had not been betrothed to Joseph, the unbelieving Jews, hostile to every good thing, would have killed her with stones. Therefore the Evangelist here called him her husband.

“‘Joseph her husband, being a just man.’ Just in word, just in deed, just in the fulfillment of the law, just in the beginning of grace. Thus, since he was just and did not wish to expose her, he wanted to dismiss her secretly. He did not wish to expose her, he did not wish to take her, he did not wish to defame her publicly, but he wished to dismiss her secretly. He wanted to send her away from himself secretly, as a pious, gentle, and merciful man.

“Since Joseph was such a man, he was thinking of dismissing her secretly. ‘While he was considering these things,’ he says. We must now ask what he had considered, so that he wished to dismiss her secretly. He was considering dismissing her. If he suspected something concerning her, how was he just? If, then, he did not suspect her, or did not consider something of that kind, why did he wish to dismiss her? He wished to dismiss her as one who was spotless and holy. Yet this too was unjust. But hear the simple meaning of this expression: Joseph was just, and that Virgin was spotless. He therefore wished to dismiss her because he recognized in her the power of the mystery and a certain magnificent sacrament, and considered himself unworthy to approach it.

“Thus, humbling himself before so great and ineffable a reality, he sought to distance himself, just as the blessed Peter, humbling himself before the Lord, said: ‘Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man’ (Luke V). Or as the centurion, sending word to that same Lord, said: ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, for I did not even consider myself worthy to come to you’ (Matthew VIII). Or as holy Elizabeth said to the blessed Mary herself: ‘And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ (Luke I).

“Thus Joseph too, rightly humbling himself in every way, was wary and afraid to bring upon himself union with such great holiness. For this reason he wished to dismiss her secretly: ‘I will dismiss her,’ he said, ‘and put her far from me, and from my knowledge. For her dignity is greater, her holiness surpasses all, and she is not suited to my unworthiness.’ Therefore he wished to dismiss her secretly.

“‘While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision, saying: Why do you hesitate, Joseph? Why do you think foolishly? Why do you meditate irrationally? It is God who is being born. You are the minister of this birth, not its giver; a servant, not the Lord; a slave, not the fashioner. Therefore minister, serve, guard, care for, and attend both to him who is being born and to her who gives birth.

“‘For although she is called your wife, and although she is said to be betrothed to you, she is nevertheless not your wife, but the chosen mother of the only-begotten God. Therefore, Joseph, son of David, who received these promises, to whom these faithful covenants were given—Joseph, son of David, not only according to the flesh but according to the spirit—Joseph, son of David: if you are a son of David, then rightly you are also his heir, as a son is heir to his father. Therefore receive as an inheritance the things promised to him, the faithful covenants.

“‘Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife. Do not fear, do not tremble, do not be disturbed. Rather, secure and undaunted, receive her according to the command of the law, called your wife but, according to the custom and union of marriage, far removed from it. Receive her, therefore, as a heavenly treasure entrusted to you: as the riches of the Godhead, as perfect holiness, as perfect righteousness; receive her as the dwelling of the Only-Begotten, as an honorable temple, as the house of God, as the special possession of the Creator of all, as the undefiled house of the king, the heavenly bridegroom.

“‘Thus, Joseph, son of David, do not fear to receive her entrusted to you and committed to your religious care. Preserve her, care for her, attend to her: flee from Herod, lead her into Egypt, and, returning again after Herod’s death, bring her into the land of Israel. Do not fear to take Mary your wife.

“When you hear ‘wife,’ do not be terrified or disturbed—not you, nor anyone who follows, until the consummation of the age. I call her wife for this reason: to conceal her virginity from the devil, to exclude and overthrow the perversity of the Jews, and not to destroy the institutions of the law. In what follows I will show that she is not regarded as your wife according to the custom of marriage, nor is the one who is born believed to be your son.

“‘For what will be born from her is from the Holy Spirit,’ because the Holy Spirit is the co-worker in this birth. For the only-begotten Son, who before the ages was ineffably born from the Father alone, now, as the end of the age drew near, came among human beings in a human body by the will of the Father, with the Holy Spirit cooperating.

“This is the one of whom Scripture foretells, saying: ‘A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us’ (Isaiah IX). For the only-begotten Son of the Father was born from the Virgin so that through that Virgin he might renew and raise up the first Eve who had fallen, and so that those who through an evil will had become sons of the devil might through the adoption of grace become sons of God.

“‘She will bear a son,’ he says, ‘and you will call his name Jesus.’ The Virgin gives birth, and you will call the one born Jesus, which is interpreted as ‘Savior.’ For he himself will save his people from their sins. ‘You will call his name,’ he says, by the name that existed before, by which he was named before the ages. You will not impose a name on him, nor establish a designation for him from yourself; rather, name and call him with rejoicing Jesus—that is, Savior.

“Bear witness that he is the Savior, and that he did not begin to save in time, but is also the most ancient Savior. ‘For he himself will save his people from their sins.’ Two distinguished things are signified by this statement: both that Christ was God and Lord before the incarnation, and that his people, to be saved by him, were already then announced.

“And therefore it was said: ‘For he himself will save his people from their sins,’ so that he might truly be God. For it belongs to the power of God to save from sins or to forgive sins. This Son of God, therefore, having his own people, came—as has been said—to free and save them from sins, whether from the Jews or from the nations. Concerning him he had already spoken through the prophet, saying: ‘The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession’ (Psalm II).

“He will save his people from their sins, redeeming all by his blood, and freeing them from the power of death by his death. ‘He will save’: that is, he is the Savior of all faithful and believing human beings.

“Now all this was done. What does ‘all’ mean? This concerning the descent of the Only-Begotten; this concerning that incarnation of the Lord; this concerning the sending of the angel to the Virgin; this concerning the betrothal and chastity of that Virgin. All this was done for the salvation of the whole world. All this was done so that one thing might be fulfilled, so that one thing might be completed. What is that? That a virgin gave birth, that a virgin remained, that she was a mother and remained an untouched virgin.

“‘Behold, a virgin will receive in the womb.’ Hear what he says, all daughters of Eve! Hear, all you who took up an inheritance of pain and sorrow after her and from her condemnation; you who bear children in sorrow—or rather, you who did not fear corruptible desire. Hear and rejoice; hear and be comforted; hear that a virgin will receive in the womb, conceiving a child not from desire.

“She was neither deceived by the serpent’s persuasion nor infected by its poisonous breath. Rather, a virgin will receive in the womb, accepting the angel’s proclamation and taking up the testimony of the prophets. A virgin will receive in the womb so that she may give birth to God, graciously made flesh, for the salvation of the world.

“‘Behold,’ he says. This very word ‘behold’ expresses wonder at the greatness of so great a mystery, so that, awakening everyone as though from sleep, he may call them to wakefulness by this saying. ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘a virgin will receive in the womb and will bear a Son.’

“She will bear a son in order to bind that armed strong one, to trample the head of the wicked serpent, to crush his powers, to seize his spoil, and to turn away the captivity of his people; to restore Adam anew; to exclude the disobedience of Eve through Mary’s obedience; to raise up the fallen race, which had been cast down through the woman’s rash credulity.

“‘And they will call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’ The angels first call his name, singing at his birth of him who comes to human beings as God of all and king of peace. Then the apostles, proclaiming the dominion and power of the only-begotten God to all nations. Then also the holy martyrs, resisting fire and sword unto death. Finally, all believers, remembering and praising this same name until the consummation of the age.

“‘And they will call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’ Who will call him thus, if not the righteous, whose name will be called new on earth—not as before in figures and images, but appearing face to face?”

“God with us. He appeared to Abraham, the father of believers, for three hours of the day, though not through the ineffable substance of the Godhead itself but rather in angelic form, from midday (Genesis XVIII). To us he appeared on earth for thirty-three years and deigned to live among human beings.

“He likewise appeared to Jacob through an angel, wrestling with him (Genesis XXXII); he allowed himself to be overcome by him so that he might rightly bless this pure-hearted man and call him Israel.

“God with us, fulfilling an even greater and more magnificent struggle on our behalf, and approaching death so that by his death he might kill death and grant blessing and immortality to the pure-hearted people who confidently say, ‘God with us’: through the preaching of the evangelists and apostles, through the sacrament of his holy body and blood, through the sign of the glorious cross.

“Through all these things, therefore, God is with us, and toward us and in us, as he himself says: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.’ He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

## Homily XXII: On the Same Feast

*(From Saint Isidore.)*

The day of the Lord’s Nativity was instituted by the Fathers as a festival solemnity to be observed for this reason: on it Christ willed to be born bodily for the redemption of the world, coming forth from the Virgin’s womb, although he was in the Father’s dominion.

The reason for his assumption of flesh is this. After that first parent, deceived through the devil’s envy, fell foolishly, he immediately, exiled and ruined, transmitted the root of wickedness and sin throughout his whole race. The whole human race grew ever more violently toward evil, with crimes spread everywhere, and, what is worse, with the worship of every kind of idol.

Therefore, wishing to put an end to sin, God counseled the world through the Word, the law, the prophets, signs, scourges, and wonders. But when the world, even after such admonition, still did not recognize its errors, God sent his only-begotten Son so that he might put on flesh, appear to human beings, and heal sinners.

He came in human form for this reason: human beings could not know him through himself alone. But in order to be seen, “the Word became flesh,” by assuming flesh, not by being changed into flesh. He assumed humanity; he did not lose divinity.

Thus the same one is both God and man: in the nature of God, equal to the Father; in the nature of man, made mortal among us. For on our behalf he remained what he was, while from us he assumed what he was not, so that he might free what he had made.

This, then, is the great solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity; this is the new and glorious festival of this day: the coming of God to human beings. Accordingly, this day is called the Nativity because Christ was born on it. We ought to observe it with festive solemnity through the recurring cycle of the year, so that the birth of Christ may be recalled to memory—Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## Homily XXX: On the Same Feast

*(From Hericus.)*

“At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: ‘Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men,’” etc. (Matthew XXIII).

The meaning of this Gospel reading appears to adhere to the preceding account. For above, our Redeemer is reported to have rebuked the scribes and Pharisees with many reproaches and, among other things, to have said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who build the monuments of the prophets and say: ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets.’” And shortly afterward: “And you,” he says, “fill up the measure of your fathers.” That is to say: “Make up what they left undone. They killed servants; you will crucify the Lord. They killed human beings; you will kill God.” And as though they might object: “We have no prophets now whom we can kill,” he adds: “Therefore, behold, I am sending you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and you will persecute them from city to city.”

Here the apostles are called prophets because, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, they possessed knowledge of future things. They are the wise in heart, because they knew how to utter speech at the appropriate time. They are the scribes, because through the Holy Spirit they have God’s law written in their hearts. Of them, then, they killed James, the brother of John, and John himself the Baptist; they stoned Stephen; they crucified Peter; they scourged the twelve apostles when they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer these things for the name of the Lord; and they persecuted them from city to city, so that, since they were not received by them, they might justly migrate to the Gentiles.

“Upon you will come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” It must be asked why the blood of all the righteous, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, is proclaimed as being required from one generation of the Jews, when it is clear that neither of these two was killed by them. Indeed, we read that innumerable martyrs existed both in the Old and in the New Testament whom they did not kill.

But it is the custom of Scripture to set forth only two generations, namely, that of the good and that of the wicked. For concerning the generation of the good it is said: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111). And: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. 23). Conversely, concerning the reprobate it is said: “Brood of vipers,” and: “A crooked and perverse generation” (Matt. 23). Thus all the reprobate who are alike in wickedness are counted as one generation; and, on the other hand, all the saints who imitate one another in virtues are said to be one generation.

Again, it must be asked who this Zechariah is who is remembered as having been killed between the temple and the altar. Some indeed think that he is the righteous Zechariah who is placed eleventh in the order of the prophets. Although his father’s name agrees with this identification—for he is called the son of Barachiah—it is nevertheless not apparent how he was killed between the temple and the altar, especially since in his time scarcely even the ruins of the temple remained.

Others understood this Zechariah to be the father of John, asserting that he was killed by the Jews because he foretold the coming of the Savior. But we understand this Zechariah, without doubt, to be the one whom Joash, king of Judah, killed between the temple and the altar, as is written in the history of Kings: “And Joash,” it says, “did not remember Jehoiada his father, but killed his son, who had rescued him from death and had secretly nourished him for seven years in the temple” (II Chron. 34).

But it is asked why he is called the son of Barachiah, when in the aforementioned history he is identified as the son of Jehoiada. The matter is resolved in this way: Barachiah means “blessed of the Lord”; Jehoiada is interpreted as “righteousness.” Therefore, one who is full of righteousness can rightly be called blessed of the Lord. Thus, according to the interpretation of the names, one and the same man may equally be understood as both Jehoiada and Barachiah. It may also have happened that Barachiah had two names and was called Jehoiada by one of them, just as the evangelist Matthew was also called Levi.

Again, it must be asked why he said that the blood of the prophets, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, was to be required from the Jews. Why he said “from the blood of Abel” is not surprising; but why “up to the blood of Zechariah” requires explanation, since many martyrs existed after him.

The answer is that through these two men—one of whom was killed in the field and the other in the temple—two orders of martyrs are designated. Through Abel, who was killed in the field, the laity are represented; through Zechariah, who was killed in the temple, those who, advancing from priestly dignity, were raised to the palm of martyrdom are represented.

He named only these two explicitly because both were innocent and were killed without any just cause; both were priests, both shepherds—one of sheep, the other of souls. And just as Abel was killed by his brother in the field, so this man was killed by his cousin and close kinsman in the temple.

“Whom you killed,” he says, “between the temple and the altar.” There were two altars in the temple: one, the altar of incense, within; the other, the altar of burnt offerings, outside. It was between the latter and the temple that Zechariah was killed. Or “between the temple and the altar,” that is, between the consent of the people and that of the priests, some of whom are signified by the temple and others by the altar.

Finally, why is Abel honored in the Gospel or the Epistles with a special testimony to his righteousness? Clearly, because it was fitting that he should be adorned with so distinguished a title by a certain privilege, since in himself he most excellently bore the figure of Christ through three eminent virtues. For he was a virgin, a priest, and a martyr.

Among so many and such varied opinions about who Zechariah was, since the historical truth cannot be investigated with certainty, we must have recourse to allegory. This is the sole resolution of those matters which are mentioned in the holy Gospel as having been said but not done.

By Abel are designated all the saints who existed from the beginning of the world until Christ’s Passion and the redemption of the human race, as the interpretation of his name itself demonstrates. For it is interpreted as “mourning,” “vapor,” “cord,” or “binding,” signifying the saints who preceded the Lord’s Passion. Considering themselves exiles and cast out from the blessedness of paradise, they were in mourning and sorrow; and, despising the present life as smoky and transitory, they hastened as quickly as possible toward the lot and cord of the heavenly inheritance.

Zechariah, however, signifies the saints from the Lord’s Passion to the end of the age. For Zechariah is interpreted as “the memory of the Lord,” or “remembering” or “recalling the Lord.” He signifies those same saints who, considering themselves redeemed by the Passion of their Lord, strive always to keep him in memory and to offer him worthy thanks.

This Zechariah was killed between the temple and the altar. The altar signifies the altar of the Lord’s cross, on which that unique Lamb was offered to God the Father for the salvation of the human race. The temple, however, expresses the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, into which all the saints will enter after judgment has been completed. Therefore, he is said to have suffered between the temple and the altar who, as has been said, signifies those who, from the time of the Lord’s Passion until entry into the heavenly kingdom, either have suffered or will suffer.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you.” By repeating the name of the city Jerusalem in addressing it—that is, by saying it again—he laments not the collapse of stones but the destruction of the people.

“You who kill,” he says, “the prophets,” such as Isaiah, whom they cut in two alive with a wooden saw, and Amos, whom they most wickedly killed in a similar manner by driving a bar through his temples; and the others whom they are reported to have afflicted with various and almost innumerable punishments.

“And you stone those who are sent to you,” such as Naboth, a righteous man, and the prophet Jeremiah in Egypt, as Epiphanius of Cyprus testifies.

“How often I wanted to gather your children”—that is, I often wanted to—“just as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.” He uses the likeness of a hen, which is moved by such great affection for her chicks that she herself also becomes weak on their behalf, her very hoarseness of voice expressing the feeling of deep compassion.

Therefore, he who elsewhere calls Herod a fox (Luke 13) rightly compares himself here to a hen. For just as a fox continually lays ambushes in order to devour hens, so Herod, thirsting for the death of our Redeemer, harassed him by pursuing him with perpetual hatred. His savagery is especially evident from the fact that when Pilate sent the Lord Christ to him for judgment (Luke 23), he and his army despised and mocked him.

This species of creature also, to which the Redeemer compares himself, has a quality harder to find in other creatures: it protects its chicks with its wings and rises against the kite. So also our mother—that is, the Wisdom of God, who is Christ—having been weakened in a certain way for us through the assumption of flesh, as the Apostle says, “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. 1), protects our weakness and resists the devil, lest he carry us away to destruction.

Yet in this defense, what the hen attempts through affection against the kite, he accomplishes against the devil through power. If, however, God is understood symbolically by the hen, her two wings are Moses and Aaron, who led the people out of Egypt; or Zerubbabel and Ezra, and Nehemiah, together with Jeshua son of Jozadak, the leaders who led them out of Babylon, under whom the same Israelite people were freed or gathered from their various captivities.

But what does he mean when he says: “How often I wanted to, and you were unwilling”? Does human will prevail over the will of God, when it is written: “Everything that he willed, he has done” (Ps. 113)?

The answer is that God bestowed free will upon human beings, and for this reason he says, “You were unwilling.” It is as though he said: “For my part I wanted to, but for your part you were unwilling.”

Alternatively: “I did indeed want to, and what I wanted I also accomplished, even though you were unwilling.” Thus she did not want her children to be gathered by him, but despite her unwillingness he himself gathered those of her children whom he wished.

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” He signifies the house of the Jews, or the city of Jerusalem, which according to the evangelist he had called a nest, or the narrow temple within it. At first, on account of their unbelief, it was deservedly abandoned by God, while the angelic powers cried: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” Then, in vengeance for the Lord’s cross, when the Romans laid it waste and plundered it like an empty nest, it was deprived of all its possessions.

“But I say to you, you will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” This was said concerning the future time approaching the judgment, when the Jews, converted to faith through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, will proclaim Christ the Lord as blessed, not merely with their voice but also by their deeds.

For after the Lord said this, we do not read that the Jews made such a confession in his praise. He said it afterward, when he entered the temple amid the praises of the crowds, while they sang this very verse in praise of Christ, as has been related above.

The Jews therefore have been granted a time for repentance, so that, if they wish to confess Christ as the blessed Son of God the Father in the name of the Lord, they may deserve to behold his face—that is, to perceive the power of his divinity with intellectual eyes and believe him equal to the Father.

They will then proclaim him blessed in the name of the Father when, having received his faith through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, as has been said, they accept it and proclaim his glory, when the Apostle’s prophecy has been fulfilled: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11).

Having set forth these things from the Gospel reading as far as we have been able, let us understand that we owe to the festival of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, which we celebrate, not only veneration but also imitation. For after his Passion the Lord Jesus chose him as the first to suffer for him, and established his unconquered love even toward his enemies as an example for all of us to imitate.

But why do we call him the first martyr, when we know that thousands of infants suffered for the Redeemer before him? He is rightly called the first martyr in the New Testament because, first of all, after the Lord’s preaching, Passion, and resurrection, he deserved to obtain the palm of heavenly recompense through the shedding of his blood and to reach the crown dedicated to his name and labor—by the favor of that same Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.
