## HOMILY XXXVIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

*(From Saint Severian.)*

The savagery of Herod has today revealed where zeal tends, where envy leaps forth, and where jealousy is carried. While it strives against the constraints of a temporal kingdom, it attempts to extinguish the birth of the eternal King.

“Then Herod,” he says, “seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, sent to Bethlehem and killed all the boys who were in it and in all its districts.” “Seeing that he had been mocked”: impiety grieves at having been mocked, cruelty expands and rages. Deceitfulness roars because it has been deceived, and fraud, turned back upon itself, is shattered.

Herod hisses as he himself falls into the snare he set; from this point he unsheathes the wickedness he contemplates. He takes up the weapons of faithless treachery; in earthly fury he seeks the one born from heaven, whom he does not believe to have been born.

He compels soldiers to encamp among the bosoms of mothers; between breasts he assaults the fortress of piety. He hardens iron against tender breasts; milk is poured out before blood. He makes them experience death before life; he casts darkness upon those entering the light. Thus acts the teacher of evil, the servant of deceit, the craftsman of wrath, the inventor of crime, the author of impiety, the plunderer of piety, the enemy of innocence, the foe of nature—worse than his own subjects, worst of all to himself—from whom Christ fled, not so that he might escape, but so that he might not be seen.

Reaching upward, he falls from on high. Striking at heaven, he enters the depths; and when he proceeds against God, he proceeds against himself. He kills himself who attempts to kill life, because salvation cannot be seized by destruction, life by killing, or eternity by an end.

O ambition, ever so blind! O presumption, so utterly wicked! O how he destroys what has been granted, who grasps at what has not been granted!

Herod, besieging an earthly kingdom, attacks the heavenly one. Yearning for earthly things, he rushes against divine things and persecutes piety itself. He had heard that a king had been born. Destined for wickedness, ready for sacrilege, prepared for crime, he does not seek the reasons for innocence; he denies justice and confounds right and wrong.

For one whose companion is wickedness, whose enemy is equity, iniquity is always a friend; one who lives by massacres, fortifies himself with blood, rages through cruelties, and whose whole existence rests upon fear, while nothing is founded upon love.

Then blind Herod seeks Christ with swords, investigates him through blood, and searches him out by cruelty. Fearing a successor, he attacks the author himself. He oppresses the innocent, wishing innocence to perish; he makes the cause of the innocent a crime against the guilty. He turns the gift of the newborn into a punishment for those born. He commands the rising of the Author to be the setting of those who are rising. He commands the saving work of the Savior to be the peril of those to be saved.

Their tongues were silent, their eyes saw nothing, their ears heard nothing, their hands did nothing—and since they had performed no action, from where did they incur death as punishment? How did those who did not yet know how to live deserve to die? Their only crime before Herod was that they had been born.

But Christ, foreknowing the future, conscious of secrets, judge of thoughts, and searcher of minds—why did he abandon those whom he knew would be sought because of him and whom he knew would be killed because of him? Born King, and heavenly King, why did he neglect the soldiers of his innocence? Why did he disregard an army of his own age? Why did he leave so abandoned the watch assigned to his own cradles, so that the enemy, seeking only the king, might run rampant against the entire army?

Brothers, Christ did not despise his soldiers but advanced them. He gave them triumph before life; he caused them to seize victory without struggle; he granted them crowns before limbs; he willed them to pass beyond vices through virtues and to possess heaven before earth.

Christ therefore sent his soldiers ahead; he did not lose them. He received his ranks; he did not abandon them.

Blessed are those whom we see born for martyrdom, not for the world. Blessed are those who exchanged labors for rest, pains for refreshment, and sorrows for joy. They live—yes, they truly live—who deserve to be killed for Christ.

Blessed are the wombs that carried such children. Blessed are the breasts that poured themselves out for such children. Blessed are the tears that were shed for such children, tears that conferred the grace of baptism.

For in different ways, but through one gift, the martyrs are baptized in their blood and the mothers suffer in the martyrdom of their children. For the sword passing through the limbs of the children reached the hearts of the mothers; and therefore those who shared the Passion must necessarily share the reward.

The little child smiled at his killer; the infant was summoned by the sword. The nursing child, in the place of a nurse, looked upon the horror of the executioner. An age ignorant of death rejoiced as it was about to die. The infant son looked upon every person not as an enemy but as a parent.

The mothers bore all that there was of anguish and pain, and therefore they will not be deprived of the joy of the martyrs, since they shed the tears of martyrdom.

Here let the hearer pay attention—let him pay attention so that he may understand that martyrdom does not rest upon merit but comes through grace. In the infants, what will was there, what free choice, when nature itself was held captive? Therefore, let us attribute everything in martyrdom to God and nothing to ourselves.

To conquer the devil, to hand over the body, to despise vices, to endure tortures, to wear out the torturer, to gain glory from insults and life from death—this is not a work of human virtue but a divine gift.

## HOMILY XXXIX. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE INNOCENTS

*(From blessed Chrysostom.)* [Col. 1176A]

A new discourse is dedicated by infants to the holy praises of Christ. The innocents open their first voice in the glory of the Lord. Those who were unskilled in speech become eloquent in praise. They offer the firstfruits of their tongue to the Lord; they sacrifice new fruits of the mouth; they taste the beginnings of words.

Infancy, which because of its age could not speak, resounded with the praises of God in joy. Those who did not know how to speak knew how to praise Christ. Those who had been unskilled in speech became skilled in praise. They display Christ through their praises; they proclaim Christ through their testimony.

Meanwhile the boys become eloquent without a teacher, instructed without an instructor, skilled without an educator. They recognize Christ and proclaim the Lord—not one whom human persuasion had taught them, but one whom Divinity inspired in the innocent.

For human things cease when divine things are being handled, because human things themselves cannot be of benefit unless they are raised up by the support of divine things. Earthly things must yield when heavenly things are proclaimed; natural powers must fall silent when virtues speak.

Thus the age of the infants is raised up in praise, an age that knew nothing of the crime of sins. One who is worthy is praised by those who are worthy, and the innocent is proclaimed through the testimony of the innocent.

For they receive from Christ and give back; they obtain and return. At one and the same time, the one who had given receives, and the one who had received gives back. I say, at one and the same time, what belongs to Christ is returned to him when his praises are offered to him by infants.

We have spoken of the praise of infants; what shall we say about the praises of nursing children? We cannot find their praise unless we know those very ones who praised. Who are they? Where are they? What praise did they offer? I ask about those who did not know how to speak.

For that age could not do what nature had not given it, nor could what instruction denied be celebrated by such people. Yet the nursing children slaughtered by Herod speak praises to the Lord; they speak in blood what they cannot speak with the tongue. Through their Passion they sing what they do not know in speech; by being killed they proclaim what, while alive, they could not proclaim.

Nor is it something new that innocent blood should either offer praises to God or reveal its own sufferings, since the blood of Abel cries out to heaven, and the souls of the slain cry out to God from the altar.

Martyrdom bestowed praise upon those to whom nature had denied speech. Those who could not narrate with their voice were permitted to cry out in blood; those who could not speak with their tongue were permitted to speak in blood. They converse with the Lord, though human words have been denied them.

But when these innocents had been killed, the words of the prophecy were fulfilled: “A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be consoled because they are not” (Matt. 2; Jer. 31).

No one denies that Rachel first represents the Church; no one who wishes to defend anything else against the truth. But I perceive two different things in her: weeping and refusal of consolation. If she wept, why did she refuse to be consoled? Or if she refused to be consoled, why did she weep? Or how is it consistent that she did not wish to be consoled, when it is consistent that she wept? Why should she not have wept, who refused to be consoled? Or why should she have been consoled, who could not weep, when it is evident that weeping is wiped away by consolation? Or, at least, why did she need to weep, when she did not need the word of consolation?

But Scripture says, “She did not wish to be consoled because they are not”—that is, she did not wish to be consoled because they are present. If she did not wish to be consoled because they are present, how did she wish to weep as though they were absent?

To give the reason for these differences briefly: the mother mourns their condition, but in the hope of glory she rejects human consolation. Affection is revealed in tears, but the glory of the slain declares a rejection of consolation. Affection and faith struggle within the mother; humanity contends with devotion. Affection laments, but faith rejoices; humanity mourns, but devotion consoles.

The mother was permitted to weep in a human manner, but was not permitted to need consolation in a human manner. For this reason the Lord Christ also wept over Lazarus, yet he himself did not need anyone’s consolation, because what wept was human, while it is clearly God who raised Lazarus.

But O blessed glory of the nursing children, to whom it was granted to dedicate martyrdoms for Christ! In one moment they complete birth and death, entrance and departure, beginning and setting, so that in that one moment, as I have said, it might be granted them both to enter the world by being born and to dedicate heaven through martyrdom.

Christ proves a new army; he appoints inexperienced soldiers; he crowns nursing legions after victory has been achieved. They become victors for Christ who were his equals in age. I say, infants become strong without struggle and victorious without battle. They know how to conquer, though they did not know how to fight.

They become possessors of victory who had been powerless because of their age. They purchase martyrdom through punishment; they acquire glory through blood; they exchange temporal death for eternal life.

That age neither feared death nor shuddered at it. For it could not fear what it did not know how to fear.

The infant Christ sends infants to heaven; he offers new gifts to the Father; he presents the firstfruits of the harvest to the Begetter. He displays the future most abundant harvest by exhibiting such fertility in the seed.

The enemy’s savagery mocked itself; it mocked itself when it thought it could disturb the plan of God, the glory of Christ, and the salvation necessary for the world. Yet it bestowed martyrdom upon many infants while seeking to kill the infant Christ.

The enemy renders service while doing harm; by killing, it grants a benefit. For it would have envied their glory if it had loved them.

But earthly battles are one thing, heavenly victories another. In Christ’s battle, one lives by dying; one rises by falling; victory is acquired through destruction.

## HOMILY XL. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

*(From the works of Saint Augustine.)*

“Today, dearest brothers,” etc. For the remainder, see in Saint Augustine, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIX, col. 2152.

## HOMILY XLI. A SERMON ON SILENCE

*(It is presented as anonymous in the Homiliary.)*

“When all things held the middle silence” (Wis. 18).

There are three silences. The first silence is ignorance of sickness; the second silence is despair of healing; the third silence is the attainment of health.

The first silence existed before the law, the second between the law and grace, and the third will exist after this life.

The first silence, then, occurred when the human being did not recognize his illness and therefore was silent and did not seek a remedy. But after the law entered and showed the sick their wounds, the silence was immediately broken, and the sick at once began to seek salvation.

But because they wanted to be saved through the works of the law, where salvation was not found, they could not find what they sought. At last, therefore, when the human being realized through the law that no one could be justified, as though exhausted by prolonged cries and now despairing, he again ceased to speak, and the second silence followed.

Then the almighty Word of God the Father, coming in the flesh, broke the silence, spoke peace, gave grace, set mercy before us, and promised forgiveness. The sick began to run to the physician and, as though with great cries, to demand a remedy through pure faith of heart and true confession of mouth.

This, then, is what is now taking place in the present life: that the human being may receive health through the grace of God. But when he has received complete health and has been brought to that blessedness of immortality, there will be nothing more for him to ask. Then that third blessed silence will follow, which will never end.

Between the first and the middle silence, many words sounded; but between the middle and final silence, one Word sounds. There were many words—the manifold commands of the law that was given through Moses. One Word is the grace of God that came through Jesus Christ—or rather, Jesus Christ himself.

Moses, the servant of God, uttered many words and many discourses; God the Father sent one Word, one discourse. But the discourses of Moses were not almighty, because they could not accomplish what they said. Therefore, when at last they fell silent, failing in the promise, then the almighty Word came—the speech of God, which not only spoke but did whatever it willed.

This speech, this Word, still speaks as long as it works its promises in the faithful. And when it has fulfilled its promises, it will, as it were, cease to speak. When the promises have been fulfilled, because there will be nothing more to ask, there will be blessed silence forever.

“While all things held the middle silence”—rightly “all things,” that is, not only those who had despaired in their petition, but also those who had failed in the promise—and the night was halfway through its course.

For in holy Scripture “night” is sometimes understood as the devil, sometimes as his members—that is, sinners and wicked people—sometimes as sin itself, and sometimes as the present life.

Therefore, by night in this passage the flow of this mortal life is signified, just as elsewhere the brightness of everlasting life is signified by day. The present life is therefore night, while the future life is day. This night has an evening; that day has a dawn.

The evening of this present night was the decline of this age; the dawn of that day is the decline of the present world. The evening of this night also began when Adam sinned, until, after receiving the sentence of death and being expelled from paradise, he went out into the darkness of this world.

The dawn of the following day is from Christ’s resurrection until the end of the age. Therefore this life is night.

But what is the course of this life? Let us see where it runs. Through mortality it runs toward death; through death it runs toward condemnation. Mortal life therefore runs downward, just as immortal life runs upward.

The upward road is in the heavens; the downward road is in the underworld. The middle stretch is the present life, which we enter by being born, traverse while living, and leave by dying.

When, then, did night have its course halfway completed, except when death dragged with it to the underworld all those whom it found on the course of the present life, and no mortal had yet been able to ascend to the life of immortals?

Or we may understand “night” as sin—that is, the night which began with original sin and runs on through actual sins. When, after the original transgression, first the transgression of the natural law and then the transgression of the written law followed, and sin had reached its greatest increase, night, as it were, had completed the middle of its course.

But when the true light appeared, this night immediately began to decline. Now, as though through a kind of alternating change, it gradually diminishes and recedes until, as the light increases, it reaches full day.

See, therefore, the plan of the most splendid divine dispensation. When every hope of recovering salvation had perished, when death was dragging everything downward with it, and sin had reached its height, then the almighty Word was sent to set free those who were to be liberated, so that the gift of divine grace might be commended all the more.

“He came,” he says. Who? From where? To where? The Word of the Most High, the Word of God, the only Son of the Father, the King, the Son of the King.

From the Father’s agreement, to endure Passion. From equality of majesty, to the gallows of the cross. From the royal throne, to the workshop of sin. From the light of heaven, to the darkness of the underworld.

But did he therefore lose his kingdom? No. By liberating those who were servants of sin, he raised them up to reign together with him.

And perhaps for this reason he came from royal seats: because in the house of his Father there are many dwelling places (John 14), and they will reign with him forever when they receive the kingdom prepared from the beginning of the age.

For he was the only son of the king; he alone possessed the kingdom. But because he came to adopt brothers who would reign together with him, he should now come not from a royal seat but from royal seats, because the kingdom to which God’s elect are called was prepared from the beginning of the age.

## HOMILY XLII. ON THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF CHRIST’S BIRTHDAY

*(From Origen.)*

“At that time Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were marveling at the things that were said about him,” etc. (Luke 11).

Let us gather together what was said and written about Jesus at his birth, and then we shall be able to know that each detail is worthy of a miracle. Therefore the father also marveled—for Joseph was so called because he had been his foster-father—and the mother likewise marveled at everything that was said about him. What, then, were the reports that had spread abroad concerning the child Jesus?

Shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and observing the watches of the night over their flock. At the very hour of Jesus’ birth an angel came and said to them: “I announce to you great joy. Go, and you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger” (Luke 2). The angel had not yet finished speaking when, behold, a multitude of the heavenly host began to praise and bless the Lord. When the shepherds had observed this in fear and the angel had departed from them, they said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this thing that the Lord has shown us” (ibid.). They came and found the child. Both they and his parents marveled at what had happened. Simeon too, as is written, increased the report and wonder, or played a major part in it. For he took the child in his arms and said:

“Now, Lord, you release your servant in peace, according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation.”

The speech of Simeon was the climax—and, so to speak, the summit—of the things that were being proclaimed about Jesus, at which his father and mother marveled. For Simeon was not content merely to hold the child and proclaim what had been written about himself; he also blessed his father and mother. He prophesied about the child himself as well, saying:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed. And a sword will also pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

What does this mean: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel”? I find something similar written in the Gospel according to John:

“For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

How, then, did he come for judgment, so that those who did not see from the nations might see, while those who previously saw from Israel might become blind? In this way he came for the fall and resurrection of many. For at the coming of the Lord and Savior, those who had previously stood fell, and those who had fallen rose.

This is one interpretation of what was said: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.” But a deeper meaning must also be understood, especially against those who bark against the Creator and, gathering here and there testimonies from the Old Testament that they do not understand, deceive the hearts of the simple. They say: “Behold the God of the Law and the Prophets; see what he is like:

‘I kill and make alive; I strike, and I heal, and there is none who can rescue from my hands’” (Deut. 32).

They hear “I kill” but do not hear “I make alive”; they hear “I strike” but refuse to hear “and I heal.” By such pretexts they slander the Creator.

Therefore, before interpreting what “I will kill and make alive; I will strike and heal” means, I shall set against them the testimony of the Gospel and speak against the heretics. There are innumerable heresies that accept the Gospel according to Luke. If the Creator is bloodthirsty, merely a judge, and cruel because he says, “I will kill and make alive; I will strike and heal,” then it is perfectly clear that Jesus is also his Son. For the same things are written about him:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.”

He is appointed not only for resurrection but also for the fall. If killing is evil, then coming for the fall must also be evil. What will they answer? Will they withdraw from his worship, or will they seek some interpretation and flee to figurative explanations, so that “he came for the fall” may sound more like kindness than severity? And how will it be just, whenever something of this kind is found in the Gospel, to flee to allegories and novel interpretations, while, whenever it occurs in the Old Testament, they immediately accuse and accept no explanation, however plausible?

Moreover, even concerning what follows—“For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”—although they may seek to explain it, they will not be able to fulfill its meaning. But I, who desire to be called ecclesiastical, not after some heresiarch but after Christ’s name; who desire to possess a name that will be blessed upon the earth; and who wish both in conduct and understanding to be and to be called a Christian, seek an equal account in both the Old and the New Law.

God says: “I will kill.” Gladly do I accept being killed. For when the old man is in me, and I still live as a man, I desire God to kill the old man in me and make me alive from the dead. For, he says, “the first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47–49).

According to this meaning, the saying “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” is also understood. We all possess within us both sight and blindness. Adam saw, and he did not see. Eve too is described as having seen before her eyes were opened. “The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food, and excellent to the eyes and pleasant to eat; and she took of its fruit, ate, and gave it to her husband, and they ate” (Gen. 3). Therefore they were not blind but saw.

Then it follows: “And their eyes were opened.” Therefore, had they been blind and not seeing, whose eyes were afterward opened? But those who had previously seen well began to see badly after they transgressed the Lord’s command; and when sin stole away the sight of obedience, they afterward lost it.

I understand in the same way what the Lord says: “Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?” (Exod. 4). There is an eye of the body, with which we behold earthly things—the eye according to the sense of the flesh. Scripture speaks of this eye: “Walking vainly and puffed up by the sense of the flesh” (Col. 2). We have another eye opposed to it and better than it, one that perceives divine things. Jesus came to make the one who was blind in us see, so that those who did not see might see and those who saw might become blind.

According to this meaning, then, what we now have before us must also be understood: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.” Is there something in me that stands wrongly, something raised up by the pride of sin? Let this fall; let this be overthrown. And if what had previously fallen falls again, it will rise and stand. My inner man once lay crushed, while my outer man stood erect. Before I believed in Jesus, what was good in me lay fallen, while what was evil stood. After he came, what had been evil in me fell, and this saying was fulfilled: “Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus” (2 Cor. 4). And also: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, idolatry, sorcery, and so forth” (Col. 3). The fall of all these things was beneficial.

Concerning this fall it is said: “Wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will gather” (Job 39). The word *carcass* derives its name from falling. This is a good fall, for which Jesus first came; nor can he bring about resurrection unless a fall has preceded it. He came first to destroy what was evil in me, so that, once it had been destroyed and put to death, what is good might rise and be made alive in me, and so that we might obtain the kingdom of heaven in him.

Luke wrote: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). The same evangelist, who clearly hands down to us that Jesus was the Son of a Virgin and was not conceived from human seed, nevertheless testifies in Jerusalem that Joseph was his father, saying: “And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were said about him.”

What, then, was the reason for mentioning as his father one who was not his father? The person satisfied with a simple explanation says: “The Holy Spirit honored him with the title of father because he had nurtured the Savior.” But someone who investigates more deeply may say: “Because the genealogy is traced from David down to Joseph, lest Joseph appear to be named needlessly, since he was not the Savior’s father, he was called the Lord’s father so that the genealogical sequence might have its place.”

His father and mother, therefore, marveled at the things said about him by the angel, by the multitude of the heavenly host, and also by the shepherds. For when they heard all these things, they marveled exceedingly.

Then Scripture says: “Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: ‘Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed. And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.’”

We must contemplate how the Savior came for the fall and resurrection of many. One who gives a simple explanation may say that he came for the fall of unbelievers and the resurrection of believers. But the inquisitive interpreter says that no one can fall who has not previously stood. Give me, then, the one who stood and for whose fall the Savior came, as well as the one who rises. For the one who rises is certainly the one who had previously fallen.

It must therefore be considered whether perhaps the Savior came not for different people, for some as a fall and for others as a resurrection, but for the same people as both fall and resurrection. “For judgment,” he says, “I came, so that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might become blind” (John 9). There is in us one thing that previously saw and afterward ceased to see, and another that did not see and afterward began to see.

For example, I do not wish to see with those eyes with which I formerly did not see and which were afterward opened to me, since after the disobedience of Adam and Eve their eyes were opened, as we discussed above.

Now, however, we must interpret what this means: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.” I must first fall, and when I have fallen, afterward rise well, lest the Savior become for me the cause of an evil fall. But he caused me to fall for this reason: so that I might rise, and so that my fall might prove far more beneficial to me than the time when I previously seemed to stand.

I stood in sin when I lived in sin. And because I had previously stood in sin, it benefited me to fall and die to sin. Hence the holy prophets too, whenever they contemplated something more exalted, fell upon their faces. They fell for this reason: so that their sins might be more fully cleansed through the fall. The Savior first grants you this very thing: that you fall.

Were you a pagan? Let the pagan in you fall. Did you love prostitutes? Let the prostitute-lover in you first die. Were you a sinner? Let the sinner in you fall, so that afterward you may rise and say: “If we have died together with him, we shall also live together with him; and if we have been conformed to his death, we shall also be conformed to his resurrection” (2 Tim. 2; Rom. 6).

This one, then, is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel—that is, of those who are able to see with a complete and rational vision.

“And as a sign that will be opposed.” Everything that history relates about the Savior is opposed. The Virgin is his mother: this is a sign that is opposed. The Marcionites oppose this sign and say that he was not born from a woman at all. The Ebionites oppose the sign by saying that he was born from man and woman in the same way that we too are born.

He had a human body, and this is a sign that is opposed. Some say that he came from heaven; others say that he had a body like ours, so that, through the likeness of his body, he might also redeem our bodies from sins and give us hope of resurrection.

He rose from the dead, and this too is a sign that is opposed. How did he rise? Did he himself rise with the same kind of body as when he died, or did he rise in a body of a better substance? There is endless dispute: some say that he showed Thomas the mark of the nails in his hands; others, arguing in the opposite direction, ask: if he had the same body, how did he enter through closed doors and stand there?

You see, therefore, how the resurrection itself is challenged by various arguments and becomes a sign that is opposed.

I also think that what was foretold by the mouths of the holy prophets is a sign that is opposed. For there are many heretics who assert that he was not foretold at all by the holy prophets themselves.

And why must I pursue the matter at length? Everything that history relates about him is a sign that is opposed—not a sign opposed by those who believe in him. We know that everything written about him is true; but among unbelievers everything written about him is a sign that is opposed.

Then Simeon said: “And a sword will pass through your own soul.”

No history teaches that the blessed Mary departed this life by the stroke of a sword, especially since it is not the soul but the body that is ordinarily killed by iron. It remains, therefore, to understand that sword of which it is said: “And a sword is in their lips” (Ps. 58)—that is, the grief of the Lord’s passion passed through her soul. Although she did not doubt that Christ, as the Son of God, willingly died and would conquer death itself, nevertheless she could not see him crucified as one born from her own flesh without experiencing grief.

Likewise, the iron said to have passed through Joseph’s soul is understood as nothing better than severe anguish of mind.

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

There were evil thoughts in human beings, and they were revealed for this reason: so that, once brought into the open, they might be destroyed; so that they might cease to exist as thoughts that had been killed and put to death; and so that the one who died for us might kill them.

As long as thoughts were hidden and not brought into the open, it was impossible to kill them completely. Therefore, if we sin, we too ought to say: “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not hidden my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity to the Lord’” (Ps. 31).

For if we do this, and reveal our sins not only to God but also to those who can heal our wounds and sins, our sins will be wiped away by him who said: “Behold, I will wipe away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. 44).

After Simeon’s prophecy, since it was necessary that women too should be saved, a woman prophetess came, of whom it is written:

“There was Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher.”

What a beautiful order! The woman did not come before the man. First Simeon came, who took the infant and held him in his arms; then came the woman, whose words are not set out in detail, but of whom it is generally said that she confessed to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.

The holy woman rightly deserved to receive the spirit of prophecy, because she had risen to this height through prolonged chastity and long fasts.

Women, observe the testimony of Anna and imitate it if it should ever happen to you that you lose your husbands. Consider what is written about her: “She lived seven years with her husband from her virginity,” and so forth. For this reason she was a prophetess. The Holy Spirit did not dwell in her casually or by chance.

It is good, first, for any woman who can possess the grace of virginity to do so. But if she cannot, and it happens that she loses her husband, let her remain a widow. Indeed, she ought to hold this intention not only after her husband’s death but even while he is alive, so that, even if the event does not occur, her will and purpose may be crowned by the Lord. Let her say: “This I vow and promise: if anything human happens to me—which I do not desire—I shall do nothing other than remain undefiled and a widow.”

“And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.”

At this point Luke passed over what he knew Matthew had sufficiently explained: namely, that after these events the Lord was taken by his parents to Egypt so that he would not be found and killed by Herod; and that, after Herod’s death, he finally returned to Galilee and began to inhabit his own city, Nazareth.

For the individual evangelists commonly omit certain matters in such a way that, whether they have seen them mentioned by others or foresee in the Spirit that they will be mentioned by others, they appear, through the continuous sequence of their own narrative, to have omitted nothing. Yet a careful reader, examining the Scripture of another evangelist, can discover where those matters have been passed over.

“But the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was in him.”

The distinction in the words must be noted. The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he was a child—that is, insofar as he had assumed the condition of human weakness—was to grow and become strong. But insofar as he was also the Word of God and eternal God, he neither needed to become strong nor could he increase.

Therefore he is most rightly declared to be full of wisdom and grace. He was full of wisdom because “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him.” He was full of grace because great grace was granted to the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ: from the moment he began to become man, he was perfect and God.

This is similar to what John wrote when he called him “full of grace and truth”; by the word “truth,” John commends the same excellence of divinity that Luke commends under the name of “wisdom.”

But you…

## HOMILY XLIII. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

*(From the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop.)*

The child is therefore circumcised. Who is this child, if not the one of whom it is written: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9)? For he was made under the Law in order to win those who were under the Law (1 Cor. 9).

He is presented in Jerusalem. What it means to be presented to the Lord in Jerusalem I would say, if I had not already explained it in my comments on Isaiah. For once vices have been circumcised, a person is judged worthy of the Lord’s gaze, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 37).

You see that the entire sequence of the ancient Law was a type of what was to come; for circumcision also signifies the cleansing of sins. But because, through a certain ready inclination toward sinning, the weakness of human flesh and mind is entangled in sins from which there is no escape, the future cleansing of every fault on the eighth day of circumcision prefigures the eighth age, that of the resurrection.

For this is what is meant by: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. 34; Luke 2). In the words of the Law, the birth from a virgin was being promised—and truly holy, because immaculate. Finally, the words repeated by the angel declare that it is he himself who would be marked by the Law:

“For what will be born from you,” he says, “will be holy and will be called the Son of God.”

For it was not sexual intercourse that opened the hidden place of the virginal womb; rather, the Holy Spirit infused immaculate seed into an inviolate womb. For among all those born of woman, the Lord Jesus alone is holy: he did not experience the contagion of earthly corruption, because of the newness of his immaculate birth, and he drove it away by his heavenly majesty.

For if we follow the letter, how can every male be holy, when it is well known that many were most wicked? Was Ahab holy? Were the false prophets holy, whom the avenging heavenly fire consumed at Elijah’s prayer?

But that holy one was signified in the figure of a heavenly mystery by the pious prescriptions of the divine Law, because he alone was to open the hidden generative place of the holy virgin Church for the bringing forth of the peoples of God, with immaculate fertility.

He alone, therefore, opened the womb for himself. Nor is this surprising. For he who had said to the prophet, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jer. 1), is the one who opened his mother’s womb so that he might emerge immaculate, having sanctified another’s womb in order that a prophet might be born.

But you…

## HOMILY XLVI. ON THE VIGIL OF THE EPIPHANY

*(From Haymo.)*

“At that time, after Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: ‘Rise, etc.’” (Matt. 2).

Because the text does not say “after the dead man” but “after the dead men,” we understand from the angel’s words that many leaders of the Jews had agreed with Herod in bringing about the Lord’s death. Therefore, by divine vengeance, it happened that many of them perished with the one with whom they had agreed to bring about the Lord’s death.

Spiritually, however, Herod’s death signifies the end of the envious conflict with which the Church now rages against the synagogue.

“He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.”

The fact that, after Herod’s death, the child Jesus returned to the land of Israel signifies that, near the end of the age, he will return to the synagogue when they come to believe in him through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah. Hence he is ordered to carry him into Egypt and commanded to flee during the night. But when he returns to the land of Israel, there is no mention of night, because those whom he now abandons to the darkness of unbelief on account of their lack of faith, he will receive into the light of faith near the end of the age.

“But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there.”

Archelaus was one of Herod’s sons. Herod had appointed him to reign after him in Judea, but later, when the Jews accused him of arrogance, he was condemned by the senate and banished into exile at Vienna [Vienne], a city of Gaul, where he ended his life.

Archelaus, whose name is interpreted as “conquering lion,” signifies the Antichrist, who for a time will have victory among the saints and will appear like a terrifying lion.

Joseph therefore did not wish to go with the child into the region in which Archelaus reigned, because Christ did not dwell by faith in that part of the Jewish people which will believe in the Antichrist.

After Archelaus’s death, Christ returns to the land of Israel, because after the Antichrist has been killed the synagogue will believe in him, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11).

But because he remains and will remain in the Church, let us hear where he lived:

“And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee; and coming there, he lived in a city called Nazareth.”

Because Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “shoot,” it signifies the Church, which possesses both the flower of purity and the shoot of righteousness. The bridegroom admired the beauty of this shoot when he said in the Song of Songs:

“Who is this that rises through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3).

Again, the bridegroom says to her:

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2).

And because the Church passes from love of the present life to heavenly desire, Nazareth of Galilee is rightly named, since Galilee is interpreted as “migration.”

As for what he added—“so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, ‘He shall be called a Nazaraean’”—this testimony is not found in the translators of the Septuagint. Some wish it to have been taken from the book of the prophet Isaiah, where it is written:

“A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean will rise from his root” (Isa. 11).

But we say that if the Evangelist had set down a definite testimony from Scripture, he would not have said “through the prophets” but “through the prophet.” For all the prophets call the Lord a Nazaraean, because they preach according to him.

He is the one of whom Daniel says: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing will cease” (Dan. 9). And David says: “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15). And again: “Know that the Lord has made his Holy One wondrous” (Ps. 4).

“After Herod had died”—that is, after the law of the letter had died, or after the devil had been shaken out of the hearts of the Jews near the end of the world. For while the Jews observe the superstitious law of the letter, the devil reigns in them, and Christ is among the nations. But after they have cast all these things away from themselves, then the Son of God, or faith, will return to them.

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph.”

The angel rightly appears to the one who believes that Christ is the Son of God and carries him in his heart:

“Rise and take the child.”

Rise from the earth, you who are abandoning earthly things. He commands him to take the child first and then the mother: first to love God, and afterward one’s neighbor. Unless he carries Christ and loves God and his neighbor, he will not be able to enter.

“For those who sought the child’s life have died.”

He speaks of the whole by referring to the part. So, at the end of the world, the law of the letter will have died.

“But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea, he was afraid to go there.”

Why did he refuse to go into Judea? Why did he not go into Judea, where he had previously lived, or to Nazareth, where he properly dwelt? He thought that the angel was ordering him to remain specifically in Jerusalem because of the Temple and the prayers that took place in Judea.

But because of the mystery, he could not turn there. For one who comes up from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of sins—cannot first go into Judea, meaning confession; nor into Bethlehem, meaning the house of bread, which signifies the Church; nor into Jerusalem, meaning the vision of peace, unless he first goes into Galilee, so that he may migrate and cross over from evil to good and from vices to virtues.

From there he must pass into Nazareth, so that he may first produce the flower and purity of good works; then he may ascend to Judea—for the flower comes first, and the fruit afterward; from there, in order, he may ascend to Bethlehem; and finally to Jerusalem, that is, to the vision of peace.

Therefore Joseph was warned in a dream by the angel not to return first to Judea.

Archelaus, whose name is interpreted as “lion seeking,” signifies the Antichrist, who reigns in place of his father Herod. In the same way the Antichrist will reign at the end of the world in place of that devil who now rules the Jews.

But among us our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, whose kingdom and dominion remain forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(From the works of blessed Gregory the Great, pope.)*
