## HOMILY LIV. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

*(From Origen.)*

“At that time, when Jesus had come down from the mountain, a great crowd followed him. And behold, a leper came and begged him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,’ etc.” (Matt. 8).

When the Lord was teaching on the mountain, the disciples came to him as eager men, as members of his household, as those near to him, as friends or brothers. Therefore the Lord also said to them: “You are the salt of the earth, and you are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). But now, when he descended from the mountain, crowds followed him—those who had been unable to climb the mountain: sluggish people, negligent people, imperfect people. Thus also the children of Israel were initially unable to ascend the mountain; they could not go to meet God because of their irreligion and impiety. Only Moses ascended, and a few of the elders of Israel with him [Col. 1189C]. So also, with the Lord, only the disciples ascended the mountain, while those who were slower remained below.

Thus even now vigilant, eager, and faithful souls—those who fear God, love the Lord, desire the heavenly kingdoms, and always follow the Lord—ascend after the Lord to that heavenly mountain, hearing the Apostle say: “Seek the things that are above; set your minds on the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3).

Now, when the Lord descended—that is, when he inclined himself toward the weakness and helplessness of the others, taking pity on their imperfection or infirmity—many crowds followed him: some because of love, some because of his teaching, and some because of their amazement and their desire for healing. And behold, one leper was among those seeking a cure, those desiring relief [Col. 1189D].

And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” You run down below and ask, O man, yet on the mountain you say nothing? Why so? Because there is “a time and season for everything under heaven”: a time for teaching and a time for healing. On the mountain he taught, enlightened, admonished, healed souls, and restored hearts. Therefore I did not wish to attempt those greater things; I allowed those highest matters to be delayed. After he had completed them, and had descended from the mountain below to heal, just as he descended from heaven and from the heavenly mountains to save those who are carnal, a leper came to him and worshiped him.

Before he asked, he began to worship; before he pleaded, he showed reverence. He worshiped him, invoking him as God and Lord for this very reason, and worshiped him. Thus also those blessed Magi first fell down and worshiped him, and only then offered him gifts (Matt. 2). In the same way this man now fell down and worshiped, and thus presented his supplication:

“Lord,” he said, “you who are rightly worshiped, who are deservedly honored, I worship you as Lord, and therefore I call you Lord. First bearing witness to your works, I then speak these words. Through you all things were made. Therefore, Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. Your will is the work; therefore, if you will, you can make me clean.

“You willed that this most unclean leprosy should come upon me—either because of my sins, so that, being corrected, I might repent; or because of your providence, so that, cleansing me wondrously, you might be glorified. You do all things with wise and provident ordering, and bestow salvation abundantly. Therefore, whether I have borne this leprosy because of my sins, forgive my offenses and cleanse me; or, because of your providence, cleanse me wondrously, so that all may glorify you. Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.

“Your will is the work, because works also obey your will; therefore, if you will, you can make me clean. I do not doubt, I am not mistaken, and I do not speak like the man who pleaded for the healing of his son: ‘If you can do anything, help us.’ Rather, I know that you can do all things. Therefore I do not ask about your power, nor seek strength—for I know that these are unfailing—but I only implore your will, and the power that follows will immediately complete this grace: ‘Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.’ For me, it will be a benefit; for you, praise; for those who see, a miracle; for those who advance, instruction [and for advancement, instruction]. Lord [Col. 1190C], if you will, you can make me clean.

“You previously cleansed Naaman, the prince of Syria, of leprosy through Elisha when he bathed in the Jordan (2 Kings 5). Therefore now also, if you will, you can make me clean.”

In response, the Lord said: “You confess that I can; you profess that, if I will, it comes to pass. Therefore I will: be cleansed. You beseech my will; you confess my power.”

“I will: be cleansed.”

You believe magnificently, and you are magnificently cleansed. You confess most fully, and you are most fully gladdened.

“I will: be cleansed.”

You did not delay in believing; I do not delay in healing. You did not postpone your confession; I will not delay in cleansing you.

“I will: be cleansed.”

So that I may also show you great grace, I extend my hand toward you.

And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: “I will: be cleansed.”

And why did the Lord touch him, when the law had forbidden touching a leper? [Col. 1190D] He touched him for this reason: to show that “all things are clean to the clean,” that the uncleanness of some does not cling to others, and that foreign impurity does not defile the spotless. But why else did he touch him? To demonstrate humility; to teach us not to reject anyone, not to shrink from anyone, and not to regard anyone as contemptible because of bodily injury or blemish sent by the Lord, whose reason for it he himself knows.

Therefore Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. “I am,” he said, “the heavenly physician; I can heal bodies together with souls. Therefore I touch everyone—not so that infirmity may cling to me, but so that I may drive it away from those who have it. For I am the sun,” he said, “incorruptible, and the moon of righteousness; therefore I draw near to all and shine upon all with my splendors for salvation, while I myself remain as I was, in the unique beauty of my holiness.”

And stretching out his hand, he touched him. “I do not disregard the law, but I heal the wound. I do not destroy the commandment, but I drive away and cleanse the leprosy. Therefore, when I extend my hand, this contamination immediately flees; it cannot approach my virtue or resist my power.”

He said, “Be cleansed,” and, extending his hand to touch him, the leprosy immediately fled. And it was found that the Lord’s hand had touched not a leprous body, but a clean one.

Let us also now consider this, dearly beloved brothers, so that no one may have the leprosy of sin in his soul, and no one retain the defilements of offenses in his heart. And if anyone does have them, let him urgently worship the Lord and say to him:

“Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. You previously cleansed Naaman, who had committed many offenses; you have had mercy from the beginning on countless others who sinned. Therefore, if you will, you can make me clean.”

And the Lord, immediately extending the hand of mercy, says: “I will: be cleansed.”

And Jesus said to the man cleansed of leprosy, to the man on whom he had had mercy, to the man who believed in the Lord and trusted in his power: “You believed; you are well. You hoped; you have been made clean. Do not forget what you were and what you have become. Do not cease giving thanks; do not be silent in confessing.”

We too, dearly beloved, ought to do this whenever we are delivered by our Lord from some danger, whenever we are saved from some pain—whether of illness, wound, or any kind of necessity. Let us not become ungrateful; let us not abandon our Redeemer. Rather, let us eagerly render him thanksgiving, and let us also present gifts according to our means, in order to honor him.

For the Lord also commanded that man to do this: “Go,” he said, “to the priest, and offer your gift.”

Then Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one.”

And why, O sweetest Lord, do you now say, “Tell no one”? “Because of my humility,” he says, “because of my gentleness, so that you too may learn, when you do something good, not to boast, not to be puffed up, and not vainly to desire to please in the sight of people—as some are accustomed to do, whether when they have done something good, when they have fasted, in almsgiving and generosity toward the poor, in the honor of the altar, or in the honoring of the saints. For they themselves wish to be glorified before people and to please themselves, thereby losing their reward before the Lord.

“See that you tell no one. For while you remain silent, this will proclaim it wondrously; while your mouth is not opened, the whole substance of your body will rejoice aloud. Yesterday unclean, today clean; a little while ago horrifying, now beautiful.

“See, therefore, that you tell no one, but go and show yourself to the priest. When they see you walking to the temple, they will marvel, and the priest, seeing you, will be terrified, because, although you were washed by him once or twice according to the law, you could not, by presenting yourself to him, be cleansed.

“Go, therefore, show yourself to the priest, so that, seeing you, he may recognize that you have not been cleansed through the observance of the law, but through the working of grace; not through the image of earthly priests, but through the splendor of the heavenly High Priest.

“Go [Col. 1192A], show yourself to the priest. Show yourself to the priest, sent by the High Priest. Show yourself to the priest, cleansed by the High Priest of God the Father. But do not appear before the Lord empty-handed. Do not appear before the priest coming to him empty-handed; you will not come before the sight of the holy temple without fruit. Rather, you will offer your gift.

“For what was then said to that man admonishes us all; speaking to him, he says to all of us that we too should not keep our gifts and offerings with ourselves, but return them to God—especially when we are delivered from some tribulation. ‘Offer your gift,’ he says.

“Why? So that all who see you both carrying and offering it may believe these wondrous things and glorify God, who had mercy on you; and so that, through this rebuke and testimony, it may become an accusation of hardness of heart against unbelievers.

“Thus also, when he raised from his sickness the man who had lain ill for thirty-eight years, he commanded him to carry his pallet and go to his house (John 5), so that, as he carried that very bed through the middle of the city, he might proclaim the one who had saved him by invoking and praising him. Thus also he sent the blind man to the pool of Siloam (John 9), so that those who saw the same blind man walking there and then returning might marvel and be astonished, and might believe in the one who performed such miracles.”

After the things stated above: “When he had entered Capernaum, a city of Galilee.”

Capernaum was so named because in it the Lord frequently displayed the magnificence of his power.

As he entered Capernaum, why did he enter there? The reason is both found and immediately made clear.

A centurion approached him. He truly approached—not half-way, but wholly; not only with the appearance of his body, but with the fullness of his soul; not merely with his face, but with an undefiled heart. A centurion approached him: foreign by birth, but a member of the household in heart; foreign by nationality, but eager in faith. A commander of soldiers, yet an even greater joy to the angels.

A centurion approached him as a rebuke to those commanders of fifty who once ascended Carmel to Elijah and were immediately consumed by fire in their unbelief (2 Kings 1), while this man was immediately assigned to Abraham’s bosom because of his faith.

A centurion approached him, pleading with him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is suffering terribly.”

At that time many people pleaded for various illnesses: one for a son, another for someone else. But no one pleaded for a servant except this man alone, and this was an increase of blessedness and a crown of glory for him.

What was this blessed man thinking? What did this centurion, full of every good quality, consider? He was saying:

“He is my servant, and I am a servant of the Creator. He regards me as his earthly lord, while I have this great Lord in heaven. If I do not have mercy on him, how will he have mercy on me? If I do not help him, how will he help me?”

Thus all who have male and female servants ought to think; thus ought they to have mercy, to sympathize with them, to plead for them, and to care for their servants and maidservants, just as that blessed centurion did.

“My servant,” he said, “lies at home.”

He was pitiable not only in one respect, because he lay there, but also in another, because he was paralyzed, and in a third, because he was suffering terribly. For by all these statements he compounded the suffering: that he lay there, that he was paralyzed, and that he was severely afflicted [Col. 1193A]. He did this both to reveal the anguish of his own soul and to move the Lord, so that he might demonstrate the servant’s torment and invite the Lord’s benevolence.

“My servant lies at home.”

“And why did you not bring him here, as they carried that paralytic to him on a bed?”

“Because,” he said, “there is no need to show him everything, since he sees everything. There is no need to bring him into the presence of one whose power is neither bounded nor confined, neither excluded nor shut out.

“He lies at home, paralyzed, and is suffering terribly.”

“What do you want, then? What do you desire? What do you seek?”

“I am not saying much,” he replied, “for I know that I am speaking to one who knows all things. I am not being verbose, for I know that I am answering one who foreknows all things.”

Therefore the one who knows hearts, responding, says: “I will come and heal him.”

“I came to Abraham and healed the aged womb of Sarah, giving them a son, Isaac, in their old age (Gen. 21); now also, coming to you, I will heal him.”

“And how, Lord, do you promise this man your coming? He neither asks nor seeks it, knowing that it would not be acceptable to him for you to come into his house. Why do you bring this up at all?”

“For this reason: so that you may prevail, become like his faith, and recognize who he is and what hidden treasure of faith is found in him.

“I also tested Abraham at the beginning—not in order to learn what I already knew, but so that you might be found like him and very strong in every trial. I tested Job in the same way. I did not test one whom I had declared righteous for that reason, but so that I might show you hope, trust, and confidence.

“Therefore I also say to this man, ‘I will come and heal him,’ so that he himself, bringing forth his great faith, may say:

“‘Lord, you have terrified me with this promise; you have disturbed me with this saying; with this word you have destroyed the strength of my soul. I am not worthy of your appearance; I am not worthy of your approach; I am not worthy of your coming near or entering. Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.

“‘That great Moses, your companion, that marvelous narrator of your works, that faithful man in all your house, humbled himself greatly, saying: “I have not been worthy since yesterday and the day before yesterday” [the wording is uncertain]. How much more should I say, Lord, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof”?

“‘I am a foreigner, a Gentile, a soldier girded with a sword, shedding blood and going out to battle. Therefore I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. But only say the word—only come by the word.

“‘Your word is your appearance; your word is a completed work. Therefore speak the word, and show, while absent in body, that you are able to accomplish the work while present in spirit. Your presence is unfailing everywhere; your appearance is present everywhere.

“‘Therefore I am unworthy of your approach and entry, while this sick man needs the visitation of your word. Speak the word, therefore, and my servant will be healed.’”

Let none of us pass over this as though it were something insignificant, just as that blessed man said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

Even now the Lord enters under the roof of believers in two forms or ways. For when holy, devout, and acceptable bishops of the churches enter under your roof, the Lord enters there through them, and you should regard it as though you were receiving the Lord [Col. 1194A].

And again, when you receive the holy food, when you partake of that incorruptible feast, when you enjoy the bread of life and the cup, when you eat and drink the flesh and blood of the Lord, then the Lord enters under your roof.

Therefore you too, humbling yourself, imitate this centurion and say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” For wherever he enters unworthily, there he enters for judgment upon the one who receives him.

But what else did that blessed man add in what follows?

“For I too am a man placed under authority, and I have soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

O prudence! O understanding of the soul! O purity of heart! Before all else, he revealed the confession of manifest charity [the reading “truth” is also transmitted], declared the mystery of the New Testament, and showed in himself an image of the Church. He became the firstfruits of Gentiles believing in the Lord.

“I,” he said, “am a man under the authority of a king or prince. Though unworthy, I have soldiers and servants under my authority; and you have angels under your authority like soldiers, and all the saints as servants. I command each one, and he acts according to my order; you command, and it is immediately fulfilled. For whatever you command and say comes to pass. You command, and it is accomplished without delay. Every creature serves you. Therefore speak the word, and it will be accomplished swiftly, and my servant will be healed.”

O the man’s faith! O the soldier’s devotion! How greatly should we glorify you, O sweetest friend of truth! The Lord marvels at you and magnifies your unfailing faith.

How did such a light proceed from the darkness of the Gentiles? How was such righteousness manifested from the error of those who did not know God? How did such clear faith shine forth from the mouth of fools serving idols?

When the Lord heard him, he marveled at him. And when the only-begotten God marvels, how great, how extraordinary, how indescribable and immeasurable must the object be? Understand this, dearest one: nothing is marvelous to God—not gold, not riches, not kingdoms, not principalities. All these things are before him like a shadow, like nothing, like a fading flower. Therefore nothing is marvelous, great, or precious in the sight of God except one thing: faith alone. This he marvels at, this he honors, this he considers acceptable to himself.

Therefore, turning to the crowds that followed him, he said: “Amen, I say to you”—that is, “Truly I say to you”—“I have not found such faith in Israel” [Col. 1194D].

This does not mean that the Lord denies having found such faith in that earlier blessed Israel, Jacob. For Jacob not only believed in the Lord but also prophesied about him, demonstrated his righteousness more openly, and foretold his manifest coming in the flesh. If he had not believed in him, how could he have prophesied about him?

The same is true of those who came from Israel. For those prophets and righteous men were also called Israel: David, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. All these clearly and openly foretold his coming. All of them had faith, and they also had prophecy. This blessed centurion had faith, but he did not have prophecy.

Therefore, while marveling, the Lord magnifies his faith above that of the Israel who existed at that time—that is, above all the tribes of Israel then living—not above him who was Israel from the beginning, nor above those who were later found to be prophets and righteous men in Israel.

“Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel as I have found among the Gentiles, among barbarians, among foreigners. The Gentiles invoke me as the omnipotent Son of God, confess me as the only-begotten, acknowledge me as Lord, love me as Lord, and worship me as one who orders all things well. But Israel did not know me, and this people of mine did not understand me; therefore they call me Beelzebub and a Samaritan, and consider me a sinner (Matt. 9).

“Jairus, a ruler of Israel, pleading with me for his daughter, who was in danger, did not say, ‘Speak the word,’ but said, ‘Come quickly, before my daughter dies.’ Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, hearing about the mystery of faith, said, ‘How can this happen?’ (John 3). Mary and Martha, who loved me greatly, said, ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died’ (John 11), as though doubting that my power is everywhere swift to be present. Therefore I have not found such faith in Israel as in this foreigner.

“But I say to you that many will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

I say to you, I testify to you, I announce to you, I proclaim to you that many will come—those about whom the prophet already spoke, saying: “Many nations will come and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and enter the house of the God of Jacob, that he may show us his ways and we may walk in them” (Isa. 2).

Many will come of whom the Lord said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

Many will come of whom it was said: “So that the children of God who were scattered might be gathered into one” (John 11). All these, therefore, will come.

From where will they come? From east and west—that is, from every nation under the sun, from east all the way to west. For just as this Gospel must be preached among all nations, so from all nations people will come to the kingdom of heaven.

Or again, those from the east are those who, immediately enlightened, pass over; and those from the west are those who endure sufferings and persecutions for the faith even unto death.

Many, therefore, will come.

“And how do you say elsewhere, O sweetest Lord, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’?”

“Many,” he says, “are called. For all the tribes of human beings have been called from the beginning of the world, and few are chosen from the multitude. Indeed, through different generations and different ages, few have been chosen. But when they come together and are gathered at the time of visitation, they are found to be many and exceedingly innumerable.”

For many will come from east and west, and will recline—not lying down bodily, but resting spiritually; not drinking temporarily, but feasting eternally.

They will recline in the kingdom of God, where there is light and hope, joy and exultation, glory and blessing, light for the eyes and the length of eternal life; where all rejoice, where all are glad; where those blessed fathers recline; where all the prophets rest; where the apostles and evangelists sit upon glorious thrones; where the multitude of martyrs rejoices in eternal glory; where the abundance of virgins exults forever, bearing the crown of spotless virginity.

O sweetest brothers: united fellowship, joyful assembly, radiant communion! This is what has been rightly proclaimed and announced from the beginning of the ages; this is the exultation; this is the rest recounted from the beginning.

All who love the Lord have hastened to go there. There all from the Gentiles who believe in the Lord and preserve their devotion are gathered. Let us all go there as well, O devout children of God; let us hasten there with all our strength. Let nothing call us back, let nothing delay us, let nothing hinder us from hastening to this desirable banquet. Let us drive all negligence from ourselves, cast away all sloth from our minds, and remove bodily impediments from ourselves, so that we may become members of this blessedness and rest [Col. 1196B], and thus be found worthy of this holy feast, as it has been said.

“Go; as you have believed, let it be done for you.”

So truly it will be done for every person according to what he has believed; this grace from the Lord will be measured out to him according to the measure of his faith.

Therefore the Lord said to him: “As you have believed, let it be done for you.”

You believed that I can do all things; you believed that I am Lord of all. As you have believed, so let it be done for you.

Let us also believe, dearly beloved brothers, that Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, can do all things, is present everywhere, and, through his indulgence, grants us forgiveness of all our sins—provided that we keep his commandments—so that each one of us may deserve to hear, together with this centurion: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done for you.”

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LV. FOR THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

*(From the same author.)*

At that time, when Jesus had entered the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves, etc. (Matt. 8).

Entering the boat, the Lord’s disciples followed him—not weaklings, but firm and steadfast in faith, gentle and devout, despising the world, not double-hearted but single-minded. These, then, followed him, not merely following his footsteps, but rather accompanying his holiness and pursuing his righteousness.

[Col. 1196D] And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. For after he had displayed many great and wondrous things on land, he crossed over to the sea, so that there too he might demonstrate still greater works, showing everyone that he was Lord of both land and sea. Having entered the boat, therefore, he caused the sea to be disturbed, stirred up the winds, and roused the waves. Why? So that he might send his disciples into fear, that they might seek his help, and that he might reveal his power to those who entreated him.

That storm did not arise of itself, but obeyed the authority of the one commanding—of him who brings forth the winds from his treasuries and who established sand as the boundary of the sea. For he said to it: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther; here your waves shall be broken within yourself” (Job 38). At his command and order, therefore, the storm arose upon the sea, for the reasons mentioned above.

A great storm arose, then, and not a small one, so that a great work, and not a small one, might be displayed. The more violently the waves rushed upon the boat, the more fear troubled the disciples, so that they might desire all the more earnestly to be delivered through the Savior’s miracles.

But the Lord was sleeping. O wondrous and astonishing thing! He who never sleeps is sleeping; he who governs heaven and earth is sleeping; he who never sleeps or slumbers is said to sleep. He was sleeping in body, but he was awake in divinity; he was sleeping in body, but he was disturbing the sea, raising the waves, and terrifying the apostles, intending to display his power.

[Col. 1197B] He was sleeping in body, just as at the well he sat tired and weary from his journey, showing that he truly bore a human body, which he had assumed in its mortal condition. In that same body he slept, while in his divinity he stirred up the sea and then calmed it again. He therefore slept in body in order to awaken the apostles and make them rise from sleep, but especially in order that we all might never sleep in spirit, neither in understanding nor in prudence; rather, let us strive to keep watch at all times, to rejoice in the Lord, and to seek salvation from him.

For he who was sleeping in body speaks that holy saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5). The disciples approached him and awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

[Col. 1197C] They were so terrified by fear, and almost beside themselves, that they rushed upon him and did not make their request calmly or gently, but woke him tumultuously, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

O blessed men, O truthful disciples of God! You have the Lord and Savior with you, yet you fear danger. Life is with you, yet you are anxious about death. Fearing the sea’s tempest, you awaken its Creator, who is present, as though, while his body slept, he could not calm or moderate the waves.

But what do these most beloved disciples reply? “We are little ones,” they say, “still weak and not yet strong; therefore we fear, therefore we tremble. We have not yet seen the cross; the Lord’s passion and resurrection have not yet strengthened us, nor his ascension on high, nor the sending or descent of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Therefore we waver in weakness, and therefore we have often heard the Lord rebuke us for our little faith.”

We willingly bear and endure this; we voluntarily submit to it. Hence the Lord now says: “Why are you troubled, you of little faith? Why do you not have strength? Why do you not retain confidence and trust within yourselves? And if death were to seize you, ought you not to endure it with the greatest steadfastness?”

[Col. 1197D] For strength is necessary in whatever may happen. In every danger or tribulation, even unto the departure of the soul, and likewise against pleasures, riches, and earthly honors, strength of spirit must be maintained, so that you may neither be exalted, O human being, nor be raised up in pride. Do not despise your enemies; do not disdain the humble; do not forget the Lord; do not abandon the Creator; do not become ungrateful.

If strength is therefore necessary in hardship and danger, so that you may bravely endure all things with faith, much more is strength necessary against pleasures and luxuries, as has been said, lest you fall into the devil’s snare.

Why, then, are you troubled, you of little faith? If you recognize me as powerful on land, why do you not believe that I am also powerful at sea? If you truly acknowledge me as God, the Creator of all things, why do you not believe that the things made by me are in my power? Why, then, did you doubt, you of little faith?

The one who believes little will be reproved; the one who believes nothing will be despised. Those weak in faith will be corrected; those altogether alien to faith will be punished. Such were the Jews and the pagans, and therefore they perished in their evils. Such also were the heretics, and therefore they will be condemned on the day of judgment.

[Col. 1198B] Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. It was written: “And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, as a mighty man overcome with wine, and he struck down his enemies behind” (Psalm 77).

And now he rises, commands the winds and the sea, and a great calm arises. He commanded the winds and the sea as Creator, as his own, as the Powerful One, as Lord. He commanded the winds and the sea first before the disciples, so that, hearing this, they might be strengthened in faith. The hidden power of his divinity commanded and threatened it; rather, he governed and calmed it, according to the saying of a certain writer: “Power has calmed the sea.”

He therefore commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. From a great wind and a great storm, with the sea disturbed and swelling, a great calm arose. For it is fitting that this great one should do great and wondrous things. Therefore, having shortly before girded himself with great power, he magnificently disturbed the depths of the sea; now, once again displaying within it the magnificence of his power, he ordered a great calm to arise.

[Col. 1198C] This happened so that the apostles, who had been exceedingly troubled, might rejoice and be gladdened with magnificent joy. Through all these things the Lord gave us an image and pattern of instruction, so that we too might maintain patience in every disturbance and insult, remain steadfast, and not abandon the faith.

Even if this whole world should boil like the sea and rise into fury; even if all the winds and whirlwinds of demons should rage everywhere; even if, as we said above, the entire storm of the sea—that is, all the principalities and powers of the world—should be stirred up and foam in the swelling of anger, raging against the saints; even if they should lift themselves up to the heavens, like malignant storms of the sea, stirring up plots and roars against any one of you: do not fear, do not be troubled, do not tremble, do not falter.

All of you who sail in the boat with the Lord in faith—all of you who, in this boat of the holy Church, float with the Lord above this wave-tossed world—even if the Lord himself should sleep, awaiting our patience and endurance in a pious sleep, or bearing with the repentance and conversion of the impious, approach him eagerly, persisting in prayer and saying with the Prophet:

[Col. 1199A] “Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever” (Psalm 44). And again: “Rise up, O Lord; help us and redeem us for the sake of your name” (ibid.).

And when he rises, he commands the winds—that is, the airy spirits of the demons. For they stir up the storms of the sea; that is, they rouse bitter and arrogant waves, meaning the rulers of the world, to inflict persecution upon all the saints and to heap insults upon the faithful. The Lord commands all of them, threatens all of them, and calms all things; he makes a great calm around body and spirit, peace for the Church, and serenity for the world.

For how often have the councils of unbelievers been stirred up against the true and steadfast Church—sometimes those of pagans, sometimes those of heretics? How often did they rush in like the waves of the sea, threatening and crushing, while these rulers of the world thought that they could utterly destroy the children of the Church?

[Col. 1199B] But the Lord rose and rebuked the winds of the demons, causing all the bold adversaries of the faith to vanish, and he gave great peace and calm to his Church.

The men in the boat were astonished. Which men? Clearly those who possessed this boat or were attending to the boat. Do not think that the apostles are signified here by “men.” For nowhere do we find the Lord’s disciples called by this name except as an honorific; they are always called either apostles or disciples.

Those men, then, were astonished—those who sailed with him, whose boat it was, those who were making their passage in that same boat. They were astonished. And indeed it was worthy of wonder that the sea, stirred from its depths, should be calmed, that its lifted waves should be quieted, and that the raging winds should be restrained.

They were astonished, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” They do not ask by saying, “What sort of man is this?” but assert that he is such a one that the sea and the winds obey him. “What sort of man is this?” That is: how great, how strong, how powerful, how mighty!

[Col. 1199C] “What sort of man is this?” Greater than Moses, more powerful than Elijah. Both of those men acted: one, by striking the sea with a piece of wood, divided it with labor; the other crossed the Jordan with a blow of his mantle. But this man, with one word, commands those who have no words, and they obey him; those who have no hearing obey; those who lack reason and understanding bow to his command. They obey, though they possess neither speech nor, as I have said, language.

For in the very substance in which they exist, they move according to their nature and serve his command, to the confusion of mortals and the condemnation of corruptible beings. He commands the sea, and it does not despise him; he speaks to the winds and storms, and immediately they are restrained. He commands every creature, and it does not transgress his command.

Yet one race of human beings—honored according to the likeness of God and endowed with speech and understanding—these alone resist; these alone are disobedient; these alone despise him. Therefore these alone will also be condemned in judgment and punished by justice, as worse than mute animals or than those creatures in this world that are without spirit and soul.

[Col. 1199D] Those men were astonished, then, because he restrained the sea and the winds were calmed.

Let us also be filled with wonder whenever the Lord displays kindness and goodwill toward us; whenever he deigns to save us from dangers; whenever he delivers us from many tumults and tribulations; whenever he rescues us from pursuing enemies. Let us wonder, and while wondering let us give thanks; while giving thanks let us obey grace; while obeying let us fear; while fearing let us love, so that we may become heirs of eternal love from him.

They were astonished, saying: “What sort of man is this?” He appears as a human being, yet he displays power as God. He is thought to be one of the carnal, yet he displays great wonders above all things carnal. He sleeps as a human being, yet commands the sea and winds as God. He sits in the boat, and by his command bends every creature wherever he wills—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LVI. ON THE FEAST OF THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

(From the works of Ambrose Autpert.)

“If the faithful carefully …,” etc. For what follows, see among the works of Saint Ambrose Autpert, *Patrologia*, volume LXXXIX, column 1291.

## HOMILY LVII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY

(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)

“When the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord,” etc. (Luke 2).

From the words of this sacred reading, the greatest condescension of our Redeemer [Col. 1200C] and the humility of his undefiled mother, blessed Mary, are commended to us: namely, that both the Lord himself and his glorious mother, although they owed nothing to the law, nevertheless willingly chose to subject themselves to its legal decrees.

For the law commanded that an infant be circumcised on the eighth day after birth and that, thirty-three days after his circumcision, he be brought to the Lord’s temple and an offering be given for him; and if he were the firstborn, he was to be made holy to the Lord.

If we examine the words of the law carefully, we shall see that not only was the Lord incarnate without sin, but that his mother too was entirely free from every subjection to the law. For the law says (Leviticus 12): “If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised; she herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification.”

By saying that a woman who gives birth after receiving seed must be cleansed together with her offspring through the offering of victims, the law clearly distinguishes her from the one who conceived without receiving a man’s seed and gave birth as a virgin. Other human beings are born with original sin because they are conceived in the mother’s womb with the pleasure of the flesh and the heat of lust.

[Col. 1200D] But the Lord Jesus Christ, because he was conceived not only without male seed but also without carnal pleasure in the Virgin’s womb, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was therefore born without sin.

But just as Christ wished to be subject to the law in order to free us from the bond of the law, so blessed Mary, although she was not under the law, did not refuse to observe the law’s provisions as an example of humility, mindful of the command that a certain wise man gave: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

When, therefore, the days of his purification—that is, either of the Lord or of his blessed mother—were fulfilled, his parents brought him to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord; that is, to set him before him and consecrate him.

For those infants who were brought from throughout the kingdom of Judah to the Lord’s temple, if they were from the tribe of Levi, were permanently retained for the ministry of the house of the Lord, because that entire tribe had been dedicated to this very temple. But if they were from any other tribe, the firstborn were redeemed by their parents after a payment was made, and were taken back to their homes.

[Col. 1201A] The purification of boys consisted in the offering of sacrifices; that of mothers, however, consisted in their being kept away from a husband’s bed and from entry into the Lord’s temple for forty days in the case of a male child, and eighty days in the case of a female child.

This does not mean that it is sinful to beget children from a lawful marriage; rather, the lawful and marital conception of the human race cannot be entirely free from the guilt of iniquity. We know that the good of marriage was divinely instituted from the beginning of the human race. Therefore the Apostle unquestionably commends “marriage honorable in all” and “the bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13).

Although marriage possesses from God, as its allotted gift, a purity founded upon faith and love, nevertheless, because it cannot be consummated without the pleasure of lust, it necessarily produces offspring tainted by the sin of the first man.

[Col. 1201B] From good marriages, therefore, what is born is so good that it is not evil even if it is born from adultery or fornication. God bestowed the gift of fertility upon human nature; the evil of lust, however, is not God’s creation but the punishment of sin.

Accordingly, a pure human being is not born from the purity of marriage, because he is conceived through the intervention of polluted lust. Conjugal chastity does not love this lust, but necessarily tolerates it for the propagation of children.

For this reason holy David, born from a lawful and faithful marriage, laments with the greatest grief the stain of carnal generation: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50).

We have said this so that we may understand that the stain of original sin lies not in lawful marriages but in the conception of infants.

As for the fact that a woman is forbidden access to the temple for forty days after giving birth to a male child, this was done literally so that the purification might last as many days as the infant is formed in the womb. Human conception, it is said, is completed in this way: during the first six days it has something resembling milk; during the following nine days it is changed into blood. Then, over twelve days, it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen days it is formed until the limbs have acquired their complete outlines. From that point until the time of birth, it increases in size throughout the remaining period.

[Col. 1201C] Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen added together make forty-five. If, therefore, we include the smaller number within the larger, we shall see that the command was for a person to be purified for approximately as many days as he is formed in the womb.

But why a longer purification is imposed for the birth of a female child than for that of a male must be investigated. For it is said: “But if she gives birth to a female, she shall be unclean for fourteen days, and she shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of her purification” (Leviticus 12).

Because the woman deceived both herself and the man, she is therefore subject to a greater curse at her birth. Physicians also report that the flow of blood lasts seven days for a male child but fourteen days for a female child, so that the weaker or inferior the sex, the more polluted it is at birth.

Moreover, fourteen and sixty-six make eighty. In this the greater number—that is, forty—is doubled, because the woman consented to the serpent’s persuasion and compelled the man to consent to her persuasion, whereas the man consented only to the woman.

Let what has been said literally about the difference in purification suffice.

[Col. 1201D] The fact that the Lord is circumcised first and then, after several days, is offered in the temple with a sacrifice signifies spiritually that no human being can be acceptable in God’s sight, nor can anyone ascend perfectly to the heavenly Jerusalem, unless he is circumcised inwardly and stripped of every remnant of mortality.

As it is written in the law of the Lord (Exodus 13 and 43; Numbers 8): “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” What it says—“every male opening the womb”—is understood both of human beings and of animals. For all firstborn were sanctified to the Lord and belonged to the priests, yet with this provision: a price was to be given to the priest for a human firstborn, while the firstborn of an unclean animal was to be redeemed for five shekels of silver.

[Col. 1202A] Spiritually, all those firstborn signified the Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he was the only-begotten Son in the nature of God the Father, became the firstborn of every creature—that is, of all human beings. He alone is truly and uniquely holy to the Lord, because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

Morally, all our firstborn must likewise be offered to God, so that whatever good we conceive in our hearts we may attribute to divine grace. And just as they redeemed unclean animals for five shekels, so we must redeem the evil deeds we commit, practicing perfect repentance for all the sins that we contract through the five senses of the body.

When, therefore, the text says “opening the womb,” it must not be believed—as the heretics have attempted to assert—that Christ deprived his mother’s womb of virginity when he emerged from it, although he had sanctified it by entering it.

[Col. 1202B] For she is the gate of which we read: “This gate shall be closed, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall remain closed,” etc. (Ezekiel 44).

For God, taking true flesh from the Virgin, assumed from her a complete human body, but did not take away from her the grace of virginity. For it was not fitting that God the Creator of human flesh, who in the first creation had bestowed virginity upon human beings, should, in redeeming what he had made, remove virginity from the flesh from which he was born.

And they were to offer sacrifices, as had been said in the law of the Lord: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” This was the offering of the poor. For the law commanded that those who were able to find a lamb should offer it for their son or daughter together with a turtledove or pigeon. But if someone could not obtain a lamb, he was at least commanded to offer two turtledoves or pigeons.

[Col. 1202C] The Lord Jesus, therefore, mindful of our salvation, although he was rich, wished to become poor for us; and he wished a poor person’s offering to be offered for him, so that by his poverty he might grant us participation in spiritual riches and the eternal kingdom.

But let us see why these birds, rather than others, were commanded to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice. The dove signifies simplicity; the turtledove signifies chastity. It loves continence to such a degree that, after losing its mate once, it does not seek another thereafter. Both birds have lamentation instead of song. Therefore they appropriately signify the weeping of the saints in this age.

Rightly, then, the turtledove and the dove are offered as a sacrifice to the Lord, so that it may be clearly shown that the simple and chaste conduct of the righteous presents a most pleasing sacrifice to almighty God.

[Col. 1203A] The dove, moreover, which flies in a flock, signifies the active life, which belongs to many. The turtledove, however, which is solitary and loves solitude, signifies the contemplative life, imitated by very few and by the rarest of people.

Morally, when, in accordance with the evangelical command, we enter our room and pray to the Lord in secret, we offer a turtledove. But when we invite others whom we can to a similar work, saying with the Psalmist, “Come, let us adore and fall down and weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94), we bring doves to the divine altar.

And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. When the Son of God came in the flesh, he received testimony of praise not only from angels and prophets but also from elders and righteous people. For it was fitting that, since every age, every sex, and every condition was to be redeemed through Christ, all should also serve him with devoted obedience.

[Col. 1203B] This man was righteous and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. He is rightly called righteous and God-fearing, because righteousness is difficult to preserve without fear of God.

In truth he was righteous, because he was awaiting not merely the consolation of his own people but that of the entire people—namely, that those who had long been oppressed by the rule of the foreigner Herod might, through the coming of the Lord Savior, be liberated and receive consolation.

And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. The holy men of old possessed a great desire to see the Lord Jesus Christ, whom they knew would come. This was granted to Simeon as a reward for the merits of the saints.

[Col. 1203C] For he received an answer from the Holy Spirit in his maturity that he would not see death before he saw the Lord. “To see” here means “to experience.”

And he came in the Spirit into the temple. When it says that he came into the temple in the Spirit, we must not suppose that he came without a body; rather, inspired by the Holy Spirit, from whom he had received the answer, he came into the temple.

And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, in order to fulfill the custom of the law concerning him, Simeon himself received him into his arms—that is, into his embrace.

Who could measure the joy of heart and indescribable delight with which Simeon was filled when he held in his own arms the Creator and Lord of heaven and earth, whom he knew had been foretold by the prophets and awaited through many prayers by all the saints of former ages?

[Col. 1203D] Figuratively, the aged Simeon signifies this world, already declining through prolonged old age. Simeon received the infant: that is, the world recognized Christ and, stripped of the oldness of sin, returned to the innocence of Christian conduct.

And he blessed God and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.” Blessed Simeon knew that those eyes would be blessed which were to see Christ. Therefore, until he himself had seen him, he did not wish to be released by death; but when he saw him, he immediately desired to be dismissed in peace.

“Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples.” He calls Christ the salvation of God the Father, whom God the Father prepared at his first coming before the face of the peoples, so that all who wished to believe in him might behold him through faith and love.

[Col. 1204A] At the second coming, this same salvation will also be prepared before the face of all peoples, so that every eye may see him and he may repay each person according to his works.

“A light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.” Christ is a light for both peoples, that is, for the Jewish and Gentile peoples; but he was especially the glory of the Israelite people, because he was foretold to them, assumed flesh among them, and performed miracles in their midst.

He was also the revelation of the Gentiles, because by the light of his illumination he revealed—that is, opened and enlightened—the eyes of their minds, which had been submerged in the profound blindness of unbelief.

Rightly, therefore, he said that Christ came first for the revelation of the Gentiles and then for the glory of Israel, because he foresaw that the Gentiles would believe before the Jews.

The Psalmist says something similar: “The Lord has made known his salvation,” and so forth, “to the house of Israel” (Psalm 97). First he says that God the Father revealed his righteousness—which is Christ—to the Gentiles; then he adds: “He has remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel” (ibid.).

Hence Paul says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

[Col. 1204B] These remarks about the Gospel reading have been stated briefly. Although it fully discloses the reasons for today’s feast, it is not out of place to investigate its name somewhat more concisely.

In Greek, ὑπαντάειν (*hypantaein*) means “to meet” or “to go out to meet.” From this the Lord’s solemnity is called ὑπαντή (*hypantē*), because on this very occasion, when the Lord was brought into the temple, Simeon and Anna, together with the other faithful persons who were there, went out to meet him at the time of his purification.

This feast is therefore celebrated at the beginning of February. The month was named from Februus, that is, Pluto, whom the pagans believed to possess power over lustrations—that is, purifications.

When the Romans had reduced the threefold world under tribute, so that each of the three parts of the world—Africa, Asia, and Europe—paid gold for five years, then silver for another five years, and likewise bronze for a further five-year period, after the fifteenth year had been completed and the census paid, the whole city was purified by the entire people in the month of February. This was done so that sacrifices might be offered to the infernal gods, by whose protection they believed they had subjugated the nations of the world.

[Col. 1204C] But Christian religion rightly changed this custom of purification. On this very day, the feast of blessed Mary, the people, clergy, and priests go around the churches with candles and hymns—not in remembrance of pagan superstition or earthly rule, but in perpetual memory of the heavenly kingdom, when, according to the evangelical parable, all the elect will go out with lamps to meet the bridegroom and bride and will enter the chamber of heavenly brightness.

The pagans always performed this purification on the fifteenth year, at the end of February—that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Later, however, as Christianity increased, it was decided that it should be transferred to the beginning of the month in honor of the perpetual Virgin.

[Col. 1205A] Following the custom of this institution, we too, according to our limited ability, intend devoutly to imitate it today, with God’s help. Let us entreat the Mother of God with humble prayers to grant us her aid, so that by her powerful intercession she may obtain from her Son the purification of our sins—she who undertook temporal purification without the stain of sin.

May she who on this day ascended with her Son to the temple of God to offer a sacrifice obtain for us entry into the heavenly city, where we may freely enjoy the sight of the divine brightness, with our Lord Jesus Christ granting it, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LX. ON THE SAME SUNDAY: HOW THE FIRST HUMAN BEING WAS PLACED ABOVE THE WHOLE OF CREATION

(From the works of blessed Chrysostom.)

The dignity of human origin is readily recognized when the sublimity of its author is considered. For it could not easily have been something insignificant or slight that the sacred hand fashioned and the heavenly hand animated with vital substance—especially since God, the same craftsman, was going to entrust to that man authority over the whole creation. He intended to make him second in rank after himself, and therefore made him complete and perfect, possessing both the dignity by which he might excel and the power by which he might rule [Col. 1206A] all living things: serving only the one by whom everything had been subjected to him, so that he might rule the world, serve God, look up to the Creator, and compel creation to obey him. He was to see that he owed the Lord as much submission as he himself demanded from creation, possessing in his own power both obedience and contempt: obedience, by which he might live; contempt, by which he might justly perish according to his deserts.

Thus it came about that, by his contempt, he fell into death, though by obedience he could have lived. When he turned the authority granted to him into contempt, he both lost the privilege of life and acquired for himself the sentence of death. Yet his creation still preserves its dominion, although he himself denied obedience to his Creator. From this it is evident how much he has taken away from his own happiness, since the merits of his sins still cannot alter the state of his condition. [Col. 1206B]

You are burdened, O man—justly burdened—and held fast by an inescapable punishment. You despise the Creator, yet command his creation. You scorn the Lord, yet demand obedience from his creation. You enjoy God’s benefits, yet do not fear his power. And while everything serves you through him, he alone is not served by you.

Twice you offend, O man, and incur a twofold and double crime: you neither obey as a servant in accordance with your condition, nor serve the Lord in accordance with the power given to you. For you, the heavens are clothed by day in the splendor of light and adorned with the rays of the sun; by night the firmament itself is illumined by the most brilliant mirror of the moon and by the varied radiance of the stars, so that through the alternation of day and night both the succession of times may be discerned and rest may be provided for wretched mortals after their daily labor.

[Col. 1206C] The seasons change in alternating succession; the forests put forth leaves, the fields become pleasant, and the meadows grow green. All living creatures, produced for different uses, bring forth offspring, obey the command, and maintain their service. Springs bubble up, all waters flow, and the seas are confined within their appointed boundaries. After winter, the mildness of spring rejoices; the heat of summer ripens the crops; drunken autumn displays its abundance; in winter the earth is weakened by rains. Everything serves according to its appointed order; man alone does not serve God.

What if all nature were constantly to declare to you:

“I have been commanded to obey you by the Lord of all things. I have been commanded to fulfill his orders concerning you, preserve his ordinances, and furnish all created things at the command of their author. In short, I obey, submit, and serve; and when you change, I do not change. I obey the rebel, submit to the insolent, and serve the contemptuous. [Col. 1206D] But if the Lord of things had commanded me to change my ordinances, pervert his orders, and withhold what is necessary, all creation would remain deprived of man, and there would no longer be anyone to despise it, because man, the despiser, would rightly and deservedly perish.”

In short, whoever you are who persist in this contempt—who command creation and do not serve the Creator, who exercise dominion and do not acknowledge the Lord—fear the patient Lord, lest you experience him as a severe judge. Let the delay granted by the one who postpones correct you, lest the judgment of the one who judges punish you. For you will easily make God favorable through your obedience, if, having turned back, you now change your vice. Whatever is accumulated through delay is repaid with interest; and what the passage of time could not remedy can no longer remain unpunished.

[Col. 1207A] “What shall I render to the Lord?” If the human condition recognizes what it owes its author, and if it understands, by considering at every moment, the countless multitude of his benefits, it will discover that it cannot equal the service of its own slavery by continual praises and unceasing thanksgiving. For the benefits he has provided and bestowed can have neither measure nor number, certainly not an end, since neither perception is sufficient to investigate them nor knowledge adequate to praise them. The immensity of his benefits surpasses the thoughts of our senses, and the countless multitude of his gifts exceeds the rapid movement of our words.

Even if the whole span of life were occupied by the service of the mouth, filled with praises, and devoted to giving thanks, you could not repay what you owe. In this matter we must strive [Col. 1207B] to exercise the devotion of our mind with all our strength in God’s service, and compel our mouth throughout all time to repeat the glories of his praise—not because what is owed is compensated by these acts, but so that the intention of our devotion may be recognized through such efforts; so that whatever our weakness takes away from completion, devotion may contribute toward acceptance; and so that you may be reckoned as having discharged your debt because you will, not because you accomplish it—not because you repay what is owed, but because you desire to obey.

For the will itself is counted, since the immensity of things does not permit us to express fully what we desire. “What shall I render,” he says, “to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115). The most holy Prophet asks by what merits he may repay divine benefits, by what kind of service he may equal the gifts he has received, by what obedience he may respond to such great gifts, and by what form of servitude he ought to match countless gifts and boundless kinds of benefits.

[Col. 1207C] Even if human merit is outstanding, preserves the rights of nature, obeys the commands of the laws, fulfills faithfulness, maintains justice, practices the virtues, condemns vices, rejects sins, and offers itself as an example to those who imitate it, whatever it has done is little; whatever it has accomplished is less. For every merit is brief in comparison with the gifts. Count the benefits, if you can, and then consider what you deserve. Weigh your deeds against heavenly benefits; reflect upon your own actions alongside divine gifts; and you will not judge yourself worthy for what you have been if you understand what you deserve.

Therefore, from the countless benefits bestowed upon you through divine mercy, choose whichever one you please: [Col. 1207D] your entire merit will not be able to compensate for it. The senses grow dull, the mind is confounded, and the spirit is disturbed when man seeks to know God. Human obedience cannot be weighed if it is compared with divine benefits; and yet we speak of the one who does not permit himself to sin, who examines the judgment of his own mind, strives to please, persists in seeking acceptance, and labors to serve.

But whoever either takes pleasure in sinning, or is so enslaved by the sluggishness of his own mind, inconsiderate actions, or the vanity of life to vices that he becomes a source of offenses, a servant of faults, and a seedbed of sins—so that he commits within himself a twofold wickedness and double crime, both failing to render the Lord the service he owes and attempting, by sinning, to repay his countless benefits with insult. [Col. 1208A]

Therefore let the righteous strive to equal their own merits with heavenly benefits, and let the sinner strive to loathe the vices he practiced. Let the righteous increase through the growth of a holy life; let the sinner, by condemning his sins, practice the justice he did not love. Let the righteous advance toward a better life; let the sinner be corrected and live. Let the righteous offer the good a saving example; let the sinner show the wicked the remedy of correction. Let the righteous await the rewards of holy merit; let the sinner, by correcting himself, avoid punishment. Thus it comes about that the righteous acquire glory by living well, while the corrected sinner receives pardon through divine mercy.

## HOMILY LXI. SUNDAY OF SEXAGESIMA

At that time, when a very large crowd had gathered and people were hastening to Jesus from the cities, he spoke by way of a comparison: “A sower went out to sow his seed,” etc. (Luke VIII).

[Col. 1208B] The reading from the holy Gospel that we have just heard, dearest brothers, etc. For the rest of this homily, see Saint Gregory the Great, *Works*, vol. II, *Patrologia* LXXVI, col. 1131.

## HOMILY LXII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY. On the Fall of the First Man

*(From the works of Blessed Chrysostom.)*

No one who exists is unaware that, in the beginning, man was so fashioned by God that he might be instructed in prudence, formed by counsel, made capable of reason, and fashioned by divine providence. He was instructed, I say, in prudence, by which he might avoid the cunning of the enemy; in counsel, by which he might seek what was wholesome and right; and in reason, by which he might understand that he ought to obey God his creator. [Col. 1208C]

For the Lord God, seeing the man whom he had made innocent, instructed, warned, and armed him, since he was going to fight with the devil and therefore had to be equipped, as it were, with certain weapons—that is, prudence, counsel, and reason. He further added a law by which man might recognize God’s will and learn what could happen to one who despised it. But this man, unwary, when he consented more readily to the devil’s persuasion than to God’s command, both lost the life he possessed and received the death he did not know.

Adam stood between his wife and the devil, between Eve and the enemy, between the woman and the serpent. The devil persuades in order to harm; Eve consents in order to perish. The devil, by the cunning of deception, ensnares the woman; the unwary woman [Col. 1208D] receives the serpent’s poison. What the devil could not accomplish by himself, he accomplished through the wife against Adam the first-formed man. Adam found destruction through the wife whom he had received from God as a helper.

Alas! Prosperous things turn to their opposite; useful things bring about ruin. In the end, Adam is wounded more by what is domestic than by the enemy’s arrows, killed more by his own sword than by a hostile one, and struck more by the woman than by an external weapon. For the subtle serpent came to deceive, and he came not to inflict his serpentine poison upon the man but upon the woman. He came, I say, so that through the consent of one he might harm both. What would have harmed both, he persuaded one to accept; what infected the mind of one with the serpent’s malice harmed both. [Col. 1209A]

In short, the consenting woman proved toward her husband to be what she had found the serpent’s malice to be toward herself. She was persuaded and persuaded others; she was infected and infected others; she was deceived and deceived others.

That woman was struck by a twofold sentence, one particular to her and one shared: the particular sentence by which she was commanded to bear children in pain; the shared sentence by which she was condemned to death together with her husband. The one sentence arose because she consented to the serpent; the other because she persuaded her husband. Through consent she fell under the sentence of death; through persuasion she deserved to bear children in pain.

This sentence, then, the one who does not know it learns while suffering; the one who is unaware feels it while being punished; and the one who ignores it recognizes it while experiencing it. Alas for the crime! The Lord’s command is despised, and the serpent’s persuasion is heard. God, who provides, is scorned, and the serpent, who deceives, is heard. Saving warnings are rejected, and poisonous conversations are welcomed.

Thus man, through contempt, is handed over to [Col. 1209B] death because he preferred to obey the serpent. They are stripped of glory and deprived of dignity; they become what they were not when they lose what they had been. The serpent rejoices greatly that he has accomplished what he wanted; he delights that he has destroyed the man whose ruin he desired. He exults that the effect of his malice has fulfilled the deception of man. Yet the wretched creature does not know that he himself is wounded while he wounds, slain while he slays—that, while he destroys man, he himself has been destroyed.

God was grieved that man had deserved the sentence of death [before] that of life, destruction before salvation, and had despised glory rather than death. Yet he was moved more by the serpent’s malice than by man’s contempt; he condemned the devil’s deceit more than man’s faithlessness. Thus the Lord God both detested the enemy’s savagery and pitied man’s fall. He shuddered at the enemy’s cruelty and grieved for the deceived man with paternal compassion. He was moved by the enemy’s ferocity and mercifully lamented the man who had been deceived. [Col. 1209C]

In the end, the Lord God said, “Where are you, Adam?” By asking, he summons him to confession. He wants him to admit his sin while inquiring what he has done. He seeks to show mercy while conversing with the guilty man about his fault. He contemplates pardon while reproving the cause of his despised law. He rebukes the fault so that he may grant pardon; those whom he could not form by instruction, he may purify through confession.

They receive garments of skins, so that those who had now confessed their offense might receive pardon through the humility of their clothing. The Lord shows by what duties offenses may be cleansed; he shows that pardon may easily be obtained through confession [Col. 1209D] and the disfigurement of one’s clothing. For just as it is defiance to conceal what you have committed with God as witness, so it is dangerous to pretend to innocence of spirit through the splendor of one’s clothing.

Therefore let no sinner conceal the vices of sin under a joy that has been abandoned to despair; let no one pour the poison of dissimulation into a mind infected by offenses. Let the vices of the mind be revealed through the sorrow of the body. If the mind is afflicted, let the body mourn, because whenever the body is involved in the matter, the mind suffers in sorrow. Certainly, just as bodily vices cannot exist without the mind’s compassion, so the vices of the mind cannot be freed from the body’s compassion. Let both grieve together, so that both may obtain pardon together, since both must necessarily be either supported by benefit or afflicted by injury at the same time.

For man is nothing other than a union of body and soul. [Col. 1210A] These two differ as definitions, but when joined together they constitute man. Just as they cannot be separated in life, so they are never separated in merit, whether good or evil. Just as the soul cannot be separated from the body’s goods, so the body cannot be separated from the soul’s evils.

If, in God’s judgment, both substances are to be cleansed either through punishment or through reward, why should they not also in this age share equally either sorrow or joy? Therefore, Christian, you have no excuse: after slavery you have been freed; after captivity you have been redeemed; after affliction you have been healed; after destruction you have been restored. You have warnings to put into practice and examples to fear.

Adam, however, neither recognized the devil’s deceit nor mourned the fall of anyone who had been deceived. Perhaps he could have escaped, [Col. 1210B] if he had not first fallen while fighting with the enemy. The Lord now instructs you; he has placed before you the examples of what happened.

“Behold,” he says, “you have been made well; do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John V). Do not sin, he says, after pardon; do not be wounded after healing; do not become defiled after grace. Consider, O man, he says, that guilt after pardon is more serious; that a renewed wound hurts worse after healing; and that a man is more grievously defiled after grace.

Therefore the one who sins after pardon is ungrateful for forgiveness; the one who wounds himself after being healed is unworthy of health; and the one who defiles himself after grace does not deserve to be cleansed. But the one who does not sin after absolution deserves a reward; the one who remains cautious after healing possesses the gift of health; and the one who keeps grace unharmed will receive the kingdom of eternity. [Col. 1210C]

It is serious for an instructed person to offend; it is more serious for one who has already been absolved to sin. A servant who offends his master after being granted freedom is worse than before. He is ungrateful for benefits who, through the arrogance of pride, despises the giver.

Therefore either gain salvation from the example, or fear a similar sentence through such fellowship, lest you experience as a severe judge the one whom you have despised as a merciful persuader.
