## HOMILY LXV. ON THE SAME SUNDAY. On the Faith of Abraham and the Sacrifice of Isaac

*(From the works of Blessed John Chrysostom.)*

Faith is the most holy foundation of religion, the bond of charity, and the support of love. It strengthens holiness, [Col. 1211A] reinforces chastity, and adorns dignities. It shines in children, flourishes in the young, and appears in the mature. It governs the sexes, advances ranks, and safeguards every duty. In the poor it is pleasing; in the person of moderate means it is joyful; in the wealthy it is honorable.

Faith preserves friendships, joins fellowships, and commends the arts. It despises no one, scorns no one, and is lacking to no one except perhaps the one who is lacking to it. Faith keeps commandments, observes precepts, and confirms [or: brings to completion] promises. Faith makes people familiar with God and establishes them as friends of Christ. For no one will receive the promises of faith unless he preserves his profession through his deeds; nor can anyone possess the rewards who has been unwilling to preserve the faith he promised, so that either the reward of fulfilled faith may be repaid to a person or the fitting punishment of violated faith may be assigned.

[Col. 1211B] Let us take the beginning of this faith from Abraham. Though he was established in advanced age, he believed that he would receive from God the son who had been promised to him; by faith he discerned in his son the reward of faith, and by that same faith he compared his offspring to the number of the stars, in which it would overflow. In the end, one son is desired for Abraham, and an immense multitude is promised to him. The consolation of a single heir is sought, and an innumerable offspring is appointed.

The Lord says: “You do not know, Abraham; you do not know what has been destined for you. But you do not know for this reason: you do not consider what you deserve. For your faith has merited so much from me, and your service has had such worth, that I both know what you desire and have determined to do what you deserve. For a son will be born to you, whose seed will spread into thousands, so that it may be compared both to the likeness of the stars and to the immensity of the sand.” [Col. 1211C]

“I believe,” says Abraham, “Lord; I believe because you are able. I trust that you will do what you promise. For I do not consider the exhausted old age of my withering life, nor attend to the sterile and barren condition of my wife Sarah; rather, I contemplate the power of your majesty. I recognize not to whom such things are promised, but by whom they are promised. Old age cannot beget children, but your command, Lord, brings it to completion. The barren cannot have children, but your power makes this possible. Nature denies it, but power commands. Age forbids it, but your power demonstrates it. That thing seems impossible to us, but not to you; to man, but not to your majesty, Lord; to nature, but not to God; to servants, but not to the Lord. Therefore I believe, [Col. 1211D] Father; I believe, Lord, that you will do what you say, because through these powers you make yourself known to all nations.”

Then Sarah conceived in her womb and bore a son destined to be the father of many nations. Isaac was born—the adornment of his race, the glory of his parents, the joy of his relatives, the honor of his family, the hope of his inheritance, the reward of faith, and the testimony of the promised offspring. In his birth the Lord fulfilled his promise, and Abraham received the desire for which he had prayed. Everyone rejoices; all are glad. Isaac is sweet when he is born, sweeter when he is nurtured. For he could not be otherwise than sweet, since his father’s faith had seasoned him and his own innocence commended him.

Sarah, once barren, also becomes a fruitful mother through her son, and will become still more fruitful through him. Youth returns to the old man; withering age is restored in the young; [Col. 1212A] and while the age of old age remains, the mother performs the tasks of youth. In the end, she caresses, nourishes, suckles, and fulfills the duties that follow—duties she might perhaps have forgotten if Sarah had been permitted to give birth at the proper time.

Then the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying: “Take your son, whom you love, Isaac, and go to one of the mountains, and offer him to me as a sacrifice” (Gen. XXII). At once Abraham decides that the heavenly commands must be obeyed as quickly as they had been divinely given. For he feared that delay might offend the promise or that tardiness might obstruct the command. In the end, he hastens to accomplish what was ordered and rushes to fulfill what was commanded. He had been glad when he received him, and was gladder when the Lord requested that he be sacrificed. Abraham showed that his son was indeed very dear to him, [Col. 1212B] but that the Lord was much dearer than his son. He did not consider the sweetness or affection of his beloved child, since he was thinking of fulfilling the command. He turned all his affections toward God, to whom he already knew himself to be devoted.

In the end, he preserved in himself the faith by which he had pleased God when he was commanded to offer his son—the same faith by which he had deserved to receive him. Isaac was present, unlike his father in age but equal to him in faith and devotion. Isaac was present, I say, and if his father had made any decision, he himself would willingly have desired it to be done. The son obeyed his father in such a way that the father obeyed the divine command: the father was secure in the son’s consent, and the son surrendered himself to his father’s will.

For there was one mind in both, one understanding, and a similar affection toward God, so that you could see the father’s nobility poured into the son and [Col. 1212C] the son’s innocence not lacking in the father; the son was a participant in his father’s faith, and the father’s sublimity overflowed from the simplicity of his son.

Relying on this security, Abraham saddled his donkey, cut wood for the sacrifice, and brought servants with him. When they came to the city, he said: “Stay here; I and this boy will go on alone. When we have worshiped the Lord, we will return to you.” At once the father set out alone with his son.

The son said to him: “Father, I see the wood; I see the knife and the fire; I am looking for the victim whom you are going to sacrifice.”

“Stop,” he said, “stop asking about what the Lord will provide for himself at the proper time, my son. Stop asking about what the Lord has already foreseen for himself.”

[Col. 1212D] A great foreknowledge on the part of the one who promises; great innocence on the part of the one who asks. Isaac, the victim, asks his father about the victim; the consequence of the sacrifice is desired. He asks about the sheep that is lacking, lest he himself, who is speaking, be sacrificed.

When they had reached the place, both climbed the mountain. The father built an altar, arranged the wood, and bound his son.

“Allow me,” he said, “my son; allow me to fulfill my vow. Allow me, I say, through you to fulfill the Lord’s command. The God who formed you demands you; the one who gave you asks for you; the one who created you desires you to be sacrificed to him. This is not parricide; this is not an act of cruelty, because it is a vow. Nor is death miserably inflicted upon you, my son, by your father; rather, provision is being made for both of us toward salvation. You will be a sacrifice all the more acceptable the more willingly you accept the benefits of a glorious death.”

[Col. 1213A] “Fulfill,” he said, “what you, as a commanded father, must do; steadfastly [or: urgently] complete what you have determined. For I neither resist nor refuse. What you wish, I wish; what you desire, I desire; what you long for, I too long for. In the end, I accept this death with the same vow with which I understand that you are willing to inflict it upon me.”

Although neither of them said these things aloud, both nevertheless displayed them all in their actions. At once the father stretched out his hand, took up the sword, and raised his right hand, wishing in devotion to cut the throat of his son and complete the sacrifice, fulfilling the Lord’s command.

But when the sword was already hanging and poised above him, the Lord said: “Spare him, spare him! I sought your faith; I did not desire that you slaughter your son. I did not wish to take away your beloved child, but to test your devotion. Now I know that you love the Lord more than your son—or rather, that you love your son more because you love the Lord. For since you did not spare your son for God’s sake, you have made him glorious with yourself before the Lord.”

[Col. 1213B] “Therefore I will heap blessings upon you and confirm that an infinite multitude of children will come forth from him for you.”

At once a ram is provided, worthy to be slain in place of holy Isaac. For it was not right that Isaac, who bore the type of Christ, should at that time be slaughtered by his father, since the perfect sacrificial victim was reserved for Christ the Lord. A ram was provided, I say, worthy to be slain in place of Isaac, so that both the father’s promise concerning the victim might be fulfilled and, after the perfect sacrifice, Isaac might be returned safely to his father.

Then both descended joyfully from the mountain: the father because he had fulfilled the vow of the sacrifice with his son safe; the son because he had willingly desired to fulfill his father’s commands. The son rejoices in his father, and the father in his son. The relatives rejoice, [Col. 1213C] and the whole family is glad; they rejoice, I say, that so great a deed has been completed and that the Lord has brought the father and son back to them unharmed.

## HOMILY LXXIII. ON THE MONDAY AFTER “INVOCAVIT”

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty,” etc. (Matt. XXV).

In the reading that precedes this one, the Lord proposed the parable of a man going abroad who, after calling his servants, distributed money among them according to what was appropriate for each: to one five talents, to another two, and to another one; and immediately he departed. After a long time, he returned and, calling his servants, settled accounts with them. He rewarded those who had worked well for the profits they had brought in, but he condemned the negligent servant [Col. 1214D], who had grown sluggish in good works. When this parable had ended, he immediately added what we have now undertaken to explain, thereby showing that the parable he had previously given referred to himself. He therefore says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty.”

Because the time of his Passion was at hand, and because at the approaching Passover he was to be seized, struck on the face, spat upon, scourged, crowned with thorns, and finally crucified, given vinegar to drink, and handed over to death, he consequently foretells that he will come in majesty for judgment, so that the great promise of glorification might compensate for the scandals that would follow from his Passion. He therefore says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him.”

It should certainly be noted that he says the Son of Man will come in majesty. By this he overturns the opinion [Col. 1215A] of certain heretics who said that, from the time of his resurrection and ascension, our Lord Jesus Christ no longer remained in the truly assumed nature of humanity. They failed to attend to what the angels said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). Here too the Lord plainly confesses that the Son of Man will come for judgment. For he is the same true Son of God and the same true Son of Man—not two, but one Son of God—who will be seen at the judgment only in his humanity. In his divinity, however, he will appear after the judgment to the elect alone, because it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI). Only the pure eyes of the saints will see the King of the ages in his beauty.

“When, therefore,” he says, “the Son of Man comes in [Col. 1215B] his majesty”—that is, in the power of his divinity, by which, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he will judge the human race, repaying the deserving with rewards and the wicked and sinners with punishments appropriate to them, according to which, as has been said, the reprobate will never be able to see him. He who once came in the assumed humanity to be judged did not cry out, and no one heard his voice in the streets, because he came so humbly that no one recognized him; now God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent. He will be accompanied by the ministry of angels, who will come with him to judgment, so that in their presence those who lived wickedly under their protection may be judged.

For angels are ministering spirits assigned to guard individual human beings. Of these the Lord says: “Their angels always see the face of the Father,” etc. (Matt. XVIII). Hence the Psalmist also says: “The heavens have proclaimed his righteousness” (Ps. XXI). The heavens will proclaim his righteousness because the holy angels will reverently proclaim God’s most just judgment.

“Then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty.” As for the throne upon which the Lord will sit in judgment, some understand it literally as that cloud in which the Lord ascended into heaven and in which he will also come for judgment. More appropriately, however, the holy Church is understood as God’s throne: the Lord will sit in it because he himself will appear glorious in his Church, glorifying her.

“And all nations will be gathered before him.” That is, all human beings, from the first Adam to the one who will be born at the end of the world—including those who have already died from the world’s beginning, and those who will be found alive in the body [Col. 1215D]. “And he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.”

Just as, he says, a shepherd separates one animal from another, so our Lord, who is the true shepherd whom his sheep recognize and follow, will separate the good from the wicked on the day of judgment. The sheep signify the saints, rejoicing in simplicity and innocence; they will be placed at the Lord’s right hand because they will be established in the hope of everlasting blessedness. The goats—petulant and wanton animals, always inflamed by lust—signify the reprobate, devoted to pleasures and enticements. They will be placed at the left because they will justly be subjected to everlasting condemnation.

But it must also be observed that he says not goats, but kids, will be placed on the left, since he has taken the goat in a good sense. It signifies the souls of the saints, who, like flocks of she-goats shorn and washed, have ascended from the washing place (Song IV), producing twin offspring and knowing no barrenness.

It should be understood that there will be two orders at the judgment, one of the good and one of the wicked; nevertheless, they will be divided fourfold. There will be two orders among the good. One will not be judged but will judge together with the Lord, as will be the case with the holy apostles and the perfect, to whom it was said: “You will sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). The other order of the good will be judged and saved; to them it will be said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. XXV).

Likewise, there will be two orders among the reprobate. One will not be judged and yet will be condemned; this will include the pagans who do not know God, of whom the Psalmist says: “The wicked will not rise in the judgment” (Ps. I). And the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III). The other order will consist of those who will be judged and condemned; to them it will be said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food.”

“Then the King will say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’” The King is Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and who on that day alone will be exalted and, by the authority of his power, pronounce the sentence. He will say this to those at his right hand—that is, to the saints who will belong to the portion of heavenly blessedness.

“Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth. This is a desirable, longed-for voice, to be received with every grace: by it the saints are called to perpetual goods and to a kingdom that will endure without end. They are rightly called blessed—that is, predestined to eternal blessing, which exists in Christ and through Christ. He calls it his Father’s kingdom, referring all power to the one whose Son he is, because from the one from whom he has his essence, from him he also has his power. Yet the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, just as their essence and majesty are one and the same.

He asserts that this kingdom was prepared for them from the world’s beginning because they were predestined and foreordained to it before the ages. The Apostle also says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. VIII).

But what merits earned such a reward, he enumerates by adding: “I was hungry, and you gave me food [Col. 1216D]. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you redeemed me.”

These words plainly express works of compassion and the generosity of benevolence, which is necessary for those enduring bodily need. But if we understand these things spiritually, we can perceive something more pleasing in the fulfillment of charity, because charity is to be shown not only toward the flesh of a brother who will one day die, but much more toward the soul that will live forever.

Therefore, whoever satisfies the hungry and thirsty with the bread of the word and gives drink from the water of wisdom fulfills the works of perfect charity. Whoever recalls one who has strayed from the way of truth by holy admonition and receives him through repentance into the house of holy Church truly performs works of compassion. Whoever, according to the Apostle, receives one who is weak in faith (1 Thess. V), and offers the consolation of compassion and words of comfort to one confined in the prison of afflictions and righteousness, certainly fulfills the obligations of true love and is therefore to be rewarded with the recompense of compassion.

Observe also that at the judgment the Lord recalls not the greatest virtues, but only works of love, which are necessary for the active life, so that he may clearly show that the kingdoms of heaven are owed to those who keep the commandments of charity; without charity, no virtue and no good work can please God.

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you [Col. 1217B], or naked and clothe you?’”

The saints will answer in this way, astonished at the immense and ineffable majesty of Christ the King. Whatever good they have done, however great it may have been, will then seem to them small and insignificant in comparison either with the magnitude of the terror that will be present then or with the abundance of the immeasurable reward.

Indeed, blessed Ephrem also says in a certain homily on the day of judgment, which he wrote full of compunction, that the saints will then ask the angels under whose protection they lived what good they have ever done, so as to be considered worthy of such glory and such a reward. And the King, answering, will say to them: “Amen, I say to you, insofar as you did it for one of these least of my brothers, you did it for me.”

Marvelous is the pious condescension of the Lord and Savior, who compensates the devotion of the righteous with such a reward that he declares himself to have been fed and clothed in the poor, and confirms that whatever has been spent on them he has received as done to himself.

Indeed, when he says: “Insofar as you did it for one of my least,” this can certainly be understood generally of every poor person: namely, that almsgiving given to anyone in need for Christ’s sake is received by Christ himself. Yet when the Lord significantly says, as though pointing to them, “for one of these least,” he shows that he is not speaking generally of just any poor people, but specifically of those who are poor in spirit, who voluntarily endure poverty for God’s sake. The faithful ought especially to assist these from their resources and make them their friends, so that they may be received by them into the eternal dwellings of the kingdom of heaven.

“Then he will say also to those at his left hand: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels [Col. 1217D].’”

To the reprobate placed at the left—who, while they lived in the world, always loved what is left, that is, transitory things, and never cared for eternal things, which are represented by the right—he says: “Depart from me, evildoers, into the eternal fire.” They are called accursed because, having consumed their lives in wickedness, they did not fear preparing themselves for eternal condemnation.

The wicked were never with the Lord, because the evildoer will not dwell beside him; yet they then seem to depart because, in the present, the wicked appear mingled with the good, from whom they will be separated at the judgment. The net of holy Church catches wicked fish together with good fish and drags them as far as the shore of the final examination [Col. 1218A]. But then, after the good fish have been gathered into vessels, the wicked will be thrown outside.

Likewise, in the Lord’s field the weeds grow together with the wheat; but when the threshing floor is reached, the wheat is stored in the granary, while the weeds are gathered into bundles and burned in the fire. Or, “depart” means that he commands them to be cast away from the presence of his vision and expelled into the outer darkness.

The accursed are therefore commanded to depart into the eternal fire, so that they may burn there without end—those who, in the present life, were unwilling to extinguish within themselves the fire of their vices. This fire was prepared for the devil and his angels because, just as God’s power prepared the kingdom for the righteous from the world’s beginning, so he ordained eternal fire for the devil, his angels, and the reprobate, in which they will be eternally tormented.

“For I was hungry, and you did not give me food. I was thirsty, and you did not [Col. 1218B] give me drink. I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me. I was naked, and you did not clothe me. I was sick and in prison, and you did not come to me.”

This sentence is greatly to be feared and dreaded. He does not say, “You seized what belonged to others,” but, “You did not give me food.” If stinginess is condemned in this way, what does robbery deserve? Or what will the one who has taken another’s property receive, if the one who has not given from his own is punished in this way? If such judgment awaits one who has not shown mercy, what will await one who has committed robbery?

“Then they too will answer, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?’”

They try to excuse themselves, as though they could deceive God, just as they once deceived human beings. But then they will have no excuse, since, while they could have been converted, they were unwilling, and they neglected to erase their sins through almsgiving.

“And answering, he will say to them: ‘Amen, I say to you, insofar as you did not do it for one of these, my least brothers, neither did you do it for me.’”

Whoever neglects to bestow a benefit on the humble and despised members of Christ is convicted of being less devoted to Christ, and consequently will never rejoice that he has given anything to him. “For whoever does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” (1 John IV).

It should be observed that here too, as above, unity is mentioned when it is said: “Insofar as you did not do it for one of my least, neither did you do it for me.” This suggests that the generosity of the one who strives to offer it with a sincere intention of heart in the unity of the Catholic faith is acceptable to God. But whoever separates himself from the unity of the faith through heretical perversity, or seeks human praise for his good work, has his mercy judged by Christ to be rejected and unworthy.

“And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

Origen teaches that all the reprobate—even the devil himself and his angels—can, after many ages, earn the forgiveness of sins and be freed from punishments. He asserts that it most fittingly accords with divine mercy that, just as God redeemed the human being, so he should also save the transgressing angel.

Yet this sentence most openly contradicts him: “These will go into eternal punishment.” But he argues on the contrary that the Lord said this to instill fear in all the perverse, so that they might dread eternal punishments and cease sinning. Against this it must be answered that, if this is not true, then neither is what Truth adds true: “But the righteous into eternal life.” But—something unlawful to say—just as he falsely threatened the former in order to strike them with fear, so he falsely promised the latter in order to deceive them with an empty hope.

Perhaps someone might say that it is unjust for a person to pay an eternal penalty for a temporal and momentary pleasure. But it should be understood that those are subjected to eternal torments who persist in evil with an obstinate will and are unwilling ever to put an end to their crimes. Moreover, even if they had lived forever, they would certainly have wished to sin forever. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, such people will go into eternal punishment.

Accordingly, God’s mercy must be sought, and our hearts must be raised together with the hands of almsgiving, so that in the present life the fire of his fear may burn away our evils. Thus, at the judgment of the dread examination, may he graciously free us from being placed among the wicked at the left and set us at the right with all the saints, and count us among the holy angels in eternal life, in which he lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIV. ON THE TUESDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

At that time, when Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, etc. (Matt. XXI).

The Lord and God, Christ, author and restorer of the human race, had chosen beforehand with the Father, before the foundation of the world, both when and where he would suffer for the salvation [Col. 1219C] of human beings. When, therefore, the fullness of that time had been completed and his Passion was already at hand, he wished to approach the place of his Passion, where he could be found by those through whom that Passion was to be carried out, lest he be regarded as though fleeing from death. For he did not fear death; rather, by his power he commanded death.

Therefore the evangelist says: “When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, saying: ‘Who is this?’” At the Savior’s entrance the city was shaken, amazed at the multitude of the people. We read something similar concerning his ascension, when the angels, seeing the Lord ascend in triumphal procession and carry his already glorified flesh into the heavens, asked in amazement: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII).

It should be noted that, as another evangelist says (John XII), six days before Passover the Lord came to Bethany, where he had raised Lazarus; and on the following day, seated upon an ass, he entered Jerusalem while the crowds acclaimed divine praises. This had formerly been foreshadowed mystically in the paschal lamb.

For it is written in the Law (Exod. XII): “On the tenth day of the first month, each one shall take a lamb for his families and households, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening.” Therefore, in accordance with this prophecy concerning the paschal lamb, the Lord Jesus entered the city of Jerusalem on the tenth day of the first month—that is, five days before Passover—while the council of the elders and rulers was conspiring against him [Col. 1220A]. He awaited the hour when, for the salvation of the world, he would offer himself to God the Father as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance.

The people were saying: “This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth.” When the proud Jews asked who he was who was entering the city with such glory, the simple crowd confessed what it knew: “This,” they said, “is Jesus the prophet.”

They called him a prophet because they were mistaken and did not know what they were saying. They did not know to call him God or the Son of God, but their error was full of perfect knowledge. For Moses had said of him: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deut. XVIII). And he himself says of himself: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII).

“Prophet” should therefore be understood in such a way that he is the Lord of the prophets, just as he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

“And Jesus entered the temple.” By entering the city and first approaching the temple, the Lord showed us the pattern of religious conduct that we ought to follow. When we enter a town, a fortress, or any place where a house of prayer has been consecrated to God, we ought first to hasten there. After commending ourselves to God through devotion to prayer, we should then proceed at once to conduct the business required by the necessities of fragile life.

“And he began to cast out those selling and buying in it, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.”

Among all the miracles that the Lord performed bodily in the world, this is the most excellent and greatest. For, as blessed Jerome says, it was a greater deed that one unarmed man cast many thousands of armed men out of the temple than that he raised Lazarus, dead for four days, from the dead [Col. 1220C]. The splendor of divinity shone forth in the appearance of humanity; and therefore, when they saw an extraordinary brightness radiating from a human face, they turned their backs to be struck and did not dare to resist.

“And he said to them: ‘It is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” but you have made it a den of robbers.’”

That house of God had first been built by Solomon, and afterward by Jesus the priest and Zerubbabel—not because God dwells in temples made by human hands, but so that his name might be invoked there, and so that he might hear the prayers of the devout people, receive their vows, and accept their gifts and offerings.

But they had made it a den of robbers because they remained in the temple for the purpose either of punishing bodily those who did not give gifts or of spiritually killing those who did give them. For the commandment of the Law was that three times a year everyone should assemble from the various regions of the Jewish kingdom at the most august and holy temple in the world: at Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths. The same Law commanded that they should not appear before the Lord empty-handed.

It often happened that those who came from more distant regions did not have anything to offer in the Lord’s sacrifice, because they could not bring their livestock with them on account of the length of the journey. Therefore the priests kept the fattest animals required for sacrificial use, selling them to those who did not have any, and then receiving the animals purchased again in exchange for the money, thus plundering the simple people.

There were also some so poor that they lacked even the money for expenses and food; they had not only no offerings, but not even the means with which to buy them. For this reason those same priests established money changers in the temple, who would lend them money on this pretext.

But because the Law prohibited interest and they could not openly demand double the money from them, they devised another fraud: they accepted various kinds of gifts in place of interest, namely raisins and fruits of different kinds. Thus they demanded in those goods that are bought with money what they were not permitted to demand in money.

They themselves called this, in their own language, *colybistae*—those who gave *colybia*, that is, cheap little gifts, which in Greek are called *tragemata* and in Latin *bellaria*.

When the Lord saw such business and fraud being carried on in the house of his Father, as blessed John says, he made a whip of cords and drove an innumerable multitude from the temple (John II).

Let the priests of the Church take heed of this and beware lest they turn the house of God into a den of robbers. A robber is one who pursues profit from religion and seeks an opportunity for business through the worship of holiness. They must therefore fear lest, just as those people were expelled from the material temple, so they may be expelled from the spiritual temple.

For every day the Lord enters the house of his Father, namely, holy Church, and drives out those occupied with shameful profits; and he regards sellers and buyers alike as guilty of one crime. Sellers are those who grant sacred orders for a payment. Buyers are those who give money for an injustice and, having paid the price to their patrons, purchase sin.

It should be noted that it says he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. What else is signified by the tables of the money changers than the altars, which, through the avarice of wicked priests, are made into tables of money changers? What else is signified by the seats of those selling doves than the dignity of teaching in the Church, which, when it turns toward profit, is itself reduced to nothing?

And what else is signified by the doves than the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove over the baptized Lord? Who are those who sell doves except those who bestow the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands in exchange for payment? But the Lord overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such people.

For any bishop who has sold the grace of the Holy Spirit, even if he now appears to shine before human beings in a pontifical vestment, has already been deprived of the priesthood in the sight of God. Hence the sacred canons anathematize the heresy of simony and command that those who seek payment for spiritual grace bestowed should be deprived of the priesthood.

Morally speaking: just as the temple in a city surpasses the other buildings, so the life of religious people surpasses that of the rest of the faithful. The mind of the faithful is therefore itself the temple of God, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. III).

If this faithful mind, abandoning innocence, brings forth perverse thoughts aimed at injuring its neighbor, it certainly becomes a den of robbers [Col. 1222A]. It is no longer called a house of prayer, but a hiding place of robbers, for it contemplates doing what may harm its neighbor.

Therefore let there be no commerce in the house of our breast, no dealings of buyers and sellers, lest Jesus enter in anger and, with the whip of stern severity, punish the accumulated filth of his dwelling.

“And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.” After expelling the unworthy and profaners of the temple, he miraculously healed the blind and the lame. By this he gave his adversaries evidence of his power and confirmed, by such testimony, the voice of the children praising him and crying, “Hosanna in the highest.” He showed by his work that they agreed with him in their voices, and also that, seeing Christ’s great power, his adversaries might be converted and believe.

He illuminated the blind before their eyes so that they might receive the light of faith; he straightened the lame so that they might cast off the lameness of their minds and begin to have better feet for right action.

“Seeing the children crying in the temple, ‘Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,’ they said: ‘Do you hear what these are saying?’”

They were indignant that they were acclaiming Christ with what seemed to be divine praises and with words that belonged to God alone. But the Lord so completely fortified his reply and so carefully measured what he said that he neither left himself open to the plots of his slanderers nor rejected those praises as though they were being offered to him by mistaken children.

He did not answer what they wished to hear: “The children speak well; they have a correct understanding of me.” Nor did he say: “The children are mistaken; you ought to pardon their ignorance.” Instead he replied: “I hear,” and thus confirmed their voices by the testimony of the Psalmist, saying: “Have you never read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise’?”

God the Father perfected praise from the mouth of infants and nursing babies because, through the simple and innocent, he bore witness to his Son, by which he most clearly confounded his enemies, the most hostile persecutors among the Jews.

“And leaving them, he went out to Bethany,” which is interpreted as “house of obedience.” By this it was already being shown that he would abandon the Synagogue and pass over to the house of obedience—that is, to the Church of the Gentiles.

At the same time, it should be considered that he was so poor that he did not even have a hut, and so flattered no one that, in so great and populous a city, no one received him. By day he preached in Jerusalem, but in the evening he returned to Bethany, where his friend Lazarus was with his sisters Martha and Mary.

Truly happy and exceedingly blessed are those who have deserved to have the Lord as their guest, at whose presence all sorrow was removed and all salutary and joyful things were provided. But those too are most happy and supremely blessed who keep themselves so chaste and free from every evil that the Lord deigns to dwell and remain among them.

Let us therefore ask this with earnest prayers and holy desires: that he may cleanse from us every vice and everything foul, everything unworthy of his sight; and that he may adorn us with the flowers of virtues, so that the Lord and our Redeemer, Jesus [Col. 1223A] Christ, may deign to make the inner chambers of our hearts a dwelling perfectly suited to himself. He lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXV. ON THE WEDNESDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

*(From the works of the venerable Bede the priest.)*

At that time the scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus, saying: “Teacher,” etc. (Matt. XII).

It is related above, etc. You may consult this homily in the venerable Bede, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 364, where it is entitled: “ON THE WEDNESDAY OF THE FIRST WEEK OF LENT.”

## HOMILY LXXVI. ON THE THURSDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

[Col. 1223B] At that time Jesus said to those among the Jews who had believed: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples,” etc. (John VIII).

Speaking to the crowds and proclaiming the mysteries of his divinity, as the holy evangelist John says above, many believed in him. Many already believed in him, though not all, because he had not yet been preached to everyone; the sound of the apostles’ preaching had not yet gone out into all the earth; nor had the apostles yet been commanded: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 28). To those, therefore, who had come to believe in him, he was speaking, saying: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” They had already been initiated into spiritual teaching; they had already begun to be there, and therefore he says: “If you remain in my word”—that is, in the faith that had begun to exist within you who believe—“then you will truly be my disciples”: disciples, certainly, of goodness, disciples of righteousness and of the highest truth.

But to what must we attain? Faith is the foundation. From this foundation, then, toward what height shall we advance? “You will know,” he says, “the truth.” Christ is the truth, and he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14). Therefore, whoever knows the truth knows the Lord. We must consider what it means to know that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2). For faith is believing what you do not see; truth, however, is seeing what you have believed. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14).

This, then, is the reward and satisfaction that the Lord promises to us who remain in his word, which the Psalmist longs for when he says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). “And the truth will set you free”—that is, it will make you free, so that, liberated from love of the world, you may securely love God, who alone is to be loved above all things, and say with the Psalmist: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72).

Then the Jews said to him: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone.” Those who had believed were not saying this, but certain others among them who did not believe. When they heard the Lord promising them liberation, they became all the more indignant at the very thing that ought to have made them grateful and submissive, as though he had designated as slaves those to whom he was promising freedom. And in truth they were slaves of sin, and they could be liberated from that most evil slavery only through the truth.

But they, thinking only of freedom according to the flesh, began to exalt themselves over the nobility of their flesh, saying: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone.” Foolish and empty pride! What do they mean by saying: “We have never been enslaved to anyone”? Joseph, certainly, served in Egypt, of whom it is written: “His hands served in the basket” (Ps. 80). The Jewish people themselves, moreover, were transported into Egypt and oppressed by Pharaoh and the Egyptians in the harshest slavery—not merely in gold and silver, but in mud and brick. Hence the Lord very frequently reproaches them by recalling that he brought them out of the house of slavery and the iron furnace of Egypt.

Perhaps, however, they might have said that their ancestors, not they themselves, had served; but to those who were speaking to him, what of the tribute they paid to the Romans? For this reason they had laid a trap of accusation for the Lord when they deceitfully asked him: “Is it lawful to pay the census tax to Caesar, or not?” Let us now hear what the Lord answered those who were lying and puffed up with empty notions of freedom: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

“Amen” is a Hebrew word; in Latin it can truly be rendered “truly.” It is, if one may so speak, the Lord’s oath. This word is found repeated from time to time only by the evangelist John, and it is found in this form among all interpreters; no one has translated it into another language, out of reverence for the Lord’s sacrament. He repeats “amen” in order, by that very repetition, to make his hearers attentive.

This statement must be heard with great fear. For who would not tremble at the Lord’s saying: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin”? What person is there who would dare to say that he is not a sinner? If, then, every human being is a sinner, certainly every human being is a slave of sin. Miserable indeed is the condition of being a slave of sin, and a slave of the devil, who is the author of sin. Human slaves, for the most part, flee harsh and cruel masters and find rest in fleeing; but the slave of sin has nowhere to flee. For an avenging conscience follows him, always clinging to him and tormenting him; it does not even cease for a moment to agitate him with the heaviest goads supplied by the memory of his sins.

Since, then, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, what hope of freedom can remain? But we have heard the Lord terrifying us; let us also hear him consoling us. For he instills fear in such a way that he brings security. It follows: “But the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever.”

The house of God is the Church of God. The Apostle speaks to the faithful, saying: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3). The slave of sin does not remain in the house forever, because whoever remains in sin does not remain in the Church. See how plainly he shows that it is one thing to sin and another to be a slave of sin. No one can fail to be a sinner, but one can avoid being a slave of sin. To remain in sin is to be a slave of sin.

The slave does not remain in the house forever because, even if the wicked appear to be placed within the bosom of the Church, they have already been cast out from the Church in the presence of God, who sees all things; and at the last, on the day of judgment, they will be separated from the company of the elect and placed on the left.

Therefore, let everyone who recognizes that he is a slave of sin strive to cast off the yoke of the harshest slavery. Let him believe in the Son of God and obey the Son’s commandments, so that he too may become a son of God. For the only Son of God has given this grace to those who believe in him and love him: that they too may deserve to become sons of God.

“If, therefore, the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.” This is the true hope: that we may be freed by the Free One; and, liberated from sin, become servants of Christ; liberated from desire, become servants of love. This is true and perfect freedom: to serve God Christ and to love him who rescued us from slavery to darkness and called us into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

But the Jews, taking pride in the nobility of their flesh, disdained becoming free, although they were slaves of sin. Therefore the Lord consequently says: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” As though he were saying: You are indeed Abraham’s children according to the flesh, but not according to imitation. I acknowledge in you the origin of the flesh, but I do not acknowledge faith.

“But you seek to kill me.” There is the source of your degeneration; there is why you are not children of Abraham. “You seek,” he says, “to kill me.” Certainly you would never be thinking of this if you were children of Abraham. “Because my word finds no place in you”—that is, it has no place in your hearts. “It finds no place in you,” he says, meaning that it is not received by you. For if it were received in you, it would certainly receive you.

“What I have seen with my Father, I speak.” What did Christ see with the Father? He saw the truth; he saw himself, certainly, because he is the Word who was in the beginning with God. He therefore saw the truth with the Father, and spoke the truth in the world, because he proclaimed himself and God the Father to the world.

“And you do what you have seen with your father.” What they would do he had told them above: “You seek,” he says, “to kill me.” But they had not seen this with Abraham their father, whom Scripture testifies to have been God’s friend. Of what father, then, is he now speaking, whose works the Jews were doing? This will be revealed most clearly in what follows. For he will say that their father is the devil—not because they had been begotten and created by him, but because they were his children insofar as they were evil. They were his children by imitation, not by creation.

With this father, then, they had seen the works they were doing, because they had become imitators of the devil: they were unwilling not only to receive the Son of God but were even plotting to kill him.

They answered him: “Our father is Abraham.” As though he could say anything against Abraham or find fault with him in any respect! But the Lord was not speaking about Abraham, because Abraham was not the kind of man who should be reproved, but rather one who should be praised by the Lord. They were provoking him to say something against Abraham, so that they might take vengeance on him as an enemy of Abraham.

But let us hear what the Lord answered them, praising Abraham and condemning them: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this.”

When the Jews boasted of Abraham on their own behalf and were constructing an accusation against the Lord on that account, the Lord did not answer what they wanted to hear. Rather, unwilling to give them an opportunity for accusation, he called himself a man—what they saw and believed him to be merely.

He therefore said: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham”—that is, you would love me and rejoice at my presence as Abraham did, who rejoiced that he might see my day, and saw it and was glad (John 14). But now you prove that you are not Abraham’s children, because you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth.

He spoke the truth to them when he proclaimed himself and the Father to them, and he had heard this truth from God because he who is the truth had been begotten by God the Father. To hear from him means nothing other than to be from the Father.

“You seek,” he says, “to kill me; Abraham did not do this.” Therefore you prove that you are not his children by doing works contrary to his. Above he had said: “I know that you are Abraham’s children,” establishing their fleshly origin. But now he shows that they are not Abraham’s children because they were unwilling to imitate Abraham’s works.

Christians are much more rightly called Abraham’s children—imitators of Abraham’s faith and works—than are the Jews, whose flesh came from him, but whose life did not.

“You do the works of your father,” he says—that is, of the devil, because he was a murderer from the beginning, and you, his followers, seek to kill me.

Therefore they said to him: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.”

Having so often put forward the nobility of Abraham’s lineage, and having so often been convicted that they were not Abraham’s children, they finally began to understand that the Lord was speaking not of fleshly generation but of similarity of life and imitation of conduct.

They were, as it were, saying among themselves: Whenever we mention Abraham, he will say: “Why do you not imitate the one whose lineage you boast of?” Let us say that God is our Father and see what he answers us. “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.”

They had read in the Scriptures that spiritual fornication is called idolatry, by which the wretched soul is subjected to demons as though prostituted to them. Therefore they said: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.” Thus they boasted that they had always worshiped God, who called Israel his firstborn.

But let us hear what answer was given to them: “If God were your Father,” he says, “you would certainly love me.” As though he were saying: You boast that you have God as your Father; recognize me at least as your brother. And if you are unwilling to honor me as God or as the Son of God, at least love me as a brother.

“For I proceeded from God and came.” This procession is eternal and ineffable, beyond time, because the Son proceeded from the Father as God, equal as Son and Word of the Father. He proceeded from God and came because the Word who was in the beginning became flesh and dwelt among us. To come belongs to humanity, just as to remain belongs to divinity. He proceeded from the Father and came because he was sent by the Father into the world, as he says: “For I have not come of myself, but he sent me.” This sending must certainly be understood as the incarnation.

“Why do you not recognize my speech? Because you cannot hear my word.” Why could they not hear his word, except because they were unwilling to believe in him and be corrected from their impiety? Why further could they not hear? Because they had chosen to remain children of the devil.

Hence it follows: “You are from your father the devil.”

He says that the Jews are children of the devil, not by birth but by imitation. For it is customary in sacred Scripture to call people children by imitation or likeness, as the prophet Ezekiel says to Jerusalem: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). Because the Jews had imitated the impieties of the Amorites, they are said to have had as parents those from whose conduct they were born, and with whom they would be condemned for similar wickedness.

Every human being, therefore, insofar as he has been created by God, is good; but insofar as, by sinning through free choice, he subjects himself to the devil, he has the devil as his father. The devil himself, insofar as he possesses natural substance, insofar as he is a creature and was made by God, is good; but insofar as he fell through pride and disobedience, he became the devil and is evil. For “devil” is interpreted as “one who falls downward.”

The Lord therefore says to the Jews, imitators of the devil: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to fulfill the desires of your father.” What the desires of their father were, he had said above: “You seek to kill me.” These were the devil’s desires, because he too envied humanity and killed; for through the serpent he deceived Eve, and through her deceived the man, and thus killed him, because he made a sinner from one who was righteous and a mortal from one who was immortal.

“He was a murderer from the beginning.” The devil came against the first man armed not with iron but with a deadly persuasion; he killed not with a sword but with iron. Therefore, whoever persuades another person to evil, drawing him into sin, kills him. Of such people the Psalmist says: “The children of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56).

“And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.” He did not stand in the truth because, having fallen away from the truth, he was unwilling to remain in the holiness of his origin. He had been made in the image and likeness of God, but through pride he retained the image, since he did not lose the nature of immortality; yet he lost the truth of likeness, because from a just and good angel he became an unjust and evil devil.

Concerning him it is further added: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar and its father”—that is understood, the father of lying. The devil was a liar from himself, because he had previously heard and learned lying from no one; he himself generated his own lie. Therefore, when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things.

And just as God is truthful and the Father of truth, so the devil is a liar and the father of lying. Why is he a liar? Because he did not stand in the truth—that is, he did not remain in God, because God is truthful.

Human beings too, because they turned away from the truth and departed from God by sinning, are called liars, as the Psalmist says: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115). And because humanity had been deceived by the devil and had become a liar, it was the devil’s child—not by nature, as was said earlier, but by imitation.

“Which of you will convict me of sin?” Because he had reproved them for their sin, he gives them the opportunity, so that, if they can, they too may reproach him for his sin.

And we must consider how great is the humility of our Redeemer. He had come to release human beings from their sins, yet he does not disdain to show that he is not a sinner—the one who, by the power of his divinity, could justify sinners.

“If I speak the truth to you, why do you not believe me?” Christ is the truth. And what else is truth than to speak the truth? He was speaking the truth when he said: “I proceeded from God and came.” Why, then, do you not believe me? Why? Except because you are from the devil and have chosen to remain in the father of lying.

“Whoever is from God hears the words of God.” To hear the words of God is to obey his commandments, which he speaks through the Scriptures. Therefore, if the one who is from God hears the words of God, and whoever is not from him cannot hear his words, let each person examine himself: whether he perceives the words of God with the hearing of his heart, and he will understand from whom he comes.

God commands us to desire our heavenly homeland, to trample underfoot the desires of the flesh, to flee the glory of the world, not to seize what belongs to others, and to give away what belongs to us. If someone recognizes that this voice of God has sounded in the ear of his heart, let him rejoice in recognizing that he is from God.

But, as may be said not without sorrow, there are some who do not deign to perceive the word of God even with the ear of the body. What else do such people openly indicate except that they are members of the devil and have chosen to remain in his lot rather than in God’s?

Every day the Lord cries out through his Scriptures, inviting us to flee the pleasures of the world that is destined to perish and to pass over, in the desires of our minds, to the joys of everlasting goods that do not come to an end. Let us therefore now strive to follow him who calls and admonishes us, lest, if we despise the words of him who speaks now, when he comes as judge in majesty we should be despised by him as unknown and alien.

Rather, let us hasten to hear him in the present and obey his commandments, so that we may deserve to be received by him into the blessed dwelling of the Father; may the same Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXVII. ON THE FRIDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

At that time there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem a pool called the Sheep Pool, etc. (John 5).

In the Gospel reading that we have just heard, two miracles have been recounted to us: one accomplished invisibly through angelic agency, the other visibly manifested through the Lord’s presence. We must therefore briefly explain the mysteries of both.

“There was,” says the evangelist, “a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.” Because God had become human for the sake of human beings, he celebrated with human beings the solemnities established by God’s law.

“Now there was in Jerusalem a pool called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes. In these lay a great multitude of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the withered, waiting for the movement of the water.”

*Probatica* in Greek is called *pecualis* in Latin, for πρόβατον means “sheep.” That pool is called the Sheep Pool because there the priests washed the carcasses of the victims that they sacrificed in God’s temple.

Mystically, the Sheep Pool, which was surrounded by five porticoes, signifies the Jewish people, protected on every side by the observance of the law so that they should not sin. For the five porticoes signify the law contained in the five books.

And fittingly that people is represented by the water of the pool, because just as the water of a pool may at one time lie peacefully in the wind and at another be disturbed when the same winds rush upon it, so that people sometimes used to preserve the purity of life and sometimes be agitated by the temptations of unclean spirits.

The same pool is also appropriately called the Sheep Pool because there were some among that people who, by virtue of a simple and innocent life, could rightly please God and say with the Psalmist: “But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture” (Ps. 94).

The multitude of the sick lying in the aforementioned porticoes and waiting for the movement of the water signifies those who, hearing the words of the law, grieved that they could not fulfill it by their own strength and therefore longed with all the desire of their souls for the help of the Lord’s grace.

“A great multitude of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the withered lay there,” he says. The blind were those who did not yet possess the light of faith; the lame were those who knew the good things that ought to be done but could not rise to accomplish them with the steps of good works; the withered were those who possessed the eye of knowledge but lacked the richness of hope and love.

Such people lay in the five porticoes, but they could be healed only when the angel descended into the pool, because through the law comes knowledge of sin, while the grace of forgiveness could be given only through Christ.

The angel who visibly descended into the pool and moved the water, imparting to it the power of healing, aptly signified this. For the movement of the water signifies the Lord’s Passion, which took place when the Jewish people were stirred up.

Therefore this angel of great counsel, that is, the messenger of the Father’s will, descended into the pool of the Jewish people clothed in flesh. He stirred them up by his miracles and teaching so that they would inflict the death of the cross upon him who was able not only to heal the human race from the illnesses of sins but also to free it from eternal death itself.

Those who descended into the disturbed water of the pool were healed because, through the Lord’s Passion—which the movement of the water signifies—we have been redeemed from the curse of the law.

The law of Moses, although it taught what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided, brought no one to perfection. It was like one who, having led people out of the dwelling places of their former ignorance, kept the sick in the porticoes but did not heal them.

The grace and faith of the Lord’s Passion, however, heal all the infirmities of our iniquities and, as though casting us out of the porticoes into the disturbed water of the pool, wash us from the sins that the law had revealed through the water of baptism, according to what the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

We must also note what is said: that whoever first entered the pool after the water had been stirred was healed, whatever illness he was afflicted with. “One,” he says, was healed from so great a multitude of sick people, because there is “one God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4).

Therefore, whoever is instructed in the mysteries of Christ in baptism within the unity of the Catholic faith is completely healed from every sickness of sins. But whoever differs from the unity of the Church does not deserve to possess the salvation that comes from the One and through the One.

Having said this about the first miracle, which was invisibly performed through the angel, let us now say a little about the next, which was visibly performed through the true Angel, Christ. In it also one person was healed.

The Lord could indeed have healed all the sick who were there, but he wished to heal only one for the sake of a definite mystery, so that he might clearly show that outside the Church there is no place of salvation.

“There was a man there who had been in his infirmity for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been ill for a long time, he said to him: Do you want to be healed? The sick man answered him: Lord, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred. For while I am coming, another goes down before me. Jesus said to him: Rise, take up your mat, and walk. And immediately the man was healed, and he took up his mat and walked.”

When the Lord was about to heal the sick man, wasting away in a long illness, he asked whether he wished to be healed—not because he was unaware that he wished it, but in order to kindle in him a greater desire for health. By lying there for so long, he had almost despaired of salvation and did not even know how to ask for his restoration.

Therefore he began to plead the cause of his inability and complain that he had no one to put him into the pool after the water had been stirred. But the Lord, taking pity on the sick man’s weakness and likewise on his simple ignorance, said to him: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.”

Immediately he recovered his strength and felt the vigor that he had lost for so long. He took up the bed on which he had lain and went to his house.

According to the spiritual understanding, this man, held by an illness of many years, represents a sinner weighed down by the multitude of many and grave crimes. The very length of time during which the sick man is said to have lain there corresponds to this meaning.

For he is said to have been ill for thirty-eight years—namely, two short of forty. The number forty, which is formed by four times ten, is usually taken in Scripture to signify the perfection of right action. For a person lives rightly who strives to fulfill the Decalogue of the law through the four books of the holy Gospel.

Whoever neglects to keep the love of God and neighbor, which the Scriptures of both the law and the Gospel commend, is short of that perfection by two.

The Lord also expressed this symbolically when, intending to heal the sick man, he commanded him: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.”

Our bed is understood to be that which has offered us consolation in bodily or spiritual infirmity. Once healed, we are commanded to carry it, so that we may also provide assistance to it in its needs.

Therefore the Lord says to the man whom he was healing: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.”

“Rise,” he says: shake off the torpor of vices that you have endured for so long in your sickness, and rise to the exercise of the virtues.

“Take up your bed”: carry your neighbor by patiently bearing his weaknesses, by whom you were for a long time and to a great extent sustained while you still groaned under the heavy burden of temptations.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6).

“Walk” through daily progress in good works; advance from virtue to virtue. Rise by abandoning sins; take up your bed by helping your brother; walk by desiring the heavenly homeland and hastening to behold the face of the Creator.

Now it was the Sabbath on that day. Therefore the Jews said to the man who had been healed: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to take up your mat.”

The madness of the Jews was astonishing and utterly astounding. When they ought to have believed in the unexpected healing of a man who had long been ill and to have praised divine power, they instead took offense and accused both the Savior and the one who had been saved.

They accused the Savior because he had healed a man on the Sabbath and commanded him to take up his bed; they reproved the healed man because he had carried his mat on the Sabbath.

They defended the letter of the law with the greatest foolishness, ignorant of the Lord Savior’s dispensation. He had once given that very law through a servant, and now, coming in person, he was preparing to change the same law into the grace of the holy Gospel, so that what had formerly been observed according to the letter and carnally by carnal people might henceforth be spiritually embraced and observed by spiritual people.

In the end, the people had been commanded to abstain from every servile work on the seventh day. But in the spiritual observance of the Sabbath—which is found in the light of the sevenfold Holy Spirit—we are commanded to rest from every sin, which is truly understood as servile work, not for one day but throughout the whole time of our life. We are commanded not only to abstain from evil deeds but also to devote ourselves to good works.

This was clearly demonstrated in the healing of this man, when the Lord commanded the one whom he was freeing from his sickness not only to rise but also to take up his bed. He was plainly indicating that those who wish to rise from the corruption of vices must, after shaking off the torpor of negligence and carrying the pledge of brotherly love, hasten at the command of their Creator; nor should they cease from the work of goodness they have begun because of the contradiction or persecution of the wicked.

This man, when the Jews contradicted him and forbade him to carry his bed, saying, “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to take up your mat,” did not put down the bed. Rather, steadfastly continuing what he had begun, he replied: “The one who made me well, he said to me: Take up your mat and walk.”

He preferred to obey the commands of the one by whom he had been healed rather than believe the false religion of those who envied his healing and the glory of their Lord.

And they asked him: “Who is this man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat and walk’?” But, as the evangelist says, he did not know who he was. He had already been saved, but he still did not know his Savior. Nevertheless, he was worthy that the Savior should reveal himself to him, since he had obeyed his command with such devotion.

But Jesus had withdrawn from the crowd gathered in that place. He had withdrawn, he says, from the agitated crowd, depriving them of divine assistance and indicating against whose powers their stubborn malice was attempting to resist.

Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him: “See, you have been healed.”

By the fact that the one who had been healed recognized Jesus not in the crowd but in the temple, we are mystically instructed that, if we desire to recognize the grace of our Creator and to attain to the vision of him, we must flee the crowd of evil thoughts and affections and carefully avoid the gatherings of wicked people. They try to hinder our good purpose either by displaying evil examples, mocking our works, or even denouncing them.

Let us devotedly take refuge in the temple of God, where we may strive to give him thanks for the benefits of his commandments and to pray for benefits yet to be received. Let us prepare ourselves as the temple of God, in which he may mercifully deign to come and make his dwelling.

We must also attend to what the Lord says to the man whom he had healed: “See, you have been healed; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you.”

By these words he showed that the man had been ill because of his sins and could be healed only when those sins had been forgiven. We must believe, however, that the Lord who healed him outwardly from his infirmity also absolved him inwardly from his crime.

Therefore the Lord carefully warned him not to sin any longer, lest by sinning again he incur the sentence of a more severe condemnation.

Illness, however, is not always given to human beings solely on account of sins. The holy doctors have identified five ways in which illness comes upon human beings.

Sometimes illness is given so that the glory of God may be revealed, as in the case of the man born blind and in the case of Lazarus, concerning whom the Lord said: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of the Son of God through it” (John 11).

At times illness is given for testing and the increase of virtues, as in the case of the blessed Job and Tobiah. Although they had been holy before the scourging, they appeared holier after the scourging and more approved through the testing.

Often illness is given for the preservation of virtues, as in the case of the blessed Apostle Paul.

Furthermore, illness is given to human beings for the correction of wrongdoing, as in the case of this man, who had lain sick for thirty-eight years, and as in the case of the paralytic to whom the Lord said: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9). Of such people it is said: “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12).

The fifth mode concerns the reprobate, to whom illness is given so that they may begin to be tormented here and pass through these temporal torments to eternal ones. This happened to Antiochus and Herod, in whom was fulfilled what is written: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17).

However divine providence may command us to become ill, let us always learn humbly to submit to the scourges of a merciful Father and to revere his most just judgments, considering that we endure less than we deserve, mindful of the saying: “Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord” (Job 5).

If we do this, we shall deserve both to be perfected in the present through chastisement and, in the future, to attain eternal rest through scourges; may our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXX. ON THE SAME SUNDAY OF LENT

*(From the works of the venerable priest Bede.)*

At that time Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon, etc. (Matt. 15).

## HOMILY LXXXI. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From the blessed John Chrysostom.)*

[Col. 1233C]

At that time Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon, etc. (Matt. 15).

The evangelist marvels. Behold the woman, the devil’s ancient armor, who drove the human being from paradise, the mother of sin, the beginning of iniquity, the material of transgression: that very woman has come, that very nature. A new and astonishing thing: the Jews flee, and the woman follows. “And behold, a woman who had come out from those regions cried out to him, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” O splendid confession! The woman becomes an evangelist, proclaiming his deity and his dispensation. For she confesses both his lordship and his incarnation.

“Have mercy on me.” Observe the woman’s philosophic soul, saying: “Have mercy [Col. 1233D] on me.” She says: “I have no consciousness of good works, nor confidence in a righteous life. I flee to mercy, to the tranquil harbor of sinners. I flee to mercy, where judgment ceases; I flee to mercy, where salvation is ineffable.”

“Tell me, woman, how did you dare, being sinful and wicked, to approach him?”

“I know,” she says, “what I am doing.” Observe the woman’s prudence. She does not ask James, does not entreat John, does not go to Peter, nor direct herself toward the apostolic choir. She did not seek a mediator, but took repentance as her companion in place of them all, and thus went to the highest fountain.

“Therefore,” she says, “he descended; therefore he assumed flesh and became human, so that I too might dare to speak to him. Above, in heaven, the cherubim tremble before him and the seraphim fear him; below, a prostitute speaks with him: ‘Have mercy on me.’” A bare utterance, yet containing an immensity of salvation: “Have mercy on me.”

“Therefore,” she says, “you came; therefore you assumed flesh; therefore you became what I am.”

O astonishing thing! Above, trembling; below, confidence: “Have mercy on me. I have no need of a mediator; have mercy on me.”

“What do you need?”

“I seek mercy,” she says.

“What do you suffer?”

“My daughter,” she says, “is grievously tormented by a demon.”

The woman has gone forth as her daughter’s advocate. She does not bring the sick girl, but presents devoted faith, bringing this within herself and saying: “The one to whom I am going is God. He sees what is absent, observes what is hidden, knows all things. Have mercy on me; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

The worst of weeping, the goad of nature, tears apart my inward parts. What shall I do, miserable woman? Observe her prudence. She did not say, “Have mercy on my daughter,” but, “Have mercy on me.” For the girl is held by an insensible affliction: she does not know what she has, does not feel the pain; she has a veiled heart, covered over by the most wicked spirit.

“Have mercy on me, who witness long-lasting evils. Every day I see my torments. Where shall I go? Where shall I turn? I do not dare go into the wilderness, nor can I leave her alone. I cannot remain at home, because the enemy is within: there are waves in the harbor; in tranquility there is a storm. I cannot find by what name to call her. Shall I call her dead? Yet she moves. Shall I call her alive? Yet she does not know what she is doing. I cannot find by what name to address her. Have mercy on me.

“If my daughter were dead, I would not suffer such things. I would surely have entrusted her body to the earth’s embrace, and when time had passed I would have forgotten my sorrows, and my grief would have subsided. But now I have a dead body that stubbornly remains alive without sensation, a pitiable spectacle: wounds of suffering that grow moment by moment, multiplied afflictions of pain [‘multiplied by pains’]. For I see her eyes turned askew, her bloodshot gaze, her twisted hands, her loosened hair, her contorted neck, her foaming mouth; I see the enemy setting things aflame [‘walking about’] though he is not visible; I see the torturer shut within, and lashes resounding; no one asking questions, while she speaks with a cry. I am present as the woman who speaks of my sorrows; I am present while nature goads me.

“Have mercy on me. A terrible storm: suffering and fear. The suffering of nature, the fear of the demon. I cannot approach or touch her. Suffering drives me on; fear thrusts me back. Have mercy on me.”

Consider the woman’s philosophy; look upon her noble soul. She did not go to diviners, did not summon magicians, did not seek amulets, did not bring impostor women, those who customarily provoke demons and increase the wound by their invocations [‘incantations’]. She abandoned all those things, dismissed the devil’s falsehoods, despised all the refuse, and came to the saving harbor of our souls.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

You know the suffering, all you who have been fathers. Help my speech, all you who have been called mothers. I cannot explain the storm that woman endured.

“Have mercy on me; [Col. 1235A] my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

You have seen the woman’s persistence; you have seen her manliness; you have seen her patience; you have seen her faith. Yet he did not answer her a word.

O new and astonishing state of affairs! The woman asks, entreats, begs, weeps over her misfortune, heightens the tragedy, recounts the suffering—and the lover of humanity did not answer. Speech is silent; the fountain is closed; the physician has withheld his medicines.

What could be so strange? What so astonishing? You summon others to follow, yet drive away this pitiable woman who follows you? But consider the physician’s wisdom: “He did not answer her a word.” Why did he not answer?
