Because he was provoking her faith still further, exercising her spirit through perseverance, and exercising the disciples’ compassion.

“For his disciples came to him, saying: Send her away, because she is crying out behind us.”

“A great voice indeed issues from her mouth,” he says, “but greater is that of her mind.”

“Send her away, because she is crying out behind us.” Another evangelist says, “before us.” The expressions differ, but the meaning is one; there is no falsehood in either account. The woman did both because of her distress: at first she cried out behind him, and when she saw that he did not answer, she ran ahead, as though licking the footsteps of her master like a dog.

“Send her away,” they say. “She will stir up a theater with her cries and summon the whole crowd.” They, being human, were embarrassed by her crying out; but the Lord knew the proper measure of his mercy.

“Send her away, because she is crying out behind us.”

But he answered and said: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house [Col. 1235C] of Israel.”

And by saying this he made her sore even worse. For he was a physician, cutting not in order to divide but in order to join.

Beloved, attend to me for a little while; I wish to investigate a hidden treasure.

“I was sent,” he says, “only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

O Lord, is this the whole matter? Is that why you became human, why you assumed flesh, why you performed such great acts of governance—that you might save one corner, while the whole world was left deserted in its ruin? And the Scythians, Thracians, Indians, Moors, Cilicians, Cappadocians, Syrians, Phoenicians—every land upon which the sun looks—have you passed through all this and come for the Jews alone? Do you disregard the nations lying in desolation, and despise those who scorn your Father, worship idols, offer incense [Col. 1235D] to them, and even consecrate their own children to demons? Do you overlook all these things and despise us wretched people waiting for you?

Indeed, all the prophets, and your own ancestor David according to the flesh, said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

And Isaiah, who contemplated you seated upon your throne of majesty, says: “And there shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI; Rom. XV).

And the patriarch Jacob says: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

The prophet Malachi also says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place pure sacrifices are offered to God” (Mal. I). [Col. 1236A]

And David himself says: “Clap your hands, all nations; shout to God with a voice of rejoicing, for God is most high, terrible, a great king over all the earth. God has gone up with rejoicing, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Ps. XLVI).

The prophet says: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Rom. XV). And all the others announced your saving coming to the nations.

For at your coming you yourself summoned the magi from the East, and through them caused the first beginnings of the Gentiles to cease, and sent them back to their own lands as evangelists. You summoned the magi by a star, while the prophets announced you to the nations.

Rising from the dead, you say to your disciples: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 1236B] XXVIII).

And now, when this pitiable and unhappy woman has come, entreating on behalf of her daughter’s illness and lamenting her misfortunes, you say: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel”?

When the centurion came and asked on behalf of his servant, you said: “I will come and cure him” (Matt. VIII). When the thief entreated you, you answered: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). To the paralytic you say: “Rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house” (Mark II). To Lazarus, dead for four days and already stinking, you say: “Lazarus, come out” (John XI). You cleanse lepers, raise the dead, strengthen paralytics, enlighten the blind, save thieves, make a prostitute chaste—and to this wretched woman you answer nothing?

O new and astonishing thing!

Beloved, consider together the woman’s constancy and manliness, and the Lord’s gracious wisdom and mercy: how his delay and refusal enriched the woman who was entreating, so that if you too pray and do not immediately receive what you have asked, you may not cease pleading.

Consider more carefully, beloved, the secret of the divine law. When the Jews had been freed from the Egyptians’ domination and tyranny, and had escaped Pharaoh’s hands and gone into the wilderness, about to enter the land of the Canaanites, filled with the worship of idols and worshiping even wood and stones, they had received the law that, once they had entered, they were not to take their daughters in marriage, nor join themselves in mutual wedlock, nor share banquets, lest through mutual association they should turn one another away from the Lord’s commandments and corrupt their morals.

“Nothing,” he says, “is to be shared by you with the Canaanites. Remain within your own boundaries; conduct your affairs among your own people and join in marriage, because you have your own language and the law given to you through Moses, which he placed like a wall and a kind of hedge between you and them” (Exod. XXIII; Deut. XXVII).

For just as a vineyard or garden is enclosed by a wall, so the law was given to the Jews, so that they could not transgress. The law therefore forbade them to mingle with the Canaanites or have any communion with them, lest friendship become an occasion of impiety.

Since the Canaanites were abominable to the Jews as idolaters and unclean people, with whom it was not lawful even to converse, and since this woman had come out from the borders of the Canaanites, she approached Christ. Yet Christ was saying to the Jews who were lying in wait for him: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII)—that I have transgressed the law?

Since, therefore, he was human and fulfilled everything belonging to the law—and since, as I have already said, the Canaanites were abominable to the Jews, who were enclosed beneath the law’s command as though behind a hedge—when Christ came, that is, when he was born of a virgin, circumcised on the eighth day, for whom an offering was performed in the temple, and all the ceremonies of the law were fulfilled, he fulfilled the law so that the Jews could not say, “He was unable to fulfill the law; therefore he abolished it.” He first completes it and afterward abolishes it, so that he might remove every opportunity for their complaint.

For he cried out and said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). Thus the Jews could not seize an opportunity to say: “We do not believe you, because you acted unlawfully by abolishing the law, because you went [Col. 1237B] to the borders of the Canaanites and conversed with them.” This was forbidden by the law.

Therefore he says nothing to the woman for the moment: while keeping the law, he delays salvation, restrains the Jews, and creates honor [“restores her”].

“He did not answer her a word.”

“I do not want to give you, O Jew, an occasion for complaint. Behold, I do not speak; behold, I do not answer. An opportunity to do good is present, and for your sake I temporarily defer my compassion. Behold, shipwreck is imminent, and the helmsman rests; as disaster increases, healing is deferred because of you, who have proved ungrateful, so that every opportunity for slander may be taken away from you. Behold, the woman has gathered a crowd through her cries, and she has not yet received an answer, lest you perhaps say: ‘You preferred the Canaanites to us, transgressed the law, and therefore we do not believe you.’”

“He did not answer her a word”—that is understood to mean because he was addressing the Jews, who were ungrateful for his benefits.

God did all these things because of his ineffable mercy, in order gradually to raise them from unbelief and remove every quibble from their minds.

For when he had healed a leper, he also said: “Go, show yourself to the priests, and offer the gift that Moses commanded for your cleansing” (Matt. VIII; Luke XIV).

O unheard-of thing! The Lord cleanses him and sends him to the law of Moses. Consider why he does this: so that the Jews would not accuse him as a transgressor of the law.

For how he cured the leper I cannot find words to express. Behold, he says: “A leper approached and begged him, saying: Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me” (Matt. VIII). And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: “I am willing; be cleansed.” It must be read in the imperative mood, not the indicative. Since the man had said, “If you are willing,” the Lord answered, “I am willing.” “You can cleanse me,” he said, and he answered, “Be cleansed.”

Under the law it was not permitted to touch a leper, because whoever touched one became unclean for the whole day. Blessed Elisha also knew this. When Naaman, a foreign leper, had come to him, sent by his king, he instructed him through his disciple, saying: “Go to the Jordan River, wash seven times, and you will be cleansed from your leprosy” (2 Kings V).

Elisha himself did not dare to go and see the leprosy or touch the man. Elisha cleansed the leper, and Christ cured the leper. Thus the Jews could not say: “What great thing has Christ done? He did what Elisha had done.”

But Elisha did not dare to touch the leper, lest he become contaminated; this man, however, touched him and cleansed him. Therefore he touched him in order to show that the one who is a servant is subject to the law, while the lord is the one who commands the law.

“I am willing; be cleansed.” And immediately he was cleansed. The evangelist could find no words to express the speed of the cure. For after saying “immediately,” he found nothing else to say. Such was the authority of the one acting that, as the word went forth, the illness fled.

Therefore he says: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer your gift for your cleansing, which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” To whom? To the Jews, so that they would not say that I had transgressed the law.

He was also secretly revealing his deity to them, so that from his works they might believe that he is the Son of God. On that day, moreover, the leper who had been commanded according to the law to offer the gift would come as a witness against them. Thus he did many things for the sake of the Jews; so now also he moderates and delays his answer to the woman’s prayers.

“Have mercy on me, because my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

His disciples approached and said: “Send her away, because she is crying out behind us.”

The Lord answered: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

The Jews might otherwise say: “You have dismissed us and gone to foreigners, and therefore we do not believe you.” Behold, people from the Gentiles come, and I do not receive them; you flee, yet I summon you, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI), and you do not wish to come? I reject this woman, and she refuses to withdraw.

Truly what is written is fulfilled: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). And elsewhere: “I appeared to those who did not seek me; I was found by those who did not ask for me” (Isa. LXV)—among whom was the Canaanite woman.

“Send her away,” they say, “because she is crying out behind us.”

Let us therefore see what the Lord says: “I was sent,” he says, “only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

Consider the Lord’s mercy. He did not say, “Go away from me,” but, “I was not sent to you.” “I did not come on account of you, but on account of the Jews, the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

When she heard this, she approached and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help me.”

He answered and said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

Consider the petitioner’s persistence and the Lord’s restraint. O mercy of the physician! He brought her to the point of despair so that she would ask more earnestly and increase her faith.

“It is not good,” he says, “to take the children’s bread.” Whose children? Clearly, the Jews. “And throw it to the dogs.” To whom? Without doubt, to you.

These words were spoken as an insult to the Jews, who had been called children but had become dogs, as Paul says: “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation, for we are the circumcision” (Phil. III). The Gentiles, however, who had been called dogs, became children: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

The praise of the Jews was an accusation against them.

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

But she said: “Yes, Lord.”

O the woman’s forcefulness! O the earnestness of her spirit! O the progress of her faith! The physician says, “No”; she says, “Yes.” The Lord says, “No”; she says, “Yes.”

She is not to be regarded as forward or shameless, but rather to be praised, because she awaits salvation.

“It is not good,” he says, “to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

“Yes, Lord. You call me a dog; I call you Lord. You insult me; I glorify you. Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. I do not reject the insult; only let me receive even the food of a dog. You speak of what is customary. Do for me what is owed to a dog. Because you call me a dog, give me crumbs.

“O Lord, you have become the advocate of my petition; by denying, you promise. Yes, Lord. For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

What follows? The one who denied, who repelled, who did not answer, who said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs,” who said, “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel”—suddenly bursts into praise of the woman, saying: “O woman!”

“Therefore,” he says, “I praise her constancy; I praise her faith, which remained firm though insulted and by her petition obtained what she sought. If I had dismissed her at the beginning, she would not have been gradually instructed, nor would you have known the strength of her soul or the hidden treasure of her faith. Therefore I suspended the gift, so that you might recognize her faith.

“O woman!”

God says, “O woman.” Let those who pray ostentatiously and entreat with distaste hear this. When I say, beloved, “Pray to God, entreat him, serve him,” he says: “I have prayed once, twice, and three times, ten times and twenty times—and what have I received?” Do not withdraw until you receive.

The petitioner’s end is the receiving of what he requests. Cease when you have received. Or rather, do not even then cease; instead, persevere in giving thanks for what you have received, so that what you have received may remain with you.

Some people enter a church and stretch their prayer out into a thousand lines, as though God needed a multitude of words, as though he did not know what you were asking, although he knows before you think.

They themselves do not know what they are saying; they merely move their lips, while the mind is without fruit and the ears of the one praying are deaf. You do not hear your own prayer, and you want the Lord to hear your petition?

“I bent my knees,” he says. You bent your knees inwardly, but your mind wanders outside. Your body is inside, but your senses are outside. Your mouth was speaking, but your mind was thinking about interest, calculating the revenues of estates, looking over the plans of houses, turning over the words of friends, observing the negligence of servants, laughing at the cleverness of parasites, and considering the appearance of women.

For since the devil is cunning, he knows that during prayer we ask for great things and often obtain them, and he hastens to obstruct unsuspecting minds. Sometimes, when we lie stretched out on our bed, we think of nothing of this sort. But when we come to prayer, clouds of thoughts overwhelm us, so that they may distract us and render us fruitless.

Knowing, therefore, that such things happen in prayer, imitate the Canaanite woman, man and woman alike, who, though a woman, asked the Lord watchfully and with the greatest wisdom, and therefore deserved to obtain her request.

But perhaps you will say: “I do not have a daughter who is possessed by a demon.”

Yet you have a soul filled with sins. And what did the Canaanite woman say?

“Have mercy on me, Lord, because my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

You too should say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, because my soul is grievously tormented by a demon.”

For sin is a great demon. The person who has it openly can be cured more quickly; but the one who hides his sins from people and does not wish to repent, but sins securely in contempt, is hateful. The former will receive pardon for the very affliction; the latter will be deprived of an answer.

“Have mercy on me.” A short utterance, but it contains an immense sea of kindness. For wherever mercy is requested, all good things are included.

If you are outside the church, say: “Have mercy on me, Lord,” not merely moving your lips, but groaning in your mind; for God also hears those who are silent. What is sought is not a place, but devotion of mind.

Jeremiah was sunk in a muddy pit, and by praying faithfully he won God’s favor (Jer. XXXVIII). Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den and inclined God’s mercy toward himself (Dan. VI). The three young men were in a blazing furnace, and they pleased God (Dan. III). The thief was on the cross, and he was heard when he faithfully made his request. The cross did him no harm; rather, his confession of faith opened paradise (Luke XXIII). Job was on a dung heap, and by his patience he made God propitious (Job II).

And if you are in the baths, pray. Wherever you are, pray. “You are God’s temple, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. III). All that is needed is the devoted will of the mind.

If you are standing in court, pray. When the king is angry, pray. God is present everywhere; he is not confined to a place. To the one who calls upon him he says: “I am here.”

When Moses had led the people out of Egypt and had come through the wilderness to the Red [Col. 1240C] Sea, the Egyptians were behind them, pursuing the people (Exod. XIV). Before them the waves roared; Moses was in distress. He was silent, but he was thinking great things in his mind. He was in the midst of tribulation: on one side, the pursuing Egyptians; on the other, the swelling sea.

Therefore he cried out to the Lord in his mind, and his voice was not heard at all. That is why the Lord says to him: “Why are you crying out to me?” He was not crying out with his mouth, but with his heart.

So when you stand before an enraged judge and a furious tyrant, pray to your Lord, and while you pray the waves will be calmed. Let the judge be before you; flee to the Lord. The judge is near you; invoke God, who is in you [or: for you].

Is he far from you, so that you must go to some place? God is not enclosed by a place [Col. 1240D], but is always near. And he who is not confined by a place is held by faith.

If you wish to ask a human being, you ask what he is doing and hear: “He is asleep,” or, “He is unavailable,” or perhaps, “His servant will not deign to answer you.” With God, none of this is necessary. Wherever you are, if you call upon him, he hears you. No doorkeeper, mediator, or servant is necessary. Say only: “Have mercy on me,” and God will immediately be present.

While you are still speaking, he says: “I am here.”

O utterance full of gentleness and kindness! He does not wait for the prayer to be completed, but immediately grants the petition.

“Have mercy on me.”

Let us imitate the Canaanite woman:

“Have mercy on me, Lord; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

“O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

Where are the heretics? Did he say, “I will ask my Father; I will entreat my begetter”? Did he need prayer? Certainly not, since he is the author of salvation, the creator of the universe, and God the Word. Therefore he said: “O woman, great is your faith,” even though he prayed according to the dispensation of the flesh.

And because the faith is great, grace was poured forth abundantly. But where prayer is necessary, there the vessel is weak.

“O woman, great is your faith.”

You did not see a dead person raised or a leper cleansed; you did not hear the prophets; you did not meditate upon the law; you did not see the sea divided into passages. You had seen none of these things from me. Moreover, you had been despised and rejected by me, yet you did not withdraw; you persevered in asking.

“O woman, great is your faith.”

The woman is dead, but her praises live. Wherever you go, you will hear Christ saying: “O woman, great is your faith.”

In Scythia, in India, in Mauritania, throughout every land upon which the sun looks, Christ cries out, and the Word does not remain silent: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

He did not say: “Let your daughter be healed,” but, “Let it be done for you as you wish.”

“You,” he says, “heal her. Be the physician. I entrust the medicine to you, so that you may apply it to her. Let it be done for you as you wish; your will heals her.”

The Canaanite woman healed her by her will, and the Son of God, as they say here, does not heal by himself.

“Let it be done for you as you wish.”

The woman neither commanded nor ordered the demon, but the woman’s will alone healed her daughter and drove away the demon.

Where are those who dare to say that Christ performed miracles through prayer? Observe what he says: “Let it be done for you as you wish.”

Consider the likeness of the utterance. He imitates his Father. For when God made heaven, he said: “Let heaven come to be,” and heaven came to be; “Let earth come to be,” and earth came to be; “Let the sun and the stars of heaven come to be,” and all things came to be (Gen. I).

The command brought forth the substance of kinship; the word revealed the communion of nature.

“And her daughter was healed,” he says, “from that hour.”

From what hour? Not from the hour when her mother reached home, but from the hour when the Lord’s word went forth. When she returned home, she found her daughter restored to sound mind, and healed by her will—or rather, by her faith.

For all these things, let us give thanks to God, through Christ our Lord, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, there is honor, glory, and power belonging equally to God the Father, throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXII. ON THE MONDAY AFTER *REMINISCERE*

At that time Jesus said to the crowds of Jews: “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin,” etc. (John VIII).

Saint John the Evangelist relates above that when the Lord was teaching in the treasury of the Temple and was openly revealing to the people the mysteries of his divinity, the Jews wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come. For his own will and the hour appointed by his dispensation had not yet come; just as he was born voluntarily, so also he suffered voluntarily.

Since, then, they wanted to seize the Lord, so that he might show that they were attempting this ineffectively so long as he did not wish it, the Lord therefore said to them what we have just heard: “I am going away, and you will seek me.” As though he were saying in other words: “You persecute me in vain; you attempt uselessly to lay hands on me. For I have predetermined the time when I must suffer for the salvation of the human race. I am going away,” he says; “I am proceeding willingly toward my passion. But even now you cannot do me any harm, because I do not wish it.”

“And you will seek me,” not out of love, but out of hatred. Finally, when Christ departed from the world, after he had made himself absent from human eyes through his passion, the Jews sought him by persecuting the apostles and the other believers. Hence it was also said to Saul the persecutor: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

The holy apostles, too, who loved him, sought him, desiring to have him present and burning with longing to see him. Let us therefore seek Christ in the manner in which the holy apostles sought him, and let us always love him. May he build up our heart, who says: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek; do not turn your face away from me.” Let us therefore seek Christ in that manner, not in the manner in which the Jews, enemies of Christ, sought him. They sought him in order to possess him; these sought him in order to destroy him.

And so, lest it be thought that they would seek him rightly, he added: “And in your sin you will die.” The one who remains in sin until death dies in his sin. Because he foresaw that they would persevere in their wickedness, he therefore said: “You will die in your sin.” And because he saw in all of them one will and a similar wickedness, he spoke in the singular: “in your sin.” But because they all wanted to destroy him with equal intent, although he had come to save them, he therefore spoke in the plural: “you will die.”

“Where I am going, you cannot come.” They could not come where he was going because they did not want to believe in him and did not love him. Therefore they could not come to that glory toward which he was hastening through death. Speaking elsewhere to the apostles, he said the same thing: “Where I am going, you cannot come now” (John XV). For at that time they could not come where he was going, because they were not yet capable of suffering for him; but afterward they would come. He did not therefore take away their hope, but foretold a delay.

The Jews, however, would never come where he was going, because they did not want to believe in him. And therefore they heard: “You will die in your sin.”

But let us hear what they answered, hearing the Lord’s words only in a carnal manner and not understanding them: “Surely he will not kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” Such was their blind mind, darkened by its own shadows. If the Lord were to kill himself, could they not follow him to death? Or were they themselves unable to die?

Therefore, when he said, “Where I am going,” he was speaking not of the place to which he was going in order to die, but of the place to which he would come after death—that is, of the glory toward which he was hastening through his passion and death. They could not reach that glory.

But now let us see what the Lord answered them: “You are from below; I am from above.” “You are from below,” he says: you think earthly thoughts, take pleasure in earthly things, and long for earthly things; you do not lift your hearts upward. “I am from above,” that is, from the Father, than whom nothing is higher, because the Father is from no one.

He was from above, that is, he was from God the Father, because he was his Word, eternally and consubstantially begotten by him before every creature, before time, and before anything that can be conceived within time.

“You are from this world; I am not from this world.” They were from this world because they were sinners, unjust, and unbelieving. But were the apostles and the other saints not from this world? They were from the world because they had been born from Adam; but they had been chosen by the Lord from the world—that is, from carnal conduct—as he says elsewhere: “I chose you from the world” (John XV).

They were therefore from the world, but they were no longer of the world, because they had been chosen from the world and belonged to him through whom the world was made. The Jews, however, because they persevered in sin, remained in the world. Therefore it was said to them: “You will die in your sin.”

“I told you, therefore, that you will die in your sin. For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sin.” He restores hope to them and shows how they can avoid dying in their sin—namely, if they believe in him. Thus, among those to whom the Lord was then speaking, there were many who would not believe and therefore would die in their sin, while others would believe and would be freed from their sins.

It should be noted that he says, “if you do not believe that I am,” without adding what he was. He did not say, “if you do not believe that I am the Christ,” or “that I am the Son of God,” or “that I am the one whom the prophets foretold.” He said none of these things, but only: “I am.” Clearly, he wished to show that he was the one who had formerly said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus III).

He used, in speaking to the Jewish people, the same verb of being that he had then used with Moses, speaking through the angel whom he was sending to liberate his people. It was as though he were saying: “I who then came through the angel in order to send Moses to liberate my people—I have now come through myself to liberate the human race.”

Unless, therefore, you believe that I am God, you will die in your sin.

But they persisted in their foolishness and did not understand the subtlety of the Lord’s words, and they answered: “Who are you?” But the Lord, in order to instruct those who would believe in him, replied: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.”

The Lord calls himself the Beginning because all things were made through him. For he is the Wisdom of God, of whom the Psalmist says to God the Father: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm CIII). If, therefore, he made all things in Wisdom—that is, in his Son—then he himself is the Beginning of all things that God the Father created through him.

The Father, too, is called the Beginning, because “in the beginning was the Word,” that is, the Son was in the Father. Yet the Father and the Son are one Beginning, because the Father and the Son are one God.

“The Beginning,” he says, “who also speaks to you.” As though he were saying: “I am God, who for your sake became humble and descended for this purpose, so that I might speak to you through the form I assumed. Believe, therefore, that I am the Beginning, because I speak to you so that you may believe this.”

“I have many things to say and to judge concerning you.” Elsewhere in the Gospel he said: “I judge no one” (John VIII). What, then, is the meaning of what he now says: “I have many things to say and to judge concerning you”?

He said the former concerning his first coming, in which he did not come to judge the world but to save it. By what he now says—“I have many things to say and to judge concerning you”—he indicates his second coming, when he will come to judge the living and the dead.

“But he who sent me is truthful.” As though he were saying: “I speak the truth because I am the Son of the truthful one. The Father is truthful; the Son is truth. And just as the Son is from the Father, so truth is from the truthful one.”

It should also be observed that the only-begotten Son gives all glory to God the Father, instructing us by such an example. If he who is the coeternal Son gives all glory to the one from whom he is, how much more ought we to glorify God in his works, since we are his servants?

“And what I have heard from him, these things I speak in the world.” What had he heard from the Father except the truth? He had therefore heard the truth and spoke the truth. He heard from the Father because he is from the Father. For having heard means nothing other than being, since he has hearing from the one from whom he has being.

“And they did not understand that he was speaking to them of his Father, God.” Why did they not understand? Because they were still clinging to carnal things and did not yet have the eyes of their hearts opened, by which they could understand the equality of the Father and the Son.

He therefore said to them: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.”

Here he calls his passion his exaltation, by which he was exalted upon the cross. For this exaltation was an abasement, not a glorification, according to which “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Philippians II).

He therefore says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.” For he foresaw there some whom he had predestined before the foundation of the world to believe after his passion. Of them we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Peter preached, three thousand believed on one day, five thousand on another, and afterward many thousands.

“Then,” he says, “you will know that I am.” As though he were saying: “For this reason I delay your faith, so that I may complete my passion. But when you have lifted me up upon the cross, just as Moses once lifted up the serpent in the desert, then you will know that I am God, of one substance with the Father.”

“And I do nothing of myself,” because “I am not from myself.” My work is from him from whom my generation also is.

“And as the Father taught me, this I speak in the world.” The Father did not teach the Son as though he had begotten one who was ignorant; rather, he taught him by begetting him knowing. For the nature of truth is simple, and for it being and knowing are the same. He has knowledge from the one from whom he has being.

“And he who sent me is with me.” God the Father sent the Son because he ordained that he should become incarnate. His mission is his incarnation. God the Father is therefore with the Son because the Father and the Son are one, possessing one substance and the same divinity, an undivided majesty.

Yet although they are together, the Son alone was sent—that is, the Son alone became incarnate—and thus the Son alone suffered. God the Father was always with the Son and did not abandon him. Nevertheless, as has been said, the person of the Son alone assumed flesh and was subject to passion and death. The person of God the Father was separate from this injury of incarnation and passion.

To indicate this by an example: when a tree receives a ray of the sun into itself and is cut with iron, the ray of the sun cannot itself be cut, nor can it be separated from the tree. So God the Father, and the divinity itself in Christ, could not suffer; only Christ’s humanity was capable of suffering.

“For I always do what pleases him.” He always did what pleased God the Father, because he fulfilled his will by accomplishing the salvation of the human race. He remained perpetually free and immune from every sin, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

Therefore, if we wish to be his members, let us strive to imitate the example of our Head. Let us do what pleases God; let us purify our spirit from every desire; let us subdue the unlawful appetites of the flesh; let us wash away with the tears of repentance the evils we remember having committed; and let us devote ourselves, as far as we can, to good works. Thus may we deserve to have God as our helper and protector amid the pressures of this age, and in the future happily to attain that supreme good: the vision of him. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIII. FOR THE TUESDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat,” etc. (Matthew XXIII).

The Lord, having repudiated the tempters as they deserved, turned his discourse toward the servants, so that their confusion might become instruction for the righteous. For a word is fruitless when one person is so confounded that another is not instructed.

“They have sat,” he says, “upon Moses’ seat.” It does not mean that the material seat on which Moses had sat was preserved among the Jews until that time. Rather, by “Moses’ seat” is understood the teaching that the scribes and Pharisees preached, although they did not practice it.

“Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works.” As though he were saying to them: “The teaching taught by Moses the lawgiver is preached and proclaimed by the scribes and Pharisees. But because they destroy by their deeds what they preach with their mouths, observe what they proclaim to you, but do not do what they do.”

With wonderful goodness, the Lord, although tested by the Pharisees, dismantles their schemes, yet nevertheless, because of the dignity of the priesthood, urges people to submit to them—not to imitate their works, but their teaching. For good teaching frequently proceeds even from a bad man, and worthless earth produces precious gold.

“For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger.”

By the heavy and unbearable burdens he means the commandments of the Law, which, especially because of the sin of the worshiped calf, are known to have been imposed upon the Jews. The scribes and Pharisees, mixing these commandments with their own traditions, placed them as exceedingly heavy burdens upon the simpler people; yet they themselves did not wish to move them with even one finger—that is, they were unwilling to fulfill even the least commandments.

Such are the indiscriminate priests in the Church today, who command the people to observe complete righteousness but themselves observe not even a small part of it. For if you place a bundle of wood upon the shoulders of someone unable to carry it, he must either throw the bundle off himself or collapse beneath its weight.

So also, when a heavy burden of penance is placed upon a person, he must either cast penance away—that is, being scandalized, sin still more. For even if we err by imposing too little penance upon sinners, it is nevertheless better to be judged according to mercy than condemned according to cruelty.

The one who wishes to appear holy should be strict concerning his own life and kind toward that of others.

“They do all their works in order to be seen by people.” The scribes and Pharisees did what they practiced for this purpose: to be seen by people—that is, to obtain outwardly the praise and favor of the populace.

Likewise, anyone who performs his works only in order to be seen by people is like the scribes and Pharisees. For the devil takes an opportunity from the intention of every person. Let us remove this vice from ourselves, so that we may not wish to be seen by them—that is, praised by them—and we shall trample down all vices without difficulty.

“They enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes.”

Because in Greek *phylattein* means “to preserve” or “to guard,” while *Torah* means “law,” he calls “phylacteries” those strips of parchment that, as though in obedience to the commandment of the Law, they wore on their foreheads, seeking popular praise for guarding the divine commandments written there. They did not understand that the divine Law should be meditated upon in the heart and not displayed upon the body.

The Law also commanded that a small and short fringe be made on the four corners of one’s cloak, so that just as they differed from the nations by the circumcision of the Law, so also they might differ by their clothing. But superstitious teachers, exceedingly desirous of popular praise, made large fringes for themselves and fastened very sharp thorns into them, so that they would frequently be pricked while walking or sitting and, as though reminded, would return to meditating upon the divine words.

From this practice it is believed to have arisen in the Church that some people customarily carry a portion of the Gospel written out, or relics of martyrs. But it should be understood that the person whom the evangelical words placed in his ears do not benefit is not saved by having them hung around his neck. For the power of the Gospel is not in the shapes of the letters but in the understanding of their meaning.

It follows: “For they love the first places at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace.”

The Lord does not forbid them to be greeted in the marketplace, nor to sit first at meals when such honor is rightfully due to them. Rather, he teaches that we must beware of those who, although they are not worthy to possess these honors, nevertheless desire them to be displayed to them beyond measure.

If these words of the Savior are understood bodily, they not only fail to build up the hearer but destroy him even more. For someone hearing that it is praiseworthy to sit in the last place sits after everyone else and not only does not lose the boasting of his heart, but seeks another boast concerning his humility, so that the person who previously desired to be seen as righteous by others may also appear humble.

But the Lord’s words should instead be understood spiritually. God does not care where a person’s body lies, but in what place the mind is situated. A person who humbles himself in position while preferring himself in his heart has humbled himself without purpose.

The scribes and Pharisees not only demanded greetings in the marketplace from the people, so that they might greet them in a loud voice, saying, “Hail, rabbi,” but also that people should bend their heads and bow down to their knees.

“And to be called rabbi by people.” They desired to be called rabbis and wanted to be teachers; they coveted the name and neglected the office.

“But you must not be called rabbi, for one is your teacher. And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven.”

In all these matters it is forbidden that what is owed to God should be given to human beings. Yet since all the commandments of divine Scripture proceed from God, many are perplexed as to why, contrary to another commandment of Scripture—“Honor your father”—he forbids people to be called fathers or teachers. Paul, too, testifies that he is a teacher of the nations.

But it is one thing to be a father or teacher by nature and another by permitted indulgence. When we call a human being father or teacher, we honor those from whom we have received growth or origin; we do not present them as the authors of our life.

Nevertheless, according to the fact that we are created and governed by God, no one else should be called father or teacher except God. He should be called Father because all things are from him; Teacher because all things are through him; or because he alone is the Teacher who inwardly instructs everyone naturally.

For when a human being teaches another, he does not provide him with understanding but merely exercises it by admonition. Teaching performs the office of a whetstone, which does not make the iron.

“The one who is greatest among you will be your servant.” As though he were saying: “Whoever wishes to surpass his brother by ruling must first surpass him by serving.”

We know that this was truly fulfilled in Christ himself. Although he is greater than all the faithful, he not only ministered outward things to them but also handed over his soul to death for them.

This is what he says: “The one who is greatest among you will be your servant.” Those set over others are especially commanded to relieve, in this way, the needs of those over whom they preside by spiritual governance and, through diligent service, to provide what is lacking in their ordinary poverty.

“But whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

We see many flourishing in the honors and riches of this age, and we observe them continuing in these things until the end. Conversely, we see some suffering in poverty and remaining in the same destitution.

Since some remain in the happiness they began with and others in their former poverty until the end of life, how can it be true that the Lord says that every person who is exalted will be humbled, and the humbled person exalted?

But because truth cannot be mistaken, we do not doubt that this will be fulfilled in the future. Everyone who exalts himself in the present life, refusing to submit to the divine commandments, will be humbled with the proud on the day of judgment and will hear from the Lord: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew XXV).

But whoever strives here to humble himself through divine love, imitating him who says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI), will be exalted by the Lord at the future judgment, when he deserves to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIV. FOR THE WEDNESDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

[Col. 1248A]

At that time, as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem,” etc. (Matthew XX).

Our Lord and Redeemer, foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be troubled by his passion, wished to proclaim to them long beforehand both the suffering of that passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying, they would also have no doubt that he would rise again, just as he had foretold.

He had often announced this very thing to them, but because what they had heard could slip from their memory as time passed, he therefore, as he was going to his passion and taking them with him, foretold the future to them again, so as to prepare them against the coming temptation, lest, when the persecution of the cross and the disgrace of the passion arrived, they should be frightened.

For evils that are foreseen do less harm. Sudden disasters, on the other hand, commonly overwhelm even the strongest.

He took, I say, his twelve disciples. At the beginning of his preaching, the Lord wished to have many disciples, from whom he chose twelve whom he also called apostles, to whom he would entrust the mysteries of the Gospel and through whom he would summon the whole world to his faith.

Elsewhere he says to them: “You are the ones who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke XXII).

Having taken these men aside, he said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death.”

It should be observed that the Lord says that the Son of Man will be handed over and condemned to death. Although the same person is the Son of God and the Son of Man, the Lord Jesus Christ, only the Son of Man—that is, the humanity—could be assumed, handed over, seized, and subjected to passion and death.

It should also be considered that in almost every passage of the holy Gospel the Lord calls himself the Son of Man rather than the Son of God, so that he may bring back to our memory what he became for us. For he who was God, exalted above all, became a humble man among all.

But the more greatly he commends the lowliness of his humanity, the more ought we to venerate and glorify the sublimity of his divinity.

“He will be handed over,” he says, “to the chief priests.” First he was brought to the priest Annas, then to the house of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.

“And they will condemn him to death.” Indeed, they condemned him to death when they cried out, saying: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew XXVI), and: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him” (John XIX).

“And they will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked.” He was handed over to the Gentiles because, as the account of his passion clearly relates, they brought him bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor, who was certainly not a Jew. Pilate, after having him scourged, handed him over to the Roman soldiers to be crucified.

It should be understood that the Lord was handed over by many. God the Father handed him over, according to what the Apostle says: “He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all” (Romans VIII).

The Son himself handed himself over, as the same Apostle says: “Who loved us and handed himself over for us” (Galatians II).

Judas handed him over to the Jews, and the Jews likewise handed him over to Pilate. Pilate, as has been said, handed him over to the soldiers.

If God the Father handed him over, and if he handed himself over, what did Judas and the Jews do wrong? What such a great crime did they commit that they should be so abhorrent and accursed to all who believe in Christ?

But in one and the same deed their intentions were different. What God the Father did with his eternal Son, he did out of love and affection for the human race. Judas and the Jews did it out of hatred and envy.

Therefore God the Father is most rightly blessed with Christ his Son and proclaimed in continual praises, while those others are condemned to eternal curse and punishment.

“He will be handed over,” he says, “to the Gentiles to be mocked and scourged.”

The Lord was mocked when, as the Gospel relates, the soldiers received him, covered his face, clothed him in purple, plaited a crown of thorns and placed it upon his head, put a reed in his right hand, and came to him saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.” And they struck him with blows (John XIX).

He was scourged and bound to a column, upon which traces of the blood poured out are said to remain visible even to this day. Since he was scourged first and then crucified, this was done according to Roman custom: they first beat with scourges those condemned and sentenced to death, and then killed them with the sword.

“And on the third day he will rise.” Divine Scripture commonly joins joyful things to sorrowful ones. Thus the Lord dispelled the disgrace of the passion he had foretold by adding the glory of the future resurrection: “On the third day he will rise.”

And rightly on the third day, because the author of life could not be held by death for long. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “He will drink from the brook by the way” (Psalm CIX), because he tasted our death in passing, and his flesh did not see corruption.

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him. He said to her: “What do you want?” She said to him: “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”

The mother of the sons of Zebedee is Mary, the mother of James and John, who is also mentioned in the account of the Lord’s resurrection.

But since the Lord is read above to have foretold his passion—that he would be handed over, mocked, and scourged—it must be asked how the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to this conception of the kingdom, so that she would ask the Lord for her sons to have the glory of reigning.

For the things that the Lord had foretold would be fulfilled in him seemed contrary to the glory of the kingdom. But because the Lord had added that he would rise on the third day, this woman thought that immediately after the resurrection he would reign in the world. She believed that what is promised for the second coming would be fulfilled at the Lord’s first coming.

Therefore, forgetful of the future, she desired present glory with feminine eagerness. Even to this day, the opinion of the Jews is that when their Christ comes, he will reign happily in the world for many years and rule over all nations; that the Jews themselves will enjoy complete peace and prosperity; and that they will be revered by all peoples.

This woman was corrupted by that opinion. Thus, through womanly error and maternal affection, she wanted to obtain a kingdom for her sons.

When the Lord asks what she wanted, he did not do so out of ignorance but as part of his dispensation, so that her request might become known to everyone and the Lord might answer her appropriately.

Jesus answered and said: “You do not know what you are asking.” Since the mother made the request, the Lord answered not the mother but the sons, because he knew that the mother’s petition arose from the will of her sons.

They did not know what they were asking: they wanted to reign and sit with Christ, although they had not yet deserved this. For they were not yet able to suffer for Christ, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy II).

They were therefore delighted by the summit of honor, but first the way of labor had to train them. They already desired to reign sublimely with Christ, but first they had to suffer for Christ.

Their desire was certainly good, but their request was ill-considered. Therefore the Lord did not condemn their will or intention, which arose from love for him; he reproved only their ignorance, saying: “You do not know what you are asking.”

“Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?”

In the holy Gospel, the name “cup,” or “baptism,” commonly designates the labor of martyrdom. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke XII).

In his passion, too, he prays to the Father: “If you are willing, take this cup away from me” (Luke XXII).

He therefore asks them whether they are able to drink the cup that he was about to drink, thereby indicating that both he and they would be brought to perfection through suffering.

Understanding this, they answered: “We can.”

And the Lord said: “You will indeed drink my cup.”

It is often asked how both brothers—John and James—drank the Lord’s cup, since we read that only James was beheaded for Christ by Herod, while John rested in peace and ended his life by a peaceful and favorable death.

But we read in histories that he too endured many things because of the name of Christ. He is found in the Acts of the Apostles to have been beaten along with the other apostles, and afterward he was placed by the emperor Domitian in a vessel of boiling oil.

It is also reported that, because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, he was exiled by the same ruler to the island of Patmos.

We therefore see that John was not without martyrdom and that he too drank the cup of suffering, even though his persecutor did not shed his blood.

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

What he says—“It is not mine to give to you”—may be understood in this sense: “It is not mine, but yours.” It is not mine to give because the kingdom of heaven lies within the power of the one who receives it.

Whoever shows himself to be such that he is worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive it, because the kingdom of heaven is attained not by a person’s status but by his life.

If, therefore, you also become such as to be worthy of receiving that kingdom, which God the Father has prepared for those who conquer and persevere in the good to the end, you too will undoubtedly receive it.

Or it may be understood in another sense: “It is not mine to give to you,” that is, it is not mine to give that kingdom to the proud and haughty—which you still are.

If you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are; that is, do not be haughty, because such people are unworthy to receive the kingdom of heaven. Therefore humble yourselves first, and then the kingdom of heaven will also be prepared for you.

“When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers.” They were not indignant against the mother but attributed this presumptuous request to the sons, since, apparently ignorant of the measure of their own worth, they had burned with immoderate desire to ask for the kingdom.

In accordance with this, the Lord above also answered not the mother, who had not made the request on her own initiative, but the sons who were reclining: “You do not know what you are asking.”

From the Lord’s response, together with the indignation of the ten apostles, it is understood that the sons had urged their mother to ask for great things.

“But Jesus called them to himself and said: ‘You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It will not be so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave.’”

The humble and kind Teacher, who is also the model of all teachers, did not rebuke the two for their immoderate and irrational request, nor the ten for the indignation and envy they held against them. Instead, he offered an example that clearly teaches that the one who truly is greater is the one who makes himself lesser, and that the one is first who becomes the servant of all.

Whoever wishes to surpass his equal by reigning should surpass him also by humbling himself. Let him defeat in service the one whom he wishes to defeat in rank.

The two were therefore seeking great things in vain, and the others were also indignant in vain at their insolent desire, since they were taught by the Lord that one ascends to the summit of supreme dignity not by power but by humility.

“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his soul as a redemption for many.”

He sets before them in himself a model of humility to be learned, so that if they disregarded the words of the teacher, they might imitate his example.

He says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served,” that is, so that others might serve him, “but to serve.”

“If I,” he says, “who, although I am the Son of God and God, became man for your sake, did not come into the world for this purpose—to seek the services or ministrations of human beings—but rather to serve you and minister to you, why do you, human beings, proudly demand services from human beings, mortals from mortals—not in order to meet the needs of nature, for which very little is sufficient, but in order to appear greater and higher than others?”

Let the superiors of churches pay attention to this and beware. Let them hear from the Lord that it belongs to the custom of the Gentiles, not to that of the Church, to lord it over subjects and exercise the domination of power over those over whom they have been placed.

Let good teachers therefore learn from this example not to exalt themselves above those beneath them through the arrogance of pride, but rather to strive to obey them and show themselves equal to them in all things, so that from him who did not come to be served but to serve they may deserve to receive heavenly authority.

The Lord ministered when, at the supper, he girded himself with a towel and washed the feet of all the disciples. The Lord also ministered when, upon the altar of the cross, he offered himself as a victim to God the Father for our redemption.

Hence it follows: “And to give his soul as a redemption for many.”

This should be committed to memory: he says that he lays down his soul not for all but for many—namely, for those who are willing to believe, for those who belong to the number of the saved and those predestined to eternal life.

But you—

## HOMILY LXXXV. FOR THE THURSDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen,” etc. (Luke XVI).

Seek the homily on the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost.

## HOMILY LXXXVI. FOR THE FRIDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

[Col. 1252B]

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples and to the crowds of the Jews: “There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge,” etc. (Matthew XXI).

The Son of God, about to suffer for the salvation of humanity, came to Jerusalem with a triumphal procession and was received by the exultant crowds, so that by such glory he might further provoke the spirits of his enemies to hasten his death. There he did not cease for five days to teach the people and, by setting forth parables, to rebuke the crimes of the Scribes and Pharisees. For since they had asked him, when he was driving them from the temple with marvelous authority, “By what authority are you doing these things?” and had laid snares for him in their speech [Col. 1252C] when, with feigned reverence, they asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not, therefore the Lord overcame them by their own arts, and in parables they heard what they had not deserved to hear more openly.

Finally, this parable embraces both the envy that the Jews had conceived against the Savior and the entire mystery of his Passion. This householder is God Almighty, who possesses human beings in the world as a master possesses his servants in a household. This is that householder who had two sons and who—according to the parable in another place—hired laborers for his vineyard; he planted the vineyard, namely the Israelite people, whom he chose from all the nations as a people specially belonging to him. This is that vineyard of which Isaiah spoke in his song and, at the end, added [Col. 1252D]: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5); of it the Psalmist likewise says: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 79).

“And he surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, and leased it to cultivators.” By the hedge, or wall, of the city he signifies angelic protection. He therefore surrounded the vineyard with a hedge because he fortified that people with the protection of walls and the aid of angels. The winepress is the altar, because just as grapes are pressed out in a winepress, so victims are sacrificed to God upon the altar. These are those winepresses whose title appears before three Psalms, thus: “For the end; concerning the winepresses.” He built a tower, namely the temple. This is that tower to which the prophet Micah speaks [Col. 1253A], saying: “And you, tower of the flock, misty daughter of Zion” (Mic. 4).

“He leased it to cultivators.” By the cultivators he means the leaders of the Jews, to whom God entrusted the city, the temple, and the whole people to govern.

“And he went away into a far country.” He went away into a far country, not by a change of place; for where can he withdraw who says through the prophet, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23), and elsewhere, “Am I a God near at hand and not a God far away?” (ibid.). Rather, he is said to have gone away because he left them free to choose whether they wished to work in the vineyard or not.

“But when the time of the fruits drew near.” The time of the fruits was when, after their enemies had been killed, they began to inhabit the land of promise in security. And he aptly says not “the yield” but “the time of the fruits,” because this vineyard produced no yield, and no fruit of good work came from that rebellious [Col. 1253B] people.

“He sent his servants to the cultivators, so that they might receive its fruits. And the cultivators seized his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another.” The servants who were first sent to the cultivators are understood as Moses the lawgiver, Aaron, and the other priests, who for forty continuous years in the wilderness demanded the fruit of the Law that God had given them. But the cultivators killed the servants sent to them, scourging them with the blows of their tongues. For it is written: “They provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord” (Ps. 105). And again: “Moses was vexed because of them, because they embittered his spirit” (ibid.).

What Moses himself thought concerning this vineyard he declares in the song of Deuteronomy, saying: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the outskirts [Col. 1253C] of Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is most bitter” (Deut. 32).

It should be noted that another evangelist says that they struck another on the head. By this servant David is understood, because he too was a servant of the householder, and he urged that same people toward heavenly desires by singing the delightful melody of the Psalms. But they struck him on the head because they rejected the discoverer of spiritual music, saying: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Sam. 20). They also handed over his noble kingdom to an ignoble man and exchanged religion for impiety. Yet he, forgetful of this insult, prayed to this householder on behalf of the vineyard, saying: “Lord God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vineyard” (Ps. 79).

“Again [Col. 1253D] he sent other servants, more numerous than the first.” By the servants sent in the second place we must understand the choirs of the prophets, who aided the people with their prophetic utterances and foretold what was about to come upon this vineyard. But they persecuted these also in the same way and killed those who foretold the coming of Christ.

Let us hear what Isaiah asks concerning the barrenness of this vineyard: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Isa. 5). “They treated them similarly,” he says (Jer. 2). For some they stoned, as Ezekiel in Chaldea and Jeremiah in Egypt. Others they killed, such as Naboth. Others they cut in pieces, such as Isaiah. Some they destroyed with an iron bar, such as Amos.

Here the patience and forbearance [Col. 1254A] of the Lord are shown: he repeatedly sent servants to the wicked tenants so that, converted by them [the text has *conventi*, “summoned/confronted,” for *conversi*], they might repent. But in their contempt they stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath.

“But finally he sent his son to them, saying: ‘Perhaps they will respect my son.’” “Finally,” he says, “I sent my son,” because, as the Apostle says, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Gal. 4). Yet he did not send him to pronounce a judicial sentence upon the wicked tenants deserving punishment, but, even after so many crimes and the impious deaths of his servants, to reserve mercifully a place for pardon.

“Perhaps they will respect my son.” The fact that he says, as though in uncertainty, “Perhaps they will respect my son,” must not be understood as though he spoke in ignorance. For God, who knows all things individually and supremely, cannot be ignorant [Col. 1254B]. Rather, he is said to doubt so that, in the name of the Son, the power of free choice might be demonstrated.

“But when the cultivators saw the son, they said: ‘This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.’” From this passage it is most plainly proved that the leaders of the Jews crucified the Redeemer not through ignorance but through envy. For they knew that he was the Son of God; they understood that he was the one to whom God the Father had said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2). They recognized that he had come into the world for this purpose: to convert all nations to his faith. Therefore, as though consulting their own interests, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him; and if we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him” (John 12).

The inheritance [Col. 1254C] of the Son is the Church, given to him among all nations. The Father did not leave it to him by dying; rather, he mercifully acquired it through his own death and, rising from the dead, possessed it under the covenant of eternal life. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Pay attention to the flock over which Christ appointed you to govern the Church, which he acquired with his blood” (Acts 20).

The wicked tenants wanted to obtain this inheritance after killing the heir, because they persecuted Christ in order to extinguish the faith that exists through him, to prefer the carnal righteousness of the Law to the righteousness of the Gospel, and to instill that carnal righteousness in all nations that were to be instructed.

“And they seized him,” he says, “threw him outside the vineyard, and killed him.” The heir of the vineyard is killed outside the vineyard because Christ was crucified outside [Col. 1254D] the city, in the place called Golgotha, that is, Calvary. Hence the Apostle says: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Heb. 13).

Or they threw him outside the vineyard and killed him because, through unbelief, they first expelled him from their own hearts and then subjected him to the punishment of the cross. This was prefigured long ago when Moses placed the altar of burnt offering in the tabernacle of God, on which the blood of victims was poured out, not inside the tabernacle but at its entrance. He indicated mystically that the altar of the cross was to be erected outside the gate of Jerusalem, and that Christ, the Son of God the Father, was not to be received in the house of the Jews—that is, in their minds—but was to be sacrificed outside.

But when the evangelist Mark, changing the order, says, “They seized him and killed him, and threw him [Col. 1255A] outside the vineyard” (Matt. 12), he indicates the stubbornness of their unbelief. They were unwilling to believe even after his Passion and resurrection, but, as though he were a useless corpse, they cast him away, excluding the preachers of his word from their territories and sending them to the peoples of the nations.

“When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those cultivators?” He asks them this, not because he was ignorant of what they would answer, but in order to condemn them by their own response.

“They said to him: ‘He will bring those wicked men to a wicked end, and will lease the vineyard to other cultivators who will render him the fruits in their seasons.’”

When the Lord came, he brought the wicked to a wicked end, because he punished the unbelieving and cruel murderers of his Son with a fitting retribution, taking away from them their place, nation, and kingdom and scattering them far and wide throughout all the regions of the world.

But he leased [Col. 1255B] the vineyard to other cultivators because he entrusted to us the mysteries of the Scriptures and knowledge of himself on the condition that we return fruit in its proper seasons—that is, that we know what it is fitting for us to say or do at each particular time.

But the words they spoke—that the lord would bring the wicked to a wicked end and lease his vineyard to others—he himself showed, by divine providence, through a prophetic example, replying: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

Those whom above he had called tenants he now calls builders, because the leaders and priests of the Jews ought to cultivate the people subject to them, as a vineyard, so that they might offer the fruits of righteousness; and they ought also to construct and adorn them as a house, so that the people might become a dwelling worthy [Col. 1255C] of the Lord. The Apostle too supports this interpretation when he says to the faithful: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3).

But they, like wicked tenants, were unwilling to return the fruit of the vineyard; and, like wicked builders, they attempted to remove from their hearers the chosen and precious stone that was to be placed either in the foundation or at the corner of God’s house—that is, they tried to take away faith in Christ.

He therefore says: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” It is as though he said: How will this prophecy be fulfilled, which says that the stone rejected by the builders became the cornerstone, unless Christ, rejected and killed by you, is preached to the nations who will believe?

For he became like a precious stone [Col. 1255D]—according to what the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)—at the head of the corner, because God joined together in one faith the two walls, circumcision and uncircumcision, and established one Church from the two peoples.

“Therefore I say to you: The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” In this passage the kingdom of God is to be understood as the holy Scriptures, which the Lord took away from the unbelieving Jews and handed over to us, so that we might produce their fruit. This is that vineyard which was once leased to cultivators, but they possessed only the name of the Scriptures and did not deserve to attain any fruit from them.

“And whoever falls upon that stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” For there is a great difference [Col. 1256A] between one who, through weakness or ignorance, sins by offending Christ and one who, through pride, denies Christ. Whoever sins while believing in Christ falls upon the stone and is broken, but is not utterly crushed, because he is reserved for repentance.

But if someone denies Christ, he falls—that is, this stone rushes upon him—and crushes him with eternal destruction, so that not even a shard remains from which a little water might be drawn from a well.

This too can be said: those who at that time despised him through simplicity and ignorance fell upon the stone and insulted him; therefore they were shattered, though not utterly crushed. But upon those who knowingly denied him as the Son [Col. 1256B] of God and, against their own conscience, attributed his works to Beelzebub, the stone will rush and crush them with everlasting destruction; it will grind them to powder, so that the wicked will be like dust before the face of the wind.

“When the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them. And seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.”

The chief priests and Scribes, convicted by their own conscience, sought to kill the Lord as though he were speaking falsely against them. Yet by doing these things they prove that what he had said was true. For he was the heir whose unjust death was to be avenged by the Father. They themselves were the wicked tenants, who could indeed be held back from killing the Son of God for a little while by human fear, until his hour came, but who never allowed themselves to be restrained by divine fear or love.

What we have explained concerning the wickedness of the Jews [Col. 1256C] in this parable can also be applied, in a moral interpretation, to each one of us. When the mystery of baptism, which a believer ought to practice through his conduct, is entrusted to someone, it is as though a vineyard to cultivate is leased to him. One servant and another, and a third, are sent to receive fruits when the Law, the prophecy, and the Psalms are read; instructed by their admonitions, he ought to return the fruits of good works.

But the servant is treated with insults and driven out when the word of God is either despised or—even worse—blasphemed. Moreover, he kills the heir, so far as lies within him, who, forgetful of the mercy of God Almighty, rejects the Son of God himself and insults the Holy Spirit by whom he was regenerated.

Therefore, when the wicked tenants have been brought to a wicked end, the vineyard is given to another [Col. 1256D], because whoever is humble is enriched by the gift of grace that the ungrateful person rejected.

But what is said of them at the end of the Gospel—that, while seeking to seize Christ, they were hindered by fear of the crowds—we see happening daily in the Church. For there are many in the Church who are brothers in name only. They are ashamed or afraid to attack the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace, which they do not love, because of the multitude of the good brothers with whom they live.

But for such people, as the Lord says to Job, when the time comes, “wings will be raised on high” (Job 39), because, having found an opportunity, they strive to persecute the Church, deliver Christ to the cross with the Pharisees, and make him an object of mockery.

We who speak must ourselves be fearful and take care lest we follow the example of the Pharisees. Let us take care diligently that we are not Christians [Col. 1257A] in name only, and that under the appearance of piety we do not conceal the title [of Christian].

Let us give thanks to the Lord, who, because of their incorrigible wickedness, took away from the Jews the Scripture in which they once flourished, and in his sole mercy bestowed it upon us. Let us venerate him not as the simple crowds did—as a prophet—but as the God and Lord of the prophets, our Savior and Redeemer, who lives and reigns, and so forth.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. ON THE SATURDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father, etc.” (Luke 15).

[Col. 1257B] The scribes and Pharisees murmured against the author of our salvation. As the reading from the holy Gospel that precedes this one declares, the Lord proposed two parables: one of a man rejoicing over a lost sheep that had been found, the other of a woman joyfully exulting over a lost drachma that had been recovered. In the conclusion of the parable he showed how great is the joy in heaven over sinners who repent. Then he also spoke this parable, demonstrating not only his own joy over sinners who repent, but also reproving the murmuring of those who were envious.

He said, therefore: “A certain man had two sons.” This man is understood as God the almighty Father, who had two sons because he is the begetter and creator of two peoples. The elder signifies the Jews, who remained in the worship of the one God; the younger signifies the peoples of the nations, who, having abandoned the Creator and worshiping the creature, went so far as to adore the devil himself, the enemy of God.

[Col. 1257C] “And the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.’ And he divided the substance between them.” The substance divided between the brothers is understood as the rational capacity attributed to human beings by God. To live, to understand, to remember, and to excel by some natural intelligence are the substance of a divine gift. The younger son sought this substance from his father when, wishing to be in his own power, he attempted to govern himself by free choice and thus, in his pride, sought to reject the Lord his creator.

He therefore divided the substance between them, because he imparted to the faithful the grace of his protection, which they truly desired; but to the unfaithful he allotted only the benefit of natural intelligence, which they thought would suffice for them.
