[Col. 1257D] “And not many days afterward, when he had gathered everything together, the younger son departed into a far country.” The fact that he departed when everything had been gathered, and not many days afterward, signifies that not long after the creation of the human race the soul came to wish to govern its own goods by itself. Yet of itself it is weak and powerless to perform good works unless it is supported by the help of the one who gave it.

“And he squandered his substance by living prodigally.” By “living prodigally” he means loving this wasteful life, which takes pleasure in spreading itself through outward pomp and does not fear becoming empty within. He departed into a far country not by a change of place but by a change of mind. For the more greatly one sins, the farther one withdraws from the grace of God the Creator.

[Col. 1258A] “And after he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country.” Famine in a far country signifies a lack of the word of God; in a far country, that is, in forgetfulness of the Creator. Concerning it the Lord threatens through the prophet: “I will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII).

“And he himself began to be in need, and he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country.” He rightly began to be in need who had abandoned the treasures of divine wisdom and heavenly riches. The one citizen of that country to whom this prodigal attached himself is the devil, whom the Lord calls “the prince of this world,” because by the merit of his perversity he has been placed over earthly desires.

“And he sent him into his farm to feed swine.” The farm signifies carnal desire. Concerning it, the man who, having been invited to go to the spiritual banquet, excuses himself by saying: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out [Col. 1258B] and see it” (Luke XIV). To be sent into the farm is likewise to be subjected to the desires of the world.

To feed swine is to perform the things in which evil spirits delight; they are fittingly signified by an animal that always rejoices in filth and mud.

“And he desired to fill his belly with the pods that the swine were eating.” The pod is a kind of legume, large and noisy in its husks but sterile and almost empty because of the scarcity of its seeds. Thus secular teachings are signified by the pods: they resound with sterile sweetness, and in them the praises of idols—that is, the tales and songs of poets—are loudly uttered. The swine, that is, demons, take pleasure in them.

This prodigal desired to be filled with these things because he wished to find in them something sordid that might pertain to blessed life, but he could not. For this is what follows:

[Col. 1258C] “And no one gave him anything.”

“But coming to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!’”

“Coming to himself,” he says. From what had he returned? Surely from those things outside him that entice and seduce through harmful pleasures; by the concentration of his mind he had returned inward to the recesses of his conscience.

“How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!” Although the nations were living in great ignorance of the truth and in error concerning the worship of God, nevertheless, when the apostles preached, they began in a certain sense to recover their senses and, having received the fullness of the word, to be recalled.

Hired servants are those who, with a view to heavenly reward, strive to perform worthy deeds. These hired servants abound in bread in their father’s house because such people are nourished in the Church by the sustenance of spiritual grace. [Col. 1258D] But those who are placed outside this father’s household perish from hunger for the word of God and desire to fill their bellies with pods, because, lacking knowledge of the truth, they seek blessed life in the pursuits of empty philosophy.

For just as bread, which strengthens the human heart, is rightly compared with the word of God, so the pod—which is bright on the outside but empty within, and which does not nourish the belly but burdens it—is compared with secular knowledge, which is empty of usefulness although sonorous in speech.

“I will arise,” he says, “because I realize that I am lying in the worst condition. I will go to my father, from whom I have withdrawn far away.”

“To my father,” he says, “I will go, because under the prince of swine I am wasting away in pitiable want.” How pious and merciful he knew his father to be, since, although offended and provoked by great crimes, he did not disdain to hear himself called “father”!

[Col. 1259A] “Father,” he says, “I have sinned against heaven”—that is, against the angels and the holy souls, which are the feet of God. “The soul of the righteous,” he says, “is the seat of wisdom.” And the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah LXVI).

He added: “And before you”—that is, in the very secrecy of the inner conscience, which the eyes of God alone can penetrate.

“And I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.” He remembers that he is a son, and in pious affection he does not doubt that everything belonging to his father belongs to him; but mindful of his former ignorance, he does not dare aspire to these things. Therefore he asks to be made like a hired servant, to serve for a reward rather than as an heir: “Make me,” he says, “like one of your hired servants.” Yet he testifies that he cannot obtain even this except by his father’s gracious favor.

[Col. 1259B] Therefore let the Pelagians be silent, who babble with presumptuous speech that a human being can be saved by his own strength without God’s help, when the Truth most plainly says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

“And rising, he came to his father.” To come to the father is to approach the fellowship of the Church through faith, where there is a legitimate and fruitful confession of sins.

“But while he was still far away”—that is, while he did not yet understand God, but was already seeking him with pious devotion—“his father saw him,” that is, had mercy on him. For God’s seeing is having mercy, just as it is written concerning Peter: “The Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke XXII).

“And he was moved with compassion; and running, he fell upon his neck and kissed him.” The father went out to meet the returning son because God was always with the only-begotten Son. [Col. 1259C] Although the Son alone assumed flesh for our salvation, God the Father always remained in him and descended with him into this pilgrimage of ours. For the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Corinthians V). Hence the Savior himself says: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone” (John VIII). And elsewhere: “The Father, remaining in me, himself does the works” (John XIV).

“And he fell,” he says, “upon his neck and kissed him.” To fall upon the son’s neck is to bend one’s arm toward his embrace. God the Father therefore fell upon the returning Son’s neck because, in immense mercy, he poured out his arm—that is, his Word—upon the lowest things of this world.

[Col. 1259D] For he kissed him, namely, he restored him through the word of grace to the hope of pardon, when through the Son he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew IV).

“And the son said to his father: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’” After he has returned to the father—that is, after he has been established in the Church—he begins to confess his sins, but he does not say everything that he had previously promised he would say.

For he said: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” but he did not add what he had earlier intended to say: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” While he was still far away and did not have the father, he desired to be a hired servant. But after he had deserved to be honored most generously by his father’s kiss, he now disdains being a hired servant.

For he understands that there is a great distinction between a slave, a hired servant, and a son. [Col. 1260A] A slave is one who abstains from vices through fear of the punishments of Gehenna or dread of worldly laws. A hired servant is one who does good through hope and desire for the heavenly kingdom. A son is one who serves God gladly through the affection of goodness and love of the virtues, out of charity.

The Apostle recalls this highest summation and perfection of all the virtues, saying: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Corinthians XIII).

This prodigal, therefore, first returning to himself like a slave, began to fear the punishments of dreadful hunger. Soon, wishing to return to his father, he began to think about the condition of a hired servant. But after the father came out to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him, he forgot the condition of a slave and forgot the hired servant’s reward; now, as a son, he became concerned only with his father’s inheritance.

[Col. 1260B] “But the father said to his servants: ‘Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him.’” The first robe is the blessed garment of innocence, which Adam, the first-created human being, received when he had been well fashioned by God, but lost after being wickedly deceived by the devil. Hence, after the guilt of transgression, the first human beings realized that they were naked and, having lost the glory of immortality, received garments of mortal skins.

The servants to whom this is commanded are the holy preachers. They brought forth the first robe when they preached that those reconciled to God were to be exalted by such great grace that they would become not only citizens of the angels but also heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ.

“And put a ring on his hand.” Secret matters are customarily sealed with a ring. By the ring, therefore, we should understand the seal of faith, by which all God’s promises are confirmed in the hearts of the faithful.

[Col. 1260C] A bride is also betrothed by a ring as a pledge of the marriage faith; therefore, by the ring is understood the pledge of the marriage between Christ and the Church. The prodigal son received the ring when, through faith, Christ joined the Church from the nations to himself. It is fitting that the ring is placed on the hand, so that works may attest to faith and faith itself may be confirmed by works.

“And put shoes on his feet.” By the shoes the ministry of evangelization is signified. For it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who preach good things!” (Romans X). The Apostle likewise says: “With your feet shod in preparation for the gospel” (Ephesians VI).

Therefore, when the son has returned to his father’s compassion, his hands and feet are adorned: [Col. 1260D] his hands, so that we, the faithful, may live rightly; his feet, so that, instructed by the pious examples of the saints, we may hasten toward eternal joys.

“And bring the fattened calf and kill it.” The fattened calf is the Son of God himself, the Lord Jesus Christ. He is rightly called a fattened calf because his flesh is excellent in spiritual richness and fruitful power, so much so that it alone was sufficient to take away the sins of the whole world.

He commanded the calf to be brought and killed, signifying that his death was to be preached through the apostles. For this calf is killed as though newly born whenever he is believed to have been killed by each individual. He is eaten when the sacrament of his Passion is received with a chaste body and a pure mind.

[Col. 1261A] “And let us eat and rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.” It should be noted that he says in the plural: “Let us eat and rejoice.” For it is shown that not only the one who had been dead and came to life again, who had been lost and found, but also the father and his servants feasted on the sacred flesh of this holy calf. The joy of the Father is our salvation, and his joy is the remission of our sins—not only the Father’s and the Son’s, but also that of the Holy Spirit, because the operation of the Holy Trinity is one, its joy one, and its love one.

This was prefigured long ago when Abraham, having received three angels as guests, is read to have killed a tender and excellent calf and set it before them. For the flesh of Christ, sacrificed for our redemption, is the joy of the whole Trinity.

“And they began to feast.” This banquet is now celebrated throughout the whole world, extended through the Church. [Col. 1261B] Every day in the holy Church this most sacred calf is offered to God the Father by the priests, and it nourishes those who receive it unto eternal life, because although it is sacrificed daily, it always remains whole, undefiled, and living.

“Now the elder son was in the field.” The elder son is the Jewish people, who first possessed knowledge of God and whom God, through the prophet, called his firstborn son. Although this people had not departed far from the father, it was not at home but in the field, because it had neither wholly abandoned the worship of the Creator on account of idols nor penetrated the inner mysteries of the law given to it. It delighted only in the surface of the letter and knew how to perform only outward, earthly works.

Hence earthly things were promised to it when the Lord said through the prophet: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah I).

“And when he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and a chorus.” It often happens that some diligent and devoted teacher among the Jews begins to investigate the secrets of the law. When, from those same Scriptures, he perceives the freedom of the Church, he recoils from the labor of servile work to which he had devoted himself by observing the letter of the law.

[Col. 1261C] This is as if to withdraw from the field and draw near to the house. He hears music and a chorus—that is, he understands that preachers full of the Holy Spirit are preaching with harmonious voices. Thus the Apostle also says: “I beseech you all to say the same thing” (I Corinthians I).

“And he called one of the servants and asked what these things were.” He calls one of the servants when he takes into his hands for reading one of the prophets, who are the true servants of this master of the household. Investigating anxiously, he asks, as it were, why the joyful feasts of the Church are taking place, since he sees that he himself has no part in them.

[Col. 1261D] Therefore the servant answers him: “Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf.” This is openly to say: “The gentile people, which until now did not know God and through error had withdrawn far from God, is now turning to him from all parts of the world, even from the ends of the earth, and for its salvation sings a new song to God with such great exultation.”

For its sake that exceedingly fat calf was also killed, to which the Psalmist says: “May your burnt offering be made fat” (Psalm XVI).

“But he became angry and was unwilling to enter.” The Jews, still obstinate in mind, remain outside and do not wish to enter the faith of the Church.

“Therefore his father went out and began to entreat him.” [Col. 1262A] At the end of the age the calling of the Jews will be fulfilled, because they will believe through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch. The father’s going out signifies this open calling of the Jews. For then he will in a certain sense go out and entreat him, so that, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel also may be saved as the younger son, although blindness in unbelief has come upon the greater part of it.

“But he answered and said to his father: ‘Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.’” Although we very frequently read that this people worshiped idols against the Lord’s command, what does it mean that he now says, “I have never transgressed your command”?

This must be understood not of all Israelites but specifically of certain ones—namely, those who always worshiped God and never turned to idols. Although such people delighted only in earthly things, as though they were in the field, they nevertheless hoped to receive those earthly goods from God alone.

This is also confirmed by the testimony of the same brother when he replied later: “And you have never given me a kid, so that I might feast with my friends.” [Col. 1262B] The kid is a foolish animal and usually bears the figure of a sinner in the divine Scriptures. But in this passage, by the name “kid” we should understand Christ, whom that people, seeing him come in the likeness of sinful flesh, judged to be a sinner.

Hence, after the blind man had been given sight, they said: “We know that this man is a sinner” (John IX). Elsewhere they blasphemously said that he was a Samaritan and had a demon (John VIII).

[Col. 1262C] Nor should it seem strange if we say that Christ is represented here by the kid, since in the law he is also read to have been called by this name. For it says: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exodus XXIII).

What he says, therefore—“You have never given me a kid”—is as though he were saying: “You have not given me the one who appeared to me to be a kid.” Because they called Christ a profaner of the law and a violator of the Sabbath, they did not deserve to rejoice in his banquets.

What follows—“so that I might feast with my friends”—must be understood as spoken from the person of the rulers, who wished to feast with their friends, that is, with the rest of the common people.

“You have not given me a kid,” that is: “For this reason you withhold him from me, because he appeared to me to be a kid.”

It may also be understood as spoken from the person of the people of Jerusalem, together with the other peoples of Judea.

[Col. 1262D] “But after this son of yours came, who has devoured his substance with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.” The prostitutes with whom he is said to have devoured his substance are the superstitions and wicked inventions of the nations. In these they expended their whole natural intelligence; and, having abandoned God, whom they ought to have had as the husband of the soul, they fornicated with the most shameful crowd of demons through a most depraved desire.

“But the father said: ‘Son, you are always with me.’” He did not rebuke him as though he were lying, but, affirming his perseverance in his service, he invited him to rejoice with him and to feast together with his son.

“And everything that is mine is yours.” Speaking to the Father in one passage, the Son says: “Everything that is yours is mine, and everything that is mine is yours” (John XVII). Behold, this sounds very similar to the present statement: “Everything that is mine is yours.” Yet the meaning is distinct and very different.

[Col. 1263A] The one who is Son of God by nature possesses everything that belongs to the Father in a more eminent way than those whom grace has made sons of God. Everything belonging to the Father belongs to the former by nature, and to the latter through God’s bestowed mercy. The former possesses all things by authority as the only Son; the latter possess them through a divinely granted adoption. The former has all things because, being God from God, he was born equal to the Father; the latter have them because they have been reborn from God.

Of course, when it is said, “Everything that is mine is yours,” it should not be understood as though those things were not also his. In an earthly inheritance there are certain limitations, and the elder brother cannot possess everything if the younger also possesses a share. But in the inheritance of spiritual and heavenly goods, perfect and immortal sons possess everything in such a way that each thing belongs to all and all things belong to each, because [Col. 1263B] charity operates in all things and knows nothing of possessing with restriction.

The Psalmist exalts this charity with great praise, saying: “I have seen the end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm CXVIII).

Let us therefore devote ourselves most earnestly to this. Through it let us learn to rejoice together as we advance in transformation.

Let us love what is above us with our whole soul, our whole mind, and our whole strength.

Let us love what is within us—that is, our inner person, namely our soul—and let us always take care to subject it to God.

Let us love what is beside us—that is, our neighbor as ourselves.

Let us love what is beneath us, namely our flesh, so that we may break its unlawful desires and compel it to obey the spirit.

Let us earnestly ask Christ, our God and Lord, to preserve our spirit, soul, and body blameless at [Col. 1263C] his coming for himself, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XCII. ON THE THIRD FERIAL DAY AFTER OCULI

“At that time Jesus, looking upon his disciples, said to Simon Peter: ‘If your brother sins against you,’” etc. (Matthew XVIII).

This entire reading from the holy Gospel instructs us by moral precepts and shows, with a most necessary admonition, how we ought to act toward those who sin against us. It should therefore be heard with all the greater attentiveness [Col. 1264B] and learned with all the greater diligence, since it is clear that without this teaching the bond of unblemished charity, by which the Church’s stability is maintained, cannot be preserved firm and unbroken.

Thus the Lord, teaching his disciples to maintain peace with their brothers, says: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone.”

It must first be noted that if a brother sins against us and wounds our spirit for any reason, we are granted the power—indeed, we are placed under the necessity—of forgiving him. For we know that our own debts are not otherwise forgiven us unless we also forgive our debtors.

But if someone sins against [Col. 1264C] God, it is not within our discretion to forgive; that belongs to God alone. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, God can be entreated on his behalf; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (I Kings II).

Yet we act in the opposite order: in avenging the insult done to God, we grow sluggish through a deadly form of piety, while in our own injuries we exercise hatred.

Nevertheless, the one who sins against us must first be rebuked privately, lest he think that what he is doing is not a sin and, having once lost his sense of shame, wish to remain in sin.

And if he listens to us, we win his soul, because through his salvation remission of sins is also granted to us, as the Apostle James says: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James V).

Thus he teaches by what order we can avoid scandals: namely, if we ourselves injure no one; if we rebuke the sinner out of zeal for justice; and if we open the depths of compassion to the penitent with our whole heart.

[Col. 1264D] When, therefore, we rebuke a sinful brother, if he does not listen to us, one or two brothers are to be brought in, so that the one who could not be corrected by one may be corrected by several, or may be convicted by their testimony.

But if he does not listen to them either, then we are commanded to tell the Church, so that he may be detested and judged by all; if he was unwilling to be corrected by shame, at least he may be corrected by the reproaches of many.

“But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a publican.” *Ethnos* is the Greek word for “nation”; from it *ethnicus*, that is, “gentile,” is derived. A gentile is one who remains as he was born and has not been reborn in Christ.

Publicans are those who sin publicly, or those who engage in public business through fraud, theft, and criminal perjuries.

[Col. 1265A] When he says that an incorrigible brother is to be treated as a pagan and a publican, he shows that the person who performs the works of unbelievers under the appearance of being faithful is guilty of a more serious crime than one who openly exists as an unbeliever and publican.

Yet this too must be carefully observed: we are commanded to forgive a brother not indiscriminately or lightly, but when he is obedient, is doing penance for his offense, and asks for pardon.

Before God, the person who refuses to correct a sinful brother when he sees him sinning, but through negligence treats the matter as insignificant, is held guilty of the same sin as the person who refuses to forgive a brother who is doing penance.

For when the Lord had said, “If your brother sins, rebuke him,” he immediately added: “If he says, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.”

Therefore pardon must be granted after rebuke—namely, to the one who has done penance and turned away from error. For forgiveness should be neither difficult nor indulgence lax:

[Col. 1265B] “Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

Because he had said that a harsh and unrepentant brother was to be treated as a pagan and a publican, lest anyone become so foolish and contemptuous through a destructive despair that he would say silently to himself, “If you despise me, I will despise you; if you honor me, then I shall certainly be honored according to my own judgment,” the Lord therefore granted the apostles the power of binding and loosing. Thus those who are condemned may know that a human judgment is confirmed by divine judgment, and that whatever has been bound on earth is likewise bound in heaven.

This power was granted especially to the holy bishops of the Church, but it is believed to have been given generally to the whole Church. For when the Lord elsewhere gave blessed Peter this power of binding and loosing, since [Col. 1265C] Peter bore the figure of the Church, there is no doubt that through Peter he granted this power to all the faithful.

“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.”

He grants the faithful great authority and confidence, and, conversely, he instills great fear in those who despise him, saying that whatever has been established on earth through the agreement of two will be done by God the Father in heaven.

First, this summons us to harmony, so that we may hasten more earnestly toward peace, since he says that he will be present among two or three who establish something together.

For it follows: “For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

“In the midst of them,” he says, “I am,” either to receive the humble penitent or to cast out the proud and obstinate. Whatever they do on earth in judging for the salvation of human beings is strengthened in heaven by my judgment from above.

[Col. 1265D] Spiritually, we may also understand this to mean that wherever spirit, soul, and body agree, and do not have among themselves the warfare of conflicting desires, with the flesh desiring against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, they can obtain from the Father whatever they ask.

There is no doubt that a petition is just and acceptable to God when the flesh desires what the spirit desires.

“Then Peter came to him and said: ‘Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?’ Jesus said to him: ‘I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.’”

Provoked by the Lord’s preceding words, the Apostle Peter approached with his customary confidence and asked how often he ought to forgive one who sinned against him—whether up to seven times.

[Col. 1266A] The Lord answered him: not merely up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven, that is, 490 times, if it should happen that he sinned that many times in a day.

For it is impossible to offend against one’s brother 490 times. This multiplication was made according to blessed Jerome.

Blessed Augustine, however, teaches that this number is to be understood simply and not multiplicatively, because the whole expression is formed by an adverb. The art of arithmetic teaches that if a number is expressed by an adverb alone or by a noun alone, it is not multiplied; but if it is expressed by a noun together with an adverb—for example, *septies septuaginta*, “seven times seventy,” or conversely *septuagies septem*, “seventy times seven”—it can be multiplied.

[Col. 1266B] Therefore, when he says “seventy-seven times,” the same teacher understands it as seventy-seven times. But now we must come to the mystery.

For it cannot be without purpose that the Lord wished to establish this particular number in forgiving the errors of brothers. It consists of seven and eleven. For whether we say seven times eleven or eleven times seven, we arrive at seventy-seven.

The number seven is a most sacred number, derived from the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit. The number eleven, however, bears the figure of every sin, since in eleven there is the transgression of ten. Whenever we sin, we certainly transgress the ten commandments of God.

Hence it is recorded that in the tabernacle of God there were eleven coverings of goats’ hair (Exodus XX). [Col. 1266C] Haircloth signifies the condition of penitents and of those who mourn for sins. In the tabernacle of God, therefore, eleven coverings of goats’ hair were ordered to be made because the holy Church exists not only from the just and undefiled, but also from penitent and converted sinners.

Recognizing the sacramental meaning of this number, the Apostle Peter, after Judas had been lost, did not wish the apostles to remain at the number eleven; instead, after Matthias had been chosen, he took care to restore the total of twelve.

Thus the Lord commanded seventy-seven times in order to show that whenever and however often someone sins, we must forgive him just as often and never cease forgiving.

[Col. 1266D] That the remission of sins is signified by this number is also made clear by the fact that blessed Luke brought the genealogy of the Lord’s generation to an end with seventy-seven generations, beginning from Joseph and reaching all the way to God the Creator himself.

Because the Son of God was coming to remove the sins of the world, his incarnation is rightly woven through seventy-seven generations, and this in ascending order. For the incarnation of the Son of God was our exaltation; and from the place to which he descended, our abasement merited to rise.

The fact that this number arises from the multiplication of seven and eleven signifies that all remission of sins takes place through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Those who refuse to forgive brothers who sin against them deserve to be deprived of the Spirit’s gifts.

Yet we are commanded to grant forgiveness differently to a penitent brother and to an enemy who persecutes us.

To the penitent brother forgiveness must be granted after he has received remission of the sin by which, although we were innocent, he injured us, so that thereafter he may share charity with us.

[Col. 1267A] To the enemy, however, forgiveness must be granted in such a way that, when he wishes evil but does it to us, we may always wish him good and, if we can, also do good to him. For as long as they persist in evil, we cannot grant them remission of their sin, even if we wish to do so.

We have two most fitting examples of this. Joseph, after salutarily chastising his brothers, forgave them benevolently (Genesis XLV). David, however, although he wept for his persecutors who were penitent yet persisted in their wickedness, could not grant them forgiveness (II Kings I).

Let us therefore diligently practice these precepts of the charity we have heard from Christ, who is the author of peace. Let us not find it burdensome to forgive small offenses, since we know that innumerable sins were forgiven us in baptism.

[Col. 1267B] But since we sin daily, let us also ask the Lord daily for forgiveness. By his own example he urges us toward the ease of pardon: he not only deigned to forgive the sins of the whole world but also to expiate them with his own mouth—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XCIII. ON THE FOURTH FERIAL DAY AFTER OCULI

“At that time the scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus, saying: ‘Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders?’” etc. (Matthew XV).

Because the Son of God had come into the world for the salvation of all, he traversed each place with swift steps, [Col. 1267C] so that he might benefit everyone, come to the aid of all, and finally provide for the common salvation of all. Indeed, as the evangelist relates above, the Lord came with his disciples into the territory of the Gerazenes, so that he might bring them, too, the relief they desired through his visitation. There the Pharisees, enemies of righteousness, persecuted him—not out of a desire to learn the truth, but in order to construct falsehood. For, as we have read:

> The scribes and Pharisees approached Jesus, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

How true is the Lord’s confession when, praising God the Father above, he had said:

> “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI).

Behold, the Gerazenes, [Col. 1267D] who were less learned, come to the Lord, bring their sick with them, and seek remedies of salvation for themselves and their own, at least by touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment. Thus, through the merit of their faith, they obtain the fullness of the salvation they desired. But the scribes and Pharisees, who ought to have been teachers of the people, gather not to hear the word, nor to receive any healing of soul or body, but to provoke quarrels over questions. They labor to reproach the disciples for unwashed hands, although they could find in them nothing of the defiling impurity they alleged. Indeed, they ought rather to have blamed themselves: though they had washed their hands with water, they bore a conscience stained by envy.

“Why,” they ask, “do your disciples transgress the precepts of the elders?” Astonishing madness! They reproach the one who is the Son of God [Col. 1268A] because he does not observe human traditions. “For,” they say, “they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

It was characteristic, and in a certain sense customary, for the Jews to wash their hands frequently, and sometimes their whole body, especially if it happened that they had spoken with any gentile. But now let us see by what judgment the sons of falsehood are refuted by Truth. He says to them:

> “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God on account of your tradition?”

As though he were saying: “Since you neglect God’s commandments for the sake of human tradition, why do you reproach my disciples because they disregard the traditions of the elders and keep the divine commands? For God said: ‘Honor your father and your mother. And whoever curses father or mother shall surely die’” (Exod. XX).

In sacred Scripture, honor is understood in two ways: not only in greeting and bowing, but also in almsgiving and the provision of necessities. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Let presbyters be considered worthy of double honor,”

so that not only the service of veneration may be offered to them, but also suitable support may be provided (I Tim. V).

“But you say,” he continues:

> “Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ and does not honor his father or mother”—and so you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition.

God, the creator and father of all, taking into consideration the weakness and age of parents, had commanded in the Law that children honor their parents and provide them with the necessities of life. The scribes and Pharisees overturned this provision of God’s Law and introduced impiety under the appearance of piety. They taught wicked children to offer to God whatever [Col. 1268C] had been assigned for the use of the poor and of their parents. Thus it happened that the offering of the children, under the pretext of the Temple, became a source of profit for the priests.

The parents themselves, knowing that what had been consecrated to God by their children could not be touched without committing sacrilege, did not wish to take it; and consequently they were afflicted by poverty and hunger. Therefore, when a needy and weak father asked his son for something, the son, instructed by teachers of iniquity, would answer him:

“O father, do not be distressed, but patiently strive to endure the hardships of this necessity, because the gift that has been offered to God from me will benefit you—not bodily, perhaps, but certainly spiritually.”

This may also be understood interrogatively:

“O father, will the gift that is from me benefit you?”

As though he were saying: “You demand that I expend for your use the gift that I was about to offer to God—and this will benefit you?” The scribes and Pharisees said this so that wretched parents would fear to accept what they saw had been offered, and would choose rather to lead an impoverished life than to touch what had been consecrated to God.

Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

The prophet Isaiah, foreseeing the Jews’ hypocrisy—that they would come against the preaching of the Gospel and resist Christ—prophesied rightly concerning them. This does not mean that what was said about them was good, but that the sacred prophecy itself corresponded most appropriately to their behavior.

He therefore speaks in the person of the Lord:

> “This people honors me with their lips.”

The Jews honored God with their lips when they studied the Law given by him [Col. 1269A] and also sang psalms and divine hymns. But their heart was far from him, because they were always carried headlong toward evil, worshiping idols in their hearts. Of them it had been written that they “turned back in their hearts to Egypt.”

They honored God with their lips when, through deceitful trickery, they said to Christ:

> “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII).

But their heart was far from him, because they said these things so that they might hand him over to Caesar’s authority. The evangelist indicated this when he first stated that, after the Pharisees had gone away, they took counsel in order to trap Jesus in his speech.

> “In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.”

They worshiped him vainly with lips and tongue, while their hearts were turned away; and they could not expect a reward with the other worshipers of God, since the Lord himself says elsewhere:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII).

They taught doctrines and commandments of men because, neglecting God’s precepts, they wished to establish their own traditions, as was shown above.

And when he had summoned the crowds to himself, he said to them:

> “Hear and understand: it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth.”

The word *communicat*—“makes common” or “shares”—is characteristic of the sacred Scriptures. The Jews, who boast that they are God’s people and portion, called “common” the foods that all people ordinarily use together, except the Jews themselves: for example, hares, oysters, pork, and animals of this kind, from which they had been commanded to abstain.

They therefore called “common” what was available for use by other people but was not part of God’s portion, and for that reason they called it unclean. Hence among them the word *communicare*, “to make common,” is used for “to pollute” and “to defile”; the translators rendered it “defiles.”

He therefore says:

> “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person.”

As though he were saying: “Nothing that is outside a person and enters into him can defile him; rather, the things that proceed from a person are what pollute him.”

Someone may reasonably object: If what enters the mouth does not defile a person, why do we not eat food sacrificed to idols? For the Apostle says:

> “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (I Cor. X).

But it must be understood that these foods themselves, and every creature of God, are clean in themselves. When they are offered to idols through the invocation of demons, however, they become unclean. For this reason they are rightly rejected by holy men.

Then the disciples, hearing this, said to him:

> “Do you know that when the Pharisees heard this saying, they were scandalized?”

They were scandalized because they saw that, with a single saying of the Lord, all the superstitious observances they practiced had been overturned. They thought that their religion consisted solely in eating or rejecting certain foods, and in washings and various baptisms, not understanding what the Apostle says:

> “Food does not commend us to God” (I Cor. VIII).

*Scandalum* is a Greek word, which we may call an offense or a downfall—that is, a striking of the foot. The Pharisees therefore were scandalized by the word of God: blinded by the obstinacy of a perverse mind, they found in Christ’s teaching not salvation but an occasion for the ruin of eternal destruction.

But he answered [Col. 1270A] and said:

> “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.”

Those who say that there are two natures in human beings—one good, from God, and the other evil, from the prince of darkness, the devil—consider this passage favorable to themselves. They take the planting that the Father did not plant to mean the evil nature.

But it must be understood that every nature is from God and is good. Because human beings possess free will, the planting of nature is good, but it frequently becomes evil through an evil will. Hence Jeremiah says:

> “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II).

Therefore, what God plants no one can uproot, unless nature itself gives its assent.

A reasonable question may arise here. If every planting that the Father did not plant will be uprooted, then will the planting also be uprooted of which the Apostle says:

> “I planted, Apollos watered” (I Cor. III)?

But we must attend to what follows:

> “God gave the growth.”

Thus, when Paul plants and Apollos waters, God cooperates with his laborers; with them he plants and waters.

> “Let them alone: they are blind guides of the blind.”

The Pharisees were blind because, observing the dark traditions they themselves had devised, they did not consider the light of God’s commandments. Of this the Psalmist says:

> “Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. CXVIII).

They are called not only blind but also guides of the blind, because such people not only fail to protect themselves from falling into the pit of destruction, but also drag those who follow them with them into the precipice of death.

Therefore the Savior commands that these men, and all perverse teachers, be left alone [Col. 1270C] and abandoned to their errors and free will, knowing that once they have fallen away, they can scarcely, or not at all, be brought back to the truth. Hence the Apostle also commands, saying:

> “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Tit. III).

Peter answered and said:

> “Explain this parable to us.”

But he said:

> “Are you also still without understanding?”

The holy apostles were still less instructed, and therefore they did not understand the words of God when they were spoken plainly. Instead, they thought that what had been said openly and was clear to the hearing had been spoken as a parable; consequently, they sought a mystical understanding of something evident.

For this reason the Lord rebukes them, because they thought that what he had spoken clearly had been expressed figuratively:

> “Are you also still,” he says, [Col. 1270D] “without understanding? Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is discharged into the privy?”

Heretics slander this statement of the Lord and reproach him as though he were ignorant of physical reasoning, because he says that all foods go into the stomach and are digested there. They say that food which has been taken in and broken up by the friction of the teeth and the neck is distributed through the limbs, veins, marrow, and nerves.

Thus we see many people who suffer continual vomiting because of a stomach disorder vomit immediately after meals what they have swallowed, and yet remain well fleshed, because at the first contact with food, the more liquid nourishment and drink are distributed through the body.

But when such people wish to criticize another’s ignorance, they display their own. For although the fluid and dissolved food may be extremely fine, nevertheless, once it has been received and digested by the limbs and veins, it flows through hidden passages—which they call pores—to cleanse the lower parts, and thus it goes into the privy.

But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the person. For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies.

It should be noted that the Lord says that evil thoughts come out of the heart. For the philosopher Plato says that the seat of the soul is in the brain; but we ought to understand the heart as the soul’s more principal seat, where, situated as though in a kind of center, it orders thoughts and supplies the bodily members with vital impulse.

By this same teaching, those who say that thoughts are injected by the devil and do not arise from one’s own will are also refuted. The devil can be an assistant and kindler of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author.

Yet it must in no way be accepted that the devil can search out the secrets of the heart. He is always lying in wait and judges what we are turning over in our minds from the posture and gestures of the body itself, since he cannot look directly into the thoughts of the heart. This power was reserved for him alone to whom it was said:

> “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (III Kings VIII).

Since, therefore, he cannot see the thoughts themselves, he detects them through certain signs and movements.

For example, if he sees us repeatedly looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the arrow of love and stimulates us through wicked suggestions to fornicate. If, by contrast, he sees us raise an angry tone of voice or a fierce look against our neighbor, he understands that the heart is wasting away with envy and thus inflames us through anger toward the crime of murder.

If, during a period of fasting, he sees us repeatedly looking toward a window and carefully marking the hour by the sun’s ray, he proves that the mind has been wounded by the vice of gluttony. If he sees us gazing ardently at the beauty of gems, gold, or any other objects, he understands that the evil of avarice lies hidden in the heart and therefore incites us to theft.

It must be observed that the Savior calls these manifest deeds “thoughts,” because desire, first conceived in the heart, is nourished by the springs of thought and is then brought to action. For this reason the Lord calls these deeds thoughts. The crafty enemy investigates their signs through certain habits of behavior, hastens to deceive the human race, and incites it to do what the divine word forbids, so that he may defile the human being created in the image of God.

Therefore, after listing the evil thoughts, the Lord added:

> “These are the things that defile a person; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

But the Pharisees accepted everything according to the letter and refused to understand spiritually the spiritual words of the prophets. Whatever the prophets commanded concerning the cleansing both of the heart and of the body, saying:

> “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I),

and elsewhere:

> “Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII),

they believed was to be observed only in bodily cleanliness.

But they washed their hands in vain, and were baptized in vain, because they scorned to be washed in the Savior’s font. What benefit is there in whitening the skin outwardly while inwardly carrying a mind made filthy by envy, avarice, and other vices?

Such people are rightly compared to whitewashed tombs, which appear white on the outside but within are full of filth and foul corpses.

Therefore, according to the Apostle:

> “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (II Cor. VII).

Let us strive to have a clean soul in a clean body, so that we may complete our sanctification in the fear of Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCIV. ON THE THURSDAY AFTER *Oculi*

At that time, Jesus rose from the synagogue and entered the house of Simon, etc. (Luke IV).

See the homily for the Saturday after Pentecost.

## HOMILY XCV. ON THE FRIDAY AFTER *Oculi*

[Col. 1272B]

At that time Jesus came into a city of the Samaritans called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Now Jacob’s well was there, etc. (John IV).

From this reading, the true humanity of our Redeemer is commended—the humanity which he assumed from us and for our sake. For although he was the true Son of God, supremely blessed and supremely happy, giving every good thing and needing nothing, he became human in order to redeem us. Thus he adapted himself to our weakness, assuming in himself, except for sin, everything that accords with our frailty.

Indeed, he who was the bread of life grew hungry; the fountain of righteousness grew thirsty; he who was the way grew tired from the journey; and he who was the light of the world permitted his limbs to yield to sleep for our sake. Thus the evangelist says: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting by the well” [Col. 1272C]. But we must consider from what journey the Lord is said to have grown weary.

Above we read that, when Jesus heard that the Pharisees had said of him that he was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—he left Judea and went again into Galilee. He therefore came into a city of the Samaritans called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob had given to his son Joseph, where Jacob’s well was; and then comes the statement, “Jesus, wearied from the journey.” For our sake, and as one of us, he could grow weary—he who in himself was always immovable in movement and mutable in condition.

He sat by the well to relieve the discomfort of weariness. He also intended to indicate the person and dignity of a teacher [Col. 1272D], for sitting is characteristic of teachers.

The Lord therefore came into a city of the Samaritans so that, while passing through, he might also bestow upon them the benefit of his teaching. But he approached the estate that Jacob had given to his son Joseph in order to show that he was the one whom the holy Joseph had prefigured: the one whom the sun and moon truly venerate, whom all the stars serve, and whom his impious brothers—namely, the Jews—persecuted with unjust hatred.

He sat by the well because he knew that the woman whom he had foreseen would believe before the ages would come there. Hence it follows: “A woman came from Samaria to draw water.” Jesus said to her: “Give me a drink.”

Why does the Lord ask the Samaritan woman for a drink, when in what follows he promises to give those who believe in him the spiritual abundance of the fountain [Col. 1273A]? He was thirsty—not so much for water as for the woman’s salvation and faith. Finally, the nature of the Lord’s thirst becomes clear from what follows, where he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father.” As his food is, so also is his drink. This, then, he desired and thirsted for: to fulfill the Father’s will in her.

But the woman was still carnal, and, understanding the Lord’s thirst carnally, she replied: “How is it that you, though you are a Jew, ask me for a drink, since I am a Samaritan woman?” She explains why she wonders, adding: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.” “Do not associate” means that Jews do not share or communicate with Samaritans; they have no use of anything in common with them and participate in nothing with them. They curse and hate them because they possess their region or because they worship both God and idols. Hence they considered it a great insult to call someone a Samaritan, and Christ is frequently recorded as having been abused by that name [Col. 1273B].

But let us hear what the Lord answered this woman, who was still wandering and living in darkness: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

What else is the gift of God than the Holy Spirit? He gave this gift to the faithful after his ascension, for “ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV). And as the same evangelist says elsewhere: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

The Lord therefore showed that he was not thirsty for the sort of water she understood [Col. 1273C]. He thirsted for her faith, and for that reason he wished to give the Spirit to her in her thirst. This is the water of which, elsewhere, standing in the temple, he said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and from his belly will flow rivers of living water” (ibid.). Explaining this, the evangelist added: “He said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

He therefore says: “If you knew the gift of God and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” She could not know Christ because she did not possess the gift of God, that is, the Holy Spirit. And because she did not know Christ, she did not know how to ask him for living water.

But the woman, still persisting in a carnal understanding, replied: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, along with his sons and his livestock?” [Col. 1273D]

It should be noted that here she calls it a well, although above he called it a fountain, since every well is a fountain, but not every fountain is a well.

Let us pass over these words, which are clear and straightforward, and hear what the Lord answered her as he explained his earlier words. He says: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst. The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

Delighted by these words of the Lord, wishing to share in so great a gift, yet still embracing the understanding of the flesh, she replied: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or come here to draw water” [Col. 1274A].

The Lord said to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.”

She answered him: “I have no husband.”

Jesus said to her: “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband.”

The Lord certainly knew that she had no husband. He spoke in this way in order gradually to draw her away from a carnal understanding and lead her to understand who it was who was speaking with her. In the end, when the woman heard what concerned her, she confessed him first as a prophet and afterward as the Christ.

But although the literal simplicity of this account is plain, a profound depth of meaning lies hidden within it. Since we have now tasted something of this gift of God and of the spiritual water, let us treat these matters spiritually. First, let us see what it signifies that the Lord is said to have come to the well at the sixth hour [Col. 1274B].

The sixth hour signifies the sixth age of the world. Then, as though in the old age of the world, the Lord and Redeemer, clothed in humanity, came to the well—to the dark depth, that is, of this world. From the height of heaven he deigned to descend to the lowest parts of the earth.

The Lord therefore came to the well at the sixth hour, when the sun began to decline toward the lower circles from the summit of heaven’s center. For, as has been said, in the last age of the world the Son of God deigned to descend to our earthly labor, so that he might teach us to put off the old man with his deeds and to put on the new, who was created according to God.

That he came weary signifies the weakness of the flesh; that he sat signifies humility. He therefore sat down weary because he assumed the weakness of the flesh for our sake [Col. 1274C] and appeared as a humble man among human beings.

Of this weakness of his flesh the prophet says: “We saw him, and he had no appearance; and we desired him, despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” (Isa. LIII). Of his humility the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

This Samaritan woman is the Church of the nations, and she is rightly called Samaritan. Samaria is commonly understood as idolatry. Hence the prophet, foretelling Christ’s incarnation, says: “Before the child knows how to call his father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isa. VIII).

Christ received the power of Damascus when the Magi offered him gold, in which that once most powerful city had formerly placed its confidence [Col. 1274D]. He received the spoils of Samaria when he brought back to the liberty of the new grace those who had been oppressed by the captivity of idolatry.

This woman is therefore appropriately called Samaritan, because before Christ’s coming the holy Church was devoted to the worship of idolatry and knew no activity except to occupy itself with the concerns of the world and empty desires. This is signified by the fact that the woman came to the well with a jar to draw water.

The Lord asked her for a drink because he thirsted for the salvation of the nations, desiring to rescue them from error and lead them to the religion of Christian faith.

The five husbands whom she had are understood as the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. By sight we see white and black and colors of every kind. By hearing we perceive harsh and melodious sounds. By smell we distinguish fragrant and foul odors. By taste we perceive both sweet and bitter things. By touch, which is diffused through all the limbs of the body, we sense hot and cold, soft and hard, smooth and rough [Col. 1275A].

Before Christ’s coming the Church of the nations was subject to these five senses. Lacking the light of the mind, it passed through a carnal life without any understanding. Since these senses were not discovered by error but were bestowed by nature, they are rightly called husbands, as though legitimate ones, to whom all human beings in the world’s first ages were subject.

But the time had now come when the soul was no longer to use those senses as rulers. Instead, it was to have a husband—that is, a rational spirit—to whom it would subject those earlier husbands, the five senses, in service. The soul was no longer to be subjected to five husbands; it was to embrace the Word of God, cleave to Christ in spirit, and enjoy not the things of the present but the love of eternal things [Col. 1275B].

But because it was still held by its former error and, after the five husbands—that is, after the period of the five carnal senses—had not yet received the Word of God, the devil possessed it, enticed by an adulterous embrace. The Lord therefore said: “Call your husband, and come here.” This means: “Remove yourself from the carnal affection in which you now live, call forth the spirit of understanding, and present yourself here.”

The spirit of a human being is, in a certain sense, the husband of the soul. It governs animal affection as a husband governs his wife. Of this the Apostle says: “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (I Cor. II).

When she answered, “I have no husband,” she heard: “You have spoken well; for you have had five husbands,” and in the first period you served the five bodily senses. The one you now have is not your husband, because you do not possess within you a spirit that understands God, with whom you could enter into a legitimate union. Rather, the devil’s error dominates you and corrupts you with adulterous defilement.

Perhaps it is relevant that, after five carnal responses, this woman names Christ in a sixth response. Her first response was: “How is it that you, though you are a Jew, ask me for a drink, since I am a Samaritan woman?” Her second was: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep.” Her third was: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst forever.” Her fourth was: “I have no husband.” Her fifth was: “I see that you are a prophet; our fathers worshiped on this mountain.”

In the sixth response she confesses Christ, saying: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ.” Yet she still errs, because she was expecting him as one who would come, while she already had him present. She had not yet called her husband, but it was near at hand that this error, like an adulterer, should be expelled and rational understanding introduced.

The woman therefore says: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.” Her understanding had begun to approach, as though a husband, but had not yet fully arrived. She thought the Lord a prophet, and in this she was not entirely mistaken. He himself even deigned to call himself a prophet, saying: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII). Long before, Moses had said of him: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him” (Deut. XVIII) [Col. 1276A].

“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.”

There was a dispute between Jews and Samaritans. The Jews worshiped God only in Jerusalem, in the temple built by Solomon; the Samaritans, who lived far away, also worshiped God, but not in that temple. The Jews therefore exalted themselves and claimed to be better because they worshiped God in a temple built by the wisest of men.

The Samaritans said to them: “Why do you think yourselves better than us because you have a temple that we do not have? Did not our fathers, who pleased God, worship on this mountain? They certainly had no temple, but worshiped here, where we also worship.”

Each side contended: the Jews on behalf of the temple, the Samaritans on behalf of the mountain; yet both were ignorant of the truth [Col. 1276B].

But let us hear what the Lord taught the woman: “Jesus said: ‘Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.’”

“Believe me,” he says. There is already in you one who believes, because you have begun to be present to understanding by recognizing me as a prophet. Believe me, then, because it is written: “If you do not believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII).

“The days are coming,” he says, “when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” He speaks of the time of evangelical grace, which was already at hand, when every shadow of legal figures would be removed and the pure light of evangelical truth would illuminate the minds of believers.

God is not confined to a place, for he fills heaven and earth; nor does he dwell in temples made by human hands, but in holy minds.

“You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know.” He grants considerable honor to the Jews, who possessed the knowledge of God and had received the Law and the Prophets, to whom belong the covenant, the legislation, and the promise, and whose are the fathers, from whom Christ came, who is blessed forever [Col. 1276C].

This is what he means when he says: “Salvation is from the Jews,” because the Savior was born from that people. He honored the Jews, but he did not reject the Samaritans. He himself was the cornerstone joining the wall from the nations to the wall from the Jews.

When he says, “We worship what we know,” this should not be referred to every individual, but only to those who were wise and teachers of the truth: the apostles, the prophets, and the others who either awaited Christ’s coming in faith or faithfully received him when he came [Col. 1276D].

The woman says to him: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ.”

Catholic piety knows well that *Messiah* is Hebrew, *Christ* is Greek, and *anointed* is Latin.

“I know,” she says, as though she were saying: “Why should we contend on behalf of the mountain and they on behalf of the temple? When Christ comes, he will reject the mountain, overturn the temple, and teach us to worship in spirit and truth.”

This woman already knew from whom she was to be taught, but she did not yet recognize the teacher. She was therefore worthy not to be delayed, but for Christ to reveal himself to her at once.

Jesus said to her: “I am he, the one speaking with you.”

Behold, the husband whom he had commanded her to call is present. The Apostle’s saying was fulfilled: “The head of a woman is man, and the head of man is Christ” (I Cor. XI) [Col. 1277A].

After she heard “I am he,” she said nothing, because she had now clearly recognized Christ.

Immediately his disciples came, and they marveled that he was speaking with a woman. The disciples, who had been in the city buying food, came. They marveled at Christ’s great condescension and immense compassion, by which he sought the lost sheep and taught a gentile and erring woman. They marveled at his mercy and immeasurable goodness; they did not suspect anything evil.

The woman therefore left her jar, went into the city, and said to the people: “Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done.”

She threw away her jar, which, because of her excessive eagerness, she now considered not useful but burdensome, so that, unencumbered and relieved of her load, she might announce Christ [Col. 1277B].

In a mystical sense, the holy Church, after coming to the faith of Christ, threw away the jar because it renounced worldly desires. That jar figuratively expressed love of the world, by which human beings, in a dark way of life sunk down to the depths, drew pleasure as though from a well. Once obtained, pleasure makes them thirst again, because pleasure, when fulfilled, does not satisfy but kindles a greater thirst for evil action.

“Come,” she says, “and see a man who told me everything I have ever done.”

She came gradually to preach Christ. At first she called him a man, so that, if she named him Christ immediately, her hearers might become angry and indignant and refuse to go out to him.

Meanwhile the disciples asked him, saying: “Rabbi, eat.”

But he said to them: “I have food to eat of which you do not know.”

His disciples therefore said: “Has someone brought him something to eat?”

What wonder is it if the Samaritan woman earlier did not understand what water the Lord was promising her? Behold, the disciples themselves now do not understand what food the Lord is speaking about.

But the true teacher instructs them—not as he instructed the woman through winding paths and circumlocutions, but openly showing that he meant spiritual food. He says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven, and to complete his work.”

The Father’s will is that we believe in his Son, as he says elsewhere: “This is the will of my Father who sent me, that you should believe in him whom he sent” (John VI).

The Father’s work is the provision of our redemption. Christ’s food, therefore, is our faith and salvation [Col. 1277D]. For this reason he fulfilled the Father’s will by teaching all to believe in him. He fulfilled his work by bringing the mystery of human redemption to maturity.

“Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes?”

The work pressed upon him, and he burned with a kind of fervor for the hastening of our salvation. He already wished to send laborers—that is, preachers—into the world.

“You say,” he says, “that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes. But I show you another harvest, already risen, already ripe, and ready to be reaped. Behold, I tell you: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest.”

It is therefore time for reapers to be sent.

This plainly means: Consider with the understanding of your mind that God is being reconciled to the world; that, after the winter of unbelief has passed, the warmth of faith is present; and that the hearts of the nations are already prepared, so that you may gather from them a harvest of righteousness through your preaching [Col. 1278A].

“For in this the saying is true: One sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap what you have not labored for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.”

The Lord did not send the disciples to sow but to reap. They were directed to places where others had already labored—that is, first to the Jews, to whom the prophets had previously announced Christ. Where there had been labor, there had certainly been sowing. What had been sown was now ripe and needed the sickle and the threshing floor.

The apostles were therefore directed to the place where the prophets had already preached. The prophets had sown what had come to this woman’s knowledge. Hence she said: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ.”

This harvest was first gathered in Judea, when, as Peter preached, three thousand believed in one day, five thousand on another, and many thousands thereafter (Acts IV) [Col. 1278B]. Those who had believed brought the value of their possessions and laid it at the apostles’ feet, so that, freed from the burdens of the world, they might follow Christ without encumbrance.

From this harvest, a few grains scattered throughout the world produced an innumerable harvest across the whole earth, which is to be gathered at the end of the age.

It should also be noted that he said above: “So that both the one who sows and the one who reaps may rejoice together.” The prophets were sowers and the apostles reapers. They labored at different times, but received one reward and gathered fruit together for eternal life.

Many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, who said: “He told me everything I have ever done.”

When the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to remain with them. He stayed there for two days, and many more believed in him because of his word. They said to the woman: “Now we no longer believe because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard and know that this truly is the Savior of the world” [Col. 1278C].

At first the Samaritans heard of the Lord’s reputation; afterward they saw him. Nor was this enough: they also asked him to remain with them for at least a few days. They no longer said that they believed because of what the woman had testified, but that they themselves had truly come to know and understand that he was the Savior of the world [Col. 1278D].

The immediate faith of the Samaritans greatly magnifies and aggravates the unbelief of the Jews. The Samaritans had certainly seen no miracle; they had not witnessed a dead man raised or experienced a passage across the sea on foot. They had heard only what the woman said: “He told me everything I have ever done.”

The Jews, however, seeing innumerable miracles every day, not only did not believe but also persecuted the author of their salvation.

The same thing happens daily among the nations. When they hear Christ preached by Christ’s friends and believe, they come to Christ as though through the reputation spread by the preaching woman. While he remains among them, they then come to know more firmly for themselves how great is the truth of the Christian faith and how great is the salvation of those who believe in Christ.

Nor is it without significance that he is said to have remained with them for two days [Col. 1279A]. Christ instructs those who believe in him by the two commandments of charity, teaching them to love God above all things and their neighbor as themselves.

He therefore remained two days among the Samaritans because he rests in the hearts of those whom he finds burning with the twofold lamp of charity.

Nor should it be overlooked that mention is made not of any night but only of the day. For what fellowship can light have with darkness? John says: “God is love” (John IV). The same writer also says elsewhere: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (I John I).

If God is love, and if God is light, then love is light. Where love is light, what place can darkness have? Conversely, where love is absent, there is no light, but everything is black with dreadful darkness.

Hence John says: “Everyone who does not love his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going. But whoever loves remains in the light” (I John II) [Col. 1279B].

Let us therefore hold fast to this love as effectively as we can, so that we may deserve to rejoice with Christ dwelling within us. Let us throw away from ourselves the jar of harmful desires, and hasten to draw others with us toward the good things that, by God’s inspiration, we have come to know.

Let us implore the mercy of our Redeemer with devout words and good works, so that he may deign to lead those to whom he has already given the knowledge of himself, together with progress in virtue, to the vision of his glory. Amen.

## HOMILY XCV. FOR THE SATURDAY AFTER *OCULI*

[Col. 1279C]

“At that time Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple,” etc. (John VIII).

The all-powerful Lord, creator and most gracious lover of humankind, our Lord Jesus Christ, whose every way is mercy and truth, had established this practice especially around the time of his passion: during the day he preached the word of God in the temple that was in Jerusalem and displayed signs and miracles by which he declared himself to be the Son of God; but in the evening he returned to Bethany and spent the nights as a guest with his friend Lazarus and Lazarus’s sisters, Mary and Martha. Thus, from time to time, at dawn he would return to Jerusalem for a similar work of preaching.

Following this customary practice, after he had preached all day in the temple on the feast of Scenopegia, that is, of Tabernacles, when the day was already drawing to evening, he went, as the holy evangelist relates, to the Mount of Olives, and from there returned to the temple again at dawn [Col. 1279D].

Mystically, the Mount of Olives signifies the sublimity of the Lord’s compassion and mercy. This is sufficiently clear from its very name, because the Mount of Olives derives its name from mercy: *eleos* (ἔλεος) in Greek means *mercy* in Latin.

The nature of oil also most appropriately corresponds to this mystery and foreshadows the grace of mercy. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

The anointing with oil ordinarily brings relief to weary and suffering limbs. The Psalmist, recalling the Lord’s mercies with grateful praise, says: “He who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases” (Ps. CII) [Col. 1280A].

The Lord therefore went to the Mount of Olives and remained there in order to establish in himself the citadel of mercy—or rather, to show that he himself is mercy, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You are my protector, O God; my God, my mercy” (Ps. LVIII).

The dawn at which he returned to Jerusalem to preach signifies the rising of the new grace, when, after the shadow of legal figures had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed to the world.

“And all the people,” he says, “came to him, and, sitting down, he taught them.”

The Lord’s sitting suggests the humility of his incarnation, through which he deigned to aid the world. While the Lord was seated in the temple, all the people came to him [Col. 1280B], because, after he had made himself visible to human beings through the humanity he assumed, many began to hear his preaching and believe in him. They did so all the more willingly because they remembered that he had made himself close to them by assuming flesh.

We say “many,” because very many, in their proud minds, rejected the salvation he had brought. Thus it had long before been foretold through the prophet: “Let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. XXXIII).

Let us therefore hear what the contemptuous did while the meek and simple marveled at the Lord’s words and listened with the greatest attention.

“Then the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery, set her in the midst, and said to him: ‘Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such women. What, then, do you say?’”

O deceitful reverence! O feigned service of a poisoned mind! O lying lips with malice in the heart, speaking deceit from the heart! They ask not in order to learn what is right, but to lay snares for the truth.

They knew that the Lord was loved by the crowds above all because he preached mercy and received sinners with the greatest kindness. Therefore, when they found a woman in adultery, they rejoiced that they had found an opportunity to test him.

They brought her to the Lord and asked what he commanded should be done with her. They said to one another: “If he says, ‘This woman must be stoned,’ then, as though he had forgotten the mercy he preached, we shall ridicule him and make him hateful to the crowds by whom he is loved. But if he forbids her to be stoned, we shall publicly seize him as an adversary of the Law and an ally of criminals and condemn him to death” [Col. 1280D].

But what can human perversity accomplish against divine power? For it is written: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord.”

Then it follows: “But Jesus bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger.”

By the fact that the Lord bent down, he showed the humility of the humanity he had assumed. By the finger, which is composed of jointed articulations and is therefore more flexible than the other limbs, the sublimity of discernment is expressed.
