By the earth, the human heart is signified, because it customarily produces the fruits of good or evil actions [Col. 1281A].

The Pharisees waited for the Lord to pronounce judgment on the adulterous woman. He did not judge immediately, but first bent down and wrote on the ground; only then, when they continued to press him insistently, did he judge. Through this example he figuratively admonishes us that, when we ourselves see the evils of our neighbors, we should not immediately condemn them rashly by reproving them. Rather, we should first turn humbly to the conscience of our own heart and investigate them carefully with the finger of discernment, determining whether they are works pleasing or displeasing to God, and then examine the matter through diligent meditation.

It is rash to judge the errors of others if you are still reproved for your own. Hence the Apostle says: “Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. IV) [Col. 1281B].

When they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

The Pharisees and scribes had laid snares on every side and believed that they could expose him either as merciless or as unjust. But the Lord easily passed through their schemes as through spider’s threads, preserving in every respect both the strictness of justice and the gentleness of compassion.

He said: “Let the one among you who is without sin”—there is the moderation of mercy.

Again: “Let that person be the first to throw a stone at her”—there is the justice of judgment.

As though he were saying openly: “You say that Moses commanded such women to be stoned, but he commanded that this be done by the just, not by sinners. First fulfill the justice of the Law, and then, with clean hands and a pure heart, come together to stone the guilty woman. First fulfill faith and mercy, that is, the spiritual commandments, and then proceed to carnal judgments” [Col. 1281C].

After giving this judgment, the Lord again bent down and wrote on the ground.

It may be understood that the Lord did this according to ordinary human custom: as though he were occupied with something else and directing his face elsewhere, he gave them a free opportunity to leave. He saw that, struck and put to shame by his reply, they would depart more quickly than they would continue questioning him.

Finally, the evangelist says: “When they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders.”

By writing on the ground before giving judgment and again after bending down, he figuratively admonished us that both before we rebuke a sinful brother and afterward, before we offer him the ministry of correction, we should carefully and humbly investigate whether we ourselves are subject either to the very sins for which we correct another or to other sins [Col. 1281D].

It often happens that someone who judges another for murder is himself held guilty of murder before the eyes of the Creator because of hatred toward his brother, since it is written: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III). Sometimes someone accuses another of fornication while concealing within himself a hidden crime of pride.

When, therefore, we correct someone who is sinning, let us carefully consider how fallen and fragile we are in ourselves if we were not sustained by divine mercy. Thus it will happen that we will not become proud against the person we correct, nor condemn him with an arrogant spirit. Instead, remembering our own condition, we will gently and meekly urge him toward the correction of his offense through salutary exhortation [Col. 1282A].

Jesus straightened up and said to her: “Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?”

She said: “No one, Lord.”

No one dared to condemn the sinful woman, because, when the Lord’s two-edged sword of speech pierced their consciences, each one saw within himself what deserved condemnation even more. But after he had cast down the accusers by the authority of justice, he raised up the woman who had been accused through the great gift of compassion.

It follows: “Jesus said to her: ‘Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on do not sin.’”

As a merciful one, he forgives her past sins; and, as a just one, he forbids her to presume to sin again. Because he was God and human, in that he was human he could show mercy to the accused woman; but in that he is God, having remitted her crime, he absolved her [Col. 1282B].

Let us therefore venerate him insofar as he is equal to God the Father, and love him insofar as he deigned to become close to us. Let us beseech his mercy with devout words and righteous works, so that he may release us from every bond of sin and grant that we sin no more. May he also kindle our minds with the flames of his holy love, so that, according to his good pleasure, Jesus Christ our Lord may make us steadfast in every good work. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVI. FOR LAETARE SUNDAY

*(From the works of blessed Pope Leo the Great.)*

“Apostolic, dearly beloved,” etc. See the remainder in Saint Leo, *Works*, volume I, *Patrologia* LIV, column 281 [Col. 1282C].

## HOMILY XCVII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

“At that time Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a great crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed on those who were sick,” etc. (John VI).

“Those who consider the signs and miracles of the Lord,” etc. See the remainder in the venerable Bede, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XCIV, column 110.

## HOMILY XCVIII. FOR THE MONDAY AFTER LAETARE

“At that time the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. And he found in the temple those who were selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money changers sitting there,” etc. (John II) [Col. 1282D].

The holy John, who wrote his Gospel last of all the evangelists, therefore took care to describe more fully and deeply those things that had been omitted by the three evangelists. For they wrote only those events that were performed by the Lord two years before his Passion, beginning from the time when John the Baptist was sent into prison. Thus, after considering the Gospel narrative most carefully, we find that the Lord and Savior came to Jerusalem twice to celebrate the paschal solemnity. Once was in the first year of his preaching, as John records; and again in the very year in which he was to suffer, when, five days before Passover, he entered Jerusalem seated on a donkey. On both occasions, however, detesting the greed of the scribes and the impiety of the priests that they practiced in the temple, he drove them out, together with all who conducted business there. From this it is clear that the reading found in Matthew and Luke is not this same one, since the same miracle occurred twice at Passover: first in the year of his preaching, which was the third year before his Passion, and secondly when the hour of his Passion was already near.

Having necessarily prefaced this by way of digression, let us now proceed in order to expound the reading of the holy Gospel.

“Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

When the Lord went up to Jerusalem as Passover approached, he plainly gave us an example of the care and zeal with which we ought to submit to divine commands. For if he who was the Son of God, appearing in the weakness of our flesh, fulfilled the decrees of the Law given by him by attending the appointed solemnities with the other people, what ought we to do, who are servants? With how much zeal ought these and the other festivals to be anticipated by good works, and celebrated with fitting reverence when they arrive?

“And he found in the temple those selling sheep, oxen, and doves, and money-changers sitting. And when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well; he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables.”

We should not think that these goods were being sold within the temple itself, but rather in the porticoes that surrounded the temple. The sheep, oxen, and doves were bought there so that they might be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice. The money-changers, meanwhile, sat there so that the price of the money could readily be assessed between the buyers and sellers of the sacrificial victims.

Thus, in a certain sense, this commerce was honorable and lawful, because the victims were bought for the purpose— as has been said—of being offered to God. What, then, do we suppose the Lord would have done if he had found them quarreling, or occupied with idle, frivolous, shameful, and indecent conversations, or engaged in any other crime, if he dealt so fiercely with those who conducted business in the temple involving things they intended to offer to the Lord?

We say this against those who enter the church but do not remain there as in the house of God, with fear and reverence. Instead, with wandering and wanton eyes they occupy themselves with empty chatter, burst into laughter, and, despising the purpose of prayer, increase the sins for which they ought to have prayed. What is more serious, if anyone dares to rebuke them for such foolish presumption, they pursue him with hatred and curses and do not fear the divine judgment, whose temple they profane by their wicked audacity.

No one who thinks rightly is unaware that what was then done bodily in the temple is done daily spiritually in the Church. For every day the Lord enters the holy Church spiritually and observes how each person conducts himself within it. We must therefore beware, and be very much afraid, lest he come unexpectedly and find something perverse in us for which we ought justly to be scourged and driven out of the Church.

Above all, we must observe this in that which is spiritually called the house of God, lest we do anything foolish there, lest what the Lord said through the prophet be spoken of us: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. II).

Nor should we forget that we ourselves are the temple of God. Therefore let us keep our conscience free from every impurity and iniquity, recalling with trembling what the Apostle says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, the Lord will destroy him” (I Cor. III).

It should also be noted that sheep, oxen, and doves were being sold in the temple. Oxen plow the earth and prepare it to receive seed. What, then, are the oxen understood to signify if not heavenly doctrine? Those sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not for their benefit, nor out of love for Christ, but with an eye to temporal profit.

Sheep are simple and gentle animals, and they provide their wool for clothing people. What, then, are signified by sheep if not works of simplicity and innocence? Those sell sheep who perform works of piety for the sake of human praise. Of such people it is said: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

What, then, is understood by doves, which lack gall, if not the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove over the baptized Lord? Those therefore sell doves who confer the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands either for payment or for the favor of the crowd, and who bestow sacred orders not for the merit of life but for the sake of favor.

The money-changers, moreover, are those who openly serve earthly things in the Church, seeking what is their own rather than what is Jesus Christ’s.

Thus, with a whip made from little cords, he drove all these people out of the temple. What is signified by the cord if not the growth of evil actions? Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with a cord of vanity” (Isa. V). And Solomon says: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V).

When a sinner piles up more serious sins upon his earlier sins, he gradually lengthens, by his actions, the cord with which he will be scourged. Therefore the Lord drove these people out; he drove out with them the oxen, the sheep, and the other merchandise, because such teaching, together with its authors, must likewise be rejected and expelled from the house of God.

The money-changers’ coins are also poured out and their tables overturned, because, when the reprobate are condemned at the end of the world, even the forms of the things they loved will be taken away from them, in accordance with what John says: “The world is passing away, and its desire” (I John II).

And to those who sold doves he said: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.”

He prohibited the sale of doves in the temple because the grace of the Holy Spirit must not be given for payment. It is received freely, and it ought to be given freely. Hence all who wish either to receive or to give it for a reward are like the scribes and Pharisees.

They make the house of God a house of commerce who, in giving or receiving sacred orders, seek payment either from the hand or from the mouth, and who carry out the ministry they have received in the Church not with a pure intention but in expectation of human recompense. They do not strive that God may be glorified in what they do, but rather that they themselves may be praised and rewarded.

Nor should we pass over without careful attention the fact that here both natures of the Lord and Savior are commended to us. His human nature is indicated because, as a human being, he went up with the others to celebrate the solemnity of Passover. His divine nature is indicated by the words he spoke to those whom he drove from the temple: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” For he openly showed himself to be the Son of God when he called the temple the house of his Father, God.

The disciples then remembered that it is written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII).

In this passage, zeal is understood in a good sense. Zeal is a kind of fervor by which the mind, having cast aside human fear, is inflamed in defense of the truth. Therefore, moved by zeal for God the Father, the Savior drove the impious traders from the temple.

Let us also, as far as we can, be zealous for the house of God, and diligently take care that nothing wicked be done in it. We act rightly in this regard if we see a brother who ought to be the temple of God swollen with pride, weakened by lust, enslaved to drunkenness, or subject to any other vice, and, insofar as our strength permits, strive to correct him and bring him back to the order of a more reformed life.

Likewise, in the very house of prayer where the most holy mysteries of Christ’s body are consecrated, where the presence of angels and of God himself is unquestioned, let us carefully ensure that nothing dishonorable or indecent is done.

“The Jews answered and said to him: What sign do you show us, since you do these things? Jesus answered them: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

The evangelist shows which temple he meant when he adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

He calls his holy body a most worthy temple, a sanctuary of divinity, because, as the Apostle says, “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II).

This temple was to be destroyed in the Passion and raised on the third day by the swift resurrection. He did not say, as they falsely represented it, “I will destroy it in the Passion,” but, using an honorable expression, he said: “You destroy it.” For it is not fitting that we should lay hands upon ourselves. “You,” he says, “destroy it,” because he was to be tortured and crucified by them.

Therefore those who had been driven from that typical temple deservedly sought to destroy the true temple of God—the one in which there could be absolutely no stain of sin—through death.

The Jews therefore said to him: “This temple was built over forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?”

They answered the Lord carnally because they understood his earlier words carnally. What he had said about the temple of his body, they thought had been said about the material temple.

When they say that the temple was built over forty-six years, they indicate not the first but the second construction. The first temple, built by Solomon during the greatest peace of the kingdom and with highly distinguished workmanship, was completed in seven years. After it had later been destroyed by the Chaldeans, it began to be rebuilt again after seventy years, at the command of the king of the Persians, when the people’s captivity had been released, by the descendants of the captivity under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua.

In this work they were so hindered by the neighboring peoples who attacked them that they held a sword in one hand and placed a stone into the construction of the wall with the other. Thus it came about that, although the temple’s construction had been begun, it could scarcely be completed over forty-six years.

This number of years corresponds most suitably to the perfection of the Lord’s body. For physical writers report that the form of the human body is completed in the womb of its mother over that many days. The seed received during the first six days after conception resembles milk; during the following nine days it is changed into blood; during the next twelve it coagulates and is transformed into the solidity of flesh; during another eighteen it is formed until the complete outlines of the limbs are established. From that point until the time of birth it continually increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, ten, and eight, added together, make forty-five. If one adds the very day on which the body, having been distinguished into its limbs, begins to increase, one finds forty-six without error. Thus the number of days in the building of the Lord’s body corresponds to the number of years we read of in the construction of the temple.

We can also find this same number in the name Adam, by calculating the numerical value of its letters. Among the Greeks, his name is composed from the principal letters of the world’s four regions. This signifies that our first parent was expelled from paradise and scattered throughout the whole world.

The names of the four parts of the world, according to the Greeks, are ἄρκτος, δύσις, ἀνατολή, μεσημβρία—that is, east, west, north, and south. The name Adam, however, consists of α, δ, α, μ. According to the Greeks, these letters have the values α one, δ four, α one again, and μ forty, which together make forty-six.

In so many days, therefore, Christ’s body was formed and perfected in the Virgin’s womb. This signified that the first Adam, scattered throughout the world, would be gathered together by the second Adam, that is, by Christ, and assembled into the unity of faith.

“When he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.”

The holy apostles did not yet understand the Scriptures, because Christ had not yet risen from the dead, nor had he yet openly given them the Holy Spirit. But on the very day of his resurrection, appearing to them, he opened their understanding so that they might comprehend everything that had been written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

Then they remembered the words they had heard the Lord speak before his Passion. “And they believed,” he says, “the Scripture of the prophets that had foretold that he would rise, and the word Jesus had spoken to them”—namely, what has just been stated: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

“When Jesus was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in him. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew them all, and he had no need for anyone to testify about a human being; for he himself knew what was in a human being.”

The reason why the Lord came bodily to celebrate the Jewish festivals is clear: namely, so that many might believe through his preaching. The evangelist says that when Jesus was in Jerusalem, many believed in him; but he did not entrust himself to them, because they did not believe in him in such a way that Christ would consider them worthy of his familiar companionship.

Although they were already thought to believe, he looked into their hearts inwardly. This is what is meant by the words, “because he knew them all.” He did not wish to be proclaimed by people whom he foresaw might be scandalized in his Passion.

“For he had no need for anyone to testify about a human being; he himself knew what was in a human being.”

These people represented the type of catechumens, who already believe in Christ, but to whom Christ does not yet entrust himself, because they have not yet been reborn through the water of baptism. For no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he has first been reborn “of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III).

Hence the custom of the Church has also prevailed that the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood are not entrusted to catechumens, although they themselves profess that they believe in Christ.

But we, who have already been reborn in Christ and initiated into the life-giving sacraments of his body, should give eternal thanks to his name and exalt his mercy with praises worthy of him, insofar as we are able. In his incomprehensible kindness he has deigned to entrust himself to us in such a way that he might remain in us and we in him.

Certainly, what we presume is great; but we are secure in his most truthful promise, in which he says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Therefore, let us carefully examine the inner chambers of our hearts, and whatever we find polluted by vices or defiled by filth, let us hasten, especially during these days, to cleanse it with prayers, fasts, and abundant tears.

Let us go before his face in confession, if we desire to behold his countenance in the future without shame. Let us journey joyfully toward our heavenly homeland, so that no obstacle of this world may impede us, neither prosperity draw us back nor adversity delay us.

For we are promised nothing worthless or perishable, but that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II). May we deserve to attain it with the help of him who has deigned to call us.

You, however.

## HOMILY XCIX. FOR THE TUESDAY AFTER LAETARE

[Col. 1287D] At that time, when the feast was already halfway through, Jesus went up to Jerusalem, into the temple, and taught. And the Jews wondered, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” etc. (John VII).

In the reading which precedes this one, the holy evangelist relates that the Lord was walking in Galilee; for he did not wish to go into Judaea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Therefore, while he was there and, so to speak, was concealing himself because of the violent persecution stirred up against him, and when the feast day of Tabernacles was near, his brothers said to him: “Leave here and go again into Judaea, so that your disciples also may see the works which you do” (John VII). Seeing that they sought the unstable and transitory glory of this world and held heavenly glory cheap, the Lord replied: “You go up to the feast; I will not go up to this feast.” When, therefore, he had said these things and many others to rebuke and confound those desirous of human praise, he then remained in Galilee.

But when the feast day was already halfway through—for the solemnity lasted eight days, as has just been read—Jesus himself also went up. And the Jews wondered, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” What is this? Before the Lord came to the festival, they were seeking him, and there was much murmuring about him. Behold, he whom they sought is present; he who was in hiding teaches; he speaks openly and is not seized. But the former was an example; the latter, an exercise of power. For he hid himself in order to teach us to flee persecution, according to what he commands elsewhere: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X).

“And the Jews wondered,” he says. They wondered, yet were not converted from unbelief. But the reason for their wonder is disclosed when it is added: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” They knew where he had been born and how he had been brought up. They had never seen him learning letters; yet they heard him disputing about the Law and adducing testimonies from the Law and the Prophets—something no one could do who had not read the Law itself. But no one could read the Law itself unless he had first learned letters. For this reason they wondered, not understanding that he was the author and Lord of the Law. If they had been willing to believe, they would by no means have wondered that he knew the Law who had himself given the Law.

Yet this wonder of theirs became for the Teacher of truth an occasion for imparting a loftier doctrine. For the Lord gave an answer that was profound and to be examined more attentively. It follows: Jesus answered them: “My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me.” In a few words the Lord seems to have said something almost contradictory. For he did not say, “This doctrine is not mine,” but, “My doctrine is not mine.” We must therefore ask what it means that “my doctrine is not mine.” For if it is his, how is it not his? But let us recall what blessed John said at the beginning of this Gospel, and there we shall be able to find the solution to this question. For he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” What, then, is the doctrine of the Father except the Word of the Father? For a word is someone’s word. Thus he called his doctrine not his own because he is not from himself, but is the Word of the Father. Therefore, when he says, “My doctrine is not mine,” it is as though he said: “I who teach am not from myself.”

For although we believe and confess that the Son is equal to the Father in divinity, and admit no difference of either nature or substance between the begetter and the begotten, nevertheless he is the Father and he is the Son. The Father is indeed from no one, because he is God from himself. But the Son is God, not from himself, but begotten from the Father; just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. And these three are one God, one light, one power, one majesty. Since he saw that not everyone could understand so profound a mystery, he gives counsel as to what they might do in order to attain to it. “If anyone,” he says, “is willing to do his will, he shall know concerning my doctrine whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.” If anyone is willing to do the Father’s will—that is, if anyone is willing to believe in his Son—he shall know concerning my doctrine; that is, he shall understand. Understanding, therefore, is the reward of faith. We are not to understand in order that we may believe, but must first believe in order that we may understand. For it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII).

Let us therefore do the will of the Father; that is, let us believe in the Son of God the Father. This is the Father’s will, as the same Son says elsewhere: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John VI). The construction of this expression must certainly be understood: for it is one thing when we say with the dative, “I believe you,” and another with the accusative, “I believe in you.” We certainly say that we believe Paul, but not that we believe in Paul. We say that we believe Peter, but not that we believe in Peter. Thus it is one thing to believe God and another to believe in God. To believe God is to give credence to his words, just as even the demons believe him and tremble. But to believe in God is, by believing, to love God; by believing, to cherish him; by believing, to be incorporated into his members. This is the faith that God requires of us, the faith that works through love. Therefore, if anyone does the Father’s will by believing in his Son, he shall know concerning Christ’s doctrine that it is not from elsewhere, not from nothing, but is from the Father, remaining in the Father and equal to the Father.

“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory.” By these words he marks the Antichrist, the treasure-house of wickedness and son of perdition, who, as the Apostle says, “opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (II Thess. II). Therefore, when he comes, he will speak from himself, saying that he has come on his own authority and has not been sent from God, and seeking not God’s glory but his own. Of him the Lord says elsewhere: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V).

“But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is truthful, and there is no injustice in him.” By these words the Lord plainly refers to himself. Although he was equal to the Father in divinity, yet, appearing in time through the form of a servant which he had assumed—he who was the Creator of time—he sought not his own glory but the Father’s. Or, indeed, by this he gave us an example of humility, so that we, who are mere human beings and cannot do any good thing from ourselves, may attribute everything to God and refer it to his praise and glory, whether we do some good or, through the generosity of his mercy, rightly understand his Scriptures. But we, on the contrary, proudly ascribe to ourselves the good that we do, while we charge our Creator with our evils, alleging that he did not make us otherwise. Christ our Lord, however, sought the Father’s glory, and therefore he is truthful and there is no injustice in him. But in Antichrist there is injustice, and he is not truthful, because he will seek his own glory, not God’s. He was not sent by God, but was permitted to come.

“Did not Moses give you the Law? Yet none of you keeps the Law. Why do you seek to kill me?” They indeed boasted that they fulfilled the precepts of the Law, but they are refuted by an evident judgment. For the Law forbids murder; how, then, were they keeping the Law when they were planning to kill the Savior? For if they had rightly read the Law and fulfilled it in deed, they would have recognized Christ in their own Scriptures and would never have plotted his death.

The crowd answered him. A crowd, he says, is always uncertain and disturbed, lacking every order of reason. “You have a demon. Who is seeking to kill you?” O inexpiable crime! O blasphemy that is to be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come! For it was worse to say this than to kill Christ: they said to him, “You have a demon,” though by his own command he cast out demons. One ought to stop one’s ears against so wicked an insult, unless we learned patience from the example of the Lord himself. Hearing these things from frenzied and disturbed people, he was not himself disturbed; but, remaining tranquil in his truth, he did not return evil for evil or reviling for reviling. If he had wished to answer them, “You rather have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken truly. For unless they were full of a demon, they could not speak so perversely about God.

Jesus therefore answered them: “I did one work, and you all wonder.” It is as though he said: “Why do you wonder so greatly at the healing of one man, when you would wonder still more if you saw all my works?” For he had done one thing: he had healed on the Sabbath the paralytic who had lain there for thirty-eight years; and they were disturbed because they did not understand that he was the author of the Sabbath (John V). He had not broken the Sabbath by healing a man on it, because the observance of the Sabbath had been given for the salvation of human beings.

“Therefore Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.” It is as though he said: “Moses convicts you.” The Law commands you to circumcise a man on the eighth day; it also commands you to keep the Sabbath on the seventh day. If, therefore, the eighth day of one who has been born falls on the seventh day—that is, on the Sabbath—what will you do? Will you refrain from work and keep the Sabbath, or will you circumcise the infant, in order to fulfill the sacrament of the eighth day? But I know that you will circumcise him, because it is a sign of salvation, and a person ought not to refrain from salvation on the Sabbath. “Now, therefore, you are angry with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath.” For he was healed so as to be sound in body, and he believed so as to be sound in soul. But if a person receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the Law of Moses may not be broken, why are you angry with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath?

That circumcision had been given especially for three reasons. First, that it might be a sign of Abraham’s great faith. Second, that through it they might be distinguished bodily from the other nations, just as they were distinguished in dress by the fringes of their cloaks. Third, that, receiving it in the male member, they might know that they ought to observe chastity of mind and body. Circumcision then had as much efficacy as baptism has in the New Testament, because through it all sins were forgiven, except that it could by no means open the gate of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore they ought not to abstain from so useful and profitable a thing because of the Sabbath’s empty idleness.

Mystically, however, that circumcision prefigured the baptism now performed in the Church, through which all sins are most truly forgiven and the heavenly kingdom is opened to believers. Circumcision was performed in the male member through which human propagation is effected, so that it might be shown that through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin. And just as every person is born with a foreskin, so every person is also generated with original sin, from which, together with all vices, we are stripped through baptism, which is the true and spiritual circumcision. People were circumcised with Peter’s knives, because, as the Apostle says, “the Rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). By the invocation of whose name the simple water of baptism is made fruitful with spiritual power, so that it may be able to bestow spiritual generation upon people.

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with just judgment.” To judge according to appearance is to consider the person in judgment. They were considering persons, because they were not angry with those who circumcised little children on the Sabbath, but were angry with the Lord because he had made the whole man sound on the Sabbath. “Judge,” he says, “with just judgment.” If you do this, you will condemn neither me nor Moses; but, once you have perceived the truth, you will by no means see my works as contrary to Moses’ precepts.

Certainly this admonition of the Lord was not given to the Jews alone: the Lord also admonished and instructed us. Let us therefore hear his words as though he were speaking to us in person. For he says: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with just judgment.” It is a matter of great difficulty to avoid this fault—that is, not to judge by regard for the person, but to render just judgment. No one can fulfill this except one who loves all equally, who in judging cases attends not to influence but to merit, and considers not who is to be judged but on what account he is to be judged. We say this not about those whom we are commanded to honor differently on account of the dignity of their ranks, but about those whose cases we are commanded to hear and decide.

Some people from Jerusalem were saying: “Is this not the man whom they seek to kill? Behold, he now speaks openly and they say nothing to him.” Those who said this knew that the Lord was being sought by the Jews, but they did not understand that he was not seized because of his own power. Thus they thought that the rulers had already believed that he was the Christ. They say: “Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ?” But they show that they had not yet believed, when they add: “But we know where this man is from. Yet when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

What does it mean when they say, “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from”? For when Herod inquired about the place of Christ’s birth, they answered that he was to be born in Bethlehem, and confirmed their very words by prophetic authority. But they knew the place of his birth and could not comprehend the generation of his divinity, as the prophet says: “Who shall declare his generation?” It is as though they said: “We know this man like one of the other human beings; we perceive nothing divine, nothing royal in him. But our Christ, the almighty God, is to come and rule the whole world.” This, indeed, would be the cause of their death. For they were unwilling to believe in Christ because they considered only his humanity and could not grasp his divinity.

Therefore the Lord answered them concerning both: namely, concerning the frailty of his humanity and the majesty of his divinity. For he cried out while teaching in the temple: “You both know me and know where I am from.” He said this concerning his humanity, according to which they knew both the place of his birth, the nobility of his parents, and the appearance of his face. They knew, therefore, that he descended from royal stock and could not be hidden as one illustrious in the splendor of nobility. “And I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.” This he referred to his divinity, according to which they were ignorant that he was the Son of God and had been sent into the world by the Father. They did not know God the Father either, who is the true begetter of truth itself. They did not know him because, in ignorance of the Son and without faith in him, they were not worthy to attain the knowledge of God the Father.

Finally he adds: “But I know him.” Therefore, if you wish to know him, ask me so that you may know, because I am from him and he sent me. Most beautifully and most briefly he embraced both his divinity and his humanity: “I am from him,” he says, because I am the Son born of God the Father. For whatever the Son is, he is from him, and he owes it to him whose Son he is. “And he sent me”—that is, he ordained that I should be incarnate; this is what you see in me, what you behold as present before you. But when we hear that God the Father sent the Son, let us not think of a dissimilarity of nature, but of the Father’s authority.

They therefore sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come. “No one,” he says, “laid hands on him”—that is, no one used force and no one dared seize him—because his hour had not yet come: the hour, namely, of his own will. For just as he was born by his own will, so he also suffered by his own will. For just as before the ages he foreordained the virgin mother from whom he would be born, so he also foreknew and chose the death he would suffer and the time when he would suffer it. Recalling this hour while he hung on the cross, he said: “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit (John XIX).

Therefore the Jews could not seize him, because he held in his own power both his death and the ministers of his death; and when he himself willed to suffer, even if the Jews had wished to refrain from killing him, they could not have done so. Thus in the one case mercy, and in the other truth, was displayed: mercy in the humility of the flesh by which he willed to suffer; truth in the power of divinity by which, until he himself willed it, he could not be seized. Both were done for our salvation, for whose sake he through whom humanity had been created became human, lest what he had made should perish.

Let us not, therefore, be ungrateful for such great benefits as we have undeservedly and unworthily received from him. Let us obey his commands, so that we may become sharers in his promise. Let us seek his countenance with spiritual desire; let us seek his face always. Let us seek him not as the Jews did, that we may kill him, but that we may be given life by him. Let us seek him not that we may drive him away from us, but that we may remain with him forever. You, however.

## HOMILY C. FOR THE WEDNESDAY AFTER LAETARE

At that time Jesus, passing by, saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” etc. (John IX).

The Son of God had come to the Feast of Booths, and on the last day of that festival, standing in the temple, he was teaching the people who had gathered for the feast. He rebuked the unbelieving Jews and instructed the faithful concerning the mysteries of his [Col. 1293B] divinity. But the wretched Jews, enemies of every good thing, unable to endure his words, fled to stones, seeking to bury the one whom they could not understand. He, however, passed through their midst. For the hour that he had appointed for his Passion had not yet come, since he had determined to suffer not at the Feast of Booths but at Passover.

As the Lord was passing by, therefore, as the Evangelist now relates, he saw a man blind from birth—that is, born blind—whom his mother had brought forth from the darkness of the womb into the night of the world. “He saw,” he says, that is, he had compassion on him. For his seeing him means having mercy on him. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke XXII).

And his disciples asked him: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” The holy [Col. 1293C] apostles knew that, for many reasons, infirmities are given to human beings by God’s dispensation: sometimes for the cleansing of sins, sometimes for testing, and sometimes for the preservation of virtues. But they did not know for which of these reasons that man had been born blind, and so they questioned the Lord as their teacher, so that they might learn from him what they did not know.

Jesus answered them: “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents.” What does the Savior mean when he says that neither he nor his parents sinned? If no human being is without sin, how did the blind man’s parents not sin? Had they not, by living and conducting themselves in the world, added many sins? If, then, both he and his parents had sin, why did the Lord [Col. 1293D] say, “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents”?

But we must understand that the Lord answered the matter about which he had been questioned. They had asked whether the blind man had been born because of his own sin or that of his parents. To this the Lord replied that neither he nor his parents had sinned in this respect—namely, so that he should be born blind. He and his parents therefore had countless sins, but he had not been born blind because of them.

Why, then? “But,” he says, “so that the works of God might be manifested in him.” The Teacher of truth teaches that he was born in this way so that the works of God might be manifested in him, in order that, by freeing him from innate blindness and restoring his sight, he might openly show to all that he was the Son of God.

“I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day.” As everywhere, so now also [Col. 1294A] he attributes all glory to God the Father, saying that he performs the works of the one whose Son he was. These were the works of God the Father for which the Son of God had come: namely, the illumination and healing of the human race. For by the illumination of this blind man, the illumination of the human race was signified.

The miracles of our Redeemer are therefore believed to have been performed literally in such a way that, when considered mystically, they indicate something that ought to be done. This blind man, then, prefigures the human race, which was blinded in its first parent, because from him we have all drawn not only the origin of death but also of iniquity. And he is rightly called not merely blind but “blind from birth,” because all human beings—except the one who was born from the Virgin—are born with original sin and come into the world [Col. 1294B] weighed down by the gravest blindness, which we contracted from the root of our first parent.

He had been created with good sight, but by obeying the devil’s persuasions he incurred blindness, which he transmitted to all his descendants. But as the Lord was passing by, he saw the blind man. For he saw him not while standing but while passing by, because he appeared in the likeness of flesh but did not stand in the way of sins; for he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth (1 Peter II).

Hence, according to the parable in another passage, the Samaritan came up beside the wounded man. What is signified there by the wounded man is signified here by the blind man. And what is said there as “he came,” is said here as “he passed by.” The Lord therefore came up beside the wounded man, and, passing by, saw the blind man, because he approached the road of our mortality but did not plant his foot in the way of sins. [Col. 1294C] For he came to take away the blindness of our sins, not to take it upon himself.

These works of the Father, therefore, he said that he ought to perform, because he had come to seek what was lost and restore what was corrupted. “While it is day,” he says. “Night comes, when no one can work.” What day he intended is clearly expressed when he adds: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

But what does he mean by saying, “I must work while it is day”? Did he work only when he was bodily present in the world? If we accept this interpretation, then after his Ascension that terrifying and dreadful night is already in the world, in which no one can work. Yet elsewhere he rightly promised: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” [Col. 1294D] (Matthew XXVIII).

If, then, he is with the saints until the consummation of the age, he certainly always works until the end of the age. For the one who was then bodily present in the world is now present everywhere in the world by divine power.

We must therefore ask what this night is in which no one can work. This night belongs to the impious, to whom it will be said: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV). This night will come when, after all the reprobate have been condemned, no place for repentance and no opportunity for pardon will remain, because in hell no one will confess to the Lord.

The Lord therefore works while it is day, because while we live here he waits for and urges us to confession, refrains from punishing, and is present to all who call upon him in truth. “The night comes in which no one [Col. 1295A] can work,” because when the world has ended, the elect have been received into heaven, and the door has been closed, labor is vain and repentance late. For when they cry, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” he will answer: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII).

Let us therefore hear the Apostle saying: “While we have time, let us do good” (Galatians VI). Now is the time for doing good; then is the time for receiving what one has done.

But let us see what the Lord did. When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and spread it over the man’s eyes. Then he said: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam,” which is interpreted as “Sent.”

The healing of the blind man, marvelous and astonishing even in its novelty, commends a great mystery if we understand it. For by spitting on the ground he made clay and anointed the blind man’s eyes. The spittle that flows from the [Col. 1295B] head into the mouth signifies the divinity of Christ, because God is the head of Christ. And Wisdom says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV). Solomon says of the same Wisdom: “For she is a vapor of the power of God, and a pure emanation of his glory” (Wisdom VII).

The clay from the earth is the flesh of Christ. By spitting on the ground, therefore, he made clay, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

Although the blind man had now been anointed, he still did not see until he came to the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted as “Sent.” It is not without a mystery that the Evangelist supplied the interpretation of this name, saying that it is interpreted as “Sent.” For who was sent except the one who says: “I have not come of myself, but the Father sent me”? Christ truly is the Sent One, because unless he had been sent, none of us [Col. 1295C] would have been dismissed from sin.

That pool, therefore, is Christ’s baptism. The blind man washed in the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted as “Sent,” and he was illuminated, because those baptized in Christ are illuminated. When he was anointed, he was made, as it were, a catechumen; but he needed to be washed—that is, baptized—in order to be illuminated. A catechumen is anointed in order to be instructed. For *catechumen* is Greek; in Latin it means “instructed.” He is baptized, however, so that he may recognize the true light and receive the remission of all sins.

And so the neighbors and those who had previously known him, because he was a beggar, were saying: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” Some said, “It is he”; others said, “No, but he is like him.” His opened eyes caused this confusion; once illuminated, he [Col. 1295D] seemed to have changed his appearance. But he, not ungrateful and not forgetful of the benefit bestowed, said: “I am he.” He confessed that he was that man.

So they said to him: “How were your eyes opened?” He answered: “The man who is called Jesus made clay from spittle, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ I went, washed, and I see.” He already saw well, since he was proclaiming the grace given to him. He was already evangelizing Christ and preaching his illuminator.

Then they said to him: “Where is he?” He replied: “I do not know.” He was still anointed and had not yet been spiritually illuminated. He was preaching Christ, but he did not know whom he was preaching. For, as he had said above, “that man,” he did not yet know how to call him God, since he was like a catechumen and still needed to be taught.

They brought the man who had been blind to the Pharisees. Now it was the [Col. 1296A] Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Again, therefore, the Pharisees asked him how he had received his sight. He said to them: “He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

Some of the Pharisees were saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Not all of them said this, but some did. For they were already being anointed, and the truth was beginning to glimmer in their hearts. But those who were criticizing the Lord were rather blind; they had neither been anointed nor seen.

They criticized the Lord for not keeping the Sabbath, although he was perpetually free from every servile work, because he committed no sin. For this is spiritually to keep the Sabbath: to be free from sin, which is servile work, because “everyone who commits [Col. 1296B] sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII).

While they were saying these things, however, others who were already approaching illumination said: “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” And there was a division among them. *Schisma* is Greek; in Latin it means “division” or “split.” They were therefore divided, because one party assented to the truth and the other applauded falsehood. Christ, the day, was divided between light and darkness.

So they said again to the blind man: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes?” They were asking what he thought of his illuminator, so that they might find an opportunity to expel him from the synagogue. But he openly and steadfastly declared what he thought of him. For he said: “He is a prophet.”

He was not yet illuminated in his heart but merely anointed. He did not know how to call him the Son of God, but [Col. 1296C] confessed him to be a prophet; yet he was not altogether mistaken. For the Lord himself says of him: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII), and, “No prophet is without honor except in his own country.”

They did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight until they called his parents, the man who had received his sight, and questioned them, saying: “Is this your son, whom you say was born [Col. 1296D] blind? How then does he now see?”

His parents answered them and said: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is of age; let him speak for himself.”

They saw that a charge was being constructed against both themselves and him, and therefore said: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But if you want to know how he now sees, you must ask him, because he is of age; he can speak for himself.” For they would rightly have been compelled to speak on behalf of an infant, since an infant, because of his age, cannot reasonably speak.

The Evangelist shows that they said this not out of ignorance but out of fear, when he adds: “His parents said these things because they feared the Jews.” For the Jews had already conspired that, if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue.

At that time it was regarded by them as a great matter if they expelled someone from the synagogue. For just as now murderers, adulterers, and those guilty of other capital crimes are expelled from the Church, so then confessors of Christ were expelled from the Jewish synagogue. The parents of the man born blind feared incurring this penalty, and therefore said: “Let him speak for himself.”

They called [Col. 1297A] the man again who had been blind and said to him: “Give glory to God.” To give glory to God means to speak the truth about some matter as though in the presence of God. But these men wanted him to deny Christ. For what else does “Give glory to God” mean than “Deny the gift you have received,” when this is certainly not giving glory to God but blaspheming him?

“We know that this man is a sinner.” They wanted him to give glory to God in such a way that, like themselves, he would call Christ a sinner. But he, so as neither to become subject to their charge nor conceal the truth, did not say, “I know that he is righteous.” Instead, he answered: “If he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.”

So they said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He had been questioned so many times and had answered [Col. 1297B] so many times that, now somewhat wearied and because of their hardness and unbelief, he replied with a kind of perplexity: “I told you already, and you heard it. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”

Because he himself already believed and had become the Lord’s disciple, he said: “Do you also, like me, wish to believe in him and cling to his discipleship?”

They reviled him and said: “You are his disciple.” May this curse fall upon us Christians! If you consider the attitude of their hearts, it was a curse, because they spoke with the intention of cursing. But if you weigh the words themselves, it is a desirable blessing. For who would not desire to be Christ’s disciple?

“We are disciples of Moses,” they said. They were deceived, misleading themselves. For if they were disciples of Moses [Col. 1297C], they would believe Moses when he proclaimed Christ and would recognize the one who had been foretold through Moses. For the Lord says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John V).

“We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.” These are the words of contemptuous people. For how did they not know where he was from, when they knew both where he had been born and to which tribe he belonged? Indeed, above they had said: “But we know where this man is from.”

Something similar is also found in the Book of Kings. When David, still a young man, had struck down Goliath, who was formidable even to brave men, Saul said to Abner: “Whose son is this boy, Abner?” (1 Samuel XVII). Certainly he had been Saul’s armor-bearer and had often played the cithara before him, yet Saul was asking who he was. It was as though he did not recognize the one in whom he despised the age of a youth and the appearance of a shepherd. [Col. 1297D]

In the same way, these pitiable men, seeing the Son of God as a human being, judged him so contemptible and insignificant that they said: “We do not know where he is from”—following the customary practice of people who say that they do not know those whom they reject.

The man answered and said: “This is remarkable: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.” It was as though he were saying: “The one whom you pretend not to know is hidden by humility but revealed by the power of his signs. It is not known where he is from, and yet, like God, he makes the blind see.”

“We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, him he hears.” He speaks as one who has been anointed but not yet illuminated: for God hears sinners also. Indeed, the tax collector was heard who, standing far off in the temple of God, lowering his eyes to the ground [Col. 1298A] and striking his breast with his fists, said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII).

By this confession he was so heard that he returned from the temple justified, although he had come to the temple unjustified. Sinners are therefore heard, as has been said, if they repent of their sins, wash away past evils with tears, and sincerely renounce being what they once were.

“From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” Great confidence, free and courageous steadfastness! The rulers were raging, but he, setting their indignation aside, confessed the truth. For who else could do such things except God? And if there are some who at some time have done such things, they received from him the ability to do them. For he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

They answered and said: [Col. 1298B] “You were born entirely in sins”—that is, with your eyes closed. They reproached him for having been born in this way because of his parents’ sins. But did not the one who opened his eyes save the whole man? And did not the one who illuminated him outwardly also cleanse his heart from every cloud of iniquity?

“You were born entirely in sins, and you teach us?” They themselves had certainly questioned him; they themselves had compelled him to say what he thought of Christ, his illuminator. And now they rebuked him for confessing and expelled him from the synagogue.

For it follows: “And they cast him out.” They were indeed casting him out, but Christ was receiving him. He deserved to know Christ all the more when he had been expelled from the company of Christ’s enemies.

God heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said to him: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” But although he saw him only [Col. 1298C] with bodily eyes, he did not yet understand him in his heart. He answered: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” By these words he showed that his heart had long been prepared to believe, but that he did not know in whom he ought to believe.

The Lord said to him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” The Lord was now washing the face of the anointed man and illuminating the eyes of his heart. Finally, having been washed and spiritually illuminated, he answered: “I believe, Lord.”

But this was not enough. It is not sufficient to believe; he also fell down and worshiped him, thereby in a certain way testifying that he believed him to be God, since he worshiped him.

But amid these events, what remains for us who read them, for whose sake they were also written? For “whatever was written,” as the Apostle says, “was written for our instruction” (Romans XV). What, then, ought we to do except [Col. 1298D] strive to imitate what we read or hear in the Scriptures?

It is a great thing to say that we should imitate the Apostle Peter, whose footsteps the sea made passable beneath him. We therefore need not set Peter or the other apostles before us as examples; let us at least imitate this beggar who, now well illuminated, was not led astray or silenced in his confession of the truth by the threats of savage rulers, by the reproach of his former blindness, or by the expulsion from the synagogue—a terrifying and dreadful expulsion not only for himself but also for his parents.

Let us hear him preaching and making his good confession: “If anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, him he hears.”

Let us therefore worship the Lord, not with the vapor of incense or the throats of lowing bulls, but [Col. 1299A] with sacrifices of faith and love, most pleasing to him. Let us do his will—that is, fulfill his commandment—and hold in our minds fear of him and the holy hope of his promises, because “the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm CXLVI).

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CI. FOR THE THURSDAY AFTER *LAETARE*

At that time Jesus went into a city called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd were going with him, etc. (Luke VII). (Seek Homily 17 for the Sunday after the Feast of Pentecost.)

## HOMILY CII. FOR THE FRIDAY AFTER *LAETARE*

[Col. 1299B]

At that time there was a certain man who was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha his sisters, etc. (John XI).

Among all the miracles that the Son of God performed in order to reveal his divinity, this one stands above the rest and holds, as it were, the chief place: the miracle he performed concerning Lazarus. Certainly, each of his works is worthy of the greatest admiration. Who would not reverently marvel that the lame walked with upright steps, that the barriers of the tongue were loosed for the mute, and that the eyes of the blind, long closed, were opened by the touch of his sacred hand? Who, considering these and many other things, would not wonder at and admire the divine power? Yet all these things seemed small in comparison with Christ’s immense majesty, [Col. 1299C] unless his friend Lazarus had died. He allowed him to die for this reason: by raising him in a new manner, admirable throughout all ages, he might declare himself to be Lord of life and death.

The singular dignity of this miracle was further enhanced by the special merit of its most worthy recorder. No other evangelist described it; it was reserved for the Lord’s beloved John alone. For so unique and excellent a matter ought to have no other narrator than the virgin most beloved by Christ.

But since this reading is for the greater part clear in itself and does not require exposition point by point, we have undertaken to explain it more by sections than word for word, so that we may come to the matters that are more necessary. We read above that, when the Lord was in the temple and teaching in the portico called Solomon’s, the Jews, unable to endure his words about his divinity, picked up stones to stone him. But the Lord came unharmed out of the temple, from among the hands of those who wanted to stone him, and went across the Jordan, where John had previously been baptizing.

While he was there, Lazarus became ill at Bethany, which was the village of Mary and Martha, near Jerusalem. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair. Since at that time there were several women of this name, she is identified by her most famous deed. She was the Mary who, as the evangelist Luke relates earlier, once came as a sinner to the Lord’s feet, anointed them, bathed them with her tears, and wiped them with her hair; thus she obtained from the Lord the forgiveness of many sins (Luke 7).

So they sent word to him, since he was absent across the Jordan, announcing that Lazarus, their brother, was ill, so that he might come to the aid both of them and of their brother, freeing the women from grief and him from sickness. But let us see what the messengers said: “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is ill.” They did not say, “Come and heal the sick man.” They certainly did not dare to say this. It was enough for them that he should know he was ill, for they knew that he would not abandon the one he loved. “Behold,” they said, “the one whom you love is ill,” as though they were saying: “It is enough, Lord, that you know this; there is no need for you to come to us and weary yourself. Command there, and here what you command will be done.”

When Jesus heard this, he said: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” Why do you say, Lord, that it is not unto death, when Lazarus was inevitably going to die? The Lord knew this as well, and he himself had willed that it should happen; but he had determined to raise him after death. What he answered, therefore—“This illness is not unto death”—has the same meaning as if he had said: “This death is not unto death.” For he is not dying in order to be held by death like other dead men, but in order to be raised in a wondrous manner.

“For the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it”—the word “illness” must be understood. This glorification did not increase him, since he is perfectly complete and cannot progress; rather, it benefited us, insofar as through this great miracle we might believe in him and escape the eternal death of the soul.

But let us examine more carefully what he said. He says, “For the glory of God,” and then adds, “so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” Therefore the Son of God is God. This is directed against the heretics who said that Christ was not God by nature but by grace. One of them accordingly said: “I do not envy Christ for having been made God; I too can become this, if I wish.”

Now Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary, and Lazarus. Lazarus was ill and they were grieving, but they had the greatest hope, because the one who consoles the sorrowful, heals the sick, and even raises the dead loved him. When he heard that Lazarus was ill, he remained in the same place for two days. The Lord did not wish to come then; he delayed healing so that he might raise him more wondrously. Thus he remained there until the four days had been completed.

After this he said to his disciples: “Let us go again into Judea.” The disciples were terrified when they heard that he wanted to return to Judea. They knew of the savage conspiracy by which the Jews were persecuting him and striving to deliver him to death. Therefore they said to him: “Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and you are going there again?”

He answered them—he who could not fear human fury: “Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks by day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks by night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

The holy disciples had heard that the Lord intended to return to Judea, and they were afraid that the Jews might seize their good teacher. As though offering him advice and wishing to turn him back from his purpose, they did not yet perfectly understand the dispensation for which he had come. For God had assumed humanity for this purpose: that he might die for the salvation of human beings.

So also blessed Peter, when he heard the Lord speaking about his passion, wishing in some way to turn him back, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; you shall not die” (Matthew 16). When the apostles therefore wished, in a manner, to advise the Lord, he rebuked them, saying: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?”

He plainly called himself the day, for he is “day from day” and “light from light,” and elsewhere says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). To show himself to be the day, he chose twelve apostles. Concerning them he now says: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” It is as though he were saying: “You who are the hours of the day, why do you wish to offer such advice? The hours follow the day and carry out their work under the day’s direction.”

But perhaps someone may say: Judas was one of the twelve. Was he also an hour of the day, although he betrayed the day itself to death? When the Lord said this, however, he was not considering Judas himself, but Matthias, who had been foreseen as his replacement. In the end, when Judas went to the place destined for him, the apostle Matthias was chosen in his place, and thus the apostolic number remained complete.

Christ, therefore, is the day, and whoever walks in this day cannot go astray. He clings to the one who said: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” For the one who is without this light can go astray; he cannot walk.

After saying this, he told them: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.” Lazarus was dead, but he lived for Christ. No one could awaken another from sleep with such ease as Christ could raise Lazarus from the tomb.

Indeed, all the dead may be called “sleeping,” if you consider the power of God, by whom they are to be raised on the last day, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep” (1 Thessalonians 4). And elsewhere: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15).

They said to him: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be saved.” They understood the Lord’s words in their literal sense and answered accordingly: “If he sleeps, he will be saved.” For sleep in a sick young man is usually a sign of recovery. The Lord, however, had spoken of Lazarus’s death, while they thought he had spoken of ordinary sleep.

Then Jesus told them plainly: “Lazarus is dead, and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.” Lazarus had been reported as ill, not dead; but what could be hidden from the one before whose eyes all things are naked and open? How could the death of Lazarus be unknown to the one who had created Lazarus himself?

He rejoiced for the sake of the disciples, who were amazed that he knew everything in this way; through this, they believed more certainly and clearly that he was the true God. Although they already believed, their faith was still of a kind that could grow, advancing as it was built up by miracles.

“But let us go to him.” Thomas, who is called Didymus, then said to his fellow disciples: “Let us also go, so that we may die with him.” These words reveal the true affection of one who loved. The apostles loved the Lord incomparably, because their life depended upon his presence, so much so that they considered it joyful either to live with him or at least to die with him.

“Let us go,” he said, “and die with him.” It was as though he were saying: “We see him hastening toward his enemies and toward death, and we cannot turn him back from such a purpose. Let us also go, so that we may die with him, lest after his death we remain both abandoned and without consolation.”

Jesus therefore came and found that Lazarus had been four days in the tomb. This was what he himself had willed; he had delayed coming earlier so that the four days might be completed and Lazarus might be raised more gloriously.

But since the literal matters are sufficiently clear in themselves, let us ascend to investigate the mystery. Lazarus signifies some sinner who has not merely sinned but has also adopted a habit of sinning. Perhaps someone may silently ask: How could Lazarus represent the sinner, when the Lord loved him so greatly? Sometimes, however, meanings are taken from opposites.

Thus King and prophet David committed adultery with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and killed his own faithful and innocent soldier by the sword of the sons of Ammon (2 Samuel 11). If you consider the historical event, who would doubt that Uriah, innocently killed, should rightly be preferred for his justice and innocence to David the adulterer and murderer? But if you inquire into the hidden mystery, Uriah signifies the devil, while David, by contrast, signifies Christ. This does not mean that the merits of the different parties are thereby diminished.

Often the name of the devil is seen written in gold, while the most radiant name of Christ is defaced with ink. Thus, as we have said, Lazarus represents some sinner. He was loved by Christ because Christ deigned to manifest his presence for sinners. For he himself said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9).

We must now ask what is signified by the four days during which the dead man lay in the tomb. Every human being who is destined to die is born with original sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Romans 5). This is the first day of death, given by the origin of our descent.

Then, as he grows by being born, a person reaches the years capable of reason and begins to possess within himself the natural law, by which human beings are naturally taught not to do to others what they do not want done to themselves. Yet they also transgress this law: they do not want to suffer theft, but they commit theft. Behold the second day of death.

After this, the law given through Moses was added. It commands: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20). This law was written, but it too is despised; thus there is now, as it were, a third day of death.

After all this Christ came, brought the gospel, proclaimed the kingdom, threatened evildoers with Gehenna, and promised eternal life to those who live well. What more is there to say? The gospel too is despised, and this is the fourth day of death.

These four days may also be explained in another way. We said that Lazarus represents a sinner who has already been buried under the evil habit of sinning and under despair. A person reaches the habit of sin through a fourfold progression. First there is a suggestion in the heart, second consent, third the deed, and fourth the habit.

Some people, when struck by an unlawful thought, drive it from their hearts so completely that they are not moved by any evil delight. Others take pleasure in certain things but are not led to consent to that pleasure. Consent then follows, and the deed breaks forth. The deed already becomes a habit, the four days of death are completed, and a kind of despair arises, so that it may be said: “He already stinks; he has been dead four days.”

When Martha learned that Jesus had come, she went out to meet him, while Mary remained at home. Martha said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

How restrained are her words, and how temperately she grieves over her brother’s death! She did not say, “I ask you to raise him,” but only: “I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” It was as though she were saying: “I am certainly convinced that you can do it; I know that unfailing power is in you. But if you wish, you will do it. I do not presume to ask you to do so, because I do not know whether you wish it.”

Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise.” Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.” The Lord was promising the resurrection of her brother in the present, but Martha thought that he was speaking of the resurrection in which all human beings will rise. She had certainly often seen the Lord raise the dead, but this was something so great that even faith itself had not dared to attempt it. She was confident about that resurrection, but remained uncertain about this one.

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life.” It was as though he were saying: “Why do you now doubt that your brother can rise, when I, who am the resurrection and the life, promise that he will rise? The one through whom the rest of humanity will rise at the resurrection can also raise him now.”

He is therefore the resurrection and the life, because through him we rise from sin so that we may live for righteousness. “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live”—that is, if he has died in the flesh, he will live in the spirit. For God is not the God of the dead.

Here he is speaking of bodily death. Whoever believes in Christ and lives in accordance with that belief, even if he dies in the flesh by paying the common debt of all human beings, nevertheless lives in his soul by clinging to Christ, who is the life of the soul.

“And everyone,” he says—understand: everyone who lives in the flesh—“and believes in me, even if he dies for a time by bodily death, will not die eternally,” because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.

“Do you believe this?” He knew what she would believe, since nothing can be hidden from him; yet he sought the confession by which she would be saved. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

She said to him: “Yes, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world.” When she believed him to be the Son of God, she believed in life and resurrection, and that everyone who believed in him would not die eternally. For earlier the Lord had asked whether she believed this.

After she had said these things, she went away and secretly called her sister Mary, saying: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” Here “secretly” means that she spoke in a subdued voice: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”

When Mary heard this, she rose quickly and came to him. Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. The Jews who were with Mary in the house and were consoling her, when they saw that she quickly rose and went out, followed her, saying that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

The Jews who had gathered to console her thought that she was hurrying to her brother’s tomb to seek comfort in tears and satisfy her grief by weeping. They followed her by divine providence, so that many might see the remarkable miracle of the raising of one dead four days and thus believe in Christ.
