When Mary came to where the Lord was, she saw him and fell at his feet, saying: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” It was as though she were complaining: “While you were present with us, neither death nor any illness dared approach us, since it knew that life was dwelling among us. But when you went away, envy appeared, and death snatched our brother, who was still living in this world, away in a bitter burial. If you had been here, your friend Lazarus could not have died.”

When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he groaned in spirit, troubled himself, and said: “Where have you laid him?”

O groaning of compassion! O disturbance destined to remove the disturbance of the troubled and to bring eternal joy! The Lord troubled himself by his power, because no one else could trouble him. He was troubled because he himself willed it, just as he died because he himself permitted death to come to him.

Yet he indicated something great in this disturbance. We said above that the four-day Lazarus signifies a desperate sinner, weighed down as if by the mass of a tomb, stinking and decomposing through his evil reputation and condition. As Christ was about to raise him, he groaned and troubled himself, to show that one who is in such a state ought to be troubled, groan, and roar inwardly in his heart; he ought to consider what he has done and say to himself:

“What has happened to me, wretched man? In baptism all my sins had been forgiven. But behold, after the holy washing I have become more filthy; after the medicine I have been more grievously wounded. I have sinned severely, yet I never wished to put an end to my sins. The mercy of God always waited for me to repent and did not wish to punish me immediately when I sinned. Yet I, most wretched and deserving of eternal torments, did not hesitate continually to provoke his most gentle patience by new and fresh crimes.”

When the sinner laments these things within himself, Christ already groans and is troubled within him. He groaned for this reason: to teach the sinner that he must groan and accuse his sins if he wishes to return to the life of the soul.

“Where,” he says, “have you laid him?” Did he not know where the one whom he wished to raise had been placed? He asks in order to show that he knows only those things that are just and holy, while he does not know the sinner because he rejects him.

Thus after Adam’s sin he is asked: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3). And to the reprobate at the judgment he will say: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13; Matthew 25). For what does it mean to say, “I do not know you,” except: “I do not acknowledge you in the light of righteousness”?

They said to him: “Lord, come and see”—that is, have mercy. For his seeing is his having mercy. And Jesus wept, because he was the fountain of compassion. Yet those tears were destined to bring forth indescribable joy.

Here Sedulius beautifully says:

> He filled his friend with tears  
> [lacuna]  
> God in majesty.

He wept for the one whom, in the humanity he had assumed, he could raise by the power of his divinity. The Lord also wept for the same reason that he had earlier groaned and been troubled: to teach sinners that they need abundant weeping and tears.

Then the Jews said: “See how he loved him.” But some of them said: “Could not he who opened the eyes of the man born blind have caused this man not to die?” The Lord certainly could have done this, but he allowed Lazarus to die so that he might be raised by a greater miracle.

Jesus, groaning again within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay over it. The stone under which the dead man was pressed signifies the law, by which the sinner is condemned. The law is rightly represented by a stone, because it was written on tablets of stone. The dead man beneath the stone is therefore the guilty person under the law.

Those who live well are not under the law, since the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and sinners (1 Timothy 1). The Lord commanded that this stone be removed when he commanded the grace of the holy gospel to be preached throughout the whole world.

Martha, the sister of the one who had died, said to him: “Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.” She was now almost despairing; she feared that removing the stone would release a stench more than she hoped that her brother could be raised.

Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”—namely, when I raise one who has been dead four days and has begun to stink.

Likewise, when someone considered hopeless is rescued from the tomb of sins, the power of God is proclaimed by those who behold it, because where sin abounded, grace abounds even more.

So they removed the stone. Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

By these words, what else was he seeking in this work, as in his other works, than the glory of God the Father? Since in his humanity he was less than the Father, he asked him to raise Lazarus and declared that he had been heard by him. He said this because of the crowd standing around, so that they might believe him, even in this way, to be the Son of God and sent by him, since the Son’s affection toward the Father compelled him to invoke the Father.

Now the underworld was being shaken; now hell, opened beneath the Lord’s feet, lay exposed. All the dead were waiting for their names to be called.

Jesus therefore cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!” By calling one person by name, the others were also recalled.

But how many things are said to have occurred in the raising of this dead man! The Lord groaned, wept, was troubled, and cried out with a loud voice, because one whom the weight of evil habit presses down rises from the death of sin only with difficulty and with a cry.

Immediately the man who had been dead came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth, and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them: “Unbind him and let him go.”

The Lord could certainly have raised any dead person he wished without a cry, but he did not wish to do so because of the hidden grace of the sacrament. The dead man rises at the Lord’s loud voice when the sinner, moved by the great grace of God, comes to repentance.

He comes out of the tomb when he confesses his sins, but he is still bound, still guilty, and cannot be absolved by his own strength. Therefore the Lord commands the disciples to unbind him and let him go, because the power to forgive sins has been given to them, to the other ministers of the holy Church, and to their successors.

For he says: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18). At the same time, the unity of Christ and the Church is commended here. Since Christ is the head and the Church is his body, Christ raises and the disciples unbind, so that it may be clearly shown that no one can be raised from the death of sins without the unity of the Catholic faith.

It must not be omitted here that the holy gospel records the Lord as having raised only three dead people. There is no doubt that he raised more dead people, since blessed John says: “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book” (John 20). But only three are related for a definite mystical reason.

First, he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue while she was still within the household walls. He did not permit anyone to enter with him except Peter, James, and John, as well as the girl’s father and mother (Luke 8).

He also raised the son of a widow who had been carried outside the gate of his city, with many people present and watching (Luke 7).

Moreover, he raised Lazarus, who had already been buried and had already begun to stink.

These three kinds of dead signify three kinds of sinful people whom Christ still raises today.

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who was raised within the house while only a few people watched, signifies those who keep sin shut up within their conscience and have not yet brought it forth into action.

For example, when someone is moved by an evil thought and considers whether the opportunity exists to fulfill what he has unlawfully desired, he is already dead, but is still shut within the house. The Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). He has not yet approached her bodily, but he has consented in his heart. He is already dead, but he has not yet been carried out.

If such a person should at some time, through divine inspiration, recognize his evil conscience, abandon his wicked consent, and return to life, this occurs in the secrecy of his thoughts.

Others, after consenting, go out to commit the crime; the dead man is, as it were, brought forth from the hiding places of the soul, so that what was concealed in secret may appear publicly. Yet such people are often admonished by God, converted, and raised to the life of the soul.

There are also some who, by doing what is evil, entangle themselves in an evil habit, to such an extent that the habit itself prevents them from understanding that what they are doing is evil. Sometimes they even defend the evil they commit and become angry when they are reproved.

These are like people already buried and crushed beneath a great mass—that is, the weight—of evil habit. The Lord deigns to come to them through the hidden impulse of his mercy, provided that they have sisters, namely the spiritual virtues of the soul, through whose intervention they can be recalled to life.

Yet the Lord reveals a certain difficulty when he groans in spirit, troubles himself, and cries out with the loudest voice, showing that strong cries of reproof are needed against one who has persisted in the habit of sinning.

We must not despair of such people. At the Lord’s voice the sick man trembled; the dead man of four days rose; the sinner was freed, even from the habit of committing offenses. First the Lord gives him life inwardly through himself; afterward he absolves him through the ministry of priests.

No sinner is to be absolved before he has been corrected through worthy repentance and has shown himself to be inwardly alive.

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary and Martha, and had seen what he did, believed in him. After a miracle so glorious and worthy of proclamation throughout all ages, it is said that not all but many of the Jews believed. This passage reveals their extremely hard unbelief and their perversity, which was readily turned toward evil.

Indeed, their sin was so great that they could not properly receive the faith of Christ unless they first killed the Son of God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek your name, Lord” (Psalm 82).

They were first filled with confusion and shame when, after Christ’s ascension, they heard his apostles preaching his resurrection. They began to blush and to consider what a great crime they had committed in killing the Savior. Thus they sought his name when, struck with fear, they said to the apostles: “What shall we do, men and brothers? Tell us.”

Blessed Peter answered them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized for the forgiveness of sins” (Acts 2).

For he had decreed before the ages that by his death he would destroy the one who held the power of death—that is, the devil—and that, though dead, he would subjugate to himself the very ministers of his death.

Therefore let us offer thanks to the renowned victor over death with the greatest exultation; let us exalt him day and night with praises; and above all let us implore his mercy, so that he may make us obey his commandments in every respect. Then, with no sin ruling within us, may we cling to him in mind and desire and happily deserve to attain the joy of the blessed vision.

## HOMILY 103. FOR THE SATURDAY AFTER LAETARE

At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life,” etc. (John 8).

After the Lord and our Redeemer had rescued the woman caught in adultery from the savagery of the Jews who wanted to stone her, and had most mercifully absolved her from the guilt of adultery, lest anyone should perhaps doubt whether the one whom they regarded as a true human being could forgive sins, he deigned to demonstrate most openly who he was through the power of his divinity. For he says [Col. 1308A]: “I am the light of the world.” The divinity was indeed an incomprehensible and unbounded light, hidden beneath the veil of the flesh he had assumed; by its authority he forgave this woman’s sins, and those of anyone else he wished.

This is that true light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I), namely, the wisdom of God, which proceeded from that eternal and unceasing light. Human frailty could not otherwise have endured its brilliance unless it had enveloped itself, as it were, in a cloud of flesh, through which the splendor of this divine light might become known to human minds as through a very clear mirror. Therefore the vision of the inner person must be cleansed and kept free from every stain of vice, like a body protected from harmful moisture, so that it may be made worthy to behold this true light.

“He who follows me [Col. 1308B] does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” As though he were saying more plainly in other words: Whoever in the present obeys my commands and, insofar as possible, imitates my example will not in the future fear the darkness of eternal condemnation, but will enjoy the light of eternal life, where, once the fear of death has been removed, he will be granted joy in perpetual existence alone.

These are the darknesses to be feared, darker than every night—not perceived by the outward eyes with which we see what is white and black, but by the inward eyes with which we discern what is just and unjust, with which we contemplate not bodily and visible forms but the truth intelligibly.

The Pharisees answered him: “You testify concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” They answered in this way as though he alone were giving testimony, and as though his testimony were not true, [Col. 1308C] although it is clear that, before the Lord came and appeared visibly in the flesh, he sent many witnesses ahead and kindled them like lamps with the spirit of prophecy. They foretold his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension.

Among these the chief and great one was John the Baptist, whose greatness the Savior himself attests, saying: “Among those born of women no greater has arisen,” and so forth (Matthew XI). Elsewhere the same Lord calls him a lamp, saying: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V). Thus he bore witness to our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “I baptize you with water, but the one who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie” (Luke III).

But the Jews paid no attention to these things and, having forgotten them, acted as though he alone were giving testimony about himself. They said: [Col. 1308D] “You testify concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” But let us hear what the Lord answered them: “Even if I testify concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.”

By these words he revealed both himself and God the Father, to whom the only-begotten Son of God ascribed all glory. “If,” he says, “I testify about myself, my testimony is true, and it is confirmed by the Father’s testimony. For I know where I came from, because I was sent by him; and where I am going, because, when the mystery of my incarnation has been completed, I shall return to the Father.”

Yet when he came to us, he did not abandon the Father, nor, when he returned to the Father, did he abandon the earth. For Christ is not a light contained by places and times, like this bodily sun, [Col. 1309A] which cannot approach the west without withdrawing from the east. We must not think in this way about that true light which is Christ, who is wholly everywhere and shines ineffably everywhere.

For elsewhere he says: “No one has ever seen God” (John I). “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.” He was speaking on earth and saying that he was with the Father; but, when he was about to depart from the world through his ascension, he promised the faithful, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII).

His testimony about himself was therefore true, because, having been sent by the Father, he had the Father’s testimony, and, having fulfilled this mission, he was returning to the place from which he had come.

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.” This must be understood of his first coming. [Col. 1309B] For there are two comings of the Lord: the first in mercy, the second in judgment. The first has taken place; the second will occur at the end of the age.

If the Lord had come to judge at his first coming, he would have found everyone deserving punishment. Mercy therefore had to come first, and judgment was to be exercised afterward. For the Psalmist also said: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psalm C); he said that he would sing mercy first and judgment afterward.

Through this mercy he became human for the sake of human beings; he endured reproaches, mockery, spitting, scourging, and finally the cross itself, in order to save the human race that had been lost. Concerning this first coming of his, in which he had come mercifully to redeem the human race, he said: “I judge no one.”

But concerning the second coming, in which he will come as judge, he adds: [Col. 1309C] “And if I judge, my judgment is true.” He reveals why his judgment would be true when he continues: “Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me”—that is, who ordained that I should become incarnate. For this sending is the incarnation.

The Son had therefore been sent by the Father, but had not departed from the Father. He came into the world through his humanity, but remained with the Father through his co-eternal divinity. His judgment was therefore true because he himself was the true Son of God.

“And in your law,” he says, “it is written that the testimony of two people is true” (Deuteronomy XVII). “In your law,” he says—that is, in the law given to you. In the same way we say every day when we pray: “Our bread,” meaning the bread that we ask to be given to us.

But we must ask how the testimony of two people can be true. [Col. 1309D] Were those two false witnesses not false witnesses who gave false testimony during the Lord’s passion? Or were those two elders not also false witnesses who, in the very book of Daniel, brought false testimony against the most chaste Susanna (Daniel XIII)?

Yet when the law says, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every matter shall stand,” the mystery of the Trinity is commended. The Trinity also supported Susanna’s chastity inwardly in her conscience through its testimony, when she was falsely accused by two elders.

The meaning is this: If your law approves the testimony of two people as true—people who can sometimes speak falsely, even if not with the intention of lying, yet deceived by error, thinking that what is false is true—if, then, [Col. 1310A] you do not dare to disapprove or reject their testimony, how do you presume to say that the testimony of me, God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, established in perfect truth, is not true? Accept our testimony instead, lest you experience judgment.

“I am the one who testifies concerning myself.” He himself testifies concerning himself and requires no other witness than himself, because he knows everything even before it happens and considers most clearly from what source each thing proceeds. For all things are naked and open to his eyes, and he does not need anyone to tell him what the life of each person is like, since he is the judge of all and will repay every person according to his works.

It follows: “And the Father who sent me testifies concerning me.” “I do not,” he says, “testify concerning myself alone, because the Father who sent me himself bears witness to me.”

[Col. 1310B] But the Jews understood Christ’s words carnally and therefore said: “Where is your father?” They saw the human being openly, but did not understand the God hidden within. “Where,” they ask, “is your father? We heard you say that you would not be alone, but that the Father who sent you would be with you. Yet we see only you; we cannot see the Father with you. Show us your father.”

And the Lord replied: “You know neither me nor the Father.” As though he were saying: If you want me to show you the Father, it is as though you already knew me; but you still know neither me nor my Father. Because you do not know me, you cannot know my Father. You must first come to know me, and then you will be able to arrive at knowledge of my Father.

[Col. 1310C] “For if you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.” There is one knowledge of the Father and the Son, whose substance is one; neither can be known apart from the other. They knew Christ according to the flesh, concerning which he said elsewhere to them: “You know me, and you know where I am from” (John VII); but they did not know his divinity.

He says “perhaps” not because he was in doubt, but to rebuke their unbelief. When this adverb is spoken by a human being, it signifies doubt; when spoken by God, to whom nothing can be hidden, it signifies rebuke. Thus, when the Apostle said: “I think that I have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians VII), he was not doubting that he had the Spirit of God, but reproving those who doubted and did not believe.

[Col. 1310D] Therefore, when he says: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also,” he rebukes the unbelievers who did not know that the Father and the Son have one knowledge, and that one cannot be known apart from the other.

For this reason he says elsewhere to Philip, who asked him to show them the Father: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John XIV). Because the Father and the Son are one, their knowledge and their understanding are one.

Jesus spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple. The treasury was a place in the temple where treasures were stored. *Gaza* in the Persian language means “riches,” while *phylasso* in Greek means “I guard” or “I keep.” Thus, by a compound name, he called the place the treasury because riches were kept there.

The Lord’s great steadfastness and immense confidence are shown here: in the very inner precincts of the temple, before the Scribes and Pharisees, his enemies, he spoke the words of his divinity without fear.

[Col. 1311A] Mystically, however, the treasuries signify the mysteries of Scripture that were attached to the temple. Christ is the temple to which all the mysteries of the law and the prophets were attached and to which they pertain; they were to be fulfilled only in him. These spiritual treasuries were to be opened after his resurrection, when he granted the apostles understanding and showed that everything had been fulfilled in him.

Hence the evangelist says that, after rising from the dead, he opened their understanding so that they might understand everything written about him (Luke XXIV). But at that time the Lord spoke in the treasury because he was speaking to those same Jews, who did not understand his parables and did not believe.

“And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come”—namely, the hour of his own will and determination. For just as he was born by his own will, [Col. 1311B] so he suffered by his own will. If he had wished, he would never have suffered; if he had not suffered, the human race would never have been redeemed; if it had not been redeemed, no human being would have been saved.

For this purpose God became human: to redeem through the weakness of his humanity those whom he had created through the power of his divinity. One and the same Son of God and Son of Man, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, without confusion and without division in word, perfect God and perfect human being: through whose eternal benefits eternal thanksgiving is due. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## HOMILY CIV. FOR PASSION SUNDAY

*(From the works of blessed Pope Leo.)*

[Col. 1311C] “The sacrament, dearly beloved,” and so forth. For the remainder, see Saint Pope Gregory, *Works*, volume I, *Patrologia* LIV, column 313.

## HOMILY CV. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From the works of blessed Pope Gregory.)*

At that time Jesus said to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: “Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” And so forth (John VIII).

“Consider, dearest brothers, the gentleness of God,” and so forth. For the remainder, see Saint Gregory, *Works*, volume II, *Patrologia* LXXVI, column 1150.

## HOMILY CVI. ON THE SECOND DAY AFTER JUDICA

[Col. 1311D]

At that time the Scribes and Pharisees sent officers to arrest Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them: “I am with you for a little while longer, and I am going to him who sent me,” and so forth (John VII).

No one can sufficiently admire how great was the hardness in the hearts of the Scribes and Pharisees. For while our Redeemer was calling them to faith through continual preaching and the working of miracles, and while the simple crowds were believing and glorifying both the Lord’s deeds and his words, they, on the contrary, not only did not want to believe in him, but were even trying to arrest him.

They had fixed the root of their hearts in love of the world; therefore they were unable to receive [Col. 1312A] the words of heavenly teaching. They therefore sent officers to arrest him. But the Lord, who had it in his power to die when and how he wished, answered: “I am with you for a little while longer.”

As though he were saying: “What you now intend to do is premature. You will do what you wish, but not now, because I do not wish it. I am with you for a little while longer, and I am going to him who sent me. First I must fulfill the dispensation of the flesh I have assumed, and then reach the place where I must undergo the passion.”

“You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am you cannot come.” By these words he indicated the time of his resurrection. Those who refused to receive him while he was speaking in their presence and proclaiming himself God through miracles sought him after his resurrection, when they saw everywhere an immense [Col. 1312B] multitude already believing, and signs and miracles being performed far and wide through the apostles—he himself working in them and through them, who says elsewhere: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

Then they sought him and did not find him, because he had already departed from the world in bodily presence and, ascending to the Father, had penetrated the heavens. “And where I am, you cannot come.” Observe that he speaks of the future when he says, “You will seek me and will not find me,” but of the present when he says, “Where I am, you cannot come.”

The Son, co-eternal and of one substance with the Father, was in the bosom of the Father. He was speaking on earth, but remained with the Father and in the Father. Those who did not wish to believe that he was equal to the Father could not come to him there. For one must come to him not by place but by faith.

[Col. 1312C] But the Jews, in their customary manner, did not understand his words and thought that he was speaking carnally. They began to complain among themselves, saying: “Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Surely he is going to the dispersion among the Gentiles and will teach the Gentiles?”

In saying this they did not know what they were saying; nevertheless, because he was indeed going there, they prophesied. For he was going to the dispersion among the Gentiles and was going to teach them, not through bodily presence but through his apostles, through whom and in whom he himself spoke, as one of them says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians XIII).

The holy preachers were Christ’s feet, as the prophet says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” [Col. 1312D] (Isaiah LII). Through these feet he was going to the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles might receive the faith and salvation that the Jews had rejected.

On the last and great day of the festival Jesus stood and cried out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says” (Proverbs of Solomon), “rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The festival of *Scenopegia* was then being celebrated, that is, the Feast of Tabernacles, in memory of the time when they lived in shelters in the desert for forty years. This festival was observed in the seventh month, which the Latins customarily call September. They celebrated it for eight days, and the eighth day, that is, the final day, was the most solemn and holy.

On this final day of the festival Jesus stood and, not merely speaking but crying out, invited them, saying: [Col. 1313A] “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” This thirst was not bodily but spiritual.

If anyone thirsts, that is, if anyone wishes to believe in and love Christ, let him come—not with bodily steps but with the affections of the mind. Let him come not by physically migrating to Christ, but by loving Christ and departing from love of the world, and let him receive the love of Christ.

“Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The evangelist necessarily took care to explain what water we should understand, adding: “He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

What, then, is this water except love, which has been poured into the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit? For the Apostle says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V).

[Col. 1313B] The belly in which we must receive this water is the inner conscience. When it has drunk this water of the Holy Spirit—that is, when it has begun to possess the love of Christ—it will have a spring of living water; indeed, it will itself become a spring.

For this spring flowing from the belly of the conscience is goodwill. Proceeding from the water of love, it wishes to benefit its neighbor. Whoever thinks that the good he possesses is sufficient for himself alone and does not strive to extend its benefit to others does not have living waters flowing from his belly. But if he wishes to benefit others from the good he has received, water flows from his belly, because his goodwill is spread among his neighbors.

This spring will not be dried up by any drought; rather, it will continually increase through its devoted flow.

“He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive.” He means the Holy Spirit, whom we venerate as [Col. 1313C] the third person in the Holy Trinity.

All the faithful must know that the whole Trinity is God and spirit, since the Lord says: “God is spirit” (John IV). The Father, therefore, is spirit, and the Son is spirit. Consequently, so that the Father and the Son may be distinguished, the third person of the Trinity is no longer called simply “spirit,” but, with an epithet, is called “the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1313D] Before his ascension he promised this Holy Spirit to the apostles, and after his ascension he sent him on the day of Pentecost in tongues of fire. Therefore the evangelist says: “Whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

The holy apostles and the other faithful did indeed have the Holy Spirit before Christ’s resurrection, but they did not receive him through such an open bestowal as they were afterward going to receive him. They had the Holy Spirit so that they themselves might live rightly and benefit certain people; afterward they received the Holy Spirit so that they might be able to convert the whole human race to faith in Christ.

By this Spirit the whole Church is universally enlightened and instructed, and amid the pressures of the world she is consoled by hope of future goods. Enumerating his most effective power, the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues,” and so forth; concluding, he says: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills.”

Let us therefore devoutly ask for this Spirit, so that he may empty our minds of all the filth of carnal desires and make us a dwelling place for himself, [Col. 1314A] with the almighty Trinity accomplishing the whole work. He lives, and so forth.

## HOMILY CVII. ON THE THIRD DAY AFTER JUDICA

At that time Jesus was walking in Galilee; for he did not wish to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him, and so forth (John VII).

Our Lord Jesus Christ, mindful in all things of our salvation, set before his future faithful in everything he did examples that they ought to imitate. Because he saw that persecution by unbelievers would be stirred up in the holy Church for the sake of his name, and knew that his weaker members could not endure the ferocity of persecution, lest such people despair of salvation and [Col. 1314B] regard themselves as alienated from Christ if, frightened, they should ever flee from suffering, the Lord deigned to provide for them by both command and example.

By command, when he permitted such people to flee in time of persecution, saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew X). By example, when, while still a child, in order to avoid Herod’s cruelty, he deigned to flee not only from one city to another but even from one region to another, being carried by his parents into Egypt.

When he had become a young man, and the leaders of the Jews wanted to kill him because of his preaching of the gospel, he often left Judea and went to other regions, so that his members would not be afraid to do what they knew had first been done by their Head, nor would anyone be charged with wrongdoing if, [Col. 1314C] overcome by fear, he sought the protection of flight.

The holy evangelist whose passage has been read says: “Jesus was walking in Galilee. For he did not wish to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.”

The Lord had not lost his power; by doing this he was comforting our weakness. For if he had wished, he could have walked safely among them—he himself testifying that he had death itself in his power—saying: “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John X).

Finally, he demonstrated this power when, at the time of his passion, at the sound of his voice those who had come to arrest him went backward and fell to the ground (John XVIII). But, ordering all things according to a most provident [Col. 1314D] dispensation, he deigned for a time to remain absent from his persecutors, in order, as has been said, to provide an example.

The Jewish festival of Scenopegia was near. Scenopegia was the Feast of Tabernacles, when all the Jews were commanded by the law, in the seventh month, to live in tabernacles, in memory of the time when they lived in the desert for forty years in tabernacles without any houses.

The day is called a festival—not because the celebration took place on only one day, for they lived in tabernacles for seven days, but because the Jews customarily called all the days belonging to the same celebration “one day,” on account of the single solemnity.

[Col. 1315A] The brothers of the Lord, in the most customary language of Holy Scripture, are understood to be his blood-relatives according to the flesh, namely his cousins. For what certain heretics have said—that the brothers of the Lord are called the sons of Joseph, the husband of the ever-virgin Mary, by a certain wife of his named Isca—has no authority to support it and therefore must by no means be accepted by the faithful. It should certainly be known that in sacred discourse brothers are customarily called in three ways: by nature, nation, and kinship. By nature, as Jacob and Esau. By nation, as all Jews, from whatever tribe, were called brothers. Hence it is said in the law: “If your brother, a Hebrew, reduced to poverty, sells himself to you” (Leviticus XXV). By kinship, as Abraham and Lot were called brothers, though Abraham was Lot’s uncle. For it is written: “Abraham said to Lot: Let there be no quarrel, I pray, [Col. 1315B] between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Genesis XIII). A fourth way, too, can be added: that of religion, according to which all Christians are called brothers, who rejoice that we have one God as our Father. Therefore, in that third way, which we said was calling brothers according to kinship, we must understand this term here and wherever we read of the brothers of the Lord. Thus James was called the Lord’s brother because he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt.

His brothers therefore said to him: “Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples may see the works you are doing. For no one does anything in secret,” and so forth. “If you do these things, manifest yourself to the world.”

The holy evangelist took care to explain why they said this when he [Col. 1315C] added: “For even his brothers did not believe in him.” They could indeed be Christ’s kinsmen according to the flesh, but they disdained to believe because of that very relationship. And because they sought worldly glory, they did not wish to believe in the one whom they knew to be a despiser of that glory.

They therefore thought that he was merely human. Measuring him by themselves, and being desirous of honor themselves, they assumed that he was by no means free from this desire. As though consoling him and offering him advice, they said: “Leave here and go into Judea, where the seat of the whole kingdom is, where the capital city and the temple venerable throughout the world are; there make yourself known to people and be glorified by everyone, so that your disciples may see the works you are doing.”

The holy disciples of the Lord did indeed see his [Col. 1315D] works, but not for the purpose they sought—namely, that they should exalt them through earthly and popular favor—for they knew that divine works must be proclaimed with divine praises.

But let us hear what the Lord answered these lovers of glory: “My time has not yet come.” They were urging him to go into Judea and make his power known to the world through miracles, lest he be regarded as obscure, undistinguished, and without glory. But the Lord replied that the time of his glory had not yet come.

First came the time of his humility, through which he had determined to reach heavenly exaltation. He therefore says: “My time,” that is, the time of my glorification, “has not yet come.” For he was first to suffer [the Passion], and only afterward, by rising again and ascending to heaven, was he to be glorified.

“But your time,” he says, “is always [Col. 1316A] ready”—namely, the time of the glory you always desire, for whose sake you think everything must be done. Although they sought worldly glory with every effort, they could not attain it, because glory pursues and embraces those who despise it, but rejects and detests those who seek it.

They are well represented by that fable in which certain people are said to have been condemned in hell to roll an enormous stone up a mountain. Just as one who pushes a stone upward slips backward toward the lower places under the stone’s weight, so all the ambitious suffer a shameful repulse and cannot rise to what they strive to reach.

The time of Christ’s glory had therefore not yet come; it will be complete at the end of the age, when the one who came to be judged will come to judge the living and the dead, and the one who presented himself in humility will appear [Col. 1316B] in majesty.

Why does the Lord say, “I will not go up,” when in what follows we read that he went up once the festival was already under way? But it must be noted that he says, “to this festival day.” “You go up to this festival day.” “Go up,” he says, “to this day on which you extend yourselves toward worldly glory and do not consider heavenly glory. I will not go up to this festival day, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” For then he did not go up with them, but after a few days of the festival had elapsed, because his time—that is, the time of his glory—had not yet been fulfilled.

My festival day will then come—not passing by on fixed days, but remaining in continuous celebration.

When he had said these things, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the festival, not openly but as though in secret.

[Col. 1316C] According to the literal sense, the Lord went up secretly because he was not seeking human favor, nor taking pleasure in the pomp of the world or in the attentions of crowds pressing around him.

Mystically, however, he went up secretly because he was hidden in those solemnities—the one who had been prefigured by the symbolic sacrifices offered there, but was not understood. Now, under the grace of the holy gospel, he has been revealed, because what was presented to them in shadow and figure is enacted for us in the disclosed light of truth.

The Jews therefore sought him at the festival because he had not gone up with his brothers. Before he arrived, they sought him and said: “Where is he?” And there was much murmuring among the crowd concerning him.

That great murmuring arose from the disagreement [Col. 1316D] among them. For, as the evangelist continues, some said: “He is good”; others, however: “No, but he is misleading the crowds.” Some asserted that he was good; others blasphemed him as a deceiver.

But what was then said about the Lord by the impious is said even today about his faithful servants. For whoever is religious and serves God with a simple heart is criticized by the irreligious and malicious, and is called by some good and by others a deceiver.

This is therefore of great consolation to us. Why should Christ’s members shrink from what was inflicted upon their Head? Let Christ’s servants not refuse to hear from lovers of the world what the Jews who murmured said about Christ.

Yet no one spoke openly about him because of fear of the Jews. When he says, “No one spoke openly [Col. 1317A] about him,” he refers only to those who said that he was good. They spoke in silence and in a very low voice, with subdued sound—that is, with their mouths restrained.

Those who said, “He misleads the crowds,” however, spoke more loudly; their noise could be heard more clearly, like the rustling of dry leaves.

But thanks be to God, the voices have been changed for the better. Although the glory of Christ that we devoutly await has not yet come—the glory through which we hope to obtain the rewards of eternity—nevertheless the Church has already grown so widely throughout the whole world and spread herself in every direction through all the regions of the earth that her praises are sung by all the faithful in a free and exalted voice, and all openly say that he is good.

If there are any heretics, few remaining like planks after a shipwreck, [Col. 1317B] they do not speak openly but whisper as though in a corner rather than speak, because, as the Psalmist says: “The mouth of those who speak wickedness has been stopped” (Psalm LXII).

With the mouths of unbelievers closed, the mouths of the faithful have been opened. They now praise the name of Christ in the choir and sing to him with tambourine and psaltery, because, exalted on the cross, he drew all things to himself, so that among all nations he alone might be worshiped and held to be God, blessed above all forever.

To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CVIII. ON THE FOURTH DAY AFTER JUDICA

At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s [Col. 1317C] Portico, and so forth (John X).

*Encaenia*, in the plural, was the term for the festival of the temple’s dedication, which the Jewish people, following the ancient custom of their ancestors, regularly celebrated each year. For *encaeniare* is said in Greek to mean in Latin “to initiate” or “to begin.” It should rightly be believed that the holy Evangelist took care to indicate also the season in which this dedication occurred, saying: “And it was winter.” By this he shows that this *encaenia* did not refer to the temple’s first dedication, but to the one that was last. For we find in the sacred writings that the temple itself was dedicated three times.

Its first dedication was carried out by Solomon, with great splendor and peace throughout the whole kingdom, in the autumn. The second, by Zerubbabel, Jesus the high priest, and the other descendants of the deportation, was completed in the spring. The third was carried out by Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers in winter; at that time it was also specifically decreed that this same dedication should be celebrated every year with solemn rites. This decree was observed until the time of the Savior, as may be understood from the reading of the holy Gospel.

That observance, begun by them, is now recognized as being rightly and reverently maintained in the Church, when, year after year in continual succession, the anniversary of the church’s dedication is devoutly honored by the faithful with divine praises. It is celebrated with all the greater eagerness and devotion because it is beyond doubt that it is especially pleasing to the Redeemer—so much so that on this day he deigned to enter the temple itself and to disclose to the people the mysteries of his divinity.

Indeed, through the harshness of winter the hardness of unbelief is signified, which at that time existed in the minds of certain Jews. To them applied what the Lord says elsewhere: “Because wickedness will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.”

“And Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico.” He calls it Solomon’s portico because that once most powerful king used to stand there to worship, and therefore it began to be called by his name. The porticoes surrounding that temple are often called by the name of the temple itself.

If, then, the Son of God at that time wished to walk bodily in the temple where the blood of brute animals was poured out, how much more will he now deign and rejoice to visit and inhabit the house of his Church, where the sacraments of his body and blood are consecrated. And if he did not disdain to walk through the portico where that king—although most powerful and wisest, nevertheless mortal and earthly—used to stand, how much more will he deign to illuminate the inner chambers of our hearts with the presence of his majesty, provided that he sees our minds as Solomon’s portico—that is, filled with his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom.

We must not think that only this building in which we gather for worship is the temple of God. We ourselves, who gather here, ought both to be called and to be the temple of God, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of the living God” (II Cor. VI).

“Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him: ‘How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.’”

It is clear why the Evangelist first mentioned that it was winter. The Jews surrounded him not out of a desire to recognize the truth, but to provoke a temptation and construct an accusation, so that they might find some way of charging him.

“How long,” they say, “will you keep our souls in suspense?” They complained that he was taking away their souls by leaving them uncertain and perplexed, although he had come for the purpose of saving the souls of those who believed in him.

“If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” The Jews believed that Christ would be merely a human being and would come as a king superior to all others; their descendants continue to do so to the present day. For this reason they have suffered extermination and been laid waste, so that scarcely any of them has dared publicly to confess that he will be a Hebrew. They continue in their utter madness to await the time when they will accept the Antichrist as Christ.

They therefore wanted the Lord to say that he was the Christ, so that they could hand him over to the governor for punishment as though he were resisting Augustus and usurping imperial power. For this reason the Lord framed his reply so wisely and moderately that he closed the Jews’ avenue to accusation, while daring to proclaim openly to future believers that he himself is the Christ.

“For he answered them: ‘I speak to you, and you do not believe.’”

Here he most plainly shows that he is the Christ. By saying, “I speak to you,” he shows that he is the Word—that is, the Son of God—coeternal and consubstantial with the Father. It is as though he were saying: “By the testimony of my works I continually declare that I am the Son of God; but you, blinded by your unbelief, neither believe me when I speak nor are willing to attend to the works that I perform. If you considered them properly, you would undoubtedly believe that I am the Son of God.”

“The works that I do,” he says, “in the name of my Father, these themselves bear witness about me.” And observe that he ascribes all the glory of his works to God the Father when he asserts that he performs them in the Father’s name.

The works he performed—giving sight to the blind, restoring paralytics to health, feeding many thousands of people with a few loaves, and even bringing the dead, including those four days in the tomb and already foul-smelling, back to life—these works, I say, bore witness that he was the true Son of God, whose glory he sought in all his works.

“But you do not believe.” Giving the reason why they did not believe, he adds: “Because you are not of my sheep.”

He calls his sheep those who are faithful and obedient to him, who love and follow him as their shepherd and, by following the footsteps of the good shepherd, reach the pastures of eternal satisfaction. Thus he said that those who were unwilling to believe in him were not of his sheep, because he saw that they were already prepared for eternal destruction and would not be purchased for everlasting life by the price of his blood.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” According to the customary usage of Holy Scripture, “to know” is used for “to choose.” Hence it is written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II). “Not to know” means “to reject.” For God is ignorant of that which he does not approve as worthy of eternal life. Hence at the judgment he will say to the wicked: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV).

Christ’s sheep therefore hear his voice because they obey his commands from the heart. He himself knows them because, as the Apostle says of himself and those like him: “He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight.”

They follow him both here, by walking in the paths of his gentleness and innocence, and afterward, by entering happily with him into the joys of eternal life. Hence it follows: “And I give them eternal life.”

These are the pastures that he promised to give his sheep: pastures that never wither through any drought, but remain eternally green with unfailing loveliness.

“And they will not perish forever,” he says, because their shepherd and Savior is such that nothing belonging to them can perish at all in his presence. The holy martyrs appeared to perish in the eyes of the foolish when they lost this mortal life through torments; but they did not perish forever, because, released from the bonds of the flesh, they received from Christ the rewards owed to them.

Therefore he adds: “And no one will snatch them from my hand”—that is, from my power. Those whom Christ has once taken to himself through predestination cannot be taken from his power by any force of diabolical temptation or by the cruelty of human persecution.

If there are some who, after receiving glory, perish from the number of Christ’s sheep, they certainly are not sheep in the eyes of God. Persecutors tried to snatch Christ’s devout confessors from his hand when, by various tortures, they compelled them to deny the faith of Christ, so as to estrange their souls from Christ. Or, overcome by the steadfastness of those who died, they handed their bodies over to be burned by fire or submerged to be dissolved by water, as though they could thereby take away from Christ the power to resurrect them.

But no one can snatch them from the hand of him who helps the saints to conquer amid their struggles and crowns the victorious in heaven. By these words he also rebuked the audacity of those who had set the snares of death for themselves. In their utter folly they were plotting his death, although they could accomplish nothing against him and could not remove even one of his own.

Yet, lest by saying this he appear to be seeking his own glory, he refers all this power to the Father, adding: “What my Father gave me is greater than all.”

What God the Father gave to the mediator between God and human beings is greater than all. He gave him to be his only-begotten Son, neither unlike in nature, nor inferior in power, nor later in time. He gave this by begetting, because God begot God. This is what is greater than all.

Therefore John himself, when speaking of the Word of God, passed beyond every angelic and human creature and reached that which is greater than all, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.”

What the Son of God possessed before the ages through divinity, he received in time through humanity. “And no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

Above he said: “No one will snatch them from my hand.” Here he says: “No one can snatch them from the hand of my Father,” so that we might clearly understand that his power is also the Father’s, and that we must believe him to be the Christ who, unlike the other saints, did not receive it in time through grace, but has always truly existed as the Son of God.

He also demonstrates this in the sentence that follows, when he says: “I and the Father are one.”

“We are one,” he says: one substance, one divinity, perfect equality. By these words he not only answered the question of the Jews, who were testing him by asking whether he was the Christ, but also showed how detestable was the madness of the heretics whose future coming he foresaw.

Sabellius teaches that the Father and the Son are one person. Christ refutes him when he says, “I and the Father,” where two persons are most clearly indicated.

But the Jews, who had patiently endured the Lord’s speech up to that point, were unable to bear the force of his words when he said, “I and the Father are one.” Because they carried hearts of stone, they ran for stones. For it follows: “The Jews took up stones to stone him.”

But because he did not then wish to suffer, nor had he determined to be stoned by them, he restrained by his command the arms that were already raised and about to strike, and continued to address them.

“Jesus answered them: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father.’”

He refers to the healings of the sick and to his constant presentation of teaching and miracles. He says that he displayed all these works from the Father, thereby showing that in everything he sought the Father’s glory.

“For which of these works,” he says, “are you stoning me?”

They answered him: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy.”

Although unwillingly and reluctantly, they confess this and cannot deny that Christ had bestowed many good benefits upon them. Yet miserable men that they were, they considered blasphemy what he had said about the equality of himself and the Father.

Consider what they say: “Although you are a man, you make yourself God.”

Behold: the unbelieving Jews understood what the Arians still neglect to understand. They understood that the Lord’s statement, “I and the Father are one,” could not mean “one” unless there were equality. They therefore regarded it as blasphemy because they believed him to be merely human and absolutely refused to believe that he was God.

Jesus answered them: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” (Ps. LXXXI).

He said, “In your law,” meaning the law given to you. It should also be noted that he calls this testimony of the psalmist something written in the law, because all Scripture is sometimes called “the law” in a general sense. At other times “the Law” is understood distinctly in itself and is distinguished from the Prophets, as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. XI).

Holy Scripture is often divided into three parts, as in the statement: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand all the things written about him in the Law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke XXIV).

“If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken,” that is, it cannot be charged with falsehood, and therefore you do not dare reject it—“do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

It is as though he were saying: “If human beings were called gods because the word of God came to them, how is the Word of God himself—the Word who was in the beginning with God—not God? If those who became participants in the word of God deserved to be called gods, why should the Word of God himself, from whom they receive their participation, not be God?”

It should be noted that he says: “Whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.” The Father sanctified the Son—not because he had ever been unholy, but because he begot him holy. For just as God begot God, the immeasurable begot the immeasurable; so the holy Father begot the holy Son. And he sent him into the world because he ordained that he should become incarnate for the salvation of humankind.

“If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

It is as though he were saying: “If I merely claim in bare words that I am the Son of God and do not also prove this by the display of my works—when by powerful majesty I restore those whom nature brought forth imperfect, vice corrupted, or infirmity afflicted—then do not believe me. But if I do what no one except the Son of God could do, then, if you do not believe me, at least believe these works.”

“So that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” He had already said, “Believe the works”; now he again says, “so that you may know and believe.” The sense is as though he were saying: “Believe, so that you may know and believe.” The meaning is this: “If you do not believe me, believe the works, so that, by believing, you may know that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

He therefore wishes to establish that what he said was true—“I and the Father are one”—and that they were wrong to wish to stone him, since he had not blasphemed as they supposed. For this reason, by reason and divine action, without fleeing or hiding himself, he restrained those who were stoning him.

We must therefore believe so that we may be able to know, because knowledge is the reward of faith. By believing, we shall enter into the powers of the Lord and shall know how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

It must be understood, however, that the Father is not in the Son, nor the Son in the Father, in the same way that God is said to be in some holy man and any holy person in God. The Son is in the Father through the equality of one and the same substance, whereas a human being is in God through participation in grace.

A holy man may indeed say that God is in him, but he cannot say, “I and God are one,” nor again, “Whoever sees me sees God.” This belongs only to the only-begotten Son, who is in the Father in such a way that he is equal to the Father and is one with the Father, with whom belongs all honor and glory, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CIX. FOR THE THURSDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

At that time a certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him. And he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table, etc. (Luke VII).

*(Look for the homily on Saint Mary Magdalene.)*

## HOMILY CX. FOR THE FRIDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

At that time the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus and said: “What are we to do, because this man performs many signs?” etc. (John XI).

After Lazarus had been raised by Christ the Savior, through so great a miracle many of the Jews who had been present and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them—whether those who had already believed in him or those who had come to Martha and Mary for the purpose of offering consolation—went to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus had done, either out of pious zeal, so that they too might believe in him, or in order to denounce him, so that they might rage against him.

At once, darkened by their wickedness and not knowing where to turn—for they saw that they were being defeated by the evidence of his signs—they gathered a council, not so that they might be converted and believe, but so that by a wicked conspiracy they might condemn him to death. They took counsel to destroy him, not to protect themselves.

“What are we to do?” they asked. Miserable men, they did not say, “Let us believe,” but, as though sharpening their hostility and encouraging one another toward his death, they said: “What are we to do, because this man performs many signs?”

Whether they wished it or not, they confessed that the one whom they despised as though he were merely human shone forth like God through signs and miracles.

“If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.”

They feared losing an earthly kingdom, but neglected to think about eternal life; therefore, by God’s most just judgment, they lost both. For forty-two years after his passion and glorious ascension, the Romans came under the rulers Titus and Vespasian and took away from them their place, kingdom, and nation, destroying them by sword, famine, and captivity. Those who had killed Christ at Passover were themselves taken captive by their enemies during that same festival.

Those who had offended the Father through the wrong they did to the Son were themselves destroyed by the Father and the Son—namely, Vespasian and Titus—and so, guilty and miserable, they passed into eternal punishments, in accordance with what the Lord had said elsewhere about them: “The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII).

“The Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.” The Jews thought that Christ’s teaching was opposed to the temple and to the traditions of their ancestors. They therefore feared that, if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to resist the Romans by fighting for the city and the temple.

But one of them, named Caiaphas, since he was high priest that year, said to them: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.”

The Evangelist goes on to show that he did not say this on his own, but prophesied because he was high priest that year, through the operation of the priestly office that he unworthily held:

“He did not say this on his own, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation.”

From this passage we learn that even wicked people often foretell future events through the spirit of prophecy. Hence at the judgment they will say to the Lord: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” (Matt. VII).

One may ask how Caiaphas is called high priest “that year,” when the Lord had commanded by the Law that there should be only one high priest, and that, upon his death, his son should succeed him and administer the priesthood in his father’s place.

It should first be understood that this arrangement was observed from Aaron until the time of King David. David, wishing to increase the temple’s services, decreed—with the Lord nevertheless directing the matter—that there should be several high priests who would succeed one another in order, each serving in turn for a year.

Hence the Evangelist Luke reports concerning Zechariah: “When he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke I).

It may also be understood that, in more recent times, this arrangement was established among the Jews through ambition for offices and disputes over rank, so that there were several high priests who served in the Lord’s temple by turns, with others succeeding them after a year. Josephus also reports concerning Caiaphas that he had purchased the priesthood for one year from Herod.

But let us examine what he prophesied.

“You do not know anything, nor do you consider that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.”

The Evangelist says that he did not say this on his own, but, since he was high priest that year, prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation—and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.

Caiaphas therefore prophesied that it was expedient for Christ to die for the Jewish nation alone. But the Evangelist knew that he would suffer for the salvation of the entire human race, so that he might gather into one those who had been predestined before the ages to be children of God and form one fold from believing Jews and Gentiles, as the Lord says elsewhere:

“I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd” (John X).

For at that time they were not yet children of God or sheep. By suffering for them and redeeming them with his precious blood, he made them children of God instead of children of the devil, and established them as innocent sheep instead of guilty wolves.

“From that day they determined to kill him.” This does not mean that they had not previously planned this, since earlier they are said to have conspired against his death and wished to seize him. Rather, it means that at that time they bound themselves irrevocably to the crime of carrying out his death and resolved to hasten their wicked plans as quickly as possible.

Therefore Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away to the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephrem, and remained there with his disciples.

Certainly he, who is Lord of hosts, could not be afraid, nor had the power of his divinity abandoned him. If he had wished, he could have continued to move openly among the Jews and suffered no harm from them. But by withdrawing and avoiding the fury of his enemies, he deigned to give us an example: if a time of persecution should arise, we should not hesitate to seek places of refuge and avoid the rage of wicked people by remaining hidden.

The fact that the Lord left the Jews and went to the region near the wilderness signifies that, because of their faithlessness and unbelief, he was about to leave those who had once been God’s people and nation of possession and pass, through apostolic preaching, to the Gentiles who had formerly been desolate and abandoned by God.

The name of the city where he stayed with his disciples also corresponds most appropriately to this meaning. For *Ephrem* is interpreted as “fruitfulness,” clearly prefiguring the holy Church from the Gentiles. Once barren and unproductive, after receiving the word of faith in Christ it strove to abound in the spiritual fruits of good works.

That land, once scorched and desolate and knowing how to produce nothing green, now offers throughout the whole world both the grace and the use of fruit-bearing trees and of various fruits. It is no longer called a wilderness, but has deserved to be called, by the better name, the garden of delights and paradise of God.

Our Redeemer therefore, knowing that the time of his passion was at hand, wished to remain for a short time apart from the Jews, waiting for the coming Passover, which was soon to arrive, when he would hand himself over to their hands to be seized and crucified, just as he had ordained before the ages.

He also admonishes us to await that solemnity with the greatest vigilance through the sacred observance of the forty days. Therefore we must earnestly implore in our prayers the mercy of him who redeemed us at the great price of his blood, so that, together with the forgiveness of sins and with his grace and mercy, he may bring us to himself as those pleasing to him—he who lives and reigns, etc.

## HOMILY CXXIV. ON HOLY EASTER DAY
There are, in fact, two lives for a human being who exists in the body: one before death and the other after resurrection. Everyone knew one of these by experience, but knew nothing of the other, and the human race directed its attention only to the life it knew. The Lord came in the flesh, and while assuming one life, revealed the other: while assuming the life known to us, he showed us the one unknown to us. By dying he lived out the life we possess; by rising again he disclosed the life we are to seek. By his example [Col. 1326D] he taught us that this life, which we lead before death, is not to be loved for its own sake, but endured for the sake of the other.

None of us would recognize what was to follow after death unless the Creator of our life had come even to the punishment of our death. For unless he had mercifully sought the lowest places, he would not justly have recalled us, lost as we were after his own image, to the heights. Hence it is rightly said to blessed Job: “Have you entered into the depths of the sea, and have you walked about in the furthest parts of the abyss?” (Job 38). It is as though he said: “I, who not only sought the sea—that is, the world—by assuming human flesh and a human soul, but also, through that flesh voluntarily placed in death, descended to the lowest region of hell, as into the depths of the sea.”

For if “sea” is to be understood—as is customary in divine speech—as “the world,” [Col. 1327A] nothing prevents “the depths of the sea” from being understood as the prisons of hell. The Lord entered these depths of the sea when he entered the lowest places of hell in order to free the souls of his chosen ones. Hence the prophet also says: “You made a way through the depths of the sea, so that the redeemed might pass over” (Isa. 51). Before the Redeemer’s coming, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it confined within itself even the souls of the good, although not in places of punishment. Yet the Lord made this depth a way, because on coming there he granted his chosen ones to pass over from the prisons of hell to the heavenly places on this day. Hence it is aptly said there: “so that the redeemed might pass over.”

What he had called “the depths of the sea,” repeating in other words, he calls “the furthest part of the abyss,” because just as the abyss of waters cannot be grasped by any sight of ours, so the hidden places of hell cannot be penetrated by any power of our thought. [Col. 1327B] We see that those who depart from here are taken away, but we do not see what recompense of punishments awaits them according to their merits. It must be carefully considered that he declares himself to have walked about in the furthest parts of the abyss. To walk about is the action of one who is not restrained but free. For when someone is bound by chains, his steps are likewise impeded.

Because, therefore, the Lord endured no bonds of sin, he walked about in hell. He came as a free man to those who were bound; hence it is written: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87). Thus for the Lord to walk about in the furthest parts of the abyss means that he found there nothing that could hold him, as Peter testifies when he says: “Having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held [Col. 1327C] by it” (Acts 2).

Or certainly, because when we walk we are led from place to place and are found present here and there, the Lord is said to have walked in hell so that it might be shown that he was present by the power of his divinity in each place among the elect souls. Hence the spirit of wisdom is also described as mobile, so that by this it may be signified that, being absent from no place, it encounters us everywhere.

The more wonderfully the Lord regards this descent of his, the more frequently he pours it into the redeemed human being. Repeating it again, he adds: “Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?” (Job 38). The gates of death are the hostile powers, which the Lord opened when he descended, because by dying he overcame their strength. They are also called “dark doors,” [Col. 1327D] because, being unseen on account of the ambushes by which they conceal themselves, they open the way of death to deceived minds.

The Lord saw these dark doors because he both beholds and restrains the fraudulent malice of the unclean spirits. Unless he himself, by seeing them, prevented them without our knowledge, our mind would understand nothing of their ambushes and, captured by those same ambushes, would perish. We too see these dark doors when we are enlightened by the rays of heavenly light. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall see my enemies” (Ps. 117). He himself sees our enemies, therefore, when by his gift he makes them visible to us.

Or certainly, the Lord saw these dark doors when, penetrating the prisons of hell, he struck down the cruel spirits [Col. 1328A] and, by dying, condemned the rulers of death. This is spoken here not only of the future but also of the past, because what he was going to accomplish in action he had already accomplished in predestination.

Since, after his death and resurrection, the Church grew and was extended among all nations, it is aptly added: “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?” (Job 38). For when he entered the narrow confines of death, he spread his faith among the nations and extended the holy Church to countless hearts of believers. To it the prophet says: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations” (Isa. 54).

This breadth of the earth surely [Col. 1328B] would not have come about unless he had first shown, by rising again, the life that we know. In his death he opened the eyes of our mind, to show what life is and what life would follow. Therefore, maintaining this sequence in the Gospel, he says to his disciples: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24).

For while he was preaching, few from the people of Israel believed; but countless peoples of the nations followed the way of life when he died. While he was still living in a passible condition, he endured the proud; but on departing from his passible life he struck them down dead. Samson aptly prefigured this in himself long ago: while he lived, he killed only a few, but when the temple was destroyed, he killed countless enemies [Col. 1328C] as he died (Judg. 16).

For the Lord destroyed a few who were raised up by the pride of arrogance while he lived, but when the temple of his body was dissolved, he destroyed many more; and all at once, by dying, he prostrated the elect from the nations whom he had endured while living. Rightly, therefore, after teaching that he had entered the regions below, he immediately added that the breadth of the earth should be considered.

Our Lord, therefore, coming for the redemption of the human race, made from himself, as it were, a hook for the destruction of the devil. For he assumed a body so that this Behemoth might desire it as bait through the death of the flesh; and when he unjustly desired that death in him, he lost us, whom he had held as though justly. He was therefore caught on the hook of the Lord’s incarnation: while desiring the bait of the body in it, he was pierced by the barb of divinity. [Col. 1328D]

For there was humanity in him, which would draw the devourer toward itself; and there was divinity, which would pierce him. There was visible weakness, which would entice him; and hidden power, which would transfix the throat of the captor. He was caught on the hook because he perished by the very thing he devoured.

Indeed, this Behemoth knew that the Son of God had become incarnate, but he did not know the order of our redemption. He knew that the Son of God had become incarnate for our redemption, but he did not know at all that our Redeemer would pierce him by dying. Lest, then, this monster lying in wait for human deaths should devour whomever he wished without limit, the hook held the captor’s jaws in this way, and he bit himself while biting it.

It remains for each one of us to submit ourselves more fully to our Creator [Col. 1329A], the more truly we consider the violent powers of the adversary against us. For what are we except dust? And what is he except one among the heavenly spirits—and, what is greater still, the highest among them? What can dust dare to do by its own strength when it fights against the prince of angels? But because the Creator of the heavenly spirits assumed an earthly body, the humble dust rightly now conquers the proud angel.

It is fitting that the one who thought himself strong after abandoning the Creator should be conquered by dust, so that in his defeat he may discover that he failed because he was lifted up. But he rages and pants fiercely because the lowest places torment him, while a human being ascends to the heights; because in that loftiness the flesh remains subject, from which such a great spirit himself lies forever cast down.

Yet the order of merits has changed the positions of minds. Thus pride [Col. 1329B] deserved to be cast down, and thus humility to be exalted, so that the heavenly spirit, by raising itself up, might be brought down to Tartarus, while humble earth might reign without end above the heavens: through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.
