## HOMILY CXXVIII. ON EASTER TUESDAY

(From the works of Saint Cyprian.)

[Col. 1329D]

The most wise Solomon, the fountain of wisdom, the arbiter of justice, and the teacher of discipline, spoke thus in the *Song of Songs*: “Where do you pasture? Where do you abide?” “At midday” (Song 1). Who was asking? It is the voice of the Spirit asking the Lord Christ: “Where do you pasture? Where do you abide?” And he replied: “At midday.”

We marvel, dearest brothers, that the Holy Spirit asks this, since he has no need of instruction, for the whole world is known to him. He existed before time and had no beginning, just as the world will one day have an end; eternity does not possess an age, nor can what knows no origin ever have an end. [Col. 1330A] Yet the Holy Spirit compels the Lord Christ to speak of his Passion so that the people who did not know might hear: “Where do you pasture?”—that is, “Where do you suffer?”

And the Lord answers: “At midday,” when at the sixth hour the fiery sun hung in the middle of the heavens in its balance, and the divided measure of the sky, with its flaming axis, gathered the shadows beneath it under a flashing shield, while the shadow of the world and of hell hung together in the night.

Thus all Judaea was clothed in blindness when they cried out with furious violence: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23). Just as all creation did not see the sun at the sixth hour, so everything lying beneath the heavens learned the majesty of Christ—I speak of a small thing—for Christ, whose tabernacle he placed in the sun, gathered all nations and entered wholly [Col. 1330B] into our consciences amid the deep night of the ages.

The Lord Christ hung upon the cross at the sixth hour, and the sun hung there as a servant. When Christ’s side was pierced by the lance, from the sixth hour until the ninth the brightness of the sun was strangled. Heaven mourned its Creator; day lost its eye; and, deprived of the fastening of the heavens, day became like night, while the sudden arrival of night blinded its brightness.

Therefore, in the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, day became like night, because in his resurrection night was revealed as day, as it is written: “For darkness shall not be darkened by you, and night shall be illumined like day” (Ps. 138). Creation would sin if it did not mourn its Creator; and day would sin if it did not tear its garment.

Judaea would rightly have committed sacrilege if, through its own crime, it had not trembled at the sixth hour and the blindness of the sun had not borne witness. [Col. 1330C] Day went before the Lord into hell; eternal night learned what it had not known. Day was terrified by the night it did not know, as David says: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18).

Christ fittingly showed his tabernacle: the cross was the lodging of his body, and in it, by a single structure, the powers of hell were slaughtered. Christ’s body still hangs upon the structure of the cross, and already hell is being defeated. Let the majesty of this stranger terrify Tartarus. Death, deceived, flees from hell; excluded from its own dwelling, death runs toward heaven and sees the night it had not known.

The stars grow pale, the earth trembles, the elements are thrown into confusion, and the dead come forth from their tombs. For no tombs could retain any portion of the bodies when all Gehenna had likewise split open.

For this reason day returned to its proper state [Col. 1330D]: the author who made this day returned to the true day, as it is written: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 117). Therefore the elements recover their proper form, because if all things had perished with the ruin of the world, there would be no one today to fear. And so, in the faith of Christ, the whole world is one place.

Indeed, this name flew across the lands and sailed over the waves, because the spirit has no road, and faith never seeks a carrier. What will Judaea say against the Lord Christ, whom a flaming star revealed when he was born, and whom the blindness of the sun made known when he suffered?

Human pride has now lost its standing, because it heard that the Lord had been born and saw him suffer. After the resurrection the people were terrified when they saw him made new, restored after hell, and, after the nails [Col. 1331A] and death, once again borne to the Father by a vehicle of light as he flew up to the heavens. The people worshiped with faces raised upward; and lest he depart altogether, through the sacrament of his body he divided himself within our hearts.

While we carry him within our conscience through faith, through blood in martyrdom, through modesty in virginity, and while all the people [the printed text has *totiusque*, apparently corrupt] worshiped—not mourning but rejoicing—he showed us the way to heaven: the Lord Christ, who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXIX. ON EASTER WEDNESDAY

(From the works of blessed Pope Gregory.)

“At that time Jesus revealed himself again to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way,” etc. (John 21.)

[Col. 1331B] “The reading of the holy Gospel that has just been read in your hearing, my brothers,” etc. For the remainder, see Saint Gregory, volume II of his works, *Patrologia* LXXVI, column 1184.

## HOMILY CXXX. ON EASTER WEDNESDAY

(From Saint Maximinus.)

The fishing of our Liberator is our liberation. In the holy Gospel we observe two fishings of the Lord—that is, occasions when the nets were cast at his word. One was earlier, when he chose the disciples; the other was when he rose from the dead.

That first fishing signifies the Church as it is now; the latter, after the Lord’s resurrection, signifies the Church as it will be at the end of the age. [Col. 1331C] In that first fishing, finally, he commanded the nets to be cast but did not say toward which side; he merely commanded that they be cast. The disciples cast them. It was not said, “to the right”; it was not said, “to the left.”

The fish signified human beings. If it had been said “to the right,” only the good would have been intended; if it had been said “to the left,” only the wicked. But because both good and wicked were to be mixed together in the Church, the nets were cast without distinction, so that fish might be caught signifying the mixture of the good and the wicked.

It is also written there that they caught so many fish that the two boats were being submerged—that is, they were being pressed down by the submerging weight. Those two boats were not actually submerged, but were endangered by the multitude of fish. This signified [Col. 1331D] that, in the multitude which the Church was to gather, discipline would be endangered.

This too was added to that fishing and is narrated: the nets were torn because of the multitude of fish. What did the torn nets signify except future schisms? Three things, therefore, were signified in that fishing: the mixture of good and wicked, the pressure of the crowds, and the divisions of heretics.

The mixture of good and wicked was signified because the nets were cast neither to the right nor to the left. The pressure of the crowds was signified because so great a catch was made that the boats were pressed down. The divisions of heretics were signified because the multitude was so great that the nets were torn.

Now consider this fishing which has been read today. It took place after the Lord’s resurrection, to signify what the Church will be like after our resurrection. [Col. 1332A] “Cast the net on the right side,” he says. The number of those who will stand at the right has therefore been distinguished.

You remember that the Lord said he would come with his angels: “All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep at his right, but the goats at his left. To the sheep he will say, ‘Come, receive the kingdom’; to the goats he will say, ‘Depart into eternal fire’” (Matt. 25).

“Cast it on the right.” It was as though he said: “I have now risen; I wish to signify the Church that will exist in the resurrection of the dead. Cast it on the right.” The nets were cast on the right, and they could not lift them because of the multitude of fish. There was a multitude, but also a definite number—and what a multitude, and what greatness! There, however, there is no number. [Col. 1332B]

But now, before the resurrection comes and the good are separated from the wicked, what the prophet says is fulfilled: “I announced and spoke; I cast the nets, and what happened? They were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39). The number belongs to the saints who will reign with Christ. They may enter the Church now beyond the number, but they cannot enter the kingdom beyond the number.

Why do I urge you to rescue yourselves from the present evil age? Why do I urge you? So that those of you who wish to live may not imitate wicked Christians. Do not say: “Why is that man not faithful, yet gets drunk? Why is that man not faithful, yet keeps concubines? Why is that man not faithful, yet commits fraud every day? Why is that man not faithful, yet consults astrologers?”

Now, if you wish [Col. 1332C] to be grain, you will then be found in the mass. But if you wish to be straw, you will be found in a great heap—but one destined to be consumed by a great fire.

Who, then, brought the nets to the shore? Peter brought the nets to the shore. When the Gospel was being read just now, you heard it. Wherever you heard “shore,” understand the end of the sea; wherever you heard “the end of the sea,” understand the end of the age.

In that fishing the nets were not drawn to the shore, but the fish that had been caught were poured out in the boats. Here, however, they drew them to the shore. Await the end of the age: a good end will come for those on the right, and a bad one for those on the left.

And what of the fish? “They drew in,” it says, “the net containing one hundred and fifty-three fish.” The evangelist added an important detail: “Although they were so many—that is, so great—they did not tear the net.”

They will be great [Col. 1332D], but there will be no heresies; indeed, there will be no heresies precisely because they will be great. Who are the great? Read the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel and you will find the great.

For he says in one place: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Amen, I say to you, whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so, by speaking good things but living badly, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

But in which kingdom of heaven? In the Church as it is now, because it too is called the kingdom of heaven. For if this Church, which gathers the wicked and the good, were not called the kingdom of heaven, the Lord himself would not have said in the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13).

But see what follows: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net [Col. 1333A] cast into the sea.” The net is the dragnet; it gathers fish of every kind. But what then? It draws them to the shore. The Lord says this in the parable. “When they have drawn it to the shore, they sit down and collect the good into vessels, but they throw away the wicked.” And he explained what he had proposed. What does he say? “So will it be at the consummation of the age.” Do you understand the shore? “The angels will come,” he says, “and separate the wicked from among the just, and they will cast them into the furnace of burning fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Nevertheless, he calls the Church the kingdom of heaven. And because, while it is still in the sea, it has good and wicked fish swimming together, in this kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church of the present time—the one who teaches good things but does evil is called least, because he too is there.

He is not absent from it; he is there in the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1333B]—that is, in the Church as it exists in this age. He teaches good things and does evil. The hired servant is necessary. “Amen, I say to you,” he says, “they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). He is of some benefit.

For if they were of no benefit because they teach good things but live badly, the Lord himself would not have said to his people: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). Why? “For they preach, but they do not practice.”

Let your charity pay attention, for I wish to explain who the great fish are. “Whoever abolishes,” he says, “one of these least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” He will be there, but he will be least. [Col. 1333C]

“But whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). And behold, these are the great fish caught on the right: the one who does and thus teaches, who teaches good things and does not contradict himself by living badly, though his good tongue bears witness to his bad life.

Therefore, whoever does and teaches in this way will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. And it follows: “For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

How do you understand the kingdom of heaven now? The one of which it is said to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Consider those scribes and Pharisees who sit on Moses’ seat [Col. 1333D], concerning whom it was said: “Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do, for they preach and do not practice.” The righteousness of the Pharisees, therefore, is to speak and not to act. Let your righteousness exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that you may speak good things and live well.

Why should I now repeat the same matter concerning the number of one hundred and fifty-three fish? You know it. This number arises by addition from seventeen. Begin with one and reach seventeen, adding all the numbers: add one to two and they make three; add three and they make six; add four and they make ten. Thus add all the numbers up to seventeen, and you reach one hundred and fifty-three.

Our entire attention, therefore, should be directed to what the seventeen signify [Col. 1334A], for in them lies the foundation of the one hundred and fifty-three. What does ten signify? Recognize the law in the number ten. Ten commandments were given. First, the Decalogue is so called because it was written on tablets by the finger of God.

In ten, recognize the law; in seven, recognize the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is commended by the number seven. Hence sanctification is not mentioned in the law except on the seventh day.

God made light, but it is not said that he sanctified it. He made the firmament, but it is not said that he sanctified the firmament. He commanded the earth to bring forth plants. He separated the sea from the land, but it is not said that he sanctified them. He made the moon and the stars, but it is not said that he sanctified them. He commanded living creatures to come forth from the waters, swimming and flying, but it is not said that he sanctified them. He commanded four-footed animals [Col. 1334B] and all reptiles to come forth from the earth, but it is not said that he sanctified them. He also made the human being himself, but it is not said that he sanctified him.

He came to the seventh day, on which he rested, and he sanctified it. By his rest God sanctified our rest. Our sanctification, therefore, will be complete there, where we rest with him without end.

For why would God rest? He was not wearied by working. If you accomplish something by a word, are you not wearied? If you command and it immediately happens, you stand and remain whole. He spoke a few words, by which he made everything, and suddenly he became tired?

Recognize the law in ten; recognize the Holy Spirit in seven. Let the spirit be joined to the law, because if you receive the law but lack the help of the spirit, you do not fulfill what you read. You do not fulfill what is commanded you, but the human being is held under the law as a transgressor. [Col. 1334C]

Let the spirit come near and help, and what is commanded is done. If the spirit is absent, the letter kills you. Why does the letter kill you? Because it makes you a transgressor, and you cannot be excused on the ground of ignorance: once you have received the law, you have learned what you should do. Ignorance does not excuse you, and the spirit does not help you; therefore you have perished.

But what does the apostle Paul say? “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). The spirit gives life because it causes the letter to be fulfilled, so that it does not kill. These are the saints who fulfill the law by God’s gift. The law can command; it cannot help. The spirit, the helper, comes near, and God’s command is fulfilled with joy and delight.

For many act out of fear; but those who fulfill the law because they fear punishment would prefer that the thing they feared did not exist. Those who act out of love for righteousness, however, rejoice in it [Col. 1334D] because they do not have it as an enemy.

Therefore the Lord says: “Be reconciled with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5). Who is your adversary? The word of the law. What is the way? This present life.

How is he your adversary? He says to you, “You shall not commit adultery,” and you wish to commit adultery? He says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” and you wish to seize what belongs to another? He says, “Honor your father and mother,” and you are insulting toward your parents? The law says, “You shall not bear false witness,” and you do not withdraw from lying?

When you see that the word commands one thing while you do another, is it not your adversary? You have an evil adversary. Do not let him enter your inner chamber with you; settle the matter while you are with him on the way.

The Lord is present to reconcile us. How does God reconcile us? [Col. 1335A] By forgiving sins and inspiring righteousness, so that good works may be done.

When, therefore, you have been reconciled with your adversary—that is, with the Decalogue of the law through the Holy Spirit—you will belong to the seventeen. When you have come to belong to the seventeen, the number grows from there to one hundred and fifty-three. You will be crowned at the right, so that you do not remain condemned at the left.

With the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXXV. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT THOMAS

“Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came” (John 20).

This one disciple was absent: when he returned, he heard what had happened; having heard, he refused to believe. The Lord came again and offered his side to the unbelieving disciple to touch, showed him his hands, and, displaying the scar of his wounds, healed the wound of his unbelief. What, dearest brothers, what do you perceive in all this? [Col. 1336A] Do you think it happened by chance that this chosen disciple was then absent, but afterward came and heard, hearing doubted, doubting touched, and touching believed? It did not happen by chance, but by divine providence. For heavenly mercy acted in a wondrous way: while the doubting disciple touched the wounds of the flesh in his Master, he healed in us the wounds of unbelief. Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more for faith than the faith of the believing disciples did, because while he was brought back to faith by touching, our mind, setting aside all doubt, is strengthened in faith.

Thus he permitted the disciple to doubt after his resurrection, yet did not abandon him in his doubt, just as before his birth he wished Mary to have a betrothed husband, although that husband did not attain the consummation of her marriage. For in this way [Col. 1336B] the doubting and touching disciple became a witness to the true resurrection, just as the bridegroom of Christ’s mother had been the unimpeachable guardian of her virginity.

He touched and exclaimed: “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” Since the apostle Paul says, “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI), it is plainly clear that faith is the proof of those things that cannot be seen. For things that appear are no longer held by faith, but by knowledge. Since, then, Thomas saw and touched, why is it said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? But he saw one thing and believed another. For divinity could not be seen by mortal man. He therefore saw a human being and confessed him to be God, saying, “My Lord and my [Col. 1336C] God.” Thus he believed by seeing: when he considered the true man, he exclaimed that this was the God whom he could not see.

What follows brings great joy: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” In this saying we are especially signified, we who retain in our minds the one whom we have not seen in the flesh. We are signified—but only if we follow our faith by works [by acting]. For that person truly believes who puts into practice what he believes. In contrast, concerning those who retain faith in name only, Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I). Hence James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. I).

Hence the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the ancient enemy of the human race: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he has confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” [Col. 1336D] (Job XL). For who is signified by the river except the flow of the human race? This race flows from its beginning to its end and, like water, runs onward from the fluidity of the flesh until its appointed limit. What is signified by the Jordan except the form of the baptized? Since the author of our redemption deigned to be baptized in the river Jordan, the name “Jordan” rightly expresses the multitude of those contained within the sacrament of baptism.

Thus the ancient enemy of the human race swallowed the river: from the origin of the world until the coming of the Redeemer, he drew the human race into the belly of his malice, with scarcely a few of the elect escaping. Hence it is rightly said: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished,” because he does not consider it a great thing [Col. 1337A] when he carries off unbelievers. But what follows is exceedingly grave: “And he has confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth,” because, after carrying off all the unbelievers from the origin of the world, he still presumes that he can deceive even the faithful. For each day he devours with the mouth of his deadly persuasion those in whom an evil life is at odds with their confession of faith.

Therefore, dearest brothers, fear this with your whole attention; consider it among yourselves with vigilant minds. Behold, we are celebrating the paschal solemnities. But we must see to it that we may deserve to reach the eternal feasts. All things that are celebrated as festive in time pass away. You who attend these solemnities, take care not to be separated from the eternal solemnity. What good does it do to attend the feasts of human beings if it happens that one is absent from the feasts of angels? The present solemnity [Col. 1337B] is the shadow of the solemnity to come. For this reason we celebrate it annually, so that we may be brought to that solemnity which is not annual but perpetual. When this celebration takes place at its appointed time, our memory is renewed in desire for that one. Therefore, through the repeated experience of temporal joy, let the mind grow warm and burn for eternal joys, so that it may enjoy the truth of joy in its homeland, having meditated upon the shadow of joy along the way.

Order your lives and your conduct, brothers. Consider how sternly the one who rose gentle from death will come in judgment. Certainly, on the day of his dreadful examination, he will appear with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, with principalities and powers, while heaven and earth burn and all the elements are shaken in terror to serve him. [Col. 1337C] Set this judge of such great dread before your eyes; fear him who is to come, so that when he comes you may see him not in fear but in confidence. He must be feared so that he may not be feared. Let his terror train us for the practice of good works; let fear of him restrain our lives from wickedness.

Believe me, brothers: we shall then be as secure concerning his sentence as we now strive to be watchful concerning our guilt. Certainly, if one of you were to be brought before my judgment tomorrow to plead a case against his adversary, he would perhaps spend the whole night sleepless, anxiously and feverishly turning over in his mind what might be said to him and how he might answer the objections. He would be extremely afraid that he might find me harsh; he would dread appearing guilty before me. And who am I, or what am I? [Col. 1337D] Surely, not long afterward I shall be a worm after man, and dust after the worm. If, then, the judgment of dust is feared with such concern, with what attention must the judgment of so great a Majesty be considered, with what fear must provision be made for it?

But since there are some who are uncertain about the resurrection of the flesh—and we teach this more effectively when we also address the hidden questions of your hearts—we must say a few things about faith in the resurrection. Many people, as we ourselves once were, when they see flesh reduced to corruption and bones to dust in the tombs, despair that flesh and bones can be restored from dust. Thus they reason among themselves and say: “When is a human being brought back from dust? When does it happen that ashes are given life?” We answer them briefly: it is much less for God to restore what existed than to create what did not exist. Or what is surprising if he restores a human being from dust, when he created all things together from nothing? For it is more wondrous to establish heaven and earth from things that did not exist than to restore the human being himself from earth.

[Col. 1338A] But attention is fixed on the ash, and its ability to return to flesh is despaired of; the power of divine action is sought as though it could be grasped by reasoning. Those who say such things in their thoughts do so because, through constant repetition, God’s daily miracles have become cheap in their eyes. For behold, within a single grain of the tiniest seed lies the entire mass of the tree that is going to be born. Let us place before our eyes the marvelous size of any tree and consider where that tree began its growth, which by growing reached such a great mass. Without doubt, we shall find its origin in a very small seed. [Col. 1338B]

Now let us consider where, in that little grain of seed, there lies the strength of the wood, the roughness of the bark, the abundance of taste and fragrance, the richness of fruits, and the greenness of leaves. The seed-grain, when handled, is not hard; from where, then, did the hardness of the wood arise? It is not rough; from where did the roughness of the bark burst forth? It is not flavorful [it does not possess flavor]; from where came the taste in the fruits? Smelled, it gives off no scent; from where does fragrance waft from the fruits? It shows no green in itself; from where did the greenness of the leaves emerge?

Thus everything lies hidden together in the seed, although everything does not emerge from the seed at the same time. From the seed the root is produced; from the root the shoot emerges; from the shoot the fruit arises; and in the fruit seed is produced as well. Let us add that seed, too, lies hidden in the seed. What, then, is surprising if he restores bones, sinews, flesh, and hair from dust, when each day he restores wood, fruit, and leaves in the great mass of a tree from a small seed?

When a doubting mind therefore seeks a rational account of the power of the resurrection, questions should be presented to it concerning those things that continually take place and yet can in no way be grasped by reason. Thus, while it is unable, through the sight of what it sees, to penetrate its nature, it may believe from the promise of divine power what it hears.

Therefore, dearest brothers, consider with me the things that endure, while those things that pass away with time should be despised as already abandoned. Hasten with your whole attention toward the glory of this resurrection, which the Truth displayed in himself. Flee earthly desires that separate you from the Creator, because [Col. 1338D] the more uniquely you love the Mediator between God and human beings, who lives and reigns, etc., the more highly you attain the sight of almighty God.
