## HOMILY CLIII. ON THE THURSDAY OF PENTECOST

*(From blessed Jerome’s exposition of the Gospel of Matthew, in various passages.)*

[Col. 1341C]

At that time Jesus, having summoned the twelve apostles, gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure illnesses, etc. (Luke IX.)

In the preceding passages of this holy Gospel, blessed Luke relates that in those days Jesus went out onto a mountain to pray, and spent the night in prayer to God (Luke 6). “And when day had come,” he says, “he called his disciples and chose twelve from among them.” Thus, O man, an example is set before you for imitation. What ought you to do for your salvation, when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What ought you to do when you wish to undertake some work of charity, when Christ first made a point of praying before sending out the apostles? [Col. 1341D]

Not everyone who prays ascends a mountain. For there is a kind of prayer that produces sin. But whoever prays well, whoever seeks God through prayer, progressing from earthly things to higher ones, climbs to the summit of the more exalted court. But whoever pleads while concerned with riches, worldly honor, or even the death of an enemy, lies prostrate in the lowest places and sends base prayers to God.

The Lord prays, not that he may plead for himself, but that he may obtain something for me. For although the Father has placed all things in the Son’s power, the Son nevertheless, in order to fulfill the role of a human being, considers that he ought to plead with the Father on our behalf, because he is our advocate. “We have an advocate with the Father,” he says, “Jesus Christ” (1 John 2). If he is an advocate, he ought to intervene for my sins. [Col. 1342A]

He pleads, therefore, not as one who is weak, but as one who is merciful. Do you wish to know that he could do everything he desired? He is both advocate and judge. In the one role his duty of mercy is displayed; in the other, the mark of his power. Do you also wish to know that he prayed for me, not for himself? “And when day had come,” he says, “he called his disciples and chose twelve from among them” (Luke 6).

Here it should be noted that evangelical and apostolic Scripture calls not only those twelve disciples of Christ, but also all who believe in him and are instructed for the kingdom of heaven through his ministry. They are called disciples from learning (*discere*); from their multitude he chose those whom he himself wished to choose, and he called them apostles. “Apostles” is Greek; in Latin they are called *missi*, “those who have been sent.” Explaining the sacramental significance of this name, the evangelist Mark says: “And he made twelve to be with him, and to send them out to preach the Gospel” (Mark 3). The Lord himself also says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20).

The twelve were rightly chosen so that the salvation of the world, which they would preach in word, might also be mystically commended by their number. For three groups of four make twelve [the printed text has *Ter enim quaterni decas dispondius*, an uncertain and apparently corrupt reading]. This is the significance of the passage in which, as a type of the Church, Solomon built a temple for the Lord and also made a bronze sea in which the priests might wash (2 Chronicles 4). He placed it upon twelve oxen, three facing north, three west, three south, and three east. In figure this indicated that the apostles and their successors would cleanse all the regions of the square-shaped world from the stain of sin through faith and confession of the Holy Trinity.

They are also rightly chosen on a mountain. The mountain on which the Lord chose the apostles signifies the height of righteousness in which they were to be formed and which they were to preach to human beings. Since he was about to send them to preach the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, he rightly wished to admonish them, by the elevation of the place where they were chosen, not to dissolve their minds in low desires, but always to raise them toward the desire for and pursuit of higher things.

Likewise, when he was about to give the law to his earlier people, he appeared on a mountain and made known from the mountain what they ought to do. But because the time had not yet come for it to be said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matthew 3), it was only said: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (Exodus 20). Although these same words figuratively promise us the eternal kingdom that exists in the land of the living, the people were by no means able to draw near to the Lord speaking on the mountain. They heard what was said from below, because they did not yet know how to ascend in a mind capable of understanding the mysteries being proclaimed. Moses alone, because he had learned to hear the law spiritually, climbed to the summit of the mountain on which the Lord was (Exodus 19).

It is rightly said that, ascending the mountain, the Lord called to himself those whom he himself wished. Their being called to the apostolate did not result from their own choice or zeal, but from divine condescension and grace. Hence elsewhere he says to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15).

Now, brothers, when the Gospel was read, we heard that, after calling together the twelve apostles, Jesus gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. The kind and merciful Lord and teacher does not begrudge servants and disciples the exercise of his powers. Just as he himself had cured every disease and every infirmity, so he also granted his apostles the authority to cure every disease and every infirmity.

But there is a great difference between possessing and granting, between giving and receiving. Whatever this one does, he does by the Lord’s power. Whatever they do, they confess both their own weakness and the Lord’s power, saying: “In the name of Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

It should be noted that, according to Matthew, the first authority to perform signs is granted to the apostles in the twelfth place (Matthew 10). Nor is it without mystery that the apostolic choir is completed by the number twelve, so that the salvation of the world, which they would preach in word, might also be commended by their number. For three groups of four make twelve. Three groups of four apostles were sent to preach, so that throughout all the regions of the square-shaped world they might baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore it is written concerning the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, that it had three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west (Revelation 21). This figuratively showed that, through the preaching of the apostles and their successors, all the nations throughout the world would enter the Church in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

The children of Israel once encamped around the tabernacle according to the same mystery, so that the camp was square on every side, with three tribes stationed on each side. Thus the primitive Church, which was in Judea, was to establish spiritual encampments for God in the faith and confession of the Holy Trinity, surrounded on every side by believers from among the nations of the whole world.

“He gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases.” After the Lord had shown that he preached against unclean spirits, he chose holy men who would both cast out unclean spirits and preach the Gospel themselves with a pure mind and tongue. He also granted them the ability to cure other illnesses and even to raise the dead, as the evangelist Matthew records (Matthew 10).

“And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.” Perhaps no one would have believed uneducated men promising the kingdoms of heaven. Therefore he first granted them the authority to perform signs, and then sent them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of their deeds might also bear witness to the greatness of their promises, and the power displayed might give credibility to their words. Those who preached new things would perform new deeds, and they would display visible miracles in the healing of diseases so that they might draw the hearts of their hearers toward faith in invisible things.

Thus even now, although the number of the faithful has increased, there are many within the holy Church who possess a life of virtue but do not possess signs of virtue, because a miracle is displayed outwardly to no purpose if there is nothing being accomplished inwardly. For according to the saying of the teacher of the nations, tongues are “for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14).

Yet the signs that were then performed bodily through the apostles are performed spiritually every day in the holy Church through holy preachers: when someone who is weak in faith is strengthened in faith by their preaching; when someone dead in sins, pierced by the grace and mercy of God, is raised through their instruction to repentance and confession of his sins, and through worthy amendment earns eternal life.

Someone led astray by the devil into fornication, or greed—which is the service of idols—or deceived by the error of certain capital crimes, all of which are judged to be leprosy of the soul, returns through the mouths of teachers, or even through examples of holiness that pierce the heart, to the bosom of Mother Church. They confess that they have continually sinned grievously, and, constantly showing their sorrow for their sins, redeem their offenses through almsgiving and other works of mercy, until, remaining in repentance, they receive amendment from the vices in which they had been entangled. Surely such people, cleansed as if from leprosy, merit eternal salvation?

“And he said to them: Take nothing for the journey, neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.”

Priests ought to have such great trust in God that they are in no way entangled in the concerns of earthly commerce or the desires of the world. Although they do not provide for the expenses of the present life, they should know with complete certainty that these will never be lacking to them if they labor faithfully in the work of God’s will and in the word of preaching, lest, while their minds are occupied with temporal matters, they provide less adequately for the eternal welfare of those subject to them. [Col. 1344C]

This demonstrates that priests ought to live a poor life, lest they appear to preach for the sake of profit. For the one who cut off riches has, so to speak, also cut off the necessities of life; and, by forbidding treasures, he also forbids gluttony when he prohibits carrying bread.

By the prohibition of a staff he admonishes us to seek help nowhere except from the Lord, so that, possessing the Lord’s help, we may not seek the support of a staff. Hence elsewhere he says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke 12).

When he forbids the bag, he shows that we must avoid worldly honors, human favor, and every kind of bodily pleasure. When he forbids bread, he urges us not to conduct ourselves in gluttony and drunkenness, and teaches us who preach abstinence to cut the vice of gluttony away from ourselves.

Mark, moreover, says that he commanded them to wear sandals (Mark 6), so that the foot would be neither covered nor bare—that is, so that the preaching would not be concealed by a desire for earthly advantage, nor would priests display corrupt examples to those subject to them.

By money, hidden wisdom is signified. Whoever possesses the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor carries it, as it were, as money locked away. Whoever accepts the office of teacher ought neither to be weighed down by the burdens of secular business, nor weakened by carnal desires, nor hide under the idleness of sluggish torpor the talent of the word entrusted to him. [Col. 1345A]

When he forbids two tunics, he warns us not to be double-minded, saying one thing with our mouths and carrying another in our hearts, but to be well-disposed and kind toward everyone.

In another Gospel it is written that the Lord forbade the apostles to possess gold or silver, or money in their belts, or a bag for the journey, and so forth (Matthew 10). This command is appropriately given to preachers of the truth, to whom he had previously said: “You received without payment; give without payment” (ibid.). For if they preach in such a way that they do not accept payment, possession of gold, silver, and coins is superfluous. If they had possessed gold and silver, they would appear to preach not for the salvation of human beings but for the sake of profit.

He also removed bronze from their purses so that the apostles, teachers of true religion who instructed that everything should be governed with foresight, might show that they themselves were to think nothing about tomorrow.

“Do not carry a bag on the journey.” By this command he also reproves the philosophers commonly called *bactroperitae*—“staff-carriers”—because, although they despise the world and regard everything as worthless, they carry a storehouse with them.

“Nor two tunics.” In the two tunics, it seems to me, he indicates a double garment—not that, in the regions of Scythia and places stiff with icy snow, a person ought to be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunic” we should understand clothing, so that, while dressed in one garment, we do not reserve another for ourselves out of fear of the future.

“Nor sandals.” Plato also commands that the two extremities of the body should not be covered and that the head and feet should not be accustomed to softness; for once these have acquired firmness, the other parts are stronger.

“Nor a staff.” Since we have help from the Lord, why should we seek the support of a staff? And because he had sent the apostles to preach, in a certain sense naked and unencumbered, and the condition of teachers seemed harsh, he tempered the severity of the command with the following statement, saying: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matthew 10). That is: “Receive only as much as is necessary for your food and clothing.” Hence the Apostle also says: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6).

“Let the one who is instructed in the word share in every good thing with the one who instructs him” (Galatians 6), so that those whose spiritual things the disciples reap may make them participants in their material goods—not out of greed, but out of necessity.

This is what we have said historically. But according to the allegorical sense, teachers are not permitted to possess gold, silver, or money that is in belts. We often read of gold as signifying understanding, silver as speech, and bronze as the voice. We are not permitted to receive these things from others, but to possess them as gifts given by the Lord.

Nor are we to accept the doctrines of heretics, philosophers, or perverse teaching; nor be weighed down by the burden of the world; nor be double-minded; nor bind our feet with deadly chains. Rather, as we enter the holy land, we must be naked. We must not have a staff that is turned into a serpent, nor rely upon any bodily support, because such a staff and reed are fragile: if you press it slightly, it breaks and pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it.

Again, “nor a staff” means that we do not need the rights of an alien power, since we possess a staff from the root of Jesse. Whatever other staff there may be will not be Christ’s.

It is customary to ask how Matthew and Luke mention that the Lord told the disciples not to carry a staff (Luke 9), while Mark says: “And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff” (Mark 6). The matter is resolved if we understand that “staff” is used with one meaning in the passage according to Mark and with another in the passage according to Luke and Matthew. The same applies to the temptation of which it is said, “God tempts no one” (James 1), and to that of which it is said, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13). The former is temptation to deception; the latter is testing.

Both statements, therefore, should be understood as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles: that they should carry no staff, and that they should carry nothing except a staff. [Col. 1346B]

For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth, he immediately added: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matthew 10). Thus he clearly showed why he did not wish them to possess or carry these things—not because they are unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way that they might understand that these things were owed to them by those to whom they announced the Gospel in faith.

It is clear that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought not to live from any other source than those who provide for them after receiving the Gospel. Otherwise the Apostle would have acted contrary to this command when he supported himself by the labor of his own hands, so as to be a burden to no one (Acts 20). Rather, the Lord gave them authority, so that they would know that these things were owed to them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is the fault of disobedience. But when authority is granted, each person may choose not to use it and may relinquish it as though it were his own right.

Thus, when the Lord established what the Apostle says he established—that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9)—he was speaking to the apostles so that, secure in their calling, they would neither possess nor carry the necessities of this life, whether great or small.

That is why he included the staff: to show that all things were owed by the faithful to his ministers, who were to ask for nothing superfluous. By adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” he completely disclosed and clarified the reason for all these instructions.

He therefore signified this authority by the name “staff” when he said that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff, so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord and signified by the staff, even those things that are not carried will not be lacking.

The same should be understood of the two tunics, so that none of them would think he ought to carry another besides the one he was wearing, out of concern that it might be needed, since through that authority he could receive one.

But when Mark prohibits not the carrying or possession of two tunics but, more explicitly, wearing them—saying, “and that they should not put on two tunics”—what does he admonish them except not to walk in a double manner but simply? Christ has been clothed upon us once for all; therefore, through the perversity of our understanding, we must not afterward be clothed in another garment, whether of heresy or of the law.

Alternatively: by the prohibition of two tunics we are warned to distribute all our excess possessions to those in need. Hence the Apostle also urges us, saying that, having food and clothing, we should be content. Let us not seek the pomp of the world or the riches of the age, but let us store up treasures for ourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys and where thieves neither break in nor steal. For wherever our treasure is, there also, necessarily, our heart will be (Matthew 6).

Therefore we ought to give to those in need whatever is left over for us, because the hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury. We, brothers, are the Lord’s stewards. Therefore let us see and consider that, with great strictness, he will require from us what he has granted us here for distribution.

We must consequently be faithful stewards, for of the substance we possess no steward is more faithful than we ourselves. While it is permitted, and while we have the time, let us give diligently. Let us remember what a certain wise man said:

> The gifts that he gives you when dying are not gifts.

He means that gifts given after death are not as pleasing to God as those bestowed while a person is still in good health. Whatever a person wishes to possess in his eternal homeland, he should prepare for himself while he remains in this present life. For what he stores up here in the hand of the poor, he will find there in the presence of the divine majesty.

It is therefore better for each person, while alive, to offer to God what he possesses than for someone else to do so after his death, since whoever neglects himself will not repent after death. Hence the Lord will say at the end to his faithful steward: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little, enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25).

The passage continues: “And whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not depart from it.” He gives a general command of steadfastness, instructing them to preserve the rights of hospitality and asserting that it is unfitting for a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run from house to house and alter the inviolable obligations of hospitality.

Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles are to enter is to be selected, so that there may be no occasion for changing their lodging and violating the obligations of hospitality. For it is written: “Whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart” (Matthew 10).

Concerning the ordination of a bishop and a deacon the Apostle says: “They must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Timothy 3). When the apostles entered a new city, they could not know what sort of person each inhabitant was. Therefore their host was to be chosen according to the reputation of the people and the judgment of their neighbors, lest the dignity of the preaching be disfigured by the disgrace of the one receiving them.

Although they were obliged to preach to everyone, one host would be chosen—not as one conferring a benefit upon the person who would stay with him, but as one receiving a benefit. For the question, “Who in it is worthy?” means that he should recognize himself as receiving grace rather than giving it.

“And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake off even the dust from your feet,” and so forth. The dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: they entered the city, and the apostolic preaching reached the people there. Or the dust is shaken from their feet so that they may receive nothing from those who rejected the Gospel—not even what is necessary for food.

Allegorically, those who listen humbly to the word, if they are obscured, as human beings, by the stains of earthly frivolity, are soon cleansed by the traces of evangelical preaching that they receive. But the fellowship of those who despise the preaching through unbelief, negligence, or even deliberate intent is to be avoided, and their synagogue is to be shunned. The dust of the feet must be shaken off, lest the trace of a pure mind be polluted by empty deeds and things comparable to dust.

Alternatively: the feet of the disciples signify the work and progress of preaching. The dust with which they are sprinkled signifies the earthly lightness of thought, from which even the highest teachers cannot be entirely free when, concerned for their hearers, they devote themselves without ceasing to salutary cares and, as though traveling along the roads of the world, scarcely lift the dust of the earth with one heel.

Those who receive the word turn the afflictions and cares of their teachers, which they endured on their behalf, into an argument for their own humility. But those who reject the teaching of their instructors turn their teachers’ labors, dangers, and weariness from their anxieties into evidence for their own condemnation.

This is also the dust that elsewhere is commanded to be wiped off against the despisers of the Gospel, and from which the feet of evangelists are commanded to be washed by good hearers—or rather, the dust from which the feet are said to have been washed by the Savior himself (Luke 10).

“Having departed, they went through the villages, evangelizing and healing everywhere.” Mark explains more fully what the apostles preached and how they healed: “They preached,” he says, “that people should repent, and they anointed many sick people with oil, and they were healed” (Mark 6).

James also says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5).

One thing is clear: this practice was handed down by the apostles themselves to the holy Church, namely, that the sick should be anointed with oil consecrated by episcopal blessing.

“They preached that people should repent.” And above: “He sent them,” he says, “to preach the kingdom of God,” because, following both the example of John the Baptist and that of the Lord himself, the Savior, they preached both things: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matthew 3). To draw near to the gates of the kingdom of heaven is for each person to repent of those things by which he had fallen away from it.

## HOMILY 154. ON THE FRIDAY OF PENTECOST.

At that time, on one of the days, Jesus was sitting and teaching. Pharisees and doctors of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was present to heal them, etc. (Luke 5).

The Lord, the Savior of humanity, visits all things in his saving course. Now in the wilderness, now in the city, now by the sea, he dispenses heavenly teaching and gifts of power to the crowds. Now he prays alone on the mountain; now he helps those laboring at sea, lest they perish. Everywhere he bestows the gifts of salvation, demonstrating that every rank and condition belongs to his grace. “Crowds,” says the Evangelist, “were coming together to hear Jesus and to be healed of their infirmities; but he withdrew into the wilderness and prayed.”

According to the mystical interpretation, after the miracle performed in the city—the complete healing of the leper, whom the Gospel passage above describes as cleansed when the Lord touched him—he withdraws into the wilderness. There he receives with kindly compassion the crowds gathering around him, to show that he loves a life more peaceful and removed from the cares of the world, and that, because of his desire for such a life, he applies himself to healing bodies.

Indeed, as though avoiding the throng of those seeking him in the human manner, he did not wish to enter the city openly. Allegorically, however, he taught that Truth does not reveal itself openly to minds agitated by carnal passions; rather, upon those whom it sees to be separated from the allurements of temporal things, it more abundantly pours the light of its gifts. Yet because heavenly compassion does not abandon even the carnal—indeed, it grants them the grace of its visitation, by which they may themselves become spiritual—after the wilderness, as Mark writes, the Lord returns to the city. When many have gathered there, he speaks the word, and, after healing the paralytic, gives many an occasion for that inward healing which is found in faith.

Alternatively: the fact that the Lord performs miracles in the city but spends the night praying in the wilderness or, as we read, on the mountain, gives us a prior example of both lives, namely the active and the contemplative. Thus no one should neglect care for his neighbors out of devotion to contemplation, nor, being excessively bound by care for his neighbors, abandon the practices of contemplation, so that neither love of neighbor impedes love of God, nor love of God casts aside love of neighbor.

To pray on the mountain is, after abandoning the cares of lowly thoughts, to hasten with one’s whole mind toward the eternal joys of heavenly contemplation. To withdraw into the wilderness and pray is to suppress the inward uproar of earthly desires as they arise and to seek within oneself a kind of secret place with the Lord, where, when the outward tumult has ceased, one may speak silently with him through inward desires.

But what is read in Mark—that while the Lord was teaching in a house so many gathered that they could not fit, not even near the door (Mark II)—properly signifies our salvation, who have come from the Gentiles to the faith. While the Lord was preaching in Judea, we were not yet able to enter to hear him. Nevertheless, although we were outside, he caused the words of his teaching to reach us, because he himself gathered us through the mouths of holy preachers and, although we were found outside the synagogue in which he preached, made us participants in his Gospel.

Having considered what the Evangelist has briefly set forth above, let us now in due order examine what follows in the Gospel, which was also read today, and say what the Lord grants us:

> “And it happened on one of those days that Jesus was sitting and teaching. And Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was present to heal them.”

Where the Lord taught while seated, and when he healed the paralytic while the scribes and Pharisees were seated with him, Luke omits for the sake of brevity. Matthew and Mark, however, who recount the event, seem to raise a question, since Matthew testifies that he did this in his own city, while Mark says it occurred in Capernaum (Matthew IX; Mark II). The difficulty would be greater if Matthew had also named Nazareth. But now either Galilee itself, in which Nazareth was situated, should be understood as the city called Christ’s city, specifically to distinguish it from the region across the sea of the Gerasenes—from which, as Matthew writes, he had crossed over and come to Galilee—or certainly Capernaum itself was called Christ’s city. He had made it his own not by being born there, but by illuminating it with his miracles.

> “And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and place him before Jesus.”

They offered him, the paralytic, lying on a bed, because he was unable to enter on his own. The healing of this paralytic indicates the salvation of the soul that, after the long inactivity caused by the allurements of the flesh, sighs for Christ. First of all, it needs ministers who will lift it up and offer it to Christ—that is, good teachers who can suggest the hope of healing and the help of intercession.

According to Mark, these men are found to have been four, either because the whole power and preaching of those who proclaim the Gospel is confirmed by the four books of the Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised to obtain wholeness. As we have learned elsewhere, we may rightly understand these as the cardinal virtues. For these virtues precede the others in rank, and the others depend upon them as upon a hinge.

Of these virtues it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom:

> “For she teaches sobriety and justice, wisdom and virtue, and nothing in life is more useful for human beings” (Wisdom VIII).

Some, changing the names, call them prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

> “And finding no way by which they could bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles.”

They desire to offer the paralytic to Christ, but because the crowd intervenes, they are shut out on every side. For often, after the soul has come to its senses and wishes to be renewed by the remedy of heavenly grace following the sluggishness of an infirm body, it is held back by the obstacle of its former habit. Often, even during prayers filled with secret sweetness and what is almost a delightful conversation with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts intervenes and blocks the mind’s vision, so that Christ cannot be seen.

What, then, should be done in these circumstances? We must not grow sluggish in our desire for salvation. Certainly we must not remain below, outside, where the crowds are clamoring; rather, we must climb onto the roof of the house in which Christ teaches. That is, we must seek the sublimity of Sacred Scripture and meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord with the Psalmist:

> “How does a young man keep his way pure? By guarding your words” (Psalm CXVIII).

> “And they lowered him with his bed into the midst, before Jesus.”

Once the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because, when the mysteries of Scripture have been opened, one comes to knowledge of Christ; that is, one descends through devotion into the humility of faith.

The house of Jesus is rightly described as covered with tiles, because beneath the contemptible covering of letters, if someone opens it, the divine power of spiritual grace is found. Hence, according to the account of another Evangelist, “they had uncovered the roof where Jesus was” (Mark II). The uncovering of the tiles in the house of Jesus is the opening, beneath the lowliness of the letter, of the spiritual meaning and heavenly mysteries.

The fact that he is lowered together with the bed signifies that Christ must be known by a human being who is still established in this flesh. According to the mystical meaning, the whole company of the Gentiles is now offered in the person of the paralytic to be healed.

We must consider the Lord’s words of healing. He does not say to the paralytic, “Be saved”; he does not say, “Rise and walk.” Rather, as Matthew writes, he says only:

> “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew XIX).

In the one Adam, sins are forgiven to all the Gentiles. He is therefore offered for healing with angels ministering; he is called “son” because he is the first work of God. From this point the soul’s sins are forgiven, and the pardon of the first transgression is received through forgiveness.

For this is what follows:

> “When he saw their faith, he said, ‘Man, your sins are forgiven you.’”

As the Lord was about to heal the man from paralysis, he first dissolved the bonds of his sins, to show that he was condemned to the dissolution of his limbs because of the bonds of his faults, and that he could be healed by the restoration of his limbs only after those bonds had been released.

So also, to the paralytic who had long awaited in vain the movement of the water near the Sheep Pool, the Lord says after healing him:

> “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

The one whose sins were being forgiven is rightly called “man,” since, precisely because he was human, he could not say, “I have not sinned.” At the same time, so that the one who forgave a man’s faults might be understood to be God, Matthew and Mark report that he was told:

> “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew IX; Mark II).

O marvelous humility! He calls “son” the man who was despised and weak, with all the joints of his limbs dissolved, and whom the priests did not consider worthy to touch. Or perhaps he calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven.

According to the tropological interpretation, the soul sometimes lies in its bodily torpor, with all the powers of its limbs dissolved, and is offered to the Lord for healing by a perfect teacher. If it has been healed by his mercy, it receives such strength that it immediately carries its own bed.

We should certainly observe how great the faith of each person is worth before God, since another’s faith was worth so much that the whole man was suddenly made well—both inwardly and outwardly—and the faults of some were released through the merit of others.

> “And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: ‘Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?’”

We read in the Prophets, where the Lord says:

> “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isaiah XLIII).

The scribes therefore rightly accuse him of blasphemy, because they thought he was merely a man and understood his words as God’s words.

The Pharisees speak truly: no one can forgive sins except God alone. God also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. Christ is therefore proved to be true God, because as God he can forgive sins.

They bear true witness to God, but because they deny the person of Christ, they fall into error. The Jews are therefore mistaken: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ.

But the Arians err far more foolishly. Though defeated by the words of the Gospel, they do not dare deny that Jesus is the Christ and that he can forgive sins; nevertheless, they are not afraid to deny that he is God. They wickedly presume to introduce this error and are not ashamed to proclaim things contrary to the words of the Christian faith.

Together with the Arians, therefore, those faithless people are judged by the Catholic Church to be outside it who harbor in their minds the erroneous belief that the Lord is neither the true Son of God and God, nor able to forgive sins.

Yet, desiring to save the faithless, he reveals himself as God both through his knowledge of hidden things and through the power of his works.

> “He answered them: ‘Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?’”

For the wisest speaker attributes to the same God who says, “I am he who blots out your iniquities,” the words:

> “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (1 Kings VIII).

“I,” he says, “possess the same majesty and power by which I see your thoughts, and by which I can also forgive human beings their sins.”

Understand from yourselves what the paralytic obtains.

> “For which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?”

There is a great difference between saying and doing. Whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven was known only to the one who forgave them. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rise.

A bodily sign is therefore performed so that the spiritual reality may be proved, although removing the defects of both body and soul belongs to the same power. We are also given to understand that many bodily weaknesses occur because of sins. Perhaps for this reason sins are forgiven first: once the causes of weakness have been removed, health may be restored.

There are, in fact, five different causes for which we are afflicted in this life by bodily troubles.

First, the righteous may be burdened by bodily illness in order to increase their merits through patience, as were the blessed fathers Job and Tobias and countless martyrs in both Testaments.

Second, they may be afflicted to preserve the virtues they have received, lest those virtues perish when pride tempts them. Thus, for the Apostle Paul, “a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan,” was given to him to strike him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians XII).

Third, illness may be given so that we may understand and correct our sins, as happened to Mary, the sister of Aaron, who was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of her rash and proud words (Numbers XII), and as happened to the paralytic we are discussing, who could not be healed of his infirmity until his sins had first been forgiven.

Fourth, it may occur for the glory of God who saves, whether through himself or through his servants. Thus the man born blind in the Gospel had sinned neither himself nor his parents, but was afflicted “so that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John IX, 11). Likewise Lazarus’s illness was said not to be for death, but for the glory of God, so that through it the Son of God might be glorified.

Fifth, it may serve as the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is proper to the reprobate, as with Antiochus and Herod. Each of them, in his own time, fought against God, and the misery of their present afflictions showed everyone what torments they would suffer perpetually in Gehenna.

To them applies the saying of the Prophet:

> “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jeremiah XVII).

Therefore, in all the adversities we suffer temporarily, we must give thanks to the Lord with humility. Conscious of our weakness, we should rejoice in the remedies granted to us. We must return to our conscience, carefully examine both our deeds and our thoughts, and purify with fitting correction whatever we discover that we have done wrong. Whatever we discover to have perished through the fault of pride among the things we believed we had done rightly, we must likewise correct through humble satisfaction.

This has often been the cause of our scourging. But for the innocent and righteous to be scourged for the increase of their rewards is a special gift granted to perfected men. To be driven by temporal blows toward eternal torments, however, is the punishment of the unrepentant reprobate.

> “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

If God is for us the one who, according to the Psalmist, has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east is from the west (Psalm CII), and, according to the testimony of the aforementioned Isaiah, blots out our iniquities; and if the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then he is both God and Son of Man. Thus Christ, as man, can already forgive sins through the power of his divinity, and Jesus Christ, through the weakness of his humanity, can die for sinners.

> “He said to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.’”

When our paralytic soul rises and recovers its former strength, it carries the bed on which it had previously lain dissolved, and carries it into the house of its virtues.

To rise spiritually from one’s bed is to draw the soul away from the carnal desires in which it had lain sick. To take up one’s bed is to deprive the flesh itself, corrected by the reins of continence, of earthly pleasures through hope of heavenly rewards.

This is the bed that David washes every night (Psalm VI): that is, for the stains of a single offense, it is chastised with a fitting stream of repentance.

To take up one’s bed and go home is to return to paradise. For paradise is the true house that first received humanity—not lost by right, but by fraud, and at last restored through him who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy.

Alternatively: the one who was sick carries his bed home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, brings itself back, together with the body, into its inward keeping, lest after forgiveness it commit anything for which it might again justly be struck.

The bed, in which the flesh rests, signifies the flesh itself; the house signifies the conscience. Because when we lie dead in our minds through vices and rest in the pleasure of the flesh, we are carried in a bed while sick. But when we have been healed in mind, so that we now resist the vices that assail the flesh, we must necessarily endure the insults of temptations because of our weakness.

Thus the one who has been wondrously restored to salvation is commanded:

> “Take up your bed,”

that is, the thing on which you were carried. For each person must bear the reproach of the flesh in which he previously lay sick.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Take up your bed and go to your house,” except: Carry the temptations in which you have lain until now, and return to your conscience, so that you may see what you have done?

> “And immediately he rose before them, took up the bed on which he had been lying, and went to his house, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God.”

Marvelous is the power of divine might, where, without any intervening delay, swift health accompanies the Savior’s command. Those who were present rightly turn their astonished hearts, after the weapons of blasphemy have been condemned, toward praise of such great majesty.

At first they fear that the Lord’s power will avenge his faithless crowd; then, when the fear of despair has ceased, honor is rendered to God because he has given such authority to human beings.

For this follows:

> “And they were filled with fear, saying, ‘We have seen marvelous things today.’”

But this was owed to Christ alone; it was familiar to him alone to do such things through communion with the Father’s substance. It should not therefore be surprising that he was able to do these things. For what is God believed unable to do? Otherwise, the praise would have arisen from one man, not from many.

The cause of the honor offered to God is that, through his Word, authority and a way were given to human beings both for the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of bodies, and the return to heaven.

But you, Lord, etc.

## HOMILY CLV. FOR THE SATURDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the exposition of the blessed Ambrose on the Gospel according to Luke, Book IV, no. 55.)*

[Col. 1354C]

> “At that time Jesus rose from the synagogue and entered the house of Simon. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever, and they pleaded with him on her behalf,” etc. (Luke IV.)

“Jewish sacrileges,” etc. For the remainder, see Saint Ambrose, *Works*, vol. II, *Patrologia* XV, col. 1629.

## HOMILY CLVI. ALSO FOR THE SAME SATURDAY

> “At that time Jesus rose from the synagogue and entered the house of Simon,” etc. (Luke IV.)

In this passage of the holy Gospel, the Evangelists did not preserve the same order. Mark and Luke, in fact, recount this event before saying anything about the leper who was cleansed when the Lord came down from the mountain (Mark I). Matthew, however, after concluding the Sermon on the Mount and mentioning the cleansing of the leper and the healing of the centurion’s servant, adds the restoration of Simon Peter’s mother-in-law (Matthew VIII).

But the diversity of narrative causes no difficulty when the same event is being reported. It should be noted that, in Matthew, the leper was the first specifically healed; second was the centurion’s servant; third, Peter’s mother-in-law suffering from fever in Capernaum; and fourth, those possessed by demons who were brought to him, whose spirits he cast out by a word, when he also healed all who were ill.

Since “through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom II), the medicine of salvation first had to operate against the author of death himself. First, the serpent’s tongue had to be closed, so that it would no longer spread its poison. Then the woman who was first deceived had to be healed of the fever of carnal desire. Third, the man who had listened to the words of his misleading wife had to be cleansed of the leprosy of his error.

Thus, in Luke’s Gospel, the order of restoration corresponds to the order of the fall. For a little earlier he reports that in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean demon. After describing his complete restoration to health, he adds what we heard in today’s reading:

> “And rising from the synagogue, Jesus entered the house of Simon. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever.”

After giving a full account of this revelation [relevationis, “raising/relief”] granted by the Lord, and inserting several other matters, he goes on to the cleansing of a man who was full of leprosy.

It is fitting that the precise place where the leper was cleansed is not stated, so that it may be shown that not the people of one particular city, but the peoples of all nations, were healed.

We have introduced these matters by way of a necessary digression, to demonstrate the mystical order preserved by the Evangelist: the order of restoration in the Lord, which had also been the order of the fall in the first-formed human beings.

Let us now direct the gaze of our mind to this Gospel passage, which has been assigned to us for exposition in today’s reading.

If we say that the man freed from the demon signifies, in the moral sense, a mind cleansed of unclean thought, then, correspondingly, the woman afflicted with fever but healed at the Lord’s command signifies the flesh restrained from the heat of desire through the precepts of continence.

For all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy are the fury of an unclean spirit (Ephesians IV). But understand fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed—which is the worship of idols—as the fever of alluring flesh (Colossians III).

> “And they pleaded with him on her behalf. And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her.”

In Matthew’s Gospel it is written:

> “He touched her hand, and the fever left her” (Matthew VIII).

At one time the Savior is entreated; at another he heals the sick without being asked. He thereby shows that, against the passions of sins also, he always responds to the prayers of the faithful, and that he either grants understanding of those things which they themselves scarcely understand within themselves, or mercifully forgives even things not understood by those who devoutly ask, according to the Psalmist’s petition:

> “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Psalm XVIII).

The woman’s hand is touched, and when her works have been healed, the sickness of her sins flees.

> “And immediately she rose and ministered to them.”

It is natural for those suffering from fever, when health begins, to remain weak and to feel the discomfort of their illness. But the health bestowed at the Lord’s command returns all at once. Not only does it return, but it is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to minister to those who had helped her.

And, according to the laws of tropology, the members that had served impurity for iniquity, so that they might bear fruit for death, should serve righteousness for eternal life.

According to the mystical interpretations also, after the centurion’s servant has been saved and the Gentiles’ faith has been praised in the centurion, Peter’s mother-in-law—that is, the Jewish synagogue—is next healed from the heat of fever.

Peter’s house signifies the Israelite people, in which, according to the Apostle Paul, Peter received the ministry of apostleship (Galatians II). Peter’s mother-in-law signifies the synagogue of that same people. It is fittingly understood as the mother of the primitive Church, like Peter’s wife, because the Church of Christ’s first disciples is known to have drawn its fleshly origin from that synagogue; betrothed, as it were, to Peter but invisibly made fruitful by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it is rightly believed on the pattern of the blessed Joseph and the Virgin Mary.

But Peter’s mother-in-law—that is, the Jewish synagogue—burns for the time being with the fever of faithlessness, until the full number of the Gentiles enters and thus all Israel is saved (Romans XI).

To touch her hand is to form good works within her, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, have been cleansed, their feverish synagogue remains lying sick.

The fever then leaves her when the manifold sickness of faithlessness departs from her. She rises and ministers when, renouncing dead works and seeking the things above, she walks in newness of life.

> “When the sun had set, all those who had the sick with various diseases brought them to him. And he laid his hands on each of them and healed them.”

Matthew writes:

> “When evening came, they brought him many who were possessed by demons; and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our weaknesses and bore our diseases’” (Matthew VIII).

All are healed not in the morning, not at midday, but in the evening, when the sun is about to set, when the grain of wheat dies in the earth so that it may bear much fruit.

The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of the one who said:

> “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John IX).

When the sun has set, more demoniacs than before and more sick people are healed, because while he lived temporarily in the flesh he taught only a few Jews; but after trampling down the kingdom of death, he transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world.

To his ministers, as heralds of life and light, the Psalmist sings:

> “Make a way for him who rises above the setting” (Psalm LXVII).

The Lord rises above the setting because from the place where he set in his passion, he manifested his greater glory by rising again.

> “Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.”

The demons confessed that he was the Son of God. As the Evangelist attests, they knew that he was the Christ, because the devil had recognized him as a man when he was exhausted by forty days of fasting, but, unable to discover by temptation whether he was also the Son of God, had now either understood—or rather suspected—from the power of his signs that he was the Son of God.

The devil therefore did not persuade the Jews to crucify him because he thought that he was not the Christ or the Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by his death.

The Apostle truly speaks of this mystery, hidden from the ages:

> “None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians XI).

Why did the Lord forbid the demons to speak? The Psalmist makes this clear:

> “But to the sinner God says, ‘Why do you recite my statutes?’” (Psalm XLIX),

lest someone, while hearing a preacher, follow one who is in error. The devil is an evil teacher, who always mixes falsehoods with truths so that, under the appearance of truth, he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

In other cases, however, it was not only the demons, who confessed unwillingly, who were commanded to remain silent about Christ. Those who were healed by him and wished to confess him voluntarily were also commanded to remain silent; indeed, even the Apostles, who were to preach him throughout the whole world after the resurrection, were commanded before his passion to say nothing at all about him. Otherwise, if his divine majesty were proclaimed, the dispensation of his passion might have been delayed; and if the passion were delayed, the salvation of the world that was to come through it would have been denied.

> “When day came, he went out and departed to a deserted place. And the crowds were seeking him, and they came as far as he was and held him back, so that he would not leave them.”

To them he said:

> “I must evangelize the kingdom of God to the other cities also.”

If the setting of the sun expresses the Lord’s death, why should his resurrection not be indicated by the return of day? When its light was revealed, he was sought by the crowds of believers; and, found in the wilderness of the Gentiles, he was held back so that he would not depart—especially since this departure, seeking, and finding occurred on the first day of the week, on which the resurrection was celebrated.

The fact that, according to Mark, the Lord went to a deserted place and prayed there (Mark I) signifies that, after the glory of his resurrection had been revealed, he went into the wilderness of the Gentiles and prayed there in his faithful people, because through the grace of his Spirit he stirred their hearts to the power of prayer.

Let us therefore, brothers, follow the example of those who faithfully sought the Lord and therefore deserved to find him, and who, captivated by the sweetness of his presence, held him back so that he would not leave them. Let us direct the gaze of our mind and, with the Lord’s help, seek the Lord.

The voice of the divine song says:

> “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Psalm LXVIII).

Let us seek him who is to be found; let us seek him after he has been found. He is hidden so that he may be sought as one who is to be found; he is boundless so that, once found, he may still be sought. Hence it is said elsewhere:

> “Seek his face always” (Psalm CIV).

He satisfies the seeker insofar as the seeker is capable of receiving, and he makes the one who finds him more capable, so that the person may seek again to be filled where he has begun to receive more.

It was not said, “Seek his face always,” in the manner of the words about certain people who are “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy III). Rather, it was said as in the words:

> “When a person has finished, then he begins” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII),

until we come to that life where we shall be so filled that we shall not become more capable, because we shall be so perfect that we shall no longer progress. Then what is sufficient for us will be shown to us.

Here, however, let us always seek, and let the fruit of finding not be the end of seeking. It is not that we do not always seek because we seek only here; rather, we say that we must seek here so that we never suppose that we may cease seeking here.

For those of whom it is said that they are “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” are indeed learning. But when they depart this life, they will no longer be learning; they will receive the reward of their error.

Thus it is as though it had been said: “Always walking, and never arriving at the way.” But let us always walk on the way until we come to where the way leads. Let us nowhere stop on it until it brings us to the place where we shall remain.

In this way, by seeking we press onward; by finding we arrive at something; and, by seeking and finding, we pass on to what remains, until, by finding, the seeking comes to an end where, after perfection, no further intention of progress remains.

This is in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom we have now received the grace of reconciliation and have access by faith, having been justified by it into the hope of the glory of the children of God; he who also gave us the pledge of the Spirit (Romans V; 2 Corinthians V). To him be glory and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, before all ages and now, throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLVII. FOR THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

*(From the works of the venerable Bede the priest.)*

[Col. 1358B]

> “At that time there was a man from the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: ‘Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher,’” etc. (John III.)

“As you have heard, dearest brothers, from the reading of the holy Gospel, the ruler of the Jews,” etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, *Works*, vol. V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 197.

## HOMILY CLVIII. FOR THE FEAST OF THE HOLY TRINITY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

[Col. 1358C]

> “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness,’” etc. (John XV.)

Seated at table with his disciples, after the Lord had sealed the mysteries of the New Testament through the consecration of his body and blood, and the hour of his betrayal was already at hand, among the other matters with which he graciously instructed them he warned them not to be terrified when the persecution of the ungodly raged against them, nor to give way when weary, but to maintain invincible strength of steadfastness in all things. He also promised the coming of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace they would be deprived of earthly fear and established by the strength of heavenly virtue.

Finally, if we consult the pronouncements of divine Scripture [Col. 1358D], we shall clearly recognize that the holy apostles, before receiving the Holy Spirit—who was sent upon them on the tenth day after the Lord’s ascension into heaven—had been less suited and capable of understanding the mysteries of divine sublimity, and also less strong for enduring the adversities of the persecution inflicted upon them. When the Holy Spirit came upon them, they received, together with an increase in divine knowledge, steadfastness for enduring the torments of suffering.

To make this clearer by an evident example, let us bring forward the blessed Peter himself, the summit of the apostolic height. Before he was strengthened by the Holy Spirit, he was so weak and fearful of mind that, at the voice of a single maidservant, he denied that he even knew the Lord [Col. 1359A] (Matt. XXVI). But after the fire of the Holy Spirit had kindled his breast, formerly chilled by fear, he suddenly conceived such strength of spirit that, above all the apostles, he emerged to preach publicly the glory of Christ’s resurrection and overcame the terrors of the rulers, saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). And again: “We cannot fail to speak of the things that we have seen and heard” (Acts IV).

Let us therefore marvel at blessed Peter preaching, whom we had mourned for denying him. For he was illumined by so great a radiance of the Holy Spirit and established by so great an authority of truth that he converted those very men who shortly before had been Christ’s executioners, so that they even desired to die for the love of Christ.

Accordingly, while speaking to the disciples and promising them the coming of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1359B] who would teach them the knowledge of divine truth and strengthen them for confidence in preaching and steadfastness in suffering, the Lord says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, and so forth.” The order of the words is this: “When the Paraclete comes, he will bear witness concerning me.”

For the Paraclete—that is, the Holy Spirit—bore witness concerning the Lord Jesus Christ because, having entered into the hearts of the apostles, he bestowed upon them the fullest knowledge of Christ’s divinity and humanity. Thus, insofar as mortal weakness permits, they knew whatever ought to be thought about him: how he was of one substance and the same majesty with the Father; how he who before the ages was God with God appeared as a human being among human beings at the end of the ages; how, having been born of a virgin, he received [materially uncertain: the object of *acceperit* is not supplied], so that the same one might be both [Col. 1359C] human and God; how, having suffered willingly, he rose from the dead by his own power; how, ascending into heaven, he sat at the Father’s right hand; and finally, how he himself would come at the end of the world as the impartial judge of all.

All these things the holy apostles learned about Christ through the instruction of the Holy Spirit. Nor were they alone: all who rightly hold any belief about Christ must likewise be believed to have attained it through the grace of this Spirit.

He also bore witness when he inspired the disciples with steadfastness to preach what they had learned—when, through one and the same Spirit, they were endowed both with the gift of spiritual knowledge and with the aid of power for preaching.

But when he says, “whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father,” this is spoken by way of an insertion, a figure called in Greek *parenthesis*, [Col. 1359D] which he wished to insert into the sentence in order clearly to show that in the Father and the Son there is one will and one operation, with a distinction of persons. Thus we are to understand that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but that in the three persons there is one and the same power of majesty.

It must also be observed that he says the Holy Spirit is sent both by himself and proceeds from the Father—not because the operation of the Father and the Son is separable, but so that the distinction between the persons of the Father and the Son may be made manifest. Yet in this distinction of persons, the Son’s one will and operation agree with the will and operation of the Father.

Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit is sent by the Son, so he is also sent by the Father; and just as he proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son [Col. 1360A]. The Holy Spirit himself, because he has one will and the same operation with the Father and the Son, is also said to come of his own accord. The Lord plainly demonstrates this where he says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III). And the Apostle, after enumerating the distributions of divine gifts, adds: “All these things one and the same Spirit brings about” (I Cor. XII).

The Lord shows the same thing in this passage when he says: “When the Paraclete comes.” Since he is sent also by the Son, the Son himself goes on to say: “Whom I shall send to you.” And to show that he proceeds also from the Father, it is added: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

For this reason, it is not unworthy of inquiry why the Holy Spirit is said to be neither born, nor begotten, nor unbegotten, but rather proceeding. The Fathers answer this question [Col. 1360B] in the following way: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but he is not called begotten, lest two Sons be suspected in the Trinity; and he is not called unbegotten, lest two Fathers likewise be believed to exist in the Trinity. He is called “proceeding” on the testimony of Christ, who says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

The distinction between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds is this: the Son is born from one, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

By his coming, the Holy Spirit bore witness concerning the Lord, because, infused into the minds of the disciples, he revealed by his clear light all that mortals needed to know about him. He plainly impressed upon them how the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1360C] neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from both; and how in these three persons there is one majesty and one substance.

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness.” The apostles bore witness to the Lord Jesus Christ when, illumined by the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, they freely preached outwardly to others, having cast away their fear, what they had inwardly recognized through his inspiration.

“Because you have been with me from the beginning.” Since they had been with the Lord from the beginning of his preaching, they were able to preach to others what they knew. It greatly benefited the apostles for preaching the faith and bearing witness concerning Christ that they had associated with him from the beginning of his preaching. Through the length of time and the constancy of their presence with him, they received heavenly instruction more fully and—as one might say—imbibed it to the marrow [Col. 1360D].

Hence they preached to others without hesitation the things they had seen and heard from him. Blessed Peter rightly confirms this, when, wishing to appoint another apostle in the place of Judas the betrayer, he decided to choose not a novice—that is, an inexperienced man—but one proven through long association, namely, from the time of the Lord’s preaching. He said: “Brothers, it is necessary to choose one of these men who have accompanied us throughout the whole time during which the Lord Jesus came in among us and went out, to become with us a witness of his resurrection to the people—one of these” (Acts I).

This means Matthias, who was one of the seventy disciples whom the Lord chose after the apostles at the very beginning of his preaching.

Elsewhere he indicates with what authority Peter preached the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 1361A], speaking thus about Christ: “God raised him from the dead and granted that he should be made manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses foreordained by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts X).

“I have told you these things so that you may not be scandalized.” The Lord foresaw what storms of persecution would arise against the apostles as they preached, and therefore graciously took care to foretell what would come afterward, so that they might more easily endure what was approaching. Evils that are foreknown affect us less, whereas unforeseen ones disturb us more severely.

It must also be noted that, after saying that they would be illumined by the coming of the Holy Spirit and would bear witness to him, he immediately added the adversities of the persecution that would follow. For the more earnestly the holy strive toward the heights of virtue [Col. 1361B], the greater the devil’s envy arises against them. It seeks to resist their progress and, whether through himself or through his members, to uproot completely the beginnings of a good work.

The Lord therefore says: “I have told you these things so that you may not be scandalized,” as if he were saying: I make known to you beforehand what will later come to pass so that, armed with the shield of foreknowledge, you may in no way be cast down from the firmness of your steadfastness.

“They will put you out of the synagogues.” In the Gospel we find that the Jews conspired so that anyone who confessed Christ would be expelled from the synagogue. Among them this was reckoned a very serious offense. No one will doubt that this custom formerly prevailed among the Jews: those who were accused either of blasphemy or of some other crime were expelled from their assembly.

For just as [Col. 1361C] now murderers, incestuous persons, and those subject to capital crimes are, by the authority of the canons, driven from communion with the Church and from the altar, so at that time confessors of the name of Christ were expelled from the synagogue. This was suffered by Nicodemus and Gamaliel, and by many others, who chose for a time to be deprived of human society so that they might adhere to Christ forever.

That they were not only expelled from the synagogues but also put to death by their fellow citizens is made clear when the Lord adds: “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

When the Jews persecuted the heralds of the holy Gospel with hatred and death, they thought that they were offering service to God, believing that by this means they were carrying out the vengeance of the Law. Hence blessed Paul also bore witness to them [Col. 1361D], saying: “They have zeal for the Law, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X).

Therefore these words of the Lord must be understood specifically not of the Gentiles but of the Jews, as if he were saying: You will suffer tribulations from the citizens of your own nation; but endure them all the more willingly, since they will try to inflict them upon you not so much out of hatred for you as through zeal for the Law of their fathers.

Yet it does them no good to defend the Law, which was given through a servant, when they refused to receive the grace of the Gospel, which came through the Son. By these words the apostles are greatly consoled, since they hear—as we have said—that the rage of persecution against them is stirred up not by hatred of them but by zeal for the divine Law.

“And they will do these things to you because they have not [Col. 1362A] known the Father, nor me.” The faith of the holy Church has already sufficiently received the teaching that the Father and the Son are of one divinity and power, and therefore that no one can possess knowledge of the Father without knowledge of the Son.

The same Evangelist says elsewhere: “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father” (I John II). And elsewhere: “Whoever loves him who begot him also loves him who has been begotten by him” (I John V).

In vain, therefore, do the Jews boast of knowledge of the Father, since they stubbornly refused to receive the Son. Let them boast as much as they wish of worshiping God the Father: if they mock our faith, which exists in Christ and through Christ, they will certainly never be pleasing to God the Father, nor will they ever be able to attain knowledge of him, unless they receive Christ through faith—in whom lies the door to attaining knowledge of the Father—and believe him to be equal in all things to God [Col. 1362B] the Father.

What benefit or relief these words of the Lord would bring to the apostles is immediately made clear when he adds: “But I have told you these things so that, when their hour comes—that is, the hour of the evils that you will suffer—you may remember that I told you.”

It is as if he were saying: I foretell to you the things you will suffer for the sake of my name so that, when their hour comes—that is, the time of the events foretold—you may recall that I predicted them to you, and thus endure the present evils, knowing that I who was able to foretell them to you will be able to deliver you when they come.

It was certainly a great kind of consolation for the apostles, amid their adversities, to remember that they had been forewarned of such things by their Teacher, from whom they undoubtedly knew that they would be rewarded for the exercises of their labors [Col. 1362C].

These words of the Lord must be weighed with the greatest care and not heard carelessly: “I told you.” I—that is, the almighty God; I who am to die for you and for your salvation, and redeem you with my blood; I who will always supply you with help in tribulation, and after your tribulations will reward you as victors with immortal prizes. I foretold these things to you—as if he were saying: When you see fulfilled the things that I foretold would happen to you, believe that I am the Son of God, who was able both to do such things after foretelling them and to foretell them before doing them.

It should also be noted that he who here foretold the future persecution promises his faithful shortly afterward assistance in that same persecution, saying: “In [Col. 1362D] the world you will have tribulation, but be confident; I have overcome the world” (John XVI).

Elsewhere, too, he promises a reward to those who lawfully strive in the same contest, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. VI).

He is accustomed both to assist his soldiers so that they cannot be defeated and, so that they may not conquer in vain, to bestow an immortal palm after the battles: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout eternal ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLXII. ON THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the works of blessed Augustine.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Do not judge, and you will not be judged,” and so forth (Luke VI).

Just now, brothers, when the Gospel was being read, we heard the Lord saying: “Do not judge,” and so forth [Col. 1363C]. For the remainder, see Saint Augustine, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XXXIX, col. 1871.

## HOMILY CLXIII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful,” and so forth (Luke VI).

The Lord God created man among all things under this condition and endowed him with such outstanding dignity that, if he had wished to persevere in the blessed state of his creation from the beginning, he would have known by himself what ought to be done and would have been carried toward its fulfillment without any resistance from an opposing force. But after he obeyed the devil’s persuasions, he suddenly experienced such [Col. 1363D] mutability within himself that he not only became mortal instead of immortal, but also found the faculty of free choice itself so corrupted and degraded that he could no longer, by himself, understand anything good—much less accomplish it in practice—without the help of divine mercy.

Since, therefore, it was impossible for the fallen human race, by its own power, to rise to the performance of what the demands of salvation require, the Lord deigned to appear under the form of man and personally to instruct the apostles whom he had chosen from the whole mass of the human race, and to show us how we might be restored to sonship with God. For earlier he had said: “Love your enemies, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5), clearly making known that the grace of divine adoption can be [Col. 1364A] merited by love alone.

And shortly afterward: “Be merciful,” he says. In this reading of the holy Gospel we are taught not only to be merciful, but also shown how we are to be merciful, when it says: “Just as your heavenly Father is merciful.”

Our Father, almighty God, is called “Father” in two ways: either because, when we did not yet exist, he created us, or because, when we were lost, he mercifully recreated us. God our Father is therefore merciful either because, in his abundant mercy, he bestows temporal goods upon the ungrateful and wicked, raining upon the just and unjust and causing his sun to rise upon the good and the wicked—for by this he also feeds the beasts—and permits them likewise to advance in temporal prosperity according to their desires in the present; or because he grants the gifts of spiritual goods by a special [Col. 1364B] grace to his elect, whom he allows to use present things in such a way that eventually he makes them enjoy everlasting goods.

This great mercy of God is set before us for imitation, if we desire to be sons of God. “Merciful” is derived from *a misero corde*, “from a miserable heart,” a term properly suited to our weakness: being subject to miseries, we learn from our own condition how we ought to show mercy to others.

Misery, however, not only cannot befall God, who remains eternally and blessedly happy in the blessedness of his nature, but does not befall a just man either when he shows mercy to another. For who would deny that the wise man ought to be free from every misery when he assists the needy, gives food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, clothes the naked, receives the traveler under his roof, and finally extends his humanity even to the burial of the [Col. 1364C] dead?

Even if he does this with a tranquil mind, moved by no goads of sorrow but led by the duty of goodness, he is nevertheless called merciful, because by suffering with others he appears to have a sorrowful heart. This name does him no harm, since the fulfillment of the divine commandments benefits him.

Almighty God is therefore called merciful by a word transferred from man to God. He is merciful to both above all his creation, which he orders and governs with kindly protection, so that it may not return to nothing but rather endure in eternal stability.

Alternatively: when God is called merciful, this in no way reveals a property of his substance; rather, it accommodates itself to our understanding. Since we can conceive of nothing concerning him as he truly is, we are led toward knowledge of him through what takes place within [Col. 1364D] us.
