God is called merciful because he mercifully governs and rules the human race, which he created with potentiality.

That we enjoy the health of our bodies, that we rejoice in the abundance of crops and are nourished by pleasant air, and that we are warmed by the heat of the sun itself—all this is undoubtedly brought about by the benefit of the most merciful God.

We must also know that the adverb “as” does not always indicate equality, but sometimes also likeness. It is obvious that we have no means of possessing as great a mercy as [Col. 1365A] God is shown to possess; but God, just as he is boundless, also displays boundless mercy.

We, who are very unlike his power, being merely human beings, should nevertheless take care to be merciful insofar as understanding and ability permit, loving and multiplying benefits not only toward the grateful and our friends, but also toward the ungrateful and our enemies.

Whoever bestows temporal or spiritual goods upon others out of divine love, whoever mercifully grants pardon to those who sin against him, just as he himself desires to obtain forgiveness from the Lord—such a person undoubtedly becomes an imitator of God.

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned.” One may ask: Since the Psalmist says, “Judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. 57), why does he here prohibit the same thing by saying, “Do not judge”?

By saying this, he does not take away from us the understanding necessary for judging; rather, he warns us not to condemn someone whose thoughts are either unknown to us or whose future character [Col. 1365B] we do not know. Nor should this be understood as prejudicing ecclesiastical judgments, by which it is customary to punish the faults of the negligent; instead, the necessary moderation of discernment is being enjoined.

This sentence is principally commanded to us so that, whenever we can doubt with what intention certain actions are performed—for some things are capable of being done with either a good or a bad intention—we may always interpret them in the better sense.

Such things include, for example, the consumption of different foods, the carefully selected variety of drinks, and other necessary treatments of the body. Concerning these the Apostle forbids us to judge: “Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat, and let him who does not eat not judge him who eats” (Rom. 14), since any kind of human food might be taken with a simple intention, without the fault of desire.

The time for judging these and similar actions, which can be performed [Col. 1365C] indifferently, will come when, as the Apostle teaches, “the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will disclose the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4).

But we are permitted to judge those things concerning which there is no doubt that they are done with a wicked intention, such as those works which the Apostle calls works of the flesh, saying: “Murders, drunkenness, fornications” (Gal. 5), and other such things, which both exclude their perpetrators from the kingdom of God and make them liable to eternal death, unless they are expiated by worthy repentance while life remains. Concerning these the Lord himself says elsewhere: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7).

There are, however, certain especially [Col. 1365D] important cases in which we must avoid rash judgment—namely, when it is uncertain, as has been said, with what intention something was done, and also when it is uncertain what someone who appears good or wicked today will be tomorrow.

For example, if someone complains of an infirm stomach and wishes to eat before the usual hour, and you attribute this not to illness but to greed, you have judged rashly. We ought not to judge him with that judgment of condemnation by which we despair of his salvation.

Again, if you recognize open drunkenness and gluttony, and rebuke the person in such a way that you despair of the correction of one subject to such a vice, you have nevertheless judged rashly.

Let us therefore not rebuke what is hidden, nor rebuke what is manifest in such a way that we despair of anyone’s amendment. Then we shall avoid the judgment [Col. 1366A] of which it is said: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.”

In this sentence all that is contained throughout the fields of the holy Scriptures concerning conduct toward enemies is gathered together with extraordinary brevity. It commands us to forgive those who sin against us, so that our sins may be forgiven us by God. It likewise commands us to give benefits, so that eternal life may also be given to us by God.

By saying, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven,” and immediately adding, “Give, and it will be given to you,” he shows that it is not enough merely to forgive those who sin against us unless we also bestow upon them whatever benefits we can.

Whoever bestows temporal or spiritual goods upon others out of divine love, whoever grants pardon to those who sin against him, just as he himself desires to obtain forgiveness from the Lord—such a person undoubtedly becomes an imitator of God.

[Col. 1366B]

“A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will they give into your lap.” Since the Lord urges us to the duty of compassion, he also indicates the measure of future recompense, so that we may devote ourselves all the more to generosity the more certain we are of a full reward.

He says: “A good measure,” that is, a just and equal one; “pressed down,” that is, full; “shaken together,” that is, stirred, or shaken from every side; and “overflowing,” that is, abundant—they will give into your lap.

Who are those who will give a good measure, unless they are the poor to whom we have given benefits? The same meaning is found in what the Truth says elsewhere concerning the poor: [Col. 1366C] “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” and so forth (Luke 16).

The poor themselves do not repay the reward to those who give them alms; rather, Christ does so, for whose love they perform these deeds. Yet the reward is said to be given into the lap by the poor, because they provided the occasion through which the donors of alms could merit that reward from the Lord: either because, being pitifully needy, or because they were importunate in asking, they were sustained by the generosity of the stronger, and some of them were even drawn to the faith of Christ by kindly benefits.

Or, to say something about enemies: many wicked people who rage against the good have been recalled to the way of upright charity by the patience or benevolence of those good people.

It should be noted that the reward is said to be given into our lap. For what we have in our lap we possess securely. Beautifully, therefore, this recompense is said to be given into the lap, so that it may be shown with what security it is to be possessed and with what charity it is to be retained.

[Col. 1366D]

“For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” By the name “measure” we understand the rule of judgment itself. Another Evangelist states this more explicitly, saying: “With what judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7).

But if we judge rashly, will God also judge rashly, though he is a just judge? Or if we measure with an unjust measure, is there also an unjust measure with God, by which it will be measured back to us?

This is said because the rashness by which you harm another must itself harm you, and the justice by which you help another must also, in turn, help you.

This may also be [Col. 1367A] understood simply concerning the giving of alms. Hence the distinguished preacher says to his hearers: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings” (2 Cor. 9). For the more merciful someone has been toward the poor of Christ in this life, the greater the reward he will receive from the Lord in the future.

What we say here concerning the giving of alms must be understood generally of everything we think, say, or accomplish in deed: each person will receive according to his works.

He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?”

The meaning of this verse is connected with that of the preceding sentence, where the command is given to distribute alms and forgive offenses. It is as though he were saying:

[Col. 1367B]

If anger has stirred you against an enemy, or avarice has closed your heart against one who asks alms from you, will you be able to cure his vice by exhorting him, especially when your own mind is held bound by the same vice?

Or do you think that only the one who injured you should be considered guilty, and that you should not also be condemned—the one who does not know how to bear an injury patiently?

Conversely, if his wickedness encounters a mind of yours that is gentle and tranquil, he will be moved to repentance, and you will be endowed with the gift of patience.

“A disciple is not above his master. But everyone who is perfect will be like his master.”

The heavenly Master and Lord of all who live piously is Christ. In him and from him is the discipline of every virtue and of religion. His disciples are all those whom the title of Christianity adorns, according to what they hear from him elsewhere: “Your one master is Christ” (Matt. 23).

[Col. 1367C]

This Master, so great and so singular, became man although he was God. He suffered injuries and did not repay injury in kind, although, being God, he could have punished his detractors by the mere command of his will. Finally, he did not consider it unworthy to undergo death, since he became the author of eternal life.

If, therefore, he who was God patiently endured the injuries inflicted upon him, why should we, his disciples, who are merely human beings and who are capable of investigating many things but accomplishing only a few, disdain to endure insults?

For if we truly wish to be his disciples, we must strive to hold fast to the standard of perfection that we learn from him. A Christian raises himself as though above his master when he disdains to hear insults and attempts to avenge himself by his own strength.

[Col. 1367D]

“But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, while you do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?”

This too must be referred to what precedes, where it is said that a blind man cannot be led by a blind man—that is, that a sinner cannot properly be corrected by one who is guilty of more serious crimes.

Many people, although proud, thieves, robbers, and harboring hatred in their hearts, if they see others disturbed even slightly by an outbreak of anger, as though struck by a speck, and changed from their customary tranquility of mind, or caught in some offense, however slight, judge them severely. They consider their own crimes trivial or nonexistent, while regarding the crimes of others as serious.

Although they possess the Lord’s command prohibiting judgment and condemnation, they, forgetful of it, prefer to judge and condemn rather than amend and correct.

Hence it continues: [Col. 1368A] “Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye?”

The eye in this passage is called the intention of the heart and the clarity of the mind. The speck is anger aroused by a sudden impulse of the soul. The beam is understood as hatred—that is, anger prolonged by lengthy reflection in the heart, as though nourished by constant rains upon a tree.

Just as there is a great difference between the size of a beam and the slenderness of a speck, so there is a corresponding difference between anger and hatred. Hatred is anger grown old, whereas anger is a sudden disturbance of the soul, which is sometimes even proved useful.

For it can happen that, if we are angry with someone, we wish him to be corrected. But it can never happen that we wish the person whom we hate to be corrected or improved.

For this reason the Lord testifies [Col. 1368B] that it is impossible for one who carries a beam in his own eye to remove the speck from his brother’s eye.

It is indeed impossible not to become angry, because man is by nature capable of anger. Hence, by apostolic indulgence, we are permitted to be angry, provided that anger itself, confined within a brief limit, does not exceed its proper bounds. For when he had said, “Be angry,” he immediately added, “and do not sin” (Eph. 4).

There is no difference, however, between hatred and murder, as John bears witness: “He who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

Therefore, as has been stated, one who carries a beam in his own eye cannot remove the speck from his brother’s eye, because no one can correct another person’s anger if he conceals hatred in his own mind.

Accordingly, such a person is rightly rebuked with sharp denunciation when it is said: “Hypocrite, remove the beam from your eye first.”

“Hypocrite” is a Greek word, [Col. 1368C] composed from *hypo* and *crisis*. It is composed of “whole” and “corrupt.” For *hypo* means “false,” while *crisis* in Greek means “judgment.” A hypocrite can therefore be called a pretender who claims for himself the name of justice only in outward appearance.

The name is also derived from paintings, which, expressed through the artificial colors of various pigments, represent only the likeness of real bodies.

A hypocrite may also be called “gilded beneath.” For *hypo* in Greek is rendered in Latin as *sub*, “under,” while *chrysos* means “gold.”

A hypocrite is called not only one who harbors one thing in his heart and does another in his actions, but also one who, although wicked, seeks to rebuke the good. Sometimes such people, though themselves full of wickedness and hatred, wish to appear as advisers of those whom they correct out of hatred.

We must guard against and observe them all the more prudently, the more easily we may be deceived by an outwardly imposed appearance of holiness.

The Lord therefore says: [Col. 1368D] “Hypocrite, remove the beam from your eye first, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

This means: First drive hatred away from yourself, since it is the more serious fault; afterward you will be able more safely to correct the minor faults of the one whom you love.

Meanwhile, we must know and watch with the utmost vigilance that whenever the usefulness of some matter requires someone to be corrected, we should first consider whether we have ever possessed the sin for which we rebuke our brother, or whether we are still entangled in the same sin.

[Col. 1369A]

If we discover that we have never possessed it, let us give thanks to God, by whose gift we were able to avoid it; nevertheless, let us recognize that we are human beings and could have possessed it.

But if we judge that we have committed such a thing and now, by God’s gift, are free from it, let the common weakness of humanity touch our minds. Let us strive to be toward our brother as we wished others to be toward us when we were still like him, and let us care for him with the same compassion by which we know that others helped us.

If, however, we discover that we still persist in the error for which our brother is being rebuked, let us neither rebuke nor reproach him, but groan together with him. Let us invite him not to obey us, but to strive alongside us, and let us hasten together to the remedy of repentance.

[Col. 1369B]

This must be provided for with the greatest care: although the force of correction should proceed in whatever manner is appropriate, its intention must nevertheless be directed toward the salvation and amendment of the one being corrected. Thus outward discipline may be severe toward our brother without the inward warmth of charity wasting away.

For when we contend for the salvation of others, it comes about that we ourselves obtain forgiveness for our sins. Hence the holy teachers, with the most prudent judgment, have placed this also among the means by which sins are loosened, with blessed James as their authority, who says: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5).

But you.

## HOMILY CLXIV ON THE SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From blessed Ambrose’s exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, book IV, no. 68.)*

[Col. 1369C]

At that time, when the crowds pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God, and he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret, etc. (Luke 5.)

Where the Lord bestowed various kinds of healing upon many, etc. For the rest, see Saint Ambrose, *Opera*, vol. II, *Patrologia* XV, col. 1633.

## HOMILY CLXV ON THE SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From blessed Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 7, no. 19.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” etc. (Matt. 5.)

After the Lord had encouraged his hearers, etc. [Col. 1369D] For the rest, see Saint Augustine, *Opera*, vol. III, *Patrologia* XXXIV, col. 1239.

## HOMILY CLXVI ON THE EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the same source.)*

At that time, when a great crowd was with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd,” etc. (Mark 8.)

The height of his divinity, etc. For the rest, see Saint Augustine, *Opera*, vol. V, *Patrologia* XXXIX, col. 1902.

## HOMILY CLXVII ON THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From blessed Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 23, no. 77.)*

[Col. 1370A]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves,” etc. (Matt. 7.)

Concerning the investigation and possession of wisdom, the Lord, etc. For the rest, see Saint Augustine, *Opera*, vol. III, *Patrologia* XXXV, col. 1304, line 45.

## HOMILY CLXVIII ON THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused to him of having wasted his possessions,” etc. (Luke 16.)

Who is the rich man except Christ? Rich in heaven [Col. 1370B] and rich on earth, rich everywhere. Rich, full of grace and truth. “And we have all received from his fullness” (John 1). Rich, with whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Rich in all things and toward all who call upon him.

The steward, however, is each Christian, who in baptism received the stewardship of himself and of his neighbor. For every Christian lives not only for his own sake but also for his neighbor, and is required to render an account not only for his own soul but also for that of the person with whom he lives in this life, exercising himself in body and soul and helping his neighbor by instruction and example.

He seeks not only what is his own, but also what belongs to others. This is the noble and holy stewardship entrusted to Christians. From this comes Christ’s dreadful judgment and the future reckoning.

[Col. 1370C]

“And this man was accused to him of having wasted his possessions.” Every day we are accused before God, because our angels always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18) and report all our deeds to him.

What, then, shall we do? Where shall we hide? Those who see our inmost selves accuse us. Those who behold us and God at every hour denounce us. They behold all our deeds and God, because by looking upon our deeds they report them to God.

There is no barrier, no darkness by which they can be prevented from seeing all our deeds, because the divine light by which they are illumined penetrates everything. For “the light shines in the darkness, and the night will be illumined like the day” (Ps. 138).

“And this man was accused to him of having wasted his possessions.” Who properly dispenses all the good things entrusted to him? Who does not at some time fall asleep?

[Col. 1370D] Sometimes good Homer nods. “In many things we all offend” (James III). And if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John I).

“And he called him and said to him: What is this that I hear about you?” The Lord calls us every day: “Come, children, listen to me” (Psalm XXXIII); “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matthew XI); and: “O men, I call to you, and my voice is addressed to the sons of men” (Proverbs VIII). Every day he speaks to us. He speaks through the prophets, through the apostles, through himself in the Gospel, through teachers, and in the conscience.

“What is this that I hear about you?” He rebukes those who think evil, those who speak evil, those who act perversely, and those who live wickedly. [Col. 1371A] “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship.” For “of every idle word that men have spoken, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew XII).

“Give an account of your stewardship”: what you do with yourself, what you do with your neighbor, what you think in your heart, what sort of word you utter, what pleases you to hear, and upon whom you fix your eyes. “Give an account of your stewardship. You are dissipating my goods; you are using my goods badly; you are giving my goods to strangers. I call, and you do not answer; I extend my hand, and you do not look back. Give an account of your stewardship.”

“For now you can no longer be steward.” You have reached the end; it is the time of judgment and of rendering an account. “Now you can no longer be steward.” You will soon depart from here; you will soon die; now you can no longer be steward. For after this life there is no stewardship. Here, by our stewardship, we serve; there [Col. 1371B] by resting, we receive our reward. Here we acquire what we shall possess there. Here there is labor; there, reward.

“But the steward said within himself: What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me?” Blessed is the one who thinks about the end; blessed is the one who thinks every day that he will die, because “the end of prayer is better than its beginning” (Ecclesiastes VII). And when the saints come to their end in this world, they become everlasting in the heavenly dwelling, for whom the end of life brings the beginning of living.

“What shall I do? How shall I escape from a stewardship badly administered? I cannot dig.” Once the stewardship of this life has ended, no activity remains after this life by which we may merit eternal life. There I can no longer dig, because there it is no longer possible to refresh the poor, visit the sick, or devote oneself to sacred vigils and prayers.

For what else is digging than to cultivate the soil of mind and body through the exercises of holy actions? We dig the earth when we uproot vices from ourselves and plant virtues. This cannot be done after this life, because that time is not suited to repentance but to the recompense of good or evil works.

“I am ashamed to beg.” Let it not be said to me what was said to the foolish virgins: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves” (Matthew XXV). There is good begging, and there is bad begging. Here there is good begging. Here we rightly beg wisdom and instruction from teachers; from the saints we beg in the litanies that they pray for us. In the other life begging is shameful. For who would not be ashamed to say: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (ibid.)? Therefore I am ashamed to beg.

[Col. 1371D] Truly it is a shameful begging, where nothing is recovered and perpetual want of every good accompanies one. Therefore I am ashamed to beg. There begging for another’s good does no good, when one’s own good is lacking altogether. Nor can anyone expect from another what he himself has not merited, since scarcely each person’s own goods suffice for him, and “the righteous man will scarcely be saved” (1 Peter IV). Therefore I am ashamed to beg.

“I know what I shall do, so that when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.” He found salutary counsel at the end, having administered his stewardship badly: namely, to give little in order to receive more, and to be received into the houses of others, since his own resources were failing.

Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” And he said: “A hundred measures of oil.” [Col. 1372A]

We have one common master, all who worship the one God, to whom we all owe whatever good we can do. But because we are all stewards, part of the master’s debt, by the law of our stewardship, is referred to us, so that we are found to be not only debtors to God but also to one another. For we are commanded to love not only God but also our neighbor. We are therefore debtors to God and debtors to our neighbor; yet we owe everything to God, including what we refer to our neighbor, so that whatever we owe, we owe to God.

We possess spiritual goods, and we possess bodily goods. Spiritual goods include faith, justice, charity, and the rest, which we owe to God and to our neighbor. Bodily goods include gold, silver, wheat, wine, and the rest, by which we serve God and help our neighbor.

[Col. 1372B] What can we understand better by oil than spiritual things? Oil is rarer and lighter than the solidity of wheat; it sustains the light and the practice of virtues, illuminates the mind for contemplating the truth, and surpasses all liquids, just as spiritual things surpass bodily things. What is meant by wheat if not bodily things? Indeed, a species often signifies a genus.

The steward first speaks to the debtor of oil, because spiritual things precede bodily things. He owes a hundred measures of oil because he owes God whatever spiritual good he possesses. There are as many measures of oil as there are kinds of spiritual good. The vessel containing a hundred measures of oil signifies all the kinds of spiritual goods. For the number one hundred often signifies fullness, and a finite number is often used for the infinite.

He therefore owes a hundred measures of oil who owes God the perfection of spiritual good. But much of what is owed to God concerns our neighbor. For we greatly offend unless we render faith, justice, and charity to our neighbor.

When, therefore, the steward orders fifty to be written from the hundred measures of oil, what is owed to God is confirmed in writing, because what is owed to him is not remitted; he does not order it to be written because it is remitted. He remits what is his own and leaves what belongs to God. With regard to what is owed to him, he makes the debtor secure; with regard to what is owed to God, he makes him anxious.

Thus it follows: “He said to him: Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” As if he were saying openly: “What you owe me, I remit to you; what you owe God, take care to record. And you who stand in pride, sit down quickly and humble yourself; and what you used to regard as insignificant or, through forgetfulness, considered worthless, write upon the tablets of your heart and keep in your memory, so that you may repent frequently and make satisfaction until that debt itself is remitted to you.”

“Sit down quickly,” that is, do not put it off from day to day. “Write fifty”: the number of repentance and remission. Hence the fiftieth year is the year of remission, and the fiftieth psalm is penitential. Fifty are therefore written, and fifty are remitted. The like number signifies a like offense against God and man.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”; this is the first and great commandment. “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XXII). For those whose love is alike have an offense that is alike.

[Col. 1373A] It follows: “Then he said to another: And you, how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.” A *cadus* is a measure of liquids, and a *corus* a measure of seeds.

We should be very fearful, since we owe our neighbors the fullness of bodily goods: we owe them, and yet we do not pay; we owe the whole, and scarcely pay a little. What, then, shall we do? If we cannot pay all that we owe to others, let us at least remit what is owed to us.

Thus it follows: “He said to him: Take your account, and write eighty.” For one who writes eighty in place of a hundred remits a fifth, because in bodily matters what is owed to one’s neighbor is what the five bodily senses demand. What is left through the number eight is entrusted in writing to divine grace.

“You have taken what is mine; you have carried off what I lent; you have denied what was entrusted to you.” [Col. 1373B] “If I remit it to you, what difference does it make to me? Write eighty,” that is, commit to memory that you still need the pardon of divine grace.

For the grace of the Gospel is signified by the number eight, just as the austerity of the Law is signified by the number seven. But one merits the grace of the number eight who keeps the commandments signified by ten. Thus, through the number eight joined to fifteen, we understand the grace implanted in the commandment, so that the one who writes eighty reaches the grace of eight through keeping the Decalogue.

And the Lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. A wondrous thing! He is a bad steward, yet he is praised; he administered badly, yet he is spared; he did not correct what he had done, yet he is forgiven. Truly he acted prudently, because he remitted little in order to receive more: he remitted temporal things in order to receive eternal things.

For he had heard: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke VI); and: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI). Truly he acted prudently who contrived to make God his debtor, so that he might demand from him the remission owed to him, because he had remitted. He acted prudently because he made the one to whom he was obligated obligated to himself; and the one whom he had had as a harsh exactor he now had as a merciful debtor, so that he could say confidently: “Forgive, because I have forgiven; repay the pardon you owe, because I have granted pardon.”

“For the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.” The children of light labor and scarcely earn their reward; they run and scarcely reach the prize; they give birth in travail and scarcely escape. The children of this age, after frauds, enticements, and unlawful behavior, merely remit, and they hold God as their debtor; they spare, and they are spared; they pardon, and they are pardoned.

Therefore the children of this age are more prudent than the children of light in their generation—that is, when they are regenerated for God and renewed by spiritual life.

“And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” Mammon, that is, riches, are called riches of iniquity because they are not acquired without iniquity, and because it is unjust to reclaim for private use what the Lord created for common use.

Hence it is written: “Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia” (Habakkuk III)—that is, because of the acquisition of riches I saw men made tents of darkness, that is, of vices and demons. Those who could have been tents of virtues by pursuing poverty have become tents of vices in order to gather iniquity.

Who does not see many people committing perjury, committing murder, plotting deceit against their neighbors, and betraying their household goods and their masters because of riches? These are the tents of Ethiopia on account of iniquity.

But since the steward has acted above with regard to both spiritual and bodily things, why does the Lord conclude his parable by speaking only of bodily things? We more quickly forgive an injury than money that has been lent; we more easily give our faith than our property; we are readier to put away hatred than to spend what is ours.

Therefore the Lord, having instructed us in mercy through the parable, concludes his discourse with that aspect of mercy which he knows is more difficult among human beings. At the end he exhorts us more earnestly to that toward which he sees us less inclined, because “the end of prayer is better than its beginning.”

Let us therefore make friends from the riches of iniquity by distributing them to the poor and by remitting them to debtors and to those who have taken them away.

But since some riches of iniquity are possessed by paternal inheritance, others are acquired through honest labor, and others are usurped through crime or impiety, friends certainly are not to be made from those that come from crime or impiety. Nor should anyone think to seek helpers for salvation from riches that he has amassed through an iniquitous trade.

For it is written: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, those offered because of crime” (Proverbs XXI). “The offering of one who sacrifices from iniquity is defiled,” and so is “the one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father.”

When, therefore, we are commanded to make friends from mammon of iniquity, we must distinguish them, so that we understand the riches that come from inheritance or honest labor. [Col. 1374C] Yet these too are called riches of iniquity, as though of inequality, because when we hold them as private property, we do not maintain equality with other human beings.

There are therefore the riches from which we are commanded to make friends: riches both of iniquity and of justice. They are riches of iniquity with respect to God, who creates all things for common use; but they are riches of justice with respect to the world, because they are possessed by human beings according to worldly justice.

Riches that are justly possessed on earth are therefore unjust with respect to divine justice and just with respect to earthly justice. Earthly justice defends each person’s ownership of his possession; through earthly justice human beings gather what is their own, while through divine justice they make their possessions common.

[Col. 1374D] But riches that arise from crime are altogether unjust. Divine justice does not approve them, and earthly justice also condemns them. Such riches, acquired through crime, must in no way be offered to God. Yet they must quickly be returned, indeed thrown away, lest the evildoer be found to persist in an evil course already begun.

“So that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.” Here he explains what he had said: “They may receive you into their houses.” The eternal mansions are the houses of those to whom mercy is shown. They are called their houses not by possession but by causation: not because they possess them, since perhaps they will not possess them, but because they are the cause whereby their benefactors possess them.

They therefore receive us into their houses when they cause us to enter the eternal mansions. We regard these mansions as theirs because we receive them only through them. They repay them to us, so to speak, for the benefits they received; and because they received temporal mercies, they become dispensers of eternal recompense, through him who rendered on their behalf what they owed: our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CLXIX. FOR THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the Works of blessed Pope Gregory.)*

At that time, when Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “For if you had known, even you,” etc. (Luke XIX.)

“I wish, if I can, to run briefly through the brief reading from the holy Gospel in a brief discourse,” etc. For the remainder, see Saint Gregory, *Works*, volume II, *Patrologia* LXXVI, col. 1294.

## HOMILY CLXX. FOR THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the Works of blessed Augustine.)*

At that time Jesus spoke a parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others, saying: “Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a publican,” etc. (Luke XVIII.)

The reading of the holy Gospel builds us up for prayer and faith, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Augustine, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XXXVIII, col. 655.

## HOMILY CLXXI. FOR THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

[Col. 1375C]

At that time two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican, etc. (Luke XVIII.)

The meaning of this reading adheres throughout to what came before, where the Lord urges his disciples to persist in prayer by introducing the parable of the judge who does not fear God and the widow who cries out, although he concluded it in this way: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” Lest anyone then improperly flatter himself on account of his faith, he immediately added a lesson in humility, showing that humility surpasses all the exercises of good works and is the mother of the virtues, just as pride is plainly the head of all vices.

To declare the singular merit of humility, therefore, he used a comparison between two men, praising humility in one and condemning pride in the other. “Two men,” he says, “went up into the temple to pray,” etc.

Seeing certain Jews exalt themselves through a feigned holiness and, on that account—as though they possessed superior merit—prefer themselves to others, he brought forward this parable, in which the virtue of humility is especially commended and presumptuous pride is shown to be something that must be avoided.

The evangelist says: “He spoke this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others: Two men went up into the temple.”

That famous temple, renowned throughout the world, which had been built by Solomon in Jerusalem at lavish expense, stood in the more elevated part of the city, namely, on Mount Moriah. It was therefore beautifully said that they “went up,” because the city of Jerusalem was situated on the slope of a mountain—on a descent—partly on the mountain and partly in the valley. The Lord’s temple, as we have said, was placed in the higher part of the city, and whoever wished to come to it had necessarily to reach it by ascending.

Hence we read below: “This man went down to his house justified rather than the other,” that is, from the temple; or the publican went down justified rather than the Pharisee, that is, in comparison with the Pharisee. And in another Gospel we read that a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke X).

The reason for their ascent is also added: “To pray.” For it is established that the temple had been built so that the people might offer there both their first fruits and the other things prescribed in the Law, and also at appointed times make petitions for themselves and the security of their kingdom.

“Of these two men who went up into the temple to pray, one was a Pharisee and the other a publican.”

The Pharisees were the clerics and priests of the Jews. Because they separated themselves from the others as though they possessed holier and greater merit, they are interpreted as “the separated,” their name being borrowed from Pharez, the son of Judah.

This man is shown to have been one of them: swollen with arrogance, he went up into the temple not so much to pray to God as to praise himself.

Publicans were so called either because they engaged in public vices, or because they served public business, paying taxes to the state—that is, tax collectors—or even because they were all those who accumulated riches for themselves by lawful and unlawful means.

Then this publican belongs among the members of the holy woman, the Church, mentioned above, concerning whom it is said: “Will God not avenge his elect who cry out to him?” (Luke XVIII.) The Pharisee, however, belongs among those concerning whom the fearful sentence is added at the conclusion: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

“The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus within himself.” The fact that the Pharisee is said to have prayed standing refers to the custom of that people, who, when they came to God’s temple, were accustomed to pray not only prostrate but standing upright with the whole body, as the posture of the body testifies.

“God, I give you thanks that I am not like the rest of men.”

[Col. 1376D] The holy teachers enumerate four forms by which every swelling of the arrogant is detected.

The first form is when a person thinks he possesses a good that he does not possess. The Apostle’s statement indirectly strikes at this, saying: “If anyone thinks that he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Galatians VI).

The second form is when someone believes that he possesses by himself the good that he does possess, plainly imitating the devil, who in his elation said: “I do not know the Lord, and I made myself.” The Apostle’s statement rebukes him: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians IV.)

The third is when someone knows that the good he possesses was given to him from heaven, yet trusts that he received it on account of his own merits, contrary to the apostle Paul, who says: “Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans XI.)

The fourth, likewise, is when someone thinks he possesses a good in a singular way and, despising others, desires to appear specially good.

The Pharisee is shown to have suffered above all from this disease. Under a kind of generalization, placing everyone below himself and weighing his own merits as greater, he preferred himself even to the praying publican.

“God,” he says, “I give you thanks that I am not like the rest of men: extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican.”

Extortioners are those who violently seize what belongs to others; the unjust are those who do not keep the law of God, which is the standard of perfect and supreme justice; adulterers are those who violate another’s marriage bed.

“I fast twice in the week.” If anyone wonders why he boasts that he fasted twice in the week, the question can readily be resolved in the following sense.

It is clear that the Jews reckoned all their days from the Sabbath in this manner: the first of the Sabbath, the second of the Sabbath, and so the remaining days from the Sabbath were named up to the Sabbath, just as we are accustomed to say “the first feria” and “the second feria.” Here the name “Sabbath” may appropriately signify the entire week, which is closed by the Sabbath. No one could be so foolish as to think that he fasted twice on one day, which is plainly impossible. Thus, “twice in the Sabbath” means that he fasted on two days of the week.

“I give tithes of all that I possess.” The Law prescribed that the children of Israel should give the Lord tithes annually from all their possessions. But the scribes and Pharisees, so that they might appear holier than those who gave tithes, tithed not only the produce of their crops but even the smallest herbs.

Hence elsewhere they are rightly rebuked by the Lord, who says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew XXIII)—that is, the higher commandments of the Law, namely love of God and neighbor, or judgment and mercy.

Here we should briefly recall that the prophet Ezekiel, in the mystical vision he reports having seen beside the river Chebar, says among other things that he saw four living creatures full of eyes before and behind (Ezekiel I). Although these creatures are filled with manifold mystical meanings, they specifically bear the symbol of the saints.

These creatures are therefore rightly said to be eyed on every side, because the activity of the saints is everywhere guarded with great vigilance. They foresee desirable goods in such a way that they carefully avoid every evil. Thus they devote themselves to earthly acts of service without separating their minds from heavenly things. Finally, they know how to enjoy temporal things while always directing their attention to eternal things. They are so watchful and prudent even in the good works they perform because they know that the frauds of the exceedingly crafty enemy can also insinuate themselves into good works.

But those who are moved by little or no concern for themselves, while attending to some matters, frequently neglect others. They differ greatly from these holy creatures because they do not prudently extend the eye of vigilance to everything.

This is shown to have happened to the Pharisee. He applied his keen eye to giving thanks to God, giving alms, and fasting, but he negligently grew sluggish in observing humility. Like one who carefully fortifies every entrance of a city but leaves behind a breach, he left a scar of pride through which he became subject to the plunder of the savage enemy.

For just as it is of no benefit that an entire city is guarded against an enemy assault if a single opening is left through which the enemy may enter, so it does no good to gather many virtues if we leave one vice in ourselves through which the devil may seize us.

“And the publican, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes toward heaven, but was beating his breast.”

As many signs of pride preceded in the Pharisee, so many indications of humility are subsequently described in the publican. The Pharisee proclaimed his merits and displayed himself as superior to others; this man, by confessing his sins, lowering his eyes, and beating his breast, wins the favor of the Godhead.

He stood far off because, truly recognizing himself as sinful and profane, he did not dare approach the sanctuary. He stood far off because he knew that by sinning he had withdrawn far from God.

He did not wish to lift his eyes toward heaven because he knew that he had gravely offended the one who is in heaven by looking upon unlawful things. He considered himself unworthy to behold God or God’s temple with the same eyes with which he had looked upon so many unlawful objects of desire. He did not yet dare to join the number of those who, trusting in the forgiveness of sins, say with the Psalmist: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens” (Psalm CXXII).

He was also beating his breast because he knew that he had thought many wicked thoughts there, by which he had offended God. As though exacting punishment from himself, he did not so much obtain forgiveness of his crimes as wrest it from the Lord.

“God,” he says, “be merciful to me, a sinner.” The prayer is very brief, but commended by wondrous and powerful devotion. It changed the judgment of the Judge and suddenly made the publican righteous from being unjust.

Hence it follows: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.”

Great confidence is rightly granted to penitents through the example of this publican. Although he came to the temple unjust, because he humbly mourned his former sins, he departed from the temple justified.

When it says “rather than the other,” the authorities explain it in two ways: either “rather than the other” means from that temple, or “rather than the other” is to be understood as “more than he.”

Since these matters are clear in their literal sense, let us seek whatever mystery remains.

These two men are types of two peoples. The Pharisee, vainly exalting himself on account of the excellence of his merits, figuratively represents the Jewish people, who swelled with pride over their observance of the Law they had received and arrogantly refused to receive the coming of their Redeemer, who came to them in humility.

Among the other things that the enormity of their sins demanded, this people arrived at the point where those who had once received angels as guests in their forefathers now heard, in the temple, those who no longer wished to dwell with them crying out: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

The publican, however, who by humbling himself and confessing his sins merited exaltation, likewise represents the Gentile people. Having received the truth of apostolic preaching, that people abandoned the portents of false gods and sought through worthy repentance to make its Creator propitious.

It was fittingly granted this people’s exaltation that the one who had previously been the devil’s slave should become a son of God. Because, having been converted by God, it recognized its sins and perfectly repented of its crimes, it received not only forgiveness but also the privilege of preceding the Jewish people in the dignity of faith.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

This sentence can be understood of both peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile. The one, as has been said, became proud of divine benefits and deserved to be humbled; the other, humbling itself devoutly in confession of sins, deserved to be exalted.

It can most appropriately be understood also of every proud and humble person, in agreement with Solomon’s statement: “Before destruction the heart of a man is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Proverbs XVIII).

Yet we see many flourishing in the honors and riches of this age and persevering in them to the end. Conversely, we see some laboring in poverty and want and remaining in that same destitution until the end of life.

Since some remain in their initial prosperity and others in their former poverty until the end of life, how is it true that the Lord says that everyone who is exalted will be humbled and everyone who is humbled will be exalted?

But because Truth cannot be deceived, we must understand that, even if this does not always appear to be fulfilled in the present, we have no doubt that it will be completed in the future.

Everyone who exalts himself in the present life by refusing to submit to the divine commandments will then be humbled on the day of judgment, joined with the proud and impious, and will hear from the Lord: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew XXV).

But whoever here strives to humble himself for the love of God, imitating the one who says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI), will be exalted at the future judgment by the Lord when he merits hearing the desired words: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew XXV).

We must gather from the humility of the publican not only an example of humility; conversely, we must also take a model of humility from the words of the proud Pharisee.

The Pharisee considered the evils of others and began to display his own good deeds. We, on the contrary, must weigh our own evils and devoutly consider the good deeds of others.

Thus, just as the Pharisee, preferring himself to the others, was humbled to his ruin because he despised them, so we, judging ourselves inferior to the good works of the faithful, may be exalted through imitating them and advance toward glory.

When we have attained such a form of devotion, let us strive to recite frequently in our daily prayers this prayer composed by blessed Bede, brief but altogether salutary:

> “Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the countless servants of yours who are exalted through contempt of the world, glorious through the merit of justice, angelic in the praise of chastity—or even like many of those who, after public crimes, by repenting have merited to become devoted to you. And even if I do anything good through the gift of your grace, I do not know with what purpose I do it, nor by what strict judgment it is weighed by you.”

But you, Lord …

## HOMILY CLXXII. FOR THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the Works of the venerable Bede, priest.)*

At that time Jesus, departing from the borders of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the borders of the Decapolis, etc. (Mark VII.)

“That deaf and mute man,” etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede the priest, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 234.

## HOMILY CLXXIII. FOR THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it,” etc. (Luke X.)

The Lord reveals the heavenly mystery: it pleased God to reveal his grace more to little ones than to the wise of this world. The apostle Paul set this forth more fully in writing, saying: “Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?” (1 Cor. 1). For since the world did not know God’s wisdom through wisdom, it pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching, to save those who believe.

Let us therefore understand by “little one” one who does not know how to exalt himself or, in ornate speeches, to flaunt the skill of his own wisdom—as most philosophers do. A little one was he who said:

> “Lord, my heart is not exalted,  
> nor are my eyes lifted up.  
> I have not entered upon great matters,  
> nor upon things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130).

And so that you might know that this “little one” was not such by age or understanding, but by his humility and a certain avoidance of boastfulness, he added: “But I have exalted my soul.” You see how lofty this little one was, how sublime in the summit of his virtues?

The Apostle wishes us to be such little ones when he says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3).

A most beautiful passage concerning faith follows, when he says that everything has been handed over to him by his Father. When you read “everything,” you acknowledge the omnipotent one—not one unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you read “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom, by nature and by right, all things belonging to the one substance are proper—not bestowed upon him by grace as a gift.

He added: “No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore he called those eyes blessed to whom it was granted to see Christ, God’s salvation.

But so that you may know that just as the Son reveals the Father to whomever he wishes, so the Father also reveals the Son to whomever he wishes, listen to the Lord Jesus himself praising Peter because he had confessed him to be the Son of God:

> “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

Closely connected with these words is the passage in which those who consider themselves learned in the law are exposed. They possess the words of the law but do not understand its force. From the very first chapter of the law he demonstrates that they are ignorant of the law, proving that from the beginning the law itself proclaimed both the Father and the Son and also announced the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, saying:

> “You shall love the Lord your God,  
> and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Therefore the Lord said to the lawyer: “Do this, and you will live.” But he, as though he did not know who his neighbor was—for he did not believe in Christ—replied: “And who is my neighbor?” Thus whoever does not know Christ does not know the law either. For how can he know the law when he is ignorant of the truth, since the law announces the truth?

> “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.”

To explain more clearly the passage set before us, let us recall the ancient history of the city of Jericho. We remember, therefore, that Jericho, as we read in the book called *Joshua son of Nun*, was a great city, enclosed by marvelous walls—walls that could be penetrated neither by iron nor by a battering ram. In it lived Rahab the prostitute. She received the spies sent by Joshua as guests, instructed them with her counsel, replied to the citizens who demanded that they had departed, and hid them on the roof. To rescue herself and her people from the destruction of the city, she tied a scarlet cord in the window. The city’s own impregnable walls, however, collapsed at the sound of the seven priestly trumpets and the united shouting of the jubilant people.

Observe how each person preserves his particular duty: the spy his vigilance, the prostitute the mystery, the victor his faith, the priest his religious service. The spies do not fear danger for the sake of praise; she does not betray those whom she has received, even in danger. Joshua is more concerned to preserve faith than to conquer, and he first commands the prostitute’s safety before the city’s destruction. The weapons of the priest are the insignia of religion.

Who would not consider it a complete miracle that, from the entire city, no one was saved except the one whom the prostitute delivered? This is the truth of the simple history [or: “the historical truth”]; but if it is considered more deeply, it signifies wondrous mysteries.

For Jericho is a figure of this world. Into it Adam, expelled from paradise—that is, from that heavenly Jerusalem—descended through the fall of transgression. He migrated from the realm of life to the underworld; and it was not a change of place but a change of conduct that made him an exile from his nature’s proper condition. Adam was changed far from the state in which he had enjoyed untroubled blessedness. When he turned aside into worldly sins, he fell among robbers—among whom he would not have fallen had he not made himself liable to them by straying from the heavenly commandment.

Who are these robbers except the angels of night and darkness, who sometimes transform themselves into angels of light but cannot persevere in that guise? First they strip away the garments of spiritual grace that we have received, and then they are accustomed to inflict wounds. For if we preserve undefiled the garments we have put on, we cannot feel the robbers’ blows.

Take care, therefore, lest you first be stripped, as Adam was stripped when he was deprived of the guardianship of the heavenly commandment and divested of the covenant of faith, and thus received a mortal wound. The whole human race would have perished in him had that Samaritan, descending, not healed his grievous wounds.

This Samaritan is no ordinary one: the man whom the priest and the Levite had despised, he himself did not despise. Nor should you despise him because of the name of his sect, when you admire him through the interpretation of the word. For the name “Samaritan” means “guardian”; that is its interpretation. And who is a guardian except the one of whom it is said: “The Lord guards the little ones” (Ps. 114)?

Thus, just as there is one kind of Jew outwardly and another inwardly, so there is one kind of Samaritan outwardly and another secretly.

This Samaritan, therefore, descended. Who is the one who descended from heaven except he who ascended into heaven—the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3)?

Seeing the half-dead man whom no one had previously been able to heal—just as the woman suffering from a flow of blood, who had spent all her resources on physicians—he came up to him; that is, by taking upon himself our condition, he became our neighbor through compassion and drew near through the gift of mercy.

“And he bound his wounds, pouring in wine and oil.” This physician has many medicines with which he is accustomed to heal. His word is a medicine. One word of his binds wounds; another soothes them with oil; another pours in wine. He binds wounds with a sterner commandment; he soothes them by the remission of sin; as wine, he pricks them through the warning of judgment.

“And he placed him,” it says, “on his own beast.” Hear how he places you upon it. He bears our sins and suffers for us, and the shepherd placed the weary sheep upon his shoulders. For man was made like the beasts of burden. Therefore he placed us upon his own beast, so that we would not be like a horse or a mule, and so that, by assuming our body, he might abolish the weaknesses of our flesh.

Finally, he led us into an inn, though we had become beasts. An inn is a place into which those exhausted by a long journey ordinarily withdraw. The Lord therefore led him into the inn—he who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap (Ps. 112).

And he cared for him, lest the sick man fail to observe the commandments he had received—in which the she-ass recognized the manger of her lord (Isa. 1).

But this Samaritan could not remain long on earth; he had to return to the place from which he had descended. “On the next day,” therefore. What is this “next day” except perhaps the day of the Lord’s resurrection, of which it is said: “This is the day that the Lord has made” (Ps. 117)?

“He brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: ‘Take care of him.’” What are these two denarii except perhaps the two Testaments, which bear within themselves the impress of the eternal king, and by whose price our wounds are healed? For we were redeemed with precious blood, so that we might avoid the wounds of the final death.

The innkeeper received these two denarii. Although it is not unreasonable to understand them also as the four forms of these books, who is this innkeeper? Perhaps the one who says: “I consider these things as dung, in order that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3), so that he might care for the wounded man.

The innkeeper, therefore, is the one who says: “Christ sent me to evangelize” (1 Cor. 1). Innkeepers are those to whom it is said: “Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature”; and: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved”—saved, certainly, from death; saved from the wound inflicted by the robbers.

Blessed is that innkeeper who can heal another’s wounds. Blessed is the one to whom Jesus said: “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you.”

Paul was a good steward. His discourses and letters overflow, as it were, beyond the account he had received. He carried out the Lord’s moderate command with almost immoderate labor of mind and body, so that through the administration of spiritual instruction he might raise many from a serious illness.

A good innkeeper, therefore, is he whose inn is the place in which the donkey recognized its master’s manger, and in which flocks of lambs are enclosed, lest, while ravening wolves growl at the folds, entry into the sheepfolds become easy.

He promises that he will repay the wages. When will you return, Lord, except on the day of judgment? For although you are always everywhere, standing in our midst and unseen by us, there will nevertheless be a time when all flesh will look upon you as you return.

Repay, then, what you owe. Blessed are those to whom you are debtor. Would that we might be worthy debtors! Would that we might be able to repay what we have received, and that neither the office of priesthood nor the ministry might exalt us.

How will you repay, good Jesus? You promised that abundant reward awaits the good in heaven; yet you also repay when you say:

> “Well done, good servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25).

Therefore, since no one is more a neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as Lord, and let us love him as neighbor. For nothing is so near as the head is to its members.

Let us also love the one who is an imitator of Christ; let us love the one who has compassion on another’s poverty through the unity of the body. Kinship does not make a neighbor, but mercy does, because mercy is according to nature. For nothing is so in accord with nature as to help one who shares our nature.

## HOMILY CLXXIV. ON THE SAME SUNDAY.

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see,” etc. (Luke 10).

It is characteristic, and in a certain sense proper, to divine Scripture to join what follows to what precedes and, from knowledge of what has already been set forth, to shape an understanding of what follows in proper order. Therefore, in order to understand the sequence of this reading fully, we must retrace what the holy Evangelist said a little earlier. There we read that, when the disciples returned from their preaching mission and, as is customary among human beings, rejoiced that [Col. 1383D] even the demons were subjected to them, the Lord said to them: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you, but rejoice because your names are written in heaven.” After a brief intervening passage, turning to the disciples, he said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.”

In these words, the chief question is whether the eyes of all who could see Christ are thought to belong to this blessedness, since not only the good and faithful but also the wicked and unbelieving could see him, and were exposed not merely to seeing him but even to inflicting insults upon him. To resolve the difficulty of this question, it is necessary to distinguish carefully between the two kinds of vision in the Lord. He appeared in one way to the spiritual apostles, and in another to the scribes, Pharisees, [Col. 1384A] and carnal crowds. The apostles and the other faithful, while recognizing that he was a human being, did not doubt that he was also true God. This is made clear by the apostle Peter, who answered the Lord on behalf of them all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

The Pharisees, however, believed only what they saw. They saw with bodily eyes and believed him to be merely an ordinary man. I say “believed” because they wanted human beings to believe this; otherwise, instructed by the Law and the prophets, they had no doubt that he was the Christ. But because they feared losing the human glory they possessed, they were afraid to confess him as the Christ. Or alternatively: the Pharisees, judging the Lord solely by bodily sight, understood nothing divine in him with their blinded minds. Consequently, they did not fear pursuing him or assailing him with injuries, insults, [Col. 1384B] and reproaches.

Therefore, it is not the eyes of those who thought him merely human that are called blessed, but the eyes of the apostles and the faithful, who were deemed worthy to behold Christ in the beauty of his divinity—that is, those who believed that he was both true God and true man. Concerning them, speaking earlier to the Father, he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI)—that is, to the humble and gentle apostles. Although they saw him surrounded by ordinary human weakness, they nevertheless believed and understood that, hidden in the man, there was one God with the Father.

Happy also are the eyes of those who, without doubt sharing this blessedness with the apostles, after every outpouring of vice has been wiped away [Col. 1384C] and every stain’s moisture has been thoroughly refined, are deemed worthy to contemplate God with the most purified vision of the mind. They hasten not only to know the Lord through faith, together with many others, but also, insofar as he permits, to contemplate wisely the nature of his divinity. For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.

He calls the saints and the righteous “kings”: those who know how to govern and order all bodily movements and all desires of the soul according to the will of their Creator, using the body as their servant under the command of the soul. But since it is evident that God was seen by the shepherds of ancient times, what does it mean when it is said: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it”?

Abraham certainly [Col. 1384D] saw God, whom he received as a guest when he appeared several times, even in the persons of three angels (Gen. XVIII). Moses too, as Scripture testifies, was accustomed to speak with God face to face, as a man speaks with his friend (Exod. XXXIII). Isaiah likewise, with his great voice, said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne” (Isa. VI). Micah and many other prophets likewise most truthfully affirm that God appeared to them. Hence they were called “seers,” and nearly the whole of the rest of Scripture demonstrates that almost all the ancient fathers saw God.

If, then, the holy fathers and prophets saw God, as Scripture testifies, what does the Lord mean when he says: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see”?

But seeing through faith is one thing, and seeing by [Col. 1385A] direct vision another. The saints mentioned above saw almighty God, but through a mirror, through images, and in created things subject to them. The teachers affirm that all the manifestations said to have been made to the fathers in the Old Testament were carried out through inferior creatures—that is, through angels. For if the saints saw God in his divinity as he is, without any images, what does it mean that Moses, as we have already said, spoke with the Lord face to face, yet earnestly entreated the Lord, saying: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me plainly, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII)? By seeking to see the one whom he wished to see plainly, he clearly showed that until then he had seen him through images and figures.

The blessed Stephen likewise says of this same Moses [Col. 1385B]: “This is the Moses who was with the angel who appeared to him in the bush” (Acts VII). But the holy apostles always had the Lord present, clinging to him with complete familiarity and with the greatest intimacy in their daily association. Whatever they wished to know, they learned by asking the Lord—not through a mirror or enigmas. Therefore, they are rightly preferred in the law of blessedness to all the saints of earlier times, hearing the Lord say: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

For all those who are said to have seen God in the Old Testament died according to faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar. It must also be understood that, as the ages advanced, the growth of divine knowledge increased. God appeared [Col. 1385C] to Abraham, but long afterward, when he appeared to Moses, he said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and I did not disclose my name, Adonai, to them” (Exod. III). By these words Moses is shown to have known something more of God than the fathers who preceded him.

The blessed David, born many centuries later, openly declares: “I have understood more than the elders” (Ps. CXVIII). This means plainly: “More subtly than all the patriarchs and prophets who came before me, I have understood something of the majesty of God.”

What, then, should be said of the holy apostles, who were taught by God’s wisdom itself and through it, and who learned fully all that human wisdom could bear concerning heavenly and divine things? The words of the ancient saints testify to what they desired most greatly: to see God present [Col. 1385D] in the flesh. They declare that with all their affections they longed to see the Son of God incarnate.

Thus Isaiah, burning with a great and incomparable desire to see God, cried out: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. LXIV). David too, burning with equal desire, said: “Lord, incline your heavens and come down” (Ps. CXLIII). Each of them desired, if it could be, to see the incarnate Son of God in his own time.

It should also be noted that those whom Luke in the present reading calls “prophets and kings,” Matthew, speaking more distinctly elsewhere, calls “prophets and righteous men” (Matt. XIII). They are the great kings who are also righteous: those who know how not to yield and succumb to the movements of their temptations, but to govern [Col. 1386A] them and rule over them.

And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and said: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” This lawyer—that is, teacher of the Law—took the occasion for testing the Lord from the Lord’s own words, which had earlier been addressed especially to the disciples: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). Hearing this and wishing his own name also to be inscribed in heaven, he asked what he ought to do in order to possess eternal life. For he understood that being written in heaven means nothing other than being inscribed in the memory of eternity.

But since the Lord had been questioned by a lawyer, it was appropriate for him to send the lawyer back to knowledge of the Law, so that he might answer himself in his own words. [Col. 1386B] Hence it follows: “Jesus said to him: What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” Since he himself was a teacher of the Law, as has been said, the Lord questioned him about the Law itself.

But the lawyer did not so much answer the Lord as untie for himself the knot of the question that had been proposed: “You shall love,” he said, “the Lord your God with all your heart”—that is, with your entire understanding—“and with all your soul”—that is, with your entire will, or with everything by which you live and understand—“and with all your strength”—that is, with all your power—“and with all your mind”—that is, with your entire memory or reason. “And your neighbor as yourself.”

After love of God, love of neighbor is rightly placed second. Its measure is now clearly determined, since we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves. For no limit is established in love of God; rather, we are commanded to love him with [Col. 1386C] all the faculties of mind and body. The apostle Paul says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. XV).

Therefore, when the Lord deigns to answer the lawyer who was testing him, he teaches our ignorance. In that answer he shows us the road to the heavenly homeland. When he says to the one who tested him and expounded the commandment of love, “You have answered rightly; do this and you will live,” he plainly declares that we can reach eternal life through love alone, provided that we keep it not merely in word but in deed: namely, by loving God with all our heart, with all our soul, with all our strength, and with all our mind.

We also love our neighbor as ourselves if we do for our neighbors everything that we wish them to do for us.

[Col. 1386D] Furthermore, it should be understood that the whole Decalogue, in which the perfection of the entire divine Law consists, is contained in these two statements of love. In the Decalogue there are three commandments pertaining to love, and seven by which the practice of love is instructed. Hence the Apostle says: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the prophets” (Rom. XV).

Therefore, no excuse based on ignorance is now available to anyone, nor is anyone left with the argument that fulfilling God’s commandments is impossible. For all the commandments of the Law and the Gospel commend love. Love alone is commanded in each commandment, and love in its entirety is commanded in all of them. Whoever maintains it in the order in which it must be observed toward God and according to God will certainly fulfill the whole sum of the Law and the Gospel, which depends upon it.

[Col. 1387A] For love alone begins the virtues, love alone advances them, and love alone perfects them. Thus it is rightly said of it by the Psalmist: “The saints shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII).

But while the Lord approves the lawyer’s answer and unties the knot of the question that had been proposed, he shows us by what path we ought to proceed toward eternal life. Yet the lawyer, seeing that the Lord had praised him and desiring still greater approval, asks again whom he ought to know as his neighbor. This is what the Gospel says: “But he, wishing to justify himself”—that is, to show himself just and wise.

He was not worthy to belong to those of whom the Lord had earlier said to the Father, “You have revealed these things to little ones” (Luke X), that is, to the gentle apostles. Rather, he belonged to those of whom he said: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent,” namely, the [Col. 1387B] scribes and Pharisees.

Because he had been praised by the Lord, as has been said, for answering well, and because he had acquired from this a small measure of conceit, he wished to show himself just and said to the Lord: “And who is my neighbor?”

This teacher of the Law asks whether the one who is related merely by blood and bodily kinship is to be understood as a neighbor, or rather every person who shows mercy to another. The Lord answered him in such a way as to teach that every person who has compassion on another is that person’s neighbor; and at the same time he clearly showed that he himself had deigned to become our neighbor through the humanity he assumed.

What the Lord did is then disclosed in order, when it is added: “But Jesus, taking him up, said.” The verb “take up” (*suscipio*) is [Col. 1387C] understood in two ways. Sometimes it means “to receive,” as in: “Simeon took Jesus into his arms” (Luke II). At other times it means “to answer,” as in the present passage, when it says: “Jesus, taking up [the matter]”—that is, answering—“said: A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.”

When the lawyer asked the Lord who his neighbor was, the Lord set before him a parable about a man going down from Jerusalem to the city of Jericho. On the road he was stripped and wounded by robbers; a Levite and a priest, who belonged to his own people, found him but passed by without wishing to show him mercy. A certain Samaritan, however, who belonged to another people, passed by, was moved by mercy, bound his wounds, placed [Col. 1387D] him on his own beast, took him to his inn—that is, to his lodging—and cared for him.

On the following day he gave two denarii to the innkeeper, namely, his host, and asked him to care for the wounded man, promising to repay him his reward when he returned.

After presenting this parable, the Lord asked the teacher of the Law which of the three had been neighbor to the man who had been wounded: the Levite or the priest, who were of the same people, indeed of the same city, but had not shown mercy; or rather the foreign Samaritan, who had shown him mercy.

The scribe’s answer plainly confirms that no one is more truly our neighbor than the one who has mercy upon us, and that the Lord commands such a person to go and strive to act in the same way.

[Col. 1388A] “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” On the literal level, he is said to have gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho because Jerusalem is situated in mountainous country, whereas Jericho lies in the plains. Therefore, one reaches Jericho from Jerusalem only by going down.
