It is reported that, along this road, robbers lurked in certain caves and pits and repeatedly preyed upon travelers.

Alternatively: it is said that, literally, between Jerusalem and Jericho there was a valley notorious for the frequent plundering and robbery of travelers, at the time when the ten tribes defected from David’s kingdom and civil wars raged between Rehoboam and Jeroboam (3 Kings XII).

The site of Jericho is also said by those knowledgeable about places [Col. 1388B] to have been remarkable. For that city was shaped like a lunar hemisphere and fortified by a sevenfold wall; hence it received the name of the moon, for Jericho is interpreted as “moon.”

But the surface meaning demanded by the letter must be touched upon in such a way that the truth of the allegory may be effectively sought and firmly adhered to.

This man, therefore, who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, is understood as Adam, and, through him, causally, the human race. The city of Jerusalem from which he is said to have descended, interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the dwelling of the heavenly homeland. The first man had been created by God to contemplate and possess it perpetually.

He fell from that happiness when, in his pride, he was expelled from paradise and estranged from the vision of divine contemplation. For as long as he was in paradise, he remained, through contemplation of the mind, in the fellowship and society of the angels. [Col. 1388C] But when, moved by the serpent’s persuasion, he grew proud against his Creator, he immediately fell both from paradise and from contemplation of his Creator.

This is signified by the present parable, which says that the man went down from Jerusalem; by the name Jerusalem, that blessedness of the heavenly homeland is designated.

Where our first parent fell after being estranged from contemplation of the heavenly Jerusalem, the Lord makes clear when he adds: “into Jericho”—that is, into this mortal life, full of labors and failings, into which unhappy human mortality was deservedly expelled because of disobedience, there to lament forever in the exile brought upon it by its most grievous presumption and pride.

The present life [Col. 1388D] is designated by the name Jericho. And rightly, through Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” the decline of our death is represented: just as the moon diminishes and wanes each month, so the life of our mortality, declining at every moment, vanishes day by day.

This man, therefore, went down from Jerusalem into Jericho when the parent of the human race, in whom we all were, sinned and fell from those immortal dwellings of paradise into this mortal life, full of misery.

“And he fell among robbers.” Let us see who the robbers were among whom the first man fell, and how, after being stripped and wounded by them, he escaped half-dead.

In former times those whom we now call attendants were called robbers, because they stood at the sides of kings. But now custom has established that robbers and thieves are so called because they hide (*latere*). [Col. 1389A]

By the robbers, who are named from hiding, evil spirits are understood. They are called robbers because they rage all the more wickedly the more secretly they do so. If they could be seen, perhaps they could to some extent be avoided. But because they are invisible, they secretly beset our road.

The man fell among these robbers because he descended. This descent is understood as nothing other than pride, concerning which the Lord says: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII). If he had not descended through pride, he would not have fallen among robbers, because he first became proud within himself and then, when tempted, yielded to his enemies.

For it is written: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. XVI). He is rightly said first to have descended and then to have encountered the robbers. He had already fallen inwardly [Col. 1389B] through pride before the eyes of God, when the enemy, tempting him outwardly, overthrew him so easily.

From this it may be inferred that no one can be driven into sin by the suggestion of evil spirits unless he is willing and voluntarily seeks opportunities to be tempted.

They also stripped him when they deprived him of the garment of immortality and innocence, making him, from righteous and immortal, sinful and mortal. For if our first parent Adam had not sinned through pride, he would have remained immortal.

This is aptly signified by the fig leaves with which they covered their nakedness—namely, the roughness of sins and the itching of unlawful pleasure (Gen. III). The condition of mortality was also prefigured in the garments of skins. This is the robe that the prodigal [Col. 1389C] son deserved to receive when he returned to his father’s mercy (Luke XV).

“And after inflicting wounds, they went away.” What are the wounds of these blows, if not the corruptions of sins that have been inflicted? Just as the flesh is injured by blows, so the soul is bloodied by sins.

The Psalmist, observing this, laments himself with mournful tears, saying: “My sins are fixed in me like arrows” (Ps. XXXVII)—all the more wickedly because through them the life of the soul, not of the body, is taken away.

After inflicting the wounds—that is, after accumulating sins—they are said to have gone away, not because they cease in any respect from attacking human beings, but because they conceal their own spiritual frauds and wickedness cunningly, so that they cannot be avoided or detected.

“Leaving him half-dead.” In the part by which a human being can know God, he is alive; but in the part by which, through sinning, he offends God, he is shown [Col. 1389D] to be dead, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

Although they killed the better part of the human being—that is, the soul—they could not altogether take away the dignity of reason and the divine image. To the extent that a human being wastes away through sins, he dies; but insofar as he is vigorous through reason and knows his Creator, he is regarded not as dead but as alive.

The robbers, therefore—that is, the demons—left the man half-dead, because they took away from him the blessedness of immortality but could not take away the reason of the soul, by which he can know God.

“Now it happened that a certain priest went down the same road, and, seeing him, passed by. [Col. 1390A] Likewise, a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by.”

The priest and Levite who saw the wounded man and passed by signify the Law of the Old Testament and the priesthood of the Jews, which once shone forth especially in priests and Levites.

Or, to speak more distinctly, by the priest is understood Aaron the priest together with all his descendants, and by the Levite Moses likewise with his succession. He is called a Levite because he was an administrator of the Law.

They descended by the same road because they all traveled through the world under the one condition of death. But, after seeing the wounded man, they passed by without producing any remedy, because the ancient Law and the priesthood were able only to reveal sins, not to free anyone from sin.

The wounds of sins could be shown through the Law and the Jewish priesthood [Col. 1390B], but they could not be healed. As the Apostle says: “It was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of brute animals” (Heb. X), until that unique sacrifice came which, offered upon the cross, wiped away the sins of the world.

Hence it follows: “But a certain Samaritan, while traveling, came near him.”

The Samaritans were not of the Jewish people; rather, they were foreigners and served idols. When the ten tribes had been transferred from Samaria by the king of the Assyrians because of their sins, the king of the Assyrians, wishing the land not to be left empty and reduced to a wilderness, sent certain foreigners—Assyrians, namely—to Samaria, which had been the capital of the ten tribes, so that they might live there and cultivate the land.

When they began to dwell there and serve idols, since they did not know [Col. 1390C] God, the Lord sent fierce beasts among them, by whose ravages they were destroyed. When this became known, the king of Assyria, having consulted with his advisers, sent them one of the Jewish priests to teach them the ordinances of the God of the land.

After he had given them the divine Law—as the history of Kings and Chronicles recounts in full—they began, compelled by fear, to worship God. But because their former unbelief still persisted, they did not cease to worship idols as well.

The Jews therefore regarded these people as objects of abomination and contempt, and called them Samaritans and full of demons, because they served demons. Hence they also hurled this as the greatest insult against the Lord Christ: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John VIII).

This Samaritan is a type of the Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 1390D] Elsewhere, when the Jews blasphemed him and said that he was a Samaritan and had a demon, he did not deny that he was a Samaritan, but showed his indignation at the false charge that he had a demon, saying: “I do not have a demon.”

He did not consider it unworthy to be called a Samaritan, because in the mark of disgrace he embraced the mystery of truth. For Samaritan is interpreted as “guardian.” No one is more appropriately understood as the guardian of the human race than the one to whom the prophet, in the person of the Church, says: “Guardian, what of the night?” (Isa. XXI), and the Psalmist: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

The same Psalmist, wishing to avoid these spiritual robbers, entreated this guardian, saying: “Guard me from the [Col. 1391A] snare “Guard me from the snare that they have set for me” (Ps. XL).

This Samaritan, therefore—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—near to us through compassion and neighbor to us through mercy, came near the wounded man while traveling. This means that he came near the human race, which had been wounded by sins, because God, who is above all, became human among all; the creator of times and places chose to be contained within time and place when, having assumed humanity, he appeared in the likeness of flesh [of sinful flesh], in order to condemn sin through sin.

He had, as it were, a road, because he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the Virgin’s womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb, rising again, ascended into heaven.

Hence in the epithalamium, in the voice of the Church, it is said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, [Col. 1391B] bounding over the hills” (Song II).

Traveling this road, the Lord saw the wounded human race—that is, he had compassion upon it. He is said to have come near the wounded man because he stood, in a certain sense, beside us when he appeared like human beings in the reality of the flesh he assumed. Of him it is rightly said: “When he saw him, he was moved with compassion.”

It belonged solely to divine goodness and mercy that he grieved over us, placed as we were under the dominion of harsh death. This overcame justice and prevailed, so that aid might be given to the wretched.

“And drawing near, he bound his wounds.” The binding of the wounds signifies the abolition of sins. The Lord bound the wounds of the wounded man when, coming into this world, he restrained the sins he found in human beings by rebuking them, saying: “Repent” (Matt. III).

He therefore bound the wounds when, removing the habit of sinning, he [Col. 1391C] fastened wounded minds with the bandage of righteousness and holiness. Hence the prophet, grieving that the sinner’s soul does not turn back from evil deeds, says: “Wound and bruise and swelling sore have not been bound up or softened with oil” (Isa. I).

“Pouring in oil and wine.” Wine poured into wounds stings, whereas oil soothes and softens. By wine, therefore, the harsh and bitter rebuke of sin is understood; by oil, gentle and kindly healing is signified.

Wine cuts away putrid flesh. In a certain sense he poured in wine when he terrified sinners and the unrepentant with the severity of punishments, saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III).

He likewise poured in oil when he promised forgiveness to the repentant, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”

[Col. 1391D] “And placing him on his own beast.” The beast is understood as the Savior’s flesh. For *jumentum*—“beast of burden”—is derived from *juvare*, “to help.” The Lord’s flesh was a beast of burden because it provided us eternal help so that we might be restored to life.

He therefore placed the wounded man on the beast when he bore our sins in his body upon the wood. And God became a beast of burden in such gracious condescension that the human being might become God’s beast of burden. Human beings were irrational beasts, to whom he says: “Do not become like a horse or a mule” (Ps. XXXI).

Thus, as though they were beasts of burden, they are led into the inn. Speaking of this assumption of humanity, the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. XIX)—that is, he will assume a body [Col. 1392A] in no way weighed down by the burden of sins.

This is what it means that he placed the wounded man upon his beast. It is signified in another parable, in which the good shepherd placed the sheep upon his shoulders and thus carried it back to the flock (Luke XV).

In the moral sense, each person is placed upon the Lord’s beast and led into the inn when, coming to baptism, he receives faith in the holy Trinity and is placed within the fellowship of the holy Church.

For it follows: “He led him into the inn.” The inn into which he led him is understood as the present holy Church. In it the holy animals of God—that is, the faithful—are continually nourished with grain, namely, the word of God, and strengthened by the most sacred bread of the Lord’s body. Of them it is said: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. LXVII).

The innkeeper signifies the order of preachers [Col. 1392B], to whom Christ has entrusted the holy Church, so that they may strive to refresh it with the nourishment of the divine word.

Travelers, exhausted from the road, also customarily enter the inn, and all the saints, wearied by the tumultuous activities of the world, rest quietly within the Church.

“And he took care of him.” It was not enough for the Lord to prohibit sins and set forth the commandments of life unless he also granted the wretched human race the means to avoid what was prohibited and fulfill what was commanded.

But this Samaritan could not remain longer on earth; he had to return to the place from which he had come. “And on the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: Take care of him.”

The first day is the time of the Lord’s incarnation, when, as it is written, “for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. IX). The second [Col. 1392C] day is the time after the Lord’s resurrection, when the splendor of eternal light, together with the glory of the Gospel, shone throughout the world upon all the nations.

The two denarii signify the two Testaments, the Old and the New, in which the name and image of the eternal King—that is, knowledge and contemplation—are contained.

On the second day, therefore, the Lord brought out the two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, because, rising from the dead, he opened the disciples’ understanding and disclosed to them the mysteries of [Col. 1392D] both Testaments for the instruction of all the nations.

The innkeeper, as has been said, signifies the order of preachers. One of them is the outstanding Paul the apostle, who, spending the denarius of the Law on the care of the wounded man, said: “I count all these things as refuse and regard them as dung” (Phil. III).

The innkeeper received the two denarii when knowledge of both Testaments was bestowed upon the apostles and they were sent out to preach, as though to care for the human race.

For what else does it mean to say, “Take care of him,” than: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI)?

“And whatever more you spend, I, when I return, will repay you.” Let us see what the innkeepers—that is, the holy preachers—spent beyond what was required.

The holy apostles spent beyond it when, in addition to the commandments of the Gospel, they contributed through their sayings and letters to the salvation of human beings.

The teacher of the nations, who was one of the innkeepers of the holy Church, fulfilled this role. He spent something beyond the account entrusted to him when he carried out the Lord’s measured command with almost immeasurable labor, and when [Col. 1393A], concerning matters about which he had received no command, he offered counsel, saying: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. VII).

Again he says: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel; but we have not used this authority among you, lest we burden any of you” (1 Cor. IX).

When he comes—that is, when at the end of the world he appears to all flesh—he will repay what was spent beyond the requirement, because, according to another Gospel parable, he will set him over all his possessions (Matt. XXV).

Great, therefore, is the merit of this innkeeper, to whom Christ is debtor. Who would not rejoice to be at least a suitable debtor of Christ? How great, then, is the one whose debtor he is—the one who has all others as his debtors? Hence he confidently glories, saying: “He who gave what was not owed will not deny what is owed.” [Col. 1393B]

Having carried the analogy this far, and now bringing to a conclusion what he had undertaken, the Lord asks the lawyer which of the three seemed to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers: whether the priest and Levite, who were neighbors by birth but strangers in mercy, or the Samaritan, who was foreign by nationality but near through compassion.

The lawyer answered what reason required: namely, that the one who had shown him mercy had been more truly his neighbor. And the Lord, urging him to perform a similar work of piety, said: “Go, and do likewise.”

This means: “To show that you truly love your neighbor as yourself, go and be ready to work for his benefit, whether bodily or spiritual, with whatever power you possess. Imitate this praiseworthy [Col. 1393C] example of the Samaritan and bestow the gift of mercy upon whomever you can.”

By this argument, let us recognize and love every human being as our neighbor, and, in loving him, let us have compassion on his need because of our kinship with him. For mercy makes a person more truly a neighbor than kinship does, because mercy is a matter according to nature. What is more according to nature than to help one who shares our nature?

Spiritually, however, no one is more truly our neighbor than Christ, who healed our wounds. He is our neighbor through divinity, because he is not far from any one of us. “For in him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII).

He also deigned to become our neighbor through humanity, because, although he was far from us—[Col. 1393D] immortal from mortals, righteous from sinners—he descended to us to become our neighbor, though previously he was distant.

Let us therefore revere him as our Lord and God, and love him as our neighbor, because he is our head. And it is certain that nothing is nearer than the head is to its members.

Let us always, as his most faithful members, look to him as our head, and from now on confidently ask for his mercy. For he cannot fail to have mercy upon his subjects, since he deigned to make himself neighbor to the undevout.

Loving those who love him, he will love them and lead them into contemplation of himself and of the Father—Jesus Christ our Lord, who reigns forever.

## HOMILY CLXXV. FOR THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 1394A]

“At that time, as Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him,” etc. (Luke XVII).

In those lepers whom the Lord cleansed in this way, when he said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests,” many questions may reasonably be raised. These concern not only their number—what it means that there were ten—but also the fact that only one of them gave thanks. Such questions may freely be asked, since, even if they are not investigated, they either do not hinder the reader’s purpose at all or hinder it greatly. But the more important question is why he sent them to the priests, so that, as they went, they might be cleansed.

Of all those to whom he granted these bodily benefits, none is found to have been sent to the priests except lepers. For he had also cleansed from leprosy the man to whom he said, “Go, show yourself to the priests, and offer for yourself the sacrifice which Moses commanded as a testimony to them” (Luke 5). Next, one may ask what spiritual cleansing can be understood in those whom he accuses of having proved ungrateful. In bodily terms, it is easy to see that a person may not have leprosy and yet not possess a good disposition. But according to the significance of this miracle, he may be called ungrateful. We must therefore ask what leprosy itself signifies.

They are not said to have been healed but cleansed, since they were freed from that condition. Leprosy is a defect of color, not of health or of the integrity of the senses and limbs. Thus lepers may not unreasonably be understood as those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, profess various [Col. 1394C] doctrines of error. They do not conceal their ignorance; rather, they bring it into the light as though it were the highest expertise and display the vanity of their speech. Moreover, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truth. Truths mingled disorderly with falsehoods in a single argument or account of a person appear like the coloring of one body; they signify leprosy, which varies and stains human bodies with patches of different colors, true and false.

Such people must be avoided by the Church so completely that, if possible, they should remain at a greater distance and call upon Christ with a loud cry, just as those ten stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” The fact that they call him “Master”—by that title I do not know whether anyone ever addressed the Lord when seeking bodily healing—I believe sufficiently signifies that leprosy is false doctrine, which the good Master wipes away.

Almost no believer doubts that the priesthood of the Jews was a figure of the future royal priesthood, which is in the Church and by which all who belong to the body of Christ, the supreme and true chief of priests, are consecrated. For now all are anointed, whereas at that time anointing was performed only for kings and priests. When Peter, writing to the Christian people, calls them “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2), he shows that both titles apply to that people, to whom the anointing belonged.

Other faults, therefore, like diseases of the limbs and of the soul’s senses, the Lord himself heals and corrects inwardly in the conscience and understanding. [Col. 1395A] But instruction—whether initiation through the sacraments or catechesis through spoken preaching and reading—is properly entrusted to the Church, where a certain true and pure color is understood, because it is ready at hand and most conspicuous outwardly. For these things are done not in hidden thoughts but in manifest actions.

Thus Paul also, after hearing the Lord’s voice, “Why are you persecuting me? I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9), was nevertheless sent to Ananias, so that through that priesthood established in the Church he might receive the sacrament of the faith’s teaching and have his true color confirmed. This was not because the Lord cannot do everything by himself—for who else performs these things even in the Church?—but so that the very fellowship of the assembled faithful, by mutually approving one another and sharing [Col. 1395B] the doctrine of the true faith in all that is spoken in words or signified in sacraments, might spread over everything one appearance of true color.

This also pertains to what the same apostle says: “Then after fourteen years I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up in accordance with a revelation, and I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, privately before those who seemed to be important, lest I should be running or should have run in vain” (Galatians 2). A little later he says: “When they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas” (ibid.). That act of mutual exchange showed one form of doctrine, excluding all variation. Paul also profitably admonishes the Corinthians concerning this, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing” (1 Corinthians 1). [Col. 1395C]

When the angel announced to Cornelius that his almsgiving had been accepted and his prayers heard, he was nevertheless commanded to send to Peter, for the sake of the unity of doctrine and the sacraments (Acts 10), as though it were said to him and his household: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” For as they went, they were cleansed. Peter had already come to them, but they had not yet received the sacrament of baptism and had not yet spiritually reached the priests. Nevertheless, their cleansing was made manifest through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the wonder of tongues.

Since these things are so, it is now easy to see that someone may attain a complete and true doctrine within the fellowship of the Church and discuss everything according to the rule of the Catholic faith, distinguishing the creature from the Creator, and thus show that he is free from the variety of falsehoods like a person cleansed of leprosy—and yet be ungrateful to God and his Lord and cleanser. Carried away by pride, he is not prostrated in the pious humility of giving thanks and becomes like those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1).

For when he says that they knew God, he shows that they had been cleansed of leprosy; yet immediately he accuses them of ingratitude. Therefore such people will remain in the number nine, as imperfect. If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed, and such a combination is formed that the number does not advance further unless it returns again to one; and this rule of number is preserved throughout infinity. Thus the nine need one in order to be joined together in a kind of form of unity and become ten. But the one does not need them in order to preserve unity.

Accordingly, just as those nine who did not give thanks, having become rejected, were excluded from the fellowship of unity, so the one who gave thanks was approved and praised as a sign of the one Church. Since the others were Jews, their loss of the kingdom of heaven was revealed through their pride, for unity is guarded there above all. But this Samaritan—whose name means “guardian”—gave to the one from whom he had received what he had received. In a manner of speaking, he sang the words of the Psalm: “I will guard my strength toward you” (Psalm 58). Through thanksgiving he submitted to the King and preserved unity with the King in humble devotion. [Col. 1396B]

But you.

## HOMILY CLXXVI. ON THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(By Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time, as Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria, etc. (Luke 17).

The most evident testimony of the holy evangelists declares that the journeys of our Lord and Savior were always full both of miracles and of mysteries. His purpose was not fulfilled merely by walking from one place to another; through this movement, provision was also made for human salvation. He traveled, passing from place to place, so that he might assist everyone, be present to everyone, meet each person, and join himself to all; by miracles he compelled some to faith, and by preaching others. [Col. 1396C]

Although he filled all things with his divinity, he nevertheless willed to be circumscribed by place in his humanity, so that, by assuming what we were, he might grant us participation in his divinity.

Yet it is not enough to understand this journey of the Lord only in a bodily sense; we must also investigate whether some mystery may lie hidden within it. The Lord’s journey, therefore, is his passage from earth to heaven. He went because, once his passion had been completed, he was hastening through the world and returning to the Father. He went because he was hastening from mortality to immortality, from punishment to glory, from contempt to kingship.

As he was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria. Mindful of human salvation, for the restoration of which he had come from heaven, and with the moment of his passion already imminent, he went to the city of Jerusalem, not fearing any savage people, however cruel, however anxiously thirsty for the shedding of his blood. Jerusalem contained the Lord’s temple; there was the priesthood of the Jews, there the worship of sacred religion. There also, three times a year, every male among the Jews appeared according to the legal commandment. Therefore the Lord often visited that city, desiring to announce the words of salvation to many there and to display his miracles.

Thus, so that his journey might not appear separated from or deprived of the proclamation of miracles, as he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee and entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him. They were separated, as the law decreed, from living together with the common inhabitants of houses and cities.

Samaria was a city or region in its own right, where the kingdom of the ten tribes once flourished [Col. 1397A] before they abandoned the worship of God and experienced Assyrian captivity. After those people had been led away from their own land into exile, foreign peoples sent by the Assyrians inhabited their territory. Galilee, on the other hand, was a large part of the Jewish kingdom; Nazareth was there, if it is permissible to call it the Lord’s homeland.

As the Lord went to Jerusalem and hastened toward the passion that was immediately to be fulfilled, he also visited these provinces in passing and illuminated them with the signs of his miracles.

“And as he entered a certain village.” Beautifully, the holy evangelist did not expressly name this village, in order to show that the lepers who met the Lord had no fellowship with human beings and possessed no fixed place in which to settle. By the decree of the law they had been separated [Col. 1397B] from the fellowship of ordinary habitation.

It should be noted that we do not read that these lepers met the Lord in a village, a settlement, or a city, but rather on the road, because the law prescribed that anyone who was leprous should be separated from all the people through the ministry of a priest. Therefore, having been segregated from ordinary fellowship, they did not meet the Lord in a village or settlement but on the road.

As the Lord entered the village, they met him because they were close to being healed. Thus they appropriately hailed him as “Master,” from whom they were to receive the commands both of bodily health and of eternal life. But the Lord, wishing to teach that the divine law must always be obeyed, carried out the commandment of the law established by him and directed them to the priests, saying: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.”

For the law prescribed (Leviticus 13) that if anyone incurred the mark of leprosy, he should be brought to the priest, so that by his judgment he might be pronounced clean or unclean.

Thus, by a provident dispensation, the Lord sent the lepers to the priests for many reasons. First, to block their opportunity for accusation, sparing those who were more concerned with their chattering objections. Second, so that, seeing lepers cleansed by the Lord—whom they themselves had been unable to cure through priesthood and law—they might either believe and be saved, or, if they did not believe, be made inexcusable concerning his coming. Third, in order thereby to commend more fully the priesthood of the holy Church.

If that priesthood, which was enacted in type and figure, was so venerable in its own time that it was honored by the Lord himself, how much more should that priesthood which is now administered not in figure but in truth be revered and honored with every honor.

Alternatively: “When he saw them, he said: Go, show yourselves to the priests.” Among all those whom the Lord is said to have healed in various ways from different illnesses, he wished to send none of those to whom he gave care to the priests except lepers.

The literal explanation of this is easy, because it is clear that he did this so that he would not seem to furnish weapons against himself to his adversaries who accused him. They might complain that he was not showing the priests the honor and reverence due to them, especially since the cleansing of lepers was specifically to be determined by the priests.

But if a spiritual meaning is sought in this deed, it is clear [Col. 1398A] that the priesthood of the Jews was a type of the royal and Christian priesthood, which now remains in the Church through God’s grace, by which all who belong as members to the true priest are cleansed and consecrated.

“And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.” Swift obedience was fittingly followed by speedy healing. It was also done with great providence that they were cleansed before they came to the priests, lest, if they had happened to be cleansed in the priests’ presence, the priests should perhaps suppose that they had been healed by their ministry and not by the power of the one who sent them.

But that these matters, which we have briefly treated literally, are full of sacraments is shown by the order of events itself. The Lord’s miracles claim this privilege especially: they are to be believed as having truly occurred according to history, and, when spiritually examined, they reveal the sweetness of mysteries hidden within. When they do this, what else are we doing than drawing forth honey from the deepest hidden recesses of divine favors?

These lepers, therefore, can not inappropriately signify heretics. Leprosy is of such a nature that it sprinkles the skin it infects with different colors. So heretics, in order to pretend that they are speaking the truth, mix truths with falsehoods and, as it were, stain a doctrine of one color with a superimposed variety. If they always pursued the truth, they would not be heretics; but if they always spoke falsehoods, no one except the most deranged would believe them.

They therefore mix, as has been said, truths with falsehoods so that, when truth is accepted on the surface, the hidden disease of falsehood may insinuate itself within, like those who offer poisons and first smear the rim of the cup with honey, so that, while the sweetness of the honey attracts attention, the potency of the drink may be consumed more eagerly. [Col. 1398C]

Alternatively: Because leprosy, mixed with different colors in one and the same skin, makes a person hideous, heretics are not inappropriately designated spiritually by the name of lepers. They lack the unity of faith and are infected with various errors.

It must be understood, however, that there is absolutely no false doctrine that is not mixed with some truth. Otherwise, if it were openly false, it would not be accepted; and if it were entirely true, it would not be heretical. Just as wounds appearing on a body’s skin cover the flesh with different colors, so falsehoods are sprinkled with truths in the doctrine of every heretic, so that under the appearance of truth the hostile falsehood may prevail. Those who offer poisons likewise first smear the rims of their cups with honey, so that through the taste of sweetness one may arrive at the cup of death. [Col. 1398D]

Such plagues must be driven away by the authority of the leaders of the Church, so that their authors, cast out from the fellowship of all Christianity, may be compelled to call upon the Lord Jesus with loud cries in order to receive salvation.

It should also be observed that the holy evangelist deliberately expressed the number itself, taking care to indicate how many there were. For he says: “Ten leprous men met him.” They were commendable in their beautiful number but deformed by their shameful skin.

Thus heretics boast that they are somehow contained within the perfection of ten, while they assert that they are fulfillers of the divine commandments received in the Decalogue and profess themselves to be teachers of the Christian faith. The number delights, but the insincerity of their sinister doctrine offends.

This is what the Apostle says of such people: “Having indeed the appearance of holiness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3). Such people must be expelled from cohabitation in the city of God—that is, from communion with the universal Church—so that at least, condemned and separated from the fellowship of all, they may eventually be wearied by the long tedium of their exclusion and be compelled to call upon Christ with loud cries and confess him as the Master of truth.

This is what the evangelist says: “They stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” They stood at a distance and did not approach the Lord because, as has already been said, they had been separated from ordinary fellowship. [Col. 1399B]

Standing at a distance, the lepers raised their voices to the Lord so that they might not be hindered in any way by the noise of a bustling crowd. They rightly call him “Master” when they are about to be healed, since they recognize that they had erred in faith and doctrine.

In the spiritual meaning, too, how appropriately heretics call Jesus “Master,” in whose words they remember having gone astray! When they hasten eagerly to return to the rule of his teaching, they soon deserve to find the benefits of the salvation they desire.

“When he saw them, he said: Go, show yourselves to the priests. And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.”

Leprosy has four kinds of meaning. It signifies the unbelief of the pagans, the faithlessness of the Jews, the error of heretics, and the stains of grave sins. Whoever desires to be purified from this manifold leprosy must approach the Church and seek the priests, so that through their ministry he may be stripped of the stains of sins, without which no one can be healed of such a sickness.

The fact that the lepers were sent to the priests signifies that converted heretics ought to present themselves to the priests or ministers of the holy Church and lay open for examination the error of their wicked doctrine, like the variation of diseased skin. Thus, instructed by them in the rules of the Catholic faith, they may be restored to their former purity and beauty.

Although the Lord, who is the supreme pontiff and true teacher, can inspire inwardly through his own instruction what must be held, he nevertheless, by a great dispensation, wishes teachers to be obeyed. Through this, those who are to be taught are established in profound humility, and once humbled they become better prepared to receive the mysteries of the faith.

For if blessed Paul, who had been instructed by divine revelations from heaven and who says that he received the Gospel neither from a human being nor through a human being but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, was nevertheless sent to Ananias so that he might receive from him the truth of the faith and fulfill the other requirements of ecclesiastical order (Galatians 2; Acts 9), what must be thought of the rest?

What does it mean that they were cleansed before they came to the priests? Perhaps it prefigures that many, with fervent faith, while seeking holy teachers for the recovery of their souls, are granted such abundant prevenient grace from God that, before they lay aside the leprosy of their souls through the washing of baptism, they deserve to be cleansed from original sins by the coming of the Holy Spirit.

This was fulfilled in Cornelius and those who were with him, of whom it is written: “While Peter was still speaking at length, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word.” And blessed Peter said: “Can anyone forbid water, so that these people should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?”

The manifold mercy of God has granted this power to the priests who preside over the Church: they may impose the discipline of penance upon those who confess and, once they have been cleansed by the same saving satisfaction, admit them also to the door of reconciliation. The safeguards of the divine will have been ordered in such a way that God’s pardon cannot be obtained without the supplications of the priests.

“But one of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice.”

That this one man was of great merit and immense faith may be inferred especially from this: while the others remained ungrateful, he alone returned to give thanks to his cleanser. He thought little of presenting himself before the priests to whom he had been sent and strove instead to present his countenance to the true priest, Christ, who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, and who is the chief priest of priests and the priest of priests.

This one man, who alone returned while the others departed ungratefully, giving thanks to the Savior, signifies the devoted humility of the one Church before God. Whoever gives thanks to God daily restrains the thoughts of his presumption, humbly considers his own weakness, attributes nothing of what he does to himself, and confesses that everything proceeds from divine mercy.

It is beautifully said that he returned with a loud voice. He returned with a loud voice because in his mind he perceived God’s great mercy toward him. Rightly he returned glorifying God with a loud voice, since in his sudden restoration he had experienced God’s omnipotence.

In this deed he showed himself to be a chief member of the holy Church: amid the blasphemies of heretics and the voices of the Jews, he does not cease daily to praise Christ and give him thanks.

The evangelist rightly adds concerning him: “Because he fell on his face, giving thanks.” This kind of falling belongs properly to the elect. The fall of the rejected, however, is always backward, according to what is written concerning the Lord’s persecutors: when the Lord said, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground (John 18). Concerning the followers of Antichrist, Jacob says under the figure of Dan: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned snake on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, and let its rider fall backward” (Genesis 49). [Col. 1400D]

Whoever falls backward falls where he does not know what deceit may be hidden. But whoever falls on his face falls where he sees everything that is present.

The rejected fall backward because, by neglecting to bring their past evils before the eyes of their minds, they later roll unhappily backward—that is, toward the eternal punishments which they refused to foresee. To fall on one’s face means to blush with shame over things committed through ignorance or negligence. To those who fall on their faces in this way the Apostle Paul says: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6).

The holy evangelist also carefully inserted the statement, “And he was a Samaritan.” We do not find this added superfluously or idly if we consider the mystery concerning the man. Samaritan means “guardian.” By this name the person is most appropriately identified who, having received the gift of health, preferred to guard it in humility and gratitude rather than lose it through pride and ingratitude.

For this reason he deserved to be blessed by the name of that true Samaritan who healed the wounds of the injured man.

“And he was a Samaritan”—that is, a foreigner. We often read in the Gospel that Gentiles came to the Lord to hear him and be healed by him and, after receiving health, strove to give thanks to God. But the Jews, continually witnessing his miracles and receiving cleansing from him, always remained ungrateful.

Spiritually, the Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” signifies the whole body of the Gentile people converted to God through faith, who possess guardianship for the preservation of humility. When the Gentile people, converted to God, attribute every good they possess to the one from whom they received it, they carefully guard the benefits bestowed upon them by God, singing with the Psalmist: “I will guard my strength toward you, because you, God, are my protector” (Psalm 58).

“Jesus answered and said: Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?”

The Savior rightly asks after those who remained ungrateful as though they were unknown when he says, “Where are the nine?” For just as he is shown to know those whom he chooses, so he is not inappropriately said not to know those whom he rejects.

Thus at the end he will say to some: “I do not know where you come from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13). This does not mean that anything is hidden from God, but that he rejects the ways of the wicked—whose figure these lepers represent—as though they were unknown.

Similarly, a truthful man is said not to know how to lie because he disdains to speak a lie—not because, if he wished to lie, he would be unable to do so, but because, out of love for truth, he scorns to speak falsehood.

The Lord therefore says: “Were not ten cleansed, and where are the nine?” If the number nine receives one as an addition, it completes a certain form of unity and rises to ten. In this number, that is, ten, such a combination is formed that no further number increases beyond it unless this same ten is repeated from the beginning, that is, from one.

One, therefore, does not need nine in order to guard its unity; the nine, however, need one so that a certain image of unity may be completed, namely, ten.

Likewise, those who have been placed within the unity of the holy Church, represented by the one, do not need the assistance of those who stand outside through unbelief. Those who are outside, however, need the help of the elect, so that through their ministry and intercession they may deserve to be incorporated into the holy Church, since otherwise they cannot be saved.

The evangelist adds concerning those who remained ungrateful: “No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner.” Earlier he asserted that ten had been cleansed; now he says that no one was found to return and give glory to God except that foreigner.

Literally, it is easy to see that a person may be healed in body and yet remain ungrateful. Spiritually, however, it is surprising that he calls those people healed who are converted by God’s grace from unbelief to faith and yet remain ungrateful.

If someone is perfectly cleansed through faith and baptism, how can he be ungrateful to God, whose mercy brought him from unbelief to faith? And if he is ungrateful, how is he clean?

It must be understood that there are certain people in the congregation of the faithful who are indeed cleansed through faith and baptism but remain ungrateful in good works. Concerning them the Apostle Paul says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1). When he says that they knew the Lord, he shows that they had been cleansed from the leprosy of unbelief through baptism; but when he adds that they did not glorify the Lord or give him thanks, they are accused of ingratitude.

“No one was found to return and give glory to God.” By this sentence he secretly strikes at the hardness of the Jews and praises the readiness of the Gentiles to believe. For in almost every passage of the holy Gospel we find that the Jews were slow to faith, while the Gentiles were eager—indeed, most ready—to believe.

This is seen in the blessed centurion, of whom it was said: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matthew 8). It can also be seen most clearly in the Gentiles who, around the time of Christ’s passion, desired to see him.

He therefore says: “No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner,” as though he were saying: “Citizens hate; foreigners embrace. The Jews persecute; the Gentiles seek and venerate. The former labor to destroy him after so many benefits; the latter strive, by giving thanks for what they have received, to prove worthy of greater gifts.”

And Jesus said to him: “Rise, go; your faith has saved you.” Rise, namely, from the vices of sins, and go to the practice of virtues. The Lord praises him as he lies there and simply worships him; by the utterance of his divine mouth he encourages him to rise and approves that, having believed perfectly, he deserved to be saved perfectly.

He also indicates what those who refused to return and give thanks deserved: if this man was saved by his faith, then surely those others were condemned by their unbelief.

Those who have already begun to be ashamed of their committed sins are likewise first commanded to rise and then to walk. We rise, as it were, when we repent of our sins, resist an evil-rooted habit, and become displeased with ourselves for having been such people. We walk when we set our feet upon the path of God’s commandments through good works and exercise the spirit, previously unaccustomed and almost sluggish, in the pursuit of virtues.

Spiritually, we may also understand that if those who remain within the holy Church were saved by their faith, then without doubt those who remain outside are condemned by their unbelief.

This is also suggested in the case of the man who lies before the Lord’s feet and is commanded to rise: those who hold the right faith together with the practice of humility and humbly submit themselves to their Creator—those whom this man represents, returning cleansed to give thanks to God—are commanded through the consolation of the divine word to rise from sins and advance toward works of virtue through disciplined practice. As their virtues increase daily, they are raised to that perfection in which they may deserve perpetually to contemplate the God of gods in Zion.

But you.

## HOMILY CLXXVI (SECOND VERSION). ON THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 1403A]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other,” etc. (Matthew 6).

These words must be carefully considered. For he subsequently shows who the two masters are when he says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Among the Hebrews, *mammon* is said to mean “wealth”; the Punic term agrees, for in Punic *mammon* means “profit.” But whoever serves Mammon certainly serves the one who, because of his perversity, has rightly been placed over these earthly affairs and is called by the Lord “the ruler of this age.” Therefore a person will either hate this one [Col. 1403B] and love the other—that is, God—or endure the one and despise the other. Whoever serves Mammon will endure a harsh and destructive master: he is entangled in his own desire, subjected to the devil, and does not love him. For who is there who loves the devil? Yet he endures him, just as someone in a great household who has attached himself to another man’s maidservant endures harsh servitude because of his desire, even though he does not love the man whose maidservant he loves.

But he said “he will despise the other,” not “he will hate him.” For no one’s conscience can truly hate God; yet a person despises him—that is, does not fear him—when he is, as it were, confident of God’s goodness. The Holy Spirit recalls us from this negligence and destructive security when he says through the prophet: “My son, do not add sin upon sin, and do not say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclus. V), while failing to understand that God’s patience leads you to repentance. For whose mercy can be believed to be so great as that of the one who forgives all sins to those who turn back and makes the wild olive share in the richness of the cultivated olive tree? And whose severity can be so great as that of the one who did not spare the natural branches, but broke them off because of their unbelief?

But if anyone wishes to love God and take care not to offend him, let him not suppose that he serves two masters, and let him unfold the intention of his heart in a straightforward manner, free from all duplicity. Thus he will think of the Lord in goodness and seek him with a simple heart.

“Therefore,” he says, “I tell you, do not be anxious in your soul about what you will eat, nor about what you will put on your body,” lest, although superfluities are no longer sought, the heart should nevertheless be divided because of necessities themselves, and our intention be twisted toward acquiring them. This happens when, while apparently acting mercifully—that is, when we wish to appear to be helping someone—we attend more to our own profit than to that person’s benefit, and therefore do not seem to ourselves to be sinning because what we wish to obtain is not superfluous but necessary.

The Lord, however, warns us to remember that God has given us far more by making and composing us of soul and body than the food and clothing whose care he does not wish us to make a cause of a divided heart. “Is not the soul,” he says, “more than food?” This is so that you may understand that the one who gave the soul will much more easily give food, and that the body is more than clothing—that is, so that you may likewise understand that the one who gave the body will much more easily give clothing.

At this point it is usually asked whether this food pertains to the soul, since the soul is incorporeal whereas this food is corporeal. But let us recognize that in this passage “soul” means this present life, whose support is this bodily food. In accordance with this meaning, the following was also said: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it” (John XII). Unless we understand this as referring to the present life—which must be lost for the sake of the kingdom of God, as the martyrs clearly demonstrated—this command will contradict the saying: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Mark XVI).

“Look,” he says, “at the birds of the air: they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into their barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not [Col. 1404B] worth more than they?” That is, you are more precious, because a rational creature such as a human being has been placed more exaltedly in the order of nature than irrational creatures such as birds.

“Which of you,” he says, “by being anxious can add one cubit to his stature?” And why are you anxious about clothing? That is, the one by whose power and dominion it has come about that your body was brought to this stature can also clothe it by his providence. That it was not by your own care that your body reached this stature can be understood from the fact that, even if you were anxious and wished to add one cubit to this stature, you could not do so. Therefore leave to him also the care of covering the body, since you see that by his care it has come about that you possess a body of such stature.

A lesson also had to be given concerning clothing, just as one had been given concerning food. Thus he continues and says: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labor nor spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?”

But those examples should not be examined allegorically in such a way that we ask what the birds of the air or the lilies of the field signify. They were presented so that greater matters might be impressed upon us through lesser ones. The same is true of the judge who neither feared God nor respected human beings, yet, because a widow repeatedly pleaded with him, finally undertook to consider her case—not out of piety or humanity, but to avoid further annoyance (Luke XVIII). That unjust judge does not in any way represent God allegorically; rather, God wished it to be inferred from the fact that not even an unjust human being can despise those who batter him with continual prayers, even in order to avoid annoyance, how much God, who is good and just, cares for those who entreat him.

“Therefore,” he says, “do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we put on?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

Here he most clearly shows that these things are not to be desired as though they were our true goods, so that we ought to do good for their sake if we do anything at all; nevertheless, they are necessary. He made clear the difference between the good that ought to be desired and the necessity that ought to be accepted when he said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

The kingdom and righteousness of God, then, are our good. They are to be desired, and in them our end must be established, so that we may do everything that we do for their sake. But because in this life we are engaged in warfare so that we may reach that kingdom—and because this life cannot be conducted without these necessities—“these things,” he says, “will be added to you; but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.”

When he said “first,” he indicated that the other things are to be sought afterward—not in time, but in rank. The one is our good, the other our necessity; and the necessity exists for the sake of the good. We ought not, for example, to preach the Gospel in order to eat, but to eat in order to preach. For if we preach in order to eat, we regard the Gospel as less valuable than food; and food will then be our good, while preaching will be our necessity.

The Apostle also forbids this when he says that he is indeed permitted and authorized by the Lord that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (I Cor. IX)—that is, that they should receive from the Gospel what is necessary for this life—but that he himself had not used this authority. There were many who desired an opportunity to acquire wealth and live according to the Gospel. Wishing to cut off that opportunity from them, the Apostle supported himself by the work of his own hands.

Elsewhere he says that he does this “to cut off the opportunity,” although, like the other apostles, he was permitted by the Lord to live from the Gospel; and he did not establish the end of his preaching in food (II Cor. XI), but rather placed the end of his own sustenance in the Gospel. In other words, as I said above, he did not preach in order to obtain food, or any other such necessities, but accepted these things in order to fulfill his mission, lest he preach unwillingly rather than willingly.

He proves the same point when he says: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these provisions” (I Cor. IX). From this he shows that it was permitted, not commanded; otherwise he would be held to have acted contrary to the Lord’s command.

Then he continues and says: “I have not written these things so that they should be done in my case. It would be better for me to die than for anyone to make my boast empty” (ibid.). He said this because he had already decided, on account of certain people seeking an opportunity, to support himself by the work of his own hands.

“For if I preach the Gospel,” he says, “I have no ground for boasting”—that is, if I preach in such a way that these things are done for me; if I preach in order to obtain them and place the end of the Gospel in food, drink, and clothing. But why does he have no ground for boasting? “For necessity,” he says, “is laid upon me”—that is, if I preach because I have no means by which to live, or in order to obtain a temporal reward from preaching eternal things. In that case necessity, not free will, would be present in the Gospel.

“For woe to me,” he says, “if I do not preach the Gospel.” But how ought he to preach? Clearly, he ought to place his reward in the Gospel itself and in the kingdom of God. In this way he can preach not under compulsion but willingly.

“For if I do this willingly,” he says, “I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me.” That is: if, compelled by poverty and by the lack of those things necessary for temporal life, I preach the Gospel, others will receive the reward of the Gospel—those who love the Gospel because I preach it—but I will not receive it, because I do not love the Gospel itself; rather, I have placed its price in temporal things. This must not happen, so that someone may not minister the Gospel as a son but as a servant who has been entrusted with a stewardship, distributing what belongs to another and taking nothing from it for himself except provisions. These are given from outside, not as a share in the kingdom, but for the support of miserable servitude.

Although elsewhere he also calls himself a steward (I Cor. IV), a servant who has been adopted into the number of sons can faithfully administer to his fellow heirs the possession in which he has obtained a co-heir’s share. But here, when he says, “If unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me,” he wishes such a steward to be understood as one who administers what belongs to another and receives nothing from it himself.

Therefore, whatever is sought for the sake of something else is without doubt inferior to that for whose sake it is sought. For this reason, the first thing is that for which you seek the other thing, not the thing you seek for its sake.

Accordingly, if we seek the Gospel and the kingdom of God for the sake of food, we make food primary and the kingdom of God secondary, so that, if there is no food, we do not [Col. 1406C] seek the kingdom of God. This, then, is to seek food first and the kingdom of God afterward: to place the one in the first position and the other in the second.

But if we seek food in order to possess the kingdom of God, let us do what was said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” For those who seek first the kingdom and righteousness of God—that is, who place this before all other things, so that they seek the others for its sake—should not be troubled by fear that the necessities of this life, which are required for the sake of the kingdom of God, will be lacking.

For he said above: “Your Father knows that you need all these things.” And therefore, when he had said, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness,” he did not say, “Then seek these things also,” even though they are necessary. Rather, he said: “All these things will be added to you”—that is, they will follow if you seek the former, without any hindrance caused by them.

And when you seek these things, do not turn away from that kingdom, nor establish two ends for yourself, so that you desire the kingdom of God for its own sake and these necessities as well. Rather, these things will not be lacking to you because of that kingdom, since you cannot serve two masters.

The person who tries to serve two masters is the one who desires the kingdom of God as a great good and also desires these temporal things. But no one can have a single eye and serve the one Lord God unless, whatever else is necessary, he takes it for this one purpose—that is, for the sake of the kingdom of God.

Just as soldiers receive their rations and pay, so all who preach the Gospel receive food and clothing. But just as not all soldiers serve for the safety of the state, but rather for the things they receive, so not all who minister to God serve for the salvation of the Church, but for these temporal things, which they obtain as rations and pay—or for both this and that.

But it has already been said above: “You cannot serve two masters.” Therefore, with a simple heart, we ought to do good to everyone solely for the sake of the kingdom of God, and in this activity we ought not to consider either temporal reward alone or temporal reward together with the kingdom of God.

By the name of all these temporal things he placed “tomorrow,” saying: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow.” For “tomorrow” is spoken only in time, where the future succeeds the past. Therefore, when we do anything good, let us think not of temporal but of eternal things. Then the work will be good and perfect.

But you.

## HOMILY CLXXVII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one can serve two masters,” and so forth (Matthew VI).

The Lord became man for this purpose: to rescue us from the power of darkness and to make us a kingdom for God the Father. For he himself says, speaking figuratively in a certain passage of the Gospel, that “a certain nobleman went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself” (Luke 19). By these words he wished no one other than himself to be understood: he deigned to come from the heavenly realms into this region of misery and death in order to destroy the devil’s dominion, which he had established through a certain pact of sin and a compact of eternal death, and to exalt his own kingdom by the laws of justice and gentleness.

When, therefore, many were already defecting from the devil’s kingdom, obeying heavenly decrees and undertaking the signs of faith with ready devotion, that most victorious king addresses them in these words: “No one can serve two masters.” It is as though, exhorting them in other words to the discipline of spiritual warfare, he said: “If you choose the authority of my rule perfectly, you must reject the service of the former master in every respect. For it is impossible to obey both at once, since what I command and what he commands are opposed to each other. I command that all things belonging to holiness and honor be fulfilled; he commands that every shameful thing and everything contrary to honor be practiced. I command my soldier gladly to take up the weapons of virtue in order to preserve gentleness and humility; he compels his followers, for the sake of pride, to inflict death upon the innocent. How, then, can equal service be rendered to both, whose dominion is unequal?” [Col. 1407D]

These words of our Redeemer instruct us to avoid the cares of this age and exhort us to despise temporal things and to strive always for heavenly things. “No one,” he says, “can serve two masters.” The meaning of this statement is perfectly clear even without explanation according to the literal sense: no one can serve two carnal masters in such a way as to please both equally and obey both equally. Hence it follows: “For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other.”

But he subsequently reveals who these two masters are in the spiritual sense when he adds: “You cannot serve God and mammon,” that is, Christ and the devil. “What fellowship is there between Christ and the devil? Or what communion between light and darkness?”

Again, concerning the two masters, it follows: “Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other.” He will hate the one—that is, the devil, who must be hated—not because he is a substance, but because he is evil; and he will love the other—that is, Christ, who, like a gentle master, commands that he be loved solely out of affection: “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22).

“Or he will endure the one,” that is, the devil, as a harsh and pitiless master. For he shakes the lovers of the world with the most severe commands, and once he has gained dominion over a person, he compels him to do evil even against his will and unwillingly; nor do they carry out his commands without the gravest hardships. They frequently endure exile, shipwreck, the loss of their property, and finally death itself for these things. Scripture says of such people: “They labored to do evil” (Jeremiah 9).

They therefore endure such a master unwillingly rather than serve him obediently, because once they have voluntarily accepted his dominion over them, they can never afterward be rescued by their own strength, except by the exceedingly powerful hand of God.

“And he will despise the other,” he says—that is, God. Here one should note the precision of the Lord’s words. Although he had first said, “Either he will hate the one and love the other,” he did not then say the reverse: “Either he will love the one,” namely, the devil, “and hate the other,” namely, God. For no conscience, however depraved, can break out to the point of saying that it hates God or loves the devil. [Col. 1408C]

“To despise” means not to fear. God is despised by those who flatter themselves, while sinning, with the hope that their crimes will go unpunished, thinking either that God does not know their crimes or that, once he has seen them, he immediately forgives them. They do not know that, by overlooking their sins, divine goodness calls them to repentance, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2). “But according to your hardness and your impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God.”

Alternatively: It is fitting that he added either that one is to be endured—that is, the devil—or that the other is to be despised—namely, God. For whoever disregards God’s commandments by contradicting them despises God, but does not hate him. He endures the devil as though he had a harsh and cruel master, but does not love him: whoever submits to him through greed for riches submits to the one who is regarded as the prince of this world, as the Lord says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

Although such a person endures him as a cruel master, he does not love him. For example, if someone in a great household were joined to the maidservant of some powerful man, even if he did not love the man whose maidservant he loved, nevertheless, because of the force of his desire, he would endure harsh servitude by submitting himself to the man whose maidservant, joined to him, he loves. So also a person who loves riches is a servant of the devil, who is the head and prince of the lovers of the world. [Col. 1409A]

To possess riches is an indifferent matter. Wealth does not harm a rich man if he uses it well, nor does poverty make a poor man more commendable if, amid filth and want, he does not avoid sins. “You cannot serve God and mammon.” Among the Hebrews or Syrians, *mammon* is interpreted in Latin as “riches”; in Punic, *mammon* means “profit.” Both expressions, however, refer to the same end.

He rightly singled out greed in particular, so that he might clearly show that servants of riches are also servants of the devil. The Apostle did not hesitate to call greed the service of idols, saying: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 5).

Here one must carefully note that he does not say, “You cannot serve God and possess riches,” but, “You cannot serve God and mammon,” that is, riches. For we read that many of the holy Fathers possessed temporal goods and riches, and nevertheless served God.

Abraham was exceedingly rich. With three hundred and eighteen household slaves, he defeated five kings in a military expedition and rescued his brother Lot from captivity (Genesis 14). Job, that great example of patience, is likewise shown by the testimony of Scripture to have abounded in riches among all the peoples of the East (Job 1). What shall we say of the most holy David, to whom both an abundance of riches and the magnificence of royal power were available, and to whom gifts were brought by the nations subject to him on every side?

Although these men possessed riches, they did not serve riches but God, because they did not entrust their hope to riches, nor guard them as servants; rather, they distributed them freely as masters, holding them for use, not for desire, and wisely arranging them as things given to them, as it were, from the side.

For this reason blessed David, when he was established on the throne of the kingdom and showed that he placed no trust in deceptive riches, said: “I am needy and poor, like all my fathers” (Psalm 108). Addressing those who were rich or might become rich, he said: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 61).

Whoever therefore guards riches as a servant, and does not distribute them as a master, is a servant of riches; and by serving riches he is compelled to serve the devil, because, entangled in greed for riches, he subjects himself to the devil, who by the merit of his wickedness has been set over earthly things [Col. 1409D] and is called by the Lord “the prince of this age.”

Therefore let the rich hear these things and choose rather to be servants of Christ than slaves of riches. Let them learn not to lean upon present things, but to plant all their hope in eternal things, and to desire to have riches for this sole purpose: that they may have something with which to relieve the needs of the poor and with which their own sins may be redeemed.

“For this reason I say to you, do not be anxious about your soul, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear.” It is as though he were saying: “Because you cannot serve God and the desires of the world at the same time, and because you must not trust in the uncertainty of riches, I therefore say to you: do not be anxious about accumulating riches, by which the mind, once entangled, is estranged from love of its Creator.”

It may be asked whether this bodily food pertains to the soul or to the body, since it is clear that the soul is incorporeal, whereas food is corporeal. But in sacred Scripture the name “soul” commonly signifies the present life, according to what the Lord says elsewhere: “Whoever loves his soul,” that is, his life, “will lose it” (John 12). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “I do not account my soul more precious than myself” (Acts 20).

Here, therefore, “soul” must be understood in this sense, so that the present life is meant—the life sustained by food and clothing. Food is a certain bond and means of preserving it, and labor must be undertaken for its support; but anxiety must be removed, so that, having food and clothing, we may be content with them (1 Timothy 6).

Or “soul” may have been used for the body itself in which it is contained, the whole being designated by a part, just as we read that Jacob went down into Egypt “with seventy souls” (Genesis 46), although it is evident that the souls did not descend without their bodies.

As for spiritual food and clothing, we ought to be exceedingly concerned about them. Nevertheless, the Lord’s own words must be weighed more carefully. He does not say, “Do not seek what you will eat or what you will wear,” but, “Do not be anxious.” Thus it is not labor but anxiety that is forbidden.

Yet since it was said to the first man, “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3), what does it mean that he commands the disciples—or rather, all the faithful—not to be anxious about what they should eat, drink, or wear? Does he forbid a person to labor, when he previously commanded him to eat bread by the sweat of his face? Certainly not. To this end he was also given the skill of working the land and plowing the fields, so that he might be nourished and clothed by his own labor.

But in these commands of the Lord, the following distinction must be observed: each person should strive to procure what is necessary for bodily food and clothing when those things are lacking which natural frailty requires, since without them he cannot continue to exist and life itself, deprived of this twofold support, would fail. He forbids anxiety about these things, by which excessive concern is understood.

The ancients therefore aptly defined anxiety as “distress of the mind accompanied by immoderate thought.” Thus anxiety, as something superfluous and excessively troubling, is removed, while labor, as something necessary, is permitted (Psalm 127). Indeed, the use of labor is not forbidden at all, since the Psalmist calls blessed the one who is nourished by his own labors, and the Apostle says that one ought to labor with one’s hands at what is good, so that one may have something to give to those suffering need (Ephesians 4).

Therefore labor must be undertaken so that necessity may be overcome; anxiety must be removed, since it serves not necessity but desire.

“Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” A human being consists of these two substances, namely, soul and body. Everything we desire, we desire either for its own sake or for the sake of something else. Wisdom, which is God, is to be desired for its own sake. For the sake of something else, for example, someone may desire to have medicines—not in order to possess medicines, but so that health may be provided for the body.

No one doubts that what is sought for its own sake is greater than what is sought for the sake of something else. It is therefore shown here that the soul is more than food, because food is required for the purpose of sustaining the present life. The body likewise is more than clothing, which is sought so that nakedness may be covered.

The Lord therefore admonishes us by this statement to remember that God has given us something much greater in making us, when we did not yet exist, from soul and body than food is: the sense is, “Since he has granted us greater things—namely, body and soul—he will certainly grant lesser things, namely food and clothing. Why, then, are we anxious about lesser things, when we have received greater ones?”

“Consider the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” He calls the birds that move throughout this air “the birds of the air.” Whatever is nearer to heaven is customarily called “heaven” in Scripture.
