The Lord leads us to consider greater works, so that through them he may more easily persuade us concerning lesser things. No one doubts that a human being is greater than any bird. Man was made in the image and likeness of God, whereas a bird is a creature lacking reason; and when it dies, both its body and its soul die. Although a human being dies in body, the soul nevertheless lives for God.

He therefore says: “Consider,” that is, observe, “the birds of the air, for they neither sow,” that is, they do not plant seed, “nor reap,” that is, they do not gather in, “nor gather into barns,” namely, granaries; “and your heavenly Father feeds them,” that is, they are nourished by God’s command.

If, then, the birds, whose soul is mortal, are nourished by the providence of God their Creator, how much more are human beings, to whom eternity is promised, governed by his generosity?

Some, desiring to be wiser than they ought, wished to examine this passage through allegorical interpretation, saying that the “birds of the air” signify angels, who live without any anxiety and enjoy perpetual security and rest. They did not consider what follows: “Are you not worth much more than they?”

If, then, divine providence supplies unfailing nourishment to these birds, which have no skill in cultivating the earth and produce no harvest from crops, it is shameful for human beings to be wearied by anxiety, when both the tempering of the elements and the fertility of the earth serve them.

The foolishness of such people is rightly restrained by the example of irrational birds, because birds claim nothing as their exclusive possession and do not know how to envy others; these people, however, defend private possessions, although they have lost what is common.

They are therefore recalled to contemplate their dignity and consider their origin when he adds: “Are you not worth much more than they?” He does not say, “Are you more numerous,” since “more numerous” pertains to number, but “worth more,” with reference to dignity: that is, “You are of greater worth and value than they.”

Those creatures are irrational and govern themselves by no understanding; when they die, they perish in body and soul. You, however, were created in the image of God, predestined for eternity, and fashioned more sublimely within the order of creation. You must therefore remember what you are, lest, while you devote yourselves too much to earthly things, you fall into what is earthly and lowly.

“Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” To persuade us more easily that certain things are possible without anxiety, he also gave an example from what is impossible: “Which of you,” he says, “by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?”

It is as though he said: “If there is someone among you who can add one cubit to his stature, so that he may appear either taller or broader, let him think and labor, if such a thing is possible, about how he will clothe and feed what he himself has added to his body. But what God has created, he has provided to clothe and feed even without your anxiety.”

Since, then, you cannot accomplish even what is least for God, leave to his providence the care of covering and nourishing the body, since it was he who brought your body to this stature.

But since instruction concerning food had been given by comparison with the birds of the air, an example concerning clothing also had to be given by comparison with the lilies of the field. Hence it follows: “And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They do not labor in growing, nor do they spin,” that is, they do not spin thread so that they may be clothed by their own labor.

By this moral instruction we are persuaded that, if even things lacking sense and reason are clothed by God’s providence, needing neither practical use nor ornament to make them pleasing, you should believe that a rational human being, if he places all his hope in God, can never be in need because he has relied upon divine favor.

It should be noted that the Lord has used “the lilies of the field” for all the plants of the field. They do not labor in growing, nor do they spin—that is, they do not twist threads to fashion beautiful garments for themselves.

Of these it follows: “But I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” He has used a particular term in place of a general one, as is made clear below, where the grass of the field is expressly mentioned.

Nor should we omit that certain teachers assert that here we are forewarned by the example of angels. They say that it should not be understood casually that a flower is compared with a human being—or, in Solomon’s case, with one greater than a human being. Because of his excellence, Solomon was in some respect more than a man: he built a temple for God and prefigured the true Solomon, that is, Christ, in mystery.

Thus the glory of the heavenly angels is expressed by the lilies. We are adorned by their brightness and delighted by the fragrance of their holiness.

These lilies—that is, those angelic hosts—are hindered by no anxiety and exercised by no labor, but preserve the grace of divine freedom through the heavenly gift of their nature.

It should also be added that lilies require no cultivation, nor, in the generation of this flower, does the anxious labor of farmers return in its cycle as it does for the yield of other fruits. Even if, once the flower has fallen, what is external appears to wither, it is nevertheless nourished internally by the strength of the root; and, as soon as it is summoned by the gentle influence of spring, it is clothed again in the beauty of its flower.

So too the angelic orders receive from the condition of their origin, which they have attained, the fact that they exist forever.

Solomon, therefore, although surrounded by great splendor, cannot be compared with these flowers, because, even if he adorned the weakness of bodily nature with a certain strength of mind and the glory of his deeds, he could in no way equal the height of the angels, who, free from human frailty, preserve the adornment of incorruptible goodness.

The Lord promises that he will give this beauty of immortality and this incorruptible garment to the elect at the resurrection, saying: “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22).

“But I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” History relates that Solomon was the richest of all the kings of Israel. Among the other riches of his dignity, he especially excelled in the beauty and variety, as well as the preciousness, of his clothing, so much so that the individual attendants, together with all those subject to him, used their own distinctive garments.

Thus, concerning the queen of Sheba, who had come from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom, we read: “When she saw the order of his attendants and the garments in which they served, she no longer had any spirit left” (1 Kings 10).

Yet although he was adorned with such honor and splendor of clothing, he was not clothed with such beauty as one of these—understand, one of the lilies. And indeed, what texture or embroidered design produced by women can equal the beauty of flowers? What is as red as the rose? What is as white as the lily? And, indeed, no purple or dye can surpass the exceedingly beautiful color of the violet.

When he says, “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these,” by “all his glory” he means the greatness of his kingdom, the splendor of his luxuries, or, as we have said, the distinction and variety of his clothing.

Why he introduced this comparison with luxuries he makes clear by adding: “If, then, God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace of fire, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?”

He calls “the grass of the field” the same thing he earlier called “the lilies of the field,” namely, all the herbs adorned with beautiful colors.

The adverb “tomorrow” does not always signify the following day in Scripture; sometimes it also signifies a future time, as in the statement made by Samuel, raised by the medium, to Saul: “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me” (1 Samuel 28). Jacob likewise says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Genesis 30).

Here too, therefore, when it says that it is “tomorrow” that the grass is thrown into the furnace, this must be understood of a future time. The meaning is: If God surrounds with such beauty things that quickly fall and wither—namely, grass, which is here today in its greenness and tomorrow is thrown into the fire—how much more diligently will he provide what is necessary for you, who have been prepared for an eternal inheritance?

Because you do not believe this as you ought, but still doubt, you are therefore “of little faith.” He calls the apostles “of little faith,” because they had not yet reached the summit of perfect faith. Hence they also said to the Lord: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17).

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’” It should be noted that he does not say, “Do not seek food or drink,” or “Do not be anxious about food or drink,” but specifically, “What you shall eat or drink.”

Here those are especially censured who, established in communities, disregard the fellowship of the others who are generally fed or clothed under one superior, and seek finer or harsher food or clothing than those with whom they live, so that by this they may be considered either more influential or stronger than the others.

Both practices are blameworthy and both deserve notice: excessive ostentation in clothing gives rise to pride, while excessively shabby and neglected dress provides, under the appearance of religious seriousness, material for praise and a desire for approval.

One must therefore walk along the royal road between the two, so that neither expensive clothing marks one as proud nor cheap clothing marks one as more religious than is proper.

For whom, then, anxiety about food and clothing is appropriate is made clear when he adds: “For the Gentiles seek all these things.” Except for the few Jews who, possessing the Law, worshiped the God of heaven, the other nations throughout the world, serving idols, were called Gentiles.

Speaking of them here, the Lord says: “The Gentiles seek all these things.” They are the people who do not know God and know how to think of nothing except earthly things. It is properly their condition to be tormented by worldly cares, since they have no hope of the future and make no account of labors, but delight only in present things. “They have been compared with foolish beasts and have become like them” (Psalm 48).

But you, formed by a different instruction and prepared for heavenly dignity, think about spiritual and eternal things. Nor should you fear that, while doing these things, you will lack the use of temporal goods; nor should you distrust God’s power, since he knows better than we ourselves what we need and provides for us far more beneficially than we know how to provide for ourselves.

Hence it follows: “For your Father knows that you need all these things.”

Some people who teach superfluously object: “If God knows what we need before we ask, what need is there to beseech him for our necessities? We are therefore speaking uselessly to one who already knows.”

They should be answered that we are not narrators but petitioners. It is one thing to tell someone who does not know, and another to beseech humbly one who knows. He wishes us to ask him, although he also knows what we ought to ask, so that our petition may receive its reward.

What we must seek with the chief desire of our minds and with the utmost earnestness is fully taught by the statement that follows: “But seek first the kingdom of God [Col. 1414D] and his righteousness.”

“First” is not used here numerically but rather quantitatively: “First,” that is, before all things and above all things, seek the kingdom of God.

The kingdom of God is understood in four ways in sacred Scripture. Sometimes it signifies the present Church, as in the statement: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 13)—that is, in the present Church—“is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

Sometimes it signifies sacred Scripture, as in: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you” (Matthew 21), that is, the understanding of the divine Scriptures.

Sometimes it signifies the heavenly homeland, as John says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3).

Sometimes it signifies the Lord Jesus Christ himself, as he says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God is among you” (Luke 17), that is, Christ in his humanity dwells among human beings. And, as he says in the present reading, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness,” he calls the joys of that heavenly city the kingdom: there are supreme peace and true tranquility, and the fruits of struggles and the rewards of labors are granted to the saints.

Let us seek this kingdom of God through the services of our life, continually sigh for it, and most willingly endure every hardship and difficulty for the sake of attaining it.

“Seek also his righteousness.” The righteousness of the kingdom of God is the fulfillment of God’s commandments. The righteousness of the kingdom of God is to despise all perishable and transitory things and to regard the loss of present goods as gain in what follows.

The person who seeks God’s righteousness is the one who, practicing good works, obeys his words and commandments in all things.

Thus, when we seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, those things—the highest and true goods—will be given to us, while these other things will be added as lesser goods. Although they may appear to be goods in the present, they are intermediate things; when compared with those true goods, they should no longer be called goods.

They are given to the saints while they still labor in the present pilgrimage, so that, relieved by them as by a kind of provision for the journey, they may reach the goods they will receive in their homeland.

Temporal things ought to be kept for use, eternity for desire. For if present goods are available, the mind must attend to them, lest their excessive accumulation weigh it down and burden it as with a weight, preventing it from reaching the homeland.

Thus we ought to use present goods sparingly and honorably, so that, after we have traveled through the stretches of this long exile, we may enjoy eternal things.

Alternatively: “And all these things will be added to you.” Since, while remaining in this life, we cannot pass through it without food and clothing, after saying, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness,” he immediately adds: “And all these things”—understand, temporal goods—“will be added to you.”

Here it should be noted that greater things are commanded to be sought—namely, the kingdom of God and his righteousness—so that lesser things may be obtained, namely, the goods of the present life. Concerning these he did not say “they will be given,” but “they will be added,” as necessary things which we are not to enjoy as an end, but which, placed as we are upon a journey, we are to use.

## HOMILY CLXXVIII. ON THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the exposition of blessed Ambrose on the Gospel according to Luke, book V, no. 89.)*

[Col. 1415D]

“At that time Jesus went into a city called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him, etc.” (Luke 7).

This passage is rich in grace on both sides, so that we may believe that divine mercy was quickly moved by the lamentation of the widowed mother, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Ambrose, volume II of his works, *Patrologia* XV, col. 1660, no. 89.

## HOMILY CLXXIX. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From blessed Ambrose [?].)*

“At that time Jesus went into a city called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him, etc.” (Luke 7).

[Col. 1416A] The Gospel sermon that precedes this one recounts how the Lord healed the centurion’s servant on account of the greatness of his faith, and how he exalted the faith of the centurion himself—or rather, the faith of all the nations in him. After relating that miracle, the evangelist continues: “After this he went into a city called Nain.” From miracle he hastens to miracle, and by a certain progression of power passes from the healing of a paralytic to the raising of the dead.

For we learned from blessed Jerome that Nain is a city in the province of Galilee inhabited by Jews, two miles distant from Mount Tabor. On that mountain the Lord taught the eight beatitudes and nearly all the commandments of the New Testament. Nain is interpreted as “wave” or “commotion.” As the Lord approached its gates, he encountered the body [Col. 1416B] of a dead man, which was being carried outside the city for burial. Chroniclers report that this city contains a church that was once the house of the widow whose son the Lord is said here to have raised.

The Lord therefore went forth to provide an opportunity for the exercise of his power; his disciples went with him—those most faithful companions of his journeys, sharers in his labors, who were nourished by his presence, instructed by his preaching, and strengthened by his miracles. The city of Nain, which, as we have said, in our language means “wave” or “commotion,” spiritually signifies this world, which, having lost its tranquility, is always subject to fluctuations and disturbances and never remains in the same condition. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “You have shaken the earth, O Lord, and troubled it,” etc. (Psalm 59).

Thus the Lord approached Nain, so to speak, when, having assumed the humanity of our weakness, he deigned to appear visibly in the world. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out: the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her.

This woman was not troubled by a simple anxiety of grief. She was a widow, deprived of the consolation of her son; and she would have endured his death somewhat more lightly if he had not been her only son, if another had survived to lessen his parent’s sorrow. Yet in this respect she was blessed: by Christ’s compassion she was soon to receive again the one whom the harshness of human fate had taken from her.

Nor did it happen without divine providence that a large crowd was present both with the Lord and with this woman, so that many might become witnesses of the miracle being performed and many also praisers of divine power. But why did a large crowd go with the Lord? The evangelist John makes this clear when he says: “Because they saw the signs that he performed” (John 6). Since the Lord performed miracles wherever he went—that is, since by preaching the Gospel he announced words of salvation—his disciples went with him, clinging to him, and a great crowd also went with him.

This deed, wonderfully accomplished by the Savior, is entirely clear according to the historical sense. Understood spiritually, however, it supplies no small edification to the minds of its hearers. For according to the spiritual or moral sense, this dead man, who was carried outside the gate of his city while many looked on, signifies [Col. 1417A] a man dead in sins and sunk into the sleep of a deadly burial in crimes. Although he is dead in soul, he no longer conceals the death of his soul in the hidden recesses of his thoughts; rather, just as through the gates of a city, so through the evidence of perverse conversation or evil action, he brings his wicked life to the notice of many by his bad example. He no longer hides his shameful sins; instead, having become bolder in evil, he presents them to others for imitation.

Of such people the prophet says: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not hide it” (Isaiah 3). And again he says to the sinful soul: “Your forehead has become like that of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jeremiah 3).

By the gate of the city through which the dead man was carried out, one of the five bodily senses is understood. For there are five well-known bodily senses, arranged by nature in their appropriate places: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The city of each soul is its body, in which it dwells as in an enclosed city. A dead man is carried out through the gates of this city when someone, displaying through one of the bodily senses an indication of an evil will, declares himself to be dead in soul.

For example, whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her, whoever raises his eyes and stretches them toward the ends of the earth, sends forth signs of his death through the gates of his eyes. When anyone opens his ear to idle words, to shameful or lustful songs, or to words of detraction, he makes such ears the gates of death for his soul. Whoever, enticed by brothel perfumes and by the skin of an exotic mouse, neglects to run after the fragrance of God’s ointments is drawn out dead through the gate of his nostrils.

But whoever opens his mouth to utter blasphemies against God and to sow discord among his brothers—whose mouth speaks vanity, and who lends his tongue not only to idle but also to harmful speech—does nothing other than reveal, carried out through the door of his mouth, the death of his soul.

Hence the prophet, lamenting that the entrances of our city are carelessly left open, says: “Death has entered through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jeremiah 9). Again the prophet says: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lamentations 3).

For just as an enemy, hurling arrows into a city through its windows, wounds and kills those shut inside, so the evil spirit, when he drives the weapon of temptation into the mind through any one of the five senses, immediately casts the soul down from its state and destroys it with a deadly pestilence. Seeking to burst into the innermost places of the soul, he adapts himself to images, mingles with sounds, inserts himself into smells, and insinuates himself into tastes; and thus, while he is guarded against with insufficient vigilance, he opens a way to death, which lies beside pleasure.

Therefore divine providence must be humbly implored to guard all the gates of our city. To prevent the raging enemy from besieging them, may he mercifully close them against the enemy’s engines and allow his praise continually to be proclaimed in our gates.

It should not be passed over without notice that this dead young man is said to have been the only son of his widowed mother. Although the Church, which is the mother of all believers, is gathered from many persons, each of the faithful who is marked with the character of the Christian faith is rightly a son of one mother—the Catholic Church, I mean. Although they differ in age and sex, they are made one in Christ by the grace of regeneration, when through adoption they become brothers of the only Son.

Moreover, every believer is a child of faith when he is instructed in its rudiments, but a mother when he raises others. Thus the apostle Paul spoke to the Corinthians with maternal affection: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4).

When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said: “Do not weep.” Since there were two substances in Christ—namely, God and man—the evangelist fittingly first demonstrates that the Lord was moved with compassion as a true man, and then records that, as true God, he raised the dead. Thus, in the compassion with which he pitied the widow, he gave us an example of the piety we should imitate; and in the effect of the miracle, he set before us for admiration and proclamation his power and divinity, by which he also raised the dead.

“Do not weep,” he said, as if he were saying: “Do not weep for him as though he were dead, since you will soon see him rise from death.”

And he approached and touched the bier—that is, the coffin in which the dead man was being carried, which received its name from carrying. By touching the bier on which the lifeless man was being carried, he gave a clear indication of his gracious condescension. Although he could have restored him to life by his word alone, he preferred first to touch the bier, both to give a sign of his compassion and to raise the widow’s spirit, which had been cast down by grief.

Those who were carrying him stood still, awaiting the marvelous effect of the power. For when they saw the Lord approaching, they who were carrying the dead man stopped, eager to see his mercy in the resurrection of the dead.

Although these matters stand out sufficiently in the literal sense, it remains for us to investigate what mystery they contain. The person of this widow cannot be without sacramental significance: commended by the dignity of her character, by the merit of her continence, and by the attendance at the funeral, she merited from the Lord the resurrection of her only son.

She plainly signifies the holy Church, the mother of all who rightly believe. Pregnant with the word of God, she does not cease daily to give birth to spiritual children for her through the washing of the divine font. [Col. 1418D]

This woman is rightly said to have been a widow. “Widow” is so called as though meaning “separated from a husband,” because the Greeks use *viduare*—“to make a widow”—for “to separate.” Our holy mother is also a widow, because she does not see her husband Christ present in the flesh. For after Christ, her husband and redeemer, departed into heaven through the assumption of humanity, the holy Church remained on earth like a widow.

Hence Solomon, speaking in the person of the adulterous woman—that is, the church of heretics, which flatters itself over Christ’s absence—says: “There is no man in his house; he has gone on a distant journey, taking the money-bag with him; he will return to his house on the day of the full moon” (Proverbs 7).

The meaning of this statement is as follows: “There is no man in his house”—that is, Christ is not present in the Church according to his humanity. “He has gone on a distant journey,” because, rising from the dead, he penetrated the heights of heaven, which are far removed from this light and from the dwelling of the vast intervening air. “He took the money-bag with him”—that is, he exalted his flesh, placed above the heavens in the treasury of divinity, and seated it at the right hand of the Father. “He will return to his house on the day of the full moon”—that is, when the number of the elect in the Church has been completed, he will return at the end of the world for judgment, to take his bride, the Church, to himself.

By the bier on which the corpse of the dead man was carried, we understand the conscience of the sinful person, in which he lay sleeping in evil through despair. The bearers who carried the lifeless man in the bier—that is, the supreme instrument of a funeral—to burial signify either the impure desires that drag a person to destruction or the evil conversations of companions who deceive him.

While they lull the soul into security by flattering allurements, encourage those who do evil, and thereby make them readier for worse things, they in a certain way cover them with earth piled over them and bury them beneath a mound of soil so that they cannot breathe. Of such people the Lord says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9). The dead bury the dead when sinners flatter sinners.

When the Lord touched the funeral bier, the bearers stopped, because when the Lord pierces the heart of a sinful person through inward inspiration, the carnal and impure desires, together with the evil conversations of deceptive companions, immediately fall silent. Thus, turning back upon themselves, they hear the Lord calling them to life and respond to his call through deeds worthy of their renewed conduct.

Some teachers understand the bier as the wood of the primordial transgression, in which we were all carried dead under the condition of that guilt by four poles, signifying the four material elements. We were carried toward destruction by these four poles when we burned with the harmful heat of desire, when the cold moisture of lust overflowed, when the sluggish dullness of the body blunted the vigor of our minds, or when our spirit, hardened by corruption, nourished a mind empty of the true light.

But when the Lord touched the bier, the bearers of that bitter funeral halted their step, because when the Lord touched mortal things and appeared in the likeness of sin, we, who were already near the tomb, were granted resurrection when the course of these bearers was stopped.

Our tomb was evil conduct; our tomb was unbelief. Our throat was a sepulcher, according to what the Psalmist says of the reprobate: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Psalm 5). We were freed from this sepulcher by the touch of Christ and the hearing of his voice.

For what does his touching mean except to come to our aid in mercy? And what does it mean for us to hear his voice except to fulfill his commands eagerly?

And he said: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” He was indeed dead, but since all things live to the Lord, he spoke to the dead as though to the living, saying: “I say to you, arise.” Between the Lord’s command and its accomplishment there is no interval. For “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148). “Whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth.”

When the Lord’s voice had been heard, the man who had been dead sat up and began to speak. After his resurrection the dead man began to speak, so that his true resurrection might thereby be shown, and he might be believed to be not a phantom but a reality.

And he gave him to his mother. Once the dead man had been raised and fully restored to health, the Lord gave him to his mother.

Spiritually, the dead man sits up when, through inward compunction, a sinner rises from the death of the soul to life and, after the deadly sleep of sin, raises himself to good works. He begins to speak when, confessing faith in the Holy Trinity, he reveals signs of his life to others, or when by the word of exhortation and the example of his conduct he invites others to repentance. He is restored to his mother when, through the priestly ministry, he is restored to communion with the Church.

All were seized with fear, and they glorified God. It was just that a new and previously unheard-of miracle should be followed by great astonishment among those who witnessed it, so that mouths previously silent suddenly opened in the praises of God.

Here a moral point may be observed. Just as the bodily resurrection that visibly took place in the body moved people to wonder outwardly, so the spiritual resurrection that occurs daily in the souls of the faithful admonishes us to strive to rise inwardly from the death of the soul. The more perilous and desperate the death from which the soul returns to life, the more people are corrected by its example and recalled to life.

For the one who falls from a higher position falls more disastrously; and the more grievous the fall, the more pleasing is the mercy of the one who raises him. Thus, when the one who had fallen more disastrously is lifted up, greater hope of salvation is generated in many.

Let us consider blessed David and Peter. One, although he was king and prophet, descended into so deep a pit of destruction that he committed adultery and murder together (2 Kings 11). The other was driven from the height of the apostolic dignity to the precipice of a threefold denial (Matthew 26). When, in repentance, they quickly rose from the death of the soul, many penitents obtained salvation.

The greater their honor and the higher their rank, the more dangerously they fell; and the more grievous their fall, the more graciously the Lord’s compassion shone forth in raising them. The more abundantly the Lord’s compassion appeared in them, the firmer became the hope of salvation for all who come to repentance.

“For a great prophet has arisen among us.” The simple crowds, ignorant of the Law and the prophets, which promised the Jews the coming of the Son of God, saw God and man dwelling bodily among human beings and performing wondrous deeds through the power of divine might. They therefore thought that he was one of the prophets who used to perform miracles among the people of Israel, and so, deceived by error, they cried out: “For a great prophet has arisen among us.”

They called him a great prophet, but not God or the Son of God, because they were still blinded by the cloud of ignorance. For this reason, in the preceding passage, they are pointedly designated by the name “crowds.” They were crowds because they had not yet penetrated, together with the apostles, into the inner mystery of his divinity.

Although these crowds were mistaken with a certain devotion of spirit, they were not altogether in error. They were mistaken in thinking that he was only a mere man; but they were not at all mistaken in saying that he was a prophet. For he truly was a prophet, because he proclaimed with complete truth what was to come. The Lord himself also testifies that he is a prophet when he says: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13). And elsewhere: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matthew 13).

He was therefore a prophet, although he was the Lord of the prophets, just as he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

They also added: “For God has visited his people.” Through this man who performs such miracles, God the Father visited his people by sending his incarnate Word into the world, so that by compassionate assistance he might redeem them and free them from the long illness—or rather, from the death—in which they had long languished.

Nor did he visit his people only at that time. Every day he visits his faithful through his Gospel, through the sayings of the prophets, and through the examples of the fathers who came before us. The Lord also visits his people when, through the administration of the Holy Spirit, the terror of eternal punishment, or the sweetness of the heavenly homeland, he reveals inwardly to each of the elect and teaches by hidden inspiration how he may rise from the death of the soul.

Or otherwise: He visits his people daily—the people whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son—when, through the inward inspiration of his word, he arouses them to love invisible things and impresses upon their minds the greatness of the joys promised to them in heaven: safety without weakness, salvation without pain, life without death; ease without impediment, security without weariness; a place where there is the holy fellowship of all the elect, an established solemnity, secure rest, true peace, and everlasting life.

Let us therefore give thanks to God the Father, our creator, who, after justly leaving our earlier fathers in unbelief because of their iniquity, confirmed his mercy toward us in the final ages of this world by sending his Son to redeem the human race.

Let us also give thanks to his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to come to us by assuming humanity and to promise heavenly blessedness to those who obey the precepts of his commandments. May he himself help us so that we may at last attain it and live happily with him—the one who visited us by his presence in the Incarnation and mercifully redeemed us by the blood of his Passion.

Meanwhile, when the narratives of the four evangelists are compared, we find three dead persons whom the Lord raised, although there is no doubt that he raised more, even if this is not recorded in writing. Many were undoubtedly raised bodily by the Lord, says blessed Augustine; but it was not without reason that three were mentioned: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, still lying dead inside the house; this young man, carried outside the gate of the city; and Lazarus, dead for four days and already stinking.

These three dead persons signify three classes of sinful people whom Christ even today raises from the death of the soul in the holy Church. But let us see what these classes of the dead are.

There are some who consent to an evil thought. They have sin inwardly in their hearts, but do not yet reveal it by an action. To signify that such people can be brought to life in him, the Savior raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue while she was still lying inside the house, representing the wickedness of sin hidden in the secrecy of the heart.

Others, clinging to a perverse thought, fall into action after consenting to sin, like one who carries a dead man outside: what was hidden in secret now appears publicly. Yet so that these people too should not despair, if they repent, of being made alive in soul by the Lord, the Lord raised the young man who had been carried outside the city gate and restored him to his mother, because, causing the soul to rise from sin, he restored it to the unity of the holy Church.

Others sin not only by thinking or doing what is unlawful, but also bury themselves, as it were, beneath the very habit of sinning. Yet so that such people too might not lack hope of pardon, provided that there are vigilant thoughts concerned for their salvation, watching over them like devoted sisters to Christ, he raised Lazarus, who had already been four days in the tomb.

At the same time, the Lord wished to show that lighter sins, which exist in the heart and thought, can be cured by the remedy of lighter penance. He therefore called the girl lying in the chamber forth by a brief and very easy command, saying: “Girl, arise” (Luke 8). On account of the ease of her rising, he had even denied that she was dead.

But to show that more serious sins—those which are shamelessly presented to others for imitation, or by which the sinner is so weighed down through long habit that he cannot rise—require a more extensive remedy of penance, he said to the young man who had been carried outside, using more words so that he might rise: “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7).

When he was about to raise Lazarus, he ordered the barriers of the tomb to be removed, groaned in spirit, groaned again, wept, and cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11).

A fourth dead man is announced to the Lord by the disciples, but he did not raise him, because there were no living people who would pray to the Lord for his life (Matthew 8). This dead man signifies those of whom John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). A sin unto death is to persist in sin until death.

Therefore, whoever recognizes that he lies in one of the three deaths of the soul mentioned above must repent of his deeds and continually implore divine mercy, joining the prayers of the faithful to his own, so that he may quickly merit to rise to eternal life.

But you.

# HOMILY CLXXX. ON THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the works of the venerable Bede the priest.)*

At that time, when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. And behold, there was a certain man suffering from dropsy before him, etc. (Luke 14).

[Col. 1423A] “Of dropsy,” etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XCIV, column 301.

# HOMILY CLXXXI. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

At that time, when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees, etc. (Luke 14).

The eternal and invisible Creator of all things, intending to save the human race, which for the long ages of this passing world had been bound under the laws of perpetual death, deigned in the last times to become man—by a wondrous order, and indeed by a wondrous birth—so that those whom justice had condemned might be redeemed by the prompting of mercy. And, in order to display a greater earnestness of his compassion toward us, he became not only man, [Col. 1423B] but also a poor and humble man, so that, by stooping to our poverty, he might grant us a share in his riches.

Finally, he became so poor for us that he did not even have a hut in which to take shelter, in accordance with what he himself says elsewhere: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). For this reason he deigned to visit human banquets—not because he desired meals prepared by mortal hands, but so that he might teach salvation and seek faith. He readily allowed himself to be invited to human feasts for this purpose: both to enlighten the guests by miracles and so that the members of the household who were occupied in service within their masters’ homes, and who had no free opportunity to approach him, might on this occasion hear the word of salvation [Col. 1423C] and recognize the author of their salvation.

For he despised no condition, nor judged any unworthy of his mercy, because he has mercy on all and hates none of the things he has made; likewise, he cares for all.

Another beginning:

The Lord approached the bodily banquets of human beings not so much to eat the outward food served by attendants as to distribute to his hearers the fare of the heavenly banquet—he who is himself the bread that descended from heaven. This is shown to be true by the fact that wherever he sat down to dine, he either taught something or performed signs. This occurred at the banquet about which the present reading is composed: there he both performed a miracle and delivered a sermon.

He also did this out of the most compassionate affection of his mercy, so that the household which, always occupied in the service of its masters, could not freely gather to him wherever he might be, might nevertheless, when he graciously came to their masters’ dwellings, enjoy his presence together, be refreshed by his teachings, and rejoice in his miracles [Col. 1423D]. At the same time, he was setting before future preachers of the New Testament an authoritative example, so that they might impart the word of salvation to masters and subjects, free persons and slaves, superiors and inferiors, to all without distinction of persons; and so that they might not shrink from receiving from those to whom they proclaimed the word of life the services of hospitality, in a fitting exchange, “so that those who sow spiritual things for them may reap their material things” (1 Cor. IX).

Therefore, in order to fulfill the duty of his dispensation, the Lord entered the house of a ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread.

[Col. 1424A] The Sabbath day was held most sacred and was celebrated with great observance according to the ancient rite. On it, abstaining from every kind of work, people devoted themselves to meditation and banquets. Christian custom more suitably transferred its observance to the Lord’s Day, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.

When the Lord had been invited to the ruler’s banquet, it is said: “And they were watching him.” This is to be understood of the scribes and Pharisees, who were present for the purpose of being able to criticize him, with a twofold malignity: whether he cured the dropsical man, they would condemn him as a despiser and violator of the Law and of the Sabbath; or whether he did not cure him, they would accuse him of impiety or inability. For just as the good followed the Lord in order to hear his preaching and see his miracles, so, on the other hand, the scribes and Pharisees [Col. 1424B] were present so that they might slander him in his actions.

We say that to watch means to guard carefully and attentively. Thus they were watching him—that is, they were craftily intent on finding grounds for accusing him. Why they were watching him can be understood from what follows. “And behold,” he says, “there was a certain man with dropsy before him.” Since it was the Sabbath, they were considering whether or not he would cure the sick man on that day. If he did cure him, they intended to say: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX). But if he did not wish to cure him, they would defame him on the ground of inability.

“Behold,” says the Evangelist, “there was a certain man with dropsy before him.” Dropsy is a disease which the Latins call *veternus*. It derives its name from water, because in Greek *hydor* means “water.” It is a subcutaneous disease arising from a rupture of the [Col. 1424C] bladder, producing swelling of the belly and foulness of breath. It has this particular feature: the more a person drinks, the more he arouses in himself a harmful thirst.

“And answering, he said to them: ‘Is it lawful to cure on the Sabbath?’ But they were silent. Then he took hold of the sick man, healed him, and dismissed him.”

That he is said to have answered those who had said nothing refers to what was stated previously: “And they were watching him.” Since he regards thoughts no less than actions, he rightly answered their thoughts as though they had been words or deeds. He questioned them not because the Lord was seeking their opinion, but so that they might be more effectively refuted by their own response or silence. Thus, seeing themselves enclosed on every side, they were rightly silent when questioned. Whatever they said, they saw that it would be spoken against them [Col. 1424D].

If they said, “It is lawful,” they would hear: “Why, then, are you watching me?” But if they said, “It is not lawful,” they could not escape in that way either. For the Lord would say to them what he subsequently brought against them: “Why do you care for your animals on the Sabbath?”

Therefore, seeing that their own conscience had struck them down and left them silent, he took hold of the sick man, healed him, and dismissed him.

The Lord healed the dropsical man in the presence of the scribes and Pharisees in order to show them that, just as that man had been healed in body, so they too, if they wished to believe in him, could be healed in soul. With wise economy the Lord cured the dropsical man before the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees and immediately afterward disputed against avarice, so that through the illness which the man suffered in his body he might signify the sickness by which they were wasting away in their minds [Col. 1425A].

Mystically, this dropsical man signifies the Jewish people themselves, who had been weighed down by a particularly evil disease of avarice and lust. No nation was more avaricious than the Jewish people, nor more inclined to lust. Balaam the diviner had foreseen them as addicted to this disease when he gave Balak such counsel as would prostitute them to idolatry through the beauty of women (Num. XXIV–XXV). We speak here truly of spiritual fornication, to which that same people was so devoted that through the prophet it is called by the name of a shameless and adulterous prostitute (Ezek. XVI).

The dropsical man who is healed prefigures the synagogue, in which part of that people was freed by faith from the harmful fluid of avarice and lust. Thus, after Christ’s ascension, as many of them as possessed houses or fields [Col. 1425B] sold what they had and brought the proceeds before the apostles’ feet, and for love of him renounced their wives and all the attachments of this age (Acts IV).

Morally also, this dropsical man signifies any avaricious or lustful person. For just as the thirst of the dropsical person is insatiable, so the avaricious person multiplies a kind of thirst: the more he acquires, the more he strives to acquire by right and wrong. Hence Solomon says: “The avaricious man is not filled with money” (Eccl. V). Since neither poverty diminishes his thirst nor abundance satisfies it, the saying agrees with this: “The avaricious man is always in need.”

Likewise, the more any lustful person satisfies the pleasure of the flesh, the more he is inflamed to commit worse acts. Thus it comes about that the very thing by which the incentive to lust is extinguished for the moment soon afterward causes a worse conflagration [Col. 1425C].

We have said that avarice is signified by the disease of dropsy: just as the dropsical person thirsts for water, so the avaricious person thirsts for money. The Evangelist shows that the Pharisees suffered from this vice when, after some parables, he adds: “For the Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and derided him” (Luke XVI).

“And answering, he said to them.” Since no one had asked a question beforehand, what does it mean that he is so often said to have answered the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees? This expression is customary in the sacred books. Scripture often introduces a statement in the voice of one answering even though no question has been asked. Thus elsewhere in the Gospel we read: “At that time Jesus answered and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth’” (Matt. XI). Certainly, in that passage no question from the Father or anyone else had preceded, so that the sacred authority could testify that he had answered.

Likewise, when the holy women were weeping at the Lord’s tomb and asking nothing, it is said of the angel [Col. 1425D] who had come to announce Christ’s perpetual resurrection: “But the angel answering said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid’” (Matt. XXVIII).

After healing and dismissing the dropsical man, he immediately attacks the avarice of his accusers. For it follows: “And he said to them: ‘Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath?’”

By these words the Lord refuted those who were slandering him in such a way as to prove that they were devoted to avarice. It was as though he were saying in other words: “If you hasten to rescue your animals on the sanctified day [Col. 1426A] when they happen to fall into a well, even with labor—not caring for the animals themselves, but attending to your avarice—why do you criticize me for healing on the Sabbath a human being created in the image of God and far superior to an animal?”

He aptly compares the dropsical man with an animal falling into a well, because an animal slipping into a well suffers from the moisture of the water, just as the dropsical man is weighed down by fluid. Likewise, elsewhere he compared the bent woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years with an animal that is untied in order to be led to water (Luke XIII).

Yet, in the very plain words of the historical account, the inward sweetness of allegory is perceptible. For by the ox and the donkey the two peoples are understood: the Jewish people and the nations. The ox, [Col. 1426B] whose neck is worn by the yoke and whose labor turns the earth opened by the plow, most appropriately represents the Jewish people, who had borne the harsh yoke of the Law; whose pride the weight of the Law oppressed; and who served God for the sake of earthly happiness and the abundance of passing things.

It was a heavy yoke for the Jews to bear circumcision, to celebrate the feasts of Tabernacles in the open air—that is, amid the harshness of rain and the heat of the sun—to observe the repose or festival of the Sabbaths, and to keep the other most burdensome obligations of the Law, in which they had been serving throughout all the preceding ages.

The donkey, however, an exceedingly irrational animal and more burden-bearing than other creatures, represents the Gentile people. Hindered by the weight of sins and by the mass of the evil habit implanted in them, [Col. 1426C] they could neither breathe freely nor resist those who imposed burdens upon them; they proceeded toward mute idols as they were led.

These animals can also signify two classes of human beings. The ox, which labors for the production of crops, represents the wise. The donkey, an ignoble and senseless animal, figuratively displays all who are foolish and lack the reasoning of the word.

Rightly, therefore, in both passages the Lord placed the ox and the donkey either slipping into a well or loosed from the manger under the signification of the Jewish and Gentile peoples. For when the mediator of God and human beings himself came into this world, he found all people—whether Jews or Gentiles, wise or dull—entangled in the harshest bonds of sins and sunk, as if in the depth of a well, in the abyss of pleasure and carnal desire [Col. 1426D].

For it is written: “Everyone is bound by the bonds of his sins” (Prov. V). And the Apostle says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

Appropriately, then, it follows concerning the Lord’s mockers: “They could not answer him concerning these things.” For they saw all the darkness of falsehood vanish before the most splendid light of truth. But when the Lord saw that they were unable to answer and yet unwilling to cease from malice and envy, he turned his discourse to the exhortation of those who had been invited, who perhaps could profit from his preaching.

For he observed that they were seeking the first places at table with an improper zeal. He said to the invited guests in a parable, teaching them how they should choose the first places, and said to them:

[Col. 1427A] “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.”

Taken literally, this admonition of the Savior, rightly understood, offers a saving lesson to all. It especially commends humility and declares that humility is praiseworthy not only before God but also among human beings.

Nor is it without reason that the holy Evangelist wished to call this Gospel reading a parable. *Parabola* is Greek; in Latin it is called *similitudo*, “likeness.” In a likeness, one thing is presented figuratively, while another is suggested according to the truth.

That the wedding signifies the union of Christ and the Church can be inferred from many passages of the holy Gospel. He says: “Can the children of the wedding fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark II). Elsewhere, speaking in a parable, he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” [Col. 1427B] (Matt. XXII).

For God the Father made a wedding for his Son when, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the holy Church to him with the dowry of faith and love. At a wedding the bridegroom is joined to the bride so that children may be begotten. Thus the only-begotten Son of God joined to himself from the nations the holy Church as his bride and made many spiritual children his by adoption.

The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the womb of the Virgin Mary, in which he graciously united his divinity to our humanity through his Incarnation.

All of us who are marked by the title of Christianity, all who are fortified by the sign of the cross, have been invited to this wedding. Whoever, therefore, has come when called to this wedding—that is, whoever through the grace of faith has joined himself to the members of the Church [Col. 1427C]—should not recline in the first place, meaning that he should not boast of his merits or prefer himself to others as though he possessed a unique privilege of merit. Rather, he should always strive to think humbly of himself.

He does not know whether someone more honored than he has perhaps been invited by the one who invited him, and whether he may be required to give up his place. The person who gives his place to one invited after him who is more honored is the one who, secure in confidence concerning his former way of life, sees himself surpassed in good works by those who were called after him with lively eagerness.

For example, those who turn to divine service from the earliest growth of their youth are often surpassed in good works by those who, returning late from the stages of worldly life, are found to be strong in holy actions. These people are invited later yet recline first, because although they come late to the practice of religion, [Col. 1427D] they teach themselves more vigorously in justice and holiness; what they lack in time [the reading *parte* is uncertain] they make up for by the liveliness of their zeal.

When he begins, with strength, to occupy the last place, he recognizes better qualities in others than in himself. Whatever he previously considered great in his own conduct, he judges weak and most insignificant by comparison with another’s merit, saying with the Prophet: “I am poor and in labors from my youth; but having been exalted, I have been humbled and confounded” (Ps. LXXXVII).

What we ought to do, and how we ought to conduct ourselves in the Church, the teacher of heavenly discipline soon made clear when he said: “When you are invited to a wedding”—that is, when you come into the fellowship of the holy Church—“recline in the last place”—that is, take care to think humbly of yourself [Col. 1428A], according to what is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Eccl. III).

Do not boast of your virtues, but consider everyone superior to you; reckon yourself the least of all, inferior to everyone. For you will be more precious in the eyes of God the more contemptible you are in your own eyes; and the more worthless you seem to yourself, the more you will please God.

Then, when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you: “Friend, move up higher.”

This saying is also evidently fulfilled in the present life. Every day the Lord of the wedding enters the wedding of the Church; he judges the appearance, company, and conduct of the banqueters. The one whom he finds established in humility he blesses by exalting him with the name of friend, saying to him: “Friend, move up higher.”

He promotes the one whom his place seemed to hold below to the highest dignity of ecclesiastical rank [Col. 1428B], so that those reclining together—that is, resting in the faith—may glorify him with great admiration and, astonished, say with the Psalmist: “But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honored” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

When the Lord Jesus Christ comes to judgment, he will glorify and exalt whoever he finds humble and will command him to ascend to higher things. For he will raise to eternal blessedness those whom he has seen in this life thinking humbly of their virtues, according to the exhortation of the Apostle Peter to his hearers: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you on the day of visitation” (1 Pet. V).

Hence it is fittingly added: “Then you will have glory in the presence of all who recline with you.” “Then”—that is, at the end of the world—you will have glory.

But because this is said not of the present [Col. 1428C] but of the future, “then” must be referred to the blessedness that will be given to all the elect at the end of the world, when each person will see God as he is. It is rightly said “then,” lest, if we do anything good, we seek praise from human beings in the present; rather, “then,” that is, in the future life, we should await our reward from God.

For it is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX). Whoever delights in the glory of the present life and desires to possess now the fullness of the glory owed in the future will undoubtedly lack eternal blessedness, which is reserved for the elect as they journey toward their heavenly homeland.

This Gospel saying can also be truly understood literally in this life. Whoever is found reclining in the last place is exalted to a higher place when the master of the house comes. For every day the Lord comes spiritually and invisibly into the company of the elect and enters his wedding [Col. 1428D]; every day, as we have said, he considers the conduct and behavior of the faithful. Resisting the proud, he often prefers those whom he finds humble to others and glorifies them with such great gifts of special grace that those who recline with them—that is, who rest in the same faith—raise them up in harmonious admiration, proclaiming with the Psalmist: “Blessed are those whom you have chosen and taken to yourself, O Lord, etc.” (Ps. LXIV).

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

This conclusion appended to the Gospel reading teaches that the preceding parable must also be understood mystically [Col. 1429A]. It is evident that not everyone who exalts himself before human beings will immediately be humbled in this life, nor will everyone who humbles himself in the sight of human beings be exalted, since the opposite sometimes occurs: a person who begins to be raised to some pinnacle of dignity may not cease to be exalted until the end of his life. Conversely, one who begins to be humble and modest may remain in that very mediocrity until the end of his life.

Therefore, since God cannot be deceived, and these are his words, if this is not fulfilled in the present life, it remains that it will undoubtedly be fulfilled in the future—namely, when the wicked and proud will be humbled with the devil in hell, hearing from the Lord: “Go into the eternal fire”; while the just and humble will be exalted by the Lord, receiving from [Col. 1429B] him the desirable voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

That we may deserve to hear this, may he himself deign to grant it to us, God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLXXXII. ON THE WEDNESDAY OF THE EMBER DAYS

*(From the works of the venerable priest Bede.)*

At that time, one of the crowd answered and said to Jesus: “Teacher, I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit; and wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams, and gnashes his teeth, and becomes rigid, etc.” (Mark IX.)

It is related in the preceding chapter of this holy Gospel, [Col. 1429C] etc. For the remainder, see the venerable priest Bede, *Works*, vol. V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 312.

## HOMILY CLXXXIII. ON THE FRIDAY OF THE EMBER DAYS

*(From blessed Ambrose’s exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, book VI, no. 12.)*

At that time a certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him. And entering the house of the Pharisee, he reclined at table, etc. (Luke VII.)

Here many seem to encounter a difficulty, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Ambrose, *Works*, vol. 11, *Patrologia* XV, col. 1671.

## HOMILY CLXXXIV. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE EMBER DAYS

*(From the works of blessed Pope Gregory the Great.)*

[Col. 1429D] At that time Jesus told the crowds this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none, etc.” (Luke XIII.)

Through his Gospel our Lord and Redeemer sometimes speaks by words and sometimes by deeds, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Pope Gregory, *Works*, vol. II, *Patrologia* LXXVI, col. 1228.

## HOMILY CLXXXV. ON THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the imperfect work on Matthew, among the spurious short works attributed to blessed Chrysostom.)*

At that time the Pharisees approached Jesus, and one of them, a teacher of the Law, questioned him, testing him: [Col. 1430A] “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” Etc. (Matt. XXII.)

The Jews frequently tested Christ with various questions, etc. For the remainder, see Saint John Chrysostom, *Works*, in our edition, vol. VI, col. 872.

## HOMILY CLXXXVI. ON THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the works of blessed Jerome the priest.)*

At that time Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city, etc. (Matt. IX.)

The present reading has shown that Christ performed divine mysteries in human actions and carried out invisible works through visible things. “He got into a boat,” it says, “and crossed over and came to his own city.”

[Col. 1430B] Is this not the one who, driving back the waves of the sea, laid bare the depths, so that the Israelite people might pass on dry ground, amid the astonished waters, as through the hollows of mountains (Exod. XIV)? Is he not the one who bent the summits of the sea beneath Peter’s feet, so that then the fluid element might offer solid service to human footsteps (Matt. XIV)? And what does it mean that he so denies himself the service of the sea that he crossed a very small lake for a boatman’s fare?

“He got into a boat,” it says, “and crossed over.”

And what is surprising, brothers? Christ came to take upon himself our infirmities and to confer upon us his remedies of health, because a physician who does not bear infirmities does not know how to heal, and one who has not been made weak with the weak cannot confer health upon the weak.

Therefore, if Christ had remained in his own powers, [Col. 1430C] he would have had nothing in common with human beings; and unless he had fulfilled the order of the flesh, his assumption of flesh in him would have been pointless. He therefore endured these necessities so that, as a true human being, he might be tested by human necessities.

He got into a boat. Christ, always calming the boat amid the waves of the world, got into it so that he might lead those who believe in him by a peaceful voyage to the heavenly homeland and make citizens of those whom he had made sharers in his humanity. Christ, therefore, does not need the boat; rather, the boat needs Christ, because without a heavenly pilot the boat of the Church cannot reach the heavenly harbor through the world’s sea, amid so many and such great dangers.

We have said this, brothers, with regard to spiritual understanding. Let us now follow the order of the historical account itself.

“Jesus,” it says, “got into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city” [Col. 1430D]. The Lord, the Creator of the world, after narrowing himself into our flesh for our sake, began to have a human homeland and to be a citizen of a Jewish city. He began to have parents, though he himself is the parent of all parents, so that love might invite, charity attract, affection conquer, and humaneness persuade those whom domination had driven away, fear had scattered, and the force of power had made outsiders.

“He came into his own city. And they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith,” he says, “he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’”

He hears forgiveness, and the paralytic is silent; he gives no thanks. [Note: [Col. 1430D] “He renders a better return,” as below, col. 1433D. EDITOR.] [Col. 1431A] For he was striving toward the care of his body more than of his soul. He lamented the temporal troubles of his weakened body in such a way that he did not lament the eternal punishments of his more deeply weakened soul, judging the present life more desirable for himself than the future.

Rightly, therefore, Christ regards the faith of those who brought him and regards the senselessness of the man lying there, so that, through the support of another’s faith, the paralytic’s soul might be healed before his body.

“Seeing their faith,” he says.

Observe here, brothers, that the Lord does not seek the will of the foolish, does not await the faith of the ignorant, and does not investigate the foolish desires of the sick, but comes to the aid of another’s faith. Indeed, brothers, when does a physician either seek or consider the wishes of the sick, since the sick person always desires and asks for what is harmful? Hence he now applies iron, now fire, now bitter potions [Col. 1431B], and imposes them on unwilling patients, so that the healthy may experience the treatment which the sick could not perceive.

And if a human being disregards insults and despises curses in order voluntarily to confer life and health upon wounded hands, how much more does Christ the physician, in divine goodness, draw to salvation even those unwilling and resisting who are wounded by the diseases of sins and afflicted by the madness of crimes?

O brothers, if only we wished—if only we wished always to see all the paralyses of our minds, so that we might perceive our soul, deprived of virtues, lying upon the beds of vices! Then it would become clear to us how Christ, who daily disregards our harmful desires, draws us toward saving remedies in order to cleanse us even when unwilling.

“Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven you.”

By saying this, he wished it to be understood that he was God, who through human form was [Col. 1431C] still concealed from human eyes. In powers and signs he was compared with the prophets, because they too had performed miracles through him. But since granting forgiveness of sins is not within human power and is a singular mark of divinity, he implanted the knowledge that he was God in human hearts.

The Pharisees’ spite proves this. For when he had said, “Your sins are forgiven you,” the Pharisees replied: “He blasphemes. For who can forgive sins except God alone?”

O Pharisee, who in knowing do not know, in confessing deny, and in bearing witness oppose! If it is God who forgives sins, why is Christ not God for you, when by one gift of his forgiveness he is shown to have taken away the sins of the whole world? “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

But if you are able to grasp greater signs of his divinity [Col. 1431D], hear how he penetrated the secret of your breast. See that he reached the hiding places of your thoughts; understand that he lays bare the counsel of your heart.

“And when Jesus had seen,” he says, “their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts? Which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven you,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins,’ he said to the paralytic, ‘Rise, take up your bed, and go into your house.’ And he rose and went into his house.”

The searcher of souls anticipates the great deliberations of their minds and demonstrates the power of his divinity by the testimony of his deed. He restores the limbs of the shattered body, tightens the sinews, joins the bones, fills out the organs, strengthens the power, and rouses to movement again, in a living corpse, the members that had already been buried [Col. 1432A].

“Take up your bed”—that is, carry the one that carried you; change the roles of the burden, so that what was a testimony of weakness may be proof of health, so that the bed of your pain may be evidence of my healing, and so that the greatness of the weight may proclaim the greatness of the strength you have received.

“Go,” he says, “into your house,” lest, having been healed by Christian faith, you should now die along the paths of Jewish faithlessness.

But you.

## HOMILY CLXXXVII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

At that time Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city, etc. (Matt. IX.).

[Column 1432B] The Lord Jesus, Creator of all things, after, for our sake, having confined himself in our flesh, began to have a homeland and to be a citizen of a Jewish city, so that he might invite to faith in himself those from whom he had assumed humanity, persuade them by love and charity, and draw them by affectionate human kindness.

Speaking, therefore, about the Lord Jesus, the holy evangelist Matthew says: “He who went up into a boat crossed over,” that is, went across the strait. A *fretum* is called a narrow sea, evidently from its heat and boiling, since the sea boils more intensely where it is narrower. Here, however, by the strait we must understand the Sea of Galilee, which the Lord often crossed by boat so that by his continual preaching he might invite to salvation the multitude of inhabitants living all around it.

The Lord’s city, according to the flesh, is said to have been Nazareth, adorned alike by his conception and his upbringing. A question certainly arises between Mark and Matthew, since Mark [Column 1432C] says that this very miracle of the paralytic was performed in Capernaum (Mark II), whereas Matthew narrates it as though, when the Lord came into his own city—which we have said was Nazareth—the paralytic was brought to him, and he cured him.

This question would be more difficult to resolve if Matthew had also named Nazareth in this passage. But since both Nazareth and Capernaum are cities in the province of Galilee, when the Lord came into Galilee he is rightly said to have come into his own city, regardless of which town in Galilee he was in. Indeed, Galilee itself—the whole province—can be called Christ’s city, since even that kingdom of the Jews, once exceedingly extensive and containing many cities, is called one house, namely Israel, and may all the more be called one city.

Why prolong this further? [Column 1432D] Christ’s Church itself, spread throughout the whole world, is also called a city. For the Psalm says: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI). Since, therefore, the Lord performed this sign in Capernaum, as Mark says, there is no doubt that he did it in his own city, especially since Capernaum itself, in Galilee—which was the Lord’s province—stood out so greatly that it was regarded as a kind of metropolis.

The teachers also resolve this question in another way: Matthew the evangelist, when he says that the Lord crossed over and came into his own city, passed over what the Lord did there and moved on to the following miracle, that of the paralytic, which took place in Capernaum. Mark, however, relates in full and in order how the event occurred. [Column 1433A]

Or certainly Capernaum is called the Lord’s city because he preached continually in it or in its vicinity and performed the greatest miracles there. Thus the Lord himself, reproaching it elsewhere, says: “Woe to you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven” (Matthew XI)—that is, by the splendor of my miracles—“you will be brought down to hell. For if the things that have been done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.”

“And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed.” The Greeks call paralysis a dissolution of the limbs. This disease completely deprives whatever part of the body it has seized of all its functions, and often attacks the entire body as well.

“And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven [Column 1433B] you.’” In saying this, he wished to be understood as God, since he was still concealing himself from people in his humanity, so that, through the fact that he could forgive sins—a power that belongs solely to God and not to man—they might advance without hesitation toward the faith of belief.

We should consider how much one person’s own faith can obtain, if the faith of others obtained so much that through their intervention it was suddenly able to gain for another person salvation of both mind and body. The evangelist does not say that the Lord saw the faith of the man who was carried, but rather the faith of those who brought him. In this matter a great and useful humility is commended to us: we should sincerely believe that through the intercession of those who are pleasing to God, those who are either less worthy to be heard on their own or are conscious of their own weakness [Column 1433C] are assisted when they commend themselves to the intercession of good people, so that through their work they may obtain from God both temporal and spiritual help.

“Take courage,” the Lord says, “son.” The humble condescension of our Redeemer is wondrous: he deigns to call “son” a feeble man, wasted throughout his entire body, whom the scribes and Pharisees did not even consider worthy to touch.

If we attend to the divine work being accomplished in the man, he rightly calls him “son,” since he absolves him from his sins. Moreover, by first forgiving the man the sins through which he had contracted the same infirmity, and afterward restoring him to health, he shows that the man had been condemned to weakness on account of the merit of his faults and could not otherwise escape bodily illness unless he were first freed from the troublesome sickness of the heart. [Column 1433D]

“Your sins are forgiven you,” he says. When the paralytic heard that the Lord promised him pardon for his offenses, he said nothing in response to Christ and offered him neither thanks nor praise, evidently because he desired bodily health more than that of the soul and judged the present life, which was more gratifying to him, preferable to the future one.

But Christ does not regard the dullness of the man lying there; rather, looking upon the faith of those who brought him, he forgives sins to an ungrateful man. And since envy is always the companion of virtue, let us hear what follows: “This man blasphemes.”

They did not say this with the voice of their mouths, but in the secrecy of their hearts. The evangelist makes this clear when he says: “And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your [Column 1434A] hearts?’” Mark explains more clearly what they called blasphemy, saying: “Some of the scribes were thinking in their hearts, saying: ‘Who can forgive sins except God alone?’” (Mark II).

They had read in the prophets that the Lord said: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isaiah XLIII). They were also indignant that Christ, whom they regarded as merely human, had promised the paralytic forgiveness of sins as though he were God.

Although they did not know it, the scribes and Pharisees speak the truth, because no one can forgive sins except God alone—who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiveness. Christ is therefore proved to be true God because he is able to forgive the sins of whomever he wishes.

“And when [Column 1434B] Jesus saw their thoughts.” God, the searcher of hearts, anticipating the evil plans of their minds, shows the blaspheming scribes that he is God, who can also clearly recognize the hidden things of their hearts. As if he were silently saying: “So that you may truly know me to be God, let it be evident to you that I also know most openly the hiding places of your thoughts. By that power of divinity through which I am able to see your thoughts, know also that I can forgive sins to human beings.”

“Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” Whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven was known only to Christ, who forgave them. But everyone present could approve by sight that he had risen and was walking. Therefore the Lord [Column 1434C] performed an external bodily sign of healing so that it might be demonstrated that he had inwardly performed the spiritual sign, namely, the forgiveness of sins.

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic: “Rise.”

It is evident that, if God has made our iniquities as far from us as the setting sun is from the rising sun, and the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, then this same Christ is both God and the Son of Man: God, who forgives sins through his divinity; the Son of Man, who through his humanity was able to die for sinners.

When he says, “Then he said to the paralytic,” these are the evangelist’s words.

“Take up,” he says, “your bed”—that is, carry the one who carried you—“so that what was a testimony of infirmity may become proof of health.”
