[Column 1434D] “And he rose and went to his own house.” Between the Lord’s command and its fulfillment there is no interval. “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm CLXVIII). “Whatever he willed, he did.”

Between our speaking and doing there is a great distance: we can speak easily, but we work with effort. Christ’s word, however, is immediately accompanied by action, because “he spoke, and they were made.”

He therefore says: “Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” It is as though he said: “Just as it is easy for me to say to a paralytic, ‘Rise,’ and he immediately rises, so it is easy to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ and they are immediately forgiven.”

When the crowds—that is, the people—saw the sign he had performed, they feared [Column 1435A] God and glorified him who had given such authority to human beings: namely, so that a human being placed among human beings might be able to grant health to whomever he wished.

Thus, after those who accused the Lord of blasphemy had been refuted, the astonished crowds rightly burst forth in praise of the Creator. At his command, without any intervening delay, swift health suddenly took possession of the whole man.

From the healing of this paralytic we are given to understand that many afflictions befall human beings on account of sins. Five different kinds of causes are handed down for which temporal troubles are divinely inflicted upon human bodies.

Either the elect are weighed down by bodily illness in order to increase their merits through patience, as happened to blessed Job and Tobit; or it is for the preservation of virtues, [Column 1435B] lest they be cast down when tempted by pride, as the thorn of the flesh was given to the Apostle Paul so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians XII); or it is for recognizing and correcting sins, as Mary, the sister of Aaron, was struck with leprosy because of her presumptuous words (Numbers XII), and as happened to the paralytic under discussion, who, in order to be cured, first needed the forgiveness of sins; or it is for the glory of God, as Lazarus’s illness was not for death but for the glory of God (John XI); or it is for the beginning of eternal damnation, which properly belongs to the reprobate, as Antiochus and Herod displayed to all by their present misery what they were to suffer in Gehenna. To them applies the prophetic saying: “Crush them with a double [Column 1435C] crushing” (Jeremiah XVII).

Therefore, since we cannot know for what reason we are scourged, it is necessary that in all adversities that we suffer temporally we humbly give thanks to the Lord. Whatever we discover that we have done wrong, we must cleanse through humble satisfaction, so that at last we may rejoice perfectly in the benefits attributed to divine mercy.

The healing of the paralytic, accomplished wondrously by the Savior, is clear according to the literal sense. But because divine mysteries always lie hidden in Christ’s human actions, we must consider what the Lord’s crossing over to his own city signifies allegorically.

The evangelist says: “Jesus went up into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city.”

Earlier, Saint Matthew narrated that after the Lord slept on the sea and, once awakened, calmed the storms, [Column 1435D] he came to the region of the Gerasenes, where he healed the man whom a legion of demons had attacked. Immediately afterward, as the present reading relates, he adds that, having gone up into a boat, he crossed over and came into his own city.

Allegorically, the boat into which the Lord went signifies the cross of the Lord’s Passion, onto which the Lord himself ascended; or the Lord’s own body, which hung upon it; or, more specifically, the soul of each believer; or, generally, the entire holy Church.

The sea that the Lord crossed signifies the present age, which is shaken by the very frequent narrow straits of tribulations, as though by certain storms.

By the city of Nazareth, in which the Lord was conceived and raised, and which is interpreted as “flower” or “guarded,” [Column 1436A] the holy Church is suitably signified: that is, the multitude of the elect, which, so that it may not lose the flower of faith or the fruit of good works, is cleansed by God’s grace from the filth of vices and guarded against the attack of plotting demons.

That the Lord, after sleeping on the sea, went to the region of the Gerasenes and, returning from there, came back to his homeland signifies that, rising from the sleep of death, he passed over to the people of the Gentiles, who were to be healed through the apostles from the assault of demons. But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, he will soon return to his own Jewish citizens through the preachers of that time.

There he healed the paralytic, namely, the Jewish people, cleansing from sins both original and actual all who have been predestined to eternal life.

Again, in another way: “The Lord went up into a boat, [Column 1436B] crossed over, and came into his own city.” Since he ascended the cross, which is signified by the boat, after conquering and trampling underfoot the waves of the disturbances of this age, he came into his own city, that is, the Church, which, as the Psalmist testifies, is called the city of God: “Glorious things,” he says, “have been spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI).

In this passage the name “city” signifies the Church, that is, the multitude of the elect. The Lord comes into his own city, the Church, when through the preaching of the apostles he ascends into the hearts of the elect.

For when the holy apostles, by their preaching, led their hearers to this faith—that they should believe that the divinity of the Son of God had been joined to human weakness in the Virgin’s womb, that he had been born in that same flesh, [Column 1436C] crucified and buried, and had risen on the third day; that he had taken that same body up into heaven and in it sat at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places; and that in it he would return at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead—the same Christ ascended in the holy Church, that is, in the hearts of believers through faith.

“And behold, they brought him a paralytic.” This paralytic lying on a bed signifies morally the unhappy soul that rests miserably in the pleasure of sin as though in a certain little bed. The healing of this paralytic represents the healing and restoration of that same suffering soul, which, after a long wandering in carnal pleasure, desires to return to its Creator.

But the soul, if it is to be saved, also needs its own bearers: good teachers, namely, who supply it with the hope of salvation [Column 1436D] through their teaching and offer it the help of intercession before the Lord through their holiness.

According to Mark (chapter II), these are rightly found to have been four, either because of the four books of the Gospels, upon which the foundation of all doctrine rests, or because of the four principal virtues upon which the health of every soul consists: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Others call these sobriety, wisdom, fortitude, and justice; nothing is more useful than these in human life.

For whatever soul has been steeped in the teaching of the four Gospels and supported by these four virtues will deserve to receive complete health from the Lord, so that it may rise, take up its bed, and return to its house.

Hence it is added: “Rise, take up [Column 1437A] your bed, and go to your house.”

By the bed is signified the body of every human being. Thus the soul rests in the body as in its bed. Or certainly by the bed our neighbor is understood, in whom, in a time of tribulation and distress, we safely take refuge as though to rest.

“And he rose and went to his own house, glorifying God.” The Lord performed this sign bodily in the paralytic at that time, and he performs it spiritually every day in the holy Church.

Just as he commanded the paralytic to rise and carry his bed, by which he had been carried, so he commands us every day, who lie in carnal vices as though delightfully in a bed, to rise. And after we have risen from sins, he commands us also to undertake to carry the infirmities of others, [Column 1437B] whether bodily or moral, just as we too were carried by our brothers at the time of our weakness.

And since we have said that the flesh is also signified by the bed, he commands those who rise to carry their little bed—that is, to strive to carry our flesh, which carried us toward vices, back toward the virtue of self-restraint. What drew us joyfully toward guilt should, when afflicted, lead us back to forgiveness.

The Lord commands this of us every day through himself, that is, through the proclamation of the Gospel, through the sayings of the prophets, and through the various and diverse examples of the saints.

The Lord therefore says to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed.” It is as though he were saying to the soul lying in sins: “Rise from vices, namely, from the vices of the flesh, to spiritual virtues; and carry your bed, that is, the flesh of your body, which carried you toward [Column 1437C] sin and guilt, and carry it back toward forgiveness.”

Or: “Carry your bed,” that is, your brother, by whom you too have been carried; “and go to your house,” that is, you who have wandered through various crimes of vice, return to the keeping of yourself.

To return home is for each person who has gone astray to return to the keeping of himself and to bind himself by the commandments of his Creator, so that the whole person—both inward and outward—may be pleasing to God.

Our home may also be understood as paradise. Since we fell from it through lack of self-restraint, it is necessary that we return through self-restraint.

But when such a soul, which had languished in sins, hastens back to forgiveness, it often happens that many who see this blaze forth in praise of God.

Hence it is added here: “When the crowds saw it, they feared and glorified God, who had given such authority [Column 1437D] to human beings.”

He says “to human beings,” either referring to the paralytic, who, exhausted by bodily weakness, was immediately able to rise at Christ’s command and carry his bed; or, rather, referring to our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone by his word was able to restore health of both soul and body to a man whose limbs had been dissolved.

The same thing happens spiritually in the soul of a sick person. When someone who had lain there for a long time is seen hastening back to forgiveness, many unbelievers glorify God, who gives such authority to human beings that after a long calamity of vices they may rise to the salvation of their souls.

Whenever health occurs, whether in body or in soul, it is granted by him. Hence Jesus himself is also called Savior, because [Column 1438A] “he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I).

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

# HOMILY CLXXXVIII. ON THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the works of blessed Pope Gregory the Great.)*

“At that time Jesus spoke this parable to the crowds: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son,’ etc.” (Matthew XXII.)

“The text of the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, etc.” The remainder may be found in blessed Pope Gregory, volume II of his works, *Patrologia* LXXVI, column 1282.

# HOMILY CLXXXIX. ON THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the same author.)*

[Column 1438B] “At that time there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son. Etc.” (John IV.)

“The reading of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, brothers, needs no exposition, etc.” The remainder may be found in the same author, in the volume cited above, column 1211.

# HOMILY CXC. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

*(From Hericus, monk of Auxerre.)*

“At that time there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum, etc.” (John IV.)

How incomprehensible and inscrutable the divine judgments are, and how far they differ from human judgments, we can observe in all the passages of divine Scripture, but especially in the present reading of the holy [Column 1438C] Gospel.

For behold: as the following discourse of this reading indicates, when the Lord and Redeemer was asked to go and visit the official’s son, he did not wish to go. Yet elsewhere, when the centurion himself resisted and protested that he was unworthy, he deigned to promise that he would come to the centurion’s servant.

Who does not know that an official is a person of greater authority than a centurion? Yet before almighty God—whose judgments are sometimes hidden but always true—the centurion’s faith had greater power than the official’s purple robe.

Thus once David, while his brothers, who were older and, according to human judgment, wiser, were rejected, was chosen for the kingdom. And at the end of the age, not [Column 1438D] orators and nobles but lowly fishermen are called by the Lord to the apostleship.

Considering this subtlety of divine judgments, the Psalmist said: “Your judgments, O Lord, are a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV). And again: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Psalm XVIII). Isaiah also prophesies of Christ: “He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears” (Isaiah XI).

But these matters will be seen more appropriately in their own place. We have not been reluctant briefly to anticipate them; now let us proceed to expound the reading of the holy Gospel.

“There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum.” He is called *regulus*, a diminutive form of the name *rex*, “king”: a little king, evidently not elevated by great power.

[Column 1439A] This name suits him well, since he asked for salvation for his son; for he is shown to have possessed not a full but a diminished faith.

Capernaum is a city of the province of Galilee, in which the Lord displayed many miracles. In it, too, the son of this official lay ill.

When he heard, therefore, that the Lord was coming from Judea into Galilee, where he had recently changed water into wine, he went to him to ask for the health of his dying son.

Although the whole land of the twelve tribes, in which the Jews lived, was generally called Judea, that part of the kingdom of the Jews in which the two tribes—Judah and Benjamin—were established was especially and specifically called Judea.

From that region, as the Lord was coming, this official approached him, asking him to come down and heal his son. [Column 1439B] Why? “For he was beginning to die,” that is, approaching death was pressing upon him.

Jesus therefore says to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

Signs are so called because they signify something; wonders are as though *porrodicia*—“things pointing far ahead”—because they indicate something in the distance.

It is entirely evident that the Jews, as though they had this custom implanted in them by nature, entrusted their faith to no matters, even divine ones, except through signs. Hence the Apostle Paul also said: “The Jews demand signs” (1 Corinthians I).

But it may be asked why the Lord says to this official, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” when he believed before seeing a sign. How could he not believe, when he asked for his son’s salvation?

But if we attend to what he asked, we clearly recognize that his faith was not complete. [Column 1439C] He asked the Lord to come down and heal his son, and thus desired his bodily presence as though the Lord could not work salvation in his son unless he were physically present.

If he had believed perfectly, he would undoubtedly have known that there is no place where God is absent. He therefore rebukes a man sluggish in faith and wishing to test who he was, or what power he possessed, in the healing of his son.

The official says to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies.” His son’s illness pressed upon him, and therefore, persevering in prayer, he asks for his recovery.

Jesus says to him: “Go; your son lives.”

As we learned from another Gospel narrative, a centurion came to the Lord, saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously [Column 1439D] tormented” (Matthew VIII). The Lord replied to him: “I will come and heal him” (ibid.).

A centurion is one who commands a hundred soldiers. Since the official is of higher dignity than the centurion, we must carefully consider why, when asked, the Lord refuses to go bodily to the official’s son, while he promises to go to the centurion’s servant even without being asked.

He does not deign to be present with the official’s son, but he does not disdain to visit the centurion’s servant. In this action, however, our own pride is specially struck down by the humility that is proposed for imitation in our Redeemer. We honor in human beings not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but honors and riches.

To show that what is exalted among human beings—that is, among the lovers of this age—must be despised by the elect, while what appears despised among human beings must not be [Column 1440A] despised by the saints, our Redeemer refused to go to the official’s son but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant.

“The man believed the word that Jesus said to him, and he went.” From this it is already apparent how much this man profited from the Savior’s rebuke. Since the Lord had said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” as soon as he heard from the Lord, “Go; your son lives,” he immediately went on believing.

As he was going down, his servants met him and announced that his son was alive. He then asked them at what hour he had improved, and they told him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”

It is not without a great mystery that the evangelist relates that the official’s son was freed from his illness at the seventh hour. Christ’s miracles, which he performed bodily, are not merely miracles [Column 1440B] for us; secret mysteries are also to be considered in his deeds.

The number seven is consecrated by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, since all the spiritual gifts that God bestows upon all the faithful are comprehended in this same number seven.

There are seven virtues of spiritual gifts, by which the condition of human beings in the present life is most suitably adorned: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.

Without God’s grace no one can be wise, understanding, a counselor, strong, learned, devout, or filled with fear of the Lord.

Since these gifts are granted to human beings only through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit himself—who [Column 1440C] is nothing other than the true God—is also called by these same names.

Just as the Son, proceeding from the Father, is called a lion because of his strength, a sheep because of his innocence, a door because through him we enter to the Father, light because he illumines every human being, and is also called truth and resurrection, along with many other names according to particular properties, so also the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is properly called by these seven names: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear.

Hence he is also called the Spirit of sevenfold grace, because of the mystery of the number seven, in which supreme perfection is understood.

Seven is composed of three and four. In three it bears the significance of the Holy Trinity; in four, [Column 1440D] of the Gospel. Whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the result rises to the number twelve, which is also known to be most perfect, because the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the teaching of the Gospel were spread through the twelve apostles into the four parts of the world: east and west, north and south.

There are also four elements of the world and, as has been said, four regions of the earth; likewise four seasons of the year; and there are four Gospels upon which the Church is established.

We may also refer the number three to our inner person, that is, to the soul, which has a threefold nature: irascible, concupiscible, and rational.

In every [Column 1441A] rational soul there are also three faculties: memory, ingenuity, and understanding.

The prophet Isaiah also foretold that the Holy Spirit would rest bodily upon the Lord when he prophesied about Christ: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse”—namely, the Lord Jesus from the stock of David—“and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah XI).

That Spirit rested upon the Lord Jesus Christ because the whole fullness of divinity dwelt most fully in his body, not in portions as in the other saints, to whom the word of wisdom is given to some, the word of knowledge to others, the grace of virtues to others, and to each according to the measure of faith.

[Column 1441B] Rather, the Spirit rested upon him in fullness and remained there in perpetual habitation.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit himself is signified by the number seven, and from him and through him all health, all strength, and all spiritual gifts are bestowed upon all the faithful, the evangelist rightly reports that the official’s son was restored to health at the seventh hour of the day. Whatever health is granted, whether of body or soul, is bestowed by that Spirit who is signified through the same number seven.

The official’s son was rightly healed at the seventh hour, because the whole person then attains perfect health when the creature recognizes its Creator and submits to him in worthy humility and service.

This is the most righteous order: the soul must be enslaved to God, but the body to the spirit.

The same number seven is also consecrated by the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, [Column 1441C] in which and through which this true health and the forgiveness of all sins are granted.

The father therefore recognized that it was the hour at which Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives”; and he himself believed, and his entire household.

A little earlier in this same Gospel we read that, while the Lord was preaching in Samaria, when a woman said, “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done” (John IV), many Samaritans believed in him through the word alone, without seeing any sign.

But in response to this great miracle performed in Judea, only the official and his household believed.

This is what the Lord had said above: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

This event also prefigured that only a few [Column 1441D] Jews would believe in God, while the multitude of the Gentiles would come to the faith.

The Jews saw the Son of God himself performing signs; they had his apostles as preachers and teachers; yet only a few of them bowed their necks beneath the yoke of faith, while the others persisted in unbelief.

Therefore, while those condemned to perpetual torments on account of their unbelief suffer, eternal blessedness is promised to us if we adorn by works what we believe by faith. The Savior says to us: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX).

The complete conversion of the Jews will indeed be fulfilled near the end of the age, when, at the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, the hearts of the fathers will be turned to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, and what the Apostle said will be fulfilled: [Column 1442A] “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

And Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah X). And again: “In truth they will be converted in Christ Jesus.” Amen.

# HOMILY CXCI. ON THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(From the works of blessed Augustine.)*

“At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,’ etc.” (Matthew XVIII.)

“Yesterday the holy Gospel admonished us, etc.” The remainder may be found in Saint Augustine, volume V of his works, *Patrologia* XXXVIII, column 514.

[Column 1442B] *(After the words “and let the others fear,” the sermon ends in Saint Augustine and continues in the Homiliary.)*
The Lord teaches that forgiven sins return when brotherly charity is absent, by means of the servant whom he found indebted ten thousand talents; when this servant pleaded with him, he forgave him everything. But when that servant showed no mercy to his fellow servant, who owed him a hundred denarii, the master ordered him to repay what had been forgiven him. The time, therefore, when forgiveness is received through baptism is, as it were, a time for rendering an account, so that all debts found to exist may be forgiven.

Yet that servant who afterward lent money to his fellow servant, which the latter could not repay, did not show him mercy; rather, he was himself indebted and had thus been spared by his master [Col. 1442C]. This is indicated by the words of the fellow servant, who said: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” Otherwise he would have said: “You had already forgiven this debt; why are you demanding it again?” The words of the Lord himself make this still clearer. For he says: “But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants, who owed him a hundred denarii.” He did not say, “to whom he had already forgiven a debt of a hundred denarii.” For if he had forgiven it, that man would not have owed him anything. Since he said, “he owed him,” it is clear that he had not forgiven him.

It would indeed have been better, and would have been more fitting for such a great debtor, who was rendering an account and awaiting mercy from his master, if he had first forgiven his fellow servant what the latter owed him, and then approached to render his account, where the master’s mercy was to be fulfilled. Yet the fact that he had not previously forgiven what his fellow servant owed him did not prevent his master, at the time when the account was to be rendered, from forgiving him everything he owed. But what did this benefit him, since, because of his perseverance in hatred, everything was immediately charged against him again?

Thus we are not prevented from receiving the grace of baptism, which forgives all sins, even if hatred of a brother continues in the heart of the person whose sins are forgiven. For the previous day is settled, and whatever remains is settled as well—even the hour and moment immediately preceding baptism and the very moment of baptism. Thereafter, however, the guilty person immediately begins (?) to be liable, not only for the days, hours, and moments that follow, but also for those that have passed, when everything that had been forgiven returns. Such things often occur in the Church.

## HOMILY CXCII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

[Col. 1443A]

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,” etc. (Matthew XVIII).

Our Savior, dearest ones, by living among human beings, taught us not only to avoid sins but also, through a pious and salutary counsel, took care to instruct us how we might be absolved from the guilt of sins. His counsel is this: if we wish to be absolved before God from the debts of our sins, we too must absolve those who offend us from the faults of which they are held guilty toward us.

He deigned to invite us to this not only by frequently exhorting us, but also by carrying it out in deed. He invited us by words when he said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI). And again: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone” (Mark XI). And once more: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI). When Peter asked him whether a brother should be forgiven as many as seven times, he said: “I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew XVIII).

By carrying this out in deed as well, he left us a great and memorable example. For what did he say when his crucifiers gave him myrrh mixed with gall to drink and raised him upon the cross? “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). Thus, brothers, the Lord Jesus Christ became for us like an eagle stirring up its young to fly and hovering over them (Deuteronomy XXXII). It seemed too little to him to urge us by words alone to fly toward that perfection in which enemies are loved and debtors are forgiven, unless he also showed us in himself an example of the same thing and, as it were, by his own lofty flight invited us to imitate him.

Certainly, for a sensible person who does not have a heart of stone, this example alone ought to have been sufficient, even if all that exhortation in words had not preceded it. Sometimes he invites us to this perfection in plain and explicit words, as is clear from the examples already mentioned; at other times, through parables, as in the Gospel that we now have before us. For he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like,” etc.

Who are the heavens, and what is the kingdom of heaven that has been compared to a king? If, as Scripture says, “the soul of the righteous is the seat of God” (Wisdom VII), it follows that the souls of the saints are the heavens. The angelic spirits are also called heavens; the Psalmist invites them to praise God, saying: “Praise him, heavens of heavens” (Psalm CXLVIII).

What is the kingdom of heaven—that is, of all the blessed—if not eternal life? Eternal life, however, is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He is the land of the living, the inheritance of the saints. He is the paradise of delight, the spacious place in which the foot of the faithful is established. He is both the king and the kingdom of the saints, in whom, with whom, and through whom all the elect reign. The kingdom of heaven, therefore, is Christ.

This kingdom of heaven is rightly compared to a king, who is said to be merciful in absolving a debtor and just in punishing an ungrateful person, since Christ is both human and King of kings: greatly merciful toward those who seek mercy, and a severe judge toward the ungrateful [Col. 1444A].

“He wished to settle accounts with his servants.” There are three servants of our King with whom he has to settle accounts concerning their debts. One is the person who neither asks nor deserves ever to be freed from his debt. Another is the person who is freed for a time but becomes ungrateful. The third is the person who is both freed and remains grateful.

The servant who is never freed from his debt is the entire people of unbelievers. Bound before their Creator by an immeasurable debt, they neither deserve nor ever find absolution, and they have already been judged by God.

The other two servants are the two classes of people who come to the faith of the Church. For when the elect and the reprobate receive the ecclesiastical sacraments daily, they are nourished together with them in the bosom of the Church, yet they do not cease to oppose them and afflict them with many sorrows; and Esau presses against Jacob in the womb of their mother. Thus there are two servants in the Church, the good and the evil, the elect and the reprobate. For that third servant of whom we spoke is outside.

All are indeed servants of the supreme King, who created them all in his image to serve and praise him; but two withdraw from his service, while one remains. What, then, is the debt that each owes his master? We can infer from this that Scripture calls sin a debt: after the Savior had taught us to pray in this way, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI), he immediately added shortly afterward: “For if you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” [Col. 1444C].

Every human being is bound by this debt to God. For we are conceived in sins, born in sins, and live in sins throughout our entire life. The Lord settles accounts with his servants when, through the mouths of preachers or even through hidden inspiration, he rebukes the faults of sinners of every kind and demands satisfaction for their sins.

That unbelieving servant hears, despises it, hardens himself against the rebuke, neither seeks nor finds pardon, and is condemned in his unbelief. The elect servant hears, is pierced with remorse, makes satisfaction, is absolved from his sins, and remains grateful, because he willingly forgives those who offend him, his fellow servants.

But what does that reprobate servant do, who lives for a time in the Church together with the elect? Let us hear from the words of the Gospel reading. He is the one of whom it is said: “One who owed ten thousand talents was brought to him.” A person guilty of many criminal sins is a debtor of many talents—sins such as adultery, homicide, sacrilege, theft, perjury, robbery, or even unbelief and similar offenses.

The name “talent” appropriately designates such things because they are extremely serious, just as this kind of weight is the heaviest among the various weights distinguished by their particular names. Hence, in the prophet Zechariah, wickedness is designated by the name of a talent, when it says: “And I saw, and behold, a talent of lead was being carried; and he cast it into the middle of the vessel, and said: ‘This is wickedness’” (Zechariah V).

Just as there are different kinds of talents, so crimes themselves differ from one another. Indeed, perhaps because he wished the name “talent” to signify the gravest sins, he did not add “talents of gold” or “of silver,” since those names signify precious things, such as virtues and knowledge; instead, he simply says, “ten thousand talents.”

Let the person who has repeated some grave sin so often that he has made a habit of it be said to owe a thousand talents. For the thousand, which is fourth in the sequence of numbers from which the progression of counting begins, can appropriately signify the habit of sin, which itself occupies the fourth place in the progress of sins.

For just as we advance in counting from one to ten by adding units, from ten to one hundred by adding tens, and from one hundred to one thousand by adding hundreds, so progress is made from the delight of sin, which is first, to consent; from consent to the act; and from the act to habit.

The person who has violated all the commandments of the Decalogue through an evil habit owes ten times a thousand talents, and has already become a despiser of all righteousness. For just as ten thousand is fifth after one thousand in the boundaries of numbers, so contempt occupies the fifth place after the habit of sin, according to what is said elsewhere: “When the wicked comes into the depths of vices, he despises.”

But if this interpretation seems burdensome to anyone [Col. 1445C], let him simply say that the person who has committed many criminal sins owes ten thousand talents, and let the number be, as commonly happens, a finite number used for an infinite one.

It follows: “But when he had nothing with which to repay, his master ordered him to be sold,” etc. When a sinner is rebuked by the Lord through the mouth of his minister or through his own conscience, he has nothing with which to repay the debt while his heart remains hardened against correction, while he is shaken neither by fear, pierced by salutary sorrow, nor inflamed even to tears.

The Lord therefore orders his ministers to sell such a person, together with his wife and children, so that the debt may be paid. This follows the manner of speaking by which those who declare souls to be alive are said to give them life, and those who testify that they are dead are said to kill them.

The ministers of the Lord may also fittingly be said to sell the sinner when, after a simple and gentle admonition, they terrify him with severe denunciation and threats of Gehenna, declaring that he has been sold into the power of Satan [Col. 1445D]. The devil’s currency is sin, for the sake of whose brief pleasure a person hands himself over to the devil when he sins.

Hence the Apostle, speaking in the person of the sinner, says: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Romans VII). And through the prophet it is said to sinners: “You were sold for nothing” (Isaiah LII). Indeed, for nothing, because the sin for which a person sells himself is of no value; it is nothing, and when people sin, they become nothing.

That the sinner’s wife is sold together with his children means that his perverse desire and the works of iniquity propagated from it are proved, by firm assertions, to have been sold for eternal torments [Col. 1446A].

We can also discern another manner of sale in this passage. Ecclesiastical discipline orders that those who are held by manifest crimes and do not accept correction be separated from communion with the Church by a sentence of excommunication and thus handed over to Satan, so that their spirit may be saved through repentance.

Is it not, then, a good kind of sale when we hand a sinner over to Satan in order to receive a righteous, repentant person? Thus the Apostle sold the fornicator of whom he speaks to the Corinthians, saying: “Though absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, that the one who has done this should, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians V).

But he receives another man in his place when he admits the corrected person to communion with the Church. Writing to the Corinthians on his behalf, he told them to console him and confirm him in charity (2 Corinthians II).

We are also ordered to sell the wife of an obstinate sinner because he must be alienated from us not only according to spiritual communion but also according to bodily association, so that he may appear wholly devoted to Satan, both in spirit and in flesh. For the name “wife” commonly signifies the flesh.

Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone who is named a brother is covetous, or a fornicator, or a worshiper of idols, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat” (1 Corinthians V). Do not some prelates, then, sell the wife of the wicked appropriately, when, for the sake of some personal association, they do not fear to associate bodily with those whom they have deprived of spiritual communion or whom they know to have been deprived of it by others?

Similarly, to sell the children means to strike with the same sentence those who consent to or associate with excommunicated persons.

Both forms of sale are dreadful, and at times they greatly disturb even the hardest hearts of the reprobate, so that, setting aside their iniquity for a time, they humble themselves with tears before the ministers of the Lord and offer whatever satisfaction is required. This is to fall prostrate before the Lord.

The servant in question belongs to this number, for it is said: “Then that servant fell prostrate and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me.’” As if he were saying: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Psalm VI) [Col. 1446D]. “And I will repay you everything.” This means: “Every night I will wash my bed” (ibid.), that is, for each of the sins by which I deserved your anger, I will strive to cleanse my conscience.

It follows: “The lord had compassion on that servant, released him, and forgave him the entire debt.” “The mercies of the Lord are over all his works” (Psalm CXLIV), because through baptism or repentance he forgave sins not only to the elect but also to reprobates who believe for a time or practice the fruits of repentance for a time, as he promises through the prophet, saying: “If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns and practices repentance from his sin, and does judgment and justice, none of all the sins he has committed shall be counted against him” (Ezekiel III).

“But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii” [Col. 1447A]. Every debt by which one human being can be bound to another is of little weight in comparison with the debt for which he is held guilty before God, just as one compares a hundred denarii with ten thousand talents.

“And seizing him, he was choking him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe.’ And that servant fell prostrate and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ But he was unwilling; instead, he went away and put him in prison until he should repay the entire debt.”

The word “choking” indicates the proud and tyrannical exacting of a debt, which occurs when, by force or harsh reproaches, a debtor is so oppressed and, as it were, strangled that he can scarcely retain the ability to respond or make an excuse.

He is sent to prison when he is brought before the judge and hemmed in on every side by strict justice, so that no opportunity of escape is left [Col. 1447B].

“When his fellow servants saw what had happened,” etc. Our fellow servants who are saddened by our wickedness and report it to the Lord are righteous men. Inflamed by zeal for justice, when they cannot correct our enormities, they sigh toward God and entrust our correction to him.

The angels of God are also called our fellow servants. They always behold the face of the Father, and, observing all our actions, report each one in God’s presence.

“Then his master summoned him,” etc. The wicked servant, who is to be judged by the Lord for his ingratitude, is summoned and handed over to torturers when he is snatched from this life by death and subjected to the power of wicked spirits to be tormented.

“He handed him over,” it says, “to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt” [Col. 1447C]. “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.”

Brothers, a sentence exceedingly terrifying and full of dread is brought before us in this passage: if we have been merciless toward our debtors, not only those sins that we have committed after receiving forgiveness, but also those that were forgiven us either through baptism or through repentance, will be punished in us.

Hence one of the Fathers says: “Whoever, forgetting the divine benefit, wishes to avenge his own injuries not only does not deserve pardon for future sins, but even the past sins that he believed had been forgiven him will be brought back for punishment.”

Again the same Father says: “The sin drawn from Adam is repaid temporally, since all die because of it; but it is not repaid eternally to those who are reborn through grace, if they remain in that grace.”

Another says: “It is clear from the words of the Gospel that if we do not forgive from the heart whatever offense is committed against us, what we had rejoiced had already been forgiven through repentance will again be exacted.”

Another likewise affirms the same thing, saying: “It must be considered that he says ‘the entire debt,’ because not only the sins a person commits after baptism will be counted against him for punishment, but also the original sins that were forgiven him in baptism.”

The same sentence is also confirmed by the words of the prophet, when it is said: “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the abominations that the wicked is accustomed to commit, shall he live? None of all his righteous deeds that he did shall be remembered” (Ezekiel XVIII) [Col. 1448A].

For if all the righteous deeds he did are consigned to oblivion, then the repentance he offered for his sins must also be reckoned as nothing. It therefore remains that the sins for which repentance had been offered should be recalled for punishment, since nothing now remains to excuse them.

But perhaps someone asks how a sin that is counted against the sinner for punishment could have been forgiven him in baptism or through repentance. To this we answer that at that time he had been established by the grace of the Lord in such a condition that, had he remained in it, his past sins would in no way have harmed him. This, of course, was to have been freed from sins.

What, then, brothers, shall we say to this? The sentence you have heard is plainly dreadful and exceedingly fearful. What benefit will it be to us to have been baptized, to have afflicted our souls repeatedly with fasts, vigils, and other works of repentance, and to have distributed alms to the poor in order to receive forgiveness of sins, if by our perversity we again stir up against ourselves the sins that God had already forgiven us through these remedies?

What benefit is there in healing a wound if, through one’s own negligence, one damages the scar and the wound opens again? Plainly, according to the Lord’s teaching and the Fathers’ assertions, we stir up to our own destruction the wounds that have already been healed by the heavenly physician—that is, the sins already forgiven us—so that, at the future judgment, each of them may inflict its own torment upon us if we harbor hatred toward our debtors and obstinately and mercilessly refuse forgiveness to those who ask for pardon [Col. 1448C].

We must also note that he does not say simply, “if you do not forgive,” but says, “if you do not forgive from your hearts.” By this addition he excluded a feigned reconciliation, which occurs when someone, overcome by the persistence of those who plead with him, pretends to make peace with an enemy while retaining hatred in his heart and awaiting a suitable opportunity for revenge.

Therefore, dearest ones, let us carefully strive to preserve that great remedy for sins which the Savior has so often commended to us with such diligence, and without which everything we do to obtain forgiveness of our offenses before God is fruitless. Let us bear the injuries of our neighbors with all gentleness; let us be gentle in forgiving our debtors and ready to show mercy to those who seek mercy, so that we too may find mercy in the presence of our strict Judge, through the gracious help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father, etc.

## HOMILY CXCIII. ON THE TWENTY-FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(From the *Opus Imperfectum on Matthew*, attributed to Saint Chrysostom among the spurious works.)

At that time, the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to entrap Jesus in his speech, etc. (Matthew XXII.)

All wickedness is sometimes confounded by the reasoning of truth, but it is never corrected, etc. For the remainder, see the works of Saint Chrysostom in our edition, volume VI, column 866.

## HOMILY CXCIV. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

(From Hericus, a monk of Auxerre.)

[Col. 1449A]

At that time, the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to entrap Jesus in his speech, etc. (Matthew XXII).

Luke the Evangelist makes it clear that, when the Savior himself was born under Caesar Augustus, a census was conducted throughout the whole world, and that among all the nations of the entire world subject to the Roman Empire, Judea too had become tributary. For this reason a great sedition was then raging among the people. Some judged that, since the Romans were constantly serving in the army for the security and peace of everyone, they ought to pay them the census tax. The Pharisees, on the contrary, who applauded themselves for their counterfeit righteousness, endeavored [Col. 1449B] to assert that the people of God, who paid tithes, offered first fruits, and observed the other decrees of the Law, ought not to be subjected to human laws. This sedition grew so strong that, after the Lord’s Passion, the Jews—persisting in this very obstinacy and rebellion—lost their place, nation, and kingdom when the Romans came on this pretext to avenge the Savior’s death; they also lost their present life and their future one. Blinded by greed, they preferred to suffer all these things rather than pay taxes to the Roman army.

Since, therefore, the chief priests could not seize the Lord because of the fear of the people, they at least tried to trap him in his speech. So the Pharisees went away and took counsel. Where did they go? To the Herodians, that is, to Herod’s soldiers who had been placed in charge of collecting [Col. 1449C] the taxes. For Caesar Augustus had appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, king over the Jews, so that he might oversee the taxes and obey the Roman Empire. From the fact that the Evangelist does not say “they were reconciled,” but “they took counsel,” and from his statement that “they came together with the Herodians,” it is evident that they discussed with them a plan of this sort for entrapping him.

For the priests were thinking among themselves: “If we go alone and question Christ, even if he says that it is not lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, nevertheless, when we make such accusations against him, no one will believe us, because everyone already knows that we are his enemies. The testimony of enemies in court, even if true, is nevertheless rejected as suspect.” They therefore did not wish to question Jesus Christ themselves, because they were already under great suspicion of hostility in Christ’s eyes, lest, as suspected persons, they should be unable to entrap him. They sent their disciples to him, therefore, pretending to be righteous, so that they might at least trap him in his speech and thus hand him over to the governor’s authority, while appearing themselves to be free from responsibility for his death.

They sent their disciples to him, therefore, as men not yet at all suspected, so that they might either easily deceive him or, if they were defeated—as indeed happened—their senders might suffer less embarrassment. For when an evil plan is exposed, the worse the person involved, the less shame results. The Pharisees therefore sent their disciples with Herod’s soldiers, the Herodians—or those whom the Pharisees, mocking them because they paid taxes to the Romans, called “Herodians,” and who were not devoted to divine worship [Col. 1450A]. Some Latins absurdly suppose that the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be the Christ, something we nowhere read at all. As we have said, he calls the Herodians Herod’s soldiers, who had been placed in charge of collecting the taxes.

So they say: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful.” They call him teacher and truthful so that, as though pleased by their flattery, he might plainly disclose to them the secret of his heart. “We know,” they say, “that you are truthful, and that you teach the way of God—that is, the law of God—in truth, and that you care about no one,” meaning that, when proclaiming the truth, you care neither about anyone’s friendship nor anyone’s hostility. Why they said this they reveal when they add: “For you do not regard the person of human beings,” that is, neither on account of the poor nor on account of the rich do you abandon the truth and speak falsehood.

“Tell us, therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay the census tax, or not?” It was as though they were saying: “We are servants of the supreme King. We received the Law from him; according to the commandments of the Law, we offer him tithes, first fruits, offerings, and sacrifices. Therefore it is unjust that we should serve earthly kings.” By saying this in a flattering and deceitful question, they tried to lead him to say that, since he feared God more than Caesar, taxes ought not to be paid to the Romans, so that those who were present might seize him as the leader of a revolt against the Jews. But if he said that the tax ought to be paid, they would slander him as a destroyer of the Law.

When Jesus recognized their wickedness—that is, when he considered their deceit and fraud—he said: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?” [Col. 1450C] It should be noted that he did not answer their fabricated words with a polite response, but, in accordance with their cruel intention, confronted them harshly, answering their thoughts rather than their words. The first virtue of one who answers is to recognize the words of those asking the question and to call them not disciples but testers.

A hypocrite, therefore, is one who is one thing and pretends to be another, that is, who acts one way in deeds and presents another way in speech. He calls them hypocrites so that, when they heard from his mouth what they themselves were thinking in their hearts, they might recognize him as a knower of human hearts, like almighty God, and might not dare to carry out against him what they were plotting.

Hypocrites are also called “sub-gilded.” For *hypo* in Greek means “under,” while *chrysos* means “gold.” Accordingly, he rightly calls his testers hypocrites, since they were striving to do one thing in deeds and pretend another in speech.

“Show me the coin of the census.” Wisdom always acted wisely, so that it might defeat its testers by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “the coin,” that is, the inscription of the denarius, or, as others say, the currency. The term *numisma* was derived from the name inscribed on the denarius. The denarius is a kind of coin counted as ten *nummi*, and it bore Caesar’s name and image.

And he says to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?” From this passage those who say that the Lord Jesus sometimes asked the Jews because of ignorance, rather than for the sake of his dispensation, may infer their position. For he asks whose image the coin bears and whose inscription it carries—not because he himself did not know what everyone who saw the denarius could know [Col. 1451A], but so that he might answer their speech appropriately.

They say to him: “Caesar’s.” Here “Caesar” should not be understood as Augustus Octavian, but as his stepson Tiberius, who had succeeded him in the Empire and under whom the Lord also suffered. It should be known, moreover, that all the kings of the Romans were called Caesars, after the first, Gaius Julius Caesar. He was so called either because he had emerged into the light from his mother’s womb by incision, or because he was born with a full head of hair.

Then he says to them: “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Render to Caesar what belongs to him—that is, the coin, the tax, and the money—and to God what belongs to God—that is, tithes, first fruits, and the other gifts commanded by the decree of the Law.

What the Lord commanded to be done, he himself also fulfilled in deed. For when he had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” He said: “Yes.” When Peter had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or the census tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” He said: “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Then the sons are free” (Matthew XVII).

It was as though he were saying: “If the sons of kings are free from tribute, I, who am the Son of the eternal King and who was born from the lineage of an earthly king, ought to be free from tribute.” Yet, so that we should not scandalize them: “Go to the sea and cast a hook; and take the first fish that comes up, and when you have opened its mouth you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (ibid.).

Regarding this passage, blessed Jerome says that he does not know what should be admired more: the Savior’s foreknowledge or the greatness of his power. His foreknowledge is shown in that he knew that the fish had a stater in its mouth and that it would be the first one caught. The greatness of his power is shown if, at his word, a stater was immediately created in the fish’s mouth, and if by speaking he brought about what was going to happen.

Therefore, as was said earlier, our Lord was the king’s son both according to the flesh and according to the spirit, either born from David’s lineage or the omnipotent Word of the Father. As the king’s son, he did not owe tribute; but, having assumed the humility of the flesh, he ought to fulfill all righteousness.

And we are wretched, who are reckoned by the name of Christ and do nothing worthy of such majesty. He endured the cross for us, yet we do not pay tribute; and, as though we were sons of the king, we are exempt from taxes [Col. 1451D]. The Lord Jesus also rendered to God the things that are God’s, since in all his works he fulfilled the will of the Father, according to what he himself says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John VI).

Spiritually, just as Caesar demands a denarius from his subjects, on which his image is represented, so God will require from us a soul marked with the light of his countenance. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV). Just as a denarius is stamped with the image of the king, so our soul is illumined by the splendor of the divine light.

For the human being was created in the image and likeness of God—not in the body, but in the spirit, that is, in the soul. The apostle Paul makes this clear when he says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Ephesians IV). By these words it is shown that the human being was created in the image and likeness of God not in the body, but in the spirit.

He was therefore created in the image and likeness of God in the soul, so that, just as God is holy, just, and true, and distinguishes between good and evil, so the human being, remaining holy, just, and true, might likewise retain discernment between good and evil. He was also made in the likeness of God so that, just as God is perpetual and immortal, so the human being too would be immortal and eternal—unless he had sinned.

Thus, as we have said, the human being was created in the likeness and image of God not in the body but in the spirit, with this distinction preserved: the image is understood in holiness, while the likeness is understood in eternity. Let us therefore strive to be renewed in the spirit of our mind and to put on the new human being, who was created according to God, so that we may deserve to render him his denarius—that is, our holy and undefiled life.

In another sense, it is evident that the Pharisees and Herodians who were sent to test the Lord had different intentions. Some thought that nothing should be rendered to Caesar; others thought that everything should be rendered to Caesar. Accordingly, these two groups of testers signify two kinds of heretics. One teaches that service must be rendered only to the body and to Caesar—that is, to the belly, which is also called an exactor in the book of blessed Job—and that one must serve only it. The other kind of heretics urges that care for the body be wholly abandoned and that attention be devoted only to the soul’s advancement, sometimes even inflicting ruin upon the body for the sake of the soul [Col. 1452C].

But the Lord rejects both positions and teaches that one must walk along the royal road. Support for the body must not be denied; attention must also be devoted to the soul’s advancement according to usefulness and circumstance, with discernment preserved in all things, so that the body may be kept subject and the spirit may not waste away through the body’s starvation.

Again, in another sense, understand Caesar as the devil, who once in paradise gave the human being the worthless coin of persuasion and daily demands from him the liability of this debt. We render the tax to him not as he demands, but as our advantage requires, when we disdain to do perverse things; when we cleanse through worthy satisfaction in penance the sin we contracted through his persuasion; when we abandon vices and renounce them together with their author, so that, once this tribute has been paid, we may thereafter live free and secure.

But after we have thus returned to the devil what we received from him, it is necessary that we restore undefiled to almighty God what we have received from him—namely, our soul, marked with the light of his countenance and adorned with good works. For we are God’s coinage; we fell from his treasury, and what had been impressed upon us was worn away by error. Therefore we must diligently strive to repair by repentance and worthy living the image of God that we corrupted in ourselves by sinning.

With his help, who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, etc.

# HOMILY CXCV. ON THE TWENTY-FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(From blessed Ambrose’s exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, book VI, no. 53.)

[Col. 1453A]

At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, a certain ruler approached and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, my daughter has just died; but come and lay your hand upon her, and she will live,” etc. (Luke VIII).

Christ had left the synagogue in Gerasa, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Ambrose, *Works*, volume II, *Patrologia* XV, col. 1682.

# HOMILY CXCVI. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

(From the exposition of the venerable priest Bede on the Gospel according to Luke, book III.)

[Col. 1453B]

At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, a certain ruler approached and worshiped him, saying, etc. (Luke VIII).

Behold, a man came whose name was Jairus, and he was the ruler of the synagogue. Following the earlier reading, in which we interpreted the rejection of the Synagogue, the faith of the Church, and then again the restoration of the Synagogue, the dying daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is appropriately added, etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, *Works*, volume III, *Patrologia* XCII, col. 411.

# HOMILY CXCVII. ON THE TWENTY-SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(From blessed Augustine [?].)

At that time, when Jesus had lifted up his eyes and had seen that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” [Col. 1453C] etc. (John VI).

The miracles that our Lord Jesus Christ performed are indeed divine works, and they admonish the human mind to understand God through visible things. Since he is not a substance of the sort that can be seen with the eyes, and since his miracles—by which he governs the whole world and administers the entire creation—had become commonplace through their continual occurrence, so that scarcely anyone deigned to attend to God’s marvelous and astonishing works in any grain of seed, in his mercy he reserved for himself certain things to do at an appropriate time, beyond the customary order and course of nature. He did this not so that people would see greater things, but so that, seeing unusual things, they would be astonished—people for whom daily occurrences had become commonplace.

For the governance of the whole world is a greater miracle than the feeding of five thousand people with five loaves, and yet no one marvels at it. People marvel at the latter not because it is greater, but because it is rare. For who even now feeds the whole world except the one who creates harvests from a few grains? He therefore acted as God acts. From the source by which he multiplies harvests from a few grains, he multiplied the five loaves in his hands. Power was in Christ’s hands; those five loaves were like seeds—not indeed committed to the earth, but multiplied by him who made the earth.

This was therefore brought before the senses so that the mind might be lifted up, and presented to the eyes so that understanding might be exercised: we were to marvel at the invisible God through visible works, and, raised up to faith and cleansed through faith, we were also to desire to see invisibly the one whom we came to know invisibly through visible things [Col. 1454A].

Yet it is not enough to contemplate these things in Christ’s miracles. Let us ask the miracles themselves what they say to us about Christ. For, if they are understood, they have their own tongue. Since Christ himself is the Word of God, the deed of the Word is also a word for us.

Let us therefore seek to understand not only how great this miracle is, as we have heard, but also how profound it is. Let us not delight merely in its surface; let us also search out its depth. What we marvel at outwardly contains something within. We saw, we anticipated something great, something splendid and altogether divine, something that could be done only by the Lord; we praised the maker on account of what had been made.

But just as, if we were looking somewhere at beautiful letters, it would not be enough for us to praise the writer’s hand for having made them equal, uniform, and beautiful unless we also read what he had conveyed to us through them [Col. 1454B], so the person who merely looks at this deed delights in the beauty of what was done and admires the craftsman. The person who understands is like one who reads.

A painting is seen in one way, letters in another. When you have seen a painting, that is, seen and praised the whole of it, everything has been done. When you have seen letters, that is not the whole matter, because you are urged to read. Indeed, when you see letters, you say—if perhaps you do not know how to read them—“What do we suppose is written here?” You ask what it means, although you already see something. Another person is going to show you what you are seeking to recognize in what you have seen. He has one kind of eyes, and you another. Do you not both see the same characters? Yet you do not recognize the signs in the same way. You see and praise; he sees, praises, reads, and understands.

Since we have seen and praised, let us read and understand. “The Lord is on the mountain.” Let us understand all the more, because “the Lord is on the mountain” means that the Word is on high. What happened on the mountain therefore does not lie low in a humble place, nor should it be passed over casually; it should be contemplated.

He saw the crowds, recognized that they were hungry, and mercifully fed them—not only by goodness but also by power. For what would goodness alone accomplish where there was no bread with which the hungry crowd could be fed? If power had not accompanied goodness, that crowd would have remained fasting and hungry.

Finally, the disciples who were with the Lord in their hunger also wanted to feed the crowds, so that they would not remain empty, but they had nothing with which to feed them. The Lord asked where bread could be bought to feed the crowds [Col. 1454D]. Scripture says: “But he said this to test him,” namely, Philip, the disciple whom he had questioned. For he himself knew what he was going to do.

Why, then, did he test him concerning the matter of food, unless he wished to reveal the disciple’s ignorance? Perhaps, in revealing the disciple’s ignorance, he signified something. It will become clear when the sacrament of the five loaves itself begins to speak to us and to indicate what it signifies. There we shall see why the Lord wished, by asking what he knew, to reveal the disciple’s ignorance in this deed.

Sometimes we ask what we do not know, wishing to hear so that we may learn. Sometimes we ask what we know, wishing to discover whether the person we question also knows it. The Lord knew both things: he knew what he was asking, he knew what he himself was going to do, and he likewise knew that Philip did not know it. Why, then, did he ask, unless to reveal Philip’s ignorance? Why he did this, as I have said, we shall understand later.

Andrew says: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?” When Philip, questioned by the Lord, had said that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be sufficient to refresh that great crowd, there was a boy there carrying five barley loaves and two fish.

And Jesus said: “Have the people sit down.” There was much grass in the place, and about five thousand men sat down. Then the Lord Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and ordered them to be broken. The loaves were broken and placed before those reclining—not five loaves any longer, but whatever the one who had created and increased them had added. There was also as much fish as was sufficient.

It is little to say that the crowd had been fed; fragments also remained, and these too were ordered to be gathered up so that they would not perish. They filled twelve baskets with the fragments.

To proceed briefly: by the five loaves the five books of Moses are understood. They are rightly not wheat loaves but barley loaves, because they belong to the Old Testament. You know that barley is formed in such a way that one scarcely reaches its marrow; for the same marrow is clothed with a covering of husk, and the husk itself is tough and clinging, so that it must be stripped away with difficulty.

Such is the letter of the Old Testament, clothed in coverings of carnal sacraments. But if one reaches its marrow, it feeds and satisfies.

A certain boy therefore carried five loaves [Col. 1455C] and two fish. If we ask who this boy was, perhaps he was the people of Israel, who carried them with childish understanding but did not eat them. The things they carried burdened them when closed, but fed them when opened.

The two fish seem to signify for us those two exalted persons in the Old Testament who were anointed to sacrifice for the people and to rule them: priests and kings. And the one who was signified through them came at the appointed time in the mystery. He came—the one who was shown through the marrow of the barley and concealed through the husk of the barley. He himself came, bearing both offices in himself, priest and king: priest through the sacrifice by which he offered himself to God for us; king because we are ruled by him, and the things that were carried closed are opened.

Give thanks to him: he fulfilled through himself what was promised through the Old Testament. The loaves were broken, and by being broken they were multiplied. Nothing is more truthful. For the five books of Moses, when they are expounded—as though by being broken, that is, by being discussed—have produced how many books!

But because the ignorance of the first people was concealed in that barley, it was said of that first people: “As long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts” (2 Corinthians III). The veil had not yet been removed, because Christ had not yet come; the veil of the temple had not yet been torn while he hung upon the cross.

Because, therefore, the people’s ignorance was in the Law, that testing of the Lord revealed the disciple’s ignorance. Nothing, then, is without significance. Everything stands out, but it requires an interpreter.

The number of the people fed also signified the people established under the Law. Why were there five thousand, unless because they were under the Law, which is set forth in the five books of Moses? Hence, from those five porticoes, the sick were brought out, but not healed. For the one who healed the sick man there was also the one who fed the crowds here with five loaves.

They also reclined upon the grass. They therefore had a carnal understanding and rested in carnal things. For “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah XL).

What are those fragments, then, except the things that the people could not eat? Certain more hidden aspects of understanding are therefore meant, which the multitude cannot grasp. What remains, then, except that the more secret matters of understanding, which the multitude cannot grasp, should be entrusted to those who are capable of teaching others, as the apostles were? Hence twelve baskets were filled [Col. 1456B].

This was done wondrously because it was great; it was also done usefully because it was done spiritually. Those who saw it then marveled; we marvel now when we hear it. It was done so that they might see it; it was written so that we might hear it. What the eyes were able to do in them, faith does in us. We see with the mind what we could not see with our eyes, and we are superior to them, because it was said of us: “Blessed are those who do not see and yet believe” (John XX).

I add that perhaps we have also understood what that crowd did not understand, and that we have truly been fed because we have been able to reach the marrow of the barley.

Finally, what did those people who saw this think? “Those people,” he says, “when they had seen the sign that he had performed, said, ‘This is truly the prophet.’” Perhaps they still thought Christ a prophet for this reason: because they were reclining upon the grass [Col. 1456C].

Yet he was the Lord of the prophets, the fulfiller of the prophets, and the sanctifier of the prophets—and also a prophet. For it was said to Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you” (Deuteronomy XVIII)—like him according to the flesh, not according to majesty.

That the Lord’s promise should be understood of Christ is clearly explained and read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts VII). And the Lord himself says of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Mark VI).

The Lord is a prophet, and the Lord is the Word of God; and no prophet prophesies without the Word of God. With the prophets there was the Word of God, and the prophet was the Word of God. Earlier ages deserved prophets inspired and filled with the Word of God. We have deserved the prophet who is himself the Word of God.

Christ the Lord was the prophet of the prophets just as Christ is the Lord of the angels. For he himself was also called “the angel of great counsel” (Isaiah IX). Yet elsewhere what does the prophet say? “Neither a messenger nor an angel, but he himself, coming, will save them,” that is, he will not send a messenger to save them, nor will he send an angel, but he himself will come.

Who will come? The angel himself. Certainly not through an angel—unless he is an angel in such a way that he is also the Lord of angels. For angels are messengers in Latin. If Christ announced nothing, he would not be called an angel. If Christ prophesied nothing, he would not be called a prophet.

He exhorted us to faith and to taking hold of eternal life. He announced something present and foretold something future. In announcing what was present, he was an angel; in foretelling what was future, he was a prophet. Because the Word of God became flesh, he was Lord both of angels and of prophets. But you, O Lord.
