# HOMILY IV. ON THE OCTAVE OF SAINT ANDREW

At that time, as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea, etc. (Matthew IV).

[Col. 1458B] It is well known to all that the Sea of Galilee is called by different names because of [Col. 1458C] the various places adjoining it. This sea, or lake, because it had pleasant water to drink and abounded in fish, therefore kept a large population around it. The Lord frequently crossed it, as we read in the Gospel, in order to display his miracles to the peoples dwelling around it and to invite them, by the word of his preaching, to the way of salvation.

Walking, therefore, beside this sea, our Redeemer saw two fisherman brothers casting their nets into the sea. But it is rightly asked why, for preaching the grace of the New Testament throughout the world, the sons of kings or scribes were not called first, but fishermen were chosen. Clearly, this was because the things that are weak in human estimation are strong with God. [Col. 1458D] Fishermen, then, and not nobles, were called, so that the powerful of this age would not grow proud and say that Christ had been able to introduce his faith to the world only through them. The uneducated are sent to preach, so that the wise of this age might be deprived of any ground for boasting, when they see that the Gospel has been spread to the ends of the earth not through eloquent but through simple preachers.

They are called in pairs because they were to preach a twofold love and also to hand down the twofold Testament to the world. Spiritually, however, the fact that the Lord, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, saw Peter and Andrew casting their nets signifies that the incarnate Son of God saw, in the sea of this world, spiritual fishermen whom he foreknew to be suited, before the foundation of the world, for the work of preaching.

[Col. 1459A] And he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” It was fitting that fishermen of fish should first be destined to become fishers of men, so that, delighted by the likeness of their occupation, they might more willingly submit their necks to the discipleship of the Savior.

But they, leaving their nets, followed him. Perhaps someone may say: “What, or how much, did these men leave behind, who possessed almost nothing?” But one must consider that they left much behind because they abandoned the will to possess. They left much behind who abandoned everything that they had, or could have had, or desired to have. For if they had possessed great wealth and extensive worldly estates, they would have left everything for the love of Christ, just as they left their boat and nets. For as much was left behind by the apostles who followed the Lord as could be desired by those who did not follow him. [Col. 1459B] Their disposition, therefore, must be weighed more than their possessions.

Porphyry and Julian Augustus, the apostate, do indeed accuse them either of ignorance of historical judgment or of foolishness: the apostles followed the Savior at the first sound of his command, as though following a man irrationally calling them, although it is written: “Do not be quick to believe” (Ecclus. VI). But if the Lord created creatures of such a kind that they are able to attract other creatures to themselves—for example, as we see in the magnet and amber, which are recognized to possess such force and power that they draw iron or straw to themselves and make them adhere to them—how much more could the Creator of all creatures himself attract to follow him those whom he wished.

For, as is known from the account of blessed Jerome, such splendor [Col. 1459C] and majesty of the hidden divinity shone forth in the human face of Christ that, at his first appearance, he very easily attracted those who came to him.

And departing from there, he saw two other brothers, and behold, they followed him. The Lord saw these apostles just as he had seen the earlier ones—that is, he had mercy on them. For his seeing is to have mercy. He called them; he called these men also. He illumined the minds of the former; he illumined the hearts of the latter. These men too left everything, just as the former had. They followed the Lord, just as the former had.

But it may be asked how he first called two—Peter and Andrew—and shortly afterward two others, James and John, as Matthew and Mark relate, when Luke says that the sons of Zebedee were Peter’s companions and that, when the boats were filled with a multitude of fish, they were called by that same Peter to draw out the nets. [Col. 1459D] There too, after the Lord had said to Peter, “From now on you will be catching men” (Luke V), it is written that, after they had drawn the boats ashore, they followed the Lord together.

It must be understood that what Luke relates happened first. At that time the Lord did not call them to follow him, but merely foretold to Peter that he would catch men; afterward, as Matthew describes, he called them two by two to follow him.

Furthermore, one should know, as the evangelist John relates, that Andrew, while still a disciple of John the Baptist, heard John himself say concerning Christ: “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John I). Immediately encouraged by this statement, he followed the Lord [Col. 1460A] of his own will together with that disciple of John whose name the Scripture does not mention. After remaining with him for one day, as the same evangelist relates, they immediately returned to their aforementioned teacher, John the Baptist, and continued to serve under his instruction until Andrew was later called by the Lord to discipleship together with Peter, as Matthew describes here in his Gospel.

It should also be noted that these disciples, intending to follow the Lord, are said to have left their nets and their father. For Zebedee is interpreted as “fugitive” and signifies the devil. The nets signify the entanglements of this world. Whoever, therefore, desires faithfully to follow the Lord must first shake his foot free from the obstacles of human affairs, that is, from the cares of the present life, and then strive with all his strength to flee the devil.

Allegorically, the four disciples [Col. 1460B] called by the Lord from the sea signify two peoples, called by the grace of God from the anxieties and unrest of this age to the stability of spiritual devotion. For Simon Peter, whose name is interpreted as “obedient” or “recognizing,” and James, who is called “supplanter,” signify the Jewish people. The Jewish people first recognized their Creator through the giving of the Law and promised to obey his commands, saying through Moses: “Everything that the Lord has spoken to us we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exod. XXIV). It also supplanted the Gentile people by despising idols and worshiping God.

Andrew, however, whose name means “manly,” and John, whose name is interpreted as “the grace of God,” designate the Gentile people. After coming to the faith, they strove to walk manfully in God’s commandments; and whatever good they did, they attributed not to their own merits [Col. 1460C] but entirely to the grace of the Savior.

Morally, too, every believer can recognize these four names in himself if he strives to observe their interpretations in the four principal virtues. Every believer is Simon Peter when, through prudence, he recognizes his own sins and, having wiped them away, offers strong obedience to the divine commandments. He is Andrew when, through temperance, he manfully endures the temptations brought against him. He is also rightly called James if he is shown, through fortitude, to supplant vices. He may fittingly be called John if, by fulfilling the commandments of the Creator through justice, he attributes nothing to himself but assigns all things to the giver of every good.

Whoever, therefore, desires to come to the heavenly homeland must necessarily strive, with Simon Peter—[Col. 1460D] whose name is interpreted as “recognizing” or “obedient”—to obey the divine commandments and acknowledge his own sins, saying with the prophet: “For I acknowledge my iniquity” (Ps. L). Let him also take care, with Andrew, to resist the devil’s temptations manfully, and, with James the supplanter, to supplant vices with every strength. Let him likewise strive, with John—whose name is interpreted as “the grace of God”—to return thanksgiving for his good works to the giver of every good, so that, attributing the good he does in every respect not to himself but to God, he may deserve to be rewarded by him in the future, who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY VIII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY.

Today, dearly beloved brothers, has brought us great joy, for on this day Christ the infant was presented in the temple. Let virgins rejoice: a virgin gave birth to Christ. Let them not think that anything of what they vowed has been destroyed in her; she remained a virgin after childbirth.

Let widows rejoice: Anna the widow recognized the infant Christ. Let married women rejoice: [Col. 1461D] Elizabeth, herself married, prophesied the Christ who was to be born. No condition has been omitted that does not bear witness to the salvation of all. Do only virgins, then, reach the kingdom of heaven? Widows reach it as well.

That holy widow Anna was of great merit. For she had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. After his death, she had reached old age, advancing in a holy old age. For, being eighty years old, she awaited the Savior’s infancy, so that, being old, she might see the little one; being an old woman, she might recognize the little one; and, as she was about to depart from the world, she might see the Savior entering it.

In the male sex also these three conditions are commended. The Lord Christ himself, born as a boy, was presented in the temple. Let boys rejoice, vowing continence to the child. He himself consecrated the integrity of childhood, [Col. 1462A] who brought fruitfulness to his mother but did not take away her virginity.

That old man Simeon had lived for a long time; his age was comparable to Anna’s. He had received the response that he would not see death before he had first seen the Christ of the Lord.

Understand, brothers, how great was the desire that the ancient saints had to see Christ. They knew that he would come, and all who lived piously would say: “If only that birth would find me alive! If only I might see with my own eyes what I believe in the Scriptures of God!” And so that you may know how great was the desire of the saints who knew from the Scriptures that a virgin would give birth, as you heard when Isaiah was read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII). The Gospel opened to us what Emmanuel means, saying: “Which is interpreted, ‘God with us’” (Matt. I).

[Col. 1462B] Therefore, unbelieving soul, let it not be incredible to you; let it not seem impossible to you that a virgin should give birth and that the virgin who gave birth should remain a virgin. Understand that God was born, and you will not wonder at the virgin’s childbirth.

And so that you may know that the ancient saints and righteous ones desired to see what was granted to this old man Simeon, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking to his disciples, said: “Many righteous men and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” This old man Simeon was very late in hearing, but mature in seeing. He did not wait to hear Christ speaking, because he saw the infant.

This alone was granted to him, already decrepit with age, as he desired and sighed, saying daily in his prayers: “When will he come? [Col. 1462C] When will he be born? Do you think I shall see him? Do you think I shall endure? Do you think that birth will find me here? Will these eyes see him through whom the eyes of the heart will be revealed?” He said these things in his prayers, and in response to his desire he received the answer that he would not taste death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord.

Mary his mother was carrying him as an infant; Simeon saw him and recognized him. Where did he know that he recognized him? He who had been born outwardly was revealed inwardly; he saw and recognized him. Simeon recognized the infant lying there, while the Jews killed the young man performing miracles.

When he had recognized him, he took him in his arms—that is, in his embrace—and clasped him. He carried the one by whom he was carried. For he is Christ, the Wisdom of God, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII).

[Col. 1462D] How great he was there, and how great, yet how small, he had become! Having become small, he sought the small. What does “he sought the small” mean? He sought not the proud and haughty but the humble and gentle. He deigned to be placed in a manger, so that he might be the food of pious beasts.

Simeon therefore took him in his arms and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace” (Luke II). You dismiss me in peace because I see peace. Why, then, do you dismiss me in peace? “Because my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid.). The salvation of God is Christ the Lord. “Announce his salvation from day to day.”

You have, then, boys, the child Christ; holy old men, the old man Simeon. But if you seek some married man to bear witness to the Lord, consider Zechariah.

Let no one, therefore, my faithful Christian brothers, seek [Col. 1463A] anything else. Whether virgin, widow, married woman, man, celibate, or married husband—whatever more someone may wish to be, he will not find anything that belongs to Christ beyond this.

But did Christ remain as he was born? He grew and reached youth, but did not decline into old age. Let your faith therefore grow; let it find strength; let it not know that it has reached old age. In this way you will belong to Christ, the Son of God: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” but “the Word became flesh” so that he might dwell among us.

Majesty lay hidden where weakness appeared. Simeon took weakness into his hands, but recognized the majesty within. Let no one despise Christ born and presented as an infant in the temple, if he wishes to be reborn.

It belonged to him to be born [Col. 1463B] for our sake; let it belong to us to be reborn in him, who came into this world to save sinners. Concerning him John says in the Gospel: “This is the Lamb of God; this is he who takes away the sins of the world” (John I), Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY IX. ON THE SAME FEAST.

(From the works of the venerable Bede, priest.)

“At that time, when the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord,” etc. (Luke II).

“The solemnity of today’s celebration,” etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, his works, volume V, [Col. 1463C] Patrologia XCIV, col. 79.

HOMILY X. ON THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER.

The institution of today’s feast received from our predecessors the name “Chair,” because it is reported that on this day Peter, the first of the apostles, received the chair of the episcopate. Rightly, therefore, churches throughout the world celebrate the birthday of that see which the apostle accepted for their salvation, the Lord saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

“Upon this rock,” he says—that is, upon the Lord and Savior, who granted his faithful confessor a share in his own name. “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” The gates of hell are the torments and blandishments of persecutors, which, by frightening some away from the steadfastness [Col. 1463D] of faith, open the entrance to eternal death.

There are therefore many gates of hell, but none of them prevails against the Church founded upon the rock. Rightly, then, is he to be honored by all the churches who is the head of the Church and who followed the solidity of the firmest rock, confounded the enemies of Christ by the authority of the Holy Spirit and triumphed through the strength of unwearied endurance. Nor did the gate of hell, as has been said, prevail against him who, confessing the King of glory, opened to himself the entrance of the eternal gate.

Or how could that life-giving gate not be open to him who, filled with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, affirmed the mystery of the one majesty of God in the Father and the Son, teaching and showing what was, in the one and same Son of God, [Col. 1464A] both the nature of the assumed flesh and the privilege of the divine nature?

He had certainly heard the Savior himself say: “I and the Father are one” (John X), and: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John XIV). This confession made him honorable on earth and glorious in heaven.

The Lord therefore named Peter, as we have said, the foundation of the Church; and for this reason the universal Church rightly honors this foundation, upon which the height of its building rises. Hence the Psalmist fittingly says: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the chair of the elders” (Ps. CVI).

It is therefore worthy that this foundation should be honored in the Church, through which one ascends to heaven. Since the birthday of the Chair is celebrated today, the priestly office is honored. It must necessarily possess that much greater dignity [Col. 1464B] in the Church, the greater the honor accorded to the priestly office.

This day, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, is rightly honored by us, because, while we celebrate the birthday of the Chair, we also venerate the episcopate of the apostle Peter. Yet because it frequently falls within the days of Lent, the reverence due to the holy days ought to make it more pleasing to us.

And God fittingly granted us the birthday of the Chair at the very beginning of the fasts, so that the day that had previously belonged to excess might now belong to sobriety; what had belonged to gluttony might belong to abstinence; and what had belonged to sin might belong to holiness.

The observance of this solemnity was introduced into the churches in the following manner. As the apostle passed through the regions disseminating the word of life and laying the foundation of the Church, when he drew near to Antioch, the whole city began to hear, through Nicias [Nicetas] and Aquila, [Col. 1464C] that Peter was approaching.

When all the people of the city of Antioch heard that Peter was coming to Antioch, they went out to meet him. Nearly all the elders and nobles sprinkled ashes on their heads, put on sackcloth, and did penance barefoot, because they had agreed with Simon Magus against his preaching.

While they recounted these and similar things, they brought him people afflicted by illnesses and tormented by demons, as well as paralytics and others suffering from various dangers. There was an immense multitude of sick people gathered together.

When Peter saw them—not only doing penance for the evil things they had thought about God through Simon, but also displaying such complete faith in God that all those suffering from different illnesses believed they could be saved through him—he stretched out his hands toward heaven and [Col. 1464D] , pouring forth a prayer with tears and giving thanks to God, said:

“I bless you, O Father worthy of proclamation, who deign to fulfill every word and promise of your Son, so that every creature may recognize that you alone are God in heaven and on earth.”

Saying these and similar things, he ascended to a higher place and ordered the entire multitude of the sick to be placed before him. He addressed them all in these words:

“Seeing that I am a man like you, do not suppose that you can recover health from me. Rather, it is through him who, descending from heaven, has shown those who believe in him the complete healing of soul and body. Therefore let this whole people bear witness to your faith: that you believe with your whole heart in the Lord Jesus Christ, so that they too may know [Col. 1465A] that they can be saved by him.”

When the entire multitude of the sick cried out with one voice that the God whom Peter proclaimed was the true God, suddenly an immense light of God’s grace appeared in the midst of the people. The paralytics began to run, healed, to Peter’s feet; the blind, having received their sight, began to cry out; the lame, their walk restored, gave thanks; the sick rejoiced at receiving health. Some who were living only by their breath, already without sense or voice, were also restored. All the lunatics and those filled with demons were likewise freed.

The Holy Spirit therefore displayed such great power of his grace on that day that everyone, from the least to the greatest, confessed God with one voice. Within seven days more than ten thousand people who believed in God were baptized and consecrated through sanctification. Thus [Col. 1465B] Theophilus, who was higher in rank than all the powerful men in the city, consecrated his great house as a basilica in the name of the Church, with every desire of eagerness.

In that basilica a chair was established for the apostle Peter by the whole people. Every day the entire multitude gathered there to hear the word and believed the sound doctrine whose efficacy brings healing to all.

Then Faustinus approached and fell at Peter’s feet, saying:

“The seeds of your word, which the field of my mind received, have now been born and brought to fruitful maturity. Place me in the Lord’s granary, making me a participant in the divine table.”

Then Peter, taking his hand with great joy, handed him over to Clement and his brothers, saying:

“As God restores sons to a father, so the sons restore you, the Father, to God.”

He then proclaimed a fast [Col. 1465C] to all the people. When the Lord’s Day came, he baptized him; and, taking his conversion as an occasion in the midst of the people, he explained all the circumstances of his case, so that the whole city regarded him as though he were an angel and showed him no less grace than it showed the apostle.

On the following day Peter ordered the people to assemble. After appointing one of those who followed him as bishop, and other men as priests, and after baptizing many and restoring to health all who had been afflicted by demons or illnesses, he remained there for another three days. When everything had been properly arranged and he had established the Church of Christ, he bade them farewell and departed for Laodicea, greatly desired by them.

After this Peter came to Rome and, through his preaching, converted many throngs of people to the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are glory and [Col. 1465D] honor forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY XI. ON THE SAME FEAST.

(From the works of the venerable Bede, priest.)

“At that time Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, and he questioned his disciples, saying: ‘Who do men say that the Son of Man is?’” etc. (Matt. XVI).

The reading from the holy Gospel which you have just heard, brothers, must be pondered with all the greater attention and continually retained without forgetfulness, inasmuch as it clearly commends to us the great perfection of faith and likewise demonstrates the great strength of that perfected faith against every temptation. For if we wish to know how one ought to believe in Christ, what could be clearer than what Peter says to him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”? [Col. 1466A] Again, if we delight to hear how powerful this faith is, what could be more explicit than what the Lord says concerning the Church that was to be built upon him: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it”? But these matters will be explained more fully in their proper places.

Now, returning to the orderly explanation of the Gospel reading, let us first examine the place where it is recorded to have occurred. “Jesus came,” it says, “into the region of Caesarea Philippi.” As Luke testifies, Philippus was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. He therefore founded a city at the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Mount Lebanon, which is the boundary of Judaea toward the north, and called it Caesarea Philippi, evidently in memory of his own name and likewise in honor of Tiberius Caesar, under whom he [Col. 1466B] reigned.

Coming into that region, Jesus questioned his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He does not inquire as though ignorant of what either the disciples or outsiders thought about him. Rather, he asks the disciples what they think about him so that he may reward their confession of the true faith with a fitting recompense. For just as, when all were questioned generally, Peter answered as one for all, so what the Lord answered Peter, he answered in Peter to them all. He asks what others think about him so that, after the opinions of those who were mistaken had first been set forth, the disciples might be shown to have learned the truth of their confession not from common opinion, but from the secret of the Lord’s own revelation.

“Who,” he says, “do people say that the Son of Man is?” He fittingly calls those “people” who knew how to speak only of the Son of Man, because they did not know the mysteries of his divinity. For those who know how to grasp the mysteries of his divinity are rightly said to be above humanity, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). After prefacing this concerning people—that is, concerning those who are wise only according to human understanding, hearing, and sight—he immediately added concerning himself and those like him things that transcend the general human judgment: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (ibid.).

The same applies here. When the Lord had asked the disciples whom people said he was, and they had produced various opinions of various persons, he said to them: “But you, whom do you say that I am?” It was as though he were separating them from the generality of human beings and indicating that they had become gods and sons of God by adoption, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

Simon Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He calls him the living God in distinction from the false gods whom the pagan world, deceived by manifold error, either established for itself from dead human beings or, in even greater madness, fashioned from inanimate matter for its worship. Of such gods it is sung in the Psalms: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak,” and so forth (Ps. 113).

Let your affection note how wonderfully it came about that, when a declaration concerning both natures of the same Lord and our Savior was to be made by the Lord himself and by his faithful disciple, the Lord himself confessed the humility of the humanity he had assumed, while the disciple displayed the excellence of his divine eternity. The Lord declares about himself what is lesser; the disciple announces concerning the Lord what is greater. The Lord says of himself what he became for us; the disciple declares concerning the Lord that he is the one who made us.

Thus in the Gospel the Lord was accustomed much more frequently to call himself the Son of Man than the Son of God, so that he might remind us of the dispensation which he undertook for our sake. But the more humbly we remember that he descended for our exaltation to the lowest things of humanity, the more necessary it is for us to venerate the heights of his divinity. For if, amid the mysteries of his incarnation by which we were redeemed, we always recall with devout mind the power of his divinity by which we were created, then we too, together with Peter, shall be granted the reward of heavenly blessedness.

When Peter had confessed him to be the Christ, the Son of the living God, let us see what follows. “Jesus answered and said: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona.” It is therefore clear that, after the true confession of Christ, the true rewards of blessedness remain. But let us look attentively at the nature and greatness of the name by which he glorifies the one who perfectly confessed his name, so that by truly confessing him we too may deserve to share in that blessing.

“Blessed are you,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jona.” *Bar-Jona* is said in Syriac, and in Latin means “son of a dove.” The Apostle Peter is rightly called the son of a dove, because the dove is a very simple creature, and he followed the Lord with prudent and devout simplicity, mindful of the command which he and his fellow disciples received from that same teacher of simplicity and truth: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10).

Or certainly, because the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, he is rightly called the son of a dove, since he is shown to have been full of spiritual grace. And the Lord rewards with fitting praise his lover and confessor when he testifies that he is a son of the Holy Spirit, by whom he himself affirms that Christ is the Son of the living God—although no believer doubts that this is accomplished in very different ways.

Jesus Christ is the Son of God by nature; Peter, like the other elect, is a son of the Holy Spirit by grace. Christ is the Son of the living God because he was born from him. Peter is a son of the Holy Spirit because he was reborn from him. Christ is the Son of God before the ages, for he is the power of God and the wisdom of God, which says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning” (Prov. 8). Peter is a son of the Holy Spirit from the time when, illuminated by him, he received the grace of divine knowledge.

And because the Holy Trinity has one will and the same operation, after saying, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona”—that is, son of spiritual grace—he immediately added: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” The Father revealed this to the son of a dove because the grace of the Father and of the Holy Spirit is one, and the grace of the Son is likewise one, as will be proved by very simple examples from Holy Scripture.

The Apostle says concerning the Father: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4). The Son himself says concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15). The Apostle says concerning the Holy Spirit: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). The Father therefore sent the Spirit; the Spirit himself breathes where he wills (John 3), because, as we have said, the will and operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. Therefore it is appropriately said that the Father who is in heaven revealed to the son of a dove the mystery of faith, which flesh and blood could not reveal to him.

“Flesh and blood” are rightly understood as human beings puffed up with fleshly wisdom, ignorant of the simplicity of the dove, and therefore wholly turned away from the wisdom of the Spirit. Concerning them it was said above that, because they did not understand Christ, some said that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “The natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

It follows: “And I say to you, You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Peter, previously called Simon, received from the Lord the name Peter because of the strength of his faith and the steadfastness of his confession. He clung to the Lord with a firm and tenacious mind, concerning whom it is written: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

“And upon this rock”—that is, upon the Lord and Savior, who gave his faithful knower, lover, and confessor a share in his own name, so that he might be called Peter from the rock—“I will build my Church.” For no one reaches the portion of the elect and eternal life except through faith and love of Christ and through receiving Christ’s sacraments, as the Apostle testifies: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” The gates of hell are wicked teachings which, by leading the inexperienced astray, drag them down to hell. The gates of hell are also the tortures and flatteries of persecutors, which, by frightening or softening the weak, remove them from steadfastness in faith and open for them an entrance to eternal death. Likewise, the wicked deeds and foolish conversations of unbelievers are certainly gates of hell, insofar as they show the way of destruction to their supporters and followers.

“For faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself” (James 2). And “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). There are therefore many gates of hell, but none of them prevails against the Church founded upon the rock, because whoever has received the faith of Christ with deep love of heart easily despises whatever external danger brought on by temptation may assail him.

But whoever among believers has lost his faith, corrupted either by deed or by denial, must be considered not to have built, with the Lord’s cooperation, the house of his confession upon the rock, but, according to the parable in another passage, to have built it upon sand without a foundation (Matt. 7). That is, he did not follow Christ with simple and true intention, but displayed the outward appearance of a Christian for some earthly and fragile reason.

It follows: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” The one who confessed the King of heaven with greater devotion than the others was rightly himself given, above the others, the keys of the heavenly kingdom, so that it might be clear to all that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven without that confession and faith. By “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” he names the knowledge and power of discernment by which one should receive the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom.

Therefore he plainly adds: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it must nevertheless be known without any doubt that it is also given to the other apostles. He himself bears witness to this when, after the resurrection and triumph of his passion, he appeared to them, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20).

Even now the same office is entrusted to bishops and priests throughout the whole Church, so that, when the causes of sinners have been recognized, they may absolve from fear of eternal death all whom they see to be humble and truly penitent. But those whom they know to persist in the sins they have committed, they are to declare bound to everlasting punishments.

For this reason the Lord elsewhere commands concerning a brother who has been corrected once, twice, and a third time, but does not repent: “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. 18). And lest anyone should consider it a trivial matter to be condemned by the judgment of the Church, he immediately added with fearful solemnity: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” Authority to bind and loose is therefore given to the whole Church of the elect, according to the measure of their faults or repentance.

But blessed Peter, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed him with true love, specially received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power, so that all believers throughout the world might understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of faith or from fellowship with him can neither be loosed from the bonds of sins nor enter the door of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must with our whole attention learn both the mysteries of the faith he taught and demonstrate works corresponding to the faith. We must with all vigilance avoid the manifold and subtle snares of the gates of hell, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may be delivered from them, according to the Psalmist’s words, and may deserve to enter the gates of the daughter of Zion—that is, the joys of the heavenly city—in order to proclaim his praises.

Let us not suppose that salvation is sufficient for us if we are made equal in faith or conduct to crowds of the negligent or to any unlearned people, for the sacred writings prescribe one rule both for believing and for living. Whenever the examples of those who err are thrust before us, let us immediately turn away the eyes of our mind lest they see vanity, and diligently search in our hearts what Truth itself decrees, following the example of blessed Peter, who, rejecting the sects of those who erred, uttered the mystery of true faith in an unwavering confession of his mouth and preserved it with inseparable care of heart.

Here we have learned of the confidence of his confession; elsewhere he himself bears witness to the power of a single love for Christ. When some of his disciples were departing from him, and he said to the Twelve, “Do you also wish to leave?” Peter answered him: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 6).

Therefore, my brothers, if we strive to imitate his example according to our measure, we too shall be able, with him, both to be called blessed and to be blessed in reality. The name Simon, that is, “obedient to Christ,” will also suit us. Because of the simplicity of our unfeigned faith and the grace of virtues received from the Lord, we shall be called sons of a dove. He himself will rejoice in the spiritual progress of our soul and say: “How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like doves’” (Song 4).

Thus, when upon the rock of faith we build gold, silver, and precious stones—that is, perfect works of virtue—no fire of tribulation will harm us, and no storm of temptations will prevail against us. Rather, tested by adversity, we shall receive the crown of life, which he himself promised us, who lives and reigns as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF BLESSED MARY, OR RATHER ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 1470C]

“You,” I say, “I address, O Jews, who to this day have denied the Son of God. Was it not your voice when you saw him performing miracles and, testing him, said: ‘How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly’” (John 10)? But he sent you to consider his miracles, saying: “The works that I do themselves bear witness concerning me,” so that not words but deeds might bear witness to Christ.

Yet you, not recognizing the Savior who was working salvation in the midst of your land, adding evil to evil, said: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8). But you did not wish to consider what he answered you: “Is it not written in your law that the testimony of two people is true?” (ibid.)

Transgressors of the law, attend to the law. You seek testimony concerning Christ? Is it not written in your law that the testimony of two people is true? (Deut. 17.) Let not merely two, but more witnesses of Christ come forth from the law and convict those who hear the law but do not practice it.

Speak, Isaiah; bear witness to Christ. “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted as “God with us” (Isa. 7).

Let another witness also come forward. You too, Jeremiah, bear witness to Christ. “This,” he says, “is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him, who discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3).

[Col. 1471A]

Behold two suitable witnesses from your law, by whose testimony your hearts have not been pierced. Let still others, and still others, be introduced as witnesses from the law of Christ, so that the hardest foreheads of his enemies may be crushed.

Let holy Daniel come also, young indeed in age, but old in knowledge and gentleness. Let him convict all false witnesses; as he convicted the shameless elders, so by his testimony let him crush the enemies of Christ.

Speak, holy Daniel; say concerning Christ what you know. “When the Holy of Holies comes,” he says, “anointing shall cease” (Dan. 9). Why, when he was present—when you insultingly said to him, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true”—did your anointing cease, unless it is because he is the one who came as the Holy of Holies?

If, as you say, he has not yet come, but the Holy of Holies is expected to come, demonstrate your anointing. But if—as is true—your anointing has ceased, acknowledge that the Holy of Holies has come.

For he is also that stone cut from the mountain without hands that cut it: that is, Christ, born of a virgin without the hands of those embracing. He grew so greatly that he became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth.

Concerning this mountain the Prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2). And David says concerning it: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain. Why do you suspect the mountains covered with cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell?” (Ps. 67.)

When the Lord Christ himself questioned his disciples about whom people said the Son of Man was, they answered: “Some say Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” And he said: “Why do you suspect the mountains covered with cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell upon it?”

Peter recognized this mountain and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). He recognized the mountain and climbed the mountain; he bore witness to the Truth, and he was loved by the Truth. Peter was founded upon the rock so that he might accept death by loving the one whom he had thrice denied through fear.

Speak also, Moses, lawgiver and leader of the people of Israel; bear witness to Christ. “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers. Every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from his people” (Deut. 18). Hear in the Gospel that Christ is called the prophet: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Mark 6).

Let holy David also come forward, a faithful witness, from whose seed he himself proceeded to whom the law and the prophets bear witness. Let David also speak concerning Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71).

Whom will they serve? Say: whom will they serve? Do you wish to hear whom they will serve? “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109).

More explicitly and by name: “Why,” he says, “did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

Let another witness come forward. You too, prophet Habakkuk, bear witness to Christ. “Lord,” he says, “I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I trembled” (Hab. 3).

What work of God did he admire and fear? Did he tremble in wonder at the creation of the world? Certainly not. But hear what he feared: “In the midst of two animals you shall be known.” Your work, O God, is the Word made flesh. “In the midst of two animals you shall be known.” How far did you descend? You made me tremble because the Word through whom all things were made lay in a manger.

“The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s manger” (Isa. 1). “In the midst of two animals you shall be known.” What is meant by “in the midst of two animals you shall be known,” unless either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of the two thieves, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah speaking with him on the mountain?

“The Word walked and went out into the fields. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). This is what Jeremiah says: “After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3).

Behold how the witnesses of truth agree with one another; behold how they convict the children of falsehood. Are these things sufficient for you, O Jews, or shall we still introduce from the law and from your own people other witnesses to bear witness to the one whom, in your deranged minds, you insultingly said, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8)?

And if I wished to gather from the law and the prophets everything that has been said concerning Christ, time would fail me more readily than material. Nevertheless, I shall introduce that old man born from your people but not left in your error, holy Simeon, who deserved to be kept in this light in his decrepit old age until he should see the true light. His age was already compelling him to depart, but he waited to receive the one whom he knew was coming, since this old man had been warned by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he had seen the Christ of God born.

Recognizing him, he went to the temple. When he saw him carried in his mother’s hands, and his holy old age recognized the divine infancy, he took the infant into his arms. He indeed carried Christ, but Christ sustained the old man. He sustained the one who was being carried, so that the other would not depart from the body before the promised time.

But hear what he said and whom he confessed—enemies, not of Christ but of yourselves. Blessing God, the old man cried out and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2).

Let the parents of John, Zachariah and Elizabeth—young in years, barren, but fruitful in old age—also bear witness to Christ. Let them say what they think concerning Christ and raise up a suitable witness for him. For they say to their little son at his birth: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High, for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1).

And Elizabeth herself said to the virgin mother: “Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (ibid.).

John understood that the mother of his Lord had come to his own mother. Still placed within the narrow confines of the womb, he greeted him by movement, since he could not do so by voice. Later John himself became the forerunner, friend, humble and most faithful servant, and a suitable witness—so much greater among those born of women as he was thought to be what he was not.

For the Jews believed him to be the Christ, but he loudly declared that he was not, saying: “I am not the one you suppose me to be; but behold, one is coming after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie” (Luke 3).

O faithful witness and friend of the true Bridegroom, how much more humble you would have been if you had said that you were worthy to untie the strap of his sandal! But by declaring yourself unworthy of this, you contradict the Jews, who were false witnesses.

These things had been said before you saw Christ. When he came to you, exalted yet humble for the sake of fulfilling his dispensation, to be baptized by you—although he had absolutely no sin—hear what you answered, whom you recognized, and what testimony you gave. Let the enemies who refuse to listen hear it: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” [Col. 1473B] (John 1). And you added: “Do you come to me to be baptized? I ought rather to be baptized by you” (Matt. 3).

The servant recognized the Lord; one bound by the chains of original sin recognized the one free from every bond of sin; the herald recognized the judge; the creature recognized the Creator; the friend of the bridegroom recognized the Bridegroom. For this too is John’s voice: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

Are these things sufficient for you, O Jews? Are so many witnesses and testimonies from your own law and your own people sufficient, or will you still dare, in your excessive shamelessness, to say that people of another race or nation ought to bear witness to Christ?

But if you say this, he answers you: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Yet, as Paul rebukes you in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first. But since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold,” he says, “we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

Let us also show that testimony to Christ was given by the Gentiles, since Truth did not remain silent but cried out even through the tongues of his enemies. Did not that most eloquent poet, amid his verses (Virgil, *Eclogue* 4),

> Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven,

bear witness to Christ?

If this should be called into doubt, let me introduce other suitable witnesses from the Gentiles, who will say still more. I shall not pass over that king who subdued your arrogance by taking you captive—namely, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

Speak, Nebuchadnezzar. Tell us what was revealed to you in the furnace into which you had unjustly cast three righteous men. Did you not say: “Did we not cast three boys bound into the furnace?” And they answered you: “Truly, O king.” Then you said: “Behold, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3).

O foreigner, where did you learn this? Who announced the Son of God to you? What law, what prophet announced the Son of God to you? He has not yet been born into the world, yet you recognize the likeness of the one who is to be born. Where did you learn this? Who announced it to you, unless the divine fire so illuminated you within that, while the Jewish captives—your enemies—were held there among you, you could bear witness in this way to the Son of God?

But since every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses, as the Lord himself, refuting your obstinacy, says: “It is written in your law that the testimony of two people is true” (John 8), let a third witness now be introduced from the Gentiles, so that the testimony of truth may be strengthened on every side.

Let us bring forward what the Sibyl also proclaimed prophetically concerning Christ, so that, by one stone, the foreheads of both groups—Jews and pagans—may be struck, and so that all the enemies of Christ may be struck down by their own sword, like Goliath. Hear what she said:

> The sign of judgment: the earth shall be drenched with sweat.  
> From heaven a king shall come, destined through the ages,  
> Present in the flesh, certainly, to judge the world.  
> Hence the unbeliever and the faithful shall see God,  
> The Most High, with the saints, when the end of the age itself has come.  
> Thus the souls whom he himself judges shall be present with flesh.  
> When the world lies uncultivated among dense thorns,  
> They shall cast away the idols of men and all wealth as well.  
> Fire shall burn the earth, the sea, and the heavens,  
> Seeking out the dark gates of Avernus and breaking them open.  
> For free light shall be given to all the flesh of the saints,  
> But the guilty shall be consumed by everlasting flame.  
> Revealing hidden deeds, each person shall then speak  
> Of secrets, and God shall open hearts to the light.  
> Then there shall also be mourning; all shall gnash their teeth.  
> The sun’s radiance shall be taken away, and the choir of stars shall perish.  
> The heavens shall be rolled up; the moon’s splendor shall pass away.  
> He shall cast down the hills and raise the valleys from below.  
> Nothing lofty or high shall remain among human affairs.  
> The mountains shall already be made level with the plains, and all the blue waters of the sea  
> Shall cease; the shattered earth shall perish.  
> Thus likewise the springs shall boil, and the rivers with fire.  
> Then the trumpet shall send down a mournful sound from the high  
> World, lamenting the wretched crime and its manifold sufferings.  
> And the earth, splitting open, shall reveal Tartarean chaos.  
> And before this Lord the kings shall all stand together.  
> Fire and a river of sulfur shall fall from heaven.

These words concerning Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and second coming were spoken in such a way that, if anyone wishes to identify the initial letters of these verses in Greek, he will find:

> Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Ὑιὸς Θεοῦ Σωτήρ

that is, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” This also appears when the same verses are translated into Latin, except that the distinctive character of the Greek letters could not be preserved to the same extent.

Let us listen with the utmost attention to other Sibylline verses that more openly demonstrate Christ’s passion:

> He shall later come into the hands of wicked and unbelieving men.  
> They shall slap God with defiled hands.  
> With unclean mouths they shall spit venomous saliva.  
> The completely innocent one shall give his back to the blows.  
> Receiving blows upon the face, he shall remain silent, lest anyone recognize  
> What the Word is, and whence he came to speak to the dead.  
> And he shall bear a crown of thorns.  
> For food they gave him gall, and for his thirst they gave him vinegar.  
> They displayed this table of inhospitality.  
> For, foolish one, you did not recognize your God,  
> Who played with mortal minds; yet with thorns  
> You crowned him with a crown and mixed the dreadful gall.  
> The veil of the temple shall indeed be torn, and in the middle of the day  
> There shall be exceedingly dark night for three hours.  
> And he shall end the doom of death, having accepted the sleep of three days,  
> And then, returning from the dead, he shall come into the light.  
> Called forth, he first showed the beginning of the resurrection.

I believe now, O enemies, Jews, that you have been so overwhelmed and refuted by the truth itself through so many witnesses that you ought neither to resist nor to inquire any further. But you—

# HOMILY XXVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(By Hericus, a monk of Auxerre.)*

“At that time Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and questioned his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say that the Son of Man is?’” etc. (Matthew 16).

Herod the Elder, under whom the Lord was born, is said to have had four sons: namely, Philip, who is mentioned here and who, as Luke relates (chapter 3), was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis; Archelaus and Lysanias; and also Herod, under whom the Lord suffered.

Therefore this Philip, as stated above, ruler of the fourth part of the kingdom of the Jews, established a city at the foot of Mount Lebanon in honor of Tiberius Caesar, where the Jordan rises from two springs. He decreed that it should be called Caesarea Philippi, in memory of his own name and likewise in honor of Tiberius Caesar. Later, after losing its former name, it was called Paneas. The ancients also report that in this city tribute was once customarily paid to kings.

He did this out of favor toward that Caesar, in imitation of his father Herod, who named a city Caesarea after Caesar; it had previously been called the Tower of Strato. Herod is also found in the histories to have founded, beyond the Jordan, the city of Ilias as a memorial to the daughter of that same Caesar.

When the Lord therefore came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples what opinion people held of him. He most fittingly wished to do this in that region, so that where an earthly king had once been accustomed to exact tribute from his subjects, there the heavenly King, on coming, might receive from his disciples the tribute of faith.

Here he set forth a model for the rulers of the holy Church, who act in Christ’s place in administering his affairs: they too should inquire of those whom, because of their faith and conduct, they esteem more familiarly than others what reputation they have among their subjects.

If they discover that they are worthy of the good reputation they have received, let them attribute the whole of it to God’s grace and strive to be such as their reputation has proclaimed them to be. But if they perceive that a testimony about them is being borne otherwise than is proper, let them correct it in themselves and strive to live so piously and in accordance with what their sacred rank of pre-eminence requires that such a splendor of holiness shine forth in them as may wipe away every cloud of evil speech and prevent their reputation from lying about them.

For he says: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He does not ask this as one who does not know, as though he could have been ignorant of what people thought about him; rather, he does so in order to reward their confession of the true faith with a fitting recompense and to free from error the people corrupted by the false traditions of the scribes and Pharisees.

For the scribes and Pharisees, who stood out among the Jewish people in honor and wisdom, saw that the people were abandoning them and following the Lord Jesus Christ because of the holiness of his life, his saving preaching, and the signs of miracles that they continually saw him perform. Driven by jealousy, they envied him.

Although they had been instructed above others in the Law and the Prophets and knew that he was the Christ, they nevertheless feared losing human glory if the people abandoned their teaching and followed the Lord’s commandments. Therefore they worked by whatever means they could to subvert the hearts of the people, lest they believe him to be the Christ who had been promised to their fathers in the Law and the Prophets.

Hence even to this day the Jews suppose that the Lord Jesus Christ has not yet come into this world, but is still to come.

Seeing, therefore, that the people were corrupted by the traditions of the scribes and Pharisees and that the people regarded him not as the Christ but rather as John, or Elijah, or Jeremiah, the Lord wished to free them from this error. For that reason, by asking what others thought of him, he required that, once the various errors of those who held opinions had been set forth, the disciples should be shown not to have learned the truth of their confession from popular opinion, but rather through the revelation of divine inspiration.

For he says: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” As though he were saying: “Of me, who am called the Son of Man—that is, the son of Mary—who do people say that I am?” He does not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “Who do they say that the Son of Man is,” so that he would not seem boastfully to be asking about the popular opinion concerning himself.

He was accustomed to call himself the Son of Man more often than the Son of God, in order to remind us of the dispensation of humanity that he assumed for our sake.

Wherever “son of man” is written in the Old Testament, blessed Jerome testifies that in Hebrew it is understood as “son of Adam.” For Adam is also interpreted as “man.”

And fittingly he calls “people” those who knew how to speak only of the Son of Man—that is, of the humanity of the Son, which they saw with their eyes, while they did not know the mysteries of his divinity. They were “people”; that is, they understood only human things about him.

But those who had already learned to speak of the Son of God deserved to be called no longer people but gods. Such were the holy apostles, who, already instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, were worthy to understand not only that Christ was the Son of Man, but also that he was the consubstantial Son of God the Father.

Therefore, after the various opinions of the people had been stated, he immediately asks the apostles who they say he is. By this he distinguishes them from the generality of other people and shows, by the privilege of their unique knowledge, that they possess a nature above the human.

The teachers of the Church ought also to observe this form of questioning. They too should inquire of their subjects what reputation they have among ordinary people and outsiders, so that, according to what they hear about themselves, they may correct their conduct and strive to conform themselves more modestly to everyone.

But they said: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”

It is not necessary here to investigate the causes of popular error—why some thought Christ was Elijah, others John, and others Jeremiah—since unbelievers could have erred about Elijah and Jeremiah just as Herod erred about John, saying: “The John whom I beheaded has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him” (Mark 6).

For just as Herod thought that Christ, who was working miracles, was John whom he himself had beheaded, so the uneducated crowd thought that this same Christ was Elijah or Jeremiah. One of these is read to have been taken up into heaven, while the death of the other is plainly recorded in canonical Scripture.

But it may be asked why the Lord Jesus Christ was regarded by Herod or by the people as John, since John did not shine with any signs of miracles, whereas Christ performed the greatest and most extraordinary signs. He cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, expelled demons from possessed bodies, restored the ability to walk to the lame and paralytics, and raised the dead—things which we know John never did.

To this it must be said that Herod or the people could have regarded Christ as John because they thought that, after rising from the dead, he could perform miracles that he had not performed previously. They held the same belief about the resurrection of the dead as we do: namely, that the works of the dead after their resurrection would be of greater dignity and glory than before.

Jeremiah could not unreasonably have been thought to be Christ because of the extraordinary holiness by which he excelled among the people, just as it is read of Jeremiah that he was sanctified in his mother’s womb and shone forth as illustrious in his own time (Jeremiah 1).

Elijah, however, could have been believed to be the Lord because the people knew that he was to come before the Savior’s arrival, as Malachi says: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers” (Malachi 4).

Jesus says to them: “But who do you say that I am?” As though separating them from the generality of human beings, he indicates those who have become gods and sons of God by adoption, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81).

As though he were saying: “While those who are people form various opinions, you who are gods and have already become sons of God by adoption—who do you say that I am?”

Then Peter, more ardent in faith and more ready than the others in his love of confession, answered in the name of all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

When all the apostles had been questioned generally, blessed Peter, taking upon himself the persons of them all, answered from the abundance of his understanding: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

And truly it was fitting that the one who was to be the head of the Church should speak with the mouth of the whole Church.

He said “Son of the living God” to distinguish him from the false gods whom pagan error established for worship, either from dead human beings or from insensible things that it created for adoration. Of these it is written: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (Psalm 113).

In this brief sentence he most suitably comprehended everything that can be said about Christ through extended courses of speech, and at the same time he exercised human curiosity, which is bold in investigating hidden things.

Why should we ask how Christ was born from the substance of God the Father, when the one who begets has never existed without the one begotten? Or how he came forth as a human being from the womb of a virgin mother and left his mother whole and undefiled? Why should we ask these and many other questions of this kind about Christ, when it was sufficient for blessed Peter simply to believe that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God?

Blessed Paul too judged that he knew nothing else except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2).

The goal of Christian faith, therefore, is established in the confession of Christ the Son of God. It is not permitted to know how he was begotten, but it is permitted to believe that he was begotten.

This too must be considered: Christ asked about the Son of Man, whereas Peter answered concerning the Son of God. We ought to venerate his divinity all the more because he humbled and subjected himself for our sake.

Now let us hear with what praise Christ addresses his confessor and herald: “Blessed are you,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

“Bar-Jonah” in Syriac means in Latin “son of a dove.” Blessed Peter the apostle is rightly called the son of a dove because he adhered to the Lord with prudent and godly simplicity.

For the dove is an exceedingly simple and innocent animal, and among birds it rejoices in simplicity above all others.

If we wish to understand this more deeply, by the dove—in whose form the Holy Spirit appeared over the baptized Lord—the grace of that same Holy Spirit is represented.

Therefore the Lord rightly called Peter the son of a dove, since he himself had filled him with the grace of spiritual gifts; under the Spirit’s instruction, Peter had learned inwardly what he so suitably brought forth outwardly.

Some simply think that this Peter had a father named John, according to the passage where the Lord elsewhere asks him: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21). They maintain that, through scribal error, “Bar-Jona” was written in place of “Bar-Joanna,” which means “son of John,” with one syllable omitted from the middle.

“Joanna,” however, is interpreted as “grace of God.”

Both names can be understood mystically in such a way that Peter is called the son of a dove—that is, of the Holy Spirit—and the son of John—that is, of the grace of God, through whom spiritual gifts are represented.

It should also be noted how perfectly appropriate the return of praise was. Blessed Peter said that the Lord was the Son of God, and Christ consequently called him the son of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when blessed Peter is called the son of the Holy Spirit, he is plainly confirmed to be the son of God. For “God is Spirit” (John 4).

Yet Christ the Son of God and blessed Peter are very different and entirely distinct. What the former possesses by nature, the latter received by grace. What is eternally proper to the former belonged temporally to the latter as an accidental gift.

When he says, “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” by the name of flesh and blood we should understand the carnal tradition and teaching of the scribes and Pharisees.

“Flesh and blood” are rightly understood as human beings puffed up with carnal wisdom and ignorant of the simplicity of the dove.

The terms “flesh” and “blood” are used with various meanings in the holy Scriptures.

Sometimes “flesh” denotes the substance of nature itself, as in Genesis: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2).

At times, by the name “flesh,” through synecdoche, the whole human being is signified, as John says of Christ: “The Word became flesh” (John 1). This plainly means: God became human.

“Flesh and blood” are also customarily used for corruption, as the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15).

Very often too, by the name “flesh and blood,” a doctrine that has become dense through the subtlety of a carnal rather than spiritual understanding is meant, as Paul says of himself: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Galatians 1).

It is in this sense that “flesh” must be understood here: namely, carnal wisdom and, with respect to God, the foolish wisdom of carnal people. The more broadly it spreads itself in investigating earthly and transitory matters, the less it reaches the entrance to intellectual and true philosophy.

Therefore flesh and blood did not reveal this to him, because he did not learn through worldly wisdom that Christ was the Son of God; he learned it through the inspiration of God the Father, who alone knows the Son.

Alternatively, as has been stated above, “flesh and blood” may refer to people who think carnally about Christ, who do not possess the simplicity of the dove, and who are therefore unworthy of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Such were those whose opinions about Christ the evangelist recounted above. Of such people the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

“But my Father who is in heaven.”

Since it is entirely certain that all spiritual gifts bestowed by the Lord upon the faithful are given by the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says, “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom,” and so on, until he says, “distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12), how does the Lord Jesus Christ say that the mystery of faith was revealed to blessed Peter by the Father?

We must understand that just as the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one, so too their operation and will are one. Accordingly, it is fittingly said that the Father who is in heaven revealed to Peter the mystery of faith, which flesh and blood could not reveal.

“And I say to you that you are Peter.”

The order of the words is: “Because you said to me, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ I say to you—not with an empty word that has no effect, but I truly say to you—that you are Peter.”

We should not believe that Peter first received this name at that moment, but rather at the time when, at the beginning of the Lord’s preaching, he was brought to the Lord by Andrew, as John testifies. There, as a great foreshadowing of his faith, he heard from him: “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as “Peter.”

Thus the Lord now called him by the name previously given to him. He does not say, “You shall be called Peter,” but “You are Peter,” referring to what had been said earlier.

Just as Christ gave the apostles a name, so that they might be called the light or the salt of the earth, so he gave his distinguished confessor, who had previously been called Simon—that is, obedient—the name Peter because of the strength of his unconquered faith. For he clung with tenacious mind to the one of whom it is written: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

The rock is so called not in essence but by signification. Just as a lion is called so because of strength, or a lamb because of innocence, so a rock is called so because of firmness: for those who hope in him, he is a tower of strength against the enemy. Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Psalm 17).

“And upon this rock”—that is, upon me, whom you have confessed with your mouth, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—“I will build my Church.”

He is that precious stone set in the foundation of the Church, concerning whom Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

Or, “upon this rock”—that is, upon this faith by which you have confessed me to be the Son of the living God—“I will build my Church.”

The one who preserves his faith unblemished builds upon Christ. The one who, through love of God and neighbor and through observance of God’s commandments, hastens to attain the lot of the elect also builds upon Christ.

He added “my” to distinguish it from the church of heretics, of which the Psalmist says: “I have hated the church of the wicked” (Psalm 25).

Of them he adds: “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

He did not say this concerning the condition of temporal death, by which we read that almost all the apostles were brought to completion through martyrdom. Rather, he calls vices and sins the gates of hell.

The deadly doctrines of heretics are the gates of hell, for by them they ensnare the unwary and drag them to the condemnation of everlasting death.

The seductive blandishments of persecutors are also gates of death, as are the harsh assaults of cruelty by which they seek, whether through persuasion or by inspiring terror, to cast the faithful down from the state of their uprightness and make them liable to eternal death.

The works and foolish conversations of wicked people are likewise gates of hell, insofar as they open an entrance to death among the faithful and show their hearers or followers the path of destruction.

But none of these gates of vices prevails against the Church founded upon the rock, because whoever has been firmly founded upon the rock, which is Christ, through faith and good works cannot be thrown down from the state of right faith by any ambush of temptations or driven to ruin by any adversity.

Whoever succumbs to temptation, however, must be believed to have built the house of his faith not upon the solid rock but upon shifting sand, because he assumed the name of Christ not out of love for the truth but for the sake of some temporal advantage.

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

We must not childishly imagine that the keys of the kingdom of heaven are made of some material, such as silver or gold. Rather, by “keys” the very judgment and power of discernment are signified—power that knows how to admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the wicked from the blessedness of its happiness.

These keys were specially given to blessed Peter the apostle, who confessed the King of heaven with a more excellent confession than the others, so that it might be clear that without that confession and faith by which he declared Christ, no one could enter the kingdom of heaven.

“And whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

Although this power of loosing and binding may appear to have been granted by the Lord to Peter alone, it was also granted generally to all the apostles in his person.

For after the noble triumph of his resurrection, appearing to them all, he plainly said: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20).

Just as, when all were questioned generally, Peter answered for all, so what the Lord answered to Peter, he answered in Peter to all.

Moreover, the same office is entrusted to all bishops and priests in the Church: after recognizing the causes of sinners, they are to exercise the power of binding and loosing according to the measure of their faults or repentance.

This must be done in such a way that, as is found even in some priests at the present time, they neither condemn those who are innocent or without guilt nor presume to make secure those who deserve condemnation, as though they had been absolved.

There are some who, when they wish to use this power carelessly and arbitrarily, deprive themselves of the office of confession, because they suppose that they can bind those who are in fact loosed in the sight of God and loose those who are held bound by their own guilt in God’s judgment.

Therefore this judicial severity must be weighed with great vigilance and great care by the holy shepherds of the Church. They must always bear in mind with apprehension what the Lord says through the prophet concerning those who think perversely: “They put to death souls that should not die and gave life to souls that should not live” (Ezekiel 13).

After examining the cause of the sin, let them declare those whom they see erasing their offenses with worthy contrition absolved from the bonds of eternal death.

But those whom they find sluggish in performing penance—those who not only do not regret their sins but wish to remain in them—they ought to assign to the punishments of everlasting condemnation, so that, through the clear condemnation resulting from prompt discipline, they may be compelled to undergo the salutary decrees of repentance and humility.

Finally, blessed Peter, as has been said, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed him with unconquered love, specially received both the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the citadel of judicial power. Thus all who believe in Christ may understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of his faith or fellowship can neither be absolved from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Since we honor his festival, recurring annually and venerable as that of the chief of the apostles, with the solemn observance of celebrated offices, let us strive, insofar as we can, to imitate his examples and ask for his assistance everywhere. Since the holy Church has been specially entrusted to him, may he deign, through his continual patronage, to help us, who are its least members, and, by his devout intercession, to lead us into the glory of the kingdom of heaven.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be praise and glory throughout all ages. Amen.
