# HOMILY XXXVIII. ON THE CHAINS OF BLESSED PETER THE APOSTLE
Simon, son of Joanna, called Peter from *petra*, after being a fisherman of fish, a fisher of men, the foundation of the Church, [Col. 1485C] confessor of the Son of God, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, once a despised bearer of the cross, now the key-bearer of heaven, celebrates three festive and solemn days throughout the yearly cycle. The first he consecrates to the chair at Antioch, the second to the glorious suffering of the cross, and the third is today’s feast, entitled “The Chains.”

Concerning this feast, many people circulate various opinions, which they devise not on the authority of truth but through the error of uncertainty. It seems to them that today’s solemnity began to be venerated because on this night the holy Apostle was freed from his prison-chain. But the sequence of events does not agree with the truth, since he is read to have been sent into prison not today but during the days of Unleavened Bread, and after Easter to have been delivered from Herod’s hand and from all the expectation of the Jewish people.

[Col. 1485D] Those who believe that Easter is properly celebrated in August should believe that Peter escaped his chains today. And if they wish to counter that the phrase “after Easter” signifies something yet to come, as though he had been kept in prison from Easter until the present day, Herod’s cruelty and the madness of the Jews confront them: scarcely would they have allowed the apostle to live even for the day on which he was arrested, had they not feared violating the Paschal feast.

There are also others who by no means believe that the apostle’s release occurred today, but that the Fathers established this day for the faithful to venerate it, just as the commemoration of the apostles Simon and Jude is held on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, although their martyrdom is recorded as having occurred on the Kalends of July. We also read of other saints that one day is assigned for their commemoration and another for their departure from this world. Many examples could be supplied, if extended speech did not produce weariness.

[Col. 1486A] But what the Fathers may have intended by arranging these matters in this way is not for the present moment to explain point by point. I shall merely touch briefly on the reason for which today’s feast came about. If what I say displeases the judgment of my readers, I do not fear being rightly reproved for falsity, since I am not publishing my own words as those of any authority, but am opening up the closed matters of others to those less able to understand them.

Antiquity celebrated the Kalends of the month of August before the coming of the Savior; the origin of this celebration should, briefly, be disclosed. Octavian Caesar Augustus ruled the Romans with the consular fasces. When Egypt rebelled against him, he undertook war against its borders. In that war he crushed Cleopatra, in whom the last kingdom of the Ptolemies had fallen, and the incestuous Antony with his forces.

[Col. 1486B] When, victorious, he gained possession of Alexandria and brought the victorious standards back to Rome, he was honorably received by the people of both sexes, as befitted a victor. And because he increased Roman prosperity through Alexandria’s resources to such an extent that he established the prices of possessions and other goods at twice what they had been before, the leading men of the state decreed that the memory of his victory should be recalled every year.

It was therefore agreed by common counsel that the commemoration should take place on the Kalends of Sextilis, so that in that very month the day of the victory might be celebrated—a day which, because the state and Caesar had been enlarged, was called by the name “Augustus.” From then onward, after extensive deliberation by the leading men, the custom grew up that every year the Roman people should gather together in honor of so great a prince; that the city, crowned with Caesar’s victories, should honor the beginning of the sixth month with applause and dances; and that no one from the assembled crowd should return home before tasting a simple offering—namely, bread and a drink of glass [*sic*].

[Col. 1486C] Thus observance of this day began in the twenty-eighth year before the Lord’s incarnation and prevailed among the pagans for four hundred and seven years, until the final years of the Christian emperor Hadrian. Then it came to an end among the pagans and thereafter passed to the Christians. It passed from unbelief to faith, from impiety to piety, from the prince of the nations to the prince of Christians, from Caesar Augustus to an evangelical fisherman.

Then it was solemnized in the temples of idols; now it is celebrated in the churches of the saints. Then it was offered to demons; now it is offered to him who is God of gods. Let the discourse proceed to explain how Christian religion changed this observance.

[Col. 1486D] The emperor Augustus Arcadius, son of the great Theodosius, governed the empire for fourteen years after his father’s death. When he was removed from this life, he left the kingdom to his younger son Theodosius, who had scarcely reached eight years of age. His mother Eudoxia, a woman of memorable life, assuming a manly spirit, energetically governed the empire. Becoming for her son a teacher of virtue, she taught him to follow the traces of his father’s life and goodness. For she instructed him in the divine laws and perfectly educated herself together with him. She was not lifted up by the heights of royal power but was instead inflamed with divine fear.

[Col. 1487A] The greatness of the benefit increased her desire to do good. She was not ashamed to lower the purple and care for the poor and the weak. She did not send servants or attendants to the dwellings of the sick; she herself came and supplied what was necessary. She prepared the food herself, broke the bread, served the meal, washed the cups, and offered the drink. With her left hand she supported the sick person; with her right she fed him. The humble queen also performed the other duties belonging to servants, desiring to earn from him the rank of one who serves well—him who declares that he is visited in his least ones.

For this reason she took the greatest care to cleanse her homeland of the sacrilegious rite of the gentiles and to shake the chaff of heretical depravity away from the grains of the Catholic faith. Amid these works of piety, she conceived the desire to visit the places of Jerusalem, to water the Savior’s footprints with tears, and, rather than seek the crucified one in the tomb among the dead, to adore him living and reigning in heaven.

[Col. 1487B] The desire inspired by the Holy Spirit achieved its fulfillment. Setting out with a royal retinue, she was received at Jerusalem as queen and mistress and honored by the Jewish people with great gifts. Among those bringing offerings, one person was present with a more valuable gift, although it appeared cheaper than the offerings of the others. Some offered silver purified seven times, others gold tested by fire, others a precious and very large stone; this man offered iron, more precious than silver, gold, and stone—namely, the chains with which Herod’s cruelty had bound Peter in prison, and which the brilliance of the angelic visitation had cast apart in the chamber by the power of its word.

[Col. 1487C] If anyone thinks it incredible that the Jews either preserved Peter’s chains as an honor or gave them as an honor—although they never ceased disparaging his sanctity—let him know that nothing is impossible for the divine will. For as long as it wished, that will allowed such a pearl to be trampled by unclean swine, until it revealed it at the time when it would become an ornament of the Church.

He who was able and willing to manifest the trophy of his soldier through a Jew, just as through a member of that same unbelieving people he revealed the marks of his cross to Helena, wished the people hostile to the truth to be covered with the greater blush of their own shame, in proportion as they themselves confessed the witnesses of the Crucified One to possess the more excellent glory.

[Col. 1487D] Who would doubt that Eudoxia danced for joy no less when she recognized Peter’s chains than Helena did when she saw the Lord’s long-desired cross? The joy of both discoverers could have been equal, yet I dare not declare the merit of the two treasures equal.

The one Helena found is of greater merit insofar as it pertains to the person of the emperor, to the person of the Lord, to the person of the teacher, to the person of the bridegroom, and to the person of the Son of God. What Eudoxia found is of lesser merit insofar as it pertains to the person of a soldier, of a servant, of a disciple, of a friend, and of a human son. Nevertheless, both are holy, both are great, and neither can be compared with any earthly riches.

The greater sanctified the greater, because person justified person: the emperor, the soldier; the Lord, the servant; the teacher, the disciple; the bridegroom, the friend; the Son of God, the human son. Christ justified Peter.

[Col. 1488A] From Christ Peter received that by which he might consecrate his chain; from himself Christ had that by which he sanctified his cross. The cross, the punishment of thieves, became the crown of the saints; the cross, the world’s rejection, became the glory of heaven; the cross, the penalty of death, became the remedy of life.

For this reason, by the privilege of freedom, the cross surpasses Peter’s chain in merit. And although the good fisherman’s chain is holy and venerable, the glorious cross of the most merciful Savior nevertheless excels it.

The queen, having obtained the desired gift, returned thanks to him from whom all good things proceed. Having arranged in her mind the purposes for which she had come, she hurried back to the Roman citadel. She brought to Latium chains that loosen the bonds of sins—chains that would no longer bind the just and holy but would release the impious from every form of ungodliness.

[Col. 1488B] She entrusted the fortunate event to silence until a suitable time for bringing it into the open should arise. She did not wish the news of the matter suddenly to thunder into the ears of the common people, lest words which might heal for an hour without deeds should pass away when the hour had passed. By a higher counsel she considered how to commend the treasure that had been found to the Romans, so that, as long as devotion to the Christian faith endured, it might possess a perpetual memorial in the holy Church.

[Col. 1488C] Heavenly grace favored her good intention, and a fitting opportunity, well corresponding to her desire, presented itself. Seeing that the faithful and the unfaithful agreed in this pagan observance—that each year, in praise of Caesar’s victory, they solemnized the Kalends of Sextilis with a great display of toga and popular ceremony—she pondered that the tender infancy of the newborn Church could quickly be stained by the filth of superstitious error unless divine mercy should hasten to put an end to such great disasters of pestilence.

She considered using the authority of royal majesty against the practitioners of the rite, but it was not easy to overturn the judgment of the court and the diligence of the leading men. It was difficult to revoke the senate’s decree from its ancient customary purpose, especially since by that time it had grown old through the long succession of so many Christian emperors.

The supporters of the same observance seemed to themselves to be doing nothing contrary to the purpose of the Christian religion in this celebration, since they neither placed sacred offerings upon altars nor burned incense to the gods, but raised applause for the public prosperity and Caesar’s triumphs with dances. And if the senatorial orders should incline toward the will of their party, the lesser body of officials would strongly resist, turning the matter into the tumult of sedition, since the destruction of their yearly leisure and celebration would be contrary to their interests.

[Col. 1488D] Therefore, as I have said, it was difficult among them to overthrow the rite of antiquity, just as even today in the Christian world many rites of empty superstition are observed, whose memory can be erased only with difficulty or not at all.

Accordingly, the queen, beloved of God, recalled her excellent purpose to her mind: she should in no way provoke a riotous people to sedition in honor of royal majesty, lest those who were poorly advised should turn to worse conduct when they seemed to be treated too harshly. She decided to obtain through humble prayers what she believed could not safely be extorted through the terror of threats.

[Col. 1489A] She disclosed the secret of her prudent mind to the bishop of the Roman see, who already shared the same desire but, being inexperienced, feared stretching out his arms against the current to the danger of the Church. She made him the spokesman of her prayer before the people, so that the Kalends of Augustus might continue with the same observance as before but be designated by the name of a more excellent prince.

The sounder part of the people therefore gave assent to the apostolic words; those who feared that the observance would be abolished attempted to stir up a popular riot. But when they learned from the former group that the petition concerned not the abolition of the observance but a change of name, the agitation of the turbulent crowd ceased, and the inscription of the more excellent name was approved with common praise.

Then Eudoxia made public declaration of the treasure brought from Jerusalem and, entering with the pope, delivered to the people a speech full of devotion and compunction concerning Peter’s chains. [Col. 1489B] She taught that in them there was a saving medicine for the health of the inner and outer person, and that through him in whose most sacred body they had been consecrated one could merit absolution from all sins, since it is very easy for him to obtain from that one whatever he wishes, from whom he has received the power to loose and bind the bonds of souls.

She also inserted into her speech a reference to the chain that the apostle carried under Nero’s custody, which Alexander, the fifth bishop of Rome after blessed Peter, taught to possess abundant powers of healing, and which he revealed to Balbina, daughter of Quirinus, for the increase of her salvation.

At the conclusion of the speech, by God’s will she obtained this result of her petition: that, as I have said, the Kalends of August should continue with the same observance, but should be designated by the name of the prince of the apostles; and that the joys of the same celebration, which until then had been called Caesar’s victory, should thereafter be called Peter’s Chains.

[Col. 1489C] To confirm this decree of the decision for all time, the empress’s expenditure and the pope’s additional contribution completed and consecrated to the Lord a church in which the chains of the most merciful Peter were worthily deposited. There they bestow abundant benefits upon those in need, and there the madness of Caesar’s applause was struck with a perpetual sentence of anathema, so that the memory of the victory of apostolic liberation might reign more freely throughout the world.

The pontiff also devised, in correspondence with the impiety, this form of piety: just as the worshipers of Augustus on this day tasted an offering of bread and wine, so should worshipers of Christ taste the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and, led out from the prison-house of death, follow the angelic guide with Peter. May he introduce us, freed from the chains of sins, [Col. 1489D] into the gate of the heavenly kingdom, where he may refresh us with the satisfaction of his presence—he upon whom the angels desire always to gaze (1 Peter 1), and to whom they proclaim without ceasing, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6), praising the one true God in Trinity, who lives and reigns without end. Amen. But you—

## HOMILY XLV. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF HOLY MARY
Many daughters have gathered riches; the mother of the Lord has surpassed them all (Prov. XXXI). Many faithful souls have stored up for themselves precious ornaments of virtue, by which they might please God [Col. 1490D]: the mother of the Lord has surpassed them all. She surpassed everyone on earth; she surpassed everyone in heaven. On the day of her pilgrimage, she exceeded all the inhabitants of earth in the beauty of her merits; on the day of her restoration, she transcended all the inhabitants of heaven in the honor of her rewards.

Daughters of Jerusalem, come and see the mother of the Lord in the diadem of her royal glory, with which her Son crowned her, on the day of the gladness of her heart (Cant. III), on the day of her blessed assumption into heaven. Clap your hands and rejoice over her, all you who love her (Isa. LXVI), for she has been exalted exceedingly and glorified beyond measure. Let us sing in wonder at her glory; let us sing [Col. 1491A] to her a song of joy, saying with King Solomon: “Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved?” (Cant. VIII).

What, or what kind, was the desert from which she came up? Where, or when, did she ascend? Overflowing with what delights? Leaning upon whom as her beloved? With her help, we shall speak.

The Jewish people were a desert, abandoned by God and deprived of the manifold grace which it had been accustomed to possess, according to what the Lord had threatened through Isaiah, saying: “Behold, the Lord, the ruler, will take away from Jerusalem and Judah the strong and mighty man, and every strength of water, and the warrior, and the judge and prophet, and the rest that follows” (Isa. V). And again: “I shall remove its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be for trampling, and I shall leave it desolate” (Isa. V).

[Col. 1491B] From this desert of lamentable misery, our glorious Θεοτόκος—“God-bearer”—ascended, on the day when the Lord remembered removing the burden of the groanings with which she lamented the absence of her Son, to a certain happier desert, full of joy. She ascended, I say, to that desert which the Savior recalls in the evangelical parable, saying: “Does he not leave the ninety-nine in the desert and go after the one that was lost?” (Luke XV).

That heavenly dwelling of the saints is called a desert because it had been abandoned by humanity; or, certainly, on account of the likeness to a desert place, since peace and perpetual tranquility are there. No man there presses upon his neighbor because of the multitude of inhabitants; no one disturbs another with any assault or noise. Indeed, on account of this same likeness, the human mind which is disturbed by no clamor of cares or vices is called a [Col. 1491C] desert by the wise.

She ascended, I say, and was exalted—whether in the body or outside the body, we do not know; God knows (II Cor. XII). How high was she exalted? To the heavens? Certainly, even above all the heavens, and above all the heavens of heavens. Certainly, even above angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim.

“This has been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. CXVII): that a fragile woman, a little worm formed in the mud of this turbulent age, should have deserved to surpass so greatly creatures so pure, so glorious, and so excellent. Yet it was worthy and entirely fitting that all things should be placed beneath the feet of her who had given birth to the Creator of all. It was worthy [Col. 1491D] that she should be the Lady of the angels who had been worthy to be the mother of the Lord of angels. It was worthy that angelic purity should be subjected to her in heaven, to whom divine purity had wholly given itself on earth. It was worthy that he who had said, “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth” (Exod. XX), should honor his mother more greatly than his ministers. It was worthy that he should love her more intimately and reward her more abundantly, since she had loved him more uniquely and more closely than every rational creature.

And who could estimate or conceive how great was the love of such a mother for such a Son? If a bad mother loves a bad son by the instinct of nature alone; if a good mother loves a good son by the instinct both of nature and of virtue [Col. 1492A], how greatly is the best mother thought to have loved the best Son? In the Son, nature, the fullness of virtues, and, beyond these, divinity supplied the cause for love; in the mother, the fullness of the Holy Spirit brought about the power to love. What limit, then, could there have been to a love in which no cause for loving could be lacking?

Since, therefore, she loved more than all others, she was rightly loved and honored by the Lord more than all others. For behold, she has been exalted above the choirs of angels, even to the right hand of her Son; she has been made the powerful mistress of the whole household of the Lord, and has been called Queen of heaven.

How powerfully she drew to herself that prophetic verse which says: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV)! And what is the gold laid over her garment [Col. 1492B] except that immeasurable ardor of charity, adorning from above the whole sanctity of her life as with a radiant color? And what is the variety of her garment with which she is surrounded? Without doubt, it is the thousand times ten thousand hosts of the heavenly armies serving her, with all of whom she is clothed and wonderfully adorned as with a garment of light—thousand thousand thousands of them.

Thus that divine exclamation by which that glorious cherub once made himself unworthy may most fittingly be turned toward her, so that it may be said: “Every precious stone was your covering, O Mary—sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. XXVIII).

Our queen is rightly said to be covered with these nine most precious gems, since, when compared individually with the nine orders of angels, she [Col. 1492C] appears so much more glorious as she surpasses them in her beauty.

Burst with envy, ancient serpent, and let your indignation tear you in two; for behold, the woman whose heel you once lay in wait for has crushed your head (Gen. III), and by the power of humility has drawn to herself the privilege of your honor, which you lost through pride. She walked perfectly in her ways, and behold, she has been placed upon the holy mountain of God, amid the burning stones, from which the Lord cast you out because iniquity was found in you, and you were reduced to nothing (Ezek. XXVIII).

But why have we assigned only the orders of the blessed spirits to the variety of her garment? Is not everything most precious that has been carried from earth to heaven surrounding her, in service of every kind of praise and honor? The venerable gray hair of patriarchs and prophets [Col. 1492D] bows before her; beneath her the apostolic columns that support the hall of God bend low. The golden splendor of martyrs and the silver brightness of confessors respectfully yield to the splendor of her beauty.

Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surround her; virginal gems rejoice in their own distinctive, sign-bearing celebration and, with her leading the song, sing their unique hymn after the footsteps of the Lamb.

Moreover, for another reason we may call those aforementioned stones the covering of our Θεοτόκος, namely, because the glorious merits represented by their properties are her precious ornaments. Sardius is blood-red and bears the figure of martyrdom; this, without doubt, was added to the ornaments of this queen in [Col. 1493A] the passion of her Son. Hence it was said to her: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke II).

Topaz is pleasing to kings and has two colors, heavenly blue and golden, signifying contemplation of divinity. Gold is adapted to divinity, and the heavenly hue to contemplation. And who could contemplate God more intimately than she who, more familiarly than every rational creature, received God into the midst of her heart and, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, clothed him in her own flesh?

Scripture also bears witness to her contemplation when it says: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke II).

Jasper is a green stone, signifying the unfading steadfastness of faith. The evangelical message also commends this quality in her, saying: “And blessed is she who believed, for the things spoken to her by the Lord [Col. 1493B] shall be fulfilled” (Luke I). Great indeed was the power of her faith: she believed so quickly the angel announcing things so incredible and unheard-of; and through this she merited at once to be made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and to conceive the Son of God.

She preserved the unfading vigor of her faith to the end; even at the death of the Son of God she did not waver in faith so as to cease believing him immortal God whom she saw dying as a human being.

Chrysolite appears sprinkled, as it were, with burning sparks. Those who excel through the Spirit in the word of wisdom resemble it. When they kindle the hearts of their neighbors with divine persuasions, what else do they pour forth but certain sparks of the fire with which they burn within?

It must likewise be believed without doubt of the blessed Virgin that, although she was full of the fire of the Holy [Col. 1493C] Spirit from the time of Christ’s conception, she never, like frivolous women, uttered idle words. Rather, every word of hers, seasoned with the salt of wisdom and suited to kindle the hearts of her neighbors, was like a spark of that fire which she carried enclosed within.

Beautifully this fire flashed forth at the beginning of her visitation, when from the fullness of the Holy Spirit she poured forth that divine song, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior,” and so forth (Luke I). What else but certain sparks did she emit when she instructed the Evangelists both about her own visitation and about the many things that took place around our Savior, her Son?

Onyx has a cloudy and almost somewhat gloomy color, resembling a human fingernail, signifying [Col. 1493D] the modesty of humility. The humility of the blessed Virgin is indeed a singular beauty. Although she had been chosen as the mother of the Lord, she called herself a handmaid; nor did she profess that anything other than humility in her had pleased God, saying: “Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I).

Beryl has an appearance like that of water struck by the brilliance of the sun. In this way the face of the virgin mind was irradiated most abundantly by the Sun of justice. At one and the same time, all its brightness was poured into her on earth, and all of it shone forth in the heights.

Sapphire has the appearance of a serene heaven and signifies the tranquility of a pure mind, which is darkened by no clouds of vices or anxieties. Hence the throne of God is said by the prophet to have the appearance of sapphire (Ezek. I), because the mind upon which God sits, as upon a throne, must be endowed with heavenly purity and tranquility.

That the blessed mind of the Virgin possessed the highest tranquility and, as it were, heavenly purity is most certain from this: when the Holy Spirit came upon her with ineffable abundance, he does not know how to rest except upon the humble and quiet person (Isa. LXVI). The power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that no cloud of human vice could disturb her serenity; and thus she became the unique throne of God above all his companions.

If, in order that they may be sons of God, it is necessary for people to be peacemakers (Matt. V), then the mind of the holy Virgin had to be wholly peaceful in every respect, so that she might merit to be not only the daughter but also the mother of God.

Carbuncle [Col. 1494B] shines by night but appears dark during the day. By a similar comparison, the holiness of the blessed mother is likened to the moon or the dawn. Before the coming of her Son—that is, while the ancient night was still completing its course—she shone uniquely in the world; and, like the rays preceding the coming sun, she was illuminated above all who were living.

This was evidently foreseen by the one who said: “A star shall rise out of Jacob” (Num. XXIV). And by the one who said: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Cant. VI).

But when the true Sun emerged from her womb and the day dawned which the Lord had made (Ps. CXVII), from that time onward, if the brightness of the mother is compared with the brightness of the Son, although it is exceedingly great, yet in comparison with his it appears in a certain manner dark, as if one were to compare a star with the sun.

Emerald [Col. 1494C] has such brilliant greenness that it even sends rays of green toward whatever is placed near it, and by its greenness affects not only dry things but also green ones. By a beautiful likeness, the noble freshness of virginity is compared with it; virginity has even derived its name from this greenness.

For just as it is customary for the corrupt to entice others willingly into corruption, so it is characteristic of good virgins, being green through incorruption, to encourage others toward the virtue of virginity, and to recall by word and example those who have been withered through corruption to the freshness of continence. Thus they affect both what is green and what is dry with their own greenness.

Among these was the one who said: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Cor. VII). And again: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord [Col. 1494D], but I give counsel” (I Cor. VII).

How many did that blessed virgin whom Jesus loved raise to the summit of virginity by the word which he spoke: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Apoc. XIV). And Jesus, the virgin and leader of virgins, said: “There are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let whoever can accept it accept it” (Matt. XIX).

The emerald therefore rightly shines among the ornaments of our queen, because the marvelous freshness of virginity, admired by all nations, remains uniquely green in her even after childbirth, and spreads the noble rays of its greenness throughout the ages.

For behold, her gracious and beloved virginity is proclaimed throughout the whole world, and many thousands of both sexes are illuminated by [Col. 1495A] the examples of her chastity, as they vow continence both to her and to her virginal offspring.

Rightly, therefore, the prophetic word is turned toward her on account of all these things: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. XXVIII). For whatever is precious, whatever is lovable, is signified by the preciousness of those stones; all of it has been divinely heaped upon her.

Certainly, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed with coverings such as these (Matt. VI).

“The fragrance of your garments, O Mary, is like the fragrance of incense” (Cant. IV). Your splendid virtues are incense of the finest fragrance in the sight of the Most High and most effective for entreating his favor. “Like Lebanon, uncut, you have filled your dwelling with fragrance.” Your incorrupt integrity has filled the whole house of the Lord with the fragrances of the best reputation and urges the minds of all to bless [Col. 1495B] and pray to God.

“Like cinnamon and balsam giving forth fragrance, you have yielded a sweet odor; like chosen myrrh, you have yielded an odor of sweetness” (Ecclus. XXIV). You breathe for us the fragrance of cinnamon in humility, of balsam in charity, and of myrrh in chastity; therefore we run after you, O Mary, in the sweetness of your perfumes (Cant. I).

Help those who run; draw along the weary; lift up the fallen, so that we too may enter with you.

“Like a terebinth, you have spread your branches over the breadth of the earth” (Ecclus. XXIV). Behold, we flee to you, so that you may be for us a shelter by day from the heat, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain.

Pay attention and see, dearest ones, what has been said about the glory of this queen, and you will clearly understand what her delights are [Col. 1495C], which the divine word notes in her when it says: “Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved?”

And who is this beloved except her most loving Son? It was fitting for her to lean upon a strong and unbending staff in her venerable old age, to complete that great and arduous journey from this valley of misery to the highest heavens, which no one had entered except her only Son.

Without doubt, he himself, her Son, the King of kings and Lord of lords, met her joyfully with the multitude of the heavenly host, placed himself beneath her as a faithful staff, and carried her—the mother who had carried him—full of days and full of every spiritual abundance beyond the fullness of the saints, all the way to the sight of the throne on high. He placed her upon the throne of ineffable [Col. 1495D] glory.

And thus she was established in Zion; likewise she rested in the sanctified city; and her power was in Jerusalem. “She took root among the honored people, and her inheritance was in the portion of her God, and her dwelling was among the fullness of the saints” (Ecclus. XXIV).

O joys of that day, worthy to be proclaimed throughout the whole world, by which all the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem were gladdened at the arrival of their queen, rejoicing with the Son in such a mother and with the mother in such a Son!

And what wonder is this? If it is a joy to the household of any insignificant human being on the day when he brings his bride to the wedding, should there not have been joy among the citizens of heaven on the day when it pleased them to lead to the wedding of their King a bride chosen from among brides, to receive as inheritance a beloved daughter among daughters, and to honor suitably as the blessed mother among [Col. 1496A] women?

At her entrance, all the heavenly trumpets sounded, and all the sons of God rejoiced. They proclaimed her most blessed, praising her victorious hand, which had most powerfully humbled the neck of the ancient deceiver.

Not so Eve, not so; but like dust which the serpent blew away from the face of paradise.

Therefore, dearest ones, if the glorious Lady is venerated and praised, if the blessed company of angels rejoices in her, it belongs to us much more to rejoice in her and to exalt her name with every honor and every praise.

For she came forth from us; she is the precious jewel of our race; our honor has been perfected through her. At the beginning, we were made vile in the sight of the angels through man and woman; but behold [Col. 1496B], both sexes have been raised above them—the male in Christ, the female in Mary.

Now they honor man and woman as companions and fellow citizens, seeing above themselves the prince of each sex. They behold above them two great lights taken from among human beings: the greater light and the lesser light, Jesus and Mary, whom it would be utterly unworthy to compare with the sun and moon.

Let us therefore rejoice and be glad in her, because she is the faithful advocate of us all in heaven. Her Son is the mediator between God and human beings; she herself is the mediatrix between her Son and human beings.

As befits the mother of mercy, she is most merciful, and she knows how to sympathize with human weaknesses, because our nature is known to her. For this reason she does not cease to intercede for us with her Son, provided that she sees us lamenting and detesting [Col. 1496C] our own sins.

Indeed, by the abundance of her mercy she anticipates our repentance and restrains the sword of her Son extended to strike, praying and asking that he patiently await our conversion.

For if the world were not supported by such great intercession, it would surely already have been overthrown by the just judgment of God, as Sodom and Gomorrah once perished by divine fire, and as the Jewish people were consumed by heavenly plagues in the desert.

For behold, the same iniquities that had been the cause of their destruction have multiplied throughout the whole world, and in far greater measure.

What, then, is this Lady who brings reconciliation, except something like a most gentle cloud overshadowing us from the face of the sun, lest we be burned by its excessive heat?

Therefore, dearest ones, let us rejoice with all our heart in this advocate of ours, so powerful, [Col. 1496D] so loving, and so faithful, who denies help to no one who asks worthily and intercedes with her Son for no one in vain.

Let us rejoice, I say, in her; let us venerate her with worthy acts of service and worthy praises, together with those sacred legions of angels; and let us beseech her favor with all the nobles of heaven.

What acts of service, then, are there by which we could worthily honor so great a Lady? Certainly, this service is most pleasing to her: that, imitating her most sacred life, we should love what she loved and avoid what she avoided.

The beauty of chastity is pleasing to her, through which she too was made gracious in the sight of the Most High. Let us therefore, out of reverence for her and for her Son, receive this virtue as a guest in our hearts [Col. 1497A], and embrace her beauty; then we shall find great favor in her sight.

For if we roll about in the filth of lust like swine, we shall be detestable before her and shall be able to do nothing worthy in her sight.

The modesty of humility is beloved by her, because of which she was exalted by the Lord to the highest summits of honor. Encouraged by her example, let us love this virtue and practice it in our deeds, and we shall render her a service pleasing to her.

For if she sees us lifted up by the arrogance of pride, we shall be unable to please her in any action, since her enemy reigns among us.

Precious in her sight is the ardor of divine charity, by which she is known to have loved God above salvation and every beauty, and for which she was loved by the Lord above every creature.

If, therefore, we strive to be like [Col. 1497B] her in this also, loving with our whole heart God and our Lord and Savior, her Son, then in that very act we shall offer in her sight a rich and most sweet-smelling holocaust; nor shall we ever be able to offer her a service more acceptable.

But if we are empty of divine charity and full of hatred and envy toward our brothers, we shall take up her praises upon our lips in vain and shall strive in vain to render her service in anything.

Judge for yourselves, brothers: if a naked servant, or one dressed in garments shamefully torn and having dirty hands, should presume to serve before some chaste and severe matron, would he not be detestable to her? Surely she would turn her eyes away in indignation and would think herself dishonored rather than honored by his service.

How then [Col. 1497C] do we dare to appear full of iniquities before that awesome Lady of the whole world, whom the entire heavenly court honors with complete reverence; to attend her festivals and proclaim her praises, when it is certain that she loves justice and hates iniquity (Ecclus. XV)?

“Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” However precious the food may be, it cannot please when offered in a filthy vessel.

Let us fear lest she also say to us: “You offered well, but you divided badly.” We offer well when we proclaim her holy praises, but we divide badly when, through an evil life, we alienate ourselves from her.

Nevertheless, however dreadful our weaknesses may be, we must not despair of her mercy if we are willing to accuse ourselves before her and, with repentant hearts, implore [Col. 1497D] her intervention.

Without doubt, we shall see her help over us, because her compassions are many, and her mercies are abundant toward all who call upon her.

Blessed be her name throughout everlasting ages. Blessed be God in the multitude of his mercy, who has given us in the heavenly court so powerful, so merciful, and so intimate with his majesty an advocate.

To our God be joyful and beautiful praise, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVI. ON THE SAME FEAST
For today glorious ever-virgin Mary ascends to heaven. I ask you, rejoice, because—to speak thus—she, ineffably exalted, reigns with Christ forever. Today the Queen of the world is snatched from the earth and from the present evil age. I say again, rejoice, because, secure in her unfading glory, she has now reached the palace of heaven. Exult, I say, and rejoice, and let the whole world be glad, because today, through the intervention of her merits, salvation has been increased for us all. For you also, who love her, greater honor, virtue, and grace are granted together with the other holy virgins.

Therefore, beloved, rejoice and praise God; for if we are commanded by the prophetic voice to praise God in his saints, much more ought we at this celebration of his blessed virgin mother to exalt him more diligently with hymns and spiritual songs, to jubilate with praises worthy of God, and to honor him with mystical gifts. There is no doubt that everything offered and solemnly attributed with due honor to his mother contributes wholly to the glory of his praise.

For this reason I am sufficiently afraid, and very greatly apprehensive, while I desire to comply with your spiritual benefit, lest I be found both presumptuous and an unworthy praiser—especially since I possess neither the holiness nor the eloquence by which I might worthily praise the blessed and glorious virgin. For, to speak truthfully, whatever can be said in human words falls short of the praise of heaven, since she has been proclaimed and praised with divine and angelic praises of surpassing excellence. She was foretold by the prophets, prefigured by the patriarchs in figures and enigmas, presented and shown by the evangelists, and reverently and most dutifully greeted by the angel. Moreover, her nature and greatness were divinely declared by that same angel when he said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke I).

It was fitting that the virgin should be endowed with such gifts, so that she might be “full of grace”—she who gave glory to heaven, infused God and peace into the earth, faith to the nations, an end to vices, an order for life, and discipline for conduct. And rightly the angel is sent to the virgin, because virginity is always akin to the angels. Indeed, to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one. Hence to acquire angelic glory in the flesh is a greater merit than to possess it. To be an angel is a matter of happiness; to be a virgin, of virtue. A virgin strives with grace and strength to attain what the angel possesses by nature. Yet both being a virgin and being an angel are the work of a divine gift, not of human accomplishment.

“Hail,” he says, “full of grace.” And rightly “full,” because grace is granted to others in portions, whereas in Mary the fullness of grace poured itself out wholly and all at once. This is what David sings: “He came down like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm LXXI). Now a fleece, although it comes from the body, does not experience the body’s passion; so holy virginity, although it exists in the flesh, knows nothing of the vices of the flesh. Truly, heavenly rain descended gently upon the virginal fleece, and the whole wave of divinity entered into the flesh when the Word became flesh; then, pressed out through the gibbet of the cross, it poured the rain of salvation upon all the earth and bestowed drops of grace upon human minds.

“The Lord is with you,” he says. A wondrous thing! He who sent the angel to the virgin was already with the virgin, and God preceded his messenger, yet did not depart from God. He could not be confined by places, who is present in all places and is wholly everywhere, without whom nothing is wholly anything. Therefore the Father’s Word, never departing from the Father, deigned to become man for us through his secret mystery, known to himself. Since he assumed everything that belongs to man, he is wholly man; and since he retained everything that belongs to God, he could not be anything other than God, who was born from Mary. For God knows all things and can do all things.

Because this is so, he knew and was able to mingle and unite himself in the virgin’s womb without corruption of himself, so that Christ might be one—God and man, one person and one substance. For this reason the mother of God, chosen and preselected, is rightly greeted and proclaimed by the angel as full of grace. Truly full, through whom every creature was flooded with the abundant rain of the Holy Spirit. And therefore the angel first venerates and greets her with profound devotion. He himself marvels at the nature and greatness of the one whom he greets. For, I confess, that greeting was neither ordinary nor customary, but worthy of all wonder. It was indeed an offering of veneration, a presentation of a gift, and a service of homage. For although grace is believed to have existed in the holy Fathers and prophets, it was not yet full to this extent. In Mary, however, came the fullness of all the grace that is in Christ, though in another manner.

“And therefore,” he says, “blessed are you among women”—that is, more blessed than all women. Thus Mary’s blessing removed everything of the curse that had been poured out through Eve. Moreover, the birth of Christ restored the grace that the whole world had not previously possessed. Therefore what nature did not possess, experience did not know, reason did not recognize, and the human mind could not grasp—heaven fears, earth is astonished, and every creature, even the heavenly, marvels at. This is the whole of what is divinely announced to Mary through Gabriel and fulfilled through Christ.

For this reason I confess that I am unworthy to speak of such a great subject. Indeed, I think no one would dare to do so unless he wholly failed to understand how great are the things being disclosed. Nevertheless, even though no one is found adequate for this, no sinner should therefore cease from praise with all his desires, although he cannot fulfill what he perceives. Thus, when the divine discourse spoke of the sinner in the Psalms, it said: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me”; and immediately added, “and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm XLIX). It is as though it plainly said: There is a way of praise leading to eternal praise that will remain without end, but no one reaches it unless I first show it.

Therefore, dearest ones, since the way of our salvation lies in the praises of the Savior, I exhort and admonish you: at this sacred solemnity of Mary, the mother of God, do not cease from praise. If you are a virgin, rejoice that you too have been worthy to be what you praise; only take care that you may be one who can worthily be praised. If you are continent and chaste, venerate and praise her, because you cannot be chaste for any other reason than through the grace of Christ, which was most fully present in Mary, whom you praise. If you are married or certainly a sinner, nevertheless confess and praise her, because from her mercy and grace flowed to all so that they might praise.

And although praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, do not cease praising, because thereby forgiveness is promised to you and to all, so that you may praise. Otherwise, unless we strive to praise God in his saints according to the measure of our understanding, how shall we praise him, as we sing, according to the multitude of his greatness? We must by no means neglect what we shall one day fulfill: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII). What we cannot accomplish with our voice, nor with eloquence, let us perform with our desires and from the depths of our hearts, because he is great, good, and immeasurable. Let us confess with mouth and spirit, for righteousness and salvation, how great and what kind of one he is—as he himself knows.

For this reason I ask that we all celebrate with the utmost devotion the feast of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, because this is a day worthy of veneration by every age, [Col. 1500B] on which she was worthy to be exalted above the choirs of angels and to reach beyond what belongs to the nature of our humanity. Here it is not the substance that is removed, but the greatness of glory that is revealed. She is raised to the right hand of the Father, where Christ entered for us as a priest made eternal, into the palace of heaven.

This, I say, is the day on which the undefiled mother and virgin advanced as far as the height of the throne and, exalted upon the royal seat, now sits gloriously after Christ. Thus the holy Church of God everywhere confidently sings that she surpassed the merits of angels and archangels—something it is lawful to believe of no other saint. For although likeness is promised to the saints, the reality is denied them. This privilege belongs not to the nature but to the grace of the blessed virgin Mary, from whom God himself was born, [Col. 1500C] both God and man.

Therefore she is superior in merits, not in nature, to both virgin and man. Hence, although the other virgins imitate her up to the conception and birth, and up to Gabriel’s service of the new greeting, from that point onward everything accomplished in her is divine, as the angel testifies, because she is overshadowed by the Holy Spirit and by the power of the Most High.

Before this event, the womb of the virgin Mary, although pure, undefiled, free from the contagion of sin, and holy, was nevertheless still clothed, so to speak, in the lowliness of humanity, like the whitest wool bleached to its own color. But when the Holy Spirit came upon it—for when that same wool is stained with the blood of the purple shellfish or murex, it is changed into purple—it too, without intercourse, was changed into a mother, so that it was no longer what it had been, but became true purple, most suitably consecrated by God for the clothing and glory of the supreme King; thereafter no one might use it for feminine purposes except God.

Indeed, to speak thus, although the blessed and glorious virgin Mary had long before been shown to be incomparable among all the virgins beneath heaven, so that she could fittingly receive within herself the mingling of divinity while both natures remained safe, yet when she was filled with grace, when she was suffused with the Holy Spirit, and when she was overshadowed by the power of the Most High, she became richer in merits, higher in sublime dignity, more beautiful in holiness, and more glorious through the prerogatives of her merits, so that she herself was now to be devoted to no uses other than divine ones.

Therefore, O holiest virgins, although you ought to imitate so great and such a virgin, it is especially fitting that you venerate her, and that she be worthily exalted with joyful praises, insofar as is lawful, in a dignity somehow beyond that of angels. As we have said, she is not rashly proclaimed today with the utmost devotion as exalted above the choirs of angels through the grace of Christ, because our Lord and Savior preceded her into heaven, truly born from her, to prepare for her, as he himself promised his disciples, a place in the heavenly dwellings.

For this reason the prophet David, long ago, rejoicing, sings to Christ: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course is as far as its summit” (Psalm XVIII). Therefore he ascended to reclaim the same glory, although he had not lost the glory he possessed previously, before the world existed. He ascended and prepared for this most holy virgin a place of immortality, so that she might reign with him forever.

And this is the feast of the present day, on which she, glorious and blessed, reached the heavenly bridal chamber. Just as the incomparable virgin is incomparable to the other virgins, so this feast is incomparable to all the feasts of the saints and even wondrous to the angelic powers. Therefore the Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the heavenly citizens and marveling at her ascension, says in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke from perfumes?” (Song of Songs III).

And rightly “like a column of smoke,” because she is slender and delicate, because she has been made thin by divine disciplines; for within she was burned as a holocaust in the fire of pious love and the desire of charity. “Like a column of smoke from perfumes”—surely because she was filled with many fragrances of virtues, and the sweetest odor flowing from her was fragrant even to angelic spirits.

She was ascending from the wilderness of the present age—the branch from the root of Jesse, long ago brought forth. But the souls of the elect marveled with joy at who she might be, since by the virtues of her merits she surpassed even the dignity of angels. Concerning her the same Holy Spirit says again in the same Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?” (Song of Songs VI).

The Holy Spirit marvels, making all who marvel at this virgin’s ascent marvel as well, because she shines in her ascent like the dawn of a new day, relying upon and surrounded by many hosts of saints. Hence it is said: “Terrible as an army set in battle array.” She was indeed made terrible by her virtues, like an army perfectly arranged, supported on every side by the protection of the holy angels.

“Beautiful,” he says, “as the moon”—indeed, more beautiful than the moon, because she now shines without any waning of herself, illumined by heavenly splendors. “Chosen as the sun” in the splendor of her virtues, because the sun of justice himself chose her to be born from her.

At her funeral, then, insofar as it is lawful to believe, the angels ministered, and all the courts of heaven rejoiced together. Nor is this surprising, because the honor of the mother belongs to him who was born from her, whom every order of heaven venerates and adores, exalted above them with the Father on the throne of the Lord’s majesty.

We read that angels have very often come to the funerals and burials of various saints and rendered service at their obsequies, and that they have carried the souls of the elect to heaven with hymns and praises. There, too, choirs of both sexes are frequently said to have been heard and to have sung praises; meanwhile—and this is even more remarkable—they sometimes shone with a much greater light, and those still living in the flesh perceived there for a long time the fragrance of a wondrous odor.

If, then, to revive hope, beloved women, and strengthen the faith of those standing by, our Savior Christ sometimes deigned, in order to establish more fully the merits of his servants, to display such great things through his heavenly ministers concerning the dead, how much more should we believe that today the army of heaven, with its hosts, came festively to meet the mother of God, surrounded her with immense light, and led her with praises and spiritual songs to the throne prepared for her long ago, even before the foundation of the world?

There is no doubt that all that heavenly Jerusalem then exulted with ineffable joy, was gladdened with immeasurable love, and jubilated with every expression of rejoicing, because this feast, which returns to us annually today, became for them a perpetual feast—and rightly so. For it is believed that the Savior of all himself, insofar as it may be understood, came wholly festal to meet her and, with joy, seated her with himself upon the throne.

Otherwise, how is it believed that he fulfilled what he himself commanded in the Law? “Honor,” he says, “your father and your mother” (Exodus XX). That he honored the Father, he himself bears witness when he says to the Jews: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges. But I honor my Father, and you dishonor me” (John VIII). Concerning his mother, the evangelist says that, when they returned, he went to Nazareth and “was subject to them” (Luke II).

But one is the nature by which God the Father is honored according to himself, and another is the nature by which he is subject to his parents. Yet in both respects the one and same Christ is rightly believed, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I): one Emmanuel, which means “God with us.”

The Catholic faith preserves this union of divinity and humanity without confusion and without division. By understanding this, let the natural and substantial concord of unity be recognized, so that neither conversion of one of the two substances into the other nor division is admitted. To believe in this way is to honor the mother of the Lord, who bore for us both God and man—neither man without God nor God without man, but one true Jesus Christ, God and man.

Otherwise she could not be called the mother of God—as many heretics have attempted to deny—unless she had borne the true God incarnate. For this reason we rightly confess two births in Christ: one from the Father, without beginning, without time, eternal and coeternal with God the Father; the other from his mother in time, when, assuming pity and mercy, he descended to us by his own will, born as the God-man. Thus, according to the truth, he who is always acknowledged as God was carried in his mother’s womb.

For this reason we also truthfully confess her as *theotocon*—“God-bearer,” that is, mother of God—and also as *christotocon*—“Christ-bearer.” This does not mean that the Word carried flesh along with himself, nor that he was joined to the previously mentioned flesh at some earlier time; rather, when the Word became flesh from the virgin’s flesh, the substance of divinity and humanity was united in the womb in such a way that Christ, God and man, is one person.

For from two natures, without confusion of either, there is found only one Jesus the Lord: remaining God in the form of God, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II), while remaining one and the same in the form of the servant that he assumed. He is wholly God in the flesh of the virgin, from whom he was born, and wholly man.

Hence the Apostle says: “In him dwells bodily the whole fullness of divinity” (Colossians II). Therefore, O daughters, be wise as serpents and innocent as doves, so that through the prudence of perfect understanding you may preserve whole and inviolate the ring of your faith and the pearl for which you abandoned everything, [Col. 1503B] lest—God forbid—you lose both the dowry and the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

Take the greatest care, then, that the simplicity of the dove, which was in Mary, may be preserved unharmed and inviolate. Concerning her Solomon says in the Song of Songs, as though in her praise: “Come,” he says, “my dove, my undefiled one, for winter has passed and gone away” (Song of Songs II). Then he says: “Come from Lebanon; come, you will be crowned” (Song of Songs IV).

And rightly she is commanded to come from Lebanon, because *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whiteness” or “whitening.” Blessed Mary was white with the many virtues of her merits and whiter than snow through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, representing the simplicity of the dove in all things. For everything that took place in her was entirely purity and simplicity, entirely grace and truth, entirely mercy and justice, which looked down from heaven. Therefore she was undefiled, because she was corrupted in nothing.

She enclosed a man in her womb, as the holy Jeremiah testifies, and received him from no other source. “The Lord,” he says, “will create a new thing upon the earth, and a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah XXXI). Truly a new thing, and a novelty surpassing every novelty of virtues, when God—whom the world cannot bear, nor anyone see and live—entered the dwelling of the womb in such a way that he did not know the body’s barriers, and was carried in such a way that he was wholly God within it. And he came forth from it, as Ezekiel declares, through a gate entirely closed.

Hence it is sung of her in the same Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your emissions are a paradise” (Song of Songs IV). Truly a garden of delights, in which every kind of flower and every fragrance of virtues was planted, [Col. 1503D] enclosed in such a way that it could not be violated or corrupted by any deceitful ambush of evil.

A sealed fountain, therefore, sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity, from which the fountain of life flows, in whose light we all see light; for, according to John, he is the one who enlightens every person coming into this world. The issuing forth from this womb is indeed the paradise of all the heavenly citizens.

Regarding this field of the womb, the patriarch Isaac, sensing its fragrance from afar, said: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a field that the Lord has blessed” (Genesis XXVII).

Some who understand too little may think that the earlier saints understood less of the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, although they too were saved by the same grace. Hence it is clear that time did not prejudice the sacrament of the united man and God, so that he was already in that one through the unity of person from the beginning of the world who had not yet been born from the virgin Mary. This is demonstrated by many indications in Scripture.

Thus the Lord says to the Jews: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII). By these words he showed that he who was speaking had always existed in the mystery of unity; and to commend this he said, “Before Abraham, I am.” “Before Abraham came to be” indicates the brevity of humanity, whereas “I am” reveals the eternity of nature. In that eternity he indicates that he who was speaking already existed through the sacrament of his incarnation.

The Apostle Jude, wishing to clarify this more openly, says: “Jesus, having saved the people from Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5). And elsewhere Paul says: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him” (1 Corinthians X). This does not mean that Jesus or Christ had already been born from the virgin Mary, but that in that one Son of God the unity of person, which was hidden in the mystery, was already being proclaimed.

Elsewhere also he says clearly: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I), because whatever God did from the beginning, he did entirely through the unity of the sacrament. Therefore Jesus was already in the Son who led the people out, and Christ was in the one who was tempted, since it is beyond doubt that through the unity of the sacrament he had always been in God.

Otherwise, if you do not believe this, either Christ will not be God at all, or, contrary to the prophet, God will appear to be recent. But lest we be shaken by such accusations, we must search the Scriptures, in which the unity of person in Christ is proclaimed—a unity that time does not invalidate, lest he always be called one.

Hence blessed Peter, speaking of the Fathers, says: “Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we shall be saved, just as they also were” (Acts V). The Lord alone led them, and no foreign god was with him. Therefore God is not recent with us either, because the one and same person who was their leader is our redeemer through the passion of his flesh.

He is one in his flesh, one in the sacrament, and one in the Spirit. Reason does not permit us to understand one Son of man and another Son of God, since he is restricted by neither time nor passion. Rather, God entirely passed into Christ and Christ into God, so that whatever belongs to the Son of God may rightly be called Christ, and whatever Christ suffered in the flesh may rightly be believed to have been suffered by God.

Otherwise, if you consider reason and human senses, divinity and human condition could never have been joined together to such an extent. They were joined in Christ, and one Emmanuel came from both.

I ask you, O virgins, and I ask you, widows: imitate Paula, the widowed mother, an example of continence and chastity; imitate Eustochium, whom you have here with you, a virgin and a model of perfect integrity. If there is less in them than in the mother of the Lord—indeed, because there is—then you possess a secondary offspring and a perpetual virgin. For just as no one is good in comparison with the Lord, so no one is found perfect in comparison with the mother of the Lord, although she may be proved outstanding in virtues.

I preferred to incur the blush of modesty rather than fail to carry out your command, since at times our God appears to obey your prayers, especially since you have with you women whom you may imitate in virtue. With them you can learn affection from me rather than the instruction you requested for the praise of this day.

## HOMILY XLVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(From the works of Saint Augustine.)*

“At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house, etc.” (Luke X).

“The words of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.” For the remainder, see volume V of the works of Saint Augustine, *Patrologia* XXXVIII, column 613.

## HOMILY XLVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(From blessed Anselm, bishop.)*

[Col. 1505B] “At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house, etc.” (Luke X).

In Sacred Scripture, one and the same thing is very often found to signify different things, such as a lion, a kid, fire, and water, or even the sun and many other things. For there is the Lion from the tribe of Judah, and there is the lion that goes about seeking someone to devour. There is the scapegoat that bore our sins, and there is the goat at the left hand that is condemned. There is the fire that the Lord sent upon the earth and wishes to burn, and there is the fire that falls upon the ungodly so that they do not see the sun. There is the water whose streams flow from the belly of the believer, and there is the water whose storm does not engulf us. There is the sun of justice, which illumines us, and there is the sun that does not scorch us by day.

Although, therefore, a castle may elsewhere signify something evil—such as that of which it is said, “Go into the castle,” where it is also added, “which is opposite you” (Matt. XXI)—and this plainly indicates what it signifies, nevertheless here we understand the castle into which Jesus entered, subject to the rule of Scripture, by analogy as the unique and undefiled Virgin, the mother of that same Jesus. [Col. 1505C]

A castle is so called because it is any tower together with a wall surrounding it. These two defend one another, so that enemies are kept away from the fortress by the wall, and from the wall by the fortress. The Virgin Mary is not improperly likened to such a castle: her virginity of mind and body enclosed her on every side like a wall, so that lust never had access to her, nor could any enticement corrupt her senses. And because, when lust cannot do so, pride usually attacks virginity, in that same Virgin there is a tower—humility—which repels every form of pride from the wall of virginity. And because, when pride cannot do so, lust usually attacks humility, the wall of virginity repels every form of lust from the tower of humility.

Thus these two—the wall, namely, of virginity and the tower of humility—fortify one another, so that in the humble Virgin there was never either the pride of virginity or polluted humility; rather, humble virginity and virginal humility always remained in her. Although what has been said is so true that the Christian faith can believe nothing truer, let us nevertheless set forth from the Gospel some testimonies to her virginity and humility.

For when the angel promised her a son, she replied, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” [Col. 1506A] (Luke I). If it were said to any betrothed virgin who had resolved in her mind to marry, “You will have a son,” she would not be astonished or ask how it would happen, since she would know that she was betrothed and soon to marry, and would expect, according to the ordinary course of nature, to be made fertile by a man. But she was rightly astonished and asked how what had been promised would come to pass, because, although betrothed, she knew with complete certainty that she would never marry or know a man. This concerns her virginity.

Regarding her humility, it must be said that when she was greeted by the angel, chosen to be the Mother of God, and taught how this would happen while her virginity—which she held in such great fear—was preserved, and was proclaimed blessed above all women, she replied, “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord.” And elsewhere: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” O exalted Virgin, Mother of God; O humble Mother, handmaid of God! What could be more exalted? What could she think more humbly of herself? [Col. 1506B]

Some think that this castle was Magdalum, from which Mary Magdalene takes her surname. If this is true, it serves the interpretation already given. For *Magdalus* means “tower” and is compared with humility. But the place is not named here; only that it was “a certain” place is stated, and we must not pass over this without examination.

“A certain” castle—that is, a unique castle—was the Virgin Mary. Although many other women possess both the wall of virginity and the tower of humility, that is, although they are virgins and humble, they cannot, while preserving virginity, also be mothers and bear children, as she alone did. Therefore this castle is rightly called “a certain,” that is, unique, because she alone was both virgin and mother—something no other woman could or can be. [Col. 1506C]

But let us grant that someone could be both mother and virgin, although this is impossible: even so, the Virgin Mary would remain unique, because she gave birth to the one Son of God, who, just as he is the only-begotten Son of the one Father, is likewise the only Son of his one Mother. Therefore, even if a virgin gives birth, no one will bear either that same Son or another like him.

There is, then, a certain castle into which Jesus entered. The gate through which he entered is faith. Because she believed, what had been spoken to her by the angel was fulfilled by the Lord, as Elizabeth said to her. Nor was this castle violated because Jesus entered it. Jesus saves; he does not violate. He repairs what is broken, but does not break what is sound. His work corresponds to his name.

“And a certain woman named Martha received him into her house, and she had a sister named Mary.” These two sisters, as the holy Fathers have explained to us most fully, signify two ways of life in the holy Church: Martha, namely, the active life, and Mary, the contemplative life. The former labors to provide every service of humanity to those in need; the latter is free to contemplate and see that God is. The one is occupied with outward things; the other contemplates inward things.

Just as the Mother of God is unique, so too the effect of these two ways of life, represented by these two sisters, was unique in her. Never did Martha work in anyone else in this manner; never did Mary devote herself to contemplation in anyone else in this manner; never did either of them display what belonged to her in anyone else in such a way. When I speak of Martha or Mary, I mean what they signify.

But let us now consider the activity of this Martha, and afterward infer the contemplation of this Mary. To make the matter clearer, let us compare what others do through Martha with what she herself did. [Col. 1507A]

Others receive an ordinary guest into their house; she received not an ordinary guest, but the very Son of God, who had nowhere to lay his head—not into a house, but into her womb. Others clothe any naked person with changeable and perishable garments obtained from wherever they can; she assumed the Word of God in that same virginal flesh, in the unity of his person, which will remain forever immutable and incorruptible.

Others refresh anyone who is hungry and thirsty with outward food and drink; she nourished God made man, who in his humanity was in need, not only with outward food and drink, but also fed him with the milk of her womb. To pass briefly over the six works of mercy, which, when performed for one of his least, God acknowledges as done for himself: she received as a guest not one of the least, but the supreme Son of God; she covered him, naked in the flesh, and even with swaddling clothes; she fed him when hungry; she gave him milk when thirsty; when he was weak through infancy and age, she not only visited him but continually bathed, warmed, anointed, and carried him. Thus it is rightly said of her, “But Martha was occupied with much serving.”

When he was seized and crucified, as though placed in prison, she was present, as it is written: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother” (John XIX). Meanwhile she was troubled and anxious when she fled with him into Egypt from the face of Herod, who persecuted such a son of hers so fiercely that he killed many boys of the suspected age. She was troubled when she learned that the Jews were plotting against him and seeking to inflict death upon him. [Col. 1507C]

Finally, she was greatly troubled, and, in accordance with Simeon’s words, a sword pierced her own soul (Luke II), when she saw such a son of hers seized, bound, scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, mocked, struck on the face, crucified, killed, and buried. Thus the saying aptly applies to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.”

Let no one doubt that the blessed Virgin Mary wished her Son to be freed from every tribulation, and wished herself to be helped in her distress by the divinity which she knew was present in that same Son through contemplation—the part belonging to Mary. This is what Martha complains of: that her sister has left her alone to serve, and she calls for her help in the ministry.

So much for Martha’s part. But concerning Mary’s part, which is declared to be the better, who could speak worthily of how great or what kind it was in blessed Mary? If it was such as we have said—or rather, because it was better than we have said—what was Martha’s part in blessed Mary, which indeed is not praised by the Lord but nevertheless is not condemned, compared with that part which Mary chose as the best, praised in such a way that it is said it shall not be taken from her? [Col. 1507D]

O how great was the abundance of God’s sweetness in the blessed Virgin when the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and she conceived from that same Holy Spirit! What did she not taste of God, in whom the wisdom of God lay hidden, and in whose womb he was fashioning a body for himself?

Christ is, as the Apostle says, “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” and in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (1 Cor. I; Col. II). But Christ was in Mary; therefore the power of God, the wisdom of God, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were in Mary.

She sat not only at the feet but also at the head of the Lord, listening to the word from his mouth. She kept all the words of the angels, shepherds, and Magi, as well as those of her own Son, pondering them in her heart. No one ever tasted as she did how gracious the Lord is. She was filled from the abundance of God’s house and given drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. XXXV). Nor is this surprising, since with her—indeed, within her—was the fountain of life, from which flowed such perfection of both ways of life.

She was occupied with many things as Martha, yet delighted in the one thing as Mary, because “one thing is necessary”: many things are offered, but one remains. Thus she uniquely fulfilled Martha’s part, and uniquely chose Mary’s better part.

But Martha’s part is taken away from her. She will no longer be anxious about serving him as a child, for all the orders of angels serve him as Lord. She will no longer be troubled as she flees with him into Egypt from the face of Herod, because he has ascended into heaven and Herod has descended into hell before his face. She will no longer be troubled by the many things the Jews did to her Son, because all things have been subjected to him. The Son of Mary will no longer be scourged or killed by the Jews or soldiers, because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. VI). [Col. 1508C]

Martha’s part, then, is taken away from her, but for her good; Mary’s part, however, is perfected in her and shall not be taken away. For she has been exalted above the choirs of angels. Her desire has been filled with good things; she sees God face to face as he is; she rejoices with her Son forever.

This is the better part, which shall not be taken away from her. May we also share in it through her merits and prayers, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns, etc.

**HOMILY XLIX. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE.**

*(From the works of the venerable Bede the presbyter.)*

“At that time there arose a dispute among the disciples of Jesus as to which of them seemed to be the greater,” etc. (Luke XXII).

[Col. 1508D] “As is ordinarily the custom in the Scriptures of the good,” etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, *Works*, vol. V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 423.

[Note: This homily is read almost word for word, except for the beginning, among the works of blessed Chrysostom in our edition, vol. VIII, col. 485, among the spurious works, with this note by Savile: “When some foolish and unlearned little Greek had discovered in the ecclesiastical historians that an oration beginning in this manner had been delivered by our John, that most shameless man attached to a human head a truly bestial body and foisted this spurious and utterly false offspring upon us in place of the Word, scarcely worthy of reading, much less of correction. We rejected the earlier Latin translation … and prepared a new one.” We give the old version which the Homiliary presents. EDIT.]

**HOMILY L. ON THE BEHEADING OF BLESSED JOHN THE BAPTIST.**

*(From the works of blessed Chrysostom [?].)*

Woe is me! What shall I do? Where shall I begin my speech? What shall I say, or what shall I leave unsaid? For I alone have not been struck with astonishment of mind, but so have all who have heard the voice of the Gospel; and they marvel with me either at John’s steadfastness, or Herod’s wickedness, or the beastlike frivolity of the impious women.
