For what have we heard? “Herod,” it says, “having seized John, put him in prison.” Why? “Because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip.” Shall I perhaps condemn Herod’s frivolity, or the madness into which he was most wretchedly led by women? What shall I say? How, I ask, shall I recount the cruel wickedness of those women?

Indeed, I think that no beast in this world can be compared with a wicked woman. But now I am speaking of a wicked woman, not of a good and honorable one. For I know many women who are good, honorable, and well adorned, ready for every good work. I ought to recall their lives for the edification of those listening and to awaken honor for good women in the minds of all. [Col. 1509B]

Therefore, no beast in this world is like a wicked woman. Among four-footed animals, what is fiercer than a lion? Yet that is nothing compared with these women. Or among serpents, what is more savage than a dragon? Even that cannot be compared with a wicked and quarrelsome woman. For both lion and dragon are inferior in wickedness.

The wisest Solomon bears witness to this speech of mine, saying: “It is better to dwell with a lion and a dragon than with a wicked and quarrelsome woman.” And lest you think that the prophet said this without reason, learn it more plainly from these examples. Lions respected Daniel in the den, but Jezebel killed that just man Naboth. The whale guarded Jonah in its belly. Delilah, however, ensnared Samson and, having his head shaved with a razor, disfigured her husband and handed him over to foreigners.

Dragons, vipers, and horned beasts trembled before John the Baptist, who lived in the desert, their natural ferocity subdued. Herodias, however, cut off his head and accepted the death of so great a man as the price of a dance.

Ravens fed Elijah on the mountain, and Jezebel persecuted him after the rain had been restored to the earth through his agency, seeking to repay him with the punishment of death, although by his prayers the famine of the human race had been driven away and she herself, unworthy as she was, continued to live (3 Kings XIX). For what did she say after that remarkable benefit? “If you are Elijah, I am Jezebel. May the gods do these things to me and add these things, unless by this hour tomorrow I make your life like the life of one of those who have been killed.”

And Elijah was afraid, and departed for his life, and went into the desert, a journey of forty days. He began, as though wearied and faint in spirit, to ask that he might die, and said: “Lord God, it is enough now; take my life, for I am not better than my fathers.”

Woe to me! What more can be said, if so great a prophet feared a woman—he who had carried in the power of his tongue the state of the whole world, the rain of heaven, and the appearance of the field; who had brought down fire from heaven and, through the power of prayer, raised the dead? Did he fear a woman? He feared her, I say. For no wickedness can rival that of a wicked woman.

Again the wisest Solomon bears witness to this saying of mine: “There is no head above the head of a serpent, and there is no wickedness above the wickedness of a woman” (Ecclus. XXV).

O woman, the supreme evil and the sharpest dart of the devil! Woman cast Adam down in paradise and drove him out of paradise. Woman armed the gentlest David to kill his innocent soldier Uriah the Hittite, so that he might send a letter by deceit. Woman hurled the wisest Solomon into the sacrilegious transgression. Woman deceived, shaved, and blinded the strongest Samson, stripping him both of the hair of his strength and the beauty of his eyes, so that he became a mockery to the enemies who had previously feared him, and, now a captive, ground grain with those over whom he had ruled undefeated. Woman dragged the most chaste Joseph, bound in chains, down into prison. Woman beheaded John, the lamp of the whole world.

And what shall I say about women? Woman brought angels down from heaven—that is, holy men who were journeying toward heaven. Woman utterly overthrew, slaughtered, killed, and crushed all things, filling them with disgrace and emptying them of honor. For an immodest woman spares no one: she does not honor a Levite, does not revere a priest, and does not show respect to a prophet. [Col. 1510B]

O evil worse than every evil, a wicked woman! Whether she is poor or rich, it is a double evil. If she possesses means that cooperate with her wickedness, the evil is doubled: an intolerable viper, an incurable poison.

I know that even vipers are calmed by the charms of enchanters, and that lions, tigers, and leopards, their ferocity tamed, become gentle. A wicked woman, whether she suffers injury, rages, or whether she receives honor, becomes swollen with pride. But if she is the wife of some powerful man, she does not cease day and night to goad her husband craftily—flatteringly, wickedly, importunately, and violently—until she drives patience from his mind and sharpens him into agreement with her madness, so that she makes her husband like herself.

She gives wicked counsel to the wicked, as Herodias did to Herod. If she has a poor husband, she likewise never ceases to incite him to anger and quarrels. If she is a widow, she despises everyone indiscriminately and is puffed up by the spirit of pride toward every lie. She does not restrain her tongue through fear of God, nor look ahead to the coming judgment, nor direct her attention toward God. She knows neither how to preserve the laws of friendship nor how to respect the faith of religion. Nothing is too much for her, not even handing her husband over to death.

Thus Job’s wife was handing that just man over to death, saying: “Say something against God, and die” (Job II). O ineffable wickedness, O impious will! She did not pity her husband when she saw all his limbs and vital organs burning with inflamed sores and his entire flesh covered with worms. She was not moved to mercy when she saw him writhing in such pains, bound by cruel tortures, struggling in a deathly agony, and singing out his sufferings in mournful howls through the strained utterances of his wasting sides.

The wife was not softened in her mind’s affection when she saw lying on a heap of dung, his body naked, the man whom she had once seen clothed in royal purple. She did not remember her former life with him, nor how she had flourished through him in glory, riches, and honors. Forgetful of all good things, listen to what she said: “Say something against God, and die.”

O marital grace! O word suited to soothing great pains! O faithful unity of love! Tell me, woman: do you think that if she had seen you placed in a similar tribulation, she could ever have spoken such a word to you, rather than wiping away your suffering with prayers and acts of kindness?

And was that grievous suffering not enough for her, unless you too came upon him, heavier than his pains and wounds, bringing upon him an everlasting punishment for the sin of blasphemy? Or do you not know that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come?

Do you wish to see another woman equal to her in wickedness? Bring me Delilah. For she too handed over her husband, the strongest Samson, shaved and bound, to the foreign enemies as spoil and a mockery. The companion of her bed, whom she had caressed most tenderly, whom she had flatteringly courted with seeming simplicity, whom she herself thought more dear than anything, whom she had embraced in unity only yesterday—today, like an enemy, she deceives.

The man whom shortly before she had touched with cunning and wickedly flattering enticements as though she loved him, shortly afterward she handed over to death in mockery. And what shall we say? For what reason of hatred had his wife come to dislike him? Perhaps he was not handsome? And who at that time seemed more beautiful than he, who wore seven locks upon his head as an image of sevenfold grace?

Or was he not strong, and was he despised with contempt for cowardice? Who was stronger than he, who met the terrible lion that came against him, and, alone and unarmed, strangled it with his intertwined hands, and, as it is written, tore it apart as one tears a kid? And who with the jawbone of an ass, one of its ancient bones, dry and withered, struck down a thousand foreign enemies?

Moreover, he was holy—indeed, so holy that, after he had grown thirsty from the labor of battle in a dry place, he prayed to the Lord in the exhaustion of his spirit, and immediately drank from water bursting forth from the very jawbone he held in his hand. From that same bone of the dead animal with which he had conquered, he quenched the heat of his thirst and was refreshed.

And such a man, so great in beauty, strength, and holiness, his wife deceived and bound as an enemy and handed over to the foreigners. How did that woman prevail over so strong a man, except through his innate simplicity and goodness and her own cunning wickedness? For she entered into her husband’s inmost heart not merely inquisitively but deceitfully; she wearied him with simple yet persistent entreaties and seductive flatteries, robbed him of that secret mystery of his strength, and, once his hair had been shaved and he had been stripped of his power, utterly overthrew him. Thus the one woman, wickedly armed with deceit and without weapons, defeated the man whom many thousands of armed enemies had not conquered.

For this reason the prophet announces to you and says: “Guard yourself from your wife, lest you reveal your heart to her.” Tell me, then: what beast has ever plotted such things against its male? What female dragon wishes to destroy its mate? What lioness has handed over her male to be slaughtered?

You see, therefore, what Wisdom foretold: “There is no head above the head of a serpent, and there is no wickedness above the wickedness of a woman.” And whoever has a wicked wife should know once and for all that he is already bearing the reward of his iniquities. This saying is not without testimonies to its truth. Hear the wise man saying: “A wicked and sinful woman will be given as a portion for evil deeds” [Col. 1512A] (Ecclus. XXV).

But let this speech of mine concerning the wicked woman end here. For now it is necessary in turn to recall good women, especially on account of those who are present. Good women regard the virtues of good women as their own, and consider their chaste labors to be their own crowns.

The good and hospitable woman was the blessed Shunammite, who asked her husband to build a lodging for Elisha, so that when he passed by and turned in to them, as he was accustomed to do, he might have a private place for refreshment. She placed a bed there for him, as Scripture declares, and a lamp and a table. The bed was not empty of coverings, but had suitable bedding spread upon it; the lamp was not merely a wick of linen, but had light with tinder and oil; and the table was not without bread, but furnished with necessary food (4 Kings IV).

What, however, can we say worthily about that blessed widow who received Elijah (3 Kings XVII), whom the poverty of her possessions did not hinder, since she was rich in good will, although she had neither grain, nor wine, nor stew, nor any other earthly food with which to console her exhausted poverty? No fruitful field produced for her the seed of bread; no vineyard brought her sweet wine through flowing veins and fruitful clusters. She had not even a palm’s breadth of ground in which to plow, nor an elbow’s space in which to plant a vine.

Instead, every year at harvest time she went out into the field and, bending forward in a slow advance, followed the reapers, cutting the few remnants of the harvested crop and gathering into her small lap the remaining or fallen ears left behind by the advancing harvesters. In this way she stored up, as though measured out and counted under careful estimation, a year’s supply of food.

To her, then, Elijah came, sent by the Lord, in a time of famine, when almost the whole world had dried up and withered through lack of rain, and, parched by the scarcity of crops, denied food to living creatures. The sky burned with fiery heat, and the thick air was darkened by vaporous clouds; the rains had been withdrawn and the restrained clouds hung suspended. No grass, flowers, or shoots were sprouting. No dewy breeze refreshed the ears of grain; the rivers, thinned into streams, flowed through narrow channels; the breasts of the springs had grown cold from the prolonged heat of the scorching sun; and the seas, deprived of the customary seasoning of bitter salt because the sweet waters of rivers and rains no longer flowed into them, had lost it.

*Then Elijah came to that needy widow, and what storms of love widows suffer even in a time of abundance.* [Editorial text as printed.]

You know the customary distress of widows, which certainly grows heavier when poverty is punished by desolation. God sent a wealthy prophet, who even in a time of famine abounded in bread, and, leaving [descending from] the mountain, came to this poor woman.

But why did the man who by his word had brought fire down from heaven not set aside bread for himself? Could he not? Certainly he could. But he did not do so for this reason: lest the widow, prepared for a good work, be deprived of the reward of hospitality; and also so that the Lord’s blessing might multiply that small handful of flour and the little trickle of oil in the mouth of the prophet who had been received.

For the prophet was not sent merely for his own rest, to be fed by the needy woman, but rather to feed the needy, and to reveal the hidden disposition of good will in her heart. The Lord himself also does this. Although he is powerful enough to feed visibly all who are in this world by himself, he nevertheless restrains his hand from providing directly, so that in a time of need he may reveal the fruits of human kindness in minds ready for good, and distinguish the dispositions of souls by the quality of their works.

If there are no people of this will or worthiness to receive God’s saints, then the Lord feeds them either through birds, as he fed Elijah in his secluded mountain place, or through a prophet sent from elsewhere, as he fed Daniel in the lions’ den, or through a sea creature, as he fed Jonah through the whale; or God himself, as shepherd, supplies nourishment, as he did for our fathers in the desert.

For when there was no one in the wilderness to receive the children of Israel, he provided manna from heaven for the hungry, and water flowed from the rock for the thirsty. But when the saints live mingled among the peoples of this world, even if he sees them suffering tribulation, he permits them to endure it so that he may give grace to those who are willing to show them human kindness, enabling them to gain eternal salvation for themselves through a present benefit.

Elijah therefore went to that widow, who had nothing in her storeroom except a handful of flour. She had prepared even this, with much labor, for herself and her children at the very time of the prophet’s arrival, having nothing left and expecting to die with her children after it was consumed.

And what did the prophet say to her? “Bring me a little water in a vessel, so that I may drink.” As she was immediately going away, he called out to her again: “Bring me also a morsel of bread in your hand.” She simply stated what she did not have, but acknowledged what she did have.

For what did she say? “As the Lord lives, I have nothing stored up except this little bit of flour and a small amount of oil” (3 Kings XVII).

It is most remarkable that, in such a great scarcity of food, she did not refuse the very little that remained to her. Yet how many people nowadays, who possess gold and silver as though they were mere mud, refuse when asked to help the needy or to lend for a time, and swear that they have nothing? And if they are ever persuaded, after much pleading, to provide assistance, they draw up contracts and securities, and write certain prejudgments stronger than iron. First they bind the hand of the borrower with crafty written agreements, and in addition they require sureties and guarantors for the money lent.

But that poor woman of ours, at the single word by which she was asked, did not deny that she had one small handful of flour. And what did the prophet reply to her? “Hurry,” he said, “and first make me a little cake baked under the ashes; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your children.”

The prophet’s word was a trial, a testing of the heart, an examination of the will. The blessed widow’s heart was as though placed on a balance, questioned by the command of the prophetic word as by the torture of an inquisition, and hanging uncertainly between two alternatives: whether she should look after herself and her children, or obey the prophet more fully.

But she chose rather to prepare refreshment for the prophet from what remained of her poverty. For she knew that “whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward,” and that “whoever gives a thirsty person a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple shall not lose his reward” (Matt. X).

But why did the prophet say, “Hurry”? Was he so hungry that he needed the woman’s haste without distinction? Certainly not. He wished to teach her to be prompt in spirit, fervent, and cheerful for the accomplishment of a good work, not to provide it with sadness or merely from necessity. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX).

“Hurry,” he said, “and make one for me first,” just as Abraham hurried at the arrival of the angels to the sheep and took a calf from them. [Col. 1514B] And just as Sarah hastened to make cakes under the ashes, so that she might receive that bread hidden in heaven (Gen. XVIII).

Hurry, and do as Abraham did with sacrifices to God—not first for yourself and afterward for me, as Cain did, and Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest, who despised the honor of God, choosing for themselves first the first portions of the sacrifices from all the gifts offered to God (1 Sam. II).

The widow therefore promptly carried out what the prophet had commanded her, and quickly filled her storehouse, foreseeing that a rich fruit was laid up for those who work in God. The prophet received the widow’s preparation, tasted it, spoke, and filled her house with good things.

“The flour in the jar shall not fail,” he said, “and the oil in the vessel shall not diminish, until the Lord gives rain upon the earth.” And why did he set the end of the blessing for that time? Quite necessarily. For when new grace came upon the earth like rain, it was necessary that the old law should reach its term, and the deed should correspond to the word.

You see how quickly the blessed widow harvested the reward of hospitality. “The fruit of good labors is glorious, and the root of prudence is unfailing” (Wis. III).

You have heard, O women, both the deeds of wicked women and the virtues of good women. Therefore trample upon the crimes of the former, but follow the examples of the latter. Curse those women, but imitate these, so that when you have followed the course and footsteps of holy women, you may be numbered with equal grace and praise among their choirs and fellowship in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY LI. ON THE SAME FEAST.**

*(From the works of the venerable Bede the presbyter.)*

[Col. 1514D]

“At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his servants, ‘This is John the Baptist,’” etc. (Matt. XIV).

“While celebrating, dearest brothers, the birthday of John,” etc. For the remainder, see the works of the venerable Bede, vol. V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 237.

**HOMILY LII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.**
Let every creature magnify the mother of the Creator; let heaven and earth and all their fullness bow before her glorious majesty. Let the sons in the Church exalt the mother [Col. 1515A] and say to her who have been redeemed by the Lord:

“We raise our minds and eyes, together with our hands, to you, queen of the world, and before the glory of your majesty we bend the knee and incline our necks; with hearts full of sighs we send our prayers up to you in heaven. Do not disdain to incline from heaven’s height your blessed eyes—those with which you continually gaze with longing upon that incomprehensible glory of eternal light—toward your suppliants, cast down from on high into this sewer of the world.

“Behold, we sinners stand before the dreadful Judge, whose terrible hand brandishes the sword of his wrath over us. And who will turn it aside? No one is so fit, Lady, to place his hand between us and the Lord’s sword as you, most loving of God, through whom we first received mercy on earth from the hand of the Lord our God.

[Col. 1515B] “Open, therefore, mother of mercy, the door of your most gracious heart to the sighing prayers of Adam’s children, who flee from every end of the earth to the shelter of your protection, away from the face of the Lord’s dread. To you, Lady, our eyes stream with tears, and with a devoted and powerful cry we beseech you: assuage toward us the anger of your Son, which we have grievously kindled by sinning, and by your prayer reconcile to us his grace, from which we ungratefully fell away.

“By his wound we were healed; again we ask for his remedy, because our scars have festered and become corrupt, and there is no health in us” (Psalm 37). Attend, Lady, and behold the pains of the wounds of our soul, for we have revealed our case to you with confidence. We have recognized you as a woman of immeasurable kindness, and truly as the mother of mercy [Col. 1515C] because you passed through this unclean and slippery world by an undefiled path and, while still dwelling among sinners, shone before God with such holiness that you alone deserved to approach the throne of the eternal King.

“You do not recoil from a sinner, however foul, nor despise him if he sighs toward you and with a penitent heart begs your intervention. With a gracious hand you draw him back from the abyss of despair, breathe into him the medicine of hope, and embrace with motherly affection one despised by the whole world; you cherish him and do not abandon him until you reconcile the wretched man to the dreadful Judge. Theophilus, restored to grace through you, is a famous testimony to this kindness of yours.

“And no wonder, Lady, if the sanctuary of your heart has been drenched with so abundant an oil of mercy, since that immeasurable [Col. 1515D] work of mercy which God predestined before the ages for our redemption was first fashioned in you by the world’s maker. For when it pleased heavenly grace to dwell in us, from whom it had long been far removed, you alone were found worthy that the King of kings and Lord of lords, coming from his royal seats, should choose his first dwelling among the children of men in your virginal palace.

“Truly it pleased God to dwell in you when, from the very substance of your undefiled flesh, as from the cedars of Lebanon, divine Wisdom built himself a house by an ineffable architecture. He supported it with seven silver columns and placed within it a golden couch. These are the seven spirits of God, and this is that unique one in whom alone he found the rest he sought [Col. 1516A] in all things, and as a sign of this he poured out all his treasures without measure.

“It rightly pleased the Holy Spirit to dwell in you, O Mary, when he deigned to consecrate your womb for such divine mysteries. For he is the consuming fire, who inflamed your most holy soul within himself and filled it with the splendor of divine majesty. In an ineffable manner he impregnated your womb and caused you to conceive and bear God and man while remaining closed, and to remain a virgin after childbirth.

“Now, therefore, the whole world venerates your womb, Lady, as the most sacred temple of the living God, because in it the salvation of the world was begun. There the Son of God clothed himself in beauty, and, splendid in a white robe, joyfully came to meet his chosen bride, the Church; there he offered the long-desired kiss [Col. 1516B] and the virgin with the Virgin in the Virgin tasted beforehand the wedding ordained from eternity.

“There the wall of enmity was first broken down which the disobedience of our first parents had built between heaven and earth. There heavenly things were joined with earthly things, and mercy and truth met one another in the kiss of peace, when divinity and humanity came together in one and the same person. And that new thing came to pass upon earth: God was man, and man was God.

“There the great Elisha contracted himself to the size required to raise a little boy. There the ancient patriarch of days clothed his chosen son in a many-colored tunic. There Rebecca, knowing beforehand what was to come, wrapped the skins of goats around the hands of her son who was to be magnified and covered his bare neck.

“There, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, the Son who was to be inherited by God [Col. 1516C] the Father among all the nations concealed the power of divine majesty beneath the likeness of sinful flesh; his face was hidden, and therefore we did not esteem him. There, by the providence of the deep counsel, the hook was baited which was cast from heaven into this great sea to draw out the ancient serpent. From there came the golden bracelet by which Leviathan’s jaw was to be pierced, so that he might vomit out the dead who were not his own, whom he had safely swallowed from the beginning of the world.

“Your most sacred womb is for us a garden of delights, O Mary, because from it we gather many flowers of joy whenever we recall in our minds how great a multitude of sweetness flowed from there for the whole world. You are a garden enclosed, holy Mother of God, into which the hand of a sinner never entered to pluck its flowers.

[Col. 1516D] “You are a bed of aromatic plants belonging to the saints, planted by the heavenly perfumer and delightfully blooming with the beautiful flowers of every virtue. Among their loveliest blossoms we marvel at three excellences in you. They are the ones whose sweetest fragrance fills the whole house of God: violet of humility, lily of chastity, rose of charity, O Mary.

“Rightly, from such a bed that beautiful flower, fairer than the flowers of paradise, came forth—the one upon whom the Spirit of the Lord rested. And to what shall we compare you, O mother of beauty? Truly you are God’s paradise, because you brought forth for the world the tree of life, from which whoever eats will live forever.

“The fountain of life, which came forth from the mouth of the Most High, sprang from the midst of your womb and from there, dividing itself into four heads, flowed out to water the face of the parched world [Col. 1517A] making glad the city of God. For whoever drinks from it will never thirst again.

“Behold, this is greater than paradise. If someone drinks of the water of that paradise, he will thirst again. O how much you have bestowed upon the world, you who were found worthy to be the channel of such health-giving water!

“O most brilliant lamp, how many have you gladdened! Illumined with such splendor of God’s glory, you brought forth that desired light by which the tenth drachma was found, for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

“Indeed, the singer of the divine wedding song saw you from afar when he burst forth in an exclamation of wonder, saying: ‘Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arranged for battle?’ (Song of Songs 6).

“You advanced into the world like a brilliantly glowing dawn, O Mary, when you went before the splendor of the true sun [Col. 1517B] with the radiance of such holiness that it was fitting for the day of salvation, the day of reconciliation, the day that the Lord has made, to begin from your brightness. You were a blessed dawn, the herald of a blessed day. Such a dawn suited such a day, and such a day such a dawn.

“And rightly you fulfilled the office of dawn. For the Sun of justice himself, about to proceed from you, anticipating his rising with a certain morning radiance, poured out upon you abundantly the rays of his light. By these you put to flight the powers of darkness which Eve had brought in, and thus you brought into the world the sun desired by all nations.

“You are called beautiful as the moon, and not undeservedly compared with it. For the moon alone among all the stars most resembles the sun, and, beautiful in its silvery brightness, shines above the other stars in heaven.

“You are the most exact image of the true sun; [Col. 1517C] among the thousands of stars serving God, you shine gloriously in heaven through virginal purity. The moon illumines the night after receiving the sun’s light into itself. You illumine our night by the virtues implanted in you by God and by your magnificent examples, which call us to imitate you.

“For whoever follows your ways will not walk in darkness but will find the light of life. You are therefore beautiful as the moon, indeed more beautiful than the moon, because you are wholly beautiful, and there is no stain in you, nor any shadow caused by change.

“You are chosen as the sun—that sun, I say, whose creator is himself the Sun. He was chosen from among thousands of men; you were chosen from among thousands of women. He was chosen from among all things that exist through him; you are terrible as an army arranged for battle.

“For what? Did not [Col. 1517D] the princes of darkness tremble when they saw a woman advancing against them, contrary to custom, equipped with all the armor of the strong? A strong woman, most skilled in warfare, whose sword is upon her thigh because of nighttime terrors. Around her stands a powerful army of spiritual virtues, each protecting the others in its appointed order, since the day persists through ordered arrangement.

“We also have no doubt that an innumerable host of blessed spirits was assigned to the service of so great a prince, so that they might guard Solomon’s most beloved bed and ensure that a dwelling prepared for the eternal King would not be invaded by a stranger guest.

“Surely fear and trembling came upon them, so that they said: ‘Behold, this is more than Eve. This is God’s camp. Let us flee from Israel.’

“You, therefore, outstanding warrior, first [Col. 1518A] courageously undertook to conquer him who first overthrew Eve. You crushed the spirit of pride by that virtue of humility which the Lord saw in you, so that for its merit he judged you worthy to be exalted above all the choirs of angels. You would never have ascended glorified above all the angels unless you had first descended in humility beneath all human beings.

“You also extinguished the burning of forbidden desire in your virginal flesh by the power of chastity, to such an extent that he in whose sight even the stars are not pure judged your flesh so clean that he did not disdain to join it to his own divine purity.

“Once you had courageously conquered these primary leaders of darkness, the entire army of spiritual wickedness was turned to flight before your face.

[Col. 1518B] “Glorious things have been spoken of you, Mother of God, but there is still room for your praise; every tongue still stammers in praising you. For throughout every nation under heaven there are neither utterances nor speeches capable of fully expressing the greatness of your glory.

“O great, O gracious, O most lovable Mary! You cannot even be named without kindling the affections of those who love you, nor thought of without refreshing them. You never enter the gates of devout remembrance without the sweetness divinely implanted in you.

“And now we follow you, Lady, crying out to you from the depths of our hearts: ‘Help our weakness; remove our disgrace. Do you see this tunic of skin that has surrounded us—the tunic of our mother Eve? This is what she once transmitted to us and clothed upon the flesh of her children, like a double garment [Col. 1518C] of her shame.

“‘From the hand of that double evil our earth received its seed; it conceived and brought forth for us thorns and thistles of iniquity in the soul, calamities in the body, and through these death in both.

“‘O unhappy inheritance, O dreadful weakness of human flesh, how long shall we suffer you? You have bent our backs greatly, for you are exceedingly heavy, and we have borne you for a long time. You have diminished us greatly from the angels and compared us with senseless beasts. You have grown far too powerful, since you could be healed only by the death of the Son of God.

“‘You raised yourself too high above us when you rashly ascended even to him who is above all. And who will free us from the miserable corruption of this garment of skin? The grace of our Savior, your Son, O Mary. To remove our weaknesses he willingly became weak; to become himself the death [Col. 1518D] of our death, he, though innocent, died for sinners.

“‘And who is so fit to speak for us to the heart of our Lord Jesus Christ as you, blessed Mary, who lie sweetly in the most secret embraces of your most loving Son in the eternal midday and rejoice in his most intimate conversation with the full joy of your heart?

“‘Speak, Lady, for your Son hears you. Invoke his good name over us, that we may be healed of the leprosy of flesh and spirit. Burn away this deadly poison which Eve gave us to drink from the remains of her fruit. Would that she, drunk with her potion, had either drunk it all or spilled it all.

“‘At your intercession, may our entire yoke rot away before the face of God’s mercy. May our youth be renewed like the eagle’s, so that, made new, with a new [Col. 1519A] voice we may sing a new song, joined to the new citizens there where all things are new, celebrating an eternal jubilee and singing together with cymbals of rejoicing.

“‘May this thick cloud be removed from our eyes, so that with unveiled face we may behold the glory of the Lord and be absorbed by the Spirit of the Lord into that immeasurable sea of divine light; and, bound to our God by the bonds of charity, may we become one spirit with him.

“‘May your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, grant this to us, O Mary, he to whom be praise, glory, and thanksgiving forever and ever. Amen.’”

## HOMILY LIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(From the works of the venerable priest Bede and, in places, from the commentary of Saint Jerome on the Gospel of Matthew.)*

[Col. 1519B]

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob,” etc. (Matthew 1).

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.” According to this generation Christ is the Son of Man, as he very often calls himself, commending to us what, in his mercy, he deigned to be for our sake. For that heavenly and eternal generation by which he is the only-begotten Son of God before every creature—because all things were made through him—is so ineffable that the prophet Isaiah’s statement is understood to refer to it: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

Although this may also have been said of his temporal birth, by which the Word became flesh, and the Virgin, made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, bore a [Col. 1519C] son and remained a virgin.

“Son of David, son of Abraham.” The order is reversed, but necessarily changed. For if he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, Abraham would again have had to be repeated in order to unfold the sequence of the generation. He therefore called him the son of these two alone, passing over the others, because the promise concerning Christ was made only to them: to Abraham, “In your seed,” he says, “all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12); but to David he said, “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Psalm 131).

“Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob.” Matthew therefore traces Christ’s human generation from the very beginning of the promise of Christ, that is, from Abraham, recalling the ancestors and carrying the line down to Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born.

Mystically, however, he shows how, from the darkness [Col. 1519D] of paganism—as from Egyptian slavery—through forty-two men, as though by the stations of that same number, one arrives at the Virgin Mary, full and flowing with the flood of the Holy Spirit, as though at the intelligible Jordan under the leadership of the Lord Jesus Christ, like Joshua son of Nun. He testifies that Christ was born from Mary; placed at the end of the genealogy like a hook at the head of a net and sent by the Father into the sea of this world, he killed the hooked, crooked serpent by being killed, and by dying he put to death the death of the human race.

Therefore, as though by a doubled cord—that is, by repeating each name—the order of the genealogy is woven in the likeness of a net, until from its beginning, namely from Abraham, one arrives [Col. 1520A] at the hook, that is, at Christ. Of him it is said to holy Job: “Will you draw out Leviathan with your hook, or pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” (Job 40).

He was caught, therefore, on the hook of Christ’s incarnation: when he desired the bait of the flesh in him, he was pierced by the barb of divinity.

“Judas begot Phares and Zara by Tamar.” It should be noted that in the Savior’s genealogy he does not take any of the holy women, but those whom Scripture censures, so that he who had come for sinners might, being born from sinners, wipe away the sins of all. Thus in what follows Rahab the prostitute, Ruth the Moabite, and Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, are also included.

At the deeper level, in all these four women the Church coming to the Lord from the error of paganism is represented. Previously alien, [Col. 1520B] full of disgrace, and considered barren, she was joined to Christ as a legitimate wife and bears more adopted children for God than the synagogue, which previously seemed to have the Lord as her own husband.

“Tamar” is interpreted as bitterness, or “one who changes,” or “palm tree.” All these meanings rightly suit the holy Church. She was formerly bitter in idolatry and turbulent conduct, but now she is sweet through tears of contrition and the devotion of pious labor. She is rightly called “one who changes,” because she has been changed from sinful into righteous, and from hated into beloved. She is properly compared with a palm tree because of the contest of labors and the reward of victory. Concerning her the Psalmist fittingly says: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Psalm 91).

“Rahab” is interpreted as breadth, or hunger, or impulse. And what [Col. 1520C] is proclaimed by this except the nobility of the holy Church? Isaiah says to her: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare” (Isaiah 54).

She therefore has hunger—not hunger for bread or thirst for water (Amos 8), but hunger to hear the word of God and to do his will. An impulse indeed enters into her, because the speed of preaching, with the Holy Spirit breathing upon it, is directed throughout the breadth of the world.

Finally, Ruth, who is interpreted as “seeing,” or “hastening,” or “failing,” rightly signifies the Church, which contemplates God in purity of heart and, according to the Psalmist, hastens to offer her hands to God. She determines, that is, she resolves to remain firmly in faith and love of God.

Bathsheba, however, who is interpreted as “the seventh well,” [Col. 1520D] signifies the abundance of the grace of the Holy Spirit brought about in the Church. Through a spiritual gift—that is, through the sevenfold gift—the Church has become a well of satiety, because in her there has been made a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.

“Naasson begot Salmon.” This Naasson is the prince of the tribe of Judah, as we read in Numbers.

“Jesse begot David the king.” He calls David “king,” not because he alone among the kings is placed in this genealogy—for several kings reigned from him until the Babylonian deportation, and are listed—but because David was the first king of the house of David, through whom the order of the genealogy proceeds.

“David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s.” It is asked why, [Col. 1521A] when the three other foreign women are given by their proper names, Solomon is not said to have been born by Bathsheba, but only by one who had been Uriah’s wife.

This is thought to have been done because, although the other three women mentioned above were guilty, in bearing the sons through whom the genealogy runs they deserved not only not to be censured but even to be praised. This woman, however, having committed adultery and murder, bore a son to King David through a marriage so blameworthy that she is rightly not seen to be named in the Savior’s genealogy.

Her husband’s name, Uriah, is given as though he were a righteous man, so that the enormity of the crime might also be recalled by the fact that he was killed on account of his wife.

Mystically, David signifies Christ; his name is interpreted as “strong of hand” and “desirable.” And what is stronger than the lion who conquered, from the tribe of Judah, the root of David? Scripture shows how he is desirable [Col. 1521B] when it says: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations will come” (Haggai 2). Peter also says: “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1).

Uriah, however, whose name is interpreted as “my light is God,” signifies the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light, daring to say to God: “My light is God, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14).

“Joram begot Joathan.” [Col. 1521C] In the Fourth Book of Kings we read that Ochozias was begotten by Joram. When Ochozias died, Jozabeth, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ochozias, took Joas, her brother’s son, and rescued him from the slaughter carried out by Athaliah. His son Amasias succeeded him in the kingdom, and after him his son Azarias reigned.

You see that, according to the historical account, three kings intervened whom this Gospel omitted. Joram did not beget Ozias, but Ochozias and the others whom we have enumerated. But since the evangelist’s purpose was to arrange three groups of fourteen in different periods of time, and since Joram had joined himself by marriage to the most impious Jezebel, his memory is removed up to the third generation, so that he would not be placed in the line of the holy birth.

It had also been said through the prophet that no one from the house of Ahab would sit upon the throne of the kingdom of Israel except in the fourth generation. Once, therefore, the stain of the foreign family had been cleansed and the three generations passed over, the royal origin is now counted in the fourth generation of those that follow.

“And after the Babylonian deportation, Jechonias begot Salathiel.” If we place the first Jechonias [Col. 1521D] at the end of the first group of fourteen, the next group will contain not fourteen but thirteen. Let us therefore know that the first Jechonias is the same person as Joakim, while the second—that is, Joachin—is the son, not the father. The former is written with κ and μ, the latter with χ and ν. Their names have become confused among Greeks and Latins through scribal error and the passage of time.

The blessed Jerome, following the historical account, explained this matter in this way. Jechonias himself is also interpreted as “preparation of God.”

Thus there are now not forty-two generations, which make three times fourteen, but forty generations, because one is counted twice—if we count Christ himself, who presides royally over the governance of our temporal and earthly life as though by the number forty.

But you, Lord…

## HOMILY LIV. ON THE VIGIL OF THE APOSTLE MATTHEW

*(From the works of the venerable priest Bede.)*

[Col. 1522A]

“At that time Jesus saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him: ‘Follow me,’” etc. (Luke 5).

“The same Levi is also Matthew,” etc. For the remainder, see the works of the venerable Bede, volume V of *Patrologia*, volume 94, column 419.

## HOMILY LV. ON THE DAY OF SAINT MATTHEW

*(From the same source.)*

“At that time, as Jesus was passing by, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew, and he said to him: ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him,” etc. (Matthew 9).

“We read the Apostle saying,” etc. For the remainder, see the volume cited above, column 249.

## HOMILY LVI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

[Col. 1522B]

*An account of the dedication of the church of Saint Michael and of the miracles displayed.*

The church, founded by the work of the blessed Michael the archangel and consecrated in his name, shows that the memory of blessed Michael the archangel is to be venerated throughout the whole world. It is commended not by the splendor of metals or by the privilege of signs, but by its form, made humble, and by its heavenly power, since the archangel, mindful of human frailty, deigned to build it with his own hand when he came from heaven to obtain for mortals there the fellowship of heavenly beings.

Situated on the summit of a lofty mountain, it appears to have been hollowed out of the mountain’s own [Col. 1522C] body in the form of a cave. The place is in the territory of Apulia, where the city of Sepontus lies between the Adriatic Gulf and Mount Garganus. The mountain rises twelve thousand feet from the city walls and bears upon its highest summit the church of the blessed archangel that I have mentioned.

A little book placed in the same church tells how this place became known to mortals.

There was in that city a very wealthy man named Garganus, who gave the mountain its name after an event involving him. While his cattle, whose number was immense, were grazing here and there along the sloping sides of the mountain, it happened that a bull, scorning the company of the common herd and accustomed to wander alone through the mountain, did not return home when the cattle came back.

[Col. 1522D] Its owner gathered a multitude of servants and searched all the byways; at last he found the bull standing at the summit of the mountain before the entrance of a certain cave. Angered, therefore, that it had wandered alone, he took up a bow and shot at it with a poisoned arrow. But the arrow, turned back as though by a blast of wind, struck the man who had shot it.

The citizens were troubled and amazed at how this had happened; for they did not dare to approach any nearer. They consulted the bishop about what should be done. He ordered a three-day fast and admonished them to seek the answer from God.

When it was completed, the holy archangel of the Lord addressed the bishop in a vision, saying:

“You have done well to seek from God the mystery hidden from human beings—namely, the reason why the man was struck by his own weapon. Know that this happened by my will. For I am [Col. 1523A] Michael the archangel, who always stands in the presence of the Lord. I have determined to dwell in this place on earth and to keep it safe, and by this sign I wished to prove that I am the inspector and guardian of everything that takes place there, including the place itself.”

When this revelation became known, the citizens made a practice of asking the Lord for favors here through Saint Michael.

They saw there two entrances. The southern one, which was the larger, could be approached by several steps descending toward the west. But they did not dare enter beyond the crypt; they devoted themselves daily to prayer before the entrance.

Meanwhile the Neapolitans, still straying in pagan rites, attempted to attack the people of Sipontus and Beneventum in war. The latter, instructed by the warnings [Col. 1523B] of their bishop, requested a three-day truce so that during a three-day fast they might implore the holy Michael’s faithful patronage and protection.

During that time the pagans, with theatrical games, invited the aid of false gods. But on the very night preceding the day of battle, Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop. He said that the prayers had been heard, promised that victory was at hand, and warned that the enemy should be met at the fourth hour of the day.

They were therefore made joyful and assured of angelic victory, and, compelled by the Spirit of the Lord, the Christians went out to meet the pagans. At the first preparation for battle, Garganus was shaken by an immense trembling; frequent flashes of lightning flew through the sky, and dark gloom covered the entire summit of the mountain. The prophecy was fulfilled that praises the Lord, saying: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Psalm 103).

The pagans fled, [Col. 1523C] driven partly by the sword of the enemy and partly by fiery arrows. Their pursuers followed them as far as Naples, cutting down everyone they encountered, until at last the survivors, dying, entered the walls of their city.

Those who escaped the danger, having learned that God’s angel had come to the aid of the Christians—for they saw that nearly six hundred of their own men had been killed by lightning—immediately bowed their necks to Christ, King of kings, and put on the armor of faith.

When they returned home as victors and brought vows of thanksgiving to the Lord at the archangel’s temple, they saw in the morning beside the northern entrance—which I said was like a small side door—what appeared to be the footprints of a man deeply impressed in the marble. They understood that blessed Michael had wished to display this as a sign of his presence.

Later, when a roof was added and an altar installed, the church itself was called Appodonia because of the signs of the footprints.

[Col. 1523D] There was much dispute between the people of Sipontus and Beneventum about what they should do with the place—whether they ought to enter it and dedicate the church there. After consultation, they built and dedicated, south of that place, a church in the name of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. In it they also established altars of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of Saint John the Baptist.

At last, having found a sound course of action, the bishops sent messengers to ask the Roman bishop what should be done. He happened at that time to be on Mount Soracte, about fifty miles from the city of Rome, which the inhabitants call by the name of Saint Sylvester because he had once hidden there in exile, praying with [Col. 1524A] his companions during the persecution of the faith.

He sent back this instruction:

“If it belongs to human beings, beloved brothers, to dedicate that basilica, it ought especially to be done on the day on which victory was granted. But if the holy guardian of the place has otherwise willed it, then especially on this day his will must be sought concerning the matter.

“Since this time is approaching, let us both undertake a three-day fast with our citizens, asking the Holy Trinity to bring to a definite completion the gifts that he has deigned to bestow upon the chief minister of his seat.”

It was done as the bishop had advised. On the final night of the appointed fast, the angel of the Lord Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop of Sipontus and said:

“You have no need to dedicate this church, which I built. For I who founded it also dedicated it. You need only enter and, with me as your patron, frequent the place in prayer. [Col. 1524B] Tomorrow, while you celebrate Mass there, let the people receive communion according to custom. It will be my task to show how I myself consecrated the place.”

In the morning they arrived with offerings and, with great persistence in prayer, entered through the southern royal entrance. And behold, there was a long portico extending northward and reaching the small side door outside which, as we said, footprints had been impressed in the marble.

Before one arrived there, however, a very large basilica appeared toward the east, reached by ascending steps. This basilica, together with its portico, seemed able to hold about five hundred people. It displayed a venerable altar, covered with a red cloth, near the middle of the southern wall.

The building itself was angular—not constructed in the manner of human workmanship with upright walls, but rough like a cave, with steep sides and many projecting [Col. 1524C] rocks. Its roof was also of varying height: in one place it could be touched by the head, while elsewhere it could scarcely be reached by hand. I believe that the archangel was teaching by this that God seeks and loves not the adornment of stones but purity of heart.

Outside, the summit of the mountain is partly covered by a hornbeam forest and partly spread out in a green plain.

When the celebration of the Mass had been completed, everyone returned to his own home, struck with immense and astonished joy. The bishop, however, appointed ministers, singers, and priests, constructed a dwelling, and ordered the entire daily course of psalms, hymns, and Masses to be celebrated there in proper order.

No one dared enter there at night, but after dawn had passed he sang the morning hymns there.

[Col. 1524D] From the very rock that covers the holy building, north of the altar, sweet and exceptionally clear water trickles down drop by drop. The inhabitants call it “the Drop.” For this reason a glass vessel prepared to receive it hangs suspended from a silver chain. It is customary for people, after receiving communion, to climb by steps to the vessel and taste the heavenly gift of the liquid.

It is sweet to the taste and health-giving to the touch. Indeed, some who have drunk of this drop during the long burning of fevers immediately obtain health through swift relief.

The sick are also frequently healed there in countless other ways, and many miracles are proved to occur there that belong only to angelic power—especially on the day of his nativity, when a crowd larger than usual streams there from the surrounding provinces, and the presence of angelic power is in some way [Col. 1525A] believed to be greater, so that what the Apostle said spiritually may be seen to happen bodily as well:

“For angels are ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation, in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Hebrews 1).

But you, Lord…

## HOMILY LVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

*(From the works of blessed Maximus, bishop.)*

[Col. 1525B]

“At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’ And Jesus called a little child and placed him in their midst,” etc. (Matthew 18).

“If you have listened attentively, brothers, to the Gospel reading,” etc. For the remainder, see among the works of Saint Maximus, volume 57 of *Patrologia*, column 445.

## HOMILY LVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL

*[From Haymo.]*

“At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” etc. (Matthew 18).

Whenever we read that the Lord’s disciples contended or asked among themselves about precedence, we ought not to attribute it to spite or envy, but to human frailty and weakness. For they were inexperienced and newly instructed; because they had heard him preaching his resurrection, and had not yet been enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they had not learned perfectly to love the heavenly kingdom. As the evangelist John says, “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7). They thought that, when he rose from the dead, he would possess a bodily kingdom and that they themselves would be raised to positions of honor.

Hence, at the time of his Passion, a dispute arose among them as to which of them would be the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. This suspicion had misled the mother of the sons of Zebedee when she approached the Lord, saying: “Lord, say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (Matthew 20). For the same reason Cleopas and the other disciple, to whom the Lord had appeared after his resurrection in the guise of a traveler, said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). And certain of the disciples, questioning him, said: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1).

The occasion for asking the Lord which of them was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven may perhaps have arisen from what came just before. For, as the evangelist related above, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” He also says: “When he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: ‘What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or the census-tax—from their own sons or from strangers?’ And he said: ‘From strangers.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Then the sons are free. But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you’” (Matthew 17).

Therefore, when the other disciples had seen Peter placed on an equal footing with the Lord in paying the census-tax, they reckoned that he had been set above them all. At that moment they approached Jesus, saying: “Who, do you think, is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”

But the teacher of humility, who says in the Gospel, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11), wishing to show that the kingdom of heaven must be sought not through pride but through humility, and that the greater person in it would be the one who humbles himself for God’s sake, called a little child and set him in their midst. He said: “Amen I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

This can be understood in two ways. We may take the little child here to be the Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he is great and greatly to be praised, and “of whose greatness there is no end” (Psalm 144), was born as a little one for us, and “a son was given to us” (Isaiah 9), in order to make us exalted. The sense is: Unless you humble yourselves according to my example—I who did not come to be served but to serve, and who became among you like one who serves, not like one who reclines—you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which has been prepared for the humble.

But if we simply understand any little child, it is readily apparent that by this example he urges us not only to humility but also to preserve simplicity. It is as though he said: Just as this child whom I have set before you as an example, when he sees a beautiful woman does not lust, does not covet another’s wealth, when injured does not retaliate, does not think one thing and say another, and when angry does not maintain lasting quarrels, so you likewise cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, prepared for the humble and simple, unless you possess in your minds the innocence that this child possesses in his body.

No proud person walks along its way; no swollen-hearted person proceeds upon it, because it is the difficult and narrow way that leads to life, and few are those who find it (Matthew 7). Therefore, when he says, “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” it is as though he had said: If an exalted position already delights you, first let the humiliation of an innocent life train you. He did not wish the apostles to be little children in body, but to possess the innocence of little children in their minds.

The Lord wanted his disciples to be such little children when he said to them: “Let the little children come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19). The apostle Paul likewise wished his disciples to have the innocence of little children, when he instructed them in his letter: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be little ones in malice and mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14).

The prophetic king knew himself to be such a one: exalted upon a royal throne but humble in mind, he said: “The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and he saved me” (Psalm 114). And again: “I will play, and I will make myself still lower than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6).

For he is a little one who displeases himself in order to please God; and before God he will be more beautiful in proportion as he is humbler in his own estimation. Hence it is added: “Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child is the greater in the kingdom of heaven.”

Let us therefore possess the virtue of humility if we wish to possess a place of exaltation in the kingdom of heaven, because, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14). Hence Scripture also admonishes us elsewhere, saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus 3). And again: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5).

And lest you should think that the one who humbles himself here for God’s sake is to be despised, he added an appropriate declaration, saying: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” This is what the Lord promised he would say in the future: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matthew 25).

He expressly says: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” Although we ought not to choose selectively those to whom, according to the word of Scripture, we should do good, nevertheless we ought to show special goodwill toward those who choose to be little and humble for God’s sake, in whose way of life we recognize Christ to be present.

Thus, when a pious father was instructing his son, he said: “Set your bread and your wine upon the burial of the righteous, and do not share them with sinners” (Tobit 4). And again: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it” (Ecclesiasticus 29). Hence the Apostle also says: “While we have the opportunity, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Galatians 6).

For whoever bestows temporal goods upon those in whose life and conduct he recognizes Christ dwelling, certainly gives to the one for whose love he bestows them. Hence it is rightly said, “in my name.” Many give temporal goods not in Christ’s name but so that they may win human praise. Of them it is written: “They loved the glory of men more than the glory of God” (John 12). And the Lord says elsewhere: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by men” (Matthew 23). And again: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6).

And lest we remain reluctant to receive guests or strangers, he promised that he himself is received in them when he said: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” Hence he also says elsewhere: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10). And again: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever despises you despises me” (ibid.).

Just as rewards are promised to those who receive others, so punishment is imposed upon the harsh and greedy, when it follows: “But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.”

Here we must consider how grave a sin it is to scandalize a brother, since such vengeance is threatened even against those who cause scandal. When he says, “It would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea,” he speaks according to the custom of the province, where among the ancient Jews capital crimes were punished by this penalty.

Let no one therefore think that the scandalizing of a brother is a light sin, since such a punishment is foretold for those who cause scandal. For, as he says elsewhere in the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5). The Apostle shows that he entirely avoids this when he says: “It is better for me not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which my brother is scandalized” (Romans 14).

He also restrains his disciples from this sin, saying: “Why do you scandalize your brother, or why do you despise him?” Therefore, insofar as we can, according to the Apostle’s admonition, we ought to avoid giving scandal to our brothers. If, however, scandal arises on account of the truth, the truth must be chosen rather than avoided for the sake of avoiding scandal.

Alternatively, by the ass’s millstone, which has weight but accomplishes no journey, the revolving love of the world is signified. When he says, “It would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea,” he excludes carnal people and lovers of the world from ecclesiastical rule. For it is better that a lover of the world, while living carnally in the world, should destroy only himself than that, placed in ecclesiastical government, he should by his perverse life drag himself and others to destruction.

For when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is also despised. While weak disciples follow the example of their patron, they too perish, and their destruction falls back upon the head of the one who is the author of the crime.

Or, alternatively, by the ass’s millstone teachers are understood. Just as a millstone breaks the grain of wheat so that its kernel may be revealed for the nourishment and refreshment of human nature, so teachers, opening the hidden meanings of sacred Scripture, make its inner sense manifest for the life and refreshment of holy souls.

“Woe to the world because of scandals.” The world to which woe is pronounced is not the world that the Son of Man came to seek and save, but the world that lies in wickedness—that is, the lovers of the world. Of this the Lord says elsewhere: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17).

Those who dwell in the world in mind and desire are rightly called “the world.” Of them John says: “The world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2). While lovers of the world, because of worldly desires, do not fear to scandalize others, they themselves nevertheless suffer scandal—sometimes in body, but always in mind. Therefore woe to them, because they spend their days in good things and in a moment descend to the underworld.

To them James says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4). To them also belongs what follows: “For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the scandal comes.”

When he says “it is necessary,” it is as though he said: It cannot be that scandals do not come. For there must also be heresies, as the Apostle says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11). And another Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27).

In a time of peace it cannot easily be determined who is good and who is evil. But when the wind of those who cause scandal has blown, it will cast the light and insubstantial away like chaff before the face of the wind, while it will gather the grains into Christ’s barns.

Woe therefore to the person who presents himself in such a way that the evil that is to come is accomplished through his ministry. Of such the Lord says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and cast them into the furnace of burning fire” (Matthew 13).

We understand this more easily if we bring forward one example: Judas, namely, the betrayer of the Lord. Of him the Lord said at the time of his Passion: “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom he will be betrayed” (Matthew 26). It was necessary that the Son of God suffer Passion for us, but woe to Judas, who made our good his own evil.

And lest anyone should think that, under the pretext of relatives or friends, he ought to withdraw from God’s way, the Teacher of truth removes every error when he adds: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna.”

How abhorrent this is according to the literal sense is readily apparent. But when we are driven beyond the letter, a spiritual sense must be sought. Since the hand, foot, and eye are necessary for our needs, the affection of relatives and dearest friends is signified here, as though the Lord said: If someone is precious to you as an eye, close to you as a foot, and necessary to you as a hand, and persuades you to withdraw from God’s way, cut off your love for him and throw it away from you.

It is better for you to enter life alone than, together with a great crowd of relatives, to be cast into eternal fire. “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Mark 8).

For example: a wife flatters, a father threatens, a mother persuades, a brother and sister weep; but you stand firm in the Lord’s way, lest by loving them uselessly you withdraw from the love of God. Rather, follow what he says elsewhere: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, follow me” (Matthew 8).

We do not say by this that we ought to be ungrateful or disobedient to parents and friends. But when they wish to remove us from God’s way, then let us cut off their love from us. When, however, we recognize that they love God, they must be loved and honored by us doubly: first because they are righteous, and then because they are our relatives. The Lord says in the Law: “Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you and you may live long” (Deuteronomy 5).

Hence the Apostle also says: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of the household of faith, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5).

How great a concern and care the Lord has for those who place all their hope in him, he makes clear when he adds: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” Those who are little and humble in the present life for God’s sake must by no means be despised.

They are little, as we have said, who are humble and despised in their own eyes. Of them the Savior says in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

Whoever therefore does not fear to scandalize such people offends God, who dwells in them, as he himself says through the prophet: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye.” And again: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Zechariah 2).

It is especially sweet what is added concerning them, explaining why they must not be despised: “I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18).

Here we learn that each of the faithful has an angel assigned to him for his protection, who both defends him from temptations and helps him in virtues, as the Apostle says in his Letter to the Hebrews: “Angels are ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1).

And the psalmist says concerning every righteous person: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways; and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 90).

We also read of Peter in the Acts of the Apostles that, after he had been led out of prison by an angel and had begun to knock at the door, the faithful who had gathered said: “It is not Peter, but his angel” (Acts 12).

The angels of the little ones therefore always see the face of the Father, because they go forth on our behalf in such a way that they never withdraw from his vision. Thus the angel Raphael says to Tobiah: “I am one of the seven spirits who stand before God” (Tobit 12). And Daniel says: “A thousand thousands served him, and ten hundred-thousands stood before him” (Daniel 7).

The angels who are guardians of our life are believed to announce our prayers and works to God. Thus the angel says to Tobiah: “When you prayed, I offered your prayers before God” (Tobit 12). And Daniel says: “From the day on which you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself in the sight of God, your words were heard, and I came because of your words” (Daniel 10).

But you, O Lord.

## HOMILY LIX. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT LUKE THE EVANGELIST

While I was diligently investigating, by reading the divine and sacred books, from what lineage the most blessed evangelist Luke arose, by whom he was instructed, which men he imitated, in what regions he wrote and taught, and where he rested and where his sacred body was carried, I found separate pieces of information in separate places. After selecting a little from many sources, insofar as my small talent was able to grasp it, I have tried partly to explain it in my own style and partly to copy what I found written by certain learned men. Our following discourse will make this clear to the attentive ears of your charity.

Therefore, the most glorious apostle and evangelist of Jesus Christ, Luke, was a Syrian of Antioch, a physician by profession, and a disciple of the apostles. He set forth their life-giving deeds, as he had seen them, in clear and eloquent language, and wrote them in a brief book to his beloved Theophilus.

Then he followed Paul, that outstanding teacher of the nations, up to the triumph of his Passion—the Paul whom he received at Rome together with the apostle Peter—and remained his inseparable companion in his travels, staying with him everywhere.

Joining the deeds especially of Paul’s journeys and sacred teaching to the book of those same apostles, he wove them together for the praise and remembrance of their names and for the strengthening of the universal Church.

While the same venerable Luke followed that most glorious Paul through many tribulations by land and sea, he deservedly earned from him the praise contained in such testimony. For, writing to the Colossians, he says of him: “Luke, my most beloved physician in the Lord, greets you” (Colossians 4). And writing to the illustrious Timothy, he says: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4).

In another place in his letter, among the rest of his greetings, he says of him to the Church of God at Corinth: “We have also sent with them our brother, whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. Not only that, but he has also been appointed by the churches as our companion in our journey” (2 Corinthians 8).

This evangelist of the Lord is, so to speak, a man praised by the mouth of everyone, since he deserved to be proclaimed by so great an apostle and teacher of the nations. Let us therefore praise him together with that apostle, dearest brothers, and let us exalt him with one voice, heart, and mouth, proclaiming him to be a true physician of souls sent by God.

All the words of his teaching seem to resound with nothing other than medicine for the ailing soul. Therefore he did not undeservedly receive such a name. “Lucas” in Aeolic, but in our language, is interpreted as “rising” or “raising up.” He is therefore rightly called “rising” or “raising up,” because, despising earthly things, he rose and lifted himself toward heavenly things, and with the whole effort of his mind followed the Lord freely and unencumbered.

Hence, while he was still held in the prison of the body, he was considered worthy both to preach his Gospel and to write to his followers. By the word of his preaching he also led many to faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

O most holy evangelist Luke, proclaiming far and wide the Lord’s true words, whose sound, first resounding in Aeolic ears, circles through the inner courts of heaven like thunder; and finally, as the psalmist says, not only extends to the western regions, but resounds throughout all the ends of the earth, a voice full of every sweetness.

O illustrious light-bearer of evangelical proclamation and life-giving grace, sending us from the eastern regions the light of faith, and clearly showing the path to those who wish to climb the way of heaven.

O healing medicine of the soul, most blessed Luke, who, smelling like precious spikenard ointment and soothing the hidden recesses of our hearts, never cease by your unwearied voice to invite us in every way to joys that will endure forever, where no sickness, no pain, and no groaning is found.

For this verse from a certain poet’s epigram can rightly be applied here:

> Traveler, do you wish to know whether the poet lives after death?  
> Behold, I speak in what you read; your voice, indeed, is mine.

When the Gospels had thus been composed—Matthew in Judea and Mark in Italy—Luke, prompted by the Holy Spirit, composed his own Gospel historically in the regions of Achaia and Bithynia, in Attic language, more from what he had heard than from command, as it had been handed down to him by those who had seen the Word of God from the beginning and had been teachers of the Word of God.

Beginning with the times of priests and kings, in this manner—“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah” (Luke 1)—he gives a full and orderly account of the history.

The teachers judged that the book of this most zealous evangelist Luke, considered together with the four books of the Gospels, is represented under the figure of a calf. A calf is a priestly victim, and this was fulfilled in the sacrifice of our Redeemer, who, suspended upon the gibbet of the cross for the salvation of the whole world, offered himself to the Father as a living sacrifice.

Concerning him the presbyter Sedulius, beautifully playing upon the subject in his description of the Paschal mystery, says in heroic verse:

> Luke holds the rights of the priest with his flourishing mouth.

And Paulinus, bishop of the see of Nola, sings in verse about this venerable man of the Lord, playing aptly on the theme:

> Luke, twice a physician: first by his profession, then by his speech;  
> Luke, twice a physician: as once he strengthened the bodily limbs  
> Of the sick, so now, in sick minds,  
> He composed twin books of medicines for life.
