Why should I say more about so truthful and outstanding an evangelist, who deserved to be praised by such great and eminent teachers—namely Jerome, Ambrose, and many others who are the walls of the churches and the fountains of eloquence?

Nor do I know what I can worthily say. Even if my voice were made of iron and all the limbs of my body were changed into tongues, I could scarcely fulfill fully, in his praise, what he deserves. But moved by love for so great a man, and not acting from the rash presumption of an ignorant person, but overcome by the charitable prayers of certain brothers, I have been compelled to write these things for your affection.

Now let us continue with what we omitted. For, so that the account of our mouth may be strengthened, we shall attach to this brief work of ours examples from that illustrious teacher Ambrose.

He says as follows:

“Most holy Luke, holding to a certain historical order, revealed many miracles of the Lord to us, yet in such a way that the history of his Gospels embraced all the virtues of wisdom.

“For what could be more excellent for natural wisdom than that he revealed that the Lord’s incarnation also came to be from the Holy Spirit? Hence David, teaching natural wisdom, says: ‘Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created’ (Psalm 103).

“He teaches moral matters in the same book of his Gospel, instructing conduct in the Beatitudes: how one should not strike, nor strike back at one who strikes; how one should do good and lend without hope of repayment, since reward follows more readily when it is not expected.

“He also taught rational matters when I read: ‘Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in much’ (Luke 16).

“What more shall I say about natural matters? He taught that the powers of heaven would be moved, that the Lord alone is the only-begotten Son of God; that at his Passion darkness came over the day, the earth shook, and the sun, withdrawing, took away the rays of its brightness.

“Thus he claims for himself all worldly wisdom and possesses the primacy of true spiritual wisdom, especially since, daring to take something upon himself, he placed the very mystery of our faith—the Trinity—in this threefold wisdom, namely natural, moral, and rational.

“If we believe the Father to be natural, because he begot the Redeemer for us; the Son to be moral, because, obedient to the Father unto death according to his humanity, he redeemed us; and the Spirit to be rational, because he infused into human hearts the understanding by which divinity is to be worshiped and life directed, then there is no difference of operations, no distinction, where there is no second fullness of power in the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.”

Now let us return to the order of the narrative. “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7), says the Lord.

Open therefore to us who knock, O Lord, who hold the key of knowledge, so that we may still be able to say something fitting in praise of your blessed evangelist Luke, for the edification of those who hear.

As the same Lord’s apostle testifies in the prologue of his Gospel, there were many who attempted to arrange an account of the Gospel concerning the events fulfilled among us, just as those handed them down to us who from the beginning saw the Word of the Son of God, ministered to him. Enduring records down to the present time show that these accounts, published by different authors, became the beginnings of various heresies. Such works include what is called the Gospel according to the Egyptians, and those according to Thomas, Matthias, Bartholomew, the Twelve Apostles, Basilides, Apelles, and others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

For the present it is enough to say that there were certain people who, without the Spirit and grace of God, attempted to arrange an account rather than weave the truth of history. To them the prophetic saying rightly applies: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart, who walk after their own spirit, who say, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when the Lord has not sent them” (Ezekiel 13).

Of them the Savior also says in the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10). He says “came,” not “were sent.” In those who come there is the presumption of rashness; in those who are sent there is the obedience of service.

The Church, however, founded upon the Lord’s rock by his voice, whom the king brought into his chamber, and to whom he secretly extended his hand through the opening of descent, like a fawn among the stags, pours forth four Gospels from one fountain, like the four rivers of Paradise. It has four rings and four corners, by which, like the ark of the Lord’s covenant, it is carried upon incorruptible wood.

This is also that chariot in Zechariah which, carried throughout the world, subjects the necks of all nations to the yoke of faith.

Moreover, the four rivers are beautifully said to proceed from one fountain of Paradise, by which the number of the four evangelists is signified, as well as the four perfect virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

For just as Paradise is watered by four wholesome and shining rivers belonging to the Lord, so our heart is watered by the four instruments of the evangelists. From this clear fountain of the Lord Jesus Christ, this holy man—namely, the apostle Luke, the interpreter of the evangelical book, concerning whom our discourse is—proceeds like the Euphrates and never ceases repeatedly to water and moisten our heart.

And just as the Euphrates is called “fertile,” or “fruitfulness and abundance,” so he too is rich in great fertility and abundance. Through the teaching of the Gospel he increases the faith of the holy Church spread throughout the whole world, and, like a ray of brightness coming from the heavens, illuminating the breasts of many people, he does not cease daily to enlighten them when his words are read in the Church as good news.

For “Gospel” in Attic, and in Roman usage, means “good news,” or “a new announcement.” It announces the incarnation and holy birth of Christ, as well as his Passion and resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and his coming to judgment with glory and a kingdom.

These are the seven seals with which John says that the book was sealed—one that no one can open, whether in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth, or loose its seals, except the Lion from the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5), that is, Christ.

Or the Gospel is called “good news” because it announces a kingdom after labor and life after death.

Therefore this very Gospel was rightly written by the evangelist Luke, as we said above, to that same Theophilus, to whom he also addressed the book of the Acts of the Apostles—that is, to one beloved by God.

It therefore also concerns you, whoever you are, O human being: if you love God, the Gospel has been written to you. And if it has been written to you, receive the evangelist’s most precious gift of pearls, and carefully preserve the pledge of a friend in the innermost chambers of your heart.

O what a gift, what a pledge, if you consider it, attend to it, and ponder it in your mind! If you preserve these things well and watchfully, they will lead you happily to joys that will endure forever, where, joined to the choirs of angels, you will rejoice without end.

This blessed Luke is also said to have been thoroughly educated in Greek eloquence. Apart from what the order of evangelical discourse demanded, he undertook a labor of the greatest necessity: first, to show the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ by a faithful account to Greek believers, lest those absorbed in Jewish genealogies should be held solely by a desire for the Law, or, deceived by heretical fables and foolish enticements, should wander beyond the truth.

Then, like a heavenly farmer sowing the seed of his teaching in the minds of countless people and breaking the soil by announcing it with the plow of his distinguished tongue, he converted them to faith in their Creator.

Doubling the talents of his Lord and bringing with him a hundredfold fruit, in order to reign forever in the jeweled halls of heaven, he hastened forward with the eager desire of an ardent spirit.

For he imposed martyrdom upon his body, wearing down his limbs with continual lamentations and frequent vigils. From the very time of his youth he persevered entirely in chastity, and he is reported to have had neither wife nor children.

Therefore, not undeservedly, he shines among the ranks of angels and the glorious choir of the apostles, among the praiseworthy number of prophets, the gleaming lilies of virgins, and the unfading roses and flowers of martyrs; and he enjoys fellowship with all the blessed saints.

Some also report that this evangelist was one of the two disciples to whom the Lord joined himself as they were going to the village of Emmaus, revealing himself to them in the guise of a traveler, opening their understanding, and wondrously bringing it about that they recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

When he was seventy years old, he died in the regions of Bithynia, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], and his body was buried by Catholic men.

After many cycles of years had passed, while Constantine Augustus was reigning, his holy body was transferred with honor to the city of Constantinople and suitably placed there.

Because we have learned nothing concerning the extent and nature of the miraculous prodigies that the Lord Jesus Christ frequently performs there, to the praise of his name, through the merits of this most glorious evangelist Luke, I shall refrain from recounting them.

This, however, is evidently what divine providence brought about: namely, that when the venerable relics of this evangelist Luke had been carried to many places, many signs of power might occur, and that more people, through remembrance of his teaching and virtue, might come together in faith and love for our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he preached.

He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout the boundless ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF ONE MARTYR

Because today the birthday of the blessed martyr has dawned, a day that the Lord has wished us to celebrate with you, dearest brothers, let us say something—since he grants it—about the glory and endurance of the martyrs. They despised worldly glory, and therefore their endurance was proved. For their glory lay hidden in heaven, because their endurance was exercised on earth. Whoever does not shrink from their endurance reaches their glory.

It is considered wretched to suffer harsh and difficult things in the flesh, because such suffering is truly burdensome. If it were burdensome to no one, it would not be glorious for the martyrs. Thus, to many pleasure-seekers and [Col. 1537D] greedy men, the holy martyrs appeared insane when they endured such things for Christ’s name. Indeed, they were pressed to deny him. Some were beaten for a very long time with rods and whips; others were struck with clubs and leaded instruments; others were torn limb from limb; others were killed with the sword; others were flayed and drenched with melted pitch and lead; others were tortured by the heat of burning coals; still others were consumed by flames; some were drowned in the sea; others were handed over to beasts; others were killed by the horror and hunger of prisons. As many kinds of punishments and deaths as the enemy could devise, so many he inflicted upon the martyrs without any pity. Yet although they suffered terrifying things openly, secretly they were crowned ineffably.

Many sought earthly glory; many brave men [Col. 1538A] considered that blood ought to be shed for their country, and did not hesitate to shed it so that after death they might also possess glory among their descendants. But what comparison can be made between their glory and that of the martyrs? What could an emperor discover that a fisherman could discover? In Rome there are the tombs of emperors, consuls, and brave men who subdued and subjected the world by arms. To whose tomb did an emperor deign to enter? And yet, after laying aside his diadem, the fisherman welcomed him praying at his tomb.

Behold: if the martyrs had desired earthly glory, they too were not deprived of it, since they sought such honor among the angels. We see their glories on earth and marvel. What would we suffer if we saw them in heaven? How great would be the astonishment of our wonder if we saw [Col. 1538B] the martyrs glorifying among the angels, whose anniversaries we see the peoples celebrating?

But we wish to rejoice with the saints and do not wish to endure the world’s tribulation with them. Whoever does not wish to imitate the holy martyrs, at least insofar as he is able, will not be able to reach their blessedness. Thus the Apostle also proclaims, saying: “If we are companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in consolation” (II Cor. I). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John XV). Whoever does not wish to endure the world’s hatred with the head refuses to be in the body.

But someone says: “Who is able to follow the footsteps of the blessed martyrs?” To him I reply that, with the Lord’s help, if we wish, we can imitate not only the martyrs but the Lord himself. [Col. 1538C] Hear not me, but the Lord himself crying out to the human race and saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Hear also the blessed Apostle Peter admonishing us: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). Similarly the Apostle Paul cries out: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. V).

What shall we answer to these things, brothers, or what excuse shall we be able to offer? If someone says to you that you ought to imitate the virtues the Lord performed, your excuse may be just, because it is not granted to everyone to perform virtues and miracles. But to keep God’s commandments is enjoined upon all of us. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself did not say: “Learn from me to raise the dead or to walk over the waters [Col. 1538D] with dry feet.” Rather, what did he say? “For I am meek and humble of heart.” And again: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V).

And although there are many other good remedies by which we ought to imitate God and the blessed martyrs, these two are nevertheless the chief ones: that we be meek and humble of heart, and that we love our enemies with all our heart and all our strength.

Concerning loving one’s enemies, dearest brothers, no one will ever be able truly to excuse himself. Someone may say to me: “I cannot fast; I cannot give all my possessions to the poor and to the churches.” Can he say: “I cannot love”? But someone says: “My enemy has done so many [Col. 1539A] evils to me that I can love him by no means.” You consider what a man has done to you, and do not consider what you have done to God. If you carefully examine and investigate your conscience, you commit, without any comparison, greater sins against God than a man has committed against you. And since perhaps you wish God to deign to forgive you much, why do you not consent to forgive a little?

But you, brothers, because every day in prayer you say to God, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” forgive, and it will be forgiven you (Luke VI). For Truth itself cries out terribly and says: “If you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

Let us therefore imitate the holy martyrs in faith, in humility, in gentleness, in [Col. 1539B] endurance, in patience, and in love. Thus we shall be able to have the martyrs themselves as intercessors before the Lord, so that our sins may be erased and eternal rewards bestowed upon us, through the gift of our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIV. ON ONE MARTYR

*(From the works of blessed Chrysostom.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves,” etc. (Matt. X).

The apostles sent by the Lord traversed the whole world. Finding it sick, they restored it to health; finding it placed in tribulation and ruin, they recalled it to [Col. 1539C] stability. They did not carry shields, draw bows, shoot arrows, distribute money, or rely upon eloquence. They were indeed naked with respect to the world, but clothed with Christ; poor, but rich; lacking money, but possessing the kingdom of heaven; without human comforts, but possessing their Lord. “I am with you,” he says, “all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

They traversed the whole world, sheep together with wolves. Who has seen this? Who has heard of it? He says: “I will send you like sheep in the midst of wolves.” What shepherd ever sends sheep into the midst of wolves? Rather, if he sees wolves, he gathers the sheep. But Christ did the opposite. He directed the sheep to the wolves, and they were not wounded by the beasts; [Col. 1539D] rather, the wolves were converted to the gentleness of sheep.

And so that they would not say, “We are sheep, and you are sending us as food for wolves,” he removed their fear with a single statement. He did not say, “Go,” for he was not sending them by their own strength; rather: “Behold, I am sending you.” You are weak, indeed, but the one who sends you is powerful.

Who are you? “I am he who stretched out heaven, who founded the earth, who bridled the sea, who dissolved death, who nailed to the cross the bond that stood against you, who changed the ancient law, who recalled you to your former homeland, who shatters the strong and strengthens the shattered.” What is stronger than the sea? Yet a little sand blunts and restrains its intolerable force.

“Behold,” he says, “I am sending you—I who have power over death and life, I who descended from heaven. Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves.” [Col. 1540A] I became a kind of wall for the sheep, so that, surrounded on every side, they might not preserve their safety even by flight. O the power of the one who sends sheep into the midst of wolves! Wolves were all around, and the wolves were changed and became sheep. For they were wolves not by nature but by will.

“Behold, I am sending you.” What then do you command us? “Be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves. But beware of men, for they will hand you over to councils,” etc.

Even if a serpent is wounded a thousand times, as long as it saves its head, it is entirely healthy. So also, if an adversary wishes to take your money, yield willingly. And if he tries to take away all your possessions, let them go. And if he desires to wrest away your very temporal life, do not resist. Only preserve the simplicity of your faith. If that remains unharmed, all the evils that assail you will be very easy to bear. [Col. 1540B]

Naked you came from your mother’s womb, and naked you will depart. Perhaps you will be sent into exile. Say: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII). Perhaps death will seize you. It is not to be feared, because it is a passage. Only preserve your faith, an unfailing treasure and everlasting riches.

The blessed martyrs, who did not lose their faith and who, after departing from the body, are stronger than the living, are witnesses to what I say. Therefore, he says, I became man; therefore I put on flesh: to save the whole world. For the Church is very dear to God—not enclosed by walls, but surrounded by faith.

For the sake of the Church heaven was stretched out, the sea spread forth, the air extended, the earth founded, paradise planted, and many miracles performed: the sea was divided [Col. 1540C] and then joined together again; the rock was split and then joined again; manna rained from heaven and was set down like a table covered with frost.

For the sake of the Church there were prophets; for the sake of the Church, apostles. And why should I say more? For the sake of the Church the only-begotten Son of God became man, as Paul says: “He did not spare his own Son” (Rom. VIII). In order to heal the Church, he shed the Son’s blood for the Church. This blood waters the Church.

Its plantings cannot wither, nor do its trees lose their leaves. It is not subject to the necessity of time, nor bound by the condition that during summer it cover itself with a crown of leaves but in winter lose them. It is not governed by the changing seasons, but the grace of the Holy Spirit guides it. [Col. 1540D] Therefore it does not grow old or contract, and it is not overwhelmed by its many assaults.

For how many attacked the Church from the beginning, when the seeds of faith were being sown and weapons were raised against it! But the more it was attacked, the more splendid it became. Now, by God’s grace, kings, commanders, soldiers, and the whole world are filled with faith.

For at the beginning, and, so to speak, in the infancy of the Church, kings were impious, commanders insane, and the people devoted to sedition. Judges’ edicts were issued everywhere; altars were burned for demons; smoke and the foulest odor polluted the very air. The earth was defiled with blood; demons raged; the devil ruled. A father disowned his son; a son dishonored his father. Nature was indeed torn apart, but piety was not [Col. 1541A] divided.

Where are now those who dared to oppose the Church? When it was new, it could not be harmed in any way. Now, when it has reached as far as heaven, do you think it can be overcome? At that time, when there were eleven apostles, no one could overcome them, and a few men captured the whole world. Now, when the earth and sea, the entire world, uninhabitable regions, cities, and all the ends of the earth are filled with piety, do you think you can contain it? You cannot.

For Christ suffered for it, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. Heaven could more easily be destroyed and the earth perish than the Church suffer any harm. Who says this? Christ himself speaks: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV). [Col. 1541B]

Good. For the word of God is stronger than heaven itself, because heaven is the work of the Word. God said, “Let there be heaven,” and the word appeared as a work. Nature proceeded; no one hindered it, because the Lord of nature commanded—he who can create and change.

“I built it,” he says, “I who established heaven. But for heaven I did not shed blood; for heaven I was not crucified; nor did I assume a heavenly body for heaven’s sake. And why should I speak of heaven? I did not assume the body of angels, so that you may learn that the Church is more honorable than heaven, than angels, and than every creature.”

Therefore, “heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” Let a Gentile be present; let a Jew be present. If these words are empty, let them refute them. But if what has been said is truth, let them worship God’s power.

Christ says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, [Col. 1541C] but my words will not pass away.” It is easier for heaven to pass away and earth to be swallowed up than for my words to fail.

But what are these words? Let us bring them forward and see whether they have perhaps perished. I do not silence doubters, but I close the mouths of heretics. What, then, are the words?

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” Which sayings? What words? “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

He said, “upon this rock,” not “upon Peter.” For he built his Church not upon a man, but upon faith. And what was the faith? “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He called the Church a rock because it receives the waves and does not waver. [Col. 1541D]

The Church receives temptations, in a certain sense, yet it is not conquered. What does “upon the rock” mean? It means upon Peter’s confession, upon the words of piety.

But perhaps you will ask whether this building receives stones, wood, or iron. No, he says; for it is not a material building. If it were such, it would be dissolved by time. But the confession of piety can be conquered neither by demons nor by any creature.

The martyrs bear witness: their sides were scraped, but their faith was not broken. O new material for a structure! The wall is dug out, but the treasure is not taken away. The flesh is torn, but the faith is not ruptured. Such indeed is the power of the martyrs.

“For upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it.”

Pay close attention to the word: [Col. 1542A] by “the gates of hell” he means dangers that produce death. What then? Does everyone enter hell when he is endangered? Yes. For just as gates are entrances to cities, so dangers are entrances to death.

And why, he says, does he not prevent temptations? In order to display the Church’s strength. If no one could attack it, they could say: “If it were attacked, it would certainly be overcome.” Therefore I permit it to be attacked, so that victory may be credited not to the weakness of those who oppose it, but to faith.

And he did not say that the gates of hell would not approach it, but that they would not prevail against it. What then? It will indeed be attacked, but it cannot be conquered. The Church receives storms, but it is not submerged; darts are hurled against it, but it is not pierced; engines of war are prepared, but it is not overthrown by the assaults of crowds.

And why do I say “the Church”? [Col. 1542B] A fisherman spoke one statement, and it remains immovable like a tower: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

How many tyrants tried to erase this word, but could not? For it was founded upon the rock. Consider tyrants, kings, diadems, sharp swords, the teeth of beasts threatening death, furnaces, frying pans, iron hands and hooks, and every device prepared. The devil emptied his quiver, but harmed the Church nothing, for the gates of hell will not prevail against it.

The event itself bears witness; the agreement of what happens bears witness: how many attacked, and no one prevailed. The attackers have been handed over to silence and oblivion, while the Church increases daily in power.

Where is Claudius now? [Col. 1542C] Where is Nero? Where is Tiberius? They are mere names; none of them remains, nor does any remembrance of them. And because they attacked the Church, they also lost their memory. But the Church shines ever more brightly.

Wherever you go—to the Indians, to the Moors, to the Britons, to the Spaniards, even to the furthest ends of the earth—you will find: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I), and everything filled with religion.

Previously, everything was filled with impiety. Now not only do cities flourish in religion and in the faith of Christ, but even the desert glorifies in the Lord’s name.

Formerly even queens danced at men’s banquets, as we read that Herodias’s daughter did (Mark VI); now scarcely would a servant girl deign to do this. In ancient times, among the Persian people, [Col. 1542D] sons were joined in marriage to their parents, and a sister was united to her brother with impunity; now they seek virginity.

Previously there was a certain people that fed upon human flesh; now they restore their souls through fasting. The Massagetae and Berbices consider those wretched who die from illness. When their parents, relatives, and kinsmen reach old age, they slaughter and devour them, saying that it is better for them to be consumed by their own people than by worms.

But now, after Christ’s passion and resurrection, they devote themselves to Christ through abstinence and chastity, and almost all peoples are prepared to shed their blood for the Lord’s name.

Previously kings were impious and persecuting; now they carry piety up to heaven. When they enter [Col. 1543A] the thresholds of the Church, they lay down their crown and paint Christ’s cross upon their foreheads.

Outside are weapons; here are the mysteries. Outside are shields; here is the celebration of the sacraments. The son of Theodosius and the father of Theodosius are distinguished by religion and piety.

Therefore, for all these things let us give thanks to the Lord, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, and to the Holy Spirit, throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXVIII. ALSO ON THE MARTYRS

*(From Pope Leo [?].)*

Whenever, dearest brothers, we celebrate the solemnities of the holy martyrs, let us expect through their intercession to obtain temporal benefits from the Lord in such a way that, by imitating the martyrs themselves, we may deserve to receive eternal benefits. For the joys of the holy martyrs’ festivals are [Col. 1543D] truly celebrated by those who follow the examples of those martyrs.

The solemnities of the martyrs are exhortations to martyrdom, so that we may not be reluctant to imitate what we delight to celebrate. But we wish to rejoice with the saints and do not wish to endure the world’s tribulation with them. Whoever does not wish to imitate the holy martyrs, at least insofar as he is able, will not be able to reach their blessedness.

Thus the Apostle Paul proclaims, saying: “If we are companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in consolations” (II Cor. I). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John XV). Whoever does not wish to endure the world’s hatred with the head refuses to be in the body.

But someone says: “Who is able to follow the footsteps of the blessed martyrs [Col. 1544A]?” To him I reply that, with the Lord’s help, if we wish, we can imitate not only the martyrs but the Lord himself. Hear not me, but the Lord himself crying out to the human race: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Hear also the blessed Apostle Peter admonishing us: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II).

Behold, Christ says, “Learn from me”; blessed Peter says that we should follow his footsteps. Similarly the Apostle Paul cries out: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. V).

What shall we answer to these things, brothers? Or what excuse shall we be able to offer? If someone says to you that you ought to imitate the virtues the Lord performed, your excuse may be just, because it is not granted to everyone to perform virtues and miracles [Col. 1544B]. But to live justly and chastely, and to preserve charity toward all, is enjoined upon everyone with the help of God.

For the Lord himself did not say: “Learn from me to raise the dead or to walk over the waters with dry feet.” He does not say this. Rather, what does he say? “For I am meek and humble of heart.”

And again: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V). And again: “You also, therefore, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (ibid.).

And although there are many other things in which we ought to imitate the Lord and the blessed martyrs, these two are nevertheless the chief: that we be meek and humble of heart, and that we love our enemies [Col. 1544C] with all affection.

Concerning loving one’s enemies, dearest brothers, no one will ever be able truly to excuse himself. Someone may say to me: “I cannot fast; I cannot keep vigil.” Can he say: “I cannot love”? He may say: “I cannot distribute all my possessions to the poor and serve God in a monastery.” Can he say: “I cannot love”?

If you say that you cannot abstain from wine and meat, we believe you. But if you say that you cannot forgive those who sin against you, we do not believe you at all, because no excuse remains for us when we are commanded to perform this almsgiving not from the storeroom but from the heart, so that we may deserve to reach our eternal homeland by the way of life.

For by these two commandments—that is, [Col. 1544D] “You shall love the Lord your God” and “You shall love your neighbor”—as though by two spiritual feet, if we wish to run along the path of true charity, we can happily reach our heavenly homeland.

Paul the Apostle ran with these feet when he said: “I therefore run, not as uncertainly” (I Cor. IX). Whoever loves his enemies fulfills in himself what the Lord said: “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Choose now what pleases you. If you love your enemies, you will deserve to be not only a friend but also a son of God. But if you do not wish to love your enemies, you cannot have God as your gracious protector, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III). And again: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because [Col. 1545A] darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II).

And another Scripture says: “The Lord brings to ruin unto death the ways of those who retain injury.” Are these my words, dearest brothers? They are drawn from catholic and sacred books.

Therefore, so that we may not be murderers or remain in darkness, let us strive to love not only our friends but also our enemies, so that with a free conscience we may approach the gracious and merciful Lord according to the bond of his promise.

For he himself said: “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

Pay close attention, brothers, and know that it is one thing to sin against God and another to sin against a human being. When people sin [Col. 1545B] against us, if we do not grant forgiveness to those who repent, we incur sin. But when someone has sinned against God, if we wish to forgive without great strictness, we become participants in their sins.

The Lord therefore says: “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.”

I ask you, brothers: what could be said more sweetly? He has placed in our power the manner in which we will be judged on the day of judgment. He did not say: “Go east and seek justice; sail as far as the west to receive forgiveness.” Forgive your enemy, and you will be forgiven; show mercy, and mercy will be shown to you; give, and it will be given to you.

Nothing is sought from you outside yourself. God directs you to yourself and to your conscience. He has placed within you what he requires. Therefore you need not seek the remedies for your wounds [Col. 1545C] far away. If you desire forgiveness for your sins, you can find it within, in the storeroom of your heart.

But someone says: “My enemy has compelled me to endure such great evils that I can love him by no means.” You consider what a man has done to you, and do not consider what you have done to God. If you carefully examine and investigate your conscience, you have committed, without any comparison, greater sins against God than a man has committed against you. And with what face do you wish God to deign to forgive you much, when you do not consent to forgive a little?

But if, as you are accustomed by God’s favor, you willingly receive these spiritual medicines that we have mentioned above, and carefully preserve them stored in the treasury of your holy conscience, then, with the Lord’s help, you will not [Col. 1545D] fear the devil’s poisons. Through hatred or anger, either bitter wounds will never be inflicted upon you, or, if they should perhaps creep in, they will quickly be brought back to their former state through charity, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIX. ALSO ON THE MARTYRS

*(From Haymo.)*

At that time Jesus, descending from the mountain, stood in a level place, with a company of his disciples and a great multitude of people, etc. (Luke VI).

Not only through the mystery of the Incarnation, descending from heaven to earth, did the Lord Jesus Christ deign to accommodate himself to human weakness, but [Col. 1546A] also, in his holy discourses, he so tempered his teaching for the instruction of human ignorance that not only the perfect but also the less perfect might be able to find the food of life. Accordingly, as the Evangelist related above, when he had ascended the mountain, his disciples followed him. There, when he had given more perfect commandments to those who were able, as it were, to grasp them, he did not wish to abandon the simpler crowds on their account; so, descending again from the mountain, he stood in a level place. By this action he showed that, in preaching, the discourse of teachers must be adapted to the capacity of their hearers. The mountain here signifies more perfect teaching, while the level places signify a humbler and more common preaching.

Those who are such that they can hear with the apostles, “To you it has been given [Col. 1546B] to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII), must be instructed in higher things. But those who, because of weakness of mind, cannot ascend to a loftier teaching must be educated in the smallest commandments, so that those who are altogether incapable of doing good may at least not be inclined to commit evil. The Lord showed this elsewhere by his example, when, in reply to a certain man who asked, “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?”—as though he were dwelling in the valleys—he said: “You know the commandments? You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property, honor your father and mother.” But when that man replied, “I have kept all these things from my youth,” he showed him the mountain of more perfect teaching, saying: “One thing is still lacking to you: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give [Col. 1546C] to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

But because those weighed down by the riches of the world can scarcely ascend this mountain, it is immediately added: “When he heard this, he went away sad, because he had many possessions” (Matt. XIX; Luke XVIII).

The apostle Paul likewise followed this example when he had ascended the mountain with his disciples, to whom he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II). But when he was dwelling, as it were, with certain unequal companions, he said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). For not everyone understands everything, nor are all instructed in the same way. The proud must be admonished in one manner, the humble in another; the chaste in one manner, adulterers in another; the drunk in one manner, the sober in another; men in one manner, women in another; the married in one manner, virgins in another; the devout in one manner, the impious in another; those who despise the world in one manner, lovers of the world in another; the peaceful in one manner, the quarrelsome in another; those who give away their own possessions in one manner, those who seize what belongs to others in another. Thus the former may hear what they should love in the promise of eternal life, and the latter what they should fear in eternal punishment.

For often what benefits one illness harms another. Poison, although it is a human being’s death, is a serpent’s life; and a gentle hiss calms horses but incites puppies. Following this example, therefore, teachers ought to temper their preaching, so that the perfect may find something they can always continue learning, while the weak may hear things from which they do not recoil.

The blessed patriarch Jacob showed this to us by his own example. When [Col. 1547A] he was tending the sheep of his uncle Laban and was to receive various animals as his wages, he took poplar and almond rods, peeled some portions of them, left other portions with their bark, and placed them in the troughs when the sheep came to drink, so that, looking at them, they might conceive offspring of varied coloring (Gen. XXX).

Jacob, the shepherd of sheep, signifies shepherds of souls, to whom it was first said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI). Water signifies Holy Scripture, according to Solomon’s saying: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing stream, a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII). The varied rods are the various meanings of Scripture. The sheep are led to drink when the faithful gather to hear the word of God. And when various [Col. 1547B] meanings are brought forward from the divine utterances, they are placed, as it were, like rods in the troughs. Some are to be peeled in part, while others are to be left with their bark, because, as we have said, the more perfect are to be instructed in the allegorical sense, whereas the simple and less understanding are to be fed according to the truth of the historical sense.

Thus, when the Lord taught the disciples on the mountain and wished to heal the crowds in the valleys, he showed that those who could not believe through the teaching of words might at least believe through the power of miracles. As we have said, the Lord made this clear by his own example when, descending from the mountain, he stood in a level place, together with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who had come to hear him. Here we should understand the seacoast as the regions of the Great Sea [Col. 1547C], especially since Tyre and Sidon, which are situated in the heart of the sea, are mentioned.

From this we learn that his powers had reached not only the kingdom of the Jews but also neighboring and foreign regions, when all were flocking together not only to hear the word of God but also to be healed of their diseases. Hence it is added: “And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.”

Many desired to touch him, from whom all power proceeds, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II). And therefore, because all power went out from him, everyone wished to touch him. For above he had also healed a leper by touching him, [Col. 1547D] and now the whole crowd sought to touch him, so that we may understand that his touch is healing.

The woman who suffered from an issue of blood for twelve years experienced this. When she touched the fringe of his garment, she was immediately healed of her infirmity (Luke VIII). At her touch power went out from him to such an extent that the Lord, as though unaware, asked: “Who touched me?” And his disciples said to him: “Rabbi, the crowds press and jostle you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But he replied: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.”

Spiritually, the person touches Christ who believes that he is the true God and confesses him with right faith. But pagans, Jews, and heretics do not touch Christ, because they scorn believing him to be the true God and do not wish to confess him with right faith. Hence, when Mary [Col. 1548A] did not believe that the Lord had risen but sought him dead among the dead and wished to touch him, she was told: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX). As though he were saying: “Because you were unwilling to touch me with the hand of faith, do not touch me with the hand of the body.”

The healing of those afflicted by demons took place not only through his presence but also through the invocation of his name in his absence, just as the disciples, rejoicing, say to the Lord: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke X).

It follows: “And he lifted up his eyes toward his disciples and said: ‘Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.’” Although the Lord was speaking generally to all, he specially lifted his eyes toward the disciples, whom he made worthy of greater grace. For Christ’s lifting [Col. 1548B] of his eyes signifies gifts of more abundant mercy. He lifted his eyes toward the disciples, whom he endowed more particularly with virtues, as we read elsewhere: when someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with you,” he himself lifted his eyes toward his disciples and said: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Mark III).

Let us hear what he says with his eyes lifted: “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” And what virtue ought to hold first place among the other beatitudes, if not voluntary poverty? For from it the other virtues derive a beginning and origin. Just as many branches and leaves grow from a single root of a tree, so many virtues are generated from voluntary poverty.

Whoever loves voluntary poverty will be merciful through generosity [Col. 1548C], not grasping through avarice. He will consequently also be meek, because one who loves poverty with humility does not seek riches through boastfulness. He will also be peaceful, because there is no occasion for quarrelling where there is no desire to acquire. He will also possess purity of heart, because just as those who love riches are troubled in spirit, so those who love voluntary poverty are concerned with the things of God and with how they may please God.

But we must carefully consider that the poverty which is praiseworthy is poverty that either does not desire to possess or, if it happens to possess, abandons its possessions for distribution on God’s behalf. Hence, to show that this poverty pertains to blessedness, the Evangelist added: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom [Col. 1548D] of heaven” (Matt. V).

Some are poor both in spirit and in possessions; others are poor neither in possessions nor in spirit; others are poor in possessions but not in spirit; others are poor in spirit but not in possessions.

Poor in possessions but not in spirit are those who have nothing yet desire to possess much. Poor in spirit but not in possessions are those who, according to the Apostle, are “as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Cor. VI). Such were Abraham, Jacob, and David, who, although exalted upon a royal throne, showed himself poor in spirit, saying: “But I am a beggar and poor” (Ps. XXXIX). And again: “I am needy and in labors from my youth” (Ps. LXXXVII).

Poor neither in possessions nor in spirit are the proud rich, who, enriched with resources, are nonetheless swollen in mind. Of them it is said in the psalm: “Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding [Col. 1549A] in this age, they have acquired riches” (Ps. LXXII).

Poor both in possessions and in spirit are perfect monks, who, leaving everything for God’s sake, do not even leave the power over their own bodies to their own discretion. And therefore, the poorer they are here for God’s sake, the richer they will be in the future life, according to the Lord’s promise: “Everyone who has left house, fields, father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children for my sake will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

“Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be satisfied.” What those who desire to attain blessedness ought to hunger and thirst for is more clearly declared by another Evangelist, who says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. V). To hunger and thirst for righteousness is to hear God’s commandments willingly [Col. 1549B] and to fulfill them even more willingly in action.

Such people will be satisfied when they are brought to behold God, whose commandments they received here with great hunger of mind, saying with the psalmist: “But I shall appear in righteousness in your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). Hence Solomon says: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I).

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Those who weep are called blessed—not those who weep because of the loss of temporal advantages or the death of loved ones, but those who weep because of the remission of sins or in expectation of the kingdom of heaven. They can truly say with the psalmist: “O God, I have declared my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight” (Ps. LV). And again: “My tears have been my bread day and [Col. 1549C] night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI).

Such people will laugh when what the Lord said is fulfilled: “Now you have sorrow, but I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI). We must not understand laughter here in a childish sense, but as exultation and joy of mind. Hence Sarah, rejoicing at the promise of offspring, said: “God has made laughter for me” (Gen. XXI). Of this laughter it is said through blessed Job: “The mouths of the truthful will be filled with laughter” (Job VIII). Of the same laughter it is also said in the praises of the Church: “She girded her loins with strength, and she will laugh on the last day” (Prov. XXXI).

Since the reward of martyrdom is attained through the merit of humility, it is rightly added after the other beatitudes: “Blessed will you be when people hate you, [Col. 1549D] and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, because of the Son of Man.”

Here it is shown that the persecution of the wicked is not to be feared but rather endured when it comes, because, as the apostle James said: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James I).

Yet this must be examined more subtly: we must not stir wicked people to persecute us, but rather, with as much justice and uprightness as we can, calm them when they have been stirred up. If they refuse to be quiet, persecution must be endured rather than justice abandoned. Another Evangelist declares this more clearly, [Col. 1550A] saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Murderers, adulterers, thieves, and invaders of what belongs to others endure many tribulations. Yet such persecution does not lead to blessedness; only persecution endured for righteousness does so. Hence blessed Peter admonishes us, saying: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an adulterer, or a robber. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name” (I Pet. IV). And again: “Who is there who can harm you, if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed” (I Pet. III).

Therefore the Savior rightly concludes, saying: “Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.” We must not grieve in persecutions but [Col. 1550B] rather rejoice, because the more harshly someone is afflicted here for righteousness’ sake, the more sweetly he will be rewarded in heaven.

Hence James also admonishes us, saying: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith is much more precious than gold tested by fire” (James I). And another Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

For this reason also the Savior, when he encouraged his disciples to endure persecution, set forth his own example, saying: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours.” And again: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

[Col. 1550C] Therefore, according to the Lord’s command and example, let us strive to bear all the adversities of this age with equanimity, knowing that if we have been chosen by him, we have been sent not to the joys of the world but to sufferings. Just as he was sent by the Father—who ordained that he should become incarnate for the redemption of the human race—so he is sent into the world for suffering.

Amid the scandals of persecutors, therefore, let endurance of sufferings be present; let us flee earthly desires that separate us from God, so that we may deserve to obtain heavenly rewards. Amen.

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “A certain man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his goods to them, etc.” (Matt. XXV).
