## HOMILY LXXXVI. ALSO ON CONFESSORS

*(From Haymo.)*

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “A certain man going abroad [Col. 1551D] called his servants and entrusted his goods to them, etc.” (Matt. XXV).

In the comparisons which the Lord proposed to instruct our ignorance, it must be carefully considered that certain things are proposed for our admonition in such a way that they apply specifically to the mediator between God and human beings himself. This is confirmed in the sequence of the present reading, where it is said: “A certain man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his goods to them.”

This man is to be understood figuratively as the Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he is God before the ages, became human at the end of the ages. Of him it is written: “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI).

This man [Col. 1552A] went abroad when, by ascending into heaven, he raised up his flesh, which he had assumed from human beings. From the time when it was first said to the first man, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III), the proper place of flesh has been earth. But this man went abroad because the flesh he assumed did not see corruption but ascended into the heavens after the resurrection.

The servants of this man are human beings, whom he created as rational creatures to serve and praise him. To serve this man is the highest freedom; to withdraw from his service is the most shameful slavery. Paul gloried in being his servant when he said: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus.” And again: “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers” (II Tim. I). And in the Psalm [Col. 1552B]: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV). And again: “I am your servant” (Ps. CXVIII).

The goods of this man are spiritual gifts, that is, virtues of the soul, which have arisen from his goodness and have been bestowed upon us through his generosity: charity, peace, patience, humility, chastity, sobriety, and things of this kind.

Therefore, as he was about to go abroad, he called his servants and entrusted his goods to them, because he granted spiritual gifts to spiritual people. And because not everyone receives these gifts equally, but one makes greater progress and another less according to the distribution of the giver, it is rightly said: “To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and he departed immediately.”

Just as a talent was weighed in various ways among the ancients, so the gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse according to the merits [Col. 1552C] of those who receive them—not in themselves, but in those who receive them. For one Lord gives different gifts to his servants, according to what the Apostle says: “To one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the gifts of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, various kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

The five talents signify the five bodily senses, through which the outward person is governed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The two signify understanding and action. And by the name of one talent understanding alone is expressed.

Therefore the person who receives two talents receives more than the person to whom five [Col. 1552D] talents have been entrusted, because there are some who perform whatever works they can through their outward senses and yet make less progress in spiritual understanding. There are also some who accomplish great things outwardly and understand even greater things inwardly. There are likewise some who receive only one talent, because they understand good things but make no effort to do them. Of such people it is written: “They are wise for doing evil, but they did not know how to do good” (Jer. IV).

That we must diligently devote ourselves to multiplying good works is made clear when it is added: “The one who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise, the one who had received two gained another two.”

We have already said above that the five [Col. 1553A] talents signify the five bodily senses, and the two signify understanding and action. To double five talents, therefore, is to serve God with the greatest devotion through the outward senses: giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, visiting the person confined in prison, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and fulfilling other works of mercy.

Talents are doubled, as it were, when certain people who are slower in understanding make progress in spiritual understanding through the practice of good works. Those who double the two talents are people who, by living well and teaching well [Col. 1553B], do not neglect to multiply the Church of God, keeping in mind what is written to Timothy: “Entrust the teaching you have received from me to people who are qualified to teach others also” (II Tim. II).

The Apostle urged spiritual servants to double the talents they had received in this way when he said: “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the measure of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, in generosity; the one who presides, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.”

But the one who had received one talent went away, dug in the earth, and hid his master’s money. He hides one talent in the earth, as it were, who occupies the intelligence he received from God in earthly activities and binds himself entirely to the love of the world.

But the time will come when spiritual people will rejoice over the profit they have acquired and lovers of the world will be ashamed of their desires. Hence it is added: “After a long time the lord of those servants came and settled [Col. 1553C] accounts with them.”

The lord is said to return after a long time because a long interval lies between the Lord’s ascension and his second coming. Then accounts will be settled with the servants, when he will strictly demand from us the gifts which he mercifully bestowed upon us, when, as the Apostle says, we shall stand before the tribunal of Christ to render an account for what we have done (Rom. XIV).

Blessed is the person who at that hour of examination is found to be such as the one who is described next: “The one who had received five talents came forward, brought another five talents, and said: ‘Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five.’”

For someone gains another five from five talents when, through the five bodily senses mentioned above, he performs whatever good he can. There are some [Col. 1553D] in the Church who, although they seem slower in intelligence, nevertheless, when they faithfully serve through outward ministry, are brought by his gift to spiritual understanding, to such an extent that they are sometimes even chosen for ecclesiastical teaching.

What reward he is to receive is made clear when it is added: “His lord said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.’”

All things of the present life are little in comparison with future goods, however great they may seem. Therefore the person who has been faithful over little is set over much, because the one who has properly distributed earthly substance will receive an everlasting reward for transitory things, hearing [Col. 1554A] from the judge himself: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

Then the one who had received two talents also came forward and said: “Lord, you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained another two.” He likewise gains another two talents who had received two from the lord, when the person who possesses understanding and action calls many to the love of God not only by living well but also by teaching well.

It should be noted that both the person who brought ten from five talents and the person who brought four from two are praised in equal words, when the lord says to each: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” which means, “Rejoice well.” How the servant rejoices with the lord is explained when it is added: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much.”

He is rightly told [Col. 1554B]: “Enter into the joy of your lord,” because he will receive a reward proportionate to the number of those whom he has won by living well and teaching well, and to the greatness of that achievement.

From these words we understand that those will receive a greater reward from the Lord in eternal life who, by living well, as we have said, and by teaching well, devote themselves spiritually to the instruction and teaching of others.

The Lord declares this more openly elsewhere, when the apostles say: “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone?” He replied: “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the lord appoints over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will set him over all his possessions” (Luke XII).

For the person who is set [Col. 1554C] over all his possessions will receive a double reward—not only because he lived holily but also because he taught worthily. Hence Daniel, speaking about the resurrection of the dead and showing that spiritual teachers will be set over all good things, says: “Those who have been instructed will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII).

Desiring to hear this desirable voice and ineffable joy, our most blessed Father, whose feast we celebrate today, strove, by teaching well and living well, to distribute the talent entrusted to him, so that he might return it doubled to the Lord—not only by admonishing the devout but also by restraining the reprobate.

And because, according to the voice of Scripture, “a wise [Col. 1554D] son is the joy of his father” (Prov. X), the merits of his joys increase in proportion to the growth of his spiritual sons.

Therefore it is necessary, dearly beloved brothers, that each one of us, following the footsteps of this most blessed Father, not hide in the earth the talent we have received from God, but strive with great desire to distribute it, so that we may return it doubled to the Lord.

And because one person has received the art of reading, another of singing, another of preaching, another of painting, and another of making things pertaining to the adornment of the church, each should strive to distribute to others what he has learned.

Not only in ecclesiastical ministries are such gifts found. There are also people in this congregation who possess various crafts by which they earn their living: some are masons, some carpenters, some smiths, and some stonecutters. Each person’s craft by which he is nourished will be reckoned [Col. 1555A] as the commendation of his talent; and if he instructs others in what he knows, he will receive a reward in the future.

The Lord shows how such a person ought to distribute the talent he has received when he says: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X).

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, each one of us must carefully and vigilantly consider how he may present to the Lord the talent he has received, doubled.

But if someone does not wish his talent to benefit others, let him fear the rebuke which the person who hid one talent in the earth heard from the Lord: “Wicked and lazy servant, why did you not give my money to the bankers, so that when I came I might at least have received what was mine with interest?”

And what follows will be fulfilled: “Take the talent from him and [Col. 1555B] give it to the one who has ten talents.” For whatever he has done without charity is not good in God’s sight, even though it may appear good before human beings.

Each person will possess a greater glory with the Lord in proportion to how generously he has distributed the talent he received for the Lord’s love. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. ALSO ON CONFESSORS

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “A certain nobleman went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return, etc.” (Luke XIX).

Since the disciples had heard above about the Lord’s Passion, [Col. 1555C] etc. For the remainder, see the venerable Bede, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* XCIV, col. 471.

## HOMILY LXXXVIII. ALSO ON CONFESSORS

*(From the works of blessed Pope Gregory.)*

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. And be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, etc.” (Luke XII).

The reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, has been opened to us, etc. For the remainder, see Saint Gregory, *Works*, volume II, *Patrologia* LXXVI, col. 1123.

## HOMILY LXXXIX. ALSO ON CONFESSORS

*(From Haymo.)*

[Col. 1555D]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, etc.” (Luke XII).

Among the other virtues that our Lord Jesus Christ taught the disciples, and through the disciples taught us, he particularly and preeminently set forth chastity. For when he had previously urged us to love voluntary poverty, saying, “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys,” he immediately added a teaching on preserving chastity, saying, “Let your loins be girded.”

That lust is located in the loins of men and in the navel of women, the Lord attests when, speaking of the devil to blessed Job, he says: “His strength is in his loins [Col. 1556A], and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). Thus, under the name of “loins,” lust is signified here when it is said: “Let your loins be girded.” We gird our loins when we restrain the heat of desire through the love of chastity.

John the Baptist had his loins girded in this way; of him it is written: “He was clothed with camel’s hair, and had a leather belt around his loins” (Mark 1). He was not among the unclean, who because of the discharge of semen were expelled outside the camp; rather, he displayed in the very clothing of his body the chastity that he possessed in his mind. Elijah likewise wore a belt around his loins (2 Kings 1).

Those who are not joined together for love of children but to satisfy lust do not have girded loins; rather, they belong to those who, because of uncleanness, are expelled outside the camp [Col. 1556B], being compared to senseless beasts. Whoever, taking the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute, certainly does not have girded loins, since, as the apostle Paul truly says, “without peace and chastity no one will see God” (Heb. 12).

How greatly incorruption of the flesh pleases God, he himself testifies through the prophet, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish” (Isa. 56). And in the Apocalypse it is said of such men: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins” (Rev. 14).

Although this must generally be observed by all the faithful, it is nevertheless specially enjoined upon ministers of the ecclesiastical order, since in the old law they were not permitted to eat the flesh of the lamb, sacrificed as a figure of the Lord’s body and blood, until they had their loins girded, the Lord saying: “Thus shall you eat it: you shall gird your loins, and you shall have shoes on your feet” (Exod. 12).

Again: “The Lord said to Moses: Speak to Aaron and to his sons: No man of your offspring in whom there is a blemish shall approach the altar. If he is a hunchback, or bleary-eyed, or has a white spot in his eye, or a skin disease in his body, or a continual itch; if he is blind or lame, if he has a broken foot or a twisted nose; if he is *poderosus* [perhaps afflicted with a foot ailment], or herniated” (Lev. 21).

Those who ought to handle the sacred mysteries with their hands and minister them to others must therefore be free from every unclean pollution [Col. 1556D], so that they may be chaste in mind and modest in body. We learn this from the conduct of David. When he came to the priest Ahimelech, he was unwilling to receive the consecrated loaves until he had testified that he and his men were clean from women—not merely from other women or concubines, but also from their own wives. For he says: “Indeed, if the matter concerns women, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before, when we set out, and the vessels of the young men were clean” (1 Sam. 21).

Therefore let each person examine his conscience; and if he recognizes himself to be incontinent in body, let him abstain from holy communion, lest he receive for judgment what was given to the faithful as a remedy, fearing that terrifying declaration of the Apostle: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

Alternatively, we gird our loins when we set aside all the impediments of the world, so that we may be able to plant the step of our mind firmly upon the way of God’s commandments. A man whose clothing is ungirded is hindered by his own garments from walking freely; but one who is girded can move freely in every direction.

A soldier girds himself for battle and carries a sword around his loins with which to strike his adversary. You, therefore, who desire to be a soldier of God, gird your loins—that is, set aside all the passing things and impediments of the world [Col. 1557B]—so that you may be able to fight not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Thus what the same Apostle adds may be fulfilled in you: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace” (Eph. 6).

In this manner the soldier Job girded his loins when he heard: “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 38). Hence also, in praise of the Church, it is said: “She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm” (Prov. 31).

Whoever is such ought to be set before others as an example for imitation, because the Lord says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” [Col. 1557C] (Matt. 5). Therefore, after he had said, “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning,” what are signified by the lamps except good works? To have burning lamps is to display good works for others to imitate, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

We must consider that two things are commanded: namely, to gird the loins and to have burning lamps, because chastity is of no benefit without good works, nor are good works of any value without chastity. We are first commanded to restrain the loins, and afterward to hold the lamps, because a person ought to be promoted as an example to others when wholesome desires are vigorous in his breast and carnal pleasure does not occupy his mind.

This was prefigured in the law, when Moses commanded that the Levites minister until their fiftieth year, and after their fiftieth year become guardians of the vessels, observing the proper age either for governance or for undertaking the office of preaching (Num. 8).

But one may ask why he commands us to hold lamps when elsewhere he says: “But when you pray, go into your room, and shut the door and pray to your Father” (Matt. 6). The answer is that those are commanded to display good works as an example to others who are so perfect that they are not puffed up when praised by men.

But to those who are imperfect, or whom human favor exalts, it is commanded: “But when you pray, go into your room [Col. 1558A], and when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

And because, according to John’s statement, “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence on the day of judgment” (1 John 3), all who have their loins girded and their lamps burning ought not so much to fear the Lord’s coming as to love it. Hence it is added: “And you must be like men waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.”

Our Lord went to the wedding when, ascending into heaven, he joined to himself the multitude of angels as a new man. He will return to his servants when he begins to be revealed in judgment.

Or otherwise: certainly the Lord comes to us every day when, through his grace, he visits our consciences [Col. 1558B] and inflames our heart with his love. He knocks when, through the distress of illness, he announces approaching death. The person who opens to him immediately is the one who leaves the body joyfully and desires to see the face of him whom he has always longed for.

He fears opening to the Judge who knocks when he recognizes that he has in no way obeyed the Judge’s commands; and he trembles at seeing him when he leaves the body, remembering that he despised him. He fears, as it were, seeing the Judge whose commands he does not recognize himself as having obeyed.

Just as the righteous love the judge’s arrival in his city, while thieves and robbers fear it, so those who know that they have in no way obeyed the Lord’s commands fear his coming. Only those love it who recall that they have lived rightly—those who preserve their life blamelessly, insofar as human frailty permits, and place their heart’s affection on the joy of the heavenly homeland rather than on earthly love.

Such was the apostle Paul, who, secure concerning his good works, said: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4). And again: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better” (Phil. 1). And again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

In this way blessed Martin was prepared to open to the Judge who knocked. When he was afflicted by the distress of illness and moved by the tears of his disciples, he said: “The struggle of labor in which I have fought until now is difficult, Lord; but if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse to undertake the labor for their sake. Let your will be done.”

What reward is prepared for such people, the Lord makes clear when he adds: “Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, will find watching.” To watch is for each person to be attentive in good works. The one watches well who believes rightly and lives rightly. The one watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light. Or certainly, the one watches who shakes off torpor and negligence and clings to the divine commandments with an ardent spirit.

In this way the apostle Paul urged people to watch when he said: “Awake, righteous ones, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). And again: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13). And again: “Watch and pray, and stand firm in the faith” (1 Cor. 16).

The character of the reward itself is further indicated [Col. 1559A] when it is added: “Amen I say to you, he will gird himself, and make them recline, and passing by, he will minister to them.”

For God’s girding himself means preparing himself for repayment. Our reclining means resting in eternal blessedness, according to what he himself says elsewhere: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8).

He is said to “pass by” when, after the judgment, he hastens to the kingdom. Or certainly, the Lord will pass by and minister to us when he leads us from the form of his humanity to the contemplation of the glory of his divinity.

At the judgment he will appear to all in the form of his humanity, to the righteous and the unrighteous alike, as it is written: “Every flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3). But after the reprobate have been condemned by just judgment, in accordance with what is written, “Let the impious be removed, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26), he will pass by only to the elect. He will raise them from the vision of his humanity to the contemplation of his divine glory, so that those who now behold merely a man may then be worthy to see God face to face, and to see in what manner the Father remains in the Son and the Son in the Father.

But because the end of the present life is uncertain for everyone, it is rightly added: “And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

The ancients divided the night into four watches, so that each watch contained three hours. The variations in the hours signify the different stages of human calling.

The first watch is the earliest period of our life, namely childhood. The second watch is adolescence or youth, which are nearly the same, as Solomon says: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Eccl. 11). The third watch is old age.

When the Lord calls some who are working well in childhood from this life, he comes, as it were, to watching servants in the first watch. When he leads others from this life in adolescence or youth, he comes as it were in the second watch.

If someone is unwilling to watch in the first watch, let him at least watch in the second—that is, if someone has been sluggish in childhood with respect to good works, let him at least in adolescence or youth shake off the sleep of torpor and exercise himself in good works while the strength of his body is vigorous.

But if someone is found to be so negligent and idle that he has watched neither in the first nor in the second watch, let him at least in the third—that is, in old age—come to his senses [Col. 1559D], and then not fear to watch, when he will have little time left for watching.

For divine mercy does not despise those who turn late. Through the prophet it says: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33). And again: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18).

But because the ancient enemy usually deceives lukewarm Christians in this respect—persuading those whom he urges toward sin that they will have a long life—the Lord, by warning us of the uncertainty of the end, adds: “But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.”

Literally, the meaning is this: if a householder who had a treasure stored in his house knew of the thief’s arrival [Col. 1560A], he would set watches, provide guards, strengthen the weaker places, and anxiously take precautions so that his house could not be broken into by any trick.

Spiritually, this householder is our mind. It sleeps in a falsely secure manner when, forgetting the day of death, it grows sluggish in good works and promises itself, as though it were long, the very short time of the present life.

The thief’s arrival is death, which comes suddenly and unexpectedly and carries the treasure of our soul away to punishment. Therefore, if we wish to guard against the arrival of this thief, we must always keep the day of death before our eyes.

It helps us greatly against sin if the end of life does not depart from our memory, as Scripture admonishes: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7).

Hence the Lord also adds by way of warning: “You also must be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect him, the Son of Man will come.”

If we knew the term of our life, we might perhaps assign one time to pleasure and another to repentance. But since the hour of death is uncertain for everyone, a conscience must not be secure from good works. For almighty God, who does not wish anyone to perish but all to come to the knowledge of truth, wished the final day to remain hidden from us so that, while one day is unknown, every day might be observed.

When he says that the Son of Man will come at an hour when we do not expect him, if we refer this to the day of judgment, it is clear that the day is uncertain and unknown to all, as he himself says in the Gospel: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone” (Matt. 13). And again: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24). And again: “As lightning comes out from the east and reaches to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (ibid.).

After his resurrection, when the disciples asked him, he said: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). Hence the apostle Peter says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (2 Pet. 3).

But what will then happen generally to all in the resurrection of souls and bodies happens daily in individual souls. For the Son of Man comes when, overtaken by sudden death, we find that the limit of our sinning is also the limit of our living [Col. 1560D].

And while we do not abandon evil things, but are abandoned by evil things, we practice late repentance, not attending to what is written: “Do not delay turning to God, and do not postpone from day to day, lest his wrath come suddenly and destroy you in the time of vengeance” (Ecclus. 5).

## HOMILY XCIII. ON VIRGINS

*(From Haymo.)*

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who found it hid, and for joy over it went and sold all that he had and bought that field,” etc. (Matt. 13).

The Virtue and Wisdom of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, not only deigned, out of compassion for humanity, to assume human nature, but also, condescending to human ignorance, frequently employed comparisons drawn from temporal things in his holy sayings, so that by comparing visible things he might stir the minds of his hearers to love invisible things.

Therefore, when he taught that heavenly glory should be loved diligently, he used the likeness of those things that people are accustomed to love most, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who found it hid.” By the name of “treasure” we must spiritually understand the love of the heavenly homeland [Col. 1561D], where there are riches that do not fail, a treasure that never withers, and where the Lord admonishes us to store up treasure, according to what he says elsewhere: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal; for where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6).

This treasure is accumulated all the more, the more diligently one spends one’s temporal treasure and resources for God. Hence it is said of the man who found the treasure: “And for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”

The field in which the hidden treasure is found is ourselves, provided that heavenly desire remains within us [Col. 1562A]. The man buys it by selling everything who afflicts his body through the discipline of the heavenly homeland, in fasts, vigils, and prayers.

The man also buys the field with its discovered treasure by giving everything who, crucifying his members with their vices and desires, follows Christ and, in a kind of spiritual exchange, transforms himself by turning away from evil and doing good.

The Lord urged someone to buy this treasure hidden in the field when he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19).

It should be noted that the treasure, once found, is hidden so that it may be preserved, so that we may understand how diligently we must avoid vainglory in good works. For the present life is like a road; the robbers beside the road are unclean spirits, who especially envy those whom they see striving toward the heavenly homeland with a spiritual treasure.

Thus the prophet says of their leader: “He sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, to kill the innocent” (Ps. 9). These robbers seize the riches of those who expose their good works before men through empty boasting.

Therefore, when we perform a good work outwardly, we must always keep our intention of pleasing God hidden, in accordance with what he himself admonishes us: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” And again: “But when you pray, go into your room, and shut the door and pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret [Col. 1562C], will repay you” (Matt. 6).

To kindle the mind in love of heavenly desire, another comparison is given when it follows: “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls; and when he found one precious pearl, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.”

By the name of the precious pearl, we understand the sweetness or splendor of the eternal homeland, which is more precious than all precious things and sweeter than every delight.

Spiritually, we are merchants who are commanded to purchase heavenly glory with earthly resources. It should be noted that he says, “He sold all that he had and bought it,” because the person who buys the one precious pearl—that is, the heavenly homeland—by giving everything is the one who renounces not only earthly resources but also his own will.

Whoever gives his possessions to the poor but still serves his own will has not yet bought the precious pearl, because he has retained what he could have offered to God as more valuable. For God does not seek our possessions, but us; he commanded us to give earthly substance only for the sake of gaining souls.

Since, therefore, we are compared both to the merchant seeking good pearls and to good pearls, we must preserve in our work what we have received in the name.

Just as earthly merchants are not prevented from pursuing their business by the dangers of the sea, are not terrified by the ambushes of robbers, are not deterred by the harsh hazards of the journey, and are held back neither by winter’s cold nor by summer’s heat, provided only that they can acquire earthly profit, so we, who are spiritual merchants [Col. 1563A], must not be held back from love of the heavenly homeland by any allurements of the world; no adversity of the world must terrify us, and no tribulation must prevent us, so that, loving the precious pearl, we may be able to say with the Apostle: “Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

Let us imitate another practice of merchants. Those who devote themselves to commercial activities have this characteristic: if they suffer losses in one business, they apply themselves more diligently to commercial activities until they recover in another enterprise what they lost in one.

So also, if we suffer damage to our soul in some circumstance, let us apply ourselves more diligently to the good work we have begun, so that what we lost through negligence we may recover through good work. Thus we may attain the profit of the precious pearl and be worthy to hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

This pearl is so precious that it cannot be compared with any earthly riches, and so inexpensive that it can be acquired by good will alone. Zacchaeus sought to purchase this precious pearl with many possessions. When he had received the giver of this pearl into his house, he said out of excessive joy: “Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19).

The widow also purchased this pearl by casting two small coins into the treasury. The Lord himself, witness to her conscience, praised its value, saying: “Amen I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all who have put into the treasury” (Mark 12). “For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in everything she had, her entire livelihood.”

The most blessed N., whose feast we celebrate today, purchased the beauty of this pearl by giving many riches, when, for love of it, she abandoned the power of a kingdom [Col. 1563D] and rejected the bed of royal marriage, devoting herself to voluntary poverty.

Therefore, without doubt, because she despised marriage with an earthly king, she became the bride of the heavenly King; and she who did not wish to reign with an earthly king in the world reigns with Christ in heaven.

And because she avoided the greetings and services of royal officials, she now ministers to Christ, joined to the companies of angels.

Therefore it is fitting that we who venerate a temporal queen with due honor should entreat this queen, pleasing to God, with devout prayers, so that, because she has gathered us together in the name of Christ by her example, she may make us joyful in the present life through her merits and prayers and render us acceptable in the future.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind.”

The Church is beautifully compared to a net, because it has been entrusted to a fisherman and daily catches human beings within the net of faith. Just as it belongs to fishermen to draw fish from the depths and whirlpools to the shore with a net, so the Church daily strives, through the teaching of preachers, to draw human minds from the world’s turbulent and bitter whirlpools back to the true light.

And because, as long as it is in the present life, the Church gathers both the good and the wicked, it is rightly added concerning this net: “When it was full, they drew it ashore, sat down, and selected the good into vessels, but threw the bad away.”

When the good and the wicked are named, the Church of the present age is signified. The good are found nowhere alone except in heaven; the wicked nowhere alone except in hell. This Church, which stands between the two, receives citizens of both homelands, as the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39).

It should be considered here that many reprobates can now enter the Church, beyond the number of the elect, but they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. Hence it is well said: “They selected the good into their vessels, but threw the bad away.”

These words plainly show that the separation of the elect and the reprobate will take place at the end of the world. Just as the sea signifies the world, so the shore of the sea signifies the end of the world.

They sat on the shore and selected the good into their vessels, but threw the bad away, because at the end of the world the elect will be taken up into glory and the reprobate separated for punishment, according to what the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel: “In that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left” (Luke 17).

Therefore, in explaining the parable, the Lord added: “So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

This is what the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin” (Matt. 13).

And when asked about the weeds that the enemy had sown among the wheat, he answered: “Let both grow until the harvest; and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn” (ibid.).

The same thing is said elsewhere by the Lord: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats,” etc. (Matt. 25).

In the statement that follows, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” the nature of the punishments is plainly described. The eyes usually shed tears because of excessive smoke, while the teeth gnash because of intense cold.

When he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows that the reprobate in Gehenna will endure both intolerable cold and immeasurable heat, in accordance with what is said through blessed Job: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat, and down to the underworld is their sin. Let mercy forget him; worms are his sweetness” (Job 24).

When the parable had been completed [Col. 1565A], the Savior asked the disciples about its meaning, showing pious teachers that, if they are to instruct others, they must sometimes ask questions. For he said: “Have you understood all these things?” When they answered, “Yes,” he rejoiced in their progress, saying: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.”

That this applies especially to the apostles is clear from the fact that they are compared to a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.

If by “new and old” we understand the Old and New Testaments, we recognize that Abraham and Moses and the other fathers who lived before the Lord’s coming did not bring forth new things together with old things. For although they foretold new things, they did not see the Lord’s new incarnation with bodily eyes, as he himself says to his disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10).

The apostles, however, spiritually understood new and old things, and they saw the new things with bodily eyes. To them he said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13).

Or otherwise: the old things pertain to punishment, while the new things pertain to glory. It was old for man, after sin, to go to punishment; but something new happened to him through the Redeemer’s coming, when glory was promised to those who worked well.

Therefore, when the Lord praises the disciples, saying, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old,” he shows teachers the order to be observed in preaching: they should bring forth old things concerning the terror of punishment and new things concerning the promise of reward.

The Lord also shows this by his example in the sequence of this reading, when in the earlier parables he stirred people toward reward and in the following ones threatened punishment. Thus, as has been said, he shows teachers that they should promise glory to those who work well while never ceasing to threaten sinners with punishment.

This was also figuratively shown in the law, when through Moses he gave the following command: “You shall not take as a pledge the upper or lower millstone, for he has pledged his life to you” (Deut. 24).

The upper and lower millstone signify hope and fear. We receive a pledge, as it were, from debtors when we receive a sinner’s confession. If we do not promise forgiveness to the penitent, we deny mercy and take away the upper millstone. But if we give the sinner security, we remove the lower one.

Both must be observed, so that we promise forgiveness to penitents in such a way that we threaten those who persist in sin with punishment, in order that those whom promised rewards do not move to do good may at least be frightened by announced punishments.

You, however—

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins [Col. 1566B] who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride,” etc. (Matt. 25).

What the ten virgins signify, etc. For the remainder, see blessed Augustine, *Works*, volume V, *Patrologia* 38, column 573.

## HOMILY XCV. ALSO ON VIRGINS

At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride,” etc. (Matt. 25).

I often admonish you, dearly beloved brothers, etc. For the remainder, see the works of Saint Gregory, volume II, *Patrologia* [Col. 1566C] 76, column 1118.

## HOMILY XCVI. ALSO ON VIRGINS

Nevertheless, although the parable has a spiritual meaning, there is no harm in interpreting it also in a literal, bodily sense. Etc. ## HOMILIES OF PAUL THE DEACON, ALSO CALLED WINFRID. (S)

## HOMILY ONE. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

*(From Martène, enlarged Collection, volume IX.)*

[Col. 1565D]

Although the merits of all the saints are worthy of veneration in our devotion, nevertheless the feast of the glorious and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, must be venerated with our whole affection. For each of the saints has brought the aid of particular intercessions in their several places. But this most blessed virgin and mother, singular in glory, has brought universal aid to the whole world, which was corrupted by the stain of sin. Yet when is a feeble intellect and parched tongue sufficient to proclaim such great praise, when not even the philosophers’ lavish eloquence could suffice? Nor is it surprising that this most holy Virgin surpasses the capacities of human speech in her praises, since she also transcended the nature of the human race by the excellence of her merits.

Nevertheless, we must not remain entirely silent about her praise, because, although the poverty of our understanding is inadequate to the task, the devotion of a devout mind is nevertheless sufficient before God; nor should we doubt that she can provide a spark of wisdom for speaking about herself, since she bore in her most chaste womb the fullness of all wisdom. She can also grant efficacy to speech when she wills, for she carried in her virginal womb the Word made flesh, through whom all things were made.

But what, dearest brethren, should we first select, or what above all, from such great virtues, since nothing insignificant or mediocre, but everything supreme, is to be said? For what virtue, beloved, could have been lacking to this blessed Virgin, when she was full of the gifts of every grace? Thus, in a manner previously unheard of, she was greeted by the angel with the highest praise: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28).

What, I ask, could this Virgin have lacked in justice or holiness, who received so abundantly the fullness of grace through a mercy so efficacious? Or what place could there have been for vices in her soul or body, when she became the Lord’s temple, as it were, in place of heaven, which contains all things?

This is truly that house of which Solomon speaks—understanding, of course, that the passage also signifies the Church in another sense: “Wisdom built her house; she hewed out her seven pillars” (Prov. 9:1). For this virginal house was supported by seven pillars, because this revered Mother of the Lord was enriched with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and the fear of the Lord.

Eternal Wisdom made her such that she would be altogether worthy for him to assume flesh from her—the immeasurable price, namely, of human salvation. What more worthy than this Virgin, dearest brethren? What holier could have arisen within the succession of the human race? No patriarch, no prophet, none of the ancients, none of those who came after, no human being at all could be compared with her. For how could anyone be judged comparable to her, when, beyond the excellence of virginity, she towers above all through the fruit of such sublimity?

Nor is it surprising that this wondrous Virgin surpasses the height of all mortals, since in this respect she also excels the merit of the blessed angels. Concerning this fruit, God the Father speaks to David, addressing him as patriarch: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11).

The most glorious of the prophets, Isaiah, foreseeing this outstanding Virgin by prophetic spirit many years beforehand, said: “A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). And how fittingly, dearest brethren, was this blessed virgin and mother signified by the name “branch”: she who both shone forth with the purpose of perfect action toward heavenly things and, entirely free from the knots of vice, gleamed with flexibility through humility.

Therefore she not undeservedly produced a flower, because she adorned the fields of the whole world with sacred blossoms. For the singular flower is our Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

In the lily, an outwardly white color and an inwardly fiery one are discerned: for our Redeemer possesses whiteness from the virginity of his flesh, and also the radiance of fire from the power of his divinity. For it is written: “The Lord our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29).

This lily is not born in the mountains but in the valleys, because Christ the Lord, abandoning the proud, is found in humble hearts. This holy Mother of the Lord can also be signified by the name “lily”; the virgin likewise can be so signified. Hence the Song continues: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2:2). Although this may also be understood of the universal Church, it can nevertheless be applied more appropriately and specifically to this Virgin.

The lily surpasses the other flowers by the extraordinary brilliance of its whiteness and is no less distinguished by the sweetness of its fragrance; hence it is very aptly compared to virginal beauty. This flower is raised from the earth from which it has sprung, and, bending outward, opens itself entirely toward the heavens. On the outside it is exceedingly white; within, however, it glows with a reddish flame, and it also has, as it were, a projecting little thyrsus in its middle.

So, indeed, sacred virginity despises earthly things with every effort and strives toward what is above. The purity of virginal flesh shines outwardly with whiteness; inwardly it burns with love of the twofold charity. It gives forth the fragrance of a good reputation through its way of life and stretches toward exalted things through the continual purpose of the heart.

But this lily of precious growth, as sacred Scripture bears witness, is found among thorns, so that venerable virgins may know that they must endure the troubles of the people among whom they live and bravely overcome the piercing trials of wicked spirits, so that through these things they may deserve to be called by the Lord “my beloved among the daughters.”

The bride had seen the bridegroom coming to gather these lilies when she said: “My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices, to gather lilies” (Song 6:1). The Lord descends into his garden when he comes either to the Church generally or to each soul individually. The bed of spices is that soul which is watered by a heavenly gift and appears filled, as it were, with various virtues like spices.

The Lord visits such minds in the Church as produce the shoots of virtues; but he comes especially for this purpose: to lead the souls of blessed virgins to the heavenly bridal chamber. For, as we are taught by the testimony of frequent readings, the Redeemer of the human race himself habitually comes in person to the sacred death of virgins. If this is believed concerning other virgins, it must be judged much more true of his most holy mother, that her own Son and Creator himself lifted her to heaven on this day.

But what tongue, what words, could ever suffice for the triumph of such a sublime and glorious ascent, when human judgment fails before the thought of such excellence? Take heed, therefore, O virgin, and be vigilant, lest you be deprived of such honor. You shine with the beauty of chastity and, having become the good odor of Christ, give forth fragrance like a lily. Do not let the poisons of the persuading enemy entice you; do not in any way diminish what shines with such brilliance.

A virgin in the flesh but not in the spirit does not obtain the reward of virginity. It is one thing bravely to resist the allurements of temptations; it is another to yield weakly when they creep in gently. Nor is modesty alone sufficient for you to receive the rewards of virginity, unless you are also endowed with other virtues.

Nor will you be able to guard so great a treasure unless your breast is possessed by continual humility. Always remember this glorious virgin mother, who deserved to be exalted to such sublimity because she was humble. Do not seek perishable riches on earth, since you will possess eternal rewards in heaven. Flee the excess of possessions; flee the joy of the world, since you are to enjoy heaven and rejoice with its angels.

Guard your heart with every care; restrain your tongue from idle words. In all things, venerable virgin, show yourself such that you may be gathered like a lily from the garden of the Church and may be worthy to be joined forever to the King of virgins.

But my speech is also addressed to you, women whom divine love has inflamed so greatly that, leaving husbands, children, property, and estates, you have come with manly courage to the service of God. Do not abandon the path once begun; do not, having once placed your hand upon the plow of the cross, look back, lest you return in your hearts to Egypt and take delight in the attractions of onions and melons. Rather, strive through humility to remain what you began to be, knowing in all things that, if you persevere to the end, you will receive the glory of rewards according to the merit of virgins.

To you also, if there is any woman who remembers that she has sinned, I give this counsel: recall the confession of Mary Magdalene. As though placed at the Lord’s feet, wash away your former stains with fountains of tears, so that you too may deserve to hear from the Lord himself: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you” (Luke 7:50).

“In my Father’s house,” as the Lord says, “there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2), and each soul is honored there according to its merits. Yet the ardor of everlasting charity will be so great there that each person will rejoice to possess in another what he does not possess in himself.

Therefore retain the good of charity with the whole effort of your minds together; exclude from your senses the plague of all envy and malice; and, according to the Apostle’s word, “rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things,” so that in this life, full of troubles and miseries, living peacefully and soberly, you may in the eternal homeland possess, through the harmony of charity in another, even what is not granted to each one of you individually.

You have as the helper of your struggle this most glorious virgin and mother, under whose protection you have taken refuge; for she who brought salvation to the whole suffering world, through her customary compassion, intercedes for all with her Son and Lord—

## HOMILY II. ON THE GOSPEL: “Jesus entered a certain village,” etc.

### 1

The sequence of the sacred reading that has flowed to us from the evangelical fountain, although small in appearance and proceeding by a shortened path, is nevertheless expanded inwardly through great stretches of usefulness. For we heard that he whom the world cannot contain according to the excellence of his divinity was received in the form of humanity within the small cottage of faithful women. One of them, called Martha, offered him bodily service; the other, called Mary, clung to him with spiritual contemplation.

But this very different service of the two women must certainly be interpreted according to mystical meanings. For two lives are practiced by good believers in this time of mortality: one is called active, the other contemplative. The Greeks called the first *praktikē*—that is, “practical”—and the second *theōrētikē*—that is, “theoretical” or “contemplative.”

These two sisters, therefore, beloved by the Lord, signify these two spiritual lives by which the holy Church is exercised in the present age. Martha signifies the active life, through which we are joined to our neighbor in charity; Mary, the contemplative life, through which we sigh toward the love of God in compunction.

One was intent upon work, the other upon contemplation; one served the active life through outward ministry, the other the contemplative life through the heart’s suspension in the word. The active life is that which is occupied in works of righteousness for the benefit of one’s neighbor; the contemplative life is that which, free from every business, is fixed upon the love of God alone.

The one consists in good conduct, the other in contemplation of unchangeable truth. The one lives by faith during this pilgrimage; the other brings those who live well to the kingdom. The rewards of the active life are great, but those of the contemplative life are greater. The active life begins with good works; the contemplative life reaches what it seeks.

The works of the active life end with the body; the joys of the contemplative life increase more fully at the end. The former, although useful and good, will pass away when rest comes; the latter is the reward of passing good works and the rest that will remain.

The contemplative life is shown by Rachel, who was beautiful but barren, because through the leisure of contemplation fewer children of works are generated. Leah, with weak eyes but fruitful, displayed the active life, because action is indeed laborious and considers less lofty things; but because it gives itself more generously to the benefit of its neighbor, it grows more fruitful in works, as though in children.

These two lives are signified by Ezekiel when it is written concerning the living creatures: “And human hands were under their wings” (Ezek. 1:8). What, then, are signified by the hands except the active life, and by the wings except the contemplative life? “Human hands were under their wings,” that is, the power of action under the flight of contemplation.

For although through the active life we do something good, nevertheless through the contemplative life we fly toward the heavenly desire. And although both these lives are gifts of grace, so long as we live among our neighbors one is necessary for us, while the other depends upon our will.

For who, knowing God, enters his kingdom unless he first acts well? Without the contemplative life, therefore, those who do not neglect the good they are able to perform can enter the heavenly homeland; but without the active life they cannot enter if they neglect to do what they are able to do.

### 2

Those who strive to come to the leisure of contemplation must first exercise themselves in the practice of the active life, so that, while they drain away the filth of sins through works of righteousness, they may present a clean heart for seeing God. For the mind that still seeks temporal glory or yields to the temptations of carnal desire is undoubtedly barred from contemplation.

Hence, when the people were receiving the Law, they were removed from the mountain—that is, from lofty contemplation—as though by the curiosity of carnal minds. And in the Gospel, the man cured of the legion of demons wishes to follow God through contemplation, but he is ordered to return home and devote himself to the work of the active life.

Even in the practice of contemplation or action there is sometimes a great difference among souls. For contemplation alone benefits some, while for others the active life alone is a consolation. For others, the middle way, composed of both, is more useful for relieving the mind’s anxieties, which are often nourished by exclusive concentration, so that the two sides may be better balanced.

When the Savior shone throughout the cities by signs and miracles during the day, he commended the active life to us; when he spent the night on the mountain in prayer, he signified the contemplative life to us. Therefore the servant of God, following Christ’s example, neither abandons the active life nor fails to practice the contemplative life. Otherwise he proceeds improperly.

For just as God must be loved through contemplation, so one’s neighbor must be loved through the active life. Accordingly, we cannot exist without both lives, just as we cannot possibly exist without both kinds of love.

The active life is to give bread to the hungry, teach the ignorant with the word of wisdom, correct the one who is in error, recall a proud neighbor to the way of humility, care for the sick, carefully distribute to each person whatever is appropriate, and provide for those entrusted to one’s care so that they may be able to live.

The contemplative life, however, is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, but to rest from outward action and cling to the desire for the Creator alone, so that one no longer wishes to do anything else. Having trampled down every care, the soul burns to behold the face of its Creator; it already knows how to bear with sorrow the burden of corruptible flesh; it longs with every desire to join the hymn-singing choirs of angels, to mingle with the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption eternally in God’s presence.

### 3

The evangelical sermon continues concerning Mary, saying: “She also sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word; but Martha was busy with much serving” (Luke 10:39).

The perfection of the contemplative life is uniform: to keep the mind stripped of all earthly things and, as far as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ. But how extensive the service of the active life is, Paul, the teacher of the nations, demonstrates. In the most frequent statements of his Epistles he recalls his labors for Christ by land and sea and his dangers.

In those same statements, while commending the Lord’s visions and revelations, he also indicates that he was perfected in contemplative virtue—something very few can imitate. Hence he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13).

“She stood and said: ‘Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me’” (Luke 10:40). In Martha’s person speak those who are still ignorant of divine contemplation and consider only the work of fraternal love, which they have learned, pleasing to God. Therefore they declare that all who wish to be devoted to Christ must be enslaved to the work of action.

And Martha is rightly described as standing, while Mary is described as sitting beside the Lord’s feet, because the active life labors in strenuous struggle, whereas the contemplative life, after the tumult of vices has been quieted, already enjoys the desired tranquility of mind in Christ.

“And the Lord answered and said to her: ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary’” (Luke 10:40). Blessed David also, defining this one thing as necessary for a human being, desires to cling continually to God, saying: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72:28).

And elsewhere: “One thing I asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the will of the Lord and be protected by his holy temple” (Ps. 26:4).

There is therefore one and only one *theoria*, that is, contemplation of God, to which all the merits of justification and every pursuit of virtue are rightly subordinated.

The text continues:

### 4

“Mary chose the better part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

And behold, Martha’s part is not condemned, but Mary’s part is praised. For he does not say that Mary chose a good part, but the best part, thereby indicating that Martha’s part was also good.

Why Mary’s part is best is immediately added when he says: “It will not be taken away from her.” Therefore, dearest brethren, we too must practice these two lives—the active and the contemplative—with unceasing devotion, applying ourselves earnestly now to one and now to the other.

We must exercise ourselves in action in such a way that, following the example of the blessed Apostle Paul, we labor with our hands, always keeping before our eyes his terrible saying: “If anyone does not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thess. 3:10).

The labor of the hands means not only cultivation of the earth or any kind of work, but everything that may be useful to the household, as well as obedience to the commands of whatever superiors we serve.

We must also devote ourselves with all our strength to the benefit of our neighbor: to admonish and restrain, to encourage good, to visit, to console, to serve, to support, to exhort, and to provide whatever services necessity may require.

When we have thus exercised ourselves on the path of the active life, we must also frequently, whenever opportunity allows, return to prayer, confession, remembrance of our former deeds, sighs and a fountain of tears, thanksgiving, and even contemplation of Christ the Lord himself.

In this way we shall both wipe away the evil we have done by good and outstanding works and, because we had turned away from God, return to him through devotion to contemplation. For now we see him in a mirror and in an enigma; one day we shall see his desired face without end.

Having briefly treated the evangelical reading, let us now turn our discourse to the sacred feast of the glorious Mother of the Lord that we celebrate.

### 5

First we must ask why this blessed Mother of the Lord, who was holier than all others, did not follow her Redeemer, Lord, and Son among the company of the disciples and the other women who were present at that time.

For, unless I am mistaken, nowhere else is she said to have been present at the Lord’s miracles except at the wedding celebrated in Cana of Galilee. Elsewhere we read that the Lord was told concerning her: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with you” (Matt. 12:47). Finally, she is said to have stood near him when he was already placed upon the cross.

But in this matter the reason is plainly apparent. For he himself, her Son and Redeemer, is said among other things to have declared: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). And elsewhere: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19:10). Also: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke 5:32).

Therefore, if the Lord was sent on account of the lost sheep, to save what had perished, and to call sinners to repentance, what need was there for this most holy mother and virgin, endowed with the light of immeasurable holiness, to cling bodily to her Lord and Son among publicans and sinners, when she is undoubtedly believed never to have been spiritually absent from him at any time?

The same reasoning also applies to the blessed John the Baptist. The Lord exalted him with the greatest and most distinguished praises, yet did not number him among the disciples, because the one whom he instructed inwardly with heavenly teaching he had left outwardly, as it were, in his own freedom.
