[lacuna]

[Uncertain reading: *nitricem* (“nurse”)], who, appearing to the world gentle and humble, did not despise those entangled in worldly desires, those bound by various crimes, publicans and sinners, prostitutes devoted to carnal pleasures, or even the robber himself, despite his hands stained with human blood.

To her, therefore, let every age and every sex hasten. Let each of you ask with full faith from her effective merits whatever he or she considers lacking or desires to possess. For she who brought forth the Redeemer of all in her chaste womb is ready to confer the help of salvation upon all.

Approach her, O virgin, who intend to consecrate both body and soul in chastity. Imitate her purpose insofar as you can; ask her protection, so that you may be fortified by her—the one who first seized and first preserved the glory of radiant virginity.

Approach her, widows deprived of husbands; hope from her for relief from your distress. She who knew no husband is as close to you in proportion as you are deprived of the comfort of a husband, and she is close through heavenly assistance.

Approach her likewise, mothers; ask from her, who is acquainted with maternal feelings, a remedy for your hardships—for she is both virgin and mother, something never heard of before her.

Let all who lead innocent lives approach her; let all whom the guilt of conscience weighs down come together before her. Rely upon the effective merits of this most splendid mother and virgin for the fulfillment of whatever you ask. For she who gave birth to Jesus Christ, God and Lord, the very fountain of mercy, receives everything from him and through him grants to all what they desire.

[Note: We extracted this homily, or rather fragment of a homily, from an old Cassinese manuscript. — Mabillon.]

## HOMILY III. ON THE HOLY FATHER BENEDICT

*(From Mabillon, Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*

Because the priest Venerable Bede composed almost his entire final homily—the fiftieth, that is—about the life and deeds of a certain Benedict, an inmate of his monastery, and because it plainly seemed scarcely suitable for our offices to read, I, Paul the deacon, the least servant of blessed Benedict, so that the number fifty itself might not be diminished from these homilies, composed this fiftieth homily, with heavenly grace assisting, for the glory of God and the praise of our most holy Father Benedict.

The reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke:

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.’” And so forth.

## Homily of Paul the Deacon and Philosopher on the Same Reading

These words of the holy Gospel, as you have heard, dearest brethren, were preceded somewhat earlier by the Lord’s statement concerning the Jews who did not believe: “This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it,” and so forth.

And after much else:

Who, dearest brethren, after the holy apostles, is more worthy to be called by the name of “salt” than this most blessed Father of ours? Separated from the city of Rome, as from the unstable and bitter waves of the sea, while he kept himself within the confines of his cave, he changed whatever small amount of the liquid of worldly instability he could possess into the solidity and rational order of salt. Scorched by the rays of the true Sun through the warmth of charity, he reached the whiteness of righteousness.

He not only then seasoned the lives of many through his bodily presence, pious words, and deeds, but, present in spirit to this very day, he instructs not only our community but his followers throughout almost the whole of the West.

[Note: Here Paul Winfrid, deacon and monk of Monte Cassino, writing toward the end of that century, testifies that the Benedictine Rule had spread, before the eighth century, especially throughout the whole West. Worthy of notice is the miracle related in this homily, in which speech was granted to a mute man; he says that it was performed through Saint Benedict at Cassino about ten years earlier. Saint Bertharius, abbot and martyr of Monte Cassino, celebrated in verse other miracles done there in his own time, that is, in the following century. From this homily we learn that the Venerable Bede composed fifty homilies for feasts and Sundays throughout the year, and that they were already being read in the ecclesiastical offices at Cassino; the fiftieth was the one he wrote on the deeds of blessed Benedict, surnamed Biscop, founder and abbot of his monastery. Because it was quite unsuitable for the Cassinese offices, Paul the deacon composed another in its place, to be recited on the feast of our holy Father Benedict. From these facts we understand that Bede’s aforementioned homilies were then arranged among the Cassinese differently than in two very ancient manuscripts of the library formerly called Thuan and now Colbertine, in which only forty-nine homilies are found; nor does the one concerning Benedict Biscop occupy the last place, but an intermediate one. — Mabillon.]

Through the salutary and rational rule of his holy institution, he restrains the life of those who are carnal and corrupted by the stain of dissolution, recalling it to salvation. Although the severity of this discipline may appear harsh, like the quality of salt, when applied to festering wounds, it is nevertheless certain that, if endured patiently, it confers heavenly medicine.

Therefore, dearest brethren, whenever we are perhaps chastised somewhat severely by a presiding Father, or by those who are placed over us by him according to the rule, we ought to accept this medicine of perpetual salvation all the more humbly, since we must undoubtedly believe that it mitigates the punishments of Gehenna for us.

Who, as we began to say, is more worthy than this guide along the narrower way, who shone upon the world like the light of day? Through the merits of his life and the multitude of his miracles, he not only shone forth then but even to the present has continued to grow and become radiant everywhere.

That recent miracle testifies to this—a miracle that speaks for itself, performed nearly ten years ago and known to many of you: a mute man had spoken before this most sacred body—that is, his ashes. As soon as he sought Benedict’s aid with all his vows, he obtained the use of his tongue. He who from the day of his birth had been unable to utter a single word began, more wondrously still, not only to speak his own language—that is, his barbarian language—but Latin as well.

There are many other things worthy of narration that Christ accomplishes through him every day; under God’s guidance, they ought to be disclosed to your charity in their proper order.

Who, then, to continue what I began, lived more simply than this man, that is, with a purer intention of heart? He always despised all things destined to perish and established his mind in heavenly things. For this reason he was immediately heard in what he desired: by the simplicity of his mind he pleased God and excluded every wrinkle of duplicity from his purpose.

And after some further remarks:

Whose body—which, as we said, signifies works—could have been more luminous than this man’s, who through the excellence of his life offered light to so many? Or whom could the splendor of his own deeds have illuminated more like a radiant lamp than this man, who, surrounded outwardly by countless lamps as he ascended to heaven, was destined inwardly to receive greater things from the vision of the Creator?

What lamp brighter than this teacher arose? Placed upon the lampstand of a loftier life, it radiated throughout the provinces of the West. If, perhaps, he had hidden himself within the narrowness of his cave, as he had begun to do, he would surely have appeared to be held beneath a bushel—that is, within the measure of his own discipline—and would have cast the locks of his ruddy radiance upon few or none.

But with God’s inspiration, placed upon the lampstand of governance, he offered splendid light to all who desired to be illumined. Even today, throughout almost every region devoted to Christian worship, when the marvels of so many miracles have been heard and the light of such great holiness recognized, the mouths of all the faithful to whom these things can reach resound in divine praises.

To mention only a few of the many things: who would not marvel to hear that he disclosed hidden things openly and foretold the future; that waters obeyed his commands; that springs emerged from rocks; that the elements so often abandoned their nature; that birds offered service; that the earth vomited forth a corpse it had received; [lacuna]; [uncertain: the text reads *cunctis terribile est, pavidare*]; that illnesses yielded to his commands; that death lost its claim to authority; that the secrets of the heart were revealed; and that, while his body remained enclosed, his spirit hastened wherever he wished?

Finally, who would not be amazed that the whole world was seen by one man, that, while placed on earth, he looked upon the citizens of heaven, and that, while still bound by flesh, he contemplated the merits of souls?

Who, hearing these things and many similar ones, would not immediately burst into praises of God the Father, who grants such gifts to his servants and, above all these things, bestows upon them a kingdom without end in heaven?

But from where did this outstanding Father earn the privilege of performing such deeds, so that he might shine with so many miracles before an admiring world like the holy apostles, unless it was because he embraced the life of those same apostles and received with a willing heart the teachings of the heavenly Teacher in order to serve him?

Neither the allurements of the flesh, nor the worldly joys that persuade toward evil, nor the enemy’s cunning counsels could bend him in any way as he hastened toward eternal rewards.

Therefore, dearest brethren, we who have hastened from different parts of the world to his teaching must learn to despise what he despised and to love what he loved. And if we desire to follow him afterward to glory, let us now follow his footsteps by imitating him, lest, if we turn aside from the pattern of his righteousness now, we later be forcibly separated from his company.

Certainly, if one of us were dragged violently from this assembly to prison, great shame and immense sorrow would oppress the person who suffered it. What do we think there would then be of shame, terror, and anguish if—God forbid—it should happen that one of us were separated forever from that splendid choir of this holy Father of ours and the brothers who preceded us, and were moreover plunged into infinite torments?

Let us therefore examine our life on every side, beloved. Let us exclude every stain and all malice from ourselves. Let us be gentle, temperate, and humble. Let us pursue the things that belong to peace and charity. Let us hold to the precepts of this Father of ours and follow his footsteps, so that with him we may likewise attain eternal joys, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## THE SAME HOMILY. ON THE EVANGELICAL SENTENCE AND ON SAINT BENEDICT

*(From Mai’s New Collection.)*

From the words of the Gospel according to Luke:

“Jesus said to his disciples: ‘No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.’”

From a most ancient manuscript once at Monte Cassino and later in the Vatican, magnificently decorated with paintings and written in Lombard script, together with the following preface by the same Paul the deacon:

Venerable Bede the priest composed almost his entire final homily—the fiftieth, that is—about the life and deeds of a certain Benedict, an inmate of his monastery, and it plainly seemed scarcely suitable for reading in our offices. I, Paul the deacon, the least servant of blessed Benedict, so that the number fifty itself might not be diminished from these homilies, composed this fiftieth homily, with heavenly grace assisting, for the glory of God and the praise of our most holy Father Benedict.

**Homily.**
At the words of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, [Col. 1577B] dearly beloved brothers, the Lord had prefaced a little earlier, speaking of the unbelieving Jews: “This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah.” And shortly afterward, announcing under the figure of the queen of the south the Church that would come to faith from the Gentiles, he said: “The queen of the south will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” Since, then, on the occasion of these words Truth had made mention explicitly of the Jews, but figuratively of the Church—and since he certainly knew that the mystery of his incarnation would benefit the Gentiles much more than the Jews—he added what has just been read, saying: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand.” The Lord lights a lamp when he fills the earthen vessel of human frailty with the flame of his divinity. This lamp, that is, the radiant faith of his incarnation, he did not wish either to hide from believers or to place under a bushel—that is, to confine it within the measure of the Law—or to restrict it within the boundaries of the single Jewish nation. Rather, he wished to entrust it to the peoples of the Gentiles who had been subjected to him, and to unite them more closely to himself by illuminating them. The lampstand signifies the holy Church, upon which he set the lamp, because he fixed the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads. Immediately indicating the reason why the lamp ought to be placed upon the lampstand, he added: “So that those who enter may see the light,” that is, so that those who wish to enter the Church faithfully may plainly behold the light of truth and [Col. 1577D] faith. By this saying the offspring of the Jews also is condemned, because, while seeking external signs, they refused to enter through faith the open door of the light.

But because the Lord had first deigned to declare himself a lamp, he makes clear, by what he adds, how the name “lamp” may also be applied to his elect, when he says: “The lamp of your body is your eye.” By “body” he means our works, which appear openly to everyone; by the “eye,” however, he means the intention of the mind that performs them. By the merit of this intention it is discerned whether those same works are works of light or of darkness, as he subsequently explained, saying: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous; [Col. 1578A] but if it is evil, your body also will be dark.” “If,” he says, “with a pure and upright intention you strive to do the good that you are able to do, the works you perform are certainly works of light, even if they seem to possess some imperfection before human beings, since, as the Apostle says, all things work together for good for those who love God. But if the intention that precedes is perverse, every work that follows is evil, however upright it may appear.” Because we must guard against this with the utmost care, Truth plainly adds an admonition, saying: “See, therefore, that the light which is in you is not darkness.” That is, take diligent care lest the very intention of the heart, which is the light of the soul, be darkened by the murk of vices; consider it carefully, in accordance with what is commanded elsewhere: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds.” It continues: [Col. 1578B] “If, then, your body is luminous, having no part of darkness, it will be wholly luminous, and it will illuminate you like a lamp with its radiance.” By “our whole body” he means all our works, because the Apostle also calls certain works that he condemns and commands to be put to death our members, saying: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, and other such things.”

“If, therefore,” he himself says, “you have performed a good deed with a good intention, having no part of a dark thought in your conscience, even if it should happen that one of your neighbors is harmed by your good action—for example, if he does something evil with the money he had received from you in his need, or suffers something because of it; or if, through the word of exhortation by which you wished to correct someone in error, he should perhaps fall into a more harmful error—nevertheless, because of your simple and luminous heart, you will be granted the grace of light here and in the future, and from the radiance of your own action you will receive the brightness of eternal recompense.” Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us also strive, by God’s grace, to be burning lamps and to offer the light of good example to our neighbors as they enter God’s house. Let us strive to serve the works of light and, with diligent care, guard against a perverse intention insinuating itself into our good deeds. May the intention of our heart always be pure and simple, so that the action of all our work may be found clear before the inner Judge and clothed in the light of a worthy reward.

We have said these things briefly in explaining the Gospel reading. [Col. 1578D] But since we are now celebrating the most sacred day of our blessed father Benedict, on which he passed to heaven by a radiant path, let us see whether the sequence of the present reading can be applied to his life or merits. First, however, it is pleasing to take a few things also from the Gospel of Matthew, which clearly correspond to this reading and support the praises of so sublime a man. For the blessed evangelist Matthew reports that, among other things, the Lord said to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth”; and again: “You are the light of the world.”

Who, dearly beloved brothers, after the holy apostles, is more worthy to be called by the name of salt than this most blessed father of ours? Separated from the city of Rome, as though from the unstable and bitter waves of the sea, while he kept himself within the confines of his cave, he transformed whatever small amount of the fluidity of worldly instability he might have possessed into the solidity and rational order of salt. Scorched by the rays of the true sun through the fervor of chastity, he attained the whiteness of justice. He not only seasoned the life of many at that time by his bodily presence and pious words and deeds, but, present in spirit to this very day, he instructs not only our community but especially his followers throughout the whole of the West. Through the wholesome and rational rule of his holy institution, he restrains a life weakened by the corruption of carnal dissolution and brings it back to salvation. Although the judgment of his discernment appears austere, like salt, to wounds that are growing inflamed, it is nevertheless certain that, when endured patiently, it confers heavenly medicine.

[Col. 1579B] Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, whenever we are chastised with due regularity, perhaps more sharply, by our Father the abbot or by those whom he places over us, it is fitting that we receive this medicine of perpetual salvation with all the greater humility, the more certainly we must believe that it mitigates for us the punishments of hell. Who, as we had begun to say, shone more brightly in the world than this guide of the narrower way, like a ray of light? By the merits of his life and the multiplicity of his miracles he not only shone forth then, but to this day continues to grow and radiate his brightness everywhere. The recent miracle of which we speak bears witness to this—a miracle performed nearly ten years ago and known to many as true: namely, that one who had previously been mute spoke before this most sacred body. For as soon as he sought Benedict’s aid with all his vows, he obtained the use of his tongue; and although from the day of his birth he had been unable to utter a single word—a fact all the more astonishing—not only did he begin to express his own speech, that is, his barbarian language, but at the same time also Latin. There are many more events worthy of being recounted that Christ performs daily through him; with God as our guide, they ought to be disclosed individually to your charity.

Who, then, to continue what we began, passed his life with a more single eye than this man—that is, with a purer intention of heart? Always scorning all things destined to perish, he made his mind firm in heavenly things. And he was immediately heard in what he desired because, pleasing God by the simplicity of his mind, he excluded every wrinkle of duplicity from his intention. Hence Solomon says of God: “And with the simple is his conversation.” We also confess, no less, that the Creator of all things that have been made is by nature altogether simple. Therefore anyone is heard more effectively in prayer in proportion as, through a simple intention, he possesses, according to his proper measure, a likeness to the divine nature.

Whose body—that is, whose works, as we have said—could be more luminous than that of this man, who displayed light to so many through the excellence of his life? Or whom more than him did the splendor of his own action illuminate like a radiant lamp? Surrounded outwardly by innumerable lamps as he ascended to heaven, he was surely destined to receive inwardly greater things from the vision of the Creator. What lamp brighter than this teacher arose? Set upon the lampstand of a higher life, it illuminated all the provinces of the West. If he had perhaps hidden himself within the narrow confines of his cave, as he had begun to do, he would certainly have seemed to scatter the locks of his gleaming radiance over few or none, as though beneath a bushel—that is, held back within the measure of his own judgment. But with God’s favor, placed upon the lampstand of governance, he offered a brilliant light to all who wished to be enlightened. And he offered it in such a way that even today, throughout almost all the regions devoted to Christian worship, the prodigies of so many miracles having been heard and the light of such holiness having been recognized, the mouths of all the faithful to whom these things can reach resound in divine praises.

To mention only a few things among many, who would not marvel on hearing that he revealed hidden things openly and foretold the future? That waters obeyed his commands; that springs emerged from rocks; that the elements so often abandoned their natural order; that birds rendered service; that the earth vomited forth a corpse it had received; that things terrible to all trembled in fear; that diseases yielded to commands; that death lost the authority of its dominion; that the secret of the heart was disclosed; that a spirit hastened wherever it wished while its body remained confined within physical barriers? Finally, who would not be astonished that one man should behold the whole world, see the citizens of heaven while still placed on earth, and contemplate the merits of souls while still bound to the flesh? Hearing these and many similar things with his ears, who would not immediately burst into praises of God the Father, who grants such things to his servants and, beyond all this, bestows on them a kingdom without end in heaven?

But by what means did this exceptional Father deserve to perform such things, so that, like the holy apostles, he might shine forth in miracles admired by the whole world, unless it was because he maintained the life of those same apostles and received with the ear of his heart the teachings of the heavenly Master, preserving them? Neither the allurements of the flesh, nor the deceptive joys of the world, nor the enemy’s cunning counsels could bend him in any way as he pressed on toward eternal rewards.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we who have hastened to his instruction from different parts of the world must learn to despise what he despised and to love what he loved. And if we desire to follow him afterward into glory, let us now follow in his footsteps by imitating him, lest, if we turn aside now from the standard of his uprightness, we should later be forcibly separated from his company. Certainly, if someone were to drag one of us from this very assembly violently to prison, great shame and immense sorrow would truly oppress the person who suffered it. What, dearly beloved, do we think the shame, terror, and anguish would be there if—God forbid—it should happen that one of us were separated forever from that most splendid choir of this holy Father of ours and of the brothers who preceded us, and were moreover plunged into endless torments? Therefore, beloved, let us examine our life on every side; let us exclude from ourselves every impurity and all wickedness; let us be gentle, temperate, and humble; let us pursue the things that belong to peace and charity; let us hold fast to the precepts of this Father of ours and follow his footsteps, so that together with him we may obtain eternal joys; through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## EXPLANATION OF THE PROLOGUE OF THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

*(From Tosti, History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino.)*

[Col. 1581A]

There are three ecclesiastical disciplines: the first is physics, that is, natural philosophy; the second is ethics, that is, moral philosophy; the third is logic, that is, rational philosophy. For physics derives its name from *physis*—*physis* in Greek, “nature” in Latin. Ethics, however, derives its name from *ethos*: *ethos* in Greek means “customs” in Latin. Logic derives its name from *logos*, for *logos* in Greek means “reason” in Latin.

For the sake of these three ecclesiastical disciplines, therefore, Solomon, wisest of all kings, composed three books. He called the first book Proverbs, the second Ecclesiasticus, and the third the Song of Songs. The first [Col. 1581B] book is suitable for children, because in it he often addresses children as sons, saying: “Hear, my son.” Hence mention is also frequently made in that book of evil things, namely prostitutes, heretics, and other things similar to these. The second book, however, properly suits adults, because in it adults are already admonished to despise the vanities of the world. Hence that book begins with vanity, saying: “Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher; vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” The third book, however, suits the perfect, because in it things joyful rather than adverse or sad are found.

Following this order of Solomon, blessed Benedict, not ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline, said: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master.” That is, just as Solomon in his first book addresses children as sons, so [Col. 1581C] he too at the beginning of his book addresses a child as a son, saying: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master,” and so forth. For it must be known that some books read *ausculta* (“listen”), while others read *obsculta*. But whether one says *ausculta* with *au* or *obsculta* with *ob*, nothing is wrong, since *auscultare* is said as though from *auribus scultare*, that is, “to hear with the ears”; *obscultare*, however, means “to hear together” or “to hear generally,” because *ob* in this place means “together.”

Now we must consider for what reason Saint Benedict, when he said “son,” prefixed *o*, when it would have been sufficient for him to say only “son,” since in the word *son* a vocative meaning is understood. But it must be known that, just as many nouns, to intensify—that is, to augment—their meaning, take certain added syllables—for example, when you say *praedives*, “very rich,” *praepotens*, “very powerful,” and *excelsus*, “very high,” with *prae* and *ex* added to mean “very rich,” “very powerful,” and “very lofty”—so Saint Benedict is understood to have intensified his form of address when he said “son,” prefacing it with *o*. For *o son* contains two vocatives, as if he had said: “Son, son.”

“Son” is used in many ways: by nature, by adoption, by imitation, by instruction, and by race. Sonship by nature and adoption is known to everyone. By imitation someone is called another’s son because he imitates that person’s works; hence the Lord says in the Gospel to the Jews: “You are from your father the devil, because you wish to do his works.” By instruction, people are called sons who are placed under teachers; hence the Apostle says: “I begot you through the Gospel.” By race, for example, was that rich man who was placed in hell and whom Abraham called his son, saying: “Son, remember that you received good things during your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise bad things.” Similarly, the rich man called Abraham “father,” saying: “Father Abraham,” and so forth.

Although “son” is used in many ways, a father is always understood there, even if he is not explicitly mentioned, since a son cannot exist without a father. In this place, then, when Saint Benedict says “son,” he shows that he has toward you the affection of a father and the discipline of a teacher. His address to you, in which he calls you “son,” makes clear what he is leading you toward: that is, it shows that he is leading you to receive the affection of a father and the discipline of a teacher. Precepts are so called because they seek a reward, since those who observe them receive rewards from them. A master is called *magister* as though from *magistratus*, that is, “more learned,” just as a disciple is named from learning.

It is also asked why Saint Benedict said “incline,” when he could have said “open.” It must be understood that many open their ears but do not incline them—that is, humble them. Therefore he said “incline,” as if he were saying “humble them.” For unless the proud had their ears and all their limbs held upright, divine Scripture would never say: “Make their ears heavy, and you will humble the eyes of the proud,” since the proud are always raised up in the arrogance of pride.

It must also be understood that the proud are not said to have proud limbs in such a way that the limbs themselves are proud; rather, because the functions of the limbs of proud people are proud, the limbs are therefore called proud. Although the other limbs too are called proud on account of their functions, pride is more commonly recognized in the eyes.

The meaning is this: when he says, “Incline your ears,” he means, “Submit your ears in order to learn humility,” because to incline is to be brought down from higher things to humble things.

Again, we must consider why, when he says “ears,” he adds “of the heart,” when it would have been sufficient for him to say “ears” without adding “of the heart.” The reason is that whenever divine Scripture says “ears,” it requires the ears of the heart. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” There he is not speaking of bodily ears, because all who were present there possessed bodily ears; and no one would have come there to hear unless he had bodily ears. But because the Lord, knowing—as God sees—that many of those present did not have the ears of the heart, he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” as if he were saying: “I address those who have the ears of the heart.”

The ears of the outer person hear sound only, but do not discern it, because our outer person is shared with beasts, whereas the inner person is shared with angels, since he has been fashioned in the image of God. Saint Benedict, however, because he was speaking to humble and simple people, added “of the heart” so that there might be no difficulty in understanding which ears he meant.

According to the understanding of the ancient wise men, *aures* (“ears”) is said as though from *audes*, because they hear. According to the understanding of the later wise men, however, *aures* is said from *hauriendo* (“drawing in”), because they draw in sound.

It may also be asked why Saint Benedict, when he said “of the heart,” added “your,” when it would have been sufficient for him to say only “of the heart.” He added it for the intensification of the heart, that is, for the heart’s greatest attentiveness. For Father Benedict said “your” with the same intention with which God says to the prophet Ezekiel, “with your eyes.” He says: “Son of man, see with your eyes, hear with your ears, and set your heart upon everything that I shall show you; for you have been brought here so that these things may be shown to you.” The Lord appropriately added “your,” because he was requiring the eyes and ears of the heart. It was as if he were saying: “Because the things shown to you cannot be seen with bodily eyes or heard with bodily ears, I therefore say ‘your,’ so that you may see them with prophetic eyes and hear them with spiritual ears.”

Thus Saint Benedict also added “your” in this passage, as if he were saying: “Because you cannot hear with bodily ears the things that I am striving to commend to you, son, I therefore say ‘your,’ so that you may hear them attentively with the ears of your heart.”

[Col. 1583]

## THE THIRD PART OF THE WORKS OF PAUL WINFRID THE DEACON: LETTERS AND POEMS

### SECTION ONE: LETTERS

[Note: [Col. 1583C] Hoeften collected various readings of this letter; he would have collected many more had he had our edition at hand. We leave this task to the reader who has leisure and inclination to compare our native edition with foreign editions, for the antiquity itself bears witness in its favor. For Codex 353 was compiled by John, abbot, less than a full century after Paul and Theodemar. Consequently, the authority of the most learned Menard, who suspects in Hoeften that this letter is not Theodemar’s, moves me not at all, since both the chronology fits well and the wording of the letter itself clearly reveals Paul as its author, in addition to the testimony of so many of our manuscripts.]

## LETTER ONE

[Note: [Col. 1583C] Beginning of the letter of Paul the Deacon. The letter is attributed to Paul because Paul composed it by his own effort and ingenuity; to Theodemar because it was written in his name.] The letter of the deacon to [Note: [Col. 1583D] To King Charles. At that time he was merely king, not yet emperor.] King Charles begins.

*(From the Cassinese Chronicle, edited by Ang. Mue.)*

[Col. 1583B]

To Charles, lord, propagator and defender of the Christian religion, wisest of kings through the power of Christ, Theodemar, the least, and the entire flock of blessed Father Benedict subject to your rule, eternal salvation in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1583D] *Tam per epistolae seriem.* Charles’s letter to Theodemar has been lost.] Having received both through the course of your letter and through the holy bishop [Note: [Col. 1583D] Adelgarius, bishop. His see is not established. “Perhaps Troyes,” says Hoeften.] Adelgarius [Note: [Col. 1583D] *Vestra famina.* Paul uses the same word in the hymn of Saint John:

“Lest you should be able to stain life  
with even a light utterance”;  

and elsewhere.] your message, we rejoiced with great exultation when we learned that your Sublimity, our lady the queen, and your children were safe and well. We shall rejoice with no less delight when we learn of the extension of your frontiers and of your victories and triumphs over your enemies. That event also increased our joy, because we have learned that your Excellence, growing from virtue to virtue, diligently excels in God’s field and brings the monastic order to a better condition. It is certain that this deed will make you more blessed, since you are offering such a gift, and one so pleasing, to our God.

Since, therefore, it has pleased your Clemency that some of the monks of that region should be instructed in the teaching and illustrious examples of our blessed Father Benedict, in accordance with your command we have sent you a copy of the rule of that same blessed Father, taken from the very manuscript that he [Note: [Col. 1583D] *De ipso codice, quam ille suis … manibus.* At that time the autograph of the Rule still existed at Monte Cassino; it later burned at Teano.] himself [Note: [Col. 1583D] *Exarabit.* For *exaravit* above, *exultabimus*, and below *coenovio* for *coenobio*, *probidentia* for *providentia*, *octabum* for *octavum*, and *devitum* for *debitum*. The consonants *u*, *b*, and *v* were interchanged reciprocally because of the Greek-influenced dialect and writing of that age.] wrote out with his holy hands. As a confirmation of that sacred rule, we have also attached the hymns that, according to the institutions of our blessed Father, ought to be sung at each office or feast.

If anyone is troubled by the question of why blessed Benedict prescribed that, during the summer season, only one section from the Old Testament should be read on weekdays at the night office, let him know [Note: [Col. 1584C] At that time it was not yet customary in the Roman Church to read the sacred Scriptures as they are read now. Hoeften thinks that Theodemar—or rather Paul the Deacon—was mistaken here, since Pope Gelasius I, long before Gregory and one generation before Benedict, had already arranged the readings for the entire year in their proper order. But whoever established the order and number of the readings, our most holy Father Benedict nevertheless most wisely organized a form of psalmody different from that of the Roman Church, so that monks would be distinguished from clerics not only by their way of life but also by the manner of their public prayers. The author of the Life of Saint Waleric, abbot, who was a disciple of Saint Columban, relates in Surius, under 3 April, that the holy man performed both courses daily: the monastic and the Gallican or clerical. Hence it is clear that the monastic rite differed from that of the clerics, even under the Rule of Saint Columban. As for the readings, our holy lawgiver appointed only one on weekdays during the summer because of the shortness of the nights. The reading of sacred Scripture that was lacking from the office was customarily supplied in the refectory. For it was a very ancient custom of monks to hear the whole of sacred Scripture each year, partly in choir and partly in the refectory, as is evident from ancient monastic ritual books.] that even then it was not customary in the Roman Church to read the sacred Scriptures [Col. 1585A] as they are read now; rather, this practice was established some time later, either by blessed Pope Gregory or, as others assert, by Honorius.

For this reason our predecessors established that here, in our sacred monastery founded beside the holy body of that man, three readings from the Old Testament should be read on weekdays during the summer, so that they would not appear to differ from the holy Roman Church. Nor should it be believed that this displeased blessed Father Benedict; rather, it would have pleased him if someone, out of love for God, took care to add to what he had instituted in God’s praises. For, as regards the division of the psalms to be sung on each day of the week, if anyone thinks a different arrangement better than the one established by the blessed Father himself, he has permission from him to sing as he considers better. Nor ought the monks—if this is pleasing to your most wise heart—who now sing psalms according to Roman custom to be compelled to divide the psalms according to the institution of this sacred Rule. If it seems appropriate to you, they may, while singing according to their accustomed practice, adopt the rule governing their manner of life.

We have also sent [Note: [Col. 1585C] *Pondo.* This should not be altered, for *pondo* is correctly used, as is *pondus*.] a weight [Note: [Col. 1585C] *Of four pounds.* “From this passage perhaps,” writes Hoeften, “the most learned Menard suspects that this letter is not Theodemar’s. For if, as the Cassinese say in their explanations, the weight of a pound is thirty-three and a half ounces, and this measure seems excessive to some, what should be said of this four-pound measure of Theodemar’s, that is, forty-eight ounces, with thirty-two assigned to the midday meal and sixteen to supper? For Saint Benedict wished one third to be reserved for those who were to dine.” Nevertheless, we are certain, from the two weights still preserved at Monte Cassino, that the daily ration of bread established by the holy Father was either thirty-nine or forty-eight ounces. Nor will that measure seem excessive to those who consider both the various bodily constitutions for which the most judicious lawgiver strove to provide and the agricultural labor in which the monks were then engaged, as well as, finally, the scarcity of accompanying dishes, which was therefore compensated by an abundance of bread, especially for those who were continually fasting. Consult our Ferrarius on chapter 39 of the Rule, where more is said.] of four pounds, to the equal weight of which the bread ought to be made, which [Note: [Col. 1585D] *Into four quadrae.* It can be divided into four parts, sections, or fragments. Servius, commenting on the passage in Book VII of the *Aeneid*, “Nor spare the broad *quadrae*,” writes: “We understand *quadrae* either as loaves or as square fragments.” Hence Juvenal, Satire 5:

“So that you may think it a great thing to live on another’s loaf.”

And Horace, Book I, Letter 18:

“And for me a loaf will be split from the divided gift.”

Martial also, Book VI, epigram 75:

When you send me either a thrush or a *quadra* of cake. [Col. 1586C] See what Scaliger wrote on *quadra* in his commentary on the *Moretum*, and Vossius in his *Lexicon*. Four *quadrae*, each of one pound, may be divided according to the text of the holy Rule. This weight, established by the Father himself, has been found in this place. We also sent a measure of drink to be supplied to the brothers at dinner, and another at supper: [Note: [Col. 1586C] “Which two measures . . . are the measure of an *emina*.” Others read “measure”; either reading can be defended. Concerning the *emina*, see the Ferrarius cited above, in chapter 40 of the Rule.] our elders judged these two measures to be the measure of an *emina*. We also sent a measure of one cup, [Col. 1585C] which [Note: [Col. 1586C] “Those who are to serve.” In the Rule, chapter 38, they are called *servitores*, namely those who serve at table or in the kitchen.] the brothers who are to serve customarily receive, in accordance with the text of the holy Rule.

Our blessed Father established that two cooked dishes be prepared for the brothers at the daily meal, and a third consisting of raw legumes soaked in water. We, however, following the institution of our elders, prepare three cooked dishes on other days, but on Wednesday and Friday only two for the brothers who are to be fed. The exception is that many of our brothers eat only bread and garden herbs on those days; most of them also drink no wine. On Sunday and on the principal feast days we add a fourth dish.

Except on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, on the other days, when the brothers dine and wine is plentiful for us, we have a flask mixed for each of them. On the greatest feasts—that is, Christmas and Epiphany, Easter and the Tuesday after Easter, when our feast is especially solemn, and Pentecost, and the feasts of Saint John, Saint Peter, Saint Lawrence, Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and blessed Benedict—we also have this mixed for them at dinner. In addition, [Note: [Col. 1586C] “In summer, after None, fruit and single bowls, etc.” I saw this ancient custom of drinking in the community after None, with fruit or cucumbers, retained at the Cassinese congregation until my youth; it is now obsolete. Among the ancient usages of the Cistercians, chapter 83 is entitled “Concerning drinking after None.” See Hoeften.] in summer, after None, if there is any fruit, we provide our brothers with single bowls.

[Note: [Col. 1586C] “The haymaking season.” Here he weighs the agricultural labors, [Col. 1586D] so that one may no longer be surprised at the enormous bread allowance prescribed for laborers. Hoeften also illuminates this passage.] When it is haymaking season, we also give the brothers who are laboring a drink made with honey at the fourth hour. [Note: [Col. 1585D] “A drink made from honey, etc.” For restoring strength, quenching thirst, and soothing and comforting the bowels. The famous saying of Asinius Pollio is relevant: when he had passed his hundredth year and Augustus, his host, asked by what means he had preserved such vigor of body and mind, he replied, “Mulsum within, oil without.” *Mulsum* is a drink prepared from honey and wine, so called because by its gentleness it soothes the veins.]

[Note: [Col. 1586D] “Birds, etc.” Besides Ferrarius, Hoeften explains this passage most fully; consult him at pages 926 and following. Certainly Theodemar, Paul, and our earlier Cassinese monks held that the legislator did not absolutely forbid monks to eat birds.] We never eat birds except on Christmas Day, if we have the means, and likewise during the days of the Easter feast. Yet our most prudent Father placed the matter of eating birds so cautiously in his Rule that, if monks wish to eat them when the opportunity arises, they are not subject to guilt; but if [Col. 1586C] their abbot does not provide them with such food, they cannot demand it as though it were owed to them.

Since you have kindly asked what garment should be understood by *cuculla*, [Note: [Col. 1587C] “The *cuculla* . . . the *casulla*, etc.” A codex of Saint Angelo at Fornias, preserved in the Cassinese archives, contains an image of Abbot Desiderius wearing a *cuculla*: a full-length garment closed on every side, not especially loose, with narrow sleeves. This was clearly the form of the *cuculla* in that period. From an earlier age we possess among us neither a painting nor a graphic description of a *cuculla*. Certainly its form was not identical in every age, although it did not wholly differ from the original. See Hoeften and Ferrarius.] we say that the *cuculla* is what we call by another name the *casula*. Hence our blessed Father prescribed one that is hairy in winter and plain or old in summer, since this type of garment is customarily woven with hair.

The garment which the Gallican monks call a *cuculla*, and which we call a *cappa*, properly designating the monastic habit, we should call a *melotes*, just as some people in this province have until now called it. Concerning this garment blessed Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*: “When the boy Placidus had been rescued from the water by the monk Maurus, he said, ‘When I was being drawn out of the water, I saw the abbot’s *melotes* over me, and I perceived him drawing me out of the waters.’” This covering [Col. 1587B] was so called because in ancient times it was made from the hide of an animal [Note: [Col. 1587D] “Because *melos* on account of the nakedness, etc.” One should read “on account of the roundness”; for the *melis*, an animal of the wild-cat kind, perhaps what is called the badger, is said by Paul also to derive from the Greek *melon*, “apple,” because its body is round like an apple. Hence *melina* garment and *melotes*.] which is called *melos* because of the nakedness of its body. Some call this little animal a badger.

Blessed Benedict said nothing about this kind of covering in the text of his Rule, evidently because he saw that most monks used the covering in different ways. The monks of Gaul wear it more loosely and at greater length; Italian monks, as you know, have this kind of garment shorter and tighter; the Greeks, apart from a covering for the head, have only a small portion hanging before the chest and behind; monks from overseas have such a covering made of fur. Therefore, because blessed Benedict saw such diversity in monastic clothing, he left it to each monk’s own judgment to choose whichever of these he preferred.

Concerning the number and quality of garments, our blessed Father so prescribed in his Rule that the abbot’s foresight should nevertheless determine how to distribute them to each according to his need. The Father himself also said that in temperate regions fewer garments are needed, and in cold regions more.

Our elders and former abbots, however, established that our brothers should have three tunics on account of their various labors: two heavier ones for winter and one lighter one for summer. Likewise, instead of *cucullae*, two garments which we call [Note: [Col. 1587D] “*Mattos*.” Others read *mantos* or *mantas*. *Matta* means a covering or mat on which monks customarily lie. Perhaps, therefore, *matta* or *mattus* was applied to a garment whose weave resembled a coarser mat.] *mattos*, made from heavier cloth, and one lighter covering for summer. We do not have *cucullae* because they are more expensive, and because our Father elsewhere commanded us to have garments of the sort that can be bought more cheaply in the province.

Our brothers also have two pairs of breeches. Many of them, however, with God’s help, exercise such restraint that they have neither breeches nor more than two garments, in accordance with the text of the Rule. The venerable Father established that monks should have scapulars for their work; hence the name *scapulare*, because it chiefly covers the shoulders, and also a *capud*, which [Col. 1588B] nearly all the peasants in this land wear. Instead of this covering we have one made of coarser fabric, resembling a *melotes*, except that its sleeves reach to the hands. [Note: [Col. 1587D] “*Capud*.” These letters *d* and *t* are elsewhere noted as having been transposed.] Besides these, we add for each person whatever he requires. Thus we give our old men fur-lined garments, [Note: [Col. 1587D] “Fur-lined *gunnas*.” Breulius reads “two furs.” Our reading is unquestionably preferable. See Hoeften.] and we allow the sick to lie on mattresses; in every case we provide each person exactly what his need demands.

Our brothers are also permitted to have towels, either for the service of the tonsure or for wrapping the books they receive for reading.

Besides the regular fasts, we fast until Vespers on the vigils of the principal feasts; and from Vespers of the vigils throughout the night and the feast day, until the office of Compline, [Note: [Col. 1588C] “We do not bend the knees.” This is how they spoke, softening the harsher pronunciation of the seventh letter so that it nearly corresponded to the third vowel; hence they wrote it in this way. [Col. 1588D] Later, when the Italians, through the contagion of the barbarians, learned to pronounce the third vowel more harshly, they changed it into the sound of *g*, so that instead of *Jesu*, *iam*, and *Joannes* they pronounce *Gesu*, *gia*, and *Giovanni*. As for the rite of the ancient Church, it was customary on Sunday and from Easter to Pentecost to pray standing rather than prostrate on the knees, in memory of Christ’s resurrection. On this subject see the canons “Si quis presbyter,” Distinction 30; “Scire debet,” Distinction 76; and “Quoniam,” *De consecratione*, Distinction 3.] we do not bend the knees.

On Sundays also, and from the Nativity of the Lord through the eighth day, and likewise from Easter to Pentecost, we do not bend the knees at the public office. [Note: [Col. 1588D] “At the public office.” *Poplicus* was formerly *populicus*, and *poplicus* occurs in an ancient inscription preserved by Gruterus, page 150; it derives from *populus*. Hence *Valerius Publicola* and *Poplicola*.]

We have also sent you, written on a small sheet within this letter, the text of the promise according to which the earlier monks used to promise the holy Rule in this place. [Note: [Col. 1588D] “The text of the promise.” In our codex we do not possess a copy of this formula, which Hoeften reports here.]

Our brother Joseb, whom, as you have kindly written to us, you intend to appoint to govern the monastery according to the path of the Rule, has, under the ordinances of the sacred canons, the means of liberality to do this; these ordinances grant monks permission even to be elevated to ecclesiastical ranks. [Note: [Col. 1589D] “Contrary to the sequence of the Rule.” Chapter 62: “If an abbot requests that a priest or deacon be ordained for him, he should choose one of his own.”] Let him nevertheless consider whether he can so restrain himself that he may benefit the brothers by his example.

For the discipline imposed upon monks in this matter is great and fundamental, and contrary to the order of the Rule, if some outsider is placed over them without their own election. Yet let your shrewd and prudent discernment arrange the matter as heavenly wisdom may have inspired your mind.

We earnestly beseech you, with humble prayers, concerning our venerable monk Optatus, that, because through the ignorance of youth he committed an excess, he may deserve release through your clemency.

When these matters have been completed, [Note: [Col. 1589D] “We commend ourselves to your sacred [person].” Supply “person,” “majesty,” or the like. A royal letter is also called “sacred.” Hoeften adds from the Trier codex this couplet:

> Farewell, salvation of your fatherland, light and glory of your people,  
> Greatest of rulers, and our exalted love.

[Col. 1590D] It is absent from our copy. For the outcome of this letter and the monks sent into Gaul, consult Hoeften, page 1090.] we commend ourselves to your sacred person, asking our Lord publicly and privately to grant us, for many years, the safety of you and yours, and always to preserve your glory everywhere. It ends.

## LETTER II. TO CHARLES THE GREAT

He dedicates his *Vocabulary* to him.

*(From Mabillon, Annales Benedictini.)*

To the lord King Charles, illustrious in the gift of generosity, wisdom, and power, most exalted of kings: Paul, the least of servants.

Wishing to add something to your libraries, since I possess very little of my own, I was necessarily obliged to borrow from another. Festus Pompeius, thoroughly learned in Roman studies, who disclosed the origins both of obscure expressions and of certain matters, extended his work to twenty lengthy volumes. Omitting from it everything excessively long and less necessary, and clarifying certain obscure points entirely in my own style while leaving other material as it had been arranged, I have offered this abridgment for your Highness to read.

If you do not disdain to read through it, you will find in its sequence some matters arranged according to grammatical art and others according to etymology. In particular, you will find clearly explained the names of your Romulean city, its gates, roads, hills, places, and tribes, as well as the rites of the pagans and various customs. You will also find expressions familiar to poets and historians, which they used frequently in their works.

If your discerning and subtle intellect does not wholly reject this little gift of my insignificance, it will, with life as its companion, encourage my poverty toward better things.

“Augustus, a holy place,” etc. A. This vocabulary ends with this word beginning with the letter N: *nequiquam*.

[Note: [Col. 1590D] There was great intimacy between Paul and Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, perhaps contracted during Paul’s retreat at Monte Cassino. Evidence for it is the letter Paul wrote to Adalhard, who had requested from him the letters of Saint Gregory. Of these Paul arranged for only fifty-five to be copied, and sent them to his friend, some corrected in his own hand, together with a preliminary letter—no more illustrious proof of mutual affection between the two could be offered.]

## LETTER III. TO ADALHARD, ABBOT OF CORBIE

*(From Mabillon, same work.)*

To my most beloved brother and lord, Adalhard, a man of God: Paul, suppliant.

My dear friend, last summer, when I was in those regions, I had wished to see your face, but, impeded by the weariness of my horses, I could not come to you. Nevertheless, with the inward eyes—the only eyes I possess—I frequently behold the sweetness of your brotherhood.

Indeed, I had wished to obey your commands earlier; but, being poor and lacking scribes, I could not do so sooner, especially since a prolonged illness so weakened me that from September until almost the day of the Lord’s Nativity I was confined to my bed. Even that little cleric who wrote these things as best he could was unable to put his hand to the inkstand.

Receive, then, although late, the letters you requested. Since I could not reread them all because of my occupations, know that thirty-four of them have been reread and corrected by me as far as I was able, except for a few passages in which I found something missing. I did not wish to supply these according to my own judgment, lest I seem to alter the words of so great a teacher. In those places I marked a *z* on the outside margin, as a sign of corruption.

If your brotherhood has the opportunity, therefore, try to reread the remaining letters in a more accurate codex and supply the passages that are defective. I nevertheless advise your holiness not to publish them indiscriminately, because some matters in them are better concealed from the less capable than known by them.

Farewell, beloved brother, ever growing in good things; and when you direct your mind toward heavenly things, remember me.

> Before the Rhine flows back to its former sources,  
> Before bright Moselle seeks its own spring,  
> Will the dear and ever-memorable name of Adalhard  
> Depart from the love in my heart.  
> You too, if you flourish by Christ’s gift,  
> Be mindful of your Paul for all time.

## LETTER IV. TO THE ABBOT THEUDEMAR

To my most beloved lord and Father, the abbot Theudemar, loved with my whole heart: Paul, your little and suppliant son.

[Col. 1590D] Although extensive distances of land separate my body from your fellowship, a tenacious love—which can never be divided—nevertheless touches me in some measure toward your community. The love of you and of my elders and brothers torments me almost every moment with such force that neither the formalities of a letter nor the brevity of its pages can express it.

When I call to mind the leisure devoted entirely to divine works, my most welcome stay in the little guesthouse, your pious and religious affection, the holy company of so many soldiers of Christ laboring in divine worship, the shining examples of each brother’s undivided virtues, and the sweet conversations concerning the perfection of the heavenly homeland, I am arrested, stunned, and languishing; nor can I keep back the tears drawn from the depths of my heart.

I dwell among Catholics and people devoted to Christian worship. Everyone receives me kindly, and abundant affection is shown me because of our Father Benedict and your merits. But in comparison with your monastery, this palace is a prison to me; beside the great peace that exists among you, my life here is a storm. Only this frail body holds me back from that homeland; with all the mind I possess, I am with you.

I seem now to be present at your exceedingly sweet harmonies; now to be seated with you at supper, satisfying myself more with your company than with food; now to observe each person’s diligence in his different duties; now to learn how the elderly or infirm are faring and the causes of their condition; now, as though in paradise, to tread the beloved thresholds of the saints.

Believe me, Father and lord; believe me, sacred and venerable phalanx: I am detained here for a time by the sight of me alone, by the compassion of your hearts alone, by the advancement of souls here alone—and, beyond all this, by the power of our tranquil king and lord.

But as soon as I am able, and the Lord of heaven through the pious prince has lowered the night of sorrow and the yoke of misery from my captors, if I can in any way earn the joyful promise of the most merciful prince, I shall soon return to your fellowship, with life as my companion and no other circumstance detaining me.

No . . . riches, no estate, no abundance of refined metal, no affection of any kind will be able to separate me from your community.

Therefore, dearest Father, and you, beloved Fathers and brothers, I beg you to ask our most blessed common Father and teacher Benedict continually on my behalf, that by his merits with Christ he may obtain that I be restored to you as soon as possible.

I trust in our God, who never allows anyone to be deprived of good desires, that he will restore me to you sooner, according to the longing of my panting heart, with appropriate fruit.

I consider it superfluous to write that you should pour out prayers for our lords and their army, since I know that you are always devoted to this very thing. For the lord Abbot Ill., as you already do, ask Christ, whose singular generosity here sustains me after the prince’s munificence.

You are present to me in such abundance, beloved ones, that if I wished to name you individually, this entire page could not contain your names. Therefore I both wish and write greetings generally to all, begging you not to forget me.

But you, my venerable lord abbot—or whatever title you bear as superior—I ask that you have someone write to me about your welfare and that of the brothers, or about what fruits the present year has brought you; and send me the names and number of those brothers who, freed from worldly bonds, have departed to Christ. For I hear that many have died, but Nonnus in particular. [Col. 1592C] If this is truly so, he has taken away with him no small part of my heart.

Farewell, most holy Father, and deign to remember your little son.
