[Col. 1591]

## POEM I. THE LIFE OF SAINT BENEDICT, ABBOT

[Col. 1591C]

See Book I of the *History of the Lombards*, chapter 26, in this volume, column 468.

## POEM II

[Note: [Col. 1591D] According to Rambach, this poem served ecclesiastical song for many centuries, though I can scarcely believe it. I have not found the hymn in any one book; nevertheless, moved by the learned man’s judgment, I have added it. The legend of Saint Benedict sheds light on many passages.]

### HYMN ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT

*(From the Treasury of Hymns.)*

Brothers, with joyful hearts,  
Come with harmonious song;  
Let us enjoy the gladness  
Of this illustrious feast.

By this golden path Benedict,  
Revealer of the narrow way,  
The Father ascended to the kingdoms,  
Gaining the rewards of his labors.

He shone like a new star,  
Driving away the clouds of the world;  
At the very threshold of life  
He despised the world’s bloom.

Mighty in miracles,  
Inspired by the breath from above,  
He shone forth in wonders,  
Foretelling the age to come.

Bringing food for many,  
He restored the vessel of bread;  
Entering the narrow prison,  
He extinguished fires with fires.

By the weapons of the cross  
He broke the cup bearing poison;  
He restrained the wandering mind  
With the gentle scourge of the body.

Rocks pour forth;  
Iron returns from the depths;  
It runs obediently across the waves;  
A boy escapes death by a mantle.

Hidden poison is exposed;  
A command is swiftly accomplished;  
Ruin crushes the enemy;  
The raging lion yields.

A great mass becomes light at the bottom;  
A phantom pyre is moved;  
Health returns to the broken;  
The departure of the absent is revealed.

Cunning ruler, you are caught;  
Unjust possessor, you flee.  
Future secrets, which the heart has not reached,  
Are foreknown.

Buildings are founded through dreams;  
The earth vomits up corpses;  
The fleeing dragon is restrained;  
The sky rains coins.

Glass resists the rocks;  
Jars flow with oil;  
A vision releases the bound;  
The dead receive life again.

The power of so great a light  
Is conquered by a sister’s prayer;  
The more one loves, the more one prevails—  
He sees her swimming through the sky.

A radiance unknown in earlier ages  
Shines forth by night;  
The whole world is seen by it,  
And the holy man is borne aloft in flames.

Amid these things, like nectar,  
He shone forth wondrously through his lyre;  
For he fittingly traced these lines  
For the followers of the sacred life.

Now, leader mighty enough for your disciple,  
Attend the sighs of your flock;  
May it grow in good things, lacking the *hydrus*;  
May it thus follow your path.

## POEM III. ON SAINT SCHOLASTICA

*(From Arnoldus Wyon, *The Tree of Life*.)*

O blessed sister of Benedict in Christ’s name,  
O blessed sister of the exceptional Father.

Serious in counsel, though then still a young girl,  
You trampled the world; serious in counsel.

Beautiful bride of God, adorned with snowy jewels,  
You will bear sacred lilies, beautiful bride of God.

You seek the heights of heaven; you despised the world’s delights;  
You seek the perpetual heights of Dindymus.

Everything hateful to you, placed beneath Phoebus’ light  
And wrongly persuaded by the sun—everything hateful to you.

You surpassed the Castalian leaders, hastening as their guide;  
Illuminated and rejoicing, you surpassed the Castalian leaders.

Behold your virginal [something] . . . [Note: [Col. 1593D] Perhaps *Christi* or *fratris* should be supplied.] you had joined to the shrine,  
So that your virginal [something] might stand inviolate.

From tender nails, exchanging the perishable for heavenly things,  
You hold the victory; from tender nails.

You bring back broad trophies, narrow [things], *spudela*, *satelles*;  
Virgin daughter of Zion, you bring back broad trophies.

In heroic verses we have formerly written your most chaste praises;  
Behold, we have written for you in heroic verses.

Who [or “to whom”] became clearly evident, touched by the light of merits,  
Perfect for all, who [or “to whom”] became clearly evident,

May suffice by prayers to conquer your brother’s vow,  
Unconquered for all, may suffice by prayers.

Now it remains to write and turn the pen toward your birthday,  
To climb where you have been commanded; now it remains to write.

On a blessed day, virgin, you entered the lights of heaven,  
In the tenth month of Numa, virgin, on a blessed day. Amen.

*(Attached to this was the following six-line poem by a certain German, composed in praise of the same virgin when he came from Germany to the threshold of blessed Benedict, our father:)*

Sweetly attend my lips, illustrious Muse,  
And with mingled melodies sweetly attend my lips;

So that I may utter her, forever and without end, blessed,  
And the virgin’s honor, so that I may utter it.

The Spirit, the Dove, flies, and breathes upon you with his gift;  
Bearing lavish gifts, the Spirit, the Dove, flies.

## POEM IV. THE LIFE OF SAINT MAURUS, ABBOT

*(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*.)*

Leader, way, life, honor, praise, glory, and strength  
For your people, Jesus, light of light, leader, way, life.

You, almighty, make mute creatures speak;  
Whatever pleases you, you make happen, almighty.

Grant, I pray, that I may recount the greatness of Saint Maurus,  
What he accomplished through you; grant, I pray, that I may recount it.

When he was twelve years old, he was entrusted to gracious Benedict;  
He despised the world when he was twelve years old.

He ceased to be a boy when he began to be a monk;  
In character, not in age, he ceased to be a boy.

Who, I ask, would not marvel at continuous fasts?  
Who, I ask, would not marvel at sleepless nights?

O tears, groans, long silences, cold,  
A straw bed, a cloak—O tears, groans.

From childhood Maurus shone with the light of virtues;  
He shone from childhood through exceptional signs.

The holy Father sees whom he should draw from the sacred house,  
He sees—and Maurus sees whom he should draw from the house.

A little boy, fallen into the waters, is seen by Benedict in spirit;  
The boy fallen into the waters is rescued by Maurus.

Reason is amazed that Maurus ran upon the river;  
Behold, another Peter is here—reason is amazed.

His parents rejoiced at one deprived of movement and speech;  
Here, by prayer, he gives him movement and speech.

After the Father’s death, Cassino hoped to have him;  
After the Father’s death, it desired the Father.

He becomes Father of Glannafol, while Cassino grieves deeply;  
By the Father’s command, he becomes Father of Glannafol.

O Benedict, your fame fills everything; your disciple  
Is sought by the Gauls—O Benedict, your disciple.

The whole assembly grieves that Gaul demands him;  
The whole assembly grieves that it is to be deprived of him.

Benedict gives him a pound, a vessel, and a little book;  
The brothers give kisses; Benedict gives them to him.

He follows the departing man as far as the gate;  
He follows the departing man with gifts beyond these.

The gracious one assigns him sacred gifts of relics,  
And, teaching him with these words, assigns them to him.

“Receive, dear son, these final gifts of your master;  
Receive the last words, dear son.

Let these, my offspring, testify to our love for you;  
Let these provide you protection, my offspring.

You will complete four times eighteen years upon the earth;  
After your deeds, you will seek the stars, four times eighteen.

Farewell as you depart; you will endure adversities;  
The Lord will be favorable—farewell as you depart.”

While Maurus proceeds, many adversities occur;  
Maurus performs many signs while he proceeds.

A man broken by a fall from a tower, with no physician attending, recovers;  
The man broken by a fall from the tower is restored while he prays.

A riding accident suddenly twisted a man’s foot;  
Maurus sets the twisted bones of the foot straight.

A blind man from birth asks for the service of sight,  
And by a touch he receives the service of sight.

A mother weeps for a half-dead boy, and this suffering woman weeps;  
Soon by prayer he gives life to the half-dead boy.

The absent man saw that the Father was seeking the stars and said so;  
An angel shows him that the Father is seeking the stars.

“O Benedict, you ascend by a wondrous road to heaven;  
Make this road for us, O Benedict.”

A certain sacristan collapsed when the wall already built fell upon him;  
He nearly died after the sacristan had fallen.

The distinguished Father carries him to the doors of the church  
And saves him by his prayers, the distinguished Father.

The strong man was astonished, not knowing who had come there;  
He was astonished that the strong man had suddenly become well.

Three builders are handed over to Satan’s spirits by a slander;  
Maurus takes them away from Satan’s spirits.

The evil angel took life from one of the three;  
Maurus rescued one of the three from death.

A blessed man recovers from this disaster after seven years;  
Soon the blessed man rises up safe from it.

Wine in a vessel increases when this man blesses it;  
The more it is drunk, the more the wine in the vessel increases.

A man with a cancerous ulcer had already lost his nose and lips;  
He is healed when the man with the cancerous ulcer is signed.

When he was preparing to enter the basilica at night,  
Satan stood before the doors of the basilica.

“Maurus, do you suppose you can drive us from our own seats?  
Come then, Maurus, and see whether you can.

Hardly any of so great a flock will remain for you;  
They are all ours—hardly any, hardly any will remain for you.

Whenever I wish, I shall lead triumphs from this people;  
I shall kill and overthrow them whenever I wish.”

The almighty God rebukes you, he said; may God rebuke you, Satan,  
And in your own words may the almighty rebuke you.

When he had spoken these words, Satan withdrew like a breath of air;  
He himself entered the house when he had spoken these words.

While he asks the Lord, heavenly consolations appear;  
An angel stands beside him while he asks the Lord.

“Put away your sadness, dearest lord,” he was commanded;  
“Satan has disclosed these things; put away your sadness.

Within a short time the greater part of your community will die;  
You too will seek the heights within a short time.

Do not fear what he said, that he would lay them all low;  
None of them will belong to him—do not fear what he said.”

The exceptional Father foresaw these things by Christ’s gift  
And explained them to the brothers.

Most of the brothers died and sought the stars after a short time;  
He himself also died and sought the stars after them all.

Buried in the tomb, he flashes with the light of signs;  
Buried in the tomb, he reigns in heaven.

From there, by the Lord’s grant, he watches over his servants;  
From there he visits and nurtures his servants.

Jacob, stricken in dreams, is a witness to this. [Note: [Col. 1595D] The monastery of Glannafol, miserably plundered by Gaïdulf of Ravenna, to whom it had been entrusted by Pippin, had begun to be restored by Rorigo, count of Anjou, and his wife Bilechildis. When they later grew somewhat lukewarm in the work they had begun, Jacob, abbot of Cormery near Tours, was warned from heaven once and again; when he neglected to urge them to continue the work, he paid the penalty to Saint Maurus. These matters should be taken from the history of the destruction and restoration of Glannafol, which we shall present in the fourth century of the Benedictine history.]  
Bilheil and Rorigo are witnesses to this.

The terrible death of Gaïdulf is also a witness to this;  
Anaguareth’s vision is a witness to this. [Note: [Col. 1596D] Anaguareth, a Breton, saw a wondrous vision at the tomb of Saint Maurus, according to the same history.]

That impious and savage man had scattered his servants;  
The impious savage man perished beneath his heel.

This pious and reverent man, Anaguareth, had approached his shrine;  
This pious and reverent man sees him while awake.

Then he gave you songs, vows, and prayers, angel Maurus;  
And you gave songs, vows, and prayers to the Lord.

“I have often watched what I should do here,” he said;  
“Having seen my servants, I have often [watched what I should do].”

Those who seize their possessions are restrained by heavenly enemies;  
They become mad—those who seize their possessions.

Twice killing a servant, he repaid the servant in his place;  
But he miserably perished, twice killing a servant.

Many miracles occur at his tomb;  
A heavenly multitude sings at his tomb.

At his tomb the action of the foot returns to the lame;  
At his tomb sight is given to the blind.

At his tomb a paralytic became well at once;  
At his tomb a voice is given to the mute.

Eight were simultaneously afflicted by various illnesses;  
There eight were simultaneously restored unharmed.

If I recount everything, time itself will fail me;  
My voice will fail if I recount everything.

Cassino itself rejoices, possessing his great gifts;  
Cassino rejoices also in his remains. [Note: [Col. 1596D] The author seems here to be referring to the arm of Saint Maurus sent to the Cassinese monks by Saint Odilo, as Leo of Marsica writes in Book II, chapter 53, of the *Cassinese Chronicle.*]

Here many are granted health through his merits;  
Many are saved here through his merits.

Here, gracious Father, be present to your servants;  
Here, gracious Father, bring aid to your own.

Here, gracious Father, mindful of your discipleship, be present;  
Be our companion here, gracious Father.

By prayer, by merits, let us overcome the wicked enemy;  
By prayer, by merits, make us your companions.

When you were Father, our company grieved, deprived of the Father;  
With you as Father, may our company rejoice with the Father.

May the whole flock and its shepherds be above the stars of heaven;  
May the shepherds be above the stars of heaven with their flock.

## POEM V

[Note: [Col. 1597D] Everywhere this hymn is placed among the hymns for the Nativity of Saint John; in very many books it is divided into two or three parts to be sung at Matins, Lauds, and Vespers, and in some it is abbreviated. The poem, through verse 32, was explained in an extensive commentary in Weitz’s *Heortology*. He thus alerts lovers of musical art to its importance and sweetness: [Col. 1598D] “It is noteworthy that Guido of Arezzo, among the foremost in musical skill in his age—he lived under Emperor Henry III—introduced six syllabic notes, delighted by the perfection of the number six: UT, RE, MI, FA, SOL, LA, which he borrowed from this hymn and transferred. He increased that number of notes and added a seventh companion to the six already accepted from our hymn, BI.”]

### ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

*(From the Treasury of Hymns.)*

That your servants may, with loosened strings, resound  
The wonders of your deeds,  
UTterly loose the guilt of polluted lips,  
Holy John.

A messenger coming from high Olympus  
Announces beforehand to the Father  
That you are to be born great,  
And declares in due order  
The course of life you must lead.

Doubting the heavenly promise,  
He lost the power of ready speech;  
But when you were born, you restored  
The organs of his silenced voice.

Placed in the hidden chamber of the womb,  
You sensed the King remaining in the bridal room;  
Hence both parents, through the merits of their child,  
Sing of hidden things.

In the caves of the desert, during tender years,
Fleeing the throngs of citizens, you sought

so that you might not stain your life

even with a light utterance.

The camel provided a shaggy covering,

the two-toothed sheep a girdle for your sacred limbs;

water was your drink, and for food

honey was joined with locusts.

[Col. 1597C] All the other prophets merely sang,

with prophetic heart, of the coming radiance;

but you point it out as the one who takes away

the sin of the world.

No one was born throughout the vast extent

of the world holier than John,

who deserved to bathe in the waters

the one who washes away the age’s wickedness.

O exceedingly blessed, and of lofty merit,

knowing nothing of the stain upon your snow-white purity,

mighty martyr and inhabitant of the wilderness,

greatest of the prophets.

Garlands crown some by thirties,

increased by additions; some are doubled,

others heaped up threefold, with a hundredfold fruit—

[Col. 1597D] sacred garlands adorn you.

Now, powerful through your abundant merits,

drive back the hard stones from our hearts,

level the rough path, and direct

the crooked tracks.

So that the merciful author and redeemer of the world,

having driven envy away from purified minds,

may, when he comes, deign rightly

to place his sacred footsteps there.

[Col. 1598A] The citizens of heaven celebrate you

with praises, O God, at once simple and triune;

and we too, suppliants, beg forgiveness:

spare the redeemed.

Let us all resound glory to the Father,

and to you, Christ, heavenly-begotten,

with whom the holy Spirit, likewise Creator,

reigns.

## POEM VI. TO PETER OF PISA

(From Leboeuf, *Dissertation on the Ecclesiastical and Civil History of Paris*.)

Bright one, whose ploughshare cleaves the loins of the field,

and whose gaze you restrain … as it wanders through the settings …,

the blessed one, mounting the fiery axis of the whole world,

[Col. 1598B] pours forth rays, and by whose light the flourishing fields—

Cynthius, restraining the clouds with his burning crown—

gives growth to the fruits and grants tranquil seasons.

It delights him to sound sweetly with the Muse,

and to compose a high-pitched song beneath a slender reed.

Unhappy is the man over whom the sky hangs

with gloomy clouds, and hail courses over his wretched fields;

his house is overturned by the cold-blowing storm.

It is not pleasant for such a man to inflate this reed at his lips,

but rather, bent down, to utter words broken by sobs

and drench the grassy ground with abundant weeping.

O if only I were the young man whom you say plays with you,

whose path the Minciad, born in the country of Stuzmyrne, could [in this corrupt passage] touch with palms and fragrant laurels—neck and foot—if he deigned and wished, and were not so unlike your condition as he is,

you would see me composing songs in mournful verse,

and filling the dense woods with sweet melody.

This is itself what I sing in a thin whisper,

after he has suffused me with the light of his own countenance

and drawn forth from my mute throat whatever voices it contained.

Still trusting in him, I rise up from hope concerning my master;

holy hope grants the kingdoms of heaven;

hope bestows everything.

Dead is whoever grows cold by wavering in hope.

Come, then, unfold the tangled knots

through the air by a many-sided account:

one who is not a father does not feel that he possesses—

for the male gives the female sex to offspring in the body;

sometimes both sexes are revealed in an androgyne.

One gives light without eyes; another, without nostrils,

[Col. 1598D] or lacking feet and hands, or with some part cut away,

begets an intact girl without blemish.

Often a mutilated ram gives horns to its brutish offspring;

thus, from a shortened father, a lamb is born with a tail.

Moreover, the various kinds of things throughout the world

bestow upon what is born from them what they themselves do not possess:

the sea does this, the earth does this;

shellfish too often practice it.

Thus far I have perhaps run in vain, striving.

[Col. 1599A] Teach me, with reverence, the solution;

I am ready to learn. Untie this little question for the ancient prophets,

not unequal to them:

tell me, I beg, who is the father, despised throughout the world,

who, though lacking chastity, begets a son of immense strength,

outstanding, whom no one can prevail against,

and whom at once the kingdoms of the world dread?

## POEM VII. TO THE KING

(From Leboeuf, *ibid.*)

Cynthius, sloping toward the western shores, was already

flying with swift horses; night was already preparing

to clothe herself more quickly in her blue mantle,

gleaming with the dew-bearing brilliance of varied adornment,

when suddenly a distinguished messenger sent to me from your court

[Col. 1599B] brought fiery missiles, as though they were the likeness of a pure gift,

from an ancient and dear companion sending his heart,

arrows penetrating even to the innermost parts of my breast.

At the new dawn we hastened to your halls,

and now almost the daylight has revolved through its daily course.

The shortness of time did not allow me worthily

to set Peter against them with missiles, spaciously,

or to play with darts.

When tomorrow’s light shone conspicuously from the East,

and Titan’s trembling purple had dyed the waves,

and golden redness wandered broadly over the roaming waters,

and all things will see while Phoebus shines throughout the world. May he expiate the slender arrows as the bow drives them away—he who pierced his beloved, as though an enemy, with sharp darts.

I marvel by what art of meter the woven fabric

of our poem did not reach its conclusion,

[Col. 1599C] which shines lofty in the divine and radiant garden.

Farewell, cedar, and reach the lofty clouds with your crown;

you too, happy cypress, rise through the field with your fruit.

## POEM VIII. ALSO TO THE KING, IN SUPPLICATION

(From Leboeuf, *ibid.*)

Attend serenely to the words of your servant, greatest king,

and look with compassion upon my weeping.

I am wretched, as I deserve, and, as much as anyone in the world,

mourning, sorrow, and a sad hour are always present for me.

The seventh year is here since your cause

has generated manifold griefs and shaken my heart.

Since then my brother has been a captive

in your territories, afflicted in heart, naked, and needy.

His pitiable wife, throughout his homeland,

[Col. 1599D] begs food in all the streets with trembling mouth.

She supports four [the words *haec vir per mixtos sustentat ab arte* are corrupt; the means of support is uncertain],

whom she can scarcely keep covered with rags.

I have a sister who, consecrated to Christ from her earliest years,

keeps vigil in distinguished simplicity.

She, holding fast to an unending gain in this lot [the phrase *Haec sub sorte pars lucrum sine fine retentans* is corrupt],

has now almost lost her sight through weeping.

Our entire little household property, however small it was,

has been taken away, and, alas, there is no one

to bring any help to the wretched.

The wife of my brother has been excluded from her father’s property,

and now we are equal to slaves in our rustic condition.

Nobility has perished; poverty has come upon the wretched.

I confess that we ought to have suffered harsher things.

[Col. 1600A] But have mercy, mighty ruler, have mercy, we beg,

and at last, merciful one, put an end to these evils.

Return the captive to his homeland and civic fields;

restore his home together with his modest possessions.

May our mind continually offer praises to Christ through the ages—

to him who alone can return worthy rewards.

## POEM IX. HYMN OF PAUL THE DEACON ON THE TRANSLATION TO BENEVENTO OF THE BODY OF THE BLESSED MARTYR MERCURY

(From Pietro Piperno, *On Magical Effects*.)

O martyr Mercury, crown with the enduring gifts

of the glory of the age to come

those who with all their vows venerate

your translation.

You who once at Rome, while Decius commanded,

[Col. 1600B] suffered much for Christ, with Christ himself granting it,

and, a man foremost in imperial valor,

fell victorious.

The emperor Constans, carrying him with him

in the manner of his predecessors, toward the borders of Apulia,

when he entered as a tyrant,

laid waste everything.

Meanwhile he devastates a wealthy city,

Samnia, truly rich,

whose violent ruin God

thus consoles.

Three cenobites, men of life pleasing to God,

grieving, sad, and sorrowful over these things,

buried there the blessed body

entrusted to them.

[Col. 1600C] The desolate city, thus consoled,

builds a temple over the blessed body,

having covered its bones with earth,

so that it may be pleasing to God.

The emperor, advancing, came to Benevento,

but, checked by the force of one resisting him,

hastened to Rome and turned away from Samnia,

the warlike power.

After many years Arechis, distinguished

prince of Samnia, moved by many signs,

transferred the martyr’s body,

with praises worthy of him, to Samnia,

giving it to a noble and splendid altar,

by whose prayer may the blessed *Poeugma* [uncertain reading]

cleanse us from every fault

and grant the desired condition.

[Col. 1600D] Honor and virtue, kingdom and power,

be yours, our God, who thus make your people rise up,

bringing aid against hostile circumstances.

Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] Doubtful.]

## POEM X

(From Tosti, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*.)

Whoever wishes to recognize the splendid teachings

of blessed Paul should read this book

with great care.

For it preserves alike a song of life and of Gehenna,

and bears the precious gifts of God’s Church.

Here too the reader will find food for souls,

and, without weariness, nourishment and blessed rest.

[Col. 1601A] If by chance you wished to know the writer’s name,

he is called Paul the Deacon, and himself a monk.

With God’s help he completed this work,

for the praise of God and of the holy archangel Michael.

I beg you, reader, do not cease to entreat the Lord,

that he may receive the writer’s vow with favor.

“Another began; I shall finish [printed *ego finibit*, grammatically irregular]. [lacuna]”

## POEM XI. EPITAPH OF ROTHAID, DAUGHTER OF KING PIPPIN

(From Duchesne, *Historians of Frankish History*, vol. II.)

Here I lie, called Rothaid [Rothaidis] by name,

and I derive my lineage from a very exalted stock.

For my brother is Charles, who subjugated

Italian nations by arms, trusting in the power of the Thunderer.

My father is Pippin, begotten of the princely Charles,

[Col. 1601B] who laid low the tyrant of the Hagarenes

in a great slaughter [or: disaster].

Pippin is my great-grandfather, than whom no one was bolder.

But my great-great-grandfather was the powerful Anschises,

who derives his name, after a long interval,

from the Trojan Anchises.

This holy and blessed bishop Arnulf,

who shines everywhere through wondrous deeds,

begot him.

Here my parents placed me,

trusting in the hope of this man.

## POEM XII. ALSO THE EPITAPH OF ANOTHER DAUGHTER, ADHELAID

(From Duchesne, *ibid.*)

Everlasting love and the cause of salvation

make the one whom an alert heart urges hasten here.

Do you wish to know why this sacred place retains

so many tombs, where the starry court of heaven is open?

This holy man of the Lord, who afterward guarded the flock,

had previously been the father of a legitimate offspring.

His descendants, trusting in their grandfather as patron,

wish to place their bodies in this holy place.

Here rests Adelaid, a pious virgin, daughter of Pippin.

Protect her and the others also, Holy Father.

## POEM XIII. EPITAPH OF QUEEN HILDEGARD, WIFE OF CHARLEMAGNE

[Note: [Col. 1601D] Paul Warnefrid, in his book *On the Bishops of the Church of Metz*, in Duchesne, *Historians of Frankish History*, vol. II, p. 202, and in Bouquet, vol. V of *Historians of the Affairs of Gaul*, p. 192, indicates in the following words that he is the author of this and the subsequent epitaphs:

“Hildegard rests near the city of Metz, in the oratory of blessed Arnulf. Since the kings already mentioned derived their origin from blessed Arnulf, they placed there the bodies of their deceased loved ones. For there were buried two daughters of King Pippin, one called Rothaid and the other Adelaid. There too were buried two daughters of the younger King Charles, namely Adelaid and Hildigard. This Hildigard, called by her mother’s name, followed her dying mother soon afterward. I have taken care to record below all their epitaphs, composed by us at the command of King Charles …”

From this it is clear that the same epitaphs were first attributed by Baronius, vol. IX of the *Annals*, under the year 786, p. 332, and afterward also by D. Duchesne himself—before this passage of Paul Warnefrid had become known to him—to Alcuin, *Works*, p. 1757. We compared this poem with the Metz manuscript, sent to us by D. Francis of the Order of St Benedict, Congregation of SS. Vitus and Hydulfus, a learned man whose scholarly pen is occupied in composing and continuing the history of the city of Metz, soon to be completed in accordance with the wishes of scholars.]

(From various editions of Baronius, Duchesne, and Bouquet, and from the Metz manuscript.)

The golden elements that gleam with yellow figures

show how brightly the buried limbs once shone.

Here lies a queen, exalted spouse of a powerful king,

Hildegard, who was happily married to Charles;

she surpassed the offspring of so illustrious a stock

by as much as the Indian gem surpasses the soil from which it was born.

[Col. 1602A] So great was the grace of her flourishing beauty

that no woman beneath the setting sun could have been more beautiful,

nor could the sardonyx, mingled with Parian roses [the wording is uncertain],

equal the delicate beauty of her.

Yet the lights of her heart surpassed this appearance,

as did the simplicity of her soul and her inward beauty.

You were gentle, wise, skillful, and gracious,

generous and adorned with every virtue.

But why should I say more, when no praise for you is greater

than that you pleased so great a man?

And when the mighty man of war joined to his ancestral scepters

the flax-bearing Po and the Roman Tiber

[Note: [Col. 1602D] Metz manuscript: *Tibrum* for *Tibrim*, both accusative forms of “Tiber”],

you alone were found worthy

to hold in your hand the golden scepters of a manifold kingdom.

[[Note: [Col. 1602D] We have restored this couplet from the Metz manuscript.] The year after the eleventh had already received you

when sweet-flowing love united you both.]

Again the year after the eleventh bore you away—

[Note: [Col. 1602D] Many interpret this as the thirteenth year, so that Hildegard, thirteen years old, married Charles and lived with him for the same number of years. She died in 783. Bouquet. Consult Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annals*, book XXV, p. 265; Duchesne, *On Frankish Writers*, vol. II, p. 203.]

Alas, mother of kings! Alas, glory and grief!

The Frank, the Suevian, the German, and the Briton himself

mourn you, together with the Hyberan company and the harsh Getae

[Note: [Col. 1602D] Printed *Hybera*, variant *Ibera*: both designate the Iberian company].

The inhabitant of the Loire laments you, the Italian land laments you,

and anxious Rome herself groans at your death.

You moved even the strong hearts of men to weeping:

behold, tears fall among shields and weapons.

Alas, with what fires you burned your husband’s wise heart,

ever firm in strength!

[Note: [Col. 1602D] Printed *Heu, quantis*, “Alas, with how great [fires]”; Metz manuscript *Heu, quantum*, “Alas, how greatly.”]

This hope consoles all who mourn,

a hope certain indeed: that, for your worthy deeds,

you possess the sacred kingdoms.

[lacuna]

Gracious Father, [grant] her to share in what is yours [the preceding text is missing].

## POEM XIV. EPITAPH OF HILDEGARD, DAUGHTER OF CHARLES AND HILDEGARD

[Col. 1602C]

Hildegard! bitter death snatched you away suddenly,

as Boreas snatches the privets in early spring.

The circle of your life had not yet completed a year,

nor had a second annual light come to you.

Little girl, you leave behind no little grief,

piercing your father’s royal heart with a dart.

Bearing your mother’s name, you renew the grief of her death [Note: [Col. 1602D] Printed *de morte*, “from her death”; variant *de corde*, “from the heart.”]

after you had lived scarcely forty days.

With sorrowful hearts we pour out rivers of tears,

while you, exceedingly blessed, seek everlasting joys.

## POEM XV. EPITAPH OF ANOTHER DAUGHTER, ADELHEID

[Note: [Col. 1603A] Adelheid and Hildegard were buried near their mother at Metz, in the suburban basilica of the holy apostles, or of St Arnulf, from whom they derived their lineage. There were also buried the two daughters of King Pippin, Rothaid and Adelaid; their epitaphs too survive, composed by Paul the Deacon, in Duchesne, in the work cited.]

[Col. 1603A]

Here lies buried in this small tomb a little girl,

called Adelheid by the sacred stream (*amne sacro*).

Her father is Charles, powerful with a double diadem,

quick of intellect [Note: [Col. 1604A] Printed *Mobilis*, “quick, agile”; Metz manuscript *Nobilis*, “noble”],

and sufficiently strong in arms.

[Col. 1604A] She had taken her beginning near the lofty walls of Pavia

when her father, seeking the Italian kingdoms, took them

[Note: [Col. 1604A] In the year 773];

but, hastening toward the Rhône, she was snatched from the light of life,

and her mother’s heart was struck with grief from afar.

She died without seeing her father’s triumphs;

now she possesses the blessed kingdoms of the eternal Father.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF PAUL THE DEACON

## [PROBLEMS]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

(From Mai, *Roman Spicilegium*, vol. V.)

Among the distinguished men of the monastery of Monte Cassino, Peter the Deacon reports, in chapter 36, Paul the Ligurian, who, he says, professed the monastic life there in the time of Pope Paschal II and composed commentaries on the Prophets, the Psalter, and the New Testament, as well as writing other volumes that had not yet come into Peter’s hands.

Mabillon too speaks of this Paul and his books, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. V, book LXIX, under the year 1100; as does Legipontius, *Literary History of the Benedictines*, vol. IV, pp. 36, 41, 46, 51; and finally Lelong, *Bibliotheca Sacra*, vol. I, p. 895, although he adds nothing to what Peter the Deacon has reported.

Marus believes that all the aforementioned little works of Paul perished, while at the same time lamenting the negligence of his age in investigating the treasures of sacred monuments.

Yet neither Peter the Deacon expressly mentions, nor Marus saw, Paul’s little work on sacred Genesis. I discovered it a few years ago in a Vatican manuscript, apparently an autograph manuscript, but certainly contemporary, since its script must be assigned to the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the twelfth century.

Whether the author proceeded also to the other books of the Pentateuch, I do not know; for the Vatican codex ends mutilated at the blessings of the patriarchs. The title of the work is: “Here begin Paul’s Problems concerning Riddles from the Canonical Books.”

They are called “problems” because most of the work turns on questions and their solutions.

The Christian authors cited by Paul, so far as I have seen, are Ambrose, Antony the Abbot, Augustine, Eucherius, Faustus, Pope Gregory, Jerome, John Cassian, Isidore, Junilius, Orientius, Origen, Orosius, Sulpicius, Theophilus, and certain anonymous writers.

Among the Hebrews he cites the Seventy Interpreters, a certain Judas, the *Annals of the Hebrews*, and, generally, Jewish writings.

Among the pagans he cites Apuleius and Virgil.

The work itself begins as follows:

“The Old Testament, Isidore says, is so called because, when the New came, it ceased.”

My sole purpose at present is to provide some knowledge of the work and the smallest specimen of it, especially from the passages of ancient authors cited in it.

[Col. 1603]

## HERE BEGIN THE PROBLEMS

[Col. 1603B] Folio 23. JUDAS says: “The authority of books is recognized from their prefaces.”

Folio 29. THEOPHILUS. “He divided the light and the darkness. He called the light day.” That is: day is the form of the formed thing; night is the deprivation of work.

Folio 30. OROSIUS. “Does the firmament stand still, or does it move? If it moves, how is it firm? If it stands still, how do the heavenly bodies travel around the world?” That is: the firmament is not called such because it stands immobile, but because of the firmness of its nature, just as the pole’s rotation is carried around the ether.

Folio 40. JUNILIUS says: “After the first day nothing is shown to have been made from things that did not exist. The human soul alone was [made thus], just as man alone was made from nothing.”

Folio 50. Concerning this paradise MATTHEW the apostle says:

[Note: [Col. 1603] Our Paul seems to have taken what follows from some apocryphal work.]

“The paradise of delights, where Adam was, higher than all mountains and near heaven; and there is found in it nothing that harms human salvation, whether among living or dead creatures; where neither lilies nor roses wither; where there is neither labor nor old age; and all animals obey the command of man, not to be slaughtered for food, but to serve the delights of angels and human beings. For there too banquets are prepared from the flesh of cattle or fish, yet no one is killed. The same is true of drinks. Nevertheless, no evacuation of waste follows. Nor is the face of heaven there said to be covered with clouds, nor are there lightning flashes; and so forth.”

Folio 57. Repeating a word occurs in three ways: in rebuke, as in, “Where are you, Adam? Where are you, Adam?”; in prohibition, as in, “Abraham, Abraham, do not lay your hand upon the boy”; and in consolation, as Antony said: “Where were you, Jesus? Where were you, Jesus?”

Folio 60. OROSIUS says that the world resembles a man lying in bed, and that it is first formed from the head—that is, from Adam’s paradise, placed in the east—and that the ocean lies between it and this world.

OROSIUS says that another island is hidden in the east, with the pleasantness of Adam’s paradise, in which Elijah and Enoch still dwell.

Codex, folio 66, where the subject is Lamech the murderer. FAUSTUS. “Or a young man,” that is, because Cain is not gray-haired and does not grow old in any way, like wild beasts that do not grow old. These things are read in the *Annals of the Hebrews*.

“Why is Lamech’s punishment greater than Cain’s? Because before Cain no murder had been committed, nor had any correction or harsh sentence been pronounced to punish it. It was not so with Lamech. Or ‘seventy-seven times,’ because this number of Lamech’s race was destroyed in the Flood. Or because vengeance rests in this number. Seventy-seven men were completed from Adam to Christ, and then the world will be dissolved and human souls will find rest,” and so forth.

SULPICIUS, however, says that he does not say this about Cain: “into my wound,” that is, “his vengeance is upon me,” recalling the word of the Lord.

Folio 94, where the subject is Isaac’s sacrifice. FAUSTUS. “They came to the place. Why did Abraham say, ‘We will return to you’? If he intended to offer his son, how could he return?” That is: he believed in hope against hope, because he believed he would offer his son, since the Lord had foretold it to him.

He also believed that his son would return, because the Lord had said to him, “Your seed shall be like the stars of heaven.”

He also believed that the one who had given him a son from a barren woman and from old age could raise him from the dead, and so forth.

# FRAGMENT OF SEXTUS POMPEIUS FESTUS ON THE MEANING OF WORDS

Transcribed from a very ancient exemplar of the Farnesian Library.

[Col. 1605]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1605A] Verrius Flaccus, a distinguished grammarian of the Augustan age, [Col. 1605B] had written, around the beginning of Tiberius’ principate, nineteen books *On the Meaning or Signification of Words*. In the third or fourth century after Christ, S. Pompeius Festus reduced them to an epitome; otherwise Festus is mentioned by none of the ancients except Charisius and Macrobius.

This work appears to have been in use among learned men until, approximately four hundred years after Festus, Paul the Deacon embraced in a narrower volume a truly golden treasury of Roman antiquity, less suited to the inertia and negligence of his contemporaries. It is unnecessary to pursue here the manner in which he handled the ancient exemplar.

[Note: [Col. 1605D] He frequently attacks Verrius sharply, for example on p. 136, under “Salva res est”; p. 137, under “Spondere”; p. 148, under “Sertor”; p. 158, under “Terentum”; p. 181, under “Orcus”; p. 184, under “Pictor Zeuxis”; p. 189, under “Tatium”; p. 191, under “Tersum diem,” and so forth. Compare what he says about his own purpose, p. 35 and following, under “Porriciam.”]

Just as Pompeius Festus’ epitome suppressed Verrius’ books, or caused them afterward to be neglected by copyists, so Paul the Deacon’s little book either suppressed the volumes of Pompeius or caused them thereafter to be neglected by copyists. This is the reason why altogether four manuscript codices of Festus are known to us, with only one surviving:

1. The manuscript that Macrobius had in his hands at the beginning of the fifth century after Christ; it no longer exists.

[Col. 1605C] 2. The manuscript used by Placidus, a grammarian of uncertain date, when he was composing the glosses recently edited by Angelo Mai; it too no longer exists.

[Note: [Col. 1605D] *Classical Authors from the Vatican Codices*, vol. III, p. 427. They were reprinted by the German editors of the *Annals of Philology and Education* in 1833. Compare Fr. Dübner in the *Rheinisches Museum* of 1835, “Inedita,” and elsewhere, no. 8. Ursinus had already frequently compared Festus’ words in his notes with Placidus’ manuscript glosses.]

3. The manuscript that belonged to Paul the Deacon, likewise lost.

4. The Farnesian manuscript, once brought from Illyria and now preserved in the Royal Library of Naples. It begins with the letter M and, in the portion that survives, is miserably mutilated and short by several leaves that were extant in Pomponius Laetus.

Certain people transcribed fragments of the Farnesian codex in the earliest period of the revival of letters; others arranged for them to be transcribed; still others seem to have read them in the archetype.

Although as early as 1489 Angelo Politian, in his *Miscellanies*, chapter 73, appealed to their authority,

[Note: [Col. 1605D] “What we are now about to report will perhaps be ridiculed and hissed down by some as uncertain and wavering, and as not yet sufficiently investigated. But I thought I ought to speak of it, lest that nearly extinguished trace of antiquity, whatever its worth, should be destroyed. Four years ago, in 1485, a Greek man named Manilius Rallus, but one highly trained in Latin letters, showed me at Rome a certain fragment of Sextus Pompeius Festus—for so it was titled—quite ancient indeed, but mostly mutilated and gnawed through by mice.

“What held me greatly was this: if those remains, whatever their value, survived from the complete volume itself that the author Festus had composed, and not from the abridged work now forcibly compressed and curtailed in our hands—apparently by some obscure and unlearned person, who in this respect too had rendered insufficient service to literature.

“Pomponius Laetus, a man exceptionally learned in antiquity and good letters, had also retained for himself some pages from the same fragment; he likewise gave them to me to read and transcribe.”]

A conjecture about the true reading of a line of Catullus follows; see p. 114. The various readings of Pietro Vettori, which A. Augustinus also cites in the preface to his edition, appeared in 1553, after Festus’ fragments had already been published and repeatedly reprinted.

It was unfortunately the case that Paul the Deacon’s epitome, copied frequently before the invention of printing and soon printed in 1471, was afterward reprinted more than ten times before the end of the fifteenth century, whereas the genuine remains of Festus were left hidden in private libraries.

In 1510, at last, a certain Conagus—I do not know who he was—was the first, while publishing Paul’s epitome, to compose from Paul and the scraps of Festus that rough and undigested miscellany. I wished to include the printer’s notice and the verses copied below, both because the exemplar is extremely rare and because it establishes a line of descent; apparently none of the more recent editors knew of it.

“Reader. If the fragments of Sextus [printed ‘Sesti’] Pompeius Festus, all of which have been found and are here attached, beginning with the letter M and continuing to the end, have not been set apart but have been joined to others, this was done deliberately, so that readers might not be wearied by repetition, and because certain things have been added that were not in the exemplar of our Pius but in another of the same kind—things so rough that they do not seem entirely correct.

“Nevertheless, to avoid rashness, and so that nothing belonging to the fragments themselves might be omitted, they have been printed according to the exemplar. If Pius himself, who because of his absence could not correct them, and could not even inspect his own exemplar while it was being printed, had been present, they would have been more correct.

“Therefore, do not attribute to Pius himself those additions that are uncorrected, taken from another exemplar; they are noted below.

“Under the letter S: ‘Satis,’ a word, especially [unclear] ‘a pterir retro.’

“Under the letter T: ‘Trium viri’; throughout the fragment, in a certain exemplar, it is joined to ‘senonas gallos,’ following ‘transalpina’ [printed corruptly].

“Under the letter S.

“Under the letter T: ‘Topper’ in some places.

‘May he attract Festus: in what manner, Conagus.’

The reader has found it; you yourself should approve the plan.

He attached the fragments that you now see added,

and took care that each should fit in its own order.

If any Latin should prove weak or rough, he confesses

that he changed nothing, lest he corrupt it.”

[Col. 1607A] The book appeared at Milan together with Varro (*On the Latin Language*) and Nonius Marcellus. The Paris editions of these three grammarians from 1511 and 1519 reproduce it. Among these, by chronological order, must be placed the Aldine edition of the *Thesaurus Cornucopiae*, published at Venice in 1513 and reprinted in the same type in 1517, then in 1527, with several notes by Michael Bentini, which all later editors neglected.

[Note: [Col. 1607D] Therefore all are mistaken who, following Augustinus, report Aldus as the compiler of the miscellany mentioned above. Nor does Aldus himself claim anything of the sort in his preface to the reader; rather, he wishes ill upon Paul and the other abbreviators of the same flour, as though he did not know that the fragments of Festus published by him certainly repair part of the damage.]

Other printers north and south of the Alps made the Aldine *Thesaurus* their own, but did so without changing anything, or at least very little, in the books of Pompeius Festus. These scholarly efforts did little for our work, however, until in 1559 Antonius Augustinus, that tireless investigator of all antiquity, obtained the archetypal codex of the fragment from the very rich library of Cardinal Ranuccio Farnese.

He arranged the whole of Paul’s epitome, placing beside it not only the surviving glosses of Festus but even the smallest fragments, in alphabetical order. All earlier editors, as well as the manuscript codices, had arranged the words by their first letter only, following ancient custom.

[Col. 1607B] He also added indexes of authors and of matters mentioned incidentally, as well as notes of no little value. Finally, he was the first to place at the beginning carefully collected fragments of Verrius Flaccus, which later editors down to the present day have been content to reprint, altering a few syllables here and there.

This is the Augustinian, or, as it is otherwise called, Venetian edition, which Joseph Scaliger adorned with commentary and supplements.

Many have judged Scaliger’s work differently; but however much the efforts of a great man may deserve credit, it must be admitted that the fragments of the mutilated pages, scattered at the editor’s discretion and with uncertain measurements of the lacunae, provided uncongenial material for conjecture, even though Paul’s authority supported him in many places.

But a man born for the good of ancient letters truly brought salvation to Festus: Fulvius Ursinus, who prefaced his notes as follows:

“On the fragment of Festus.

[Col. 1607C] “It is now twenty years since Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, compared the fragment of Festus—which the memory of our forefathers records as having been brought from Illyria and which is preserved in the Farnesian Library—with the published texts much more carefully than others had done, and was the first to transcribe the second, mutilated portion of the book and publish it at Venice, with commentary by himself and the work of Carlo Sigonio.

“But since at that time he was one of the fourteen judges at Rome, occupied with lawsuits and other more serious concerns, some things escaped that distinguished man, who had deserved so well of letters, while the pages were being transcribed.

“Learned men afterward followed that edition and restored so much in it that from what they published at Paris it can easily be understood what they would have done if they had obtained a more correct codex.

“We, therefore, who have often had the opportunity not merely to inspect these remains of antiquity but also to handle them at our discretion, observed from a comparison of several passages that, if the pages of this fragment were reproduced faithfully from the archetypal exemplar,

[Col. 1607D] all students of antiquity would more easily and more certainly conjecture what is mutilated and incomplete in them. We therefore arranged for the pages themselves to be transcribed with as much care as possible, in the order in which Festus wrote, with the number of lines on each page and the number of letters in each line, neither increased nor diminished, but exactly as they are in the exemplar.

“Moreover, we restored the mutilated part of the pages in countless places, taking account of the space that had to be supplied. We borrowed much from the writings of those named above and added much from ourselves—not because we believe these additions true or think Festus wrote them in this form, but in order to stir the ingenuity of learned men to do this fragment good service.

“We distinguished these supplements from the ancient text by differences in lettering and by certain signs. We also separated from it those leaves which Pomponius Laetus is said to have received from Marullus, because their archetypal exemplar does not survive; and because the other part of the pages, which had been mutilated by fire near the margin, was omitted by those who then transcribed the fragment and is now missing.

“As for the pages we have published, they were transcribed from the hand of a most learned man and are not only more accurate than the other editions but also fuller in several places. Thus, if anything beyond these pages appears in the published texts, it must clearly be believed not to belong to Festus, but to have been taken from Paul’s epitome or from elsewhere.

“To all this we added at the end some very brief notes on only those matters that seemed to have been overlooked by others. Since the additions supplied from Paul’s epitome or from the commentaries of others are readily available to everyone, we thought it superfluous to record them here, except where something may have slipped in through our own inadvertence.”

[Col. 1608B] There can scarcely be any doubt that Fulvius Ursinus was extremely careful in transcribing the work. Yet the text, difficult in itself and corrupted by every kind of error, was treated most badly by the printers.

The editor’s notes suffer from the same defect. The index of glosses, compiled, I think, by some schoolman, teems with every kind of mistake.

There is another difficulty: the leaves that reached Ursinus were short by several glosses, so that certain matters are absent from the Roman edition and, despite his protest to the contrary at the end of the preface, must now be recovered from the ancient sources.

I learned from catalogues that the Ursinian book was reprinted at Paris in 1583, perhaps in a more corrected form, but I was not permitted to inspect this edition.

Soon afterward Dionysius Gothofredus, in his *Authors of the Latin Language*, arranged for the Augustinian compilation and the pages of the Farnesian codex and its leaves to be reprinted from the Roman edition, so that learned men might not lack anything while reading through the remains of Festus. In this he made insufficient use of the printers’ care;

[Col. 1608C] for, to omit other defects, they sadly disturbed the arrangement of the lines on many pages.

Dacerius follows Augustinus (1681), as do Dacerius’ Dutch editors (Amsterdam, 1700 or 1701), except that they reprint the fragment from Ursinus, but on square pages, breaking the arrangement of the codex’s pages and lines.

How many blemishes this text, so often and variously handled by editors, has had to contract, competent judges of such matters will readily understand. For my part, I pass over examples, lest the preface grow into a commentary. I shall openly confess this much: apart from Lindemann’s edition [Note: *Latin Grammarians of the Old School*, vol. II. Leipzig, 1832, quarto.], there is scarcely another that deserves any confidence, especially in the mutilated pages of Festus. Yet Lindemann himself—whose services to Paulus and Festus are many and distinguished—restored the order of the manuscript codices in the epitome of Paulus, but in the separately printed fragment of Festus did not take sufficient account of critical considerations. He did not arrange his pages so that they corresponded with Ursinus’s, but marked their beginnings and endings only with his own numbering. For squared paper can scarcely accommodate an exact measurement of lacunae; without that, every attempt at supplementation becomes a frivolous game of chance. Add that he did not everywhere correctly distinguish Ursinus’s supplements from the text of the Farnesian manuscript, while elsewhere he was an excessively careful imitator of the old book.

When I noticed these things, and when the bookseller kept insisting that purchasers especially demanded Festus as a companion to Varro, I thought it would be worthwhile to undertake a more accurate edition of the Farnesian text, based on the Roman edition, correcting the errors I have noted above [Col. 1609A] and adding the necessary indexes. Moreover, since the time of Antonius Augustinus no one had either added anything to or corrected anything in the fragments of Verrius [Note: [Col. 1609D]

I except Foggini, who appended to his explanation of the Praenestine Calendars fragments of Verrius that were not fuller, but arranged in a different order:

1. pp. 87–89: “Historical narratives which, as ancient writers testify, existed in his books.”

2. pp. 90–95: “The meanings and orthography of certain words from Verrius Flaccus in Festus and other ancient writers, arranged according to the alphabetical order.”

That Foggini also compiled the Farnesian remains, although it would have been better to transcribe them in full, was nevertheless appropriate. But what advantage accrues to editions of Festus if everything this grammarian discussed concerning the meanings of words under the added name of his Verrius is read again at the beginning of the book, I certainly do not see; for Festus in its entirety is nothing other than an extremely long fragment of Verrius Flaccus.]

I have completely rewoven this fabric, nevertheless omitting what was already found in Festus and adequately indicated in the index of authors.

You will not be surprised, benevolent reader, if you find conjectures transferred from the margin to the end of each page; typographical abbreviations made somewhat differently; brackets introduced in place of different letters; the beginnings of glosses distinguished by a straight obelus; and a definite, easier system of punctuation adopted in place of an uncertain and crude one. We did not wish to detract from the elegance of our little book by anything that would not add to its reliability. We seem all the more deserving of pardon in this respect because we corrected Ursinus’s text not only from its errors and from a collation of his notes, but also from Augustinus and the older books preceding Augustinus. We did so rarely and only under the greatest necessity, especially in the excerpts, since Ursinus edited them with less care. To attempt anything further would have been beyond either our purpose or our ability [Col. 1609B], particularly since Festus is the kind of author in whose correction a grammarian’s hand can scarcely restrain itself within the limits imposed by the work.

In Ursinus’s supplements, just as we often recast the wording so that, without altering the sense, the lines of the Roman edition could be represented in a more recent typographical format, so wherever a sentence ended in a faulty restoration we thought it better to refrain from new conjectures—except that in one or two places we did not wish to reject a new reading supported by the authority of monuments. (See p. 95, line 6, and the comparison of the interpreters at Dion Cassius, p. 36, line 30.) The conjectures that Ursinus assigned to the margin—often false, as on p. 188, *Cornificius* (see the Index of Authors, s.v.), and sometimes useless, as on p. 190, *deditione*—we have treated with considerable leniency. There were, however, cases in which manifest errors necessarily had to be removed (see, for example, p. 184, *pretii* for *auctoris*). Notes relating to the writing of the Farnesian manuscript have been added for this purpose, so that critics could not complain that anything had been omitted by which the truth of a good or bad reading might in some way be established.

[Col. 1609C] Complete indexes to Pompeius Festus did not yet exist. Here, benevolent reader, you will have indexes that, if not new, are at least renewed and enlarged. But what I have accomplished in this part of the little book is better shown by comparison with earlier editions [Note: [Col. 1610D] For example, see the Index of Authors and Monuments, s.v. *Cato*, *Lex*, *Lingua*; and the Index of Subjects, apart from the Greek words, s.v. *aedis*, *sacellum*, *sacra*, etc.] than described in my own words.

As for publishing the epitome of Paulus and the commentaries on Varro and Festus, although I have already resolved to undertake something, I prefer first to await your judgment.

Written on the Ides of October, 1838.

[Col. 1609]

## [On the Meaning of Words]

M.

### Page 1

**[par] Mutum** we call something either because it produces no sound when it comes into contact with these letters.

**[par] Metaphor.** What the Greeks call *metaphora*, we call *translatio*, that is, “a transferred word,” from *domo mutuatu verbum*: “which,” says Verrius, “we use in speech, especially when a suitable and significant word is lacking, so that we may indicate a thing by a more attractive [Note: *speciosiore*], and likewise more expressive word than the proper term.” [lacuna] “returns to its own.” [lacuna] “the transferred term will remain where it has arrived.” [lacuna] “as something foreign, just as if it were its own, from…” [lacuna]

**[par] Metaplastics.** Among poets this is used for what they customarily change because of metrical necessity; the same is called a barbarism [Col. 1610A] when writing in prose. [lacuna] **[par] Meta—** [lacuna] “from the more costly…” [lacuna] “having arrived…” [lacuna] “which Ennius says…” [lacuna] “that is…” [lacuna] **[par] Meta—** [lacuna] “as…” [lacuna] “for the sake of…” [lacuna] “necessity.”

**[par] Metonymy** is a trope in which what contains is signified by what is contained, or a superior by an inferior, and an inferior by a superior. What contains is signified by what is contained, as in Ennius, when he says: “Africa trembles, a terrible, rugged land, with tumult.” What is contained is signified by what contains, as when one says, “the wine-jar has been drained.” A superior by an inferior, as Ennius says: “With great uproar the wind drives Vulcan.” An inferior by a superior, as in: “The god persuaded the mind to wine, who is greatest by far.”

**[par] Masculine and feminine** nouns are better said according to Greek usage, [Col. 1610B] for the Greeks do not call them *andrika* (ἀνδρικά) and *gynaikeia* (γυναικεῖα), but *arsenika* (ἀρσενικά) and *thēlyka* (θηλυκά).

### Page 2

**[par] “Gold was returned to the matrons.”** Sinnius Capito says this; it seems to mean that the gold was restored to the matrons, from which the Roman People had made a bowl and sent it to Apollo at Delphi, as is attested by the inscription on a tablet. The matrons had indeed given the gold after removing it from their own adornment, so that the vow to Apollo might be discharged. Some say rather that the statement should be understood of the gold which the matrons once contributed for the liberation of the Capitol from the Senonian Gauls; it was later returned to them by the Roman People.

**[par] Magisterare.** The ancients used this for “to rule” and “to govern.” But some use *magisterare* for [lacuna].

**[par] Muta.** [lacuna] “by voice…” [lacuna] “much…” [lacuna] [Col. 1610C] “understand…” [lacuna] “the matter…” [lacuna] “are called…” [lacuna] “to whom rather…” [lacuna]

**[par] Mille.** The ancients used it in the singular, whereas we now use it differently when we say *mille nummum* (“a thousand coins”).

**[par] Municas.** Likewise [Note: *id.*] from *communicas*, Verrius says, from *munia*, that is, “duties,” or rather from *co—* [lacuna].

**[par] Mancipatus.** One adopted in such a way that he was heir to his own father was called *mancipatus*. For the adopted son is heir to the one who adopts him as though he had been born from him, while of his natural father he is almost as though he were not in another’s power. Thus he is a legitimate and natural heir, as is clearly shown by what Servius Sulpicius says in the speech he wrote and delivered on behalf of Aufidia.

**[par] Multifacere.** The ancients used this as they used *magnifacere*, and likewise *parvifacere*. M. Cato is a witness in the speech he wrote against Q. Minucius Thermus concerning the Ten Commissioners: “He sets no great store by faith, oath, or chastity.” [lacuna] This expression rightly fell out of use, because quantity is not estimated in this way [Note: “quality”], nor does the matter require multitude or consist in number.

### Page 3

[Col. 1610D] **[par] Magistri** are called, in every matter, those who are more powerful than the others: thus *magistri equitum* (“masters of the horse”) and *magistri populi* (“masters of the people”). The ancient usage also spoke of the games of Apollo in this way, which are now called otherwise, as Cato shows in the speech he delivered against [lacuna].

[Col. 1611A] **[par] Maledictors.** The ancients called *maledictores* those whom we call *maledici* (“slanderers”). When Cato was setting out for Spain [Note: *Hispaniam*]: “Slanderers must be removed.” [lacuna]

**[par] Mihipte** for *mihi ipse* (“I myself”) Cato used when he said [lacuna] talents [lacuna] [lacuna].

**[par] Mansues.** Cato said *mansues* for *mansuetus* (“tame”) in a letter to [lacuna]: “mansues” [lacuna].

**[par] Meritavere.** Cato often said *meritavere* for *meruere*. In Book IV concerning the Carthaginians: “The Suffetes immediately summoned all the cohorts, and all those who had served.”

**[par] Magnificius.** Cato used *magnificius* for *magnificentius* in the work he wrote [lacuna]: “what man [lacuna] more beautifully cleanses or more splendidly [lacuna].” We now say *magnificentius*, since *magnifice* is its positive form.

But his grandson, in the work he wrote [lacuna], says: “Nevertheless, when he was curule aedile, he celebrated the games of the Great Mother more splendidly than the others.”

**[par] Magnificior** [Note: *Munificior*.] also seems to have derived this from *munifice*, since we now say *munificentior*, although *munificens* is not used in our language. Cato, in the work he wrote, says [lacuna]: “no one more munificent.”

**[par] Mediocriculum.**

### Page 4

Cato used this in the speech he delivered during his consulship: “A rather small number of men conducting a laughing magistracy, and a moderately small army advancing to meet them.” [Note: *gerere*, “to conduct,” rather than *genere*.]

**[par] The shrine of Mutunus Titinus** stood on the Velian Hill [Note: *Veliis*], opposite the Mustelline Wall, in the alley [or harbor], from which, after its altars had been removed, a bathhouse was made into a house. It had remained inviolate from the foundation of the city until the principate of Caesar Augustus, and had been reverently and properly maintained, as is clear from the books of the Pontiffs. [Col. 1611C] It now has a small shrine at the twenty-sixth milestone from the city, on the right-hand side of the road beside a crossroads, where it is still worshiped; women sacrifice there, wearing bordered garments [Note: *velatae*, “veiled”].

**[par] Matrons** were not removed by the magistrates, so that they might not appear to be struck or touched, or so that pregnant women might not be shaken. For this reason Verrius also says that “their husbands, rather than being seated with their wives, were forced by the magistrates to descend from the essedum” [Note: *essedo*], because husband and wife ride in the same vehicle.

**[par] Mourning is diminished for the people** by the dedication of a temple; when the censors have completed the lustrum; when a public vow is discharged; and, for private persons, when children have been born; when honor has come to the family; when a parent, child, husband, or brother, captured by the enemy, returns home; when a betrothal has taken place; when someone more closely related than the person being mourned has been born [Note: *is*]; and when it is the festival of Ceres, and for every celebration [Note: *gratulatione*].

**[par] The Flamen Dialis** is of the highest rank among the fifteen flamines, although the others too possess their particular distinctions of dignity. The least important is considered the Flamen Pomonalis, because Pomona presides over the least valuable produce of the fields, namely apples.

**[par] Mundus.** As Ateius Capito says in Book VII of the *Pontifical Matters*, the *mundus* is customarily opened three times a year, on these days: the day after the Volcanalia and the sixth day before the Ides of November. Why it is so called he reports in the following way.

### Page 5

Cato, in his *Commentaries on Civil Law*: **[par] Mundus.** “The name *mundus* was given after the *mundus* that is above us. Its form is such, as one who entered it could understand, that the lower part resembles that upper one, as though consecrated to the Spirits of the Dead. The ancients decreed that it remain closed at all times except on the days written above; they also judged those days religious, because at that time the things belonging secretly and in concealment to the worship of the Spirits of the Dead were, as it were, brought into the light and revealed. They therefore wished nothing to be done in the state during that period. Thus, on those days, they did not engage the enemy in battle; no army was enrolled; no assemblies were held; and nothing else was conducted in the state except what the utmost necessity required.”

**[par] Mos** is an ancestral institution, that is, a custom belonging to the memory of the ancients, especially in matters of their religious observances and ceremonies.

**[par] Milium.** Some think that *milium* took its name from the greatest sum of money, which is one thousand; others judge it to be of Greek origin, since the Greeks call it *kenchros* (κέγχρος), just as they call panic grass *melinē* (μελίνη).

**[par] Municipal rites** are called those which people had from the beginning, before they received Roman citizenship, and which the Pontiffs wished them to observe and perform according to the custom in which they had existed in ancient times.

**[par] Smaller temples** are made by the augurs when certain places are enclosed with boards or linen cloths so that they open through no more than one entrance, the boundaries being defined by prescribed words. Thus a temple is a place so pronounced or so enclosed that it is open on one side and has an angle [Col. 1612B] fixed to the ground [Note: “angles fixed,” or perhaps “fixed boundaries”].

**[par] Manalis spring.** The augurs call a perennial well *manalis*, yet it does not seem to be one that must be inspected, because the water that flows of its own accord into a stream is what is inspected.

**[par] Manes.** The augurs invoke the Manes as gods because they are believed to flow through all heavenly and earthly things [lacuna].

### Page 6

**[par] The same.** The upper and lower gods were called by the same name; the augurs invoked them for this reason, because the former were thought to favor the life of human beings.

**[par] Munus.** Verrius says that *munus* means the administration of the state; likewise a magistracy, prefecture, command, or province, when something is entrusted to someone by the agreement of the entire multitude and by the lawful assembly of the people gathered together, through votes, so that he may undertake it when it has been assigned by order of the people, either for a fixed period or according to his own good faith, and administer it continuously until a definite time [Note: *ad*, “until”].

**[par] Monstra** are things that exceed nature’s regular order: a serpent with feet, a bird with four wings, a human being with two heads, or a liver that has split while cooking.

**[par] Muta exta** are called entrails from which no divination or response is obtained. By contrast, *adjutoria* are those signs that indicate that something definite will happen, whether warning us to beware of a fire or poison, or portending or indicating that some definite and manifest danger is impending, or indicating a diminution of boundaries.

**[par] Lesser and greater auspices.** Messala explains which are called greater and which lesser. He says that the auspices of consuls, praetors, and censors are greater, and those of the remaining magistrates lesser, since the former are customarily called greater magistrates and the latter lesser magistrates.

**[par] Tables** take the place of altars in sacred houses, because by the laws governing all such places the tables too are sacred, so that they occupy the position, as it were, of altars or sacred couches. Private persons also commonly have them in the very places where they intend to hold sacred observances [Note: *sacra*], such as a commemoration of the dead, not a sacrifice. [lacuna] “held the altar.” [lacuna]

### Page 7

**[par] Mille.** Veranius says in the book he entitled *On Ancient Words* that “the people of a thousand cities stood in place of a kingdom” was said [lacuna]. He thinks that the Greek expression *chiliās* and *chiliades* (χιλιάς, χιλιάδες) gave rise to and occasioned this usage, though not everyone uses it.

**[par] Mute letters and semivowels.** The ancients used to double them in writing or reading. Ennius, he says, wrote them in the work he composed on [lacuna], from which the doubling of mute letters first arose [lacuna].

**[par] Manumission.** A slave was said to be manumitted for sacred purposes when his master, holding now his head and now another part of the same slave, proclaimed: “I wish this man to be free; and in exchange for him pay twenty [units] of my pure, genuine, non-sacred gold, so that before I depart he may be made legally independent.” With these words he sent the slave from his hand and made the man free [Note: *emittebat*, “sent out,” rather than *mittebat*].

**[par] Mosculis.** Cato used this for *parvis* (“small”) in the work he wrote [lacuna].

**[par] To move a table.** Because the table was sacred by the laws governing it and had been placed for the gods in a temple, moving it was considered inauspicious among the ancients, and the punishment of the person who moved it followed.

**[par] Tables.** Some say that tables used to be placed at crossroads and were called *triviales* (“of the crossroads”).

**[par] Mente captus.** A person is called *mente captus* (“deprived of mind”) when his mind has departed from human control. The same person is called *demens* (“out of his mind”), because he has departed from his own mind and gone away from his mind.

**[par] Manare.** Verrius says that the ancients used to say *manare* of the sun when the rays of the rising sun had begun to cast their brightness; and therefore the first part of the day was called *mane* (“morning”). It is more commonly said, however, that the word derives from *manu bonum* (“good by hand”), from *mane*, that is, from *mature* (“ripe, timely”), because what is mature is good. Hence *Matuta* too seems to have been called *Mater* (“Mother”).

**[par] Mamertines** were called [Col. 1613B] for the following reason. When a severe pestilence had fallen upon the whole of Samnium, Sthennius Mettius, the leading man of that people, summoned an assembly of his fellow citizens and explained that in sleep he had seen Apollo commanding that, if they wished to be freed from the calamity, they should vow a sacred spring—that is, that they would sacrifice to him whatever should be born in the following spring.

### Page 8

After they had done this and had been relieved, a pestilence of the same kind attacked them again after twenty years. Accordingly, when Apollo was consulted a second time, he replied that they had not fulfilled their vow, because human beings had not been sacrificed. If they expelled the people concerned, he said, they would certainly be freed from the disaster.

Thus, when ordered to leave their homeland, they settled in that part of Sicily which is now called Taurominium [Note: *Taurominitana*]. By chance, when the Messanians were struggling in a new war, they came to their aid voluntarily and freed them from it. The inhabitants, wishing to repay their service, invited them into their community and into a share of their lands, and gave them a single name. They were called Mamertines because, when the names of twelve gods had been cast by lot, the name Mamers happened to come out; in the Oscan language this signifies Mars. The author of this story is Alfius, in Book I of his *Carthaginian War*.

**[par] Murrata.** That the ancients used a drink called *murrata* is shown by the fact that even now the aediles add it to the sacred couches of the gods during supplications, and by the provision of the Twelve Tables that it should not be placed with the dead, as Varro says in Book I of his *Antiquities*.

**[par] Muger.** The camp men are accustomed to say *muger*, as though it meant “mucous,” of one who plays such a game badly [Note: *is*, “he is,” rather than *his*].

**[par] Muries.** As Veranius explains, *muries* is made from dirty salt, ground in a mortar and thrown into an earthen vessel, which is then covered, plastered with gypsum, and baked in a furnace. The Vestal Virgins cut it with an iron saw and put it into a jar kept inside the shrine of Vesta in the outer storeroom. They add running water—or any water except that which comes through pipes [Note: *addunt*, “they add,” rather than *addent*]—and finally use it in sacrifices.

### Page 9

**[par] It is considered unlawful for the Flamines** to make shoes or sandals from the hide of a dead animal. They may use the hide of an animal killed in some other way or sacrificed, because everything that perishes by its own death is polluted.

**[par] Me.** The ancients used *me* for *mihi* (“to me”), as Ennius says in Book II: “If anything human should happen to me, so that you may preserve…” Lucilius likewise says: “Now I return to you, so that whatever matter threatens me may be dealt with.”

**[par] The greatest of the lesser Pontiffs** is called the one who entered that college first; likewise the least is the one who entered it last.

**[par] Malevoli.** The sign of Mercury called *Malevolus* was near the Janus; it was likewise in the territory of the Turduli [lacuna], and was also called by the name *Malevolus* because it looked toward no shop.

**[par] Malluvium.** In the commentary on sacred rites, *malluvium* signifies something with which one washes the hands; from it come *malluviae*, “the things with which the hands are washed,” just as *pelluviae* are the things with which the feet are washed [Note: *quia*, “because,” rather than *qui*].

**[par] The greatest praetor.** Some think this means the one who possesses the greatest power; others, the one of the greatest age within the college. But it has been decreed by the college of augurs that, in the augury of Salus, greater and lesser praetors are named—not with reference to age, but to the force of their authority [Note: *qui*, “because,” rather than *quia*].

**[par] A stipulation on account of death** is thought, as Antistius Labeo says, to be one made in such a way that it is confirmed by the death of the promisor; or, as some have said, one whose cause was death.

**[par] Marspedis**, or *Maspedis* without the letter *r*, is a customary word in the prayer of the Arval Brothers; even the augur Messala says in his *Explanation of the Auguries* that he was unable to discover what it means.

**[par] The greater consul.** L. Caesar thinks this means either the one who possesses the fasces or the one who was elected first. The greater praetor is the urban praetor; the others are lesser.
