### Page 10

**[par] Mendicus.** Verrius thinks *mendicus* (“beggar”) derives either from the mind of one whom fortune has deceived, or because he asks each person to remedy his life with food.

**[par] Mater, Matuta, manes, mane, matrimonium, materfamilias, matertera, matrices, materiae.** Verrius says these seem to have been named because they are good—namely, of the kind that things which are mature possess. Or rather, they derive from *mater* (“mother”), which is of Greek origin: *mētēr* (μήτηρ).

**[par] Modo quodam.** That is, “in a certain manner” or “by a certain method.” From *modus* come *commoditas*, *commodus*, *commodat*, *accommodat*, *modice*, *modestia*, *moderatio*, and *modificatio*.

**[par] Naenia** is a song sung at a funeral, for the purpose of praising the deceased, to the accompaniment of a flute. Afranius used the word in *The Materterae*. They used to sing a *naenia* during the funeral procession. Some have believed that the word signifies a pledge.

Plautus, in [lacuna]: “Go away, then.” [lacuna]

The same author, in *The Truculent Man*: “To this man my mistress said at home, and among us let there be a *naenia* concerning property” [Note: *mesto*, “let there be mourning,” rather than *esto*, “let there be”].

Some say that *naenia* is so called because the sound is more like the lamentation of those who weep. Others say that the name *naenia* derives from a word for the lower end of the intestines. To prove this they use Plautus, in the *Bacchides*: “If you have a sword, a vervain-stalk is at home for us, with which, when you have provoked me, I shall make you more pierced than a mouse’s *naenia*.”

Whether it is called *naenia* because we bring forth that final sound while weeping and lamenting, or because the Greeks call the extreme end *neaton* (νέᾱτον), or because the last string is called *nētē* (νήτη), they named the final sound of a song *naenia*.

**[par] A shrine of the goddess Naenia** had been dedicated beyond the Viminal Gate; now it possesses only a small chapel.

### Page 11

**[par] The naval crown** is awarded to the man who first armed himself and leapt onto an enemy ship, or through whose effort or hand an enemy ship was captured. M. Terentius Varro obtained one in the Pirate War, presented by Cn. Pompeius Magnus [Col. 1614D]. Others obtained it as well, among them A. Atilius [Note: *Atilius*], in the war fought against Nabis. This is recorded in a Saturnian poem, which the commanders themselves customarily placed on public tablets, naming those who had been awarded the naval crown.

**[par] Neuqua** is used for *nullatenus* (“in no way”), and for *non ita* (“not so”); it also signifies “and not,” as in *nec*.

**[par] Nefrendes.** Q. Mucius Scaevola asserts that rams are called *nefrendes* because they cannot grind with their teeth. Ateius Capito says that they are infants who have not yet begun to grind, that is, to break. Livy, in the old *Odyssey*: “Whom I nourished, not yet grinding, with milking nourishment.” [lacuna] And [lacuna] for *nefrendibus*.

As the ancients said, *rienes* is what current usage calls *renes* (“kidneys”). Some think that *nefrendes* refers to the testicles, which the people of Lanuvium call *nebrundines*; the Greeks call them *nephroi* (νεφροί), and the Praenestines *nefrones*.

**[par] Necerim, nec eum.** *Nemora* signifies pleasant woods, for it has the same meaning. The author of this word is Homer, who says in the *Iliad*: “In the shady pasture, and the god cast upon him…” [lacuna]. There is no doubt that he designates a place having fields and pastures. The Greeks called *nemos* (νέμος) by this name because “there are pastures in it” (*dia to nomas einai en autō*, διὰ τὸ νομὰς εἶναι ἐν αὐτῷ).

**[par] Nemut.** This means “unless,” “also,” or “indeed.” Cato used it in *On Tribunician Power* [Note: *Tribunicia*], when he says [lacuna] “the hardships.”

**[par] Neminis.** Cato used this genitive case when he said: “And who would say it, since it belongs to no one?” He likewise used it of magistrates created improperly: “and no one’s…” [lacuna]

Ennius, in *Erechtheus*: “Many have hearts of stone, whom no one’s suffering moves.”

### Page 12

**[par] Nemo.** The word *nemo* seems to be composed of *ne* and *homo* (“not” and “man”). This is further confirmed because it is always used of a person and is not normally formed in the plural, since it is understood as meaning “for no one.”

**[par] Given over to death.** Properly speaking, a person is said to have been given over to death when he has been killed without a wound, as by poison or hunger.

**[par] Necessarium.** Opillus Aurelius says that something is *necessarium* when one must not cease from it, or without which one cannot live, or without which one cannot live well, or which cannot be prevented from happening.

**[par] Necessarii.** As Gallus Aelius says, these are relatives or relations by marriage, toward whom necessary duties are performed in preference to others.

**[par] Nec legens.** A person is called *nec legens* (“not choosing”) who is not reading, or who has no choice regarding what he ought to do, having neglected the reasoning proper to his duty.

**[par] Nec.** Grammarians generally say that *nec* is a disjunctive conjunction, as in “he neither reads nor writes.” But if one examines the matter more carefully, as Sinnius Capito did, it can be understood that the ancients used it for *non* (“not”), as in the Twelve Tables: “But let him not be a guardian”; likewise: “If he worships by theft, which will not be manifest”; and in Plautus, in *The Ghost*: “Nor rightly, if you should say it to him”; and in Turpilius, in *Demetrius*: “Nor is it rightly said to me, what I have been hearing for a long time.”

**[par] Nec unquam, necunquam, quemquam.** “Never,” “never,” and “anyone.”

**[par] Nequalia.** Losses or disadvantages.

**[par] Nequinont.** Used for *nequeunt* (“they cannot”), just as the ancients said *solinunt* and *ferinunt* for *solent* (“they are accustomed”) and *feriunt* (“they strike”).

Livy, in the *Odyssey*: “Partly they wander, nor now can they return to Greece” [Note: *nequinont*].

**[par] Nequitu and nequitur.** The ancients used these for *non posse* (“not to be able”), as Pacuvius says: “But since I cannot contend, the wound must be stretched.” [Note: *tum*, “then,” rather than *ut*.]

Plautus, in *The Satyr*: “It cannot be drawn back, wherever it has once advanced.”

Cato, Book I of the *Origins*: “There were several shrines in that place. He removed their augural consecration, except for the shrine of Terminus; that one could not be deprived of its consecration.”

**[par] Nequiquam** means the same as *frustra* (“in vain”), as is clear from examples of many authors.

**[par] Nectere** means “to bind,” and is frequent in very many authors. It is also used in the commentary on sacred rites in this manner: “The lesser Pontiff shall bind from straw the *napurae*” [Note: *napuras*], that is, “make little cords with which the sows are to be tied.”

**[par] Nectar.** In Greek, *nectar* signifies the drink of the gods. Hence Vergil says: “They pack and fill the chambers with sweet nectar”; likewise Lucretius, Book II: “and the flower of nard, which breathes nectar from its flowers” [Note: *naribus*, “nostrils,” rather than *floribus*].

**[par] Non pridem.** “Not long ago” is said equally correctly and frequently as *jampridem* and *quampridem*.

**[par] Nequa.** Gold that envelops the ears with excessive force. Sinnius Capito says that this verse of Lucilius means that gold is harmful when it injures the ears—either because of the weight of earrings, when the softest part of the ear is cut, or because gold is to be understood as money, in relation to which and through excessive greed human beings are led to sin.

**[par] Neither a woman nor one’s lap should be trusted.** This is a proverb, because a woman is of uncertain and fickle character, and because things placed in one’s lap commonly fall out when they have been forgotten, instead of being quickly lifted up [Note: *propere*, “quickly,” rather than *pro*].

**[par] Nexum.** As Gallus Aelius says, *nexum* is whatever is conducted through bronze and scales. It is said to be *necti* (“bound”), and examples of this are the making of a will, the giving of a *nexus*, and the liberation of a *nexus* [Note: *datio*, “giving,” rather than *dando*; *liberatio*, “liberation,” rather than *liberanto*].

**[par] Nervus.** We also call *nervus* the iron bond by which the feet are hindered. Although Plautus says that the neck too can be bound by it: “Captured treacherously, by Pollux, he proves his neck with that iron bond” [Note: *aedepol*, “by Pollux,” rather than *epol*].

**[par] Nexum aes.** Among the ancients, money that was bound through a *nexum* was called *nexum aes*.

**[par] Negumate.** In the song of [lacuna], the prophet Marcius, it means “deny,” as he says: “However much the two [lacuna] move, deny…”

**[par] Negritu.** In augural language, *negritu* means illness.

**[par] Nebulo.** As Aelius Stilo says, a person is called *nebulo* who is worth no more than mist, or whose character cannot easily be discerned—“a worthless fellow, a trifler.”

**[par] Negibundum.** The ancients used this for *negantem* (“denying”). Cato, in the work he wrote [lacuna]: “negibundus” [lacuna].

**[par] Neutiquam.** This is said for *nullo modo* (“in no way”), as is shown by [lacuna], who says: “But my heart by no means agrees, when I look with my eyes.” Cicero: “You cannot indeed be indissoluble; nevertheless, you will by no means be dissolved.”

**[par] Nepos.** Among the Etruscans, *nepos* means “luxurious” or “dissipated.” For men of luxurious life were called *nepotes*, because they take no more care of their family property than those whose father and grandfather are still alive. The word is derived from the fact that a *nepos* is born after his father, later than a son.

Some, including Aristarchus, the interpreter of Homer, wanted the word to be Greek; they cite from Apollonius: “ready for those feet of yours” (*teoisi nepodessin hetoimē*, τεοῖσι νεπόδεσσιν ἑτοίμη).

**[par] Nephasti.** The days marked *N* were called *nefasti*, because on them it is unlawful for the praetor before whom a case is being heard to pronounce the three words “I give, I declare, I adjudge.”

**[par] Nep.** The sign *N. P.* is customarily used to designate the days preceding the *nefasti*, whose earlier part is *fas*. On these days slaves are manumitted, levies are held, armies are enrolled, and it is permitted to go to the provinces. Sacred institutions are also established, vows that have been made are discharged, and temples are consecrated.

**[par] Nepa.** In the language of the Africans, *nepa* is the constellation which we call Cancer, or, as some have wished, Scorpio. Plautus, in *Casina*: “I shall withdraw to the wall and imitate a scorpion.”

**[par] Nepus.** This means “not pure.”

**[par] Nesi.** This was used for *sine* (“without”) in the law concerning the dedication of the altar of Diana on the Aventine.

**[par] Nautea.** Opillus Aurelius says that *nautea* is a kind of herb with black grains, which tanners use. Its name seems to derive from *nausea*, because it causes nausea, through the exchange of the letters *T* and *S*, a practice familiar to the ancients.

Plautus, in *Artemo*: “The ointment which would have made the noses of muleteers smell of *nautea*…” [lacuna]

[lacuna] “and of spices.”

The same author, in *Curculio*: “For every ointment, compared with yours, smells like *nautea*.”

In *Casina*, a greased goat smelling of *nautea* is substituted for the prostitute.

Labeo, in his commentary on pontifical law, says that *nautea* is a certain red substance with which some garments of the Pontiffs are dyed.

**[par] Nat io.** Cincius says that among the ancients *natio* signified something born there: a class of people who had come from nowhere else but were born in that place. He also says that *natio* was used not only collectively of all people, but also separately of individual persons. Sinnius Capito, however, says that nearly all kinds of human beings are divided into nations, such as the Cures, Sabines, Hernici, Aequi, and likewise the Volscians. Among animals too, a good offspring expected in the future is called a good *natio*.

**[par] The family of the Nautii** is descended from the Trojans. Their ancestor was Nautes, who brought to Rome the bronze image of Minerva, to which the Nautii later used to sacrifice. Veturius.” When they had remained for some time in a certain town to restore their strength, the Bruttians—who at that time had a treaty with the Romans—immediately stopped the war there. Hence, from their leader Nautes, the family was called Nautia.

**[par] Nati.** *Natio* was said to mean “trade,” and *natinatores*, derived from it, “seditious persons conducting business.” M. Cato, in [lacuna]: “the multitude of Macedonia.” Etruria, [lacuna]

The surviving inherited fragment reads: “Samnites, Lucanians, to *natinari* among themselves, and to constitute factions” (*Samnites, Lucanos inter se natinari, atque factiones esse*). No governing lemma or secure syntactic connection is visible in the supplied text.

**Naccae.** Fullers are commonly called *naccae*, as Curiatius says, because they are *nauci*—that is, of no value. Cincius holds the same view. Some say that, because nearly all work is done from wool, the Greeks call wool-work *nacae*. [Col. 1617: *Nauci.*]

**Naucum.** Ateius Philologus says that *naucum* is used for “trifles.” Cincius derives it from the inside of an olive or nut—that is, what is within it. Aelius Stilo says it means the shell of every object. The glossators, or their writers, say it means the part of a bean-grain that clings to the bean-thread [Note: “the bean’s hilum”]. Some say that, from the Greek *ναὶ καὶ οὐχί* (“yes and no”), it denotes a fickle person. Some say it means the central partition of a walnut, which Verrius calls *juglandam* [Note: *juglandam*].

Plautus, in *The Lazy Parasite*: “Both washed with great praise; finally, both of us are *non nauci*”; likewise in *The Haunted House*: “What I should call that word *nauci*, I do not know”; and in *The Truculent Man*: “You love a man who is *non nauci*.” Naevius, in *The Little Tunic*: “To spend his night as *nauco*.” But Ennius: “There is that worthless trifler, a man *non nauci*” [Note: “there, or thereabouts”]. [Col. 1617]

**Nares.** They think the nostrils are called *nares* because through them we breathe every kind of scent by the openings of the nose [Note: “we smell”].

**Narica.** A kind of small fish. Plautus: “But I see in the tin vessels a good and gray *narica*, and five shells of *taguma* made into fish-pools.”

**Nacitor.** In the Twelve Tables: “Whatever he shall have acquired, let him have it as booty” [Note: “whatever he shall have taken as booty”]. Likewise in the Latin treaty: “Whoever acquires money, let him have it; and if he acquires any pledge” [Note: “shall acquire it”], “let him have it for himself.”

**Nare.** Cornificius says that *nare* is derived from *navis*, because water is carried along floating, like a ship [Note: “or perhaps *navis*”]. Ennius, Book VII: “One longs to swim, another is preparing to fight.” Plautus, in *The Pot of Gold*: “Like boys who are learning to swim, he puts on a wicker raft.” Thus *natare* is formed from *nare*, just as *dictitare* from *dicere* and *factitare* from *facere*.

**Navus.** “Quick and energetic”; it seems to have been named from the speed of ships. Ennius, Book VI: “A vigorous man was found, a Greek-born man, a Greek king.” And Book XVI: “To preserve the command of the vigorous is to preserve what cannot be overcome.” Plautus, in *The Frivolous Woman*: “One must act vigorously in whatever one does, and not be led along.” [Col. 1617C; Pag. 17]

**Navalis scriba.** The naval clerk, who served on a ship, was considered a clerk of the lowest rank among the several kinds of clerks, because his service was also subject to dangers [Note: “was exposed to dangers”]. Plautus: “I know you, you shameless naval clerk of the dovecote.” This may be because the places on a ship from which the oars project are called *columbaria* [Note: “from which the oars emerge”], or because the profits of the *columbarii* were rash and uncertain.

**Nassiterna.** A kind of handled, open water-vessel, such as is commonly used for washing down horses. Plautus, in *The Two Bacchises*: “Who is bringing this most filthy fellow out with a *nassiterna* and water?” And in *The Nervolaria*: “Who is bringing a *nassiterna* here with water, without asking permission?” Cato, in the speech he composed against Quintus Sulpicius: “How often I saw *truili*, *nassiternae*, pierced water-vessels, and pitchers without handles” [Note: “pierced”]. [Col. 1617D]

**Nassa.** A kind of fishing vessel [Note: “fishing vessel”] from which, once a fish has entered, it cannot escape. Plautus: “By Hercules, I shall never today seek food from that *nassa*.”

**Napuras.** “Tie up,” as the Pontiff says; they are cords made from straw.

**Naustibulum.** The ancients called a vessel resembling a trough by this name, evidently from its resemblance to a ship.

**Navia.** A trough carved from a single piece of wood, like a ship, used during the grape harvest. A fig tree in the Comitium is also called *Navia*, after the augur Attus Navius. For when Tarquinius Priscus wished to alter the tribes instituted by Romulus, and was deterred by Attus through an augury, he asked him, in order to test his skill, whether what he had conceived in his mind could be done. When Attus, with the augury permitting it, had answered that it could be accomplished, the king ordered a whetstone and a razor to be brought out. When they had been brought out, he asked the augur whether the stone could be cut with that razor. When Attus answered that it could, he suddenly cut the whetstone with the razor.

After this, since Tarquinius dared do nothing further against him, the king ordered that the razor and whetstone should be buried beneath a consecrated place. A fig tree was planted there within the area enclosed by the sacred boundary. Whenever it happened to wither, he ordered it to be replanted and cuttings to be taken from it. In the course of time so many other fig trees sprang up in that place that, after they had been uprooted and removed from the sacred ground, all the trees that then stood there—except that one fig tree—were expelled by a fatal warning and, above all, by the command of the haruspices. Divine responses also promised that, as long as it lived, the liberty of the Roman people would remain unharmed. For that reason people began from that time to tend and replant it. [Col. 1618A; Pag. 18]

**Nauscit.** When a bean-grain opens in order to germinate, because it resembles a ship in shape.

**Navitas.** According to uncorrupted usage, those whom we now call sailors were formerly called *navitae*. Cato is a witness in the speech he wrote when departing for Spain: “Of the wine and oil which the sailors had carried with them, I used only so much.”

**Naevia silva.** Verrius says that a grove outside the city, at the fourth milestone, was called the Naevian Grove because the house of a certain Naevius stood there; from him the grove was also called *Naevia*. The ancients were accustomed to cast this name up as a reproach, because dissolute and worthless men had been accustomed to stay there. M. Cato is a witness in the speech he wrote against M. Caelius, if he had called it thus: “I had begun my journey from the Naevian Gate, and from there to the Naevian Grove, far from the Naevian house.” Hence, Verrius reports, the proverb “from the Naevian house” arose. [Col. 1618B–C; Pag. 19]

**Nudius tertius.** It seems to be compounded from *nunc* (“now”) and *die tertio* (“on the third day”).

**N. …** In the countryside they are called …, whom they call by another name, denoting the whole from a part; as though they had been called from this … They are called pa— … The hollow sky is called …; dam— is called … [the supplied text is lacunose]. [Col. 1618C]

**Nupta nova.** Some wish *nupta nova* (“newly married woman”) to have been named in the same way as women who take part in weddings are called *pronubae*, namely from *nubere* (“to marry”). Others have said that it was so called because the Greeks call a new bride *νέαν νύμφην* (“a new bride”). Others, because Homer calls a wife *νυὸν* (“wife”), according to the ancient Greek manner of speaking, when he says:

> “From a distant land, the wife of spear-bearing men.”

[Col. 1618C]

**Numere and numero.** The damaged text says that *numere* and *numero* are used alike, but treats *numere* as apparently present-tense and *numero* as alien to a past use. It offers two uncertain explanations: an ancient customary pronunciation of such verbs, or a fixed treatment of final vowels, illustrated from Sextus Pompeius by a vocative final syllable said to be lengthened and elsewhere shortened in *-e*. The syntax and several forms are broken.

Sinnius Capito is said to have explained *numero* as “too much,” but the alleged quotation survives only in fragments: “… you are least … unless *numero perbiterint*, unless quickly …”; the proposed explanatory words are likewise corrupt [Note: “quickly”]. “You are dead from this,” as though one were painting the expression: “Why have you died so quickly?”

Likewise in *Neleus*: “We shall never make [something] *numero* for our mother” [Note: “pleasantly”]. That is, “We shall never do too much.” In Naevius: “I have never seen anyone who knew *numero*.” Whoever knows, that is, knows the task—namely, knew too much. Or did Antonius Panurgus mean *numero* as “too much, too quickly,” that is, “excessively rapidly”? Thus Plautus, in *The Cauldron*: “What do you want, my maidservant? You say ‘too much, too quickly’ far too often.” Accius, in *Oenomaus*: “That I might be related to you, not that I might destroy you, I sought your daughter; fear clears you of the charge too quickly.” Afranius, in *The Suspected Woman*: “Because of a falsehood believed by you, too quickly”—that is, “far too rapidly.” Caecilius, in *The Aethrion*: “Ah, wretched man, why so? He has come too quickly; flee home” [Notes: “*Aethrione*”; “flee”]. Afranius, in *The Pretender*: “Ah, wretched woman, too quickly and in vain I gave thanks” [Note: “Ah!”]. [Col. 1618D; Pag. 20; Col. 1619A]

**Numera senatum.** A senator says this to the consul when he wishes to obstruct the passage of a senatorial decree and requests that either the matters brought forward be divided [Note: “be referred”], or that the senators be consulted one by one; or, if there are not enough senators, that the number required for issuing a decree be prescribed [Note: “recorded”].

**Nupta verba.** The ancients called words which a maiden was not permitted to say *nupta verba*. Thus Plautus, in *The Misanthrope*: “I am a virgin; I have not yet learned to speak married women’s words.” [Col. 1619B]

**Nuptiae.** Santra says that *nuptiae* was so called because what the ancient Greeks called *nymphaea* they called *gamon* (*γάμον*); hence *νέαν νύμφην* (“new bride”). Cornificius says it was so called because new marriages are sought. Curiatius says it was because a new agreement [Note: “pact”] is made. Aelius and Cincius say it was because the bride’s head is covered with a flame-colored veil, which the ancients called *obnubere* [Note: “*obnubarunt*”]. For the same reason, the law also orders a person who has killed a parent to cover his head—that is, to veil it [Note: “funeral”].

**Numerius.** It is said that the praenomen *Numerius* had never previously existed in a patrician family, although Fabius—who alone survived after the three hundred and six had been killed by the Etruscans—was led by the greatness of his wealth to marry Otacilia, the daughter of a woman from Maleventum, as the place was then called. The condition was that whoever was first born should be called Numerius, after his maternal grandfather. [Col. 1619]

**Non omnibus dormio.** A proverb said to have arisen from a certain Scipio, called *Pararhenchon*, because he pretended to be asleep, so that his wife might commit adultery with impunity. Lucilius mentions him. [Col. 1619C]

**Nuncupata pecunia.** Cincius says, in Book II of *On the Duty of the Jurist*, that money is *nuncupata* when it is named, fixed, and declared by its proper names: “When he makes a *nexum* and a transfer of ownership, whatever he has named with his tongue, so let it be law” [Note: “that is, whatever he has named or said, so let it be law”]. Vows are called *nuncupata* when consuls or praetors make them as they depart for a province; they are recorded on tablets in the presence of many people. But Santra, in Book II of *On Ancient Words*, gathers from numerous examples that *nuncupata* does not mean simply “named” in the strict sense, but “promised,” and, as it were, “declared under witness,” “delimited,” and “accepted”; this is more appropriate also in the case of vows being *nuncupated* [Note: “which”].

**Nusciosum.** Ateius Philologus says that a person who saw poorly because of an eye defect was commonly called *nusciosus*. Popilius [Note: “Opilius”] Aurelius says that *nuscitiones* are night-blindnesses. Aelius Stilo says the term refers to someone who saw better in the evening than at midday, but recognized nothing unless he brought it close to his eyes. [Col. 1619C–D]

**Nonas.** Some derive *Nonae* from the new moon, because the beginning of the moon fell upon them. Others say that they were always the ninth day before the Ides, and that the first syllable of the name should therefore be written with an added *u*.

**Nundinae.** The ancients wished the market day to be a day of holiday, so that country people could gather for buying and selling; they also made it *nefastus*, so that, if public business were permitted, the market-goers would not be interrupted.

**Nundinal cook.** Plautus says in *The Pot of Gold*: “That cook is a market-day cook; he usually goes on the ninth day” [Note: “That man is a market-day cook”]. The cooking and the cook, elsewhere called *novendialis*, plainly indicate what he meant by *nundinal*: one who cooked on the ninth day. [Col. 1619D; Pag. 22; Col. 1620A]

**Nuculae.** The ancients called the people of Praeneste *Nuculae*, either because, when they had been enclosed by the Carthaginians at Casilinum, they sustained themselves with nuts through hunger; or because a great many small nuts grow in their territory [Note: “are born”].

**Numus.** He thinks that *numus* was derived from the Greek word *νοῦμμος*, and that it has the same value among us and among them, since we have received many names from the Greeks, of which this is one.

**Nutius.** This word denotes both a person and the thing itself. Of a person: “A messenger has arrived”; of a thing: “A message has been brought.” C. Caesar seems to have made this distinction in his *Commentaries*.

**Nuper.** As though *noviper*, we say *novissime* (“most recently”). It belongs to past time, but the remainder of the passage is lacunose: “…” [Col. 1620A]

**Numen.** It is said to mean, as it were, the nod and power of a god.

**Numella.** A kind of fetter by which quadrupeds are tied. They are usually made of sinew or, most often, raw oxhide.

**Numidae.** We call those whom the Greeks call *Νομάδες* (“Nomads”) *Numidae*, either because that kind of people conducts business in livestock, or because they live on herbs like animals.

**Nuts.** Nuts are demanded for brides and thrown to children, so that, when the new bride enters her new husband’s house, the omen may be favorable and auspicious. [Col. 1620B]

**Numa.** They say that Numa Pompilius lived on the Janiculum, where his chest was found, together with books bearing Numa’s name, by a certain scribe named Terentius while he was digging over a field.

**Nonuncium.** This term, which the schoolmasters commonly call a *nonuncium*, signifies nine ounces; a *teruncium* signifies three half-ounces, since each of the three consists of half an ounce.

**Nomen.** It is said either to be derived from the Greek *ὄνομα*, or to be formed as though from *novimen*, because it produces knowledge. It also denotes a family name, as in *Teretius*. It is also used for a debt: thus we say that a debt *was a name* when money has been exacted from a debtor. [Col. 1620B–C; Pag. 23]

**Noctua.** It seems to have been named from the time of night, at which it customarily hoots or flies. Among the Greeks Minerva is called *γλαυκῶπις*, “owl-eyed,” because the owl has gray eyes [Note: “gray-eyed”].

**Noneolae.** He calls the teats that hang from the throats of she-goats *noneolae*.

**Noctiluca.** When Lucilius says *noctiluca* in Book II, he means something obscene: “*noctiluca* … medical …” [the supplied context is lacunose]. [Col. 1620C]

**Noverca.** A woman is called a *noverca* when, after children have been taken away, a man takes a new wife for the purpose of restraining—that is, controlling—the household. The first such woman is mentioned among the ancients [Note: “the ancient Annia”], who married … [the source breaks off].

**Aventinus.** It is said to have received its name because, in the reign of Servius Tullius, the Aventine, cut off by marshes, was approached by boats; or because Aventinus, an Alban king, was buried on the Aventine.

**Novale.** Aelius Gallus and Opilius Aurelius say that a *novale* is what the Greeks call *νειός*. They also use Homer as a witness, who says:

> “Striving to reach the deep-ploughed fallow.”

Cincius, however, says that it is a place where the clod has been broken open and left for new sowing. [Col. 1620C]

**Nauti consulatu et T. Sicini.** When the Volsci, in the consulship of [the text is fragmentary] and Titus Sicinius, had entered a fierce battle against the Romans, the military tribunes are said to have been burned and buried on the steps immediately beside the Circus. The place was later paved with white stone. Those who fell there for the republic were Opiter Verginius Tricostus, [Valerius] Laevinus Postumus, Cominius Auruncus, Mallius Tolerinus, Publius Veturius Geminus, Aulus Sempronius Atratinus, Verginius Tricostus, Mucius Scaevola, and Sextus Fusius Medullinus. [Col. 1620D; Pag. 24]

**Noxa.** As Servius Sulpicius Rufus says, it signifies “damage.” Among poets and orators, however, it is used for “fault”; *ad noxam* means “to sin,” or “for a sin,” and also “punishment for a sin” [Note: “punishment”]. Accius, in *Meleager* [Note: “*Meralippo*”]: “That you are liable to this offense.” Likewise: “When the law orders someone to be surrendered for an offense, it orders him to be surrendered for the crime.” Caecilius, in *The Substitute Chaerestratus* [Note: “*Chaerestrato*”]: “For that offense is more womanly than manly” [Note: “is a woman’s offense rather than a man’s”].

**New Curiae.** The new Curiae were built by Fabricius near the crossroads [Note: “nearby”], because the old Curiae built by Romulus were too small. In them he had divided the people and the sacred rites into thirty parts, so that they might perform those rites there. When these rites were transferred from the old Curiae to the new ones, the rites of four Curiae could not be transferred because of religious scruples [Note: “seven Curiae”; “four”]. Therefore the sacred rites of the Foriensis, Rapta, Veliensis [Note: “Vellensis”], and Velitiae Curiae are performed in the old Curiae [Note: “Curiae”]. [Col. 1621A]

**Nothus.** The Greeks call a child born of a non-legitimate wife *nothus*; among us he is said to be born of a *spurius* father. The text connects this with Servius Tullius, king at Rome, who is said to have been born from the concubine of Spurius Tullius [the following designation is corrupt]. Or perhaps we should prefer to believe that he was born of Oclisia Corniculana, a captive, while his mother was enslaved [Note: “while she was enslaved”].

**Nota.** *Nota* sometimes signifies a mark, as on animals, tablets, books, or individual or paired letters; at other times it signifies disgrace.

**Nobilis.** The ancients used *nobilis* for “known,” and indeed wrote it with the letter *g* [Note: “with the letter *g*”]. Plautus, in *Pseudolus*: “He has the face of a foreign and unknown man” [Note: “unknown”]; and: “An unknown person is placed before my eyes” [Note: “unknown”]. Accius, in *Diomedes*: “Therefore I shall return to Argos, for here I am known” [Note: “for here I am unknown”]. Livius, in *The Virgin*: “The unknown walk about in distinguished dress” [Note: “they walk about in distinguished attire, unknown”]. [Col. 1621A–B; Pag. 25]

**Noegeum.** Some say that *noegeum* is a kind of garment edged with purple; others, that it is white and translucent, as though from *navum*, because the shell of certain fruits is extremely thin and not without whiteness. Thus Livius Andronicus says in the *Odyssey*: “As soon as he wiped tears from his *noegean* face”—that is, from his white face.

**Nixi di.** Three statues in the Capitol before the shrine of Minerva are called the *Nixi* gods. They are shown resting on their knees, as though assisting women in the straining of childbirth. Those who have handed down the story say that, after King Antiochus of Syria had been defeated, Marcus Acilius removed them from the Roman people and brought them to the place where they now stand; others say that they were brought here after Corinth was captured, having been placed beneath a table there.

**Nictare.** The ancients used *nictare* of repeatedly attempting something by the exertion of the eyes or other limbs. Thus Lucretius, in Book IV: “Here, where they cannot blink and stand upon their wings” [Note: “blink”]. Caecilius, in *The Hymn-Singer*: “They hurl themselves against the talkative healers without blinking at the poles.” Novius, in *The Macchus Copo*: “You will write at once, when you are bound upon the sinew” [Note: “you will blink”].

Hence some used *nictatio*, others *nictus*, as Caecilius does in *The Boxer*: “Then, while praising him, to strike this timid blinking with trembling eyelids; here to rejoice and marvel.”

A dog *nictit*—that is, yelps softly—while smelling the tracks of wild animals, as Ennius says in Book X: “Just as a hunting creature, *venenox* [‘venomous,’ or corrupt], when fastened in chains, is accustomed, if it has by chance perceived [something] with its keen nostril, to *nictit* and howl there in a sharp voice” [Notes: “*venox*”; “*nictit*”; “and it is”]. Hence the whining itself is also called *nictus*. [Col. 1621C]

**Niquis scivit.** This is a century said to have been established by King Servius Tullius, in which a person who had not cast his vote in his own century could vote, so that no citizen might be deprived of the right to vote. For *sciscito* means “state an opinion” [Note: “*scisco* means ‘I inquire’”], and *suffragium ferto* means “cast a vote” [Note: “*fero*”]; hence *Scita Plebis*, “the resolutions of the plebs.” In this century, however, no one is assessed, no centurion is appointed, and no one can belong to the century, because no member of that century is individually determined. *Nequis scivit* is therefore *nisi quis scivit*, “unless someone has voted.”

**Ningulus.** “No one,” as Ennius says in Book II: “You who threaten with iron, and [corrupt: *inte ninculus*] can cure” [Note: “*ningulus*”].

**Niger lapis.** The Black Stone in the Comitium signifies a place of ill omen, which some say was destined for the death of Romulus. [Col. 1621D; Pag. 26]

It did not happen, however, that Romulus was buried there. Rather, Faustulus, his foster father, is said to have been buried there, together with Quintilius, the grandfather of the man who followed Romulus’ cause; his family was called Quintilia after him.

**Nanus.** The Greeks call *nanus* a low and hollow water-vessel, commonly called a “bearded bucket” [Note: “low”]. From this short or dwarf people are called *nani*, “dwarfs.”

**Necem.** Verrius suspects that *necem* is derived from the Greek, for the Greeks call a dead person *neky*. Hence we say *neci dare*, “to give to death.”

**Nivem.** Verrius interprets *nivem* as “new,” from the Greek, who call it *neon*. The remainder is lacunose.

**Nequinates.** The people of Narnia are called *Nequinates*, because, after the colonists had been expelled from the town of Nequinum, they settled there in ancient times [Note: “the people of Narnia”]. Cato, in his speech against Thermus [Note: “against Thermus”]: “Among ten men …” [the remainder is lacunose].

**Negotium.** It is so called because it is not *otium*, “leisure.”

**Navus.** We use *navus* from the speed of a ship, which is extremely swift.

**Numidae.** They are called *Nomads*, and are said to live longer than others. Hence Cato said in [a lost work]: “The Numidians are long-lived,” because they live for a great age.

**Nuts.** Sinnius Capito says that people customarily say that nuts are sent at the Cerealia when they wish to signify that missiles are being thrown at the Circus during the Cerealia. Since it was customary to throw nuts, we designate the whole by a part, because nuts are valued above all the other missiles, especially since the nuts scattered there are burned by the flame. [Col. 1621; Col. 1622B]

**Novendial festivals.** They are said to have been instituted by King Tullus Hostilius [Note: “Hostilius”], at the prompting of an omen, to expiate prodigies on the ninth day during the Latin Festival. This was either because stones had rained on the Alban Mount [Note: “custom”], or because a voice had been heard commanding the Albans to perform according to their rite the sacred rites they had omitted. For at that time those rites were recalled from the Albans, whose state had been lost and almost utterly destroyed [Note: “after the state had been lost and nearly destroyed”], and which they had begun to neglect in the subsequent period. [Col. 1622B; Pag. 26]

## N–O

**N. …** They are said to have been invented by the consul Marcellus: devices which, once applied, would make Syracuse easier to capture.

**Naval Gate; Naval District.** Both seem to have received their names from their proximity to the naval installations.

**The day after the Nones, Ides, or Kalends.** These days are considered unlucky. Likewise, for a new bride, the fourth day before the Kalends, Nones, or Ides was thought to dawn dark, because the Pontiffs had decreed these days dark: whenever Roman commanders had offered supplication on them for the sake of waging war, they had conducted the republic’s affairs badly. [Col. 1622C]

**Sextus Pompeius Festus, *On the Meaning of Words*, Book XVI, begins successfully.**

**Ob.** As a preposition, it sometimes means “around,” as when we say that a city is *obsidered*, *obsigned*, or *obvallated*—besieged, sealed, or surrounded. Sometimes it takes the place of the preposition *propter*, “because of,” as in *ob merita*, “because of services,” and *ob superatos hostes*, “because of conquered enemies”; hence *obsides*, “hostages,” as though *obfides*, because a pledge is given for the state. Sometimes it means “toward,” as in Ennius: “He began to lead the legions toward Rome by night,” and elsewhere: “He led [them] toward Troy.”

**Oculissimum.** Plautus: “The dearest doorway of the little house.” In *Curculio* he uses *oculissime*, meaning “clearly visible,” as though “he looks clearly.” In *Pseudolus* he uses *oculatum* [Note: “*oculatum*,” “eyed”] for “in broad daylight,” when he says: “Buy olives on a dark day, by Hercules; sell them on an *oculata* day”—that is, on a day seen by the eyes. Elsewhere he says *oculatum Argum*, “Argus with eyes everywhere,” because his whole body has eyes. Again: “One witness with many eyes is better than one with ears”—that is, someone who says that he saw it. Verrius says that this form is derived from the word for “eye.” [Col. 1622C–D; Pag. 27]

**Oculitus.** It is formed like *funditus* and *penitus* and signifies that something is as dear as an eye, or is eye-like.

**Odefacit.** The ancients said *odefacit* for *olefacit*, “smells,” by an old habit of changing letters. This book contains many such forms; some think the word is derived from the Greek *ὀσμή*, “scent.”

**Porticoes of Octavia.** Two porticoes are so called. One, nearer the Theater of Marcellus, was built by Octavia, the sister of Augustus. The other, nearer the Theater of Pompey, was built by Gnaeus Octavius, son of Gnaeus, who had been curule aedile, praetor, consul, and one of the decemvirs for performing sacred rites, and who had celebrated a naval triumph over King Perseus. After it was burned, Caesar Augustus undertook to restore it. [Col. 1623A]

**Ogygian walls.** When Accius calls them the Ogygian walls in *Diomedes*, he means Thebes, because tradition says that Ogyges founded that city [Note: “Ogyges”].

**Occasio.** An opportunity is a favorable moment arising by chance.

**Occasus.** It means destruction, or the setting of the sun when it falls from above the earth beneath it. Ennius used the word for an opportunity in Book II: “This opportunity was given, but Horatius was renowned for his leap.” Likewise in Book V: “He attacks in anger, holds him; the opportunity helps the affair.” And in Book VIII: “Or when opportunity, or the time, restrained him from daring.”

**Occisum.** Some distinguish *occisum* from *necatum* by saying that the former is done by striking and a blow, while the latter is done without a blow. Thus it is written in the laws of King Numa Pompilius: “If someone kills a man by lightning, do not lift him above the knees.” And elsewhere: “If a man has been killed by lightning, no funeral rites ought to be performed for him.” [Col. 1623A–B; Pag. 28]

**October horse.** The horse sacrificed in the Campus Martius in October is called the October horse because it is the right-hand horse of the victorious team of two that is sacrificed annually to Mars. There used to be a serious dispute over its head between the Suburans and the Sacravians: the latter wished to fix it to the wall of the Regia, while the former wished to fix it to the Mamilian Tower. Its tail was carried to the Regia with such speed that blood dripped from it onto the hearth, so that it might share in the sacred rite.

Some say that the horse is consecrated to Mars, the god of war, as a sacrificial victim—not, as the common people think, because punishment is inflicted upon it for the fact that the Romans are descended from the Trojans and the Trojans were captured in the form of a horse.

That horses were counted among sacrificial victims by many peoples is shown by the Lacedaemonians, who sacrifice a horse to the winds on Mount Taygetus and burn it there, so that its ashes may be scattered as widely as possible across the borders by their blowing; and by the Sallentines, among whom a living horse dedicated to Jupiter is thrown into the fire [Note: “alive”]; and by the Rhodians, who throw a four-horse chariot consecrated to the Sun into the sea every year, because he is said to travel around the world in such a chariot. [Col. 1623B–C; Pag. 29]

**Occidamus.** Plautus uses this for *cedamus*, “let us yield,” although many other prepositions are more familiar with this verb.

**Occentassint.** The ancients said *occentassint* for what we now call “they have reviled.” It is done loudly and with a certain musical tone, so that it can be heard from a distance. It is considered shameful because it is thought not to be done without cause. Hence, I think, they call it a *cantilenam*, since I do not think that its song possesses any pleasantness.

**Ocris.** As Ateius Philologus reports in his *Book of Glosses*, the ancients called a rugged mountain *ocris*. Thus Livy: “But who are these men climbing the high *ocris*?”; and: “The lofty *ocres*, the rotten fields, and the great sea.” Also: “The lofty *ocres* of Taenarum”; and: “Not such as Chiron taught on Mount Pelion.” Hence perhaps unevenly swollen boots were also called *ocreae* [Note: “*ocreae*”].

**Occare; occator.** Verrius thinks that *occare* and *occator* are derived from *occaedere*, because the harrow cuts up the clods of earth; Cicero most elegantly says that it comes from “blinding” the sown crops.

**Ocius.** The comparative *ocius* and then the superlative *ocissime* have been frequently used. Some say that these forms in our language are derived from the Greek *ὠκέως*, “quickly,” whose positive form, from which a comparative ought to proceed, is not present among us. Plautus is an authority for the superlative, whose examples are greater, in *The Nervolaria*: “That we may be free as quickly as possible …”

From Caelius’ *History*: “… are aroused as quickly as possible …” Aelius Lamia, in [a lost work]: “… Lamia ought …” [the supplied passages are lacunose]. [Col. 1623C–D; Pag. 30]

**Ocimum.** A Greek word; it is said to derive its name from the speed of its growth.

**Occupaticius field.** The ancients called a field *occupaticius* when, after its own cultivators had ceased to frequent it, it began to be occupied by others. This occurred in Campania. When Hannibal wished to reward the Capuans who had deserved well of the Carthaginian state, he publicly ordered that the fields which had been occupied and devastated should be restored to them as though recovered from an enemy. But when he heard the common complaint of those whose land had been occupied by private persons, he ordered that fields be given—not those which the complainants had previously possessed, but *occupaticii* fields. [Col. 1624A]

**Orchitis.** Ateius Philologus [Note: “Ateius,” not Accius] says in his *Collections* that *orchitis* is a kind of olive, derived from the Greek *ὄρχεις*, “testicles,” because it is the size of testicles; hence it is called *orchitis*. [The remainder is lacunose.]

**Orchestra.** A place in the theater where those actors who are now called *planipedes* were formerly not admitted, except for as long as the plays were being explained—plays that could not be explained without them. They wore *ricinia*, so that they might appear in more suitable dress and derive their name from it.

**Orca.** A very large kind of sea monster. Vessels shaped like it are also called *orcae*: they are rounded and of an ugly form. [The remainder is lacunose.] [Col. 1624B; Pag. 31]

**Oriri.** To be born, or to rise.

**Orba.** Among poets, *orba* means a woman deprived of some beloved person; among orators, a woman who has lost her father or mother [Note: “mother”]. As Servius Sulpicius says, a woman who has lost her children is *orba*, since children are, as it were, her eyes. [The subsequent citations from Gallus Aelius and Cornificius are severely lacunose: “… before … stronger … in that book … pontificate … a girl without … sacred … married … if she had belonged to someone … Cornificius … insert … having obtained …”] [Col. 1624C]

**Ortygia.** The island now called Delos is called *Ortygia*.

**Orbius Clivus.** It seems to have been named from *orbes*, “curves,” along whose winding turns Tullia, daughter of King Servius Tullius, and Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Servius’ son-in-law, hurried after the king had been killed, aiming together at possession of the royal house. The hill began to be called *Orbius* because, being steep, it led over the Esquiline Hill in curves [Note: “because it led”]; hence *Orbius* was named from those curves.

**Oratores.** Some think that *oratores* is derived from the Greek *ἀρητῆρες*, because those who were sent by the Roman people to kings and nations on behalf of the republic customarily called the gods to witness in prescribed words, *ἀρᾶβθαι*—that is, “to testify.” [The source is lacunose here.] [Col. 1624D; Pag. 32]

Some Romans call such men *legati*, “envoys,” as Cato says in the speech he wrote *On His Own Achievements against Thermus*: “I was sent as envoy to the consul Marcus Fulvius in Aetolia, because many Aetolians had come saying that the Aetolians wished for peace; envoys departed for Rome concerning this matter.” And in Book I of the *Origins*: “Because of this, Coelius, the Alban praetor, began the war; he sent envoys to Rome with …”

At other times *oratores* means “intercessors,” as in Terence: “I come as an advocate; see to it that I become one who obtains the request.” Afranius likewise, in *The Emancipated Man*: “If … then if something arises …”

At other times it means eloquent and articulate people, from the fact that the ancients used *orare* for *agere*, “to plead” or “to act.” For this reason their speeches are also called *orationes*. [Col. 1625A]

**Orata.** A kind of fish, named from its golden color, because country people called gold *orum*, just as they said *oriculae* for “little ears.” For this reason they also say that a certain very wealthy Sergius, who wore two large gold rings, was called *Orata*.

**Orae.** The outermost parts of lands—that is, the coastal regions—are called *orae*. Hence the outermost parts of garments are also so called, although these may likewise be called the first parts. Caecilius uses the word for the beginning of an affair in *The Aethrion*: “I cannot find any beginning from which I might extricate myself” [Note: “from which I might”].

**Oreae.** The bits of a bridle that are put into the mouth. Titinius, in *The Woman from Setina*: “Even if she is silent, she will still be glad that the bits are entrusted to her” [Note: “that the bits are permitted”]. Naevius, in *The Fortune-Teller*: “But put the bits on the lion” [Note: “if you put the bits on the lion”]. Cato, Book III of the *Origins*: “He answered concerning the horses: ‘Give me the bits from there; take the whip for yourself.’” Coelius, speaking for himself before the people: “A horse had been killed beneath my thighs; I removed the bits while Lucius Stertinius watched” [Note: “the horse, which …”; the omitted passage is supplied in the *Schedes*, page 172, line 20, through page 187, line 29]. [Col. 1625A–B; Pag. 32]

**Oreos.** Liber Pater and the nymphs called *Oreades* are so named because they frequently appear in the mountains.

**Ordinarius.** Oppius says that an ordinary man was customarily called a *scurra*, a buffoon.

est, when he says: “When the magistrates dare order nothing, lest the consul destroy anything under the auspices.”

### *Perihodos*

*Perihodos* is used both of a certain section in lyric poetry and of a sentence circumscribed by words in prose. In gymnastic contests, one is said to have won the *perihodos* when one has won at the Pythian, Isthmian, Nemean, and Olympic games, from the circuit of those spectacles.

### *Perempta* and *interempta*

Poets commonly use *perempta* and *interempta* in place of the perfect forms of *interficere* (“to kill”). [Note: *interfectis*.] Lucretius: “When at once the body and the nature of the mind have been destroyed.”

### *Perpetem*

The poets used *perpetem* for *perpetuo*, “continuously” or “without interruption.”

### *Persillum*

The priests call a small pitch-coated stick *persillum*. With this ointment the Flamen Quirinalis [note: *Portunalis*] anoints the arms of Quirinus.

### *Persicum portum*

When Plautus says *Persicum portum* (“the Persian harbour”), he seems to mean the Euboean Sea, because the Persian fleet is said to have been stationed there, not far from Thebes.

### *Personata fabula*

A certain play of Naevius is entitled *Personata*. Some think that it was first performed by masked actors [note: “performed”]. But since comic and tragic actors began using masks only many years later, it is more plausible that this play was performed as a new work by the Atellans, who are properly called *personati*, because they have the right not to be compelled to put on a mask on stage, whereas the other actors must endure this.

### *Persicus*

*Persicus* seems to signify “very shrewd,” as in Plautus: “He understands nothing of conciliating himself, unless he is clever in this way” [note: *sibi*, “for himself”; *persicus*]. Naevius: “And whoever was shrewd is present at the reckoning” [note: *carpeti*; the reading is uncertain, perhaps *adest, ratio*].

### *Perpetrat*

“Carries through,” “completes,” or “accomplishes.” Pacuvius in the *Teucer*: “Nor can he accomplish it by prayers, who … the commands of his father” [note: “nor can he accomplish it at a price”; and in the *Niptrae*]: “He insists on returning to Sparta; if he accomplishes that.” They also used the word without a preposition, since this usage has now passed into common practice.

### *Perpulit*

“Persuaded” or “impelled.”

[Several examples are lost: **[lacuna]** “by speaking he persuaded me … namely, compelled …”]

### *Pertisum*

The ancients said *pertisum* for *pertesum*.

[The surrounding example is fragmentary: **[lacuna]** “who somewhat … persuaded, impelled.”]

### *Puteum*

The ancients said *puteum*, from which *puticuli* may be derived.

### *Puticuli*

The *Puticuli* were called a very ancient kind of burial, because people were buried there in pits. Such was the place where corpses are now thrown outside the Esquiline Gate. Aelius Gallus thinks that they were called this because the bodies there putrefied.

Aelius Gallus says that it was an ancient custom for heads of households to throw worthless slaves into a public place outside the town; because the bodies thrown there putrefied, the name *Puticuli* arose.

### *Putu*

The ancients, he says, used *putu* for *puro*, “pure.” Hence vines from which what impeded them had been cut away were called *putatae*. Cornificius says this, and Ennius understood the word in the same way when he wrote in the *Alexander*:

[The quotation is lost: **[lacuna]**]

Plautus: “This parasite is purely and utterly …”

[The remainder is lost: **[lacuna]**]

Gold also is commonly called *putatum* when it has been purified, and a reckoned account is *putata*, that is, made clean.

[Example lost: **[lacuna]** “he reported to the heirs …”]

### *Putitium*

Plautus used *putitium* for “foolish”: “He is more foolish than a barbarian.”

The reason is this. When Potitius had learned from Hercules the ritual of sacrifice, he is said to have taught it for fifty thousand asses of heavy bronze to the public slaves of the Roman people [note: “public slaves”]. After this, within thirty days, all the Potitii—there had been twelve members of that family—perished.

### *Pubes*

A young man who is already capable of begetting children is called *pubes*. Its opposite is *impubes*, “underage” or “not yet sexually mature.”

*Pubes* is also used of several people of the same age.

### *Puteoli*

Some say that Puteoli was so called from the stench of its hot water; others, because many wells were made there for the sake of those same waters.

[The remainder of this entry is fragmentary: **[lacuna]** “but when … this … of that …”]

### *Pugnus*

The fist (*pugnus*) is so called from *punctio*, that is, striking or stabbing.

### *Pegasus*

The poets relate that Pegasus was a winged horse. It is said that his hoof brought forth a spring called Hippocrene.

[The remainder is fragmentary: **[lacuna]** “verses of another … Lucina Juno … beautiful …”]

### *Prospera*

The ancients used certain nouns in *-a*, declined in the first declension, with the final syllable lengthened, such as *praefiscine*, evidently to ward off the evil eye, as L. Cincius says. The same practice was also customary in the ritual purification of a household.

### *Porca praecidanea*

A *porca praecidanea* is a sow customarily sacrificed beforehand. This kind of victim was called *praecidanea* because it was slaughtered before the new grain was harvested.

### *Placenta*

A *placenta* is a kind of cake made from three pottages. Others say it is a kind of pottage made with three offerings.

### *Porriciam*

The ancients used *porriciam* for *porro iaciam*, especially of entrails. Plautus in the *Pseudolus*: “And meanwhile I shall hold the entrails in my hands, so that I may cast them before the place” [note: *interea*, “in the meantime”].

What is to be consecrated and dedicated to a god is cast upon the hearth and altars. Conversely, what is profane is consumed in the sacrifice. Thus Verrius writes in the same book of the *Meaning of Words*:

“Let me speak freely, if I have said anything contrary to him: he thinks that entrails are cast upon the altar and hearth for this reason, that, since they are profane, it is necessary that they too—that is, things dedicated to the god—be consumed.”

It is not at all necessary to refute this opinion, either here or in many other matters, since I intend to pass over, in the considerable number of his books, words that have already died and been buried and that, as he himself often admits, have no use or authority, and to condense the remainder into a very few books. Those matters on which I disagree will be found set out in these books of mine, plainly and briefly, as far as I have understood them. They are entitled *Ancient Words with Examples*.

*Page 36.*

### *Porigam*

The ancients seem to have said *porigam* for *porrigam*, following their practice of not doubling letters. The word may be derived from *porro regam*, “I shall rule forth”; or, if that seems frivolous, from the fact that it was plainly derived from *e rivo regam* [note: *rivo regam*, “I shall direct from a stream”]. The ancients also said *porga* for *porrigam*.

### *Porcae*

*Porcae* are the widely spaced furrows made in fields to divert water. They are so called because they “prevent” (*porcant* [note: *porcent*]) water from harming the grain. More closely spaced furrows are called *lirae* [note: *lirae*].

### *Postliminium receptum*

Gallus Aelius, in the first book of his *Meanings Pertaining to Law*, says that *postliminium receptum* applies to a free man who has gone from one state into another and returns to the same state, under the law established concerning return from captivity. Likewise, a slave who has come from us into the power of the enemy and later returns to us comes under the power of the person whose slave he previously was, by the law of *postliminium*.

The same rule applies to horses, mules, and ships as to slaves. Whatever classes of property return to us from the enemy by *postliminium* may likewise return from us to the enemy. With free peoples, allied peoples, and kings, *postliminium* applies to us in the same way as with enemies.

[The concluding sentence is incomplete: **[lacuna]** “Those nations that are under our authority …”]

*Page 37.*

### *Provorsum fulgur*

A lightning flash is called *provorsum* when it is not known whether it occurred by night or by day. Thus sacrifices are made to Jupiter the Lightning-Bearer and to Summanus, since Jupiter’s lightning is considered to be diurnal and Summanus’s nocturnal.

### *Propatulum*

*Propatulum* means widely extended and open. *Patuli* oxen are those whose horns extend in different directions above their heads.

### *Propriassit*

“Has made his own.”

### *Properus*

That the ancients used *properus* for “swift” is shown by the adverb *propere*, “quickly.”

### *Prophetae*

In the *Adrastus*, Julius calls *prophetae* the priests and interpreters of shrines and oracles:

“The prophets command them to veil their heads with green laurel, they who duly and purely prepare the sacred rites.”

### *Propter viam*

A sacrifice is made *propter viam*, “because of the road,” for the sake of setting out, to Hercules or to Sancus [note: *Sango*], who is evidently the same god.

### *Prodigia*

The word *prodigia*, “omens,” arose from an alteration of the letter *g*, for what is now called *c* was called *g* by the ancients.

### *Produit*

*Produit* means “he will give forth,” as in the censorial law: “He shall provide the colonnade with its roof and repairs; he shall give forth”; elsewhere it means “he will have given forth.”

### *Prodegeris*

“Exhausted,” “consumed,” or “squandered.” Caecilius in the *Hymnides* [note: *Hymnide*]: “To squander is, when you have nothing, to make a laughing-stock of yourself.”

Plautus in the *Nervolaria*: “It is fitting that a productively extravagant man should be a prodigy as a lover” [note: *producte prodigum*; “in me”].

### *Prodinunt*

“Go forth,” as Ennius writes in Book III of the *Annals*: “The servants go forth; then the bright lights shine.”

### *Probrum*

“Disgrace,” “sexual misconduct,” or “shameful offense.” Accius in the *Hellenes*: “Who consider everything except disgrace to be blameless.”

Caecilius in the *Davus*: “Then, having been confined, she bears a boy for him and disgrace for herself.”

### *Probrivum*

Apparently equivalent to *prohibitum*, “restrained”: those who restrain themselves from wrongdoing.

### *Prodigiatores*

Soothsayers, interpreters of prodigies.

### *Prodita*

“Gives forward to memory,” and “deceives.” It also means “proceeds from an inner place.” It also means “destroys,” as in Ennius, Book XVI:

“Not eagerly hoping to reveal the highest things.”

### *Punicum*

The word *Punicum* is said to have been transferred from the Carthaginians. The same thing was called *probum* [the surrounding text is fragmentary; “the sweetest in the other books, because it seemed …”]. *Punicum* is also the name of a garment.

### *Pro*

*Pro* signifies “in,” as in *pro rostris* [note: *pro rostris*, “before the speaker’s platform”], *pro aede*, “before the temple,” and *pro tribunali*, “before the tribunal.”

### *Progener*

A grandfather calls his granddaughter’s husband *progener*.

### *Profanum*

That which is not from a temple is called *profanum*. Plautus: “May you have the sacred thing from the profane; it is valued little.”

Livy [the quotation is lost: **[lacuna]**].

Pacuvius in the *Periboea* [the quotation is lost: **[lacuna]**].

Hence, Verrius says, the word *profanatio*, “profanation,” is derived.

### *Pro*

The preposition *pro* is used to enlarge or make something public, as in *prodi*, “come forth,” *provoca*, “challenge,” and *propelle*, “drive forward.”

Elsewhere it expresses the power of taking away, as in *propudium*, “preventing disgrace,” because in both cases it denies the presence of shame and power.

Elsewhere it has other meanings, such as *apud*, *ob*, or *ab*: *pro pecunia*, “for money”; *pro praedio* [note: *praede*], “for an estate”; *pro consule* [note: *consilio*].

Sometimes it expresses wonder, as in *pro Jupiter!* “By Jupiter!” Accius in the *Menalippus* [note: *Melanippo*]:

“By Jupiter! … from everyone’s hand …”

[The remainder is lost: **[lacuna]**]

Plautus in the *Condalio* [the quotation is lost: **[lacuna]**].

Sometimes *pro* means “before,” as in *pro hostio*, “before the doorway.” Sometimes it means “in,” as when we say *promittere barbam et capillum*, “to let beard and hair grow.”

### *Profundum*

That which is deep and has its bottom far below is called *profundum*. Pacuvius in the *Medus*:

“Nor the deep …”

### *Profesti dies*

The days called *profesti* are so called because they are far removed from the religious observance of the divine name. Caecilius in [a lost work]:

“What we do on a workday, you have done just as much on a holiday.”

Afranius in the *Privignus*:

“Equally on a workday, in contrast to when you celebrate.”

### *Profusus*

*Profusus* meant “extravagant beyond measure.” Terence in the *Adelphoe*: “Let him squander, waste, perish—it makes no difference to me.”

It also means “cast down” or “lying.” Pacuvius in the *Teucer*:

“Overcome with groaning, I mutter, yawning …”

### *Plauti*

*Plauti* are dogs whose ears are drooping and floppy, so that they appear to be spread more broadly.

[The remainder is fragmentary: **[lacuna]**]

### *Plantae*

Seeds of vegetables are called *plantae* because they are flat, just as the soles of our feet are called *plantae* for a similar reason.

### *Plancae*

Flat boards were called *plancae*, on account of their flatness. For the same reason people whose feet are flatter than usual are called *planci*.

### *Plaustrum perculi*

The ancients said *plaustrum perculi* of someone who struck a wagon loaded with goods with his foot—that is, overturned it. The expression later passed into a proverb. Plautus records it in the comedy *Epidicus*:

“Epidicus was my teacher; I am ruined. I almost overturned the wagon.”

### *Plebeius magistratus*

No one may assume a plebeian magistracy unless he is of the plebs. Every magistracy called by this name is of this kind.

### *Plutei*

*Plutei* are hurdles stretched with raw hide [note: “covered”]. They used to be placed in front of soldiers engaged in work and were called military screens. Now boards behind which something is sheltered are also called by the same name.

### *Plebeii Aediles*

The Plebeian Aediles were established no less by the vote of the people than by the plebiscite that provided for the creation of that magistracy, so that they might preside over the sacred buildings. They are said to have been assistants of the tribunes of the plebs.

They are said to have been assistants of the tribunes of the plebs. When the plebs seceded from the patricians, these men, created together with the Plebeian Aediles, made the shops which he calls the New Shops. We say that there were five, though seven are reported; they are called plebeian from the class of magistracy. M. Junius Brutus and Q. Oppius, Plebeian Aediles, saw to their construction.

### *Plexa*

*Plexa* means “bound together.” It comes from Greek; we add the preposition to it when we say *perplexa*, “entangled.”

### *Plentur*

The ancients also said *plentur* without prepositions.

### *Plera*

That the ancients said *plera* is shown by Pacuvius:

“The greater part is ruined.”

### *Ploximum*

Catulus says that a box in a carriage was called *ploximum*, or *capsa*, when he wrote:

“Indeed, he has the gums of an old *ploximum*.” [Note: *capsamve*, “or a box.”]

### *Plorare*

Now *plorare* means “to weep” or “to call out.” With a preposition, *implorare* means “to invoke”; among the ancients, it plainly meant “to call out.”

In the laws of King Romulus and Tatius:

“If a daughter-in-law is sacred to the gods of her parents …”

In the law of Servius Tullius:

“If a boy beats his parent, and that parent cries out, the boy shall be sacred to the gods of his parent” [note: *estod*, “let him be”]; that is, “if he has cried out.”

### *Pedulla*

What we call *pedullae* [note: *nos, ea*, “we call them thus”], the Greeks plainly call *πέδιλα* (*pedila*), “sandals.”

### *Pax*

Sinnius Capito thinks that *pax*, “peace,” is derived from the making of agreements, since the conditions of the pact must be observed by both peoples toward one another.

### *Penis*

The ancients called the penis *coda*, “tail.” From that ancient usage, even today a piece of pork with its tail, served at solemn dinners, is called *offa penita*. The brushes with which shoes are cleaned are called *peniculi*, because the ancients made them from the ends of tails and used them to wipe things.

The word may perhaps be derived from *pendere*, “to hang.”

Naevius in the *Tunicularia* [note: *Cunicularia*]:

“You call Theodotus, who, sitting in a booth at the crossroads festival, painted the household gods, covered around with mats, playing with a large ox-tail.”

This means “with a large brush,” that is, a tail.

### *Propius*

A cousin’s son is *propius* to me, as is the daughter of my cousin, and my father’s cousin, and my mother’s cousin.

*Page 41.*

### *Possessio*

As Gallus Aelius defines it, *possessio* is a certain use of land or a building, not the estate or field itself; for possession is not [lacuna] in respect of things which can be touched. [The text is damaged.] One who says that he possesses something may truly say this.

Therefore, in the actions brought under the law, no one among those who dares call the possession his own proceeds directly by that claim; rather, he comes to the interdict, so that the praetor may use these words:

“As you now possess this estate, concerning which the matter is in dispute, which neither of you possesses by force, secretly, or by permission of the other, so may you possess it. I forbid force to be used against this.”

### *Praefecturae*

In Italy, *praefecturae* were places in which justice was administered and markets were held, and which possessed a certain form of Roman commonwealth, although they did not have their own magistrates. Each year prefects were sent to them under these laws to administer justice.

There were two kinds. In the first were the places to which the four-and-twenty prefects, elected by popular vote, customarily went:

Capua, Cumae, Casilinum, Volturnum, Liternum, Puteoli, Acerrae, Suessula, Atella, and Calatia [note: *Calatiam*].

The second were those to which the urban praetor sent men each year under the laws, such as Fundi, Formiae, Caere, Venafrum [note: *Venareum*], Allifae [note: *Allieas*], Privernum, Anagnia, Frusino, Reate, Saturnia, Nursia, Arpinum, and many others.

### *Parret*

The word *parret*, which occurs in legal formulas, ought to have been pronounced with the first syllable lengthened and written with a single *r*, so that it would be *paret*, “is found,” as in *comparet*, “appears,” and *apparet*, “is evident.”

### *Portum*

Almost everyone agrees that *portum* in the Twelve Tables was used for *domum*, “home”:

“Whoever lacks a witness shall go about crying out at the door for three days.”

### *Patrocinia*

The term *patrocinia* began to be used when the plebs was distributed among the patricians, so that it might be protected by their resources.

### *Postica linea*

In the division of fields, Servius Sulpicius called the line facing from sunrise to sunset the *postica linea*.
