### *Pontina tribus*

The Pontine tribe was named from the city of Pontia; from the same place the Pontine Marsh was also named, near Terracina.

### *Papiria tribus*

The Papirian tribe was named from Papirius, or from the name of the land situated around Tusculum. The Pupinian tribe was so closely joined to it that it once undertook a war over their boundaries.

When the war had been declared by the fetials, and the leaders [the text is damaged], the two tribes were about to enter battle with their armies drawn up, but since the leader of one side had already withdrawn from the conflict, heralds were sent to both armies before the signal was given. They announced that the matter would be left to the judgment and authority of the armies themselves. Thus, without any battle, peace was made by the vote of both armies.

### *Pupinia tribus*

The Pupinian tribe was named from the name of the land called Pupinus, around the city of Tusculum.

[The remainder is fragmentary: **[lacuna]**]

### *Popillia tribus*

The Popillian tribe was one of the thirty-five tribes—there were that many. It was named from a woman named Popillia, whose name was favorable; similarly, the Pinaria tribe was named either from the sister of Pinarius or from his name.

### *Populus*

*Populus*, “the people,” has a common vote with the plebs in passing laws. The centuriate assemblies consist of patricians and plebeians divided into centuries. But when the plebs meets without the patricians in tribal assemblies, what the plebs has voted is called a *plebiscitum*, “decree of the plebs,” for this reason.

The patricians’ vote is shared with the people.

By votes of this kind a *populiscitum* is made.

*Page 43.*

### *Prorsi limites*

In land measurement, *prorsi limites* are the boundaries laid out directly toward the east.

### *Pugio*

The dagger (*pugio*) seems to have been so called because it fights by stabbing [note: *pungat*, “stabs”].

### *Propilia*

The Propilian tribe [note: *Poplilia*] derived its name from that of its female ancestor. Tribes were customarily named not only from men but also from women.

### *Praebia*

*Praebia* are remedies for treating an illness, namely, things supplied for the purpose of a cure.

### *Parare inter se munus*

They said *parare inter se munus* when a drawing of lots was held among Roman magistrates to determine which magistrate should undertake which task, or when they reached an agreement among themselves about a matter assigned by law.

Thus, in the senate and also in the assembly, they used to draw lots or arrange matters among themselves to determine whether they ought to go out or remain at home.

For consuls, just as for new praetors, it was necessary to go to a province and administer its affairs; conversely, the magistrates of the previous year had to depart.

The law also provided that within a fixed number of days the designated magistrates should arrange among themselves the provinces.

### *Peregrinus praetor*

The *peregrinus praetor* was so called because justice was administered differently to citizens and to foreigners. Therefore, according to the law, at first there was only one [note: *fous*, so printed], and later two praetors were created.

### *Praemetiri*

*Praemetiri* means “to measure beforehand,” as though it were *prae-essum*, “a preliminary offering,” for the purpose of a preliminary rite.

### *Protelare*

*Protelare* means “to drive far away.” It is evidently derived from Greek τῆλε (*tēle*), “far away.”

### *Privato sumptu*

Before they received pay, Roman soldiers supported themselves at private expense. This practice continued almost until the time shortly before the Roman state was captured by the Gauls; from that point onward soldiers were not employed without public pay.

### *Porci*

An image of a pig held fifth place among the military standards, because when a war had been concluded and peace made between peoples, the treaty was customarily confirmed by the sacrifice of a pig.

### *Polimenta*

Verrius says that the ancients called the testicles of pigs *polimenta* when they castrated them, deriving the term from the polishing or cultivation of crops or clothing, because those organs were treated in a similar way.

*Page 44.*

### *Pater patrimus*

Among the ancients, a man was called *pater patrimus* when he himself was already a father but still had his own father living.

### *Portisculus*

As Aelius Stilo writes, a *portisculus* is an implement that gives the fleet its rhythm in harbour. It is a hammer, mentioned by Cato in his speech opposing King Attalus and the revenues of Asia:

“C. Licinius the praetor enrolled Roman citizens as oarsmen; they came scattered, under the *portisculus* and under the whip.”

### *Pro scapulis*

When Cato says *pro scapulis*, he means “in return for an injury from blows,” since many laws had been proposed concerning citizens by which the penalty of flogging was established.

In the speech against M. Caelius he indicates that he had prevented many of his fellow citizens from suffering this:

“If I struck them, I often went away unharmed; moreover, for the republic, for their backs, and for the treasury, I benefited the Roman people greatly.”

### *Primanus tribunus*

A *primanus tribunus* is mentioned by Cato in the speech *On His Own Virtues*, against Thermus:

“It is one thing to hurry, another to hasten. Whoever completes each task at the proper time is hurrying; whoever begins many things at once and completes none is hastening.”

### *Prorsus*

*Prorsus* means “straight ahead,” unless it comes from Greek πρός [note: *πρός*, “toward”].

Cato, in *On the Junian Law concerning Usury*, writes:

“The Camerini, our citizens, possessed a beautiful town, excellent and most beautiful land, and the most prosperous circumstances. When they came to Rome, they went straight to their friends as guests.”

### *Prohibere comitia*

“Preventing the assembly” is said of rendering the day invalid through illness. The condition is commonly called *maior*, but for this very reason it is also called *comitialis*.

Cato, in the speech he wrote *On Sacrilege Committed*:

“When we take the auspices at home, I wish that I had shown due honor to the immortal gods. If a slave or maidservant, while beneath a blanket, made a noise that I did not notice, this does not invalidate the auspices for me. If the same thing happened there to a sleeping slave or maidservant, even that does not invalidate them for me.”

*Page 45.*

### *Penatores*

Those who carry provisions are called *penatores*. Cato, in the fourth speech against M. Acilius:

“After I had brought *nativitas* [uncertain reading] out from the ships, I did not make fishermen, provision-carriers, and [lacuna] out of soldiers and sailors, but gave them food.” [Note: *feci, sed cibum dedi*.]

### *Pilates*

*Pilates* is a kind of stone. Cato, Book V of the *Origins*:

“A stone whiter than *pilates*” [note: *pelastes*].

### *Peregrina sacra*

Foreign rites are called *peregrina sacra*. They are either rites brought to Rome when foreign gods were summoned during the assault on cities, or rites sought during peacetime for reasons of religious observance, such as those of the Great Mother from Phrygia, of Ceres from Greece, and of Aesculapius from Epidaurus. Their customs are observed because they are worshiped in the manner of those from whom they were received.

### *Peculatus*

*Peculatus*, “embezzlement of public property,” began to be called public theft from *pecus*, “cattle,” because this kind of fraud began with cattle.

Before coined bronze or silver existed, the heaviest penalty for an offense was two sheep and thirty oxen. T. Menenius Lanatus and P. Sestius Capitolinus, as consuls, established this by law. After the Roman people began using coined bronze, the Tarpeian law provided that an ox should be valued at one hundred asses and a sheep at ten.

### *Potitius and Pinarius*

When Hercules came to the altar that is still called the Greatest, after profaning the tenth part of the cattle that he was driving from Geryon’s land at Argos into his homeland, he taught the ritual of sacrifice.

The Potitian and Pinari­an families continued to perform it until the censor Appius Claudius gave them fifty thousand asses of heavy bronze to teach the public slaves the sacrificial rite. After this, all the Potitii—there had been twelve members of the family—perished within thirty days [note: “of that family”; “perished”].

Because Pinarius had not attended the sacrifice, it was later provided that no member of the Pinarii should eat from that sacrifice.

### *Plebeiae Pudicitiae sacellum*

The shrine of Plebeian Chastity is in the Long Street. Verginia, a woman of patrician birth, had married L. Volumnius, a plebeian consul. After a quarrel had arisen between the patricians and the plebs—

*Page 46.*

[The continuation is fragmentary: **[lacuna]** “for by that right …”]

### *Portorium*

*Portorium* was the name of the tax paid to the *portitores*, the contractors who collected it.

[The remainder is fragmentary: **[lacuna]** “when it had been divided in half … in the tax contracts, the collection of the portoria was leased to two …”]

[Further fragmentary text: **[lacuna]** “and Ti. Coruncanius, son of Tiberius, the censors … within a fixed period … something … with censorial dignity despised … sureties …”]

### *Primigenius sulcus*

The *primigenius sulcus* is the furrow cut by a bull and a cow when a new city is founded, because this kind of animal was used as though it were a team.

[The remainder is fragmentary: **[lacuna]**]

### *Parilia*

Romulus founded the city on the Parilia, a festival day especially observed by young men.

### *Praetexta pulla*

No one except the person conducting a funeral was permitted to wear the black *praetexta*. The same right belonged to a magistrate who held public games in some place; he wore the *praetexta* and usually had a secretary because of the games he conducted.

The right to wear the *praetexta* was also granted to consuls and praetors when they proclaimed vows, because of their ignorance of newly instituted sacred rites [note: “new sacred rites”].

The same right was granted to those fulfilling a vow. Valerius Vicanius, however, began to be criticized when he used it while leaving the senate wearing the plain toga.

*Page 47.*

### *Pilae*

Both male and female effigies were suspended at the crossroads during the Compitalia from wool. They thought that this festival belonged to the gods of the underworld, whom they call the Lares. On that day as many woolen balls as there were slave-members of the household, and as many effigies as there were free members, were placed there, so that the Lares might spare the living—for that is how they are invoked—and be content with the balls and images.

### *Punicae Fortunae aedes*

Cornelius Scipio is said to have vowed a temple to Punic Fortune when he was besieging Carthage, so that he might not suffer misfortune from that Fortune.

He likewise vowed a temple to Venus, said to have borne the title *Genetrix*, which he dedicated as soon as he had captured Carthage, the rival of the Roman state. Others say that he dedicated it several years later.

[The account is damaged: **[lacuna]** “when, as consul, he had failed to arrange for the temple of Punic Fortune, which he owed by his vow, to be dedicated first.”]

### *Pueri*

Boys are called *impuberes* (“not sexually mature”); Atta uses *pueri* in this sense. Atta uses the word in [a lost work], and in several verses he shows this meaning.

A bronze statue of an underage boy was once set up at the salt works. They say that the statue had been brought from [a lost place]. Some attempted to carry it away, but no one was ever able to wrench it from its base.

Others say that certain people removed the base while leaving the statue itself behind; they carried away only the base. Still others relate that, after removing the statue itself, they erected it in the Tibur­tine territory at the fifth milestone from the city.

### *Plena*

They sacrificed a pregnant sow (*plena sus*) to Mother Earth, because that kind of animal was considered especially hostile to sown grain, since it damaged the seed by digging with its snout.

### *Ploti*

The Umbrians were called *Ploti* because they had flat feet. For this reason the half-soles worn by hunters, allowing them to place their feet more flatly, are called *semiplotia*. For the same reason the poet M. Accius, because he was from Sarsina in Umbria, was first called *Plotus*, “flat-footed,” and later came to be called *Plautus*.

*Page 48.*

### *Postumus*

One born after the death of his father is called *postumus*. Plautus in the *Aulularia*:

“When a man in middle age brings a middle-aged wife into his house, and, if he is an old man, happens to make the old woman pregnant, why do you doubt that the name *Postumi* is ready for such children?”

### *Porcae*

Varro says that the furrows made between two [note: “two”] other furrows are called *porcae* because they extend grain.

### *Parmulae*

Soldiers used to fight with small shields called *parmulae*. C. Marius abolished their use and gave Bruttian shields in their place.

### *Porca aurea and argentea*

Ateius Capito says that a golden and a silver *porca* were so called. Although they are not counted among the number of sacrificial victims, they nevertheless bear that name: one made of gold and the other of silver are used in the sacrifice of Ceres.

### *Pulcher*

An ox brought to an exceptional degree of fatness is called *pulcher*, “handsome.”

### *Propudi*

A pig called *propudi* [note: *propudianus*] was, as Ateius Capito says, used in the sacrifice of the Claudian family as an expiation and atonement for all incurred religious pollution.

### *Parum cavisse*

A magistrate declares that someone appears to have “taken insufficient precautions” when, following the opinion of his council, he is about to condemn [him on a capital charge; the text breaks off]. [Note: *patravisse*.]

### *Piscatorii ludi*

The *Piscatorii ludi*, or Fishermen’s Games, are held each year in June across the Tiber by the urban praetor for the Tiber fishermen. Their profits do not go to the market but mostly to the area of Vulcan, because that kind of live fish is offered to that god in place of human lives.

### *Publicius clivus*

The Publician Rise is called after the two brothers L. and M. Publicius Malleolus [note: *Malleoli*], curule aediles. They paved it with money that they had collected from persons convicted of cattle theft [note: *ceperant*, “had seized”], so that vehicles could travel to the Aventine [note: *vehiculis*; *Velia*; “might be able”].

### *Praedia*

Verrius says that *praedia* [note: *praebia*, or *praebia*] are the remedies that Caia Caecilia, the wife of Tarquinius Priscus, is believed to have discovered and mixed into her girdle.

Her statue, girded with it, was set up in the temple of the god called Dius Fidius [note: *Sancti*]. From that girdle those in danger take shavings.

He says that these are called *praedia* [note: *praebia* or *proebia*] because they prevent misfortune.

*Page 49.*

### *Priscae Latinae coloniae*

The old Latin colonies were so called to distinguish them from the new colonies that were later established by the people.

### *Praetor*

The praetor is now saluted at the harbor by those who depart for a province as propraetor or proconsul. Cincius says in his book *On the Power of Consuls* that the custom originated as follows.

The Albans held power until the reign of Tullus. After Alba was destroyed, down to P. Decius Mus [note: *poectum*], the Latin peoples customarily met at the head of the Ferentine spring [note: *caput Ferentinae*], below Mount Albanus, and administered their common authority by common deliberation.

Therefore, in the year when it was first necessary to send Roman troops to the army, by order of the Latin nation many of our men customarily performed the auspices on the Capitol from sunrise.

When the birds had given the favorable sign, the man sent by the common Latium [note: *Latii*]—the man approved by the birds—was accustomed to salute the praetor who held that province in the name of the praetor.

### *Patricii*

Cincius says in his book *On the Assemblies* that those whom we now call *ingenui*, “freeborn,” used to be called *patricii*.

### *Possessiones*

*Possessiones* are fields extending broadly, public and private. They were held not by formal conveyance but by use; and whoever had occupied one cultivated it [note: *colebat*, “cultivated,” for *collidebat*].

### *Potestur*

Scipio Africanus used *potestur* in the speech *On the Command of D. Brutus*.

### *Poteratur*

C. Gracchus used *poteratur* in the speech in which he employed the word [note: *usus*].

### *Probrum of a Vestal Virgin*

The law that provided that the crime of a Vestal Virgin should be punished capitally, and that the man who had violated her chastity should be beaten to death, was posted in the Atrium of Liberty. Along with many other laws, it was consumed by fire, as M. Cato says in the speech entitled *On the Augurs*.

He also adds that the Vestal Virgins were removed from the priesthood—

*Page 50.*
[Col. 1633C] [Those] condemned for incest were buried alive because they had polluted the sacred rites of Mother Vesta; yet, although guilty, they were not buried outside the city, but in the field nearest the Colline Gate, which is called the Criminal Field. Some say that *privilegium* means a private law. Cicero, in the speech he wrote *On His House before the Pontiffs*: “… men … [lacuna] … consuls … [lacuna] … in that … [lacuna] … lictors … [lacuna] … by your judgment … [lacuna] … but you … [lacuna] … no one … [lacuna] … The Senators, Equites, and Treasury Tribunes condemn; the thirty-five Tribes condemn. By what law, by what custom, by what precedent have you individually carried a law concerning the life of a citizen who had not been condemned? The sacred laws forbid it; the laws of the Twelve Tables forbid a penalty to be imposed upon private persons. The thirty-five Tribes as a whole do not condemn poisoners, because they themselves are killed in the case in which they are accused.

**Punici.** They are called *Punici*, not *Poeni*, although, as Verrius says, the word derives from the Phoenicians; likewise, the Punic war, not the Poenic war, although the Carthaginians are called *Poeni*. For what the ancients used to pronounce with a long syllable through *pu*—Ennius pronounced *Poeni* in the poem—should be said *Poenos*. But because of the scribal error by which words belonging to the feminine gender are written in the masculine, and because the Greeks themselves speak in the same way, saying *philologos*, *philargyros*, and *pheias*, the scribe, supposing that *Poenos* referred to men, changed it, since Ennius had not explained the word by an added form. Yet nouns of this kind are often used in the masculine as well as pronounced in the feminine gender.

**Dicius.** Thus we say both *hic lapis* (“this stone”) and *haec lupus* (“this she-wolf”); [note: *lupus*, “wolf”]. Even those words that are called participles—which for the most part signify someone or something in an order of events, and which receive case, number, gender, tense, and person—are expressed in both genders.

[Col. 1634A] **Page 51**

… [lacuna] …

**Portumnus.** Portumnus, also called Palaemon, was worshiped by the Romans among the gods who preside over the sea.

**Poenas pendere.** This was said specifically of one who paid money for an offense, because formerly weighed bronze was used.

**Pullariam.** Plautus seems to have used this for the right hand in … [lacuna].

**Procedere.** Sometimes it means “to follow,” sometimes “to move behind.”

**Pertusum dolium.** When we say “a perforated jar,” we mean poison.

**Pes.** … [lacuna] … Ennius, Book I of the *Annals*: … [lacuna].

**Polit.** He said *polit* for “plays with a ball” … [lacuna].

**Petreia.** A *petreia* was the figure that preceded a procession in colonies or municipalities and imitated a drunken old woman. It was called *petreia*, apparently from a defect of the soil.

**Procilli**, or **Praecilli.** Cato said in … [lacuna]: “I shall turn to that … [Col. 1634B] … more shameless … [lacuna] … embassies … [lacuna] … witness.”

**Pelliculatione.** Cato used *pelliculatione* for “induction,” from *pellicere*, “to induce,” in the speech he wrote *On …* [lacuna]. The ancients often said *contra*, *robosem*, and *arboses* in place of forms with *r* … [lacuna] … the sea properly requires … [lacuna].

**Praemiosa.** This means “wealthy.” Cato said in the speech he wrote … [lacuna]: “… shamelessness rich in rewards.”

**Pascales oves.** He used *pascales* for *pascuales*, ignorantly, in the work he wrote … [lacuna]: “He forbade a pascal sheep.” The same author calls a Tarentine sheep *pellita* in the speech he wrote … [lacuna]: “A sheep covered with wool at Tarentum is worth more than one hundred thousand sesterces, although I did not know …” [note: “in the Tarentine field”]. What is pastured in the territory of Tarentum is called *Taretia*. Cato says: “I have been endangered.”

**Page 52**

—in the speech he wrote to the censors’ tablets [note: *notas*].

**Parsi.** “I did not spare,” says Cato in the same speech: “I know that prosperity is accustomed to breed negligence; and, so far as it was in my power to prevent this, I did not spare my labor.”

**Praedonulos.** Cato used this diminutive in the *Letters*: “Because little robbers often seem useful.”

**Praece.** The singular *prece* [note: *precem*, “prayer”] is used by the same author in the work *On the Conspiracy*.

**Pulchralibus.** Likewise, for *cupediis* [note: “delicacies”], in the work *On the Olive-Oil Trade*.

**Punctatoriolas.** Cato calls light skirmishes *punctatoriolas* in the work he delivered *On the Military Affairs of Histria*.

**Proaedificatu.** This is said of what has advanced from private ground onto public land.

**Percunctatu patris familiae.** Cato says that it was enacted by law that no one should send a slave without questioning the head of the household, in the speech in which he opposed the Orchian Law.

**Prodidisse.** This is said not only of those who betrayed their country to the enemy, but also of making time longer. Thus Cato: “You, Gaius Caecilius, betrayed the soldiers of the Third Legion by day, although they had no treachery in mind” [note: *prodisse*, “to have betrayed”].

**Pavimenta Poenica.** Cato uses this to signify pavements laid with Numidian marble, when he says in the speech he delivered *That No One Should Be Consul Twice*: “I can say whose villas and houses, built and polished with the greatest care, stand furnished with citrus wood, ivory, and Punic pavements.”

**Prolato aere.** Ennius used *prolato aere* of Achilles in Aristarchus’ *Achilles* [note: “in Aristarchus’ *Achilles*], meaning a shield extended before him.

**Poenita offa** [note: *penitam*]. Naevius calls a piece of meat with a tail an *absegmen*; the ancients called a lump cut off in the shape of a ball an *offa*, like porridge rounded by hand.

**Privatae feriae.** These are called the rites belonging to individuals, such as birthdays, days of ritual activity, and funeral days.

**Pronubae.** Women who have married only once are employed at weddings, as auspices of the permanence of the marriage [note: “the perpetuity of the marriage”].

**Pudicitiae signum.** In the Cattle Market there is a shrine where the wife of Hercules had lived [note: “there is a shrine”]. Some think that it belongs to Fortuna. Likewise, on the Latin Road, at the fourth milestone, there is a shrine of Fortuna Muliebris; it is religiously forbidden to touch it except by a woman who has married only once.

**Page 53**

**Patrimi et matrimi pueri.** Three children wearing the bordered toga escort the bride: one carries a torch made from white thorn, because she was married at night; two hold the bride.

**Pilentis et carpentis.** It was permitted for matrons to ride through the city in *pilenta* and *carpenta*. When gold was needed for the vow which Camillus had made to Delphic Apollo, they contributed it.

**Prima aut secunda hora.** They conducted the betrothal rites at the first or second hour [note: “dedicated”], for the sake of an omen, so that the outcome might be as favorable and fortunate as possible.

**Praetextu sermone.** Some think this expression is used because it is religiously forbidden for boys wearing the bordered toga to use obscene language; others because, when brides have laid aside their bordered togas, obscene words are shouted by the crowd of boys.

**Palatualis Flamen.** The Palatual Flamen was established because the Palatine was under the protection of that goddess.

**Portenta.** Some have thought that portents are serious and prodigies favorable; others that certain portents are favorable and certain prodigies gloomy. They call them *portenta* because they indicate what is being directed onward, and *ostenta* because they merely display monsters; they also prescribe remedies.

**Postularia fulgura.** These are flashes of lightning that demand [note: “indicate”] that the religious obligation of vows or sacrifices has been neglected.

**Pestifera.** These are signs that indicate death or exile.

**Peremptalia.** These are flashes that destroy earlier flashes, such as portents—that is, they remove them [note: “take them away”].

**Pullus Jovis.** Quintus Fabius, whose surname was Eburnus, was called Jupiter’s “chick” because of his whiteness, since one of his buttocks had been struck by lightning. The ancients also called a boy whom someone loved his “chick.”

**Peregrinus ager.** Land that is regarded as neither Roman nor enemy territory.

**Publica sacra.** Rites performed at public expense on behalf of the people, and for mountains, districts, curiae, and shrines; as opposed to private rites, which are performed for individual persons, families, and clans.

**Perenne.** A person is said to take auspices *perenne* when he crosses a river, or water arising from a sacred source, after taking auspices.

**Puls.** Porridge is given especially to the sacred chickens during the taking of auspices, because something could fall from it onto the ground and make a *tripudium*, that is, a *terripavium* (*pavire* means “to strike”), from which they could derive knowledge of the future. For if the chickens by whom they took the auspices did not eat, they thought danger was imminent; but if they ate, they considered it a favorable omen, provided that something fell from their mouths while they were eating.

**Page 54**

**Portenta rerum.** Portents of things are said to occur when solid bodies rarely appear, such as comets, whirlwinds, chasms, and thunder produced in a clear sky.

**Pedestria auspicia.** They thought that auspices were pedestrian when derived from a fox, wolf, serpent, horse, or other four-footed animals.

**Proptervia.** Auspices were called *proptervia* when they displayed themselves beside the road.

… [lacuna] … weak … [lacuna] …

**Piacularia.** Auspices were called *piacularia*, that is, sacrifices, according to an ancient linguistic custom, when either the victim escaped from the altar, or, after being struck, gave a bellow, or fell onto a part of the body other than the one required.

**Pestifera auspicia.** These occur when the heart is missing from the entrails, or the head from the liver.

**Pullarium.** Some think it was named from the chickens, because its special feature is that a bird is watched for the taking of auspices.

**Praepetes aves.** Birds are called *praepetes* when they fly before the person taking auspices; for the ancients used *praepetere* for “to go before.”

**Pecunia.** They said that a sacrifice was made *pecunia* when, for the sake of crops and fruits, pure meal was offered in sacrifice, because all household property—which we now call *pecunia*—consisted of these things.

**Projecta sacra.** Sacrifices performed when the sky is struck by lightning are called *projecta*. They are performed to avert the harmful flashes of lightning or to procure favorable ones.

**Parilia.** Women who have recently given birth themselves privately judge that the Parilia festival must be observed, administering the rites at home in bed [note: “at home, in the beds”], so that, by giving birth, they may be made firm, as it were [note: “may be stabilized”].

**Parilia festa** … [lacuna].

**Page 55**

… [lacuna] …

**Publici Augures.** The Public Augurs did not have the same legal status as the other augurs. For although there were more of them in number, the Public Augurs surpassed the others in official dignity. Their origin is ancient and therefore obscure. One thing is clear: they were accustomed to be selected by lot, and were called the Public Augurs of the Roman People, the Quirites, in the augural books. They took auspices after marking out the regions of the sky as a *templum*, which they marked out with the lituus called Quirinal, in the pomerium outside the city … [lacuna] … you have done …

**Picus rex.** King Picus used the woodpecker as an omen, as Verrius says, and was named from that augury. He fathered King Fatuus, whom others call Faunus, and Fatua. From them Latinus was born, and he treated the Trojans with the highest honor: he even received their king Aeneas, fleeing from the Argives, as a guest, gave him citizenship, and joined his daughter to him in marriage.

**Polubrum.** Some think that this was what we call a *pelvis*. It has the same form as a *polubrum* and is held in the left hand, as its meaning indicates.

**Patres.** The men from whom the Senate is composed are called *Patres*. At the beginning of the city’s foundation Romulus selected one hundred men and called them by this name, so that the republic might be administered and governed by their counsel and wisdom. He assigned portions of land to each, to the poorer citizens as though to children, and distributed money. For from the time of Romulus they were already accustomed to use coined gold and silver and foreign currency, as both public and private accounts show.

**Publica pondera.** The public weights customarily used by the Roman people are discussed by Junius in … [lacuna]. He says that the two Silii, Publius and Marcus, tribunes of the plebs, proposed the following words:

**Page 56**

“By the public weights which at this time the Roman people usually use, let everything be carefully brought into equality, so that a *quadrantal* of wine shall weigh eighty pounds. A wine *congius* shall be ten pounds. Six *sextarii* shall make a *congius* of wine; fifty-two *sextarii* shall make a *quadrantal* of wine. A *sextarius* shall be equal to the wine-pound; sixteen pounds shall make a *modius*. If any magistrate shall act contrary to these public weights, *modii*, and public vessels, or shall order them to be made smaller or larger, or shall introduce fraud so that this occurs, any magistrate who wishes may impose a fine on him [note: “may fine him, as he wishes”], provided that he assesses it at the lesser portion for a head of household; or, if anyone wishes to declare it sacred, he may do so.”

**Pecuum.** When Marcus Cato used *pecuum* in the genitive, he formed it from the singular nominative form used by the ancients, namely *pecu*, just as *testu*, *tonitru*, *genu*, and *veru*. The genitive of all these, in the plural, doubles the letter *u*. This is not because *pecus* should be understood like *pectus*; in declension we follow the form that is in ordinary use.

**Praeteriti senatores.** Formerly senators who had been passed over were not objects of reproach. Just as kings selected and enrolled those whom they wanted to have in their public council, so, after the kings had been expelled, the consuls and tribunes with consular authority selected as their closest associates first patricians and then plebeians. This continued until the tribunician Ovinian Law intervened, by which it was enacted that the censors should select the best man from every order, tribe by tribe, for the Senate. As a result, those who had been passed over and removed from their place were regarded as disgraced.

**Pro censu classis juniorum.** In the description of the centuries, when Servius Tullius used this expression, it should be understood as “in the census,” as Marcus Varro says in Book VI of *Human Affairs*: just as one says “in place of the temple of Castor,” “in place of the tribunal,” and “in place of testimony.”

**Page 57**

**Procu** [note: *patricium*] in the description of the classes established by Servius Tullius signifies *procerum*, “of the foremost”; for these are the leading men. *Proci* are those who seek something in marriage, in Greek μνηστῆρες, “suitors.” For *procare* means “to ask,” as in the expression used when appointing a judge: “If you seek another, or if you seek him”—that is, “if you ask for him.” Hence prostitutes are also called *procaces*, “forward” or “shameless.”

**Praerogativae centuriae.** These centuries are so called, as Varro teaches in Book VI of *Human Affairs*, so that the Roman country people, who did not know the candidates, might observe them more easily. Verrius judges more plausibly that the reason is this: when the candidates had been designated by the *praerogativae*, the people began discussing who was worthy or unworthy, and the others became more attentive in casting their votes concerning them.

**Peculium.** The slaves’ private property was named from *pecus*, “livestock,” just as the head of a household’s property was named from *pecunia*, “money.”

**Puelli.** This is a diminutive formed from *pueri*, “boys.” Thus Ennius says: “The Carthaginians were accustomed to sacrifice their little boys”; Lucilius: “And since this man is so handsome, and a little boy worthy of you”; and Plautus: “Once this little boy used to sell himself.”

**Praeciamitatores** [note: *praeclamitatores*]. These are said to go before the Flamines Dialis, Quirinalis, and Martialis and shout during public festivals that people should abstain from work, because it is religiously forbidden to see anyone working on those days.

**Pedum.** This is indeed a crooked staff used by shepherds to catch sheep or goats, from *pes*, “foot.” Vergil also mentions it in the *Eclogues*: “But you, take up your staff.” But in the verse of Ennius’ *Iphigenia*: “Do you hesitate to bring forth the *pedum* and advance a step? Make an effort,” Verrius says that the same weapon is signified [note: “staff”]. I cannot sufficiently marvel at this, since the order and meaning are clear.

**Pone.** The ancients used *pone*, with a grave sound, for the meaning of *pro loco* [note: “in place of”]. But they also placed the word before … [lacuna].

**Page 58**

… [lacuna] …

**Perimit, adimit, tollit.** “It destroys, removes, takes away.” Hence *peremptus*, “killed.”

**Pure lautum.** The ancients said this of something washed with pure water.

… [lacuna] …

**Pura vestimenta.** The priests of the Roman people were accustomed to wear pure garments when they sacrificed—that is, garments not soiled, not struck by lightning, not associated with death, and not stained—for this reason … [lacuna].

**Proculato.** This is also used for *provocato* and *pro citato*, “challenged” or “summoned.”

**Praefericulum.** A bronze vessel without a handle is called a *praefericulum*. It is open at the top, like a basin, and was used for sacrifices in the shrine of Ops Consiva.

**Patellae.** Small, pitch-coated vessels, also suitable for making sacrifices, shaped somewhat like small *capidulae*.

**Pantices.** They called the folds of the belly *pantices* … [lacuna].

**Procincta classis.** An army arranged and prepared for battle was called *procincta*. It was not lawful for the Flamen Dialis to see such an army. The ancients said *procinctus miles*, just as we still do when an army is drawn up. It was called *procincta* because men used to go into battle girded in their togas. Hence wills made by those about to go into battle were called *testamenta procinctu*.

**Prosimurium.** Antistius says in his commentary on pontifical law that this means the pomerium, that is, the place nearest the wall. Cato says: “Formerly everyone took auspices outside the Aventine; now they do so even within buildings.” The word is formed as though from *promoerium*, “before the wall.” The right of extending the pomerium is usually granted especially to those who have enlarged the Roman people through territory captured from the enemy.

**Page 59**

The most ancient pomerium of Romulus ended at the foot of the Palatine Hill. King Servius Tullius extended it. Likewise, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the dictator, apparently imitating King Tullius, attempted to extend it. But although the pomerium is a place that marks the boundary of the urban auspices, enclosed within a field defined by fixed regions for the taking of auspices, and although it may be extended, no one nevertheless enclosed the Aventine within the walls, even though the pomerium had been extended to it. The accepted reason is that Remus took auspices there and the birds proved unfavorable. In a later age, they say, it was enclosed. If the pomerium had been touched by private persons, a penalty had been established.

**Pontificale pomoerium.** They called this the place and field behind the wall where the Pontiffs established their auspices. When the pomerium was extended, the Public Augurs of the Roman People were accustomed to recite these words:

“Guardian gods of the city, do not make this pomerium smaller or larger; but extend it according to the regions by which it has been bounded.”

The word *pomoerium* seems to have been formed as though from *post muros*, “behind the walls,” that is, what lies behind and within the walls of the city.

**Proptu.** Labeo says that *proptu* appears to be used for what someone prepared at his own expense … [lacuna] … concerning whose expense you reported … [lacuna] … “ready grain” in your commentary. But some say that it means “brought forth,” the same as *promptum*. He says, however, that properly what has been prepared for future use is called *promptum*. This meaning is opposed by *penus*, especially since *penus* and *promptuarium* are different things; a *pantoleion* [note: “a store of bread, oil, and wine”] is mentioned by Plautus in the *Trinummus*.

**Potitus servitute.** The ancients used this of one who serves slavery, as Labeo says. Such usages are closest to the Greek custom. In the same way the ancients said *potitus hostium*, “having come into the power of the enemy.”

**Penus.** This is the innermost place in the temple of Vesta, closely enclosed, and opened only on certain days around the Vestalia. Those days are regarded as religiously restricted.

**Planta oliaginea.** A leafy branch taken from an olive tree by planting.

**Pomonal.** This is in the Solonian territory, on the Ostian Road, at the twelfth milestone, reached by a turning from the eighth milestone [note: “at a turning”].

**Pubes.** *Pubes* is also one capable of begetting offspring. This condition begins at fourteen years for a male and at twelve for a female; some think the term applies to a man capable either of intercourse or of undergoing it.

**Prandicula.** The ancients used this for what we now call *jentacula*, “breakfasts.”

**Prodignae hostiae.** As Veranius says, these are victims that are consumed; hence extravagant people are also called *prodigi*, “prodigal.”

**Petronia.** The Petronia is a stream flowing into the Tiber, which magistrates cross after taking auspices when they wish to conduct some business in the Campus. This kind of auspice is called *peremne*. The ancients expressed *amnis*, “river,” in the feminine gender.

**Penetrale sacrificium.** A sacrifice performed in the inner part of a shrine. Hence the innermost chambers of any place are called *penetralia*, and *penes nos* means “in our power.”

**Puri, probi, profani, sui auri.** These words are used in manumission for the sake of sacred matters. *Puri* means that which has not been used for a filthy pig [note: *spurco*]. *Probi* means that which has been properly cooked and purified. *Profani* means that which is not sacred and has been released from every religious obligation. *Sui* means that which does not belong to another.

**Pacione.** The ancients used *pacione* for what we now call *pactionem*, “agreement”; hence *pacisci*, “to make an agreement,” and *paceo* still remain in use.

**Presan** [note: *praesentanea*]. As Veranius says, a sow is called *praesentanea* when it is sacrificed to Ceres for the purification of a family, because a part of that sacrifice is performed in the presence of the dead person whose funeral is being arranged.

**Pateram perplovere** [note: *perpluere*]. In sacrificial language this means that the vessel is perforated.

**Pastillum.** In religious rites, a kind of round cake.

**Puilia saxa.** Fabius Pictor says that the *Puilia* rocks are beside the harbor along the Tiber. Labeo thinks that this is the place where Ficana stood, on the Ostian Road at the eleventh milestone.

**Page 61**

**Paveri frumeta.** The ancients called grain *paveri* when it did not emerge properly from the husk.

**Paludati.** In the augural books, as Veranius says, this signifies “armed” and “adorned.” For all military ornaments are called *paludamenta*.

**Purimenstrio.** Those who, for the sake of religious rites, remain in ceremonies throughout the entire month are said to be *purimenstrii*—that is, pure because they abstain on specified days.

**Prox.** A favorable word, apparently signifying something in advance [note: “they think it signifies”], as Labeo says in Book XI of *Pontifical Law*.

**Penatis.** Antistius Labeo thinks that *Penatis* can be used in the singular, because *Penates* is plural; proportion also permits *Penas*, just as *optimas*, *primas*, and *Antias*.

**Proculiunt.** Antistius says in Book IX of *Pontifical Law* that this signifies “they promise.”

**Popularia sacra.** As Labeo says, these are rites performed by all citizens and not assigned to particular families: the Fornacalia, Parilia, Laralia, and the *porca praecidania*.

**Pollucere.** The goods that may be offered are spelt, *polenta*, wine, leavened bread [note: “fermented”], dried figs, pork, beef, lamb, cheese, mutton, *alica*, sesame, oil, and fish with scales, except the *scarus* [note: *squarus*]. For Hercules, however, all edible and drinkable things may be offered.

**Profestum est facere.** This means “to treat as profane,” that is, to do something on a day that is not a festival; or, as some have said, to do something as though it were not a festival; or to do something that is not permitted on festival days. Thus a *profestus* day is a day without festivals.

**Profanum.** That which is not held by religious obligation.

**Procubitores.** These are almost the same as *velites*: soldiers who keep watch at night in front of the camp when the enemy camp is nearby, as Marcus Cato says in the work he wrote *On Military Affairs*.

**Properam.** That the ancients used *properam* for “swift” and “energetic” is shown by Cato, who says in his work *On Military Affairs*: “The third withdrawal from the camp is swift and successful” [notes: *castris* for *fastris*; *properaque* for *prosperaque*].

**Pro … sta dolia.** Labeo says that this means … [lacuna].

**Page 62**

… [lacuna] …

**Priveras mulieres.** They called private women *priveras* … [lacuna].

**Pube praesente.** This means “with the people present.” By synecdoche (*συνεκδοχικῶς*), the entire people are signified by those who are pubescent … [lacuna].

… [lacuna] … the remaining places … sacred flashes … [lacuna].

**Pecunia.** Money distributed for games and spectacles is called *lucar*, because it is collected from sacred groves [note: *lucar*, “hence”] … [lacuna]. In the same book I said … [note: “is said”] … He thinks this, and Valerius Messalla holds the same opinion in his explanation of the Twelve Tables.

**Pipulum.** This was called a lamentation.

**Promellere.** Verrius says that this signifies “to advance a lawsuit” [note: “to advance a lawsuit”].

**Purime tetinero.** This is written for *purissime tenuero*, “I shall have held most purely.”

**Publicus ager.** Public land was so called because it belongs to the public [note: “of the public”], as the Oscan inscription at Veii indicates; for it belongs to the use and legal authority of the augurs.

**Prodicere diem.** This means *prodere*, “to announce”; for *prodictio* is *proditio*, which, as Verrius says, applies to the present.

**Patronus.** Why the ancients called him *patronus* is clear: just as fathers are accustomed to be counted among the masters of their sons, so patrons were accustomed to be counted among the masters of their clients.

**Pristina**, or **priustina** [note: *pristina*]. Thus they also used *prior* and other words of this kind, formed from *prius*, “earlier.”

## P–Q

**Page 63**

… [lacuna] …

**Praesagitio.** This word is so called because *praesagire* means “to perceive acutely.” Hence old women are called *sagae*, “wise women,” because they know many things, and hounds are called *sagaces* because they perceive the lairs of wild beasts.

**End of Book XVI of Sextus Pompeius Festus. Beginning of Book XVII. Successfully.**

**Quirinus.** Romulus was called Quirinus for this reason: he used a *curis*, that is, a spear, and the Romans called Romulus by that name.

**Quirinalis porta.** This was also called the Colline Gate, as we read in ancient authors. One name is found used in place of the other because at first the two were joined so closely that they seemed to have been only one gate. Santra says that it was called the Colline Gate because the Quirinal Hill lies near it. They call it the Quirinal Gate either because one goes by it onto the Quirinal Hill, or because the shrine of Quirinus is near it. Thus, apparently, a usage arose and two names were applied to the same thing.

**Quirites.** The Sabines were called *Quirites* from the goddess Cures, to whom they were accustomed to sacrifice water and wine. Some, however, say that they were called from *curis*, the spears with which they perform her rites; Verrius rejects this opinion. From the name of the same goddess, the Sabine spears also seem to have been called *curres* [note: *Cures*], with which that people was powerful in arms. Now the name is used individually of both the Sabine and Roman peoples, as is shown by the herald who customarily announces at funeral proclamations:

“He of the Quirites has been given over to death” [note: “some read ‘that Quiris’”].

**Page 64**

The term *Quirites*, after the treaty struck by Romulus and Tatius, indicates the union and partnership of the people.

**Quirinalia.** A day in February on which rites are performed to Quirinus. The same day is called the Festival of Fools. The damaged text connects it with the Sabines coming from Cures and moving onto the hill after the treaty between Romulus and Tatius; those ignorant of the day of their own Fornacalia rites perform the sacred ceremony especially on that day [note: “day”; note: “Agonus”].

**Quirinalis collis.** The hill now called the Quirinal was formerly called the *Agonus* [note: “Sabine”], before the Sabines coming from Cures moved onto it after the treaty made between Romulus and Tatius. It received this appellation from them, although some think that it was so called because the temple of Quirinus was built there.

**Quirina tribus.** The Quirina Tribe seems to have derived its name from the people of Cures among the Sabines.

**Quiritium fossae.** These are the ditches with which Ancus Marcius surrounded the city that he founded beside the mouth of the Tiber, and from which he also founded Ostia. Because he had made them through the labor of the people, he called them the Ditches of the Quirites.

**Quincentum.** The ancients used *quincentum*, lengthening the first syllable and writing it with the letter *c*. Later this seemed less satisfactory, and it came to be pronounced as we pronounce it now.

**Qui patres, qui conscripti.** Those called “the Fathers” and “the Enrolled” were summoned into the Senate-house at the time when, after the kings had been expelled from the city, Publius Valerius, the consul, because there were too few patricians, enrolled 164 plebeians among the senators, in order to complete the number of three hundred senators, and thereby designated two classes.

**Quispiam.** That *quispiam* means “someone,” and *quaepiam* means “some woman” [note: *quae*], just as *qui* and other words of the same kind do, is beyond doubt. But where the following part of the discussion began cannot be discovered.

**Quinquatrus.** Some think that this festival was called *Quinquatrus* from the number of days on which it is celebrated. They are as wrong as those who say that the Saturnalia lasts four days and the Compitalia the same number, since sacrifices are performed on each individual day of all these festivals. The form of the word was expressed according to the usage of many Italian peoples, because it is a festival day after the fifth day of the Ides, as among the Tusculans there are *Triatrus*, *Sexatrus*, and *Septematrus*, and among the Faliscans *Decimatrus*. They think the day was dedicated to Minerva because her temple on the Aventine was consecrated on that day.

**Page 65**

**Quinquertium.** The ancients called this what the Greeks call πένταθλον, “the pentathlon,” as this verse shows:

“He surpassed everyone equally in the pentathlon.”

Livy likewise calls the athletes themselves *quinquertiones*: “The herald calls the pentathletes into the middle.”

**Quisquiliae.** This is thought to mean whatever falls from trees in the form of small twigs or leaves—whatever falls [note: “falls”]. Caecilius says: “Remembering the spoils of the flying wind, mere rubbish”; and Novius in the *Togularia*: “Get away from the crowd, you worthless man. What is it?”

**Quintipor.** This was a common slave-name among the ancients, derived from the master’s praenomen, like *Marcipor*, *Gripor*, and *Caipor* [note: *Caipor*]. Some, however, think it was so called from the number of children born to a slave woman, because he was the fifth.

**Quippe.** That *quippe* means “why not?” is shown by Ennius, Book XI:

“For surely all kings are accustomed to do so in prosperity.”

The same author, Book XVI:

“For surely it is not enough that ancient men be moved to war.”

Many others use it likewise.

**Quianam.** This was used by the ancients for *quare* and *cur*, “why,” as in Naevius’ poem *The Punic War*:

“O highest ruler of the gods, why [this] race …?”

And in the *Satire*:

“Why did you drive away the Saturnian people?”

And in Ennius, Book VII:

“Why has our judgment been turned by our words?”

**Quid nisi.** That the ancients used this expression is shown by Afranius in the *Epistle*: “At my advice you will refrain, mother—why not?”

**Quietalis** [note: *Quietalus*]. The ancients called Orcus by this name.

**Quintia prata.** The Quintian Meadows were named after Quintius Cincinnatus. When his son had been condemned and he had sold everything, Cincinnatus acquired four *iugera* of land across the Tiber. While he was cultivating that land, the Senate, having appointed him dictator, sent a messenger to greet him. After accomplishing the matter successfully and celebrating a triumph, Cincinnatus immediately returned to his private affairs, laying down the dictatorship and engaging in farming and household management; in this he was himself an object of emulation to the Romans.

… [lacuna] … because by that … [lacuna] …

**Quinctiliani Luperci.** They seem to have been called *Quinctiliani* after Quinctilius, who was placed in charge of the Luperci, just as the Fabiani were named after Fabius. Likewise, the Luperci over whom he had been placed in charge received the name. Many think that both groups, the Fabiani and the Quinctiliani, were established in the time of Romulus. Their number was later often increased, because many people were enrolled among the Luperci as an honor.

**Quintana classis.** Verrius says that the *Quintana classis* was so called because King Servius Tullius, when he distributed the multitude according to the census, made five classes when he organized them. The reason for the name *classis* is that those who were assessed possessed nothing except themselves and their own head. Lucilius mentions it thus:

“Whatever … [lacuna] … he obtained.”

**Querquera fever.** A severe and intense fever. Some wish to derive the name from *quercus*, “oak,” because that kind of tree is both heavy and hard and also grows to enormous height. Aurelius Opilius, however, says that it is called *frigid*, and that it causes trembling with shivering. Santra derives it from the Greek word κάρκαρον, which they use for a tremor of this kind; from this, he says, *carcer*, “prison,” is also derived.

Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*:

“For me there was a bilious, oak-like cough.”

Lucilius, in Book … [lacuna]:

“Throwing me about as an oak-like fever terrifies.”

Elsewhere:

“An oak-like fever follows, and of the head …”

## Fragmentary Lexicon: Q–R

*The supplied text begins and repeatedly continues in a physically damaged state. Brackets and ellipses below preserve the surviving boundaries; no missing wording has been conjecturally supplied.*

[Col. 1642A] The opening fragment preserves only: “pains … [right … which … for which under the laws there was an action for fourfold damages] … from him … to the people … the Calabrian Curia … name of the laws … under the dominion of the people ….”

### *Quando rex comitiavit, fas* [Col. 1641]

“When the king has held an assembly, it is lawful”: writers on the monthly festivals say that a day was marked thus in the calendar in honor of the king of sacred rites, for the festivals proclaimed by the king in the Curia on the Nones of February. [Variant: *comitiavit*, “held the assembly”; *edicuntur*, “are proclaimed.”] Many writers have transmitted them. On the day when the king comes into the Comitium, its earlier part is *nefas*, a time when public business is forbidden, while its later part is *fas*, lawful, because after completing the rites he departs. If someone else, such as the pontiff, acts in the Comitium for the king that day, the whole day is *fastus*, lawful for public business. [Variant: *is*, “that.”]

### *Quando stercus delatum, fas*

“When the refuse has been carried away, it is lawful.” A day is similarly marked in the calendar when the temple of Vesta is cleansed and its refuse is carried from Vesta’s temple to the Capitoline hollow. [Variants: *aedes Vestae*, “temple of Vesta”; damaged *oli vum* for the hollow.] [Col. 1642B] Once this has been done, the praetor may pronounce the three formal words.

Quaestors were so called because they investigated capital cases; hence those who conduct such investigations are called “quaestors of parricide.”

### *Quando*

When pronounced with a grave accent, *quando* means “because” or “since” and is a conjunction. Plautus writes in the *Menaechmi*: “For this reason, because I wipe the table when I eat”; in the *Pseudolus*: “I shall give it when the time comes.—Lead her away when you have it”; and Ennius, Book XVI: “When night shall fly girdled with the central constellations.” In the Twelve Tables the same word is written with final *c* [variant: *e*] and has the same meaning.

### *Quadrata Roma*

The place on the Palatine before Apollo’s temple is called “Square Rome.” Objects customarily used for a good omen in founding a city were deposited there, because at first it was fortified with stone in a square shape. Ennius mentions the place [variant: *meminit*] when he says: “And who had arisen to reign in square Rome” [variant: *extiterat*, “had arisen,” for the damaged main reading].

### *Quadrurbs*

Accius called Athens a “four-city,” since the inhabitants of four towns—Brauron, [Col. 1642C] Eleusis, Piraeus, and Sunium—brought their dwellings together into one.

### *Quaeso; quaesere*

Just as *quaeso* means the same as “I ask,” ancient writers used *quaesere* for *quaerere*, “to seek.” Ennius, Book II, writes: “The fortified harbor … makes places ready [variant *munda*, ‘clean’] for beautiful ships and for sailors seeking their livelihood upon the sea.” In the *Chresphontes* [variant spelling: *Cresphonte*]: “He takes me as wife for the sake of seeking children for himself”; and in the *Andromeda*: “Your mother, for the sake of seeking a child for the family.”

### *Quadrantal*

The ancients called *quadrantal* what is called an *amphora* in Greek, because the vessel was a square foot and held forty-eight sextarii. Plautus in the *Curculio*: “This old woman is thirsty.—How little does she thirst?—She is moderate: she holds a quadrantal.” Cato against Oppius: “You bought the wine; you gave estates worth sixty quadrantals of wine to the public [variant *publicum*]; you did not give the wine.”

### *Quaxare; quartarii*

Frogs are said to *quaxare* when they utter their cry [variant *quoaxare*]. The ancients called hired muleteers *quartarii* because they received a fourth of the profit. Lucilius: “Moreover, worthless men, a rogue like a *quartarius*, [Col. 1642D] gather all the boundary stones.”

### *Quatenus; quatinus; quatenoc*

*Quatenus* means “to what boundary,” as *hactenus* means “to this boundary”; *quatinus* means “since.” The ancients said *quatenoc* [variant *quatenos*]. Scipio Africanus, in the speech written after his return from Africa: “As the situation had arisen, our camp was fortified to such an extent that you could lead away part of the army.”

### *Quande; qua mox; quatere; quassare*

The ancients used *quande* for *quam*, as many old authors attest. The source’s attribution is damaged [variants: “then, Ennius,” or “then also Livy”]. It quotes: “Jupiter, relying upon the wall, rather than … the strength of his hand” [variant *manu sui*]; “Rather than all your legions and fellow citizens”; and Lucretius: “Famous for an obscure style, rather among the empty-headed than the serious Greeks [variant *inter Graios*], who seek truth.” [Col. 1643A]

*Qua mox* means “how quickly”; *mox* by itself means “a little later” or “afterward.” *Quatere* means the movement of something suspended and near another thing, not “to strike,” as Verrius thought, since *concutere* is compounded from *con-* and *quatere*. *Quassare* means to shake repeatedly.

### *Querquetulanae; virae*

The Querquetulan nymphs are thought to be those presiding over a flourishing oak grove. The name shows that this kind of woodland once stood inside the gate called Querquetularia after it. [Variant: *virae*.] The ancients called women whom we call wise women or prophetesses [variant: *sagas nos*] *virae*. The words *virgines* and *viragines* still preserve the form.

### *Ques; qui hoc censetis; quot servi*

The ancients said *ques*. Its declined dative *quibus* remains, for *qui* [variant *quis*] makes *quibus*, as *isti* makes *istis* and *illi*, *illis*.

“Those of you who approve this, pass over there; those who approve everything else, come to this side.” This wording is used for the sake of a good omen, so that the presiding official need not say, “those who do not approve.”

“As many slaves, so many enemies” is a proverb. [Col. 1643B] Sinnius Capito thinks that an error arose because most people reversed the wording. It is likelier that the original was, “As many enemies, so many slaves,” [variant *quod*, “because”] since captives were generally reduced to slavery. The continuation through [Col. 1643C] is almost wholly lost: “Hence also chattels … [many broken lines] … Sinnius Capito … as they report … of beneficent virtue … to all … maidservants … every … rule … fixed more deeply ….”

### *Quota; quod; quinquennales; five kinds of augural signs*

*Quota*, Verrius says, meant among the ancients not only “because” but also “after,” because Greek ἐπεὶ [variant ὅτι] has both meanings. *Quod* can also mean “something,” besides its common use, just as the Greeks say τὶ.

Censors were called “quinquennial” because they completed the lustrum every fifth year, from which they began to receive the name. Public augurs observed five kinds of signs: from the sky, birds, sacred feeding, quadrupeds, and dire portents, as stated in the Augural Books.

### *Rufuli; ructare; respersum*

Military tribunes appointed by the consul rather than by the people were called *Rufuli*. Rutilius Rufus carried a law about their jurisdiction that protected them in many ways. [Col. 1643D] Their right was thus elevated, while those elected by popular vote were then being reduced in standing. They were called *Rufuli* from Rutilius’s surname and afterward *Rutili*. The following page is badly broken. It preserves a statement that Verrius said one should say *ructare*, not *ructari*, followed at [Col. 1644A] by a fragment of Valerius Flaccus: “You would see others belching and spitting out most splendidly in their pride.” Cicero nevertheless used *ructaretur* in the second *Philippic*.

Among the ancients *respersum* meant wine, because at the nine-day funeral rites the dead person’s tomb was sprinkled with wine. The rest of the entry is lost.

### Roman games

The Romans appear at first to have used no work of professional performers. When they first began to hold games, performers were summoned from Etruscan cities. All the games now celebrated by the Romans were instituted late. Some place the Roman Games first; others the Megalensian Games of the Great Mother and the popular games of Ceres. Some say Roman boys played “Troy” in equestrian contests. Others say that riding, throwing, jumping, and racing were instituted at the festival of the Parilia, [Col. 1644B] and that performers likewise held theatrical contests.

### *Rubidus; Porta Romana; rutabulum*

Bread that is underbaked, reddened with a red color, is called *rubidus*. Plautus in the *Casina*: “Put it into the oven and toast it there for reddish bread.” Wrinkled leather flasks of the same color are likewise called *rubidae*.

The people call “Roman Gate” the place where water flows down from the architrave. The ancients called it the Statue of Cincia because the family’s tomb stood there. But Romulus established the Porta Romana at the lowest [variant *in imo*] slope of Victory, a place shaped into a square by steps. It was called Roman chiefly by the Sabines because it was the nearest approach to Rome.

A *rutabulum* is the implement farmers use [variant *utuntur*] for raking forward the fire to bake bread. Novius in the *Picus*: “What was I to do, idle [variant *otiosus*]? I was gnawing the fire rake.” Naevius [variant *Navius*], describing a man’s obscene member [Col. 1644C], says that even a woman hoping to marry a young man [variants *viro*, *adolescentulo*] may handle an old, worn-out *rutabulum*.

### *Ruta caesa; rutilum; rutrum; rotunda Vestae aedes*

*Ruta caesa* are things that the seller of an estate cut down for his own use and gathered by digging them out [variant *extraxit*]. *Rutilum* [variants *Rutilius*, *Rutilus*] means red. Ancient women too favored this color and took the surname *Rutilae* [variant *Rutilias*], as Afranius often indicates.

On the Capitol stands the image of a youth holding a mattock, an ephebe turning up sand for exercise in the Greek manner. Pompeius Bithynicus brought the statue from Bithynia to Rome among the royal furnishings.

King Numa Pompilius appears to have consecrated Vesta’s round temple because he believed Vesta to be the earth by which human life is sustained, and the earth to have the shape of a sphere, so that the goddess might be worshiped in a temple resembling her.

### *Ruscum; rupitias; rodus or raudus*

Verrius says *ruscum* is a little larger than grass and more slender [variant *exilius*] than shrubs and fruit-bearing bushes [variant *fructicibusque*], and resembles a rush. [Col. 1644D] Cato, *Origins* VII, records that women used things of its color [variant masculine *solitus*]: “Women covered in gold and purple; a golden [variant *auri*] diadem adheres; golden crowns, russet in appearance [variant *facie*], linen bracelets [variant *galbeas*], skins, and necklaces.”

In the Twelve Tables *rupitias* means “shall have caused damage” [variant second person *dederis*].

*Rodus* or *raudus* means a rough, unfinished thing. Poets also call a stone *raudus*. Accius in the *Melanippus* [variant spelling *Menalippo*]: “He stood [variant *constitit*], recognized, perceived [variant *sensim*], and placed himself upon a high spot. From here take up in your hands a great and heavy rough stone [variant *rodus*].” In the *Chrysippus*: “No one was without weapons; whatever met each man [variant *obvium*], iron or a rough stone [variant *saxum rodum*]….” [Col. 1645A]

Common speech used *rodus* not only for unworked bronze, as in Lucilius—“a small [variant *pauxillum*] lead peg, a *rodus*, and a skein [variant *metaxam*] of flax”—but also for coined bronze. In a conveyance, when the formula says, “Strike the scale with the small bronze,” the scale is touched with an as. Cincius, *On Ancient Words*, says that just as almost every unshaped material is called *rudis*, such as unpolished cloth, so unworked bronze is *rudusculum*. Cast bronze lay by Apollo’s temple and was called *adrudus*. In censorial valuation unworked bronze is called *rudus*.

### *Rudiarii; rudis; rudentes; ruspari*

From the same word, those who polish new cloaks are called *rudiarii*. We call an inexperienced person *rudis*. *Rudentes* are nautical ropes, and also donkeys when they bray. *Ruspari* means to search with a sieve [variant *crebro*, “often”], as the verse shows: “And I shall go, searching out hiding places, to examine the best ones.”

### *Rustica Vinalia; rustum*

The Rustic Vinalia are celebrated on 20 August, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, a festival of Jupiter. While fighting Mezentius, the Latins dedicated to that god the libation of all their wine. On the same day temples were consecrated to Venus, one at the Circus Maximus and another in the grove of Libitina [variant *Luco Libitinensi*], because gardens are under that goddess’s protection [variant *in ipsius*]. [Col. 1645B]

The entry *rustum ex rubus* then breaks off across pages 74–76; only the end survives: “… where he might lie down for the purpose of repeating the auspices.”

### *Rogatio*

A *rogatio* is a proposal on which the people are consulted concerning one or more persons when it does not apply to everyone, or concerning one or more matters when it does not enact a rule for all matters. [Col. 1645C] What the people ordain concerning all persons or matters is called a law. Gallus Aelius therefore says the difference is that a *rogatio* is a kind of law, though a law is not automatically a *rogatio*. A *rogatio* [editorial supplement] cannot fail to be a law, provided it was proposed in lawful assemblies.

### Romulus and the name of Rome

Some very foolishly said that Romulus was named from the Ruminal fig tree, others because he was nourished at the she-wolf’s teat, *ruma*. It is credible that he and his brother were instead named from their greatness of strength.

Cephalon of Gergis, who seems to have written about Aeneas’s arrival in Italy, says Rome was named from a companion of Aeneas. This man occupied the hill now called the Palatine [variants *Palatinus* or *Palatium*], founded a city, and named it Rhoma. Apollodorus in the *Euxenis* says Aeneas and Lavinia bore Maylles, Mylus, and Rhomus, and the city took its name from Rhomus. Alcimus says Aeneas had a son Romulus by Tyrrhenia, from him came Alba, Aeneas’s granddaughter, and her son Rhodius [variant *Rhomus*] [Col. 1645D] founded Rome. Antigonus, writer of an Italian history, says a man named Rhomus, conceived by Jupiter, founded a city on Rome’s Palatine and gave it his name.

The author of the Cumaean History says some Athenians departed for Sicyon and Thespiae [variant *Thespiasque*]. Because dwellings were scarce, many left those cities for foreign regions and came to Italy. After long wandering they were called Aborigines. The damaged continuation says that men of exceptional strength subjected others and named the Palatine, where most settled, *Valentia* from the ruler’s strength. When Evander and Aeneas came to Italy with many Greek speakers, the name was translated and began to be called *Rhome*.

Agathocles of Cyzicus says [Col. 1646A] that Aeneas, prompted by Helenus’s prophecy, sought Italy and brought his granddaughter Rhome, Ascanius’s daughter. When the Phrygians gained Italy, especially the regions near the present city, she was the first [variant accusative *primam*] to consecrate on the Palatine a temple of Faith. When the city was later founded on that hill, she appeared a just cause for its name because she had earlier dedicated the place to Faith. Agathocles also says several authors report that Aeneas was buried in Berecynthia by the river Nolon, and that a descendant named Rhomus came to Italy and founded the city called Rome.

Callias [main damaged form *Caltinus*], who wrote the deeds of Agathocles of Sicily, thinks that among the Trojans fleeing after Ilium’s capture was a man named Latinus with a wife, Rhoma; after gaining Italy he founded a city and called it Rhoma. Heraclides Lembus thinks that some Greeks returning from Ilium [main singular *quendam*; variant plural *quosdam*, “some Greeks”] were driven by storm [Col. 1646B] to Italy, followed the Tiber to the site of Rome, and, weary of sailing, had their fleet burned by captive women at the urging of a mature maiden named Rhome. Forced to remain, they founded a city and named it chiefly for her, whose counsel had secured their settlement. Galitas writes that after Aeneas’s death rule in Italy passed to Latinus, son of Telemachus and Circe; by Rhome he [variant *isque*, “and he”] had sons Rhomus and Romulus, which caused the city founded on the Palatine to be called Rhoma above all.

The next account is transmitted with broken left margins. Diocles of Peparethus says Ilia, daughter of Numitor king of Alba, bore twins. Faustulus, a royal servant, exposed them at the lowest bank of the Tiber near the fig tree later called Ruminal by Romulus. A she-wolf suckled them there and a woodpecker of Mars fed them; afterward Acca Larentia, Faustulus’s wife, found and raised them. [Col. 1646C] Most say Numitor knew and supplied their food, because Ilia asserted that Mars had fathered them. They were secretly instructed at Gabii in letters and every liberal discipline, spent early boyhood in music, and surpassed their peers in height and beauty. One was called Romulus, the other Remus. When they learned they were Ilia’s sons, had been exposed beside the Tiber, suckled by the wolf’s teat, found by Faustulus, and raised, they were named chiefly from *ruma*, “teat.” After learning who their father was, they first restored the kingdom to their grandfather Numitor. Then they used augury to decide which would found and name a city. With manifest divine approval Romulus founded it and called it Roma [Col. 1646D], rather than Romula after himself, so that the broader sense of the word might promise greater prosperity to his country.

Terentius Varro says Rome was earlier called Romula after Romulus and that the vowel was afterward altered and letters worn away. Verrius says the reason for this naming was forbidden to be published. The Roman Gate was formerly called Romulan, and afterward named from Rome.

### *Romulia tribus* and damaged transition

Dionysius says the Romulian tribe was named from Romulus because it was enrolled on land he had captured from the Veientines. Terentius Varro says it was so named because it was nearest Rome. The remainder through [Col. 1647A] is mostly lost, preserving isolated words including “*ruma*, that is, breast,” “Capitol,” and “called.”

### *Rumex; rumitant; Ruminal fig; rumen; rumentum*

*Rumex* is a kind of weapon resembling the Gallic *sparum*. Lucilius: “Then spears, then *rumices*, and afterward the javelin are carried.” *Rumitant* means “they spread rumors,” as Naevius says: “At the same time, from different directions, they spread rumors among themselves” [variant *sese*].

Varro says the Ruminal fig tree near the Curia beneath the Old Shops was so called because beneath it the she-wolf gave Remus and Romulus her *ruma*, that is, breast. A breast is called *rumis*; hence farmers call suckling kids *subrumii*, [Col. 1647B] since they are still beneath the teats. Others [variant *alii*] think cattle customarily ruminated beneath the tree.

*Rumen* is the part of the neck through which food is swallowed; hence the ancients said *rumare*, now *ruminare*. In the Augural Books *rumentum* appears to mean an interruption or breaking off: “While he recites the words for moving the sacred shields, if meanwhile a bird [variant *avis*] sings, let there be *rumentum* in that auspice and augury just as before.”

### *Rhegium; Rhodesicadion; rhinoceros*

Verrius says *Rhegium* should denote the town in the strait off the region [variant *regione*] of Sicily, since its name comes from “breaking,” Greek ρῆξαι [corrupt main Greek ῥαταιαι]. This is especially so because the place in Cisalpine Gaul where the Forum of Lepidus stood is called Regium.

When Lucilius said *Rhodesicadionque* [variant *Rhondon Icadionque*], he supplied names of pirates [variant *cognomina piratarum*, “surnames of pirates,” for the main text “banks”] and described his body and health as hostile to himself as those men were to sailors’ safety [variant *illa esset*, “they were”]. Some say the rhinoceros is an Egyptian ox.

### *Redemptores; redibitum; redivia*

In strict ancient usage, *redemptores* were those who contracted [variant *conduxerant*] to make or provide something publicly [variant *aut*], completed it, and only then received their money; ancient usage employed “buy” for “receive.” [Col. 1647C] Now those who contract to provide something for use are called *redemptores*.

*Redibitum* [damaged main form *redibiturtu*] properly denotes something returned and rejected by the person who gave it [variant *ei*], who is therefore compelled to possess again what he possessed before.

Some call the skin that peels back around a fingernail *redivia*, others *reluvium*, because *luere* [main *ruere*] means “to loosen.” Titinius in the *Setina*: “Weariness, a fellow slave’s hangnail, and a whip”; and Livius: “Stumbling in reading over something rough or over a hangnail.”

### *Redhostire; redamptruare; redivivum*

*Redhostire* means to return a favor. Novius [main *Navius*] in the *Lupus* has a badly damaged quotation: “The … orders King Amulius [variants *salvere jubet*, *Amulium*] to be greeted; Menalus in return requites the wise old companion.” Accius in the *Amphitryon*: “Come, does anything requite you [variant *redhostitum*] more readily when you delight yourself in it?” [variant supplies that clause.] They also used *hostire* for “to make equal.” Ennius in the *Cresphontes*: “Listen, and add an equivalent to what you hear”; [Col. 1647D] in the *Ransom of Hector*: “What my sword and spear can match at close quarters in an enemy’s [variant *hostiris*] hand”; and Pacuvius in the *Teucer*: “Unless I restrain insolence and match ferocity.”

In the dances of the Salii, *redamptruare* [main *redatruare*] is said when, after the leader has *amptruavit*, that is, performed movements, the same movements are returned in turn [variants *amptruavit*, *et*]. Lucilius: “When the leader dances, the crowd afterward danced in response” [variants *redamptruavit*]. Pacuvius has a damaged phrase, “a favor to be earned” [variant *Promerenda*], and: “When I see that the Greeks respond in no moderate fashion and pursue with their utmost resources.”

*Redivivum* is something renewed from old material. Cicero, *Against Verres* III [main Book I]: [Col. 1648A] “Do you think it less labor to make one entirely new column, using no reused stone?”

### *Redarguisse; redimiculum; reus*

Scipio Africanus, son of Paulus, is said to have pronounced *redarguesse* with *e* [main *redarguisse*], and likewise *pertisum*. Lucilius says: “So that you may seem wittier and know more than others, they say [variant *ferunt*] *pertisum hominem*, not *pertaesum*.” [The ending “for the gender …” is lost.] Women call the little chain used especially for adornment a *redimiculum*.

Today *reus* means one who pleads a case, and likewise one who promised or guaranteed something and owes it. Gallus Aelius, Book II of *Meanings of Words Pertaining to Law*, says: “A *reus* is one who has formally joined issue with another, whether he [variant *is*] brought the action or the action was brought against him.”

A *reus stipulando* is the same as the stipulator, since he stipulated from another in his own name [variant *qui stipulatus*], rather than being one who joined another’s stipulation [variant *is*]. A *reus promittendo* is one who promised something to another in his own name, or [variant *quive*] promised something for another.

Ateius Capito [main damaged *Capito Actus*] holds the same opinion but supports the interpretation with an example. “For” [variant *Nam*], in the second table, second law, it is written: “If one of these has an impediment [main *unum*, variant *vitium*]—judge, arbiter, or party—let that day be postponed” [variant *dies diffissus*]. [Col. 1648B] Now both litigants [variant *actor reusque*] are called parties in a trial [variant *rei*], and by ancient custom an accuser is likewise summoned from the road [variant *de via citu*; main text “accused of violence”].

### *Rivus; repanda; ritus; rite; retractare*

Commonly *rivus* means a slender flow of water made not by a channel or artificial trench [variant *specu inciliove*] but by its natural impulse. Yet man-made channels too are called *rivi*, whether dug above ground or carried through a tunnel below it [variants *ii*, *subter*]. The word’s origin depends upon Greek.

Streams of the Pomptine region [variants *retanda*, *Pomptina*] are leased as *repanda*, that is, to be cleared. *Retae* are trees projecting either from riverbanks or standing in the channels.

*Ritus* is a manner or custom. *Rite* means “well and correctly.” The continuation at [Col. 1648C] is fragmentary; it includes Plautus, *Menaechmi*: “Surely this woman, standing in the manner of a donkey, is dreaming …,” followed by broken references to a person, a weapon, another thing, missiles, and an oar. *Retractare* means to handle again.

### *Rabidus; ravus; rates; radere; rabula*

*Rabidus* is named from *rabies*, the canine disease. Catullus, concerning Berecynthia and Attis: “The raging frenzy of the mind departs into soft repose.” Plautus calls people of a *ravus* color *ravistelli*: they are between yellow and blue-gray. The continuation after *ravo sub-* is lost [variant *colore*]. The source calls this the worst kind of people and quotes the *Epidicus*: “But who is this little woman, and that gray-yellow fellow who comes?”

*Rates* are timbers bound together and driven over water; the word sometimes also denotes ships. Afranius in the *Epistula*: “… a vessel struck by wind.” The same word also denoted oars [variant *significarunt*]. Accius in the *Neoptolemus*: [Col. 1648D] “And I strike back the sea with oars”; elsewhere: “But now the oars propel the blue sea.”
