The Twelve Tables forbid “scratching the cheeks,” that is, tearing them with the fingernails. A *rabula* is a person intent on [variant *intentus*] many affairs and ready to scrape away and remove something; or the name comes from being rather fierce in conducting business, almost rabid. The remainder of page 83 is lost.

### *Porta Rodusculana; runa; rasores*

The Rodusculan Gate appears to have been named because [Col. 1649A] it was left rough and unpolished, or because it was bound with bronze. Varro says in the *Antiquities* that bronze was called *raudus*, whence the conveyancing formula: “Strike the scale with the small bronze.”

*Runa* is a kind of missile. Ennius: “He withdraws after being struck with a *runa*, that is, a javelin.” The description of another poisoned type is almost wholly lost. The ancients called lyre players *rasores*, “scrapers,” because, Verrius says, they seem by a certain art to scrape the strings with the stroke.

### *Ratitus quadrans; ravim; ratus*

Tarquitius, in a book whose title is lost, and Opilius Aurelius [main *Oppius*] think a quarter-as was called *ratitus* because it and the triens bore the image of a raft, as the as bore a ship. Antonius mentions a *ratitus* triens. [Col. 1649B] He thinks trientes were called *ratiti* because “raft” was the designation of a third of an as, while there was no such designation [variant *nulla sit*] for a fifth or another fraction, unlike numerical names such as *sextans*. The corrupt continuation says that *ratis* was used only of a three-part unit and cites one “raft” of the legions [variant *legibus Numae*, “laws of Numa”] as meaning a triens, because trientes were paid when accounts were reckoned with creditors.

The ancients used *ravis* for hoarseness. Plautus: “If we ask anything there, let us ask until we are hoarse”; and: “By Hercules, I shall clear everything out [variant *Expurgabo*] to the point of harsh hoarseness.” A fragment from the *Artemo* is lost. Caecilius in the *Hypobolimaeus*: “You will be asked until you are hoarse before you make the cake.”

*Ratus sum* means “I thought”; elsewhere *ratus* and *ratu* mean “firm, certain.” Ennius: “Romulus will be slain when he securely gains the booty.” Accius in the *Melanippus*: “What you say is not established, nor is there a place for saying what you are doing.”

### *R.R.; Ravillae; Porta Ratumena*

In many speeches the two letters **R. R.** are customarily written when the acts of someone are discussed [variant *disseritur cujuspiam*]. They mean *rationum relatarum*, “accounts rendered,” because by those tablets judges are shown what was publicly paid and received [variants *iis*]. [Col. 1649C]

*Ravillae* [main *Raviliae*] comes from gray-yellow eyes, just as *Caesullae* comes from blue-gray eyes.

The Ratumena Gate was named for a young man of distinguished Etruscan [variant *Etrusci*; main damaged *clarusci*] family. Victorious in a chariot contest, he was thrown from terrified horses at Veii [variant *Veiis*; main damaged *vehis*] and died at Rome. The horses reportedly did not stop before reaching the Capitol and seeing the clay chariot on Jupiter’s pediment. The Romans had contracted for it with a Veientine [variant *Veienti*; main *vegenti*] skilled in pottery. It had been recovered in war, because in the kiln it grew so large that it could not be removed. The prodigy seemed to portend that the city possessing it would become the most powerful of all.

### *Reciperatio; reciprocare; recellere; recinium*

Gallus Aelius says *reciperatio* occurs when a law is agreed between the Roman people and foreign kings, nations, and cities, establishing how property is to be returned and recovered through arbiters and how the parties may pursue private claims against one another. [Col. 1649D]

The ancients used *reciprocare* for asking back and forth, because *procare* means “to ask.” Pacuvius in the *Teucer* has a corrupt line: “Rapidly, reciprocally, violently, narrowly, to drive, straight … to move back and forth,” followed by a broken phrase about placing and fastening under laps. Plautus in the *Astraba*: “As though you were moving a lifting beam [variant *tollenonem*] or a Greek pestle back and forth on a level road.”

*Recellere* means to bend back; *excellere*, to raise on high. Those who interpreted the Twelve Tables said *recinium* was every square garment, a man’s toga [variant *virilem togam, qua*] which women used, bordered [variant feminine *praetextam*] with a purple stripe. The supplied chunk ends at page 85.
from which the *reciniati mimi planipedes* [“flat-footed actors wearing *recinia*] derive their name; Santra carefully discusses this matter in Book II of *On the Antiquity of Words*.

**Reconductae.** [The manuscript reading is *reconderit*.] He will have made again [*refecerit*], and “to found a city” means “to make” or “to build,” as Cincius attests in his *Book on Ancient Words*.

**Ricae** and **riculae** are small *ricinia*, that is, little cloaks made for use on the head. Granius indeed says that it is a woman’s headband, with which the Flaminica is bound instead of a fillet.

**Rectae** are called the men’s garments that fathers arrange to have made for their sons, as an omen. The term is used because they are woven upright and lengthwise, by people standing.

**Remancipata**, says Gallus Aelius, is a woman who has been mancipated by the man into whose *manus* she has entered.

**Rienes**, which we call kidneys, the ancients called *nefrundines*, because the Greeks call them νεφροί (*nephroi*). Plautus in *The Satyr*: “I see that things have gone badly for you; he was smooth as a kidney.”

**Refriva faba** [“refriva bean”; the note reads *faba*], says Cincius, is a bean that is customarily brought home from the field for a sacrifice, as though the crops were being called back home. Thus beans are taken from the wheat-field for the performance of a religious rite. Aelius is uncertain whether it is the bean that is carried into the field and brought back home, or one that is *refrigatur*, that is, roasted. Cincius’s view is supported by the fact that, in public sacrifices, when bean porridge is offered to the gods, it is called *refriva*.

**Remeare** means “to return,” just as *comeare* means “to go back and forth.” Hence *commeatus* is said of the time during which one may go and return. Afranius, in *The Emancipated Man* [the note reads *in Emancipato*]: “He forbade me to return to the school without payment,” [with the name *Paccius* or *Paucius*].

**Remeligines** and **remorae** are said to derive from *memorando* [the note reads *a morando*, “from delaying”]. Plautus in *The Dish*: “Why are those *remeligines* still delaying inside so wonderfully long?” Afranius in *The Betrayer*: “I have been sent as a *remeligo* from the household gods to this place, to check the ship’s course.”

**Remora**, or “delay,” is so called because it causes hindrance. Plautus in *The Trinummus*: “Those things which obstruct many affairs, and are hateful, cause delay to private and public business.” Lucilius: “What voice, resounding from you, causes delay in my progress?”

**Remurinus ager**, the Remurian field, was so called because it was occupied by Remus; Remus’s dwelling was likewise called *Remuria* on the Aventine. They say that Remus chose the Aventine as the place where he would live. Hence, they say, the place at the summit of the Aventine was called *Remuria*, where he had taken the auspices concerning the founding of the city. The same place was once called **Remorium** or **Remonium**, as a [lacuna] witness [lacuna].

**Remores** are also the birds in an augury that compel someone to delay an action [lacuna].

**Rimari** means “to search out thoroughly,” as in “also in the cracks” [lacuna], “the one who searches you out” [lacuna]. Ennius, Book XI [lacuna] “and the men” [lacuna].

**Remillum** is said to mean something like *repandum* [“bent backward”] [lacuna]. Lucilius [lacuna]. Suda [lacuna] *remilium*; and Afranius, in [lacuna]: “I shall stretch out along the hip” [lacuna].

**Remorbescat** seems to have been used by Ennius to mean “may he relapse into illness.”

**Refutare** means “to refute” or “to rebut.” Pacuvius in *Hermiona* [the note reads *Hermiona*] [lacuna] “which glory and [lacuna] human [lacuna]”

**Rictas** is composed from *fando* [“speaking”], with the letter *a* changed into *u*, just as happened in *caludo*, from which comes *recludere* [“to open”] [lacuna].

**Renanciscitur**, according to Verrius, means “he recovers” or “he regains.” Hence we still say *nanciscitur* and *nactus*, that is, “he obtains” or “having obtained.”

**Reor** means “I think” or “I judge,” and so do all the forms derived from it; their passive usage is authoritative.

**Remulco** is the act of dragging a large ship by oars from a small boat.

**Rigidum** signifies both “cold beyond measure” and “hard” [lacuna]. [The note reads *rigido* rather than *ugido*.] [lacuna] “with hard iron” [lacuna].

**Regifugium.** The day called *Regifugium* is marked in the calendars as the sixth day before the Kalends of March, as Verrius says. It was so called because King Tarquinius fled from Rome on that day. Cincius, in his *Book of Calendars*, argues that this is false, as does Julius in *On Festivals*. They say that the Salii and the virgins of the Salii attend the *Rex sacrorum* when he performs the sacrifice in the Comitium; immediately afterward he flees. This will be understood correctly by anyone who has read in the calendars the days marked in the following manner: **Q. REX. C. F.**, that is, “When the king has gone to the Comitium, it is permitted”—in other words, he goes to the Comitium. For only on these festival days is the *Rex sacrorum* permitted to go to the Comitium, and not on other days. This custom seems to have been adopted from Etruria.

The day called *Regifugium* is also marked in the calendars on the Kalends of June. Since that day is not wholly *nefastus*, it should be written with the sign **N'**, not **N.**, because the day changes from *nefastus* to *fastus*.

**Regia** was so called either because, for the sake of religious rites, those summoned by the Pontiff gathered there, or because the sacred rites of the *Rex sacrificulus* were customarily performed there.

**Regiae feriae** seem to be days observed in a city for the sake of courts, assemblies, and markets by a priest who possesses royal authority. They were not always held for this one reason alone, since the care of sacred majesty was also assigned to him when a lightning-struck place had to be purified or when a similar prodigy had to be expiated; on such occasions *Regiae feriae* were likewise customarily held.

When Plautus says **reglescit**, he means “increases,” in this verse: “I scarcely survive the pain that day by day, alas for wretched and ruined me, grows more and more.” Hence dormice (*glires*) also seem to have received their name, because their bodies increase with fat.

**Reapse** is the same as *re ipsa*. Pacuvius in *The Judgment of the Arms*: “If what I have done well is not unwelcome in reality.”

Poets use **regimen** for *regimentum*. Ennius, Book XVI: “The old man was the first [lacuna] skilled in the conduct of war.”

**Relegati** are properly those who, for the sake of disgrace or punishment, are required by law, a decree of the Senate, or an edict of a magistrate to remain away from the city of Rome or from some other place, as Gallus Aelius also indicates.

**Religiosus** is not only someone who highly reveres the sanctity of the gods, but also someone dutiful toward human beings. *Religious days* are those on which it is considered unlawful to do anything except what necessity requires. Among them are the thirty-six days called *Atri*, the Alliensian days [the note reads *et Alliensis*], and those on which the *mundus* is open.

Gallus Aelius says that something is **religiosum** when it is not permissible for a person to do it, so that, if he does do it, he seems to act against the will of the gods. Examples include a man’s entering the temple of Bona Dea; bringing a law before the people contrary to the law governing the auspices; and conducting legal proceedings before the praetor on a *nefastus* day.

He gives an excellent account of the differences among **sacred**, **sanctified**, and **religious**. A **sacred building** is one consecrated to a god. A **sanctified wall** is one surrounding a town. A **religious tomb** is one in which a dead person has been buried or interred; this, he says, is sufficiently clear.

Yet, in a certain respect and at certain times, the same thing may appear to possess all these qualities. What is sacred may also be considered sanctified by law or ancestral custom, so that it cannot be violated without penalty. It may likewise be religious, since it is something that a person is not permitted to do anything to; if he does so, he seems to act against the will of the gods. The same rule must be observed with a wall and a tomb, so that they may become simultaneously sacred, sanctified, and religious, in the manner explained above when we discussed sacred things.

**Repotia** are celebrated on the day after a wedding, when dinner is held at the new husband’s house, because the drinking is, as it were, renewed. Pacuvius in *Iliona*: “Driven away from the breast by him, [lacuna] receives [lacuna]; such [lacuna] is pleasing” [the note reads *repotialis*].

**Repagula**, says Verrius, are objects fixed in such a way that they may be removed to open something, whereas those fixed against them from the opposite side prevent opening. Cicero in *Against Verres*, Book IV: “After tearing out the bars and breaking the doors, they tried to demolish the statue and weaken it with crowbars.” Poets sometimes call these objects *repages*.

Verrius says **repudium** is so called because it is made on account of something shameful. Accius: “Rejected and cast out from Argos, I have long been an exile.”

**Repedare** means “to withdraw” or “to step back.” Pacuvius: “Step back a little, son, from the vestibule.”

**Repastinari ager** is the name given, according to Verrius, to land whose nature is changed by digging: woodland is cleared by excavation, or stony ground is softened by breaking, so that it may become suitable for pasture—whether for animals’ grass or for human cultivation. Cato, in the work he wrote *On His Own Virtues against Thermus*: “From the beginning I devoted all my youth to frugality, endurance, and industry; I occupied myself with cultivating the land, with the Sabine rocks, with breaking up and gathering flints.” Afranius in *The Rejected Man*: “The old man plants after breaking up the ground; you flee” [the note reads: “You, old man, sow after breaking it up”].

**Reluere** means “to redeem,” “to release,” or “to recover from a pledge.” Caecilius in *Carine*: “Let her redeem the gold and clothing that belonged to her mother, which, while alive, she herself had pledged.”

The ancients used **resignare** for “to write back” or “to reply in writing,” just as we still use *subsignare* for “to subscribe.” Cato, *On Spoils*, concerning the rule that nothing should be fixed in place except what had been captured from enemies: “But when they have been divided, let them return, with the tribute recorded again” [lacuna].

[lacuna]

**Resultare** often means “to spring back” or “to rebound.”

**Restibilis ager** is land that is sown continuously for two years with grain bearing an awn. Those who lease estates customarily stipulate that this must not be done.

**Reses** and **residuus** mean “sluggish” or “idle,” because such a person remains seated. Accius [lacuna]: “I hate the idle, devoted to sleep and inactivity.” Afranius in *The Rose*: “Besides, many idle men” [lacuna]. Pacuvius in *The Judgment of the Arms* [lacuna]: “And you would rather remain idle and wish yourself away, while we are here engaged in labor” [lacuna].

**Resecrare** means “to release from a religious obligation.” When a defendant had appealed to the people in the assembly by the gods to free him from the danger, the magistrates ordered him to perform *resecrare*. He would then persist in asking that they free him, arguing that he was innocent and guiltless and, above all, begging that they not set another day for him or decide to take action against him a second time. When the assembly had to be dismissed [lacuna].

[lacuna]

Plautus: “And I beseech you, mother, concerning what I had begged you earlier” [lacuna]. [The following fragment contains *resecror*, “I beseech again.”]

**Res conperendinata**, says Verrius, is a case scheduled for the third day.

Verrius says that **ravam vocem** means a hoarse, insufficiently clear voice, sounding almost like the barking of a dog. Hence a lawyer who spoke combatively was called a **rabula**, as in Lucilius [lacuna]. [The surviving fragment includes *travilla* and *ravistelli*.] We may prefer to say that these words derive from *ravi*, as in Plautus, who says in *The Pot of Gold*: “If we ask for anything, let us first ask for it until hoarse.” Elsewhere: “By Hercules, I shall clear everything out until I am hoarse.”

**Rosea** is the name of a plain in the territory of Reate, because its fields are always sown while moist with dew.

Cornificius says that the shrine of **Rediculus** stood outside the Capena Gate. It was called *Rediculus* because Hannibal, when approaching the city, turned back from that place after being frightened by certain apparitions.

Verrius says **reserari** is used of things that become open when the bar is removed from the door hinge; hence things that have been opened and unclosed are called *reserata*. The *serae* are not called the wooden bars placed against closed doors [the note reads: “for the wooden bars placed against closed doors are called *serae*”]. Pacuvius in *The Judgment of the Arms*: “Now open the doors, remove the bars, so that I may embrace him.”

**Remanant** means “flow back” [the note reads *revitant*, “return”], and **reptent** means “crawl” [the note reads *repetant*, “return/repeat”]. Ennius, Book I: “They forsake the streams and fields” [the note reads “they return to them”].

When we say **refert**, Verrius says that we are speaking incorrectly. The proper form is *rei fert*, with *rei* in the dative, not the ablative. But usage has now established the form.

**Ridiculus** properly means someone who is laughed at for disgraceful behavior.

## Book XVII of Sextus Pompeius Festus

## Book XVIII

**“I laugh,” says Galba, “at the packhorse.”** This is a proverb that Sinnius Capito interprets as applying to those who lose courage at the beginning of some undertaking. When Sulpicius Galba was leaving for his province and noticed that his packhorse had fallen at the very gate, he said: “I laugh at you, packhorse: you are already tired, though, since you are going to travel such a long road, you have scarcely begun it.”

**Retricibus.** When Cato says, in the work he wrote after delivering the review of the censorship of Fulvius Nobilior, he refers by this name to a watercourse above the Ardeatine Way, between the second and third milestone, by which the gardens below the Ardeatine and Asinarian Ways are irrigated as far as the Latin Way.

**Recepticius servus.** In Cato’s *Speech in Support of the Voconian Law*, the term refers to a slave returned because of a defect: “When she became angry, she ordered the man to pursue and demand back the defective slave.”

**Rogat** means “he consults the people” or “he asks them to vote for what he proposes.” Hence in ordinary usage we also use it for “to ask” and “to entreat.” Cato, in his speech opposing the repeal of the Baebian Law, says: “I shall rather do what this man asks.”

**Restat**, according to Ennius, is used for *distat*, “is distant,” in the following: “The attack is not far away in the regions between” [the note reads *Ennium* and *haud*].

One should say **ruri esse**, not *rure esse*. Terence attests this in *Phormio*, when he says: “He kept himself in the country; there was the field belonging to our father.”

For some people it is a matter of religious scruple to leave by the Carmental Gate and to hold the Senate in the temple of Janus outside it. For the three hundred and six Fabii who left by that gate were all killed at the Cremera, when the Senate’s decree ordering their departure had been made in the temple of Janus.

**Retiario.** When a net-fighter battles a *murmillo*, the following song is sung: “I am not seeking you; I am seeking the fish. Why do you flee me, Gaul?” The *murmillo*’s type of armor is Gallic, and the *murmillones* were formerly called Gauls; their helmets bore the image of a fish.

This type of combat seems to have been instituted by Pittacus, one of the Seven Sages. When he was about to fight Phrynon over a boundary dispute between the Athenians and the Mytilenaeans, he secretly carried a net and entangled Phrynon with it.

**Resignatum aes** is said of a soldier whose pay is entered in the records as withheld by order of the tribune of the soldiers because of some offense [the note reads: “so that his stipend is not paid”]. The ancients sometimes used *resignare* for “to write.”

The **Rituales** are called the books of the Etruscans in which it is prescribed by what ritual cities are to be founded, altars and temples consecrated, with what sanctity walls are to be protected, by what law gates are to be opened, and how tribes, curiae, and centuries are to be distributed and armies established and organized. They also contain other matters of this kind pertaining to war and peace.

**Rutilae canes**, that is, dogs not far removed from red in color, are sacrificed, according to Ateius Capito, in the *canarium* sacrifice, to avert the severity of the Dog Star for the sake of the crops.

Particular religious importance is assigned to **censorial majesty**. In his books *On the Life of the Roman People*, Varro offers the following examples:

When M. Fulvius Nobilior was made censor together with M. Aemilius Lepidus, although he had previously been very hostile to Lepidus and had often been involved in lawsuits with him, he immediately, once the office had been conferred, set aside his enmity toward the man for the sake of the state—a consideration that is regarded above all others. This judgment of his character was pleasing and approved by everyone.

When A. Postumius and Q. Fulvius were made censors, Fulvius had lost two sons while they were serving in Illyricum and, because of a serious disease of the eyes, could not perform the censorship. Postumius therefore advised that the Sibylline Books be consulted and that public supplication be offered for the health of his colleague.

When Ti. Sempronius’s censorial reputation was being undermined by Rutilius, a tribune of the plebs, Rutilius had become angry over a demolished wall belonging to a private house and had prosecuted his colleague Claudius on a fixed day. Sempronius arranged that the same centuries which had condemned him should acquit him.

The censorships of L. Aemilius Paulus and Q. Philippus were religiously exemplary. Paulus suffered from a serious illness and was nearly lost during his tenure.

That of P. Cornelius Scipio Nasica was likewise exemplary. His colleague was M. Popilius [lacuna]. Although he had stood surety, it is established that he was released by the Roman people.

M. Valerius Messala and C. Cassius Longinus were censors whose moral authority had been overturned during their magistracy, and they became notorious. For it is said that a palm tree which had sprung up during the Persian War on the Capitol, on the very altar of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, was then found lying overturned; and a fig tree that had grown there made notorious once again those censors who had acted without any regard for moral integrity.

The censorship of L. Cornelius Lentulus and C. Censorinus follows. Lentulus had been convicted in a public trial for extortion. Many therefore, after obtaining the censorship, remitted the penalty of his condemnation.

The censorship of P. Africanus and L. Mummius was notable, though Mummius was marked by sluggishness in carrying out his duties. He removed Asellus from the *aerarii* without imposing any penalty, to the ridicule of Africanus’s severity, since Africanus had made him an *aerarius*.

The censorship of Q. Fulvius Nobilior and his colleague Appius Claudius was also exceptionally distinguished, because the nobility was branded with three extremely severe marks.

In the censorship of Q. Pompeius and Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus, the Senate was reviewed; only three senators were removed, men of such distinction that they might have overshadowed the brilliance of others.

**Redinunt** means “they return.” Ennius [lacuna]: “They return to their homeland” [lacuna].

**Regium** is what belongs or belonged to a king, as in “royal slave” and “royal house,” such as the house of Numa Pompilius. **Regale facinus**, however, is an action worthy of a king.

In Book XI, Ennius calls the Romans **Greeks**, when he says: “They contend [lacuna]; they are accustomed to call themselves Greeks, Graii” [lacuna]. “Because the Greek language, over long stretches of time, [lacuna] Spaniards” [lacuna; the note reads *Hos pavi*].

He does not mean that the Romans spoke Greek, since Romulus, the founder of the city, spoke in the words of the Latin language. Rather, he means that in former times the language of the Greek people was the same as Latin, differing only slightly in pronunciation. Its origin seems to indicate that this is true, since it appears to be a Greek usage. 

**Rigido tum caerula suro.** When Ennius says this, he seems to be playing upon the etymology of the word *caerulus* [“blue”]. It derives from the word for the sea [the note reads *maris*]. He uses the same word with the same meaning in Book II: “He carries himself through the blue meadows of the cheerful fields.” He called the sea itself *caerula* elsewhere: “From there they traveled by ship through the blue sea” [the note reads *ambullabant*]. He is referring to the island of Paros.

Likewise: “One *surus* can nevertheless carry a *surus* and defend [it]” [the note reads *possent*]. *Suri* are rustic staffs [the note reads *fustes*], and *surculi* is their diminutive.

**Reque eapse.** Scipio Africanus, son of Paullus, used this compound expression in his speech *Before the Temple of Castor*: “I have often deserved well of these men, in many places, by my efforts, actions, counsels, and by the matter itself, and I have often [lacuna] hope” [the note reads *siem*], that is, “and in reality itself.”

C. Gracchus used **res publicae**, in the plural, in the work he wrote *On the Law of P. Ennius* [the note reads *Penni*] and foreigners, when he says: “Those nations, through greed and folly in other matters, lost their own states.”

**Recto fronte ceteros sequi si norit** means “if he knows how to follow the others with a straight brow”; Cato uses it in his *Speech on the Consulship*. This was an ancient usage, as Ennius also says: “From the highest stock”; “On that day, the grandson”; “A she-wolf pregnant”; and “No fear.” The pontifical commentaries likewise frequently contain such expressions as *hic ovis* [“this sheep,” masculine] and *haec agnus* [“this lamb,” feminine], and *porcus* [“pig”]. We should regard these not as errors but as evidence of ancient usage.

**Recipie** occurs in Cato for *recipiam*, “I shall receive,” as do many other forms of this kind.

**Redemptitavere**, like *clamitavere*. Cato, in the speech he delivered *On Statues and Paintings*: “They tried to purchase honor” [the note reads *emptitavere*], “and did not redeem evil deeds with good deeds” [the note reads *malefacta*].

**Repulsior**, in a second comparison, Cato used in his speech *Against Cornelius before the People*: “Who is more uncultivated, more scrupulous, more deserted, more rejected from public affairs?” [the note reads *Ecquis*].

**Ratissima** likewise derives from the forms we call *rata* [“settled” or “valid”], from which *rationes* also comes. Cato, in [the speech] against Thermus [the note reads “Q. M.,” that is, Minucius]: “Toward the republic, many benefits, most firmly established and most welcome.”

**Regillis** are white tunics and yellow netted garments, both [lacuna], woven vertically from standing threads. Virgins put them on and went to bed on the day before their wedding, as an omen; the same practice is observed when men are given the toga virilis.

A maiden is symbolically **carried off** from her mother’s lap—or, if her mother is absent, from her nearest relative—when she is handed over to her husband [the note reads *traducitur* or *trahitur*], because this event turned out favorably for Romulus.

The **torch** by whose light the new bride is led is customarily snatched away by the friends of both parties. This is done so that either the wife may not place it beneath her husband’s bed that night or the husband may not arrange for it to be burned in a tomb; in either case, it is thought that the death of one of the two is being sought.

**Ritus** is an approved custom in the administration of sacrifices.

**Receptus mos** is a custom that a community has adopted voluntarily from elsewhere.

**Religiosi** are those who exercise discernment, according to the custom of the community, in performing or omitting religious acts and who do not entangle themselves in superstitions.

**Renovativum fulgur** is the name given to a renewal of lightning when, after some lightning has occurred, a similar bolt appears that signifies the same thing.

To **referre diem prodictam**, that is, to move a proclaimed day earlier, is a religious offense, as Veranius says in his work on the auspices concerning assemblies. He confirms this by the example of the censors L. Julius and P. Licinius, who did this without any decree of the augurs, and for that reason the *lustrum* was not very successful.

**Regalia exta** are the entrails that promise an unexpected honor to powerful men; to private and humble people, inheritances; and to a son still under paternal authority, mastery.

**Respicere avem** is used in taking the auspices when someone returns to the place from which he observed a bird.

Everything that is a temple or shrine is both **religious and sacred**, and such places are also called consecrated. But something may be religious in itself without necessarily being sacred, as with tombs, since tombs are religious, not sacred.

**Reus**, when used for either party, as Sinnius says in the work he entitled *On the Defendant*, may refer to someone speaking on his own behalf or acting against another; he may use the other person’s oath.

People who are perfectly accomplished in every art are commonly called **Roscii**, just as the comic actor Roscius was perfect in his own art, lacking nothing required for excellence, as Cicero says in Book I of *On the Orator*.

The **Rustic Vinalia**, held in August according to the calendars, were celebrated for Venus, because a temple of that goddess had been consecrated on that same day. Draft animals and market gardeners ceased work, because all gardens are said to be under Venus’s protection.

Verrius says that those called **rauci** appear to derive their name from dryness or from a certain resemblance to the awn of an ear of grain. For Verrius also teaches that, in ears of grain, yellow grain is called *rava*.

A **rica** is a square, fringed, purple garment that the Flamini­cae used instead of a small cloak or a head covering, according to Verrius. Titinius: “Clad in a *rica* of raw, white wool.” Others say that it is a triple cloak made by freeborn maidens whose parents are both alive, dyed blue, and washed in pure water. Others say it is the garment with which the Flaminica wraps her cap.

A bird was called **respici** when, after the sacrifice had been completed—as though the desired outcome had been obtained and the assembly completed—the priests ordered the *reus* to be taken up according to their custom. After the other rites had been completed in the sacred grove where they were performed, the *reus*, kneeling and bent forward by the *calatores*, had wine poured over his head with a solemn prayer.

With the army **dismissed**, the augur whom the consul had used in taking the auspices during the war is also ordered to depart. Once he has departed, it is certain that the army too has been dismissed, so that, when necessary, it may depart whenever it wishes. For, as Appius Pulcher says, consuls and censors do not make permanent use of the presence of the augurs, but only during the taking of the auspices. The augur is then dismissed by the person from whom the legal axes had previously been received. Antistius Labeo says that this person is also the prior one, and that the same law indicates that he is first in taking the auspices, as Labeo says in his *Book on the Office of the Augur*.

An augur may perform this act in the council or in another place where he is seated. When the chickens are eating their mash, he takes the auspices only there. If he wishes, he may do so within the *pomerium*; otherwise he takes his position in the temple.

**Repertum** means the same as recovering something lost, as though from *repartum* and *reparatum*.

**Rictus**, **rixae**, and **rixosae**, as well as **ringitur**, seem to derive from the idea that things are split apart in opposite directions and are contrary to what is straight. The word may more suitably appear to derive from *regere*, “to direct.”

**Sesopia** are called, in the Augural and Salian hymn, what we otherwise call *esopia*, meaning “seats”; the word remains in use today.

**Susque deque** is frequently used for “more or less.” It signifies what the ancients were accustomed to express with *usque*.

**Sonivio**, in the Salian and Augural hymn, means “sounding” or “resounding.”

**An inheritance without sacred obligations** is a proverbial expression used when something comes to a person without any troublesome appendage. In former times people administered not only public but also private sacred rites with the greatest care, and an heir who inherited money also inherited the sacred obligations; it was therefore necessary to administer them with the utmost diligence.

The ancients said **suppum** for what we now call *supinum*, evidently substituting the letter *s* for the aspiration of the Greek form, just as they say *hylas* where we say *silvas*; likewise Greek ἕξ, “six,” and ἑπτά, “seven.” Lucilius also mentions the word: “If you give what he asks, and if you offer it, supine.”

The **Sempronian granaries** were a place where, under the law of Gracchus, public grain was stored and guarded.

A **statua** is the statue of that *ludio* [the note reads *ludionis*] who was once struck by lightning in the Circus and buried on the Janiculum. Later, in response to prodigies and oracular answers, the Senate decreed that his bones be brought inside the city and buried in the Volcanal, above the Comitium. A column bearing his likeness was placed over them.

The **Servilian Lake** was named after the man who had arranged for it to be made. It stood at the beginning of the Vicus Jugarius, adjoining the Basilica Julia. In that place M. Agrippa set up an image of a hydra.

**Sonticus morbus**, in the Twelve Tables, means a genuine illness accompanied by a legitimate cause, as Aelius Stilo says. Some think it is an illness that causes harm, since *sontes* means “harmful” or “guilty.” Naevius says: “The cause must be a genuine one, on account of which you destroy the woman.”

Some think the **Sacred Way** was so called because a treaty was concluded on it between Romulus and Tatius. Others think it was so called because priests used that route when preparing sacred objects. It should therefore not be called the Sacred Way only, as the common people suppose, from the Regia to the house of the *Rex sacrificulus*, but also from the house of the *Rex* to the shrine of Strenia, and again from the Regia to the Citadel. Verrius says that it should not be written as one word, but separately, like the other roads—Flaminia, Appia, and Latina—so that it should not be *Novamviam* but *Novam viam*.

**Scita plebis** are the measures that the plebs enacted by its own vote without the patricians, when proposed by a plebeian magistrate.

**Solitaurilia** signify the sacrifice of three victims of different kinds: a bull, a ram, and a boar. They are so called because all are whole and sound in body, unlike [the note reads *contrari*] [lacuna] wethers [the note reads *verveces*] and boars [the note reads *maiales*]. In Oscan, *sollum* means “whole” and “solid.” Hence certain weapons are called *soliferrea*, entirely made of iron; a person skilled in the liberal arts is *sollers*; and things that are not loosened or hollow in any part are called *solida*, “solid.”

Among these victims the bulls are entirely uninjured [the note reads *caeditur*, “is slaughtered”], specifically in the part involved in castration. Some think that the name is derived especially from the solid bull, since it is the largest of the three victims. Others have said that the names of all three—*sus*, *ovis*, and *taurus*—were combined to produce a single designation for the group as a whole.

If the name is derived from *sollum* and *tauri*, referring to these victims, it is not surprising that it is pronounced with a single *l*, according to ancient usage, since at that time no letter was doubled in writing. Ennius is said to have changed this practice, being a Greek who followed Greek usage, because the Greeks, both in writing and in reading, doubled mute, semivowel, and liquid consonants.

**Secordia** was used by some for “idleness.” M. Cato used it for “stupidity” in Book VII of the *Origines*, when he says: “[lacuna] the cause was excessive cowardice and stupidity, so that no public or private business was conducted.”

The formation of **semis**, **semimodius**, and **semuncia** is comparable to other words derived from Greek in which our letter *s* represents their aspiration [lacuna], such as ἑπτά, *septem*, and ὕλαι, *silvae*. These forms likewise seem to derive from the Greek term ἥμισυ, “half.”

Some think that the **Sublician Bridge** was named from *sublices*, a special Volscian word for beams extended across their width. The Formians call such beams by the same name as books. Other writers call them *sublices* because flowing water passes beneath them. This was the opinion of [lacuna], who also mentions the Sublician Bridge; and of Naevius, who says in Book [lacuna] of the *Punic War*: “[lacuna] crosses the flowing river at the Sublician Bridge,” and elsewhere [the note reads *ab*] “from the planks,” which still preserve the name [lacuna]. Sallustius, in Book IV of his *Histories*: “[lacuna] of the Sublician Bridge” [lacuna]. “[lacuna] hollowed out with *sublices*” [lacuna].

**Supervacaneum**, as Verrius seems to think, is distinguished from *vacuus*, “empty.” Something is called *vacuus* only when it is sufficient and adequate for a household; what exceeds that amount is called *supervacaneum*, “superfluous.”

The ancients called **strufertarii**, according to [lacuna], hired men who, in expiation of offenses committed at trees struck by lightning, performed certain sacrifices of *strua* [the note reads *strue*] and *fertum* with the traditional formula: “I beseech you, Jupiter, that you be willing and favorable toward me.” The rite could also be performed without a *strufertarius*.

**Suberies** is a kind of tree from which bark used for swimming is stripped. Lucilius [lacuna] “of the winter shelter” [lacuna].

**Silicernium** is a funeral meal, which writers call by another name *exsequium*. But [lacuna] and Verrius think that *silicernium* is what we call a *farcimen* [“sausage”], by which the family was cleansed of mourning; for the person in whose name the rite was instituted would already be “seeing silence.” Caecilius, in *The Obolostater*: “I believed I would eat his funeral meal.”

Verrius says **sudum** means *subudum*, “somewhat damp.” But almost all examples from the authorities require *sudus* to mean “dry.” *Sudum* is formed as though from *se-udum*, “without moisture,” just as *securus*, “free from care,” is formed from *sine cura*, “without care.”

The ancients called **sublesta** weak and insubstantial. Plautus in *The Persian*: “To”

If disgrace attaches itself to poverty, poverty becomes more grievous and credit less secure—that is, weaker. In the *Nervelaria* he likewise calls wine *sublestissimum* (“very weak”), because it makes people weak either in body or in spirit.

*Satur* (“full”), *vir* (“man”), and *caro* (“flesh”) do not have [the expected form].

In the nominative case, *supellex*, and in the genitive, *supellectilis*, were said in a manner that now seems contrary to the rule of formation [Note: [Col. 1659] “proportion”], since all words ending in the letter *x* acquire a syllable through the oblique cases. These two words, however, depart from that rule, as do several others [Note: [Col. 1659] “many others”]; this should not therefore invalidate the principle.

Verrius most absurdly says that *scurra* (“buffoon”) is derived either from Greek, namely *σκιρτάζειν* [Note: [Col. 1659] Greek: *σκιρτᾶζειν*, “to leap”], or from *sequendo* (“following”), a derivation to which he is more inclined. People of humble fortune, and others who followed someone as a mark of honor, were accustomed not to precede but to follow him. Thus Lucilius says:

> Our Cornelius, son of Publius, a Scipio by name,  
> bends time itself toward idleness and delights,  
> toward painted lights, the catamite,  
> and even toward his own Follower—  
> so that you may more correctly say:  
> “He happened to be going home; many of us followed,  
> in a crowd and in full numbers,”

since he wants them to appear to have followed because of their quarrels, not because of their customary service.

**Page 105**

*Secus* (“otherwise”): Valgius thinks it comes from the Greek *ἑκάς* (“far off”), absurdly enough, for the examples of nearly all who use the word plainly show a different meaning.

*Stipe* (“with a coin”): that it means stamped money is shown both by the money given as a soldier’s pay and by the fact that, when money is promised, this is called *stipulari* (“to stipulate”).

*Sobrinus* (“cousin”) is, as Gallus Aelius says, the son of my father’s cousin or the son of my mother’s cousin. A woman, for the same reasons, uses the terms “brother,” “paternal cousin,” “cousin,” *propius consobrinus* [Note: [Col. 1659] *sobrinus*, “cousin”], and “female cousin.” The same degrees of relationship exist among female cousins as well.

A *sororium tigillum* (“Sister’s Beam”) is so called for the following reason. By agreement between King Tullus Hostilius and Mettius Fufetius [Note: [Col. 1659] Mettius Suffetius], leader of the Albans, the three Horatii and the three Curiatii [Note: [Col. 1659] Curiatii] fought, so that whichever side won would possess the supreme power. Our Horatius prevailed and returned home victorious. His sister, meeting him and learning that her betrothed had been killed by her brother’s hand, turned away from his kiss. For this reason Horatius killed her. Although his father released him from the charge of the crime, he was nevertheless accused of parricide before the duumvirs, condemned, and appealed to the people. By their judgment he was victorious: he passed beneath two beams, with a third laid across the top, which his father had set up, as though sent beneath a yoke. After altars had been consecrated there to Juno Sororia and Janus Curiatius, he was freed from all guilt for the crime, with the auspices approving it. From this the beam was called the *sororium tigillum*.

The breasts of girls are called *sororiae* [Note: [Col. 1659] *sororiare*] when they first begin to swell, just as boys’ breasts are called *fraterculare*. Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*:

**Page 106**

> Then the little breasts began to resemble sisters;  
> but I meant to say, they began to resemble brothers.  
> What need is there for many words?

*Surrexit* (“he rose”) and *sortus* were used by the ancients for *surrexit*, and its participle as though it were *surrectus*. L. Livius [Note: [Col. 1659] Livius] frequently used these forms.

*Sors* (“lot”) also means patrimony, whence we say *consortes* (“joint heirs”), and it means the answer or outcome that falls to each person in the drawing of lots.

*Soracum* is the name of the object on which theatrical costumes are carried. Plautus says in the *Persa*:

> I have a little bookcase full of books and a *soracum*.

Some think that the *Sobrius Vicus* (“Sober Street”) was so called by Cloatius and Aelius because there was no room in it for a tavern or an inn. Others say it was because Mercury was customarily worshiped there with wine, not milk.

*Sonivium* is a *tripudium* (“auspicious feeding-omen”), according to Appius Pulcher, because it makes a sound when more than [the expected amount] falls from the beak of a chicken or from the mouth of a four-footed animal [Note: [Col. 1659] *puls*, “porridge”].

*Sons* means “guilty,” just as *insons* means “innocent.”

Some think that *sodales* (“companions”) were so called because they sat together and were together. Others think it was because they customarily ate food from their own provisions. Others, because they advised one another about what was useful. The same people think that, because they frequently come together and assemble, they are called *congerae* [Note: [Col. 1659] *congeras*], from the Greek word *γέρρα*.

*Sodes* means “if you please,” from *si audes* (“if you dare”), and *illico* means “on the spot,” from *in loco*. Terence says in the *Andria*:

> Tell me, please, who had Chrysis yesterday?

**Page 107**

They used *surus* (“stake”) for the word from which *surculus* (“small stake”) was formed by diminutive derivation. Plautus says in [the *—*]:

> You have no *surus*.

They also called a stake *surus*. Since the Circus was enclosed with small stakes, they selected a long *surus* and then shaped it with an axe [lacuna]. Ennius says:

> One *surus* could carry another *surus* and still defend [it].

*Surremit* means “he took up.” He likewise says:

> And into his hand he took up the spear.

He also used *surempsit* for “he appropriated,” as in “he took up the boy.”

*Surium* [lacuna]. He said that it was so called because, when he excelled the noblest men both in the Academy and in the Lyceum and had therefore always been regarded as pre-eminent, he established that, whenever a discussion took place, the person who was more worthy than he should be chosen first. Hence [lacuna] he called him *σκύριον καὶ οὐκέτι σύριον* (“Scyrion and no longer Syrion”), because, had he been warned, he sometimes refuted Socrates in debate—arguments that he had collected in a book he wrote and entitled *Scyrius*, after the person for whose sake he had given the work that name.

They called *summussi* (“murmurers”) those who muttered. Naevius says, “I hate *summussi*.” Thus he clearly explains what it is that you fear. Ennius says in the sixth book of the *Annals*:

> Quintus was muttering secretly.

Accius says in the *Andromacha*:

> Speak—the mother is no longer here;  
> for now [Note: [Col. 1659] *jam*] muttering is unnecessary.

Caecilius says in the *Anagnorizomene* [Note: [Col. 1659] *Anagnorizomene*]:

**Page 108**

> What you can, be silent, conceal, hide away, cover up, keep quiet, mutter, remain still.

*Sum* was used by Ennius for “him.” In Book I:

> But you ought not to preserve the whole matter as he does [Note: [Col. 1659] “the highest”].

And in Book II:

> But himself he, whom he had given, from the borders of light [lacuna].

The Oscan word *sollō* means what we call “whole.” Lucilius says:

> Even the vessels altogether separate no *sollō* of two asses;

that is, “not the whole” [Note: [Col. 1661] *solla*, “whole”]. Livy uses it likewise.

*Sollicuria* means “careful in every matter” [Note: [Col. 1661] “curious”].

*Solliferreum* is a kind of weapon made entirely of iron.

*Sollers* also means “wise in every matter.”

*Sollemne* means what must be performed every year.

Seats are called *solla* [Note: [Col. 1661] *solia*], on which no more than one person can sit; hence those who spread such seats are said to *soliare sternere*. These are called *sollisternia*, and Babylonian *solaria* are likewise named for coverings spread in the same way. Verrius says that all these words derive from *solium* (“seat”). Hollow basins constructed for washing, into which individuals descend, are also called *solla*. They seem, however, to have been named from ascending [Note: [Col. 1661] from sitting] rather than from *solum* [Note: [Col. 1661] *sollum*, “floor”].

Ap. Pulcher says in Book I of his *Augural Discipline* that a *sollistimum* is a *tripudium* in which either [Note: [Col. 1661] a bird] falls out of what the bird is carrying, or a solid stone, or a living-rooted tree falls—objects that neither on account of a defect nor through human force have been cut down, thrown down, or pushed away [Note: [Col. 1661] “or by human force”].

*Solum* means “earth” or “ground.” Ennius says in Book III:

> He gave Tarquin both the kingship and the ground of the kingdom.

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1661] “elsewhere”]:

> But after he had traversed for a while the ground of the lands.

According to Verrius, *solea* is not only what is placed beneath the sole of the foot, but also a piece of strong wood [Note: [Col. 1661] “strong”] upon which a wattle wall is built.

*Solox* means coarse wool, and an animal that grazes everywhere in the open, without shelter. Titinius says in the *Barbatus* [Note: [Col. 1661] *Barbatus*]:

> From coarse wool to purple cloth I have given [it].

Lucilius says:

> With pastoral and mountain cattle, shaggy and coarse.

The ancients used *sos* for *eos* (“them”), as Ennius says in Book I:

> Then the goddess of the gods stood near that place beside them.

In Book III:

> And around them are great and wealthy nations.

In Book VII:

> While they think to terrify them less, or encourage them.

In Book XI:

> They strive to call them Greeks; they usually remember the Greeks.

At times they used it for *suos* (“their own”), as when the same Ennius expresses it with the dative case:

> After good Ancus left the light of his eyes.

*Sultis* means *si vultis* (“if you wish”). Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*:

> Follow me this way, if you please, all the legions of Laverna.

And in the *Rudens*:

> Take care of these matters with the greatest diligence, if you please.

M. Cato, speaking for L. Caesetius, says:

> Listen, soldiers, if you please. If any of you survives the war, if anyone has not found money, he will be in need.

The ancients are shown to have used *solari* (“to console”) without a preposition by Pacuvius, who says:

> He consoles me, helps me, and encourages me.

*Solatum* is the name generally given by country people to a kind of disease, which Afranius also mentions in [lacuna]:

> To cure the *solatum* [lacuna],

whose name derives from *aurigo* [Note: [Col. 1661] *aurigo*].

*Solipunga* is a kind of harmful little creature, which becomes more violent and active through the sun’s heat, from which it takes its name.

*Sospes* means “safe” in nearly all authors. Afranius says in the *Epistola*:

> May the gods keep you safe for your own people.

Vergil, Book VIII of the *Aeneid*:

> Greatest leader of the Teucrians, while you are safe, never [shall this happen].

Ennius in [lacuna]:

> Gods, preserve the father and the fatherland safe.

Accius in [lacuna]:

> If he had safely reached his homeland in due form.

Ennius seems to use *sospes* in the sense of “savior” when he says:

> While he is safe, I am free.

Verrius says that *sospitare* means “to inspire with good hope” or “not to disappoint a good hope.”

*Succrotilla* was said of a thin, high-pitched voice. Titinius in [lacuna]:

> To speak in a feminine, shrill little voice.

Afranius in the *Epistola*:

> He was speaking seriously in a shrill voice.

Plautus, describing women’s slender legs in the *Syro*:

> With ankles twisted outward, with little legs like little companions [Note: [Col. 1661] *todellis*], beautifully formed,  
> so that they would not walk on their feet.

A *sucula* is a kind of machine made of round, bored, thick material. Just as piglets surround a sow’s udder and turn it by pulling on a hauling rope, so it is operated. The same name is given to the five stars which are otherwise called the Hyades because of rain. The Greeks call them *Ὑάδες*. Since our people thought they were named from *sus* (“pig”), they called them *Suculae* in Latin speech [Note: [Col. 1661] “in the manner of speaking, they called them”].

The ancients called a belt *succingulum*. Plautus says:

> From Hippolyta he took Hercules’ belt,  
> though by no means without great danger.

*Succerda* meant pig manure [lacuna]: “succerda manure.” Titinius says:

> What do you have except a single chest without a key?  
> Into it you store *succerdae*.

By another name *succerda* is called *opicerda* [lacuna]. “An *opicerda* man” [lacuna] means a man whom the sun sees among the *opicerdae*.

The Suburan tribe was formerly called the Succisana [Note: [Col. 1661] Succusana], with a *c*, from the name of the district; for they also report that the lower part of that district was called Succusana. Verrius, however, says he was surprised that it was not named from the village of the Succusani, where soldiers used to train.

A *succidanea hostia* (“substitute victim”) is the victim slaughtered second, so called because it is, as it were, cut down after another. Some think it was named from *succedere* (“to follow”), not *succidere* (“to cut down”).

Some think that *sugillatum* (“a bruise”) derives from a Greek word, because that part beneath the neck is called by them *κύλον*.

Some think that *sycophantae* (“sycophants”) were so called for the following reason. They say that certain Attic youths were once accustomed to break into the gardens of others and strip off their figs. A law was therefore enacted [Note: [Col. 1661] “provided”] that whoever did this should be punished capitally [Note: [Col. 1661] “with a capital penalty”]. Those who prosecuted such offenders over petty losses were called *sycophants*.

**Page 112**

*Sulci* (“furrows”) are the lines along which a plow is drawn, whether for sowing, founding a city, or digging a straight-sided trench in which trees are planted. The track left by lightning is similarly called a *sulcus*. Some think the word was formed from the Greek *ὁλκόν* (“a furrow”).

*Suasum* is the name of a color produced by a smoky drip on a white garment. Plautus says:

> Because, shameless woman, you stained your little cloak with *suasum*.

Some, however, read *in suaso* (“in the *suasum*”), and there are others who say that every color produced by dyeing is called *suasum*, because it is, as it were, persuaded to pass from white into another color [Note: [Col. 1663] “is made to pass”].

Gallus Aelius defines *saltus* in Book II of *Meanings Pertaining to Law* as follows:

> A *saltus* is a place where there are woods and pastures, for whose sake there are also huts. If some portion of that *saltus* is plowed for the sake of shepherds or guards, that fact does not destroy its name as a *saltus*, any more than a farm situated in cultivated land loses its name as a farm because it contains a building for its use, even if some portion of it has woodland.

*Superescit* means “will remain.” Ennius says:

> So long as even one Roman remains in the toga [Note: [Col. 1663] “at Rome”].

Accius says in the *Chrysippus*:

> Indeed, if he remains here [Note: [Col. 1663] “if”], I hand over Sparta and Amyclae.

By itself *super* means “above,” as when we say, “he yields above him” [Note: [Col. 1663] “he sat above him”]. But, following Greek usage, it is also used for *de* (“about”), as the Greeks use *ὑπέρ*. Plautus says in the *Miles Gloriosus*:

> Through my efforts concerning this neighbor whom I am now arranging for you.

In the *Phasma*:

> At last I understand that you are speaking about our affairs.

Pacuvius says in the *Medus*:

> Concerning what matter did you say that Hippotes was killed?

Cato, against Annius:

> No one before now has dealt with this magistrate about such a matter.

Afranius says in the *Virgo*:

> You began with other matters, about [Note: [Col. 1663] *re*, “the matter”].

The *supercilium* (“eyebrow”) is what is above the *cilium* (“eyelid”), that is, the upper covering of the eye.

Enemies are said to be *sub iugum missi* (“sent beneath the yoke”) when, after all their arms and weapons have been taken away, they are ordered to pass beneath two spears fixed in the ground, with a third tied across their tops.

Ennius used *subices* for *subjecti* (“placed beneath”) when he said in the *Achilles*:

> Through the gods I [lacuna] moist clouds placed beneath, from which rain arises with dreadful sound and rushing breath.

*Superstites* [Note: [Col. 1663] “those present”] means “present witnesses.” Evidence of this is that, when the witnesses are present, the parties to a dispute are ordered to take possession of the disputed property. Plautus says in the *Artemo*:

> Now I may say whatever I wish; no witness is present here.

In ordinary usage [Note: [Col. 1663] “ordinary custom”], it is used for those who are more than sufficient.

Surviving children are also called *superstites* in relation to their parents [lacuna]. For this reason I would wish to continue living longer, although I would wish all my children to survive me.

The augurs call a bird *supervaganea* when it gives its cry from the very top of a summit, because it is, as it were, wandering in the highest regions and above everything; hence the name.

They thought that the eyebrows were under Juno’s protection. Women are said to possess them in particular because the eyes, through which we enjoy the light granted by Juno, are protected by them. Hence the goddess herself also seems to have been called Lucina.

Those are called *suppernati* whose thighs have been cut in the manner of a pig’s hams. Ennius says in the *Annals* [Note: [Col. 1663] “these”]:

> He cut off the hams in the unjust pride of the Carthaginian.

Catullus says to Colonia:

> Ligarius lies in the ditch, his thigh cut through by an axe.

*Suppremum* sometimes means “highest,” as when he says:

> Father, highest in war, and Mars, powerful in arms.

Plautus says:

> You have always regarded me as supreme in your affairs.

At other times it means “last,” as in the Twelve Tables:

> Sunset shall be the final time.

[Lacuna] “with your final crime.” Hence we say that someone is buried on his final day [lacuna]. And:

> As mourners, with their faces turned toward the final hour [lacuna].

Cato, concerning [lacuna], says that he had never denied a defendant before the praetor the final plea [lacuna]. Elsewhere *suppremum* means “greatest,” as when they called two sheep and thirty oxen the greatest fine.

**Page 115**

*Subsidium* (“reserve support”) was said of soldiers who took position in the rear line and came to the aid of a wavering line. This class of soldiers consisted of those who had completed their service but nevertheless retained their place in the army. It was the third line, that of the *triarii*, as Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*:

> Come now, all of you take your places in reserve, as the *triarii* [Note: [Col. 1663] *triarii*] customarily do.

In the same way those stationed before them, or assigned to another position, were called *praesidiarii* (“support troops”).

Things that are *subsolaneae* are called those that concern the lowest ground, and the term does not apply only to the name of one particular thing. Those who cultivate the lowest soil are called *subsolanei*, as are those who work the earth; those above are *supersolanei*. From this comes *solidum*, meaning the bottom layer of soil, upon which the sole of the foot rests.

*Subsilles*, otherwise called *ipsilles* [Note: [Col. 1663] *ipsulices*], are thin plates necessary for sacrifices, said to be especially useful for the sacred rite, in the form of male and female figures.

The ancients called *substillum* the time before rain, when the ground was already almost wet, and after rain, when it was not yet completely dry—when it was still dripping or had not yet ceased to drip [Note: [Col. 1663] “had not yet ceased”].

*Subscudes* are called all wedge-shaped tablets [Note: [Col. 1663] “wedge-shaped”] by which boards are fastened together, because the place into which they are inserted is struck from below. Pacuvius says in the *Niptrae*:

> No *subscus* holds the join of the basin together.

Plautus says in the *Astraba*:

> Let it be thoroughly bored, and add *subscudes*.

Those who are said to “come beneath the crown” are so called because captives customarily come crowned. Cato says in his work *On Military Matters*:

> So that his own people, for a deed well done, may go crowned to offer supplication rather than come crowned after a deed badly done [Note: [Col. 1663] “come”].

This is a sign that nothing is being granted by the people [Note: [Col. 1663] “by anyone”]. Plautus likewise indicates this in the *Hortulus*:

> Let the herald be present there with a crown; let anyone who wishes come [Note: [Col. 1663] “come”].

*Sublime* means “raised to a height.” Ennius says in the *Thyestes*:

> Look upon this shining height, which everyone calls Jupiter.

Vergil says in Book I of the *Georgics*:

> Here the summit is always lofty for us [Note: [Col. 1665] “sublime”].

*Cato* used *sublimavit* [Note: [Col. 1665] “Cato”], meaning “he raised on high,” in Book II of the *Origines*:

> He raised him to the greatest honor and the most exalted renown.

The word is said to derive from the upper threshold, because that is above us.

*Subcenturiare* means to fill out a century by supplying or substituting men. Plautus says in the *Saturio*:

> A substitute century of a hundred—look for someone at home who will delight you.

Caecilius says in the *Triumphus*:

> Now my military stratagem requires a substitute century [Note: [Col. 1665] “a substituted century”].

Kids are said to *subrumari* (“suckle beneath”) when they are brought to the teat, because it was called a *rumis* [Note: [Col. 1665] “it was called a *rumis*”], or because they draw the *rumina* while sucking milk.

A *subulo* is called a flute player in Tuscan. Thus Ennius says:

> Once a flute player stood beside the sea-shores.

Verrius says in another book that *Subura* was named from the village of the Succusani. He supports this especially by the authority of those who say that both the district of the city and the tribe were so called from a permanent military post that used to come to the aid of the Esquiline when the Gabines attacked that part of the city. Proof is provided by the fact that even now the tribe is written with the letter *c*, not *b*.

*Subverbusta* means “burned by blows,” as Plautus says:

> Ulcerated, shackled, beaten, filthy.

*Suboles* (“offspring”) comes from *olescere*, “to grow,” just as *adolescens* (“young man”), *adultus* (“grown”), and *indoles* (“nature, character”) do. Lucretius says in Book V:

> Whether the offspring is male, or whether its origin is female.

Vergil says:

> Dear offspring of the gods, great increase of Jupiter.

Aelius Stilo and Cloatius explain in nearly the same words that *subucula* is so called because it is given to the gods from *halica* [Note: [Col. 1665] *halica*], oil, and honey. Its meaning as a kind of tunic, however, is known to everyone.

*Sub vos placo*, used chiefly in prayers, means what *supplico* means (“I beseech”). Thus in the laws:

> Cross over, and lament as you proceed [Note: [Col. 1665] “within”].

*Suffiscus* was the name of the little sac of a ram’s testicles, which was commonly used as a purse. Perhaps *suffiscus* was so called because of its resemblance to a *fiscus* (“pouch”).

**Page 118**

*Subacti* means “softened.” Elsewhere it means “forced” or “compelled,” as when we say that cattle have been driven beneath a tree. Elsewhere it means “conquered.”

*Supplicium* differs from *supplicia*, as usage shows. In common usage we say “this belongs to the gods, that to human beings”; but when *supplicium* is imposed on someone, the matter concerns the punishment of a person who is ordered to be beaten.

*Supplicia* are objects carried by the *caduceatores* (“heralds”). They were taken from the lucky vervain tree [Note: [Col. 1665] *felici*], for it was not religiously permitted to take the *supplicia* from any other vervain [Note: [Col. 1665] *verbenis*]. Sinnius Capito says that, when a citizen was put to death, it was established that a sacred rite should be performed for the Semones with a two-toothed sheep, so that by this sacrifice the punishment might be paid for the safety of the citizens [Note: [Col. 1665] “for the release”]; the head of the condemned man and the property from which anything had been taken were to be made sacred to the god. Hence it became customary that, because the king of the sacred rites then came out into the Forum for the purpose of supplication, the act was called *supplicium*. But many have always reported this differently [Note: [Col. 1665] “often reported otherwise”]. By this example he shows that *supplicia* means “supplications.” Nowadays *supplicia* generally means “punishments.”

*Sufes* was the name of a Carthaginian magistrate, as *Mediastuticus* was among the Oscans. Calidius, in his speech against Quintus Caecilius, says:

> Do you not seem to see, judges, fire and smoke following you, and flame? The Senate resolved this when the *sufetes* made the motion.

**Page 119**

A soldier is said to throw spears *sub vitem* (“beneath the vine”) when he throws them upward from beneath his hand. Lucilius says:

> Like a good soldier who beneath the vine has set up his spears [Note: [Col. 1665] “has lowered them”].

Soldiers are said to fight *sub vite* when they fight beneath a military vine. Lucilius says:

> And equally to advance into the open, to fight, far from beneath the vine.

Soldiers are said to throw stakes *sub vineam* when, with the centurions standing by, they are compelled to throw stakes.

*Supparus* was the name of a girl’s linen garment, also called a *subucula*. Pomponius says in the *Fullonia*:

> [Lacuna] Every garment made of linen is called a *supparum*.

Naevius calls a purple garment a *supparum* in the *Punic War*, and in the *Nautae* he calls the garment consecrated to Neptune a *supparum*. But now we call *suppari* linen sails stretched crosswise [Note: [Col. 1665] “linen”]. Afranius says:

> I do not seem to be a girl if I am dressed in a *supparum*.

*Supa* [Note: [Col. 1665] *sipat*] means “throws”; hence *dissipat* (“scatters”), *dejicit* (“throws down”), *obsipat* (“throws against”), and *insipat* [Note: [Col. 1665] *injicit*, “throws in”]. [Lacuna] he throws meal into a pot [Note: [Col. 1665] *ollam*].

*Sutelae* are deceitful tricks, so called from their resemblance to the work of sewing.

*Suspectus* has several meanings; it derives partly from *suspicor* (“to suspect”) and partly from *suspicio* (“suspicion”). It is therefore not surprising that it cannot be assigned a single meaning.

*Sutrium*, as though from *eant* (“let them go”), has passed into a proverb for the following reason. During a Gallic disturbance, an order was issued that the legions should be ready at Sutrium with their own food. The expression began to be used of people who performed a service from their own means and resources for those to whom they were obligated. Plautus says:

> But make sure, while the blackbird sings through the verses, that you remember to gather what it sings; make each person come with his own food [Note: [Col. 1665] “*colax*, with food, and also these”], as though they were going to Sutrium.

*Suopte* means “his very own” [Note: [Col. 1665] *suo*, “his own”], as *meopte* means “my very own,” and *tuopte* “your very own.”

The poets have handed down that the swine species is hated by Venus because Adonis, whom the goddess loved, was killed by a boar. Others say it is because pigs are the filthiest of all domesticated animals and are extremely lustful, so that the expression became an insult applied to women when they are said to *subare* and *subire*.

The proverb “The pig teaches Minerva” is used when someone teaches another a thing of which he himself is ignorant. Rather than report the matter simply—as they say, laid out in the middle—Varro and Euhemerus preferred to wrap it in foolish myths.

*Strues* are kinds of loaves, resembling joined fingers, held together by a cake laid across them.

The ancients called constructions of all kinds *struices*. Plautus says:

> He provides cereal banquets, lays out the tables in such a way, and arranges such great piled dishes.

Livy says:

> Where the Castalian stream falls through rocky structures.

**Page 121**

The ancients used *struere* for “to add” or “to increase.” Thus M. Cato rightly says:

> One ought to use law, right, liberty, and the commonwealth collectively; each person has built up glory and honor for himself in his own manner.

Or in the Twelve Tables:

> If he plays false or advances his foot, let him throw in his hand.

Some think it means “to go backward,” others “to move in another direction,” others “to flee” [Note: [Col. 1667] “to flee”], others “to lengthen one’s stride,” and others “to shorten it.” Alternatively, it may mean that he scarcely places one foot before the other, goes slowly, or delays.

According to Ateius Philologus [Note: [Col. 1667] Adeius], *stroppus* is what is called in Greek *στρόφιον* [Note: [Col. 1667] *στρόφιον*]. Some say that the emblem worn by priests on the head is a crown, or that an emblem such as a *strophium* is placed on the head in place of a crown. Thus among the Faliscans there is a festival called *Struppearia*, because people walk about crowned. Among the Tusculans, the *strophium* placed on a cushion is called the *struppus* of Castor [Note: [Col. 1667] “day”].

In mimes, *strutheum* chiefly means the obscene male member, presumably from the lustfulness of the sparrow, which the Greeks call *στρουθός*.

We call *strena* the gift given on a sacred day as a favorable omen. Its name derives from a number indicating that a second and a beginning [Note: [Col. 1667] “a third as well”] of a similar benefit will come, like *trena*, with an *s* prefixed, as the ancients customarily did in *locus* and *litis*.

Plautus uses the Umbrian term *strebula* for the haunches of sacrificial victims, which the Greeks call *μηρία* and which were customarily placed on altars. He says in the *Frivolaria*:

> Hold the lamb’s haunches [lacuna] with the [lacuna].

*Stlata* was a kind of vessel, broader than it was high, so called from its breadth, following the usage by which the ancients said *stlocum* for *locum* and *stlitem* for *litem*.

*Stlembus* means heavy and slow. Lucilius called the horse of Apulidae *stlembus* in [lacuna], referring to a sluggish and slow horse.

They say that *stellio* [Note: [Col. 1667] *stellionem*] is a kind of lizard. Verrius says it was named because poison drips from it onto its food, rather than, as others say [Note: [Col. 1667] “elsewhere”], from its resemblance to stars, because it is mottled.

The ancients called stamped money *stips*, because it was packed together; hence *stipulari* (“to stipulate”) is said of the person who, when questioned, promises a *stips*, that is, bronze money.

The ancients used *stirps* in the masculine gender for “seed” or “stock,” metaphorically using the form which poets now express in the feminine gender. Livy says:

> They report that the families of certain Romans were produced from Trojan stock before Rome was founded.

The same Livy says:

> They relate that a certain Ostrymon arose from Greek stock.

Ennius in the *Annals*:

> Pyrrhus by name, as they relate, from the highest stock [lacuna].

[Lacuna]:

> Recall the brother born from the same stock; applaud.

Gallus Aelius defines it as follows:

> *Stirps* is the propagation of a family, so that it is the stock from which someone is born [Note: [Col. 1667] “*stirps* is”].

By metaphor, *stirpes* are named after those roots which grow beneath the lowest parts of trees.

**Page 123**

*Stipatores* were called the bodyguards whom the ancients called *latrones*, that is, mercenaries who surrounded the bodies of kings with weapons as though with iron.

A *stipes* is a stake fixed in the ground. Afranius says in [lacuna]:

> How honorably he acted when he drove him against a stake [Note: [Col. 1667] “doorpost”] of the enemy; I appeal to your loyalty, who are present [lacuna].

[Lacuna] “that forest, and [lacuna] struck my side with an enemy’s cast” [Note: [Col. 1667] “throw”], so that, once the stake had been torn away, the soldier who had struck the shield with a powerful throw [lacuna]. Unless he intended *stipes* to mean a weapon or spear. Accius says in the *Bacchae*:

> Is there some firwood or alder stake [Note: [Col. 1667] “firwood”] [lacuna]?

Ennius [lacuna]:

> Firwood stakes [Note: [Col. 1667] “firwood”] [lacuna].

[Lacuna] “he killed him with the stake, wherever [lacuna] he seized the stake.”

The ancients used *strittavus* for *tritavus* (“great-great-grandfather”), who is the father of the great-grandfather and great-grandmother, just as they used *stlis* for *lis* (“lawsuit”).

In the poem of Naevius, *strigores* is found for *strigosi*, meaning people with dense muscles [Note: [Col. 1667] “men”]. Elsewhere *strigores* means people worn down by exercise.

*Strigae* were called rows of things placed continuously beside one another, named from *stringere* (“to draw tight”). Verrius says that the Greeks call *strigae* *syrnia*, a name given to wicked women whom they also call flying women. Thus the Greeks customarily ward them off with these words:

> *ΣΥΡΡΙΝΤΑ ΡΟΜΡΕΙΕΝ ΝΥΚΤΙΚΟ ΜΑΝ ΣΤΡΙΝΤΑΤΟΛΑΟΝ ΟΡΝΙΝ ΑΝΩ ΝΥΜΙΟΝ ΩΚΥΡΟΡΟΥΣ ΕΡΙ ΝΗΑΣ.*

[This is a corrupt Greek apotropaic formula, approximately invoking the removal of a night-mad, people-devouring strix—a bird—and referring to swift-footed beings upon ships; several words are materially uncertain.]

**Page 124**

A *statuliber* is a slave whom a will orders to be free once a specified condition has been fulfilled. If the heir is responsible for preventing the *statuliber* from fulfilling the condition he must fulfill, the slave nevertheless appears to be free [Note: [Col. 1667] “if the condition remains in force”].

A *status dies* (“fixed day”) is a day appointed for a legal proceeding involving a foreigner. In ancient usage people of this sort were called *hostes* (“enemies” or “foreigners”), because they possessed equal rights with the Roman people; *hostire* was used for “to make equal.” Plautus says in the *Curculio*:

> If a fixed day agreed with a foreigner intervenes, nevertheless one must go where they command, however unwillingly.

Some think *stagnum* (“pool”) is so called because water always stands in it. Others say that the place is called by the Greeks *στεγνός* (“watertight”) because it holds water well.

*Satura* is both a kind of food prepared from various ingredients and a law packed with many other laws. Thus the enactment of laws includes the clause:

> Let no law be repealed or diminished *per saturam* (“by way of a miscellaneous measure”).

T. Annius Luscus, in the speech he delivered against Tiberius Gracchus, says:

> The power which the plebs had granted *per saturam* was repealed.

C. Laelius, in the speech he delivered on his own behalf, says:

> Then, on the following day, after votes had been gathered as though in a miscellaneous collection, he was received into surrender.

**Page 125**

An image of the *Stata Mater* was worshiped in the Forum after it had been purified [Note: [Col. 1669] “illuminated”], so that the stones would not be damaged by the fire that was burning there in great quantity at night. A large part of the people carried the worship of that goddess back to their respective neighborhoods.

Caecilius seems to mean a kind of earring by *stalagmium* in the *Carine*, when he says:

> Then I have at home a *stalagmium* from her ear.

*Stolidus* means “stupid” or “foolish.” Ennius says in Book I:

> For foolish swine are accustomed [Note: [Col. 1669] “accustomed”] to fight by force.

And in the *Alexander*:

> He calls him a man because, foolishly licentious, he does not understand.

Caecilius says in the *Hypobolimaeus*:

> Go away from here, you fool; there [Note: [Col. 1669] “there,” not “to him”], so that he may be your father.

And in the *Androgynus* [Note: [Col. 1669] *Androgynus*]:

> But I am a fool; I ought to have come first to offer congratulations [Note: [Col. 1669] “I ought”].

It is clear that the ancients used *stuprum* for “shame” or “dishonor” in the poem of Naevius:

> Every day I am chastised for foulness and dishonor.

And in the *Sententiae* of Appius:

> That he may possess his mind [lacuna], lest it produce any fraud, dishonor, or violence.

Naevius says:

> They would rather perish there than return to their own people with dishonor.

Likewise:

> If they abandon those bravest men, they will continue to inflict great dishonor upon the people [Note: [Col. 1669] “you will continue”].

The Greeks of Doris call unworked flax *stuppa*.

**Page 126**

The *Stura* is a river in the territory of Laurentum, which some [lacuna].

They call it **Astura**.

**Suber.** A tree, and *suberies*—the cork with which they swam in the baths. [Note: *thermis*, “in the baths.”]

**Sterilis.** They called a barren woman *sterilis*, whom the Greeks call στεῖρα (*steira*), one who does not conceive the generative seed. [Note: *concipit*, “conceives.”]

**Seplasia**, or **Seplasium.** A place where costly perfume was sold. Pomponius, in *The Adelphi*:

> May the infernal gods destroy you, Antipho, because you ask where this perfume comes from. And yet, where could fine perfume come from, except Seplasia?

**The festival of fools.** The Quirinalia were so called. It was a festival of Quirinus, because on that day those who, on the appointed day, had either been unable to perform the sacred rite or had neglected it sacrificed to Quirinus. They had failed to observe the day of the Fornacalia rites assigned to their own guilds, and atoned for the offense of delay; moreover, what they had not done for their own guilds, during whose festival it was permitted, they performed then.

**Sanctum.** Opilius Aurelius says that something is called *sanctum* which is neither sacred (*sacrum*) nor religious (*religiosum*). Aelius Stilo says that it appears to be both—sacred, of course, and religious. Most people, however, say that because a penalty or fine has been imposed upon anyone who violates it, the word is used only in the sense of *sacred*. Hence the word *sanctio* is also derived from laws; and a law, as well as the motion by which it was proposed, is called *sancta*. Likewise, a proposal is called *sancta*; and so is the tribune of the plebs who proposed it before the assembly. [Note: *quique*, “and whoever.”]

**Sanqualis avis.** The Sanqualian bird is so called, which in the augural commentaries is called *ossifraga* (“bone-breaker”), because it is under the protection of the god Sancus.

### Page 127
