**Saccomorum** [Note: *Sycomorus*, “sycamore.”] is a kind of tree, which Pomponius says was named from the fig and the mulberry, because it is both a fig and a mulberry; hence its name was formed from the Greek words μόρον (*moron*, “mulberry”) and σῦκον (*sykon*, “fig”).

**Solem** [Note: *Solem*, “the Sun.”] Verrius says it is called so because it is alone. In the same way the Sun is sometimes called Sol and sometimes Apollo:

> You are Apollo,

as it appears in the *Carmen Saeculare*.

**Sacrem.** Verrius says that a pig is called *sacer* once it is considered pure after giving birth, and that the name is derived from this circumstance. He adds that point, though it is of little use, but omits the etymology of the word. Plautus:

> Young man, at what prices are these sacred, unblemished pigs sold?  
> —One coin.  
> —Here, take it from me; order yourself to be purified at my expense.

And in *The Rope*:

> There are lambs and sacred pigs at home.

Cato, against Quintus Minucius Thermus:

> After … he slaughtered a sacred pig in his lap.

It is sometimes used for a sacrificial victim. Ennius:

> With the sacred victim’s blood poured out.

**Sacrima.** The sacrifice made for the first grapes was called *sacrima* by the ancients. According to Aelius Stilo and Cloatius, it was must placed in an amphora at the Liberalia, for the purpose of sacrifice, in place of grapes and wine, which are, as it were, sacred when the rite is performed for Liber, just as *praemelium* is offered to Ceres.

**Sacrificulus Rex.** The *Sacrificulus Rex* is the man who performs the rites that kings used to perform. The first one mentioned after the expulsion of the kings is Sicinius Bellutus.

**Sacella.** Shrines are called *sacella*: places consecrated to the gods without a roof.

### Page 128

**Sacrosanctum.** Something is called *sacrosanctum* when it has been established by the interposition of an oath, so that anyone who violated it would pay the penalty with his life. The tribunes of the plebs and the aediles of the same order belong to this class; Marcus Cato affirms in the work he wrote that the plebeian aediles were *sacrosancti*.

**Sacratae leges.** The sacred laws are those by which it was decreed that anyone who acted against them should be made *sacer*—forfeit to one of the gods—together with his family and property. Some say that the laws are called *sacratae* because the Plebs, having sworn an oath on the Sacred Mount, enacted them.

**Seclusa sacra.** These were called *seclusa sacra*, which the Greeks call mysteries.

**Scaena.** By some it is called *scaena*, by others *sacena*: a pontifical *dolabra* (pickaxe or adze).

**Sarissa.** A type of Macedonian spear.

**Sacer mons.** The Sacred Mount is called the hill beyond the Anio, a little more than three miles away. When the Plebs seceded from the Patricians and appointed tribunes of the plebs to assist them, they consecrated the mountain to Jupiter as they departed.

A *sacer homo*, however, is a person whom the people have condemned for some offense. It is not religiously permissible to sacrifice him, but anyone who kills him is not condemned for parricide. For the first tribunician law provides that if anyone kills a man who has been made *sacer* by that plebiscite, he is not to be considered a parricide. From this it has become customary to call any bad and wicked man *sacer*.

### Page 129

Gallus Aelius says that anything consecrated in any manner or by any institution of the state is sacred: whether a temple, an altar, an image, a place [Note: *locus*, “place.”], money, or anything else dedicated and consecrated to the gods.

But when private persons dedicate any of these things to a god for the sake of their own religious observance, the Roman pontiffs do not consider the object sacred. If, however, private rites have been undertaken which, according to the pontiffs’ regulations, must be performed on a fixed day or at a fixed place, those rites are called sacred, as though they were a sacrifice. The place where those private rites must be performed scarcely appears to be sacred.

**Sacrani.** The people who originated at Reate were called *Sacrani*. They drove the Ligurians and Siculi out of the Septimontium; for they had been born from a *ver sacrum* (“sacred spring”).

**Sagmina.** *Sagmina* are called *verbenae*, that is, pure herbs, because they were taken from a sacred place by a consul or praetor when envoys were setting out to make a treaty or declare war; or the name may come from *sancire*, “to confirm.”

Naevius:

> They took up staffs and sacred herbs—  
> the sacred law of Jupiter to be sworn by means of the sacred herb.

**Sagaces.** People of great and skillful intelligence are called *sagaces*. Afranius, in *The Brundisian Woman*:

> Who has a heart so keen and an intellect so extraordinary?

### Page 130

Lucretius, Book II:

> Nor is this keen mind less able to understand these things.

He also spoke of a keen dog:

> The unconquered dog, keen, relying on powerful strength.

**Saga.** A woman skilled in sacred rites is also called a *saga*. A wise man is called *sagus*, with the first syllable lengthened, perhaps to avoid ambiguity.

**Sanates.** They were called *Sanates*, as though *sanati*, “those who have been healed,” that is, healed in mind.

Sulpicius Rufus, however, and Opilius Aurelius think that *Sanates* refers to peoples of an inferior status, such as the Tiburtines and others who lived with the Tiburtine people in the Tiburtine territory—that is, foreigners and peoples of inferior rank.

Thus it is written in the Twelve Tables:

> For the bound man and the freed man, and for the Fortes and Sanates, let the same law apply—

that is, the law of the good, and also of the foreigner belonging to the lower-ranking colonies that were established among the Old Latins, which King Priscus brought together along the coast, above and below Rome, into the Latin communities. He called them *Sanates* because, contrary to expectation, he had prepared and healed them, and had been able to make a treaty with them, as Cincius says in Book II *On the Office of the Jurist*.

### Page 131

Valerius Messala did not omit this point in his explanation of the Twelve Tables. Yet in the book whose title he writes as *On Obscure Sayings* [Note: *inscribit*, “he titles.”], he says that the Fortes and Sanates were two neighboring peoples, concerning whom this law was written, by which it was established that they should have openly the same right as the Roman people.

He thinks that the law refers to no others than the Fortes and Sanates, understanding it in this way. Many people dislike later what they once approved; therefore, he says, *sant forcti* [Note: “made sanate”; the text appears corrupt] means “healed madmen.”

**Sarpta.** A vineyard that has been pruned—that is, purified. The small branches left behind usually obstruct the vines, and therefore they are cut away.

For this reason, writers also think that *sarmenta* are so called; for the ancients used *sarpere* in the sense of “to clear.”

**Sarte.** In the augural books, *sarte* is used for “whole” or “sound”:

> To hear and see safely and soundly.

For this reason public works that are contracted on the condition that they be delivered intact are called *sarta tecta* (“repaired and roofed”); for *sarcire* means “to make whole.”

**Sarra.** The region now called Epirus was formerly called *Sarra*.

**Sardare.** It means “to understand.” Naevius, in Book … of the *Punic War*:

> Which the fools cannot understand sufficiently.

**Sardi venales.** “Sardinians for sale”—that is, one worse than another. This proverb appears to have arisen from the fact that at the Capitoline Games, which are held by the neighboring communities [Note: *vicanis*, “by the inhabitants of the villages.”], an auction of Veientine boys [Note: *Veientium*, “of the Veientines.”] usually takes place. In it each last and worst old man is brought forward by the auctioneer, wearing a purple-bordered toga [Note: *praetexta*, “purple-bordered toga”] and a golden amulet, the dress in which the kings of the Etruscans used to appear.

### Page 132

They are called Sardinians because the Etruscan people originated at Sardis in Lydia. For Tyrrhenus set out from there with a large force and occupied that part of Italy which is now called Etruria.

Sinnius Capito, however, says that the consul Tiberius Gracchus, colleague of Publius Valerius Falto, conquered Sardinia and Corsica, and that nothing except slaves was captured as booty; these formed a very cheap multitude.

**Sarcito.** In the Twelve Tables, Servius Sulpicius says that *sarcito* means “pay the damages” or “make good.”

**Sardanapalus.** He was a king of the Assyrians, given to unparalleled luxury, always and at every moment occupied among women and banquets.

**Sargus.** A kind of fish, which is generally found in the Egyptian sea. Lucilius:

> What will move him—the splendid *helops*, or the Egyptian *sargus*?

**Saturnia.** Italy, and the hill that is now the Capitoline, were called *Saturnian*, because they were thought to be under the protection of Saturn. Those who lived in the fortress at the foot of the Capitoline slope were also called *Saturnians*. An altar dedicated to that god appears to have stood there before the Trojan War, because people supplicate at it with their heads uncovered.

For the Italians, following Aeneas, cover their heads. When Aeneas was performing a sacred rite on the shore of the Laurentine territory to his mother Venus, he covered his head so that Ulysses would not recognize him and interrupt the sacrifice; in this way he avoided being seen by the enemy.

### Page 133

**Saturno.** A festival is celebrated for Saturn in December, because a temple was dedicated to him at that time, and he appears to preside over the cultivation of the fields; the sickle is therefore also his emblem.

The very ancient verses in which Faunus is thought to have sung the fates to human beings are called *Saturnian*. Naevius wrote the *Punic War* in this meter, and many others composed further works in it. In the *Salian Hymns* the god is called *Saturnus* [Note: *Satirnus*], evidently from sowing.

**Sas.** Verrius thinks that *sas* means “those,” citing Ennius, who says in Book I:

> For every Roman has his own virgins at home—

although it appears more likely to mean “their own,” as in Book IV of the same author, where it must have that meaning:

> Nor had anyone seen philosophy—which the Latin language does not possess—as the wisdom that is proclaimed, in dreams, before he began to learn it.

In the same way, when he says *sapsam*, meaning *ipsam* (“herself”), he does not use any other form, in Book XIII:

> Where the matter itself displays itself and gives its command.

Pacuvius, in *Teucer*:

> For the matter itself will restore the kingdom to Teucer. [Note: The alternative reading is “The matter itself will restore the kingdom to Teucer.”]

**Scaeva.** The common people use the word both in a good and in a bad sense when they speak of a good or bad *scaeva*. Writers, however, have usually used it in a bad sense, as it is also found among the Greeks. Hostius used *scaevus* for “left” in Book … of the *Histrian War*:

> … he perceives the left …  
> … has gone completely away …

### Page 134

**Saperda.** A kind of very poor fish; it also means “wise,” as Varro says:

> Brave, witty *saperdae*, though we are all alike.

**Sanderaca.** He says that *sanderaca* is a kind of color, which the Greeks call σανδαράκη (*sandarake*). Naevius:

> A blackbird of sanderaca color.

**Sabini quod volunt somniant.** “The Sabines dream whatever they wish” is said to be an old proverb. Sinnius Capito says it arose from the fact that whenever a sacrifice was performed beside the road, they used to bring a Sabine man into attendance. He promised to dream on their behalf; and after he awoke, he told those performing the rites everything he had seen in sleep, provided it was relevant to the religious observance of the sacrifice.

Hence the proverb appears to have arisen: “The Sabines are accustomed to dream whatever they wish.” But because certain old women, through their eagerness to drink, were trying to obtain that dream, the saying “An old woman dreams what she wishes” also became widespread. For generally whatever we desire in our waking minds tends to appear to us in sleep.

**Sambyca.** A kind of musical instrument; women who play it are called *sambycistriae*. By analogy, they also called by this name the machine with which cities are stormed: just as strings are stretched on an instrument, ropes are stretched on the siege machine.

### Page 135

**Samnites.** The name is said to have been derived from spears, because of a kind of spear which the Greeks call σαυνία (*saunia*). Others say that this people, expelled beyond the borders by the Sabines in fulfillment of a vow made during a sacred spring, occupied the hill called Samnium under the leadership of Comius Castronius; hence the name *Samnites*.

**Salaria via.** It is said to begin at the gate now called the Colline Gate, from the Quirinal Hill. It was called the Salt Road because permission had been obtained to transport salt by it from the sea to the Sabines.

**Salacia.** She was called *Salacia* because she stirs up the sea. The ancient poets, however, are said to have used the word for water itself. Pacuvius, in …:

> Hence we flee the violence of Salacia, and gladly feed on Ceres’ gift; afterward I am laid in a chamber, enclosed all around by a wall, so that no mortal can then carry me away from there.

**Salutaris porta.** The Salutary Gate was named from the Temple of Salus, which was nearby; others say it was named from greetings.

The *Megalesia* are the games now so called; formerly they were called theatrical games. Historians have recorded that they were first instituted by Gaius …lius and Marcus Popilius, son of Marcus, curule aediles. During these games mimes used to appear in the orchestra while the acts of the play were being arranged inside, performing obscene verses.

**Salva res est, saltat senex.** “The matter is safe; the old man is dancing.” Verrius gives the reason why the parasites of Apollo continually repeat this expression in Book V, whose first letter is P. When C. P. Sulpicius and C. N. Fulvius were consuls, and Marcus Calpurnius Piso was urban praetor and producing the games, the performers suddenly went out to take up arms because the arrival of the enemy had been announced [Note: “when the enemy’s arrival was announced.”]. After their victory they returned to the theater, anxious lest the interruption of the religious observance should cause offense. The games had to be renewed, and there they found Gaius Pomponius [Note: *Pompinius* in the text], a freedman mime, advanced in years, dancing to the flute player. Therefore, the cry celebrating the unbroken religious observance is still repeated today.

But in this book he reports the words of Sinnius Capito, who says that these Apollinarian Games were held under the consuls Claudius and Fulvius, instituted on the basis of the Sibylline Books and the prophecy of the seer Marcius [Note: *M.* expanded as *Marcii*]. No Pomponius is mentioned, and he absurdly gives here a reason for the name “parasites of Apollo,” although he had passed it over in that account. He says that they were so called because Gaius Volumnius, who danced to the flute player, played the secondary role—the parasite being a character introduced in nearly all mimes.

I have reported this inconsistency of our Verrius not without embarrassment.

**Salii.** Although there can be no doubt that the Salii were named from *salire*, “to leap” or “to dance,” Polemon says that there was an Arcadian named Salius, whom Aeneas brought from Mantinea to Italy and who taught the Italian youths the ἐνόπλιος (*enoplios*), “armed dance.”

### Page 137

Critolaus, however, says that Saon came from Samothrace with Aeneas and brought the household gods, the Penates, to Lavinium; he established the type of dancing called *saliare*. From him the Salii were named. Since lavish banquets are provided for them on every day and wherever they stay, any other lavish banquets are also called *saliares*.

**Salmacis.** A nymph named Salmacis, daughter of Heaven and Earth, is said to have given her name to the water of the spring at Halicarnassus. Anyone who drank from it was softened by the vice of unchastity. The entrance to the spring, narrowed by walls, gave reckless young men an opportunity to violate the boys and girls approaching it, because no escape route was open.

Ennius:

> Salmacian spoils, won without blood or sweat.

**Saliae virgines.** Cincius says that the *Saliae virgines* were hired women who were brought to the Salii, wearing the *apex* and the military cloak. Aelius Stilo wrote that they performed a sacrifice in the Regia, clothed and equipped with the *apex* in the manner of the Salii.

**Spondere.** Verrius thinks that *spondere* was so called because something is promised voluntarily, that is, by one’s own will. Then, forgetting this, he says in a later section that *sponsus* and *sponsa* were named from the Greek because they perform σπονδαί (*spondai*), “libations” or “solemn agreements,” with sacred rites interposed.

**Salix.** He says that this is the name not of a tree but of a kind of shrub, and he absurdly interprets it as having been so called because it grows with such speed that it appears to leap.

**Salinum.** On the dining table a *salinum* was customarily placed in place of a water-vessel, together with a small dish, because salt is nothing other than water.

**Salentini.** The Salentines are said to have been named from the sea: Cretans and Illyrians who, sailing together with the Locrians, established an alliance in that region of Italy which they …

### Page 138

**Saeculares ludi.** The first secular games were held in the territory of King Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated to Mars by the consul Publius Valerius Poplicola. The Roman people had previously found there, and preserved, an altar also dedicated to Dis and Proserpina, sunk nearly twenty feet underground at the far end of the Campus Martius, in a place called Terentum. At that altar the Roman people were accustomed to perform sacrifices for averting evils.

Later, Popillius Laenas, one of the two men responsible for sacred rites, began to celebrate secular games there every one hundred and ten years. In these games he sacrificed dark-coloured victims over three days and as many nights; afterward it was established that they should be held every hundred years. Hence they appear to have been called *saeculares*, because a period of one hundred years is considered an age or generation.

**Scutilum.** A thin and lean person is called *scutilus*, from the Greek, just as when we call a man *scutilus* we indicate someone so emaciated that only a thin skin remains. In a procession we use *scutilus* in another sense, so that it appears to be derived from *scrutillus*, with the letter *r* worn away, and to denote someone able to investigate by virtue of his character. But the name *scutilus* is formed from Greek when we mean something made of leather.

**Squalidum.** Verrius says that *squalidum* means unkempt and filthy. He says it was so called because it closely resembles the scales of fish, especially those of fish hidden in the depths of marshes, which are particularly rough. Hence Ennius, in *Telephus*:

> How squalidly dressed, enclosed in a single robe.

**Squarrosos.** He says they were named from the same resemblance to fish scales: their skin rises in bumps because of continual filth. Lucilius:

> The rough, shapeless snouts of Varro’s and the cliff-dwellers’ kind.

**Schoeniculae.** Plautus appears to call little prostitutes *schoeniculae*, because they used *schoenum*, a very inferior kind of perfume. Thus he says:

> Diabolical little *schoeniculae*, little wonders,  
> with worn-out ankles and tiny, battered legs.

The same author:

> Bakers’ mistresses, remnants of flour-bins,

**Scorta.** Prostitutes are called *scorta*, following the usage of country people who, as in the old Atellan plays, used to say that they had brought a little skin in place of a prostitute [Note: *pelliculam*, “a little skin.”]. For everything made from skins is called *scorteum*.

**Scortes.** Verrius says that the testicles of rams are called *scortes*, that is, “skins,” for the same reason and from the same leather-related terminology.

**Scandulaca.** A kind of herb harmful to crops, because it kills them by entangling them like ivy.

**Scaptensula.** A place in Macedonia where silver is dug out. It was so called from digging, which in Greek is σκάπτειν (*skaptein*). Lucretius:

[Note: The manuscript reading has *rumices* rather than *murices*.]

**Scitum Populi.** A decree of the People was called a *scitum* when the entire patrician order, without the Plebs, ordered something by its votes at the proposal of a patrician. But when something was enacted after a question had been put by someone and the Patricians and Plebs had voted, it was already called a written law.

A *plebiscitum*, however, is what a tribune of the plebs proposed to the Plebs without the Patricians—that is, what he asked them about—and the Plebs enacted.

**Plebes.** The Plebs consists of all the people except the senators and the patricians.

**Scita facie.** Poets use this expression for “with a good face,” and elsewhere *scita* for “good.” Terence, in *Phormio*:

> “Quite pretty,” he says.

And in *The Self-Tormentor*:

> But if you knew how cleverly it occurred to me.

Ennius, Book VI:

> Light … a clever driver.

**Scena.** It is clear that *scena* was a kind of knife, but it is disputed whether it was an axe or an adze. Cincius, in Book II of his work *On Ancient Words*, says that it was a pontifical adze. Livius, in *The Lydian*:

> He collapsed as though struck by a *scena*, scarcely otherwise.

**Sextus Pompeius Festus, *On the Meaning of Words*: Book XVI ends; Book XIX begins.**

**Spectio.** In the augural books, *spectio* is used for “observation” and “announcement,” because those who possess all authority over sacred matters have it. The augurs had *spectio* alone, by whose advice the magistrates conducted affairs, but they did not have the power to obstruct them by making announcements. After they had seen enough, *spectio* was granted without *nuntiatio*, so that they themselves might conduct the matter according to the auspices rather than impede others by announcing what they had seen.

**Scripturarius ager.** A *scripturarius ager* is public land on which a fixed payment is required for grazing animals, because the public contractor prepares the account in writing with the herdsman.

**Scribae.** The ancients called both copyists and poets *scribae*, as well as those whom we now call *librarii*. Nowadays *scribae* are specifically the copyists who write the public accounts on tablets.

Thus, when Livius Andronicus composed a poem during the Second Punic War which was sung by maidens, because the Roman state thereafter began to fare more prosperously, a temple of Minerva on the Aventine was publicly assigned to the scribes and actors, where they might assemble and place offerings in Livius’ honour, because he both wrote plays and acted in them.

**Scraptae.** Worthless and contemptible women were called *scraptae*, as Verrius says, from things called *screa*, that is, what one usually coughs up, insofar as one purges oneself by doing so. Titinius, in *Prilla*:

> By Castor, today I saw the bed of Postuma Piculeta made up by a filthy woman.

**Sceleratus campus.** The “Accursed Field” is near the Colline Gate. The Vestal Virgins who committed incest were buried alive there.

**Scribonianum.** The Scribonian *puteal* is the place before the atria made by Scribonius, who had been commissioned by the Senate to investigate sacred shrines that had been struck by lightning. He took care of it because a shrine at that place had been struck by lightning.

Some people did not know where the lightning had been buried—for once this is known, it is impious to cover it. Therefore the sky is always visible there through an open hole.

**Sceleratus Vicus.** The Accursed Street is so called because, when Tarquinius Superbus had arranged for King Servius Tullius, his father-in-law, to be killed, his daughter drove over her father’s fallen body in a carriage, hurrying to take possession of her father’s house.

### Page 143

**Scelerata porta.** Some call it the Accursed Gate; it is also called the Carmental Gate because a shrine of Carmenta was nearby. For this reason entering or leaving through that gate is considered an omen.

**Schedia.** A kind of makeshift vessel, made only from beams fastened together, in which merchants transport goods after losing their ship. Hence *schedia* is also used of poems and verses that are not sufficiently finished [Note: “finished.”]. He called something *schedium* when he said:

**Sexagenarii.** In former times, sixty-year-old men were thrown from the bridge. Manilius gives this as the reason: the Aborigines who first inhabited Rome were accustomed to sacrifice each year to Father Dis a man who was sixty years old. They ceased doing this upon the arrival of Hercules. Later, out of respect for the ancient custom, they began to throw wicker effigies of men from the bridge into the Tiber in the old manner.

Others say that, while Hercules was delayed in Italy, some of his companions lived along the riverbank and called themselves Argei after the Argives. Their memory was renewed by the following rite: a certain Greek envoy named Argeus had been sent from Greece and had remained a long time at Rome with them. When he died, the priests established that, after he had reported the affairs of the state, a wicker effigy should be sent through the river and the sea to his homeland.

### Page 144

Some say that after the city had been freed from the Gauls, because of a shortage of food they began throwing sixty-year-old men into the Tiber. One of them, hidden through his son’s filial devotion, often benefited his country by giving advice while appearing in the person of his son. When this became known, the young man was said to have been unaware of it, and the lives of the sixty-year-olds were spared.

His hiding place, by which he had protected [Note: *arcuerit*, “had warded off”; the text reads *arguerit*] and concealed the old man, was considered worthy of reverence and was therefore called *Argaea* [Note: *Argaea*].

But the following explanation is the most firmly established. When people first began voting at the assemblies by crossing the bridge, the younger men shouted that the sixty-year-olds, who no longer held any public office, should be thrown from the bridge, so that they themselves rather than the old men might choose their commander. Sinnius Capito also holds this view.

Afranius confirmed the mistaken notion about the Tiberine bridge in *The Rejected Woman*.

**Secus** [Note: *sexus*, “sex”]. It means “otherwise,” and also *sexus*, “sex,” in the sense of nature and bodily constitution, from the Greek ἕξις (*hexis*, “condition” or “disposition”). Afranius, in *The Stepson*, says:

> A childless man adopted a son of the male sex.

Pacuvius, in *Atalanta*:

> He begets offspring threefold in the male sex.

**Simpludiarea.** *Simpludiarea* are funerals at which only games and basket-bearers are present. Some have said that these are funerals at which neither category of games is present. *Indictiva* funerals, however, are those at which there are not only games but also horse-leapers; these are the most elaborate.

**Sex suffragia.** The “six voting groups” are so called among the centuries of the equestrian order. They were added to the number of centuries established by King Priscus Tarquinius.

**Sestertius.** A *sestertius* is a quarter of a *denarius*. At the time when the *denarius* was worth ten asses, this amounted to two asses and a half.

### Page 145

**Sinistrae aves.** “Left-hand birds” and *sinistrum* refer to the left side of the auspices, that is, to what permits something to happen. Varro, in Book V of the *Epistolary Questions*, says:

> When you look southward from the seat of the gods, the eastern regions of the world are on the left, and the western regions on the right. I think it happened for this reason that the left-hand auspices were considered better than the right-hand ones.

Sinnius Capito and Cincius hold nearly the same view.

**Sentinare.** It means “to be busy” or “to be fully occupied,” and is derived from *sentina*, the bilge-water which endangers a ship when it takes in a great quantity of water. Caecilius, in *Aethrio*:

**Senatores.** It is sufficiently well established that *senatores* derives from *senectus*, “old age.” Romulus initially chose one hundred men, by whose counsel he would administer the state; hence they were also called *Patres*, “Fathers.”

Today, when senators are ordered to attend, the term refers to those who are permitted to give their opinion in the Senate. For those who, after the census had been established, received office from among the younger men and gave their opinion in the Senate are not called *senatores* until they have been enrolled among the elders.

**Senatus decretum.** Aelius Gallus distinguishes *senatus decretum* from *senatus consultum* by saying that a decree is a portion of a senatorial resolution—for example, when a province is assigned to someone—although that assignment itself is also a senatorial resolution.

**Senis crinibus.** Brides are adorned with six locks of hair because this was the most ancient form of adornment for them. Some say it is because the Vestal Virgins are so adorned, and because they promise their chastity to their husbands [the text is fragmentary].

**Sentes.** Since it is established that *sentes* means “thorns,” and Afranius said in *The Abducted Woman*:

it must be understood in the sense of “thorny.”

> at least by sipping.

**Senones.** Verrius says that the Gauls are thought to be called *Senones* because they came newly from the transalpine region. They were first called ξένοι (*xenoi*, “foreigners”), and later *Senones*.

**Septentriones.** The seven stars are called *Septentriones* from seven yoked oxen, which farmers call *triones* (“plow-oxen”), because, yoked together, they plow the earth, as though they were *terriones*.

Some derive the name from the seven stars because the Greeks call that constellation ἅμαξα (*hamaxa*, “wagon”), since it has a part shaped like a wagon pole. Hence Ennius says:

But natural philosophers, having contemplated the arrangement of the seven stars, say that they are called *septentriones* because the stars are positioned so that groups of three form what appears to be triangles.

**Scensas.** The ancients called what are now *caenae* (“dinners”) *scensae*. What are now called *prandia* (“luncheons”) they regarded as dinners, while they called dinners *vespernae* (“evening meals”).

**Signa.** As the objects themselves are called *signa*, so too are stones, objects made of clay, and anything else of that kind. Sculpted images are also called *signa*. Cups, too, in which figures are stamped in relief, are called *signa*.

**Sequester.** A *sequester* is someone who stands between parties engaged in a dispute, holding a deposit between them according to their agreement and returning it to the person who establishes by law that it is owed to him. Cato, in the speech he delivered *On the Indigites*:

> They allow wretched men to perish so that they may seize their property; or, if the survivors make a claim, they betray them by giving them over to a sequester. [Note: “they give them to a sequestrator.”]

And Plautus, in *The Merchant*:

> No, rather, it was given to me in sequestration …

**Sepulchrum.** According to Gallus Aelius, a *sepulchrum* is the place in which a dead person has been buried. The ancients called it a *bustum*. It is marked out for the dead by boundary stones or by some other object, within which the burial has taken place.

*Taxatio* is the term for an assessment made for a fixed sum. That it is also said to derive from *tangendo* (“touching”) is attested by the stage performers who are called *taxatores*, because one attacks another with insults.

*Tabernacula* (“tents”) is so called from its resemblance to *tabernae* (“booths”), which themselves were so named because they were formerly made of boards—not, as some think, because they were enclosed with boards.

*Tagit*: Pacuvius in *Teucer*: “So that I, if anyone touches me, may also touch”; and the same author in *Hermione*: “Or I shall not see unless I touch.” He undoubtedly used the form according to ancient custom. For today these forms are not used without prepositions, as in *contigit* (“touched”) and *attigit* (“reached, touched”).

*Tablinum* is the name of a place immediately beside the atrium, because ancient magistrates, in their official authority, kept their tablets…

### Page 167

Three kinds of *manubiae* (“bolts of Jupiter”) are believed to exist. The first are the smallest, which give warning that the gods are appeased. [Note: [Col. 1689] *quaedam*, “some (of them).”]անալ the second are larger, arrive with a crash, and shatter or tear apart whatever Jupiter’s will and the counsel of the gods are believed to send them against; the third are larger than these and come with fire. Although no lightning-bolt is without fire, these have a distinctive character: they either burn, disfigure with soot, or set things alight—things whose condition is altered by the counsel of the higher gods.

*Maniae*: Aelius Stilo says that these are figures made from flour in the shape of human beings, because they are made ugly; others call them *maniolae*. The *maniae* with which nurses frighten little children are ghosts, that is, the gods and goddesses called *Manes*, who either flow from the underworld to the upper world, or else *Mania* is their maternal grandmother. There are authors in support of both opinions.

*Mamercus* is an Oscan praenomen, from the fact that the Oscans call Mars *Mamers*.

The family of the *Mamilia* is said to have originated from Mamilia, the daughter of Telegonus, whom he fathered at Tusculum when he himself had founded that town.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *fuit*, “was.”]

*Mantare*: to remain frequently. Caecilius in *Epistola*: “Now do not remain so long.” “Now see this: whether blind, [lacuna] arrival torments the mind.”

The use of *manticulae* (“little purses”) for poor people to store coins in existed even in our own age. Hence those who handled little purses for the purpose of stealing were called *manticulari*. From this poets also used the verb for acting deceitfully. Pacuvius:

“He approaches with cunning in order to pick the purse, for he knows what he has earned: he picks the purse of the poor man; [lacuna] Thus I, overwhelmed by the deed, am crushed beneath the yoke.”

Then elsewhere:

“I shall approach the king with cunning; I must pick the purse”; and:

“You begin a new contrivance: with the touch of a purse—or are you speaking more sacred oaths?”

Plautus seems to mean this: “By which small offenses are wiped away every day.” For among the ancients mantles were commonly used for wiping the hands.

*Moeson*: A comic character is called *Moeson*, whether a cook, a sailor, or someone of that sort. It is said to derive from its inventor, the comic actor Moeson, as Aristophanes the grammarian says.

*Maeniana* were named after the censor Maenius, who was the first to project beams beyond the columns in the Forum, so that the upper viewing-places might be enlarged.

*Major Greece* was the name given to Italy, either because the Sicels once occupied it, or because many large cities in it had been founded by people who came from Greece.

The month of *Maius* seems to have existed in several Latin communities before the founding of Rome. For this reason, it is uncertain whether it was named from the *maiores* (“elders”), just as *Junius* was named from the *juniores* (“younger men”); or from Maia, because religious rites were solemnly performed for Mercury, her son; or because sacrifices were made to the goddess herself in many Latin communities during that month.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *ipso mense*, “in that very month.”]

*Monstrum*, as Aelius Stilo interprets it, is derived from *monere* (“to warn”), as though it were *monestrum*. Sinnius Capito likewise says it is so called because it shows what is going to happen and warns of the will of the gods. The same explanation applies to *prodigium*, as though it were *praedictum* (“foretold”), because it foretells the same things; and to *portentum*, because it portends and signifies them. From the same meaning it is clear that a fourth term should be added, especially since it depends on the same signification and is obvious to everyone: *ostentum*, which is likewise derived from *ostendere* (“to show”).

*Monitores* are those who prompt actors on the stage; the word is also used where commentaries are added, which are called books.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *par Monitores*; *libri dicuntur*, “they are called books.”]

*Monile* (“necklace”) is the name for a woman’s ornament of the sort which the stories say Eriphyle possessed; hence an ornament hanging from a horse’s neck is also called a *monile*.

### Page 169

*Molucrum* is not only the object on which millstones are rubbed—the Greeks call it *μύλικρον*—but also a swelling of the belly, which can occur even in virgins. Afranius mentions it in *The Virgin*:

“Usually, for a virgin, just as for a pregnant woman, the uterus is called a *molucrum*; it passes away without pains.”

Cloatius and Aelius also say in the *Books of Sacred Matters* that a *molucrum* is a certain square wooden object on which the victim is sacrificed. The same Aelius, in his explanation of the Saliar songs, says that the object placed beneath the millstone is called by the same name. Aurelius Opilius says that it is the place where grain is ground.

*Mola* is also the name for roasted grain sprinkled with salt, because victims are sprinkled with it after it has been ground. Some foolishly think that *molae aviae* (“grandmotherly molae”) was the correct expression.

*Mundus* can also refer to a woman’s adornment. [lacuna] Accius: “With a maiden’s adornment, secretly from her father.” Ennius: “Likewise, in that place, on lofty ships, with a clean face [or: ‘he makes a clean face’], and also with the bronze of Ceres.”

The *mundus* that is said to open three times a year is opened on the third day before the Kalends of September, the fourth day before the Nones of October, and the third day before the Ides of November. It is perhaps called *mundus* because the earth is moved.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *id omne*, “all of that.”]

*Mamphula* is the name of a kind of Syrian bread which, as Verrius says, falls onto the coals and ash in an oven before it is fully baked. Lucilius mentions it:

“If money supplies me with a strong baker, add an *empleuron*, one who knows how to make *mamphulae* for everyone.”

*A municipes* is, as Aelius Gallus says, a person born free in a *municipium*. It also means someone who has performed public service after coming from another class of people. It likewise means one who has freed himself from slavery in a *municipium* through a *municeps*. Again, *municipes* were people who had come to Rome from other communities and were not permitted to hold magistracies, but only a share in public duties.

### Page 170

[Col. 1690C]

Servilius, however, said that at first the term referred to those who had become Roman citizens on the condition that they would always maintain their state separately from the Roman people: the people of Cumae, Acerrae, and Atella, who were likewise Roman citizens and served in the legion but did not hold offices.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *Ser. filius*, “the son of Servilius.”]

Some think that *mutas* was formed from the letters, because, when placed at the ends of words, they force the speaker to fall silent. Others think it is because they have a small and weak sound, as when we call an orator or tragic actor “mute.”

Some think that *multa* is the Oscan word for a penalty. Marcus Varro says that it is a penalty, but a monetary one, concerning which he gives a detailed account in Book I of the *Epistolary Investigations*.

*Mullei* are said to be a kind of shoe first used by the kings of Alba and later by the patricians. Marcus Cato, *Origins*, Book VII:

“Whoever had held a curule magistracy wore *mullei* with tanned leather [or: ‘tanned’ or ‘crescent-shaped’]; the rest wore *perones*.”

Likewise Titinius in *The Setine Woman*:

“Now you have shown yourself in the *mullei* which you put on your feet.”

They think the term was derived from *mullare*, that is, “to sew.”

The ancients used *multifariam*, evidently because something could be spoken of in many places.

*Manius Egerius* consecrated the Nemi territory to Diana, from whom many distinguished men arose and continued for many years.  
[Note: [Col. 1689] *Aegerius agrum*, “Aegerius [consecrated] the territory.”] Hence the proverb: “Many Maniuses at Aricia.”

Sinnius Capito has a very different view. He says that ugly and deformed people are meant, because deformed figures are called *maniae*, and that a kind of cloth made at Aricia is called *manicum*.  
[Note: [Col. 1691] *panis*, “bread.”]

Ennius used *moene* in the singular:

“By the marketplace in the field of the enemy, before the wall.”

*Mutire*: to speak. Ennius in *Telephus*:

“To speak openly is a sin for a commoner.”

*Moenia* are walls and the other things made for fortifying a city, as Accius says in *The Hellenes*:

“He orders the standards immediately to sound, and weapons to be brought before the walls.”

It also signifies public duties. Plautus in *Nervolaria* [or: *Stichus*]:

“And other walls forbid me from performing the duties that are mine, [lacuna] a kind of myrrh…”

### Page 171

*Manuos* in the Sacular songs [or: Saliar songs], Aelius Stilo says, means “good.” The gods below are called *Manes*, meaning “good,” by those who worship them humbly out of fear of death; similarly, *immanes* is used to mean “very great,” not “good.”  
[Note: [Col. 1691] *Inferi di*, “the gods below.”]

The ancients pronounced *muscerdae* with the first syllable long, meaning “mouse dung.”

*Mapalia* are called Punic huts. Because nothing private exists in them, the word is customarily thrown at people who live without restraint. Cato, *Origins*, Book IV:

“They are called *mapalia* where they live; they are, as it were, round enclosures.”

*Metalli* are called, in the military law, something like mercenaries. Accius, *Annals*, Book XXVII:

“Grooms, servants, mercenaries, and camp-followers.”

From this class of people he thinks the cognomen of the Caecilian family was derived. [lacuna]

“Between the hand and the chin” is a proverb taken from Greek, namely:

“Much lies between the cup and the edge of the lip.”  
Greek: *Πολλὰ μεταξὺ πέλει κύλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρου.*

Some augur, passing by Calchas as he planted vines, told him that he was mistaken: it was not permitted for him to [lacuna].

*Minusculae Quinquatrus* (“the Little Quinquatrus”) is the name given to the Ides of June, because that day is the festival of flute-players, who worship Minerva. The goddess’s proper festival is the Quinquatrus in March.

*Muli Mariani* (“Marius’ mules”) are so called from an institution of Gaius Marius. His soldiers were accustomed to carry their baggage on a forked pole, with a pack-board placed on it.  
[Note: [Col. 1691] *superposita*, “placed above.”]

## Book XIII of Sextus Pompeius Festus begins

*Mulus* (“mule”) is used for the vehicle of the Moon, either because the Moon is as barren as a mule, or because, just as a mule is born not from its own kind but from horses, so the Moon shines with the light of the Sun rather than with her own.

The shrine of the goddess *Murtia* [lacuna].

The month of *Martius* was the beginning of the year both in Latium and after the founding of Rome, because the people were especially warlike at that time. Evidence of this is that the later months, which complete the year, are named by number, the last being December.

When Gracchus used *malo cruce* (“on the gallows-cross”), with *malus* in the masculine gender, in his speech against Publius Popillius, he likewise represented ancient usage. In the same way the ancients said *hunc frontem* (“this forehead”) and *hunc stirpem* (“this stock”), and again *hanc lupum* (“this wolf”) and *hanc metum* (“this fear”). Likewise, when the same author said in the speech against Popillius and Matho:

“By that precedent and institution, he deserved to perish on the cross…”

[lacuna]

“…and the worthless man who lingered continually in lawsuits and for that reason stood in line among those approaching the Praetor.”

Aelius Stilo, however, who did not live according to strict order, says in the speech he wrote *On His Own Virtues against Thermus*:

“What would become of me if I had not always earned all my years of service in orderly succession?”

Some even believe that *manipularis*, because it referred to the lowest rank, was called *ordinarius*.  
[Col. 1692A]

*Ornatus* means furnished with good accomplishments and having obtained honors from the people; it also means well equipped, as a soldier, gladiator, or actor about to perform plays. Yet *ornatus* also means the dress itself with which someone is adorned, as when we say that someone comes out in tragic or comic costume.

[lacuna]

*Orestiades* are nymphs, inhabitants of the mountains.

The order of the priests is assessed according to the majesty of the gods, so that each is considered greater in proportion to that majesty. The King seems to be first, then the Dialis, after him the Martialis, in fourth place the Quirinalis, and in fifth place the Pontifex Maximus. Thus at banquets the King reclines above all; likewise the Dialis above the Martialis and Quirinalis, and the Martialis above the next. All likewise rank above the Pontifex.

The King ranks first because he is most powerful; the Dialis because he is the priest of the whole universe, which is called *Dium*; the Martialis because Mars is the father of the founder of the city; the Quirinalis because Quirinus, from Cures, was adopted as a partner in Roman rule; and the Pontifex Maximus because he is regarded as judge and arbiter of divine and human affairs.

*Ordiri* means to make a beginning of something; hence the beginnings of a robe are called *exordia*.  
[Note: [Col. 1691] *exorditae*, “begun.”]

*Opaca* means shady.

*Opalia* are the festival days on which prayers are offered to Ops. One of them [lacuna].

*Optutu*, as though *optuitu*, comes from the verb *tueri* (“to look at”) and means “I see.”

An *optata hostia* (“chosen victim”) is what others call an *optima hostia*: the victim which the aedile, after three victims have been set before him, chooses to be sacrificed.

*Opima spolia* (“rich spoils”) are said to derive originally from *Ops*, the wife of Saturn, because he is regarded as a cultivator of the fields, named from sowing and represented holding a sickle, the emblem of the farmer. Thus she is also called *Consiva* and is thought to be the Earth. For this reason she is worshiped by the Roman people in the Regia, because the earth grants all wealth to the human race. Hence the wealthy are called rich in earthly possessions; *opimae hostiae* are especially fat victims; and *opima* means magnificent and ample.

### Page 174

Consequently, spoils are also called *opima* when a Roman commander has stripped them from the enemy commander. Such spoils are so rare that within a period of only a few years they have occurred three times in the Roman state: the first, which Romulus took from Acro; the second, which the consul Cornelius Cossus took from Tolumnius; and the third, which Marcus Marcellus fixed up for Jupiter Feretrius after taking them from Viridomarus.  
[Note: [Col. 1691] *Virdumarus*.]

Marcus Varro says that the spoils are *opima* even if a common soldier has stripped them from the enemy, provided that they are taken from the enemy commander. [lacuna] They are not [lacuna].

That they are placed at the temple of Jupiter Feretrius is attested by the books of the Pontiffs, in which it is written:

“For the first spoils, an ox; for the second, *solitaurilia*; for the third, a lamb, is to be publicly provided.”

There is also said to be a law concerning the *opima spolia*:

“Whoever, under whose auspices, with the army drawn up, takes the opima spoils shall give them to Jupiter Feretrius, and let him who took them sacrifice an ox and pay two hundred asses. Let him who takes the second spoils sacrifice at the altar of Mars in the Campus the *solitaurilia* of whichever kind he wishes. Let him who takes the third spoils sacrifice a male lamb to Janus Quirinus, and let the one who took them give one hundred asses; and let him under whose auspices they were taken offer an expiation to the gods.”

No law of this shrine survives, nor is it known whether it has a temple. The formula “according to the best law” is also customarily added when certain magistrates are elected. [lacuna]

*Obscum* has two different and contrary meanings. Cloatius thinks that by this word something sacred is signified, since sacred laws are also called *obscatae*. In nearly all ancient commentaries *Opicum* is written for *Obscum*, as in the fifth play of Titinius:

“Those who speak Oscan and Volscian, for they do not know Latin.”

From this, too, indecent and inflated words are called *obscena*, because the Oscans made very frequent use of filthy sexual expressions. But the same name is also given to a place in the Veientine territory which the Roman augurs are reported to have been accustomed to enjoy.  
[Note: [Col. 1693] *publici populi*, “of the public people.”]

The ancients used *obigitat* for *ante agitat* (“drives before”), as in *obambulare* (“walk about”).

*Obinunt*: they go around, perform, or undergo (*obeunt*).

The ancients used *objurare* for “to approach,” as in [lacuna] *Penthesilea*. “They were afraid to approach.” [lacuna]

*Ob vos sacro* occurs in certain prayers instead of *vos obsecro* (“I beseech you”), just as *sub vos placo* occurs instead of *supplico* (“I supplicate you”).

*Opportune* is said to derive from the fact that harbors are especially useful and desirable to sailors.

*Obherbescere*: to grow grass over, to become overgrown with grass.

*Oboritur*: is born, arises. For the preposition *ob* is customarily used in place of *ad*, as this verse demonstrates:

“So great a joy arises from the greatest tumult.”

And Ennius:

“He began to lead the legions by night toward Rome.”

*Obnectere*: to bind, a term especially common in connection with marriage.

A person is said to have *observasse* when he observes what he ought to do for a particular reason. Thus someone who observes another is said to have honored that person.

*Ommentans*: Livy in the *Odyssey*, when he says:

“You will arrive at Pylus, or remain there.”

It means “remaining beside,” but in the sense in which something is often said to happen; that is what *mantare* means.

*Ops*: the ancients used this for what we now call “wealthy,” as is shown not only by its opposite, *inops* (“poor”)… [lacuna]

### Page 176

“…he yields; I have arisen needy.”

The *obsidional crown* is given to a commander who has freed from the enemy those who were under siege. It is made from green grass, generally cut from the place where the besieged had been confined. We have shown by several examples that among the ancients grass was a sign of victory. This crown possessed great authority.

For two crowns were given to Publius Decius: one by the entire army, the other by those who had been besieged in the garrison. Lucius Sergius Dentatus, who was regarded as the Achilles of Rome and is said to have fought one hundred and twenty times on behalf of the republic, was awarded twenty-six crowns: among them eight golden, fourteen civic, three mural, and one obsidional.

The difference between the obsidional and civic crowns is this: the former is a sign of the saving of a single person; the latter of the saving of several citizens.  
[Note: [Col. 1693] *universorum*, “of all.”]

*Obstitum*: Cloatius and Aelius say that this means “violated and touched from heaven.” Cincius says that it refers to one who has stood in the way of a god or goddess—that is, one who has seen something which it was impious to see.

*Obstinato*: resolute, firm, persevering, so that one can hold fast. Pacuvius:

“Having arisen resolutely…”

Accius in *Amphitryon*:

“Though you rely on your mind so obstinately…”

Cato, in his speech against Quintus Thermus concerning the ten men:

“He made rumor and reputation worthless, while he pursued sexual crimes and, obstinate in notorious offenses…”

Naevius in *Lycurgus*:

“You who stand there obstinate…”

*Obstrudat*, *obsatulent*: they block by thrusting the gum forward greedily, without taking food; hence also *obstrudulentum*. [lacuna] Titinius said:

“Something obstructive, which [lacuna] while I sit; or something bright—or something handsome but cold.”

*Obsidium*, like *praesidium* and *subsidium*, is correctly used. Gaius Laelius is also an authority for this in his speech *For Himself before the People*:

“So that they might simultaneously establish a blockade against us by land and sea.”

And Sallustius, *Histories*, Book I:

“After completing great works, he began a blockade through the agency of Lucius Catiline, his lieutenant.”

### Page 177

*Obstitum*: oblique. Ennius, Book XVI:

“With mountains set obliquely—standing in the way—night arises.”

And in Book VIII:

“To increase still further the sun’s oblique [or: ‘with slanting light’]…”

Caecilius in *Imbros*:

“Lying on his back, with his head tilted, he made wind for himself with his little tunic.”

Lucretius:

“Everything must necessarily be done wrongly and obliquely.”

*Obsalutare*: the ancients used it for offering greetings, as in *consalutare* and *persalutare*.

An *obvaricator* was someone who came in another’s way and prevented him from completing his journey in a straight line.

The *Oufentina* tribe originally took its name from the river Oufens, which is in the Privernian territory, between the sea and Tarracina. Lucretius [or Lucilius]:

“From Privernum comes the Oufentina, and from the river Oufens.”

Later, the censors also enrolled others from different communities in the same tribe.

*Oscillum*: Santra says that it is so called because things “oscillate,” that is, incline and are carried headlong. Cornificius says that *oscillantes* are so called because they used to carve a face on masks, out of modesty, those who practiced this kind of game.

The origin of this swinging is said to be as follows. King Latinus disappeared during a battle fought against Mezentius, king of Caere. He was judged to have become Jupiter Latiaris. Therefore, on his festival days, free persons and slaves seek him not only on earth but also wherever the sky seemed accessible through swinging. This was like an image of human life, in which the highest are sometimes brought down to the lowest and the lowest raised to the highest. For that reason memory of the beginning of life is also renewed through the movement of cradles and the nourishment of milk, since during those festival days people are moved on swings and use milk as nourishment.

Nor are there lacking those who think that the Italians followed the example of the Greeks. Among the Greeks, after Icarus had been unjustly killed, his daughter Erigone, driven by grief, perished by hanging, by way of imitation [lacuna].

### Page 178

*Ostentum* is not only customarily used in place of *portentum*, but is also used participially. Pacuvius in *Medus* attests this:

“And look, at that very moment, an old man appeared as an omen.”

And Accius in *Bacchae*:

“You laugh at us while present and ready, and he has voluntarily offered himself as an omen.”

*Oscinum tripudium* is an omen which signifies by the song of the mouth what is going to be portended, when a raven, crow, owl, *parra*, or woodpecker sings.

The ancients used *obstinet* for what is now *ostendit* (“shows”), as in the ancient songs:

“But now, as the dawn withdraws from the sky, it shows its father…”  
[Note: [Col. 1693] *candens*, “shining white.”]

According to Appius Claudius, *oscines* are birds which make an omen by singing with the mouth, such as the raven, crow, owl, or *parra*; *alites* are those which make an omen by their wings and flight, such as the buzzard, *sanqualis*, eagle, *immissulus*, and vulture. The magpie, or else the woodpecker, and the *Martius*, *Feronius*, and *parra* are reckoned among both the *oscines* and the *alites*.  
[Note: [Col. 1693] *alites*, “winged birds.”]

King Ancus Marcius is said to have founded the city of Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber where it flows into the sea and to have given it a feminine name. Whether this refers to the city or to the colony later founded there, neither certainly ought to be expressed in the plural.

*Osculana pugna* (“the Osculan battle”) occurs in a proverb signifying that the defeated are victorious, because in the same battle the Roman commander Valerius Laevinus had been defeated by Pyrrhus, and shortly afterward Sulpicius had defeated that same king. [lacuna] “and our commander likewise.” Titinius recalls the matter in this way:

“This is, in a way, an Osculan battle.” [lacuna] “otherwise, because in flight he gathers spoils from this side.”

[lacuna]

### Page 179

A kiss is also signified by *osculum*, as in Plautus’ *Nervolaria*:

“A kiss is enough for me… [lacuna] both of them, my father.”

This custom was instituted by the ancients among relatives and close kin, especially among women. [lacuna]

When the phrase *optima lex* (“the best law”) was used in creating a *Magister Populi*, who is commonly called a Dictator, it signified that his authority was to be as full as possible. This was the case with Manius Valerius, son of Marcus, of the Volusian family, who was the first *Magister* elected by the people. But after an appeal from that magistracy to the people was granted—an appeal that had not existed before—the addition “according to the best law” ceased to be used, since the authority of the earlier *Magistri* had been diminished.

In giving his *Origins* the title “Books of Origins,” Cato does not seem to have embraced a sufficiently complete title for his undertaking, since he gives greater weight to the events in the history of the Roman people.

The man now called an *optio* was formerly called an *accensus*. An assistant was assigned to the centurion by the military tribunes; from that time onward it was permitted to the centurions to choose whichever assistant they wished, and the name itself was derived from the act. Plautus in *Asinaria*:

“By whatever means you can, bring around me, my wife, or your slave Saureas; carry him off. I promise you that, if you accomplish this, it will not harm you. Take Leonidas as your *optio*.”

Ennius in *Telemon* supports the view that *obsidionem* should be said rather than *obsidium*, when he says:

“You knew Ajax, born free, for whom you prepare a siege.”

Elsewhere:

“I yield, since he does not cease to draw a siege-line around us.”

*Orare*: the ancients used it for *agere* (“to conduct, perform”). This is shown by the terms *oratores*, and those who are now called envoys but were then called *oratores*, because they conducted the business entrusted to them by the state. Ennius likewise says in Book I of the *Annals*:

“But to do what your father asks of you with prayers…”

### Page 180

Verrius says that those whom we call *Oscans* were formerly called *Opsci*, as Ennius attests when he says:

“The Opscan is conducting the business from the walls.”

He further adds that indecent acts arising from illicit lust are called *obscena* because the custom of that people introduced the term. I am not sufficiently persuaded that this is true, since among almost all ancient peoples things regarded as bad omens were called *obscena*. Virgil’s testimony provides examples, so it is unnecessary to cite the examples of earlier authors:

“The obscene birds, the Harpies”; and:

“And obscene hunger.”

The ancients used the preposition *ob* for *ad*, as Ennius attests in Book XIV:

“All were killed and set alight in the clear night,”

that is, “kindled.”  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *lucenti*, “shining.”]

And in *Iphigenia*:

“I shall go to Acheron,”

where the treasures of death lie nearby.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *objacent*, “lie beside.”]

That *obferre*, *obtulit*, *obcurrit*, *oblatus*, and *objectus* are of the same type does not sufficiently persuade me.

That *ostentum*, which we sometimes use in place of *prodigium*, was also customarily used participially is made certain by Gaius Gracchus in his speech on the laws he promulgated:

“What is brought to us as an omen is brought to them for use.”

*Occisitantur*: they are often killed. Thus Gaius Gracchus said before the Rostra in his speech against Publius Popillius:

“Free men are now being slaughtered in the town.”

*Osi sunt*: that the ancients declined *odi* (“I hate”) in this way is shown by Gaius Gracchus in his speech on the Minucian law:

“It would be surprising if these men had suffered any wrong, since they have always been hated.”

The form is still common with a preposition, when we say *perosi* (“thoroughly hateful”).

*Ostende*, *ostendam*: “show,” “I shall show,” as is clear from very many other examples of this kind.

*Optionatus*, like *decurionatus* and *pontificatus*, is a title or office. Cato says in the speech he delivered before the equites:

“Our ancestors separately established different rewards for the good and the brave: *decurionatus*, *optionatus*, decorated spears, and other honors.”

### Page 181

*Ob os* means “to the mouth.” [lacuna] This is also attested by the examples cited above.

*Obsonitavere*: they often feasted. Cato in his speech urging that the Orchian law not be weakened:

“Those who formerly feasted extravagantly afterward feasted at the rate of one hundred [asses].”

It means “to banquet.”

*Ostentas*: you often display, for the sake of boasting. But it must also be used, and has been used, participially in the feminine gender.

Among the ancients people were fined two sheep for lesser offenses and thirty oxen for greater ones; the fine did not exceed this number. After the state began to use stamped bronze and the animals used for fines were spoiled through neglect, the crime of embezzlement also began to be used as a term. The livestock fine was assessed in money: oxen at one hundred asses and sheep at ten. Hence the supreme fine, that is, the greatest, is called three thousand asses. For lesser offenses there is also *vicessis*.

The ancients used *olivitam* when olives were harvested, just as *messis* was used for grain and *vindemia* for grapes. This word ought rather to have been commonly used, since otherwise we would have no term for that meaning, although some call it *olivitatem meam*.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *olivitatem eam*.]

Cicero, Book I of *On Glory*, gives the origin of *oppida* (“towns”) very well. He thinks that the name was derived from *opem* (“aid”), because they provide assistance, adding this in imitation of the Stoics’ absurdities.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *ineptias*, “absurdities.”]

Verrius says that the underworld god whom we call *Orcus* was called *Uragu* by the ancients, because they pronounced the sound of the letter *u* as *o*; nevertheless, in the shape of the letter *c* they used *g*. But he gives no examples that would lead us to believe this, except that this god presses upon us most severely.

The ancients used *obmoveto* for *admoveto*, as in the other examples that have been reported.

Titius says that *offendices* are knots by which the priestly cap is fastened and loosened. Antistius Labeo says that *olvatum* is a kind of measure.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *Olvatium*.]

*Occultu offerre* means “to place almost beneath the earth.”

*Objacuisse* was formerly used for *jacuisse* (“to have lain”).

*Praeceptat* occurs in a Saliar song and often means *praecipit* (“he commands”).

*Pa* is used for *parte* (“in part”), and *po* for *potissimum* (“especially”) in a Saliar song.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *populo*, “for the people.”]

*Promeneruat* likewise means *monet* (“he warns”).

*Praedotiot*: *praeoptat* (“he prefers”).

*Prospices*: “look ahead.”

*Pesnis*, or *poesnis*, means *pennis* (“wings”), just as *Casmenas* was used for *Camenas* and *Caesnas* for *caenas* (“dinners”).  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *Poenis*.]

*Polteo* means *ulteriore* (“farther, on the other side”).

*Polet*: *pollet* (“is powerful”), because the ancients had not yet doubled consonants.

*Plisima*: *plurima* (“very many”).  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *Plusima*.]

*Pretet tremonti*: *praetemunt*, “they pass before.”

*Perfines*: *perfringas* (“you may break through”).  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *perstringas*, “you may touch lightly.”]

*Promerion*: a special merit surpassing that of others; or it may mean *promedium* (“for the middle”), that is, “shares in”; or we use it for something held undivided.  
[Note: [Col. 1695] *promorion*; *medio*, “for the middle”; *ut*, “as.”]

*Priviclioes*: *privis*, that is, “to individuals.”

*Petila sura*: commonly interpreted as “dry and tightened.” Scaevola says that this is what an equine hoof is called when it is white.

*Pilumnoe poploe*, in a Saliar song, refers to the Romans, as though they were accustomed to use spears, or because they especially strike their enemies with shields.

Some say that *praepetes* are birds so called because they provide an auspice by flying past in front; others because they indicate things that we anticipate, or because they fly past; or they think the word was taken from Greek, because they fly before our sight. These explanations are foolish: they combine a Latin preposition with a Greek word. Poets, for the rest, use the term indiscriminately for all birds.

*Pilare*: to plunder. Some say that it is of Greek origin… [lacuna]

### Page 183

Some people are called *picati* whose feet are shaped like sphinxes, because the Dorians call such things *phicae*.

*Petulantes* and *petulci* are also names for those who attack with a brazen impulse and repeatedly assail others in order to harm them. Virgil in Book IV of the *Georgics*:

“Nor may the wanton sheep and kids trample the flowers”; and:

“They know the horned mothers… and the wanton lambs.”

Afranius in *Ida*:

“Our meeting, assembly, sport, mischief, and wantonness.”

At times the ancients seem to have used the word for “swift,” as may be understood from this verse:

“He sprang out like some sort of swift creature and shook his feet.”

*Petrae* are of two kinds. One is a natural rock projecting into the sea, which Ennius mentions in Book XI:

“Brought down from high above and covered with other huge rocks,”

and Laevius in *Centaurs*:

“Where I often [sat] upon the rocks.”

The other is made by human hands, as Aelius Gallus explains: a *petra* is a place whose right and left sides fill out an arch up to the level of the crown of the arch.

The ancients used *petissere* for *petere* (“to seek, attack”), in the same form as *lacessere* and *incessere*. But, as it seems to me, when they meant “to seek” more frequently, they used forms such as *petessant*, “they seek more frequently.”

*Petrones* generally refers to rustic people, because of their old-fashioned character and because they are rough and abrupt. [lacuna] Fields are now called *petrae*, just as *rupices* is derived from *rupes* (“rocks”).  
[Note: [Col. 1697] *a rupibus*, “from rocks.”]

Lucilius seems to think that *petauristae* were named from the *petaurum*, when he says:

“Just as mechanics leap high out of a *petaurum*.”

Aelius Stilo, however, says that they fly through the air, when he says:

“*Petaurista* properly, in Greek, because they fly *πρὸς ἀέρα*—‘into the air.’”

*Petoritu* is thought to be both a Gallic vehicle and to have received its name from the number four, namely its four wheels. Others think it is Oscan, because the Oscans also call four *petora*; others think it is Greek, but used in an Aeolic form.

*Petimina* are sores on the shoulders of pack animals; this is the common usage, and Lucilius also [mentions them].
