Licinius Imbrex*, for *Caecilius in Imbros*; *tunicula*, “little tunic,” for *cunicula*; *inter mare, et*, “between the sea and,” for *mare intra et*; *Lucilius*, for *Lucretius*; *efferantur*, “are carried up,” for *afferantur*; *ei*, “him,” for *eis*; *candens*, “shining white,” for *cedens*; *alites*, “birds of flight,” for *aut*; *picus autem*, “but the woodpecker,” for *picam aut*; *per sex eos. f. scilicet eos* is a corrupt alternative reading for the clause concerning his festival days.

[Col. 1693–1695] *amabo*, “please,” for *ambo*; *Volusinae*, for *Volusuinae*; *populi*, “of the people,” for *a populo*; *post*, “after,” for *propter*; *data*, “granted,” for *dicta*; *is*, “he,” for *his*; *ne legi Orchiae derogaretur*, “that the Orchian law should not be weakened”; *XXX bob.* means “thirty oxen”; *vicessis*, an alternative to *vincesis*; *colligebatur*, “was gathered,” for *cogebatur*; *nullam ... causam*, feminine forms for *nullum ... causa*; *olivitatem eam*, “that olive-harvest,” for *oblivitatem meam*; *ineptias*, “absurdities,” for *inertias*; *Urgum*, for *Uragu*; *Olvatium*, for *Olvatum*; *populo*, “for the people,” for *potissimum*; *Poesnis* and *Poenis* are alternative spellings for *Pesnis* and *pennis*; *Plusima*, for *Plisima*; *perstringas*, “you may touch lightly,” for *perfringas*; *promorion*, *medio*, and *ut* are alternative readings for *Promerion*, *medium*, and *aut*; *privicloes*, for *priviclio es*.

[Col. 1695–1697] *humeris*, “shoulders,” for *his*; *pedicus*, for *pedibus*; *petrisque*, “with rocks,” for *ceterisque*; *Laevius*, for *Levius*; *quae Jovis*, “which of Jupiter,” for *qui locus*; *expletura est*, “is about to fill out,” for *expletur usque*; *a rupibus*, “from rocks,” for *a rupicis*; and *is*, “they,” for *his* in the explanation of *petaurista*.

He mentions this when he says: “So that the petimen touches the nose, or the loins the neck.” Naevius also testifies that this name was customarily applied to the part between the two shoulders of a pig, which is called the *nectos* [Note: alternatively, *pectus*, “breast”], in his description of the sow [Note: alternatively, *sulliae*], when he says: “With the fish-petimen, which he had earned.”

**Pennas.** It is said that the ancients called feathers *peenas*, from the Greek, since the Greeks call things that are more winged *πετηνά* [Col. 1697B]. They likewise called them *pesnas*, as they called *caesnas*.

**Pictor.** Zeuxis the painter died of laughter while laughing uncontrollably at an old woman whom he had painted [the word *anum*, “old woman,” is supplied]. I do not see why this was reported here by Verrius, since he had undertaken to write about the meanings of words; yet he also included some verses, and tolerated rather foolish ones, under the pretended name of no author [Note: alternatively, “he reported this matter, and the verses are sufficiently foolish and belong to no author”]. They are as follows:

“What sort of thing will he finally do in his laughter? Unless he wants to become a painter, who died of laughter.”

**Picta.** The *picta*, which is now called the *toga*, was formerly called *purpurea*, and it was without pictorial decoration. Evidence for this is the painting in the temples of Vertumnus and Consus: in one, M. Fulvius Flaccus; in the other, T. [Note: alternatively, L.] Papirius Cursor are depicted in triumph. The *tunica palmata* was so called from the breadth of its purple stripes, whereas now it is named from the type of decoration.

**[Editorial interpolation.]** Verrius says that *impetum*, *industrium*, and *indulgentem* are formed on the same principle as *impune* and *immunis*. I am not sufficiently convinced by him.

**Pietati.** They say that a temple was consecrated to Pietas by Acilius [Note: Acilio] at the place where a woman once lived who secretly nourished her father, imprisoned there, with her breasts. For this deed, immunity [Note: alternatively, *impunitas*, “impunity”] was granted to her.

**Picus.** Some think that the bird *picus* was named from Picus, king of the Aborigines, by whom [lacuna].

**Piscatorium aes.** In the ancient manner, the money that is paid for fish on the Alban Mount is called “fishing-money.”

**Pedam.** It is commonly found in certain commentaries that the ancients called a human footprint, and especially the footprint of a foot, a *peda*.

**Pescia.** Aelius Stilo says that in the Saliar hymn *pescia* means head-coverings made from lambskins, because the Greeks call skins *pesce*, neuter plural.

**Pestiferum fulgur.** A “pestilential lightning-bolt” is so called when death or exile is customarily signified by it.

**Pisalitem.** Naevius calls Pantaleon a *pisalites*, that is, a tyrant born at Pisa, although those who originate there are otherwise now called *Pisani*, “Pisans.”

**Pedibus obsitum.** Titinius calls one covered with feet—that is, with lice—*pedicosus*, as follows: “He will be driven from the country, louse-ridden and filthy.”

The ancients used *pedes* for lice. Thus Plautus reports in the *Curculio*:

“Another kind, in my opinion, among human beings: flies, gnats, bedbugs, lice, and fleas.”  
[Note: alternatively, “another kind of pimps.”]

Livy likewise says in the *Gladiolus*: “Are they fleas, or bedbugs, or lice? Answer me.” Lucilius says: “When he saw me, he scratches his head and picks out lice.”

**Pesestas.** Among the other words spoken during a prayer when a farm is purified, *pesestas* seems to signify pestilence, as may be understood from the other words, when one says: “May you avert disease, death, defilement, mist, and skin disease.” [Note: alternatively, “which the curse-priests say during a curse.”]

**Pedum.** A *pedum* is a kind of crooked staff, as Virgil says in the *Bucolics*: “But take up the shepherd’s staff,” when he often asked me to do so.

**Pedem struit.** In the Twelve Tables this means “he flees,” as Servius Sulpicius says.

**Pistum.** The ancients used *pistum*, “polished by pounding” [Note: alternatively, “made smooth by pounding”], more often than we now use the corresponding word.

**Pedarium senatorem.** Lucilius uses this expression when he says: “Agipes began to cast his vote.” He is called this because, silently passing over to the person whose opinion he approves, he indicates what he thinks.

**Piscatorii ludi.** The “fishermen’s games” are so called because they are customarily held across the Tiber in June for the profit of fishermen.

**Piscinae publicae.** The name “public baths” still survives today, although the baths themselves no longer exist. The people used to come there both to swim and otherwise for exercise; hence Lucilius says: “A boxer with a blunt face, a sluggish fellow from the public bath.”

**Pectenatum tectum.** A roof divided into two parts in the likeness of a comb is called *pectenatum*, just as one divided into four parts is called *testudinatum*.

**Piari.** Verrius says, as though using a word peculiar to himself, that those who are insufficiently spirited, when they are not in possession of their minds, are *piari*, and that by certain words they are released from this disadvantage.

**Pignosa, pignora.** These forms arose in the same way as *Valesii* and *Auselii*, and *Pinosi* and *Palisi* [Note: *Pinasii*, *Papisii*].

**Pectuscum.** The Palatine district of the City was called *Pectuscum*. Romulus placed it facing that side where the Roman territory extended most broadly toward the sea, and because the city could be approached there most easily. The Tiber separated the Etruscan territory from the Roman; the other neighboring communities had certain hills set opposite them.

**Peculatus.** Today *peculatus* means any kind of public theft, but the word was derived from *pecus*, “cattle,” just as *pecunia*, “money,” itself was. Moreover, offenders too were fined in cattle, because there was not yet an abundance of bronze or silver. Hence the highest fine is still called the *suprema multa*.

**Piatrix.** A priestess who customarily performed expiation was called a *piatrix*. Some call her a *simulatrix*, others a *saga*, and others an *expiatrix*; the expiatory substances she uses are called by some *purgamenta*.

**Piacularis porta.** The “piacular gate” is so called because certain expiations were performed there; or, as Cloatius says, because when someone is released from a sacred obligation through an act of expiation, a sacrifice is offered there for the purpose of expiating and propitiating.

**Pigere.** *Pigere* is sometimes used for “to be delayed,” and sometimes for “to repent.”

**Pangere.** *Pangere* means “to fix.” Hence plants are said to be *pangi*, “fixed,” when they are planted in the earth.

[lacuna] **Permutatur.** This properly seems to be said of something transferred from one place to another; *commutatur*, however, refers to one thing being substituted for another. But the two words are now used indiscriminately.

## P.-T.

### Page 187

**Pierides.** The Muses seem to have been called *Pierides* because of the pleasantness and solitude of Mount Pierius, where they delight in secluded places because of their liberal studies.

**Perconctatio.** *Perconctatio*, “questioning,” seems to have been named from nautical usage, because sailors test and discover the depth of the water with a pole. For this reason Verrius says that its second syllable is also customarily written with *o*. This seems false to me: the word is *percunctatio*, because one who asks something inquisitively “goes through all things” (*per cunctas res it*), and therefore it is correctly written with the letter *u*.

**Perfugam.** Aelius Gallus says that a *perfuga* is a free person, slave, or enemy who has voluntarily gone over to his enemies. The same person is also called a *transfuga*, although some think that a *perfuga* is not so much one who flees from others as one who takes refuge with someone in hope of advantage.

**Perfacul.** The ancients said *perfacul* and *per se facul* for what we now call *facile*, “easily.” From this, *facultas* has remained in usage.

**Peremptalia fulgura.** Gracchus [Note: Granius] says that lightning-bolts are called *peremptalia* when, by their force, they destroy earlier lightning-bolts or omens in two ways: either by removing the earlier ones, or by means of a greater *manubia*, so that a third yields to a second and a second to a first. For just as all omens are overcome by a lightning-bolt, so a lightning-bolt that has struck is overcome by the *manubiae*.

**Perediam and bibesiam.** Plautus coined *perediam* and *bibesiam* in his customary fashion when he wished to express a desire to eat and drink.

**Peremere.** Cincius says in his book *On Ancient Words* that *peremere* means the same as “to prohibit”; Cato, however, used it in his book *On Military Matters* for “to damage” [Note: “The passages that should follow are given above, p. 33.”].

[lacuna] **Tabem.** The ancients used *tabes* for something that causes wasting. Sallustius also uses it frequently, as in the *Catiline*, when he says: “When a wasting disease had invaded the minds of most of the citizens”; and in Book IV of the *Histories*: “That custom, as a wasting disease, had gathered into the city” [Note: alternatively, “had been cast into the city”]. Cornificius [Note: Corvinus] uses it for Liburnia: “Because of this wasting disease and destruction of the entire household.”

**Tabellis.** The ancients used tablets instead of sheets of writing. By means of them they informed absent persons of whatever needed to be communicated back and forth, privately or publicly. Hence messengers are still called *tabellarii*, and tablets sent by emperors are so called.

**Tagax.** *Tagax* means “thief,” from *tangere*, “to touch” [Note: *tagere*]. Lucilius mentions the word: “And to be able to scratch the penis with his hand, boldly” [Note: alternatively, “to scratch with his hand, *tagacem*”].

**Tages.** A boy named Tages, son of Genius and grandson of Jupiter, is said to have given the twelve peoples of Etruria the discipline of haruspicy.

**Taminia.** *Taminia*, a kind of wild grape, seems to have been so called by Verrius because it is as wondrous (*tam mira*) as vermilion (*minium*).

**Talus.** *Talus* seems to have been used as a praenomen among the Sabine names.

**Talentorum.** There is more than one kind of talent. The Attic talent is six thousand denarii; the Rhodian [Note: “and seven thousand”]; the cistophoric, four thousand five hundred denarii; the Alexandrian, twelve [Note: thousand] denarii; the Neapolitan, six [Note: thousand] denarii; the Syracusan, three [Note: thousand] denarii; and the Rhegian, victoriati.

**Tane.** Aelius Stilo and Opillus Aurelius interpret *tane* as “to such an extent.” Thus Afranius says: “Is your little chest so full of spiders?”

**Thaleae.** Some say that the name *Thalia* [Note: *Thaleae*] was derived from the flowering of youth; others, because poems always flourish.

**Talipedare.** The ancients used *talipedare* for “to stagger in the feet from weariness,” as though one dragged one’s feet and seemed to stand on one’s ankles, or repeatedly lifted one’s feet.

**Tam.** *Tam* has this meaning when we use it as a kind of antecedent, to which we add *quam*, as when we say: “So excellent a work was bought at so small a price”—that is, “in such a way”; just as in Greek one says *οὕτως ἀγαθόν*, “so good.” Conversely, we say: “As bad a poet as Homer is, so good is Choerilus” [Note: *Choetilus*].

The ancients also used *tam* for *tamen*, “nevertheless.” Naevius says: “What if he is silent, while he watches, nevertheless he knows what has been written” [Note: alternatively, “Who, if he is silent …”]. Ennius says: “Those things of mine nevertheless enabled me to attain peace.” Titinius says: “When we do well, nevertheless we suffer so badly, as certain men report.” He also says: “Although you are worthless, nevertheless, by Castor, I have looked after you as you eat” [Note: alternatively, “yet, by Castor, I have looked after you.”]

### Page 189

**Tandem.** When *tandem* means “at some time,” it is sometimes added redundantly, as in Terence’s *Phormio*: “So then, did Antipho marry a wife against my orders?” Here it does not indicate any time. Cicero even doubles its temporal meaning when he says *tandem aliquando*, “at long last.”

**Tauri verbenaeque.** In a commentary on sacred rites, *tauri verbenaeque* signifies figurines made of flour.

**Tama.** A *tama* is said to occur when, through the exertion of travel, blood descends into the legs and produces swelling. Lucilius [Note: alternatively, Lucretius] says: “A swelling appears in the groin; pimples; *tama*; let not a *boa* harm [you].”

**Taenias.** Verrius interprets the Greek word *taeniai* as meaning a woolen ornament for the head of an honored person. Thus Caecilius says in the *Androgynus*: “A tomb full of ribbons, as is customary”; and elsewhere: “While he was binding the wound with a ribbon.” Ennius says in the *Alexander*: “Flying down from heaven with a crown and ribbons.” Accius says in the *Neoptolemus*: “It is better to adorn [it] than to strip the city of its ribbons” [Note: alternatively, “of its ribbons,” *e taeniis*].

**Taedulum.** The ancients sometimes used *taedulum* for “disagreeable,” something that was a nuisance to everyone.

**Tatium.** Laniuvius [Note: alternatively, Lavinius] says that Tatius was killed by the friends of those ambassadors whom the bandits Tinini [Note: alternatively, Tatiani] had killed, but that he was buried in the laurel grove on the Aventine. This has no more to do with the meaning of words than do many other matters, both those already passed over and those that will be reported hereafter.

**Taurorum specie.** Rivers are represented in the form of bulls—that is, they are fashioned with horns—because they are fierce, like bulls.

**Talionis.** Verrius says that the Twelve Tables mention *talio* as follows: “If he breaks a limb, unless he makes an agreement with him, let there be retaliation” [Note: *rapsit* for *rapit* is an alternative reading]. He does not explain what the term means, I think because it is well known: the law permits equal vengeance.

**Tarquitias.** It is commonly thought that the stairs made by King Tarquinius Superbus were called *Tarquitiae* in abhorrence of that name.

**Tarpeiae.** Some think that a likeness of Tarpeia in the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus was called *Tarpeia*, in memory of the maiden who, after making a bargain with the Sabine enemies that they should give her what they carried in their left hands, admitted them with King Tatius. Later, when peace was being made, he stipulated with Romulus that the place should always be open to the Sabines [Note: *esse*, “to be,” or alternatively *etiam*, “also”].

**Tam perit quam extrema faba.** “It perishes like the last bean” is a proverb, because the last bean is generally crushed or plucked off by passers-by.

**Tappulam.** Valerius Valentinus composed, under a fictitious name, a convivial law in a humorous poem. Lucilius quotes it as follows: “They laugh at the Tappulan law, collecting the rich man’s provisions” [Note: *congere* for *congere*].

**Termonem.** Ennius, following Greek usage, said *termo* for what we now call *terminus*, “boundary,” as follows: “He advances at great speed to where the boundary has been restored”; and: “Before the good exhorter, rather than at the boundary.”

**Trientem.** T. Quintius, Dictator, wrote that he had given Jupiter as a gift a golden crown weighing two pounds and a third, after he had captured nine cities in nine days and a tenth, Praeneste, by surrender [Note: alternatively, “the surrender of Praeneste”]. Cincius says in Book II of the *Mystagogicon* that this means two pounds and a third, an expression still used today when we say that a piece of wood is *bes alterum*, that is, has a breadth of one foot and two-thirds. Likewise, *sestertium* means two asses and a half, the third.

Also, when there are three asses and a fourth part [Note: “a quadrans”], the fourth is called a *quadrans*.

### Page 191

[lacuna] **Tersum diem.** The ancients used *tersum diem* for a clear day; he says that he has no authority for the expression.

**Teretinatibus.** [The name was derived] from a river [lacuna].

**Tripudium.** [lacuna] “he dances in triumph” [lacuna] “because the earth must be stamped”: for *pavire* means “to strike,” from which *pavimenta*, “pavements,” is also derived. This comes from the Greek, since they say *παίειν* for what we call “to strike” [lacuna].

**Taminare.** *Taminare* means “to violate” [lacuna], and *contaminare*, “to defile,” was evidently derived from it [lacuna].

**Teres.** Something rounded in length is *teres*, such as the beams that nature supplies.

**Temetum.** *Temetum* means wine. Plautus says in the *Aulularia*:

“Are you going to prepare a wedding here for Strobilus, Ceres?”  
“Why?”  
“Because I see that no wine has been brought.”

Pomponius says in the *Decima*: “Not much wine, but very much.” Novius says in the *Duobus Dossenis*: “Follow, drink deeply; follow, fear of wine.” The same author says in the *Funus*: “Come, go out, carry away the drunken man” [Note: alternatively, “drunkenness”]; and in the *Surdus*: “I have drunken daughters, but look, I see them coming.” Afranius says in the *Consobrini*: “By Pollux, more than that drunken, worthless woman.”

**Tintinnare.** Naevius uses *tintinnare* [Note: alternatively, *titinnire*] as follows: “There they made such a clatter with the millstones; the fetters were jingling.” Afranius says: “I hear the doorkeeper’s impediments jingling.”

**Tributorum conlatio.** In addition to the assessment mentioned elsewhere at the beginning of the account, there is another kind of levy based on the census. It is called a rash or emergency levy, such as was collected after the city had been captured by the Gauls, because during the preceding fifteen years there had been no other census [Note: alternatively, “no other people”]. Likewise, in the Second Punic War, when M. Valerius Laevinus and M. Claudius Marcellus were consuls, the Senate and the People contributed to the treasury whatever they had [Note: alternatively, “whatever they could.”]

**Tentipellium.** Artorius thinks that *tentipellium* is an iron shoe or instrument by which hides are stretched, and that Afranius therefore said in the *Promo* [Note: alternatively, *Primo*]: “I believe I have those tentipellia in my hands.” Verrius says that Titinius thought it was a cosmetic by which wrinkles are stretched, when he says: “The tentipellium is applied; the wrinkles on the face are stretched.” In that passage he used the word metaphorically (*τροπικῶς*).

**Tignum.** *Tignum* is called not only the timber used in buildings but also timber used in vineyards, as in the Twelve Tables: “A beam joined to a building or vineyard—let no one remove it” [Note: alternatively, “let no one remove it by the stake”].

**Tela.** *Tela* properly seems to refer to missiles, the name having evidently been transferred from the Greek, since the Greeks call things sent from afar *τηλόθεν*, whereas we call them *eminus*, “from a distance.” Similarly, weapons held in the hands and hanging from the shoulders are called *arma*, since that part of the body should be thought to be called the *armus* among us no less than [lacuna].

**Tigillum Sororium.** [lacuna]

**Vici.** Communities begin to be called *vici* when they arise in the countryside and do not have villas there, as among the Marsi and Peligni. Some of these villages partly possess a commonwealth and are said to possess legal jurisdiction; others possess none of these things, yet markets are held there for conducting business, and annually village magistrates and *pagi* magistrates are appointed.

In a second sense, the term defines those buildings that are contiguous within towns whose parts are separated from one another by roads and districts and distinguished by different names for the sake of differentiation.

In a third sense, it defines buildings that a private person constructs in a town—that is, each person on his own property—in such a way that there is a passage through the building by which the inhabitants have access to their respective dwellings. These people are not called *vicani*, “villagers,” as are those who live either in the town’s *vici* or in the countryside.

### Page 193

**Viget.** The word seems to have been derived from *vim agere*, “to exercise strength,” but not in hostile actions; rather, it refers to things that, with a swift [Note: “swiftly”] and energetic spirit, strive toward good fruit [lacuna].

**Voisgram.** A bird that plucks itself is called *voisgram*. The augurs call the same bird *fucillans* [Note: alternatively, *fecilitra*] [lacuna].

**Vigintiquinque.** In the Twelve Tables, *vigintiquinque poenae* signifies twenty-five asses.

**Victima.** Aelius Stilo says that a *victima* is a calf, because of its strength. Others say it is an animal led bound to the altar, or one sacrificed because of conquered enemies [Note: alternatively, “on behalf of conquered enemies”].

**Vectigal.** *Vectigal* is the name for money owed to the people as tribute, military pay, equestrian tax, and ordinary tax.

**Viae.** Roads are both public, on which everyone may travel, and private, which others are forbidden to use except those to whom they belong [lacuna]. “They shall construct the roads; the stones are [lacuna], and let him drive his animals wherever he wishes.”

**Viatores.** *Viatores* are called those who attend upon magistrates. The reason is that at the beginning all the tribes had fields near the City and people were constantly engaged in rural work; consequently their services were more frequently needed on the road, since the magistrates generally summoned people from the fields.

**Verticulas.** When Lucilius says *verticulas*, he calls vertebrae, “spinal joints,” by this name.

**Vernae.** Those born in the villas in spring are called *vernae*, because spring is the season assigned by nature to reproduction. At that time Numa Pompilius established a religious rite for Mars, to secure peace and concord between the Sabines and Romans, so that the *vernae* might live and not conquer. The Romans called those born there *vernae*, that is, “born in that place”; for the Sabines, who were allied with the Roman People, considered it a disastrous choice to conquer them.

**Vergiliae.** The Pleiades are so called because with their rising spring ends and summer begins.

**Vastum.** *Vastum* means “great,” but it is also used for “empty.” Accius says: “Now Peleus will make this city vast with iron”; Pacuvius says:

“What sort of things, rough and uncultivated in their vastness …”

### Page 194

**Ve victis.** “Woe to the conquered” is thought to have entered proverbial use when, after Rome had been captured by the Senonian Gauls, gold was being weighed out according to an agreement and treaty so that they would withdraw. When Appius Claudius complained that the barbarians were demanding it with unfair weights, Brennus, king of the Gauls, added his sword to the weights and said: “Woe to the conquered.” Later, Furius Camillus pursued him and cut down his forces after surrounding him by ambush. When Brennus complained that this was being done contrary to the treaty, Camillus is said to have repaid him with the same words.

**Vegrande.** Some say that *vegrande* means “badly great,” as *vecors* means “of an evil heart” and *vesanus* “of one who is badly sound.” Others say it means “small” or “little,” as when we say *vegrande frumentum*, “a small quantity of grain.” Plautus says in the *Cistellaria*: “Who, unless you go, advances with an excessively small step.”

**Vecors.** *Vecors* means “disturbed” and “evil-hearted.” Pacuvius says in the *Iliona*: “Who, in swift superstition, with a mad wife”; and Novius says in [lacuna]: “He drives sorrow and madness from his heart.”

**Vapula Papiria.** *Vapula Papiria* was an ancient proverb. Sinnius Capito reports that it was customarily said when people wished to signify to those making threats that they despised and disregarded them, relying on the right of freedom. Plautus says in the *Feneratrix*:

“Hey, you—the freedman is said to have done in barbarian country what he did to his patroness; that is why I say … freedwoman, greetings: ‘Vapula Papiria.’”

“Barbarian country” means Italy. Aelius says that *vapula* is used here for *dole*, “suffer pain.” Varro says it means *peri*, “perish,” as Terence shows in the *Phormio*: “Do you not come to your senses, you scoundrel?” And Plautus in the *Curculio*:

“Will you return the woman, or shall I throw you before this sword of mine—rascal?”  
“Vapula, then—I emphatically order you to be beaten, so that you do not frighten me.”  
[Note: alternatively, “I order you to be beaten.”]

### Page 195

**Vacerram.** Aelius and many others say that a *vacerra* is a post to which horses are customarily tied. Ateius Philologus, however, says that the word signifies an extremely harsh insult, like *vecors* and *vesanus*. Livy is cited as saying: “Mad and with a destructive madness” [Note: alternatively, “wickedly mad, *vacerra*.”]

**Vagorem.** *Vagor* is used for “wailing.” Ennius, Book XVI: “What a clamor of the attacking army, a flying wail.” Lucretius, Book II: “And the wailing prevails and mingles with the funeral.”

**Valvoli.** The pods of beans were called *valvoli*, as though *vallivoli*, because they are shaken out when a *vallum* is made [Note: alternatively, “when broken”].

**Vagulato.** In the Twelve Tables, *vagulato* means a legal inquiry accompanied by abuse: “If anyone lacks a witness, let him go and make a public outcry at the doorway on the third day.”

**Valgos.** Opillus Aurelius [Note: Opilius] and many others say that a person with unequal calves is called *valgus*. Plautus says in the *Miles Gloriosus*: “You see most people with malformed ankles, crooked and twisted.” In the *Silitergo* he says: “If she later bears me marked children, whether bow-legged, knock-kneed, with joined legs, squinting, or thick-lipped.”

**Viere.** *Viere* means “to bind,” as this verse demonstrates: “They went, weakly binding a sacred wreath.” Hence come *vimina*, “withies,” and wicker vessels, which are bound together.

**Vermina.** *Vermina* are bodily pains accompanied by a kind of minute movement, as though the flesh were being cut apart by worms. This pain is called in Greek *στρόφος*.

**Veruta pila.** Javelins are called *veruta* because they have points fixed onto them [Note: alternatively, *verua*]. Ennius, Book X: “[They covered] five hundred courses, often with javelins” [lacuna].

**Uruat.** Ennius uses *uruat* in the *Andromeda* to mean “surrounds.” The word comes from the furrow made by the plowshare in founding a city, whose shape is very like a hook because of the curvature of the plow-beam and the tooth to which the plowshare is attached. He says: “It surrounds the head on every side, up to four hundred feet from the ground.”

**Ungulus.** In the Oscan language, *ungulus* means “ring,” as in [lacuna]: “If she has found anything worth preserving as a memorial, for whoever should seek them, it is the ring he took from her while drunk.” Pacuvius says in the *Iliona*: “While he resisted, I forcibly removed this ring from him”; and in the *Atalanta*: “I display the ring hanging from my left arm.”

### Page 196

**Unciaria lex.** The law introduced by L. Sulla and Pompeius Rufus began to be called the *Unciarian Law*. It ordained that debtors should pay a tenth part [lacuna].

**Venenum.** The ancients used *venenum* for a substance whose color changes when it is used to dye something, as Ennius says: “With that substance in which it has already once been soaked.”

**Ventabant.** It is plausible that the ancients said *ventabant*, especially when the preposition was added [lacuna], meaning *adventabant*, “they were approaching.”

**U.ntupum.** [The word] means [lacuna], what the Greeks call *ὕειν*, “to rain” [lacuna].

**Venditiones.** In ancient times the leases of the censors were called *venditiones*, because the produce of public places was, as it were, sold.

**Viminalis.** Both a gate and a hill are called *Viminalis*, because there seems to have been a grove of willows (*vimina*) there; there is also an altar consecrated to Jupiter Viminius.

**Vindex.** *Vindex* comes from *vindicare*, “to claim,” because it prevents one who has been seized from being held by another.

**Vineae.** Verrius teaches that *vineae* are so called because they are rich in wine; certain military engines are also called *vineae* because of their resemblance to vineyards.

**Vivatus and vividus.** Poets use *vivatus* and *vividus* for “vigorous,” deriving them from great strength.

**Vindiciae.** *Vindiciae* are things concerning which there is a dispute. More properly, however, the word *ius*, “right,” is used, because the matter arises between those who are contending [Note: alternatively, “*vindiciae* are rather said to arise between those who are contending.”]

Cato says in the work he wrote to L. Furius *On Water*: [lacuna] “The praetors award possession according to the people.” Lucilius says: “No one here respects a claim, a sacred rite, or divine power.”

Cincius says of this word: “In former times those objects were called *vindiciae* that had been taken from an estate and brought into court.” Servius Sulpicius, however, says that *vindicia* was formed in the singular, and means the matter concerning which there is a dispute, from *vindicare*, “to claim” [lacuna].

In the Twelve Tables: “If he has brought a false claim, and if the other party wishes it, let the praetor appoint three arbiters; by their decision [lacuna], let the damage be deducted twofold from the produce.”

[Note: The beginning of the fragment consisted of the word *Manubiae* and extended to *Malo cruce*. These passages are found in the *Schedes*, pp. 167–172. After *Malo cruce* came *Mutum*, etc., which is placed on p. 1 of the Fragment as far as *Ordinarium hominem*, p. 32. After *Ordinarium* follow the passages found in the *Schedes*, pp. 172–182. The rest is complete in the Fragment as far as *Tablinum*, p. 164. After *Tablinum* follow the passages beginning with the word *Tabem*, p. 187, [Col. 1703B] and continuing through the word *Vindiciae*, which was the end of the Fragment. URSINUS.—“The end of the Fragment,” the learned man correctly says; not, however, the end of the Farnesian Codex, which, as they testify, is also mutilated at the end. Apart from the final words of the gloss *Vindiciae*, the words *Vehere* and *Veredos*, to be noted below, make this still clearer. The final part of Paul’s *Epitome* also more fully supplements the glosses *Vindicium* and *Vindicia* in the excellent Paris manuscript no. 7662, which none of the editors so far appears to have consulted. Lindemann, certainly, is as ignorant of it as he is of the other manuscripts of Paul preserved in our Royal Library. But more on these matters elsewhere. E. E.]

### Notes concerning the text of the Farnesian Codex

[Note: Passages not marked with a name are to be attributed to Fulvius Ursinus.]

**P. 4, under *Mundus*.** After the word *Volcanalia* add, from Paul’s *Epitome*: “On the third day before the Nones of October.” [Ursinus: The editors before Augustine had already indicated the lacuna with their customary note, “defective” or “fragment.” Compare *Redarguisse*, p. 81.]

**P. 7, under *Manumitti*.** We have restored this formula of manumission to its original integrity, if I am not mistaken, using the wording in which it was formulated, since the Augustinian edition omitted some words and distorted others.

**P. 10, under *Mater Matuta*.** The words of Festus that follow must be repaired from Paul’s wording. One letter, however, is different: *manis* has been written instead of *manes*, in my opinion through the copyist’s error. A. AUG.

**P. 10, under *Naenia*.** Glossary: “*Noenia*, *ἐπιτάφιος ᾠδή*,” “a funeral song.” The Greek words added at the end are exactly what is read in the exemplar. It is well known, however, what *νήτη* is.

**P. 12, under *Nec*.** *Nec escit* should be written instead of *nec esit*. For the ancients said *escit* for *erit*, “will be,” and *superescit* for *supererit*, “will remain.”

**P. 17, under *Navalis*.** “What if the oars project?” Should we write this instead as “What if the oars flash forth”? Certainly we shall come closer to the ancient reading, which is *rem geminent*.

**P. 18, under *Naevia*.** I do not know what the fragment following *Naevia*—[lacuna]—belongs to. Varro, Book I of *On the Latin Language* (V, 19), says that *cavum*, “hollow,” comes from *chaos*, from which everything arose, and that *caelum*, “sky,” was named from *cavum*.

**P. 20, under *Nuptias*.** It seems that *legem quoque funestam*, “also a deadly law,” should be read instead of the corrupt word *parenstam*.

**P. 21, under *Nucupata*.** The exemplar has this form, *nucupata*, instead of *nuncupata*, following the ancient spelling convention, which is contradicted by *formonsus* and *gnefonsus*. The remainder should be read as we noted in the margin of the page: “*Nominata cerca* etc.; when he makes the bond and names the slave with his tongue, let that be the law”—that is, “as he named him.”

**P. 23, under *Noverca*.** Since the Fragment has *veterannia*, not *ecterannia* as others have transcribed it, we have derived from that reading *veteres Annia*, “the elder Annia.” Whom this Annia married remains to be investigated.

**Ad p. 23.** The Farnesian Codex was written in two columns on paper of considerable width, but fire consumed almost one third of it. The first and fourth columns of each folio are intact; of the second, the left portion survives, and of the third, the right portion, with approximately half-lines remaining. The end of the lost writing follows no definite line but corresponds to the course taken by the fire.

Here, on folio VI, column 3, if one offsets the losses against one another, approximately half a line is missing—that is, in each line about sixteen to nineteen letters. At the beginning of this gloss, however, a space of fifteen letters is empty because two of them belong to the preceding gloss. Having explained this, I transcribe the gloss below with my supplements:

“—The nine opponents] T. Sicinius and Volscius being consuls, when they had entered into a conspiracy] against him. They are said to have been burned by the Roman People in the cir]cus and buried in that region] which is immediately around the place where there is a site paved with white stone. Their names were:] Opiter Verginius Tricostus, … Valerius] Laevinus, Postumus Cominius Auruncus, …]ilius Tolerinus, L. Vetusius Geminus. Sempr]onius Atratinus, Verginius Tricostus, Mu]tius Scaevola. Sex. Fusius Fusus.”

(Niebuhr, *Roman History*, vol. II, p. 143. We shall examine elsewhere how he defends his conjectures. E. E.)

**P. 24, under *Nixi di*.** After the word *mensae*, the exemplar adds *tripedi*, “three-footed,” but in another hand. I think it was added by way of a scholium (*σχολιαστικῶς*).

**P. 27, under *Oculissimum*.** In the Augustinian edition this passage is so faulty and distorted that Festus’s meaning is scarcely perceptible in it.

**P. 31, under *Ortygia*.** Since in the exemplar the adverb *nunc* had been written by the copyist with two letters (*nc*) placed above the line, an error arose in the Augustinian book: *nunc* was not printed, and the entire sentence was altered because one sentence had slipped away.

**P. 32, under *Orae*.** In place of *quam expediam*, we emended in the margin to *qua me expediam*, and we consider this the correct emendation.

**P. 33, under *Persicus*.** The verse of Plautus in the exemplar has *persibus* instead of *persicus*; Varro likewise has it in Book VI (VII, 107) of *On the Latin Language*.

**P. 35, under *Porriciam*.** Varro, Book V (VI, 54) of *On the Latin Language*: “What has been profaned,” he says, “is what has been consumed in sacred rites; hence formerly everything that had been profaned was consumed in temples …” These words belong under *profanata*, which we derived from the two words *profana ea*. Since the rest of the Augustinian edition has been displaced from its proper place, we restored it according to the exemplar and restored many mutilated passages.

**P. 37, under *Oratores*.** On inspecting the exemplar more carefully, we restored much that is missing from the Augustinian edition. In addition, we changed the corrupt word *propte* to *propterea*, and *decretoribus* to *deprecatoribus*.

**P. 40, under *Plorare*.** The exemplar has *od* in the law of Numa.

**P. 43, under *Parare*.** The exemplar writes *acere* instead of *agere*, following the ancient convention by which *c* was used for *g*.

**P. 43, under *Peregrinos*.** We repaired Festus’s passage from the words of the *Digest*, Book I, title 11. In the Augustinian edition it had been incorrectly joined to the word *parare*.

**P. 44, under *Primanus*.** This is exactly what appears in the exemplar. The remainder may have been added either by Paul or by someone else who wished to illustrate the passage with an example and explanation.

**P. 45, under *Potituim*.** The exemplar has *decimam bovum*, “a tenth of cattle,” in the ancient spelling, as it has *foro bovario* below.

**P. 49, under *Praetor*.** This entire passage was absent from the other books. A. AUG.

**P. 49, under *Potestur*.** The exemplar plainly reads: *in ea qua vocis cum*, so that it may perhaps need to be emended to *in ea quae est*. The word *est*, however, appears to have been added by another hand.

**P. 51, under *Pascales*.** The exemplar initially had *Tarentino*; later *Terentino* was written over it.

**P. 55, under *Publica Pondera*.** It is difficult to determine whether the exemplar reads *Oetier* or *oïtier*, because the letters are fading.

**P. 57, under *Praeclamitatores*.** The exemplar plainly reads: “so that people may abstain from work.”

**P. 63, under *Quirites*.** The exemplar plainly has [lacuna] “there is a herald, who at funerals …,” so that it seems necessary to read: “The evidence is the herald who [acts] at proclaimed funerals.”

**P. 79, under *Rumentum*.** The exemplar has [lacuna] *erim vis canerit*, not, as the Augustinian edition has it, *crimen avis canerit*. Here he has certainly made an already obscure passage from antiquity still more obscure.

**P. 81, under *Redarguisse*.** After the word *genus*, the pre-Augustinian editors place *FRAG.*, as they customarily do wherever the writing of an ancient fragment fails. Something does indeed seem to have dropped out here. Compare p. 4, under *Mundus*.

**P. 85, under *Refriva*.** The word *tevirfico* is corrupt; others have replaced it with *e tritico*, “from wheat.” Perhaps *revertantur*, “let them return,” should be written.

**P. 87, under *Procul Patricium*.** I think the word *patricium* was added.

**P. 88, under *Relegati*.** Since the exemplar has *Senatui que Consulto*, not *Senatus consulto*, I prefer *magistratuus* to be read instead of *magistratus*.

**P. 92, under *Rideo*.** In the ancient book this passage reads *Sex. Pomp. Festi, lib. XVIII*. A. AUG.

**P. 94, under *Religionis*.** The Festus Fragment plainly has [lacuna] *in ara*, “on the altar.”

**P. 96, under *Recipie*.** The exemplar has *recipiem*.

**P. 104, under *Satur*.** Some material is missing at the end. I think the word should be *obliqua*, “sloping,” rather than *pro portione*, “according to proportion.” For it should have said *saturis, viris, caronis*, not *saturi, viri, carnis*. See Charisius, Book II. A. AUG.
[Col. 1705D] p. 109, s.v. *Solatum*. In the exemplar it reads *arquato*, so that he appears to have called jaundiced persons *arquati* from the color of gold, because country people are said to be *solati* from the color of the sun; for that passage . . . . *rigine* is plainly *aurigine*.

p. 110, s.v. *Sospes*. In the Augustinian edition this fragment is so badly mutilated that no sound sense can be extracted from it.

p. 110, s.v. *Sucula*. Here too the passage has been handled exceedingly badly in the Augustinian edition. We published it according to the exemplar’s authority, making *quinque* out of the corrupt word *ruintque*, and emending *loquenti* to *loquendi*. This spelling practice is found both in ancient monuments and very frequently in this very fragment, where one finds *set* for *sed*, *adque* for *atque*, *quodannis* for *quotannis*, and countless other forms of the same kind. Cf. the note on p. 155.

p. 112, s.v. *Sulci*. See whether *fictum* should better be read for what is written in the exemplar.

p. 112, s.v. *Suasum*. Perhaps one should write *persuadeatur* for *persuadetur*; for in the manuscript *Epitome* it is *persuadentur*, showing that *persuadeatur* was written there as well.

p. 114, s.v. *Suppernata*. Politian recognizes Festus’s reading in the *Miscellanies*, chapter 73, and transcribed *suppernata*. I am therefore surprised that Antonius Augustinus wrote that Politian was mocked by Marullus because he substituted *expernata* for *suppernata* in Catullus.

p. 118, s.v. *Sub vitem*. In the exemplar Lucilius has *subsit*, as we printed it, not *subit*; for the latter Paulus has *submisit* in the *Epitome*.

p. 120, s.v. *Struere*. *Adicere*, rather than *adjicere*, is written in the exemplar, according to the ancient spelling practice.

p. 123, s.v. *Stipes*. *Ostium* should be written without the mark of aspiration, although the exemplar has *hostium*, just as above in *Scrupi* it has *hostreis* for *ostreis*.

p. 126, s.v. *Sterilem*. The word *cipit*, which occurs in the exemplar, may be accepted, if you prefer it to *concipit*.

p. 126–127, s.v. *Sycomorus Saccor*. Perhaps *Saccorum*; for I cannot think what else could be said. A.A. — Isidore, XVII, 7: “*Sycomorus*: *ficus* (‘fig’) and *morus* (‘mulberry’) are Greek names.” In the printed editions, however, *sicut* has been corruptly written for *ficus*. URS. — Ursinus therefore read *Sycomorus*, at least in the margin, which we restored. In the editions of Augustinus and Scaliger, the torn fragments of this gloss, displaced from their proper position, can scarcely be recognized; Dacerius did indeed complete it from the Roman edition, but, contrary to the principle of alphabetical order—which all editors after Augustinus profess to follow—inserted it at the beginning of the letter S. E.E.

p. 127, s.v. *Sacrem*. . . . . The exemplar plainly has *ine* (?) and from this we made *sanguine*.

p. 127, s.v. *Sacrificulus*. I think that those final letters found in the exemplar, . . . . *utus*, indicate the name of Sicinius, who was called Bellutus. For it is possible that Verrius followed historians other than Livy and Dionysius, who report Marcus Papirius as the first *Sacrificulus*.

[Col. 1706C] p. 129, s.v. *Sagmina*. We added in the margin, from the *Epitome*, the verse of Naevius that is missing from the exemplar. [Ennius apud Cicero, *On Duties* III, 29]: “O nourishing Faith, fitted with wings, and oath of Jupiter.” URS. — Yet I do not see that Festus’s text is thereby correctly established, and Paulus does not remedy the matter in the other fragment of this gloss. Lindemann is certainly mistaken in presenting to us the words “the sacred law of Jupiter by means of *sagmen*” as a verse of Naevius. But I shall discuss this and other matters of the same kind elsewhere. E.E.

p. 137, s.v. *Salentinos*. The exemplar has *quam d . . . .*, which, through the fault of the printers, was not reproduced with complete clarity. From this fragment we made *quam dicunt*. URS. — Elsewhere, at Ursinus’s suggestion, we corrected the text, as at p. 126, s.v. *Sycomorus*, and p. 152, s.v. *Sacramento*. Nevertheless, we often restored the division mark by conjecture wherever it was plainly absent before or after a Greek word, although it was uncertain whether it belonged to the manuscript reading or to the supplements. E.E.

p. 140, s.v. *Spicit*. Pomponius Laetus read Ennius’s verse as follows:

> When the king from the lofty mountains looked down upon them of his own accord.

The exemplar certainly has: *Quos ubi rex . . . . ulo spexit de contibus celsis* (“When the king . . . . ulo looked down from the lofty *contibus*”), so that *sedulo* or *paulo* should be read.

p. 140, s.v. *Spintyrnix*. The name of the poet whose words are quoted is missing. A. AUG. — We added the lacuna mark, as elsewhere, although Ursinus was silent. E.E.

p. 142, s.v. *Scrutillus*. From *sullus* we made *suillus*, and for the corrupt word *ivillum* we emended to *scrutillum*. There can be no doubt about *suillus*, since in this exemplar the letter *l* is often written in place of *i*. I remember having read of *scrutillus*, but I do not have time to investigate where.

p. 142, s.v. *Scrupi*. The verses of Ennius cited here by Festus, from the *Andromache*, survive in Nonius under *Scapres*. The exemplar has: “Ennius in An. . . not [Col. 1707A] Ar . . . . . .” Hence arose the error by which some wrote “in the *Judgment of the Arms*,” although the verse is from the *Andromache*. In the same exemplar the reading is likewise *asperi*, not *aspera*.

p. 143, s.v. *Scelerata*. The exemplar plainly has . . . . . *s. i.* “She is called Carmentalis” (so?).

p. 144, s.v. *Sexus*. The old book has *secus* at the beginning, but *sexus* in the examples. A. AUG.

p. 147, s.v. *Sifus*. We think that the word whose final letters alone remain in the exemplar was *praetoris*: that much space has been left. Or, if one prefers, *curatoris*. Both occur in ancient fragments of laws.

p. 147, s.v. *Seplasia*. The exemplar has . . . . *on M. Cicero*, which I think belonged to “Cicero mentions in the *In Pisonem*.”

p. 147, s.v. *Saticula*. The exemplar plainly has . . . . *iam*, from which we made *coloniam*.

p. 148, s.v. *Segesta*. Hermolaus, in his commentary on Pliny III, 8, read *obsceno omine* for the exemplar’s *nomine*.

p. 149, s.v. *Servorum*. The exemplar has *cervos*, where others printed *servos*. We retain the ancient reading.

p. 149, s.v. *Sispitem*. What Festus says is true: the ancients called Juno *Sispes*, except that on coins the form is *IVNO SISPITA*. Thus here too it appears that one should read *Sispitam* and *Sospitam*.

p. 151, s.v. *Sontica*. Agellius cites Cato on the Floridian affair at IX, 12 and X, 13. Since the exemplar has . . . . “there the *sontica* cause . . . .,” it is sufficiently clear that the case of *A. Atili* is to be supplied.

p. 151, s.v. *Spiciunt*. Cato’s speech *Against Thermus concerning the Ten Men* is frequently cited by Festus and by Agellius, XIII, 24. I have found no reference to “the Seven Men,” so perhaps *decem* should be written here as well in place of *septem*.

p. 154, s.v. *Silatum*. The exemplar has *jantaculum et jajuni*. The glossary likewise has: *Jantat*, “he breakfasts,” *ἀκρατίζει* (“he drinks unmixed wine”); *Jantaculum*, “breakfast,” *ἄκρατον* (“unmixed wine”). We have seen this spelling in other manuscript books as well.

p. 155, s.v. *Secespitam*. *Rediculo* is written in the exemplar for *reticulo*, according to that old practice of using *d* for *t*, discussed above (in the note on p. 110). The same exemplar also has *tubae*, not *nubae* as in other editions. *Tubae* is used for *tubis*. The word *cancella* somehow entered the supplement to this fragment through a copyist’s error. [For *repagula*, which appears in the *Errata*, and which we restored. E.E.]

p. 159, s.v. *Tullios*. Paulus’s manuscript *Epitome* reads: “Some have said that the *Tullii* were *Silani*, others *rivi*, others violent projections of blood flowing in an arc,” and the rest as in Festus. In an old Latin–Greek lexicon *Silvanus* is explained by *Κρουνός* (“spring”), and perhaps that should therefore be read both here and in Cornelius Celsus. What if, instead of *sanguinis* (“of blood”), we read *amnis* (“of a river”), since what follows is “such as are at Tibur”? But nothing should be changed rashly.

p. 160, s.v. *Topper*. We placed *mature* (“in due time”) in the margin for *temere* (“rashly”), because that is the reading below. We also read *homonem* for *humanum*, from Ennius’s verse, “He was feeding a wretched man”; and above, in the *Epitome*, s.v. *Hemona*, it reads: “They called a man *homonem*.” Attius’s verse in the *Io* may perhaps be read: “Quickly, as happens, does the father’s anger drive him out?” or “The father drove that woman out.” The word *inferinuntur*, which the ancients used for *inferuntur* (“are brought in”), has been omitted in the Augustinian edition.

p. 161, s.v. *Tutulum*. The exemplar plainly has: *formâ e tali*; hence the Augustinian edition printed *forma e tali*, although it should have been written *forma metali*.

p. 168, s.v. *Monstrum*. At the end of this gloss we indicated a lacuna in which the word *Monitores*, certainly explained by the following verses, has disappeared. A. Augustinus remarks on this passage: “You will understand Festus’s truncated words from those of Paulus: ‘Monsters are called,’ etc.” Scaliger, Gothofredus, and Dacerius, here and elsewhere, present the text as two glosses, although it is a double transcription of one gloss. Moreover, the gloss *monitores* is entirely absent from the pre-Augustinian editions. E.E.

p. 173, s.v. *Opima*. We wrote *Pompeli regis* in the margin instead of *Pompili*, because the ancients said it that way, just as *Dueli* for *Duili*; and the *Schedae* have *Pompelli*.

p. 179, s.v. *Optima lex*. In the *Schedae* enough space has been left to restore the two words that we noted in the margin. We think one should read *magister populi* for *a populo*, and likewise *magistrorum* for *magistratuum*, as the *Schedae* have it.

p. 182, s.v. *Praedotiun*. This is how it stands in the *Schedae*, and correctly, etc.

p. 183, s.v. *Petrarum*. The *Schedae* have *Levius* for *Livius*; hence I suspect that *Laevius* is meant, etc.

p. 184, s.v. *Pictor Zeuxis*. In the *Schedae* these words are so corrupted that they nevertheless almost lead one by the hand toward the true reading. They read, in corrupt form: *cum versiculos quoque adhaereret tulerit et septos pati*. Then follows *nullius praetoris praetexto nomine*. We emended it as follows: *cum versiculos quoque ea de re rettulerit, et ineptos satis et nullius pretii, praetexto nomine* (“since he had also reported some little verses on that matter, sufficiently foolish and entirely worthless, under a pretexted title”). [But is this correct? I think I have corrected it more easily. E.E.]

p. 181, s.v. *Impetum*. This is merely a gloss by Paulus’s epitomator, which we included above among the Verrian fragments, p. 24, n. 39. How it entered the text is uncertain. The Augustinian and pre-Augustinian editions are entirely free of this interpolation. E.E.

p. 185, s.v. *Pisalitem*. This is how it stands in the *Schedae* instead of *Pisatilem*, and it appears that it should be read so.

p. 190, s.v. *Talionis*. The manuscript book has *rapit* for *rupit*, so perhaps *rapsit* should be read.

p. 191, s.v. *Tripudium*. These words are missing from the other editions; see above under *Puls.*: . . . “*Tripudium* was said in the taking of auspices” appears to have stood in the exemplar. Festus then gave an example from some writer on the augural discipline.

p. 191, s.v. *Tintinnare*. In the *Schedae* the reading is *molae* instead of *molle*, or *mollem*, as others have emended it; this is the true reading.

p. 191, s.v. *Tributorum*. I think the exemplar originally had *census populus*, and that the word *poplus* was subsequently changed to *alius*. Traces of the ancient reading survive in the *Schedae*.

p. 191, s.v. *Tentipellium*. *Indeq.* is found in the *Schedae* for *idem*, and is preferable.

p. 192, s.v. *Vici*. The complete and emended reading is found in the *Schedae*. For *paci* was written, according to the ancient spelling practice, in place of *pagi*. The rest is also more correctly given in the *Schedae*: “another, when that kind of building is defined which is continuous with those towns that are divided by roads and districts for the sake of distinction.” At the end, the *Schedae* have *in oppidi vicis* and *vicani* in both places.

p. 193, s.v. *Victimam*. The *Schedae* have *ob hostes victos* for *ad hostes victos*, a small change; for the Augustinian emendation *hostibus victis* is too far removed from the ancient reading. In the *Schedae* the reading is *victa* for *vincta*, so perhaps *vitta* should be written.

p. 193, s.v. *Viae*. This word is missing from the other editions.

p. 194, s.v. *Vecors*. The examples from Pacuvius and Novius are missing from the other editions.

p. 194, s.v. *Ve victis*. The *Schedae* have *Brennus rex* (“King Brennus”); in the margin, however, another hand—perhaps that of the person who collated those *Schedae* with the ancient exemplar—has noted *dux* (“commander”) for *rex*, and *pensum* for *apenderetur*.

p. 195, s.v. *Viere*. These passages too are missing from the other editions. Ennius’s verse survives in Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language* [V, 62], where the reading is *malaci*, as in the *Schedae*.

p. 195, s.v. *Uruat*. Placidus in his glosses: “You enclose with a city, you encircle; derived from *urbs*, ‘city.’” The *Schedae* have a more correct version of Ennius’s verse.

p. 195, s.v. *Ungulus*. *Nacta* should be read, even if anyone should ask why. For the corrupt word *elirio*, the *Schedae* have *ebrio*, which is the true reading.

p. 196, s.v. *Unciaria*. It must be investigated what the following material belongs to. The words following *ventabant* are likewise uncertain.

p. 196, s.v. *Vindiciae*. In the quotation from the Twelve Tables that Festus adduces at the end, the *Schedae* have, before *arbitros*, more than half of the word *tor*. It may therefore have been complete as follows: “Let the praetor appoint three arbitrators.”

[Col. 1709]

## Back matter of the volume

[Col. 1723]

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS TO THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF BEDE

Roman numerals designate the book; Arabic numerals designate the chapter or page of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

## A
## A

Aaron and Julius, martyrs, I, 7. Acca: goes to Rome with Wilfrid; relates the miracles of Saint Oswald, III, 13; IV, 14, and Wilfrid’s vision, V, 19. In the bishopric of Hagustald, he succeeds Wilfrid. His praises, deeds, and education, V, 20. He was bishop of Hagustald when Bede brought his History to a close, V, 23. His chasuble, 357. His relics, including his shroud and the same chasuble, 358.

Acha, Edwin’s sister, mother of King Oswald, III, 6.

Adamnan, abbot: receives the Catholic Easter observance as envoy to Aldfrid; corrects many of the Scots from their error; writes from Arculf a book on the Holy Places; presents it to Alchfrid; dies, V, 15 and 21.

Adamnan, monk: his penance; vision concerning the burning of the monastery of Coludi, IV, 25.

Adbaruae. See Baruae.

Ad Candidam Casam. See Candida Casa.

Ad Caprae Caput. See Caprae Caput.

Adda, brother of Utta, one of the four priests sent to convert the Middle Angles, III, 21.

Addi, a companion whose boy Bishop John recalled from death by prayer, V, 5.

Adgefrin. See Gefrin.

Adlapidem, a place in the province of the Jutes where the king Arwald’s brothers were crowned with martyrdom, IV, 16.

Ad murum, a royal settlement of King Oswiu, where Peada and Sighberct were baptized with their followers, III, 21 and 22.

Adtuifyrdi, beside the river Alne. Synod held there under Theodore, at which Cuthbert was elected bishop, IV, 28.

Aduluald. See Eadbald.

Aebba, aunt of King Ecgfrith, abbess of the monastery in the city of Coludi, IV, 19. Her devotion during the burning of the monastery and her death, IV, 25.

Aebbercurnig, monastery; its location, I, 12. Trumwine’s withdrawal from it, IV, 26.

Aecci, one of the bishops of the East Angles substituted for Bisi, IV, 5.

Aedan, king of the Scots, defeated in battle by Aethelfrith, I, 34.

Aedan, bishop: three of his teeth, 358; his cross, 358; his head, 360.

Aedan, bishop, comes to the English; his character and opinion concerning Easter; receives a see on the island of Lindisfarne, III, 3. His life, almsgiving, devotion, humility, and the occasion of his mission, III, 5. He gives to a poor man the horse presented to him by King Oswin; foretells the king’s death; himself dies, III, 14. Three of his miracles, III, 15–17. His burial, way of life, and judgment concerning Easter, III, 17. What he endured patiently, 25. For how many years he held the episcopate, III, 26. He recalls Hilda from Cale and consecrates Heiu, IV, 23. The kind of life he established among the monks, IV, 27. Part of his bones brought back to Scotland by Colman, III, 26.

Aeddi, Stephen, master of singing, IV, 2.

Aedgils, priest from whom Bede learned the history of the burning of Coludi, IV, 25.

Aedibald, king of the Mercians, to whom all the southern provinces as far as the Humber were subject, V, 23. His charter, 390.

Charter of Aedbald, or Eadbald, king, concerning Northbourne, 586.

Aethelberht, king of Kent: how he received Augustine and his companions, I, 25. Pope Gregory I arouses his zeal by letters and sends him gifts, I, 32. He builds and richly endows the church of Peter and Paul at Canterbury, where the bodies of bishops and kings may be placed, I, 33. He rules over all the English peoples as far as the Humber. He builds the church of Saint Paul in London and that of Saint Andrew in Rochester. He adds estates to both churches, as also to the church at Canterbury, II, 3. He receives letters from Pope Boniface, II, 4. His death, rule, laws, genealogy, and burial. [Col. 1724] The state of the Christian faith after his death, II, 5.

Aethelberht, son and heir of Wihtred, king of Kent, V, 23.

Aethelberg, illegitimate daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, abbess of the monastery at Brie. Her incorrupt body transferred to the church of Saint Stephen there, III, 8.

Aethelberg, also called Tate, daughter of King Aethelberht, married to Edwin; brings the Christian faith to the kingdom of the Northumbrians, II, 9. Receives letters and gifts from Pope Boniface, II, 11. After Edwin’s death, returns to Kent, II, 20.

Aethelberg, abbess of the monastery at Barking, built by her brother Bishop Earconwald, IV, 6. Her holiness and miracles at her death and after it, IV, 9.

Aethelfrith, king of the Northumbrians. His deeds: he defeats Aedan, king of the Scots, in battle, I, 34. He lays low the Britons and their monks at the City of the Legions, II, 2. He pursues Edwin by force and treachery. He is killed by Raedwald on Edwin’s account, II, 12. He was of the province of Bernicia, III, 1.

Aethelhere, brother of King Anna, killed, III, 24.

Aethelhild, abbess, heals a demoniac with the dust in which Saint Oswald’s bones had been washed, III, 11.

Aethelhun, son of King Edwin by Queen Aethelberg, baptized and buried at York, II, 14.

Aethelhun, brother of Aethelwine. His vision concerning his companion Ecgberht; his death, III, 27.

Aethelred, king of the Mercians, husband of Osthryth. His devotion to Saint Oswald, III, 11. He devastates Kent and receives the province of Lindsey, IV, 12. During his reign the synod of Hatfield was held, IV, 17. Battle with Ecgfrith and treaty, IV, 21. At last, as abbot, he reconciles his successor, King Coenred, to Wilfrid, V, 19.

Aethelthryth, daughter of King Edwin by Queen Aethelberg. Baptized and buried at York, II, 14.

Aethelthryth, queen, daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, IV, 3. Her life, death, incorruption, and so forth, 31, 37; IV, 19. Hymn concerning her, IV, 20.

Aethelwalh, king of the Mercians, baptized; gives Selsey to Wilfrid, IV, 13.

Aethelwald, king of the East Angles, brother of Anna; receives Suidhelm from the holy font, III, 22.

Aethelwald, bishop of Lindisfarne, V, 13.

Aethelwine, bishop in the province of Lindsey, III, 11; IV, 12. Instructed in Ireland, III, 27.

Aethelwine, prefect of King Oswiu; kills Oswin, III, 14.

Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, born in the province of Deira, III, 1. Fifth among those who held the greater authority in Britain, II, 5, 9. Wounded by an assassin. He defeats the king of the West Saxons, II, 9. Receives letters and gifts from Pope Boniface, II, 10. While pursued by Aethelfrith, he is urged to believe through a vision concerning the acquisition of the kingdom, II, 12. With Raedwald’s help he becomes king. By what counsels he embraces the faith, II, 13. Baptized at York, he begins the church of Saint Peter there, but is killed, II, 14. He persuades Earpwald to abandon idols, II, 15. He is present when Paulinus baptizes at Tiowulfingacaester, II, 16. The peace, prosperity, and excellence of his reign, II, 16. Receives an exhortatory letter from Pope Honorius, together with a decree concerning metropolitan jurisdiction between Canterbury and York, II, 17. He is killed, II, 20. His head is buried at York, ibid. His body is at Streaneshalch, III, 24. His vessels, cross, and chalice are carried by Paulinus to Kent, II, 20.

The Egyptian custom concerning Easter, III, 25.

Aelfleda, also called Aelbfled, daughter of King Oswiu; after Penda’s defeat, dedicated to God, III, 24. She enters the monastery of Heruteu and becomes abbess of Streaneshalch, III, 24; IV, 26.

Aelfwine, brother of King Ecgfrith, killed, IV, 21.

Aella, king of the province of Deira, whose name Pope Gregory I alluded to, II, 1.

Aelli, the first to hold authority over the English south of the Humber, II, 5.

[Col. 1725] Aeodbaldus. See Eadbald.

Aesica, a boy dying in the monastery at Barking who invokes a virgin who is also dying, IV, 8.

Charter of Aethelred, duke of the Mercians, 376.

Aetherius, bishop to whom Pope Gregory wrote concerning the kindly reception of Augustine, I, 24. By him Augustine was ordained, I, 27.

Charter of Aethelred, king of the Mercians, 370.

Aetius, consul to whom the Britons send their lament, I, 13. Killed by the emperor Valentinian, I, 21.

Aetla, bishop of Dorchester, from the monastery of Streaneshalch, IV, 23.

Agatha, IV, 20.

Agatho, pope: receives Biscop and Ceolfrith at Rome; sends John the Singer with them to investigate the faith of the Britons, IV, 18. Holds a synod against the Monothelites at Rome, at which he absolves Wilfrid, V, 20.

Agatho, priest of Agilberht, III, 25.

Agilberht, a Gaul, coming from Ireland, becomes bishop of the West Saxons. On this occasion he returns to Gaul and becomes bishop of the city of Paris. Recalled by the king of the West Saxons, he sends another in his place, III, 7. He visits Alchfrid in the province of the Northumbrians; attends the synod at Streaneshalch concerning Easter; substitutes the priest Wilfrid, whom he had made priest, for himself in the discussions, III, 25. He returns home, III, 26. He consecrates Wilfrid, III, 28. He receives Theodore, IV, 1. See again concerning the same man, V, 19.

Agnes, IV, 20.

Agricola, son of Bishop Severianus, introduced the heresy of Pelagius into Britain, I, 17.

Aidanus. See Aedan.

The Alans rage through Gaul, I, 11.

Alaric, king of the Goths, invades the Roman Empire, I, 11.

The time of Alban’s martyrdom, 297. He was crowned with martyrdom no earlier than the nineteenth year of Diocletian, ibid. Under Constantius, father of Constantine, 298.

Albanus. The history of his conversion and martyrdom, I, 7. Some relics of other saints were placed on his tomb by Germanus and Lupus, and a mass of sepulchral dust was removed, I, 18.

Albinus, abbot, instructed by Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian; Bede’s source for his account of the deeds in the province of Kent, Preface. Hadrian’s successor. His expertise in Scripture and languages, V, 21.

Alchfrid, son of King Oswiu, IV, 16. He attacks his father, III, 14. He persuades Peada, king of the Mercians, to accept the faith, III, 21. He accompanies his father against Penda, III, 24. His judgment concerning Easter, III, 25. He first gives the Scots, and later Wilfrid, a monastery at Ripon, III, 25; V, 20. He sends Wilfrid to Gaul to be ordained, III, 28; V, 19. He recovers the kingdom of the English, IV, 26. He hears Dricthelm recounting his vision, V, 13. He receives from Adamnan the book of Arculf on the Holy Places, V, 16. He dies, V, 19.

Alcluith, a city of the Britons. Its location, I, 1, 12.

Aldberht, one of the two bishops of the East Angles when Bede completed his History, V, 24.

Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians after Ecgfrith, V, 1. His death, V, 19.

Aldhelm, abbot of the monastery at the town of Mailduf. Bishop of the West Saxons; wrote a book on Easter and on virginity. His praises, V, 19.

Charter of Aldred, sub-king of the Hwiccas, 371.

Aldwine, bishop of Lichfield, attends the consecration of Archbishop Tatwine, V, 23.

Aldwine, brother of Aethelwine, abbot of the monastery of Peartaneu, III, 11.

Aldwulf, king of the East Angles, II, 15. During his reign the synod of Hatfield was held, IV, 17.

Aldwulf, after Tobias, bishop of Rochester. He attends the consecration of Archbishop Tatwine of Canterbury, V, 23.

Alectus. He holds the island of Britain, I, 6.

Charters of Alexander I, king of Scotland, 367.

Charter of Bishop Alhwin of the Hwiccas, 374.

Alne, river, beside which the synod was held at Adtuifyrdi, IV, 28.

Alric, brother and heir of Wihtred, king of Kent, V, 23.

Ambrosius Aurelianus, leader of the Britons, I, 16.

Amfleat, a bay of the sea in which Peter, first abbot of Canterbury, was drowned, I, 33.

Dust of the martyr Amphibalus, 357.

Anatolius, whose writings concerning the date of Easter the Scots and Picts followed, III, 3, 25.

Andhun, leader of the king of the West Saxons; he expelled Caedwalla from the province, IV, 15.

Andilegum, a monastery in Gaul to which English virgins were sent, III, 8.

Andrew, apostle; his sacristy in the city of Rochester, III, 14.

[Col. 1726] Andrew, an Italian monk, put forward by Abbot Hadrian to the Roman pontiff for the archbishopric of Canterbury, IV, 1.

Androgius, leader of the Trinovantes, surrendered to Julius Caesar, I, 2.

The Angles invited into Britain, I, 15, 16. They accept the faith, I, 23.

The East Angles, I, 15. They accept the faith, II, 15. Their kings are called Wuffings, II, 15.

The Middle Angles, I, 15. They become Christians, III, 21.

Anna, king of the East Angles, son of Eni, successor of Ecgric, III, 18. He receives Coinualch, king of the West Saxons, as an exile and converts him to the faith. His character, III, 7. He adorns Cnobheresburg with buildings and gifts, III, 19. He is killed by King Penda, III, 18. He had daughters, Aethelthryth and Sexburga, IV, 19.

Difference in years between the Hebrew authority and that of the Seventy-two translators, III, 24.

Indulgence of Thomas Appleby, bishop of Carlisle, 387.

Arculf. Author of the book on the Holy Places. Extracts from his book, V, 16–18.

Arles, where Constantius, the count, killed Constantine II, I, 11. They commend to the bishop of that city their apostles departing for Britain, I, 24, 28; IV, 1.

The Armorican Tract, reputed homeland of the Britons, I, 1.

Arius; his heresy infects Britain, I, 8.

Arwald, king of the Isle of Wight. His brothers crowned with martyrdom, IV, 16.

Asclepiodotus. He recovers Britain, I, 6.

Asser of Menevia says nothing about the university of Oxford, 346. A clause concerning King Alfred is inserted into his book in bad faith, 347. Asser of Menevia and Asser of Sherborne are the same person, 352.

Asterius, bishop of Genoa, consecrates Bishop Birinus, III, 7.

Attila, king of the Huns, keeps the consul Aetius occupied in wars, I, 13.

Audubald. See Eadbald, II, 11.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo. He responds to Pelagius, I, 10.

Augustine and the other monks, persuaded by the letters of Pope Gregory I, set out, I, 23. Their arrival in Britain, I, 25. Their conduct and success, ibid., I, 26.

Augustine is ordained bishop at Arles. His questions to Gregory, with the responses, I, 27. He receives the pallium and other things from Gregory, I, 29. He is instructed concerning what he should do about temples, festivals, and sacrifices of idols, I, 30. He receives an exhortatory letter warning him not to boast of his virtues, I, 31. He restores the church of the Savior in the royal city and establishes a monastery to the east, I, 33. He summons the bishops of the Britons to a conference at a place called Augustine’s Oak. A miracle occurs there involving a blind man. At a second synod he proposes terms of peace. When they reject them, he threatens vengeance by the English and foretells it, II, 2. He makes Mellitus bishop of London and Justus bishop of Rochester. His death. His epitaph, II, 3.

Augustine baptized many thousands not in the neighborhood of York but in Kent, 316.

Aurelianus, Ambrosius, leader of the Britons, I, 16.

Auxerre, the seat of Bishop Germanus, I, 17.

## B

Badon, a mountain. Its siege, I, 16.

Badudegn, a brother in the monastery of Lindisfarne, healed at the tomb of Saint Cuthbert, IV, 30.

Baduini, one of the bishops of the East Angles substituted for Bisi, IV, 5.

Bede dedicates his History to King Ceolwulf. He identifies his sources, Preface. His candor in the Easter controversy, III, 17. His tunic, 358.

Baldhild, queen of Gaul, orders Bishop Dalfinus to be killed, V, 19.

Bancornaburg, monastery of the Britons. The number of its monks; their way of life; their slaughter at Chester, II, 2.

Hair of the hermit Bartholomew of Farn, 357.

Baruae, a monastery in the province of Lindsey, given by King Wulfhere to Chad, IV, 3. Wynfrith departed from it and died there, IV, 6.

Bassianus, emperor, son of Severus, I, 5.

Bassus, a soldier of King Edwin, leader of Paulinus and Aethelberg when they returned to Kent, II, 20.

Beardaneu, a monastery in the province of Lindsey to which the bones of King Oswald were brought, though with difficulty, III, 2.

Bebba, queen, from whom Bebbanburg takes its name, III, 6, 16.

Bebbanburg, the royal city of Bernicia; whence its name, III, 6, 16. In its church of Saint Peter the relics of the holy King Oswald were placed, III, 6, 12. Besieged by Penda and delivered from the fire by Aidan’s prayers, III, 16.

Begu, a nun of Hackness. Her vision concerning Hilda’s death, IV, 23.

Benedictus. See Biscop.

Bercta, queen of Aethelberht. Her lineage and religion, I, 25.

[Col. 1727] Berctgils, also called Boniface, bishop of the East Angles, III, 20.

Bercthun, leader, expelled Caedwalla from the province of the West Saxons. He was later killed by him, IV, 15.

Bercthun, abbot of the monastery at Inderauuda, relates the miracles of Bishop John, V, 2–4.

Berctuald, abbot of Reculver, after Theodore archbishop of Canterbury, V, 8, 12. He receives Wilfrid, V, 19. He consecrates Aldwulf bishop of Rochester. He dies, V, 23. He is buried in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul, II, 3.

Berctus, under whose leadership King Ecgfrith devastated Ireland, IV, 26.

Barking, a monastery in the province of the East Saxons, built by Bishop Earconwald for his sister Aethelberg, IV, 6. Miracles there, IV, 8–10.

Bernicians. Concerning them, see III, 4, 6; V, 5, 15. Aethelfrith arose from this province, III, 1. The first cross was erected there, III, 2.

Bernwini, Wilfrid’s cleric and kinsman, to whom he entrusted part of the Isle of Wight, IV, 16.

Bethlehem: its location, description, and holy places, V, 17.

Betti, one of the four priests sent to convert the Middle Angles, III, 21.

Birinus, bishop: how he came to Britain. He preaches the faith to the Gewissae. He receives a see in the city of Dorchester. He is buried there and transferred to Winchester, III, 7.

Biscop Benedict builds a monastery at the mouth of the river Wear. He comes to Rome and receives a letter of privilege. He brings John the Singer to Britain, IV, 18. He goes with Wilfrid to Rome, V, 20.

Bisi, bishop of the East Angles, successor of Boniface, attends the synod of Hertford. Because of his illness, two bishops are substituted for him, IV, 5.

Blecca, prefect of the city of Lincoln, converted by Paulinus, II, 16.

Bledla, king of the Huns, I, 13.

Blithryth, wife of Pippin, obtains an island on the coast for Suidberht, V, 12.

Boisil, prior of Mailros, V, 10. Cuthbert’s teacher, IV, 27. He foretells that Cuthbert will be bishop, IV, 28. In a vision he forbids his disciple Ecgberht to go to Germany, V, 10.

Book of Boisil, 356. His garments and hair, 358. His head, 360. His hair shirt, ibid. His comb, ibid.

Boniface, pope, predecessor of Deusdedit, II, 6. He summons a synod of the Italian bishops. He sends its decrees, together with a letter to Archbishop Laurence and King Aethelberht, through Mellitus, II, 4. He obtains the Pantheon from Phocas, II, 4. He sends the pallium to Justus and a letter, II, 6. He sends letters and gifts to Edwin, II, 10. He sends letters and gifts to Queen Aethelberg, II, 11.

Boniface. See Berctgils.

Boniface, archdeacon at Rome and Wilfrid’s teacher, V, 10.

Boulogne, a city of Gaul where Peter, abbot of Canterbury, was buried, I, 33.

Boructuarians, V, 10. Brought to the faith by Suidberht. Conquered by the ancient Saxons, V, 12.

Bosa, bishop of the Deirans at York, IV, 12. From the monastery of Streaneshalch, IV, 23. His death, V, 3.

Bosham, a monastery in the province of the South Saxons, IV, 13.

Bosel, first bishop of the Hwiccas, IV, 23.

Bothelm, a brother of the church of Hagustald, healed of a broken arm by a piece of the wood of Saint Oswald’s cross, III, 2.

Bregusuid, Hilda’s mother. Her dream concerning her, IV, 23.

Bridei, son of Meilochon, king of the Picts, III, 4.

Brie, a monastery in Gaul to which English virgins were sent, III, 8.

Britain: its description and so forth, I, 1. Its condition after the persecutions up to the Arian madness, I, 8. After the departure of the Romans, I, 12, 14. After the victories of the Saxons, I, 15. After the Pelagian heresy, I, 22. The plague, III, 27.

The Britons, compelled by hunger, repel their enemies. Those who grow luxurious amid abundance perish. They summon the Saxons to their aid, I, 14. They are reduced by the Saxons to misery, I, 15. Under the leadership of Bishop Germanus they defeat the Saxons and Picts, I, 20. They refuse to preach the faith to the Saxon people, I, 22. Their bishops reject Augustine’s authority. They are slaughtered by Aethelfrith, king of the English, II, 2. They regard the religion of the English as worthless, II, 20. Their bishops attend Chad’s consecration, III, 28. Part of them recover their freedom, IV, 26. Some under the rule of the West Saxons accept the true Easter, V, 18. Most reject it, V, 22. The condition of the people when Bede completed his History, V, 23.

Briudun, monastery from which Archbishop Tatwine of Canterbury came, V, 23.

Brocmail, defender of the monks of Bangor, turns his back in the battle at Chester, II, 2.

Buchanan is mistaken when he writes that Severus’s wall was built between the Firth of Clyde and the Firth of Forth, 303.

[Col. 1728] Burghelm, one of the priests who baptized the people of the South Saxons, IV, 13.

Burgred, king of the Mercians. Agreement between him and Wulfrid, 375.

Buscfrea. See Uuscfrea.

## C

Caecilia, V, 19. Her church, V, 11.

Caedmon. His gift of singing; revelation concerning his death, IV, 24.

Caedwalla, king of the Britons. His character. He kills Edwin, II, 20. He kills Osric and Eanfrith. He himself is killed by Oswald, III, 1.

Caedwalla, of royal descent among the Gewissae, an exile. Later, as king of the Gewissae, he kills King Aethelwalh and subdues the province of the South Saxons, IV, 15. He gives Wilfrid a quarter of the Isle of Wight, IV, 16. After abandoning the kingdom, he goes to Rome. He is baptized and dies, IV, 12; V, 7.

Caelin, brother of Bishop Cedd, ministers the word and sacraments to King Oidilwalh of the Deirans, III, 23.

Cair Guorthigirn, 293. Municipality, ibid. Meguaid, ibid. Ebrauc, ibid. Maunguid, 294. Ceint, ibid. Peris, ibid. Legion, ibid. Segeint, ibid. Guent, ibid. Lerion, ibid. Pensauellcoit, ibid. Celemion, ibid. Guintguic, 295. Ligualid, ibid. Colun, ibid. Custeint, ibid. Grant, ibid. Lundein, ibid. Guiragon, ibid. Daun, 296. Guricon, ibid. Legion guarusic, ibid. Brithou, ibid. Darithou, ibid. Urnach, ibid. Luitcoyt, ibid. Glou, ibid. Cei, ibid. Ceri, ibid. Dorm, ibid. Dauri, ibid. Merdin, ibid. Cair: what it signifies, 296, 297.

Calcaria. See Kalcacester, IV, 23.

The Council of Chalcedon accepted in the synod of Hatfield, IV, 17.

Cale, a monastery in Gaul to which English virgins were sent, III, 8; IV, 23.

Campodonum, where there was a royal villa and a basilica built by Paulinus, but burned by the pagans, II, 14.

Candida Casa, the see of Bishop Ninian. The location and religion of the place, III, 4.

Candidus, a priest commended by Pope Gregory to Bishop Aetherius, I, 24.

The Cantware: whence Bede obtained what he reported concerning their province, Preface. They alone were exempt from Edwin’s rule, II, 5. The condition of the kingdom after Hlothere’s death, IV, 26.

Caprae Caput, a monastery of the priest Utta in the kingdom of the Northumbrians, III, 21.

Carausius, emperor. How he occupied the Britains, I, 6. He is falsely said to have restored Severus’s wall, 309.

Chester, a city near which Aethelfrith, king of the English, laid low the Britons and killed the monks of Bangor, II, 2.

Cataract, a village nearby where Paulinus baptized, II, 14.

Chad, brother of Bishop Cedd and abbot of Lastingham, III, 23, 28. He is ordained bishop of York. His character, teacher, and learning, III, 28.
