His reordination and withdrawal to Lastingham, IV, 2, 3. He is given the bishopric of the Mercians and Lindsey, the third bishop, III, 24, IV, 3. He establishes the monastery of Baruae. He dies and is buried in his episcopal see at Lichfield. Revelation concerning his death; exhortation to the brothers; fear of the Lord in the winds; miracles of healing at his tomb, IV, 3.

Chad’s dwelling, which he built for himself, 362.

Cearl, king of the Mercians, father of Quoenburga, II, 14.

Ceawlin, or Caelin, king of the West Saxons, second English emperor south of the Humber, II, 5.

Cedd, one of the four priests sent to convert the Middle Angles, III, 21. Sent to convert the East Angles, he returns home. He receives the episcopal rank from Finan. He completes the work begun. He foretells Sigberct’s death and baptizes his successor Suidhelm, III, 22. He revisits the northern province. He establishes the monastery of Lastingham. His death, burial, and brothers. The story of an unbaptized boy, III, 23. He attends the synod of Streaneshalch and converts to the Catholic Easter, III, 26. The story of his brother’s soul taking Chad’s soul up to heaven, IV, 3.

Ceolfrith, after Benedict, abbot of Wear and Jarrow. He sends architects and letters concerning Easter and the tonsure to King Nechtan, IV, 18. He urges Adamnan to observe the Catholic practice, V, 21.

Ceollach, a Scot who, after Diuma, abandons the episcopate of the Middle Angles, III, 21, 24.

Ceolred, son of Aethelred, king of the Mercians after Coenred, V, 19.

Ceolwulf, after Osric, king of the Northumbrians, to whom Bede dedicates his History, Preface. Brother of Coenred. The state of his kingdom, V, 24. His head, 360.

[Col. 1729] Cerdic, king of the Britons, under whom Hereric, Hilda’s father, lived in exile, IV, 23.

Cerotesei, a place in the region of the South Gyrwe where Bishop Earconwald built a monastery for himself, IV, 6.

Hebron, V, 17.

The twenty-eight cities of Britain, 293.

Claudius’s crossing to Britain, I, 3.

Clement, pope, consecrated by Saint Peter as his assistant and successor, II, 4.

Clement. See Wilbrord.

Clofeshoh, a synod ordered to be held there annually, IV, 5. Synod under Biornwulf, king of the Mercians, 373.

Clyde, the river beside Severus’s wall, I, 12.

Cnobheresburgh, a fortress containing Fursa’s monastery, III, 19.

Celestine, pope, sends Palladius as bishop to the Scots, I, 13.

Coenred, father of Aethelred, king of the Mercians, 365. He vainly urges a despairing soldier to do penance, V, 13. He becomes a friend of Wilfrid. After abandoning the kingdom, he dies as a monk at Rome, V, 19. In his time the people of Iona accept the Catholic Easter, V, 22. Osric succeeds him, V, 24.

Coifi, pagan high priest of King Edwin. By what arguments he recommends the Christian faith. He destroys the altars of idols, II, 13.

Coinualch, king of the West Saxons, rejects the faith and repudiates his wife. He loses the kingdom. In exile he accepts the faith and is restored to the kingdom. He receives Agilberht as bishop, introduces another in his place, recalls Agilberht, and receives the other sent by him, III, 7.

Coldingham. Certain charters concerning the estate of Coldingham, 366.

Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne. His dispute concerning Easter, III, 25. He returns to Scotland. He obtains from King Oswiu that Eata be made abbot of Lindisfarne. He takes part of Aedan’s bones with him. His frugality, continence, and so forth; the devotion of that age, III, 26. Those whom he took with him, IV, 4.

Colonia, where the bodies of the two Hewalds were buried, V, 10.

Coludi, a city where Aebba’s monastery stood; Aethelthryth was veiled there, IV, 19. It was destroyed by fire, IV, 25.

Columba. Who he was, V, 10. When he came to Britain, he preached the faith to the northern Picts. He founded the monasteries of Iona and Dearmach. He rests in the former, III, 4. The source of the Scots’ Easter custom, III, 25. His monasteries reformed by Ecgberht, V, 10. His bones, 357, 358.

Columbanus, abbot, observes Easter in Gaul according to the custom of the Britons, II, 4. Among others, Pope John sends him a letter concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

Compendium, a royal village in Gaul where Wilfrid was consecrated, III, 28.

Constans, son of Constantine II, killed by a monk calling himself Caesar, near Vienne, I, 11.

Constantinople, oppressed by famine, plague, and ruin, I, 13. Disturbed by the heresy of Eutyches. A synod held there was accepted in the Council of Hatfield, IV, 17.

Constantine I, proclaimed emperor in Britain, I, 8.

Constantine II, killed, I, 11.

Constantine, son of Heraclius, II, 18.

Constantine, pope. During his pontificate King Coenred became a monk at Rome, V, 20.

Constantine I, emperor, dies in Britain, I, 8.

Constantius the Count kills Constantine II at Arles, I, 11.

Cromanus, one of the bishops to whom Pope John sends a letter concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

Cromanus, one of the priests to whom Pope John sends a letter concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne. Whence Bede obtained what he wrote concerning his life, Preface. He warns King Ecgfrith not to attack the Picts, IV, 26. His entry into the religious life, character, episcopate, miracles, death, incorruption, relics, tomb, IV, 27–32.

Banner of Saint Cuthbert, 356. Silver image, ibid. Cloak in which he lay on the ground for eleven years, ibid. Checkered garment, ibid. Piece of cloth on which he lay for 418 years and five months, and part of the chasuble in which he lay for eleven years, 357. Gloves, 358. Book containing the Gospel text, 359. Life of Saint Cuthbert, 360. Wax-impregnated cloth that had wrapped this saint’s body in the tomb, and his garment, 361. Linen of double weave that had wrapped his body in the tomb, ibid. Cloth with which his body was sewn, ibid. Indulgence granted to those visiting his body by the bishop of Dunblane, 387.

Cuduald, abbot under whose governance Wilfrid died in the monastery of Oundle, V, 19.

Cwichelm, king of the West Saxons, sends an assassin to kill Edwin, II, 9.

Cwichelm, after Putta, bishop of Rochester, IV, 12.

[Col. 1730] Cyniberct, Bede’s source for the deeds in the province of Lindsey, Preface.

Cy[lacuna], fourth bishop of Lindisfarne, IV, 12. He held office when Bede brought his History to a close, V, 23.

Cyniberct, abbot of Hrentford, obtains baptism before death for the brothers of King Arwald, IV, 16.

Cynibil, brother of Bishop Cedd, III, 23.

Cyniburga, daughter of Penda, wife of Alchfrid, king of the Northumbrians.

Cynifrid, physician, testifies to the incorruption of Aethelthryth’s body, IV, 19.

Cynigils, king of the West Saxons: baptized; gives the city of Dorchester to the Church; Coinualch succeeds him, III, 7.

Cynimund, priest, relates to Bede a miracle of Aidan, III, 15.

Cynuise, queen of the Mercians, with whom Ecgfrith, son of King Oswiu, was held hostage, III, 24.

Cyril: the doctrines of Theodore and Theodoret, and Ibas’s letter against him, condemned at the synod of Hatfield, IV, 17.

## D

Dacore, a river beside which Suidberht’s monastery stood, IV, 32.

Daegberct, king of Gaul, to whom Uuscfrea and Yffi were sent to be fostered by their mother Aethelberg, II, 20.

Dagan, bishop, refused to eat with the Romans, II, 4.

Dalfinus, bishop of Lyons, unsuccessfully attempts to retain Wilfrid in Gaul. His death, V, 19.

The Dalreudi: whence they came, I, 1.

Damian, after Ithamar, bishop of Rochester. Consecrated by Deusdedit, III, 20. Putta succeeds him, IV, 2.

The Danes, V, 9.

Daniel, after Haeddi, and together with Aldhelm and Forther, bishop of the West Saxons, V, 18, 23. He sent Bede in writing some information concerning the ecclesiastical history of his own province, that of the South Saxons, and the Isle of Wight, Preface. He added the Isle of Wight to his episcopal see, IV, 16. He attends the consecration of Archbishop Tatwine of Canterbury, V, 23.

Charters of David, earl and later king of Scotland, 368.

Dearmach. The reason for the name; foundation of the monastery, III, 4.

Deda, abbot of Peartaneu. Baptized by Paulinus, II, 16.

Deglastan, where Aethelfrith defeated Aedan, king of the Scots, in battle, I, 34.

Denisesburna, where Oswald killed Caedwalla, III, 1, 334.

Derauuda. See Inderauuda, V, 2, 6.

Deira, also Deiri. Pope Gregory’s allusion to the name, II, 1. One of the two provinces of the Northumbrians. The homeland of King Edwin, III, 1. Joined in peace with the other province by King Oswald, III, 6. Its own bishop was given to it by King Ecgfrith, IV, 12.

Derwent, a river beside which Eumer the assassin attempted to kill King Edwin, II, 9. Godmundingham is situated beyond it, II, 13.

Derwent, a river at whose source the anchorite Hereberht lived, IV, 29.

Deusdedit, pope, predecessor of Boniface, II, 7, 8.

Deusdedit, archbishop of Canterbury, successor of Honorius. Of what nation he was; by whom he was ordained. He consecrates Damian bishop of Rochester, III, 20. He dies, III, 28; IV, 1.

Dicul, priest, to whom Fursa left his monastery, III, 19.

Dicul, a Scottish monk who possessed the monastery of Bosham, IV, 13.

Dinnaus, one of the Scottish bishops to whom Pope John sends letters concerning Easter, II, 19.

Dinoot, abbot of the monastery of Bangor, II, 2.

Diocletian, emperor, in whose time the Britons preserved the Christian faith in peace, I, 4, 6.

Diuma, one of the four priests sent to convert the Middle Angles. He becomes bishop of them and of the Mercians. Ordained by Finan. He dies, III, 21, 24.

Domnoc, the see of Felix, bishop of the East Angles, II, 15.

Dorchester, the first see of the bishops of the West Saxons, III, 7.

Durobrivae, Rochester, the see of Bishop Justus. The city’s location in relation to Canterbury; the foundation and endowment of the church there, II, 3.

Canterbury, the metropolitan city of the kingdom of King Aethelberht. He gave Augustine a residence there, together with a see and possessions, I, 25, 26; II, 3. The church of Saint Martin there existed before Augustine’s arrival, I, 26. Augustine consecrated it in the name of the Holy Savior. The monastery in which Aethelberht founded the church of Peter and Paul. Tomb of bishops and kings, I, 33. The city was seized by fire and saved by a miracle, I, 6.

Dricthelm, rising from the dead, relates what he had seen. His life after restoration, V, 12.

Charter of Duncan, king of the Scots, 366.

Index of the relics of the church of Durham, 356.

[Col. 1731] Duunchad, abbot, under whose governance the people of Iona accepted the Catholic Easter and related observances, V, 22.

## E
## E

**Eaba**, queen of the East Saxons, wife of Aedilvach, from the province of the Huiccii. Her lineage. Baptized, IV, 13.

**Eadbald.** See Aduluald, Audubald, and Aedbaldus, son of King Aedilberct. Unbelieving. Incestuous, II, 5. How he was converted to the faith. His piety. He builds a church of the Blessed Mother of God in the monastery of St. Peter, II, 6. He receives a testimony of faith from Pope Boniface, 2, 8, 10, 11. He gives his sister Aedilberg in marriage to King Aeduin of the Northumbrians, II, 9. He receives Paulinus returning with Aedilberg, II, 20. He leaves the kingdom to his son Earconberct, III, 8.

**Eadberct**, duke of the Mercian people. Uulfhere raises him against Osuiu, III, 24.

**Eadberct**, bishop of Lindisfarne, successor of Cudberct in the see and in the tomb, IV, 29. He covers the church with lead, III, 24, 25.

**Eadberct**, abbot of Selaeseu, the first Anglo-Saxon bishop, V, 18.

**Eadberct**, son and heir of King Uictred of Kent, V, 23.

**Eadfrid**, son of King Aeduini by Quoenburga. Baptized by Paulinus, II, 14. Put to death by King Penda of Mercia, II, 19.

**Eadgar**, third bishop of Lindisfarne, IV, 12.

Charters of King Eadgar of England, 379.

Charters of King Eadgar of Scotland, 366.

**Eadgyd**, a virgin in the monastery at Berecingum, invoked by a dying boy when she was about to die, IV, 8.

**Eadhed**, priest of King Osuiu. Bishop of the church of Rhypum. Sent with Uilfrid to Kent, III, 28. Ordained the first bishop in the province of Lindisfarne, IV, 12.

Charter of King Eadred of England, 377.

**Eafa**, duke of Mercia. Uulfhere raises him against Osuiu, III, 24.

**Eanfleda**, daughter of King Aeduini, II, 9. The first of the Northumbrian people to be baptized; she returns to Kent with her mother, II, 20. She returns as wife to King Osuiu, III, 15. She asks him for Getlingum in memory of King Osuini. Buried at Streaneshalch, III, 24. Observes the true Easter, III, 25. She commends Uilfrid to King Erconberct for his mission to Rome, V, 19.

**Eanfrid**, son of Aedilfrid, an exile among the Scots, where he was converted to the faith. He succeeds Aeduini in the kingdom of Bernicia. He returns to idolatry. He is put to death, III, 1.

**Eanfrid**, father of Eaba, IV, 13.

**Eanheri**, brother of Eanfrid, IV, 13.

**Eappa**, one of the priests who baptized the Anglo-Saxon people, IV, 13. He presides over the monastery of Selaeseu, IV, 14.

**Earcongota**, daughter of King Earconberct of Kent. Sent to the monastery at In Brige. A miracle at her death, and another at her tomb, III, 8.

**Earconberct**, king of Kent, son of Eadbald. He destroys idols. He commands the Lenten fast. He marries Sexburga, daughter of King Anna of the East Angles, III, 8. He dies, IV, 1. He sends Uilfrid and Benedict to Rome, V, 19.

**Earconuald**, bishop of the East Saxons. His holiness. Miracles at his bier. Which monasteries he built, IV, 6.

**Eatpuald**, king of the East Angles, son of Reduald. He accepts the faith. He is killed, II, 15.

**Eata**, one of Aedan’s twelve boys, bishop of the Bernicians, in Hagustald and Lindisfarne, III, 26. At last he held only Hagustald, IV, 12, 27, 28.

**Ebba.** See Aebba.

**Eboraca.** At which Emperor Severus died, I, 5. By its episcopal constitution, Gregory’s metropolitan see, I, 29. By the constitution of Honorius, equal to Doruvernum, II, 17, 18. King Aeduin baptized there, II, 14. His head buried there, II, 20.

**Ebroinus**, mayor of the royal household in Gaul. He grants Theodore and his companions permission to cross to Britain. He detains Hadrian in Gaul, IV, 1.

**Ecgberct**, king of Kent, son of Erconberct. After consulting Osuiu, he sends Uighard to be ordained bishop of Doruvernum, III, 29. He sends a prefect to Gaul to bring Theodore, IV, 1. He dies, IV, 5.

**Ecgberct**, an English priest, brings the monks of Iona to the true date of Easter, III, 4; V, 22. His piety, vow, and recovery while dying, III, 27. He recounts a vision concerning the soul of Ceadda, IV, 3. He advises King Ecgfrid not to attack the Scots, IV, 26. Wishing to preach to the Germans, he is sent by a vision to the monasteries of Columba, V, 9. He dies on Easter Day, V, 22, 23.

**Ecgfrid**, son of Osuiu, hostage among the Mercians, III, 24. He succeeds his father, IV, 5. In the eighth year of his reign, a comet appears. He hates Uilfrid, 364. He expels him. He substitutes two bishops. He obtains the province of Lindisfarne after expelling Uulfhere, IV, 12. During his reign, the synod of Haethfelda, IV, 17. In his presence, the synod of Ad Tuifyrdi, IV, 28. He had Aedilthryda as his wife, IV, 19. He engages in battle with Aedilred, IV, 21. He ravages Ireland. While leading an army against the Picts, he is killed, IV, 26.

[Col. 1732] King Ecgfrid gives St. Cuthbert the estate of Creec and Lugubalia, 387.

**Ecgrice**, kinsman and successor of Sigberct, king of the East Angles. Killed in battle against Penda, III, 18.

Charter of Bishop Ecguini, 371.

Cloak of Edmund the Confessor, 357.

**Edric**, son of Ecgberct. He joins the Anglo-Saxons against Hlother and kills him, IV, 26.

**Eduin.** See Aeduin.

Rib of King and Martyr Edward, 358.

**Edwini**, archbishop: cuirass, 359.

**Elafius.** He meets St. Germanus, who restores his son to health, I, 21.

**Eleutherius**, Roman pope, to whom Lucius, king of the Britons, sends a letter concerning the reception of the faith, I, 41.

**Eleutherius**, bishop of the West Saxons. See Leutherius.

**Elge**, a region in the province of the East Angles. Its description. A monastery of Aedilthryda there, IV, 19.

**Elli.** See Aelli.

**Elmete**, a forest in which was the monastery of Tryduulfi, II, 14.

Silver bier and hood of Elphegi, 360.

**Emme**, bishop of the Senones. He receives Hadrian when he comes to Britain, IV, 1.

**Eolla**, the second Anglo-Saxon bishop, V, 18.

The Council of Ephesus accepted at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Ercunualdus**, patrician of the Franks. He receives Furseus and preserves his body, III, 19.

**Esus**, abbot, Bede’s source for the *De Gestis* concerning the province of the East Angles, preface.

**Etherius.** See Aetherius.

**Etheldreda.** Stole which she gave to St. Alfrid, 360.

The insanity of Eudoxius condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Eufemia**, IV, 20.

**Eulalia**, IV, 20.

**Eumer**, an assassin sent to kill Aeduini, II, 9.

The heresy of Eutyches condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Eutychius**, bishop of Constantinople. His heresy refuted by Pope Gregory I, II, 1.

## F

**Fara**, abbess. She built the monastery at In Brige, III, 8.

**Farn**, an island. Its location. Retreat of Bishop Aedan, III, 16. Bishop Cudberct’s retreat; he also died there, IV, 27, 29. Oidiluald’s retreat; he also died there, V, 1.

**Faro**, bishop of the Meldi. He receives Hadrian, IV, 1.

**Felix**, Roman pope, great-grandfather of Gregory the Great, II, 1.

**Felix**, bishop of Burgundy. He preaches the faith to the East Angles, II, 15; III, 18. He receives the see at Domnoc. He dies, II, 15; III, 20.

**Feppingum.** See Infeppingum.

**Finan**, bishop of Lindisfarne, successor of Aedan, III, 17. He baptizes Peada, king of the Mercians, with his people. He ordains Diuma bishop of the Middle Angles and Mercians, III, 21. He baptizes King Sigberct of the East Angles with his people. He ordains Cedd bishop of the East Angles, III, 22. He builds a church of timber on the island of Lindisfarne, III, 24. He is steadfast in his position concerning Easter, III, 25. How many years he held the episcopate, III, 26.

**Fortheri**, bishop of the West Saxons, V, 19. But only in part, V, 24.

**Franks.** They ravage the coasts, I, 6. They are driven out by the barbarians, I, 11. They serve as interpreters for Augustine in Britain, I, 25. English virgins are sent to their monasteries, III, 18.

**Frisia, Frisians.** Uictberct preaches the faith to them without success, V, 9. The nearer part is conquered by Pippin, V, 10.

**Frisian.** To him an unshackled captive was sold, IV, 22.

**Frigyd.** She presided over the monastery of Hacanos, IV, 23.

**Frodheri.** A soldier killed by the dagger of Eumer, II, 9.

**Fullanus**, brother of Fursaeus, to whom he left his monastery, III, 19.

**Furseus**, from Ireland. He establishes a monastery among the East Angles. His vision. His voyage to Gaul. He builds a monastery at Latiniacum. His body is preserved incorrupt at Perrona. His little book, III, 19.

## G

**Gaul.** Many English virgins visit its monasteries, III, 8. Its metropolitan archbishop ordains the archbishop of Kent, V, 8. It is ravaged by the Saracens, V, 23.

**Germans**, corruptly called by the Britons, V, 9.

**Gebmundus**, bishop of Rochester, IV, 12.

**Gefrin**, an estate in the province of Bernicia, where Paulinus baptized, II, 14.

**Germany**, its peoples, V, 9. Those who came from it to Britain, I, 15.

**Germanus**, bishop of Auxerre, sent with Lupus to Britain for the first time against the Pelagian heresy, I, 17. The crossings, delay, disputation, miracles, and battle of the two men, I, 17, 18, 19, 20.

[Col. 1733] Germanus’s return with Severus, arrival at Ravenna, death, I, 21. One of his bones, 357.

**Gerontius**, count. He kills Constans, I, 11.

**Gessoriacum**, the shore of the Morini, I, 1.

**Geta**, son of Emperor Severus, dies, I, 5.

**Gethlingum**, where King Osuini was killed. A monastery there, III, 14, 24.

**Geuissae**, a people of the West Saxons, III, 7. They overthrow King Eadbald in battle, II, 5. They receive the faith, III, 7. In the city of Venta, the Anglo-Saxon people are subjected to their bishop, IV, 15.

**Gildus**, British historian cited by Bede, I, 22.

**Gleni**, a river in the province of Bernicia, at which Paulinus baptized, II, 14.

**Gobbanus**, priest to whom Furseus left his monastery, III, 19.

**Godmundingaham**, a place of idols, polluted by its own priest. Its location, II, 13.

Beard of Godric, 357, 359. Belt, 360. Cuirass, 361.

**Goduine**, metropolitan of Gaul. He ordains Berctuald archbishop of Canterbury, V, 8.

**Gordianus**, father of Pope Gregory I, II, 1.

Charters of Count Gospatric of Dunbar, 369.

**Goths.** They break Rome, I, 11.

**Grantacaestir**, where a small coffin for Aedilthryda’s body was found, IV, 19.

**Gratianus**, killed by Maximus, I, 9.

**Gratianus**, a municipal official and usurper, is created and killed in Britain, I, 11.

**Gregory I**, Roman pope. Mention of his letters and those of his disciples, preface. Author of ecclesiastical chant, 333. He sends exhortatory letters to those struck with fear, I, 23; also to the bishop of Arles concerning the reception of Augustine, I, 24; and to assist him in discipline, I, 28. He replies to Augustine’s questions, I, 27. He sends him the pallium, vessels, vestments, relics, and books, I, 29. Through Mellitus he informs him what he should do concerning shrines, festivals, and sacrifices to idols, I, 30. He warns him not to glory in miracles, I, 31. By letter he stimulates King Aedilberct’s zeal and sends him gifts, I, 31. His conversation with merchants, through which he undertook the conversion of the English. He arranged for Masses to be celebrated over the bodies of the apostles. He arranged for the words “Diesque nostros” to be added to the Mass. His father, great-grandfather, devotion, pastoral care, office as *apocrisiarius*, writings, illness, death, burial, and epitaph, II, 1. An altar is dedicated in his honor in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul at Doruvernum, II, 3.

**Gregory II**, Roman pope, during whose pontificate King Ini went to Rome, V, 7. With whose permission Nothelm brought the papal letters from Rome to Bede, preface.

**Gregory III**, Roman pope, during whose pontificate Bede dedicated his *History*, preface.

Grymi’s grave, 303.

**Gudfrid**, abbot of Lindisfarne. Freed from a storm through the prayers of Oidiluald, V, 1.

**Gyrvii.** Thomas, bishop of the East Angles, was from their province, III, 20. The monastery of Medeshamstedi is situated in their region, IV, 6. The Southern Gyrvii, IV, 19.

**Gyruum**, a monastery beside the river Tina, V, 22. See Ingyrvum. So called because water from the Tina there “turns” in part (Wessington manuscript, *De Origine Ordinis Monachorum*, etc., p. 26).

## H

**Hacanos**, a monastery built by Hild. Its location. A vision there concerning Hild’s death, IV, 23.

**Hadrianus**, abbot of Hiridanum. His praises. Designated by the Roman pope for the archbishopric of Doruvernum, he first proposes Andrew and then Theodore. He accompanies the latter to Britain. He is detained for a short time in Gaul by Ebroinus. He receives the monastery of St. Peter from Theodore, IV, 1. He dies, V, 20.

**Hadulac**, the second bishop of the East Angles, at the point where Bede’s *History* closes, V, 23.

**Haede**, bishop of the West Saxons in the city of Venta, III, 7. Consecrated by Theodore, IV, 12. While he was bishop, King Caedualla abandoned the kingdom, IV, 12. His praises. His death, V, 18.

**Haenigils** testifies to Dricthelm’s vision, V, 12.

**Haethfelda**, the synod held there. Profession of faith, IV, 17.

**Haethfelth**, a plain where King Aeduini was killed, II, 20.

**Hagustald.** The church given as the seat to the bishop of the Bernicians, IV, 12. Dedicated to St. Andrew, V, 20. The devotion of the brethren on the eve and morning of the killing of King Osuald, III, 2.

**Hearnius (Thomas)**, 302.

**Hebron.** See Chebron.

**Hefenfelth**, where Osuald, after erecting a cross, defeated Caedualla, III, 2, 334.

**Heiu**, a nun, the first among the Northumbrians. Founder of the monastery of Heruteu, IV, 23.

**Helena**, concubine of Constantius, I, 8.

**Hengist**, leader of the English. His lineage, I, 15; descendants, II, 5.

Charters of Henry, earl and son of David I, king of Scotland, 368.

Boundaries of the provinces of the Heptarchy, 291.

[Col. 1734] **Heraclius**, emperor, II, 18.

**Heraclius**, Caesar, ibid.

**Herebald**, cleric of John, bishop of York. Crushed by an accident and recalled from death through his bishop’s prayers. At last abbot of the monastery at the mouth of the river Tina, V, 6.

**Hereberct**, priest. Indulgence is granted to those who have traveled to his island out of devotion, 387.

**Hereric**, nephew of King Aeduini, father of Hild. How he received the faith. An exile, he perished by poison, IV, 23.

**Heresuid**, mother of Alduulf, king of the East Angles, sister of Hild, and an example of the regular life in the monastery of Cale, IV, 23.

**Heriburg**, abbess of Vetadun, V, 3.

**Hermianus**, one of the priests to whom Pope John and others sent letters concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

**Heruteu**, a monastery founded by Heiu. Hild was its abbess, IV, 23. Aelfleda, dedicated to God, entered it, III, 24.

**Herutford**, council held there, IV, 5.

**The two Heuualdi**, preaching the faith among the Saxons, were killed. Their bodies were buried at Cologne, V, 10.

**Ireland.** Its description. Homeland of the Scots, I, 1; III, 19. It resounds with the miracles of St. Osuald, III, 13. A plague there. Many withdraw there from England for the sake of learning. They are struck by the disease, III, 27. Ravaged by King Ecgfrid, IV, 26. From there preachers go to Germany, V, 9, 10. For the most part it accepts the true Easter, V, 15.

**Hiddila**, a priest. He ministers the word on the Isle of Wight, IV, 16.

**Jerusalem**, V, 15, 16.

**Iona**, an island. Its monastery, III, 3, 21. The authority of its abbots. Its observance of Easter, III, 4. Aedan came from there, III, 3. Colmann returned there, IV, 4. Its monks refuse to accept the Catholic Easter from Adamnan, V, 15, 21. Ecgberct is sent there by a vision, V, 9. From him they receive it, V, 22.

**Hilarius**, Roman archpriest, together with John, the elected Roman pope, and others, sends letters to the bishops and to the Scots concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

**Hild**, abbess, first of Heruteu and later of Streaneshalch, III, 24. At the synod held there concerning Easter, she is on the Scottish side, III, 25. Her life and death, IV, 23.

**Hildilid**, abbess at Berecingum after Aedilburga, IV, 10.

**Hiridanum**, a monastery in Campania, whose abbot was Hadrian, IV, 1.

**Hloduius**, king of the Franks. He receives Furseus, III, 19.

**Hlotharius.** During his reign the synod of Haethfelth was held, IV, 17.

**Hlothere**, king of Kent, brother and successor of Ecgberct, IV, 5. He redeems an unshackled captive, IV, 22. Wounded, he dies, IV, 26.

**Homelea**, a river in the region of the Geuissae. The tide extends beyond its mouth, IV, 16.

**Honorius**, emperor, I, 9, 10, 11.

**Honorius**, Roman pope and successor of Boniface. He sends Paulinus the pallium and letters to Aeduini, II, 17. He likewise sends letters to the Scots concerning Easter, II, 19. On his advice Birinus comes to Britain, III, 7. He honors Aidan, III, 25.

**Honorius**, archbishop of Canterbury. Consecrated by Paulinus, II, 16, 18. He sends Felix to preach to the East Angles, II, 15. From Pope Honorius he receives the pallium and letters concerning metropolitan jurisdiction between the bishops of Doruvernum and Eboraca, II, 18. He receives Paulinus returning to Kent with Aedilberg, II, 20. He ordains Ithamar bishop of Rochester. He ordains Thomas bishop of the East Angles, III, 14. He substitutes Berctgils in his place. He dies, III, 20.

**Horsa**, leader of the English. His monument, I, 15.

**Hrenus**, a river crossed by the barbarians, I, 11. The bodies of the Heuualdi were thrown into it, 5, 10. On its island, the monastery of Suidberct, V, 11.

**Hreutford**, a monastery of Abbot Cyniberct in the province of the Jutes, IV, 16.

**Hrof**, from whom Hrofaescaestrae takes its name, the see of Bishop Justus. The church of St. Andrew, II, 3. Paulinus becomes its bishop, 2, 10. Buried there, III, 14. The succession of bishops from Paulinus to Tobias, III, 20; IV, 12; V, 8. A fortress of the Cantuarii, IV, 5. Laid waste by Aedilred, king of the Mercians, IV, 12.

**Hrypum.** See In Rhypum.

**Huiccii.** Augustine and his companions are at their frontier, II, 2. Their bishop, IV, 23.

**Humbra**, a river, II, 16; V, 23.

**The Huns** drive the Goths from their settlements, V, 19.

**Hunuuald**, a count. He betrays King Osuini, III, 14.

**Hygbald**, abbot in the province of Lindisfarne. He recounts, on Ecgberct’s authority, the vision concerning the soul of Ceadda, IV, 3.

## I

**Ibas.** His letters were condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Idla**, a river on the borders of the Mercian people, beside which Aedilfrid was killed, II, 12.

**Iffi.** See Yffi.

[Col. 1735] **Iiudi**, a city in the eastern gulf of the sea, near the Wall, I, 12.

**Imma**, a captive whose chains were loosened when Masses were sung, IV, 22.

**Immin**, duke of Mercia. Uulfhere raises him against Osuiu, III, 24.

**Incompendio.** See Compendium.

**Incuneningum**, a region in the province of the Northumbrians. Dricthelm’s vision occurred there, V, 12.

**Inderauuda**, the monastery of Bishop John of York, V, 2, 6.

**Infeppingum**, a region of the Middle Angles in which Diuma died, III, 21.

**Inguald**, bishop of the East Saxons at London. He attends the consecration of Archbishop Tatuini, V, 23.

**Ingyrvum**, a monastery beside the river Tina, V, 21.

**Inhrypum**, first given to the Scots and later to Uilfrid by King Alchfrid, III, 25. It has Bishop Eadhed, IV, 12. The burial of Uilfrid, V, 10.

**Ini**, after King Caedualla of the West Saxons, goes to Rome, V, 7.

**Inisbofinde**, an island, the monastery of Colmann and others, IV, 4.

**On the shore**, the island of Hrenus, where Suidberct built a monastery for himself, V, 11.

**Irmenricus**, father of King Aedilberct, II, 5.

**Ithamar**, bishop of Rochester, III, 40. He ordains Deusdedit archbishop of Canterbury. He dies, III, 20.

**Ithancaestir.** See Ythancaestir, III, 22.

## J

**Jacobus**, deacon and minister of Paulinus, II, 16. Left behind at York. His zeal and death, II, 20. He observes the true Easter. He attends the synod of Streaneshalch, III, 25. The first teacher of Roman chant, II, 20; IV, 2.

**Jareth**, II, 45.

**Jaruman**, bishop of the Mercians, III, 24. He brings the East Saxons back to the faith, III, 30.

**John of Bridlington.** Bone, 360.

**John the Evangelist**, cited by the Scots concerning their observance of Easter, III, 25.

**John the Martyr.** His relics were sent by the Roman pope to King Osuiu, III, 29.

**John**, elected Roman pope after Severinus. He sends letters to the Scots concerning Easter and the Pelagian heresy, II, 19.

**John**, Roman *primicerius*, associated in the same letters with John the elected pope, II, 19.

**John**, Roman counselor, in the same letters, ibid.

**John**, archbishop of Arles. He receives Theodore, commended by the Roman pope, IV, 1.

**John the cantor.** He attends the synod of Haethfelth. He dies on the return journey and is buried at Tours, IV, 18.

**John**, after Eata bishop of Hagustald. After Bosa, bishop of York. His *History*, V, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

**John**, Roman pope after Agatho. He absolves Uilfrid. He sends letters concerning him to the kings, V, 19.

**Julianus of Campania**, associate of Pelagius, I, 10.

**Julius Caesar.** His arrival in Britain, I, 2.

**Julius and Aaron**, martyrs, I, 7.

**Justinus Minor**, emperor, I, 4.

**Justus**, sent by Pope Gregory I to Augustine in Britain, I, 29. Appointed by Augustine bishop of Rochester, II, 3. He sends a letter to the Scots concerning Easter, II, 4. He leaves Britain with Mellitus. He returns, II, 5. He succeeds to the archbishopric. From the Roman pope he receives the pallium and a letter authorizing him to ordain bishops. He ordains Paulinus, II, 7. He dies, II, 17, 18.

**Jutes**, the part of Britain in which they settled, I, 15; IV, 16.

## K

**Kaelcacaestir**, Hild’s retreat, IV, 23.

## L

**Labienus**, a tribune, killed, I, 2.

**Laestingaeu**, a monastery. Its brethren supplied Bede with material for the *De Gestis* concerning the provinces of Mercia and the East Angles, and for the life and death of Cedd and Ceadda, preface. Description of the place, consecration of the monastery, and related matters, III, 23. Its abbot was Ceadda, III, 28. Retreat of Ceadda and Ouini, IV, 3.

**Laistranus**, one of the Scottish bishops to whom Pope John sent a letter concerning Easter and related matters, II, 19.

**Latiniacum**, a place in Gaul where Furseus built a monastery, III, 16.

**Laurentius**, martyr. His relics were sent by the Roman pope to King Osuiu, III, 29.

**Laurentius**, priest, sent by Augustine to Pope Gregory, I, 27. Augustine’s successor. He consecrates the church of Peter and Paul at Doruvernum, I, 23; II, 4. His letter to the Britons and Scots concerning Easter, II, 4. When he leaves Britain, he returns after being scourged by the apostle Peter. He converts King Eadbald to the faith. His death and burial, II, 5.

**Legacaestir**, where the Britons were routed by King Aedilfrid, II, 2.

[Col. 1736] At what time three embassies were sent by the Britons to the Romans, 311.

**City of the Legions**, whose inhabitants Aaron and Julius were martyrs, I, 7.

Charter of Bishop Leofsini, 383.

**Leptis**, an African town, from which came Emperor Severus, I, 5.

**Leutherius**, nephew of Agilberct, sent in his place to the bishopric of the West Saxons, III, 7. He attends the Council of Herutford, IV, 5. He dies, IV, 12.

Books which Gregory the Great sent to Britain, 313, 315.

**Lilla**, minister of King Aeduini. Killed for the Lord, II, 9.

**Lindisfarne**, an island and the seat of the Scottish bishops, III, 3. In the cemetery of its church is the head of St. Osuald, III, 12. Aedan is buried there, III, 17. Following the rites of its church, the monastery of Laestingaeu was established, III, 23. A basilica there, made of timber and dedicated to St. Peter, first roofed with reeds and later with lead. Aedan’s bones were transferred into it, III, 17, 25.

**Province of Lindisfarne**, III, 24.

**Lindissis.** From this source Bede drew what he wrote about the province, preface. Its location and conversion, II, 16. Its bishops, IV, 12.

**Lindocolina**, a city, II, 16, 18.

**The shore.** See On the shore.

**Loidis**, a region in which there was formerly a royal estate, II, 14. In it Osuiu defeated Penda, III, 24.

**Lothere.** See Hlothere.

**Lucius**, king of the Britons. A Christian, I, 4.

**Lugubalia**, a city where Brother Hereberct met St. Cuthbert, IV, 29.

**Luidhard**, bishop of Queen Bercta, I, 25.

**Lundonia**, metropolis of the East Saxons, II, 3. According to Gregory’s arrangement, its bishop ought to receive the pallium, I, 29. Its inhabitants, inclined toward idolatry, reject the bishop, II, 5.

**Lupus**, bishop of Troyes, sent with Germanus to Britain against the Pelagian heresy, I, 17.

**Lyccidfelth**, the see, burial, translation, and tomb of Ceadda, IV, 3.

Charters of Lyfingi, bishop of Worcester, 384.

## M

**Maban**, cantor, V, 20.

**Macedonius.** His heresy was condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Maelmin**, the site of a royal estate in the province of Bernicia, II, 14.

**Mageo.** See Muigeo.

Masters of the Church, 362.

**Maildufi**, a town containing Aldhelm’s monastery, V, 18.

**Mailros**, a monastery of which Eata was abbot, III, 26. Cudberct was provost, IV, 27. Dricthelm’s retreat, V, 12.

Comb of Archbishop Malachy, 360.

**Mambre**, V, 17.

**Marcianus**, emperor, I, 15.

Cross of Queen Margaret of Scotland, 356. Tooth, 357.

Church dedicated to the Virgin Mary at Lichfield, IV, 3.

**Martinus**, bishop. The church at Doruvernum is dedicated to him, I, 26; and also the church at Candida Casa, III, 4.

**Martinus**, Roman pope. During his pontificate, the Roman synod was accepted by the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Maserfelth**, the place where King Osuald was killed, III, 9.

**Massilia**, through which Theodore came to Britain, IV, 1.

**Mauritius**, emperor, I, 23.

**Maximianus Herculeus**, begins the tenth persecution in the West, I, 6.

**Maximus**, emperor, killed at Aquileia, I, 9.

**Province of the Meanwari**, in the territory of the West Saxons. Given by King Uulfhere to Aedilualch, IV, 13.

**Medeshamstedi**, a monastery in the region of the Gyrvii, built by Sexuulf, IV, 6.

**Middle Angles**, I, 15; III, 21.

**Meilochon**, father of Bridius, king of the Picts, III, 4.

**The bishop of the Meldi.** He receives Hadrian, IV, 1. Uilfrid dies there, V, 19.

**Mellitus**, sent by Pope Gregory I to Augustine in Britain, I, 29. Appointed bishop of London by Augustine, II, 3, 4. He sends a letter to the Britons and Scots concerning Easter. He goes to Rome on the affairs of the English Church. He sits in the synod of the bishops of Italy. He brings its decrees to Britain, II, 4. Refusing Eucharistic bread to the sons of Saberect, he is expelled. He comes to Kent. He leaves Britain. Recalled by King Eadbald, he is rejected by the people. He becomes archbishop, II, 6. He consecrates the church of the Holy Mother of God built by Eadbald in the monastery of St. Peter, II, 5. He receives exhortatory writings from Pope Boniface. By prayer he extinguishes the flames consuming his city. His death and burial, II, 6.

**Mercians.** From them Bede drew what he wrote about this province, preface. The part of Britain in which they settled, I, 15. Their pagan people attack the northern regions, III, 14. Southern and northern Mercians. Defeated by Osuiu. They receive the faith. They recover their freedom, [Col. 1737] III, 24. Succession of their bishops to Uynfrid. Their sees, IV, 3. Their king’s provinces south of the Humber are subject to him, V, 23.

**Mevaniae**, islands subjected to English rule by Aeduini. Their location and description, II, 5, 9.

**Middle Angles**, that is, the Mediterranei Angli. They receive the faith, III, 21. Their bishops, IV, 12.

**Morini**, I, 1.

**Muigeo**, also Mageo, a monastery of the English in Ireland, founded by Colmann, IV, 4.

**Wall.** See Admurum.

**Pictish Wall**, or rampart, I, 5, 12.

Hadrian’s Wall, 302.

The wall of Lollius Urbicus under Antoninus Pius, ibid.

Severus’s wall, 303.

Its location, ibid.

It was made of turf, 306.

The distinction between the Wall and the Rampart, ibid.

The turf wall in Scotland was not converted into stone by the Romans when they were already abandoning Britain; but the wall in Northumbria was, 307.

Severus’s wall was not restored by Carausius, 309.

Under Valentinian I, the rampart of Antoninus was renewed, 310.

## N

**Naitan**, king of the northern Picts. With his people he is brought to a correct judgment concerning Easter and the tonsure. He receives letters from Abbot Ceolfrid concerning the same matters, V, 21.

**Nero**, emperor, almost lost Britain, I, 3.

The heresy of Nestorius condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Nicene Council**, concerning the Arian heresy, 23, 34; I, 8. Concerning Easter, III, 25. Accepted at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17.

**Nid**, a river beside which the synod was held at which Uilfrid was restored to the episcopate, V, 19.

**Niridanum.** See Hiridanum.

**Northumbrians.** From them Bede drew what he wrote about this province, preface. Who they are, I, 15; II, 7. The condition of the people after Aeduini, II, 20. The condition of its Church in the time of Osuiu, III, 26. Pestilence, III, 27. The condition of the people when Bede brought his *History* to a close, V, 23.

**Nothelm**, priest of the church of London. He brought the letters of the popes to be inserted into Bede’s *History*, preface.

## O

**West Saxons**, IV, 15.

**Octa**, grandfather of King Aedilberct, II, 5.

Charter of King Offa of the Mercians and Aldred, sub-king of the Huiccii, 372.

Charter of King Offa, 373.

**Offa**, son of King Sigheri. He becomes a monk at Rome, V, 91.

**Oftfor**, bishop of the Huiccii. From Hild’s monastery. His life, IV, 23.

**Oiddi**, one of the priests who baptized the East Saxons, IV, 13.

**Oidiluald**, king of Deira, son of Osuald, uncle of King Osuiu. He attacks his uncle, III, 14, 24. He gives the monastery of Laestingaeu to Bishop Cedd, III, 23.

**Oidiluald**, priest of Inhrypum. He calms a storm by his prayers. He dies on the island, V, 1.

**Oiscingae**, the royal family of Kent. From it, II, 5.

**Mount of Olives.** Church of the Ascension, V, 17.

**East Angles.** See Angles, I, 15.

**East Saxons.** See Saxons, I, 15.

**Orric**, also called Oisc, great-grandfather of King Aedilberct, II, 5.

**Osfrid**, son of King Aeduini by Quoenburga. Baptized by Paulinus, II, 14. He fell in battle, II, 20.

**Osfred**, son and successor of Aldfrid, king of the Northumbrians, V, 18. During his reign Uilfrid was received back into his Church, V, 19. After Coinred was killed, he assumed the kingdom, V, 22.

**Osric**, son of Aelfric. An exile among the Picts. Converted to the faith. He succeeds Aeduini in the kingdom of Deira. He returns to idols. He is killed, III, 1.

**Osric**, king of the province of the Huiccii, IV, 23.

**Osric**, king of the Northumbrians after Coenred. He dies, appointing Ceoluulf as his successor, V, 23.

**Osthryda**, sister of King Ecgfrid and wife of Aedilred, IV, 21. Queen of Mercia. Devoted to St. Osuald, III, 11.

**Osuald**, the sixth ruler in Britain, II, 5. Successor of Aeduini. He completes the church of St. Peter at York, II, 14, 20. He kills Caedualla. Before the battle he erects a cross and prays, III, 1, 2. He receives Aedan as bishop from the Scots. He gives him the island of Lindisfarne as the seat of his bishopric. He interprets the bishop’s words for the people. Churches are built. Monasteries are established, III, 3. His rule, lineage, almsgiving, and the miracle involving his hand and arm, III, 6. He receives Cynigils, king of the West Saxons, for baptism, and later his daughter as a wife. He joins himself to him by the gift of the city of Dorcic, III, 7. He is killed. Miracles of the place and of his relics, III, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. His annual commemoration, IV, 14.

Ivory scepter of Osuald, 356. Banner, 357. Cuirass and cross, 358. Ivory horn, 359.

[Col. 1738] **Osuini**, king of Deira. His lineage, virtues, and killing. An example of humility, III, 14. His flesh, 357.

**Osuiu**, brother and successor of Osuald, III, 14. He makes the Pictish and Scottish peoples tributary, II, 5. Attacked by his enemies—the Mercians, Alchfrid, and Oidiluald—he kills Osuini, III, 14. He marries Eanfleda, daughter of King Aeduini, III, 15. He gives his daughter Alchfleda in marriage to Peada, king of the Mercians. He receives the Mercian kingdom, III, 21. At his urging the East Saxons receive the faith, III, 22. His vows and victory against Penda. Burial at Streaneshalch. His rule. He transfers the southern Mercian kingdom to Peada, III, 24. His judgment concerning Easter at the synod of Streaneshalch, III, 25. He sends Ceadda to Kent to be ordained, III, 28; V, 19. He and King Ecgberct send Uighard to Rome to be ordained bishop of Doruvernum. He receives a letter and other items from the Roman pope, III, 29; IV, 1. At Theodore’s request, he gives Ceadda to the Mercians as bishop. He extends Uilfrid’s episcopate to the boundaries of his own rule, IV, 2. His death, IV, 5.

Charters of Oswold, bishop of Worcester, 378. Of the same, archbishop of York, 382.

**Ouini**, monk of Queen Aedilthryda. He enters the monastery of Laestingaeu. Witness of the revelation concerning Ceadda’s death, IV, 3.

The University of Oxford does not, on sufficiently certain grounds, claim Alfred as its founder, 346. Nothing concerning it is found in the little book of William of Malmesbury on the antiquity of the monastery of Glastonbury, 349; nor in his book on the kings, 350; nor in Constantius’s *Life of St. Germanus*, ibid.; nor in the *Life of St. Gildas*, ibid. All the arguments by which Alfred is shown to have been the founder of that university are overturned, ibid. The university’s three halls were not founded by Alfred, 353. Ingulph was educated at this institution, 356.

## P

**Padda**, one of the priests who baptized the Anglo-Saxon people, IV, 13.

**Palladius**, the first bishop sent to the Scots, I, 13.

Relics of Pancratius, sent by the Roman pope to King Osuiu, III, 29.

**Easter**, controversies that arose in the Church in every age concerning its celebration, 317.

Bones of Patrick, 357.

**Paulinus**, sent by Pope Gregory I to Augustine in Britain, I, 29. Ordained bishop by Justus. He comes with Aedilberg to Aeduini, converts the king and the Northumbrian people to the faith. He asserts that through his prayers he obtained a daughter for the king, II, 9. By the spirit he learns of King Aeduini’s vision, I, 12. He receives the episcopal see of York. He preaches and baptizes. He builds a basilica at Campodonum. The miracle of the altar escaping the fire, II, 14. He preaches the faith in the province of Lindissi. He builds a church in the city of Lindocolina. He consecrates Honorius archbishop there. He baptizes in the river Treenta. His portrait, II, 16. He returns to Kent with Queen Aedilberg. He becomes bishop of Rochester. Dying in that church, he leaves behind the pallium, II, 20. In what year he dies and where he was buried, III, 14. While he was preaching, Hereric received the faith, IV, 23.

Church of the apostle Paul built at London, II, 3.

Tonsure, IV, 1.

**Peada**, son of Penda, king of the Middle Angles. He seeks Alchfleda, daughter of King Osuiu, in marriage. He receives the faith, III, 21. He receives the kingdom of the Middle Angles as a gift from King Osuiu. He is killed, III, 24.

**Peanfahel**, also Penneltun, I, 12.

**Peartaneu**, a monastery in the province of Lindissi, II, 16; III, 11.

**Pecthelm** recounts to Bede the vision of a despairing man, V, 13. Witness of Haeddi’s miracles, V, 18. The first bishop of Candida Casa when Bede brought his *History* to a close, V, 23.

**Pegnalech**, a monastery in which Tuda was buried, III, 27.

**Pelagius**, a Briton. His heresy, I, 10, 17, 21. Letter of John, the elected Roman pope, against it, II, 19.

**Penda**, king of the Mercians and a pagan. He aids Caedualla against Aeduini, II, 20. He deprives King Coinualch of the kingdom because of the repudiation of his daughter, III, 7. He ravages the northern regions, III, 15. He attacks the city of Bebbanburch with army and fire without success. He burns the village where Aedan died, except for one house left untouched, III, 17. He kills the kings Sigberct, Ecgrice, Anna, and others of the East Angles, III, 18. He himself is killed by Osuiu, III, 24.

**Pente**, a river of the East Angles, on whose bank Ythancaestir stands, III, 22.

**Perrona**, a village in Gaul where Furseus’s body was preserved, III, 19.

**Peter**, apostle. He rebukes Archbishop Laurentius, II, 6. His church at York, II, 14. Another at Bebbanburch, III, 6. Another at Lichfield, IV, 3. A monastery dedicated to him at Uiuraemuda, IV, 18.

Church and monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul at Canterbury, I, 33; II, 3. Their relics, III, 29. Their monastery at Uiuraemuda and Ingyruum, V, 24.

**Peter**, deacon of Pope Gregory I, II, 1.

**Peter**, a monk sent by Augustine to Gregory, I, 27. Priest and abbot of the monastery of Peter and Paul at Doruvernum. Legate to Gaul. He is drowned. Buried at Boulogne, I, 33.

**Phocas**, emperor. He establishes the Roman see as supreme, I, 34. He turns the Pantheon into a church of the Blessed Mary and all the martyrs, I, 32.

**Picts.** Their origin, I, 1, 12. Where they settled, I, 1; III, 4. Their custom concerning the female line of kings, I, 1. They invade the Britons, I, 12. Tributary to Osuiu, II, 4. They receive the faith from the Scots. Their observance of Easter, III, 4. Northern and southern Picts, III, 4. The jurisdiction of the church of York over them in the time of Uilfrid, IV, 3. The province of the Picts is subject to English rule, IV, 12. Attacked by Ecgfrid. It recovers its freedom, IV, 26. The condition of the people when Bede brought his *History* to a close, V, 23.

**Pippin**, duke of the Franks. He brings the faith to conquered Frisia. He buries the bodies of the Heuualdi at Cologne, V, 10. He gives Suidberct an island on the shore. He gives Uilbrord a see at Ulltaburg, V, 11.

**Puch**, a count near Inderauuda, whose wife Bishop John healed with blessed water, V, 4.

**Putta**, bishop of Rochester. Skilled in Roman chant, IV, 2. He attends the Council of Herutford, IV, 5. When his church is devastated by Aedilred, he receives another from Sexuulf. He taught the chants of the Church. He ended his life in peace, IV, 12.

## Q

**Quentauic**, a port of Gaul from which Theodore sailed to Britain, IV, 1.

**Quoenburga**, daughter of Cearl, king of the Mercians, and wife of Aeduini, II, 14.

**Quoenburg**, a virgin of the monastery at Vetadun, healed by Bishop John, V, 3.

## R
Racuulf, monastery: its location. From it Berctuald [became archbishop], V, 8. Relics of Radagundis, 360, 361. Raedfrid, prefect of King Ecgberct, sent to Gaul to receive Theodore, IV, 1. Rathbed, king of Frisia, to whom Uictberct preaches the word in vain, V, 9. Expelled by Pippin, V, 10. Rathmelsigi, monastery of Ireland in which Ecgberct lived, III, 27. Reduald, king of the East Angles. Fourth overlord of the southern English, II, 5. He killed Aedilfrid. He raised Aeduin to the kingship, II, 12. Father of Earpuald. Instructed in the sacraments of the Christian faith. Nevertheless, he served idols. His lineage, II, 15. Regenheri, son of King Reduald, killed in battle, II, 12. Catalogue of the relics of the church of Durham, 356. Relics sent by St Gregory to Augustine, 315. Rendlesham, royal village of the East Angles, where Cedd baptized Suidhelm, III, 22. Reuda, leader of the Scots, I, 1. Rhine. See Hronus. Rhof., Rhofcestre. See Hrof. The church of Ripon. See Inhrypum. Ricberct, by whom Earpuald was killed, II, 15. Ricula, sister of Aedilberct, II, 3. Hair and hair-shirt of Robert of Stanhope, 357. Charters of Robert, bishop of St Andrews, 370. Rome, shattered by the Goths, I, 11. The Romans ceased to rule in Britain, I, 11. They return to Britain’s aid. They built a stone wall in place of Severus’s rampart, III, 2. They bid farewell to the Britons, I, 12. Romanus, bishop of Hrofescaestre after Justus, II, 8. He was swallowed by the waves, II, 20. Romanus, priest of Eanfled, attended the synod of Streneshalch, III, 25. Ronan, a Scot and defender of the true Easter, III, 25. Rufinianus, sent by Pope Gregory I to Augustine in Britain, I, 29. The Rugini, V, 9. The harbor of Rutupiae, I, 1.

## S

Saberct, king of the East Saxons, nephew of Aedilberct, II, 3. Called “Saba” by his sons. After his death, his sons, being pagans, gave free rein to the idols. They were forbidden the holy offering. They expelled the bishop. Going out to battle, they fell, II, 5. The river Sabrina. Which peoples beyond it have a bishop, V, 23. Saethrid, daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles; a nun and abbess of Brie, III, 8. The Saracens ravage Gaul, V, 23. Saranus, a teacher, or abbot, among the Scots, to whom, among the other bishops, Pope John sent a letter concerning Easter, II, 19. The southern Saxons, I, 15. Converted to Christ, IV, 13. Subject to the West Saxons, IV, 15. They have their own bishop, V, 17. The West Saxons, or Gewissae, receive the faith, III, 7. Their kings Caedualla and Ini went to Rome, V, 7. The East Saxons. Their metropolis is London, II, 3. They fall away from the faith, II, 5. They receive the faith, III, 22. Falling away again, they are recalled from error, III, 30. [Col. 1740] Scellanus, one of the Scottish priests to whom Pope John sent a letter concerning Easter, etc., II, 19. Schools in Gaul under the Roman emperors, 336. Schools in the Gallic bishoprics, 337, and in the monasteries, 338. Likewise in other places, 339. The school of Canterbury, most flourishing in the liberal arts, ibid. Schools in several places in England besides Kent, 340. The Kentish school, most celebrated under Archbishop Theodore, 340, 341. Schools among the Gauls excelled in liberal studies, 341, and that at Canterbury under Theodore, 343. The boys of Sigberct’s school, 344, 346, and their teachers, 345. That Sigberct’s school was at Cambridge can be proved by arguments no less cogent than those establishing Alfred’s school at Oxford, 346. It is rightly doubted whether Alfred founded the school at Oxford, 350. Alfred’s school was not established at Oxford but at the royal court, 353. Whether Sigberct’s school was at Cambridge, 354. If not at Cambridge, where it was located, 356. The homeland of the Scots was Ireland, I, 1. The Scots in Britain, I, 1, 34; V, 22. When the Romans departed, they ravaged Britain, I, 12. The erroneous Easter observance of the northern Scots, II, 4, 19; III, 3, 25. The southern Scots observe the tonsure and Catholic Easter, III, 26. The conduct of the Scottish bishops, III, 26. War between Ecgfrid and the Scots, or Irish, IV, 26. The Scots adopt Catholic rites, V, 14, 21. The black cross of Scotland, 356. Sebbi, king of the East Saxons. Faithful, III, 30; IV, 6. His piety. Vision. Death. Miracle in his sarcophagus, IV, 2. Sedulius, after whose example Aldhelm composed his book *On Virginity* in verse and prose, V, 18. Segeni, one of the Scottish priests to whom Pope John sent a letter concerning Easter, II, 19. Selaelseu, its description. Given to Uilfrid, IV, 13. The vision of the boys there, IV, 14. Emma, bishop of Sens, with whom Hadrian spent the winter on coming to Britain, IV, 1. Sergius, pope of Rome. During his pontificate King Caedualla was baptized at Rome, V, 7. Suidberct and Uilbrod were ordained bishops for Frisia, V, 11. Severianus, bishop and father of Agricola, who introduced the Pelagian heresy into Britain, I, 17. Severinus, Roman pontiff and successor of Honorius, II, 19. Severus, emperor, was brought to Britain. He constructed the rampart. He died at York, I, 5. The Romans lived near the rampart but possessed the territory beyond it by right of rule, I, 11. Severinus, bishop of Trier, a disciple of Lupus, joined Germanus on his return to Britain against the Pelagian heresy, I, 21. Sexburg, daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, wife of Earconberct, III, 8. After her sister Aedilthryda, abbess of Ely, IV, 19. Sexuulf, abbot of Medeshamstede, ordained bishop of the Mercians in place of Uynfrid, IV, 6. He gave Putta, bishop of Hrof, a church for a place of retirement. At the same time bishop of the Mercians and Middle Angles. Expelled from Lindsey, IV, 12. Sigberct, brother of Eorpuald, an exile in Gaul, received the kingship as a Christian. He brought the province of the East Angles back to the faith and founded a school, II, 15; III, 18. He gave a site to Fursa’s monastery, III, 19. He entered the monastery. He was led out from it to battle and killed, III, 18. Sigberct, king of the East Saxons, baptized. He requested teachers and was killed by his own people; the occasion of the massacre, III, 22. Sigberct’s school: where it was located, 335. Sighar, son and successor of Sebbi, IV, 11. Sigheri, king of the East Saxons, an apostate, III, 30; IV, 6. The ancient seal of the Durham convent, 334. The Solent, the sea lying between the Isle of Wight and Britain: its width and tides, IV, 16. Sprot (Thomas), 315. Stanford, land there given to Uilfrid, V, 19. Stilicho established a Roman legion on the frontier of Britain, 311. Stillingfletus is mistaken about the date of the three embassies sent by the Britons to the Romans, ibid. Strenaeshalch, Hilda’s monastery. After her, Aelfleda presided over it. In it she herself, Osuiu, Eanfled, Aeduini, and others were buried, III, 23. The origin of the name. A synod concerning Easter was held there, III, 23. Five bishops came from it, IV, 23. Trumuini’s withdrawal, IV, 26. The river Sualua in the province of Deira, in which Paulinus baptized, II, 14. Sudergeona, a region beside the river Thames, in which is Cerotaesei, IV, 6. Suefred, brother of Sighard and his fellow-partner in the kingship, IV, 11. The Suebi rage throughout Gaul, I, 11. [Col. 1741] Suidberct, abbot of the monastery at Dacore, IV, 32. Suidberct, bishop of the Frisians. Ordained by Uilfrid. He preached the word to the Boructuarii. Withdrawing, he built a monastery on the shore. He died there, V, 12. Suidhelm, king of the East Saxons, son of Sexbald. Successor of Sigberct, baptized, III, 22. Symmachus, consul, I, 13.

## T

The river Thames: its ford, crossed by Caesar despite the opposition of the Britons, I, 2. It separates the East Saxons from Kent, II, 3. Tilaburg lies on its bank, III, 22. Cerotaesei lies beside it, IV, 6. Tanatos, an island at which Augustine and his companions landed. Its description, I, 25. Tarsus, a city of Cilicia and Theodore’s homeland, IV, 1. Tate, also called Aedilberge, II, 9. Tatfrid, from Hilda’s monastery, elected bishop of the Hwiccians. He died before his consecration, IV, 23. Tatuini, after Berctuald, archbishop of Canterbury. His homeland, praise, and consecration, V, 23. Tecla, IV, 20. The bones of Theobald, archbishop of York, 358. His vestment, ibid. Cloth dipped in his blood, ibid. The doctrines of Theodore and Theodoret condemned at the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 17. Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. His nation, praises, ordination, and arrival in Britain, IV, 1. He consecrated Leutherius bishop of the West Saxons, III, 7. He consecrated the church of Lindisfarne to St Peter, III, 24. At Canterbury he opened a school, not at Cricklade, 344. He entrusted the monastery of St Peter at Canterbury to his companion Hadrian, III, 24. His deeds in Britain. He completed Ceadda’s consecration and requested that he be appointed bishop of the Mercians. He consecrated Putta bishop of Hrof, IV, 2, etc. He substituted Uynfrid for Ceadda, IV, 3. He convened the council of Herutford. He ordained Bisi bishop of the East Angles, IV, 5. He deposed Uilfrid and substituted Sexuulf. He appointed Earconuald bishop of the East Saxons, IV, 6. He ordained Haeddi of the West Saxons; Cuichelm, Gebmund of Hrof; Eadhead; Eata; Bosa of York; Tunberct of Hagustald; and Trumyini of the Picts as bishops, IV, 12. He presided over the synod of Haethfelth, IV, 16. He presided over the synod of Adtuyfyrdi. He consecrated Cudberct bishop of Lindisfarne, IV, 28. He made peace between Ecgfrid and Aedilred, IV, 21. His skill in medicine, V, 3. His death, epitaph, and successor, IV, 23; V, 8. Theodosius fortified the Britains with frontier defenses, 309. Theodosius the emperor restored Valentinian, I, 9. Theodosius the Younger, emperor, I, 13. The blood of Thomas of Canterbury, 357. Flesh and fat, 358. One pair of bedes belonging to Thomas, earl of Lancaster, 357. Thomas of Hatfield, 361. Thomas, deacon and successor of Felix, bishop of the East Angles, III, 20. The charter of Thor Longi, 369. Thruidred, priest of the monastery at Dacore. He cured the eye of a young man with Cudberct’s relics, IV, 32. Thryduulf, abbot and priest, in whose monastery the altar of the basilica at Campodunum is preserved, II, 14. Tiberius Constantinus, emperor, assisted Pope Gregory of Rome against the heresy of Eutyches, II, 1. Tilaburg: examination of the religious; its location, III, 22. Tilheri, bishop of the Hwiccians, 371, 372. Tillemont is mistaken in writing that Severus’s wall was built between the Clyde and the Forth, 304. Tilmon, one of the companions of the Heualds, to whom a vision concerning their bodies appeared, V, 11. The river Tinus, beside which is the residence of Bishop John, V, 2. The monastery of Ingyrvum, V, 21. Tiouulfingacaestir, a city beside the Trent, where Paulinus baptized, II, 16. Titillus, notary at the council of Herutford, IV, 5. Tobias, after Gebmund, bishop of Hrof. Ordained by Berctuald, V, 8. His education, praises, burial, and successor, V, 23. Tomianus, one of the Scottish bishops to whom Pope John sent a letter concerning Easter, etc., II, 19. Tondberct, prince of the southern Gyrvii, first husband of Aedilthryda, IV, 19. Tondheri, a soldier of Osuini who was killed with his lord, III, 14. The tonsure of the clergy and its origin, 327. When the clerical crown was introduced, 328. On the controversy concerning it between the Britons and the Romans, 330. Torctgyd, a sister in the monastery at Berecing. Her visions, IV, 9. Trajectum, the seat of Uilbrord’s bishopric, V, 11. Trecasena, a city and the see of Bishop Lupus, I, 17. The river Trent: Paulinus baptized in it, II, 16. Beside it a battle took place between Kings Eugfrid and Aedilred, IV, 21. Trinovantum, a British city that surrendered to Julius Caesar, I, 2. Trumberct instructed Bede in Scripture. He used to recount Ceadda’s piety amid the winds, IV, 3. [Col. 1742] Trumheri, a kinsman of King Osuiu, abbot of Ingethlingum. After Ceollach, bishop of the Middle Angles, III, 21, 24. Trumvini, bishop of the Picts, IV, 12. He persuaded Cudberct to accept the bishopric, IV, 28. He withdrew with his people to Strenaeshalch. He died, IV, 26. Tuda, after Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne. His learning and judgment concerning Easter, III, 26. A plague. His burial, III, 27. Tuifyrdi. See Adtuifyrdi, IV, 28. Tunberct, bishop of Hagustald, IV, 12. Deposed, IV, 28. Tunna, abbot of the monastery founded by him. Tunnacaestir, IV, 22. Tytilus, father of King Reduald of the East Angles, II, 15.

## U

Ualchstod, bishop of the peoples beyond the Sabrina when Bede brought his History to a close, V, 23. Ualdheri, bishop of London, gave King Sebbi the religious habit. He alone attended him at his death, IV, 11. Charter of Uhtred, sub-king of the Hwiccians, 372. The Hwiccians, mentioned at II, 2. Uictgils, father of Hengist and Horsa, I, 15. Uictred, king of Kent, son of Ecgberct, restored the kingdom, IV, 26. During his reign Berctuald was elected archbishop, V, 8. He died, leaving three sons as heirs of the kingdom, V, 23. Charter of Uictred, 390. Vienna: Count Gerontius killed Constans there, I, 11. Uighard, bishop. Taken away by death, III, 29. Uilbrord, a kindly bishop of the Frisians, V, 10, 11. Witness of the miracles of St Osuald, III, 13. Uilfaresdum, where King Osuini dismissed his army, II, 14. Uilfrid I. A monk of Lindisfarne who went to Rome and stayed with Uilbrord, III, 13. Also with Dallinus, archbishop of Lyons, from whom he received the tonsure. He received the monastery of Inhrypum from King Alchfrid. He disputed with Colman about Easter, III, 25. He was sent to Gaul to be consecrated bishop. Having remained there too long, he found Ceadda ordained bishop of York, III, 28. Until Theodore’s arrival, he ordained priests and deacons in Kent, IV, 2. He administered the bishopric of York. He extended his jurisdiction over Northumbria and the Picts, IV, 3. He attended the council of Herutford through representatives, IV, 5. Expelled from his see by King Ecgfrid, he sought Rome, IV, 12, 13. In his absence Theodore added two bishops to Northumbria, IV, 12. Driven by the wind to Frisia, he administered the faith to the people and baptism to the king. He was absolved twice at Rome, V, 19. On his return he preached the faith to the Anglo-Saxons. Miracles involving rain and fishing. He received Selaelseu from the king, IV, 13. He was recalled home, IV, 15. A fourth part of the Isle of Wight was given to him by Caedualla, IV, 16. He bore witness to Queen Aedilthryda’s virginity. He veiled her, IV, 19. He held the bishopric of the Middle Angles, IV, 23. While he was in exile in the regions of Mercia, Oftfor became bishop of the Hwiccians, IV, 23. He ordained Suidberct bishop of Frisia, V, 11. He served as bishop of Lindisfarne for one year after Cudberct, IV, 29. His life and death, V, 19. Uilfrid II, bishop of York, V, 6; and when Bede brought his History to a close, V, 23. Uilfrid, bishop of the Hwiccians, when Bede brought his History to a close, V, 23. Uiltaburg, Uilbrord’s see. See Trajectum, V, 11. Uini, bishop of the West Saxons, in the city of Venta. He succeeded Agilberct. Expelled from there, he purchased the see of the city of London, III, 7. The only canonical bishop in Britain, he consecrated Ceadda, III, 28. The river Uinuaed, beside which Osuiu defeated Penda, III, 24. The river Uiuri, at whose mouth Biscop built a monastery, IV, 18. On its northern side Abbess Hild lived the monastic life, IV, 23. Ceolfrid was abbot of its monastery, V, 21. Ultanus, brother of Fursa and his companion in the eremitical life, III, 19. Undalum, the province in which Uilfrid died, V, 19. Uoden, great-grandfather of Hengist and Horsa, I, 15. Usserius is mistaken in believing that Severus’s wall was of stone, 306. Utta, priest, sent to Kent to bring Eanfled to King Osuiu. He calmed a storm with oil given by Aedan, III, 15. Brother of Adda. Abbot of the monastery at the Goat’s Head, III, 21. Uuffa, grandfather of Raeduald, king of the East Angles, from whom the kings of the East Angles descended, II, 15. They were called Uuffings, II, 15. Indulgence of William, bishop of Dunblane, for those visiting the body of St Cudberct, 389. William of Malmesbury interpolated by Twyno, 349. He says nothing about the academy at Oxford, 350. The tooth of William of York, 360. Uulfhere, king of the Mercians, son of Penda. How he was raised to the kingship, III, 24. He sold the episcopal see of London, III, 7. During his reign Trumhere was bishop of the Middle Angles, III, 21. The kings of the West Saxons were subject to him. He restored part of their province, which had fallen away, to the faith by sending Jaruman, III, 30. He gave Ceadda land for the monastery at Adbarua. The boundaries of his kingdom, IV, 3. Driven into flight by King Ecgfrid, IV, 12. King Aedilualch of the Anglo-Saxons, received by him from the baptismal font, was given the Isle of Wight and the province of Meon, IV, 13. Concerning his sons Uulfadus and Ruffinus, 362. Uulfstan. Agreement between Wulfstan, archbishop of York, and Wulfric, 383. Uuscfrea, son of King Aeduini by Aedilberga. Baptized by Paulinus, II, 14. He returned to Kent with his mother, II, 20. At the urging of Kings Eadbald and Osuald, he was sent to Gaul. He died there in childhood, II, 20. Uynfrid, bishop of the Mercians, the Middle Angles, and Lindisfarne, III, 24. Ordained by Theodore, IV, 3. He attended the council of Herutford, IV, 5. Deposed by Theodore, he ended his life in the monastery at Adbarua, IV, 6.

## V

Valens, emperor, I, 9. Valentinian, emperor, I, 9, 21. The Vandals rage throughout Gaul, I, 11. Vantsumu, the river separating the island of Thanet from the mainland, I, 25. On the golden and silver vessels given by St Gregory to Augustine, 315. Vecta, the Isle of Wight. Its location and size. Subjugated by Vespasian, I, 3; IV, 16. Given by King Uulfhere to Aedilualch, who had been baptized, IV, 13. Captured by King Caedualla. A fourth part of it was given to Uilfrid. How it received the faith, IV, 16. Its jurisdiction belongs to Danihel, bishop of Venta, V, 23. Vecta, great-grandfather of Hengist and Horsa, I, 15. Venta, the Saxon Uintancaestir, the second see of the bishop of the West Saxons. The church of the Apostles Peter and Paul there, III, 7. Verlamacaestir, the city near which St Alban suffered martyrdom, I, 7. [Col. 1744] Vespasian, emperor, subjugated the Isle of Wight, I, 3. Vestments sent by Gregory the Great to England, 314. Vetadun, the monastery where Bishop John cured a virgin dying from bloodletting, V, 3. Victbert: who preached in Frisia in vain, V, 9. Virgilius, bishop of Arles. To him Gregory sent a letter concerning the admission of Augustine into the fellowship of instruction, I, 28. Vitalian, Roman pontiff. His letter to King Osuiu concerning the sending of a bishop in place of Uighard, III, 29. He sent Theodore, IV, 1. Vitra, grandfather of Hengist and Horsa, I, 15. Vortigern, king of Britain, I, 14.

## W

Wood (Anthony), in his *Antiquities of Oxford*, falsely asserts that Sigberct’s school was merely a grammar school, 341. He wrongly denies that Theodore opened a school at Canterbury, 343. He is ungrateful toward Alfred, whom the Oxonians call the founder of that academy, 345. He understood the Saxon language either not at all or very badly, ibid. He unhappily denies that boys, and even infants, studied at Alfred’s school, 346. Everything he writes about the Alfredian professors lecturing on the arts and theology at Oxford is refuted, 349, 352. Charter of Werfrith, bishop of Worcester, 376.

## Y

Yffi, son of Osfrid, son of Aeduini by Quoenburga, baptized by Paulinus, II, 14. He returned to Kent with his mother, II, 20. Ythancaestir, a city of the East Angles. Its location. The churches established there by Cedd, III, 22.

[Col. 1743]
